### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the utmost care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, by which the reader can readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the modest price; and above all, this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; but the Eastern authors are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## [Note: [Col. 0011A]]

**Line 4.**—He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the City, should use the pallium, and that the bishop of the city of Rome should be consecrated by him. The pallium, which is the insignia of the fullness of pontifical office, is by right conferred only on archbishops, canon 1 and following, distinction 100, chapter 4 *On Elections*. Nevertheless, by special favor, it was also granted by the supreme pontiffs to certain bishops—for example, to Mark, bishop of Ostia, because of the consecration of the supreme pontiff, which he possesses by ancient custom; and to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, by Gregory, concerning whom Gregory himself speaks in Book VII, Letter 5, and elsewhere.

Hence arose the custom that the bishop of Ostia should consecrate the supreme pontiff, as Robert, abbot, reports in the supplement to Sigebert under the year 1180:

> “The bishop of Ostia, by ancient custom, ordains and consecrates the Roman pontiff. This custom arose from the fact that, after Blessed Sixtus had been martyred, together with Saint Lawrence his deacon, Blessed Justin the presbyter, with the Roman clergy, elected Dionysius as Roman pontiff, and Maximus, bishop of Ostia, consecrated him. From this custom it has subsequently followed that the bishop of Ostia ordains and consecrates the Roman pontiff, and has the pallium only for those matters that pertain to the ordination and consecration of the Roman pontiff.”

Augustine mentions the same rite in the *Brief Report of the Conference* of the third day, chapter 16:

> “The Roman pontiff is customarily ordained by three bishops, the first of whom is the bishop of Ostia.”

Anastasius, in the Life of John V, says:

> “He was consecrated by three bishops—the bishop of Ostia, the bishop of Porto, and the bishop of Velletri—just as his predecessor, Pope Leo, had been.”

[Col. 0011C] **Line 6.** He built two basilicas, one on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests, and another in the city of Rome, near Pallacina. The common reading must be retained: Baronius wrongly read “Palatine.” Pallacina was the name of a sewer in the City, located near the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, which Anastasius mentions below under Nicholas I:

> “From there it began to run into the sewer which is near the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, which is called Pallacina.”

Likewise under Leo III:

> “And in the monastery of Blessed Lawrence the Martyr, which is called Pallacina.”

Likewise under Benedict III:

> “From there, the Tiber, rushing in, began to run into the sewer which is near the monastery of Saint Sylvester and Saint Lawrence the Martyr, which is called Pallacina.”

Likewise under Gregory IV:

> “He also made, in the monastery of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, which is called Pallacina, six baskets of silver.”

Gregory calls the same place Palacina in Book V, Letter 44:

> “A shop in this City, which is situated near Palacina.”

## [Note: [Col. 0011D]]

**Line 4.**—He established that the bishop of Ostia … The custom by which the bishop of Ostia is accustomed to consecrate the Roman bishop appears to be older than this period. For Pope Dionysius is said to have been consecrated by Maximus, bishop of Ostia. Saint Augustine, in the *Brief Report of the Conference* of the third day, chapter 16, while arguing against the Donatists, mentions this rite as extremely ancient.

**Line 5.**—Should use the pallium. The word *pallium* is understood differently in canon 12 of the Council of Gangra and here. There it means the garment worn by those who professed a stricter monastic life and had renounced the flesh and the world. Here it means the vestment and insignia of the Roman supreme pontiff, signifying his highest honor and full authority; it was also customarily granted by him to metropolitan bishops for serious and reasonable causes. Elsewhere this is called the *Phrygium*, perhaps because it is usually woven with crosses in Phrygian workmanship. Baronius, year 336, no. 63.]

## [Note: [Col. 0012A]]

# Chronological Notes

To Blessed Mark, besides eight months and twenty-one days of episcopate, the older catalogues, together with the paintings of Saint Paul, also assign two years, with the exception of the Liberian Catalogue: namely, the catalogue under Felix IV, and the catalogues of Cava, Farfa, Lucca, and Colbert, all cited above in the Prolegomena in the series of the Roman pontiffs, as well as the text of the Librarian. Yet both the Liberian Catalogue and the one immediately following it, that of Felix IV, the Librarian, and the fourth Ocriculan codex assign him one and the same pair of consuls—that is, all those which record a consular date. The consuls named during Mark’s pontificate are Nepotianus and Facundus, who marked the year 336 of the common Christian era.

Under these consuls the Roman pontiff was elected fifteen days after the death of his predecessor Silvester—for the Farfa Catalogue, together with the Librarian, counts that many days—which had closed his life on the final day of the Roman year, 31 December, in the consulship of Constantius and Albinus, in the year 335 of the Christian era, as I have already shown in the Chronological Notes on Silvester. He was solemnly brought to the apostolic see on Sunday, 18 January, and celebrated the one Easter in the same consulship of Nepotianus and Facundus; before that consulship had ended, he departed to heaven on the Nones of October. Therefore, might the two years of pontificate mentioned above pertain to a vicariate exercised by him in the extreme old age of Silvester? The need for assistance in carrying out pontifical duties, owing to Silvester’s advanced age, would have required a vicar in the peace of the Church no less than the continual persecution under earlier pontiffs had required the frequent precautions explained above in the notes to their lives.

Other causes also persuaded the Roman pontiffs, especially in this fourth century after Christ, with which we are now concerned, to establish in the City a vicar—sometimes a presbyter, sometimes a bishop—to perform several acts. Thus, in the Acts of Liberius, Damasus, then a presbyter, is said to have been appointed vicar by Liberius. It may also be observed that, as the fourth century progressed, the use of vicars was wisely adopted in the Roman Church as circumstances required, but in many Churches degenerated into abuse, since it had to be restrained by the Nicene canons, as Augustine testifies. From him we learn, in Letter 110, that even after those canons had been enacted long before, and although Valerius, bishop of Hippo, and Augustine himself were ignorant of them, Augustine had been appointed by Valerius as vicar with a future succession, contrary to the law of those canons.

Thus we readily understand not only that the legitimate use of a vicar was frequent in many Churches, but also that in some it deteriorated into the corrupt practice of appointing a vicar under an agreement of succession. The Roman Church neither admitted this kind of corruption and abuse—appointing vicars with succession—in its own case, nor approved it in others. But it used the legitimate office of a vicar, whether presbyter or bishop, as the pontiff wished, without the right of future succession, in the same fourth century, and retained it in subsequent centuries. It continues to retain it in our own age with the greatest prudence, without any violation of the canons, indeed with very great benefit and economy for ecclesiastical discipline. It had employed the same office in the centuries preceding the fourth, and had received examples of it from the very beginning of its institution, from Peter, prince of the apostles, in Linus, Cletus, and Clement, as we have explained in their proper place.

If, then, we move back to earlier times from 7 October 336, the day on which Blessed Mark died, by eight months and twenty-one days, counting both extremes, the date of his enthronement in the Roman episcopate falls on Sunday, 18 January, the feast of the Roman Chair, in the same year 336, the Dominical Letter D indicating that day. He must, however, have been ordained bishop two years earlier, either to exercise pontifical duties under Silvester or to preside over one of the churches nearer the City, founded long before and shortly afterward enlarged in basilica and revenues by Constantine the Great.

If we assume the day of ordination indicated in the aforesaid date to have been Sunday, 20 January 334, only two years, eight months, and nineteen days would elapse from it to 7 October 336, counting both extremes; one day would therefore be lacking from the total of twenty days counted in the Liberian Catalogue and others. Nevertheless, this slight reduction may be restored by moving back the day of his election to the Roman pontificate, or of his enthronement, which we have assigned to 18 January 336, nearly a full two years after his episcopal ordination.

This two-year period of episcopal dignity and vicarial ministry is gathered from the catalogue of ordinations preserved for us by Anastasius. For Mark is said to have held ordinations twice in December, at which he consecrated twenty-five presbyters, six deacons, and twenty-seven bishops for various places. Yet no December elapsed while Mark held the chair of Peter, whom we say was either elected or placed on the Roman throne on 18 January 336 and died in the same year on 7 October. The two ordinations which the *Liber Pontificalis* says he performed in December must therefore have been held by him during the lifetime of his predecessor Silvester, while he was acting in the pontifical office’s place and, at Silvester’s command, promoting to the aforementioned orders and to the episcopate men designated by Silvester.

As the number of newer episcopal sees founded through Constantine’s zeal and generosity increased, Silvester would have arranged for those whom he was establishing as the first bishops in those sees to remain longer in the City, to be formed for the governance of souls, and, once formed by urban examples, to be initiated and ordained here by a vicar assisting him in the pontifical office. This would have occurred whenever illness or the burden of advanced age prevented Silvester from attending promptly to so many concerns and duties, or from being present to those requiring a more vigorous old age.

# Historical Notes

**Line 4.**—He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the City, should use the pallium. Cardinal Baronius, commenting on these words of the Librarian under the year 336, no. 63, observes that in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* the pallium is here first mentioned as an indication of supreme honor and the fullness of authority.

> “Here for the first time,” he says, “in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs there is mention of the pallium as an indicator of supreme honor and fullness of authority. The same thing is also called the *Phrygium*, since it was especially the insignia of the Roman pontiff and was customarily granted by him on occasion to metropolitan bishops. The Greeks testify that such a *Phrygium* was conferred by Pope Celestine of Rome on Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, when he delegated his functions to him.
>
> “But why the *Phrygium*, which is woven with crosses, should be called a pallium, when the form of the ancient pallium was very different and larger—as what has been said above in both the first and second volumes of the *Annals* sufficiently demonstrates—I do not think I have fully established. I shall nevertheless state what conjecture has suggested. First, just as in the ancient Hebrew priesthood there was the distinctive breastpiece of the high priest (Exodus 28), which it was forbidden for any other priest or pontiff to wear, and of which we have often spoken in the first volume, so in the priesthood of the Christian religion that kind of garment which we call the pallium came into the exclusive use of the supreme pontiff, although it was shared for important reasons with several bishops. It was also called the *Phrygium* because it was customarily woven with crosses in Phrygian workmanship.
>
> “Since it was attached, while the pontiff performed sacred rites, to that garment which—as was demonstrated in the first volume—bore before it the appearance of a pallium, but which we now call the *planeta* or chasuble, perhaps this caused the *Phrygium* itself, the chief ornament of the priestly pallium, to be called a pallium. Otherwise, the word *pallium* was customarily used to signify every covering in sacred matters.
>
> “Hence Venantius Fortunatus calls the veils erected in the church by Gregory, bishop of Tours, before the holy cross *pallia*, since they too were woven with images of crosses, as he himself explains in these verses:

> “Finally Gregory offers these temples to the holy cross,  
> while he covers them with pallia bearing the signs of the cross.  
> The divine power of Christ suddenly gave the gifts;  
> soon the second cause of the pious vow was present.  
> The pallia are worthy: beautiful things woven with the cross;  
> by their services the holy cross possesses crosses.  
> Silk, to which a white foil is joined in woven cloth,  
> and the work is magnified by woven crosses.  
> Thus devoted good will quickly gave this to the pontiff,  
> and the white veils dedicated to the cross are pleasing.”

The documents cited by that most learned cardinal lend such authority to his observations and conjectures that it might seem superfluous to add new support to them. Anyone wishing to know fuller material, gathered both from Baronius’s sources and elsewhere, should consult the notes collected below under the section on Saint Celestine, where the pallium sent by Celestine himself to Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, mentioned here by Baronius, will be discussed at greater length. Nevertheless, it will not be burdensome to anticipate a few points in confirmation of the matters presented in Baronius’s passage concerning the pontifical pallium, which we shall explain more fully under Celestine.

The shoulder-piece (*superhumerale*) proper to the ancient priesthood, belonging to Aaron and his successors in the high priesthood, was transferred to Christians through the supreme priesthood of the Son of God. It was fitting that it be represented in the pallium of Peter and his successors—namely, by a broader veil wound around the shoulders, to which a border was attached, bearing symbols of the greatest authority entrusted by Christ the Lord to the prince of the apostles, to his chair, and to the Roman pontiffs who legitimately succeed to that authority.

Just as I observed above in the notes on Saint Stephen, no. 24, line 9, that the *cappa*, called the priestly garment, was composed from the ephod of the Levites and the priestly headpiece joined together, so the pontifical breastpiece, together with the band and pendants of the tiara, appears to have coalesced in the earliest period into a single covering of the shoulders and head. Later it seemed more convenient to employ these separately in the Phrygian ornament of the mitre and among the insignia of the supreme priesthood in the pallium.

In that pallium of Peter, therefore, the first faithful appropriately chose to express the supreme authority of that priesthood by the symbol used by Christ the Lord: the keys of the kingdom of heaven, entrusted by the eternal Priest and our Lord Christ to his vicar on earth. Thus we see in ancient Christian reliefs and paintings the handing over of the keys by Christ the Lord to Peter represented as though the keys had been placed in his pallium.

This is how they sculpted them under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, that is, in the year 359 of the Christian era, on the sarcophagus of Junius Bassus, which, dug up intact from the Vatican crypts, is again preserved opposite the confession in the Vatican basilica. On the silver vessel for sacred ministry, which we mentioned in the notes on Saint Urban, the Lord likewise places the keys of heaven in Peter’s pallium.

Other examples of the same symbol may be seen in Alamannus, *On the Lateran Walls*, pages 56, 61, and following. On the occasion of explaining the same emblem—the keys enclosed in the pallium of the Apostle Peter, represented in mosaics, paintings, coins, and seals of charters—he also adds testimonies of the Fathers, by which we learn that this symbol is applied to Peter and his successors in the Roman see.

> “The testimonies of the Fathers,” he says on page 62, “by which Peter’s keys are claimed for the Roman pontiffs are innumerable. For the present purpose, there is the address of Theodore the Studite to Leo III, and another to Paschal I, his successor. These addresses, in Greek, explain the Latin images on these coins:
>
> “Ἀκούε, κλειδοῦχε τῆς οὐρανῶν βασιλείας etc.
>
> “Hear, O key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, rock of faith upon which the Catholic Church has been founded; for you are Peter, who adorn and govern the see of Peter.”

Thus Theodore the Studite addressed the Roman pontiff in his letter to Leo III. In another letter to Paschal I he wrote:

> “Τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οὗ σὺ τὰς κλεῖς ἔδεξω etc.
>
> “The Gospel of Christ, whose keys you received from Christ himself through the chief of the apostles and through those who successively preceded your most sacred head down to your predecessor; and, concerning the Roman Church, he there likewise declared:
>
> “Κορυφαῖος θρόνος, ἐν ᾧ ὁ Χριστός ἐθήκε τὰς κλεῖς τῆς πίστεος:
>
> “The chief seat in which Christ the Lord placed the keys of faith.”

In this breastpiece, or pallium, the symbol of apostolic primacy, antiquity expressed the emblems of supreme authority by the keys of the kingdom of heaven placed in it by Christ the Lord.

In ages close to the apostles, additions were made to this pallium of the supreme pontiff: an orarium, or white border or band marked with crosses. Ancient mosaics and paintings of the supreme pontiffs, from the third and fourth centuries to the twelfth, represent this band running around the edge of the pallium over the shoulders and hanging down to the feet.

The portion of the same covering or pallium turned back toward the nape, which formed the priestly headpiece, retained the same Phrygian ornament when decorated with the same Phrygian band, even after the headpiece was separated from the pallium and became what we call the jeweled mitre. The pallium also retained, along its front edge, the same cross-marked border descending from the neck and shoulders to the feet. Beneath it, the supreme hierarch extends his hand to receive the kisses of the princes of the sanctuary.

The Phrygian band marked with crosses, which could be more easily attached and removed, was fitted during sacred ministry over the shoulders and breast. It retained the name of the pallium to which it was attached, as well as the indication of the supreme authority of the priestly office.

The same happened with the *laticlave*, the insignia of the authority of provincial governors and higher magistrates among the Romans. During the same periods, this kind of toga, woven at its edge with a broader purple band or border, transmitted both its name and the indication of its greater authority to the purple band sewn around the end of the second century and in subsequent ages over the shoulders and breast. It was attached at the place where the fold of the toga was customarily gathered and suitably thrown back over the shoulder by all toga-wearers who professed a more refined dress, as Quintilian testifies in his books *On the Orator*, when he gives instructions for arranging the toga before magistrates so that public decorum may be observed.

This matter will become clearer in the notes on Saint Celestine, where we reserve the presentation of ancient documents concerning this purple *laticlave* sewn over the shoulders and breast of the presiding officer of a council or province. It distinguished his toga from the dress of the other assessors by this ornament, which did not appear on the others.

In the age of Constantine, the use of some breast-band approaching the form of the *laticlave* just described is found to have been extended to several judges, as is clear from the relief preserved on Constantine’s triumphal arch at Rome. It displays the court enclosed by railings before the emperor’s tribunal beside the basilica in Trajan’s Forum, or in the Palladian Forum, with judges and curial magistrates standing near the emperor.

I reproduced an image of this relief in the preceding volume, in the notes on Saint Cornelius, where I indicated that the learned bishop Giovanni Ciampini presents the same relief in his book *On the Cancellarius*, interpreting it similarly as authority attributed to those who wear that breast-garment, which is very close to the *laticlave* of provincial governors.

Thus, in the sacred principate of the priestly hierarchy, I find that the Roman pontiffs likewise extended the use of their own breast-band marked with crosses, or pontifical pallium, to those bishops whom Blessed Peter, the other apostles, or the successors of Peter established as heads of ecclesiastical provinces, or metropolitans, when the Churches were first founded; and also to those whom the Roman pontiffs themselves appointed as presidents in their place over fuller councils.

This was done by Siricius in the case of Ambrose and by Celestine in the case of Cyril. The pallium was therefore a token of the greater authority communicated by the Roman pontiff to such bishops, appointed to govern one province or several provinces, or delegated to preside in his name over fuller synods of priests, so that they might judge by sacred authority beyond what metropolitan rights allowed.

That pallium, taken from the body of Blessed Peter, as though drawn from his pontifical band and pallium, is properly received from Peter’s successors by metropolitan prelates, so that they may exercise over the bishops of their province a share of the apostolic care and authority.

Accordingly, Pope Mark is said to have communicated the insignia of the pallium to the bishop of Ostia so that the latter, appointed to consecrate the elected Roman pontiff, might appear to excel the bishops of his province by this prerogative of honor, assigned uniquely to the bishop of Ostia—as though he himself were acting in the place of the apostle within the college of prelates, a role entrusted to him by the predecessors of the one whom he was to consecrate and ratified by that same man, who wished the supreme shepherd of the Catholic Church to be consecrated through his ministry.

**Line 7.** *Near Pallacina.* Reading C, corrected in the margin of the text of Volume I, writes *Pallatinas*. But the name *Pallacina* should be retained, even if it perhaps arose in a later age through the barbarization of the Latin language. This is shown by an ancient inscription cited by Aringhius, Volume II of *Subterranean Rome*, page 288. It was erected in the year 343, under the consuls Philippus and Salia, namely under Pope Julius, the immediate successor of this Mark of whom we are speaking. There Anti[us] is called “lector of Pallacina”; it reads as follows:

> “Peter was buried on the eighth day before the Ides of March. He lived eighteen years; ‘DE P.’ [uncertain abbreviation]. In peace, under the consuls Philippus and Salia. The two brothers: Antius, reader of Pallacina; ‘DEP.’ [uncertain abbreviation], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.”

## [Note: [Col. 0016D]]

**Line 1.**—He held office for two years, eight months, and twenty days. This is an error. Saint Mark held office for eight months and twenty-one days, as Jerome testifies in the *Chronicle*, and Sozomen in Book II, chapter 29. He was created on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, which falls on 16 January of the year 336, under the consuls Flavius Popillius Nepotianus and Facundus, eminent men.

**Line 5.**—Should use the pallium. The pallium is an indicator of supreme honor and the fullness of authority. But why it was customarily made from the wool of sheep or lambs, rather than from linen, byssus, cotton, or silk, although it was an insignia of great honor, Isidore of Pelusium explains. Writing to Herminus in Book I, Letter 136, he says:

> “This, my dear friend, which the priest carries on his shoulders and which is woven from wool, not linen, represents the skin of that sheep which the Lord sought when it had gone astray and, having found it, lifted upon his shoulders. The bishop, who bears the figure of Christ, performs Christ’s office and, by the garment itself, shows everyone that he is an imitator of that good and great Shepherd who undertook to bear the weaknesses of the flock.”

Thus Isidore of Pelusium disclosed the little-known mystery of the pallium.

**Line 6.**—He built two basilicas, one on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests, and another in the city of Rome near Pallacina. The first basilica is now called Saint Balbina’s, at the foot of the Aventine Hill. Pope Gregory III restored it, as recorded in the Life of Nicholas I, where the cemetery of Saint Mark is discussed.

The other was founded in the more frequented part of the City, near the Palatine places, in the year of the Lord 336. Today it is called Saint Mark’s, after its founder. Pope Adrian I mentions this basilica in writing to Charlemagne in defense of the images:

> “From that time until now, the holy churches of the pontiffs—namely, those of Silvester, Mark, and Julius—of marvelous size have been depicted among us, both in mosaic and in the other histories adorned with sacred images.”

## [Note: [Col. 0017B]]

# In the Year of the Lord 336

Saint Mark, a Roman by nation, son of Priscus, succeeded Saint Silvester after an interregnum of seventeen days. He was ordained on Sunday, 18 January of the year 336, on the sacred feast of the Chair of Saint Peter.

The *Liber Pontificalis* credits him with establishing that the bishop of Ostia, consecrator of the Roman pontiff, should use the pallium. After creating five presbyters, six deacons, and seven bishops for various places in a single ordination, he died on 7 October of the same year, as the *Chronicle of Damasus* testifies, after occupying the see for eight months and twenty days.

His burial is indeed recorded in the Hieronymian Martyrology on 6 October; but this must be understood as referring to some translation of his remains performed on that day. For he is also commemorated on 7 October in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory. He was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way.

In the second volume of the Works of Saint Athanasius, pages 623 and following, two letters are reported. The first bears this title:

> “Letter of Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops to Pope Mark concerning copies of the Council of Nicaea, because the Arians had burned their copies.”

The title of the second is:

> “Reply of Pope Mark concerning the sending of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea to Athanasius and all the Egyptian bishops.”

The latter presupposes that the Egyptians, afflicted by the dreadful persecution of the Arians, had suffered the loss of the Nicene canons, which, together with all their other books, had been burned by those same Arians, and that they had requested a copy from the Roman Church.

But the Egyptians suffered no persecution from the Arians under Constantine; they suffered one only under the rule of Constantius. Moreover, it asserts that seventy canons were enacted by the Council of Nicaea, contrary to the evidence of the Alexandrian codex sent by Saint Cyril to the African prelates, which contained only twenty.

Furthermore, in the year 336, during which Pope Mark occupied the see, Saint Athanasius was already living in exile in Gaul. He therefore could not have written from Alexandria to Mark, Roman pontiff, as this letter supposes that he did.

These indications of its fictitious character also apply to the first letter. Certainly Baronius rejects both as pure and utter fabrications; for each was stitched together from various statements of Celestine I, Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, Saint Leo, and Agatho.

From the fact that Anastasius writes that Saint Mark gave the pallium to the bishop of Ostia, the consecrator of the Roman pontiff, Caeconius, in his account of Leo II, and Sigonius, in his *History of the Kingdom of Italy* under the year 682, write that the bishop of Ostia alone was the consecrator of the Roman bishop until Leo II, who was ordained by three [Col. 0018A] bishops—namely, those of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri. But in the pontificate of that same Leo we shall show that the Roman pontiffs were always ordained by three bishops, among whom the first place was held by the bishop of Ostia, the second by the bishop of Porto, and the third by the bishop of Albano. For although both Leo II and John V were ordained by the bishops of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri, the bishop of Velletri was nevertheless not one of the ordinary consecrators, but was added on those occasions to the bishops of Ostia and Porto because, as Anastasius says in his account of Leo II, the see of Albano was vacant.

This custom later ceased, at a time unknown to me, and another took its place: namely, that the senior cardinal bishop, together with two other bishops chosen from among the older bishops, performed that office. Augustine Patricius, *Book I, chapter 3, section 2 of the Rites of the Holy Roman Church*, nevertheless observes that in his own time the ordination of Sixtus IV alone had been performed not by the senior cardinal bishop, but by the cardinal of Rouen, who was bishop of Ostia.

[Col. 0018B]

The first bishop whom we know to have been honored with this distinction, so that he might use the pallium, was the bishop of Ostia, who received it from Pope Mark. For the pallium belongs only to patriarchs and archbishops. Later, however, the Roman pontiffs granted it to other bishops, either in consideration of their merits or for some other legitimate reason. It was granted to Siagrius, bishop of Autun, by Gregory the Great, whose Letter 114 of Book VII to him on this matter is extant; and to Actard, bishop of Nantes, by Adrian II, as is clear from the same pontiff’s letter addressed to him. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, and many others also possessed this privilege. On these matters Cardinal Bona should be consulted, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 24, no. 16, where he adds that today the bishops of Lucca and Pavia in Italy, and the bishop of Bamberg in Germany, use it as a perpetual privilege.

The Roman pontiff, whose supreme right and full authority extend over all the Churches, always and everywhere uses the pallium. The others—both archbishops and bishops—may not use it except within the church, on certain specified days, when they celebrate the solemn rites of [Col. 0018C] Mass. This is in accordance with an ancient custom indicated by Gregory the Great in Book II, Letter 54, to John, archbishop of Ravenna, and in Book IV, Letter 50, to Virgil of Arles.

[Col. 0018C]

The origin of the pallium in both the Western and Eastern Churches is extremely ancient. Baronius considers it older than Pope Mark. He must, however, be corrected in passing on one point: in the year 430, no. 26, he believed that Pope Celestine had sent Cyril of Alexandria the insignia of vicarial authority—that is, the *phrygium* or pallium, or head-covering called the mitre. This is indeed reported by more recent Greek writers, but without testimony from the ancients, and it is rejected by John Garnerius in Dissertation 2, *On the Synods Held in the Case of Nestorius*, p. 350.

Isidore of Pelusium, who flourished around the year 412, mentions the pallium in Book I, Letter 136, to Herminius, and discusses at length both its use and its mystical significance.

The pallium is a white woolen band approximately three fingers wide, woven in the form of a circle [Col. 0018D] and placed over the shoulders. From this circle another similar band hangs down in front over the chest, another hangs downward at the back, and two descend over the shoulders. These bands are marked with purple crosses. The pallium itself is fastened with three golden pins or brooches.

It is made from the wool of spotless white lambs, which every year, on the feast of Saint Agnes, are customarily offered at the solemn Mass in her church on the Via Nomentana and blessed, then entrusted to the apostolic subdeacons and raised in some convent of nuns until the time comes to shear them. Pallia are woven from their wool. They are brought to the Vatican basilica and laid over the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul on the vigil of their feast; they remain there throughout the night and on the following day are handed over to those appointed to guard them.

Cardinal Bona, mentioned above, says more about the pallium; much of the foregoing has been excerpted from him.]

[Col. 0009]

## 49

Mark, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, occupied the see for two years, eight months, and twenty days [Note: [Col. 0009] B: eight days fewer.]. He lived in the time of the consuls Constantine, Nepotianus, and Secundus [Note: [Col. 0009] B: Facundus], from the day of the Kalends of February until the day of the Kalends of October.

He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the City, should use the pallium [Note: [Col. 0009] *The pallium. See Baronius, under the year of the Lord 336, at the end.], and that the bishop of the city of Rome should be consecrated by that same bishop; and he issued a regulation concerning the entire ecclesiastical order.

He built two basilicas, one on the Via Ardeatina, where he rests, and another in the city of Rome near the Pallacines [Note: [Col. 0009] C: *palatinas*].

At his prompting, Constantine Augustus offered to the basilica which he established as a cemetery on the Via Ardeatina [Note: [Col. 0009] C: omitted] the estate of the Roses, together with all the surrounding open land, yielding forty solidi.

To the basilica in the city of Rome he offered the following: one silver paten weighing thirty pounds; two silver *amas* (vessels; the term is uncertain) weighing twenty pounds; one silver cup weighing ten pounds; three silver ministerial chalices weighing two pounds each; one silver crown weighing ten pounds; the Antonian estate on the Via Claudia, yielding thirty solidi; the Vaccanas estate on the Via Appia, yielding forty solidi and two tremisses [Note: [Col. 0009] C: *tremisses*]; the Orrea estate on the Via Ardeatina, yielding fifty-five solidi and one tremissis [Note: [Col. 0009] C: *tremissis*].

He held two ordinations [Note: [Col. 0009] Baronius, at the place cited, thinks that he held none] in the month of December: twenty-five priests, six deacons, and twenty-seven bishops for various places.

He too was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Via Ardeatina, on the second day before the Nones of October [Note: [Col. 0009] CB: the day before], and the episcopate was vacant for twenty days.

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Mark: eight months and twenty days. He too lived during the consulship of Constantine, Nepotianus, and Facundus, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February until the Nones of October, the consuls being the same.

## XXXVI. SAINT JULIUS. A.D. 336, THE 31ST YEAR OF CONSTANTINE
