[Note: [Col. 0019B]

Line 5.—“He also built three cemeteries.” This passage can be understood in two ways: either that he ordered the ancient cemeteries of the martyrs, once discovered, to be opened to the faithful Christians in his time; or that he ordered underground places, that is, sand-quarries or crypts, to be adapted for the burial of Christians. Julius may be said to have built cemeteries in either sense. But in which manner he did so is not known to me.]

[Note: [Col. 0021A]

Line 8.—“And that a record which concerns all matters of ecclesiastical faith should be collected in every respect, and that all documents should be recorded in the Church through the first notary, whether legal instruments, documents, donations, exchanges, transfers, wills, or claims.”

During the persecution, the duty of the notaries in the City was to collect the acts of the martyrs. When the persecution ceased, so that they would not be left without an official function, they were assigned the task of maintaining a record of ecclesiastical affairs—that is, of drawing up all ecclesiastical documents. These documents were reported to the first notary, who was the chief of the seven and was called the first notary, just as the chief of the lesser clergy is called the first notary in the canon *Perlectis*, under the words “To the first notary,” Distinction 25.

To the first notary, I say, all ecclesiastical acts were reported: legal instruments, that is, documents pertaining to lawsuits or ecclesiastical judgments; donations, exchanges, and transfers, namely, those made for the acquisition of ownership, such as purchases and sales; wills; or delegations. Thus, I think that *delegationes* should be read instead of *allegationes*. Delegated things are bequests, or judgments expressing any final wishes.

Anastasius, in his account of Innocent I, writes: “In that place the most blessed Innocent, by delegation from the illustrious woman Vestina, established a Roman title.” Augustine, *On the Seasons*, Sermon 76: “Besides, it is a great loss when the Lord has given you this responsibility so that you may dispense what has been entrusted to you, yet you do not preserve what has been delegated to you.” Optatus of Milevis, *Against the Donatists*, Book I: “A small quantity of gold and silver is handed over to Caecilianus, who was seated, just as it had been delegated by Mensurius, with witnesses present.”

[Col. 0021C]

Or that the clerics’ manumissions should be recorded in the church through the archivist of the holy see.

Julius is reported to have decreed that manumissions should take place in the church before the archivist of the apostolic see. But it is more accurate to say that this was introduced by Constantine’s constitution: manumissions were to take place in the church, as stated in Book I, *On Those Who Manumit in the Church*, and as Sozomen mentions in Book III, chapter 9.

Manumissions took place in the church before the bishop and were entered into the church records, so that the grant of freedom might be more secure. Augustine, Sermon 2, *On the Life of Clerics*: “Nevertheless, before he became a cleric, he had bought some little slaves from his earnings; today he will manumit them in the presence of you and of the episcopal records.”

At Rome, manumissions took place in the church before the archivist of the apostolic see, because they were entered into the archive—that is, the church’s record office, whose custody belongs to the archivist of the apostolic see—chapter *Ad audientiam*, *On Prescription*.]

[Note: [Col. 0021D]

Line 3.—“He was in great tribulation.” In the old martyrology of Regina, as Holstenius observes in his notes on the martyrology, similar words are found: “On the day before the Ides of April, at Rome, the burial of Julius, bishop and confessor, who endured tribulations and exiles for ten months under Constantius the Arian, son of Constantine; after his death he returned with great honor to his own see.”

Julius was never sent into exile. Moreover, after Julius had been condemned, Constantius ruled for several more years. These words, as I think, were ancient acts concerning Liberius—material which ought to have been inserted into the additions to the acts and brief catalogues of the Roman pontiffs. Through the carelessness of the scribes, however, as we have observed in the acts of other pontiffs, they were inserted under Julius.

If this addition is transferred to Liberius, the remaining passages should be deleted, namely, those which improperly and falsely insert material about communion with the sect of the Rebaptizers. Just as the truer acts are restored when these passages are deleted from Julius, so the acts of Liberius will be more impressive when they are restored to him.]

[Note: [Col. 0022A]

Line 3.—“He was in great tribulation and exile for ten months.” It is beyond doubt that Pope Julius expended much labor on behalf of the exiled bishops Athanasius, Marcellus, and many others, in order to restore them. But, apart from Platina, who follows the error of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, no one, so far as I know, has until now asserted that Julius himself endured exile for any period.]

[Note: [Col. 0022A]

### Chronological Notes

The catalogue of the age of Liberius not only gives the consulship of Titianus and Felicianus—the well-known epoch of the death of Constantine the Great—which establishes the first Easter of Julius’s pontificate; it also indicates the day marked as the beginning of that see, namely 6 February, which in the year 337, under those same consuls, fell on a Sunday suitable for episcopal consecration.

An error nevertheless entered the total period assigned to Pope Julius. The total is inconsistent with the same catalogue, since, besides assigning complete years, it gives one month and six days, and counts that total from the aforementioned 6 February, or the eighth day before the Ides of February, to the day before the Ides of April.

The missing month, subtracted by the scribes when the total was written, is supplied by the paintings preserved in the basilica of Saint Paul, which distinctly show two months. The same two months are also expressed in four catalogues of the oldest Italian manuscript codices, in the Belgian codex of Papebrochius, and in almost all the Colbertine codices, as well as in the manuscripts of Anastasius.

Yet in both the paintings and the catalogues that preserve the corrected number of months, the number of years has been corrupted. Only eleven seem to be assigned there to Pope Julius, whereas the Liberian and Felician catalogues assign him fifteen years, also indicated by a consular note—namely, the consulship of Constantine Augustus V and Gallus Caesar [Col. 0022C] (A.D. 352), reckoned from the previously mentioned consulship of Titianus and Felicianus in 337. Between these two dates there is a complete fifteen-year period.

We may therefore conjecture that the numerical signs were somewhat worn away in the exemplar from which both the scribe of the fourth-century catalogue under Liberius and the author of the paintings in the following century, during the age of Leo the Great, copied them. From *XV.... l. VI*, the scribe of the catalogue may have written *XI.... II VI*, while the painter produced *XI II VI*.

The epoch should therefore be restored not so much from the shapes of the numerals as from the words expressing the period in the Liberian catalogue: from the eighth day before the Ides of February, under the consulship of Titianus and Felicianus (A.D. 337), to the day before the Ides of April, under the consulship of Constantine V and Gallus Caesar (A.D. 352). This correctly comprises fifteen complete years, two months, and six days.

The reading of the catalogue is confirmed by another work likewise belonging to the fourth century, namely the *Depositio episcoporum*, presented above in the Prolegomena from Bucherius. There Julius’s burial is assigned to the same day, the day before the Ides of April, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, in the cemetery of Callistus.

It should be observed that this does not refer to the cemetery of Callistus situated on the Via Appia, but to the cemetery on the Via Aurelia in which Pope Callistus was buried. According to the author, it was called the cemetery of Calepodius, as is explained above under the entry for Callistus.

Once the numerical signs of the epoch have been restored by this observation, the other catalogues presented in the Prolegomena to Saint Julius in the series of the Roman pontiffs—especially the Italian catalogues, which, as we have said, were copied from the paintings of the basilicas—also recover their integrity. They assign to Pope Julius fifteen years, two months, and six days.]

### Historical Notes

Line 3.—“He was in great tribulation and exile for ten months, and after the death of this Constantius he returned in glory to the see of the blessed apostle Peter.” [Col. 0023A]

Cardinal Baronius rightly asserts under the year 352 that this addition should be removed from the section on Julius, since it was improperly inserted into the text of the Librarian and is known to conflict with its context.

For since the Librarian’s text assigns Blessed Julius eleven years and two months in the see, and begins that total under the consulship of Felicianus (A.D. 337), mistakenly assigning Maximus as his colleague instead of Titianus, it follows that it considers Pope Julius to have died in the year 348, and therefore not to have survived Constantius the Arian, who lived until the year 361.

Certainly nothing whatever is found in the catalogues concerning the exile of Pope Julius. The passage therefore appears to be an excerpt from the acts of Pope Liberius, Julius’s successor, which a copyist imprudently placed in the margin where it did not belong, after which another, equally unskilled, thought that it should be inserted into the text corresponding to the marginal annotation.

If Pope Julius perhaps did endure ten months of exile under Constantius the Arian—though no evidence of this is supplied elsewhere—his return to his see would more likely have occurred after Constantius departed than after he died. The error would then have arisen in the rendering of *ex quo obiit Constantius* (“after Constantius died”), when the reading should have been *ex quo abiit Constantius* (“after Constantius departed”).

Nevertheless, until Julius’s exile is established from another source, the more probable view is that these words were imprudently excerpted from the history of Liberius, his successor, or that something concerning the exile of Blessed Anastasius was cut off and attached to this section on Blessed Julius.

Line 5.—“He built two basilicas in the city of Rome, one near the Forum, etc.” Adrian I asserts in his letter to Charlemagne on the veneration of sacred images that Julius himself adorned this basilica with sacred paintings and mosaics. The letter is to be read in the general councils, in Labbe’s edition, volume VII, p. 955, and in the earlier edition of Binius, volume III, second section, p. 126, where we read:

“The holy churches of the holy pontiffs Sylvester, Mark, and Julius, of marvelous size, have been painted among us both in the museum and in the other histories, together with sacred images.”

Line 9.—“And that all documents, drawn up in the Church through the first notary, should be recorded, etc.; whether legal instruments or donations, etc., and that the clerics should record them in the church through the archivist of the holy see.”

That this was done for many centuries is demonstrated by the archives of the City and of places near the City. I shall give an example from the eleventh century, from the Farfense documents dated to the fifth year of Pope Benedict [VII] and of the Emperor Henry III, in the fifteenth indiction, which correspond to the year 1017.

In these documents, the archpriest and clergy of the diaconia of Saint Eustachius transfer to Lord Hugo, abbot, houses situated in Rome, in the ninth region. The transfer is recorded through the archivist of the holy Roman Church in the following words:

“IN N. D. D. SAL. N. I. X. (*In the name of our Lord God our Savior Jesus Christ.*)

“In the year, by God’s favor, the fifth of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter; and in the third year of our lord Henry, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor; in the fifteenth indiction, on 23 January.

“It is certain that we, Peter, the religious archpriest of the venerable diaconia of Saint Eustachius, holy martyr of Christ, which is called ‘in the Plane Trees,’ and John, the second, and Eustachius, the third, religious priests of the aforesaid diaconia, with the consent of the entire congregation of the priests of God of that same true diaconia of Saint Eustachius, have on this day ceded and transferred, etc., the houses, etc., situated in Rome, in the ninth region, in Scorticlari, between the Alexandrian Baths, and within these boundaries.

“On one side they are held by Benedict, priest, who belongs by right to our diaconia of Saint Eustachius, and by the oratory of your Savior, which is above, Lord Hugo, humble abbot and exchanger, etc.

“We have requested that this document be written by the archivist of the holy Roman Church in the month and indiction stated above, the fifteenth.

“+ Peter, archpriest of the diaconia of Saint Eustachius, holy martyr of Christ, transfers this here.

“MM. (*By my hand.*)

“+ John, second priest, MM. SS. (*I have subscribed with my own hand.*)

“+ Eustachius, third priest, MM.

“+ Benedict, priest, MM.

“+ Adrian, priest, MM.

“John, by God’s will, judge.

“+ I, George, by the grace of God treasurer of the holy apostolic see.

“+ Marinus, brother of Crescentius, prefect of the city of Rome.

“I, Peter, archivist of the holy Roman Church, who am mentioned above, the writer of this document, have completed and finalized it through the three subscriptions and the transfer that was made.”

I have chosen to insert this document not only because it will serve as an example of the preservation, from the fourth century to the eleventh, of the law requiring transfers and exchanges of estates belonging to the churches of the City to be recorded by the archivist of the holy apostolic see, with the signatures of the contracting parties, the judge, the notary of the holy see, and a nobleman such as the brother (*germanus*) of the prefect of the City—perhaps he was present as a witness. It therefore demonstrates the careful administration of properties belonging to the titular churches and diaconiae of the City.

It will also provide later generations with evidence of the never-interrupted custom of dividing the City into fourteen civil regions, established by Augustus and used in legal documents. The diaconia of Saint Eustachius was situated in the ninth region. It also confirms the names of the Baths of Alexander and of the oratory of Saint Saviour, names that have survived to our own time together with the Plane Trees, from which the diaconia of Saint Eustachius, then called “in the Plane Trees,” received its additional designation.]

[Note: [Col. 0024B]

Line 3.—“He was in great tribulation and exile for ten months.” This fiction is disproved, for he is never reported to have undergone exile, and he himself died before Constantine’s death. Anyone can learn this very clearly both from Greek and Latin writers and also from Athanasius.]

[Note: [Col. 0024B]

Saint Julius, a Roman by nationality and son of Rusticus, succeeded Saint Mark. He was ordained on 6 February, which in the year 337 fell on a Sunday.

During his pontificate the entire East was in turmoil because of the Arian heresy and the Arians’ hostility toward Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

In the year 341 the Council of Antioch was held. The occasion for it was the dedication of the Antiochene church, begun by Constantine the Great and completed under Constantius. Hence Athanasius says in his book *On the Synods*: “At Antioch they convened a new synod on the pretext of the *Encaenia*,” that is, the dedication festivities.

Accordingly, the Arian emperor Constantius, under the pretext of this dedication, summoned the bishops of the East. Baronius considered this synod an Arian assembly, and all who followed him did so until Schelestratius. In his book on the holy Council of Antioch, Schelestratius showed that the Antiochene synod had been attacked under four headings:

First, that it had been an Arian assembly;

second, that it had deposed Athanasius;

third, that it had perverted the faith;

fourth, that it had attacked ecclesiastical discipline.

But the very learned author shows in the same work that these four charges do not apply to the beginnings of the Antiochene synod, which was celebrated by ninety Fathers, but to the outcome, or final acts, of the Antiochene assembly held by approximately forty Eusebians.

Before that council, Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, had sent an embassy to Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, asking him to act as judge in the case of Athanasius. Julius summoned Saint Athanasius and the Eusebians to Rome.

When Athanasius arrived, Julius sent his priests Elpidius and Philoxenus to the East to summon the Eusebians to the Roman synod. The Eusebians, cited by them to come to Rome and plead their case, were so terrified when they heard the name of an ecclesiastical court that they resorted to their customary tactics. They delayed Julius’s priests beyond the day appointed by Julius for the synod and offered empty excuses, [Col. 0025A] claiming that, because of fear of war with the Persians, they were unable to travel to Rome.

Julius therefore held the Roman council, which had already been announced, in the year 342. Fifty bishops attended it, together with Vitus, an envoy of Pope Sylvester who had once served at the Council of Nicaea.

There the case of Saint Athanasius was brought to examination, and he was judged worthy of communion and of the episcopate, as innocent of the crimes that the Eusebians had fabricated against him.

At the council a letter of the Eusebians to Pope Julius was read, written in the name of the Antiochene synod. It had been composed in an insolent and contentious style and contained a lengthy complaint against the pontiff. The pontiff replied to it in the name of the council. His letter, which Saint Athanasius reports in his second *Apology Against the Arians*, is a notable treasury of ecclesiastical discipline.

Marcellus of Ancyra, who in the year 336 had been deposed from the episcopate and condemned to exile at the Council of Constantinople, where Saint Athanasius had been ordered into exile, had returned to his see and had again been accused of heresy. He had been condemned at the aforementioned Council of Antioch.

In this Roman synod he pleaded his case before Pope Julius and was declared innocent. For Athanasius writes concerning him in his letter to the solitary monks:

“He went to Rome and demonstrated that he was innocent.”

Julius did not restore him to communion, however, until Marcellus had given him a written confession of faith. Epiphanius reports it under Heresy 72.

Baronius is correct in thinking that this confession of faith is not the one that Julius reports as agreeing in every respect with the Catholic Church. Although it contains much for refuting the impiety of the Arians, the term “consubstantial” does not occur in it, even though that was the principal point demanded of a Catholic confessor.

Marcellus should not, however, be blamed for that silence, since no one accused him of denying consubstantiality, which he had subscribed to and defended at the Council of Nicaea. The error charged against him was of another kind, namely, the error of the Sabellians and of Paul of Samosata.

Although some have vainly attempted to free Marcellus from suspicion of heresy on the basis both of this Roman synod and of the Council of Sardica, from which he was shortly afterward acquitted, he was nevertheless acknowledged as a heretic by Athanasius and later by everyone. This may be seen in Baronius’s critical discussion under the year 347 and in Schelestratius, Dissertation III, *On the Holy Council of Antioch*, chapter 5, where it is observed that his heresy did not become known until many years after his death.

After the Roman synod, the Eusebians again employed criminal audacity in disturbing the Churches and laying snares for Athanasius. Pope Julius therefore referred Athanasius’s case to the emperor Constans and urged him to act with his brother Constantius for Athanasius’s restoration to his see.

Constans wrote to his brother Constantius about this matter, and both emperors summoned a council at Sardica—a city bordering Illyricum, Moesia, and Thrace—for the year 347. This is manifest from Athanasius’s second *Apology*, from his letter to the solitary monks, and from the synodical letter of the Fathers of the synod to all the bishops.

Athanasius states in the aforementioned letter to the solitary monks that approximately three hundred bishops attended this synod. At it, Saint Athanasius, Marcellus of Ancyra, Asclepas of Gaza, and others unjustly condemned by the Eusebians were acquitted.

A synodical letter was written to Pope Julius. It contains these noteworthy words, by which the primacy of the Roman pontiff is splendidly asserted:

“For this will seem best and most fitting: that from each and every province the priests of the Lord should refer all matters to the head, that is, to the see of the apostle Peter.”

The same is evident from the synodical letter to the Church of Alexandria and from the synodical letter to all the bishops, both of which are reported by Saint Athanasius in his second *Apology*.

The Greeks count twenty canons enacted by that synod; the Latins count twenty-one. The third, fourth, and seventh canons assert the right of appeal in episcopal cases to the Roman pontiff, in honor of the memory of the holy apostle Peter.

Some people infer from these canons—but falsely—that the right of appeal to the Roman see was not confirmed but instituted by the Council of Sardica. Since the Roman pontiff is by divine right the first of all bishops, superior to the others in jurisdiction, and head of the Church, it follows that bishops may appeal to him when they suffer injustice.

Thus the right of episcopal appeal to the Roman see is an appendage of the pontifical primacy. Indeed, Cardinal Perronius says in his *Reply to the Response of the King of Great Britain*, chapter 3:

“If that right had been instituted by the Council of Sardica, how could Julius, the Roman pontiff, have written the following to the Eusebians several years before that council?

‘Judgment ought to have been given according to the canon, and not in this manner. It was necessary to write to all of us, so that what was just might be decided by all. For they were bishops, and not ordinary churches, who were suffering these things, but churches which the apostles themselves had instructed in the faith. Why, then, did you wish to write nothing to us in the first place concerning the city of Alexandria? Are you unaware that it is customary for a letter to be written to us first, so that what is just may be determined from here? Therefore, if such a suspicion had arisen against the bishop, the matter ought to have been referred here, to our Church.’”

Peter de Marca, Book VII of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 3, believes that the right sought for the Roman bishop at the Council of Sardica was entirely different from a judgment on appeal, and that nothing else was granted to him except the power to order a retrial of the case.

But learned men have already observed that this synod not only granted the right to order a review, but also asserted and confirmed for the Roman pontiff the power to judge appeals brought to the Roman see by deposed bishops.

The arguments that the very learned author brings against this have been refuted by others. It has been shown that the practice of appeals was frequent both in the Eastern and in the Western Church after the Council of Sardica, and that its origins were wrongly pushed back by that prelate to the time of the Council in Trullo in the Greek Church and to the eighth century in the Latin Church.

On these matters Natalis Alexander should be consulted under the fourth century. Christianus Lupus explains the canons enacted at this Council of Sardica in Part I of his *Decrees and Canons of General and Provincial Synods*.

Ursacius and Valens were Pannonian bishops—the former of Mursa, the latter of Singidunum—who had fallen under suspicion of Arian heresy and had therefore been condemned by the Council of Sardica. In the same year, 347, they presented a petition to the Council of Milan, where the perfidy of Arius and Photinus was condemned, and they were received into communion.

This synod was held in the presence of Pope Julius’s legates, as Saint Hilary testifies in his fragment *On the Synods*, or in the presence of priests of the Roman Church, as the letter of the Council of Ariminum teaches. It was held in order to investigate the case of Photinus, heretical bishop of Sirmium, as Hilary states in the same place.

The synod must have been large, since it dealt with the status of a metropolitan bishop and with a matter of faith.

Photinus was first condemned at this Council of Milan; the condemnation was repeated by Pope Julius at the Roman synod held two years later; and finally at the Council of Sirmium in the year 351, four years after the Milanese council. At this last council Photinus was condemned and deposed for the first time. The dates of these three synods have been carefully discussed in Baronius’s critical work.

The following were the principal points of Photinus’s heresy.

First, he rashly declared that God is solitary and should be confessed in the Jewish manner. He thought that neither the divine Word nor the Holy Spirit was a person, but preached that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit had one single operation.

Second, he asserted that Christ had his beginning from Mary and was merely a human being. This is established by Epiphanius, Heresy 71; Theodoret, Book III of *Heretical Fables*; and others.]

Pope Julius did not long survive the Council of Sirmium. He died on 12 April in the year 352, after having occupied the see for fifteen years, two months, and six days, as is read in the chronicle of Damasus.

He was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the cemetery of Calepodius, and was later transferred from there to the basilica bearing his name, namely, Saint Mary across the Tiber.

In three ordinations held in the month of December, he ordained eighteen priests and four deacons; in addition, he ordained nine bishops for various places.

Of all the writings of Pope Julius, only two letters remain, both reported by Athanasius in his second *Apology*: one addressed to the Eusebians and the other to the Church of Alexandria.

Two decretal letters circulated under his name and are printed in editions of the councils as having been written to the Easterners. They, together with the letter of the Easterners to Julius, are spurious and were patched together by the fabricator of the decretals from various fragments of Latin writers.

John, archbishop of Nicaea, relates in his letter on the Nativity, which Combefis translated from Greek and elucidated with notes, that Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, sent letters to Pope Julius warning that it was impossible for the memory of three solemnities to be celebrated on the feast of the Epiphany in sacred places separated from one another. Among these celebrations, since the Nativity of the Lord was involved, it happened—whether by the tradition or permission of James, the Lord’s brother—that, after the matter had been carefully investigated at Rome and the necessary calculations had been diligently made, it was established that the true day of the Lord’s Nativity fell on 25 December:

> “And in this way,” he says, “Julius, the Roman patriarch, harmonized the Hebrew and Roman months. From that time the Roman Church began to celebrate the Savior’s Nativity with joyful rejoicing on 25 December, and he handed down that it should be celebrated by all the Churches.”

He adds that St Basil not only marked the Savior’s Nativity on 25 December in his *Moralia*, but also instructed Gregory of Nazianzus to promulgate and celebrate it on 25 December at the Council of Constantinople, although some did not agree. Finally, under Arcadius and Honorius, when the latter occasionally came to Byzantium, with the assistance of St John Chrysostom and St Epiphanius, summoned from Cyprus, it was also determined in the East that the Nativity of the Lord should be celebrated on that same day, 25 December. The other patriarchs subsequently agreed.

He describes the Nativity feast, already being celebrated at Rome under Honorius with solemn rite, as follows: “The Romans celebrated the Lord’s Nativity on its proper day, with the readings completed and with many troparia and melodies.” This letter of John of Nicaea is found in volume II of the *Auctarium of the Library of the Fathers*, p. 311.

These things agree with what Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, says at the beginning of his funeral oration for his brother St Basil. After speaking of the feasts that preceded Christ’s manifestation, or Nativity, he writes:

> “But I do not count the first celebration together with the others. For the feast established because of the divine manifestation of the Only-Begotten Son through the birth from the Virgin is not simply a holy celebration, but the holy of holies and the celebration of celebrations. Let us therefore number those that follow it. First, the spiritual company of the apostles and prophets established the beginning for us; these are Stephen, Peter, James, John, and Paul. Then, after them, preserving their order, the shepherd and teacher inaugurates the present celebration”—namely Basil, whose feast the Greeks celebrate on 1 January.

According to Gregory of Nyssa, the feast of Christ’s manifestation through birth from the Virgin preceded that day. After it came the solemnity of St Stephen the Protomartyr, immediately followed by the feast of the apostles Peter, James, John, and Paul, which was celebrated on one and the same day, as the same St Gregory teaches in his oration on the praises of St Stephen. The celebration of St Basil on 1 January followed thereafter.

Gregory of Nazianzus likewise testifies that this same practice of celebrating the Nativity and Epiphany existed in his Church. In Oration 49, on the Epiphany, p. 632, he expressly affirms that the feast of the Lord’s Nativity and the adoration of the Magi, on which he delivered a special oration, was distinct from the feast of the Epiphany:

> “The Nativity of Christ was first celebrated with an appropriate solemnity by the leader and initiator of the feast, and by you, indeed by all—both those who live in the world and those who are higher than the world, etc. But now another action of Christ follows, and another mystery”—namely the Epiphany, which was therefore celebrated after the Nativity.

John of Nicaea’s account is also confirmed by Chrysostom in Homily 35 on the Nativity of Christ, found in volume V of his works, p. 466. He says that ten years earlier this same feast of the Lord’s Nativity had begun to be celebrated separately from the Epiphany, on 25 December.

At the time when St John Chrysostom delivered that oration, he was not yet a bishop but only a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, as Combefis shows in his notes to the aforementioned letter of John of Nicaea. Whether he delivered the oration at Antioch or at Constantinople, he nevertheless teaches that scarcely ten years had passed since the true day of the Lord’s Nativity had become known:

> “Indeed, it is not yet the tenth year since this very day became clearly known to us.”

He then relates how the celebration returned from the Western Church, where there was an ancient tradition of the Nativity feast, to the Eastern Church, so that the celebration was introduced there, although not everyone immediately welcomed the idea that the Lord had been born in December:

> “This day, although known from the beginning to those who dwell in the West, has only now, and not many years ago, been transmitted to us.”

He later says that learned men disagreed about the matter: some rejected it as a novelty, while others argued that it should be accepted and restored as consonant even with the antiquity of the Easterners, though it had long fallen into disuse.

Gretzer, in his commentary on chapter 8 of Codinus, denies that this homily belongs to St Chrysostom. Nevertheless, both Casaubon, in *Exercitation* 2 against Baronius, and Combefis, in the place cited, support its attribution with the strongest arguments. On this matter Florentinius should be consulted in his notes to the *Hieronymian Martyrology*, *Exercitation* 2, pp. 195 ff., where he also discusses at length the vigil of the same feast. Zacagnius should likewise be read in the preface to volume I of his *Collection of Ancient Monuments of the Greek and Latin Church*, no. 33. He believes that the words of St Chrysostom quoted above should be understood of the Churches of the patriarchate of Antioch, where, following Egyptian custom, the feasts of the Epiphany and Nativity had formerly been celebrated on one and the same day.

I am not unaware that the cited Combefis writes that the letter of John, bishop of Nicaea, on the Nativity is novel and full of fables. Whatever the truth of that matter, however, the material we have quoted from it above cannot be counted among the fables, since it appears to be confirmed, in a manner of speaking, by the two holy Gregories, of Nyssa and Nazianzus, and by St Chrysostom in the places cited.

In any case, the precise time when the feast of Christ’s Nativity began to be celebrated remains entirely uncertain. It is certain, however, that in the time of Clement of Alexandria—therefore toward the end of the second century—the feast was either not yet celebrated or had not been assigned to a particular day, at least in Egypt, where he lived, and in the neighboring provinces. I infer this from Book I of the *Stromata*, where near the end he writes:

> “There are some who investigate the Lord’s Nativity more curiously, adding not only the year but also the day. They say that it was in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus, on 25 Pachon—that is, on the twentieth day of our month of May—not on the fifteenth day, as some wish. For the Egyptian month Pachon begins on the twenty-sixth day of our April.”

A little later he adds:

> “Some of them even say that he was born on 24 or 25 Pharmuthi—that is, on the nineteenth or twentieth day of our April. For the Egyptian month Pharmuthi begins on the twenty-seventh day of our March.”

From this it necessarily seems to follow not only that the Lord’s Nativity had not been assigned to a particular day, but also that it was not then celebrated, as his baptism was celebrated. Clement of Alexandria records the latter in the same place:

> “The followers of Basilides also celebrate the day of his baptism, spending the entire preceding night in readings.”

Nevertheless, it is certain that in the early periods of the Church, and after Clement of Alexandria, the feast of the Epiphany was the same as the feast of Christ’s Nativity—namely, the occasion on which our Savior presented himself to mortals to be seen. The Epiphany signified both Christ’s Nativity, the arrival of the Magi, and Christ’s baptism. Dionysius Gothofredus demonstrates this from the holy Fathers in his commentary on Law 5 of Theodosius the Younger, *On Spectacles*, issued in the year 425.

The feast of the Epiphany was celebrated in both the West and the East on 6 January. Ammianus Marcellinus, a pagan writer, testifies to the Western practice in Book XXI, chapter 2. For the East, the witnesses are Epiphanius, Book III, and Cassian, *Conferences*, Book X, chapter 2. When Chrysostom delivered his first oration on Pentecost, only three feast days, apart from Sunday, were celebrated: Easter, Pentecost, and the Epiphany, or Nativity of Christ.

Later, the people of Constantinople, instructed by the Romans, added a fourth feast and distinguished the day of the Nativity from the day of the Epiphany. This occurred shortly after St Chrysostom had delivered the aforementioned first oration on Pentecost, which is found in volume V of his works.

From that time the feast of Christ’s Nativity began to be celebrated in the East in December, while the earlier solemnity of the Epiphany remained in January. Other explanations for the name and character of that feast then began to be offered. The day that had previously been honored or celebrated as Christ’s Nativity was now regarded as representing his baptism and the arrival of the Magi. On this subject Chrysostom’s oration on the Baptism of Christ and Jerome’s Book I commentary on Ezekiel should be consulted. These matters are taken from the cited Gothofredus, where more information may be found.

That these two celebrations had then been divided is also clear from the aforementioned law of the emperor Theodosius the Younger on spectacles; in it the emperor expressly distinguishes the Nativity and Epiphany of Christ.

This institution, however, was not accepted by all Eastern peoples. Abulpharagius, in his *History of Dynasties*, p. 94, mentions a letter written by the emperor Justinian to the bishops in the year 551, from which we learn the following:

> “In the twenty-fifth year of his reign, he wrote to all the bishops everywhere that they should celebrate the feast of the Nativity on the twenty-fifth of the earlier Canun—that is, our December—and the Epiphany on the sixth of the later Canun—that is, January. They obeyed his command, except for the Armenians. They retained their former custom, by which they celebrate both feasts on the same day.”

The Armenians, incidentally, who refused to obey the decree of the emperor Justinian, had received the Christian faith as early as the time of Gregory the Illuminator, around the time of Constantine the Great. In the year 536, however, they separated themselves from the Church and professed the Eutychian heresy. On this matter the author of the *Critical Commentary on Baronius* should be consulted under the year of Christ 535.

[Note: Further notes, written by Claudius Sommier, may be found with his notes on St Liberius in column 29.]

## 50

Julius, a Roman by nation, son of Rusticus, held the see for 11 years, 2 months, and 7 days. He lived during the time of Constantius the heretic, son of Constantine, from the consulship of Felicianus and Maximus.

[Note: B: 15 years, 5 months, 17 days.]

[Note: B: From the consuls Nepotianus and Facundus, under Constantius 5 and Gallus Caesar.]

He endured great tribulation and exile for ten months.

[Note: *After many tribulations, in exile.]

[Note: B denies that he was an exile until the year 352.]

After the death of this Constantius, he returned with glory to the see of blessed Peter the Apostle.

He built two basilicas in the city of Rome, one near the Forum and another on the Via Flaminia. He also constructed three cemeteries: one on the Via Flaminia, another on the Via Aurelia, and a third on the Via Portuensis.

He established that no cleric should conduct any legal case in public except in a church; that records, which are required of everyone for the sake of ecclesiastical faith, should be collected by notaries; and that all documents prepared through the chief notary should be authenticated in the church, whether lawsuits, instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, wills, pleadings, or manumissions.

[Note: B: obligations; C: bonds.]

[Note: *Scrinium*, or holy scrutiny.]

These acts were to be authenticated by the registrar of the holy see in the church.

He held three ordinations in the city of Rome during December: eighteen presbyters and four deacons; he ordained nine bishops for various places. He was buried on the Via Aurelia in the cemetery of Calepodius, at the third milestone from the city of Rome, on the day before the Ides of April, and the episcopate ceased for 25 days.

## Catalogue under Liberius

Julius: fifteen years, one month, and eleven days. He lived during the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, from 6 February until the day before the Ides of April, when Constantius V and Constantius Caesar were consuls.

He constructed many buildings: the basilica on the Via Portuensis at the third milestone; the basilica on the Via Flaminia at the second milestone, called Valentini.

[Note: Or perhaps *Valentinus*, to whom the following Calendar is inscribed. Bucherius. See him.]

He built the Julian Basilica, in Region VII near the Forum of the divine Trajan; the basilica across the Tiber, in Region XIV near Callistus; and the basilica on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone near Callistus.

## XXXVII. Saint Liberius. A.D. 352, year 16 of Constantine

[Note: From the same source, the Freher manuscript.]

Number 51, line 1: B has “three months and four days.” Line 3: A and B have “Constantius”; A and B have “three years.” Line 4: A has “then the priests assembled.” B has “and, assembling the priests with their council, Liberius appointed Felix in his place.” Line 7: A has “and expelled”; B has “condemned.” Line 13: A and B have “should rebaptize; then they recalled Liberius from exile; but when he returned.” Line 18: A has “who was from the dregs”; B has “but so.”

Number 52, line 8: A has “adorned with marble plates”; B has “with stonecutters’ work.” Line 11: A has “nineteen presbyters.” Line 14: A and B have “six days.”

From the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts:

Number 51, line 1: “Son of Ligustus,” corrected in Augustinus to “son of Aug[ustus]” (M: Ligustus); he held the see six years, three months, and four days. He lived in the time of Constans, the heretical son of Constantine (M: “in the time of the heretical Constantine”).

Line 4: “and he was in exile”—the published reading is better.

In the same line: “Therefore, when the priests had assembled with their council, they appointed as bishop in his place the presbyter Felix, a venerable man.”

This Felix held a council with 48 bishops and found two presbyters, Ursacius and Valens, agreeing with Constantius Augustus. He separated them from the Church.

After a few days Ursacius and Valens, moved by evil zeal, asked Constantius Augustus to recall Liberius from exile and to share with him only one communion, according to the baptism.

[Note: M: “that is, according to baptism.”]

Then, after authority had been sent through Catulinus, an *agens in rebus*, they came together. Line 12: “so that he might agree with the heretic in one participation in communion only, so that they might not rebaptize.” Then they recalled Liberius from exile.

When Liberius returned, he lived in the cemetery of St Agnes, near the sister of Constantius Augustus, until, after the emperor’s death or return, he might again come back to the city.

But Constantia Augusta, because of her faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, summoned certain men who were of the party of Felix, and, after holding a council, sent for Liberius from the cemetery of St Agnes and expelled Felix, who was Catholic, from the episcopate.

[Note: M: “And Constantius Augustus entered Rome at that very hour and held a council with the heretics, together with Ursacius; he also expelled Felix, who was Catholic, from the episcopate and recalled Liberius. From the same source, etc.”]

Number 52, line 1: “From that day there was persecution against the clergy, so that within the churches the presbyters and deacons”—M adds “and clerics”—“neither … *et m. cor.* [abbreviated and uncertain] …” Then Felix …

Line 3: “where he rests in peace, 4 Kalends of August.” “Liberius, 4 Nones of August: when Constantius the heretic entered Rome, Liberius, although not rebaptized, gave assent and held …”

[Note: M: “he is a heretic.”]

Line 6: “and the basilica of St Paul, and also the Constantinian basilica for seven years. There was a great persecution in the city of Rome, so that clerics and priests could enter neither churches nor baths.” Liberius adorned the cemetery of St Agnes with marble plates. He built a basilica …

Line 10: “of Lydia.” All the years of Felix are counted in his ordination. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome.

Last line: six days.

At Holstenius and Schelestratius:

Line 4: both Florentian manuscripts: “and, assembling the priests with their council, Liberius appointed Felix in his place.” Anselmus: “And the priests assembled with the council of Liberius.”

Line 7: Anselmus and Florentius: “and condemned them,” etc.

Line 9: Cassianus: “so that he might share only one communion.”

From this point they recalled Liberius from exile.

Line 15: Florentius: “Constantia.”

Line 17: Florentius: “who had approved the council of deceit.” In the same line, the second Florentius: “because she had perceived the council.”

Line 18: Vatican manuscript and Florentius: “from the dregs.”

Line 19: Florentius and the Vatican manuscript: “Augustus.”

Number 52, line 4: manuscript codices: “Roman.”

Line 7: the second Florentius: “the clergy.”

Line 8: Florentius and the Vatican manuscript: “the tomb with marble plates.”

Line 9: Florentius: “in his ordination.”

Line 11: Florentius: “5 September.” In the ancient Martyrology of St Cyriacus: “9 Kalends of October: the burial at Rome of St Liberius, bishop.”

At Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript:

Number 51, line 12: “having been instructed that there should be one participation.”

Line 14: “in the cemetery of St Agnes, at the sister of Constantius Augustus, so that, as it were …”

Line 15: “intervention,” or “at the request.”

Line 17: “she had perceived the council.”

Line 18: “from the cemetery.”

Number 52, line 4: “in the city of Rome.”

Line 13: “in the cemetery.” Thus it is almost always written incorrectly in what follows as well; from now on we shall cease noting it.

[Note: Number 51, line 13—“Only so that they should not rebaptize.” That the Arians rebaptized those who came to their sect from the Catholics in the time of Pope Liberius is clear from this passage, which the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* copied from the second catalogue. When the Arians began to rebaptize is not yet known. It is nevertheless probable that they adopted the practice of rebaptizing from the Donatists, and that the Donatists, so that they would no longer be said to lurk in a corner of Africa, entered into union with the Arians before the time of Liberius.]

[Note: Number 51, line 10—“Then, after authority had been sent through Catulinus, an *agens in rebus*, Ursacius and Valens came together to Liberius.” Letters and imperial commands were conveyed by the *agentes in rebus*, and those who were to be summoned to the emperor’s court were summoned through them. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book II, chapter 27: “The form of the rescript was read; the directive of the master of offices had been established; an *agens in rebus* was in attendance.” And Symmachus, Book VII, Letter 59: “Julius, an *agens in rebus*, presented the imperial letters to me.”]

[Note: Number 52, line 6—“And there was a great persecution in the city of Rome, so that the clerics and priests were allowed entry neither into the churches nor into the baths.” Under Constantius, one form of persecution inflicted on the clergy was the prohibition of churches and baths. Christians of better times also used baths, not for luxury but for health. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 41: “I bathe at an honorable and healthful hour.” The apostle John himself did not abstain from the bath. Once, when he entered a bathhouse to bathe and heard that Cerinthus was inside, he immediately rushed out, lest he bathe with a heretic; this is reported by Eusebius, Book III, chapter 22, and Book IV, chapter 13, and by Epiphanius in the *Panarion*, heresy 30, section 24. Augustine himself bears witness that after his mother’s death he used the bath to relieve his grief, *Confessions*, Book IX, chapter 12: “It also seemed good to me to go and bathe, because I had heard that the bathhouse was so called because the Greeks say *balaneion* (βαλανεῖον), something that drives anxiety from the mind.”]

[Note: Line 8—“Here Liberius adorned the old tomb of St Agnes the martyr with marble plates.” The tombs of martyrs and of the great were customarily adorned with marble crusts; hence *marmoreae memoriae* are frequently mentioned. Augustine, on Psalms 33 and 48: “*Platinae* are marble slabs.” Anastasius calls them *platoniae* in his Life of Damasus: “He built a *platonia* where the bodies of the apostles, that is, of blessed Peter and Paul, lay, and he adorned it with verses.” The same author, in the Life of Sixtus III: “He placed silver grilles above porphyry *platoniae*, weighing three hundred pounds.” And below, in the same work: “He built a *platonia* in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, where he wrote the names of the bishops and martyrs together with their memorials.” The same author, in the Life of Leo III: “Above the lilies he placed *platoniae* made of marble metals.” Both words derive from the Greek *platynō* (πλατύνω), “I broaden” or “I extend.” Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book III, Letter 9: “Above the aforesaid *platoniae*, or columns.”]

[Note: Number 51, line 12—“Who agreed with the commands of Constantius.” Here there is a remarkable corruption of the events, an incoherent sequence of circumstances, and the chimerical heresy of rebaptizers allegedly promoted by Constantius. All these things are shown to be contrary to the truth by contemporary and trustworthy writers, and should therefore be regarded as the addition of some petty scholar or of someone animated by the worst hostility toward Liberius.

These materials appear to have been fused together and arranged from additions taken from the accusations brought against Liberius by the Luciferians and the schismatics under Felix and Ursicinus. Someone collected these accusations, inserted them into the margins of the catalogues, incorporated them, and interpolated the acts of Liberius.

This will be established with certainty if we say that the earlier addition under Julius actually belongs to Liberius. For it speaks there about Liberius’s exile and restoration and suits him, although it is wrongly attributed to Julius. When the compiler saw that this addition did not agree with another that he found in other catalogues, he attributed the first to Julius and assigned the second to Liberius; both are false.

If the complete Life of the presbyter Eusebius still existed, our conjecture might perhaps be confirmed; Baluzius preserves only a fragment of it, volume II of the *Miscellanea*, p. 141. Meanwhile, it is clear that the material was taken from those acts, since among the surviving monuments it is found nowhere except in the Eusebian fragment, which says the following about communion and rebaptism.

The fragment begins as follows:

> “At the same time when Liberius had been recalled from exile by Constantius Augustus the heretic, in that one doctrine only, so that they should not rebaptize the people but contaminate the populace by one communion.”

These words have been attached to the acts of Liberius and taken verbatim from the Life of Felix III, which survives complete in several manuscripts of the Colbert Library, as Baluzius testifies. It appears to have been written by Eusebius, since many things read in the Eusebian fragment are also found in the Life of Felix.

In these acts, however, many extremely false statements occur, especially the claim that Valens and Constantius were presbyters, although they were certainly bishops; the surviving sentence of deposition removes them from the episcopate. Nor could they have been present at Rome at that time, any more than Constantius could, as is proved by those who have examined Constantius’s actions more carefully.

Indeed, in the manuscripts of the Life of St Felix the Roman presbyter, Valens and Ursacius are named. The interpolator of these acts omitted the word “Roman.” The two readings are as follows. In Migne, the passages from the *Liber Pontificalis* through “forty-eight bishops” and from the Life of St Felix through “in the presence of forty-eight” are printed in parallel.]

### *Liber Pontificalis*

“And Felix held a council and found two presbyters agreeing with Constantius Augustus the Arian, named Ursacius and Valens, and expelled them at a council of forty-eight bishops.”

### Life of St Felix, according to Baluzius’s edition

> “The same Felix held a council and found two Roman presbyters agreeing with Constantius Augustus the Arian, named Ursacius and Valens, and condemned them at a council in the presence of forty-eight bishops who had been assembled. He declared Constantius, son of Constantine, a heretic, and said that he had been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia, near Nicomedia at the estate of Aquilone. For this declaration St Felix was expelled from his episcopate by Constantius Augustus, son of Constantine Augustus.”

The compiler of the acts of Liberius and Felix—or rather, the interpolator—inserted the earlier words taken from the Acts of Felix in full into the Life of Liberius. The words beginning “He declared,” together with what follows, he inserted into the Life of Felix. The false, foolish, and senseless lies that he pours forth about Felix will be considered in their proper place.

[Note: Line 9—“They should share in one communion only.” The *Liber Pontificalis*, taking this from the acts of Eusebius and Felix, places Liberius’s fall in the fact that he became a transgressor by communicating with the Arian heretics and entering into one communion with them. It nevertheless says that he did not share their doctrine concerning rebaptism; although Constantius and his partners in perfidy adhered to that doctrine, Liberius was alien to it.

The notes below will discuss the fiction of rebaptism. For the present, from the asserted cause of Liberius’s fall—his entering into one communion with the Arians—there arose the suspicion that these acts, or rather the deeds of Eusebius and Felix, had been elaborated either by some Luciferian or by a schismatic follower of Ursicinus.

For Lucifer of Cagliari had been given an occasion to separate himself from communion with the other fallen bishops by the indulgence granted to the bishops of Ariminum who had fallen. The Luciferians called the communion that had been granted an act of treachery.

This was first publicized and confirmed by Liberius, who, in confirming it, silently rebuked the Luciferians. Among the fragments of Hilary there survives a confirmation of the earlier papal decree. It declares that the Ariminian bishops were restored to their see after publishing their renunciation of the Ariminian decree and their profession of the Catholic faith, and adds:

> “Through this profession, even if it seems slight and lenient to some, he may recover what had been lost through guile from rectitude.”

He had said earlier:

> “For if some who make it their concern should perhaps rashly judge that what had been provided for by reason ought to be destroyed by a harsher judgment, and that what had already been secured by apostolic authority should be renewed …”

Liberius therefore recalls what had already been done and decreed, and censures those who had called the decree slight and lenient. By this he wounds the Luciferians, who, as is recorded there, proclaimed that mercy should not be shown to those who had acted unknowingly at Ariminum.

Faustinus and Marcellinus, supported by the presbyter Gregory, and others, presented a petition to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius. There they defended the Luciferians’ cause and accused of adulterating the Catholic truth those bishops who communicated in any way with the Arians—as they believed the fallen bishops of Ariminum had done. They boldly asserted that through this indulgence the whole Church had become guilty of treachery, while only a few with Lucifer retained the purity of the faith. They likewise affirmed that all who had subscribed to the decrees of the Arians ought to be regarded as transgressors.

They describe their own party and the Catholic party as follows:

> “Meanwhile, because among some people the multitude is preferred to the truth, since it has only a few followers, and because we are distressed that we follow the inviolable faith among the few and avoid the many on account of their impious heresies and the sacrilegious subscriptions of transgressors, what do you judge in this matter, most just emperors and defenders of the Catholic faith? To which of these two parties do you give your approval? One party contains many bishops. But where there are many, there the sacred faith of Christ, formerly always defended, has been violated through treachery; there, through fear of the law, the impiety of Arius, formerly always condemned, has been embraced. But where there are very few, there the faith of Christ is defended through exiles, tortures, the shedding of blood, and death itself, while the impiety of Arius and every heresy are execrated as the supreme evil.”

They therefore distinguish those who had justly been discredited on account of heresy or treachery, and regard as transgressors all who, even if they did not embrace the Arian heresy, nevertheless communicated with the Arians in any way.

Offended by Liberius, whom they regarded as the author of the condemnation of the Luciferians, these men fabricated the story that Liberius had communicated with the Arians and differed from them only in refusing to defend the doctrine of rebaptism. In this way they could show Liberius to be an unworthy pontiff, as well as his successor Damasus, whom Liberius had appointed his vicar when he was carried into exile, and so advance the cause of Ursicinus, whom they regarded as the true pontiff.

Just as the Donatists fabricated the fall of Marcellinus in order to weaken especially the judgments pronounced against them by Melchiades and Silvester, and to present Victor of Garba as the true successor of Peter’s chair, so these men fabricated this account.

The conjecture is strengthened by the words of the Eusebian fragment, where Eusebius is described as having been questioned by Liberius in the presence of Constantius. He says, p. 141:

> “We trust in the Lord that Christ will find us faithful, just as we were baptized, and we hold the blessing that we received from blessed Julius.” Liberius said: “Whose office do we hold? Is it not that of our predecessor Julius?”

This clearly shows that the Luciferians taught that the Church had fallen through these communions and that all the bishops were to be regarded as transgressors, while they themselves were free from that guilt because they had been consecrated by Julius, not by Liberius. Thus our conjecture becomes manifest.

These men therefore, first defending Felix and then Ursicinus, either wrote or interpolated the acts and filled them with these futile inventions. It is not surprising that they could safely circulate such things, since the emperors, having been deceived by them, issued a favorable rescript addressed to Cynegius, the praetorian prefect, in which they commend them as follows:

> “Nevertheless, when our clemency was petitioned by Faustinus and Marcellinus, priests most complete in faith, we feared that, if no answer were given by us to those who made the request, we might seem to approve those who, contrary to our purpose, had added something to the divine law that we serve. We therefore regulate both matters in such a way that we honor the petition that has been presented, but neither wish nor command anything to be added to the faith at our discretion. No one has ever been so profane in mind that, although he ought to follow Catholic teachers, he himself determines for the teachers what ought to be followed. And indeed the praise of the petition is credible and just, since it has embraced almost the entire sequence and order of heretical superstition, which is contrary to the Catholic faith. For it has disclosed both where it arose and by whose author it was advanced.”

Gregory, who was the author of the Life of Eusebius, as he himself testifies at the end of the cited fragment, was, I think, the same man who is praised by the schismatics in the petition. Whether he was the same person who later became bishop of Baetica and is numbered among the followers of Lucifer is a matter for another discussion.

For the present it is enough to note that the history and fall of Liberius—represented as a transgressor through communion entered into with the Arians, while rejecting only their rebaptism—was fabricated from these schismatic petitions. Whether it was unjustly imposed upon Pope Liberius that he communicated with the Arians must be investigated by those who have treated this question expressly.]

[Note: Line 10—“Apart from the second baptism.” In the Life of Felix I, the schismatics—who are unique in this account—fabricate the claim that in the time of Liberius the Arians promoted a second baptism, namely that they rebaptized those who transferred their allegiance from the Catholics to their camp.

For neither Athanasius nor Hilary nor any of the others who expressly described the errors of the Arians accuses them of promoting rebaptism. The first among the Arians to disseminate this error was Eunomius, and that only after the death of Liberius. Out of hatred for the earlier Arians and Semi-Arians, he became the head and leader of those who taught that the Word differed in essence from the Father. After the year 380 he universally promoted the rebaptism and reordination of all who came to him either from the Catholic religion or from other sects.

This is clear from Philostorgius, who, recounting the deeds of the Eunomians under Theodosius, writes in Book X, chapter 4, section 136:

> “The Eunomians separated themselves so completely from the aforementioned heresies that they accepted neither their baptism nor their ordination.”

The falsehood of the schismatics is thereby exposed, as is the origin of this claim; and the interpolation of these acts is likewise proved.]

[Note: Line 18—“Liberius recalled from the cemetery of St Agnes.” These words are taken from the Acts of Felix and have been inserted here by the compiler of the Life of Liberius, with a few changes of wording.]

### Line 18

**“Constantius entered Rome and, at that very hour, convened a council.”** After Liberius had been recalled, Constantius was not in Rome. For while the more exact chronologists place Liberius’s return in the year 358, they report that Constantius spent that entire year at Sirmium, was occupied in war against the Quadi and Sarmatians, and that in the same year the council returned—at which the Persian envoys had entered Constantinople on 23 February (according to the Chronicle of Idacius under the year 358), and for the purpose of hearing them he finally prepared to depart. Hence the falsity of the Acts of Felix must be noted; and consequently the interpolator who attached to Liberius what he took from those Acts, without applying any critical judgment, did not hesitate to assert both that Constantius delayed in the city while Liberius was returning from exile and that a council subsequently took place in Constantius’s presence.

There are, however, other incontrovertible arguments that Constantius was not in Rome in that year, drawn from the publication of laws. At the end of the year 357 he was at Milan, where he issued law 5 under the title *On Sorcery* in the Theodosian Code, as well as law 14 *On Bishops*, also there, dated 9 December at Milan. In the same place he issued law 9 *On the Public Post*. That he went to Sirmium and was there at the end of the year is indicated by law 27 *On Appeals*, which was published at Sirmium. Philostorgius reports that Liberius’s recall from exile was deliberated not at Rome but at Sirmium, when, continuing his account of Constantius’s actions, he writes in book IV, chapter 3, §65:

> “He himself went to Sirmium and conducted affairs there; there, too, he recalled from exile Liberius, the bishop of the city of Rome, whom the Romans ardently desired, and restored him to them when they demanded him.” (Book XVI, p. 455.)

Marcellinus removes all doubt. Describing Constantius’s stay in the city in 357, and adding that he had been greatly delighted by the city’s magnificence for thirty days, he writes:

> “Therefore, wishing to remain longer in the most august of all seats, so that he might enjoy purer leisure and pleasure, the emperor was alarmed by repeated messages and reliable reports indicating that the Suevi were invading Raetia as far as Valeria, and that the Sarmatians—a people highly skilled in banditry—were ravaging Upper Moesia and Pannonia Secunda. Disturbed by these reports, on the thirtieth day after his entry, 29 May, he departed from the city and hastened into Illyricum by way of Tridentum. Thereupon, having sent Severus to replace Marcellus—a man strengthened by experience in war and maturity—he ordered Ursicinus to come to him. And the latter, having gratefully received the letter, came to Sirmium.” [Col. 0037C]

### Number 52, line 1

**“From that same day there was persecution among the clergy.”** What the interpolator inserted here is taken from a fragment attributed to Eusebius, but in such a way that the entire cause of the persecution is referred to Liberius’s return. In the Eusebian Acts, however, Constantius is, with an even worse error, named as the author, as though he were present at Rome. Baluze, p. 142, gives the following:

> “From that same day, whoever was found within the churches by order of the emperor Constantius not confessing or participating in the same manner as Liberius was to be punished with the sword without trial. Therefore, in the streets, in the alleys, in the churches, and even in the baths, they were being killed by the sword, while Constantius, together with Liberius, persecuted Christians.”

And the *Liber Pontificalis* shortly afterward says:

> “And there was a great persecution in the city of Rome, so that the clergy and priests had access neither to the churches nor to the baths.” [Col. 0037D]

Faustinus and Marcellinus, in the treatise cited above, expose these lies fabricated by the Luciferians. They assert that a persecution took place at Rome, but attribute it neither to Liberius nor to Constantius, rather to the people’s hostility toward the Luciferians. For after saying, “Where there are many, there the sacred faith of Christ was violated through betrayal . . . there impiety was accepted through fear of the law of Arius,” they immediately add:

> “But where there are very few, there the faith of Christ is vindicated through exiles, through torments, through the shedding of blood, and through death itself.”

Apart from the fact that no such persecution in the City is recorded anywhere by secular writers, they are also refuted by the fact that this alleged great persecution could have been exercised only against a very small number of people, as the Luciferians themselves testify; in relation to those people, scarcely even a portion of the punishments they invented could have been inflicted.

What makes the author of the Eusebian fragment still more flagrantly mendacious is that he adds at the end:

> “After Liberius died, Damasus was raised up, and in a public declaration condemned Liberius, having held a synod with twenty-eight bishops and twenty-five presbyters; and the persecution ceased, though not for very long.” [Col. 0038A]

Who would dare believe such nonsense, when the Acts of Damasus establish that Damasus had been appointed Liberius’s vicar, and that Saint Damasus was the pontiff’s companion in the very cemetery of Saint Agnes?

From these lacunae the interpolation of Liberius’s deeds emerged. Hence every sensible person will recognize that these interpolations deserve no greater credence than either the Eusebian fragment or the Acts of Saint Felix, which were composed by Luciferians offended with Liberius. They regarded him as the first author of the indulgence published for the bishops who had lapsed at Ariminum, and that indulgence had given occasion to the Luciferian schism.

### Line 8

**“Here Liberius adorned the tomb of Saint Agnes with slabs of marble.”** The schismatic presbyters had said that the Catholics possessed temples gleaming with precious marble. The splendor of churches had already become widespread under Constantine, especially through such kinds of ornamentation—not only at Rome but also throughout the churches of the rest of the world.

It is reported of Nectarius that, after becoming bishop of Constantinople in 381, he never ceased during his lifetime to gather marble for adorning the church of Saint Anastasia. Since these materials were later lost—we do not know by what accident—they gave slanderers the opportunity to fabricate the claim that they had been sold by Saint Chrysostom. For at the synod numbered 7 in Photius, among the other accusations, this too was brought forward:

> “That he himself had sold the marbles of Saint Anastasia, which Nectarius had left to that church for the purpose of adorning it.”

[Col. 0038B]

### Note

### Number 51, line 5

**“They ordained the presbyter Felix in his place.”** The heretics’ accusation that Liberius had been infected with the Arian heresy is false, since he wrote or taught nothing contrary to the orthodox faith. We readily concede that, by communicating with the Arians, by unjustly condemning Athanasius, and by subscribing to a formula of faith lacking the term *consubstantial*—although that formula was Catholic—he incurred a justified suspicion of heresy in the external forum and was for that reason rightly avoided by the Catholics. See Baronius, year 355, numbers 5 and following, and year 357, numbers 46 and following; Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book IV, chapter 9.

### Line 12

**“He consented to the commands of Constantius.”** That is, he was compelled by force, torture, and the weariness of exile.

### Number 52, line 2

**“They would be crowned with martyrdom.”** It seems that at this time Eusebius, a Roman presbyter, was shut inside a room by Constantius’s agents and, remaining there for seven months, breathed his last, consumed by hunger. Baronius, notes on the Martyrology, 24 August.

### Line 4

**“He consented to the heresy of Constantius, but was not rebaptized.”** This seems to indicate that, although Liberius communicated with the Arians, he did not become an Arian through the second baptism by which they were accustomed to baptize again those Catholics who defected to them. [Col. 0038D] But this statement is superfluous and was added by someone; for the Arians had not yet begun to rebaptize. Indeed, at this time the Church did not reject the baptism of the Arians, as Saint Jerome testifies in *Against the Luciferians*. Baronius, year 357, number 41.

### Line 6

**“There was a great persecution in the city of Rome.”** Those who did not communicate with Liberius abstained not only from the church but also from the public baths, lest they bathe together with them. They knew from the teaching of John the Evangelist that one ought not to share the washing of the bath with heretics; for that reason the magistrate raged against them. Baronius, year 357, number 58.

[Col. 0038D]

## Chronological Notes

From the catalogue of that age—the most ancient of all—we understand that the beginning of Liberius’s pontificate was on 22 May, in the consulship of Constantius Augustus for the fifth time and Constantius Gallus Caesar. In that same year his predecessor Julius is also recorded in a fourth-century work as having died on 12 April. At this point the catalogue ends, thereby proving its antiquity.

The end of Liberius’s life is made no less certain by the *Book of Petitions* presented to the emperor Theodosius by the two presbyters Faustinus and Marcellinus toward the end of the fourth century. Baronius assigned it to the year 367, while Schelestratus published it in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, volume I, book II, chapter 9, no. 2, from Vatican Codex 4903. Panvinius had earlier cited it in volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History* from a manuscript preserved in the same Vatican library. He states that the codex was written in uncial letters and was preserved in the library of the monastery of Santa Croce at Fonte Avellana; in it, he says, the following is read:

> “And so, on 24 September, in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus, Liberius was taken from human affairs.”

The consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus belongs to the year of Christ 366. Therefore, since Liberius assumed the Roman pontificate in 352, on 22 May—the day on which he was elected, unless one should read 24 May, the Sunday on which he was ordained—and since he was taken from human affairs on 24 September 366, in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus, it is necessary to assign to his tenure of that see fourteen years, four months, and two days.

It may therefore seem strange that, although the limits of Liberius’s pontificate are so certain, no chronological period corresponding to that total is found among the calculations assembled in the prolegomena. There I nevertheless noted that three years must be subtracted for the exile in which Liberius was detained by Constantius Augustus. Part of that period must also be assigned to his legitimate successor, Saint Felix, pope and martyr, as will be shown in this and the following section. This is demonstrated both by the paintings in the basilica of Saint Paul and by catalogues that assign to that see ten years, seven months, and three days.

Moreover, when Felix was ordained in Liberius’s place by Liberius’s decision, while Liberius himself was being taken into exile—as is expressly stated in line 9 of Anastasius, number 52—all of Felix’s years are counted from the time of his ordination. Although Felix’s legitimate pontificate should not be extended beyond one year, three months, and two days, as I indicated from Schelestratus’s second dissertation, chapter 9, in the same folio 105 of the *Prolegomena*, column 2, the catalogue under Felix assigns Felix a full three years of exile, which are taken away from Liberius.

The Librarian mentions that Liberius spent two years in exile before Felix was ordained at his persuasion. Line 4, number 51:

> “Here he is taken into exile by Constantius because he was unwilling to consent to the Arian heresy, and he spent two years in exile; and the priests assembled, with Liberius’s advice, and ordained the presbyter Felix as bishop in his place.”

If to these two years one adds the one year, three months, and two days assigned to Felix, the total is three years, three months, and two days. Subtracting this from the fourteen years, four months, and two days counted from the beginning of Liberius’s pontificate to his death according to the documents of the fourth century leaves eleven years, one month, and no days:

> 14 years, 4 months, 2 days  
> minus 3 years, 3 months, 2 days  
> = 11 years, 1 month, 0 days. [Col. 0039D]

The paintings of Saint Paul and several catalogues, together with the Librarian, assign ten years, seven months, and three days to Liberius’s pontificate. Thus five months and twenty-seven days must be assigned to his exile in addition to the two full years.

If from these two years, five months, and twenty-seven days of exile, and from Felix’s legitimate pontificate of one year, three months, and two days, together with the ten years, seven months, and three days assigned to Liberius’s see, the total is calculated, it comes to fourteen years, four months, and two days. This corresponds to the interval from 22 May 352, in the consulship of Constantius Augustus for the fifth time and Gallus, when Saint Liberius assumed the pontificate, to 24 September 366, in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus, when he died.

In which years Liberius was driven into exile can be gathered from line 3 of this section, since the Chronicle of Jerome and other writers report that Liberius was ordered into exile a second time. The passage reads:

> “He was in office during the time of Constantius, the son of Constantine, up to Constantine Augustus for the third time. Here he is taken into exile by Constantius because he was unwilling to consent to the Arian heresy, and he spent two years in exile, etc.”

In the words “up to Constantine for the third time,” where I think one should read “up to Constantius for the third time,” the third consulship of Constantius Gallus together with the seventh consulship of Constantius is indicated, if I am not mistaken, in the year of Christ 354. This consulship appears in many laws of both the Theodosian and Justinianic Codes—sometimes incorrectly designated as the seventh consulship of Constantine, where the seventh consulship of Constantius should be read—as well as in the Alexandrian Chronicle, the *Fasti Florentini*, the *Fasti Maiores* and *Minores*, the *Fasti of Idacius*, Prosper’s Chronicle, the *Fasti of an Anonymous Author*, and those of another anonymous author collected by Reland in *On the Urban Prefecture*.

It seems, then, that the first law against Liberius’s exile belongs to this period. In the year 355, in the consulship of Arbittio and Lollianus, he was driven into exile on 13 August, as Panvinius gathered from the most ancient Acts of the pontiffs; see Schelestratus, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 2, chapter 9, no. 3. This was three years, two months, and twenty-one days after his ordination.

Two years later, after returning from exile, he is said to have found Felix, formerly an archdeacon and then a presbyter, made pontiff contrary to his oath and elected by the clergy—as is also reported in the chronicle prefixed with Jerome’s name—having first been intruded by the faction of the Arians, although he himself was a Catholic.

Thereafter, in varying alternation, Liberius and Felix were harassed by the Arian prince and by the Roman Senate and people: now Liberius, now Felix, they were driven from the City and recalled in turn. At that time, whether through the consent of Liberius, who was again in exile, or through the rumor brought to Rome that he was said to have consented to Constantius in accepting the Sirmian formula, it is clear that Felix was lawfully elected as Liberius’s successor.

He, seated legitimately on the apostolic Chair, resisted Constantius with such remarkable firmness of faith that, after one full year, three months, and two days—the period assigned to his legitimate see in the paintings of Saint Paul, in the catalogues, and in the other documents cited in the *Prolegomena*—some say that he was driven from the City and secretly put to death by Constantius’s command on 10 or 11 November. Others say that he was indeed expelled from the City and ceased to hold the pontificate on 11 November, but that he continued to live until the year 365, since the *Book of Petitions* of Faustinus and Marcellinus reports that he died in the consulship of Valentinian and Valens.

After Felix’s death or resignation, the episcopate was vacant, according to the Farfa catalogue, for thirty-seven days—from 12 November to 20 December.
