According to the Librarian, who perhaps includes the dates of Felix’s death and Liberius’s re-election, it was vacant for thirty-nine days—from 11 November to 21 December of the same year, 359.

Liberius was then elected Roman pontiff again on 21 December and is said to have held the three patriarchal basilicas—the Constantinian, Vatican, and Pauline—for seven years (section 52), namely until the year 366 of the Christian era, when he died on 24 September, in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus.

After his second election he held office for 6 years, 9 months, and 3 days. Before his first exile he had held office for 3 years, 2 months, and 21 days. The total is 9 years, 11 months, and 24 days. If the 7 months and 9 days that elapsed from 2 August to 10 March of the following year are added, the result is 10 years, 7 months, and 3 days, assigned to Liberius by the Bergamo catalogue and the two Colbert catalogues, IV and VI, with the paintings of Saint Paul likewise in agreement, as I reported above in the *Prolegomena*.

The chronology of the two pontiffs, Liberius and Felix, must therefore be arranged from the documents cited as follows:

- **352, 22 May:** On Sunday, Liberius is ordained Roman pontiff.
- **355, 13 August:** Liberius is driven into exile.
- **356:** Felix is intruded into the Roman see on an unspecified day.
- **357, 2 August:** Liberius returns from his first exile.
- **358, 10 March:** Liberius goes into exile again, after seven months and nine days counted from his return, and relinquishes the pontificate.
- **358, 8 August:** Saint Felix is lawfully elected as successor.
- **359, 11 November:** Saint Felix is expelled and either martyred or resigns the pontificate.
- **359:** According to the Librarian, the episcopate is vacant for thirty-nine days, from 11 November to 21 December; according to the Bergamo catalogue, for thirty-seven days, from 11 November to 20 December.
- **359, 21 December:** Liberius is elected Roman pontiff again and presides over the Apostolic [Col. 0041B] See until his death on 24 September 366.
- **366:** In the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus, Saint Liberius closes his final day on 24 September, having held the Roman see for nearly seven years after his second election.

## Historical Notes

### Number 51, line 1

**“He held office for ten years, seven months, and three days.”** I explained shortly above, in the chronological notes, how this total is calculated. In the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark one reads: “He held office for six years, four months, and three days.” I suspect that this was taken from an older exemplar in which perhaps six years, nine months, and three days were written. That total defines the period from Liberius’s second election to the end of his life, rounded to seven years by the Librarian in the following section.

This period of Liberius’s tenure was interrupted by a second exile, broken by his resignation and the consent he gave to Felix’s election, and finally resumed through his second election to the Roman See. It renders the chronology of his times so complicated that it eludes the calculations of nearly all historians and chronologists, or at least exhausts the patience of those attempting to establish the chronology of that see.

The difficulty is increased by the need to separate in Liberius’s history the events that occurred earlier from those that followed after his recall. Thus Baronius himself, the author of the *Annals*, observes under the year 357 that the earlier events must necessarily be combined with the later ones so that a complete picture of the deeds of that pontiff may emerge. His unconquerable strength in affirming the Catholic faith and the holiness of his conduct, commended by the Fathers who were his contemporaries, becomes evident when his earlier and later periods are compared.

The sufferings he endured as a human being during the intervening period—when, worn down by the tedium of exile, he subscribed to the sentence against Athanasius and to the formula deceitfully presented to him, although it did not dissent from the Catholic faith—cannot themselves be separated from the sequence of the many events involving other formulas that followed and differed from that one. The accusation of subscription cannot be fastened upon him with respect to those formulas.

It should therefore not seem at all surprising if Liberius’s deeds appear somewhat obscure and confused to us in this *Book of the Pontiffs*. They could not be related by the more diligent historians and chronologists without mixture and entanglement. The reader will nevertheless find them clarified in the earlier studies, especially in Baronius under the year 357, then in the younger Pagi’s section on Liberius, and perhaps more elegantly in Somier’s *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*. This will be evident from the following sample of selected notes, drawn here from his commentary.

### Number 52, line 10

**“Here he built a basilica in his own name near the market of Livia.”** The more appropriate place to discuss this will be under Sixtus III, who enlarged the Liberian basilica.

### Line 13

**“He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.”** Several pontiffs from the time of Saint Marcellus through Siricius are recorded as having been buried in this cemetery of Priscilla: Marcellinus, Marcellus, Silvester, Liberius, Siricius, and Celestine.

Aringhius, who lists them in *Subterranean Rome*, book IV, chapter 28, no. 10, also observes that it is clear from a letter of Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne that this cemetery had been decorated with paintings by Celestine. He adds, in no. 12, that Pope Paschal transferred the relics of several of them into the City, when they had to be rescued from the attacks and injuries of the Saracens and heretics. This is shown by the marble tablets attached to the title of Saint Praxedes, where he deposited the relics of the holy pontiffs Siricius and Celestine; Aringhius also displays their funerary inscriptions, which had been published by Baronius and Gruter.

We also know from another source that the cemetery of Priscilla was famous in Liberius’s time because of the solemn baptism administered there by that same pontiff when he was forbidden to enter the City. This occurred at Damasus’s urging, with the entire gathering of presbyters assembled there, as Aringhius records from the ancient Acts of Liberius in the cited book IV, chapters 30 and 31. There he explains the parts of the cemetery of Priscilla called the cemetery of Novella and the Ostian cemetery. I indicated this above in volume II, in the notes to Saint Marcellinus, p. 259.

Moreover, Damasus, who is named in the Acts as Liberius’s presbyter and vicar while Liberius was still alive, later became his immediate successor. In that same cemetery of Priscilla, where he buried his predecessor Liberius, he adorned the tomb of Pope Marcellus with verses, which may be read in Baronius, *Appendix*, volume III, p. 309; Gruter, p. 1172; and Aringhius, book IV, chapter 28, no. 7.

[Col. 0042B]

### Note

### Line 3

**“Here he is taken into exile by Constantius.”** Liberius is sent into exile by the emperor as far as Beroea, a city of Thrace, because he was unwilling to subscribe against Athanasius and to communicate with the Arians.

### Line 5

**“They ordained Felix in his place.”** Felix, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was installed in Liberius’s place through the efforts of the Arians, especially Acacius, the leader of the Arians. Nevertheless, he was orthodox, not an Arian. In matters of religion he was free from reproach, although he openly communicated with those who were striving to undermine that religion and subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation.

The authorities are Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Acacius; Theodoretus, book II, chapter 10; Sozomenus, book IV, chapter 10; and others. While Saint Liberius was alive, Felix could not have been elected as anything more than a chorepiscopus, lest there be two bishops of one Catholic Church and, disgracefully, two heads protruding from one body.

### Line 8

**“They had access neither to the churches nor to the baths.”** The clergy and priests who had adhered to Felix avoided the church where Liberius assembled his followers and also abstained from the baths, lest they bathe together with them. They knew from the teaching of John the Evangelist that one ought not to share the washing of the bath with heretics.

[Col. 0042D]

### Note

### Line 3

**“By Constantius.”** Saint Liberius, a Roman by birth and the son of Augustus, ascended the pontifical see after an inter-pontificate of two months and several days. He was ordained on 21 June, which was a Sunday in the year 352.

Immediately the Eastern bishops attempted to draw him over to their side, but Liberius replied to the Easterners that he could not agree with them, and for a long time he steadfastly refused to condemn Athanasius. Therefore, in order to confront the persecution that was threatening—not so much against Athanasius as against the entire Catholic Church and especially the Western bishops—in the year 353 he sent legates to the emperor Constantius, who had halted at Arles after defeating Magnentius. These were Vincent of Capua, Marcellus of Campania, and several others. He instructed them to obtain from Constantius the convocation of a general council to be celebrated at Aquileia, [Col. 0043A] where the matter of the faith would first be considered and then the case of Athanasius.

On the occasion of Liberius’s legation, a council was convened at Arles. There, at the instigation of the Arian bishops Ursacius and Valens—who, after the Council of Milan, discussed under Julius, had returned to their vomit—and together with Saturninus, the also-Arian bishop of Arles, the emperor forced most of the orthodox bishops, and especially Vincent of Capua himself, Liberius’s legate, to subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation.

This was the same Vincent who had served as Silvester’s legate at the great Council of Nicaea and who had also sat as a judge with other bishops at the great Council of Sardica to hear and judge Athanasius’s case. He had often cast a white vote into the urn for Athanasius’s acquittal, as they say. Yet afterward he remained unshaken against those same Arians in defense of the Catholic faith, as we shall say when speaking of the Council of Ariminum.

Almost alone among the orthodox bishops at the council of Arles, Paulinus, bishop of Trier, gave a display of unconquerable courage. Because he had defended the faith and Athanasius’s innocence with outstanding strength and bravery, he was deposed by the Arians and sent by Constantius into exile in Phrygia, where he died in 358 as a glorious confessor. The history of this council is drawn from Liberius’s letter to Constantius, Saint Athanasius’s first apology, and other sources.

On the other side, about thirty Arian bishops assembled at Antioch in a synod in the year 354 and, as Sozomenus writes in book IV, chapter 8,

> “wrote letters to all the bishops established everywhere, asserting that Athanasius had returned to Alexandria contrary to the laws of the Church, not because he had previously been declared innocent in a synod, but through the contentiousness of those who shared his opinions; and they urged them neither to communicate with him nor to write to him.”

After Liberius learned what had happened to the legates he had previously sent to the emperor Constantius, he sent another legation to the same emperor in the year 354. The legates chosen for so important an undertaking were Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia; Pancratius, a presbyter of the Roman Church; and Hilary, a deacon of that same Church. At the command of the same pontiff, Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, joined them. They brought Liberius’s letter to Constantius, who was still in Gaul. The letter survives in the fragments of Saint Hilary and in Baronius.

They obtained what they requested from Constantius: namely, the convocation of a general council for the following year, 355.

In that year, and indeed before it had advanced very far—before the end of May—several bishops from the East and more than three hundred from the West, as Socrates and Sozomenus testify, assembled at Milan. Lucifer of Cagliari and his colleagues, the legates of the Apostolic See, as well as Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, foresaw the tyranny that the Arian emperor Constantius would exercise in this synod. They approached it with great reluctance, especially Eusebius.

Nevertheless, after being summoned to the council by two letters—the first from the Arians and the second from the same legates—Eusebius attended it, although he had hesitated for ten full days, as Saint Hilary testifies in his letter to Constantius. These two letters, published by Baronius from the Acts of Saint Eusebius and from the archives of the Church of Vercelli, are preserved in the first volume of the councils.

After Eusebius of Vercelli and the apostolic legates had been admitted into the church and synod, the Arians, who were plotting the overthrow of the Nicene faith and the exile of all bishops who would not subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation, demanded that they subscribe against Athanasius.

But, as the cited Hilary adds, Eusebius replied:

> “It is first necessary to establish the faith of the priesthood. He had discovered that some of those present were contaminated by heretical pollution. He placed in their midst the faith set forth at Nicaea, promising to do everything they demanded if they would write in support of the profession of faith. Dionysius, bishop of Milan, was the first to receive the sheet and began to write his profession. Valens violently snatched the pen and paper from his hands.” [Col. 0044A]

Then, out of fear of the people of Milan, who were preserving the Catholic faith with remarkable zeal, the Arians moved the synod from the church to the palace. There, as Sulpitius Severus says in book II of his *Sacred History*:

> “They issue a letter in the emperor’s name, filled with every kind of wickedness. Their purpose was this: if the people received it with willing ears, they could bring forward what they desired with public authority; but if it were received otherwise, all the odium would fall upon the emperor, and the matter itself would be pardonable, since even then a catechumen could rightly seem not to have known the sacrament of faith. Accordingly, when the letter was read in the church, the people rejected it.”

[Col. 0044B]

Since Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari, Pancratius, and Hilary—the apostolic men who were defending the faith and justice with courage—refused to subscribe to Athanasius’s condemnation, the emperor Constantius condemned them to exile. Hilary was savagely beaten with scourges through the evil machinations of Ursacius, Valens, and Constantius’s eunuchs, as we learn from Saint Athanasius’s letter to the solitaries.

Dionysius, bishop of Milan, who had imprudently subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation, later joined the apostolic legates in the glory of confession and was sent into exile with them. He died there, and the emperor Constantius intruded the Arian Auxentius into his see.

Not content with this, the emperor summoned Pope Liberius to Milan. When Liberius arrived, he refused, in accordance with the emperor’s wishes, to consent to Saint Athanasius’s condemnation: first, because Athanasius’s innocence and the Arians’ hostility toward him were known to Liberius; and second, because he saw that the Nicene faith was being attacked by underground passages while its vigorous defender, Saint Athanasius, was being persecuted.

Therefore, when Constantius attempted to extort this consent from him, Liberius replied:

> “I ask first that a general subscription be made confirming the faith set forth at Nicaea. Then, after our brothers have been recalled from exile and restored to their sees—if those who are now stirring up disturbances in the churches appear to have agreed with the apostolic faith—let us all assemble at Alexandria, where both the accused man and his accusers, as well as his defender, are present; after their case has been examined, let us deliver a unanimous judgment.” [Col. 0044C]

These words are preserved in the dialogue that the emperor held with Liberius at Milan, reported by Theodoretus in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16. Worthy of being engraved in cedar are the words with which Liberius replied when Constantius threatened him with exile:

> “I have already said farewell to the brothers who are at Rome. Ecclesiastical laws are more important than a residence at Rome.”

After several days had passed, the emperor summoned Liberius again. When Liberius did not depart from his position, Constantius ordered him to be relegated to Beroea in Thrace.

After two years of Liberius’s exile had elapsed, Constantius went to Rome. There, as Theodoretus says in book II, chapter 17, the Roman matrons petitioned him to order Liberius’s return from exile. The emperor,

> “after consulting with his bishops, promised that he would restore the man to them if he agreed with the opinion of his bishops.”

Liberius, overcome by weariness and burning with an uncontrolled desire to recover his see, and having also suffered force and blows, condemned Athanasius and subscribed to the formula of faith offered to him by the Arians.

Therefore, in the year 358, as Jerome says in his *Chronicle*, Liberius entered Rome in triumph, and indeed on 2 August, as Anastasius records:

> “Liberius entered the city of Rome on 2 August.”

It cannot be said that his return to Rome occurred in 357, since he was not recalled from exile before he had subscribed to the formula composed by the third Council of Sirmium, held in 358.

Certainly, in December 357, Liberius was not yet in Rome, since law 14 of the Theodosian Code *On Bishops*, issued at Milan in December, was addressed to Felix, bishop of Rome. Liberius therefore had not yet been restored to his see.

The formula to which Liberius subscribed appears to be the one that Hilary calls in his fragments “the treachery composed by the Arians,” and which Liberius calls Catholic. In his letter to the Easterners, he says that Demophilus presented it to him and that he accepted it.

Since, after the third Council of Sirmium in 358—as may be read in Baronius’s *Critique*—the formula of faith to which Liberius subscribed had been composed, and since that council seemed to have established not so much peace among the Easterners as new disagreements among them, the emperor Constantius summoned an ecumenical council at Ariminum to be held in 359.

At the advice of the Arians, however, he divided it into two parts, [Col. 0045B] so that the Easterners would meet at Seleucia in Isauria and the Westerners at Ariminum in Emilia.

About 160 Eastern bishops assembled at Seleucia. Since they harassed one another with mutual accusations, the council split into two factions. A new formula of faith was issued by Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine and leader of the first faction. In it, after rejecting the terms *consubstantial* and *of equal substance* as abhorrent to Scripture, he acknowledged a similarity of the Son to the Father and condemned the term *dissimilar* with an anathema.

The bishops of the other faction, the semi-Arians, rejected this formula. They defended the Son as similar to the Father in substance, not merely in will, as Acacius did. Therefore the Acacians withdrew. The semi-Arians, assembling in the church, deposed and excommunicated those who refused to be present.

On these matters one should read Saint Athanasius, *On the Synods*; Socrates, book II, chapter 31 and following; Sozomenus, book IV, chapter 21; and Severus Sulpitius, book II, who writes that Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was present at this synod. Hilary himself therefore gives a more detailed account of what occurred there in his book *Against Constantius*.

Four hundred bishops attended the Council of Ariminum, according to the same Severus Sulpicius in the passage cited above. Once the bishops had assembled, the letters of the emperor Constantius were read, in which he ordered that only the matter of the faith be discussed. Valens and Ursacius, the Arians, brought forward a third formula of faith, the Sirmian formula, which taught that the Son was like the Father according to the Scriptures; but although it pleased the emperor, it was nevertheless rejected by the Fathers. Then the Nicene faith was approved by the unanimous vote of the Catholic bishops, and it was judged sufficient for every purpose. Ursacius, Valens, and four other Arian bishops were condemned, and a synodal letter was sent to Constantius Augustus; Athanasius reproduces it in his work *On the Synods*. In this letter the Fathers ask the emperor to receive the delegates whom they send with kindness. Finally, they plead that he order the bishops—[Col. 0045D] whom both the burden of age and poverty afflict—to be returned to their homeland, lest the churches, in the absence of their bishops, be left deserted. But Ursacius and Valens, who had arrived before the orthodox delegates, so embittered the emperor’s mind that the bishops sent by the council were unable to bring back any reply. Theodoret testifies that all these things were accomplished by the schemes of the Arians, so that, after wearing down the orthodox bishops by a prolonged delay and crushing them with disgust, they might compel them to destroy the decrees which they had issued against the heresy and its defenders. But the Catholic prelates, in letters sent to Constantius, declared that they would never depart from their earlier purpose and judgment, and that they had given the same instructions to the council’s delegates. Yet when the bishops sent by the council were forced to subscribe to the Arians’ perfidy and to communicate with them, they were not alone in being led into that transgression; nearly all the bishops of the orthodox party were also drawn into it. On their lapse, see Saint [Col. 0046A] Athanasius in his letter to the Africans, Saint Hilary in the fragments, and others.

Pope Liberius and Vincent, bishop of Capua, who had previously appeared to have been weakened by Arian contamination, returned to a better course and stood fearlessly for the Catholic faith, refusing to subscribe to the Arians’ perfidy. This is clear from the letter of Pope Damasus and the Roman synod to the Illyrians, reported by Theodoret in Book II, chapter 22, and from the delegation of the Council of Lampsacus sent to Liberius himself. For when, after the death of the emperor Jovian, the bishops of the Hellespont and Bithynia, together with other defenders of consubstantiality, had celebrated the Council of Lampsacus—a city in the Hellespont—in the year 364, and had decreed that the doctrine asserting that the Son was like the Father in substance should be upheld, they sent a delegation to Pope Liberius after the council. They instructed the delegates not at all to disagree with Liberius concerning the faith, but to communicate with the Roman Church and to ratify the faith of *consubstantiality*. [Col. 0046B] When the delegates arrived in Rome, they presented the council’s letter, but Liberius did not wish to receive it, because he suspected them of the Arian heresy. They, however, professed that they were Catholics and presented him with a petition in which the very words of the Nicene Creed had been written. This is established by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 7, and by Socrates, Book IV, chapters 4 and 11. In the latter passage Socrates also appends the petition delivered to Liberius by the aforementioned delegates. In it they profess that they hold and preserve the Catholic faith confirmed by the most holy Council of Nicaea, in which the word *consubstantial* (*homoousios*) was set down in a holy and devout manner to overthrow Arius’s perverse doctrine. Next, they curse and condemn Arius, his impious doctrine, and the supporters of his error. Third, they pronounce anathema by name upon the formula of faith recited at the Council of Ariminum, since it conflicts with the Nicene faith. Fourth, they set out their own faith, which is in every respect the Nicene faith. By means of this petition Liberius, as though binding the delegates by their pledge, received them into communion, [Col. 0046C] and then dismissed them with letters. This is certainly a firm argument for Liberius’s orthodox faith.

Saint Athanasius likewise relates in his letter to those living a solitary life that Eusebius, the Arian eunuch of the emperor Constantius, offered many gifts to Blessed Peter, but Liberius, the custodian of that same church, sharply rebuked him for allowing them to be brought into the church and ordered that they be cast out of the Church as unlawful and accursed. But why should we hesitate, when Pope Siricius supplies us with the most certain evidence of Liberius’s orthodoxy in the letter he wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, which will be discussed shortly? For in its first chapter he expressly asserts not merely that Liberius, with great courage, resisted the brazen insolence of the Arians in those most disastrous times by refusing to subscribe to the Arian formula of faith recited at the Council of Ariminum—as nearly everyone writes—but that he went further and declared that council invalid and annulled it. The words of Siricius are quoted below, no. 15.

[Col. 0046D] Certainly Liberius enjoyed a great reputation in the Catholic Church, as Saint Ambrose’s eulogy proclaims. In Book III of *On Virgins*, which he wrote to his sister Marcellina, he says: “Since in the preceding two books we have arranged what we had to say, it is time, holy sister, to recall the teachings of Liberius, of blessed memory, which you are accustomed to discuss with me, so that the more holy the man, the more welcome the discourse may become.” He later inserts a discourse of that same Liberius delivered at Marcellina’s spiritual nuptials, when she dedicated herself to God in perpetual virginity. But, to bring the matters concerning the Council of Ariminum to a conclusion, Natalis Alexander demonstrates in a separate dissertation, in the fourth century, that the bishops of that council should not, because of a lapse so deeply to be mourned, be branded with the mark of heresy.

After Pope Liberius had annulled the Council of Ariminum, he sent general decrees to the faithful of Christ. These have not reached us, but they are mentioned in a letter written by Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, in the year 385. [Col. 0047A] For in its first chapter we read as follows:

“Thus, at the very beginning of your letter, you indicated that many who had been baptized by the impious Arians were hastening to the Catholic faith, and that certain of our brothers wished to baptize them again. This is not permitted, since both the Apostle forbids it, and the canons contradict it; moreover, after the Council of Ariminum had been annulled, the general decrees sent to the provinces by Liberius, my predecessor of venerable memory, prohibited it. We unite such people, together with the Novatians and other heretics, to the Catholic assembly, as has been established in the synod, by the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the laying on of the bishop’s hand. This is observed throughout the whole East and West. You too must henceforth deviate in no way from this path, if you do not wish to be separated by judgment from our synodal college.”

Here, however, it should be observed in passing that in the time of Gregory the Great heretics in the West were received by the laying on of hands alone, but in the East with the addition of chrism, as can be seen in his Letter 61 of Book IX, to the bishops of Ireland. Pope Innocent likewise asserts that Arians were received into the Roman Church by the laying on of hands [Col. 0047B], in Letter 18 to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, chapter 3.

After Liberius had, in two ordinations held in December, ordained eighteen priests and five deacons, and had additionally ordained nineteen bishops in various places, he exchanged this life for death on 23 September 366. He was buried on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla. The *Chronicle of Damasus*, which was composed before Liberius’s death, does not record the year or day of his death; it shows that an empty space was left for the day and year on which Liberius would die. We obtain the year of his death from the *Chronicle of Eusebius*, according to Pontacus’s edition, and from the preface to the petition of the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus, Luciferians, addressed to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius. There they record the day of his burial, namely 24 September, as it is also given in Bede’s *Martyrology*. [Col. 0047C] In the Hieronymian Martyrology, however, the day of his death is recorded, namely 23 September, as also in the ancient *Martyrology of Saint Cyriacus*. He therefore occupied the see for fourteen years, three months, and three days. Among his letters is one addressed to all the bishops, and another to Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt. Learned men regard these as spurious, since they are patched together from letters of Siricius, Leo, Martin I, and others.

[Note: [Col. 0047C]

The reader should understand why the notes of the Most Reverend Archbishop Somier on the histories of both pontiffs—Julius and Liberius—are presented together: the reason is the case of Athanasius.

Because of the exile mentioned in no. 50, it seemed useful to select from Father Pagi the preceding notes, and from the Most Reverend Archbishop Somier the following ones, dealing with the exile imposed on Saint Athanasius by the evil schemes of the Eusebians who had assembled at the Council of Antioch [Col. 0047D], as well as with the revocation of that most wicked decree, subsequently brought about by the authority of Pope Julius. He consistently extended apostolic protection both to Athanasius and to Marcellus of Ancyra, as well as to other bishops similarly expelled on account of the Catholic faith. From this the reader will be able to judge whether the summary concerning the exile inserted at this point was extracted from the acts of Liberius, which a copyist had inadvertently transferred from the margin, or whether his words were truncated and confusedly combined with the account of the acts of Julius in the investigation of the exile unjustly decreed against Blessed Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, as some suspect. We have therefore thought it appropriate to excerpt the following from *Dogmatic History*, Book III, chapter 5.]

## On Julius

Pope Julius made the glory of his pontificate illustrious by his vigorous defense and exercise of the authority of his see, and by the constant protection he extended to bishops who suffered persecution [Col. 0048A] in defense of the faith. It was his good fortune to see the outcome of his labors crowned almost everywhere with a favorable result: his own Western patriarchate remained always faithful and obedient; the good cause, although harassed in the East, continually prevailed over the plots of its enemies; and the heretics were perpetually confounded, even though they were unsuccessfully supported by their own devices and by the supreme power of the princes who protected them. We shall demonstrate these points in the following chapters.

The faction of the Arians always found the principal support of its sect in Eusebius of Nicomedia, and for that reason his associates were called Eusebians. Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was the principal target against whom their weapons were directed, since by his zeal in defending the truth—which they themselves were attempting to overthrow—he surpassed all the others. The Eusebians therefore left no deceitful device, crime, or slander untried in their effort to obtain his deposition from the episcopate at the cabal of Tyre. But when the manifest injustice of the sentence they had pronounced against him became too [Col. 0048B] evident, and they consequently could not easily hope that it would be confirmed by those authorities whose power was recognized as necessary for carrying out the penalties decreed against him, they reached such a degree of malignity and cunning that they did not fear to accuse him of treason in letters sent to the Great Constantine and to induce the emperor to drive him into exile without a hearing. Constantine later excused this action by confessing that he had done it in order to protect Athanasius and remove him from the envy of his enemies, rather than to punish any crime, since he acknowledged that Athanasius had been found guilty of none; and when he indicated that he was ready to recall Athanasius from exile, he was overtaken by death. The three Caesars who succeeded their father fulfilled his wishes. The Eusebians were rejected with shame, and the lies they had told were refuted by the delegates sent by Athanasius (Saint Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*). But when the Eusebians claimed that Athanasius’s restoration had been carried out against the laws of the sacred [Col. 0048C] canons, they even dared to ordain Pistus as bishop in his place—something they had never attempted while Constantine the father was alive. They did not even fear writing to Julius, the Roman pontiff, asking him to act as judge of the decrees enacted at Tyre concerning Athanasius (Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 7); and Pistus himself, intruded into the see in opposition to Athanasius, came to Rome to defend the validity of his election. But the defenders of Pistus, “since they were not the equals of the presbyters sent by Athanasius and were continually convicted and refuted by them, asked Julius to summon a council and to send letters both to the Eusebians and to Athanasius at Alexandria, by which they would be summoned, so that the case might be examined before everyone in a just judgment. For then, they said, they would prove against Athanasius what they could no longer prove” (Saint Athanasius, *Apology* 2). Together with these delegates Athanasius had sent to Rome a synodal letter from the bishops of his patriarchate, by which the Eusebians’ calumnies were utterly overturned. Those who supported [Col. 0048D] Athanasius resisted the devices of the opposing faction briskly and with complete confidence, so that the latter were left speechless and utterly confounded. Julius neither allowed Pistus to be brought before him nor wished to communicate with him. The Eusebians’ delegates therefore, in order to evade the danger threatening their cause, claimed that they had not yet had sufficient time to collect their legal proofs and begged Pope Julius to summon a council at which an end might be put to this controversy.

The Roman pontiff, although he already knew from the first exchanges that everything fabricated against Athanasius had been contrived by unjust means, nevertheless, wishing to have the whole matter thoroughly investigated so that no one could later object or suspect that he had been forestalled by either party, ordered the council they requested to be convened at Rome. As Theodoret writes in Book II, chapter 4: “Following the canon of the Church, he ordered them [the Eusebians] to come to [Col. 0049A] Rome, and he summoned the divine Athanasius to answer on his own behalf in the court.” The Eusebians’ delegates, although they had obtained the holding of a council, were so enraged and shaken by the fact that Pistus had not been admitted to appear before Julius, and by the overwhelming arguments of Athanasius, which demanded that the intruder be treated accordingly, that three of the principal delegates—Macarius, Martycius, and Hesychius—although afflicted with serious illness, departed suddenly during the night and took flight. Julius had adopted and maintained his decision to convene the council all the more firmly because many bishops had been harassed by the Eusebians just as Athanasius had. “For,” says the holy Father in *Apology* 2, “not only did the bishops Athanasius and Marcellus come here with complaints about the injuries inflicted upon them, but many other bishops also came from Thrace, Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine.” We read in ancient writers that the case of these Eastern bishops was brought before the tribunal of Julius, the Roman pope, after the Council of Antioch had considered it, with Eusebius himself sending delegates to Julius so that he might confirm whatever had been decreed against [Col. 0049B] Athanasius (in Photius, *Codex* 257 and 258). Socrates also asserts this in Book II, chapter 11. This sufficiently demonstrates how firm and unshaken the supreme authority of the Roman see was regarded by the ancients. For by this example the bishops confirm that authority when, in the synodal letter of the Council of Italy to Theodosius Augustus, they write:

“By right and by the custom of our ancestors, just as Saint Athanasius of venerable memory, Peter, formerly bishop of the Alexandrian Church, and many of the Eastern bishops did, so that they might be seen to have taken refuge in the council of the Roman Church, of Italy, and of the whole West.”

But, leaving aside the sequence of this chronology, what is especially established by the event is the following: the disputed case was brought before the tribunal of the Roman pontiff; the Eusebians humbly professed that they would obey the judgment of the Roman pontiff; Saint Athanasius was summoned and came here as quickly as possible; “the Eusebians were ordered to appear [Col. 0049C] for judgment on a fixed day; and they were greatly disturbed because, contrary to their expectation, Athanasius had come to Rome, while they had contrived futile and empty excuses by evasive argument” (from Saint Athanasius, *Apology* 2). I shall explain this more clearly after first removing a difficulty that someone might raise concerning certain expressions used by ancient writers. Those hostile to the authority of the Roman see misuse these expressions to suggest to their readers that the bringing of the case before the tribunal of Pope Julius ought to be understood as nothing more than the consensual appointment of an arbitrator by the Eusebian party, while Athanasius, without consenting to that arbitrator, had looked to Rome as an asylum. But if the nature of the case is considered, together with the selection of documents gathered by Julius to inform his judgment and the method he employed to decide the controversy, all these things abundantly show that Julius’s judgment was awaited by virtue of the supreme authority entrusted to this see by Christ the Lord [Col. 0049D] over the whole Church. Tribunals are indeed asylums and places of refuge to which the weak and unjustly oppressed may withdraw and from which they may seek aid against the oppression of the powerful. Saint Athanasius and his companions, persecuted by the Eusebians, came to Rome not only to live in a safer place and withdraw from the fury of their enemies, but also to obtain from the supreme judge the legitimate assignment of their rights. Together with the other Easterners, they appealed to this tribunal not to obtain favor, but to receive justice against the disturbers of the law, with the proper legal order observed, and so forth. Finally, Julius himself openly declares that the right to decide that controversy belonged to him and that nothing could legitimately be determined without consulting him:

“Do you not know that this is the custom: that we should first be written to, so that from here what is just might be determined? Therefore, if such a suspicion had arisen there against a bishop, it ought to have been referred here to our Church.”

In the same place [Col. 0050A], from a letter of Pope Julius preserved by Athanasius, shortly before the end.

“The firmness of spirit which Saint Julius displayed here in defending the supreme authority of the apostolic see, and how he exercised it in the events that followed, is explained more fully by the same Archbishop Somier in chapters 6, 7, and 8, in connection with the Council of Sardica, which he demonstrates was summoned by the supreme pontiff. There, in his customary learned manner, he discusses appeals properly brought, and to be brought, to the holy see. It is enough to present here a selection of his material, which we have sampled as an illustration of the steadfastness of so great a pontiff in asserting the primacy and authority of the Roman see over the others.”

## On Liberius

Line 3.—“Here in exile,” etc. To provide a true and distinct understanding of the pontificate of Liberius, we shall do several things. First, we shall explain his concern [Col. 0050B] for the defense of the Catholic faith. Second, we shall indicate the evils he suffered and the persecutions he endured for the same reason. Third, we shall show that Liberius’s lapse detracted nothing from the authority of the holy see. Finally, it will become clear that, after being restored from what he had suffered as a human being, he subsequently emerged more vigorous and more useful to the Church, which thereafter he administered with the greatest praise.

Among the fragments of Saint Hilary’s works there is an edited letter under the name of Liberius to the Eastern bishops. It states that this pontiff had excommunicated Blessed Athanasius because Athanasius had refused to come to Rome to answer accusations once again brought against him near the end of the preceding pontificate. Protestant writers derive much of the substance of their error from this letter. It must therefore be stated that, as is clearly established by all the ancient records, this letter is not the work of Liberius. Baronius demonstrates this with conclusive arguments [Col. 0050C] in Volume III of the *Annals*, and it is perfectly clear that the letter was fraudulently inserted into the works of Saint Hilary by some Arian and substituted for another letter wholly contrary to it. This is manifestly inferred from what that holy Father immediately adds, which shows that Saint Hilary at that time was closely attached to the party of Athanasius. For the letters sent at that time by the Egyptian bishops to the same Roman pontiff asked not that Athanasius be restored to his see, but that he be declared to remain in communion with the Church, since he had been received by Julius, his predecessor.

It cannot be denied that, at the beginning of his pontificate, Liberius was greatly pressed by the Eastern bishops to exclude Athanasius from communion. But when, at the same time, a letter arrived from seventy-five Egyptian bishops whose judgment concerning Athanasius contradicted the earlier letters of the Easterners, Liberius communicated both letters to his clergy [Col. 0050D] and ordered that they be read at a synod. Moved by the testimony of the Egyptians, he also indicated to the Italian bishops: “It appeared contrary to divine law, when the number of Egyptians supporting Athanasius was greater, to give any measure of agreement to those who accused him” (letter of Pope Liberius to Constantius Augustus). He replied in accordance with this judgment.

Even then he foresaw that, through the cunning of the Arians, who enjoyed influence with the emperor, a terrible storm was about to overtake the Church. The whole West had persisted and still persisted in the constancy of orthodox doctrine. The vigilance of the Roman pontiffs, by protecting from their nearby station—or rather, from the center which they occupy—the surrounding provinces against the corruption that had infected the more distant East, had preserved them from it. The West was also protected from the contagion of that plague by the piety of the emperors Constantine and Constantius. Since they had received this part of the empire in a fraternal division, they defended, especially in their own dominions, the truth of the Nicene faith [Col. 0051A], to which they firmly adhered, with their patronage. But when these pious princes died before Constantius, and the whole empire was brought under his authority, while the tyrants who had divided certain regions were also eliminated, it was obvious that this emperor, freed from fraternal restraints and from fear of his rivals, would burst forth without restraint into the unbridled license of solemnly professing and disseminating Arianism everywhere. There was also reason to fear that, if any hidden supporters of the same heresy had previously existed in the West, they would now find in a prince who openly professed it the opportunity to exercise with impunity and freedom the same acts of violence whose sole theater had until then been the East, though not without some alternation in the policy of moderation.

To meet these impending evils in time, Liberius sent delegates to Constantius, who, after the destruction of Magnentius, was staying at Arles. The delegates—Vincent, bishop of Capua, and Marcellus, likewise a bishop in Campania—had been instructed to obtain [Col. 0051B] from the emperor his consent to convening a council at Aquileia. They met Constantius at Arles and found there a number of bishops, most of them Arians, who had recently condemned Athanasius. After that sentence, the emperor had ordered that no bishop residing within the imperial boundaries should communicate with Athanasius, and exile had also been decreed for those who disobeyed. Constantius did not even allow the delegates’ request concerning the celebration of a council to be brought forward. Instead, he treated them harshly with threatening words and hostile actions and compelled them to sign, in their own handwriting, an unjust decree against Athanasius. Liberius’s grief at this is shown by his letter, in which he confessed that the sorrow had nearly caused his death.

Nevertheless, the pontiff persisted in his plan to have a general council convened, which he regarded as the sole remedy for averting the evils threatening the Church. He therefore prepared a new delegation to Constantius, adding to it Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, Pancratius [Col. 0051C] the presbyter, and Hilary the deacon. He ordered them to lodge with Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, a prelate of notable holiness, and to secure his participation as their companion in that delegation and petition, since Eusebius was devoted to the Roman see with unbroken zeal and reverence.

He added a letter to Constantius Augustus which displayed no less apostolic firmness than the respect due to the emperor. It showed the necessity of a council both for bringing the case of Athanasius to an end and for defending the doctrines of the faith, and so forth. In it he also set out what secular authorities ought to provide for the convocation and celebration of councils and for the execution of their decrees. They ought to employ their authority for the preservation of public peace, so that those assembled, enjoying the emperor’s protection, might quietly discuss everything and freely establish decisions according to the order of the laws; and so that what had been confirmed by the judgment of the priests of God might, with the assistance of the rulers, be obediently received by the peoples [Col. 0051D] and diligently carried into execution.

The later delegates obtained from the Caesar the convocation of the council that had been denied to the earlier delegation. A synod was permitted to assemble at Milan. The emperor wished to be present there, not to preserve ecclesiastical freedom, but to suppress it and replace Catholic doctrine with Arianism. “For this reason,” writes Saint Athanasius in his letter to the Solitaries, “in place of an ecclesiastical court he established his own palace as the tribunal for these cases, and made himself the supreme ruler and author of these lawsuits.” And again: “When he learned of the freedom of Paulinus, Lucifer, Eusebius, and Dionysius, the bishops, … he drove them into exile; but, becoming more violently enraged against Athanasius, he promulgated an even harsher edict against him—namely, that he too must suffer his penalties, that the churches must be handed over to the Arians, and that he [Constantius] would leave them free to do whatever they wished.” What could the pastor and head of the Church do in such a difficult [Col. 0052A] condition of the times? Only this remained for him: to groan and console the afflicted at the same time through letters, to make himself a participant in their sufferings for the name of Christ, and through their prayers, by their common faith and hope, to await grace and glory from them for undertaking martyrdom together with them. This he certainly did in his letter to the exiled Confessors, in which we read:

“Placed between grief at your absence and joy in your glory … I ask you to believe that I am present with you. And because you have been brought nearer to God, raise me, your fellow priest and servant of God, to the Lord by your prayers, so that I may be able to bear with endurance the attacks which, as they are announced day by day, inflict ever more serious wounds,” and so forth.

The second matter which we promised to address concerning Liberius was to show the extent of the persecution he endured from the Arians who had been stirred up against him. For he did not long remain immune from the storms [Col. 0052B] that he had foreseen. Christian and pagan writers alike who mention these events also testify that the authority of the Roman see in the Church was the principal reason why the Arians sought it above all others and feared it above all others. Ammianus Marcellinus writes in Book XV, shortly after the middle:

“Liberius, the bishop of the Christian law, was ordered by Constantius to be brought to the imperial court, as though he were resisting the emperor’s commands and the decrees of the association of many of his own people … When the emperor ordered that he, agreeing in this with the others, should reject [Athanasius] by subscription from the priestly see, Liberius, after being warned, steadfastly persisted, repeatedly proclaiming that it was the height of impiety to condemn a man whom he had neither seen nor heard. He was plainly resisting the emperor’s decision. For although the emperor knew that Athanasius’s condemnation had been completed, he nevertheless strove with ardent desire to have it strengthened by the authority possessed by the bishops of the Eternal City. When this was not obtained, Liberius, with difficulty and out of fear of the people—who burned with love for him—was carried away in the middle of the night.”

Saint Athanasius, who understood much more deeply than Marcellinus what had been done concerning the cause of his religion and what affected his own affairs, and who knew the actions of the Arians against Liberius and of Liberius on behalf of faith and justice in opposition to them, explains the matter more fully in the frequently mentioned letter to the Solitaries:

“First, the Arians did not spare even Liberius, the Roman bishop. They were moved by no reverence, whether because that see was apostolic or because Rome was the capital of Roman rule … nor did they remember that they had called those apostolic men by that name in their letters. When they saw that Liberius was orthodox, a hater of the Arian sect, and zealous in drawing everyone away from that heresy, the impious men deliberated among themselves as follows: ‘If we draw Liberius over to our opinion, we shall soon overcome them all.’ They therefore brought the matter before the emperor. He, hoping that through Liberius he could draw everyone over, sent a certain eunuch, Eusebius, with letters and gifts, and so forth. [Col. 0052D] The bishop, however, argued against this in words and asked how such a thing could be done against Athanasius, whom not one but already two synods had clearly pronounced free from every crime, and whom the Roman Church had dismissed in peace. This is not the ecclesiastical canon, nor have we ever received such a tradition from the Fathers, who themselves received it from the blessed and great Apostle Peter,” and so forth.

When Constantius saw that his earlier attempts were failing, “he writes to Rome; once again palace officials, notaries, and counts are dispatched, and letters are sent to the prefect ordering him either to lure Liberius from Rome by deceit and send him to the camp, or to use force in persecuting him … Liberius is therefore dragged before the emperor. When he arrived there, he also made use of great freedom of speech.” In the same place Theodoret preserves the sequence of that conversation and records the thoughts of Constantius and Liberius in Book II of his *History*, chapter 16.

Constantius: “Does so great a part of the whole world rest upon you, Liberius, that you alone dare to come to the aid of an impious man and disturb the peace of the earth and of the whole world?”

Liberius: “Suppose that I alone am concerned; nevertheless, the cause of the faith is not thereby made weaker.”

Constantius: “There is one thing at issue. I want you to embrace communion with the churches and then return to Rome. Therefore, have regard for peace; subscribe, so that you may return to Rome.”

Liberius: “I have already said farewell to the brothers who are in Rome. For I consider it more important to observe the ecclesiastical laws than to have a dwelling in Rome.”

Two days later Liberius was banished to Beroea in Thrace.

Among ancient writers, and likewise among more recent writers today, there has been uncertainty as to whether Felix, a deacon of the Roman Church whom the Arian faction arranged to be created in place of Liberius, the pontiff driven into exile, was ever a legitimate pontiff. On both sides, very weighty evidence from the events is produced to increase the force of the respective positions. We can affirm without danger of error that Felix’s election was entirely illegitimate, since it is absolutely certain that the Roman see was in no way vacant during Liberius’s exile. As for Felix’s having been regarded in good faith as Roman pontiff for some period of time—namely, when, from the external fact that Liberius had subscribed to Athanasius’s condemnation and communicated with Athanasius’s adversaries, some had become convinced that Liberius had departed from the Nicene faith—that opinion was soon removed from people’s minds. The Church quickly perceived that the supposed apostasy of Liberius rested on a false suspicion. Thus, when Liberius returned, Rome received him with an extraordinary expression of joy and honored him as supreme pontiff until the end of his life, just as it had previously held and honored him before he was driven into exile. From this it follows that nothing was lost from pontifical authority, nor was the glory of the Roman see diminished in any way by Liberius’s lapse. I shall now continue his history with a brief examination, in order to complete the third point I proposed [Col. 0053C].

Liberius’s constancy was at last weakened by weariness and the hardships of exile, as is testified by letters he wrote to Vincent of Capua and to the other bishops of Campania, asking them to work for his return; these letters are read in Hilary’s fragments. The letter circulated by some under the name of Liberius and addressed to Ursacius, Valens, and Gannius is nevertheless spurious and fraudulently fabricated. It states that Athanasius had been separated from communion with the Roman Church by Liberius before Liberius reached the emperor’s court. We have seen that this directly conflicts with Athanasius’s own testimony quoted above and with the other documents preserved by Theodoret in his *History*.

The Arians, in order to induce Liberius to condemn Athanasius, employed as an instrument of their fraud Fortunatian, bishop of Aquileia, previously celebrated for his steadfast adherence to the Nicene faith, though he had abandoned it shortly before; and also Demophilus of Beroea, with whom Liberius was living in exile. Each of these men insinuated to the pope that Athanasius’s case had nothing in common with the cause of the Church. Therefore, while the peace of the entire East had to be safeguarded, the private affair of one man should be set aside; but as for the cause of the faith, nothing was more consistent with Catholic doctrine than the formula composed at Sirmium and subscribed by all the Fathers who had assembled there. These suggestions, then, made to Liberius—already severely shaken by the distress and misery of exile, as well as by the threat of death imposed at the emperor’s command—so weakened his constancy that he removed Athanasius from the communion of the faithful, according to the wishes of those same adversaries, and subscribed the formula placed before him. This is evident from Liberius’s own letters to the Easterners and from Athanasius’s letter to the Solitaries.

No one will deny that Liberius sinned by subscribing to the condemnation of Athanasius, who had deserved nothing of the kind, and by admitting Athanasius’s enemies to communion. Yet this was a fault of conduct, not of teaching, as Tertullian warns in his book *On Prescription* concerning what Paul reproached in Peter. Athanasius’s enemies, seeking an opportunity to persecute him and prepare his proscription, never accused his faith, although the true cause of their persecution lay in his profession of the faith, which they hated. They accused him of violence, extortion, sorcery, and machinations against the emperor and the security of the state. Because of these crimes—although Liberius knew, or ought to have known, that Athanasius was far removed from them—he unjustly condemned that innocent man.

As for the communion established with the Easterners, it must be observed that Liberius granted it because they had subscribed the Sirmian formula, just as he himself subscribed it, regarding it as an act consistent with Catholic doctrine. It is preferable, however, to investigate what this formula of faith actually was and in what terms it had been expressed, since it is the subject under discussion.

Three formulas of faith are distinguished as having been composed at Sirmium.

The first was framed against Photinus, bishop of that place. It begins:

> “We believe in God the Father almighty, creator and maker of all things, etc., and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, etc., begotten from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, etc. The holy and Catholic Church therefore considers alien to herself those who say that the Son came into existence from what did not exist, or from another subsistent reality, and not from God; or that there was a time or an age when he did not exist.”

(See St Athanasius, *On the Synods*. See also St Hilary, *On the Synods Against the Arians*, who recognizes it as thoroughly orthodox.)

The second formula of faith, composed by Valens, Ursacius, Geminius, and men of the same sort, declares that the terms “substance” (*οὐσίας*) and “consubstantial” (*ὁμουσιοῦ*), or “similar in substance” (*ὁμουσιοῦ*), ought not to be used when speaking of the generation of the Son of God, etc.

> “No one ought to be led into doubt that the Father is greater; nor should anyone doubt that the Father is greater in honor, dignity, divinity, and even in the very name of ‘Father.’ The Son, together with everything that the Father subjected to him, is subject to the Father.”

St Hilary calls this the blasphemy of Hosius and Potamius, in *On the Synods*. (See also St Athanasius, *On the Synods*.)

The third formula of belief was composed at Ancyra and from there brought to Sirmium, as an antidote to counteract the poison administered in the second formula by the Arians. It therefore contains Catholic doctrine, expressed in the following statements found in St Hilary, *On the Synods Against the Arians*:

> “The Son is the perfect image of the Father. Yet perfect likeness does not make the Son the Father. The Son is proclaimed the image of the Father through the truth of likeness; he does not differ in substance from the substance of the Father, whose image he is,” etc.

St Hilary, who presents this formula, calls its authors:

> “Men devoted to apostolic and evangelical teaching, whom the fervor of faith kindled amid such great darkness of heretical night, etc., who steadfastly beat back the assault of audacious unbelief. ... Thanks be to the Lord, because the emperor, warned through you, recognized his ignorance and, through these statements of your faith, acknowledged the error to be not his own but that of those around him.”

Besides these formulas, another was signed at Sirmium to be carried to Ariminum, where it had been decided that a synod should be held. In this last Sirmian formula, after the confession that the Son was begotten by God before all ages from the Father alone, and the affirmation—according to the Scriptures—that the Son is God from God and like the Father who begot him, it is added that the term “substance,” though simply introduced by the Fathers, caused offense to many because it was commonly unknown among the people. Accordingly, it seemed useful that it be removed and that no mention be made of the word “substance” when speaking of God:

> “For the sacred Scriptures make no mention at all of the substance either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we say that the Son is like the Father in all things, since the sacred Scriptures affirm and teach this.”

This last Sirmian formula is described in this way by Socrates, *History*, book II, chapter 29.

It is certain that Liberius never subscribed the second of the formulas mentioned. For he did not subscribe it at Beroea: the formula that was composed there and presented to Liberius by Demophilus had been drafted by bishops, most of whom opposed him—namely, Basil of Ancyra, who is known to have proscribed it in the synod he held there; Silvanus of Tarsus, who openly attacked it in the synod of Seleucia; Cecrops of Nicomedia; and other Easterners whose names have been preserved for us by blessed Hilary (*in the fragments*), and whom we know to have been only semi-Arians. We also know that Theodore of Heraclea, who had belonged to that group, died before Liberius’s exile and therefore before the formula was composed; for it was drafted after Hosius’s fall, while Liberius was in exile. Finally, it is clear from St Hilary’s catalogue of those who had dictated it that neither Hosius, Potamius, nor Geminius is mentioned, although they had undoubtedly subscribed it.

Nor should it be said that Liberius, while at Sirmium, received and subscribed that second formula when he was summoned there from his exile at Beroea, at the request of the legates whom the bishops of the West had sent to the emperor (as Sozomen testifies, book IV, chapter 14), and was thereafter sent back to Rome. For, agitated by the rumor that the Arians had deliberately spread—namely, that Liberius, while staying at Antioch, had followed the example of Hosius, condemned the term “consubstantial,” and professed the Son unlike the Father—Liberius, shaken, I say, by this false rumor, himself composed a confession of faith and had it subscribed by all the bishops, both Eastern and Western, who were then staying at Sirmium. In it he declared those alien from the Church who asserted that the Son was not like the Father in substance and in all things.

Likewise, he did not sign the third formula either at Beroea or at Sirmium, since it had not yet appeared by the time of his return to Rome. For Liberius returned to Rome and was received within the city on 2 August of the year 357 (according to the *Petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus* and Anastasius in his account of Liberius), whereas the third formula is recorded as having been composed and subscribed at Sirmium in the consulship of Flavius Eusebius and Hypatius, on 29 May—that is, on the eve of Pentecost in the year 359 (Socrates, book II, chapter 29; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 75.22).

It remains, therefore, to say that Liberius, while at Beroea, subscribed only the first of the formulas explained above, the one directed against Photinus. If, while at Sirmium, he subscribed something else, as Sozomen narrates, compelled by the emperor at the urging of Basil of Ancyra and the other bishops then residing in the imperial entourage, it was certainly nothing other than a combination or collection of decrees against Paul of Samosata and Photinus of Sirmium, together with the formula of faith issued at the dedication of the church at Antioch. This collection had been assembled to overthrow the errors of certain men who, under cover of the term “consubstantial,” were attempting to strengthen their private heresies.

It is certainly established that the decrees against Paul of Samosata, who blasphemously asserted that there was in Christ the Lord only one human nature, and those against the Photinus mentioned above, are orthodox. The same must be thought of the formula of faith published at Antioch at the dedication of the church, which Sozomen mentions—whether by it he means the one that the Eusebians produced before the celebration of the synod in order to deceive the Catholics and remove from themselves every suspicion of a faith differing from ours (a version of it is found in St Athanasius, *On the Synods*: “There is one God of the whole universe, in whom they believe, and one only-begotten Son of God, existing before all ages and coexisting with the Father,” etc.); or whether he is speaking of that formula, or of the two formulas, composed and received at the same council by the unanimous agreement of the Fathers.

One of these begins in St Hilary, *On the Synods*, as follows:

> “We believe in one God, the Father, etc., and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, God, through whom all things were made, etc.”

The other is formulated in St Athanasius, *On the Synods*, in this way:

> “I believe in God the Father, etc., and in his only-begotten Son, God the Word, etc., our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, etc., begotten from the Father before the ages, perfect God from perfect God, existing with the Father in person, etc.”

If this second of the last two formulas contains certain words which, in St Hilary’s time, many thought conveyed a meaning different from the Catholic one—for example, when the names “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” were said carefully to signify the proper substance, order, and glory of each person named, so that they were three in substance but one in agreement (St Hilary, *On the Synods*)—Hilary removes every difficulty by showing that the council of Antioch had not been convened against the heresy that dared to preach that the three divine persons were of unlike substance, but against the heresy which, after the Council of Nicaea, had advanced to the point of wishing to assign three names to the Father.

> “Therefore, wishing that the holy synod assembled should destroy this impiety ... they said that there were three substances, teaching by ‘substances’ the persons who subsisted; they did not separate the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by a difference of unlike essence.”

In the third formula this is made clear when it says that the Son exists with the Father in person. St Athanasius explains the matter more lucidly in *On the Synods*, where the word “hypostasis” (*ὑπόστασις*, *hypostasis*) is used, corresponding to the word “substance” employed by Hilary to signify the person. Thus, according to Athanasius, the proper person (*ὑπόστασις*), order, and glory of each are understood, so that there are three with respect to persons but one through concord—that is, through unity of essence.

Afterward, by the age of blessed Augustine, common usage—at least among the Latins—established the fixed meaning of these terms: the word “substance” came to signify “essence.” It was no longer permitted to say that there was one essence and three substances in God; instead, one essence or substance and three persons had to be professed. St Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VIII, chapter 9:

> “But because our Latin manner of speaking has now established that when we say ‘essence’ this is understood in the same way as when we say ‘substance,’ we do not dare to say ‘one essence, three substances,’ but ‘one essence or substance, and three persons.’”

As for the suppression of the term “consubstantial,” which some reproach Pope Liberius for omitting as though it were the sign and token distinguishing Catholics from Arians, it must be observed that in the period immediately following the Council of Nicaea it had not been commanded that this term always be used in formulas professing the faith. For it does not appear in the formula that Marcellus of Ancyra, Valens, and Ursacius presented to Pope Julius. Nor is it found in the other formula that St Ambrose wished to be issued by Palladius and Secundianus in order to remove the suspicion of Arianism brought against them at the Council of Aquileia. Nor does it occur in the first or third of the formulas composed at Sirmium, or in the three Antiochene formulas mentioned above.

During that period, therefore, the explicit expression of the term was not considered necessary for distinguishing Catholic from heterodox meaning. Consequently, Liberius must not be judged guilty of heresy because he omitted a term that was not yet necessary from the formula he subscribed. This suspicion is even more remote from Liberius because the thing signified is denoted more explicitly even though the word “consubstantial” is omitted. For by declaring in the Sirmian formula that those who deny that the Son is like the Father in substance and in all things are alien from the Church, he certainly asserts that the Father and the Son are of the same substance—which has the same meaning as saying “consubstantial.” A perfect image and complete likeness include unity of substance, since there is neither likeness in all things nor perfection of likeness where difference is admitted.

Liberius’s immunity from the stain of Arianism is confirmed by the fact that those who admitted perfect likeness of substance in the divine persons did not thereby acknowledge three gods. According to their position, however, they would have been compelled to admit three gods if they had recognized in the persons three different divine substances rather than unity of substance, or consubstantiality, in them. Certainly, blessed Athanasius conceived this necessary consequence when he objected to certain Arians that they rejected the term “consubstantial” in vain, since they admitted that the Son was an image in no way differing from the substance of the Father.

> “If you, Acacius and Eudoxius,” he says in *On the Synods*, “do not reject the faith published at the Encaenia, and if it is written there that the Son is an image of the Father’s substance, undifferentiated from it, why then do you write to the Isaurians: ‘We reject the term consubstantial’? For if the Son is not like the Father according to substance, how could he be the image of the Father without any dissimilarity at all?”

Nevertheless, care must be taken not to confuse what Liberius did with what the heretics just mentioned did. Liberius subscribed a formula in which the term “consubstantial” was not explicitly read; yet the formula did not on that account lack an orthodox meaning. The Arians, on the contrary, of whom blessed Athanasius speaks, had subscribed a formula that was notoriously and openly heretical, independently of the suppression of that word and term.

Liberius, without condemning the term “consubstantial,” consented that it not be expressed in the profession of faith offered to him—which was otherwise orthodox—being moved by the consideration that the heretics against whom the profession was directed might misuse that term to support their errors. The Arians, however, directly attacked the term “consubstantial,” since their principal aim was to overthrow the faith concerning the mystery for which that word evokes the proper and true idea. Nothing is asserted here for which we have not produced documentary evidence.

We do not deny that history records a persecution having been stirred up in the Church after Liberius’s return to Rome, when a portion of the clergy that disagreed with him refused to enter either the church or the baths if they knew that Liberius’s supporters were staying there. A false rumor had spread widely, even as far as the East, concerning Liberius’s defection to the Arian party. Therefore, several men, zealous for the defense of the faith from which they thought Liberius had fallen, judged it appropriate to withdraw from him as one deposed and to join the antipope Felix. Felix had renounced the Arian party, which he had supported shortly before, and had condemned Constantius Augustus as a heretic. He consequently underwent the same fate as Liberius: he became the object of their persecution, just as did the presbyters of his communion.

For this reason, when revising its Martyrology in the sixteenth century of the Redemption, the Roman Church judged that Felix’s titles of pope and martyr—of which he had enjoyed possession—should be preserved. Yet those rumors raised against Liberius’s faith quickly vanished, so that afterward the Romans honored and followed him just as they had honored and followed him when he was being sent into exile.

Moreover, the dreadful curses and anathemas directed against Liberius that are found inserted into fragments of the works of St Hilary must not be regarded as having been composed by him. Apart from the fact that that book is full of lacunae and corrupt readings in many places, who would say that Hilary wished to rage so unjustly against Liberius, already restored to his own see and defending the Nicene faith so gloriously, while opposing the Arians so vigorously, especially in rejecting and abolishing the Ariminian Formula?

When St Jerome (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 97) recalls that Liberius was compelled by the detestable Fortunatian, broken, and forced to subscribe to heresy, and when in his *Chronicle* he states, “Liberius, overcome by the weariness of exile, subscribed to heretical depravity,” etc., he is speaking according to the rumor circulated and commonly accepted concerning him, because Liberius had broken communion with Athanasius and entered communion with the Arians, as though he had accepted their formula. Alternatively, Jerome may have chosen to call those formulas signed by Liberius “heretical depravity,” because, although by their own nature they were not heretical, they had nevertheless been craftily proposed to him by heretics so that the use of the other formulas—those containing the doctrines of the faith that the Arians rejected—might be abolished.

It is only to these formulas that Liberius can be affirmed to have subscribed, while maintaining right judgment and professing the orthodox faith concerning the divinity of the Word, even with the omission of “consubstantial.” The deficiency caused by that omission was supplied by the additions that immediately followed, although the Arians deliberately suppressed the clear term designating the true idea of the dogma they denied. They considered that they had made sufficient progress toward gradually abolishing belief in the truth contained in that word if it were omitted thereafter.

For this reason, the ancient writers do not accuse Liberius of abandoning the faith by subscribing. Rufinus, *History*, book I, chapter 27, doubts whether Liberius was sent back to Rome by Constantius because he had yielded to the emperor’s will by subscribing, or because the emperor sought to gratify the Roman people, from whom Liberius had departed only after being entreated. Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, says that Liberius’s restoration was granted in order to suppress the Roman disturbances by his return. Socrates, book II, chapter 29, says that Liberius was recalled from exile and restored to the city because, after a revolt had broken out, the Roman people expelled Felix from that church.

Theodoret narrates that the emperor’s mind was swayed by noble Roman women to decide that both men—Liberius and Felix—should jointly govern that church:

> “All cried out with one voice: ‘One God, one Christ, one bishop.’ When these cries had been poured forth by the devout people with piety and justice, Bishop Liberius returned. Felix, however, secretly withdrawing from Rome, migrated to another city.”

To Sozomen’s testimony, cited shortly before concerning Liberius’s subscription at Sirmium—which detracts nothing from the Nicene faith—must be added the same historian’s account of the manner of Liberius’s return:

> “The emperor grants Liberius permission to return to Rome. The bishops assembled at Sirmium then write to Felix, who was at that time bishop of the Roman Church, and to the clergy of that church, instructing them to receive Liberius and for both of them jointly to administer the apostolic see. ... Not long afterward Felix died, and thereafter Liberius alone presided over that church. This happened not without divine providence, so that the see of Peter, governed by two bishops—a condition plainly marking division and contrary to the sacred laws of the Church—might not be stained by any mark of infamy.”

Finally, although Liberius had abandoned Athanasius, St Athanasius vigorously came to his defense, saying:

> “After spending two years in exile, Liberius was bent and induced by threats of death to subscribe.”

He asserts that this very violence directed against Liberius is evidence of Liberius’s aversion to Arian impiety and his inclination toward Athanasius:

> “But that very event,” he says, “sufficiently proves both their violence, Liberius’s hatred of heresy, and his support for Athanasius when he possessed freedom of feeling. For those things that were extorted by tortures against his former judgment must be attributed not to the will of one who feared, but to the will of those who compelled him.” (Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*.)

We said that the fourth matter to be demonstrated concerning Liberius was how beneficially he presided over the Church after returning to his see and recovering from the lapse he had suffered in subscribing against Athanasius.

After Liberius’s return to Rome, the council of Ariminum took place. It cannot be honored with the name of a council, since neither its convocation, its celebration, nor its outcome proceeded lawfully. The emperor, who ought in his office to have acted as the Church’s defender, forgot the duty of a protector and assumed the roles of pontiff and high priest, which in no way belonged to him. Thus he convened a general council to calm the storms that he himself was raising, arrogating to himself the governance of the Churches.

> “He gives orders,” says Sozomen, book IV, chapter 15, “that ten bishops from the Western regions and an equal number from the Eastern regions, whom the council should choose by common agreement, should come together to his palace and explain to him what had been decreed. His purpose was not merely to determine whether they had agreed with one another in accordance with the sacred Scriptures, but also to decide what seemed best to do.”

Then, at the urging of the Arians Eudoxius, Acacius, and others, whose counsels he followed, he judged it expedient to divide the council into two: the Eastern bishops were to meet at Seleucia, and the Western bishops at Ariminum.
