> “The emperor writes to the bishops,” as Sozomen states in the same passage, together with Athanasius, *On the Synods, “instructing them first to decide the matters that seemed ambiguous in the faith and finally to discuss the cases of bishops who complained and to judge their accusations carefully ... Once everything had been decided, ten from each side were to approach the court and report to him what had been done.”

Thus, both in prescribing laws for the council concerning the subject and order of judgment and in drawing to himself the cause of the judgment, he assumed the role of supreme judge in the Church.

It is certain that Pope Liberius attended neither council; and it is equally certain that he did not consent to that convocation under the ridiculous conditions proposed by the emperor Constantius. Nor can we suppose that Vincent of Capua, who is said to have taken part in the assembly at Ariminum, attended that gathering as a legate of the apostolic see, as some more recent writers gratuitously assume.

In both assemblies the method of procedure was so alien to the rules of the Fathers that it could scarcely be believed that a synod had been gathered in the name of Christ, or therefore by the authority of him who exercises the place of Christ the Lord in his Church. Official magistrates sent by Augustus throughout the provinces—as Sulpicius Severus indicates, *History*, book XX—some of whom had even been enticed by the hope of the consulship if they did not dismiss the bishops before they had agreed upon one faith, gathered at Ariminum, like armed agents, more than four hundred Western bishops, not merely summoned but dragged there. Taurus, the chief among those officials, held the bishops as though under guard, so that none of them could slip away before subscribing to the emperor’s position.

The Catholic bishops acted steadfastly for some time, especially at Ariminum, where they constituted the larger number. Nevertheless, wearied at that station, they succumbed and became an unhappy testimony for posterity to the axiom that the Spirit of Christ, who cannot lie, was not dwelling in their midst; for, gathered without the head of the Church, they could not adequately represent the body of the Church.

Thus, anyone of sound and orthodox judgment who remained in the assembly at Ariminum easily foresaw the direction of the emperor’s plans and what the outcome of the convocation would be. The Catholics had no use for the Arians’ false peace or for the tranquility promised by their protector of the Church. They quickly judged that true concord could not be established with the enemies of truth, since the Arians would accept no agreement without the subversion of justice, and they openly pronounced in favor of the ancient faith confirmed by the Council of Nicaea.

They further give the reason for their judgment, explaining that those who remove peace cannot proceed peacefully, and that the other Churches, especially the Roman Church, would rightly cry out against them:

> “For how will those who remove peace be able to act peacefully?” the Fathers of Ariminum write in their letter to Constantius, preserved in St Athanasius, *On the Synods*, and in Sozomen, book IV, chapter 17. “Rather, contention and disturbance will arise from them both in the other cities and in the city of Rome.”

It should be noted that by “the other Churches” the Fathers here mean those whose delegates were not present at that assembly, just as delegates from the Roman Church were not present.

The event proved that the bishops’ conjecture was correct. Weariness at the long delay at Ariminum, the adversaries’ stratagems, fear of exile, and the evils threatened by the emperor bent their minds toward subscribing a formula composed in ambiguous language. The Arians afterward took from it the support for their error by which they sought to eliminate the true doctrine of the Church.

Rome did not fail to oppose those pernicious innovations with vigor. Liberius’s successor, in his *Synodical Letter to the Illyrians* (in Theodoret, book II, chapter 22), asserts that:

> “The very large number of bishops assembled at Ariminum ought not to possess the force of a precedent, especially since that formula was composed without the Roman bishop, whose judgment ought to have been awaited above all others, and without Vincent, who had exercised the episcopate with integrity for so many years, or without the others who agreed with him.”

This constancy of Liberius again provoked the persecution of the Arians against him. They had obtained from the emperor the power to compel all bishops to subscribe the formula of faith they had composed and to expel from their churches those who resisted. Their exercise of this license began against Liberius, bishop of Rome, who was forced to take refuge in the crypts of the martyrs, where the clergy came to him to deliberate concerning the needs of the Church.

The ancients remembered this second expulsion and withdrawal of Liberius, especially Sozomen, who also gives its true date, although less accurate writers wrongly confuse it with the pope’s earlier exile at Beroea.

Liberius spent some time in this hiding place until the emperor Julian, elected at the very beginning of his reign, permitted the bishops expelled or exiled by his predecessor Constantius to return to their own sees.

Liberius’s first concern during this period of inactivity was to proclaim and grant a general amnesty to the bishops who, having been ensnared by the Arians, had subscribed their deceptive formula. He therefore issued an encyclical letter to the bishops throughout Italy, explaining that it belonged to his apostolic authority to weigh everything with moderation and not to forget mercy when condemning the authors of evils, especially toward those who, overcome by ignorance and having fallen into error, should repent after being recalled by the apostolic words he addressed to them.

He orders that such men be restored to their own sees. But if anyone should refuse to convert, “let him be judged a traitor to the Church, as the author of treachery, and punished with spiritual strength” (Liberius’s letter to the bishops of Italy, in Hilary, *in the fragments*).

At the same time, a synod was held at Alexandria, where it was likewise declared that, in order to obtain pardon, those who had not been the authors of the error but had been compelled by necessity and violence should be admitted and retained in the ecclesiastical dignities they held.

> “It seemed to them,” he says, “that these men should be forgiven and restored to the rank of the clergy.” (See Athanasius’s letter to Rufinus, in the Second Council of Nicaea, session 1.)

This decision was also communicated to Rome, and it is established that the Roman Church approved everything.

It should be believed that the visitations of the Eastern Churches then undertaken by Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, and Lucifer of Cagliari, together with the acts of jurisdiction exercised by both, were carried out by mandate and authority of the apostolic see.

When Lucifer of Cagliari arrived at Antioch, while the parties were still divided, he hastily installed Paulinus, a Catholic and holy man, wholly worthy of the priesthood, as bishop of that see, as Rufinus says, book I of his *History*, chapter 27, etc.

As Eusebius of Vercelli traveled through the Eastern regions, Socrates writes, book III, chapter 7, “he restored those who were weak in faith to complete health, like an excellent physician; he instructed and educated them in ecclesiastical doctrine,” etc.

Finally, as Gregory of Nazianzus relates in his *Oration in Praise of Basil*, “there were certain bishops from the West who drew all the orthodox over to their side.” Simple bishops could certainly not have attempted and accomplished such things unless they had been endowed with a higher authority, and that authority could have been none other than that of the Roman see.

The same conclusion must be drawn from what St Gregory of Nazianzus reported in his *Monody*, where he writes:

> “The bishops Lucifer and Eusebius were sent from the city of Rome to Caesarea to calm the sedition that had arisen in the Church at Caesarea.”

The Eastern semi-Arians likewise recognized this authority of the apostolic see, for they organized an embassy to Liberius in order to obtain union with the orthodox. Recognizing that they were being attacked by the Arians, they preferred the course of approaching—or, as St Basil says, pretending to approach—the Roman faith, judging this preferable to communicating with those same heretics.

> “They send Hypatian to request,” says Sozomen, book VI, chapter 7, “that permission be granted them to assemble together in order to establish the doctrine of the faith properly. When he came to Valentinian and explained the bishops’ requests to him, Valentinian replied that, since he was one of the laity, it was not lawful for him to involve himself in such matters. ‘Therefore,’ he said, ‘let the priests and bishops, who are responsible for these matters, assemble separately by themselves wherever they wish.’”

After this reply had been given to Hypatian’s embassy, they convened the council of Lampsacus. From that council they sent three bishops to the West with instructions to follow in all things the teaching and judgment of Pope Liberius, to receive communion with the Roman Church, and to subscribe to the doctrine that the Son is consubstantial.

Socrates, book IV, chapter 11, relates the matter as follows:

> “These men, driven into straits by fear, or rather by force, sent envoys from one city to another and declared that they had to flee for refuge both to the emperor’s brother and to the bishop of Rome; that they ought to embrace the faith of those men rather than communicate with Eudoxius. Accordingly, they sent Eustathius, etc., and instructed them not to disagree in any way with Liberius, but to communicate with the Roman Church and to ratify the faith concerning the Son’s consubstantiality.”

Sozomen, book IV, chapter 10, does not disagree, reporting the following:

> “They write letters both to Liberius, the bishop of Rome, and to the other bishops of the West, since they preserved firm and secure the faith derived from the apostles and, above all others, ought to safeguard religion. They wished the bishops to explain how far it lay within their power to assist their envoys and to confer with them concerning what ought to be done, and what seemed best for establishing the condition of the Church.”

Eustathius of Sebaste, one of the three envoys, proceeded to the holy see so that he might be restored to the episcopate from which he had been deposed in a council, as St Basil testifies in Letter 74:

> “Eustathius, expelled from the episcopate because he had been deposed in the synod at Melitene, devised a means of being restored: namely, that he should travel to you.”

All these things are certain testimonies that pure doctrine and authority to govern the other Churches had been entrusted to the Western Church, and therefore to the Roman see, which alone possesses this privilege over the Eastern Church.

Liberius at first “refused to receive the letters presented by the envoys [Col. 0062A]” (says Socrates, Book IV, chapter 11), for he declared that they were supporters of the Arian sect . . . . . They replied that, moved by repentance, they had recognized the truth, confessed the Son to be like the Father in all things, and held that the word “like” differed in nothing from “consubstantial.” After they had said this, Liberius asked them to commit a declaration of their opinion to writing. They presented him with a document in which the words contained in the creed issued at Nicaea had been prescribed, and so forth:

“If anyone, after this faith has been set forth by us, brings any charge either against us or against those who sent us, let him come with a letter from Your Holiness to the orthodox bishops whom your piety shall approve; let him debate the matter with us before them; and, if it is established that anything has given offense, let punishment be imposed upon its author.”

When this had been done, the pontiff admitted them to communion and, when they returned to their homeland, furnished them with letters of recommendation addressed to the Eastern bishops. In these he congratulated them on their return to the unity of the Church [Col. 0062B] and to the faith of the apostolic see and of the other Western Churches. He concluded the letter with a declaration of anathema against those who persisted in Arian impiety and in the sect of Arius’s followers.

Liberius also dictated a special letter on behalf of Eustathius, in which he ordered that Eustathius be restored to his see at Melitene. Saint Basil gives abundant testimony to this in Letter 74, saying:

“But what was proposed to him—Eustathius—by the most blessed bishop Liberius, and to what he consented, is unknown to us, except that he brought a letter by which he was to be restored.”

When the envoys had returned to the East, the bishops who, under the emperor Jovian, the predecessor of Valentinian and Valens, had held a synod at Antioch for the defense of the doctrine of consubstantiality held a council at Tyana. There the letters of Liberius and of the Western bishops were read. They brought the Fathers such extraordinary joy that they subsequently sent an encyclical letter to all the Churches of the East, urging that the decrees of the Western Church and the letters of Liberius and of the other bishops, brought by the envoys, be carefully read among them [Col. 0062C]. They urged the Easterners to observe that the number of Western bishops who had written the same statement was much greater than the total number of those who had assembled at Rimini. They advised them to accept the doctrine of their communion, to declare in writing that they would not thereafter depart from it, and to assemble on an appointed day at Tarsus in Cilicia for a council. At this council, when Liberius’s letters restoring Eustathius had been read, Eustathius was immediately admitted to his episcopate at Sebaste.

At the same time a great disturbance arose in the East concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. When news of this had reached Rome, Liberius thought it appropriate to issue a decision. He promptly sent his judgment to the Eastern Churches, with a warning that they should hold the same view as the Western Church, which taught that the three divine persons were consubstantial [Col. 0062D] and equal in glory. Or, to use the words of Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 21, and Nicephorus Callistus, Book XI, chapter 30:

“They were to consider, together with the priests and bishops of the West, that the Trinity was consubstantial and equal in glory. When this had been done, each of them acquiesced in matters once judged by the Roman Church; and the controversy seemed to have come to an end.”

Thus Liberius, after accomplishing so many distinguished deeds, left the Church a memory of himself that was especially precious when he departed this life. Three men of great holiness who survived him gave him an illustrious testimony in writing. Saint Ambrose calls him holy and a man of holy memory (Book III, *On Virginity*). Saint Basil, in Letter 74, and Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 75, call him blessed and most blessed. The Martyrologies of Bede and Wandalbert also place him among the saints.

[Col. 0029]

## 51

Liberius, a Roman by birth, son of Augustus [Note: [Col. 0029] B: fifteen years, four months, one day.], occupied the see for ten years, seven months, and three days. He lived from the time of Constantius, son of Constantine, until Constantine Augustus III [Note: [Col. 0029] B: “during the reigns of Constantius, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, and Valens, emperors, from the consulships of Constantius V and Gallus to those of Lupicinus and Jovinus.”] [Note: [Col. 0029] C: “Constantius.”] [Note: [Col. 0029] C: “eighth.”]. He was carried into exile by Constantius [Note: [Col. 0029] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 355.] because he refused to consent to the Arian heresy. He spent two years in exile [Note: [Col. 0029] C: three.], and the priests, assembling with Liberius’s approval, ordained in his place Felix the presbyter [Note: [Col. 0029] B approves only that he was elected by the heretics, not with Liberius’s approval.], a venerable man, as bishop. Felix held a council and found two presbyters consenting to Constantius Augustus, the Arian, Ursacius and Valens, and he expelled them [Note: [Col. 0029] * “ejected.”] [Note: [Col. 0029] * “condemned.”] at a council of forty-eight bishops. [Note: [Col. 0029] See Baronius under the year 357.]

After a few days, however, moved by zeal, Ursacius and Valens asked Constantius Augustus to recall Liberius from exile, so that they might share one communion only [Note: [Col. 0029] B denies that the Arians rebaptized him at that time, in the year 357.], without a second baptism. Then, by authority sent through Catulinus, an *agens in rebus*, Ursacius and Valens came together to Liberius [Note: [Col. 0029] On Liberius’s lapse, see Baronius under the year 357.]. Liberius consented to Constantius’s commands, so that communion with the heretics alone might be shared, provided that he was not rebaptized.

When Liberius returned from exile [Note: [Col. 0029] Baronius refutes this in the place cited.], he lived in the cemetery of Saint Agnes near Constantius’s sister, so that, through her intervention or entreaty, Liberius might be restored to the city. Then Constantia Augusta, who was faithful to the Lord Jesus Christ, refused to ask her brother Constantius Augustus, because she had perceived the deceitful plan.

At the same time Constantius, together with Ursacius and Valens, summoned certain men who were Arians and, as though a council had been held, sent for Liberius and recalled him from the cemetery of Saint Agnes [Col. 0031]. Constantius entered Rome and at that very hour held a council with the heretics, together with Ursacius and Valens. He expelled Felix from the episcopate, although Felix was Catholic, and recalled Liberius.

## 52

From that day there was persecution of the clergy, so that presbyters and clerics were killed within the church and crowned with martyrdom. Felix, deposed from the episcopate, lived on his little estate on the Via Portuensis, where he also [Note: [Col. 0031] See Baronius, in the place cited, concerning the cause of the persecution. Baronius, under the year 357, proves that he was a martyr.] rested in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Liberius entered the city of Rome on the fourth day before the Nones of August and consented to Constantius [Note: [Col. 0031] Baronius, in the place cited, proves that he did not consent to the heresy.]. Liberius was not, however, rebaptized, but gave his consent, and held the basilicas of blessed Peter the Apostle and blessed Paul, and the Constantinian basilica, for seven years. There was a great persecution in the city of Rome, so that clerics and priests were permitted entrance neither into the churches nor into the baths.

This Liberius adorned the tomb of Saint Agnes the martyr with marble slabs [Note: [Col. 0031] C: “with bronze plates.”]. Thus all the years of Felix were counted within his ordination. He built a basilica in his own name beside the market [Note: [Col. 0031] “of Livia.” The Basilica of Saint Mary Major, according to Baronius.] of Livia.

He held two ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: eighteen presbyters, five deacons, and nineteen bishops for various places. He too was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopate was vacant for seven days [Note: [Col. 0031] CB: six.].

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Liberius lived during the time of Constantine, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June until . . . . ., under the consulships of Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.

## XXXVIII. SAINT FELIX II. YEAR OF CHRIST 355, THE 19TH OF CONSTANTINE

[Note: [Col. 0063B]

Line 2.—“This declared Constantius.” In Felix’s life according to Mombritius, these words, together with the other preceding words, are inserted verbatim from the life of Liberius. There, after recounting Liberius’s deportation into exile and Felix’s substitution, the text adds:

“Felix, being a Catholic man, fearing God, and a just man, held a council and found two Roman presbyters consenting to Constantius Augustus the Arian, named Ursacius and Valens, and condemned them in a council before forty-eight bishops who had been assembled. This declared Constantius.”

What did the interpolator of the acts do? He took the earlier passage, removing its opening words, and inserted it among the acts of Liberius. But these words—“This declared Constantius,” and so forth—he inserted into Felix’s life.

Yet Felix’s deeds refute the falsity of this account, because in the years 357 and following Valens and Ursacius were not in Rome. At that time they were promoting the formulas issued at Sirmium in the years 357 and 359. For Ursacius and Valens subscribed to the first formula issued at Sirmium [Col. 0065A], as Hilary records in *On Synods*, in these words:

“But the perfidy drawn up at Sirmium . . . These are those who composed it: Narcissus, Theodorus, Basilius, Eudoxius, Demophilus, Cecropius, Silvanus, Ursacius, Valens, Evagrius, and others.”

He similarly calls the other formula composed there, in his book *Against Constantius*, “the ravings of Hosius and the advances of Ursacius and Valens.” Socrates, Book II, chapter 24, and others show that these men were at Sirmium during those same years. That Ursacius and Valens continued at Sirmium to promote the perfidy until the year 359 is proved by the letter of Germinius, which discusses the third formula issued at Sirmium in 359. It says, in a fragment:

“For under the emperor Constantius, of blessed memory, when disagreement concerning the faith had begun to arise among certain persons, in the presence of that same emperor, with George, bishop of the Alexandrian Church; Pancratius, bishop of the Pelusians; Basil, then bishop of Ancyra; and Valens himself, Ursacius, and my humble self also present, after we had debated the faith until nightfall and agreed upon a definite rule, and so forth.” [Col. 0065B]

Epiphanius has the same account in *Against Heresies* 73, which concerns the Semi-Arians, number 22. These facts therefore brand this passage as false, just as they confirm the earlier observation concerning the fictitious stay of Constantius in the City. For from the year 357, from its end until 359, when the last Sirmian formula was issued, Constantius was not in Rome, as we have shown; nor could Valens and Ursacius have been Constantius’s permanent attendants during those years.

“And baptized a second time there.” The schismatics, enlarging the fabrications in Felix’s life, add that Constantius introduced the doctrine of rebaptization and, more remarkably, that he himself was rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia in the Villa of Aquilone, and that by his command Felix, by whom he had been declared a heretic, was condemned to martyrdom. Everyone can see that these claims are false.

For it is certain that Constantius had not been baptized in the year 357. Hilary, an eyewitness who carefully weighed all Constantius’s deeds, states that in the year in which the first Sirmian formula was issued, the bishops of Sirmium “deceived the ignorant emperor, so that, occupied with wars, he might set forth the faith of such perfidy and impose upon the Churches a form of belief, although he had not yet been regenerated” (*On Synods*, p. 1194).

Furthermore, if during the time of Liberius and Felix the emperor had promoted a doctrine of rebaptization, Hilary, in his books *Against Constantius*, would certainly not have ceased attacking the memory of the wickedness he defended. Philostorgius likewise, being an Eunomian and therefore one who ought especially to have promoted the rebaptization of all sects, would not have omitted an account of Constantius’s rebaptization if it had truly occurred. He would have used it to support his own perfidy. Yet he simply says that Constantius was baptized, stating of him:

“When he had reached Moysucrones, he was seized by illness, and after that was baptized by Euzoius; he left both the empire and life, as well as synods, to impiety.” (*Book VI*, chapter 5.)

Thus the heap of lamentable fictions in the acts of Felix published by Mombritius becomes apparent. The interpolator took these materials [Col. 0065D] and inserted them into the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs.

Line 3.—“By Eusebius of Nicomedia”: a most foul falsehood of the same kind as the alleged rebaptization. Eusebius of Nicomedia died in the year 342, as Valesius demonstrates in his notes on Socrates, Book II, chapter 13, whereas Constantius was baptized in the year 361. Euzoius’s baptism of Constantius is asserted not only by Philostorgius but also by Saint Athanasius, *On Synods*, p. 698, and by Socrates, Book II, final chapter.

Lines 3–4.—“And by this he was declared.” The text here assumes that time intervened between the rebaptization and Constantius’s death, so that Felix learned of the rebaptization; after learning of it, he summoned a council at Rome and declared Constantius a heretic. It further assumes that additional months intervened, during which news was brought to Constantius and he again sent men to crown Felix with martyrdom.

The evidence already cited proves these claims false, since Constantius died after receiving baptism. Felix therefore could not have done these things while Constantius was alive, as the account asserts [Col. 0066A].

Line 4.—“He is crowned with martyrdom.” The Eusebian fragment, written after Liberius’s death, says nothing about martyrdom and mentions only exile. It represents Eusebius as reproaching Constantius and Liberius in these words:

“As for you, the madness of the devil and the envy of your superstition led you to send into exile, as a cause of condemnation, Felix the bishop, whom you yourselves did not hesitate to acknowledge as Catholic and as a pure priest, invoking the Lord Jesus Christ, declared so by all; yet he is occupied with prayers on his little estate.”

Since the author of the fragment had undertaken to commend the deeds of Eusebius and Felix, and testifies that he wrote after Liberius’s death—Liberius having survived Constantius’s condemnation by several years—he would not have failed to record Felix’s martyrdom had it occurred while Constantius and Liberius were still alive. Since he mentions only exile [Col. 0066B] and is completely silent about Felix’s martyrdom, there is consequently good reason to doubt the claim made here that Felix was a martyr.

Moreover, the declaration by which Felix supposedly pronounced Constantius a heretic is assumed, in one and the same context, to have been made in Felix’s acts according to Mombritius, and therefore in the year 357, when Liberius was led into exile. Yet in that same year Constantius stayed in Rome for thirty days, as we have seen from Marcellinus. Before the end of that year, at Milan, Constantius issued Law 15 concerning bishops in the *Theodosian Code*, addressing it to Felix, the Roman bishop. It is therefore clear that Constantius could neither have been rebaptized in that year nor have been offended by Felix, to whom the emperor sent a law.

This addition must therefore be regarded with the other refuse taken from the acts of Felix, fabricated, as I believe, by schismatic Luciferians. Accordingly, these additions, as wholly inappropriate, must be removed from both accounts, as having been inserted into the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs by an ignorant interpolator.

The account of Felix’s death given in the life of Liberius should therefore be followed, where it says:

“Felix, deposed from the episcopate, lived on his little estate on the Via Portuensis, where he rested in peace.”

Philostorgius agrees with this. After saying that Liberius had been recalled from exile, he adds:

“But Felix, who had meanwhile been ordained bishop at Rome, recovered his episcopal dignity, although thereafter he was placed in charge of no particular church.” (As above.)

The Luciferians, moreover, believed that all the bishops of Rimini had lapsed and had in some manner communicated with the Arians, and therefore that they were not bishops and that those ordained by them ought not to be received; they even held that the Church had thereby become the synagogue of Antichrist. This is proved by the Luciferian interlocutor in the dialogue *Against the Luciferians* published by Saint Jerome, who mocks them as declaimers of canine eloquence against all the Catholic bishops then in existence.

It consequently happened that, at the end of the Eusebian fragment, the schismatic—who, as I believe, was a Luciferian—added the utterly false accusation that Damasus had publicly denounced Liberius as a heretic. He did this to show his own adherents that Liberius’s decree concerning the reception of those who had lapsed at Rimini should be treated as worthless, since it had proceeded from a heretic condemned by a council.

Anyone of sound judgment will readily affirm that the acts of Felix published by Mombritius were fabricated by the same method. But what should be said about Felix’s episcopate? Pagius should be consulted in his critique of Baronius.]

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

Line 4.—“He is crowned with martyrdom.” After Felix’s death no one was substituted in his place. For Liberius, having entirely broken off the Arian communion which had intervened for the sake of recovering his see, was recognized and accepted by everyone as the legitimate pontiff of the Roman Church, just as he had been before.

It is therefore more deserving of laughter than refutation that certain recent historians, willingly followed by the Magdeburgians, have invented the claim that a certain Leo, an Arian, succeeded Felix II. They say that Leo was hostile to Saint Hilary, who, arriving late at the synod, was ordered to sit on the ground as punishment; and that therefore, by the same punishment with which God the avenger had struck Arius, Leo breathed out his soul together with his entrails.

But since the testimony of all the most ancient authorities places Leo I in office at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, and since, without any mention of this matter, all authorities unanimously substitute Damasus after the deaths of Liberius and Felix, you should know that this is not history but a fable, perhaps devised by later writers, who falsely imagined that Liberius, after Felix II had been expelled, raged against the Catholics in the manner attributed to Leo. See Baronius, year 357, number 69; Bellarmine, Book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0067A]

### Chronological Notes

The paintings on the Via Ostiensis in the Basilica of Saint Paul, together with the Italian and foreign catalogues reviewed above in the Prolegomena [Col. 0067B], agree in assigning one year, three months, and two days to Felix’s legitimate tenure.

The catalogue under Justinian alone assigns Felix a full three years, the following figures having been worn away. It may therefore be suspected that a copyist confused the units of months with the preceding unit under the column of years, so that from I, III he incorrectly punctuated III, I . . . . Alternatively, when the unit indicating the year had been worn away, the copyists of the manuscript may have transferred the three months that followed to the number of years.

If the author of the catalogue assigned Felix three years, he attributed to him the two years of his predecessor Liberius’s exile and confused them with the year of Felix’s legitimate tenure that followed, after the election had been completed with the consent of Liberius, who made the chair vacant by his departure.

In the chronological notes to number 51 of Liberius’s life, documents were brought forward that establish the certain duration of Felix’s legitimate pontificate as one year, three months, and two days. This is so whether he was beheaded by Constantius’s command on the fourth day before the Ides of November for his defense of the Catholic faith, as the Ocriculan manuscript states; or whether for the same reason he was beheaded by that emperor near the walls of the City, beside the aqueduct of Trajan, on the following day, namely the third day before the Ides of November, and subsequently buried by the clergy under the care of the presbyter Damasus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, as the Bibliothecarius states in line 12 of this number; or whether he was ordered into exile and, voluntarily yielding the pontificate, prolonged his life until the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, as the presbyters Faustinus and Marcellinus explain in their *Book of Petitions*—although Baronius, under the year 357, number 48, and Papebrochius, in his chronological-historical essay on the lives of the pontiffs, dissertation 9 on Saint Felix, think that several things in this little book were fabricated by these schismatic presbyters—and as the Bibliothecarius seems to indicate in number 52, line 3, under Liberius.

However these testimonies may be reconciled, the period of the legitimate see assigned to Felix in the Pauline paintings and in the manuscripts of Anastasius and others mentioned above is closed by one year, three months, and two days, from 8 August 358 to 10 December 359, as we explained above at the end of the chronological notes on the life of Liberius.]

### Historical Notes

Line 2.—“This declared Constantius, son of Constantine, a heretic, and rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia.” Many of us believe that this repeated baptism, which was transferred through the slander of the Arians from the life of Constantius the son into the life of Constantine the father [in the notes on Silvester, volume II, p. 293], is attributed by the Bibliothecarius to Constantius; nevertheless, it is denied by several most serious writers.

Baronius leads their ranks under the year 357, number 49. That eminent writer not only opposes the assertion of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, but thinks that the contrary is demonstrated and confirmed by clear testimonies of Fathers contemporary with Constantius Augustus, such as Athanasius among the Greeks and Hilary among the Latins. In Hilary’s *On Synods*, Constantius’s boldness is rebuked because, although not yet regenerated, he dared to prescribe a form of belief to the Churches.

The difficulty Baronius raises concerning Constantius’s repeated baptism is increased by the material Pagius gathers in his critique under the year 324, number 5. Pagius thereby establishes, contrary to Baronius’s opinion, that the baptism was received by the great Constantine when death was approaching, at Nicomedia.

But concerning the baptism administered at Rome to the great Constantine by blessed Silvester—not at Nicomedia by any bishop—which, eighteen or twenty years before Constantine’s death, his mother Helena and those who were of Constantine’s family (συγγενεῖς αὐτοῦ, “his relatives”), as well as many friends and members of his household, received together with that emperor, we seem to have established Baronius’s position sufficiently from the history of John Malalas, and from the older *Chronographer* cited by him, as well as from other documents, against Pagius, in volume II of the notes on [Col. 0068B] Silvester, p. 293.

As for the claims made by some concerning Constantine’s repeated baptism, we have shown that they are falsely asserted and have said that they appear rather to have been fraudulently transferred by the Arians from the deeds of Constantius into the life of Constantine.

But another difficulty must here be resolved concerning Constantius’s repeated baptism. Writing against that emperor five years before the Arian emperor died—others think even later—Saint Hilary plainly says that he had not yet been regenerated. Athanasius also supports this in his book *On Synods*. From this it is understood that Constantius remained a catechumen not merely when he was advanced in years but even when he was already close to death.

Yet it scarcely seems credible that these Fathers, who had so often seen and addressed Constantius, were unaware of a baptism supposedly received by him long before, according to those who believe that he was rebaptized. The force of the authority alleged against this view cannot be concealed.

Nevertheless, the student of truth must also weigh the contrary evidence. Once the chronology of Constantius’s baptism has been carefully considered, together with this prince’s exposure to Arian influence—first, when he was imprudently drawn into it at his aunt’s house, and afterward, following his father’s death, when he was inflamed more fiercely through the influence of a presbyter of the same sect who was a familiar of Constantia, the sister of Constantine [see Socrates, *History*, Book I, chapter 19, and Book II, chapter 2, as well as Theodoret, Book II, chapter 3]—it is not difficult to understand why some say that Constantius was rebaptized, while others hold that even in the final years of his life he was only a catechumen and had not yet been regenerated.

We accept the day and year of Constantius’s death from Socrates at the end of Book II. “He died,” Socrates says, “on the third day before the Ides of December, in the consulship of Taurus and Florentius,” namely in the year 361 of the Christian era and in the forty-fifth year of his age. Jerome and the other writers agree, saying that he was born on 6 August, in the consulship of Gallicanus and Bassus, that is, in the year 317, as Cangius shows in the *Byzantine Families*.

Above, in the notes on Silvester, we saw that the baptism received by Constantine the Great at Rome together with his mother and the rest of his family should be assigned to the year 319, when, returning from Illyricum to Rome, he was increased by a third son, Constans, born to Fausta.

Since οἱ συγγενεῖς—“the relatives”—were baptized together with their father Constantine, his sons also, who above all were συγγενεῖς, members of his family, must have been granted the sacrament of baptism. Thus, just as Constantine’s sister Constantia and Crispus, the son of his former wife Minervina, are counted among those baptized with Constantine—Constantia by the Bibliothecarius in *Silvester*, number 43, and Crispus by Theophanes in Cangius, p. 44—so too the sons born from his marriage to Fausta must have been washed in the sacred font together with their father.

Numerous documents prove that Crispus was regenerated in Christ, as does a coin which we presented in volume I and which we take care to reproduce here again, bearing several marks of the Christian religion.

[Col. 0069]

[Col. 0069A] Since Constantine and Constans, the brothers of Constantius by the same mother Fausta, as well as his sisters Constantina, Saint Constantia, and the younger Helena, were washed with the saving water at an early age, why should Constantius not also have been baptized when he was already two years old at his father’s baptism?

For Saint Constantia is read to have been baptized by blessed Silvester in the church of Saint Agnes together with her aunt of the same name; that aunt died long before Constantine’s death. We can therefore scarcely doubt that baptism was administered to Constantius either as an infant or as a child.

His subsequent instability in the faith he had received, and even his later aversion from the Catholic assembly, was, I think, the reason why, with his own consent and deliberate concealment, doubts later arose concerning his baptism—especially in the East, where he ruled. There the Arian presbyters instilled new interests in him through their conversations, as did his aunt Constantia.

The reception of the second seal, confirmation, having been postponed—perhaps under the pretext of his father’s example, mentioned above, or through a feigned desire to receive it after he had been made better instructed by fuller catechesis—he gradually withdrew from the Catholics and also abstained from the mysteries, professing himself a catechumen.

What followed while he administered the empire for twenty-four years and more, and from the time he assumed the dignity of Caesar for thirty years, especially his conduct against the Catholic bishops, sufficiently reveals the testimony of writers who, with Jerome, lamented under that prince: “The whole world was astonished to find itself Arian.”

It should therefore not seem strange that, under his rule, when almost the whole world had forgotten the Catholic faith in so many provinces, the East did not know of the prince’s baptism received in childhood and deliberately concealed by his long abstention from the sacred rites. Nor should it seem strange that the bishops who approached him and saw him profess himself a catechumen for forty years likewise remained unaware of it.

The Roman Church, however, carefully reviewed the deeds of its own pontiffs and of the great Constantine while he was staying there. It preserved those deeds not only in books but also, more enduringly, engraved in the marble of so many churches that he had founded and endowed, and retained them more deeply impressed in human memory [Col. 0069C]. It could not so easily forget the sacrament conferred upon Constantine the Great and his children.

Therefore, while preserving the authority of the Fathers who wrote of the prince’s profession as a catechumen—what they themselves saw him publicly do and proclaim—one must not deny credence to the Romans, who, on the basis of archival documents, maintained that this child’s first baptism had taken place and called “repeated baptism” the baptism conferred upon him when he was already close to death, in the forty-fifth year of his age [Col. 0070A], by Euzoius, an Arian bishop recently advanced to the see of Antioch. The copyist’s error substituted Eusebius, a member of that faction, for Euzoius.

It is much more difficult to reconcile the baptism of Arian impiety, requested and received by the prince when he was near death, with the praise given him after death by Saint Gregory of Nazianzus.

Baronius nevertheless reconciles these matters under the year 361, numbers 21 and following, especially number 31, by excusing Gregory on the ground that, being ignorant of what had happened, he thought Constantius repentant.

If Gregory of Nazianzus could be ignorant of what the dying Augustus had done publicly, in his own vicinity, and could regard him as a penitent Arian, when writing less than four years after his death, no one should find it surprising that, after at least forty years had elapsed since Constantius’s first baptism in the West as an infant or child, Athanasius and Hilary were unable to know what the prince, living in the East, did not profess to have received—or perhaps vainly thought had been conferred upon him as a child—after he had withdrawn to the Arian party [Col. 0070B].

These matters have been said in order to weigh the arguments on both sides before making any more severe judgment concerning the supposed error of the Bibliothecarius and the reliability of the monuments that testify to Constantius’s repeated baptism.

In any case, the declaration attributed to Pope Felix against Constantius refers to the Arian heresy asserted by that prince. That is all that was expressed by the old inscription found together with the body of Saint Felix II in the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Baronius, under the year 357, number 1, Aringhius, and others discuss the body of Saint Felix, pope and martyr, who condemned Constantius.

The addition made in the Bibliothecarius’s text concerning the repeated baptism, since the repetition occurred after the death of this Pope Felix II, should not be referred to Felix’s declaration. Rather, it expresses the historian’s conception, so that the meaning is:

“This Felix II declared that Constantius was to be regarded as a heretic, as the outcome demonstrated, although some excused him, when he repeated the baptism administered to him by Euzoius, the Arian recently advanced to the see of Antioch, at the urging of Eusebius of Nicomedia.”

Line 5.—“He built a basilica on the Via Aurelia,” and so forth; and line 11: “His body,” and so forth, “was buried in the aforesaid basilica, which he himself built on the Via Aurelia at the second milestone.”

The site adjoins the cemetery of Calepodius, not far from the Church of Saint Pancratius, on the Via Aurelia. On this, see Panvinio, Aringhius, and Boldetti, Book II, chapter 18, observations on the cemeteries.

The body was transferred from there to the titular church of Saints Cosmas and Damian within the City, although the portion enclosed beneath Gregory VII was transferred with other relics into a marble slab that formed the altar table when the chapel of Saint Pastor was consecrated. At that time the chapel, together with its titular church, had been renewed from the foundations.

This slab can now be seen attached to the wall inside the chapel of Saint Peter, after the new chapel of Saint Pastor had been magnificently erected by the illustrious Gaetani family.

The inscription of Benedict, titular priest of the same church under Gregory VII, is as follows:

In the time of Gregory, the seventh blessed bishop,

The distinguished presbyter, the illustrious man Benedict,
The customs of the Church he thoroughly renewed,

Which the same sacred Cardinal caused to be consecrated,

And which he made for the same sacred title under the pope,

On the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

In the name of the Shepherd and of John the Forerunner.

On account of the cross, the garment of God, this place is held sacred,

A portion of the garment of Saint John also being joined to it (the Evangelist),

Of the martyr Stephen, under the papal name of the first,

Of the martyr and pope Felix, honored as the second,

[Col. 0071B] Nor less of Hermes, prefect and martyr of the City,

And of Tranquillinus, Marcus, and Marcellianus.

This celebrated place is established by their relics.

Here also [are relics] of many others, whose names we could

Tell, if there were room for them on this tablet.

Through the merits of these, may we return to the stars of heaven.

] [Note: [Col. 0071B]

Line 1.—“Felix, Roman by nationality.” Ciaconius removes Felix from the number of the Roman pontiffs for the reasons given above, no. 51.]

[Note: [Col. 0071B]

Saint Felix II, Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius Liberius, whose deacon he was, was appointed Roman pontiff in the year 355, as we have seen, after Liberius had been driven into exile; and indeed he was appointed by Arian men in the palace of Constantius, since he could not be appointed by the Catholics. He occupied the see for approximately three years, until 29 June 358, on which day he is said to have been deposed from the episcopate in the fuller catalogue of the ancient pontiffs—four days, that is, before Liberius entered the city of Rome, which, as we said, occurred on 2 August of the same year. After Felix had been deposed from the episcopate, as that catalogue records, he lived on his small estate from 30 July.

Marcellinus and Faustinus, schismatic priests of the Roman Church, write in the preface to the petitions that they presented to the emperor Theodosius: “In the third year Liberius returned; the Roman people went out to meet him with joy. Felix, denounced by the senate and people, was expelled from the City.” They add: “After eight years”—that is, from the time Felix was expelled from Rome—“when Valentinian and Valens were consuls” (that is, in the year 365), “Felix died on 22 November.” Although those priests were otherwise exceedingly mendacious, they may safely be trusted in this matter, since they relate events that took place before the eyes of the whole City.

It is disputed whether Felix was truly Roman pontiff. Cardinal Perronius, in his response to the king of Great Britain; Bellarmine, in his defense of Pope Felix; and Henschenius, in the appendix attached to volume III of the Saints’ Acts for April, show that Felix was a true pontiff, because the ancient catalogue of pontiffs—and even the *Liber Pontificalis*—states that, when Liberius was being led into exile, the priests assembled with the counsel of Liberius and appointed Felix in his place. Hence, on the inscription of Felix’s sarcophagus, discovered in 1582 under Gregory XIII in the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, one reads: “Here lies the body of Saint Felix, pope and martyr, who condemned Constantius the heretic.” Nor can this be understood of Felix I, for he did not suffer martyrdom, as we stated in the account of his pontificate, since he departed to God before the persecution of Aurelian.

Nevertheless, because what Anastasius and, following him, Ado and other martyrologies transmit about the martyrdom of Felix II appears fabulous, while the aforementioned Marcellinus and Faustinus state that he died a natural death, one must say, with the author of Baronius’s *Criticism*, that Felix II was called a martyr because he endured many things for Christ. This expression was commonly used in the earlier centuries of the Church, and does not mean that he was killed on Christ’s account. Thus Fronto, a canon regular of the Order of Saint Augustine, writes that there exists a litany in a manuscript written seven or eight centuries ago in which Felix II is numbered among the pontiffs under the title of saint and confessor.

Although the Fathers of the Council of Sirmium wrote to Felix the bishop and to the clergy of the city of Rome that they should receive Liberius on his return, and that the two of them—Felix and Liberius—should administer the episcopate together, which Theodoret reports in book II, chapter 17, that the emperor Constantius had likewise decreed, it is nevertheless certain from Theodoret in the same place and from the petition of Faustinus and the aforementioned Marcellinus that, when Liberius returned to Rome, Felix went elsewhere and lived on his small estate, where he died.

Christian Lupus, in the fifth part of his commentary on the decree of Gregory VII, and other learned men, argue on the contrary that Felix II was not a true pontiff. Each opinion has its supporters and its reasons, and nothing certain can be said about the controversy. It is certain, however, that Felix is venerated as a martyr in the Roman Breviary and Martyrology on the day of July assigned to him, as also in the Martyrology of Ado and elsewhere; and that in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory an office is read in the Mass of Saint Felix and pontiff.

On the Roman episcopate of Felix and on his martyrdom, Papebrochius should be read in his *Chronological-Historical Essay*, where he also rejects many things related by the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*.]

[Col. 0063]

### 53.

Felix [Note: [Col. 0063] Baronius, under the relevant year, proves that he could not have been Roman bishop], Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, occupied the see for one year and two months. He declared Constantius, son of Constantine, a heretic, and said that he had been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia near Nicomedia, in a northern estate [Note: [Col. 0063] Baronius, under the year 357, denies that this was the cause of Felix’s death]; and for this declaration, by order of that same Constantius Augustus, son of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0063] This conflicts with what is said about Liberius], he was crowned with martyrdom and beheaded.

While serving with the honor of the presbyterate, he built a basilica on the Via Aurelia. At the same basilica he purchased a plot of land near the site and offered it to the church that he had built, two miles from the city of Rome. He held one ordination in the month of December: twenty-one priests, five deacons, and nineteen bishops for various places.

He also suffered in the city of Corana [Note: [Col. 0063] C has *Corona*; B has *Cora.], together with many clergy and faithful, secretly brought near the walls of the City, at the third milestone of Trajan’s aqueduct, on 11 November [Note: [Col. 0063] C has “the lake”]. His body was then taken away at night by priests and clergy, together with the priest Damasus, and was buried in the aforementioned basilica that he himself built on the Via Aurelia, on 20 November, at the second milestone, in peace. His episcopate ceased for thirty-nine days [Note: [Col. 0063] *38].

Lines 2 and 3: “amid the contest.” Line 16: “an embossed cup”; another interlinear reading added above it is *anaclifum*. Line 21: “folio 120 and a tremissis. The estate of Antonianus in the territory of Cassinum, worth 103 folles.”]

[Note: [Col. 0075A]

Line 7.—“Near the theater,” namely, that of Pompey.]

[Note: [Col. 0075A]

Line 23. “He established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches,” and he commanded this of priests, bishops, and monasteries. Sigebert likewise attributes this to Damasus in his *Chronicle*, under the year 382.

The institution of singing psalms day and night in the churches is falsely attributed to Damasus, since this practice had existed from the earliest beginnings of the rising Church. What may be credited to Damasus is the Psalter which, according to the Septuagint translators, was sung in all the churches after being corrected by Jerome, and which Damasus handed over to the Gallican churches to be sung. Hence it was called the Gallican Psalter; the Romans retained the Psalter according to the Septuagint translators, and hence it was called the Roman Psalter. This is what Sigebert says in the passage just cited:

“This Psalter Pope Damasus, at the request of Jerome, established to be sung in the Gallican churches, and for this reason it is called Gallican, while the Romans retain for themselves the Psalter according to the Septuagint, for which reason it is called Roman.”]

[Note: [Col. 0075B]

Line 11. “He made a constitution concerning the Church.” In the customary phrase of the *Liber Pontificalis*, which indicates the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, the subject of the constitution is omitted.

In my opinion, however, this constitution of Damasus should be understood as the one he issued when Gratian, after the death of Valens, the most vehement enemy of the Nicene faith, published an edict to address the condition of the Eastern churches, which had been disastrously disfigured by various sects under Constantius, Julian the Apostate, and Valens. By this edict he decreed that the churches of each city should be governed by those who agreed in communion with Damasus.

Accordingly, Damasus issued a celebrated *Tome*, or profession of faith, which he sent through Paulinus to Meletius of Antioch. Meletius was the first of more than 150 Eastern bishops to sign it, in the year 378 at the Council of Antioch, followed afterward by the others at the Council of Constantinople. Holstenius first published fragments of it in the first part of his Roman collection. The Chalcedonian Fathers discuss it in their splendid address to Marcian, and we shall prove the matter at greater length in our commentary on that address, which, God willing, we shall publish.]

Line 23.—“He established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches.” This means alternately. The singing of psalms had already been introduced at Rome and throughout the churches of the world from the apostolic age and had become universal, as Cardinal Bona learnedly proves in his treatise *On Psalmody*.

Shortly before these times, the monks Flavian and Diodorus had introduced at Antioch the practice of reciting in alternating voices; this custom spread throughout the East. Theodoret, speaking of those monks in his *Ecclesiastical History* (book II, chapter 24), says:

“They diligently stirred everyone to the practice of piety by night and by day, and were the first to divide the choirs of those singing psalms into two parts, handing down the hymns of David to be sung alternately. This practice, begun first at Antioch, spread everywhere and traveled even to the remotest parts of the earth.”

Since he adds that they made this known to all the bishops, it seems that Saint Ambrose introduced the practice into his own church. Saint Augustine indicates this when, describing events around the year 387, he writes (*Confessions*, book IX, chapter 7):

“Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to celebrate this kind of consolation and exhortation, with great zeal, as the brothers sang together with voices and hearts. It was, of course, about a year, or not much more, since Justina, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, was persecuting the holy man Ambrose on account of the heresy into which she had been led by the Arians. The devout people were keeping vigil in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant.”

That they sang alternately is shown by the words he adds:

“Then it was established that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people might not waste away from the weariness of grief.”

That was the Eastern custom described above. Cyril also frequently mentions the practice of singing alternately, day and night and at the appointed hours, in his *Life of Saint Sabas* preserved by Cotelerius (vol. III of the *Greek Monuments*, August, p. 242). In describing the various exercises of the monks, he especially praises the recitation of psalms at fixed hours, saying at no. 37:

“On another night the blessed Sabas came out of his cave alone and proceeded to the torrent, reciting the psalms of David verse by verse.”]

[Note: [Col. 0076A]

Line 2.—“With him Ursicinus was ordained amid the contest.” Since Damasus had been elected by the larger part of the clergy as the successor of Felix and Liberius after the Council of Ariminum, the opposing party, unwilling to endure this, created Ursicinus a pseudo-pontiff some time later and occupied the Basilica of Sicininus. “When this had happened,” Rufinus says (book II, chapter 10), “such sedition—or rather, such wars—arose, with the peoples defending one side or the other, that the places of prayer were filled with human blood.”]

Line 4.—“They expelled Ursicinus from the City,” namely, by the authority of Praetextatus, prefect of the City.

2

Line 8.—“He built a Platonia.” A *Platonia* is a pavement elegantly laid with marble slabs of various shapes. See Baronius, under the year 384, no. 17.

Line 11.—“He was maliciously accused.” Since the schismatics could not undermine the legitimate ordination of the pontiff by any slander from hostile enemies, and since the same accusations were known to the emperor and the magistrates, they turned to false and exceedingly shameful charges. As is clear from the letters, they accused that most holy and pure man—whom Saint Jerome calls “a virgin and teacher of the virgin Church”—of adultery.

Line 23.—“He established that psalms, etc.” The ecclesiastical custom of gathering in church and singing psalms day and night is extremely ancient and has been handed down to us from the institution of the apostles. Therefore, what is written here—that Damasus established that psalms should be sung in the church day and night—is false and was added by someone, unless we interpret it as referring to some particular form of psalmody prescribed by him. Baronius, under the year 384, no. 20.]

[Note: [Col. 0076C]

### Chronological Notes

The epoch of Blessed Damasus was firmly established by contemporary and autograph documents, which we presented above in volume II, pp. 67 ff. and 106, in the *Prolegomena*. Since Saint Liberius died on 24 September, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaiphus, as was demonstrated above in his chronology, his episcopate ceased for seven days, as the Librarian counts at the end of the account of Liberius.

Thus, on 1 October of the same consulship, in the Christian era 366—a day that fell on Sunday—Damasus was ordained and began his pontificate. Since he continued it until 11 December 384, in the consulship of Ricimer and Clearchus, as Prosper, his contemporary, testifies in his chronicle, and as the church records presented in the *Prolegomena* to volume II, p. 68, confirm, it follows that eighteen full years, two months, and ten days must be assigned to his tenure of the see. This is the period assigned to him by the surviving paintings in the Basilica of Saint Paul, by the catalogues, and by the other numbered codices listed in the same *Prolegomena*, folio 106.

In the catalogue of Felix IV, a copyist’s error is readily recognized: he transferred the unit removed from the column of years into the neighboring column of months and wrote:

The documents cited on p. 67 of the same *Prolegomena* should be consulted, where Damasus’s epoch is clearly demonstrated.

### Historical Notes

Line 2.—“Ursicinus amid the contest.” “After taking counsel with the priests, they appointed Damasus, etc., and expelled Ursicinus from the City and appointed him bishop of Naples.” From the Florentine manuscript of Anastasius I presented in the *Prolegomena*, volume II, folio 61, a catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Naples, in which Ursus is numbered as the thirteenth bishop and is said to have been of the same age as Saint Damasus and to have occupied the same episcopate for four years:

“XIII. Bishop Ursus occupied the see for four years. He lived in the time of Pope Damasus and of the emperors Valentinian and Gratian.”

Some maintain that this same Ursus should be identified with Ursicinus, also called Ursinus, who was ordained at Rome during the dispute against Damasus. They rely on the testimony of John the Deacon—whom most people consider to have been a deacon of the Neapolitan Church—who explicitly makes this identification.

Others deny it, following Baronius under the year 381; among them is Ughellus in *Sacred Italy*. They argue, first, from the difference in the names; second, from the fact that Ursicinus, who had been ordained by a faction and then exiled to Gaul, stirred up disturbances against Damasus even fifteen years after Damasus’s election; and finally, from the fact that the supporters of that faction, namely the priests Marcellinus and Faustinus, mention nothing in their petition about a Neapolitan episcopate supposedly conferred upon him.

Baronius, under the year 368, does indeed record a rescript of Valentinian and Valens Augusti, dated 12 June in their second consulship, by which the followers of Ursicinus were permitted to live wherever they wished without injury to their religion, although the city of Rome alone was forbidden to them. For this reason, some think that Ursicinus’s four-year episcopate at Naples can be reconciled with the evidence: after he was driven from there and exiled to Gaul, he could have remained alive and capable of stirring up disturbances fifteen years after the beginning of the pontificate of Blessed Damasus.

In that rescript, however, the emperors establish nothing concerning Ursicinus, who had been ordained in schism after Damasus. It is therefore difficult to believe that the imperial indulgence could be transferred to the principal author of the faction in such a way that he was not merely permitted to live near the City, but could also have been appointed to govern the Neapolitan Church by the legitimate pontiff Damasus, whether with Damasus’s consent through the bishops of the province or through the clergy of Naples.

As for the testimony of John the Deacon, which originated several centuries after that dispute, they argue that the writer could easily have been deceived by the similarity of the names Ursus and Ursicinus, by the proximity of their ages, and could have confused the deeds of the two men no less than their names.

Some think that the following passage was copied from John the Deacon into the *Liber Pontificalis*. Since Henschenius omits it, however, this indicates that it is absent from certain manuscripts: namely, where the ordination of Ursicinus amid the dispute is mentioned, but nothing is added about an episcopate at Naples having been conferred upon him.]

[Col. 0077D] Line 6.—“He was in the time of Julian.” Here we have another sentence, or a clause belonging to another sentence, which some suspect was taken from the corrupted acts of Liberius. The emperor Julian had already died on 26 June 363, as the *Life of Liberius* consistently shows. Therefore a full three years intervened between Julian’s death and the election of Pope Damasus on 1 October 366.

Damasus had indeed been appointed priest and vicar of Pope Liberius in the time of Julian, if we follow those same acts, but he had not yet been promoted to the episcopate. The expedition against the barbarians, followed by the threats made against Liberius—that, on his victorious return, his flesh would be offered to the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth—seems to refer to Julian the Apostate, not to the Arian Constantius. Saint John Chrysostom mentions it in *Against the Pagans*, as Baronius observes under the year 363; so do Saint Jerome in his *Chronicle*, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus in Oration II against Julian, [Col. 0078A] and the historian Theodoret in book III, chapter 18.

At that time Damasus, priest and vicar of Liberius, urged Liberius to administer baptism in the Ostrian cemetery. It therefore appears that some abbreviator of those acts condensed the following line, in which the Librarian says that Damasus was living in the time of Julian. He ought to have added that Damasus was then a priest and vicar, and not yet bishop or successor of Liberius. That occurred only after the three years following Julian’s death had elapsed, while Valentinian governed the Roman Empire.

Line 7.—“He built two basilicas, one near the theater of Saint Laurence, and another on the Via Ardeatina.” Several writers have illuminated the Basilica of Saint Laurence at the Theater of Pompey. We had been expecting shortly a fuller history of it from the illustrious and reverend bishop Fonseca, recently promoted from the canonry of that basilica by our holy lord Benedict XIII to the episcopate of the Church of Jesi.

The columns excavated from the ruins of the Theater of Pompey and from the adjoining Curia—where they say that Caesar the dictator was stabbed—are said to adorn the basilica in the magnificent buildings of the Apostolic Chancery. So too does the statue of the Great Pompey, now preserved in the distinguished museum of the Marquis Clement Spada.

We read in Gruter, folio 111, no. 8, an inscription excavated near the basilica in which the name of the Genius and the name of the Theater of Pompey appear. That the theater extended around the area now called the Campo de’ Fiori is shown by enormous columns discovered a few years ago in the foundations of the neighboring buildings of Cardinal Pio of Carpentras, and from there extending through houses toward the street named after the ironworkers.

We infer that the stage of the theater stood there from the magnificent marble architraves excavated in various places opposite the church of Saint Andrew della Valle, corresponding at the end of that street to the area of Saint Charles at the Catinari. There, too, recently discovered fragments of enormous columns of porphyry confirm the magnificence of the ancient structure.

A portico followed, leading to the deaconry of Saint Angel, from the modern Fish Market. This part of the district is adorned by arches and by an inscription of Septimius Severus and Caracalla, still surviving and decorated with greater splendor under those same Augusti. An inscription discovered there, which Gruter reproduces on folio 111, no. 6, indicates that it was called the Portico of Jove under Diocletian during its restoration.

In an eighth-century work on the regions of the city of Rome, published by the illustrious defender of antiquity Mabillon in his *Analecta*—and to which we have again given a place, with a new edition and expanded notes, in the *Prolegomena* to our Anastasian edition—no. 1 describes the route from the gate of Saint Peter to Saint Paul. Along that route, after the title of Saint Laurence at Damasus, as sections 2 and 3 indicate more explicitly, comes the Theater of Pompey. The text then adds: “and through the portico as far as Saint Angel and the temple of Jove”—that is, the Capitoline temple—as we noted in the same place.

That this Basilica of Saint Laurence was adorned by its founder, Blessed Damasus, with sacred images and histories is shown by Pope Adrian in his letter to Charlemagne, inserted in the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea by Binius, volume III, second part, p. 126, at the end of column 1, and by Labbe, volume VII, column 955.

I published evidence of the consecration of the same basilica by Saint Damasus—a document perhaps the oldest genuine evidence of this kind of rite—in no. 35 of the preface to volume I. It was found among ancient marbles collected by Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, who held the title of Saint Laurence as Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and adorned that basilica with many structures, especially at the high altar, and with ornaments. The following letters are engraved on the marble tablet:

[Col. 0079A] I think they should be expanded as follows. “In the name of Christ, I, Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, consecrated this house, dedicated in the ninth region, in the month of September: Saint Paul, Saint Peter.”

The names *Damasius* and *Damasus* were used interchangeably, either according to the preference of those pronouncing them differently or through the ignorance of stonecutters in marble inscriptions and of copyists and scribes in manuscripts. This can be observed both on this stone and in the ancient lectionaries of the Liberian Basilica within the City and of the Church of Otricoli in the Sabine territory, in the ninth region of the Augustan division, which was called the Circus Flaminius.

We know from Publius Victor that the area of this basilica extended toward the Theater of Pompey. Above, in the notes on Saint Julius, we showed that the same district extended as far as the deaconry of Saint Eustachius and was called by that name in public records still signed in the eleventh century.

The dedication of this Laurentian basilica, now called “at Damasus,” is recorded on the Kalends of September. Its date in both recent and ancient records agrees with the inscription on the stone. Finally, the last sigla, F P A and F P E, leave no one in doubt that they represent the names of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and were placed as a seal, a practice familiar to the pontiffs of the Roman Church both in charters and in the custody of sacred objects.

Twenty years ago, when, by order of Clement XI, a reliquary chest found in the small compartment of an altar beneath the high altar of the deaconry of Saint Mary in Domnica was opened, a large part of the bones of Saint Balbina was found, together with a circular lead tablet inscribed: “BODY OF SAINT BALBINA, VIRGIN.” On the lid of the chest containing other relics, different from the bones of the virgin, images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul were impressed. No other seal was used more frequently on glass dishes prepared for sacred ministry and for collecting the blood of martyrs, or affixed to their small reliquaries, than the two heads and names of those apostles.

For this reason also, the fact that the name of Paul is placed before the name of Peter on this stone indicates that the sculptor varied the order at will, as Aringhius, Fabretti, and Bonarota observe on circular glass objects. Sometimes Paul is placed on the left, as we see on the lead seals of bulls, both ancient and recent.

The reverse side of this marble tablet displays the names of the saints whose relics, according to custom, were placed beneath the altar table at the consecration of the same church.

“Here rests the head of Saint Crescentinus the martyr, and the relics of Saint Superantius.”

Saint Crescentinus was a Roman soldier. It is recorded that his body, without the head, was transferred to Urbino in the year of our salvation 1068, under Maynard, bishop of that city, who had obtained it from Fulco, bishop of Tifernum. Crescentinus had suffered under Diocletian on the Kalends of June. He is also called Crescentianus, as in the office printed for him at Rome and Fano in 1657, with the authorization of the Sacred Congregation of Rites.

On the same day, the ancient Antwerp Martyrology records at Rome the passion of Saints Juventius, Cyriacus, and Superantius. The martyrologies of Florentius and of the monastery of Corbie call the latter Exuperantius, as Florentius himself reported under the Kalends of June.

Whoever compares this titular tablet of the church’s dedication and seal of the sacred relics—which Pope Damasus placed beneath the altar of the dedicated basilica—with the parchment document customarily enclosed by the bishop consecrating a church together with the sacred relics beneath the altar table, will certainly see that the rite instituted by our ancestors in this holy Roman Church has been retained with complete constancy for fourteen centuries and more, from Blessed Damasus down to our own age.

As I write this, our most holy lord Pope Benedict XIII, four days ago, namely on Sunday, 17 September of this year 1724, solemnly dedicated the titular Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. It had begun to be restored from its foundations under Clement XI, who had laid its foundation stone on 27 February 1702. Benedict enclosed the following inscription:

“On 17 September in the year of the Lord 1724, the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, the feast of the Impression of the Sacred Stigmata in the body of Saint Francis, I, Benedict XIII, bishop of the Catholic Church, formerly Brother Vincent Maria, Cardinal Ursinus of the Order of Preachers, archbishop of Benevento, consecrated this church in honor of the Twelve Holy Apostles and this altar under the name and memory of the holy apostles Philip and James; and I enclosed in it the relics of the holy martyrs Donatus and Severinus. To each of Christ’s faithful who visit it today, and to those who visit it on the anniversary of this consecration, I granted a plenary indulgence and, in the customary form, an equal indulgence of fifty years and the same number of forty-day periods. This is the first church, and this the first altar consecrated by me, though unworthy, together with it, in the first year of my pontificate, in addition to 356 other churches, 1,463 fixed altars, and 620 portable altars, which I solemnly dedicated with the same sacred rites while simultaneously holding the dignity of cardinal and archbishop.”

The other basilica founded by the same Pope Damasus outside the City on the Via Ardeatina was destroyed by the common disaster that overtook many other suburban sacred buildings. When the barbarian flood poured in and encamped around the City, most of the suburban shrines were not merely despoiled but utterly demolished and leveled to the ground by the destroyers. Thus, to prevent the injuries they inflicted everywhere upon the sacred relics, the best pastors judged it necessary to remove many bodies of holy martyrs and confessors and transfer them within the City, lest they be scattered by impious hands.

On this occasion the body of Blessed Damasus, which had rested in the same basilica that he founded outside the walls—as we read in this no. 54, lines 7 and 8—was also transferred to the earlier Laurentian basilica called “at Damasus” after its founder. There it is piously preserved and venerated beneath the high altar, inside the altar established in the church’s underground chamber.

Line 8.—“He built a Platonia, where the bodies of the apostles lay.” Ado of Vienne used the same words in his *Chronicle*, as Cangius observes in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under the word *Platonia*. In explaining the idea signified by this term, he proves that it refers to precious marble cut into thin slabs, with which the interiors of buildings were magnificently covered. So too above, in the account of Liberius, no. 52, line 8: “Here Liberius adorned with marble plates the tomb of Saint Agnes the martyr.”

[Col. 0080D] Line 10.—“Whose shrines he also decorated with verses.” Among the ancients, the sacred cemeteries where martyrs were buried were called *concilia*, as Baronius observes in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 23 June, and Boldetti in *On Sacred Cemeteries*, book II, chapter 19, p. 585, citing the acts of Pope Saint Stephen and Jerome’s epitaph for Nepotianus.

Blessed Damasus had many inscriptions composed by himself engraved in the sacred cemeteries and in the churches erected over those cemeteries. Cardinal Baronius frequently reproduced them in his *Annals*; Martius Milesius collected them and published them together with the surviving works of the same pontiff. Some of them can still be seen intact: for example, the inscription of the fountain in the Vatican crypts; the inscription of Saint Eutychius the martyr in the Basilica of Saint Sebastian on the Via Appia; and another on the pavement of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin in the Hills. In each of these the name of Damasus is engraved.

### Line 11.—“Here he established a decree concerning the Church.”

[Col. 0081A] What the Librarian understands by the expression *decree concerning the Church* is explained more clearly in the following item concerning Siricius, line 2, where we read: “Here he established a decree concerning the whole Church, or against all heresies, and disseminated it throughout the whole world, so that it might be kept in the archives of every Church as a weapon against all heresies.” The writers of the *Liber Pontificalis* customarily use the expression *decrees concerning the Church* for apostolic constitutions issued by Roman pontiffs concerning faith or morals.

The constitutions which Damasus issued both in the four Roman councils held in the City and in the approval of the ecumenical synod of Constantinople have been so celebrated in the writings of ancient and modern historians, and so suitably collected by Baronius, Binius, and Labbe in their *Annals* and *Councils*, as well as in the notes of Pagi and Somier, that here only the principal points of the chief matters need be indicated.

At the first Roman council celebrated by Damasus at the beginning of his pontificate, in the year 367, “Valens and Ursacius, and the other manifest Arians, [Col. 0081B] were condemned,” as Athanasius writes at length to the African bishops: “Thanks ought to be given to the piety of Damasus himself and to the others who assembled at Rome, because, after Ursacius and Valens, together with their associates of the same opinion, had been expelled, they preserved the harmony of the Church.”

In the third year of his pontificate Damasus held a second council in the City, at which Auxentius, the Arian bishop of Milan, was deposed, and Ursicinus, the schismatic, was condemned. The synodal letter of this council, addressed to the bishops of Illyricum, is still extant.
