The third Roman synod under Damasus, attended by Peter, bishop of Alexandria, condemned the heresy of Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, who had been transformed from a defender of the Nicene faith into an author of heresy; and on the same occasion it struck with repeated anathemas his disciple Vitalis, who had been intruded by a faction into the see of Antioch. The same anathemas were renewed against Arius, Sabellius, Macedonius, Eunomius, and Photinus. See the letter of Pope Damasus to the Easterners in Theodoretus, book V, chapter 10. The presence of [Col. 0081C] Peter of Alexandria shows that Damasus celebrated this synod after the seventh year of his administration.

Finally, the fourth Roman synod, which Damasus had summoned as ecumenical, admitted the excuses of the Easterners. Through legates sent from the Council of Constantinople to Damasus, they acknowledged the authority of the Roman pontiff, by which he had the right to summon them to his ecumenical synod, as they testify in the synodal letter addressed to him, preserved in Theodoretus, book V, chapter 9. The letter is to be referred to the year 382, when they complained that their Churches were endangered by heretics if, because of the journey to Rome, they were absent from them for too long.

The same Roman synod, after first bearing witness to its primacy, confirmed the order of the ancient patriarchal sees—namely, those of Alexandria and Antioch—without counting Constantinople, although the ambition of certain Greeks contends that an appendix was added to the canons of the Council of Constantinople assigning the [Col. 0081D] bishops of that see the second place in the sessions. Baronius refutes them under the year 381. And although both Pagis disagree with Baronius in asserting the authenticity of the canon, the younger Pagi nevertheless concludes in his discussion of Damasus, no. 14, in these words:

> “But whatever the case may be, it is certain that that canon was not received by the Roman Church, and that it was expressly proved before Innocent III, who, in canon 5 of the Fourth Lateran Council, counted the see of Constantinople second among the patriarchal sees and assigned to it a dignity second only to that of Rome.”

These matters, therefore—those concerning faith which Damasus affirmed, and those concerning the discipline of the Church which he established—are to be recognized in the Librarian’s very brief sentence: “He established a decree concerning the Church.”

### Line 11.—“Here he was maliciously accused,” etc.

Another event that occurred at a council under Damasus ought to be added above. It should not, however, have been listed among the decrees concerning the Church, since it was a personal act of his: namely, the pope’s voluntary vindication of himself at the council [Col. 0082A] against the calumnies of factions. See the notes of Somier.

I shall add only this observation: the utterly shameless audacity of the heretics and schismatics of that age against the holiest men was no less unrestrained in the East than in the West. In the East they brought charges of sexual misconduct and magic against Athanasius, while against Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus they alleged the heresy which both of them vigorously persecuted; see Baronius under the year 371.

Nor were they more lenient toward Jerome, accusing him of an infamous intimacy with holy women whom he was training in Christian virtues at Rome and in Syria, or disgracefully branding him with the charge of heresy, although he was the hammer of heretics. Thus, in accordance with their character, they did not cease contriving calumnies against Damasus: they not only insinuated rumors of violated chastity, but also muttered about the impiety of offering incense and betraying the faith, which they falsely claimed he had shared with Marcellinus, Marcellus, Melchiades, and Silvester. [Col. 0082B] Augustine refutes them in *On Baptism against Petilianus*, chapter 16.

I have silenced their slanders together with the holy Doctor in the notes to Marcellinus. Apart from the authorities cited there, the importance that should be attached to defending Marcellinus’s innocence may also be demonstrated by the dissertation of Our Most Holy Lord Benedict XIII, inserted in the Beneventan synodical collection and published while he governed the same Church of Benevento as archbishop. It is entitled *On the Body of Saint Bartholomew*, folio 75.

### Line 12.—“A bath beside the titular church.”

In my defense of the parochial rights of the same basilica of Saint Lawrence in Damasus, of whose chapter I was a member, published in 1706, part II, section I, no. 6, I observed that, in the oldest titles of the city of Rome, sites were generally chosen for their foundation where an abundant supply of water was available for baptism by immersion, which was then the customary practice. The titles were founded “as dioceses for the baptism and penance of the many who were converted from paganism, [Col. 0082C] and for the burial places of martyrs,” as we saw above in the discussion of Marcellus, no. 31.

Accordingly, I noted that in the earliest titles one finds nearby baths or water outlets, and indeed that the ruins of baths still survive at several of them. The title of Pastor, or of Saint Pudentiana, famous for the hospitality shown to the apostles, is situated at the Baths of Novatus. The title of Saint Prisca on the Aventine still displays in its underground chamber both the baths and the mosaic decorating them. Beside the Baths of Titus stood another lodging of the apostles, where the title of Eudoxia was later established; the title of Saint Clement is joined to these as well.

The three titles immediately adjoining the Baths of Diocletian are those of Pope Caius, Saint Susanna the virgin, and Saint Cyriacus. The same number of titles almost touches the Baths of Antoninus: namely, Saint Balbina; the title called Fasciola, of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; and Saint Sixtus, also called Tigridis, where there was likewise a baptismal pool. Beside the outlet of the Marcia aqueduct stood, on one side, Saint Eusebius and, on the other, Saints Silvester and Martin, also called *Equitius*. Saint Marcellus was situated at the conduits of the [Col. 0082D] Aqua Virgo. Near the Transtiberine *naumachia* were Saint Chrysogonus and Saint Cecilia, where the mounds of the baths can also be seen.

Thus, in the title of Damasus, the proximity of a bath demonstrates the deliberate selection of a suitable place for opening a baptismal font there, since the Roman Church’s titles were chiefly intended for this ministry, as I indicated above in the notes on Saint Dionysius.

### Line 14.—“Here he established a title in the city of Rome,” that is, the basilica which he himself founded.

In the notes on Saint Cletus I collected a considerable amount of material concerning the number of titles, originally fixed at twenty-five by order of the prince of the apostles and preserved by his successors during the persecutions. It was later increased to twenty-eight, during the peace of the Church, by Silvester, Mark, Julius, and Damasus, while Liberius had recently enlarged the number of basilicas.

There I also discussed the division of the priestly districts of the Roman clergy and the assignment of seven titular clergy members to perform the sacred mysteries in a fixed order and sequence in [Col. 0083A] each of the basilicas which later writers called patriarchal. These basilicas represented the universal Church established in this Roman see, the mother and sovereign of all, through the chair of Peter, which transmitted the right of supreme priesthood to its lawful successors seated upon it.

Although I brought together much material both in the discussion of Cletus and in that of Dionysius concerning the increase of the patriarchal churches in the City shortly before the celebration of the ecumenical Council of Constantinople under Damasus, it nevertheless seems useful to add something here in order to present that system more clearly, lest matters insufficiently explained by an author seeking brevity should cause confusion for those proceeding further.

I had therefore said that the number seven was anciently assigned to the bishops and cardinal priests who constituted the leaders of the priesthood, together with the deacons, likewise fixed at seven as an index of the whole body, in this holy Roman [Col. 0083B] Church. They were assigned to each of its patriarchal basilicas for the daily celebration of the sacred mysteries, in priestly rotations returning in a fixed order throughout the week, just as, in the Church of the Mosaic Law, twenty-four priestly divisions returned at appointed times, as described in 1 Chronicles 24.

I added that the Christian Church, gathered both from the nations and from the circumcision, possessed this increase in extent beyond the narrow limits of the Mosaic Church, so that it might gather the whole world into the true worship of God, in the unity of one faith and one congregation of the faithful, under one head, though its divine ministries were performed in different places.

God willed three sees to stand out and to be endowed with broader authority through the prince of the apostles. Of these, he made the Roman see pre-eminent, conferring upon it a singular privilege above the others: namely, to exercise the fullness of power over the entire body of the Church.

This catholic bond of the hierarchy, displaying the one Spirit of Christ by whom all the members, animated by one head, are governed under one [Col. 0083C] authority, seemed so outstanding to the wise men and architects who cared for the structure of the Christian body that, in the Roman Church established as the head of all, they never ceased presenting its image both to minds and to eyes.

The mark that Peter had impressed in the foundation of the twenty-five titles, entrusted to his immediate successors, by which all the priestly divisions gathered into one Church could be recognized, the other pontiffs faithfully retained until Silvester. Whenever the number was reduced by the persecutors, they restored it.

After the foundations of the Roman Church had thus been firmly laid and strengthened through the first three centuries, while the precious stones of this heavenly Jerusalem were compressed within the narrow spaces of the crypts, peace was at last restored to the Church under Constantine. This gave an opportunity to bring the structure of the Church out of the underground and to display it more magnificently before the eyes of all in the royal masses of the basilicas.

The chief concern, however, was always that the work should surpass the material, and that the fitness [Col. 0083D] of the mystery should exceed the dignity of the structure—namely, that it should indicate, as the Church speaks, the wisest interpreter of her own work, “that just as she advanced through temporal spaces, so she should seek from God an increase through spiritual growth.”

The principal Roman basilicas founded by Constantine in the fourth century and dedicated by Silvester therefore did not lack their own mystery. Innocent III explained it, and predecessors of Innocent much earlier confirmed it in that harmonious division of basilicas and titles which showed the Roman see to be the seat of God and of the Lamb among the patriarchal thrones of the Christian world: a center of unity, a type of the catholic whole, and a crown of all the Churches, gathering into its maternal embrace the offerings presented to Christ by the harmonious choir of the elders, or by the ordered hierarchy of priests.

We have already set forth that idea of the universal Church expressed in this Roman Church, both in the words of Innocent III in the notes on Saint Dionysius [Col. 0084A] and in those of Cardinal Rasponi in the notes on Saint Cletus. I shall therefore not dwell on it longer here.

Only the following explanation remains to be given. How did the three principal sees of the Christian world, founded by the authority of Peter and possessing widely extended jurisdiction, correspond to an appropriate image in the three principal Roman basilicas constructed in the age of Constantine the Great? At that time the ancient number of twenty-five titles, prescribed by blessed Peter, established by Cletus, and retained by his successors until Silvester, was still in force.

And when, shortly after the age of Silvester, the number of titles was increased to twenty-eight, and two basilicas were added to the three principal ones representing the three patriarchates, receiving their own weekly rotations of titular priests, and appearing—according to the view of Innocent III and Cardinal Rasponi—to represent two other sees almost equal to the patriarchates in honor, although they were not endowed with any new jurisdiction during the fourth and fifth centuries, from the time of the First Council of Constantinople to that of the Council of [Col. 0084B] Chalcedon, how, I ask, could this fivefold number of basilicas enjoying a sevenfold assignment of titles represent, by the decision of the Roman pontiffs, the image of those five sees?

For from Damasus to Leo—that is, from the Council of Constantinople to the Council of Chalcedon—the Roman pontiffs resisted the claims of the two sees of Constantinople and Jerusalem, which sought an equal rank alongside the primary group of the three patriarchal sees founded by Peter: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.

The opposing tendencies appear to conflict. On the one hand, there was the prohibition against increasing the ancient number of three patriarchates; on the other, there was a concession that, in the image of the Christian world, not merely three but five sees should be represented as superior in dignity to the other episcopal thrones.

To begin removing the appearance of contradiction in this last comparison, the very learned author and interpreter of the ancient and new discipline, Thomassinus, aptly warned that one must [Col. 0084C] distinguish the honorary right of sitting in the more honorable place, of using certain insignia, and of enjoying similar distinctions—an external form indicating the Church’s special reverence toward certain sees—from the right of exercising power, whether by coercing or directing entire provinces, exarchates, and dioceses as subjects.

The Roman pontiffs resisted vigorously, especially in the fourth and fifth centuries, any disturbance of this second kind of right. They restrained the audacity of the prelates of Constantinople and Jerusalem if they attempted anything belonging to the foreign directive or coercive authority of the three ancient and primary patriarchates founded by Peter’s authority: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.

They forbade the transgression of the limits established by the Fathers. From the age of Damasus especially to that of Leo the Great, they decreed the recovery of such usurped rights for the ancient sees whenever they perceived them being gradually appropriated, above all by the bishops of Constantinople: first the authority of the metropolitan of Heraclea, then [Col. 0084D] the jurisdiction of the exarchate of Pontus, then that of the see of Alexandria and Antioch, and later even that of Rome. Thomassinus clearly explains this series of events in part [uncertain], book [uncertain], chapter 10, where he recounts the attempts of Hilary, Atticus, Sisinnius, and their successors.

The Roman pontiffs firmly resisted this disturbance of the ancient authority, even entrusting their legates at the council with the order “to forbid, and by forbidding to invalidate, whatever the bishops might attempt as a new measure that could either harm the apostolic see or increase one Church at the expense of another.” Thomassinus collected this passage there, no. 14, from session 15 of the Council of Chalcedon.

This honorary right, however, was very different from the former. It consisted solely in the assignment of a more honorable place after the bishop or legates of the Roman see. Just as the bare precedence of the title honored the bishops both of Jerusalem and of New Rome, so the supreme pontiffs indulgently allowed councils to decree it. They not only did not order their [Col. 0085A] legates to invalidate it, but also insisted that, once granted by decree, it should remain permanently in force.

Accordingly, at the Synod of Chalcedon, the papal legate Paschasinus complained that, in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, a more honorable place had not been assigned to the bishop of Constantinople above the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch. Everyone at Chalcedon expected and approved that Anatolius should be placed before them.

We have treated this matter sufficiently in the notes on Dionysius, where, together with Thomassinus, we observed that the Council of Nicaea acted similarly with the bishop of Jerusalem. In canon 7 it granted him “a due sequence of honor, while preserving the proper dignity of the metropolitan see of Caesarea.”

Thus, while the integrity of jurisdiction belonging to the three genuine patriarchal sees founded by Peter as their author remained intact, the Council of Nicaea granted the see of Jerusalem, and the synod celebrated at Constantinople granted the see of Constantinople, a rank of honor almost equal to that of the patriarchal sees. Nor was there any contradiction in the Roman pontiffs’ granting them the summit immediately below themselves, provided that no power taken from the three patriarchal sees was added, whose ancient rights they ordered to be preserved inviolate.

With this jurisdiction preserved, and with the power of those sees thereby firmly [Col. 0085B] established and represented by the three principal Roman basilicas—the Lateran, the Vatican, and the Pauline—nothing prevented Damasus and his successors from presenting in the Roman Church, which displayed the entire system of the Christian world to the faithful, images also of those two sees, added in name and by the title of honor to the order of the three patriarchal sees.

Whether that division and the assignment of six cardinal bishops to perform daily rotations in the Lateran basilica, with the supreme pontiff fulfilling the seventh, or first, place on Sunday, and likewise the assignment of twenty-eight cardinal priests to four sevenfold rotations corresponding to the four basilicas nearest the Lateran, was instituted while Damasus was seated on the pontifical throne or after his death by his successors cannot be determined so easily. Both Cardinals Baronius and Rasponi discuss these arrangements [Col. 0085C] from ancient ritual books.

Under Damasus, the number of titles was indeed completed at twenty-eight, when he “established as a title in the city of Rome” the basilica of Saint Lawrence which he had constructed, as we read in line 14 of this item. Before Damasus, the number had already exceeded twenty-five: under Silvester the title of *Equitius* had been added, and under Mark another title bearing his name had been added in the Palatine district.

That under Damasus several bishops, priests, and monks had already been associated with the clergy in singing the psalmody within the city churches is inferred from this very item, where it is stated in line 23: “Here he established that they should sing psalms day and night throughout all the churches; he prescribed this for priests and bishops, or monasteries.”

As far as I can determine by conjecture, it seems that the Lateran basilica, as the chief of all and as the place where Silvester had resided from its foundation as though in his episcopal palace, was assigned a weekly [Col. 0085D] honor: the duty of celebrating the sacred rites for the supreme pontiff and the cardinal bishops, whom a later age therefore also customarily called Lateran bishops.

Among these I find the bishop of Tivoli listed in the year 1138 under Innocent II, in an ancient stone in the church of Saint Stephen near the walls of the city of Poli, now assigned to the Religious Fathers of the Pious Schools and fixed to the wall on the left as one enters the church. Its complete text is given here, since it contains several matters worthy of remembrance, together with the errors contrary to the orthographic rules of its own age:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, at the prayers of Lord Odo the count, and of John, bishop and archpriest of this holy church, and of the other faithful of God, Lord Guido, cardinal and bishop of the Lateran, consecrated this church with two altars on the eleventh day of March, from the relics of the holy martyrs Celsus, Tiburtius, Stephen the pope, and other saints, for the holy Church of Tivoli. He consecrated [Col. 0086A] the great altar in honor of blessed Stephen the protomartyr and blessed Nicholas, and the altar of the portico in honor of blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Thomas the apostle, and blessed Giles the confessor. And he established that every year, on the anniversary of the dedication, whoever should come devoutly to this dedication should receive one year remitted from his penance and a fourth part of his venial offenses; and, if he had five or more years, one year of penance should be remitted, and the remaining years should be remitted to him, together with a fourth part of his venial offenses.”

This designation of bishops as “Lateran bishops,” recorded on this stone and agreeing with the Roman Order produced by Cardinals Baronius and Rasponi to demonstrate the assignment of the weekly office performed by bishops in the principal basilica of all, shows that this custom continued into the twelfth century of Christ.

Its origin, however, must be traced back to the fourth century, indeed to the very foundation of the basilica. Several examples from that age suggest that bishops resided with the supreme pontiff in the Lateran [Col. 0086B] patriarchate. Eusebius reports that Constantine the Great always had several bishops attached to his retinue, whom he wished to be his table companions, advisers, and companions on his journeys. See book I of *The Life of Constantine*, especially chapter 42, entitled “Honors Conferred upon Bishops.”

It was much more fitting for several suburban bishops to remain at the side of the supreme pontiff. Their presence was not thereby withdrawn from their own parishes, given their proximity to the City, just as the prelates of extensive dioceses are considered to remain with their own churches even when they are much farther from the boundaries of those dioceses, provided that they reside at their centers.

Moreover, the examples of the prince of the apostles employing bishops as assistants in the City, together with the custom of his successors of retaining nearby bishops with them for longer periods and of summoning even those living far away to the apostolic thresholds at fixed intervals, made it easy for Constantine, while residing at Rome, to have at least neighboring bishops as companions in his own buildings. The same facility therefore remained for Silvester, in the buildings [Col. 0086C] donated to him by Constantine, to retain these Lateran bishops to perform the sacred rites with him.

The selection of six bishops to complete, with the supreme pontiff, the number seven, and to perform the divine mysteries in rotation on each weekday, also suits the age of Silvester. He is said to have established the practice by which the individual days following the Lord’s Day were designated by the name of weekdays, so that the clergy might understand that every day they were to cease from worldly concerns and devote themselves to God, having been enrolled in the lot of the Lord.

Calendars marked in advance with weekly letters among Christians belong to the same period and practice. Bucherius published them together with the Latin paschal cycle, recently elucidated by Cardinal Norisius. Thus it is entirely clear that whatever concerns the sevenfold divisions of divine ministry, once publicly displayed after peace had been restored to the Church, must be referred to the age of Silvester or to a time very near it.

The most ancient [Col. 0086D] apostolic institution had already foreshadowed this arrangement: at Jerusalem, through the seven deacons; at Rome, through an equal number of deacons, subdeacons, regions, and notaries; and in Asia, through seven bishops, corresponding to the seven spirits of God standing before the throne and to the seven lampstands of the Apocalypse. This number was especially suited to divine ministry, since it had been employed to signify the whole, from the time when the Creator of all things established the period of his works by this very number of days.

I would not, in fact, deny that the three bishops whom the prince of the apostles is said to have employed at Rome as assistants, together with the twenty-five titular priests whom we saw established in the City by his command through Cletus, exactly equaled four complete groups of seven.

Therefore, if the image of the three patriarchal sees instituted by Peter had to be displayed in this Roman Church through three principal basilicas, and if the fourth throne, that of Jerusalem, having acquired a due sequence of honor by title in the Council of Nicaea, had expressed a type in the [Col. 0087A] fourth basilica through the care of Silvester, the number of priestly rotations could most suitably be completed by three bishops selected from the six bishops nearest the City, together with the twenty-five priests corresponding exactly to the original total.

A similar honor was later conferred in the Constantinopolitan synod upon the bishop of that see. It therefore required a fifth basilica to represent his image with the others, and likewise demanded a fifth group of seven for the performance of the sacred ministry there.

The fifth group of seven is found in the age of Damasus, when the titles had increased to twenty-eight, if the threefold number of the three nearest bishops is doubled and joined with the supreme hierarch, the head and prince of all.

Such a choir of bishops was rightly assigned only to the Lateran basilica, which represented the Roman see. The other basilicas, however, were assigned groups of seven priests, so that the dignity of the first see would be recognized as unequalled by the others even from the rank of the senior priests who celebrated the divine mysteries there, as compared with the junior priests who celebrated them in the other basilicas.

This division should therefore be referred either to the age of Silvester or to that of [Col. 0087B] Damasus, both because of the arguments given above and because, after the Council of Constantinople, providential care made it especially necessary to sketch through figures a system displaying the universal Church and the primacy of the Roman see above the others.

Any suspicion of contradiction therefore disappears when one admits a figure consisting of the three patriarchates possessing ancient jurisdiction and the two later additions possessing, by title alone, the sequence of honor conferred by general councils. Under Damasus this figure is to be joined with his constant rejection of the attempted invasion by the two sees seeking to usurp the rights of the three patriarchates. For in the arrangement of the figure, the privilege of Rome always stands out: Rome exercises primacy over all, contains the others within its office, and orders that the rights of the three sees established by Peter be preserved, while permitting the honorary title to be shared with others.

### Line 23.—“Here he established that they should sing psalms day and night [Col. 0087C] throughout the churches; he prescribed this for priests and bishops, or monasteries.”

The younger Pagius, no. 22, thinks that the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* falsely asserts this, as though he were claiming that Damasus was the first author of this institution. The two highly learned cardinals, Baronius and Bona, however, establish that the custom of singing psalms in the daytime and at night during the liturgy was already in force in the Eastern and Western Churches long before Damasus.

With due respect to that learned writer, I would think that nothing contrary to the antiquity and practice of nocturnal and diurnal psalmody—which rightly belongs to the very beginnings of the nascent Church—is being affirmed here by the Librarian. He appears instead to be speaking of the discipline established by Damasus in all the collegia of the urban clergy: that psalmody should be performed in fixed rotations, and that a definite rite should be employed in the daytime and nighttime prayers of the basilicas, titles, and monasteries.

Everything read in this item from line 14 to its end concerns the particular affairs of this Roman Church, [Col. 0087D] not general practices common to all the Churches of the world.

It therefore appears that Damasus divided the priestly rotations to be performed according to the Roman Order in all the sacred buildings within the City and in the bishopric of the City, whether situated in the suburban region—namely, in basilicas, titles, deaconries, monasteries, and cemeteries. Some rotations were performed by the bishops assisting him, others by priests, the urban clergy, and monks.

He also assigned each day certain psalms, verses, and antiphons for the nocturnal and diurnal liturgy, enlisting Jerome’s assistance in this care. Jerome transferred here some instructions drawn from the examples and traditions of the Church of Jerusalem, as we learn from book VII, letter 64 of Gregory the Great, a passage noted by the cited Cardinal Bona in *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 16.

If that same cardinal warns that blessed Gregory’s assertion must be understood cautiously, the caution required here is that the practices which Damasus, after consulting Jerome, restored or added to the ancient rites of the Roman Church must be [Col. 0088A] distinguished from other practices added or restored by Damasus, by his predecessors, or likewise by his successors. These latter practices were drawn from the new or ancient discipline of various apostolic Churches and seemed, by their usefulness and appropriateness, likely to be especially suitable for this Roman Church.

In this fourth century, when peace was restored to the faithful and public worship became possible, the vigilance of bishops, having acquired the freedom to act, did not cease to uphold in their own Churches the ancient customs properly introduced by apostolic men. They directed those customs according to definite rules that did not conflict with the common practice of the universal Church. The opportunity provided by general councils enabled them to learn that practice from their colleagues.

Thus, just as Athanasius in Egypt, Basil in the East, and John Chrysostom were organizing their customs for liturgical use in their own bishoprics and dioceses, so blessed Damasus wished to prescribe in this Roman [Col. 0088B] bishopric a definite order, especially one to be maintained in psalmody. According to the assertion of this *Liber Pontificalis*, he assigned bishops, priests, and the monks from the monasteries then increasing in number at Rome to sing and attend properly to the divine praises in the Roman basilicas and titles throughout the day and during the nocturnal vigils.

It naturally followed that, once peace had been restored to the Church and the magnificence of the emperors increased the number, size, and adornment of the sacred buildings, the religion and concern of so many prelates should also provide for the order, number, rotations, and offices of the ministers, as well as for the definite rites by which the divine duties were to be discharged.

The manner in which, especially under Damasus, the number of basilicas and titles was completed so that it might correspond most suitably to a division into sevenfold rotations adapted to the mystery of universality was explained shortly above.

Truly, however, what Damasus chiefly accomplished in organizing psalmody (the subject of this section) was the correction of copies of the sacred text of Scripture, undertaken through Jerome by collating the Italian version with the Greek of the Seventy translators, as Jerome himself testified in the later preface to the Psalter, when some years afterward he prepared another version from the Hebrew source at the urging of Paula and Eustochium. For he spent nearly the final three years of Damasus’s life in Rome (that is, from the year 382 to the end of 383), as he himself relates in Letter 99 to Asella. During that time he both restored the Italian version from the Septuagint and, at Damasus’s urging, contributed many other things toward the provision of divine worship.

Marianus Victorius gathered these matters together in his Life of Jerome, prefixed to the Roman edition of the works of the same holy doctor, in these words:

> “He not only arranged all these things while remaining in Rome, and ensured that all the duties of the Church were performed honorably and devoutly; he also took care that whatever good practice existed either at Antioch, from which Peter, chief of the apostles, had come to Rome, or at Jerusalem, where that same apostle had also founded a church and afterward left it to James to govern, should likewise be observed at Rome, where Peter’s see remains. At his insistence, as Saint Gregory testifies, the Alleluia began to be sung at Rome according to the custom of the Church of Jerusalem; and, following the usage of Antioch, ‘Glory be to the Father’ began to be sung at the end of all the psalms. Through his correction, Rome adopted the psalms of the Seventy translators for reading and singing in the church. At the request of Damasus, he was the first to correct from the Greek the New Testament that the Roman Church thereafter always read. He was also the first, as Cassiodorus, Usuard, and Ado testify, to gather together briefly the accounts of the martyrs’ deaths that are recited in the churches.”

Thus far Marianus concerning Jerome.

In this provision and ordering of psalmody, and in the selection of sacred rites, a common praise belongs to Damasus and Jerome. It was the vigilant care of the pontiff both to entrust these matters to Jerome and to adapt them, along with many other things, to the daily use of the Roman clergy. These practices were brought together from apostolic churches everywhere by the most holy bishops whom Damasus summoned to the City, or by guests whom he received.

When I consider that Peter of Alexandria, while Damasus was seated in the Roman see, was not merely present with him in the City but also attended the third of the councils held at Rome by Damasus; that Paulinus of Antioch was likewise received by him as a guest together with Jerome; and that many other such lights of the distinguished churches of the world shone before both groups of clergy and monks and gave them laws—I mean Eusebius of Vercelli, Hilary of Poitiers, and Epiphanius, bishops of Salamis—there can be no doubt about Damasus’s zeal, asserted by the Librarian, in establishing many practices from the rite and discipline of the ancients that constitute no small part of the Roman order, later enriched by his successors, especially Leo, Gelasius, and Gregory the Great.

The same conclusion is suggested by Damasus’s particular care both to provide, through the most experienced presbyters of the Roman Church, for the discipline that was to be devoutly maintained in the remaining provinces, and to imitate the examples of individual bishops in cultivating studies directed toward and promoting the worship of God.

The first point is evident from his selection of the presbyter Simplicianus, sent from the Roman title over which he presided to Ambrose, who had been made bishop of Milan while still a catechumen, so that Simplicianus might assist him as a kind of director and teacher in pastoral care. Augustine testifies that he experienced such guidance with his own eyes, in Book VIII, chapter 2, of the *Confessions*, cited by Baronius under the year 375.

The second point is clearly gathered from the surviving minor works of Damasus, compared with the books of the holy bishops and writers of the same age. In that century Nazianzenus expressed in verse the mysteries of the faith and the deeds of the saints, so that among Christians the study of literature might be nourished—something Julian was trying to destroy by his murderous edicts. Damasus too expressed such matters in verse.

At that time hymns were being composed throughout the Eastern Church by Ephrem the Syrian; in Egypt by Synesius; and in the West by Paulinus of Nola, Hilary of Poitiers, and Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Saint Basil the Great was then organizing both the liturgy for clergy and priests and a rule of prayer and life for monasteries. John Chrysostom was likewise reducing his liturgical rites to written form.

He assigned particular psalms to night offices and to funeral processions for the dead, and hymn melodies for dawn. He established sacred stations in the churches; in monasteries he appointed choirs of angelic ranks; and in convents of virgins he appointed groups of women imitating Mary, completing the task set by the Davidic Psalter and adding to it the praises of their own song. He writes this explicitly in Homily VI *On Repentance*, cited by the cardinal Thomasius of venerable memory in his preface to the Psalter.

Damasus certainly did not neglect these laws and studies when he distributed the priestly offices throughout the City, whose basilicas had been increased by those he founded, and when he employed the presbyter Jerome to introduce the customs of monastic life to Roman men and women—indeed, to distinguished men and women—who were inflamed with zeal for Christian perfection. Before their eyes stood splendid models in the many most holy Egyptian, Palestinian, Syrian, Greek, and Latin fathers whom Damasus repeatedly summoned to celebrate councils in the City.

Thus it came about that the heavenly ardor which had begun under Damasus did not cool under his immediate successors, Siricius, Anastasius, and Innocent. The clergy of the City, learned men, and noble virgins and matrons of both sexes received the books of both Testaments, corrected according to genuine copies at Damasus’s command, explained in Jerome’s words, and confirmed by the conduct of Jerome himself, Paulinus, Hilary, Eusebius, and Epiphanius. That same heavenly ardor impelled the holy women Paula and Eustochium, descendants of the Gracchi and offspring of the Scipios, together with countless other groups of noble men and women who had undertaken the beginnings of a more holy life at Rome under that pastor, to profess that life at Jerusalem.

### [Col. 0090A]

We must therefore attribute to Damasus’s pastoral care not the original institution of the singing of psalms—for this had always flourished in the Christian Church from its foundation, having been commended by the Lord and Master of all to his disciples—nor the original formation of the doxological verse “Glory be to the Father,” which had already long been found in explicit form. Rather, we must attribute to him that division and distribution, according to fixed turns, of the daily and nightly task of such divine praises, individually assigned on the basis of earlier custom and thereafter to be sung from corrected books, together with a selection of hymns, verses, and collects. Damasus prescribed these things to bishops, presbyters, clergy, and the monasteries then increasing in the West, according to the testimony of this *Pontifical Book*—a testimony strongly supported by the customs and history of that same age.

### Line 27

“He was buried on the Ardeatine Way in his own basilica. He rested there until he was transferred to another basilica of his title within the City. This occurred before Saint Adrian I renewed the roof of that same basilica, as we read below, no. 324. He is preserved there beneath the high altar, in the altar of the confession, or hypogeum, his sacred head having been granted to the Vatican Basilica, where it is venerated in the sacristy among the selected relics.”

### [Note: Col. 0090B]

#### Line 2

“And with him Ursicinus was ordained amid dispute.”

In the same year Ursicinus was acclaimed pontiff during the schism. The dissension that had begun under Liberius and Felix, within the Roman clergy, through Felix’s substitution—although Liberius had tried to settle it by receiving into the clergy and uniting with the others those who had been ordained by Felix—had spread secretly and flared up again on the occasion of the new pontiff. While some tried to ordain a pontiff on Felix’s side and others on Liberius’s side, the conflict broke out anew.

### [Note: Col. 0090B]

Saint Damasus, a Spaniard, son of Antonius, succeeded Liberius after a vacancy of seven days in the see, as Anastasius says. He was ordained on the first day of October in the year 366, which was a Sunday. His election, however, was disturbed by Ursicinus, a Roman deacon who was elected in schism against Damasus, who had been elected by legitimate votes, as will shortly be explained.

### Line 3

“And a council of priests having been held.”

At the very beginning of his pontificate, before the end of the year 366, or at least at the beginning of the year 367, he held a synod at Rome against Ursicinus the antipope and against Valens and Ursacius, together with other heretics already condemned. Its synodal letter was incorrectly included by the collectors of the councils among the acts of the Illyrian synod. Its inscription is in fact as follows:

> “To the most beloved brothers throughout Illyricum who retain the ancestral faith, the bishops of Italy send eternal salvation in the Lord.”

In it those bishops write that they are sending the rejection of the Council of Ariminum, and they add:

> “It is evident that the authors of the Arian or Aetian heresy, Valens and Ursacius, together with the rest of their associates, are not now what they have begun to reveal themselves to be in Illyricum, but that they were condemned long ago.”

This synodal letter was sent to the Illyrians because Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum had been bishops in Illyricum before their deposition.

Thus Saint Athanasius says in his letter to the Africans:

> “We give thanks both for his piety—that is, Damasus’s—and for that of the other bishops who were with him, because, after Ursacius and Valens with their associates had been expelled as sharing the same judgment, they preserved the concord of the Church.”

That the synod was a large one is inferred from the same letter of Athanasius. Before the words just quoted, it reads:

> “The writings of our beloved fellow minister Damasus, bishop of great Rome, and of so many bishops gathered with him, are sufficient.”

Moreover, that this synod was convened at the beginning of Damasus’s pontificate is proved by the fact that the author of the synodal memorandum writes that, as soon as Damasus had obtained the pontificate, he immediately convened a synod. Certainly Saint Hilary, who died in the year 367, cites its synodal letter among his fragments.

### Line 11

“He established a regulation concerning the Church.”

Damasus convened a second synod at Rome against Auxentius the Arian, who had intruded into the see of Milan, in the year 372. The synodal letter of this council, addressed to the bishops of Illyricum, is reported by Theodoret in Book II, chapter 22; Sozomen in Book VI, chapter 23; and Nicephorus in Book XI, chapter 31.

According to the imperial rescript, no fewer than ninety-three bishops attended this synod, as appears in the heading of the Roman synodal collection published by Holstenius. It dealt at length with the consubstantiality of the Holy Spirit with the Father, as can be read in the synodal letter mentioned above and in the fragments of Damasus’s letter appended to it in the same Roman collection and reproduced from it in volume II of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, page 893.

The heresy of the Macedonians was therefore first condemned in the West at this Roman council. For the claim made by some that it was first proscribed in the West by the fathers of the Illyrian council cannot stand, since it is clear that the Illyrian synod was assembled after it had received the synodal letter of this second Roman synod held under Damasus, as can be read in Baronius’s critical discussion.

This Macedonian heresy was later proscribed at the first ecumenical Council of Constantinople, discussed below. Its beginning was as follows. After Eusebius of Nicomedia, the usurper of the see of Constantinople, had died, Macedonius was ordained bishop of that church by the Arians in the year 342. But when he was deposed in 359 on account of many crimes, he founded a new heresy, asserting that the Holy Spirit was not a participant in the same honor as the Father and the Son, but was the minister of both—and a creature.

Consequently, not only at this council but also at the fourth Roman synod under Damasus, the consubstantiality of the Holy Spirit was discussed. At the latter council anathemas were pronounced against several heretics and specifically against the Macedonians:

> “We anathematize,” Damasus says in the letter he sent to Paulinus from this synod, “the Macedonians, who, coming from the stock of Arius, have not changed their perfidy, but only their name.”

And below:

> “If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a created thing, or was made through the Son, let him be anathema. … If anyone does not say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one divinity, power, majesty, might, glory, dominion, one kingdom, one will, and one truth, let him be anathema. … If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be adored by every creature, just as the Son and the Father are, let him be anathema.”

This second Roman synod, convened chiefly against Auxentius, appears to have been the result of a warning given to Pope Damasus by Saint Athanasius. After holding a synod in Egypt in the year 371, Athanasius wrote to Damasus, as is clear from Athanasius’s letter to the Africans. In it he says that he had written to Damasus against Auxentius, the intruder into the Church of Milan, and expressed his astonishment that Auxentius had not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church.

A third Roman synod was held by Damasus in the year 375. Peter, bishop of Alexandria and successor of Saint Athanasius, attended it. Sozomen, speaking in Book VI, chapter 25, about the two Apollinarii, father and son, says:

> “When Damasus, the first bishop of the city of Rome, and with him Peter, bishop of Alexandria, learned that this heresy—namely, that of the Apollinarists—was spreading more widely, they convened a council at Rome and decreed that it was alien to the Catholic Church.”

The anathemas against the Arians and other heretics found in a letter of Pope Damasus cited by Theodoret in Book V, chapter 11, are not to be referred to this synod, as Baronius believes. Nor is the letter of Damasus beginning “He who exhibits the reverence due to the apostolic see,” which is recited by the same Theodoret in Book V, chapter 10, a synodal letter of this council, as Baronius and others after him thought. It is instead a decretal letter of Damasus himself, written much later, as Valesius noted in his annotations on Theodoret.

Finally, the synodal memorandum concerning this third Roman synod says:

> “Peter, after he had been expelled from Alexandria, hastened to Rome. When he had been received, Pope Damasus convened a divine and holy synod at Rome. It branded that madman Apollinarius, together with his disciple Stephen—which should read Timothy, who was a disciple of Apollinaris—and the robber Lucius, with an anathema.”

From this it is also clear that the heresy of Apollinaris was first condemned in the West by Pope Damasus.

The principal error of Apollinaris was that he considered Christ’s human nature incomplete, that is, lacking a soul, whose place, he claimed, was taken in the body by the Word himself, who had become flesh.

Second, the Apollinarists asserted that Christ’s body was consubstantial with the divinity. From this it followed that the divinity of the Word was passible, and in fact that it had suffered torments and death.

Third, they asserted that the divine Word had not taken flesh from the Virgin but had brought it from heaven.

Fourth, they loudly proclaimed that the very substance of the Word had been changed into flesh.

Finally, Apollinaris also erred concerning the Trinity, devising certain degrees of dignity: great, greater, and greatest. Thus the Holy Spirit was called great, the Son greater, and the Father greatest.

Other ravings of Apollinaris may be read in Natalis Alexander’s account of the fourth century.

Damasus convened a fourth synod at Rome in the year 378, both against various heretics and against bishops belonging to the faction of Ursicinus the antipope. In a letter of Damasus reported by Theodoret in Book V, chapter 10, whether it is considered synodal or decretal, Damasus says:

> “Why have you again requested the deposition of Timothy, who here too, by the judgment of the apostolic see, in the presence also of Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, was deposed together with his teacher Apollinaris?”

It is therefore evident that Apollinaris and Timothy had already been condemned in the third Roman council in the year 375, and that this letter of Damasus must accordingly be referred to this fourth Roman council.

The anathemas against the Arians and other heretics are likewise to be referred to this synod. They occur in a letter sent by Damasus to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, while Paulinus was at Thessalonica, and are cited by Theodoret in Book V, chapter 11.

After recounting the death of the emperor Valens, which occurred on the ninth day of August in the year 378, the synodal memorandum states:

> “Gratian, the son”—namely, of Valentinian, of whom it had been speaking—“became emperor of the West and the East and recalled the devout bishops from exile. At that time the blessed Damasus also convened a sacred synod at Rome against the Arians, the Pneumatomachi, and many other heretics; and he sent to Paulinus at Thessalonica the exposition of the divine articles, which, by divine providence, accomplished the greatest things everywhere and persuaded all that the Trinity is consubstantial and to be adored.”

What we have said about the Macedonians in connection with Damasus’s second Roman synod must be referred to this Roman synod as well.

The fathers of this fourth synod wrote to the emperors Gratian and Valentinian concerning the condemnation of the schismatics and the faction of Ursicinus. Their letter is reported in volume II of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, together with the rescript of Gratian Augustus, issued to Aquilinus, the vicar of the City, in accordance with that letter.

Although Ursicinus had been banished to Gaul in the year 374 by the judgment of the emperor Valentinian, he and, following his example, certain bishops continued to occupy churches. Ignoring or driving away the duly appointed officials, many members of that faction retained their churches. The emperors therefore ordered that the sentences previously issued against the seditious be enforced.

This is an appropriate place to speak about the schism of Ursicinus.

## The Schism of Ursicinus against Saint Damasus

In the year 366, after the death of Pope Liberius, Ursicinus, a Roman deacon, disturbed the Roman Church by a criminal schism. He was ordained bishop against Damasus, who had been elected by legitimate votes, and he drew many members of the clergy and Roman people over to his side.

So violent a sedition arose that, if Ammianus Marcellinus in Book XXVII is to be trusted, 137 citizens were killed in a single day in the Basilica of Sicininus. When the schismatics were unable to overturn the legitimate election of the pontiff, they turned to calumny and accused the most holy man Damasus of adultery. Saint Jerome calls him “a virgin and teacher of the virgin Church” in Letter 50 to Pammachius, while the ancient writers of ecclesiastical history—Socrates, Theodoret, and Sozomen—praise his unimpeachable conduct.

### [Col. 0093B]

The Catholic emperors worked by their authority to extinguish the schism of Ursicinus. Praetextatus, prefect of the City, expelled him from Rome under Valentinian Augustus, as Ammianus, cited above, testifies. Praetextatus also received from that emperor a rescript ordering that the basilica occupied by the schismatics be restored to Damasus and that they themselves be expelled from the City.

Moreover, as was just stated, Valentinian, in order to provide for the peace of the Church, sent Ursicinus into exile in Gaul. He was recalled under the condition that neither he nor the supporters of the schism could set foot either in Rome or in the suburban regions.

After Valentinian’s death, Ursicinus again attempted to invade the Roman see. Bishops ordained during the schism, and deposed by the judgment of the Catholic bishops, retained the churches they had seized. Consequently Gratian Augustus expelled Ursicinus to Gaul and, at the request of the fathers of the fourth synod held at Rome under Damasus, restrained the insolence of the schismatics by a formal law, as is clear from the synodal letter of that council and from Gratian’s rescript, discussed above.

### Line 5

“And Damasus remained.”

The fathers of the Council of Aquileia, held in the year 381 under the presidency of Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, afterward petitioned the same emperor in a letter preserved in volume II of the Councils. They implored the emperors not to lend a ready ear to Ursicinus, who, after his condemnation, was attempting to reclaim the Roman see.

After Damasus’s death, however, Siricius was substituted in his place amid some disturbance instigated by Ursicinus, as we shall say there.

In any case, the author of the *Pontifical Book*, as Baronius himself admits, falsely writes that, after being expelled from Rome, Ursicinus was consecrated bishop of the Church of Naples. For the rescript issued by Gratian and Valentinian the Younger in the year 378 makes clear that Ursicinus was then suffering distant exile. Nor does Marcellinus, who supported his party, report this in the memorandum he presented to the emperor Theodosius, nor does any ancient writer.

## The First Council of Constantinople, the Second General Council

In the fifteenth year of Pope Damasus, the emperor Theodosius summoned the bishops of the East to Constantinople, chiefly against the heresy of Macedonius, without consulting Damasus. For this reason Damasus did not send legates to the council to preside over it in his name.

Accordingly, this council was not initially regarded as ecumenical in itself, but only afterward, when Damasus conferred that dignity and authority upon it by his consent. Although ecclesiastical rules forbid synods to be held and decrees to be enacted in the churches without the authority of the Roman pontiffs, they do not prohibit national synods, or even councils of the entire East, from being convened without that authority. Such councils are not ecumenical by virtue of having been summoned by emperors, patriarchs, or metropolitans; nevertheless, they acquire that authority if the assent of the Roman pontiff is added.

In the year 380 Damasus had announced a council at Rome to examine the case of Maximus the Cynic, who had invaded the throne of the Church of Constantinople. When the Eastern bishops declined to attend, the bishops of Italy, after the Council of Aquileia in the year 381, again asked the emperor Theodosius that a general synod of Eastern and Western bishops be assembled at Rome.

The Eastern bishops, summoned to it by Damasus, excused their delay at Constantinople on the grounds that the crises of their churches detained them in the East and prevented them from traveling to Rome, adding the pressure of limited time. Nevertheless, they acknowledged the authority of the Roman pontiff, by which he was lawfully summoning them to his council, as can be read in their synodal letter. This letter was issued by the Eastern bishops who had gathered again at Constantinople in the year 382, while the synod was being held at Rome. In it, through legates, they sent Damasus and the Western bishops a report of the matters conducted and decreed at the ecumenical council held in the year 381.

This synodal letter is reported by Theodoret in Book V, chapter 9.

Thus 150 Eastern bishops, presided over by Timothy of Alexandria, celebrated an ecumenical synod in May of the year 381. At it Maximus the Cynic, the intruder into the see of Constantinople, was deposed, and the see was confirmed to Saint Gregory Nazianzen. Gregory, however, resigned it for the sake of peace. In his place Nectarius, a man of senatorial rank who was still a catechumen, was appointed at the same council.

Second, the heresies of Macedonius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius were condemned, and a creed was issued against them by which the Nicene faith was more fully explained and confirmed. We have discussed the heresies of Macedonius and Apollinaris— the former in connection with the second Roman synod and the latter in connection with the third Roman synod under Damasus. Baronius’s account in volume IV of the *Annals* should be consulted for the blasphemies of Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus.

Finally, canons concerning the administration of the churches were issued. Seven Greek collectors transmit them. It is much more probable that only three were issued at this council, while the others were enacted at another Constantinopolitan synod at a different time and attributed to this council by those who composed the code of the Greek Church.

The third canon, concerning the second place of the bishop of Constantinople in the Church and the primacy of honor after the Roman see, is not spurious, as Baronius thought. All the ancient manuscripts and all the collections of the Middle Ages and later centuries contain it; moreover, Socrates in Book XII, chapter 13, testifies that it was enacted.

That the third canon did not conflict with the second, and indeed took nothing away from the rights of the Church of Alexandria, can be seen in Baronius’s critical discussion under the year 381. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the Roman Church did not receive this canon. This was explicitly demonstrated before Innocent III, who in canon 5 of the Fourth Lateran Council counted the see of Constantinople second among the patriarchal sees and assigned to it a dignity second only to that of Rome.

The council’s completion on the ninth day of July is inferred from the fact that the canons bear that date. Certainly, on the thirtieth day of the same month Theodosius issued Law 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Catholic Faith*, in which Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, is mentioned as having been ordained at the council. From this law, and from Law 8 of the same code, *On Heretics*, it is deduced that the council had already been concluded on that day.

Immediately after the council was held, the fathers requested its confirmation from the emperor Theodosius—not because they considered such confirmation necessary for an ecumenical council, but so that by this means they might bind the emperor to protect the faith, suppress heretics, and secure observance of the canons by his own laws as well.

As already stated, the fathers of the Constantinopolitan council held in the following year, 382, informed Pope Damasus by synodal letter of the matters decreed at the ecumenical synod. In Theodoret, Book V, chapter 9, it bears the inscription:

> “To our most beloved and most religious lords, brothers, and fellow ministers, Damasus, Ambrose, Britton, Valerian, Ascholius, Anemius, Basil, and the remaining holy bishops gathered in the great city of Rome,” and so forth.

In that letter the fathers request confirmation of the matters enacted at the ecumenical synod, whose report they were sending, when they say:

> “Since these matters have been established among us canonically and legitimately, we urge your Reverence also to rejoice in them, through the intervention of spiritual charity, and through fear of the Lord, which restrains every private affection and places the building up of the churches above personal goodwill and favor toward individuals.”

This synodal letter was sent to Damasus by three bishops: Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscianus. In it they explained why they had not come when summoned to Rome and sent the acts of the ecumenical synod held at Constantinople in the preceding year to the Roman pontiff for examination. These acts were confirmed by him. From that time onward they were always held in the highest veneration as having been approved by the apostolic see.

As for the Constantinopolitan Creed, as soon as it appeared it was substituted by all the Greek churches for the Nicene Creed, although its name was not changed. Thus all the later Constantinopolitan synods and fathers, whenever they speak of the Nicene Creed, commonly mean the Constantinopolitan Creed, yet they do not call it Constantinopolitan but Nicene.

Even today we call what we sing at the solemn celebration of Mass the Nicene Creed, although it is in fact the Constantinopolitan Creed, as Lupus observed in volume I of the Councils, chapter 4. He adds that the Church of the city of Rome preserved the ancient custom of reciting the Apostles’ Creed, since no heresy had originated there.

By the same right the African, Italian, Gallican, and all the Latin churches retained the Apostles’ Creed without addition, as is clear from Augustine, Chrysologus, and other Latin bishops, who are recorded as having delivered only this creed to catechumens.

Since, according to the testimony of Theodoret, Sozomen, and Socrates, the Arian heresy had never been able to cross the borders of Illyricum, there was no need among the Europeans for a new token of profession. The churches of Spain must nevertheless be excepted. Having been overrun and occupied by Goths, Arians, Vandals, and Suevi, they changed the Apostles’ Creed into the Nicene Creed, that is, the Constantinopolitan Creed, just as they changed the triple immersion of baptism into a single immersion.

This is clearly recorded in the Third Council of Toledo, held in the year 589, at which, on the advice of Reccared, king of Spain, it was decreed:

> “That throughout all the churches of Spain and Gaul the Creed of the Council of Constantinople be recited according to the form of the Eastern churches.”

Later, certain Gallican churches under Charlemagne imitated this practice. Others, however, and the royal chapel itself, did not dare to imitate them until they had obtained permission from Leo III. For the Roman Church had not yet adopted this same custom of singing under John VIII. Later, however, so that it would not differ from the churches of Spain and Gaul subject to it, which were unwilling to abandon the custom, it sang that creed during the solemn celebration of Mass.

Edmund Martene, in Book I, chapter 1, article 2, no. 10, of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, believes that after the First Council of Constantinople the Nicene Creed was delivered to catechumens before baptism. He proves this from the Council of Constantinople held under Menas in the year 536, where, in the fifth session, it reads:

> “For specifically the creed of the 318 holy fathers, in which we are baptized, was harmoniously confirmed by those three holy synods.”

But since, as has been said, the Constantinopolitan Creed was substituted for the Nicene Creed without a change of name, I suspect that in this and the other passages cited by Martene the reference is to the Constantinopolitan Creed, which is called Nicene because the Nicene faith was more fully explained and confirmed in it.

Martene himself therefore admits that in the commonly used Roman order, in the Gelasian order, in the Salzburg Pontifical, in the very ancient Rheims manuscript dating from 900, and in the first order of scrutiny in the Gellone Codex, the Constantinopolitan Creed, not the Nicene Creed, is identified.

Indeed, it seems more suitable that the Constantinopolitan Creed was delivered to catechumens so that they might be instructed concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which was not clearly expressed in the Nicene Creed but was clearly expressed in the Constantinopolitan Creed.

### [Col. 0096B]

The Constantinopolitan Creed is as follows:

> “We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.
>
> “And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages, God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father—that is, of the same substance as the Father—through whom all things were made.
>
> “For us human beings and for our salvation he came down from heaven; and he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became human. He was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried; and on the third day he rose again according to the Scriptures. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.
>
> “We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified, who spoke through the prophets.
>
> “And in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church.
>
> “We confess one baptism for the remission of sins.
>
> “We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.”

Pope Damasus, after enduring many labors for the Church, departed to God on the tenth day of December in the year 384, after having occupied the see for eighteen years, two months, and ten days.

Saint Jerome preserved the day of his death in the *Martyrology*. The expanded *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* preserved the years, months, and days of his tenure. The year of his death is inferred from the epitaph of his successor Siricius, reported by Baronius’s annotator, from which it is clear that Siricius attained the pontificate in the year 384.

Damasus held five ordinations in December, ordaining thirty-one presbyters and nine deacons. He consecrated sixty-two bishops in various places and was buried on the Ardeatine Way in his own basilica. He erected many basilicas of the martyrs, adorned the tombs of many of them with verse, and composed an epitaph for himself.

He is counted among the saints, renowned for miracles, and among ecclesiastical writers.

He had Saint Jerome of Stridon as his assistant in composing letters and in ecclesiastical affairs; at his command, Jerome likewise rendered the New Testament into conformity with the Greek text. Jerome writes of him in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, possessed an elegant talent for composing verse; he published many brief works in heroic meter, and died nearly eighty years old under the emperor Theodosius.” His works were collected by Martius Milesius Sarazanius. But Letter VIII, said to have been written to Stephen, archbishop of the Council of Mauritania, and to all the bishops of the African province, is spurious, as its subscription shows: “Given under the consulship of Flavius and Stilicho, eminent men, for the fifth time.” For Flavius Stilicho is the same man who held the consulship in the year 400, with Aurelian as colleague, and again in 405, with Anthemius. Moreover, the letter is prefaced: “Damasus, servant of the servants of God, and by his grace bishop of the holy Church of the city of Rome”; yet before Gregory I the Roman pontiffs did not call themselves “servants of the servants of God” in their letters. [Col. 0097A]

The *Book of the Pontiffs*, or *Pontifical*, inserted in the volumes of the Councils, is likewise wrongly attributed to Damasus, as scholars generally agree. Nor should Jerome’s letter to Damasus, or Damasus’s letter to Jerome, be counted among Damasus’s works, as Schelestratius shows in the second part of *Illustrated Antiquity*. As for the catalogue of the ancient pontiffs, which we used down to Liberius, where it ends, and which we have called the *Chronicle of Damasus*, Baronius correctly recognized that it was not Damasus’s work, just as he correctly recognized the falsity of what is read about it in the *Book of the Pontiffs*: namely, that Damasus established that psalms should be sung in churches day and night, as though he had been the first author of that sacred practice. [Col. 0097B] For, as Cardinal Bona proves in chapter 16 of *On Divine Psalmody*, Saint Ambrose instituted this alternating manner through antiphons in the Western Church, and Damasus confirmed it by apostolic decree. On this matter more may be read in Bona himself, where, on page 458, he also says that what Gregory the Great writes in Book VII, Letter 64, as cited by Baronius, must be understood cautiously: namely, that Pope Damasus received from the teaching of Saint Jerome the practice that, in imitation of the Church of Jerusalem, the Alleluia should be sung in Rome. For, Bona says, the Alleluia did not begin to be sung in the Roman Church at that time; rather, since it had previously been sung only during the Paschal season, it was then decreed that it should also be used outside that season.

In the same place, on page 447, Bona further says that many otherwise highly credible teachers attribute to Pope Damasus the rule concerning the singing of the doxology, “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning,” and so forth, at the end of the psalms; they claim that he issued a decree on this matter at the urging of Saint Jerome. But they were misled [Col. 0097C] by Jerome’s letter to Damasus, which, as we have just said, is adulterated. The Second Council of Vaison, or Vasio, held under Felix IV in 529, decreed in canon 5 that in the Church, after “Glory,” one should say “as it was in the beginning,” against those who blasphemously claim that the Son of God began to exist at a particular time. Nor was Damasus the author of the decree concerning the divine Scriptures and the works of the holy Fathers received in the Catholic Church—that is, the decree concerning books to be received and not received—even though, through a scribal error, that decree bears Damasus’s name in the collection of Cresconius; for many of the authors of the works mentioned there lived and wrote after Damasus. More on this matter may be found under Gelasius.

[Note: [Col. 0097C]

Line 2.—“Ursicinus is ordained amid contention,” etc.; line 11: “He was accused of plots,” etc.

We consider it necessary to pursue the sequence of this history exactly, so that the mouths of the enemies of the Roman See may be closed—those who seek an opportunity from it to impress upon people’s minds a false idea concerning the authority of that See. [Col. 0097D]

It has never rightly been open to doubt that Damasus’s election to the supreme pontificate was entirely legitimate and properly conducted. Saint Jerome, who was then living in Rome and studying rhetoric when Damasus was elected, writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 369: “Damasus is ordained thirty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church.” Rufinus, a contemporary of those times, says in Book II, chapter 10 of his *History*: “After Liberius, Damasus received the priesthood in the city of Rome by succession.” All the ancient histories agree about this event. In Socrates, Book IV, chapter 24, we read: “Damasus succeeded Liberius in the administration of the Roman episcopate.” Theodoret, Book V, chapter 2, says: “This Damasus was bishop of Rome, the successor of Liberius in the administration of that Church; a man truly distinguished by the adornments of an exemplary life, who continually defended apostolic doctrine.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 22, records: “After Liberius died, Damasus assumed the see of the Church of Rome. In this election Ursacius the deacon was his competitor; when he was passed over in the voting, he bore it with an embittered spirit.” [Col. 0098A]

This Ursinus, called Ursinus by Rufinus and Ursicinus by Marcellinus, “unable to endure Damasus’s being preferred to him, burst into such a frenzy that, after persuading a certain bishop who was quite inexperienced and rustic—namely Paul of Tibur—he gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men in the basilica called Sicininus and extorted his own ordination as bishop, in defiance of law, order, and tradition.” Rufinus, *History*, Book II, chapter 10.

This schismatic ordination provoked serious disturbances and considerable bloodshed in the City. To avert them, the Roman magistrates, having no doubt about Damasus’s legal right, compelled the antipope to go into exile: “When Ursicinus and his followers had been driven out,” says Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, “a profound peace, already desired by the Roman citizens, was beginning to grow in a manner most suitable to the circumstances.” Yet the followers of his faction attempted to prevent that peace from lasting. Having found patrons at the court of the emperor Valentinian for their petitions, they obtained permission to return on condition that they would suffer heavier penalties if they caused new disturbances. When they were found to be recklessly inclined toward the same movements, they were again banished to Gaul; and the seditious associates were deprived of the only church that had remained for their assemblies. Marcellinus, although a pagan author, reports that the magistrate then governing Rome, the likewise pagan Praetextatus, gave just and truthful support to the cause of Damasus by expelling Ursicinus. [Col. 0098B]

Meanwhile Damasus, exercising his pontifical authority to abolish the schism, issued a sentence of condemnation against its author and his accomplices in the crime. He removed them from communion with the faithful, and in the council that he held at Rome in the third year of his pontificate, for the deposition of Auxentius of Milan, he did not cease to repeat against them the sentence previously issued. It is precisely these decrees of the Apostolic See that the emperor Valentinian mentions when writing to Ampelius, prefect of the City, and Maximinus, *vicarius* of the Venerable Prefecture, concerning the schismatics in question.

To facilitate execution, Valentinian had established by ecclesiastical law that the cases of other bishops were to be judged by the Roman pontiff, since cases of faith, as well as matters of ecclesiastical government, belonged to men of that order—so that priests should judge priests. See Saint Ambrose, Letter XIII, to Valentinian; also Baronius under the year 386, Letter XXXI of Saint Ambrose; and the *Collection of Councils*, volume II, under the year 378.

After Valentinian’s death, the restless ingenuity of Ursicinus and his followers devised new plots against Damasus, employing calumnies. When they realized that nothing could easily be brought forward against either his doctrine or his allegedly mismanaged administration, they spread a false rumor about his private life. But when the calumnies were quickly exposed, Ursicinus, who had long been banished to Gaul, was confined more strictly at Cologne Agrippina within a narrower place of retreat; and Isaac was shut away in a remote corner of Spain under the title of condemnation. Thus the emperors Gratian and Valentinian state in their rescript to Aquilinus, *vicarius* of the prefecture.

Damasus, however, sufficiently secure in the testimony of his conscience, could have been content to despise the accusers’ futile attempt, or could have safeguarded his public reputation merely by declaring his innocence, as we read that his successors did more than once. Instead, he preferred to prove his innocence in a council and in the presence of the emperor’s entourage. It is very important here to demonstrate that this action of Damasus in no way prejudiced the unshaken rights of the supreme priesthood of the Roman See, which inviolably maintains that on earth it is judged by no one.

[Col. 0099A] There is no need to seek elsewhere a demonstration of this claim, since ample evidence is supplied by the Roman council of Damasus itself, of which we are speaking. That council, we say, rightly issued a testimony rather than a decree concerning the integrity and heroic virtues of the holy pontiff. Evidence is also supplied by the rescript of the emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, addressed to the *vicarius* and to the prefects of the praetorian prefecture of Gaul and Italy (see Baronius under the year 381), ordering them, by exercising their authority, not to fail to uphold firmly the sentences pronounced by the judgment of the Roman bishop and to carry them exactly into due execution.

The council of which we are speaking—at which Damasus’s innocence was fully examined and publicly celebrated against the calumnies of the schismatics—sent a synodal letter to the emperor. After first offering thanks to that prince for having asserted in his laws as well the authority of the Roman pontiff to judge other bishops, they complained of Ursicinus and of certain bishops deposed by Damasus who, following the example of their leader, were fostering schism in the Church. [Col. 0099B] They assert that the plans and deceptions of such lost schismatics were directed toward this end: “that, while the man who had been appointed judge over all was himself pleading his case, there might be no one to judge those who had fallen or those factious invaders of the episcopate.” (*Synodal Letter of the Roman Council to Gratian.*)

They make it clear that, in this state of affairs, the pontiff had wished of his own accord “to submit himself to the more severe judgments of priests” . . . so that “the holy man,” they say, “desired rather to contribute to your piety than to serve himself, and not to detract from anyone but to add honor to the emperors.” They add that Damasus wished to follow the example of his predecessor, Pope Sylvester, “who, accused by sacrilegious men before your ancestor Constantine, pursued his own case.”

In their reply, the emperors condemn the lazy, inert, and negligent conduct of the magistrates, as well as the indolence of judges who patiently permit religion “which we rightly venerate,” they say, “to be disturbed,” and they attribute the cause of such tumults and evils to this negligence. Then they add concerning the schismatics: “Hence those persecutors of the most holy See, after the man of most holy mind had been examined and found—by the divine will alone, which would have been enough, and also by judicial inquiry—to be innocent, and after this had likewise been confirmed to the divine father Valentinian, did not shrink from disturbing Bishop Damasus with the most disgraceful calumnies. When they despaired of being able to strike him, they disturb the people for whom he is a hostage before the Divinity.”
