They therefore order that the factious men who were disturbing the peace of the cities be expelled by those authorities and kept one hundred miles from the city of Rome. “Whoever, moreover, has been condemned by the judgment of Damasus, etc., and whoever, having been summoned to priestly judgment, has failed to appear through contumacy, shall be sent by the illustrious prefects to episcopal judgment, whether by the proconsuls or by the *vicarii*, so that he may reach the city of Rome under escort, etc.; or, if he himself is a metropolitan, he shall necessarily proceed without delay to Rome or to those whom the Roman bishop has appointed as judges . . . But if the integrity of a metropolitan bishop or of any priest is suspected, or if favoritism is suspected, it shall be permitted to appeal to the Roman bishop or to a council summoned from fifteen neighboring bishops—provided that, after the inquiry has been held, what has been decided is not overturned.”

In this way, therefore, the emperors, by a solemn declaration and an express law, recognized the right vested in the Roman pontiff to judge bishops and to receive appeals to his Apostolic See. The universal Church had previously recognized this right openly and authoritatively at the Synod of Sardica.

**Line 11.—“He established a decree concerning the Church.”**

A kind of fatal contagion had infected the principal Churches of the East so thoroughly that the sees of Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople were suffering from schism at the same time that the Roman Church in the West was likewise being disturbed.

[Col. 0100A] The schism of the Church of Antioch had arisen while Liberius was seated at Rome. For the Arian bishop Eudoxius, preferring the patriarchal see of Constantinople—which he had seized, and which was endowed with a richer patrimony—to the see of Antioch (see Socrates, Book I, chapter 34), had his faction’s followers establish Meletius, formerly bishop of Sebaste and then bishop of Beroea, upon the Antiochene throne. “For they thought,” says Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 27, “that because of his reputation and esteem he would in the future draw not only the inhabitants of Antioch but also the neighboring cities, and especially the former Eustathians—who held the same doctrine about God as the Council of Nicaea had transmitted—entirely over to his sect.” Rufinus adds, *History*, Book I, chapter 24, that Meletius’s translation was contrary to the laws of the sacred canons.

When the Arians realized that their expectation had been frustrated—for Meletius had explicitly professed that he stood for the Nicene faith—they induced the emperor Constantius to send him into exile and to substitute for him [Col. 0100B] Euzoius, an open Arian and one of Arius’s principal disciples. The ancient Catholic community at Antioch, which had steadfastly preserved the faith in the consubstantial, and which was called Eustathian, was not moved by Meletius’s declaration. They refused to recognize him as bishop and to communicate with those who adhered to him, “for two reasons,” says Socrates in the passage cited: “first, because Meletius himself had been chosen for the priestly office by the votes of the Arians; and second, because his followers had received the washing of baptism from them.”

Lucifer of Cagliari found the Church of Antioch in this condition when, after the death of the emperor Constantius, he visited it, as we mentioned above in the notes on Liberius. He hoped that the two Catholic groups, the Eustathians and the Meletians, could be reconciled and brought together into one assembly, “if such a bishop were chosen,” writes Rufinus, Book I, chapter 27, “as would be welcomed by not one people only, but by both. Therefore, in excessive haste, he installed as bishop a Catholic and holy man, in every respect worthy of the priesthood, Paulinus.” But the Meletians refused to accept him, so that the schism continued for many years, with both parties proceeding to new elections whenever their respective leaders died.

Saint Basil informed Pope Damasus of these disturbances. At the same time, in Letter 52 to Blessed Athanasius, he wrote as follows: “It seemed to me appropriate that a letter should be written to the bishop of Rome, so that he might consider what is happening here and express his judgment. And since it is difficult for some people to be sent from there by a common and synodal decree, let him himself, using his authority in this matter, choose men capable indeed of bearing the hardships of the journey, but also suitably equipped for this task, so that by gentleness and good judgment they may correct those among us who are distorted and crooked, carefully and prudently adapting their speech, and carrying with them everything that was done at Rimini, in order to rescind what was there carried out by force and violence.”

In his letter to Damasus, no. 220, whom he calls “most revered Father,” he explains the vastness of the regions shaken by these disturbances and the remedy to be expected from the Roman See. “Whatever,” he says, “extends from Egypt as far as Illyricum is struck by a violent storm and the agitation of the waves . . . We certainly think that the sole remedy for these evils is the visitation and solicitude of your mercy . . . We have descended to this point, that through our letters we might provide ourselves with a little consolation, if you, finally aroused by our situation, would undertake our care and send here some men of the same confession as ourselves—men able either to reconcile the parties at variance with one another or to restore the Churches of God to friendship and unity, or at least to expose publicly those who were the causes of this upheaval. In every other respect, it should be clear to all of you with whom you ought ultimately to enter into communion.”

[Col. 0101A] Saint Jerome, living in that province, was being urgently pressed to join openly the party of Paulinus, or of Meletius, or of a certain Vitalis, whom Apollinaris—the covert heretic of whom we shall have to speak below—had caused to be chosen as a third bishop by certain Catholics separated from the Meletian group. Saint Jerome, I say, writing to Blessed Damasus, expresses himself as follows in Letter 57: “Following no one as first except Christ, I am joined in communion to Your Beatitude, that is, to the chair of Peter; I know that the Church is built upon that rock. Whoever eats the Lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the flood reigns . . . Nor can I, with so many regions lying between us, continually seek the holiness of the holy Lord from Your Holiness. Therefore here I follow your Egyptian confessors, and beneath the cargo ships I conceal myself in a little boat. I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius; I am ignorant of Paulinus. Whoever does not gather with you scatters; that is, whoever is not of Christ is of Antichrist . . . Deign to send me a written reply, and at the same time tell me with whom at Antioch I ought to communicate.” And in Letter 58: “From this quarter the Arian madness of the world, supported by false defenses, rages; from that quarter the Church, split into three parts, hastens to drag me to itself . . . Meanwhile I cry out: If anyone is joined to the chair of Peter, he is mine. Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus claim to adhere to you. I could believe it if only one asserted this. But now either two are lying, or all of them . . . Therefore I implore Your Beatitude, by the cross of the Lord, etc., to tell me in your letter with whom in Syria I ought to communicate.”

Damasus preferred Paulinus, calling him the bishop of Antioch in his letters. For Paulinus’s faith was not yet suspect to the Roman Church; the faith of his competitors, however, was open to suspicion.

Saint Basil, chiefly devoted to Meletius, unsuccessfully arranged for his letters to be carried to the magistrates of Antioch and to others, asserting that falsehoods were being circulated against Meletius in the West; and he appealed to Athanasius that the Antiochene see be entrusted to Paulinus by Roman judgment. After Meletius’s death, Flavianus was appointed as his successor in vain, contrary to the agreement signed by Paulinus and Meletius that, when either of them died, the survivor should hold the Antiochene chair, and contrary to the support of Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, who was indignant at the Easterners’ inclination toward schism (*Carmen* 1). At the council held by Pope Damasus at Rome, he decreed that Paulinus should be maintained in possession of the dignity he had assumed. He also sent him a synodal letter, whereas he never sent one to Flavianus and did not recognize the titles conferred upon him by his supporters. “Indeed, the Roman pontiff regarded the bishops who had ordained him as excommunicated, and many Western priests shared his view,” says Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 11. See Letters 10, 272, 321, 325, and 349 of Saint Basil.

After the death of Saint Athanasius, the Alexandrian Church [Col. 0101D] was afflicted by schism more cruelly than the Church of Antioch. Peter had been elected and had been received by unanimous agreement both of the clergy and of the magistrates and people. He had written to Damasus about his election, and from Damasus he received, through a deacon of the Roman Church, letters of consolation and communion (according to Theodoret, Book IV, chapter 20). The Arians, who had at last permitted Saint Athanasius to complete in peace, in his own see, so many years of persecution, could not tolerate Peter’s succession, especially since Athanasius himself had previously designated him. They expelled him by armed force and installed in his place a certain Lucius, whom they had earlier ordained for this purpose. Peter withdrew to Rome as to an honorable and secure asylum against the fury of the emperor Valens and his ministers, who, together with Lucius the pseudo-bishop, were inflicting every kind of cruelty upon the Alexandrian Catholics. After the persecution had subsided, “Peter returned from Rome to Alexandria with a letter from Damasus, bishop of Rome; this letter,” says Socrates, Book IV, chapter 30, “confirmed both the faith of the Homoousians and Peter’s appointment.” The people, therefore, trusting in that letter, expelled Lucius and installed Peter in his place.

At approximately the same time, the Church of Constantinople, which had been groaning for nearly forty years under the tyranny of the Arians who had seized that see, was visited by Saint Gregory of Nazianzus. The few Catholics who remained in the imperial city, supported by the protection of orthodox bishops living in the surrounding region, had brought him there. Impelled by the earnest prayers and persuasion of both groups, and above all by the divine Spirit, he cultivated that field of the Lord for two or three years with happy success, as Gregory the priest recounts in his *Life*, without assuming the episcopate. Meanwhile a certain Maximus the Cynic, having gathered clients around himself and having won the favor of the holy Gregory by an appearance of exceptional integrity—which the crafty hypocrite merely pretended—insinuated himself so successfully [Col. 0102B] that he was ordained bishop by stealth. He had drawn several bishops over to his side, including Peter of Alexandria. Nazianzenus alludes to Peter’s denial followed by weeping and says of him in his oration against Maximus: “It happened that Peter also denied me; and perhaps he did not weep bitterly, in order to heal his sin.”

But when Damasus learned of this Cynic’s intrusion, he labored so diligently and persistently—with efforts attested by several of his letters that had not yet been lost in the time of Nicholas I—that Maximus was expelled from Constantinople. “After much effort had been expended by Pope Damasus concerning Maximus, as his letters to various persons indicate, Maximus was expelled from Constantinople.” Letter of Nicholas to the emperor Michael. The ecumenical synod subsequently held there (Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 2) declared that Maximus neither was nor had ever been a bishop. After it had first elected Saint Gregory to that same chair and then, when Gregory declined it, Nectarius, the Fathers of the council wrote to Damasus, who was at that time holding a council in the City, and begged him in their synodal letter to approve and graciously accept whatever had been done and decreed in accordance with the laws of the sacred canons. The emperor Theodosius likewise requested confirmation of that election from Damasus through his envoys, as Boniface I writes in his letter to the bishops of Illyricum: “The emperor Theodosius, of most merciful memory, did not consider the ordination of Nectarius valid, because it had not been within our jurisdiction. Therefore he sent courtiers from his own side together with bishops and formally requested that a document be regularly sent from the Roman See, one that would strengthen his priesthood.”

There were also schismatics elsewhere, in various provinces, who sent representatives to the City; indeed, they even attempted to establish at Rome bishops from among their own sectarians, acting as apes of the true and Catholic Church, whose summit of glory the chair of Peter not only illuminates but also strengthens. Such mimics were the Luciferians and the Donatists. Blessed Damasus moved every stone to restore these wandering sheep also to unity. Optatus of Milevis, writing against the latter, demonstrates from the novelty of their Church the falsity of an institution deprived of its foundation because it is not made firm in Peter; the unbroken succession of bishops from Peter’s chair displays the certain mark of the true Church of Christ. “Nor did Caecilianus depart from the chair of Peter or of Cyprian; rather, Majorinus departed from it, and you occupy a chair which had no origin before that Majorinus.” (Optatus of Milevis, Book I.)

In Book II he adds: “Among the endowments, the chair is the first. We must see who first sat there. In the city of Rome, the episcopal chair was first bestowed upon Peter, and in that one chair unity was to be preserved by all, so that the other apostles might each defend his own individual chair, and so that anyone who set up another against that single chair would already be a schismatic and a sinner. Peter sat first, and Linus succeeded him, etc.; Liberius was succeeded by Damasus, with whom the whole world agrees with us through the exchange of official letters in the one fellowship of communion. Yet you also claim to possess some portion in the city of Rome. It is a branch of your error, extended from falsehood and not from the root of truth.”

“In the other patriarchates as well, Damasus exercised these functions, conscious of the right attributed by Christ the Lord to the Roman See through the prince of the apostles—namely, that it should be the custodian of the divine faith. How greatly this axiom was celebrated under Damasus, both by the Fathers and by the princes, belongs to be explained here, so that the force of the concise narrative may be understood more clearly: ‘He established a decree concerning the Church,’ a phrase often employed by the Librarian both of Damasus and of his predecessors and successors. In chapter 16 of Book III, the lord archbishop Somier demonstrates that this same axiom prevailed under Damasus.”

After the death of Valens, while Gratian alone governed the reins of the Roman world, “he offered to God, the governor of all things, as it were the first fruits of the entire empire,” writes Theodoret, Book V, chapters 2 and 3. “For he composed a law by which he ordered both that the shepherds who had been expelled into exile should return and be restored to their flocks, and that the holy churches should be handed over to those who embraced communion with Damasus. This Damasus was bishop of Rome . . . And, in order that the law I have mentioned might have greater authority, he sent with it the commander Sapor. When Sapor arrived at Antioch and displayed Gratian’s law, Paulinus firmly affirmed that he stood on the side of Damasus. Apollinaris likewise affirmed this, while concealing the sickness of his error . . .” Theodoret, Book V, chapters 2 and 3.

Since the Antiochene Church was thus divided into three parts, Paulinus, Apollinaris, and Meletius, each at the head of his own party, professed to stand with Damasus. Paulinus vigorously defended his rights. Apollinaris, concealing his errors, fought no less fiercely for his own election. Flavianus, the client and supporter of Meletius, sought to establish the rights of the man under whose patronage he lived. He therefore argued that neither of Meletius’s adversaries or competitors enjoyed communion with the Roman pontiff, since they did not follow Damasus’s doctrine. Thus, in the passage cited, Theodoret has Flavianus ask Paulinus, in the hearing of the commander: “If you embrace the communion of Damasus, my friend, demonstrate clearly to us your agreement and kinship with his doctrine, and take possession of the churches, as the law commands.” Then he addresses Apollinaris: “I am amazed, my friend, that you not only wish so shamelessly to resist the truth, although you know with certainty that Damasus, a truly remarkable man, affirms that our complete nature was assumed by God the Word, but that you also teach the contrary opinion . . . Embrace the doctrine of Damasus and take possession of the holy churches.”

The matter came to this: once it had become clear that Paulinus and Meletius admitted no faith other than the Roman faith, while Apollinaris was far removed from it, Apollinaris was ordered to withdraw from all ministry in the Church of Antioch. For the sake of peace, however, the two orthodox men, Paulinus and Meletius, with the consent also of the emperor’s delegate, were permitted to preside over the portion of the flock that followed each of them separately. See Theodoret, chapters 3 and 4 of the same book.

Theodosius, whom Gratian had taken as his colleague in the empire, was no less zealous in displaying his devotion to sacred doctrine, whose guardian he knew the Roman See to be. He promulgated to the people of Constantinople the celebrated law found in the Theodosian Code, under the title “On the Catholic Faith,” Book II: “We wish all the peoples whom the empire of Our Clemency governs to live in the religion which the religious tradition, transmitted by the divine apostle Peter to the Romans, still declares to have been handed down by him; and which it is clear that Bishop Damasus follows, together with Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness—namely, that according to apostolic and evangelical doctrine we should believe one deity of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, under equal majesty and within the holy Trinity,” etc.

But lest anyone suppose that such laws, prescribed for the entire empire and received throughout the whole Church of Christ, concerned the individual person of Damasus separated from his pontifical character, or that they referred only to the privileges of the See that he occupied—lest, I say, anyone suppose this, witnesses of the highest authority and contemporaries of those times must be produced. They explicitly confirm that this right was inherent in the authority of that august See, so that believers might thereby be strengthened in the faith. These witnesses are Saints Jerome and Ambrose.

In Letter 57, Jerome writes as follows: “Since the ancient East, riven by the fury of its peoples, tears apart the Lord’s seamless tunic, woven from above, into fragments . . . so that it is difficult to discern where the sealed fountain and that enclosed garden may be, I have judged that I ought to consult the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth. From there I now seek food for my soul, from the place where I once received Christ’s garments,” etc. In Letter 58 he thus addresses Damasus, after first describing the dissensions in the East: “From this quarter the Arian madness of the world, supported by defenses, rages; from that quarter the Church, split into three parts, hastens to drag me to itself. The ancient authority of the monks dwelling around me rages against me. Meanwhile I cry out: If anyone is joined to the chair of Peter, he is mine . . . Tell me in your letter with whom in Syria I ought to communicate.”

The same Father’s advice to Demetrias is also well known, in Letter 8: “I have learned that poisonous nurseries still live and flourish in certain people. I think I ought to warn you in the devout affection of charity to hold the faith of Saint Innocent, who is the successor and son of the apostolic chair and of the aforesaid man; and not to accept a foreign doctrine, however wise and clever you may think yourself.”

No less famous is the statement he made in Book III against Rufinus: “Know that the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic mouth, does not admit such deceits; and even if an angel should announce something other than what was once preached, fortified by the authority of Paul it cannot be changed.”

Saint Ambrose, likewise a contemporary of Damasus, writes in his commentary on 1 Timothy, chapter 3: “Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house, whose ruler today is Damasus . . . There, necessarily, it must be called the house of God and truth.”

From this we readily grasp the judgment of so great a Father concerning the authority and character of the man whom he regards as the director and infallible arbiter of truth. These words declare the idea of the privileges of the See, not a particular effect of virtue arising from the man’s personal character. That Ambrose thought and felt this way most deeply concerning the privilege of the Roman See—that it should be the herald and guardian of faith and truth—we understand clearly also from what he said when he related that his brother, Blessed Satyrus, had been preserved from shipwreck and had reached the shore in a region frequented by schismatics. “He summoned the bishop to himself,” he says, “and asked him whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops, that is, with the Roman Church,” etc. (*On the Death of His Brother*, approximately halfway through). For Satyrus and Ambrose, therefore, it was one and the same thing to agree with the Catholic bishops and with the Roman Church.

Ambrose confirms these views when, in his synodal letter to Damasus, he calls him “the faithful guardian of the Lord’s flock, worthy for the Lord’s sheep to hear and follow . . . Let them believe the Creed of the Apostles, which the Roman Church has always preserved and keeps undefiled.” There too he calls the Roman pontiff “the Teacher of bishops and of councils.” “But why say more before the Master and Teacher?”—whose judgment they conform to: “Know that Jovinianus, Auxentius, and the others whom Your Holiness condemned have also been condemned among us according to your judgment.”

But concerning the judgment of heretics and causes exercised by Damasus with complete authority, and concerning the sentence of condemnation pronounced against them, let us now join together the distinguished evidence.

The synodical letter which Blessed Athanasius, together with ninety bishops of his patriarchate who were sitting with him in council, sent to the African bishops has preserved for us the memory of another synod, which Blessed Damasus celebrated at Rome at the beginning of his pontificate for the eradication of Arian perfidy. From this letter we learn that a great number of Fathers had assembled there, so that the truth of the faith concerning the consubstantial Word—handed down by the Lord himself to the apostles and solemnly professed by the Church through the apostles in the Council of Nicaea—might be firmly established. We are taught that the council took the greatest care to expose those who supported the indicated heresy and all who had fallen into it. Finally, from the same letter we understand that the decrees of Pope Damasus, issued in that council, were sufficient to confirm the faith of the Church.

“The writings of Damasus,” says Athanasius, together with the Egyptian synod in that synodical letter, “our beloved fellow-minister and bishop of great Rome, and of all the others assembled there in such number, are indeed sufficient. No less sufficient are the writings of the other councils, held partly in Gaul and partly in Italy, for establishing the faith that is in us, which Christ bestowed, the apostles preached, and the Fathers who had come from every part of our inhabited world to Nicaea handed down. The greatest care was taken on account of the Arians, so that those who had fallen into that heresy might rise again and its authors be detected” [Col. 0105B]. From this it is gathered that Damasus had written to Athanasius concerning the judgment he had pronounced against the Arians and concerning the deposition of Valens and Ursacius.

“We give thanks both for his piety and for the others who assembled at Rome, because, after Ursacius and Valens, together with their associates, had been expelled under the same sentence, they preserved the harmony of the Catholic Church.”

When the bishops of the Alexandrian patriarchate thanked Pope Damasus for what he had done on behalf of the Church, they brought him complaints against “Auxentius, the invader of the Church of Milan,” declaring that he was not only in communion with the Arian sect but was also guilty of many crimes, which he had committed together with Gregory, his associate in impiety; and they wondered why he had not yet been deposed and expelled from the Church. There.

When reports from the bishops of Gaul and Venetia were added to these complaints of the Egyptians, stating that this Auxentius and several others were not only infected with the Arian disease but had also forged a new heresy against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, Damasus immediately summoned a council at Rome, calling together bishops of different nations. Auxentius was condemned there. A sentence of excommunication was issued there against the enemies of the consubstantial and divine Spirit. It was declared there that no synod, however great the number of its bishops, could have a valid or authoritative sentence unless the consent of the Roman pontiff were added, whose judgment was to be awaited before all others.

“The number of bishops who had assembled together at Rimini ought not to have the force of a precedent, especially since that formula had been composed without the Roman bishop—whose judgment ought to have been awaited before all others—and without the others who agreed with him.”

Synodical letter of the Council of Rome to the Illyrian bishops, in Theodoret, book II, chapter 22, and in Sozomen, book VI, chapter 23.

We learn these things from the synodical letter of the Roman council under Damasus, which the Illyrian prelates afterward passed from hand to hand to the bishops of Asia, Phrygia, and the other provinces. In their memorandum they stated [Theodoret, book IV, chapter 8] that the same letter had been brought to them from Rome, which is the head of the empire, and that they were sending it to them with their colleague Egidius, so that they might learn whether their preaching was in fact of such a character or not.

The emperor Valentinian and his brother Valens, who had not yet been corrupted into following Arian impiety, added to it a law dictated in the form of a letter, ordering that the decrees issued in both councils, the Roman and the Gallican, should be received.

“But we do not think otherwise than the two councils: one of which has already been held at Rome, the other in Gaul.”

Letter of the emperor Valentinian to the Asian diocese, in the same Theodoret, book IV, chapter 7.

Saint Basil, both in his own name and in that of the other orthodox Eastern bishops, brought three leaders of the factions before the tribunal of the Western Church, as before that authority which alone could offer help in the danger threatened by these sectarians.

“We have no reason,” says the holy Doctor, “to expect help from anywhere else, unless the Lord sends healing through you, by whom he is sincerely worshiped. The wicked and shameless heresy of the Arians has plainly been cut off from the body of the Church and remains fixed in its own error; it harms us little, because its impiety is known to everyone. But those who, wearing sheep’s clothing, outwardly pretend to gentleness and calm, while inwardly they cruelly tear apart Christ’s flock—and who, because they proceed from our own fold, easily injure the simpler-minded—are those destructive men who cannot so easily be guarded against. We ask that through your diligence they be publicized and exposed to all the Churches of the East, so that either, entering the right path, they may be sincerely joined to us; or, if they persist in being perverse, may keep their pestilence to themselves alone, lest thereafter, through careless communion, they be able to infect those nearest to them.”

Saint Basil, Letter 74 [Col. 0106B].

The three leaders of the factions accused by Saint Basil were Eustathius of Sebaste, Paulinus of Antioch, and Apollinaris. Eustathius, who had been restored to the episcopate of Sebaste by the authority of Pope Liberius, had made a profession of faith at Rome, as we have said, but had fallen back into Arianism; indeed, he had embraced the heresy of those who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit. With the utmost shamelessness he dared to bring countercharges against Blessed Basil and to level a calumny against the faith of the great Doctor, as Basil testifies in Letter 74. But he quickly fell under divine vengeance and, by a just decree, suffered an unhappy end to his life.

Paulinus of Antioch was accused of having accepted the doctrine of Marcellus of Ancyra and of a heresy that confused the three divine Persons. Nevertheless, the fact that this accusation was held to be worthless at Rome did not prevent Paulinus from always being regarded by the Roman Church as the legitimate bishop of Antioch, while Meletius—whom Saint Basil tolerated—was excluded; nor did it prevent those whose faith was suspect from swearing, at the command of the Apostolic See, their profession of faith in the hands of Paulinus.

“Apollinaris also wrote certain things about the resurrection, composed in a fabulous—or rather Jewish—manner, in which he says that we shall return again to the worship prescribed by the Law … Then also concerning the incarnation …”

Saint Basil, Letters 74 and 77.

“To remove the mind from Christ’s incarnation, and to assert that he assumed flesh only together with a soul, but by no means a mind … Apollinaris of Laodicea was the author and defender of this teaching.”

Saint Epiphanius, Heresy 87. See Theodoret, book V, chapter 3.

Damasus condemned this heresy in a council held at Rome and deposed its author, Apollinaris, together with his disciple Timothy. When, after this judgment, the heresiarch and his followers pretended among Catholics that they were alien to that sentence and boasted that they were in communion with the Roman See, the Eastern bishops wrote to Damasus concerning the matter, asking him to condemn and depose such sectarians.

Vitalis in particular, whom Apollinaris had made bishop of his faction among the Antiochenes and who boasted that he shared in Roman communion, was reported to the most blessed Damasus. Saint Gregory of Nazianzus writes that, when he was accused in this way [Letter 2 to Cledonius], he was compelled to go to Rome and set forth his faith in writing. He did so in such a way that at first sight it appeared sound and orthodox, for the words had been attached in forms so carefully adapted to different interpretations that they could serve equally to conceal the errors of his sect and to express Catholic truth.

Damasus therefore replied to the Eastern bishops in the following sense, according to Theodoret, book V, chapter 10:

“Because your charity, most honored sons, accords the Apostolic See the respect that is its due, this is also a very great honor to yourselves. For although, since the holy Church in which the holy Apostle, seated there, taught us how to handle the helm of government that we have assumed, the first place is assigned to us, nevertheless we confess that we are far inferior to him in that degree of dignity … Know, brothers, that we long ago renounced that profane Timothy, the disciple of the heretic Apollinaris, together with his impious doctrine; and for this reason we believe that his remains will henceforth have no importance … Why, then, do you again ask me to renounce Timothy, who here also, by the judgment of the Apostolic See, in the presence of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was renounced together with his master Apollinaris?”

When, therefore, Damasus had received the profession of faith made by Vitalis, he issued no decision concerning his person. Instead, he sent him back with a letter to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, so that Paulinus might judge whether he was acting sincerely.

“I had sent you a written reply through my son Vitalis,” he says, according to Baronius, Annals, year 373, no. 5, “leaving everything to your will and judgment; and through the presbyter Petronius I briefly indicated that, at the moment of his departure, I had already been moved to some extent by his case. Therefore, lest any scruple remain with you, and lest your caution—if you wished perhaps to join him to the Church—be delayed in receiving approval, we have sent our profession of faith, not so much to you, who share communion in his faith, as to those who, by subscribing to it, may wish through you—that is, through us—to be joined to you, dearest brother. Therefore, if the aforesaid son of mine, Vitalis, and those who are with him, wish to join themselves to you, they must first subscribe to that exposition of the faith” [Col. 0107C].

The formula of faith sent by Damasus to Paulinus anathematizes those “who dare with profane mouth to say that the Holy Spirit was made through the Son”; it pronounces an anathema upon all “who do not freely proclaim that the Holy Spirit is one and the same with the Father and the Son both in essence and in power,” and so forth, according to Theodoret, book V, chapter 11.

This formula was like a touchstone by which heretics could be distinguished from Catholics. Vitalis, as well as the others, refused to subscribe to the formula. Thus his persistence in error was exposed at Rome, and he was struck with anathema together with men of the same sort, without regard to that earlier deceitful profession which they had presented in writing.

Blessed Damasus also made illustrious the zeal of his faith and the authority of his see against the heresiarch Priscillian and his followers.

Their heresy was a compendium, or combination, of the errors of the Manichaean and Gnostic sects. Saint Epiphanius seems to indicate its origin when he relates [Heresy 26, toward the end] that, while he was still in the vigor of youth in Egypt, certain infamous groups were brought to the attention of the bishops. When those who had assembled there attempted to outrage his chastity, they were expelled and dispersed by the vigilance of the bishops.

One of these criminals, named Marcus of Memphis, withdrew to Gaul and seduced many noblewomen, especially women attracted by the enticements of pleasure, with which he seasoned his doctrines. He also infected Spain, where, through a distinguished woman and a professor of rhetoric—who had been his first disciples—he gathered a powerful band of followers, over whom Priscillian, who gave the sect his name, was placed. See Saint Jerome, Commentary on Isaiah, chapter XLIV.

“According to the description of Sulpicius Severus, History, book II, he was of noble family, exceedingly rich, energetic, restless, eloquent, learned through extensive reading, and exceptionally ready in discussion and disputation. Fortunate indeed would he have been if he had not corrupted his excellent intellect through a perverse zeal. In him one could see many good qualities of mind and body: he could remain awake for long periods and endure hunger and thirst; he was by no means greedy for possessions and was extremely sparing in their use. Yet he was also exceedingly vain and more puffed up than was proper by his knowledge of profane matters; indeed, it was believed that he had practiced magical arts from adolescence.

“When he undertook his destructive teaching, he attracted many noblemen and even more common people into his society by his persuasive authority and his art of flattery. In addition, women desirous of novelties, unstable in faith, and gifted with a cunning mind for every matter flocked to him in crowds. For by displaying the appearance of humility in his speech and dress, he had inspired everyone with honor and respect for himself. Gradually the corruption of this perfidy spread through much of Spain; and certain bishops also became depraved, among them Instantius and Salvianus, who received Priscillian not only with agreement but under something like a conspiracy.

“When Hyginus, bishop of Córdoba, learned of this while living nearby, he reported it to Idacius, a priest of advanced age. But Idacius, attacking Instantius and his associates without restraint and beyond what was proper, added a kind of torch to the fire that was beginning, so that he exasperated the wicked rather than suppressing them. Accordingly, after many conflicts among them, some worthy of remembrance, a synod was assembled at Caesaraugusta; Aquitanian bishops were also present. The heretics, however, did not dare submit themselves to judgment. A sentence was therefore issued against them in their absence, and the bishops Instantius and Salvianus, as well as the laymen Helpidius and Priscillian, were condemned,” and so forth [Col. 0108B].

To strengthen his sect against the Council of Caesaraugusta, the sect appointed Priscillian, still a layman but the chief of all the evils, as a bishop. When the Catholic bishops had obtained from the emperor Gratian an edict expelling the heretics from the cities and provinces, Priscillian and his fellow bishops went to Rome “so that they might clear themselves before Damasus, who at that time was bishop of the city. But their route passed through inner Aquitania” [Sulpicius Severus, History, book II], “where, being received with great honor by the ignorant, they scattered the seeds of perfidy; and especially corrupted the people of Elusa, who at that time were truly good and devoted to religion, through wicked preachers,” and so forth [Col. 0108C].

Several ancient Fathers review their errors. See Saint Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 70; Saint Jerome, Against the Pelagians, addressed to Ctesiphon; Orosius, in Saint Augustine, Consultation on the Error of Priscillian; Saint Augustine, Against Lying; Saint Leo, Letter 93 to Turibius; and others.

Sulpicius continues at the place cited:

“When they reached Rome, wishing to clear themselves before Damasus, they were not even admitted to his presence. Returning to Milan, they found Ambrose equally opposed to them. Then they changed their plans. Since they had not deceived the two bishops—whose authority at that time was supreme—by bribing and soliciting them, they sought to extort from the emperor what they desired. Having corrupted Macedonius, then master of the offices, they secured a rescript ordering that, disregarding what had previously been decreed, the churches should be restored to them. Relying on this, Instantius and Priscillian returned to Spain,” and so forth [Col. 0108D].

As for Damasus, he steadfastly resisted both them and the new monster of heresy called Helvidius, which rose up against the counsel of evangelical virginity and, with horrible blasphemy, dared to direct against the ever-undefiled Virgin Mary that foul breath which struck the ears of the Catholic Church. He affirmed that, after Christ the Lord had been conceived through the operation of the divine Spirit and brought forth without injury to her virginity, she had children by Saint Joseph.

Against this infamous heretic, Blessed Jerome—who was then living at Rome—took up his pen and published a splendid book in defense of the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God. Jerome declares that Pope Damasus—an outstanding man, learned in the Scriptures, himself a virgin, and a teacher of the Church’s Virgin—found this work free from every reproach.

To these examples, therefore, of Damasus’ unshaken constancy against heretics and of his apostolic authority in asserting the doctrine of the Catholic Church and exercising ecclesiastical judgments, correspond the other demonstrations of the same pontifical authority that he gave in convoking the ecumenical Council of Constantinople. Some modern writers have boldly called these into question, but Archbishop D. Somier has vigorously asserted and confirmed them in book III, chapter 18, of his History of the Dogmas of the Holy See. We refrain from repeating more of them here in the notes to this number, which the excerpts already given sufficiently illuminate. In the same chapter you will find collected whatever may usefully clarify the ecclesiastical history of those regions concerning the apostolic vicars appointed by Damasus throughout Illyricum.]

[Col. 0071]

54

Damasus, a Spaniard by nation, son of Antonius, sat [Note: [Col. 0071] B, year 17, month 3, day 4. See Baronius, year of the Lord 367.] for eighteen years, two months, and ten days; and Ursicinus was ordained at the same time amid contention. After a council of priests had been held, they appointed Damasus, because the stronger and much larger multitude was on his side; and thus Damasus was appointed, while they expelled Ursicinus from the city and appointed him bishop of Naples. Damasus remained in the city of Rome as prelate in the Apostolic See. He lived during the time of Julian. [Note: [Col. 0071] B: under Valentinian, Valens, Valentinian the Younger, and Theodosius, from the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus to that of Ricimer and Clearchus.] [Col. 0073]

He built two basilicas, one beside the theater [Note: [Col. 0073] He dedicated it.] to Saint Lawrence, and another on the Via Ardeatina, where he rests in the catacombs. He also built a platonia, where the bodies of the apostles, that is, of blessed Peter and Paul, had lain, and adorned it with verses [Note: [Col. 0073] See Baronius, year 384, concerning the meaning of “platonia.”]. He sought out many bodies of holy martyrs, and decorated their [Note: [Col. 0073] C: shell-work and tombs.] shrines with verses. He issued a constitution concerning the Church. [Note: [Col. 0073] See Baronius, year 367.] He was maliciously accused and charged with adultery; and when a synod had been held, he was cleared by forty-four bishops, who also condemned Concordius and Callistus, the deacon accusers, and cast them out of the Church.

He established a title-church in the city of Rome, namely, the basilica which he himself had built, where he donated a silver paten weighing fifteen pounds [Note: [Col. 0073] C: twenty]; an embossed cup weighing ten pounds [Note: [Col. 0073] C: silver]; five silver ministerial chalices, each weighing three pounds; five silver crowns, each weighing eight pounds; a bronze, wax-coated hanging vessel weighing sixteen pounds; houses around the basilica yielding fifty-five solidi [Note: [Col. 0073] C: 355]; the Papirian estate in the territory of Ferentinum, with its adjoining ancient lands [Note: [Col. 0073] C: adjacent properties], yielding two hundred and twenty solidi and a tremissis [Note: [Col. 0073] 120 and a tremissis]; the Antonian estate in the territory of Cassinum, yielding one hundred and three solidi; and a bathhouse beside the title-church yielding twenty-seven solidi [Note: [Col. 0073] Baronius, at the cited place, denies this].

He established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches; this he enjoined upon priests and bishops, or monasteries. In one ordination at Rome during the month of December he ordained thirty-one priests, two deacons, and sixty-two bishops for various places. He was also buried on the Via Ardeatina in his own basilica, on the third day before the Ides of December, beside his mother and sister. The episcopate then remained vacant for thirty-one days.

XL. SAINT SIRICIUS. A.D. 385, THE TENTH YEAR OF VALENTINIAN, THE SEVENTH OF THEODOSIUS.

[Note: [Col. 0109C]

Line 10.—“Unless only by confinement in a monastery.” Since the heresy of the Manichaeans was not only exceedingly wicked but also obscene, Siricius judged that no lighter penalty should be imposed upon them than perpetual penance to be carried out in a monastery. From this two things follow: that monasteries existed before Siricius, and that perpetual penance was imposed for graver offenses; with this qualification, however, that provision for the journey was granted to those who were at the point of death.]

[Note: [Col. 0111A]

Line 2.—“He issued a constitution concerning the whole Church, or against heresies, and spread it throughout the whole world, so that it might be kept in the archive of every Church because of the opposition against all heresies.”

Siricius established that pontifical constitutions against heretics should be entered into the archives of all the Churches, so that they might be known to everyone. Pontifical constitutions and letters were preserved in the archive of the Roman Church.

Jerome, Against Rufinus, book II: “If you suspect that I fabricated the letter, why do you not seek it in the chartary of the Roman Church?”

Anastasius, in his account of Celestine: “He issued a constitution concerning the whole Church, which is preserved to this day in the archive of the Church.”

The same author, in his account of Leo: “Again the most blessed Archbishop Leo sent many letters concerning the faith, which are preserved to this day in the archive.”

The books of Gelasius against Eutyches and Nestorius were placed in the archive of the Church for safekeeping. Anastasius, in his Life of Gelasius: “He also wrote books against Eutyches and Nestorius, which are preserved to this day in the library and archive of the Church” [Col. 0111B].

Boniface II deposited in the archive of the Church the chirograph—that is, the written sentence of anathema—issued against Dioscorus the schismatic. Anastasius, in his Life of Boniface: “The Church archive enclosed that chirograph, as though condemning Dioscorus.”

The Roman synod held under Martin was placed in the archive of the Church. Anastasius, in his account of Martin: “That synod is preserved to this day in the archive.”

The same author, in his account of John V: “Their chirograph is kept in the archive of the Church.”

Line 4.—“He established that no presbyter should celebrate Mass throughout the week unless he received the consecrated [bread] designated by the local bishop, which is called fermentum.”

Siricius decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Mass before receiving from the bishop the fermentum, that is, blessed leavened bread. This is the fermentum which, by the institution of Melchiades, the bishop customarily sent through the Churches as a symbol of the Church’s communion.

A notable trace of the same rite is found in Innocent I, Letter to Decentius:

“As for the fermentum which we send on Sunday to the title-churches, you have wished to consult us unnecessarily, since all your Churches are situated within the city. Their presbyters, because on that day they cannot come together with you on account of the people entrusted to them, therefore receive from us, through the acolytes, the fermentum that we have prepared, so that they may not consider themselves especially separated from your communion on that day. I do not think that this should be done through the parishes, because the sacraments ought not to be carried over long distances, nor do we send them to the different cemeteries where presbyters have been established; rather, their presbyters possess the right and permission to prepare them.”

Formerly, in the Eastern Church, the Eucharist was sent to other Churches on the feast of Easter; the Council of Laodicea prohibited this in canon 14.

Line 9.—“He established that if anyone converted from the Manichaeans returned to the Church, he should in no way be admitted to communion, unless he were kept subject to confinement in a monastery for the days of his life.”

Siricius decreed that converted Manichaeans should not be admitted to holy communion except at the end of life, and that they should be thrust into monasteries for the sake of penance. Confinement in a monastery for the sake of penance was a familiar punishment for clerics: canon “If a bishop,” distinction 50; the final canon, distinction 55; canon “If any cleric,” and canon “It has been said,” distinction 81; canon “Clerics,” question 23, chapter 8.

Innocent I used the same punishment against the Cataphrygians. Anastasius, in his account of Innocent: “He found many Cataphrygians in the City, whom he relegated to exile and monasteries.”]

[Note: [Col. 0111D]

### Line 2.—

Here he established a provision concerning the whole Church, or against all heresies. These words, and their very expression, confirm the observations already made concerning the manner of explaining papal constitutions. Although their subjects are by no means individually specified, they nevertheless indicate published constitutions relating to the Churches and circulated as general decrees. Such was this provision of Siricius, which concerned all the Churches, and whose subject matter concerned all heresies.

The occasion on which it was issued must now be examined, so that this ecclesiastical observation may become more firmly established. In both the preceding and following events recorded in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, papal constitutions are frequently praised, while their subjects are usually omitted; these passages explain how such constitutions are to be understood. Accordingly, the provision of Siricius which is here said to have been circulated throughout the whole Church against all heresies must be understood as the one issued by Pope Siricius with the patronage of Theodosius, while the emperor was present at Rome in the year 388, in the fifth year of Siricius’s pontificate, when the emperor was celebrating his triumph over the defeated tyrant Maximus.

For it was customary for emperors to establish festivals on their quinquennial, decennial, and vicennial anniversaries and, just as they attracted and rewarded the people with largesses or similar solemnities, so too they proclaimed sacrifices for the prosperity of the empire and promoted more devout religious observances; they did the same on the occasion of triumphs. Hence persecutions against Christians were conducted on such days, as Diocletian did, as noted above. After Constantine embraced the Christian religion, and the emperors who followed him did likewise, they became accustomed to promote more diligent observance of the Christian religion and to grant privileges on those same days.

For when Constantine was celebrating his twentieth anniversary, which, according to Sozomen, fell on 25 July, he promoted the celebration of the Council of Nicaea in order to cleanse the Church of the stain of the Arians, and conducted the following proceedings with the bishops amid the very pomp of the festival:

> “When these things had been decreed by the council, it happened by chance that Constantine’s twentieth anniversary was being celebrated at the same time. For it is the custom of the Romans to celebrate a public festival every tenth year of each emperor. The emperor therefore, considering the occasion to be conveniently at hand, invited the bishops who had taken part in the synod to a banquet and honored them with appropriate gifts.”

Thus Constantius, at his fifth anniversary, wished the Eastern bishops to be summoned to Seleucia and the Western bishops to Ariminum, in order to settle the many disputes concerning the faith. He acted similarly at Antioch in 341 and at Sardica in 347.

Theodosius, however, on each of his victories considered nothing more important than to offer gifts to God, their giver and benefactor, through the more abundant promotion of religion, by issuing highly beneficial edicts either for the restoration of the Church or for the destruction of idolaters and heretics. In the year 380, after defeating the Alans, the Huns together with the Goths, and after being baptized at Thessalonica, he immediately issued a law against the heretics who, by possessing several churches in each city of the East, belonging to various sects, were provoking the greatest hatred against the Catholics.

He therefore decreed that in every city only the bishop who embraced the communion and faith of Damasus should reside, and that the churches should be taken away from the others:

> “We desire,” says the emperor in the law, “that all the peoples ruled by the moderation of our clemency should practice that religion which the religion established by the divine apostle Peter declares to have been handed down to the Romans and preserved until now.” … Following this law, we command that they embrace the name of Catholic Christians; but the others must bear the disgrace of the heretical name in their madness, and their assemblies must not receive the name of churches. They are to be punished first by divine vengeance and afterward by the penalty of our own action, which we shall undertake by heavenly judgment.”

Philostorgius, who was then living at Constantinople in the twentieth year of his life, describes the restoration of the Catholic bishops and churches and the expulsion of the heretics that followed the publication of this law. He writes:

> “The emperor Theodosius, having engaged the barbarians near Sirmium—for immediately after he assumed the empire necessity required him to depart thither—and having been victorious in war, proceeded magnificently from there to Constantinople. He entrusted the care of the churches to those who professed the *ὁμοούσιον* [*homoousion*, “of the same substance”]; but he expelled the Arians and Eunomians from the city, among whom was Demophilus,”

and so forth. The leading representatives of the heresies then spreading are listed, and are described as having been expelled from their seats and wandering elsewhere. This strengthens still further the earlier observation made concerning Damasus: that the same pontiff issued a doctrinal constitution on the occasion of another edict promulgated by Gratian.

And since the bishops of the Eastern Churches were present and followed the faith and communion of Damasus, Theodosius, in another law issued after the year 380, decreed that henceforth no bishop should be appointed in the Eastern provinces unless he were in communion with those bishops who professed the faith and communion of Damasus. For when Book 3 of the same title in the *Theodosian Code* had listed the bishops belonging to the Catholic communion, it added in their proper names:

> “But all who dissent in the faith of communion from those whose special mention has been made must be expelled from the churches as manifest heretics, and from this time forward they must in no way be permitted the authority or power to retain churches.”

Although the ecumenical Council of Constantinople, celebrated in 381, appeared to have provided for the Churches of the East, nevertheless, because those men were clamoring and seeking a new hearing, he permitted them, out of indulgence, to assemble. The leaders of the heresies came to Constantinople in 383, among them Eunomius, who published a more extensive exposition of his impiety. Valesius reports it in his notes on Socrates, p. 61, and Baluzius in his new collection of councils.

The gathering took place in June of that year. Socrates discusses it in Book V, chapter 10, and Sozomen in Book VII, chapter 12. When Theodosius recognized the treacherous purpose of their most obstinate minds, he issued another law in which he decreed that they should be restrained as follows:

> “All those whom the error of various sects disturbs—namely, Eunomians, Arians, Macedonians, Pneumatomachi, Manichaeans, Encratites, Apotactites, Saccophori, and Hydroparastatae—must not assemble in any circles, nor display private walls in imitation of churches; they must carry out nothing, either publicly or privately, that could oppose the Catholic ordinance.”

Another law was issued again in the year 384, so that from that time onward the efforts of the heretics who had torn the bosom of the Church from the year 319 to 383 were suppressed along with idolatry.

In response to the various formulas of faith that the heretics had presented at the gathering in Constantinople, it was therefore necessary for the Church, in its purity and catholicity, to respond and oppose suitable remedies to each of them, so as to uproot their impiety from its foundations. Meanwhile, the empress Justina was obstinately attached to the Arians and, out of hatred conceived against the Catholics, to the other sects as well.

But she was condemned in the year 388, the same year in which the emperor, with favorable success, won a glorious victory over the tyrant Maximus and immediately entered Rome to celebrate a triumph over his various enemies. It is credible that there Siricius was urged to undertake deliberation and issue a formula of faith against all heresies.

The fact that this was praised by the *Book of the Pontiffs* and was issued at that time, even if it has perhaps perished or remains concealed, is established by the sequence of events related above. The author of the *Miscellany* reports that Theodosius went to Rome after Maximus had been defeated and, after the war with Maximus, adds:

> “Then, therefore, the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, having completed the victory, came to Rome.”

Pacatus, in the panegyric delivered at Rome on the occasion of the triumph, gives a fuller account of Theodosius’s arrival in Rome and of his actions there. Rufinus, who was then alive, testifies that from that moment Theodosius devoted all his efforts to restoring the Catholic faith. After relating Maximus’s machinations against Gratian, Rufinus adds:

> “Theodosius was present, mindful of Gratian because of his loyalty to the empire, his goodness, and his benefactions; and, rising with all the strength of the East to avenge him, he avenged the righteous blood. Meanwhile, the impious mother of Valentinian had died, and he restored the Catholic faith, which she herself had violated, as well as the kingdom, after expelling the tyranny. Then, after he had entered Rome in a splendid triumph, he returned again to his own kingdoms.”

The most fitting and appropriate occasion had arrived for Siricius, while advancing Theodosius’s zeal, to issue a constitution against all heresies, aimed at completely uprooting the formulas of faith and the propositions advanced by the heretics in the Constantinopolitan gathering.

The appeal of the tyrant Maximus may also have moved Theodosius. Maximus, in his reply to Siricius, stated that he had resolved to eradicate heresies and put an end to dissensions. A letter survives in which Maximus announces this to Siricius:

> “We have received the letter of Your Holiness, which was most welcome to us and which plainly accorded both with the name of a priest and with the dignity of the most splendid City. As for the Catholic faith, concerning which you wished to consult Our Clemency, the greater and more particular experience I have of divinity in my own case, the more I confess that I must take care of it—since I ascended to imperial power immediately from that saving source, and since God has always shown himself my supporter in all my endeavors and successes, and may he deign to be its protector and guardian today and, as I hope, forever. … For the rest, we declare that our mind and will are directed toward this: that the Catholic faith, with every dissension removed, and with all priests in agreement and all serving God unanimously, should remain unharmed and inviolable.”

For if Siricius had promoted the eradication of heresies with Maximus in the preceding year, and the tyrant had made this promise, then when Theodosius, pious and victorious, was present at Rome in the following year, it is certain that Siricius both promoted this work and promulgated a constitution against all heresies. This is even more certain because, from the year 380 to 392, Theodosius issued so many laws and worked to enforce them in order to crush every effort of the heretics. He truly did so, and the faith flourished again most abundantly. At the same time, Siricius obtained from Theodosius the destruction of the temples of the idols at Rome, as Prosper reports in his *Chronicle* and as Saint Augustine records.

### Line 3.—“He disseminated it throughout the whole world.”

With the patronage of Theodosius, Siricius could have communicated this constitution to all the provinces, just as Damasus, while the leaders and protectors of heretical depravity were still alive, sent his *Tome* to the East, and it was signed by the bishops to whom it had been sent.

In such circumstances the Roman pontiffs were accustomed, because of their more powerful primacy and their care for all the Churches, to send encyclical letters declaring what ought to be believed and what ought to be rejected. Thus, according to Lerinensis, Stephen replied to the bishops in the controversy over rebaptism with the words that nothing new should be introduced, but that what had been handed down should be retained.

His successors, persevering in the same solicitude, as we shall explain in the appropriate places, sent throughout the provinces to the bishops a formula of faith, which that age called a *rule* or a *Tome*, together with the obligation that each recipient should communicate it to the nearest bishop.

That this practice was observed, among other places, in the Spanish council which some number as the First Council of Toledo, is clear from these words among its acts:

> “Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, at the command of Pope Leo of the City of Rome, to Balonius, bishop of Galicia.”

For the other rules of faith transmitted by the pontiffs, see the following notes.

### Same passage.—“So that they may be kept in the archive of every Church as a weapon against all heresies.”

From this ecclesiastical diligence, formerly maintained with religious care—that encyclical letters should be preserved in the archives of the Churches—I believe it happened that the compiler of these Lives omitted to record the subjects of the Constitutions, since those matters were preserved in the encyclical codices.

Conversely, the subscriptions of the bishops appended to a published constitution were sent to the apostolic see and stored in its archives. This is noted at the end of the Holstenian fragment concerning the *Tome* of Damasus signed by the Eastern bishops.

Regarding the preservation of apostolic constitutions, perhaps collected in some codex, and their communication—as concerning an established practice—Zosimus writes to Hesychius, bishop of Salona:

> “We are therefore surprised that the statutes of the apostolic see were not delivered to your diligence.”

Innocent I likewise requires the bishops to prove that these things had not been communicated. Writing to Exsuperius of Toulouse, he says:

> “For if it cannot be proved that, to certain persons, that ecclesiastical rule of life and discipline which was sent from Bishop Siricius to the provinces likewise reached them …”

I say that Innocent demands proof, since the apostolic see was extremely diligent in this matter. The same Innocent left testimony to this when he reminded Rufus of Thessalonica:

> “For we have made this will of ours sufficiently manifest, as was fitting, throughout each province.”

When the bishops had received this notification through the care of the metropolitans, the metropolitan was obliged to inform the pontiff of the subsequent obedience of the bishops. This is made clear by Innocent’s successor Boniface, who writes to the same Rufus:

> “You have said that you presented our letters to the notice of each of those to whom we had already written concerning the path they ought to guard. Many priests, mindful of the sacred traditions, have professed that they commend their due consent to these letters.”

He says that this obligation flows from sacred tradition. It is therefore clear why the observation made here is correct: that these papal constitutions were preserved in the archives of the Churches.

Such professions and subscriptions—whether of synodal or encyclical letters—preserved in the archives were a powerful proof of the truth. Thus, when the African bishops had condemned the Sirmian impiety by common agreement, Constantius, then most miserably deceived by the utterly corrupt bishops Ursacius and Valens—the earlier leaders of the impiety and authors of the entire Sirmian tragedy—endeavored to seize these subscriptions from the archives of the African churches.

Hilary mocks their tyrannical assault in his book *Against Constantius*:

> “For you have subjected the Eastern bishops to your will—not to will alone, but also to violence. You command that the subscriptions of the Africans, by which they had condemned the blasphemy of Ursacius and Valens, be returned to you. You threaten those who resist and finally send men to plunder them. What? Do you think that Christ judges only by a written document, and that God is moved by a little slip of paper to call a will to account?” Or that what was once written down and violently seized by you can be erased from the conscience of divine power?”

### Line 4.—“Here he decreed that no presbyter throughout the entire week should celebrate Mass unless he received the consecrated bread designated and identified by the bishop of the place.”

This constitution coincides with the provisions of Melchiades and Zepherinus. Siricius, however, appears to have extended the decree to the universal Church in view of the circumstances of the time.

Indeed, that this custom was practiced after Siricius is taught by the decretal letter of Innocent I cited above. There the pontiff responds to Decentius of Gubbio, who had asked whether the Eucharist should be sent to priests established outside the city in the parishes, just as it was sent to the presbyters of the city’s churches. He therefore clearly presupposes that this custom had been established throughout the Churches by a decree of Siricius.

This constitution must be considered particularly appropriate to the circumstances in which both East and West had been polluted by various crowds of heretics, and in which a Catholic bishop had been installed in each Church, while the heretical leaders had been expelled. Siricius wished the rectors of the remaining Churches, the presbyters, to be recognized as united with the Catholic bishop in one profession of faith and communion; he therefore ordered that they receive nothing except the Eucharist consecrated by the designated bishop, as though the other priests were to be recognized by this definite token of unity.

The word “designated” also seems to confirm this interpretation, meaning the Catholic bishop who, after the expulsion of the bishops of the various sects residing in the same city, alone had been designated, by the profession of the *Tome* of Damasus or Siricius, to occupy the see. Other codices show that the word “designated” belongs with “bishop,” since they omit the word “place.”

That this practice was observed among the other Churches is taught by the letter of Latinius Latinius, which Charles Macri published in his *Hierolexicon*. Siricius appears to have read of this special token of the Mass, since the clergy of the other sects assembled in the churches of the Catholics, but did not participate in the Eucharist.

Philostorgius had observed this. In recounting Arian practices, he asserts that they were accustomed to assemble with the Catholic congregation in the churches, but never to participate in the sacrifice. He writes:

> “Although the Arians differed in their opinions from those who proclaimed the *homoousion*, nevertheless they shared with them in prayers, hymns, discussions, and almost everything else, except the mystical sacrifice.”

That Siricius was speaking here about participation in the Eucharist is inferred from another decree of Siricius in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, which immediately follows. There the pontiff—or the *Book of the Pontiffs*—plainly speaks of the same Eucharistic participation, specifying to whom it should be given and to whom it should be denied:

> “Here, concerning the Manichaeans whom he sent into exile, he established that they should not share communion with the faithful, because, with their mouths polluted, they were not permitted to handle the body of the Lord.”

He could have carried this out with the assistance of Theodosius, whose stay at Rome was prolonged for three years. During that period he issued the law preserved under the same title in the *Theodosian Code*, which reads:

> “Those who hold the leadership of a savage doctrine—that is, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and readers—and those who attempt to stain Religion under the veil of the clergy, or who belong to any heresy or error, if they appear to come from their wicked assemblies, whether within the city or in the suburbs, must be expelled altogether.”

### Line 6.—“What is called the leaven.”

Nicetas, archbishop of Nicomedia, attempted from this passage and another passage concerning Melchiades to prove that, in the primitive Church, the matter of the Eucharist was leavened bread.

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg and ambassador of Lothair to John Comnenus, replied:

> “This constitution of the Roman pontiffs Melchiades and Siricius appears to be understood not of a leavened host, but rather of the *Eulogiae*, which are ordered to be distributed throughout the Churches every Sunday.”

Many follow Anselm’s interpretation, but they are mistaken. In the passages cited, consecrated bread is plainly mentioned; and Innocent I, who explained the constitution of Siricius, stated that it was not to be understood as a ceremonial distribution of the *Eulogiae*, but of consecrated bread. He gives the reason why the Eucharist should not be sent by the bishop to presbyters established in the parishes:

> “Because the sacraments are not to be carried far; nor do we send them through different cemeteries to presbyters who have been established there, but the presbyters possess the right and authority to consecrate them.”

Nor does the word “leaven” support the Greek error. The text does not say that the bread is leaven; rather, the consecrated bread of the bishop is called “leaven.” For, during the time of persecution, in order that the Eucharist might not be recognized, they referred to it as “leaven.” Hence the passage says “what is called leaven,” namely, among the faithful, who understood the Eucharist by that term.

### Notes on Lines 6 and 7.—

“Here, concerning the Manichaeans whom he had deported into exile,” and so forth.

The pontiff established these measures against the Manichaeans because they could scarcely be distinguished from Catholics. They held only secret assemblies and, by means of perjury and lies, claimed to be Catholics. After being convicted of heretical falsehood and perjury, they pretended to perform penance and outwardly condemned their own heresy, while inwardly continuing to be Manichaeans. In order not to be exposed, they attended Catholic churches and participated with Catholics in the sacred Eucharist.

They were therefore rightly and deservedly detected and punished with exile; or, if they performed penance, they were admitted to participation in the sacred Eucharist only at the end of life.

## Chronological Notes

Our papal chronology has now reached a firm foundation. Once the certain date of the death of Saint Damasus had been fixed as 11 December 384, an equally certain beginning of the reign of his successor Siricius is revealed by the latter’s decretal letter to Himerius of Tarragona, which everyone accepts as genuine. It is dated 11 February, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto—that is, in the common Christian year 385.

Since Siricius, in this letter, responds to a letter sent shortly before by Himerius to his predecessor Damasus, and begins his reply by referring to his recent succession, it is clear that the beginning of Siricius’s succession to the Roman see after the death of Damasus must be assigned to a date between the death of Damasus on 11 December 384 and 11 February 385, the date on which the letter was written.

The *Bibliothecarius* and the catalogues state that the see was vacant for thirty-one days after the death of Damasus. Siricius’s election to the Roman pontificate therefore fell on 12 January 385, which was a Sunday, suitable both for episcopal ordination and for enthronement (*ἐνθρονισμός*, *enthronismos*).

That the date should be attributed to the enthronement rather than to the ordination is suggested by ancient documents, confirmed both by the *Chronicle* of Prosper of Aquitaine, a contemporary of that age, in which the beginning of Siricius’s episcopate is assigned to the same consulship of Ricimer and Clearchus in which Damasus died, and by the *Chronicle* of Marcellinus Comes, in which it is recorded under the immediately preceding consuls, Merobaudes II and Saturninus, who belong to the year 383.

These two statements can be reconciled if we suppose that Siricius, while still a presbyter, was ordained bishop in the year 383, under the consulship of Merobaudes for the second time and Saturninus, to whose consulship Marcellinus assigns his episcopate. We may further suppose that in the following year, 384, the year in which Damasus died, under the consulship of Ricimer and Clearchus, Siricius acted as Damasus’s vicar and performed the pontifical functions. He may perhaps also have received ordination in December, when Damasus completed his mortal life so that he might enjoy immortality.

That the epoch of Siricius’s episcopate should indeed be referred to a full year before the death of Damasus—whether he was ordained to relieve the difficulties of that age, or to govern a Church near the City, from which he was summoned to Rome, just as others in that century are reported to have moved from one see to another when the needs of the Church required it—is demonstrated by comparison with the certain dates of the two immediately subsequent pontificates, those of Saint Anastasius and Saint Innocent. These dates are preserved in the surviving paintings from the Leonian cycle in the basilica of Saint Paul.

The comparison proceeds as follows.

1. The date of Saint Innocent’s death is made certain by establishing the indisputable beginning of the see of his successor Zosimus shortly before Easter of the year 417, under the consulship of Honorius Augustus XI and Constantius II. Easter was celebrated on 25 March; the burial of Innocent occurred on 12 March according to the oldest martyrologies; and the *Bibliothecarius* and the catalogues state that the see was vacant for twenty-one days after his death.

2. The letter of Paschasinus to Leo the Great concerning the date of Easter, published by Bucherius together with the canon of Victorius on p. 75, testifies as follows:

> “In the time of my lord Zosimus, of blessed memory, the predecessor of Your Apostolate, in the eleventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius, when it was being considered that Easter should not be kept on 22 April, it was celebrated on 25 March.”

That year was the common Christian year 417, and the same letter repeatedly affirms that Easter in that year was celebrated under Zosimus.

If Zosimus’s election and ordination are placed on Sunday, 11 March of that year, and if that pontiff began his office with acts of piety toward his predecessor by arranging his funeral on the following day, 12 March, until he was transferred to the cemetery of Ursus Pileatus on 28 July, according to the *Bibliothecarius* at the end of no. 58, then all the chronological dates asserted by Anastasius and recorded in the catalogues and paintings from Saint Siricius to Saint Innocent agree exactly.

They show that Siricius’s ordination to the episcopal office must be assigned, with the *Chronicle* of Marcellinus, to Sunday, 24 September 383, under the consuls Merobaudes and Saturninus, while his elevation to the Roman pontificate after the death of Damasus, with the see vacant for thirty-one days, must be aligned with Sunday, 12 January 385.

If, from the date established for Siricius’s episcopal ordination, 24 September 383, we count the fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty-five days expressed both in the paintings of Saint Paul and in nearly all the more important catalogues, as shown in the *Prolegomena*, Siricius’s life and pontificate conclude in the year 399, under the consuls Theodorus and Eutropius, on 19 September.

The see is said to have been vacant for twenty days after his death, according to the *Bibliothecarius* at the end of no. 55. The election and ordination of Anastasius, his successor, therefore fell on Sunday, 9 October of the same year, 399.

The papal chronology of Anastasius, as I shall show in the following section, is fixed at two years and twenty-five or twenty-six days. Saint Anastasius therefore died around 3 November 401. After his death, the *Bibliothecarius* counts twenty days during which the apostolic see was vacant. Accordingly, the election and ordination of Saint Innocent, his successor, is assigned to Sunday, 24 November of the same year.

Finally, the numbers fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty days, which are utterly clear in the last image of Saint Innocent—the image that closes the surviving Leonian series in the basilica of Saint Paul—are confirmed by the agreement of almost all the catalogues and codices, or at least of the principal ones, as shown in the *Prolegomena*. They show that the end of his pontificate and mortal life must be placed in the year 417, under the eleventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius, on 14 February.

Since, according to the *Bibliothecarius*, twenty-two days of vacancy followed before the election of Zosimus, his successor, we arrive at 9 March, which must be assigned to the election of Zosimus. He was ordained two days later, namely on Sunday, 11 March, Passion Sunday. Paschasinus, a contemporary of that time, affirms in his letter to Saint Leo the Great that Zosimus, already pontiff, celebrated Easter on 25 March.

On the day after his ordination, 12 March, Zosimus began his office with acts of piety toward his predecessor and arranged the earlier burial of Innocent. We find this burial recorded on that same day, 12 March, in the ancient martyrology of Florentinus and in the other sources cited above.

The sum of the period and the order of the dates may be set before the eyes more briefly as follows.
