This total of thirty-three years, five months, and fourteen days, calculated from the dates of these three pontificates as marked in the paintings and catalogues and from the vacancies of the see recorded by the *Bibliothecarius*, is separated by only two days from the exact reckoning of the period extending from the episcopal ordination of Siricius on 24 September 383 to the election of Zosimus on 9 March 417.

Those two days must be added to the vacancy of the see after the death of Innocent, so that the total becomes entirely exact. They may perhaps have been worn away through the deterioration of the manuscripts. Thus every source confirms the distribution of the period and the assignment of the dates in the order given.

That the end of this interval falls in the year 417 of the common Christian era, marked by the eleventh consulship of Honorius, is demonstrated by the letter of Paschasinus, which, as we have said, reports that Easter was celebrated on 25 March. The Sunday date and the positions of both heavenly lights support this conclusion.

There is also another chronological marker, publicly observable in the following year, namely 418, and mentioned by historians, which confirms the correctness of this chronology. In the official lists, after the consulship of Honorius XI and his colleague Constantius II, by whom the year 417 is marked, there follows the twelfth consulship of Honorius Augustus, held with Theodosius the Younger Augustus VIII, under indiction I, in the year 418.

Marcellinus assigns a solar eclipse to this indiction and consulship in his *Chronicle*. The so-called Sicilian chronicle agrees with Marcellinus and gives the date, as Idacius does, as 19 July. Astronomical tables show that on that day and in that year an eclipse of eleven and a half digits was visible at Rome, twenty-six minutes after midday, according to Petavius; and that an eclipse of twelve digits was visible at Reims at 1:20 before midday, according to Calvisius.

Since Marcellinus places the beginning of Zosimus under the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II, in indiction XV, it is clear that he aligns it with the year 417 of the Christian era. Paschasinus’s testimony likewise refers the Easter celebrated on 25 March to that same year.

Since both termini of the total period collected above and divided among the three pontiffs according to the years, months, and days assigned to each in the Leonian paintings and catalogues are shown by the certain chronological markers recorded by historians and chronologists, the total period lying between those same termini must likewise be judged to have been correctly distributed according to the division confirmed by equally strong evidence.

Now that the total period has been established, we must inquire into its parts, so that it may be demonstrated that each pontiff has rightly been assigned his proper portion of that threefold period. It is preferable to move backward from the endpoint of Innocent, demonstrated by so many documents, and to confirm by cumulative proofs each of the dates already established from the surviving numbers in the Leonian series.

Just as the end of the rule of Saint Innocent has been established from the beginning of the rule of his successor Zosimus, and the year of the Christian era and the consulship have been made certain by the movements of the heavenly lights observed in the solar eclipse, so the beginning of Innocent’s pontificate is confirmed by a similar observation.

Petavius noted in *De doctrina temporum*, Book II, chapter 50, from the *Fasti* and *Chronicle* of Idacius, another solar eclipse recorded under the consulship of Arcadius V and Honorius V, on 11 November, feria II (which he correctly emends by writing III). The astronomical tables show that on that same day, at Rome, an eclipse of ten and a half digits occurred at three in the morning. They demonstrate that it belongs to the year 402 of the Christian era.

In that same year, when Idacius’s *Chronicle* records the consuls, the brothers Arcadius and Honorius, both Augusti, together with the eclipse, it also records the beginning of Innocent’s pontificate. Prosper and Marcellinus likewise place the epoch of this pontificate under the same consuls, both because Innocent celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate under those consuls and because Marcellinus, proceeding by indictions that begin to be counted from the month of September, assigns the events to the year in which those consuls entered office and associates the preceding autumn months with them.

In any case, Innocent must be said to have sat in the chair of Peter for approximately forty days before the two Augusti brothers, Arcadius and Honorius, began their fifth consulship—that is, in the year 401 of the Christian era, on 24 November. Thus the complete total of his pontifical period is fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days, a figure confirmed both by the paintings of Saint Paul and by the other documents that we have already produced in Volume II of the *Prolegomena*, folio 107.

Having therefore established both limits of the consulships to which the pontificate of Innocent I was referred, we must now attempt to trace the certain evidence that leads back to the beginning of his predecessor, Anastasius.

The character of this beginning, together with the endpoint of Pope Siricius, who had died immediately before him, is preserved for us by the First Council of Toledo, dated by the Spanish Era 438. Pagius, under the year 400, no. 4, excuses Idacius for assigning the same event to Abraham’s year 2316 [Col. 0120B], or A.D. 399, as though he were contradicting the reliability of the Acts—unless he inconsistently reckoned his years sometimes from the Kalends of September and sometimes from the beginning of October. With due respect to so eminent a man, I would affirm that the year marked by Idacius, a contemporary of that period, is correctly reckoned according to the customary system of indictions from the Kalends of September and corresponds with the common Christian year A.D. 399. This is indicated by the Spanish Era 438 itself, reckoned from the year 4675 of the Julian Period, from the foundation of the City, according to our tables, 715, beginning with the Parilia of that year, as we demonstrated in volume II, in the Prolegomena, and in our chronology. There we place the consulship of the two Gemini and all the preceding consulships a full year earlier, on the basis of certain demonstrations of the chronology of the times, established by eclipses and other evidence.

The Acts of the Fathers in September, after the council had been held on the Kalends themselves, and on the third day before the Nones, the eighth day, and the third day before the Ides of that same month, in Spanish Era 438, must, I say, be referred to this very year of the common era, 399. For this is not contrary to the reliability of the Acts; indeed, it corresponds so precisely with the events [Col. 0120C] that the death of Pope Siricius, and the vacancy of the apostolic see that immediately followed those days, can be recognized as having occurred after those same September Ides. This is also expressly understood from the council’s letter, issued before the report from Toledo of the election of his successor had been received during the month of October.

For the copy of the definitive sentence appended to those Acts, which the Fathers issued shortly afterward, after mature consideration of the circumstances and after granting the accused time to come to their senses, indicates that Siricius was already dead, since it calls him “Siricius, pope of holy memory”; and it shows that news of his successor had not yet reached the council. For when the sentence prescribes the conditions for penitents to be restored to communion, it includes among them the requirement that the rescripts of the Roman pontiff be awaited, as well as the replies of Simplicianus, bishop of Milan and Ambrose’s successor both in the episcopate and in the papal delegation to investigate this case.

It names Simplicianus explicitly [Col. 0120D]; but because the Roman pontiff had not yet been elected when that sentence was written—or at least because the Fathers at Toledo had not yet been informed of the election following Siricius’s death—they could not name him in either place. Instead, the Fathers consistently indicate him by the same general formula: “the pope who is now in office.” The words of the sentence are:

> “Awaiting, in like manner, what the pope who is now in office, what Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and what the other priests of the churches may write in reply.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We decree, moreover, that before communion is restored to them by the pope or by Saint Simplicianus, they shall ordain neither bishops, nor presbyters, nor deacons.”

From these formulas, which do not indicate the pope’s name, it is known that the copy of the sentence was dictated after the earlier Acts of September, while the apostolic see was still vacant—that is, before news of Anastasius’s election had reached the Fathers during the autumn of the year 399. This is consistent with Spanish Era 438, correctly reckoned by Idacius [Col. 0121A], and corresponding to the year demonstrated in our Chronology.

Thus these matters also agree with the epoch of Pope Anastasius, recorded in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul and in the catalogues, which assign him two years and twenty-six days, reckoned from 9 October 399 to 3 November 401. As for the other deposition, at Ursus Pileatus, that work was undertaken at the appropriate time, together with the construction in the cemetery, in the following May, as the Librarian records.

The years, months, and days of these three pontiffs, therefore, as expressed in the Pauline paintings, will conform to the chronological evidence derived from eclipses and consulships, as well as to the public Acts of the councils, if they are arranged as follows.

## Historical Notes

### Line 1.—Saint Siricius

Saint Optatus of Milevis appended a continuous series of the Roman pontiffs, from blessed Peter the apostle to Siricius, in Book II, in these words:

> “Therefore there is one chair, which is first among the gifts. Peter sat first; Linus succeeded him; Clement succeeded Linus, and so forth. Liberius succeeded Julius; Damasus succeeded Liberius; Siricius succeeded Damasus—he who is today our associate.”

### Same line.—He sat for 15 years, 11 months, and 25 days

This is read distinctly in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, where the letters are entirely intact and clear in the case of this pontiff [Col. 0121D]. The four oldest catalogues of Italy, together with others published in the Prolegomena of volume II, fol. 106, agree with it.

When Grimaldus, the notary, came upon the nearly vanished colors in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Peter, which had been dispersed under Paul V—as is clear from his own words, quoted on fols. 72 and 74—although he was trying, merely as an example, to reproduce the epochs of six pontiffs, he found the traces of the letters so obliterated that he indicated the gaps of the others only by dots, while reproducing only Siricius’s years, months, and days. It is therefore not surprising that, in the eleven months, he saw only the upper half of the numeral ten in the letter for 10, and substituted a five for it; and that, in the expression of the days, he omitted the entirely lost letter for five after twenty.

For he wrote: “Siricius sat 15 years, 5 months, 20 days,” whereas from the complete inscription preserved in the Pauline basilica one can clearly read:

> “SIRICIUS SAT 15 YEARS, 11 MONTHS, 25 DAYS.”

These facts wonderfully confirm the innocent error of those visitors who hastily copied into their papal catalogues corrupted numerical examples, even though they consulted the autograph paintings of the Roman basilicas, where the true numbers had formerly been depicted but had almost been effaced by the long aging of the centuries, or obscured by dust to those looking up from the pavement, as well as by the lack of more vivid light, as I have already shown in its proper place [Col. 0122A].

### Line 2.—Here he established a constitution concerning the whole Church, or against all heresies

The oldest surviving decretal letter of a pontiff of the Roman see, and the one regarded by critics without controversy as genuine, is the letter of Pope Siricius written to Himerius of Tarragona. On this, consult both Pagius and the most illustrious Somier, archbishop of Caesarea, in his notes on this pontiff. I shall indicate the principal points of that letter, together with the passages in their Notes that individually elucidate those points.

Siricius, therefore, replying to the consultations sent from Spain to his predecessor Damasus, in order to provide the laws of ecclesiastical discipline that were to be observed, makes use of regulations already established by Damasus himself and by his other predecessors; but, wherever necessary, he adds to those ancient provisions his own safeguards, to be observed by all the churches. Thus this single letter of Siricius preserves for us both the memory and a considerable part of other letters issued by earlier pontiffs, which have perished through the ravages of time [Col. 0122B].

He also shows that similar general decrees had proceeded from Liberius, from which no one who did not wish to be separated by episcopal judgment from the body of Christ could lawfully depart. Before Liberius, he teaches, similar decrees had been established by his predecessors and by their predecessors, as circumstances and the necessities of safeguarding faith or discipline required, and had been transmitted to the provinces as papal laws to be observed by all.

See in Somier’s Notes the beginning of Siricius’s Decretal, where he teaches that it belongs to the inheritance of the Roman see that the authority to establish a rule to which all priests must obey—an authority handed down by the apostle Peter to his successors in that see, together with the care of the entire flock—should remain intact [Col. 0122C].

The care with which Siricius provided for the individual regions of the Christian world, or of the Church spread throughout East and West, while exercising his apostolic responsibilities in both, is clearly perceived in the Notes of Pagius and Somier. For what he contributed to Spain concerning discipline, see Pagius no. 11 and Somier, pp. 2–5. What he provided for Africa in matters of faith and discipline is treated by Pagius in nos. 3, 4, and 5; Somier continues from pp. 5–7. What he gave to the churches subject to the see of Milan for extinguishing the heresy of Jovinian, and what he ordered to be carried out in Illyricum, both in suppressing the errors of Bonosus anew and in establishing an apostolic vicariate there, should be sought in Pagius, nos. 6, 7, and 8, and in Somier, Book IV, chapter 3, p. 15.

What he further established for the provinces of the Antiochene throne, and for freeing the whole East from the schism and usurpation of Flavianus, can be found elegantly summarized in Pagius no. 12 and treated more fully in Somier, chapter 2; still more extensively in Baronius’s Annals; and in Florentinius’s Ancient Martyrology, under 26 November, fol. 1001. There the celebrated Florentinius proves that the holiness of this pontiff was also commended by blessed Jerome, and that the two holy men gave one another mutual testimonies of esteem—something that certain writers failed to understand.

As for the manuscripts distinguished by their antiquity in which Siricius’s decretal letters are read, see the codex numbered 800 in the monastery of the title of Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the City. Finally, what Siricius accomplished at Rome, whether for eradicating the remnants of pagan superstition or for asserting the dignity of the apostolic see, may be seen in Somier, chapter 3, pp. 18–21 [Col. 0122D].

### Line 5.—An example is given from the more distinguished cases

Finally, “the consecrated portion of the bishop,” etc., which is called the *fermentum* [Col. 0123A]. It is evident that by the name *fermentum*, both here and in the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, the most sacred sacrament of the Eucharist is meant.

For the same meaning in the aforementioned letter of Innocent, see Mabillon, *Musaei Italici*, volume II, p. 1, on the Roman Order, where he proves the antiquity of his book on the Roman Order from this very meaning of *fermentum*. How ancient this designation was can be gathered from what we presented in the preceding volume, under Melchiades, following Schelestratius on the discipline of the secret (*disciplina arcani*).

Above all, however, the venerable Cardinal Thomasius clearly explained the true meaning of the Eucharistic sacrament in this term *fermentum* in his Notes on the Ancient Book of Masses, chapter “Gospel,” no. 160.

There is also another meaning of the word *fermentum*, by which *eulogiae* are signified—that is, loaves not consecrated, although endowed with a blessing from the priests. On these matters, see Macer in his *Lexicon* and the authors whom he cites.

### Line 9.—He established that if anyone converted from the Manichaeans, etc.

Somier discusses the deceptive practices of the Manichaeans in feigning the Catholic religion, and Siricius’s vigilance in exposing and rejecting their deceptions, on p. 7 of volume II. They had long before adopted this false resemblance in their fasts under Melchiades; it was likewise necessary to provide means by which they could be distinguished from Catholics. See our Notes under Melchiades [Col. 0123B].

### Line 10.—Unless only by confinement in a monastery

Schelestratius aptly observes here the growth of monastic profession in the West during the pontificate of Siricius. In the East, however, although monasteries had begun to be founded and frequented much earlier, they did not cease during Siricius’s own age to provide vigorous assistance in the provinces where the faith of many was wavering and had to be rescued from the frauds of heretics.

The single community of Maronite monks, gathered during this period by the blessed abbot Maron on a hill of Syria purified from pagan superstitions between Apamea and Emesa, near the river Orontes, sent out so many colonies of ascetics educated there that they subsequently established numerous monasteries throughout the East. Thus, although the Catholic faith in those provinces was harassed over time by the followers of Macedonius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Jacobus, as well as by other heretics, it was preserved among them undefiled through the work of these Maronites. Among the Syrians, it became practically equivalent to say “Catholic” and “Maronite.”

On this matter, see Pagius, p. 120, no. 46, in the historical observations on the lives of the Roman pontiffs. Siricius therefore rightly established that those Manichaeans who had been recalled from error to the Catholic Church should provide perpetual assurance of constancy in the Catholic faith by being confined within monasteries. There they were to learn the discipline of a penitential life, in a place where the Catholic faith, strengthened by examples of every virtue, offered a pattern equipped with all the precepts and counsels of evangelical holiness [Col. 0123C].

### Line 16.—In the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way

That his relics were removed from there by Paschal I and deposited in the title-church of Saint Praxedes, together with the remains of the other holy pontiffs listed there, on 20 July, in the tenth indiction—that is, in the year of Christ 817—is shown by an ancient marble tablet affixed near the chapel of Saint Zeno in that same church. Baronius reproduced its funerary inscription [Col. 0123D].

### Note: [Col. 0123D]

#### Lines 6 and 7.—The Manichaeans whom he sent into exile, etc.

The Manichaeans are said to have had secret associations in the City, but to have been harassed and driven out everywhere both through the efforts of Pope Siricius and through the laws of the emperors.

#### Line 16.—He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way

All the lists have it so, although Bede places Siricius’s death on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

### Note: [Col. 0123D]

#### Line 2.—Here he established a constitution

At the very beginning of his pontificate, on the third day before the Ides of February in the year 385, he wrote that celebrated letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, in which he replied to the report sent to Damasus. It consists of fifteen chapters, by which ecclesiastical discipline was restored, and in which he required these decrees to be observed not only in the province of Tarragona but also in Carthaginensis, Baetica, Lusitania, and Gallaecia [Col. 0124A].

This is the first of the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs that scholars generally recognize as genuine, and the first that is found in the ancient collections of the Latin Church.

It is a constant and indisputable opinion among scholars that, in the first centuries of the Church, the sacrament of baptism was administered only on the solemnities of Easter and Pentecost. Since the Spaniards had added not only the day of Christ’s Nativity and Epiphany but also the feast days of the apostles and martyrs, Siricius, in the letter mentioned above to Himerius, relying not only on the authority of the apostolic see but also bringing forward the custom of all the churches, writes, moved by this matter, as follows [Col. 0124B]:

> “There follows the unacceptable and correctable confusion concerning the baptism of those who are to be baptized, according as each person has wished—something which, as we say with grief, is presumed by our fellow priests not through any reason grounded in authority, but by sheer rashness: namely, that innumerable peoples, as you report, receive the mystery of baptism indiscriminately and freely on the Nativity of Christ, or on his Manifestation, and likewise on the festivals of the apostles or martyrs. Yet this privilege is claimed for the Lord’s Pascha, together with Pentecost, both among us and among all the churches; and on these days alone during the year, when people gather for this purpose, it is fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be administered.”

This occurs in the second decree of that letter; on it, see also what will be said under Leo. As for the first decree, concerning the non-rebaptizing of Arians, see what was said under Liberius.

In the year 386, in the month of January [Col. 0124C], Siricius held a synod of eighty bishops at Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter. There survives a synodal letter addressed to the African bishops, issued at Rome in the council of eighty bishops, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after the consulship of Arcadius Augustus and Bauto, illustrious men and consuls.

By the nine chapters established by Pope Siricius in this synod, he attempted to restore ecclesiastical discipline, which had collapsed in Africa. First, provision was made concerning the Novatians and Montenses, so that those coming to the Church would be reconciled by the imposition of hands. By “Montenses” he means the Donatists, so called because at Rome they had first established their church on a hill. On this decree, see what was said under Liberius.

He further warned that priests and deacons who were married should not remain with their wives after they had been ordained. Pope Innocent mentions this decree in his letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse. The author of the *Baronian Criticism*, under the year 418, no. 66, says that at the fifth Council of Carthage, held in the year 398, when the matter of clerical incontinence was reported, the Fathers agreed that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should abstain from their wives according to earlier statutes—that is, according to the decisions of the preceding councils [Col. 0124D].

But because the incontinence of the African clergy was considerable, two letters of Siricius—one of which has not reached us—were reread at the Council of Zellum, convened in 418. In accordance with their prescription, several points of discipline were again decreed, a summary of which Ferrandus reported in his *Brief Summary of the Canons of the Roman Church*, chapter 60. On canon 9, in which Siricius exhorts presbyters to continence, see Marca, Book I of *On Concord*, chapter 8, and Schelestratius, Dissertation 3 on the African Church, chapter 12.

Papebrochius, in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt on the Catalogue of the Ancient Pontiffs*, suspects these two letters—to Himerius of Tarragona and to the African bishops—of being spurious. But the author of the *Baronian Criticism*, in the first volume, shows that there is no ground for doubting their authenticity. In the second volume he likewise establishes the authenticity of the later letter on the basis of Schelestratius and Natalis Alexander, against Quesnellus, who incorrectly believes both that letter and the Council of Zellum, at which it was read, to be forgeries [Col. 0125A].

### Line 3.—And scattered them throughout the whole world

Siricius certainly fought against the Manichaeans and the Priscillianists, who agreed with them on many points. Since he could not uproot all of them completely, especially at Rome, he obtained a law from Theodosius the Great by which they were to be suppressed through secular penalties; Baronius also conjectures this under the year 389, no. 64.

He also fought against Flavianus, the less legitimate occupant of the see of Antioch and disobedient to the synod, by sending repeated letters to the emperor and summoning the Council of Capua for this reason, as Baronius testifies in the same place, no. 68. Finally, he condemned Jovinianus, the Christian Epicurean, as well as Bonosus, bishop of Sardica, as has just been stated. Florentinius, already cited, will furnish more material against all the charges brought against Siricius.

After Siricius had labored greatly for the faith and for eradicating the remnants of paganism, having obtained from Theodosius the Great a law that the temples of idols in Rome should be destroyed—a measure carried out during his pontificate, as Prosper in his *Chronicle* and Augustine attest—he passed to God on 26 November [Col. 0125B].

### Line 4.—Against all heresies

In the year 382, the monk Jovinianus left the monastery at Milan, where for some time he had concealed himself under a Catholic name and monastic habit. Jerome excellently describes how loosely and impurely he lived in Book I Against Jovinianus, chapter 2. Jerome adds that this heresiarch held that virgins, widows, and married women possessed equal merit; that those reborn in full faith through baptism could not be overthrown by the devil; that abstinence from food had no merit; and that all who had preserved their baptism would receive one and the same reward in the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0125C].

According to Saint Augustine, in his book *On Heresies*, Jovinianus said that all sins were equal. From the same source we learn that he was driven to such impiety that he denied that the most holy God-bearer Mary remained a virgin in childbirth, claiming that she was violated in the manner of other women.

When he spread these errors at Rome, he drove several nuns—whose chastity had previously been beyond suspicion—into marriage. The senator Pammachius, son-in-law of Saint Paula, reported him to Pope Siricius, as is clear from Saint Jerome’s Letter 50, addressed to that same Pammachius, the most ardent defender of the Catholic faith.

Jovinianus was therefore condemned by Siricius and expelled from the Church in a Roman synod, as is evident from Siricius’s second letter to the Church of Milan. That letter was sent through the legates Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander, who were to secure the condemnation of that heresy and of the heretics at the council to be held at Milan.

Saint Ambrose received Siricius’s letter and the legates with honor and convened a council at Milan [Col. 0125D]. At that council, in accordance with Siricius’s judgment, Jovinianus and his followers were condemned, as is evident from the synodal letter of that council, which is read among the letters of Saint Ambrose. It is uncertain, however, whether Jovinianus was condemned at the council held at Milan in 390 or at another council.

Bonosus, bishop of Sardica, asserted that Christ was a mere man and recognized two sons in the Savior, one eternal and the other temporal. He further asserted that the Virgin God-bearer, after Christ’s birth, had other children. He was condemned by Anysius of Thessalonica and the other bishops of Illyricum, to whom the Council of Capua, held around the year 389, had entrusted the investigation of his case.

Pope Siricius also condemned his error, as is evident from his letter to Anysius and the other bishops established throughout Illyricum. Nevertheless, Marius Mercator, in his Dissertation on the Twelve Anathemas of Nestorius, writes that this heresiarch had already been condemned by Damasus. Garnerius, in his Notes on that dissertation, believes this should be understood to mean that Bonosus had been condemned by Damasus under the names of Marcellus and Photinus, whose heresy he had renewed. Those men had been proscribed in the Roman synod from which the profession of faith was sent to Paulinus of Antioch; we discussed that Roman synod, held in 378, under Damasus [Col. 0126A].

But although this is true, the heresy of Photinus had already been condemned in three councils under Julius—the councils of Milan, Rome, and Sirmium—before Damasus. If Marius Mercator had been referring to the heresy of Photinus, he would have said that Bonosus had been condemned beforehand not by Damasus but by Julius. Therefore Mercator was referring only to the heresy of Marcellus. In fact, the heresy of Marcellus, and consequently that of Bonosus, who renewed it, was condemned in that Roman Council under Damasus in these words, according to Theodoretus, Book V, chapter 11:

> “We anathematize those who assert two sons, one before the ages and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.”

Nevertheless, the Photinians were later called Bonosians, as is clear from Audentius, a Spanish bishop, who, as Gennadius reports in Book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14, wrote:

> “He wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, and especially, with particular intent, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosians,” etc. [Col. 0126B]

### Line 4.—That no presbyter should celebrate Masses, etc.

In the *Pontifical Book* concerning Siricius, we read:

> “He established that no presbyter throughout the entire week should celebrate Mass unless he received from the designated bishop of the place the consecrated portion, identified by the name *fermentum*.”

We discussed a decree issued by Pope Melchiades, from the same *Pontifical Book*, under that pontiff. It also concerns the *fermentum*, which Baronius, under the year 313, nos. 49 and following, thought should be understood as *eulogiae*, or blessed bread.

Now, however, scholars agree that both in those two decrees and in another decree, which we shall discuss under Innocent I, the subject is a custom of the primitive Church by which the bishop sent the sacraments to the presbyters of the city who could not be present at the Sunday sacrifice. Schelestratius noted this in his work on the discipline of the secret, chapter 7, article 5. See what was said under Melchiades and what will be said under Innocent, where the decrees of Melchiades and Siricius are explained more fully [Col. 0126C].

### Line 9.—That if anyone converted from the Manichaeans, etc.

The same author of the *Pontifical Book* records another decree issued by Siricius in these terms:

> “He established that if anyone converted from the Manichaeans returned to the Church, he should in no way be admitted to communion unless he were held bound only by confinement in a monastery for the days of his life, so that, weakened by fasts and prayers and tested under every examination, they might remain so until the final day of their passing; and, out of the Church’s humanity, Viaticum might be granted to them.”

On these words Schelestratius, in Part I of *Illustrated Antiquity*, p. 463, says:

> “Since the heresy of the Manichaeans was not only exceedingly depraved but also obscene, Siricius judged that no lighter punishment should be imposed upon them than perpetual penance [Col. 0126D] to be carried out in a monastery. From this two conclusions follow: that monasteries existed before Siricius, and that perpetual penance was imposed for more serious crimes; with this qualification, however, that Viaticum was granted to those who had been placed under the final sentence.”

### Line 16.—Who was also buried, etc.

Baronius, uncertain about his holiness, did not place him in the Roman Martyrology. He was moved to this both by the reasons already given and because he did not accept that Siricius, following the example of Damasus in composing letters, had not made use of Jerome’s work or supported Jerome as was fitting.

Certainly it cannot be denied that Jerome was not held in high regard by Siricius at the beginning of his pontificate. Several Roman clerics, burning with envy and hatred of the holy teacher, stirred up persecution against him and brought some grave accusation against him; this can be gathered from Jerome’s letters, and Baronius notes it under the year 385, no. 8.

Nor was it difficult for those men to become increasingly angry with him, since, while he was at Rome and in letters sent to his friends after his departure, he openly rebuked them. He attacked them vehemently, calling them the senate of the Pharisees and accusing them in plain terms of ignorance and depraved morals [Col. 0127A].

Thus Siricius, perhaps surrounded by malicious reports against Jerome, did not retain him at Rome in order to calm the disturbances, but allowed him, inflamed by his ardor for the holy places and for study, to return to Jerusalem.

There was also the fact that, when the holy teacher attacked Jovinianus with great force of pen, he seemed to exalt virginity so highly that he might be thought in some sense to condemn marriage. Although this was entirely contrary to his intention, it was nevertheless the common opinion at Rome at that time. Consequently Pammachius was likewise compelled at Rome to withdraw copies of Jerome’s works against Jovinianus. Saint Jerome, in Letter 52 to Pammachius himself, prudently and affectionately praised this action.

Baronius also infers from the first letter of that same holy man, now fifth in order [Col. 0127B], to Sulpicius Severus, that Siricius was less favorably disposed toward Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola. Paulinus, grieving over the fires of jealousy among the Roman clergy while he was at Rome, adds:

> “But your young servants, our fellow servants, could more fully indicate how much the proud discrimination of Pope Urbicus is harming the grace of the Lord.”

From these words, Baronius infers that Siricius was hostile to Paulinus, either because he refused to count him among his own clergy or because he disliked him on the ground that Paulinus, a consular and senatorial man in Spain, had suddenly become a presbyter from a layman, although unwillingly.

Yet Paulinus could easily have been slandered to Siricius by members of the clergy and the Roman curia, and envy could have been stirred against him, just as against Jerome, because, although already a monk, he inveighed against clerics of looser conduct.

It must also truly be admitted that Paulinus, for human reasons, was not always the best judge of men and of their character when he accused Siricius of proud discrimination. Jerome, in turn, almost accused Siricius of excessive simplicity and innate goodness. Although Paulinus excelled in holiness of life, he may be regarded as less penetrating in judgment, since, presuming good of everyone—as did Siricius—he thought highly even of Rufinus of Aquileia when Rufinus departed from Palestine in peace and with Jerome’s embrace; he praised Vigilantius without recognizing him during the long journey through Spain; and he called Melania, a leader of Origenist errors, holy and loaded her with many praises, as Baronius observes under the year 397, no. 3 [Col. 0127C].

Since these things did not harm Paulinus’s holiness, the matters noted by Baronius on the same account do not detract from Siricius’s holiness either.

For more on Siricius’s holiness, see the aforementioned Florentinius. To his discussion I add that it should not seem surprising that Siricius trusted what the Roman clergy said against Saint Paulinus and Saint Jerome, or vice versa. Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, whose reputation was so great among kings and supreme pontiffs, innocently attached himself to the faction against Saint William, elected and consecrated bishop of York. In Letter 234 he calls him “the idol of York,” and in Letter 360 “the common plague,” because even great and most pious men are sometimes deceived by false reports.

But just as the fabricated accusations against William of York did not prevent Honorius III from enrolling him in the catalogue of the saints, so it must be said that what Saint Paulinus wrote against Siricius in no way harmed Siricius’s holiness.

With Siricius, the learned Jerome concludes his supplement to the Eusebian Chronicle [Col. 0127D].

### Note: [Col. 0127D]

#### Line 2.—Here he established a constitution concerning the whole Church

Somier, *Ecclesiastical Dogmatic History*, chapter 1, no. 8, at the end.

After complaining about the negligence of the metropolitans regarding ordinations, Siricius forbids the diaconate and presbyterate to be conferred upon bigamists, and declares that his decrees concerning what must be done or avoided are to be laws [Col. 0128A] for the universal Church:

> “By a general pronouncement we decree what must henceforth be followed by all the churches and what must be avoided,” etc.

He declares that those metropolitans who do not obey such laws will be rigorously punished by the apostolic see. He also shows that all the churches, as members of that body of which Rome is the head, are bound to know and obey the laws of that head:

> “Henceforth the chief bishops of all the provinces shall know that, if they promote anyone contrary to the canons and our prohibitions, an appropriate sentence must be issued by the apostolic see . . . .”

> “Concerning these matters you have referred to the Roman Church, as to the head of your body . . . . We urge you to ensure that what we have written in reply to your consultations be brought to the knowledge of all our bishops—not only those established in your diocese, but also all the Carthaginians, Baeticans, Lusitanians, and Gauls, or those who border your provinces on every side . . . .”

> “Although no priest of the Lord is free to be ignorant of the statutes of the apostolic see, it is nevertheless more useful if, through the care of your unanimity, they are brought to the knowledge of all our brothers, so that what we have beneficially established—not rashly, but prudently, with the utmost caution and deliberation—may remain inviolate, and so that access to every future excuse, which can no longer be open to anyone before us, may be closed,” etc. [Col. 0128B]

Siricius’s letter to all the orthodox concerns the discipline of sacred ordinations, which this pontiff orders all the churches to observe. At the very beginning he declares that the care of all the churches has been entrusted to him, etc.

During the pontificate of Siricius, the Third Council of Carthage was held. Its canon 26 decrees:

> “The bishop of the first see shall not be called the chief of priests, or the high priest, or anything of that kind, but only the bishop of the first see.”

This decree of a national council cannot have referred to the Roman bishop [Col. 0128C], as certain innovators contend; it could refer only to the bishops of Africa, whose jurisdiction encompassed several provinces forming that portion of the Western patriarchate which was subject to the primate of Carthage.

This is clearly demonstrated by canon 26 of that same council, where the metropolitan also, in relation to the suffragans of his province, is called the bishop of the first see:

> “Bishops shall not travel across the sea unless they have consulted the bishop of the first see of their respective province,” etc.

See also chapter 2, p. 11.

[Col. 0128D] Having established discipline through these exertions, Siricius turned his attention to abolishing the schism that had long afflicted the Church of Antioch. In the preceding pontificate we related the origin of that schism: contrary to the agreement reached between Paulinus and Meletius—each of whom governed the portion of the flock by which he was recognized as pastor, so that when one of them died the survivor would assume full authority—the followers of Meletius, after his death, substituted Flavian. The Roman See, which had condemned this election, had approved the election of Evagrius, who had been chosen as Paulinus’s successor. Siricius first wrote about this matter to the emperor Theodosius, and soon afterward addressed him in person—for Theodosius had come to Rome to celebrate his triumph after his victory over the tyrant Maximus. He spoke so forcefully against Flavian that, when the emperor returned to the East, he ordered Flavian to go to Rome and await judgment on his case at the Council of Capua. Flavian avoided this, and so forth.

Saint Ambrose, a contemporary writer who took great pains in judging cases of this kind, explains the evasive tactics employed by Flavian in Letter 9 of Book I, addressed to Theophilus of Alexandria, whom the Council of Capua had appointed, together with the Egyptian bishops, as a judge:

“Let Flavian have something to fear; that is why he avoids the examination, and so forth. We certainly think that the matter should be referred to our holy brother, the bishop of the Roman Church, [Col. 0129A] since we presume that you will judge only those things which could not displease him. In this way the judgment will be usefully consulted, so that, once we know that what has been done has undoubtedly been approved by the Roman Church, we may gladly obtain the fruit of such an examination.”

From this letter of Ambrose we learn several things.

1. Flavian took pains to prevent the case concerning his acquisition of the see of Antioch from being examined, because he had the greatest distrust of that examination.

2. The Council of Capua referred this judgment to Theophilus of Alexandria and to the bishops of his patriarchate. Here, however, one must observe that this could not have been done unless the authority of the holy See had yielded the matter to the council of Capua, since the power of delegation is an act of jurisdiction and cannot be exercised except by a superior.

3. Flavian attempted to evade judgment by employing secular power.

4. The intention of the Fathers of the Council of Capua was that the dispute should be settled while the communion of the parties remained intact.

5. The apostolic See had to approve what had been approved by the judges, so that the sentence might be carried out.

[Col. 0129B] Line 4.—“Against all heresies.” See Somier, p. 18. It is absolutely certain that the holy pontiff Siricius condemned the heresy of Jovinian at Rome and saw to it that it was also proscribed at Milan, where it had arisen. The sectarians who professed the monastic life there withdrew to Rome in order to disseminate throughout the city their writings infected with errors of this kind. For, placing continence before marriage, they publicly disclosed their blasphemies in a reckless written statement—as the letter attributed to Siricius and addressed to the Fathers of the Church of Milan records—teaching that the profession of virginity did not surpass marriage; that the Virgin Mother of God was indeed a virgin before childbirth, but did not remain a virgin after giving birth; and they condemned the practice of fasting.

The authors of such blasphemies and errors were nevertheless reported to Pope Siricius, and the faithful who reported them—men of excellent birth and distinguished religious character—also presented the sectarians’ writings to him. [Col. 0129C] Siricius, having convened a solemn council of the Roman clergy, condemned Jovinian and his followers by formal judgment, since they taught a doctrine contrary to the teaching of the apostolic See, which is identical with Christian law. He declared that, by divine sentence and by our judgment, they were condemned in perpetuity and would [Col. 0130A] remain outside the Church. It is entirely worth noting that the Roman pontiff speaks of his decision in the same way that the Council of Jerusalem, assembled under the Apostles, announced its own decrees: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” The pontiff says: “By divine sentence and by our judgment.” He sent the law of his judgment to the Church of Milan, so that it might receive and preserve the same decision.

That Church obediently complied at once by summoning a council. For the Fathers who had assembled there, in a synodal letter addressed to the Roman pontiff, affirm that they had already followed his judgment and likewise condemned those sectarians with their errors. In the same letter they testify that they recognized Siricius as the universal shepherd of the whole Church:

“Who faithfully guards, with pious solicitude, the gate entrusted to him and Christ’s sheepfold; worthy that the Lord’s sheep should hear and follow him . . . . . Let the Apostles’ Creed be believed, which the Roman Church has always preserved undefiled . . . . . But why say more before our teacher and doctor . . . . . [Col. 0130B] Therefore, know that Jovinian, Auxentius, and the others whom Your Holiness condemned have also been condemned among us in accordance with your judgment.”

Maximus, who, while Siricius sat at the helm of the Church, had seized the empire from Gratian, replied to the letters of that same pope, in which Siricius entrusted him with the defense of the Catholic Church and demanded from him a profession of the same faith. Maximus calls him “most beloved Father” and “an apostolic man,” plainly answering to the name of priest and to the dignity of the most splendid city.

“As for the Catholic faith, concerning which you wished to consult our Clemency, I confess, most beloved Father, that I take the greatest care of it,” and so forth.

In another letter, which Maximus himself had earlier sent to the emperor Valentinian Augustus, he removes him from adherence to the perverse counsels of the innovators, to the prejudice of the Catholic faith—a faith established and confirmed over many centuries in Italy, Africa, Gaul, Spain, and especially at Rome, which had become the leading city of the world no less by the title of true religion [Col. 0130C] than by the power of the empire:

“All Italy and Africa believe by this sacrament; Gaul, Aquitaine, and all Spain glory in this faith; venerable Rome herself, whose primacy also exists in this matter.”

[Col. 0109]

55

Siricius, a Roman by nation, the son of a man from Tibur, held the see for 15 years, 11 months, and 25 days. [Note: [Col. 0109] B: 13 years, 1 month, and 14 days, from the consulship of Arcadius Augustus and Bauto to that of Honoratus IV and Eutychian.] He issued a decree concerning the whole Church, or against all heresies, and disseminated it throughout the entire world, so that it might be kept in the archives of every Church for use against the attack [Note: [Col. 0109] C: “attack”] of all heresies.

He decreed that no presbyter should celebrate Mass throughout the week unless he received from the designated bishop of the place a consecrated and identified portion, called the fermentum [Note: [Col. 0109] See Baronius, volume II of the Annals, on the fermentum.].

He decreed concerning the Manichaeans whom he had deported into exile [Note: [Col. 0109] See Baronius, volume V, under the year 398.] that they should not share communion with the faithful, because it was not permissible for the Lord’s holy body to be handled by a polluted mouth.

He decreed that if anyone converted from the Manichaeans returned to the Church, he should in no way be admitted to communion, unless he were kept under the obligation of confinement in a monastery for the rest of his life, so that, chastened by fasts and prayers and tested through every examination until the last day of his passage from life, he might finally, because of the Church’s kindness, be granted the viaticum.

He decreed that a heretic should be received by the laying on of hands in the presence of the entire Church.

In the month of December he held five ordinations in the City: 31 presbyters, 16 deacons, and 32 bishops for various places.

He was also buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March; and the episcopate was vacant for 20 days.

XLI. SAINT ANASTASIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 398, THE FOURTH CONSULSHIP OF ARCADIUS AND HONORIUS.
