[Note: [Col. 0131B]

Line 2.—“He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bowed down.” Anastasius decreed that, when the Gospel is read, the clergy should stand. When the Gospel is read, we stand, so that by this posture of the body, prepared for a journey, we may signify that we are ready to follow God and his faith attested by the Gospel.

That this was the custom of the Eastern Church is attested by John Chrysostom, *On the Different Places in the Two Testaments*, “On the Circus.” In the Eastern Church, when the Gospel was read, candles were lit. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*:

“Throughout all the Churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lamps are lit while the sun is already shining—not, of course, to drive away darkness, but to display a sign of joy.”

The same practice was observed at Rome. Anastasius, in the life of Leo III:

“He made two cast lamps of the purest silver, and he also decreed that on Sundays or on holy solemnities they should stand on either side beside the reading desk, and that, when the sacred readings were read, they should shine with the splendor of their light.”]

[Note: [Col. 0131C]

Line 5.—“And he also decreed that under no circumstances should a man from overseas be received into the honor of the clergy unless he produced a letter of recommendation from five bishops, because of the Manichaeans.” Because of the Manichaeans, who were especially numerous in Africa, Anastasius decreed that clerics should not be ordained without autograph letters—that is, letters of recommendation—from five bishops. Canon *Transmarinos*, Distinction 98; this was repeated by Gregory I and Alexander III, Canon *Afros*, in the same distinction, chapter 1, *On Clerics from Abroad Not to Be Ordained*.

Line 9.—“He was buried in his cemetery at the Bear with the Cap.” This was the name of the district in which the cemetery of Anastasius was located, perhaps derived from a Bear with a Cap, which served as its emblem. The shops around the forum were distinguished by signs. Quintilian, Book 6, *Institutes*, chapter 3, says that he pointed with his finger to the image of a Gaul painted on the Cimbrian shield of Marius. The shops, however, were around the forum, and that shield had been placed there as a sign.

[Col. 0131D] Pliny, Book XXXV, chapter 4, adds that on the shield of Marius there was an image of a Gaul sticking out his tongue:

“Showing in a painting a Gaul sticking out his tongue in a most ridiculous manner.”

Signs were placed for amusement, to provoke laughter; so it is not surprising that in this place the capped Bear may have appeared as a sign, like an emancipated slave. Anastasius, at the end of his life of Innocent I, reports that Innocent was buried in the same cemetery at the Bear with the Cap.

Anastasius also mentions the same cemetery at the Bear with the Cap in his life of Nicholas I:

“And he also restored the cemetery on the same road at the Bear with the Cap.”

The district of the Bear with the Cap was in the fifth region of the City, that is, the Esquiline region. Sextus Rufus, *On the Regions of the City*. Similarly, in the fourth region of the City there was a place called “At the White Hens,” which Sextus Rufus mentions in his little work *On the Regions of the City*. Gregory, Book II, Letter 17:

“A house situated in this City, in the fourth region, beside the place called the White Hens.”

[Col. 0132B] Perhaps it was named from the white hens that were a notable feature of this place. The villa of the Caesars, which stood beside the Tiber near the ninth milestone on the Flaminian Way, was called “At the Hens,” because the offspring of a white hen was preserved there. An eagle flying overhead had dropped it from above into the lap of Livia Drusilla, who was sitting in the open air; Pliny, Book XV, chapter 30.]

[Note: [Col. 0132B]

Line 3.—“He issued a decree concerning the Church.” The Origenist doctrine, introduced and disseminated by certain people through evil practices, should be understood as the subject of the Anastasian decree praised by the *Book of the Pontiffs*. The occasion was provided by a denunciatory letter from Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the errors of the Origenists and the activities of certain monks who, fraudulently introducing themselves into houses, administered poison.

Two letters of Pope Anastasius relate to the memory of this decree; ecclesiastical writers mention them, and Saint Jerome discusses them at length in his apologies against Rufinus, who is counted among the leaders of the Origenists. [Col. 0132C] Jerome writes that the pontiff issued a threatening and decisive letter against Rufinus:

“And you flee so greatly from the judgment of the Roman City that you would rather endure a barbarian siege than the sentence of the peaceful City.”

He then exposes Rufinus’s evasions by which Rufinus sought to avoid judgment. One of these was the claim that Jerome had fabricated the pontifical letter. On that occasion Jerome recalls another letter of Anastasius, in which the pontiff, writing to the Easterners, attacked the errors of Origen. Thus Jerome writes in the cited passage:

“Suppose that I fabricated a letter in the past year. Who sent the recent writings to the East? In them Pope Anastasius heaps such praises upon you that, when you read them, you begin to wish to defend yourself rather than accuse us.”

[Col. 0132D] The pontifical writing was therefore addressed to the Easterners, in that region where the monks had disseminated the poison by their artifice. Concerning this judgment the emperor Justinian, writing to Menas of Constantinople, says:

“Let us also hear the holy Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from a discourse written to certain monks who agreed with Origen. For he says:

‘Why do we anathematize Origen and the other heretics, following our own example and that of Anastasius, bishop of the holy Roman Church, who, renowned for his ancient struggles, was appointed leader of the most noble people, and whose synod of all the blessed bishops of the West also follows the judgment of the Alexandrian Church delivered against the impious man and accepts and approves it?’”

[Col. 0133A] Saint Jerome also praises him and commends the fame of the decree in a letter to Pammachius:

“May the preaching of the chair of Mark the Evangelist be confirmed by the preaching of the chair of Peter the Apostle. Although it has been spread abroad by a famous saying that blessed Anastasius also, with the same fervor because he has the same spirit, will pursue the heretics hiding in their pits; and may his letters show that what was condemned in the East has been condemned in the West. We pray that he may live many years, so that through his zeal the renewed plantings of heresy may wither and die over a long period.”

He writes similarly to Demetrias:

“I nearly passed over what is perhaps the most important point. While you were still a little girl and Anastasius, of holy and blessed memory, was governing the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the regions of the East was compelled to pollute and shake the simplicity of the faith praised by the Apostle’s voice. But the man of the richest poverty and apostolic solicitude immediately struck down the noxious head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra. And because I fear—or rather, because I have learned by report—that poisonous plantings are still alive and flourishing in some places, I think I should warn you in the pious affection of charity to hold fast to the faith of holy Innocent, who is the successor and son of the aforesaid man in the apostolic chair.”

Jerome also observed that these Anastasian decrees had been disseminated throughout the Christian world and that the Origenists had been pursued through them, when he objected to Rufinus:

“What will [Col. 0133B] the letters of Bishop Theophilus do? What will those of Pope Anastasius do, pursuing the heretic throughout the whole world?”

From this it may be concluded that, alongside the Councils of Alexandria and Cyprus, which were held against the Origenists during this pontificate, a Roman council must also be included, according to the words of Saint Jerome quoted above:

“Whom the entire synod of the blessed bishops of the West also follows.”

Its memory has been omitted by the editors of the councils.

The following considerations suggest that this council was first celebrated at Rome and that its decree was then sent throughout the provinces, announced and subscribed in particular synods under the individual metropolitans.

1. It instituted an examination of the kind solemnly conducted in councils. The examination was occasioned by Marcella’s zeal, as Jerome explicitly testifies in his letter to the virgin Principia, which is a funeral inscription for the widow Marcella. After praising Anastasius and his efforts against the Origenists, he writes of the subsequent examination:

“You may ask what this has to do with Marcella’s praise. This was the beginning of the condemnation of the heretics: she brought forward witnesses who had first been instructed by them and afterward had been seized by the heretical error; she showed the multitude of those who had been deceived; she produced the impious volumes *Peri Archon*—‘On First Principles’—which were displayed as corrected by the hand of Scorpius; and when the heretics were summoned by repeated letters to come and defend themselves, they did not dare to appear. So great was the force of conscience that they preferred to be condemned in their absence rather than be convicted in person.”

These proceedings show that a conciliar examination had been instituted.

That Western bishops were informed of the condemnation issued by Anastasius, accepted it, strengthened it with their subscriptions, and announced it to their peoples is likewise attested by Anastasius himself in a letter addressed to John, bishop of Jerusalem. In it he mentions both the issued decree and the fact that he had announced it to the bishops, especially to Venerius, one of the principal primates of the Western region. This appears from a letter published by Garnerius among the works of Mercator, where the pontiff says:

“We have written the letter of condemnation to our brothers Venerius and Chromatius.”

[Col. 0133D] The particular conciliar acts are recalled there in the synodal letter of condemnation:

“Therefore know what sort of letter our humility sent, written with most diligent care to our brother and fellow bishop Venerius.”

As for what he did with the other bishops of the world through encyclical letters announcing the condemnation, and how the emperor’s edicts followed, he writes:

“Certainly I shall not lack care to preserve the faith of the Gospel among the peoples entrusted to me, and, insofar as I can, to address in letters the portions of my people scattered through the various regions of the earth, lest some beginning of profane interpretation creep in and, by casting its darkness over them, attempt to weaken devoted minds. Nor could I remain silent about the matter over which I rejoice: responses have come from the most blessed princes, by which every person serving God is recalled from reading Origen, and the one whom profane reading has exposed is declared worthy of condemnation by the judgment of the princes. Thus far the form of my judgment has proceeded.”

[Col. 0134A] Among the Origenists, Primopilus Rufinus was summoned to the pontifical examination, at least among the Westerners. Jerome asserts this in the apologies published against him, and Rufinus himself bears witness in a letter to Anastasius.

These things, then—the Roman synod and its proceedings, here noted only briefly—gave occasion for saying that the synod had been solemnly convened and that the words of the *Book of the Pontiffs* applied to it: “He issued a decree concerning the Church.” Since this decree was then especially famous and conspicuous among the other decrees of the pontifical book, the compiler thought it sufficient to allude to it while leaving its subject unstated.

Thus he had written most accurately that the Origenists were condemned in a twofold synod under Anastasius and Theophilus, Western and Eastern:

“Therefore the blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius, Crematius, and the entire synod of Catholics, both of the East and of the West, denounce that heresy to the peoples with one judgment because they possess one spirit.”

[Col. 0134B] Line 5.—“And he also decreed that under no circumstances should a man from overseas be received into the honor of the clergy.” By “men from overseas,” the Africans understood Italians, just as the Romans understood Africans by that expression. This can often be observed in Saint Augustine and in the Councils of Carthage of the same period, where the expression is repeatedly found.

Thus clerics arriving at Rome were not admitted to the offices of the Church unless they came with episcopal testimonials; hence the following line.

Line 6.—“Unless they produced an autograph letter from five bishops.” Not from all the bishops, but from five; and, as I think, from those bishops who gave authority to ecclesiastical documents. They were the primate, the metropolitan, the senior bishop in the province, the diocesan bishop, and the bishop nearest to the city when the proper bishop had died. That these customs had become established in the African Church is shown by the canon book of that same Church.

Line 7.—“Because of the Manichaeans.” Africa was then suffering from a multitude of Manichaeans. To avoid being detected, they pretended at will to practice the religion, even resorting to perjury. Saint Augustine discusses this hypocrisy at length in Book XXVI of *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*.

For this reason Siricius, Anastasius’s predecessor, had decreed that this pestilence of men should never be admitted to communion unless tested through every examination. Since clerics arriving according to their rank were invited to join the clergy at the sacrifice, and since Manichaean clerics pretended to practice the religion, Anastasius therefore wished and decreed that all clerics arriving from Africa should bring testimonials subscribed by one of the bishops mentioned above, so that no sacrilegious participation might occur.

Leo the Great speaks of the Manichaeans’ simulation in participating in sacred rites, and condemns it again, warning all the faithful as follows:

“Although, to conceal their infidelity, they dare to attend our mysteries, they restrain themselves in the communion of the sacraments in such a way that sometimes, lest they be entirely hidden, they receive Christ’s body with an unworthy mouth, but altogether refuse to drink the blood of our redemption. We make this known to your Holiness so that such men may be exposed to you by these indications and so that those whose sacrilegious simulation has been detected may, by priestly authority, be expelled from the fellowship of the saints.”

The remaining passages there, in which the holy pontiff discusses the morals of the Manichaeans, should also be read.]

[Note: [Col. 0134D]

Line 2.—“He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bowed down.” The occasion for sanctioning this decree seems to have arisen as follows.

During the time of Anastasius, a serious dispute arose at Rome between the presbyters and the deacons. The deacons, administering the affairs of the Church, became arrogant and despised the presbyters. The presbyters rose up against them and, in accordance with the custom prescribed by the Roman Church, maintained that while the presbyters were seated the deacons ought to stand.

The dispute, however, advanced so stubbornly that even when the deacons stood before the people to read the Gospel, the presbyters would not rise from their seats. Anastasius therefore rightly detested this behavior and thought that it had to be corrected by such a decree.]

[Note: [Col. 0135A]

Chronological Notes

In addition to what we established above concerning the pontifical epoch of Saint Anastasius—deriving it from the consulships of Theodorus and Eutropius, in the year of Christ 399, on Sunday, 9 October, and extending it to the consulships of Vincentius and Fravitta, in the year of Christ 401, on 3 November—two testimonies of writers must be considered. They calculate the total period first from the century of Christ to the consulships of this period and can therefore greatly illuminate the pontifical chronology, which is so closely connected with the consular chronology.

The first testimony is taken from Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapters 53 and 54. He counts [Col. 0135B] 365 years from the Ides of May under the two Gemini as consuls—that is, the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, or Pentecost, from the beginning of the Apostles’ preaching—to the Ides of May in the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus.

Pagi, under the year 398, no. 4, observes that Augustine’s calculation does not support Baronius’s chronology or his own. He thinks that the blessed Doctor’s calculations have been improperly performed, since, whether the two Gemini consuls are placed with Baronius in the year 31 of the common Christian era or in 29 with Pagi under the year 398, the total of 365 does not work out.

Nevertheless, when the entire context of chapters 53 and 54 of blessed Augustine is carefully considered, it can be gathered that the holy Doctor correctly argues against the pagans from the period of time which, according to their assumptions, they themselves had defined—from the false response of demons to the supposed end of Christian worship.

For the pagans had invented the following:

“I do not know what Greek verses, as though poured forth by a divine [Col. 0135C] oracle to someone consulting it,” he says in chapter 53, “in which they indeed make Christ innocent of this supposed sacrilegious crime, but add that Peter performed magic so that Christ’s name might be worshiped for 365 years; then, once the aforesaid number of years had been completed, it would immediately come to an end.”

He gives the reason for inventions of this kind in the same place:

“When they saw that the Christian religion could not be destroyed by so many and such great persecutions, but had rather gained greater growth through them,” the worshipers of empty gods resorted to false oracles fabricated by themselves, in order to deceive the adherents of their superstitions by a false expectation and prediction of our downfall and to nourish a vain hope in them.

Therefore, in order to refute and utterly overturn their deceit, the holy Doctor shows in those two chapters, 53 and 54, that, by whatever method they count the same 365 years—whether from the baptism of Christ the Lord, from his Passion, or from the coming of the Holy Spirit—they cannot extend them beyond the consulship of the year 398, that of Honorius and Eutychianus.

[Col. 0135D] He then adds that, in the consulship immediately following, that of Manlius and Theodorus, namely in the year of Christ 399—which I have shown must be connected with the beginning of the pontificate of Anastasius, the subject of our discussion—not only did the Christian rites not cease, “but in the most famous and eminent city of Carthage in Africa, Gaudentius and Jovius, counts of the emperor Honorius, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, destroyed the temples of false gods and broke their images.”

Augustine’s inference against the presumed claims and lies of the pagans is legitimate and evident, regardless of the point from which they chose to begin the magic they had invented concerning blessed Peter and the total of 365 years that they had set as the limit for the destruction of our religion.

Pagi observes that this total cannot be altered, since it is reported by all copies of the works of blessed Augustine, with no variant reading that could cast doubt upon it. Its retention is also recommended by the familiar superstitions both of Mithra among the pagans and of the Gnostics among the heretics. [Col. 0136A] These had been drawn from the same sources and renewed in those times by Julian; they had falsely promised their deranged followers victory over Christian worship under the mystical number 365, expressed by the letters in the words ΑΒΡΑϹΑΞ (*Abrasax*) and ΝΕΙΛΟΣ (*Neilos*).

Augustine’s intention, then, is to demonstrate that the 365 years had been completed entirely in the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus, regardless of the distorted measure of events and consuls that the inventors might use. The indicated series of 365 years does not proceed beyond that limit, which is entirely true.

But if we ask from which year the beginning of the indicated period must be taken in order for the 365 years to be completed exactly in the consulship of the year 398, it must plainly be reckoned from that notable enlargement and proclamation of our faith which opened the door to the nations for receiving the grace of Christ—not from Peter’s imaginary magic, but from the heavenly vision shown to him, which brought Cornelius the centurion to him and invited the prince of the Apostles to establish the see of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians.

[Col. 0136B] Our chronology, explained and proved above, assigns that year to the thirty-third year of the common Christian era. If 365 years are added to it, the year 398 results: the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus, which Augustine indicates as the limit fixed by the false expectation of the pagans for the destruction of the divine worship of Christians, but which was ennobled by the new and splendid triumph of our religion. At that time, by a public imperial decree, the temples of the empty gods at Carthage were destroyed under the following consulships, just when the ridiculous fabricators of such oracles were threatening our sacred rites with their final day and destruction.

The second testimony illuminating the chronology of Pope Anastasius concerns the final year of the fourth century, when Stilicho was consul. It is taken from Sulpicius Severus, a contemporary of the same period, who writes:

“The Lord was crucified under the consuls Fufius Geminus and Rubellius Geminus. From that time until Stilicho was consul there are 372 years.”

This total corresponds exactly to the chronology established by us. For if, with Victor of Aquitaine and with the Fathers who commonly refer the Lord’s Passion to the eighth day before the Kalends of April in that same consulship, we assign Christ’s Passion to the leap year 28 of the common Christian era, when the two Gemini were consuls, and add the 372 years which Sulpicius reckons from that point to the consulship of Stilicho, the year 400 of the common Christian era results. This was the second year of Pope Anastasius, to which the consulship of Flavius Stilicho and Aurelianus must be assigned according to the judgment of all the chronologists of our time.

Historical Notes

Line 1.—“Anastasius,” and so forth. Saint Augustine, Letter 164 to Gratiosus, lists the succession of the Roman pontiffs from blessed Peter up to Anastasius, the pope under discussion here.

Line 3.—“He issued a decree concerning the Church.” This law, which he proposed to the whole Church, was the just condemnation of the Origenists. The origin of that error is given in the notes of Somier and Pagi.

[Col. 0136D] John, bishop of Jerusalem, had been reported to Pope Siricius by Saint Epiphanius because he had extracted several errors from Origen’s books entitled *Peri Archon*—“On First Principles”—and introduced them to the Christian people. They were contained in eight principal propositions, which Saint Jerome enumerates individually in Letter 61.

Rufinus of Aquileia—see Pagi’s notes on Anastasius, no. 2, and on Siricius, 11—a most vehement defender of Origen, had translated into Latin the books of Origen in order to disseminate those same errors at Rome, and had published them in the year 398, offering the Romans poison in a golden cup.

While this Origenist heresy had not yet been exposed, Rufinus obtained from Pope Siricius a letter of communion. But when those pernicious doctrines were discovered not long afterward and reported to the apostolic See, which Anastasius occupied, Jerome, then residing in the East, was entrusted with the task of faithfully rendering Origen’s *On First Principles* into Latin, as he himself testifies in Letter 64 to Oceanus.

[Col. 0137A] What followed may be read both in Pagi’s notes, numbers 2 and 3, and in Somier’s notes, chapter 4. The substance is this:

“Anastasius proscribed the books of the *Periarchon* [Pagi, no. II], disciplined Rufinus the translator, terrified the peoples with the edicts of the princes, and accused John, bishop of Jerusalem, a supporter of Rufinus and Origen, solemnly warning him not to allow himself to be deceived by a defender of error. These facts are established by that celebrated letter of apostolic vigor, sent by Pope Anastasius to the aforesaid John, bishop of Jerusalem. In it the pontiff speaks as follows:

‘We have indeed condemned the writings and errors of Origen. As for the translator, since he has not sufficiently cleared himself either in his preface to Origen’s books [Col. 0138A] or in the apology sent to us—and indeed perhaps he really agrees with those same errors—we summoned him to Rome for the judgment of the apostolic See; and when he refused to come, we included him in the same sentence. We have written the letter of condemnation to our brothers Venerius, bishop of Milan, and Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia.’”

The cathedral archive of Verona preserves the most ancient copy of this letter among the distinguished codices collected in the ninth century by Pacificus, archdeacon of the holy Church of Verona. We think that a specimen of its script should be exhibited here, so that it may be entirely clear by what genuine documents the acts of the pontiffs are confirmed, since we can present their letters inserted in codices of such great antiquity.

[Col. 0137] Specimen of the script of several codices of outstanding antiquity, preserved among many others in the Cathedral Church of Verona, in the Archive and Library of the Most Reverend Chapter.

No. 1. From a parchment codex written in capital letters, containing various letters of the holy Fathers. At no. XXIII the following letter of Saint Anastasius, the first pope of that name, is found:

No. 2. From a codex likewise written on parchment, containing the thirty-five books of Saint Gregory the Great on Job. The form of its script displays beginnings of books very similar to those of Augustine Petavius in Mabillon, p. 355; the body of the books, however, resembles the diplomas of Clovis in the same author.

[Col. 0139] Imitation of the script in which the codex was written, formerly in the Library of Justellus and now preserved in the Bodleian Library at Oxford; from it Justellus himself published the *Canons of the African Church* in 1615.

After the consulship.

[Col. 0139A] We observe nearly comparable antiquity in the parchment manuscripts of the councils of the African Church, formerly belonging, as I have learned, to Christophorus Justellus, an especially noble, devout, and learned editor of the code of canons of the African Church published 110 years ago, but now preserved in the famous Oxford library. I am pleased to append a specimen taken from them in the year 1713. I shall address the information concerning these parchments in the note immediately following that on Saint Zosimus. It is preferable, however, to present here, together with the specimen of the Veronese manuscript, these records of events from the same period—namely, of the councils of the African Church—which sent a delegation to that same Pope Anastasius, of whom we are speaking, in order to obtain an interpretation of the apostolic constitutions concerning clergy who had withdrawn from the Donatist schism and were seeking to be received and enrolled in the Catholic clergy. On these matters see also the notes of Pagius and Somier.

**Line 4.**—The basilica called Crescentiana, in the second region, on the Mamertine Way [Note: [Col. 0129] C: *Mamurtina*. *Mamurrina*.], in the City of Rome. When we attempted to establish something about the site of the cemetery at Ursus Pileatus [Col. 0139B], we were required not to neglect an investigation of this Crescentian basilica. Its site is designated in the second ecclesiastical region, which comprised three of the fourteen regions established by Augustus: namely, II, VIII, and XI—the Caelian Hill, the Roman Forum, and the Circus Maximus—as we determined with Nardini in the *Prolegomena*.

In so extensive a region, the location is difficult to determine. Although the difficulty seems to be reduced by the evidence concerning the Mamertine Way, which Nardini, on the basis of several documents, has shown must have been laid out at the foot of the Capitoline slope toward the fora of Augustus and Trajan, running from the Arch of Septimius Severus and the prison of Saint Peter—also called the Mamertine Prison—to the title of Saint Mark, nevertheless the profound silence concerning that Crescentian basilica among writers contemporary with its founder’s age prevents us from saying anything certain about it. The nearby invasion of the Goths and the sack of the City may perhaps have devastated that recent building, as they did many others [Col. 0139C]. Nor should we be surprised if traces of its construction have been confused among the ruins of the City, since, of the more than three hundred churches counted in the City by the *Roman Ordo* written by Cencius Camerarius in the twelfth century (see Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 192), several dozen have since disappeared—either levelled to the ground or converted to other uses, such as monasteries and hospitals, or having acquired different titles through new constructions. It is therefore more probable that this basilica stood not far from the Roman Forum, in the district extending from the xenodochium of Saint Mary of Consolation toward the church of Saint Martina, where the name Mamertine Way has not entirely disappeared.

**Line 9.**—He was buried in his own cemetery at [Col. 0140A] Ursus Pileatus. Careful narrators of the sacred crypts—Bosius, Aringhius, and Boldettus, together with Florentinius in the *Ancient Martyrology* under 12 March and 21 December—distinguish two cemeteries celebrated among the ancients by this name. Under 21 December is recorded the burial of Saint Innocent, the immediate successor of this Anastasius. The ancient Vatican manuscripts cited there from Aringhius likewise agree, recording both pontiffs, Anastasius and Innocent, as buried at Ursus Pileatus on the Portuensian Way: that is, first buried outside the City on the Portuensian Way, at the cemetery of Ursus Pileatus; then transferred to another cemetery within the City, likewise distinguished by the name Ursus Pileatus, but situated a considerable distance from the first, namely near the church of Saint Bibiana on the Esquiline.

We also know from our Librarian, no. 491, that the relics of these pontiffs were placed by Sergius II, together with many others, beneath the sacred altar in the new dedication of that title, which he himself restored from its foundations. Yet those sacred remains are not said [Col. 0140B] to have been removed at that time from the cemetery on the Portuensian Way, but only to have been placed beneath the altar at the dedication. It must therefore be understood that these relics—or portions of the bodies of several saints—were taken from various cemeteries and churches, both within and outside the City, as is indicated there.

Accordingly, it is not contradictory to affirm that the bodies of the holy pontiffs Anastasius and Innocent were first deposited at the church of Saint Bibiana when they were brought from the cemetery on the Portuensian Way called Ursus Pileatus into the City, so that they would not suffer injury from the Saracens ravaging the Roman countryside. They were brought there together with many other holy martyrs and confessors, who were likewise to be rescued from danger and reburied at the same church. Their great number is displayed on an ancient stone. Hence some suppose that the name “cemetery at Ursus Pileatus” was communicated to that church together with the sacred relics of so many heavenly beings.

Then, after several generations, Sergius II and other Roman pontiffs requested portions of the sacred bones from that new cemetery of Ursus Pileatus within the City [Col. 0140C], on the occasion of the dedications of altars and churches. As for the name Ursus Pileatus, given to both cemeteries, I observe that the one within the walls, belonging to Saint Bibiana, was situated at the street of Ursus Pileatus mentioned by Sextus Rufus in Region V of the City, as Nardini observes, book IV, chapter 2, p. 162. It therefore scarcely seems possible that the cemetery outside the walls on the Portuensian Way could have borrowed the name from it.

I shall nevertheless indicate an occasion for the designation which, I suspect, caused the name to adhere to one cemetery from the other. This suggestion is provided by an ancient inscription on a marble tablet preserved in the Vatican basilica’s archive. It concerns that togatus Ursus who first played with a glass ball under the emperor Verus. The tablet was taken from a dismembered monument—whether tomb or statue—and a cenotaph, and was used as a foundation beneath the sarcophagus of a Christian, as often happened in later centuries [Col. 0141A]. The sarcophagus had been placed near the high altar of the old Vatican basilica. Grimaldus, the notary assigned to record the demolition of the old basilica in his *Diary*, attested this, reporting it on folio CLXIII:

> “The discoverer of the game of the togatus Ursus with the glass ball, and the inscription in praise of him—outstanding to the point of wonder in the time of the Caesars—which had been engraved on a marble tablet and originally placed beneath the statue he had earned for that achievement: this tablet, after it had later been laid beneath the burial chest of a Christian when foundations were being laid for the pavement near the high altar of the Vatican basilica, was dug up in the year 1591 and is preserved in the archive of that basilica.”

Ursus lived in the time of the emperor Verus.

> **URSUS THE TOGATUS, WHO FIRST PLAYED WITH THE GLASS BALL,  
> SKILLFULLY, WHILE THE PEOPLE PRAISED ME  
> WITH THE GREATEST SHOUTS,  
> IN THE BATHS OF TRAJAN, THE BATHS OF AGRIPPA  
> AND OF TITUS, AND MUCH IN THOSE OF NERO.  
> IF YOU BELIEVE ME, I AM [AS I SAY; THE SENSE IS ELLIPTICAL]; COME, REJOICING BALL-PLAYERS, AND, FRIENDS, CROWN MY STATUE  
> WITH FLOWERS, VIOLETS, ROSES, AND ABUNDANT FOLIAGE,  
> AND LOAD IT WITH WILTING PERFUME, LOVERS;  
> POUR OUT BLACK FALERNIAN, OR SETINE, OR CAECUBAN WINE,  
> AND SING OF URSUS WITH HARMONIOUS VOICE—  
> AN OLD, CHEERFUL, JOCULAR, BALL-PLAYING SCHOLAR  
> WHO SURPASSED ALL HIS PREDECESSORS  
> IN JUDGMENT, BEAUTY, AND MOST SUBTLE ART.  
> NOW LET US SPEAK TRUE WORDS IN VERSE:  
> I CONFESS THAT I, AN OLD MAN, HAVE BEEN DEFEATED—  
> BY VERUS, THREE TIMES CONSUL, MY PATRON,  
> NOT ONCE BUT OFTEN;  
> I AM GLADLY CALLED HIS *EXODIARIUS*—HIS PERFORMER IN AN AFTERPIECE.”**

This Ursus, then, the freedman of Verus whom the inscription describes as a *togatus* after he had obtained freedom and the toga from his patron Verus, three times consul, must also have been a *pileatus*, as indicated by another sign of freedom and by the custom of placing a cap upon a freedman. A statue was erected to him with this inscription and together with an account of his invention of the glass playing-ball, in a street on the Esquiline within the City, near the Baths of Titus mentioned there. In my judgment, this gave the common people occasion to call the street after that statue of Ursus Pileatus—just as the statue popularly called Pasquilli, which is actually that of a gladiator in the Parione region, gives its name to a street near the Agonal Circus—even when Festus was writing.

This seems much more probable than imagining a statue of a cap-wearing bear, such as lies there today, broken apart and fashioned in the sculpture of a later age. In the Esquiline district, at the crossroads extending from the fortress of the Aqua Martia, commonly called after the Trophies of Marius, toward the churches of Saint Bibiana and Saint Crucis, an ancient marble was once placed. It was later transferred to the portico of Saint Bibiana, where we read the following inscription:

> “This is the road by which one goes to the place that in ancient times was called Ursus Pileatus and in modern times the monastery of Saint Bibiana. In this place were buried five thousand two hundred and sixty [Col. 0141D] bodies of holy martyrs,” etc.

The often-mentioned Canon Boldettus testifies to this in his observations on the *Cemeteries*, book II, chapter 18, p. 537. He also asserts that, despite every diligence, he was never able to uncover any traces of subterranean crypts around that church, even after sending into a nearby well excavators skilled in such investigations.

He therefore rightly concludes that this cemetery was constructed above ground at a time when a suitable place was being sought to receive the bodies of holy martyrs from the suburban crypts. Cemeteries of this kind are likewise occasionally mentioned at the title of the Twelve Holy Apostles and at the collegiate church of Saint Mary of the Martyrs, marked by the relics of saints.

Indeed, he aptly observes that when repositories for martyrs were constructed in those sacred buildings, the name of the cemeteries from which the relics had been transported there was transferred to the buildings themselves. Thus, at the title of the Holy Apostles, the name of the cemetery of Apronianus was adopted when many relics of saints were brought there from the cemetery of that man, situated on the Latin Way [Col. 0142A].

Conversely, the name of a new cemetery arose from the particular church where relics brought from one or more cemeteries were deposited, as happened at Saint Mary of the Martyrs. At the beginning of the seventh century, under the emperor Phocas, Saint Boniface IV deposited there the sacred remains of several cemeteries during the dedication of that church.

Sometimes, however, the name of a new cemetery was applied to designate an older one, in whose place it had been substituted for the protection of the bodies of the saints. That this occurred at Saint Bibiana’s, at Ursus Pileatus, is shown by the observation of the same writer, who reports that Cencius Camerarius described it as follows: “The cemetery at Ursus Pileatus at Saint Bibiana.” He also lists among the certain and distinguished martyrs buried there Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice. Their sacred bodies and an ancient inscription were preserved by the altar of our Liberian basilica, having been brought from the church of Saint Bibiana, and are still retained there. They had been transferred [Col. 0142B] by Pope Simplicius from the Portuensian Way, as Baronius testifies under the year 1123.

Thus the name Ursus Pileatus could equally have been applied to the cemetery on the Portuensian Way, so that it would be understood that the cemetery of Ursus Pileatus at Saint Bibiana contained those martyrs who were excavated from the former cemetery after it had been so stripped on the Portuensian Way.

Let this be said to indicate the origin of the later cemeteries in the City, where Roman law prohibited the burial of the dead during the earlier centuries of the Christian era, and to clarify the names of the two cemeteries at Ursus Pileatus, where the ancient church lists and our Librarian report that the holy pontiffs Anastasius and Innocent were buried.

[Note: [Col. 0142B]

**Line 1.**—“Anastasius,” etc. He held office for two years. As Jerome says to Principia, Rome did not deserve to have him for long, lest the head of the world should be struck down under such a bishop; for not long after his death Rome was captured by the Goths.

**Line 5.**—“Via Mamertinia.” This is an error: it should be *Mamurrina*, from the houses of Mamurra located there.]

[Note: [Col. 0142C]

**Line 3.**—“He enacted a decree concerning the Church.” We have already said, in the section on Siricius, that Rufinus of Aquileia, the most vigorous defender of Origen, spread his errors at Rome and, after translating his books *Periarchon* into Latin, served the Romans poison in a golden cup. For this reason Saint Jerome exposed the perfidy of Rufinus’s translation and refuted Rufinus’s version in Letter 65, addressed to Pammachius and Oceanus.

Rufinus attempted to repel Jerome’s accusations in a twofold apology, to which Saint Jerome likewise opposed a twofold apology. As the dispute grew heated and divided the Romans and other Christians throughout the world into opposing parties, Pope Anastasius branded the errors of Origen with the mark of heresy. Theophilus of Alexandria testifies to this in a letter to certain monks, quoted by Justinian in the *Treatise to Menas*, and Saint Jerome does so in book II of his *Apology*, chapter 6.

Moreover, Anastasius summoned Rufinus to Rome to give an account of himself. Rufinus evaded the pontiff’s summons with frivolous excuses and sent him a profession of faith instead. Anastasius therefore proscribed the books *Periarchon*, corrected and condemned Rufinus the translator, condemned Origen the author, alarmed the people by imperial edicts, and accused John, bishop of Jerusalem and supporter of Rufinus and Origen. He seriously warned him not to allow himself to be deceived by a defender of error.

These facts are established by that celebrated letter, full of apostolic vigor, which Pope Anastasius addressed to the aforementioned John, bishop of Jerusalem. In it the pontiff speaks as follows:

> “We have indeed condemned the writings and errors of Origen. As for the translator, since he has not sufficiently cleared himself either by his preface to Origen’s books or by the apology sent to us—and indeed perhaps in reality agrees with the same errors—we summoned him to Rome for judgment before the apostolic see; and when he refused to come, we included him under the same sentence. We have written the letter of condemnation to our brothers Venerius, bishop of Milan, and Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia.”

There can be no doubt about the authenticity of these letters, since Saint Jerome, in book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*, writes that Anastasius sent letters by which he pursued Origen throughout the world; and that, after receiving them, he compelled Venerius of Milan and Chromatius of Aquileia to convene synods in which, with the same judgment and therefore with the same spirit, they denounced Origen as a heretic to the people.

Anastasius also sufficiently demonstrates that he had condemned Rufinus by the final words of the letter: “Let him himself see where he can be absolved.” A little earlier the letter says:

> “I could not remain silent about this also, which I rejoice has happened: responses have come forth from our most blessed rulers, by which everyone serving God may be recalled from reading Origen; and the sentence of the rulers has thus preceded the form of my own judgment against anyone whom profane reading has revealed to be guilty.”

Regarding these words, Garnerius, in his notes on that letter, printed in volume I of the works of Marius Mercator, p. 109, says: “Jerome mentions the imperial rescripts against the Origenists in these words, *Apology I against Rufinus*: ‘The rescripts of the emperors ordering that the Origenists be driven from Alexandria and Egypt were also drafted at my suggestion.’”

The Annotator of Baronius proves that this condemnation of Origen and Rufinus occurred in the year 401, and that the letter was likewise sent by Pope Anastasius in that year, in the note for that year, no. IX and following.

In the same year, 401, Baronius reports that a delegation was sent to Pope Anastasius from the Council of Carthage, after another council had also been celebrated at Carthage on the Ides of September [Col. 0143C] of that year, from all the provinces of Africa. The earlier council had been celebrated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July; Baronius believes that this latter synod was convened at the suggestion of Anastasius himself.

Since both synods were convened in the same year, they are presented under the name of a single Fifth Council in the ancient Collection. On both synods one should consult Marca, *Dissertation on the Ancient Collection*, chapters 8 and 9, and Schelstratius, dissertation III, *On the African Church*, chapter 10, who gives further details about the canons enacted in those synods. Baronius adds that the letter which the pontiff wrote to the African bishops is missing.

The *Liber Pontificalis* writes concerning Saint Anastasius:

> “He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but should stand bowed.”

Baronius believes that this decree was occasioned by the dispute that had arisen at Rome in those times between priests and deacons. The deacons, administering the affairs of the Church, despised the priests; the priests, however, rose up against them and maintained, according to the rule prescribed by the custom of the Roman Church, that while the priests were seated, the deacons ought to stand.

But the dispute advanced so far that even when the standing deacons read the Gospel before the people, the priests would not rise, thereby humiliating the deacons still further. Pope Anastasius corrected this by a decree, if credence is to be given to the *Liber Pontificalis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0143D]

**Line 3.**—“He enacted a decree concerning the Church.” Namely, in the case of the Origenists. On this matter see Somier, book IV of the *History of the Dogmas of the Holy See*, at the end of chapter 3 and chapter 4.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius and in his *Apology against Rufinus*, relates that John, bishop of Jerusalem, was reported to Pope Siricius by Saint Epiphanius as a supporter of Origen’s errors, and that Rufinus, imbued with the same errors, cleverly disguised himself so that he obtained from that pontiff letters of communion, which he used everywhere. Under the pontificate of Anastasius the fraud was detected, and its author was proscribed by the apostolic see.

The Origenism chiefly at issue here consisted of eight principal articles, on which John, bishop of Jerusalem, was accused by Saint Epiphanius as having drawn them from Origen’s works. Rufinus had brought the same errors from the East. “Eight heads of accusation have been brought against you,” says Saint Jerome (Letter 61). “First: it is held to be unknown that the Son can see the Father,” etc.

Before judgment was rendered at Rome against Rufinus, who had been accused on these same matters, the apostolic see, with its customary prudence in such cases, prepared the case. Letters were sent to Jerome, then working in the East, requesting from him a faithful translation of Origen’s book *On First Principles*, or *Periarchon*. It was of the greatest importance to know its legitimate meaning, since Rufinus was accused of having rendered it perversely.

Several people were heard who, after being led by Rufinus into his errors, had later returned to the sound doctrine of the Church. Pope Anastasius himself wrote to Rufinus more than once, ordering him to appear before the apostolic tribunal and clear himself of the charge that he shared a false doctrine.

After these preliminaries, Anastasius formally proscribed Origenism, as Saint Jerome explained in his letter to Pammachius and Marcella:

> “Although it has been spread abroad in a celebrated discourse that the blessed Pope Anastasius also, with the same fervor—for he possesses the same spirit—pursued the heretics hiding in their pits, and although his letters show that what was condemned in the East was condemned in the West, we pray that he may live many years, so that, through his efforts, the resurgent plantings of heresy may wither and die after a long time.”

The churches of Milan and Aquileia, to which the decision was sent [Col. 0144C], received Anastasius’s definition against Origenism with the obedience and eagerness that were due; soon the entire Christian world received it with the same reverence and joy.

Rufinus, uselessly prolonging the matter by various tricks, finally sent his apology and profession of faith to Pope Anastasius. It was full of confidence but empty of that detestation of the errors which he was especially expected to express:

> “I judged it equitable,” he says, “to satisfy Your Blessedness by my letter—not to wipe away the stain of suspicion from your holy mind, which, like a sanctuary of God, receives nothing unjust, but to offer you, against those who perhaps bark at me out of rivalry, a kind of staff of my confession by which they might be driven away.”

But the pontiff perceived that Rufinus’s apology did not sufficiently clear him of contamination by the errors of Origen, on account of which the trial had been instituted. He therefore struck down the contumacious man with a sentence of condemnation, as is expressed in the letter Anastasius sent to John, bishop of Jerusalem. That letter contains a splendid testimony to the steadfastness of the Roman Church in preserving the deposit of faith:

> “With this thought, therefore, I have granted that the man who exposed to the people of our City the transferred reading of Origen, as though casting upon pure minds a kind of cloud, sought by crooked winding paths to dissolve the faith of the apostles, established by the tradition of our forefathers. I approve him if he accuses the author and exposes his detestable deed to the people, so that the man whom rumor had long since bound may at last be held by rightful hatred. But if the translator shows himself satisfied with the errors of so many evils and exposes impious doctrines for the people to read, he has built by his labor nothing other than an attempt, as though by the judgment of his own mind, to overturn under the title of an unexpected assertion this faith—which alone and first among Catholic Christians is held as true from the apostles down to the present time. Let this be far from the Roman Church; let Catholic discipline never admit it. It will certainly never happen that we admit by any reasoning what we rightly and deservedly condemn. Therefore, may the providence of Christ our God, spread throughout the whole world, deign to approve that we cannot accept anything that stains the Church, overturns established customs, wounds the ears of those standing by, or arranges quarrels, anger, and dissensions,” etc.

Those who write about ecclesiastical affairs ought certainly to keep these distinguished marks of pontifical authority before their eyes and present them to others, rather than disseminating truncated or ambiguous testimonies, which they foolishly strive to spread among the public in order to undermine that authority against all right.

**Line 5.**—“He decreed that no foreigner should be received into the clergy in any manner unless he produced the written attestation of five bishops, on account of the Manichaeans.” See Somier, chapter V, under the year 401. Two councils were celebrated at Carthage, the first on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June and the second on the Ides of September, in which we find distinguished testimonies.

Pope Anastasius, together with Venerius of Milan and other bishops sitting in council, had forbidden clerics of the Donatist Church to be received into the Catholic clergy, even if they renounced the schism. But the African Fathers gathered at Carthage for the council on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, considering the extreme need of the churches established throughout Africa for clergy to be supplied to them, sent delegates and letters to Saint Anastasius, and likewise to Venerius, asking them to relax something of the discipline of the decree until they could be relieved from the shortage of ministers in the African Church.

“Let letters be sent to our brothers and fellow bishops, and especially to the apostolic see,” etc. From these testimonies it is clear that the African churches recognized a superior authority in the region beyond the sea, in Italy. They acknowledged that laws could be given to them by that authority, and understood and promised that they themselves had to obey them completely—in this case, to observe them exactly concerning the Donatists. For the rest, see the notes of Pagius.]

[Col. 0129]

**56**

Anastasius, a Roman by nation, son of Maximus, held office for two years and twenty-four days. [Note: [Col. 0129] B: four years, one month, and thirteen days, from the consulship of Honorius IV and Eutychianus to that of Honorius and Arcadius V.] He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, [Note: [Col. 0129] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 402, p. 159.] the priests should not sit but should stand bowed. He enacted a decree concerning the Church. He built the basilica called Crescentiana in the second region, on the Mamertine Way [Note: [Col. 0129] C: *Mamurtina*. *Mamurrina*.], in the City of Rome. He also decreed that no foreigner should be received into the rank of the clergy in any manner unless he produced the written attestation of five bishops, on account of the Manichaeans.

He held two ordinations in the month of December: nine priests [Note: [Col. 0129] C, B: eight], five deacons, and eleven bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 0129] C, B: ten]. He was buried in his own cemetery at Ursus Pileatus on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopate remained vacant for twenty-one days.

No. 57, line 3.—“And concerning the rules of monasteries.” From where the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* took the statement that Innocent I issued a decree concerning the rules of monasteries is entirely unknown to me, for there is nothing on this matter in the Second Catalogue, compiled in the time of the emperor Justinian [Col. 0149C]. Lucas Holstenius notes concerning these words: “Here the writer’s ignorance is apparent.” Nevertheless, I am surprised that a learned man noticed this, for monks had come to Rome since the time of Damasus under the leadership of Saint Athanasius, and Saint Jerome had instructed Roman virgins and matrons in the practices of female monasticism. Thus Innocent I, who flourished long after Damasus, could have issued statutes concerning the rules of monasteries, especially since Siricius, Innocent’s predecessor, had wished those returning from the Manichaean heresy to be confined in monasteries to perform penance, as we noted above.]

[Note: [Col. 0149C]

No. 57, line 2.—“He enacted a decree concerning the whole Church and concerning the rules of monasteries.” Innocent I gave rules to the monks, which are now missing. At that time Augustine gave a rule to religious women. We have Augustine himself as a witness in Letter 109, which contains the rule. [Col. 0149D] Before Siricius, monks were outside the clergy. Siricius I wished and ordered monks to be ordained as clerics, in canon “Monks,” question 1, canon 16.

**Line 25.**—“Three silver baptismal chalices, each weighing [an unspecified number of] pounds.” Innocent offered silver chalices for baptism. In the churches there were chalices dedicated to baptism—that is, for administering Holy Communion to the baptized—because the baptized were admitted to Holy Communion immediately after baptism, under both kinds, as was customary in that age. Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 9:

> “He also then receives for the first time a ring, with which, after being questioned concerning the pledge of faith, he seals it; and thereafter he feeds upon the abundance of the Lord’s body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149D]

No. 57, line 2.—“He enacted a decree concerning the whole Church.” He then briefly reviews what Innocent decreed. Since the compiler of these additions to the catalogues presents the matter as though it were well known, he did not state the subjects of those constitutions, because their memory had been preserved somewhere in an accessible codex. That this was a particular codex of Innocent, called by him the *Book of Rules*, in which these decrees were contained, seems to be proved by the words of Innocent himself to Vitricius of Rouen, written at the very beginning of the letter [Col. 0150C]:

> “It will be your duty, through the neighboring parishes and our fellow priests who preside over their own churches in those regions, to make this book of rules known diligently, as a kind of little textbook and guide, so that they may both know our practices and, by diligent instruction, be able to shape the conduct of those who come together in faith.”]

### Line 3.—And concerning the rules of monasteries

Heterodox writers, and some even among our own, consider this addition unreasonable, since it asserts that monasteries were then multiplying, whereas they believe that there were no monasteries at all in the City. But this is foolish. The destruction of the pagan shrines by the law issued by Theodosius at Sirmium could have provided an opportunity for the associations located beside those shrines to be converted into monasteries. For no one who has even tasted learning with the tips of his lips can be unaware that there were spacious houses at Rome serving as residences for the leaders of religious associations. The most famous among these was that of the Salii. There were also groups called “brothers,” and their inscriptions [Col. 0150D] show their locations and associations, which learned men have elucidated.

That monks then existed in Italy is taught by the letter that the aged Jerome wrote to Paulinus concerning the establishment of a monk. It is expressed more clearly in Letter 16 to Principia, where he writes:

> “The suburban estate was your monastery, and the chosen countryside your solitude; and you lived in this way for so long that, in imitation of you, we rejoiced that Rome had become Jerusalem. There were frequent monasteries of virgins and an innumerable multitude of monks, so that, because of the number of those serving God, what had formerly been a disgrace afterward became a glory.”

### Line 4.—He banished them to monasteries

This was what Siricius had previously decreed concerning the Manichaeans, from which their practice may be established. The penalties of exile and relegation could more easily be carried out in the circumstances of that period, since after the year 388 the laws of Theodosius had been promulgated, imposing exile and relegation upon all heretics.

**Ibid.: “And here he found Pelagius.”** The *Liber Pontificalis* recounts all these matters in a single [Col. 0151A] period, by which it seems to indicate that those matters too were preserved in the *Book of Constitutions*. It is said that he found Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, first through the private letters of bishops and of others who had initially learned of the matter, then through their synodical letters, and finally condemned them.

Private letters were, as it were, exhortatory letters urging that some action be taken. Saint Augustine distinguishes them from synodical letters in a letter written to Paulinus, or Boniface, explaining that the synodical letters contained reports addressed to the apostolic see, while others were addressed to Innocent. He begins as follows:

> “Accordingly, reports concerning this matter were sent from the two councils, the Carthaginian and the Milevitan, to the apostolic see . . . . . . We also wrote to the pope Innocent of blessed memory, on account of the reports of the councils, a private letter in which we dealt somewhat more fully with the matter itself. He replied to everything in the manner in which it was right and proper for the bishop of the apostolic see to reply.”

Just as there were distinctions among the letters that were sent, so the pontiff responded appropriately in the same manner. Catholics made use of this distinction at the celebrated conference, when the letters of Mensurius, primate of Carthage, to Secundus of Tigisis were produced. For, as Saint Augustine states in the brief account, chapter 13, at the end:

> “The Catholics patiently listened while these letters of Mensurius and Secundus were read to the end, although they testified that they were private letters and did not pertain to the cause of the Church.”

They gathered the distinction, of course, from the customary features of the letters. Thus the discovery of the heresiarchs was made through private letters; but an authoritative condemnation followed, at the request of the bishops, after reports had been made to the apostolic see. For the Carthaginian and Milevitan councils, having examined the case, made the pontiff better informed through their synodical reports, so that he might confirm the acts of the council by his own authority and supreme right.

The Carthaginian Fathers state in their synodical report:

> “We judged that the authors of this kind of persuasion, Pelagius and Coelestius, ought to be anathematized.”

This was done so that the authority issuing from the apostolic see might be accepted by the whole world, as the following words of the synodical letter imply:

> “We therefore thought that this act, brother lord, ought to be made known to your holy charity, so that, for the protection of the salvation of many and the correction of the perversity of certain others, the authority of the apostolic see might also be applied to the decisions of our mediocrity.”

In the same sense the Milevitan Fathers wrote in their synodical letter:

> “Because the Lord has placed you in the apostolic see through the special gift of his grace, and has given you such a position in our times that, if we remain silent before your reverence about what ought to be suggested for the Church, this will count against us as the guilt of negligence more than it could count against you if you received these things either with disdain or negligently, we ask that you deign to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers of Christ’s weakened members,”

and so forth. The remaining passages that are cited likewise show that the distinction assigned here is well established.

Prosper confirms this explanation in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, when he writes concerning the Pelagians:

> “The Roman See of Peter first cut down  
> the advancing pest,  
> that, made the head of the world in pastoral honor,  
> holds by religion whatever it does not possess by arms.”

In the same sense the Fathers of the council of Jerusalem under John had proceeded. Orosius, in his *Apology*, after reporting the proceedings in chapters 2, 3, and 4, brings the debate to an end as follows:

> “At last Bishop John, after our final request and proposal that brothers and letters be sent to blessed Innocent, the Roman pope, with all agreeing to follow whatever he should decide . . . . we all agreed upon this judgment: after giving thanks, making peace, and completing a prayer as a testimony to peace, we departed.”

Although Jansenius calls these Acts spurious, Garnerius, in Dissertation 2 addressed to Marius Mercator, in his notes on Book I of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 7, and most recently the Benedictine Fathers in the preface to volume X of the works of Saint Augustine, defend them [Col. 0152A] against such an accusation. What Innocent did is clear from the sentence he pronounced against the heresiarchs.

### Line 6.—He must be reborn again through baptism

By these words the pontiff proscribes the first error of the Pelagians. Since they denied original sin, they consequently considered the administration of baptism useless for its remission. This error was, as it were, the foundation of all the others. Marius sets it forth in the preface to his book of annotations as follows:

> “The progenitors of the human race, Adam and Eve, were created mortal by God; and none of their descendants was harmed by their transgression, but they harmed only themselves and were themselves alone guilty before God—nothing else at all.”

Innocent therefore declared that baptism had been instituted for the remission of original sin, and that no one should be regarded as a Christian unless, having died to original sin, he were reborn through baptism. Hence the fifth proposition of Coelestius proscribed by Zosimus was:

> “Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

From the *Commonitory* of Mercator.

### Line 8.—Through the devotion of a certain distinguished woman, Vestina . . .

The acts here recorded, consisting of gifts of movable property, and the possessions afterward assigned to the Church and listed below, could have been extracted by the *Liber Pontificalis* from documents preserved in the Church itself, where ordinarily both wills, gifts offered to the Church, and benefactors are recorded. The distinguished editor, born to illuminate secular and sacred learning, explained this in detail in the preface to the preceding volume.

Among the pagan peoples, such numerical lists of gifts and property were found engraved on tablets. Gruter supplies several examples. We have selected one that was found mutilated at Smyrna and belonged to the Smyrnaean Gymnasium, where Lucius Vestinus is also mentioned. The fragment reads:

> “During this praetorship, the following made promises: Claudius Bassus, president of the contests, to roof the palace of Nemesis; Fuscus, to execute work costing eight minae; Chersiphron, Asiarch, the gardens at the Palm Grove; Lucius Pompeius, five minae for the Palm Grove. Lucius Vestinus, to roof that part of the palace adjoining the curia and to make bronze doors. Smaragdus, prytanis, to construct the shrine of Fortuna at the Palm Grove; Claudianus, to gild the roof of the place designated for anointing the senators. Others likewise promised, in the sanctuary’s *pulvinar*—that is, the place of supplication—a column with a twisted capital.

> “Nymphidia the chief priestess; Claudius Artemilla; Claudius Polla; Claudius Niceta; Theudianus; Stephanophorus II; Flavius Asclepa; Isidorus the Sophist; Antonia Magna, one mina; Claudius Ariston; Albidia Magna, one mina; Claudius Hedia, one mina; Claudius Charis, one mina; Claudius Leontion, one mina; Claudius Aurelia: three twisted columns for the Palm Grove. The Jews who had recently arrived, one mina. Metrodorus, son of Nicanor. Dicenus, seven denarii for the Palm Grove. C.I.C. S. Murruus and Cilianus, two minae.

> “And what we received from the lord Caesar Hadrian through Antonius Pelomon, in accordance with the senatorial decree, at the time when we had twice been appointed keepers: a sacred contest; immunity; theologians; singers of hymns; one hundred and fifty myriads; columns for the place of anointing, seven hundred and three Synnadic, twenty Numidian, and ninety porphyry columns. A sundial was also constructed by Sextus, the pontifex maximus.”

Such was the care of an earlier age in preserving the memory of benefactors. Christians, reforming this practice according to a better institution, gave it a place; and from this the *Liber Pontificalis*, whether through the labor and diligence of its compiler or of later additions, preserved for memory the fragments collected from books, marbles, inscriptions, and similar sources.

### Number 58, line 19.—To be carefully governed, administered, and adorned by the presbyters Leopardus and Paulinus

Here we first encounter mention of several presbyters governing the same Church, and indeed exercising authority, as the following words make clear: “And by the disposition of Vestina, authority was granted to the presbyters of the aforesaid title.”

From this it also seems necessary to infer that, when the number of deacons and presbyters is assigned in the lives of individual pontiffs, this should be understood only of the ordination of persons to rank and to the designation of churches, or titular churches, and not as meaning that he ordained only those persons and no others.

For when several presbyters are mentioned, while the number of ordained deacons does not exceed seven, it would follow that the presbyters who were appointed had not previously been deacons—something wholly foreign to the customs of the Church. Moreover, it is certain that subdeacons, acolytes, and lectors existed in the Roman Church, as the letter of Cornelius to Fabius most clearly attests; nevertheless, their ordination is not recorded.

Thus others were ordained along with those whom the pontiffs appointed to care for the churches, so that there would be several available in due time to be advanced to the dignity either of presbyter or of deacon in the Roman Church, while the others remained in their proper ministry. This is clearly indicated here because Leopardus and Paulinus—certainly to be read as Ursicinus—had previously been simple presbyters, and by Vestina’s disposition had received authority over the basilica of Saint Agnes [Col. 0153B]. That authority is explained here by the words “to govern, administer, and adorn”; and they became presbyters of the title of Saint Agnes, that is, they obtained that dignity. Their responsibility for revenues, properties, estates, and so forth will be noted below and is certainly presupposed here.

[Note: [Col. 0153B]

### Number 57, line 2.—He made a decree concerning the whole Church

That is, a decree pertaining to the universal Church.

### Lines 4 and 5.—He found Pelagius and Coelestius

Concerning this condemnation, Saint Prosper, in his work *Against the Collator*, reports the following from the words of Pope Zosimus:

> “We have established that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Innocent, issued from the see of the most blessed Apostle, shall remain in force until they openly confess the grace of God,”

and so forth.

### Lines 6 and 7.—To be baptized, which Pelagius condemned

[Col. 0153C] In his letter written to Innocent, as Augustine relates in *On Original Sin*, chapter 17, Pelagius complained that he was being maliciously defamed on this point. “He says,” Augustine writes in the passage mentioned, “that he is defamed by people who claim that he denies the sacrament of baptism to infants and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption.”

Accordingly, when it is said here that Pelagius denied baptism to infants, this must be understood to mean that, even if not in words, he could nevertheless appear to have denied it in practice, since he denied original sin, on account of which baptism is necessary for infants.

[Note: [Col. 0153C]

## Chronological Notes

There is no need to add more in order to confirm the chronology of the pontificate of the blessed Pope Innocent I, since it has been sufficiently demonstrated in number 55, concerning Saint Siricius, where the periods of the three pontiffs are established by clear evidence.

[Col. 0153D] One difference remains to be disentangled from the reckoning of this period in the Chronicle of Idacius, a difference long ago noted by several chronologists.

“Bishop Idacius,” says Cardinal Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, Book I, chapter 11, p. 72, “who lived in his youth under Innocent, marks the beginning and end of Innocent’s pontificate by two celestial signs. In the eighth year of Arcadius, a solar eclipse occurred on the third day before the Ides of November, on the second day of the week. Innocent is recorded as the thirty-eighth bishop of the Roman Church. He designates the year of Innocent’s death by another eclipse: in the twenty-fourth year of Honorius, a solar eclipse occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, which was the fifth day of the week. Zosimus is bishop of the Roman Church XXXIX.”

The beginning of Innocent’s pontificate is correctly placed in the eighth year of Arcadius—who began to rule with his brother Honorius on 17 January 395—namely, in the year 402, and so forth.

The most learned cardinal corrects three matters in the text of Idacius. First, he corrects the weekday of both solar eclipses. He shows that the first, on the third day before the Ides of November, should be assigned to the third day of the week, not the second. He likewise advises, together with the principal chronologists, especially Petavius, that a similar correction be made in the weekday of the second solar eclipse, in the year 402, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, where the fifth day is incorrectly given instead of the sixth. [Col. 0154A]

The second error of Idacius concerns the number assigned in the succession. Cardinal Noris shows that Innocent ought to be called the fortieth pontiff from blessed Peter in the Roman chair, and Zosimus the forty-first. We likewise judge this correction necessary.

The third matter he presents for correction concerns the year in which Innocent began his administration. Noris supposes that he was elected in the year 402, but we do not accept this, since it has been established that his predecessor Anastasius died before the end of the year 401—as was proved shortly beforehand and can be confirmed by the evidence cited in Pagi’s *Annals* under the year 402, numbers 16 and 17, and also under 417, number 4, although I do not agree with him concerning the day of the death—not around the end of April in the year 402, as writers of the preceding century believed, and as Noris followed them in believing, since the ancient Martyrology edited by Florentinius had not yet been published.

[Col. 0154B] From this we learn again that the deposition of Saint Innocent the pope is assigned to 12 March, as the elder Pagi gathered from several Martyrologies under the year 417, numbers 5 and 6; and that one of the translations of his relics belongs to 28 June, the day on which it is celebrated.

We, without changing the day of his deposition as asserted in these Martyrologies, assigned his death, on the basis of the documents previously produced in the chronological notes concerning Siricius, to 14 February of the year 417, in which year Zosimus is now known to have succeeded him and to have celebrated Easter.

We therefore accept, with Noris, that one day should be added to the number of each weekday in Idacius. I maintain that the eighth year of Arcadius could also have been associated there with the first year of Innocent’s pontificate during the first quarter of the year 417, before Easter, according to the customary method of the chronologists of that age. They commonly referred the years of emperors, especially Eastern emperors, to the turning of the indiction in September, but the years of Roman pontiffs to the epoch of the Easter festival celebrated by them.

Since Innocent succeeded Anastasius around the end of the year 401, the first year of his pontificate was still running at the next Easter, in the year 402. At that time the eighth year of Arcadius could also have been marked, with the indiction noted as beginning in his eighth year and still running at Easter 402.

For Theodosius, the father of Arcadius, assigns a date of the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February in the year 394, while indiction VII was running—the indiction that had begun in September 393—and this year was attributed to his father Theodosius, whose life had continued into its beginning. The following indiction, VIII, which began in September of the year 394, affected the first year then running of Arcadius’s reign.

Therefore, after seven years had elapsed from that point, namely in September of the year 401, indiction XV began to be numbered. It then coincided with the eighth year of Arcadius’s reign and continued until September of the year 402. Thus the Roman year 402, from the Kalends of January, presented an indiction coinciding with the eighth year of Arcadius and with the first Easter year of Innocent, who had not yet celebrated the second Easter of his pontificate.

[Col. 0154D] Thus, by reckoning the time of Easter in the case of pontiffs and the indiction in the case of emperors, it comes about that the eighth year of Arcadius coincides in Idacius with the first year of Innocent, and the twenty-fourth year of Arcadius with the first year of Zosimus, who succeeded Innocent before Easter in the year 417.

## Historical Notes

### Number 57, line 2.—He made a decree concerning the whole Church, etc.

Pagi observes, from number 3 through number 18, that Innocent’s principal constitutions are contained in three decretal letters of his. The first is dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus VI and Aristaenetus, namely in the year of Christ 404, and is addressed to Victricius, bishop of Rouen. The second was issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius—that is, in the year 405—to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse. The third is dated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus VII and Palladius, in the year of Christ 416. For the rest of his decretals, see number XIX [Col. 0155A] below. Other letters of Innocent, besides the decretals, remain; Pagi examines them in the following numbers.

### Line 3.—And concerning the rules of monasteries

It is certainly remarkable that sensible men should be found who maintain that Innocent could not possibly have written rules for monasteries, when it is clear from the books of the holy Fathers that, both in the East and in the West, the principal monastic rules were being formulated in this same age of Innocent.

To say nothing of the legislators of the Eastern monks who were contemporaries of Innocent—Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Athanasius, and Cyril—among the Western teachers of monks Jerome alone displays a whole phalanx in Gaul. There he indicates to the monk Rusticus that Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, was a teacher; to him Innocent had shortly before sent the famous decretal mentioned by us. Alongside Exuperius he presents the holy and learned bishop Proculus, who, he says, “surpasses our little writings by his living and present voice and directs your path through daily discourses.”

In Gaul, Hilary and Martin opened schools for monks and handed down rules in the age of Jerome and Innocent. Eucherius, Maximus, and Lupus, together with the Hilary already mentioned, learned the same rules under Honoratus on the island of Lérins near Marseille, as Cardinal Noris proves in *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 1.

What more is needed? At this time almost every bishop was establishing a manner of coenobitic life among his clergy. Thus Augustine did so in Africa, Patrick in Ireland, Germanus among the people of Auxerre, Paulinus at Nola, and others in various places. See the notes of Schelestratius and Pagi, note 11 on this number.

### Lines 3 and 4.—And he found many Cataphrygians in the City, whom he banished into exile and to monasteries

The heresy of the Cataphrygians, disseminated by Montanus from Phrygia, held impious opinions concerning the divine Persons among its other errors, as we learn from Letter 54 of Saint Jerome. Baronius shows that their baptism was rejected both by the Council of Laodicea and by the Council of Nicaea under the years 314 and 325.
