It is clear that survivors of this group remained in the City from the letter of Jerome cited above, since a certain follower of Montanus had whispered to Marcella testimonies from the Gospel of John twisted to support his heresy.

Against these plotters against the Catholic religion, therefore, Innocent’s apostolic care exercised the authority of judicial power. Accordingly, Socrates writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 9:

> “Anastasius was succeeded by Innocent, who was indeed the first to begin persecuting the Novatians living at Rome and deprived them of many churches. He punished the obstinate with exile; those who repented he confined in monasteries”—as Jerome indicates in Letter 4 to Rusticus—“so that there they might practice, under the obedience of a superior, a strict way of life according to the approved rules of the holy Fathers, which would be highly beneficial to them, since they had previously followed the superstitious fasts of Montanus and had thus imposed upon themselves punishments that were not only ineffective but hateful to God.”

Nor was there no monastery near the City at this time. Cardinal Noris points out that a monastery constructed outside the Angelican Gate, one mile from the City, called Pinetum and described by Rufinus, existed during this period. See *History of Pelagianism*, p. 19, at the end of chapter 2.

### Lines 4 and 5.—And here he found the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius, and condemned them

For a defense of Innocent’s letters and acts against the unjust censures of Erasmus and Vossius, see the vindication undertaken and successfully advanced twelve centuries earlier by Augustine in the passages cited by the most eminent Noris from the works of that Father, *History of Pelagianism*, Book I, chapter 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0155D]

### Number 57, line 1.—Innocent, by nationality an Albanian

In the Roman Martyrology he is called a martyr. He may have been given this name because of his admirable virtue and supreme steadfastness, comparable to the courage of martyrs, which he displayed in every struggle for the defense of the faith and the protection of the Church. His deeds indicate this, and illustrious testimony is provided by Chrysostom; Palladius of Helenopolis, his disciple; Theophilus of Alexandria; Saint Jerome in his letter to Demetrias; Saint Augustine in many letters and in his book *Against Julian*; and also by the Fathers of the Carthaginian and Milevitan councils.

### Number 58, line 23.—Buried at Ursus Pileatus

That the body of Saint Innocent was buried at Ursus Pileatus, at Saint Bibiana, and was afterward transferred to the title of Equitius—that is, to Saints Martin and Sylvester on the Esquiline—is taught by an ancient inscription placed there.]

[Note: [Col. 0156A]

### Number 57, line 2.—He made a decree concerning the whole Church and concerning the rules of monasteries

Regarding these words, Holstenius notes that they reveal the ignorance of the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*. Schelestratius, however, in a note on those words, wonders that a learned man could have made such an observation:

> “For,” he says, “in the time of Damasus, monks had come to Rome under the leadership of Saint Athanasius; and Saint Jerome had taught Roman virgins and matrons the institutions of nuns, to such an extent that Innocent I, who flourished long after Damasus, could issue regulations concerning the rules of monasteries—especially since Siricius, Innocent’s predecessor, wished those returning from the Manichaean heresy to be confined in monasteries to perform penance, as we said under Siricius, number 10.”

Accordingly, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, Innocent decreed in the tenth decree that monks promoted to the clergy should remain firm in their purpose and observant of monastic discipline.

I am not unaware that heterodox writers attack, or even entirely reject, Innocent’s letter to Victricius of Rouen because it contains certain decrees that are word for word the same as those in a letter of Siricius. But since decrees 12 and 13 of Innocent’s letter, of which the heterodox writers speak, are contained in Innocent’s letter at the Third Council of Tours, held in the year 566 or 567, and were approved there, and since Innocent could not have done better than to transmit the institutions of his predecessors, no one can rightly doubt the authenticity of that decretal letter of Innocent, which Dionysius Exiguus inserted in full into the *Code of the Roman Church*, just as no one can doubt the letter of Siricius, which was praised by the Council of Zell and by Ferrandus.

Innocent the pope wrote this decretal letter to Victricius in the year 404. In it he urges him to make it known to the suffragan bishops and neighboring Churches, so that the practice of the Roman Church might be understood. Innocent calls that letter the *Regulatory Book*, which appears to be none other than the collection of decrees so closely joined to the letter itself that they seem to constitute a part of it.

It contains thirteen decrees. In the third he establishes that cases involving clergy, both of the higher and of the lower order, are to be judged by the bishops of the province according to the Nicene canons, “without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in every case.”

In the twelfth he establishes:

> “Those who have specially married Christ and have deserved to be veiled by a priest, if afterward they marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from this world. Those who, while their husband is still alive, marry another are to be regarded as adulteresses, and permission to perform penance is not to be granted to them unless one of the two has died.”

Finally, in the thirteenth and last decree he establishes:

> “Those who have married after promising that they would always remain in their profession of virginity are to perform penance for a considerable time, even if they have not been veiled.”

The other decrees should be read in the volumes of the Councils.

The second decretal letter of Innocent was issued in the year 405 to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, and contains seven decrees or canons. In the first, he decrees that incontinent clergy, namely priests and deacons, are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor, and he confirms the most sacred law of celibacy imposed upon them by his predecessor Siricius.

In the seventh, he sets out a list of the canonical books and testifies and declares that they have been received by the Church as sacred and divine. When Calvinists and Lutherans read this list, they will recognize themselves as alien from the sense and faith of the ancient Church with respect to the number of canonical books. For Innocent is not merely expressing his own opinion; he is transmitting the doctrine and tradition of the Church, derived from the apostles to his own time and preserved in the Roman Church.

But, to return to Innocent’s letter to Decentius of Gubbio, it proves that the discipline of the Secret was carefully observed in the earliest centuries of the Church. For Innocent, writing to a Catholic bishop, was unwilling to write even about the form of consecration, and likewise not about the form of confirmation. Speaking of this latter sacrament in chapter 3, he says:

> “I cannot state the words, lest I seem to disclose more than to answer the consultation.”

This provides an occasion to discuss that discipline. The well-known statement of Augustine in *Tractate 96 on John* is relevant:

> “The sacraments of the faithful are not disclosed to catechumens.”

Also well known is the statement of that same great doctor of the Church:

> “Catechumens do not know what Christians receive.”

So too the statement of Chrysostom, *Homily 27 on Matthew*:

> “Only the initiated know the mystery of the Eucharist . . . .”

And the statement of Cyril of Jerusalem in his first *Catechesis* to those preparing for baptism:

> “The initiated know the power of this cup; you too shall know it shortly afterward.”

Schelestratius, cited above, demonstrates from Iamblichus, *On the Life of Pythagoras*, Book II, chapter 82, and from Clement of Alexandria, Book V of the *Stromata*, that among the philosophical sects themselves, long before Christ’s coming, it had been observed that the profane were kept away from sacred matters.

Moreover, everyone agrees that this discipline was observed for catechumens, Jews, and pagans, but not for the faithful, or baptized persons, to whom all the mysteries of the Catholic religion could be explained without any circumlocution.

The Fathers believed that they had to follow Christ’s solemn command in Matthew, chapter 7:

> “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw pearls before swine.”

Since the holy Fathers unanimously assert, on the basis of Christ’s words just cited, that the discipline of the Secret was introduced, it is clear that it arose from apostolic tradition. The common agreement of the Churches did not originate in a decree of some particular or general council; rather, all the Churches throughout the world observed the same discipline, without its beginning being traceable to any definite time. Therefore, according to the rule of Saint Augustine, this is one of those things that have reached us through apostolic tradition.

Protestants say that, among the Orthodox, the discipline of the Secret formerly consisted merely in concealing the rites. But there are many testimonies of the holy Fathers from which it can be shown with the greatest clarity that the ancient discipline of the Church was concerned not only with concealing the symbols of the sacraments and their rites, but also with concealing the realities signified by them, or their contents.

There is an especially celebrated testimony from all Italy, which Julius I transmitted in his own name to the Eusebians and which Athanasius presses against those same men in his second *Apology*. The Eusebians were accused not only of having spoken about the chalice and the table in the presence of the prefect, with both pagans and Jews present, but also of having discussed the blood and body of Christ before those same people, with catechumens present as well.

The bishop of all Egypt laments this in these words, in a synodical letter to the whole Church under heaven:

> “In the presence of pagan men they held discussions about the Church, the chalice, the table of the Lord, and the holy of holies.”

For “the holy of holies” must be understood as the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ, which were to be concealed from pagans, Jews, and catechumens, not made public.

[Col. 0158A] Schelestratius then proves from Origen, Book I *Against Celsus*, that the same discipline of the Secret concerning the mystery was received in the Church both with respect to doctrine and with respect to rites.

There Origen enumerates the doctrines that were preached publicly, such as the Incarnation, the Passion, and the Lord’s Resurrection. But he does not speak of the mystery of the most holy Trinity, or of the sacrament of the Eucharist, or of the other sacraments, because these belonged among the things not communicated to everyone, and concerning which the discipline of the Secret had to be observed. He expressly warned of this when he was about to treat of the mystery of the Eucharist in *Homily 13 on Exodus*.

Chrysostom too, in *Homily 40 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, professes that he does not dare to speak about the form of baptism and the Creed, in which the mystery of the most holy Trinity is expounded:

> “I do not dare,” he says, “because of those who are not initiated. They make our exposition more difficult, since they compel us either not to speak openly or to disclose the secrets to them. [Col. 0158B] Nevertheless, I shall say what I can, discreetly and in shadowed form,”

and so forth.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem also, discussing in *Catechesis 6* the mysteries contained in the Creed, says:

> “The Church now discloses these mysteries and sacraments to the one who is departing from the ranks of the catechumens; nor is it customary to explain them to pagans. For we do not declare the mysteries concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to any pagan, nor do we speak openly among catechumens about the mysteries. Rather, we often speak many things secretly, so that the faithful who possess the reality may understand, while those who do not possess it may not be harmed.”

From this discipline of the Secret it arose that, in the first centuries of the Church, no treatises were written on the seven sacraments, of which mention is so frequent in our own times.

Protestants indeed say that the earlier Fathers abstained from commentaries on the seven sacraments because they did not accept that number of sacraments. But this can easily be refuted by the agreement of the Eastern schismatic Church and the Western Orthodox Church. For the Eastern schismatics would not have agreed with the orthodox Latins in one and the same opinion for eight hundred years unless they had received it from their predecessors.

Another explanation must therefore be sought. When treatises on the seven sacraments are published, it is necessary to explain their rites and to determine the matter and form by which they are effected; the doctrine itself concerning everything relating to the consecration and administration of the sacraments cannot be concealed. Yet the ancient discipline of the Church carefully hid these things from the eyes and ears of pagans, Jews, and catechumens. Fearing their profanation, the ancients abstained from discussing them in sermons, took care to avoid them, and did not treat of them in writing.

By contrast, after that discipline had been abolished in the sixth century of the Church, mention of the sacraments became frequent, not only among the Greeks but also among the Latins, at least from the time of Charlemagne. Among the Greeks this occurred after the time of Photius, who, in his *Bibliotheca*, celebrates, on the basis of the monk Jobius, the seven most holy mysteries of the Church of Christ.

The discipline of the Secret, therefore, was the reason that during the first six centuries of the Church Catholic writers abstained from treatises on the sacraments, wrote about them more rarely and obscurely, and were not concerned to enumerate their number.

We have thought it not inappropriate to extract all these matters, on the occasion of the decretal letter of Pope Innocent to Decentius of Gubbio, from Schelestratius’s dissertation cited above. For through this discipline several statements of the Fathers that Protestants bring forward against Catholics can be explained.

Furthermore, we shall discuss approximately when this discipline ceased, both in the East and in the West, in the pontificate of Pope Eugene I.

There is also another decretal letter of Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nucera, consisting of five canons, and another to the bishops of Macedonia. It is quite clear that all of these are extremely rich witnesses to ecclesiastical discipline. Their canons should be read in the *Collection of Councils*. As for the Decretal which he [Col. 0159A] addressed to the Council of Toledo, in order to remedy the collapse of discipline in Spain, especially the abuses of ordinations, in which the canons were being violated with impunity, it was not addressed to the Council of Toledo held during the consulship of Stilicho—for that belongs to the year 400, when Anastasius, not Innocent, was pope—but to another Council of Toledo, convened while Innocent was pope, whose acts have perished.

While Innocent was pope, a great tumult arose at Constantinople in the year 403, and schism was introduced into the Church because of the hatred which Eudoxia Augusta, wife of the emperor Arcadius, bore toward Saint John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople. She was offended because he had delivered an address to the people containing a general denunciation of women. Thinking that the insult had been directed at herself, the Augusta arranged for a council to be convened against him. As Socrates says in book VI, chapter 15, those who were hostile to John for various reasons flocked to it in particular. That assembly was called “at the Oak,” a suburb [Col. 0159B] of Chalcedon. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, presided over it, and thirty-six bishops were present. John was deposed there and sent into exile by the emperor. Shortly afterward he was recalled by imperial order and, when the people asked him to resume his episcopal see and, according to customary practice, to offer the greeting of peace, he replied that this should be done by decree of the judges, and that those by whom he had been condemned ought to reverse their decision and absolve him, as Socrates reports in the cited chapter 16.

For he knew that at the Council of Antioch held in 341 this decree had been enacted: “A bishop deposed by a synod, if he has dared to celebrate the sacred rites, has no permission to return.” Therefore he did not wish to recover his see without the judgment of a greater synod, so that, however the Antiochene canon might be interpreted, he might appear to have observed it. In the end, however, he yielded to the people’s demands. In his edition of the Councils, Baluze composed a history of this synod from an account written by a man who at that time was constantly with Saint Chrysostom—namely Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, whose dialogue on the life of Chrysostom we now possess complete and intact through the efforts of Emeric Bigot.

In the year 404 a new council was convened at Constantinople, at which Saint John was again deposed and again condemned to exile by the emperor Arcadius. At that synod canon 4 of the aforementioned Council of Antioch was read. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria and Chrysostom’s principal adversary, had sent it. It stated:

“If any bishop or presbyter, whether unjustly or justly deposed, returns to the Church on his own authority without a synod, he shall have no place for an excuse, but shall be expelled altogether.”

Yet the canon of the Council of Antioch does not contain the adverb “unjustly.” Chrysostom used a twofold reply. First, he attempted to show that he had satisfied the Antiochene canon. Then, when he still could not escape his adversaries’ accusations, he replied that the canon in question did not apply to the Church of the Catholics [Col. 0159D], but to the Church of the Arians, since the canon produced by Theophilus was entirely different from the canon of the Council of Antioch. For Theophilus’s canon had not been issued by Catholic bishops assembled at Antioch, but by the Eusebians alone after the Antiochene synod, out of hatred for Athanasius. Hence George, patriarch of Alexandria, calls the canons transmitted by Theophilus “adulterated writings bearing a false name.” Schelestratius discusses this matter more fully in Dissertation 5, *On the Council of Antioch*, chapter 6.

That Chrysostom appealed to Pope Innocent after being expelled from his see is clear from the letter of the emperor Honorius to Arcadius, ruling in the East, preserved in Baronius under the year 404, numbers 80 and following. There it is reported that both Chrysostom and Theophilus sent legates to Innocent to convey his judgment concerning the sentence passed against Chrysostom:

“Legates were sent to the priests of the eternal City and to Italy from both sides. A sentence capable of establishing the rule of discipline was awaited from the authority of all. Nothing should have been altered, and everything ought to have remained intact while the considered decision was proceeding. Meanwhile, however, a strange precipitate rush of haste broke out: without waiting for the letters of the priests who had been consulted through the mutual embassies of the parties, and without examining the facts, the bishops were sent into exile, subjected to punishment before they had experienced the judgment of an episcopal tribunal. Finally, the matter itself proved how premature that condemnation had been. For those whose authority had been awaited—namely, the Roman pontiff and his advisers—permitted John to remain in peaceful communion, judged that reconciliation should be effected, and thought that no one ought to be excluded from fellowship before judgment.”

That Innocent rescinded and annulled the sentence of deposition pronounced against Chrysostom by Theophilus of Alexandria and his associates in the year 403, at the synod held at the Oak, is evident from the testimony both of Palladius and of Innocent himself. Palladius [Col. 0160B], in his *Dialogue on the Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, writes:

“To this the blessed Pope Innocent replied. Having admitted both parties to communion, he decreed that the judgment of Theophilus was cancelled and void. He said that another irreproachable synod of Western and Eastern priests ought to be convened, with the friends of the council withdrawing first, and then the enemies; for, in general, neither party’s judgment is entirely sound.”

Innocent, in Letter 31 to Theophilus, which Palladius likewise quotes, writes:

“Brother Theophilus, we have decreed that both you and our brother John belong to our communion, just as we stated clearly enough in our earlier letters. Now, persisting in the same judgment and intention, we write the same things again. And whenever you write, unless a due and appropriate judgment follows, because of the things that have been done with such great disgrace, it is impossible for us to withdraw from communion with John.”

Chrysostom did not appeal to the Roman pontiff only concerning the judgment pronounced against him by Theophilus in the year 403 [Col. 0160C], as we have said; he also appealed concerning the judgment which other bishops, at Theophilus’s instigation, pronounced against him in 404. When the bishops hostile to Chrysostom had condemned him again, he appealed once more to Innocent’s tribunal, as is shown by these words of his letter to Innocent, reported by Palladius:

“Write, I beg you, and decree by your authority that such unjust acts, carried out while we were absent and not avoiding judgment, have no force whatever. Moreover, subject those who committed such acts to ecclesiastical censure. As for us, innocent men who have neither been convicted, nor accused, nor apprehended, nor proved guilty of any crime, command that we be restored to our churches, so that we may enjoy charity and the customary peace with our brethren.”

That Innocent likewise rescinded the sentence pronounced against Chrysostom in this second judgment is demonstrated by Natalis Alexander in Part II of the fourth century, Dissertation 27. In Palladius’s *Dialogue* [Col. 0160D], Theodore, a deacon of the Roman Church, reports the words of the *Commonitorium*—the directive given by Innocent to the legates whom he sent from his side to Constantinople, so that they might attend the synod which he greatly desired to be held for a fuller discussion and final determination of this case. Among other things, this *Commonitorium* states:

“John ought not to enter upon judgment unless the Church and communion were first restored to him, so that, with every occasion for delay removed, he might enter the council of his own accord.”

Theodoret likewise writes in book V, chapter 34:

“The bishops of the West refused to communicate with the bishops of Egypt, the East, the Bosphorus, and Thrace until they had entered the name of that most holy man”—namely John Chrysostom—“in the registers containing the names of deceased bishops; and they did not even deign to greet Arsacius, his successor.”

But Innocent could not decree that the name of Chrysostom, which had been erased from the Church’s registers by decree of the Eastern council, should be restored to those same registers [Col. 0161A] unless the sentence passed against him had first been rescinded.

For this reason Innocent did not admit Alexander, patriarch of Antioch, or Acacius, bishop of Beroea, to apostolic communion until they had made satisfaction for Chrysostom’s memory and restored his name to the sacred diptychs, as is clear from Innocent’s Letter 17 to Alexander and Letter 19 to Acacius of Beroea, in which he decrees the same thing. Hence Pope Gelasius, writing to the bishops of Dardania in Letter 13, testifies that Chrysostom was absolved by the judgment of the apostolic see alone, without any synod. Finally, Facundus, in book VI, teaches that Chrysostom’s condemnation was rescinded by Innocent.

This proof, drawn from Chrysostom’s appeal, is all the more powerful for demonstrating the use of appeals after the Council of Sardica because his case did not concern the faith but merely discipline. Therefore the distinction devised by certain learned men must not be accepted: they admitted that cases of faith could always be referred to the apostolic see through appeals by deposed bishops, but denied this of cases of ecclesiastical discipline. For Natalis Alexander, the authority cited above, demonstrates that this practice prevailed in the Church, both Eastern and Western, for many centuries after the Council of Sardica.

It should nevertheless be observed, with the same learned author, in Part I of the fifth century, chapter 4, *On National and Provincial Councils*, article 2, that Innocent wished Chrysostom’s appeal to be judged by a definitive decision at an ecumenical synod. He made every effort to have such a synod convened because of the danger of schism that threatened if so grave a case were judged with only the bishops of Italy, or even of the entire West. Since most of the Eastern bishops, the emperor Arcadius, and the empress Eudoxia regarded Chrysostom as lawfully deposed, while they revered Arsacius and afterward Atticus, intruders into his see, as legitimate bishops of Constantinople [Col. 0161C], it was to be feared that the Church of the East would completely sever communion with the West if the Roman pontiff reduced Arsacius and then Atticus, the invaders of the see of Constantinople, to proper order and imposed the severity of the canons upon Theophilus and the other bishops allied with him in wickedness and unjust counsels—canons which they had violated with impunity.

Nevertheless, by a provisional decree Innocent rescinded the predatory synod held at the Oak. Finally, by a definitive decree, when no hope remained of holding an ecumenical synod, he compelled the Easterners to restore John Chrysostom’s memory among the bishops of Constantinople in the Church’s diptychs. He did not restore communion with the Easterners until they had carried this out. He then proves at length that communion between the Eastern and Western Churches had been suspended rather than broken, and that the matter had not proceeded as far as schism [Col. 0161D]; only the exchange of *formatae* letters had been interrupted.

**Line 5.—“And he condemned them.”**

During Innocent’s pontificate, a council was convened at Carthage in the year 416 against that heresy. The errors of Pelagius and his disciple Coelestius were condemned there by anathema. Immediately afterward a synod of Numidia was held at Milevis, attended by Augustine; following the example of the Carthaginian synod, it condemned the same errors, although the Fathers of both synods spared the persons of Pelagius and Coelestius. Perhaps this was because Pelagius had fraudulently obtained acquittal at the synod of Diospolis in Palestine in the year 415, or rather because through frequent lies he had avoided condemnation. For Augustine and others present the synod of Diospolis as the first victory over this heresy, although Pelagius was so far from having been absolved there that he rather condemned himself by his own mouth [Col. 0162A], as Augustine frequently reproaches the Pelagians for doing.

After examining the matter, both synods—the Carthaginian and the Milevitan—sent a report to Pope Innocent, so that he might confirm by his authority what the bishops had judged concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius and their heresy. “They reported,” says Marca in *Dissertation on the Ancient Collections of Canons*, chapter 14, “to Pope Innocent, so that he might decide with supreme authority.”

These are the words of the Carthaginian synod:

“We have judged that the authors of this persuasion, Pelagius and Coelestius, ought to be anathematized.”

They define what appears necessary, but they do not pronounce judgment; they reserve this to the supreme see, whose authority extends throughout the whole Church. The following words teach this:

“Accordingly, brother lord, we have thought it necessary to bring this action to the notice of your holy charity, so that, for the protection of the salvation of many and the correction of the perversity of certain others, the authority of the apostolic see may also be applied to the determinations of our modest station.” [Col. 0162B]

The synodical letter of the Council of Milevis has the same purpose. It says that the bishops would be at fault if they kept silent about matters that ought to be brought before the apostolic see for the benefit of the Church. Accordingly, concerning the new heresy they write to Innocent, asking him to apply pastoral care to great dangers:

“Because the Lord has placed you in the apostolic see through the special gift of his grace, and has granted you to our times in such a way that, if we were to remain silent before your veneration about matters that ought to be brought forward for the Church, this would rather count against us as the fault of negligence than that you could receive them either with disdain or carelessness, we beg you to apply pastoral care to the great dangers of Christ’s weak members. For a new and exceedingly dangerous heresy is attempting to rise up, the enemy of God’s grace.”

In addition to the synodical letters of the councils of Carthage and Milevis, five bishops—Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius—wrote other, private letters in their common name to the same Innocent [Col. 0162C]. In them they explained Pelagius’s case, asserting that it was especially Innocent’s concern to remedy so great an evil, because many followers of Pelagian doctrine were in Rome. In his letters to Valentinus—Letter 215, formerly 47, and Letter 186, formerly 106, to Paulinus—Augustine calls these letters not synodical but private.

In the former, he says:

“What was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, at the council of the province of Carthage and by the council of Numidia, and somewhat more carefully by the five bishops,” and so forth.

In the latter, in section 2, he says:

“We also wrote to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, in addition to the reports of the councils, private letters in which we dealt at somewhat greater length with the case itself.”

Pope Innocent replied to the cited synodical letters of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis and to the private letter of the five bishops on the sixth day before the Kalends of February in the year 417 [Col. 0162D]. First, he praises the Fathers of those councils, both because they had formerly pronounced judgment in this case—namely, against Coelestius—and because they now preserved the reverence due to the apostolic see by consulting it and referring everything to its judgment. Innocent is astonished that the Fathers of Diospolis had omitted this. He then adds that the bishops had examined the question and condemned the heresy, but had not yet promulgated their decision, which undoubtedly required the decree of the apostolic see in order to bind everyone.

Finally, after a lengthy discussion, Innocent established two things. First, he condemned Pelagius’s impious doctrine as contrary to the rule of faith:

“Whoever, therefore, appears to assent to this opinion, by saying that we have no need of divine assistance, declares himself an enemy of the Catholic faith and unworthy of its benefits,”

as he says in his letter to the Carthaginian synod.

Next, he separated the authors of the heresy from communion until they should repent. He names them in his reply to the Council of Milevis:

“Therefore, by the authority of apostolic vigor, we judge that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, the inventors of new expressions which, as the Apostle says, produce no edification but are accustomed to give rise to the most empty disputes—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will. Meanwhile, they are not to be received into the Lord’s fold until they are willing to abandon the path of the perverse life which they have followed.”

Since the five bishops named above had warned him in their private letter that Pelagius’s cause was being supported by many people in Rome, and that the synod of Diospolis had been deceived by Pelagius’s ambiguous account of grace, they also added their advice: either that Innocent summon Pelagius to Rome or correspond with him so that he might explain what he understood by grace.

To this letter Innocent replied, as the cited Marca reports, that he did not know whether there were people in Rome who favored Pelagius’s doctrine; at least they were keeping hidden and making no such claims. As for the purgation of Pelagius carried out in the East, he had indeed received episcopal acts brought to him by laymen, but he doubted whether they were genuine. Innocent took no account of the proceedings of the synod of Diospolis and did not regard Pelagius as absolved and cleared of the accusation brought by the Gallican bishops, even if he had been absolved by the synod of Diospolis. He did not summon Pelagius to Rome or correspond with him, as the five bishops had advised; instead, he deprived him of communion after convicting him by his own book.

“Someone may think this impious and contrary to judicial procedure,” Marca continues, “to condemn a man without hearing him. But if one considers the ancient practice, one will find that a person convicted by witnesses of some crime, homicide for example, was immediately excluded from communion, without any prior admonition summoning him to clear himself. The purpose was that, compelled by this censure, he might approach the bishop either to prove his innocence or, by acknowledging the crime, to seek the benefit of penance. This had to be observed all the more carefully in the case of heresy, the disease being one that required more diligent treatment. Accordingly, Innocent rightly and in accordance with that ancient custom adds, speaking of Pelagius:

‘If he has confidence, and knows that what he says is not worthy of our condemnation, namely, that he has now completely rejected everything he had said, he ought not to be summoned by us; rather, he himself should hasten so that he may be absolved’—

that is, from the excommunication with which Innocent had struck him.”

Garnerius thought that all these letters sent by Innocent to Africa had been issued at some Roman synod convened by him. He based this on the assumption that it had been customary for Innocent’s predecessors and successors to write decretal letters, especially on matters of doctrine, at a council and then send them throughout the world. Marca holds the same opinion in book VII, chapter 12, number 5, of *On the Harmony of the Canons* [Col. 0163D].

But because none of the ancients mentions this Roman synod, the author of the Baronian critical work agrees with neither of them on this point. He says that Augustine, in book IV to Boniface, chapter 12, replying to the Pelagians who, after being condemned by Pope Zosimus, appealed to a council, writes:

“Was a synod really necessary for an obvious evil to be condemned—as though no heresy had ever been condemned except by the gathering of a synod? In fact, very few heresies are found for which such a necessity arose. There are far more, and incomparably more, which, once they arose, deserved to be rejected and condemned where they appeared, and from there could become known throughout the other lands as things to be avoided.”

Indeed, after the Pelagians had been declared heretics by Innocent and later by Zosimus, they are found to have complained only about the Roman clerics, as may be seen in Augustine, book II to Boniface, chapter 3 and following.

Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, suggests that the apostolic see was the first to condemn the Pelagian heresy, in these verses:

> The See of Peter, Rome, first cut down  
> The plague that was invading.  
> It had become the head of pastoral honor  
> For the world, and whatever it did not possess by arms  
> It held by religion. From there the care  
> Of the rulers of the East shone forth no less:

These verses are not easy to explain, since Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, proscribed the Pelagian heresy in the year 412, five years before Innocent. Various learned men, including Baronius and Garnerius, have adopted different opinions on this matter. Setting these aside, I think Marca’s view more probable. In his dissertation *On the Ancient Collections of Canons*, chapter 15, he resolves the difficulty as follows.

He thinks that the doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius was first proscribed by the apostolic see through a general decree, as contrary to the Catholic faith. For the Carthaginian synod under Aurelius did indeed exclude Coelestius from the presbyterate and from the communion of the Church [Col. 0164B] because he was spreading errors. But this was a private censure directed against the man, which he thought he had evaded by appealing to the Roman see. The Africans themselves had therefore judged that the matter should even then be referred to Rome, from which the final decision of the entire case was expected. Prosper was thus not without reason in attributing the first condemnation of the Pelagian heresy to the Roman see.

A greater difficulty is caused by what Prosper adds concerning the judgment of the Palestinian bishops in the East—that is, of the synod of Diospolis—which he says also condemned the Pelagian doctrine. Since this took place in the year 415, whereas Innocent’s replies to the African synods were promulgated in 417, those bishops appear to have been the first to decide the matter.

“But the answer is easy,” says the cited Marca. “They did not condemn Pelagius; through ignorance of the facts they absolved him. Although they approved Christ’s grace and presented themselves as its defenders, they did not condemn the errors hidden from them by Pelagius’s cunning.” Their efforts therefore benefited the Church by affirming grace, but the heresy, unknown to them, could not be explicitly proscribed by any decree of theirs.

The difficulty arising from a single word in Prosper is more serious, and even the most learned Petavius could not resolve it. For Prosper seems to indicate that, after Pelagius’s heresy had been condemned, the Palestinian bishops in the East passed judgment:

“From there the care of the rulers of the East shone forth,”

whereas it is certain that the judgment of Diospolis preceded the Roman pontiff’s decree by two years.

Therefore, in this verse, “from there” indicates not time, as some think, but place. Prosper was writing in the West, and, taking account of geographical direction, he says:

“From there the care of the rulers of the East shone forth,”

as though he were saying: “Here in the West the plague against grace was cut down, and from there in the East the Palestinian bishops also took care of the same matter.”

All of this is copied from Marca. Anyone wishing to learn more about the Pelagian heresy should read the cited Marca; Cardinal Noris, in his *History of the Pelagians*; Garnerius, in his dissertations on Marius Mercator; and the author of the critical work on Baronius, from whom we have drawn the preceding account chiefly.

After Siricius, Anastasius and then Innocent entrusted their vicariate power to the bishop of Thessalonica throughout the Illyrian provinces. Anastasius’s action is clear from Innocent’s letter to Anysius of Thessalonica, in which he expressly asserts this, as preserved by Holstenius in the *Roman Collection*.

After Anysius’s death, Innocent entrusted the same authority to Rufus, bishop of that see, who had rendered good service to the apostolic see. Holstenius records the following words in the same place, page 48:

“Therefore, since this grace, divinely going before, teaches me that provision must be made for Churches separated from me by such long distances, I judge, with the assent of Christ the Lord, that the care and the cases which may arise throughout the Churches of Achaia, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus and Crete, Riparian Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalis should be entrusted to your prudence and gravity. Indeed, in accordance with his most sacred instructions, we impose this responsibility upon the foresight and virtue of your distinguished sincerity—not establishing this for the first time, but imitating our apostolic predecessors, who wished these duties to be entrusted, according to their merits, to the most blessed Acholius and Anysius.”

A little later he adds:

“Take up, therefore, dearest brother, in our place, throughout the Churches mentioned above, the care of them, while preserving their primacy. Among those primates, be first, so that whatever they need to send to us they may not request without your judgment. For either the matter, whatever it may be, will be settled through your experience, or we command that it be brought to us through your counsel.”

It must not be omitted here that Innocent deprived many churches of the Novatians living in Rome. Socrates writes in book VII, chapter 9:

“Anastasius is succeeded by Innocent, who was indeed the first to begin persecuting the Novatians living in Rome and deprived them of many churches.”

Later Coelestine took all their remaining churches away from them and compelled their bishop to gather the people secretly in private houses, as we shall say under that pope.

**Line 19.—“A silver stag for pouring water.”**

In addition to what was narrated above at the beginning of this pontificate, the *Liber Pontificalis* writes that Innocent made, for the adornment of the baptistery, a silver stag for pouring water, weighing fifteen pounds. This was because, when the water had once been blessed, it could not suffice for the multitude of those to be baptized—which in the larger cities could amount to several thousand people. Thus, as soon as the pontiff began to immerse the person being baptized in the sacred font, water conveyed through channels immediately flowed into it.

According to the same Anastasius, he also made a silver vessel for chrism oil weighing five pounds, as well as certain other objects that should be read in the same author. He made these things in the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which he dedicated.]

[Note: [Col. 0165C]

**Number 57, line 2.—“He established a decree concerning the whole Church.”** Somier, book IV, chapter 6, page 37.

The pontificate of Innocent I is rich in events that make the authority of the holy see manifest. The definitions of faith issued by this pontiff against the heresies and heretics that arose in his time, the disciplinary laws which he established in the Churches of his Western patriarchate, and the judgments which he exercised in cases involving bishops of the other patriarchates, which constitute the Eastern Churches, demonstrate that authority.

Let us begin with the acts of jurisdiction which he exercised over the Eastern Churches—specifically, over those which first stirred up disturbances against the authority of the holy Roman see.

It is well known that Saint John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, was unjustly deposed in the assembly at the Oak through the faction of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, supported by the favor of the imperial court. The first report of the matter reached Rome through an Alexandrian cleric sent by Theophilus with letters to Innocent, to inform him of John’s deposition. Shaken by Theophilus’s audacity and by the disgracefulness of the deed, the pontiff did not even think such letters worthy of a reply, since they did not set out the sequence of events.

Three days later three further letters were delivered to him: one from John Chrysostom, another from the forty bishops who adhered to him, and a third written by the clergy of Constantinople. Four bishops and two deacons, whom John himself had sent as legates to Innocent, brought them.

From these letters Innocent learned the full account of what had occurred in the assembly at the Oak and of the disturbances that followed. In his own letter Chrysostom indicated that the illustrious legates would explain everything more clearly, so that His Holiness might as quickly as possible provide counsel for the afflicted condition of the Church:

“Wrongful acts,” he says, “must not only be lamented but also corrected. Therefore I beseech your charity to be moved to compassion and to do everything necessary to bring these evils to an end.”

Among the remedies he proposed, he urgently requested that Innocent declare in writing, by his authority, that the judgment pronounced unjustly against him in his absence, although he had not refused to submit to a lawful judgment, was void and without force; that the unjust judges should be punished by canonical penalties; that he be granted letters of communion with the apostolic see and the others, with which communion had never been interrupted; and that he, who had been expelled, be restored to his church.

“By your authority,” he says, “decree that these acts, carried out so unjustly while we were absent and while we did not avoid judgment, have no force, just as by their very nature they have none. Let those who acted unjustly be subjected to the penalty of the ecclesiastical laws. As for us, who have neither been convicted, nor accused, nor regarded as guilty, grant us through your letters and your charity, as well as that of all the others whose fellowship we previously enjoyed, permission to enjoy that fellowship, and command that we be restored to our churches.”

“To this,” Palladius says, “the most blessed Pope Innocent replied. Having admitted both parties to communion, he decreed that the judgment of Theophilus was cancelled and void. He said that another irreproachable synod of Western and Eastern priests ought to be convened, with the friends of the council withdrawing first, and then the enemies. For, in general, neither party’s judgment is sound.”

“A few days later a certain Peter, a presbyter of Theophilus, arrived together with Martyrius, a deacon of the Church of Constantinople, carrying Theophilus’s letters and certain brief commentaries as well. These appeared to show that John had been condemned by thirty-six bishops, twenty-nine of them Egyptians and seven others from different regions.

“When Pope Innocent had read these commentaries and discovered that the charges were not serious, that John had not been present, and that he had not been reproved face to face, he increasingly abhorred the madness of Theophilus, who had uttered so savage and merciless a sentence against an absent man. Having dismissed these men with severe letters,” and so forth.

A little later Theotechnus, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, arrived in Rome, bringing letters from the bishops who stood with John. They had been frequent participants in the council, numbering approximately twenty-five or thirty, and informed Innocent that John had been expelled by the emperor Arcadius from his Constantinopolitan see and banished to Cucusus.

Innocent sent letters of communion to all those bishops and urged them to endure their adversity patiently. He grieved that he could not provide the relief he wished, because powerful adversaries were opposing his efforts. He nevertheless refused to receive an envoy of the bishops belonging to the faction hostile to Chrysostom, who had come to fabricate accusations, and did not even consider his audacity worthy of a reply.

Finally, several bishops and presbyters, together with other ecclesiastical men expelled from their churches because they had preserved communion with John, came to Rome.

“Demetrius, bishop of Pessinus, came for the second time,” Palladius says. “He had travelled through the East preaching the communion of the Roman Church with Bishop John, as was witnessed by the letters of Pope Innocent. He brought letters from the bishops of Caria, who embraced communion with John; from the presbyters of the Church of Antioch, who follow the discipline of the Romans there, praising the integrity of the judgment and execrating as unlawful and impious the ordination made among them of Porphyrius.”

Innocent replied both to John and to the faithful members of his clergy who adhered to him. To John he urged constancy in acting for justice, “since a good conscience is truly a firm defense against all undeserved misfortunes,” and so forth.

To the others he indicated that he himself was suffering with them. He declared Atticus to have been violently intruded into the see of the expelled John, contrary to the canons of Nicaea, and his ordination void. He also declared that he was giving serious consideration to how an ecumenical synod might be convened [Col. 0167A], through which, by divine will, these turbulent disturbances might be calmed.

In fact, the pontiff wrote to Honorius and obtained an order that the Western bishops should assemble for a synod. A council was held in Italy.

“The bishops of Italy, gathered together, begged the emperor to write to his brother Arcadius and order that a council be held at Thessalonica, so that both parties from East and West might more easily come together. Moved by this, the emperor wrote to the Roman bishop, asking him to send five bishops, two presbyters of the Roman Church, and one deacon, who would carry his letters to his brother.”

When Innocent arranged this embassy, he attached to it, together with Honorius’s letters to Arcadius, a *Commonitorium* of the Western bishops. It instructed that Bishop John should not submit to judgment until he had first been firmly restored to his own see and restored to communion with all the Easterners.

“After receiving the *Commonitorium* of the Western council”—Palladius says, “of the entire West”—“the directive was as follows: John ought not to enter into judgment unless the Church and communion were first restored to him, so that, with every occasion for delay removed, he might enter the council of his own accord.”

Some more recent writers render that word *Commonitorium* as “Instruction.” This is indeed the sense in which it is accustomed—and ought—to be understood in certain cases: for example, when someone sends another person away and, as an aid to memory, gives him in writing an outline of what is to be done, so that he may not forget his instructions. Here, however, *Commonitorium* means the same as a law prescribed by the person issuing the command, so that it may be carried out as something advised and deliberated by one who possesses the authority to decide and command. In this sense the word is commonly used by authors. This particular case is expressly cited by Du Cange in his *Glossary* among several examples of the same meaning.

This preliminary judgment is a manifest confirmation [Col. 0167C] of that jurisdiction which the Western Church exercises over the Eastern. But why should the Western Church thus prevail over the Eastern, unless because the Roman pontiff, who presides over both, has his see in the West?

When John’s opponents learned of the legation, they laid ambushes for the envoys on the road in order to frustrate it, and, after subjecting them to insults and violence, compelled them to return without accomplishing their mission, having forcibly taken away the letters they were carrying.

Chrysostom, learning of these events from his exile, sent a second letter to Innocent:

“We give you perpetual thanks,” he says, “because you have shown toward us a fatherly goodwill. For, insofar as it depended upon your piety, everything would already have been settled and corrected, all scandals would have been removed, and the Church would be rejoicing in tranquil and sincere peace; everything would plainly have turned out well, and neither the laws would have been despised nor the constitutions of the Fathers violated.”

The most devout exile then turns to asking mercy for his own enemies [Col. 0167D], so that they might not be separated from the assembly of the faithful. He was moved by the consideration that he foresaw how much danger would thereby come upon all the Churches, since almost the whole world was being divided into opposing parties:

“Let them not be afflicted,” he says, “nor cast out from the assembly, when the magnitude of so great an undertaking is taken into account. For that struggle is, in large measure, the struggle of the whole world.”

Chrysostom’s enemies brought it about that the holy bishop, afflicted by extraordinary evils and calamities on his journey, should die a hastened death. It is reported that, when Pope Innocent learned of his death, he separated the Emperor Arcadius Augustus and Eudoxia from communion with the faithful. Others deny that this happened, especially more recent critics, who argue from the defective chronology and other features of the document that the letters serving as witnesses to the event are spurious.

Whatever judgment may be formed concerning this last assertion, it is certain that blessed Innocent never abandoned [Col. 0168A] Chrysostom’s cause, even after his death. The justice which death, by hastening John’s end, had prevented from being administered to him while alive in a full council was publicly secured for his memory by Innocent’s steadfastness. The apostolic man, vigorously contending in defense of his office, declared that he would communicate with none of the Easterners who were waging war against Chrysostom, unless, in an ecumenical synod, the diseased members of those who had carried out these actions were healed.

“This,” says Palladius, “is the judgment of the Roman Church: not to communicate to the end with the Eastern bishops, and especially with Theophilus, until the Lord grants a place for a universal synod and, through it, heals the diseased members who carried out these actions.”

The African Fathers of the council intervened in vain on behalf of the Easterners. Neither Innocent nor any of the Western bishops could bring himself to enter into concord with the bishops of Egypt, the East, the Bosporus, and Thrace, or with those of the Antiochene patriarchate, until they had restored Chrysostom’s name to the ecclesiastical diptychs [Col. 0168B], in which, according to episcopal custom, the names of bishops who had died in communion with the Church were recorded.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, was the first of all to carry out this command of the Roman See, as Theodoret attests in book 5, chapter 35. When, after the death of Porphyry, who had been hostile to Chrysostom, a successor had been elected, he immediately sent a legation to Innocent and

“requested and obtained peace,” says Innocent, “so that he might receive the Evagrians into their orders and places, with the integrity of the ordination which they had received from the aforementioned Evagrius [Porphyry’s predecessor, who had supported Chrysostom] . . . . The bishop of that city, my brother Alexander, promised that he would recite the name of the aforesaid bishop [John] among the bishops who are at rest. Know, dearest brother, that we have extended our hands to this undertaking and received them into our inmost being, lest members which had sought healing should for a long time be regarded as alien from the unity of the body.”

At the intervention of this same Alexander, Acacius, bishop of Beroea, was also decreed admissible to the desired communion on this condition: that, following Alexander’s example, he should

“drive far from his disposition every hostility and every rivalry, both concerning the name of Saint John, that admirable bishop, and concerning all the participants in his communion, etc., and that you should confess with your own mouth, before our beloved mediator Alexander, everything that has been confirmed by these acts, as is proper for one who is entering communion,”

says Innocent (*Epistle* 19 to Acacius).

By obeying this condition, Acacius not only obtained grace from Innocent for himself but also labored on behalf of Atticus of Constantinople, urging him to obey the apostolic decree. The bishop Maximianus of Macedonia also wrote in favor of Atticus’s reception. Innocent replied to him as follows (*Epistle* 166):

“Suspended communion is restored to one who demonstrates that the causes by which it had been suspended have now been cleared away, and who professes that the conditions of peace have been fulfilled. We make this known, and we show it by a great avenue to all who will seek the same peace, provided that they likewise show that, in accordance with their position, they have at some time done or fulfilled what has been examined and completed, and that communion should be granted to them, as these men [the Antiochenes] have solemnly requested through a legation sent for that purpose. We therefore await both the profession of the aforesaid man concerning the fulfillment of all the conditions which we have previously stated at different times, and his request for communion, so that we may rightly restore it to one who both requests it and proves himself worthy of receiving it.”

Atticus delayed for a long time, even sending envoys, until he had rendered due honor to Chrysostom’s memory. He could not obtain peace before he had entered John’s name in the lists.

“But Atticus,” says Theodoret, book 5, chapter 34, “who succeeded Arsacius, and who had often sent envoys to them and often requested peace, was finally received after he had written John’s name in the lists.”

While Innocent was carrying out these measures to preserve or restore unity in the Eastern Churches, he watched with equal [Col. 0169A] concern in the West both over the preservation of apostolic discipline through decretal letters and over the protection and liberation of the purity of the Catholic faith from the contagions of Coelestius and Pelagius. Thus, because he exercised throughout the world this threefold care of unity, discipline, and faith, the Bibliothecarius is rightly said to have stated of him: “He made a constitution concerning the Church.” The first of these concerns, unity, has been treated above in Somier’s Notes. What follows concerning the next two matters has been extracted from the same author’s *History of Dogma*, book IV, chapters 8 and 9.

From chapter 7, concerning discipline:

To Victricius, bishop of Rouen in Gaul, who was earnestly requesting the norm of the Roman Church, Innocent sent in his letter (*Epistle* 2) an organized set of rules for a reputable life and conduct, “so that,” he says, “the peoples of the Churches in your region may learn by what practices and regulations the life of Christians in each person’s calling ought to be governed, and what discipline is observed in the Churches of the city of Rome. It will be your responsibility, through the neighboring peoples and our fellow priests who preside over their own Churches in those regions, diligently to introduce this book of rules, as a sort of instructional and admonitory work, so that they may both become acquainted with our practices and, through assiduous teaching, be able to form the conduct of those who flock to the faith. . . . These are the matters which, with the divine judgment in view, every Catholic bishop ought thereafter to observe,” etc.

Among the other rules he includes this one concerning the referral of more serious cases to the apostolic see:

“But if more important cases should have arisen, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, just as the synod [of Sardica] decreed and venerable custom requires.”

To Exsuperius of Toulouse (*Epistle* 3), in addition to the norm of discipline, he wrote in his Decretal a canon concerning the books of both Testaments, excluding from the number the apocryphal writings which were falsely circulated under the names of the apostles.

He replied from Spain to the Fathers of the Council of Toledo concerning ordinations. To the bishops of Macedonia he sent a Decretal concerning several rules of the sacraments. To Aurelius, primate of Carthage in Africa, he commanded:

“I wish you to send these writings to be read throughout all the African Churches.”

To Decentius of Gubbio he recalled the traditions of the Roman Church:

“Who does not know, or who fails to understand, that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, the prince of the apostles, and is still preserved today, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing ought to be superimposed or introduced which either lacks authority or appears to take its example from elsewhere? Especially since it is manifest that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, together with the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read, if another of the apostles is found or reported to have taught in these provinces. But if they do not read this, because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves; there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it. Otherwise, while striving after foreign assertions, they may appear to omit the source of their institutions.”

He commended Felix of Nuceria because, following ancestral custom, he judged that the definition of doubtful matters ought to be sought from this source:

“We cannot fail to admire that your affection follows the institutions of our ancestors and refers to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, everything that may admit of some doubt, so that the apostolic see, having been consulted, may pronounce from the doubtful matters themselves what ought certainly to be done. We gladly accept this, and we approve your affection as mindful of the canons” (*Epistle* 4).

And, to pass over the remaining matters, he required zeal for discipline from John, bishop of Jerusalem (*Epistle* 32), admonishing him to devote himself more earnestly to the defense of the monasteries:

“See, brother, the snares of the ancient enemy, and keep vigilant with the spirit of a good ruler, so that those matters which have been brought to us more by rumor than by explicit accusation may either be corrected or restrained, lest ecclesiastical law compel the one who has not defended the matter to answer for causes that have been shaken.”

The repeated declaration and confirmation of the apostolic vicariate throughout Illyricum may also be included among the disciplinary constitutions. Saint Damasus had first conferred upon Saint Aelius, bishop of Thessalonica, vicariate authority of the Roman See over several provinces of Illyricum. After his death, Saint Anysus, his successor, received similar authority from four Roman pontiffs: Damasus, Siricius, Anastasius, and Innocent. When Anysus died, Rufus was appointed as successor, and Innocent transferred the same authority to him. Both of Innocent’s grants are found in letters, a copy of which survives in the Acts of the Third Roman Council under Boniface, the second pope of that name.

“Innocent to his dearest brother Anysus:

“Those eminent and distinguished men who were my predecessors—namely, Damasus of holy memory, Siricius, and the aforementioned man Anastasius—conferred this authority upon you in such a way that they entrusted to your holiness, which is full of justice, the cognizance of everything that might be done in those regions. You ought to recognize that my own humility likewise maintains this judgment and possesses the same will. For it was not right that I should attempt to act against the judgment of such good men, in whose place I am recognized as having succeeded, nor that anything should appear to be denied to your merit, to which those distinguished men seem to have granted so great a favor of this authority. I therefore declare that I recognize this very office as having been reserved for my own humility also, so that, with equal judgment and in a similar form, I may grant to your goodness and to your affection what you deserve.”

“Innocent to his dearest brother Rufus:

“Thus the wholly wondrous Paul entrusted to Titus the matters he should attend to in Crete and to Timothy those he should arrange throughout Asia, as we learn from reading the sacred letters. Therefore, by this grace proceeding from God, I judge that care should be taken of Churches separated from me by such great distances, by entrusting to your prudence and gravity, with Christ the Lord’s approval, the care of and cases arising among the Churches of Achaea, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus, Crete, Mediterranean Dacia, Ripuarian Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalitana, etc.

“Receive, therefore, dearest brother, in our place, the care of the aforesaid Churches, without prejudice to their primacy; and, as first among the primates, let them seek your judgment before petitioning us concerning whatever they need to send to us. For we direct that every matter be either settled through your experience or brought to us through your counsel. Know also that, with the favor and permission of the apostolic see, it is lawful for your fraternity, whenever any ecclesiastical matter must be handled or investigated either in your own province or in those mentioned, to take with you whatever bishops you wish as associates from any Churches. By their faith and moderation, decide whatever necessity and the case require, as the best and chief arbiter; and, chosen by us, make the determination as our intermediary,” etc.

[Col. 0170D] From chapter 99, concerning the faith, one learns of the condemnation of the Pelagian heresy requested from the two councils of Africa.

Eight principal heads of error constituted the substance of the Pelagian heresy: “by not defending free will, but rather elevating it into sacrilegious pride, they leave no place for the grace of God,” as the Fathers of the Council of Carthage wrote to Innocent in their synodical letter. That these errors were first proscribed by the Roman See is taught by the contemporary author Saint Prosper in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 2:

> The Roman See of Peter first cut down  
> The plague that was invading,  
> Which, made the head of pastoral honor  
> For the world, holds by religion  
> Whatever it does not possess by arms.

By the plague, or the name of the Pelagian sect, which was first cut down or condemned at Rome, Prosper here understands Jovinian, Rufinus, and Evagrius Ponticus. Their errors, condemned by Damasus and Siricius, were revived by Pelagius, as Jerome teaches in the preface to book IV of his commentary on Jeremiah:

> When suddenly the heresy of impassibility and sinlessness, which had once been strangled in Origen and, not long ago, in his disciples Grunnius and Evagrius Ponticus, as well as in Jovinian, began to come back to life and to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also in those of the East.

The first judgment directly instituted and pronounced against the sect properly called Pelagian after its author, and against Coelestius, his associate, was delivered in an African council held in the year 412. Since its Acts have been lost, another council, assembled five years later in Carthage from the same province, supplies the record, writing in its synodical letter to Innocent:

“We have recognized Pelagius and Coelestius as the authors of this wicked error. Hence it came about that we asked for a review of what had been disputed here, in the Church of Carthage, nearly five years earlier concerning the name of Coelestius.”

Marius Mercator recounts what Coelestius subsequently did:

“The bishops of that region,” he says, “resisted Coelestius and ordered him to condemn the same propositions, because they were heretical in meaning. But Coelestius in no way agreed; rather, by resisting those proceedings, he was deprived of ecclesiastical communion. He believed that he ought to appeal from that judgment to the examination of the Roman bishop. But, once that appeal had been disregarded, he soon went to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there he dared, by stealth, to seek a place in the presbyterate.”

Several years later Pelagius, who had withdrawn to the East, was brought before the Council of Diospolis in Palestine.

“Pelagius himself,” says Saint Augustine (*Epistle* 107), “condemned the Pelagian opinion against the grace of God with a feigned heart, but nevertheless fearing the Catholic judges, etc. Pelagius himself deceived the Palestinian judgment, and therefore he appears to have been acquitted there. But he could not in any way deceive the Roman Church, where you know that he is very well known, although he also attempted both of these things,”

adds the holy doctor in *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapters 8 and 9.

Shortly after the Council of Diospolis in Palestine, two councils were held in Africa, namely the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, where that heresy and its authors were condemned. The Fathers of Carthage address Innocent in their synodical letter:

“We have therefore thought it necessary, lord and brother, to make this action known to your holy affection, so that, for the protection of the salvation of many and the correction of the perversity of some, the authority of the apostolic see may be added to the decisions of our moderation . . . . There are also countless passages which, if we wished to gather them from all the Scriptures, could not be contained in a single volume. And we fear that, by mentioning them to you—who proclaim with greater grace the authority of the apostolic see—we may appear to act improperly.”

The bishops of Milevis likewise, having expressed nearly the same things concerning the errors condemned by them, request with equal reverence confirmation of their proceedings:

“But we judge,” they say, “with the assistance of the mercy of our Lord God Jesus Christ, who deigns both to guide you when you give counsel and to hear you when you pray, that those who hold such perverse and destructive opinions will more readily yield to the authority of your holiness, drawn from the clear light of the Scriptures, so that we may rejoice rather in their correction than grieve over their destruction, most blessed lord.”

In his reply to both councils, Innocent praises them for having

“preserved the examples of ancient tradition and, together with the vigor of our religion, now strengthened ecclesiastical discipline with no less reverence in consulting us than formerly, when you pronounced judgment, since you approved that the matter should be referred to our judgment. You know what is owed to the apostolic see—for all of us who occupy this position desire to follow the Apostle himself—from whom the episcopate itself and the entire authority of this name arose. Following him, we know how both to condemn such evils and to approve what deserves praise. You also do not judge that the institutions of the Fathers, which we preserve in the priestly office, ought to be trampled underfoot. They decreed this not by a human but by a divine judgment: that, whatever might be done, even in separated and distant provinces, should not be considered concluded before it had come to the knowledge of this see, so that its just pronouncement might be confirmed by the full authority of this see. From it the other Churches should draw, just as all waters proceed from their native spring and, through the various regions of the whole world, flow pure and uncorrupted from their source.”

After these preliminary remarks, he confirms the judgment of the council and pronounces the condemnation of the same heresy. He replies to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis in nearly the same sense and by the same method:

“You therefore consult carefully and appropriately for the honor of the apostolic see—for the honor, I say, of him who, in addition to those matters that are external, bears the concern of all the Churches, and who must determine what judgment is to be maintained concerning anxious matters. You have followed the form of the ancient rule, which you know has always been observed throughout the whole world together with me . . . . You have also confirmed this by your action, knowing that answers always flow from the apostolic fountain to those who seek them throughout all the provinces, especially whenever the matter of faith is under discussion,” etc.

He then proceeds to confirm the Acts of the council and to condemn the heresies.

Besides these synodical letters, Innocent also received private letters from several of the Fathers, especially from five bishops, among whom was Augustine. They suggested that he summon Pelagius to Rome and compel him to abjure the heresy and to anathematize his writings in which it was contained. Innocent replied that he had sufficiently declared both what he had pronounced concerning the errors against the grace of God and the proper judgment of condemnation which the councils had issued against them [Col. 0172C]. Pelagius, whether he claimed to be innocent or confessed his offense as a penitent, ought to come to the apostolic see either to clear himself or to obtain pardon. But he would accomplish neither unless he anathematized the errors that had been proscribed by the Church.

“But if he obstinately wishes to persist in this impiety, action must be taken so that help may be given, at least, to those whom not their own error but rather this man’s error has led astray.”

Augustine highly commends Innocent’s replies:

“He replied to all our questions,” he says (*Epistle* 106), “in the very manner in which it was right and fitting for a bishop of the apostolic see to reply.”

The holy doctor certainly holds a different and better view than certain more recent writers who dare to assert that Innocent usurped and attributed to himself rights which in no way belonged to his see. The conduct of that outstanding Father and doctor toward the holy see is likewise entirely different from the practice now adopted by those same modern writers, who nevertheless boast that they are Augustine’s disciples. With incredible obstinacy they refuse to obey the apostolic judgment, which was supported and confirmed by genuine and solemn authority, if ever any judgment was. Yet the teacher under whom they boast of having been formed solemnly declares, in a sermon publicly read to his Church (*Sermon* 2 on the Words of the Apostle, at the end):

“The Acts of the two councils of Africa, which we mentioned shortly before, were sent to Rome so that they might be confirmed by the apostolic see; and replies came from there; and thus the matter was concluded.”]

[Col. 0145]

57

Innocent, an Albanian by nationality and the son of Innocent, sat for fifteen years, two months, and twenty days [Note: [Col. 0145] B: one month, ten days, from the consulships of Arcadius and Honorius V to those of Honorius XI and Constantius II]. He issued a constitution concerning the whole Church, the rules of monasteries, Jews, and pagans. He found many Cataphrygians in the city and banished them to exile and monasteries [Note: [Col. 0145] CB: into the exile of the monastery]. He also found the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius and condemned them. He further decreed that anyone born of a Christian woman should be reborn through baptism, that is, should be baptized—a doctrine Pelagius condemned [Note: [Col. 0145] Baron: not in words but in fact, because he denied original sin].

At the same time he dedicated the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. The work was carried out by the priests Cusicinus [Note: [Col. 0145] C: Ursicinus] and Leopardus, and by the deacon Libyanus, through the devotion expressed in the will of a certain distinguished woman named Vestina. The woman mentioned above arranged in the text of her will that the basilica of the holy martyrs should be built from ornaments and pearls sold at fair valuations; it was built to completion.

At that place the most blessed Innocent, acting under the commission of the distinguished woman Vestina, established a Roman titular church and, in that same sacred place [Note: [Col. 0145] C: in the same house], offered two silver patens, each weighing twenty pounds; twelve silver crowns, each weighing fifteen pounds; two silver basins, each weighing twenty pounds; one silver *pharus-can­tharus*, weighing twenty-two pounds; four silver *cerostrata*, each weighing thirty-five pounds; a silver tower with a paten, and a gilded dove weighing thirty pounds; for the adornment of the baptismal font [Note: [Col. 0145] C: the baptistery], a silver stag pouring out water, weighing twenty-five pounds; a silver vessel for chrism oil, weighing five pounds; another vessel for exorcized oil, weighing five pounds; two patens for chrism, each weighing four pounds; an embossed silver cup [Note: [Col. 0145] C: an embossed vessel], weighing ten pounds; another silver cup, weighing ten pounds; five silver chalices, each weighing three pounds; three silver baptismal chalices, each weighing two pounds; and many other gifts. He also gave silver water vessels, each weighing sixteen pounds; sixteen bronze *phara-can­thara*, each weighing ten pounds; and likewise twenty bronze *pharae-can­tharae cerostratae* [Note: [Col. 0145] *cerostrotae*] within the basilica, each weighing forty pounds.

>[Col. 0147] |

58

Houses beside the Libyan basilica, yielding 32 solidi [Note: [Col. 0147] C: 85]; a house on the Clivus Salutis, a bathhouse [Note: [Col. 0147] C: *Balneatae*], yielding 88 solidi and a *tremissis* [Note: [Col. 0147] C: *tremissem*]; the Corras estate [Note: [Col. 0147] C: Sarras] in the territory of Clusium, yielding seventy-one solidi and a *tremissis*; the Corviana estate in the territory of Clusium, yielding eighty-eight solidi; the Fundan estate in the territory of Fundi, with fifteen adjoining holdings, yielding one hundred eighty-one solidi and a *tremissis*; the Figlynas estate in the territory of Casinum, yielding sixty-three solidi [Note: [Col. 0147] C: 58] and a *tremissis*; the Antoniana estate in the territory of Clodius, yielding forty-two solidi [Note: [Col. 0147] C: 62]; the Amandanus estate, which the distinguished woman Vestina gave to her cousin, in the territory of Veii, yielding forty-six solidi and a *tremissis*; the houses of Emeritus on the Clivus Mam­morius [Note: [Col. 0147] C: Mamuri] within the City beside the basilica, yielding sixty-two solidi; a house on the Clivus Patricius, assessed as a house beside the basilica on the Long Street, known as “at the Lake,” yielding eighty-two solidi; a house at the Floriana stone chair, yielding fifty-eight solidi; the bakery [Note: [Col. 0147] C: *pistrinum] on the Long Street, known as Castoranus, yielding sixty-one solidi; a bathhouse on the Long Street, known as the Temple, yielding forty solidi; three *siliquae*, three ounces at the Numentine Gate [Note: [Col. 0147] *Numentanae*], yielding seventeen solidi and a *tremissis* [Note: [Col. 0147] C: 22, and a *tremissis*].
