He decreed [Note: [Col. 0147] See Baron, year 417] that a fast should be observed on Saturday [Note: [Col. 0147] CB: diligently and worthily], because on Saturday the Lord was placed in the tomb and his disciples fasted. He decreed that the basilica of blessed Agnes the martyr should be carefully administered, governed, and adorned by the priests Leopardus and Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0147] C: covered]. By Vestina’s arrangement, the priests were granted authority over the aforesaid titular church. He held four ordinations during the month of December: thirty priests, twelve deacons [Note: [Col. 0147] CB: fifteen], and fifty-four bishops in various places. He too was buried at the Bear with the Cap, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, and the episcopate remained vacant for twenty-two days.

XLIII. SAINT ZOSIMUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 417, THE THIRTEENTH OF HONORIUS, THE TWELFTH OF THEODOSIUS

[Note: [Col. 0173A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher codex.

No. 59, line 2, B: “he established many things concerning the Church.” Line 6, B: “he held ordinations in the city of Rome.” Line 9, A: “ten days.”

Line 1: “Abramius,” with one year, three months, and twelve days. Line 2: “Here he established many things in the Church, and he made . . .” Line 3: “linostumis.” Lines 3 and 4: “Permission was granted through the parishes for the blessed candle.” This too he decreed: “that no . . .” Line 6: “in the city of Rome during the month of December.” Line 8: “is the Tiburtine Way, beside . . .” “Seven days before the Kalends,” and the episcopate remained vacant for eleven days.

Line 2: “three months, eleven days”; “and he established many things in the Church.” Line 3: “covered on the left.” Lines 3 and 4: “through the parishes permission was granted for the candle to be blessed” [Col. 0174A], “and he ordered that no . . . should be served to the common people, but only in the cells of the faithful.” Line 2: “He held ordinations during the month of December.” Line 4: “seven days before the Kalends of January,” and the episcopate remained vacant for eleven days.

In Holstenius and Schelestratius.

Line 2: “three months, twelve days.” Thus the Florentine manuscript. Line 3, Florentine: “here he established many things concerning the Church.” Line 8, Cassinese and Florentine: “candle.” Line 4, Florentine: “seven days before the Kalends.”

In Penia, from the Cavensis codex.

Line 1: “his father Abramius.” Line 3: “so that the deacons should have their left arms covered with linosthinus cloths.” Lines 4 and 5: “that no cleric should serve a drink in public, but only in the cells of the faithful, especially of clerics.”]

[Note: [Col. 0173B]

Lines 2 and 3.—“And he decreed that the deacons should have their left arms covered with *linosthinus* cloths.” Zosimus is credited with the decree that deacons should carry on the left hand *mappulae*, which are linen garments or cloths, according to canon *Illud*, Distinction 93. Today they are called the maniple.

Lines 3 and 4.—“And permission was granted through the parishes for candles to be blessed.” Zosimus is credited with a decree concerning the blessing of the Paschal candle. Sigebert likewise says under the year 417: “Pope Zosimus decreed that the candle should be blessed throughout the churches on Holy Saturday.” From that time the candle is solemnly blessed and lit on Holy Saturday. Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book III, chapter 31: “He set up a silver column upon a porphyry base, on which a great candle, to be blessed on Holy Saturday, might be solemnly placed.”

Lines 4 and 5.—“And he ordered that no cleric should serve a drink in public, but only in the cells of the faithful [Col. 0173C], especially of clerics.” The decree of Zosimus forbade clerics to enter a tavern or inn for the purpose of eating or drinking. The same prohibition appears in the Fourth Synod of Carthage, canon 27, except when necessity required it during a journey, canon *Clerici*, Distinction 44. Clerics are likewise not permitted to operate an inn. Sixth Synod, in Trullo, canon 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0173C]

Line 2.—“Here he established many Churches.” It should be read, with Baronius and others: “Here he established many things in the Church” [Col. 0174B]. For the subject is published constitutions, not the construction of churches, as the following words make clear, since they add “and he decreed,” which belongs to the same period and indicates the subject. The same wording is repeated in the entry on Coelestine: “Here he made many constitutions, and he decreed.”

It should be observed that the first words, which express the existence of constitutions without indicating their subject, refer to general decrees concerning faith or morals, contained in the accessible codex preserved in the archives of the Church, as will be shown below in the case of Coelestine. Since these matters were known to all, their specific content is omitted. When the phrase “and he decreed” is added with a particular subject assigned to the constitution, I think this is because the decrees were particular constitutions, or because they were not preserved in that codex. The existence of a Codex of Constitutions will be proved in its proper place.

Among the constitutions concerning the faith issued by Zosimus, the first place is occupied by that solemn proscription of the errors, especially those of Coelestius, which he condemned. When the heresiarch persisted in evasion, Zosimus issued, as Coelestine says in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, a celebrated *Tractoria* to all the bishops of the world, in which he condemned the Pelagian doctrine. Marius Mercator arranged briefly but accurately in his *Commonitorium* the articles, evasions, condemnation, and *Tractoria* sent by the pontiff to the bishops.

After recounting the earlier events, he speaks as follows concerning the condemnation and promulgation of the judgment:

“For this reason he was previously condemned in writing by the bishop Zosimus of blessed memory, in an extensive and very lengthy document. In it are contained the very articles on which he had been accused [Col. 0175A], and the entire case, both concerning the aforementioned Coelestius and concerning Pelagius, his teacher, appears to have been narrated in greater detail. We also have copies of these writings here. We further report that similar writings were sent to the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, to Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem.”

Apostolic constitutions were directed to these patriarchal or primatial sees so that, through them, they might be communicated to their suffragans, as was observed above. When Marius says that all the delusions of the Pelagians were condemned in the longest and most extensive writings, he sheds light on the cited statement that Zosimus “established many things concerning the Church,” since he took care to overthrow all the errors. Marius continues:

“All the aforesaid articles—for he had previously listed five errors—are contained in that letter of the bishop Zosimus of blessed memory which is called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned. It was sent both to Constantinople [Col. 0175B] and throughout the whole world, and was strengthened by the signatures of the holy Fathers,” etc.

Saint Prosper, explaining the reasons for the judgments issued by Innocent and Zosimus, wrote:

“Then the devices of these men were broken; then they collapsed together with the companions and leaders of their pride, when Innocent of blessed memory struck down the heads of the wicked error with the apostolic sword; when he compelled the synod of the Palestinian bishops to pronounce judgment against Pelagius, upon himself and his followers; when Pope Zosimus of blessed memory added the force of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils and armed the right hands of all the bishops with Peter’s sword for the cutting down of the impious, etc.”

Gennadius also wrote: “Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, issued a decree addressed to the Churches of the West and East. After him, his successor, Pope Zosimus, promulgated it more widely.”

Augustine should be consulted in his books against Julian, the follower of Coelestius. Among these constitutions, I believe there was also one concerning appeals to the apostolic see, which had now begun to be debated and which broke out again with greater force under his successor Boniface.]

### Lines 3 and 4

Permission was granted throughout the parishes for candles to be blessed. Zosimus established only that the same candle, which previously used to be lit exclusively in the larger basilicas, should likewise be permitted in each parish. For the blessing of the Paschal candle had existed earlier in the Church, as Prudentius demonstrates, since he composed a hymn about it. Baron, year 418, no. 27.

### Line 6

For the month of December. Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, states that he occupied the see for one year, nine months, and nine days; therefore, from 18 March 417 to 26 December 418.

## Chronological Notes

Zosimus’s beginning, shown from the letter of Paschasius to belong to the consulship of Honorius Augustus XI, in the year of Christ 417—in which Paschasius himself celebrated Easter on 25 March—is inferred from the date of his ordination, Sunday, 25 February. Accordingly, it is also recorded under those same consuls in the *Chronicle of Marcellinus*. The endpoint, however, must be extended to the immediately following consulship, that of Honorius XII and Theodosius the Younger VIII, in the year of Christ 418, a consulship famous from the African councils, whose acts are prefaced with those same consuls.

The Oxford library preserves a notable manuscript of those acts, written in capital letters and formerly kept in the library of Christophe Justel, from which he had prepared his edition of the book of canons of the African Church 110 years ago, as I related above. I was permitted to transcribe the portion edited by Justel when, on 26 January 1713, I was most courteously conducted by the most distinguished men, the vice-chancellor Gardiner and the librarian John Hudson—renowned among scholars for his editions of the ancient geographers and his new translation of Josephus—to view the illustrious monuments of Greek and Latin antiquity in the Arundelian marbles placed near the Sheldonian Theatre. They also allowed me, at will, to examine and transcribe the ancient coins of that celebrated treasury and the outstanding manuscripts of that excellent library—men always intent upon showing hospitality to their guests.

Similarly, in London, the distinguished earl Thomas of Pembroke and the eminent knights Fountaine and Germain permitted me to inspect the domestic treasuries of great value that they possessed; and in the Royal Library and the Cottonian Library, their most courteous custodians did likewise. All of them abundantly confirmed the singular benevolence toward a guest and the devotion to letters of that illustrious English nation, which I had already long experienced.

Through their kindness, therefore, I took care to append a specimen of the script of those manuscripts belonging to the African councils held under Innocent and Zosimus, in order to establish more fully the reliability of the chronology [Col. 0176B] and of pontifical history on the basis of documentary evidence. The antiquity of the manuscript undoubtedly reaches the eighth or ninth century, as is made clear by an image of its script compared with Mabillon’s specimens in diplomatic studies.

The agreement of the older catalogues—the Farfensis, the Cavensis, and three Colbertine catalogues, 1, 4, and 5—together with other very ancient catalogues, in assigning to him a tenure of one year, eight months, and twenty-five days (only the Bergomensis, among the four Italian catalogues selected, reducing the number of months by one, perhaps through a scribal error), advises us to agree with the Librarian, who calculates the same total. We should therefore fix the end of Blessed Zosimus’s mortal life and the beginning of his immortal life on 13 December; his burial, occurring ten or eleven days later, should be assigned to the 25th, or, according to other manuscripts, to 26 December—the same day on which Anastasius is commemorated and on which his own memory is celebrated.

The vacancy of the see, prolonged for only a very few days, is asserted not only by the Librarian, who fixed it at either two or eleven days, [Col. 0176C] but is also confirmed by the ancient martyrology of Florentinius. In it the ordination of Boniface, his successor, is recorded on 19 December, indicating that in that same year, 418, Sunday fell under the dominical letter E. If the vacancy lasted only two days, Boniface, elected on 15 December, postponed his ordination until the following Sunday. But if it lasted eleven days, he was elected on Christmas Eve and received episcopal ordination on the following Sunday within the octave of Christmas, 20 December, as the Librarian and the ancient Martyrology report. I shall show in the next entry that the beginning of Boniface’s pontificate must be sought from this point.

Besides those already listed, there are other distinguished chronological indications relating to Zosimus’s pontifical ministry, although it was confined within a short interval. For example, a solar eclipse on 19 July, a Friday, is recorded by Marcellinus Comes under the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, with other chronologists and historians agreeing; astronomical tables likewise place it in the same year, 418.

[Col. 0176D] In the same year—the twenty-fourth of Arcadius and Honorius—in which he records the aforesaid eclipse, Idacius adds a brief account that not only illuminates the year through a notable, though disastrous, event, namely an earthquake that shook Palestine, but also indicates that Zosimus’s deeds were committed to writing:

“During the episcopate of the one mentioned above”—Zosimus, whom Idacius himself numbers as the thirty-ninth bishop of the Roman Church—“the holy places in Jerusalem were shaken by a very severe earthquake, concerning which the written records of that same bishop provide information.”

## Historical Notes

### Line 2

Here he established many things in the Church. Of the many things established by Zosimus, the Librarian reported only a few, and did not choose what ought to be regarded as the most important. Perhaps he knew, as Idacius did, that Zosimus’s deeds had been committed to writing.

These included the letters sent to the African Fathers—and indeed to all the bishops—concerning the case of Coelestius and Pelagius; the letters to the bishops of Gaul concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles; the appointment of an apostolic vicar in three of those provinces; and the renewed condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius after their flight, by which they had withdrawn from the judgment of the Roman see, even though they had been ordered to appear before it.

The matters concerning appeals from overseas, begun under Zosimus and completed by his successor Boniface, and similar actions, must certainly be regarded as much more extensive and weighty than regulations concerning the linen-bordered pallia of deacons, the blessing of candles throughout the parishes, and the prohibition against clergy publicly serving drinks. Although these matters too deserved pontifical attention and were worthy of remembrance and later use—and were therefore rightly included by the Librarian—nevertheless, he ought not wholly to have omitted those things that concerned the preservation of the Catholic faith, which is the principal matter of all, and the administration of the duties and rights of the properly ordered hierarchy within the priesthood.

I must not, however, leave unexplained the omission. I would like two considerations above all to be weighed, [Col. 0177B] either to satisfy a reasonable criticism or to provide an opportunity for concealing, with some degree of censure, the deficiency.

The first is that, over time, different librarians collected the deeds of each pontiff and indicated them briefly, so that the collection itself resembled a summary or gleaning of acts more than a history. Hence some thought it appropriate to omit entirely matters already contained in larger volumes, or substantial materials that would themselves constitute a complete book of suitable size—for example, matters that would have a place in other catalogues of decretal letters or in similar collections arranged in another class, where they could easily be found.

The compiler who composed the account of Blessed Gregory the Great in this book followed this rule. He passed over twelve entire books of Gregory’s letters, although elsewhere he enumerated other writings of the holy teacher. He thought those books belonged rather to the registers of letters than to an epitome of the saint’s life.

The author of this account concerning Zosimus acted in the same way. He did not wish, in this brief summary of Zosimus’s pontifical deeds, to enumerate individually the decretal [Col. 0177C] letters that were already known from another collection of canons, or rules and decretals of the supreme pontiffs. He pursued instead the smaller decrees that he thought would be more difficult to find in the larger volumes containing all the letters.

Other collectors and librarians, however, adopted a different policy. They thought it appropriate to name explicitly even those matters that were found at greater length in the acts of councils and in the rules and books of the Fathers. Hence the condemnation of heresies, the division of provinces, and other more substantial acts are expressed differently according to each compiler’s judgment and the plan of his particular work.

The second point to be observed is that this *Pontifical Book* arose from catalogues of the Roman Church, as we demonstrated with Schelestratius and others in the *Prolegomena*, and was subsequently enlarged by later writers through the insertion of information relating to the particular use and history of this holy Roman [Col. 0177D] Church.

Hence its compilers are found to have devoted special attention to listing the foundations, endowments, and adornments of the basilicas, titular churches, and cemeteries of the City or its environs; the ordinations of the presbyters and deacons serving in them; the rites practiced there and transmitted through it to the other Churches of this Western patriarchate; and, at times, also decrees issued by it for all the Churches of the Christian world, together with actions concerning the condition of the whole Christian commonwealth.

The same thing occurs in our own age in the daily books, or sacred journals, of the Roman pontiffs. These are customarily dictated by the masters of sacred ceremonies of the same Holy See, or written by notaries and officials responsible for consistorial affairs. Although both kinds of record are intentionally devoted chiefly to rites and pontifical acts carried out in the City by the supreme hierarch of the entire Church, or in places where he happens to be staying, it nevertheless remains open to the authors of those journals to insert among such acts matters relating to this bishopric, this province, and this patriarchate of the Western diocese, as well as other matters concerning the universal Church spread throughout the world, including laws, legations, and constitutions issued by the supreme pontiff, the successor of Peter, for its governance. Alternatively, they may pursue exclusively those matters relating only to sacred ceremonies or to the summary of consistorial affairs.

This point, once noted on the occasion of this entry concerning the pontificate of Zosimus, should be applied to the others as well. It should be observed that, according to the discretion of the Librarian who was writing at the time, actions of one kind are sometimes recorded in one place and omitted elsewhere. This variety should be attributed to the different tendencies and concerns of the minds of those who, in various periods, presided over the pontifical library, the public archives, and the record offices.

### Line 3

So that the deacons might have their left sides covered with linen-warped pallia. This had already been established by Silvester. See no. 35 and Alteserra’s notes on that passage.

From the notes of that distinguished scholar, however, a question arises: should those linen-warped pallia worn by the deacons on the left be called *mappulae*, which we now call maniples, or rather *oraria*, which are now more commonly called stoles? Alteserra seems to include both under that decree of Silvester renewed by Zosimus.

Dominicus Macri treats the matter at greater length in his *Sacred Lexicon*, under the word *Linostima*, where he thinks that *oraria* are also meant:

“The linen-warped pallium,” he says, “which Pope Saint Silvester granted to deacons, Gavantus thinks was the maniple, but this is also common to subdeacons. I nevertheless believe that it was the stole, which the Greeks called *orarium*, concerning which I shall speak in its proper place. They wear it over the left shoulder, folding its front part back toward the arm and leaving the rear part hanging.

“The Carthusians observe the same practice, but according to the Latin rite they fasten it on the right side and gather the longer part on the arm in the manner of a maniple. This opinion is confirmed by the very ancient image of Saints Peter and Paul, which belonged to Pope Saint Silvester and is preserved with great veneration in the Vatican Basilica. In its lower part the same supreme pontiff is depicted baptizing Constantine, assisted by two deacons. The deacons are dressed in the ancient *colobium*, and from their shoulders hangs a stole, or sleeve, which in reality can be nothing other than the linen-warped pallium.

“Our opinion is confirmed a second time by the words of Rudolphus, proposition 23, where, speaking of this decree of Silvester, he says: ‘That deacons should use the dalmatic in church, and that their left side should be covered by the linen-warped pallium.’ Therefore it is a stole, which formerly hung on the left, as on the part that was then, as stated in the aforesaid bull, the more honorable.

“Some have ingeniously derived its etymology from the Greek λινοστῆμον, that is, ‘the warp of linen,’ perhaps to distinguish it from the stole, which in those centuries was made with a woolen warp.”

Charles Macri, the brother of Dominicus Macri, adds in his supplement to the notes that the linen-warped pallium seems to have been an *orarium*, or stole. We may infer this, he says, from the fact that the ankle-length Median garment, which Herodotus in Book VI, Xenophon in Book VIII, Plutarch in his *Alexander*, and Arrian in Books IV and VI call *stolē* (στολή), Quintus Curtius in Book III calls a *pallium*, while Horace, *Satires* 1.2, used *pallium* for a band, saying:

“Her stole descended to her ankles, and a pallium was wrapped around it”;

and Seneca, *Troades* 25:

“Let the pallium gird the loosened tunics.”

These observations of learned men lead us to recognize an affinity between the priestly vestments of the new law and the priestly ornaments prescribed by God in the old law. I treated this affinity in the *Prolegomena* sufficiently for an understanding of the general class of all garments pertaining to the service of the altar. Here it will be enough to touch upon those that relate specifically to the insignia of deacons in this entry.

We have seen, therefore, from Blessed Jerome and from Josephus, whom Jerome cites in his letter to Fabiola, that the priests of the Mosaic law shared certain garments with the high priests, in addition to the round cap or hemispherical tiara. These three other garments were:

1. Linen undergarments, or breeches.
2. A linen, ankle-length tunic, fastened to the body like a military shirt.
3. A belt, or girdle, woven like a serpent’s skin with a ground of scarlet, purple, hyacinth-blue, and fine linen thread.

Jerome observes that this belt was four fingers wide, tied around the chest between the navel and the breast, and hanging down on one side toward the legs. When greater freedom of movement was required for sacrifice, it was customarily thrown back over the left shoulder.

Just as the measurement of this Levitical belt has been retained [Col. 0179B] in the stole that Christians call the deacon’s stole, so its throwing back over the left shoulder is visibly expressed in the arrangement prescribed for deacons, both by Silvester above in no. 35 and here by Zosimus.

It is placed over the left shoulder both in the Latin Church and among the Greeks. Among the Greeks, the rear part hangs freely and descends toward the legs, while the front part is fastened to the arm. Among our Latins, however, for the sake of carrying out the ministry more freely, the hanging part is fastened around the belt by a clasp or knot on the right side. On the left arm, instead of wrapping around the other end of the same band, a segment of similar width—cut as though from a longer sash or belt—is doubled so that it can be inserted at the left elbow. This type of ornament we call the maniple.

The same applies to the great pallium of our pontiffs, that band signifying the extent of their authority. Until the tenth century it was arranged around the shoulders, with each end flowing in front from the chest and behind from the back all the way to the feet, as all the ancient mosaics preserved in the Roman basilicas and titular churches demonstrate. After experience showed that it repeatedly gave the pontiff celebrating an opportunity to stumble and fall while ascending and descending the steps of the altar and throne, it began, as we shall say below in another entry, to be prudently shortened, until in our own age it scarcely reaches below the ribs. Thus the pontiff’s ministry is made more convenient and free from the danger of falling, without diminishing either its symbolism or its dignity.

So much for its form. We must now discuss the material of that deacon’s ornament, established by the repeated decrees of Silvester and Zosimus.

Silvester prescribed that deacons should wear a linen pallium on the left shoulder. Zosimus likewise prescribed a garment woven with linen warp and threads—that is, *linostimum*—for the reason that linen was so closely associated with priestly vestments that it occupied a place in almost every one of them. The breeches are linen; the ankle-length tunics are linen; and the priestly and Levitical belt is woven from byssine thread, that is, the finest linen. Hence, when our pontiffs are anointed, linen bands are used, and linen mitres are used for bishops when they assist the supreme pontiff.

No one explains more successfully the reason why such a garment was prescribed for deacons in the age of Silvester and Zosimus than Chrysostom, who lived into the age of Zosimus. Goar reports his testimony in the homily on the prodigal son, in the *Euchologion*, part II, under the ordination of the Greeks, no. 23:

“You know,” he says, “those spiritual delights, you who have tasted them, and you remember the dread mysteries of the divine sacrifice, and those who imitate angels’ wings with fine linen stoles placed upon their left shoulders and move about in the Church.”

Besides this origin of the deacon’s stole in the Levitical belt turned back over the left shoulder, interpreters of the sacred rites also derive its symbolism from the beginning of the new covenant. They identify the linen garments as *mappulae* worn on the left arm, on the basis of the *Roman Order* VI in Mabillon; and they identify the linen-warped pallia worn by deacons on the left on the basis of this entry and the preceding no. 35, as I noted in the annotations to Saint Stephen.

They think that this symbolism proceeds from the linen cloth with which Christ the Lord, the true High Priest, chose to gird himself when he instituted the sacrifice and priesthood of the new law. We therefore pointed out that even before Silvester these linen garments and other sacred vestments had been assigned to our Levites and priests, when we explained the decree established by Pope and martyr Stephen: that priests and Levites should not use sacred vestments in everyday life, but only within the Church for the service of the altar.

What, then, was the reason for establishing a decree under Silvester and Zosimus, if before Silvester Stephen had already legislated concerning the sacred garments of priests and deacons, and among those garments were the linen pallia and the *oraria* of Christ the Lord, taken from linen?

We shall understand the reason [Col. 0180B] if we consider the greater cultivation of sacred vestments, more broadly explained after the restoration of peace to the Church under Silvester through Constantine. In that age, consular robes, royal purple, palm-patterned garments, and triumphal vestments, frequently offered by rulers professing the faith of Christ, were properly dedicated to God by the pontiffs as insignia of Christ’s royal priesthood. The pontiffs placed the insignia of Christ’s cross upon them and did not disdain to cover the golden and embroidered ornaments of royal treasure with the woolen apostolic pallium. These garments were devoutly brought into the sanctuary by the emperors, who submitted themselves and their kingdoms to Christ.

Since due attention had therefore been given to the dignity of the ancient pontifical symbols in the ornaments of the higher priesthood, Silvester and Zosimus likewise wished due attention to be given to the insignia of the Levitical office as originally instituted—namely, to the linen *mappulae* customarily placed on the shoulder, even when dalmatics woven with gold and purple were assumed during the peace of the Church.

Indeed, such was the determination not to abandon the sacred symbols of these ancient pallia, or *oraria*, and borders that even then, and still today, deacons may not appear for the service of the altar without this ornament, including on those days when the dalmatics must be set aside. Nor may subdeacons approach to perform the duty of their order in the sacrifice unless they are dressed in those linen garments and equipped with the *mappulae* on the left, even if on certain days they remove their outer and costly tunics during the ministry.

Anyone who wishes to learn more about these ornaments should consult what we have brought together in the *Prolegomena* concerning the cultivation of sacred vestments.

### Lines 7 and 8

Buried beside the body of Blessed Lawrence on the Tiburtine Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Certainly he must be said to have been alive after the fifth day before the Nones of October, since a letter of his survives that was signed and addressed on that day—his *Commonitorium* to the priests of Ravenna—under the consuls Honorius XII and Theodosius, that is, in the year of Christ 418.

It is read in a ninth- or tenth-century parchment manuscript preserved at Rome in the library of the titular church of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, which we discussed shortly before on page 35. There it is preceded by another letter sent by Zosimus to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March under the same consulship.

### Note

#### Line 1

A Greek by nationality. Not, as some have said, a Cappadocian from Caesarea, but a Reatinus from Magna Graecia, now called Calabria.

#### Line 2

Here he established many churches. Another reading: “Here he established many things in the Church.”

Coelestius, having heard of Innocent’s death, immediately hurried from the East to Rome, as Marius Mercator testifies in his *Commonitorium* in these words:

“The aforesaid Coelestius, although expelled from here also”—that is, from Constantinople—“went with all speed to the city of Rome under Zosimus, the bishop of blessed memory.”

When he reached Rome, Pope Zosimus held a hearing in the Basilica of Saint Clement, and everything that had been done in his case up to that day was examined. Coelestius was also brought in, and his written statement was read, by which he testified to his faith, as Zosimus writes in his letter to Aurelius and all the bishops of Africa, sent in the year 417. The consuls are given in that letter, but the day and month are lacking.

Coelestius’s profession appeared Catholic to Zosimus—not because Zosimus himself approved the doctrines it contained, but because Coelestius showed himself entirely ready to embrace the judgment of the Apostolic See.

“In a man of exceptionally keen intelligence,” Augustine says in Book II, chapter 3, of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, “who, if corrected, would certainly have benefited many, the willingness to reform was approved, not the falsity of the doctrine.”

Zosimus nevertheless did not think that Coelestius’s written statement ought to be sufficient for him. He probed his mind through various questions, as is clear from the aforementioned letter of Zosimus to the African bishops.

Nor did he judge that Coelestius should be released from the bonds of excommunication with which he had been bound:

“But after an interval of two months, until a reply should come from Africa, an opportunity to repent was granted him under a certain leniency of a medicinal sentence,”

says Augustine in Book II, chapter 7, of *On Original Sin*. Zosimus communicated this to Aurelius and the other African bishops in a letter dated the eleventh day before the Kalends of October of that same year, 417. In that letter he rebuked those holy prelates rather harshly, grieving over the cases of Pelagius and Coelestius, who, although they possessed Catholic understanding, had been condemned as heretics.

After Zosimus wrote to the African bishops on behalf of Coelestius, Pelagius also sent a letter in which he sought to remove from himself the charge of heresy, together with a profession of faith. In it he claimed sincerely to declare what he believed and what he rejected.

Following Coelestius’s example, he discussed at length certain points about which no one had accused him. But when he came to the question of baptism, he said:

“We hold one baptism, which we affirm is celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults.”

These words nevertheless did not bind him to confess original guilt. Nor did he specify what grace he acknowledged to be necessary. From what Augustine relates about the deceptions of the Pelagians, we understand that this exposition of faith, in which nothing at all seems to appear except what is orthodox, opened the door to all their errors.

Nevertheless, after receiving it, Zosimus wrote to the African bishops the letter mentioned above, dated the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. In it he said that Pelagius clearly cleared himself and expounded his faith with such clarity that he left no room for malicious interpretations.

Yet Zosimus later corrected the error he had imprudently committed, and Augustine therefore excused him as far as he could.

The African bishops, after receiving the letters of Pope Zosimus, held two councils in the year 418. Saint Augustine always calls the first of them the African Council, although it was held at Carthage. Two hundred and fourteen bishops attended it.

From that council a remonstrance was sent to Pope Zosimus. In it the Fathers of the council protested seriously against Zosimus because, setting aside the judgment of both the African Church and the Roman Church under Innocent, by which the case of Coelestius had been concluded, he had recalled it for a new examination.

Then, when they understood from Zosimus’s letters that he was hastening to absolve Pelagius and Coelestius unless their accusers came to Rome and proved the charges against them, they submitted a petition of protest. They demanded that their rights be preserved and that nothing be changed in the sentence pronounced against the two men, but that everything remain in its existing condition—at least until they could send one of their number to Rome with suitable documents concerning the case, by which the heretics’ practices could be exposed and it could be shown how lawfully and canonically they had been condemned.

From that council, therefore, all the proceedings in the case of Coelestius were sent to Zosimus.

When matters had reached this point, Zosimus examined what had thus far been done against Coelestius both at Rome and in Africa, and summoned him to a fuller hearing and supreme judgment. But when the heresiarch saw that his devices were becoming apparent and that no means of evasion remained, he withdrew from the examination.

When his flight became known, a definitive sentence was immediately issued against him and Pelagius. Zosimus then wrote to all the bishops of the world that lengthy letter which Marius Mercator calls the *Tractoria*, of which only some fragments remain.

Mercator says the following about the matter in his *Commonitorium*:

“When the bishops from Africa replied and explained the whole case that had been dealt with among them, and when the proceedings that had then been completed with him or concerning him had also been sent, he was summoned to a fuller hearing, so that he might hasten to fulfill what he had promised—that is, after those aforesaid points had been condemned, that he might be released from the sentence of the African bishops by which he had been deprived of communion.

“He not only failed to appear, but also fled from the aforementioned city of Rome. Consequently, he was condemned by the aforesaid Zosimus, bishop of blessed memory, in extensive and very lengthy writings. In them are contained the very points of which he had been accused, and the whole case, both of the aforementioned Coelestius and of Pelagius, his still more wicked teacher, appears to have been recounted. We ourselves also possess copies of these writings.

“We shall add that similar and identical writings were sent to all the Eastern Churches, to the diocese of Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem, and to the bishops.”

Zosimus sent his *Tractoria* and the acts of the African synod to the emperor Honorius, who was residing at Ravenna, requesting that Coelestius and all the Pelagians be expelled from the City and regarded as heretics throughout the Christian world.

After receiving these documents, Honorius issued a rescript, which Baronius inserted in his *Annals* from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Vedastus under the year 418. Salmasius later published it, as did Usserius in Book I of *On the Beginnings of the British Church*, and Baluzius in the appendix to Salvianus. More recently Garnerius gave a more accurate text, partly through collation of printed editions and partly with the help of manuscripts, in Dissertation 3, *On the Imperial Constitutions Issued in the Pelagian Case*.

In that rescript, addressed to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium of Italy, Honorius says:

“Let your Illustrious Authority know that we have established by a law destined to endure for all time that, after the first heads of this accursed doctrine—Coelestius and Pelagius—have been expelled from the City, any other followers of this sacrilege who may henceforth be found in any place, or who may again utter anything in support of the condemned perversity, shall, when apprehended by anyone, be dragged before the competent judge.”

The praetorian prefects—Junius Quartus Palladius of Italy, Monaxius of the East, and Agricola of Gaul—carried out the imperial edict by their orders. In a decree that still survives, they commanded that Pelagius and Coelestius be expelled from the City and that all convicted of their error be stripped of their property and punished with perpetual exile.

Honorius’s rescript is said to have been issued at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of May, under the names of Our Lords Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, Augusti and consuls. It therefore belongs to the year 418, specifically one month and several days after Zosimus had written his third letter to the Africans on 21 March. Within that interval he both summoned Coelestius for the final time to judgment and issued his *Tractoria* against the Pelagians to all the bishops of the world.

The African bishops assembled at Carthage in the council that Saint Augustine calls plenary received Zosimus’s *Tractoria* and wrote him a congratulatory letter, in which, as was fitting, they congratulated Zosimus on the condemnation of the Pelagians.

This letter and Zosimus’s *Tractoria* are mentioned in chapter 8 of the chapters commonly appended to Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. Celestine, to whom those chapters are attributed, says:

“That all the efforts, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, since no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has given. The regular authority of Pope Zosimus of blessed memory directs us to this judgment when, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says:

‘But we have referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise.’”

The African bishops venerated this statement, shining with the light of the most sincere truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man:

“But that which you placed in the letter that you took care to send to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, at God’s prompting,’ and so forth—we understood your statement to mean that you cut down, with the sword of strict truth, as though passing swiftly by, those who exalt the freedom of human choice against God’s assistance.

“For what did you attribute more freely to free choice than the fact that you referred everything to the conscience of our humility? And yet you faithfully and wisely recognized, and truthfully and confidently declared, that this had been done at God’s prompting:

‘For the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children through paternal inspirations so that they may do something good. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Thus we do not fail to recognize the presence of our own choice, yet in each movement of the human will toward good we do not doubt that his assistance is the more powerful.’”

Thus Celestine.

The letter praised above must have been written by the African bishops assembled in plenary council, where they received Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, since Zosimus ceased to live toward the end of the year 418 and no other council was assembled in Africa before his death.

### Lines 3 and 4

“So that the deacons might have their left sides covered with linen-warped pallia, and permission was granted throughout the parishes for candles to be blessed.”

The *Pontifical Book* attributes to Zosimus the granting of permission for the Paschal candle to be blessed in each parish. Cardinal Baronius says that this should not be understood as though Zosimus had been the first to institute the use of the Paschal candle. Rather, Zosimus established only that the same candle, which had previously been lit only in the larger basilicas, should likewise be permitted in every parish. For Prudentius demonstrates that the blessing of this candle was earlier in the Church, since he composed a hymn about it.

The same *Pontifical Book* asserts that Zosimus established that deacons should have their left sides covered with linen-warped pallia. By the name of this pallium we should understand the deacon’s stole, woven from linen and wool, which deacons wear over the left shoulder, in contrast to the priestly stole, which hangs from the neck down the front of the chest.

This practice had already become customary from the time of the Council of Laodicea, held around the year 363, so that deacons used the stole in sacred ministries. Canon 32 states that subdeacons should not assist wearing *oraria*, and canon 23 that lectors and singers should not perform their office wearing *oraria*.

Regarding the latter canon, an anonymous author in his notes on the canons of the councils observes that lectors and others were forbidden to use *oraria* so that the ranks of the orders would not be confused. The *orarium* was the same as the stole—or, as others hold, the *sudarium*, a cloth with which the mouth was wiped—which eventually became the maniple.

It is more probable, however, that *orarium* here means the stole, which formerly covered the shoulders by its width and of which we have retained only the border worn around the neck. The Greeks differ from the Latins in this respect: among the Greeks, the *orarium* is crossed before the chest and behind the back in the form of a cross.

Line 2.—“Here he established many churches.” Another reading: “Here he established many things in the Church.” No one can testify more securely to what Zosimus did in the Pelagian controversy than Zosimus himself in his letters, together with the testimony rendered concerning him by St. Augustine. Zosimus’s [Col. 0184A] third letter is as follows:

“Zosimus to Aurelius and to all throughout Africa, etc. ‘A great weight of examination demands a great [standard], so that the scale of judgment may not be inferior to the matters themselves that are being dealt with. To this is added the authority of the Apostolic See, to which the decrees of the Fathers, in honor of the most blessed Peter, have established a special reverence. . . . The presbyter Caelestius presented himself for our examination, requesting that those matters which had been reported concerning him to the Apostolic See otherwise than they ought to have been might be cleared up. . . . Having set everything else aside, on the day of the hearing we took our seats in the basilica of St. Clement. . . . Accordingly, we examined everything that had previously been done. . . . When Caelestius had been admitted, we ordered his written petition, which he had submitted, to be read aloud. Nor were we satisfied with this: we repeatedly investigated whether he was speaking from his heart or merely with his lips what he had written.’”

St. Augustine testifies that, in the profession of faith which Caelestius presented to Zosimus, he declared: “If perchance, as happens to human beings, some error arising from ignorance has crept in, let it be corrected by your judgment.” St. Augustine, *On Original Sin*, chapter 6: “Moreover, when Caelestius was attempting to clear himself, he constrained him, through repeated interventions, to agree with the aforesaid letters of the Apostolic See, that is, of Pope Innocent.” The same author, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 3: “Nevertheless, he was not yet believed to have been released from the bonds of excommunication; but, with a period of two months interposed until a reply should come from Africa, an opportunity for repentance was granted him under a certain leniency of medicinal judgment.” The same author, *On Original Sin*, chapter 8.

Pelagius, too, had diligently sought remedies in letters by which, if possible, he might evade the Roman pontiff’s careful investigation of this case. For he had written to Innocent a profession of his faith, borrowing true statements from the Apostles’ Creed and not openly mixing his errors into them; indeed, he asserted free choice and that we always need divine assistance. He concluded everything in this way:

“This is the faith, most blessed pope, which we have learned in the Catholic Church, and which we have always held and do hold. If anything has perhaps been stated in it with insufficient skill or inadequate caution, we especially desire that it be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your apostolate, whoever wishes to stain me will prove himself ignorant, malicious, or even non-Catholic; he will not prove me a heretic.”

Prailus, bishop of Jerusalem, had also added his own letters to Zosimus, in which he attacked the accusers of Pelagius and Caelestius. He portrayed Pelagius as so obedient to the Apostolic See that, when the letters of the commendatory writer and of the person commended were read publicly, the holy men of the Roman Church who were present could scarcely restrain their tears from joy, as Zosimus states in his fourth letter.

Meanwhile, judgment by the pontiff was held in suspense between the Roman and African Churches through letters sent back and forth, until fuller evidence could be brought by the African Fathers. Zosimus had communicated to them the materials transmitted by Pelagius and Caelestius.

“For although,” says Zosimus in his tenth letter to Aurelius, “the tradition of the Fathers has granted such authority to the Apostolic See that no one would dare dispute its judgment, and although it has always preserved this authority through canons and regulations, and ecclesiastical discipline, still operating under its own laws, renders in the name of Peter—whose institution it also descends from—the reverence that it owes, etc.; nevertheless, since we possessed such authority that no one could reopen our judgment, we did nothing that we would not voluntarily report to your knowledge in our letters. We granted this to fraternity, so that, consulting together, we might act in common—not because we did not know what ought to be done, or because we would do anything that, contrary to the welfare of the Church, would be displeasing—but because we wished to deliberate together with you concerning the man who, as you yourselves state in your letters, had been accused among you and had come to our see, claiming himself innocent and not refusing judgment after his earlier appeal. He had voluntarily demanded his accusers and condemned the crimes which, as he said, had falsely been alleged against him through rumor, etc. Therefore let your fraternity know that, after the letters which we received above from you, we have changed nothing, but have left everything in the same condition in which it had long been when we announced this to your holiness in our letters, so that the formal request which you had sent to us might remain.”

At last the case was brought to a conclusion by the Apostolic See. This is shown by several authors and, above all, by St. Augustine, who writes in *Against the Second Letter of Pelagius*, book II, chapter 3, that the African bishops advised Zosimus not to be satisfied with the general agreement which Caelestius claimed to render to the letters of Innocent, but to require of him specifically “that he should openly anathematize the wrong things which he had set down in his petition. Otherwise, if he did not do this, many people of limited understanding would believe that those poisons against the faith in his petition had been approved by the Apostolic See, because the See had said that his book was Catholic, rather than that they had been corrected because he had replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent. Therefore, when his presence was demanded, so that either the man’s cunning or his correction might become clear through definite and lucid answers, and no ambiguity might remain for anyone, he withdrew and refused to submit to the examination.”

When, by this method, the cunning of one who pretended readiness to obey and to submit himself to judgment had been exposed, St. Augustine (*Letter* 47 to Valentinus and *Letter* 157 to Optatus), St. Prosper (*Book against the Collator*), Marius Mercator (*Memorial to Theodosius*), and others testify not only that a sentence of condemnation was pronounced against Pelagius and Caelestius by Zosimus as well, but also that Zosimus took care, through circular letters sent to all the bishops throughout the world, that what he had decreed should become known to everyone.

Most especially one should read Paulinus, deacon of the Church of Milan, in the short work which he presented to Zosimus as an act of thanksgiving. There he describes the sequence of the judgment and the sentence pronounced by Zosimus against Caelestius, after the earlier sentence issued by Innocent:

“I give thanks to God and to Christ the Lord, who willed that the case of the Church should be conducted in such a way that the Apostolic See, by whose mouth the heresy ought to be condemned through the judgment of two pontiffs, ordered those things to be condemned which had been brought forward by me against Caelestius.”

But in what manner the will to amend had previously been approved in Caelestius—he claimed that, being uncertain about many matters, he wished to be instructed—rather than the falsity of his doctrine, which he did not then acknowledge that he professed, is shown by St. Augustine in book II *To Boniface*, chapter 3.

Zosimus had ordered in his encyclical to the bishops that, in condemning the Pelagians, the condemnation should be subscribed by everyone, and he imposed the penalty of deposition upon those who resisted, according to Marius Mercator in the *Memorial*. The law of the emperor Honorius proved so supportive of this pontifical constitution in the matter of faith that it ordered a public accusation to be instituted everywhere and the penalty of exile to be decreed against rebels.

Julian, bishop of Eclanum, and seventeen others experienced the just coercion both of pontifical and imperial authority. Because they refused to subscribe, they were deprived of communion by the Apostolic See and driven into exile by the judgments of the emperors, as is clear from Zosimus’s second letter.

The measures of Zosimus which we have discussed thus far are recognized as pertaining to the government of the universal Church entrusted to him. The particular measures which he ordained in the regions of the Western patriarchate were these: the primacy over the three provinces of Gaul—namely, Viennensis, Narbonensis I, and Narbonensis II—was confirmed to the bishop of Arles, to whom it had also previously been granted, with the office of Apostolic Vicar over all Gaul added to it (*Letters* 5 and 6).

In his Decretal letter to Hesychius of Salona (*Letter* 1), he prescribes that the same decrees concerning ordinations which he transmitted to Gaul, Spain, and Africa should be observed in the province of Dalmatia.

He also established several regulations in the African provinces. In Byzacena he rebuked the bishops because they were not ashamed to subject priests to the judgments of laymen.

He compelled Augustine to go to Mauretania Caesariensis in order to settle the needs of the Church, according to Possidius in the *Life of Augustine*, chapter 14, and according to St. Augustine’s *Letter* 157 to Optatus, when the case of the Donatists and appeals to the Apostolic See were under discussion.

On these matters, see the sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 2:

“Certain matters have been enjoined upon us by the Apostolic See. . . . This concerns the Nicene canons, that they be observed.”

The canon under discussion there was in fact a canon of the Council of Sardica, although the pontiff called it a Nicene canon. The reason was that those two councils, Nicaea and Sardica, were joined together and completed in a single book, since an explanation of the Nicene canons was also found among the Sardican canons; consequently they were commonly cited under the name of Nicaea, especially in that period and in the many works that followed.

The African Fathers testify in their synodical letter to Boniface, Zosimus’s successor, that they had professed the reverence which they owed to Zosimus, as will be shown below.]

[Col. 0173]

## 59

Zosimus, a Greek by nation, the son of Abrahamius, sat for one year, eight months, and twenty-five days [Note: [Col. 0173] B: four months and seven days, from the consulship of Honorius XI and Constantius II to that of Honorius XII and Theodosius B.]. Here he established many churches [Note: [Col. 0173] “Here he established many things in the church,” C and B.]. He also issued a decree that deacons should have their left shoulders covered with linen-woolen pallia, and, permission having been granted throughout the parishes, that candles be blessed [Note: [Col. 0173] C: “he granted.” C and B: “the Paschal candle.”]. He ordered [Note: [Col. 0173] B and C: “so that no drink should be offered to any cleric in public”] that no cleric should offer a cup in public, except only in the cells of the faithful, especially of clerics.

He held one ordination in the City during the month of December: ten priests, three deacons, and eight bishops for various places. He was also buried beside the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence on the Tiburtine Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [another reading: June] [Note: [Col. 0173] C: the seventh], and the episcopate remained vacant for eleven days [Note: [Col. 0173] Baronius: one day].
