## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

A little earlier I said that the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Boniface should be referred to the consulship of Monaxius and Plintha. His ordination is recorded in the ancient martyrology of Florentius as having occurred three days before the Kalends of January, which opened the year 419 in the course of those same consuls.

A contemporary witness from the same period is Prosper in his *Chronicle*, critically edited by Schelstratus in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, page 466, where the following is read:

“Under the consuls Monaxius and Plintha, Boniface exercises the fortieth episcopate of the Roman Church.”

This is supported by a letter of Boniface himself, sent to the bishops of Gaul on the Ides of June in the consulship of Monaxius, and by another letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, dated in the same consulship, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, according to Holstenius.

A copy of the former is found in the celebrated codex of the library of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, subscribed as follows:

“Given on the day of the Ides of June, while the most illustrious man Monaxius was consul.”

Another letter follows, sent three years later to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne. Its opening is: “Indeed, we find it difficult to lend credence to complaints”; its conclusion is: “Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February, while our lords Honorius XIII and Theodosius X, Augusti, were consuls.”

In calculating the total period during which Boniface sat, even the opinions of ancient writers appear to disagree, assigning different numbers of months and days, as is evident from the variant readings of the text of Anastasius.

More careful critics, however, appropriately observe that this difference in months and days must be referred to the months of the schism which were added to the solid three years attributed to him. During those months Eulalius, supported by the false insinuations of Symmachus before the emperor Honorius, who was residing at Ravenna, disputed the election with Boniface.

The chronology of that dispute, collected in the notes of the younger Pagi from number 2 through number 11, is found there and removes every discrepancy. It must be admitted that three or four months were spent in dispelling the accusations of Eulalius and Symmachus. During this period Boniface was ordered to abstain from exercising pontifical functions in the City. Finally, through several letters of Honorius sent from Ravenna up to the third day before the Nones of April—which Baronius reports under the year 418—Boniface obtained peaceful possession of the Roman See, after Eulalius had been expelled.

For this reason some codices assigned to Boniface’s see, counting from the legitimate election by the clergy, as was proper, more than three years, eight months, and thirteen days. Others assigned three months and thirteen days beyond the three years; these seem to begin that epoch from some imperial rescript.

In the martyrology of Florentius, the day of his deposition is fixed as the fourth of September. This agrees exactly with the total period defined by codex B from the day of his ordination, the twenty-ninth of December, if the seven days explicitly numbered in the catalogue of the Palatine-Vatican codex of the year 865 are read as we have given them in the Prolegomena, following Schelstratus, and as they occur in several copies of Anastasius’s work cited by both Pagi.

Thus, beginning from Boniface’s ordination, recorded, as we have seen, on the twenty-ninth of December, the exact calculation of the months and seven days assigned to this pontiff beyond the complete three years is established.

How illustrious this three-year administration of Boniface was, as shown by the letters of the Fathers and by the councils, is indicated by the notes of others and by our own; consult them.

It remains for me to show why I record Boniface’s death in the year 422 rather than 423, although Cardinal Norisius, an elucidator of history and chronology, thought it should be assigned to 423 in book I of his *History of the Pelagian Controversy*. At the head of chapter 22 he places this title: “The emperor Honorius dies, and afterward Pope Boniface.” The chapter itself begins:

“In the year 423, on the fifteenth day of August, the emperor Honorius died”; and five lines later he adds: “On the twenty-fifth day of October, when Boniface the pontiff had also died, Caelestine was substituted.”

I would defer to the authority of so great a writer, unless Prosper and Marcellinus Comes, who were still alive at that time, indicated otherwise.

Marcellinus arranged the events under the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus in this way. In the sixth indiction: “Caelestine was created bishop of the Roman Church, the forty-first; he lived nine years.” After recounting the other events of that same year, he places the death of Honorius last.

Prosper likewise, in his *Chronicle*, under the same consuls, first records the beginning of Caelestine’s pontificate, writing: “Caelestine presides over the Roman Church as its forty-first bishop for nine years, ten months, and fifteen days.” He then reports that Lamissus became the second king of the Lombards and concludes the events of the year with the death of Honorius and the tyranny of John.

The testimony of contemporary writers therefore not only does not place the death of Honorius before Boniface’s death; it places the beginning of Caelestine’s pontificate before the death of Honorius.

Moreover, if Honorius died in August—which cannot be doubted, both from the testimony of the historians cited by Ducange in *Christian Constantinople* [Col. 0190B] and from the laws of the Theodosian Code issued during that consulship, namely, law 61 on the sixth day before the Ides of August, concerning heretics; law 19, concerning appeals; law 5 of book XI, concerning donations, compared with the preceding law; and law 7 of title 19, book II, concerning wills—and if the beginning of Caelestine’s pontificate is counted among the first events of that year, although he began his pontificate on the twenty-fifth of October, then we must certainly conclude that this October belonged to the sixth indiction.

During that indiction, as the consulship began on the Kalends of January, Asclepiodotus and Marinianus entered office in the Christian year 423, whereas the indiction itself had begun in September of the year 422, shortly before Caelestine’s pontifical accession.

Again, from the nine years, ten months, and fifteen days assigned to Caelestine, his election is calculated to have occurred in the same year, 422. His death cannot be postponed beyond the period of the year 432. Therefore, if ten years, ten months, and the additional days are assigned to him, the beginning of his pontificate cannot be taken from the year 432 but must necessarily be connected with the year 422.

[Col. 0190C]

## HISTORICAL NOTES

No. 60, line 5.—“When the Augusta Placidia, with her son Valentinian Augustus, heard this while they were sitting at Ravenna, she reported it to the emperor Honorius, who was sitting at Milan.”

To prevent the history from being obscured by the complicated expression of the names Placidia and her son Valentinian, to whom the title “Augustus” is attributed in this passage earlier than is appropriate, one should observe the following.

Placidia Augusta, daughter of Theodosius the Great and sister of the two emperors Arcadius and Honorius, after the death of her first husband, Athaulf, king of the Goths, was given in marriage to Constantius the Patrician in the year of Christ 416, during the consulship of Theodosius VII and Palladius. From this marriage she gave birth to Valentinian III on the sixth day before the Nones of July in the year of Christ 418, during the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, according to Prosper in his continuation of the *Chronicle of Eusebius.

Boniface was elected Roman pontiff in the immediately preceding year, as it was drawing toward its end—namely, on the twenty-ninth of December in the year of Christ 418. On that same day the faction of the schismatics installed Eulalius in the Lateran patriarchium, while Placidia was then at Ravenna with her husband Constantius, who had been admitted into a share of imperial power and the dignity of Augustus.

This occurred either in that same year, under the consulship of Monaxius and Plintha, as Idacius reports, following Besoldus as corrected by Rupertus, page 426; or in the year 420, whose beginning coincides with the schism of Eulalius.

As long as Honorius lived—and he lived until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 423, during the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus—Valentinian, still a child, did not obtain the dignity of Augustus. His father Constantius had received and retained that dignity from Honorius until the final day of his life, the second of September in the year 421.

After the death of his uncle Honorius, Valentinian was named Caesar and Augustus by his cousin Theodosius the Younger on the eighteenth of October in the year 425, and the Western Empire was assigned to him.

Therefore, to prevent the Bibliothecary’s text from disturbing the history, it should be understood as presenting Placidia at the election of Pope Boniface as residing at Ravenna together with her son Valentinian, who was still an infant—not as sitting there with him as Augustus, but rather with her husband Constantius, to whom the dignity of Augustus had been granted in that same year.

Placidia, therefore, Honorius’s sister, and Constantius, Placidia’s husband, wrote to that same emperor Honorius concerning the schism of Eulalius. When this passage says, in line 14, that Eulalius was ordered by both Augusti to leave the City after the Paschal festival, we understand that these Augusti who imposed the sentence of exile upon Eulalius were Honorius and Constantius.

Line 20.—“So that no woman or nun should touch or wash the sacred pallia, or place incense in the church.”

A decree not unlike this was issued by Soter; the reason for its enactment is indicated in note 12 under St. Soter, namely, that the heresy of Marcion was admitting women of its sect to the ministry of the altar.

I believe that the occasion for renewing that decree arose under Boniface. After peace had been restored to the Church under Constantine, as monastic institutions began to flourish in the City during the course of the fourth century—as we explained above under Damasus—and consecrated virgins had decided to establish and inhabit certain rudimentary monasteries, they also received definite rules: in the East from Basil the Great, throughout Africa from Augustine (*Letter* 109), and in the West from Innocent and other Fathers.

Altaserra observes in his notes to Innocent that Siricius wished monks to be chosen for the clergy, according to the canon *Monachus*, distinction 16, question 1. It therefore came about that those consecrated virgins too were admitted to the register of the Church’s distributions, to receive them together with the clergy, since they had been entrusted to the bishop’s care.

For this reason they are sometimes called “canonical” virgins by Chrysostom: women who had professed chastity under a fixed rule. See Thomassinus, *On the Ancient and New Discipline of the Church*, part I, book III, chapter 42, number 12.

Likewise, pious women who assisted at the burials of the faithful, singing with the acolytes, received a share in the Church’s regular provision. See the same Thomassinus, chapter 51, number 7.

Therefore, lest from the rationale of the canon and from their association with the lower clergy in singing there should at some point creep into their minds an idea, or an ambition, that they had been assigned an equal ministry with the clergy for service at the altar, Boniface judged that the decrees of his predecessors should be recalled and carefully confirmed, in order to uproot every source and occasion of such an error and ambition: no woman or nun was to touch the sacred pallia.

No. 60, line 7.—“He was also buried in the cemetery of St. Felicitas on the Salarian Way.”

A very distinguished man, following Ciaconius, charges the Bibliothecary with falsehood:

“Since it is clear,” he says, “from Ciaconius that the cemetery of St. Felicitas was near that of Callistus on the Appian Way, where today there is a chapel of that same martyr, in which an inscription of Boniface I, pope and confessor, is read, and his coffin is visible, in which his body was once deposited.”

The illustrious author will nevertheless pardon me if I undertake to vindicate the Bibliothecary from certain documents which demonstrate that the cemetery of St. Felicitas was situated on the Salarian Way. These documents do not conflict with the first burial of Pope Boniface on the Salarian Way, just as that burial does not conflict with his later translation to the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, with portions of his relics also divided among various churches of the City, where they are preserved and venerated.

The fact that the cemetery of St. Felicitas was located on the Salarian Way, and that the churches of St. Silvanus the martyr and of St. Boniface the pope and confessor were adjacent to it, is taught not only here by the biographer but also in the *Life of Pope Hadrian*, number 345. He says that the same neighboring cemeteries, basilicas, and buildings were restored by Hadrian himself:

“He restored with wondrous magnificence the cemetery of St. Felicitas on the Salarian Way, together with the churches of St. Silvanus the martyr and of St. Boniface the confessor and pontiff, all joined together in one place. He also renewed the basilica of St. Saturninus, situated on the aforesaid Salarian Way, together with the cemetery of the saints Chrysanthus and Daria, and renovated the cemetery of St. Hilaria. Indeed, he also restored anew the cemetery of the Jordanians, namely, those of the saints Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis the martyrs, or of the seven holy virgins. Likewise, on the same Salarian Way he renewed the cemetery of St. Silvester the confessor and pontiff, together with that of many other saints, which had fallen into ruin.”

In this passage I think the copyist’s error in the final lines should be corrected, so that they perhaps should read:

“Indeed, he also restored anew the cemetery of the Jordanians, namely, those of the saints Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis the martyrs, or of the seven holy brothers”—for the ignorant copyist, I think, substituted the sigla “VII VV.” for “VII FF.”, interpreting them as “seven virgins.”

These names—Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis—belong to three of the seven brother martyrs, who were likewise sons of St. Felicitas, as is clear from the Acts reprinted among the *Sincere and Select* works by R. P. Ruinart.

Ruinart also observes that in the very ancient Bucherian martyrology, belonging to the fourth century of Christ, these names, together with those of the remaining brothers and the same depositions, are recorded in the following words:

“On the sixth day before the Ides of July: Felix and Philippus in Priscilla’s cemetery; and in the cemetery of the Jordanians, Martialis, Vitalis, and Alexander; and in that of Maximus, Silvanus”—read “Silvanus,” for the Novatians stole this martyr—“and in Praetextatus, Januarius.”

In the Prolegomena we published this with Bucher’s marginal note, asserting: “They are the seven sons of St. Felicitas.” There, too, instead of “the Novatians stole this martyr,” he rightly thinks that one should read: “the Novatianists stole this martyr.”

Accordingly, on the Salarian Way, at the first milestone from the City, there are three neighboring cemeteries: those of Priscilla, the Jordanians, and Maximus. Six of the sons of St. Felicitas were buried in them, while the first of the seven, named Januarius, was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.

See also the ancient capitulary of the Gospels and the notes of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius under the month of July, page 183.

The seven sons of St. Felicitas were named as follows:

1. Januarius  
2. Felix  
3. Philippus  
4. Silvanus  
5. Alexander  
6. Vitalis  
7. Martialis

Only Januarius is recorded as having been buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Praetextatus. Felix and Philippus were buried in Priscilla’s cemetery; Martialis, Vitalis, and Alexander in the cemetery of the Jordanians; and Silvanus in the cemetery of Maximus.

That the cemetery of Maximus was situated on the Salarian Way, around the first milestone from the City, is proved not only by other documents but also by a fragment of a marble tablet excavated there in the vineyard of Dr. John Baptist Sintes, a physician, ten years ago. He gave it to me together with several Christian inscriptions from that same cemetery. Some of them, as was customary, give, as was customary, the consulships in which the faithful there mentioned were buried.

The tablet, a representation of which I have arranged to present here, has a mutilated inscription, since part of the marble is missing. Its elegant form of lettering reveals a sufficiently cultivated age, such as appears in other monuments of the third century of Christ. It also displays two seated figures on chairs furnished with cushions.

The names are added to the figures: Maximus to one and Secundinus to the other. Between the two figures [Col. 0192D] rises a more ornate and higher seat with a decorated back, on which no one is seated. I think this is an episcopal cathedra.

To the right of that seat sits Maximus, a bearded man dressed in a tunic and pallium. To the left sits Secundinus, beardless, likewise wearing a tunic and pallium.

Maximus raises his right hand, extended, in the manner of a priest giving a blessing: two fingers, namely the index and middle fingers, are extended, while the others are folded toward the palm. Thus Maximus appears to be represented as a presbyter conducting a Christian gathering with Secundinus and celebrating sacred offices in the cemeteries of the martyrs during those gatherings before dawn about which Pliny writes to Trajan in book X, letter 97.

Certainly Maximus imparts a blessing by the same ritual and sits in the same way in a more distinguished place near the episcopal seat as the weekly priest sits among us in the choir and, when we are beginning the reading at the morning prayers, pronounces the blessing and makes the sign of the cross with his hand.

[Col. 0193]

[Col. 0193A]

The Bibliothecary mentions Maximus, presbyter and martyr during the persecution of Decius, both in the *Life of St. Fabian*, number 21, and in the acts of St. Cornelius, number 22.

In the *Life of St. Fabian* he writes:

“After his passion—which occurred under the consuls Decius for the second time and Gratus, in the year of Christ 250—Moses and Maximus, presbyters, and Nicostratus, a deacon, were arrested and sent to prison. At the same time Novatian came from Africa and separated Novatianus and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses the presbyter died in prison, where he had been for eleven months, as had many others.”

Then in the *Life of St. Cornelius* he adds:

“After this had happened, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius together with Maximus the presbyter, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church and became faithful confessors.”

Whether this presbyter Maximus, a faithful confessor who was with the presbyter Moses under Cornelius—that is, in the year of Christ 252—survived for another six years and suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Valerian in the year 258, when the edict mentioned by St. Cyprian in letter 82 was issued, ordering that bishops, priests, and deacons should be punished immediately; and whether therefore he is the same presbyter Maximus whom the Roman Martyrology commemorates on the tenth of November and declares to have been crowned during the persecution of Valerian, is not clear to me.

Certainly his age is consistent with the form of the letters and the drawing represented on this marble.

Concerning Secundinus the martyr, buried on this same Salarian Way—or at least venerated there together with Saints Cyriacus the deacon, Largus, Smaragdus, and their companions, later transferred from the Salarian Way to the Ostian Way by St. Marcellus—see Florentius in the older martyrology under the eighth of August.

After collating the Pisan, Antwerp, Corbie, and Queen of Sweden codices—now Vatican—which mention both roads, the Salarian and the Ostian, he writes:

“The confusion which now appears in our books and in the Corbie martyrology is easily removed, since the holy martyrs were both buried and venerated on the Salarian Way and on the Ostian Way.”

That is, some of them were later transferred from the Salarian Way, where they had first been buried, to the Ostian Way by the blessed Marcellus.

The cemetery of Maximus, therefore, and that of St. Felicitas and her sons, situated on the Salarian Way around the first milestone from the City and restored by Hadrian I, was the place where St. Boniface, pope and confessor, the first of that name, was buried.

Nothing in this contradicts the Bibliothecary’s statement that his first burial took place in the cemetery of St. Felicitas on the Salarian Way, where, while he was alive, he had constructed so many restorations. His body was later transferred from that subterranean cemetery to another cemetery on the Appian Way, as happened with so many other martyrs and confessors who were transferred from there, as I have mentioned.

“Above we warned, in the notes on Zosimus, that in this Anastasian collection the more important decrees are repeatedly missing—decrees which, although they were recorded in books of a different character and were well known, the abridger of these Lives perhaps thought should not be repeated here. In addition to the reasons already indicated for the omission of earlier constitutions, the Life of Boniface supplies another: in it the Librarian does not enumerate the judicial decisions and laws enacted by Boniface through his *tractoriae* on matters of the greatest gravity, both in the cause of the faith and in disciplinary legislation—whether in condemning Pelagius and Celestius or in establishing apostolic vicariates. Since Boniface’s predecessors had treated these same matters of faith and discipline, and his successor Celestine later continued them, the compiler of the Lives, as I suppose, deemed it sufficient to indicate in one or another section the constitutions then issued, while the remaining ones were contained in the collection. For us, however, it seems useful to distinguish the proper acts of each pontiff on the basis of the notes of those who treated the matter carefully, especially Pagi and Somier, which we shall customarily transcribe here. From the work of Archbishop Somier, however, for the sake of brevity we shall condense the substance of what he says, without reproducing every word where this is unnecessary.”

[Note: [Col. 0194C]

No. 60, line 2.—“Here, during the dispute with Eulalius, he was ordained on the same day.” A schism arose between Boniface and Eulalius. Symmachus, prefect of the City, being inclined toward Eulalius, misrepresented Boniface’s case to the emperor Honorius, who was then staying at Ravenna. He claimed that Eulalius had the better rights and had himself been duly and legitimately ordained, whereas Boniface was spurious and illegitimate; and that, on the basis of Symmachus’s false report, Boniface, because he had intruded himself tyrannically, ought to be expelled, so that peace and ecclesiastical discipline might be safeguarded. But when the matter had truly become known and established, the emperor Honorius, replying against Eulalius, favored Boniface: he restored the latter to the see and expelled the former from the City.

Line 9.—“Of Felicitas the martyr. Beside her body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0195A]

No. 60, line 15.—“They recalled him to the City by imperial authority.” Once restored to his see and seated there peacefully, Boniface appealed to the emperor Honorius to provide for the future peace of the Church, so that it would not be divided by a new schism after his death. The most religious emperor granted the holy pontiff’s request and decreed that, if two men had been elected through canvassing, neither of them would be pontiff: “Only he shall remain in the apostolic see whom divine judgment and the consensus of the whole body, through a new ordination, shall have chosen from among the clergy.” This is established by Honorius’s rescript to Boniface, preserved in Baronius under the year 419, no. 12. At that time Eulalius, together with his supporters, was living in exile at Antium, not far from the City, awaiting the death of Boniface, who was broken and weakened by advanced age and poor health. The author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, however, writes that Eulalius later became bishop of the Church of Nepi.

Boniface not only provided for the future peace of the Church; he also seems to have obtained from Honorius a constitution against the Pelagians, since Prosper, in *Against the Collator*, chapter 41, writes: “Boniface of holy memory enjoyed the Catholic devotion of the most pious emperors, and against the enemies of God’s grace he used not only apostolic edicts but also royal ones.” Honorius himself mentions this constitution in a letter given at Ravenna on the fifth day before the Ides of June to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. In it he indicates that he had renewed the constitution which he had issued in 418 against Pelagius and Celestius, and had also decreed that anyone who knowingly failed to denounce or expel them, wherever in the world he might act, should himself be driven into exile. This constitution, sent to Aurelius with the aforesaid letter, has not come down to us. After receiving it, Aurelius sent letters to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana on the Kalends of August. In them he distinguishes the imperial constitution from the letter addressed to him and urges them all to subscribe to the condemnation of Celestius and Pelagius, as Honorius commands in the aforesaid letter.

[Col. 0195D] It is very important to note the words of this letter. “For never before,” Garnerius says in Dissertation III, where the overthrow of the heresy is discussed, “as far as we know, had any constitution of the Christian emperors been issued requiring all bishops to be summoned—whether those who had been absent from a council at which a formula of faith had been established or a heresy, together with its authors, condemned, or even those who remained quietly in their own sees and were not suspected on account of heresy—to subscribe to a sentence issued by the Church against a particular person. Certainly there is no such constitution in the entire Theodosian Code, nor in the ecclesiastical historians; for the measures alleged concerning Eusebius and Theognis in the Arian controversy have an entirely different character.” This constitution may therefore rightly be regarded as the model for many subsequent ones. The law requiring subscription was first enacted by sacerdotal authority and then by imperial authority, as is clear from the words of Prosper about Boniface quoted above and from other testimonies of writers of the same century, cited by the same Garnerius in his dissertation on subscriptions from the records of the Pelagian controversy.

Just as, in the Eutychian controversy, there was no other formula of faith than the letter of Saint Leo on the Incarnation to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, so in the Pelagian controversy there seems to have been no other than the *Tractoria* of Pope Zosimus to all the bishops of the entire world. This is clearly attested, among others, by Marius Mercator in his *Commonitorium*, in these words: “All the chapters written above, as has already been said, are contained in that letter of Bishop Zosimus of blessed memory which is called the *Tractoria*. In it Celestius and Pelagius were condemned; it was sent both to Constantinople and throughout the whole world and was confirmed by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers. Julian and his other accomplices, however, refusing to subscribe and unwilling to show themselves in agreement with those Fathers, were not only deposed and deprived of office by imperial laws and sacerdotal decrees, but also expelled from all Italy.”

Line 21.—“Nor should a slave be made a cleric or be liable to the curia.” While Boniface was seated in the see, Theodosius, emperor of the East, issued a rescript on the day before the Ides of July in the year 421, by which he extended the rights of the episcopate of Constantinople also to Illyricum. He therefore removed the Illyrian diocese from the Roman pontiff and transferred it to the patriarchal jurisdiction of the imperial city. At the request, however, of his uncle Honorius, Theodosius rescinded the same law in 422, as is clear from the rescript of that same Theodosius in reply to a letter from Honorius, published by Holstenius in the Roman collection, page 81 and following. That law had been issued at the insistence of the Illyrian bishops; for Theodosius says in his rescript to Honorius: “Having removed every surreptitious petition of the bishops supplicating throughout Illyricum, we decree that what the ancient apostolic discipline and the old canons declare shall be observed. Concerning this matter, according to the form of the oracle of Your Perpetuity, we have sent written instructions to the illustrious prefects of the praetorium of our Illyricum, so that, once the bishops’ surreptitious petitions have ceased, they may take particular care to preserve the ancient order.”

When Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica and vicar of the Holy See throughout Illyricum, had consulted Pope Boniface concerning certain points of ecclesiastical discipline, and Boniface had replied to his questions with the authority of the apostolic see, Rufus encountered opposition from some bishops of those provinces while attempting to execute Boniface’s commands. Rufus therefore wrote back to Boniface asking him not to attribute to him the unfortunate outcome of these constitutions. Boniface, in order to encourage him more strongly to preserve the reverence due to the apostolic see, delegated his own powers to him, as earlier pontiffs had done, in a letter addressed to him on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, during the consulship of the illustrious Monaxius, that is, in the year 419. These letters are preserved by Holstenius, page 54.

[Col. 0196D] In those letters Boniface does not state what the constitutions were which some bishops of those regions had refused to accept. They must therefore be recovered from elsewhere, specifically from other letters of the same Boniface. From these it can be gathered that Rufus reported to him that those bishops, without consulting him, had summoned a synod at Corinth to reopen the case of Perigenes. Perigenes had been ordained bishop of Patras, but because the inhabitants of that city refused to accept him, he had been established by the supreme pontiff in the metropolitan see of Corinth. Rufus had also added that the vicariate granted to him was being held in contempt, and that this contempt also redounded against his own person. Boniface therefore replied that the Illyrian bishops’ new attempts, being contrary to antiquity, could have no force; that causes decided by the apostolic see could not be reopened in the provinces; that the status of Perigenes, metropolitan of Corinth, could not in any way be disturbed; and that councils could not be assembled within Illyricum without Rufus’s knowledge. Consequently Rufus was to be honored on account of his apostolic vicariate, without whose authority bishops could not be ordained throughout those provinces.

“Boniface was especially concerned,” says Baluzius in his supplement to Book V of Marca’s *On Concord*, chapter 24, “about the case of Perigenes—not indeed merely because of his affection for a man devoted above all others to the apostolic see, but chiefly because the definition of the Roman judgment had been shaken by the Illyrian bishops, who afterward attempted to judge the case again in the Corinthian council.” This can be seen in a letter sent by Boniface to the bishops throughout Illyricum on the fifth day before the Ides of March in 422 and quoted by the same Holstenius. In this matter there were two offenses against the majesty of the apostolic see. First, they dared to reopen a case that had been judged by the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff. Second, they were planning to hold that synod without the consent of Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, who was vicar of the Roman see throughout all the provinces of Illyricum. Boniface included these two points in a letter to Rufus, sent on the same day as the preceding one, namely, the fifth day before the Ides of March:

“To the synod which is said to be unlawfully assembled concerning our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes, whose status, as we have written, cannot in any way be disturbed, we have sent such letters that all the brethren may understand, first, that they ought not to have assembled without your knowledge and, second, that what has been judged by us is not to be reconsidered. For it has never been permitted to deliberate again about what has once been established by the apostolic see.”

This matter had taken such deep hold of Boniface’s mind that, when writing the aforesaid letter to the Illyrian bishops who were going to assemble at the Corinthian synod, he openly threatened abstention if they brought Perigenes’s case forward again for discussion. After the sentence of the Roman pontiff, his honor could not possibly be doubtful or uncertain according to the rules:

“Let the synod therefore be assembled,” he says, “so that we may return to the case of this injury, and let the council, always keeping what is dear in its deliberation above all else, recognize its hidden purpose; and what absolutely cannot be done according to the rules will take place: the honor of our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes, whom our sentence placed in the see of the aforesaid Church, will become doubtful and uncertain.”

And below:

“Coming together, as is fitting, brethren, let no one who wishes to remain in our communion bring forward again for discussion the name of our brother and fellow priest Perigenes, whose priesthood the apostle Peter has already once confirmed by the prompting of the Holy Spirit.”

Pope Boniface was therefore displeased by the audacity of the Illyrian bishops, who presumed to assemble councils without Rufus’s knowledge. Pope Innocent had granted Rufus that whenever a case arose requiring an assembly of priests, he could summon whatever bishops he wished from any Churches and settle disputes with them. [Col. 0197D] Boniface went further and decreed that the Illyrian bishops were not permitted to assemble—that is, to celebrate councils—against the knowledge of that same Rufus. Thus, when he learned that those bishops had summoned a synod at Corinth to reopen Perigenes’s case, he was, as he himself says in the same letter, moved and agitated. He ordered that the synod be celebrated only on Rufus’s authority and that the judges be chosen by Rufus:

“Since, however, the accuser must be given his place,” Boniface says in the same letter, “lest we seem altogether to provoke a hearing, if anything is alleged to have been done by him against discipline and the priestly purpose after he had been established as bishop by our authority, our fellow bishop Rufus, to whom we entrust everything in our place, shall undertake, together with the other brethren whom he himself chooses, to hear the case, and shall report to our knowledge everything that the course and order of events have shown to belong to his examination.”

The authority of the apostolic see in the case of Perigenes is clear from the fact that he always retained his dignity. That Boniface decreed that the ordinations of bishops could not be celebrated without Rufus’s knowledge is shown by the same letter to the Illyrian bishops and by another letter given by Boniface on the same day to the Thessalian bishops.

Boniface restored the rights of the Church of Narbonne, which had been diminished by his predecessor Zosimus, in Letter 3 to Hilary of Narbonne. He also restrained Patroclus, bishop of Arles, at whose request Zosimus had subjected the Church of Narbonne to that of Arles and who had ordained a bishop for the Church of Lutuba in lower Aquitania, belonging to the province of Narbonne. Boniface ordered the execution of the Nicene canons, which established that each province should be governed by its own metropolitan.

When the clerics of the city of Valence brought before Pope Boniface the bishop Maximus, whom they knew to be accused of various crimes, especially the Manichaean heresy, and to whom they knew that the more serious cases were to be referred according to ecclesiastical discipline, the pontiff, in Letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul, entrusted the investigation of this affair to the bishops of the seven provinces:

“We have decreed,” he says, “that judgment concerning you must take place within the province and that a synod must be assembled before the Kalends of November, while the right of referral to the apostolic see is nevertheless preserved, to which an appeal could be made from the national councils themselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0198B]

No. 60, line 2.—“Here, during the dispute with Eulalius, etc.” The election of Boniface, the first of that name, to the Roman see was disturbed by the intrusion of Eulalius, archdeacon of this Church. During the first conflicts, which stirred up the factions on both sides, the emperor Honorius had already been influenced by the supporters of Eulalius. The larger and sounder part of the Roman clergy, however, which had elected Boniface, presented a supplicatory petition to the emperor, asking him to order the earlier measures to be removed—namely, the rescripts he had issued—and to summon Eulalius to the court, that is, to call him to Ravenna, where Honorius resided. They promised that Pope Boniface would come with his priests. Honorius willingly received the petition that had been presented. Nevertheless, he did not claim for himself the power of ecclesiastical judgment.

Indeed, he wrote back that he would summon bishops from different provinces “so that, once the matter had been brought into question, the dispute of many before us might resolve it” (*Rescript of Honorius to Symmachus*).

But Eulalius’s attempted actions, described by the Librarian in this number, line 10, removed the need for an episcopal judgment. Eulalius was expelled from the City by order of the emperor, as a recalcitrant, through Symmachus, prefect of the City. Boniface was brought back into the City, and the people acclaimed him as the legitimate pontiff, “since all orders have yielded to divine judgment and to the will of Your Majesty,” as the same prefect wrote back to Honorius.

[Col. 0198D] In Africa, however, the examination of the cases begun under Zosimus was continued by the bishops gathered in a national council at Carthage from seventeen provinces, in the presence of legates sent by Zosimus.

As for appeals by bishops to the Roman see, Pope Zosimus, in support of its defense, had produced the fifth canon of the Council of Sardica under the name of Nicaea. At that time, as we said above, these two councils were regarded as one, both for the reasons given above and also so that the true council celebrated by Catholics at Sardica would not be confused with the council of Arians held at Philippopolis. This matter was not sufficiently clear to the Africans. Alipius, one of the Fathers of the council, denied that this decree was found at all in the acts of the Council of Nicaea. They therefore thought that copies of the Nicene synod should be requested and that Bishop Boniface should be asked to send some people who could produce, in accordance with his letters, the copies of that Nicene council. In the meantime, while they awaited them, they said that they would observe the commands conveyed by Boniface’s legates.

The matter of appeals by presbyters was also discussed. In this affair, when Faustinus, the legate of the Holy See, protested that the rights of that see must not be diminished, Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, said:

“In addition to the very matters which we have promised in the acts, it is also necessary that we communicate fully, in a letter from our humble selves, each matter we discuss to our holy brother and fellow priest Boniface.” (*Council of Carthage VI*, chapter 5.)

They not only did this, but, following the example of the earlier synods under Zosimus, they clearly explained the power of the Holy See over the African Churches, leaving it to the judgment of the Roman pontiff either to delegate his envoys with authority to investigate or to leave the settlement of the dispute to the judgment of the provincial bishops, and so forth.

It is therefore clear from what has been said that the African Fathers did not deny the right of appeal to the Roman see; [Col. 0199B] rather, they disputed the manner in which that right was to be pursued and exercised, when the Roman legates produced chapters 4 and 5 of the Council of Sardica:

“If any bishop, etc., let the Roman bishop be written to; and if he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let him appoint judges,” chapter 4.

“And let no other bishop be ordained in the same seat after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop,” chapter 5.

He also consistently defended the rights of the apostolic vicariate throughout Illyricum, which he had established and which he had granted, at the request of the Corinthians, in the case of Bishop Perigenes. He had first remitted the examination, together with his support, to the bishop of Thessalonica, whom he had appointed his vicar in that region. This occurred when factional promoters of a new jurisdiction—usurped by the bishops of the Church of Constantinople on the occasion of a law issued by the emperor Theodosius, by which he detached the provinces of Illyricum from the Roman patriarchate and assigned them to the judgment of the bishop of Constantinople—had summoned a council at Corinth, without consulting the apostolic vicar, to judge Perigenes’s case.

The letters Boniface sent, both to Rufus himself and to the other bishops of Macedonia, testify with what courage and vigilance he opposed these attempts and likewise strengthened Rufus of Thessalonica, who was similarly affected, against the violence of the usurpers. They are read in the Third Roman Council under Boniface II:

“Blessed Peter the apostle,” he says, “to whom the citadel of the priesthood was granted by the Lord’s voice, is raised to immeasurable joy whenever he foresees that the sons of the unblemished peace granted to him by the Lord are guardians of the honor entrusted to him.”

And in another letter to the same man:

“Therefore, dearest brother, relying on the authority subscribed by you long ago, arm yourself as a capable minister of God against the hostile bands . . . He does not permit the privilege of his see to perish while you, fisherman, are laboring . . . Exercise against the others who are contumacious the right of the power granted to you . . . Concerning the synod said to be unlawfully assembled over the case of our brother and fellow bishop Perigenes, whose status, as we have written, cannot in any way be disturbed, we have sent such letters that all the brethren may understand, first, that they ought not to have assembled without your knowledge; and second, that what has been judged by us is not to be reconsidered. For it has never been permitted to deliberate again about what has once been established by the apostolic see . . .”

Likewise, in the following letter to the same Rufus and the other bishops of Macedonia, he writes:

“No one has ever boldly laid hands against the apostolic dignity, whose judgment may not be reconsidered; no one has rebelled in this matter except one who wished judgment to be passed upon himself.”

In addition to these letters, Boniface also sent legates to the emperor Honorius to obtain his protection, by which the usurpations and prejudicial measures attempted by the Greeks might be averted. Honorius wrote to his imperial colleague, Augustus Theodosius, and obtained from him, in a later rescript, the annulment of what the Illyrians had earlier obtained by fraud against the rights of the Roman Church. He preserved for that Church the full enjoyment and exercise of its ancient power:

“Having removed every surreptitious petition of the bishops supplicating throughout Illyricum, we decree that what the ancient apostolic discipline and the old canons declare shall be observed. Concerning this matter, according to the form of the oracle of Your Perpetuity, we have sent written instructions to the illustrious prefects of the praetorium of our Illyricum, so that, once the bishops’ surreptitious petitions have ceased, they may take particular care to preserve the ancient order, lest the venerable Church lose the privileges established for the most holy City by the ancients, privileges which have consecrated to us the perpetual empire of its name.” (*Rescript of Theodosius A to Honorius A.*)

This law ought to have been inserted into the body of the law, in place of the other law abrogated by it. But the cunning of the compilers carefully arranged matters so that whatever they observed to be advantageous to the Roman Church they excluded from their collection, in order that they might sell and promote the usurpations of Constantinople with greater confidence.]

[Col. 0185]

## 60

Boniface, a Roman by nation, son of the presbyter Jocundus, sat for three years, four months, and thirteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0185] B: five years, minus two months and three days, from the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII to the consulship of Marinianus and Asclepiodorus.]

Here, during the dispute with Eulalius, he was ordained on the same day, and there was dissension in the clergy for seven months and fifteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0185] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 418, at the end.]

Eulalius, however, was ordained in the Constantinian basilica, while Boniface was ordained in the Basilica of Julia. At the same time, when the Augusta Placidia heard of this while she was seated at Ravenna with her son, the Augustus Valentinian, she reported it to the Augustus Honorius, who was seated at Milan. At the same time both Augusti, by an authority jointly issued, ordered that both men leave the City. When they had been compelled to depart, Boniface lived in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas the martyr on the Salarian Way. Eulalius, however, lived in the city of Antium at Saint Hermes.

When the following day of Easter arrived, Eulalius, because he had been ordained in the Constantinian basilica, presumed to enter the City; [Col. 0187] he baptized and celebrated Easter in the Constantinian basilica. Boniface, however, following the custom, celebrated the baptism of Easter in the basilica of Saint Agnes the martyr. When the two Augusti heard this, they sent orders, expelled Eulalius, and, by an authority issued from them, recalled Boniface to the City and established him as bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0187] See Baronius under the year 419.]

They sent Eulalius away into Campania. After three years and eight months Boniface died. The clergy and people requested that Eulalius be recalled, but Eulalius did not consent to return to Rome. He too died in the same place in Campania, one year after Boniface’s death.

This Boniface decreed that no woman or nun should touch or wash the sacred hangings,

[Note: [Col. 0187] The consecrated pallium.]

or place incense in the church, unless it were done by a minister; nor should a slave be made a cleric or be liable to the curia or to any other obligation.

## 61

Here he built an oratory in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas beside her body, and adorned the tomb of Saint Felicitas the martyr and of Saint Livanius

[Note: [Col. 0187] C: Sylvanus.]

where he also placed the following: a silver paten weighing twenty pounds; a silver cup weighing ten pounds; a silver vessel weighing thirteen pounds; two smaller silver chalices weighing four pounds; and three silver crowns weighing fifteen pounds. He held one ordination in the month of December: thirteen presbyters, three deacons, and thirty-six bishops in various places. He too was buried in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas the martyr on the Salarian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November; and the episcopate was vacant for nine days.

[Note: [Col. 0201B]

Lines 2 and 3.—“So that the 150 psalms of David might be read before the sacrifice.” Lucas Holstenius notes in the margin: “before the Canon.” Romuald understands this as the entrance of the Mass. Yet 150 psalms were never sung at that point, but only part of a single psalm. Hence this passage could more correctly be understood of Matins, at which nearly all the psalms of David are sung antiphonally over the course of the year. The author took these words from the second catalogue, from which the Palatine-Vatican catalogue differs somewhat. In the latter it reads that an antiphon should be sung before the sacrifice; some words are missing at that point. Nor was the entrance rite formerly sung antiphonally from Davidic psalms by the clergy in the churches; rather, it was Matins, instituted by Celestine, as can be gathered from the *Liber Pontificalis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0201B]

Line 2.—“Here he enacted many constitutions and decreed that the one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, something that had not previously been done; only the letters of the apostle Paul and the Holy Gospel were recited, and thus Masses were celebrated.” Sigebert likewise reports this under the year 426.

Lines 13 and 14.—“Twenty-four silver wax-bearing vessels in the body of the basilica, each weighing twenty pounds.” “In the body of the basilica” means in the choir or middle of the church. Anastasius, in the Life of Sylvester: “Fifty silver wax-bearing vessels in the body of the basilica.”]

[Note: [Col. 0202B]

Line 3.—“The psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice.” Some understand Celestine to have decreed that antiphons should be placed before the psalms; others, that at the entrance of the Mass an antiphon selected from the psalms should be recited. This is found in the Palatine-Vatican catalogue, where under Celestine it reads: “He decreed that an antiphon should be sung before the sacrifice.” I think, however, that the holy pontiff decreed that throughout the entire week the psalms should be divided among the days, with a fixed number of them assigned to each day, and that they should be sung in the churches. Formerly assemblies were held on Saturday and Sunday, as appears from Cassian, Palladius, and others who describe the rites observed by the monks. The pontiff could also have divided the number of psalms to be recited at Matins, some being recited alternately, and others before the sacrifice.

The occasion for this constitution and for introducing the custom may have arisen from the evil practice of the Arians. To infect the people, they composed hymns in which Arian perfidy was mixed. At night they sang these hymns antiphonally within the city walls; then in the morning they proceeded in groups to a church outside the gates. For by a constitution of Theodosius, issued in 388, churches were taken away from heretics within the cities. Socrates, describing the customs of the Arians living in Constantinople, relates the matter as follows:

“Whenever feast days occurred each week—that is, Saturday and Sunday, on which assemblies are customarily held in the church—they gathered within the city gates, near the public porticoes, and sang hymns appropriately composed for the Arian heresy, responding antiphonally to one another. They did this for most of the night. At dawn, singing the same antiphons, they proceeded through the middle of the City and, going out beyond the gates, made their way to the place where they celebrated their assemblies.”

To restrain their insolence, he could have instituted the singing of psalms antiphonally in the church on each day, so that the words of the psalms, which proclaim Christ, might break the pattern of the heretical hymns and disperse the forest of their errors.

### Line 5

“He made a decree concerning the whole Church, especially concerning the region.” It is better and more correctly read, with other manuscripts, “concerning religions.” To understand the formulas of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, one should note what was said above. Here the text reads, “He made many decrees, and he decreed,” omitting “concerning the Church,” as is found everywhere in what precedes and follows, even when the subject of the decree is omitted. This was done to show that the earlier statutes had been particular, whereas the later ones concerned faith and morals pertaining to the universal Church. He generally lists the earlier decrees because they had been issued in particular letters or similar writings; the later ones, however, because they were preserved in the book of decrees and in the archives of the churches, and were therefore known and manifest. Since priests could not be ignorant of them, mention of the matter previously discussed was omitted.

It is well known that Coelestine issued many decrees concerning regions, or concerning the faith, especially against the Pelagians, Nestorians, and Eastern schismatics. He restrained the heresiarch Celestius, who was renewing the earlier heretical statutes by his customary schemes, especially when he was attempting to obtain a hearing. He not only checked his audacity in seeking a reconsideration of the sentences issued by Innocent and Zosimus, but expelled him from all Italy, as Prosper testifies:

> “The pontiff Coelestine, of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that the condemned ought to be granted not a judicial examination but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Celestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the case had not been examined, to be driven beyond the boundaries of all Italy. So inviolably did he judge that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees must be observed, that he absolutely refused to allow reconsideration of what had once deserved to be cut off.”

Then, when Julian and his associates had approached Nestorius, whom they knew to be offended with Coelestine and Cyril because they opposed the impious opinions which he had conceived and defended, this occasioned the Roman synod convened in 424 or 425, as Garnerius demonstrates in his dissertation on synods convened in the Pelagian controversy. There the synod again condemned both the old and the new opinions of the Pelagians, confirmed Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, and decreed that they were not to be received unless they made an explicit profession and subscription to it.

These conciliar acts, sent by the pontiff to the Fathers at Ephesus, were accepted by common agreement, as the Fathers testify in the fifth session:

> “When the records of the proceedings concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Celestians had been read in the holy synod, we judged that the decrees and decisions which your Piety had issued concerning them must also remain solid and firm.”

That the holy pontiff fought against the Pelagians is also shown, apart from his letter to the bishops of Gaul, by what Prosper records in his *Chronicle*, under the year 429:

> “The Pelagian Agricola, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, corrupted the churches of Britain by introducing his teaching. But through the action of the deacon Palladius, Pope Coelestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place; and, after the heretics had been driven out, he directed the Britons to the Catholic faith.”

He had as his companion Lupus, bishop of Troyes. Concerning him, the Anonymous author of his life adds under the year 428, when he was chosen bishop:

> “After a period of two years had been completed, he departed for Britain with Saint Germanus against the Pelagian heresy, which attacked the sound faith.”

What he did against the Nestorians, Eastern schismatics, and Semi-Pelagians is clear; consequently it is certain that Coelestine issued many decrees concerning religion. The title “decree concerning religions” is understood to denote a decree of faith for the use of that period, as is clear from the synodical letter of the Roman council, which quotes the words of the rescript of the emperors Valentinian and Gratian:

> “Concerning the other priests of the churches, let the Roman bishop conduct the examination, so that the pontiff, together with his colleagues, may judge concerning the religion of religion.”

### Line 6

“Which are today kept stored in the archive of the Church.” These words prove and confirm what was said above: namely, that these apostolic decrees of faith, because they were contained in an accessible book and preserved in the archives, were not expressly set down in the *Book of the Pontiffs*. The same is said below concerning the decretal letters of Saint Leo: “Which are today kept stored in the archive.”

That general decrees were readily available and preserved both at Rome and in the archives of the patriarchal sees and other churches is made certain by Acacius, who wrote to Pope Simplicius concerning decrees issued by the apostolic see for the Alexandrian Church. He asserts that these decrees were kept both in the Roman archives and in the most distinguished archives:

> “As it was found in our archives, so, if you deign to inquire in your own repositories, you will be able to learn what subsequently occurred concerning the same matter and what was reported from the bishop of Alexandria to Rome and from one side to the other.”

When Pope Anastasius had sent Rufinus a letter of admonition, and Rufinus, seeking to evade its force, accused Jerome of having fabricated it, Anastasius, among other replies aimed at overturning the accusation, addressed Rufinus as follows:

> “If you suspect that I fabricated the letter, why do you not seek it in the record office of the Roman Church?”

That these letters bore reliable identifying marks is shown by the following words of Saint Jerome:

> “We demonstrate that the letter is his—that is, Anastasius’s—against you; the whole world acknowledges it, and it has clearly come into your hands as an authentic document. I marvel at the shame—or rather, at the shamelessness—with which you deny what you doubt is true.”

The diligence of the apostolic see in issuing these letters and preserving copies with the same identifying marks is described by Nicholas I in letters sent to the emperor Michael; he also gives the reason for this diligence: so that the letters might not be falsified by wicked men.

### Line 7

“After the Raetian fire.” The Florentine codex of the Library of Saint Mark reads “after the Getic fire.” This seems to indicate the disaster inflicted on the city in 410 by the Getae—whom we also call Goths—under Alaric. The pontiffs took the greatest care to restore what had been carried away, especially the sacred vessels belonging to the ministry of the Church. Hence, in the account of Leo:

> “He renewed, after the Vandalic disaster, all the sacred silver furnishings melted down throughout the titular churches.”

[Note: [Col. 0204C]]

### Line 1

“Coelestine.” By the authority of this pontiff, Britain, Scotland, and Italy were cleansed of the Pelagian heresy; the Eastern Churches of the Nestorian heresy; and the Burgundians and Hibernians were converted to the faith of Christ. Everyone can therefore understand how foolishly Laurentius Valla, a grammarian wholly ignorant of ecclesiastical affairs, asserted that Pope Coelestine—who was the first of all to condemn Nestorius at Rome and who arranged, through his legates, for him likewise to be expelled by the ecumenical Council of Ephesus—had been infected with the heresies of that same Nestorius. These statements are drawn from Prosper, Bede, and Baronius, under the years 423 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

## Chronological Notes

The pontifical eras of Coelestine, Xystus, and Leo are demonstrated from the date of the birth, or ordination, of Hilary, who succeeded Leo. In the acts of the Roman council of 465, under the consuls Flavius Basiliscus and Herminericus, and in Hilary’s letter issued under the same consuls, the anniversary of his episcopal ordination is assigned to 19 November, four years before that council. For the beginning of that period is marked by Marcellinus in his *Chronicle* under the consuls Severinus and Daglaifus in 461, together with the death of the emperor Majorian, which is also known to have occurred under the consulship of Severinus from Letter 11 of Sidonius, Book 1.

From that Sunday, 19 November 461, the anniversary of Hilary’s accession to the chair, one proceeds backward through each of his predecessors to Boniface, assigning to each the period of his pontificate expressed in the historical records and adding, day by day, the interval during which the see remained vacant after his death. The total period is thereby established. These periods and intervals are recorded by Anastasius and other writers.

From 4 September 422, therefore—the day on which Saint Boniface departed this mortal life—let thirty-nine full years, two months, and twelve days be counted, according to the preceding computation, properly assembled. The terminal date of the calculation is 4 November 461, the last day of the vacancy of the see after the death of Leo the Great. The following day, 19 November, marked with the Sunday letter A, provides the most suitable time for the ordination of Blessed Hilary, which, according to the acts of the council and the letter of the same pontiff already mentioned, he himself was accustomed to commemorate annually on that day.

Besides the terminal points of this total period, which agree exactly with the documents, let the intermediate epochs of Saint Xystus III and Saint Leo the Great also be compared, as I shall show below in the individual accounts of each. Thus, from this division and assignment, which remains consistent everywhere, the epoch of Coelestine emerges as firmly established.

## Historical Notes

### Line 2

“He made many decrees”; and Line 5: “He made a decree concerning the whole Church, especially concerning religions, which are today kept stored in the archive of the Church.”

It is evident that the librarian of the Roman see, here and in the sections concerning the other pontiffs, wished merely to indicate that the decrees and decretal letters of these supreme pontiffs must be sought in other codices of the Roman Church, together with the more important sanctions concerning the faith and other serious matters, issued in councils or transmitted to the provinces. Since the *Brief Summary of Lives*, compiled in the form of the old catalogues, undertook to extract only a few items, it included matters pertaining to the particular condition and adornment of this Roman Church: such things as titles and basilicas founded, endowed, or enriched with gifts; ordinations held there; and other matters of this kind.

More important works pertaining to the condition and government of the universal Church are generally indicated briefly by the generic clause, “He made a decree concerning the Church.” Concerning Coelestine it states: “He made many decrees.” Certainly he made many, both in the Roman councils and at Ephesus against Nestorius; in Italy, Britain, and Africa against the Pelagians and Novatians; and in decretal letters issued concerning discipline, the establishment of individual metropolitans throughout the provinces, the promotion of men to the episcopate, and many other matters. Since these are discussed in the notes of the illustrious Lord Somier, archbishop of Caesarea, and collected by Pagianus, they need not be repeated in ours. Concerning the churches in the City which Coelestine took away from the Novatians, see Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 11.

### Line 2

“He caused David’s one hundred and fifty psalms to be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice.”

What it means to sing a psalm antiphonally is explained above all with great learning and clarity by the late Cardinal Thomasius, who quotes this very passage of the Librarian both in the preface to the *Responsorials and Antiphonaries of the Roman Church*, page 21 and following, and in his discussion of ancient rites concerning the singing of the Mass, prefixed to the *Ancient Books of the Masses of the Roman Church*, page 10 and following.

In the indicated preface to the *Responsorials and Antiphonaries*, after defining an antiphon as a reciprocal voice by which two choirs of singers alternate their singing, he distinguishes the ancient rite—introduced into the Mosaic Church from the time of David—of singing psalms alternately through three choirs of singers: the Kohathites under Heman, the Gershonites under Asaph, and the Merarites under Ethan (1 Chronicles 6). From there the practice passed to the Christian Church. He observes, on the basis of Eusebius, *History*, Book II, chapter 17, that in the earliest times the more frequent custom was to sing responsorial psalms, with the entire choir responding to a single leader. Then, on page 22, he says:

> “The first to establish that psalms should be sung by two choirs were Flavianus and Diodorus, contemporaries of Saint Athanasius.”

> “For these men were the first—as Bishop Theodoret of Cyrrhus writes in the *Tripartite History*, Book V, chapter 32—to divide the choir of singers into two parts and teach them to sing David’s melody antiphonally. This first began to be done at Antioch, and from there it spread as far as the ends of the whole world.”

See Saint Basil’s letter to the clergy of Neocaesarea; Sidonius, Book V, Letter 17; Cassiodorus on Psalm 33, no. 3; and others in many places.

> “The kind of alternating song in question is chiefly comprised within the ecclesiastical rite in which the choirs indeed alternate the melody, but do not sing one and the same psalm or canticle in succession. One choir sings the melody of a verse of a psalm, while the other choir sings something else, apart from the psalm or canticle itself, between the individual verses. This element, which is more frequently repeated by the other choir, is generally called an antiphon by the Latins, but among the Greeks an antiphonal *troparion*.” In this sense, therefore, an antiphon is a shorter and more concise song, or a properly formed combination of words serving as an interpolated sentence, which one choir sings between the verses while responding to the other choir that is singing the psalm.”

This is the kind of antiphon of which Socrates speaks in Book VI, chapter 8—not the alternating singing of psalms first instituted by Flavianus and Diodorus, as we have seen above from Theodoret. The two accounts can easily be reconciled in the manner just described. The learned priest Petrus Gussanuillaeus wished this reconciliation to be supplied in the preface to the *Antiphonary of Saint Gregory*.

Socrates writes as follows, from the old translation of Epiphanius Scholasticus, *Tripartite History*, Book X, chapter 9:

> “It must nevertheless be explained from what source the practice of singing antiphons in the Church took its beginning. Ignatius, the third bishop of Syrian Antioch after the Apostle Peter, who also lived with the apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels, how they sang hymns to the Holy Trinity antiphonally. He is therefore shown to have transmitted the manner of that vision to the Church of Antioch, and from there it passed to all the churches.”

That Socrates understood by the term “antiphon” a composed hymn sung responsively may be inferred from the fact that what he relates about Saint Ignatius indicates that it belonged to this category, as did the other antiphons first used by the Arians at Constantinople and subsequently introduced among the Catholics by Saint John Chrysostom. The Arians sang their antiphons, composed according to Arian doctrine, and frequently sang this impious one:

> “Where are those who say that he is one in threefold power?”

By contrast, the antiphons of the Catholics were hymns proclaiming the *homoousion*. See chapter 10 of the *Tripartite History*.

> “Saint Ambrose was the first to institute antiphons in the Church of Milan,” for Paulinus says in his *Life of Ambrose*: “At this time antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan. The devotion of this celebration has continued to the present day, not only in that Church but throughout almost all the provinces of the West.”

Saint Augustine confirms this in *Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 7:

> “At that time it was established that hymns and psalms should be sung, according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people might not waste away from the weariness of grief.”

I believe these statements have the force of showing that not only were psalms sung alternately, but that certain hymns, or selections from sacred songs, were also sung responsively. For the hymns mentioned there are not the sacred songs which, chiefly on the authority of Ambrose, we use today. The Easterners do not use them in the manner in which our Westerners employ them. Therefore, by the name “hymns,” I think those sacred little songs should be understood which Paulinus had previously called antiphons: the former word explaining the manner of singing, the latter the thing that was sung.

> “As far as can be learned from ancient writers, the Roman Church attributes the use of antiphons to Pope Saint Coelestine.” See the very learned Henschenius, *Acts of the Saints*, 10 April, day 6, page 544.

Once the practice had been received, the Roman Church retained it consistently, as is plainly shown by Book 7 of the *Daybook of the Roman Pontiffs* and by the antiphonaries of Saint Gregory, both for the Mass and for the offices. Concerning the use of antiphons in the other Churches of the West, the various ancient councils of the nations and the ancient constitutions of the monks should be consulted. We must hasten to pursue what writers on ecclesiastical rites have treated less clearly than they ought: namely, the circumstances of the antiphons, that is, the manner and rite according to which they are sung in the Church.

> “An antiphon, then, as we said, is a verse or interpolated sentence which is sung together with some or all of the verses of a psalm or canticle in an interpolated melody, in precisely the order in which ecclesiastical responsories are sung. The antiphon differs from the responsory in this respect: in responsories the choir responds to one singer, whereas in antiphons one choir sings in response to another. In a responsory, one singer sings a verse, while the choir always inserts the responsory; in an antiphon, one choir sings the verse and the other choir responds with the antiphon.”

Rabanus, *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, Book I, chapter 33:

> “The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person sings the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses.”

When, therefore, Pope Coelestine instituted the antiphonal singing of psalms in the Holy Roman Church, as we read in this section, it follows that he contributed substantially to the arrangement of the divine office, both nocturnal and diurnal. For psalms sung antiphonally permeate nearly all the parts of the daily task required of the clergy in the praises of God.

### Line 5

“He made a decree concerning the whole Church, etc. ‘Which are today kept in the archive of the Church,’ etc.”

The remaining decrees of this blessed pontiff must be sought in his decretal letters and in the acts of the councils. Ancient copies of these letters survive in the often-mentioned codex of the title and monastery of Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the City. One letter is dated under the consuls Florentius and Dionysius, on 21 July—that is, in the year of Christ 429—which Coelestine wrote to all the bishops established throughout the province of Viennensis (that is, Vienne) and Narbonensis. It begins: “We would indeed wish,” and so forth.

Among the councils, the most celebrated is the letter produced at Ephesus by his legates in the second session, which shows how great and how extensive was the care the blessed pontiff exercised for all the churches of the world:

> “Bishop Arcadius, legate of the Roman Church, said: ‘Let your Blessedness command that the letters brought from the City of the holy and most reverently named Pope Coelestine, bishop of the apostolic see, be read aloud. From them your Blessedness will be able to learn what care he exercises for all the churches,’” and so forth.

The acclamations that followed sufficiently demonstrate the Fathers’ judgment:

> “All the most reverend bishops acclaimed together: ‘This is a just judgment. To the new Paul, Coelestine; to the new Paul, Cyril; to Coelestine, guardian of the faith,’” and so forth.

Those letters were given to Coelestine on 8 May, under the consuls Bassus and Antiochus—that is, in the year of Christ 431.

The acclamations of the Fathers at the Council of Ephesus, which bear celebrated witness to Coelestine’s exceptional care in defending the truth of the Catholic faith, also commend his wholly apostolic firmness in consolidating the ancient discipline and exercising the authority of the Roman see over the entire Christian people and over the leaders of the Christian people—that is, all the pastors of the churches—in order to keep them in the fulfillment of their duty.

For this reason, Peter, a presbyter of the title of Saint Sabina, thought that the primacy of that see, so splendidly asserted in his judgments and laws, should be commemorated above all other monuments of the period in a mosaic work dedicated in the title of Saint Sabina. It still survives in almost complete integrity and is considered the most ancient of the Christian mosaics preserved through twelve centuries. Several writers have published it, and the most devoted student of sacred antiquity, Bishop Joannes Ciampinus, reproduced it with an engraving on copper in the first volume of his work.

Among other things, it displays the Church from the Gentiles and the Church from the circumcision. Since the Apostle Peter established the primacy of his chair in both, Coelestine, heir to that chair and authority, likewise did not cease to exercise his office by defending its rights in the general councils. An inscription rising above these figures and covering the entire wall speaks of Coelestine, who administered and steadfastly defended this primacy, as follows:

> “When Coelestine held the apostolic summit,  
> First among bishops, he shone throughout the whole world,”  
> and so forth.

For the rest, consult what we prefixed in the prolegomena to this volume concerning the splendid assertion of the primacy of the Roman see during the centuries encompassed by this volume, both from the preliminary dissertation of Archbishop Somier and from our observations presented there.

### Line 7

“He dedicated the Basilica of Julia.”

Cardinal Rasponus demonstrated that this basilica must be sought within the Lateran patriarchate, *On the Lateran Patriarchate*, Book IV, chapter 14, page 332. He writes:

> “In an ancient ritual codex, in which the coronation of the Roman emperor is discussed, this basilica is mentioned very frequently. It is stated that the emperor Constans, having been brought to the City, proceeded on Saturday to the Lateran and reclined in the Basilica of Julia.”

He also observes that it had shortly before been read, in section 60 concerning Saint Boniface, that during the schism provoked by the supporters of Eulalius, who were hostile to Boniface’s election, Boniface was created pontiff in the Basilica of Julia, while Eulalius was elected by the faction in the Constantiniana.

He therefore thinks that the Basilica of Julia should be identified with a chapel of the Lateran patriarchate located near the oratory and chapel of Saint Sylvester, which took its name from Pope Julius, its founder. The statement that Julius’s basilica was founded near the Forum does not prevent its being understood as this very basilica erected near the Lateran Forum.

The Librarian describes it as situated there in the account of Siricius, section 158, as Rasponus and Famianus Nardinus observe. When the apostolic see was vacant after the death of Conon, part of the clergy elected Theodore the archpresbyter, who occupied the inner part of the Lateran palace. Paschal the archdeacon, however, brought forward to the pontificate by another faction, occupied the outer part of the patriarchate, from the Oratory of Saint Sylvester, and “the basilica of the house of Julia, which faces the Campus.”

This also removes the difficulty caused by the two names, the Basilica of Julius and the Basilica of Julia attributed to this oratory, which had troubled Cardinal Rasponus in the place cited. For the Librarian’s testimony clearly shows that both the Basilica of Julius and the Basilica of Julia were called after Pope Julius, their founder—that is, the house of Julia, of which the basilica was a portion and member.

When Saint Sylvester received the Lateran buildings as a gift from the Great Constantine, to inhabit them himself and to be used by his pontifical successors, he undertook to arrange them so that they would be suitable for the needs of the clergy living with him. During the eight-month pontificate in which Marcus succeeded Sylvester, scarcely any addition could be completed. Julius, however, Pope Marcus’s successor, enlarged the buildings acquired by Sylvester by adding the new House of Julia. This was either a paternal inheritance belonging to Julius because he was a Roman, or a property purchased for a price, or a building constructed from its foundations on land belonging to him.

The same thing occurred in the pontifical palace at the Vatican, where its various parts are called after the pontiffs who founded or embellished them during their respective administrations: the Innocentian, Borgia, Clementine, and Sixtine sections.

When Julius added these buildings to the patriarchate under the name of the House of Julia, he also included an oratory called the Basilica of the House of Julia. In the same way, the great Sixtine and Gregorian chapels in the Vatican and the Pauline Chapel in the Quirinal pontifical palace still retain the names of their founders and are regarded as more distinguished than the other smaller chapels erected within those palaces by various pontiffs for more private use or for the service of the Palatine household.

We likewise call these chapels by the names of their founders: those of Saint Pius V, Sixtus V, Clement VIII, and Paul V.
