This usage was inherited from their predecessors, according to the more convenient practice of each pontiff in praying, celebrating private Mass, or storing sacred relics, as the circumstances of the time suggested. Thus the oratories of Hilary, John, and Theodore survive within the Lateran patriarchate.

It is unnecessary to add further examples of this matter, since almost every bishop retains the same practice in his own episcopal residence.

### Line 12

“To Saint Peter the Apostle, a *pharus* weighing twenty-five pounds, of the purest silver; twenty-four wax-coated silver *canthari* in the body of the basilica, each weighing twenty pounds.”

I think that the name and form of this kind of sacred furnishing, used to support lights in basilicas, can be derived from an ancient marble of exceptionally elegant workmanship. It is now seen in the Alban gardens, once belonging to the Sabelli princes and now to the heirs of the late Cardinal Paulutius, and, as I believe, surviving from the celebrated villa of Domitian.

A type of candelabrum is represented on it, showing why the names *cantharus* and *pharus* are joined. A *cantharus* is a handled vessel, generally used for holding wine and presenting the appearance of a very broad mixing bowl—a drinking vessel attributed by the Greeks and by Latin pagan authors to Bacchus and Hercules.

The shape of the vessel is very similar to that of a broad, round, open-mouthed pot, also used to retain fire during winter in the halls of noblemen. Such vessels are commonly made of beaten silver today and were used in the same way by the ancients. I remember having noted one at Naples in an ancient relief of elegant workmanship preserved among numerous monuments of learned antiquity in the atrium of the house of the Carafa princes. There Bacchus’s companions are shown carrying staffs and various symbols used in his rites; two of them carry fire placed on a tray in such a handled *cantharus*, for sacrificial use.

For this reason, in many representations of sacrifices, vessels resembling broad mixing bowls and *canthari* are shown, placed upon a tripod to contain coals, over which the sacrifice was offered. Yet the use of such a handled pot, or *cantharus*, to illuminate the darkness of night with an everlasting flame was common among the ancients in the arrangements for nocturnal festivals, and it is not omitted in our own times when roads must be illuminated by the pouring of pitch, oil, tallow, or thick fatty substances. In ordinary popular usage during peace, and in military operations during war, such pans are called *padelle* by the makers of fireworks.

In sacred buildings, where costly wax torches or balsam mixed with bronze are accustomed to burn during the sacred vigils according to the ancient custom of the Church, precious supports are likewise procured to hold those fires and lights. Candelabra of bronze or silver support wax candles and torches, sending their light in every direction from their elevated position.

Other, equally elevated supports were required by the ancients to contain balsam, spikenard oil, and wax melted together in such handled vessels or *canthari*. These supports acquired the name *phari*, in imitation of that celebrated Alexandrian tower which illuminated the harbor with fires suspended from it.

From the two terms, therefore—*pharus*, which refers to the support, and *cantharus*, which refers to the vessel into which the material feeding the flame was placed above—came the word *pharacanthara*. This designated tall candelabra intended to support melted wax mixed with balsam, spikenard oil, and other fragrant substances in the vessels described, as may be seen in the Alban relief.

For other candelabra supporting wax formed into rounded cylinders, which we call wax candles or tapers, the name *pharus* is more appropriate than *pharacantharus*. Thus, in this section, candelabra are distinguished from *canthari* and *pharacanthari*.

It may be observed in passing that the Great Constantine provided for this use of nocturnal light during the sacred vigils celebrated in churches. In the endowments of the City’s basilicas and of the sacred Lateran font, among the various annual supplies which the provinces and estates assigned to them were required to furnish, there are listed spikenard oil and as much as three hundred pounds of balsam, in addition to wax.

The practice is indicated in the account of Sylvester, section 36, verse 50, where we read the following among the gifts assigned to the Lateran basilica:

> “In the middle of the font are porphyry columns supporting a golden basin, in which there is a candle weighing fifty-two pounds of the purest gold. On the days of Easter, two hundred pounds of balsam burn there, with a wick of asbestos tow.”

The use of balsam for a perpetual light, just as in the ancient sanctuary that represents our Eucharistic sacrament, is preserved in the pontifical chapel. There the clergy appointed to this duty pour wax melted with balsam into round metal vessels, in the manner of a lamp fixed to the candelabrum of the Old Testament, although candles are used in the celebration of the divine offices.

### Line 16

“He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.”

Subsequently, his relics were gathered and transferred into the City by Pope Paschal and deposited in the title of Saint Praxedes, as the frequently mentioned marble attached to that church indicates. Later they were divided by his successors among several churches, especially the Basilica of Saint Paul outside the Walls on the Ostian Way.

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

### Line 4

“Which had not previously been done.” For formerly the sacrifice was concluded with the Epistle and the Gospel. Martinus Casinus reports: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause,” which is said at the beginning of the sacrifice, was discovered by Coelestine. The same pontiff also instituted the Gradual of the Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

### Line 2

“He made many decrees”; and Line 4: “He made a decree concerning the whole Church.”

Saint Coelestine, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, broke the efforts of the Pelagians and expelled them from all Italy. They were accustomed to test each of the bishops of the Roman Church craftily at the beginning of their pontificates, and they attempted to insinuate themselves into Coelestine’s favor by the same methods. But they found him far more hostile to them than his predecessors.

When, under Boniface, they had been ordered to reside beyond the hundredth milestone from the City by a decree of the emperor Constantius, reported by Baronius under the year 420, section 2, although it belongs to the year 421, when Constantius was declared emperor, Coelestine drove them far beyond the borders of Italy, as Prosper teaches in Book 41 of *Against the Collator*:

> “The pontiff Coelestine, of venerable memory, to whom the Lord granted many gifts of his grace for the protection of the Catholic Church, knowing that the condemned ought to be granted not a judicial examination but only the remedy of repentance, ordered Celestius, who was requesting a hearing as though the case had not been examined, to be driven beyond the boundaries of all Italy. So inviolably did he judge that the statutes of his predecessors and the synodal decrees must be observed, that he absolutely refused to allow reconsideration of what had once deserved to be cut off.”

For this reason the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus say in Part II, session 5:

> “When the records of the proceedings concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians and Celestians had been read in the holy synod, we judged that the decrees and decisions which your Piety had issued concerning them must also remain solid and firm.”

Garnerius, in his dissertation on the synods held in the Pelagian controversy, thinks that Coelestine convened a synod at Rome in 424 or 425 against the Pelagian bishops who stubbornly refused to subscribe to the formula of faith prescribed by Zosimus. But, just as the date of that synod is uncertain, so too is the synod itself.

Coelestine attempted to eliminate the Pelagian heresy not only from Italy but also from Britain. Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*, under the consuls of the year 429:

> “The Pelagian Agricola, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, corrupted the churches of Britain by introducing his teaching. But through the action of the deacon Palladius, Pope Coelestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place; and, after the heretics had been driven out, he directed the Britons to the Catholic faith.”

Saint Germanus undertook this legation together with Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes. An Anonymous author wrote the latter’s life and says:

> “After a period of two years had been completed”—that is, from the episcopate of Lupus, to which he had been elevated in 428—“he departed for Britain with Saint Germanus against the Pelagian heresy, which attacked the sound faith.”

Concerning Germanus’s legation, one should consult Constantius the presbyter in his *Life* as printed by Surius under 30 July, and Bede, Book I, chapter 17.

In the following year, 431, Coelestine gave the Scots as bishop that same deacon Palladius, at whose urging he had sent Saint Germanus to Britain. For Prosper writes under the consuls of that year: “Palladius is ordained by Pope Coelestine for the Scots who believe in Christ [Col. 0211D], and is sent as their first bishop.” Bede also records this in Book I, chapter 13, saying that it occurred in the eighth year of the younger Theodosius—that is, reckoning from the death of the Emperor Honorius.

There is a major controversy between the Irish and the Scots concerning Palladius’s apostolate. The Irish, whom it is certain were called Scots by the ancients, contend that Palladius was sent to their island; the Scots, or, as we now say, the Scottish Britons, claim him for themselves. The difficulty is increased by Prosper, who writes in Book Against the Collator, chapter 41, concerning Pope Coelestine:

> “Nor did he free Britain from this same disease—namely, the Pelagian heresy—with less care, when he excluded even from that hidden region of the Ocean certain enemies of grace who occupied only the land of their origin, and, having appointed a bishop for the Scots, while striving to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian Christian.”

The Romans designated by the name “barbarians” all peoples alien to their dominion and culture [Col. 0212A]. Hence Prosper’s words, “he also made the barbarian Christian,” are interpreted by some of Scotland and by others of Ireland. On this matter one should consult Usserius, *On the Antiquities of the British Church*, chapter 16; Alford, in the *British Annals* under the year 431; and other English and Irish writers, who dispute among themselves concerning this mission of Palladius.

But whatever the truth of this controversy may be, it is certain, and universally agreed, that around this time Saint Patrick was sent to Ireland and ought to be called the apostle of Ireland. For the Irish owe it to him that their homeland became an island of saints and, at one time, a center of letters and learning. Although some seeds of Christian teaching had been scattered in Ireland before him, and Saint Palladius is therefore said to have been sent to the Scots believing in Christ, the honor and title of Ireland’s conversion belong solely to Patrick. Through him not merely a few individuals or people from the common ranks, but kings and princes, and whole peoples in groups, having been washed with saving baptism, submitted their necks to the yoke [Col. 0212B] of faith.

He veiled Saint Brigid; he convened several councils reported by Spelman; and through his work very many churches were founded in various places, in which bishops were ordained. Bollandus presents the life of Saint Patrick, bishop, apostle, and primate of the Irish, under 18 March, and in the preliminary commentary, where he discusses at greater length his three captivities, monastic life, and journeys. He considers Patrick’s death to have occurred in the year 460, although Marianus Scotus, Sigebert, and others assign it to the year 491. Although many things resembling fables have entered the lives of the Irish saints, Bollandus nevertheless arranged the chronology of Patrick’s history on the basis of plausible conjectures.

Pope Coelestine continued the vicariate of the apostolic see throughout Illyricum through Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica. For Holstenius, in the *Roman Collection*, presents a letter of Coelestine addressed to Perigenes and nine other bishops [Col. 0212C] established throughout Illyricum, without day or consular date. From it we learn that Felix, bishop of the province of Dyrrachium, had been surrounded and nearly overwhelmed by the faction of certain accusers, had not Coelestine’s diligence intervened.

On that occasion Coelestine informs the Illyrian bishops that from antiquity the apostolic see had transferred a portion of its solicitude to the Illyrian provinces, and that their care had always been entrusted to the Church of Thessalonica. He says that he had confirmed this authority to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, and commands them to obey him in all ecclesiastical matters:

> “Without his counsel,” says Coelestine, “let no one be ordained; let no one, without his knowledge, presume to gather the bishops of the province entrusted to him, except with his consent; and through him let any matter be referred to us.”

He immediately threatens with the penalty of excommunication those who should not obey these ordinances of the apostolic see:

> “By this command let them also understand that whoever thinks he ought to resist our authority or his command [Col. 0212D] is to be separated from the fellowship of the brethren, since he has himself separated from it.”

This letter was recited in a Roman synod held under Boniface II. Dyrrachium is a city of Macedonia, situated on the western shore of the Ionian Sea, between Brundisium, a city of Italy, and Thessalonica.

## The Beginning of the Nestorian Heresy and the Council of Ephesus, the Third Ecumenical Council

During the pontificate of Coelestine, the heresy of Nestorius arose. It was condemned in a Roman synod convened before the Council of Ephesus. It is useful to describe briefly here the origin of this heresy and the councils held against it under Coelestine.

When Sisinnius, bishop of Constantinople, died near the end of 427, and the Constantinopolitan clergy were divided while deliberating over his successor, the Emperor Theodosius decided to summon Nestorius from the Church [Col. 0213A] of Antioch. Nestorius was a native of Germanicia, a small town in Syria, and, as Evagrius writes, had embraced the monastic life in the monastery of Saint Euprepius near Antioch. John, later patriarch of Antioch, and Theodoret, later bishop of Cyrus, were living there. His teacher was Theodore of Mopsuestia, from whom he learned to hold erroneous opinions concerning the Incarnation of the Word.

Since Nestorius cultivated an impressive appearance of holiness, he was summoned by Theodosius to Constantinople and ordained bishop on the Kalends of April 428. He came there with the presbyter Anastasius, his associate in all his counsels, whom he later used as an instrument of his hatred for the Mother of God.

In the very year of his ordination Nestorius disclosed his heresy, though the writers recount its first manifestation differently. Cyril, in his letter to Acacius of Beroea, says that while a large crowd was present in the church and Nestorius was seated in the church’s chair, a certain bishop named Dorotheus [Col. 0213B] rose and dared to exclaim in a loud voice: “If anyone says that Mary is the Mother of God, let him be anathema.”

Socrates, however, relates the matter in Book VII, chapter 32, as follows:

> “The presbyter Anastasius, who had come there from Antioch together with him—that is, with Nestorius—and was constantly in his company, was held by him in great honor and served as his adviser in the conduct of affairs. On a certain occasion he taught in the church that Mary ought to be called the Mother of God by no one; for she was a human being, and God could not be born from a human being.”

These words greatly disturbed everyone’s minds, both clergy and laity. However the matter occurred, Nestorius not only patiently tolerated Anastasius and Dorotheus speaking impiously, but himself also delivered a sermon in the great church, where a large assembly of every rank was present, on the Lord’s Incarnation. It contained the whole poison of the impiety he had then first revealed:

> “God has a mother,” Nestorius said, among other things [Col. 0213C]; “therefore paganism is excusable for introducing mothers among the gods. No, excellent man, Mary did not give birth to God, and so forth; she gave birth to a human being, an instrument of divinity,” and so forth.

Marius Mercator reproduces this sermon in Garnerius, volume II, page 5. Against this blasphemy of Nestorius, Proclus wrote a panegyrical oration on the praises of the Virgin Mother of God, of which more will be said shortly; Cyril wrote a letter to the monks of Egypt; and Cassian published seven books, which he therefore entitled *On the Incarnation*, because in them he fought against Nestorius’s treatise *On the Incarnation*.

When everyone shuddered at so great a blasphemy of Nestorius, the indignation of the hearers was such that on the very day the sermon was delivered, a certain simple monk, as soon as the sermon had been delivered—for he was burning with zeal for the faith—went forward into the middle of the church while the assembly was being celebrated and attempted to prevent the herald of impiety, as a heretic, from entering. But this holy man, overcome by Nestorius’s power, was publicly beaten with whips and sent into exile, as the monks of Constantinople testify in the supplication [Col. 0213D] presented to the emperor. It is extant in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30. There, in chapter 14, Saint Cyril’s letter to Coelestine is reported, in which he testifies that the monks, the senate, and most of the people of Constantinople soon began to abstain from the assemblies, lest they contaminate themselves by communion with Nestorius.

Nestorius therefore had two principal errors. The first was that the human being formed in the Virgin’s womb was someone other than the only-begotten Word of God; that the Incarnation was merely the indwelling of the Word of God in a human being as in his temple; and consequently that God had not been born, suffered, or died, and that Christ was not God but merely God’s temple. His other error was that he denied that the blessed Virgin Mary was the Mother of God, as has already been stated.

Hence the Nestorian heresy has the greatest affinity with the heresy of Ebion and of Paul of Samosata, and with the doctrines of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Garnerius explains this affinity at greater length on page 306 and following.

[Col. 0214A] After that first sermon, Nestorius delivered another in the year 429, ostensibly against the Arians and Macedonians but in reality against the Catholics, by which he seemed to confirm the earlier one. At that time something remarkable and daring occurred, which Cyril recounts in Book I of the *Contradictions*, concerning Eusebius, an advocate of causes who was later appointed bishop of Dorylaeum on account of his singular learning and piety.

While Eusebius was among the laity, he dared to rebuke publicly in words a bishop who was speaking impiously in a sermon, and he gave an example of his faith and courageous firmness against heresies. Nestorius delivered a third sermon shortly afterward, ostensibly against the Apollinarists. In it he concealed the poison somewhat more artfully and infused it into the people with greater harm, since he appeared to be attacking the Apollinarists, a name then offensive to Catholics because they confused the natures in Christ. Nevertheless, he could not refrain from expressing his own heresy concerning Christ as a mere human being, differing from other human beings only by superiority [Col. 0214B].

Against this sermon the same layman Eusebius publicly presented a protest. By this action he inflamed everyone’s zeal for the faith against Nestorius, who was renewing the heretical doctrines of Paul of Samosata. This protest of Eusebius is reported in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 13.

Following the example of the laity, the presbyters, inflamed with zeal, began to attack the corrupt doctrine in the church called Irene Maritima. Immediately, however, they were ordered to be silent by the threats and authority of the bishop, who was raging. Consequently, when the people demanded the customary preaching of the faith, they cried out publicly: “We have an emperor; we do not have a bishop,” as is read in the supplication of Basil in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30.

Proclus, bishop of Cyzicus, continued to teach the people as before. During a very large assembly he delivered, before a great gathering of every rank, a panegyrical oration on behalf of the Virgin Mother of God and against Nestorius. Although he did not name his opponent, out of reverence for the bishop present, he nevertheless refuted the heresy [Col. 0214C] known to all with the greatest applause from his hearers.

The oration was delivered on a more solemn feast day, and therefore probably on a feast of Christ or of the blessed Virgin, most likely on 25 March. Although all gave Proclus great applause as he spoke, Nestorius nevertheless dared, immediately afterward and according to his custom, to address the people. With the greatest shamelessness and impiety, he criticized and even condemned as blasphemous Proclus’s principal statements.

Not content with this, Nestorius delivered three further sermons at three successive assemblies after Easter. In them he attacked three principal statements of Proclus: that God had suffered and died; that God was our high priest; and that the blessed Virgin ought to be called the Mother of God.

Nestorius had sent his first treatise on the Incarnation, together with several other homilies, through trusted men into the provinces in order to spread the plague more widely. When these writings reached Egypt, Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, was compelled to write to [Col. 0214D] the monks so that they might confront the evil, which could be feared on account of the uninstructed simplicity and credulous fickleness of certain people into whose hands the writings had come.

Cyril recounts the matter in this way to Pope Coelestine in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14. When copies of Cyril’s letter to the Egyptian monks had been brought to Constantinople, they were so helpful that many members of the magistracy wrote to Cyril to thank him for it. This provided Nestorius with fuel for the anger he had conceived against Cyril.

Accordingly, since certain Egyptians were living in the imperial city against whom the Alexandrian bishop had taken canonical action on account of the infamy of their lives, Nestorius bribed them to fabricate accusations against Cyril and to submit to him and to the Emperor Theodosius written petitions charging Cyril not merely with administering the Church badly, but also with stirring up disturbances in Egypt against the emperor and the magistrates. This may be seen in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 12, and in Cyril’s *Apology to Theodosius*.

[Col. 0215A] When Coelestine learned that not only Constantinople but the whole East had been disturbed on account of Nestorius’s sermons, he was offended by this. Together with the other bishops, in whose assembly he had wished a report to be made concerning everything, he decided to consult Cyril on the matter, asking whether events were really as rumor proclaimed. Cyril mentions these letters of Coelestine in his first letter to Nestorius.

Meanwhile Nestorius attempted, by a letter sent once and again to Coelestine, to win over his mind. Saint Cyril feared that Nestorius might impose upon the Roman pontiff, and therefore informed him about Nestorius’s errors and about what Nestorius had thus far done against him.

The letter is addressed: “To the most blessed and most beloved Father Coelestine, beloved of God, greeting in the Lord.” The Alexandrian prelate, bishop of the second see, calls him the Roman Father, clearly out of reverence for the primacy.

Two points in that letter deserve notice. First, Cyril testifies that it is the custom of the Churches that heresies arising anywhere in the world [Col. 0215B] be referred to the apostolic see:

> “The ancient custom of the Churches,” he says, “urges that matters of this kind be communicated to your Holiness.”

Second, he says that he had not dared, without consulting Coelestine and before awaiting the judgment of the apostolic see, to withdraw himself from communion with Nestorius:

> “We shall not openly and plainly abandon his communion before we have indicated these matters to your Piety. Therefore deign to prescribe what you think should be done here, so that it may be clearly established whether we ought to communicate with them or whether we should freely declare to him that no one should communicate with one who fosters and proclaims such erroneous doctrine. Moreover, the mind of your Integrity and your judgment concerning this matter must be clearly set forth in writing to the most devout and God-dedicated bishops of Macedonia, and likewise to the prelates of the whole East. For we shall give those who desire it an opportunity to remain, with one mind, in one judgment, and to give assistance to the right faith, which is now under attack.”

[Col. 0215C] In the year 430, after receiving Nestorius’s letters and the quaternions (quires), which contained manifest blasphemy, Coelestine was further angered by the fact that Nestorius was assisting the Pelagian bishops. He therefore delayed his reply for some time. After receiving letters from Cyril of Alexandria, which reported Nestorius’s errors, he immediately sent a forceful letter to Nestorius, rebuking him as a patron of the ancient heretics and, in addition, as the author of a new heresy.

Coelestine did not wish this letter to be conveyed directly to Nestorius. Instead, he sent it through Possidonius, a deacon of the Church of Alexandria, to Cyril in Egypt, so that Cyril might later transmit it to Constantinople.

These letters were issued in a Roman synod that Coelestine celebrated at the beginning of August. In it a sentence of excommunication and deposition was pronounced against Nestorius unless, within ten days of the denunciation, he condemned his errors in an open and written [Col. 0215D] confession. Those who had been expelled by Nestorius on account of the faith were also restored to communion with the Church. Finally, the Alexandrian prelate was entrusted with executing the sentence.

The Pelagians were condemned in the same synod, so that, because they were joined to Nestorius by fellowship in error, they might be struck by the same sentence. Finally, seven letters were written from the synod by the supreme pontiff: to Cyril, so that he might act in this matter in the place of the apostolic see; to Nestorius, so that he might return to repentance; to the Constantinopolitan clergy, so that they might remain steadfast in the faith; to John of Antioch; to Rufus of Thessalonica; to Juvenal of Jerusalem; and to Flavian of Philippi—that is, to the bishops of the principal Eastern sees—so that they might act vigorously in the cause of the faith.

These letters are recited in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 15, 17, 19, and 20. They bear the same date, 13 August, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, and therefore belong to the year 430.

[Col. 0216A] After receiving the letters of Pope Coelestine, Cyril convened a council in Egypt, specifically at Alexandria, and from there sent a synodical letter to Nestorius. It contained three things: an exposition of the faith, twelve anathemas to be subscribed, and notification of the sentence issued by Coelestine. This is reported in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 36.

The synod sent four bishops to deliver Coelestine’s letters and the synodical letter to Nestorius, the Constantinopolitan clergy, and the archimandrites. They were Theopemptus of Cabasa, Daniel of Darna, Potamion, and Macarius. It was customary, when bishops of the principal sees were summoned to judgment, for them to be summoned by at least three bishops, as Garnerius proves by various examples on page 338.

In this synodical letter of Cyril and the Alexandrian council there is a notable passage in which the real presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist and the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass are asserted:

> “Moreover,” says Cyril, “I cannot fail to add here, together with the Fathers of the synod, this point: while we proclaim the death of the only-begotten Son—that is, of Jesus Christ—and his resurrection from the dead, and confess his ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the Church an unbloody sacrifice and approach the mystical blessings, and by this means are sanctified, having become participants in the sacred flesh and precious blood of Christ [Col. 0216B], the Savior of us all. For we do not receive it as common flesh—far be such a thing from us—nor again as though we had received a divine indwelling, or had been joined to him merely by a word of dignity, but as truly life-giving and belonging properly to the Word himself.”

And so forth, as may be read in Baronius under the year 430, number 55.

Before Coelestine’s sentence was conveyed to Nestorius, Nestorius sent a third letter to Coelestine. After attacking Cyril, he informed him of the general synod summoned by the Emperor Theodosius, doing so craftily, as though taunting the pontiff because his own sentence had been rejected:

> “It has pleased the most devout [Col. 0216C] emperors,” he says, “with the Lord’s help, also to convoke, without excuse, a synod of the entire world, for the investigation of other ecclesiastical matters.”

That expression, “without excuse,” and the imperial letter to the metropolitans indicate this clearly, says Garnerius, who was the first to publish this summons of Nestorius and the form of the summons communicated to him.

Since the summons of the Council of Ephesus is dated 19 November, that letter was issued not long afterward, and indeed before 30 November, when Coelestine’s definitive letter was delivered to Nestorius. For Coelestine’s letter is not mentioned in it—something that certainly would not have been omitted had Nestorius already received it.

While these events were taking place at Constantinople, the four bishops sent by the Alexandrian synod arrived there, delivered to Nestorius Coelestine’s apostolic letters and Cyril’s synodical letter, as Coelestine’s vicar, on 30 November, as Theopemptus, one of the legates [Col. 0216D], related to the Fathers of Ephesus in Part I, Act I:

> “On Sunday,” he said, “after the assembly had ended, we went up to the episcopal residence. There, in the presence of the entire clergy and with nearly all the distinguished men standing by, we handed Nestorius the letters in question. After receiving them, he arranged that we should speak with him on the following day. We therefore departed. But when we returned the next day, he did not admit us, nor did he give any satisfaction concerning the letters. Instead, he publicly proposed in a sermon the same doctrines as before, and doctrines even worse than those.”

This occurred on 6 December, the day on which he delivered that sermon, which Garnerius reproduces on page 85. On page 93 he also reproduces another sermon delivered by Nestorius on the following day, Sunday, 7 December.

[Col. 0217A] After receiving the letters of the Roman and Alexandrian synods, Nestorius immediately sent a copy to Antioch, to his friend John, bishop of Antioch. He asked John to arrange for the most learned bishops of his party—especially Andrew, bishop of Samosata, at that time renowned among the Easterners for the reputation of his learning and piety, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus—to write against Cyril’s twelve anathemas contained in his synodical letter, on the pretext that they renewed the heresy of Apollinaris or Arius.

Those anathemas contain nothing other than the judgments of the Fathers, and nothing is found in them that all had not taught everywhere and always. They can all be reduced to four propositions.

First, that the Son of God truly became human.

Second, that the same person, and not another, is the Son of God and the son of man, and thus that God was born from a woman, and that the Word had two births.

Third, that the Virgin is the Mother of God.

Fourth, that the Immortal endured death, and that the one who was crucified is the same one who is to be adored.

Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrus wrote against Cyril’s anathemas. Before Easter of the year 431, however, Cyril answered their objections in two Apologies: one against the Eastern bishops and the other against Theodoret. Both are extant in Garnerius, pages 133 and 178.

[Col. 0217B] Meanwhile, when Nestorius saw that Cyril’s anathemas were aimed at his doctrine like so many weapons, he too composed twelve anathemas, each corresponding to one of Cyril’s. They are recited in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 29.

Before the letters of Pope Coelestine, issued by the Roman synod, and Cyril’s synodical letter were delivered to Nestorius, John, bishop of Antioch, had sent him letters written to himself by Coelestine and Cyril. When Nestorius understood from them what storm threatened his own head, he attempted to turn it upon Cyril.

After accusing Cyril before Theodosius both of impiety toward God and of a crime against the emperor, he requested that a general council be convened in which judgment might be instituted against the accused. At Nestorius’s urging, Theodosius summoned that council and called bishops from all the dioceses [Col. 0217C] to Ephesus for Pentecost of the year 431. He sent letters to the bishops of the principal sees: Coelestine of Rome, Rufus of Thessalonica, Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Capreolus of Carthage.

He ordered each of them to come without excuse or delay, together with those whom they knew to be suitable. At the same time he forbade anyone to introduce any innovation privately before the synod had been convened and a common judgment had been issued concerning all:

> “No innovation is to be made privately by anyone before the synod has been convened and its common judgment, which was to be given concerning all matters, has been issued.”

This is read in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30. The measure was plainly advantageous to Nestorius, whom the sentence of the apostolic see would otherwise have removed from his throne.

The edict of Theodosius was issued at Constantinople on 19 November, in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, Augusti and consuls, and therefore in the year 430.

[Col. 0217D] That the council was not summoned at Coelestine’s advice is clear from the fact that Coelestine’s letters were delivered to Nestorius only on 30 November, twelve days after the council had been summoned. Otherwise Coelestine would have held contradictory positions at the same time: on the one hand, he was issuing a definitive sentence of condemnation against Nestorius and sending executors of that sentence; on the other, he was committing the matter to a council.

Moreover, Nestorius himself admits that he had requested the council. For this reason he is called the petitioner for the council by Coelestine and by the legates of the apostolic see. The presbyter Philip himself, one of the apostolic legates and especially zealous in asserting pontifical dignity, testified that the council had been summoned not by Coelestine but by the emperors, and that it had been assembled at the time when the pontiff’s sentence against Nestorius was to be put into execution. Coelestine entrusted that execution to Cyril, not to an ecumenical synod. This is plainly established by the letters of Nestorius and Coelestine and by the Acts of the council.

From these facts collapses the opinion of Peter de Marca, who says in Book IV of *On Concord*, chapter 4, [Col. 0218A] number 1, that Nestorius seems to have appealed to the emperor and obtained from him a rescript by which the sentence of both the Roman and Alexandrian synods was either suspended or entirely set aside. I say that this opinion collapses because it rests on what Marca assumes: that the sentence of both synods had first been announced to Nestorius, and that he then either appealed to the emperor or requested that a council be summoned.

This conflicts with the imperial letter of Theodosius, with the authority of Marius Mercator, and with Nestorius himself. Since the sentence of the apostolic see was not announced until after the council had been summoned—a fact that escaped Marca—it ought rather to be regarded as having been anticipated than as having been suspended by the edict, if we wish to speak precisely.

[Col. 0218B] When Coelestine received the imperial letter in the year 431, he summoned the Western bishops to Rome at the beginning of May. They assembled there and, as the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus say in their report to the emperors, proclaimed the correct judgment concerning the faith with great unanimity. They declared that those who held otherwise were entirely alien to the priesthood, the clergy, and ecclesiastical rank.

In that Roman synod, legates were chosen to represent Coelestine at Ephesus: Arcadius and Projectus, bishops, and Philip, a Roman presbyter. Coelestine gave these legates mandates or instructions. Although they are not extant, Baronius gathers from Coelestine’s letter to the Council of Ephesus that Coelestine and the Roman synod sent the legates to the East not so that, after the decrees issued by the same pontiff against Nestorius had been annulled, Nestorius’s case might undergo a new examination, but rather so that the legates themselves might execute the sentence Coelestine had issued against Nestorius.

Baronius would certainly have asserted this more confidently had he seen Coelestine’s memorandum, recovered by Baluzius from two manuscript codices, one Colbertine and the other Vatican. For it clearly establishes that the legates of the apostolic see were sent to the Council of Ephesus to execute what Coelestine had already decreed [Col. 0218C] concerning Nestorius and to add the weight of apostolic authority to the council’s decrees.

This memorandum is dated 8 May, in the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus, and therefore belongs to the year 431.

Although it is established from Coelestine’s letter to the synod itself and from Cyril’s letter to certain members of the Constantinopolitan clergy, extant in volume II of the Councils, page 562, that the most devout emperors had set the sacred day of Pentecost as the limit for the Council of Ephesus, and therefore 7 June, the Fathers of the council say in their letter to the emperors, on page 570:

> “On the twenty-second day of June, according to the Romans, we assembled.”

John, bishop of Antioch, who deliberately prolonged his journey and delayed with the Easterners, was responsible for this postponement. Nevertheless, while he was only five or six days’ journey away, he sent two bishops to Cyril. They repeatedly testified that John had instructed them to say that the holy synod should not be postponed if he happened to be delayed any longer.

Since he had been awaited in vain for sixteen days [Col. 0218D], the synod began. It was immediately divided into two communions: the smaller part adhered to Nestorius, while the larger and sounder part adhered to Cyril, especially Memnon, bishop of Ephesus.

Before continuing this account, however, something should briefly be said here about the president and the number of Fathers of the synod.

John Launoy, a doctor of Paris, denies that Cyril occupied the place of Pope Coelestine in the council. But, as Baluzius notes in his annotations to Marius Mercator, page 488, there can be no room for evasion, since in the records “which were conducted at Ephesus in the presence of those bishops and presbyters who had come from Rome,” Cyril is said to have been “also presiding in the place of the most holy and most blessed archbishop of the Roman Church, Coelestine.”

Cyril therefore attended both as bishop of Alexandria and as Coelestine’s vicar, just as shortly afterward Flavian, bishop of Philippi, participated both in his own name and in the name of Rufus of Thessalonica [Col. 0219A].

Certainly, in the Acts of the council Cyril is everywhere honored by this title, even after the arrival of the legates of the Roman see. This is clear from Action IV, where the Roman legates are named immediately after Cyril and before all the other bishops.

Indeed, even before the legates arrived, Cyril had presided in Coelestine’s place, as is clear from the First Action:

> “When the most religious and holy bishops were seated in the most holy church called Mary—Cyril of Alexandria, who also occupied the place of Coelestine, the most holy and most sacred archbishop of the Roman Church, and Juvenal of Jerusalem,” and so forth.

This was not unjust, since Coelestine had delegated to Cyril the authority of the apostolic see for executing the sentence against Nestorius issued in the Roman synod, and this was the matter being handled in the Council of Ephesus.

The ancient writers do not agree about the number of bishops who attended the synod. But the cited Baluzius correctly asserts that the opinion which says there were two hundred [Col. 0219B] or approximately that number appears more probable. In the Cresconian collection, the bishops who attended the Council of Ephesus are named and numbered as 190. The same number is found in the Greek codex of the Royal Library, number 206.

Therefore, as Baronius rightly maintains, we should stand by the testimonies of Cyril and of the bishops of the Council of Ephesus, which plainly show that the bishops who attended this synod numbered no more than 218.

In the First Action of the council, celebrated on 22 June, a Monday, all the documents were read. Among them was Nestorius’s letter to Cyril, which begins, “The insults contained in your remarkable letter,” and so forth. It was rejected by the unanimous judgment of the Fathers, and Nestorius was condemned as a heretic and struck with anathema.

Coelestine’s letter to Nestorius was also read, as was Cyril’s synodical letter to Nestorius, which had been delivered to him by the bishops Theopemptus, Daniel, Potamion, and Macarius [Col. 0219C]. The testimony of those bishops was then heard. They asserted that Nestorius had given no satisfaction either to Coelestine’s letters or to Cyril’s and the Alexandrian synod’s letters, but had publicly proposed in a sermon the same doctrines as before, and doctrines worse than those.

A sentence of deposition and excommunication was then issued against Nestorius, who had been convicted as guilty of and responsible for a wicked heresy. It is especially noteworthy that, in issuing it, the synod says that it had been convened by the sacred canons and by the letter of the most holy Father and fellow minister Coelestine, bishop of the Roman Church.

This sentence was communicated to Nestorius on the following day, 23 June.

John, bishop of Antioch, arrived on the fifth day after the sentence against Nestorius had been issued, on Saturday, 27 June. On that same day he held his own little council. As the report of the Fifth Action to Pope Coelestine states:

> “As soon as John entered Ephesus, before he had shaken off the dust gathered on the journey [Col. 0219D], before he had removed his clothing, he dared to undertake an impious act. For he composed a private document and attached to the most holy Cyril and the most learned Memnon the charge and disgrace of deposition. He also inflicted an insult upon the entire synod in the name of excommunication. In addition, he deposited these matters in a public written document, to be read by anyone, affixing it to the walls of the theater so that he might display the spectacle of his impiety.”

Then, as can be read in chapter 12 of the synodical tragedy against Irenaeus, John of Antioch, in the presence of his synod and of Count Candidian, who had been sent by the emperor to the council to ensure that order was maintained, said that Cyril and the other bishops against whom he had pronounced sentence intended to celebrate the liturgical assembly of the Eucharist, and asked His Magnificence to go to them and warn them “not to trample upon ecclesiastical sanctions and pious decrees, nor to celebrate the assembly—men some of whom had justly been deposed, while others had been deprived of communion because of heretical madness, inexplicable and unlawful disturbances, and contempt for pious sanctions.” Candidian later reported these matters to the synod:

“I made my request on that very Saturday toward evening, and on the following day, going very early to the most reverend Bishop Cyril—that is, on Sunday, and therefore on 28 June—I did not cease asking and entreating him to grant my petition. But they did not comply; they went out and held the assembly. I was unable to contend with them further.”

It is clear from the synodal Acts that, after hearing Candidian’s report, John concluded that Cyril and his associates had again acted treacherously and had violated the fourth canon of Antioch; he threatened to report the matter to the emperors.

Immediately after the first session of the synod, Candidian, who favored Nestorius, had reported to the emperor what had been done at the council. Nestorius had also made a report, but so falsely that they stirred the mind of Theodosius—already favorably disposed toward Nestorius and hostile to Cyril—against the entire synod. After Candidian’s report had been read at Constantinople, Theodosius immediately sent a rescript through Palladius, the *magister*, ordering that everything be rescinded as having been conducted improperly, and that the doctrines be examined by common deliberation, so that all might agree more easily. He also ordered that no one be permitted to leave Ephesus, either for his homeland or for the imperial court, before everything had been properly concluded, so that the matter might be brought to completion without delay. The synod complained that Candidian’s machinations had so far concealed the truth from the emperor, and asked that he summon them, together with five bishops who could explain in person what had been done by both sides and in what manner.

Meanwhile, on 10 July, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, together with Philip, the presbyter and legate of Pope Celestine, arrived at Ephesus. They were received by the council, and on the same day the second session of the ecumenical synod was held. Celestine’s letter was read with solemn ceremony, and the Fathers acclaimed him:

“To the new Paul, Celestine!”
“To Celestine, guardian of the faith!”
“To Celestine, in harmony with the synod!”
“The entire synod gives thanks to Celestine!”

The third session was held on the following day. The proceedings that had previously taken place in the deposition of Nestorius were read, and the sentence against Nestorius was pronounced separately by each of the three legates. The synod then reported to the emperor the arrival of the legates and the agreement of both Churches in condemning Nestorius; finally, it requested permission to depart, as though everything had been completed.

The fourth session was held on 16 July. Cyril and Memnon presented a petition in which they complained before the holy synod of the injury inflicted upon them by the Orientals and requested that John of Antioch be summoned. When he failed to appear, the Fathers declared invalid everything that John’s synod had done against Cyril and Memnon. They decreed that the matter should be reported to the emperor and that John should be summoned a third time before legal proceedings were initiated against him.

The fifth session was held on 17 July, and John was summoned for the third time. When he refused to hear the episcopal legates in person, the synod pronounced sentence of excommunication against him and his bishops, and again declared invalid everything that had been done against Cyril and the others.

Meanwhile, John attempted to influence the emperor’s mind through letters and asked that the synod be summoned either to Constantinople or at least to Nicomedia, from which messages could more quickly be carried to the imperial city. Count Irenaeus, whom John had sent to the emperor, arrived at Constantinople and arranged for Cyril’s condemnation to be published in the Church. But when John the physician, Cyril’s *syncellus*, arrived, the court was divided into two factions. The view prevailed that one of the leading men should be sent to order, in the emperor’s name, that the three deposed men—Cyril, Memnon, and Nestorius—be treated alike as deposed and that all should be brought together into one synod.

Accordingly, Count John of the Sacred Largesses was sent with letters from the emperor addressed by name to all the bishops of both parties, ordering them to initiate a gathering into one synod. From the report sent to Celestine, it is evident that in this fifth session the Fathers of Ephesus confirmed the deposition of the Pelagians decreed by the apostolic see.

The sixth session was held on 20 July, in which Theodore’s creed was condemned. Finally, the seventh session was convened on the last day of July.

Meanwhile, Count John of the Sacred Largesses arrived at Ephesus and summoned the bishops of both parties to his lodging. John of Antioch and Nestorius appeared with their associates; Cyril also appeared with other bishops. An argument arose: some denied that Nestorius ought to take part, while others insisted upon it and rejected Cyril. The count placed Nestorius and Cyril under guard and informed the emperor that the bishops’ minds were irreconcilable.

In these difficult circumstances, the emperor ordered Nestorius to withdraw from the council and instructed legates from both parties to come to the imperial city. The holy synod elected its legates, and the Oriental faction elected its own. The latter, in a letter to their associates, testify that they were at Chalcedon on 4 September.

The emperor heard the legates of the schismatics five times at the Rufiniana villa, apparently with considerable benevolence. But he ordered the legates of the synod’s Catholic party to accompany him, so that they might ordain a bishop at Constantinople, while the Orientals were left at Chalcedon. At last, after receiving permission to depart, the Orientals sent word to their associates at Ephesus that the cause of Nestorius had been ruined and that the followers of Cyril had deceived everyone by tyranny, flattery, and gifts.

The Acts do not report what the ecumenical synod received from its own legates. They merely state that Cyril arrived at Alexandria on 30 October and was received by his people as though he were the leader of a victorious army. This is the general account of what occurred after the seventh session.

The bishops whom the ecumenical synod had sent to the emperor Theodosius arrived at Constantinople on 25 October, four months after the abdication of Nestorius had elapsed. They ordained as bishop of Constantinople Maximianus, a presbyter who had been a monk—not especially cultivated in letters, but a man of approved faith and piety.

Theodosius sent Nestorius away to his monastery of Saint Euprepius, situated before the gates of Antioch. From there he was later transported to other places, and his books were burned by order of Theodosius, as may be read in the *Annals* of Baronius and in his *Critica*.

Immediately after his ordination, Maximianus, in the Constantinopolitan synod, sent letters according to custom to the principal sees and also to the bishops of Old Epirus, whom the schismatics were attempting to deceive as though they enjoyed communion with the holy synod, although they had not withdrawn from their former position.

In the letter that the Ephesian synod sent to all the Churches of the world, it enumerates the bishops whom it had deprived of rank or of Christian communion. Among them it mentions John, patriarch of Antioch; Dorotheus, metropolitan bishop; Helladius of Tarsus; Himerius of Nicomedia; and Eutherius of Tyana. Since these men had been deposed by the Ephesian synod because of their extraordinary obstinacy, their deposition was confirmed in this Constantinopolitan synod of Maximianus.

The synod reported this decree to Celestine for confirmation, and Maximianus sent synodical letters from that synod to Celestine.

Celestine, however, on 15 March of the year 432, in his reply to Maximianus’s synodical letters and to the report of the Ephesian synod concerning Maximianus’s merits and virtues, did not judge that decree worthy of confirmation in every respect. He held that all the adherents of Nestorius, and the bishops condemned at Ephesus, should not be expelled from their sees, nor should every hope of pardon and restoration be cut off from them.

He therefore considered the decree excessively harsh and contrary to an ancient canon once issued by the Roman Church at the urging of Saint Athanasius. According to that canon, only heresiarchs, even if penitent, were deprived of the hope of recovering their former rank. Celestine wished this canon to be observed with regard to the Nestorians, and with a further extension—namely, with regard to those who, together with the authors of the heresy, were known to have been condemned by the subscription of all the brethren.

The pope then asserts that this clemency had not merely been introduced by the Roman Church but had also been established by imperial laws. Accordingly, returning bishops who had come out of the Nestorian heresy could not fail to be treated in this way: they were to anathematize Nestorius and his doctrine and thus be restored to their Churches. This profession was also to be required and made by bishops who had deceived the emperor and who had recovered their Churches through secular authority.

When Celestine speaks of John of Antioch and the other bishops condemned at Ephesus, whom Theodosius, on allowing them to return to their own places, had judged orthodox and innocent, he orders that they too be compelled to make this profession. Finally, he orders that the same clemency be applied to John of Antioch, although he was the head of the faction and had been condemned by the votes of all, because he had been condemned not on account of heresy but on account of disturbance and obstinacy.

The beginnings of Semi-Pelagianism are assigned to the year 428, when Saint Augustine wrote Letter 217, formerly numbered 107, addressed to Vitalis of Carthage. Augustine knew that Vitalis, an educated man, taught that the beginning of faith was not a gift of God. He protested vigorously and said:

“They”—that is, the Pelagians—“attribute everything pertaining to the faithful and pious life of human beings to free will, so that they consider these things to be obtained from ourselves and not to be requested from the Lord. But you, if what I hear about you is true, contend that the beginning of faith, in which there is also the beginning of good—that is, pious—willing, is not to be attributed to God but is to be possessed from ourselves, so that we begin to believe. As for the remaining goods of religious life, you agree that God grants them by his grace to those who, already believing, ask, seek, and knock.”

Augustine refutes Vitalis by appealing to the prayers of the Church and proposes twelve rules concerning the Church’s faith in the question of the grace of God.

When the faction of the Semi-Pelagians, which had arisen in Africa, grew stronger in Gaul, Prosper of Aquitaine, later the notary of Pope Leo, and Hilary, a layman who had undertaken to defend Augustine’s teaching, went to Rome to Pope Celestine. Around the year 432 they obtained from him a letter addressed to the bishops of Gaul, in which he rebuked them more sharply because they granted presbyters such license that, bringing undisciplined questions before the public, they obstinately preached doctrines opposed to the truth.

In the same letter he restrains those who spoke against the name of Saint Augustine and adorns Augustine with the praise due to him. The letter appears in volume II of the Councils, but without a day or a consular date, although Augustine is spoken of in it as dead. It was therefore written either in 431 or in the following year.

In most manuscripts, authorities of earlier bishops of the apostolic see concerning the grace of God and free will are appended to this letter. In the Labbe edition, however, these are rightly distinguished from Celestine’s letter. The style of these ten chapters is plainly different from the style of the letter.

Sirmond, in volume I of the *Gallican Councils*, denies that these chapters belong to Celestine, but does not dare to propose a certain author for them. Quesnell, in volume II of the works of Saint Leo the Great, dissertation III, considers Saint Leo the Great to be their true author. Cardinal Noris, however, in chapter 8 of the *Augustinian Vindications*, thinks that the chapters belong to Prosper of Aquitaine. Antelmius, in his dissertation *On the True Works of Saints Leo the Martyr and Prosper of Aquitaine*, overturns Quesnell’s opinion and, by comparing in detail the expressions and forms of speech usually employed by Prosper with the words of this little collection, shows that one and the same Prosper states in his preface to the objections of Vincent of Lérins that he composed these chapters at the command of the apostolic see.

The condemnation of the Semi-Pelagians will be discussed under Boniface II. On their errors, Natalis Alexander is to be consulted in the fifth century.

Celestine’s second letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne establishes several matters.

First, he reproves clerics who had introduced a novel form of dress, walking about wearing a cloak and girding their loins. He orders them to retain the habit they had received from their forebears, since it was better to display priestly dignity through morals than through clothing.

Second, he prohibits the denial of penance to the dying:

“I shudder, I confess, to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though he could not at any time assist one who hastens to him, and free a human being endangered beneath the burden of sins from the very weight by which he desires to be released,” and so forth.

Third, he wishes bishops to be promoted through the ecclesiastical grades, not taken from among the laity, and not to be criminals.

Fourth, he decrees that each province should be content with its own metropolitan, confirming Boniface’s constitution concerning the Churches of Narbonne and Arles.

Fifth, he forbids anyone to be given as bishop against the will of the bishops or consecrated without the consent of the clergy and people. He orders that the clergy of a vacant Church be preferred to outsiders, as in sacred elections. He commands that no digamist and no husband of a widow be ordained, and declares ordinations of such persons illegitimate.

Finally, he delegates to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne the case of the bishop of Marseilles, who was said to have congratulated the murderer of one of his fellow bishops.

Italy expelled not only the Pelagians but also the bishop of the Novatians from Rome. Socrates, who in book VII, chapter 9, had said that Innocent began to persecute the Novatians living in Rome and deprived them of many churches, later writes in chapter 11 of the same book:

“Celestine succeeded him”—that is, Boniface. “He too took away from the Novatians the churches that they had in Rome and compelled Rusticula, their bishop, to gather the people secretly in private houses.”

[Note: [Column 0223C]

Line 5.—“He made a constitution concerning the Church, and especially concerning religion” (or “the region”), and so forth. In the preceding pontificate we discussed the appeals made by Africans to the holy see, especially that of Antonius, bishop of Fussala, who had been established in that see through Augustine’s efforts, since it had therefore been separated from the see of Hippo. Antonius, accused of crimes, had been deposed from the episcopate by the synod of the province. He appealed from the synod’s sentence to the Roman pontiff Boniface. Boniface subsequently died, and Augustine wrote to his successor Celestine. He entreated and asked him, adducing arguments and recent examples, not to weaken an episcopal judgment supported by a just cause. He said that, after the transmitted acts had been examined, he would recognize that the bishops had perhaps pronounced a sentence against Antonius that was less severe than it ought to have been.

Moved by these considerations, Celestine appears to have acted in accordance with Augustine’s suggestions and requests.

A second example of an appeal had been provided by the presbyter Apiarius under Zosimus and Boniface. Under Celestine, however, after being accused of new crimes, he failed so completely that, even before the legate Faustinus sent by the holy see to carry out his restoration, he confessed himself guilty and thus gave the African bishops an opportunity to obtain certain moderating laws concerning appeals. These laws did not infringe or diminish the power of the apostolic see but introduced a more exact observance of the discipline properly established by the canons. This is clear from the synodical letter of the bishops.

Above all, the authority of the Sardican canon was preserved. It declares the power of the Roman bishop as follows:

“If the one who asks that his case be heard again should, by his petition, move the Roman bishop to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be in the power of the bishop to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. And if he decides that those should be sent who will judge in the presence of the bishops, having the authority of the one by whom they were sent, it shall be at his discretion.” (Council of Sardica, canon 7.)

[Column 0224A] This remained so firmly established that, although the Africans attempted by whatever strategy to withdraw from transmarine appeals, the discipline of the ancient law nevertheless continued to prevail—the discipline customarily exercised throughout Africa by the holy see in ecclesiastical judgments—as long as the form of ecclesiastical government survived there. This was openly affirmed by the synod held in Africa in 646 concerning the reform of ecclesiastical judges in the provinces. It wrote to Pope Theodore:

“Above all, and most justly, the matter ought to be examined by the apostolic summit itself, whose ancient concern it is both to condemn what is evil and to approve what is praiseworthy. For the ancient rules have decreed that whatever is done, even in distant provinces, should not first be handled or accepted unless it has been brought to the knowledge of your venerable see, so that a just judgment might be confirmed by its authority.” (Synodical letter of the Africans to Pope Theodore.)

[Column 0224B] Celestine declares that his apostolic care extended to all the provinces in a decretal letter addressed to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, in order to confirm the ancient discipline:

“We have been appointed by God as watchmen, so that, demonstrating the diligence of our vigilance, we may cut away what must be restrained and establish what must be observed. Spiritual care does not fail even in regard to the most distant places, but extends everywhere that the name of God is preached; nor do matters escape our knowledge when, through the authority of a novel presumption, attempts are made to overturn the rules.”

In another letter to Perigenes and the bishops established throughout Illyricum, he declares the authority of the apostolic vicar whom he had appointed, writing:

“Whatever is done concerning cases is to be referred to him, dearest brothers. No one is to be ordained without his counsel. No one, without his knowledge, is to usurp the province entrusted to him. They must not presume to gather bishops except with his consent. Through him, too, anything that arises is to be referred to us.”

[Column 0224C] More than all other provinces of the western region, Britain and Ireland displayed the apostolic care of Celestine, present and active for all, as Prosper relates in his *Chronicle*:

“Nor did he free Britain from this same disease”—that is, Pelagianism—“with more sluggish care, when he excluded from that secret region of the Ocean certain enemies of God’s grace who occupied only the place of their origin.”

He adds the method of the cure, writing:

“The Pelagian Agricola, son of the Pelagian bishop Severianus, corrupted the Churches of Britain by the insinuation of his doctrine. But at the urging of the deacon Palladius, whom Pope Celestine had sent from the Roman Church for this purpose, Pope Celestine sent Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in his place, so that, after the heretics had been expelled, he might direct the Britons toward the Catholic faith.”

This Germanus is the same man whom a contemporary writer of those times states was sent by the Gallican bishops together with Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, for the same reason that Celestine had in view and Prosper explains (*Against the Conference*, at the end):

“By the ordination of Palladius as bishop for the Scots, while he sought to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian Christian.”

There is no doubt that Celestine suggested to the bishops of Gaul nearest to Great Britain that they should select from their own number those who appeared better suited to undertake the task in that province. To those who had thus been designated and chosen, he entrusted the office of apostolic vicars: “Pope Celestine sends him in his place.”

Accordingly, Palladius was ordained by Pope Celestine for the Scots who believed in Christ and was sent as their first bishop. Prosper, under the year 432 in his *Chronicle*, calls Palladius the apostle of the Scots. He later went to Ireland by order of the Roman pontiff, but died shortly afterward. He was succeeded by that Patrick who became famous for his holiness and, after converting the island to the Christian faith, deserved to be called the apostle of Ireland.

While these things were being done in the West by Celestine, the ruin threatening the Eastern Churches exercised his vigilance and zeal. He prudently averted it, assigning corresponding responsibilities to blessed Cyril.

The disastrous origin of the Nestorian heresy threatened this ruin. There is no reason to repeat here the summary of its history, prefaced shortly before from selected notes of Pagi and taken from the learned Archbishop Somier.]

Celestine, a Campanian by nationality [Note: [Column 0199] C. B: Roman.], son of Priscus, sat for *nine years, one month, and nine days [Note: [Column 0199] B: eight years, five months, and three days, from the consulships of Mariniana and Asclepiodotus to those of Aetius and Valerius].

He enacted many constitutions and decreed that the one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice [Note: [Column 0199] C: antiphonally], which had not previously been done. Before that, only the Epistles of the Apostle Paul and the holy Gospel were recited, and then Mass was celebrated.

He made a constitution concerning the whole Church, especially concerning religion [Note: [Column 0199] C: concerning religious matters], which is preserved today in the Church archive [Note: [Column 0199] C: which is kept in the archive].

Thus he dedicated the Basilica of Julia [Note: [Column 0199] C: Julia], in which, after the fire of the district [the transmitted text is uncertain], he offered the following gifts: a silver paten weighing fifteen pounds; two silver cups, each weighing eight pounds; two silver vessels, each weighing ten pounds; [Column 0201] two silver candelabra, each weighing thirty pounds [Note: [Column 0201] C: seven]; fourteen bronze candle-bearing vessels, each weighing thirty pounds [Note: [Column 0201] C: twenty-four]; likewise ten silver crowns, each weighing ten pounds.

To blessed Peter the Apostle [Note: [Column 0201] C: Paul], a silver *pharus* or lamp-bearing vessel weighing twenty-five pounds of the purest silver.

Twenty-four silver candle-bearing vessels within the body of the basilica, each weighing twenty pounds.

He held three ordinations in the month of December: thirty-two presbyters, twelve deacons, and forty-six bishops for various places.

He was also buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, and the episcopate was vacant for twenty-one days [Note: [Column 0201] C: twenty].

XLVI. SAINT SIXTUS III. A.D. 432; THEODOSIUS 25; VALENTINIAN 8.

Number 63, line 1.—“He sat for eight years.” After sitting for eight years less thirty days, he departed this life on the fifth day before the Kalends of April in the year of Christ 440, which was the thirty-third year of Theodosius and the sixteenth of the Emperor Valentinian. (Saint Prosper in his *Chronicle*; Baronius, under the year 440.)

Number 64, line 1.—“He built the Basilica of Saint Mary, which was formerly called Liberius’s.” Perhaps he restored it in a larger form and adorned it with more extensive decorations in praise and honor of Mary, the Mother of God, for whom, triumphing over the blasphemies of Nestorius, he may have wished to erect so magnificent a triumphal arch.

Number 65, line 5.—“What had been taken away by the barbarians.” From this we clearly understand that, while the Goths occupied the City, they did not refrain from stripping the ornaments of all the churches, but only those that they knew belonged to the basilicas of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

Lines 26 and 27.—“Which he also adorned with verses.” In this octagonal structure he inscribed two verses on each of the architraves. Since they contain a Catholic assertion concerning original sin against the Pelagian heresy, it seemed appropriate to reproduce them here, so that verses promulgated throughout the whole world for beneficial purposes might be preserved for all eternity:

*A sacred people is born here for the heavenly city from a life-giving seed,*  
*whom the Spirit brings forth from the fertilized waters.*

*The Virgin Church, a mother through virgin birth, bears the children*  
*whom she conceives as God breathes upon her and brings forth from the stream.*

*Hope for the kingdom of heaven, reborn in this font:*  
*the blessed life does not receive those who have been born only once.*

*This fountain is life, and it washes the whole world,*  
*taking its beginning from the wound of Christ.*

*Immerse yourself, sinner, to be cleansed in the sacred stream:*  
*the water receives you old and brings you forth new.*

*If you wish to be innocent, cleanse yourself in this washing,*  
*whether you are burdened by ancestral sin or by your own.*

*There is no difference among those who are reborn, whom one font,*  
*one Spirit, and one faith make one.*

[Column 0231A] *Let neither the number nor the form of your sins terrify anyone:*  
*whoever is born in this stream will be holy.*
**Line 32.—“He was buried.”** The injuries which, as we said above in the notes to the first letter of Sixtus I, the first Sixtus, Roman pontiff and martyr, suffered after his death, according to Jerome, were also endured—indeed, more severely—by Sixtus III, with whom we are here concerned. For just as a book by Sixtus, or Sextus the Pythagorean, was published under his name by the Origenists, so three volumes were written by the Pelagians under this Sixtus’s name: the first, *On Wealth*; the second, *On Evil Teachers, Works of Faith, and Future Judgment*; and the third, *On Chastity*. Baronius demonstrates that these works are filled with Pelagianism in the year 440, no. 7 and following, on the grounds that the first volume contains the Pelagian proposition that a rich man cannot be saved unless he distributes all his possessions to the poor; the second attributes nothing to divine grace and everything to free choice in good works; and finally, the third mocks those who maintain that the good of chastity proceeds from the grace of God. Having been unmistakably painted in these colors, this little book, recently printed under the name of Sixtus, was not without grave danger to the faithful. Reader, recognize it as such, lest you drink poisons from Babylon’s golden cup, ennobled by an illustrious name.

**Line 33.—“The episcopate ceased for twenty-two days”; more accurately, forty-two.** For thus Saint Prosper writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 440:

> “When the pontiff Sixtus had died on the Kalends of April, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting the arrival of the deacon Leo with extraordinary peace and patience. At that time he was being detained in Gaul between Aetius and Albinus, commanders of the Roman army, in order to restore their friendship.””

## Chronological Notes

The epoch of Xystus III, besides the indication which we saw emerge from the total reckoning of time in the preceding number and from the assigned portions of that total from Boniface to Hilary, is also confirmed by a letter of the same Xystus to Cyril of Alexandria, reproduced in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, edited at Cologne by Binius, p. 456. There the holy pontiff congratulates Cyril on the peace concluded between him and John of Antioch and with the Church. He states that the news had been brought to him when, on the occasion of his *natale*—that is, the anniversary of his consecration—a synod of bishops was being held at Saint Peter’s:

> “O report,” he says, “worthy of the one who sent it, worthy of the assembly! The judgment of heavenly joy ought to have such assessors, and so forth. The whole brotherhood gathered to the blessed Apostle Peter. Behold assistance suited to the matter, and hearers suited to what was to be heard. Our bishops had as witness to their congratulation the one whom we have as the beginning of our honor. For he himself presided over the holy and venerable synod which my natal day, with the Lord’s favor, had assembled—for this must be believed—since it is proved that he was absent neither in body nor in spirit. He was present at the palm, who was not absent from the contest,” and so forth.

He repeats nearly the same things in a subsequent letter to John of Antioch. Both letters were dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus—that is, in the year of Christ 433, on 17 September, namely, the second month after his natal day according to our view of the beginning of Xystus’s pontificate, which assigns the date of his ordination to Sunday, 10 July 432.

## Historical Notes

**No. 63, line 2.—“Here, after one year and eight months,” etc.** No one who has read Augustine’s letters 104 and 105, addressed to this same man when he was serving as a presbyter of the Roman Church under Zosimus, is unaware that the calumnies fabricated against Xystus—and fabricated with the utmost shamelessness by the Pelagians—were refuted by the holy teacher. Augustine congratulates him that these calumnies had been driven back by a holy man with abundant profit for Catholic truth, since the enemies of divine grace found in him, when he pronounced an anathema against them, the very leader whom they had falsely celebrated as the patron of their distinguished cause.

Moreover, inspired by his most learned writings and by an unmistakably pastoral love for the Lord’s flock, he fought so vigorously against the rising errors in defense of grace that Augustine asks what could be read or heard more excellent than his writings. But that, eighteen years later, after Xystus had been raised to the pontificate, curses were again spread by the former consul Bassus—of the sort that an unchaste woman had concocted against Athanasius—so that a venerable man judged it necessary to employ the remedy of voluntary purification in a council, is not established by sufficiently reliable evidence. Certain acts of a Roman council were indeed circulated, from which the Bibliothecarius perhaps extracted his account, and which others copied from the Bibliothecarius. But the learned Spondanus, Baronius’s abridger, gives his judgment on what should be thought of such acts under the year 433, no. 3; the prudent reader may consult him.

**No. 64, line 1.—“Here he built the basilica of Saint Mary, which the ancients called Liberius’s, near the market of Libya.”** Above, no. 53, in the Life of Liberius, the founder of the basilica, I stated that it would be more appropriate to defer to this place what had to be said about the foundation, enlargement, and various names of this basilica. For documents concerning the different names assigned to this sacred building—Liberian at its foundation, Major in its enlargement, and *ad Praesepe* after the acquisition of the sacred pledges of the Lord’s Nativity brought here from Palestine—provide a collected record of events. These documents not only confirm the history of the basilica but also illuminate the history of relics of the same kind brought from the East to the principal churches of the City.

Such a discussion can scarcely be considered useless, since the knowledge of most of these matters is confused and, deprived of written records by the obscurity of time and made still more obscure by our great distance from them, requires a more exact interpreter.

To begin, then, the history of our basilica with its names, the Bibliothecarius appropriately observes that in ancient times it was called by Sixtus III the Basilica of Liberius, after its founder. But when Sixtus enlarged its area—and may therefore be regarded as its new founder—it surpassed all the other churches in the City dedicated to God under the invocation of the Virgin Mother of God, to such an extent that the Basilica of Saint Mary was designated, in a kind of antonomasia (*ἀντονομαστικῶς*), simply as “Saint Mary,” and was distinguished from the others by the surname “Major.”

How much increase and ornament it received through Sixtus is sufficiently shown by the mosaics encompassing scenes from both Testaments, which clothe the whole basilica in the principal nave of the church. There the arch called the triumphal arch displays, at the dedication of the pontiff, the name:

> **XYSTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI**  
> **Xystus, bishop for the people of God.**

An ancient inscription preserved in the *Gruteriana*, folio 1170, no. 7, further indicates that, besides the mosaic scenes mentioned, many sacred images of martyrs were also executed by him, with the distinctive emblems of the sufferings each had bravely endured for Christ:

> **VIRGO MARIA TIBI XYSTUS NOVA TECTA DICAVIT**  
> **DIGNА SALVTIFERO MUNERA VENTRE TUO.**  
> **TU GENITRIX IGNARA VIRI: TE DENIQUE FOETA**
