> **VISCERIBUS SALVIS EDITA NOSTRA SALVS.**  
> **ECCE TVI TESTES VTERI SIBI PRAEMIA PORTANT**  
> **SVB PEDIBVSQVE IACET PASSIO CVIQVE SVA.**  
> **FERRUM FLAMMA FERAE FLVVIUS SAEVVMQUE VENENVM**  
> **TOT TAMEN HAS MORTES VNA CORONA MANET.**

> Virgin Mary, Xystus has dedicated new roofs to you,  
> worthy gifts for your life-giving womb.  
> You, Mother who knew no man—yet fertile—our Salvation,  
> brought forth with your womb unharmed.  
> Behold, witnesses of your womb carry their rewards for themselves,  
> and beneath their feet lies each one’s own passion.  
> Sword, flame, wild beasts, river, and savage poison—  
> yet one crown awaits all these deaths.

Almost every column supporting the central nave bears, near the bottom of its shaft, the name of Rufinus, cut into it in ancient times. This seems to show that the columns were placed not by Liberius but by Xystus. Perhaps they had been taken from those prepared for Rufinus, the guardian of Arcadius, when he was planning the construction of some splendid building. After Rufinus had been declared an enemy of the state and, following his death, most of his property had been confiscated for the imperial treasury by the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, they may have been assigned, at Xystus’s request, to enlarge this sacred church.

Whatever may be the truth about the name of Rufinus engraved upon them, Pope Hadrian I does not hesitate to affirm, in his letter to Charlemagne on the veneration of sacred images, read at the Second Council of Nicaea, that the basilica was not merely adorned by Xystus but actually made by him—that is, enlarged and embellished to such a degree that it may be considered rebuilt through his agency:

> “The blessed Xystus,” he says, “made the basilica of the Most Holy Mother of God, called Major, which is also called *ad Praesepe*, adorning it with golden metalwork and with images depicting various sacred histories.”

Thus, besides the second surname, “Major,” it had already acquired a third in Hadrian’s time, namely, *ad Praesepe*. Since this name is not heard of either under Liberius or under Xystus, but first appears attached to it under Pope Theodore—below, no. 126—it gave rise to the question whether this basilica had been enlarged at that time solely through the acquisition of the relics of the Lord’s manger and swaddling clothes.

I undertook this investigation all the more willingly because I foresaw that it might shed light on the transfer of many sacred relics which the West possesses, having been brought from Palestine and the other provinces of the Eastern Church into these regions, especially into the City. The inquiry inserted here will show how far I have so far been able to proceed through careful examination and comparison of the monuments. I wished it to be set out under its own title, outside the series of notes, and divided by marginal numbers, so that, freed from the constraints of brief annotations, it might range more freely in investigating both the origin and the cause of so singular and memorable a name and acquisition.

*(See the dissertation promised here at the end of all the Notes to the Life of Saint Xystus III. There is also added there another dissertation by the same author concerning the mosaics constructed by Saint Xystus III in the Liberian basilica after the sacred ecumenical Synod of Ephesus.)*

## Notes

**No. 63, line 2.—“He was accused and indicted.”** Namely, he was said to have violated a nun named Chrysogonitis. For this reason the pontiff himself voluntarily wished his case to be judged in a synod.

**No. 64, line 1.—“Here he built the basilica of Saint Mary, which the ancients called Liberius’s.”** Pope Hadrian mentions this church in a letter to the emperor Charlemagne, in these words:

> “Sixtus, successor of Celestine, made the basilica of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, called Major, which is called *ad Praesepe*.”

**No. 65, lines 26 and 27.—“Which he also adorned with verses.”** In the octagonal structure, with two verses inscribed on each architrave, as they now exist after their renewal by Gregory XIII.

## Notes

**No. 63, line 1.—“He sat for eight years,” etc.** Pagius summarizes the events at the beginning of the pontificate as follows. Once Sixtus had been called pontiff, he omitted nothing that might bring Nestorius to condemn his own heresy. For Gennadius, in book 54 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says:

> “Likewise Sixtus, the successor of Celestine, sent judgments on the same matter, both to Nestorius himself and to the bishops of the East, in order to cut down his error.”

Hence Sixtus himself, in a letter sent to John of Antioch in the year 433 and quoted by Baronius in that same year, writes:

> “I believe that the course and order of events has been reported to Your Love: how we wished to come to his aid by our admonition; how we held back him who was rushing headlong and was about to be plunged into the depths beneath the weight of his blasphemies.”

When, toward the end of 432, peace had been arranged between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch, John wrote to Pope Sixtus and sent synodal letters from the Synod of Antioch, at which John assented both to the condemnation of Nestorius and to the ordination of Maximian as bishop of Constantinople. In addition to those synodal letters addressed to Sixtus, Cyril, and Maximian, John and Cyril each reported the matter to Sixtus in separate letters.

John of Antioch’s report to Sixtus has perished, but it is indicated in Sixtus’s reply to that same John, in which he states that the report had been solemnly read in the synod assembled by his natal day. Sixtus greatly rejoiced over this peace, as is clear from his letters to John and Cyril.

Helladius of Tarsus and Eutherius, metropolitan of Tyana, after seeing that they had not only been excluded from the peace but that the settlement made by the Synod of Ephesus and confirmed by the Constantinopolitan synod of Maximian was also approved and accepted by the patriarch John, and that nothing now remained for them except exile—for the emperor Theodosius was defending the peace by every means and extending a protective hand to its opponents—appealed to Sixtus, the Roman pontiff, not only against the peace but also against all the acts of the Council of Ephesus.

This is taught us by a letter of Eutherius of Tyana to Alexander of Hierapolis and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, which is read in chapter 116 of the synodal work against the tragedy of Irenaeus. From it one also concludes that this appeal was interposed before Sixtus’s confirmation of the peace that had been concluded. Eutherius and Helladius of Tarsus ask Alexander and Theodoret to send to Rome this common form of appeal, to which many other bishops had likewise adhered. That this was done is clearly shown by another letter of Eutherius and Helladius to Pope Sixtus, also found in chapter 117 of the same synodal work.

In this letter to Sixtus, Eutherius and Helladius bring forward various charges against Cyril and against his *capitula*, which they say contain a blasphemous novelty of expression. They claim that Cyril ordered Nestorius to subscribe to them, on pain of deposition; that Nestorius refused to consent to heretical stratagems and was condemned for that reason alone by the Synod of Ephesus, and indeed before the arrival of many of the bishops who were expected, so that the condemnation occurred without a synod.

They also bring forward various charges against John of Antioch, especially that he later retracted what he had done justly and fell into manifest betrayal by admitting Cyril to communion without repentance and without an anathema against his *capitula*. Against the Council of Ephesus they produce still more arguments, particularly that it admitted Cyril, who was himself accused, to the presidency; that it condemned Nestorius without due examination and before the arrival of the bishops who had been summoned; that it brought bishops to subscribe the sentence against Nestorius by promises, threats, and fraud; and that it condemned even those who refused and appointed others over them.

Finally, the appellants do not refuse to condemn Nestorius, but they wish this to be done judicially and in accordance with the sacred canons.

> “We ask,” they say, “and prostrate ourselves at the holy feet of Your Reverence, that you extend a saving hand, remove the shipwreck of the world, command an investigation of all these matters, and impose heavenly correction upon these unlawful proceedings. Let the holy pastors who have been unjustly driven from their sheep be recalled, and let order and the ancient harmony be restored to the flocks.”

They ask that they and the other bishops who had either been expelled or deposed be restored to their former status, that the pope retract everything, and that he also define the matter.

They then continue:

> “We would indeed have hastened to Your Holiness, we who come from different regions—that is, from Euphratesia, both Cilicias, Second Cappadocia, Bithynia, Thessaly, and Moesia—unless the terror of the wolves had detained us, as they lie in wait for the flocks for plunder, error, and every kind of adversity. Therefore we have been compelled, in our place, to send highly reverend clerics and monks to take our place.”

From this it is clear that bishops of various provinces adhered to this appeal.

What Sixtus did after the appeal was lodged we read neither in the synodal work mentioned nor elsewhere. Lupus, in his notes on chapter 117 of the synodal work, maintains that the pontiff accepted it and, before sending the letters to Cyril and John of Antioch by which he confirmed the peace, promptly reconsidered everything. He supposes that Sixtus even reconsidered the Constantinopolitan synod of Maximian and granted the appellants’ requests not in every respect but in certain matters, and he attempts to prove this from the two letters of Sixtus.

Yet nothing in those letters does not suggest the opposite, as the author of the Baronian critique says. It should therefore be believed that the pontiff wished the decrees of the Council of Ephesus to take effect, except that he restricted certain acts of Maximian’s synod and restored four metropolitans who had been deposed from that dignity, provided that they subscribed to the articles of peace.

This outstanding monument of antiquity further shows how greatly those men were mistaken who wished to claim that the Eastern bishops had never formerly appealed to the Roman pontiffs but always to a general synod of the whole Church. Indeed, the same author of the Baronian critique writes under the year 433 that Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis, appealed to Sixtus together with his entire province, and that Irenaeus, the author of the synodal work—although a Nestorian and therefore hostile to the Apostolic See—approved Roman appeals. He also writes that the practice of appealing from a pontiff who had been inadequately informed to one better informed, in order to seek a reconsideration of an apostolic judgment, is most ancient and was directed not to a general synod but to that same pontiff or his successor.

**Line 4.—“And when an assembly had been held.”** Acts of the Roman synod concerning the case of Sixtus III, accused by the former consul Bassus of having defiled himself through sexual misconduct, are circulated. They say that he was acquitted in the presence of the clergy, the senate, and the emperor. But these acts are recorded with a false consular date and are riddled with anachronisms, which expose their fabrication.

Nor do they gain any authority from Sixtus’s letter to the Eastern bishops, since it is composed from passages of the Eighth Council of Toledo, Felix III, Gregory the Great, Hadrian I, the Theodosian and Justinianic Codes, the Arian interpreter, and Sixtus the Pythagorean.

Acts of the same sort are those concerning the synodal accusation and purification of Polychronius, bishop of Jerusalem, which are said to have taken place at Rome under the pontificate of Sixtus. For throughout the whole period of Sixtus’s see, Juvenal governed the Church of Jerusalem, and nothing is more absurd than those acts. The accusation and purification of Sixtus are indeed reported in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, but since other fables are also recounted there, both histories must be regarded as of doubtful reliability.

**No. 65, line 1.—“A golden image with twelve gates or divisions,” in the manner in which images were fashioned in antiquity.** The images of other saints were set within them. See Ciampini and other antiquaries who reproduce representations of images.

**Line 6.—“During his times Valentinian Augustus made the confession of the blessed Apostle Paul from the purest silver, weighing two hundred pounds.”** The *confessions* of apostles, martyrs, and saints are their tombs.

Anastasius, below, under the same entry:

> “Likewise Bishop Sixtus made the confession of Saint Lawrence the martyr with porphyry columns, and adorned the screen and the altar, as well as the confession of Saint Lawrence the martyr.”

The same author, under Hilary:

> “He made the confession of Saint John the Baptist from silver.”

And below:

> “He made the confession of Saint John the Evangelist from silver.”

And again:

> “In the oratory of the Holy Cross he made a confession, where he placed the Lord’s wood, together with a golden cross set with gems.”

Likewise, in Anastasius II:

> “He made the confession of the blessed Lawrence the martyr from silver.”

Likewise, under Honorius:

> “And he covered the confession of the blessed Peter with pure silver.”

**Lines 8 and 9.—“And he adorned the screen and the altar.”** *Transenna* means a passage or crossing. Likewise, in Stephen IV:

> “And after a few days they threw the presbyter Waldipertus out of that same custody and, casting him to the ground beside the screen of the Lateran field, dug out his eyes.”

It can mean a *pergula*, a structure through which one passes. Paulinus, letter 12:

> “This basilica is opened by three equal arches, with a screen shining before them.”

Macrobius, book II, chapter 10:

> “Sitting in the screen.”

Or it can mean a rope stretched across a passage. Servius, commenting on the passage in Book V of the *Aeneid*:

> “And the dove flying across the stretched rope.”

Hence *transenna* can mean a stretched rope.

It can also mean a lattice or device by which birds are caught. Plautus, in the *Rudens*:

> “In human life many screens are made, where people are deceived by tricks.”

The same author, in the *Bacchides*:

> “Now this thrush seeks a worm from the screen.”

And in the *Persa*:

> “Today I shall lead this man into the screen by clever tricks.”

**Lines 18 and 19.—“Silver vessels for baptism or penance, weighing ten pounds.”** *Ministeria* means sacred vessels. Likewise Anastasius, under Hilary:

> “Ten pounds of silver vessels for baptism.”

The same author, under Gregory:

> “He also made a marble ambo in the same church and endowed it with various linens and vessels.”

Later writers call this a chapel. Einhard, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, uses *capella* for an ecclesiastical treasury or collection of sacred vessels.

# First Dissertation of Francesco Bianchini

## On the Translation of the Sacred Cradles and Manger of the Lord Jesus Christ, as well as the Body of Blessed Jerome, from the Bethlehemite Church to the Liberian Basilica

Divided into the following sections.

## Index of Sections

**I.** The occasion for investigating the manger of the Lord’s Nativity, together with his infant cradle and swaddling clothes, transferred here, arising from the name Saint Mary *ad Praesepe*, which was added to the Liberian basilica under Pope Theodore.

**II.** The assignment of a new name indicates the acquisition of the object signified by that name, together with matters belonging to that principal object.

**III.** The question is proposed concerning the translation to our basilica of part of the Lord’s manger and the relics associated with it—namely, Christ’s cradle and the body of Saint Jerome.

**IV.** The obscurity of the history of the translation, arising from the scarcity of historians in that period, is increased by writings of uncertain date and by works fabricated by other authors.

**V.** With Cardinal Baronius, the false account of the first translation of Saint Jerome’s body, attributed by Petrus de Vineis to Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, is rejected, since Cyril died more than thirty years before Saint Jerome.

**VI.** With the same cardinal, the translation of part of the Lord’s manger and its associated relics into our basilica around the middle of the seventh century is accepted as genuine.

**VII.** At that time the name Saint Mary *ad Praesepe* was added to this basilica and thereafter remained attached to it continuously; previously it is not found attributed to the basilica.

**VIII.** The year of the translation can be approached more closely if it is placed between 640 and 650. The history of the Saracens’ invasion of Palestine and of their new rule in that region, arranged according to the sequence of years and compared with the events of the same period in the Eastern and Western Empires, seems to require that date for the translation.

**IX.** Under the pontificate of Pope Theodore, from 642 to 649, the occasion and the strongest indications for the translation of the Lord’s manger are found.

**X.** The translation is said by the writers to have taken place at the same time as the translation of the body of Blessed Jerome.

**XI.** To make the translation of the Lord’s manger more clearly known, it is first established what is meant by the name “the Lord’s manger” from the age of Saint Jerome to our own. The manger is the innermost part of the cave of the Nativity, where the Lord, newly born from the Virgin Mother, was laid.

**XII.** Saint Jerome had been buried at the entrance of the cave—that is, at the entrance to the cave of the Lord’s Nativity.

**XIII.** The Lord’s manger is likewise understood by later travel writers as the innermost recess of the cave of the Nativity.

**XIV.** The relics of the Lord’s manger are said to be the rubble and stones that formed that inner recess of the cave. Accordingly, this rubble—or portion of the innermost recess of the cave of the Nativity—was transferred to the Liberian basilica. These are the relics of the Lord’s manger preserved here from the age of Pope Theodore.

**XV.** After being kept for approximately 529 years in the ancient altar of the old chapel, they were transferred by Sixtus V in 1585, together with the altar itself, and deposited beneath its table in a leaden chest. They were moved to the new Sistine chapel, magnificently built by him, where they are preserved today.

**XVI.** Ancient documents of our Church correctly affirm that the relics of Saint Jerome were transferred together with the Lord’s manger, after Palestine had been almost stripped of the relics of its saints.

**XVII.** The translation of these relics under Pope Theodore, who himself came from Jerusalem, appears to have been carried out on the advice of Saint Sophronius, the last Jerusalem patriarch after the Saracen invasion.

**XVIII.** The cult given to the Lord’s manger in the Liberian basilica from the age of Theodore, when that sacred pledge was transferred from Palestine, increased day by day under Theodore’s immediate successors.

**XIX.** On the sacred cradles of Christ transferred from Palestine to the Liberian basilica, where they are preserved today.

**XX.** In Palestine, two kinds of sacred relics pertaining to the principal events of our religion can be distinguished: first, immovable relics; second, movable relics.

**XXI.** Churches were founded over the immovable relics in the age of Constantine the Great, especially over the place of the Lord’s Nativity and the Lord’s Resurrection.

**XXII.** Relics of the second kind, namely movable relics, were preserved in those same basilicas.

**XXIII.** What principal movable relics were preserved in the basilica of the Resurrection?

**XXIV.** What relics were preserved in the basilica of the Nativity? Here the Lord’s cradle is discussed as distinct from the manger.

**XXV.** By the name “cradle” are understood both infants’ beds and the bands, cloths, and fastenings used to wrap infants and hold them firmly in the cradles so that they would not fall out. In Greek, *σπάργανα* (*spargana*) refers both to the bands and to the other equipment mentioned, which includes the cradles themselves.

**XXVI.** After this explanation of the Latin and Greek terms signifying bands, cloths, fastenings, cradles, and the entire equipment and furnishing of infants’ beds and childbirth, it is shown that such furnishings, used at the Nativity of Christ the Lord and during his infancy and called in Latin *cunabula* and in Greek *σπάργανα*, were preserved in the Jerusalemite and Bethlehemite churches until the fourth century after Christ, together with other sacred relics rendered venerable through contact with Christ the Lord, the Mother of God, and other saints.

**XXVII.** This continued until Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, traveled to Palestine, and Emperor Marcian, on the occasion of the Council of Chalcedon, obtained from the patriarch of Jerusalem that a portion of the bands and cradle of Christ’s infancy be given to them. Brought to Constantinople, it was deposited in the celebrated churches dedicated to God under the titles of the Virgin Mother of God of the Guides and *ad Blachernas*. From these, a portion reached the kings of the Franks in the thirteenth century and the churches of Spain.

**XXVIII.** The Eastern Church granted a portion of this cradle—or of these bands—and of the furnishings of Christ’s infancy to those emperors in the same way that some portion of other Palestinian relics was also granted in the fourth century both to emperors and empresses and to most holy bishops who requested those relics, especially on the occasion of journeys to Jerusalem undertaken by them.

**XXIX.** This facility in distributing relics, which prevailed in the Jerusalemite Church, especially after repeated Persian invasions, caused Palestine to be almost deprived of its other movable relics when it fell prey to the Saracens around the year 610. Thus the portion of the Lord’s manger, the surviving cradle and part of its furnishings, and the body of Blessed Jerome were then the last of the sacred pledges that could be transferred to the West.

**XXX.** When the relics of the manger and cradle and the body of Saint Jerome were fortunately transferred to our basilica during those same years under Pope Theodore, they did not undergo diminution. For the discipline then prevailing in the Roman Church—and asserted by Pope Gregory forty-five years before Theodore’s pontificate—would not readily permit the division of sacred relics, at least of the principal ones, as the Jerusalemite Church did.

**XXXI.** From the portion of the Lord’s cradle that survives among us it is inferred that more than half of that sacred furnishing, or little bed of Christ’s infancy, consists of five boards reverently preserved in a silver reliquary. Every year it is displayed above the altar of the Most Holy Manger on the night of the Lord’s Nativity and, on the day of the Nativity itself, above the high altar of the basilica for the veneration of the faithful. If the thicker boards of the same cradle, deposited by Sixtus V beneath the altar table in the larger chapel established for the manger, are added to these, nearly the entire body of the sacred cradle preserved in this basilica is constituted.

**XXXII.** For this reason, the practice of preserving the ancient discipline is commended even in our own age. It forbids the diminution, division, and distribution of fragments of such sacred pledges, since when they are preserved intact they provide a more excellent testimony for stirring more vividly the pious feelings of the soul toward the mystery celebrated in them.

**1.** Since the history of the *Book of the Pontiffs* in no. 64 reports the various names of the basilica of Saint Mary, founded by Liberius and enlarged by Xystus III of that name, consideration of another designation must not be separated from this passage, although it was assigned later, two centuries after Xystus, under Pope Theodore. In Theodore’s Life it is first called Saint Mary *ad Praesepe* (no. 126); thereafter the name remains under Theodore’s immediate successors, as can be seen in the Life of Saint Martin (no. 132), where it is likewise indicated:

> “The basilica of Saint Mary, the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God, which is called *ad Praesepe*.”

**2.** The addition of this name is evidence of the translation of the principal pledges among the sacred relics from the Bethlehemite church to this place: namely, the manger and cradle of the infancy of Christ the Lord, and the sacred body of blessed Jerome, who had once been buried there in the fifth century of the Christian era and now rests in this Liberian and Sistine basilica, near those same venerable pledges deposited and reverently preserved among us.

In order to enjoy them more closely, and to water them with his most devout tears, sing continually, and pray without ceasing—as he himself recalls in his letter to Marcella, inviting her to visit them—Saint Jerome gladly abandoned the broad porticoes of the City and Rome’s gilded ceilings. In the cave and manger of the Savior he established his delights, and in the little dwelling of Christ and the lodging of Mary he established his palaces and Capitols.

**3.** I hope that I shall do something worthwhile if I endeavor to gather from genuine documents the period and occasion on which these Bethlehemite trophies of our religion were transferred to the City and placed thereafter for preservation in the Liberian basilica, thereby acquiring for it the new surname Saint Mary *ad Praesepe*. I also hope to disclose this to the devout worshipers who flock here to adore them, insofar as the historical evidence permits, concerning those centuries which not only scarcity of writers removed far from the sight of later generations but which the incursion of the barbarians and the overthrow of the Roman Empire in the West, and in the East its disfigurement and mutilation, enveloped everywhere in dense darkness.

### 4.

The account of such translations is certainly recognized as obscure among historians of our own time, undoubtedly because of the lack of contemporary writers who recorded the events. Hence even those among more recent authors who have attempted to write about the sacred relics of the Liberian Basilica have gone off in different directions, consulting only commentaries either of uncertain date or close to their own period. To pass over Octavius Panciroli, who treats these matters rather meagerly in *The Hidden Treasures of Rome*, and others who scarcely touch upon them while surveying the seven churches of the City, Abbot Paolo de Angelis—who in twelve books set forth a description of the Liberian Basilica, magnificently adorned with copper engravings under Paul V, a pontiff no less devoted to its embellishment than to its worship—devoted the whole of chapter four of his sixth book to clarifying the translation of the body of Saint Jerome.

Yet he seems not to have completed the task assigned to him with much success, since he employs mutually contradictory testimonies and assertions drawn from codices of uncertain age and unknown authors, reported among the books called *passionaries*, or lectionaries, to which we shall shortly refer. The codex of the monastery of Saint Cecilia, which he cites on page 18 and page 115, column 1, asserts that Pope Liberius, at the first foundation of the basilica, placed there the Lord’s manger, the cradle, the hay, and the cloths of Our Lord and Redeemer beneath the altar of that same manger, together with many other relics of the saints.

In other books, however, both of the Liberian Basilica and of the Vatican, he observes it asserted that the body of Blessed Jerome—whom we know to have been buried at the Lord’s manger around the year 420, the year of his death, when Theodosius IX and Constantius III were consuls, according to the chronicle of Prosper, who was then living, namely half a century after Liberius’s pontificate—remained for a long time in the Bethlehem church after it had been stripped of all its relics, when, because the sins of men provoked God’s just scourges, Palestine fell prey to the Persians and Saracens, shortly after the beginning and around the middle of the seventh century of the Christian era. It is then said to have been secretly removed from there by a monk at the prompting of a heavenly vision and transferred clandestinely to the city of Rome.

To pass over the other defects in both accounts, I consider here only their contradiction and opposition to one another, on the basis of documents that are by no means uncertain. For how could Pope Liberius have placed in the basilica he built at Rome the Lord’s manger and the cradle of Christ the Lord, when Jerome, surviving Liberius by approximately half a century, was buried at the Lord’s manger in Palestine? After returning there following the death of Liberius and of his successor Damasus, he was present there as a teacher of the solitary life for the Roman virgins and matrons whom he had summoned from the City; and, pointing with his finger toward the Lord’s manger and the cradle there, he indicated the sanctity of these relics—sometimes to encourage the religious devotion of those most pious women, sometimes to instill horror of crimes in the most wicked deacon Sabinianus—as is abundantly clear from his letters, which will be produced below.

### 5.

There is an equal error of history and chronology in Peter de Natalibus, who attributes to Cyril of Jerusalem, on the basis of an old manuscript, the first translation of the body of Blessed Jerome. For, as Baronius observes in his notes on the Martyrology, under 9 May, when Cyril departed this life in the year 386, the holy doctor survived him for thirty-three years, namely until the ninth consulship of Theodosius the Younger, which was in the Christian year 420.

Since, therefore, the most learned cardinal rightly determines that that premature translation of the relics of Saint Jerome, placed at the end of the fourth century at Cyril’s death, must be rejected as false, since Jerome was still alive, the supposedly later deposition of the Lord’s manger and cradle in the Roman basilica under Liberius is overturned with even greater reason. For the holy doctor was buried much later in the Bethlehem church beside those sacred relics.

### 6.

Having excluded this fictitious translation, falsely attributed to the fourth century both of the body of Blessed Jerome, who had not yet died, and of Christ’s sacred cradle and manger, which had not yet been removed from the Bethlehem church, we turn to establishing—on the authority of Baronius in his notes on the Martyrology—the true translation of those sacred relics around the year of Christ 640, when, as the Saracens invaded Palestine, the most holy remains previously kept there had to be withdrawn from the barbarians’ assaults.

The aforementioned Cardinal admits as the first translation of the sacred body of Blessed Jerome to Rome from Palestine the one that Peter de Natalibus, in *Catalogue*, book IV, chapter 145, calls the second, and assigns to the period of the Saracen incursions into Palestine.

We not only agree with Baronius’s view but also say that the translation of the relics of the Lord’s manger and of the sacred cradle of our Savior, together with many other relics of the saints brought to Rome, belongs to the same period. Among these were the bodies of Blessed Jerome and of the apostle Matthias from Palestine, placed within the Basilica of Saint Mary Major by Pope Theodore. It was at this time, in fact, that the same Liberian Basilica received the new designation of Saint Mary at the Manger.

### 7.

As I observed in the first section, we do not find this title attributed to the basilica before that time. Thereafter, however, I have shown from the text of the Bibliothecarius that this designation, Saint Mary at the Manger, was used continuously. The sacramentaries, antiphonaries, and missals arranged before Pope Theodore under Gregory the Great—who preceded Theodore’s pontificate by forty years—agree, having been published by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius. Whenever a station at Saint Mary Major in the Liberian Basilica is prescribed, the additional title Saint Mary at the Manger is never appended.

The same is true in the register of the letters of that same Blessed Gregory, book II, near the beginning, where the sevenfold litany is ordered. The title is given in the surviving document as follows: “Concerning the Greater Litany in the Basilica of Saint Mary.”

Under Pope Theodore, however, and under the pontiffs who immediately followed him, Martin and Eugenius, the name is explicitly found. It also appears in Gregory III, nos. 196 and 202; in Leo III, sections 383 and 386; in Paschal I, sections 450 and 451; and elsewhere throughout.

The Roman *Ordo*, compiled during the twelfth Christian century from older sources and inserted into the *Book of Censuses* by Cencio, then cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in Orthea and chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, who was later elected pope and took the name Honorius III, states the following in no. 2 of the Mabillon edition:

> At the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, in the morning the lord pope goes to the Basilica of Saint Mary Major to sing Mass, and in the evening to celebrate Vespers; and he remains there that night, celebrates the vigils, and after the vigils celebrates Mass there at the MANGER.

### 8.

The matter must nevertheless be treated more closely, and, if possible, the year in which the title Saint Mary at the Manger was assigned must be established as nearly as possible. By comparing the events of that year with those of the immediately preceding years, it may be determined whether the occasion for forming the new name arose from the conveyance of the cradle and the relics of the manger, made illustrious by the Lord’s Nativity, from the Bethlehem church to the Roman Liberian Basilica.

We have already seen that this title began to be assigned under Pope Theodore, who occupied the Roman See from November of the year 642 until April of the year 649. It is not difficult to investigate, from the Eastern chronicles of the Greeks, Arabs, and Syrians, and even from the annals of our Western writers, what took place in Palestine during these seven years and the years immediately preceding them.

Moreover, since several distinguished chroniclers and historians gathered the sequence of events from those times, and their abbreviators reduced it to an epitome, while the critics of the annals—especially Pagi—carefully examined it, only a small amount of labor is required for the shorter account that I append here. I follow Pagi, who seems more diligent than the others in examining and correcting the difference of two or three years admitted by some histories in dating such events. From this account the occasion for carrying those sacred relics from Palestine to the West may be recognized.

Scarcely, therefore, had the year 629 of the Christian era arrived—Cedrenus assigns it to the nineteenth year of Heraclius—when the emperor Heraclius restored to the holy city the Lord’s cross, recovered from the Persians together with Zacharias, patriarch of Jerusalem, and the other faithful captives who had been led into Persia fourteen years earlier. He restored it with that solemn procession whose memory the Church annually commemorates on 14 September.

Four years later, namely in the year 633, the Arabs, following the institutions of Muhammad, the false prophet and impostor who had died in the preceding year, 632—Cedrenus assigns his death to the twenty-first year of Heraclius—began war against the emperor Heraclius.

In the years 633 and 634, the Arab Saracens, under Euberus—called Abubacharus by some and Abubacrus by others—the successor and kinsman or relative of Muhammad, invaded and ravaged the region of Gaza. They killed Sergius, commander and governor of Palestine, near Caesarea. (*Theophanes*, in the twenty-third year of Heraclius.)

When this Abubacharus, the principal Saracen commander, or *amir*, died on 23 August 634—according to Pagi, following Elmacinus—Omar, or Umar, began to reign that same day, according to Theophanes and Cedrenus under the twenty-fourth year of Heraclius. He appointed Othman commander for the war against the Persians, occupied Arabia, and took Damascus. He struck such terror into Heraclius, who was awaiting the outcome of affairs near Edessa, that Heraclius, as though all hope were lost, abandoned Syria and withdrew to Constantinople, carrying thither from Jerusalem the venerable wood of the life-giving cross. (*Theophanes* and Cedrenus at the place indicated.)

In the year 635 the Saracens invaded all Phoenicia. Advancing victoriously as far as Egypt, they subjected the region of Syria, besieged Jerusalem, and reduced the Egyptians to servitude.

In the year 636, while the siege of Jerusalem had not yet been lifted, Saint Sophronius, the patriarch, was prevented from visiting the Bethlehem cave of the Nativity and the Lord’s manger during the Christmas festival, in order to celebrate the sacred rites there with the people, as he had previously been accustomed to do.

In the year 637, after Umar had captured Jerusalem, he granted it to the patriarch Sophronius and was so favorably disposed toward the Christians that they were permitted to perform the sacred rites according to their ancestral worship. Blessed Sophronius, however, did not long survive. When no successor was duly chosen for him in the patriarchate at his death, Sergius of Joppa violently invaded his position.

The Saracens, having driven out Yazdegerd, took Mada’in and the royal treasures stored there. Their caliph Umar, having weakened the two empires through his dominion—namely that of the Romans, from whom he had taken Egypt and Syria, and that of the Persians, whose Chaldea, Media, and Persia itself he had almost entirely occupied—was granted by his followers the new title *Amir al-Mu’minin*, that is, “commander of the believers.”

In the year 638, after Antioch had been subdued by Umar, Muawiya was appointed commander and *amir* of the entire Saracen dominion from Egypt to the Euphrates. (*Theophanes.*)

In the year 639, according to Elmacinus, the Saracens took Memphis, the capital of Egypt.

In the year 640, after the death of Pope Severinus, John IV, a Dalmatian by nation, was appointed pontiff of the Roman Church; he was to survive for less than two complete years. Theophanes assigns to this year—the thirtieth year of the emperor Heraclius, in the Christian era 640—the flight of Yazdegerd into inner Persia out of fear of the Saracens.

In the year 641, in the month of March, in the fourteenth indiction, the emperor Heraclius died after thirty years and ten months of imperial rule. (*Theophanes*, with whom the other historians agree.) Constantine, the son of Heraclius, survived his father by only 103 days and, having been poisoned by his stepmother Martina, as Cedrenus and Theophanes believe, left as his successor Heraclius, the son of that same Martina. But after six months his rule was terminated, and Constans, the son of Constantine and grandson of Heraclius, was substituted in his place.

In the same year the Saracens took Alexandria in Egypt, according to Elmacinus.

In the year 642, when John IV, the Roman pontiff, died, he was succeeded by Theodore, whose father was Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem, as the Bibliothecarius relates in section 121.

This Pope Theodore founded in the Lateran patriarchate an altar of Saint Sylvester, subsequently called the altar of the Holy of Holies, adjoining the chapel of Saint Lawrence. Both he himself and succeeding pontiffs brought to it especially important relics, particularly those conveyed from Palestine. On this matter see Panciroli, *The Sacred Treasures of the City of Rome*, Region 2, no. 12, where he refutes another reading of Anastasius concerning the title of that altar, found in other codices and called by Cardinal Rasponi the altar of Saint Sebastian.

Whether the altar was called Saint Sylvester’s or Saint Sebastian’s, it formed part of the pontiffs’ chapel, constructed to store the most precious relics of all. Besides this chapel founded by Theodore—which proves his care in procuring sacred remains that would lend distinction to the chapel of the Holy of Holies—documents also attest to his exceptionally devoted zeal in honoring, with sacred buildings and gifts, the relics of Christ’s martyrs and of other saints. These include the churches of Saint Valentine at the Milvian Bridge and of Blessed Euplius at the Ostian Gate, as well as the gifts offered to Saints Primus and Felicianus in the title-church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian, mentioned by the Bibliothecarius in his *Life*, no. 128.

The recent example of Theodore’s predecessor, John IV, further increased the pontiff’s zeal. John had wished to provide for the shrines of his homeland by transferring to Rome the sacred bodies of the holy martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, Maurus, and their companions from the province of Dalmatia. He had seen Illyricum frequently ravaged by the incursions of Arabs, Slavs, and Hungarians under the emperors Maurice and Heraclius, until the whole region was deprived of its inhabitants and reduced to the appearance of a wilderness, as D. Ducange gathered from the Byzantine historians in *Byzantine Families*, page 270.

The circumstances were especially favorable for Pope Theodore to transport sacred relics from Palestine to Rome through Stephen, bishop of Dora, who sailed back and forth from there to Italy in order to present himself to the Roman pontiff, report to him the dangers threatening his paternal homeland from both heretics and barbarians, and implore assistance from the providence of the Apostolic See amid the present disasters.

As he approached death, Blessed Sophronius had taken this bishop, who was pre-eminent among his fellow provincials under the patriarch of Jerusalem, with him to the sacred Mount Calvary. By his command and under oath, binding him by the holiest memorials of our redemption that they beheld with their eyes and touched with their hands, he had compelled him to sail to Rome as quickly as possible and humbly to seek assistance for the afflicted affairs of the Christians, and above all for divine worship, from the father and shepherd of the universal Church, Christ’s vicar on earth.

The bishop of Dora diligently fulfilled the task entrusted to him. He sailed to Rome and explained to Pope Theodore what he had so religiously undertaken to carry out at the request of the patriarch Sophronius, who was near death. In the Roman pontiff he found equal vigilance and ardor of spirit to meet the dangers and needs of that province, which had been adorned by Christ the Lord with the principal mysteries of our religion.

Theodore therefore entrusted Stephen of Dora with the authority of the apostolic vicar over the vacant see of Jerusalem after Sophronius’s death, both to resist the Monothelite heretics courageously and to safeguard the other sacred matters there.

What Stephen, as apostolic vicar, accomplished in that province, both under Pope Theodore and under his successor Martin I, may be seen in the letters of Pope Martin to John, bishop of Philadelphia, which Baronius reported under the year 649. It may also be seen in the synodal acts of the Roman council under the same Pope Martin, investigation 2, where Stephen of Dora clearly states the matters I have just recounted and records them in a petition. Returning to Rome a second and a third time with that petition, he presented himself at the apostolic feet. (*Roman Council under Martin I*, investigation 2.)

He was the spokesman for the common desire of all the orthodox Eastern priests of that region, as well as of the aforementioned Sophronius of holy memory, on 6 October, a Tuesday, in the eighth indiction. These are the chronological markers of the year 649, after Theodore had been received into heaven before the Ides of May and Martin had succeeded him in July.

### 9.

During this seven-year period of Theodore’s pontificate, reckoned from 642 to 649, the need—if ever at another time—for the Catholic bishops of Palestine, and for Stephen of Dora, was extraordinarily urgent. Sophronius had bound Stephen by oath and mandate on Mount Calvary, while the Roman pontiff, after Sophronius’s death, had ordered him to exercise the rights of that see by vicarious authority. They therefore had to ensure not only the protection of the faith attacked by the Monothelites but also the careful preservation and security of every sacred object, both from the injuries of the barbarians and from the seizures of the heretics.

The sacred relics deposited in the churches of the Jerusalem episcopate, both in the holy city and in the neighboring places, were among the principal treasures that had to be withdrawn from the attack and power of those enemies. This was especially so when, in the year 643, the new ruler Umar undertook the restoration of the Jerusalem temple in order to convert it into a shrine of Muhammadan worship and, influenced—I do not know by what persuasion of the Jews—ordered the cross dedicated by the Christians on the Mount of Olives to be removed. (*Theophanes* and Cedrenus; see Baronius under the same year.)

This was certainly a disastrous indication of the violence to be feared against the holiest relics of our religion. From such an omen Stephen ought to have realized that he must, as soon as possible, arrange for those relics to be withdrawn from the sight and power of profane men and placed in safety—those relics that had always been regarded as the more august and venerable ornaments of the Jerusalem church, the Bethlehem church, and the neighboring churches.

For when the emperor Heraclius had once and again recovered the Lord’s cross from the Persians and the Saracens, and, after restoring it to the holy city in 629, had five years later, when a more serious danger arose under Umar, carried it back to Constantinople for its preservation, although he was still able to assemble an army by land and sea to recover the provinces, the unarmed bishop, guardian of such treasures, ought much more quickly to have provided for their safety by a prudent removal and placed them in the safest possible location before Umar’s hostile spirit, and that of his counselors, toward the Christian cross turned to burning or violating with sacrilegious assaults the memorials and instruments of the mysteries of our salvation.

But what place in Asia or Africa still remained for receiving and safely guarding such treasures? Antioch, Jerusalem, and Alexandria—the three patriarchal sees—had been subjected to the victories of the Saracens, and were occupied by the violence of heretical bishops and intruders. In the imperial capital of the East, where the Monothelites were seated upon the patriarchal throne, and where rulers of that sect, reduced to order by frequent tragedies within the space of a few months, could neither display nor promise themselves any stability in possessing and protecting the imperial dignity, what refuge could appear worthy, in the eyes of Stephen of Dora, for the relics of the saints, the Lord’s cradle, and the manger?

No holier or safer place could indeed present itself to the guardian of such treasures and the vicar of the patriarchal see, as he looked around, than the sanctuaries of the city of Rome. A very extensive opportunity for bringing to safety whatever relics he had gathered presented itself, since during the aforesaid seven-year period he was compelled to sail three times from Palestine to Italy in order to appear before the Roman pontiff.

And this was Pope Theodore, the son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem, who, as the Bibliothecarius records, knew particularly well whatever sacred objects from Palestine might have been brought here and left behind. These journeys from the Jerusalem Church repeatedly brought Stephen before Pope Theodore, who recalled the recent example of his predecessor, John IV the Dalmatian, who had rescued from the incursions and injuries of barbarous nations the bodies of the holy martyrs of that same region, his birthplace.

In the Lateran patriarchate, near the Constantinian fountain, sacred images of the martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, and Maurus, of Domnio, and of others whom John himself had arranged to have brought here from Dalmatia were still depicted in mosaic work, which we continue to see. That province had been exposed to repeated incursions “under Maurice and Heraclius by the Avars or Hungarians, Slavs, and Croats, repeatedly ravaged and so emptied of inhabitants that they reduced it to the appearance of a wilderness,” as Du Cange gathered from the Byzantine historians in *Byzantine Families*, page 270.

Theodore had these very recent examples of his immediate predecessor before his eyes in the Lateran patriarchate, where he himself founded his basilica and the chapel of the pontifical palace, dedicated to Saint Sylvester. There he would store the holiest relics, and his successors would add to them, so that the place would later be called the Holy of Holies.

Why, then, should he not also have added among the other duties entrusted to Stephen, bishop of Dora, this one: that the choicest relics remaining from the Jerusalem and Bethlehem churches, which had to be withdrawn from the barbarians, should be carried into the maternal bosom of this new Jerusalem—namely, the Roman Church—as into the safest refuge?

That this was indeed done with a portion of the Lord’s manger and with Christ’s sacred cradle under Theodore is indicated by the new title, as we have said, Saint Mary at the Manger. This title was then heard for the first time appended to the ancient names of our Liberian Basilica. In that basilica the pontiffs who immediately followed began to celebrate Mass annually at the Manger on the Lord’s Nativity and adorned that sanctuary with the most precious gifts, to indicate the excellence of that sacred treasure.

Thus Paschal I covered the altar of the Manger and the confession—after the model of Solomon and the temple constructed at Jerusalem—with solid gold on every side, as the Bibliothecarius testifies in no. 450:

> He wonderfully embellished and adorned the altar of the manger of the aforesaid basilica, or the venerable confession, throughout, inside and out, with the purest gold and various scenes, weighing 254 pounds and 4 ounces.

### 10.

Ancient documents, expressed in the books of the basilica, also prove that the body of Blessed Jerome, resting beside the cave of the Bethlehem manger in Palestine, was brought here on the same occasion. From these documents it is known that the translation of the holy doctor to the Liberian Church, celebrated in the Martyrology by annual sacred rites, was long ago noted from the same books by Peter de Natalibus and recognized by Cardinal Baronius.

Peter de Natalibus observed that in these Roman Chronicles the translation of the sacred body of Blessed Jerome from Palestine to the city of Rome is reported to have occurred:

> after many cycles of years, he says, following the death of the glorious Jerome, when Jerusalem had been destroyed and occupied by the Saracens, and had been almost entirely deprived of the relics of the saints, with only the body of Blessed Jerome remaining in those regions.

The notice that this removal took place at the same time when the treasures of nearly all the relics had been extracted from the holy city occupied by the Saracens confirms that the date of the translation of the holy doctor’s relics to Rome must be connected with the conveyance of the Lord’s manger.

Peter de Natalibus not only asserts this, but so does Marianus Victorius in his *Life of Jerome*. He prefixed this life to the Roman edition of the holy doctor’s works, prepared under the keen judgment of Cardinal Sirleto and dedicated to Pope Pius IV. Victorius had collected it with the greatest care from Jerome’s writings and from other documents of recognized authority. He also presented the life itself in a special dedication to Pius’s nephew, Saint Charles Borromeo, archpriest of the Liberian Basilica.

This distinguished author, who had examined ancient codices in the Roman archives and libraries relating to Jerome’s writings and memory, describes the joint translation of the Lord’s manger and the body of Saint Jerome as follows:

> After his death he was buried in Bethlehem, his funeral rites having first been duly celebrated according to Christian custom, as he himself reports that Antony had done for Paul. He was later transferred from there to Rome together with the manger of Christ our Savior, on the seventh day before the Ides of May—that is, on the day when the feast of his teacher Gregory of Nazianzus is celebrated. Pope Pius II later transferred the day to the vigil of the Ascension, so that it might be celebrated with greater festivity and more frequently; on that day a plenary remission of sins was granted to those visiting his tomb. The most blessed man, greater than every proclamation, for whom all the ages sigh, lies above the Esquiline, in an altar erected for him beside the Lord’s manger, where his sacred tunic is still preserved, in the Church of Saint Mary Major, and so forth.

This joint translation of the Lord’s manger and the body of Saint Jerome is to be assigned to the earlier years of Pope Theodore’s pontificate, on the basis of the occupation of Jerusalem by the Saracens mentioned by the ancient codices seen by Peter de Natalibus and Marianus Victorius. That occupation occurred in the year 637. The same conclusion follows from the added notice that nearly all the relics had already been transported away, so that only Jerome’s body remained to be carried out together with the manger.

How strong an indication this is for determining the period is sufficiently shown by the sermon of Blessed Sophronius, delivered on the Lord’s Nativity in the presence of the Bethlehem manger, which was then occupied by the Saracens—namely, in the year 636, while they were besieging Jerusalem. Since they had pitched their camp on Bethlehem soil, Sophronius himself was prevented from approaching the sacred cave and manger, where on Christmas night he desired, as was customary, to offer the solemn sacrifice to God.

The holy bishop complains:

> He and his hearers had been excluded from there like the sinful Adam, who could see the garden of paradise with his eyes—for he lived opposite it—yet could not return to it, prevented by the sight of the revolving flame and sword. So he and his hearers were made exiles from the nearby city of Bethlehem, which lay before their eyes, while the dagger of the Hagarenes threatened slaughter; and he was forbidden to enter the manger that received God and the heavenly cave toward which he longed to fly and was carried with the full force of his soul, so that he might behold the mystery hidden within it and utter that angelic hymn, “Glory to God in the highest,” in praise of the one newly born.

Thus, in the year 636, when the patriarch Sophronius delivered this conclusion, there were still preserved at Bethlehem not only that cave made heavenly by Christ’s Nativity but also the very manger that received God, when he was laid in the manger.

### 11.

Those two things must be distinguished: the cave, or grotto, in which a stable had been opened according to the local custom of that region, and the manger, namely the innermost recess of that same stable and cave, where animals were accustomed to take their fodder. It was there that the Word made flesh, at his first appearance, willed to be laid by his Virgin Mother.

The bishop of Gaul Arculphus, who traveled there during those same years, described both parts of that sanctuary. From his dictated account Adamnanus, a monk and priest of Scottish-Irish origin, took notes and transmitted the account to posterity. In the following century, the Venerable Bede incorporated a commentary on the situation of Jerusalem, expressed in nearly the same words as the description of Arculphus and Adamnanus.

These are Adamnanus’s words, recently reprinted by the distinguished writer Jean Mabillon in section III of the Benedictine edition, part II, page 512:

> In the eastern and farthest corner of that same city, Bethlehem, there is a kind of natural half-cave. Its innermost and furthest part is called the Lord’s manger, in which the mother laid the child after he was born. Another place, adjoining the manger mentioned above and nearer to those entering, is properly said to have been the site of the Lord’s Nativity. That Bethlehem cave of the Lord’s manger has been entirely adorned within, for the honor of the Savior himself, with precious marble. Above this half-cave, on a stone upper chamber, the Church of Saint Mary has been built and founded with a great structure, precisely over the place where the Lord is specially said to have been born.

All who have traveled among and written about the holy places of Palestine describe this basilica, built over the cave of the Lord’s manger by Blessed Helena, the mother of the great Constantine, in addition to Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapters 41 and 43. Among more recent authors, João Ciampini, a prelate highly distinguished for his service to sacred antiquities, has clearly described its adornments in volume II of his *Ancient Monuments*.

The distinction between the cave and the Lord’s manger given in the description of Arculphus and Adamnanus corresponds to the distinction set forth two hundred and fifty years earlier by Jerome, the custodian of the Bethlehem shrine, in letters 17 and 18 to Marcella. Paula and Eustochium invited Marcella there and celebrated the lodging of Christ and Mary in these words:

> In what speech, with what words, can we set forth for you the cave of the Savior? And that manger must be honored in speech.

And a little farther on:

> Behold, in this small opening in the earth the creator of the heavens was born; here he was wrapped in swaddling clothes; here he was seen by the shepherds; here he was revealed by the star; here he was worshiped by the Magi.

The Venerable Bede, the next writer after Adamnanus, follows nearly the same words and traces.

The next surveyor of that sacred journey after the bishop Arculphus, the monk Adamnanus, and the priest Bede was Bernard, a monk of Frankish origin. In the year 870, having obtained permission to make the pilgrimage from Pope Nicholas I together with an apostolic blessing, he was first conveyed to Alexandria in Egypt and then proceeded to Palestine with his companions.

Having committed his recollections of the journey to writing, the aforementioned P. Mabillon made them public in the indicated volume of Benedictine history, after Adamnanus, folio 523.

When Bernard reached Bethlehem, he records the following, section 16, as having been seen there:

> Bethlehem, therefore, has a very large church in honor of Saint Mary. In its middle there is a crypt beneath a single stone; its entrance is on the south, while its exit is toward the east. In it the Lord’s manger is shown, toward the west of the crypt. The place where the Lord cried is toward the east. There is an altar there where Masses are celebrated. Beside this church, to the south, is the church of the blessed martyred Innocents. Finally, one mile from Bethlehem is the monastery of the holy Shepherds, to whom the angel of the Lord appeared at the Nativity of the Lord. Finally, thirty miles east of Jerusalem is the Jordan, and above it is the monastery of Saint John the Baptist. Many monasteries are situated in these places, and so forth.

### 12.

Before proceeding further to present the observations of this monk Bernard, or of others who wrote about the sanctuaries of Palestine after his time, I wish to note two matters that contribute greatly to establishing the time when the body of Saint Jerome, together with a portion of the Lord’s manger, was translated to the West.

First, by comparing the descriptions of Adamnanus and Bernard, it is learned that in the time of the former—that is, Adamnanus, or rather of the bishop Arculphus, whose journey and survey of the holy places occurred around the year 670—the tomb of Saint Jerome was customarily shown in a separate church outside the walls of Bethlehem, in the valley adjoining the southern slope of the Bethlehem hill.

Adamnanus writes:

> When we inquired with similar concern about the tomb of Saint Jerome, Arculphus said: “The tomb of Saint Jerome, about which you ask, I saw myself. It is located in another church built outside that same little city, Bethlehem, in a valley adjoining the southern side of the ridge of the aforementioned Bethlehem hill. That tomb of Jerome, constructed in a manner similar to David’s monument, has no ornament.”

Arculphus and Adamnanus do not add this last detail without purpose. The absence of ornament indicates that Jerome’s sacred bones had been carried away from there a few years earlier to Pope Theodore. After Umar the caliph removed the crosses from the Mount of Olives, suspicion arose in the mind of Stephen of Dora, who was exercising there the office of apostolic vicar by command of the same supreme pontiff Theodore. He feared that the body of Blessed Jerome—almost the only sacred relic remaining on Bethlehem soil after the other holy remains had been removed from there—might be scattered by the impious counselors of Umar, just as, according to the accounts, had happened to the bones of the Lord’s precursor under the apostate Julian.

Indeed, one may even wonder whether the tomb shown to Arculphus in a church somewhat removed from the cave and manger of the Savior was rather a second repository of the body of the holy doctor, and a temporary one at that. It may have been used so that the body could be removed more cautiously when it was taken from its first burial place—which he had chosen beside the cave itself, at the entrance to the sacred grotto—and, under the pretext of depositing it in a church, the second translation beyond Palestine, by which it was conveyed to Rome, might be accomplished more securely.

[Col. 0247A] Certainly, later travelers to Palestine scarcely remembered that tomb of Jerome, so far removed from the cave of the Lord’s manger, in their accounts of the venerable places shown to them. Bernard, a monk of Frankish origin who went there in the year of Christ 870 with the approval and blessing of Pope Nicholas I, speaks of Jerome’s monastery—and indeed of the bed and cell shown to him. But he does not report having been shown the holy doctor’s tomb in that church, although he does mention tombs that he saw both around Jerusalem and around Bethlehem; indeed, in Egypt, outside the walls of Alexandria, he recalls being shown the tomb of Saint Mark the Evangelist, though, as he expressly notes, it had been removed from there by Venetian merchants fifty years earlier.

Nor does Marinus Sanutus, who described the same holy places after seeing them himself in 1321, when he presented his book to the Supreme Pontiff under the title *The Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross*. There he merely indicates [Col. 0247B] that blessed Jerome had been buried not far from the Lord’s manger. Certainly, in an ancient parchment codex of the archive of the most holy Liberian Basilica, where Jerome’s life is collected from his own writings and those of other Fathers, the following is said concerning his earlier burial:

> “Moreover, blessed Jerome, while he was still alive, made a tomb for himself by cutting into the rock at the entrance to the cave of the Lord’s manger, not far from the tomb of the aforementioned holy women, Paula and Eustochium. After he had conquered the power of the world, he was buried there on the day before the Kalends of October.”

I shall review Marinus Sanutus’s book below.

The one indication of Jerome’s tomb that I have seen after the time of Arculphus survives in Brocardus, or Brucardus, a writer of the thirteenth century. He too places the tomb beside the Lord’s manger, where, he says, the monastery and the holy doctor’s bed were shown to pilgrims, together with his tomb and those of Paula and Eustochium—not, however, [Col. 0247C] in the church situated in the valley below. It is worthwhile to give this author’s text from the recent edition inserted into the *Sacred Geography* of Nicolas Sanson, geographer to the Most Christian King, p. 184.

**13.** Bocardus, therefore, or Bruchardus of Strasbourg, of the sacred Order of Preachers, who lived for some time in Palestine and carefully described toward the end of the thirteenth century what he had seen, describes the cave of the Nativity and the Lord’s manger as follows:

> “At the eastern extremity, beneath a certain cliff that stood beside the city wall of Bethlehem, there was, according to the custom of that country, a place used as a stable. It had a manger cut into the rock, where the Savior of the world was born of the Virgin and laid down, since there was no more suitable place in the lodging than the manger in which the Creator and Redeemer of the world might be placed (Luke 2:7). Today a most noble chapel has been built there, paved with marble and raised upon marble columns, so that scarcely any sacred place more beautiful than this can now be found. The Sultan even attempted to carry away from it the columns and other marble facing with which the walls shine; but, when a serpent suddenly appeared and struck terror, he was compelled to abandon the plan he had undertaken. Near this church, too, certain remains of a monastery may be seen, in which the bed and tomb of Saint Jerome are shown to pilgrims, and so also the tombs of Paula and Eustochium, not far from this church.”

Finally, Marinus Sanutus Torsellus, in the book that he himself presented to the Supreme Pontiff in the year of Christ 1321 under the title *The Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross*, left us the following account of the Bethlehem cave of the Nativity in Part XIV, Book III, chapter 11:

> “On the eastern side there is a cave in the rock beside the city wall. It appears, according to the custom of that country, to have been a place used as a stable, with a manger cut out, as it is customary there to make mangers. With what praises shall I exalt this cave, where Christ was born [Col. 0248A] of the Virgin, and so forth? Note also that beside the aforementioned rock, in which Christ was born, there is another cave, larger than the first and only four feet distant from it. Beneath it was the manger in which that sweetest child, immediately after birth and wrapped in cloths, was laid beside the ox and the ass. It appears that the two caves were originally one continuous cave, divided only by a constructed doorway and by the ascent through which one goes up from the chapel to the choir.

> “The hay of the manger was brought to Rome by Queen Helena and decently preserved in the church of Saint Mary Major. Jerome was buried not far from the manger. One descends from the church to the chapel of that sweetest Nativity by ten steps. The chapel is entirely decorated within in mosaic work, paved with marble, and constructed at very great expense. Mass may be celebrated above the place where the blessed Virgin gave birth, upon a marble slab located there. A portion of bare stone can also be seen where Christ was born. Likewise, a part of the manger in which he lay has been left uncovered.”

These places are visited with the greatest devotion and reverence [Col. 0248B]. Scarcely any more beautiful church, or one equally worthy of devotion, can be found in the world. It contains extremely noble marble columns arranged in four rows, remarkable also for their astonishing size. Moreover, the nave of the church, from the columns above to the beams, is made of the most beautiful and distinguished mosaic work. All the histories from the creation of the world to the coming and judgment of Christ are depicted there, and so forth.

In this church of Saint Mary of Bethlehem, on the wall to the left, there is also the place where the Lord’s umbilical cord and circumcision were placed; on the right side of the choir, toward the south, is the place where the Holy Innocents were buried, and an altar has been constructed there. A certain Sultan ordered the precious panels and columns of this venerable church to be carried away for the construction of a palace for himself in Babylon, and so forth. “Here he recounts that he was prevented from carrying them away by a prodigy sent to him from heaven.” He then adds:

> “The Saracens indeed venerate all the churches of the blessed and glorious Virgin, but this one especially” [Col. 0248C].

After a short interval he continues:

> “At the northern exit of this church there is a cloister of monks, reached by ascending several steps. In a certain crypt a cell is shown in which blessed Jerome afflicted himself with penance and labored greatly in the translation and exposition of Sacred Scripture. His bed is also shown, as are the workshops of the cloister over which he presided. Almost a stone’s throw from the aforementioned church, toward the east, is the church of Saint Paula and her daughter Eustochium, where they performed penance. Their tombs are shown there as well.”

I have thought it appropriate to present together the testimonies quoted thus far, from writers succeeding one another from the seventh to the fourteenth century in their descriptions of the Bethlehem sanctuary and its surroundings, so that it may be clear what is to be understood by the name “the Lord’s manger” and by the relics of that same manger transferred to the Liberian church together with the body of blessed Jerome. Once these matters have been defined and [Col. 0248D] confirmed by the consistent testimony of so many centuries, both the reason and the time of the translation can no longer remain obscure.

According to Arculphus and Adamnanus, Bede, and indeed blessed Jerome himself, the Lord’s manger is that innermost part of the cave of the Nativity—or of the Bethlehem recess—that is, the interior and narrower portion of the sacred cave (which Jerome therefore called “a small opening in the earth”), assigned as a stable for animals, in which the most holy Virgin laid down the Son of God whom she had borne. According to Sanutus’s measurement, this recess, or manger, was separated by only four feet from the more spacious area of the cave, which they call the cave of the Nativity.

In that narrow recess of the manger, deliberately cut into the rock according to the custom of the region, as the writers mentioned above observe, an altar was erected in such a way that the altar table would not obstruct the entire view of the rock where Christ was born. Moreover, a portion of the rock where he was born was intentionally left uncovered, [Col. 0249A] as was a portion of the manger in which the Savior of the world was laid.

**14.** Since this is the understanding of the Lord’s manger consistently handed down by writers from Jerome’s age to our own, it follows that, when the relics of the Lord’s manger are said to have been transferred, this must mean some portion of that rock which had formerly constituted the Lord’s manger in the recess of the cave: a portion cut out from there and carried away. The name “Christ’s manger” therefore applies to it most appropriately, since it was a part of the whole that had previously been formed there together with the other portions left behind.

For the portions remaining there and separated from the portion extracted, and for that portion of the rock which was left bare so that devout worshipers might see it, the name “manger” is used just as it is for those portions of the same rock torn away and carried elsewhere.

When, therefore, the name “Saint Mary at the Manger” was first heard in the Liberian Basilica under Pope Theodore, the nature of the object indicated by that name requires us to understand that this august title had been given to the sanctuary because of the venerable portion of rock brought there, where the Savior, born of the Virgin Mother, had been laid.

**15.** Where the segments of the Lord’s manger cut from Bethlehem were placed is not obscure. Dominico Fontana, architect to Pope Sixtus V, to whom the pontiff entrusted the task of transferring the old sanctuary into the part of the basilica enlarged by him through the magnificent construction of the Sistine Chapel, expressly reported that they had been placed in a leaden chest beneath the altar table, just as they had formerly been arranged.

In the books he published concerning the structures he completed at the command of Sixtus, where he discusses the chapel of the most holy manger, he reports the following on p. 40:

> “The place where this chapel was to be installed was excavated underground for greater devotion. Above it an altar of fine marble was constructed, with steps around it, covering the entire chapel. Upon that altar His Holiness celebrates the Mass of the night and, on the day of the Nativity, celebrates pontifically with all the cardinals and the court. Directly below it another altar has been placed in the middle of the ancient chapel. Within it are the most holy relics of the manger, placed in a leaden chest, and every priest may celebrate upon it.”

This chest and the relics of the Lord’s manger enclosed in it were known to the architect, who states that the altar had been removed from its former position: “That altar, which had formerly stood sideways, was removed from its previous location and is now turned to face the said chapel.”

When the altar was therefore removed from its former position and transferred to the new one, which was seventy palms distant from the place it had previously occupied—as the same architect states on the page cited—the leaden chest enclosed beneath the altar table was examined according to custom. It contained the relics of the Lord’s manger, brought here from the Bethlehem cave together with the sacred body of blessed Jerome, when Palestine had fallen as plunder to the Saracens; when Umar had converted the site of the Jerusalem Temple into a building of Muslim superstition; and when he had removed [Col. 0249D] the sacred crosses from the Mount of Olives.

There was just cause to fear that, under the influence of the same advisers whose counsel he had obeyed in removing the standard of our religion from that place, he might also be driven to overthrow the memorials of the Bethlehem cave and block its sacred entrances. Thus the enemies of our faith who urged such acts might wish to renew the examples witnessed and lamented under Julian: insults against the tombs of the saints and the burning of their remains, so that the sacred ashes might be scattered.

**16.** The reason why the body of blessed Jerome should be counted among the last of the sacred relics that, as the ancient books testify, were removed from Palestine and taken to a safer place becomes clear from the same writers. These men traveled there out of pious devotion and committed to writing the fact that a particular reverence for this Bethlehem church of the Virgin Mother of God had taken root in the minds of the Saracens. The church, dedicated to the Mother of God, stands over the sacred manger, just as the chapel of Sixtus V in the Liberian Basilica stands over the ancient chapel of the manger, transferred to the center of that same basilica.

I have already quoted the words of Marinus Sanutus, who expressly writes:

> “The Saracens venerate all the churches of the blessed and glorious Virgin, but this one especially” (Saint Mary of Bethlehem).

Both he and other descriptions of the holy places of Palestine record this not only of the Saracens of their own age but also of those who preceded them. They relate that the Sultan refrained from removing the columns and marbles of that church at the site of the Lord’s Nativity, magnificently constructed by Helena, the mother of Constantine Augustus, when he was contemplating transferring those ornaments to Babylon.

Once this disposition and restraint, which remained in the minds of the Saracens, had been observed—their willingness to spare churches dedicated to the Mother of God, and especially this Bethlehem church—it inspired such confidence in the minds of our Christians that they considered the sacred relics preserved in that same church [Col. 0250B] sufficiently safe from injury. Among these, the body of blessed Jerome was especially counted, so long as the decrees of the prince Umar refrained from destroying the crosses.

Moreover, the ancient codices of the archives, brought forward by Paolo de Angelis in Book IV, chapter 4 of his description of the Liberian Basilica, and supported by Peter de Natalibus, whom Baronius follows in his notes to the Martyrology, relate that the faithful did not dare remove the relics of that holy doctor from there until a monk, after being warned and rebuked three times in a vision for his disobedience, was divinely commanded to take them from the tomb and transfer them to Rome.

Whether, therefore, by the vision seen by the monk the Lord intended to signify that the body of the holy doctor ought to be transferred in those times when fear of the powerful barbarians had persuaded the Emperor Heraclius to withdraw the sacred pledges from their hands—even though the protection of the Bethlehem chapel might have made the Saracens more lenient toward the ornaments placed in that asylum—or whether Pope Theodore, a fellow countryman of the Palestinians, acted through providence to safeguard such great relics, taking the opportunity to arrange through Stephen of Dora, the vicar he had appointed, those matters which the blessed patriarch Sophronius had entrusted to him to carry to the Roman See before his death [Col. 0250C]—all these circumstances prove that the bones of the holy doctor did not remain much longer in the Bethlehem sanctuary of Palestine after nearly all the relics of the saints resting in that province had been carried away in that same period either to Constantinople or to the city of Rome.

They also confirm the zeal of Pope Theodore and his successors in restoring the worship and veneration owed, for the sake of Christ the Lord, to the manger itself through the transfer of a portion cut from that manger and carried to the Liberian Basilica together with the body of Saint Jerome. Thus, by means of the Roman pontiffs, who would offer sacrifice to God over that same manger brought to Rome on the night and day of the Lord’s Nativity, whatever the blessed Sophronius had wished to accomplish in the customary manner in that sanctuary was fulfilled, when the barbarians had prevented him from doing so there—as we saw from the homily of his cited above. This was especially appropriate since they perceived that Saracen rule had already spread so far over all the empires of the East that the captivity of Palestine was destined to be extremely long.
