**17.** Moved by this zeal, Pope Theodore—devoted no less to the piety of Sophronius than to that of his episcopal father and to the pious devotion with which his native city of Jerusalem had been formed toward the Lord’s manger and the relics of blessed Jerome deposited there, which had not yet been removed from Saracen captivity, although the region of Palestine had been almost stripped of all the other sacred relics previously preserved outside the Bethlehem asylum—resolved to designate a chapel in the Liberian Basilica in which worship might be offered to such pledges of our salvation, plainly resembling the Bethlehem chapel.

In the Roman sanctuary he wished to restore whatever had been removed from the devotion of the faithful in Palestine, whose free access to the cave consecrated by so many mysteries had been obstructed by the Saracen invasions.

**18.** Under the auspices, therefore, of the piety and zeal of Pope Theodore, the name “Saint Mary at the Manger” began to be heard in Rome, in the Liberian church. The relics of the rock where Christ had been laid by his Virgin Mother were brought here together with Jerome, that faithful worshiper of the cave. They were placed beneath the altar table, so that the divine sacrifice might be celebrated there, as had been customary in the Bethlehem chapel. The place was adorned with mosaic work, as in Palestine.

Gifts, ornaments, and the name itself recalled the birthplace of Christ, bestowed upon the Roman city—or rather, to use Jerome’s words, Rome happily transformed into an inn for Christ and Mary.

The colony of Christ’s Nativity, if one may so call it, successfully transferred under Theodore from the portion of the manger, received remarkable growth from his successors. Pope Saint Martin, the first after him, began at this manger the martyrdom that he was to complete elsewhere. For it is read that, when he was destined to death by the exarch Olympius because of his courageous defense of the Catholic faith, plots were laid against him while he was celebrating the solemn Mass in this church of Saint Mary at the Manger. Thus this new Palestine found, in a certain sense, its own Stephen in Rome.

I do not, however, derive Martin’s confession here from an imitation of the Bethlehem chapel and its worship. I infer it from the solemn Masses immediately instituted and frequently celebrated here as soon as the name and relics of the Lord’s manger had been introduced.

The same was observed under Martin’s successor, Pope Eugenius, when the zeal of the clergy and people for religion shone forth. As a condition and token of the Catholic faith required of those who came to perform divine offices in this basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger, anyone who did not produce that token of faith in its entirety was entirely excluded.

The principal worship of solemn Masses established there at the first translation of the sacred pledges under Theodore, Martin, and Eugenius according to the model of the Bethlehem sanctuary was followed by the addition of other decorations bestowed upon these relics by succeeding pontiffs. In them there is always evident a particular effort to attest the genuine authority of the Bethlehem manger, a substantial part of which had been preserved here.

As in the age of Chrysostom that manger was enclosed and preserved with gold and silver so that the mystical gifts of the kings might be revealed by sight alone, so throughout the ages the pontiffs vied in embellishing this one with every kind of precious metal. The same zeal of priesthood and empire was thereby displayed: every age saw them submitting their insignia to the humble host of the manger in which the Lord was born, until the magnificence and devotion of Sixtus V omitted almost nothing that could complete the ornament and declaration of its dignity.

The comparison may now appear less significant: in the august basilica, in both places, the first fruits of royal gold are offered—there by the Magi of the East, here by the Indies of the West—and [are offered] to the King, the Man, and God; in both places the chapel of the Lord’s manger is clothed with columns, mosaics, and choice marble facing—there by Constantine, here by Sixtus; and the memory of the Virgin Mother is honored there by Helena and here by Paul.

There, the altars shine with the golden and silver gifts of Eudoxia and Placidia; here, with those of the bishops of the Apostolic See, Leo III (377, 379, 401, 409) and Paschal I (450, 451). Their piety and magnificence have been imitated by the Spanish king Philip IV and Queen Catherine, and by the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, James Colonna and Peter Ottoboni, vice-chancellor and archpriest. In this very jubilee year in which I write, 1725, solid silver skillfully represents the sacred histories and clothes on every side the principal altar, upon which the sacred cradles of Christ the Lord’s infancy—made precious by his touch—are displayed for the veneration of the faithful.

Leaving aside these later matters and pursuing only what the pontiffs nearest to Theodore contributed to the worship of the sacred pledges during the waning seventh century, when the aforementioned name was introduced together with the relics of the Lord’s manger into our basilica, it is sufficient to mention the more than one thousand solidi contributed by Agatho for furnishing the lights [Col. 0252A] (146), when the influx of the crowds attending vigils for the Lord’s Nativity was greatest after those Bethlehem relics had been deposited here.

One should also mention the litanies instituted by Sergius at Saint Mary at the Manger for the four solemn feasts of the same Mother of God—the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Dormition, and the Presentation (§ 164)—as well as the monasteries and hospice added by Gregory II (§ 178), so that the basilica might resound day and night with divine praises, having in a certain sense become heir to the treasures of Jerusalem and Bethlehem’s piety.

**19.** The plan of the discussion requires that the memories of the sacred cradles, likewise transferred from there to our basilica, be joined to the Lord’s manger. To condense what would otherwise require a more extended treatment, I shall have two tasks. First, it is necessary to indicate how they were preserved in Palestine before they came to us. The second task [Col. 0252B] will be to investigate their translation.

**20.** To avoid having to pursue individually the history of the principal relics preserved in Palestine before the invasions of the Persians and Saracens, it will be sufficient to observe generally that, among the sacred relics relating to the mysteries of our redemption and to the principal deeds of Christ the Lord and his saints, two categories can be distinguished.

The first consists of bodies or objects that are immovable or difficult to remove; the second consists of those that could easily be moved from one place and carried elsewhere.

To the first category belong, I would say, Mount Tabor, Zion, the Mount of Olives, and Calvary; and the caves consecrated to the mysteries of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection. Objects that are difficult to move and transport—such as houses, tombs, and similar structures made venerable by the deeds or burials of Christ, the Mother of God, the apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and other saints—may likewise be assigned for the most part to this category.

The second category consists of relics that can easily be transported [Col. 0252C]: the actual instruments of the events, which human beings carry in their hands—for example, the cradles and infant clothing of Christ the Lord; his garments, cross, crown of thorns, lance, and similar objects; as well as the garments of the Mother of God, Peter’s chains, the episcopal chair of the apostle James preserved among the people of Jerusalem, or that of the Evangelist Mark preserved among the Alexandrians, and other such things.

The bones of the saints are also included in this category, whether deposited in their tombs or preserved in altars. There is no difficulty in carrying them away once the repositories in which they are kept have been opened.

**21–22.** I observe, therefore, that it had become customary at Jerusalem and in the churches of its patriarchate, from the time when the public worship of our religion began to be practiced there in the peace of the Church under Constantine, for magnificent sacred buildings to be erected in the very places consecrated by the celebration of our mysteries, where the immovable relics of the first category were situated.

These buildings enclosed within their walls both those same venerable and immovable relics and the memorials of the deeds of the Lord [Col. 0252D] and his saints, so that God might be honored there with the greatest solemnity of divine sacrifice, where he appeared to have chosen a seat from which to exercise his mercy toward humanity.

The relics of the second category—that is, those capable of being transported and pertaining to the same deeds, which were specifically to be commemorated within the churches designated for that purpose—were hung in and preserved in reliquaries and small compartments of those same sacred buildings.

We read in Eusebius that blessed Helena, the mother of Constantine, was asked by her son Augustus to go to Jerusalem in search of the Lord’s cross and the other instruments of our salvation, which the enemies of the faith had buried in the earth. By God’s gift she brought to light relics of both categories.

After the caves of the Lord’s Nativity, tomb, and Resurrection had been discovered and properly cleansed of the sacrilegious profanation of Hadrian and the other rulers and persecutors who had erected pagan idols over them so that the faithful would not visit them in the future, basilicas of Christian worship were founded through the zeal of that same empress. These basilicas contained within themselves those immovable sanctuaries.

She left some of the movable relics at those churches to be preserved there, as we said earlier, and carried others with her to her son Constantine, both to enrich the basilicas and sanctuaries that he had constructed in Rome and to enrich those in other principal cities of the Roman Empire.

Most of the relics that she left in Palestine are therefore found to have been enclosed within the sacred walls of the churches mentioned above, or adorned with precious reliquaries deposited in those churches, and preserved there during the fourth and fifth centuries.

**23.** In the Basilica of the Resurrection, where the cave and tomb of our Redeemer can still be visited unmoved, Bishop Arculphus relates that around the middle of the seventh century linens were suspended opposite the tomb. Beneath them was another altar cut from half of the stone that had been rolled to the entrance of the Lord’s monument at his burial.

Adamnanus, a writer of that same century, testifies that Arculphus, who had inspected these things with his own eyes, reported this to him (no. 4).

Between the church of Golgotha, where the Lord’s cross had been fixed, and the nearby basilica also named the Basilica of the Martyrdom by its founder Constantine, three distinguished instruments of the Lord’s Passion were preserved in Arculphus’s time. Adamnanus writes this in his account, no. 8.

The first was a silver cup with handles on both sides, which, after blessing it, the Lord is said to have used at the supper to give the sacrament of his blood to the apostles and to dine with them after the Resurrection. A sponge was preserved in it, which, filled with vinegar, a soldier had offered to the thirsty Lord on the cross.

In the portico of the same Constantinian church, Arculphus reported seeing “the lance of the soldier with which he himself had pierced the Lord’s side as he hung upon the cross.” He describes it as having been preserved in this manner:

> “This same lance is kept in the portico of Constantine’s basilica, enclosed in a wooden cross. Its shaft has been cut into two parts, and the whole church of Jerusalem likewise kisses and venerates it frequently.”

He then adds the following concerning the veil of the sweat-cloth:

> “We have also learned from the account of holy Arculphus, who saw it with his own eyes, concerning that most sacred sweat-cloth which had been placed in the tomb over his head. He further reports that it was preserved in a chest of the church, wrapped in another linen cloth, whose length he gives as eight feet.”

Arculphus also saw another, larger linen cloth in the same city of Jerusalem. It was said to have been woven by holy Mary, and for that reason the entire people venerated it with great reverence in the church (no. 11).

But blessed Paulinus may serve as a summary of all these things. In Letter 34 he lists what, in his own age—namely, the fourth century of Christ—was displayed in Palestine:

> “The manger of the one who was born, the river of the one who was baptized, the garden of the one who prayed, the courtyard of the one who was judged, the column of the one who was scourged, the thorns of the one who was crowned, the wood of the one who was suspended, the stone of the one who was buried, the place of the one who was raised, and the memorial of the one who was taken up.”

See Gretser, *On the Cross*, Book I, chapter 95.

**[Col. 0253D] 24.** We therefore know that so many immovable and movable relics were preserved until the time when the Saracens entered Palestine shortly before the middle of the seventh century. Thus, in the single Basilica of the Resurrection and in the nearby churches of the Passion and the Tomb at Jerusalem, all these objects were displayed: the linens of the tomb and the sweat-cloth; the stone that had closed the entrance, turned into an altar table; the cup of the Lord’s Supper; the sponge offered to the thirsty Lord; the lance thrust into the side of the dead man; and, in addition, a portion of the Lord’s cross recovered from the Persians.

To these we must add a portion of the crown of thorns, seen by the monk Bernard in the year 870, hanging in the church on Mount Zion, where a column supporting the portico and stained with Christ’s blood was also shown to Paula, according to Jerome.

In the Bethlehem church there was likewise no lesser abundance of movable sacred pledges, especially during the fourth and fifth centuries, relating to the mystery and events of the Lord’s Nativity.

The cradles, distinct from the cave of the Nativity but preserved there, seem to be indicated by the letter of blessed Jerome to the deacon Sabinianus. Rebuking the wicked desires expressed by him in that sanctuary, Jerome uses these words:

> “That angel, the doorkeeper of Mary’s chamber, guardian of the Lord’s cradles, and bearer of the infant Christ, before whom you were doing such things—he himself exposed you.”

The Church certainly distinguishes the cradles from the manger. Just as, from the Gospel, it knows that the Lord, born of the Virgin Mother on that same night, was laid in the manger, so, with Leo the Great, it shortly afterward recites that he was adored by the Magi in the cradles.

The skilled craftsman and nourisher, blessed Joseph, designated together with the angels as the bearer of Christ, surely did not fail to prepare those cradles, having discovered that there was no room for him in the lodging and realizing that he would soon have to move to another dwelling.

Thus the Lord whom the shepherds had received as the infant whom they were to seek during the night, wrapped in cloths and lying in the manger, was worshiped by the Magi several days later in the cradles.

The Fathers and Christian poets also sing of the distinction in carefully chosen language: when Christ was born and adored by the shepherds, they mention only the manger; when he was adored by the Magi, they mention both the manger and the cradles.

Ambrose, in the hymn for the day of the Lord’s Nativity:

> “Your manger now shines forth,  
> and the night breathes a new light.”

And Juvencus the presbyter, Book II, verse 168:

> “This sign I shall proclaim: the child whom you wish to see  
> may now be seen filling the mangers with his slender voice.”

And verse 176:

> “The shepherds hasten and see the child lying  
> in the lap of the manger.”

And Sedulius the presbyter, in his hymn concerning Christ:

> “He endured lying upon hay;  
> he did not shrink from the manger.”

And Venantius Fortunatus, Book II, hymn 1:

> “He endured being placed in a manger;  
> beneath his mother he put on the swaddling cloths.”

And Prudentius, in the *Enchiridion*, Letter 28:

> “The manger was a cradle for the one who lay there.”

But when they speak of the one adored by the Magi and sought by Herod for death, they mention the cradles together with Prudentius in the hymn for the Epiphany, verse 100:

> “Soldier, go, seize the sword;  
> stain the cradles with blood.”

Or, if they mention the manger, they do not omit the cradle and cradles already prepared for Christ and guarded by his nourisher and bearer, the spouse of the Virgin Mother, where the Chaldeans worshiped him:

> “O holy cradles of your manger,  
> eternal King,  
> entrusted as sacred through the ages  
> even to peoples who cannot speak!

> “The dumb cattle adore these things,  
> that is, the unlearned crowd;  
> the mindless race adores them,  
> whose power lies in feeding,

> “But with faithful spirit  
> let pagan people and the four-footed creature  
> come together at the mangers,  
> and let what was brute acquire understanding.”

For what Prudentius asserts—that these holy cradles of the manger are sacred to peoples throughout the ages—should not be taken as a poetic statement but as a historical one.

We saw that, according to Jerome, an angel was assigned both to the manger and to the cradles as Christ’s bearer, whether he means the angel who protected the sacred cave or Joseph, guardian and spouse of the Virgin and bearer of Christ in his infancy.

I therefore indicate the cradles together with Jerome all the more readily, and not merely the “cradle,” so that it may be fully understood that Prudentius’s prayer concerned both kinds of infant furnishings and the venerable relics of Christ’s infancy: that they should be held sacred by peoples throughout every age.

**25.** I know that among the Latins *cunae* are sometimes distinguished from *cunabula*: *cunae* properly being movable beds, generally resting on swinging supports, for moving infants back and forth so that they may more easily surrender to sleep; while *cunabula*, or *incunabula*, are the ties and swaddling bands with which infants placed in cradles are bound, and by which cloths are fastened around their little bodies.

This is inferred from Plautus, *Truculentus*, verse 13:

> “There is need of swaddling bands, cushions, cradles, and cradle-bands.”

And in *Amphitruo* I, 52:

> “Nor could anyone bind him in the cradle-bands.”

The author of the *Lexicon of Antiquity*, who collected these points learnedly, observes that Plautus would have repeated himself ineptly if *cunabula* meant swaddling bands. Accordingly, together with Ferrarius, *Select Readings* 1120, he concludes:

> “It is therefore credible that *cunabula* were swaddling bands, straps, or ties by which infants wrapped in swaddling cloths were bound in cradles, as is done today, so that they would not fall out.”

This is indeed credible; but it is established and certain [Col. 0255B] that the word *cunabula* was understood to mean both those swaddling bands, cloths, and straps, and the cradles themselves.

To pass over numerous passages of ancient writers that support this, and to give a selection from Claudian alone—namely, in the *Consulship of Probinus and Olybrius*, verse 144; in the third *Consulship of Honorius*, verse 17; in the fourth *Consulship of the same*, verse 21; and in *The Marriage of Honorius and Maria*, verse  — 

> “Now the welcome changes have returned; he weighs the cradles,”

—which the interpreter Pyrrhus, in the edition *ad usum Delphini*, explains as “he repays her for the cradles and his upbringing”—

to pass over, I say, these authorities and many similar ones, I certainly cannot omit the clear definition of Isidore, who in the *Etymologies* teaches not only the force of the word *cunabula* but also its etymology.

“*Cunabula*,” he says, “are beds in which infants were accustomed to lie. They are so called because they were used for childbirth, as though *cynabula*”; for among the Greeks **κύειν** (*kyein*) means “to give birth.”

Isidore took both points from Servius’s commentaries on Virgil, *Eclogue* IV, verse 23:

“The cradles themselves will pour forth gentle flowers for you.” On this Servius writes as follows: “Cradles: little beds in which infants customarily lie, or places where they are born; for among the Greeks κύειν means ‘to give birth.’”

It is therefore clear from the authorities cited that *cunabula* is used generically and indiscriminately for the whole equipment and furniture associated with childbirth and infancy—namely, for cradles, swaddling bands, cloths, straps, and fastenings employed to cherish infants, wrap them, bind them, and protect them while they sleep—although at times it can or must be understood specifically of cradles, and at other times of swaddling bands alone.

What occurred among the Latins in the usage of the word *cunabula* likewise occurred among the Greeks with the term σπάργανα (*spargana*), which corresponds exactly to both meanings of *cunabula*, according to the writer’s preference: namely, so that it may signify both the bands by which cloths are bound around the tender bodies of infants, as well as the straps and fastenings by which infants already wrapped and bound in those cloths are tied within the same cradles, lest they fall out; and also the cradles themselves, in which the infants, enclosed and fastened, are kept for their safety.

For this reason Screvelius, in the Latin-Greek Lexicon under the word *cunae*, correctly places alongside it, as synonyms, κόιτις and σπάργανον. Other Greek-Latin lexicons likewise explain that the Greek word σπάργανον corresponds to the two Latin words *fascia* and *cunabula*, as we read in the lexicon of Scapula and in others.

It must therefore be accepted that the Greek term σπάργανα corresponds to the Latin word *cunabula*, as we see in the sacred Council of Chalcedon, session two, Roman edition, p. 207, D. There, when Pope Leo’s letter to Flavian was publicly read, the Latin original expressed Leo as saying of the birth of Christ the Lord, “The infancy of the little child is displayed by the humility of the cradles”; this was rendered in Greek: καὶ ἡ μὲν νηπιότης τοῦ Βρέφους, διὰ τῆς τῶν σπαργάνων εὐτελείας ἐπιγιγνώσκεται—“and the infancy of the child is recognized through the lowliness of the swaddling bands.”

Indeed, interpreters of the sacred Scriptures in both languages confirm this meaning of the word when they translate the Hebrew expression in Job 38:9. That expression is formed from a root properly meaning “to wrap in swaddling bands,” with the pronoun “his” added; taken literally, it would yield, “his swaddling band.” Thus the verse would sound, in Hebrew idiom: “When I made the cloud its garment and darkness its swaddling band.” The Vulgate Latin version most correctly explains it: “When I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it, as though in the cloths of infancy, with darkness.” The Greek Septuagint renders it equally successfully: Ὀμίχλῃ δὲ αὐτὴν θαλάσσαν ἐσπαργάνωσα—“But with mist I swaddled it”—that is, “I wrapped it, namely the sea, as though in the swaddling bands (or cradles) of infancy.” Symmachus elegantly draws out the force of the metaphor from the circular constriction of infants by swaddling bands and cloths of infancy, and from the cradles or fastenings in which they are held within the circumference of their cradle. All these things are σπάργανα; hence the verb σπαργανόω, “I wrap in swaddling bands.” The likeness between infant swaddling bands and mists is remarkably apt: the mists encircle the circular surface of the Ocean on every side and embrace the enclosed body in the manner of a cradle. Symmachus, in the Vatican edition of Sixtus V, has: ὡς νεφέλῃ περιείλησα αὐτὴν—“I enclosed it as with a cloud,” that is, “I surrounded the sea with a cloud.”

Thus in Greek, σπάργανα, just as in Latin *cunabula*, means both the bands, cloths of infancy, straps, and fastenings, and the cradles themselves—or, if one prefers, the little beds—used to surround and cherish infants’ bodies, so that they may sleep more safely and be protected on every side from external blows and disturbances.

**26.** I have thought it necessary to dwell at somewhat greater length on the meaning of the various words by which these instruments of childbirth and infancy are designated in Greek and Latin, so that every ambiguity may be removed when one investigates in writers of either language what was done with such cradles and σπάργανα used both to receive the most sacred body of Christ at his Nativity and to prepare it for the adoration of the Magi in the cave at Bethlehem, and also to guard and cherish it elsewhere during the course of his infancy—namely, during the flight into Egypt and the return to Palestine—in accordance with the customary care of the Virgin Mother and of her undefiled spouse, the blessed Joseph, the foster-father of Christ. They prepared these things with no less skill than was appropriate to the care of the infant Savior, and preserved them diligently after he had passed beyond the cradle and advanced in age and wisdom before God and men.

For if the care of the first believers was so great in preserving at Jerusalem the chains of the Apostle Peter, later transferred by Eudoxia to Old and New Rome after the passage of many centuries, and in preserving the chair of James until the age of Eusebius—as he himself writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 19—then surely the most prudent Virgin and Seat of Wisdom understood much more keenly the value of such furnishings, already rendered most sacred by divine contact with Christ and destined to be transmitted with honor to future ages, as Prudentius sings:

> O holy cradles  
> Of your manger,  
> Eternal King,  
> Sacred among the peoples throughout the ages;

and entrusted, as Jerome testifies, to the guardianship of angels in Christian churches, as the holy doctor exclaims against the sacrilegious Sabinianus.

**27.** That these same cradles and σπάργανα were in fact preserved and guarded among the successors of the Apostle James in the Jerusalem see—under whose authority lay the adjacent church and town of Bethlehem, six miles away, together with the Lord’s manger—is established by Nicephorus’ history. Nicephorus, in book XIV, chapter 2, relates that the Empress Eudocia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, journeyed to Jerusalem and sent to Constantinople three sacred gifts collected there. She wished them to be guarded as a heavenly treasure in the celebrated church of the Holy Virgin Mary, called τῶν ὀδηγῶν, “of the Guides,” magnificently built by the Empress Pulcheria, sister and guardian of Theodosius.

Those three gifts were as follows:

1. An image of the Mother of God, painted, he says, by the Apostle Luke; he also discusses it in book XV, chapter 14.

2. A sacred distaff, namely, one used by the Mother of God in domestic weaving to prepare cloth and garments for her divine Son, and for herself and her spouse.

3. The swaddling bands of the Savior himself. Thus the Latin translator, the Rev. Fr. Fronto Ducaeus, renders what the Greek historian calls σπάργανα.

Whether one calls these relics swaddling bands, cloths of infancy, and fastenings; or cradles; or even cradles in the narrower sense, it amounts to the same thing. For from this testimony we establish that, toward the end of the fifth Christian century, the furnishings associated with the birth and infancy of our Savior were preserved in the Jerusalem episcopate, and that Eudocia transferred part of them from there to Constantinople.

From whom, however, these gifts had originally been received may be learned from the same historian, when he again discusses Pulcheria’s zeal in magnificently constructing sacred buildings, in book XV, chapter 14. He teaches that the Empress Pulcheria asked Juvenal, archbishop of Jerusalem, and the bishops of Palestine who had gone to Chalcedon for the celebration of the ecumenical council, to give her the body of the Virgin Mother of God, which she had heard was deposited at Jerusalem.

Juvenal replied that the most sacred body had indeed been carried away and deposited near Jerusalem at Gethsemane, amid both angelic and apostolic hymnody; but that, when the tomb was opened on the third day, only the burial bands were found, emitting an extraordinarily sweet and heavenly fragrance. The body, however, had been received into heaven by divine power and endowed with immortality before the general resurrection:

> “The rulers themselves asked him—Juvenal the patriarch—to send them her holy tomb (σόρος), together with the sacred garments (ἀμφία), properly sealed by him. Juvenal accordingly sent it, and they consecrated and deposited it with devout hands in the greatest church they had built at Blachernae, near the sacred and divine altar.”

**28.** It is therefore established from the Greek historians that in the fifth Christian century the σπάργανα of the infancy of Christ the Lord were preserved at Jerusalem—by which term we understand the whole equipment associated with childbirth and infancy—as well as garments, linens, and the tomb in which the body of the Mother of God had lain for three days, together with many other sacred relics of which we are speaking.

It is also established that these sacred pledges were customarily guarded by the patriarch of Jerusalem, and that parts of them were sometimes distributed to emperors who requested them, properly secured with the same seal, as treasures. Relics were also divided among bishops who came to Jerusalem for prayer, as is known from sermon 17 of Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia. His works were recently published under the auspices of the most eminent prince, Cardinal Giovanni Francesco Barbarigo, enlarged by the learned notes of the distinguished Paul Galleard, canon of Brescia.

The holy bishop reports that, on his journey to Jerusalem, he was also given relics by sacred virgins, sisters of Basil the Great. These relics had once been entrusted to them by Basil himself:

> “They prayed to God that so precious a possession might pass to such heirs as would cultivate it with equal faith and diligence, and who would prove both successors to and enlargers of their zeal and veneration.”

The Emperor Justin also distributed to the blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, who was returning from the sacred places of Palestine and had asked only for relics of the saints, some thorns from the crown of our Lord Jesus Christ and relics of the Holy Innocents from among those which the emperors possessed after they had been transferred from Jerusalem, as Aimo reports in book III, chapter 18 of his *History of the Franks*.

Thus it is confirmed that these gifts, entrusted by the bishops of the Jerusalem Church to the greatest rulers and carefully guarded by the holiest bishops in the Eastern Church, gradually began to be subdivided, with the precaution that so precious a possession should pass to heirs who would preserve and advance its veneration with equal diligence.

Not to be excessive in appending a catalogue of the other relics preserved at Jerusalem during that and many succeeding centuries, it is enough to indicate the relics belonging to the cradles of Christ, with which we are here specifically concerned—namely, the furnishings of his birth and infancy. It is established that the portion acquired by Eudocia at Jerusalem, transferred by her to Constantinople, and there deposited in sacred buildings dedicated to God under the name of the Mother of God, those of the Guides and of Blachernae, was preserved there until the twelfth century and the beginning of the thirteenth. For the Emperor Baldwin sent to Philip Augustus, king of France, among other sacred gifts, a relic of the linen in which Christ the Lord had been wrapped in the manger, as Rigord relates in Spondanus under the year 1200, no. 1, and as Joannes Ferrandus notes in *Investigation of Relics*, book I, chapter 1, p. 9.

**29.** Since the bishops of Jerusalem, beginning in the age of the Empress Eudocia, had been exceedingly generous in handing over a large portion of such sacred pledges to her, which she then transferred to enrich the churches of the imperial city of Constantinople; and since they did not cease distributing the portions of the same sacred furnishings that remained with them whenever venerable bishops arrived, whether on the occasion of some council or because they had traveled to Palestine on a sacred pilgrimage; and since they repeatedly consoled the devotion of pious rulers and royal women who came there by again dividing their diminishing supply of such precious bundles—it should by no means seem surprising that, when the Saracen invasion occurred toward the end of the seventh century, not very much remained among the portable sacred relics that could easily be transferred.

Thus, by about the year 640, almost the last items of this kind to be removed were thought to be those associated with the virginal childbirth of the Mother of God, apart from the stones to be cut from the cave at Bethlehem belonging to the Lord’s manger, portions of the cradles and *cunabula*, and other sacred relics of the same church at Bethlehem. Of these, the only object still available to be transported westward with them was the body of Saint Jerome.

For rulers had enriched not only the kingdoms of the Eastern Empire with sacred relics of Palestine received from the bishops of Jerusalem; they had also at times enriched Western churches with such gifts. From the archives of my own homeland—Verona, that is—from which, one hundred and fifty years ago, the learned and most devout Cardinal Augustine Valerius, then its bishop, compiled a sufficiently extensive catalogue, I could produce illustrious examples by enumerating the many relics brought there from Palestine, especially to the church of Saint Stephen, formerly the cathedral. There, among other things, are preserved a portion of the Lord’s cross, relics from the hair of the Virgin Mother of God, relics from the body of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and the bodies of four of the Holy Innocents.

The arrival of these relics from Palestine is readily understood as having been due to Galla Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III and widow of Olybrius, the last emperor of the West. After her husband’s death she journeyed to Palestine, returned to Italy, lived at Verona, and, as Panvinius relates in *Veronese Antiquities*, book IV, chapter 19, followed by D. du Cange in *Byzantine Families*, p. 76, died there in the greatest holiness. The archives of that church likewise establish this, for she is honored as buried there; the Roman Martyrology also records her memory on 11 October. In his notes, Cardinal Baronius makes use of the testimony of Augustine Valerius.

What I observe in the sacred buildings of my homeland, others will recognize in many churches throughout Italy and indeed throughout the western regions of Europe: it is altogether evident that the historians are right in indicating that, around the time of the Saracen arrival in Palestine, the greater part of the portable treasury of sacred relics had already been distributed. God providentially arranged this so that so many venerable monuments would not be scattered by impious hands. The same providence also acted when disaster from those barbarians was already imminent, arranging for the final removal to Rome of the Lord’s manger and cradles, as well as the body of Blessed Jerome, to the Liberian basilica.

**30.** At that time, however, we know that the bishops of Palestine followed a different discipline in distributing relics from the one maintained among us. Such division was not so readily admitted here as among the Easterners, as is clear from the response of Gregory the Great to the Empress Constantina. This response is frequently cited by the leading writers on relics, collected by the often-mentioned Boldetti in *The Sacred Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs*, book II, chapter 2. They present the practice maintained at that time by the Roman Church in its frugal distribution of such sacred pledges.

Although Blessed Gregory seems in other letters to indicate that he himself distributed not only *brandea* and keys applied to the sacred ashes of Christ’s martyrs, but also certain small portions of bones, everyone nevertheless acknowledges how sparingly such gifts were distributed both by him and by his predecessors. God’s provident plan, that is, disposed the Eastern bishops toward distribution and the Western bishops toward restraint, so that the relics might be more easily carried away from places exposed to barbarian violence, while here they could be more safely guarded, where they were to be preserved for the future.

From this discipline of the Roman Church all Westerners certainly received the benefit that the most distinguished instruments of the mysteries of our redemption and the monuments of the saints, which confirm the constancy and glory of divine grace in his Church, were preserved for later generations.

**31.** As for the sacred cradles of Christ of which we are speaking, or the little bed of his infancy, preserved in the Liberian basilica: once each year we remove it from the marble compartment suitably placed above the top of the altar, beside the Pauline chapel and before the presbytery, and expose it for the veneration of the faithful. On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity we place it above the altar of the inner sacristy; at night, above the principal altar of the Sistine chapel, above the Lord’s manger; and on the day of the Nativity itself, above the papal and principal altar of the basilica, where the supreme pontiff Clement XI, while celebrating the sacred rites, delivered a homily to the people more than once according to ancient custom.

As I say, with regard to these cradles of the Lord’s infancy, enclosed in a silver case through the munificence of Philip IV, Catholic King of Spain, so that their material and form can easily be recognized through the crystals, we have learned from examining them that more than half of the sacred cradles has come down to us, and that they were collapsible, of the kind which several men returning from Palestine report that poor people there still use today.

In our case five boards can be seen, cut from ordinary fir. Their length is approximately four and a half Roman palms, and their width is nearly half a palm. Two of them have been deliberately pierced by a square opening near the outer part of their length, so that a crossbeam could be inserted through it to hold the entire little folding cradle firmly in its framework, as the accompanying figure demonstrates. By means of that figure we show that the complete body of the cradle could be assembled from these boards, with the additional pieces that are now missing. I readily think that they were enclosed in the leaden box found beneath the altar of the Lord’s manger by Sixtus V—a box seen by his architect Fontana, who mentions it in his book on that pontiff’s buildings, fol. 40.

The structure of the cradle is found to be as follows. Two boards, marked in the figure by the letters A B and C D, are to be erected. The first supports the infant’s head; the second is placed at the feet. For easier transport, both are made collapsible at the middle by means of iron straps or small hinges E F, such as everyone knows are commonly attached to ordinary chests in order to turn the lid.

These hinges are fixed transversely to a central crossbar H I, which passes through the middle of the boards A B and C D. The boards, or supports, are cut in this manner. From the center +, at a distance of one and a half palms, a circle is described passing through the points C H D I. It is divided in two by a saw cut along the horizontal diameter H + I, so that the two semicircles may be folded—namely, so that the upper semicircle + C may fall upon the lower one + D whenever necessary and remain suspended by the small hinges or straps E and F.

Along the diameter of the cut of the lower semicircle, the horizontal crossbar H I, which is never to be separated from it, is fastened externally with nails. Then both the upper and lower semicircles are suitably hollowed at S, Q, Z, and K, so that at K the nurse’s foot, moving back and forth, may depress and raise the sides of the cradle in alternation, thereby inducing sleep in the infant.

Another board, A B, similar to and parallel with the board C D cut in this manner, is erected at a distance A C, or B D, of approximately four palms above the horizontal plane B D, on which both must stand in order to support the cradle.

The body of the cradle is composed of seven small boards, each approximately four and a half palms long and three or four fingers wide. The two upper boards, H L and the parallel board to be placed at I, are made passable at both ends by means of a notch or square opening at H and L, to receive the end of the transverse crossbar H I. In that position they are held firmly by a wooden peg inserted at H, which may be removed as desired.

Another board of similar length, forming the bottom of the cradle, is used at M N as a transverse crossbar. It projects through a notch at M O, and likewise at N, and is secured by a wooden peg at O.

The body of the folding cradle may thus be understood to have been constructed with ease. For holding it more firmly, three iron rods may be fitted above it—P Q, A C, and R S—which can also support a canopy to temper the air for the infant in the customary manner. Let the boards T V and X Z be parallel to I H, with the corresponding boards Y and K on the other side, so that they may support the hay or bedding.

A framework of this kind can be very easily completed, dismantled, and restored. The cradle preserved in the Liberian basilica is understood to have been of this sort, if we carefully consider the five surviving small boards out of the seven that composed the semicylinder of the cradle: L H, T V, N M, K, and Y I—although perhaps five would have been sufficient. One of them, pierced at H, shows the place where the crossbar was inserted; the straps and small chains hanging from it indicate that it was fastened to the neighboring board T V.

Thus the only missing pieces are the perpendicular boards A B and C D. Either they were formerly given to the empresses Eudocia and Placidia and transferred to Constantinople together with part of the remaining furnishings of the cradles, or τῶν σπαργάνων, as we established above from the Greek historians under number 1; or else they were enclosed in the leaden box together with the stones cut from the grotto of the Lord’s manger. That box was discovered beneath the altar table by Sixtus V and restored there when the chapel was moved, under the direction of the architect Domenico Fontana, who described it in the cited book.

[Col. 0261]

**[Col. 0261A]** It is made highly probable that a cradle of this structure was prepared by the foster-father of Christ the Lord, the blessed Joseph, who was also a carpenter—namely, a collapsible cradle that could be carried during the return to Nazareth and even used during the journey into Egypt. This is suggested both by examination of the surviving boards and by the custom of the Eastern peoples, reported to us by trustworthy travelers, as well as by careful consideration of the need to conceal the infant’s flight, which had been entrusted to Joseph so that, through his care, the divine infant might be removed from Herod’s search and anger.

A folding little bed caused the least inconvenience and attracted the least attention from those encountered along the road. For if a carpenter carries boards bundled together, he gives the impression rather of a craftsman transporting nearby beams for some work than of someone undertaking a long journey to move away from persecutors with his wife and son.

Moreover, such a cradle could easily be made within an hour or two. I wished to test this by having boards prepared to the same measurements, in order to imitate the prototype of the sacred cradles. When the pious spouse of the Virgin was forced to descend into the stable because no place was available in the inn for the Virgin, who was about to give birth, and when he saw the infant after his birth placed in the manger, it is credible that he immediately seized some boards and constructed a portable cradle for the Son of God. In the poverty of such lodging, he could at least use the aid of his craft to protect the divine child from the harshness of winter.

But whether the holy patriarch constructed a portable and folding cradle in the cave at Bethlehem, or whether, as the Lord grew, he adapted the same cradle for the journey into Egypt or for the return to Palestine, these surviving pieces show more than half of the structure and form of the whole body of that cradle, now visible because of the discipline maintained by the Roman Church. This discipline did not readily permit the division of these primary pledges, rendered venerable by contact with Christ the Lord and the Virgin Mother. We would not possess this benefit if the Jerusalem bishops’ practice of dividing the same relics into smaller fragments over the ten centuries since they came to us had been brought here together with the cradles.

**32.** It is therefore entirely right that the custody of such relics and the discipline that resists their division should flourish among us, so that the treasury of the sacred cradles may be preserved for posterity with the same devotion with which our ancestors handed it down to us. Experience shows that the attentive faith of the faithful is stirred more vividly to recall the mystery celebrated in these objects when so large a portion is seen together, proving the united devotion of preceding centuries, joined with our own in carrying out the same religious acts.

In the same way, when those traveling to Palestine, or to the tombs and trophies of the apostles, or to the cemeteries of Christ’s martyrs, go there to pray and contemplate the memories of Christ’s servants, a certain sweet feeling arises—a feeling shared with them of faith, hope, and charity toward God. The letters of Jerome express this clearly enough: he invites the scion of the Gracchi [*Gracchorum*; OCR uncertain], Eustochium, Paula, and Marcella, to the Lord’s manger and the little village of Christ, and commends their common devotion with his contemporaries in frequenting the martyrs’ crypts on Sundays.

The pious sentiments of that blessed doctor of the Church are wonderfully answered by the exhortations of Clement XI of holy memory, who, twelve centuries after Jerome, addressed us during the solemn celebration of Mass in his patriarchal Liberian basilica in these words. Their most gentle sound will awaken in the hearts of his children an enduring imitation of the paternal meditation and devotion both of Clement himself and of his predecessors:

> “Let us rejoice, beloved, in our happiness. It has been granted to us in this most sacred temple, at this very altar at which we offer sacrifice, almost to see and venerate the sacred cradles of the Savior. Here the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father, reclining in the manger, appeared made in the likeness of human beings and found in human form. Here, amid the icy darkness of a winter night, the little child who was born for us and the son who was given to us grew stiff with cold. Here he was warmed by the alternating breaths of the animals, whose warm spirits blew their foul-smelling breath from their breasts. Here he was wrapped by his mother in cloths; here he was seen by the shepherds; here he was pointed out by the star; here he was adored by the Magi. Here the sharp grasses laid beneath his tender head prefigured the harsher thorns that would later crown his brow. Here the divine infant poured forth abundant tears, the first beginnings of the blood he would one day shed for our redemption. Here, received into virginal arms, the trembling child softened in the embraces of his most chaste mother the bonds of cruelty that he knew were being prepared for him by the traitor’s kiss.

> “But, as blessed Jerome says—once for a long time, while he lived, an inhabitant of the cave at Bethlehem, and now buried near the Bethlehem manger in this basilica—‘That manger in which the infant whimpered should be honored more by silence than by the poorest words.’”

(Clement XI, in his homily for the Lord’s Nativity, 1714.)

# FRANCIS BLANCHINI’S SECOND DISSERTATION

## On the Mosaic Images Placed by Pope Sixtus III in the Enlargement of the Liberian Basilica after the Ecumenical Synod of Ephesus

**[Col. 0263B] INDEX OF SECTIONS**

I. The care of the supreme pontiffs in selecting the ornaments which they established in basilicas and sacred buildings founded or dedicated by them.

II. An illustrious example of this care is perceived in the sacred images executed in mosaic by Saint Sixtus III in the Liberian basilica, which he enlarged and adorned after the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, held at the end of the pontificate of his predecessor, Saint Celestine, against the heresy of Nestorius.

III. Pope Saint Hadrian, in his letter to Charlemagne read at the Second General Council of Nicaea, mentions this work of Sixtus and the papal care and policy of adapting such ornaments to the history and doctrines of faith established by those same general councils.

IV. It was also customary in the Eastern Churches to dedicate memorials of general councils on the walls of churches, as is clear from the church at Bethlehem founded in the age of the Great Constantine, from the church at Constantinople, and from others.

V. In the mosaics placed by Sixtus III in the Liberian basilica there is displayed not only a memorial of the Council of Ephesus and of the Catholic doctrine defended there against Nestorius, but also the principal testimonies of both Testaments which the Fathers of that council used to confirm that Catholic doctrine.

VI. Sixtus placed the testimonies drawn from the New Testament in the arch of the central nave of the same basilica, which is called the triumphal arch. The testimonies drawn from the Old Testament, which the same Fathers brought forward to illustrate the type or figure of the doctrine, he arranged on both walls forming the same nave. Moreover, on the triumphal arch one sees a dedicatory votive tablet of the council, which the age of Anastasius seems to have called *votarea*.

VII. The principal testimonies of the New Testament produced by the Fathers of Ephesus and expressed by Pope Sixtus III in the mosaic of the same arch, to confirm the Catholic doctrine defended there, are enumerated individually. The first is taken from the Annunciation made to the Virgin Mother of God by the archangel Gabriel.

VIII. The second is taken from the presentation of the child Jesus in the temple.

IX. The third is taken from the adoration of the Magi.

X. The fourth is taken from the slaughter of the innocent infants.

XI. The fifth is taken from Christ the Lord’s disputation among the doctors.

XII. Since all these subjects concern the infancy and childhood of Christ the Lord, Sixtus carefully selected them in order to display those things which, in the very event and mystery of the Incarnation and Nativity, declare Christ the Lord to be God and man, and which rightly establish the most holy Virgin as his mother and Mother of God, against the blasphemies of Nestorius, who denied both.

XIII. The figures of this doctrine, selected from the Old Testament by the holy Fathers of Ephesus, especially by Blessed Cyril, in the name of Pope Celestine, who presided over the same council, are represented in Sixtine mosaics placed above the columns in the central nave.

XIV. The first is derived from Genesis, chapter 14, where Melchizedek, king and priest, blesses Abraham and offers bread and wine.

XV. The second is taken from Abraham’s receiving the three visitors as guests and worshiping one of them. Genesis 18.

XVI. Lot and Abraham depart in different directions with their flocks. Genesis 13.

XVII. Isaac blesses Jacob. Genesis 27.

XVIII. Jacob’s service in the house of Laban in order to obtain Rachel as his wife. Genesis 29.

XIX. The separation of Laban’s and Jacob’s flocks. Genesis 30.

XX. The deeds of Jacob and his sons at Shechem, and Jacob’s divinely commanded migration to Bethel. Genesis 34 and 35.

XXI. The figures on the opposite side of the basilica’s nave recount the history of Moses from Exodus, chapter 2, beginning with his rescue from the Nile River. Why does the account begin with Moses?

XXII. The marriage of Moses to Zipporah. Exodus 2.

XXIII. Moses is sent back to Egypt by divine command to lead his brothers out of slavery into freedom. Exodus 4.

XXIV. The Paschal law given through Moses to the Israelites who were to depart from Egypt. Exodus 12.

XXV. The first encampments of the Israelites as they proceeded toward the Red Sea. Exodus 12.

XXVI. The passage of the Hebrews through the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh. Exodus 14.

XXVII. Waters sweetened by the casting in of wood; and the rain of quail, together with the manna sent down from heaven. Exodus 15 and 16.

XXVIII. Water brought forth from the rock by the striking of Moses’ staff. Exodus 17.

XXIX. The battle of the Israelites against the Amalekites and their victory, when Moses lifted his hands while standing upon the rock. Exodus 17.

XXX. Moses and Aaron, cast down by the glory of the Lord, face the rebellion of the people, who attempt to overwhelm them with stones. Numbers 14.

XXXI. Deuteronomy is handed over to the Levites to be guarded in the Ark. Joshua is declared leader of the people, to lead them into the promised land. Moses’ death on Mount Nebo. Deuteronomy 31 and 34.

XXXII. Under Joshua’s leadership, Jericho is besieged. Rahab the prostitute, who had received the spies as guests and displayed a scarlet cord, is spared from destruction. Joshua, chapter 2.

XXXIII. The people cross the Jordan under Joshua. Twelve stones are set up there as a memorial, and an equal number are carried away. The same, chapters 3 and 4.

XXXIV. While Joshua is besieging the city of Jericho, he worships a man who appears to him by divine power and hears that he has been appointed by God as commander of the army. Joshua, chapter 5.

XXXV. The Ark of God is carried around the city seven times, while the priests sound their trumpets by Joshua’s command; the walls of Jericho fall, and the city is given as plunder to the victorious Israelites. Joshua 6.

XXXVI. While Joshua is fighting, the sun and moon halt their course, and great stones hurled from heaven like hailstones strike down the enemies of the Israelites. Five kings allied against those same Israelites flee into caves; from there they are brought out by Joshua’s command and subjected to the final punishment. The same, chapter 10.

**1.** A second dissertation is owed to this place in order to illuminate the history of the pontiffs from Saint Sylvester to Blessed Gregory the Great. It is inserted here especially for the reasons that will now be stated.

[Col. 0264C] Once the persecutions had been removed, the Christian Church experienced that peace which not only allowed the faithful to exercise divine worship publicly in the City, but also permitted them to display the royal throne of our peaceful Solomon, Christ the Lord, in basilicas raised and adorned no less religiously than magnificently through the piety of bishops and the munificence of princes, and to set it before the worship of the whole world. Many of Silvester’s immediate successors dedicated new buildings to God, so that by their example they might lead the rest also in this religious duty—those whom they surpassed and outshone by the practice of every virtue, as well as by the grandeur and authority of their office.

The wise architects, since they were engaged in building the body of Christ, which is the Church, also carefully considered the arrangement of the parts and ornaments of the basilicas they founded—basilicas which were intended both to represent that same Church of God through mystical imagery and to gather the peoples for the true worship of God, duly performed through prayers and sacrifices. They weighed each detail with such provident [Col. 0264D] and mature deliberation that they placed almost nothing there which did not refer to the purpose assigned to the structure: namely, to raise the minds of the faithful so that they might perform the duties prescribed by religion in holiness and order.

Accordingly, in their emblems and ornaments they sought to provide the minds of those who looked upon them with two chief supports: the history of an accomplished event, and the lesson, drawn from that history, concerning the true worship and adoration of God which, by the divine revelation of our faith, must be rendered by all. These two purposes, commended to us by the pontiffs in the tradition of sacred images so displayed in churches, fill both sections of the acts of the Seventh Synod, that is, the Second Council of Nicaea, as becomes clear to anyone who reads through them.

Thus Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, read in the synod, act 4, in Binius’s edition, p. 50, col. 1 CD:

> “What historical narration teaches through hearing, silent painting displays through imitation. For, as Basil the Great says (in the sermon on the Forty Martyrs, likewise read in act 2, p. 16), from both things we are stirred to courage. A brief narration—if I may put it so, made in summary—and an illustrative representation of deeds expressed in an image through painting are useful to us who contemplate them.”

And in act 6, p. 67 of the same edition, the deacon Epiphanius, in his refutation of the false synod of the Iconoclasts, after reciting canon 82 of the Sixth Synod under Justinian—which decrees that, according to ancient tradition, the type of Christ the Lord designated by the Forerunner is to be represented in the form of the Lamb—reads the following:

> “Therefore, embracing the ancient types and shadows handed down by the Church as symbols and prefigurations of the truth, we venerate grace and truth. We see and understand that, both before the six holy synods and after them, paintings of the saints were handed down in the Church no differently from the sacred reading of the Gospel. For what is read, once it reaches the ears, we then read inwardly in the mind and transmit it; and what we see with our eyes in paintings, that too we embrace in our minds. Through these two things, mutually corresponding—reading, I mean, and painting—we acquire one knowledge by which we arrive at the remembrance of things that have happened.

> “Hence, from these two highest senses one may find an effective conjunction in the Song of Songs: ‘Show me your face, and let me hear your voice. For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful.’ To these words we too appropriately sing that other verse from the Psalm: ‘As we have heard, so also have we seen.’”

I shall pass over the other testimonies of the Fathers which concern sacred images generally, and which teach that their veneration is to be referred to the prototype represented through them. I shall instead gather more closely those relevant to the subject of our dissertation: namely, to show that from these most ancient images, adorning the Liberian basilica at the command of Xystus III, it can be understood that he himself, and the other Roman pontiffs, adopted such a selection when adorning their basilicas and titular churches, so that the sacred images they caused to be painted there might set before the Church both the memory of an accomplished event and the dogma of faith [Col. 0265C] revealed by God—two supports especially effective for arousing the minds of the faithful to praise God.

Accordingly, just as a reader was not rashly permitted to choose whichever books or sections he preferred to read publicly in church, but was commanded to recite those designated by the bishop, so too it was not lawful for a painter to draw on the walls of sacred buildings whichever histories he preferred according to his own judgment. Rather, the arrangement and selection were reserved to the foresight of the pontiffs, while the art of coloring obeyed it.

> “The antiquity of the events themselves bears witness,” says Basil the Great, likewise read in the same act 6, “and the teaching of the Fathers led by the Spirit: for, seeing these things in venerable temples, they themselves received them and, when dedicating venerable temples, took care to paint them.… Therefore the conception and tradition belong to them, not to the painter. The painter’s is merely the art; the arrangement plainly belongs to the holy Fathers who dedicated them.”

**2.** What kind of selection the Roman pontiffs therefore used in arranging these things before their eyes, so as to set forth the memory of an accomplished event and to confirm through that same memory the dogma of true worship, is shown above all by the mosaics added by Xystus to the Liberian basilica, which he had enlarged. More than any others, these mosaics have been preserved through the religious devotion of so many centuries and by a special kind of protection for our own age; for, through the most recent zeal and generosity of the most holy Father in Christ, Benedict XIII, in this very year in which the dissertation is being printed, after the entire roof and the structures of the chapels had been repaired and every trace of squalor removed, they have been restored to their former splendor.

**3.** To attain more successfully an understanding of the memory of the events represented in these mosaics, and of the dogma of faith expressed in them by the command and selection of Xystus, it is useful to attend to what I had stated earlier in the Prolegomena from the letter of Pope Adrian to Charlemagne, written concerning the veneration of sacred images: namely, that the Roman pontiffs customarily dedicated, after each ecumenical council had been successfully completed, monuments of the Catholic victory achieved through God and rescued from the snares and attacks of the heretics, both in thanksgiving to God and as future trophies commemorating the well-conducted struggle, as well as splendid incentives for the faithful people to offer the sacrifice of the established worship to the Giver of all good things.

Adrian enumerates the individual ecumenical synods celebrated by his predecessors and points to the sacred buildings adorned in this way: by Silvester after Nicaea, in the Lateran; by Damasus after Constantinople, in his titular church; and by Celestine and Xystus after the successful completion of Ephesus. These examples will suggest to us that their works commended to these walls both the memory of the accomplished event and the dogma of divine worship steadfastly asserted in it, represented through the same documents of Scripture in the mosaics of the Liberian basilica just as in the council they were represented through the sacred books.

**4.** I think it should likewise be recalled that from ornaments plainly similar, placed not only in the West but also in the [Col. 0266B] East in sacred buildings magnificently constructed by Constantine the Great or by princes who succeeded him immediately, and solemnly dedicated by the pontiffs, it is clear that the bishops were concerned to insert the memory of the synods in those buildings, so that the Church of God might more readily repeat the religious acts established in those synods under the inspiration of the divine Spirit.

Let the Church of Bethlehem, founded by Constantine the Great and subsequently restored together with its mosaics around the end of the seventh and beginning of the eighth century, serve as an example of all. This is evident from the inscriptions placed there not only in Greek and Latin, but also in Armenian and Arabic, and published by Bishop Giovanni Ciampino in his book on the sacred buildings constructed by Constantine the Great, chapter 24.

The image and memory of several councils are displayed there. The image is expressed by a mosaic altar on which, according to custom, the sacred Gospel book is placed as though seated upon its throne—that is, in the very manner in which it was displayed in sacred councils as the supreme [Col. 0266C] judge and oracle of faith. The memory and indication of each council are expressed by an inscription attached to the individual images, generally in Greek letters. Thus, in the third panel, concerning the Council of Ephesus—the same council whose relevance to the Liberian basilica we have demonstrated—the memory is presented as follows:

> + Η ΑΓΙΑ ΣΥΝΟΔΟϹ Η ΕΝ ΕΦΕ ϹΩ ΤΟ ΠΡΟΤΕΡΟΝ ΤΩΝ Ϲ ΑΓΙ ΝΩ etc. — “The holy synod at Ephesus, the former [synod] of two hundred holy Fathers …”

Ciampino renders it into Latin:

> + “The holy synod of Ephesus, previously convened under Theodosius the Younger by two hundred Fathers, was assembled against Nestorius, who divided Christ into two persons and did not acknowledge the Mother of the Lord as God-bearer. The holy synod defined and confessed that the Only-Begotten of God had descended from heaven, had become incarnate [the supplied text reads *incarna um*], by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, and had become man according to the hypostatic union; that she who bore him was God-bearer; and it struck Nestorius with an anathema.”

[Col. 0266D] What had been expressed in the Church of Bethlehem in writing concerning the sacred councils around the end of the seventh century had been represented much earlier in painting by several Eastern churches, so that the painting of four or six of the earlier general synods had its own name. We shall observe this in sections 174 and 179 of the Bibliothecarius—whether it should be called *Botarea*, or *Pancarea*, as others correct it, or, as Macro thought, *Bolarea*, from the Greek word Βουλῆς (*boulēs*, “of a council”), meaning something connected with a council.

The emperor Philippicus, an Iconoclast, had removed that image of the six general councils painted in the Church of Constantinople; Theodosius the Younger restored it. Bibliothecarius, section 179:

> “As soon as the aforesaid Theodosius entered the royal city, he immediately restored to its former place that venerable image in which the six holy synods had been painted and which Philippicus had removed, though he should not even be named.”

See Baronius under the year 711. But as soon as the Romans perceived the heretical opinions of Philippicus after his elevation to the imperial power, they were inflamed with zeal for the faith and, as the Bibliothecarius says in section 174,

> “erected in the church of blessed Peter the image which the Greeks call Votarea, containing the six holy and universal synods.”

The churches situated farther away venerated the memory of such synods, dedicated to them in those images, to such an extent that the Greeks and the Moschi frequently represented them also in their Menaea, which may be consulted in the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, volume I, May.

The importance of displaying before the eyes of the faithful, for veneration and recollection, both the memory of what had been accomplished in the councils and the dogmas of faith there rescued from the attacks of heretics was always considered so great that this was done both for those who knew letters and for those who did not, through paintings, mosaics, reliefs, and inscriptions intended to recall the dogmas themselves and the memory of the events to the minds of the faithful.

**5.** Let us now return to the letter of Pope Adrian, which asserts that anyone may recognize that Xystus accomplished in the Liberian [Col. 0267B] basilica after the Council of Ephesus what Silvester had already accomplished after Nicaea in the Lateran, and Damasus after Constantinople in his titular church: namely, to dedicate the memory of a successful event in the council, to arouse faith in the dogma asserted there, and to render more ready the other duties of religion, which the sight of venerable images ordinarily facilitates by providing the minds of those who contemplate them with an occasion for being raised to God.

Moreover, what had been established in the Council of Ephesus against the blasphemies of Nestorius, according to the rule of faith concerning the Only-Begotten Son of God hypostatically united in the Virgin’s womb to the human nature he assumed, and concerning the title “God-bearer” to be attributed to that same Virgin, is not merely expressed here. The more important passages of divine Scripture are also displayed, from both the New and the Old Testament, which the Ephesian Fathers employed to prove the truth of those same dogmas and of the revelation handed down to us.

**6.** The passages selected from the New Covenant fill the principal arch of the basilica, which is called the triumphal arch. At the top of this same gable, where Xystus placed the inscription **XYSTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI**—“Xystus, bishop, to the people of God”—a circular panel has been represented, displaying the apparatus of the council: namely, the sacred volume of the Gospels sealed with seven seals, as an indication of the New Testament drawn from the Apocalypse, and placed upon a platform according to the council custom mentioned shortly before. You will read of this custom being observed at Ephesus in Cyril’s *Apology to Theodosius*, printed with the acts, Roman edition, p. 624 D.

There is also shown an episcopal seat furnished with curtains, an altar table with crowned offerings, an upright title of the cross, and sacred images of the apostles Peter and Paul placed on either side near the pontifical seat. All these things are carefully enumerated and explained by Ciampino, together with a special figure of this circular panel so that each detail may be seen distinctly, in the cited volume I of *Ancient Monuments*, p. 200.

The holy apostles Peter and Paul, the chief heralds among us of that Testament through which the truth revealed to the Church is made manifest, support this panel as though it were a votive tablet—perhaps the term which a later age barbarously inflected as *Votarea*, when Anastasius used it—in an offering of thanksgiving to God. Through tradition, testimony, and the judgment of the Fathers gathered in councils in Christ’s name under the primacy of Peter and his successors, that Testament casts down and destroys every heresy.

The four evangelists are likewise represented around the heads of the apostles by the customary symbols of the four animals known from the descriptions of Ezekiel and John. Destined to draw the chariot of God’s glory throughout all nations through the impetus of that same Spirit, they are like a heavenly quadriga dedicated in the triumphal arch. They raise to the summit of praise the divinity and humanity of Christ the Lord, wonderfully subsisting in the single person of the Word and adored in the council through the confession of the whole Church. At the very top of the arch this is expressed by Christ’s monogram, adorned with the letters Α and [Col. 0268A] Ω, showing that he is both the beginning of all things and the end to which they are referred. To him the heavenly beings sing, and every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth bends. See Plate, letter A.

This inscription of dedication, and the subject of the history—both the events accomplished and the worship which the faithful ought to learn—are presented together so concisely in the votive image placed by Xystus after the Council of Ephesus that, in the same triumphal arch, he paints the testimonies of the New Testament by which above all the Ephesian Fathers, and especially Cyril, who presided in the name of the Apostolic See, taught through explicit oracles that the divine person of the Word is to be adored in Christ. On the side walls he adds the agreement of the Old Testament, under various figures which foreshadow the same mystery, selecting from among them especially those which the Ephesian Fathers, and Cyril above all, employed both in the sessions of the council and in the books they published to demonstrate that same Catholic truth.

**7.** We need only enumerate them, therefore, in order to recognize that the principal testimonies of the New Testament declaring the Catholic faith established at the Council of Ephesus are represented in the great, or triumphal, arch. We shall then review in the lateral mosaics the figures from the Old Testament produced by those same Fathers, which, according to the tradition of the ancestors, signified the same mysteries.

The oracles of the New Testament which manifest to us the truth of those dogmas begin with the Annunciation of the angel Gabriel to the Virgin designated as the Mother of God, taken from the Gospel of Luke, chapter II. Xystus arranged for the mosaic to display the angel greeting, the Virgin responding, and the Holy Spirit descending and divinely overshadowing her. Plate 1, letter B.

To this Gospel history Xystus added in the mosaic the revelation of the worship then offered by the angels to the Word taking flesh from the Virgin, recorded in Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews, chapter I, in words confirmed by the testimony of the Psalm:

> “And when he again brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him.’”

He therefore added figures of angels standing reverently, such as John saw before God’s throne in Apocalypse, chapter VIII, no. 2.

Both testimonies—the first, Gabriel’s announcement to the Virgin that the one taking flesh from her womb was the Son of God, and the second, Paul’s proclamation of the worship then rendered by the angels at God’s command to the Word taking flesh from the Virgin—were produced at the Council of Ephesus to prove Christ’s divinity and the single person of the Word, henceforth subsisting in two natures. This occurred in the first session, and indeed in the first testimony of the Fathers produced there, in the Roman edition of the Councils, p. 352, col. 1: the testimony of Peter, bishop and martyr of Alexandria, recited again in act 6, p. 434.

Christ’s divinity and the single person of the Word are demonstrated from the archangel’s words:

> “The Lord is with you,”

that is, the Word of God is now with you. For Gabriel’s greeting indicates that the Word of God was born in the virginal womb and became flesh. Hence it is also written:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of God.”

We learn from Cyril, in his explanation of the Eighth Anathema, that the worship of the angels was brought forward from Paul’s Letter and that it was therefore also reported in part III of the Council of Ephesus, Roman edition, fol. 509, in these words:

### ANATHEMA VIII

> “If anyone dares to say that the man assumed is to be worshiped together with the Word of God, and glorified together with him, and called God alongside him as one alongside another—for the particle ‘with,’ when added, invariably and necessarily carries this meaning—and does not rather honor Emmanuel with one worship and attribute to him one glorification, insofar as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.”

### EXPLANATION VIII

> “We have been baptized into one God, the almighty Father, and into one Son, and also into one Holy Spirit. Do you not know, brothers,” says blessed Paul (Romans VI), “that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.”
>
> “Therefore we believed and were baptized into one—as I have said, Son—the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the incarnate Word of God the Father, made man. We have been taught to adore the one existing God, and the heavenly powers with us. For it is written in Hebrews I: ‘And when he again brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship him’ (Psalm XCVI). The Only-Begotten became Firstborn when he appeared like us.”

**8.** To this, then, belongs the explicit history of the Annunciation of the God-bearer, which proves from the words of the archangel Gabriel and from the worship of the angels that the Word of God, when he became flesh in the Virgin’s womb, did not cease to be what he was; and therefore that he is to be worshiped as God and Son of God, born in this way from the Virgin, and that the Virgin is to be called God-bearer.

The mosaic also includes the figure of Zechariah hearing from the same angel Gabriel the oracle concerning the son, John, who was to be born to him and who was to be the Lord’s forerunner, filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb. Thus it displays the whole of the first chapter of Luke’s Gospel, in which the angel, the priest, and Elizabeth all testify to Christ’s divinity.

Speaking to Zechariah about John, the angel Gabriel foretells that he will be great before the Lord, but not the Lord or the Son of the Most High. In announcing Jesus, who was to be born from the Virgin, he calls Christ not merely great but the Son of the Most High, the Son of God (Luke I).

The priest Zechariah, following the angel’s instruction, says the same things about his own John: that he will be a prophet who prepares the way for the Lord. But concerning the Lord Christ, who visited us, rising from on high, he speaks much more exaltedly when he says that those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death are to be enlightened by him who thus rose from on high through the merciful compassion of God.

The other evangelist, the beloved disciple of Christ, explains this more fully. Speaking of John, he says (John I) that he was not the light which enlightens every person, but that this light was the Word, who was God in the beginning with God, and became flesh and dwelt among us.

Cyril, in the homily delivered at Ephesus against Nestorius and printed in part I of the Council, act 1, p. 387 of the Roman edition, refers to Zechariah’s testimony and finds an assertion of Christ’s divinity in the words cited, when he says concerning the Virgin God-bearer:

> “Through her the Only-Begotten Son of God shines forth as light for those who were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death.”

Elizabeth, the wife of Zechariah, confesses with her husband that the Virgin Mary is the Mother of God when she addresses her:

> “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb”;  
> “And from where is this granted to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me?”

See plate 1, letter C.
