**9.** On the opposite gable of this arch, Saint Xystus also arranged for the presentation of the child Jesus in the Temple to be displayed: there the aged Simeon and the widow Anna are made witnesses to his divinity, with the Holy Spirit speaking through their mouths, so that, as Ambrose reminds us in his commentary on Luke II, every age, both sexes, and the miracles of the events might establish the faith. Plate 1, letter D.

So many proclamations of Christ’s divinity are expressed in the first and second chapters of Luke and selected from them by the Ephesian Fathers, especially Cyril, that Pope Xystus judged that they should be collected in the upper series of this mosaic as the chief weapons of our faith, by which the victory of truth was won against the blasphemies of the heretics.

[Col. 0270A] In the second series of the same arch there follows the adoration of the Magi, who approached the newly born Lord at the sign of a star sent from heaven. No one is unaware that, by the consensus of the Fathers, we have been taught that the divinity of Christ the Lord is proved in this Gospel history, which is recounted in Matthew II.

It is enough to read Jerome, who quotes the verses of the presbyter Juvencus:

> “They bring gifts—gold, myrrh, and frankincense—to the King, the Man, and God.”

And the verses of Prudentius, which Ciampino quoted in his description of this mosaic, *Ancient Monuments*, chapter 22, volume II, p. 208:

> “Here the Magi bring precious gifts to Christ the child beneath the Virgin’s breast:  
> myrrh, frankincense, and gold.  
> The Mother marvels at so many honors of her chaste womb,  
> and that she has borne God, a man, and the supreme King.”

We are not now investigating what has been stated elsewhere about this mystery and history. We are considering what was drawn by the Ephesian Fathers from this chapter of the Gospel [Col. 0270B] to establish the dogma of faith against Nestorius. See plate 1, letter E.

In act 1, p. 351, these words are read from Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium:

> “Since he is both King and God, and tasted death in the dispensation of his passion, the gifts are signs of the mysteries: the Magi offer gold, recognizing that he is King; they offer frankincense, for they know that they are offering it to God; they offer myrrh on account of death, in the mystery of the passion.”

Among the other writings of the Fathers, the homily of Theodotus, most holy bishop of Ancyra, delivered on the Nativity of our Savior Jesus Christ, was likewise read at the Council of Ephesus. It is printed on p. 602 of the Roman edition. This holy bishop explains the dogma under discussion as follows:

> “For the Magi also offered frankincense to him who was seen, as to God, neither separating nature from nature nor dividing in thought what had once been united. Rather, recognizing by a single wonder that he who appeared was God, they offered frankincense, indicating his divine dignity by that gift. Nor did the angels separate, in their understanding, what had been born from the Word of God; but, knowing that he was one and the same, visible and intelligible, they cried out, saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men.’ They did not say one thing while thinking another, as you do; they did not confess one Christ Jesus in words while dividing the same Christ in thought, as you do, possessing thoughts opposed to your words. Rather, they glorify one and the same God.”

Theodotus adds many further arguments against the errors of the Nestorians, who sought support for their own heresies from this very history, wrongly explained. Cyril too did not pass them over in silence in the same edition of the Councils, p. 513. He produces the opposition of the Easterners and responds to it on p. 514:

> “They say that the gifts brought by the Magi were appropriate both to him who was understood and to him who was seen, again dividing the one Lord Jesus Christ into two after the union. He who is understood became visible, not through a change of nature but through union with the body that was seen.… Those gifts, therefore, were appropriate to the one person, that is, to Christ; for in the same person he is at once God and man. For this reason, when he himself was born, the choirs of the holy angels sang, and the hosts of spiritual beings said that he himself was Savior and Redeemer.”

Both Cyril and Theodotus include the worship of the angels and the Magi. Xystus includes it in his mosaic as well. For, in addition to representing the Magi offering gifts, he wished angels to be shown standing beside the child Christ just as they stand beside God’s throne. Ciampino observes in his description of this mosaic that Christ the Lord is not represented there as an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger, but rather as a child seated on a royal throne rather than on a little bed.

Ciampino notes that the divinity of Christ the Lord is represented in this way even in the child Jesus, with reference to Psalm CIX; therefore, he says, the painter was concerned here more with the mystery than with the history. I would prefer to derive this same expression of the mystery from the Ephesian Fathers rather than from the painter’s judgment.

Thus Theodotus continues in the homily cited shortly before:

> “The Magi were seeking him as King, asking about the birth of the King and saying to the Jews: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him.’ You seek a king, O Magus? And why do you offer frankincense as to God? But I know him to be both King and God. Therefore I offer him both gold and frankincense, designating by my gifts both God and King.”

> “But he who then drew the Magi to piety by ineffable power has established this joyful festival today: no longer placed in a manger, but set upon this saving table. For that manger became the mother of this table. For this reason he was placed in it, so that in this one he might be eaten and become saving food for the faithful; but that manger designated this glorious table. The Virgin, however, brought forth these choirs of virgins. The poverty of the Bethlehem lodging built these glorious temples, and so forth. You see poverty made the parent of such riches. Why do you reproach Christ with Bethlehem’s lowliness? Why do you bring poverty forward without comparing with it the profits thereby won for the whole world?”

Theodotus responds in these and many other passages to the Nestorians, who impiously divided Christ’s single person into two because things which the Word made flesh suffered as a man seemed to them inconsistent with God’s dignity. Xystus therefore displays in the mosaic the throne of God, which Theodotus also recognizes in the manger, so that the Ephesian proofs of the Catholic dogma might shine everywhere in this mosaic and be set before the holy people of God who gaze upon these images.

**10.** In the same section of the mosaic and of the triumphal arch there is also the slaughter of the Holy Innocents, plate I, letter F: the infants whom King Herod ordered to be killed, from two years old and under, in Bethlehem [Col. 0271C] and its territories, after he seized upon the arrival of the Magi—who were seeking the newborn King of the Jews—as an opportunity to gather the priests and scribes, and heard from them that the prophetic oracles testified that he was to be born in Bethlehem of Judah.

He was struck with fear lest this child should dislodge him from the royal throne. The holy Fathers present this fear of Herod, inflicted upon the armed king and his retinue, who raged with impunity through slaughter, by the Lord Infant born in swaddling clothes and in a manger, as an argument for Christ’s divinity: even while in infant bands he was shattering the heads of his enemies.

At the Council of Ephesus, however, Roman edition of the Councils, volume II, pp. 354 A–355 B, this passage is employed with an explanation by Theophilus of Alexandria, the sixth in his first Paschal Letter, to refute the blasphemy of Nestorius, which revived the heresy of Paul of Samosata—as Pope Celestine writes to the clergy and people, and as the same clergy attest, Council of Ephesus, Roman edition, volume I, pp. 283 D and 268 D.

Nestorius said that there was one Christ who was born from the Virgin, the son of that same Virgin, and another Son of God who, before Mary and before the ages, was the Father’s Word. For this reason, he taught that this Son of God and Word had not truly suffered and had not truly become incarnate, but only apparently and imaginarily, as the most impious Manichaeus taught.

Against these heresies contained in Nestorius’s blasphemy, or certainly following from it, among the other oracles of Scripture testimonies from the New Testament are employed to prove that the child Jesus, even in infancy, demonstrated himself at once to be true man and true God, while suffering all the weaknesses of our lowliness and of the flesh he assumed, sin alone excepted, and at the same time exercising and manifesting the power and force of the divine nature, which he never abandoned. Roman edition, p. 355. Theophilus says:

> “Although he differed from us in the manner of his birth, he nevertheless judged that he should embrace our likeness in all things, sin alone excepted. For he is born, wrapped in swaddling clothes, suckled, and placed in a manger; and finally he experiences all the weaknesses of our nature on account of its antecedent sins. Yet, while he was still an infant, he terrified the enemy and his cohort, brought the Magi to repentance, and fearlessly caused them to disregard the command of the king from whom they had received their instructions.”

Before Theophilus wrote these things, Irenaeus had used these same testimonies concerning the infancy of Christ the Lord to silence the mouths of the heretics of his own time and to prove from them that the divine and human nature subsisted in the one person of Christ, namely, the Word of God. He did so in book III, chapter 18, against those who say that Christ appeared merely in semblance.

After bringing forward the Scriptures already related to establish the truth of Christ’s divine and human nature—namely, the announcement of the angel Gabriel and the adoration of the Magi—he also adduces the slaughter of the infants killed by Herod in Bethlehem out of fear for the kingdom of the Christ who was being born. [Col. 0272B] The Church venerates them from those earliest centuries as flowers of the martyrs and witnesses to this truth, made so not by speaking but by dying, as these very testimonies of Irenaeus, the homilies of Origen, and those of other Fathers demonstrate.

But lest we wander beyond the proper course of the passages which the Ephesian Fathers employed from these Scriptures to confirm the Catholic dogma against Nestorian errors, it is enough to have shown, from Theodotus’s homily recited there and confirmed by the acclamation of the Fathers, why Xystus represented in the mosaic, together with the adoration of the Magi, the remaining parts of this same history: namely, Herod’s inquiry into where Christ would be born and the slaughter of the infants.

These events prove that the child ought to be worshiped with the Magi as God, since the prophets had foretold through so many signs that Emmanuel would be born in Bethlehem; and at the same time that he ought to be regarded as truly human, since it was announced that he would be conceived by a Virgin from the line of David and, as one truly born [Col. 0272C] within the borders of Bethlehem, was sought for death among the infants of two years and under, his fellow countrymen.

I must not pass over one point which adds glory to Xystus’s work, and much more to the Catholic faith, through these images: namely, that in this selected Gospel history and in our Ephesian confession, Xystus repeatedly presents what his immediate successor in the chair, Leo the Great, taught no less, as did all his most worthy successors. In their name, and in his own after thirteen centuries, Clement XI, educated in this school, gathered and taught us to repeat the same thing in his homilies on the Lord’s Nativity (from Saint Leo the Great, homily 8 on the Nativity of the Lord):

> “The Lord became David’s son, and from the fruit of the promised lineage a child was born without a man, with two natures meeting in one person: so that our Lord Christ might be begotten by the same conception and the same birth, possessing true divinity for the miracles of his works and true humanity for enduring sufferings.”

Clement XI, homily of 1704 on the Nativity.

[Col. 0272D] **11.** The parts of the Gospel history represented by Xystus in the remaining section of the same mosaic of the arch are fitted to this confession, plate I, letter G: namely, the child Jesus found among the teachers; his growth in age and grace; and his return with the Virgin Mother and Joseph his foster-father, so that he might be subject to them (Luke II).

Xystus did not recall this history without purpose when displaying the triumph of the Council of Ephesus. The impious Nestorius had abused this Gospel testimony, as he wrote in the sixth quaternio, publicly read in the holy synod, first session, p. 363, as though it confirmed the blasphemy by which he asserted that Christ had gradually advanced to pontifical dignity, and that this pontiff, subject to suffering and progress, was therefore far removed from the Word of God, perfect and impassible by his own nature.

The Fathers’ indignation rightly rejected this perverse interpretation of Scripture. They punished its author with anathema and deposition from the episcopate, in accordance with the judgment of Celestine. Cyril expounded the legitimate meaning of the Gospel text [Col. 0273A] in his defense of the Fourth Anathema against the objections of the Orientals, p. 523, comparing his interpretation with Paul’s Epistles (the First to the Corinthians and the Epistle to the Romans). “The choir of the holy Fathers,” he says, “agrees with this,” and he demonstrates it by producing the written statements of Atticus of Constantinople and of the two Roman pontiffs, Julius and Felix. It is therefore clear from every consideration that Xystus’s selection of images for this mosaic, drawn from Gospel history to adorn the arch, contains the dogmas of the Council of Ephesus, and that the proofs of those dogmas set forth in the council are displayed here as though secured by the seal of faith, with the Fathers rightly acclaiming their agreement, p. 405:

> “To Celestine, a new Paul; to Cyril, a new Paul; to Celestine, guardian of the faith; to Celestine, in harmony with the council; the whole council gives thanks to Celestine. One Celestine, one Cyril, one faith of the council, one faith of the whole world.”

### 12.

The Gospel history represented in this mosaic [Col. 0273B] does not proceed beyond the infancy and childhood of Christ the Lord. The reason is that the principal point at issue in the definition issued against the Nestorian heresies was to demonstrate that, from the very beginning of his conception, he who was born in the Virgin’s womb was both man and true God. Once this had been established by the events of the Annunciation of the Mother of God, the birth of the Child, the adoration of the Magi, the presentation in the temple, the disputation with the doctors, and the return with his parents to Nazareth, it followed that the remaining acts of the Lord’s life, death, and resurrection—which declare his human and divine nature eternally subsisting in the Word—would likewise show that the rule of Catholic doctrine understood Christ in this way throughout all the stages of his life. Nestorius had departed from that rule when he asserted (Prosper, *Chronicle*):

> “Christ was born from Mary merely a man and not also God; and divinity was conferred upon him according to his merit.”

Therefore [Col. 0273C], together with Gregory of Nazianzus, quoted in the first session, it must be held (Roman edition, p. 357):

> “If anyone should say that he who was perfected through his works, whether after baptism or after the resurrection from the dead, merited adoption as a son—just as the pagans introduce adopted sons—let him be anathema.”

Thus, since the Virgin conceived Christ, God and man, by the Holy Spirit, and carried and gave birth to him while remaining inviolate, she must rightly be called the Mother of God. The council accordingly established these matters concerning the events of Christ’s life, and Xystus confirmed them in the mosaic. The revelation of the same dogma is sufficiently established by the Lord Savior’s infancy and childhood, without any need to represent the events that followed that age.

Ciampinus thought that, in the lowest small panel on the right side of this triumphal arch, above the image of the city of Jerusalem—which is also identified by the name *Jerusalem*—the deadly sentence pronounced by Herod against John the Forerunner was represented in the figures showing a seated king among several others, with the name [Col. 0273D] *Herod* written above him. In fact, this Herod is Herod the Great, who receives the approaching Magi when they ask, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” Before him three Magi are represented in foreign dress and girded for travel. It is therefore entirely clear that this is part of the history of the Magi’s adoration, in which, just as in the other scenes, there are presented proofs of the Lord’s infancy confirming that the child Jesus was God and man, as we have said—proofs employed at the Council of Ephesus in support of the Catholic dogma. See Table I, letters II and I.

### 13.

Having thus considered the histories and proofs drawn from the New Testament and presented by the Ephesian Fathers, and arranged by Xystus on the principal arch of the basilica above the high altar, let us now turn to the remaining images arranged by the same Xystus along both the right and left walls, rising from the presbytery toward the front of the church above the columns. In these we shall recognize the events and mysteries [Col. 0274A] taken from the Old Testament and employed to confirm the faith of the dogmas defended by those same Fathers, whether seated in the council or read and approved there.

Cyril will be especially useful, not only because he was present at the council, but also because he exercised there the position and functions of the Roman pontiff Celestine. Celestine explicitly declares that he held precisely the same views as Cyril after he had read Cyril’s exhortatory letters calling Nestorius back from heresy; Celestine therefore entrusted him with the exercise of his own functions at the council. The agreement between Celestine’s and Cyril’s doctrine was so great that Celestine admits that, although he wished to add certain points, he refrained when he recognized that all the meanings of his own faith were manifested in Cyril. On p. 273 he writes:

> “Indeed, beloved brother, we too would have added certain things, unless we had perceived that you likewise understood and held everything that we ourselves understand and hold.”

Since the pontiff Celestine therefore adopted Cyril’s views [Col. 0274B], especially on the subject that gave the council its occasion to declare the common faith, and since the Fathers of the council subscribed and acclaimed the same judgment, p. 405:

> “One Celestine, one Cyril, one faith of the council, one faith of the whole world,”

it makes no difference whether the doctrine suited to establish this dogma and represented in the mosaic is drawn from Cyril, from the council, or from Celestine.

Let us therefore turn to the side of the basilica nearest the images of the New Testament events already explained in that part of the arch facing south. We shall set forth one by one, from the history and oracles of the Old Testament, the figures of the same dogma described above, admitted and approved by the Ephesian Fathers, and explained according to the unanimous sense of the Fathers who there testified, in writing or by voice, that this was the faith of Celestine, the faith of Cyril, and the faith of the whole world.

Twenty-two square panels are visible above the line of columns on this wall, corresponding to the same number properly arranged and elegantly [Col. 0274C] decorated on the opposite wall. Mosaic work fills the panels. In some it has been lost and replaced by painting; in others it remains wholly intact or has required only slight pictorial supplementation. Only those that remain intact or have been restored in only a small part need be reviewed, since they belong to the age of Xystus, from which proof is sought for the Catholic dogma then defended at the Council of Ephesus and recognized in these figures. Xystus, Celestine’s successor, placed them here as a perpetual memorial of the matter and as an example of the worship that had been established, adding them to the Gospel truth clearly expounded at the council and represented in the arch of our basilica through the histories of the Incarnation of the Word and the infancy of Christ the Lord already discussed.

The first panel in order, namely the one joined to the corner of the triumphal arch and the presbytery, from Genesis, chapter 14, represents the history of Abraham returning from battle after defeating King Chedorlaomer and his allies. Melchizedek, king of Salem, met him on his return with his victory and brought him bread and wine. He was [Col. 0274D] priest of God Most High, and Melchizedek blessed him.

Cyril had to bring forward this figure from the Old Testament as a preliminary image of Christ the Lord, signifying his eternal priesthood, because Nestorius had shamelessly twisted it to serve his own views and his followers likewise abused it, although they knew that the Lord Jesus himself had indicated the dogma of his divinity from Psalm 109 by presenting the verse, “The Lord said to my Lord.” In the same context follows the title, “Priest according to the order of Melchizedek,” attributed by the Lord to that same Lord and Son of David: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Concealing and neglecting this legitimate and divine interpretation, Nestorius, p. 363, wickedly bent both the oracle of the psalm and Paul’s Epistle, which speaks of the same priesthood, to suit his heresy, impiously defiling both Scriptures with his customary blasphemies. The Fathers, who heard them recited in the first session from his sixth memorandum, condemned them, and a sentence of anathema and deposition was pronounced against Nestorius [Col. 0275A].

Cyril vindicated this image of our eternal pontiff’s priesthood, prefigured in Melchizedek and rightly cited by the Apostle Paul, from the calumnies of the heretics. In agreement with the teaching of the Fathers, he showed that it must rightly be understood of Christ the Lord, both in his *Book on the Right Faith to the Queens*, printed in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 240, of which there will soon be discussion, and in Book II of the *Glaphyra on Genesis*, in the section entitled “On Abraham and Melchizedek.” That title may serve for the panel and image we are contemplating.

Thus, when Cyril was treating Melchizedek as a type of Christ and of the excellence of his priesthood, set before us as superior to all legal worship and rightly explained by the Apostle Paul, he wrote:

[Col. 0275B]

> “You see, then, the types of perfection through Christ shining forth clearly in Melchizedek, and the measure of the legal worship shown to be inferior. For it is beyond doubt that what is lesser is blessed by what is greater and more excellent, according to Scripture. Now the divine Abraham was, in a sense, the root of the Israelites, and Levi, adorned in him with the glory of the divine priesthood, was still hidden in his loins. For blessed Abraham was by his power the father of those who in the course of time would arise from him. I think this was wisely said concerning Levi. He was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met him. Thus the legal righteousness was blessed through the worship found in Christ, whose type is Melchizedek. No one, surely, will doubt that the blessing which possesses the power to bless is incomparably more useful than that which lacks this power.”

Cyril then proceeds to a fuller explanation of this type [Col. 0275C]. First, he briefly reviews certain varied and futile opinions about Melchizedek:

> “Perhaps the person most eager to learn will ask who Melchizedek was. Those who are imprudently captivated by various absurdities and are not well acquainted with the usage of divine Scripture invent various opinions about him.”

After reporting and refuting these absurdities, he says:

> “Away, then, with this absurdity of thought. Melchizedek was a man, not the Holy Spirit.”

A little later, moving toward an explanation of the true meaning of this type from the Apostle Paul, he writes:

> “Paul, since he knew the law exceptionally well, did not deal with the Jews by means of simple arguments, but by the Mosaic writings, to which it was likely that even against their will they would yield, since they knew how to resist the truth. He therefore established Melchizedek as the likeness and type of Christ, because he is called the King of righteousness and peace. This applies, in a mystical sense, only to Emmanuel. For he became the author and giver of righteousness and peace to mortals. We have indeed been justified through him (Romans 1 and First Corinthians 6) [Col. 0275D], having shaken off the yoke of sin. We have also obtained peace with the Father and God, and so forth. Thus the divine Paul fittingly applied these things, drawn from the clear and manifest likeness of Melchizedek, to Christ. He established as the symbol, or type, of the priesthood superior to the legal priesthood the blessing bestowed on Abraham and the offering of wine and bread. For we have been blessed by Christ, the great and true priest, in no other way.”

Finally, Cyril shows that Paul, being learned in the law, took care there to refute two Jewish prejudices: that the legal commandment of Moses could not be superseded, and that the priesthood could not be transferred from the tribe of Levi.

> “Paul therefore attempts,” Cyril says, “to prove from sacred Scripture itself that both the newness of the law and the transfer of the priesthood had been foretold, and that the significance of both had been announced beforehand in types.”

Nestorius impiously denied that Christ was God the Word, man, priest, and pontiff [Col. 0276A]. His sectarians echoed him in the objections reported in Part III of the Council of Ephesus, p. 532 of the Roman edition, under the Tenth Anathema:

> “If anyone should say that our pontiff and apostle is not himself the Word of God after he became flesh and a man like us, and so forth, let him be anathema.”

Cyril, following the teaching of the earlier Fathers, dispelled the Nestorians’ sophistries, which arose from their erroneous interpretation of the history of Melchizedek and ran contrary to the tradition of the Fathers. Jerome, for example, writes to Marcella:

> “You will find Melchizedek, king of Salem, to be the prince of this city. Already then, in a type of Christ, he offered bread and wine, and consecrated the mystery of Christians in the blood and body of the Savior.”

Justin Martyr does not differ from this in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 9, F, col. 2 of the Latin edition. Again, Cyril, in the *Book on the Right Faith to the Queens*, included in Part I of the Roman edition of the Council of Ephesus, p. 238, no. 37, and in his exposition of the Tenth and Eleventh Anathemas of the same council, Part III, p. 511, agrees with Jerome. Both follow [Col. 0276B] the Apostle Paul, who teaches in Hebrews 7:10 and 18, and chapter 10:13, that the type of Christ’s pontificate and of the superior priesthood is prefigured in Melchizedek, king of Salem, above the Levitical priesthood. For this reason Christ the Lord is called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and not according to the order of Aaron.

Cyril therefore concludes in *Glaphyra*, Book II, p. 63, E:

> “He therefore establishes that Melchizedek was a priest not from the tribe of Levi. Then he shows that he was indeed priest of God Most High, but that he offered bread and wine. Thus he says of him: ‘Consider how great this man was, to whom even the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest things.’ The descendants of Levi, who receive the priesthood, have a commandment according to the law to take tithes from the people—that is, from their brothers—even though they too came forth from the loins of Abraham. But he whose descent is not counted among them took tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises,” and so forth.

[Col. 0276C]

> “It has therefore been demonstrated in Hebrews 7, through Melchizedek, that the priesthood exercised according to the law by one tribe must be transferred, and that the form and law of another priesthood must arise. … For this reason, when the divine Paul discusses these matters, he says: ‘If, then, perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood’—for the people received the law under it—‘what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, rather than to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, the transfer of the law must also take place.’ And again: ‘It is even more evident if another priest arises according to the order of Melchizedek, who has not been made according to the law of a carnal commandment but according to the power of an indestructible life.’ For he testifies: ‘Because you are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

[Col. 0276D]

Supported by this apostolic interpretation, the Latin Church commemorates the sacrifice and priesthood of Melchizedek as a type of the eternal priesthood of our Savior God—not only in the solemn office of this institution, composed five centuries ago at the command of Urban IV by Blessed Thomas Aquinas, where it begins with the Vespers antiphon prefixed to Psalm 109, “Christ the Lord is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek; he offered bread and wine,” but also in the canon of the Mass, which was written in the Church’s earliest centuries.

It is found expressed both in the *Sacramentary of Gregory* and in the time of Blessed Ambrose, who quotes it in Book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 6. There he explains the relation of this type to the priesthood of Christ, God and man, together with the Apostle Paul, in almost the same words and certainly with the same meaning as Cyril in the passage cited.

Xystus III therefore rightly places among the monuments of the victory won by Catholic truth against the blasphemies of Nestorius—blasphemies that denied Christ the Lord’s divine nature and eternal priesthood [Col. 0277A], and that are recorded in these mosaic works adorning the basilica of that Mother of God—the images of Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, offering bread and wine and blessing Abraham. These images accord with the interpretation handed down to us by the Apostle Paul, enshrined in the canon of the Mass, attested by [Col. 0278A] Ambrose and Cyril, and defended by Jerome against the inventions of the Nestorian heretics, who distorted the history and priesthood of Melchizedek to suit their own opinions.

[Col. 0277B]

### 15.

The next panel represents Abraham receiving as guests the three men who had appeared to him, preparing a table for them, and receiving from God the promise of the Messiah.

Cyril, the defender of the Catholic faith against the Nestorians, explains this same history in the next chapter of the *Glaphyra* cited above, immediately after the chapter in which he had explained the type of Abraham and Melchizedek. He begins Book III, chapter 1, which he entitles “On Abraham [Col. 0278B], and on the Promise through Isaac, and on the fact that the mystery of faith was prefigured through them,” as follows:

> “The divine Paul writes that Christ was made pontiff and apostle of our confession,” and so forth.

He reveals the matter even more explicitly in his earlier book *Against Julian*, writing in such a way as to establish that the proper character of divinity is ineffable, since anything that can be explained in human language falls below its dignity. For this reason, through types and figures, as through a mirror or an enigma [Col. 0279A], we are taught in the sacred writings concerning divine things—such as the consubstantiality of the three divine Persons in the type of the three men who appeared to Abraham as his guests.

> “Thus, finally,” he says, “we affirm that the divine Abraham was instructed, since this is written concerning him: ‘God appeared to him by the oak of Mamre as he sat at the entrance of his tent. When he looked up at noon, he saw with his own eyes, and behold, three men stood before him. When he saw them, he hurried to meet them and, falling prostrate before the entrance of his tent, worshiped, saying: “Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant.”’ After other words, he said to him: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ He answered: ‘Behold, she is in the tent.’ Then he said: ‘I will return to you at this time, and at the proper time Sarah your wife shall have a son.’

> “Behold, he most clearly says that God was seen by him, but that three men were observed. Yet divine Abraham, running to meet them, did not say, as though to three persons, ‘Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servants,’ but called the three uniquely [Col. 0279B] ‘Lord,’ as though they were one, and asked them to turn aside to him. And since they were also as one, the three spoke as though from one person: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ and, ‘I will return at this time next year.’ Observe, then: three were seen, each existing with his own subsistence, yet all comprehended in one by the principle of consubstantiality, and deliberately interweaving their conversations with one another.

> “Such images, however, are obscure in a certain sense and far below the truth, except insofar as they are useful for leading us by the hand, as it were, toward knowledge of realities that surpass mind and speech. For the light of the divine vision enters only pure minds, and from things perceptible to the senses we soar toward things far greater than our senses and the power of reason. The nature of divinity is one, by the agreement of all, and is above all, through all, and in all. In understanding, however, it extends into the holy [Col. 0279C], venerable, and consubstantial Trinity: into the Father, I mean, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet each of these Persons also subsists separately, each existing in reality and truly as what it is said to be; nevertheless, the principle of consubstantiality gathers them into an undifferentiated nature.

> “The Son is begotten from the Father, and is from him and naturally in him. The Spirit also proceeds as one who exists personally from God and the Father, and likewise from the Son. For the Father sanctifies through him that which is suited to be sanctified. Our forefather Abraham therefore did not fail to worship in the Holy Trinity the architect of earth and heaven and of all things, with whom rests all power.”

(He confirms this in Book VIII, p. 268.)

Thus, in the type represented by faithful Abraham, the consubstantial Trinity is presented for worship, while the Son of God—God remaining eternally and becoming man in time—is promised as one who will be born of the Virgin. Soon Isaac, the son of Abraham and Sarah, will become the type of that mystery. The faithful [Col. 0279D] is thereby accustomed to worship one God subsisting in three hypostases and to confess one Christ, God and man, displaying in the single person of the incarnate Word two natures—not confused, but united in the hypostasis of the Word.

Whether the Word of God appeared to Abraham under the form of three men—that is, the second Person of the Trinity, the Son, accompanied by two angels, as Justin Martyr preferred in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 35, and Irenaeus in *Against Heresies*, Book IV, chapter 23 (for Paul the Apostle establishes in Hebrews 13 that some of these were angels), and as Hilary writes in Book IV of *On the Trinity*:

> “God speaks there to Abraham and promises that Sarah will give birth. After this, three men stand beside the seated man. He worships one and confesses him to be God. The same one, both worshiped and seen by him, promises that he will return at the appointed time and that Sarah will have a son. Although Abraham saw a man, he nevertheless worshiped him as God, recognizing the mystery of the future embodiment [Col. 0280A]. Nor did such great faith lack testimony, since the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.’ The man who was seen therefore promises that he will return. Consider the fulfillment of the response. Remember, however, that the one who makes the promise is a man. What then does Scripture say? ‘And the Lord visited Sarah.’ This man, then, is the Lord, of whom Scripture says that he accomplished what he had promised. What follows? ‘And God did for Sarah as he had spoken.’ He is called a man in his speaking, signified as Lord in his visitation, and proclaimed God in the deed.”

—or whether, with these Fathers, one should say that the only-begotten Son of God, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, appeared to Abraham between two angels and promised that he would come; or whether, with Augustine, one should prefer to say that the three men who appeared to Abraham were three angels, one of whom, returning an answer at God’s command, spoke in the name of the God who commissioned him, as Augustine holds in his books *On the Trinity* and in Book XVI [Col. 0280B] of *The City of God*, chapter 29—the point is the same with respect to the argument that Pope Xystus intends us to recognize in the type of this history. It demonstrates the divinity of the Word taking flesh in such a way that the Lord, who remains what he is and exists before all ages, became man in the fullness of time. Christ was therefore not a man who carried God, as Nestorius blasphemed, but the Man-God, as the Catholic Church confesses—a truth revealed, handed down, and always publicly professed, especially at the Council of Ephesus.

Accordingly, the mother and Virgin of that God-Man was truly called the Mother of God, as the true Mother of that Son who subsisted through the one divine hypostasis of the Word of God, and not through a created hypostasis, as the impious arch-heretic and his followers imagined. They divided the divine hypostasis of the Word into two, as Vincent of Lérins writes, and were reluctant to have Christ called God. Instead, they insisted that he should be called an instrument and tool of divinity, a man who bore God, and other notions still more foolish. They rejected the word *Theotokos* and refused to call the holy Virgin the Mother of God, as Cyril complains in his exhortatory letters addressed to the same Nestorius, which are to be read in Part I of the Council of Ephesus, p. 255 of the Roman edition [Col. 0280C].

After the oracles of Scripture had thus been explained to us by the apostles of Christ and their legitimate successors, Pope Celestine rightly wrote to Cyril and congratulated him for “feeling and holding in the same way everything that we feel and hold,” and for the fact that this was a great triumph of their faith, since Cyril had both proved Celestine’s position so powerfully and explained its opposite so effectively through the testimonies of the divine Scriptures.

Xystus, Celestine’s immediate successor, therefore rightly displays for the people of God to see near the triumphal arch of his basilica these triumphant types of our faith, expounded by Cyril while exercising the functions of the Apostolic See at the Council of Ephesus and made more splendid by the agreement of the Fathers. The basilica was enlarged and adorned on this occasion with monuments recalling the mysteries of the incarnate Word and the title of the Virgin Mother of God [Col. 0280D], so that it might testify both to the memory of what had been accomplished and to the Church’s universal practice of the worship that was owed.

### 16.

Lest I seem excessive in treating an argument likewise confirmed by each of the individual images adorning both the right and left sides of the basilica, it will suffice to enumerate the surviving ancient mosaics of Xystus and to indicate the testimonies of the Fathers and councils, especially the Council of Ephesus. From these, anyone will be able to recognize that the figures were selected chiefly from the Pentateuch of Moses and from the Book of Joshua, his successor. They present the dogmas of faith declared at the Council of Ephesus and confirmed by Celestine and Xystus in such a way as simultaneously to recount the historical event and prescribe the norm for worship.

We continue along the southern side, where the first and second figures, those of Melchizedek and Abraham, have already been explained. The third follows. From Genesis, chapter 13, it depicts Lot withdrawing, because of quarrels among the shepherds, from the company of his uncle Abraham, the father of all believers, and choosing a dwelling near the fertile fields of Sodom—a disastrous choice, since he observed the crimes of its inhabitants, who shortly afterward would experience divine vengeance [Col. 0281A].

The indication of Blessed Ambrose the Doctor is sufficient for recognizing in this figure a type of the events that took place in his own age in the cause of faith. At that time he himself was contending against the Arian heresy, which was not greatly different from the Nestorian heresy, since both denied Christ’s divinity, although their deception and method differed somewhat. He employed both the oracles of the New Testament and the types sketched in the Old Testament.

The holy Doctor therefore explains the figure of Lot and the quarrels between his shepherds and Abraham’s shepherds:

> “Let us consider, then, who these shepherds are, whose animals they tend, and what quarrel occurred between the shepherds of Abraham and the shepherds of Lot. The shepherds are teachers of flocks. Who, then, are the shepherds of the senses, except instructors and, as it were, rulers of flocks—their leaders—or those who advise us [Col. 0281B] in speech, or the thoughts of our mind? If they understand and hold firmly to pastoral discipline, they do not permit the flock of the senses to wander too far or cling to useless and novel pastures. Rather, as prudent teachers, they call it back, apply the reins of reason, and resist those who struggle against them. But bad teachers, or teachers of useless disputation, allow them to be carried along by their own impulse and to rush into ruin and danger,” and so forth.

Through this type, Xystus, together with Ambrose, teaches that we must not depart from the true doctrine handed down to us by the father of believers, manifested through the only-begotten Son of God, who became among us the firstborn of many brothers in faith, adopted by him as sons of his Father, and entrusted by him to the shepherds of the peoples. We must cling firmly to this doctrine, lest we be involved in a common ruin with the wicked offspring of alien peoples.

### 17.

In the images placed immediately afterward, he proceeds to sketch the type [Col. 0281C] of the heirs of the Abrahamic family—the heirs of paternal blessing and teaching—and to hand on to the people of God the Catholic truths concerning the mystery of the Word taking flesh from the Virgin, confirmed by the Ephesian Fathers.

The three successive panels, together with their mosaics, were entirely destroyed during the construction of the Pauline chapel. We are therefore left only with a desire to know the histories once represented in them. We think that they concerned the sacrifice of Abraham and Isaac and the remaining acts of Isaac up to the final blessing, since types of this kind occur in the same order in Cyril’s books of the *Glaphyra*, as well as in Ambrose’s works arranged according to the sequence of Genesis.

The surviving series therefore expresses the figure of Isaac, the father, conferring a blessing upon his son Jacob, as the sacred text describes it in chapter 27. Cyril explains it in Book III of the *Glaphyra*, especially near the end, where he treats the blessing pronounced by Isaac over Jacob:

> “The power of blessing is transferred once again to Emmanuel himself: ‘Let nations [Col. 0281D] serve you,’ he says, ‘and princes worship you, and be lord of your brother.’ Emmanuel was called the firstborn when he became like us and was numbered among many brothers. Yet for this reason he loses nothing of being God and Lord of all. We worship him as Lord, and he exercised dominion as the God of those who by grace were called to brotherhood. For who, he says, among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, and who shall be like him among the sons of God? Emmanuel therefore exercised dominion as God over those who were brought into brotherhood; and every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth shall bow to him, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

Anyone can understand from Cyril’s words and from the type of the blessing bestowed by Isaac on his son Jacob—explained with the confirming authority of Scripture—that the Nestorian heresy is nailed to the cross. For in the letter to the Queens, contained in Part II of the Council of Ephesus [Col. 0282A], Roman edition, p. 213, Cyril, after citing the testimony of the Epistle to the Philippians mentioned above, concludes:

> “How, then, is he not God who has until now been proclaimed to exist in the glory of divine majesty?”

### 18.

The next figures, continuing through the last two surviving panels on the same wall, encompass the history of the patriarch Jacob. Cyril, the faithful interpreter and likewise the defender of Catholic truth against Nestorius, combines this history almost throughout his commentary with the types of the same dogmas previously examined.

In the ninth panel—for the mosaic of the eighth has perished and was replaced by a recent painting—Jacob the patriarch, received into Laban’s household, promises Laban seven years of service tending the flock in order to obtain Rachel in marriage, and complains that Leah was given to him instead of Rachel. He endures a second seven-year period of labor, represented in the tenth panel, which nevertheless has lost half its mosaic because of the excessive collapse caused by age. Finally, Rachel’s marriage follows, represented in the eleventh mosaic [Col. 0282B].

In all these events Cyril recognizes a figure of Christ, both in his *Book on Worship in Spirit and in Truth*, p. 65 of the Paris edition, and in Book IV of the *Glaphyra on Genesis*, p. 125. Irenaeus preceded Cyril in explaining these matters in *Against Heresies*, Book IV, chapter 38. Justin Martyr, in his *Dialogue with Trypho* against the Jews, near the end, agrees with both. I gladly cite this Father, both because he lived close to the apostolic age and because he provides a kind of model to which Cyril adhered in the method of his explanation. Paul the Apostle had already pointed out the prototype to both of them in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, where through the deeds and faith of the patriarchs, the leaders of Moses’ people, the judges, and the other prophets, he teaches that the mysteries of Christ were prefigured, and that Christ’s two natures—the divine and the human, subsisting in the person of the Word—were presented in these same types. The following figures likewise refer to them, namely:

### 19.

In the twelfth panel, the separation of Laban’s and Jacob’s flocks, from Genesis, chapter 30; and in the thirteenth, the abundance of parti-colored [Col. 0282C] sheep born to Jacob after he had set before them branches of plane trees, stripped of their bark and thrown into the channels where the animals drank.

Cyril clearly explains this figurative application to Christ the Lord in *Glaphyra on Genesis*, Book V, p. 148, beginning with these words:

> “The rod, by figuring him for us, again sketches Emmanuel. Hence he adds: ‘God has taken away all the livestock of your father and given it to me.’”

He then shows that this corresponds perfectly to the divine event:

> “For Christ brought to himself all who are in the world, enclosed the flocks of believers in his own sheepfolds, and possesses riches suited to God and preeminent glory. For he says somewhere to the Father and heavenly God: ‘All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them.’”

Irenaeus had explained it no differently in Book IV, chapter 38:

> “The various sheep that became Jacob’s wages became a type of Christ’s reward, because people from varied and differing nations, coming together into one company of faith, become what the Father promised him: [Col. 0282D] ‘Ask of me,’ he says, ‘and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.’”

In the lower space of the same thirteenth panel is represented Jacob’s meeting with Esau. The same Cyril teaches that this is to be referred to the mystery of Christ in *Glaphyra on Genesis*, Book I, p. 162.

20. The fourteenth and fifteenth mosaic panels belong to the history of Jacob dwelling in the tents at Shechem, when his sons Simeon and Levi, after avenging by the slaughter of the Shechemites the wrong inflicted upon their sister Dinah, are rebuked by their father. He, however, is ordered by God to ascend to Bethel, abandoning the Shechemites, and there to erect an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him when he was fleeing from Esau. Obeying this command, the patriarch ordered all the idols of the nations to be removed by his people; then, after everything had been purified, he built an altar at Luz, naming the place Bethel—that is, “house of God.” Saint Cyril demonstrates that all these events are to be referred to the type of Christ the Lord [Col. 0283A], in book VII of the *Glaphyra on Genesis*, p. 221, when he examines the episode of Dinah and the vengeance of Simeon and Levi.

Blessed Ambrose, however, in *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, book II, chapter 7, after considering Jacob’s gentleness and mercy in the avenging of Dinah—he had received with grief that scene of exacted vengeance—draws out the following interpretation, attested by the same explanations:

> Hence a divine response was given to him who was prophesying the coming of the Lord Jesus: “Arise, ascend to the place of Bethel,” that is, to the house of bread, where Christ was born, as the prophet Micah testified, saying: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata, are not the least among the princes of Judah. For from you shall go forth the ruler of Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” Truly it is the house of bread, which is the house of Christ, who came to us from heaven as saving bread, so that no one might now hunger, acquiring for himself the food of immortality. There the patriarch is commanded to dwell; there to make an altar to God who had appeared to him, etc. How great are the mysteries, since there is the Church of God, in which God appears and speaks [Col. 0283B] with his servants. There the images of the nations are at once removed and hidden. For the faith of the Church has abolished every observance of paganism.

Thus Ambrose. But Cyprian, more briefly than all the others and with testimony especially suited to our subject, confirms the matter when he employs this figure against the Jews, in book II, chapter 6, to prove Christ’s divinity, in these words:

> That Christ is God. In Genesis: “And God said to Jacob: Arise and ascend to the place of Bethel, and dwell there, and make an altar there to that God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of your brother Esau.”

These figures, then, were employed by blessed Xystus in his mosaics and by Cyril to demonstrate Christ’s divinity against the heretics of his time; they had previously been employed by Cyprian against the Jews to establish the same article of faith from the mysteries of the Old Testament.

21. Since the mosaics that followed on this side of the basilica had fallen away, Cardinal Pinelli adorned their panels with recent paintings. We therefore omit them and turn to the remaining figures from the Old [Col. 0283C] Testament brought forward by Xystus and employed by the Ephesian Fathers to signify the doctrines of faith concerning the two natures in Christ, subsisting in the person of the Word, as declared by the authority of that council against the heresy of Nestorius.

Just as, therefore, on the side considered thus far, histories and mysteries had been selected from Genesis to signify this article of faith—mysteries formerly set forth among the Jews and later recognized by the Fathers of the council—so on the opposite side Xystus selected, from the remaining books of the Pentateuch and also from the book of Joshua, events and mysteries that had likewise been examined by the Ephesian Fathers, especially by Cyril in defense of that doctrine.

The first panel on this side, its mosaic having been consumed by age, can no longer display the figures it contained in the time of Xystus. The second, however, and the others preserved down to the nineteenth, show the continuation of Xystus’s work. The second, therefore, divided into two parts, displays in its upper section Moses [Col. 0283D], the infant drawn out of the Nile, presented to Pharaoh’s daughter, and, at her command, nourished by his mother (Exodus II).

Cyril begins his books of the *Glaphyra on Exodus* from this point. In his preface to Palladius he states that he had demonstrated in the preceding books what manner of worship in spirit and in truth should be understood; in the present work, the *Glaphyra on Exodus*, he had reserved those matters by which the mystery of Christ might, as far as possible, be displayed beforehand as though in shadows.

Having set forth, therefore, the history of Moses, born of the tribe of Levi and enclosed by his mother in a basket, floating safely upon the Nile until Pharaoh’s daughter, moved by the infant’s crying, ordered him to be drawn out, preserved, and brought up by his mother, Cyril carefully applies each detail to the type of Christ the Lord:

> Moses, he says, lowered and exposed in a basket of rushes by the hand of his mother, is a clear type of this event. For the synagogue of the Jews also alienated Emmanuel from itself. But Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—even if she had Satan as her father [Col. 0284A], found him at the waters, which bear the type of holy baptism, through which and in which Christ is found.

And so forth. Cyril had drawn this from the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews XI:

> By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful; and they did not fear the king’s decree.

The lower section of the same panel continues with the earlier deeds of Moses as an adult, undertaken in defense of his countrymen, which blessed Paul appended in the passage just cited:

> By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary pleasure of sin, regarding the reproach of Christ as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt . . . By faith he abandoned Egypt, not fearing the king’s wrath.

Accordingly, in this lower part of the panel Moses is shown summoned before the tribunal to answer for the killing of an Egyptian man, whom he had slain in defense of his fellow countryman; sought by Pharaoh for execution, he withdraws into the land of the Midianites [Col. 0284B].

Stephen the protomartyr, in Acts VII, describes this Moses as powerful in words and deeds, but rejected and repudiated by his own people, who said to him: “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?” This Moses, he says, “whom they denied, God sent as ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.” From this Moses they later heard: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.” Blessed Stephen sufficiently explains the direction of this figure and promise concerning Moses by indicating Christ. Following Stephen, Cyril, in the passage of the *Glaphyra* cited above, refers this type to Christ the Lord.

In selecting these figures and presenting them to the Christian people, however, both the Ephesian Fathers and Xystus had before their eyes not only the resemblance of the figure to its prototype. They also established another purpose for their choice: namely, to teach that Christ the Lord, figured in those types, was a light infinitely more excellent than the shadows by which he was foretold.

Hence, among the other testimonies of the Fathers [Col. 0284C] recited at the Council of Ephesus, there is the clear testimony of Theophilus the bishop (p. 203 of the Roman edition of the Council of Ephesus):

> In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages.

There is also the second oration of Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Right Faith to the Queens*, where, from the same Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, an argument is developed from that opening passage. It demonstrates that, from the relation of resemblance previously present in Moses to signify Christ’s high priesthood, Christ the Son and Lord possesses a much greater glory than Moses the minister and servant, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house:

> Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house.

He therefore indicates that through these types the resemblance is contemplated in Christ’s human [Col. 0284D] nature assumed by the Word, but the superiority of the prototype in the same person of the Word and in his divine nature, which he did not abandon; for this reason Christ is truly called God.

> For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God,

namely, that Son of whom Paul had said at the beginning of the Epistle, “through whom he made the ages.”

The entire purpose, therefore, of employing these figures of Christ prefigured in Moses, and also of Joshua son of Nun, which will follow later on this side of the basilica, is the same as that of the Ephesian Fathers when they selected these figures to illuminate the catholic doctrine concerning Christ’s divine and human nature. This doctrine had been foreshadowed in many parts and in many ways by God speaking through the promises of the Law to the fathers through the prophets, but in these last days was openly manifested in the Son himself, who spoke to us, through whom he made the ages, and who, having assumed flesh from the stock of David and Abraham, deigned to dwell among us.

The Roman Church offers us [Col. 0285A] this same testimony of Paul to be read at the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. The Ephesian Fathers wished it to be recited as testimony to the doctrine, and Xystus judged that throughout the entire history of Moses it should also be represented before the eyes of the faithful in the mosaics of the basilica of the Mother of God.

Therefore, as many figures as have here been selected from the deeds of Moses, so many documents of the types of Christ’s divine and human nature do we count as dedicated by Pope Xystus, in accordance with his own teaching, that of his predecessor pontiffs, the Ephesian Fathers, and the whole Church.

22. The mosaic of the next panel depicts Moses celebrating his marriage with Sepphora and the same Moses as a shepherd, feeding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, also called Raguel. Cyril interprets this name as “flock of God” (*Glaphyra on Exodus*, p. 259, Paris edition).

Cyril explains both matters as referring to Christ. First, concerning Sepphora, he says near the end of book II of *Worship in Spirit and in Truth*, p. 78B:

> She was called from the Gentiles while she was following the Law, and, as though joined in marriage with [Col. 0285B] Moses the pedagogue, who most effectively leads to the mystery of Christ. For the Law is a kind of elementary teacher, leading to the beginnings of the sayings of God and implanting in us, through riddles and shadows, certain seeds of the knowledge by which the mystery of Christ is perceived.

Regarding Moses’ pastoral care of the flock of his father-in-law Jethro the priest, who was subsequently called Raguel—that is, “flock of God”—Cyril likewise finds the mystery of Christ in the name:

> For he came under the hand of that supreme prince of all shepherds, namely Christ Jesus, through whom and with whom glory belongs to God the Father, together with the Holy Spirit; hence it is called “the flock of God.”

(*Glaphyra on Exodus*, book I, p. 259E.)

23. In the fourth panel there follows Moses’ return to Egypt with his wife and children, to lead his brethren out of Pharaoh’s slavery. He carries before him the staff which the sacred text calls “the staff of God”: “carrying the staff of God in his hand” (Exodus IV:22). For this reason Cyril and other [Col. 0285C] very ancient Fathers, including Justin Martyr in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 24, regard it as a type of Christ:

> Moses was sent with the staff to redeem the people, and, carrying it in his hand as he went before the people, he divided the sea.

Cyril says:

> The staff, therefore, is the Son of God.

And, indicating this staff in Moses’ type, he says:

> For that was the true sign in which we all believed: that the Word, having become like us, came down to us. This is what the staff thrown upon the ground signifies.

(*Glaphyra*, book II, p. 298C.)

Again, in the scholion *On the Incarnation*, part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 15, Roman edition, fol. 581, where he proves the catholic doctrine that the Word of God remained God even after becoming man, from the symbol of Moses’ staff, he writes:

> “And the staff became in his hand, and he said to him: Do this, so that they may believe you, because the Lord God of your fathers has appeared to you, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Observe in these words the Son of God in nature and truth, as though he were a staff belonging to the [Col. 0285D] Father. The staff is an emblem of royal power. In the Son he possesses authority over all things. Therefore the divine David also says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever, and the staff of uprightness is the staff of your kingdom.” But he threw it upon the ground, that is, he surrounded it with an earthly body, or sent it into the earth through his humanity.

For this reason Xystus’s mosaic displays peoples worshiping in the presence of that same staff, as the sacred text recounts in the same fourth chapter of Exodus:

> And he performed signs before the people, and the people believed; and they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel and had looked upon their affliction, and, bowing down, they worshiped.

24. The fifth panel shows Moses standing among several men dressed in long garments; he addresses them, and a lamb is placed upon an elevated platform. Hence the distinguished Ciampinus thought it was the calf cast by Aaron from the earrings of the Israelite women while Moses was absent.

But the sequence of the Mosaic history ought not to refer to [Col. 0286A] the idol of the calf cast in the desert (Exodus XXXII) before recounting the drowning of Pharaoh, which is narrated in chapter XIII. Nor does the figure of the animal placed upon the elevated base represent a calf; it represents a white lamb.

Therefore, as I believe, it refers to the Paschal law, recounted in Exodus XII: “Let each one take a lamb according to his families,” and so forth. No figure of Christ from the Old Testament is celebrated more frequently by the Church than the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb. Thus this type requires no authorities from individual teachers for its confirmation.

25. In the sixth mosaic, represented by Ciampinus in plate LVII, no. 2, Moses orders the heads of the families, intent upon selecting a lamb from the flock for slaughter, to depart. Below, three stopping-places appear, while Moses preaches from a platform to his countrymen, who have not yet been led to the sea. It seems to depict, from chapter XIII of Exodus, the journey and encampment through those three stopping-places which, according to Jerome in his work to Fabiola on the forty-two stopping-places, the Israelites traversed before the appearance of the pillar of fire by night and the cloud [Col. 0286B] by day—namely, Rameses, Succoth, and Etham.

In precisely the same style we have seen the itineraries of the Roman world arranged on the Peutinger Map by the painters of the age in which Xystus’s mosaics were being composed. Jerome, in that treatise, or Letter CXXVII to Fabiola, proves from Psalm LXX and from the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter X, that all these matters refer to the mysteries of Christ: namely, the departure from Egypt into the wilderness, and the number of forty-two stopping-places, corresponding to the equal number of generations in Christ’s genealogy according to Matthew, are not without this kind of type and figure:

> The Apostle declaring that all these things happened to them in figure, and that all our fathers were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.

26. These final words of the Apostle sufficiently explain the seventh history of Xystus’s mosaic, in which the Hebrews’ passage through the Red Sea is represented, with Pharaoh drowned, from Exodus XIV [Col. 0286C].

The Crypt of the Holy Martyrs, the ancient sarcophagi of Christians of this period, the ritual books, and all the most ancient monuments of the Roman Church very frequently employ this history of Moses to make manifest to the faithful the benefits of our Deliverer and Savior God, and the sacraments formerly shadowed forth in these figures for the Hebrews.

We therefore need no private interpreter in order to understand the intention of Pope Xystus in displaying this event, since the public authority of the Church supplies its explanation through so many documents.

27. The history of the eighth panel is taken from chapters XV and XVI of Exodus. There, when the people murmured against Moses because they were suffering both from a lack of sweet water and from scarcity of food, the Lord appeared to Moses and, in provident mercy, came to the aid of both needs. He showed him a piece of wood, which, when thrown into the water, made the bitter waters sweeter; and he rained quail and manna from heaven for them to eat, so that the ungrateful might cease distrusting and murmuring [Col. 0286D].

There is likewise such an abundance of the Church’s testimonies and such agreement among the Fathers in understanding the mystery of Christ in these figures that they scarcely require explanation. Cyril, in the *Glaphyra on Exodus*, entitles the relevant chapter “On the Manna and the Quail.” After narrating the history, he develops the type as follows:

> Experience and the events themselves most certainly taught them, he says, that God can even now give and prepare a table in the wilderness. Thus, in truth, our Lord Jesus Christ also performed similar miracles when, from five broken loaves, he satisfied a great multitude in the wilderness, filling twelve baskets besides with the fragments.

Cyril then relates the Jews’ undutiful loathing, by which they preferred Egyptian meat to food supplied from heaven, to the rejection of Christ’s teaching and sacraments, transmitted to later generations:

> Something similar happened to the wretched Jews in the time of the Savior. For those things that had then been shown beforehand were shadows and types of what was to come [Col. 0287A]. Since they preferred to the true manna—that is, to Christ, who descended from heaven, can nourish us all, and promises eternal life—the foul and tasteless use of earthly things, they necessarily offended not only God but also Moses himself. For it is written: “The anger of the Lord was kindled against his people,” and Moses also regarded it as evil.

Cyprian had preceded Cyril in this interpretation, writing in Letter LXXVI to Magnus:

> We see the sacrament of this equality celebrated in Exodus, when manna rained down from heaven and, as a prefiguration of future things, displayed the nourishment of heavenly bread and the food of the coming Christ.

Jerome agrees with both of them, writing in the fifth stopping-place, in his work on the forty-two stopping-places:

> Understand Marah as the waters of the western letter. If confession of the cross is cast into them and the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion are joined to them, everything that appears unbearable, sad, and harsh is changed into sweetness.

[Col. 0287B] But let us not weary ourselves searching in the Fathers for what the Lord himself deigned to reveal in the Gospel—both concerning the figure of his sacraments previously presented in the manna and concerning the excellence of his bread, which gives eternal life, over the Mosaic food that did not deliver from death.

He indicates the resemblance when he declares: “This is the bread that came down from heaven.” He attests the difference and superiority of his living bread over the Mosaic bread, which does not rescue from death, when he adds:

> Not as your fathers ate the manna and died. Whoever eats this bread will live forever.

(John VI.)

This had to be explicitly represented in these mosaics, which were to express the deeds of the Council of Ephesus and the documents of its doctrine. For in Act I, p. 363, the impious arch-heretic Nestorius, in Quaternio 4, absurdly explained this promise of our Redeemer and built his blasphemies upon it. The Fathers, on the other hand, opposed this poison with the remedy of legitimate interpretation—both in Theophilus’s exposition against the Origenists, in the chapter entitled “That Christ Is Life and Life-Giving” (p. 189), and in Cyril’s eleventh anathema [Col. 0287C]:

> If anyone denies that the Lord’s own flesh is life-giving, let him be anathema.

(p. 306; and its defense, p. 537), where the doctrine is clearly expressed.

28. The subject of the ninth mosaic is the miracle performed by God through Moses’ staff at the waters of contradiction. None of the Fathers doubts that Moses, the staff, the rock, and the waters drawn from it pertain to the mystery of Christ.

Blessed Cyril, however, most aptly interprets these matters for the argument concerning the catholic doctrine asserted against Nestorius, in the letter addressed to Anastasius and the other monastic Fathers, printed in part III of the Council of Ephesus, Roman edition, p. 703. His words must be given here.

He says concerning Christ the Lord:

> He manifested the truth to us, bringing that worship which existed in shadows and figures to an end.

Then, descending to this event of Moses and to the words of divine [Col. 0287D] Scripture that describe it, he finds an expressed symbol and testimony of the divine and human nature subsisting in him after the flesh had been assumed by the Word:

> They tested him in the testing; they quarreled against him at the waters of contradiction. O marvelous thing! By calling him a man, he immediately declared him God—the one whom Israel provoked and tested both in the wilderness and at the water of contradiction. The Psalmist will confirm this, saying: “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great abyss; he brought water out of the rock and led waters forth like rivers.” And what follows? “They tested him in their heart,” he says, “and spoke evil of God, and said: Can God indeed prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?”

You understand, therefore, how they quarreled against God who was performing miracles, whom Moses also calls a man. For the divine Paul, understanding the matter in the same way, writes:

> They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.

The man, therefore, against whom they quarreled was himself the one who was being tested by the Israelites, not yet incarnate. For it is not the case, as some dare to say, that there was one Son before the flesh and another, different from him, from the seed of David; rather, there was one and the same Son: before the incarnation, the still unembodied Word; after his birth from the holy Virgin, incarnate and made man, as those holy and divine Fathers wrote.

Moses also confirmed this by another sign. For as though someone were asking and wished to learn of what man he had spoken, whom he said had been tested and rebuked by the Israelites, he all but points directly to Jesus and says, “etc.”

29. In the tenth mosaic of Xystus there follows the battle of the Israelites against the Amalekites. Moses raises his hands, supported by Aaron and Hur upon the stone of assistance; Joshua, meanwhile, fights courageously according to Moses’ command [Col. 0288B].

To Palladius, who asked for the mystery of the event—“What is the meaning of this Scripture?”—Saint Cyril, whom I chiefly cite among the Ephesian Fathers, responds in *Worship in Spirit and in Truth*, book III, p. 88:

> I think that nothing is difficult for those who wish to understand. For if someone considers that Moses commanded Joshua, what else can he suspect than precisely this: that, although the Word was God, he became subject to the Law, which pertains to the condition of humanity, and was in a certain manner subjected to Moses’ commands? This occurred in many ways: at one time he endured circumcision according to the flesh, at another he paid the didrachma, and so forth. Although he became subject to the Law on account of his human nature, he was nevertheless even then God, Savior, and Redeemer of the whole people. For when he had chosen powerful men from the whole people of Israel and from every nation—namely, the holy apostles and those who were called through faith, and so forth—he entered into battle [Col. 0288C] with them against the ruler of this world.

The remaining mysteries of this event disclosed there concerning Christ may be seen both in Moses and in the rock upon which he sat, and in the altar he erected:

> When Moses extended his hands, he displayed the form of the cross; and Amalek, in my opinion, signifies precisely those who, through that venerable cross, conquer Satan and prevail against their enemies.

A little later, approaching the words, “They took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side and the other on the other”:

> The precious, chosen, approved cornerstone is Christ. Resting upon him—for sitting signifies rest—those from Israel who are more obedient and teachable, that remnant according to the election of grace, extend their hands, that is, receive the cross. Christ strengthens and sustains them, signified by Hur and Aaron; he is understood as both Judge and high priest. For Hur [Col. 0288D] was a most upright judge, while Aaron was the high priest.

Finally, when the battle and victory were complete, Moses came to the altar he had erected and said:

> After Amalek had been routed and defeated, Moses erected an altar to God and gave it this name: “The Lord is my refuge.” This too presents a figure of Christ. For our Lord became our refuge when he defeated the ruler of this world, trampled upon the dominion of death, and offered himself for us as an immaculate sacrifice, a fragrance of sweetness to God the Father. That altar, therefore, was a figure of Christ, whose fitting and true name is “My Lord, my refuge.”

Before Cyril, Cyprian had recognized the figure of Christ in these same types. In book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 16, he writes:

> This is the stone in Exodus upon which Moses sat at the summit of the hill, when Joshua son of Nun fought against Amalek; and through the sacrament of the stone and the stability of the sitting, Amalek was overcome by Joshua—that is, the devil was conquered by Christ.

And in chapter 21 of the same book:

> By this sign of the cross Amalek was conquered by Joshua through Moses. In Exodus Moses says to Joshua: “Choose men for yourself, go out, and engage Amalek tomorrow. Behold, I shall stand at the summit of the hill, with the staff of God in my hand,” and so forth. “And Joshua routed Amalek and all his people.” And the Lord said to Moses: “Write this for a memorial in a book, and place it in the ears of Joshua, because I shall utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from beneath heaven.”

Jerome also accepts this mystery, writing to Fabiola at the eleventh stopping-place:

> Moses ascends the mountain; Joshua fights against Amalek; by the sign of the cross the enemy is overcome.

Older than both these Fathers, Justin Martyr had agreed with the same interpretation in his *Dialogue against the Jews*, p. 26:

> When the people were waging war against Amalek, and the son of Nun, who was called Joshua—that is, called by the name of Jesus—was in command of the battle, Moses himself prayed to God with his hands extended toward heaven. Aaron supported them throughout the whole day, so that, when he grew weary, he would not lower them. For if he relaxed at any point from that figure which imitates the cross, then, as it is written in Moses, the people were defeated. But if he remained in that position and figure, Amalek alone was defeated, and the people were made strong by the cross. It was not, therefore, because Moses prayed in this manner that the people were superior, but from the beginning of the battle, when the name of Jesus was present, he himself displayed the sign of the cross.

30. In the eleventh panel of Xystus’s mosaics the people’s rebellion is represented. It was caused not by the punishment of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, as Ciampinus thought, but by the return of the spies from the promised land, who had brought back false reports in order to instill terror in their countrymen, as described in Numbers XIII and XIV.

The learned prelate was surprised to see the people in this mosaic driven by fury and lying there, hurling stones against men fleeing to the tabernacle and protected within the cloud by divine assistance [Col. 0289C]. In the sacred text, however, he did not otherwise read that Moses or Aaron had been stoned during the rebellion that arose after the punishments inflicted for the recklessness of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram and of the two hundred and fifty men whom avenging fire had consumed in Numbers XVI. He therefore thought that this was the sedition depicted here.
