In his explanation of plate LX, no. 1, where he arranged for this representation of the Xystine mosaic to be engraved, he remains uncertain about several elements expressed in the mosaic painting that he does not find stated in the sacred text, especially the people attacking with stones the men who had taken refuge within the cloud. He supposes these men to be Moses, Aaron, and Hur, but adds:

> For a long time that group of men troubled me—not merely rushing upon the fugitives, but attacking them with stones; yet this is not at all consistent with the sacred text of any version. Since this appears to be a genuine stoning, etc., I could find no stoning that suited these figures better than the one in which Joshua, chapter VII, destroyed Achan together with his entire household,

and so forth.

He excludes this interpretation from the image of the mosaic because it occurred after the death of Moses; moreover, the Lord’s protection would not have rescued those who were stoned, since they were sources of guilt and were subject to the same punishment under divine law; nor was the place of Achan’s punishment at the tabernacle, but outside the camp. He therefore concludes that the image does indeed represent Moses and Aaron attacked by a rebellious people after the death of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, but that the throwing of stones, which is not mentioned in that rebellion, was added by the painter’s own decision in order somehow to display the fury of the foolish crowd.

With due respect to a prelate who rendered such excellent service to sacred antiquities, I would say that, once his mind had been preoccupied by the opinion he had adopted concerning the later rebellion represented in this panel—the one that followed the destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—he failed to notice that the image should be referred to another rebellion, one that preceded not only the punishment but even the crime and sacrilege of those three men, who rashly advanced to priestly functions not granted to them [Col. 0290A].

There is another rebellion which God declares in Numbers XIV:22 to have been the tenth since these rebellious Israelites had been led out of Egypt. Because they murmured, he excludes them from the number of those who would be brought into the promised land:

> They have now tested me ten times and have not obeyed my voice; they shall not see the land for which I swore to their fathers.

It is therefore established that the history of that tenth rebellion is represented here, since the individual circumstances of the narrative are faithfully recognizable—especially the hurling of stones by the enraged people not only against Moses and Aaron, the leaders of the expedition, but also against Joshua and Caleb, who had been sent to inspect the land. The people continued doing this until those men fled to the tabernacle and were protected by divine assistance. This is how they are represented here—not through the painter’s arbitrary decision and recklessness, but through the careful diligence of Pope Xystus, who prescribed to the mosaicist the outlines of the history from the divine writings.

The sacred text says in Numbers XIV:2:

> All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying, “Would that we had died in the land of Egypt,” and so forth. “Let us appoint [Col. 0290B] a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt.”

When Moses and Aaron heard this, they fell prostrate upon the ground before the whole assembly of the children of Israel. But Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephone, who had also explored the land, tore their garments and spoke to the entire assembly of the children of Israel:

> The land which we traversed is exceedingly good, etc. Do not rebel against the Lord . . . The Lord is with us; do not fear.

And when the whole multitude cried out and wanted to overwhelm them with stones, the glory of the Lord appeared over the roof of the tent of covenant to all the children of Israel. The Lord said to Moses:

> How long will this people insult me? How long will they refuse to believe me, despite all the signs that I have performed before them? etc. In this wilderness your corpses shall lie.

When we consider the words employed by the sacred text in the history of this rebellion and compare them with what blessed Cyril wrote in the explanation just given above, it is clear that the same mysteries of Christ’s divinity, foreshadowed in both passages, are applicable in both cases [Col. 0290C]. The rebellion against Moses is also called a rebellion against the Lord God—that is, against Christ the Lord, signified in the same type of Moses, Aaron, and Joshua as lawgiver, high priest, and leader of the people who were to be brought into the promised land.

The rebellious and unbelieving Jewish nation was considering the appointment of another leader, by whom it might be brought back to Egypt, the land of slavery and darkness. Accordingly, the mysteries detected by Cyril above apply equally to this rebellion:

> You understand, therefore, how they quarreled against God who was performing miracles, whom Moses also calls a man.

Cyril confirms this explanation from the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, which also confirms the matter. For when Paul begins, in the third chapter of that Epistle, to prove that Christ, as the Son of God, is far more excellent than Moses, the servant in God’s house, he proceeds to a serious admonition that we should not depart from faith in Christ by imitating the unbelief and rebellion of the Jews [Col. 0290D] against Moses, expressed in the event from Numbers just recited and represented in the mosaic.

He introduces the same words from Numbers XIV:37 to indicate the hardness and provocation of the rebels against the Lord, which we must avoid:

> We have become partakers of Christ, Paul says, if only we hold the beginning of his substance firm to the end . . . For some who heard provoked him, but not all who came out of Egypt through Moses. And with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

### 31

In the twelfth panel, which Ciampinus reproduced on Plate LX, no. 2, Moses hands over to the Levites the scroll of Deuteronomy, to be kept in the ark, as we read in Deuteronomy 32:

> “After Moses had written the words of this law in a scroll and completed it, he commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, saying: ‘Take this book and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, so that it may be there as a testimony against you.’”

In that scroll, which is called the second law, or Deuteronomy—its very name also indicating the new law of Christ, which was to serve as a testimony against the unbelieving Jews concerning the things previously set forth in the first law—it was shown, in these words, that the people would be led into the promised land through Jesus and not through Moses:

> “And Moses summoned Jesus and said to him before all Israel: ‘Be strong and courageous. For you shall enter before this people into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers that he would give them, and you shall distribute it to them by lot; and the Lord himself will go with you. He will not abandon you or forsake you. Do not fear, and do not be afraid.’”

After Cyril had quoted this from Deuteronomy 31, p. 429, he adds an exposition of the type and mystery fulfilled in Christ Jesus:

> “When the excellent Moses,” he says, “was about to depart from human affairs and afterward be transferred to the dwellings above, the divine Jesus was in a certain sense substituted for him and succeeded him in authority. For when the old and ancient letter, together with the legal worship, had, as I have already said, almost come to an end, the Only-Begotten descended to us from heaven and became man. Although, as God, he was Lord of all and possessed from the beginning the splendor of dignity in this matter, he nevertheless humbled himself in such a way that, because of his likeness to us, he seemed to have been called to the beginning of kingship. Hence he himself says: ‘I have been appointed king by him’—namely, by God and the Father—‘upon his holy mountain of Zion, declaring his commandment.’ Therefore let no one again bring Moses back to us, for he has yielded to Christ’s glory; nor let types continue to prevail, nor let anyone put forward a shadow.”

This single exposition of Cyril’s, which agrees in every respect with the other symbols expressed in these mosaics—and especially with the first, concerning Abraham and Melchizedek, which presents the same argument as Paul the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews, written concerning the divinity of Christ the Lord and the infinite superiority that follows from his divinity over the Mosaic types—is, I say, by itself sufficient to prove that these mosaic images executed in the Sistine [Xystine] church refer to the Catholic doctrine defended at the Council of Ephesus against the Nestorian heresy. At that council the Fathers, especially Cyril, who presided, employed testimonies of this kind collected from both Testaments.

> “With Moses therefore removed,”—to return with Cyril to the image under discussion, in which Moses hands the second law, or Deuteronomy, to the priests and appoints Joshua in his place—“and taken away from their midst, Christ arose in a certain sense and was declared our leader. Through him and in him, having been transferred to the kingdom of heaven, we shall obtain eternal and genuine happiness, leading a holy life free from every fault.”

He rightly observes that, once Moses has been removed, Jesus is substituted as leader of the Israelites. This too is represented by the Sistine mosaic panel. For in it we see Moses, in the low plains of Moab, handing the scroll of Deuteronomy to the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, so that it might be enclosed in the ark and reread every seventh year, when the year of remission came around, at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 31). In the same mosaic panel Moses is shown, summoned by God, proceeding toward Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah opposite Jericho (ibid., 34), where, in accordance with the revelation previously announced to him, he completed his life.

This symbolic prefiguration of the Christian law through Deuteronomy enclosed in the ark, and of the superiority of Jesus, our God and Leader, over Moses, the faithful servant, could be confirmed by numerous testimonies of other Fathers: namely, Irenaeus, book IV *Against Heresies*, chapters 2 and 3, who says, “The words of Moses are the words of Christ”; and chapter 50 of the same book, a passage I shall cite in the exposition of the next image; and Jerome, who writes in his letter to Paul: “Deuteronomy also is a second law and a prefiguration of the evangelical law,” etc.; and Justin Martyr, who, in his dialogue with Trypho, speaks as follows concerning Jesus Nave, Moses’ successor and a type of Christ:

> “Just as he introduced the people into the holy land—not Moses—and just as he divided it by inheritance among those who entered with him, so Christ also will convert the dispersion of the people and distribute the good land to each person, though not in the same manner. For the former gave them an inheritance that would last for a time, since he was neither God nor the Son of God; but the latter, after the holy resurrection, will give us an eternal possession.”

These testimonies, I say, could be collected from such Fathers, who were earlier than Cyril, to prove that the interpretation of the figure was not invented by Cyril, but was given in accordance with the consensus of the Fathers. It was therefore also reported by Xystus among the selected testimonies of so great a man, whether acting in the synod in the place of Celestine or as his representative, in defense of the doctrine there championed by the Catholics.

The lower part of the same mosaic displays the Levites carrying the ark of the covenant, with the scroll of Deuteronomy enclosed within it according to Moses’ command, and the mystery of Christ shut up, as it were, in the ark for the unbelieving people of the Jews; but opened for us in the Gospel after the year of redemption and freedom, when we were happily called to the tabernacles of the children of God.

### 32

We come to the thirteenth image of the Sistine mosaic, in which the history of Joshua is represented as he begins the leadership entrusted to him after Moses’ death. Justin Martyr, cited shortly before, is an apt interpreter of the figure of Christ the Lord signified by Joshua’s succession:

> “Thus he reproved the unbelieving Trypho. ‘Jesus,’ as I said earlier, who is often called *Auses*, was the one who, together with Caleb the scout, was sent into the land of the Canaanites and was called Jesus. You do not ask why this was done; you do not hesitate or desire to learn. Therefore you do not know Christ, and, though reading, you do not understand. Even now, when you hear that Jesus Christ is our own, you do not reflect or conclude that this name was given to him neither without reason nor at random. But you discuss why one letter was added to Abraham’s earlier name; and likewise, with polished argument, you debate why one letter was added to Sarah’s name. Yet you do not ask why the name Auses, which the son of Nave had from his father, was changed entirely into the name Jesus. Nor, in the same way, do you ask why not only his name was changed, but also why, after he had succeeded Moses, he alone of those who had left Egypt at that age led the people into the holy land.’” etc.

Irenaeus agrees with Justin in chapter 50 of book IV *Against Heresies*:

> “The entire departure of the people from Egypt, which was brought about by God, was a type and image of the departure of the Church that was to come from the Gentiles. For this reason, bringing her out at the end, he leads her into her inheritance—not Moses, the servant of God, but Jesus, the Son of God, will give it to her as an inheritance.”

Justin reports that he received this from the more ancient presbyter John, who was almost of apostolic times. Tertullian also agrees with them in *Against the Jews*, p. 116 of the edition.

This same mosaic panel contains, from the earlier deeds of Joshua, the episode in which the scouts sent by him to Jericho were received in the house by Rahab. She took precautions for the safety of her guests when, after being lowered through the window so that they might not be captured by the ruler’s guards and subjected to the ultimate punishment, they used the very scarlet cord by which they had been lowered to secure their escape. They left it hanging in the window as the sign by which their female hostess was to be rescued from the destruction of her fellow citizens, when the victorious Israelites entered and plundered the captured city (Joshua 2).

Although the authority of the Apostle Paul amply proves that the symbol of this figure refers to faith in Christ—for in the Epistle to the Hebrews, among the other beginnings of Christ’s mysteries prefigured in the ancient law, he enumerates this one, saying in chapter 11, verse 31, “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace”—nevertheless, interpreters, including the ancient Fathers, approach the Apostle’s concise style not inappropriately. Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue* recently employed to explain the preceding figures, p. 31B, says:

> “For the sign of the scarlet and purple cord which the scouts gave to Rahab the prostitute at Jericho—those scouts who had been sent by Jesus the son of Nave—advising her to tie it to the window through which she had lowered them, so that they might depart secretly without the knowledge of their enemies, likewise signified the sign of Christ’s blood. Through that blood, those who were once adulterers and unjust among all the nations, having received remission and forgiveness of sins, now obtain salvation by no longer committing sin.”

Three doctors of the Church adhere to Justin Martyr’s interpretation: Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine. Jerome does so in his letter to Nepotian on the life and conduct of clergy, p. 13 of the Roman edition, vol. I; Ambrose in book V *On the Faith*, chapter 4; and Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 86, whom the Council of Ephesus and Pope Xystus reach in time; Pope Xystus,

> “adding the weight of his support to theirs in this mosaic,” so that we might recognize the mysteries of Joshua, Moses’ successor, and the sacrament of the Lord’s blood, displayed in the scarlet cord, with Rahab representing the Church by faith, in the window—so that her house might be saved,” as Jerome says, “while Jericho perished.”

From this point, therefore, the sequence of Joshua’s deeds begins to be laid beneath the footsteps of Christ, who impressed these temporal signs of eternity upon the law in order to lead us from the shadow of death into the splendor of the saints and into his own wondrous light.

### 33

The fourteenth panel in its mosaic preserves for us the image of the crossing of the Jordan under Joshua, described in chapters 4 and 5 of his book. In the dried bed of the Jordan stand the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord. At that place twelve stones are seen, set up by Joshua as a memorial of the event, while an equal number, taken from there, are carried on the shoulders of the Israelites to be set up at Gilgal, as a future memorial for posterity of the Lord’s mighty hand, which thus led his people across the streams of the Jordan on dry ground.

It was in this river, according to Augustine (vol. X, *Appendix*, sermons 25 and 36), that Christ’s teaching began. The Israelite forces

> “follow Jesus, their leader, carrying the ark of the Lord, with the cloud withdrawn as though the veil had been removed”

(the same Augustine, *Questions on Joshua*, question 3).

Everything is filled with types of Christ the Lord. It would be lengthy to compare each one with the harmonious exposition of the Fathers. Let us stay with Cyril, since he was the standard-bearer of the Ephesian Fathers in defending the divinity and humanity of our Savior God. He not only, together with Celestine, Xystus, and those Fathers, produced clear testimonies of the New Covenant, brighter than the sun; he also extracted from the Old Testament these types and shadows, prefigured in the law and the prophets, of the truth to be manifested at the coming of the Son of God.

Cyril therefore, in the *Glaphyra* on Deuteronomy, p. 426, observes that the collection of twelve large stones from the bed of the Jordan, which Joshua was commanded to carry out, had been prescribed by God through Moses (Deuteronomy 27):

> “When, therefore, you have crossed the Jordan, set up the stones which I command you today on Mount Ebal, and smooth them with plaster; and write upon the stones all the words of this law plainly and clearly.”

Cyril explains the mysteries expressed in nearly every verse, prefacing them with this general conception received from the Apostle Paul:

> “For this reason,” he says, “the divine Moses also placed a veil over his face. By this, I believe, he signified to those who were more discerning that the law is twofold, that the truth lies hidden within, and that a shadow has been cast over it like a mask; and that external things are a kind of superfluous covering of the inner and hidden things. The book of Deuteronomy therefore teaches us that the teachers of the new covenant in Christ will indeed employ the discourse given through him for a time, and that they will lead people to the truth and provide a clearer exposition of the letter by interpreting it spiritually.”

From this he proceeds to the individual symbols of the law and revelation of Christ the Lord, written upon the twelve great stones. He interprets them as the choir of the apostles, who, after the crossing of the Jordan—that is, after receiving the saving baptism of Christ the Lord—clearly reveal his divine mysteries to us. Through them we received the right of eternal inheritance, handed down to us by our leader Jesus, so that his promises might not fail.

Rightly, therefore, did Celestine rebuke Nestorius because

> “he had removed from the symbol handed down by the apostles those words which promise us the hope of the whole of life and salvation. For these things,” he says in Celestine’s letter to Nestorius, published in the Roman edition of the Council of Ephesus, p. 278, “were handed down to us by the apostles fully, completely, and openly; they admit neither addition nor diminution. We read in our books that nothing ought to be added and nothing taken away.”

Cyril teaches that these same meanings are expressed in the twelve stones taken from the Jordan, which bear the type of Christ’s apostles:

> “These great stones,” he says in the passage cited, “set in their place signify the choir of the holy apostles, etc. The stones, coated with plaster, bear Scripture, namely, the law, in a very explicit form. For in the holy apostles we shall find the contemplations of the law subtly and clearly—not any longer shadowed by the letter, nor possessing a dark veil and shadow, but radiance and purity.”

### 34

Next, in the fifteenth panel, from the same history of Joshua, he is shown approaching the city of Jericho to besiege it. He sees a man and hears from him that he has come as the commander of the army of the Lord. Joshua prostrated himself and worshiped him, in order to carry out his commands. Again the Lord appears to Joshua and promises that the city will be captured by him. Joshua, chapters 5 and 6.

Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue*, p. 18, greatly illuminates this type, showing that it concerns Christ the Lord. Indeed, he inclines toward the view that the divine Word himself, under the appearance of an angel and a man, presented himself as the commander of the army and prefigured his coming in our flesh, which he was to assume at the appointed time:

> “I shall bring you testimony from the Scriptures, by which I shall show that God, in the beginning, before all created things, generated from himself a certain rational power participating in reason. This is also called by the Holy Spirit the glory of the Lord, sometimes the Son, sometimes Wisdom, sometimes an angel, sometimes God, at other times Lord and Word. It is also occasionally called the commander of the army, when it appeared in human form to Jesus the son of Nave, etc. The Word of Wisdom testifies that this very one is God, begotten from the Father of all things, and that he is the Word, power, and glory of the one who begot him, as Solomon said these things, among others, etc.”

After inserting a few words, he again affirms that this very God, the Son of God the Father and Wisdom, appeared to Jesus the son of Nave near the closed and fortified city of Jericho, just as Xystus represents him in this mosaic, based on Joshua 5:

> “When Jesus was at Jericho, he saw a man standing near him, and, approaching, asked him, ‘Are you one of ours or one of the enemy?’” etc.

There Justin joins together several such apparitions reported in the Pentateuch and Heptateuch: the one made to Abraham at the oak of Mamre in Genesis; Jacob’s wrestling with the angel; the one seen by Moses in the bush in Exodus; and this one near Jericho in Joshua. In each he observes that the one who appeared is called equally a man, an angel, and God. From this he concludes that it was truly the divine Word who appeared under the form of a man, an angel, or a commander, while at the same time asserting himself to be God. Thus those holy men who were trained by faith in expectation of the coming Christ might become accustomed, through these types and figures, to worship God and man—the one person of the Word—who through the mystery of the incarnation was promised both to them and to us.

From this doctrine, confirmed by Justin in the several apparitions mentioned, Cyril selects one—to indicate through one the meaning of the others—in his exposition of the Creed, which is read in the first part of the first session of the Council of Ephesus, Roman edition, p. 702. It is the apparition during Jacob’s wrestling, where a man is said to have appeared wrestling with him, and where Jacob subsequently calls that man God: “I have seen God face to face.” Cyril then adds the cause of the mystery and symbol, which is likewise applicable to the others together with Justin’s interpretation:

> “For God was indicating beforehand to the patriarch that his Only-Begotten Word would at some time become man.”

After a few intervening words he adds:

> “Nevertheless, consider this: when a man wrestled with him, he says that he saw the Lord face to face, and he calls him the form of God. For the Word of God, even after becoming man, remained in the form of the Father, according to the spiritual image, and wholly unchangeable according to nature.”

Justin recognizes these same meanings in the other apparitions and, indeed, in the one represented here in the mosaic: Joshua sees a man near Jericho, worships him, and calls him Lord. When Trypho asks him to show that the Word of God, the Son and Wisdom, wished to be born as man from a virgin, Justin answers:

> “This too has already been demonstrated by me in those passages of the prophecies which I have previously cited.”

The last of those passages had been this very apparition of a man to Joshua, commanding him to remove the sandals from his feet and promising victory over the besieged city of Jericho. Xystus therefore rightly joins this apparition in the mosaic to the others produced by Cyril and the other Ephesian Fathers, according to ancient tradition, in defense against Nestorius of the Catholic doctrine that, after the incarnation, the one person of the Word subsists in two natures and constitutes one Christ, God and man.

### 35

In the sixteenth panel the walls of the city of Jericho, besieged by the Israelites under Joshua, are seen collapsing and falling while trumpets sound and the priests carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord around the city seven times. The Apostle Paul explicitly relates this symbol to faith and the mysteries of Christ:

> “By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days” (Hebrews 11:30).

Jerome, a distinguished interpreter of the mystery, approaches the same interpretation in book I *Against Jovinianus*, Roman edition, p. 505:

> “Because the Lord’s army was armed in this way with priestly trumpets, as though for evangelical preaching, the world is overthrown under the type of Jericho.”

Jerome says much in the same passage to present the symbolic relations of Joshua to Christ the Lord. From these we shall also illuminate the remaining mosaic panels that follow.

For the present, however, let us rest with the explanation given shortly before by Jerome: the priestly trumpets sounding seven times around Jericho and the ark of the Covenant being carried around it seven times signify the powerful sound of evangelical preaching and the unconquerable strength of the Word of God, carried into the Church as into an ark by the gathered priests, for the destruction of the fortifications of the enemies. This type is all the more aptly applied to the events of the Council of Ephesus because the total number of circuits of God’s ark around the walls, or strongholds, of the enemies of the truth corresponds precisely to the number seven of the council’s sessions.

The conquest of the city of Jericho represented in this panel must also necessarily be connected with the apparition of the man worshiped by Joshua in the preceding panel. For the Fathers cited above, who believe that the Son of God himself then appeared under the form of a man in order to prefigure the mystery of the incarnation, recognize in the human form in which he appeared a type of the human nature to be assumed by the Word. In the same way they testify that the divine nature was indicated by the prediction and promise concerning the city’s conquest, which he soon confirmed by deed.

Other Fathers, however, believe that it was not the person of the Word who spoke with Joshua, but an angel sent by God—namely, the archangel Michael, according to most interpreters—since he is called the Prince of the army of the Lord (Joshua 5:14). They likewise refer the episode to the confession and symbol of the divine and human natures to be joined, at the appointed time, in the one person of the Word through the mystery of the incarnation. Since the angel then displayed, in a certain sense, a representative image of that person, he appeared as a man; and at the same time Joshua was seen prostrate at his feet, so that he might worship the majesty of the Lord, from whom he understood that the angel sent to him displayed the figure of the one who was to come, the angel of the Great Counsel, and our leader, as Jerome writes on Psalm 76:

> “Jesus himself, our leader, holds the sword; he always goes before us, fights for us, and conquers our adversaries.”

In a word, these two visions are, so to speak, twin visions: the man wrestling with Jacob at Luz and the man appearing to Joshua at Jericho. Justin Martyr recognizes the same symbol in both, namely, Christ the Lord, prefigured as God and man.

The same mystical meaning therefore applies to both, which Cyril explains concerning the first in the *Scholion on the Incarnation*, part III of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 25, Roman edition, p. 584:

> “The sense of the Scriptures is indeed mystical,” he says, “etc. Nevertheless, it is certain that the one who wrestled with Jacob was a man, since Jacob called him the face of God. Nor was that all: he knew that he was truly God. ‘I have seen God face to face,’ he says, ‘and my soul has been saved.’ For Emmanuel is God by nature. He is also called the face of God, for he is the form of the Father’s substance. He called himself this among the Jews when he said concerning God and the Father: ‘You have neither seen his face nor do you have his word remaining in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent.’ That the man who wrestled with Jacob was truly God is again confirmed by the sacred writings. For, it says, the Lord spoke to Jacob: ‘Rise, go up to the place of Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.’

> “The other vision, too—that of the armed man seen by Joshua and asked, ‘Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?’—reveals the notion of a man. This notion is joined to the notion of God when Joshua, worshiping the same man, says: ‘My Lord speaks to his servant.’”

Both symbols therefore refer equally to the doctrine of faith declared at the Council of Ephesus and vindicated there against the Nestorian heresy. For this reason Xystus included them among the other documents expressed in his mosaics.

### 36

The seventeenth panel is adorned with the battle undertaken by the Israelites under Joshua against the five Amorite kings, described in chapter 10 of his book. In it the camps of the allied kings were thrown into confusion not only by the swords of the Israelites and by strength confirmed by God, but also by enormous stones sent from heaven like hail.

Two succeeding panels also belong to the history of that same chapter 10, and they are the last of those preserved from the ravages of time. In one, the mosaic represents the sun and moon, the two lights, commanded by Joshua to stand still until he had destroyed the enemies. In the other, the five fugitive kings who had withdrawn into caves are brought out at the command of the victorious Joshua.

We shall explain the three panels together, since they belong to the same history of the defeat of the five kings who stood in the way of the Israelites’ attaining the inheritance of the promised land designated for them by God, which Joshua was to distribute to them individually.

Pope Celestine seems to have had this episode in mind when, after the Council of Ephesus, he congratulated the common victory of the faithful people in his letter to the clergy and people established at Constantinople, Roman edition, p. 64:

> “For Nestorius—incited, as we read, by him from whom he derived [the wording is uncertain]—was attempting to take away from you, the legitimate sons of God, your inheritance. We believe, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, that because of your faith you will be both heirs of God and co-heirs of our Christ. He was therefore not permitted to carry off the palm from you; rather, you triumphed over him through the arms of faith. You are victors—or rather, this is the victory of the common King over the enemy. The excluded tyrant speaks of victory. He whose divinity was thought capable of being made uncertain has conquered in you.”

Joshua had worshiped the divinity of the man who appeared, declaring himself to be the commander and prince of the Lord’s army. At his command Joshua carried the ark of the Covenant around Jericho, and, according to Jerome, raised the priests’ trumpets, the heralds of evangelical preaching, to sound. When the walls of Jericho had been thrown down, he destroyed its hostile king and offered to God as anathema all the spoils of the enemies. Soon afterward he defeated and routed the five allied kings in a single battle and through many miracles, so that they sought hiding places in caves. Then he ordered them to be brought out and trampled under the feet of the victors, and finally, after they had suffered the ultimate punishment, to be thrown dead into the same cave in which they had hidden as fugitives.

That all these deeds and prodigies accomplished by the outstanding leader Joshua are to be referred to the type of Christ the Lord is so certain from the consensus of the Fathers that it requires no proof. The leader’s very name is an evident indication of this relationship, as interpreters observe when they read his praise in the book of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 46:

> “Strong in war was Jesus the son of Nave, successor of Moses among the prophets, who was great according to his name, greatest for the salvation of God’s elect.”

For the name Jesus, or Joshua, means “Savior,” and is referred to God’s elect. The manner in which Joshua was greatest for the salvation of God’s elect follows in the words added by the Church:

> “To defeat the enemies who rose up, so that they might obtain the inheritance of Israel.”

Saint Cyril explains Joshua as a symbol of Christ in his work *Against Julian*. Saint Jerome, however, presents this most brilliantly in several places, especially in book I *Against Jovinianus*, p. 504. I shall give only the beginning of his extensive comparison here, so as not to transcribe several pages of the holy doctor on an argument sufficiently clear:

> “I shall proceed,” he says, “to Jesus the son of Nave, who was formerly called Ause, or, as it is more correctly found in Hebrew, Osee, that is, ‘Savior.’ For, according to the Epistle of Jude, he saved the people of Israel and led them out of Egypt and brought them into the promised land. This Jesus, as soon as he came to the Jordan,” etc.

From the blessed doctor and from other Fathers who lived close to or before the time of Xystus, I shall select shorter statements that relate the type of Joshua to the doctrine concerning Christ the Lord defended at the Council of Ephesus.

Jerome, therefore, in his commentary on Isaiah 28, in the *Epitaph of Paula*, and in *Against Jovinianus*, concisely designates the image of Christ in Joshua through the miracle of the heavenly bodies stopping their courses at Joshua’s command, so that the Israelites’ victory over the Amorites might be completed:

> “Jesus spoke with confidence in the God dwelling within him; the sun stood still.”

Here it must be observed that Jerome was speaking of Joshua as a mere man and as an imperfect figure of Christ when he said of him, “He spoke with confidence in the God dwelling within him,” and that the sun stood still. He understood that something different must be said of Christ the Lord, who accomplished these things not through confidence in God dwelling within him, but through the divine power proper to himself, since he himself existed as God—as Athanasius says, cited by Cyril in defense of the eleventh anathema of the Council of Ephesus, fol. 539.

For Jerome too, together with Athanasius, had learned from the Apostle Paul what he wrote to the virgin Principia: that in Christ “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). He did not receive, as did his servants Noah, Moses, and the other righteous, a grace received from another distinct from himself; rather, he himself, from his own divine substance, poured out grace and power upon all, so that through his gift they might accomplish what he himself, by his own power, as Lord of grace and nature, brought about by commanding both grace and nature.

The likeness of the type, therefore, lies in the authority to command that Joshua exercised when he represented Christ. For this reason, in the faith and figure of Christ, he commanded both heavenly lights, indicating the complete authority to command that is inseparable from Christ the Lord and innate in him by nature. He himself said, and they came to be, since he is the Word through whom all things were made. He communicated such authority to his servants, who among human beings bore a temporary and shadowy type and image of his majesty.

Concerning the five kings defeated by Joshua and displayed in the final panels proposed by Pope Xystus from the surviving mosaic, blessed Jerome, directing attention to the type of Christ expressed through Joshua and to his victory, by which obstacles to attaining the promised inheritance are removed for us who have been called to it, writes in book I *Against Jovinianus*:

> “To pass over countless matters—for it is not my present purpose to disclose all the mysteries of the Old Testament—the five kings who had previously resisted and opposed the evangelical army in the promised land were defeated while Jesus fought.”

The order of the victory was this: when the Israelite army first rushed against the fleeing enemies, enormous stones sent from heaven like hail crushed the fugitives and killed many more of them by their blows than the swords of the victors had previously cut down. This part of the victory is represented in the penultimate panel.

The final panel depicts the five kings being brought out of their caves and placed before Joshua, so that the mighty leader might inflict punishment upon the defeated. After the soldiers had been struck by the swords of the Israelites and by the heavenly hail, such terror seized the kings that they sought hiding places in caves. Joshua ordered that they be discovered by careful search and brought before him. The remaining portion of the mosaic has been lost through the damage caused by its great age.

It is highly probable that, in the few panels enclosing the circuit of the central nave, the end of Joshua’s history and the succession of the principal Judges were represented: Gideon, Barak, and Samson. Blessed Paul enumerates these in the cited chapter 11 of the Epistle to the Hebrews among those who through faith conquered kingdoms. That is, as figures of Christ, they would announce beforehand to posterity the truth of the Catholic doctrine defended at the Council of Ephesus, concerning the divinity and humanity of Christ, which are to be worshiped.

For it was customary, both for Cyril and for the Fathers who flourished before him, to borrow mystical testimonies from the Old Testament concerning that doctrine which, in the New Testament, had been set forth more clearly through the truth manifested by the Son of God.

Thus Justin, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, where he argues against Jews who denied Christ’s divinity, imitates Paul and Stephen by enumerating the figures of Christ prefigured in the patriarchs, leaders, judges, priests, and kings of the Old Testament. Tertullian did the same in *Against the Jews* and *Against Marcion*. Cyprian followed him, as others have noted (de la Barre, at the end of the argument of Tertullian’s work *Against the Jews*, p. 98A), in his treatise *To Quirinus*.

Cyril, however, perhaps more successful in method than the others and more abundant in the number of types, carried this out splendidly both in the *Glaphyra* and in his books *Against Julian*. He was given the opportunity to illuminate through figures of the ancient covenant that doctrine which he had confirmed at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius with so many oracles of the New Testament.

The Roman See found Cyril’s views so consistent with those of the apostles and with its own that Pope Celestine, who had been declared president of the council in his own name, wrote to him:

> “Indeed, beloved brother, we too would have added certain things, unless we had seen that you likewise think and hold all the same things that we think and hold.”

And Xystus, Celestine’s successor, gathering in these mosaics the testimonies of the Council of Ephesus and of the Catholic truth defended there by Cyril, seems to subscribe to Celestine’s letter through these images dedicated in our basilica:

> “This is truly a great triumph of our faith: namely, that you have so powerfully proved what is ours, and so forcefully defeated through the testimonies of the divine Scriptures the things opposed to it.”

(*Letter of Saint Celestine to Saint Cyril*, in the Roman edition of the Council of Ephesus, p. 274.)

These were the matters I had to treat in this dissertation concerning the ornaments added by Saint Xystus to the Basilica of Liberius during its enlargement—not only to illuminate the history of this pontiff and his works, but also to place in the same light the care and foresight of his predecessors and successors in selecting the ornaments of sacred buildings. Through venerable images these ornaments would kindle minds toward the true worship of God, both impressing upon them the memory of what had been accomplished and displaying revealed doctrine, according to which our faith renders the offerings of due worship.

### Note

**[Col. 0299A]**

No. 63, line 4—“And when the assembly had been held,” etc. Somier, p. 259. Certain ancient acts (in Baronius under the year 433, no. 320 and following) mention a judgment pronounced by Pope Xystus in his own case, just as a similar opportunity is reported in the case of other pontiffs, against Bassus and Martinianus, his calumniators. The *Liber Pontificalis* touches on these matters to some extent.

Other acts, however, report a judgment pronounced by the same pontiff against Polychronius, bishop of Jerusalem (in Binius under Xystus III), and against another bishop, Euphemius. But since such Acts contain certain features indicating that their reliability is suspect, we shall refrain from using them here [Col. 0299B]. For we have determined, amid the almost infinite abundance of events that we examine, to employ only testimonies of indisputable certainty.

In the history of Sixtus, however, these documents, which are subject to no doubt, must be taken into account; they are listed in chapter 24 of Book IV by the same Archbishop Somier, namely, Augustine’s Letters 104 and 105 to the same Sixtus concerning the Pelagians. In the first, the holy Doctor declares that those who, after the condemnation pronounced by an unmistakable judgment of the Apostolic See, had suddenly fallen silent concerning those pernicious errors but nevertheless did not provide a sufficiently secure proof of their healing, must be compelled not only to remain silent about those false doctrines but also to defend the truths opposed to them with the same zeal with which they had been accustomed to defend the falsehoods. In the second letter, he praises the letter sent by Sixtus to Aurelius of Carthage, which clearly displayed Sixtus’s own firmness against the aforesaid errors. Here [Col. 0299C] Augustine’s splendid observation concerning the letter sent by the Apostle Paul to the Romans must also be noted: he commends the grace of God so greatly “that from there his preaching, as though from the head of the world—that is, Rome—might spread throughout the whole world.”

Sixtus’s own letters to John of Antioch and Cyril of Alexandria must also be considered: they bear witness to his exceptional eminence, and to the plainly apostolic providence and solicitude demonstrated in those same letters [Col. 0300A]. Sixtus orders that they be transmitted through those bishops for the information of the other bishops, “so that they may learn about so great a matter and, even if everything was once most fully defined, the Apostolic See nevertheless does not cease. For concern for all the Churches does not permit us to be at rest from such cares.”

Vincent of Lérins, in the final chapter of the *Commonitorium against Heresies*, speaks of Sixtus’s letter to John of Antioch as an outstanding defense of the ancient doctrine against the plots and errors of innovators:

“We have added,” he says, “the twofold authority of the Apostolic See . . . Pope Sixtus, in the letter which he sent to the bishop of Antioch concerning the case of Nestorius, says: ‘Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, there is one faith, let us believe what has evidently prevailed, and let us declare what must be held.’ Finally, after setting out what must be held and believed, he says: ‘Let innovation have nothing further permitted to it, because nothing should be added to antiquity. Let the clear faith of our forebears, and their belief uncontaminated by any admixture of mud, remain undisturbed.’ It was wholly apostolic [Col. 0300B]: it adorned the belief of the forebears with the light of clarity, but portrayed new profanities as an admixture of mud,” and so forth.

Saint Prosper noted the following in his *Chronicle* under the year 440 concerning Sixtus’s zeal and providence against the Pelagians:

“At this time,” he says, “Julian of Arles, a most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for the episcopate he had long ago lost was driving onward, attempted by various arts of deception, while presenting the appearance of correction, to creep back into the communion of the Church. But Pope Sixtus, vigilantly meeting these plots at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no entrance to the pestilential designs. Thus he made all Catholics rejoice at the downfall of the deceitful beast, as though he had then for the first time cut down the most arrogant heresy with the apostolic sword.”

The same Saint Prosper, at the end of his work *Against the Collator*, speaks as follows of Sixtus’s successful labor:

“Let this portion be reserved for this shepherd: and just as his predecessors, Innocent, [Col. 0300C] Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, drove away manifest wolves, so may he drive away those who are concealed.”

In our own age Clement XI renewed, by Sixtus’s example, the ancient victories of the Apostolic See against the enemies of God’s grace and human freedom. His predecessors, Innocent X and Alexander VII, defeated the declared defenders of Jansenism concerning the feigned abjuration among the adherents of that same sect.
