[Note: [Col. 0303B]

Number 66, line 8.—“Two hundred and fifty-six priests were assembled, and others, whose autograph was circulated by 406 bishops.” According to this statement, therefore, the Fathers of Chalcedon numbered 622, although the Acts enumerate 630. These men are placed in two groups: those who signed the dogmatic letter before the celebration of the synod, and those who did not sign it but nevertheless attended the council. If one had to guess, I would say that the number denotes the bishops of both parties who are recorded in the first session of Chalcedon as standing in that dispute.

The Catholics stood on the side of the legates together with Anatolius. They were all Eastern bishops who had been marked out for deposition by Dioscorus at the Robber Council of Ephesus. Theophanes speaks of that deposition; after recounting the Acts of the Robber Council of Ephesus, he immediately adds in his *Chronicle*, p. 87: “Moreover, Dioscorus deprived Theodoret, Ibas, and Andrew, as well as Domnus of Antioch and all the bishops of the East, of ecclesiastical authority.”

[Col. 0303C]

The followers of Dioscorus repeatedly call these men “Nestorians” in the first session, as may be read there. The opposing party stood with Dioscorus and consisted of Egyptian, Illyrian, and Palestinian bishops. A dispute arose between the two parties in the first session, until the Palestinian and Illyrian bishops went over to the Catholic side, leaving Dioscorus with only thirteen Egyptian bishops. The *Liber Pontificalis* therefore says that the former party consisted of 406 bishops and the latter of 256.

This could be recognized from the dogmatic letter subscribed before the council in the year 450 by the Eastern bishops under Saint Abundius. It was sent to Rome and deposited in the archive, thereby giving the compiler an occasion to record the number. For the authentic subscriptions were carefully preserved in the archive of the Apostolic See, as is observed concerning the subscriptions of the Council of Antioch in 378 to the Tome of Damasus, in the fragment of Holstenius at the end of that work.

The expression “whose autograph was circulated”

[Col. 0303D]

appears to refer to the decree issued by Leo in his dogmatic letter to Flavian. Among other things, this is shown by the similarity of the wording, which has often been examined in the case of Sylvester when the Nicene decree was under discussion.

This subscription was made at the Council of Constantinople. It was signed by those who were present and then sent to those who were absent; this is what is expressed by the phrase “whose autograph was circulated.” The subscribed autograph was again examined at the same synod.

That this concerns the Council of Constantinople under Saint Abundius, Saint Leo’s legate throughout the East, is most clearly demonstrated by a fragment of the Life of Abundius, where we read as follows:

[Col. 0304B]

“Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, the New Rome, after receiving the letter of Saint Leo the pope concerning the confession of the Catholic faith against the madness of the heretics, assembled a council of bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, and deacons. Before the sight of all, the letter of Saint Leo the pope was read, which the blessed Abundius presented in the presence of everyone. With the testimonies of the Roman and Greek Fathers in agreement, Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, assented with complete devotion and subscribed to this letter of Saint Leo the pope, which contained the truth of the Catholic faith, with the testimonies of the Fathers sent by that same Apostolic See in agreement. He pronounced an anathema against Eutyches and Nestorius, and against their doctrine and their followers. The bishops, presbyters, archimandrites, and deacons who were present did the same.”

Leo rejoiced at this subscription and shortly afterward wrote to Paschasius, bishop of Lilybaeum. Quesnellius was the first to publish the letter, number 68:

“You should know that the whole Church of Constantinople, together with all the monasteries and many bishops, gave its assent and, by its subscriptions, anathematized Nestorius and Eutyches together with their doctrines.”

At the same time, the same letter was sent to the metropolitans who were seated in the provinces. They subscribed to the letters sent to them and forwarded the subscribed autograph to the council of Constantinople, which was still being convened. This is read in the fourth session of Chalcedon, p. 30:

“When only a few had assembled at Constantinople, the letter of the blessed Archbishop Leo was sent to the metropolitans who were everywhere, and it was subscribed.”

Hence, in that same session, the bishops repeatedly say during the exchanges that they had already subscribed to the letter.

A specimen of the other subscriptions appears in Theodoret’s letter in reply to Saint Abundius, who had sent him the dogmatic letter for subscription. Theodoret writes:

[Col. 0304D]

“I gave thanks to almighty God that the religion which was in peril has been renewed through your holiness. We learned this from the letters of our lord Leo. For we read what he wrote to Flavian, of holy and blessed memory, and we gave thanks to God that we had found an advocate and defender of the truth. Therefore I assented to these letters and attached copies of them to my own letter, to which I also subscribed. Likewise my lord Ibas and my lord Aquilinus.”

The 406 Catholic bishops in this party therefore possessed a special prerogative at the Council of Chalcedon because they had subscribed to the dogmatic letter. At the very beginning of the second session, when the judges asked the bishops about the rule or decree of faith that was to be composed, Cecropius, bishop of Sebastopolis, boldly replied on behalf of all who had subscribed, p. 286:

“The matters concerning Eutyches arose, and on these a form was issued by the most holy archbishop of the city of Rome. We follow him, and we all subscribed to the letter.”

That they regarded Saint Leo’s letter as the rule of faith, and that after their subscription they rejected every other revision, is revealed in the same session. When the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops promoted a reconsideration and comparison with Saint Cyril’s letter, and the judges assented, the subscribed bishops opposed their petitions, saying, p. 307:

“All the most reverend bishops cried out: ‘This is what we believe. As Leo believes, so do we believe; none of us doubts it. We have already subscribed.’”

Thus, when, through the indulgence of the judges, instruction was permitted to the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops, lest that permission prejudice the profession already issued by the bishops who had subscribed, Bishop Florentius, praising the statement of Cecropius, protested:

“Although, as regards our own person, we who subscribed to the letter of the most holy Leo do not need correction.”

This subscription was therefore held in such high regard by the Catholic party and was repeated in so many professions that it must have been an authentic testimony to the truth. Since it was also recorded in the ecclesiastical annals, the compiler could insert it and preserve the number of those who subscribed.

Line 9.—“Those who were assembled together with the Tome, that is, with the faith of the Apostolic Church of Rome, with the autograph of the holy Archbishop Leo.”

These words admit of a twofold interpretation. The first may be explained as follows: “Those who were assembled with the Tome, which contained the subscriptions

[Col. 0305B]

of the bishops of the West who had subscribed to the letter and testified that this was the common profession and faith of the Apostolic Church of Rome; and with the autograph that had been circulated, which contained Saint Leo’s letter and the subscriptions of the Eastern bishops.” Or they may be understood in this way: “Those who were assembled with the Tome, or dogmatic letter, which was an exposition and declaration of the faith concerning the disputed article of the Apostolic See, written by Saint Archbishop Leo, and with the autograph that had been circulated throughout the East before the celebration of the Council of Chalcedon.”

Both interpretations gain strength from the observations made above and from the surviving letters of the Western bishops among Saint Leo’s letters, whose authors subscribed to the dogmatic letter before it was sent to the East. It was neither new nor unusual for letters from the Western bishops to be sent to an ecumenical council, where the mind of the whole Church was to be examined.

The first interpretation is confirmed by a later action of the same Leo the Great. When he saw the authority of the Council of Chalcedon being attacked by refractory monks and Eutychians in the year of Christ 457, he wrote to the metropolitans and patriarchs to rouse them to its defense. This is testified by a letter sent to Aetius, a presbyter of Constantinople, published by Quesnellius. It reads as follows, Letter 121:

[Col. 0305C]

“We have also decided to send general letters to the metropolitan bishops, so that their spirit may be strengthened and confirmed, and so that they may know that they must strive with equal zeal and harmonious unity to defend the Council of Chalcedon. Of these letters, if it seems good to you all together, you will send one to Antioch and another to Jerusalem. We have also already sent similar writings to the Illyrian bishops.”

Concerning the letters received from the Western bishops, Leo writes that copies should be sent to demonstrate their unanimous agreement in defending the Council of Chalcedon and to present that agreement to the emperor and the others:

[Col. 0305D]

“We have likewise sent copies of the letters which the Gallic bishops and the Italian bishops sent to us with harmonious belief, so that it may not remain unknown how their faith is also one with ours,” and so forth.

Line 10.—“But in the presence of the Catholic ruler the council was assembled, numbering 400 bishops.”

These words seem to denote the fifth and sixth sessions, in which the decree of faith, finally elaborated, was published in the presence of Marcian. The *Liber Pontificalis* adds: “who set forth the Catholic faith,” and so forth.

It is certain that not all the bishops were summoned to compose the decree, but only part of them. Since the text says that 400 were assembled, while it had been said above that these men had subscribed before the council’s celebration, we infer, according to this testimony of the *Liber Pontificalis*, that these same 400 were selected to formulate the decree. The facts that not all were summoned and that the subscribers were selected support this conclusion.

For in the fifth session, p. 447, we read:

“Asclepiades, a deacon of great reputation of the most holy Church of Constantinople,

[Col. 0306A]

read the definition. It does not seem appropriate to insert it in these Acts. After the reading, when some were hesitating, John, bishop of Germanicia, stepping into the middle, said: ‘The definition is not satisfactory; it must be made complete.’”

These words clearly show that all the bishops were not present for the compilation of the decree. Otherwise those who hesitated, and who were not afraid to oppose it publicly, would have acted foolishly, since they could have done so more conveniently in the assembly.

Moreover, it is evident that the greater part of the Eastern bishops attended the gathering, because the cry was heard: “Send out the Nestorians; send out the enemies of God.” This was uttered by John, bishop of Germanicia, and those who were hesitating agreed with him. In the preceding session, the Easterners who had frequently been marked with that condemnation were likewise addressed in these terms.

In general, Saint Leo informs us that the Catholics accused the Eutychians of Nestorianism in his letter to Proterius, first published by Quesnellius. He writes, Letter 103:

[Col. 0306B]

“Therefore, dearest brother, out of concern for the common faith I warn you that, since the enemies of the cross of Christ lie in wait for all our words and syllables, we must give them no, even slight, opportunity to pretend that we agree with the Nestorian position.”

Led by this reasoning, we think that the 400 who set forth the faith were those who had previously subscribed, and that this is what the *Liber Pontificalis* intended to indicate.

Line 14.—“Together with his wife, Augusta Pulcheria.”

Some copies of the Latin edition of the Council of Chalcedon agree with this, in the sixth session, where p. 463 reads:

[Col. 0306C]

“With the most devout and most Christian queen, Augusta Pulcheria, also present, through divine zeal and the fervor of faith.”

The *Breviculum of the Eutychians* agrees, where the same proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon are reported and it is added:

“In which he himself and Pulcheria also sat, together with the whole senate and the officials.”

Baluzius, however, shows that these words, just as they are absent from all the Greek copies, are likewise absent from the older Latin copies. Therefore the addition was made by a later hand, as also in the *Liber Pontificalis*.

(In the new collection of the Councils, p. 1264.)

Line 17.—“And again the emperor Marcian Augustus, together with his wife Pulcheria Augusta, setting forth their faith in their own handwriting, requested the holy council to direct it to the most blessed Pope Leo, asking him to expound the Catholic faith.” This repeated exposition of the council’s faith and its being sent to Leo seems to indicate something other than the decree of faith, which Marcian and Pulcheria considered necessary, and which the Fathers of Chalcedon carried out and Leo the Great approved. What this decree was is difficult to explain. Yet if conjecture—indeed, conjecture drawn from the circumstances of the time—is admissible, we may say, not implausibly, that these words refer to the splendid address of the Council of Chalcedon to Marcian, published to counter the rumors spread by the Eutychians.

At the time of the council’s celebration, the fundamental principle of the Eutychians was that no other formula of faith was to be retained or professed except the Nicene one, and that every other formula, issued by any ecclesiastical tribunal whatever, was to be rejected as alien; both those who issued such formulas and those who professed them were to be punished by deposition. Dioscorus advanced this principle alone at the robber council of Ephesus. He saw to it that the Ephesian canon was read, by which he declared this to be prohibited, and those present who were followers of Dioscorus joined their votes in agreement.

For this reason he prohibited the reading of the dogmatic letter and deposed Flavian, because at his earlier council in Constantinople he had proposed to Eutyches and the Fathers that another formula should be professed. Then, in still greater madness, when he saw the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo being received, professed, and solemnly subscribed throughout the provinces of the world, he dared to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against Leo himself.

Theodosius, by a law obtained through court influence, strengthened this heretical foundation and decreed that it be followed throughout the provinces of the empire. But when the adherents of Dioscorus—especially the monks in Palestine, where Theodosius’s wife, namely Eudoxia, was residing at Jerusalem—heard that the robber council of Ephesus had been rejected by Chalcedon because it had upheld the dogmatic letter, and that Dioscorus had been punished by deposition, they surrounded the widowed empress and represented the Fathers of Chalcedon as insulting the law published by her husband Theodosius, indeed as enemies of the decrees of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus.

Under the leadership of the monk Theodosius, they began to regard all the Fathers still residing at Chalcedon as deposed, according to the provision of the Ephesian decree, because they had dared to receive a new formula, although, as the Eutychians imagined, this had been entirely prohibited by the Ephesian canon.

Theophanes reports these events, which occurred during the Council of Chalcedon and specifically through the Eutychian monks with Eudoxia’s support, in his *Chronicle*, recounting the beginnings of this disastrous tragedy, p. 92:

> “The monk Theodosius, a destructive man, after the Council of Chalcedon had been completed—that is, after the first six sessions had been held—was rapidly taken to Jerusalem. When he learned of Eudoxia Augusta’s affection for Dioscorus, who had been deposed by the council, he began to cry out and declaim against it as though it had perverted the true faith. The Augusta, having been drawn to his view, and the monks likewise having been deceived, he resorted to the murders familiar to him and, in barbarous fashion, intruded himself upon the episcopal throne, even with the assistance of the Augusta’s own household in carrying out this invasion, while Juvenal, the legitimate bishop of Jerusalem, was sitting in the synod of Chalcedon. He appointed bishops in the cities while their bishops were still sitting in the council—that is, in the Council of Chalcedon. When Severian, bishop of Scythopolis, refused to agree with his wicked errors, he expelled him from the city and killed him. He stirred up persecution against those who rejected his communion: some he put to death by torture, while he ravaged the houses of others with fire, so that within the city he displayed the appearance of a city devastated by barbarians. Finally, he cruelly killed Anastasius, deacon of the Holy Resurrection, who had attacked his extreme impiety with insults and rebukes, and he dragged the holy man’s body publicly through the city and threw it to the dogs in mockery.”

Thus he seized the patriarchal see of Jerusalem. He declared the other bishops sitting at Chalcedon to be deposed, by right of the disposition of the Ephesian canon and of the robber council under Dioscorus, and he was able to win the Augusta over under the pretext of defending the edicts that had been published by her husband.

The letters preserved in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon pursue at greater length what was done through the tragic contrivance of this impostor and his adherents. Indeed, with equal audacity in their crimes, they dared not only to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon but also Saint Leo. Marcian charges them with this in his letter to the same men (ibid., p. 671):

> “But in addition to what you formerly dared to do with swords and other cruelties, you did not hesitate to impose necessity upon very many, so that they would consent to your perverse doctrines and, by their cries and subscriptions, anathematize that same holy synod, the most holy patriarch of the apostolic see of great Rome, Leo, and the other most holy Fathers.”

When these rumors had been brought to the emperor and the council, the Fathers initially thought that sufficient provision had been made through the proceedings of the first session, in which the robber council of Ephesus had been read and annulled. Nevertheless, since the Theodosian constitution concerning the preservation of the robber council and the Ephesian canon still existed and remained in force, and since it required an interpretation—that is, an authoritative declaration—the emperor, as is said here, again entrusted the matter to the assembled Fathers for discussion.

They produced the splendid address to Marcian in which, first, they prove—even against the unwilling Dioscorians—that it must be admitted that various formulas of faith had been written and professed from the Council of Nicaea to the time of Chalcedon. They identify ten of the more distinguished formulas, some of which the heretics admitted, thereby proving that from the very celebration of Nicaea the Church had issued new declarations of faith according to the circumstances of the heresies, and that these declarations had been accepted without hesitation.

Indeed, after the Ephesian canon, a peaceful letter had been issued by Saint Cyril, the author of the disputed Ephesian canon, and subscribed by Catholics and schismatics alike with unanimous agreement. In this way they overturn the heretical foundation of the Eutychians.

Second, they explain the true and genuine meaning of the Ephesian canon and show that neither the Council of Nicaea nor the Ephesian canon could deprive the Church of the power to defend the faith.

Third, they undertake the defense of Saint Leo’s dogmatic teaching and examine the earlier custom of declaring the dogmas of the faith through such letters.

The Acts present the subject of this address in the following terms (p. 643):

> “Address of the holy and universal Council of Chalcedon to Marcian, the most devout emperor and lover of Christ. The most holy archbishop Leo has now written a letter to Flavian of holy memory, bishop of the imperial city of Constantinople, not introducing anything new against the faith of Nicaea, but following the holy Fathers, who, after the great Council of Nicaea, likewise refuted the heresies that arose in each period.”

That this was issued after the sixteenth session seems likely both from what is said here—namely, that the council was assembled again—and from the fact that in all copies the address occupies the first place among the records following the sixteen sessions that had been held.

Finally, Marcian published a law in 452 by which he annulled the Theodosian law that decreed that the robber Council of Ephesus was to be received as ecumenical. It is preserved in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon under the title:

> “On invalidating what was unjustly pronounced against Flavian, bishop of the imperial city of Constantinople, of holy memory, and confirming what was afterward decreed concerning him by the holy Synod of Chalcedon.”

This law follows the Theodosian law bearing the heading:

> “Interpretation of the law promulgated by Theodosius the Younger, after he had been deceived by Chrysaphius, against Flavian and his associates on behalf of Eutyches; this was destroyed by the law subsequently issued by the most religious emperor Marcian.”

This occasion, arising from the disturbances of the monks—which were increasing through the Augusta’s favor and her patronage of Dioscorus and his adherents—must certainly have moved the emperor to entrust the clarification of the matter to the Fathers of Chalcedon. The bishops who were still assembled diligently carried out the task assigned to them. In the celebrated address they accomplished this by sending it to Leo.

The *Liber Pontificalis*, therefore, seems to be referring to this second assembly.

Moreover, that Eudoxia promoted the cause of the robber Council of Ephesus and the seditious monks with stubborn determination for four full years is shown by Nicephorus, when he writes about Eudoxia in Book XIV, chapter 50:

> “She spent eleven years at Jerusalem. From that time she lived four years scarcely accepting the Acts of the universal Council of Chalcedon; but after she had approved and welcomed the decrees of that council, she spent another four years, and at last died.”

The decrees of the Council of Chalcedon praised here are nothing other than the decree of faith, the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo, and the address to Marcian. When Eudoxia acknowledged these and examined their weight, she not only abandoned her patronage of heresy but also recalled Juvenal and the Catholic bishops, defended the Catholic religion, and died in that faith.

Saint Leo praises these three decrees and, through them, shows that all the heads of Eutychianism had been sufficiently cut off. He presents this to Theodoret, and therefore the authority of the address must be evaluated in the light of this confirmation by Leo.

Thus, in 453, he writes to Theodoret about the Eutychian perfidy in Letter 93:

> “In the letter of the apostolic see, confirmed by the agreement of the universal holy synod, we know that so many testimonies of divine authority have been assembled that no one can any longer doubt, unless he prefers to bring upon himself the darkness of error. For the synodal proceedings—both those in which the definition of faith was first read as having been confirmed and those in which the aforesaid apostolic letter was received—have also been defended through the zeal of your Fraternity. Most especially, the address of the whole council to the most devout emperors has been strengthened by so many testimonies of the Fathers who preceded it that it may persuade even an impudent and stubborn mind, unless it has already been condemned with the devil on account of its impiety.”

That Eudoxia’s adoption of the Eutychians’ cause was the greatest impediment, apart from the disasters and tragedies that followed in Palestine, is shown by Marcian’s efforts. He employed Leo as an advocate in order to bring the Augusta to better counsels, and the pontiff stirred up Valentinian, Eudoxia’s son-in-law, so that he might admonish the Augusta.

Thus, in the letter to Julian of Cos, first published by Quesnellius, Letter 88, p. 306:

> “And because the most merciful emperor graciously deigned to instruct me more privately through our son Paul concerning the admonition of our most merciful daughter Eudoxia, I did what he wished, so that she might learn from a letter how beneficial it would be for her to favor the Catholic faith. I also obtained that she be admonished about this by a letter from her most merciful son. I do not doubt that he too will labor earnestly so that the authors of the seditions may recognize the purpose of their profession; so that, if they do not understand the preaching of those who teach, at least they may fear the power of those who punish.”

I believe that it was on this occasion that Marcian sent Leo’s letter, which Quesnellius published from the Boldeian codex G. L. After its opening, on p. 307, it reads:

> “We are greatly astonished that, after the synod celebrated at Chalcedon and the letters of the venerable bishops sent to Your Piety, in which they set forth the entire sequence of the matters done in the synod, those letters were in no way sent forth by Your Holiness, although, when read in the holy churches, they ought to have come to the knowledge of all. Consequently, a great doubt has been cast into the minds of some who still pursue the false opinion and depravity of Eutyches: whether Your Blessedness has confirmed what the synod decreed. Therefore may Your Piety deign to send letters by which all the Churches and peoples may know that the Acts of the synod have been approved by Your Blessedness, and so forth.”

And the remainder contained there, from which this note in the *Liber Pontificalis* appears even more clearly.

This, then, is the second letter of Marcian requesting from the pontiff an authoritative confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon, and it seems to be what the *Liber Pontificalis* is discussing here.

Line 20.—“Leo sent the volume of the Catholic faith and expounded it.” That he approved the address that had been sent is shown by the letter addressed to Theodoret. That he gave further confirmation through the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon he writes in his letter to Marcian, published as Quesnellius’s Letter 89.

That he sent a volume in which the Catholic faith was expounded in a fuller treatment is shown by Letter 97, addressed to the monks of Palestine. In it he examines the mystery of the Incarnation at greater length against Nestorius and Eutyches and explains the Catholic truth.

Therefore, in the letter addressed to Juvenal, Letter 110, in which he rejoices that Juvenal has been restored to his see, he presents the dogmatic letter to be followed, together with the address by which the defense of that same letter had been undertaken:

> “You clearly recognize, in accordance with the antiquity of your priesthood, by how many authorities of both the New and the Old Testament this truth is declared, since the faith of the Fathers and my writings addressed to Flavian of holy memory, which you yourself mentioned, together with the confirmation of the universal synod, are sufficient.”

Line 21.—“Condemning all heresies.” That Leo issued a treatise in which, by setting out each heresy individually, he explained the rule of faith to be followed is attested by Justinian. Pope Vigilius commends such a work of both Celestine and Leo in his letter to the emperor. In that letter, while Justinian’s profession of faith was extant, Vigilius declares that Justinian acted rightly in condemning all heresies according to the method observed by Celestine and Leo, Roman pontiffs. Baronius, year 540, p. 304:

> “For this reason, venerable emperor, we receive with devoted reverence and thanksgiving what you have sent us, inflamed by the ardor of faith and moved by a gracious indignation, together with pious words in which you have commemorated with praiseworthy affection Celestine of blessed memory and Leo, prelates of the apostolic see, who, condemning each heresy through the synodal assembly entrusted to them by divine dispensation, have established what all Christians ought generally to follow, by a law that will endure forever.”

Line 22.—“Which are kept to this day deposited in the archives.” This gives further support to the preceding observations: namely, that the established faith of the Roman pontiffs was carefully preserved in the archives, and that, because this was obvious, the *Liber Pontificalis* omitted the subject matter of the constitutions.

Line 23.—“He frequently confirmed the Council of Chalcedon through his letters.” The number of letters is recorded with necessary care, and the *Liber Pontificalis* mentions fifty-one.

The necessity of confirmation is revealed by the aforementioned letter of Marcian, extracted from the Boldeian codex, which asks for confirmation a second time. Indeed, as the emperor writes at the end of the letter, p. 307, so that every cause of disagreement might be removed:

> “Therefore may Your Venerable Dignity signify this everywhere as soon as possible by letters, which may show most fully that you regard the Council of Chalcedon as ratified, so that no suspicion of disagreement or discord may remain concerning the judgment of Your Holiness.”

I think that these letters were collected later on the occasion of Timothy the Cat, who, under the emperor Leo in 457, promoted the reconsideration of Chalcedon, as though the council were not to be received as ecumenical. To settle this controversy, letters were sent to the bishops of the entire world. In particular synods, through encyclical letters, they professed that they had received and did receive the Council of Chalcedon as ecumenical. From these materials the encyclical book of the Council of Chalcedon was formed, and several letters are preserved in Part III of that council.

The Roman Church, moreover, gathered a separate codex of Leo’s letters, in which the pontiff confirmed the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. This was a necessary precaution to counter the evasions of the Eutychians.

Simplicius writes that this codex was also known to be preserved in the imperial archives, in his letter to Basiliscus—not to Zeno, as the received reading has it, concerning which more below—when the emperor, favoring the Eutychians, was considering the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon.

Thus the pontiff writes:

> “There are abundant documents available to Your Clemency—if you order them to be sought in the archives of your palace—containing the definitions of our assemblies and of the Fathers. For it cannot be believed that your conscience is unaware of what was disseminated throughout all the provinces of the East from the citadel of your empire: namely, the responses which my predecessor Leo sent to the inquiries of Marcian and Leo, both of august memory, and to those of the Council of Chalcedon, of blessed memory.”

Number 67, line 6.—“He renewed the basilica of blessed Paul.” In some codices, “after the divine fire” is added. Concerning this restoration and the painted images, Adrian I writes to Charles on behalf of the Second Council of Nicaea, volume IV of the Councils, p. 812:

> “Concerning the sacred Fourth Council, the distinguished and wondrous preacher, Saint Pope Leo, who himself also built churches and decorated them with mosaics, painting various histories or images, did even more in the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle. There he made the larger arch and painted in mosaic our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, together with the twenty-four elders, adorning them with their names and verses. From that time until the present these works have been faithfully preserved by us.”

[Note: [Col. 0310D]

Number 66, line 1.—“Leo, a Tuscan by nationality.” In the year of the Lord 440, the thirty-third year of the emperor Theodosius and the sixteenth of Valentinian, after an interregnum of more than forty days, according to Prosper, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, Leo, an Etruscan by nationality and deacon of Pope Sixtus, was appointed in his absence to the place of the deceased.

Sophronius relates of Leo in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 149, that he remained for forty days at the tomb of the blessed Apostle Peter, devoting himself to vigils and prayers and asking the apostle to intercede for him before God, so that his sins might be forgiven. When the forty days had been completed, the Apostle Peter appeared to him and said:

> “I have prayed for you, and all your sins have been forgiven as regards their punishment, except for the laying on of hands”—that is, the promotion of certain unworthy men to sacred orders—“for this alone will be required of you, whether you acted well or perhaps badly.”

Saint Gregory further relates, in Book III, Letter 30, that at this time, when certain Greeks were doubting the authenticity of a *brandeum*, Pope Leo brought scissors and cut it, whereupon blood flowed from the incision.

He explains shortly beforehand what a *brandeum* is:

> “Let the most tranquil lady know what the Roman custom is. When they give relics of the saints, they do not presume to touch anything from the body; rather, a *brandeum* is placed in a small box and laid upon the most sacred bodies of the saints. When it is taken up, it is deposited with veneration in the church that is to be dedicated. Through this, such great miracles occur there that it is as though their bodies themselves had specifically been brought to that place.”

Gregory of Tours, *Miracles*, Book I, chapter 28, also mentions the very ancient custom of placing cloths or handkerchiefs over the tomb of the Apostle Peter, so that they might be received enriched by blessing.

Number 67, line 11.—“He decreed that a nun, etc.” In imitation of and at the exhortation of Saint Leo, the emperor Marcian promulgated an edict against those who forced unwilling virgin daughters to receive the sacred veil and to be consecrated to God in perpetual virginity. He prohibited any virgin offered for this purpose by her parents from receiving the sacred veil before the age of forty, so that until that time she would be free and could marry if she wished.]

[Note: [Col. 0311B]

## Chronological Notes

The fixed point for opening the true chronology of the supreme pontiffs from Celestine to Hilary turns on the date of Hilary’s accession to the see, or of his episcopal consecration, a date known to us from the Roman council. As we said above in the chronological notes on Celestine I and Sixtus III, we showed there that this date falls on Sunday, 19 November 461, and we shall establish it again in the Life of Hilary.

The ancient catalogues, together with the Librarian, testify that the see remained vacant for seven days from the death of the predecessor to the election of Hilary. Florentinius observes this in his notes on the tenth of November in his *Martyrology*, where he found recorded in that same *Martyrology* the burial at Rome of Saint Leo the bishop.

The same author also produced the very ancient Hieronymian *Martyrology* of the canons of Lucca, in which the feast of Saint Pope Leo is recorded on the same day, the fourth day before the Ides of November. Likewise, in Rubeus, one reads: “At Rome, the burial of Saint Leo the bishop,” on the fourth day before the Ides of November.

It is remarkable that the seven-day vacancy of the see agrees with the day of the burial of Leo the Great, 10 November; that the election of his successor Hilary follows on the seventeenth of the same month; and that the coronation, or *enthronism* (*ἐνθρονίσμος*), follows two days later, on Sunday, 19 November.

To answer the objections that might be raised from the feast of Saint Leo the Great, assigned to 11 April in the Roman *Martyrology*, the learned author observes that in the ancient Sacramentary of blessed Gregory the feast of Saint Pope Leo falls on a different day, namely the fourth day before the Kalends of July. Both Pagis remark that the celebration of Saint Leo’s feast was assigned to 11 April in the Roman *Martyrology* only from the time of Gregory XIII.

He therefore concludes that the feast assigned to 11 April was connected with the solemn translation performed on that day—perhaps the translation carried out by Pope Sergius, when the bones of the blessed pontiff, which had been kept for two hundred and thirty years in the lower sacristy of the basilica, were placed inside the basilica in a suitably arranged oratory. Shortly afterward, Leo III clothed its altar in gilded silver, and Saint Leo IV adorned it with other gifts. Both were their predecessor’s *syncellites*, as we shall say below in their Lives, together with the Librarian.

Once the end of the mortal life of Saint Leo the Great and the date of his burial have thus been established as 10 November 461, in the consulship of Severinus and Dagalaiphus, it follows that the beginning of his pontificate—lasting twenty-one years, one month, and twenty-six days—fell around the second week of September 440, in the consulship of Valentinian and Anatolius.

This total is given by Anastasius and by the older and more accurate catalogues, those of Farfa, Cava, and Bergamo, with only a difference of two days noted in the last. Most of the Colbertine catalogues also support it.

Prosper of Aquitaine, who was living at that time, records the election of Pope Leo under those consuls. He does not give the month or day. But we can readily ascertain both from the stated period of more than forty days after the death of Sixtus, during which the Roman Church was without a bishop, according to Prosper’s testimony. For he writes in his *Chronicle*:

> “In the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fifth time and Anatolius, after the death of Bishop Sixtus, the Roman Church was without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with remarkable peace and patience the arrival of the deacon Leo. At that time the Gauls detained him between Aetius and Albinus for the purpose of restoring friendship, as though he had been led away for a longer period so that the merit of the elected man and the judgment of those electing him might be tested. Therefore Leo the deacon was summoned by an official embassy and, having been presented to his rejoicing country, was ordained the forty-third bishop of the Roman Church.”

This agrees exactly with the date we have assigned for the death of the blessed Sixtus, 29 July. Thus, up to Sunday, 8 September, on which we say that Leo the Great was ordained bishop after being summoned from Gaul and restored to his country, there is the interval defined by Prosper.

Nor does our Librarian Prosper contradict this testimony when he assigns twenty-two days of vacancy to the Roman see after the death of Sixtus. For if he reckons the term of the vacant see either from the election or from the consent of the elected man, the election or consent could have occurred on 20 August, three weeks after the death of his predecessor. The remaining interval would then bring the period to the forty days and more during which the Aquitanian writes that the Roman Church was without a bishop and awaited Leo’s arrival in remarkable peace. Even if the see was not technically vacant for the entire period, the Roman Church was nevertheless deprived in some sense of its pastor, since it had a bishop who had been elected but not yet ordained.

With the dates of Leo’s election and ordination in 440, and the end of his most holy life in 461, thus firmly established, numerous intervening years of his twenty-one-year pontificate are confirmed by the consulates expressly given by Leo himself in his letters. A particularly valuable example of these letters, owing to its antiquity, is preserved in the library of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem in the City, among the select codices collected there from the most ancient monasteries of the Reverend Fathers of the Cistercian order. In the same title they display no less evidence of the most religious worship than of outstanding learning, especially in sacred literature. The library itself, recently enlarged and elegantly adorned, is diligently and assiduously maintained and frequented.

A clear testimony concerning the events of Leo the Great’s pontificate and the chronology of his age also survives in the Council of Chalcedon, the Fourth General Council, in the paschal letters sent by Proterius of Alexandria to Leo, and in the paschal cycle published by Victor of Aquitaine in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus, in the year of Christ 457. Victor sent it to Hilary, then archdeacon of the Roman Church and, four years later, Leo’s successor, when questions had arisen concerning the date of Easter in the years 444 and 445.

This cycle, composed with a total of 532 years and illuminated by the most learned commentaries of Bucherius, gives for each year, in addition to the consular indication, the weekdays on which the Kalends of January fall each year.

In a work that I composed twenty-four years ago, when the correct reckoning of Easter was being discussed in the sacred congregation convened by Clement XI under the prefecture of Cardinal Noris, I placed the title *Solution of the Paschal Problem* before a table of Easter celebrations drawn from the testimonies of the holy Fathers. There one can see the characteristics of several years and of the Easters belonging to the age of Saint Leo, by which the chronology of the great pontiff is illuminated.

I do not think this document is unrelated to the proof undertaken here. Therefore I have taken care to insert the same table here.

[Col. 0313B]

Established by the authority of the sacred Council of Nicaea, produced by Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, and confirmed by the practice and teaching of Saints Athanasius, Ambrose, Augustine, Cyril, Proterius, Paschasinus, and Pope Leo.

(The mean full moons have been calculated from the Ricciolian Tables for the meridian of Rome.)

## By the Same Bianchini

Number 66, line 3.—“Here he discovered two heresies, the Eutychian and the Nestorian, etc.” The Librarian lists the new heresy of Eutyches, which he joins to the ancient heresy of Nestorius, both equally deserving condemnation, although one opposed the other.

In addition to this new heresy, Leo discovered the ancient heresy of Manes, which was secretly spreading in the City. Beginning the care of the Lord’s flock by restraining this hidden pest, he says in Letter 2 to the Italian bishops:

> “Our investigation discovered in the City very many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety; our vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them.”

He presents a method involving this threefold activity—investigating, exposing, and restraining heretics—which was to serve as an example to others, in the words that follow:

> “I exhort, implore, and admonish your Charity to keep watch with the diligence that you ought and are able to exercise, in order to investigate them, lest they find anywhere an opportunity to conceal themselves.”

He also prescribes a balance between provident charity and necessary severity, from whose examples others might profit:

> “Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected, so that they would condemn Manichaeus together with his preachers and disciples by a public profession in the Church. We compelled them to do this by the subscription of their own hand, and after they had confessed in this way that they had been in the pit of their impiety, we relieved them by granting them penance. But certain others had sunk so deeply that no remedy brought to their aid could help them. They were therefore subjected to the laws, according to the enactments of Christian rulers, and were sent into perpetual exile by public judges, so that they would not pollute the holy flock with their contagion.”

After purging the City and Italy, Leo devoted no less vigilance to protecting Spain from the errors of the Priscillianist sect, which was propagated as a kind of offshoot of Manichaeism.

When he was informed by the bishop of Astorga of the remnants of the pestilence that were sprouting in those regions, he sent him letters (Letter 93) and, as he says in chapters 16 and 17, “to our brothers and fellow bishops, the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia,” proposed the remedies of synods. In the first place, he ordered that those bishops who were polluted by the contagion of heresy should unquestionably be separated from communion if they were unwilling to condemn the most impious sect in all the perversities of its teaching.

Prosper, in *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, chapter 6, testifies that Leo exercised his strength with equal fervor against the Pelagians, especially Julian. The most eminent Noris confirms this in *History of Pelagianism*, Book II, chapter 13, at the end, on the authority of Pope Gelasius, and commends Leo with this eulogy:

> “The most holy pontiff died in the year of salvation 461. He had overthrown the Manichaeans, Nestorians, Eutyches, and other plagues, and with a final blow had all but slain the Pelagian heresy as well. Pope Gelasius, in his letter to Bishop Honorius, places Leo last among the Roman bishops who condemned the Pelagians. ‘Or perhaps,’ he says, ‘do you not know that this heresy of which we speak was long ago struck down by the apostolic see through Innocent of blessed memory and afterward through Zosimus, Sixtus, and Leo, by continuous and unceasing judgments?’”

The other examples and writings of Leo the Great that offer posterity a method for abolishing heresies and that are suitably applied in the Church are summarized briefly by the archbishop D. Somier in Book V, chapter 1, of his *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*. We borrow several matters from him, as well as the following:

From Prosper’s *Chronicle*, under the year 444, concerning the public condemnation and disclosure of errors that were to be issued by heretics doing penance:

> “At this time, the diligence of Pope Leo revealed that very many Manichaeans were hiding within the City. He brought them out of their secret places and exposed them before the eyes of the whole Church, and made them both condemn and disclose all the shameful doctrines of their creed.”

Moreover, from Leo’s decretal letters he derives rules and instructions given by Leo to bishops concerning the obtaining of such subscriptions from guilty penitents before they were admitted to communion, and concerning the drafting of formulas of condemnation. These formulas were to state that the penitents embraced and approved in every respect all the synodal decrees confirmed by apostolic authority for the destruction of the sect, in full, open, and personally subscribed declarations.

Letter 86 of Leo the Great, to the bishop of Aquileia.]

**Line 8.**—“And 256 priests, and others, were assembled, etc.” The number of 406 bishops is asserted in the synodical report of those same Fathers to Pope Leo, which is read in Part III of the Roman edition of the Council of Ephesus, p. 459D, to have been 520. But since the proceedings comprise sixteen sessions, and many attended one session [Col. 0317A] who did not attend another, different numbers may be given for different sessions. On the number, however, see Cardinal Baronius, under the year 451, and Pagi, no. 35.

**No. 66, line 9.**—“Together with the volume,” that is, with the apostolic faith of the Roman Church, bearing the autograph of the holy Archbishop Leo. Concerning the doctrinal letter of Leo the Great signified here—which, as a rule of faith complete in every respect, was received with the praise of all the Fathers—see the history most diligently compiled in Somier’s notes. **The same writer.**

**Line 23.**—“Here he frequently confirmed the Council of Chalcedon in his letters.” The Most Reverend Archbishop Somier illustrates this kind of confirmation in Book V, chapters 6 and 11, of his *Dogmatic History*. See the notes selected from it for this *Life*.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

**No. 65, line 4.**—“He made the apse of the Constantinian basilica, [Col. 0317B] adorned another apse of blessed Peter, and renewed the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle.” In the three patriarchal basilicas, Saint Leo adorned the *camera*, or apse of the presbytery, commonly called the tribune. In the basilica of blessed Paul on the Ostian Way, however, he established the principal monuments of his constructions and decorations. Therefore Pope Hadrian, in his letter to Charlemagne on the veneration of sacred images, expressly mentions this work, as we reported in chapter 4 of the dissertation on the ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs, and in the second dissertation following the notes on the *Life of Saint Sixtus III*.

What we observed in that dissertation, following the authority of Pope Hadrian, while examining the history of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, was that the testimonies of both Testaments produced by the Fathers of that council to confirm the article of faith concerning Christ’s two natures—divine and human, subsisting in the one person of the Word—had been carefully expressed in the sacred images of the Liberian basilica [Col. 0317C]. We could likewise show that this doctrine was represented in the paintings, historical scenes, and mosaics of the basilica of Saint Paul by Leo the Great.

But lest we seem to repeat what has already been done, or detain the reader longer than is appropriate, we shall merely indicate the apses, or vaulted chambers, and principal arches of the patriarchal basilicas of the City listed here by the Librarian, even though, after Leo the Great’s restoration, they were repeatedly renewed by later pontiffs, his successors, and indeed in centuries very far removed from one another. Nevertheless, they have always retained—and still retain—the memory of the first four universal councils and the documentary evidence of the doctrines of faith defended there, expressed in the testimonies of the divine Scriptures.

Let it be permitted to indicate these matters briefly. In each of these basilicas, an image of the prince of the Apostles is seen, generally formed in mosaic in the apse or vaulted presbytery, together with the testimony to the divinity of Christ the Lord, which is set forth as the foundation of faith [Col. 0317D]:

**YOU ARE CHRIST, THE SON OF THE LIVING GOD.**

In the Lateran basilica, restored by Sixtus IV after the fire, this was not omitted, but was observed and expressly represented in the customary manner. It may be seen elegantly engraved in an image of that same mosaic and inserted in a book recently printed, namely in the year 1723, *On the Present State of the Same Holy Papal Lateran Church*.

In the apse of the Vatican basilica, Innocent III likewise restored it in the form shown by Ciampini in his image of the mosaic adorning that apse, in his book *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by the Great Constantine*, p. 43. In the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, Pope Honorius III, about five hundred years ago, similarly expressed the same confession of Peter.

Although the old apse of the Vatican basilica was destroyed, together with its mosaic, in the construction of the new building, that same confession did not cease to be represented in the bronze ornamentation of the cathedra placed there by Alexander VII. There the giving of the keys is represented, followed by [Col. 0318A] Peter’s confession. This handing-over of the keys and the subject of the confession are also carved in an ancient relief preserved in the most sacred place of the Vatican crypts, before the burial place of the holy Apostles, which we call the Confession. There, a sarcophagus discovered in the same crypts in 1607 and represented by Aringhi in Book II, chapter 10, p. 293, displays among other images taken from the sacred Scriptures this very testimony of the Apostle Peter to Christ’s divinity, which was entrusted to the teaching office of the Church. Thus the holy Apostle seems, in a certain manner, unwilling ever to be separated from the ashes of this document of his confession.

In the apse of our Liberian basilica also, Nicholas IV, its restorer, represented blessed Peter with the oracle of his confession:

**YOU ARE CHRIST, THE SON OF THE LIVING GOD.**

In this single confession the Nicene doctrine of Christ’s divinity against the blasphemies of Arius, the Constantinopolitan Creed, the teaching of Ephesus against Nestorius, and the truth of Chalcedon [Col. 0318B] against Eutyches are firmly established.

In the apse of the Lateran, the image of the Virgin Mother of God is adorned with Greek letters assigning her the title **MOTHER OF GOD**. The Vatican dome and the very ancient image of the Liberian basilica in the Pauline chapel likewise display her, as a distinguished monument of the faith of Ephesus against Nestorius.

In the Lateran and Liberian basilicas, Saint John the Evangelist bears the beginning of his Gospel:

**IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.**

By this the Arian impiety and the heresies related to it were refuted at the Council of Nicaea and at the councils that followed.

In the Vatican basilica restored by Innocent III, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, offered as a victim for us and pouring out upon us the sacraments of his body and blood, was represented. We likewise saw that typical lamb, marked on the forehead with the name of Christ, represented in the ancient Vatican sarcophagus mentioned shortly before.

How many conciliar decrees concerning faith this single image encompasses is sufficiently clear to anyone even slightly acquainted with ecclesiastical history [Col. 0318C]. It is therefore often displayed in Roman titles, as in those of Saints Cosmas and Damian under Felix IV, Saint Mark under Gregory IV, and Saints Praxedes and Cecilia under Paschal I, as may be seen in Ciampini.

In the Pauline basilica on the Ostian Way, besides the apse emblems restored by Honorius III, there remain, through the design and command of Leo the Great, on the arch crowning the apse, the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse adoring, and the four mystical animals proclaiming the divinity of Christ to our Savior. Hadrian indicated these in the oft-mentioned letter read at the Seventh Ecumenical Council concerning the veneration of sacred images. The name of the pontiff and of Placidia Augusta is also inscribed there as follows:

> **THE DEVOUT MIND OF PLACIDIA REJOICES THAT THE WHOLE GLORY**  
> **OF HER FATHER’S WORK SHINES THROUGH THE ZEAL OF POPE LEO.**

In the Vatican and Pauline basilicas, Saint Leo III—according to Anastasius, sections 410 and 411—had placed two silver shields [Col. 0318D] inscribed with the Creed, one in Greek letters and the other in Latin, above the entrance to the body of the church. From this Creed, naturally, the faith of all the councils takes its beginning.

What Leo established in these basilicas, we preserve today on the individual altars. In the apse of the Lateran, the Holy Spirit is represented in the form of a dove, just as in the Vatican above the cathedra, hovering over the four rivers of Paradise. These signify Christ’s baptism and the grace received from it, with the river Jordan placed beneath them, as though indicating through them Christ’s washing.

This same symbol of baptism may be seen in the old mosaic of the Vatican apse, restored, as we said, by Innocent III, in Ciampini’s aforementioned work, chapter 4, p. 43, where its figure is engraved.

The palm and the phoenix are seen in the Lateran as types of the death and resurrection of Christ the Lord, together with other symbols enumerated by Cardinal Rasponi in Book I, chapter 9, *On the Lateran Basilica*. The palm and phoenix—an ancient emblem of the mysteries of Christ [Col. 0319A], also found on the coins of the Christian Caesars of the fourth and fifth centuries, as antiquarians know—were likewise displayed in the Vatican apse when it was renovated by Innocent III.

Ciampini, *On Sacred Buildings*, chapter 4, p. 43, represented them insufficiently distinctly in his image of that mosaic. But that portion of the mosaic, preserved together with the likeness of Innocent III and now displayed in the church of the city of Poli, adjoining the magnificent palace of the counts who are dukes of that city, clearly shows the symbol of the phoenix.

For the full presentation in the presbyteries of Rome’s patriarchal basilicas of the complement of the apostolic symbol, together with the articles of faith already indicated—which encompass the faith of the Holy Trinity and the divine and human nature of our Savior, as well as the mysteries of the Incarnation, birth, Passion, death, and resurrection—the expectation of the coming Judge and of our resurrection is recalled and expressed in the Lateran mosaic by the words of the Apostle Paul, together with an image of that Apostle:

**WE AWAIT THE SAVIOR, OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST,** [Col. 0319B] etc.

Moreover, the unity and communion of the Catholic Church are displayed in the images and inscription of the Vatican mosaic restored by Innocent III, and in the Lateran inscription. The same appears in another mosaic under Celestine I in the title of Saint Sabina, represented by images and inscriptions:

**THE CHURCH FROM THE CIRCUMCISION AND FROM THE NATIONS,**

gathered under the one vicar of Christ on earth and prince of the shepherds.

Finally, the confession of the last doctrines of the Apostles’ Creed is added: the remission of sins, in the keys entrusted to Peter, which became the insignia of the patriarchal basilicas; and eternal life, indicated in the Innocentian apse of the Vatican by the book of eternal life in the hand of Christ the Lord seated upon the throne, according to the type of the Apocalypse—as Ciampini notes on p. 43 of the work cited above—and by the Lamb taking away the sins of the world.

This is also indicated by the words of the Forerunner beneath that symbol in the Liberian basilica, where Saint John the Baptist holds in his right hand an opened scroll inscribed in letters:

**BEHOLD THE LAMB OF GOD.** [Col. 0319C]

In that same basilica, we have seen contained, expressed in panels from both Testaments and produced at the general councils, the symbols and documentary evidence of the Altar and the sacraments, of the cathedra, and of the other mysteries, together with the doctrines of faith.

Thus it is entirely clear that the patriarchal basilicas of the City, cultivated by the supreme pontiffs from Sylvester onward—from their foundation through their subsequent restorations down to the present age—are for the faithful peoples like that book of the Apocalypse, chapter 5, which John saw written within and without in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne, and opened by the Lamb possessing the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth: that is, the sevenfold grace of the divine Spirit, everywhere among the nations in the profession of the Catholic doctrine, which summons the peoples to acclaim:

> “To him who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power, forever and ever.”
>
> “And the four living creatures said: Amen.”
>
> “And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshiped him who lives forever and ever.”

With this symbol of the vision [Col. 0319D] described by John in the Apocalypse, Leo the Great certainly marked the triumphal arch of the patriarchal basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. His own name was also added, and the mosaic remains preserved after almost thirteen centuries. Later, at the beginning of the ninth century, Saint Paschal I imitated this example and had the same vision of the twenty-four elders adoring and offering their crowns before the throne of God represented in the titles of Saints Praxedes and Cecilia, as may be observed in Ciampini, *Ancient Monuments of the Roman Church*, vol. II, chapter 25, plate 46, fol. 147; and chapter 27, plate 51, p. 151.

**Line 7.**—“The basilica of blessed Cornelius, bishop and martyr, beside the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way.” Today this suburban holy building is sought in vain, as are many others in the same stretch of the Appian Way and in nearby areas, constructed by different pontiffs [Col. 0320A] above the cemeteries in which the holy departed had been laid.

The suburban churches of Urban and Mark on the Appian Way, of Damasus on the Ardeatine Way, and others like them are sought in vain, since for many centuries the incursions of the barbarians around the City, especially those of the Saracens, destroyed almost all the sacred buildings outside the walls of Rome.

Concerning the cemetery of Saint Cornelius the pope on his own property beside the Appian Way, see what we noted above from the Librarian in the notes on his *Life* and on Saint Pius.

**Line 9.**—“And he freed all Italy from the danger of its enemies.” Victor of Tunnuna, writing a full century after the holy pontiff but not far removed from him in time, records the embassy of the holy pontiff and its successful outcome three years earlier, under the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.

Moreover, Prosper, blessed Leo’s notary—as he is called by Ado, following Marcellinus—in the edition of the *Chronicle* by Du Chesne, reported almost word for word what is read in Victor.

**Line 10.**—“Here he established a monastery at Saint [Col. 0320B] Peter, etc.” We have already said above that monks existed long before Leo’s pontificate. In Rome and around Rome, from the time of Saint Jerome, we have also seen monks and rules for monasteries prescribed by Saint Innocent.

Yet we have not so far read that monasteries were built by the supreme pontiffs near the basilicas of the City before Leo the Great. Leo therefore appears to have been the first author of this practice when he constructed near the Vatican a monastery of Saints John and Paul. His immediate successors imitated him.

For Hilary, elected as his successor from among Leo’s deacons in the year 461, “made monasteries at Saint Lawrence and within the City at the *Luna*” (below, no. 71).

Saint Simplicius succeeded him in the year 467: “He dedicated the basilica of blessed Andrew” the Apostle “beside the basilica of Saint Mary” (below, no. 72), namely the church of Saint Andrew, called *Cata Barbara*, near the Liberian basilica, where the church and monastery of Saint Anthony of Egypt are now seen. Sixty years ago there still existed there a mosaic bearing the name of Pope Simplicius, published by Ciampini in *Ancient Monuments*, vol. I, p. 243.

That a monastery existed there, restored 250 years later by Gregory II, is testified by the Librarian, section 178, in these words:

> “He established the *Gerocomium* [or *Gerontocomium*], which is situated behind the apse of the holy Mother of God at the manger, as a monastery; and he organized the monastery of the Apostle Saint Andrew, which is called Barbara’s and had been reduced to extreme desolation, so that not even one monk was present, by bringing in monks, so that both monasteries might sing praises to the holy Mother of God every day and night.”

From this we also learn the reason for founding such monasteries around the basilicas and more distinguished titles: namely, so that the monks, together with the clergy, might perform the daily and nightly office of psalmody in these most celebrated sanctuaries.

Leo promoted the monastic rule not only in the City and within the monasteries he himself built around it, but also established and enlarged it in the western provinces [Col. 0320D].

The people of Marseille boast that the monastery of Saint Victor—regarded among the most celebrated and ancient monasteries of the Western Church—had Cassian as its founder, Cassian being a very close friend of Leo the Great. Bringing the rules of Saint Pachomius and of other Egyptian Fathers into the West, Cassian also erected two churches together with the monastery.

The historians of Marseille, especially the elder and younger Ruffus, report that these churches were dedicated by Saint Leo the Great, in Book XI, chapter 1, no. 5. They say that the upper church was distinguished by the title of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and the lower by the invocation of the Mother of God and Saint John the Baptist. Hence, they assert, the churches initially bore the name of those Apostles, although in later times, because the relics of Saint Victor were buried there, the church, abbey, and monastery came to be called Saint Victor.

They hold that Leo carried this out at Cassian’s request [Col. 0321A], in order to repay the favor for the distinguished work written by Cassian at Leo’s urging, *On the Incarnation of the Lord against the Nestorian Heresy*. Cassian had dedicated this work to Leo while serving as deacon of Sixtus III in Gaul.

It is highly probable that Pope Leo, while staying in Gaul, had attentively observed the excellent fruits of the monasteries he saw there, which served as nurseries of most holy bishops. With the same hope of preserving and advancing a stricter discipline among the clergy through the proximity and, so to speak, companionship of monks, he conceived the idea of establishing monasteries near the basilicas in the city of Rome.

A distinguished document of the abundant fruit produced in the clergy by the promotion of discipline through the foundation of monasteries is supplied to us by a notable marble inscription, cut during the time of Leo the Great in the church of Narbonne. It was published by the same Ruffuses in their aforementioned *History of Marseille*, Book X, chapter 1, from the collections of Baluze relating to the works of Salvian.

The inscription is as follows:

> **+ BY THE MERCY OF GOD AND CHRIST, THIS THRESHOLD [Col. 0321B], etc.**
>
> By the mercy of God and Christ, this threshold was installed in the fifth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Rusticus.
>
> Rusticus, bishop, son of Bishop Bonosus and nephew on his mother’s side of Bishop Arator, companion of Bishop Venerius, fellow presbyter in the monastery of the Church of Marseille, in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day of the year and the third day before the Ides of October, began, together with the presbyter Ursus, the deacon Hermes, and their companions, to remove the wall of the church formerly destroyed by fire. On the thirty-seventh day, the squared stone began to be laid in the foundation, etc.

There would be much worthy of note in this inscription: the careful reckoning of episcopal periods in the same age, the rite of restoring a church, and other matters of this kind useful for confirming pontifical history.

Passing these over, however, I wish only that one point relevant to the subject of the present work be observed: namely, the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline promoted in that period by the Gallican bishops among their clergy through the proximity of monasteries to their episcopal sees [Col. 0321C]. These monasteries seemed to become nurseries of excellent clergy, since from them priests and bishops distinguished for holiness were repeatedly chosen.

Rusticus and Venerius are here called *syncellites* (fellow cell-dwellers). That Rusticus is the man to whom Saint Jerome’s Letter 4 is still extant, while he was a monk; he was afterward elected a presbyter of Marseille and finally became bishop of the Church of Narbonne. The celebrated decretal Letter 92 of Leo the Great was also addressed to him.

Venerius, initially Rusticus’s fellow presbyter and colleague from the monastery, first became a presbyter of the Church of Marseille and then its bishop. He is named with Rusticus in Letter 52, sent by Saint Leo to the bishops of Gaul after the Council of Chalcedon, and he subscribes with Rusticus in the response of their colleagues to Leo the Great, published after Letter 51 of that pontiff.

Blessed Martin in Tours, Hilary in Poitiers, another Hilary in Arles, Germanus in Auxerre, Eucherius in Lyon, Lupus in Troyes [Col. 0321D], and many others had proved, or were proving, by their own experience how greatly the sight of ordered monastic life contributed to forming an excellent clergy. For this reason the bishops brought monasteries close to their episcopal sees, just as Leo began to bring them close to the patriarchal basilicas in Rome.

**Line 13.**—“He established over the tombs of the Apostles guardians, called *cubicularii*, from the Roman clergy.” In addition to the doorkeepers, appointed for the service of the church and for certain altar duties, Leo the Great established *cubicularii* at the tombs of the Apostles.

The former generally had to stand at the entrance and doors of the church; the latter were entrusted with guarding the interior parts of the chamber of the church, namely the choir and presbytery, or even the chapels. This is how Cardinal Baronius understood the matter under the year 461, no. 11, explaining this passage of the Librarian:

> “Those who are called *cubicularii*. These are what we now call chaplains. For we have noted in the Martyrology that among the ancients a *cubiculum* meant the same as what among us today [Col. 0322A] is called a chapel; otherwise, the Roman Order also teaches that some of the *cubicularii* were laymen.”

Charles Macer, in his brother Dominic’s *Hierolexicon*, under the word *Cubicularius*, adds that among the Latins *capellanus* and *cubicularius* are synonyms, and among the Greeks so are *pastophoros* (Greek: **παστοφόρος**) and *pastophorion*; and that *pastophoria*, choir, bridal chamber, and bedroom all signify the same thing.

The *cubicularii* established by Leo must therefore be understood as chaplains who guarded these interior parts of the church—the chapels or chambers—and the area of the choir and presbytery around the tombs of the Apostles. They were therefore to be chosen from the clergy.

Later Gregory the Great also recommended that clergy be assigned to the bishop’s chamber, in *Decretum*, Distinction 2, Question 7, chapter 58, so that clergy or monks, rather than laymen, might perform the office of *cubicularius*. The same appears to be understood of the *cubicularii* of the Apostles established by Leo from among the clergy.

Since Leo had founded a monastery near the basilica of the prince of the Apostles so that the monks might recite the nightly vigils and daily prayers alternately or jointly with the clergy [Col. 0322B], he also wished them to serve with the clergy as guardians of the chambers, chapels, bridal chamber, and choir, in the station assigned to them around the tomb of the Apostles.

The same arrangement still exists in the Ambrosian basilica: the daily services of the altar and choir are performed both by clergy and by monks.

**Line 17.**—“He was buried beside the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle.” The burial of Saint Leo the Great in the Vatican basilica has been illuminated by many writers, both ancient and modern, on the occasion of three translations of the same sacred body.

The first took place from the entrance of the old sacristy within the basilica, under Pope Sergius I of that name, about 240 years after Leo’s death. An ancient inscription engraved by Sergius to commemorate the event was first published by Gruter from the Palatine manuscripts in the Appendix to the *Thesaurus Inscriptionum*, fol. 1170, and afterward by Cardinal Baronius in volume X of the *Annals*, appendix, p. 919.

The second translation was occasioned by the construction of the new Vatican basilica over the old one, which was enclosed within it. Gregory XIII, concerned that the erection of the massive structures supporting the largest vaults, and the demolition of the Leonine chapel built by Sergius over the tomb, might cause some accident and damage the sacred remains, judged that they ought to be transferred to a safer place.

The translation was postponed, however, until the pontificate of Paul V, when the masses of the new basilica had reached a height at which the chapels could be completed without danger of collapse. Then, in May 1607, the sacred body was solemnly removed from the old tomb and placed beneath the altar-table of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Column, where it was to remain until the decoration of the neighboring altar, bearing the name of Saint Leo but not yet firmly established under Paul, had been completed.

When all the decoration in that part of the basilica had finally been completed under Clement XI [Col. 0322D], the opportunity for the third translation arose in April 1714. We were not only permitted to attend it, but also to see and venerate the relics of the sacred body at close range and to draw the arrangement of the bones that remained in their places, together with the clothing in which they were wrapped.

This seemed likely to contribute considerably to determining the arrangement of certain priestly vestments according to the usage of Leo’s age, especially the pallium drawn around the shoulders and fastened with pins, as well as the covering of the head, from what was observed when his coffin was opened.

I would insert here the entire history, with observations arranged in several chapters, were it not more suitably reserved for the final volume of this work, when the Librarian’s text leads us to the *Life of Sergius I*.

We must nevertheless point out that the image of the sacred body of Leo the Great, which the Reverend Fathers Henschenius [Col. 0323A] and Papebrochius faithfully reproduced from the autograph of Grimaldus preserved in the canonical archive of the Vatican basilica, in the *Propylaeum* to volume I of the May saints, does not correspond to the original.

For Jacobus Grimaldus, selected to record the proceedings, could not so readily have become a painter through the appointment by which he was declared a notary. In the image drawn together with the acts, he represents the saintly pontiff’s entire head covered with a round papal mitre; but in the written description he corrects the wandering of his pen.

For he clearly declares that Saint Leo’s head had been consumed and reduced to fragments of bone—indeed, to very small fragments, as we ourselves saw. No round mitre, or *regnum*, as it is called today, appeared above those fragments of bone; only folds of a veil bent around the crown of the head and rising from the same fold of the garments, which covered both shoulders and the breast, as though continuous with it.

Here are Grimaldus’s own words, copied from the autograph, fol. 148:

> “When the coffin was opened, the sacred body itself of Saint Leo the Great was seen by all who were present there—namely, by the several bishops and canons whom he names—still intact; that is, none of the principal parts of the bones was missing or displaced, except for the head. It was seven palms and three quarters in height. As could be conjectured, although it had been considerably consumed by the length of time and antiquity, this holy pontiff had been slender and emaciated in body.
>
> “He was dressed in pontifical vestments: a *planeta*, or broad *casula* in the ancient style, of chestnut-colored purple. His hands were folded and covered by the *planeta*; they had been reduced to bones. His right leg had fragments of the tunic and dalmatic, and his feet likewise were seen reduced to bones.
>
> “The head had been consumed into several fragments of bone and was blackened. The remains of the pontifical mitre could be seen, torn and darkened by extreme age. Around the neck, and likewise above the hands, certain golden threads gleamed. A small red cross, which belonged to the pontifical pallium, remained above the right shoulder. He also held another, somewhat longer cross of the same pallium near the breast on the right side [Col. 0323C]. In the middle of the breast one golden pin of the pallium could be seen fastened into the *planeta*. Nothing remained of the pallium itself. The *planeta* reached to the feet. Everything dissolved at the touch, both because of the antiquated material and because of the damp place, although it had been very well sealed,” etc.

The appearance shown to us 107 years later of the same sacred body and the clothing with which it was covered corresponds perfectly to this description by Grimaldus. The breast and shoulders were entirely covered, while the lower limbs appeared clearly beneath the folds of the garments, which were thinner there and largely dissolved.

The exposed vertebrae of the neck and loins could be seen. The ilia, the bones of both thighs, and the tibiae could be distinguished. The fibula had been moved slightly from the left tibia, while all the other bones remained exactly in their places.

The head was as follows. Of the bones of the skull, only a few small fragments remained, fallen among the remnants of the coverings. Part of the left side of the lower mandible remained intact. The eminent Pauli, the papal chief physician, summoned to the inspection by command of His Holiness, noted that a tooth had fallen from it and dictated by name to the notary the bones that appeared.

The fallen and displaced process of the right humerus lay not far from the remaining part of the humerus, which protruded from beneath the folds of the garments in its proper position. Therefore no portion of the skeleton had been moved from its place, except for the dissolved skull and the few other bones mentioned.

I shall also give the words dictated by the papal chief physician to the notary who was committing this solemn recognition of the sacred relics to the public records:

> “When the enclosure of the tomb of Saint Leo, the first pope of that name, had been opened so that his venerable relics or the form of his body might be inspected, at a first, untrained glance there appeared a mass of crumbled garments and consumed flesh. Indeed, because of the long duration of the centuries, we found the limbs so diminished and almost consumed [Col. 0324A] that scarcely any opportunity remained for even an anatomical, and that only a superficial, description.
>
> “Nevertheless, it did not escape our careful examination. The position of the head, raised into a heap of bone fragments, was clearly visible; above all, the segment of the lower jaw was intact in comparison with the other parts of the head, with a tooth lying above it outside its socket.
>
> “The thorax, as well as the arms, was covered with garments torn and largely consumed, so that the parts could scarcely be distinguished from one another.
