The vertebrae of the neck and loins, however, appeared to be situated in their natural positions. Around the lower end of the sternum, here and there, lay two scraps of a golden strip, or traces of some other ornament.
>
> “The more elevated iliac bone and the bones of both thighs projected distinctly once the coverings, long since torn, had been removed. The tibiae also appeared intact to their extremities, except for the left one, whose broken fibula lay not far from the tibia.
>
> “We were unable to inspect the tarsal, metatarsal, and toe bones. Nevertheless, we considered it most probable that they lay wrapped among the ashes of the garments and flesh [Col. 0324B], or had settled here and there on the bottom of the coffin after it had been shaken several times.
>
> “Two other fairly distinct fragments also appeared there, lying near the position of the head. One resembled a clavicle, precisely at the part by which it is joined to the shoulder; the other was quite certainly one of the bones of the skull. It is, however, highly probable that these two fragments had fallen from the upper coffin of the three holy Leos. For the lead and wooden lid of Saint Leo’s coffin, loosened and compressed by the aforementioned upper coffin of the three holy Leos, could have allowed the fragments to enter.”

Here he is speaking of the coffin of the three successors and namesakes of Leo the Great—namely, Leo II, Leo III, and Leo IV—which contained their ashes in three separate compartments and had formerly been placed above the coffin of Saint Leo I described earlier. Anyone may learn the details more fully both from Grimaldus’s acts under Paul V and from the recent account of the translation [Col. 0324C] of the four holy Leos, printed in Rome under Clement XI in the year 1715.

One thing was lacking in that Roman edition of 1715: the image printed with it ought not to have been taken from the one that Grimaldus had had made by an unskilled draftsman, which did not correspond to his description; rather, he should have had it formed solely from the original, visible to everyone. Once we had carefully reproduced this image after examining it in the presence of the sacred body on 2 April, and again comparing it with that same sacred body on 11 April, when Clement XI descended to the tomb of the holy predecessor, then kept in the chapel of Saint Nicholas, and, after the sacred rites had been performed there, knelt with several most eminent and most reverend cardinals, as well as most illustrious and most reverend bishops and prelates, before the venerable bodies of the four holy Leos, he ordered public records on the matter to be drawn up by Cosmas Antonius de Bernardinis, a public notary by apostolic authority and specially appointed by the same supreme pontiff as notary of the Congregation of Sacred Rites [Col. 0324D] to record those proceedings—and once the image had been approved by the most illustrious lord Michael Angelus de Paulis, papal chief physician and honorary member of the pontiff’s privy chamber, who examined the position of each individual bone and dictated its name to the recorder—we have thought it not inappropriate to insert it here.

For it displays the position of that same sacred body, the form of the bones remaining in their places, and the folds of the garments, from which it is not difficult for those versed in Roman antiquities and in the civil and ecclesiastical customs of the Leonine age to discern the form of the vestments. For the longer, gathered folds extending from the lower part of the legs toward the arms, while retaining the same arrangement even in the tattered garments, show the shape of the ancient planeta, reaching almost to the ankles and surrounding the body in the manner of an episcopal cope, from which bishops and priests [Col. 0325A] performed the sacred rites with their arms projecting.

Above the breast, however, the gathering of several coverings displays something resembling the innermost hood of an episcopal birrus, and also that cleaner garment which the supreme pontiff uses while celebrating, thrown back above the planeta from the opening at the neck—called the phano—extending from the top of the clavicles and throat to the ends of the elbows. That a pontifical pallium marked with purple crosses had been fastened to this garment—as the surviving images of supreme pontiffs in the mosaics of the Leonine age and of later periods, in Roman basilicas and titular churches, demonstrate—is shown by the long, gilded pin seen above the breast both by Grimaldus and by us.

The coverings drawn back above the head, which in this tomb retained their folds and rose from the shoulders toward the position of the bregmatic and temporal bones, although the skull had collapsed into fragments of bone, demonstrate either that some part of the phano was customarily drawn back from the nape in the manner of a hood over the crown of the head—from which the origin of the mitre must be derived, as I shall show in its proper place in my dissertation on sacred priestly vestments—or that some veil had been placed over the face of the holy pontiff while his funeral was being arranged.

Grimaldus records on folio 45 of his Acts, from the written account of Jacobus Herculaneus, canon of Saint Peter, preserved in the canonical archive, that on 4 February 1543 a tomb was discovered near the chapel of Saint Petronilla in the Vatican basilica. It was the tomb of Maria, wife of Honorius Augustus, in which garments woven with gold were seen. Among them he lists a golden cloth wound several times around the head, and, distinct from it, another cloth placed over the face and breast. From this the custom of that age in burying the bodies of princes and distinguished men and women may be recognized. Herculani’s words are:

> “Be it remembered that on 3 February 1544 a tomb was discovered in Saint Peter’s, in the chapel called Saint Petronilla, formerly that of the kings of France, while the foundations of the new structure were being dug. The tomb was a large marble sarcophagus covered with a slab of similar thickness, one palm and three quarters; its length was fourteen palms and its width eleven palms. In it was the body of Maria, wife of Honorius, emperor of Constantinople. The body was clothed in a garment made of gold, as it is commonly called, *orotirato*. On its head it had a golden cloth wound several times, and another spread over the face and breast. This gold, cast in the form of a loaf, weighed thirty-five pounds,”

and so forth. He describes other ornaments found with these, which I do not list here, since the subject is only the veils placed over and wrapped around the head, whose use in the burial of high-ranking persons flourished in the age of Saint Leo and immediately thereafter.

Besides, therefore, the vestments of the priestly *casula*, or planeta, falling down to the feet and gathered into the bend of the elbows in the manner of episcopal copes, as well as the phano, the pallium, and the head-covering in the manner of a hood—from whose cut-off border and title the mitre appears to have arisen—the golden threads seen in Saint Leo’s tomb around the throat and around each wrist indicate to us a border for the insertion of the head and for the opening of the sleeves of the subdiaconal tunic and the diaconal dalmatic, used in the same way among Latins and Greeks, with a form midway between the two rites to be inferred from the insertion of the sleeves.

But there will be a more suitable opportunity to discuss these matters at greater length below, in a special dissertation prepared by us for this purpose while the sacred body of Leo the Great was being uncovered. We shall record its appearance in the present notes to his Life.

[Col. 0326A] **View of the Sacred Body of Saint Leo the Great, after his tomb had been opened and again sealed by order of Pope Clement XI on 2 and 11 April 1714 during his solemn translation.** Only small fragments remained from the skull, together with half of the lower jaw. The remaining bones had stayed in position, except that the upper process of the right humerus and the fibula of the left tibia had been displaced. They were visible beneath garments of saffron color, thinned by age and decently gathered in broad folds, in the manner of a cope, both above the head and around the breast and lower limbs. Above the sternum was a gilded pin for fastening the pallium; and around the joints of the wrist and elbow golden border-threads were visible. The length of the sacred body was seven Roman palms and three quarters.

[Note: [Col. 0325D]]

**No. 66, line 16.—“Where they also condemned Eutyches.”** At Constantinople, in the presence of three apostolic legates, a council of 150 Fathers was convened, in which an anathema was pronounced against Eutyches, who said that in Christ the Lord there had been two natures before the incarnation but only one nature after the incarnation; and against Nestorius, who asserted that the Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, was merely human and was not also born God.

**No. 67, line 8.—“He went to the king of the Huns, named Attila.”** After suffering defeat in the Catalaunian Plains near Toulouse, Attila advanced bloodily upon Italy. He besieged Aquileia, situated on the borders of the province, for three years. When, his fortunes having become desperate, he was considering lifting the siege, he saw storks carrying their young from the city into the countryside. Moved by this omen, he attacked the city more fiercely, eventually captured it, plundered it, and burned it, sparing no class of people and calling himself the Scourge of God. He destroyed Ticinum and Milan, royal cities. Then, after laying waste to many places all around, when he was also preparing to overthrow Rome, Pope Leo the Great, urged on by the emperor Valentinian, went out to meet him and rendered him so mild that, having immediately promised the firmest peace, he proceeded without intending to return beyond the Danube. He had been terrified by the threatening death of two men, swords drawn above his head, unless he obeyed the words of the holy pontiff. Peter and Paul were believed to have been those who, in so great a crisis, stood as protectors of Italy and Rome. As a result of this destruction of Aquileia, the Venetians migrated to the islands, while the people of Padua occupied a deep channel; thus Venice began to be inhabited and founded amid the waters.]

[Note: [Col. 0327A]]

**No. 66, line 3.—“Here he discovered two heresies.”** According to Pagi, he also encountered and suppressed other heresies that deserve mention. After Africa had been devastated by the Vandals, many Manichaeans came to Rome. There they mingled secretly with the Catholics, held meetings, and seduced many by their impious doctrine. Leo’s first confrontation was against them, and Prosper relates that many whom his diligence had uncovered were exposed in the consulship of the year 443. Countless books of theirs were burned at Rome, and many of the Manichaeans themselves were restored to soundness.

Then, in the following year, 444, Saint Leo, in Letter 7—formerly numbered 2—to the bishops throughout Italy, dated 3 Kalends of February, warned that many Manichaeans had been detected in the city of Rome through his vigilance and that they should be investigated with equal diligence by those bishops. This letter was sent through the provinces to all the bishops, as Idacius, a contemporary of those times, writes: “Through the bishop then presiding at Rome, proceedings concerning the Manichaeans are sent through the provinces.”

Later, in the year 447, he suppressed the same Manichaeans in Spain, as well as the Priscillianists, whose errors were partly shared with the Manichaeans and partly peculiar to themselves. He crushed the sect of the Priscillianists in a letter sent to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, Letter 93, in which he separately refutes each of the sect’s principal errors and summons Turibius and the bishops of Galicia and Lusitania to a council, so that together they might see what ought to be done against the spreading heresy. Those who wish to know the impious practices of the Priscillianists should read this letter of Leo. Saint Leo attacked not only the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, but also the Pelagians.

**Line 10.—“With the autograph of the holy archbishop Leo.”** While Saint Leo was seated in office, the Eutychian heresy arose. Its beginnings and the councils held against it must here be presented briefly. Eutyches, a presbyter and archimandrite, or abbot, of a very celebrated monastery in the imperial city of Constantinople, according to Liberatus, chapter 2, fell into the blasphemous impiety of Apollinaris through excessive hatred of Diodore, once bishop of Tarsus, and Theodore, once bishop of Mopsuestia. He “corrupted the dogma of the mystery of the Incarnation, calling both the divinity of the Only-Begotten and his humanity one nature, asserting that a commixture and confusion had occurred, and attaching the saving Passion to the immutable Deity itself,” as Facundus writes in book VIII, chapter 5, quoting a fragment of a letter from the lord bishop of Antioch to the emperor Theodosius.

Thus Eutyches asserted that Christ was from two natures, but not in two natures—that is, that there had been two natures before the union and one afterward. The consequence was that Christ was not consubstantial with us according to the flesh. Since the letter of the lord bishop of Antioch to the emperor Theodosius was written around the year 442, the beginning of the Eutychian heresy must be dated from that year. Hence Saint Anastasius Sinaita writes: “About ten years afterward”—that is, after the Council of Ephesus—“a certain Eutyches, an archimandrite, arose at Constantinople, saying that the whole Christ was one nature.”

Pope Gelasius, in Letter 16 to the bishops of Dardania, dates the beginning of the Eutychian heresy from the year 448, because in that year Eutyches was summoned to judgment before Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, after being accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum in Phrygia Salutaris and a friend of Eutyches. The matter is mentioned in the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists*: “When Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, found Eutyches advocating such things, he reported him to Bishop Flavian out of zeal for the faith—a zeal that he had also displayed when he was an *agens in rebus*, for he had in due time rebuked Nestorius as well when he was preaching sacrilegious things in the Church.”

The accusation deeply offended Eutyches. He therefore complained to Saint Leo that the Nestorian heresy was again flourishing through the efforts of certain persons. Leo praised his zeal and kindly replied on 12 Kalends of March in the year 449. Hence the Acts of the Fifth Council say: “Leo, pope of elder Rome, of holy memory, both received Eutyches and replied, approving him; yet afterward he condemned and anathematized him as a heretic.”

But before Eutyches was brought before episcopal judgment, an accusation concerning the revival of the Apollinarian heresy through the efforts and machinations of Eutyches had already been brought to the emperor Theodosius by the lord bishop of Antioch. This is clear from the aforementioned synodal letter of the lord bishop to Theodosius, preserved in Facundus, book VIII, chapter 5. From it we learn who those persons were whom Eutyches was tacitly defaming before Saint Leo as followers and supporters of Nestorius. It is clear that he was speaking of Domnus, Theodoret, and others of that sort, who had complained to Theodosius about Diodore and Theodore, whom Eutyches had anathematized.

A synod was immediately convened at Constantinople by Bishop Flavian, on 6 Ides of November in the year 448. It was not an ordinary synod, but consisted only of those bishops who happened to be present at court. The occasion for convening it was a dispute that had arisen between Florentius, bishop of Sardis and metropolitan of Lydia, and two bishops of his province. Once that matter had been concluded, the synod dealt with Eutyches, who had formerly labored with the holy monk Dalmatius to overthrow the Nestorian heresy.

Eutyches had repeatedly been admonished in friendship by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, to abandon his error, but had obstinately persisted in it. When, moreover, he asserted at the synod that there had indeed been two natures before the union but one after the union, he was condemned by the synod. The eunuch Chrysaphius, administrator of the empire, achieved nothing on his behalf; he was driven less by love for Eutyches than by hatred of Flavian. The heretic evaded the judgment, though he was convicted from his own writings.

The synod was completed in seven sessions, and all the bishops, thirty-two in number, subscribed to it, along with twenty-three archimandrites. The bishops subscribed with this formula: “I, Basil, bishop of N., having judged, have subscribed.” The archimandrites subscribed: “I, N., presbyter and archimandrite, have subscribed to the deposition of Eutyches.” The reason was that bishops attend councils as judges, whereas abbots attend as honorary observers: the former pronounce the sentence, while the latter assent to the sentence issued by the bishops.

The sentence against Eutyches as a heretic was pronounced in these words:

> “We have decreed, with tears and mourning, his complete destruction through our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed; that he is excluded from every priestly office, from our communion, and from the primacy of the monastery.”

When Eutyches saw that, with the authority of Chrysaphius and the protection of Augustus Theodosius, he could not keep his doctrine secure and intact, he fled to the Roman pontiff, since it was easy to surround someone who was absent. His letters are read in the synodal collection against the tragedy of Irenaeus, published by Christianus Lupus, chapter 222. At their end Eutyches says:

> “I have appended to these letters of mine both documents: the one presented to the synod by my accuser, and the one prepared by me but not accepted.”

Yet that letter contains no mention of an appeal by Eutyches. Chapter 223 of the same synodal collection then contains a protest petition submitted by Eutyches in the city of Constantinople, as the words of Leo in Letter 8 to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, make clear.

Saint Leo, since Flavian had not informed him of what had taken place at Constantinople—lest he condemn an innocent man or acquit a guilty one—wrote to the emperor Theodosius and to Flavian. Flavian immediately replied to the supreme pontiff and sent him the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod in the case of Eutyches, together with his letter.

After receiving Flavian’s letter, Leo promised his aid and assistance against Eutyches. He sent through the illustrious man Rhodanus a letter that Quesnell first published as number XXII. This was followed by another to Theodosius, numbered XXIII, in which Leo professes adherence to the Nicene faith, condemns the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches, and requests that a synod be convened within Italy.

In that letter he promises that a longer letter would be delivered by Flavian’s messenger. This was the celebrated letter to Flavian, formerly numbered X and now XXIV, praised at Chalcedon, approved by the Fathers, and retained as an exposition of the Church’s faith concerning the Incarnation of Christ, so that, like a Lydian stone, true and adulterated faith might be tested by it.

That letter was once read in its entirety in the Roman Church during Advent. Quesnell also establishes from a manuscript of the Royal Library that it was customarily read in the churches of Gaul. In the year 449 Leo’s legates brought it to the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, of which more will be said shortly.

Meanwhile Eutyches submitted supplicatory petitions to the emperor and accused the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod of having been abridged and falsified. The emperor, deceived by the speeches of the eunuch Chrysaphius, ordered the proceedings to be reviewed, to determine whether anything had been omitted, mutilated, or corrupted.

For this reason he ordered the same bishops who had celebrated the preceding synod at Constantinople to assemble again in the year 449. He placed Bishop Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia over them, removed Flavian of Constantinople, and deprived him of the right to sit. The synod therefore began on 5 Ides of April. The Acts were recalled for examination; nothing corrupted or altered was found, and everyone approved that everything had been written exactly as it had occurred.

When Eutyches understood that this route had closed every avenue of escape, he sought the protection of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria and an enemy of Flavian. Dioscorus wrote to the emperor and requested another synod, which the emperor ordered him to preside over by letter. Theodoret, who was hostile to Dioscorus and openly opposed to Eutychian doctrine, was excluded from that assembly.

A synod was therefore summoned at Ephesus on 3 Kalends of April in the year 449, before the proceedings of the Council of Constantinople held in 448 had been reviewed, so that it might begin on the Kalends of August. Saint Leo, invited by the emperor, sent as his legates Julius, bishop of Puteoli; Renatus, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement; and Hilary, a deacon.

The synod began only on 8 August. One hundred and thirty bishops attended, and Dioscorus of Alexandria presided. Eutyches was immediately introduced and presented a confession of faith full of falsehood and pretense, confused by an ambiguity of words. His condemnation was then reviewed, and he was declared innocent and released from the bond of excommunication.

Flavian, the defender of the faith, was condemned, together with Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum. Many pontiffs were proscribed and condemned, among them Ibas, bishop of Edessa; Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus; and, last of all, Domnus of Antioch.

Indeed, while everything was being turned upside down, and the assembled bishops, with a sword as it were held to their throats, were signing decrees of this kind, and everything was being done contrary to law and equity, Flavian—who had appealed to the supreme pontiff—was subjected not only to insults but also to blows and wounds. He gave up his spirit to God at Epipae, a city of Lydia, to which he had been sent into exile, whether death overtook him there or was inflicted upon him, in the same year, 449, as Marcellinus records in his chronicle.

In such a desperate state of affairs, the legates of Pope Leo firmly resisted the efforts of the heretics against Flavian’s condemnation and were consequently placed under guard. Because of these proceedings the synod was rightly called predatory, or a robber synod.

When Hilary the deacon, Pope Leo’s legate, had escaped from the pseudo-synod of Ephesus after overcoming countless dangers to his life and had arrived at Rome, Pope Leo received him. After hearing his account of events as they had occurred, Leo convened a council at Rome in which he condemned and annulled everything that had been done at Ephesus.

He then repeatedly insisted in letters that Theodosius and Augusta Pulcheria should act, so that by common agreement another synod might be convened within Italy to erase the disgrace and stain of Ephesus. He also went out with many bishops of Italy to meet Augustus Valentinian, who was coming to Rome with his mother Galla Placidia and his wife Eudoxia for religious reasons, to the threshold of the apostles. By his prayers he compelled both the women and Valentinian to write to Theodosius and bring it about that, in another council, the wrongful acts committed at Ephesus should be reviewed.

But Theodosius’ mind, entangled in the fictions and deceits of the Eutychians, could be bent neither by letters, nor by prayers, nor by any appeal to his own relatives. Rather, by public laws he condemned Flavian and ordered that the predatory synod of Ephesus be placed on a level with the Council of Nicaea.

Yet he did not escape either lightly or belatedly from the punishment for so great a crime. Not long afterward, while he was riding, his horse collapsed; he was violently thrown, severely injured, and died on 28 July in the year 450, leaving no heir.

After the death of the emperor Theodosius, his sister, Augusta Pulcheria, with the support of the senate and army, took control of the Eastern Empire and gave herself in marriage to Marcian, a most distinguished senator of Thracian origin and the son of a man who had pursued a military career.

When Marcian had assumed the empire, he considered convening a general council at the urging of Saint Leo. In the meantime he ordered a synod to be held at Constantinople, at which that famous letter of Saint Leo to Flavian—formerly numbered 10 and now 24—was read. All confirmed it by their subscriptions. It was then sent to the other metropolitans, who approved it together with the bishops of their provinces.

Anathema was pronounced against Nestorius and Eutyches, and their heresy was proscribed at Constantinople, as Saint Leo testifies in Letter 68 to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, dated in July of the year 451.

But Baronius is wrong, and after him the anonymous author of *A Selection of the Acts of the Universal Church*, or *New Summary of the Councils*, in asserting that at that synod it was forbidden that the names of Dioscorus of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Eustathius of Berytus should be recited from the diptychs. For Saint Leo, in Letter LX—formerly XL—to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, also dated on the Ides of April in the year 451, says:

> “As for the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius, it is not fitting that your Reverence should maintain that they are not to be recited at the sacred altar, on the ground that our men established there said this ought to be done.”

Therefore, as Quesnell correctly observes, Leo writes to Anatolius not as though reporting something already done, but only concerning something that his legates and Anatolius were to settle.

Although Saint Leo preferred that the ecumenical synod be postponed and held in Italy, the emperor Marcian, pressed by circumstances and by the wishes of the Easterners, began preparations for convening a synod. By his edict he ordered the bishops to come to the city of Nicaea on the next Kalends of September in the year 451.

After receiving the emperor’s letters, Saint Leo immediately considered sending legates. He wrote to him in Letter LXIX, formerly XLIX, and announced that he was sending Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum; Boniface, a presbyter; and Julian of Cos, to act in his place. The letter was dated 6 Kalends of July. On the following day he added two others to those legates: Lucentius, a bishop, and Basil, a presbyter.

Meanwhile, when Attila, king of the Huns, had been defeated in Gaul and had begun to march toward the East, and when the emperor had learned from the letters of the prefects that all Illyricum was being thrown into confusion by fear of the approaching barbarians, he could not go to Nicaea. He therefore transferred the council from Nicaea to Chalcedon, which lies only seven stades from Constantinople, and communicated this to the bishops by an edict issued on 10 Kalends of October.

The transfer was also prompted by the entreaty of the legates of the Apostolic See, who had earnestly begged the emperor to be present at the holy council and had declared that they would not go there in his absence. This is clear from the letters of the emperor Marcian to the synod that had assembled at Nicaea, reproduced in Part I of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 41 and following; from Liberatus, chapter 13 of the *Brief Account*; and from Evagrius, book II, chapter 2.

Natalis Alexander correctly proves that the synod was first summoned by Augustus Marcian to Nicaea and then transferred by him to Chalcedon with the consent of Saint Leo. He also shows that Saint Leo presided over the synod through the legates Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, Lucentius of Asculum, and Boniface the presbyter, to whom he added Julian of Cos as a participant in the deliberations rather than as a fellow legate.

The synod began on 8 Ides of October in the year of Christ 451, in the very spacious basilica of the holy virgin and martyr Euphemia, situated in the suburbs of the city.

In the second session discussion of the faith began. The Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds were publicly recited; then the letters of Cyril to Nestorius and to John of Antioch, written when peace had been established between them; and then Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian. To it the bishops acclaimed in these words: “Peter has spoken thus through Leo”; “The apostles taught thus.”

In the fourth session they returned to establishing the formula of faith and to Leo’s letter. When the Fathers were asked what they thought of that letter, they replied in their proper order that it agreed with the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds and also with the faith expounded by Saint Cyril in his letters; for that reason they had subscribed to it.

The eleventh session, concerning Domnus, bishop of Antioch, is not fictitious, as Quesnellus supposes in Dissertation 11 of his edition of the Works of Saint Leo. Baluzius, in his Preface to the Council of Chalcedon, no. 32 and following, solidly demonstrates that Quesnellus was deceived on this point and responds to all his arguments.

Domnus, bishop of Antioch, was deposed by the bishops of the robber synod of Ephesus, and Maximus was ordained in his place by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at the command of the emperor Theodosius. Saint Leo annulled all the proceedings of that robbery and restored the bishops who had been expelled from their sees. He did not restore Domnus alone; indeed, he confirmed the episcopate of Maximus, who had been imposed over him. With the permission of the synod, Maximus granted Domnus an annual allowance from the resources of the Church of Antioch.

**Line 23.—“He frequently confirmed the Council of Chalcedon in his letters,” etc.** In the fifteenth session, the clergy of the Church of Constantinople requested that the Fathers establish certain provisions concerning the see of Constantinople. The legates said that they had no instructions regarding this matter. The judges, however, declared that it belonged to the synod, and immediately withdrew; the legates followed them.

Nevertheless, in the absence of both parties, the Fathers enacted several canons. Greek codices contain thirty; Latin codices, twenty-eight. The twenty-eighth of these confirms the patriarchal privileges granted to the Church of Constantinople by the First Council of Constantinople under Damasus: namely, that it should enjoy the honor of rank immediately after the Roman see, and should possess right and authority over the dioceses of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia and their metropolitans, and should additionally ordain the bishops of the barbarians.

When the apostolic legates heard this in the sixteenth and final session, held on the Kalends of November, they demanded that the canon concerning the see of Constantinople, enacted in their absence, be reread. After it had been recited, together with the subscriptions of nearly all the Fathers, Lucentius, the legate of the Apostolic See, addressed the judges:

> “Let Your Glory first consider by what deception this was done with the holy bishops, so that they were compelled to subscribe to canons that had not been written down, although they had mentioned them.”

Everyone shouted: “No one was compelled.”

Since there was controversy concerning the canons, the judges ordered that the canons produced by both sides be brought forward. After this had been done, they again confirmed the canon that had been read, by their authority, while the Fathers acclaimed: “This is a just sentence”; “We all say this,” and so forth.

But Lucentius, the legate of the Apostolic See, protested, and rightly so. Saint Leo therefore became extremely indignant at this definition, since it overturned the Nicene canons, attempted to invalidate the third canon of the First Council of Constantinople, and falsely asserted that the Roman Church possessed the privilege of primacy only after receiving from the Fathers what it holds over the universal Church. From this it followed that the see of Constantinople, now made equal to the Roman see, ought to be granted the same privilege.

Therefore, just as Saint Leo was the most steadfast approver of what they had decreed against the heretics, so he showed himself the most vigorous defender against ambition, refusing absolutely to allow the rights of the Churches established by the Nicene Fathers to be changed.

Thus he rejected that canon, number 28, which the Greeks themselves also removed from the number of the canons. The remaining canons of the council he approved, at least by tacit consent, and the universal Church received them. The synod, celebrated by 630 Fathers, was concluded at the beginning of November in the year 451.

**Line 25.—“Eighteen letters to the bishops throughout the East.”** In the year 453 Saint Leo wrote to Julian, bishop of Cos, that, acting in his place, he should assume special care lest either the Nestorian or the Eutychian heresy revive in any part of the world. That letter, formerly numbered 56 and now 86, is the one in question.

In Letter 84 to the emperor Marcian, speaking of the same Julian, Leo says:

> “I have delegated my authority to him against the heretics of our age; and, for the protection of the Churches and of peace, I required that he not be absent from your court.”

It was dated on 6 Ides of March, during the consulship of Opilio, a man of consular rank, and therefore in the year of Christ 453.

From these and similar words, Marca, in book V of *On Concord*, chapter 15 and following, and Quesnellus, in his notes on the same letters, derive the origin of vicars—or, as we now commonly say, envoys—of the Apostolic See serving at the imperial court.

In establishing this institution, Saint Leo followed the practice of the Eastern patriarchs. From the time when the seat of empire was transferred to Byzantium, they sent *apocrisarii* to the Eastern emperors. In many respects, however, Leo distinguished himself from them according to his own prerogative.

The holy pontiff had seen the Eastern Churches tossed by terrible storms through the new heresy of Nestorius, scarcely—or perhaps not at all—brought to rest by the decisions of the Council of Ephesus. He also knew that the bishop of Constantinople, relying on the canon of the Second General Council, was devoting all his strength to enlarging his power and would not end his efforts until he had subjected the greater primates to himself. Once those primates had been subjected, there was reason to fear that he would eventually consider diminishing the authority of the Roman see as well.

He therefore judged that someone should be sent to the imperial city to watch over the faith and ecclesiastical peace and to act with the emperor to restrain efforts contrary to that faith and peace.

In the earlier age, the office of *apocrisarius* was entrusted to clerics or presbyters. For this reason it was established in the first place, and confirmed by imperial edicts, that bishops should not come to the imperial court, as is clear from Justinian’s *Novella* 6, chapter 11. Now, however, that office is often entrusted to bishops.

For an account of the legates, *apocrisarii*, or representatives of the Roman pontiffs to the emperors, appointed to conduct the affairs of the universal Church, Marca, already cited, should be read. Concerning the origin of the envoys of the Apostolic See at the court of the Frankish kings, see what will be said under Gregory III.

**No. 67, line 1.—“He renewed [the churches] after the Vandal disaster,” etc.** In the year 455, when Genseric, king of the Vandals, unexpectedly attacked and entered the city of Rome, Saint Leo went out to meet him. Addressing him at length, he obtained that he should abstain from the fire and sword with which he had intended to destroy the city and be content with plunder alone, as Prosper reports in his *Chronicle*:

> “Genseric took possession of the city of Rome, entirely deprived of every defense, when Saint Leo, bishop, met him outside the gates. His supplication, through God’s agency, so softened him that, although the city had been delivered into his power and everything was his, he nevertheless abstained from fire, slaughter, and torture.”

After fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its wealth by a secure and unrestricted search. Many thousands of captives, together with the queen and her daughters, were carried away to Carthage.

Saint Leo defended the three principal basilicas from plunder. When he then turned his attention to repairing the damage after the disaster, he ordered the silver vessels of great weight that Constantine had formerly given to the three basilicas—the Constantinian basilica, Saint Peter’s, and Saint Paul’s—to be melted down and distributed among the churches of the city, as the *Pontifical Book* records. That work also recounts that, through his piety and diligence, many basilicas were built and restored.

**Line 17.—“He was buried at the basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle,” etc.** After Saint Leo had occupied the see for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days, he departed to God on the fourth day of November in the year 461 [Col. 0333C], as the Annotator of Baronius proves under that year of Christ; there he also shows that it was only from the time of Gregory XIII that his feast was assigned to the eleventh day of April. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, as the *Book of the Pontiffs* records.

Three later translations of his relics took place. By which pontiff the first was carried out is unknown; but the second was made by Pope Sergius I of that name, in the year 688, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the first indiction. This is established by his epitaph, in which one reads:

> “Deposited on the third day before the Ides . . . and translated here again by Blessed Pope Sergius, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the first indiction.”

In the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Vitus at Verdun, cited by Mabillon, volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 431, the following is added:

> “He sat in the episcopate for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days.”

The third translation of the same holy pontiff was carried out by Paul V. For Henschenius, under the eleventh day of April, on which he is commemorated, quotes the *History of the Elevation and Translation of His Body* from a manuscript catalogue of the Church of Saint Peter, in which one reads [Col. 0333D]:

> “That sacred body, together with the bones of the other Leos—Second, Third, and Fourth—was transferred with solemn rite into the new church on the aforesaid twenty-seventh day of May, the Sunday within the octave of the Ascension, 1607, after Vespers had been sung. Those present at this translation were,” etc.

Our most holy lord, Pope Paul V, wished to see the bodies of these same saints, and he saw them with great consolation of spirit. That history also records that, before this translation, the body of Saint Leo the Great had been placed in a wooden chest, in which rested the body of the most blessed Leo the Great, Pope Leo I, deposited there by Sergius I.

[Note: [Col. 0333D]]

**No. 66, line 1.—“Leo, a Tuscan by nation,” etc.; and line 21.—“Many letters concerning the faith,” etc.** Saint Leo is called the first of his name “the Great” because he stands out among the pontiffs by singular merit. Since he was endowed with all the qualities necessary to form a supreme pontiff, and since he encountered very many opportunities to exercise them, he raised the glory of the pontificate to the highest summit of praise.

From the beginning of his administration he showed clearly that the greatness and sublimity of the office entrusted to him were thoroughly known to him. He judged that one must begin with the sacrifices of the Lord’s praise, after imploring divine assistance (*Sermon on His Assumption*), and relying upon those powers which Christ the Lord permanently strengthened in the Prince of the Apostles and which the inheritance of the chair transmits to his successors through enduring faith:

> “And just as what Peter believed in Christ remains, so what Christ established in Peter remains” (*Second Sermon 2*).

Of this dignity, he says, “even in an unworthy heir it does not fail . . . him whom they should know to be not only the primate of the bishops of this age, but of all bishops.”

He therefore both asserted and exercised this supreme power: first in condemning and uprooting heresies (chapter 1), and then in establishing Catholic faith and discipline (chapter 2).

Among his outstanding contributions concerning the faith is the fact that he was the first in the Church to give explicit and formal testimony concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. In his letter 93 to Turibius of Astorga, chapter 1, *On the Holy Trinity*, he writes:

> “How impiously they think—the Priscillianists, etc.—as though there were not one who begot, another who was begotten, and another who proceeded from both.”

(Somier, p. 268, volume II.)

As a defender of discipline, traditions, and canons, especially in the administration of the sacraments, he removed the abuse of requiring penitents to make public confession of hidden crimes:

> “Since the guilt of consciences is sufficiently disclosed to priests alone by secret confession” (letter 80), “that confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and then also to the priest, from whom the sinner receives penance for his offenses.”

He prohibited the solemn administration of baptism outside the appointed days of Easter and Pentecost. In the same place, in letter 91, chapter 5, he sets forth the rules and practice for reconciling penitents who, because of illness, are prevented from speaking.

As for the ordinations of bishops, he so prohibited their disturbance—even by holy bishops such as Hilary of Arles—that they should remain within the boundaries established for each by his predecessors. Thus he fixed definite limits between the provinces of Vienne and Arles: assigning to Vienne the four neighboring towns of Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble, while assigning the remaining cities of that province of Narbonese Gaul to Arles (letter 109; Somier, book V, chapter 3).

**Line 20.—“But Blessed Leo directed and expounded the *Tome of the Catholic Faith*.”** This refers to the dogmatic letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. After the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds had been recited in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon, that letter was received with the acclamations of the Fathers, who testified that it was itself the standard of right faith:

> “This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the Apostles. We all believe thus. The orthodox believe thus. Anathema to him who does not believe thus. Peter has spoken thus through Leo. The Apostles taught thus.”

It is worthwhile at least briefly to review the sequence of events that preceded this, so that the clearest example may shine forth of the authority of the pontiff, everywhere preserved and prudently employed, in accordance with what we touched upon in the analytical dissertation on the primacy of the Holy See among the *Prolegomena* to this volume, article 6.

Eutyches, an archimandrite, or superior of a monastery in the imperial city of Constantinople, fabricated a new heresy while attacking the Nestorian one. For when Nestorius impiously asserted two persons in Jesus Christ—one, namely, the eternal Son of God, and the other a son of the Virgin Mary fabricated by himself and different from the former—Eutyches thought that he would introduce the truth opposed to this error if he likewise taught one nature in Christ, just as there is one person:

> “He therefore presumed to drag many into his own impiety,” as Flavian wrote to Saint Leo, [Col. 0335A] “saying that before the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures, divinity and humanity, but after the union there was made one nature . . . He added another impiety, saying that the Lord’s body, which was made from Mary, was not of our substance nor of human composition; for he calls it human, indeed, but not consubstantial with us, nor with his mother according to the flesh,” etc.

This new heresiarch was condemned in the council held at Constantinople as a reviver of the errors of Valentinus and Apollinaris. When, however, he obstinately refused to withdraw from the errors he had adopted, he was deprived of communion, deposed from the priesthood, and removed from the governance of his monastery.

After appealing to the Apostolic See, Eutyches, falsely proclaiming that he had been accused of heresy, was compelled to submit memorials of protest against Bishop Eusebius, by whom he had been accused. Through the eunuch Chrysaphius he ingratiated himself with the emperor Theodosius so successfully that he obtained from him letters recommending him to Pope Leo.

He also attempted to win over the Western bishops in advance against Saint Flavian, by whom he had been deposed. Among them he sought especially to anticipate Saint Peter Chrysologus, but without success. For the holy archbishop replied to Eutyches:

> “In all things, however, we exhort you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written by the blessed pope of the Roman city. For Blessed Peter, who both lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of the faith to those who seek it. We cannot, for the sake of peace and faith, hear cases outside the consent of the bishop of the Roman city.”

When Blessed Leo learned from the emperor’s letters of the disturbances that had arisen in the Church of Constantinople from this controversy, he praised the emperor’s zeal, since he had found in him not only a royal but also a priestly spirit; and he requested time to be informed about the matters concerning which the emperor judged that he should be admonished.

He also sent forceful letters to Flavian:

> “We are astonished,” he wrote, [Col. 0335C] “that your Fraternity concealed from us whatever scandal may have occurred. But, looking to the cause of what you have done, we wish to know the reason and for everything to be brought to our knowledge, etc. And therefore, since your Love sees that we are necessarily concerned about so great a matter, let it hasten to indicate to us, as it ought previously to have done, everything with the greatest possible fullness and clarity.”

In obedience to this letter, Saint Flavian informed Leo through a careful and exact account of the events, and confirmed everything by the authority of the Apostolic See:

> “Having therefore been moved, most holy Father . . . treat his own cause as a common one; deign to decide jointly and according to rule against him by your own letters . . . For the case needs only your support and defense, by which you ought, through your own agreement, to bring everything to tranquility and peace. Thus the heresy that has arisen, and the disturbances caused by it, will most easily be destroyed, with God cooperating, through your most sacred letters. The council that is being announced as imminent will also be removed, so that the most holy Churches may nowhere be disturbed.”

What he adds here concerning the removal of the council refers to what Eutyches and his faction were attempting: namely, that a council be convoked in the East, where he expected to have many supporters.

Nevertheless, Saint Leo consented to a council being held at Ephesus, at Theodosius’s request, and he sent his legates there. When he informed the emperor that he had sent his dogmatic letter to Flavian, which he himself had written, he stated that through it the emperor could learn “what the Catholic Church universally believes and teaches concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation.”

Accordingly, after the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds had been recited in the customary manner during the second session, the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon read this letter with the acclamation mentioned above.

We do not think that the remaining events of the Council of Chalcedon need to be repeated here in the notes of Archbishop Somier, since we have already related them above from Pagіus. We shall nevertheless select several events, both before and after the council, which are happily observed in the abundant sequence of facts presented in the following chapters of the same archbishop’s fifth book.

From chapter 8, p. 337: the policy of the court of Constantinople in seeking a general council at Ephesus was entirely different from the zeal of Pope Leo in ensuring that the authority of the same convocation was properly maintained. The intrigues of the court—devised by the powerful eunuch Chrysaphius, their inventor, an enemy of Saint Flavian and a patron of Eutyches—were directed toward dissolving what Flavian had rightly judged, while preserving the appearance of justice.

After various efforts had been unsuccessfully attempted, it finally occurred to them to admit Dioscorus of Alexandria into the faction. With the powerful support of the Empress Eudocia, who was hostile to Flavian, Dioscorus could easily increase his influence with Theodosius, a prince readily surrounded and drawn toward their wishes.

Therefore, so that they might dominate the council, they arranged for it to be convoked far from the sight of Pope Leo and under the eyes of Theodosius, excluding bishops who favored Flavian. To keep the Westerners away as well, they took pains to have the letters of convocation delivered to them late.

They advised that Leo himself be summoned; but since they considered that he would not leave Italy during those difficult times, they hoped that the presidency would be offered to Dioscorus of Alexandria. They thus drew the unwary emperor, according to their prearranged plan, into assigning the leading role to Dioscorus, as though he were following the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

The council convoked at Ephesus therefore degenerated into a council of plunderers. Saint Leo did send his legates so that, in the customary manner, they might supply his presence and preside over the synod. He also instructed them by letters sent to the emperor Theodosius, to the Empress Pulcheria, and to the bishops, so that everything might be conducted according to the order of law. In these letters he exercised the right proper to apostolic care: namely, prescribing to general councils the questions to be decided in them and directing the judgments to be rendered concerning them.

Nevertheless, all Leo’s care was eluded not only by hidden tricks but by open violence and tyranny, which Dioscorus, supported by the favor of the powerful, arrogated to himself. The court’s magnates had occupied the entrance to the council under arms, ostensibly to ward off disturbances and defend the freedom of the Fathers, but in reality to suppress that freedom and increase the disturbances they themselves had stirred up.

This was made clear at the very beginning of the session. For Dioscorus, contrary to law, advancing into the place customarily assigned to the legates of the Roman Church while they were present, ordered them to sit beside him. The legates, who held the place of Pope Leo, refused to sit beside him because, as Liberatus says in the *Breviary*, chapter 12, “the presidency of the Holy See had not been given to them.”

They were therefore made spectators, outside the proper order, of the events that subsequently took place. Even while wishing, if possible, to avert the worse developments of that unfortunate assembly, they saw everything burst forth into open violence. [Col. 0336D] Leo’s letters were not admitted; Eutyches’s memorial was received; and, with Dioscorus leading the acclamation, the author of the memorial was restored. Flavian, together with other Catholic bishops, was accused of heresy and thrown into chains. When he appealed to the Apostolic See, Dioscorus—having changed from a bishop into an executioner—struck him with so many punches and kicks that, after three days in exile, he died in the greatest agony from his wounds. Thus, among later generations, these unhappy events acquired not the name of a synod but of the Ephesian Robbery.

> “Those who were sent,” says Leo the Great of his legates in letter 26 to Pulcheria, “protested in the synod as was proper, declaring that what was being done through force and fear could not prejudice the sacraments of the Church or the Creed established by the Apostles, and that they themselves could not be separated by any injury from that faith which they had brought to the Holy Synod fully and carefully expounded and arranged by the See of Blessed Peter the Apostle. Since its recitation was not admitted when the bishops requested it,” etc.

From chapter 7, entitled: **Letters written by the ruler of the Western Empire and by the August ladies, in which the Roman pontiff is recognized as the supreme and legitimate judge in matters of faith and of bishops.**

When Theodosius, having been deceived by the Eutychians, had arrogated to himself an authority over the Ephesian synod that did not belong to him—namely, the authority to decide as arbiter concerning the presidency and decisions of the council—he consequently usurped also the right to confirm the council itself. He did this by means of an edict, in which these attempts are expressly recorded in the third session of the sacred Council of Chalcedon.

Saint Leo, prudently confronting so many evils and scandals through the authority of his office, took care not only of what he himself undertook but also that sounder counsels should be conveyed to the emperor, who had been deceived by the Eutychians, through the emperor Valentinian, Theodosius’s son-in-law, and through Galla Placidia, Theodosius’s mother.

The letters of this son-in-law and mother, published in part I of the collection of the Council of Chalcedon, are extensive documents concerning the authority of the Roman See, recognized even by Caesars and Augusti.

> “We must defend with every fitting devotion the faith handed down by our ancestors,” says Valentinian, “and preserve inviolate in our own times the dignity of veneration belonging to the Apostle Blessed Peter, so that the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church, to whom antiquity assigned the primacy of the priesthood over all, may possess both the place and the power to judge concerning faith and priests,” etc.

He suggests that a general council be convoked within Italy, etc.

Writing to the same person, Galla Placidia asks

> “that, according to the form and decision of the Apostolic See, which we too venerate as pre-eminent—just as Constantine the Great, the founder of our line, venerated it—Flavian, while the priestly order remains wholly unharmed, be sent to the judgment of the Apostolic See for a council. In that See the first man who merited to receive the heavenly keys established the primacy of the episcopate,” etc.

Eudoxia also, the wife of Valentinian and daughter of Theodosius, makes a similar request:

> “that whatever was established in that tumultuous and most wretched council”—the Ephesian council of Dioscorus—“be removed with all vigor, and that, with everything preserved intact, the matter of the episcopate be sent to the Apostolic See, in which Blessed Peter, the first of the Apostles, who also held the primacy of the priesthood after receiving the keys of the heavenly kingdom, presides.”

To these testimonies of the Augusti, so clearly advancing the supreme authority of the Holy See, one may add letter 119 of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, in which he appeals to Saint Leo after having been deposed in the Ephesian assembly:

> “If Paul, the herald of truth and trumpet of the most holy Spirit, ran to the great Peter so that he might bring from him a resolution for those who were disputing at Antioch, how much more should we, who have been cast down and are insignificant, run to your Apostolic See. For it is fitting that you should be first in all things . . . I await the judgment of your Apostolic See; I entreat and implore Your Holiness that, when I appeal, your just and righteous judgment may bring me aid, and that you command me to come to you and show that my doctrine follows the footsteps of the Apostles.”

And in letter 116:

> “For that most holy See—the Roman See—possesses the leadership and primacy of all the Churches throughout the world, for many reasons,” etc.

The Great Leo therefore exercised this authority also when Theodosius sought the admission of Anatolius to the episcopate of Constantinople. He sent legates for this purpose, instructing them to require definite conditions: that Anatolius publicly make a proven confession of the Catholic faith; condemn the heresy of Nestorius; admit Cyril’s dogmatic letter, approved by the Holy See, in which the substance of the Nicene faith is explained and the most distinguished testimonies of the holy Fathers are asserted in support of that Catholic faith; and likewise admit Leo’s own dogmatic letter, conformable to ancient tradition.

Theodosius appears to have made some reparation for the damage he had ignorantly inflicted upon the Church when he finally sent the eunuch Chrysaphius into exile and did not strongly resist the withdrawal of his wife Eudocia into solitude. He would perhaps have been close to carrying out the other measures suggested by Leo, had he not been overtaken by death and unexpectedly ceased to live.

From chapter 8, where the convocation of the general Council of Chalcedon is discussed—a council convoked and celebrated by the authority of the Roman See—as well as the testimonies advanced in support of that authority.

The excellent prince Marcian, successor of Theodosius, having properly begun his imperial rule by defending the Catholic religion, which Theodosius had pursued with insufficient care, writes to Leo the Great, recognizing his authority to convoke and celebrate an ecumenical synod:

> “For the stability and condition of our empire,” [Col. 0338B] “may Your Holiness implore the eternal Divinity, so that we may possess such a purpose and desire: that, with every impious error removed, through the celebration of a synod under your authority, the greatest peace may be established among all the bishops of the Catholic faith, pure from every crime and remaining undefiled,” etc.

No less clearly does the Empress Pulcheria, Marcian’s wife, speak in a letter published with the preceding one in the first part of the Council of Chalcedon:

> “Therefore may Your Reverence deign, in whatever manner you judge appropriate, to signify that all the bishops of the entire East, of Thrace, and of Illyricum—as has also pleased our most pious lord, my husband the emperor—may quickly assemble from the Eastern regions in one city; and there, under your authority, may they decide in the holy council concerning the Catholic confession and concerning those bishops who were previously separated, as faith and Christian piety require.”

Exercising this authority, Leo the Great, after convoking the council at Chalcedon, orders his legates to attend [Col. 0338C], and writes to the Fathers of the council:

> “Let the vain unbelief of those who err be utterly silenced, once the audacity of disputing against the divinely inspired faith has been completely rejected. Nor may what may not be believed be defended. For, according to the evangelical authorities, the prophetic voices, and the apostolic teaching, it has been declared most fully and clearly in the letter that we sent to Flavian of blessed memory what the pious and sincere confession concerning the mystery of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ is . . . Let the decrees of the earlier Ephesian synod, presided over at that time by Cyril of blessed memory, remain in force specifically against Nestorius, lest the impiety then condemned flatter itself in any way merely because Eutyches is struck by a just condemnation. For the purity of the faith and doctrine which we proclaim in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers equally condemns and pursues the wickedness of Nestorius and of Eutyches, together with their authors.”

The council was therefore celebrated at Chalcedon. As is expressly read in the first session and those that follow, the pontifical legates presided over it in the customary manner. They are always named first, and in the third session they testify concerning Leo:

> “He who is the Catholic Pope Leo commanded our lowliness to preside in his place over this holy council,” etc.

In the first session they expressly declare that they have in their hands the commands of “the most blessed and apostolic man, the pope of the city of Rome, which is the head of all the Churches,” by which his Apostolate had deigned to command that Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, should not sit in the council but should be admitted for examination:

> “We must observe this . . . He must necessarily give an account of his judgment, because, although he did not possess the status of a judge, he presumed to act as one and dared to hold a synod without the authority of the Apostolic See—something that was never permitted and never done,” etc.

The commands of the Roman pontiff immediately found ready execution. The Alexandrian bishop descended from the judges’ bench that he had previously occupied and came forward into the middle as an accused man. Eusebius of Dorylaeum, his accuser, insisted that he be compelled to answer in the council concerning matters which, he said, had been brought forward by him and left in that holy council as records of his acts against them. These matters, he said, could show that Dioscorus was alien from the Catholic faith, had strengthened a heresy filled with impiety, and had deposed Eusebius unjustly.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus, previously deposed by Dioscorus in the assembly, was ordered to enter, despite the protests of Dioscorus’s faction of bishops, so that he might participate in the synod, since the most holy archbishop Leo had restored his episcopate, etc.

The acts of the Ephesian assembly were examined. Dioscorus was ordered to answer why the letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, which the bishops had insistently demanded to be read, had not been read, although he had repeatedly promised under oath that it would be read. From his answers and those of others who had been present at that convocation, it became known that the letter had deliberately been suppressed.

Dioscorus was convicted of interpolating the records and of using open violence against the bishops. It was declared that Flavian, bishop of holy memory, had been unjustly condemned by heretics; his faith agreed with the Apostolic See and with the tradition of the Fathers. It was therefore concluded that the sentence ought necessarily to be turned back upon those who had condemned him. At the end of the session, a sentence of deposition was proposed against Dioscorus and his associates, and praise was given to the letter of Pope Leo, since it had been written against Eutyches’s unbelieving doubt, which had arisen in opposition to the Catholic religion.

The beginning of the second session was devoted to the profession of the Catholic faith according to the formula received in general councils, and to the declaration of the Fathers together with Cecropius, bishop of Sebastopolis, who testified:

> “The matters concerning Eutyches came forward, and a form was given concerning them by the most holy archbishop of the city of Rome. We follow him, and we have all signed the letter.”

The most reverend bishops cried out:

> “We all say this. What has been expounded is sufficient. It is not permitted to make another exposition . . . The faith was rightly discussed by the 318 holy Fathers and confirmed by the holy Fathers Athanasius, etc., and now again through the most holy Leo. We ask that these things . . . be recited.”

After the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds had been read, as well as Cyril’s letters to Nestorius and to John of Antioch, the bishops cried out:

> “We all believe thus. Pope Leo believes thus. Anathema to him who confounds and to him who divides . . . This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the Apostles. Peter has spoken thus through Leo; the Apostles taught thus . . . Why were these things not read at Ephesus? Dioscorus concealed them. We believe thus. We all believe thus. None of us doubts. We have already signed.”

In the third session, Paschasinus, presiding over the council in the customary manner as the pope’s legate and presenting the matters to be treated, said:

> “The Catholic Pope Leo commanded our lowliness to preside in his place over this holy council. Therefore it is necessary that the matters brought forward be discussed through our intervention. For this reason, let the memorial presented by our most religious brother and fellow bishop Eusebius, which he has received, be read.”

After a triple canonical admonition, Dioscorus offered various excuses for not appearing before the synod. He was struck by a sentence of deposition, which all the Fathers of the council asked the pontifical legates to pronounce against the convicted defendant:

> “We therefore ask Your Holiness—you who possess, or rather you who possess collectively, the place of the most holy Pope Leo—to pronounce and deliver against him the sentence implanted in the canons. For everyone, and the whole universal synod, agrees with the sentence of Your Holiness.”

Finally, the synod assented to and signed the sentence pronounced by the legates. In its report to Pulcheria it used this formula:

> “With Christ prosperously guiding our understanding, who showed the truth in the wondrous Leo—for just as He uses the wise Peter, so He uses this man as its defender.”

[Col. 0340A] From chapter 9. In the fourth session, when the imperial commissioners asked what the synod had established concerning the Catholic faith, they replied:

> “The representatives of the Apostolic See, through the most reverend Paschasinus, said: The Holy Synod follows and holds the rule of faith established at Nicaea by the Fathers. But also, etc. Thirdly, the writings directed by the most blessed and apostolic man, Pope Leo of the universal Church, condemning the heresy of Nestorius and Eutyches, have expounded what the true faith holds. Likewise the Holy Synod holds and follows this faith; it can neither add anything further nor subtract anything . . .”

The bishops cried out:

> “We all believe thus. Thus we were baptized. Thus we baptize. Thus we believed. Thus we believe.”

They added by spoken testimony the written record of their subscription:

> “The letter of the most holy Leo agrees with the faith of the 318 Fathers of Nicaea, etc., and I have subscribed to it.”

It is almost embarrassing to report the entanglements woven by certain recent writers concerning this subscription [Col. 0340B]. They contend that Leo’s letter was subjected to examination and that the Fathers pronounced, by way of investigation, upon its conformity. But no one can say this without abusing the words of the council.

From what we have brought forward thus far, it is clearer than daylight that the Fathers of Chalcedon never proposed to deliberate on whether Leo’s dogmatic letter should be received and signed by them. Rather, the Fathers began with its acceptance. One of the principal grounds on which Nestorius was condemned was precisely this:

> “That he did not permit the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo to be read; and because it was not read, they brought scandal and injury upon the Holy Church of God throughout the whole world” (Act 3).

In the second session, where the letter was read and received by the council, certain doubts arose among the bishops of Illyricum and Palestine concerning some statements in it. But this was not after a prior judicial examination; rather, the letter was received with acclamations and expressions of praise.

The council paid no significant attention to these doubts—apart from the fact that one of the bishops and one of the deacons alleged certain similar points from Cyril’s letter to Nestorius—and again acclaimed:

> “No one doubts,” etc.

Thus it showed that no one retained any doubt concerning the supreme authority of this letter.

Moreover, when the imperial commissioners suggested that “a special meeting could be held with Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the faith might be discussed jointly, so that those who doubt might be instructed,” all the most reverend bishops cried out for the third time:

> “We believe thus. We all believe thus. As Leo believes, so we believe. None of us doubts. We have already subscribed.”

Finally, the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops themselves testified in writing during the fourth session that the difficulties that had arisen for them came from nothing other than the obscurity of a language unknown to them:

> “Those who hold the place of the Apostolic See explained to us what the obscurity of the language had marked out as separating . . . We consented to this letter and subscribed to it . . . Certain words from it stood in the way . . . We heard from the most holy Fathers, etc., that they say there is no division . . . For this reason we consented and subscribed to the *Tome*.”

I also grant that thirteen Egyptian bishops refused to subscribe, alleging as their reason that, since the Alexandrian See to which they were subject was vacant, they could not sign after their archbishop in the customary manner:

> “The most reverend Egyptian bishops said . . . We consent to what your authority has decreed. We do not contradict it. But choose an archbishop. We await him until he is ordained.”

The Fathers of the council, however, judged that these petitions and offers should not be granted sufficiently. They were already inclined to institute a judgment against the Egyptians on suspicion of heresy, unless the legates of the Apostolic See had intervened. Paschasinus said:

> “If Your Glory commands, and if you order that some humanity be shown to them, let sureties be given, and let them not leave the city itself until Alexandria receives a bishop.”

The judges and the senate replied:

> “Let the judgment of the most holy Paschasinus stand firm.”

This, then, was the honor with which the Council of Chalcedon received the dogmatic letter of Leo the Great, whatever Neotericus may mutter (Nat. Alex., section I, dissertation 13). He imagined that the council had received and approved it only after a juridical and judicial examination, having first tested it against the rules of faith. He contends that he would incur guilt of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit if he attributed another method of acceptance to the universal synod:

> “If I were to attribute that blind manner of proceeding to an ecumenical council, I would seem guilty of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit” (there).

Another recent writer, treating the same matter, attributes to the bishop of Lycaonia a vote that he never expressed, namely: “If anyone should find something objectionable in the exposition of the faith declared by Leo’s letter, I would not concern myself with it; for I regard it as settled that it does not contradict the exposition handed down by the Fathers of Nicaea.”

But if one attends to the words of that Neoptolemus, bishop of Lycaonia, they indicate a judgment far different from that of the recent writer:

> “From the beginning,” he says, “our country was pure of every heretical stain and free from questions and disputes of this kind. We believed more simply, following the faith of the Fathers expounded in the city of Nicaea, which Cyril of blessed memory later interpreted and which Leo, the most holy and most religious archbishop of the city of Rome, again declared. We likewise do not oppose these expositions. But if anyone thinks he has some occasion for contradicting the exposition of Blessed Bishop Leo, let him himself seek and contend for it, while we contradict or resist nothing in the exposition of the 318 Fathers or of those 150 most holy Fathers who came after them.”

This differs greatly from the insinuation that Neotericus thrusts forward against the authority of the Roman pontiff. For through these words of Bishop Neoptolemus—words that expressly indicate his approval equally of Leo’s letter, Cyril’s letter, and the Nicene Creed—the recent interpreter teaches that dissent from Leo’s letter would be permitted without penalty.

The same recent writer, with excessive confidence, draws into his system, opposed to pontifical authority, Leo’s words in which he glories in the Lord:

> “He did not permit us to suffer any loss among our brethren; rather, what He had previously defined through our ministry, He confirmed by the irretractable assent of the whole brotherhood.”

From these words the theorist concludes that only the irreversible judgment of an ecumenical synod is being described, and that it is not to be recalled for examination; whereas all other judgments, even if they belong to the Roman pontiff, are subject to reform.

We, on the contrary, observe that Leo does not speak of that acceptance of the council as a judgment, but as assent: “he confirmed it with the irrevocable assent of the whole brotherhood.” [Col. 0341D] When this assent is called irrevocable, it is called so because, once given, it can in no way be withdrawn, nor is it permissible to depart from it. It in no way appears to signify that a decision of an ecumenical synod could be opposed to another decision issued by the Roman See, or that the Chalcedonian definitions concerning the faith could be opposed to his dogmatic letter. Surely his memory had not failed so badly that he could forget what he himself had written so many times concerning the decisions of the Holy See before the council was summoned. See what we cited in the preceding chapter. If it is permissible to repeat it here, let only those words be indicated which he writes to the Fathers assembled at the threshold of the council:

“Therefore, dearest brothers, once the audacity of disputing against the faith divinely inspired has been wholly rejected, let the unbelief of those who err fall silent; nor may what may not be believed be defended.”

But let us not depart from the letter to Theodoret. Does Leo not declare in it that his own letter to Flavian is God’s very definition, God making use of the ministry [Col. 0342A] of the pope?

“What the Lord first defined through our ministry . . . so that he might show that what had first been formulated by the first of all sees and had received the judgment of the whole Christian world had truly proceeded from him: so that in this also the members may agree with the head.”

What fully confirms that Leo’s decision was not subjected by the council to juridical examination, but that the council believed it was its duty to accept the dogmatic letter and to conform its own judgment to the pontifical judgment, is what took place in the fifth session. A definition of faith was proposed there, and all applauded it with acclamations, except for certain Eastern bishops and the legates of the Roman See. They argued that something was lacking from the proposed definition, since it did not express everything contained in Leo’s letter concerning the confession of two natures in Christ after the hypostatic union, without confusion. When the bishops persisted in affirming that nothing was lacking from the definition, but that it was in conformity with Leo’s letter, they said:

“We have received the letter of the most holy Leo, [Col. 0342B] and have subscribed to it . . . Archbishop Leo believes as we believe. Let the definition be subscribed. The definition contains everything. The definition has the faith. Leo said the same things as Cyril; Celestine confirmed what Cyril said. Xystus confirmed what Cyril said.”

The legates replied:

“If they do not agree with the letter of the apostolic and most blessed man, Pope Leo, order written replies to be given to us, so that we may return to the West and a synod may be held there.”

When Emperor Marcian also lent his support to this protest of the legates, his commissioners asked the bishops:

“Dioscorus said that he accepted what is from two natures, but did not accept two natures. The most holy Archbishop Leo says that two natures are united in Christ, without confusion, without change, and without division, in the one-begotten Son, our Savior. Whom, then, do you follow: Saint Leo or Dioscorus?”

The venerable bishops cried out:

“As Leo believes, so do we believe. Those who contradict him are Eutychianists. [Col. 0342C] Leo has explained the matter correctly.”

The most magnificent and most glorious judges said:

“Then add to the definition that two natures are united in Christ, without change and without confusion.”

When they had inserted this very assertion of Leo into the definition—asserting that it was consistent with the faith of Nicaea and Constantinople and with Cyril’s letters to Nestorius and to the Eastern bishops, and that it was “in agreement with the confession of that great Peter” and “a common pillar against those who think perversely”—both the apostolic legates and all the Fathers subscribed to the definition thus conformed, for the confirmation of orthodox doctrines. In fact, from the more ancient centuries onward, the decisions of the Roman See have been held in such honor that they have been compared with the definitions of universal synods and placed immediately alongside the very oracles of divine Scripture.

In the final session of the council, which was the sixteenth, the legates of the Apostolic See reported that on the previous day, after their departure from the council, certain matters had been discussed with the imperial commissioners [Col. 0342D] against the sacred canons and the discipline of the Church. The archdeacon of the Church of Constantinople replied that, before their departure, the legates had been asked by the clergy of that Church to deign to examine, together with the Fathers, certain matters that they wished to propose. When the legates replied that they had received no instructions from the Apostolic See concerning the matters which the aforementioned clergy wished to propose, and therefore left the council, the imperial commissioners had been asked to hear the clergy, and their petitions had been referred to the council Fathers. As the Fathers proceeded to examine the petitions, they established certain provisions, which the same archdeacon read from a written document, concerning the rights of the Church of Constantinople, bringing them almost level with the dignity of Old Rome, especially by granting it the ordination of the metropolitans of the three exarchates of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace.

The legates strongly opposed this decision as contrary to the sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea and to the rights of the Roman Church, [Col. 0343A] and protested that it had to be annulled:
