“If our opposition should otherwise remain attached to these proceedings,” they said, “let it be so that we may know what we ought to report to the apostolic man, the pope of the universal Church, so that he himself may pass judgment either concerning the injury done to his see or concerning the overturning of the canons.”

After the sessions had been completed, the council Fathers addressed Emperor Marcian and then wrote to Pope Leo, lavishly praising him:

“God has provided us with an invincible defender against every error and has prepared the pope of the Roman Church for victory, girding him on every side with the teachings of truth, so that, just as Peter was fervent in affection and this man contended with still more fervent affection, he might lead every perception and understanding toward God.”

Council of Chalcedon, part III, no. 1. They wrote to Leo himself:

“Regarding you as the leader and author of so great a good, we have shown to the sons of the Church, for the common advantage, the inheritance and portion of truth . . . To these five hundred and twenty of us, you presided as head over members [Col. 0343B] who were holding your rank.”

After praising the pontiff and his legates, they proceeded to the canon established for the Church of Constantinople and explained the reasons for establishing it, saying that they knew that “your Holiness also, upon learning of it, would approve and confirm the same.” They again stated the plausible reasons by which they hoped Leo’s mind would be moved to grant confirmation of their acts and decrees in their entirety, although his legates had opposed the matter most recently proposed. Letters expressing the same position were sent to Leo by Emperor Marcian, Pulcheria, Anatolius of Constantinople, and Julian of Cos.

## From chapter 11

Leo confirms everything established at the Council of Chalcedon concerning the faith, rejoicing that “the holy synod, consenting in religious unanimity to the writings of our humility, strengthened by the authority and merit of my Lord, the most blessed Apostle Peter, has cut away from the Church of God the diabolical inventions of diabolical thoughts.” He therefore replies:

“Let the brotherhood and the hearts of all the faithful know that I am present with you in my own judgment, not only through the brothers who carried out my role, but also through the approval of the synodal proceedings, solely in the matter of the faith—as must often be said—for which it pleased the general council to be assembled, both by the command of the Christian princes and with the consent of the Apostolic See,” etc.

Pope Leo therefore confirms the decrees concerning the faith, not by simple consent and adherence to the definition as though it were ratified independently of his approval, but by the authority of confirming which resides with the Apostolic See, as Leo expresses in the wording used in Letter 77 to Anatolius:

“Thus let Atticus profess that he will observe in every respect the definition of the faith of the Chalcedonian symbol, to which your Devotion also consented by subscribing, and which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed.”

[Col. 0343D] As for canon 28, concerning the patriarchal jurisdiction granted to the Church of Constantinople over the exarchates of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace, and concerning its place immediately after the Roman See, blessed Leo so completely denied his consent that in his letter to Anatolius he expressly calls it a violation of the Nicene canons and grieves and marvels that:

“By unheard-of excesses, never before attempted, the holy synod, assembled to extinguish the sole heresy and to confirm the Catholic faith, is being drawn by Anatolius into an occasion for ambition, as though what the multitude had illicitly desired could not be rejected, and as though that condition of the Nicene canons, established through the Holy Spirit, could ever be dissolved in any part.”

In the letter also sent to the emperor, he vigorously resists this perversion:

“Let it be enough for Anatolius that, through the aforementioned assistance of your Piety and the assent of my favor, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city. Let him not disdain the royal city, which he cannot make an apostolic see; nor let him hope in any way that it can be enlarged through the offenses of others.” [Col. 0344A]

And in his letter to Pulcheria he completely invalidates and annuls the consent of the bishops given to that decree against the Nicene canons:

“We set it aside as void, and by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle we wholly cancel it by a general definition.”

In his encyclical letter to the bishops who were petitioning on behalf of Constantinople, he replies:

“No one will be able to obtain assistance from me through patronage in such a way that I should consent, by trampling upon the constitution of the Fathers, to what he requests.”

He earnestly warns each of them:

“Do not wish to ask me, for anyone’s sake, for something which, without guilt on the part of both of us, it is neither lawful for me to grant nor for you to obtain.”

What he writes to Maximus of Antioch and to Theodoret of Cyrrhus agrees with this, full of apostolic steadfastness in defending the rules of the Fathers and the examples of his predecessors. Finally, in the letter sent to Proterius of Alexandria—who had been appointed in place of Dioscorus after Dioscorus’s deposition at Chalcedon—he promises, just as he had written to Maximus of Antioch, that he would not permit [Col. 0344B] the rights of their sees to be prejudiced.

He rightly writes that the decree had emerged through the underhanded action of certain persons, since no one was defending the rights of the Alexandrian Church, which was then vacant, while the Antiochene Church also remained silent so as not to incur the displeasure of Anatolius. Thus the cause of the principal Churches would have been entirely abandoned unless the apostolic legates had resisted.

Anatolius not only did not take Leo’s opposition badly, but rejoiced in it, since he sought from it an opportunity to spread the claim that the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon had been disapproved by Leo. Leo, however, prudently confronted this serpentine slander by sending letters to the Fathers of the council, to Emperor Marcian, and to others, in which he clearly separated those matters concerning the faith that he had rightly confirmed from those matters concerning a change in discipline that he had prohibited as attempts against the Nicene canons.

## From chapter 12

The vigilance of Leo the Great is presented in the publication and establishment throughout all the Churches of his dogmatic letter and of the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon that he had confirmed. It shines forth in the letter sent to Ravennius of Arles, together with a copy of his dogmatic letter to Flavian, so that Ravennius might arrange for it to be circulated among all the bishops of Gaul.

How eagerly and reverently it was received by everyone is shown by the letters of three bishops sent to Leo. In them, his paternal care and apostolic teaching are not only commended with fitting praise, but he is also humbly asked to inspect the copies of that letter which they had had scribes transcribe, and, if anything were missing through a scribal error, to correct it; or, if he had later added anything, to order that it be inserted, so that for present and future times an intact memorial of the teaching and vigilance of so great a shepherd might be preserved, a future protection even for places where error had not yet entered, lest an unexpected enemy come upon the unsuspecting, and lest careless security provide an opening for injury. [Col. 0344D]

A synod of bishops held in Gaul shortly afterward, giving abundant thanks for the same dogmatic letter sent to them, says that the letter was received with such eagerness that many recited it from memory, no differently from the creed:

“Whoever does not neglect the mysteries of redemption has inscribed the writings of your apostolate upon the tablets of his heart, as he does the creed, and has committed them to a tenacious memory, so that he may be more prepared to confound the errors of heretics.”

This synodal letter is subscribed by forty-three bishops, with Rusticus of Narbonne presiding.

While Leo was replying to these matters, he learned that his letter had been received at the Council of Chalcedon with the acclamation mentioned above. Therefore he ordered the bishops of Gaul to arrange that it also be brought to the bishops of Spain. It was received with equal rejoicing in Insubria, as the synodal letter of that province sent to Leo testifies. Leo did not cease writing to Maximus of Antioch and to Theodoret [Col. 0345A] of Cyrrhus so that knowledge of that dogmatic letter might reach everyone. For there the need for a remedy was more urgent.

The monks of Palestine, for the most part Eutychians, had stirred up such disturbances that, after Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, had been expelled, they intruded into his see a certain Theodore, their fellow monk, who enjoyed the favor of the Empress Eudoxia, the widow of Theodosius III. Relying upon this support, they did not spare any excess in acting against the Catholics, so that they might renounce both the Roman pontiff and the Council of Chalcedon.

At first the remedy was attempted by milder measures, through letters sent both by Leo and by Marcian. But the hardened obstinacy of the seditious compelled the emperor to send military forces, by which the rebellious Eutychian monks were forced to remain confined in monasteries, and some of them were even punished with death. Leo sent a congratulatory letter to Juvenal after his restoration to his see, but seasoned it with a serious admonition that he should care more diligently for the flock entrusted to him, lest it should thereafter be infected by the breath of such a pestilence.

[Col. 0345B] The churches of the Egyptian patriarchate were no less the object of Leo’s care than those of the East. He considered that caution was necessary both regarding the monks and regarding Proterius, who had been appointed in the place of Dioscorus and had been his disciple. But after Proterius had sent Leo a truly Catholic profession of faith, Leo recognized that there was nothing to fear from him; he congratulated him and added rules for recalling the Eutychians from their errors.

The partisans of Eutyches had abused Leo’s dogmatic letter, corrupting several of its passages and inserting Nestorian errors into it. They had also brought the Council of Chalcedon into disrepute on account of the injury inflicted upon the Alexandrian see, since the Fathers had placed Constantinople before it.

Leo confronted the first slander by sending a letter to Marcian, in which he asked him to arrange for his dogmatic letter to Flavian to be faithfully rendered into Greek by competent men and published in the Alexandrian diocese, so that it could be compared with the teaching of the bishops of that see—Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril. He met the second pretext by writing to Proterius how vigorously the legates of the Apostolic See had objected and protested against the Chalcedonian decree, which granted the bishop of Constantinople what the Nicene canons and the discipline of the Church forbade. He declared that he would remain steadfast in asserting the due rights and privileges of the Alexandrian Church, following the example of paternal antiquity.

While these matters were being successfully advanced, the death of Emperor Marcian interrupted the progress that had been hoped for. Timothy the Cat, after the murder of the holy Proterius, was intruded into his place and erupted into such insolence that he did not shrink from hurling an anathema against Leo and against the supporters of the Council of Chalcedon.

Saint Leo, informed of so many crimes, did not cease urging Leo Augustus, Marcian’s successor, to extend his protection to the Catholic Church. The Cat did not cease employing his cunning and every art of deception [Col. 0345D] in order to bend the unwary emperor toward summoning a new council.

Saint Leo, asked by the emperor about this matter, replied:

“Since, therefore, the universal Church has become a rock through the building of that principal rock, and since blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, heard from the voice of the Lord, ‘You are Peter, and [Col. 0346A] upon this rock I will build my Church,’ who is there, unless he be Antichrist or the devil, who would dare to assail an unassailable truth? . . . They desire to cloud the splendor of your Serenity with a certain contagion, when sacrilegious parricides dare to ask for what even the innocent are not permitted to obtain.”

Leo acted through his letters so that another bishop might be given to the Alexandrian Church in place of the Cat, namely Timothy, surnamed Solofaciolus. When Timothy wrote to Leo, Leo warned him to eliminate every remnant of Nestorian and Eutychian error from his episcopate.

He also thought it necessary to warn Anatolius of Constantinople to see that the same errors were more diligently uprooted from the imperial city. He made the same request of Anatolius’s successor, Gennadius, when he wrote that the Cat’s disguised conversion had to be guarded against in such a way that he should warn that the wicked man be excluded from every private or public conversation.

## From chapter 13

The pontificate of Leo the Great is therefore an epoch memorable above all others that appear in ecclesiastical history. During it, God’s visible protection was extended to the Apostolic See [Col. 0346B], especially in the most difficult times, when the flood of barbarians and the prevalence of heresies were mingling and confusing all human and divine things and striving to overthrow them. With what success Leo fought against heresies, with the same majesty he suppressed the incursions of Attila and Genseric.]

[Note: [Col. 0346B]

No. 67, line 11.—“Here he established that a nun,” etc. Here a sentence has been omitted, which both manuscripts of the Florentine Codex preserve:

“Here he established that within the action of the sacrifice it should be said: ‘the holy sacrifice, the spotless offering.’”

As noted in Velser’s Mainz edition, these words were also found in two German manuscript codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0346B]

No. 67, line 11.—“Here he established that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-covering unless her virginity had been proved at sixty years of age.” Leo’s decree was that a nun—that is, a virgin—should not be veiled before her sixtieth year. By the Council of Agde, canon 19, and the Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 40, the age before which they were not to be veiled was set at forty; by the Third Council of Carthage, canon 4, at twenty-five; by the canon “Sanctimonialis” and the following canon, at twenty, in Gratian, Causa 20, question 1.

Line 13. “Here he established over the tombs of the apostles custodians, who are called cubicularii, from the Roman clergy.” By Leo’s decree, custodians were placed over the tombs of the apostles, chosen from the order of clerics, who were called cubicularii. Cubicularii are servants who are assigned to the service of a bedchamber. Suetonius, in Julius, chapter 4: “With one physician and two cubicularii.” Hence the custodians of the bodies of the apostles were called cubicularii, as though they were the apostles’ chamber-servants, or because they were taken from the pontiff’s bedchamber or chamber.

By the same analogy, Ottho of Freising accepted the term cubicularii for the custodians of the church of Saint Martin, in Chronicle, book IV, chapter 32, and Sigebert, under the year 509. Abbot Uspergens calls them matricularii, as does Vandalbert the deacon in the Life of Saint Goar, in Surius, 6 July:

“Custodians or matricularii of the church.”

The chapels or oratories added to churches are called cubicula:

Anasias, in his Life of Sergius: “He carefully adorned the roof and the chambers which surround that basilica on every side.”]

[Col. 0299]

## 66

Leo, a Tuscan by birth, son of Quintianus, sat for twenty-one years, one month, and twenty-six days. [Note: [Col. 0299] B: twenty-one years less thirty-two days, from the consulship of Valentinian V and Anatolius to that of Severinus and Dagalaiphus.]

During his time Demetria, a servant of God, built a basilica to Saint Stephen on the Latin Way, at the fourth milestone, [Note: [Col. 0299] *: three.] on her own estate.

He encountered two heresies, the Eutychian and the Nestorian, through certain bishops. He established precepts by his own authority and sent them to Marcian Augustus, the faithful Catholic ruler. After a conference with that ruler, the bishops assembled, and [Note: [Col. 0299] See Baronius, under the year of the Lord 431, p. 138.] a holy council of bishops was held at Chalcedon, [Note: [Col. 0299] *: Chalcedonia.] in the martyr’s shrine of Saint Euphemia. [Note: [Col. 0299] C: Euphemiae.]

Two hundred and fifty-six priests and others assembled, while the subscription of their signatures extended to 406 bishops. They assembled together with the Tome, [Note: [Col. 0299] C: Tomo.] that is, with the apostolic faith of the Roman Church, bearing the signature of the holy archbishop Leo.

A council of 400 bishops was also assembled in the presence of the Catholic ruler, Emperor Marcian. [Note: [Col. 0301] C: 1,200; others: 600. Baronius gives 600, on the basis of Leo’s Letter 52.] Together with Emperor Marcian, they set forth the Catholic and apostolic faith: two natures in the one Christ, God and man at once.

At that point the most devout Emperor Marcian, together with his wife, the Empress Pulcheria, laying aside their royal dignity, set forth their faith before the sight of the holy bishops. There they also condemned Eutyches, Nestorius, and Dioscorus.

Then Emperor Marcian Augustus and his wife Pulcheria Augusta again set forth their faith in their own written declaration and asked the holy council to send a letter to the most blessed Pope Leo, requesting him to set forth the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0301] See Baronius under the year 450.]

Blessed Leo sent the Tome of the Catholic faith and set it forth, condemning all heresies. Again the most blessed Leo sent many letters concerning the faith to the archbishops; they are preserved to this day in the archive. [Note: [Col. 0301] C: of the Roman Church.]

He frequently confirmed the Council of Chalcedon in his letters: twelve letters to Emperor Marcian, thirteen letters to Emperor Leo, eight letters to Bishop Flavian, [Note: [Col. 0301] C: nine.] and eighteen letters to the bishops throughout the East, through which he confirmed the faith of the synod.

## 67

After the Vandal disaster, he renewed all the sacred silver vessels that had been melted down throughout the titular churches: six water-jars, two for the Constantinian basilica, two for the basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle, and two for the basilica of Blessed Paul the Apostle. Constantine Augustus had offered them, and each weighed one hundred pounds. He renewed all these sacred vessels.

He constructed the vaulted ceiling of the Constantinian basilica and adorned another vaulted ceiling in the basilica of blessed Peter. He also renewed the basilica of blessed Paul the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0301] CB: after the divine fire, that is, the conflagration.], and he built a basilica for blessed Cornelius, bishop and martyr, beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

For the sake of the Roman name, he undertook an embassy and went to the king of the Huns [Note: [Col. 0301] “by lightning.”], named Attila. [Note: [Col. 0301] “of the Huns.” See Baronius under the year of the Lord 452, p. 178.] He freed all Italy from the danger of its enemies.

He established a monastery near Blessed Peter the Apostle, called that of Saints John and Paul. [Note: [Col. 0301] CB: “Here he established that within the action of the sacrifice it should be said: ‘the holy sacrifice, the spotless offering.’”]

He established that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-covering unless her virginity had been proved at sixty years of age.

He established over the tombs of the apostles custodians, who are called cubicularii, [Note: [Col. 0301] B: “who are now called chaplains,”] from the Roman clergy.

He held four ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: eighty-one presbyters, thirty-one deacons, and 185 bishops for various places.

He too was buried beside the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on the third day before the Ides of April; and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days. [Note: [Col. 0301] B: “refutes this.”]

# XLVIII. SAINT HILARY. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 461, THE FIFTH YEAR OF LEO, THE FIRST OF SEVERUS

[Note: [Col. 0349A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript.

No. 68, line 1: B, Hilarius. In the same place A, seven years. Line 4: B, “and the Tome.” Line 6: B, “and confirming the dominion of the holy Catholic and Apostolic See.”

No. 69, line 7: B, “the Lord’s lamb.” Line 14: AB, “which are called hecaton, pentalaica, and concastriata.”

No. 70, line 9: AB, “five silver vessels.” Lines 16 and 17: AB, “five pounds.” Line 18: A, “another golden cup, weighing five pounds, a golden one with gems.” Lines 25: AB, “two.” B, “a silver altar weighing forty pounds, ten silver lamps weighing twenty pounds, basins.” Lines 26 and 27: B, “forty pounds.” Line 27: A, “twenty-four.”

From the Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane codices.

No. 68, line 1: Hilary, [nationality uncertain: “n. S.”], son of Crispinus, held office for seven years, three months, and ten days. Here he made a decree and spread it throughout the whole world, and letters confirming the Catholic and apostolic faith. (M: “confirming,” singular.) Line 5: D, “and all that follows,” etc.; “and all heresies”; “confirming the dominion and primacy of the holy Catholic and [Col. 0349B] Apostolic See.” Here he made an ecclesiastical constitution at Saint Mary’s. This was in the consulship of Basiliscus and Hermenericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

No. 69, line 2: “and John the Evangelist.” Line 3: “precious.” He made the confession of blessed John (M: holy John) the Evangelist from silver, weighing one hundred pounds, and so forth, in both oratories. He made bronze doors overlaid with silver. Line 6: There he placed the wood of the Lord enclosed in a golden cross (in M the word “enclosed” is absent), with gems, weighing twenty pounds. (M: Above the confession he made a golden arch.) In the confession he made silver doors, each weighing fifty pounds; above the confession he made a golden arch weighing four pounds. Line 10: two pounds. He also made a golden crown before the confession, weighing ten pounds; a silver beacon with dolphins, weighing five pounds. (M: two pounds. In the confession he made silver doors, each weighing twenty pounds. He also made, etc.) Four golden lamps, each weighing two pounds. (M: four pounds.) Line 14: “which are called hecaton.” He made pentalaica and two striated shells, and porphyry columns with perforations (in M “and” is absent), surrounding a water basin, with waxen grilles on the right and left, [Col. 0349C] and columns. Line 18: “in mosaic” (M: “in mosaic work”). Line 19: delete the question mark. In the same place: “He made a crown for John.” Line [same]: “a silver beacon or basin,” weighing twenty-five pounds.

No. 70, line 4: a golden column weighing two pounds, in the Constantinian basilica (M: thirty pounds; a silver tower with dolphins, weighing sixty pounds; a golden column [Col. 0350A] weighing twelve pounds, in the Constantinian basilica). He made, etc. Line 7: ten pounds; four silver cups, each weighing five pounds; ten ministerial silver chalices, each weighing two pounds (M: four silver cups, each weighing six pounds; two golden cups, each weighing six pounds; ten ministerial silver chalices, each weighing two pounds). Line 14: ten pounds. At Saint Peter the Apostle, a golden cup weighing five pounds; another golden cup with precious gems, weighing four pounds; ten ministerial silver chalices, each weighing two pounds; silver basins. Line 15: a golden one with gems, weighing ten pounds (M: five pounds). Line 16: ten ministerial chalices, each weighing twelve pounds (M: two). Line 17: “at Saint Lawrence.” Line 19: ten pounds; two golden lamps, each weighing fifteen pounds; a golden basin or beacon, weighing two pounds; a golden tower with dolphins, weighing five pounds; four silver cups, weighing twenty-four pounds; twelve ministerial silver chalices. Line 24: each weighing ten pounds. In another basilica of Saint Lawrence he made silver beacons. Line 27: ten silver ministerial vessels for the baptistery, weighing ten pounds. Line 28: fifty bronze beacons, twenty-six bronze basins; he also made twenty-five small cups, each weighing ten pounds; a golden cup weighing eight pounds; fifty ministerial chalices, each weighing four pounds, which he ordered to be stored at Saint Mary Major. [Col. 0350B] (M: golden cups weighing eight pounds.)

No. 71, line 1: “In the city of Rome he established vessels for the stations that had been established around the city.” A station cup (M: stationary cup), weighing eight pounds; twenty-five silver cups for the titular churches, each weighing ten pounds; twenty-five silver basins, each weighing ten pounds. He also built the oratory of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery. He also built two libraries in the same place. Likewise, he built a monastery in the city at Luna. Here he held two ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December: twenty-five presbyters and five deacons. Line 12: “of blessed Sixtus,” etc.

No. 69, line 1: “the confession of Saint John the Baptist from silver.” Line 4: “a golden confession of Saint John from silver.” Line 5: “in both oratories, bronze doors clad with silver.” Line 7: “the wood of the Lord, a golden cross with gems.” [Col. 0350C] Line 8: “thirty pounds”; from silver he made doors for the confession, weighing fifty-eight pounds. [Note: [Col. 0351B]

No. 68, line 2.—“Here he made a decretal,” etc. Hilary did two things: first, he composed a decretal letter; then he circulated other letters concerning the Catholic faith. The ancient catalog of the Roman pontiffs joined these together; the compiler of the expanded catalogs subsequently identified separately the decretal that was published and that is designated in line 8 by the names of the consuls. We shall identify it below.

The first mention of the decretal letter occurs in the *Liber Pontificalis*, which distinguishes it from the letters concerning the Catholic faith. Siricius called every decree issued by the Apostolic See a decretal enactment, volume I of the Councils, chapter 15, p. 851. Thus, writing to Himerius of Tarragona, he said:

“Now we incite your brotherly spirit more and more to observe the canons and defend the decretal enactments.”

What is meant by the name *decretal* he indicates by adding:

“And although it is not permissible for any priest of the Lord to be ignorant of the statutes of the Apostolic See or of the venerable definitions of the canons.”

In this passage, what he had first called “decretal enactments” and “canons” he subsequently calls “the statutes of the Apostolic See” and “the venerable definitions of the canons.”

Later, usage became established whereby the rules of councils were called “definitions,” while the decretals of the Roman pontiffs were called “decretals.” Hilary, who will be praised below, speaks in the same way in his Roman synod, where he calls decrees, as it were, legislative enactments proceeding from the Apostolic See, and calls canons the constitutions of councils.

In the same manner, Simplicius writes to Zeno, bishop of Seville, using the same formula of speech, volume II of the Councils, p. 803:

“Therefore, since you glory in such judgments, we have deemed it fitting that you be supported by the vicarious authority of our see; fortified by its strength, you must in no way permit the decrees of apostolic institution or the boundaries established by the holy Fathers to be transgressed.”

In the same sense Saint Nicholas I wrote to Photius:

“As for what you say—that you possess neither the Council of Sardica nor the decretals of the Roman pontiffs . . . the decretals, however, which have been established by the most holy pontiffs of the first see of the Roman Church, by whose authority and sanction all synods and holy councils are strengthened and receive stability—why do you say that you neither possess nor observe them, unless because they contradict your ordination?”]

Line 2.—Letters on the Catholic faith. In addition to the decretal letter, he sent letters to all the bishops, in which he again confirmed the four synods as ones to be professed as ecumenical, condemning the heresies. This was necessary at that time, when the Eutychians had declared war not only against the Council of Chalcedon but also against the Catholic faith, so that he might make both matters known to the bishops throughout the East, strengthening and confirming them, and showing that the apostolic see remained constant in its profession of the ecumenical synods.

He had learned the necessity of this profession from St. Leo, who wrote to Julian of Cos in a new letter published by Quesnell, Letter 88, p. 306, concerning the apostolic and authoritative confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon, to be published throughout all the Churches:

> “What, therefore, the most merciful emperor considered necessary [Col. 0352A], I have willingly [Col. 0352B] fulfilled, so that I might send writings to all the brothers who were present at the synod of Chalcedon, by which I might demonstrate that I approved what our most holy brothers had confirmed concerning the rule of faith—especially on account of those who, as an opportunity for concealing their perfidy, wish the decrees of the council to appear weak or doubtful, which have not at all been strengthened by the assent of my judgment . . . . . Therefore let Your Dilection take care to remind the most pious prince by frequent appeals that, with his own letters added, he should order the writings of the apostolic see to be delivered to the priests of each province, so that no enemy of the truth may hereafter presume to excuse himself on the grounds of my silence.”

Concerning this subterfuge of the Eutychianists, the letter of Marcian to the same pontiff should be read; G. L. first published it there, p. 307, among the letters of St. Leo in the new edition. Hilary therefore issued these letters; and I believe that from this arose the practice whereby recently elected Roman pontiffs and bishops, in their professions of faith, expressly professed that they received and venerated the ecumenical councils [Col. 0352C]. See the Roman *Diurnus* and the letters of St. Gregory the Great.

Line 3.—Confirming three synods: Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon. In some manuscripts, “four” is found instead of “three.” Our reading, however, should be retained. Nor can it be inferred from this that Hilary removed the Second General Council of Constantinople from the number of the ecumenical councils. For when, in Acts II, IV, and VI, the entire Constantinopolitan Creed was read and inserted into the decree of faith with the suffrage of all the bishops, Hilary, by confirming the Council of Chalcedon, consequently professed and confirmed the Council of Constantinople as well, since that synod had declared it ecumenical.

Concerning the faith of the Constantinopolitan Creed, Gregory the Great wrote from the standpoint of the Roman Church, Book VI, Letter 121:

> “The Roman Church, however, has neither possessed nor accepted the canons or acts of that synod up to the present; but it accepts that synod in this respect: that by it a definition was made against Macedonius” [Col. 0352D].

The name “Nicene” was applied to the Constantinopolitan Creed. This is deduced from the Council of Toledo, vol. II of Aguirre’s *Councils*, p. 340, which King Reccared attended and where he subscribed to a profession of faith containing the Constantinopolitan Creed, which is designated as the Nicene Creed.

The profession issued by Hilary appears to have mentioned only three councils. This may be inferred from the Roman synod under Felix, which, in sending a synodical letter to the eastern clergy and monks, and prescribing a profession for them to issue after the Roman model, describes it as follows, vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 855:

> “So that Your Charity may recognize that we hold the venerable synods of Nicaea, the First of Ephesus, and Chalcedon against Nestorius and the most impious Eutyches.”

But when the Council of Constantinople was mentioned separately in other professions, the Roman pontiffs not only did not disapprove, but confirmed it by their own approval; see Baronius, in the place cited above. For this reason Vigilius [Col. 0353A], praising the profession issued by Justinian and communicated to the Churches of the East for their profession, wrote as follows:

> “Your Piety has accomplished this with the greatest strength: throughout all the parts of your kingdom and throughout the whole world, you order that the faith which is known to have been irreproachably established through the venerable synods that Christian confession must always embrace—Nicaea, Constantinople, the First of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—be preserved in unshaken peace.”

Line 6.—Confirming the authority and primacy of the apostolic see. Because of the scarcity of the Acts, it is not clear what Hilary did more particularly to vindicate the authority of the see. Perhaps he restrained the ambitions of the patriarchs of Constantinople and, in the letters concerning the Council of Chalcedon that the bishops of the East were required to profess, considered it especially necessary to invalidate what the patriarchs of Constantinople had presumptuously claimed in Act XVI—namely, the first place among the other patriarchs of the East.

This conjecture of ours can be strengthened by several considerations [Col. 0353B]. In particular, Emperor Leo did not fail, at the request of the clergy of the Church of Constantinople, to promote the ambition of the patriarch of Constantinople; and when that patriarch saw Leo and Hilary persisting in their resolve to defend the Nicene canons establishing patriarchal rights, he attempted to extort the same concession from Simplicius, who succeeded Hilary.

Simplicius, however, resisted more vigorously and opposed his attempt. He sent Probus, bishop of Canusium, as a legate to Constantinople for this purpose and restrained the ambition, as Gelasius writes in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania:

> “Nevertheless, under the holy pope Simplicius of blessed memory, the legate of the apostolic see, Probus, bishop of the city of Canusium, was sent there and, at the request of the emperor Leo, demonstrated in his presence that this could in no way be attempted. Nor did he give his consent to these things at all. Therefore they should observe appropriately not the quality of any particular city, but the measure of the Church’s administration established by the tradition of the Fathers.”

Hilary therefore [Col. 0353C] did not permit the Nicene statutes to be removed, in accordance with the zeal of his predecessor. Rather, he defended his own authority and that of the patriarchs and resisted the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople.

Certainly Gennadius, the successor of Anatolius, made no attempt, either on his own initiative or through the emperor. Acacius, however, who succeeded Gennadius in 471, claimed this for himself; and at his urging Leo attempted to obtain it from Simplicius, though without success. Acacius did not cease promoting the privileges of the see of Constantinople, especially so that it might be ranked second after the Roman see and hold the principal place among the eastern patriarchs.

This continued until Zeno was restored to the imperial power in 477, when Acacius obtained from him the law that appears as chapter XVI of the Code of Justinian, under the title *On Holy Churches*. In it, in accordance with the decrees of the Councils of Constantinople and Chalcedon, the privileges are said to be restored. Since they are said to be restored, it is implied that they had previously been denied by the unanimous judgment of Leo, Hilary, and Simplicius.

Indeed, during this intervening period the patriarchs of Constantinople [Col. 0353D] claimed for themselves, in accordance with Act XVI of Chalcedon, jurisdiction over three exarchates, especially that of Ephesus; and Evagrius, Book III, chapter 6, shows that the other patriarchs opposed this presumed right.

In recounting the edicts of Basiliscus against the holy Council of Chalcedon, which Basiliscus had ordered to be condemned in 476, Evagrius relates that Timothy the Cat, the obstinate Eutychian and murderer of St. Proterius, was released from the exile imposed upon him by the emperor Leo. While he was hastening to recover his see and asserting the privileges of the second see throughout the East, he restored to the bishop of Ephesus the rights of the exarchate that had been taken away by the bishop of Constantinople through the decree of the Council of Chalcedon, Act XVI.

On the authority of the rhetorician Zacharias, Evagrius says:

> “The same writer relates that Timothy, after leaving Constantinople, proceeded to Ephesus and installed Paul as bishop of that city. Paul had long before been appointed by the bishops of the province, as the ancient custom of the Church requires [Col. 0354A], but had subsequently fallen from the see. Timothy also restored to the Church of Ephesus the right of the patriarchate, which the Council of Chalcedon . . . had taken away from it.”

From these facts it is clear that the *Pontifical Book* rightly says that Hilary confirmed the prerogative of the apostolic see; among his other distinctions, the pontifical records present this as one of the things commended in him.

Line 7.—“He issued a constitution concerning the Church.” Since the consular date is added, two conclusions may be drawn.

First, since there once truly existed a codex of the constitutions of the pontiffs, the *Pontifical Book* omitted the contents of those constitutions and considered it sufficient to mention the constitution issued, which anyone could find in that codex. This is evident in the case of the present constitution, which was most recently published in a more correct form in the synodical collection, Cassinese manuscript, chapter 227, p. 471, by Lupus from the Vatican manuscript, where the same consular date is found.

Second, the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs had various additions, and one and the same item was sometimes recorded briefly and sometimes at greater length. Thus this constitution is read in the ancient catalogue as: “He issued a decretal.” A later hand added and explained which decretal had been issued by appending a chronological note.

The date noted here and the consuls coincide with the Roman synod first published by Lupus. That synod bears the following heading:

> “Here begin the regulations of Pope Hilary . . . In the consulship of the most illustrious men Flavius Basiliscus and Herminericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, while the venerable Pope Hilary was presiding in the basilica of St. Mary.”

The constitution was issued concerning sacred ordinations and elections; ecclesiastical discipline and the Churches of Spain were also treated there.

At the very beginning, the pontiff lays down two things to be observed: the Nicene canons and the decrees of the apostolic see. He distinguishes the two as follows:

> “Since the religious assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges us to treat with more diligent care whatever concerns ecclesiastical discipline, if it pleases you, brothers, let us establish firmly, at the Lord’s command and for all time, those matters that pertain to the order of ordinations, in accordance with the precepts of divine law and the constitutions of the Nicene canons, so that no one may presume to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see without endangering his own status. For the guilt of such transgressions falls upon us, who administer the offices of the chief priesthood, if we are found negligent in the matters of God.”

From this it may also be observed that, just as in the particular case of Spain he decreed that the sacred Nicene canons were to be confirmed inviolably by the apostolic see under threat of divine judgment, so he acted in the letters distributed throughout the East concerning the profession of the Catholic faith, especially concerning the Council of Chalcedon. When the clergy of Constantinople sought to humble the apostolic see through the ambition of Anatolius and, contrary to the provisions of the Nicene canons, to overturn the order of the patriarchs, the pontiff, following the example of his predecessor Leo, had to strengthen the primacy of the apostolic see by his authority [Col. 0354D] and annul what had been wrongly done.

Since the *Pontifical Book* calls this constitution “concerning the Church,” it indicates—as has often been noted—that it concerned the universal Church; or it designates a decree sent to the Churches throughout the world. Hilary’s words at the end clearly demonstrate this, where he decrees:

> “Hilary, bishop of the Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said: Since we decree that the form of the present definition, established according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, is to reach the knowledge of all the Churches, and since no one may be permitted, on account of ignorance, to do what is not permitted, the diligence of the notaries shall see to it that the proceedings are published.”

The notaries, therefore, were to prepare authentic copies and send them to all the Churches.

## Note: [Col. 0354D]

Number 68, line 1. Hilary. After an interregnum of approximately seven months, on the day before the Ides of November in the year 461, the fifth year of the emperor Leo, Hilary, a Sardinian by nationality [Col. 0355A], formerly a deacon and legate at the Ephesian assembly, was appointed in the place of St. Leo.

At the beginning of his pontificate he confirmed what had been decreed by the three ecumenical councils against the Arian, Nestorian, and Eutychian heresies. He also arranged for a new Paschal cycle of 542 years to be produced by Victorius of Aquitaine, then easily the leading authority in that field, on the testimony of Gennadius and Marianus Scotus.

Gelasius writes in Letter 11 to Dardanus:

> “When the emperor Anthemius of the West, with the Macedonian Philotheus urging him, Philotheus being supported by Anthemius’s intimacy, wished to introduce new assemblies of divided sects into the city, he openly restrained him before the blessed apostle Peter, declaring in a loud voice that this must not happen, to such an extent that the emperor promised, with an oath, that these things would not be done.”

During Hilary’s pontificate at Constantinople, when a certain painter attempted to paint Christ in the form of Jupiter, his hand withered. After he confessed the crime and offense, Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, healed him. [Cedrenus, in the *Compendium*.]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The agreement between the catalogues of Italy that we published in volume II of the *Prolegomena* and the more celebrated catalogues from Gaul cited by both Pagius, together with the text of the Librarian, in assigning a total of six years, three months, and ten days, removes every doubt concerning the amount of time to be assigned to Pope Hilary’s tenure.

His letter and the Acts of the Roman council mentioned above, in the chronological notes on Celestine, section 62, establish that his election fell on November 11 and his ordination on the following day, November 12, which was a Sunday in the year 461. It follows that his death should be assigned to February 21, 468. This is confirmed by Pagius, numbers 10 and 13, in his notes on this section.

Marianus Scotus—Pagius the Elder notes this in his critical remarks on Baronius, year 467, number 3—correctly records the death of St. Hilary on February 21, in agreement with the *Florarium of the Saints* and with the martyrologies of Maurolycus, Galesinus, and Caninius cited by Bollandus.

Bollandus must nevertheless be corrected concerning the year of the holy pontiff’s death. He thought it was 467 on the basis of several documents, especially the letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops of Dardania, where it is stated that St. Hilary resisted Anthemius. Anthemius was elevated as emperor on the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Priscus and John, as the chronographer published by Cuspinianus writes. Pagius the Younger observes this in his notes on the Life of Hilary, number 12, and the Paschal Chronicle also agrees, assigning the same consuls.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

Number 68, line 6.—“He issued a constitution concerning the Church in the holy basilica of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, in the consulship of Basiliscus and Herminericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.”

This indicates the decretal letter on ordinations issued by Hilary at the end of the council held at Rome under the same consuls in the Liberian basilica. Baronius discussed the Acts of that council under the year 465, as did the editors of the councils.

A copy of that letter, signed in the same consulship on the third day before the Kalends of January, is found in a parchment manuscript of a collection of canons among the manuscripts of the library of the monastery of Santa Croce in Jerusalem. The manuscript is approximately eight or nine hundred years old. The proceedings of the council can be found in summary form in the notes of Pagius and Somier.

Number 69, line 1.—“He made three oratories in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica: one of St. John the Baptist, one of St. John the Evangelist, and one of the Holy Cross, etc.; and in both oratories”—that is, those of St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist—“he installed bronze doors sheathed in silver.”

These silver-sheathed bronze doors, bearing letters expressing the dedication and Hilary’s name, survive in the oratory of St. John the Baptist. The inscription reads:

> “In honor of the blessed John the Baptist, Hilary, bishop [Col. 0356A] and servant of God, offers this.”

An ancient mosaic also survives in the vaulted ceiling of the oratory. Its center is occupied by the image of a lamb, by which Christ the Lord was signified by the Forerunner. In the lunettes around the windows, images of the four Evangelists, each bearing his proper name, can be seen in the same mosaic work. Ciampinus published drawings of them in *Old Monuments*, vol. I, chapter 26.

At the entrance to the oratory, Hilary the pontiff is likewise carved in the *zophorus* above the columns that adorn the doorway:

> + HILARY, BISHOP OF THE HOLY PEOPLE OF GOD. +

In the opposite oratory of St. John the Evangelist, a marble inscription carved above the columns in the architrave preserves both Hilary’s name and the memory of his fortunate escape from the danger prepared for him by the plots of the heretics during the brigand assembly at Ephesus. At that time, while he was a deacon, he was sent as the representative of Leo the Great, together with his colleagues, to preside over the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon.

Because he had been rescued, by God’s favor, from the hands of the enemies of the faith, he reported this to the protection of the blessed John the Evangelist, writing:

> “To his liberator, the blessed John the Evangelist, Hilary, bishop and servant of Christ.”

The bronze doors of this chapel likewise survive, though they are not the ancient ones installed by Hilary, as in the preceding oratory, but later ones, repaired during the pontificate of Pope Celestine III.

Cencius, cardinal chamberlain of the most noble Sabelli family, later elected pontiff and called Honorius III—as Ciampinus writes, p. 239—restored them. An inscription was added:

> “In the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Celestine III, pope, at the command of Cencius, cardinal of Santa Lucia and chamberlain of the same lord pope, this work was carried out.”

Cardinal Rasponus testifies that the third oratory, that of the Holy Cross, survived until the time of Sixtus V. In his work on the Lateran basilica, Book III, chapter 9, he reports:

> “Toward the west, beside the baptistery, there was formerly an oratory of the Holy Cross, likewise built by the pontiff Hilary, to which there was access through the door of the same baptismal font. This oratory still existed in the time of Sixtus V. In front of it was a small enclosure surrounded by a portico, supported by seven columns and three pilasters. The doorway of the peristyle was supported by two fluted alabaster columns, and on the *zophorus* there was this inscription:
>
> ‘I shall enter your house, Lord, and I shall worship toward your holy temple in your honor.’
>
> The doors were bronze, inlaid with silver, and the small building itself, square in structure and resembling the form of a cross, was so elegant and skillfully constructed that there are very distinguished authors who report that Michelangelo derived the design of the Vatican basilica from this oratory,” etc.

A magnificent portico belonged to this oratory of the Holy Cross, so elegantly constructed by Pope Hilary. The Librarian mentions it together with the oratory erected by the same pontiff and supported by enormous columns, specifically porphyry ones [Col. 0356D]. Several of these columns can still be seen, although the portico itself has been destroyed. They form one side of the oratory of Saints Venantius, Rufina, and Secunda and retain the name “Portico of St. Venantius,” as the aforementioned Cardinal Rasponus demonstrates in Book III, chapters 5 and 6.

There he also records the sacred rites customarily celebrated here by the Roman pontiffs in the solemn administration of the Paschal baptism. Our most holy lord, Pope Benedict XIII, continued to perform them every year while he resided in Rome; after his election to the Roman see, he became a model of pastoral conduct for the other bishops.

The magnificence of Pope Hilary in constructing the oratory of the Holy Cross is evident everywhere, whether one considers the external structure or the internal decoration.

Externally, the façade displayed a three-sided portico supported by enormous porphyry columns, as we have said. From it there was an entrance to the fountain, itself adorned with porphyry. Around it he placed grilles, columns, architraves, and pediments cast in bronze, together with mosaic work.

The parts relating to the fountain should be seen in the Life of Sixtus III, who enlarged the fountain and adorned it with an octastyle enclosure containing porphyry columns that supported the architraves and the *zophorus*. They may also be consulted in Cardinal Rasponus, who elegantly describes each part and the ancient inscription in Book III, chapter 1.

The interior of the chapel of the Holy Cross contained and guarded the instrument of our salvation—the Lord’s wood—enclosed within a golden and jeweled cross weighing twenty pounds. Above it rose a golden arch resting on onyx columns. Silver doors weighing fifty pounds were assigned to this shrine, and golden lamps and crowns were hung all around it.

The silver tower and golden dove mentioned by the Librarian in the chapels attached to the baptismal font should be understood as belonging to the custody of the Eucharistic sacrament [Col. 0357B]. It was customary to preserve the Eucharist in such towers and doves, a practice already introduced in the time of Basil the Great, as various writers observe together with Cardinal Baronius under the year 57, number 152. They also indicate that the practice still exists in some churches, as we ourselves saw in the metropolitan church of Paris, where a golden dove hanging above the high altar guards this heavenly pledge of eternal life.

Such a repository for the Lord’s Body had to be established near the sacred font, since after the sacrament of baptism had been administered to those reborn and confirmed at the sacred font, the Eucharistic sacrament was also given to them, as the ritual books commonly teach. These may be read in the work of the distinguished Edmund Martene, volume I, where on p. 647 the practice of keeping the Eucharist in golden or silver towers and doves is also explained.

Line 14.—*Hecatonpenta*. Nardinus, *Ancient Rome*, Book IV, chapter 4, p. 178 of the new edition, reads *hecatompeda*. There he also shows that *nymphaeum* was often used for a fountain.

The meaning, therefore, is that these porphyry-stone columns were called “hundred-foot” columns. They may be called *hecatompedes* not because they rose to a height of one hundred feet, but because they were extremely lofty and exceeded the dimensions commonly observed in other objects made of the same stone.

Bellorius likewise observes in his notes on the *Vestiges of Ancient Rome*, p. 53, that a portico was called *hecatonstylon* when it was supported by a large number of columns, even if the number was not one hundred. The number one hundred is often used to signify a very great quantity, as Virgil’s line demonstrates:

> “Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths.”

The same is shown by the name of Thebes, the city of the hundred gates, *hecatompylai*—“hundred-gated”—because it was passable through a great number of gates.

Number 71, line 1.—“He appointed ministers who would go around the customary stations.” Macer included this passage of the Librarian in his lexicon under the word *statio*, to prove that the use of stations was much older than the time of Gregory the Great.

There, drawing on St. Ambrose, he defines a station as the observance of fasting and prayer; and he distinguishes this from a station understood as the place designated at fixed times for carrying out those rites.

On the same occasion he explains that the ministers mentioned here should be understood as clergy assigned to serve at the sacred rites in the places where the station was celebrated.

He correctly derives the name *station* from military terminology. The Church, which professes to serve God in this world as a soldier, did not disdain to borrow numerous words from military usage.

At the end of the *Appendix to the Prolegomena*, on the occasion of the Greek inscription from Puteoli reproduced there from the Museum of the eminent Cardinal Alessandro Albani, we observed that the inscription records a public act of the Tyrians in the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus—indicating the year 174 of Christ—and in the 300th year of the Tyrian era. We observed that the word *station* is used there to signify the assembly, college, or corporate body of the people of that nation, possessing the right to perform sacred rites according to their ancestral custom [Col. 0358A].

For this reason we said that, from almost the very beginning of the Christian Church, the word had been appropriately transferred to designate the rite and custom of Christian stations. Among the Romans, the word already carried the idea of an assembly of many people gathering at a fixed place to perform sacred rites according to ancestral custom.

Thus, in the *tituli*, where Christians had customarily gathered even during the persecutions, and where the supreme pontiffs had assigned the right to administer the sacred rites to the presbyters established there, public stations were celebrated after peace had been restored to the Church, as the Roman order declares.

For the performance of sacred rites there at appointed times, especially on days of solemn fasts or feasts, both ministerial clergy and station subdeacons were present. The sacred furnishings to be carried for the use of the pontiff who visited those stations were also prepared according to the selection and care of the same pontiffs, especially Hilary.

[Col. 0358B] Line 6.—“He made a monastery at St. Laurence, and a bath and a praetorium, etc. Likewise, a monastery within the City at Luna.”

I shall begin by investigating this second monastery established by Hilary.

In a garden belonging to the title of St. Eusebius, situated on the Esquiline, approximately twenty years ago we saw the walls of a church and an adjoining building uncovered about twenty palms below ground level. Columns and an architrave were then extracted, bearing an inscription identifying Hilary, at that time archdeacon, as the builder under the patronage of blessed Laurence. The architrave is now preserved in the stone collection of the eminent Cardinal Alessandro Albani, with this inscription:

> + WITH THE HELP OF THE LORD OUR GOD JESUS CHRIST, WHILE THE BLESSED MARTYR LAURENCE INTERCEDES, HILARY THE ARCHDEACON MADE THIS. +

In the Esquiline region Panvinius mentions a shrine of Luna. The remains of a temple of the Sun Mithras, discovered in the garden of the Marquises of Palombara opposite the same title of St. Eusebius approximately fifteen years ago, suggest that it was not far from the title. Several reliefs and images belonging to that superstition were found there.

Worshipers of the Sun were accustomed not to separate the shrine of the Moon from that dedicated to the Sun. Thus Sextus Rufus, in the City itself, records in the region of the Temple of Peace a temple of the Sun and immediately adds the temple of the Moon.

On the old Capitol an altar was established for each of the two heavenly bodies, as well as a temple of Apollo and Clatra—Nardinus, p. 190. In the palace, where Varro mentions a temple of the moon that shines by night, there is also a temple of the Sun. Likewise, in the Circus, one obelisk was dedicated to the Sun and another to the Moon.

Elsewhere, temples and altars dedicated to the Sun and Moon stood near one another under different names: Janus and Jana, Apollo and Diana, Aglibolus and Malakbel, and similar pairs. These may be consulted in the works of antiquarians, in Macrobius among the ancient authors, and in Vossius’s work *On Idolatry* among more recent writers.

Since the monastery founded by Hilary is said to have been “at Luna,” and since in this part of the Esquiline there are remains of a monastery and a small church adjoining it, together with Hilary’s inscription dedicating the work to God under the protection of the prayers of blessed Laurence, I believe that this is the monastery within the City at Luna indicated by the Librarian.

The buildings—which he calls the *praetorium*—constructed together with the monastery and bath at St. Laurence, should, in my judgment, be sought at St. Laurence Outside the Walls, to whom the designation of St. Laurence properly belongs.

That suburban district, however, had been so disfigured and devastated by many disasters, even before the basilica of Laurence was restored by Pelagius II, that it is useless today to search its ruins for evidence of Hilary’s constructions.

It may be considered sufficient for our memory that the Librarian preserved the matter through the inscription quoted above, found on the Esquiline within the City at St. Eusebius. There Hilary, then archdeacon of Leo the Great, clearly demonstrated his singular devotion to the blessed martyr Laurence [Col. 0359A]. After becoming pontiff, he chose a place near Laurence for his burial and added monasteries to the martyr’s basilica, following the example of his predecessor Leo, whom we have seen establish a monastery at the basilica of St. Peter and recommend similar care to his successors.

Line 8.—“He made two libraries in the same place.” On these, consult Cardinal Rasponus, *On the Lateran Sacred Church*, Book III, chapter 14. There he also reports the excellent passage by our Panvinius, who, with his customary abundant and solid learning, illuminates not only these libraries built by Hilary but also the older libraries erected by Christian bishops near their churches.

## Note: [Col. 0359A]

Number 68, line 1.—“A Sardinian by nationality, from Cagliari.” Through his disregard for wealth and the greatness of his counsels, he shone among the exalted pontiffs; rich in merits, he deserved the conversation and greeting of the angels.

He performed the duties belonging to an excellent pontiff: constructing and adorning churches, teaching, admonishing, correcting, and giving abundant alms wherever necessary.

His gold and silver gifts are reckoned to have exceeded 102,983 of our gold scudi, apart from the labor of the craftsmen, the expenses of the buildings, and the annual revenues that he assigned to them.

These facts clearly show what the wealth of the Roman Church was, since such lavish expenditures were made on sacred vessels and the adornment of the churches.

## Note: [Col. 0359B]

Number 68, line 2.—“He issued a decretal.” In the year 467, Leo, the emperor of the East, sent the patrician Anthemius to Rome and appointed him emperor. As the chronographer published by Cuspinianus writes, he was elevated as emperor at Rome on the day before the Ides of April, under the consuls of the year 467.

With the Macedonian Philotheus urging him, Philotheus being supported by Anthemius’s intimacy, Anthemius wished to introduce new assemblies of various sects into the city of Rome. Hilary resisted him with apostolic firmness and, as Pope Gelasius says in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania, “openly restrained him before the blessed apostle Peter, speaking in a loud voice so that this would not happen, to such an extent that the emperor promised, with an oath, that these things would not be done.”

This single passage, even if all other proofs were lacking, destroys the opinion of Papebroch, who wrote in his *Chronological-Historical Essay on the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs* that Pope Hilary passed to God on February 21, 467.

Although it is true that his death should be assigned to February 21, it must nevertheless be postponed to the year 468, after he had faithfully administered the Roman Church for six years, three months, and ten days, as stated in the *Pontifical Book*, in the six catalogues prefixed to the first volume of Baronius’s critical edition, in the Vatican-Palatine catalogue, and in several authors cited in the same critical work under the year 467 [Col. 0359D].

If he had died on February 11, 467, Gelasius would falsely have written that he resisted the emperor Anthemius at Rome, since Anthemius is said to have become emperor at Rome on April 12 of that same year. This also confirms the chronology of the earlier Roman pontiffs.

Line 7.—“He issued a constitution concerning the Church.” In the year 465 Pope Hilary held a council at Rome in the basilica of St. Mary on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, as stated in the Acts, which were published in a more correct form than previously by Christian Lupus at the end of volume I of the Cassinese letters.

The council dealt with ecclesiastical discipline and the Churches of Spain. Five canons, or decrees, were enacted there:

1. The Nicene canons and the decrees of the apostolic see must be observed [Col. 0360A].

2. Bigamists, men married to widows, and men married to women who had been defiled were not to enter the ecclesiastical orders.

3. Penitents, illiterate persons, those deficient in bodily members, and those lacking something because of mutilation were not to advance to a higher order.

4. Whatever a bishop or his predecessor had illicitly ordained was to be corrected by the bishop who remained.

5. No bishop was to choose his own successor.

This last decree was issued because, as is clear from the second letter of the Spanish bishops to Hilary, Nundinarius, bishop of Barcelona, had designated a successor for himself with the consent of the bishops of the province of Tarragona.

Therefore, in his second letter to Ascanius, metropolitan of Tarragona, and the other bishops of the province of Tarragona, Hilary, acting according to the judgment of the Roman synod issued on December 30 of the same year, 465, wished Irenaeus to be excluded from the governance of the Church of Barcelona:

> “Lest,” he said, “episcopal honor be thought to be an hereditary right, since it is conferred upon us solely by the kindness of our God.”

This was so even though the bishops of the province and Ascanius the metropolitan supported Irenaeus, and the leading men and the people had requested him as a man distinguished by his merits and integrity of character.

Furthermore, Silvanus, bishop of Calahorra in the same province of Tarragona, had promoted a foreign presbyter over his own bishop in that same Church. The Spanish bishops brought this unusual action before the apostolic see, while the leading men of Calahorra and the neighboring cities offered excuses for it before the Roman pontiff.

Hilary granted Silvanus pardon for the violation of the canons, as also to the other bishops who had complained of him, since some had ordained bishops for certain cities without the consent of the metropolitan.

Therefore the Spanish bishops brought Silvanus’s case before the Roman pontiff because it was a cause of schism; and a principal function of the primacy of the pontiff is to preserve the unity of the Church intact. “Accordingly,” they say, “because these presumptions, which divide unity and cause schism, must be resisted promptly, we ask your See that we may be instructed by apostolic utterances concerning what you wish to be observed in this matter.” In the same letter the Spanish bishops display their religious reverence toward the apostolic See when they write:

“Although there had been an ecclesiastical necessity, we truly ought to have sought that privilege of your See by which, after the Savior’s resurrection and the reception of the keys of the kingdom, the singular preaching of the most blessed Peter looked to the illumination of all peoples throughout the world. His vicariate’s authority, just as it excels, is likewise to be feared and loved by all. Accordingly, worshiping God wholly in you, we have recourse to the faith praised by the apostolic mouth, seeking an answer from the place where nothing is commanded through error or presumption, but everything through pontifical deliberation.”

[Note: [Col. 0360C]

Number 69, line 1.—Here he built three oratories in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica: those of Saint John the Baptist, [Col. 0360D] Saint John the Evangelist, and the Holy Cross. The first two oratories can still be seen in the baptistery of the Lateran basilica, with an inscription of Pope Hilary.]

[Note: [Col. 0360D]

Number 69, line 12.—A nymphaeum and a three-sided portico before the oratory of the Holy Cross, where there are columns of extraordinary size called Hecaton-penta. Nymphaea are public buildings in which those without houses celebrated weddings. See Zonaras, on Leo the Great. Elsewhere, nymphaea are fountains adorned with marble columns, usually placed before sacred buildings for ornament, as this nymphaeum was placed by Hilary before the oratory of the Holy Cross. Before the basilica of Saint Peter there was a cantharus adorned with columns, pouring forth rising waters, concerning which Paulinus writes in Letter 33:

“Therefore, beyond the gleaming courtyard, the vestibule is spread out, where a dome of solid bronze, raised high, adorns and shades the cantharus, which with its mouths and hands serves up and pours forth flowing waters—not without mystical significance—[Col. 0361A] encompassing the leaping waters with four columns. For such an ornament befits the entrance of a church, so that what is carried out within through the saving mystery may be signified by a visible work before the doors.”

And Anastasius, in his Life of Symmachus:

“And he adorned the cantharus of blessed Peter, together with its four-sided portico, with marble.”

Nymphaea were built in various places in the City. Ammianus, Book XV:

“At the Septizonium, a celebrated place where the emperor Marcus built a nymphaeum of ambitious workmanship.”

And Capitolinus, in his Life of Gordian the Younger:

“No works of Gordian remain at Rome except certain nymphaea and baths.”

Line 14.—Two *trientes*—basins and conchae (printed *triantas*)—with netted, pierced porphyry columns, pouring forth water. Basins were stone pools beside the doors of buildings, containing water for watering animals and for suppressing fires. Donatus, in his commentary on the *Adelphoe*:

“Varro teaches that a basin was always added to gates, namely for the use of animals going out and coming in, and also so that aid against hostile fire might be supplied from nearby to the gates.”

Tranquillus, in *Galba*, chapter 7:

“To the basin [Col. 0361B] where he was accustomed to water himself.”

Lines calls it *L. Lines*, Digest, Book 19, concerning the action for purchase. Basins were stone vessels that received water from the pools. Basins are almost always joined with pools, as here and below in the same work:

“And in the middle a porphyry basin with an adjoining concha, pouring forth water in the middle.”

Read *assita* or *adsita* [“set beside”], rather than *assirta*. Concerning conchae, see below under Paschal. Around the pools and conchae located in the vestibule of buildings, marble or stone columns were placed for ornament. For the most part the columns were marble and, so that they would be safe from injury, were *ragiatae*, that is, covered with nets of iron or bronze, or with cords. Ulpian, in the Digest, *L. Fundi*, paragraph “Reticuli”:

“Nets around columns, balustrades around walls, and likewise curtains of buildings are not [part of the sale].”

Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book 3, chapter 5:

“Between the exterior columns, nets of cords serve as a wall, so that what is in the forest may be seen through them, and so that no bird may pass through.”

*Ragia* means a net; from it the vernacular *rejat*, “an iron grille,” unquestionably derives. Pools and conchae of this kind [Col. 0361C] poured out water through openings, that is, through pipes called pierced pipes, because the projecting ends of the pipes pour water through the mouths of lions’ heads. Sidonius, Book 2, Letter 2:

“Into this pool, therefore, six pipes draw a stream from the brow of the mountain and pour it forth through simulated lions’ heads.”

From the Latin *forare*, “to pierce.” Frontinus, *On the Water Conduits*, Book 2:

“For it concerns not only the safeguarding of the waters themselves but also the protection of the reservoir, which is consequently damaged without reason when pierced.”

And this is what the same author earlier called an opening:

“They place a new opening onto the reservoir and leave the old one, through which they extract water for sale.”

The text says *trientas* pools and conchae; read *trientes*. Pools and conchae were called *trientes* from the measure of water, because they held one-third of a finger’s breadth of water conveyed from the forms of the aqueducts by imperial authority. Frontinus, *On the Aqueducts*, Book 1:

“Thus the module of an ounce has a diameter of one finger and one-third of a finger.”

Line 17.—In the middle, adorned on every side with bronze railings, columns with pediments [Col. 0361D] and architraves, mosaic work, and Aquitanian columns. Mosaic work is tessellated work, that is, variegated with marble cubes. Augustine, *City of God*, Book 15, chapter 8:

“And the other races of human beings, or beings resembling human beings, which are painted in mosaic on the seaward [Col. 0362A] pavement of Carthage.”

Paulinus, Letter 12:

“He brightens the apse, paved in marble on floor and walls, with a vault illuminated by mosaic.”

Anastasius, in his Life of Symmachus:

“And he adorned the cantharus of blessed Peter, together with its four-sided portico, with marble, and made from mosaic lambs, crosses, and palms.”

Pliny calls it *museum*, Book 36, chapter 21:

“These stones, too, are called *musea* when they are cut away in buildings.”

Aquitanian columns are columns of Aquitanian marble, which is quarried in the Pyrenean mountains contained within the borders of Aquitania. Sidonius, Book 2, Letter 10:

“Proud with Aquitanian supports.”

Vitruvius, Book 3, chapter 1:

“Concerning Aquitanian supports.”

Pediments were added to columns. The pediments of columns are their capitals or capitals’ upper members. Pliny, Book 26, chapter 23:

“In the temple of Diana at Ephesus, bases were first placed beneath the columns and capitals were added.”

Leo of Ostia, Book 3, chapter 28:

“In the capitals of that church’s columns.”

Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, Book 2, chapter 109:

“Scripture seems to call the bases of columns not only those by which columns are supported from below, [Col. 0362B] but also the upper parts that we call capitals.”

For ornament, angels of silver or gold were placed above the capitals of columns. Anastasius, in his Life of Leo III:

“In the same way, in the basilica of that apostle he made four cherubim of the purest silver, gilded, which stand above the capitals of the columns.”]

Number 71, line 1.—In the city of Rome he established *ministeriales* who would circulate among the appointed stations. Stations were fixed prayers at the memorials or tombs of martyrs. Tertullian, *To His Wife*, Book 2:

“So that, if a station is to be observed, the husband may arrange a bath for the day.”

The same author, *On Fasting against the Psychics*:

“Likewise, neither do the stations—which themselves indeed have their appointed days—belong to Wednesday and Friday.”

Anastasius, in his Life of Gregory III:

“He also established that an annual station should be held in the cemetery of Saint Petronilla.”

Stations were appointed for particular days and particular places. Therefore Hilary appointed *ministeriales*, that is, clerics who would make the rounds—that is, visit—the stations, namely the places and altars designated for stations.]

[Col. 0362C] Line 7.—“He also made an oratory of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery.” Hilary dedicated an oratory in the baptistery of the Lateran basilica. In baptisteries, oratories—that is, altars—were customarily dedicated. Anastasius, in his Life of Symmachus:

“Likewise, at the font in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, an oratory of the Holy Cross made of silver.”]

Line 8.—“He also made two libraries in the same place.” Hilary established two libraries in the Lateran baptistery. The greater churches had libraries. Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, addressed to Pammachius:

“Make use of the libraries of the churches.”

Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 14, mentions the Jerusalem library established by Bishop Alexander; Jerome mentions the Caesarean library in his letter to Titus and in Book 3 of *Against the Pelagians*. The books of Gelasius against Eutyches and Nestorius were deposited in the library of the Roman Church. Anastasius, in his Life of Gelasius:

“Here he wrote books against Eutyches and Nestorius, which are still kept today in the library [Col. 0362D] and archive of the church.”]”

Among the offices of the Roman Church was that of librarian. Anastasius, in his Life of Gregory II:

“The care of the library was entrusted to him.”]

[Col. 0345]

68

Hilary, a Sardinian by nation, son of Crispinus, sat for six years, three months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 0345] B: ten months, two days fewer, from the consulship of Severinus and Daglaiphus to the consulship of Pusaeus and John]. He issued a decretal letter and scattered throughout the whole East letters concerning the Catholic and apostolic faith [Col. 0347], confirming the three synods—Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—or [Note: [Col. 0347] C, etc.] the tome of Saint Archbishop Leo—and condemned Eutyches, Nestorius, and Dioscorus, or all their followers, and all heresies, while confirming the authority [Note: [Col. 0347] C: “dominion”] and primacy of the holy apostolic See. He issued a decree concerning the Church in the basilica of the Holy Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, during the consulship of Basiliscus and Hermenericus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [November 16].

69

He made three oratories in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica: those of Saint John the Baptist, Saint John the Evangelist, and the Holy Cross, all of silver and precious stones. He made the confession of Saint John the Baptist of silver, weighing one hundred pounds, and a golden cross. He also made the confession of Saint John the Evangelist of silver, weighing one hundred pounds, and a golden cross; and in both oratories he made bronze doors plated with silver. In the oratory of the Holy Cross he made a confession, where he placed the Lord’s wood, with a golden cross set with gems, weighing twenty pounds. He made doors of the purest silver for the confession, weighing fifty pounds; above the confession, a golden arch weighing four pounds, supported by onyx columns, on which stands a golden lamb weighing two pounds; a golden crown before the confession; *phari* with dolphins, weighing five pounds; four golden lamps, weighing two pounds; a nymphaeum and a three-sided portico before the oratory of the Holy Cross, where there are columns of extraordinary size called *hecaton penta*; two basins and two conchae [Note: [Col. 0347] *castriatas*. C: *cithariacas*] with radiating porphyry columns [Note: [Col. 0347] C: *soraitis*], pierced [Note: [Col. 0347] C: “perforated”], pouring forth water; and in the middle a porphyry basin with an adjoining concha [Note: [Col. 0347] *raita*], pouring forth water in the middle, surrounded on the right and left; in the middle, bronze railings and columns with pediments and architraves, adorned on every side with mosaic work, and Aquitanian, Tripolitan, and porphyry columns. Before the confession of blessed John, a silver crown weighing twenty pounds; a *pharocantharus* [Note: [Col. 0347] that is, “silver”] weighing twenty-five pounds.

70

Likewise, at Saint John, within the holy font, a golden lamp with ten fittings [Note: [Col. 0347] *lychnis*, B: *mixis*] of lights, weighing five pounds; three silver stags pouring forth water, weighing thirty pounds each; a silver tower with dolphins, weighing sixty pounds; a golden dove weighing twenty-one pounds. In the Constantinian basilica, a silver *pharacantharus*, of which ten hang before the altar, each weighing twenty pounds; a golden cup weighing six pounds; golden chalices, each weighing one pound; two silver cups [Note: [Col. 0347] “five”], each weighing ten pounds; another golden cup weighing five pounds; twenty silver ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds; five silver jars, weighing ten pounds.

At blessed Peter the apostle: a golden cup weighing fifteen pounds; another golden cup with green and hyacinth-colored gems, weighing four pounds; ten silver ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds; two silver jars, each weighing eight pounds; twenty-four silver *pharacanthara*, each weighing five pounds.

At blessed Paul the apostle: a golden cup weighing five pounds; four silver cups, each weighing six pounds; ten silver ministerial chalices, each weighing seven pounds; two silver jars, each weighing ten pounds.
