At blessed Lawrence the martyr: a golden cup with green and hyacinth-colored gems, weighing four pounds; a golden lamp with ten fittings, weighing five pounds; a purest golden cup weighing five pounds; two golden lamps, each weighing one pound; a golden *pharacantharus* [Note: [Col. 0347] “a golden *pharocantharus*”] weighing two pounds; a silver tower [Col. 0349] with dolphins, weighing twenty-five pounds; three silver cups, each weighing thirty-four pounds; twelve silver ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds; a silver altar weighing forty pounds; ten silver lamps, each weighing two pounds; two silver jars, weighing ten pounds.

In the basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr: ten silver *pharacanthara*, each weighing ten pounds; twenty-six bronze *canthara*; silver vessels for baptism, ten pounds; a bronze *phara*, fifty pounds.

71

In the city of Rome he established *ministeriales* who would circulate among the appointed stations. A handled golden cup weighing eight pounds; twenty-five silver cups for the titular churches, each weighing ten pounds; twenty-five silver jars, each weighing ten pounds; fifty silver ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds. He stored all these things in the Constantinian basilica or at Saint Mary’s. He built monasteries at Saint Lawrence, the Bath, and the Praetorium [Note: [Col. 0349] C: “of Saint Lawrence”] of Saint Stephen. He also made an oratory of Saint Stephen in the Lateran baptistery. He also made two libraries in the same place. Likewise, within the City, a monastery at the Moon [Note: [Col. 0349] C: “one”]. He carried out an ordination in the City during the month of December: twenty-five priests, six deacons, and twenty-two bishops in various places. He was also buried at Saint Lawrence in the crypt beside the body of blessed Bishop Sixtus; and the episcopate was vacant for ten days.

XLIX. SAINT SIMPLICIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 467, OF LEO 2, OF ANTHEMIUS 1.

[Note: [Col. 0363A]

From Fabrotus, based on the Freher manuscript.

Number 72, lines 1 and 2, month 1, A: six days. Line 7, B: “week.” Lines 8 and 9, B: “the third region at Saint Lawrence, the first and seventh regions at Saint Peter.”

From the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts.

Number 72, line 1: sat for fifteen years, one month, and seven days. Here he dedicated the basilica of Saint Stephen in the City, in C. m. Line 5: Lucinianus. Line 6: at Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Lawrence the martyr, weekly periods, so that the priests might remain there. Line 13: “constructed.” “At that time the Roman Church, that is, the first apostolic See, was executive.” For Simplicius, the bishop, heard this about Peter the bishop of Alexandria, because Acacius had reported and affirmed it concerning him. Line 17: Timothy and Acacius sent a written reply. Line 19: “nevertheless, when his time of repentance had expired.” Line 21: sixteen silver *canthara*. Line 22: “ordained.” Line 15, A B: “concerning whom Achatius.” Line 23, A B: 58. Line 24, A: 36; B: 88. [Col. 0364A] 2. Line 23: priests, 58. Line 24: 86 places; “who was also buried.” Last line: twenty-six days.

From another Thuane manuscript.

Number 72, line 1: 15 years, 1 month, 7 days. Line 7: “weeks.” Line 13: “At that same time the Church, that is, the first apostolic See, was executive.” Timothy. Line 16: “concerning whom Acacius.” Line 21: Peter, 16. Line 23: priests, 68; deacons, 10. Line 24: 26. Last line: two days.

In Holstenius and Schelestratius.

Line 1: Flor.: “Castorio”; Flor. 2: “Casto.” These two manuscripts add “one month.” Line 5, Florentius 2: Licinianus. Line 7: Deusdedit and Florentius: “weeks.” Line 14: in Florentius, “bishop” is absent. Line 15, Florentius: “concerning whom.” Line 18, Florentius: “priests.” Line 23, Florentius: 94. Line 24: cardinals; Deusdedit: 36; and he adds: “After his death, a decree concerning the whole Church was made by the priests and deacons.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363B]

Line 6.—“He established at Saint Peter the apostle, Saint Paul the apostle, and Saint Lawrence the martyr weekly periods, so that priests might remain there for penitents and baptism.” The third region at Saint Lawrence; the first region at Saint Paul; the sixth or seventh region at Saint Peter. In the churches of Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Lawrence, Simplicius established priests who would administer penance and baptism on a weekly basis; hence they were called *hebdomadarii*, or weekly ministers. Anastasius, in his Life of Gregory III:

“And from the weekly priests, the solemn celebrations of Mass.”

The same author, in his Life of Stephen IV:

“He established that every Sunday the solemn celebration of Mass should be performed upon the altar [Col. 0364B] of blessed Peter by seven cardinal bishops serving weekly, who attend in the church of the Savior.”

Following this example, at the Lateran Council held under Innocent III, penitentiaries were established in each cathedral and conventual church to hear confessions and impose penances, as stated in chapter *Inter cetera*, concerning the office of ordinaries. Otto of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, cardinal deacon and legate of the apostolic See in England, established penitentiaries—that is, confessors—in each cathedral church at a council held in 1239 in the church of Saint Paul in London, as Matthew Paris reports:

“We command that general confessors be established in the cathedral churches.”

Thomas of Cantimpré reports that he himself held the office of penitentiary for several years in the church of Cambrai, *The Book of Bees*, Book 2, chapter 30.]

Line 10.—“During his episcopate a report came from Greece from Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and [Col. 0365A] it affirmed that Peter of the city of Alexandria was a Eutychianist heretic, following a petition made by Bishop Acacius and drawn up in his own handwriting.” Here *report concerning heresy* means a denunciation made under the seal of the denouncer’s own handwriting. Anastasius, below, in his Life of Felix III:

“During his episcopate a report again came from Greece: Peter of Alexandria had been recalled by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.”

And below, in the same place:

“After three years another report came from the emperor Zeno, that Acacius should return as a penitent.”

The same author, in his Life of Gelasius:

“In his time another report came from Greece, because many crimes and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius.”

The same author, in his Life of Anastasius:

“Then the senators Festus and Probinus sent a report to the king and began to act so that the king might appoint a visitor for the apostolic See.”

The same author, in his Life of Boniface II:

“At the same time a report came from the African bishops concerning the decree that the bishop of Carthage should do everything with the counsel of the apostolic See.”

In legal books, *report* has another meaning: a consultation submitted to the emperor by a governor or judge in doubtful [Col. 0365B] cases. “Digest, *To the Emperor*; *To the Emperor*, concerning appeals and reports.” Augustine, Letter 137:

“Just as judges do in secular affairs, when the uncertainty of a case is referred to a higher authority, so that while the report is pending they may dare to alter something concerning it.”

Optatus of Milevis, Book 1, *Against the Donatists*:

“A report was sent; a rescript came.”

Line 13.—“At that same time the first Church, that is, the executive Church of the apostolic See, existed.” Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, acknowledged the primacy of the Roman Church when he brought Peter, bishop of Alexandria, before the apostolic See on a charge of heresy. That See is called “executive” for this reason: when Acacius made the denunciation, Pope Simplicius, after hearing the case, condemned Peter of Alexandria. Jerome acknowledged the primacy of the Roman Church in his letter to Damasus:

“For this reason I judged that I should consult the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth; now I ask nourishment for my soul from the place from which I once received Christ’s garments. [Col. 0365C] Let envy of the Roman summit cease; let ambition withdraw: I speak with the successor of the fisherman and the disciple of the cross. Following no first one except Christ, I am joined in communion to Your Blessedness—that is, to the chair of Peter. I know that the Church is built upon that rock.”]

[Note: [Col. 0365C]

Line 1.—Simplicius. From the time of this pontiff the most dreadful Acacian schism began, and it tore apart all the churches of the East until Hormisdas. But what is more grievous, whether through the ignorance or negligence of the compiler, amanuensis, or scribes, the acts of Simplicius, Felix, and Gelasius lie so disfigured that, apart from intolerable anachronisms, it is scarcely possible from them to distinguish what belongs to each in its proper setting or to understand what was done by the Roman pontiffs during that schism and the disturbed condition of the Eastern churches, if the account is weighed against the sequence of the *Book [Col. 0365D] of the Pontiffs*.

Therefore, applying ourselves to careful examination, we follow the conjecture that we have often mentioned: namely, that the acts were interpolated through various additions, which were later reinserted, but not by an accurate and diligent hand. For the additions, at will, attributed actions belonging to one pontiff or another, confused them, overturned their order, and produced an utterly false sequence and narrative of events and persons.

When, therefore, I compared and weighed whether the disorder had arisen from additions that had been made and had not been suitably placed in their proper locations, at last light dawned. I recognized that, if those things inserted here and there thoughtlessly were restored to their proper places, times, and persons, not only would nothing false remain, but the principal matters of apostolic concern devoted to suppressing the Acacian depravity would receive very considerable illumination.

Accordingly, first we shall clarify with notes those passages in the acts of Simplicius in which the *Book of the Pontiffs* correctly reports, in proper order, the beginnings of Acacius’s affair. Then, after rejecting an entire period taken from the acts either of Felix or of Gelasius [Col. 0366A] and inserting it into the acts of Simplicius, we shall demonstrate that it was wrongly attributed to Felix or Gelasius and that, when restored to Simplicius, it represents the careful concern of the pontiffs in overthrowing the Acacian schism.

### Line 10

During his episcopate a report arrived from Greece from Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and declared Peter of Alexandria a Eutychianist heretic. The Acacian report, announcing to Simplicius that Peter Mongus was a Eutychianist heretic and therefore to be condemned, is the fundamental evidence by which it is proved that Acacius thereafter communicated with the same condemned heretic, persisted in communion with him even after the warnings of the Apostolic See, and was consequently excommunicated; and that from this he fomented a schism and wrongfully, with rebellious intent, insulted the Apostolic See.

The *Liber Pontificalis* therefore begins its account of the unfortunate events of this schism with this report, which was made in the year 476, the ninth year of Simplicius, at the time when Odoacer, having occupied Italy, established the kingdom of the Goths [Col. 0366B]. Marcellinus writes concerning that year: “The Western Empire of the Roman people, which Octavian Augustus, the first of the emperors, began to hold in the seven-hundredth year from the founding of the city, perished with this Augustulus in the 522nd year from the reigns of the preceding emperors, after which the kings of the Goths held Rome.”

Peter Mongus, however, had seized the see in the following circumstances. Timothy Aelurus, the murderer of Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, had already been expelled and sent into exile at Cherson by the emperor Leo, and Timothy Solophaciolus had been elected in Proterius’s place. In the year 476 the tyrant Basiliscus seized the imperial power, published an edict against the Council of Chalcedon, and restored the hostile bishops of that council who had been exiled. The edict and the catalogue of those restored are preserved in Evagrius. Aelurus finally died in 477, and Peter Mongus, or Moggus, Aelurus’s associate, was consecrated by a single deposed bishop, while Timothy Solophaciolus was still alive.

When Zeno, restored to the imperial power, heard this, he ordered Mongus to be deposed [Col. 0366C] and Solophaciolus to be regarded as patriarch of Alexandria. But when the latter died in the year 481, John Talaia—called by the Greeks Tabennesiotes because he belonged to the number of the monks of Tabennesis—was elected.

The earlier succession, before the election of Mongus, is described by Theophanes in his *Chronicle*. After reporting that Basiliscus, having driven out Zeno, had seized the empire, he adds:

> “But immediately, chiefly impelled by the words of Zenobia, he declares war against the orthodox faith. Therefore, after publishing an edict, he recalls Timothy Aelurus from exile and restores Peter the Fuller, who was hiding in a monastery, to his see. All those, however, who rejected the holy Council of Chalcedon as adversaries attacked the truth with complete freedom.”

Concerning the recall of Aelurus he later writes:

> “Thereafter Basiliscus, having secured him with an imperial diploma and hostile to the decrees of the council, sent him to Alexandria, and Peter the Fuller to Antioch, their minds embittered against the truth and strengthened in that disposition by his persuasion.”

Concerning Acacius’s zeal when he saw these things, he writes as follows [Col. 0366D]:

> “Basiliscus, having issued an edict publicly, abolished the Council of Chalcedon and ordered Acacius of Constantinople to carry out the same measure. But the whole population of the city, even women and children, gathering together and rushing against Basiliscus, prevented the crime in the church. Acacius, however, wrapped his own body, then the throne, and finally the altar in black cloth. The great Daniel, also inflamed with wholly divine zeal, descended from the column on which he had been sitting and, together with Acacius and a great multitude of the people, was constantly present at all the ecclesiastical assemblies.”

The author of the *Life of Saint Daniel the Stylite* writes thus about Acacius (in Surius, 2 December, chap. 41):

> “Basiliscus indeed seized the scepters, but immediately hissed terribly against the Church of God and babbled certain blasphemous and adulterous things about the dispensation of the flesh assumed by Christ. He wished to punish by an unjust death Acacius, who at that time occupied the pontifical see, who defended the orthodox doctrine and vigorously resisted the storm of Basiliscus’s doctrines with ardor of spirit [Col. 0367A] and freedom of speech.”

The earlier reports of Acacius to Simplicius, therefore, concerned the impious attempts of Basiliscus, Zenobia, and Aelurus, and at the same time the restoration to their own sees of the bishops who had overthrown the Council of Chalcedon. Among these leaders of impiety were counted Peter the Fuller, usurper of the see of Antioch, and Paul of Ephesus.

Prompted by Acacius’s warnings, Simplicius wrote a letter to Basiliscus, who was then promoting the condemnation of the Council of Chalcedon and the withdrawal of the definition that had already been issued and received (ibid., chap. 5). So great was the damage suffered by the Eastern Church through the decree published by Basiliscus that Evagrius states:

> “It is reported that Anastasius also, who later became bishop of Jerusalem after Juvenal, subscribed to the letters written by Basiliscus to everyone generally; and that many others besides him, approximately five hundred in number, did likewise.”

With such a number Basiliscus and Aelurus could have uprooted the Catholic faith throughout the East by the council they had summoned [Col. 0367B].

That Acacius sent this report to Simplicius is suggested by a letter of Simplicius to Acacius, first published by Holstenius. In it Simplicius speaks as follows about these earlier disturbances and reports (in *Collectio Romana*, part I, p. 194):

> “In the letter of your Dilection, which you sent through our son Epiphanius, a deacon of approved faith, you have explained more fully what our most religious sons, the presbyters and archimandrites, had previously written in brief. You reported it in a lengthy volume, indeed, but in language required by the matter, so that we might learn what had been done by the heretics at Constantinople and in the other regions. You placed before our eyes each of the things committed anywhere against the Catholic faith itself, so that it might be seen by what remedy the Churches might also be assisted—those Churches to which, under the pretext of tyrannical domination [namely, that of Basiliscus], and through the absence of the most Christian ruler [Zeno], the pernicious robber [Timothy, namely Aelurus] and the re-emerging usurper of the Alexandrian Church inflicted the injuries of exile.”

Stirred by this first and extensive report [Col. 0367C], Simplicius replied to Basiliscus by letter in the year 476, the ninth year of his pontificate. Baronius, relying on a corrupt manuscript, thinks that this letter was addressed to Zeno; yet Labbe and others prove that it was sent to the tyrant, with the support also of the Verdun manuscript, where it is said to have been given to Basiliscus.

After receiving these letters, Acacius stirred up the monks so that the people would not hesitate to rise against the tyrant, as is clear from Evagrius. The agitation was in fact so great that Basiliscus was compelled to tear up the impious edict by a contrary law and to revoke the letters summoning the council that had been announced.

Evagrius reports the edict as follows:

> “The contrary letter of the emperor Basiliscus. The emperors and Caesars Basiliscus and Marcus: We decree that the apostolic and orthodox faith, preserved in the Churches from the beginning and continued even to our empire, guarded by us despite our present opposition and to be guarded forever, in which we were baptized and in which we believe, is to be retained alone, whole, and firm, and, as it has been retained in all the Catholic and Apostolic orthodox Churches, is to be perpetually preserved; and that no other faith is to be sought. For this reason we order that the letters obtained by us, whether written generally to all or otherwise, and anything else that may have been issued by us for the sake of the faith or ecclesiastical order, be declared invalid and abolished; and that an anathema be pronounced against Nestorius and Eutyches, against all who hold the same opinion as they do, and finally against every heresy; and that no council be summoned and no investigation of the faith be conducted.”

That Basiliscus was broken by the warnings of the Apostolic See is testified by Gelasius in his letter to the bishops of Dardania, where he reveals the stratagems of Acacius the schismatic, whom those bishops were following:

> “Why, then, when Acacius saw this happening, did he not take care—as he had already done under Basiliscus—to report it to the Apostolic See, so that, if he himself could not prevail alone, then, with the counsels and deliberations joined to those of that see before the emperor [Zeno, under whom the schism was fomented], they might present what was appropriate to religion? For if Basiliscus, as has been said, a tyrant and a heretic, was broken by the writings of the Apostolic See and recalled from many excesses, how much more could a legitimate emperor, who wished to appear Catholic, have been guided together with the Apostolic See by the measured advice of all the bishops? It is known that Pope Simplicius of holy memory, and after him Felix of holy memory, repeatedly rebuked not only the tyrant Basiliscus but also the emperor Zeno for those same excesses, with unrestricted authority.”

Zeno, therefore, restored to the imperial power, having heard from Acacius of the wounds inflicted upon religion, celebrated a council at Constantinople. There he labored to have Timothy Aelurus, Peter the Fuller, John of Apamea, and Paul of Ephesus condemned, and he sent a second report together with the synodal acts. Felix III relates this in his letter to the clergy and monks of the East; after listing those heretics, he adds (in Baronius, year 483, no. 52):

> “At that time the hypocrite Acacius caused them to be condemned by the Apostolic See in such a way that even the name of Christians was taken away from them, as the acts conducted before him make clear” [Col. 0368B].

In the following year, apparently, a Roman council was summoned by Simplicius. At it the Fuller, Aelurus, and others were condemned. Letters 3 and 4 concerning the condemnation are preserved in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*. They are wrongly assigned to Felix, although they must be attributed to Simplicius, as more discerning writers, together with Pagi in his criticism of Baronius for the years in question, have demonstrated.

Finally Acacius sent Simplicius a third report, in which he reviewed the proceedings against Peter Mongus, declared him a heretic, and sent Simplicius a letter announcing his condemnation. Beforehand he had obtained from Zeno an edict, preserved by Evagrius, imposing the penalty of death upon Mongus if he persisted in his intrusion.

A record of Acacius’s letters is found in the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists* (in Sirmond and volume IV of Labbe’s *Councils*):

> “As long as the emperor Leo lived, Timothy [Solophaciolus], bishop of Alexandria, lived in piety. But when Basiliscus had seized the empire, he began to condemn the Council of Chalcedon and persecute the Catholics. Then that condemned Timothy [Aelurus], having received his freedom, came to Constantinople and restored the condemned heretics to their own places. He came to Alexandria; Timothy the Catholic fled . . . Zeno the emperor returned to the kingdom, and Basiliscus was overthrown. He was sent to Alexandria so that, after the persecutor had been driven out, Timothy the Catholic might be restored to the Church. But since Timothy was forestalled by death, Peter [Mongus], his associate, was ordained by a single heretical Alexandrian bishop. Nevertheless the most Christian emperor ordered him to be deposed and Timothy the Catholic to be brought back, as is contained in the letters of Acacius of Constantinople.”

We have thought it necessary to review these reports separately, because without them the following notes could scarcely be understood. The *Liber Pontificalis* praises the third report in order to show that the sentence of deposition pronounced by the Apostolic See against Acacius was just. Acacius had communicated with and defended the condemned heretic, who had been publicly declared such by the letters he himself had issued, while excluding the legitimately elected patriarch [Col. 0368D].

### Line 12

“After a petition had been made by the bishop Acacius, composed in his own handwriting.”

The Acacian letter containing the report of Peter Mongus’s condemnation and declaring him a heretic belonged to the class of letters called *denunciatory letters*. Through such letters, heresy and condemned heretics were announced to the Churches so that they might be avoided. Several forms of these letters survive. It is enough to read the one issued by the Council of Sardica, at the end of which heretical bishops are denounced and the reason for the denunciation is stated. The bishops subscribed this letter; and because it was an encyclical, according to the usage received in the *Liber Pontificalis*, it is called a *chirograph* (volume II of the *Councils*, p. 812).

Felix III recalls this letter and its contents to Acacius in a *Commonitorium*, when he reviews the earlier proceedings and the reports made concerning both Peter the Fuller and Peter Mongus, as well as the other condemned heretical bishops:

> “Especially when these matters were being promulgated to the most Christian ruler, upon his return, with God’s assistance, to the imperial authority, you did not fail, by sending letters here [an authentic testimony of the reports made and sent to the Apostolic See], to devote your efforts most earnestly and in a manner worthy of a Catholic bishop. You gloried that all who had attempted to act against your see, against the Council of Chalcedon, and against the preaching of the Apostolic See had been overthrown.”

Acacius’s petition was not merely intended to confirm, by his own judgment, Simplicius’s sentence against Peter Mongus, whom Acacius himself had denounced as a heretic and whom Zeno had declared liable to death. It also sought to have the pontiff confer vicariate authority upon Acacius, so that no one in the East could resist the Apostolic See’s authority over the stubborn insolence of the bishops. This is indicated by the words that follow immediately, where we read:

### Line 13

“At the same time the first Church—that is, the executor of the Apostolic See—was [the Constantinopolitan Church].”

An error has entered the text. It should be read as follows: “At the same time in which the petition was made by Acacius, the Constantinopolitan Church was the executor of the first Church, that is, of the Apostolic See, throughout the East, for the overthrow of the Eutychianist bishops”—namely, by a concession from Simplicius.

Gelasius describes the matter vividly in his letter to Faustus, when he discusses the condemnation of the aforementioned Eutychianist bishops:

> “In this very case Timothy of Alexandria [namely, Aelurus], Peter of Antioch [called the Fuller], Peter [Mongus], Paul [of Ephesus], John [of Apamea], and the others—not merely one but many, and not bearing even the name of the priesthood—were deposed solely by the authority of the Apostolic See. Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness of this matter, since he was the executor of this command.”

And in the aforementioned letter to the bishops of Dardania, Gelasius says the following about Acacius and the Apostolic See:

> “When this see had learned from certain indications that Acacius had deviated from Catholic communion, it did not readily believe it for a long time, since it knew that he had often been the executor of necessary measures against heretics” [Col. 0369C].

He immediately adds:

> “Nevertheless Acacius had indicated in his own letters that he had very readily fallen back, without consulting the same Apostolic See, into communion with Peter of Alexandria, whom he himself, as executor of the authority requested from the Apostolic See, had condemned, and whom he had declared to be outside Catholic communion.”

It is therefore most correctly noted here that Acacius requested the place of the Apostolic See, obtained it, and acted as its executor in condemning the bishops.

### Line 15

“He asserted innumerable crimes.”

To advance his petitions, Acacius set forth Mongus’s crimes. The *Liber Pontificalis* also considered it necessary to review them, in order to make it certain that the Acacian schism arose from Acacius’s evil character. He had condemned Mongus as a heretic and had ensured that he was condemned by describing and announcing to everyone, in his encyclical, the innumerable crimes committed by Mongus.

### Line 16

“At the same time Timothy the Catholic and Acacius replied.”

Acacius did not cease replying against Mongus’s depravity. Together with Solophaciolus, he warned the pontiff that Timothy Aelurus had had Mongus as an accomplice in the killing of Saint Proterius.

Certainly Mongus’s crimes were serious, and the punishment that Zeno initially imposed upon him, after the crimes had been reported to the emperor, makes this clear. It was a capital punishment, as Evagrius states:

> “Timothy, however, not long afterward paid the common debt of nature. After his death the Alexandrian bishops, on their own authority, chose Peter, surnamed Mongus, as their bishop. When this reached Zeno’s ears, it greatly disturbed him. Therefore he condemned Peter to death.”

That Solophaciolus replied to Simplicius, and that through letters sent from both sides he asked the Apostolic See to prescribe the manner and formula for receiving the heretical bishops who were then returning to the Church, is testified by Simplicius himself in a letter sent to Acacius in the year 478:

> “But so that we might rejoice with perfect joy, our brother and fellow bishop Timothy himself sent us an example of the libellus of satisfaction of those who, having been led away from the truth of the Catholic faith by the terror of the condemnation inflicted by Timothy [Aelurus] and Peter [the Fuller], both condemned, were asking pardon. He desired, with priestly compassion, to assist those who had fallen; and, in view of the divine mercy, which wishes no one to perish, we did not consider this to be rejectable” [Col. 0370A].

### Line 18

“Then Archbishop Simplicius, concealing [the matter].”

This addition has been inserted wholly inappropriately into the acts of Simplicius and has no connection or coordination with the Acacian acts that have thus far been praised. We therefore thought that something needed to be supplied. On carefully examining the acts of Felix and Gelasius cited below, we perceived that an ignorant copyist had inserted into the account of one pontiff and another, in no order but rather in confused interpolation, the material that should have been attributed to Simplicius, thereby disfiguring it with enormous chronological inconsistencies.

In order, therefore, to restore these acts, once we had recognized the sequence of events from pontifical letters and other reliable records, it was easy to place the additions belonging to each pontiff under their proper headings, so that every ambiguity might be removed and, indeed, the more hidden secrets of sacred learning and history might remain disclosed [Col. 0370B].

### The Acts of Simplicius, Illustrated by Additions Wrongly Inserted into the Acts of Felix and Gelasius and Now Restored

> “At the same time Timothy the Catholic and Acacius replied, saying that Peter had also been permitted to participate in the death of Proterius the Catholic” [from the acts of Felix]. “During his episcopate a report again came from Greece, that Peter of Alexandria had been recalled by Acacius of Constantinople” [from Gelasius]. “At the same time John of Alexandria, fleeing, came to Rome to the Apostolic See. At that time blessed Simplicius received John” [from Simplicius, in the passage cited above]. “Then Archbishop Simplicius, concealing the matter, never replied to Acacius, but condemned Peter while awaiting a time for repentance.”

The acts of Simplicius, restored in this way, not only reveal the certain sequence of the following events but also explain what was missing in the account of Simplicius for the explanation of the later acts of this pontiff against Acacius. Acacius finally appeared, after laying aside his mask, as an extremely hostile enemy of pontifical authority.

In presenting the notes on the acts restored by us, we therefore offer both the acts themselves and their order for the benevolent reader to examine more carefully.

### During His Episcopate a Report Again Came from Greece

The report should be regarded as having been sent to the Apostolic See either by John himself or by the monks. The Catholic monks fought courageously in this matter of the faith. Thus, when Basiliscus published his impious edict:

> “That remarkable man Daniel the Stylite, together with a crowd of monks and people and with certain devotees of divine matters whom he had taken with him, went to Basiliscus and spoke before him with great freedom.”

So Theophanes relates.

Before Acacius approached Simplicius with his reports, the pontiff had already been informed by the monks, as he writes in a letter published by Holstenius. Felix III likewise, when legates were departing for the East, instructed them to reconsider all the counsels of the monks [Col. 0370D]. Both Simplicius and his successors chose the monks to repair the impending evils of the Eastern Church, as anyone can clearly see from the letters sent to them.

Before we weigh the later acts of John of Alexandria together with those of Simplicius, however, John’s election must be examined. We touched upon it above; it should now be recalled more fully from Evagrius, who states that he learned it from the rhetorician Zacharias:

> “John the presbyter, to whom the administration of the august temple of the holy John the Baptist and Forerunner of the Lord had been entrusted, came to Constantinople, impelled by the advice of certain persons, in order to ask the emperor that, if the bishop of Alexandria should happen to die, he might be permitted to nominate as bishop for the citizens of that city whomever he wished. As Zacharias reports, he was discovered to be seeking the episcopate for himself; and after binding himself by oath never to seek the Alexandrian episcopal see, he returned home. Therefore, when Zeno later determined that a bishop should be chosen whom the clergy and the multitude of the laity would elect, not long afterward, upon Timothy’s death, John—having paid a sum of money, as the same Zacharias reports, and having disregarded the oath he had given the emperor—was elected bishop of the Alexandrians” [Col. 0371A].

A second and more urgent occasion, arising from Acacius’s ambition and assigned as the origin of the quarrels, was that the newly elected bishop failed to send Acacius the synodical letter concerning his election, although he sent it to Simplicius and to Calendion of Antioch.

From the beginning of his patriarchate Acacius, walking in hypocrisy, directed everything toward having the Constantinopolitan see regarded as the first among the patriarchal sees and toward its occupying second place after the Roman bishop. Hence, in the year 472, he extorted from the emperor Zeno a privilege by which he would hold the second see in the East after Rome and exercise patriarchal rights over the three dioceses of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace [Col. 0371B]. This privilege had previously been denied by Leo and Hilary.

During the Eastern disputes he compelled Basiliscus to withdraw the edict issued against the Council of Chalcedon. And when Timothy Aelurus had restored to John of Ephesus the right of exarchate according to the ancient institution—a right Acacius had already usurped, as was observed above from Evagrius—Acacius wished the imperial edict to state that these rights belonged to the see of Constantinople. Thus the edict reads in Evagrius (book III, chap. 7):

> “Furthermore, let the appointment of those bishops whose creation belongs to the see of this royal and illustrious city be restored to the most reverend and most holy patriarch Acacius; and let the bishops who already preside over those provinces retain their own sees, so that after their death no prejudice may arise from this matter against the right of ordination belonging to the holy see of this royal and distinguished city.”

On the authority of this provision, after the destruction of Basiliscus, Acacius claimed for himself the case of the bishops of the diocese of Asia, as Evagrius reports in the same work, chapter 9 [Col. 0371C].

Thus Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops of Dardania, censures this sort of Acacian ambition as follows:

> “He, puffed up with an exceedingly proud spirit, attempts to raise the throne of humility higher than was fitting, and by his presumptions seeks an entrance from every side. At the same time, by right and wrong alike, he tramples upon and passes beyond the inviolable statutes of the saints. Together with the author of pride whom he imitated, he was cast down into the deepest ruin; and he left this to the Church, so that the peaceful might mourn and the humble might weep.”

Driven by the same ambition, he insolently rose first to disturb the rights of the Alexandrian see and then those of Antioch. He also expelled from the Alexandrian see John, called Talaia, and, without any prior investigation, declared Peter Mongus—whom he had denounced as a heretic and whom, at the request of the Apostolic See, he had wished to be appointed executor for expelling from the see—as the legitimate patriarch, and communicated with him before his absolution.

This is briefly reported in the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists*:

> “After this Timothy, the bishop, died, John the Catholic Oeconomus was ordained by Catholic bishops. When, according to the custom of the elders, he had sent synodical letters to the Apostolic See, Uranian Subadjuva arrived, carrying against John, who was already bishop, a sacred document from the ruler [namely, Zeno]. John was suspended from confirmation in that episcopate. And because in that same imperial document he had mentioned the restoration of Peter [Mongus], whom he himself had condemned, this part was entirely rejected. Hence it appears that the most merciful emperor was offended.”

Liberatus reports that orders were given to Pergemius, duke of Egypt, and to Apollonius, the Augustal prefect, to expel John and substitute Mongus, with whom Acacius had communicated without taking account of the earlier condemnation.

### At the Same Time John of Alexandria, Fleeing

The *Brief Account of the Eutychianists* describes John’s arrival in the city as follows:

> “That same holy bishop John arrived, and, as was fitting, was received by the Apostolic See” [Col. 0372A].

Liberatus, chapter 18, writes:

> “John Talaia, expelled from the Alexandrian see because of Peter Mongus, went to Calendion, patriarch of Antioch, and, having received from him synodical letters of intercession, appealed to the Roman pontiff Simplicius, just as blessed Athanasius had done. He persuaded him to write to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople; and indeed Simplicius was prepared in mind and will for this.”

Simplicius was certainly prepared in mind, but he wished first to reply to Zeno, as Evagrius says:

> “John, fleeing from Alexandria, hastened to ancient Rome, where he stirred up great disturbances . . . Therefore, when Simplicius, bishop of ancient Rome, was greatly troubled, he sent letters to the emperor Zeno. Zeno replied and charged John with the crime of perjury, asserting that he had been deprived of the episcopate for that reason and not for any other.”

The pontiff refrained from writing to Acacius about John, as I think, so as not to encourage Acacius’s ambition. Acacius sought to appear, as it were, to have the cause of the deposed John of Alexandria within his own control, like a primate—a position he was pursuing among the patriarchs of the East [Col. 0372B]. He would also know that Acacius was offended with John because John had failed to send him the synodical letter that should have been sent after his election.

### Line 18

“Then Archbishop Simplicius, concealing the matter.”

The restoration made by us, examined in light of the nearest ecclesiastical records, both clarifies the sequence of Simplicius’s acts against Acacius and demonstrates that a shameful interpolation was made in the acts of Felix and Gelasius and that they have been freed from chronological inconsistencies.

What is said here—that Simplicius concealed the matter from Acacius and did not reply to him—should be understood as follows. When the pontiff heard, through Uranian, the legate sent in the emperor’s name, the charges brought against John, and received John upon his arrival in Rome, where John asserted many crimes against Acacius, Simplicius thought that he should conceal the matter until he became more certain of the charges reported.

Meanwhile, however, through letters of admonition he advanced what was beyond doubt: that Acacius should withdraw from communion with Mongus. He thought that John’s restoration would be easy if he induced Acacius to withdraw from communion with Peter Mongus.

That he did indeed do this is shown by the letter sent to Acacius after Acacius had promoted Mongus’s restoration. The letter assumes that Acacius had asked the pontiff to confirm Mongus’s restoration (volume II of the *Councils*, p. 916). Simplicius writes there:

> “That which your same letters contained made me not a little astonished: namely, that Peter—who is demonstrably the former associate and leader of the heretics, a fact which we remember is not hidden from the conscience of your Dilection, and whose refutations we confidently believe you know; who, moreover, is unquestionably still outside Catholic communion, and concerning whom it is certain that we have often written about expelling him from that city—that this man should be considered eligible for promotion to the government of the aforesaid Church, and that you should promise that he agrees with the definitions of the orthodox faith.”

The pontiff also assumes that Acacius had given Simplicius the acts of the restoration, in which it was read that Mongus had been sought by the people, when he identifies those who supported Mongus’s restoration. He writes:

> “Finally, it is said that the bishop was requested by those same people from whom he was formerly separated by participation in the Catholic faith. Thus it is sufficiently clear that they do not desire the orthodox faith, but seek power for themselves in the bishop of their own abominable doctrine; nor can a trustworthy peace arise from this between them and those who think truly. Hence the destructive condemnation of heretical minds increases, together with the pitiable captivity of Catholics” [Col. 0372D].

That the time of Acacius’s condemnation was prolonged for three years and was then published by his successor is written by Gelasius to the emperor Anastasius (volume II of the *Councils*, p. 895):

> “For this reason we rightly say that Acacius must also be removed from our fellowship. He preferred to pass into the lot of perfidy rather than remain steadfast in the sincerity of Catholic and Apostolic communion, although he had been suitably instructed for almost three years by the letters of the Apostolic See, lest this should happen.”

Liberatus, chapter 18, and the *Brief Account of the Eutychianists* contain the same account.

### Line 23

“During the months of December and February.”

Amalarius, in book II of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 1, writes:

> “The first pontiffs always administered ordinations in the month of December, in which the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, until Simplicius . . . He was the first to consecrate in February.”

The *Micrologus* repeats the same statement, adding that it is found in the Roman *Pontifical*, that is, in such a book of the Lives of the Pontiffs.

But, as was noted above, this must be understood only of ordinations to rank and to ministries exercised in the Roman Church. It is certain that at other times the remaining members of the clergy were ordained for the ministries required by the Churches. Gelasius supposes this when, shortly afterward, he retained the see.

A decree of Gelasius survives with the heading (volume II of the *Councils*, p. 956):

> “The Constitutions of Pope Gelasius, which the bishops receive at their ordination.”

One of these was:

> “Ordinations of presbyters and deacons, however, are to be held only during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months. They are also to be celebrated at the beginning and in the middle of Lent, on the evening of Saturday.”

Another letter of Gelasius, published by Holstenius, also survives. In identical words it inculcates this observance upon the bishop who is writing (in the *Collectio Romana*, p. 241).

Pelagius I, writing to the bishop of Centumcellae, assigns the middle period as the time for carrying out an ordination (ibid., p. 241):

> “When the middle week of Easter arrives, if the Lord wills and if we live, do not delay promoting each person through the offices we have mentioned.”

It is enough to add that from the beginning and down to these times the Apostolic See sent ecclesiastical letters through the provinces by means of deacons. The care of the estates of Saint Peter was also entrusted to them; these estates were scattered throughout the regions of the entire world. To fulfill these ministries, the small number of ordained deacons listed in the preceding acts was wholly insufficient.

Therefore, on the other Saturdays of the fasts, ministers were ordained for sacred and other ministries, the memory of which is omitted because only those offices connected with rank were recorded in the brief lists [Col. 0373C] (in Baluze, *New Councils*, p. 334).

Indeed, in Augustine’s *Brief Account of the Conference at Carthage* we read:

> “The Catholics could easily have replied that, among such a multitude of Roman clerics, it was nothing surprising if two or three were found who were not only *stratores* but also Cassians.”

The Roman clergy was therefore more numerous; accordingly, besides those ordained and counted in the Lives of the pontiffs, there were others who were ordained for other purposes.

[Note: [Col. 0373C]

### Line 6

“Here he established a weekly division, so that the presbyters might remain there for the penitents and baptism, etc.”

Saint Simplicius established that, because of the increasing crowds, presbyters should always wait in the designated churches in weekly rotations and be prepared to hear confessions of sins and to administer the other sacraments as the needs of the faithful required.

Those who performed this duty were called *hebdomadarii*, or “weekly ministers,” because they succeeded one another in rotation. It is therefore clear that sacramental confession of sins, instituted by Christ the Lord, had been practiced continuously in earlier centuries down to this time.]

[Note: [Col. 0373D]

### Chronological Notes

In establishing the chronology of Simplicius at fifteen years and seven days, the Bibliothecary agrees with the oldest catalogues among our own manuscripts, although the Farfensis adds one month, as do three Colbertine manuscripts cited by Pagi. Pagi nevertheless produces and follows four others from the same library that agree with ours.

We celebrate the feast of Simplicius in the patriarchal basilicas of Rome on 2 March, the day on which the Bibliothecary writes that he was buried at Saint Peter’s in the Vatican. If we count backward seven days from that date, we arrive at 24 February, which must be assigned as the beginning of his pontificate in the leap year 468, the year in which we place Hilary’s death on 21 February [Col. 0374A].

The text of Anastasius extends the vacancy of the see to ten days, whereas we reckon it as two or three days. Either the two signs for units, II, were misread by the copyists as 10, expressing ten instead of two, or the elected pontiff postponed his ordination for a full week and thereby gave the writers of the catalogues an opportunity to assign to the vacancy after Hilary’s death not only the three days completed in the election of Simplicius but also the additional seven days inserted between his election and his ordination.

This slight difference of one week does not deserve further investigation in defining this period. Its beginning is 24 February 468, and its end 2 March 483.

It is certain that the life of blessed Simplicius continued until 28 May of the year 482, when Severinus was consul. This is demonstrated by a letter of his addressed to John, bishop of Ravenna. In a manuscript approximately eight hundred years old, often cited by us in the library of the venerable monastery of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem, the copy is dated “the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Severinus, a man of consular rank” [Col. 0374B].

Moreover, another reply addressed to Acacius declares that Simplicius was still alive on 6 November of the same year. Binius published this letter in the *General Councils*; it was dated on the same day and in the same consulship.

### Historical Notes
Line 3.—And the basilica of Saint Andrew the Apostle beside the Basilica of Saint Mary. Where the church, monastery, and hospital of Abbot Antony now stand, in the Exquilian Forum extending before the façade of the Liberian Basilica, in Platina’s time there still remained the ruins of this church of Saint Andrew, dedicated by Simplicius, which the Librarian mentions. The most learned bishop and student of sacred antiquities, Joseph Ciampini, saw a surviving part of its dome less than eighty years ago. In the first volume of his *Veterum Monumentorum*, chapter 27, he described it and showed us an image of the mosaic work, not yet cut away, together with the inscription once read in full by Platina. In the portion that we print here in capitals, Ciampini supplied the letters in smaller characters [Col. 0374C] elsewhere, reserving the part that Platina had seen but which had already disappeared in Ciampini’s time:

> **HAEC TIBI MENS VALIDE DECREVIT PR[AE]DIA XPE**  
> This resolute mind has firmly decreed estates for you, O Christ.
>
> **CVI TESTATOR OPES DETVLIT ILLE SVAS**  
> To whom that testator brought his own wealth.
>
> **SIMPLICIVS QVAE PAPA SACRIS CAELESTIBVS APTANS**  
> Pope Simplicius, fitting these things for the heavenly rites,
>
> **EFFECIT VERE MVNERIS ESSE TVI**  
> made them truly to be your gift.
>
> **ET QVOD APOSTOLICI DEESSENT LIMINA NOBIS**  
> And because the threshold of the Apostle was lacking for us,
>
> **MARTYRIS ANDREAE NOMINE COMPOSVIT**  
> he arranged it under the name of the martyr Andrew.
>
> **VTITVR HAEC HAERES TITVLIS ECCLESIA IVSTIS**  
> This church, an heir, enjoys its rightful titles,
>
> **SVCCEDENSQVE DOMO MYSTICA IVRA LOCAT**  
> and, succeeding to the house, establishes its mystical rights.
>
> **PLEBS DEVOTA VENI PERQVE HAEC COMMERcia DISCE**  
> Come, devout people, and through these exchanges learn
>
> **TERRENO CENSV REGNA SVPERNA PETI**  
> that the heavenly kingdoms are sought by earthly tribute.

We have thought it right to present to the reader the more important portion of this sacred mosaic, faithfully reproduced from Ciampini’s drawing. Anyone wishing to learn more about the name “Saint Andrew *Catabarbara Patricia*,” added to this church from the illustrious matron of patrician lineage who lived nearby—Severanus also asserts that the body of Saint Severinus was transferred to Naples—and likewise about the designation of the monastery of Saint Andrew, as well as the name “Siciniana Basilica,” formerly given to this splendid building before it was dedicated to God under the name of the Apostle Andrew, should consult Ciampini himself, chapters 7 and 27 of the work cited. There he will see representations of the ornaments discovered here, both sacred ones belonging to the church of Saint Andrew and secular ones that remained in the Siciniana Basilica.

Among these are especially famous two panels transferred from there to the palace formerly belonging to Cardinal de’ Massimi, now the distinguished Albani residence at the Four Fountains. They are assembled from cut marbles imitating a painting and are perhaps the only surviving ancient example of that art. Our marble-workers and sculptors now practise it, restored with happy ingenuity, especially for decorating sacred buildings; at Florence, however, it has been brought to the highest summit of elegance in the grand duke’s lapidary museum.

The Librarian mentions this church and monastery of Saint Andrew *Cata-Barbara* [Col. 0375A] in the sections that follow.

Line 3.—And another basilica within the City, beside the Licinian Palace, of the blessed martyr Bibiana, where her body rests. The canons, to whom Pope Eugene IV had assigned this church to the Liberian Basilica, had begun to restore it during the reign of Urban VIII. The Lord, mercifully answering their prayers, granted that the body of the holy virgin and martyr should be discovered. Urban’s piety was thereby aroused, and he enriched the sacred building with magnificent ornaments, enclosed her relics in an exceptionally costly onyx vessel together with her companions in martyrdom, Demetria and Dafrosa, solemnly transferred them, and ordered that the clergy of the basilica should visit them every year in solemn procession.

The place is venerable not only because these relics were deposited there, but also because of the more ancient memory of the cemetery *ad Ursum pileatum*, about which we spoke above in the notes on Saint Anastasius.

[Col. 0375B] Line 6.—Here he established, and so forth, a weekly rotation, so that the priests might remain there on account of the penitents and baptism; the third region at Saint Lawrence, and so forth. In the preceding volume of our edition, in the historical notes on the Life of Saint Cletus, while discussing the established number of the titular churches and priests in the City, and their distribution in weekly rotations for performing sacred ministry in the patriarchal basilicas after those basilicas had been founded and enlarged in proportion to the number of patriarchates established throughout the Christian world, we explained this passage of Anastasius. We showed that around the middle of the fifth Christian century, in the Laurentian Basilica outside the walls, a representation of the Jerusalem patriarchate had been given form, since at that time the decree of the Council of Chalcedon attributed to the Jerusalem Church that corresponding rank of honor; hence that see began to be numbered among the patriarchal sees.

We explained this more fully in the notes on Saint Dionysius. From Innocent III we observed that the Roman Church had always made it its distinctive practice to express the Catholic Church through a certain symbolic form, gathering the other sees and crowns beneath the primacy of that see in which, according to the Apocalypse seen by John, the throne of God and of the Lamb is represented in the chair of Peter. For this reason the supreme pontiffs repeatedly took care to express the image of the whole community of believers, obedient through this hierarchical unity to Christ the Lord and to his vicar on earth, in the mosaics and paintings of sacred buildings: the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse offer crowns to the one seated upon the throne and to the Lamb. We see this expressed by Leo the Great in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, by Paschal I in the titles of Saints Praxedes and Cecilia, and elsewhere.

From the same vision of the Apocalypse they also borrowed another image of the whole community, namely the seven lampstands, which, by being represented in that number, signified universality. Felix III—who is called Felix IV—in the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, together with the elders, most of whom have now been cut away, and Innocent II in the Basilica of Saint Mary across the Tiber, expressed this in mosaic. What painting displayed on the walls of sacred buildings, they represented in the ministry of the Roman clergy by assigning to the patriarchal churches of the City, which are like the major dioceses, seven cardinal priests chosen from the Roman titular churches, one for each day of the week, so that they might perform the sacred rites there.

They likewise employed the same number of bishops at the Lateran, which is regarded as the mother, summit, and apex of all the churches throughout the world—as we cited above in the notes on Saint Cletus, in the words of Cardinal Damiani together with another cardinal, namely Rasponi—and which represents the Roman see itself as the chief of all sees and the earthly throne of our Lord and Savior.

While making these observations, I showed that the rights of the ancient institution were always preserved for the three greater patriarchs. From the age of Damasus through Leo the Great, Simplicius, Felix, and their successors, the Roman pontiffs employed the greatest perseverance and care to restrain the ambition of the Constantinopolitan bishops, who sought to invade provinces belonging to others and attempted to exercise primacy over the dioceses themselves. They nevertheless allowed both the Constantinopolitan and Jerusalem patriarchs to receive the title of honor and the place of session among the patriarchs, while preserving the primordial right of jurisdiction and authority owed to the Alexandrian and Antiochene patriarchs in their own regions.

In the notes on Saint Dionysius I said that, also from this arrangement of Simplicius, who instituted weekly rotations at Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Paul the Apostle, and Saint Lawrence the Martyr, and chose priests from the first, third, sixth, and seventh of the City’s seven ecclesiastical regions to administer the sacred rites in those churches, I had shown that the universality of the priesthood spread throughout the Christian world was mystically outlined at the Roman see by the titular churches and basilicas of the City. These represented the major dioceses of the individual patriarchs, and, beneath them, the nearby sees of exarchs, metropolitans, [Col. 0376B] and bishops, arranged in hierarchical connection under the successor of Peter. Over all these the Roman pontiff exercises the primacy divinely entrusted to him, while, as the Fathers of the Council of Arles testify—together with Schelestratius and Thomassinus, whose testimony we produced there—he exercises unalterable jurisdiction over all the other patriarchs.

We shall see in the notes that follow that Simplicius also exercised this authority, as did Archbishop Somier, Pagius, and ourselves. Here he provides for the honor of the three patriarchal basilicas situated outside the City’s boundary, assigning to each weekly rotations and selecting priests from the titular churches within the City to minister there daily. Therefore the beginning of that weekly division may safely be assigned to the pontificate of Simplicius in the three basilicas then situated outside the walls. The assignment of each group was also appropriately arranged from those regions which, being nearer to the patriarchal basilica to which they were assigned, offered easier access for carrying out the ministry.

For the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, a weekly clergy [Col. 0376C] was assigned from the first ecclesiastical region, which contained two of Augustus’s ancient regions, called the Capena Gate and the Aventine, 13. See the little work on the regions of the City among the prolegomena. The titular churches situated in this region are Saint Sabina, Saint Prisca, Saint Balbina, Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and Saint Sixtus. Panvinius, in *On the Seven Churches of the City*, counts them among the legitimate seven assigned to that basilica.

To the Basilica of Saint Peter were assigned weekly clergy from the sixth ecclesiastical region, which had been Augustus’s fourteenth, namely the Transtiberine region. There are located the titular churches of Saint Mary across the Tiber, Saint Chrysogonus, and Saint Cecilia, which in that division are mentioned among those assigned to the Vatican. From the seventh ecclesiastical region, which comprises two Augustan regions—namely the Via Lata, 7, and the Circus Flaminius, 9—come the titular churches of Saint Lawrence in Damasus and Saint Mark, likewise listed among the number assigned to the Vatican.

Finally, from the third ecclesiastical region, which contains two Augustan regions, namely the Isian and Serapian region, 3, and the region called the Esquiline, 5 [Col. 0376D], the titular priests assigned are those of Saint Praxedes and Saint Peter ad Vincula. Added to these are the cardinal priests from the Coelimontine region: Saints John and Paul, Saint Stephen Rotundus, the Four Crowned Saints, and Saint Cross in Jerusalem.

I also read that Saint Lawrence in Lucina was counted among the titular churches, but it is not clear to me whether, as a later alteration, it was substituted for nearer churches perhaps assigned in this first division of Simplicius. That division mentions only that the clergy of the third region was assigned to the Basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the walls for these ministries.

This discipline of regional division, for carrying out weekly rotations in the patriarchal basilicas through the cardinal priests of the titular churches, was preserved until the eleventh Christian century, as is clear from a letter of Saint Peter Damian preserved by Baronius under the year 1057. Indeed, it is known to have continued into the twelfth century, until Honorius II, from Pandulf of Pisa’s Life of Gelasius II. Panvinius also notes it in *On the Seven Churches of the City*, chapter 2, as does Carlo, Abbot Piazza, in *On the Cardinal Titles*, page 358; consult these works. You will find the reason why that discipline then failed, when, as the peace of Church and empire was disturbed, Honorius ceased creating cardinals, so that their sacred College was almost reduced to a solitary remnant, in the accounts of the same Panvinius and Piazza.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from understanding that in the age of Leo the Great and Simplicius the Roman Church established an image of the five patriarchal sees—the number to which they had been increased, at least in title, by the addition of Jerusalem at the Synod of Ephesus—by establishing weekly rotations also in the Laurentian Basilica outside the walls. I repeat: nothing prevents us from understanding these honorary additions as having been admitted by the same pontiffs who restrained the ambition and audacity of the new patriarchs. Neither the honor conferred and the title, nor the appearance of such an arrangement, infringed the primordial rights of authority consistently preserved for the three ancient patriarchs by Leo [Col. 0377B] and Simplicius, just as those rights had been preserved by their predecessors from Damasus through Leo the Great. See the notes of Pagius and Sommier.

Before we remove our hand from the tablet, while discussing this weekly division of titular clergy for administering the sacred rites in the three patriarchal basilicas then outside the walls—Saint Peter in the Vatican, Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, and Saint Lawrence in the Veran Field—it seems necessary to say something about the assignment of titular clergy to the ministries performed in the two remaining patriarchal basilicas enclosed within the City, namely the Lateran and the Liberian. We cannot doubt that these also fulfilled their weeks with an equal number of cardinal clergy, since ancient monuments express this, as produced in the works of Baronius, Panvinius, and others.

It is clear from the Librarian, section 284, that under Stephen IV seven bishops performed the weekly rotation in the Lateran. The historian reports that this pope renewed the ancient rite:

> “He renewed the Church’s former rite in the various honors of the clergy. He established that every Sunday the solemn Mass should be celebrated upon the altar of blessed Peter by the seven cardinal bishops serving weekly, who attend in the Church of the Savior.”

As to the age preceding Stephen IV to which the origin of the rite restored by Stephen should be referred, neither the Librarian teaches this openly, nor does any other writer, so far as I know, give a hint. Nevertheless, in the notes on Pope Cletus, 38, I attempted to investigate when the number of cardinal priests—which had once been fixed at twenty-five by the Apostle Peter and completed by Evaristus, then renewed during the persecutions by Dionysius and Marcellus—was increased to twenty-eight, namely four groups of seven, so that one group of seven could be assigned to each of four basilicas.

I showed that the number of titles was completed at twenty-eight under Damasus, when Silvester added the ancient title of Equitius, while Mark and Damasus each added one title named after himself. From Anastasius’s Life of Damasus I also observed, on the same page 38 of the notes, that a certain arrangement had then been established for bishops, priests, and monasteries, by which sacred psalmody was to be performed throughout all the churches day and night.

Since, therefore, by the end of the fourth century the number of four groups of seven existed among the titular churches, and an orderly rule for chanting had been entrusted to bishops and priests throughout all the churches, it seems that some weekly division began, at least from the age of Damasus, also in the basilicas founded within the City’s boundary during that same century. Damasus’s successors gradually completed it thereafter, employing nearby bishops—who were later called cardinals—as synkellites, or household clergy, in the Lateran patriarchate, so that they could perform the sacred rites whenever they were able to come to the City in rotation, and supplying the absence of bishops through the nearby titular clergy of the Coelimontine and Esquiline regions, should the bishops happen to be absent.

In the Liberian Basilica they likewise employed cardinal priests from the nearer titular churches, namely Saint Pudentiana, or Pastor; Saint Eusebius; Saint Vitalis, or Vestina; Saints Apostles; Saint Cyriacus in the Baths; Saint Clement; and Saints Marcellinus and Peter. These are also known to have been assigned to the Liberian Basilica in the division that remained in force until Honorius II. Their equal antiquity in the fifth century cannot be doubted, since at the Roman council under Symmachus priests are read as having subscribed from all these titles.

The weekly assignment, therefore, of seven bishops in the Lateran and of an equal number of priests in the four remaining Roman patriarchal basilicas seems to have received its first beginnings under Damasus and to have obtained its completion under Simplicius.

Line 13.—At the same time the Church was first, that is, the executor of the apostolic see. We recognize the character of the barbarous age in the wording of this sentence, which I fear may have been rendered obscure by the copyists’ errors. It seems, however, that it should be restored as follows:

“At the same time the Constantinopolitan Church was the executor of the apostolic see.”

This restoration is made certain by Gelasius’s fourth letter, in which the pontiff mentions that Timothy Aelurus in the Alexandrian patriarchate, Peter Mongus in the Antiochene, and others who had been deposed were removed solely by the authority of the Roman see, while the execution of that authority had been entrusted to Acacius of Constantinople. Gelasius’s words are:

> “In this very matter Timothy the Alexandrian, Peter the Antiochene, Peter, Paul, John, and the others—not merely one but several, certainly bearing the name of the priesthood—were deposed solely by the authority of the apostolic see. Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness of this matter, for he was the executor of this command.”

See Sommier’s notes on the conclusion of the whole history. From them you will understand that the Biographer’s intention was, by compressing the deeds of Simplicius into a brief sentence, to express that the authority of his see, chief of all sees, had been exercised in deposing the bishops of the principal other sees who had fallen from that rank through heresy. Acacius of Constantinople had been selected by him to carry out his command and sentence, although Acacius later sought the primacy, even though he knew that the authority to depose had merely been delegated to him by the primate of the entire episcopate, in whose name he acted.

[Note: [Col. 0378C]]

Line 3.—The Basilica of the blessed Apostle Andrew. This basilica, founded and dedicated by Pope Simplicius, is now seen joined to the church of Saint Antony near Saint Mary Major. It preserves an ornament in vermiculated, or mosaic, work of great elegance, in which an image of Christ, Saint Andrew, and several other apostles may be seen. Some call this same church Saint Andrew *in Barbaris*, because various images of wild beasts are represented on its walls—Diana the huntress and Hippocentaurs—partly in tessellated work made from different marbles and partly in vermiculated work.

[Col. 0378D] Line 7.—A week. Such men were called weekly ministers because, owing to the influx of the people, they customarily succeeded one another in rotation. But these weekly ministers, established for four regions, were seven in number because the other three regions were occupied by the Heruli, who did not in the least communicate with the Catholic Church, since they belonged to the Acacian sect.

[Note: [Col. 0378D]]

Line 15.—He condemned Peter of Alexandria, and so forth. Timothy Aelurus, as we stated in the section on Saint Leo, had invaded the Alexandrian Church while Saint Proterius was still its bishop and had arranged for Saint Proterius to be killed. But in the year 460, at the command of the emperor Leo, he was expelled from that see and sent into exile at Cherson. In his place another Timothy, Salophaciolus, a bishop and defender of the Synod of Chalcedon, had been ordained.

When Basiliscus invaded the empire of the East in 476, however, he began to condemn the Synod of Chalcedon and persecute Catholics. Accordingly, he recalled Timothy Aelurus from exile by an edict. After Timothy had again invaded the Alexandrian Church, Timothy Salophaciolus was compelled to hide in a monastery. To remedy this evil, Simplicius wrote three letters in the year 476: the first to Basiliscus, number 4 in Labbe’s *Collection of the Councils*. In it Simplicius asks the emperor Basiliscus to restrain by royal authority Timothy Aelurus, who had occupied the Alexandrian see and was secretly spreading his heresies from Constantinople.

The heading of this letter was written by the copyist as “To Zeno Augustus,” but the author of Baronius’s critical work shows that it should be read “To Basiliscus Augustus,” dated to the year 476. He also shows that this letter, together with two others—the fifth of Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and the seventh to the priests and archimandrites of Constantinople against Timothy Aelurus—was written not in January but in June.

On the other hand, Peter the Fuller, who had begun to disturb the Church of Antioch in 463, later invaded it. Moved by this audacity, the emperor Leo ordered a synod of bishops to be held in 471. At that synod the Fuller was deposed and condemned, and, by Leo’s command, was deported to the Oasis. In 476, however, he was restored to the Antiochene see by the tyrant Basiliscus, and was again expelled from it in 477.

Holstenius published in the Roman collection a letter of Pope Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, which bears neither day nor consular date. From it we learn that Simplicius, having been informed by Acacius about a synod that Acacius had summoned at Constantinople, asked that the heretics be condemned there. This letter appears in volume 4 of the Councils, page 1039. Thus, in 478, Acacius held a synod at Constantinople and Simplicius one at Rome. Timothy Aelurus, Peter the Fuller, John of Apamea, and Paul, bishop of Ephesus, were condemned at them.

For Felix III, the successor of Pope Simplicius, says in a letter to the Eastern clergy and monks, preserved by Baronius under the year 483, number 52:

> “Those whom the hypocrite Acacius then caused to be condemned by the apostolic see in such a way that even the name of Christians was taken from them, as the acts held before him make clear.”

These words can refer only to synodal acts.

Peter the Fuller was condemned in the Constantinopolitan and Roman synods because he had added this clause to the *trisagion*, the hymn customarily sung in the Church and composed only of the words, “Holy God, holy Strong One, holy Immortal One, have mercy on us”:

> “Who were crucified for us.”

He added it so as to introduce the heresy of the Theopaschites, with which the Fuller was infected, and to attribute suffering to the Triune God, to whom the preceding words referred.

This is established by a letter of Pope Simplicius to Peter the Fuller beginning, “Who will give water to my head,” and so forth. In the collection of the Councils it is wrongly attributed to Felix III; it is number 3. It is also established by another letter to the same Fuller beginning, “Since you are imbued with pestilential doctrines,” and so forth, number 4 among the letters of Felix. These two letters should be restored to Simplicius, as may be seen in Baronius’s critical work.

In these letters Simplicius attacks the Fuller because he had introduced that addition into the *trisagion* prayer. The execution of the sentence by which Peter the Fuller was condemned and deprived of the Antiochene episcopate was entrusted to Acacius, as Pope Gelasius teaches in the frequently cited letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania and in his *Commonitorium* to Faustus. Speaking there of Timothy of Alexandria, Peter the Fuller of Antioch, and other bishops, he says:

> “They were deposed solely by the authority of the apostolic see; Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness of this matter, for he was the executor of this command.”

As stated above, after Peter the Fuller had been removed from his dignity in 477, John of Apamea was ordained bishop of Antioch. After John too had been expelled three months later, Stephen, a distinguished man, was promoted to the episcopate of Antioch. When Stephen died in 481, he was succeeded by Stephen the Younger, as Theophanes writes:

> “The enemies of the faith, arming him with madness for the support of their inclination toward Peter the Fuller, pierced him with sharp reeds in the baptistery of the holy martyr Barlaam, killed him, and threw him into the Orontes River. Zeno, wishing to avenge the attempted crime, ordered Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, to create a bishop for Antioch. Acacius consecrated Calendion.”

Theodorus Lector also explicitly states that Calendion, not Stephen the Younger, was ordained bishop of Antioch at Constantinople. Simplicius, for his part, took grave offense at the killing of Stephen the Younger and at the ordination of Calendion, performed at Constantinople contrary to the rule of the Nicene canons and ancient custom.

Nevertheless, at the request of the emperor Zeno, he granted a dispensation, or pardon for the violation of the canons, on the condition that the consecration of the Antiochene bishop usurped by Acacius should not be made a precedent, and that the canons should be preserved, so that the Antiochene bishop and his election would be reserved to the synod of the Eastern diocese. This is clear from Simplicius’s letters 14 to Zeno and 15 and 16 to Acacius, which the same author of Baronius’s critical work proves to have been written in 482.

From this act of Simplicius the primacy of the Roman pontiff over all bishops is clearly demonstrated, since he dispensed even with the Eastern patriarchs concerning the canons of councils, including ecumenical councils.

When Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, had been expelled from the episcopate by Timothy Aelurus in 476, and Timothy Aelurus had himself been expelled by the emperor Zeno in the following year, Timothy Salophaciolus restored, and the restored Timothy had nevertheless died in that same year, 477, Peter Mongus, or Mongos, Timothy Aelurus’s associate, was ordained bishop of Alexandria by a single heretic.

The emperor Zeno nevertheless ordered that he be deposed and that Timothy Salophaciolus be recalled. But when Timothy died in 481, John Talaia, called by the Greeks *Tabennesiota* because he belonged to the number of the Tabennesiot monks who had lived near Canopus in a monastery since the time of Cyril, was ordained bishop of Alexandria by the Catholics. He immediately sent synodical letters, according to custom, to Pope Simplicius and to Calendion, bishop of Antioch, as is clear from the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* and from Liberatus.

He neglected to send synodical letters to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, either because he trusted in Acacius’s friendship with the master of the offices, or because he had long been hostile to Acacius. This affair deeply disturbed Acacius and embittered the emperor against John.

The emperor first wrote to Pope Simplicius through the subdeacon Uranius. In the letter he judged John unworthy of the priesthood as guilty of perjury, a fact which he claimed was also known to Bishop Acacius. He said that it would be preferable for Peter Mongus to be restored to the Alexandrian see in order to secure unity and concord among the churches of Egypt.

After receiving the emperor’s letter, Pope Simplicius—who had already been prepared to receive John Talaia’s envoys into his communion and to confirm John’s ordination by his own decision—restrained himself, lest he appear to have acted hastily against the emperor’s testimony. Soon afterward, through the same Uranius, he replied to the emperor that, as far as John’s ordination was concerned, he had suspended its confirmation after reading the emperor’s testimony; but as for the restoration of Peter Mongus, he neither could nor ought to restore him, since he was a heretic, sought by heretics, condemned by apostolic judgment, and still persisting in his former error.

These letters of Simplicius have perished. There survives, however, a letter that he wrote at the same time to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, dated on the Ides of July in the consulship of Severinus, and therefore in the year 482. It is number 17 in the collection of the Councils.

The emperor Zeno, disregarding Pope Simplicius’s reply, wrote to Pergamius, governor of Egypt, and to Apollonius, the Augustal prefect:

> “So that John might be expelled from the Alexandrian see, as though he had seized it contrary to his oath, which he had given in the imperial city; that he [the governor] might cooperate with Peter Mongus so that Peter might remain in the see; but that he should not do this before Peter accepted the emperor’s *Henoticon* and sent synodical letters to Acacius of Constantinople, to Simplicius of Rome, and to the other archbishops.”

Liberatus continues:

> “Acacius, when Peter promised to make unity but had not yet fulfilled his promise, permitted his name to be legitimately recited in the diptychs, as though he had already been placed in the apostolic see as bishop of Alexandria.”

John, as we read in the *Brief History of the Eutychianists*, came to Rome and, as was proper, was received by the apostolic see to which he had appealed. While he was at Rome, he persuaded Pope Simplicius to write to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, on his behalf against Peter Mongus. Simplicius did this promptly and willingly.

When Acacius received Simplicius’s letter, he replied that he did not at all recognize John as bishop of Alexandria, but that he had received Peter Mongus into communion at the command of Zeno Augustus. Deeply disturbed by this letter, Simplicius replied that Acacius had acted neither rightly nor procedurally in receiving Peter into communion, since Peter had been condemned by a common judgment.

While John Talaia was preparing to offer Simplicius a document containing various charges against Acacius, Simplicius was overtaken by death before Acacius had replied to his final letters, as Liberatus reports in chapter 18.
