This holy pontiff died on the second day of March in the year 483 and was buried on the same day in the Basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, according to Anastasius, after having sat for fifteen years and six days. This is the reading in one Colbertine manuscript of Anastasius, in catalogues 4 and 5 prefixed to volume 1 of Baronius’s critical work, and in Marianus Scotus.

Line 23.—During the months of December and February, and so forth. Mabillon, in his preliminary commentary on the Roman Order, paragraph 16, made the following observation about Simplicius:

> “The first apostolic men,” says Amalarius in book 2, chapter 1, “always administered ordinations in the month of December, in which the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, until Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth from blessed Peter. He was the first to consecrate in February.”

The *Micrologus* gives the same testimony from the Roman *Pontifical*, by which name it understands the book *On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*. Certainly, among all the pontiffs who performed ordinations up to the end of the ninth century, only Leo II performed ordinations in May, and Gregory the Great performed one in September; after Simplicius, all the others did so either in December or in the first or middle week of Lent. None, so far as is known, did so on Holy Saturday.

“The author of Baronius’s critical work says that Mabillon is correct, except in asserting that Leo II performed an ordination in May. In his pontificate we shall show that Leo performed his ordination in June.”

But after carefully examining this question concerning the time of sacred ordinations, it seems to me that both Amalarius and the most learned men are mistaken when they write that Roman pontiffs always performed ordinations in December until Simplicius. For just as after Gelasius, who first assigned them to the Ember Seasons, Roman pontiffs were not bound by this common rule but ordained deacons, priests, and bishops on any Saturday, as we shall show in the case of Leo II, so before Simplicius they were not bound, because of their sovereign dignity, to perform ordinations in December. Rather, whenever necessity required, they promoted men to sacred orders in other months.

Anastasius indeed records all ordinations performed by Roman pontiffs up to Simplicius as having taken place in December. Yet, as Edmund Martene writes in book 1 of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 8, article 4, number 5, he does not deny that ordinations were also celebrated during the fasts of the other Ember Seasons, either by the pontiffs themselves or by bishops acting on their orders.

This conjecture gains strength [Col. 0382A] from the fact that the Chronicle attributed to Damasus—than which, as has been stated elsewhere, no older monument concerning the duration of the Roman pontiffs survives—explicitly says that Pope Eusebius sat for only four months and sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September. He therefore saw no month of December during his pontificate, yet Anastasius testifies that he performed an ordination in December.

This error of Anastasius does not appear in the Chronicle of the Queen of Sweden, either in Papebroch’s edition in the *Attempt at a Historical Chronicle* or in Schelestratius’s *On the Antiquity of the Church*. In both, Eusebius is said to have performed three ordinations, with no mention of December. It necessarily follows that he performed the ordinations in a month other than December.

The same must be said of Pope Mark, who, according to the same Chronicle of Damasus, sat for eight months and twenty days—from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February until the Nones of October—and therefore could not have conferred sacred orders in December, as Anastasius writes. Hence Baronius, under the year 336, number 61, says:

> “Everything concerning the two ordinations held by Mark in December vanishes.”

Moreover, among the fifty-six pontiffs mentioned in the aforesaid Chronicle of Queen Suecia, fifteen are found whose ordinations may be said to have taken place in a month other than December, although that month is omitted. They are Anacletus, Evaristus, Sixtus, Pontianus, Anterus, Cornelius, Sixtus II, Eusebius, Liberius, Siricius, Anastasius, Sixtus III, Hormisdas, John I, and Felix IV, with whom that Chronicle ends.

Indeed, since that Chronicle contains no mention of ordinations performed by Simplicius, Symmachus, and Felix IV in February, it appears that its author either did not know, or rather deliberately omitted, the times of ordinations performed outside December and therefore outside the common rule. Anastasius, who is believed to have used that Chronicle, may consequently have thought that all ordinations performed by the pontiffs took place in December, because no other month was expressed in the Chronicle and because general ordinations were customarily performed in December according to ancient rules.

The Roman bishops, however, were exempt from these rules. They ordained deacons and priests on any Saturday, and even bishops on any day, including days that were not Sundays. We have an illustrious example of this in Pope Agapitus, who, while staying at Constantinople in the year 536, consecrated Menas as patriarch of Constantinople on the thirteenth day of March, which that year fell on a Thursday.

I submit this conjecture to the examination of learned men, prepared to change my opinion if they judge it unsound. See what will be said concerning Gelasius and Leo II.

[Note: [Col. 0382C]]

Line 10.—Under this bishopric a report arrived from Greece, and so forth. It fell within the period of the pontificate of Simplicius, which displayed grave dangers everywhere, dangers that could not be contemplated without tears. For he saw the empire of the West overthrown, and its last five emperors either murdered or driven from power—namely Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Nepos, and Augustulus. Like actors brought onto a temporary stage and snatched from it in the blink of an eye, they left Italy under the rule of the barbarian and Arian prince Odoacer, king of the Heruli. He also saw the empire of the East handed over to two Augusti infected with heretical pollution or favoring heresies, Basiliscus and Zeno. He likewise saw two Arian kings of the Goths exercising dominion through Gaul and Spain, and tyrannical Vandals of the same sect raging cruelly in Africa. Finally, he saw the abomination of desolation in the holy place, when he observed wicked men occupying patriarchal thrones everywhere: Aelurus and Mongus on the Alexandrian see; Peter the Fuller on the Antiochene see; Gerontius on the Jerusalemite see; and Acacius on the Constantinopolitan see, repeatedly renewing his complaints concerning the patriarchate and his ambition for the second place in the Catholic Church—an ambition attempted by his predecessors through decrees extorted in general councils, which the apostolic see had nevertheless not confirmed.

Acacius attempted, at the very beginning of Simplicius’s election, to extort from him the confirmation denied by Simplicius’s predecessors, relying on the patronage of the emperor Leo. But Simplicius’s steadfastness fully answered the firmness of the Roman see’s bishops, which had been equally maintained from Damasus to Hilary. For, through the words of his legate, he replied to Leo Augustus—as Gelasius reports in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania—that “it could in no way be attempted, nor had he in any respect given his consent to these things; and therefore they should not look to the distinction of any particular city, but should fittingly observe the mode of ecclesiastical administration confirmed by the tradition of the Fathers.”

With the same steadfastness he resisted the letters and laws of Leo Augustus issued at Acacius’s suggestion and inserted in Book 16 of the Code, *On the Holy Churches*. Indeed, with apostolic freedom and authority, Simplicius himself, and afterward his successor Felix III, more than once rebuked the man who attempted such things, as Pope Gelasius says in the passage cited above:

“Pope Simplicius, and after him Pope Felix of holy memory, are known often to have rebuked the emperor Zeno with free authority for these very excesses. He could have been brought to submission, had not the bishops of Constantinople been inflamed by instigation—he who, having become a participant in eternal communion, necessarily continued to foster what had already occurred, preferring to persist in the obstinacy of his transgression rather than return, once healed, to wholesome things, as the outcome of events itself proved.”

Simplicius’s vigilance shone forth as brightly as his steadfastness in settling the affairs of the Eastern patriarchates. Timothy Aelurus, once expelled from the Alexandrian see, was striving to creep back into the same see a second time. To avert this danger from the churches, Simplicius sent to Zeno Augustus a letter worthy of an apostolic bishop, expressing the following judgment:

“Therefore, most glorious and most merciful son, Emperor Augustus, having discharged the duty of greeting you, I must neither remain silent nor can I remain silent concerning the scandals which, it is said, are once again being committed in the churches of the East through the renewed brigandage of heretics.”

After recounting the crimes, he continues:

“These things, Emperor Augustus, although my spirit shudders that they could have been attempted even by so great a gladiator, I confess that I am held in still greater astonishment that they could have been committed under the eyes of your piety . . . For amid all public occupations, a religious prince must take the greatest care of whatever protects his principate, and the rectitude of heavenly observance must be preferred to all other things, without which nothing can stand rightly. Nor should it be thought that what has spread throughout all the provinces of the East from the citadel of your empire is hidden from your conscience—those matters, namely, which directed the counsels of Marcian of august memory, and likewise of Leo, as well as of my predecessor of blessed memory, concerning the Council of Chalcedon . . . For this same apostolic norm of teaching persists in his successors—the norm to which the Lord entrusted the care of the entire flock; to which he promised that he would in no way fail to remain until the end of the age; and against which he promised that the gates of hell would never prevail. Therefore, all the more, in the voice of the blessed apostle Peter, I, whatever minister of his see I may be, adjure you not to allow the enemies of the ancient faith to rage with impunity—those who desire to have your subjects under their control.”  
*Simplicius, Letter 4 to Zeno Augustus.*

To this letter he added another to Acacius and a third to the clergy of Constantinople. In the first, when Aelurus was pressing for a new synod to be held at Chalcedon against the earlier council and against the dogmatic letter of Leo the Great, he writes:

“Since, through the enduring teaching of our predecessors of holy memory—against which it is impious to dispute—whoever appears to think rightly does not need to be instructed by new assertions, but everything is full and complete by which one deceived by heretics may be instructed or one to be planted in the Lord’s vineyard may be formed. Once the faith of the most merciful prince has been invoked, see to it that the proposal to hold a synod is rejected,” and so forth.

In the other letter he laments that the scandal and conflagration already extinguished by the judgment of the universal council and the authority of the Holy See were being rekindled in their assembly:

“After the tradition of so many priests of the Lord, who long before us defeated these heresies throughout every part of the world, our predecessor Leo of blessed memory, in many discourses of instruction, asserted what the integrity of Catholic truth follows and what it rejects. Since this instruction has laid the foundation, there is no need for contention, as though judgment were still to be rendered concerning doubtful matters.”

In another letter to Acacius, who had written to him about whatever the heretics had done at Constantinople and in the provinces and about the remedies that ought to be brought against them, he directs his vigilant attention to bringing to an end the prolonged delay of the Fathers who had assembled at Constantinople, “so that no one uncertain in reasoning and trembling in mind might await the reconsideration of some new thing contrary to their own definitions.”

The manner in which he entrusted Acacius with carrying out the sentence of deposition against Peter the Fuller, Aelurus, Mongus, Paul, and John is evident from Gelasius’s letter to the bishops of Dardania.

The legitimate bishop Timothy Salofaciolus, restored to the Alexandrian Church, came in a solemn embassy to Simplicius. He asked pardon for his earlier error—namely, that, previously terrified, he had recited the name of Dioscorus the Eutychian during the celebration of the sacred rites. He also requested that assistance be given to Aelurus and Mongus, penitents who were offering a written statement of satisfaction, although they had fallen. This was certainly a great and outstanding proof of the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff, before whom the patriarch of the Church’s second see and penitents from his clergy presented themselves suppliantly in order to obtain grace with indulgence.

In the Church of Antioch as well, he did not cease to provide proofs of his authority through the dispensation from observance of the Nicene canon when, through Acacius of Constantinople, a new patriarch of Antioch was chosen in place of Stephen, who had been impiously murdered. He granted this in response to the emperor’s request, taking care that the election should not fall upon a heretical man if it were carried out by the clergy; but he granted it, I say, on the condition that it should not be drawn into an example or a right for those who came afterward, and that subsequent elections to the Eastern patriarchates should thereafter be conducted in the customary manner according to the definitions of the canons.

Nevertheless, the Alexandrian Church was shaken by new disturbances in the election of John Talaia after the death of Salofaciolus. John, as was customary, sent Simplicius a synodical letter concerning his election, so that it might be confirmed. The emperor Zeno, forestalled by John’s enemies, had sent letters against John to Simplicius and had also proposed the restoration of Mongus. This almost stunned Simplicius, and the pontiff delayed his reply to John; but he openly denied Zeno’s request for Mongus’s restoration. Angered by the refusal, the emperor dictated that disastrous *Henotikon* which introduced such a flood of evils into the churches, ordering the prefect of Egypt to ensure that John accept the *Henotikon* and, once it had been accepted, be expelled from his see.

A more recent writer, Natalis Alexander, has vainly attempted to free the *Henotikon* from heresy (*Part* I, century V, chapter 3, and Dissertation 18), since it was always rejected not only because it had been composed by a lay prince who possessed no authority to judge matters of faith, but also because, by suppressing the decisions of Pope Leo and of the sacred Council of Chalcedon, it favored the Eutychian heresy, against which that great pontiff and the ecumenical synod had pronounced.

After accepting the *Henotikon*, Mongus, restored to the Antiochene see by Zeno’s order, wrote to Pope Simplicius that he persisted in the faith of Chalcedon. John, however, expelled by force, first withdrew to Antioch. After conferring with Calendion, the bishop of that see, and being furnished with letters, he fled for refuge to the Roman see as one of the expelled, following the example of Athanasius. Simplicius received John with the honor that was fitting; and, because of letters written by Simplicius to Acacius, John also appeared likely to receive assistance from the emperor.

But Acacius, having followed the party of Mongus and of Zeno’s *Henotikon*, a course for which Simplicius reproached him, first replied arrogantly; then he sent Simplicius a written accusation against Acacius, to be presented to him. This document, however, was delivered to Felix, his successor, since Simplicius had meanwhile been removed from human affairs. What followed will be related in the notes on Felix. In the meantime, Simplicius’s firmness and apostolic vigilance are evident from all his acts.]

[Col. 0361]

## 72

Simplicius, a native of Tibur, son of Castinus, sat for fifteen years and seven days.  
[Note: [Col. 0361] B: five months and ten days, from the consulship of Pusaeus and John to that of Anicius Faustus.]

He dedicated the basilica of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill in the city of Rome; the basilica of blessed Andrew the apostle beside the basilica of Saint Mary; another basilica of Saint Stephen beside the basilica of Saint Lawrence; and another basilica within the City, beside the Licinian Palace, of blessed martyr Bibiana, where her body rests.

He established at Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Paul the Apostle, and Saint Lawrence the Martyr a weekly station, so that priests might remain there on account of penitents and baptism.  
[Note: [Col. 0363] “Weekly stations”: C, B. See Baronius under the year 483.]

The third region was assigned to Saint Lawrence;  
[Note: [Col. 0363] See Baronius under the year 478.]

the first region to Saint Paul; and the sixth, or seventh, region to Saint Peter.

Under his episcopate a report arrived from Greece from Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and it declared Peter of the city of Alexandria a Eutychianist heretic, with a petition having been made and drawn up in Acacius’s own handwriting. At that time the Church was first—that is, the executor of the apostolic see.  
[Note: [Col. 0363] “The Roman Church, that is, the first see, executor of the apostolic see.”]

Then, when Bishop Simplicius, the pontiff, heard this, he condemned Peter of Alexandria because Acacius alleged innumerable crimes against him, yet in such a way as to reserve a period for repentance. At the same time Timothy the Catholic and Acacius sent a reply, saying that Peter had also been involved in the death of Proterius the Catholic. Then Archbishop Simplicius, withholding his response, never replied to Acacius, but condemned Peter while awaiting a time for repentance.

He made in the Roman Church a gold cup weighing five pounds. He also made sixteen silver vessels for blessed Peter the Apostle, each weighing twelve pounds.

He held three ordinations in the city of Rome, in the months of December and February: fifty-nine priests; eleven deacons; and thirty-seven bishops in various places.  
[Note: [Col. 0363] C, B: eight priests.]  
[Note: [Col. 0363] C, B: six bishops.]

He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Nones of March, and the episcopate was vacant for six days.

## L. SAINT FELIX III. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 476, THE TENTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR ZENO, THE EIGHTH YEAR OF KING ODOACER

Line 6.—“Then the venerable Felix, archbishop of the apostolic see of the city of Rome, sent a defensor with the counsel of his see.” Defensores were subdeacons of the Roman Church whom the pontiff employed either to administer the patrimony of the Roman Church, to undertake embassies, or to judge ecclesiastical matters and persons. See canon *Valde necessarium*, Distinction 94; canon *Pervenit*, Question 1; canon *Probinum*; and canon *De praesentium*, Question 1, Distinction 16.

Line 22.—“And after his death, the priests and deacons established the following rule for the whole Church: no one should ever presume to show haste in that matter which must eventually come to examination when it is demanded.” When the Roman see was vacant through the death of Felix, the Roman clergy decreed that no one in the meantime should hasten to examine the matter which would eventually have to be examined when demanded—namely, the case of Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Alexandria, which Felix had begun to address. When the see is vacant, nothing is to be innovated. See chapter *Novit ne sedes vacet*.]

[Note: [Col. 0387B]

The order and sequence of the acts have been disturbed, and matters that certainly belong to Felix are read under Gelasius. Therefore, as with Simplicius, we have judged that Felix’s acts must first be arranged and afterward elucidated, so that everything may readily be explained in such a sequence.

Acts of Felix III supplemented and arranged from Gelasius’s deeds, with additions improperly made there.

*(From the deeds of Gelasius.)* “At that time blessed Felix received John.”

*(From Felix.)* “After three years, a report again arrived from the emperor Zeno that Acacius should return as a penitent. Then Pope Felix sent two bishops, Misenus and Vitalis, so that, if they found Acacius an accomplice of Peter, they might condemn them. When they entered the city of Heraclea, they were corrupted by money given to the aforesaid bishops, so that they would not act according to the command of the apostolic see. When they came to Rome to the apostolic see, at that same time the venerable Pope Felix held a synod, an investigation was conducted, and he found both bishops, Misenus and Vitalis, guilty and corrupted by money; and he excluded Bishops Misenus and Vitalis from communion. Then Bishop Misenus did not conceal that he had been corrupted.”

*(In Felix.)* “Then the venerable Felix, archbishop of the apostolic see of the city of Rome, sent a defensor; after holding a council with his see, he condemned Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Alexandria.”

*(From the deeds of Gelasius.)* “Yet he awaited the satisfaction of the apostolic see according to the humanity of the first see of the Church.”

*(From the same deeds of Gelasius.)* “During his time a report again arrived from Greece, saying that many evils and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius.”

*(Later in the same place.)* “And he sent again and condemned Acacius and Peter perpetually if they did not repent.”

*(In Felix.)* “This occurred in the time of King Odoacer.” And the rest, as it is read in Felix. The fact that the arrangement was made and the sequence of the acts should be assigned intermediate moments will be demonstrated below.

“At that time blessed Felix received John.” Other manuscripts add: “to whom he also granted the second see”—that is, he recognized him as patriarch of the second see—in order thereby also to break Acacius’s ambition, since Acacius was usurping throughout the East the prerogative formerly granted to the Alexandrian see without dissent. Felix further granted him the place among ecclesiastical offices owed to the patriarch of the second see.

This reception ought to be regarded as having been established in a Roman synod, which is mentioned by Evagrius; and we call this the first Roman synod under Felix. Its acts must be briefly described.

## First Roman Synod under Felix

We have assigned this synod to Felix. It is confused with another synod, held in the already advanced first year of the pontificate, 483, at which legates of the apostolic see were chosen to go to Zeno and urge Acacius to adopt better counsels. Because they think the two synods were one and the same, they distort the acts of both. We show that there were two.

We suppose that Felix was created pontiff on 6 March 483 and that the synod was assembled either to celebrate his ordination according to the earlier custom by which an ecclesiastical gathering was assembled on the anniversary day of the pontiffs—as is read in the acts of the Roman synod under Hilary in 465—or that it was the same synod which Simplicius had convened before his death in order to hear John Talaia, the Alexandrian fleeing from his own see because of Mongus’s intrusion. At his arrival, according to Evagrius, John immediately presented written petitions to both Simplicius and Felix, and, by right of appeal, his case was to be examined in a synod by the first see.

The reasons for beginning the synod under Simplicius on account of the Alexandrian Church are evident to us because the author of the brief account of the examination instituted under Simplicius expressly testifies to them. He says that, when the letter of Acacius was read in which John, called Codonatus, bishop of Apamea, had been condemned by Acacius’s own judgment:

“When the aforesaid John, bishop of Alexandria, had read this again, he could not remain silent about the fact that Acacius had condemned that John—namely Codonatus—with Peter, that is, the Fuller, and without a remedy of repentance had caused him to be condemned by the apostolic see; and yet, after so many condemnations, he had sent him to preside over the Church of Tyre.”

From this observation concerning John, two crimes necessarily emerge as having been committed by Acacius during the examination. The first was that he had received into communion the man whom he himself had condemned as a heretic, and indeed together with a decree of the apostolic see, without consulting the apostolic see. The second was that he had given the metropolitan see of Tyre to be governed by him, although this belonged to the rights of the patriarchate of Antioch; and therefore he had usurped the ecclesiastical rights of the provinces.

These matters, as I think, once proved and strengthened by other supporting evidence, which will shortly be discussed, gave Felix the occasion to complete immediately what Simplicius had begun at the start of his pontificate.

This circumstance, already discussed before the second Roman synod, at which the apostolic legation was dispatched, is recalled by this synod when, together with the legates, it writes back to all the priests and archimandrites residing at Constantinople and throughout Bithynia:

“It was also added at that time, while these matters were being examined, that Acacius had caused that John to preside over the Church of Tyre who had been ordained bishop at Apamea by Peter the tyrant of the Antiochene Church, the Fuller.”

The word “at that time” shows that the examination had been instituted before the second synod, at which the legates were selected, and that John had been restored while Peter Mongus had again been condemned by Felix. All these matters were dealt with briefly in this earlier Roman synod, and must be reviewed and weighed together.

The year of its celebration, then, was 483. Those present were either the bishops who had gathered under Simplicius or those who were present for the solemn ordination of the pontiff. There were petitions from the Catholics of both Alexandria and Constantinople. The Alexandrians testified to John’s orthodoxy, his legitimate ordination, and Mongus’s tyranny; the petitions of the Constantinopolitans were directed toward restraining Acacius, whom they loudly proclaimed to be the destroyer of the entire East.

Evagrius testifies to the embassy of the Catholic Alexandrian Church when he writes:

“The letter of the Egyptians concerned not only Peter, but also the fact that John was orthodox and had been ordained as the laws of the Church require; whereas Peter had been appointed by only two bishops infected with the same depravity of error as himself. Finally, it reported that after John’s flight he had inflicted every kind of punishment upon the orthodox. They say that all these matters were made known to Acacius by certain persons who had come to Constantinople, and that Acacius assisted Peter in everything he attempted.”

The Alexandrian legates who followed Mongus are attested by the Alexandrian *apocrisiarii*, who, continuing to defend Mongus as a heretic, came to Constantinople under the emperor Anastasius and presented a written petition to the legates of the apostolic see residing there. Baronius was the first to publish this petition.

In it the followers of the heretic Mongus complained as follows:

“Our Church arranged for legates to be sent to the city of Rome. But there a certain man from our city was found to dissent from the true faith—thus they accuse John Talaia—and to be alienated from it for various reasons. He appeared to have done this so that no opportunity would be offered for receiving the legates. They were not admitted even to the point of a personal greeting and returned without achieving anything.”  
(Volume II of the Councils, p. 953.)

The acts and decrees of this first Roman synod under Felix therefore appear to have been as follows.

First, the case of John and Mongus was examined, and the Alexandrian see was adjudicated to John. In addition, the pontiff declared that this was the second see. This was necessary in order to overthrow what Acacius had extorted from the emperors Zeno and Basiliscus—decrees enacted against the Nicene canons, and especially against Leo the Great and Hilary, in order to restrain ambition.

Thus, in Anastasius’s codex of Freher, according to Fabrottus, the following words were erroneously read under Gelasius, although they belonged to Felix—for under Gelasius Acacius and Mongus had already died:

“At that time John, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, fleeing, came to Rome to the apostolic see. Blessed Felix received him with honor and also granted him the second see.”

Or, rather, Felix recognized and proclaimed him the true and legitimate patriarch of the second see.

Gelasius presupposes that this confirmatory decree had been issued, since in each of his letters he designates John as bishop of the second see. For this reason he writes that John, adorned with this prerogative, was rightly judged by the first see, and he entirely disapproves of Acacius’s ambition in the deposition of John of Alexandria.

He writes to the bishops of Dardania that Felix, in his earlier letters, had admonished Acacius as follows:

“While appealing to him, both by persuasion and by threats, not to cut himself off from the body of Catholic unity, he also urged him—since John, the bishop of the second see, was pressing him with serious accusations—to come or to send someone to the hearing of the first see. Although the synod did not need to be repeated, it would nevertheless be fitting that the bishop of any city should not avoid the judgment of the first see, to which the bishop of the second see had appealed. He could not be heard except by the first see, especially since, their minds having been prejudiced, he had been excluded by the Greeks without any synod, and could neither state nor ought to state his case before them at all. For, being superior to lower bishops, he could be examined only by the first see, as has been said.”

Hence Gelasius said to Faustus, p. 885:

“And the bishop of the city of Constantinople, which certainly received no designation among the sees through the canons.”

Zacharias the rhetorician reports (p. 492) that Felix gave to a certain monk who had brought Acacius’s crimes to Rome a sentence of abdication; Acacius nevertheless did not accept it. Evagrius relates:

“John, who had fled for refuge to Rome, admonished Felix, who became Roman bishop after Simplicius, concerning the deeds of Peter, and urged him, as Zacharias relates, to send Acacius a letter of abdication because he had communicated with Peter. This had been done against the canons of the Church. Certain men who were leading the monastic life in the monastery of those called *ἀκοιμήτοι*—the ‘Sleepless Ones’—brought that letter. Acacius refused to accept it.”  
(Evagrius, Book III, chapter 18.)

These facts were disclosed by Zacharias. Although Evagrius says that Zacharias reported them only from a rumor that had circulated, they nevertheless show that before Felix sent the legation of Vitalis and Misenus he had already been planning something against Acacius. They also show the stratagems and diligence employed to circumvent the apostolic legates before their arrival in the imperial city—matters to be discussed shortly—and reveal that Acacius knew something of Felix’s earlier actions before the apostolic legation.

That John’s case was examined in a synodal judgment is attested by Gelasius, who says of John:

“He could not be accused in a competent judgment, since there were no evident grounds either to convict him beforehand or, afterward, to appeal.”  
(Volume II of the Councils, commentary to Faustus, p. 885.)

Gelasius likewise testifies that the original decree of condemnation against Peter Mongus was confirmed and that a reply was sent to those bishops who had written letters in favor of Peter’s confirmation. He says this in a letter to the emperor Anastasius, who appears to have promoted Peter’s cause:

“If they should perhaps assert that all had reported to the apostolic see, with one harmonious voice, regarding Peter’s reception by Acacius, they themselves acknowledge that through the same man a reply had been given to them with an equal voice.”

That is, in this first Roman synod, when Felix recognized John as the legitimate patriarch, he announced this to Acacius and at the same time declared that Mongus was to be regarded as an intruder and a heretic according to the earlier condemnation.

Gelasius calls the letter by which Felix did this a “preliminary warning.” He testifies in the letter mentioned above to the bishops of Dardania, speaking of Acacius:

“Since he had long proposed not to answer these matters with the silence that was due, an episcopal legation was also sent, and nevertheless a letter was dispatched to warn him that he ought to remember his previous deeds and look back to what he had originally labored for in defense of the Catholic faith.”

By these words the pontiff intended to say that Acacius had not replied to the repeated admonitions of Simplicius and Felix with due silence—as another reading has it—but had rejected them all with contempt. Evagrius, who will shortly be cited, also attests this.

Finally, synodical letters were issued in this council to Zeno and Acacius. Evagrius preserves only their memory. Speaking of Felix’s actions against Acacius before the legation was arranged at the subsequent Roman synod, he writes:

“Furthermore, other letters were written by Felix, both to them—that is, to the monks and others who had reported on the condition of the East—and to Zeno. In these he recalled to them not only the Council of Chalcedon but also the persecution that had been stirred up in Africa under King Theodoric. He also wrote another letter to Acacius.”

This was evidently the preliminary warning mentioned above by Gelasius.

These letters, which have perished and which, as Evagrius testifies, had been bound together in the record-book of Pope Felix’s proceedings in the case of Acacius, must have been different from those which he issued when he held the second synod and sent the legates Vitalis and Misenus, since the surviving letters contain no mention of the persecution.

I therefore think that when Hunneric, already in the year 483, summoned all the bishops of Africa so that at the beginning of the year 484—an event that occurred in February—they might hear his heretical edicts, and when twenty-eight bishops among the others fled, some taking refuge with Felix in Rome, they informed the pontiff of these matters.  
(Volume II of the Councils, p. 877.)

For African bishops are recorded as having been present at the Roman synod under Felix: Victor, Donatus, Rusticus, and Pardalius, Africans.

At the beginning of his pontificate Felix could have taken the opportunity afforded by the synod to warn Zeno because Hunneric was summoning the bishops for the purpose of making them swear that, after the king’s death, they would recognize his son Hilderic as successor—something harmful to the Roman Empire—and, in addition, to swear that they would not send letters across the sea, namely to the apostolic see, as Victor of Vita reports.

The difference between these earlier letters, sent before the legates, which have perished, and the later surviving letters, in which the dispatched legates are mentioned—and the fact that all of them were, according to Evagrius, enclosed among Felix’s Roman acts against Acacius—was the reason why we have transmitted the memory of this earlier synod held under Felix, although others omitted it.

Accordingly, the earlier letters, which have been lost, must be attributed to the first synod under Felix. In them John was recognized as patriarch of Alexandria and bishop of the second see; Mongus was condemned and destined for condemnation; and the Council of Chalcedon was to be retained.

Moreover, by warning Zeno about Hunneric’s tyranny, Felix urged him to rescue the African Churches from that oppression. For Victor himself reports:

“When Hunneric, before the month of June, was already planning to initiate a disputation concerning religion, Saint Eugenius of Carthage first warned the tyrant, saying: ‘He ought also to acknowledge all those from every transmarine region who share our religion or communion.’”

And below:

“I too will write to my brothers, so that my fellow bishops may come and be able to demonstrate to you, together with us, our common faith—and especially the Roman Church, which is the head of all the Churches.”

In the meantime, the king is reported to have replied:

“Make the whole world subject to me, so that the entire world may be brought under my power, and I will do what you say, Eugenius.”

The circumstances of the events suggest that these matters were reported to Felix by Eugenius. It follows clearly that, at the beginning of Felix’s pontificate, the Africans informed him of such miseries, and that Felix informed Zeno of Hunneric’s schemes. For this reason, in that same year, 483, before the edicts were published, Zeno sent legates to the tyrant, as Victor of Vita relates.

Therefore, these petitions of the Africans, reread in this earlier synod, gave Felix occasion to make the emperor specifically aware of the matter in his synodical letter.

For Felix’s letters in which the African persecution is mentioned cannot refer to the second synod held at Rome after the month of June, since before that month the emperor’s legates were already at Carthage, having been sent to restrain the storm that had already arisen against the Catholics.

In contempt of the imperial legate and of the petitions for the mitigation of the persecution, Hunneric ordered the edict to be read before Regino, as Victor says in that passage:

“For on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, with Regino, the legate of the Emperor Zeno, present, he ordered Bishop Eugenius to have the command read in the middle of the Church.”

Three years later a report again came from the emperor Zeno, requesting that Acacius return as a penitent. A rumor was already being spread repeatedly in the East that Acacius wished to submit to the Apostolic See. Hence, under Gelasius, the Acacians accused the Apostolic See of excessive severity, because it had rejected the penitent Acacius. (Volume II of the Councils, p. 886.) To frustrate this slander, Gelasius wrote the following in his memorandum to Faustus:

> “For it is exceedingly shameless that they pretend that Acacius asked pardon and that we proved difficult. Our brother Andromachus is a witness: he was abundantly instructed by us—he speaks in the person of the Apostolic See, since at that time Acacius had already been condemned during the pontificate of Gelasius—to urge Acacius, after laying aside his obstinacy, to come to his senses and return to the fellowship of the Apostolic See. He also testifies under oath that he exerted himself greatly with Acacius, yet could not bend him toward what was right, as the outcome of events proves. Let the judgment certainly be produced: when did he send [a message], when did he ask pardon, and when did he promise us that he would present his correction?—unless, perhaps, he entertained the disposition which we see his successors have had, namely, that, if he asked pardon, he wished it to be granted to him in such a way that he would nevertheless remain in error. In that case he would plainly seem not so much to be received by us as rather to be drawing us over into his power.”

It is nevertheless credible that he pretended to wish to unite himself with the Apostolic See and induced Zeno to write these things to Felix, in order to restrain the zeal of the Catholic monks, who had already written to Felix. Acacius was especially well known from their activities, since, because of their agitation, Basiliscus had first been compelled to revoke the edict already published against the Council of Chalcedon, as was related above from Evagrius (Book III, chapter 7). Indeed, Gelasius himself notes that Acacius had acted throughout in hypocrisy, a point he repeats frequently. Thus, in his treatise *On the Schism*, Gelasius writes (Volume II of the Councils, p. 818):

> “When he had been placed in the dignity of the supreme priesthood—whether unwillingly and against his will, one may doubt, for his fickleness and inconstancy made us doubtful—he pronounced a most truthful judgment against the enemies of God.”

Theophanes explicitly testifies that under Basiliscus Acacius had pretended to stand in defense of the Council of Chalcedon, under the year 477:

> “In this year, while the clergy and monks of Constantinople were contending in a great body on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon, Acacius, terrified, pretended to adopt their opinion and for that reason spoke against Basiliscus and Zeno from the pulpit of the church. When Basiliscus learned of this, fearing the fury of the people, he withdrew from the city . . . For the people were already preparing to lay waste to the city with fire.”

On that occasion the emperor, through Acacius’s machinations, may have announced that Acacius was entirely ready to satisfy the Apostolic See and that harmony among the Churches could easily be restored if Acacius subscribed to Zeno’s *Henotikon*, promulgated through Acacius’s fraud. In it Nestorius and Eutyches were said to be anathematized.

Theodore the Reader assumes that Zeno intended this document for the pope’s approval when he reports the following under the year 518:

> “When all the other patriarchs had consented to Zeno’s *Henotikon*, Felix, bishop of the city of Rome, alone refused to communicate with it.”

If he refused, then it had been offered by Zeno at no other time than when he reported Acacius’s feigned repentance to Felix—indeed, when he had heard of Felix’s election and requested legates to restore peace in the East and among the Churches, so that he might more easily induce the pope to adopt his intended measures. . . .

Moreover, the three years are to be counted from John’s flight and the intrusion of Mongus up to the second Roman synod. During that period Acacius began to grow obstinate and to make light of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Just as a rumor of repentance and reception by the pontiff was circulated concerning Acacius, so at the same time a similar rumor was circulated concerning Peter Mongus, as the same Gelasius teaches somewhat later (ibid., p. 918):

> “But it is said of Peter—although it is said without approval, especially concerning a man of the greatest intelligence, who for thirty years had been a notorious champion against the truth—that he was received into the Church after performing penance. Could he, then, have performed penance for thirty years, unless it was at that time when he was burning with love of the episcopate and with the fervor of ambition?” etc.

Then Pope Felix sent two bishops.

The word “then” indicates that there was an immediate motivating cause by which the pontiff, responding to the emperor’s requests and promises concerning the establishment of peace, chose bishops to act as legates. Gelasius’s words in the frequently cited letter to the bishops of Dardania (p. 907) assume that this request, together with the promise given concerning the legates’ safety, was made both by Acacius and by the emperor:

> “But Acacius not only refused to satisfy the requests; he also deceived the very embassy of the Apostolic See with blandishments, rewards, and perjuries, by which he promised it, together with the emperor, that the case of the Apostolic Bishop would be fully preserved in every respect.”

We therefore regard this request of the emperor, together with Acacius’s case and the circumstances that occasioned it, as the cause of the following synod, which we now undertake to examine.

## The Second Roman Synod under Felix in the Case of Acacius

The occasion of this synod was provided by further reports from John Talaia arriving from the East; by Zeno’s letters concerning the repentance of Acacius and Peter, and concerning the request for legates; by the promise of immunity for the pontifical legates; and by the hope of future concord among all the Churches.

For the author of the brief account writes:

> “After holy Pope Felix learned that not only had the letters of his predecessor accomplished nothing, but that certain mockeries were being perpetrated by Acacius for the overthrow of the entire ecclesiastical discipline, having chosen Vitale,” etc.

I believe that these “mockeries” were nothing other than pretended acts of repentance, satisfactions, and similar devices. Acacius carried them all out in hypocrisy, directing them toward the advancement of other wicked plans.

The synod was celebrated in the year 483, and indeed toward the end of that year. This is suggested by the complaint of the monk Cyril, who accused the pontiff of delay, according to Evagrius (Book III, chapter 19):

> “But before Vitalis and Misenus came to the emperor, Cyril, who presided over the monks called *Acoemeti* [ἀκοίμητοι, ‘the sleepless’], sent to Felix to accuse him of delay, although such grave offenses against the true faith had been committed.”

Cyril’s observation of the pontiff’s delay—he had been elected on 6 March of that same year—clearly shows that the synodal proceedings were prolonged until the year was already advancing.

The solemnity of the council is demonstrated by the selection of two bishops representing the judgment of the Western Church, together with Felix the deacon representing the Apostolic See. Nevertheless, they were to act first in their collective capacity and then as representatives of the pontiff. For this custom is repeatedly attested both in general councils and in more urgent affairs.

The brief account preserves the episcopal sees of the legates. After the words cited above, it says:

> “Vitalis, bishop of Truentum from the region of Picenum, and Misenus, bishop of the Church of Cumae from the region of Campania, were chosen.”

The summons also praises the office of the episcopal legates and explains the role of Felix the deacon in these words (Volume II of the Councils, p. 830):

> “For this purpose we have sent from our college our brothers and fellow bishops, Vitalis and Misenus, together with our most faithful Felix the Defender of the holy Roman Church, whom we have sent from our side by the ordination of the Apostolic See.”

Thus the bishops represented the college, or the consensus of the Westerners, while Felix represented the ordination of the Roman Church.

The brief account states the legates’ instructions as follows:

> “Under this commission he sent them so that Peter might be expelled from the Church of Alexandria, so that Acacius might answer the libel of holy John, bishop of Alexandria, and so that he might anathematize Peter.”

Evagrius gives the same account in chapter 18. In the preceding chapter he had said:

> “Felix therefore wrote to Misenus that he should undertake nothing before he had conferred with Cyril and learned from him what ought to be done.”

(*Chronicle*, p. 113.)

The synod was held in the Church of Saint Peter, according to Theophanes:

> “Accordingly, Felix, having convened a synod in the temple of the chief of the apostles, sent two bishops and, together with them, a Defender to Constantinople, and informed Zeno and Acacius by letter that they should expel Peter Mongus from Alexandria as a heretic.”

The same temple of Saint Peter is assigned as the place where the purification, or formal hearing, was to take place in the summons (ibid., p. 829). The legates carried the summons to Acacius, together with letters to Zeno and Acacius.

### When they had entered the city of Heraclea

Perhaps the pontiff had decided that Acacius’s case should be examined in the East according to the canons, and therefore ordered it to be conducted in Heraclea, the chief city of Thrace, to which the Church of Constantinople was subordinate.

Acacius, therefore, in order to avoid such a danger—and to avoid losing among the people what he had promoted through such great arts, with the assistance of Zeno and Basiliscus, namely, that the see of Constantinople should be declared the second see, to which the Church of Heraclea itself was subordinated by an extorted privilege—wished to corrupt the episcopal legates there. This indeed happened, since the *Liber Pontificalis* adds that they were corrupted by money and that, by forestalling the judgment, he overturned the entire proceeding.

Thus the legates remained at Heraclea only long enough to be diverted by money from holding the trial; they then went to Constantinople. In that city Acacius kept them under close guard in his house, so that they could not deliver the pontifical and synodal letters to the Catholics.

That Felix certainly wished, in accordance with the regulations of Leo and Hilary, to restrain Acacius’s ambition and restore the primatial rights of Heraclea over Constantinople is clear from the sentence of excommunication pronounced against Acacius in the third Roman synod. In listing his crimes, it states at the very beginning of the sentence (Volume II of the Councils, p. 831):

> “You are found liable for many transgressions, and you have often shown contempt for the venerable Council of Nicaea; you have rashly claimed for yourself the rights of other provinces.”

This refers especially to what the Council of Nicaea decreed in canon 6 concerning the division of provinces and the preservation of the rights of the primates, among which, at the time of the Council of Nicaea, was the exarchate of Heraclea.

Hence the sentence continues:

### And they did not act according to the instruction of the Apostolic See

It is well known that, when the Apostolic See selected legates to carry out a commission, it customarily gave them personal memoranda in addition to the common letters directed to the assembly, as will be noted below in the case of Hormisdas.

Among other instructions, the legates charged with handling the Acacian case had been ordered to hold a meeting at Heraclea and to confer on all matters with Cyril, the head of the Acoemeti and defender of the Catholic faith.

But just as, after being corrupted by money, they did nothing about the first instruction, so, when they went to Constantinople, they conducted everything according to Acacius’s wishes.

Meanwhile they went to church with Acacius and Peter’s *apocrisarii*, or representatives, and did not fear taking part in the solemn celebration of the Mass, although the orthodox protested—especially the monks—and repeatedly declared, the first, second, and third time, that this was a betrayal and the outright destruction of the faith.

First, they tied a protestation written on a small strip of parchment to a hook and hung it on one of the legates. Second, they inserted one into a book. Third, they placed another in a basket of vegetables and sent it to the legates.

Theophanes relates the matter as follows (p. 114):

> “He softened the apocrisarii of Felix, the Roman pontiff, with blandishments and enticed them with money, bringing them into communion with Peter contrary to the law of the instructions imposed upon them, while all the Catholic parties protested and objected. First, they tied a hook with cords around it and publicly hung it on one of them; second, they inserted a book; third, they even placed it in a basket of vegetables.”

Liberatus writes in his *Breviary*:

> “They went to Constantinople, and the aforementioned bishops were placed under guard, their papers having been taken away so that they could not be returned to the Catholics to whom they had been written. Later Acacius brought them out of custody and made them proceed with him, so that they might be dismissed as though Peter’s priesthood had been confirmed.”

For Acacius avoided the meeting at Heraclea, lest, if he were condemned by the judgment of the Eastern Catholics, he should utterly collapse. Since many bishops in the East adhered to the schism, it was enough for him to entice two Western legates, who represented the opinion of the rest, so that he might show his followers that both he and Peter had been received into communion with the approval of all the bishops of the entire world.

Hence, when Acacius was condemned in the following Roman synod, the Acacians blamed it on the fact that the action had not been taken after an examination by both parts of the world. Gelasius refutes this in his letter to the Eastern bishops, where he writes (Volume II of the Councils, p. 924):

> “Do they grieve over Acacius because he was not refuted in a special synod?”

That is, in a synod where both parties had assembled and, after examination and voting, had published a judgment.

A hearing and conciliar examination were not required after three admonitions, or summonses, had been issued by the Apostolic See, since personal letters existed in which the crime, the confession of the crime, and the contumacy were all made known.

Gelasius continues:

> “When he himself had disclosed his own crime in his letters, and after voluntarily confessing he ought no longer to have been heard, do they not grieve that so many Catholic pontiffs were excluded without any examination?”

The pontiff proceeds from a fundamental principle: since the Alexandrian patriarch, by virtue of the privilege of the second see, could not be examined except by the first see. He writes (ibid., p. 922):

> “For since Acacius was supported by no privilege—namely, one arising from the law of the canons by which, as holder of the second see, he could pronounce judgment—he could not lawfully condemn anyone. Likewise, unless he had received authority from the first see, he had neither the right to examine Peter nor the full power to receive him.”

It follows that Felix most properly established, on the basis of the supreme authority of the canons, that a meeting should be held at Heraclea to examine the Acacian case. Acacius forestalled the judgment and, after the legates had been corrupted with money, drew them away from Heraclea to Constantinople and enticed them into his wickedness.

That letter should be read in which this observation of ours is more firmly illustrated, together with a full account of Acacius’s machinations to claim primacy for himself in the East—not merely to govern three exarchates, but even to overturn the rights of the remaining patriarchs at will.

### When they came to Rome

Before the legates’ arrival in the City, reports from the monks had preceded them. The monks had informed the pontiff of the legates’ misconduct.

“Eventually the legates return; but the monks had preceded them and were gravely accusing them of betrayal,” says Liberatus in chapter 21.

What happened to Felix the Defender is explained by the same pontiff in the sentence of excommunication pronounced against Acacius. Because illness had forced him to follow later, he was received so insultingly by Acacius that Acacius did not even tolerate admitting him into his presence (Volume II of the Councils, p. 832):

> “You also judged Felix the Defender, our most faithful servant, unworthy of your eyes because necessity caused him to follow later.”

Liberatus adds that he was thrown into prison and that his papers were taken from him because he refused, as the fallen legates had done, to communicate with Peter Mongus.

## Pope Felix held a synod

It has already been demonstrated from the completed and restored acts of Felix that Felix held three synods in the Acacian case. We must now discuss this synod, in which Acacius was condemned.

According to the established order, the three summonses that the Church customarily issued before a condemnation can easily be understood and identified.

The first occurred at the first Roman synod, when letters were sent to Zeno and Acacius, according to Evagrius; these letters have perished.

The second was delivered through Misenus and Vitalis. It begins as follows (ibid., p. 829):

> “Sent with episcopal diligence and admonition, together with Zeno’s letter,”

which survives among the acts of the councils. To this must be added the other letters sent through the same legates to Acacius and Zeno (ibid., pp. 811 and 814).

At the end of the letter to Acacius, Felix again orders that an admonition be sent, just as he says that he had repeatedly urged him with increasingly forceful exhortations.

Liberatus recalls the third admonition in chapter 18:

> “Eventually the legates return, but the monks had preceded them. They were heard face to face and, convicted by the very letters they had brought, were removed from their offices.”

The legates therefore brought Zeno’s and Acacius’s letters, and by those letters they were convicted of betrayal.

Liberatus clearly shows shortly afterward that the pontiff replied to the letters and issued a third admonition:

> “When Acacius had therefore been fully exposed as a heretic, Pope Felix wrote the following in his synodal letters to Acacius: ‘You have sinned; do not add to it, and plead concerning your former offenses.’ After receiving this letter, Acacius persisted, neither withdrawing from communion with Peter nor openly urging him to accept the Council of Chalcedon and the *Tome* of Pope Leo.”

I therefore conclude that the letter of Acacius brought by the legates was nothing other than praise of Peter Mongus because he had subscribed to Zeno’s *Henotikon*. In that document the heretic Eutyches is anathematized, but there is a profound silence concerning Chalcedon and the dogmatic *Tome* of Saint Leo.

This is suggested by Liberatus’s words:

> “Nor did he openly persuade Mongus to accept the Council of Chalcedon and the *Tome* of Pope Leo.”

That these Acacian letters, given to the legates on their return to Rome, dealt with the matter indicated is clearly shown by the words of Gelasius. After describing this embassy, Acacius’s machinations, and the fall of the legates, he adds in his letter to the bishops of Dardania (p. 907):

> “Nevertheless, Acacius had indicated in his letters both that he had fallen back into communion with Peter of Alexandria and that he was presenting, in his own words, an accusation against John and praises of Peter. If he was confident in these matters, he ought rather to have come or sent someone, so that he could refute John, who was present, concerning the lies he uttered, and reasonably defend the praises of Peter that he had set forth.”

In the sentence against Acacius, Felix likewise says of Peter and his crimes:

> “Nor have you ceased to praise him and to exalt him with many commendations, so that you even asserted that his condemnation, which you had previously reported, was not true.”

Gelasius then infers from the order preserved in these prior admonitions that the sentence against Acacius, who despised them and remained contumacious, had been most justly pronounced.

The third admonition, which began according to Liberatus, “You have sinned; do not add to it, and plead concerning your former offenses,” and which is considered lost, was communicated to Acacius through the Acoemete monks, as I believe. In this Acacian case they had energetically undertaken the defense of the Apostolic See.

The order preserved by Liberatus proves that this was the final admonition, since he immediately adds:

> “When Pope Felix learned this, he sent the document of condemnation through Totus [more correctly, Tutus] the Defender, whose opening is: ‘You are found liable for many transgressions.’”

This was done in the Roman synod, whose ordered sequence, according to the supplement to Felix’s acts, must now be briefly explained.

## The Third Roman Synod under Felix in the Case of Acacius

The occasion of the synod, the fathers, the date, and the proceedings must be reviewed, and finally the sentence pronounced against the fallen legates and Acacius.

The arrival of the legates was the first occasion for Felix to convene a council. Reports from the monks concerning their fall had preceded them, according to Evagrius (Book III, chapter 20):

> “Those who came to Felix from the monastery of the monks called *Acoemeti* accused Misenus and Vitalis for this reason: until their arrival at Constantinople, Peter’s name had customarily been read quietly and secretly in the sacred registers; from that time until the present, however, both Misenus and Vitalis had communicated openly and publicly with Peter.”

In the basilica of Saint Peter, in the year 484, sixty-seven bishops assembled with the pontiff, as Felix’s letter to Acacius states at its conclusion, where Acacius is excommunicated (Volume II of the Councils, p. 832).

First, the emperor’s and Acacius’s letters were presented by the legates. Evagrius gives a fragment of Zeno’s letter in these words (ibid.):

> “You must know for certain that both our Piety and the most holy Peter, of whom it has been spoken, and all the holy Churches embrace and venerate the holy Council of Chalcedon. That council agrees in faith with the Council of Nicaea.”

Acacius’s letters, however, were full of insults against John Talaia and contained praises and commendations of Mongus, as Gelasius reported above.

Next, the letters of the Acoemete monks and of the monk Cyril were introduced. As witnesses to the proceedings in the imperial city, they testified before the synod against the fallen legates, according to Evagrius’s account (chapter 21):

> “These matters were further strengthened by the testimony of the monk Simeon, who belonged to the number of those called *Acoemeti* and had been sent by Cyril to Felix. For Misenus and Vitalis had been rebuked by him because they had communicated with heretics, while Peter’s name, like that of a heretic, was publicly recited in the sacred registers. By this means many simple people were led into error by the heretics, who did not hesitate to assert that Peter had been received into communion by the Roman bishop.
>
> “Simeon also added that, when certain questions were put to him, Misenus and his supporters had refused to allow any orthodox person to come to conference, to deliver letters, or carefully to examine anything that had been done against the true and sincere faith.
>
> “The presbyter Sylvanus was also brought forward. He had been in Constantinople together with Misenus and Vitalis, and he confirmed the monks’ statements.”

Next Acacius’s letters to Simplicius were produced. In them he had declared and reported to the pontiff that Mongus had been pronounced a heretic:

> “Furthermore, Acacius’s letter to Simplicius was read. It stated that Peter had long before been deposed and declared a son of darkness.”

From this denunciatory letter of Acacius, which was directed to Simplicius and thereby confirmed by him, the bishops of the entire world were to regard Mongus as a heretic. The fathers of this synod, and later Gelasius, drew their arguments from it as a most powerful weapon for pronouncing the sentence of excommunication.

“Behold,” says Gelasius, citing Acacius’s letter (Volume II of the Councils, *On the Schism*, p. 918), “the most powerful testimony of Acacius concerning what he thought about Timothy and about Peter.”

Then, after the examination had been conducted, the first decree was issued, as the *Liber Pontificalis* states. In the public council Misenus confessed that he had accepted money, and a sentence of deposition was pronounced against him.

Evagrius relates it as follows:

> “For these reasons Misenus and Vitalis were removed from the rank of the priesthood and separated from the holy and pure communion, by the judgment of the entire council.”

The case of Peter Mongus and of Acacius was carefully examined, and the proven crimes were individually listed in the sentence of excommunication sent against Acacius (ibid., p. 831).

The council issued a decree distinct from the sentence against Acacius, fragments of which Evagrius preserves. The council pronounced the following:

> “Peter, a heretic, long ago condemned by the judgment of the Holy Apostolic See, prohibited from the Church, and struck with anathema, is not received by the Roman Church. Even if no other crime were charged against him, this would certainly have sufficient weight: he cannot preside over the orthodox because he was ordained by heretics.”

Concerning Acacius, another fragment of this synod states:

> “The same judgment of the council also included the following: the very facts have shown that Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, is worthy of the gravest crime. For although he wrote a letter to Simplicius and called Peter a heretic, he nevertheless failed to disclose the same thing to Zeno, when certainly, if he loved Zeno, he ought to have done so. But it is more expedient to satisfy the emperor’s desire than to care for the faith.”

Among the many letters sent to Simplicius, the acts of this council report that one was examined in which Acacius denounced Peter Mongus as a son of darkness and as anathematized.

This matter was examined specifically because the letter, as a denunciation protected by the subscriptions of bishops according to the accepted custom, made Acacius’s former opinion of Mongus fully established.

In the letters given to the legates, however, Acacius not only praised Mongus but also “exalted him with many commendations, so that he even asserted that his condemnation, which he had previously reported, was not true,” as Felix reproaches him in the sentence of condemnation.

Gelasius says the same in his letters to the Easterners and to the bishops of Dardania.

These were the proceedings and the careful examination of this most celebrated council.

## Then the venerable Felix . . . sending the Defender

This was Tutus, as was stated above from Liberatus.

When the text adds “with the council of your see,” it means that, after the council had been held, it condemned Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Alexandria.

The sentence must be understood in this way, lest the selection of the person who was to deliver the sentence be exposed and subjected to the frauds of the Acacians. The appointment was not made by the entire council, but by a selection of certain advisers of the Apostolic See, who secretly sent Tutus to the city of Constantinople.

The subsequent words refer to the synodal sentence of the council, by which Acacius and Peter Mongus were announced throughout the Churches as excommunicated through the sending of encyclical letters.

That Tutus’s selection was made secretly is shown by Gelasius’s words in his letter to the bishops of Dardania (p. 915):

> “Although this sentence, directed against Acacius, is shown to have been issued in the name only of the Apostolic Bishop, whose legitimate authority it certainly was, it appeared especially necessary that it be sent secretly, lest, with guards everywhere being set out, a salutary disposition should be obstructed by various difficulties and fail to achieve the necessary effect.”

Liberatus explains what Tutus did after the words cited above:

> “After letters of this kind had been given to Acacius, he did not receive them, relying on the emperor’s protection. Thus those who brought them were forced, through a certain Acoemete monk, to hang the very document of condemnation on his cloak as he was entering to celebrate the sacred rites, and then depart.”

## Nevertheless awaiting the satisfaction of the Apostolic See

Just as in the third summons Felix had admonished Acacius to plead with the Apostolic See, so, when he sent the sentence of deposition, he left room for a plea if Acacius should satisfy the offended Apostolic See.

Gelasius repeatedly mentions that this was done in his letters. The Acacians claimed that the matter ought to be remitted to them without any prior satisfaction, a claim which Gelasius reproaches in his memorandum to Faustus (ibid., p. 884).

Euphemius, who had formerly adhered to the Acacian schism, likewise argued that he ought to be received, as Gelasius writes to Euphemius himself (p. 883).

The sentence, therefore, was not like the one Acacius had pronounced against Peter of Alexandria, whom Acacius had reported to Simplicius as condemned and never to be received as bishop of Alexandria: it was the condemnation of the second death, with which those said to have relapsed deserved to be punished for the gravest crimes.

Acacius too was later punished with this penalty in the fourth Roman synod, which must now be discussed.

## During this period a further report again came from Greece

After the condemnation of Acacius by Felix and the Roman synod, further crimes were committed. These gave the Catholic monks occasion to report the fall of Tutus, the raging of Acacius, his persecution of all the orthodox, and—what was most serious—the restoration of Peter Cuaphaeus, called the Fuller, to the Church of Antioch.

Acacius himself had condemned Peter together with Simplicius: Simplicius had condemned him in the Roman synod, and Acacius in the Constantinopolitan synod. Pagius proves this with compelling arguments in his critical notes on Baronius under the year 478, paragraph 4 and following.

The *Liber Pontificalis* presupposes this restoration of the impious heretic and merely records the report and the renewed sentence of condemnation against Acacius and the Fuller.

Gelasius discusses the deposition of Calendion and the fraudulent intrusion of the Fuller, as well as Acacius’s ambition, on the basis of the report of the Eastern orthodox to the Apostolic See. In his letter to the Easterners he examines Calendion’s tragedy, revisits the Acacian case, and responds to the objections circulated by the Acacian Eastern bishops, who misrepresented the sentence of excommunication pronounced against Acacius.

Thus, speaking of Calendion’s removal and the evils promoted by Acacius after it, he adds (p. 926):

> “What the report of the Catholic priests and of the others who remain in the Catholic faith contains cannot be hidden from the conscience of the entire East.”

## Because many evils and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius

It is clear that the report speaks of Peter the Fuller, because these evils occurred after Acacius’s condemnation. Gelasius especially laments the evils promoted through the Fuller in the passage cited above, where he presents to the Easterners the tragedy carried out by Acacius and Peter the Fuller (p. 921):

> “Indeed, if the same case is investigated more broadly, such a great tragedy and such great errors are found there . . . For it is openly and clearly shown there that nothing else was sought except a means by which, after any Catholic bishop had been driven out, access might be granted to the heretic Peter [of Antioch] . . . Heretics were being substituted, and no one resisted . . . What of the countless Catholic priests throughout the East who were driven from their own sees and whose places were unquestionably given to heretics?”

Theophanes likewise writes in his *Chronicle*:

> “Peter the Fuller, having entered Antioch, perpetrated many unspeakable acts: the execrations of the synod, the removal of bishops, the intrusion of guilty men, and unlawful ordinations.”

More must be noted below concerning Acacius and the crimes committed after his condemnation, when the sentence of the fourth Roman synod is related.

Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that Peter is mentioned without qualification. Gelasius does the same: when he lists both Peters together, he calls the first Peter of Alexandria, whereas he almost always refers to the Fuller by the name alone.

Indeed, after this *Liber Pontificalis* had earlier stated that the condemnation of Mongus was confirmed, it added “the Alexandrian” in order to indicate that what had been narrated concerning Peter up to that point belonged to Mongus, whereas what followed concerned the Fuller, who was distinguished by the name Peter alone.

Since there are disputes among the more learned concerning this condemnation, the date of the Fuller’s condemnation, and the synods that were held, and since we wish the order of Felix and his proceedings to be understood, the matter of this synod must be reconsidered here, so that the authority of the *Liber Pontificalis* may also show that this was the preserved order of the synods under Felix.

## The Fourth Roman Synod under Felix against the Fuller and Acacius, condemned with the sentence of the second death
After the Constantinopolitan and Roman synods, in the year 477, Fullo was driven from the Antiochene patriarchate and lived in exile away from the see until Calendion. When rumors had spread and, perceiving an opportune moment in the Acacian affair for the plans he had conceived, he joined Acacius; with Zeno’s approval, he seized the see after Calendion had been sent into exile. Theophanes describes the matter thus (in the *Chronicle*):

> “The emperor Zeno, freed from the tyrants who were oppressing him, expelled Calendion the Antiochene from the Church and banished him to Oasis, and restored Peter Fullo to the see.”

Evagrius asserts that a charge was imposed upon Calendion and that he was accused of treason, where he discusses Calendion (Book III, chapter 16):

> “He was afterward condemned to inhabit Oasis because he supported against Zeno the party of Illus, Leontius, and Pamprepius. But Peter, surnamed Cnapheus . . . recovered his own see; [Col. 0399B] and he subscribed a letter to Zeno concerning concord, and wrote synodical letters to Peter Mongus, bishop of Alexandria. Acacius, likewise bishop of Constantinople, was reconciled to this Peter.”

What Illus, Leontius, and Pamprepius were doing against Zeno may be seen in the same author, chapter 27, and in Jordanes, Book I, *On the Succession of Kingdoms and Times*. Having escaped this danger, Illus soon withdrew toward the city; hostile to Zeno, he invaded the East.

> “Against him Leontius was sent. Enticed by flattering words, he seized the diadem; and at the same time Leontius and Illus, having become enemies of the state and tyrants, were raging through parts of Syria and Isauria . . . but not long afterward they were captured and beheaded by Zeno’s army.”

The author of the *Brief History* notes that the restoration was arranged by Acacius. After recounting Acacius’s condemnation, he adds:

> “In his audacity, committing still worse deeds, he also sent Peter the Antiochene to the Antiochene Church, after expelling Calendion, whom he himself [Acacius] had ordained.”

[Col. 0399C] Thus Zeno, freed from those whose military influence was more favorably disposed toward imperial authority, laid aside his mask and allowed the Eutychians to rage against the Council of Chalcedon; and as long as he lived, he fostered the Acacian schism. Under Justinian’s rule, and afterward on many occasions, emperors who served the interests of the moment supported that religious party toward which the soldiers were more favorably inclined. Justinian did the same with the empress Theodora, as Procopius observes in his *Secret History*.

Gelasius appears to assert in his letter to the bishops of Dardania that Calendion had erased the name of the emperor Zeno from the sacred diptychs because he was showing excessive indulgence toward the Eutychians:

> “But let it be granted that Calendion removed the emperor’s name . . . Were those who were said to have sinned against the emperor, without any synod intervening, to have been deposed?”

How the matter was conducted is unknown. It is certain, however, that three utterly depraved patriarchs in the East sounded the trumpet against the Catholic religion, although in different spirits. The defection of Tutus also inflamed the pontiff’s mind; Tutus eventually yielded to gifts [Col. 0399D] and betrayed the legation, as we shall see when the acts are reviewed.

The synod was held in the year 485, not 484, as some have maintained after Baronius. The consuls’ names and the date clearly show that this synod was distinct from the third, whose acts were examined above, and that it belonged to a different year. The third synod was held to pronounce sentence against Acacius and to confirm Mongus’s condemnation; the present synod was held to drive Fullo from the Antiochene see, which he had invaded. This could not have happened until after Acacius’s condemnation, as the authors cited above assert, and after Tutus’s defection. Acacius’s condemnation bears this date:

> “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Venantius, a man of illustrious rank.”

The consulship of Venantius coincides with the year 484. The synodical letter of the present council likewise bears the date “the third day before the Nones of October, in the consulship of Symmachus, a man of illustrious rank.” Symmachus’s consulship belongs in the official lists to the year 485. It is therefore entirely certain that the synods must be distinguished by year.

The second reason is that sixty-seven bishops were present with Felix at the third synod, [Col. 0400A] whereas only forty-two are listed at the present one. The third reason is that the earlier synod dealt only with Mongus and Acacius; nothing was contemplated concerning Fullo, who had already been deposed and was also living in exile by arrangement of the Constantinopolitan synod and the Roman synod of 477.

At the present synod Acacius and Peter Mongus are presumed to have been condemned, and a sentence of condemnation is again pronounced against Fullo. Thus the bishop of Tibur and others subscribed similarly (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 856):

> “I, Candidus, bishop of the city of Tibur, following the authority of the apostolic see and the Catholic deliberation pronounced by us in accordance with the condition of the Church, have subscribed, declaring anathema against Peter, the usurper of the Alexandrian Church; against Acacius, formerly of the Church of Constantinople; and also against Peter the Antiochene, who long ago were justly and deservedly separated from the episcopate and from the number of Christians, together with all their followers.”

There are other considerations of the same carefully weighed kind, which show that this synod was distinct and was held in a different year. These matters can be further confirmed from the acts of the council.

[Col. 0400B] The acts of this synod were as follows. It was held in the church of Saint Peter, and forty-two bishops were present with Felix, as is stated in the synodical letter addressed to the Eastern clergy and monks, in which the acts are briefly reviewed (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 854).

First, the synodical acts previously issued against Vitalis and Misenus were read, and they declared that the two had been punished by deposition for their betrayal.
