They briefly described the legates’ betrayal: how they had conducted themselves with Acacius and what evil had arisen in the East from the fall of the legates. They asserted that the legates had therefore rightly been condemned and that they continued under the deposition already published.

Second, they declared that Acacius, already condemned and now insulting Catholics with new and more stubborn crimes, remained under the earlier sentence of condemnation:

> “We have judged Acacius, who more perniciously thirsts for the members of Christ and disperses throughout cities and provinces the one Church of the Catholic faith, not to be numbered among the holy bishops or among Christians.”

Third, since Zeno was promoting [Col. 0400C] the *Henoticon* and, because Fullo had subscribed to it, had restored him to the Antiochene see, the synod accordingly prescribed the formula they followed:

> “And so that your Charity may recognize that we hold the venerable synods of Nicaea, the First of Ephesus, and Chalcedon against Nestorius and the most impious Eutyches.”

The copyist omitted the formula of the Roman Church. Yet it was necessary that it be sent, so that the pontiff might oppose Zeno’s *Henoticon*, which was being imposed throughout the East as though it were the one formula to be subscribed by all.

Fourth, they testify that together with the acts they were sending the sentence of condemnation beginning, “Of many transgressions,” which had already been sent through Tutus in the preceding year. At the same time they respond to the Acacians’ objections. Their first objection was that the sentence ought not to have been delivered through Tutus, but through bishops who jointly represented the apostolic see and demonstrated the judgment of the Westerners. They made this objection in order to weaken the sentence, as though it had been published by an illegitimate procedure.

[Col. 0400D] They therefore assert that they are sending again the sentence which they had sent through Tutus. They had not decided that either that sentence or the present sentence against Acacius and both Peters should be delivered through bishops, since the Acacians’ plots prevented an easy and safe passage:

> “After that sentence which was pronounced against Acacius, the disturber of the entire Eastern Church, now also, with these men gathered together, we add [or: have added] by letter the sentence previously mentioned, which it pleased us to send through Tutus, defender of the Church, to Acacius, lest some, wishing to circumvent the truth, should deceive even the simpler-minded with their most malicious flatteries. For if snares had not been laid against the orthodox by land and sea, many of us could have come with that same sentence against Acacius.”

Thus they overturn the Acacians’ first objection. The meaning is not, as some incorrectly assert, that this synod again sent Tutus; rather, Tutus’s name is attached as a distinguishing reference to the pontifical sentence against Acacius, which Tutus had delivered [Col. 0401A] and which had already been fastened to Acacius’s garment by a monk, as Theophanes and Liberatus testify in the passages cited.

For Tutus had perhaps been deposed at the present synod because he finally agreed with Acacius, as Felix himself writes in a letter addressed to the bishops of Rome, Constantinople, and Bithynia. Sirmondus was the first to publish this letter; Labbeus inserted it most appropriately into his collection, while Hardouin omitted it (*Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1085). Yet the letter represents the acts of this council and is, as it were, a synodical letter. It is characteristic of Hardouin to pass over such acts relating to celebrated councils.

Another device used by the Acacians against the sentence of condemnation delivered through Tutus was that it was said to have been issued not in the name of the council of the Westerners but only in Felix’s name. The Fathers reject this objection as follows:

> “Accordingly, we have now hastened once again to report to your Charity the case of the Antiochene Church, gathered before blessed Peter the apostle, according to the custom that has always prevailed among us. Whenever the Lord’s priests gather within Italy for ecclesiastical matters, [Col. 0401B] especially matters of faith, the custom is maintained that the successor of the bishops of the apostolic see, acting on behalf of all the priests of Italy and in accordance with the concern that belongs to him for all the churches, should establish all things; he is the head of all. For the Lord said to blessed Peter the apostle: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it’ (Matthew 16:18). Following this saying, the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers gathered at Nicaea transferred to the holy Roman Church the confirmation and authority of these matters; and all their successors, by Christ’s grace, have preserved both down to our own time. What, therefore, was approved by the holy synod gathered, as we have said, before blessed Peter the apostle, and what the most blessed man Felix, our head, pope and archbishop, judged, is contained below.”

[Col. 0401C] The Fathers therefore say in their synodical letter that although the sentence delivered through Tutus was issued in the name of the Roman pontiff alone, it must nevertheless be understood according to the ancient custom: because the Roman Church is the head of the Churches, the pontiff confirms the decrees of councils by his authority and publishes them in his own name.

When they add, “What, therefore, was approved by the holy synod before blessed Peter the apostle, as we have said, through Tutus, defender of the Church,” and so forth, the words appear to have been transposed and should be explained thus:

> “What, therefore, was approved by the holy synod celebrated before blessed Peter the apostle, what was delivered, as we have said, through Tutus, defender of the Church, and what now, or at the present synod, the most blessed man Felix, our head, pope and archbishop, judged, is contained below.”

This follows the ancient custom concerning which the Council of Carthage under the primate Boniface speaks, when liberty was restored to the churches from the Vandals in the year 525. At that council, the Fathers, striving to restore the ancient practices, decreed among other things that this custom should be observed (*Councils*, vol. II [Col. 0401D], p. 1079):

> “It was said by all the bishops that if any letters were approved for drafting in the council, the venerable bishop who presides over this see—namely, the see of Carthage—should deign to dictate and subscribe them in the name of all.”

They say that this provision had been issued in another Council of Carthage under Aurelius. Indeed, it is also said to have been added there:

> “It was likewise approved, at the request of all the bishops, that Your Holiness subscribe all letters to be issued by the council.”

They therefore assert that both sentences were delivered: the first through Tutus, and the second issued at the present, fourth synod. But just as the copyist omitted the profession of faith issued by the present synod, so he also left out the rescript delivering the Acacian condemnation through Tutus. Moreover, the Fathers assert that just as the first sentence was inscribed only in Felix’s name, so the second was issued at the present synod.

In the encyclicals of earlier times, there are frequent references to letters, professions of faith, and other documents that, [Col. 0402A] through the carelessness of unlearned copyists, were separated from the context and later perished together with the complete acts, as is discussed at length in the commentary on the address of the Chalcedonian Fathers.

This appears to be the authentic interpretation of those words. For how could the pontiff send Tutus when, in the letter mentioned above and issued in this same year, he asserts that Tutus had been deposed because he had defiled the apostolic legation, and when the reports of Rufinus, Thalassius the archimandrite, and the other monks concerning Tutus’s lapse were extant? Or could the Fathers of the council be certain of Tutus’s faith when they had already learned from the reports that he had defected?

In the meantime, it is certain that after the words of the synodical letter cited above and the sentence again issued against Acacius by the present synod, there is a lacuna and the passage is corrupt, as anyone who reads it will immediately see. Therefore, I think that the earlier condemnation delivered through Tutus was inserted here, together with the sentence issued by this synod. The latter is itself mutilated at the beginning and reads as follows:

> “Thus did Acacius extend the impiety of his deadly condemnation, so that even when cast down he might insult; so that, [Col. 0402B] though cut off, he might not cease to rage; and although he is altogether held outside the body, he nevertheless rends its members and shows that what is written of him applies: ‘When the impious man has come into the depths of evil, he despises it.’ Adding worse things to those that came before, by persecuting the dead, his soul, grievously sinning, incurs the condemnation of the second death. For when the holy bishop Calendion had recently been expelled, as we have learned, he sent Peter—whom he himself had so often condemned—into Calendion’s Church, with the result that many, if it is true, of the Catholics withdrew, leaving their own sees, and that the pearls of our Church were cast before swine and dogs. Nevertheless, let no one be frightened that condemned Acacius does not remain quiet. Satan has been struck down, yet he is at work. Christ has conquered and conquers, and the enemy has still not ceased. And because we are certain that you too remember the prophetic reading and have no fear regarding the camp that remains standing, we most appropriately exhort you, while awaiting the Lord, to persevere—as we do—to [Col. 0402C] the end, and to retain with steadfast spirit the sentence that you find below.”

The sentence issued in Felix’s name, which the Fathers admit that they added here, likewise perished. It was joined to the subscriptions of the bishops. The subscription of the aforementioned Candidus, bishop of Tibur, presupposes that it was issued in Felix’s name; it reads, “following the authority of the apostolic see.” The subscriptions to the sentence show that the words cited presuppose an authoritative sentence issued by the apostolic see.

A portion of this same sentence exists in the *Brief History of the Eutychianists*. It must certainly be regarded as belonging to the sentence about which the Fathers speak and which they say they inserted into the letter; it bears Felix’s name. It reads there as follows:

> “Edict of the sentence of Pope Felix on account of the condemnation of Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. Acacius, who, after being admonished by us a second time, did not cease to be a despiser of salutary statutes and believed that I was to be imprisoned among my own people, God, by a sentence issued from heaven, has expelled from the priesthood. Therefore, if any [Col. 0402D] bishop, cleric, monk, or layman, after this condemnation, communicates with him, let him be anathema, with the Holy Spirit carrying out the sentence.”

This fragment agrees with what the Fathers of our Roman synod assert in their synodical letter. The Acacians’ objections—that the earlier sentence against Acacius should not be admitted because it bore only Felix’s name and had not been sent to the East through the bishops of the West or in their name—are demonstrated by the frequently cited letters of Gelasius, where he vigorously dismantles these objections and blows away the rest.

The letter containing these three things—(1) the profession of faith; (2) the first sentence pronounced against Acacius by the third Roman synod; and (3) the second condemnation pronounced against Acacius by the fourth Roman synod, namely the condemnation of the second death directed against Acacius and Peter of Alexandria and Peter of Antioch—was an encyclical and was sent to the monks so that they might disseminate it throughout the East. Whether antiquity or the ignorance of copyists begrudged the preservation of these three items, the Fathers testify as follows:

> “But so that nothing hostile in the letter might be [Col. 0403A] changed or interpreted otherwise by the most depraved minds, we first petitioned the most merciful emperor, as was proper, and sent this same letter of ours to your Charity, to the clergy and people, and to the most distinguished senate. We all subscribed it individually and collectively, asking divine assistance that, with the snares avoided—those of the Acacians, that is—he might cause what has been written to you to reach you.”

The vow of Candidus of Tibur is then added, followed by the statement:

> “Forty-two bishops likewise subscribed.”

Regarding both condemnations, and therefore also these two synods, the Holstenian Catalogue states in the margin on page 83:

> “At that time he held a synod and sent [the sentence] throughout the region of the East; and again he sent it and condemned Acacius and Peter forever.”

Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*, reports that the sentence delivered to Acacius by the Acoemete monks Bassianus and Pius was carried to him, and he speaks of this synod:

> “Acacius of Constantinople, Peter of Alexandria, and Peter of Antioch, enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, are condemned by Felix, bishop of the Roman Church, at a synod held in Italy; [Col. 0403B] and the condemnation itself is brought to Acacius of Constantinople by legates sent through the monks of the monasteries of the Acoemetes, Bassianus, and Pius.”

Here, therefore, it is very aptly noted from reports arriving from Greece that Peter the Antiochene and Acacius were condemned because of the continuation of their crimes, and indeed by that condemnation which is called the condemnation of the second death. Hence the following is added:

> “He condemned them forever, unless they should repent.”

Some manuscripts should be read: “While they did not repent.” This reading agrees better with the double published condemnation after the many crimes committed by Acacius. The author of the *Brief History* expressed it thus:

> “He caused him to be condemned by the apostolic see without the remedy of repentance.”

In the synodical letter of the aforementioned fourth synod, the Fathers say that Fullo and Acacius incurred the condemnation of the second death. Pope Felix, in his letter to Bishop Vetranio, which concerns Peter Fullo’s second invasion of the Antiochene see, also [Col. 0403C] asserts this concerning Acacius:

> “Therefore the aforementioned Acacius was rightly expelled by repeated excommunication.”

That this declaration entails a kind of indissolubility is stated by Nicholas I as follows:

> “Pope Felix not only deposed Acacius of Constantinople but also bound him with the unbreakable bonds of anathema.”

How this was done, and why it was deserved, Gelasius examines in his treatise *On Anathema*, where he shows how Acacius incurred anathema, defends the justice of the sentence issued, and vindicates it against the Acacians’ objections.

[Note: [Col. 0403C]

**Line 1.—Felix, etc.** After an interregnum of six days—during which Basil, the prefect of the praetorian guard and acting in Rome as the representative of King Odoacer, attempted to interfere with the election of the Roman pontiff by secular authority, as the acts of the fourth Roman synod under Symmachus report—Felix was created pontiff on 8 March [Col. 0403D] in the year of the Lord 483. He was Roman by birth, the great-great-grandfather of Saint Gregory the Great, as Gregory himself testifies in *Homily 38 on the Gospels* and *Dialogue* IV, chapter 16.

**Line 9.—After three years.** It is clear from Felix’s sixth letter, which contains the sentence issued against Acacius, that these men had been appointed and sent away before Acacius’s condemnation. It is therefore false that they were sent to Constantinople three years after Acacius had been condemned.]

[Note: [Col. 0403D]

## Chronological Notes

The first of Felix III’s letters, cited by Binius and other editors of the councils, was addressed to the same Acacius of Constantinople to whom his predecessor Simplicius had written his last three letters. In it Felix indicates that he had been appointed Simplicius’s successor.

Although the day and year on which the letter was issued do not appear in the copies examined so far, [Col. 0404A] nevertheless, since we know that it was written on the occasion of the council held at Rome at the beginning of Felix’s pontificate, and since we subsequently know of another letter addressed to the same Acacius, which is sixth in order in the Binian edition, in which a sentence of deposition and excommunication is pronounced against him and subscribed as follows:

> “I, Felix Coelius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed.”

It was dated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Venantius, a man of illustrious rank—that is, in the year 484 of the common Christian era. The many acts recounted there, on account of which Acacius was deprived of office, show that the earlier letters were issued by Felix in the preceding year, namely 483, with all the zeal of a pastor of the Gospel, in order to restore the erring sheep to Christ’s fold, entrusted to Peter and his successors.

Felix’s beginning can therefore be established quite clearly by reference to the Sunday of his ordination, namely 6 March in the year 483, during the consulship of Faustus the Younger; or to the weekday preceding that Sunday if the epoch is reckoned from his election rather [Col. 0404B] than from his ordination.

The end of the pontificate and life of Saint Felix III is correctly placed on 25 February in the year 492, the day on which he is commemorated, under the consulship of Anastasius Augustus and Rufus. It was under these consuls that Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*, reports Felix’s death and Gelasius’s succession; the pontifical catalogues support him when they assign eight years and eleven months to Felix’s tenure of the same see, as does Anastasius, who also gives twenty-three days.

Most catalogues, however, especially the Colbertine ones, list only eighteen days. Apparently the lower part of the numeral was cut off by copyists: from the sign for twenty-three, they copied eighteen.

In an old codex of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem, together with Felix’s synodical letter recited at the Roman council of the year 487, during the consulship of Boethius, a note of the immediately following consulship of Dynamius and Sifidius, belonging to the year 488, is also read at the end of the letter. This was either because the letter was retained for a long time at Rome before being sent to Africa, [Col. 0404C] as Binius observes, or because a copy of it was carried away later or transmitted again in the year indicated.

## Historical Notes

**Line 8.—He condemned Acacius, etc.** Although the series of the acts sufficiently shows that Felix employed in Acacius’s trial a balance between vigilant concern, which did not abandon correction, and paternal gentleness, which awaited repentance—something that anyone may observe in the notes of Archbishop Sommier and in the documents selected there—R. P. Dom Simon Mopinot nevertheless says that this is demonstrated still more clearly in the epistolary synopsis prefixed to the new edition of the letters of the supreme pontiffs, recently prepared by R. P. Dom Constantius, a monk of the same Congregation.

I shall reproduce his words. They blunt the more aggressive criticism of certain minds that arrogate to themselves the authority to brand Felix with an indiscriminate severity of zeal. On the basis of the documents brought forward by Constantius, Mopinot judges Felix [Col. 0404D] to be free from every charge of untimely fervor directed toward destruction rather than edification.

> “Certain acts of Felix II”—he calls him the second, following Hilary, whereas we call him the third—“are explained by Henry Valesius and others who follow Valesius in such a way that, besides seriously offending against history, they portray Felix himself, whether they intend to or not, as carried away by excessive zeal. For otherwise prudent and learned men suppose that after the sentence pronounced against Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, toward the end of July in the year 484, the pontiff immediately pronounced another similar sentence at a synod held four days later—at a time, that is, when Acacius had not yet heard anything about the first. But is such conduct consistent with Felix? Both his letters and the monuments of history persuade us otherwise.

> “Constantius [Col. 0405A], so that no charge of rashness might be branded upon so devout and upright a pontiff, assigns a definite date to each judgment. He places the first, with Valesius, in July of the year 484, but the second in October of the following year. It thus clearly appears that the anathema was repeated only for serious reasons and after Acacius’s obstinacy had been investigated and tolerated for a long time. The learned author supports this with arguments neither weak nor few, in a fuller dissertation at the end of which I read these words: ‘To have investigated and demonstrated this matter more carefully will not have been without benefit; for although it is always important to know the truth, it is especially important here, lest Felix appear to have been rash in pronouncing and repeating a sentence of such importance.’

> “VI. I should also like to present here in full another inquiry in which he proves that three letters attributed to the same pope—one addressed to the emperor Zeno and the other two to Peter Fullo—are to be regarded as spurious. One would see the religious [Col. 0405B] critic’s sagacity in distinguishing the true, and especially his diligence in defending the reputation of the supreme pontiffs.

> “The same task had been undertaken by Valesius, whom I have just praised, but his arguments, although highly probable, did not possess sufficient force to persuade. This gave Antonio Pagi the opportunity to construct a new system. Constantius shows that this system rests on no foundation whatever, since it can never be reconciled either with the ancient books, whether published or handwritten, or with the very wording of the letters.

> “Accordingly, without despising Valesius’s arguments but leaving them aside, he produces other arguments, both weightier and more numerous, which make the matter entirely convincing. To report each one would be tedious; to select only the chief ones is difficult, for they are so closely connected and interwoven that they cannot be separated without considerable loss.

> “I shall merely observe that it matters greatly, both for historical truth and for the praise of Felix II, that such letters not be counted among the genuine ones. For in them the pontiff is falsely represented [Col. 0405C] as having agreed with Acacius in condemning Peter Fullo. No chronological point can be assigned to this agreement anywhere in the whole pontificate of Felix, whether one considers its beginning, its end, or the intervening period; indeed, its falsity is obvious from the genuine letters of the same pope.

> “Next, Acacius is falsely represented as being honored with the title of archbishop, so that Felix is made to acknowledge the bishops subject to Acacius’s jurisdiction—Acacius, I mean, as bishop of a city which Gelasius, Felix’s successor, calls a parish of the Heracleian Church and observes not even to be counted among metropolitan rights. It is therefore utterly contrary even to the appearance of truth that Felix should have confirmed, by such approval, the privileges of the see of Constantinople based on canon 28 of Chalcedon.

> “Finally—and this is the more serious point, which ought to have been mentioned first—Felix is falsely represented as having written to Peter Fullo as though he were the legitimate pastor of the Antiochene Church and as having addressed him in these words:

> ‘Consider that you have been appointed to be a light to those who are in darkness and an instructor [Col. 0405D] of the foolish . . . See that through you the peoples, once enlightened, who have tasted the good word of God, may be enlightened.’

> “As though it were credible that the most holy pope could have been so forgetful both of ecclesiastical discipline and of himself as to wish to admit to his communion, address in honorable terms, and recognize as the legitimate bishop of the Antiochenes a most bitter enemy of the Council of Chalcedon, a sacrilegious plunderer of the Antiochene Church, recently condemned by his predecessor Pope Simplicius, and finally stripped of the name Christian—Fullo, who, if he had been healed by legitimate treatment, as Felix himself says concerning Peter Mongus, ought to have been received into pardon, not into the dignity of the priesthood.

> “Nor was the learned man content merely to deny this class of adulterine writings to Felix. He further investigated who their architect was, where he came from, in what age he lived, and for what purpose he produced them. Having explained these matters thoroughly, he concludes that the man was a Greek and a devotee of Acacius who, in order to refute more effectively the opinion of the Scythian monks concerning the one [Col. 0406A] crucified person of the Holy Trinity, invented the claim that the same doctrine had been condemned in Peter Fullo by the Roman pontiff Felix II.

> “Such was the authority of the pontiff at Rome,” Constantius says, “that even the Greeks themselves, whom the storm of the Acacian schism had severed from communion with the apostolic see, concealed themselves beneath his covering.

> “I could select from various notes and admonitions many points that converge upon the same conclusion, but we must hasten to other matters. I cannot, however, pass over the fact that several lengthy fragments, hitherto unpublished, belonging to one and the same letter of Felix, are about to come to light. The subject of that letter is a warning to the Easterners not to contaminate themselves by communion with Acacius, together with a promise that Acacius himself, if he abandons his undertaking, will be restored to ecclesiastical fellowship.

> “The latter point is useful because it explains certain somewhat obscure words [Col. 0406B] of the sentence pronounced against Acacius by the same Felix, as they were afterward explained by Gelasius; and nothing then remains in these passages that seems inconsistent with the pontiff’s charity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0406B]

**Line 1.—Felix III.** Ciaconius calls him the second, since the man created in schism against Liberius cannot legitimately be called pope.

**The same line.—Roman by birth.** He belonged to the most noble house of the Anicii, later called the Frangipani; he was the great-great-grandfather of Pope Gregory the Great, as Gregory himself relates in *Homily 38 on the Gospels* and *Dialogue*, Book IV, chapter 16.]

[Note: [Col. 0406B]

**Line 1.—Felix III, etc.** Saint Felix, the third of this name, Roman by birth and son of Felix the presbyter, the great-great-grandfather of Saint Gregory the Great, was appointed successor to Simplicius after an interval of five days between pontificates [Col. 0406C]. He was ordained on Sunday, 6 March of the same year, 483, as will be clear from the duration of his see.

Baronius rightly proves in his *Annals* and in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* under 25 February that Felix III, not Felix IV, was Gregory the Great’s great-great-grandfather. On this matter, see what will be said under Felix IV.

**Line 5.—A report came from Greece, Peter of Alexandria, etc.** John Talaia, bishop of Alexandria and then residing at Rome, as we stated under Simplicius, prepared a petition to present to him containing various charges against Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. He presented it to Felix, as Evagrius reports in Book III, chapter 18:

> “When the petitions presented by John to Felix had been brought against Acacius, on the grounds that he was communicating unlawfully with Peter—that is, Mongus, who had been intruded into the see of Alexandria—and was committing certain other acts contrary to the prescriptions of the sacred canons, Felix sent the bishops Vitalis and Misenus to Zeno, requesting that the Council of Chalcedon be confirmed, that [Col. 0406D] Peter be expelled as a heretic, and that Acacius be sent to Rome to give an account of the matters John had brought against him.”

From the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* we learn the sees of which Vitalis and Misenus were bishops. Vitalis is called bishop of Truentum in the Picene region; that town, called Truentum, is now destroyed. Misenus is called bishop of the Church of Cumae, in the region of Campania; Cumae was a city of Campania and is likewise now entirely ruined.

They were sent with the following instructions, as the same *Brief History* records:

> “That Peter should be expelled from the Alexandrian Church, that Acacius should answer the petition of the holy John, bishop of Alexandria, and that Acacius should be instructed to anathematize Peter.”

Acacius’s summons is preserved in *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1098.

Felix instructed the legates to do nothing before they had consulted Cyril, superior of the Acoemete monks, and learned from him what ought to be done, [Col. 0407A] as Evagrius says in the cited chapter 19.

When the legates reached Abydos, they were seized there by the emperor’s agents, their documents were taken away, and they were committed to custody, as Theophanes writes. At first the emperor threatened to kill them unless they communicated with Peter and Acacius. When threats accomplished nothing, however, he turned to flattery and attempted to corrupt them with gifts and bribes.

Indeed, after adding an oath, both he and Acacius promised them that the case would be preserved intact for the apostolic see and that no prejudice would arise against it if the legates entered into communion with Acacius and Peter. Pope Gelasius testifies to this in his thirteenth letter to the bishops of Dardania, near its beginning:

> “But Acacius not only refused to satisfy the demands; he also brought it about that the very legation of the apostolic see, deceived by flatteries, rewards, and perjuries—by which he had promised together with the emperor that the entire case of the apostolic pontiff would be preserved intact in every respect—should return polluted by communion with Peter.”

[Col. 0407B] When Vitalis and Misenus had therefore been deceived by various devices, they were brought out of custody and proceeded to the church together with Acacius and the representatives of Peter Mongus, where they celebrated the solemnities of the Mass. The orthodox protested, however, and declared once, twice, and three times that this betrayal was the destruction of the true faith.

The first written protest they tied around a cord and hung on one of the legates like a hook; the second they placed inside a codex; and the third they inserted into a basket of vegetables and sent to the legates, as Theophanes writes.

Having thus conducted themselves, the legates returned covered with disgrace and dishonor: not only had they failed to accomplish what they had been sent to do, but they had also polluted themselves by entering into communion with Peter Mongus, whom they had been sent to expel. On their return to Rome they brought with them Zeno’s and Acacius’s letters, which those men had sent in reply to Pope Felix, filled with insults against John Talaia and with praises and commendations of Peter Mongus. [Col. 0407C] Evagrius, book III, chapter 20, reports part of Zeno’s letter. Felix the pope, the Roman synod, and the author of the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* mention Acacius’s letter. After the departure of the legates, Felix, the defender of the Roman Church, whom Pope Felix had sent as his personal legate—for Vitalis and Misenus had been chosen from the priestly college—followed the legates somewhat later, compelled by the necessity of illness. Acacius received him with such insult that he did not even deign to admit him to his presence, as Pope Felix testifies in the sentence condemning Acacius. Liberatus adds that he was thrown into custody and that his papers were taken away, because he had refused to communicate with Acacius and Peter, as Vitalis and Misenus had done.

Before the legates had returned to Rome, report, arriving ahead of them, had spread their treachery everywhere. Therefore Pope Felix assembled a synod of sixty-seven bishops in the year 484 [Col. 0407D] in the basilica of Saint Peter. There, when Vitalis and Misenus were ordered to give an account of the legation entrusted to them and resorted to empty excuses, Pope Felix first deprived the bishops Vitalis and Misenus of their priestly office and communion. He then declared Peter Mongus of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople alienated from the priestly college and from ecclesiastical communion. This was Acacius’s first condemnation in a Roman synod, held on 28 July, with Venantius [as consul]; hence, in the year 484. Today only one fragment of this Roman synod survives, namely, part of the sentence issued by the whole synod against Peter and Acacius. It appears in volume IV of the *Councils*, p. 1073, and begins, “of many transgressions,” etc. What the Greeks objected to in it, and what the Romans replied, may be read in Baronius’s critical discussion under that same year.

The sentence against Acacius, issued by the Roman synod, was sent through Tutus, the defender of the Roman Church, [Col. 0408A] as was also the letter to Zeno Augustus, in which the bishops asked him to obey the synod’s decrees. Tutus, having received the sentence and the letters, sailed eastward. He delivered the sentence of condemnation that he had brought to Acacius between the altars and fastened it to his pallium, as Victor of Tunnuna, Liberatus, and Theophanes write. He also displayed Pope Felix’s edict for public reading throughout the city of Constantinople. After faithfully carrying out all these tasks, he was ensnared by Acacius’s deceptions. For, as is clear from Pope Felix’s letter to the monks of Constantinople and Bithynia, which is found in volume IV of the *Councils*, p. 1085, an old man named Maronas was sent to Tutus and promised him a large sum of money if he would disclose to Acacius everything that was being done against him at Rome. But the archimandrites Rufinus and Thalassius, together with the other monks in Constantinople and those settled throughout Bithynia, as soon as Tutus had returned to Rome, wrote to Pope Felix and also sent Tutus’s [Col. 0408B] own letters. When these were read in the assembly of bishops, Tutus was deprived both of his office and of the most holy communion in the year 485.

Meanwhile, when Felix the pontiff saw that affairs in the East were so disturbed that there was absolutely no hope of restoring John Talaia, bishop of Alexandria, to his see, he appointed that same prelate to the distinguished Church of Nola in Campania. The deacon Liberatus testifies to this in the *Breviary*, chapter 18:

> “John Talaia, however,” he says, “retaining the dignity of a bishop, remained at Rome. The pope gave him the Church of Nola, which is in the region of Campania. He resided there for many years and died in peace.”

Acacius, committing still worse offenses, had Calendion, the catholic bishop of the Church of Antioch, whom he himself had ordained, expelled. He then arranged for Peter the Fuller—who had invaded that see, had been expelled from it, and had been condemned in the Roman and Constantinopolitan synods under Simplicius—to be restored to that see by the emperor Zeno, while Calendion was expelled and exiled to the Oasis. From this [Col. 0408C] it happened that access was opened to the Eutychian heretics and that heretics were substituted in place of catholic prelates, as Pope Gelasius testifies both in the frequently cited letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania and in letter 15, which he wrote to the Eastern bishops. When Pope Felix learned of this calamity of the Church of Antioch, he convened a synod of bishops at Rome in the year 485, on 5 October. Its surviving record is Felix’s letter 5 to Zeno Augustus. In it Felix announces to the emperor that Peter the Fuller had been condemned by synodal judgment and the sentence of anathema, and that communion with him must therefore be avoided. He further urges the same emperor to expel the deposed Fuller from the Church of Antioch. There also survives a letter of Pope Felix to the presbyters and archimandrites residing in Constantinople and Bithynia, in the collection of the *Councils*, p. 1124, with this heading: “Letter of the Roman synod to the Eastern clergy and monks”; and finally another letter of the same pontiff to Vetranion, bishop, in the same collection, p. 1092. In this synod, therefore, Peter the Fuller, who had tyrannically occupied the Church of Antioch, was struck with anathema; and Acacius of Constantinople, together with Peter Mongus, the invader of the Church of Alexandria, was condemned by a renewed excommunication.

**Line 21.—“And after his passing,” etc.** When the emperor Zeno, in the year 482, had issued the *Henoticon*, or unitive edict, either at Acacius’s persuasion or at his dictation, and had sent it to the bishops, monks, and Christian people of the Egyptian diocese with the intention of reconciling peace and securing the unity of the Churches, it displeased both Simplicius and his successor Felix. They attempted, in very serious letters, to recall the insufficiently religious prince to his duty and to rouse him to the defense of the faith. Yet neither Felix himself nor the Church explicitly condemned that edict, partly lest they embitter Zeno’s mind and thereby give rise to more serious schisms and evils whose healing would be more difficult, and partly because Zeno did not explicitly condemn the Council of Chalcedon or affirm any heresy in his *Henoticon*. Indeed, he condemned the Eutychian doctrine and, in private letters sent elsewhere to the Roman pontiffs, especially to Felix III, professed the Council of Chalcedon; Evagrius, book III, chapter 20, reports a fragment of one such letter:

> “You must know for certain,” Zeno says in Evagrius, “that both our piety and the most holy Peter mentioned above, together with all the most holy Churches, embrace and venerate the most holy Council of Chalcedon, which is entirely consonant with the faith of the Council of Nicaea.”

From this letter and from the words of the *Henoticon* itself, Natalis Alexander, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Century*, dissertation 18, demonstrates that it contains no heresy. In it Zeno decrees that no creed other than the Nicene Creed is to be admitted. He approves the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril. He condemns Nestorius and Eutyches with anathema. Nevertheless, the Church rightly rejected it, not only because lay rulers cannot decide matters of faith, but also because, by suppressing in silence the definition of the Council of Chalcedon and Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian—received with the supreme agreement of the whole synod—as well as the expressions “from two [natures]” and “in two natures,” by which they had struck down the Eutychian heresy, Zeno, in his policy of accommodation, condescended to the heretics who abhorred those expressions. Hence, after his death, Zeno’s name was erased from the sacred diptychs, when peace was made between the Eastern Church and the Roman Church under the pontificate of Hormisdas.

When Saint Pope Felix had occupied the see for eight years, eleven months, and eighteen days, as stated by the Colbertine manuscript of Anastasius, various catalogues, Regino, Martin of Poland, Liutprand, and Hermannus Contractus, he passed to the heavenly homeland on 24 February in the year 492. After his death, Saint Gregory himself relates that Felix appeared to his virgin great-niece Tarsilla, the sister of Gordian, Saint Gregory the Great’s father, and called her to the heavenly kingdom, in his *Homily on the Gospels* 38 and *Dialogues* IV, chapter 16.]

[Note: [Col. 0409C]

**Line 4.—“Under this episcopate,” etc.** In this section the Bibliothecarius appears to have gathered Felix’s actions in the case of Acacius of Constantinople from Felix’s own letters. The distinguished archbishop D. Somier collected and arranged them more clearly in book VI, chapters 6 and 7, of his *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*, through the material that follows.

**From chapter 6.** As soon as Felix III ascended the throne of the Church, his first concern was devoted to administering justice in response to the petitions and complaints that John of Alexandria had submitted to the apostolic see against Acacius of Constantinople.

> “For when John had presented petitions to Felix against Acacius, on the ground that Acacius was communicating unlawfully with Peter [Mongus] and was committing certain other acts contrary to the laws of the sacred canons, Felix sent the bishops Vitalis and Misenus to Zeno.” [Col. 0409D]

Evagrius (book III, chapter 18) adds letters to the same emperor and also to Acacius. In the letter sent to Zeno he begins as follows:

> “The venerable confession of the Apostle Peter presses upon you with maternal appeals and, never ceasing to address the confidence of your piety, especially as one of his sons, cries out: Christian prince, why do you permit me to be cut off from the course of charity by which the universal Church is bound together? Why do you break in me the agreement of the whole world? I beg you, most devout son, since the Lord’s tunic, woven from above throughout, signified the indivisible Church of Christ as one body under the universal governance of the Holy Spirit, do not permit it to be violated in any way; and do not allow that integrity which remained even among those who crucified the Savior to appear divided in your time.

> “Is it not my faith that the Lord himself showed to be one and alone, incapable of being overcome by any adversity, when he promised that the gates of hell would never prevail against his Church founded upon my confession? [Col. 0410A] I ask that these things, which God willed to be spoken through the bishop of the aforesaid see—or through the lowliness of my order, which judged that they ought to be brought forward for the sake of your security—may make you, as though admonished by the authority of the present apostle, look more deeply upon both the paths of divine reverence and the condition of human affairs, so that, God forbid, you may not prove ungrateful to the author of the happiness entrusted to you . . . Look to your predecessors of august memory, Marcian and Leo. As their legitimate successor, you ought to embrace the faith of such great rulers and their agreement in religion, whose memory you ought to revere. Have the writings of your palace reviewed, and carefully investigate those writings which, as your piety was returning to the summit of supreme power, you sent to my predecessor as a common expression of congratulation,” etc. Second letter of Pope Felix III.

In the letters written to Acacius as well, Felix professes the zeal for preserving the faith throughout the universal Church entrusted to him as Peter’s successor. He also demands from Acacius an account of why he had not reported to him, in accordance with the admonitions of his predecessors, the disturbed state of the faith both in the Alexandrian and in the Eastern Church:

> “Indicate to us for what reason your affection, although repeatedly invited not only by the many opportunities that have continually arisen but also by letters from my predecessors, has never wished, as though under a stubborn silence, either to consult us about anything in this matter or to report anything . . .”

He then seriously warns Acacius not to confirm by obstinacy the suspicion that had arisen concerning the danger in which he was involved:

> “Therefore, since we love you with greater urgency and with sincere charity, we urge you through repeated exhortations to turn away from these things hereafter, which show that you are separated from the entire household of Christ.”

Besides these letters, Felix also sent two separate documents, one to be delivered to Zeno Augustus and the other to Acacius. Evagrius, book III, chapter 18, appears to mention both and the articles expressed in them:

> “In the former, he demanded [Col. 0410C] that the Council of Chalcedon be confirmed, that Peter [Mongus] be expelled as a heretic, and that Acacius be sent to Rome to give an account of the matters that John [of Alexandria] charged against him.”

In the second document, addressed to Acacius, he wrote as follows:

> “Your affection ought, as episcopal diligence admonishes, to have followed established custom and reported what the response of my predecessor of holy memory, delivered through the devoted subdeacon Uranius to the most merciful prince, and what his letters to you also, accomplished in the case of the Church of Alexandria. You ought also to have labored with every effort to advance the concern of which he rightly wished you to be a participant, so that the catholic faith, strengthened at the Council of Chalcedon and again confirmed by the replies of all the Lord’s priests who had sat in that council, might not, as unexpectedly once more disturbed by the perversity of heretics, be allowed to lie oppressed beneath the power of its own enemies. Since this was omitted for a long time, our fellow bishop John, driven out by the heretical invaders of the see of Alexandria, brought us the petition that he had prepared for presentation to my predecessor of holy memory, as you will recognize from what follows. We could not reject it, following the example of his great predecessor, the blessed Athanasius, and of our earlier predecessors. Therefore, after the following matters have been read, dearest brother, hasten to respond concerning what you recognize to have been set before the blessed Apostle Peter, to whom you see that prayers are offered through us and whom you cannot deny to have received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing. Respond also in the assembly of our brothers and fellow bishops, so that, ordering what justice provides for either side, removing the scandals of the Churches that we see being torn apart, restoring harmony, and preserving the integrity of the faith, we may with pure minds make acceptable offerings of reconciliation, which we offer on behalf of the whole Christian people and the salvation of the most glorious emperor. For this purpose we have sent from our college our brothers and fellow bishops Vitalis [Col. 0411A] and Misenus, together with our most faithful Felix, defender of the Holy Roman Church, whom we have sent from our side by official appointment. They must not be delayed, lest, by provoking the Lord’s indignation, matters requiring correction grow stronger through procrastination.”

Felix’s prudent care was frustrated by the disgrace and negligence of the legates. At their first arrival, they were imprisoned by Zeno’s command. There, when they were tested by blandishments and rewards to bend them, and by threats and intimidation to prevent them from carrying out Felix’s orders, they were also deceived by Acacius’s perjuries, “by which he promised him, together with the emperor, that the entire case of the apostolic prelate would be preserved in every respect for the bishop of the Roman see.” Thus they completed their legation polluted by communion with Peter [Mongus], as Pope Gelasius records in his letter to the bishops of Dardania, with the agreement of Evagrius, book III, chapter 20, and the *Brief History of the Eutychians*.

When Felix was informed of the legates’ treachery, he convoked a council upon their return at [Col. 0411B] Saint Peter’s. There, with the proper legal procedure observed, the most blessed pope suspended Vitalis and Misenus, the legates, from office and communion, and condemned Acacius. (*Brief History of the Eutychians*, at the end.)

He sent the sentence of condemnation to Acacius through Tutus, the defender of the Roman Church. He also instructed him to publish the judgment by publicly posting an edict of this kind:

> “Acacius, who, having been warned a second time by us, did not cease to despise salutary statutes and believed that I should be imprisoned because of them: God, by a sentence proved from heaven, has made this man an exile from the priesthood. Therefore, if any bishop, cleric, monk, or layman communicates with him after this denunciation, let him be anathema, with the Holy Spirit carrying out the sentence.”

Felix wrote many other letters concerning this matter, especially to Zeno Augustus, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, and to the monks of that city and of Bithynia. We shall set out here the principal points of them.

In his letter to Zeno he says:

> “It will be established as contrary to divine reverence that the legation of the blessed Apostle Peter was held as though brought back into captivity, and that its documents were violently taken away, so that it was brought out of custody to communicate with heretics—that is, with the representatives of Peter of Alexandria, against whom it had gone . . . For even among barbarian nations, and among those ignorant of the deity itself, the sacred freedom of any legation is regarded by the law of nations as inviolable when human affairs are being conducted. How much more, then, ought it to have been preserved undefiled by a Roman emperor and Christian prince, especially in divine matters.”

> “I leave it to your judgment whether anyone should choose communion with the blessed Apostle Peter or with Peter of Alexandria . . . I think, however, that your piety, which prefers even to be overcome by its own laws rather than resist them, ought to obey heavenly decrees. It ought to recognize that the height of human affairs has been entrusted to it [Col. 0411D] in such a way that it nevertheless does not doubt that divine things are to be received through dispensers divinely appointed . . . For it is certain that it is salutary for your affairs that, when God’s causes are at issue, you strive to subject the royal will to the priests of Christ according to his own decree, rather than place it above them; and that through their prelates you learn the sacred matters rather than teach them. Follow the form of the Church; do not impose upon it humanly devised laws to be followed, nor seek to rule over her decrees, to whose authority God willed your clemency to bow in pious devotion, lest, while the measure of heavenly dispensation is exceeded, you proceed to insult the one who orders all things.”

In his letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople he says:

> “Let your sentence preserve the proper rank of our son, the presbyter Solomon, whom Acacius thought he should deprive of his rank in order to please the heretics; or let it declare that all those who may have been expelled by the aforesaid man should remain in their places and in our communion. Although we know the zeal of your faith, [Col. 0412A] nevertheless we warn you that all who wish to share in the catholic faith should abstain from his communion, lest, God forbid, they undergo a similar punishment. Since there is no doubt that some among your monasteries have been deceived and have passed over to the enemies of God, either voluntarily or under compulsion, we command you to observe the following concerning such persons: whoever among you, in any place, has either voluntarily given himself over or has been corrupted by payment must be wholly excluded from your fellowship . . . But the case of those must be treated differently who are shown to have been afflicted with harsher punishments in order to force them to defect. Toward these you ought to show greater humanity, so that they may return under the discipline of penance to their cells and may expiate their fall through more faithful tears, until, after the enemies and perverters have been excluded, the catholic Church is cleansed.”

**From chapter 7.** After salutary warnings and the infliction of just penalties, Acacius fell into worse conduct and dared to exercise in the Church of Antioch the same actions that he had carried out in Alexandria. For, abusing the influence he possessed with the emperor, he secured a decree of deposition and exile against Calendion the patriarch, as though he were guilty of treason and of a falsely alleged conspiracy against the ruler, and arranged for Peter the Fuller to be substituted for him. After learning these things, Felix, in a second council held at Rome, struck Acacius with a renewed anathema, together with Peter Mongus; and in letters sent to Zeno he warned and commanded:

> “Let the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God read this, so that it may not receive into communion one who has been deposed by it for the reasons stated above, but that, through the divine letters of your serenity, you may drive him from the borders of Antioch.”

In the synodal letter that the Roman council sent to the Eastern clergy and monks, published in Labbe’s collection of the *Councils*, p. 1124, the following is read:

> “Now, having gathered again at the blessed Apostle Peter concerning the case of the Church of Antioch, we have hastened, in accordance with the custom of your affection that has always prevailed among us, to make known the following. Whenever the Lord’s priests gather within Italy on account of ecclesiastical matters, especially matters of faith, the custom is maintained that the successor of the bishop of the apostolic see, acting on behalf of all the priests of Italy and according to the concern that belongs to him for all the Churches, should determine everything, since he is the head of all; as the Lord said to the blessed Peter: ‘You are Peter,’ etc. Following this saying, the 318 holy Fathers gathered at Nicaea conferred both confirmation of ecclesiastical matters and authority upon the holy Roman Church. By Christ’s grace, all successions have preserved both of these down to our own age . . . But Acacius stretched out the impiety of his deadly condemnation so far that, although cast down, he still insults; although cut off, he does not cease to rage; and, although held entirely outside the body, he nevertheless tears apart its members. After the holy bishop Calendion had recently been expelled, he introduced Peter into his Church. I, Candidus, bishop of the city of Tibur, have subscribed, declaring anathema, following the authority of the apostolic see and in accordance with the catholic deliberation pronounced by us according to the state of the Church, against Peter, the invader of the Church of Alexandria, and against Acacius, formerly of the Church of Constantinople, and also against Peter of Antioch, who were long ago rightly and deservedly separated from the episcopal and Christian number, together with all their followers. Forty-two bishops subscribed in the same manner.”

When Acacius, persisting in schism, departed this life, Flavitas the presbyter was ordained after him. He did not consent to be enthroned without the Roman pontiff, but sent a synodical letter to Felix, the Roman pope, as Liberatus writes in the *Breviary*, chapter 18. He arranged for the letters to be carried by Constantinopolitan clerics accompanied by legates from the monasteries of that city—men who had remained steadfast in communion with the Roman see. In them he professed that he was carrying out the matter according to the rules:

> “Since it is being regularly sent to the apostolic see, through which, by Christ’s generosity, the dignity of all priests is made firm. Your letter itself, in which you confess that the blessed Apostle Peter is the summit of the apostles, the rock of faith, and the dispenser of the heavenly mystery through the keys entrusted to him, bears witness to this. Finally, it testifies that, so that we may be more fully united, you wish to have agreement with us in the orthodox faith.”  
> —Pope Felix III, letter 13 to Flavitas of Constantinople.

Felix thus placed confidence in Flavitas’s sincere disposition on the basis of the mission of the legates, whom he knew to be orthodox. He supposed that Flavitas would submit to the judgment of the apostolic see and, in accordance with its pronouncements, regard Acacius and Mongus as excommunicated, and would therefore have erased their names from the sacred diptychs. But when the legates’ questioning produced no evidence of such agreement, Felix wished to delay their admission to the communion they desired, as he records in the same letters:

> “Since these matters appear to be no small indications from which we believe that our hopes concerning your mind may proceed, a greater testimony was added when our sons, the religious monks, endowed with a confession of the true faith, came here as well. When we saw them, we judged that they had been sent for no other reason than that the names of the condemned, from whose communion these men stood apart, had already been removed from the Church of Constantinople. Therefore we saw that nothing remained except that those who carried your synodical letter should enjoy participation in apostolic communion. But while we dealt with them more carefully, so that, if they preferred to receive the communion of the blessed Apostle Peter with faithful hearts, they might declare either that they themselves or that your affection would henceforth be wholly alienated from the recitation of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius, they replied that no such instruction had been given to them and refused to consent to our salutary offer. Disturbed by this change in them, although the letters that had arrived and the very arrangement of events seemed to promise something else, and the report of those men offered communion in a manner very different from what had been hoped, we sorrowfully postponed our communion with them. [Col. 0413C] We desired it without ambiguity and hoped that it would come with the fullness of catholic faith, together with the agreement concerning orthodox faith which he had promised to share with us. Otherwise, no blame can be assigned to us if, when the bonds of charity have embraced the fellowship of the blessed Apostle Peter, the fellowship of Peter of Alexandria is preferred.”

He sent virtually the same reply to Zeno Augustus. Zeno had professed in letters sent to Felix that the purity of the faith and the harmony of the Church were the sum of his desires, and he had requested confirmation of the bishop of Constantinople by the bishop of the Roman see, since he wished to be supported from the place whence, by Christ’s will, the grace of all bishops flows. (Letter 12 of Felix III to the emperor Zeno.)

Finally, Felix addressed Thalassius, archimandrite of a monastery in Constantinople, as follows:

> “After the letters that we sent through our sons, men of religious purpose, to be delivered to your affection, we judged that your charity should also be warned, so that more vigilant care might provide nothing less for the protection of the catholic faith. Even if, by the favor of our God, the names of the condemned—that is, Peter of Alexandria and the unhappy Acacius—have been removed from the Church’s recitation, so that persons of similar ruin may not presume to assume the dignity of the priesthood, your affection, or the congregation that you govern, or whoever may in the future be pontiff of the Church of Constantinople, must not decide that he is excommunicated before all matters have been reported to the apostolic see, either through the letters of the man who has been appointed bishop or through the communications of your affection. For just as, through your catholic profession, you followed the form of the apostolic see by suspending yourself from communion with the condemned, so you must follow the example of the blessed Peter, so that when communion has been reported on his authority, you may then know that your fellowship also must be joined to it. Let no one persuade your affection at all that our communion has already been entrusted to those regions, since you see that matters still remain in doubt and that among us everything concerning the bishop created there is entirely uncertain. Nor could communion be joined to one whose honor we have not yet approved as received from us, and whose faith and imitation have not yet been confirmed. Let your affection therefore await the command of the apostolic see, and then unite itself in sacred communion with the Church of Constantinople, if it desires to remain in participation with the blessed Peter and with catholic truth.”  
> —Letter 14 of Pope Felix III to Thalassius the archimandrite.

After such clear testimonies, can it be maintained—as some modern writers dare to assert—that someone, even if cut off from communion with the Roman Church, can still remain in communion with the body of the catholic Church? Those who are not afraid to advance this claim would undoubtedly wish to form from the catholic Church—which is the kingdom, the household, and the mystical body of Christ Jesus—a kingdom without a head, a household without a father, and a body without a soul.

Flavitas did not survive his election by more than a few days beyond three months. When Euphemianus, appointed as his successor, had received Felix’s letters, he erased the name of Peter Mongus from the sacred diptychs; nevertheless, he did not wish to remove Acacius’s name from them. Evagrius, book III, chapter 23.]

[Col. 0385]

## 73

**Felix III**, a Roman by nationality, son of Felix the presbyter, of the title of Fasciola, occupied the see for eight years, eleven months, and twenty-three days.

[Note: [Col. 0385] B: nine years, less twelve days, from the consulship of Anicius to the consulship of the emperors Anastasius and Rufinus.—B denies this.]

He lived in the time of King Odoacer and into the time of Theodoric. He built the basilica of Saint Agapitus beside the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr. During his episcopate a report again arrived from Greece that Peter of Alexandria had been restored by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0385] See Baronius under the year 483.]

Then the venerable Felix, archbishop of the see of the apostolic city of Rome, sent the defender together with a council of his see. After the council had been held, he condemned Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Alexandria. Three years later a report again arrived from the emperor Zeno that Acacius should return as a penitent. Then Pope Felix sent two bishops, Misenus

[Note: [Col. 0385] C: Misenus.]

and Vitalis, so that, if they found Acacius an accomplice of Peter, they might condemn them. When they had entered the city of Heraclea, they were corrupted by money given to the aforesaid bishops and did not act according to the command of the apostolic see. When they came to Rome, to the apostolic see, at that same time the venerable Pope Felix held a synod. An investigation was conducted, and it found both bishops—namely Misenus and Vitalis—guilty and corrupted by money.

[Note: [Col. 0385] * After an investigation, both bishops were found guilty.]

[Note: [Col. 0385] See Baronius under the year 484.]

He expelled the bishops Misenus and Vitalis from communion. Then Bishop Misenus did not deny that he had been corrupted by money. This occurred during the reign of King Odoacer. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, during the month of December: twenty-eight presbyters, five deacons, and thirty-one bishops for various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Paul, and the episcopate was vacant for five days. After his passing, the presbyters and deacons established a decree concerning the whole Church, that no one should ever presume to act hastily in such a matter, since a matter that must at some time be investigated ought not to be rushed.

## LI. SAINT GELASIUS. A.D. 482; FIRST YEAR OF THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS; SIXTEENTH YEAR OF KING ODOACER.

[Note: [Col. 0415A]

Likewise two books against Arius. He also wrote two books against Arius. He also composed prefaces and prayers of the Sacraments in guarded language, and many letters on the faith in polished language” [Col. 0416A]; “He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, in January and December”; line 22: “sixty-seven places”; line 23: “December, and the episcopate was vacant for seven days.”

In Holstenius and Schelestratius.]

Num. 74, line 2: Florentius and Cassiodorus: eighteen days. Florentius omits: “In his time … Gargano.” Line 6: Florentius has: “He recalled Mesena, the bishop, from the synodal proceedings, with tears and after a written statement of satisfaction had been purged; he restored him to his church, although he had sinned in the affair of Acacius.” Line 8: Florentius omits *cleri* (“of the clergy”), and line 9, *famis* (“of famine”). Line 10: Florentius and Cassiodorus add “at Constantinople” before “Greece.” Line 12: after *the apostolic see*, Florentius adds: “whom the said blessed Gelasius received with honor, and to whom he also granted the second see.” During those times he held a synod, sent [letters] throughout the East, sent again, and condemned Acacius and Peter forever, unless Peter, repenting and submitting a written statement of satisfaction, should seek penance [lacuna]. Here also Florentius has: “He dedicated the basilica of Saint Euphemia,” etc. Florentius II likewise. Line 18: “In Villa Pertusa.” He also made provision for alms [*alim.*; abbreviated and uncertain]. Thus Florentius. Line 13: Florentius omits “February,” etc. Line 20: “What is found here, by months,” etc., is read in the Florentine manuscripts after the words “twentieth from the city.” For they read as follows: “Here he composed two books against Nestorius and Eutyches; he also composed hymns in the manner of blessed Ambrose” [Florentius II adds: “and also two books against Arius”]; “he also composed the prefaces of the Sacraments, prayers in carefully guarded language, and many letters of faith in polished language. During his episcopate,” etc.

According to Penia, from the Codex Cavensis.

Line 25: “which today is called the library and church.”

[Col. 0417A]

Lucas Holstenius, in his notes on the Life of Gelasius, writes: “Concerning the studies and character of Pope Gelasius there is an excellent account by Dionysius Exiguus, abbot, in the preface to his decretal letters addressed to Julian, priest of Saint Anastasius, in a Vatican manuscript.”

[Col. 0417A]

Line 3.—“In his time the church of Saint Michael was discovered on Mount Gargano.” During the time of Gelasius, the crypt of Saint Michael the Archangel was discovered on Mount Gargano; hence his memory is celebrated every year with a more solemn festival. Sigebert relates the matter under the year 488, according to a mistaken reckoning of the years, since Gelasius did not occupy the see before 492.

Line 5.—“He burned their books before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary.” The Manichaeans were expelled from the city, and their books were burned before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary. Symmachus did the same. Anastasius, in his Life of Symmachus, says: “After all these things, blessed Symmachus found Manichaeans in the city of Rome, and burned all their images and books together before the doors of the Constantinian basilica.” According to a constitution of Theodosius, the books of heretics were to be publicly burned, book VI, *On Heretics*. Books of disapproved reading—for example, magical books and similar works—were likewise to be destroyed, book IV, section 1, *Digest*, title *Familiae erciscundae*. Augustine relates that the books of the astrologers were publicly burned after their conversion, in his commentary on Psalm 61: “Therefore this man, now sought, found, and brought forward, carries with him the books destined to be burned, through which he himself had been destined to be burned.”

Line 23.—“Here he composed treatises and hymns like blessed Ambrose the bishop.” Treatises are expositions of Scripture. Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book I: “For you attempted not only to strip me of their discipleship by your words, but you also produced your own treatise.” Nemesianus and others, in the letter of Cyprian 78: “For in a treatise you are greater than all men, and in speech more eloquent.” Hence a *treatise* is a sermon delivered to the people after the reading of the Gospel during the solemn rites of Mass. Ambrose, letter 33: “On the following day, which was Sunday, after the readings and the sermon, when the catechumens had been dismissed, they handed over the creed in the baptisteries of the basilica to certain candidates.” Thus celebrating Mass and preaching are different activities. Victor of Vita, *On the Persecution of the Vandals*, book II: “You have free choice in your churches either to celebrate Mass or to preach.” Hence preachers were called *tractatores*, expositors of Scripture. Augustine, letter 11: “All the ancient interpreters who preceded us in the Lord and interpreted the sacred Scriptures interpreted either obscure passages or manifest ones.” The same author, on Psalm 102: “He calls through the reader; he calls through the preacher.” The same author, *Sermon on Time* 220: “The preacher, or the disputing bishop, says that from his own mouth.” The same author, on John, chapter 22: “When all the readings, pages, and the voice of the reader and preacher have been removed.” Hymns are songs in praise of God that are sung in the Church. Gelasius composed hymns after the example of Ambrose.

[Col. 0417D]

Line 10.—“In his time.” What is inserted here concerning John of Alexandria, Mongus, and Acacius belongs to the acts of Simplicius or Felix; these additions were inserted tumultuously among the acts of Gelasius by an ignorant compiler. Besides the evidence already cited, the chronological notices prove this. Gelasius was elected pope in 492. Acacius had died in 488 and Mongus in 490. It is therefore certain that these additions, just as they were wrongly attached to the acts of Gelasius, must with still greater certainty be restored to the acts of Simplicius and Felix.

As a concluding confirmation of what has been said, Cyril of Scythopolis should be heard in the Life of Saint Sabas. He records the whole sorrowful history of Peter the Fuller, including his second invasion and this new anathema pronounced against him by Felix III. This adds weight to the observations already made and helps illuminate the *Liber Pontificalis*. He writes as follows, according to Cotelier, volume III, page 264:

“Since some of them”—he is speaking of certain monasteries into which the heresy of the Fuller had penetrated—“attempted to sing the thrice-holy hymn, or Trisagion, with the addition devised by Peter surnamed Gnapheus, or the Fuller—‘who was crucified for us’—the divinely inspired elder, rightly angered, ordered that the Greeks themselves should sing the hymn according to the ancient tradition of the Catholic Church, and not according to the innovation of the said Peter. This Peter agreed with Eutyches in the same opinions, invaded the see of Antioch twice in tyrannical fashion, and was expelled by ecclesiastical decrees. Then, for a third time, after Illus—or Ilius—had assumed tyranny in Isauria under the rule of Zeno, Peter, by imperial authority, wickedly held the same throne, although the anathemas pronounced against him had not been rescinded; and he disturbed the whole East. Finally, he was struck with an anathema by the Roman pope Felix, both because of his perverse and alien doctrines and because of the aforesaid addition to the Trisagion. Therefore our father rightly and piously alone rejected the addition devised by him and followed the ecclesiastical tradition.”

These things were thus left to posterity by a contemporary writer. Just as they prove that the Fuller was condemned by three anathemas, so they show that the final anathema was pronounced against him by Felix at this synod, after the deaths of the tyrants Illus and Leontius.

Line 23.—“Here he composed treatises and hymns.” Gregory the Great praises these works, book III, chapter 2; according to John the Deacon in Gregory’s Life, he arranged them in a more suitable form: “But from the Gelasian book concerning the solemn rites of the Mass he removed much, altered a little, and added certain things.”

Peter the Fuller had given the pope an occasion for this. Theodore the Reader reports, in book II, that Peter instituted the following practices: “that the sacred chrism should be consecrated in the Church before all the people; that the invocation over the waters should take place in the evening on the feast of the Epiphany; that in every prayer the name of the Mother of God should be pronounced; and finally, that the creed should be recited at each collect.”

Since Peter might therefore have inserted into the hymns certain expressions capable of supporting his own error, just as he had done in the Trisagion, Gelasius wished to prevent the danger and to regulate the solemn rites of the Mass. Whatever may have been the reason for their institution, the Gelasian books remained in use among the churches beyond the year 800. In the Chronicle of the Abbey of Centula of Saint Richarius, where the books of the sacristy are discussed, we read as follows, book III, chapter 3, according to Bacher’s *Spicilegium*, volume IV:

“Concerning the books of the sacristy that serve the ministry of the altar. Three Gregorian missals: a Gregorian missal, and a Gelasian missal arranged in modern times by Albinus. Nineteen Gelasian missals.”

See Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 25, section 10.

[Col. 0418C]

Line 2.—“Of King Theodoric.” Although Theodoric was an Arian, he nevertheless held Catholics in esteem and deserved well not only of Catholic bishops but also of the apostolic see itself. Theodoret, Nicephorus, Zonaras, Cedrenus, and others write that he beheaded a certain Catholic who, out of regard for him, was passing over to the Arians, saying: “If you have not preserved sincere faith toward God, how will you provide a sound conscience for me, who am only a man?”

Line 2 and 3.—“Of Zeno Augustus.” Anastasius, the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, is mistaken. The authority of Marcellinus Comes, Cassiodorus in his Chronicle, Evagrius, Cedrenus, and other writers establishes that the emperor Zeno, during the consulship of Olybrius, in the year of the Lord 491—the ninth year of Pope Felix—was seized by epilepsy so severely that he appeared to be dead and was buried alive. Thus, as a just punishment from God, he received the proper reward of his pretended piety and religion.

Pope Hormisdas arranged and ordered that his name, although he had already been dead for many years, be erased from the list of Catholic emperors by the emperor Justin. This was not to condemn him as dead, but to declare that a heretic who had died without repentance was alien and unworthy of that communion in which the Catholic Church communicates with the dead through certain prescribed rites. See Baronius, under the year of the Lord 491, sections 2 and following.

[Col. 0419A]

Line 23 and 24.—“Here he composed treatises and books against Eutyches and Nestorius.” Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14, testifies that this was a substantial and distinguished volume, in these words: “Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote against Eutyches and Nestorius a substantial and distinguished volume, together with treatises on various Scriptures and on the Sacraments, in polished language,” and so forth.

It is therefore clear that the little book *On the Two Natures against Eutyches and Nestorius*, found in the *Library of the Holy Fathers* and beginning, “It was also necessary …,” cannot be attributed to Gelasius, Roman pontiff. It is only a small work, contained within a single book. Moreover, the author of that little work greatly praises the writings of Eusebius of Caesarea, although Pope Gelasius listed Eusebius among the apocryphal writers in the acts of the Roman council. The author also adduces many testimonies from the Greek Fathers but few, or none, from the Latin Fathers; he therefore appears to have been Greek rather than Latin.

Although he cites fifteen Greek Fathers, he produces only two Latins, Ambrose and Damasus, while omitting Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Innocent, Leo, Prosper, and other similar writers whom Pope Gelasius, being thoroughly familiar with them, would never have omitted. After a lengthy investigation of the matter, Baronius most diligently concludes that the author of this little book *On the Two Natures against Eutyches* and of the *Acts of the Council of Nicaea*, which are printed in volume II of the councils, is one and the same. He bases this conclusion both on the fact that in each work the author admits that he composed both works and on the fact that he greatly praises Eusebius of Caesarea and entirely frees him from suspicion of Arianism, as is evident from the preface to each work.

[Col. 0419C]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Gelasius succeeded Felix during the consulship of Anastasius and Rufus—that is, in the year of Christ 492—as Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, a nearly contemporary author, testifies in his Chronicle. Marcellinus Comes, however, places the succession two years later, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

In this pontifical chronology, one should trust the bishop of Tunnuna, who wrote about his Western patriarch and was close to him, rather than Marcellinus, a layman living at Constantinople and somewhat more distant both in place and in time. The testimonies of the manuscripts and catalogues that we cited above concerning the chronology of Felix demonstrate this. The facts themselves also prove it, as is shown in Gelasius’s letters.

His eighth letter to the emperor Anastasius was written before the emperor had openly professed himself an Eutychian heretic and leader of the Acephali sect, as Binius observes in his notes under the year 494. In this letter Gelasius clears himself of the charge that he had not sent letters to the same prince through the envoys of King Theodoric, who had gone there and returned to Rome around the end of 493. Therefore, when the envoys departed, Gelasius was already governing the Roman Church.

His seventh letter, written by Gelasius on the Kalends of November during the consulship of Albinus—that is, in the same year, 493—to all the bishops throughout Picenum, clearly proves that the beginning of his pontificate must be placed before the consulship of Asterius. It must be placed, with Victor of Tunnuna, in the year 492. Since Saint Felix III died on 24 February, the day on which he is commemorated, and the see remained vacant for five days according to the *Bibliothecarius*, it follows that Gelasius was ordained Roman bishop on the Kalends of March, which in that year fell on a Sunday.

In some copies of Anastasius, in the Codex Cavensis, and in one of the Colbertine manuscripts, his tenure is given as four years, eight months, and nineteen days.
