Some manuscripts subtract one day from this total, others ten days. From this it is inferred that his death should be assigned to 19 November. Bede and Usuardus record the date in this way.

Anastasius writes that he was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter two days later, namely on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December. His memory is likewise kept on that day in the very ancient Hieronymian Martyrology of the canons of Lucca, edited by Florentinius, page 1053: “On the Kalends of December, Pope Gelasius,” as it now appears in Baronius’s *Roman Martyrology*.

Because the patriarchal basilicas of the city of Rome, on account of the feast of the Presentation of the Mother of God celebrated on the same day, 21 November, commemorate Pope Saint Gelasius on the 26th, that day is the octave of his departure to the Lord.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

Line 9.—“Here he issued a decree concerning the whole Church.” Among the decrees of Gelasius that concern the universal Church, the most prominent is the one celebrated by so many writers: namely, the decree concerning the canon of the books of sacred Scripture, which Gelasius confirmed at a Roman synod with seventy bishops, on the basis of the tradition received from his predecessors. I say “confirmed,” not “first fashioned.”

In the historical notes on the section concerning Clement I, we demonstrated that from the very beginning of the nascent Church the catalogue of the divine Scriptures had been entrusted to this holy Roman Church, the mother and teacher of all the others, once it had become the see of Peter. From it an authoritative judgment—and, as it were, a seal—was sought concerning the word of God written in both Testaments, as we showed from blessed Augustine in book IV and V of his work *Against the Letter of the Manichaeans*.

No one should therefore be surprised that Gelasius, following the example of Clement and the constant care of Peter’s successors, reviewed the canon of the divine Scriptures once more and ordered it restored to the true text through Jerome at the command of Damasus. During Gelasius’s time, as the *Bibliothecarius* mentions in this number, line 4, Manichaeans were found in the city of Rome.

The Manichaean heresy rejected many books of the Old Testament, especially the Prophets, as is clear from the Fathers and particularly from Augustine, formerly one of their adherents but later their vanquisher. The truth handed down by the Church therefore had to be opposed to the impious blasphemy of those who denied the Scriptures, together with the key of knowledge by which they could be brought forth and interpreted.

To produce the canon of the Scriptures was as ready and familiar to the Roman Church as displaying its sanctuaries, the crypts of the martyrs, and the walls, apses, and ornaments of its titular churches and basilicas. In all these places, the entire collection of the books of the Old and New Testaments is presented for recognition by the faithful, just as in libraries and archives—or rather, it is displayed more openly in sacred buildings than in chests and libraries.

Even those who do not know letters, and therefore cannot be instructed by chests and libraries, can establish the canon of the divinely inspired Scriptures by looking upon the histories and images taken from the sacred writings, used to adorn the tombs of the faithful and the crypts of the martyrs amid the fierce heat of the persecutions, and later, after peace had been restored to the Church, to decorate the titular churches and basilicas.

The place requires me to select, as briefly as possible, something from each of the books of both Testaments that was dedicated either in the cemeteries of the holy martyrs or in the sacred buildings of the earliest titular churches and basilicas, from the apostolic age itself down to the pontificate of Gelasius. Thus, anyone wishing to hand on the canon of the sacred books need only point to these precious monuments of the first five centuries of the Christian era preserved by the Roman Church.

The Basilica of Liberius, in the mosaics of Sixtus III, as we have already seen in another dissertation appended to the notes, displays a sequence of events narrated both in the Pentateuch of Moses and in the books of Joshua and Judges.

A single sarcophagus of Junius Bassus, bearing the date of the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius—that is, the year 359 of the Christian era—was placed in the crypts of the Vatican basilica before the confessio of the holy apostles. It presents to us from Genesis the fall of our first parents and the sacrifice of Abraham, together with selected passages from Job, Daniel, and other books of divine Scripture.

In the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, decorated by Saint Leo the Great with mosaics, paintings, and scenes, the oracles of the sacred books are displayed from Genesis to the Apocalypse. The Prophets are listed along the uppermost gable of the walls, and their names—Hosea, and so forth—are written in foot-high letters beneath their images.

Accordingly, on the bronze doors made for the same basilica in the eleventh century, both the so-called Major and the Minor Prophets are listed. This is clear from the surviving inscriptions of several of both groups, still visible there:

ΒΑΡΟΥΧ — Baruch, who is joined to Jeremiah;

ΙΕΖΕΧΙΗΛ — Ezekiel;

ΔΑΝΙΗΛ — Daniel;

ΙΩΗΛ — Joel;

ΑΒΔΙΑΣ — Obadiah;

ΙΩΝΑΣ — Jonah;

ΝΑΥΜ — Naum;

ΑΒΒΑΚΟΥΜ — Habakkuk. Here it should be noted that the name Habakkuk is written as it appears in the Greek manuscripts, Αββακούμ, *Abbakoum*;

ΣΟΦΟΝΙΑΣ — Zephaniah;

ΖΑΧΑΡΙΑΣ — Zechariah.

The images and names of the others have been destroyed.

From this there spread and persisted through later generations the custom of painting and carving the images and names of these same Prophets, and sometimes also their sayings, on the doors of basilicas, on the apses and walls of titular churches, deaconries, and baptisteries, and on vessels and ornaments.

On the bronze doors of the same Pauline basilica, made at Constantinople in the eleventh century of the Christian era and published by the often-mentioned prelate Giovanni Ciampini in *Ancient Monuments*, volume I, chapter 4, other prophets are also engraved. Their deeds are recorded in the Books of Kings and Chronicles: Elijah, number 35, and Elisha, number 44. The oracles of others are represented in volumes, such as the volume of the Prophet David, number 33, which bears the verse from Psalm 44: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear.”

On Jeremiah’s small tablet, number 36, is written: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him,” from Baruch, chapter 3.

On the volume of Habakkuk—whose name is engraved in Greek letters, ΑΒΒΑΚΟΥΜ—is carved the verse from chapter 3, verse 3: “God shall come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the mountain.”

In Isaiah’s hands appears verse 14 of chapter 7: “Behold, a virgin,” and so forth.

Zephaniah presents the expectation of the resurrection from chapter 3, verse 8; Jonah presents the hope of heavenly assistance from chapter 2, verse 3; and the same method is observed with the others.

In the chief of all the deaconries, Saint Mary’s on the Via Lata, where there is an ancient tradition that the apostle Paul held catechetical instruction with the evangelist Luke and that Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles, images of the Prophets can be seen, colored with their ancient paintings. The same is true in the underground chamber beneath the presbytery of the deaconry of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

I pass over many other paintings in the cemeteries, which may be viewed in Aringhi’s *Subterranean Rome*. From them the entire canon of the sacred Scriptures can be gathered, adorned by the martyrs and confessors of Christ themselves, as well as by the predecessors of Gelasius.

Nor did the generations immediately following the age of Gelasius show less zeal in carefully preserving the sacred inheritance of the divine writings in the Roman titular churches through their priests. One titular church may stand for all: that of Saint Clement.

As we write, the principal altar of this church is being restored with greater magnificence by the most illustrious and reverend Lord Annibale, Cardinal Albani, Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church. Following the example of his great-uncle Clement XI, who cultivated the same sacred building, he found a marble slab more precious than all gold and silver. It had anciently been turned into the front of the altar, and on it the zeal of Gregory, priest and cardinal of the same titular church under the holy pope Zacharias, is attested: he dedicated books of both Testaments within the library or sacristy of his titular church. The inscription reads:

> The Israelite people offered gifts from the countryside:
>
> One, indeed, gold; another, silver;
>
> One, bronze; another, the hair of goats.
>
> But I, unhappy Gregory, chief priest
>
> Of the nourishing apostolic see and keeper of this titular church,
>
> And supreme client of blessed Clement,
>
> Offer these small gifts to you, O Christ, from your treasures,
>
> In the time of Zacharias, the supreme bishop,
>
> Through your martyr and saint Clement,
>
> Through whose merits may I deserve
>
> To be freed from my sins
>
> And enter into blessed eternal life.
>
> [AISTI: reading and sense uncertain], how much the kingdom of heaven is worth.
>
> Receive these, Lord, I beg, like the widow’s mite:
>
> The books of the Old and New Testaments,
>
> The Octateuch, the Books of Kings, the Psalter, and the Prophets,
>
> Solomon, Ezra, and the books of the histories,
>
> Full and complete. Reader, seek the sequence
>
> Of these syllables.

[Col. 0421C]

The final verse of this inscription indicates that another marble tablet had been placed not far from the first, on which Gregory the priest had caused the verses that followed to be engraved. It is difficult to interpret the final words otherwise, since they are carved in smaller letters at the bottom of the tablet, where the reader is instructed to seek the continuation of the preceding sentence: “Reader, seek the sequence of these syllables.”

It is to be regretted that the continuation of this donation has been lost. There Gregory presumably enumerated, after the books of the Old Testament, all those belonging to the New Testament and thus the complete canon of sacred Scripture—or else other gifts offered along with the books listed above. This would be so if, as the penultimate verse indicates, he had given his titular church a complete copy of both Testaments, or if he had offered additional gifts together with the books already enumerated.

[Col. 0421D]

With complete justice, the most eminent Cardinal Albani removed this stone from its place and displayed Gregory’s inscription to everyone. Builders of a more primitive age had imprudently concealed it by turning the letters toward the center of the altar and presenting to the spectators the uninscribed surface of the marble.

As the most equitable appreciator of this precious monument, he moved the stone to the middle aisle of the same titular church, decorated it with a magnificent border and a cornice skillfully assembled from the finest marbles, and presented it for clear viewing by us and by posterity.

The most illustrious and reverend prelate Justus Fontaninus, archbishop of Ancyra, reported the same inscription three days after the stone was discovered, among the additions to his most learned commentary *On Christian Discipline*. The most reverend Father de Vitriaco prepared the inscription with equal speed in a most learned study while illustrating the tomb of Titus Flavius Clemens, martyr of Christ and a man of consular rank.

After the abundant harvest gathered by such great men, there remains for us a worthwhile gleaning: to collect what can be learned from the enumeration of the sacred books recorded in this inscription, although we treated the matter more fully in a letter to the eminent and reverend Cardinal Albani, titular of the church.

[Col. 0422D]

The sequence of the books of the Old Testament is expressed there in correspondence with the Hebrew canon. First it lists the Octateuch, then the Books of Kings, third the Psalter, fourth the Prophets, afterward Solomon, then Ezra, and finally the books of the Histories.

The cardinal of venerable memory, Thomas, whom the Roman Church should rightly employ to adorn its precious monuments with equal piety and ecclesiastical learning, teaches from Cassiodorus’s *Institutions of Divine Learning* that this custom of the Christian Church should be referred especially to the fifth century—that is, the Gelasian age of which we are now speaking. It concerns the edition of the sacred books according to the translators of the Septuagint and the ancient titles used by Saint Jerome.

Cardinal Thomas begins with the Octateuch, just as this Gregory, priest of Saint Clement, does in his inscription:

“Concerning the titles of the Octateuch,” he says, “that is, the eight volumes of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, Cassiodorus writes as follows in book I of *On Divine Learning*: ‘So that the text of the aforementioned Octateuch might be opened to us by a certain brief outline, at the beginning of the books we believed that titles from the entire sequence of reading should be set down, transcribed in their proper order by our predecessors,’” and so forth.

Then he continues:

“Concerning the titles of the Books of Kings and Chronicles, the same Cassiodorus speaks in such a way that the ancients appear to have possessed titles for the Books of Kings, while he says that he himself added new titles to the Books of Chronicles,” and so forth.

Cassiodorus lists the third codex as that of the Prophets and the fourth as that of the Psalter. Our Gregory, however, retaining the same division in the titles of the codices, places the Psalter before the Prophets in the sequence, following the order of time preserved by the Greek edition of the Septuagint in the very ancient Vatican manuscript of the Sixtine edition, although the Hebrew Bible places the Psalms and the books they call the Hagiographa after the Prophets.

As his fifth codex, Cassiodorus has Solomon, just as this Gregory, the priest of Saint Clement, does. As Cardinal Thomas observes, Gregory includes in it five books: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus.

In the sixth codex Cassiodorus gathers eight books, expressed under the mixed designation of Hagiographa and historical books: Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, two books of Ezra, and two books of Maccabees.

These correspond in number and order to the ancient codex of Alexandria called that of Thecla, except for the first book, Job, which that Alexandrian codex joins to the Psalms and places before Solomon’s books, adding also Third and Fourth Maccabees before the Psalter.

Gregory the priest mentions Ezra and the Histories more briefly, joining the historical and hagiographical books together with the canonical books of Ezra. For Saint Cyril of Jerusalem and Saint Gregory of Nazianzus place Job with the Psalter, as belonging to the class of metrical books, together with Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Ferrandus, *Summary of the Bible*, book I, final chapter, and others who discuss the canon of Scripture make the same observation.

The two books of Maccabees finally complete the catalogue of the historical books. They are therefore indicated by the name of the genre or class, or by the term “histories.” In this way, on the tablet, we see the canon of the Old Testament gathered and distributed into the same classes and sequence according to the custom of the edition of the Septuagint translators.

Through these illustrious monuments, dedicated throughout the titular churches, basilicas, and cemeteries of the Roman Church from the earliest centuries, the genuine canon of the sacred Scriptures, gathered from the apostolic age and handed down continuously through the care of the Roman pontiffs, remains active on our altars, mosaics, and marbles just as in libraries and archives. We saw this above in the notes on Clement. The canon is the same as that approved by the Roman council held under Gelasius and by the decree concerning the Church that the *Bibliothecarius* records.

While these matters were being prepared for the press, the engraver was making arrangements on this day, the tenth day before the Kalends of July. The eminent and reverend Lord Cardinal Albani, Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church, had arranged for the sacred body of Titus Flavius Clemens, martyr of Christ, to be transferred on the following day. He had magnificently adorned the same titular church, restored it to brilliant condition throughout, and ordered that the pavement, constructed about three hundred years earlier from intermingled marble in mosaic work, be carefully polished.

It happened opportunely that, while I was examining numerous fragments of ancient inscriptions then being fitted and adapted to such work, I recognized a fragment of another marble tablet. On it Gregory the priest had listed the books he had donated to this titular church.

Only a few words are legible, since the fragment is square and less than a palm in size; but those few words are sufficient to show that this marble tablet was a portion of the second tablet whose existence the final verse of the first had indicated by the instruction: “Reader, seek the continuation of these syllables.”

The letters engraved on this fragment are arranged as follows:

[Col. 0424B]

The shape and size of these letters, as well as the intervals or distances between the lower and upper lines, correspond exactly to the inscription on the preceding tablet discovered at the altar. It can scarcely be doubted, therefore, that this is a portion of the second tablet, on which Gregory the priest warned that the continuation of the syllables should be sought.

Since it mentions a *book* and a *sacramentary*, I think that the writings of Augustine, Ambrose, and other Fathers were also listed in the preceding line and donated by Gregory himself, together with the books of both Testaments, to this titular church for the use of the clergy.

There is a comparable example in the famous marble tablet formerly belonging to the deaconry and now the basilica of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. The late Cardinal Thomas published it in the appendix to his *Ancient Responsorial and Antiphonal Books of the Roman Church*, page 448; it was republished with learned notes by the distinguished Giovanni Maria Crescimbeni, archpriest of the same basilica, in his history of that basilica, page 82.

On that tablet Theobald gives estates to the Church of Saint Valentine—namely, a house, a cell, a vineyard—and, in addition, books for the use of the clergy serving there:

> ONE MISSALE;
>
> TWO ANTIPHONARIES;
>
> ONE BOOK OF THE DAY-OFFICE;
>
> TWO OTHER BOOKS OF THE FERIAL NIGHT OFFICE;
>
> ONE BOOK OF GENESIS WITH THE CANONICAL HISTORIES;
>
> A PASSIONARY;
>
> A DIALOGUE;
>
> A SCINTILLARY;
>
> TWO HYMNARIES;
>
> BOOKS FROM THE MORAL WORKS.

After the books he lists the sacred vessels, namely “a gilded silver chalice with its tube and paten, a silver hand censer,” and so forth.

This donation of Theobald belongs to the year 902 of the Christian era, on the day when the church was consecrated, as expressed in these verses:

[Col. 0424D]

> In the time of the ninth and supreme pontiff John,
>
> This hall was consecrated on the final day of November,
>
> While the fifth indiction was running its course.

The titular priests of the Roman churches, and the heads of the deaconries and other sacred buildings, therefore took care that, together with carefully corrected copies of the divine Scriptures, liturgical books, ritual and pontifical books, and approved works of the holy Fathers according to the catalogue and decree of Gelasius, should be deposited in the archives and libraries of those same churches.

Thus, just as Gregory the priest, under Zacharias in the eighth century of Christ, brought into the titular church of Saint Clement the books of both Testaments, a sacramentary, other ritual books, and the works of the holy Fathers, so Theobald, eighty years after the pontificate of Zacharias, gave the Church of Saint Valentine the books of Genesis and the canonical histories, along with ritual and liturgical books, the Dialogues of Saint Gregory, and the books of the *Moralia*, as recorded in the inscriptions mentioned above.

[Col. 0425A] Nor were the distinguished men of the Gelasian age less zealous in enriching churches near the City with such sacred literary equipment, as is clearly shown by the charter of the archive of Tivoli, called the Cornutian charter, published more than once by eminent scholars—first by Suaresius at Rome, then by Mabillon at Paris in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*. He places it before the others as the most ancient, since it is dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, under the consulship of Lord Leo, Pope Augustus, for the fourth time, and Probia[nus], a man of senatorial rank—that is, in the Christian year 471.

In that charter of donation, Flavius Valia, Quintus Theodosius, a man of senatorial rank, and Julius, count and master of both military services, grant estates to the Cornutian Church, together with sacred furnishings, vessels, vestments, and finally sacred books—namely, the four Gospels, the Apostle, the Psalter, and the *Comes*. I have arranged for a copy of that charter to be printed among the *Prolegomena*.

Yet of all men, the one who most diligently followed these Roman examples and the decrees of Gelasius in enriching the cathedral church of the Holy Church of Verona, which must forever be revered by me under the title of venerable mother, was that celebrated archdeacon Pacificus. He is said to have furnished its library with two hundred and eighteen books composed by himself, together with a gloss on the Old and New Testaments, as is recorded in the funerary inscription set up under Louis the Pious around the year 820. In the judgment of the great Panvinius, he was a supreme theologian and an outstanding student of many other disciplines. Panvinius gives this judgment of him in *Antiquitates Veronenses*, Book VI, page 153, where, speaking also of the library founded by him and of a considerable part of it reverently preserved in the chapter archive, he writes:

> “In my judgment he founded the most celebrated library in the whole world. Traces of it still exist at Verona in the monastery of the canons of Verona, adorned with nearly two hundred books written in large capital letters on parchment.”

From the age of Panvinius down to our own, there have been no lack of guardians of so great a legacy who preserved it for posterity. But above all our contemporaries deserve congratulations, and immortal thanks are owed to the generosity and zeal of the most illustrious members of the chapter now flourishing. They have raised from its foundations a more spacious hall and are striving not only to care more diligently for the same codices, which were almost hidden in a dark and cramped archive, and to bring them into the light of public use, but also to add a library that can compete with many others in the abundance, elegance, and selectness of its printed books. This work is promoted by their most deserving archpriest, Giovanni Francesco Musello, a Veronese patrician, under the auspices of the most illustrious and reverend bishop Francesco Trevisiani, who, by ancestral nobility, cultivation of letters, and patronage, is among the bishops of the Venetian Republic especially distinguished.

Of the books selected nearly nine hundred years ago by the archdeacon Pacificus and written in capital letters, I have seen many containing the text of the sacred Scriptures, the Acts of the councils, the letters of the Roman pontiffs, the works of the holy Fathers, and ritual books according to the custom of the Roman Church. I shall not append here their lengthy catalogue, which seems entirely unnecessary. I shall mention only one codex published by us in the *Prolegomena* of this same volume: namely, the *Roman Order*, which displays the pontifical rites and the administration of the sacraments. It is known to have been written in the age of Louis the Pious, as I proved in that place.

On this occasion it pleased me to show, by means of the decree of Gelasius and the Roman inscriptions under Zacharias, how carefully the supreme pontiffs and the priests and ministers of this Church selected sacred codices for the instruction of the clergy and kept them available in their titular churches. From this there arose an imitational influence throughout the other churches of the West, especially those which, from the age of Charlemagne onward, after the barbarism of the Lombard period had been dispelled, brought such an abundant supply of sacred writings into their bookcases.

If anyone, after recognizing the canon of the sacred books both in the letter of Pope and martyr Clement in the first century and in the marble inscriptions of the title of Saint Clement in the eighth century, still wishes to know the individual books of divine Scripture in other monuments of equal antiquity belonging to the Roman Church, he will find the Heptateuch represented in the mosaics of the Liberian Basilica built by Saint Sixtus III. He will recognize the Books of Kings and Chronicles in the scenes depicting David as a slinger, painted in the third chamber of the cemetery of Callistus, panel I, no. 3; and Elijah and Elisha carved on the sarcophagus of the Vatican cemetery, p. 305, in Aringhius’s *Rome Underground*, Book II, chapter 10. He will find the history of Job on the sarcophagus of Junius Bassus, discovered in the Vatican crypts and placed there at the Confession of the holy Apostles, as well as in many other monuments encountered in Aringhius.

He will recognize the Major and Minor Prophets depicted in the Basilica of Saint Paul and in the other titular churches, deaconries, and cemeteries mentioned above. He will find the history of Tobit and the fish in the painting of the cemetery of Callistus, panel III of the third chamber, no. 11, where the prophet Jonah is also depicted sleeping beneath the gourd. In sculpture, Jonah appears in many sarcophagi: swallowed by the sea-monster, cast up on the shore, and restored to life.

Ezekiel’s proclamation to those rising again is likewise observed in a relief in the Vatican, in Aringhius, vol. I, p. 327. Daniel praying among the lions frequently appears, as on the sarcophagus of Junius Bassus in the Vatican crypts. The three boys unharmed in the furnace, and the chaste Susanna vindicated from the outrage and accusations of the elders, likewise appear in many paintings and reliefs of the cemeteries described by the same Aringhius—namely, in the Vatican cemetery, that of Callistus, and that of Saint Agnes.

Finally, Shaphan offering Josiah the book of the law discovered by Hilkiah is carved in relief on an ancient sarcophagus found in the cemetery of Lucina and subsequently transferred, together with the relics of the holy Innocents, by Sixtus V to the chapel within the Liberian Basilica, magnificently built by him, at the altar of Saint Lucy. Aringhius reproduced its image in *Rome Underground*, vol. I, p. 423, together with many histories of both Testaments represented there.

Apart from these most ancient documents, which indicate the books received into the canon of divine Scripture, the Roman Church displays in the *Roman Order* the readings of individual books prescribed for its clergy according to the cycle of the year. From this it is known that the sacred codices were transmitted continuously from hand to hand and reverently kept in each of its basilicas and titular churches. From this source they were distributed to the other churches of the West, which note on the very front and titles of their codices—written out over ten centuries and more—that copies of the *Roman Order*, just like the sacramentaries, had been transcribed from the authentic book of the library of the papal chamber.

The Roman Church, therefore, always had these documents ready as the teacher of the other churches for distinguishing the divine writings that it had received by apostolic authority. For this reason Gelasius, among the other measures established for the government of the whole Church, took particular care of this chief matter: that he should preserve intact for posterity the inheritance received from the Fathers. He published a canon concerning the sacred Scriptures and purified the writings of other authors, which are usefully employed for understanding those Scriptures and for instructing the people of God.

[Col. 0426D] Line 23.—“He composed treatises and hymns, like blessed Ambrose the bishop,” etc. I shall add, both for the elucidation of this passage and of the preceding one, some learned observations recently published by the Reverend Father Dom Simon Mopinot, cited in a letter of his to the Reverend Father Dom Charles Conrade, no. 8, in these words:

> “I come to Gelasius. His writings, and especially the treatises embedded in them, require a man capable both of applying remedies to what has been corrupted and of defending what has been called into doubt. So many ugly blemishes everywhere disfigure the text; so many convolutions and conflicting judgments of critics hold the reader’s mind in suspense.
>
> “Constantius brought to the completion of this work everything that study and labor, everything that the use and assistance of manuscript books could provide. His thirty-third letter, or *Decree concerning the Books to Be Received*, is a witness to this: he restored it to its ancient integrity and vindicated it for its own author. He proves, of course, that the decree is neither a fabrication of Isidore Mercator, as occurred to William Cave and others, nor composed by Damasus, Leo the Great, or Hormisdas, as others think, but was issued by Gelasius in a Roman synod. This is the opinion of the learned men Baronius, Norisius, and Fontanini.
>
> “Fontanini had already established this point by proofs; Constantius adds many others of his own, everywhere supported by the testimony of manuscripts. The principal points of his notable dissertation are these:
>
> “1. As I have already said, the author of the decree is no one other than Gelasius.
>
> “2. The decree grew through additions made by Hormisdas, though not many—only a very few, and finally only those which cannot belong to the time of Gelasius.
>
> “3. These additions themselves were rashly attributed to Gelasius in printed books, since they are absent from all, or almost all, handwritten copies, except those which bear this same work under the name of Hormisdas.
>
> “4. The fragments of the Roman synod that Baronius more than once cited under the name of Damasus and that Lucas Holstenius brought to light ought to be referred to the first part of the decree. To these should then be joined the canon of Scripture, which also belongs to Gelasius. Thus we shall possess the decree not only in a purer form but enlarged through the greater part of its substance.
>
> “5. Finally, the chronological notice, which has given rise to so many disputes, ought to be expunged, since it rests upon no sufficiently firm authority and was in fact rashly imported from another letter of Gelasius.
>
> “After explaining these points at length in his preliminary notice, he unfolds many other matters in the notes that satisfy the criticisms, or at least the observations, of the critics.
>
> “He maintains and proves that the treatise *On the Two Natures*, a wholly golden work attributed by some to Gelasius of Cyzicus, belongs to Pope Gelasius I. The learned Jesuit priest Peter Francis Chiffletius had previously done the same. Constantius completes the matter in his customary manner—that is, with new arguments that correct even Chiffletius’s mistakes.
>
> “He revised and purged, on the authority of manuscripts, another treatise entitled *On the Bond of Anathema*, which has been so mutilated by errors that one might think it almost a single wound. He devoted the same labor to the treatise in which the errors of the Pelagians are refuted.
>
> “Finally, to say nothing of other matters, he gathers more than forty fragments of letters by the same pope, partly from books written by hand and partly from canonical compilers. These appear neither in the Roman editions of the papal letters nor even in the editions of the councils, if one subtracts the twelve collected by Labbe.
>
> “The learned man wished all these materials to be arranged in a proper order and illuminated with notes relating to history and ecclesiastical discipline, so that the reader might obtain the proper fruit of their usefulness—not from the entire harvest, perhaps, but at least from the gleaning.”]

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

Line 3.—“On Mount Gargano.” The discovery of the cave of Mount Gargano in Apulia, near Manfredonia, formerly called Sipontum, is placed in the second year of Gelasius, that is, in the Christian year 493.

Line 14.—“If they did not repent.” It was the custom of the primitive Church to wait longer for those who might eventually return to the embrace of its mercy.]

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

Line 2.—“In the time of King Theodoric and the Emperor Zeno.” After his election to the pontificate, he announced it by letter, in Letter 3 of the Collection of Councils, to the bishops of Dardania, whom he urged not to communicate with the Eutychianists. That letter, however, was not sent at the beginning of his pontificate; for, as he himself says, he was delayed by the continuing storm of wars. Since peace between Theodoric and Odoacer was concluded in the year 493, it is probable that the letter was written in that same year. For Letter 12, also written to Aeonius, bishop of Arles, concerning the beginning of his pontificate, was sent in the year 494, specifically on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.

Line 6.—“Here, after the synodical proceedings,” etc. Pope Gelasius held his first synod at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of March, during the consulship of Flavius Viator, a man of senatorial rank, and therefore in the year 495, as is recorded in the Acts.

At that synod Misenus, formerly legate of the Apostolic See to Constantinople under Pope Felix, had been infected by communion with Acacius and had consequently been deprived by Felix, together with another legate, Vitalis, of the priesthood and communion. He now begged the mercy and communion of the Apostolic See. His case was examined, and he was reconciled with the Church by Gelasius, while the other legate, Vitalis, had already died under excommunication. Gelasius says in the synod:

> “Misenus therefore having regularly professed that he detests all heresies, especially the Eutychian heresy together with Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy the Cat, Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople, and Peter of Antioch, or all their successors, followers, and communicants, and that he strikes them with perpetual anathema, shall receive the grace of communion with the Apostolic See and the priestly dignity, which he received through Catholic tradition.”

All fifty-five bishops subscribed to this decree.

In the autumn of that same year, 495, or more probably in the year 496, Gelasius held a second synod at Rome. For when the Church had for several years been burdened with many apocryphal books and needed a healing hand to distinguish the genuine from the spurious, Pope Gelasius convened a council at Rome and arranged the order of the books that the Roman Church accepted, rejected, or regarded as doubtful.

That decree concerning the divine Scriptures and the works of the holy Fathers received in the Catholic Church greatly presses the heterodox, who reject tradition and mutilate the number of canonical books at will, for the advantage of their sects. The books of Job, Tobit, Judith, and Maccabees are mentioned in it, as are the Letter to the Hebrews, the Apocalypse of John, the two letters of Peter, the three of the apostle John, and the one of Jude—in a word, all the books of both the New and Old Testaments.

The same council then establishes the order of the patriarchal churches, namely, the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene churches, and likewise mentions four general councils. It also lists certain works of the holy Fathers approved by the Church, followed finally by a notice of the apocryphal books that the Church does not receive. Seventy-two bishops subscribed to this decree.

Catholics do not agree among themselves concerning the author of this decree. Some attribute it to Damasus, others to the Roman pontiff Hormisdas. But the author of the Baronian criticism demonstrates that Gelasius is its certain and undisputed author.

For, first, as regards Damasus, the decree cannot be attributed to him, since most of the authors of the works mentioned in it lived and wrote after Damasus. When the catalogue of condemned books is drawn up, the books of Cassian and Faustus of Riez are listed in this form:

> “The apocryphal works of Cassian, priest of Gaul.”
>
> “The apocryphal works of Faustus of Riez, of Gaul.”

Cassian and Faustus, however, lived and wrote after Damasus.

Nor can the decree be attributed to Pope Hormisdas. For at the beginning of the sixth century, when a controversy arose concerning the books of Faustus, not only in the West but also in the East, Possessor, an African bishop sent into exile by Trasamund, king of Africa, was staying at Constantinople. Having been consulted about those books, he himself consulted Pope Hormisdas as to what should be thought about them.

Possessor’s report to Hormisdas is found in vol. IV of the Councils, p. 1529, and is said to have been received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, during the consulship of Rusticus, a man of senatorial rank. It was therefore in the year 520.

Hormisdas replied to Possessor on the thirteenth day of August, in Letter 70, where, among other things, he says:

> “The venerable judgment of the Fathers, acting not without foresight, defined for faithful posterity what the Catholic doctrines were. Under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, it also established with certainty which ancient books should be received as authoritative, lest a reader, indulging his own opinion, should assert not what suited the Church’s edification but what his own pleasure had conceived.”

These words clearly imply that the decree concerning books to be received and not received was issued not by Hormisdas but by one of his predecessors in a Roman synod. It was not issued by Anastasius or Symmachus, who followed Gelasius and preceded Hormisdas, since no one has ever asserted this and no manuscript bears the name of either of them. Rather, it was issued by Gelasius, to whom innumerable codices attribute it. Whoever wishes to know more about this matter should read the criticism of Baronius under the year 494.

Line 13.—“And he condemned Acacius and Peter forever, if they did not repent.” Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning whom we have spoken above under Simplicius and Felix, died outside communion with the Church in the year 489. Flavitas was appointed in his place. But when Flavitas too died after three months, Euphemius was appointed as his successor.

According to Evagrius, Book III, chapter 23, Euphemius accepted and honored the Council of Chalcedon and regarded Peter Mongus with hatred because Peter had anathematized that council. When Euphemius learned of Gelasius’s election, he wrote to him, according to ancient custom, inserting a profession of his faith so that he might deserve to obtain communion with the Catholic Church.

Although Gelasius found Euphemius’s profession of faith entirely consonant with Catholic truth, he nevertheless discovered in Euphemius something worthy of reproach: namely, that he had by no means removed the name of his predecessor Acacius from the diptychs, but allowed it to be recited in the sacred services together with the other orthodox bishops. Therefore Gelasius refused to honor Euphemius, although he was in every respect a Catholic man, or the other bishops of the East with the honors of communion, unless they removed Acacius’s name from the diptychs.

This is clear from Letters 1 to Euphemius, 13 to the bishops of Dardania, and 15 to the bishops of the East. Gelasius also wrote a very weighty and eloquent letter to the emperor Anastasius, urging him to obey the Apostolic See and to restore peace to the churches by condemning the name of Acacius. That is Letter 8.

Line 23.—“He composed treatises and hymns,” etc. He also arranged the order of the Mass, and his missals were still extant in the year of the Lord 831 in the abbey of Centula, or Saint Riquier. They are listed in this way in the chronicle of that monastery, Book III, chapter 3, vol. IV of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, in the catalogue of the library’s sacrary books that serve the ministry of the altar:

> “Three Gregorian missals; one Gregorian and Gelasian missal arranged in modern times by Albinus; nineteen Gelasian missals.”

John the Deacon writes in the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, Book II, chapter 12, that Gregory compressed the Gelasian codex into a single volume, removing much from the solemn celebrations of the Mass, adding some things, and altering a few. All writers on ecclesiastical matters assert, and ancient monuments prove, that Gelasius was the first author of the Collects used in the Mass.

In the *Pontifical Book*, concerning Gelasius, we read:

> “He composed the prefaces and prayers of the sacramentary in carefully considered language.”

Regarding these words, Schelstratius writes in his notes:

> “There exists in the Palatine-Vatican Library a manuscript sacramentary approximately a thousand years old, containing prefaces received into use in the Roman Church before the time of Gregory. These may perhaps be the prefaces mentioned in this passage; hence that sacramentary is not improperly called Gelasian.”

Thus Schelstratius. From this passage some attribute to Gelasius the institution of the prefaces. Cardinal Bona, however, in Book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 10, concedes that several prefaces were edited by Gelasius, but nevertheless maintains that it is certain that the use of prefaces already existed in the earliest beginnings of the Church, and that their institution should be attributed either to the apostles or to apostolic men. He proves this at greater length afterward.

There is another codex, the sacramentary of Pope Gelasius, consisting of three books: one concerning the cycle of the year, one concerning the birthdays of the saints, and one concerning Sundays and various occasions. Its antiquity is clearly shown by the fact that the word *Filioque* is absent from the Creed; that several Masses customary in the seventh and eighth centuries are missing; and finally that fewer saints’ birthdays are celebrated than in other liturgies.

That codex, after the Floriacensian library was plundered and dispersed in 1562, came into the hands of Paul Petau, a Parisian senator, and eventually passed into the library of Christina, queen of the Swedes. From her, Thomasius received it and published it at Rome in 1680. In his preface he notes that it was written a short time after Gregory the Great.

To it he added three very ancient missals, namely the Gothic, Frankish, and Old Gallican missals. John Mabillon later had these three reprinted, together with observations on the Gallican liturgy, at Paris in 1685.

As for the canon of the Mass, beginning with the prayer *Te igitur, clementissime Pater* and continuing to the Lord’s Prayer, which is recited aloud after the canon has been completed, some make Pope Gelasius its author; others attribute it to Musaeus, a priest of Marseille; and others to Voconius, bishop of Castellane in Mauretania, who, according to Gennadius, composed sacramentary books.

Bishop Anselm, in *On the Praises of Virginity*, chapter 23, thinks that it was edited by Gregory the Great. Gregory himself, however, in Letter 64 of Book VII, says that it was composed by Scholasticus. Whoever this Scholasticus may have been, it is certain that he was earlier than Gelasius and the others mentioned above.

Nor should we believe Polydore Vergil, who asserts in Book V, chapter 10 of *On the Inventors of Things*, that the canon was assembled by many pontiffs. Even if some added a few words, nevertheless, as Pope Vigilius says in his letter to Eucherius, we received the canon from apostolic tradition. The Council of Trent, Session 22, chapter 4, likewise teaches that the canon consists of the very words of the Lord, the traditions of the apostles, and the institutions of the holy pontiffs.

Nevertheless, with the cited Cardinal Bona, chapter 11, we must observe that no pontiff after Gregory the Great added anything to the canon or altered it. The clause that Anastasius says was added by Gregory III will be discussed in its proper place.

In Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, we find Gelasius’s canon against those who, having received only a portion of the sacred Body, abstained from the chalice:

> “We have learned,” says Gelasius, “that some, having received only a portion of the sacred Body, abstain from the chalice of the sacred Blood. Since, without doubt, they are bound by some superstition—I do not know what—we decree either that they receive the entire sacraments or that they be excluded from the entire sacraments, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without great sacrilege.”

The superstition of the Manichaeans was that wine was the gall of the prince of darkness and had been created by the devil. For this reason they refused to receive communion under the form of wine, as Leo the Great testifies in Sermon IV on Lent.

Thus, in order that those hiding under the Catholic name might be exposed, Gelasius employed the same remedy that Leo had earlier used, ordering that all should communicate under both forms. This was so that Catholics who abstained from the chalice would not make themselves suspected of the Manichaean heresy, and so that the Manichaeans themselves could not escape detection by doing what Catholics did when they communicated under the form of bread alone.

When Gelasius says that the division of the mystery cannot occur without great sacrilege, he is attacking those same Manichaeans who rejected the drink of wine as the devil’s gall. By mutilating the divine mysteries, they plainly bound themselves to great sacrilege.

This account is taken from Baronius and from Cardinal Bona, Book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 18. There he shows that communion under both forms was neither divinely instituted nor ever taught by the ancient Fathers to be necessary for salvation, although from the beginnings of the Church until the twelfth century the faithful always and everywhere communicated under the forms of bread and wine.

That this remedy was effective for detecting the Manichaeans is plainly taught by what the author of the *Pontifical Book* says concerning Gelasius:

> “In his time Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome. He ordered them to be carried away into exile, and he burned their books before the doors of the Basilica of Saint Mary.”

Gelasius published a treatise entitled *On the Bond of Anathema*, in which he undertook to prove that the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon were valid only insofar as the Apostolic See had approved them; that the measures established against Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, by Felix III were just; and that Peter Mongus, the usurper of the see of Alexandria, could have been absolved only by the Apostolic See. It is found in vol. IV of the Councils, and was commented on by Augustine Barbosa in his *Collections of the Doctors*, Part I, decree 15, chapter 3, and by Diego Covarrubias, Book IV of *Various Resolutions*.

In volume IV of the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers* there appears, under the name of Pope Gelasius, a work *On the Two Natures*, against Nestorius and Eutyches. Some attribute it to Gelasius of Cyzicus, others to Gelasius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine.

But, as Spondanus noted in the margin of the *Epitome of Baronius* under the year 496, that book is cited under the name of Pope Gelasius by Saint Fulgentius, himself an African and a contemporary of Gelasius, in his *Book on Five Questions*, chapter 18, preserved by Ferrandus the deacon.

Labbe adds, in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, that it is also cited by Pope John II in a letter to Avienus and the other senators, in which he confirms the faith concerning Christ’s divinity and incarnation with testimonies drawn from every direction, as well as by other later writers. He says that Sirmond is witness that, in manuscripts of good quality, this work is found copied among the undisputed letters of Gelasius. Finally, Gennadius of Marseille, chapter 94 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Honoratus of Autun, following him, in Book II, chapter 93, as well as the author of the *Pontifical Book* himself, attribute it to Pope Gelasius.

As for the argument that heterodox writers draw from this work to prove that the substance of bread and wine remains in the Eucharist, they have already been sufficiently answered by Baronius under the year 496, no. 11 and following; by Catholic authors who have treated the controversies; and recently by Natalis Alexander, Part I, *The Church of the Fifth Century*, pp. 680 and following.

Nevertheless, I cannot omit mentioning a single recent author, Joseph Pamphilius, bishop of Segni, who was living in the year 1579 and attributed this work to Pope John, on page 22 of his *Augustinian Chronicle*.

Finally, the author of the *Pontifical Book* and the aforementioned Gennadius write that Gelasius composed hymns in imitation of Bishop Ambrose. Those hymns, however, have perished, as have his commentaries on the thirteen letters of Saint Paul, which were not free from Pelagian dregs, being either forged or corrupted by heretics, according to Cassiodorus, *On Divine Scripture*, chapter 8.

Valesius, in Book I of his *Ecclesiastical Observations on Evagrius*, chapter 1, and throughout his notes on that same Evagrius, attributes to Pope Gelasius a treatise entitled *A Brief History of the Eutychianists*, or, as the old title has it, *Deeds concerning the Name of Acacius*.

There can be no doubt, however, that he was mistaken. For the first part of this little book is copied word for word from the *Breviary* of Liberatus the deacon, who composed that work under the emperor Justinian; while the second part was collected from Gelasius’s own letters, as is clear to anyone who reads it.]

[Note: [Col. 0431D]

Line 9.—“He established a constitution concerning the whole Church.” The following should be noted from chapter 11 of Book VI of the Most Reverend Archbishop Sommier, to clarify this passage.]

[Col. 0432A] In the decretal letter of Innocent I to Exuperius of Toulouse, the Apostolic See had given the canon of the sacred Scriptures. Gelasius published it again in the council held at Rome, whose beginning is:

> “The order of the books of the Old Testament, which the holy and Catholic Roman Church has received and venerates, arranged by blessed Pope Gelasius with seventy bishops.”

After enumerating the individual books of both Testaments, it adds:

> “We also think it necessary to make this known: although all the Catholic churches throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church has not been set above the other churches by synodal constitutions. Rather, by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior it obtained the primacy, when he says, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock’ (Matthew 16:18), etc. It also received the fellowship of blessed Paul the apostle, the chosen vessel, who—not at a different time, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on the same day—was crowned in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero by a glorious death after striving together with Peter. Together they consecrated the aforementioned holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and, by their presence and venerable triumph, placed it before all cities throughout the whole world. Therefore the first see of the apostle Peter is the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind (Ephesians 5:27).
>
> “The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and Evangelist, etc. The third see, likewise honorable in the name of the most blessed Peter, is at Antioch, because he lived there before coming to Rome, and there the name of the Christian people, a new nation, first arose,” etc.

After establishing the canon of the sacred Scriptures and listing the order of the patriarchal churches, which they obtained by the authority and foundation of the apostle Peter, the decree turns to enumerating the writings that, after the divine oracles of both Testaments, occupy the next class in the Catholic Church—those to be admitted and received. These are the four holy ecumenical councils: Nicaea, with 318 Fathers; Constantinople; Ephesus; and Chalcedon.

It then enumerates the holy Fathers approved by the Catholic Church in those councils, together with their works. None of these Fathers departed in any respect from fellowship with the holy Roman Church or separated themselves from its faith or preaching; rather, by the grace of God, they remained participants in that communion until the final day of their lives.

> “Likewise the letter of blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople: if anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema. Likewise the decretal letters that the most blessed popes, at various times, sent from the city of Rome in response to consultations from various Fathers, and which are to be received with reverence.”

These writings already constituted, as it were, a body of canon law in the Church.

[Col. 0432D] After enumerating the writings in which the truth of the doctrine handed down by the Church is recognized, he lists another class of writings in which caution must be exercised, lest apocryphal and unreliable works be received as genuine and trustworthy.

Line 10.—“In his time a report again came from Greece, because many evils and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius.” The following notes on this passage are taken from Book VI, chapter 8, of the Most Reverend Archbishop Sommier.

As soon as Euphemius of Constantinople learned of Gelasius’s elevation to the Roman pontificate, he wrote to him. From Gelasius’s reply we learn that Euphemius was working toward the reconciliation of the Eastern Church, but on the condition that Acacius’s name remain in the sacred diptychs. He sent another letter concerning the same matter. Here I shall give part of the reply addressed by Pope Gelasius to him.

“If you have truly attained the understanding that these things were divinely entrusted to me, then follow the exhortations of one who does not need to be taught, and, in accordance with the heavenly ordering of the One who observes all things, [follow] the things that pertain to the unity of the churches, and who, as you say, resists vigorously the devil, the disturber of true peace and harmony. If, then, you make these declarations about me, you must either follow what, as you maintain, was established by Christ; or openly acknowledge—God forbid—that you oppose Christ’s ordinances; or you are recognized as making these boasts about me in the vein of lustful desire. . . . But then you connect this with the claim that I am capable of condescending and, by an excellent arrangement, restoring harmony. Since, therefore, you frequently use this word, let me investigate what it means. For the excellent disposition of the Catholic and apostolic Church is to condescend by advancing toward better things, not to descend to lower things and fall away.

“. . . As you say—to omit the rest for now—the Lord himself descended from heaven. He certainly descended, but in order to free humanity from error, not to mingle with its error. . . . In order that one who lies may be raised up, it is fitting for the compassionate person to bend down, not to be hurled with him into the pit. For those whom Acacius baptized and ordained, we offer without difficulty a remedy prepared according to the tradition of our predecessors, true, and in harmony with the principal religious custom. To what further depths do you want us to descend? . . . Perhaps that we should consent to have admitted the names of heretics and condemned persons who communicate with them or their successors? This is not condescension for the sake of helping, but plainly a plunge into hell.

“. . . Have you not often indicated in letters sent here that, together with the other heretics, you also reject Eutyches? If this is true, either likewise repudiate those who communicated with the successors of Eutyches, or admit those who communicate with the successors of the other heretics.”

St. Gelasius, Letter 1 to Euphemius, and shortly afterward:

“You perceive that the apostolic see does not shun peace, but shuns the footsteps of heretics and condemned persons. You too, taking this into rational consideration, think that I must be admonished because the people of Constantinople do not permit the names of the faithless to be removed. Who, I ask you, could hear this in the Church of God? For surely the flock ought to follow the shepherd who recalls it to salutary pastures, not a shepherd leading the flock astray through byways.

“. . . Tell me, I ask you: will the flock render an account on your behalf, or will you render an account on behalf of the flock? We shall come, brother Euphemius, before that fearful tribunal of Christ. There it will not be a matter of denials, informers, or evasions, but it will be demonstrated most plainly whether the glorious confession of blessed Peter has taken anything away from the salvation of any of those whom he received to govern—or whether obstinate ruin, unwilling to heed it, has rebelled even at its own peril. There it will certainly become clear whether I am—as you think—bitter, harsh, excessively severe, and difficult for you, when I labor with reason for your salvation and cry out: ‘Even if the antidote seems harsh, accept it, I beg you; drink it; live; I do not want you to die’; or whether it is you who, although prevented from harmful things, consider physicians worthy of execration—indeed, who want the physicians to become sick with you rather than to restore you to health.”

Some writers of our own age, adopting the outlook of those ancient alienated persons, accuse Gelasius’s disciplinary policy of an unteachable harshness in which neither charity nor prudence shines forth; indeed, they say that everything tends toward breaking off all intercourse, just as intercourse was in fact broken off between the supreme pontiff and Euphemius. But whatever such writers may care to say—writers whose prejudices against the Roman see are sufficiently well known—the prudent reader understands clearly enough that Gelasius’s policy in defending the faith and discipline of the Fathers carries its own defense with it.

The same Gelasius sent a formula of faith to the bishops of Illyricum, at the request of one of them, as a kind of medicine of faith under which they were to live, according to the decrees of the Fathers (Letter 2 to Laurentius). He likewise sent to the bishops of Dardania a rule for preserving the unblemished communion handed down by the Fathers, namely, that the names of those who had transgressed were not to be recited in the Church (Letter 3 to the Bishops of Dardania). From their reply it may be gathered how reverently and beneficially they received and observed these salutary admonitions:

“We have received, with the devotion that is fitting, the most salutary commands of your apostolate, delivered by Trypho, our religious son, and we render the greatest thanks to almighty God and to Your Beatitude, holy, apostolic, and most blessed Father, because you have deigned to visit us with pastoral admonition and evangelical teaching. For it is our desire and vow to obey your commands in all things; and, just as we received them from our Fathers, to preserve inviolate the commands of the apostolic see, which has been entrusted to you on account of your life and merits, and to guard with faithful and blameless devotion, insofar as the understanding of our rusticity permits, the orthodox religion whose preachers you are.

“For before your command, too, we avoided Eutyches, Peter, Acacius, all their followers and associates, as so many pestilential contagions; and now, much more after the admonition of the apostolic see, it is necessary for us to abstain from the same pollution. If any others have followed, or now follow, the sect of that same Eutyches, or of Peter and Acacius, or deem themselves to be joined with their accomplices and associates, they must by every means be avoided by us, who desire to serve the apostolic see blamelessly, according to the divine commands and the statutes of the Fathers. And if any persons—something we neither think nor desire—should, with perverse intention, believe that they are to be separated from the apostolic see, we declare that we are strangers to their association.

“For, as it has been said, by observing the commands of the Fathers in all things and following the inviolable ordinances of the holy canons, we strive to obey your apostolic and uniquely distinguished see with common faith and devotion.”

Reply of the bishops of Dardania to Pope Gelasius.

[Col. 0434C] Since Andrew of Thessalonica had been unwilling to follow at all the example of his fellow bishops of the province of Illyricum in demonstrating due submission to the apostolic see, Gelasius wrote to the bishops of Illyricum and Dardania as follows:

“Let your fraternity know that the bishop of the Church of Thessalonica, although repeatedly urged by our exhortations, has never wished to avoid the contagions of external communion, nor to condemn, by an appropriate profession, the name of Acacius or of other foreign faithless persons like him and those who communicate with them. Therefore it is clear that he has not received communion from the apostolic see, since we neither can nor ought to offer the Church’s communion, [that of] blessed Peter the apostle, except to those with pure dispositions and free from every wicked association.

“. . . You must not participate at all in the purity of the Lord’s table with any of them—a purity that our predecessors always carefully kept separate from heretical pollution. Nor should anyone attempt to deceive you by saying that the dispute concerns not religion but morals, or that the apostolic see is not dealing with the cause of Catholic communion and faith but grieving over the insult because it appears to have been despised by Acacius. For those who remain in error do not cease scattering such claims and others like them in order to deceive even the simple.

“For you see that, if the names of transgressors are believed to be recited in the Church, the contagion of transgression is introduced at the same time. The apostolic see, however, is so far from grieving over an insult that it defends the faith and sincere communion: so that today it receives with the whole affection of its heart all those who appear to have burst into contempt for it, if they return to the integrity of faith and Catholic communion by the regular paternal path, coming with their whole heart and full charity.”

From Chapter 9 of the same Book VI.

Pope Gelasius sent a lengthy letter to the bishops of Dardania concerning the schism begun by Acacius and continued on his account. We shall quote from it the principal passages, which contain a clear testimony in favor of the authority of the apostolic see, and so forth.

“Our Fathers,” he says, “wished whatever they had once established, after assembling according to the path of Scripture and the preaching of their predecessors, to remain thereafter unshaken and firm; nor did they permit what had been decreed in the same matter to be reconsidered through any subsequent presumption. They foresaw most wisely that, if anyone were permitted to repeat salutary decrees, no established order of the Church would remain stable against each successive error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by recurring outbreaks of the same madness. . . . We are confident that no one who is now truly a Christian is unaware that the decree of each synod, once approved by the assent of the universal Church, ought to be carried out by no other see before the first, which both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it with continuous moderation, in accordance with its primacy—a primacy which the apostle Peter received from the voice of the Lord, and which, with the Church following after, he has always held and still holds.

“Since John, bishop of the second see, pressed Acacius with serious charges, he summoned him to the hearing of the first see, either to come or to send someone. But Acacius not only despised the request to give satisfaction; he also tried, rather, through his legates, to draw the apostolic see into external communion. The first see rightly removed Acacius himself from its communion. He had no right to reject the judgment of the first see, to which, according to the canons, he was summoned at the appeal of the bishop of the second see in our cause.

“Nor do we conceal what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the see of blessed Peter the apostle has the right to release those bound by the judgments of any bishops, since it has the authority to judge concerning the whole Church, and no one is permitted to judge its judgment. Indeed, the canons have wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to it, while no one is permitted to appeal from it.

“Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, as has been said, frequently, in the manner of our predecessors, even without a preceding synod, has had the authority both to absolve those whom a synod had unjustly condemned and to condemn those who ought to be condemned when no synod existed.”

The blessed pontiff proves this same point by the examples of St. Athanasius, St. John Chrysostom, St. Flavian, and Dioscorus.

He also touches on a matter worthy of consideration concerning the prerogatives of the churches. If their dignity is questioned, he says: “The dignity of the priests of the second and third sees is greater than that of the city which is not only hardly counted among the sees but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights.” He is referring, of course, to the claims of the people of Constantinople, who, although their Church is not among the patriarchal sees of the first order—those, namely, in which the Prince of the Apostles either personally or through his disciple Mark sat—seek to claim over those patriarchal sees an authority of precedence.

“One power,” he says, “belongs to secular kingship, another to the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities. . . . We laughed when they wished Acacius’s prerogative to be compared with that of others because he was bishop of a royal city. Was there not an emperor resident for many years at Ravenna, Milan, Sirmium, and Trier? Did the priests of those cities ever usurp for themselves, on account of their dignities, anything beyond the measure anciently assigned to them? If they flatter themselves because of the emperor’s presence and therefore think that the person of the bishop of the city of Constantinople can be made superior, let them hear how Marcian, the prince of that same city, after the city’s enlargement, when an intercessor came forward on behalf of its priest, could obtain nothing against the rules, and praised Pope Leo of holy memory with the highest commendations because he had in no way allowed the rules of the canons to be violated.

“Let them hear Anatolius, bishop of that same see, confessing that the clergy of Constantinople had rather attempted such things than he himself, and declaring that the whole matter had been placed in the power of the apostolic bishop. Let them hear how the blessed Pope Leo himself, bishop of the apostolic see, whose authority confirmed the Council of Chalcedon, nullified by an appropriate refutation whatever, beyond what had been delegated by him for the sake of the Catholic and apostolic faith and communion, appeared to have been attempted through the pretext of that assembly by a new action, contrary to the canons of Nicaea. And he also demonstrated, under Pope Simplicius of holy memory, when Leo, the legate of the apostolic see, was present at the request of Prince Leo, that such a thing could in no way be attempted.” —In the same place.

Finally, he adds that a council had been held in Italy concerning the divisions then existing. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the Catholic Church and the Roman see had omitted nothing belonging to the restoration of fraternal communion in its purity and sincerity.

“But the Eastern ecclesiastical leaders of the present day, because without the authority of the apostolic see they indiscriminately confuse the rights of all the churches, choosing to persist in error rather than surrender the power of their presumptions, loving the license of their usurpations more than they keep in their hearts a regard for divine judgment, refuse to have Christian unity restored by legitimate treatment.”

In this letter Gelasius had promised that he would explain more fully, in a separate treatise, the matters he was then touching upon hastily. He published two treatises, of which some fragments survive. He also wrote specifically concerning the anathema, where there are many proofs of his priestly steadfastness. From Chapter 10.

Nothing, however, declares more excellently the firmness of the apostolic heart—a firmness that everywhere shone forth in Gelasius, intimately joined to the charity of the common Father of the whole Church—than the letter he himself wrote to the emperor Anastasius in these words:

“Faustus and the others, while carrying out a public embassy, returned to Rome and said that Your Clemency had asked why I had not sent writings conveying my greetings. I confess that this was not according to my own custom; but since, some time ago, they had spread throughout the whole city that, by your commands, they had been denied permission either to see me or to speak with me concerning the Eastern Fathers, I thought I should refrain from writing, lest I should appear burdensome rather than dutiful. You see, therefore, that this did not arise from any dissimulation on my part, but from appropriate caution, lest I inflict annoyance upon minds that rejected it.

“But when I learned from those men that Your Serenity’s benevolence had been discovered, and that you had graciously sought a conversation with my humility, I truly understood that it would rightly be charged against me if I remained silent. For, glorious son, I love, honor, and receive you as a Roman loves, honors, and receives a Roman prince; and, as a Christian, I desire to possess with one who has zeal for God according to knowledge a zeal for the truth. As whatever kind of vicar of the apostolic see I may be, whenever I discover anything lacking in the fullness of Catholic faith, I strive, according to my ability, to supply it with timely suggestions.

“For the dispensation of the divine word has been entrusted to me, and woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel. If the apostle Paul, the blessed vessel of election, feared this and cried out, how much more must I, insignificant as I am, fear it if I withhold the ministry of preaching divinely inspired and transmitted with paternal devotion. I beg Your Piety not to regard the duty of divine reason as arrogance. God forbid, I ask, that a Roman prince should consider the truth communicated to his understanding an insult.

“Two things, august emperor, principally govern this world: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. The burden of priests is the heavier, inasmuch as they will render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves. For you know, most merciful son, that although you preside over the human race in dignity, you nevertheless devoutly bow your neck to the leaders of divine things, seek from them the causes of your salvation, and recognize that, in receiving the heavenly sacraments and arranging them as is fitting, you must be subject to them by the order of religion rather than preside over them.

“You know, therefore, that in these matters you depend upon their judgment, not that they are to be directed according to your will. For if, insofar as it concerns the order of public discipline, the leaders of religion recognize that the empire has been divinely bestowed upon you and therefore themselves obey your laws, lest they appear to oppose your judgment even in worldly matters, with what affection, I ask, ought you to obey those who have been appointed to dispense the venerable mysteries? Accordingly, just as a grave danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent about what is fitting for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a no less serious danger rests upon those who, although they ought to obey, despise them.

“Although the hearts of the faithful ought rightly to submit to all priests who handle divine matters correctly, how much more must agreement be offered to the bishop of that see which the supreme divinity willed to stand before all priests and which the continuing piety of the universal Church has celebrated? Hence Your Piety clearly understands that no one can ever raise himself by any merely human plan against the privilege or confession of him whom the voice of Christ placed before all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and devoutly holds as primate.

“Those things established by divine judgment can be attacked by human presumptions, but they cannot be overcome by the power of anyone. And would that the audacity of those who resist were not as destructive as it is; for what was fixed by the very Author of sacred religion cannot be shaken by any power: ‘The foundation of God stands firm.’ Now, when religion has been attacked by certain persons, how much novelty could have overcome it, if it had not remained all the more unconquered precisely insofar as it was thought capable of succumbing?

“Let some persons, therefore, I ask you, cease in your times, taking advantage of ecclesiastical disturbance, rashly seeking what is not permitted, lest they neither obtain what they wrongly desire nor preserve their proper standing before God and men. Therefore, in the sight of God, I purely and sincerely beseech, implore, and exhort you not to receive my petition with indignation. I ask, I say, that in this life you hear me as one pleading rather than—God forbid—encounter me as one accusing you at the divine judgment.

“Nor am I unaware, august emperor, that your zeal for piety was present in your private life. You have always desired to become a participant in the eternal promise. Therefore, I beg you, do not be angry with me if I love you so greatly that I wish you to possess eternally the kingdom you have attained temporally, and that you, who rule in this age, may reign with Christ. . . . I ask you not to consider burdensome the things said for the eternity of your salvation. You have read the words: ‘The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy.’ I ask Your Piety to allow the affection with which I speak to be impressed upon your understanding in the same measure.

“Let no one deceive Your Piety. It is true what Scripture figuratively testifies through the prophet: ‘My dove is one, my perfect one is one.’ There is one Christian faith, which is Catholic. That faith is truly Catholic which is separated in sincere, pure, and unblemished communion from all the faithless, from their successors, and from their associates. Otherwise there will be not a divinely commanded distinction but a pitiable confusion, and no reason will remain why, if you wish to admit this in any contagion whatsoever, we should not open access and a door to all heresies.

“This is what the apostolic see takes the greatest care to avoid: since the glorious confession of the Apostle is the root of the world, it must not be stained by any crack of depravity or any contagion whatsoever. . . . Therefore, glorious emperor, do I not desire the peace of the churches—a peace which, even if it could be achieved at the cost of my blood, I would embrace? But I ask you to weigh with a truly Christian mind what kind of peace it ought to be, not merely whether there should be peace. For how can that be true peace from which unblemished charity is absent?

“And the Apostle clearly teaches us what charity ought to be when he says: ‘Charity is from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith’ (1 Tim. 1:5). How, I ask you, can it be from a pure heart if it is infected by an external contagion? How can it be from a good conscience if it has been mixed with perverse and evil things? . . . Therefore, just as, when a communicator in perversity is received, perversity itself cannot fail to be approved along with him, so perversity cannot be rejected if an accomplice and follower of perversity is admitted.

“Certainly, according to your laws, those conscious of crimes and those who receive robbers are bound by the same judicial penalty; nor is one considered free from the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless accepted the friendship and alliance of the one who committed it. Accordingly, since the Council of Chalcedon, celebrated for the truth and communion of the Catholic and apostolic faith, condemned Eutyches, the author of detestable madness, it was not satisfied unless it also struck his associate Dioscorus and the others.

“In the same way, since it is not doubtful that this has always been done or is done in every heresy, it subsequently struck down their successors Timothy, Peter, and the other Peter of Antioch—not by holding another council individually against each one, but by the rule established once by the synod.

“How, then, is it not evident that all are likewise bound by the same standard, and that those who were their communicants and accomplices, and all of them altogether, are rightly separated from Catholic and apostolic communion? For this reason we also rightly say that Acacius must be removed from our association, since he preferred to pass into the lot of faithlessness rather than remain in the sincerity of Catholic and apostolic communion, although for nearly three years he had been properly instructed by letters of the apostolic see so as not to enter into that course. . . . Therefore, either let him be shown to be free from heretical participation, with whose communion he associated himself, or he cannot fail to be rejected together with them.

“For, august emperor, if anyone should perhaps attempt something against the public laws—God forbid—he could not be allowed to do so in any way. Do you not think that it concerns your conscience that the people subject to you be brought back to the pure and sincere devotion of the divinity?
