Let them therefore permit themselves to be treated by suitable remedies; otherwise—God forbid—by passing into their destruction, we may perish with them, though we cannot save them.”

Many things could be noted and applied from this letter to the circumstances of the present time. One point especially deserves attention: the subtle criticism constructed by certain recent authors in order to attack those Greeks, like writings of similar character recently disseminated, has excessively stirred up, or at least fostered, the spirit of schism; and it has enabled that spirit to insinuate itself more deeply into minds already ill-disposed.

The memory and exhortation of the same Gelasius in his letter to Rusticus of Lyons should be recalled here:

“Consider how great a persecution we endure on account of the most impious Acacius, but we shall not fail. . . . Do what you can, dearest brother, so that your affection, and that of your people, toward us—or rather toward the apostolic see—may not cease. Those who are made firm upon the Rock will be exalted with the Rock.”

From Chapter 12 of the same Book VI.

Besides the constitutions of Gelasius already presented, the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* relates that, when Manichaeans were discovered in Rome during his pontificate, the pontiff arranged for them to be punished with exile, and asserts that their writings were publicly burned before the doors of the Liberian Basilica. Among the errors of this sect was the teaching that wine was an invention of the devil; they therefore rejected participation in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood under both species. They were detected in this, although they sought to remain hidden, because, when they were observed receiving only the portion of the sacred body under the species of bread, they abstained from participation in the chalice.

He therefore issued a decree, reported by Gratian, by which he ordered that those who refused to communicate under both species be kept away from the sacred table. Such a decree offers no support whatsoever to the error of those who think that communion under both species is necessary for attaining salvation, as Cardinals Baronius and Bona clearly demonstrate; they should be consulted on this question, Baronius under the year of Christ 406, and Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book II, Chapter 18.

In abolishing the superstition of the Lupercalia, which a certain senator sought to preserve from pagan impieties, with the still worse pretext that the sterility of the land suffered by the Romans resulted from the interruption of such rites, the zeal for religion with which he contended is shown by the treatise that survives on this matter against the senator Andromachus, in which the following is read:

“It is fitting for me to declare that these things are unquestionably harmful and deadly to Christians. . . . I do not doubt that my predecessors also perhaps did this and attempted to have these things removed before imperial ears. And since it is not evident that they were heard, while these evils continue even today, for that reason those very empires have failed; for that reason also the Roman name, without the Lupercalia having been removed, has reached every extremity.”

[Col. 0413]

## 74

Gelasius, an African by birth, son of Valerius, sat for four years, eight months, and nine days [Note: [Col. 0413] B has “nineteen days.”]. He lived during the reigns [Note: [Col. 0413] B: “of the emperor Anastasius, King Odoacer, and Theodoric, from the consulships of Anastasius Augustus and Rufinus to that of Paulus.”] of King Theodoric and Zeno Augustus.

During his pontificate the Church of Saint Michael on Mount Garganus was discovered. During his pontificate the Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0413] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 496.], and he ordered them to be deported into exile. He burned their books in a fire before the doors of the Basilica of Saint Mary. [Note: [Col. 0413] Synodal Acts.]

At a synodal proceeding he recalled Bishop Mesena to communion, restored him to his own Church after he had submitted a written statement of satisfaction, and, after he had been cleared, received him. He was a lover of the clergy and the poor, and increased the clergy. He freed the city of Rome from danger and famine. He issued a constitution concerning the whole Church. [Note: [Col. 0415] B states that Peter and Acacius had died long before.]

During his pontificate a report again came from Greece that many evils and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius. At the same time the illustrious John of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0415] Catholic bishop, number 13.] came to Rome to the apostolic see. At that time blessed Gelasius received John, sent him back, and condemned Acacius and Peter in perpetuity if they did not repent. Nevertheless, while awaiting the satisfaction of the apostolic see, he acted according to the humanity of the Church of the first see.

He dedicated the Basilica of Saint Euphemia the Martyr in the city of Tibur, at the twentieth milestone from the city of Rome. He also dedicated the Basilica of Saints Nicander and Eleutherius on the Lavican Way, on the estate called Villa Pertusa [Note: [Col. 0415] B: “in Villa Petrosa.”]; and another Basilica of Saint Mary on the Laurentine Way, on the estate of Crispinus [Note: [Col. 0415] “on the estate.”], at the twentieth milestone from the city of Rome.

Under his episcopate the clergy grew. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, in the months of February and December: thirty-two priests, two deacons, and sixty-seven bishops for various places. He was also buried in the Basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

He composed treatises and hymns, like blessed Ambrose the bishop, and books [Note: [Col. 0415] CB: “five books.”] against Eutyches and Nestorius, which are now kept in the library and the archive of the Church. After his death, the episcopate remained vacant for eight days [Note: [Col. 0415] CB: “seven days.”].

## LII. SAINT ANASTASIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 497, THE SEVENTH OF THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS, THE FIFTH OF KING THEODORIC

M. from the silver weight of 100 pounds; at that time.” Line 5: “they removed his own, because.” Line 6: “of the priests and clergy.” Line 8, [Col. 0440B] “and he was not able.” “He was struck by divine will.” Line 9: “who was also buried.”

[Note: [Col. 0439B]

Line 4.—“At the same time many . . . of the clergy raised themselves from his communion.” This addition should, I think, be regarded as extracted from the acts of the schismatics who, while favoring the party of Laurentius against Symmachus, rose up in hatred of Anastasius, the predecessor of Symmachus, and fabricated this—as usually happens wherever partisan prejudices prevail.

The falsehood of the addition—whether concerning Pope Anastasius promoting association with the Acacians and communion with them, or concerning Photinus of Thessalonica—is easily demonstrated from the letter of that same pontiff to Zeno, which he sent through Cresconius and Germanus, bishops and legates of the apostolic see to the emperor. He did indeed promote the conversion of the Acacians and promised them pardon, provided that they erased the name of Acacius from the sacred diptychs. (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 949, ch. 3.)

“Therefore we beg Your Clemency that the name of Acacius in particular be left unmentioned. . . . But lest it seem burdensome to Your Clemency for me to report individually how many excesses and presumptions Acacius possessed, I have given Your Clemency, through the brothers and fellow bishops Cresconius and Germanus, whom we sent to Your Serenity concerning the individual matters of Acacius, a full account of what he was like, for more particular review if Your Piety should wish to investigate the matter more carefully, lest the truth appear to have been lacking in any respect because of our representations. Thus, in accordance with your divine wisdom, you may clearly see that the judgment passed against such an Acacius did not proceed from pride or arrogance on the part of the apostolic see, but was extorted by definite crimes—so far as we can judge outside that judgment which alone cannot err—rather by zeal for the divinity.”

How could the pontiff, after the embassy and the denunciation of Acacius’s crimes delivered to the emperor through the legates, enter into an alliance with the Acacians and restore them to communion without any prior satisfaction? This is especially impossible because, from the final sentence of the Fourth Synod under Felix, the Church of Constantinople separated itself from the Roman Church, as Liberatus writes in the passage cited above after relating the acts of that synod:

“Since these things had occurred and Acacius remained in communion with Peter, the apostolic see separated itself from the Constantinopolitan see,” and so forth.

Nor could he have been admitted unless contumacy had been abandoned and satisfaction had been made. Moreover, Zeno—by whose fraud the synod of Heraclea, which he had pretended to promote under Hormisdas in order to conceal his crime, was dissolved—gave Hormisdas a letter in which he writes of two matters promoted by himself.

First, he had sought that the Alexandrian Church remit the anathema that it publicly pronounced against the Council of Chalcedon and the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo:

“For on this matter the divine letters sent to Alexandria, not once but many times, bear witness. Through them we reproved them for not thinking that the doctrinal statement of faith sent to them could be sufficient, and yet did not withdraw from the anathema against the Council of Chalcedon and against Leo, bishop of venerable memory. Hence there remains among us no small zeal and dispute, so that we may draw them away from the aforesaid anathema and join them to the holy universal Church.”

Second, the removal of Acacius’s name from the sacred diptychs could not be accomplished without a great sedition:

“As for the chapter which alone appears to remain, our will would perhaps comply with your request for the sake of the unity of the churches, unless we thought that other scandals would thereby be renewed in the venerable Church. Now consider what must be done, since Your Clemency judges that it would be a serious matter for living persons to be expelled from the venerable Church on account of the dead; nor do we know that what you write can be arranged without much shedding of blood.”

If Anastasius, his predecessor, had thought that union with the Church of Constantinople and the restoration of harmony should be achieved by leaving Acacius’s name in place and communicating with the Acacians who defended his acts, Zeno would have proposed this to Hormisdas: namely, that Pope Anastasius, his predecessor, had deliberated about making union with the Acacians while leaving Acacius’s name in place and erasing the synodal decrees published and established against him.

These matters should therefore be considered fabricated and stitched onto the acts of Anastasius, drawn from the accusations manufactured against Pope Anastasius and Symmachus, which the compiler did not hesitate to add here without first applying any critical judgment. But an even more enormous interpolation concerns Photinus.]

### Line 5

“Had communicated … with Photinus, a Thessalonian deacon [Col. 0441C] by name, who was in communion with Acacius.” Other manuscripts read better: “the communion of Acacius.” The Thessalonian was the vicar of the apostolic see throughout the East. Either Gelasius or Anastasius employed him to settle the disputes that had broken out in the East on account of Mongus and Acacius.

That Photinus had been at Alexandria and had worked vigorously on behalf of Saint Leo’s doctrinal teaching is attested by the representatives of the Alexandrian see in the pamphlet mentioned above, which they gave to Cresconius and Germanus, legates of Pope Anastasius who were still staying at Constantinople. They write there about Photinus as follows (vol. II of the Councils, p. 953):

> “Since the devout deacon Photinus of the holy Church of Thessalonica recently discussed with us the peace of the Churches, and said that shortly before he had been sent by the most holy Archbishop Andrew of the Church of Thessalonica to the Roman pontiff Anastasius, he affirmed that, concerning the matters that greatly offend us, he had received satisfaction in the translation of the letter from the aforesaid bishop of the Roman Church—namely, that the errors had been confirmed in the translation of the letter, whereas the Latin letter itself had been composed according to the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. Moreover, he reported that certain things had been related as having been said by that same bishop, things directed toward censuring what had been inserted in the translation, and toward censuring those who had attempted to fabricate such things in order to satisfy those who do not neglect to preserve the right and undefiled faith. Since these matters had been fully remedied, and since we desired to restore our former concord, we preferred to learn from you whether those things were true that the devout deacon Photinus had reported to us; and we wished to approach your holiness and confer with you about all these matters.”

If Photinus took his stand for the Council of Chalcedon and exposed the false persuasion of the Alexandrians in rejecting the Council of Chalcedon and Saint Leo’s letter, then Mongus—who was the leader of these heretics and remained in communion with Acacius until his death—is rightly shown to have been a condemned heretic. Consequently, Acacius could not be recalled, nor could his communion be restored as though he were innocent and free from every heretical contamination—whether by Photinus, or, what is even more extraordinary, by Pope Anastasius.

Furthermore, many learned men hold that the *commonitorium* addressed to Festus belongs to this pontiff, not to Gelasius, who is commonly thought to be its author. Anyone can perceive this from what is said about Acacius and about the entirely just sentence of condemnation pronounced against him.

Our observation concerning Anastasius, which we touched on above, must be clarified further. In the *Lives of the Pontiffs* we said that whenever a schism arose in the Roman Church, some compiler, accustomed to extracting passages from prejudiced writers, would insert them unaltered among the pontifical acts and defile their sequence. Matters that sometimes belonged to an antipope were imposed on the legitimate pope, or were falsely fabricated by schismatics, as was noted in the case of Liberius.

Laurentius, the invader of the apostolic see, is thought to have subscribed, after Pope Anastasius, to Zeno’s *Henoticon*, which Pope Anastasius absolutely refused to sign. Theodore the Reader expressly testifies to this (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II). He relates that the Roman senator Festus, sent by the Roman Senate to Zeno on certain civil matters, had been instructed to persuade the pope to subscribe to the *Henoticon*. Theodore writes:

> “Festus, secretly—as they say—had suggested to the emperor that he should persuade the Roman bishop to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon*. But when he came to Rome, he found Bishop Anastasius already dead. Therefore he worked to have the man promoted through schism subscribe to that edict.”

The man promoted through schism after Anastasius was Laurentius. To subscribe to the *Henoticon* meant to enter into association with the Acacians, since Acacius was regarded as the author, advocate, and promoter of the *Henoticon*. What properly belonged to the antipope may perhaps have been falsely imposed on Anastasius by the schismatics because of the pope’s friendship with Festus. They published these claims, and an ignorant compiler [Col. 0442C] inserted them among the acts of Anastasius.

Meanwhile, if the *commonitorium* ought to be entitled “To Festus,” rather than “To Faustus,” and if Anastasius is to be vindicated as its author, it can be understood from it how he consistently regarded both Acacius and the Acacians as condemned, and how vigorously he dissolved all the Acacians’ evasions and emptied their subterfuges of force.

Certainly Theodore indicates that Festus favored Laurentius and supported the schismatics, and therefore intended only to please the emperor, who above all wished everyone to be united in subscribing to the *Henoticon*. This confusion gave the compilers of the *Liber Pontificalis* occasion to attribute to Anastasius what properly belonged to the antipope Laurentius.

Certainly, if this had been presumed by Anastasius—and specifically upon the admonition of the entire clergy—such a favorable disposition toward the Acacians could not have been concealed. Accordingly, under Symmachus, when the emperor Anastasius had been excommunicated because of the support he had undertaken on behalf of the Acacians and because of his fabrication of calumnies against Symmachus, he would not have failed to produce this intention and policy of the pope [Col. 0442D]. Yet he did not do so. On the contrary, he drew an argument from the example of his predecessor to show that they themselves had stood invincibly against the Acacians.

Thus Pope Symmachus wrote in an apologetic letter to the emperor Anastasius:

> “You say that, with the Senate conspiring with me, I excommunicated you. I did so indeed, but without doubt I follow what my predecessors reasonably did. We did not excommunicate you, emperor, but Acacius. Withdraw from Acacius, and you will withdraw from his excommunication,”

and so forth. See the remainder.

The predecessors were Gelasius and Anastasius. Hence this fictitious addition was attached by an ignorant compiler to the acts of Anastasius. Still more foolish is the addition that follows, where the compiler’s ignorance and anachronism are evident, namely:

### Line 8

“Because he wished to recall Acacius and could not; he was struck down by divine will.”

Acacius had already been condemned when Anastasius assumed the pontificate, as was noted under Gelasius. Hence the little tale collapses. The words “who was struck down by divine will” are transmitted in other manuscripts as follows, with the punctuation placed earlier:

> “Here he was struck down by divine will.”

This addition must be regarded as one of the customary interpolations hastily attached to the *Acts of the Pontiffs*. It did not belong to the *Acts of Anastasius*, nor did it concern Pope Anastasius; rather, it concerned Hormisdas, during whose pontificate the emperor Anastasius died. The *Liber Pontificalis* assigns the following cause of his death:

> “Anastasius Augustus, filled with fury against Pope Hormisdas, wrote among his other sacred documents: ‘We wish to command, not to be commanded.’ At that same time, struck by the will of the Godhead, the emperor Anastasius was struck by divine lightning and died.”

Thus, whatever had been read somewhere about the emperor Anastasius Augustus, some unlearned person thought it should be attached to Pope Anastasius. Perhaps he was misled by the *Chronicle of Theophanes*, from which the *Liber Pontificalis* was expanded in Latin through additions of this sort. There, under the year 518, we read:

> “In this year, in the fortieth indiction, on the ninth day of April, the foolish emperor Anastasius died. He had ruled for twenty-seven years and seven months, in the two-hundred-and-thirty-fourth year from the reign of Diocletian. In his place Justin, the pious emperor, a man of advanced age and experienced in affairs, was appointed. He had begun with military service, had risen to the rank of senator, and was an Illyrian by birth. Some, however, report that Anastasius, struck by lightning from heaven, died in a stupor of mind.”

It has already been shown, and will be shown more fully below, that the customary compiler of additions extracted such material from various authors and inserted it into the catalogues. These passages, I think, gave an ignorant compiler or copyist, who had read the name Anastasius, the opportunity to attach them to the acts of Pope Anastasius.

[Col. 0443B]

## Note

### [Col. 0443B]

### Line

“Because he secretly wished to recall Acacius.”

The first letter of Pope Anastasius in the acts of the Council indicates neither that Acacius’s name was to be restored to the sacred diptychs nor that Acacius himself was to be recalled to the see of Constantinople. In that letter he plainly requested that the name of the deceased be completely erased and removed.

The heretics of our own time boast that Anastasius was convicted of error and perfidy because he communicated with Photinus, a supporter of the Acacian sect, without a council of bishops. Yet everyone can see how foolish this claim is. Anastasius could have absolved a repentant man from excommunication without the authority of any council and could have communicated with him without any danger of sin. Indeed, if he had requested from a man who was excommunicated and plainly schismatic a service necessary for the whole Church, he would not only have lost none of his faith, but would not thereby have incurred any sentence of anathema.

See Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*; Baronius, year 479, no. 27; the editors of Gratian’s *Decree*, in their notes on the canon “Anastasius,” distinction 19; and Covarruvias, vol. II, book IV of the *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13. They prove that these claims are altogether fabricated, chiefly on the following grounds: Acacius, as Nicephorus (book XVI, chapter 12) and Evagrius (book III, chapters 18 and following) testify, died during the pontificate of Felix III; and Anastasius himself, in chapter 1 of his letter to the emperor Anastasius, wrote that Acacius was already dead and stood together with Felix before Christ the Judge.

That Acacius was not recalled by Anastasius is therefore entirely certain. The same cannot be asserted with equal confidence about Photinus’s communion, since the contrary may be inferred without obscurity from a letter of that same pontiff.

### Line 8

“Who was struck by divine will.”

The heretics spread the claim that Anastasius died from a divinely inflicted illness because, in the same letter, he approved the baptism and sacred orders conferred by Acacius. As usual, however, they do so through calumnies, lies, and fables.

What Bede, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Paul the Deacon write in the life of the heretical emperor Anastasius—that he was struck by lightning around this time—they do not hesitate to transfer to Pope Anastasius, relying on no authority other than that of a single mendacious Librarian [Col. 0444A].

See Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 10; Sander, *On the Visible Monarchy of the Church*; and Hosius, book III, *Propositions of Catholic Doctrine*.

## Chronological Notes

### [Col. 0444A]

After the death of Gelasius, the Roman see was vacant for seven days, according to the Librarian, as most manuscripts read—including the Regius, Thuani, and Mazarine manuscripts, counting the terminal days. The election, or perhaps also the ordination, of Anastasius II of this name should therefore be placed around 24 November 496, since the indicated day was a Sunday and the corresponding Dominical Letter was F.

Since he is said to have held the see for one year, eleven months, and twenty-four days, his life as pope extended to 17 or 18 November 498. The final verse of this section states that he was buried at Saint Peter’s on the tenth day of that same month [Col. 0444B]. The enumeration of the days is therefore sufficiently exact. If it varies by one day in some manuscripts or catalogues, the difference is not important enough to delay us in establishing the epoch of Anastasius’s pontificate, both at its beginning and at the end of his priestly office.

## Historical Notes

### [Col. 0444B]

### Line 4

“At that time many clerics,” and line 7, “And because he wished secretly to recall Acacius,” etc.

The learned Cardinal Baronius and Bellarmine correctly observe at this passage of the Librarian, as does Archbishop Sommier, who follows them in the notes given below, that such memories were fabricated by the faction of the schismatics under the succeeding pontificate of Blessed Symmachus. They were circulated among the people, together with many false reports about both pontiffs, through the efforts of the patrician Festus and others devoted to the antipope Laurentius.

After committing these claims to writing, they used them to deceive the emperor Anastasius, who was displeased that Zeno’s *Henoticon* was not being subscribed to by Pope Anastasius and Symmachus, and to inflame his mind more violently against the legitimate and holy pontiffs, as though they were factious, turbulent, and accused of crimes.

Regarding Anastasius’s premature death, they thought they had devised a milder story by fabricating a tendency on his part to tolerate the recitation of Acacius’s name and the admission of Photinus of Thessalonica, a supporter of Acacius.

Such writings, commissioned by the faction of Laurentius, were so widely disseminated that some fragments of them reached later generations and eventually came to the attention of the Librarian’s contemporaries. The Librarian, collecting indiscriminately in a later age the life of Anastasius and the following life of Symmachus, trusted these fabricated stories about both men and mixed them into the truthful documents of their other deeds.

What Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine and other recent scholars prove by irresistible arguments is also confirmed by the discovery of fragments belonging to those schismatics. Their ancient script shows that they are older than Anastasius the Librarian and therefore reveals to us that the compiler of the Lives was not entirely without monuments close to the age of Symmachus, but lacked the necessary critical judgment to distinguish the devices and calumnies of the schismatics from the true narratives of Catholics.

It is useful to append here a surviving fragment in an ancient-character parchment gathering, apparently written about a thousand years ago and bound together with Saint Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and other short works. Among these are letters of the supreme pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, and others. It is preserved in the archive of the cathedral Church of Verona, in one of the codices collected eight hundred years ago by Pacificus the archdeacon, as I mentioned elsewhere, where it is numbered 25.

The style of the book indicates the age of Symmachus. The author of this fragment fabricates the following account about him, after perhaps first committing to writing the false claim—spread by the schismatics—that Pope Anastasius had connived in these matters. The following words seem to indicate this:

> “The emperor Anastasius was supported by letters sent through Cresconius and Germanus, so that whoever reads this attentively, under divine fear, may recognize that until now such a wicked schism has vainly continued between the Churches of the East and Italy.”

The *Life of Symmachus* then follows in that gathering, fraudulently composed in the style of the same period:

> “The fifty-second pope, Symmachus, held the see for fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. At that time Laurentius, a presbyter of the Roman Church, had been ordained bishop, and such a savage discord seized the Roman clergy and people that neither consideration of God nor fear of the king restrained the factions from cutting one another apart. Then both men—Symmachus and Laurentius—were compelled to seek the court in order to submit to the king’s judgment.
>
> “There Symmachus prevailed through large sums of money, while Laurentius was sent to govern the Church of Nuceria, a city of Campania, compelled by many threats and promises. After some years, however, Symmachus was accused before the king of many crimes. The king, under the pretext of the Easter season, because Symmachus had not celebrated with the whole community … summoned the court … by reason of the disagreement concerning the feast, and caused him to remain at Ariminum … He stayed there for some time with his clergy. One afternoon, walking along the seashore, he saw women passing by, with whom he was accused of having committed a crime; they were going to the court by royal command.
>
> “Pretending not to know what he had seen, at midnight, while everyone was asleep, he fled with only one confidant and returned to Rome, shutting himself inside the precincts of Blessed Peter the Apostle. Then the presbyters and deacons, as well as the rest of the clergy whom he had taken with him, approached the king and testified that Symmachus had fled without their knowledge. Through them the king sent instructions both to the Senate and to the clergy concerning his condemnation, in some sense [Col. 0445C].
>
> “He was also accused by the entire Roman clergy of having squandered ecclesiastical estates, contrary to the decree observed by his predecessors, and thereby of having entangled himself in the bonds of anathema. For the Easter days, nearly everyone requested from the king the venerable man Peter, bishop of Altinum, as visitor of the Roman Church. After the holy feast, a synod was convened in the city of Rome by order of the king, according to the will of the Senate and clergy, to judge his offenses. The matter was handled by certain bishops and senators … so that Symmachus … should be subjected to a hearing, while others openly cried out in his defense that no Roman pontiff could be heard by anyone, even if he were such as he was accused of being.
>
> “But the more distinguished bishops, both out of regard for religion and because of the royal command, judged that so serious a matter, already almost universally known, could not be abandoned without examination. Since the synod, amid this disagreement, was instead providing more fuel for discord between the parties, it finally decided that the indictment which Symmachus’s accusers offered should be received and solemnly entered into the acts. After this had been done, Symmachus was immediately summoned by the bishops to appear for judgment.
>
> “But when his presence was denied by the clerics who served him, the bishops admonished him a second and a third time, according to the rules, to appear before the synodal hearing. He did not deign to give any response. Then, when some bishops saw that they were accomplishing nothing in the case, they admonished the clergy who had withdrawn from Symmachus’s fellowship, once and again, to return to him without waiting for an examination. They replied that they could by no means do this before he had been subjected to a regular investigation on such serious charges and either acquitted if innocent or removed from the priesthood if guilty.
>
> “But delays … when they saw the factions of division growing more and more, they made what decisions seemed useful for Symmachus’s person, and thus abandoned the city in complete confusion. The more distinguished clergy and Senate, who had avoided Symmachus’s fellowship, sent a petition to the king on behalf of Laurentius, who at that time was staying at Ravenna to avoid Symmachus’s violence and persecution. They requested that Laurentius himself preside over the Roman Church, where he had formerly been ordained supreme pontiff, since this was also established by the canons: that each man should remain where he was first consecrated bishop, or, if he had been removed from there by some device, that he should be recalled by every means.
>
> “Thus Laurentius came to Rome and held the Roman Church for about four years. What civil wars were fought or how many murders were committed during that time need not be disclosed in the present account. While the factions clashed with one another in mutual dissension and repeatedly sought royal protection for their causes, Symmachus finally sent a petition to the king through Dioscorus, the Alexandrian deacon. He claimed that a great injustice was being done to him, especially concerning the titles of the churches that Laurentius held within Rome, and that the king’s mind had been softened toward this … by the patrician F …”

[Col. 0446B]

Here the fragment of the gathering attached to the parchment codex ends. It is certainly to be valued very highly on account of its unquestionable antiquity, if used for the purpose for which one may suppose it was assembled by some skilled and devoted student of ecclesiastical history.

Although the fragment is recognized as part of a pernicious writing, composed by some ordinary partisan of the faction of Laurentius against Symmachus—and written in a style of expression that is not inelegant for that period—it appears to be the work of a man who was not of the lowest rank, employed by the patrician Festus or by some other person of respectable standing to court the favor of the same schismatic faction and of the emperor and his consort, at the expense of pontifical reputation and authority.

The fragment attributes crimes to Symmachus and, not obscurely, to his predecessor Pope Anastasius a disposition to connive with the Acacians concerning the recitation of Acacius’s name, as though this were an innocent and suitable remedy for removing the schism of the Easterners from the Latin Church. It also heaps up many false and detestable claims concerning judgments brought or to be brought against the head of the Church of God.

Although, I say, this fragment is recognized as a portion of a pernicious and very ancient writing, it could nevertheless usefully have been collected and inserted by a student of ecclesiastical history, pontifical authority, and immunity, together with the letters of the holy pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, and Anastasius to Acacius and Acacius’s replies, bound in the same codex.

These genuine documents had to be produced against the fraud, curse, and imposture of the adversaries by anyone wishing to refute those same impostures, frauds, and curses through other genuine writings of the supreme pontiffs and councils, which demonstrate the truth and rights of the matter—as the writings of heretics were also produced in ecumenical councils when their blasphemies were being condemned.

Those poisonous writings had therefore been usefully collected and bound together with their antidotes, lest, if read in isolation, they obscure the minds of the uninstructed [Col. 0446D].

But through the injury of time and the negligence of later generations, as commonly happens, such ancient papers were carelessly treated and scattered. Once the integrity of the codex had been destroyed, the surviving gathering happened by chance to preserve mutilated fragments of the schismatic writing that resembled a pontifical catalogue. These fragments could then be used quite differently by some unlearned writer or compiler of a later age.

Seeing them bound together with the highly regarded books of Blessed Jerome and Gennadius, and with the letters of the holy pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, and Anastasius preserved there, such a writer could have accepted without examination the anciently written catalogue fragments—whose author was not evident—and without collating them with other genuine documents of the period, as historical truth requires, he could have received them rashly as authentic monuments by a contemporary writer.

From this polluted source the same calumnies and tales of forgers could have flowed into the text of the *Liber Pontificalis* [Col. 0447A], causing later generations difficulty in separating them from historical truth.

I thought it worthwhile, on the occasion of the dispute that has arisen among learned men concerning the acts of Anastasius, to identify the source of that false stream. The writers of our time mentioned in the notes of Archbishop Sommier have seized upon the dispute, and Sommier himself has refuted them with strong arguments. From this source the writer who inserted into the life of Anastasius II the incongruous passage concerning his inclination to connive at the recitation of Acacius’s name drew his rivulet.

Both that passage and similar passages sometimes found interspersed in the Librarian’s text could have been copied thoughtlessly from fragments of very ancient codices—such as the Veronese codex cited here—especially in periods afflicted by the barbarism introduced into the liberal arts and by a scarcity of learned men capable of comparing such mutilated papers, lacking title and author, with monuments of truthful writers.

Such men could have determined whether the papers had been written by sensible persons free from partisan zeal or rather by factional men devoted to advancing a bad cause. Inspection of that codex, so bound together, teaches us sufficiently that the origins of the notions used by the biographers of Anastasius must be investigated—not because we distrust that they were drawn from ancient documents, but because there is good reason to doubt whether they were collected incautiously from fragments of calumniators, rashly stitched together with the works of the Fathers and previously examined by more expert men, so that the very words expressed by the opponents could be refuted.

The age of Gelasius abounds in such disreputable fabrications of doubtful credibility, heaped up everywhere by heretics and schismatics. He therefore considered it necessary, after summoning a council, to establish a catalogue of approved books and to separate genuine, complete, and approved writings from apocryphal and corrupted ones.

Given the abundance of writings of defective origin disseminated during the times of Gelasius, Anastasius, and the neighboring pontiffs by enemies of our faith on the occasion of the heresies and schisms that had arisen, it is not surprising if later and less capable compilers sometimes fell asleep at their task and rashly adopted from ancient fragments indiscriminately scraped together from the miscellany of contending parties hostile calumnies transformed with remarkable skill into historical style.

Where narratives of known truth should have been substituted—narratives whose reasoning and authority would overturn those same calumnies—these compilers instead adopted the calumnies themselves [Col. 0447C].

## Note

### [Col. 0447C]

### Lines 4 and 5

“They raised themselves from his communion.”

The emperor Anastasius was deceitfully working to discover some way of inducing the Roman pontiff to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon*. To accomplish this, he sent Festus as an envoy.

Festus was a Roman senator sent by the Senate to the emperor Anastasius to conduct certain civil matters. He secretly promised the emperor that he would persuade the Roman bishop to subscribe to Zeno’s concord. When he came to Rome, however, he found Bishop Anastasius dead, as Theodoretus and Nicephorus (book III, chapter 35) agree in reporting.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that Pope Anastasius remained whole and sincere in the Catholic faith and died before Festus could attempt such treachery against him. We know that divine providence often arranged matters in this way, since it has always been especially accustomed to preserve the integrity of the Catholic faith: the man who was about to bring Catholic purity into danger was punished by death as quickly as possible.

### Line 8

“He was struck by divine will.”

He is said to have been struck by leprosy. Others report that, while obeying the necessities of nature, he discharged his intestines into a latrine.

## Note

### [Col. 0448A]

### Line 7

“And because he secretly wished to recall Acacius,” etc.

At the very beginning of his pontificate, Pope Anastasius sent Germanus of Capua and Cresconius, bishop of Trent, as legates to the emperor Anastasius in Constantinople, in order to recall him from heresy to a better mind. He sent with them a letter requesting that the name of Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, who had died outside the communion of the Church, be completely erased from the diptychs.

The pope also wished the emperor to admonish the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and Catholic peace. The emperor was likewise admonished to obey the constitutions of the apostolic see.

The holy pontiff achieved nothing in this most pious undertaking. The emperor, however, deceitfully detaining the legates at Constantinople, worked with great effort through fraud and deception to induce the Roman pontiff himself to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon*.

For this purpose he employed a certain Roman senator named Festus [Col. 0448B]. According to Theodore the Reader, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, Festus had been sent to the emperor Anastasius on certain civil matters and, through the emperor’s favor, obtained permission for the sacred memorial of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—formerly neglected by the schismatics—to be celebrated with greater honor and magnificence:

> “Although it had previously been celebrated, after Festus’s petition the festival was henceforth conducted with far greater splendor.”

A little later he adds:

> “Festus, secretly—as they say—had suggested to the emperor that he should persuade the Roman bishop to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon*. But when he came to Rome, he found Bishop Anastasius already dead. Therefore he worked to have the man promoted through schism subscribe to that edict.”

The man in question was the schismatic Laurentius, elected against Symmachus.

It is therefore clear that Pope Anastasius died whole and sincere in the Catholic faith before Festus could attempt such treachery against him.

It is wholly false and foolish, therefore, that the *Liber Pontificalis* states that Pope Anastasius wished to recall Acacius—or at least restore his name to the sacred diptychs—although Acacius had already been condemned by Felix III and Gelasius, his predecessors, and had been dead for many years under Felix III. It is equally false that, at the same time, many clerics and presbyters separated themselves from Anastasius’s communion because he had communicated, without a council of bishops, presbyters, or clergy, with a Thessalonian deacon named Photinus, who had communicated with Acacius.

These claims have been demonstrated to be altogether false by what has been said. Baronius, under the year 497, further shows that Pope Anastasius entered into no agreement with the emperor Anastasius, but rather detested him.

### Line 9

“Sixteen bishops in various places.”

Since the Librarian omitted several notable acts under Anastasius—especially concerning the conversion of King Clovis in Gaul and the ordination of bishops—the history must be supplemented from Pagi, numbers 6 and following.

[Col. 0448D]

While Anastasius was seated on the Roman throne, no Christian Catholic ruler at all could be found anywhere in the whole world. The emperor Anastasius, who for a long time had hidden under a covering of orthodox faith, was now openly known to be a heretic.

At Rome and in Italy, King Theodoric; in Gaul, Alaric of the Visigoths; and Gundobad of the Burgundians were entirely Arian, as were the Suebi and any others in Spain. In Germany and Britain the people were still pagan.

King Clovis of the Franks, after obtaining victory over the Alemanni through invoking the name of Christ, was baptized by Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims—not in 499, as Baronius believed, but in 496, at the very beginning of Anastasius’s pontificate, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. This is established by the letter of Avitus, bishop of Vienne in the kingdom of Burgundy, written to Clovis and preserved in volume IV of the Councils, p. 1266. Avitus writes:

> “Therefore, since the Lord’s Nativity is celebrated, let it also be yours, on which you were born to Christ and Christ was born to the world; on which you consecrated your soul to God, your life to those living now, and your fame to posterity.”

On the same day as Clovis, “his sister Albofledis was also baptized.” Then, writes Hincmarus in the *Life of Saint Remigius*, “his other sister, named Lantechildis, who had fallen into the Arian heresy, was converted; after confessing the Son and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father, she received chrismation.”

This practice of baptizing at the Lord’s Nativity continued among the Franks after the conversion of King Clovis. For King Guntram, according to Gregory of Tours, book VIII, chapter 9, is said to have postponed the baptism of his nephew beyond the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity.

When Pope Anastasius learned that Clovis had been regenerated through baptism, he immediately sent him a letter of congratulation through the presbyter Eumerius, published by Dacherius in volume V of the *Spicilegium*. He wrote:

> “We rejoice that your beginning in the Christian faith has coincided with the beginning of our pontificate. For the see of Peter cannot fail to rejoice on such an occasion, when it sees the fullness of the nations hastening toward it with swift step and, as time passes, the net being filled which that same fisher of men and blessed keeper of the keys of the heavenly Jerusalem was commanded to cast into the deep.”

Since Anastasius was ordained Roman pontiff in November 496, Clovis’s baptism belongs to the Nativity of Christ in that same year, and Anastasius’s letter to Clovis was written around the beginning of 497.

Anastasius issued a decree in a dispute between the bishops of Arles and Vienne. Pope Symmachus, in his first letter to Aeonius, bishop of Arles, written on the third day before the Kalends of October in the year 500, says:

> “It is evident that a certain dispute has arisen between the Church of Arles and the Church of Vienne concerning the ordination of bishops in neighboring cities. The matter arose because our predecessor, Anastasius of holy memory, while addressing the disorder of the province, ordered certain things to be observed contrary to ancient custom, transgressing, under whatever necessity, the ordination of his predecessors, which ought not to have happened,”

and so forth.

He then commands that the ancient decrees of the apostolic see be observed. Anastasius’s decree, however, is found nowhere. This and another letter of Pope Symmachus to Aeonius concerning the same dispute will be discussed under Symmachus.

## Note

### [Col. 0449C]

### Line 1

“Anastasius,” etc.

Saint Anastasius II, who succeeded Gelasius, wrote to the emperor Anastasius concerning his election, using the following words, which also declare his vigilant care for the Catholic religion in the government he had undertaken:

> “I announce the beginning of my pontificate and its first fruits by the peace offered to the peoples; and consequently, as a humble suppliant for the Catholic faith, I approach your piety. In this I trust that divine favor has first drawn near to me: that now the harmony of your august name undoubtedly provides assistance to me, so that, just as the lofty name of your piety shines throughout all nations and across the whole world, so, through the ministry of my humility, the see of Blessed Peter may retain in the universal Church the primacy assigned to it by the Lord God, as it always has.
>
> “[May it be arranged] that the name of Acacius in particular be suppressed; that you may cause the Alexandrians to return to the Catholic and sincere faith through the authority of your wisdom and your divine admonitions; and that, as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit dictates, obedience may be offered to our admonitions, that is, to those of the apostolic see.”

(*Letter I of Anastasius II to Anastasius Augustus.)

The holy pontiff also writes to Clovis, king of the Franks, who was the first of those kings to receive the sacraments of the Christian religion:

> “We rejoice, glorious son, that your beginning in the Christian faith has coincided with our beginning in the pontificate. For the See of Peter cannot fail to rejoice on so great an occasion, when it sees the fullness of the nations hastening toward it with rapid steps, and the net being filled through the passage of time—the net which that same fisher of men and blessed key-bearer of the heavenly Jerusalem was commanded to cast into the deep. We wish to make this known to your Serenity through the priest Eumerius, so that, when you have heard of the Father’s joy in good works, you may complete our joy and be our crown, and so that Mother Church may rejoice in the progress of so great a king, whom she has recently borne to God.

> “Make your mother joyful, therefore, glorious and illustrious son, [Col. 0450B] and be for her a pillar of iron; for the charity of many is growing cold, and our little vessel is driven through savage waves by the cunning of evil men and pierced by the foaming waters. But we hope against hope, and we praise the Lord together, who has rescued you from the power of darkness and, in so great a prince, provides for the Church one who can protect her and put on the helmet of salvation against the assaults of those who seek her ruin.

> “Go forward, therefore, beloved and glorious son, and may almighty God accompany your Serenity and your kingdom with heavenly protection; may he command his angels to guard you in all your ways, and grant you victory over your enemies on every side.”

*(Pope Anastasius II, Letter II, to Clovis, king of the Franks.)*

It should be observed that almost all the rulers of that age were unbelievers or had corrupted the Christian faith through heresy, with the single exception of Clovis, who was then being baptized for the first time in the West. The kings Theodoric, Alaric, Gundobad, and the other rulers of Gothic, Visigothic, Suevic, or Vandal origin all professed and maintained the Arian heresy. They ruled the provinces of Spain, Gaul, Africa, and Italy, from which they had expelled the Romans. Germany, moreover, and the island of Great Britain obeyed kings infected with idolatry.

Line 7.—He secretly wished to restore Acacius. The Bibliothecary states that Pope Anastasius II secretly wished to yield to the obstinacy of the Greeks, who refused to remove Acacius’s name from the sacred diptychs; but, struck down by divine judgment through a sudden death, he did not carry out this plan. The same author adds that, for this reason, certain members of the clergy withdrew from communion with the pope, and also because he had admitted to communion, without consulting the assembly of bishops, priests, and clergy, a Thessalonian deacon who had been in communion with Acacius. Some more recent writers, however, deny that this occurred, maintaining that the Bibliothecary incorrectly relied on memoirs stitched together by the faction of the antipope Laurence, whom the Greek faction opposed to Anastasius’s successor. On this matter see Cardinal Baronius under the year 497, and Bellarmine, *Controversies*, book IV, chapter 10, in the section “On the Roman Pontiff.” Others, with Tillemont in his *Ecclesiastical History* under the same year, suppose that Anastasius wished to deal more leniently with the Greeks; yet, although the author is full of errors, they consider Anastasius too unreliable a witness for confirming that conclusion.

[Col. 0439]

75.

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter, from the Fifth Region, at the head of the Taurus district, occupied the see for one year, eleven months, and twenty-four days [Note: [Col. 0439] B: two years less seven days, from the consulship of Paulinus to that of Paulinus and John]. He lived in the time of King Theodoric. He made the silver confessio of blessed Laurence the martyr, which weighed one hundred pounds [Note: [Col. 0439] Scytha consul: C, eighty]. At the same time many clerics and priests withdrew themselves from his communion [Note: [Col. 0439] They “withdrew” or “recoiled.” See Baronius under the year 497], because he had admitted to communion, without a council of the bishops, priests, or clergy of the whole Catholic Church, a Thessalonian deacon named Photinus [Note: [Col. 0439] C: Photino], who had been in communion with Acacius [Note: [Col. 0439] B: Acacius’s communion], and because he wished secretly to restore Acacius but could not; for he was struck down by divine will. He held one ordination in the city of Rome, in the month of December: twelve priests and sixteen bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, and the episcopate was vacant for four days.

Number 78, line 3: “to exercise [violence] out of envy.” “Those who had been found privately and publicly in communion with Symmachus” [line 5], “indeed the holy…” [line 6], “they wounded [him]: therefore every day they fought against the Church…” [line 7, Col. 0455C] “and also killed many priests, among them Gordianus, a most worthy priest, whom they murdered with clubs and swords at Saint Peter in Chains, the Apostle. They also killed many Christians, so that no member of the clergy could safely walk publicly through the city by day or night. Faustus, however, the former consul, fought on behalf of the Church. After all these things Symmachus found Manichaeans in the city of Rome, all of whose books he burned in a fire before the doors of Constantine’s basilica.” Line 14: “to the council of the elder.”

Number 76, line 1: The Cassinese, Florentine, Roman, Romualdian, and Deusdedit manuscripts read “Sardinian.” Line 1: “seven months” in the Florentine, Cassinese, and Vatican manuscripts. Line 8: “the Florentine and Vatican manuscripts read ‘he found.’” Line 9: after the word “he recognized,” the Florentine manuscript adds “to favor.” Line 10: “the same [manuscripts read] ‘nevertheless.’”

The Oratory of Saint Sossius, made of silver.” Line 9: “The Oratory of the Holy Cross.” Line 14: “with a quadriporticus adorned with marble work.” Line 17: “beneath the steps in the area” (perhaps it should be read “in the courtyard”).
