[Note: [Col. 0457A]

Number 76, line 1.—Symmachus. After an interregnum of four days, in the year of Christ 498, which was the final year of the deceased Anastasius, Laurence, a Roman, was elected pontiff by the votes of a few, while Symmachus, formerly a deacon, was elected by the suffrages of the majority. Through the care and efforts of the senator Festus, who had promised the emperor that he would induce the Roman pontiff to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henoticon*, arrangements were made for Laurence to be elected in schism against the whole Church; Festus knew that Laurence would comply with the impious demands. Strength was added to the Laurentian schism by the fact that it had as its supporter and promoter Paschasius, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, a man outstanding in learning and holiness. Of him Saint Gregory relates in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4, that Germanus, a bishop, having entered the Baths of Angulana on the advice of physicians for the sake of his bodily health, found the aforementioned Paschasius standing amid the heat. When asked what he was doing there, Paschasius replied:

> “I have been assigned to this place of punishment for no other reason than that I took Laurence’s side against Symmachus. But I ask you to pray to the Lord for me; and you will know that your prayer has been heard if, when you return here, you do not find me.”

Accordingly, the man of God Germanus devoted himself earnestly to prayer and returned after a few days, but he found the aforementioned Paschasius no longer in that place.

Same line. He occupied the see for fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-six days. Baronius proves that he occupied it for fifteen years and eight months less four days, from the consulship of Paulinus and Scytha to that of Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus, in the year 514, number 6.

Line 2.—He lived in the time of Theodoric. From the seventh through the twelfth year of Theodoric’s reign in Italy; from the ninth through the twenty-fourth year of Anastasius’s reign in the East.

Line 6.—And after a dispute had arisen, the parties decreed this. An importunate and ill-advised necessity, ignorant of laws, demanded that these things be done contrary to laws and canons.]

[Note: [Col. 0457C]

Number 77, line 1.—At the same time Pope Symmachus convened a synod. The first Roman synod, at which the Roman pontiff was recognized and approved by all the bishops who were present.

Line 8.—So that the king might appoint a visitor to the apostolic see. Someone who would investigate the accusations brought against Symmachus. Since the authors of the schism could find no grounds for troubling Symmachus concerning the illegitimacy of his election, they turned to slanders and lies and fabricated the most serious charges against him. They sent the king a written accusation against the pontiff and asked Theodoric, an Arian king, to appoint a visitor. Peter, bishop of Altina, was assigned this office. At the request of the Catholics, Theodoric agreed to the council’s proposal and judged it necessary to present himself at a suitable time to the City, which was endangered by civil war after his presence had long been delayed. Baronius, in the year of Christ 500.

Line 10.—From a false charge. It is remarkable that, although the synodal acts of three councils survive, none of them contains even the slightest mention of the charge on which the pontiff was accused. From this, reader, you may learn that all the bishops wisely wished those marks of infamy—which the adversaries had attempted to brand upon Pope Symmachus—to be buried in deep silence and erased by oblivion; and that they took every care to prevent any stain upon the supreme priest of the whole Church from being recorded in public acts and transmitted to posterity on any occasion.

Number 78, line 1.—At the same time Faustus was head of the senate. Ennodius declares in his little book that those killed in this schism were worthy of the crown of martyrdom, and that those who had suffered anything for this reason were ennobled by the glory of confession. He follows the judgment of the great Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 37, where he says:

> “It was necessary to suffer every hardship rather than to divide the harmony of God’s Church. But that martyrdom which someone suffers so that the confession of the Church may not be broken certainly has, in my judgment, no less—and indeed much more—commendation than that which is undertaken so that no sacrifice at all may be offered to idols.” [Col. 0458A]

Line 11.—After all these events blessed Symmachus found Manichaeans, etc. The accusation by the emperor Anastasius, by which he had defamed Symmachus on the charge of Manichaean heresy, was therefore futile.

Number 79, line 1.—He made the basilica of Saint Andrew the Apostle, etc. It is a matter of great wonder that so much could have been accomplished by a Roman pontiff under a barbarian king, under whom the City itself seemed in some sense to be held captive. This is especially remarkable because Symmachus, with pastoral generosity, did not fail to redeem captives and support the African bishops banished to Sardinia, but supplied everything abundantly.

Number 81, line 4.—He redeemed captives throughout Liguria, etc. Not with King Theodoric’s money, but with the alms of the Roman Church. Baronius, year 496, [Col. 0458B] number 56.]

[Note: [Col. 0458B]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

That Symmachus’s pontificate should be assigned to the year 498, three days after the death of Anastasius, with John (Scytha) consul in the East and Paulinus consul in the West, is established by the clearest evidence. For the acts of the Roman synod convened under his presidency in the Vatican basilica are dated as follows:

> “After the consulship of Paulinus, a most illustrious man, on the Kalends of March”—the date belongs to the year 499—“in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the most blessed Pope Symmachus presiding over the synod, Fulgentius the archdeacon said…”

Moreover, two letters of Symmachus are subscribed with the same indication of year, namely, after the consulship of Paulinus: the first was issued on the third day before the Kalends of October, and the second on the third day before the Kalends of November. A third, likewise in Binius’s edition, is dated the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, although the consular notation is not given. Since, however, it records the eighth indiction, which began in September of the same year 499, it shows that Symmachus entered upon the pontificate in 498.

The Bibliothecary assigns him fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-five days; the Cassinese and Vatican manuscripts agree with this, as does the seventh Colbertine catalogue. The Bergomian and three Colbertine manuscripts, however, add one day; others add two days. Some also add one month, both on the basis of the Anastasian manuscripts and on that of the catalogues.

The dispute is settled by the date of his deposition, which is expressly given in the Freher, Royal, Mazarine, and Thuane manuscripts as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, and in the second Thuane manuscript as the nineteenth of July; these dates are identical. Since Anastasius II died on 17 or 18 November 498, and Symmachus was elected—or even ordained—four days later (for the Sunday letter of that year, D, indicates Sunday, 22 November), it follows that, counting fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days from that date, the total designates 19 July [Col. 0458D] 514, in the consulship of Senator. This was the end of the pontificate and mortal life of blessed Symmachus, as is likewise expressly stated in a fragment of a very ancient manuscript of the canonical archive of the holy Church of Verona, which will be discussed below.

The same date is assigned to his commemoration in the Roman Martyrology and in the offices of the patriarchal basilicas of the City. Our Liberian basilica alone transfers it to the following day, because of the occurrence of the feast of Saint Epaphra, companion of blessed Paul the Apostle, who was buried together with Saint Matthias at the principal altar.

That the consulship of Cassiodorus should be assigned to Pope Symmachus, who survived until 10 July, and to his successor Hormisdas after the election that followed, is made certain by the letters produced by the compiler of the *Annals* under that same year. These include a letter of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, dated the third day before the Ides of June in the consulship of Senator, a most illustrious man, and a letter of Anastasius Augustus to Hormisdas, whom he calls [Col. 0459A] “the most holy and most devout archbishop and patriarch,” dated the fifth day before the Kalends of January in the consulship of Senator, a most illustrious man.

HISTORICAL NOTES.

Number 77, line 5.—Those accusing blessed Symmachus. The character of the shameless written accusation composed by the schismatic faction can be learned from the insults reported in a fragment sewn into the ancient manuscript of the Veronese archive mentioned above, in the notes on the Life of Anastasius II, number 75.

Number 78, line 11.—Faustus alone, the former consul, fought on behalf of the Church. Two former consuls named Faustus may have survived under Pope Symmachus: the one who held the consulship alone in 483, the year in which blessed Simplicius died, and Faustus the Younger, who was consul with Longinus in 490. See our chronology in the Prolegomena for the years mentioned.

[Col. 0459B] Line 14.—From the consulship of Paulinus to that of Senator. The consulship of Paulinus corresponds to the common era year 498, with John Scytha as his colleague; the consulship of Senator without a colleague corresponds to 514, the year in which Symmachus’s final letter, dated the third day before the Ides of June, and the emperor Anastasius’s first letter to Hormisdas, the successor of Symmachus, dated the fifth day before the Kalends of January, were issued, as we said above in the chronological notes.

Number 79, line 1.—He made the basilica of Saint Andrew the Apostle at blessed Peter. Martinellus, in his *Sacred Rome*, page 341, identifies the site of this oratory, which the Bibliothecary generously calls a basilica.

> “The church of Saint Andrew,” he says, “in the Vatican, was erected by Pope Symmachus in the year 498. John VI made an ambo for it; Gregory III made the roof and the vault. Stephen III and IV, Adrian I, and Leo III and IV bestowed gifts, according to the Bibliothecary. The same author calls it an oratory: ‘Leo IV made in the oratory [Col. 0459C] of blessed Andrew the Apostle, which adjoins the church of Saint Peter, a vestment, etc.’ Jacobus Grimaldus writes that today it is the sacristy of the Vatican basilica.”

Line 6.—The Oratory of Saint Apollinaris. The same Martinellus, folio 312, writes that this oratory was called *ad Palmata* in the portico of blessed Peter, citing the Bibliothecary under Honorius I:

> “He made the basilica of Apollinaris the martyr in the city of Rome, in the portico of the blessed apostle Peter, which is called *ad Palmata*”—another manuscript reads *Palmaria*—“from the ground where he bestowed many gifts.”

And below:

> “The litany goes out from blessed Apollinaris to blessed Peter the Apostle.”

Grimaldus wrote about it: “The church of Saint Apollinaris *ad Palmata* in the portico of blessed Peter.” Thus the Bibliothecary under Honorius I says:

> “He made the basilica of the blessed Apostle, which is called *ad Palmata*”—another manuscript reads *Palmaria*—“from the ground where he bestowed many gifts.”

And below:

> “The litany goes out from blessed Apollinaris to blessed Peter the Apostle.”

Grimaldus wrote the following about it:

> “The church of Saint Apollinaris, built by Honorius I, stood on the site where there is now a stable with several houses belonging to the archpresbyterate of Saint Peter, beside the steps of the basilica. These houses form an island in front of the forum. On one side is a street leading toward the Holy Office; on the other, a road leading toward the Gate of Turrio; behind is the public road of the Holy Spirit.

> “From this church,” Anastasius says, “by decree of Honorius, a litany went out every Saturday to the basilica of Saint Peter, and it was called *ad Palmata*. It retained the ancient name of the circus because of the victorious palm-bearers honored there with gifts in the circus games. For the end or head of the circus was there, made of certain squared stones arranged in a semicircle.

> “In 1616, when the steps of Saint Peter were removed, ancient, thick, reticulated walls appeared. They seemed to have belonged to the ruins of the circus towers. A bronze coin of Agrippina Augusta was found there. When this other part of the Vatican church was founded under Paul V, it was determined that the circus had been 720 palms long and 400 Roman palms wide. The area where the games were held was 230 palms wide. It began at the lowest steps of the basilica and ended where the church of Saint Martha now stands behind the apse, toward the west. An obelisk stood in the middle; that site is now behind the choir chapel.

> “The outer double-columned wall of the basilica of the Most Holy Crucified One and of Saint Andrew had been founded above the three great walls of the aforementioned circus of Gaius and Nero. It resembled the Circus of Caracalla, most of which still exists today. It was enclosed on both sides by high walls, three on one side, above which stood the mentioned naves of the Crucified One and Saint Andrew, and three on the other, where the cemetery of the Campo Santo now lies. Extending lengthwise, these brick walls formerly supported the arched vaults on which the seats for spectators were located. Between the two walls was a space forty-two and a half palms wide.

> “From head to foot there was no obstruction; rather, what could be seen among the ruins themselves resembled walkways and passageways. When the earth of the choir foundations was removed, I arranged for the rear wall facing the circus to be measured. [Col. 0460B] The wall itself was thirty-one and a half palms high from the ground; it was fourteen palms wide and thirty palms deep at the foundation.

> “The front façade of the ancient Vatican basilica built by Constantine the Great, its apse and outer walls, and those rising above the columns that supported the roofs with their heavy weight, were constructed from fragments of brick and tufa taken from the collapsed circus and adjacent buildings, with rapid labor and crude workmanship. Direct observation showed that Constantine had completed the basilica itself in a short time. Some capitals were finished, others unfinished; many bases differed from their columns; the windows were first made of brick in an arch, and later in the German manner, of marble.

> “The thresholds were made from large marble blocks. The lower part, buried in the earth, indicated that they had been removed from the ruins of the circus or of another building. Beneath one of them, which was slightly arched, roses had been carved; on another, the letters *CUM SPECULATOR* could be read. It was judged that these letters perhaps designated the arch or the place for the watcher in the circus itself.

> “So much for the circus. The church of Saint Apollinaris [Col. 0460C] was said to be in the portico, for the portico leading to the basilica of Saint Peter began at the church of Saint Mary *in Transpontina* and ended at the aforementioned church of Saint Apollinaris.”

Line 8.—Likewise, at the fountain in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, [he made] the Oratory of the Holy Cross, with a silver confessio, etc. Martinellus likewise writes on page 353 that there can be no doubt that the Oratory of the Holy Cross at the Fountain of Saint Peter was an altar or chapel. The Bibliothecary says the same under Symmachus. Under Leo III, however, he calls it the Oratory and Monastery of Jerusalem. Under Leo IV he calls it the venerable Monastery of Jerusalem beside the church of blessed Peter. Grimaldus writes:

> “It stood to the north, and under Alexander III it was called Saint Vincent. This church was demolished in 1611 for the sake of the new temple and had already long since been converted to the use of a wine cellar. Although narrow because of its age, it had an east-facing doorway, from which nearly eighteen columns of intact veined marble, about twenty [Col. 0460D] palms long, were recovered.”

Line 22.—He made the basilica of Saint Pancratius. On this subject one should likewise read the same Martinellus, page 265, who discusses both the original foundation under Symmachus and later repairs under Honorius I, Adrian I, and others; after him, Charles Piazza in his *Cardinal Hierarchy*. Both writers mention that in the same church, on 21 November 1204, Peter, king of Aragon, was anointed by Peter, bishop of Porto, and crowned by the hand of Pope Innocent III. He was afterward led to the Vatican basilica, where the same pontiff armed him for the defense of the Catholic faith and made him swear an oath of fidelity, reported by Ciaconius in his Life of the aforementioned Innocent.

Beneath the church of Saint Pancratius lies the very ancient cemetery called that of Calepodius, mentioned above in several places, for example in the Life of Saint Callistus and that of Saint Julius.

Number 80, line 1.—The basilica of Saints Silvester and Martin. The Bibliothecary indicates that the church whose title was founded under Silvester at Equilius was enlarged by Symmachus with a new foundation. Paintings of the same period still survive today in the underground part of that titular church, as Martinellus observes on page 256. In the first crypts on the right at the entrance are sacred images of Christ the Lord seated among the apostles Peter and Paul, and of the martyrs Processus and Martinianus; on the opposite wall are images of holy virgins. The names that remain are: “Saint Paul,” “Saint Processus,” “Saint Agnes.”

Line 6.—Likewise, at Saint Mary, the Oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Martinellus, often cited above, speaks of this same oratory under Leo III, number 405, saying:

> “In the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which is situated beside the Nativity scene, he made a silver basket, etc.”

Martinellus adds that this oratory later took its additional name from Saint Luke, the patron of the art of painting, until it was demolished under Sixtus V. Grimaldus places it at the foot of the Esquiline Hill. Paul de Angelis, in Book V, chapter 2, on the Liberian basilica, thinks that it was a chapel erected within that same basilica, but he speaks of it very briefly; he cites only this passage of the Bibliothecary and passes over the other testimony, which Martinellus skillfully brought forward from Leo III, number 405.

Martinellus’s account that the little church stood near the basilica and was demolished under Sixtus V is supported by Octavius Pancirolius in his *History of the Church of Saint Martina*. The guild of painters was transferred to that church. He writes:

> “It happened in the year 1588 that Pope Sixtus V, wishing to adorn the City with splendid buildings, leveled the church of Saint Luke, situated near the basilica of Saint Mary Major and assigned to the painters’ guild. In place of the demolished church he gave that guild this church of Saint Martina, whose title the same society arranged to have restored jointly to its patron, the holy Evangelist.”

Number 81, line 1.—He decreed that every Sunday, or on the birthdays of the martyrs, the angelic hymn should be sung. Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book II, chapter 4, numbers 4 and 5, shows that the angelic hymn *Glory to God in the highest* is older than Symmachus, since blessed Athanasius quotes it verbatim near the end of his book *On Virginity*. It is written in Greek in a fourth-century Christian manuscript from Alexandria, called the Codex of Thecla, together with Athanasius’s creed, in the royal library at London.

Therefore both Cardinal Bona and more recent liturgical writers attribute to Telesphorus the initial institution of singing the Gospel words of this hymn on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. They attribute the remainder of the hymn’s composition, along with the Fourth Council of Toledo, to ecclesiastical teachers of approximately the fourth century: Hilary among the Latins and Athanasius among the Greeks.

They attribute the practice of singing the hymn in its entirety to the decrees of Symmachus, but only on Sundays and on the birthdays of the martyrs. They credit Stephen IV, on the basis of Anastasius, number 284, with the following practice:

> “That on every Sunday it should be celebrated by the seven cardinal bishops serving weekly, who observe the solemn rites of the Mass in the church of the Savior, upon the altar of blessed Peter, and that the *Glory in the highest* should be said,”

because Symmachus had reserved this to one bishop, just as he had reserved the rite of announcing peace at the first greeting of the people with the words, “Peace be with you.” See Cardinal Bona at the place cited.

Line 3.—Every year throughout Africa or Sardinia he provided for the bishops who had been confined in exile, etc. An ancient chronicle, a sixth-century work edited by R. P. Ruinart in Part I of his *Vandalic History*, folio 115, reports almost the same words concerning Pope Symmachus:

> “Every year throughout Africa or Sardinia he supplied money and clothing to the bishops who were in exile.”

Victor, bishop of Vita, in Book IV, number 4 of his *History of the Vandal Persecution*, published by the same Ruinart on page 71, explains why and how the confessing bishops had been banished during the persecution of Genseric and his successor kings—some to Africa, others to Corsica and Sardinia—because they had vigorously and steadfastly defended the Catholic faith.

The chronicle mentioned above counts [Col. 0462A] more than 330 Catholic bishops driven into exile by Hunneric, and 220 banished by Thrasamund to Sardinia, on page 115, shortly before Symmachus’s pontificate. An ancient catalogue printed there on folio 123 lists their names individually.

Under Pope Symmachus, the persecution of King Thrasamund was raging in Africa. Therefore, as Ruinart observes, the same pontiff,

> “having received news of so savage a storm against the Catholic Church, and considering it his duty to strengthen his brothers placed amid tribulations and hardships, composed an excellent letter to them,”

which he transcribes from Ennodius, Book II, letter 14, on page 579, adding on page 582 what follows:

> “But Pope Symmachus, whose consoling letter we have quoted above, aided the confessors of Christ not only by voice or pen, but also in deed and action. Following the example of his predecessors, he shared in the sufferings of Christ’s holy confessors by supplying them with what was necessary for food and clothing. ‘He,’ says Anastasius, ‘every year throughout Africa or Sardinia supplied money and clothing to the bishops who had been confined in exile.’” [Col. 0462B]

The same words occur in the brief chronicle that we published above at the end of Victor of Vita, on page 112.

We have a third witness to this matter, namely the author of the Life of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, which the learned Philip Labbe extracted from an ancient manuscript and published in volume I of his *New Library*, page 693. There we read:

> “In the time of this blessed Avitus, a most severe persecution of the Vandals and of the other peoples in Africa broke out, and Pope Symmachus supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to five hundred and fifty bishops who were in exile.”

The author of the *Miscellaneous History*, writing under the name of Paul the Deacon, Book XVII, says that blessed Symmachus did not cease supplying them with daily assistance.

I omit Ado in his *Chronicle*, Hermannus the Contracted, and other later writers, [Col. 0462C] who copied the ancient authors.]

[Note: [Col. 0462C]

### No. 76, line 3

“He was ordained amid a dispute on the same day as Laurentius.” For Faustus, the legate of the emperor Anastasius, in order to fulfill what he had secretly promised the emperor, had undertaken to persuade the Roman pontiff to subscribe to Zeno’s *Henotikon*, or “Instrument of Union.” When he came to Rome and found that the bishop Anastasius was dead, and all hope of accomplishing this with Anastasius himself had vanished, he worked to have a successor elected who could easily be persuaded to undertake it and would comply with his wishes. Having corrupted many with money, he achieved this: contrary to custom, a certain bishop who was Roman by nationality, named Laurentius, was elected.

### No. 79, line 1

“He built the basilica of Saint Andrew, etc.” It is plainly worthy of admiration that so much could have been accomplished by a Roman pontiff under a barbarian king, under whom the City itself seemed in a certain sense to be held captive—especially since the same Symmachus, with pastoral generosity, did not fail in redeeming captives and in feeding the two hundred and twenty African bishops exiled in Sardinia by Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, but supplied everything in abundance.

### No. 76, line 3: “He was ordained amid a dispute,” etc.

Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, who, after defeating and killing Odoacer, king of the Heruli, had brought Italy under his own power, employed at the court of the Eastern Empire a Roman senator named Festus as his agent. In order to win the favor of the emperor Anastasius, Festus had promised that he would bring about the acceptance and subscription of Zeno’s *Henotikon* by the Roman pontiff. Returning from his journey to Constantinople, he found Rome deprived of its shepherd. He considered this opportunity especially suitable for accomplishing what he had undertaken.

“Accordingly, having corrupted many with money” (as Theodorus Lector writes in Book II of his *Collections*; see also Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 36), “he achieved the election, contrary to custom, of a certain bishop who was Roman by nationality, Laurentius. Thus two were ordained: Symmachus was ordained by the majority from the diaconate, while Laurentius was ordained by the others. Because of them, killings, robberies, and countless other evils were perpetrated at Rome.”

Necessity compelled both competitors to overstep the rules and induced them to submit the judgment of the affair to the king—and to a king who was an Arian—although the nature of the case required that it be treated in a council. Both therefore went to Ravenna, where Theodoric had established the seat of his kingdom. When their claims had been presented before him, he pronounced an equitable judgment: the one should sit as bishop who had either been ordained first or been elected by the greater number of votes. Since these conditions were found in the case of Symmachus, he himself was made bishop.

Symmachus began his administration by convening a council, which he himself presided over. There he was asked by all the Fathers to deign to establish provisions concerning ecclesiastical liberty and the peace and harmony of the whole Church. He replied:

> “The council of your charity, while our concern for the Church’s security disregarded the severity of winter, has especially brought us together so that, through common deliberation, we may firmly and vigorously cut off for the future the episcopal rivalry, the uncertainty of confusion, or the popular tumult which, through the devil’s deception and the usurpation of certain persons, is known to have arisen at the time of my ordination . . . decreeing what ought to be observed concerning the ordination of the Roman bishop.”

*First Roman Synod under Symmachus.*

The following matters were therefore decreed in the council:

1. If anyone, while the pope is still alive, is found in any way to offer favor to anyone for the Roman pontificate, he shall be deprived of the rank of his office.

2. If the election inclines unanimously toward one person from the whole ecclesiastical order, the elected man shall be consecrated bishop. But if the preferences of those among whom the dispute has arisen begin to be divided, the judgment of the greater number shall prevail.

3. If anyone brings to ecclesiastical notice the plans of those who have engaged in a canvass for the pontificate contrary to this synod, and proves them by reasonable evidence, he shall not only be cleared of every fault as an accomplice in such an action, but shall also be supported by a reward that is not undeserved.

“Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, consenting to these synodal constitutions, approved and confirmed by me, have subscribed. I have consented to the synodal constitutions, and I profess that I remain in this judgment. Caelius, archpriest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed and consented to these,” etc.

### No. 77, line 2: “But after four years,” etc.

Certain members of the clergy and some of the senate—above all Festus and Probinus—accused Symmachus by fabricating charges against him. Having secretly summoned Laurentius, they renewed the schism. The trickery of Festus and Probinus advanced so far that they obtained from King Theodoric the appointment of a visitor of the apostolic see, or commissioner, to reduce these matters to writing: Peter, bishop of Altinum, who favored the intruder Laurentius. He, “making the king’s command out of the priest’s wish,” as Ennodius writes in his little work in defense of Symmachus, openly attached himself to the schismatics and thereby increased the disturbances.

Symmachus, having convened a synod of one hundred and fifteen bishops, judged that provision had to be made for the unity and liberty of the Church, which had been violated by the schismatics with such shamelessness. After first offering in the synod a voluntary clearing of the crimes brought against him, he issued a sentence of condemnation against Laurentius of Nuceria, the invader of the apostolic see, and against Peter of Altinum, the assistant of the same faction.

King Theodoric had indeed intervened with his authority so that the synod might be held. But when he was seriously admonished by the bishops whom he had summoned—as we read in the acts of the synod—that the task of convening a council belonged to Symmachus himself, who was said to be the accused, and that the bishop of Peter’s see ought not to be subject to the judgment of his inferiors, he replied that the pope himself had also shown by letter his willingness to convene the synod.

At the first session, the holy pope Symmachus declared that he was willing to submit himself to the authority of the order for correction, but on this condition: before anything else, the royal visitor or commissioner should be dealt with outside the council, until Symmachus, the bishop of so great a see, had been restored to his former position; only then would he permit these matters to be treated, and he would not come to the case before that time. This appeared wholly just to the Fathers.

When new difficulties were reported to Theodoric, the king declared:

> “It belongs to the synod’s discretion to prescribe what should be followed in so great a matter, and nothing concerning ecclesiastical affairs pertains to me except reverence; whether they wish to hear the proposed case or not, let them deliberate about what they judge more useful, provided that, through the venerable council’s foresight, peace may be restored in the Roman city to all Christians.”

When the Fathers of the council understood that “it is not for sheep to anticipate the wolves’ ambush, but for the shepherd,” after weighing by heavenly inspiration all the circumstances of the case in secret, they decreed:

> “That Pope Symmachus, bishop of the apostolic see, accused of such proposals, be, as far as human beings are concerned—since, because of the obstacles specified above, the matter is known to have been left to divine judgment—immune and free; and that, without any presentation concerning the charges brought against him, he may in all his churches belonging to the right of his see administer the divine mysteries to the Christian people. For we have recognized that he could not be bound by the accusation of his opponents because of the causes specified above . . . Reserving the whole case to God’s judgment, we exhort everyone to receive holy communion from him, as the matter requires, and to remember God and their own souls.”

*In the Roman Synod under Symmachus.*

The same Fathers declared in a synodal letter to King Theodoric:

> “It is a new thing among us that the pontiff of that very see—that is, the Roman see—should be heard: no example is known.”

At the end of the same synodal letter.

The spirit of schism, whose character is obstinacy and pride, just as in heresy, published a little work entitled *Against the Inappropriate Absolution of the Synod*. In it the Fathers were accused because, among other things, they had declared that the right to convene a council did not belong to secular powers but only to the pontifical authority; and because they had pronounced that the Roman pontiff was not subject to the judgment of other bishops, since they were his inferiors. The schismatics argued that to assert that such a privilege had been bestowed by Christ the Lord upon Peter and his successors was the same as saying that the ability to sin with impunity had been divinely granted to them.

The synod was convened again and deputed Ennodius to refute the arguments of this little work. He did so in his *Apologetic*. In it he teaches that the authority to convene a council “is a prerogative divinely assigned to the Holy See . . . Or do you perhaps think that something else was meant when it was said that he himself ought to convene the synod, whose task it was, by his office, to strike you with the divine sentence through a pontifical examination—you whom insane fury had cut off from the structure of your head to the detriment of salvation . . . I say that the author of a law is not confined within the limits of his own enactment unless he wishes it . . . Perhaps God wished human beings to determine the cases of other people; but He reserved without question to the discretion of the bishop of that see the case of its bishop. He wished the successors of blessed Peter to owe their innocence to heaven alone and to present an inviolate conscience to the scrutiny of the most subtle examiner. Do not suppose that those souls have no fear of investigators whom God has reserved above all others for His own examination. The accused has no support before Him from the brilliance of an argument when he has as a witness of his very deeds the One who is Judge,” etc.

*The same work.*

D. Dupin, never failing to seize opportunities to diminish the privileges and rights of the Roman see, lists Ennodius’s statements among the paradoxes—namely, when Ennodius seems to assert that a man is either holy or immediately made holy as soon as he is promoted to the summit of the Roman pontificate. Dupin maintains that Ennodius uses no other argument to exempt the Roman pontiff from the jurisdiction of a council than this assertion, which is wholly incapable of serving as a defense.

But whatever this modern critic may assert, it is easy to recognize that Ennodius in no way attributes what is called impeccability to the Roman pontiffs, and one need only weigh the words we have cited. Does he not assert the exact opposite when he writes that those who are raised to this supreme height of the Church militant are not free from fear because their examination has been reserved to God alone? The most reverend Bishop Fleury judges Ennodius’s statements more accurately when he observes that most of the Roman pontiffs counted up to his own time had lived so innocently and holily that they seemed capable of giving occasion for such a thought.

He departs still farther from the truth when he says that the sole means devised by Ennodius for freeing the pontiffs from the jurisdiction of a council was the impeccability just mentioned. Ennodius plainly says that the legislator, although he is not subject to the law enacted by him, nevertheless has an internal law of integrity and mind which chastises the person living without the law. He also adds that judgment over the Roman pontiff had been reserved by God to Himself, although he does not wish that pontiff to be judged by a human being in the manner of other people.

Finally, the council itself, which had entrusted Ennodius with composing that apology, gave the writing such complete approval that it strengthened it with the same authority by which it fortified the acts of the synod:

> “Let this little work be held by all in its entirety as a synodal document, and let it be inserted among the acts of our fourth and fifth synods; let it be regarded in the same way as the decrees of those synods, because it was written and confirmed with synodal authority.”

*Fifth Roman Synod under Symmachus.*

It had already been declared in the preceding council—namely, the Third under Symmachus—that the primacy of Saint Peter, the law of the Lord, and the authority of councils had granted his Roman see a unique power over all the Churches; that the bishop of the aforesaid see was not subject to the judgment of his inferiors; and that for this reason his cases were reserved to God’s judgment alone, nor was he obliged to answer the accusations of opponents in a council. Accordingly, several grounds were available, apart from Ennodius’s alleged opinion concerning impeccability—grounds that could be produced, indeed had been produced, and are read in the acts of the council—to assert the Roman pontiff’s exemption from the judgment of a council.

Moreover, Avitus of Vienne, in the letter to the senators of Rome, Faustus and Symmachus, which he wrote in the name of all the bishops throughout Gaul, asserts that this manner of conducting the council was greatly to be condemned if the Fathers, instead of offering consolation to the chief priest, had attempted to judge him:

> “We understand,” he says, “that if the holy pope Symmachus had first been accused before the world, he ought rather to have received the consolation of his fellow priests than their judgment . . . It is not easily understood by what reason or law one who is inferior may judge one who is superior. The synod itself, perceiving this, reserved to divine examination the case which it had almost rashly undertaken to investigate . . . In the case of other priests, if something should perhaps waver, it can be corrected; but if the pope of the City is called into doubt, it will seem that the episcopate, not the bishop, is tottering. He who presides over the Lord’s sheepfold will render an account; but it is not the flock’s role to frighten its own shepherd—it is the judge’s.”

### No. 78, line 12

“He found Manichaeans,” etc., whose images and books alike he burned in a fire before the doors of the Constantinian basilica.

From the notes on chapter 10.

Symmachus’s elevation to the Roman see was in no way welcome to the emperor Anastasius. Festus had promised that he would bring about the signing of Zeno’s *Henotikon* by the Roman pontiff; this hope had already been removed when Festus’s schemes and efforts on behalf of the antipope Laurentius had failed. Anastasius therefore refused to send Pope Symmachus a letter concerning his accession to the see of Peter, although this was customary among Christian rulers.

Nevertheless, Symmachus did not cease writing to the same Augustus. Indeed, he judged that he ought to use this occasion to recall the emperor to sounder counsels and remove him from the protection and communion of heretics.

The emperor not only failed to receive the shepherd’s voice with receptive ears or to obey him, but, driven by sharper goads toward impiety, sent military force throughout all the provinces of the empire so that Catholics everywhere would be compelled to communicate with heretics. Pope Symmachus therefore observed the actions of the emperor, who was daily falling into worse conduct and surrendering himself completely to those excommunicated because they were devoted to the memory of Acacius and hostile to the sacred Council of Chalcedon. He proceeded to excommunicate him, urged also by the Roman senate.

This inflamed the emperor’s mind extraordinarily, so that he attempted, in a written attack against the pontiff, to defame him by charging him with every crime. How laudably the pontiff replied according to the prescription of evangelical perfection may be judged from the collection of statements worthy of that apostolic man which we append. Since the letter contains their harvest, we gather here a few ears from it:

> “I,” he says, “instructed in the teachings of the Lord and the apostles, strive to return blessing for your curses, emperor, to repay insults with honor, and to return love for hatred. See, I ask you, lest from the One who says, ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ as much as is released from me, so much more abundantly be demanded from you . . . Therefore, emperor, as for the insults which you think are directed against my person, would that they could not burden you as much as they are glorious for me! Certain people said to my Lord: ‘You have a demon, you glutton, born of fornication.’ And you think that I ought to grieve for myself because of this? . . . Because you are emperor, do you think that there is no judgment of God? I say nothing of the fact that it is not fitting for an emperor to be an accuser . . . You say that I am a Manichaean. Am I perhaps an Eutychian, or do I defend the Eutychians, whose madness chiefly supports the Manichaean error?”

*Symmachus, Pope, against the Emperor Anastasius, Apology or Letter VI.*

> “These things do not wound me; but they openly and plainly show that you have thought of rejecting the honor which blessed Peter bestowed through his intervention. Because you are emperor, do you strive against Peter’s power? And while you receive Peter of Alexandria, do you attempt to trample upon the blessed apostle Peter in whatever vicar of his he may be? Let us compare the honor of the emperor with the honor of the pontiff: the difference between them is as great as that between one who cares for human affairs and one who cares for divine affairs . . . Perhaps you will say that it is written that we ought to be subject to every authority. We accept human authorities in their proper place, so long as they do not raise their wills against God. But if every authority is from God, then all the more is that authority which is to preside over divine matters . . . You say that I excommunicated you with the senate conspiring with me. I certainly did so, but without doubt I follow what my predecessors did reasonably.”

*The same work.*

> “I, however unworthy a vicar of the apostolic see, do not cease in my own voice to admonish you, ruler of human affairs, to remember that you are a human being, however great the power of the world may support you. Look around at all those who, from the beginning of Christ’s teaching, have attempted with differing intentions to persecute or afflict the Catholic faith: those who inflicted such things, though they prevailed for a time, have themselves failed; orthodox truth has prevailed all the more when it was thought to have been oppressed. Just as it is shown to have grown under its persecutors, so it is known to have crushed those who persecuted it . . . What difference is there between a pagan and one who is worse—one who, under the Christian name, attempts to violate the true and uncorrupted tradition of the apostolic rule and rushes into such blindness that, while all heresies in those regions have public permission to profess their opinions, the freedom of Catholic communion alone is thought by those who consider themselves religious to be something that must be overthrown? If this is considered an error—which is not permissible—then let it be allowed to act along with the other errors to which permission is granted there. But if it is judged to be integrity, it ought rather to have been followed than devastated by violent persecution.”

*The same work.*

> “God has so departed from human minds that they obstinately refuse to look upon His will; and after the course of this life they will not fail to stand before that fearful tribunal, under which the aims of the wicked, examined in every detail of their actions, will be exposed and, once exposed, punished—unless there are people who do not believe these things at all, or who trust that they can commit them with impunity . . . All Catholic rulers, whether when they assumed the reins of empire or when they recognized that new pontiffs had been appointed to the apostolic see, immediately sent their writings to it, to show that they were partners in it. Therefore, those who have not done this declare themselves alienated from it; we could establish this even from your own documents . . . It is not surprising that they rage against the orthodox when they can agree with all heresies; being friends to every error, they cannot help being enemies only to those who do not err.”

*The same work.*

### Line 12

“Blessed Symmachus found Manichaeans in the city of Rome, whose images, etc.”

Pope Symmachus was so far removed from and innocent of the crime of Manichaeism falsely charged against him that the history of the Librarian records that, at his command, the books and images of the Manichaeans were burned before the doors of the Constantinian basilica, and that the Manichaeans themselves were driven into exile.

### No. 77, line 1

“He convened a synod.”

The pontiff celebrated many synods. Pagi accurately set forth their sequence, dates, and distinctions in his critical notes on Baronius, assigning each of them to its respective year.

### No. 79, line 25

“He placed a silver image with the Savior and the twelve apostles.”

This expression illuminates the manner in which the image constructed by Valentinian, discussed above under Sixtus, was made: it had twelve doors with the apostles. These images contained other images within their circumference and served as the principal ornaments placed in the center.

### No. 80, line 10

“He established dwellings for the poor.”

More convenient and of greater scale. The occasion for undertaking this work was that, when Theodoric came to Rome, he assigned annual revenues for relieving the needs of the poor. The contemporary, or nearly contemporary, anonymous author published by Valesius gives the following account:

> “At the same time a dispute arose in the city of Rome between Symmachus and Laurentius; both were consecrated. By God’s ordering, the one who was worthy of this honor, Symmachus, prevailed. After peace had been made in the City and the Church restored, King Theodoric came to Rome and approached blessed Peter with the utmost devotion, as though he were a Catholic. Pope Symmachus, together with the whole senate and the Roman people, met him outside the City with common rejoicing. Then, entering the City, he came before the senate and addressed the people at the Palm, promising, with God’s help, to preserve inviolate everything that the Roman rulers of earlier times had established. On the third day after his entry, he entered the palace amid the people's triumphal acclamations, providing the Romans with circus games. He also gave the Roman people and the poor, every year, one hundred and twenty thousand measures of grain; and for the restoration of the palace, or the recovery of the city walls, he ordered two hundred pounds each year to be given from the wine treasury.”

The Valesian anonymous author is considered contemporary by Valerius, and the author of the deeds of the subsequent pontiffs inserted many additions from him. For the words “At the same time a dispute arose” are found in exactly the same form in certain manuscripts of Anastasius. This was a formula used at Rome at that time.

Thus Hormisdas, in the memorandum given to the legates departing for the synod of Heraclea, says, among other things, concerning Macedonius, expelled from the see of Constantinople, and Timothy, who invaded it, that “there is a dispute,” or contention, between the two persons.

Similarly, in the contemporary writer Cassiodorus, in the letter of Athalaric to John II—which opposes the simoniacal canvassing customarily admitted in the election of the pontiff—the words *dispute* and *altercation* are explained as one and the same:

> “When a dispute concerning the consecration of the apostolic pontiff has perhaps arisen and the altercation of the peoples has been brought before our palace.”

In Cassiodorus, Book IX, Letter 15, page 589. Likewise, in Sigonius, Book II of *The Kingdom of Italy*, at the end of page 76, in the edict of King Rothari, one reads:

> “. . . lest any fraud be introduced into this edict through a copyist’s error; if any dispute should arise, no other copies are to be trusted,” etc.

More specifically, Procopius bears witness that the royal alms and generosity were applied to the poor gathered near the basilica of the Vatican, and that Symmachus enlarged the buildings, when he writes about Theodoric:

> “To the poor who have their dwelling near the temple of the apostle Peter, he assigned every year thousands of measures of grain from the public stores.”

Moreover, the hospitality of the apostolic see toward those who came to the thresholds of the apostles was exceedingly lavish. Accordingly, Anastasius, companion of Saint Maximus the martyr, in his letter on the sufferings of Saint Martin the pontiff, while reporting his deeds and how Martin was questioned by the emperor’s judge whether he had received Pyrrhus of Constantinople when he came to Rome and had practiced the duties of hospitality, explains the pontiff’s custom in these words:

> “Do you not know, my lords, the Roman Church? I tell you that whoever comes there, a wretched man seeking lodging, is provided with everything necessary for his use, and Saint Peter repels no one who comes there without giving him his gifts. The purest bread and various wines are given not only to him but also to the people belonging to him. If such things are done for wretched men, what expense must be incurred to receive someone honorable, such as a bishop?”

And Saint Martin himself, while in exile, when he was in the greatest poverty and expecting assistance from the clergy, writes:

> “For although the Church of Saint Peter may not have gold, by the grace of God it is not lacking in expenses for grain, wine, and other necessities.”

### No. 77, line 1: “He convened a synod,” etc.

The acts of the synod state: “After the consulship of the illustrious Paulinus, on the Kalends of March, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the most blessed Pope Symmachus presiding over the synod,” etc. Paulinus’s consulship fell in the year 498. Therefore, the synod was held on 1 March 499.

### Line 2: “But after four years,” etc.

In the year of Christ 500, Symmachus convened a second synod at Rome, the acts of which have not reached us. In order that the schismatic Laurentius might cease disturbing the Church, this synod declared him bishop of Nuceria. For the aforementioned Theodorus Lector writes:

> “When a disturbance of this kind had continued for three years in the city of Rome—namely, from the year 498—Theodoric the African, who was then ruling at Rome, although an Arian in sect, nevertheless assembled a synod. He confirmed Symmachus in the bishopric of the city of Rome and appointed Laurentius bishop of a certain city called Nuceria.”

In Theodore’s Greek text, however, it is not said that the disturbance lasted for three consecutive years, but only that it was of three years’ duration. Laurentius did not stir up disturbances throughout that entire three-year period, since, as we have already said, he subscribed to the first Roman synod. Moreover, Hermannus Contractus, in Canisius’s edition, accurately connects this second Roman synod with the year 500, although he does not state what number it was in sequence.

In the years 501 and 502 everything in Rome was peaceful, because Laurentius the schismatic—who, in the year 500, was created bishop of Nuceria “out of consideration for mercy,” as the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* puts it—did not again invade the Roman see before the year 503. In the year 502, however, Symmachus celebrated a third synod at Rome, commonly called the Palmaris, although, as will soon be said, the Palmaris Synod was celebrated only in the year 503. This third Roman synod is found in volume IV of the *Councils* [Col. 0471A] and begins with these words: “In the consulship of Flavianus [read: Flavius] Avienus the Younger, a man of illustrious rank, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, etc. Since your brotherhood has indeed obeyed the ecclesiastical laws,” etc.

The reason for celebrating this synod was the repeal of the law of Odoacer, king of Italy, by which Basilius, the prefect of the Praetorium, had decreed, first, that an election of the Roman pontiff could not take place without the consent of the king of Italy; and, second, that the supreme pontiff might not alienate anything from the Church’s possessions. These provisions were declared null because they had been enacted by a lay ruler. Nevertheless, by his own authority and that of the synod, Symmachus decreed that no Roman pontiff, nor any priest placed in charge of a titular church, might alienate or exchange any ecclesiastical estates, or even grant their usufruct, except to captive and foreign clerics. Sixty-four bishops attended this synod, among whom the most prominent were Laurentius of Milan, Peter of Ravenna, and Eulalius of Syracuse.

[Col. 0471B] Anastasius, or the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, after reporting that Laurentius the schismatic had been appointed bishop of Nuceria, relates what happened in the year 503:

“After four years”—that is, from the year of Christ 500, in which the aforementioned Laurentius was made bishop of Nuceria—“certain members of the clergy, and others from the senate, especially Festus and Probinus, moved by zeal, accused Symmachus and suborned false witnesses. They sent them to Ravenna to King Theodoric, accusing the blessed Symmachus; and, after a petition had been composed at Rome, they secretly recalled Laurentius, created a schism, and the clergy was again divided. Some communicated with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. Then the senators Festus and Probinus sent a report to the king and began to work for the king to appoint a visitor for the apostolic see. Then the king appointed Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum—or rather Altina—which the canons prohibited.”

Thus a second schism arose under Symmachus in the year 503, and Peter, bishop of Altinum, was sent by Theodoric, king of Italy, to Rome to suppress the disturbances. Peter of Altinum went to Rome and showed Symmachus no reverence, although the king had expressly commanded him to do so. He showed no concern for ecclesiastical peace, but, drawn over to the side of the schismatics, disturbed everything, as Ennodius of Ticinum testifies in his *Apology for Symmachus*. Altinum was a city situated near the coast of Venetia. After it had been destroyed, its bishopric was transferred in the seventh century to Torcellum, not far distant from it.

To put an end to these disturbances, Theodoric, king of Italy, ordered a synod to be held at Rome, which was attended by 115 bishops. This synod was the fourth Roman synod under Symmachus and was called the Palmaris from the place where it was held. That this was the fourth Palmaris Synod is proved by the author of the critical examination of Baronius’s work from a manuscript codex written in the time of Charlemagne at Saint-Germain. After the three Roman synods under Symmachus have been recorded, it reads: “The fourth synod, [Col. 0471D] held at Rome, the Palmaris.” Its beginning is: “The holy synod, etc.,” as in the collection of the *Councils*, p. 1323, where it is incorrectly called the third synod; in the same place a chronological note has also been wrongly added, although it is absent from the aforementioned manuscript codex of Saint-Germain.

That the synod was convened by King Theodoric with the consent of Symmachus is clear from its acts:

“The aforesaid pontiffs,” say the acts, “to whom an opportunity for presenting an accusation was offered, suggested that the man who was said to have been accused ought himself to have convened the synod. They knew that, through the merit or primacy of the first apostle Peter, and then through the authority of the venerable councils that followed by the Lord’s command, a singular power had been entrusted to him in the Churches; nor did any precedent of a similar kind testify that the bishop of the aforesaid see had been subjected to the judgment of inferiors. But the most powerful [Col. 0472A] prince indicated that the pope himself had also shown by letter his willingness to assemble the synod. Therefore pages were requested from his gentleness, since it was known that they had been sent by him; and he decreed that they should be delivered to the priests without delay.”

## Number 78, line 13.—“He found Manichaeans in the city of Rome, whose…”

It is uncertain in which of the synods mentioned above Anastasius the emperor was excommunicated by Pope Symmachus. Only this is certain: Symmachus published his *Apology* against the emperor’s accusations after the fourth Roman synod, called the Palmaris, since in that *Apology* he says: “I escaped whole amid showers of stones.” Since Symmachus was attacked with stones while this fourth synod was being celebrated, that *Apology* was therefore issued by him after the year 503.

From this *Apology* it is clear that Emperor Anastasius, who shared the views of Acacius of blessed memory and favored the heretics who were enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, was excommunicated by Pope Symmachus. Enraged by this, the emperor published a defamatory document against the pontiff, in which, among other insults, he called him a Manichaean. Symmachus replied to this document in the aforementioned *Apologetic Letter*, in which he says the following about Anastasius’s excommunication:

“You say that, with the senate conspiring with me, I excommunicated you. In this matter I unquestionably follow what my predecessors did, though it was done reasonably. We did not excommunicate you, emperor, but Acacius. Withdraw from Acacius, and you withdraw from his excommunication. Do not involve yourself in his excommunication, and you are not excommunicated by us. If you involve yourself in it, you are excommunicated not by us but by yourself.”

In the same *Apology*, Symmachus compares pontifical authority with imperial dignity and shows that pontiffs are superior to kings and worthy of their reverence. He teaches that rulers must not be obeyed when they command anything contrary to the law of God.

It is likewise uncertain in what year Symmachus convened the sixth [Col. 0472C] synod at Rome, because no chronological indication is recorded in it. Baronius and the collectors of the councils associate it with the year 504, and there is no sound basis for departing from them. That it was the sixth of the synods held under Symmachus is evident from the fact that it begins with these words:

“When the holy sixth synod, canonically convened at Rome by the blessed Symmachus, had assembled in unity at the blessed apostle Peter’s and was sitting in session,” etc.

This synod was held against those who seized ecclesiastical property, and it decreed that, unless they restored such property, they should be anathematized as manifest heretics and admitted to ecclesiastical communion only after making satisfaction. It was added that the same judgment applied to all who had obtained the Church’s resources under the pretext of royal generosity, since it does not belong to kings to dispose of the Church’s property. Nor is an emperor or king permitted, contrary to the divine commands and the enactments of the Fathers, to usurp anything for himself by any means.

[Note: [Col. 0472D]

## Number 98, line 3.—“Through Africa or Sardinia”

As Marcellinus Comes relates in his *Chronicle*:

“In the consulship of Theodoric and Venantius, a cruel persecution of the Catholics arose throughout Africa under Huneric, king of the Vandals. For after more than 334 orthodox bishops had been exiled and driven away, their churches were closed.”

These bishops were compelled to live in exile, some in different parts of Africa far from their own sees, others in Sardinia, as Victor of Vita teaches in his history of the Vandal persecution; this may also be gathered from the catalogue of exiled bishops published by Jacob Sirmond. To these bishops, therefore, who remained in exile until the pontificate of Hormisdas, Pope Symmachus sent money and clothing.]

[Col. 0451]

## 76

Symmachus, a Roman by nation [Note: [Col. 0451] C, B: a Sardinian.], son of Fortunatus, occupied the see for 15 years, [Note: [Col. 0451] B, manuscript: 8 months less 4 days, from the consulship of Paulinus and Scytha to that of M. Aurelius Cassiodorus.] 8 months, and 26 days. He lived in the time of King Theodoric and of Augustus Anastasius, from the tenth day before the Kalends of December to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was ordained on the same day as Laurentius, amid contention: Symmachus in the Constantiniana basilica, but Laurentius in the basilica of the blessed Mary. For this reason the clergy was divided [Note: [Col. 0451] See Baronius, under the year of the Lord 498.], and the senate was split. Some sided with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. After the dispute, the parties decided [Note: [Col. 0451] C: *construxerunt*, “arranged.”] that both should go to Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0451] “That both parties should go.”] for the judgment of King Theodoric. When both had entered Ravenna, they found this equitable judgment:

“Whoever had first been ordained, or wherever the greater party was found to lie, he should sit on the apostolic see.”

In the end, equity found in Symmachus a recognition of the truth [Note: [Col. 0451] C: “and recognition.”], and Symmachus was installed as bishop.

## 77

At the same time Pope Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0451] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 499.] convened a synod and appointed Laurentius bishop of the city of Nuceria [Note: [Col. 0451] C: “in the city of Nuceria.” See Baronius under the year of the Lord 502.] “out of consideration for mercy.”

After four years, certain members of the clergy, and others from the senate, especially Festus and Probinus, moved by zeal, accused Symmachus and suborned false witnesses. They sent them to Ravenna to King Theodoric, accusing the blessed Symmachus. After a petition had been composed at Rome, they secretly recalled Laurentius, created a schism, and the clergy was again divided. Some communicated with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. Then the senators Festus and Probinus sent a report to the king and began to work for the king to appoint a visitor for the apostolic see. Then the king appointed Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum [Note: [Col. 0452] D: “of Altinum.”], which the canons prohibited.

At the same time the blessed Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0451] “Symmachus was cleared in the synod.”] convened 115 bishops. When the synod had been held, he was cleared of the false accusation. Peter of Altinum [Note: [Col. 0451] “Altinensis.”], the invader of the apostolic see, was condemned, as was Laurentius of Nuceria, because while Bishop Symmachus was alive they had seized his see. Then the blessed Symmachus was restored to the apostolic see by all the bishops, priests, deacons, and the entire clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0451] C: “was restored.”], so that he might sit as bishop in glory at the blessed Peter’s.

## 78

At the same time Festus, former consul and head of the senate, and Probinus, former consul, began to fight within the city of Rome against the other senators, especially Faustus, the former consul. Out of envy, slaughter and murders were committed among the clergy. Those who rightly communicated with the blessed Symmachus, whenever they were found publicly within the city, were killed by the sword.

They even seized holy women and virgins, stripping them from their monasteries or dwellings; exposing their female bodies, they wounded them with blows, and every day they fought against the Church in the middle of the city. They also killed many priests, among them the most worthy priests Dignissimus and Gordianus, at the shrine of the blessed apostle Peter and at the shrine of Saints John and Paul; they killed them with clubs and the sword [Note: [Col. 0451] “Among them, Gordianus, a most worthy priest, at the shrine…”; “Whom they killed with clubs and the sword.”], as well as many other Christians, so that no member of the clergy could safely walk through the city by day or night.

Only Faustus, the former consul, fought on behalf of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0451] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 503, at the end: the books of the Manichaeans were burned.]

After all this, the blessed Symmachus found Manichaeans in the city of Rome. He burned all their images and books together before the doors of the Constantiniana basilica, and sent the Manichaeans themselves into exile. His episcopate extended from the consulship of Paulinus to that of the senator.

## 79

He built the basilica of the holy apostle Andrew at the shrine of the blessed apostle Peter. There he made a silver canopy [Note: [Col. 0451] CB: “ciborium.”] and a confessio weighing 120 pounds; three silver arches, each weighing 60 pounds; an oratory of the holy apostle Thomas in silver, weighing 300 pounds; in the confessio, 20 pounds; a silver arch weighing 16 pounds; a silver confessio of Saint Cassianus and Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, weighing 20 pounds; a silver arch weighing 12 pounds; an oratory of Saint Apollinaris in silver, with a silver confessio and arch, weighing 30 pounds; and an oratory of Saint Sosius [Note: [Col. 0453] C: “Sosius.”] in silver at the confessio, weighing 20 pounds.

Likewise, at the fountain in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he made an oratory of the holy cross in silver, with a confessio, and a gold cross with gems, in which he enclosed the Lord’s wood. The gold cross itself weighed ten pounds.

He made two oratories, one of Saint John the Baptist and one of Saint John the Evangelist, and in their confessio he placed silver arches weighing 30 pounds [Note: [Col. 0453] “and chambers,” according to another witness.]. He constructed all these chambers completely from their foundations.

He adorned the basilica of the blessed Peter with marble. He adorned the cantharus of the blessed Peter and its four-sided portico with marble, and decorated it with mosaic lambs, crosses, and palms [Note: [Col. 0453] “He made.”]. He joined together the entire atrium. He enlarged the steps before the doors of the basilica of the blessed Peter and built other steps beneath the roof, on the right and left. In the same place he built episcopal residences on the right and left. Beneath the steps in the atrium he placed another cantharus outside, in the public area of the Campus, and made it for ordinary human needs. He also made other steps for those ascending to the blessed Andrew and placed a cantharus there.

He built the basilica of Saint Agatha the martyr on the Via Aurelia, on the estate of Lardarius [Note: [Col. 0453] “on the estate called Lardarius.”], constructing it from its foundations with a fountain, and placed there two silver arches.

At the same time he built the basilica of Saint Pancratius and made there a silver arch weighing 15 pounds. In the same place he built a bathhouse.

At the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, he renovated the apse, which was threatening to collapse, and adorned the area behind the confessio with paintings. He made a chamber and a matroneum, and above the confessio he placed a silver image of the Savior with the twelve apostles, weighing 120 pounds. Before the doors of the basilica he made steps in the atrium and a cantharus. Behind the apse he brought in water and built a bathhouse there from its foundations.

## 80

Within the city of Rome he built from the foundations the basilica of Saints Sylvester and Martin, beside the Baths of Trajan. There he made above the altar a silver canopy [Note: [Col. 0453] C: “ciborium.”] weighing 120 pounds, twelve silver arches, each weighing ten pounds, and a silver confessio weighing 15 pounds.

At the shrine of Saints John and Paul he made steps behind the apse. At the shrine of the archangel Michael he enlarged the basilica, made steps, and brought in water. At the shrine of Saint Mary he built from the foundations an oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

On the Tiburtine road, at the twenty-seventh milestone from the city of Rome, at the request of the illustrious Albinus and Glaphyra [Note: [Col. 0453] “the administrators.”], who were financing the work from their own resources, he dedicated to the blessed Peter a basilica built from its foundations on the estate of Pacinianus.

He built dwellings for the poor at the shrines of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the holy martyr Lawrence.

At the shrine of the blessed Peter he made twenty silver canthari, each weighing 15 pounds, and 22 arches, each weighing 20 pounds.

He repaired the basilica of Saint Felicitas [Note: [Col. 0453] “which was threatening to collapse.”], which was already in danger of ruin. He repaired the apse of the blessed Agnes, which was threatening to collapse, and renovated the entire basilica.

## 81

He established that the angelic hymn should be sung every Sunday or on the birthdays of the martyrs, namely:

> Glory to God in the highest.

He improved the cemetery of the Jordani because of the body of Saint Alexander.

Every year he supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the bishops who had been confined in exile. He redeemed captives with money throughout Liguria, Milan, and various provinces [Note: [Col. 0453] “with funds.”], multiplied gifts, and released them.

He held four ordinations in the city of Rome, during the months of December and February: 92 priests, 16 deacons, and 107 bishops for various places [Note: [Col. 0453] CB: “17.”].

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. The episcopate remained vacant for seven days. He also rested in peace as a confessor.

## Number 82, line 2.—“From the consulship of the senator”

He means Cassiodorus, under whom the clergy and people, seditiously divided into various factions, unanimously proceeded to the election of Hormisdas. Hence Cassiodorus also attributes this good fortune to his own consulship in his letter to Theodoric:

> “In my consulship, to the praise of your times, when clergy and people were united, the desired harmony returned.”

The *Liber Pontificalis* adds very appropriately concerning Hormisdas:

> “He reconciled the clergy.”

This does not mean, as Blondellus supposed, that he then introduced some new form for the first time, but that he recalled the clergy, which had been agitated by seditions up to that point, to unity [Col. 0477D] and compelled it to observe the earlier institutions of the canons and of the apostolic see, adding further decrees to prevent future disturbances.

## Line 5.—“At the same time, according to the decision of the synod, he sent to Greece”

Here the legations sent by the apostolic see to suppress the Acacian schism, by which Greece was troubled, have been confused. Therefore both the legations and the words must be restored to their proper places.

The first legation was instituted by the pontiff at the urging of Anastasius. When Anastasius heard of Hormisdas’s peaceful election, he sent him a letter asking him to send legates to the council that he himself had summoned at Heraclea to settle the disturbances in the East. The letter is extant in volume IV of the *Councils*, in Labbe’s edition, with this date:

> “Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of January at Constantinople, in the consulship of the senator V. C., etc.”

It therefore belongs to the very year in which Hormisdas was elected. In it the deceitful emperor writes:

> “Divine matters must be placed before all other affairs. For, with almighty God propitious, we trust that the republic will both be preserved and improved. Since, therefore, certain doubts appear to have arisen concerning the orthodox religion in the regions of Scythia, it has especially pleased Our Clemency that a venerable synod should be held in the city of Heraclea, in the province of Europe. Therefore, may Your Holiness, together with whichever most reverend bishops you choose—bishops whom you have judged suitable and instructed in the orthodox religion from among those appointed over the Churches under your priestly care—deign to come to the aforementioned city of Heraclea before the Kalends of July,” etc.

In another letter to the same pontiff, the emperor explains why he had interrupted the exchange of letters with the apostolic see and solemnly declares why the judgment of the apostolic see was awaited. He writes as follows:

> “Previously, indeed, the harshness of those to whom the administration of the episcopate that you now hold had been entrusted caused us to refrain from sending letters. But now a favorable report about you, reaching our ears, has brought back the goodness of paternal affection, so that we may seek those things which our God and Savior taught the holy apostles by divine speech, and especially the blessed Peter, in whom he established the strength of his Church. [Col. 0479A] With these beginnings set forth, therefore, we urge Your Apostolate to act as mediator in the matters that have arisen in the regions of Scythia, from which we have understood that a council is also to be held, so that, once controversies have been cut away, holy unity may be restored to the Churches,” etc.

These passages therefore belong to the earlier legation. Before its acts are reported, however, certain matters concerning the councils of Sidon and Heraclea must be examined here, so that what follows may be revealed more clearly and explained on firmer grounds.

## On the synods of Sidon and Heraclea convoked by the emperor Anastasius, and on the Roman synod convoked by Hormisdas

Just as recent writers generally pass over these synods superficially, it is especially necessary to know about them in order to illuminate Hormisdas’s actions. Their nature and the reasons for which they occurred must therefore be discussed.

Anastasius had declared war on the Council of Chalcedon and attempted to seize the authentic acts of that council, which were preserved in the archives of the Church of Constantinople. For Theophanes recorded the following under the year 511 in his *Chronicle*:

> “The impious emperor was attempting, with the help of the master Macedonius, to obtain and tear apart the authentic records of the proceedings at Chalcedon. Macedonius placed them, marked with his seal, on the altar; but Calepodius, the eunuch and steward of the Great Church, eventually stole them secretly and carried them to the emperor,” etc.

Once the impious ruler had obtained these acts, he attempted to abolish and utterly destroy all confidence in the council. In the East there still remained as defenders the bishops Flavian of Antioch and Elias of Jerusalem. To overwhelm them, he entrusted Eutropius the tribune with the task of convening the Synod of Sidon and compelling everyone to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon. See the *Synodicon* of Pappus and Theophanes under the year 512.

Cyril gives a fuller account of the same events in his *Life of Sabbas*, among the monuments of the Greek Church, p. 298, in these words:

> “The emperor Anastasius, acting with unbridled madness against Flavian and Elias, the patriarchs, ordered a synod of Eastern and Palestinian bishops to be held at Sidon. He ordered that the synod should be presided over by Soterichus of Caesarea in Cappadocia and Polixenus of Hierapolis—bishops who especially anathematized the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and supported Eutyches and Dioscorus, together with their perverse and alien doctrine,” etc.

Polixenus is the same man as Xenias, the worst scourge of the East. Under his leadership the defenders of the Chalcedonian faith suffered the gravest evils. Evagrius describes his character in book III, chapter 31.

With these leaders of treachery, eighty bishops of the same kind met at Sidon. They proposed anathemas against the sacred council and subsequently adopted other determinations contrary to the true faith. Although Flavian and Elias, the patriarchs, resisted their efforts with such zeal that their impious plans came to nothing, Marcellinus briefly recorded these events in his *Chronicle*, preserved by Sirmondus, volume II:

> “Then Anastasius, renewed in wickedness, ordered an infamous and ridiculous synod to be held at the city of Sidon—ridiculous names having been prefixed from its name—with nearly eighty treacherous bishops assembled against the orthodox bishops. Flavian, the Catholic patriarch of Antioch, and John, bishop of the town of Plataeae, because they rejected this sacrilegious gathering, were sent into exile to a fortress called Petra. There Flavian, the confessor of Christ, rested in the Lord,” etc.

That these two patriarchs courageously resisted the tyrant is shown by the emperor’s words to the abbot Sabbas, whom Elias had sent after the synod to bring him to a better disposition. It also appears from this that Anastasius had worked among the metropolitans of the East to have the anathema pronounced by the members of the Synod of Sidon accepted by everyone.

Thus Cyril, in the *Life of Sabbas*, presents the emperor as speaking as follows (chapter 507):

> “Since the doctrine of Chalcedon was already to be struck down by a Catholic and universal anathema by the synod that has now been assembled, he alone prevented it, having settled the matter together with Flavian of Antioch, and, as he supposed, mocked our empire … and, as he thought, deceived us by this speech, when we had decreed that the synod should be dissolved with its business unfinished,” etc.

But in order to subvert the Council of Chalcedon by another method, he devoted all his efforts to ensuring that men declared enemies of the Council of Chalcedon would be installed in the major sees. Severus, of whom more will be said shortly, after being made patriarch of Antioch, defended the worst cause with the greatest fervor. Consequently, everything in the East was hastening toward the betrayal and destruction of the faith.

Source/review notes: The Trisagion quotation is singular in Latin (*Qui crucifixus es*): “Who was crucified for us.” The draft’s two plural renderings should be corrected, but the requested schema requires exact draft replacements; both occurrences are retained above pending that singular correction.
