The occasion of the Council of Heraclea must be traced further back, both so that the emperor’s crafty strategy may be brought into the open and so that a more accurate explanation may be supplied from the events reported in the *Liber Pontificalis* and from the embassies themselves. Severus, a most wicked monk who had been expelled from his monastery on account of the gravest crimes, ensnared the emperor by skill and fraud and easily gained his favor and goodwill because he was an exceedingly fierce enemy of the Council of Chalcedon. He was the one who advised that an addition be made to the *Trisagion*, by which the Eutychian heresy would be received. It was believed that this kind of *Trisagion* had proceeded from an angelic revelation and was therefore sung publicly. Jobus, Book VI, in Photius (*cod.* 222, chapter 24, p. 610), writes of it:

> He also relates this … As it is reported by other writers also, for example by Blessed Proclus, who was bishop of Constantinople, the composition of the aforesaid hymn was revealed to him through a vision, when the angels were singing this sacred hymn; and he was the first to draw the same teaching from it …

From the time when it was promulgated at Constantinople under Proclus, it was thereafter sung by everyone in daily and continual use, in the particular and solemn gatherings of the Church. Accordingly, at Severus’s urging, this clause was added: “Who were crucified for us, have mercy on us,” so that the Passion might be attributed to the whole Trinity and the mixing of the natures introduced by Eutyches might be confirmed by common usage.

Sotericus, metropolitan of Caesarea in Thrace, who had long before been ordained by Macedonius as a Catholic, had subsequently become a slave of the court, was hostile to the Catholic faith, and clung most basely to the emperor’s every nod. Therefore Severus, the author of all these policies, wrote to Sotericus instructing him to promote the addition by a special edict among the bishops subject to him and in the other churches. The people of Constantinople, however, urged on by the patriarch Macedonius and tenacious of the ancient practice, fiercely resisted the addition. Although Macedonius was removed from his see on that account, the emperor, persisting in his plan, became afraid for his power, indeed even for his life. Evagrius, Book IV, chapter 44, reports the matter as follows:

> At Constantinople, when the emperor wished to add these words to the *Trisagion* hymn—“Who were crucified for us”—a most serious revolt broke out, as though the Christian religion were being utterly overthrown. Severus writes in a letter to Sotericus that Macedonius and the clergy of the city of Constantinople were the leaders and authors of this revolt. He wrote that letter before he had attained the episcopate, while he was still residing in the imperial city, at the time when, as we related above, he was expelled from his monastery together with several others. I believe that Macedonius was expelled from his see on account of this accusation, in addition to the other reasons that I mentioned earlier …

In Macedonius’s place the emperor appointed Timothy, an Eutychian and supporter and promoter of the same heretical corruption.

This, then, was the first opportunity for the wily emperor to promise the rebellious people that he would convene an ecumenical council from East and West, presided over by the Roman pontiff. For after Macedonius’s expulsion and the election of the heretical Timothy, the revolt increased. Evagrius writes in the same place:

> For this reason the populace was stirred up, and since it could no longer be restrained, many of the noble and honored came into the greatest danger, and many distinguished places in the city were consumed by fire …

And after some intervening material:

> Moreover, the revolt, laying waste to everything and prevailing over every force set against it, grew so greatly that the emperor, compelled by necessity, went in a pitiable manner without the imperial crown to the equestrian contest that was to be held in the circus, and sent heralds to the people to proclaim that he was quite willing to surrender the empire …

Accordingly, he promised that he would restore everything, although deceitfully, in order by these promises to calm the people’s agitated spirits. His subsequent actions, both at the Synod of Sidon and in the election of Severus—who, after becoming patriarch of Antioch, devised still worse schemes against the Catholic faith with the assistance of Timothy of Constantinople and John Nicaeota of Alexandria—showed him to be perjured. This three-headed faction then launched a savage persecution against the Catholic bishops, punishing them with exile unless they consented to its impiety. Such was the condition of the East after the Synod of Sidon.

[Col. 0481B] Thrace, however, was free from these errors. It therefore seems that the people summoned Vitalian so that he might undertake the cause of the faith. Having assembled an army, he first gained possession of Thrace and the neighboring provinces in victory, and then led his army toward the city of Constantinople. Theophanes writes in the same place:

> In this year Vitalian, having occupied all Thrace, Scythia, and Moesia, and leading with him a huge number of Huns and Bulgarians, captured Anchialus and Odessus, and also seized Cyril, the *magister militum* of Thrace, carrying off booty in every direction as far as Byzantium; and, while sparing the city, he pitched his camp at Sosthenium …

Vitalian knew that the people adhered for the most part to Catholic doctrine, and therefore did not wish to hand the countryside over to his victorious army for plunder.

Fearing both Vitalian’s power and the people of Constantinople themselves, Anastasius once again renewed, among the terms of peace agreed with Vitalian and with an oath also added, the promise he had made to convene an ecumenical council at Heraclea. Theophanes reports it in these words:

> Anastasius, when his affairs were desperate, sent certain members of the senatorial order to ask Vitalian to negotiate peace, and swore, together with the entire Senate, that he would recall the exiled bishops to Heraclea in Thrace. Vitalian added that the head of each schola should likewise affirm the same under oath; that Macedonius and Flavian, unjustly expelled from their own thrones, should be received back, and the other bishops likewise restored to theirs; and that only then should a council be convened, to which the Roman pontiff and all the bishops should come, so that by this means whatever had been wrongly decreed against the orthodox might be subjected to the examination of a common judgment. When the emperor, the whole Senate, the remaining magistrates, and the people likewise contributed their oaths, and pledged themselves, after the terms had been set out, to carry out the matter in due order, peace was concluded, and Vitalian himself returned home …

Meanwhile, while the emperor was serving the moment until Vitalian dismissed his army, he sent the aforementioned letters to Hormisdas, so as to appear to obey the holy conditions and to restore the peoples to tranquillity. Vitalian also wrote to Hormisdas.

The pontiff, therefore, moved more by the prayers of Vitalian than by those of the emperor Anastasius, and unwilling to fail in the solicitude owed by the Apostolic See, but wishing to bring aid to the faith that was endangered in the East, sent letters to the bishops of the West, intending to convene a synod at Rome. He followed the ancient and accepted custom by which pontiffs were accustomed, before any ecumenical council, to hear the consultations of the Western bishops, either by summoning them to Rome or by having them assembled by the metropolitans in particular synods throughout the dioceses, so that the opinion of each might be sought. From these consultations they then selected legates who would bring the agreement of the Westerners and preside over the councils in the name of the Apostolic See and direct their decrees. This is clear from the heading of the letters that were delivered to the legates. Thus Agatho, before the Sixth Synod, convened a gathering of this kind in the West, and wrote in a letter: “Agatho, bishop and servant of the servants of God, together with all the synods subject to the council of the Apostolic See.”

We owe the memory of the Roman synod held under Hormisdas to the *Liber Pontificalis*, which states at line 5: “By decree of the synod he sent [them] into Greece …” Thus a Roman synod was held by Hormisdas at the same time. At it the letters of the emperor and of Vitalian were read; an order was established for bringing about the union of the Eastern churches; petitions were examined; and, after the legates had been chosen, instructions were given to them. They subsequently undertook the journey to Anastasius.

That particular synods were held by the metropolitans of the West is shown by the following evidence. First, it is demonstrated by Avitus of Vienne, exceedingly distinguished for his learning. He himself indicates that he had been admonished by Pope Hormisdas in a letter in which he asks whether the schism of the East had come to an end. The letter is found in Volume II of Sirmond’s works and contains, among other things, the following:

> Since you perceive that it accords with the state of religion and with the full rules of the Catholic faith that the flock entrusted to you throughout all the members of the universal Church should be shaped by the ever-watchful care of your exhortation, last year, if you deign to remember, you visited the province of Vienne by letters sent to my humility. Those letters reached me through the clergy of the Church of Arles, as opportunity allowed, and indeed with the fullest pastoral solicitude. In them, just as you summoned us to joy through the conversion of the provinces—that is, of Dardania, Illyricum, and Scythia—to communion, so by a most cautious admonition you instructed us concerning what might overtake us through ignorance. The condemnation of Eutyches and Nestorius, whom the authority of your holy See had long ago trampled down through your most blessed predecessors, was conveyed to our knowledge some time ago through the apostolic diligence exercised toward us …

From this letter we learn that Hormisdas sent the primate of Arles a letter for the purpose of discussing the same matter, and that the primate sent it through the Church’s couriers to Vienne. The entire subject of the consultation was that the Nestorian and Eutychian causes should be completely abolished together with the schism, and that the Gallican bishops replied in agreement with the preceding papal constitutions. There is scarcely any room for doubt that Arles did the same (Labbe, Volume IV of the *Councils*, p. 1474).

A letter of Hormisdas to the same recipient is extant. In it he mentions the conversion of the provinces which, at Vitalian’s urging, had abandoned the schism and received communion with the Apostolic See:

> Nearly all the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum, seeking communion with Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through written requests and dispatched embassies, have affirmed that they obey the apostolic rules, so that they may not be condemned on account of their former error …

And in a letter to Avitus the same pontiff writes (in Sirmond, same place, p. 123):

> The metropolitan of Epirus, that is, the bishop of Nicopolis, recently separated from the impious together with his synod, came to apostolic communion with a profession expressly formulated for that purpose. We have therefore judged that these things should be committed to writing in the present letter, so that, just as it is fitting for us to grieve over the lot of those who perish, so we may likewise rejoice over the salvation of those who return; and so that the faithful who have been established farther away may be instructed by them concerning the care with which they must flee their poison, since they see that those men are avoided even by their own people with such just abhorrence …

These same records suggest that the pontiff also sent the Gallican bishops an encyclical announcing a council, either to be held at Rome or, according to the ancient custom, in whatever provinces the encyclicals were circulated, containing the votes and replies of all and sent back to the pontiff himself. Indeed, he sent it not only to the Gallicans but also to all the other primates of the West. This is suggested both by Hormisdas’s singular zeal and by the selection of the legates who, in accordance with the decree of this synod and of the Westerners, were sent to the Council of Heraclea.

[Col. 0483A] The cause of the conversion and repentance of the Illyrians was the fall of the primate of Thessalonica. Theophanes writes of it in the same place:

> When the bishop of Thessalonica, through fear of the emperor, maintained communion with Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, forty bishops of Illyricum and Greece assembled together and, using written documents as witnesses, declared that they were separating from him as from their metropolitan. They sent the documents to Rome and promised to maintain communion with the Roman pontiff …

The legates therefore proceeded to Constantinople with instructions and with a document of faith, or profession, to be issued by the heretics and schismatics, which Hormisdas had drawn up with the consent of the Roman synod. But when Vitalian had dismissed his troops, Anastasius returned to his customary perjuries and rendered the assembly at Heraclea void. Theophanes gives the following account of its empty outcome in the same place:

> Moreover, Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, having been solicited by Theuderic and wishing to repay Vitalian in kind, sent Bishop Evodius and Vitalian the archdeacon as legates after announcing a council at Heraclea. About two hundred bishops from various places also joined them …

Such, then, is the account of the beginnings and proceedings of these three councils. We shall pursue the outcome of the Council of Heraclea itself in what follows.

**Line 5.—“Showing the Apostolic See’s humanity.”**

Among the provisions of the synod was one that the lapsed bishops should be treated with leniency. By the strict rule of the canons, schismatics and heretics who were obstinate in either offense were to be punished by perpetual deposition. Just as, after the common shipwreck of all the bishops at Ariminum, all those who had lapsed, singing a recantation, were absolved and restored to their own sees through the humanity of Pope Liberius—as stated in his letter preserved among the fragments of Saint Hilary—and as Saint Athanasius also supported in another letter, which the Greeks call canonical and which has therefore been inserted among the other canonical letters in the body of the law of the Greek Church, a matter also mentioned by Saint Jerome in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians—so* Hormisdas judged that the same course should be followed in this case with the lapsed bishops of the East. From him, therefore, we learn that the praised provision originated in the Roman synod.

The pontiff was especially inclined to show this humanity because Anastasius had accused him of having caused the Easterners to be separated from the Roman Church through the harshness of his predecessors. Cyril also noted this not obscurely in the *Life of Sabas* (in Cotelerius, Volume III, p. 295):

> When Elias, patriarch of Jerusalem, had obtained the pontificate, in the third year of the reign of Anastasius the Church of God was thrown into confusion and divided into three parties, with the Roman pontiffs separated from the Byzantines because the name of Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, had been inserted in the sacred diptychs, although he had not followed their exact diligence and strict discipline.

Hormisdas therefore decreed that a moderate rule should be applied toward the lapsed bishops, so as to remove every cause of dissension.

**Line 8.—“With the counsel of King Theoderic.”**

Theophanes says the same in the passage cited, adding more explicitly that the pontiff had been solicited by Theoderic. Indeed, the king himself also sent the legate Agapitus to attend the council. Concerning his careful selection, the following appears in a letter preserved by Baronius (*Annals*, year 515, p. 644):

> Although every embassy requires a wise man to whom the welfare of the provinces and the condition of the entire kingdom may be entrusted for defense, it is now nevertheless necessary to choose the wisest man, one who can argue against the most subtle opponents and act in the assembly of learned men in such a way that so many cultivated minds cannot overcome the cause he has undertaken. It is a great matter to speak against skilled men and to accomplish anything among those who think that they foresee everything.

**Line 11.—“And going to Anastasius Augustus, they accomplished nothing.”**

The council had been announced, and two hundred Eastern bishops had already gathered at Heraclea. But once the emperor was free from Vitalian, it came to nothing. Theophanes continues in the same place:

> Deceived both by the wicked emperor and by Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, they withdrew without having accomplished anything. For the impious emperor, having violated his agreements, secretly informed the pope that he should not come to Rome; but elsewhere he had given Vitalian a sacred letter, by which he deceitfully invited the pope to attend the celebration of the council at Heraclea.

Although this earlier embassy is said to have been unsuccessful, this must be understood with respect to the emperor, not to the other bishops, very many of whom signed the document of faith sent by the Roman synod, as Baronius rightly and at length argues. Among these, the Illyrians deserve praise. They sent a letter to Hormisdas, testifying that, while residing at Constantinople, they had subscribed to the proposed formula (in Labbe, same place, p. 1440):

> Very many of us were in imperial Constantinople while your most holy representatives, the bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, Venantius the presbyter, Vitalis the deacon, and Hilary the notary, were engaged in the struggle of piety.

These final words suggest that the legates endured many struggles from the perjured emperor. They then add that their metropolitan too had subscribed in the full Illyrian synod:

> With us also was Father and Archbishop Alcyson, numbered among the holy men, who, using petitions with every confidence, was made worthy in the presence of your blessedness to share communion with your Apostolic See.

The suffragan bishops were required, when they subscribed to a public decree issued to someone, to notify their metropolitan of the same decree, according to what Tharasius observed in the fourth session of the Second Council of Nicaea, and according to what we have discussed at length in the earlier treatise on encyclical letters. Therefore, on returning from the imperial city, they carried to the metropolitan, as was customary, a copy of the document proposed by Hormisdas and signed by them.

Hormisdas testifies in his letter to the metropolitans of Arles and Vienne that the bishops of Dardania, Thrace, and Scythia likewise professed the same document. Newly elected bishops, moreover, were required to issue a profession of faith according to Hormisdas’s document. After the death of the metropolitan Alcyson, when John was appointed in his place, he wrote a letter with the following heading:

> To my lord, most holy in all things and most blessed Father of Fathers, my fellow minister and prince of bishops, Hormisdas: John sends greetings in the Lord.

In the same letter he presented a summary of the formula:

> I … fittingly join myself to your prayers, and according to the custom of your Apostolic See, which has the care of all the churches and which you deign to exercise over the Nicopolitans, in accordance with your ancient spiritual arrangement … It is my desire to follow your teaching, just as my predecessor Alcyson stood among the saints. I anathematize Dioscorus, and Timothy called Aelurus, and Peter his successor; and Acacius, who was mingled with these through Peter’s communion; and Peter, who disturbed the Church of Antioch. In all things I follow the synodical and apostolic letters written by the true bishop, Pope Leo of Rome.

I believe that the custom requiring suffragans to inform their metropolitan arose from the fact that all were required to stand united with the primate in preserving the deposit and instructing the peoples. Thus, at the Council of Chalcedon, session 4, when a profession of faith was to be issued, Beronicianus said:

> Let each bishop make his faith known through his metropolitan, so that no doubt or disagreement may remain …

For this reason the decisions of the council were sent to the metropolitans, so that through them they might be communicated to all the suffragans. Thus the African bishops, first exiled and then recalled, when restoring the former order of the clergy at the Council of Carthage, enacted the following:

> According to the dispositions of Nicaea, confirmation of what is done in the council is to be given to the metropolitan of each province.

So it is read in the Acts of that synod, Volume II of Hardouin’s *Councils*, p. 1079.

Although Anastasius had ordered the Council of Heraclea to be annulled, he nevertheless issued a profession of faith, preserved in Labbe, p. 1433, lest the people who had remained on the Catholic side should again stir up disturbances. In it he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and admits that their doctrines are perverse. The crafty and treacherous ruler pretends that he venerates the Council of Chalcedon, whose condemnation he had promoted with such enormous effort. As for Acacius, he writes that he could not be removed from the diptychs without stirring up greater seeds of dissension in the churches of the East.

He sent all this to Hormisdas through two legates: Theopompus, *comes domesticorum*, and Severianus, *comes* of the Sacred Consistory (in Labbe, same place, p. 1430). Such an embassy of laymen, who were to discuss ecclesiastical matters and matters of faith in particular, seemed improper to Hormisdas: first, because according to the custom of the Church those who were to deal with matters of faith ought to have been chosen from the clergy; and second, because Anastasius himself had promised the contrary when he announced the Council of Heraclea to the pontiff.

We read the following in Hormisdas’s letter to Avitus (in Sirmond, Volume II, p. 131). Avitus had been awaiting and requesting the acts of the Council of Heraclea and, in addition, the outcome of the embassy sent by the Apostolic See and the Western synod. The pontiff first explains the perfidy of the schismatics and the perjuries of Anastasius, and then adds:

> For what else does it mean that, although through our brother and fellow bishop Ennodius they had promised that they would send priestly men to confirm what the Apostolic See had requested, and although they had promised many things that we had sought for the correction of their perversity, they not only did not send religious men through whom a full understanding of their case could exist in accordance with their own decrees, but, as though the matter were insignificant, sent laymen and persons foreign to the ecclesiastical body? They did not try to free themselves from the mire in which they are immersed; rather, while the brightness of the Catholic faith was shining forth, they believed—God forbid—that they could darken it by their own obscurity. This was the reason for our silence, a reason that your spiritual prudence also revealed to you. For what could I indicate in letters sent to you concerning this matter, when I saw that they were obstinately guarding their perfidy in its established condition? …

From this we also learn that, after the pontiff had received the opinions of the Westerners through an encyclical, he explained the outcome of the embassy through other letters as well. In order to do this, he awaited the fruit of the second embassy to the East, so much so that Avitus broke his silence; in this letter the pontiff explained to him the reasons for the delay.

**Line 7.—“Under John, bishop of Constantinople.”**

These words must be removed and restored to p. 84, line 1, where the text should read:

> Then Bishop Hormisdas, with the counsel of King Theoderic, sent Germanus from the Apostolic See under John, bishop of Constantinople.

This transposition occurs frequently; it has been noted in its proper place. For those legates were at Constantinople when John was appointed to the episcopate, since at the time of the earlier embassy the pseudo-bishop Timothy was still the Eutychianist bishop.

**Line 11.—“He sent the same man a second time.”**

Hormisdas mentions this embassy in the aforementioned letter to Avitus, in Sirmond. The pontiff had received an opportunity from the conversion of several Eastern bishops. In order to assist them, he prepared a second embassy with new instructions added. At the same time, the fear inspired by Vitalian continued, a fear which Cyril dispels in the *Life of Sabas*:

> Anastasius … detained by Vitalian, who followed barbarian customs, began for the time being to maintain quiet and silence in this matter …

(Same work, p. 320.)

**Line 13.—“In this document Augustus refused to agree.”**

The substance of the document is briefly set out in the instructions given to the legates, which prescribe the manner in which the profession of faith was to be issued (in Labbe, p. 896):

> The bishops who consent should also proclaim the following in the presence of the Christian people assembled in the church: that they embrace the holy faith of Chalcedon and the letters of Saint Leo the pope, which he wrote against the heretics Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus, and also against their followers Timothy Aelurus and Peter, and against those who are held liable in that same cause; likewise, they should anathematize Acacius, who was formerly bishop of the Church of Constantinople, and Peter of Antioch together with his associates. Having written these things in their own hand to the chosen venerable men, they should act according to the text of the document that we issued through our notary …

From this it is also clear that a notary was always present in these embassies of the Apostolic See, who subsequently recorded the subscriptions and professions, which, as we have seen elsewhere, were carefully preserved in the archives of the Roman Church.

**Line 13.—“Secret declarations.”**

In addition to the letters sent to the emperor and to others during this second embassy, Hormisdas, foreseeing the emperor’s and the pseudo-bishop Timothy of Constantinople’s skill in circulating documents, gave the legates nineteen secret declarations. If the emperor prevented the statutes of the Apostolic See from being openly published throughout the East, they were to work through selected men so that these declarations, or threats, might secretly be posted at the principal sees throughout the region.

We are taught by the Acts of the Council of Ephesus an illustrious example of this kind of declaration, when Nestorius began to publish his depraved doctrine. Since, relying on the power of the court, he was everywhere threatening the defenders of the truth with threats and exile—a matter mentioned by Coelestine in his letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople, in which he delivered his judgment against Nestorius, and described more fully by the monks in their petition presented to Theodosius, preserved in the first part of the Council of Ephesus, as well as by Socrates, Book VII; Evagrius, Book I; and Liberatus, Book I—Eusebius, then a Scholasticus and later bishop of Dorylaeum, and subsequently a vigorous defender of the Catholic faith at the Council of Chalcedon, seeing that the heresiarch was becoming more outrageous each day and that everyone else was afraid, published a secret declaration. He suppressed his name, but from its reading everyone could recognize that Nestorius was condemned in it. He sent it to the bishops and to all Catholics, adjuring those who read it by the Holy Trinity to ensure that it reached everyone’s knowledge.

It is preserved in chapter 1 of the first part of the Council of Ephesus in Hardouin’s edition and bears the following title:

> Declaration publicly presented against the clergy of Constantinople and announced in the church, because Nestorius was a follower of Paul of Samosata, who had been anathematized 160 years earlier by the orthodox bishops …

The declaration begins as follows:

> I adjure the person who receives this document by the Holy Trinity to make it public to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers, and laypeople living in Constantinople, and moreover to provide them with a copy, for the rebuke of the heretic Nestorius, because he holds opinions like those of Paul of Samosata, who was anathematized 160 years earlier by the orthodox bishops …

There follow the statements of Paul and of Nestorius, so that readers may conclude that Nestorius, teaching the same doctrine as Paul of Samosata, must be condemned and regarded as a heretic. The ancient translator added this note at the end:

> This declaration was publicly posted in Constantinople while Nestorius still held the see of Constantinople and was teaching wickedly …

Thus declarations of this kind were publicly posted by faithful defenders of Catholic doctrine whenever a prohibition issued by the rulers, or some superior authority, prevented the publication of such discussions.

Marius Mercator, in his scholia on the third sermon of Nestorius, observes that Eusebius was the first to oppose the heresiarch when he was publicly blaspheming:

> When Nestorius was using profane novelties of expression in the midst of the church, by which he attacked both the term *Theotokos*—θεοτόκον, “God-bearer”—and the twofold birth of Christ, a certain thoroughly good man, who was still among the laity but had nevertheless gathered remarkable learning for himself, moved by fervent and religious zeal, cried out in a louder voice and said that the Word, who existed before the ages, had also undergone a second generation, namely that according to the flesh and from a woman …

That this layman was Eusebius and that he publicly rebuked Nestorius is stated in the *Breviculus* of the Eutychianists:

> When Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, found Eutyches persuading people of such things, he acted out of the zeal for the faith that he had also displayed when he was a *agens in rebus*. For he too, at the proper time, rebuked Nestorius when he was preaching sacrilegious things in the church …

Eusebius therefore suffered persecution, perhaps even exile, as the beginning of the declaration suggests, since the same declaration was published in Constantinople by others, not by Eusebius himself; he is therefore presumed to have been absent. That he suffered many hardships after that first public rebuke is proved by the words of Leontius of Byzantium, Book III *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*:

> A refutation of both men—Paul, that is, Paul of Samosata, and Nestorius—was publicly presented, as they say, on the testimony publicly produced by Eusebius, who was then flourishing in the exercise of judgment and was afterward made head of the Church of Dorylaeum. Inflamed, as they testify, by divine zeal, he rebuked and convicted the heresy of Nestorius and Eutyches, having been exposed to innumerable dangers on behalf of piety …

He then recites the declaration cited above.

The *Liber Pontificalis* therefore praises these declarations, which Hormisdas, foreseeing the coming struggle, gave to the legates. In earlier times, when persecution had forbidden Christians to publish apologies, Tertullian nevertheless published one; because it was anonymous and secret, he called it a “silent little book” at the very beginning.

Indeed, not to depart from the matter of Nestorianism, similar secret declarations were circulated throughout the East against Saint Cyril by the Nestorians. Cyril himself mentions them (Volume I of the *Councils*, Hardouin’s edition, Part I, Council of Ephesus, chapter 12):

> They sent two documents to Baphas the martyr and deacon, who was in charge of ecclesiastical affairs: one from Photios, or from someone of the same sort, composed against the memorandum that I had written to the monks; the other in the form of a quire, with an entirely new and absurd heading, as follows: “Against those who, on account of the union, either destroy the divinity of the Only-Begotten or deify his humanity …”

The custom also continued in the age of Saint Gregory the Great, as he writes in Book V, Letter 30:

> In the silence of night he placed in a public place of the city a declaration speaking in accusation against him.

### No. 83, line 5.—With soldiers and magistriani

The perjured emperor not only failed to release the envoys, but ordered them to be put to death and afflicted with hardships. He handed them over to the custody of soldiers and, in addition, employed prefectiani and magistriani, who both took care that they speak with no one and proclaimed imperial edicts to the cities, expressly forbidding them to receive envoys of the apostolic see.

Indeed, many sources show that edicts of greater importance were customarily published through magistriani and prefectiani. When John of Antioch came to Ephesus, he used their services to announce his arrival to Count Candidianus, so that Candidianus might report it to the bishops assembled in council. Thus Nestorius writes in his letter to Theodosius, preserved in the Cassino manuscript, chapter 8, page 30, concerning Candidianus:

> “For when his Magnificence recognized that the most holy John . . . and those who are with him had drawn near—for the prefectiani and magistriani sent by him clearly made this known . . .”

In the controversies conducted with acute contention of minds between the legitimate council and the Eastern schismatics, the emperor’s letters are repeatedly said to have been brought by these officials; this may be seen throughout the Acts. Likewise, when the emperor Leo sought the opinions of all the bishops, magistriani carried the Encyclical to the metropolitans of the whole world.

We read the following in the synodical letter of the Sardican synod, in the third part of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 22, page 729, in Hardouin’s edition:

> “Since, by divine ordinance, we were summoned in the city of the Sardians through Eudoxius, a devoted man and magistrianus, who delivered the imperial command to our most religious metropolitan Eutherius, in accordance with the letter sent by that same most holy man, our metropolitan; and when we had assembled in the aforesaid city, a letter from Your Piety was sent . . .”

From this you may reasonably infer that, after being instructed by the magistriani, the metropolitan compelled the suffragan bishops, by full right, to assemble in synod, where the magistrianus explained the prince’s demands. Consequently, the synodal action belonged entirely to the bishops, whereas the princes’ demand was merely a request.

We read that the same thing occurred in the synod of Rhodes, chapter 25, page 736: the magistriani handed a letter to the synod and, when they were about to return, demanded back the document attesting that they had delivered it.

It was also the duty of the magistriani and prefectiani to receive and deliver all public edicts and acts. Thus, in the Cassino manuscript, in the edict edited by Christianus Lupus, chapter 133, page 274, Theodoretus says of the wicked deeds of a certain Anastasius:

> “But in the royal city he has many who witnessed his seductions—prefectiani, magistriani, and public officials of the city—whose written testimonies, presented to us at Chalcedon, we have read.”

In order to settle the controversy that had arisen between the Fathers at Ephesus and the Orientals, Theodosius ordered, through a magistrianus, that both contending parties return to their own sees. He sent a special message to John the patriarch, so that John might disclose the emperor’s will to the other metropolitans.

John carried this out and gave the letter he had written to the magistrianus sent by the emperor, so that he might deliver it to Alexander, metropolitan of Hierapolis. When Alexander was unwilling either to read it—or even to receive it—the magistrianus read it aloud and handed a copy to Alexander’s notary. He also received a written testimony from Alexander, which he was to show to John.

A record of this ancient custom is preserved in the Cassino synodical collection, chapter 127. It deserves to be recalled as evidence of the hierarchical order, since it is clear that the emperor’s requests were made known to the metropolitans through the primates; and it is likewise clear that the bishops were obliged to subscribe to letters sent by the metropolitan for the good of religion, so that the documents expressing the bishops’ agreement on each matter might be kept with him.

Accordingly, whenever the bishops themselves could not subscribe, they subscribed through notaries. Thus, among the subscriptions of the Council of Ephesus, we find the following in Baluzius’s new collection of councils, page 633:

> “Venantius, bishop of Hierapolis, have subscribed through my notary Theodore.”

From all this it plainly appears how the encyclicals issued to settle controversies became known to the Churches, and how the agreement of the bishops expressed in them could easily be recognized.

Add to the foregoing that Palladius the magistrianus, sent by Theodosius to the bishops of both parties contending at Ephesus, brought back from both sides, upon his return, letters to the emperor in which they all testified that they had received the imperial letters delivered by that same magistrianus.

Moreover, whenever the emperor sent anything to be published by the provincial prefects, he likewise ordered them to write back and testify that they had published it. Thus, at the end of the edict which he published throughout the empire against Porphyrius, Nestorius, and Irene, preserved in the third part of the Council of Ephesus, he gives the following order to the prefects:

> “When Your Magnificence has understood the purpose of Our Piety, let it take care that these things are observed and that the completed proceedings be returned at the earliest opportunity.”

The execution of the same command is also recorded, with the following note added:

> “These things were read in the church of the Solitaries, on the twenty-third of Pharmuthi—that is, April—in the fourth indiction, in the year 164 of Diocletian.”

And when Count Candidianus sent a protest to the holy synod of Ephesus, ordering it to desist from what it had undertaken, he added at the end:

> “Know, therefore, that a copy of this document has also been sent to our most pious lord the emperor.”

In another hand:

> “It was posted on the tenth day before the Kalends of July in the city of Ephesus.”

This is preserved in the Cassino synodical collection, chapter 9.

The *Pontifical Book*, therefore, agrees with the established practice when it records that soldiers were sent with the envoys to keep them from all contact with the Orientals and to prevent them from going anywhere else, requiring them to return directly to Rome; and that magistriani and prefectiani were sent to inform the cities that no one might receive the envoys’ writings or dare to confer with them in any way.

### Line 7.—More secretly

Acacius, whose party Anastasius supported, is said to have been the first to station guards along the roads so that the apostolic writings might not be circulated through the Churches of the East. For this reason the Roman pontiffs were compelled to publish secretly the sentence issued against Acacius.

Gelasius testifies in his letter to the bishops of Dardania that the following measures were taken by the apostolic see in the Acacian affair (*Council of Councils*, vol. II, page 915):

> “Although this sentence directed against Acacius appears to have been issued only in the name of the apostolic bishop, whose legitimate authority it certainly was, especially since it seemed necessary that it be sent secretly, lest, with guards posted everywhere, the salutary arrangement should be obstructed by various difficulties and fail to achieve the necessary effect, nevertheless, because the orthodox had everywhere been cast down and only the heretics and their associates remained in the East, the Catholic pontiffs either no longer existed at all or possessed no freedom of action.”

Just as the pontiff’s decrees in the Acacian affair, although issued secretly, were nevertheless read as bearing the name of the Roman bishop, so, although the protests were secretly posted by monks throughout the principal cities of the East, they bore the name of Hormisdas and the consent of all the Westerners. We shall note this below.

### Line 7.—The aforesaid nineteen letters of faith

The protests mentioned above he here calls letters of faith. Both designations are appropriate, as Theophanes observes under the year 516 and therefore approximately at this time:

> “The monks inhabiting the deserted places of Palestine, inflamed by divine fervor, issued four written protests of faith. They sent two of them to the emperor, one to the governor of the province, and another to the bishop of Jerusalem. They openly professed that they would in no way depart from the holy Council of Chalcedon, nor would they enter into communion with the impious Severus, even if they themselves were destined to see the holy places consumed by fire and were prepared for death.”

These statements are also read in the *Life of Saba*, page 313, in the same work. From this the use and purpose of the protests are evident.

### Line 7.—Through the hands of the monks

In the great struggles over the faith, it was certainly through the zeal of the monks that the profession of the defined Catholic doctrine stood firm. On this subject the earliest ecclesiastical writers speak frequently.

It will be sufficient to recall what Sozomen has in book VI, chapter 20, where he explains that Lucius, the false bishop of Alexandria, could not safely retain his see because of the faith of the monks:

> “Lucius, taking with him the commander of Egypt and a large force of soldiers, undertook an expedition against the monks living in the desert. For he thought that, if he harassed men who loved tranquility with greater severity, he would make them obedient to him, and by this means especially would bring over to his side the Christians living in the cities . . . The multitude of the populace adhered to their testimony and professed the same doctrine of faith as they did. For the people neither wished nor knew how to debate and chatter about doctrines, but believed that the truth belonged to those who professed virtue by their deeds.”

He adds in chapter 27 that the East would easily have turned toward the doctrines of Eunomius and Apollinaris if the monks had not resisted:

> “For the people in those regions, greatly admiring the monks . . . because of their virtue and works, believed that they held the right opinion; but those who thought otherwise they shunned as people stained by adulterated opinions.”

Philostorgius repeats the same account in book III, number 18.

Theodoretus, sent as an envoy to Theodosius to defend the cause of the schismatics, writes to Alexander of Hierapolis in the Cassino synodical collection, chapter 20:

> “But the entire clergy, together with those good monks, is violently opposing us,” etc.

Indeed, he complains that through their efforts it was not even possible to conduct the collections in the Church.

At this same time, when Anastasius had sent orders after the synod of Sidon to Anastasius, governor of Palestine, that he should expel John the patriarch from his throne, recognize Severus of Antioch as patriarch, and have everyone anathematize the Council of Chalcedon, the patriarch requested and obtained several days for deliberation.

Meanwhile,

> “he summoned the entire body of monks to the holy city and gathered them from every direction; some who counted the multitude reported that the procession contained ten thousand monks.”

When they were standing in the church and the governor was present, John, preparing to answer,

> “ascended the ambo, taking with him Theodosius and Saba, the leaders and commanders of the monks; and the entire people cried out for many hours: ‘Subject the heretics to anathema! Confirm the synod!’ Immediately, therefore, with one harmonious voice, the three of them anathematized Nestorius, Eutyches, Severus, Soterichus of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and everyone who would not receive the Council of Chalcedon. After the three had proclaimed these things and descended, the abbot Theodosius returned and addressed the people: ‘If anyone,’ he said, ‘does not accept the four synods as he accepts the four Gospels, let him be anathema.’ After these events, the governor, terrified by the multitude of monks, fled to Caesarea.”

Thus, through the monks, the envoys of the apostolic see worked to have their protests posted in the principal cities of the East. The obstinacy of the Acacians and their devotion to a wicked cause impelled the apostolic see to provide for the defense of the faith that had been attacked in this manner.

### Line 9.—Who were Anastasius’s accomplices

These were, of course, the Acacians, bitterly hostile to the apostolic see and following in the footsteps of Acacius, whom we have identified as the first to forbid the publication of apostolic rescripts. They removed the autograph letters of faith from every place and sent them to the emperor.

### Line 10.—As a crime

These words refer to the edict sent to the cities through the magistriani and prefectiani, forbidding anyone to speak with the envoys or receive apostolic writings. Or, if you prefer, they refer to what Basiliscus, Zeno, and Anastasius provided by edict: that no one should dare to post the decrees of the apostolic see.

The Acacians therefore reported the secret publication of Hormisdas’s letters to the emperor as a crime; for this reason he sent a harsher rescript to the pontiff, as we shall soon relate.

The patriarchs of Constantinople had introduced the rule that no ecclesiastic should approach the emperor unless he were presented by the patriarch. Hence Hormisdas himself, in the instructions delivered to the envoys, warns them not to offer the apostolic decrees to the emperor in the presence of Timothy of Constantinople, nor, while Timothy persisted obstinately in heresy, to seal any decrees.

This servitude was imposed by the Acacians so that, knowing what the apostolic rescripts decreed, they might circumvent the rulers at will.

Yet although the Acacian party regarded such secret publications as a crime, the populace thought otherwise. The people, more fervently devoted to the truth, attacked the emperor, as we shall soon note from Theophanes.

Indeed, after Anastasius had died and Justin had been elected, nothing did the people demand more vehemently amid their acclamations than this:

> “Let the Roman synodical letters now prevail.”

These were undoubtedly the nineteen letters of faith that had been posted and that the Acacian informers had sent from Constantinople to the emperor. Justinian too, while still a count, wrote to Hormisdas about them as follows:

> “For we know what the letters of Your Beatitude and of your predecessors, sent to the East, contain concerning this same matter.”

### Line 10.—Filled with fury

At the urging of the Acacians, the emperor Anastasius treated these writings of faith harshly, representing them as incitements to rebellion; and then, freed from fear of Vitalianus, he first began to rage against the Roman pontiff.

This was the Acacians’ doing. But when the people had recognized the emperor’s perjuries and bad faith, they were provoked against him, especially when they heard that the envoys of the apostolic see had been badly treated and that the emperor had dissolved the synod at Heraclea.

Theophanes relates these events as follows:

> “The entire populace and the whole Senate attacked Anastasius with insults as a perjurer. To this the wicked man replied most shamelessly that there was a law which ordered an emperor, when placed in necessity, to swear falsely and to lie. Thus spoke that criminal, the disciple of the Manichaeans,” etc.

You may suppose that Thomas Hobbes drew from this the destructive maxims concerning religion and even kingdoms which he set down in great number in his book *On the Citizen*.

Hormisdas briefly reports to Avitus the perverse strategy of the Acacians and of the other courtiers of Anastasius (in Sirmondus, same work, page 131):

> “But as regards the Greeks, their lips present vows of peace more readily than their hearts do, and they speak more of what is right than they do it. In words they boast that they wish for what their deeds show they do not wish; they neglect what they have professed and pursue what they have condemned,” etc.

But he launched a savage persecution especially against the monks, whom he knew to be its principal agents, under the leadership of Severus of Antioch and Peter of Apamea, false bishops. The monks reported this slaughter to the pontiff Hormisdas and, among other things, wrote as follows (in Labbe, page 1461):

> “Since Christ our God appointed you and your holy angel as prince of shepherds, teachers, and physicians of souls, it is fitting to set forth the sufferings that have befallen us and to expose the merciless wolves who are destroying Christ’s flock. Who these men are, and who have armed themselves against us, Your Beatitude has certainly heard. They are that Severus and Peter, who have never been counted among Christians; each day they attack the holy Council of Chalcedon and our most holy and blessed Father Leo with a public anathema; disregarding the judgment of God and trampling upon the venerable canons of the holy Fathers, they mock the aforesaid holy synod and afflict it with immeasurable punishments. As we were going to the monastery of the Lord Simeon on the Church’s behalf, these lost and polluted men ambushed us on the road, descended upon us, and killed 350 of our number. They wounded some; others who were able fled to the altars to worship there, but they killed them even there and burned the monasteries,” etc.

The memory of these monks is commemorated on July 31. Concerning them, see the reports of the monks in the Constantinopolitan council under Menna, volume II of the councils.

### Line 12.—Anastasius was struck by divine lightning

Cyrillus speaks of his death in the *Life of Saba*. He relates that the holy abbot undertook a journey to console Bishop Elias and records both the manner of Anastasius’s death and the day predicted by the holy bishop.

For Cyrillus says:

> “When he had returned to Jerusalem, he learned that, on the night of the tenth day of the month of July, when the vision shown to Patriarch Elias had occurred, while thunder and flashes of lightning rolled around the palace, the emperor Anastasius had been almost entirely consumed while utterly alone. His mind collapsing, he fled from place to place, but in one of the small chambers he was overtaken by divine wrath, struck down and killed, so that he died suddenly.”

These words agree perfectly with what has been related above. Theophanes gives the same account, as does Zonaras, *Annals*, book XIV, section 57.

Therefore the words inserted by an ignorant copyist into the *Life of Pope Anastasius* must be restored here and referred, as they ought to be, to the emperor Anastasius. The circumstance recorded there indicates that an error and transposition have intervened, since it says that he was struck while he was supporting the cause of the Acacians during the time of Pope Anastasius. Yet it was the Acacian informers whom he heard concerning the protests secretly posted by Hormisdas; for that reason he sent harsher rescripts to Hormisdas and supported the cause of the Acacians while subjecting the Catholics to a savage persecution.

### Line 14.—His authority

The Greeks required imperial rescripts to bear, among other things, the mark of authority. Thus in Liberius we read:

> “Then he sent Catulinus, an *agens in rebus*, with authority.”

And in Marculphus, book I, formulas 3 and 4:

> “So that this authority may retain perpetual force, we have confirmed it with our own hand,” etc.

Strictly speaking, therefore, an *auctoritas* was a letter which the emperors sealed with their own hand.

Traces of this ancient custom are also to be noted in Justin. He sent a letter to the newly elected Roman pontiff together with his profession of faith, sealed with his own hand. Gregory II speaks of this in his letter to Leo the Isaurian, affirming that letters bearing the emperor’s own signature were still preserved in the archives of the apostolic see near Saint Peter.

Such a seal was necessary, since through it and through the other letters sent to the patriarchs, the edicts of Anastasius against the Council of Chalcedon were annulled, and bishops were recalled from exile on account of the same faith.

Cyrillus mentions this same authority in the *Life of Saba*:

> “After Anastasius had died in this way, Justin, as soon as he assumed the empire, immediately issued laws ordering that all those whom Anastasius had driven into exile be recalled; likewise, that the Council of Chalcedon be inserted into the sacred diptychs,” etc.

But since this authority of Justin, sent in every direction throughout the East, became the cause of numerous synods being summoned and of bishops everywhere issuing encyclicals in order once again to approve the Council of Chalcedon, in the same manner as had occurred under the emperor Leo according to the form of the encyclical tome preserved in the third part of the Council of Chalcedon, this matter must be examined before we continue with the notes, in order to clarify it. The Palestinian synod, which the compilers entirely pass over, must therefore be considered.

## On the Palestinian synod under John, patriarch of Jerusalem

After Justin had obtained the empire, he did two things immediately: he sent a profession of faith to Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff, and published edicts throughout the empire ordering that people subscribe to the libellus, or letters of faith, secretly posted by the monks.

When the bishops, having been given the opportunity, assembled in synods and issued a subscribed libellus containing everything that the pontiff had given in his instructions to the envoys departing for the East under Anastasius, the same libellus must necessarily have been set forth in the posted letters, with a protest added, so that anyone who did not subscribe to it would be separated from communion with the Catholic Church. The emperor likewise ordered that it be subscribed.

Concerning John of Jerusalem, to whom these orders were conveyed as primate, Cyrillus writes in the *Life of Saint Saba* (same work, page 326):

> “When these orders of Justin had been delivered to Jerusalem, an infinite multitude of monks and laypeople assembled. Saint Saba also came, together with the council of bishops. After the feast had been celebrated, the divine commands were promulgated on the sixth day of the month of August, and the four synods were placed in the sacred diptychs.”

Since this synod was convened on August 6 in the year 518, and since Anastasius died during the night between July 9 and 10, it follows that the celebration of the synods began immediately after Anastasius’s death, before the pontiff had prepared a new embassy or sent a new libellus of faith.

John of Jerusalem presented these same acts to the bishops of Caesarea and Scythopolis in the Palestinian synod. Hence Cyrillus adds:

> “Then John, archbishop of Jerusalem, persuaded our holy Father Saba to proceed to Caesarea and Scythopolis with certain other leaders of the desert, in order to disclose the emperor’s letters and insert the four councils in the sacred diptychs throughout the cities. When they reached Caesarea, Saint John Chuzibita, who at that time held the episcopate of that city, came to meet them. After completing there what had been commanded, they also proceeded to Scythopolis. All the citizens, together with the most holy metropolitan Theodosius, went out to meet them at the apostolium, or church, of Saint Thomas. Returning with psalms, they celebrated the synaxis in the old holy church. Then the divine letters were published, and the four synods were entered in the sacred diptychs,” etc.

Before the Palestinian synod, the Constantinopolitan synod was celebrated, in response to the demands of the people, who would not permit John the patriarch to depart unless he first did these three things:

1. Restore the four ecumenical synods to the sacred diptychs.
2. Pronounce an anathema against Nestorius and Eutyches.
3. Anathematize Severus.

Accordingly, during the acclamations they cried out:

> “Let the Roman synodical letters now prevail!”

That is, the protests that had been secretly posted and that the Acacians had forbidden to be put into effect.

Since the pontiff had expressly commanded these three things in the letters of faith, and since the people in the full Constantinopolitan synod solemnly demanded that the patriarch publish the same things—and he did so from the ambo—it is clear that, through the particular synods assembled by order of the metropolitans, a solemn profession of the rescripts of the apostolic see was issued, especially through the Constantinopolitan synod mentioned above, by whose means peace was established between the Eastern and Western Churches.

Avitus of Vienne had not yet received any report from either Hormisdas or John of Constantinople concerning what had been done. For this reason he wrote a letter to John, first published by Sirmondus in volume II, page 41. After its opening, the following passage deserves notice:

> “Since we longed for you with a just desire as for the chief priest, the illustrious Laurentius increased our esteem for you by informing us in his letters that every cloud which, in a doubtful darkness, had obscured the peace of the Eastern peoples had been wiped away by the brightness of restored peace; and that you were enjoying with the Roman bishop such harmony as it would be fitting to assign to the world as belonging to the twin leaders of the apostles. For who, if he may be called a Catholic, would not rejoice at the peace of such great and such important Churches, which the world awaits as a sign of religion set in heaven, like a double constellation? Who would not rightly take delight in the return of those who had been infirm, and in the state of those who are safe, when, with the other sheep saved within the enclosures, the one that had strayed through the fault of erring judgment is recalled, while the heavenly folds applaud with joy? Therefore, as Fathers, guard the ecclesiastical discipline entrusted to you, even over us. Your concord requires as much authority as example. How shall we commend charity to the peoples if we do not know it among our rulers? What can appear sound in the body, or what can fail at the head? Therefore give those who are returning a pious proclamation, lest anyone perish through his purpose. Take care that the signs you have observed are not ravaged by so savage a beast, if Rome should break away from the unity of your mind. Remember us: for if the sun should set upon your disagreement, the loss belongs to the East. Confirm by a written reply for our knowledge the most prosperous report that I mentioned, so that the Western Church, awaiting from your words the gift of the heavenly oracle which it rejoices to have received through its fellow disciple, may rejoice that it is multiplied for her through the teacher,” etc.

The Tyrian synod did the same, as is clear from its synodical letter preserved in the synod under Menna. The Illyrian synod also did so; its letter of reply to Hormisdas is preserved in volume II of the councils among the letters of Hormisdas.

When the envoys of the apostolic see arrived, the bishops of the individual cities immediately offered subscribed libelli. This is stated at length in the reports of Dioscorus, the legate of the apostolic see, preserved among the pontiff’s letters and in Baronius.

This solemn profession, made through encyclicals issued by the Eastern bishops in the affair of the Three Chapters, together with the second confirmation made through them, is presented by Rusticus the deacon as the judgment of the Church and an unquestionable argument of faith (*Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*, volume X, page 382).

When he counts the number of synods and the bishops subscribing in their own sees, he writes:

> “Although the single authority of the universal synod would be sufficient for you—a synod which surpasses all others in number and which has so often been confirmed by the harmonious judgment of all the Churches, both through the encyclicals under the reign of Leo and through the libelli of perhaps two thousand five hundred priests under Justin, after the schism of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople,” etc.

Nor will it seem surprising that the number of subscribers and libelli could have become known, since Dioscorus testifies in his report that all the subscribed libelli were sent to the apostolic see. When Hormisdas received the synodical letter of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, who had been appointed in place of the deceased John, he instructed him in his reply to advance the cause of the faith and to receive repentant bishops kindly:

> “Provided, however, that those who have been united to communion with the City make known to us, either through them or through the apostolic see, your letters, in which the contents of the libelli they have offered are also to be included,” etc.

This precaution was necessary so that, from the subscribed libelli—which were to be preserved in the archives—the unanimous agreement of the Church might be discerned.

As for the period of the schism, the disturbances stirred up in the East by the Acacians, and the way in which they were settled and suppressed through the encyclicals subscribed by so many bishops everywhere, Facundus notes the following in his work *Against Mocianus* (same work, page 109):

> “Since the aforesaid Zeno, despising the decrees of the apostolic see, communicated with the aforesaid Acacius and compelled all the Churches established within the boundaries of his kingdom to do the same, and since Anastasius subsequently succeeded to the empire and to a similar presumption, the whole East, except for a very few who remained hidden within that multitude, continued separated from communion with the apostolic see for nearly forty-nine years, until the time of Justin,” etc.

This, then, concerns the synods subsequently celebrated by the bishops so that the Council of Chalcedon might be confirmed and unity at last established between the Roman and Eastern Churches.

### No. 84, line 14.—Here Pope Hormisdas

He had previously said that Hormisdas sent the embassy with the counsel and consent of Theodoricus. He now adds that Hormisdas went to Ravenna so that, with the king’s advice, he might send the embassy and his authority.

For he knew that Theodoricus was not opposed to establishing unity and peace with the Easterners. Jornandes writes of him:

> “He appointed Athalaric, the son of his daughter Amalasuntha, as king, and gave him instructions, declaring as though with testamentary authority that they should always keep the Eastern prince appeased and favorable,” etc.

### Line 15.—And the bond of the autograph document

I believe this signifies that the cause of Acacius’s condemnation was discussed more fully and at greater length. Earlier Gelasius had published a treatise on the bond of anathema, in which he demonstrated that Acacius had been condemned according to the canons.

Since the Acacians, as is soon reported, argued that an account had to be rendered and that the cause and justice of Acacius’s condemnation had to be explained, the pontiff wished to instruct the envoys more fully so that they could show that Acacius had deservedly been struck with anathema.

Justin, for his part, earnestly urged the bishops to accept this condemnation once it had been published (letter 31). Hormisdas had written to the emperor, expressing the greatest thanks for the edicts previously published, and adding:

> “While giving thanks for so great a magnanimity, we earnestly beg, with all the insistence we can muster, that the name of Acacius, together with his followers, be removed according to the order of condemnation, so that the joy of the Churches’ complete unity may be secured,” etc.

Justin replied and made the following statement concerning Acacius:

> “It has been decreed that henceforth no memory of Acacius the transgressor, formerly bishop of this city, be made among the divine mysteries; nor of the other priests who either first acted against the apostolic constitutions or became successors in error, without correcting themselves by repentance until the last day of their lives,” etc.

He therefore published a second set of edicts. Dioscorus recalls an example of these in his report, speaking of John of Constantinople and his clergy, who expressly struck Acacius with anathema in their libellus:

> “We have said that imperial decrees are to be sent everywhere, so that they may imitate the example of the royal city,” etc.

When the pontiff read these things, he wrote back to John the patriarch, urging him to persuade the emperor to send these writings everywhere (letter 44):

> “To accomplish what he has deigned to promise in his royal letters, so that, by sending edicts to those whom erring error still leads away from the breasts of Mother Church, he may restrain the devil’s deceit both by the authority of religion and by the moderate power of imperial rule,” etc.

Therefore, since he was so concerned about the condemnation of Acacius, he could indeed have produced a fuller treatise—or autograph document—on the bond of the anathema pronounced against Acacius, in order to silence the voices of the obstinate.

### Line 17.—Here he found Manichaeans

Their treachery had grown through the favor and following of Anastasius. For this reason, suppressing them too would have fallen within Hormisdas’s zeal.

In the East, the men who chiefly conspired against Justin were Manichaeans. Marcellinus writes about this in his *Chronicle* (in Sirmondus, volume II, page 378):

> “Justin was elected emperor by the Senate and immediately installed. Amantius was appointed superintendent of the palace; Andreas, Misael, and Ardabur were chamberlains. The supporters of the Manichaeans and the traitors of the emperor Justin were discovered. Two of them, Amantius and Andreas, were killed by the sword; Misael and Ardabur were sent into exile at Sardica,” etc.

During the acclamations, when the people demanded that the Roman synodical letters prevail, they also shouted many things against Amantius, among them:

> “Cast out the new Isumas! The new Isumas is Amantius. Cast the buffoon out of the palace,” etc.

This appears to indicate that the conspiracy against Justin was advanced at the beginning of his reign, when such acclamations were made by the people.

That Amantius was killed within this same period is shown by other acclamations in which the people congratulate the emperor. In the same source:

> “Amantius, the rebel against the Trinity, has died,” etc.

Meanwhile, this treachery, which had long spread throughout the East and was not eradicated from the roots, became the source of the Mohammedan impiety that infected the East at the beginning of the following century, and later of Iconoclasm under Leo the Isaurian.

### Line 19.—In his time in Africa

Concerning the date of these bishops’ return to Africa, Norisius has collected much material with great learning in *Pelagian History*, book II, chapter 21.

### No. 85, line 1.—At the same time

This is one of the customary transpositions made by copyists, since what is related here belongs to the deeds of another pontiff.

Clovis died in the year 511, as the Frankish writers establish. Hormisdas, however, was created pontiff in the year 514.

The “kingdom,” or crown, refers to votive gifts that were sent to adorn the tombs of the apostles. Such gifts, offered in the form of a crown, are frequently recorded in the temples of both pagans and Christians.

Meanwhile, the fact that the tomb of the prince of the apostles was frequented and loaded with gifts at this same time is shown by a letter of Hormisdas to Epiphanius, the recently elected bishop of Constantinople. Epiphanius had sent gifts with his synodical letter, and Hormisdas himself added the following at the end of his letter:

> “We have received a golden chalice, a silver paten, another silver chalice, and two veils, sent by your charity for the service of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.”

[Note: [Col. 0495C]

### No. 82, line 5.—At the same time, by decree of the synod, he sent into Greece, etc.

Once the Catholic faith had been restored and freed from the bonds of schism, this benefit followed: it brought the king and people of the Lazes, hitherto strangers to the true religion, to embrace the Christian faith. (*Miscellaneous Author*, book XV.)

[Col. 0495D] Line 13.—Text of the memorandum. It exists among the letters of Hormisdas, beginning as follows: “The first salvation is,” etc. Among other sacred statements he wrote this: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” This letter exists among the other letters of Hormisdas, beginning as follows: “Although it is something great.” Near the end of this letter he says: “We can endure being insulted and nullified; we cannot be commanded.” And the heretical emperor, very like Pharaoh, in order to avoid the sword of Vitalian drawn against him and escape the scourges of God pressing upon him, craftily pretended that he wished to obey the Roman pontiff. Thus he bowed his iron neck only in appearance; but when he saw that these dangers had been removed, he despised Moses together with God, and the pontiff together with Christ, with hardened obstinacy. What happened afterward in the East may be seen from the report of the archimandrites and monks of the Second Syria, which is found among the letters of Hormisdas after the twenty-second, in the general council.

Num. 83, line 13.—“Justin was orthodox, and he directed,” [Col. 0496A] etc. This was done by decree and by the council of the Synod of Constantinople, as is clear from the acts of that synod and from the letters written to Hormisdas by Justin, John of Constantinople, and Justinian.

Num. 84, line 1.—“Then Hormisdas, etc., sent Germanus from the apostolic see,” etc. Through this legation the Easterners were received into union and communion with the Roman Church, after they had obeyed the command of the Roman pontiff, removed the names of Acacius, Euphemius, and Macedonius from the sacred diptychs, made an integral profession of the Catholic faith, and removed the memory of the heretics Zeno and Anastasius from the list of emperors. Their names are still found prefixed elsewhere to various laws in Justinian’s Code, because Tribonian, a pagan and impious man, compiled that same Code. This reconciliation of the Eastern Church with the Roman Church took place during the consulship of Justin, in the year of the Lord 519, the sixth year of Hormisdas’s pontificate.

[Col. 0496B] Line 19.—“During his time the episcopate in Africa was restored, which had been exterminated by the heretics.” By the authority of certain Vandal kings it had been decreed that Catholics in Africa should not ordain other bishops in place of those who had died. But Hilderic, son of Huneric, who succeeded to the kingdom after King Thrasamund’s death in the ninth year of Pope Hormisdas—that is, in the year of Christ 522—ordered, according to Isidore in his Chronicle, that Catholic priests should be recalled from exile and that the churches should be opened. He did this before he became king, so as not to violate the obligation of the oath by which he had promised his predecessor Thrasamund, already dead, that he would open no churches to Catholics in his kingdom and restore none of their privileges. God willed to increase the most blessed pontiff by this blessing also, so that, after the restoration of the Eastern Church to Catholic communion, he might likewise see the African Church—long harassed by persecution and most recently trampled underfoot by King Thrasamund after all its bishops had been expelled—restored to its former splendor.]

[Note: [Col. 0496C]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

The Librarian fixes the vacancy of the see after Symmachus’s death at seven days. Hormisdas, therefore, was elected as his successor on July 26 and ordained on Sunday, July 27, of that same year, 514. The Librarian extends his pontificate from the consulship of Senator to the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius; for he assigns the consulship of Maximus, in which Hormisdas died, to Pope John, his successor. He defines the total period as nine years—this is what the better manuscripts give: the Freherianus, Regius, Mazzarinus, and first Thuaneus of Fabrotti; the Cassinensis and Vaticanus of Holstenius and Schelestratius; and the Cavensis of Peña, although in other manuscripts the unit is missing, through the customary fault of copyists—and twenty-seven days. I think, however, that these should be read as thirteen, so that they correspond with the year and day of his deposition, stated in section 86, lines 11 and 12. “He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on August 6 [Col. 0496D], during the consulship of Maximus. And the episcopate ceased for seven days.” Nine years and twelve days, counted inclusively from July 26, 514, reach August 6, or the eighth day before the Ides; on this date not only the Roman Martyrology but also Bede’s Martyrology commemorates this pontiff.

Besides the authors mentioned above, an ancient Vatican marble inscription, still preserved today in the sacred crypts of the basilica and published by the Most Eminent Cardinal Noris in his History of Pelagius, book II, chapter 21, page 329, testifies that Hormisdas survived until the year 523. It states that, during the consulship of Flavius Maximus, a burial place was granted by Pope Hormisdas to certain married couples. Several letters of this pontiff preserve the consulship in which they were issued and thus provide exact chronological evidence for his pontificate, as may be seen in the Prolegomena to those same years.

[Col. 0497A] HISTORICAL NOTES.

Num. 82, line 3.—“Here he organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms.” Why Hormisdas is said to have organized the clergy was explained most aptly at the beginning of the notes of the distinguished Bencinus. His other deeds, too, narrated in this and the following section by the Librarian, have been clearly demonstrated by him, by the Reverend Father Pagius, and by the Most Illustrious Archbishop Sommier in their commentaries. I therefore will not dwell further on illustrating them. I think that only one word should be corrected: “and instructed them in the psalms.” Here there is an obvious error; I believe it should read, “and instructed them by his letters.” Just as he organized the Roman clergy, previously divided into factions, and the Eastern Church, separated from the Western by schism and disunited by heresy, after peace and unity had been restored, so also by his letters he instructed them in that same Catholic doctrine and in the preservation of peace, which he commends and strengthens through so many written testimonies. Mopinot, no. 12, of the little work cited, concerning the new edition of the letters of the Supreme Pontiff, prepared by Father Constantius, says: “Nor did the diligent editor fail to vindicate Hormisdas’s letters written concerning the controversy of the Scythian monks. To this defense he devoted not merely additional notes, but a Dissertation in two parts and widely extended. In the first part he explains certain difficult points of the History and proves that nothing was asserted by the most holy pope that was contrary to the Catholic faith; and that nothing was rejected, or at least suppressed in silence, except what the love of ecclesiastical peace and the consideration of Christian prudence required to be rejected or at least kept silent,” etc.

Num. 84, line 19.—“During his time the episcopate in Africa was restored after seventy-four years,” etc. Read “84”; for in the year 439 Genseric invaded Carthage and drove Bishop Quodvultdeus, together with most of the clergy, into exile by placing him on an old ship, stripping Carthage of its shepherd, clergy, sacred places, and senate, as Cardinal Noris proves from Victor of Vita and other historians in his History of Pelagius, book II, chapter 21, and after him Ruinart in the chronological index to the edition of Victor of Vita. In the year 523 he notes the following from the same historians: “After Thrasamund’s death, Hilderic, the son of Huneric, succeeded him; he restored peace to the African Church by recalling the bishops from exile. There are eighty-four years from 439 to 523.”

The most distinguished author should also be consulted in chapter 12 of his History of the Vandal Persecution, where he treats most carefully the deeds of the African Church on the occasion of the peace restored to it. Since these matters greatly illuminate the restoration of the episcopate mentioned here by the Librarian, and the pontificate of Hormisdas during which it occurred, we have thought it appropriate to transcribe here some passages from Ruinart’s chapter 12.

“CHAPTER XII. Peace Restored to the African Church.—1. After Thrasamund’s death the whole appearance of the African Church changed. ‘Wondrous indeed was the goodness,’ says the author of the Life of Fulgentius, chapter 28, ‘of Hilderic at the beginning of his reign: restoring freedom to the Catholic Church established throughout Africa, he gave the people of Carthage their own bishop and, with most merciful authority, ordered that episcopal ordinations be carried out in every place.’”

That Hilderic ordered Boniface to be ordained in the Church of Saint Agileus near Carthage at the beginning of his reign, after freedom had been restored to all Catholics, is attested by Vitus, the author of the fragment appended to the chronicle of Tiro in Canisius. Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, however, maintains in his chronicle that Hilderic had arranged this before he assumed the kingdom, because he had been bound by an oath to Thrasamund, as we said above, not to restore freedom to the Catholics after he had obtained the kingdom.

“‘Hilderic,’ he says, ‘who was born from the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, captured by Gaiseric and joined to Huneric, reigned for seven years and three months.
