Since he had therefore been bound by an oath to his predecessor not to open churches to Catholics in his kingdom or restore their privileges, before he reigned, so as not to overstep the terms of his oath, he ordered the Catholic priests to return from exile and the churches to be opened; and, at the request of the entire Church of the city of Carthage, he consecrated Boniface, a man sufficiently energetic in divine doctrines, as bishop.’”

Isidore likewise attests this in his brief chronicle of the Vandals, in the year 553 of the era. Moreover, Hilderic’s great benevolence toward the Catholics persuaded some that he had professed the Catholic faith, which he had received from his mother Eudoxia. Others, however, think that this should rather be attributed to his innate gentleness, since, according to Procopius, he was never burdensome to anyone, whether Catholics or others.

“2. The devotion of the people of Carthage, with which they joyfully welcomed the holy confessors returning from exile, especially Fulgentius, is described by the author of the Life of that same Saint Fulgentius, chapter 29: ‘Divine praise,’ he says, ‘resounded from every tongue. For the people, following and preceding him to the basilica of Saint Agileus, celebrated the noble triumph of the blessed confessors.’

“But the affection of all for blessed Fulgentius was exceptional. ‘When,’ says the author of his Life, [Col. 0498B] ‘the face of Fulgentius appeared, an immense shout arose. Everyone argued over who would be the first to greet and recognize him, who would place his head beneath the hand blessing him, who would deserve to touch him as he passed, if only with the tips of the fingers, and who would be able to see him even while standing at a distance. But when an immense rain came upon them at the same time, the crowd’s procession was not obstructed. Indeed, the faith of the nobles grew so greatly that, spreading their cloaks gratefully over blessed Fulgentius, they repelled the rain and ingeniously fashioned a new kind of tabernacle.’”

Here it is worth observing the religious devotion of the blessed confessors. Returning from a long pilgrimage, as soon as they reached the shore, they immediately left the ships and hurried to the church of Saint Agileus to offer public thanksgiving to God. Indeed, as the cited author of the Life says somewhat farther on, “as evening was scarcely approaching, having scarcely been presented to Bishop Boniface of holy memory, they all gave the blessing and together praised God.”

“3. After a few days Fulgentius departed for Ruspa, [Col. 0498C] finding greater joys along every road of the long journey, as crowds everywhere hastened to meet him with lamps, torches, and leafy branches, giving thanks to the ineffable God. . . . Through all the churches he was received as their own bishop. Restored to his see, he lived together with his monks, but in such a way that he did nothing concerning the affairs belonging to the monastery without the knowledge of Abbot Felix. He often took monks into ecclesiastical service, regulating everything so carefully that no dispute ever arose between the monks and the clergy. The same author of the Life says much more about Fulgentius’s diligence in governing the people and about the various books he published in defense of the Catholic faith. But it is not part of our purpose to discuss these matters at greater length.

“Yet it is not permissible to omit the outstanding example of the greatest humility reported by the author of his Life in chapter 29. When, after returning from exile, the Fathers of Byzacena had assembled at the Council of Tunca to restore ecclesiastical discipline, Fulgentius was preferred by the judgment of all to Bishop Quodvultdeus, who considered himself senior to him. At that time the blessed bishop accepted this silently, lest by making excuses he seem to diminish the authority of the council. But shortly afterward, at the Synod of Sufes, he offered humble prayers before all the Fathers that Quodvultdeus should be placed before him, since he wished this to be done. He feared that, because of his own honor, scandal might arise for his brother, and he judged it better to become lesser through charity than to be greater without charity.

“While he devoted himself entirely to repairing the ruins of his Church—a work that Boniface, bishop of Carthage, was also arranging throughout Africa by convening a general council of all Africa, held in the year 525—and while he longed for the better life, he withdrew with a few brothers to the island of Circina out of a desire for greater perfection. There, shortly afterward, remaining sound in mind until his final hour, says the author of his Life, ‘on the Kalends of January themselves, after Vespers had been completed, he departed this life,’ in the twenty-fifth year after he had been placed over the Church of Ruspa, and in the sixty-fifth year of his age. Henry Noris proves in book II of his History of Pelagius, at the final chapter, that these words indicate the year 533 of the common era. The more recent as well as the ancient Martyrologies commemorate Fulgentius on January 1; the Catholic Church rightly venerates him as a most holy teacher, a most vigilant bishop, and an unconquered confessor of Christ.

“4. The peace granted by Hilderic, however, was only a kind of prelude to that supreme tranquility which the African Church attained a few years later. For Gelimer, born of Gelilaris, the son of Genseric, to whom the kingdom of the Vandals was owed after Hilderic’s death, impatient of delay, drove out Hilderic and seized the kingdom in the year 531. Hilderic’s character favored his rebellion; he was so timid that he could not even endure the sight of a sword. Moreover, Hilderic had alienated the minds of the Goths from himself because of the death of Amalafrida, the daughter of Theodoric the Great. She had married Thrasamund; but after her husband’s death, as Victor of Tunnuna relates, when she fled to the barbarians and was intercepted after a battle near Capsa, she died in custody shortly afterward.

“Athalaric, the grandson of Theodoric through his daughter Amalasuntha, who ruled the Ostrogoths in Italy, took this badly; in Cassiodorus’s Variae, book IX, in a letter addressed to Hilderic, he complains of it. There he says that Amalafrida’s death had been violent and threatens that he would soon avenge with arms the killing of the queen born from the blood of Amal, unless satisfaction were given to him and to the entire Gothic people. Procopius writes in book I of his History of the Vandal War that Amalafrida was held in chains and that all the Goths were killed by the Vandals, having been accused of plotting revolution to the ruin of the king and kingdom.

“We do not, however, read that the Goths attempted anything against Hilderic at that time. Perhaps shortly afterward Hilderic was easily thrown from the throne by Gelimer, and that tyrant, aspiring to the kingdom, had undoubtedly appeased their minds. [Col. 0499C] The cited Procopius testifies that Theodoric did not avenge these injuries because he judged that his fleet was not strong enough to undertake an expedition against Africa.

“Justin Augustus favored Hilderic, as did Justinian, who shortly afterward obtained the imperial power, because Hilderic, born of Eudoxia, was related through his mother to the Roman emperors. Indeed, after Justinian became emperor and Gelimer had overthrown Hilderic, he broke the treaty once concluded between Zeno and King Genseric. Having assembled a vast army, he recovered all Africa through the general Belisarius, after Gelimer had been defeated and captured and shortly afterward led to Constantinople for the triumph, as Procopius relates at length in his books on the Vandal War.

“The same author admirably represents the triumph of Belisarius. On that occasion Gelimer furnished, both in deed and in speech, a striking example of the fragility of human affairs. He was led to the circus with the princes of the royal family and the other leading Vandals, who were distinguished by their birth or even by their stature. As soon as he saw the emperor seated on a lofty throne, he considered the misfortunes to which he himself had come and, without breaking down in tears or lamentations, burst into these words taken from the sacred books: ‘Vanity of vanities, vanity.’

“Procopius lists the more valuable spoils brought from the Vandals and carried in the triumph. ‘They included,’ says the cited author, ‘the objects with which it was customary to serve the Vandal king: golden thrones and carriages that had transported the royal matron; besides these, the incredible splendor of jewels; golden vessels and whatever else displayed the luxury of the royal table. There were also several hundred thousand pounds of silver and other things of immense value, which Gaiseric had stolen after plundering the Roman palace. Among these were the objects that Titus Vespasian had formerly brought to Rome after the capture of Jerusalem.’

“Emperor Justinian testifies in the Code, book I, title 27, that all the imperial ornaments which Genseric had carried to Africa after the capture of Rome were restored to him. In the following year, [Col. 0500A] which was 535 of the common era, Belisarius, having obtained the consulship, celebrated a triumph in the manner of the ancient consuls. He was carried on the shoulders of captives and placed upon a chariot; then, as Procopius relates, he scattered among the people objects from the Vandal spoils—silver vessels, golden belts, and various instruments of royal luxury—which the populace received with great applause.

“5. The greatest fruit of this victory, however, was peace for the African Church. For no one denies that the persecution—which some hold to have intensified under Gelimer’s tyranny—was at that time completely extinguished. Certainly no one will persuade himself that Gelimer favored the Catholics, since everyone agrees that he was exceedingly savage even toward his own people, to say nothing of Hilderic, an excellent prince, whom he ordered to be cruelly killed along with his other relatives, as Victor of Tunnuna testifies in his Chronicle, under the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus. That author repeatedly observes that many of the nobles of Africa were killed by the same king, after which he plundered their property by lawful and unlawful means.

[Col. 0500B] “From Procopius we infer that he was especially devoted to the sect of the Arians. In book II of his Vandal War, Procopius reports that Gelimer, although Justinian had given him splendid estates in Galatia, where he lived with his relatives, did not obtain the dignity of patrician because he was unwilling to depart from the doctrines of Arius.”

“6. Africa was therefore recovered by the Romans in the twelfth indiction, during the consulship of Justinian Augustus for the fourth time and Paulinus—that is, in the year 534 of the common era—after one hundred and seven years had passed since it had been occupied by the Vandals. At the same time the city of Carthage was restored to the empire in the ninety-fifth year after it had been captured by Genseric.

“Justinian Augustus offered public thanksgiving to God Almighty on this account in the constitution concerning the office of the praetorian prefect of Africa, found in Justinian’s Code, book I, title 27. There he congratulates himself on such a great benefit granted to him by God:

“‘What thanks or praises we ought to offer to our Lord God Jesus Christ, neither can our mind conceive nor our tongue express. We have indeed previously received many gifts from God, and we confess that innumerable benefits have been bestowed upon us, for which we recognize that we have done nothing worthy. Yet above all, this deed, which Almighty God has now deigned to display through us for his praise and for his name, surpasses all the wondrous works that have occurred in the world: that Africa, previously held captive by the Vandals for ninety-five years—who were at once enemies of souls and of bodies—should through us recover its freedom in so short a time.

“‘For they transferred souls to their own impiety by rebaptizing them, since they could not endure the various torments and punishments; but bodies distinguished by free birth they subjected most harshly to the barbarian yoke. They also stained the very holy churches of God with their impieties, and some of them they turned into stables. We saw venerable men who, after their tongues had been torn out by the roots, spoke of their sufferings miserably [I would prefer to read “miraculously”]. Others, after various torments, scattered throughout various provinces, spent their lives in exile. By what speech, then, or by what deeds can we offer thanks worthy of God?’ etc.

“In this constitution the emperor wishes Africa, restored to its former condition, to enjoy the same privileges that it had previously possessed. Besides the praetorian prefect, whom he ordered to reside at Carthage, he also appointed other officials who were to have their own residences in the larger cities throughout the various regions of Africa, and he assigned stipends individually to all of them. He divided the African diocese into seven provinces: Tingitana, the province formerly called Proconsularis, Carthage, Byzacena, Tripolitania, Numidia, Mauretania, and Sardinia. He wished the first four to be administered by consular governors and the last three by presidents. In the following constitution he treats of military offices and judges, assigning the places in which the commanders of the soldiers appointed throughout the various provinces of Africa were to have their residences.”

“7. Nor was the emperor satisfied with these measures. In order to restore Africa to its former splendor, he built new cities, renewed old ones, fortified others with walls, and finally both adorned and protected the entire region with magnificent buildings and necessary monuments against the barbarians, as Procopius relates at greater length in book VI of his Buildings, from chapter 3 to the end.

“Among these works he lists Vada, a city newly built in Byzacena, and Tucca in the Proconsular province. He surrounded Leptis Magna, the metropolis of Tripolitania, which had almost fallen into ruin, with walls; there he restored the old palace, once built by Augustus Severus, who had been born there, but which had almost completely collapsed. He ordered Carthage to be called Justiniana, and he gave the same name to Hadrumetum, the metropolis of Byzacena, formerly called, as Pliny notes, Black Sissa. That city had been so neglected by the barbarians that it scarcely retained a shadow of its ancient splendor.

“Bagum, in the Proconsular province, previously scarcely known, he made into a true city, says Procopius. Its citizens, so as not to seem ungrateful, called it Theodorias in honor of Theodora, Justinian’s wife. The baths of Theodoriana, worthy of inspection, were also named from that same empress, says the same author. For other public buildings constructed by the same emperor in other parts of Africa, see the cited author.”

Num. 85, line 1.—“The kingdom came with precious gems from Clovis, king of the Franks,” etc. With divine grace working through Saint Clotilda, his Christian wife, Clovis was converted to the faith. As may be gathered from Gregory of Tours, Aimoinus, and other Frankish historians, he imitated Constantine, who offered golden crowns among other gifts, both in the Basilica of the Savior, in the Vatican Basilica, and in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way.

In the Constantinian Basilica, or Basilica of the Savior, no. 36, line 12: “He offered four crowns with twenty dolphins, each weighing fifteen pounds of the purest gold.” In the Vatican, no. 38, line 21: “A golden crown before the body [of blessed Peter], where there is the Pharmecantharus, with fifty dolphins weighing thirty-five pounds.” And in the Basilica of Saint Paul, no. 40, line 5: “He arranged all the sacred vessels of gold and silver or bronze just as in the Basilica of the Apostle Saint Peter; so too he arranged them in the Basilica of the blessed Apostle Paul.”

Both princes should be considered to have had in mind the vision of the elders in the Apocalypse, who professed the divinity of our Redeemer by offering their crowns before his throne. Pliny also testifies that, long before this, among the ancients crowns had been offered to God alone, in book XVI, chapter 4; hence the custom arose of crowning priests, altars, and victims. By this rite people acknowledged that they were offering divine worship to the one whom they regarded as God.

Thus, just as the emperor Augustus Constantine dedicated crowns to Christ our God before the principal altars of the basilicas, so did Clovis. In this way he expiated the insignia of his kingdom from the superstition of his predecessors. His pagan ancestors had attributed them to false gods; he, having acknowledged the true God, subjected them solely to his protection and to government under the supreme power.

All the princes of Clovis’s lineage before him had been devoted to the errors of pagan superstition. This is attested not only by all the historians but also by the golden treasures and gems found in the tomb of his father, which Chiffletius illustrated in a learned commentary in his Anastasis of King Childeric. There, in chapter 10, he displays a representation of Apis, or the Sun, fashioned from gold and gems and derived from Egyptian superstition to the pagan Franks of that period; in chapter 15 he discusses the superstition of the buried horse.

The sons of Clovis, however, made a very different use of gold and gems from their father’s superstition, providing an example of our most holy religion for their august posterity. For just as he, fourteen centuries ago, dedicated the first fruits of kings to Christ in the crown offered at the altar of Christ’s first vicar, so the continued rights of blood and ancestral piety among Clovis’s successors display before the altar of Our Lady of Loreto two golden crowns of the greatest value, which Louis XIII sent in 1639 with this inscription of dedication:

> Christ gave me scepters; to Christ I return the crown.

On this matter, see the historical commentary, rich in learning, on crowns, published in 1712 by Martin Schemeizel, chapter 6, article 30, page 69.

Line 9.—“From a cloak, or from an imperial robe, a *suffitorium* [substratorium] over the confession of the blessed apostle Peter.” An extremely ancient copy of the Librarian preserved in the Laurentian Library has: “From a cloak, or from an imperial robe, a *subsistorium* over the confession of the blessed apostle Peter. All these things were offered by Justinian Augustus the orthodox as votive offerings.”

Observing from other manuscripts that the wording varies, Cangius, in his Lexicon of Medieval Latin, correctly concludes that it should be rendered *substratorium*. “For,” he says, “a *substratorium* is the altar cloth upon which the corporal is spread,” as he proves by the testimony of the Roman Ordo.

The concern of the most pious princes of this age was therefore to place and dedicate their royal insignia to Christ the Lord, the King of kings, who was raising a throne for himself upon their altars. Thus, just as King Clovis offered a crown hanging before the altar, so Emperor Justinian offered the robe of imperial dignity as an altar *substratorium*. From this derive the precious textiles which, extending down over the front of the altars according to a usage that has reached our own age, we also call *pallia* and *pallae*, or, in Italian, *paliotti*.

From the imperial and royal cloak, offered in ancient times for the use of the royal priesthood of Christ, some portions passed into the vestments of ministers and others into the ornamentation of the altar itself, as we shall show more fully below in the discussion of priestly vestments.

From the age of Clovis and Justinian this custom has been faithfully preserved, especially in Gaul, so that the modern royal cloak used at the coronation of the Most Christian Kings at Rheims is subsequently offered at the Church of Saint-Denis to be preserved among the sacred treasures; from it priestly *pallia*, or copes—we commonly call them *pluvialia*—are made for use on solemn feasts.

In the same way, Greek and Eastern prelates, displaying their *sticharia* and precious *pallia* made from their imperial robe as a token of the royal priesthood of Christ, spread these same garments over the altar table, as *substratoria* for the Lord who would descend upon it. Their pious meaning is no different from that of the children of Jerusalem, who spread garments beneath him on the road during the triumphal entry by which the only-begotten Son of God proceeded to accomplish the redemption of the human race.]

[Note: [Col. 0502C]

Num. 82, line 1.—“A Campanian by nation.” By origin, from Venafrum.]

[Note: [Col. 0502D]

Num. 82, line 8.—“He also sent Ennodius,” etc. A portion of the Eastern Catholics, unable to endure the tyrannical persecution by which they were oppressed under Anastasius, incited Vitalian, master of the cavalry, to rebellion. Having gained control of several places and advanced as far as the gates of the imperial city, he compelled the emperor to request peace from him. Among the conditions were these: first, that a general council should be summoned under the authority of the Roman pontiff, at which the just petitions of the Catholics would be satisfied. Both parties—that is, Vitalian as well as the emperor—sent letters to Hormisdas, who had succeeded Symmachus.

The emperor’s letter contained the following:

“‘We have judged it opportune to entrust to your hearing the disturbances that are being stirred up among us under the appearance of religion. Previously, indeed, the harshness of those to whom the administration of the episcopate that you now hold had been entrusted prevented us from sending letters. But now the favorable opinion of you that is spreading has brought to our memory the goodness of paternal affection, so that we may seek those things which our God and Savior taught the holy apostles by divine speech, and especially blessed Peter, in whom he established the strength of his Church.

“‘With these introductory remarks, therefore, we urge you to act as mediator in the matters that have arisen from the regions of Scythia, concerning which we have recognized that a council should also be convened, so that, once the disputes have been cut away, the unity of the holy Church may be restored.’”

(Anastasius the emperor’s first letter to Pope Hormisdas. See also his fifth letter to the same.)

Hormisdas replied in this sense: He gave thanks to God that he saw the emperor in a disposition from which hope could be entertained for peace in the Church—a work certainly of the heavenly mercy of God, which his predecessors had always sought with prayers poured out to the Lord. Their conduct also showed them to have been ministers of the paternal tradition and guardians of the right faith.

[Col. 0503B] Since such peace is the origin, mother, and guardian of all good things, and since nothing is more effective than it for preserving the norm of the true faith, anyone counted as a Christian by profession ought to do everything and endure everything so that it may be kept intact.

He then sent to that same ruler two bishops, one presbyter, and one deacon to Constantinople, together with a memorandum of the matters they were to handle and instructions for conducting themselves publicly and privately both with the bishops and with the emperor. These instructions dealt especially with the recall of bishops expelled into exile for the sake of religion; their judgment was to be reserved to the Apostolic See, as was also the judgment of other prelates accused of having persecuted Catholics, and the restoration of those orthodox men who, although they had never been separated from communion with the same Holy See, had been forcibly expelled from their own sees.

There was also included a formula of profession, to be presented as a preliminary, both by the emperor and by the Eastern bishops, concerning acceptance of the holy Council of Chalcedon, the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo, and approval of the anathema pronounced against Nestorius and Eutyches, as well as against their sectarians and adherents Acacius and Peter of Antioch and those associated with them.

*Memorandum of the Legates of Hormisdas to Anastasius Augustus.*

In the letter to Anastasius to be delivered by the legates, Saint Hormisdas states:

“‘No subject for triumph can be more pleasing to you, most exalted Lord, than the subjugation of impiety, provided that the definition of our ancestors and the teaching of the holy Fathers remain unshaken in their foundations.’”

(Epistle 3 of Saint Hormisdas.)

“‘The emperor’s unstable faith mocked all the care of the blessed pontiff. The people and senate [of Constantinople] assailed Anastasius with every kind of insult, calling him, as Theophanes says in his Chronicle, a perjurer. To them that wicked man responded with extraordinary shamelessness that there was a law requiring an emperor placed in necessity to commit perjury and lie.’

“To break off all communication with Hormisdas, he sent him a brief letter, muttering in confused language about the mercy of God. In it he declared that henceforth he would cease to seek anything from Hormisdas, whom he knew to be hardened in his obstinacy of refusal:

“‘From the present time we suppress our request in silence, judging it unreasonable to show the kindness of entreaty to those who stubbornly refuse to be entreated. For we can endure being insulted and nullified; we cannot be commanded.’”

(Anastasius the emperor’s letter after the twenty-second letter of Hormisdas.)

That Anastasius was entirely untouched by any sense of religion was demonstrated even more clearly by the letter of the monks of the Second Syria to Hormisdas. In it they indicate the killings, plunderings, and burnings inflicted upon the Churches and upon themselves, and complain that these sacrileges and crimes had been perpetrated by the emperor himself through his agents. It is worthwhile to reproduce the words of the letter.]

> “To the most holy and blessed patriarch of the whole world, Hormisdas, occupying the see of the chief of the apostles Peter: the entreaty and supplication of the least of the archimandrites and of the other monks of your province of Second Syria. Since Christ our God truly appointed you and your holy angel as chief of shepherds, teachers, and physicians of souls, it is fitting to set forth the sufferings that have befallen us and to expose the merciless wolves who are destroying Christ’s flock, so that by the staff of your authority he may drive them from among the sheep; and by the word of doctrine heal the soul and soothe it with the medicines of prayer . . . John and Sergius, whom we had sent to Constantinople, thinking that vengeance would be taken for the things that had been committed. But he did not deign even to address them; rather, he expelled them with great insult and threatened those who presented these matters. Hence we have at last, though late, come to recognize that the whole perversity and boldness of such evil deeds committed against the Churches was contrived at his instigation.”  
> *(Report of the archimandrites, etc., following [Col. 0504B] Hormisdas’s Letter 22.)*

> “We therefore implore you, most blessed father, entreating and begging you to rise up with fervor and zeal and to grieve justly over the lacerated body, for you are the head of all; and to avenge the despised faith, the trampled canons, the blasphemed Fathers, and such a synod assailed with anathema. God has given you the power and authority to bind and loose . . . To you, true shepherds and teachers, to whom care for the salvation of the sheep has been entrusted, the flock itself comes, recognizing its shepherd after being freed from the most savage beasts and following the shepherd’s voice, as the Lord says: ‘My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me’ (John 10:27). Moreover, for the perfect knowledge of your holy angel, in this same supplication of ours, which possesses the force of a libellus, we anathematize all the libelli cast out and excommunicated by your apostolic see.”  
> *(Ibid.)*

To this Pope Hormisdas replied, exhorting them to patience. Then he added:

> “Those who are worldly cannot hold Churches, because it is more appropriate for them to learn than to teach. For it is impious to introduce foreign offerings to holy altars, since our God prescribed fixed boundaries for religious discipline at the very beginnings of his worship: he divided the duties between the Levites and his people. One is the power of men, another the ministry of priests. He provoked the Lord rather than appeased him who, as a profaner of sacred rites, introduced strange fire into the divine sanctuaries. For who could presume to assume authority to command in institutions belonging to another, when it is beyond doubt that the honor due to the one making the offering is punished solely for the presumption of office? Uzziah would have remained in royal office with reverence and proper administration if, warned by that example of such severity and by the ordinances of religion, he had attempted better things by permitting rather than assuming them. But while the obstinate profaner stood firm despite the temple worshipers’ warnings, he was struck amid the altars by the horror of leprosy and lost both the offices and authority of the kingdom while invading the priest’s ministry.”  
> [Col. 0504D] *(Pope Hormisdas, Letter 33.)*

> “Let them know, therefore, that what presumptuous men take upon themselves from his commands is not accepted by God, since he preserved one as a display of the divine judgment through the punishment of living disgrace, while swift fire consumed others . . . Indeed, we did not fail in our care. For in the duty of two embassies we conveyed whatever was humble in our petitions, reasonable in our argument, and salutary in our instructions. But surely we must not for that reason abandon the path of justice, with which [the emperor] Anastasius, in the obstinacy of his faithlessness, is enamored. We must not be joined to the downfall of those who are falling; without our contamination, let those perish who do not withdraw from their impieties even after their error has been corrected.”  
> *(Ibid.)*

Around this time Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, wrote to Hormisdas that rumors were circulating about the reconciliation of the Easterners with the apostolic see. Therefore, both in his own name and in that of his fellow bishops, [Col. 0505A] he urgently requested that Hormisdas deign to write back and say what ought to be done. For neither he nor the bishops of Gaul would then hold an opinion differing from that of the Roman see.

> “Whether the fervor of the aforementioned schisms has been extinguished by a correction worthy of you, speaking—as you do—with Christ’s favor . . . we have learned from various reports that Greece boasts of the reconciliation or concord of the Roman Church. Just as this is to be embraced if it is truthfully reported, so it is to be feared lest it be craftily feigned. We therefore all beg your service: instruct me what I should answer to your sons and my brothers, that is, the Gauls, if I am consulted; for, confident—let me not say in the devotion of Vienne, but in that of Gaul—I promise that all will seek an authoritative judgment concerning the state of your faith. Pray that, just as the feigned profession of the lost does not deceive us, so recognized truth may not separate us from the unity over which you preside.”  
> *(Letter of Avitus of Vienne, following Hormisdas’s Letter 9.)*

Hormisdas replied:

> “They display before the Greeks, more with their mouths than in their hearts, their vows of peace; they speak more justly than they act. In words they boast that they desire what their deeds show that they do not desire.”  
> *(Pope Hormisdas, Letter 10 to Avitus of Vienne.)*

**No. 84, line 1.**—“Then Bishop Hormisdas, etc.” and line 16: “He restored them to the unity of the apostolic see, condemning Peter and Acacius, or all heresies.” From Book VI, chapter 19, of Archbishop Sommier.

After Anastasius’s death, Justin, his successor in the empire, sent the letters announcing his election to Pope Hormisdas, beginning with these words: “Although the benefits of God ought to be reported to many, they are especially appropriate to the highest pontiffs.” Hormisdas replied:

> “The Catholic Church, most glorious son, sends the venerable first fruits of your reign to the place of a gift, together with its congratulations; through them it trusts that, after so great a weariness of discord, it will find the rest of peace. You have returned the due first fruits of your empire to Blessed Peter the Apostle. We have therefore received them with devotion, because through you we confidently believe that the Churches will soon attain concord.”  
> *(Hormisdas, Letter 28.)*

Thereupon Justin, through the count Gratus, whom he sent to Hormisdas, requested that Hormisdas send suitable ministers to Constantinople to restore the unity of the Churches. Justin sent letters to this effect, as did the bishop of Constantinople, who made the same request. In these letters the latter inserted a profession of faith and acceptance of the four ecumenical councils. Justinian also, the count and nephew of the emperor, wrote the same things and indicated that everything was working toward peace, and that no dispute now remained except concerning the memory of Acacius, regarding which a special instruction from Hormisdas was expected.

The Roman pontiff, after expressing his joy at the arrangements reported as tending toward peace, replied:

> “To receive the Council of Chalcedon, to follow the letters of Saint Leo, and still to defend the name of Acacius—this is to vindicate mutually contradictory things.”  
> [Col. 0505D] *(Hormisdas’s Letter 29.)*

In Letter 24 he says:

> “We exhort you, brother, to separate yourself from every contagion of the heretics by condemning Acacius and his followers, and to be nourished with us by communion in the Lord’s body. If you preach all things together with us, why do you not condemn all things together with us?”

He expresses similar sentiments in Letters 21 and 22, where he also adds:

> “Why is there any need to speak of matters already judged, when all that should properly concern us is to exhort them, after removing the simulation expressed above, to desire peace with complete purity, since they are the ones making these statements?”

The pontiff sent these letters to Justin with an imposing embassy. He indicated his congratulations on Justin’s reign,

> “because almighty God has raised him up for this purpose, according to his sacred writings: so that, in accordance with what has been established by the prelates of the apostolic see, with God as author and his reign lending its support, the peace and unity of the Churches desired in these times might come about.”

[Col. 0506A] He gave the legates the text of a libellus under which they were to receive the bishop of Constantinople and the others approaching Catholic unity under that profession. Through encyclical letters they themselves were to exhort these men to concord.

Blessed Hormisdas attained, by God’s generosity, the joy he had hoped for, when he saw peace restored in nearly all the Churches according to his wishes. The first bishops encountered by the legates on their journey—the bishops of Aulon, Scampia, and Lychnidus—signed the formula presented in the form accepted and subscribed by the bishop of Constantinople:

> “I accept that the most holy Churches of God—that is, that of your elder Rome and that of this new Rome—are one; I define that the see of the Apostle Peter and that of this august city are one. I assent to everything enacted by these four holy synods, namely, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, concerning the confirmation of the faith and the state of the Church, and I do not permit myself to waver concerning what has been rightly judged. I also know that those who strive and exert themselves to disturb even a single point of what has been decreed have fallen away from the holy, universal, and apostolic Church of God. Using your rightly spoken words with complete clarity, I say in this present writing that the first salvation is to preserve the rule of faith and in no way to deviate from the tradition of the Fathers; for the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be set aside: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.’ The truth of these words is proved by the effects of events, because religion has always been preserved inviolate in the apostolic see.”  
> *(Libellus of John, bishop of Constantinople, following Hormisdas’s Letter 40.)*

> “Therefore, desiring not to fall from this faith and following in all things the ordinances of the Fathers, we anathematize all heresies, especially the heretic Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, and the rest. Likewise, we anathematize Acacius, their accomplice and follower, as well as those who persist in their communion . . . We approve and embrace all the letters of Blessed Leo, pope of the city of Rome, which he wrote concerning the true faith. Therefore, as we have said above, following the apostolic see in all things, we preach everything decreed by it. For this reason I hope that I shall be with you in the one communion which the apostolic see proclaims, in which there is the integrity of Christian religion and perfect solidity. We promise that in the future the names of those separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not agree in all things with the apostolic see—are not to be recited during the sacred mysteries. But if I should attempt to doubt in any respect my profession, I declare that I am the associate of those whom I have condemned, and that through my condemnation I am their accomplice. I have subscribed this profession with my own hand and sent it in writing to you, holy and most blessed Hormisdas,” etc.  
> *(Ibid.)*

Together with this profession the Roman pontiff received congratulatory letters from the bishop of Constantinople, from Justin Augustus and his wife, [Col. 0506D] from the count Justinian, and from the leading men of the court, concerning the unity of the Churches and the extinction of the schism that had been rooted among the Easterners for thirty-five years. Hormisdas returned praise for these services and urged perseverance upon those who had joined in or labored to secure this union. He urged the emperor not to cease working, through their united efforts, to recall the Alexandrians and others as well.

His exhortation was not fruitless. At length many joined that unity, whom the pontiff enumerates in Letter 51, writing:

> “We have sent a libellus under which, if any of the Eastern clergy should seek your communion, he may be admitted to it. It is according to this same rule that it is now established that many have been received from Thrace, Scythia, and Illyricum, as well as from Old Epirus; and likewise many from Syria are already known to have been received, rejoicing to converge upon what is right and to have turned away from what is deviant.”  
> *(Hormisdas, Letter 51 to all the bishops of Spain.)*

Some monks from Scythia almost disturbed this peace, intending to introduce another schism through a novelty which they obstinately promoted: that one of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh. When they had first presented an examination of this thesis to the legates of the apostolic see at Constantinople and had been deprived of the hope of approval, they sent to Rome to seek from the pontiff himself authorization for their formulation. Hormisdas, warned by the legates, prudently postponed the matter until their arrival and judged that no further step should be taken. He had learned that the monks’ delegates, wearied by waiting, had departed from the city; moreover, he had discovered that, if discussion were opened concerning such a useless formulation, division and scandal rather than the edification of the Church would be expected. *(See the letters of Justin Augustus and others following Hormisdas’s Letters 65, 67, and 71; also Hormisdas’s Letter 70.)*

This last matter reveals the praiseworthy prudence of so great a pontiff in avoiding such entanglements and removing them from the minds of the faithful, so that they might devote themselves to more substantial pursuits and follow the teachings of the Fathers and established judgments. Concerning the books of Faustus submitted to him, he replied:

> “Let those whom you have indicated in your letter to have consulted us concerning the statements of a certain Gallic bishop named Faustus have this answer: neither is that accepted, nor can any person whom the examination of Catholic faith or the discipline of the Church does not receive among the authorities of the Fathers generate ambiguity or establish a prejudice against religion. The institutions which the Fathers fixed for the faithful to follow remain firm . . . Why, then, was there any need for accusers to extend questions beyond the established limits of the Church and to stir up disputes concerning statements that are accepted as statements, as though they had not been spoken? Christian faith is bounded by a stable and unshaken limit in the canonical books, synodal precepts, and the regular decrees of the Fathers.”  
> *(Hormisdas, Letter 70 to Possessor.)*

**No. 85, line 1.**—“From Clovis, Christian king of the Franks.” It is known that Blessed Hormisdas followed the same firmness of ancient discipline that he proposes should be sought in the writings of the Fathers, also in his administration of the Churches. He entrusted apostolic authority throughout Clovis’s entire kingdom to Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, through whom King Clovis had approached the Christian faith, while preserving the rights of the metropolitans that they had held from ancient times. He also ordered Remigius to observe the paternal rules and decrees defined by all the holy councils. *(Hormisdas, Letter 1 to Remigius.)*

With comparable commendation he appointed John of Tarragona as apostolic vicar in Nearer Spain, and Sallustius of Seville in Baetica and Lusitania. *(Letter 24 to John of Tarragona.)*

In the East as well, he conferred upon Epiphanius of Constantinople the vicariate authority of the Roman see, so that he might receive and associate with the unity of the Church those who, through a conversion not feigned but genuine, came from the errors of heretics and the company of schismatics into the Catholic assembly. He had clearly observed Epiphanius’s diligence and prudence through many documents. *(Hormisdas, Letter 80 to Epiphanius of Constantinople.)]

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

**No. 83, line 10.**—“Anastasius Augustus, filled with fury against Pope Hormisdas, wrote among other sacred documents: ‘Imperial letters are called sacra.’” Anastasius himself, in his Life of Constantine, writes: “At the same time the aforementioned emperor sent a sacra to Pope Constantine, by which he ordered him to ascend to the imperial city.” And below: “The emperor Justinian, hearing of his arrival, was filled with great joy and sent a sacra from Nicaea in Bithynia, full of thanksgiving.” And further: “Constantine received his sacra, containing a written statement of the perverse doctrine.” Again in the same work: “After some time Scholasticus, the chamberlain, patrician, and exarch of Italy, came to Rome and brought with him the sacra of the emperor Anastasius.” The same author, in his Life of John IV: “Through them he sent a sacra, by which he summoned the aforementioned pontiff.” Augustine, *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 31: “They carry the sacra of many emperors; we carry only the Gospels.” Pelagius, *Letter to Laurentius*, Letter of Centumcellae: “They suggest that they have obtained a sacra from the most merciful emperor.” Canon *Principali*, Distinction 83.

**No. 84, line 4.**—“The text of the libellus of penance.” That is, the formula of the profession of faith and renunciation of heresy which was to be made by Peter, bishop of Alexandria, and Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. Above he simply said, “the text of the libellus.” *Textus* means a book or codex. Gregory, Book VII, Letter 49: “In the text of the Heptateuch.” The same author, Book XII, Letter 30, says at the end, “the codex of the Heptateuch.” Leo of Ostia called it “the text of the Life of the monk Guinizus of Cassino” in Book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 47.

**No. 84, line 6.**—“In which the emperor Justin and the consul Vitalianus also met them with splendor and praise.” The emperor Justin and the consul Vitalianus met the legates of the apostolic see with splendor and praise—that is, with crosses, candles, and hymns of praise. The citizens of Constantinople met Pope John with the same pomp. Anastasius, in his Life of John, writes: “When they had proceeded with Pope John, the whole city met Blessed John at the twelfth milestone with candles and crosses, in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.” Agapitus was received at Constantinople with splendor. Anastasius, in his Life: “And Agapitus was received with splendor.” The people of Constantinople met Vigilius together with Justinian with hymns. Anastasius, in his Life of Vigilius: “That people sang before him all the way to the Church of Holy Sophia: ‘Behold, the Dominator, the Lord, has arrived,’” and so forth.

When Henry III, king of the English, came to Paris, the Parisian scholars proceeded to meet him solemnly and with pomp, carrying candles and wearing festive garments, which they call *comitissae*. Matthew Paris, under the year 1254: “They bought candles, festive garments, which they call *comitissae*, and everything that could testify to their joy.”

**Line 17.**—“Here he found Manichaeans, whom, after examining them by means of scourging, he also deported into exile.” The Manichaeans were beaten with whips and expelled from the City. Augustine reports that the Baetican heretic was condemned and flogged in his commentary on Psalm 122: “For who could doubt that, most recently, as we heard from the brothers who were present with our fellow bishops, that Baetican barking against the Lord was deservedly flogged?”

**No. 85, line 1.**—“At the same time a crown with precious gems came from Clovis, Christian king of the Franks.” Clovis received from the emperor Anastasius the documents of the consulship, together with a golden crown, which he himself offered to Blessed Peter and which was called a *regnum*, perhaps because it had been offered by a king. Sigebert, under the year 510:

> “King Clovis received from the emperor Anastasius the documents of the consulship, a golden crown with gems, and a purple tunic; from that day he was called consul and Augustus. The king himself sent to Rome, to Saint Peter, a golden crown with gems, which is customarily called a *regnum*.”

From that time every golden crown began to be called a *regnum* at Rome. Anastasius, in his Life of Constantine: “On the day when they saw one another, the most Christian Augustus prostrated himself with the *regnum* on his head and kissed the pontiff’s feet.” The same author, in his Life of Leo III: “That most blessed pontiff made a *regnum* of the purest gold in the basilica of Blessed Andrew; likewise, above the altar of Blessed Petronilla, he made a golden *regnum* with the most precious gems.” Further: “In the title of Holy Mary, Mother of God, which is called that of Callixtus, he made a *regnum* of the purest gold.” Further: “A *regnum spanoclystum* of the purest gold.” The same author, in his Life of Gregory IV: “One golden *regnum*, which to this day hangs above the altar.” In his Life of Sergius II: “A very precious golden *regnum* with green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems.” Further in the same work: “A silver *regnum* with little bells.” In his Life of Leo IV: “He offered a *regnum* of the purest silver, with the most precious gems, having a cross in the middle.” Further in the same work: “A *regnum* hanging above the high altar, made of the purest gold, sculpted, and without gems.”

**Line 3.**—“And the Gospels with golden covers and precious gems.” It was customary for a Gospel codex to be placed in a golden chest adorned with gems. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 63:

> “Then he ordered a chest to be made for enclosing the holy Gospels, and a paten and chalice of pure gold and precious stones.”

Anastasius, in his Life of Leo IV: “And also a Gospel with silver covers.” Leo of Ostia, Book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 30: “A Gospel with a cast silver cover in repoussé work.”

**Line 8.**—“Purple *pallia olovera*, with gold-covered panels, made from a *chlamys* or an imperial *stola*.” Purple *pallia olovera* are silk garments dyed with pure or true shellfish dye or *murex*, that is, purple. Anastasius, in his Life of Felix II: “Four *pallia olovera* woven with gold.” Private persons were forbidden to possess these, according to the final law of the Theodosian Code, concerning *vestes oloverae*. *Blattea* derives from the Latin *blatta*, which is a kind of worm that, when caught, stains the hands red. Thus Vopiscus, in his Life of Aurelian, called it a *pallium blatteum* and a *blattea tunica*: “When his wife asked him to wear a single purple silk cloak.” Shortly afterward: “He likewise permitted matrons to have purple tunics.” Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book II, chapter 38: “Accordingly, he received from the emperor Anastasius the documents of the consulship and, dressed in a purple tunic, entered the basilica of Blessed Martin.”

**No. 86, line 8.**—“Six silver station chalices with crosses, each weighing six pounds.” Station chalices were those carried before the stations by acolytes, as were the calices. Anastasius, in his Life of Leo III:

> “That same bishop made for Blessed Peter the Apostle a golden chalice adorned with various precious stones, which precedes the stations and weighs thirteen pounds.”

And further in the same work:

> “He made communion vessels of the purest silver for each district, to precede the stations in the hands of twenty-four acolytes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0509C]

**No. 83, line 12.**—“At that time, struck by a divine blow through the nod of the Deity, the emperor Anastasius was struck by divine lightning and died. Orthodox Justin assumed the empire, etc.” After the death of the emperor Anastasius on the ninth day of April in the year 518, Justin, the great defender of the Council of Chalcedon, was appointed in his place. On the Kalends of August he informed Hormisdas that he had been elected emperor; then, by another letter dated at Constantinople on the seventh day before the Ides of September, he asked Hormisdas, through the count Gratus, to send legates to Constantinople to reconcile the Eastern Church to peace and to receive those who had fallen.

John, bishop of Constantinople, sent through the same Gratus to Hormisdas a profession of faith in which he testified that he accepted the Council of Chalcedon. After the names of Saint Leo and Hormisdas himself had been restored to the sacred diptychs, he opened the way to unity. In his reply, Letter 29 to John, Hormisdas promised that he would admit him to communion with the Church if he erased the name of Acacius from the sacred diptychs:

> “These things are praiseworthy if the result of perfection follows, because to receive the Council of Chalcedon, to follow the letters of Saint Leo, and still to defend the name of Acacius is to vindicate mutually contradictory things.”

In the year 519, therefore, Hormisdas, having no doubt that the emperor Justin and John the Cappadocian, bishop of Constantinople—who had celebrated a synod at Constantinople in the preceding year, in which, after the excommunication of the Eutychians and their defenders, the Council of Chalcedon was received together with the letter of Saint Leo, whose name was restored to the sacred diptychs—were sincerely pursuing peace, sent to Constantinople the bishops Germanus and John, the presbyter Blandus, and the deacons Felix and Dioscorus as legates. He gave them a memorandum of matters to be handled and letters to be delivered to the emperor Justin; to Euphemia Augusta, his wife; to John, bishop of Constantinople; to the archdeacon and clergy of Constantinople; to Justinian, count of the domestics, later Justin’s colleague and successor in the empire; to certain patricians; to the praetorian prefect of Thessalonica; and to certain highly distinguished senatorial women. All these letters are preserved in Volume IV of the Councils, pages 1476–1484.

He also issued a libellus of faith and gave it to the legates. The bishop of Constantinople and the other prelates were to subscribe it before they were received into communion with the apostolic see. In that libellus, Acacius was anathematized, but not Euphemius and Macedonius, bishops of the same see and predecessors of John. Hormisdas judged that their condemnation should not be demanded from the bishops; it was enough that their names be erased from the sacred diptychs. This is clear from the memorandum given to the legates, reproduced in the same volume on page [Col. 0510B] 1476.

When the legates reached Constantinople, John, bishop of Constantinople, subscribed the libellus of faith presented to him by them. He pronounced anathema against Acacius and erased from the Church’s records the names of those bishops who had persisted in Acacius’s communion—namely, Euphemius and Macedonius—as well as the names of the emperors Anastasius and Zeno. On these conditions peace was established and communion was restored between the Church of Constantinople and the Roman Church in the same year, 519.

These facts are established by John of Constantinople’s libellus to Hormisdas, preserved in the same volume of the Councils on page 1486. Accordingly, in Letter 45 to John, Hormisdas praises him for returning to the unity of the Church and urges him to secure the union of the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch. In Letter 44 to Justin he congratulates him that, through his efforts, peace prevailed at Constantinople, and he likewise urges him to ensure that the same be done at Antioch and Alexandria. “The legates of Pope Hormisdas,” says Theophanes in his *Chronicle*, “ratified this peace, relying on the power of Vitalianus, who was still alive, and on the diligence of John the Cappadocian, bishop of Constantinople, who likewise still survived.”

Although the names of Euphemius and Macedonius were erased from the sacred diptychs, those bishops were not thereby separated from Catholic communion. This is clear from the aforementioned memorandum given by Hormisdas to the legates. In section 5 Hormisdas says:

> “If the bishop of Constantinople, agreeing concerning the anathema of Acacius, should say that his successors are to be recited because some of them were deported into exile on account of the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, you will explain that you can remove nothing from the form of the libellus given to you, in which the followers of the condemned are likewise included. But if you cannot turn them away from this intention, at least agree to this: after Acacius has been specifically anathematized in the libellus we gave you, let there be silence concerning the names of his predecessors, their names having been erased from the inscription of the diptychs. Once this has been done, receive the bishop of Constantinople into your communion.”

Hormisdas therefore did not judge that Euphemius and Macedonius should be anathematized. Indeed, when in 520 the emperor Justin requested, in a letter preserved in Volume IV of the Councils on page 1527, that after the name of Acacius and the authors of the error had been condemned, the names of the others should remain in the diptychs, Hormisdas, replying to him in Letter 78, remained steadfast in his former judgment and refused the request. Nevertheless, lest it appear that force was being brought against the Churches of Constantinople, Pontus, Asia, Palestine, and especially the entire Eastern diocese or patriarchate of Antioch, he entrusted the whole matter in 521 to the prudence of Epiphanius, then bishop of Constantinople. For that reason he delegated to him the vicariate of the apostolic see by Letter 80, dated on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, during the consulship of Valerius Vir Clarissimus.

The Eastern bishops were therefore eventually admitted into communion with the apostolic see, although they had not condemned Euphemius and Macedonius and had not permitted their names to be erased from the diptychs. Certainly, that the name of Macedonius remained in the diptychs in which it had been inscribed, and that it was restored when it had been removed, is indicated by the sacred worship offered to him by the Greeks and confirmed by their *Menaea*.

**No. 84, line 4.**—“When they came near Constantinople, etc.” In the year 519, while the legates of Pope Hormisdas were staying at Constantinople, the Scythian monks, among whom John, surnamed Maxentius, was prominent, insistently promoted—even to the point of sedition—the proposition that “one of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh,” which everyone was to believe and defend.

The deacon Victor and many others vigorously resisted them, being offended that they were proposing a new thesis to the people, as though the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon were insufficient. Since Faustus’s books were defended by some not only in the West but also in the East, while others fiercely refuted them, the same monks condemned them as heretical, whereas many at Byzantium asserted that they were Catholic. Hence disputes grew without limit and divided even eminent men into opposing camps.

Vitalianus, who held the consulship in 520, favored the monks. Justinian, however, nephew of the emperor Justin, opposed them in this question. When the Scythian monks saw that their opponents were contemptuously representing them as Eutychians, they presented a libellus of faith to Hormisdas’s legates, in which they explained their faith concerning Christ at length. Everything they said nevertheless converged upon the aim that the legates should receive the thesis inserted there: “One of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh.” They then explained what they thought concerning divine grace against the Pelagians and Caelestians. At the end they concluded against Faustus’s position:

> “We also abominate those who dare to say, against the Apostle’s words, ‘Our willing is ours, but the accomplishing is God’s,’ since the same teacher testifies that both willing and accomplishing are a divine gift.”

[Col. 0511C] The legates said that they had received no instructions from the pontiff concerning these matters; indeed, they had been expressly commanded not to involve themselves in other cases. But, compelled by the intervention of the emperor Justin, they finally gave ear to the monks. After hearing them repeatedly, together with the deacon Victor, the leading man of the opposing faction, they eventually gave this response in order to free themselves from the men’s persistent demands:

> “What was not written by Pope Leo we do not accept.”

They judged that inculcating new theses concerning Christ upon the people beyond the Council of Chalcedon, and adding this article—“One of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh”—to the council as an appendix, as the legates suspected, came close to rashness and insolence. Nothing, however, was debated before the legates concerning grace and free will or concerning Faustus’s books.

Enraged by this rejection, the monks decided to send an embassy to Hormisdas at Rome. Four monks were chosen to undertake it. But as soon as it became known that they had set out for Rome, Justinian and the legates sent letters to Hormisdas [Col. 0511D] informing him of what had been done with the monks in that dispute and urging the pontiff to drive the monks from the City, far from his sight. The letter of the legates, dated on the third day before the Kalends of July in the year 519, and Justinian’s letter, are read in Volume IV of the Councils, page 1516.

Hormisdas suspended his judgment for some time. But when he had decided to send the monks to Byzantium and had delegated the case to John, patriarch of Constantinople, this greatly displeased the apostolic legates. They did not want the case transferred to John’s tribunal, whom they suspected of having been won over to the monks by Vitalianus.

Later Hormisdas learned that not only Vitalianus but also Justinian, having changed his position, were supporting the monks, and that Justinian was acting on their behalf as a vigorous intercessor, although he had previously been their accuser. On the other hand, he received a letter from Dioscorus, one of the pontifical legates, accusing John—perhaps because he had been bought over—of betraying the faith of the monks. He therefore ordered the entire case to remain pending until the legates’ return.

When this became known to the monks’ representatives who were in Rome, they, impatient with a longer stay in the City, attempted secretly to withdraw from Rome. Hormisdas, however, prevented them, as is clear from his Letter 63 to the legates, dated on the third day before the Nones of December. These events occurred in the year 519.

Moreover, when the legates had written to Pope Hormisdas that the monks expressed the thesis in this form—“One of the Trinity was crucified”—and that they had therefore been suspected, as though they were preaching one nature only in Christ, the monks protested that this wording was bringing them into disrepute. Their assertion was rather:

> “One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh.”

Accordingly, they wrote in their libellus of faith:

> “We believe that God the Word, the Only-Begotten Son of the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered in the flesh for us, is one of the three subsistences of the one Divinity.”

In the year 520 Justinian, who protected the Scythian monks, again wrote to Pope Hormisdas in their favor. In his letter he emphatically affirmed that they were thoroughly Catholic and maintained that the dispute was merely verbal. He again asked Hormisdas at last to dismiss them with a response, asserting publicly that their doctrine was in accordance with the tradition of the Fathers.

Hormisdas replied to Justinian’s letter in Letter 67. In it he reproves Justinian, who had changed his judgment in the Scythian case. Nevertheless, he urges him to act with the emperor so that Victor and the others accused by the monks might be sent to Rome, where the case could be handled more effectively. The emperor Justin also wrote to Hormisdas on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, during the consulship of Vitalianus and Rusticus, and therefore in the year 520, concerning the same matter.]

The Scythian monks, lingering longer in Rome and ordered to await the papal legates, tried, by sending a legate with a booklet of their profession of faith, to win over to their side the African bishops who had been carried into exile in Sardinia by Trasamund, king of the Vandals. By common agreement they produced a booklet divided into eight chapters [Col. 0512C] and sent it through John the deacon to the African bishops. In that booklet, through chapter five inclusive, they set out their own faith concerning the person of Christ the Lord; in the fourth chapter, however, concerning that highly controversial thesis, they write:

> “The same God the Word, even with his own flesh, is one of the Trinity—not because his flesh is of the substance of the Trinity, but because the flesh belongs to the Word of God, who is one of the Trinity.”

Having defended the thesis that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, from chapter six to the end of the book they explain in the same booklet what they believe concerning grace and free will. Then they discuss at length and learnedly original sin and its punishments, and the grace by which the human race is restored, in accordance with the teaching of Saint Augustine. At the end of chapter six they teach especially that faith is given by God, and predestination without merits.

The African prelates, of whom there was a great number in Sardinia, after reading the booklet of the Scythian monks [Col. 0512D], not only commended their faith in its entirety, but also composed a second volume of their own, with the same title, *On the Incarnation and Grace*. In it they approved all the opinions of the Scythians and fortified them with further, stronger arguments. They were fifteen bishops, whose names are listed at the beginning of the book; nevertheless, that volume appears to have been composed by the pen of Fulgentius of Ruspe, who surpassed the others in learning, as is inferred from the disciple of Saint Fulgentius in chapter 20 of his *Life*. The commendation of the monks’ faith appears immediately at the beginning:

> “We have come to know both your zeal and your faith, and your salvation; indeed, in the recognition of your faith our salvation has become known to us.”

From chapter 17 onward they sharply refute Faustus’s opinion that the beginning of faith arises from the powers of nature; nevertheless, they do not censure Faustus, for they had not yet seen his books.

While these things were taking place in Sardinia, the Scythian legates, realizing that Dioscorus—one of the papal legates, whom they had always found to be their most hostile enemy—would shortly arrive in Rome, left the City. They repeatedly claimed that they could not remain in Rome any longer, lest they be crushed by his authority. Before, however, they escaped from Rome, they hung on the statues of the emperors booklets and copies expressing their opinion concerning the Trinity and divine grace, so that this might provide some pretextual cover for their withdrawal. Hormisdas writes to Possessor that they also shouted at the statues of the emperors, hoping thereby to move the Roman people to pity; yet, according to the same authority, their cries passed through the Romans’ deaf ears.

Possessor was one of the African prelates whom Trasamund had sent into exile, and at that time he was staying in Constantinople. Vitalian and Justinian induced him to consult Pope Hormisdas concerning the books of Faustus of Riez. Hormisdas received Possessor’s letter through Justin the deacon, who acted as its bearer, at a time when he was bitterly disposed toward the monks and was rightly indignant at their recent departure [Col. 0513B]. The letter was given on the Ides of August. In his reply to Possessor, Hormisdas inveighed at length against the monks in the first part of his letter and all but called them heretics. Concerning Faustus he gave the following judgment:

> “But concerning those whom you indicate in your letter to have consulted us about the sayings of a certain Gallic bishop Faustus, let them have this answer: neither is he to be received, nor can anyone whom the examination of the Catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline does not receive among the authority of the Fathers generate ambiguity or inflict prejudice upon the religious.”

Since it was commonly said that Faustus had written against Saint Augustine, that same holy Pontiff, having stripped Faustus’s books entirely of authority, imposed the last volumes of Saint Augustine upon them as books to be read, pointing them out as the purest springs from which they should draw Catholic doctrine concerning free will and the grace of God.

All this is described in summary from Book II, chapters 18 and following, of Cardinal Noris’s *Pelagian History* [Col. 0514A]. There it is also demonstrated that the Scythian monks were not only free from the Eutychian heresy, but also proved to be vigorous opponents of that heresy, although their obstinate zeal—by which they clung to a preconceived opinion even to the point of contempt for the others—was not without blame. Natalis Alexander may also be consulted, sixth century, dissertation 2.

Moreover, in the year 534 John II approved this proposition of the Scythian monks, as will be said under his pontificate. Hormisdas, however, judging it inopportune and more suited to disturbing than to building up the Church, did not even wish to examine it, leaving it untouched and undiscussed. He foresaw that its proclamation would at that time be harmful, because it seemed, at least outwardly, to have some affinity with the recently condemned doctrine of Peter the Fuller, and because, without its assistance, the Council of Chalcedon had already crushed the heresies of Eutyches and Nestorius.

[Note: [Col. 0514B]

**Number 84, line 19.**—The episcopate in Africa was restored after seventy-four years. The bishops to whom Symmachus supplied clothing and money each year were recalled from exile under Symmachus’s successor, after they had spent seventy-four years in exile. Thus says the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. This is not contradicted by Marcellinus Comes, who, under the consulship of Justinian IV and Paulinus, reports that the province of Africa and Carthage were recovered in the ninety-fourth year from their destruction, after the Vandals and their king Gelimer had been expelled. For that statement must be understood of the Vandals driven from Africa and the cities recovered by Justinian, whereas the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* is speaking of the Catholic bishops being restored; that restoration took place long before, as Onuphrius Panvinius notes in his manuscripts of the *Annals*. He says that after Trasamund’s death, Hilderic, son of Eudoxia, disregarding his father’s cruelty, brought back all the orthodox whom Trasamund had banished, especially the bishops. This took place under Hormisdas.]

[Col. 0473]

## 82

Hormisdas, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus, from the city of Frusino [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *Frusinona*.], held the see for eight years and seventeen days [Note: [Col. 0473] Fusinona. B B: nine years and ten days, from the consulship of Cassiodorus to that of Maximus.]. He lived during the reign of King Theodoric and the reign of Augustus Anastasius, from the consulship of Senator to the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius. He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *psalmis*.]. He built a basilica in the Alban territory, on the estate of Fontis [Note: [Col. 0473] B: *Mefontis*. C: *Mesontis*.].

At the same time, in accordance with the decree of the synod, he sent legates to Greece, showing the apostolic see’s benevolence, because the Greeks were bound under the bond of anathema on account of Peter of Alexandria and Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, under John, bishop of Constantinople, with the council of King Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0473] See Baronius, under the year 515.]. He also sent Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum; Fortunatus, bishop of Catenna; Venantius, a presbyter of the city of Rome; Vitalis, a deacon of the apostolic see; and Hilarius [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *Hilarium*.], notary of the aforesaid see. They went to Augustus Anastasius but accomplished nothing.

A second time he sent Ennodius himself and Peregrinus, bishop of Mesenna [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *Mesenatem*.], carrying letters of encouragement [Note: [Col. 0473] B: *confirmatory letters*.] concerning the faith, nineteen secret declarations, and the text of a booklet. Augustus Anastasius refused to consent to that booklet because he too had communicated with the Eutychian heresy.

## 83

He therefore wished to corrupt the same legates by means of a reward [Note: [Col. 0473] See Baronius, under the year 517.]. But the legates of the apostolic see, despising Augustus Anastasius, absolutely refused to accept money unless it brought about the satisfaction of the apostolic see. Then the emperor, filled with fury, expelled them through a small gate [Note: [Col. 0473] “From the city through a postern.”] and put them on a dangerous ship [Note: [Col. 0473] “On a dangerous vessel.”] with soldiers, magistrates, and prefects [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *prefects*.], named Heliodorus and Demetrius [Note: [Col. 0473] *Eliodorus and Demetrius*.]. The emperor Anastasius gave them this order: they were not to enter any city.

The legates of the apostolic see, however, secretly distributed the aforesaid nineteen letters concerning the faith through the hands of orthodox monks throughout all the cities. Yet the bishops of the cities, who were accomplices of Augustus Anastasius, out of fear sent all those letters concerning the faith to Constantinople as a criminal matter [Note: [Col. 0473] See Baronius, at the cited place, p. 677, and at the end of volume VI.].

Filled with fury against Pope Hormisdas, Augustus Anastasius wrote among his other sacred documents as follows: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” At the same time, by the will of God, the emperor Anastasius was struck by a divine thunderbolt and died. Justin the orthodox therefore assumed the empire and sent his authority to Pope Hormisdas of the apostolic see through Gratus [Note: [Col. 0473] Read: “through Gratus, an illustrious man.”], an illustrious man, hoping that peace among the Churches might be restored by the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0473] C: *restored*.].

## 84

Then Bishop Hormisdas, with the counsel of King Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0473] See Baronius, under the year 518.], sent from the apostolic see Germanus, bishop of Capua; John and Blandus, presbyters; Felix and Dioscorus, deacons of the apostolic see; and Peter, the notary. They were instructed in every aspect of the faith and in the text of the booklet of penitence [Note: [Col. 0473] “Instructed in every aspect of the faith and in the text of the booklet of penitence.” C: “fortified.”]. When they came near Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0473] “When they arrived.”], such grace of faith shone forth [Note: [Col. 0473] C: “shone upon them.”] that a very great multitude of orthodox monks and distinguished men came out to meet them. Among them were the emperor Justin and the consul Vitalian, who met them from the Round Castle [Note: [Col. 0473] C: “to the castle.”], which is said to lead [Note: [Col. 0473] C: “which leads.”] all the way into the city of Constantinople, with glory and praises.

They entered together with Gratus, the illustrious man, and were received with glory by Justin Augustus, the orthodox emperor. All the clergy, together with John, bishop of Constantinople, rejoiced, perceiving that they had been received graciously [Note: [Col. 0475] C: “perceiving that he had received them graciously.”]. The accomplices of Acacius, however, also perceiving what had happened, shut themselves inside the principal church, which is called Holy Sophia. After taking counsel, they sent word to the emperor, saying:

> “Unless an explanation is given us why our bishop Acacius was condemned, we absolutely do not consent to the apostolic see.”

Pope Hormisdas went to King Theodoric at Ravenna and, with his advice, sent his authority to the emperor Justin, together with the bond of the *chirograph* [Note: [Col. 0475] C: “with the bond.” See Baronius, under the year of Our Lord 523.] and the text of the booklet. He restored them to unity with the apostolic see, condemning Peter and Acacius, as well as all heresies.

He found Manichaeans, whom, after investigating them and examining their wounds, he sent into exile. He burned their books before the doors of the Constantinian basilica. During his time the episcopate in Africa, which had been destroyed by heretics, was restored after seventy-four years.

## 85

At the same time a royal gift came, with precious gems, from Clovis, Christian king of the Franks, as a gift to blessed Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0475] C: “a royal gift.” See Baronius, under the year 514.]. During this bishop’s pontificate many vessels of gold and silver came from Greece, as well as Gospels with golden tablets and precious gems, weighing fifteen pounds; a golden paten with hyacinths, weighing twenty-five pounds; a golden cup with gems, weighing eight pounds; a golden cup surrounded with a crown [Note: [Col. 0475] “With gems.”], weighing eight pounds; three gilded silver cups, weighing five pounds each; two silver patens, weighing twenty-five pounds; an electrum *gabata*, weighing two pounds; two golden cases of Cyre, weighing six pounds each; and purple *pallia olobera* [Note: [Col. 0475] C: *olofora blatea*. B: *oloserica*.] with gold-covered tablets, made from a cloak or imperial robe, a covering [Note: [Col. 0475] C: “a *succinctorium*.”] over the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle. All these things were offered by Justin Augustus, the orthodox emperor, as fulfillment of vows.

## 86

At the same time King Theodoric offered blessed Peter the Apostle two silver candelabra (*cerostrata*) [Note: [Col. 0475] C: *cerostrata*.], weighing seventy pounds. At the same time Pope Hormisdas made a beam at blessed Peter the Apostle and covered it with silver; it weighed one thousand and forty pounds. He made in the Constantinian basilica a silver arch before the altar, weighing twenty pounds; sixteen silver *canthara*, weighing fifteen pounds each.

Likewise, at blessed Paul he made two silver arches, weighing twenty pounds each; fifteen silver *canthara*, weighing fifteen pounds each; three silver vessels, weighing ten pounds each; and six station silver cups with handles [Note: [Col. 0475] B: “with crosses or chalices.”], weighing six pounds each.

He held ordinations in the city of Rome: twenty-one presbyters in the month of December and fifty-five bishops in various places. He was also buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Maximus [Note: [Col. 0475] B: “Symmachus.”], and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days.

## LV. SAINT JOHN. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 523, THE SIXTH YEAR OF EMPEROR JUSTIN, THE THIRTY-FIRST OF THEODORIC
