[Note: [Col. 0517D]

**Number 87, line 3.**—“He was summoned by King Theodoric,” etc. It is clear that Anastasius the Librarian translated many acts of the pontiffs into Latin and made them his own, with only slight alterations, from what Theophanes had written in Greek in his *Chronicle*, as anyone can see by comparing the two. He also seems to have taken something from the Anonymous author who composed a chronicle extending from Constantius Chlorus to Theodoric. Valesius published it in his edition of Marcellinus. The words of the Anonymous author should be compared with those of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, and it will be clear that the narrative—and indeed the words—were taken from the Anonymous author. For he writes as follows:

> “Believing that the emperor Justin feared him, he sent for and summoned John, bishop of the apostolic see, from Ravenna and said to him: ‘Go to the emperor Justin at Constantinople and tell him, among other things, to restore the reconciled heretics to the Catholic Church,’” etc.

For many of the Arians were converted through Justin’s efforts. Theodoric believed that they should be restored to the Arian communion and to the Church which he vigorously defended, and he demanded that the pontiff restore them. The pontiff rejected the unjust demand in the following manner, according to the same Anonymous author:

> “Pope John answered him thus: ‘King, do quickly what you are going to do. Behold, I stand in your presence; I do not promise you that I will do this, nor will I say it to him. In other matters which you may entrust to me, I shall be able, God willing, to obtain the result from him.’ The angry king therefore ordered a ship to be prepared and, having placed him on board with other bishops and senators, sent him to Constantinople. But God, who does not abandon his faithful worshipers, brought him there safely. When the emperor Justin came to meet him, he received him as though he were blessed Peter. After hearing the embassy, he promised to do everything except restore to the Arians those who had been reconciled and had given themselves to the Catholic faith,” etc.]

**Line 5.**—“Because … Justin … wished to disentangle the heretics.” That is, to free the East from every heresy. Thus in Plautus, *Epidicus* 1.2.49:

> “By some means I shall free myself; by some means I shall disentangle myself.”

And in Horace, *Odes* III.5.31:

> “Polished pearls”—that is, cleansed and thoroughly refined.

Vinnius likewise, in his note on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* 5.10: “I still cannot disentangle anything concerning your Dionysius.”

Thus, in order to settle the East, which had been thrown into confusion by such a multitude of sects, the emperor had decided to uproot all heretics. He also had Saint Sabas as an instigator. When Sabas approached Justin at the beginning of his reign to request certain things on behalf of the monks, which he obtained, he foretold to him in a prophetic spirit the following [same work, p. 344]:

> “And I believe and trust that God will add to your empire, in return for these works which you have freely undertaken for them, Africa and Rome, and all the rest of Honorius’s dominion, which those who ruled before your most pious serenity lost. Moreover, that you may remove from the midst the Arian heresy together with the Nestorian and that of Origen, and free the Churches of God from the plague of these three heresies,” etc.

Why, however, did Sabas foretell that Justin would eliminate only these three heresies? Cyril explains it in the same place:

> “Concerning Arius’s heresy: since the Goths, Visigoths, Vandals, and Gepids, who were Arians, dominated the whole West, he knew in his mind, through inspiration, that the emperor would conquer them.”

Justin therefore began his work with the extermination of the Arians. How successfully this would benefit the Catholic faith was shown when the Arians of the East sought the patronage of Theodoric.

Concerning the fulfillment of the prophecy, the same Cyril writes below, chapter 74:

> “But God bestowed an infinitely multiplied reward upon the emperor and brought the old man’s prophecy to fulfillment. Shortly afterward the emperor raised two trophies and carried off the crowns of two victories, such as none of the preceding emperors had yet achieved. For he recovered Africa and Rome, which had been held by rebels, and saw two kings brought to Constantinople. Thus, in a short time, he restored half of the land and sea to the Roman Empire. Then, after the whole West had been freed from the servitude of the aforesaid tyrants, who were Arians, he decreed by divine enactments that the churches should everywhere be taken away from the Arians, in accordance with the divine command—or prophecy.”

[Col. 0519C] **Line 14.**—“They came out to meet him … with candles and crosses.” In that age it was customary to receive distinguished men in this kind of solemn procession. In the *Acts of the Council of Ephesus* there survives a letter of the bishops living in Constantinople to the legitimate synod. They recount how Dalmatius had defended the Ephesian Fathers before the emperor Theodosius; after he had disclosed the acts to the emperor and bent his mind, the people came out to meet him with candles and led him to the church.

Likewise, under the emperor Justin, the legates of Hormisdas were received with a similar procession when they entered the cities. Dioscorus testifies to this in his report, and Hormisdas in his letters. For, describing their arrival at the city of Scampum and the procession of the bishop Troius, the clergy, and the people, they say that “almost all came out to meet the legates: men with women, soldiers with crosses, received us in the city,” etc. The legates add in the same place that they found Stephen, a relative of Vitalian, and Leontius [Col. 0519D], sent by the emperor to escort the legates of the apostolic see.

The same custom was observed at the election of metropolitans. Thus, when Saturninus was elected metropolitan by Maximian of Constantinople, the following is read concerning the people’s procession in the Cassinian *Synodicon*, chapter 115, p. 238:

> “Preparing for one person to come out to meet the people with crosses and candles,” etc.

In this manner the cities of Italy received an exarch when he entered them; and the Romans received Charles with the same solemnity, as is related below under Adrian I, where this too is noted:

> “As is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician,” etc.

Gregory of Tours speaks of the same custom, *History* VI.11:

> “Both entered the city—the duke and the bishop—with standards and praises, and with various banners of honor,” etc.

Indeed, at this very time, when great men went to meet the king to give thanks and perform their duty, they used candles. Let us hear Theophanes in his *Chronicle*, under the year 522:

> “In this year a Roman woman of senatorial rank, named Juvenilia, approached Theodoric, who was reigning as king, and addressed him in these words: ‘For three years now I have had a dispute with the patrician Firmus; see that I am freed from it.’ The king summoned the judges of both parties and said: ‘Unless you give judgment by the appointed day and dismiss the litigants, I shall punish you with death.’ After they had confronted one another for two days and judgment had been given according to the laws, they dismissed both parties. Then Juvenilia approached the king with lighted candles to give thanks because she had been released from the dispute. But the king became angry and summoned the judges: ‘Why,’ he said, ‘did you prolong for three years what you completed in two days?’ He then struck both judges with the sword, and from this great terror arose among the others,” etc.

**Number 88, line 1.** “He humbled himself, prostrate.” The Valesian Anonymous has the same wording, from which this passage appears to have been copied and inserted here. The same is also read concerning Justinian in the *Life of Agapetus*:

> “He humbled himself before the holy apostolic see and adored the most blessed pope.”

In the letters written and sent to the Roman pontiffs at this time, Justinian’s expressions provide illustrious evidence of the Eastern Church’s veneration for them. While still a count, Justin addressed Hormisdas as follows:

> “To my most holy lord Hormisdas, first archpontiff and pope of the city of Rome, Justinian the count sends greetings,” etc.

Pompeius, the grandson of the emperor Anastasius, writes to him in this manner:

> “To my most blessed and apostolic lord and father Hormisdas, archbishop of the universal Church, greetings,” etc.

Juliana Anicia, a distinguished woman, was present among those offering congratulations when Anastasius urged Hormisdas to permit his legates to remain a little longer in the East, for the sake of strengthening the peace, which could be secured only through the assistance of the apostolic see.

Theodoritus of Lignida likewise writes in the heading:

> “To my lord, holy, blessed, praiseworthy, and to-be-adored apostolic Father Hormisdas, pope of the city of Rome, your humble servant,” etc.

In the letter itself he says:

> “With little and insignificant sheets of paper, [he] presents himself at the feet of Hormisdas, worthy of praise and adoration,” etc.

[Col. 0520C] **Number 89, line 1.**—“At the same time.” The same forms of narrative occur in the Valesian Anonymous:

> “Therefore Pope John returned from Justin, whom Theodoric received deceitfully and ordered to be in his displeasure; after a few days he died,” etc.

**Line 8.**—“The heretical king Theodoric suddenly perished,” etc. The Valesian Anonymous adds who was the author and instigator of these actions against the Catholics, as well as the edict by which the churches were to be taken away from the Catholics:

> “Therefore the Jewish scholasticus Symmachus, at the command not of a king but of a tyrant, drafted the orders as follows: On Wednesday, the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the fourth indiction, in the consulship of Olybrius, so that when Sunday arrived the Arians might invade the Catholic basilicas.”

Thus in the East, edicts against the Arians were put into execution through Justin’s zeal. This provoked the angry king to assign all the churches throughout his dominion to the Arians by a public edict, on one and the same day. The Anonymous author nevertheless adds:

> “But he who does not allow his faithful worshipers to be oppressed by foreigners immediately passed judgment upon him according to Arius, the founder of his religion. He contracted dysentery, and when within three days he was called away, on the same day on which he rejoiced that he would invade the churches, he lost both his kingdom and his life,” etc.

Saint Gregory the Great agrees with this in *Dialogues* IV.36. Hence I suspect that the Anonymous author was a secretary of the apostolic see, whose duty it was to collect these acts; Gregory the Great may therefore have copied his history. From these records, assembled by contemporary writers, additions appear to have been made to the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs.

**Line 19.**—“The episcopate remained vacant for fifty-eight days.” After John’s death, besides Theodoric’s edict concerning the seizure of the Catholic churches, I believe another specific order was written to the Roman clergy, requiring the pontiff to be elected with the king’s approval and consent. Hence the long vacancy between pontificates, while the people resisted these new presumptions of the king, and finally yielded for the common good and the peace of the Churches [Col. 0521A]. This is shown by a letter of his successor Athalaric to the Senate of the City, preserved in Cassiodorus, *Variae* VIII.15, where the king says, among other things:

> “We declare with the greatest gratitude that you have responded to the judgment of our glorious grandfather—namely, Theodoric—in the election of the bishop. For it was right to obey the decision of a good ruler who, after wise deliberation, although belonging to another religion, appears to have chosen such a pontiff that no one could rightly be displeased with him. You should recognize that this was his principal desire: that religion might flourish through good priests in all the churches. You have therefore received one commendably established by divine grace and praised by royal examination. Let no one still be held by the former contention. The defeated man has no shame when his wish has been overcome by the prince,” etc.

Here lie the beginnings of lay presumptions concerning the confirmation both of pontiffs and of other bishops. These practices were introduced by the Arian kings of Italy, and, after Italy had been cleansed and recovered, the emperors of the East did not at all abolish them, as the *Book of the Pontiffs* notes in its proper places.]

[Note: [Col. 0521B]

**Number 87, line 1.**—John, Tuscan by nationality, etc. After the apostolic see had been vacant of a shepherd for seven days, John the Etruscan, son of Constantius the presbyter, was appointed in Hormisdas’s place by the unanimous consent of the entire clergy, on the Ides of August in the year of Christ’s birth 523, which was the sixth year of Justin’s reign and the thirty-first year of Theodoric’s Italian kingdom. During his time a great multitude of Ethiopians joined the Church. Many of the Manichaeans were killed by the emperor Justin and by Cabades, king of the Persians. The Augusta Euphemia, who had rendered the Catholic faith excellent service, departed this life.]

### 87

**Line 9.**—At the same time Pope John, ill with sickness, went on his way amid tears. Moved by the threats of King Theodoric, the pontiff unwillingly and contrary to the custom of his predecessors undertook the embassy. While he was on the journey, there occurred to him what Saint Gregory recounts in Book III, Chapter 2 of the *Dialogues*, in these words:

> “In the time of the Goths, when John, a most blessed man and pontiff of this Roman Church, was traveling to the elder Justin, the emperor, he came into the region of Corinth, where it was necessary that a horse should be obtained for him to ride during the journey. When a certain nobleman there heard of this, he offered him a horse which, because of its great gentleness, his wife was accustomed to ride—yet in such a way that, when he had reached another place and another horse could be found, the one he had given was to be sent back for his wife. And it happened that, when the aforesaid man had been carried as far as a certain place on that horse, he promptly returned the one he had received as soon as he found another. When the wife of the nobleman wished, as usual, to ride it, the horse was no longer able to do so: after carrying so great a pontiff, it refused to carry the woman. It began, in fact, with immense crying and snorting, and with the ceaseless movement of its whole body, as if in disdain, to make known that after carrying the pontiff’s limbs it could not carry a woman. When her husband prudently observed this, he immediately sent the horse back to that same venerable man, begging earnestly that he himself should keep the horse which, by his riding it, had been dedicated to his rightful possession.”

Of the same man Saint Gregory also says:

> “It is customary for a marvelous event to be related by our elders: when he came in the city of Constantinople to the gate called the Golden Gate, and crowds of people came to meet him, he restored sight to a blind man who asked him in the sight of all, and, laying his hand upon the man’s eyes, dispelled their darkness.”

### Number 88, line 7

**“At the same time, when these men mentioned above—that is, the pope, etc.—…”** When Theodoric heard that Pope John had done nothing toward restoring the churches to the Arians, but rather had dedicated the churches taken from the Arians to divine worship, he turned the sword against the most distinguished senators at Rome. The same facts are attested by the author of the *Miscella*, Book 15, and by Gregory of Tours in the place cited above.

**Line 11.**—*Symmachus.* Symmachus was Boethius’s father-in-law, a man of consular rank and highly learned in every branch of knowledge, especially theological matters. Boethius wrote his book *On the Trinity* for him and called him the judge of his writings. The grammarian Priscian, teaching at Constantinople, dedicated to him his book *On Weights and Measures*.

**On the same line, Boethius.** Severinus Boethius, consul for the second time, married Rusticiana, the daughter of Symmachus. By her he had two sons of consular rank, whom he took care to train in the best moral principles. He was an eminent philosopher, theologian, and mathematician. Because he had defended the senate when it was accused by calumny of the crime of lèse-majesté, Theodoric banished him to Ticinum, where, after many hardships in prison, he finally subjected him to capital punishment and crowned him with glorious martyrdom. On his writings, see Baronius under the year 526 and Possevinus in the *Sacred Apparatus*.

### Number 89, line 18

**“Buried on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.”** It should be read: “on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.” For he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June; but on the sixth day before the Kalends of July he was transferred to Rome and buried in the Vatican basilica.

**Line 19.**—*The episcopate was vacant for fifty-eight days.* Throughout this interval of fifty-eight days, while the see was vacant, there was a dispute at Rome concerning the election of the pontiff. Although the votes of the electors had agreed upon another candidate, it nevertheless happened, by order of the Arian King Theodoric, that they had to elect the Felix whom he had designated, Felix IV. Thus, just as the Arian emperor Constantius, after Liberius had been banished, substituted Felix II in his place, so the Arian ruler Theodoric imposed Felix IV of the same name. On this occasion it came about that, after these times, the Eastern emperors likewise permitted no other pontiff to be elected by the Roman clergy except one whom they themselves confirmed by their assent. For this reason Saint Gregory laments most bitterly in many passages.

## Chronological Notes

In the consulship of Maximus—that is, in the year of Christ 523—after the see had been vacant for seven days following the death of Saint Hormisdas, from 6 to 12 August, Saint John was ordained Roman pontiff on the thirteenth, which fell on a Sunday, as Anastasius and Ordericus write. The duration assigned to his see is two years, eight months, and sixteen days in the Anastasian manuscripts of the Regius, Mazarin, and two Thuani codices, and likewise in several distinguished catalogues, the Palatine-Vatican and the Bergomensis apud Schelestratus. The Lucensis, Cavensis, and Farfensis add one day, while the Bergomensis subtracts one day from the months.

Nevertheless, the date of his death at Ravenna in custody is recorded by the Librarian, section 89, line 6, as the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June; and his body is said to have been brought from there to Rome and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Olybrius—that is, on 27 May in the year 526. In the Roman Martyrology and that of Usuard, his memory is commemorated on the same day. In the Martyrologies of Bede and Ado, however, it is given on the following day, 28 May.

From this we can gather why, in addition to two years and eight months, sixteen days are assigned to his pontificate. Although from 13 August, when he began his pontificate, to the day of his death, 18 May, only five days elapsed beyond the complete months, those who recorded his memory on 28 May counted sixteen days from the day of his ordination and beginning, 15 August, to the 28th, counting both terminal days. Thus, in reality, from the day of his ordination, 13 August 523, to 18 May 526, when he died a martyr at Ravenna in custody, there were two years, eight months, and five days—or, counting both terminal days, six days.

## Historical Notes

### Number 87, line 1

**“John, a Tuscan by nationality, etc.”** To illustrate the birthplace of this blessed and illustrious pontiff and martyr, the citizens of Siena contribute the following documents.

Lilius, or Hieronymus Gigli, writes the following in his *Diary of the Sienese Festivals* under 28 May, translated by us into Latin:

> “All writers who have published Lives of the Pontiffs assert that John was an Etruscan. Sigismundus Titius supposes that he was born at Populonia; when barbarians destroyed that city, he says that John migrated to Siena with many others. He therefore states that John subsequently honored Siena, which he regarded as his homeland, by occupying its episcopal see. Malevoltius agrees with him. Yet we have established an earlier Sienese episcopal see from the evidence which we cited on 3 February, on the feast of Saint Blaise. The Reverend Father Ugurgerius reports that certain writers, declaring this holy pontiff to have been our fellow citizen, are supported by the tradition accepted among us. Nor are there lacking those who say that even the village of Fontebranda, then recently counted among the suburbs, was ennobled by being his residence. In the hall of the Bailiwick of Siena, among the other pontiffs born in the Sienese colony, Saint John I may be seen.”

Besides those cited by Lilius, other learned men are also put forward as supporters of this tradition: Julius Piccolomineus in his book entitled *Illustrious Sienese*, Jugurthas, Orlandus, Tommasius, Malavoltius in Part I of his *History of Siena*, John Bisdomini in his unpublished *Chronicle of Sienese Affairs*, a twelfth-century writer, Hildobrandinus, a thirteenth-century author, Maccabrunius in *On the Praises of Etruria*; Gallacis Petri in another unpublished chronicle; and Father Peter Castruccius, of the Order of Preachers, a Florentine, in his *Historical Week* printed at Todi in 1655. In the metropolitan cathedral church, among the distinguished relics of this holy martyr and pontiff, his jawbone is preserved.

### Number 89, line 6

**“He died at Ravenna in custody, a martyr, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.”** This is how the date of the holy pontiff’s death is recorded. The feast, however, concerns the commemoration of his translation, when his sacred body was brought from Ravenna, where he fell in glorious martyrdom, to Rome. Cardinal Baronius notes this in the Martyrology under 27 May, on which day it is celebrated.

**Line 10.**—*Of Felix and Adauctus.* We discussed a notable part of this sacred cemetery, discovered ten years ago near the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, above the hill close to it toward the Ardeatine Way, in Volume II of the *Prolegomena*.

**Line 15.**—*Fifteen pallia woven with gold, which John himself brought, etc.* Shortly before this, in the notes on Saint Hormisdas, we said that such precious textiles, taken from an imperial or royal robe, were customarily offered by the piety of emperors to sacred altars.

## Additional Note

### Number 87, line 9

**“Ill with sickness, he went on his way amid tears.”** When the most blessed pontiff John was traveling to Constantinople and had reached the city of Corinth, a horse was sought for him to ride on that journey. A certain nobleman offered a gentle horse which his wife was accustomed to mount, but he asked that it be returned when another had been found, for the use of his wife, who greatly enjoyed its gentleness. As the journey proceeded, another horse was found, and the first was appropriately returned to its owner. When the nobleman’s wife wished, as usual, to sit upon it, the horse would not tolerate anyone else mounting it; it became wild and kicked because the most blessed pontiff had ridden it. When the nobleman noticed this, he sent the horse as a gift to the holy pontiff, begging that he retain it permanently in his service. Thus Saint Gregory the Great relates in Book III, Chapter 2 of the *Dialogues*.

### Number 88, line 7

**“From whose hands Justin Augustus was crowned with glory.”** Before Pope John departed from Constantinople, Caesar Justin wished first to be crowned by him with the imperial diadem, since he was the first emperor to be consecrated with the imperial insignia by a Roman pontiff, and John was the first of the Roman pontiffs to travel to Constantinople.

## Additional Note

### Number 87, line 4

**“Whom the king himself sent, after requesting him, on an embassy.”** From Book V, Chapter 20.

Emperor Justin, moved by his zeal to preserve the Catholic religion from every contamination and mixture with any false belief, so that no opposing sect might flourish at all, enacted a law by which exile and death were decreed against the Manichaeans, while all other heretics, Jews, and pagans were excluded from every public office. At first he treated the Arians more leniently, lest King Theodoric, who professed the same heresy, should be provoked to rage violently against the Catholics in Italy, which he held. A little later, however, disregarding this danger, he judged that the Arian perfidy should be restrained by the same sanction applied to the other heretics, and he ordered that their churches be cleansed of all profanation by being dedicated according to the Catholic rite.

Theodoric, enraged for this reason, considered taking revenge for the severity of the law through the ruin and slaughter of the Italians, and eliminating all Catholics from this seat of religion. Nevertheless, he decided to deal more moderately with Justin Augustus and, by letters sent to him, to seek as if in friendship the withdrawal of the law enacted against the Arians.

To obtain this more effectively, he resolved to use an embassy such as had never before been heard of and therefore deserved to be celebrated above all others: namely, one which would compel the supreme pontiff himself to undertake the journey to Constantinople for the purpose of pleading on behalf of the Arian churches.

Pope John, who had succeeded Hormisdas, judged that he should act in order to avert from Italy the disaster threatening it from the heretical and barbarian king, just as he had read that Leo the Great had acted before Attila when he undertook an embassy on behalf of the Romans—even though the city might seem to be redeemed by the excessive humiliation of the pontiff, whom people would now commonly say had been sent away to act as the agent of a secular ruler and had become entangled in affairs undertaken against Christian interests.

The holy pontiff, however, carefully weighing the almost infinite evils that threatened from the heretical usurper and could be averted by this one intervention with Justin—namely, by persuading him to leave the heretics in possession of their own obstinacy and to reject the judgment of their perverse stubbornness—did not refuse to undertake the embassy.

We have thought it necessary to distinguish these instructions and the purpose of the embassy somewhat more fully, so that the credibility of the historians may be safeguarded, since it has seemed to many not to be consistent. Three witnesses deserve particular attention: a certain Anonymous published at the end of Ammianus Marcellinus with the notes of Valesius; the Librarian; and Theophanes.

When the testimony of these three is weighed, it can be gathered that three objects of the embassy are proposed. The first is stated by the Anonymous: that those who had abandoned the Arian sect and joined the Catholic faith should be compelled to return to Arianism. The second is expressed by the Librarian: that the churches taken from the Arians and assigned to professors of the Catholic rite should be restored to their former possessors. The third is reported by Theophanes: that thereafter no one should be compelled by force to renounce the Arian perfidy.

Pope John not only refused to discuss the first article with Justin; he is also said to have replied to the Arian king, who was threatening slaughter, in the following words, recorded by the Anonymous:

> “To him Pope John replied: ‘Do quickly what you are going to do, O king. Behold, I stand before you. I neither promise you that I shall do this nor shall I tell him to do it. For in other matters which you may entrust to me, I shall be able, with God’s consent, to obtain his agreement.’”

Thus he courageously permitted the king to inflict upon himself whatever punishment he preferred, rather than undertake to present to Justin a petition unworthy of a pontiff.

He is said to have persisted in the two final articles, adopting such a course amid the dangers threatening the orthodox on both sides that he always turned away the more harmful danger. God approved this arduous care of the pontiff in undertaking the journey and embassy by producing through his servant the miracle of restored sight to a blind man at the entrance to the imperial city. Saint Gregory commemorates this in Book III, Chapter 2 of the *Dialogues*. God also approved it by the honorable reception which the Librarian describes in this section:

> “The entire city came out to meet Blessed Pope John from the twelfth milestone, with candles and crosses, in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul,” etc.

Justin Augustus, who prostrated himself on the ground and worshiped this vicar of Christ, although he had already been solemnly crowned by Epiphanius, patriarch of Constantinople, wished to be crowned a second time by the successor of Peter. Besides the Librarian, Aimoinus also relates this in Book II, Chapter 1.

Theophanes adds that the same John, who had humbly undertaken the embassy for the sake of public salvation, when invited by the patriarch Epiphanius, “refused the meeting until he himself, being the Roman pontiff, should occupy the first place in the assembly.” Marcellinus confirms this when he writes of John in his chronicle:

> “The right hand occupied the right-hand throne of the Church, and on the Lord’s Day he celebrated the prayers of the Romans with a full voice in honor of the resurrection of our Lord.”

From the emperor he obtained the two final articles of the petition, the first of which he had openly declared to Theodoric that he would never present. Justin likewise had denied that he would grant that first article even if it were requested of him, since he had perhaps learned of it from Theodoric’s letters.

For it is not reasonable to suppose that the senators whom Theodoric wished to add as companions to John’s embassy held a petition different from that of the Roman pontiff, since the Librarian bears witness to their religious concern, writing:

> “Pope John and the senators, religious men, deserved everything, and Italy was freed from Theodoric.”

The author of the *Miscella* likewise asserts:

> “Justin granted them what was requested.”

And it is clear from the Anonymous mentioned above that Justin promised to do everything except permit those who had converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith to relapse into heresy with impunity.

This was precisely what Theodoric desired, but John, the leader of the embassy, openly denied that he would ever request it, and the senators accompanying the embassy, religious men, preferred to follow the example of the supreme pontiff rather than the desire of the heretical king.

When the ambassadors returned to Italy, they received a reward for having obtained from Justin a more lenient clemency toward the Arians that was entirely different from any reasonable expectation. For the barbarian king, when both Pope John and the senators arrived at Ravenna, handed them over to a grim prison, intending in due course to proceed to the ultimate punishments, unless he had feared Justin’s indignation.

Nevertheless, he increased the hardships of imprisonment with such an addition of cruelty that John, worn down by suffering and surrendering his life, was crowned with that martyrdom. When a demon-possessed man was brought to his bier, he was immediately freed. Therefore senators and people alike vied with one another to obtain his relics by means of their veils.

All these facts prove that John stood by his promises. He had declared that he would vigorously resist Theodoric concerning the first article of the petition; and neither he nor the senators are found to have undertaken that request or presented it to Justin. The honors of the highest kind that had been bestowed upon Pope John and the Roman senators at Constantinople increased Theodoric’s suspicion, since the king interpreted those honors as having been given so that the senate of the City might be stirred by sharper goads to cast off the Gothic yoke.

History certainly reports that Theodoric, driven by the same suspicion, inflicted death upon Symmachus and Boethius, men who were especially distinguished in the senate.

## Additional Note

### Number 88, line 7

**“From whose hands Justin Augustus was crowned with glory, etc.”** Although Justin Augustus had already been crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople, as is clear from that same John’s letter to Pope Hormisdas, he nevertheless wished to be crowned again by Pope John. Besides Anastasius, Aimoinus explicitly attests this in Book II, Chapter 1, writing of Pope John:

> “He placed the imperial crown upon Justin Augustus as the vicar of blessed Peter.”

Nor was it unusual in later centuries for emperors and kings to be crowned a second or even a third time. Before Justin, certain emperors, beginning in the time of Theodosius the Younger—who, according to Theodore the Reader in Book II, was crowned by Proclus, patriarch of Constantinople—received the imperial crown from bishops. But before Justin no one had received a solemn blessing from a Roman pontiff.

Before emperors were endowed with pontifical blessing, they made a profession of faith. On this and on the rite by which they were consecrated, see Edmund Martène, Book II, Chapter 2, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*. On the blessing of the emperors of the West after the renewal of the empire, see what will be said under Leo III; and on the blessing of kings, what will be said under Zacharias.

## 87

John, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius, occupied the see for two years, eight months, and twenty-two days [B. m. 9, d. 14], from the consulship of Maximus to the consulship of Olybrius, in the time of King Theodoric and Justin Augustus the Christian.

He was summoned by King Theodoric to Ravenna. [See Baronius under the year of the Lord 525.] The king himself, after requesting him, sent him on an embassy to Constantinople to Justin, the orthodox emperor, because at that time Justin, a religious man, wished with the greatest ardor and love for the Christian religion to remove the heretics. In the highest Christian fervor he adopted this policy: to consecrate the churches of the Arians as Catholic churches.

When the heretical king Theodoric heard of this, he became enraged [B: “When the heretical king heard this, he became enraged”] and wished to destroy all Italy by the sword. At the same time Pope John, ill with sickness, went on his way amid tears, and the senators and consuls went with him, namely Theodore, Importunus, Agapitus, a former consul [C: “former consuls”], and another Agapitus, a patrician. They had received this instruction: that the churches in the Eastern regions should be restored to the heretics; otherwise he would destroy all Italy by the sword.

While they were traveling with Pope John, the entire city came out to meet Blessed John at the twelfth milestone, with candles and crosses in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. For the ancient Greeks bore witness to this, saying that from the time of Constantine Augustus and blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see, down to the time of Justin Augustus, the regions of Greece had not deserved to receive the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter with honor.

### 88

Then Justin Augustus, giving honor to God, humbled himself prostrate [C: “on the ground”] and worshiped the most blessed Pope John.

At the same time Blessed Pope John, together with the senators mentioned above, begged Justin Augustus amid great tears that the embassy might be acceptable in his sight. Pope John and the senators, religious men, deserved everything, and Italy was freed from King Theodoric the heretic.

Nevertheless, Emperor Justin was filled with joy because in his own time he had deserved to see the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter in his kingdom. From his hands Justin Augustus was crowned with glory.

At the same time, when those mentioned above—that is, Pope John with the senators, Theodore the former consul, Importunus the former consul, and Agapitus the former consul (Agapitus the patrician having died at Thessalonica)—were in Constantinople, King Theodoric the heretic seized two distinguished senators and former consuls, Symmachus and Boethius, and killed them, slaying them with the sword. [See Baronius under the years of the Lord 525 and 526.]

### 89

At the same time, when the venerable Pope John and the senators were returning with honor, having obtained everything from Justin Augustus, the heretical King Theodoric received them—Pope John and the senators—with great deceit and hatred. He also wished to kill them with the sword, but feared the indignation of Justin Augustus. Nevertheless, he afflicted and tortured them all in custody [C: “wearied them”], so that the most blessed John, bishop and pope of the first see, weakened by his sufferings in prison, died.

He died at Ravenna in custody, a martyr, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [C: “the twelfth”; see Baronius, year 526]. After this event, by the will of almighty God, on the ninety-eighth day after the most blessed John died in custody, the heretical King Theodoric suddenly perished and died.

This Pope John established the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Nereus and Achilleus on the Ardeatine Way. He also restored the cemetery of Felix and Adauctus; likewise, he restored the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.

At that time an ornament of emeralds and hyacinths was placed above the confession of the blessed apostle Paul.

Also in his time Emperor Justin offered a golden paten with jewels, weighing twenty pounds; a golden chalice with jewels, weighing five pounds; five silver cups; and fifteen pallia woven with gold, which John himself brought to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to Saint Mary and Saint Laurence.

He ordained fifteen bishops in various places.

His body was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Olybrius. The episcopate was vacant for fifty-eight days.

# LVI. SAINT FELIX IV

**Year of Christ 526; ninth year of the Emperor Justin; thirty-fourth year of Theodoric.**

## Textual Variants

## Additional Note

### Line 1—“Felix, etc.”

Theodoric, the murderer of John, having rashly usurped for himself the right to choose and nominate the bishop of the apostolic see, after a dispute concerning this matter had lasted for fifty-eight days, nominated Felix, a man highly esteemed in the Roman clergy, so that no opportunity might remain for resistance to his will.

This nomination, and its explicit approval by the entire clergy, took place on 24 July in the year of the Lord 526, the ninth year of the reign of the Emperor Justin and the thirty-fourth year of King Theodoric’s reign in Italy.

But without delay God struck down the author of so great a crime, Theodoric, a savage, barbarous, and harsh tyrant, by a sudden vengeance sent from heaven, and, after hastening his dreadful death, banished him forever to the underworld.

“While he was dining,” says Procopius in Book I of *The Gothic War*, “and his servants had placed before him the cooked head of a fish of extraordinary size, the head of Symmachus, recently killed, seemed to him to appear, with its teeth fixed and projecting from the lower lip and its eyes glaring fiercely, threatening him in fury and bitterness. Terrified by this vision, he fell ill and died not long afterward.”

Saint Gregory relates in Book IV, Chapter 30 of the *Dialogues* that a certain solitary saw him, stripped and barefoot, with his hands bound, being led between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, whom he had killed, and thrown into Vulcan’s cauldron.

### Line 1—“He occupied the see for four years.”

From the beginning and end of his pontificate it is inferred that he occupied the see for four years, two months, and eighteen days.

### Line 11—“The pontificate was vacant for one month and fifteen days.”

From the death of Felix until the election of Boniface II, three days intervened. It is nevertheless read here that the see was vacant for one month and fifteen days; this must be understood of the period when, after the schism had been removed, Boniface was recognized by everyone as the legitimate pontiff.

## Chronological Notes

The catalogues of Lucensis and Farfensis, together with the Librarian, define the vacancy of the see after John’s pontificate as fifty-eight days. Since, however, the Librarian in this number, line 3, places the beginning of the see of Felix IV, who succeeded John, on the fourth day before the Ides of July—which in the year 526 was a Sunday and suitable for episcopal ordination—Pagius correctly infers that the vacancy of the see lasted fifty-five days.

Above, in the consulship of Olybrius, the year of the death of Saint John was stated to be 18 May, and consequently the election of Felix took place in July of the same year. Nevertheless, the Librarian assigns the consulship of Mavortius to the beginning of Felix’s pontificate, placing it in the following year, 527, according to the custom noted above of assigning to a pontiff’s see the consuls during whose magistracy he celebrated Easter.

With these points established concerning the beginning, the chronology of Felix IV’s rule proceeds without difficulty for four years, two months, and thirteen days. All the principal catalogues—the Palatine-Vatican, Farfensis, Lucensis, Cavensis, and Bergomensis—record the same figures, as do most of the Librarian’s manuscripts, although some add one day.

The holy pontiff therefore died on 25 September, although his sacred body was buried in the Vatican basilica on the fourth day before the Ides of October, as the Librarian testifies. Since the Librarian and the Farfensis and Lucensis catalogues say that the see was vacant for three days, the election of Boniface, his successor, should be assigned to 28 September of the year 530, and his ordination to the following day, 29 September, which was a Sunday.

This chronology is nevertheless troubled by the subscriptions of apostolic letters and councils, as observed by the two most learned cardinals, Baronius and Norisius, who disagree with one another because of those subscriptions.

The Second Council of Orange, held against the Semi-Pelagians and Massilians by Caesarius, bishop of Arles, was subscribed on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the consulship of Decius the Younger—that is, in the year 529 of the Christian era. Caesarius sent the Acts of that council to Rome for confirmation by the apostolic see, addressed to Pope Felix, carried by Armenius, a presbyter and abbot.

While Armenius was continuing his journey, or while he was staying at Rome, Felix IV died and Boniface was substituted in his place. In his letter of confirmation of the council, Boniface replied to Caesarius and announced that he had succeeded Felix, dating the letter on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes—namely, in the year of Christ 530.

Sirmondus writes:

> “Following the chronology of Baronius, he thinks that it should be read: ‘after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,’ which is the year 531.”

Cardinal Baronius, following Anastasius, places the beginning of Boniface’s pontificate in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in October, but its end on 17 October after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, namely in the year 531. In both cases, however, it is certain that he was mistaken.

For, after the Second Council of Orange had been held on the fifth day before the Nones of July in the year 529, Caesarius requested confirmation of it from Pope Felix and sent Armenius to Rome, etc. The letter of Boniface replying to Caesarius is then cited, dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men, in which mention is made of the council held by Caesarius.

“Who,” he says, “could believe that Caesarius wrote to the apostolic see after a year had passed, saying that he had convened a council at Orange?” Therefore he must be understood to have informed Pope Felix in the same year, 529, of the council which he himself had held.

While Armenius was bringing the letters to Rome, Felix died, and Boniface succeeded him in that same year. Boniface replied to Caesarius in the following year, on 25 January. Certainly the subscriptions of Felix’s letters, which are given as dated in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, must be corrected on the basis of this subscription of Boniface, especially since Baronius himself says that another letter to Sabina, dated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, must be corrected by the same erasure.

Nor is the end of Boniface’s pontificate correctly placed by Baronius and the others, generally following Anastasius, on 17 October in the consulship after that of Lampadius and Orestes. For this is proved to be plainly false by the Acts of the Roman Council held by Boniface himself and published by Luca Holstenius, where the first session begins:

> “After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the church of the blessed apostle Andrew, with the venerable Pope Boniface presiding,” etc.

From these words it is clearly demonstrated that Boniface lived until December 531 [source text: “521”].

Thus, whether one follows the opinion of Baronius or that of Norisius, several subscriptions of letters must be corrected. Baronius considers Boniface’s letter to Caesarius to have been wrongly dated “on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, 530,” and asserts that the correct reading is “on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in the year 531.”

Norisius maintains that the subscription of Felix’s letter, “on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,” must be corrected; both likewise maintain that the subscription of another letter of the same Felix to Sabina, “on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,” must be corrected.

Since, therefore, in either view several letters are found to have been incorrectly transcribed in their chronological indications and require correction, we can scarcely trust those indications. For this reason, the chronology of Felix—which is confirmed elsewhere by Anastasius and the catalogues—cannot be destroyed on the basis of a single testimony from these subscriptions requiring correction.

This is especially so because, once the single correction to the date of Boniface’s letter to Caesarius is admitted—a correction accepted by Baronius and Sirmondus, so that it should be dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, rather than “in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes”—everything proceeds correctly.

The Council of Orange is said to have been held in July 529. Confirmation was requested from the apostolic see in the autumn of 530. Norisius objects to this one-year delay on the part of Caesarius.

But if one takes into account the cruel wars then disturbing Gaul, during which the wife of Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, accused her stepson before his father of “coveting his father’s kingdom, intending to obtain it by his murder and to extend it as far as Italy, so that he himself might possess the kingdom which his grandfather Theodoric had held in Italy,” and when bloody battles were being fought everywhere—as Petavius gathers from Gregory of Tours, Aimoinus, and Procopius in his *Chronology* under the year 528—it should not seem surprising that the Catholic bishops delayed for a year the preparation of their embassy to the Roman pontiff, lest, amid such widespread suspicion and frequent military disturbances, their petitions directed to Italy should be presumed to have some other purpose.

With prudence and the delay granted, Caesarius sent a letter to Felix during the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in the year of Christ 530, around the beginning of autumn. When the envoy Armenius arrived in the city, he found Felix dead and Boniface elected; from Boniface he received a reply to Caesarius, together with the desired confirmation of the proceedings, dated the eighth day before the Kalends of February in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes—that is, 25 January 531. We leave untouched the dating of Felix’s letter to all the bishops, dated the Kalends of March in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes. Nor do we alter this consulship in another letter of that Felix to Sabina, provided it is read as “the twelfth day before the Kalends of September,” although it is recorded as the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. Boniface’s letters require no correction other than the single one already indicated and accepted by Baronius and Sirmond.

The chronology of the proceedings of the Roman synod celebrated by this same Boniface, and edited by Luca Holstenius, is certain. There the first session begins:

> “After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the consistory of the blessed apostle Andrew, with the venerable lord Pope Boniface presiding…”

This is so, provided that, with Anastasius and the catalogues, we accept that Boniface occupied the see until November of the year 531. Again, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, as we shall say in the following notes.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Line 4.—The Basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, etc.

The Sacred Way beside the temple of the city of Rome. The bishop Ciampini, whom we have often cited, in volume II of *Veterum Monumentorum*, chapter 7, settles the disputes among antiquarians concerning the Temple of Romulus, or the temple of the city of Rome situated there on the Sacred Way. The church of Saints Cosmas and Damian was erected there by Christians and was restored and adorned more magnificently by Felix IV, with sacred images added in mosaic work, which he caused to be made and set on display. Beneath the images appears the following inscription, contained in a six-line hexameter poem:

> The hall of God shines, splendid with radiant metals,  
> In which precious light gleams with greater faith.  
> From the physician-martyrs a sure hope of salvation  
> Comes to the people, and the place has grown through sacred honor.  
> Felix, bishop, offered this worthy gift to the Lord,  
> That he might live in the heavenly citadel of the sky.

Besides the image of Christ the Lord, and those of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of the holy martyrs Cosmas, Damian, and Theodore, that mosaic also displays a figure of Felix IV, adorned with a *colobium* or priestly chasuble and pallium, offering a *proplasma*, or model, of this sacred building, which he himself founded and endowed. But this figure is more recent, having been restored under Urban VIII, since the older one had perished, as Ciampini relates in the same place.

A ground plan of the city of Rome under the emperor Severus, engraved on marble tablets and set by Severus in the pavement of the temple of the city of Rome, as Bellorius demonstrates, was broken during the barbarian ages and recklessly affixed to the walls of this round temple—which is now the vestibule of the sacred church of Saints Cosmas and Damian—without any order or connection being preserved. It was found about 150 years ago, according to Flaminio Vacca, who was present when the masons uncovered it. The Farnese princes rescued it from a second destruction and preserved it in their palace at the Campo dei Fiori in such a way that Cardinal Camillo de’ Massimi could have that precious relic engraved on bronze plates drawn from the original and, adorned with the notes of the distinguished Giovanni Pietro Bellori, commend it to posterity.

### Line 7.—Who was also ordained peacefully, etc.

The Librarian’s words are not idle when he asserts that Felix IV was ordained “peacefully.” For the violence inflicted by the Gothic kings upon the freedom of elections—which Baronius deplores under the year 526, citing from Cassiodorus Athalaric’s letter to the Senate, book VIII, letter 15—had provoked disputes during that two-month vacancy of the see, disputes tending toward the danger of schism. This was the schism that Dioscorus soon afterward provoked at Felix’s death and Boniface’s election, unless the clergy’s votes, by some moderating arrangement and with the prince’s consent, had been harmonized in such a way that the merit of the distinguished candidate was weighed rather than the king’s presumption.

[Note: [Col. 0530D]]

### Line 4.—Here he built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, etc.

This basilica still exists in the city, on the Sacred Way, in the Roman Forum, beside the ruins of the Temple of Peace.

[Note: [Col. 0530D]]

### Line 1.—Felix, by nationality a Samnite, etc.

Giovanni the Deacon, in *Life of Saint Gregory*, book I, chapter 1, thought that Felix IV was the great-great-grandfather of Saint Gregory the Great, the Roman pontiff; after him, Leo of Ostia held the same view in *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 1, near the end. But Baronius, both in the *Annals* and in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* for 25 February, leans toward the opinion that it was not Felix IV but Felix III who was Saint Gregory’s ancestor. “Felix III,” he says, “was a Roman, whereas Felix IV was a Samnite by nationality and a native of Beneventum; and it is clear to everyone that Saint Gregory did not derive his origin from the Samnites but from the ancient Roman senators.” Giovanni the Deacon himself confirms this without hesitation.

Moreover, if we consider the times in which the two Felixes lived, it is more fitting to call Felix III than Felix IV Saint Gregory’s ancestor. For if one counts the years from Felix III’s death to the election of Saint Gregory as pope, one finds that 101 years intervened; but if one counts from the time when Felix IV departed this life to the pontificate of the same Saint Gregory, one counts only sixty years. From this Baronius concludes that it seems more reasonable to call Felix III his ancestor rather than Felix IV, who held the pontificate when Saint Gregory had already been born.

### Line 2.—From the consulship of Mamertinus, etc.

In volume IV of the *Councils* there is a letter of Pope Felix to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, concerning the prohibition against promoting laymen to the priesthood before they had been examined. Baronius had assigned it to Felix III under the year 48, because earlier editions of the *Councils* stated that it was dated on the third day before the Nones of February, after the consulship of M. Severus Boethius, an illustrious man; that consulship falls in that year. But Sirmond restored the true reading of the subscription from the Arles manuscript, which reads:

> “Given on the third day before the Nones of February, after the consulship of Mavortius, in the year 527 of the consul.”

Accordingly, the letter was written not by Felix III, during whose pontificate Caesarius was only a monk, but by Felix IV in the year 528.

Since the faction of the Semi-Pelagians was at that time more powerful in Gaul than episcopal strength could overcome, Caesarius, bishop of Arles, implored the aid of Felix IV, so that he might strike the enemies from a higher position and, once they had been overthrown, preserve Catholic doctrine safe and sound in that most noble province. So writes Cardinal Norisius in book II of his *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 23, where he carefully explains the proceedings of the Second Council of Orange.

A very famous assembly was being held at Orange, at the dedication of the basilica built by Liberius, formerly prefect of the praetorium. Liberius was a close friend of Caesarius, by whom he was restored to health after being wounded by a mortal blow, as Messianus relates in book II of the *Life of Caesarius*, chapter 5. Not only sacred bishops but also the most distinguished men had flocked to Orange. Caesarius therefore seized the opportunity and, having convened a council of bishops and illustrious men, produced the decisions transmitted to him from the apostolic see. This is gathered from the preface of the Second Council of Orange, celebrated on the fifth day before the Nones of July in the year 529, where the following is recited:

> “It has come to our attention that there are some who wish to think about grace and free will less cautiously and not according to the rule of the Catholic faith. Therefore it has seemed right and reasonable to us, in accordance with the authority and admonition of the apostolic see, that we should present for observance by all, and subscribe with our own hands, a few chapters transmitted to us by the apostolic see, chapters collected by the ancient Fathers from specific books of Scripture and especially concerning this matter, so that those who think otherwise than they ought may be instructed. Once these have been read, let anyone who until now has not believed about grace and free will as he ought not delay inclining his mind toward what accords with the Catholic faith.”

Thirteen bishops subscribed to this synod.

Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, presided over this Second Council of Orange as delegate of Felix IV, Roman pontiff, as Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, explicitly teaches in his book *On Predestination*, chapter 12, where he says:

> “For this reason they are called elect: they are elected by grace from the mass of perdition, possessing no merit before they are elected; their very election is the mercy of God, just as in the Council of Orange, over which the blessed Caesarius presided by delegation of the apostolic see, and presented the chapters sent by the apostolic see for all to subscribe and hold. In chapter 14 it is said: ‘No wretched person…’”

Hincmar repeats in the same words that Caesarius presided over the Council of Orange by delegation of the apostolic see, in chapter 22, pages 134 and 142 of Sirmond’s edition. We shall discuss the confirmation of that synod, as well as of the Council of Valence celebrated in 530, under Boniface II, Felix’s successor.

### Line 4.—He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, etc.

It is especially regrettable that Felix’s deeds have been handed down to us so meagerly because of the injuries inflicted by time. The author of the *Book of the Popes*, or Anastasius, says only this about him:

> “He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the city of Rome, at the place called the Sacred Way, beside the temple of the city of Rome. During his time the basilica of Saint Saturninus the Martyr on the Salarian Way was consumed by fire; he restored it from its foundations.”

Since the names of Saints Cosmas and Damian are also recited in the canon of the Mass, we should observe here, following Cardinal Bona, book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 12, section 3, that there were three pairs of saints with the same names, Cosmas and Damian: one pair of martyrs in Arabia, another pair of confessors in Asia, and a third pair of martyrs who suffered martyrdom at Rome. The memory of the first is celebrated in the *Menaea* on 17 October, that of the confessors on 1 November, and that of the Romans on 1 July.

All were physicians by profession and were called *Anargyri*, “the moneyless,” because they treated the sick without payment. From this similarity of profession and names, confusion and mistaken identification could easily arise. It is credible that, after the acts of Cosmas and Damian, the Roman martyrs, had been lost, the Arabs—whose passion was more celebrated—were substituted through ignorance or negligence, so that they began to be honored on 25 September. Florentinius discusses all these matters in his notes on the *Hieronymian Martyrology* for that same day. He observes that Felix IV dedicated this church to the Romans, not the Arabs, and believes that their feast was assigned to 27 September both in the ancient Calendar and in Saint Gregory’s *Book of Sacraments*. These, he considers, are undoubtedly the saints named in the canon of the Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0532C]]

### Line 7.—Who was also ordained peacefully. From book VI, chapter 22.

After King Theodoric had brought about the death of Pope John through the suffering of imprisonment, he arrogated to himself the power of choosing a successor to the apostolic see. To evade the opposition of the Romans more easily, he nominated a man whom he thought would receive the highest dignity by unanimous vote: Felix, of course, the fourth of that name, so distinguished among all for the reputation of his merits that no one could dislike him.

Nevertheless, the clergy, and even the Senate and Roman people, resisted King Theodoric’s tyrannical usurpation with all their strength, as long as they could, until they decided that they had to yield to circumstances, at least on the following condition: that elections in the future should be held by the clergy according to custom, but that the elected man should not exercise the rights of his government until confirmation had been requested from Theodoric or his successors.

The Roman Church groaned beneath the tyrannical yoke that Odoacer had once dared to impose in the election of a pontiff; but Pope Symmachus vigorously shook it off in a Roman council, abolishing the most unjust law. This harsh condition imposed by Theodoric’s overwhelming power was later removed when freedom was restored after the destruction of the Lombards, as we shall say in its proper place.

[Col. 0525]

## 90

Felix, a Samnite by nationality, son of Castorius, occupied the see for four years, two months, and fourteen days [Note: [Col. 0525] B: eighteen days.]. He lived during the reigns of Justin [Note: [Col. 0525] C: and Justinian, emperors,] and of Athalaric, king, from the consulship of Olybrius to that of Lampadius and Orestes. He was also in the time of King Theodoric and of Justin [Note: [Col. 0525] C: Justinian] Augustus, from the consulship of Mamortinus [Note: [Col. 0525] C: Maburti. B: Mavortius] until the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, from the fourth day before the Ides of July until the fourth day before the Ides of October.

He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the city of Rome, at the place called the Sacred Way, beside the temple of the city of Rome. During his time the basilica of Saint Saturninus the Martyr on the Salarian Way was consumed by fire, and he rebuilt it from the ground up.

He was also ordained peacefully and lived until the time of King Athalaric. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, during the months of February and March: fifty-five priests, four deacons, and thirty-nine bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 0525] CB: twenty-nine.].

He was also buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the fourth day before the Ides of October, and the episcopate was vacant for one month and fifteen days [Note: [Col. 0525] CB: three days.].

## LVII. BONIFACE II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 530, THE FOURTH OF JUSTINIAN, THE FIFTH OF ATHALARIC

[Note: [Col. 0533A]]

### In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript

Number 91, line 1: *a Sivigundo* (“from Sivigundus”). Line 2: B reads *Justini* (“of Justin”).

Number 92, line 14: A reads “the fifteenth day before the Kalends”; B, “the seventeenth day before the Kalends.” Line 15: V reads “two months, fifteen days”; indiction 11, “one month, fifteen days.”

### From the manuscripts of the Royal Library, Mazarin, and Thuani

Number 91, line 2: A reads *et Justini* (“and of Justin”). Line 3: “Dioscorus was ordained amid contention in the Constantinian basilica”; B instead reads “in the Julian basilica.” Thus there was dissension among the clergy, people, and Senate for twenty-eight days, until Dioscorus died on the second day before the Ides of October. Line 6: “moved by zeal, after holding a synod, he condemned Dioscorus by a written instrument under the bond of anathema”; and he reconciled the clergy who had consented to Dioscorus’s ordination. He placed that written instrument in the archive of the church, although no one subscribed to it during his episcopate.

Number 92, line 1: “silver dishes to the deacons, subdeacons, and notaries, from the acquired inheritance” (*de adept. h.*). Line 4: “a decree drawn up with the priests’ written declarations, and he exacted an oath from them before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, that in the election of the deacon Vigilius after him they would consent.” At that time another synod was held; and because the priests and all the presbyters had consented, out of reverence for the holy see, and because it was contrary… Line 8: “of treason,” concerning what he had done by his written instrument before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter: the subscription of the deacon Vigilius (M reads *in diaconi*, “in [that] of the deacon”). Therefore, in the presence of all the priests, clergy, and senators, the decree itself was burned in the consistory. Number 92, line 1: *scutellas* (“small dishes”). Line 3: “that they should appoint a successor for him,” which he established with written declarations. Line 7: “of the apostolic see.” Same line: “with reference to him.” Line 14: “on the seventeenth day of October, in the consulship.” Line 15: “the episcopate, two months and fifteen days.”
