A. Petri ipsum constitutum*; abbreviations uncertain).

[Note: [Col. 0535A]]

### Number 91, line 4.—And there was dissension among the clergy and Senate

The Senate defended the rights of the prince. For, as is clear from Athalaric’s letter, it had been commanded that the election of a successor should be conducted under the king’s scrutiny. The Roman clergy, however, defended the freedom of election; hence the whole dispute arose.

The clergy supported Dioscorus—Dioscorus, that is, as I believe, whom Hormisdas had sent as legate to the East during the reign of Justin, whose reports of that completed legation are also extant among Hormisdas’s letters. The Senate, on the other hand, seems to have supported Boniface, because he was Gothic by birth, as the name Sigibuldus, who is said to have been Boniface’s father, indicates.

When Boniface had designated Vigilius as his successor without consulting the prince, the Senate opposed him. There survives the sentence of anathema pronounced by Pope Silverius against Vigilius for this reason:

> “Because, contrary to the canonical laws, during the time of the holy-memory Pope Boniface, while he was still alive, you attempted to have yourself designated, unless the justice of the most distinguished Senate had opposed you…”

Thus two things obstructed the designation presumed by Boniface: the canonical laws and “justice,” that is, the royal presumption, which permitted no pontiff to be designated without the king’s scrutiny.

To prevent the servitude of kings, the clergy believed that it would be more prudent for the pontiff to designate his own successor. Silverius implies that such a designation had not been declared invalid by the pontiff, for he adds:

> “Then, through pastoral prudence and pontifical authority, your already execrable beginnings ought to have been cut off. But while the wicked wound in you was neglected, the incurable abscess grew…”

Yet below it is said that Boniface was compelled, by order of the Senate, to confess himself guilty of treason—page 99, line 9:

> “Because, by his own written subscription, and before the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, he had constituted the deacon Vigilius as his successor…”

That is, guilty of treason against the royal majesty, since the Gothic kings had provided by edict that no other pontiff should be approved without their own consent and scrutiny.

Silverius wished Boniface rather to have determined by his edict that the election of a successor could never be made by anyone or in any circumstances. Meanwhile, writers of the period observe that the Goths had introduced a heavy servitude into all episcopal elections, to such a degree that they claimed the scrutiny for themselves and assessed elected candidates in money.

With regard to the Roman pontiffs, Athalaric wrote the following in a letter to John II, given in Cassiodorus, book IX, number 15:

> “And because everything ought to be regulated according to reason, and things that are excessive cannot be called just, when concern regarding the consecration of the apostolic pontiff has perhaps arisen and the dispute of the people has been brought before our palace, we decree that, when they petition us, we should receive within three thousand solidi, together with the collection of documents…”

He had written earlier:

> “We also wish this to apply to all patriarchal and metropolitan churches…”

Accordingly, he also assesses the confirmation of the other bishops there.

That the exarchs, after Italy had been recovered by the Greeks, awaited the documents of completed elections is taught by Pelagius in a letter addressed to Valerianus, the patrician of the emperor Justinian:

> “For your Eminence ought to remember what God accomplished through you at that time in Istria and Venetia, while the tyrant Totila was in possession and the Franks were devastating everything. Yet you did not permit a bishop of Milan to be made until you had reported the matter from there to the most merciful prince, received again from his written reply what ought to be done, and, amid enemies raging everywhere, both the man who was being ordained and the man who had been ordained were brought to Ravenna by the foresight of your Eminence…”

The origin of this servitude in sacred elections must therefore be attributed to the barbarian Goths and Arians, and even to the Paulianists, who were the first to dare to bring such disputes before the emperor Valerian. Yet these quarrels ought to have been settled either by the apostolic see or by the primate together with his bishops assembled in synod, according to the canonical decrees.

### Line 8.—Yet no one subscribed to him in the episcopate, etc.

Here there was a major controversy, pursued with great contention of spirit, first by the Acacians and then, at this very time, in both East and West: namely, whether the dead could be subjected to anathema.

Some of the Roman clergy had adopted the opinion that the dead ought not to be subjected to anathema. Rusticus, Dioscorus, and others among the Westerners held this view, as their writings testify, showing with what craft the advocates of both sides argued.

Among the arguments of the Acacians, by which they refused to subscribe to the anathema against the already deceased Acacius, their principal argument was that Acacius, while alive, had been condemned only by a bishop belonging to the apostolic see, whereas he had died before other bishops had pronounced an anathema against him.

The previously mentioned Gelasius had already refuted all this, asserting that the East had refused to subscribe to Acacius’s condemnation because the stronger party adhered to his schism and, by its power, obstructed the roads everywhere with guards so that the apostolic rescripts could not be publicly presented.

Thus, when Boniface pronounced a sentence of anathema against the dead Dioscorus, a large part of the clergy, favoring Dioscorus, refused to subscribe to Boniface. Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, gathers much material concerning this controversy in the twelve books published in defense of the Three Chapters. In the catalogue of twelve authors commonly appended to Isidore’s little book *On Illustrious Men*, one reads:

> “Ferrandus, in response to Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons who consulted him about whether it is permissible to condemn anyone after death, issued a rescript in which he spoke as follows, among other things: ‘What benefit is there in disturbing the Church for those who sleep? If someone, accused and condemned while still in this body of death before he deserved to be absolved, has been taken from the Church, he cannot thereafter be absolved by human judgment. If someone accused before the day of sacred examination has been forestalled by a sudden summons, he is to be understood as preserved by divine judgment within the bosom of Mother Church. No human being can pronounce a manifest sentence concerning this. If God has granted him pardon, our severity does him no harm; but if God has prepared punishment, our kindness is of no benefit.’”

From this consultation of Roman deacons and Ferrandus’s reply, it is clear that the controversy was being fiercely debated during Boniface’s pontificate. Facundus discusses the same matter in book IV, chapter 3, where he treats the entire history of the question at length, in volume II of Sirmond’s edition, page 524.

[Note: [Col. 0536C]]

### Number 91, line 1.—Boniface

After a three-day interregnum, in the Basilica of Julius in the year of the Lord 530—the fourth year of Justinian and the second of Athalaric, king of Italy—Boniface II, a Goth by birth, was created pontiff on 15 October. Ado writes in his *Martyrology* that he dedicated a church constructed in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel at the summit of the circus.

### Number 92, line 2.—He convened a synod

Since the Gothic kings had impiously usurped for themselves the election of the Roman pontiff, Boniface judged that the Church should be provided with a means of wresting this presumed and forcibly usurped license from Gothic hands: namely, that he should choose a successor for himself, leaving no vacancy in the see. Although this might have displayed some appearance of justice, it was afterward rejected by everyone.

### Line 5.—At that time another synod was held

This refers to the second Roman synod, by which the acts of the earlier council were rescinded and invalidated.

### Line 13.—The bishop of Carthage

At this time Bishop Reparatus presided over the Church of Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0537A]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

All the catalogues, together with Anastasius, report that Boniface II occupied the see for two years and twenty-six days. We have seen that he was ordained on Sunday, 19 September 530. His death must therefore be assigned to 25 October. The Vatican catalogue, six hundred years old, prefixed to the decree of Anselm of Lucca and edited by Schelestratus in the appendix to volume I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, page 647, states that he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, that is, 27 October. The difference of two days is easily explained as an error admitted by copyists.

The letters he sent to Caesarius of Arles on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, show that he succeeded Felix during that same consulship, around the end of September, since the see was vacant for only three days after Felix died on 25 September.

The Roman synod subscribed after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, shows that Boniface was still alive in the year 531.

Finally, an ancient inscription preserved in the title of Saint Peter ad Vincula shows that in the year called 532—“again after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes”—John, surnamed Mercury, succeeded Boniface after his death, as Cardinal Norisius observes in the cited place, book II of the *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 23. He transcribes the inscription there; we shall provide a more accurate version from the original.

[Col. 0537B]

The succession of Pope John took place in the same year 532, again after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, as that year was drawing to a close. For if Boniface died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, as the testimony of the catalogues asserts, and if the see was then vacant for one month and fifteen days, as the Lucca catalogue published in the *Prolegomena* to volume II, page 19, maintains—namely, until 11 December—then twenty days of that same year remained, during which the inscription could have been dedicated by the priest Severus, while Pope John was still alive, after his election.

Norisius rightly adds that the inept scholiast of Ciaconius should be corrected. The scholiast thinks that the year 531 is designated here by the note “IT PC,” *iterum post consulatum*, “again after the consulship.”

> “Certainly,” says Norisius, “I laugh at Ciaconius’s scholiast, who wittily notes in the margin that the ancients used that abbreviation IT. That is, he says, *iterum*, ‘again,’ meaning the year 531. Absurdly so: for this year is after the consulship; the following year is ‘again after the consulship of Lampadius.’”

## HISTORICAL NOTES

[Col. 0537C] ### Number 92, line 11.—At that time a report came from the African bishops, etc.

This passage should have been transferred by the copyist to the pontificate of John II, Boniface II’s successor, since Boniface died in the year 532 and was succeeded by John II, ordained on 23 January 533.

The council of African bishops held at Carthage—after the recovery of that city, when Gelimer had been defeated by Belisarius in 534—could have been held under Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, only in that same year, 534, or in 535.

While the synodical letters and consultations sent from that council to Pope John concerning the reception into the Church of Arian priests who renounced the Arian heresy were being carried to Rome by the legates, John II died. Therefore Pope Agapetus, John’s successor, ordained on 2 June 535, received the legates and replied to the synodical letter of the African bishops’ council.

For this chronology, consult Ruinart, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part II, chapter 12, number 9.

[Col. 0537D] See also Pagi’s notes on John II, number 11, with which Archbishop Sommier also agrees in *Dogmatic History*, book VI, chapter 26, near the end.

The approval of the Second Council of Orange by Pope Boniface II ought rather to have been inserted here, and it is indeed worth remembering, since, as Cardinal Norisius notes, it put an end to the long struggle of the Semi-Pelagians, which had divided Gaul into factions for more than a hundred years.

The chronology of that synod, badly mishandled by many writers, was successfully restored from reliable documents by the learned Cardinal Norisius, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 22. He arranged the history and showed what Pope Felix IV and what Boniface II, Felix’s successor, decreed in this matter.

For Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles,

> “observing that the faction of the Semi-Pelagians in Gaul was more powerful than it could be overcome by his own strength or that of his colleagues, implored the aid of Felix IV, so that he might strike the enemies from a higher position and, once they had been overthrown, preserve Augustinian as well as Catholic doctrine safe and sound in that most noble province. Felix brought assistance to the petitioner, and he had no need to deliberate long about where aid should be sent to Gaul. For, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, he selected from the ecclesiastical archives the golden statements of Saint Augustine concerning divine grace and free will and sent them to Caesarius, greatly enhancing the renown of Augustine’s name.”

That these chapters, selected from Augustine’s statements and transmitted by the apostolic see, were presented by Caesarius for all to observe and for the Fathers of the council to subscribe is shown by the canons composed from them. Caesarius subscribed to them with the others on the fifth day before the Nones of July, during the consulship of Decius the Younger, an illustrious man—that is, in the year 529.

Thus, as Sirmond writes in volume I of the *Gallican Councils* concerning this synod:

> “The Second Council of Orange ultimately brought an end to the grave and prolonged controversy that for a hundred years and more exercised the holiest and most learned men on both sides in Gaul; it settled the entire dispute concerning grace and free will according to the teaching of Saint Augustine.”

Norisius continues:

> “Caesarius made Felix IV aware of everything he had accomplished in that matter…”

But Pope Felix died on the fourth day before the Ides of October, and he was succeeded by Boniface, Caesarius’s own friend, who replied after receiving the letters from Armenia on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

I shall give the beginning of Boniface’s letter to Caesarius:

> “Through our son Armenius, priest and abbot, we received the letters of your Fraternity, which, as appears, without knowledge of the priesthood entrusted to me—for thus Holstenius read the passage from a very ancient Vatican manuscript—you had sent to us in the charity by which we are bound in God. In them you had believed that you should request that what you had sought from my predecessor, Pope Felix, of blessed memory, for the firmness of the Catholic faith, should be made clear through my intervention. But what has the supernal will arranged? What you had hoped to obtain from him through us, you should rather obtain from us, and so forth.

> “For you indicate that certain bishops of Gaul wish the faith by which we believe in Christ to be of nature and not of grace, although all other good things have already come to them by the grace of God; and they wish that faith to have remained in human beings from Adam by free will—which it is impious to say—and not also now to be conferred upon each person by the generosity of divine mercy. You ask us, in order to remove this ambiguity, to confirm by the authority of the apostolic see your confession, in which you define, in accordance with the truth of the Catholic faith, that the right faith in Christ and the beginning of every good will are inspired in the minds of individuals by the prevenient grace of God…

> “Many Fathers, and especially Augustine, bishop of blessed memory, as well as our predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see, are reported to have discussed this matter so extensively that no ambiguity ought to remain concerning it: faith itself also comes to us by grace…

> “We rejoice that, after consultation with certain priests of Gaul, your Fraternity has understood this in accordance with the Catholic faith, especially in those matters in which, as you indicated, they defined by common agreement that the faith by which we believe in Christ is conferred by the prevenient grace of the divinity. They added also that absolutely no good thing according to God can anyone will, begin, perform, or complete without the grace of God, as the Savior himself says: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15), and so forth.

> “Therefore, greeting you with fitting affection, we approve the confession written above as consistent with the rules of the Catholic Fathers…”

The letter is subscribed:

> “Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men.”

There is also mention there of the synod celebrated by Caesarius.

Who could suppose that Caesarius wrote to the apostolic see after a year to say that he had convened a synod at Orange? Therefore he must be understood to have informed Pope Felix in the same year, 529, of the council he had celebrated.

While Armenius was carrying the letters to Rome, Felix died in that same year, 529, and Boniface succeeded him. Boniface replied to Caesarius in January of the following year.

Certainly the subscriptions of Felix’s letters, which are dated in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, must be corrected from this subscription of Boniface, especially since Baronius himself says that the other letter to Sabina, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, should be corrected by the same erasure.

But Baronius and the others, commonly following Anastasius, also establish the end of Boniface’s pontificate incorrectly, on 17 October after the consulship of Lampadius. Their view is refuted by the evident falsehood of the *Acts of the Roman Synod* celebrated by Boniface himself and edited by Luca Holstenius, where the first session begins:

> “After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the consistory of the blessed apostle Andrew, with the venerable lord Pope Boniface presiding…”

From this it is clearly demonstrated that Boniface lived until December of the year 531.

[Col. 0539D]

> “Hence it came about that, through the decrees of these two pontiffs—Felix IV and Boniface II—the errors of Cassianus, Faustus, and the other men of the same teaching were afterward rejected by all orthodox Christians as heresies and could no longer be numbered among indifferent matters. Thus the very long controversy, which had divided Gaul into factions for a hundred years and more, was finally brought to an end by both pontiffs, the case having been adjudicated in Augustine’s favor.”

[Note: [Col. 0539D]]

### Number 91, line 2.—He was ordained with Dioscorus amid contention

Dioscorus was substituted for the deceased Felix by the clergy, which had split into two factions, not without a suspicion of simony, as King Athalaric openly reports to John II, Roman pontiff. He appeared likely to have greater influence in the Roman pontificate than Boniface; but a great revolt among the clergy and the death of Dioscorus brought the contest to an end.

[Col. 0540A] No. 92, line 4. “So that they might appoint a successor for him.” The Gothic kings ruling Italy had impiously claimed for themselves the election of the Roman pontiff. But in order that the Roman Church might wrest from Gothic hands this license, presumed and usurped by force, Boniface used this pretext to undertake a new course, one not previously attempted by his predecessors—namely, that a pontiff, when selecting a successor, should leave no vacancy in the vacant see. Although this indeed had some appearance of justice, it was later rejected and rescinded by everyone.]

[Note: [Col. 0540A]

No. 92, line 1. “Here he offered to the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and notaries small distributions from inheritances acquired, and aided the clergy, endangered by famine, with many provisions.” Monthly *sportulae*, or grain allowances, were distributed to priests, deacons, and the lesser clergy. Cyprian (*Epistle* 34): “Moreover, you should already know that we have designated for them the honor of the presbyterate, so that they may be honored with the same allowances as the presbyters, and that the distributions may be divided in equal quantities according to the measure” [read *mensurnae*, “monthly”]. Hence clerics who received monthly allowances from the Church’s storehouse were called “allowance-sharing brothers.” The same author (*Epistle* 66): “In honor of the allowance-sharing brothers, let them receive from the altar and sacrifices as though they were receiving tithes from the fruits, and let them not withdraw.” Or “measure-sharing brothers.” The same author (*Epistle* 28): “Meanwhile, let them abstain from the division among those who share the measure, not as though they seemed deprived of ecclesiastical ministry, but so that they may be brought intact in every respect into our presence.”

Such grain allowances, or *sportulae*, were distributed to the clergy by means of *scutulae*, or *scutellae*—that is, by tokens or signs called *scutulae* or *scutellae*, because they were shaped like a shield or little shield. *Scutella* is a diminutive of *scutula*, which means a sign shaped like a shield or little shield. Cassian (*Conferences* I, chapter 5): “They strive to hurl darts or arrows into a very small shield, which contains within itself a painted representation of prizes.” And this is what Boniface is said here to have offered to the priests and clerics: *scutellae* from the Church’s goods—that is, portions of the goods accruing to the Church through the testament or donation of the faithful—for this kind of distribution was made by means of *scutellae*, that is, by signs or tokens. Hence the distributions of provisions, or the provisions themselves, were called *scutellae*. It is a case of the sign being used for the thing signified, just as in the books of law grain tokens are taken for the grain allowances that were provided by means of a token: *Lex Mortuo*, § 1; *Lex Titia*, *De legatis* 2. Elsewhere *scutella* means the vessel in which stew is placed. John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 23: “To whom you gave twelve gold pieces and a silver dish, which your blessed mother Sylvia had sent you with legumes poured into it.”]

Line 3. “Here he convened a synod in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle and issued a decree that he should appoint a successor for himself.” Boniface II, in a Roman synod, issued a decree permitting him to designate his successor, and chose the deacon Vigilius as successor, after obtaining a written pledge and oath from the Roman clergy. But Boniface, repenting of what he had done, rescinded the action in a second synod, because it had been carried out contrary to the canons. A Roman pontiff cannot designate his successor: canon “If anyone is a pope,” final canon of Distinction 29; canon “To the Bishop,” and following, Question 8, chapter 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0540D]

No. 92, line 3. “He convened a synod in the basilica of blessed Peter,” etc. Baronius explains from Anastasius two Roman synods held under Boniface. In the first, convened in the basilica of Saint Peter, Boniface “issued a decree that he should appoint his successor; and by that decree, with the written pledges of the priests and an oath before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, he appointed the deacon Vigilius”—that is, as successor. Baronius writes that, since the Gothic kings had impiously usurped for themselves the election of the Roman pontiff, Boniface judged it advantageous to the Church, in order to wrest this usurped license from Gothic hands, that he should choose his own successor without leaving a vacancy in the see. Although this did have some appearance of justice, it was later rejected and rescinded by everyone.

For, as the same Anastasius adds, “at the same time”—or, rather, not long afterward—“a synod was held again, and all the priests judged this” [cancelled it] “out of reverence for the holy see, because this had been done contrary to the canons, and because the fault rested upon him, in that he had appointed a successor for himself. Pope Boniface himself confessed that he was guilty of treason against the majesty of the state, because he had appointed the deacon Vigilius as his successor by his own written subscription before the confession of blessed Peter, and he burned that very decree in the presence of all the priests, clergy, and senate.”

Baronius also says that Boniface could have appeared guilty of treason against majesty to the Goths because he had appointed a successor for himself against the will of the king, to whom Theodoric had assigned the election of the Roman pontiff. But what he adds—that this decree had been made by Boniface in the earlier Roman synod through the ambition and advice of Vigilius—cannot stand, as is clear from the decree of anathema issued by Pope Silverius against Vigilius, since, as will be shown below in the section on Silverius, that decree is spurious.

After Baronius’s death, Lucas Holstenius, prefect of the Vatican Library, published in the *Roman Collection*, from the Barberini Library, a third synod convened at Rome by Boniface II. It consists of two sessions. It was held after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, and therefore in the year 531, in the case of Stephen, bishop of Larissa and metropolitan of Thessaly. Stephen had been canonically elected and ordained, but soon, through the faction of Probianus, one of his suffragans, and other wicked men, had been irregularly deposed by Epiphanius, patriarch of Constantinople, and had appealed to the Apostolic See.

Stephen sent his petitions of complaint [Col. 0541C] and appeal through Theodosius, bishop of Echinium in Thessaly, enclosing letters of the Roman pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Innocent I, Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo. By these he proved that the Roman pontiff had always governed the churches of Illyricum by patriarchal right, in addition to the right of primacy by which he presides over the universal Church. The same Theodosius, bishop of Echinium, distinguished these two powers very well in Session II, saying:

“For it is established that the venerable pontiffs of your see, although the Apostolic See rightly claims for itself the primacy of the churches throughout the entire world, and although it is necessary to appeal to it alone from everywhere in ecclesiastical cases, have nevertheless specially claimed the churches of Illyricum for their own administration.”]

Line 13. “He was buried,” etc. “In the consulship of Lampadius,” etc. At the end of the pontificate of Felix IV, a synod was held at Valencia. Around August of the year 530, Caesarius sent the abbot Armenius to Rome to obtain from Felix IV confirmation of what had been defined in the synods of Orange and Valencia. That the latter synod was confirmed by Boniface is expressly stated by the author of the *Life of Saint Caesarius*, who, after the words cited above, adds:

“Boniface, pope of the Roman Church, of blessed memory, having learned of the same struggle, trampled the designs of the disputants and confirmed Saint Caesarius’s case by apostolic authority.”

Felix IV had already died and Boniface II had been ordained when Armenius arrived in Rome. In his letter to Caesarius, which appears in volume IV of the councils, p. 1687, Boniface says:

“Through our son Armenius, priest and abbot, we received a letter from your Fraternity, which, as appears, you had sent to us, still unaware of the priesthood entrusted to me, in the charity by which we are bound in God. In it you believed that you should request that what you had sought from our predecessor, Pope Felix, of blessed memory, for the security of the Catholic faith, might be fulfilled through my diligence. But since heavenly will arranged that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us, you should rather obtain from us, we did not delay giving a Catholic answer to your petition, which you conceived with praiseworthy concern for the faith.”

And below:

“Therefore, greeting your confession with fitting affection, we approve the confession set forth above as consonant with the regulations of the Fathers.”

By these words the Second Synod of Orange is confirmed. Hence, in the Fossatensis and Laudunensis manuscripts, the cited letter of Boniface II to Caesarius is placed before the Second Synod of Orange, with this note:

“In this manuscript is contained the Synod of Orange, which Saint Pope Boniface confirmed by his authority.”

Moreover, the statement at the end of the letter that it was issued “on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, illustrious men”—that is, in the year 530—was added to the letter, because Felix IV died only on 18 September of that year, and Boniface was substituted for him three days later. On these matters, see Baronius’s critical discussion under the years 529 and following.

Anastasius writes that Boniface I [sic] occupied the see for two years and twenty-six days, and that he was buried in the basilica [Col. 0542B] of blessed Peter the apostle on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Lampadius. But it should be read, “again after the consulship of Lampadius,” by which formula the year 532 is indicated, as is demonstrated in the same critical discussion of Baronius under the year 531. Therefore, since Boniface began his pontificate on 21 September 530, he died on 16 October 532 and was buried on 17 October of the same month.]

[Note: [Col. 0542B]

No. 92, line 11. “A report arrived from the African bishops concerning the decree,” etc. It is appropriate to recall that the African bishops consulted the Apostolic See about more serious matters, as we shall see in the immediately following pontificate of John II. Meanwhile, it should be observed, on the authority of the distinguished Archbishop Sommier, that under this Boniface other metropolitans and bishops likewise did not cease to vindicate the rights of the Roman see—both by reason of its primacy over all the churches and by reason of its Western patriarchate, which included the provinces within this region—from the attacks and presumptuous acts of usurpers.

He produces an illustrious document concerning the provinces of Illyricum in Book VI, chapter 23, of the *Dogmatic History*, where he is discussing events under Boniface II. He explains it as follows:

“In the council held at Rome concerning the appeal to the Holy See lodged by Stephen, metropolitan of Larissa in Thessaly, whom the patriarch of Constantinople had deposed, the petition of that metropolitan was read, composed in these words:

“‘Since no ecclesiastical order can surpass that power of yours which has been conferred upon you by the Savior of all and the first shepherd, nothing is too small or humble for your providence to consider. Since you surpass everyone before God, you must reflect all the more deeply, because this is the proof of those who love God; and after God, Saint Peter, father and teacher of the holy Church—both yours and that of the whole world—bears witness to this, etc.

“‘While Probus, of blessed memory, who had been made bishop of the Church of Larissa, was at rest . . . the holy synod of the province, the possessors of the entire city, and the whole body of the Church assembled; and by the common testimony of all, with nothing taken away from custom, I was ordained bishop . . . But, I do not know how incited, Antonius the priest, Probianus, bishop of the city of Demetrias, etc., suddenly departed for the royal city. They composed an accusation and laid complaints before Epiphanius, archbishop of that same city, saying that my ordination was in no way consistent with the sacred canons. He sent a written warning to the province of Thessaly, ordering me to withdraw from sacred ministry, as one not ordained according to the canons.

“‘But I, looking to the primacy over the holy churches entrusted to you, said that if I had to answer some accuser, or if anything concerning my ordination had to be judged, it was necessary for me to state my case not before him who deigned to judge it, but elsewhere, before one under whom the law of the sacred canons is preserved and the custom maintained to this day. I invoked the memory of your holy head and of the Apostolic See, saying that you are the lords of this examination.

“‘Nor could these measures suffice for my peace. Against my will I was led to the royal city . . . I am guilty of no offense except that I agreed with those who elected me, and because I stated confidently that if any examination had to be conducted, it ought to be conducted by him who had been established as the lord of this examination. I confess that I expect worse things from those who threaten me: condemnation, exile, and undeservedly every kind of criminal punishment . . . Therefore I beseech you to bring me your assistance, remembering your own blessed see and that of your predecessors, for they have never suffered any unjust harm from anyone. This is your task, most blessed one: day and night to preserve the laws and decrees of the holy Fathers and of your venerable and Apostolic See in all the churches, but especially in your province of Illyricum.

“‘Some of those who elected me and repeatedly confirmed their election in their letters, so that I might be judged worthy of the priesthood, seeing that it was my purpose to restore the ancient custom in our holy churches, accused me separately before the most blessed bishop of the holy Church of the royal city. He, accepting the accusation without first examining anything that ought to be investigated concerning an accused bishop, immediately separated me from all ecclesiastical ministry . . . When the most religious man who was carrying the order came to Thessalonica, I immediately said to him: It is proper that the Apostolic See—that is, your blessedness—both hear and settle the cases of our province. But the most holy archbishop of the royal city did not desist; he even ordered that I be brought before him contrary to the canons. When I arrived, he convened the bishops residing there, and I did not delay once again making this appeal, imploring the see of the holy and blessed head, your Apostolic See, and declaring that the custom which has prevailed in our province until now ought not to be overthrown. I begged that the authority of the Apostolic See—which was given by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the sacred canons, and which has likewise preserved the ancient custom—not be violated in any respect.

“‘But he was unwilling to withdraw from his purpose . . . Those who, as I believe, are plotting against my life, sensing that you vindicate the order of the holy churches, used every effort to accomplish their will before any decision of yours could arrive. I begged that no sentence be pronounced before the proceedings were reported to your blessedness, so that the examination of the case might be reserved to you. This statement incited them still further against me, since they thought that something was being taken away from the right of the churches of the royal city, because I appeared to have named your Apostolic See.

“‘For I said that the authority of the Apostolic See, which was given by God and by our Savior, the supreme one among the apostles, surpasses all the privileges of the holy churches, and that all the churches of the world rest in its confession. After the sentence had been read, I again implored a just hearing before you, since no dispute by anyone could disturb your justice . . . When the sentence had been reread, I was immediately handed over to custody, to men who profess to love God and to be defenders of the sacred Church, so that I could not hasten to the feet of your blessedness.

“‘Let no one, following this example, dare to say anything about the rights of our holy churches, or to mention their antiquity or the rights that they have held until now, because their purpose is to make us wretched through the subordination and jurisdiction of the holy Church of the royal city. For all these things we pour out tears day and night before Jesus Christ, our God and Savior of all, mourning and displaying our miserable gray hairs, beseeching you not to allow us to be delivered into their hands. For these reasons we appeal both to your blessedness and to the Apostolic See, hoping that you will deign to correct these matters with suitable correction and grant a remedy, so that the man who loves God and who, striving to preserve the rights of the Apostolic See, appears to have endured such great dangers, may be restored to his office by apostolic authority. Look also to the future, so that the custom of the holy churches of our province may in no way be overthrown . . . for their purpose does not cease with Stephen, the man who loves God. They will do these things to many others as well, and they will not rest until they have brought their desires to fulfillment.’”

One of the bishops delegated by the provincials said the following orally:

“From the report contained in the petitions, your blessedness learns what has been done against the sacred canons and the ordinations of your predecessors. For it is established that the venerable pontiffs of your see, although the Apostolic See rightly claims for itself the primacy of the churches throughout the entire world, and although it is necessary to appeal to it alone from everywhere in ecclesiastical cases, have nevertheless specially claimed the churches of Illyricum for their own administration.”

It is therefore evident that both rights—the right of the Western patriarchate and that of the supreme pontificate—were recognized in one and the same person, the Roman pontiff, through the petitions recited here and through the declaration of the Greek bishop. The latter assembled the testimonies of earlier Roman pontiffs, as well as imperial laws, plainly declaring that Illyricum, along with the other provinces, was considered part of the Western patriarchate. We have presented these documents above in the sections on the holy pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Boniface I, Celestine I, Sixtus III, and Leo the Great.

Although no judgment of Boniface II concerning this case survives, there can nevertheless be no doubt that they pronounced the requests of the bishop of Larissa, metropolitan of Thessaly, just.]

[Col. 0533]

91

Boniface, a Roman by nationality, son of Sigilbuld [Note: [Col. 0533] C: Sigebuld. B: Sigisvulthus.], occupied the see for two years and twenty-six [Note: [Col. 0533] B: one year, two days, from the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes to the year 531, with the consulship vacant.] days. He lived during the reign of Athalaric, the heretical king, and of the emperor Justinian. He was ordained in a contested election together with Dioscorus. Dioscorus was ordained in the Constantinian basilica, while Boniface was ordained in the basilica of Julius. There was disagreement in the clergy and senate for twenty-eight days [Note: [Col. 0533] C: twenty-nine.]. At the same time Dioscorus II died [Note: [Col. 0533] C: on the preceding day.] on the Ides of October [Note: [Col. 0533] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 530.]. During those days Boniface, led by zeal and deceit, reconciled the clergy under the bond of an anathematizing written pledge, with great bitterness. He shut that written pledge away in the Church archive [Note: [Col. 0533] C: closed it up.], as though condemning Dioscorus. And he assembled the clergy. Yet no one subscribed to him in the episcopate, although a very large multitude had supported Dioscorus.

92 Here he offered to the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and notaries a small distribution [Note: [Col. 0533] C: small distributions.] from inheritances acquired, and aided the clergy, endangered by famine, with many provisions. Here he convened a synod in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle and issued a decree that they should appoint a successor for him [Note: [Col. 0533] See Baronius under the year 531.]. By that decree, with the written pledges of the priests and an oath before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, he appointed the deacon Vigilius [Note: [Col. 0533] “Appointed,” namely, as successor.]. At the same time another synod was held, and all the priests judged this [Note: [Col. 0533] B: cancelled it.] out of reverence for the holy see. And because this had been done contrary to the canons, and because the fault rested upon him in that he had appointed a successor for himself, Pope Boniface himself confessed that he was guilty of treason against majesty, because he had appointed the deacon Vigilius as his successor by his own written subscription before the confession of blessed Peter the apostle; and he burned that very decree in the presence of all the priests, clergy, and senate. At the same time a report arrived from the African bishops concerning the decree that the bishop of Carthage should do everything with the counsel of the Apostolic See. He too was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle on the sixteenth [Note: [Col. 0533] C: seventeenth.] day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Lampadius, and the episcopate was vacant for six days [Note: [Col. 0533] C: two months and fifteen days.].

LVIII. JOHN II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 531, THE FIFTH YEAR OF JUSTINIAN, THE SIXTH OF ATHALARIC.
