[Note: [Col. 0545A]

Line 3. “At the same time the religious man Augustus sent his profession of faith, written in his own hand, to the Apostolic See through bishops,” etc. The emperor Justinian sent a profession of faith to Pope John II, in accordance with ancient custom. Pope Symmachus, in his *Apology against Anastasius*:

“All Catholic rulers, whether when they assumed the governance of the empire or when they recognized that new pontiffs had been instituted for the Apostolic See, immediately sent their writings to it, so that they might show themselves to be participants in it. Therefore, those who have not done this declare themselves alienated from it; and we could also establish this from their own documents before you, unless we were avoiding you as a rival, an accused party, an enemy, and a judge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0545B]

Line 4. “He sent his profession of faith.” In former times the emperors of the East, when they were about to assume the rights of imperial rule, were required to present to the patriarch of Constantinople and to the Apostolic See a public profession of their faith, subscribed with their own hand as well. This custom is mentioned by Evagrius, Book III, chapter 32, where he speaks of the emperor Anastasius:

“But there were other matters that secretly troubled Anastasius. For when Ariadne [Col. 0545C] wished to clothe Anastasius in the imperial purple, Euphemius, bishop of the royal city, refused to give his consent until Anastasius had given him a written guarantee, written in his own hand and confirmed by oath, in which he promised that, if he obtained the empire, he would preserve the faith undefiled and introduce nothing new into the holy Church of God. He had entrusted this document to Macedonius, keeper of the sacred vessels. He had done this because many believed Anastasius to be devoted to the sect of the Manichaeans. After Macedonius had obtained the episcopal see, Anastasius wanted his guarantee returned to him, claiming that it was an insult to the empire if the aforementioned written document continued to be kept in the Church. But when Macedonius resisted with great firmness and denied that he would betray the faith, Anastasius attacked him with every kind of plot in order to deprive him of the episcopate,” etc.

In the end he obtained this by employing various stratagems. Such importance did the emperor’s profession have for exposing his deceptions. Hence the great care exercised by the churches in retaining and preserving ecclesiastical documents entrusted to the person who guarded the Church’s most precious possessions.

Symmachus boldly asserts that both Anastasius and his predecessors had sent their profession of faith to the Apostolic See. In his seventh letter to Anastasius he writes:

“All Catholic rulers, whether when they assumed the governance of the empire or when they recognized that new pontiffs had been instituted for the Apostolic See, immediately sent their writings to them, so that they might show themselves to belong to that institution,” etc.

Felix III likewise charges the same emperor with perjury committed against the profession of faith previously sent to the Apostolic See (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 815):

“I bring to the recollection of your piety your profession and conscience. Have the archives of your palace reviewed, and diligently investigate those documents which your piety, returning to the height of supreme power, sent to my predecessor in common congratulation,” etc.

Justin did the same with Hormisdas, and now Justinian has done so with John II. That such authentic imperial professions were carefully and reverently preserved at Constantinople in the repository of the sacred vessels, and likewise at Rome, is testified by Gregory II, who writes the following to Leo the Isaurian (*Councils*, vol. IV, p. 2):

“We carefully preserve the letters you sent, deposited in the holy Church at the threshold of the confession of Saint Peter, glorious and chief of the apostles; there too are the letters of your predecessors who ruled as emperors and loved Christ,” etc.]

Line same. “Written in his own hand.” This was an authority intended as testimony and to provide an indisputable document, as was noted above from Marculphus. He calls it “written in his own hand” not because the letter was merely subscribed by the imperial hand, but because it was also written in imperial ink. That this was the characteristic of imperial documents Gregory states in the same place:

“But this is especially important: your letters are carefully sealed with the imperial seals, and the internal subscriptions are accurately written in cinnabar by your own hand, as it is customary for emperors to write.”

Thus the distinguishing feature of an imperial rescript—or the means by which one could detect that a document was written by the emperor himself—was the use of cinnabar. Procopius, revealing Justin’s ignorance of letters, takes the opportunity to describe imperial ink, saying that it was a mixture of cinnabar and other liquids, from which writings were called “Phoenician,” [Col. 0546D] and he adds (*Secret History*, p. 26):

“The reed, colored with the dye with which emperors customarily write,” etc.

These colors sometimes occur in very ancient manuscripts. They are suitable for preserving letters from the ravages of time because of the perfection of the mixture. Indeed, in manuscripts such Phoenician letters often remain while the rest, written with another mixture, have disappeared.

The mixture is described by the same Procopius in the same place. Hence Anastasius, in his marginal notes on the Acts of the Eighth Synod, asserts that it was always the duty of a court official of a particular rank to prepare this imperial ink and preserve it for the emperor’s use:

“The superintendent of the *caniclium* is the one who manages and guards the *caniclium*, that is, the inkstand from which the emperor writes Phoenician letters on documents,” etc.

It also appears in the *Code*, Book VI, under “Various Rescripts”:

“Whatever sacred utterances the authority of our mildness writes in any part of the pages, it commands that they be displayed with no other appearance or color than a purple inscription—that is, marked with the brilliance of boiled murex and crushed shell. No one is permitted or authorized to possess this sacred encaustic,” etc.

On this matter, see Salmasius on Solinus. The dignity of this office was called that of the *Caniclinus*, concerning which Pachymeres writes in Book VIII, chapter 32, and Book IX, chapter 24, and frequently elsewhere among Byzantine authors.

The rescripts called “sacred utterances” issued by the emperor Leo were of this sort. The law is repeated in Book IV of the *Code*, under “Various Rescripts”:

“He ordered that they be displayed with no other appearance or color than an inscription alone, so that they might be marked by the brilliance of boiled murex and crushed shell. Only those documents in which the prince’s notation and subscriptions had been impressed on sheets or parchment were permitted to be produced or called rescripts in any court,” etc.

This was the law of Leo the Elder, who first devised the practice for rescripts. The ancients, however, were accustomed to write with red lead. On this Pliny writes in Book XXXIII, chapter 7:

“Red lead is also used in writing volumes, and it makes the letters more distinct, whether on gold, or even on marble, including on tombs,” etc.

M. Crusius testifies in his *Turco-Graecia*, p. 191, that he saw a council of Constantinople in which the subscription of John Cantacuzenus was in cinnabar, while those of the bishops were in ink. Among the Colbert manuscripts there is also preserved a subscription of John Palaeologus in the same ink.

The vessel in which it was stored was golden and decorated with precious stones, as we learn from Nicetas, in *Manuel*, Book III, no. 4:

“A golden inkstand adorned with pearls and the most precious gems,” etc.

On this matter one should also consult Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 13.]

[Note: [Col. 0547C]

Line 1. “John, surnamed Mercury.” According to an ancient inscription at Saint Peter ad Vincula, John, surnamed Mercury, was elected Roman pontiff toward the end of that year, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes—that is, in the year 531 from the birth of Christ, the fifth year of the emperor Justinian and the sixth of Athalaric, king of Italy.]

[Note: [Col. 0547D]

Line 4. “He sent his profession of faith.” This refers to the profession of faith contained in Justinian’s letter to Pope John, not to the longer edict prefixed in the Surian edition with the following faulty title:

“Edict of the most devout emperor Justinian containing a confession of faith and a refutation of the heresies opposed to the Catholic Church of God, transmitted to Pope John II, as is clear from the life of that same pope in the *Book of the Pontiffs*.”

I have said that this title is faulty because it is established that the edict—or rather, the tract—was written in the time of Vigilius. Theodorus, bishop of Caesarea, induced the emperor himself to issue it against the Three Chapters, as Liberatus testifies in chapter 24 of the *Breviary*.]

[Note: [Col. 0547D]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

The dates of John II, surnamed Mercury, and of his successor Agapetus can be established more securely if they are joined together. For the manuscripts of Anastasius and the catalogues agree both in assigning John a reign of two years, four months, and six days; in counting six or seven days of vacancy of the see from his death to the election of Agapetus; and in assigning Agapetus a total of eleven months and eighteen or nineteen days. The Librarian records that Agapetus departed for Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May—although others think that “the tenth day before the Kalends of March” should be read—and that there, overcome by illness, he died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May in the following year. His body was therefore brought back to Rome and buried in the Vatican basilica on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, on which day his memory is commemorated.

Thus a total of three years and four months must be reckoned from the beginning of John’s pontificate to the death of Agapetus. A few days must be added to this total, namely the days between Agapetus’s election and ordination, if the historian reckoned his epoch from the day of consecration rather than from the day of election.

We have demonstrated in the preceding section that John’s beginning should be placed on 12 December, following his election in the year 532. Since the death of Agapetus must be fixed on the tenth day before the Kalends of May—that is, 22 April—as the manuscripts of Anastasius have it, and since it is assigned to the year 536, as we have assigned it, the interval from the beginning of John to the end of Agapetus is three years, four months, and ten days.

From this total we assign John two years, four months, and six days, reckoned from his election on 12 December 532 to 18 April 535. To Agapetus we assign eleven months and eighteen days, counted backward from the certain date of his death, 22 April 536, to 6 May 535.

The seventeen days that intervened in the year 535 between John’s death on 18 April and the consecration of his successor Agapetus on 6 May—which was a Sunday—should therefore be divided as follows. With Anastasius, we assign seven days to the vacancy of the see, from the day of John II’s death, 18 April, to 25 April 535. We assign the election of Agapetus to the following day, 26 April; from that date to 6 May, the ten remaining days elapsed between the election and the ordination of Agapetus.

Since, therefore, the total of the two periods agrees when joined at both ends, and since the manuscripts of Anastasius agree with the catalogues in assigning John two years, four months, and six days, anyone who, like us, places the beginning of John on 12 December 532 must place his death on 18 April 535. Anyone who then counts seven days of vacancy of the see to the election of his successor Agapetus, assigning that election to 25 or 26 April, correctly places the ordination of Agapetus after a further ten days, on 5 May. That day was the fourth Sunday after Easter in that year; Easter had been celebrated on 8 April.

Near the end of the Librarian’s section, the text reports that John was buried in the basilica of the chief of the apostles on the sixth day before the Ides of June, again after the consulship of Lampadius. Through the negligence of a copyist, the note concerning the consulship was transferred from the election and ordination by which he assumed the episcopate to the end of his pontificate and life. For the year 532 of the common Christian era, which bears the designation “again after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,” belongs to the beginning of John’s assumption of office. Clear evidence of this survives in the ancient marble inscription of Saint Peter [Col. 0548D] ad Vincula, which has often been published by other chronologists and historians. I would reproduce it here from my prolegomena to volume I, no. 42, were it not that I quoted it two pages earlier with Norisius in the chronological notes on Boniface II.

HISTORICAL NOTES.

Line 1. “John, surnamed Mercury.” In the Laurentian Anastasius of the Laurentian Library of Florence, this pontiff is called Mercury.

Line 3.—“The religious man Augustus, etc. He sent his confession, etc.” I shall not repeat what you can read, learnedly gathered in the notes of Pagi and Sommier, concerning John II’s approval of these letters of Justinian. I shall indicate only one addition from the epistle of Mopinot mentioned above: toward the end of section 12, he tells us that Constantius composed another dissertation in which he “demonstrates that the expression ‘One of the Trinity was crucified’—which John II approved, although Hormisdas had refused to use it—was nevertheless not a point on which either pope opposed the other; indeed, that the faith and intention of both were the same, since, given the different circumstances of the times and controversies, one had necessarily to adopt a different course of action from the other.”

[Note: [Col. 0549A]

Line 1.—“John, who is also Mercury.” This pontiff is mentioned in an ancient marble tablet placed in the basilica of St. Peter ad Vincula.]

[Note: [Col. 0549A]

Line 2.—“He sat for two years.” During the interregnum, several men had squandered the Church’s goods in order to prepare a way for themselves to attain the pontificate, while others had corrupted certain senators with money. The senate, indignant at this, promulgated a senatorial decree against those who had thereby disgracefully accepted something. Pope John, however, after his election, acted with King Athalaric so that those who trampled upon the ecclesiastical canons might be terrified by the king’s edict. Through the Church’s defensor, he asked Athalaric to exercise royal power against such Simoniacs and to restrain them by secular penalties—men whom neither fear of God nor ecclesiastical censure could correct. Athalaric issued an edict against the Simoniacs, by which the senatorial decree of which we spoke at the beginning of the pontificate of Felix IV was confirmed. It is preserved in Cassiodorus, book IX, letter 15, and in Baronius under the year 533.

Line 4.—“He sent his confession in a handwritten document, etc.” Under the pontificate of Hormisdas we said that the Scythian monks endured many hardships of travel and many labors in defense of the proposition, “One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh.” This proposition was eventually approved by John II. The Scythian monks were vigorously opposed by other monks called Ace­metes. When these saw that the Scythians’ cause was prevailing, and that the proposition was approved both by the Eastern bishops and by the emperor Justinian, they were inflamed by a kind of rivalry and sent envoys to John II in the year 533—Cyrus and Eulogius—to defend before the Apostolic See the opinion, or error, into which they had been carried by the heat of the struggle, and to obtain its approval from the supreme pontiff.

The error of the Acemetes consisted in their denying that “one of the Trinity was incarnate and suffered in the flesh,” and that blessed Mary was truly and properly the Mother of God. Against them Justinian sent to Rome Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, and Demetrius of Philippi, to consult the Apostolic See on these questions and to obtain approval of the emperor’s faith—indeed, of the faith of the entire Eastern Church—as set out in his letter to the Roman pontiff, which is preserved in volume IV of the Councils, page 1742.

Pope John, therefore, after receiving the letters of the emperor Justinian and his embassy, about which we shall speak shortly, examined in a Roman synod this proposition, “One of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh.” He approved the profession of faith inserted in the emperor’s letters, as well as the edict of faith which the emperor had promulgated before sending the embassy, lest the Acemete envoys contrive some accusation against him. “Accordingly,” John says in his letter to Justinian, dated 25 March under the consulship of Justinian Augustus and Paulinus, and therefore in the year 534, preserved in volume IV of the Councils, page 1744, “we have received, with customary reverence, the letters of Your Serenity conveyed by Hypatius and Demetrius, most holy men, my brothers and fellow bishops. From their report we have also learned that you proposed to the faithful peoples a decree motivated by love of the faith and by the removal of heretical controversy, in accordance with apostolic teaching and with the consent of our brothers and fellow bishops. Since it accords with apostolic teaching, we confirm it by our authority.”

In the same letter the pontiff deprived the Acemete monks, who persisted obstinately in error, of communion unless they returned to sound understanding: “Among them,” he says, “observing what had been decreed by their own pontiff, we did not receive them into our communion, and we ordered them to be separated from the whole Catholic Church unless, after condemning their error, they should promptly follow our teaching and attest this by a regular profession.”

In the same year, 534, Pope John, for the same reason, wrote to Avienus, Liberius, and other senators. These letters are preserved in the same volume of the Councils, page 1751. In them he reports that the emperor had submitted three questions to him, concerning which disputes had arisen.

The first was whether Christ our God could be called “one of the Trinity”—that is, one person of the three persons of the Holy Trinity. The second was whether Christ God had suffered in the flesh while his divinity remained impassible. The third was whether Mary, ever-Virgin and the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, ought properly and truly to be called Mother of God.

John II writes that he had approved these propositions as consistent with the Catholic faith, and he confirms them with testimonies from Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers. Finally, when Pope Vigilius was unwilling to consent to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, he testified in an encyclical letter, in order by some means to appease Justinian’s mind, that he approved the proposition mentioned above: “The Son of God suffered in the flesh for us; he was crucified in the flesh and died in the flesh.”

The same proposition was also defined in the year 553 at the Fifth Council, session 8, canon 4 and following. These extracts are taken from Baronius’s critical work. On the Scythian monks, see what was said under Hormisdas.]

[Note: [Col. 0550B]

Line 3.—“The religious man Augustus … sent his confession, written in his own hand, to the Apostolic See, etc.” From Sommier, book VI, chapter 25.

Under Hormisdas we saw the controversy raised in the Church by the monks of Scythia concerning the theme of “one of the Trinity suffering in the flesh,” as well as that pontiff’s prudent care in cutting short such useless questions. Other monks of the East, therefore, whom they called Acemetes—that is, “non-sleeping,” because they continually performed the divine office in choir, relieving one another in psalmody in uninterrupted succession—decided to turn aside from and oppose those earlier monks on the opposite side. They said that we ought not to affirm that one of the Trinity had been incarnate and suffered in the flesh, nor that the blessed Virgin had truly and properly been Mother of God.

These latter monks therefore sent men to Rome to seek a definition concerning the article they had proposed. Emperor Justinian likewise decided to write to Pope John about this matter. John had only recently succeeded Boniface, and Justinian wrote as follows:

“Rendering honor to the Apostolic See and to your holiness—which has always been and remains our desire—and honoring, as is fitting, your blessedness as a father, we have hastened to bring to the knowledge of your holiness everything that concerns the condition of the Churches. For it has always been our great concern to preserve the unity of your Apostolic See and the condition of the holy Churches of God, which until now it has maintained and which remains undisturbed, with no opposition intervening. Therefore we have hastened to subject and unite all the priests of the entire Eastern region to the See of Your Holiness.

“Since matters have now been stirred up which, although manifest and beyond doubt, have always been firmly preserved and proclaimed by all priests according to the teaching of your Apostolic See, we have judged it necessary that they should reach the knowledge of Your Holiness. For we cannot permit anything that concerns the condition of the Churches—even when the matter being raised is manifest and beyond doubt—not also to become known to your holiness, who are the head of all the holy Churches.”

(Epistle of Emperor Justinian to Pope John II, letter 8, title “On the Supreme Trinity.”)

After this, the emperor explained the error of the Acemetes, whom he calls followers of Nestorius, and issued a profession of faith:

“Indeed,” he says, “all the priests of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, and the most reverend archimandrites of the holy monasteries, following Your Holiness and preserving the condition and unity of the holy Churches of God which they possess from the See of your Apostolic Holiness, without changing anything whatsoever in the ecclesiastical order that has existed and still exists, unanimously confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, born before the ages and timelessly from the Father, descended from heaven in the last days; that he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and born from the holy and glorious Virgin and Mother of God Mary, and became man; and that the one who was crucified is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. … Therefore we also say that the holy and glorious Virgin Mary is properly and truly Mother of God—not because God the Word took his beginning from her, but because in the last days he descended from heaven, was incarnate from her, became man, and was born. … Thus teaches and proclaims your Apostolic See.

“For this reason we have hastened to bring this to the knowledge of your holiness through Hypatius and Demetrius, most reverend bishops, so that it may not remain hidden from your holiness what has been wrongly and judaically denied by a few monks according to the impiety of Nestorius.”

The pontiff declared this profession of faith transmitted by the emperor to be orthodox. See what follows in Pagi’s notes on this section and below, under Agapetus.]

[Col. 0543]

93

John, who is also Mercury, a Roman by birth, son of Projectus, from the Caelian Hill, sat for two years [Note: [Col. 0543] B, three years], four months, and six days. He lived in the time of King Athalaric and Justinian Augustus [Note: [Col. 0543] See Baronius under the year 533]. At the same time the religious man Augustus, out of his supreme love for the Christian religion, sent his confession, written in his own hand, to the Apostolic See through the bishops Epazius [Note: [Col. 0543] C B, Hypatius] and Demetrius.

In those days the most Christian emperor Justinian Augustus offered to the blessed apostle Peter a golden chalice encircled with green and white gems, and two other silver chalices; a chalice weighing five pounds; silver chalices, each weighing five pounds; and four golden-woven olovéra hangings [Note: [Col. 0545] C, “but four small hangings”]. He held an ordination [Note: [Col. 0545] C B, “one ordination”] in the city of Rome during the month of December [Note: [Col. 0545] C, “the Kalends”], ordaining fifteen priests and twenty-one bishops in various places. He was also buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Ides of June, after the second consulship of Lampadius [Note: [Col. 0545] B, “under the consuls of Belisarius”], and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days [Note: [Col. 0545] C, six].

LIX. SAINT AGAPETUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 535, THE NINTH OF JUSTINIAN, THE SECOND OF KING THEODAHAD.

[Note: [Col. 0553A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher codex.

Number 94, line 8: B, Amalasuntha.

Number 96, line 5: A, “from which,” B, “because of which.” Line 9: A, “ordination” 1; B, “ordination.” Line 10: A, “three deacons”; line 10, B, “one month, 25 days.”

From the Royal Mazarin and Thuane codices.

Number 94, line 2, 19: here, at the beginning, E, “his little book, which through zeal of envy.” Line 3: “against” D (M, “against”). Line 6: “because at the same time the emperor was indignant against Theodahad, because he … the Amalanian queen”; and shortly afterward: “which made him king.”

Number 95, line 1: “But the lord pope proceeded to Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May and entered the city, being received with honor; and first he held a conference with the most pious king, that is, the emperor Justinian, concerning the religion of the faith. To him Pope Agapetus, in accordance with the apostolic faith, gave a confession concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, God and man—that is, that there are two natures in one Christ. While the dispute was continuing” (M, “the intention”; and this, it seems, was what was read in R, but “dispute” was corrected [Col. 0553B]), “the Lord so assisted him that the bishop of Constantinople, named Anthimus, was found to be a heretic.

“But when the dispute had continued for a long time between Augustus and Pope Agapetus, Justinian Augustus said to him: ‘Either agree with us, or I shall have you deported into exile.’ Then Pope Agapetus, responding joyfully, said to the emperor: ‘I am indeed a sinner.’” Line 12: “I found: nevertheless he did not fear the threats.” Pope Agapetus said to him again: “Know that you are not fit [the abbreviated words are uncertain], unless your bishop confesses that there are two natures in Christ.” Then, at the emperor’s command, Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, was summoned, and “he was examined by the father, and … confessed the Catholic doctrine in response to the questions” [Col. 0554A]. “When the pope had defeated him, Agapetus was glorified.”

Number 96, line 1: “The Augustus, filled with joy, humbled himself before the Apostolic See and prostrated himself before Pope Agapetus. Then Anthimus was excluded from communion and expelled into exile. Justinian Augustus asked the most blessed pope to consecrate another Catholic bishop in his place, named Mennas. At the same time the venerable pope obtained from the emperor everything for which he had been sent. After being held by illness for several days, he died in Constantinople.” Line 8: “He was buried on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.” “He held one ordination in the city of Rome.” Line 10: “one month, 28 days.”

From a second Thuane codex.

Number 94, line 9: Amalasuntha.

Number 95, line 4: “apostolic.” Line 6: “intention.” Line 7: “Anthemus.” Same line: “and when the intention.” Line 15: “Anthemus.” Line 16: “in this doctrine.”

[Col. 0554B] Number 96, line 2: “the pope, so that in place of Anthimus he might consecrate a Catholic bishop named M.” Line 10: “the month of the bishop, to the lord: one month, 28 days.”

In Penius, from the Cavensis codex.

Number 94, line 1: Agapetus. Line 3: Boniface. Line 8: Theoderic.

Number 95, line 1: Magius. Line 5: “man, that is, two natures in one Christ.” Line 9: “you agree.” Line 11: “Diocletian in V, which.”

Number 96, line 1: “he humbled himself before the holy Apostolic See and blessed Pope Agapetus.” Line 4: “he consecrated Anthimus the bishop as a Catholic.” Line 5: “he obtained.” Line 7: Magius.]

[Note: [Col. 0553C]

Number 94, line 5.—“He was sent by Theodahad … because he had killed Queen Amalasuntha, etc.” It is easy and obvious to anyone who compares these passages with what we have reported from Theophanes that Anastasius drew very extensively from the works of Greek writers which he translated into Latin. He appears to have written this account of Amalasuntha’s murder from Procopius’s books on the Gothic War, where Procopius relates similar events. Anastasius perhaps did not see Procopius’s Secret History, in which Procopius corrected what he had written incorrectly in the Gothic books and disclosed the truer cause of the murder.

The passage from the Secret History should be quoted, so that our observations concerning later additions of a subsequent hand may be confirmed by the earlier catalogues, and so that it may be clear from which sources these materials emerged. Procopius had described Amalasuntha’s intention of prolonging her stay in Constantinople and, after choosing a residence there through her servants, of living under the common rights of citizens. He immediately adds:

“Her noble birth, royal dignity, singular beauty, and keen and industrious intelligence at once came before Theodora’s eyes. For this reason she did not doubt that she would have to fear both the majesty of that woman’s manly spirit and the fickleness of her own husband. Nor did she reveal this rivalry lightly; she plotted the queen’s ambush and death and immediately persuaded her husband to send Peter to her in Italy.

“Caesar, as he was departing, gave him the orders which I have related in their proper place. But the Augusta—through fear of whom there was then no opportunity to tell the true story—gave him this one commission: to arrange and hasten Amalasuntha’s death, holding out the great hope of rewards if he obeyed her commands. He crossed immediately into Italy, prompted either by the hope of honor or of wealth. For the human mind cannot approach wicked murders in moderation. He drove Theodahad, by means obscure to me at least, to the murder of Amalasuntha.

“Afterward Peter was raised to the rank of Master with great power but to everyone’s hatred. Such was the end of Amalasuntha’s affairs,” etc.

He repeats below that Peter was the instigator and author of the murder, describing his character in these words:

“These men experienced Peter’s enormous and almost daily plundering in his office as Master. Although he was of a mild and scarcely harmful disposition, he was nevertheless the last of thieving men and full of disgraceful profit; he was also, as I explained above, the author of the murder of Amalasuntha, the daughter of Theodoric,” etc.

On the same matter, see Jordanes, On the Gothic Affairs, page 175. In his chronicle Theophanes also notes that, on Peter’s advice, the frontier troops were reorganized, to the ruin of the empire: for the Saracens repeatedly invaded the provinces of Asia and soon separated them from the Eastern Empire.

Line 8.—“Entrusted to him,” namely by her father Theodoric, who, according to Jordanes in the same place, page 173, had ordered this. “But when he had reached old age and recognized that he would soon depart from this life, he summoned the Gothic counts and the chief men of his people and appointed as king Athalaric, the still infant son—scarcely ten years old—of his daughter Amalasuntha, who had been deprived of his father Eutharic. He charged them, as though speaking with testamentary authority, to honor the king, love the senate and people of Rome, and always keep the Eastern prince appeased and favorable. Thus, while Athalaric was approaching the hope of youth, he commended both his own adolescence and his mother’s widowhood to the prince of the East,” etc.]

Line 2.—“And first he began to have a dispute.” Justinian, having settled domestic and public affairs, turned his attention to religious controversies. Procopius, a very free but not unjust critic of events, says this in the Gothic War, book III: “He continually sits without guards until late at night in the Museum with the senior priests, investigating with the greatest attentiveness the secrets of Christian doctrines,” etc.

He was not sufficiently even-tempered in entering into controversies of faith with various priests and therefore also with Agapetus, the Roman pontiff. It was an unusual preconceived policy of the Eastern emperors Zeno, Anastasius, and others to favor in disputes that party among Christians which was more powerful and had the larger number of adherents. Thus, when the Eutychian party was gaining strength, those worst of princes sided with the Eutychians—not because Anastasius followed the deliriums of the Eutychians, since, as we noted above, he advanced their cause even though he had given his name to the Manichaeans, but because they had the greater number of bishops and peoples. Zeno acted so that, once both parties had been weakened by these disputes, he might restore idolatry.

Similarly, as Procopius observes in the Secret History, Justinian—happy because he had nearly subdued the world by arms and governed it by holy laws, but happier still had he not had Theodora as a partner in counsels and actions—agreed with Theodora that he himself would support the Catholics, while she supported the Eutychians; and whichever party ultimately prevailed, both would follow it.

After describing Theodora’s deceitful character, Procopius proceeds to the matter (page 47 of the Secret History):

“Now let us consider the totality of the deeds performed by her and her husband. For in conducting affairs they did everything jointly, although for a long time and with great effort they made everyone believe that they held differing opinions and pursued contrary aims. At last it was discovered that they had deliberately assumed this appearance of pretense, lest their subjects, once their counsels had been shared, should stir up rebellion while opinion about them remained uncertain. At first, by means of these simulated opposing interests, they stirred up Christians against one another with controversies, as I shall explain shortly; afterward they divided the people among the factions,” etc.

And shortly afterward, on page 49:

“By these arts, while they had in fact agreed among themselves but openly feigned disagreements and led the minds of their subjects in different directions, they established their tyranny more firmly for themselves,” etc.

They had seized control, of course, over civil affairs together with the empire, and with much greater intensity—though more secretly—over ecclesiastical statutes and laws, with unrestrained license. Hence his disputes with Agapetus and his cruelty toward Vigilius, the Roman pontiff. He used religion as a Lesbian rule, measuring piety according to the private interests of imperial and public affairs; nor did they concern themselves greatly with what was rightly thought or taught about God when circumstances demanded otherwise.

Evagrius has an excellent passage on this subject, book IV, chapter 10:

“Justinian vigorously defended those who had assembled at the Council of Chalcedon and everything that had been set forth by them. His wife Theodora, however, took the side of those who asserted one nature in Christ—either because they truly held that opinion … or through a certain pretense,” etc.

John Langius translated this as “by a deliberate agreement,” etc.; Christophorsonus as “deliberately”; and, finally, Valesius most aptly as follows:

“Either through a certain pretense they had so agreed among themselves that one of them would defend the party which said that after the union there were two natures in Christ God, while the other defended those who asserted only one nature,” etc.

The aforementioned Procopius disclosed the reason for this: namely, that Justinian had good reason to fear the enormous number of those who were of Anastasius’s lineage and supported his party. Thus Procopius writes in book I of the Persian War, chapter 11:

“After Anastasius died, Justin took up the empire, excluding all Anastasius’s relatives from the succession, although they were both numerous and highly distinguished,” etc.

Line 7.—“He found Anthimus to be a heretic.” In the Acts of this pontiff, as also in those of the subsequent pontiffs, down to the point at which the deacon Paul carried his history, Anastasius inserted entire chapters of the same material, often in the same words, into his Lives of the Pontiffs. Thus Paul the Deacon writes in book XVII, page 675:

“After holding a conference with him concerning the faith, he found that he had fallen into the doctrine of Eutyches. At first the blessed bishop endured serious threats from him. But when Anthimus perceived his unshaken constancy in the Catholic faith—for he had gone so far in words that he heard such things from the bishop as these: ‘I desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor, but I found Diocletian,’” etc.

These very Acts prove that Justinian undertook the defense of the Catholics not sincerely but in order to serve the circumstances. Evagrius had written in the same work, chapter 9, that the emperor had left certain provinces free under the rule of heretics. For this reason Anthimus had been transferred from the Church of Trebizond to the bishopric of Constantinople, although it was known to everyone that he was stained by Eutychian perfidy.

For this reason Liberatus observes in the Breviarium that Justinian and Theodora simultaneously asked Pope Agapetus to communicate with Anthimus:

“When the rulers requested that the pope receive Anthimus in greeting and communion, he said that this could be done if Anthimus proved himself orthodox in a written statement and returned to his own see. He said that it was impossible for a transferred man to remain in that see. But while the Augusta was secretly promising many gifts and again threatening the pope, the pope persisted in this and refused to heed her request,” etc.

Number 96, line 1.—“Justinian … humbled himself.” Seeing the faith of the clergy and people of Constantinople and Agapetus’s outstanding reputation among them, Justinian, in order to show himself a defender of the Catholic faith, sent the pontiff a profession of faith signed by his own hand, which begins as follows (in Labbe, volume IV of the Councils, page 182): “The first salvation is right faith.” The pontiff received and approved it, and wrote back to the emperor, praising both this second profession and the earlier one sent to his predecessor. He accepted it, however, on this condition:

“Not because we admit authority of preaching in laymen, but because we confirm and strengthen your devotion to the faith, which accords with the regulations of our fathers,” etc.

The pontiff’s words should be carefully noted. Justinian sent this confession, issued at Constantinople, to the various provinces in his third consulship, in the year of Christ 533. It survives both in Greek and Latin in the Code, On the Supreme Trinity, 50.6. The pontiff approved it in such a way that he wanted it regarded as nothing more than the confession of one who held correct beliefs, not as the rule of a person proposing a profession of faith—a claim Justinian had on several occasions been known to make for himself.

Facundus speaks of the same matter and in the same sense, beginning book I as follows:

“I have always approved the confession of your faith, most merciful emperor, as consonant with the definitions of the great Council of Chalcedon, and I have defended it against the opposition of many,” etc.

He then proceeds to show how Justinian’s profession both destroys the heresy of the Nestorians and Eutychians and contains the Chalcedonian faith in its entirety, with the relevant statements brought together.

Line 2.—“He expelled Anthimus.” Liberatus reports this deposition in the following words:

“When Anthimus saw that he had been removed, he returned the pallium which he had received from the emperors and departed, while the Augusta protected him by her patronage. Then, with the prince’s favor, the pope ordained Mennas as bishop in his place, consecrating him with his own hand in the basilica of St. Mary,” etc.

Here the pretense of both rulers is conspicuously revealed: Theodora never ceased protecting Anthimus, although he had been deposed from the see of Constantinople as an Eutychian; Justinian, on the other hand, who concealed none of his plans from Theodora, wished to appear wholly dependent on the pontiff’s gestures. Indeed, in Novel 42, preserved in volume IV of Labbe’s Councils, he expressed sentiments of this kind. Concerning Anthimus, on page 1400, he says:

“He was deposed from the see of this royal city by Agapetus, of holy and glorious memory, pontiff of the holy ancient Church of Rome, because he had intruded himself into the see in a manner entirely unsuitable to him and contrary to all the sacred canons. He was also condemned and deposed by the common judgment first of that holy man of glorious memory and then of the holy synod held here, because he had departed from sound doctrines,” etc.

See the Council of Constantinople under Mennas.

Line 5.—“He consecrated a Catholic bishop named Mennas.” This appears to have been taken from Theophanes, who writes as follows:

“Agapetus went to Constantinople in this year and convened a council against the impious Severus, Julian, bishop of Halicarnassus, and all the other Theopaschites. Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, as a participant in their opinion, was deprived of office and deposed after holding the see for ten months. Mennas, a presbyter and superior of the hospice called N., was ordained in his place by Agapetus, the Roman pontiff.”]

[Note: [Col. 0557B]

Number 94, line 1.—“Agapetus.” In the year of Christ 535, during that very winter, Agapetus, an exceptionally learned archdeacon, was substituted for Pope John, as is clear from Agapetus’s letters written in that year to Emperor Justinian and to Reparatus, bishop of Carthage.

Line 2.—“He sat for eleven months and eighteen days.” Baronius proves from letters written to Agapetus and from his replies that Agapetus sat for more than one complete year.

[Col. 0557C] Number 95, line 1.—“He traveled to Constantinople.” The pontiff, undertaking an embassy, departed for Constantinople. Since he lacked the expenses for the journey, he had to pawn the sacred vessels to the imperial treasury; he recovered them through the same agency of Cassiodorus. While traveling, he healed a man who was both mute and lame, to the great astonishment of those present, in the regions of Greece. (St. Gregory, Dialogues 3.3.)

Number 96, line 6.—“He died at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.” Everyone agrees that he died in the year 536. But since his memory is celebrated in the Church on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, the information which Anastasius gives here concerning the time of his death and the vacancy of the see lacks credibility. You will find the story of Agapetus reported by Sophronius in the Spiritual Meadow, chapter 150, in Baronius under that year, number 66 and following.]

[Note: [Col. 0557C]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

It was sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding section that the beginning of Agapetus’s pontificate must be reckoned from 25 or 26 April for his election, and from 6 May 535 for his ordination. The agreement of the Bibliothecarius manuscripts and catalogues in assigning his tenure eleven months and eighteen or nineteen days proves that it ended with his life around the anniversary of his election, 25 April 536.

The year is identified by the consulship of Belisarius, and in the West it is also described as after the consulship of Paulinus Junior. Several letters of Agapetus are subscribed in this way; they are dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August and the fifth day before the Ides of September. After the consulship of Paulinus Junior, Justinian sent the same pontiff a profession of faith—not “in the consulship of Belisarius V. C.,” but, as Binius notes should be corrected, “after the consulship of Belisarius,” since it was dated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April.

Cardinal Norisius demonstrates from a Vatican codex, in his treatise On One of the Trinity Who Suffered, that the true reading of the letter and its subscription is the one Binius conjectured. Pagi observes this in his criticism of Baronius under the year 535, number 5, and under the year 536, number 4. The same is also made clear from the Acts of the Council of Constantinople under Mennas.

Those Acts likewise demonstrate that St. Agapetus died at Constantinople before 2 May, on which day the council was being celebrated, since they call Agapetus “of holy memory,” as Pagi notes under the year 536, number 5. We saw above that his death must be referred to 15 or 25 April; all the documents agree with this.

HISTORICAL NOTES.

Number 94, line 2.—“He sat for eleven months.” Pagi composed an encomium worthy of so great a pontiff when, comparing his extensive achievements with the short time divinely assigned to him for governing the Church, he wrote at the end of number 13:

“Hardly any other pontiff can be found who, presiding over the Catholic Church for so short a time, accomplished such great and numerous things, and whose praises are equally extensive and loudly proclaimed among Westerners and Easterners.”

His deeds, both in the West before the embassy which he undertook to Constantinople and in the East on the occasion of that journey, have been so fully explained and illustrated in the notes of Sommier and Pagi that they require no repetition from us. Indeed, the providential effect of his governance seems to have been prolonged beyond his life through the authority of his legates. By entrusting that authority to men approved by his own choice, he made them effective in benefiting the Church even after his death.

How greatly they advanced the cause of the faith and Catholic unity at the council held at Constantinople under Mennas after Agapetus’s departure from life—both the holy patriarch Mennas and the papal legates, all of whom had been selected and promoted to those offices by Agapetus—is best shown by borrowing from Pagi Junior’s number 14 on Agapetus:

“Before Agapetus undertook his journey to Constantinople, he sent there Sabinus of Canusium, Epiphanius of Asculum, Asterius of Salerno, Rusticus of Fiesole, and Leo of Nola, bishops whom he had appointed legates of the Apostolic See. He left them at Constantinople with their authority undiminished when he died.

“After consulting with Mennas, bishop of Constantinople, their chief concern was that the Eastern bishops should bind themselves in their own words to observe the measures established by Agapetus while he was alive. Accordingly, a council was held at Constantinople by Mennas himself and the apostolic legates on the sixth day before the Nones of May in that same year, 536. Fifty bishops attended it. It was decreed that the measures enacted by Agapetus against Anthimus and the Acephali heretics should be carried out.

“Anthimus, Severus, Peter of Apamea, and Zoaras were condemned again. Justinian ordered the execution of Agapetus’s decrees and those of the synod in Novel 42 and sent those heretics into exile. The document was issued on the eighth day before the Ides of August after the consulship of Belisarius V. C., as is read in the Acts of the council, whose fifth and final session was held on the day before the Nones of July.

“Baronius and others with him think that this council was assembled in the monastery of the celebrated archimandrite St. Dius. Henry Valesius, however, demonstrates in his notes on book IV of Evagrius, chapter 3, that it was held in the western atrium of the venerable church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”]

[Note: [Col. 0558D]

Number 94, line 1.—“Because he had killed Queen Amalasuntha, daughter of King Theodoric.” This woman was so well versed in Greek and Latin literature that she dared to engage in debate with any learned man. Moreover, she knew the languages of all the barbarians so thoroughly that she could speak with all those who had then invaded the Roman Empire without an interpreter.]

[Note: [Col. 0558D]

Number 94, line 2.—“The libelli of anathema which, through the deceit of envy, etc.” We said under Boniface II that this pontiff anathematized Dioscorus, the antipope, and that Anastasius mentions this anathema in his Life, attributing it to rivalry and deceit. Emperor Justinian likewise writes in his edict against the Three Chapters that Dioscorus was anathematized after his death for a financial reason—that is, for the crime of simony. When Agapetus obtained the pontificate, he removed that anathema as unjust, as the same Anastasius reports in his Life. For what reason the excommunication imposed by Boniface upon Dioscorus the antipope appeared unjust to Agapetus cannot be determined at all from the ancient records.]

## No. 95, line 1

“On the tenth day before the Kalends of May, he entered Constantinople.” Agapetus had already reached Constantinople in the middle of March of the year 536; for the confession of faith which Justinian presented to him while he was in Constantinople is dated in the Vatican Codex, in Cardinal Noris’s *Historical Dissertation on the One of the Trinity Who Suffered in the Flesh*, to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of consular rank, and therefore to 16 March 536. Indeed, he was already in Constantinople on 13 March, as will soon be seen.

While Agapetus was on his journey, in a certain place in Greece he caused a man born mute and lame to walk and speak through the offering of the most holy sacrifice of the Mass. The unequivocal witness to this is Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 3. Clearly, what once happened to the first Roman pontiff, and likewise to the prince of the apostles, Peter, also happened to Agapetus: when a lame beggar asked him for alms, he bestowed upon him, instead of the money he lacked, a healing more precious than all gold.

Anastasius writes that Agapetus obtained from the emperor Justinian everything for which he had been sent. But this is refuted by Liberatus, a writer of that period, who, in the passage cited, says that the emperor did not at all comply with Agapetus, who was asking for peace on behalf of Theodahad, because he had already expended a great amount of money in assembling an army. Therefore, deprived of hope of peace, the pontiff began to carry out the mission of Christ.

Anthimus, the intruded heretical bishop of the Church of Constantinople, had been transferred to that Church from the bishopric of Trebizond after the death of Patriarch Epiphanius, through the agency of the empress Theodora, who was attached to the Eutychian party, whose leader was Anthimus. Agapetus refused to receive him into greeting and communion unless he first proved himself orthodox by submitting a written statement and returned to his own see at Trebizond. Nor could Agapetus ever be moved from this decision, although the emperor—who had not yet discovered that Anthimus was a heretic—pressed him strongly to do so, and although the empress Theodora likewise demanded it and even threatened him with exile when he refused.

On that occasion Agapetus replied most steadfastly to the emperor:

> “I, a sinner, desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor; but now I have found a Diocletian. Nevertheless, I do not fear your threats.”

After this, Anthimus was questioned by the emperor in his presence. When Anthimus refused to confess two natures in Christ, the same emperor, once the fraud had been discovered, “humbled himself,” says Anastasius, “before the apostolic see, and adored the most blessed Pope Agapetus.”

Agapetus then deprived Anthimus of the priesthood and of Christian communion. In his place he appointed and consecrated as bishop of Constantinople Menas, the presbyter and superintendent of the great hospice, as Liberatus relates in the *Breviary*, in the cited chapter 21:

> “When the princes asked that the pope receive Anthimus in greeting and communion, he replied that this could happen if Anthimus proved himself orthodox by a written statement and returned to his own chair. He declared that it was impossible for a transferred man to remain in that see. But while the empress secretly promised many gifts and again threatened the pope, the pope persisted in refusing to heed her request. Anthimus, seeing himself rejected, returned to the emperors the pallium he had received and withdrew to a place where the empress might protect him by her patronage. Then the pope, with the favor of the prince, ordained Menas as bishop in his place, consecrating him with his own hand in the basilica of Saint Mary.”

That ordination was carried out by Agapetus on 13 March. For in the cited Vatican Codex, on page 45, one reads:

> “Copy of the written profession of the presbyter Menas and superintendent of the hospice, who was made bishop of Constantinople on the third day before the Ides of March, again after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, a man of consular rank.”

From this it is clear that what we said above is true: Agapetus had already reached Constantinople on 13 March. Therefore, in Anastasius, where it is read that he reached Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, one must read “the tenth day before the Kalends of March.” Moreover, the Roman pontiff could not have exercised the primacy more gloriously than by deposing the heretical patriarch of Constantinople and appointing another in his place, and by doing so without convening a synod.

Before Menas was ordained by Pope Agapetus, he publicly issued and subscribed to his profession of faith, the same profession which, as we have said, Pope Hormisdas formerly prescribed for all Easterners seeking Catholic communion. After he had been ordained, he again presented to the Roman pontiff Agapetus, according to ancestral custom, a written profession of faith in which he condemned all heresies and professed the Catholic faith. Pope Vigilius explicitly asserts this in his letter to Justinian, which appears in volume V of the Councils, page 314.

When all these things had been accomplished, the same pontiff Agapetus informed all the Eastern bishops of them by a circular letter. A copy of it, addressed to Peter, bishop of Jerusalem, is preserved in the same volume of the Councils, page 47. There Agapetus also counts among the prerogatives of Menas’s dignity the fact that, since the time of the apostle Peter, the Eastern Church had never received another bishop ordained by the hands of the Roman see.

The day after Menas’s ordination, the emperor Justinian sent a letter to Agapetus beginning: “Before this time, in this royal city…” In it the emperor says that he had published an edict against the Acephalites, Nestorius, and the Eutychians, and had inserted the substance of that edict into the letter he had written to Pope John. He says that “your aforementioned predecessor, gladly welcoming it with joyful approval for the integrity of the faith, confirmed it by his own assent and that of the whole Roman Church.” Here he is referring to the decrees issued by Pope John II against the Acephalous monks, about whom we spoke during his pontificate.

The emperor asks Agapetus to confirm by his authority the decrees issued by John. That letter appears in volume IV of the Councils, page 1788. It ought to be dated the day before the Ides of March, that is, 14 March. Later, on 16 March, the emperor sent the same pontiff a profession of faith signed by himself. It begins with the words: “The first salvation is right faith…” and appears in the same volume of the Councils, page 1801. Agapetus approved Justinian’s letter, together with the letter inserted in it to Pope John II, by a reply addressed to the same prince. Agapetus’s letter begins: “We rejoice, venerable emperor,” and appears at the cited place, page 1789.

Agapetus signifies to Justinian that he too approves and embraces the exposition of the faith which Justinian had sent through envoys to his predecessor, Pope John, and which that pontiff had confirmed. He adds:

> “Not because we admit that laymen possess the authority to preach, but because we confirm and strengthen your zeal for the faith, which accords with the regulations of our fathers.”

He then declares all who resist that profession of faith, which had again been confirmed by the present definition, to be excluded from holy communion. Next he says:

> “Accordingly, we in no way permit Cyrus and his followers, who have already been suspended from communion with the Catholic Church on account of this madness, to be restored to sacred communion unless they repent.”

He calls the obstinate perversity of the Acephalites “madness”: in opposition to the definition issued by John II, they denied that Christ is one of the Trinity. On this matter, see what was said under Pope John.

Finally, Agapetus inserts the emperor’s letter to John II and concludes:

> “And whoever dares to contradict this faith must know that he is excluded from Catholic communion. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of consular rank.”

Cardinal Noris restored the chronology of these letters and professions of faith from the Vatican Codex in the dissertation cited above, as may be read in Baronio’s critical notes under the year 535 and following.

## No. 95, line 2

“And first he began to have a dispute…” Pope Agapetus was compelled by Theodahad, king of the Goths, to go to Constantinople so that he might dissuade the emperor Justinian from his plan of recovering Italy, after he had recovered Africa. But this entreaty was ineffective with the prince, who was reckoning the very heavy expenses of military preparation. Therefore, the pontiff devoted himself exclusively to conducting affairs of religion.

The empress Theodora, who secretly favored the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, had arranged for Anthimus, the bishop of Trebizond, who was counted among that party, to be transferred to the patriarchal see of the imperial city. When Anthimus realized that suspicion had arisen concerning him, as though he did not profess the true faith, he promised the emperor:

> “He would do everything that the supreme pontiff of the great apostolic see should decree; and he wrote to the most holy patriarchs that he would follow the apostolic see in all things.”

(*Fifth Synod*, session 4.)

Relying on these precautions, and also moved by the persuasion of his wife Theodora, who possessed great influence with him, Justinian asked Agapetus “to receive Pope Anthimus in greeting and communion.” Agapetus replied that this could happen if Anthimus proved himself orthodox by a written profession and returned to his own chair—that is, the see of Trebizond. He declared that it was impossible for a transferred man to remain in that see, the see of Constantinople.

Liberatus, *Breviary*, chapter 21:

> “But while the empress secretly promised many gifts and again threatened the pope, the pope persisted in refusing to heed her request.”

The emperor himself, who thought that Anthimus shared the Catholic faith, began to threaten the pope with exile. But, moved by Agapetus’s reply, which displayed priestly steadfastness, he ordered Anthimus to be summoned in order to examine his faith. The Librarian explains what happened next.

When Anthimus was asked by the blessed Agapetus whether he confessed two natures in Christ, he never agreed to this doctrine of the Catholic Church. Justinian, therefore, realizing that Anthimus’s perfidy had been exposed by the holy man, fell at Agapetus’s feet, moved by reverence for him. All who were present glorified God and recognized the majesty of the holy see.

The Roman pontiff, whom Zonaras says in his *Annals of Justinian* appeared to have been sent by God to confound the perfidy of Anthimus and his fellow-members, just as Peter had been sent to Rome to overthrow the tricks of Simon Magus, instituted a trial against Anthimus. Several leading priests and archimandrites of monasteries accused him. Although the empress Theodora vainly brought the protection of her patronage to bear, Anthimus was convicted and declared to have been intruded into the see of Constantinople by evil arts, and he was deposed from the episcopate by the sentence of Agapetus.

Who, then, after these events, could doubt the authority and power of the Roman pontiff over all the Churches, both in episcopal cases and in the other matters which our ancestors call greater cases? Without convening a council, Pope Agapetus deposed the patriarch of the imperial city from the principal see of the Easterners and advanced another man in his place who had been lawfully presented.

This man was Menas. Concerning his ordination, Agapetus sent an encyclical letter to the Eastern bishops, correcting them with paternal charity because, without consulting the apostolic see, they had consented to the intrusion of Anthimus. He then praises Menas and observes that the dignity bestowed upon him included something that had happened to no Eastern bishop since the time of the apostle Peter: namely, that he had been ordained bishop by the hands of the successor of that same prince of the apostles.

> “And perhaps,” he says, “whether for the demonstration of his praise or for the destruction of his enemies, so great an event has now occurred that he may appear similar to those whom the choice of the Prince of the Apostles once ordained in these regions.”

(Pope Agapetus’s Letter 8, in the synod under Menas, session 1, at the end.)

The Catholic bishops and archimandrites who were then present in the imperial city presented supplicatory petitions to Agapetus, bearing these titles:

> “To our most holy and most blessed Lord, Father of Fathers, archbishop of the Romans and patriarch, Agapetus, from the bishops of the Eastern diocese, etc.; to our most holy and most blessed Lord, archbishop of ancient Rome and universal patriarch, Agapetus, from Marianus and the other archimandrites,” etc.

(Ibid.)

At their insistence, Saint Agapetus condemned Severus, the pseudo-patriarch of Antioch; Peter of Apamea; and the monk Zonaras the Syrian—heretical Acephalites. After Agapetus’s death, the emperor Justinian drove them into exile by Novel 42, ordering that the pontiff’s decrees be carried out.

This imperial law was issued after the synod held under Menas. In its fourth session the synod declares:

> “Fulfilling what was enacted by the most holy pope in the synodal letter, etc., and following what was carefully examined by the most blessed pope, we see that he [Anthimus] is alien to all sacred dignity and authority, and, according to the judgment of that most holy pope, to the Catholic designation.”

As for Severus and the other sectarians, whose condemnation was being enforced in accordance with the sentence already pronounced by Agapetus, the patriarch Menas replied:

> “We, like your charity, follow and obey the apostolic see; we regard its communicants as our own, and those condemned by it we also condemn.”

(Ibid.)

The sentence pronounced by the Fathers concerning Severus and his associates speaks as follows:

> “They indeed despised the Roman Church, the successor of the apostles, which pronounced sentence against them … Therefore, following the judgments of our holy Fathers against Severus, Peter, and Zonaras, and against all who share in their impiety, and against their accomplices … we reject them as wolves rushing into Christ’s sheepfold and strike them with a similar anathema.”

(Ibid., session 5.)

## Note on No. 96, line 7

“Whose body was carried in a leaden coffin as far as the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.” The bodies of the great were customarily placed in leaden coffins. Anastasius, under John III, concerning Narses: “Whose body was placed in a leaden coffin.” Likewise Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 11. Among the ancients, *loculus* meant a coffin in which the bodies of the dead who were not cremated were placed. Pliny, book VII, chapter 2, concerning the thumb of King Pyrrhus: “They say that it could not be burned with the rest of the body, and that it was placed in a coffin in a temple.”

## [Column 0551]

### 94

Agapetus, a Roman by nation, son of Gordianus the presbyter, a cleric attached to Saint John and Saint Paul, sat for 11 months and 18 days. [Note: Baronio wishes him to have lived more than a year.] At the beginning of his episcopate, he burned the anathema-pamphlets which Boniface had extorted from the presbyters and bishops by the deceit of envy, contrary to the canons, when all had been assembled in the midst of the Church against Dioscorus; and he released the whole Church from the envy of the treacherous. [Note: See Baronio under the year of the Lord 536.]

He was sent by Theodahad, king of the Goths, on an embassy to the lord Emperor Justinian, because at that same time the lord Emperor Justinian Augustus was angry with King Theodahad because he had killed Queen Amalasuntha, daughter of King Theodoric, who had been entrusted to him and had made him king. [Note: Malasuntha.]

### 95

“Agapetus, who went to Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, entered Constantinople, and Bishop Agapetus was received with glory. First he began to have a dispute with the most pious prince Justinian Augustus concerning religion. To him the most blessed Bishop Agapetus, with the steadfast faith of the apostles, gave this answer, saying: Our Lord Jesus Christ is God and man; that is, there are two natures in one Christ. And while the dispute was taking place”—[Note: B: “was being carried on.”]—“the Lord was present in such a way that he found the bishop of Constantinople, named Anthimus, to be a heretic.

And while the dispute was taking place between the emperor and Pope Agapetus, the emperor Justinian said this to him: ‘Either you agree with us, or I shall have you carried away into exile.’ Then the most blessed Pope Agapetus replied joyfully, saying to the emperor:

> ‘I, a sinner, desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor; but now I have found a Diocletian. Nevertheless, I do not fear your threats.’

“And again the venerable Pope Agapetus said to him:

> ‘Yet, so that you may know that you are not suitable for the Christian religion, let your bishop confess two natures in Christ.’

“Then, at the emperor’s command, the bishop of Constantinople, named Anthimus, was summoned. When the examination had revealed the truth”—[Note: “had been made known.”]—“he never wished to confess, in accordance with the teaching of the Catholic answer, when questioned by the blessed Pope Agapetus, that there are two natures in the one Lord Jesus Christ. Holy Pope Agapetus convicted him, and was glorified by all Christians.

### 96

“Then the most pious Emperor Justinian, filled with joy, humbled himself before the holy apostolic see and adored the most blessed Pope Agapetus. At the same time he expelled Anthimus from communion and drove him into exile. Then the most pious Emperor Justinian asked the most blessed Pope Agapetus and consecrated in Anthimus’s place a Catholic bishop named Menas.

[Note: Baronio denies this, under the year 536.]

“Agapetus the pope obtained everything for which he had been sent. But after several days, having been seized by illness”—[Note: C: “having fallen ill.”—]—“he died at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. His body was carried in a leaden coffin as far as the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, where he was also buried, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October. He carried out two ordinations in the city of Rome: four deacons and eleven bishops in various places; and the episcopate was vacant for twenty-four days.” [Note: C: “one month and 28 days.”]
