## Note

Although Schelestratius’s notes on the catalogues and Lives of the Roman pontiffs collected by the Librarians end with Felix IV, after the third dissertation, page 496, nevertheless, in the chronological series prefixed by him to his notes at the end of the second dissertation, he adds very brief notes—either his own or those of Holstenius—from after Felix IV, who died in the year 530, up to the beginning of the eighth year of John III, the Christian era 566. We append the more noteworthy of these to the first number of each pontiff.

Since he himself did not publish the variant readings of the Librarian’s better codices beyond Felix IV, we shall at least ensure that those are inserted here which we carefully extracted from the Farnesian Codex—judged by him and Holstenius to surpass the others in antiquity—after collating it ourselves with Velser’s edition in the years 1720 and 1726. Since, however, the Farnesian Codex, as has been indicated elsewhere, lacks its beginning, so that everything written before Pope Silverius is missing and even the beginning of Silverius’s Life has been lost, we shall reproduce from number 99 the variant readings that survive, without omitting even those that differ only in faulty spelling.

Although such variation does not pertain to the evidence of history, it is nevertheless useful for demonstrating the codex’s antiquity, equal to the age of Anastasius, when the barbarism of the Goths and Lombards had not yet been forgotten in the pronunciation and writing of Roman words. It is also fitting that a codex of such great antiquity should supplement the monuments of the older catalogues, which end approximately where the surviving portion of the Farnesian Codex begins.

Schelestratius writes at the end of his chronological series, page 326, adding this observation under the year of Christ 566, after the twenty-fifth consulship of Basil:

> “Here the consular Fasti end. For although Marius, bishop of Aventicum, in his appendix to the Chronicle of Eusebius, extends the consular Fasti as far as the second year of Tiberius, which coincides with the common year 386, and although the Greek tables, which Vossius attributes to Heraclius, continue the consular Fasti as far as the year 630, nevertheless they do not assign individual consuls. Therefore, omitting these Fasti, I bring them to an end with the year in which Justinian died, in which year several catalogues of the supreme pontiffs also end.”

As a supplement, therefore, to the several catalogues that end here, there will follow the readings of the codex judged the oldest of all by such authorities, selected from the several copies of the Librarian that he himself examined in the most celebrated libraries of Italy and beyond Italy.

## Note on No. 97, line 1

“Silverius, etc.” The events narrated here appear to have been copied from Paul the Deacon, as will be clear to anyone who compares the cited passage. As for the way in which the common manuscript of Anastasius went wrong by placing only twenty-four days between the death of Agapetus and the ordination of Silverius—a period that does not even seem sufficient for the news of the death to be sent from Constantinople to Rome—Papebrochius explains how this should be emended in his *Chronological-Historical Essay on the Catalogue of the Pontiffs*, under Silverius, page 79, and in dissertation 13, *On the Ordination and Abdication of Saint Silverius and the Substitution of Vigilius*.

### Line 9

“Guitiges went to Ravenna, etc.” These words, and nearly everything that follows, are read almost verbatim in Paul the Deacon, at the same place, page 676. A comparison of the two works clearly shows from where the additions to these deeds of the pontiffs were taken. Jordanes reported the same matter as follows, at the same place, page 177:

> “A few days earlier, King Witiges had departed, gone to Ravenna, and taken Mathesuntha, daughter of Amalasuntha and granddaughter of the former King Theodoric, as his wife.”

[Column 0570B]

### Line 11

“Because she had been entrusted to him as queen, etc.” Justinian was seeking pretexts by which he might free Italy by arms from the war and tyranny of the Goths. Witiges, without consulting Justinian, had taken as his wife Amalasuntha, the granddaughter of Theodoric, in order to secure his kingship among the Goths by this bond. For this reason the emperor declared that marriage invalid, since it had been celebrated without consulting him, the man to whom her grandfather had entrusted both the kingdom and his daughter; and by force of arms he compelled Witiges to abandon the queen and the kingdom.

Indeed, Paul the Deacon writes that Witiges, taking Mathesuntha away with him by force, was captured and made a patrician, and that the emperor assigned her an administration near the Persian frontier; while Witiges, remaining in exile, ended his life, etc.

Concerning Mathesuntha’s later marriage, Jordanes says at the same place, page 179:

> “The emperor joined Mathesuntha, [Witiges’] wife, to his own brother, the patrician Germanus. From them was born a son, Germanus, likewise Germanus [the son or descendant of Germanus; the wording is corrupt]. In him, with the race of the Anicii joined to the stock of Amala, the hope of both families, by the Lord’s favor, still promises something.”

Thus the powerful kingdom and the long-reigning Gothic nation were finally defeated and destroyed by Belisarius in the thirteen-hundredth year, as Jordanes records at the same place.

## Note on No. 97, line 1

“Silverius, etc.” When, at the end of the year of Christ 536, the Romans learned that Pope Agapetus had died, King Theodahad, as Anastasius says, by force and fear intruded Silverius, a Campanian. The Roman clergy, having previously rejected him, shortly afterward received and approved him in order to avoid a schism. It cannot be stated with sufficient certainty on what day and in what month he was created.

### The same line

“From his father Hormisdas, etc.” Bishop Liberatus, in the *Breviary*, chapter 22, asserts that Silverius was the son of Pope Hormisdas. Nevertheless, he was undoubtedly born lawfully from a preceding legitimate marriage; otherwise he would have been entirely unqualified for so great a dignity.

[Column 0570D]

### Line 3

“Theodahad, corrupted by money given, etc.” It can be inferred that what Anastasius writes here about Silverius’s simoniacal entry is false: first, because Liberatus, who lived at that time and is therefore more worthy of confidence, when narrating Silverius’s creation in the passage cited above, makes no mention of this matter even in a single word; and especially because Silverius, in the written statement of sentence that he composed concerning the condemnation of Vigilius, his usurper, vigorously charges Vigilius with the crime of simony. He surely would not have acted so freely if he himself had been guilty of the same crime.

### Line 8

“The tyrant Theodahad is extinguished, etc.” Theodahad, having fled from the City and traveling toward Ravenna, was overtaken and killed by soldiers sent by Vitiges, leader of the Goths, after he had reigned for three years, as Procopius testifies.

### Line 13

“Hearing that the Goths had made themselves a king, etc.” Anastasius is mistaken. For after Naples had been occupied, the Goths defected from Theodahad and chose Vitiges, as is clear from Procopius.

## No. 98, line 2

“Belisarius entered the City on the fourth day before the Ides of December.” Concerning this matter Evagrius, book IV, chapter 18, writes:

> “The city was surrendered to Belisarius without a battle, and Rome was again subjected to the Romans after sixty years, during which it had been occupied by the Heruli and the Goths—not from the day of Apelles, that is, the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the eleventh year of Justinian’s reign.”

That was the year of Christ 537, the sixtieth year after Augustulus was conquered by Odoacer, king of the Heruli.

### Line 7.—“King Witiges entered against Rome,” etc.

During this siege, the first remarkable point is that, throughout the entire year of the siege, they never attempted to storm the City at the place where the wall had been split from top to bottom and leaned downward as though already about to fall. The second, and still more remarkable, point is that the enemies of the Roman Church, although Arians, inflicted no insult or damage upon the very basilicas of the apostles situated outside the City; there, as Procopius testifies, they allowed the sacred rites to be celebrated freely according to the Catholic custom. In this they acted very differently from the recent heretics of our own time, who have never thought of anything before devastating and demolishing by fire and plunder the sacred monuments of the saints, consecrated to God.

### No. 100, line 10.—“Then the Empress, having taken counsel,” etc.

Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, book I, and Liberatus, *Breviary*, chapter 22, relate this same history. What has been omitted by Anastasius and Procopius may be seen in Liberatus at the place cited.

### Line 20.—“Who promised us that he would restore Anthimus.”

Add the promise of two hundredweight of gold, if, after Silverius had been removed, he would arrange for Vigilius to be ordained.

### No. 101, line 12.—“He sent him into exile,” etc.

What the heretical woman had requested, the ambitious deacon had procured; Belisarius, worse than Pilate, carried it out with extreme impiety. He deservedly merited being cast down from the highest glory into the deepest misery and poverty.

### Same line.—“And sustained him with the bread of affliction,” etc.

Liberatus says that Silverius, after being handed over to two defenders of Vigilius and to their servants, perished from starvation under their custody. For this reason, pestilence, famine, and wars arose, concerning which Baronius writes under the year 539.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The better manuscripts of Anastasius, together with the more authoritative catalogue, determine that Silverius occupied the see for one year, five months, and eleven days when he was driven into exile. Indeed, he was expelled into exile while Rome was being besieged by Witiges. Witiges began to besiege the City around the spring equinox, while the fifteenth indiction was drawing to a close, as Procopius writes; and he persisted in the siege of the City for a full year and nine days, without success.

At that time, a false accusation was fabricated against Silverius in order to satisfy the hatred of the Empress Theodora against him. The pontiff was banished by Belisarius to the Pontine Islands, as though he were an ally of the Goths, and Vigilius was intruded in his place—an antipope established through simony by the overwhelming power of the Empress Theodora. He was ordained on 22 November 537.

Silverius was driven from the City three days before the ordination of Vigilius; for, counting from Sunday, 8 June 536, he had occupied the see for one year, five months, and eleven days, which brings the reckoning to 19 November 536. The blessed pontiff survived in exile until June 538, when he completed his martyrdom, according to the *Bibliothecarius*, section 101. He was buried on 20 June, the day on which his feast is celebrated.

While Silverius had hitherto been the true pontiff and Vigilius an intruder, after Silverius’s death the clergy’s consent to the promotion of Vigilius in his place transformed him from an intruder into a legitimate successor.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

At the end of the life of Felix IV, and in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in the common era of Christ 530, we were abandoned by the second catalogue of the Roman pontiffs under Justinian. Schelestratius showed us two copies of it: one belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, now the Alexandrian Vatican copy, and the other the Colbertine copy. Schelestratius therefore ended his edition there, adding only at the end that both the Colbertine and the Alexandrian-Vatican copies contain the names and dates of the succeeding pontiffs down to Pelagius II, arranged as follows:

57. Boniface occupied the see for two years and twenty-five days [Colbertine: twenty-six].

58. John occupied the see for two years, three months, and twenty-five days [Colbertine: four months and twenty-six days].

59. Felix occupied the see for four years, two months, and twelve days.

60. Boniface occupied the see for two years and twenty-six days.

61. John occupied the see for two years, three months, and five days [Colbertine: six days].

62. Agapetus occupied the see for eleven months and seventeen days [Colbertine: eighteen days].

63. Silverius occupied the see for one year, five months, and eleven days.

64. Vigilius occupied the see for sixteen years [Colbertine: seventeen years], six months, and twenty-six days.

65. Pelagius occupied the see for four years, ten months, and eighteen days.

66. John occupied the see for twelve years, eleven months [Colbertine: ten months], and twenty-six days.

67. Benedict occupied the see for four years [Colbertine adds: one month and twenty-eight days].

68. Pelagius occupied the see for ten years, two months, and ten days.

Since this third volume of our edition is to end with Pelagius II, whose successor is Saint Gregory the Great [that is, of the Roman-Vatican edition], we provide from the appendix to that second catalogue the succession of the pontifical chronology, confirmed by the following testimony.

As for the continuation of the history from the second catalogue—which ends there with Felix IV, and with the consuls Lampadius and Orestes, in the year of Christ 530—we shall substitute for the catalogue the reading of the very ancient Anastasian manuscript. Lucas Holstenius and Schelestratius assert that this is the Farnesian manuscript, a specimen of whose writing we gave in the prolegomena.

For the appendix of the names and dates after Felix IV, recorded in that catalogue down to Pelagius II, see what we wrote in chapter 4 of our dissertation on the *Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*. We shall now supply the catalogue’s defect from the variant readings of the most ancient manuscript of the *Bibliothecarius*, which are here to be added to the editions of Velser and Fabrotti. Schelestratius did not provide these variant readings after Felix IV, whereas we carefully transcribed them from the Farnesian original while staying at Colorno in the years 1720 and 1726, with the gracious permission of the most serene Duke Francis of Parma. A few years earlier, that manuscript had been transferred to Parma from Rome, where Holstenius and Schelestratius had compared it with the Velserian edition.

We shall therefore present the text of the *Bibliothecarius* from this No. 99, where the Farnesian manuscript preserves for us the surviving reading of that exemplar, following the practice maintained in the edition of the first volume. We shall also append the variant readings of the Farnesian manuscript, adding to them the readings of another manuscript of the Laurentian Library. In the immediately preceding year, 1726, after observing that this manuscript was commendable for its antiquity and had been copied with less barbarism than the others of comparable age, I arranged for a carefully collated copy to be sent to me through the efforts of the most learned and dearest friend, D. Antonio Gori, celebrated for the corrected edition of the ancient inscriptions existing in Etruria, recently published with learned observations.

We shall therefore mark the variant readings of the Farnesian manuscript with the letter F, and those of the Laurentian copy with the letter L.

## No. 97, line 2.—“He was raised up by the tyrant Theodatus,” etc.; and line 7.—“Afterward the presbyters thus subscribed,” etc.

When the death of Pope Agapetus had been heard of at Rome, and the sacred election according to ancestral custom was already being held to create a new pontiff, Theodatus, king of the Goths, as Anastasius relates in his account of Silverius, arranged by force and fear for Silverius—by nationality a Campanian and formerly the son of Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff, born of a lawful marriage before his father’s pontificate—to be ordained pontiff, although many of the clergy opposed his election. Nevertheless, they later subscribed to it in order to avoid a schism.

Hence the appearance of the later accusation that Silverius favored the Goths. The same Anastasius wrongly brands him with the stain of simony. For Liberatus, in his *Breviary*, chapter 22, where he discusses Silverius, who, as he himself writes, was elected pontiff from the subdeaconate, says nothing at all—and neither does any other ancient writer—about money contributed by Silverius.

Silverius was ordained on 8 June, on which date Sunday fell in the year 536. Although the manuscripts of Anastasius vary concerning the interregnum after the death of Agapetus, the reading of those that give the interregnum as one month and twenty-eight days nevertheless seems preferable, though they count one day too many. For from the time at which he occupied the see it follows that he was ordained on 8 June, and consequently that the interregnum lasted forty-seven days, as recorded in Catalogues 1 and 3 prefixed to the first volume of Baronius’s critical edition.

Meanwhile, as Liberatus relates in the cited passage, Vigilius, the deacon of the deceased Agapetus, was living at Constantinople. He secretly negotiated with the Empress Theodora in order to obtain the pontificate, promising her that, if he were elected pope, he would abolish the Council of Chalcedon and restore to communion Anthimus, Severus, and the other Acephali allied with them.

## No. 98, line 1.—“At the same time there was a very great war,” etc.

These events occurred during the siege of the City of Rome, as Procopius relates in book I, chapter 25, of *The Gothic War*, and therefore in the year 537, when Rome was besieged by King Witiges. This is confirmed by Anastasius in his account of Silverius and by the Continuator of Marcellinus, who state that these events occurred in the fifteenth indiction, which was running in the year 537.

Silverius was deposed on 18 November, as will be clear from the duration of his pontificate. Vigilius, however, was ordained on 22 November, or 10 Kalends of December, which was a Sunday, as Anastasius testifies in his account of Vigilius.

## No. 101, line 12.—“And sustained him with the bread of affliction,” etc.

This holy pontiff, worn out by hardships in exile and consumed by hunger, died on 20 June. The Church celebrates his memory annually on that day under the title of martyr.

He was buried, as Anastasius says, in the same place, and a multitude of sick people customarily came to his tomb and obtained healing. His death is unjustly attributed to Vigilius. For Procopius, in the *Secret History*, chapter 1, speaking of Antonina, the wife of Belisarius, says:

> “There was a certain servant named Eugenius, an accomplice in the crime, who had also been an attendant in the sacrilege committed against Silverius.”

Here Alemannus observes in his notes on that book that Procopius indicates that Silverius was killed by the sword or by some other bloody human method. He further observes that Liberatus wrote that Silverius died of starvation, which he had learned from others, whereas Procopius wrote what he himself had seen.

As for the year of Silverius’s death, Baronius believes it was 540. Baronius’s annotator assigns it to 538. But since both Anastasius and the catalogues conclude Silverius’s pontificate at his deposition, whichever of those years was the year of his death does not affect the pontifical chronology. Although he remained the legitimate pontiff until his death, Anastasius nevertheless restricts the duration of his pontificate to one year, five months, and eleven days. From this it follows that what we said above is correct: namely, that he was deposed on 18 November 537.

In volume V of the Councils there is a letter from Pope Silverius to Vigilius, in which Silverius reproaches him for ambition concerning the apostolic see and for the crime of simony, and condemns him by a sentence of anathema. Four bishops subscribe to it: the Terracinian, Fundanian, Firman, and Minturnian bishops. Baronius supposes that they held a council with Pope Silverius on the island of Palmaria and pronounced a sentence of anathema against Vigilius.

In fact, that letter, which begins, “Entangled in many transgressions,” etc., is spurious, as is shown by the barbarity of its style, its false consular date, and its borrowed sentences from the letter of Felix II to Acacius. Moreover, what Silverius relates about Vigilius is confirmed by no historical testimony: namely, that he had sought the Levitical office with bloodstained hands, had intruded upon his predecessors, and had been restrained by the justice of the Senate.

Finally, it is incredible that Silverius—whom Liberatus testifies was immediately after his deposition held under the custody of his enemies and deported into exile—should have summoned a gathering of bishops and pronounced a sentence of anathema upon the usurper of his see. Nor could this have occurred at the time when the pontiff, expelled from his homeland and deprived of his see, was living at Patara, since Italian rather than Asian bishops subscribe to this decree of anathema. After Silverius’s return, no one would have called Vigilius excommunicated. Silverius was immediately handed over to his rival Vigilius and deported to Palmaria, or to a Pontine island, where it is not credible that he could have evaded the watchful eyes of his guards, summoned synods, enacted canonical sanctions, or hurled anathemas against his adversaries.

## No. 98, line 2.—“Belisarius entered the City,” etc.

Belisarius, a tyrant and sacrilegious man against the Chair of Peter and the whole Roman Church, afflicted and profaned it barbarously and tyrannically with injuries and damages, laying a violent hand upon the Roman pontiff himself and disfiguring and dishonoring the visible head of the Church, placed in the position of Christ.

This was indeed a great and horrifying tempest in the Roman Church: stirred up by a raging heretical woman, procured by an ambitious deacon, and impiously completed by Belisarius. But the unhappy man paid the penalty. The emperor whom he had attempted to win for himself through the Empress Theodora became, by the same route, an emperor most hostile to him, and Belisarius was miserably reduced to order by that very emperor. After committing so great a crime, and in order to reconcile the offended divine power to himself, he soon arranged for a church to be built at Rome. Before its doors he ordered the following inscription to be carved as an everlasting memorial of the crime he had committed.

> This church the patrician Vilisarius, friend of the City,  
> Built to obtain pardon for his guilt.  
> Therefore, you who set foot in this sacred house,  
> Pray often to God that He may have mercy on him.  
> This is the gate of the temple, defended by the Almighty Lord.

Today, after that church was destroyed, the marble tablet bearing the inscription remains set into the wall of the church of the Crucifers at the Aqua Virgo, opposite the Quirinal Hill.

## No. 99, line 5.—“Within the City there was a great famine, so that water was sold at a price, unless the remedy of the nymphs had come to the rescue.”

With Rome besieged by the Goths, such scarcity of everything arose that water would have been sold, unless the City had been aided by the remedy of the nymphs—that is, by the water supply of the nymphaea, meaning the baths, which were more numerous at Rome.

## No. 100, line 7.—“At that time Vigilius was a deacon and *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople.”

The *apocrisarii*, or responsales, were envoys or legates who were always in the emperor’s retinue in the name of the Roman pontiff, in order to attend to the affairs of the Church. That Gregory held this office at the Constantinopolitan court in the time of Pelagius is testified by John the Deacon in his *Life*, book I, chapter 26:

> “Not long afterward he was sent by Bishop Pelagius to the city of Constantinople on ecclesiastical business.”

Today they are called apostolic nuncios. Through the *apocrisarii*, pontifical instructions were conveyed to the patriarch of Constantinople.

Anastasius, in his account of Theodore:

> “Then the most holy Pope Theodore wrote to Paul, patriarch of the imperial city, both asking and regularly reproving him, and also sending *apocrisarii* for this very purpose, who admonished and formally warned him in person.”

The same writer, in his account of Martin:

> “These *apocrisarii*, by order of the authority of the Apostolic See, warned him to withdraw from such a heretical purpose.”

And in his account of Nicholas:

> “He immediately sent Arsenius, bishop and *apocrisiarius* and envoy of this venerable Apostolic See.”

## No. 101, line 2.—“And he detained all the clergy at the first and second veil.”

Silverius entered to see Belisarius inside the Pincian palace, while the clerics who accompanied him were detained at the first and second veil—that is, at the first and second doors. This is clear from the present passage and from Silverius’s letter to Amator, which is found in canon Gulisarius 23, question 4.

Veils are used for doors because the entrances of splendid or larger buildings were closed off by curtains. Suetonius, in his *Life of Claudius*, writes:

> “He hid himself among the curtains spread before the doors.”

Anastasius, in his account of Gregory IV:

> “Three Alexandrian curtains hanging before the main doors, bearing figures of men and horses.”

Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*:

> “So many curtains of the gates.”

Anastasius, in his account of Leo III:

> “And three other larger white silk curtains, hanging before the imperial doors at the entrance.”

Sidonius, book I, letter 2:

> “A crowd of fur-clad attendants murmurs before the doors, excluded by curtains and enclosed by barriers.”

Curtains were also placed at the doors of churches. Jerome, *To Heliodorus*:

> “A doorkeeper constantly at the door, curtains always at the entrances.”

Nor were even the doors of schools without curtains. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 25:

> “Although he was a pagan grammarian, he was better at the curtain than at the chair.”

Alexander Severus is praised because people greeted him at home as a private citizen, with the curtain open and the ushers dismissed. Lampridius, in his *Life of Alexander*:

> “He was greeted as though he were one of the senators, with the curtain open and the ushers dismissed.”

This is also what the law says: “with the curtain raised,” in the Code, title *On Shipwreck*.

## Line 6.—“John, a regional subdeacon of the first region, took the pallium from his neck.”

When Pope Fabian appointed notaries throughout the seven regions of the City to collect the acts of the martyrs, he added an equal number of subdeacons to serve as witnesses. Hence they were called regional subdeacons, as here and below in the same work:

> “Then Sixtus, regional subdeacon of the sixth region.”

## Line 12.—“And he sent him into exile in the Pontine Islands.”

Silverius was banished into exile on the island of Pontia, situated on the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is recorded in the *Roman Martyrology*, 7 May, that Flavia Domitilla was exiled there under the persecutor Domitian.

## Line 13.—“He died after wasting away and became a confessor.”

Silverius, who died in exile on the island of Pontia, is reckoned among the confessors. The same is said of Martin, who died in exile on the island of Chersonesus, in Anastasius’s *Life* of him:

> “And there, as it pleased God, he ended his life in the peace of Christ as a confessor.”

Confessors differ from martyrs in this respect: martyrs are those who suffered the ultimate penalty for the faith, whereas confessors are those who suffered something for the faith—exile, imprisonment, or tortures, for example—but not to the point of death.

Optatus of Milevis, book I, *Against the Donatists*:

> “For nearly sixty years and more, the storm of persecution swept through all Africa; it made some martyrs and others confessors.”

Cyprian also approves this distinction, letter 5:

> “But how, in order to provide the necessary expenses, without those who have confessed God with glorious voice and are confined in prison,” etc.

## No. 100, line 7.—“But the Empress, grieving,” etc.

What the *Bibliothecarius* relates here in barbarous style, Liberatus, a contemporary of those events, presents in more polished form in chapter 22 of his *Breviary*. D. Archbishop Sommier, book VI, chapter 30 of his *Dogmatic History*, notes this and summarizes the sequence of events as follows.

The only monument that remains for us, but a most glorious one, of the pontificate of Saint Silverius, who succeeded Agapetus, is his exile and martyrdom, bravely endured in defense of the Catholic faith.

The Empress Theodora, intensely intent on promoting Eutychianism, immediately after the death of Agapetus seduced the deacon Vigilius, who was then the representative of the Roman See at the imperial city. She made a bargain with him concerning the highest pontificate, the restoration of Anthimus and his followers, and the annulment of the holy Council of Chalcedon.

Armed by her with letters of recommendation to Belisarius, then master of both armies, Vigilius hastened to Italy. But he found that Silverius had already been given to the Apostolic See as pontiff. Belisarius, who had liberated Rome from Gothic servitude, turned his attention to carrying out Theodora’s secret commands—whether the machinery was to be directed toward the deposition of Silverius or toward extorting from him the promises made by Vigilius, namely, the abolition of the Council of Chalcedon and the restoration of Anthimus and the Acephali to communion.

The deacon Liberatus, a contemporary author, relates that Belisarius, then residing in the City, summoned Silverius and reproached the blessed pontiff with the crime of treason, as though he had sent letters to the king of the Goths urging him to recover Rome by treachery.

> “For it is said,” Liberatus writes, “that a former scholasticus named Marcus and a former praetorian official named Julian composed forged letters in Silverius’s name and sent them to the king of the Goths. From these letters Silverius would be convicted of wishing to betray the Roman state.  
>   
> “In private, Belisarius and his wife persuaded Silverius to fulfill the Empress’s command: that the Council of Chalcedon should be abolished and that he should confirm the faith of the heretics by his own letter. Silverius, having implored the help of heavenly aid and poured out prayers to God, was brought before Belisarius again. Belisarius admitted him alone, after excluding the pontiff’s retinue, and removed Silverius from the sight of everyone.”

Liberatus continues:

> “The next day, having summoned the clergy, he ordered them to elect another pope. While they hesitated and some resisted, Vigilius was ordained through the influence of Belisarius. Silverius, however, was sent into exile to Patara, a city of the province of Lycia. When the bishop of that city came to the emperor after Siricius had arrived at Patara, the venerable bishop protested before him and called upon God’s judgment concerning the expulsion of the bishop of so great a see. He said that there were many kings in this world, but that there was not another pope like that one, expelled from his see over the whole Church of the world.  
>   
> “When the emperor heard him, he ordered Silverius to be recalled to Rome and directed that judgment be rendered by his own letters.”

Thus far Liberatus the deacon.

The Empress Theodora, however, wishing to nullify the emperor’s command, prevented Silverius from returning to Italy. The emperor’s order prevailed, but Belisarius nevertheless did not desist from his injury. Since Vigilius, conscious of Silverius’s innocence, feared for himself, he persuaded Belisarius to hand Silverius over to his custody, threatening that otherwise he too would withdraw from the conditions of their agreement.

> “Thus Silverius was handed over to two defenders of Vigilius and to his servants. When he had been brought to the island of Palmaria, he perished of starvation under their custody.”

## 97

Silverius, by nationality a Campanian, son of Hormisdas, the Roman bishop, occupied the see for one year, five months, and eleven days.

[Note: B reads “three years.”]

He was raised up by the tyrant Theodatus without a formal decree. Theodatus, corrupted by money—

[Note: “after money had been given.” Baronius denies that money was given.]

—introduced such fear among the clergy that anyone who did not consent to his ordination would be punished by the sword. Certain priests—

[Note: C reads “some priests.”]

—did not subscribe to him according to the ancient custom, nor did they confirm the decree before the ordination.

[Note: C reads “and they did not.” See Baronius under the year 536.]

But after Silverius had been ordained under force and fear, the presbyters afterward subscribed in this manner, for the sake of the unity of the Church and the faith.

Two months later, by divine will, the tyrant Theodatus was destroyed, and Witiges was raised up as king.

[Note: “Vbigites”; B and C: “Vitigis.”]

At the same time Witiges went to Ravenna and forcibly took Amalasuntha’s daughter as his wife.

[Note: C reads “Amalasuntha.”]

The lord Emperor Justinian Augustus, indignant at this because Theodatus had killed the queen entrusted to him, sent the patrician Belisarius with an army to free all Italy from Gothic captivity.

Then the aforesaid patrician came into the region of Sicily and remained there for some time. When he heard that the Goths had made a king for themselves against the will of the lord Justinian Augustus, he came into Campania, near the city of Naples, and besieged it with his army, because the Neapolitan citizens refused to open the city to him.

[Note: See Baronius under the year 537.]

At the same time, while fighting, the patrician entered the city. Carried away by rage, he killed the Goths and all the Neapolitan citizens, sent away the plunder, and did not spare even the churches in his looting. Wives were present while their husbands were killed by the sword; their sons were taken captive, and the wives of nobles were driven into exile.

[Notes: C reads “would kill”; C reads “would drive into exile.”]

He spared no one—not priests, not servants of God, and not consecrated virgins.

## 98

At the same time there was a very great war, when Witiges came against the patrician Belisarius and against the city of Rome.

[Note: * Belisarius, here and below.]

Belisarius entered the City on 10 December. He surrounded and fortified the Roman City with guards, fortifications, or structures of the walls, and by repairing the ditch. On the very night when the patrician Belisarius entered, the Goths who were in the City or outside the walls fled, left all the gates open, and fled to Ravenna.

After this, King Witiges gathered a multitude of Gothic troops, returned against Rome on 21 February, established his camp at the Milvian Bridge, and began to besiege the Roman City.

Then the patrician Belisarius, who stood for the Roman name, shut himself inside Rome and guarded the City.

## 99

During those days the City was so besieged that no one could leave or enter. All private property, whether belonging to the treasury or to the Church, was consumed by fire, while people were killed by the sword. Those whom the sword killed, the sword killed; those whom famine killed, famine killed; those whom disease killed, disease killed.

For the churches and the bodies of the holy martyrs were destroyed by the Goths. Within the City there was a great famine, so that water was sold at a price, unless the remedy of the nymphs had come to the rescue. There were also very great battles against the City.

During those days the patrician Belisarius, fighting against King Witiges and the multitude of the Goths, protected the Romans and by his guardianship saved the City and the Roman name.

The City was then besieged for one year, as was the Roman port, by the Goths. The venerable patrician Belisarius defeated the Goths in battle, and afterward, after one year, the Goths fled to Ravenna.

## 100

At the same time there was such a great famine throughout the whole world that Datius, bishop of the city of Milan, clearly reported in his account that in the region of Liguria women had eaten their own children because of the famine. He said that these women belonged to the household of his Church.

[Note: * “and he reported this concerning a certain woman from his Church’s household.”]

At the same time the patrician Belisarius went to Naples and organized it. Afterwards he came to Rome, where he was kindly received by the lord Silverius. The patrician Belisarius went to the Pincian palace—

[Note: * “to the Pincian palace.”]

—on the Ides of May—

[Note: * “six days before the Ides of May.”]

—in the fifteenth indiction.

At that time Vigilius was a deacon and *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople.

But the Empress was grieved on behalf of Anthimus the patriarch, because he had been deposed by the most holy Pope Agapetus, who had found him to be a heretic and had appointed in his place Menas, the servant of God.

[Note: See Baronius under the year 538.]

Then the Empress, having taken counsel with the deacon Vigilius, sent her letters to Pope Silverius at Rome, asking and entreating him:

> “Do not delay to come to us, or at least restore Anthimus to his place.”

When the most blessed Silverius had read the letter, he groaned and said:

> “Now I know that this matter has brought about the end of my life.”

[Note: C reads “brings about.”]

But the most blessed Silverius, placing his trust in God and in the blessed Apostle Peter, wrote back to the Empress:

> “Lady Empress, I will never do what you ask: restore to his place a heretical man condemned in his wickedness.”

Then the indignant Empress sent commands to the patrician Belisarius through the deacon Vigilius, containing these instructions:

> “Find some pretext against Pope Silverius and depose him from the episcopate, or else send him to us without delay. Behold, you have Vigilius, our dearest archdeacon and *apocrisiarius*, who has promised us that he will restore the patriarch Anthimus.”

The patrician Belisarius then accepted the command, saying:

> “I shall indeed carry out the command, but the man who is involved in the death of Pope Silverius will himself give an account of his deeds to our Lord Jesus Christ.”

As the command pressed upon them, certain false witnesses came forward and said:

> “We have often found Pope Silverius sending letters to the king of the Goths: ‘Come to the gate called Asinaria, beside the Lateran, and I will hand over to you the City and the patrician Belisarius.’”

[Note: * “more frequently.”]

When Belisarius heard this, he did not believe it. For he knew that such things were being said about Silverius out of envy. But when many persisted in the same accusation, he became afraid.

## 101

Then he caused the blessed Pope Silverius to come to him in the Pincian palace.

[Note: B reads “in Pincis” or “in Pincii.”]

He detained all the clergy at the first and second veil.

When Silverius entered with Vigilius alone into the mausoleum, the patrician Antonina was lying on a bed, and Belisarius was sitting at her feet.

[Note: * “the patrician Belisarius.”]

When the patrician Antonina saw Silverius, she said to him:

> “Tell us, Lord Pope Silverius, what have we and the Romans done to you, that you should wish to hand us over to the Goths?”

While she was still speaking, John, a regional subdeacon of the first region, entered, took the pallium from Silverius’s neck, and led him into a chamber. He stripped him, clothed him in a monastic garment, and hid him.

[Note: * “monastic.”]

Then Sixtus, regional subdeacon of the sixth region, seeing that Silverius had already become a monk, went outside and announced to the clergy:

> “The lord pope has been deposed and has become a monk.”

When they heard this, they all fled. Vigilius the archdeacon nevertheless received Silverius under his supposed protection and sent him into exile in the Pontine Islands.

[Note: C reads “to the Pontine Islands.”]

He sustained him with the bread of affliction and the water of anguish.

[Note: See Baronius under the year 538.]

He wasted away, died, and became a confessor. He was buried in the same place on 20 June. A multitude of sick people came there, and they were healed.

He held one ordination in the month of December: fourteen priests, nineteen bishops in various places, and the episcopate remained vacant for five days.

# LXI. VIGILIUS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 540, THE FOURTEENTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN, THE FOURTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF WITIGES

## From the Farnesian manuscript and the Silverius manuscript

### No. 102

Line 2: Six months, twenty-five days.

Line 4: The master of the soldiers, surnamed Sanguinarius, seized him and brought him to Vigilius at Rome.

Line 6: In the Basilica Julia, so that they might lead him safely.

Line 7: To Constantinople.

Line 10: Had appointed him. Then the emperor and the Empress gave thanks to him. After restoring him to his rank, he sent him to Africa against Gundaric, king of the Vandals, so that he might do in Africa what he had done in Italy.

Line 14: Then the patrician Belisarius, returning from the spoils of the Vandals, offered it at Rome.

Line 16: With gems weighing one hundred pounds, on which he wrote his victories. Eleven larger silver-gilt *cirostata* (perhaps candelabra), which still stand today.

## Notes

### No. 102, line 7

“And he made him a patrician and count,” etc. The dignity of the patriciate was the summit of dignities. Nevertheless, the dignity of the comitiva, or countship, was sometimes added to the patriciate, as an accession and completion of all dignities.

Synesius, *Letter* 144:

> “You have written concerning the Count; I understand you to mean the man who has obtained the prefecture of the soldiers in his homeland.”

Constantine added the honor of the comitiva to Joseph, the superintendent of the construction of the churches of Tiberias. Concerning him Epiphanius writes, *Against Heresies* 30:

> “He obtained the rank of the Counts.”

The name “count” was given to all who were selected from the sacred retinue, as is clear from the *Notitia Dignitatum Imperii*. The name and dignity of count was also customarily added to honored men, that is, to those who had successively and in due order performed all the offices of the state. See *Codex Theodosianus* 6.75, “Concerning Decurions.”

### No. 104, line 3

“When this was heard, the Augusta sent Anthemius the *scribo* with her commands.”

The office of the *scribones* was varied, involving the transmission and execution of the emperor’s orders. Anastasius, in his Life of Theodore:

> “He sent *boiatos* to Ravenna through the hands of Maurinus the *scribo*.”

See further Gregory, book VIII, letter 36, and book XII, letter 30.

### No. 104, line 7

“Anthemius the *scribo*, coming to Rome, found him in the church of Saint Cecilia on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. When the people asked for him, he was seized; for it was his birthday, and he was giving gifts to the people.”

Vigilius is recorded as having been in the church of Saint Cecilia on his birthday and as having given gifts to the people. This passage may be understood of the Eucharist, because the Greeks call it *τὸ δῶρον*, *τὰ δῶρα*, or *τὰ ἅγια δῶρα*—“the gift,” “the gifts,” or “the holy gifts.”

### No. 104, line 10

“But the plebs followed him, shouting that they might receive a prayer from him. When the prayer had been given, all the people answered, ‘Amen.’”

When the prayer had been given, the Roman pontiff blessed the people. Anastasius, in his Life of Stephen IV:

> “There, after the bishop had given the prayer to them according to the ancient custom and had bestowed peace upon all, they brought everyone together into the Lateran patriarchium.”

The same author, in his Life of Sergius II:

> “And after the aforesaid holy pontiff had given the prayer over the people, all returned together from the church.”

When the priest blesses, the people answer, “Amen.” Ambrose, on Psalm 40:

> “For just as, when the priest blesses, the people answer, ‘Amen,’ confirming for themselves the blessing which the priest implores from the Lord for the people, so in the Psalm the response is, ‘Let it be, let it be,’ as though ‘Amen, amen.’”

### No. 105, line 2

“He sent back to Rome Ampliatus the presbyter and his *vicedominus*.”

A *vicedominus* is the bishop’s deputy in temporal matters. See canon *Diaconum*, canon *Volum*, distinction 89, and canon *Salvat*, question 3.

### No. 105, line 5

“He entered Constantinople on the vigil of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Vigils, accompanied by fasting, precede the greater solemnities—for example, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, the feast of John the Baptist, and the feasts of the Apostles. They were so called because, for the sake of prayer, vigils were customarily celebrated during the night.

See *Quaestivit* in the *Decretum*, Ambrose, sermon 60, *On the Feasts of Easter and Pentecost*:

> “For then, just as we have done now, we fasted on Saturday, celebrated vigils, and devoted ourselves to prayer throughout the night.”

Gregory, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book II, chapter 25:

> “For when, on the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity, we had completed the sacred vigil and were proceeding from the church, intending to go to the basilica of the saint…”

Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book III:

> “It became day: Peter, day: Paul. It was night when fewer gathered for the vigils.”

Although the vigils themselves later ceased, the name remained, as did fasting on the vigils. The author of the sermon *To the Brothers in the Hermitage*, sermon 25, on the Nativity of John the Baptist:

> “This feast has a vigil not only among the faithful but also among unbelievers. On this feast especially, pagan unbelievers used to gather at their church and keep vigil. But although those vigils have been abolished, we still retain the ancient name, because while we fast, we call it a vigil.”

### No. 108, line 3

“Then the clergy assembled and asked Narses to petition the ruler together with his report.”

A *suggestio* is an inducement or admonition. Anastasius, in the same passage:

> “Then the Romans made their representations against Vigilius.”

The same author, in the Life of John III:

> “Then the Romans, led by envy, made a representation to Justinian and Sophia.”

And below:

> “When Pope John learned that they had sent their representation against Narses to the emperor…”

*Suggestio* has the same meaning in Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book II:

> “The impending calamity found no remedy except that a reasonable recommendation should be presented by Saint Eugenius, if it might move the barbarian heart, written out in such a document.”

And below:

> “And because, after the second answer, I promised that I would bring forward a recommendation…”

## Further Notes

### No. 102, line 16

“The golden cross,” etc. These words are taken from Paul the Deacon, who reports the matter in the cited passage as follows:

> “When Belisarius reached Africa, he immediately killed Guntharith by a fraudulent peace agreement and subjected the remaining Vandals to the yoke of the republic. Belisarius then came victoriously to Rome and brought to blessed Peter, through the hands of Pope Vigilius, a golden cross of one hundred pounds, adorned with the most precious gems, on which he had inscribed his victories,” etc.

This was evidently in accordance with the ancient custom of heroes and commanders, who hung shields on the most celebrated altars when their victories and trophies had been inscribed upon them. Pausanias discusses this matter in several places.

### No. 107, line 1

“Then the Goths,” etc. What is narrated here is read almost word for word in Paul the Deacon.

The pressures and persecutions which Vigilius endured at Constantinople reveal Justinian’s devious religious dissimulation. He favored whichever side was stronger in the number of its adherents and provinces, and received the pontiffs sometimes with favor, sometimes with stratagems and hardships.

For this reason, I believe, the records of so many distinguished men who flourished in the same age were suppressed and allowed to fall into oblivion. Thus the statement of Facundus, writing at this very time, may appropriately be applied, book X, in Sirmond, volume II, page 728:

> “No one can know or remember everything, because not everything that has been committed to writing has continued to the present,” etc.

Since the East was divided among so many sects, most of them opposed to the Catholic faith, while Justinian hesitated more and more over which he should follow, very many Catholic writings were obliterated.

Vigilius himself seems not obscurely to have indicated this in his letter, writing as follows:

> “And therefore, if the cause of the Church is being arranged so that he may now restore to it the peace which his most pious uncle established in his time, I have no need of oaths, but shall depart immediately,” etc.

### No. 102, line 1

“Vigilius,” etc. When, through the favor of the Augusta Theodora, Vigilius had been intruded into the Apostolic See in place of Silverius, who had been forcibly deposed and driven into exile, he secretly abdicated the pontificate after Silverius’ death, perhaps in the hope that he would be lawfully elected through the influence of Belisarius. The clergy of the Roman Church, however, who were about to elect a new pontiff, were seized by fear: if they elected Vigilius, notoriously stained by many crimes, they would offend against the sacred canons; but if they passed him over, they would provide an occasion for schism and the most dangerous heresy.

After lengthy consultation, perhaps by divine inspiration and with the consent of all, Vigilius was elected to avert the danger of schism and heresy: Catholic indeed, but, because of ambition, polluted by association with heretics. After he had issued a confession of faith and anathematized every heresy, he was raised to the pontifical throne on the fourth day before the Kalends of July in the year of Christ 540, the fourteenth year of Justinian.

The outcome proved that all these events had occurred by God’s will. In an astonishing example, the man who had earlier been induced to curse the people of God was converted to bless that same people. The man whom the empress Theodora had elevated to restore Anthemius to the pontifical seat, after his own legitimate election, again confirmed the anathema pronounced against Anthemius and his heretical associates.

### Same line

“He held the See for seventeen years,” etc. Baronius writes that Vigilius occupied the Apostolic See for sixteen years, in the year 555.

### Line 10

“The emperor and Augusta thanked him,” etc. That Justinian was not aware that Anthemius was being recalled to his See, but that all these things had instead been arranged through a secret plot between the Augusta Theodora and Vigilius, is indicated by Justinian’s letter to Menna. At its conclusion, among the heretics to be cursed and condemned, he lists Anthemius, bishop of Trebizond.

It is therefore clear that the emperor himself did not thank Belisarius in this matter, unless perhaps he had been persuaded that Silverius had been condemned by a just sentence and that Vigilius had legitimately succeeded him.

### Line 11

“He sent him again to Africa,” etc. These events seem to have occurred during the pontificate of John II, in the year of Christ 533.

### Line 15

“From the spoils of the Vandals, coming to Rome,” etc. This offering, which the author of the *Miscella Historia* also mentions, may have been made during the pontificate of Silverius, in the year of Christ 537, when Belisarius, after defeating the Goths, brought Rome under his control.

If any donation was made to Vigilius, however, it must have been offered by Belisarius’ agents during his absence. For Procopius shows that Belisarius himself did not enter Rome during the fourth year of the Persian war.

### No. 104, line 1

“Likewise he gave his niece.” The history contained in this section, and in the preceding section 103 beginning with the words “Then the Romans made their representations,” is proved by Baronius, under the year 546, number 54, to be historically suspect.

## Observations of Thomas Aceti

### No. 104, line 4

“Except in the Basilica of Saint Peter, spare him. For if he is in the Lateran, bring him to us,” etc.

Observe how highly the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles was regarded at that time, even by a heretical woman: there alone the Roman pontiff could find protection against the Augusta’s boiling anger and remain unharmed.

### No. 105, line 5

“On the vigil of our Lord.”

Procopius, *Gothic War*, chapter 3, writes that, when winter had passed and the suitable season for sailing had returned, Vigilius departed from Sicily and reached Constantinople. This agrees better with the preceding words of Anastasius.

For if he had received his ordination shortly before the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as the text says, in December, how could he have reached Constantinople on the vigil of that same Nativity? Baronius, under the year 547, number 36.

### No. 106, line 7

“Then he slapped him,” etc.

The events which follow occurred after Theodora’s death, in the year of Christ 551. When persecution against him was again stirred up through Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, Vigilius had to flee to Chalcedon, to the Basilica of Saint Euphemia, as is clear from Vigilius’ letter written to the universal Church.

Accordingly, the confused and disordered material which Anastasius subsequently recounts concerning the Augusta Theodora, who had already been dead for three years, should be restored by the reader to its proper places.

### No. 107, line 1

“Totila descended upon Rome and besieged it,” etc.

The siege began in the year of Christ 546. In the following year the Isaurian soldiers betrayed the city to Totila, while the Romans, oppressed by terrible famine, were reduced to the most sordid necessities and many fell dead.

After Totila had occupied the City, he began to demolish it and turn it into pasture for sheep. But after repeatedly reading Belisarius’ letters, which wisely dissuaded him from this plan, he abandoned the project.

Belisarius recovered the City after defeating Totila again in a battle in the plain in the same year, 547.

### No. 108, line 1

“At the same time Justinian sent Narses the eunuch.”

In that year, when the emperor, at the insistence of Pope Vigilius, revoked the edict concerning the Three Chapters and presented himself as obedient to the Roman pontiff, Narses, commander of the Roman army, relying by God’s help on the intercession of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, routed and killed Totila together with his entire army in the tenth year of Totila’s reign, as the monk Saint Benedict had foretold to him.

He recovered the City a second time after it had been occupied by Totila a second time, namely in the year of Christ 553.

According to Procopius, Narses sent the keys of the city gates to Justinian the emperor at Constantinople. Thus the emperor obtained the keys of the City at the very time when he recognized the keys of Peter in Vigilius.

### Line 10

“Do you wish to receive Vigilius,” etc.

Here Justinian sacrilegiously usurps the confirmation and deposition of the Roman pontiff. How great a loss this caused to the whole empire will become clear below.

It is lamentable that the Roman clergy promised the people who were demanding it that, after Vigilius’ death, no pontiff would be appointed except one whom the emperor had presented. By this policy the mistress of nations was led into captivity and the queen of provinces was made tributary.

### Line 16

“Vigilius died,” etc.

The deacon Pelagius fell under suspicion of having killed Vigilius. He nevertheless cleared himself of the charge brought against him, as is shown below in the Life of Pelagius.

## Chronological Notes

Although Vigilius was an invader of the Roman See—having been introduced by the faction of the Augusta Theodora in place of Silverius, who had been forcibly deposed and sent into exile—his pontificate ought properly not to be reckoned from any point except his legitimate election, by which, after the death of Silverius, he was appointed in his place by the votes of the clergy. Nevertheless, the period during which Silverius lived in exile among the Pontine Islands was also popularly attributed to him.

The Bibliothecary and the catalogues assign him eighteen years and five months; several codices read six months and twenty-six days, others twenty-five.

According to Panvinius, whose view Holstenius follows in his chronological diagram and in his notes on the Roman synod under Boniface II, Vigilius died on the fourth day before the Ides of January, that is, 10 January. Cardinal Noris likewise adopts this date in his discussion of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 8, toward the end.

Since the Christian year 555 had begun in the second indiction, which had already commenced in the preceding September of 554, that date of Vigilius’ death is correctly reconciled with the chronology. For Marcellinus, in his Chronicle, reports that in the thirteenth consulship of Basil, corresponding to the Christian year 554, and in the second indiction, which began to be counted from September, Pope Vigilius began at last to be released from exile by the Roman emperors, Justinian and the younger Justin, and to return to Rome.

This agrees with his arrival in Sicily around the end of autumn of that same year. There he was seized by illness and died in the following January, with which the year 555 began. This assignment of the dates also agrees with the chronology and history of John Malalas, who wrote under the same Justinian.

For on page 230 he relates that, in August of the fifteenth indiction—which was the year 552:

> “Narses, the chamberlain and exarch of the Romans, sent news of his victory to Rome. For after Narses had engaged Totila the Goth in battle and prevailed over him, he killed him and sent his bloodstained garments to Constantinople.”

Marcellinus’ Chronicle supports this, placing Totila’s slaughter in the fifteenth indiction, in the twelfth year of Basil’s reign.

Two years after that victory, Marcellinus’ Chronicle records the free release of Vigilius, who had previously been detained by the emperor in the royal city of Constantinople, so that he might return to Rome with his companions.

During those two years after Totila’s death, Narses was occupied with recovering Italy, especially Rome, and driving the Goths out everywhere. This continued until Teja, whom the Goths had chosen as Totila’s successor, fought bravely on the bridge over the River Draco, while Vesuvius near Naples was collapsing, and was killed in battle.

After all the Goths had been driven from Italy, with their lives spared by agreement, peace was firmly re-established throughout the empire.

Thus, once the occasion for suspicion and accusation had been removed—the occasion by which Vigilius and the Roman nobles had sometimes been attacked—permission to return was granted. According to Anastasius, the Romans obtained this from Justinian, who offered them the choice either of restoring Vigilius or of substituting Pelagius for him; they chose that Vigilius should be restored to his own See.

Since the complete expulsion of the Goths from Italy occurred two years after Totila’s death, namely in 554, Vigilius’ release and the departure of the Romans returning to Italy are correctly placed in that year, around autumn; and Vigilius’ death in Sicily on 10 January 555.

If his seventeen years in the See, together with five or six months and twenty-five days, are counted backward from 10 January, his accession falls in June or July of 537. Yet, as we have said, in that year Pope Silverius was ordered into exile in November, on the nineteenth.

I therefore believe that the number of months must be reduced in the chronology of Vigilius, which I think should be reduced to seventeen years, one month, and twenty-five days.

I believe that the months were increased for the following reason. Since Vigilius’ legitimate pontificate began only with the death of Silverius and Vigilius’ new election—that is, from July—it remained in everyone’s mind that the true beginning of Vigilius’ See was to be reckoned from that month.

The number of years, however, which ought to have been reduced by one—since Silverius remained in exile until June of 538—was not preserved so clearly in human memory as the season in which Vigilius died. It is therefore not surprising that, in the catalogues, during an age filled with so many wars and with the city alternately captive and free, the number of years was marked for Vigilius from the usurped See, while the number of months was marked from the legitimately possessed See.

We assign to him sixteen years, six months, and seventeen days of legitimate tenure of the See, reckoned from approximately 24 June 538. We allow four days between 20 June, when Silverius completed his martyrdom on the island of Pontia, exhausted by hunger, and the arrival of the report of his death in the city and the clergy’s celebration of Vigilius’ legitimate election. This period extends to 11 January 555, the date of Vigilius’ death.

Before those sixteen years, six months, and seventeen days, Vigilius had usurped Silverius’ See from 22 November 537 to 24 June 538: seven months and two days. Added to sixteen years, seven months, and seventeen days, these yield a total of seventeen years, one month, and nineteen days.

With the additional four days from Silverius’ death to Vigilius’ legitimate election, the total becomes seventeen years, one month, and twenty-three days. This should be reckoned from the third day after Silverius’ exile, but it was incorrectly increased by four or five months and assigned to him as seventeen years and three or six months, with twenty-five or twenty-six days, through the error already indicated.

## Historical Notes

### No. 102, line 1

“From his father John, the consul,” etc.

John, surnamed Gibbus, was consul of the West in the year 499 of the Christian era. There was another John, surnamed Scytha, consul in 498, but he was consul of the East. I believe that John Gibbus should be regarded as Vigilius’ father.

Flavius John, consul of the West in 456, seems too far removed from Vigilius’ age to be considered his father. The same is true of Flavius John, who entered the consulship in 467 with Flavius Pusaeus: he seems somewhat too remote for the age of the pontiff to have survived as his son after ninety years.

Flavius John Palladius Eutychianus, a man of senatorial rank, count and prefect in 536, is so named in the Acts of the Council of Constantinople under Menna; Menna signed the consular registers two years later. Since Palladius was an Easterner and of Vigilius’ generation, he should not be regarded as Vigilius’ father.

Apart from these men, no other consul named John is found in the registers for this period. I therefore think that Vigilius’ origin should be traced to John Gibbus.

### No. 102, line 14

“Then Belisarius the patrician, from the spoils of the Vandals,” etc.

Some criticize the Bibliothecary, denying that Belisarius came to the City and that such gifts were offered during Vigilius’ pontificate. Cardinal Baronius is among them, under the year 545.

Yet, with all due respect to so great a writer, the matter is sufficiently established. Procopius, who accompanied Belisarius in the war and was assigned to him by Justinian as secretary, expressly describes in the first book of the *Gothic War* the sequence of events accomplished by Belisarius day by day, as well as the time and manner in which he entered Rome after recovering it for the empire and remained there for a full two years, partly during the pontificate of Saint Silverius and partly during that of Vigilius, first the usurper and afterward his legitimate successor.

After Procopius had related the recovery of Carthage in the second book of the *Vandalic War*, he records Belisarius’ return to Constantinople, his consulship, and the triumph granted him by Justinian. This occurred in the Christian year 535, as is clear from the consular registers.

In that same year of his consulship, Belisarius was sent with a fleet to Sicily. Through his prudence and valor the island was recovered for the empire, so that on the final day of his consulship Belisarius entered Syracuse in triumph. Procopius, *Gothic War*, book I, chapter 4.

Soon afterward the energetic commander turned to the siege of Naples and captured it within twenty days by a stratagem. Then he proceeded to recover Rome.

Vitiges, who had been appointed successor to Theodoric after Theodoric’s death, thought that Rome would remain in Gothic power. He left a garrison there and brought several senators with him to Ravenna as hostages; he also compelled Pope Silverius, together with the Senate and people, to swear an oath of loyalty.

Vitiges had scarcely reached Ravenna when Belisarius, finding the inhabitants favorably disposed, brought his army along the Latin Way toward the City. When the Goths voluntarily withdrew, he gained possession of Rome.

A copyist’s error assigned this to Justinian’s eleventh year, whereas it should have been called the tenth, just as a few lines earlier the name of Liberius was wrongly inserted for Silverius.

The sequence of events proves that this was the year immediately following Belisarius’ consulship. For that commander entered Syracuse on the final day of his consulship—that is, 31 December 535—and, after a few months of the year 536 had passed, took Naples, proceeded directly to Rome, captured it without opposition, restored its walls, prepared himself and the Romans to withstand a prolonged Gothic siege, and sent commanders to recover Tuscany.

As the year 537 was passing, Vitiges established his camp before the City and continued the siege for a full year and nine days, until he was forced to withdraw after his attempt had failed, in the summer of 538. Belisarius therefore remained in the City for a full two years, from autumn 536 to autumn 538.

During that same two-year period, the Roman pontificate was administered by Saint Silverius from 8 June 536 until 19 November 537. On that day, wickedly expelled into exile through the cunning of Theodora, he endured a prolonged martyrdom on the island of Pontia until 20 June of the following year, 538, when his triumphant passage from mortal to immortal life was marked.

Vigilius, however, after Silverius had been expelled by Belisarius at the command of that same Theodora, was made an intruder and occupied the Roman See unworthily throughout Silverius’ exile. Afterward, transformed from usurper into legitimate successor a few days after Silverius’ death, with the consent of the Roman clergy—around the end of June 538—he could bring into the Vatican Basilica the gifts offered by Belisarius, which the Bibliothecary records.

It should be presumed that this offering took place after the siege of the City had been lifted, around the beginning of autumn 538, as a testimony of thanksgiving to God for the great success granted to the empire, the City, and the commander in driving the Goths from the principal part of Italy, after Sicily and Africa had been liberated.

### No. 103, line 3

“To this Vigilius replied: ‘Far be this from me, Augusta Lady,’” etc.

How Vigilius, transformed from a criminal usurper into the legitimate successor of the Apostolic See and an example of pontifical steadfastness by the favor of divine grace and through the votes of the clergy properly conferred upon him, acted so that the Church of God would not be divided by a terrible schism, has been shown so clearly by Cardinal Baronius under the year 540, and is further illustrated by the notes of the Most Reverend Archbishop Sommier and of the distinguished Bencini and Pagi, which are to be inserted here with his Life, that no room remains for our own elucidation of the Bibliothecary’s text.

We shall mention only one addition to the reflections of so many distinguished writers, drawn from Dom Constant’s new edition of the letters of the supreme pontiffs. Concerning this, Dom Monpinot promises the following in his preliminary letter, no. 13:

> “XIII. As I linger over each pontiff, I feel that I am exceeding the proper measure and limits of a letter. Therefore, passing over the others, I shall stop with Vigilius.
>
> “No one is unaware how many troubles Vigilius endured for the faith, or with what strength of spirit he stood against the Eutychians. And yet, if we listen to ancient and modern writers, the prelude to so many sufferings and so many outstanding deeds was a sorrowful betrayal of the faith.
>
> “The pontiff is harassed and denounced as guilty of sacrilegious traffic: as though, setting aside all shame, he had entered into a wicked alliance with heretics, trampled upon the laws of the Church, renounced the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, and invaded the Roman See.
>
> “This stain has so settled and grown old upon his name that I think there is no one today who holds a different opinion concerning the beginning of his pontificate. I admit that it is an unpopular undertaking to oppose everyone and resist the common judgment. But if love of truth demands it, and especially when the reputation of great men is at stake, no sensible person will condemn the effort.
>
> “Constant therefore undertook to repel the calumny imposed upon the most holy pope. I shall briefly indicate the method by which he did so.”

### XIV

The learned man has little regard for Isidore’s letters and the pseudo-Damasus, or *Liber Pontificalis*, as grounds for discrediting the narrative. He further examines what the African writers—Facundus of Hermiana, Victor of Tunnuna, both bishops, and Liberatus of Carthage, a deacon—say about Vigilius. For this is the central point on which the whole story turns. He thoroughly investigates their accusations, I mean, and utterly demolishes them after comparing them both with one another and with other historical records. He also investigates the reasons for Silverius’s expulsion into exile; the grounds for promoting Vigilius in his place; the beginnings of Vigilius’s pontificate; by whose authority, and at what time, the controversy over the Three Chapters began to develop; and what the same pontiff intended first by defending and then by condemning them. Finally, he carefully examines all his actions, assigns a chronological note to each, accurately separates the certain from the uncertain and the true from the false, and submits these various arguments of historical criticism to such examination that there is none from which he does not extract something toward the refutation of the calumny.

1. What we read in the *Lives of the Pontiffs*—that Boniface II had arranged that Vigilius should be chosen as his successor while he was still alive, something that was forbidden—Constantius proves not even to bear the appearance of truth. He likewise shows that the letter addressed to the afflicted Silverius must be considered in the same connection. In it the holy pontiff marks Vigilius as though he had already burned with desire for the primatial see when he had not yet advanced beyond the rank of deacon.

2. The documents in which Facundus, Victor, Liberatus, and others claim that Vigilius had promised that, if he were made pontiff in place of Silverius, he would condemn the Three Chapters must likewise be dismissed as calumny. Vigilius neither ever made such a promise nor could have made it, since he had obtained the pontificate before anyone had even begun to think of condemning the Three Chapters. Nor is the letter attributed to the same pope any more trustworthy. In it he is falsely said to have granted his communion to the leading Acephalous leaders—Theodosius, Anthimus, and Severus—and to have done what he was said to have promised in written pledges. This principal part of the story is refuted by the clearest testimonies of the Africans themselves, of the Roman clergy, of the emperor Justinian, and finally of Vigilius himself, to say nothing of other evidence.

3. This letter was not produced before the end of the year 548, that is, at the time when Vigilius issued his *Judicatum*. Nor did it have any authors other than the Acephali. Since they had been unable to break the constancy of that pope by either secret or open force, they finally concentrated all their efforts on stirring up hatred against him, spreading the most disgraceful rumors throughout the provinces and forging writings in his name, by which he was said to have formerly passed treacherously to the Eutychian party. The African defenders of the Three Chapters then lent credibility to the calumny and accepted as true things which they could scarcely have known for themselves—being partly carried away by zeal, and moreover having been driven into exile and alienated from Vigilius’s communion because of the condemnation of the Chapters. Whatever they report about the written pledges and the letter, they report so variously and confusedly that Facundus above all and Liberatus cannot be reconciled either with one another, or with the reliable records of that age, or even with themselves.

4. It is indeed not altogether clear that no canons were violated by Vigilius’s promotion: for no one can deny that it occurred while Silverius had been driven into exile but was still alive. Nevertheless, there are considerations that persuade one that it was legitimate. As witnesses to this Constantius cites not Vigilius alone, but also the Roman clergy, the Gallic and Spanish bishops, and even the Easterners. If their acts and statements are correctly interpreted, they prove that Vigilius was regarded as the legitimate pontiff immediately at the beginning of his pontificate, while Silverius was still alive, and that his rescripts were counted among the rescripts of the Apostolic See.

5. Whatever the pseudo-Damasus relates about that pope’s journey to Constantinople, especially about the reason for his journey and the taunts of the Roman people, although these things scarcely needed refutation, are nevertheless refuted in their proper place, and not without some worthwhile effort. The interpolations in the Fifth Synod are examined with equal care, as are the wickedly attached oath imposed on the pontiff, two letters falsely marked with his name and addressed to Justinian and Theodora, and other matters of this kind, which cast no slight blemish upon his integrity.

6. Nor is omitted what some writers, partly ancient and partly recent, transmit: namely, that Vigilius sinned, if not by defending error, at least by frivolity; if not by deliberate deceit, at least by impatience of exile, in consenting to the condemnation of the Three Chapters. Constantius refutes both groups by a plain and simple exposition of the facts, and rejects as empty both this tale of exile and the reproach of frivolity. In a word, whatever the malevolence of falsifiers disgracefully fabricated, and whatever the credulity of people indulgent toward preconceived opinions carelessly admitted, this diligent editor has refuted by disentangling and exposing it.

Friends urged him to publish this treatise separately, both because it is sufficiently close in size to a book—it contains more than eighty pages—and because it could provide a taste of the rest of the work. But the prudent man preferred to preserve it in its proper place, judging—and this is the fact—that there is such a close relationship between it and the letters of Vigilius that each sheds mutual light upon the other, and that they cannot be separated without great inconvenience to the reader.

[Note: [Col. 0592B]

No. 102, line 1.—“Vigilius, a Roman by birth,” etc. This Vigilius’s accession was scarcely legitimate, since, contrary to the ecclesiastical regulations, while his predecessor Silverius was alive and removed from the administration of the pontificate, he seized the Roman pontificate by force; and therefore the sixth schism is noted, which ended with Silverius’s death. Beyond doubt Vigilius had long been afflicted by the spirit of ambition. For shortly before, under Pope Boniface II, he had arranged to be made assistant and successor in the pontificate; and when this had then turned out according to his desire, some time later he invaded Silverius’s place, as Anastasius records in the passage cited above. Silverius, in exile, strongly reproaches him for all this in a certain letter printed in volume II of the *Councils*.]

[Note: [Col. 0592C]

Line 10.—“How he entered Silverius’s place,” etc. Vigilius, a Roman by birth, son of John, a deacon of the holy Roman Church and apocrisiarius of Pope Agapetus at Constantinople, returned to Rome in the year 536, after Agapetus’s death, with letters from the empress Theodora, so that he might be chosen Roman pontiff. Through the agency of Belisarius, he arranged for the holy Silverius, already ordained and seated at Rome, to be sent into exile by Belisarius in the year 537, on 18 November. He himself, intruded in Silverius’s place, was ordained antipope on the twenty-second of the same month, as we related in the account of Silverius.

It is certain that the see remained vacant for several days after Silverius’s deposition. This may be gathered from Procopius, book I of *The Gothic War*, chapter 25, where, after saying that Belisarius sent Silverius into Greece, he adds: “And shortly afterward he advanced Vigilius to the pontificate.” Liberatus, too, after narrating Silverius’s deposition, says: “He was not seen again by his own people. And on the following day Belisarius summoned the presbyters, deacons, and all the clergy and ordered them to choose another pope for themselves.” From this it may be inferred that Vigilius was chosen on 19 November of the year 537, the day after Silverius’s deposition, and that his ordination was deferred until the following Sunday, namely 22 November. Procopius had this date in mind when he wrote that, shortly after Silverius had been sent into exile, Vigilius was raised to the pontificate.

Hence two of the catalogues prefixed to volume I of Baronius’s critical work state that the see was vacant for one day, referring to Vigilius’s election. Anastasius, referring to the ordination, wrote that the see was vacant for five days; but the unit was undoubtedly added by copyists. For Anastasius himself makes clear that Vigilius was ordained on 22 November, when he writes that this was the day of his birth. From that day until Silverius’s death, Vigilius was an antipope. On this, see what was said concerning Silverius.

Three letters of Vigilius as antipope remain. We dealt with the first in the account of Silverius. The second is said in the collection of the councils to have been written to Eutharius against the Priscillianists and Arians.
