But Baluzius, in volume I of the new *Collection of the Councils*, p. 1468, demonstrates that it ought to be addressed to Profuturus, who at that time was bishop of Braga. He establishes this on the authority of several manuscripts in the Colbert Library. Moreover, Profuturus is mentioned under that name in the acts of the First Council of Braga, where the letter is said to have been written in response to his inquiry and to have been omitted from the acts because of its length.

From this letter we learn that the error of those who rebaptized—formerly condemned by the holy Pope Stephen I of that name, later condemned at the Council of Nicaea, and opposed by Saint Augustine in Africa—was revived in Spain at the beginning of the sixth century by the Arians and Priscillianists. The same Baluzius restored the date of the letter from a Colbert manuscript, in which it is said to have been given at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Flavius John, a man of illustrious rank. In the collection of the Councils, however, it is said to have been given on the Kalends of March, during the consulship of Volusianus and John, men of illustrious rank. Yet no Volusianus held the consulship at this time, while John alone, without a colleague, entered the consulship in the East in the year 538, as all the *Fasti* record and as is also stated in the following letter of Vigilius.

Baronius thought that, after learning of Silverius’s death and the miracles that followed it, Vigilius, moved by repentance, renounced the pontificate he had wrongly usurped and, after six days, as Anastasius records, was again elected Roman pontiff by a free election of the clergy. But from what has been said it is clear that Anastasius is not speaking there of the vacancy of the see that occurred after Silverius’s death, but of the vacancy that occurred from 18 November of the year 537, after Vigilius had been deposed from the pontificate, until the day of Vigilius’s ordination, which was performed five days later, namely 22 November.

After Silverius later died, the clergy did indeed consent to Vigilius’s pontificate and declared him the legitimate shepherd of the Church by their votes, compelled both by the power of Belisarius and by concern for ecclesiastical peace and unity. But the claim that any abdication occurred is gratuitous and unsupported by the testimony of any author.

Thus Vigilius was suddenly transformed into another man. Through the action of the Holy Spirit, who governs the Church, he erased by a solemn profession of faith what he had previously written sacrilegiously to the empress Theodora concerning the faith of the Council of Chalcedon. This can be seen in his fourth letter to the emperor Justinian, in which he professed that he accepted the four Ecumenical Councils and the letters of Saint Leo and of other predecessors, and believed according to them. He also confirmed the deposition of Anthimus from the see of Constantinople by Pope Agapetus, as well as the condemnation of the other Acephali.

Vigilius wrote on the same matter to Menna, bishop of Constantinople, in his fifth letter. He congratulates him on embracing the four holy universal councils after the condemnation of the heretics, and decrees that those who repent of heresy ought to be received, provided that they anathematize those who do not follow the four councils mentioned above in matters of faith or do not wholly confess the venerable decrees of Saint Leo the pope.

At the end we read:

“Flavius Dominicus, a man of illustrious rank, count of the household troops, former consul and patrician, having reread, compared, and agreed with these documents concerning the faith, produced by the most blessed and apostolic Pope Vigilius and addressed to our lord Justinian, the most devout and most Christian prince, as well as to Menna, the most blessed man and archbishop of the city of Constantinople, have signed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, during the consulship of Justin, a man of illustrious rank.”

This occurred in the year of Christ 540. Accordingly, both letters—to Justinian and to Menna—were written by Vigilius, who delivered them at Rome to the aforementioned lord, as is clear from the letter to Menna.

### No. 103, line 1.—“The empress Theodora wrote to Pope Vigilius,” etc.

The controversy concerning the Three Chapters must now be explained. On its account the Fifth Ecumenical Council, the Second Council of Constantinople, was held. The account here follows Cardinal Norisius, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapters 3 and following.

Pelagius, the apocrisiarius of Pope Vigilius at Constantinople, wishing to weaken the power and reputation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a great patron of the Origenists who enjoyed considerable favor and authority with Justinian, persuaded Menna, bishop of Constantinople, and Justinian to accept the booklets against Origen and his followers that had been presented by monks, and to condemn Origen.

“Then,” says Liberatus in chapter 23, “the emperor readily agreed, rejoicing that he was able to pass judgment on such matters. By his order a condemnation of Origen and of those Chapters was drafted. Those found at Constantinople subscribed to it together with Menna, the archbishop, and it was then sent to Vigilius at Rome, to Zoilus at Alexandria, to Ephrem at Antioch, and to Peter at Jerusalem. When these men received and subscribed it, Origen was condemned after his death, although he had already been condemned while alive.”

Justinian therefore wrote an encyclical letter to the five patriarchs of the world. In it he reports Origen’s errors concerning the mystery of the Trinity, the pre-existence of souls, the soul of Christ, and other matters, and attacks them with testimonies from the holy Fathers. A summary of these arguments is contained in nine canons, which he appended to the letter and which Lupus has illustrated with notes in his commentary on the Fifth Synod. Once this letter had been published and, according to the Liberatus cited above, subscribed by Pope Vigilius and the other patriarchs, a serious wound was inflicted upon Origenian doctrine. These events took place after the year 540 and before the year 544.

From Origen’s condemnation arose the controversy concerning the Three Chapters, which became the source of immense disturbances and calamities. For when their defense of Origen had been rendered hopeless, the Origenists deceitfully turned their minds toward revenge.

Theodore, metropolitan of Caesarea, surnamed Arcidas, whom we have said was a great patron of the Origenists, persuaded the emperor Justinian that the Acephali could be brought by a shortcut to subscribe to the Council of Chalcedon if he corrected only three matters that especially offended them.

First, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia and teacher of Nestorius, should be condemned, even though his praises occur in the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, which had been read at the Council of Chalcedon. Second, the books of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, against the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril, ratified at the Council of Ephesus, should be prohibited. The Fathers of Chalcedon had not condemned those books, being content with Theodoret’s anathema against Nestorius, which he pronounced while present. Finally, the aforementioned letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian should be rejected, since in it Ibas praises Theodore, accuses Saint Cyril, and charges the Council of Ephesus with having issued, without examination, a hasty judgment against Nestorius.

Theodore, the metropolitan of Caesarea, suddenly promised that, once these Three Chapters had been proscribed, the Acephali would be united.

Yet Theodore seems to have offered this advice to Justinian with the intention of contriving a correction of the Council of Chalcedon—a correction which Pelagius, the apocrisiarius of the Roman See, together with the Western Church, wished to preserve wholly intact, down to the smallest iota.

The empress Theodora, who openly favored the Acephali, pressed upon Justinian the very proposal made by the Caesarean prelate. But the wicked woman was plotting a crime with this aim: once a correction had been made in some matters concerning the Council of Chalcedon, its authority as a whole would collapse and become worthless, since it would have been shown to have erred somewhere.

“When the emperor heard this,” says Liberatus at the end of his *Breviary*, “and failed entirely to foresee their painful deception, he willingly accepted their proposal and most readily promised to carry it out.” He later adds: “The prince agreed to these things, gladly promised that he would fulfill them, and, abandoning his proper undertaking, composed a book directed solely toward the condemnation of the Three Chapters, notorious to us all because of our sins.”

This was the first edict issued by the emperor Justinian against the Three Chapters. It no longer exists, as will soon be seen.

Stephen the deacon, who served as apocrisiarius with the emperor after Pelagius had been summoned by Vigilius to Rome, openly resisted the edict. He rebuked Menna, the bishop of Constantinople, as guilty of violating the faith because he had given his consent. Several bishops also gave him booklets to transmit to Vigilius, in which they protested that they had subscribed only because they had been compelled by the bishop of Constantinople.

Facundus of Hermiana, however, in book IV, chapter 4, writes that Menna of Constantinople, Peter of Jerusalem, and Ephrem of Antioch, although unwilling and reluctant, subscribed to the edict.

Pelagius the deacon, who was then staying at Rome and who was an opponent of the Origenists, rose up against the edict, as did the African bishops. The Church was therefore divided into factions. The East accepted the edict, while the Westerners—the Illyrians, Italians, Gauls, Spaniards, and, as already stated, the Africans—fought in defense of the Three Chapters.

Vigilius and the other Western bishops therefore refused to subscribe to the edict against the Three Chapters, believing that this could in no way be done without serious injury to the Council of Chalcedon. Accordingly, when a year had passed amid such divisions among the Churches, Justinian arranged for the question to be discussed in a full synod in the imperial city.

To draw the patriarchs there more easily, however, he pretended that his purpose was to restore the sect of the Acephali to Orthodox communion. Vigilius too was summoned by the emperor to the synod, but he did not go directly to Constantinople. Instead, he went to Sicily, intending that a synod should be convened there.

He remained in Sicily for a long time. For Procopius, book III of *The Gothic War*, chapter 6, speaking of his arrival at Constantinople, says:

“Vigilius, the Roman pontiff, came to Byzantium at the emperor’s summons from Sicily, where he had already spent a long time because of that journey.”

The length of Vigilius’s stay in Sicily is also demonstrated by the embassies that he received there. The bishops of Africa and Sardinia, through representatives, begged him not to submit to Justinian’s new decrees against the Three Chapters, as Facundus testifies in book IV, chapter 3.

Vigilius left Rome around the end of the year 544, specifically on 22 November, according to Anastasius, who writes that this was the day of his birth. Although Anastasius includes much that is fabulous about Vigilius, it does not follow that he was also false about the day on which Vigilius left Rome.

The year is established from Victor of Tunnuna, who reports his departure after the fourth consulship of Basil, a man of illustrious rank—according to his method of reckoning, the year 544. Moreover, Vigilius himself, in an encyclical letter dated 5 February 552, says that he had stated through a messenger, to be conveyed in his name to Justinian:

“We departed from our city in haste to your piety seven years ago in such a way that we had no private business.”

Since he counts seven years from his departure from Rome, this confirms what Victor, cited above, writes: that he left Rome in the year 544, and indeed toward its end, as we have said from Anastasius.

The same Victor of Tunnuna, in the passage cited, shows that Vigilius undertook that journey unwillingly and under compulsion. He writes:

“Emperor Justinian, stirred up by the deceptions of the Acephali, subtly compelled Vigilius, the Roman bishop, to hasten to the imperial city, under the pretext of gathering those who were separated from communion with the Church, in order to condemn the Three Chapters.”

The clergy of Italy likewise wrote in a letter to the Frankish envoys departing for Constantinople in the year 552:

“When the most blessed Pope Vigilius came there—that is, to Constantinople—six years ago, or rather, to speak more truthfully, was brought there almost by force.”

This too confirms that Vigilius left Rome in the year 544.

These statements do not, however, support Anastasius, who writes that Vigilius was seized at Rome on the order of the empress Theodora by Anthimius Scribo, placed on a ship, and forcibly taken to Constantinople. Baronius observed that this and many other things narrated by Anastasius are merely fabulous. Certainly Justinian, who wished to draw Vigilius over to his position, could not have ordered him to be treated disgracefully. Hence Victor of Tunnuna says only that he was subtly compelled, while the Italian clergy says that he was brought away almost by force.

While Vigilius was lingering in Sicily, Datius, the metropolitan, came to him from Constantinople. He had been staying there either because he had fled to escape the bloody hands of the Goths, as Baronius says, or because he had been detained there on account of the faith, as Saint Gregory the pope writes in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4.

From Datius Vigilius learned that Menna, the patriarch of Constantinople, had subscribed the sentence issued by Justinian against the Three Chapters. He also learned that, as a result, not only Stephen, Vigilius’s apocrisiarius before Justinian, but also most of the bishops and laypeople had separated themselves from Vigilius’s communion.

Thus Vigilius writes in a letter to Menna, which Facundus quotes in his book against Mocianus:

“While we were staying on the island of Sicily, we learned from our brother and fellow bishop Datius that he himself, several of our fellow priests, and many sons of the Christian Church had likewise withdrawn themselves from your communion.”

Accordingly, when Facundus speaks of Vigilius’s departure from Sicily, he says that Vigilius rebuked Menna by letter for having subscribed to Justinian’s edict. How he later conducted himself toward Menna at Constantinople will be related below.

Vigilius therefore remained in Sicily for a long time, not only to obtain permission for a synod to be held on that island, where bishops from the East, the West, and Africa could gather by an easy voyage, but also so that he would not appear to abandon Rome, which was besieged by the Goths, during dangerous times.

At last, in the year 546, apparently when the year was already well advanced, he made a landing in the Peloponnese and proceeded overland to Constantinople. Facundus, book IV, chapter 3, says that he made the same journey through Hellas and Illyricum.

At Thessalonica he met Sebastian, a deacon of the Apostolic See and quaestor in Dalmatia. Vigilius ordered him to return to his province, instructing him not to proceed to Constantinople until he had collected the revenues of Praevalis.

Vigilius entered Constantinople on 25 January of the year 547, as the Continuator of Marcellinus records under that year of Christ.

Vigilius was received with the highest honor by the emperor Justinian, as Theophanes testifies in his *Chronicle*. He adds:

“Honored by the emperor with such signs of distinction and respect, he became so emboldened that he imposed upon Menna, bishop of Constantinople, the punishment of exclusion from communion for four months.”

But the empress Theodora reconciled Menna with Vigilius. Theophanes continues:

“Vigilius, likewise asked by the empress Theodora, restored peace to Menna, the patriarch of Constantinople, on 29 June, the day sacred to the holy apostles.”

Since Menna was suspended from communion for four months, he had been excluded from it by Pope Vigilius around the end of February.

The same Theophanes demonstrates that this occurred in the year 547 when he writes:

“In that same year, on 11 May, the Saturday of holy Pentecost, while circus games were being celebrated,” etc.

This Paschal dating indicates the year 547, for Easter was celebrated in that year on 24 March.

Vigilius also promulgated a decree against the Acephali, although the empress Theodora favored them, as Saint Gregory the Great testifies in book II, letter 36, to the bishops of Ireland.

Meanwhile Vigilius was learning how prudently the pontiffs before him had refrained from attending the synods of the Greeks. Such great violence was being inflicted upon him that, on one occasion, he is said to have burst out publicly with these words:

“I protest: although you hold me captive, you cannot make the blessed apostle Peter captive.”

An Italian cleric bears witness to this in a letter, or supplicatory booklet, presented to the envoys of Childebert, king of the Franks, who were departing for Constantinople. They were earnestly asked to undertake Pope Vigilius’s cause.

As we said above, Vigilius asked only this: that an Ecumenical Council should be held in Sicily, or somewhere else closer to the West, to which the Latins could travel conveniently. But Justinian’s decree required that the matter be debated in the imperial city.

Accordingly, when the emperor pressed for a synod, Vigilius convened a council of some bishops at Constantinople in the year 548. “About seventy bishops,” says Facundus in his book against Mocianus, “assembled with the Roman bishop.”

But when Vigilius noticed that matters were proceeding otherwise than he had hoped, while Facundus and certain other Africans were defending the Three Chapters with increasing vigor, he interrupted the proceedings of the synod and decided to issue a judgment on his own.

Impatient with his prolonged stay in the imperial city and broken by Justinian’s acts of violence, he wrote his *Judicatum* to Menna, patriarch of Constantinople. In it he condemned the Three Chapters, which he had hitherto defended, suddenly changing his position, but added the clause: “With the reverence of the Council of Chalcedon preserved in all respects.”

Vigilius himself relates the matter in a letter against Theodore, metropolitan of Caesarea:

“To restrain the scandal, we condescended to the minds of certain people whom we believed could be moderated by some accommodation, because you had inflamed them for several years as an exceedingly restless instigator. We therefore judged that certain measures should be arranged medicinally for the time being, on this condition: that, once all future disturbance had been put to rest, no one should presume to do anything further in this matter, either by word or by letter.”

Vigilius had already begun to see that the Greeks were right in warning that the Three Chapters did not concern the Council of Chalcedon. That council had already been completed before the Chapters were named, and Leo the Great had given no judgment concerning them, since he had approved the acts of the council only up to the definition of the faith.

Vigilius delivered his *Judicatum* to Menna on Holy Saturday, that is, 11 April, as he himself states in his letter to Rusticus and Sebastian, deacons of the Roman Church.

Vigilius thought that he had satisfied both sides: the Greeks, by condemning the Three Chapters; the Latins, by declaring that he had done so while preserving the Council of Chalcedon.

Among others, Rusticus and Sebastian, extremely learned deacons of the Roman Church, were present with Vigilius. Both of them praised the *Judicatum* in the highest terms.

But Facundus, bishop of Hermiana, who was also present at Constantinople, accused Vigilius of lying, betrayal, collusion with the Acephali, ambition, and venality, as may be seen especially in his book against Mocianus.

The Africans not only refused to approve the *Judicatum*, but deprived those who consented to it of ecclesiastical communion. The Illyrian bishops did the same. The whole West raged, and not only the bishops but entire peoples openly resisted Justinian’s orders.

The emperor therefore understood that the *Judicatum* of Vigilius had caused the disputes to increase immeasurably, although he had hoped that they would be settled by that document.

Accordingly, Vigilius took care for his reputation. In letters sent at the beginning of the year 550 to two noble bishops—Valentinian, metropolitan of Tomi in Pontus, and Aurelian of Arles—he explained that in his *Judicatum* he had done nothing contrary to the reverence due to the Council of Chalcedon. Both letters are inserted in the acts of the Fifth Synod, Collation VII.

In the year 549, Rusticus and Sebastian, deacons of the Roman Church and, as we said in the preceding section, those great heralds and praisers of the *Judicatum*, were won over by the persuasions of Felix, an African monk and abbot of the monastery of Gillitanum. They abandoned their former judgment and, with hardened faces, separated themselves from Vigilius’s communion, increasing the number of his opponents.

They disseminated letters in every direction in which they stated that Vigilius had written something that was contrary to the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon. Vigilius himself bears witness to this in the sentence issued against them in the year 550, after 18 March, as the author of Baronius’s critical work demonstrates under that year, no. 4.

Vigilius, justly angered against them, and having learned that they were unwilling to return to a better course, struck both with an anathema and removed them from their dignity and rank. The sentence issued against them by Vigilius is inserted in the acts of the Fifth Synod, Collation VII.

Rusticus was the nephew of Pope Vigilius. Baluzius, in volume I of the new *Collection of the Councils*, in the preface to the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 25, and on p. 1228, shows that this Rusticus was the same man who compared the earlier Latin translation of the Council of Chalcedon with ancient manuscripts.

In the same year, 549, the Illyrian bishops, as soon as Vigilius’s *Judicatum* reached them, convened a synod and jointly undertook the defense of the Three Chapters. Victor of Tunnuna testifies to this in his entry for that year:

“The Illyrian synod writes in defense of the Three Chapters against Justinian Augustus and condemns Benenatus, bishop of the First Justiniana, as a detractor of those same Three Chapters.”

“It is not surprising,” says Cardinal Norisius in the same *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4, “that Benenatus alone among the Illyrian metropolitans held an opinion against the Three Chapters, for he was bishop of New Justiniana, which had been established by the emperor Justinian.”

In the year 550 the African bishops, led by Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, ventured upon a great outrage. They not only rejected the *Judicatum* but also subjected Vigilius himself to anathema. Victor of Tunnuna bears witness to this in his *Chronicle*. He inserted the events in the case of the Three Chapters more fully than the other writers in his chronological tables:

“After the consulship of Basil, in the tenth year, and therefore in the year 550, the African bishops synodically excluded Vigilius, the Roman bishop and condemner of the Three Chapters, from Catholic communion, while reserving for him the possibility of repentance; and they sent to the emperor Justinian, through Olympius the *magistrianus*, letters sufficiently suitable for the defense of the aforementioned Chapters.”

From this it is clear that the African bishops went so far in their rashness as to strike the Roman pontiff himself openly with anathema.

Vigilius had also punished them with the same penalty, for the detractors of the *Judicatum* were subjected to anathema by that very fact. This is understood from what is read in Vigilius’s sentence against Rusticus and Sebastian:

“Because they had written against our *Judicatum*, it was established through the text of that same *Judicatum* that they had already been suspended by us from communion.”

After the emperor Justinian received the synodal acts of the Illyrian bishops, in which they had defended the Three Chapters in the year 549, and the acts of the council convened in Africa for the same purpose in the year 550, he issued a rescript against the Illyrians and Africans. Isidore teaches this in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 12:

“Emperor Justinian also composed a rescript against the Illyrian synod and against the African bishops, in which he endeavored to condemn the Three Chapters.”

Nothing increasingly distressed Vigilius more than the fact that he had issued the *Judicatum*, a document of which he more than once repented. He saw that the Westerners had rebelled on that account, laying aside all reverence for the Apostolic See.

Therefore, acting with prudent foresight, he dealt with Justinian so that the *Judicatum* might be returned to him by Menna. The matter could then be treated anew in a full synod, as though from the beginning, and no prescription arising from that earlier decree could bind the Fathers when they gave their judgment.

The Italian clergy, in the booklet delivered to the Frankish envoys, testifies that Vigilius received his *Judicatum* back from Menna and thereafter, until the council, forbade all discussion of the Three Chapters under penalty of anathema. Vigilius himself says the same in the sentence issued against Theodore.

Cardinal Norisius, cited above, proves in chapter 4 that not even a single copy of that *Judicatum* remained with Menna. He argues that when, at the Seventh Collation of the Fifth Synod, the Greek Fathers later attempted to demonstrate from Vigilius’s writings that the Three Chapters had been condemned by the Apostolic See, they put forward the sentence against the Roman deacons Rusticus and Sebastian and the letters to Valentinian, metropolitan of Tomi, and Aurelian, bishop of Arles, but did not produce the *Judicatum*.

Thus Cardinal Norisius.

Yet after publishing that dissertation on the Fifth Synod, Baluzius carefully compared the published acts of the Fifth Council with the Beauvais and Paris manuscripts in his new collection of councils [Col. 0599B]. From these he noted many variant readings and, in addition, published various fragments of great importance. Among them he supplied a notable fragment from Vigilius’s *Judicatum*, which had not come down to us, and completed Justinian’s sacred imperial letter, which is read in mutilated form in all editions of the councils.

In this letter—or fragment of a letter—Justinian says that Vigilius anathematized the Three Chapters in his *Judicatum* in these words:

> “And since in the writings submitted to us under the name of Theodore of Mopsuestia many things contrary to the true faith are read, we, following the admonition of Paul the Apostle, who says, ‘Test everything; retain what is good,’ therefore anathematize Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, together with all his writings, and those who defend him. We also anathematize the impious letter said by Ibas to have been written to Maris the Persian, as contrary to the true faith of Christians, and all who [Col. 0599C] defend it or say that it is orthodox. We also anathematize the writings of Theodoret that were written against the true faith and against the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril.”

“And these things,” Justinian says in the aforesaid letter, “were inserted in what is called the *Judicatum*.” From this it is clear that Justinian, and consequently the patriarch Menna, retained a copy of Vigilius’s *Judicatum* in their possession. It was not read in the Seventh Collation, however, because Vigilius had issued his *Constitutum* on 14 May, twelve days before that Collation, which was held on the 26th of the same month. In the *Constitutum* he defended the Three Chapters, and therefore the *Judicatum* was considered to have been revoked by him.

When Justinian learned that the name of Theodore had been erased from the sacred diptychs of the church of Mopsuestia, of which he had once been bishop, he sent letters on 17 June 550 to John, metropolitan of Justinopolis in Lesser Cilicia, and to Cosmas, bishop of Mopsuestia, ordering that the matter be investigated in a synod assembled from the province, [Col. 0599D] so that it might be determined when this had happened. With John the metropolitan there were eight other bishops, senior clergy, and the city’s nobles.

The diptychs of the church of Mopsuestia were produced. In them the names of the bishops of that see were found inscribed as follows:

> “For the repose of the bishops Protogenes, Zosimus, Olympius, Cyril, Thomas, Bassianus, Auxentius, Palatinus, Jacobus, Zosimus, Theodore, and Simon,”

the last two of whom had died shortly before.

After this diptych had been read, the presbyter Stephen, who was sixty-nine years old, said:

> “I have neither known nor heard that Theodore, who was once bishop in our city, was named in the sacred diptychs. But ever since I was enrolled among this clergy, I have known that, after he was removed, Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, was at some time inserted in his place in the sacred diptychs of the bishops who had fallen asleep; and to this day he is proclaimed there in his stead.”

The other clergy and the noble citizens likewise testified to the same thing. Thus Theodore had formerly been read in the sacred books between Olympius and Thomas [Col. 0600A], but afterward he was erased from them. This erasure indicated that Theodore had died in communion with the Church, but that after his death he had been accused and convicted of error and deprived of communion.

Accordingly, the Synod of Mopsuestia pronounced the following judgment concerning Theodore, after carefully examining his case:

> “Now the truth has been revealed and made very plainly evident: Theodore, in ancient times, was outside the preaching of the divine mystery, was expelled from the sacred diptychs, and in his place the name of Cyril of holy memory was entered.”

The Fathers immediately informed the Emperor Justinian of this by letter, and, as the emperor had ordered, they also notified Vigilius. The letter to Vigilius is preserved in the Fifth Collation of the Fifth Synod.

The year 551 proved disastrous for Vigilius because of Justinian’s fury and the injuries inflicted upon the apostolic see. Theodore, metropolitan of Caesarea, impatient with the truce and unable to keep faith, had a book against the Three Chapters publicly read before many bishops in the palace [Col. 0600B]. When Vigilius learned of this, he condemned the man’s insolence and resolved to inflict a heavier punishment upon him. But since Theodore was especially dear to Justinian, Vigilius adopted a milder course: he summoned him and reproved him for the crime he had committed.

Theodore, whose disposition was naturally inclined to fabrication, humbly begged forgiveness for his deed and obtained it. Vigilius later reproached him for this in the sentence pronounced against him. But the pontiff’s excessive readiness to pardon made Theodore more prepared to attempt graver crimes, as will appear from what follows.

In this same year, 551, the African bishops who had been summoned arrived in Constantinople: Reparatus and Firmus—the former proconsular, the latter primate of Numidia—together with Primasius of Hadrumetum and Verecundus of Nicaea, all most obstinate in defending the Three Chapters. A particularly forceful pressure was brought to bear on Reparatus, primate of all Africa, but he was swayed neither by favor nor by threats; instead, he steadfastly defended the Three Chapters [Col. 0600C]. Therefore the emperor sent him into exile, where he lived until the year 563. Nevertheless, he never consented to receive the Fifth Synod, which the Roman pontiffs had signed, but died in schism.

Firmus, primate of Numidia, was corrupted by the emperor’s gifts and assented to the condemnation of the same Chapters, as Victor of Tunnuna records. Primasius long resisted Justinian: in that same year he signed the decree against Theodore, and in 553 Vigilius’s *Constitutum*. But after Justinian banished him, when he heard of the death of Boethius, primate of Byzacena, he gave his name to the condemnation of the Chapters so that he might succeed him. Having returned to Africa and disturbed the condition of the Church by plunder and violence, he was deposed by a provincial synod, as Victor of Tunnuna writes under the year after the twelfth consulship of Basil.

Verecundus of Nicaea, having withdrawn from Justinian’s fury, fled to Chalcedon, where he died, as will be related below.

[Col. 0600D] Justinian had ordered the more distinguished bishops of each province to come to Constantinople. But since the Africans defended the Three Chapters, the Illyrians refused to come, and he also saw that few Westerners were attending the synod, while Vigilius was unwilling to decide anything without the Western bishops, he published an edict against the Three Chapters in the same year, 551, at the instigation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, and ordered it to be publicly hung in the church of the imperial city and elsewhere.

> “At Constantinople,” the Italian clergy say in their memorial, “they again began to compel the most blessed Pope Vigilius, so that, if the African, Illyrian, or Dalmatian bishops were unwilling, he himself might condemn those Chapters with the Greek bishops. But when the most blessed Pope Vigilius absolutely refused to comply, they caused edicts in the emperor’s name to be hung both in the Constantinopolitan church and in various places, by which the same Chapters were condemned.”

It has already been proved above that this second edict of Justinian against the Three Chapters differed from the first, issued in 544 [Col. 0601A]. Cardinal Norisius, cited above, demonstrates in chapter 5 that this edict was posted around 14 July 551.

In this edict Justinian established the Church’s doctrines against Arius, Nestorius, and Eutyches, and accepted the four ecumenical synods. He then established nine canons against the Nestorians and Eutychians, all of which were almost word for word approved by the Fifth Synod. He afterward included this canon:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, and Eutyches, and all who have thought or think like them, let such a person be anathema.”

Since Origen’s name is not found in this canon, Baronius rightly concludes that the author of the edict was Theodore of Cappadocia, the leader of the Origenists. Since the heresy of the Acephali is also proscribed at length in the same document, Cardinal Norisius correctly infers that this Theodore was not an Acephalus, although Liberatus states in the *Breviary* [Col. 0601B], chapter 24, that he belonged to that sect.

Justinian then turns to the Three Chapters. After condemning them under the penalty of anathema, he begins an extended disputation against their defenders and demonstrates that heretics, or schismatics, may be condemned even if they are dead.

The authority for saying that the Acephali were those heretics who followed neither Saint Cyril of Alexandria nor John of Antioch nor the Eastern bishops is Liberatus in the *Breviary*, chapter 9. Speaking of the Eastern bishops’ defense of the two natures of Christ, composed by Cyril, he says:

> “I think that those who at that time did not receive it at all were the founders of the Acephali, who have neither Cyril as their head nor anyone whom they follow.”

Leontius, however, in his book *On the Sects*, writes that heretics began to be called Acephali only after the Council of Chalcedon. Garnerius, in his *History of Theodoret*, chapter 6, wishes to establish harmony between the two authors; his discussion may be consulted there.

But to return to the Three Chapters: when Vigilius learned that the emperor’s edicts against the Three Chapters had been publicly posted [Col. 0601C], he ordered both the Latin and Greek bishops to come to the Placidian residence and warned them as follows:

> “Whoever wishes to give assent to these edicts should know that he is suspended from communion with the apostolic see.”

So says the Italian clergy.

Vigilius himself, in the encyclical letter he wrote in 552, testifies that in this same year, 551, he had publicly uttered the following words in the presence of bishops from various provinces and the Constantinopolitan clergy in the Placidian residence:

> “Ask the most pious emperor to deign to remove his edicts, which he ordered to be hung up, and to await a common *Constitutum*—that is, either that the bishops of the Latin tongue, who have been scandalized, should come to the synod, or at least, with all violence removed, should declare their judgments in writing. But if he should perhaps refuse to hear our prayers, give your assent to nothing that tends toward division, and do not act against the *Constitutum* because of any threat. But if, which we do not believe, you should do this, [Col. 0601D] know that from this day, through the ministry of my voice, you are to be regarded as suspended as transgressors against the Apostle Peter.”

After the words just quoted, the Italian clergy add:

> “But Saint Datius, bishop of Milan, also lodged a protest before everyone, with loud outcry, saying: ‘Behold, I, and the part of all the priests among whom my Church is established—that is, of Gaul, Burgundy, Spain, Liguria, Emilia, and Venetia—protest that whoever gives assent to these edicts will be unable to have the bishops of the aforesaid provinces as his communicants. For it is clear to me that those edicts disturb the holy Council of Chalcedon and the Catholic faith.’”

Nevertheless, Victor of Tunnuna records in his *Chronicle* that Datius of Milan subscribed to the condemnation of the Three Chapters before his death, which occurred in 552. The annotator of Baronius, however, shows that this is very doubtful.

Zoilus, bishop of Alexandria, who refused to give assent to the edict, was deposed, and Apollinarius was substituted in his place, indeed before September of that same year, 551, as may be read in Baronius’s critical notes [Col. 0602A].

Theodore of Cappadocia, however, the author of the edict, bringing a crowd of Greeks with him, went to the church where the edicts had been hung and celebrated the sacred mysteries. Justinian, enraged that Vigilius not only opposed the emperor’s edicts but also deprived those who obeyed them of ecclesiastical communion, ordered that Vigilius be taken into custody.

Fearing for himself, Vigilius withdrew together with Datius, bishop of Milan, into the church of Saint Peter at Hormisdas. Not only the Italian clergy but Vigilius himself recounts this in the aforesaid encyclical:

> “When in that same church we were dragged from the holy altar of the saint by the feet by a force sent by the praetor, with a multitude of armed soldiers arriving as if drawn up for war, and when even the altar table itself had fallen upon us, it would have crushed us had it not been supported by the hands of our clergy.”

There he also states that this violence was inflicted upon him in August [Col. 0602B].

Therefore Vigilius, judging that not soothing remedies but iron must now be applied, reviewed before an assembly of Italian bishops the many injuries inflicted by Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, upon the apostolic see, and committed them to writing. He then pronounced the following sentence against him:

> “We decree, by the promulgation of a sentence, that Theodore, formerly bishop of the city of Caesarea in Cappadocia, has been stripped of priestly honor, Catholic communion, and every episcopal office and power.”

He suspended Menna, patriarch of Constantinople, and the bishops who agreed with him from sacred communion alone.

This sentence was issued on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, under our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in his twenty-fifth year, and in the tenth year after the consulship of Basil; therefore it was issued on 14 August 551. Vigilius nevertheless decided that the sentence should not be published, fearing that it might again drive Justinian—whose fury he had already experienced [Col. 0602C]—into madness, especially since Theodore was doing everything according to his own will.

There is preserved in volume five of the councils an encyclical letter of Vigilius, formerly mutilated but now complete, in which the pontiff sets forth the sequence of his calamities. While he was staying at Saint Peter’s in Hormisdas, Belisarius, Cethegus, and Peter, former consuls, together with Justin, the emperor’s nephew, and Marcellinus the quaestor, came to Vigilius. They demanded that, after an oath had been received, he come to the Placidian residence; otherwise he was to be dragged from the church by force.

But when he had withdrawn there and nevertheless observed that, despite so sacred a pledge having been disregarded, he was being treated more harshly day by day, he protested once, twice, and three times to Belisarius and the other judges, asking them to bind themselves by the religious obligation of an oath so that, as he says, “we might suffer no disturbances or hardships, just as had been sworn to us.”

Meanwhile Justinian, fearing that Vigilius might again flee from the Placidian residence to the church, secretly sent soldiers and ordered the building to be carefully guarded. When this was reported to Vigilius [Col. 0602D], he planned his escape two days before Christmas. In the dead of night he left the Placidian Palace by hidden paths, crossed over to Chalcedon, and took up residence at the dwelling of Saint Euphemia.

Datius of Milan followed Vigilius, as did other Latin bishops, among them Verecundus, bishop of Nicaea in the province of Byzacena, who, Victor of Tunnuna writes, died there shortly afterward.

In the year 552, Justinian, seeing that Vigilius’s steadfastness had already been sufficiently tested by experience, set aside his threats and approached him through envoys. Belisarius and the others mentioned above carried out this embassy on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

They asked Vigilius to return to Constantinople after receiving a renewed public guarantee. The pontiff replied as follows:

> “If the affairs of the Church are being arranged so that the most pious prince may restore its peace, which he established in the time of his uncle—that is, the emperor Justin—then I have no need of oaths, but will [Col. 0603A] depart immediately. But if the affairs of the Church have not been settled, I likewise have no need of oaths, because I have no intention of leaving the basilica of Saint Euphemia unless the scandal has been removed from the Church of God.”

When Justinian received this reply from the envoys, he sent Vigilius a letter—or, as Vigilius calls it, a document—filled with lies and insults. Peter the *referendarius* delivered it on the day before the Kalends of February. But since it was not signed by the emperor’s hand, and since Peter was unwilling either to write his name on it or to mark the day on which it had been delivered, Vigilius judged that no credence should be given to it.

Nevertheless, lest he appear to reveal a guilty conscience by keeping silent before the uninformed, he testifies in his encyclical letter that he had most vigorously refuted all the crimes brought against him.

On 5 February of the same year, Vigilius sent that famous letter to the whole Church, by which all that had happened was made known. In it he explains the reasons for his withdrawal to Saint Euphemia and what he had done there with Justinian’s envoys [Col. 0603B]; he also inserts a confession of his faith.

Concerning the sentence pronounced against Theodore of Cappadocia, by which he was deposed from the episcopate, he writes near the end:

> “Out of consideration for your gentleness and in hope of his conversion, as has been said, we delayed making it public.”

This encyclical is said to have been issued on the Nones of February, under our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in his twenty-fifth year, and in the tenth year after the consulship of Basil. But “the eleventh year” should be read, as is made clear by the conjunction of Justinian’s twenty-fifth year with the month of February. It is number fifteen among Vigilius’s letters in the *Collection of Councils*.

Justinian, eager to hold the synod, at last began to lend an ear to Vigilius, for he saw that nothing firm could be settled in this matter while the Roman pontiff resisted. Therefore he was no longer hostile in his disposition toward Vigilius. When Menna of Constantinople, Theodore of Caesarea, and the others understood this, they composed a profession of faith and presented it to Vigilius, who was still staying in the church of Saint Euphemia.

In it, after a straightforward [Col. 0603C] profession of faith according to the decrees of the four general synods, they asked Vigilius for forgiveness for what had been done, in these words:

> “As for whatever injuries were inflicted upon Your Beatitude or your see, I did not inflict them. But because every means must be used to hasten peace in the Church, I ask forgiveness as though I had inflicted them myself. And because during the time of discord I received into communion those who had been excommunicated or not received by Your Beatitude, I likewise ask forgiveness.”

Menna of Constantinople, Theodore of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Andrew of Ephesus, and others subscribed the document.

After this Justinian revoked the edicts, and now, with the Fathers coming to Constantinople for the synod, the case of the Three Chapters was left to be judged anew. Meanwhile, at approximately the beginning of December of that same year, 552, Menna died. Saint Eutychius was immediately appointed in his place.

At the beginning of the year 553, when he had become the new patriarch of Constantinople [Col. 0603D], Eutychius sent Vigilius a profession of faith. In it, after praising the four general synods and the letters of Saint Leo, he asked Vigilius at last to begin the council concerning the Three Chapters.

The letter was subscribed by Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinarius of Alexandria, Domnus of Antioch, and Elias, metropolitan of Thessalonica. Vigilius praised their faith in his reply on the eighth day before the Ides of January. To their request that the case of the Three Chapters be examined, he responded:

> “We agree that concerning the Three Chapters, from which the question has arisen, after a regular assembly has been held and equity has been preserved, we should hold a conference with our united brethren in the presence of the holy Gospels, so that an outcome pleasing to God and consistent with what was defined by the four holy councils may be reached.”

By those clauses—“after a regular assembly has been held” and “with equity preserved”—the pontiff consented to the convocation of the synod on the condition that Latin bishops should be present in equal number, so that they would not afterward oppose the synodal decrees.

Cardinal Norisius, cited above in chapter 6, shows that Vigilius left Chalcedon and again sought Constantinople after receiving Eutychius’s letter on the day of the Epiphany [Col. 0604A].

When Vigilius therefore understood that the Western bishops were unwilling to attend because of fear of Justinian, he denied that he could settle the matter with only a few Italians and Illyrians in such a way that no subsequent contradiction would arise from the Western bishops. At last it was agreed that the synod should be composed of equal numbers of Latins and Greeks. The same Cardinal Norisius, cited above in chapter 7, observes that this was established before Easter, celebrated on 20 April 552.

Vigilius himself says in his *Constitutum* to Justinian:

> “Afterward, and with the greater agreement of our brethren, the bishops of our party, Your Piety recently decreed, before the holy day of Easter, that, with an equal number of these bishops who are present in the city of Constantinople, we should undertake the examination of the Three Chapters, concerning which the dispute has arisen, according to the profession of our brother bishops designated above” [Col. 0604B].

But when the Greek bishops learned of this, they began to protest tumultuously. They had come from distant provinces for the sake of an ecumenical synod; its authority and name would be diminished if it were celebrated by only a few. Many highly learned men would be excluded if they were required to meet with the Latins in equal numbers. Very numerous synods had been held by Greeks alone. At Chalcedon, in the assembly of six hundred and thirty Fathers, only the legates of Pope Leo had been present among the Latins. The venerable Council of Nicaea had been composed entirely of Greeks. The Westerners’ obstinacy in defending the Three Chapters was well known; if the Easterners entered into disputation with them on equal terms, with votes balanced on both sides, the Council would be dismissed with nothing accomplished.

When Justinian heard this, he departed from the prior agreement and convoked the synod for 5 May, according to the Beauvais and Paris manuscripts, not for 4 May, as it is read in the printed manuscripts. On this matter see Garnerius, *Dissertation on the Fifth General Synod*, chapter 5, and the author of the critical notes on Baronius under the year 553, number 11 [Col. 0604C].

Accordingly, on 5 May 553, the first Collation of the synod was held. Three patriarchs were present: Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinarius of Alexandria, and Domnus—or Domninus—of Antioch; Jerusalem was represented by vicars. The Fathers numbered 165 in all.

Justinian’s sacred imperial letter, delivered to the synod by Theodore the *silentarius*, was read. In it the emperor declared that nothing was more important to him than, after eliminating heresies, to give peace to the Church following the disturbances stirred up by the Acephali. He urged the Fathers to examine the Three Chapters and to pass judgment upon them, since they had already been condemned by the *Judicatum* of the Roman pontiff.

Next the letters of Eutychius, the recently inaugurated bishop of Constantinople, addressed to Vigilius were read. They contained his profession of faith and his most humble request that, with Vigilius presiding, the controversy over the Three Chapters might be brought to an end. Vigilius’s letters to Eutychius and to the bishops subject to him, of which we have just spoken, were also read [Col. 0604D].

But since the Greek bishops knew that, without the Roman pontiff present, the synod would have no standing among Westerners and could not be regarded as ecumenical unless the Roman pontiff were present at least through his legates, they sent to Vigilius a most distinguished embassy consisting of the three patriarchs, all the autocephalous primates, and other bishops. They asked him to attend the synod and to dispute with them concerning the Three Chapters, as he had promised in his letters to Eutychius.

Vigilius replied:

> “Because of bodily infirmity, I am unable to respond to this request; but on the following day I promise to make known what I think about such an assembly.”

It should be noted that those envoys brought Vigilius not summonses but petitions:

> “Coming to the most holy [Col. 0605A] Pope of senior Rome,” they say, “we asked His Beatitude to meet and dispute with us concerning the Three Chapters.”

Thus the first Collation came to an end.

On the following day, 6 May, the same patriarchs, primates, and bishops again approached Vigilius, earnestly asking him to come to the synod. He replied that he could not meet with them, because the Western bishops who adhered to him were fewer in number than the Easterners. He would therefore give his judgment concerning the Three Chapters separately in writing and send it to the emperor; for this reason he had requested a truce.

But Justinian refused to grant the twenty-day truce Vigilius had requested, because the other bishops complained of the inconvenience of a longer stay in the imperial city. Therefore the most illustrious judges, in the emperor’s name, ordered the bishops to hold the synod even in Vigilius’s absence.

The Second Collation was therefore held on 8 May. At it, the envoys appointed at the previous Collation reported Vigilius’s responses [Col. 0605B]. The Fathers invited the bishops who were awaiting Vigilius’s patriarchal authority to attend the synod; they steadfastly refused to be present without Vigilius.

On the following day, 9 May, the Greek bishops again assembled and held the Third Collation. In it they professed the faith of the four synods, together with their definitions and the teaching of the holy Fathers whom the Church venerates as teachers. The opinion, deeply rooted in many people, that the Three Chapters could not be condemned without injury to the Council of Chalcedon was also censured. Thus the Third Collation was held.

Three days later, on 12 May, the Fourth Collation began to examine the case itself [Col. 0605C]. Several passages excerpted from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia were read. The Jewish creed that had formerly been attributed to Theodore by Charisius, a presbyter of the church of Philadelphia in Lydia, and that Marius Mercator had attacked at length around the year 431, as having been composed by Theodore, was also read.

The Fathers pronounced an anathema against those blasphemies and against Theodore himself:

> “Satan composed this creed,” the whole synod exclaimed. “Anathema to him who composed this creed. The First Synod of Ephesus anathematized this creed together with its author. Anathema to Theodore of Mopsuestia. He rejected the Gospels; he insulted the divine dispensation. Anathema to those who do not anathematize him. His defenders are Jews; his followers are pagans.”

The Fifth Collation was held on 17 May, as Baluzius demonstrates in his new *Collection of Councils*, page 1510. At it were read the writings that the holy Fathers had composed against Theodore of Mopsuestia and the measures enacted against him by the emperors’ laws.

The testimonies of Saint Cyril, in which he censured the errors of the aforesaid Theodore, were reviewed. A petition presented to Saint Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, by the bishops, clergy, and monks of Greater Armenia and Persia against Theodore was read [Col. 0605D]. So too was a fragment from the volume written by Saint Proclus to the Armenians; various letters of Saint Cyril of Alexandria, by which it was proved that Nestorius had drawn his heresy and blasphemies from Theodore’s source; the letter of Rabula, bishop of Edessa, against Theodore; and a fragment from the ecclesiastical history of Hesychius, a presbyter of Jerusalem, from which Theodore’s impiety was established.

The laws of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian against the name and teaching of Theodore and Nestorius were read. A fragment of letters from Theophilus of Alexandria to Porphyry of Antioch and from Saint Gregory of Nyssa to Theophilus was also read.

The testimonies of Theodoret were read, by which, while defending Theodore against Saint Cyril, he himself established that the errors which Cyril attributed to Theodore truly belonged to Theodore. Finally, the Synod of Mopsuestia was ordered to be read. From its acts it was proved that Theodore’s name had long before been erased from the diptychs of the Church [Col. 0606A] and that Saint Cyril’s name had been substituted in its place.

After this the question was discussed whether the dead could lawfully be condemned by anathema. It was proved by weighty arguments that this was lawful and at times necessary. It is likely that various letters of Saint Augustine were read in this Collation, for in the definitive sentence pronounced against the Three Chapters in the Eighth Collation the Fathers say:

> “Various letters of Augustine, of religious memory, who shone among the African bishops, were read, showing that heretics ought to be anathematized even after death.”

Those testimonies were produced in the synod by Sextilianus, bishop of Tunnuna in Africa, the legate of Primasius, the newly appointed bishop of Carthage, who had been ordained in place of the exile Reparatus. They were received with a great proclamation by Benignus, bishop of Heraclea in Pelagonia in Macedonia and vicar of Elias, metropolitan of Thessalonica, who added that this was the Church’s perpetual tradition.

[Col. 0606B] In the same Fifth Collation they afterward moved on to examine the second Chapter, namely the writings of Theodoret, from whose works many passages against Saint Cyril had been extracted. His letters to Andrew of Samosata and to Nestorius after peace had been established between the Easterners and Saint Cyril were reviewed.

Finally, there was his letter to John of Antioch after Cyril’s death, in which he expressed his joy at Cyril’s death and loaded him with many curses. Baronius and many other learned men after him, believing that this letter had been falsely attributed to Theodoret, wrote that the Fathers of the Fifth Synod had been deceived by an error of fact.

Garnerius, however, in the *Appendix to Theodoret’s Book of Letters*, page 99, demonstrates that the letter was not addressed to John but to Domnus of Antioch, John’s successor, and that it is genuinely the work of Theodoret. His arguments should be read in his work and in the author of the critical notes on Baronius under the year 444, numbers 7 and following.

From the year 553, therefore, the words that entered number 13 through a lapse of memory should be removed [Col. 0606C]:

> “But the Fathers of the synod, and the rest,”

through the end of the number. In their place the following should be substituted:

> “But the Fathers of the synod were not deceived by an error of fact, as Baronius maintains, since that letter, written by Theodoret to John of Antioch—or rather to Domnus, John’s successor—was not spurious, as we have shown in its proper place.”

This may be noted in passing.

After examining Theodoret’s doctrines, the synod said:

> “From what Theodoret impiously wrote, the subtlety of the holy Council of Chalcedon is astonishing. For although it knew his blasphemies and had first repeatedly used many exclamations against him, it would afterward have received him in no other way than after he had anathematized Nestorius and his blasphemies, which he had previously defended in writing.”

On 14 May, between the Fourth and Fifth Collations, Vigilius issued his *Constitutum*. In it the pontiff complained that the synod had been convened contrary to the agreed conditions. He then began a discussion of the Three Chapters and condemned sixty statements said to be Theodore of Mopsuestia’s, which the emperor had sent him through Benignus, bishop of Heraclea in Macedonia.

He proved by many arguments that Theodore’s person and name could not be condemned. From these arguments he drew the following conclusion concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia:

> “We do not dare to condemn him by our judgment, nor do we permit him to be condemned by anyone else.”

Nevertheless, he added that he absolutely refused to admit—whether in judgment or even by hearing—any chapters or writings that did not agree with the doctrines of the Gospels and the Apostles, the four holy synods, and the apostolic see.

As for Theodoret, Vigilius decreed that his writings should not be condemned specifically, since at the Council of Chalcedon he had pronounced an anathema against Nestorius, which was the only thing the Fathers had demanded of him. Therefore Vigilius said that it was unworthy for any Nestorian doctrines to be condemned under Theodoret’s name, since he had condemned Nestorius himself and his doctrines together with the Fathers, and that this would amount to an injury to the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0607A].

Accordingly, he concluded:

> “Having therefore weighed the truth of these matters, we establish and decree that nothing should be done or uttered by anyone, under the charge of his name, to the injury or disparagement of the most approved man of the Council of Chalcedon, Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus. Rather, with reverence for his person preserved in all things, we anathematize and condemn whatever writings or doctrines, published under whatever name, are shown to agree with the errors of the wicked Nestorius and Eutyches.”

But lest, by defending Theodoret, he should fall under suspicion of Nestorian heresy, Vigilius struck it with five anathemas.

Finally, he did not think that Ibas’s letter should be condemned under Ibas’s name either. This was so, first, because, when the letter was reread at the Council of Chalcedon, Ibas was judged orthodox; and second, because he subscribed to the decrees of that most holy synod and to the letter of Saint Leo. Consequently, with the agreement of the Fathers’ votes, he was restored to his see.

For it was impious to reopen matters that had been judged by the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0607B]. Vigilius proves from his letter—or *Judicatum*—concerning the Three Chapters, addressed to Menna, that he had always wished the decrees of that council to remain unshaken.

He closes his Constitutum with these words:

> “We establish and decree that no one belonging to the ecclesiastical orders and dignities may write, state, compose, or teach anything contrary to what we have asserted or established in this present Constitutum concerning the aforesaid Three Chapters, or raise any further question after the present definition. But if anything concerning those same Three Chapters, contrary to what we assert or establish here, has been or shall be done, said, or written in the name of anyone belonging to the ecclesiastical orders and dignities, and is found anywhere by anyone, we reject it in every respect by the authority of the Apostolic See, over which by God’s grace we preside.”

Sixteen bishops subscribed this Constitutum of Vigilius, almost all of them those who had also subscribed the same judgment against Theodore of Cappadocia: three from the diocese of Illyricum; and, among the Greeks, the metropolitan bishop of Iconium in Lycaonia and Vincent, metropolitan of Claudiopolis in the Pontic province of Honoriadis.

Although Vigilius issued his Constitutum on 14 May, and the fifth session was held on 17 May, it was not read there—either because the emperor had not yet received it, or because he pretended not to have received it. Indeed, Peter de Marca rightly proves that the Constitutum was not read in the other sessions of the synod either, in his dissertation *On the Decree of Vigilius for the Confirmation of the Fifth Synod*, where, in section 12, he refutes Baronius’s opinion that the Constitutum had been sent by Justinian to the synod. For if it had been read again in the synod, its recitation would have been recorded in the Acts, in which even readings of lesser importance have been inserted.

Moreover, publication of the Constitutum would have been contrary to the emperor’s purpose and prudence. Since he was entirely intent upon condemning the Three Chapters, he ought not to have obstructed his own aims by bringing forward, on Vigilius’s authority, a document that disapproved his desire. Rather, in order to obtain more easily the outcome he had proposed for himself, and so that no one might await what Vigilius would answer the emperor—for Vigilius had promised that he would do so—Justinian, through Constantine, quaestor of the sacred palace, suggested at the seventh session of the synod that Vigilius’s position had been sufficiently explained by what he had repeatedly taught on this matter, both in writing and orally.

Peter de Marca, already cited, assembles many further arguments on this point and responds to Baronius’s reasons. He shows that Justinian, knowing well that in ecumenical synods the first opinion had always been that of the Roman pontiff, and that nothing was ordinarily decreed without awaiting it, did not wish Vigilius’s authority to appear neglected in this affair. He therefore suppressed the Constitutum but presented to the synod other earlier statements of Vigilius, issued by him in preceding years, so that everything might appear to have been conducted properly and solemnly in the Acts. Yet Marca is mistaken in seeming to think that Vigilius’s *Judicatum* was presented by Justinian to the synod and read there; it was soon shown that this is contrary to the truth.

On the basis of Baronius’s opinion, innovators have inferred that the writings of the Roman pontiff were not only discussed in the synod but also refuted, and that a definition contrary to his was issued with anathema in the promulgated decrees. But from the true account of what happened, it is clear that this inference is frivolous.

The sixth session was held on 19 May. In it the Third Chapter was discussed, namely, the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian. The letter of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, to John, bishop of Antioch, was reviewed. In it Proclus wrote that Ibas had been accused before him of favoring the doctrines of Nestorius, and of translating into the language of the Syrians certain chapters of the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia and transmitting them everywhere. For this reason he had been accused repeatedly and had likewise been cleared at the synod of Berytus.

Most of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus were reread: the letters of Saint Cyril to Nestorius and of Nestorius to Cyril; the letters of Pope Celestine to Nestorius; the twelve anathemas of Saint Cyril; the letter of Saint Leo to Flavian, together with the votes of the Chalcedonian Fathers approving it; the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds; and finally the definition of faith of the Council of Chalcedon.

When Ibas’s letter was compared with these documents, it was convicted of error, and all the bishops exclaimed:

> “The letter is heretical. We all condemn the letter called Ibas’s. We all anathematize it. The letter is alien to the synod. The letter is contrary to the definition; the whole letter is heretical. The whole letter is blasphemous. Whoever does not anathematize it is a heretic. Whoever accepts it does not confess that God the Word became man. Whoever accepts it does not accept Cyril. Anathema to Theodore, Nestorius, and the letter called Ibas’s.”

At the seventh session, held on 26 May, Constantine, quaestor of the sacred palace, was sent by the emperor to the synod with documents proving that Vigilius had always detested and condemned the Three Chapters. The anathema pronounced by Vigilius against the Roman deacons Rusticus and Sebastianus, opponents of the *Judicatum* and the most obstinate defenders of the Three Chapters, was therefore read aloud.

Letters written by Vigilius concerning this controversy to Valentinian, bishop of Tomi in the province of Scythia, and to Aurelian, bishop of Arles, were also read. From all these documents it was evident that Vigilius had condemned the Three Chapters more than once. After all these documents had been read before the assembly of the Fathers, the final judgment concerning the Three Chapters was postponed until the following Monday, 2 June.

At the eighth and final session, held on that date, 2 June, the synod briefly reviewed everything previously done and issued its definitive sentence against the Three Chapters. Among other things it declared:

> “We condemn and anathematize, together with all the other heretics who have been condemned and anathematized by the aforesaid four councils and by the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, and his impious writings; also what Theodoret wrote impiously against the right faith, against the twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril, and against the First Synod of Ephesus, and what he wrote in defense of Theodore and Nestorius.
>
> “In addition, we anathematize the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Maris the Persian. It denies that God the Word was incarnate and became man from the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary; and it slanders Cyril of holy memory, who taught correctly, as though he were a heretic and as writing in the same manner as Apollinarius. It also censures the First Synod of Ephesus as though it had deposed Nestorius without examination or inquiry, and calls the twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril impious and contrary to the right faith. It defends Theodore and Nestorius, together with their impious doctrines and writings.
>
> “Therefore we anathematize the aforesaid Three Chapters: that is, the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, together with his abominable writings; what Theodoret wrote impiously; the impious letter called Ibas’s; and their defenders.”

Fourteen anathemas follow the sentence. The last three strike at the Three Chapters. The twelfth attacks not only Theodore’s impious writings but also his name and person, as well as his defenders. The thirteenth and fourteenth attack Theodoret’s writings and Ibas’s letter, together with their defenders; but they do not attack Theodoret himself or Ibas, orthodox bishops who had died in the peace of the Church.

All these decrees were subscribed by Eutychius, patriarch of Constantinople and president of the council; Apollinarius of Alexandria; Domnus of Antioch; and the others in their proper order.

The Fifth Synod condemned not only the Three Chapters but also the Origenists. Cedrenus, under the twenty-sixth year of Justinian, reports a letter from that emperor to the Fifth Synod in which he urged the Fathers to condemn Origen:

> “We exhort you, most holy Fathers, gathered together, to examine the exposition set forth below and each of its chapters, and to condemn, together with Origen, all who hold the same opinions.”

Moreover, in the second profession of faith found in the *Book of the Day* of the Roman pontiffs, after the four earlier ecumenical synods have been mentioned, the following is added:

> “This holy and universal Fifth Council also followed the four holy and universal councils already mentioned, and was assembled under the pious emperor Justinian at the city of Constantinople, etc. In it Origen, together with his impious disciples and followers Didymus and Evagrius, and those who pursued the Creator of all things, God, and all His rational creation with pagan fables, were consigned to everlasting condemnation.”

It follows from this that Origen and his followers were condemned under Justinian not only privately, as Garnerius writes in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, but also in the universal Council of Constantinople.

Theophanes and the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle indicate that the investigation of Origen and his condemnation preceded the condemnation of the Three Chapters, when they write that the synod was convened first and chiefly against the errors of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus, and only secondly against the Three Chapters.

Moreover, as Cardinal Norisius, cited above, says in chapter 6, the synod declares in its eleventh canon, or anathema:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Origen together with their impious writings, and all the other heretics who have been condemned and anathematized by the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, etc., let him be anathema.”

Fourteen canons were issued at the eighth session. Since this was the final session concerning the case of the Three Chapters, it is evident that the case of Origen had already been examined; otherwise he would have been condemned without a hearing.

Finally, Theodore of Cappadocia, a patron of Origen, attempting to prove that Theodore of Mopsuestia could rightly be condemned although he had long been dead, addressed the synod in the fifth session as follows:

> “We have also found many others anathematized after death, including Origen. If anyone goes back to the time of Theophilus of holy memory, or even earlier, he will find someone anathematized after death; and this your Holiness and Pope Vigilius, the most religious bishop of elder Rome, have now done in the case before us.”

Thus, by the admission of the leader of the Origenists, Origen was condemned by the Fifth Synod and by Pope Vigilius, and indeed before the inquiry into the Three Chapters had been concluded.

Baronius and others, following Anastasius, have handed down the report that Vigilius did not immediately approve the council and was therefore sent into exile by the emperor Justinian. Anastasius deserves credence in this, although Eustathius, in his *Life of Saint Eutychius, Bishop of Constantinople*, and Victor of Tunnuna, in his *Chronicle*, do not say a word about this exile. Anastasius should not therefore be denied credibility, since a negative argument unsupported by anything else is extremely weak.

Certainly Justinian would have been all the less willing to allow Vigilius to remain in Constantinople after the celebration of the Fifth Council, to which Vigilius had opposed himself, since he not only sent into exile or deprived of office other bishops opposed to the council’s definition, as Liberatus writes at the end of his *Breviary*, but also sent letters to the Fathers at the seventh session forbidding the name of Vigilius to be recited in the sacred diptychs. Baluzius reports these letters in his new *Collection of Councils*, p. 154. Thus Justinian had no more scruple about sending Vigilius into exile than about forbidding his name to be recited in the diptychs. The Continuator of Marcellinus, soon to be cited, also explicitly affirms Vigilius’s exile.

The same Anastasius reports that the Roman clergy asked Narses, commander of the imperial army in Italy, to join them in entreating the emperor that Vigilius might return from exile. After receiving the report both from Narses and from the Roman clergy, the emperor recalled Vigilius and his presbyters from Proconnesus, a small island of Asia and Lesser Mysia in the Propontis. The Continuator of Marcellinus says that this occurred in the year 554:

> “At last Pope Vigilius, having been released from exile by the Roman emperors and by Narses…”

Where the manuscript reads *librarius*—“the copyist”—in place of “the Roman emperor,” it should read “the Roman emperors.”

Evagrius, book IV, chapter 37, and Pope Pelagius II, in his lengthy letter to the bishops of Istria, preserved among the fragments of the Fifth Synod in volume V of the *Councils*, p. 615, testify that Vigilius consented to the synod and approved it before he was released from exile.

In the dissertation already cited, *On the Letter of Vigilius for the Confirmation of the Fifth Synod*, Marca reports a letter of Vigilius to Eutychius, archbishop of Constantinople, and to the assembled synod. It is said to have been given before the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, eternal Augustus, and in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus. Marca therefore considers it to belong to the year 553 and thinks it was the letter Vigilius issued to confirm the Fifth Synod.

But some learned men have regarded this letter as suspect of being forged. Baluzius, already cited, p. 1551, found in an old manuscript of the Colbert Library a Constitutum of Vigilius for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, dated February 554. At its end one reads:

> “Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, and in the thirteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus, at Constantinople.”

This Constitutum appears to be the genuine and authentic document by which Vigilius confirmed the Fifth Synod and sent it to Constantinople both to the emperor and to the bishops. It contains nothing that conflicts with Vigilius’s style. In it Vigilius explains, refutes, and condemns the Three Chapters at length and learnedly, and finally concludes:

> “Therefore we anathematize and condemn the aforesaid three impious Chapters: that is, the letter called Ibas’s to Maris the Persian, in which the abominable blasphemies identified above are contained; the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, together with his abominable writings; what Theodoret wrote impiously; etc. Whatever has been brought forward in my name or in the name of anyone else in defense of the three aforesaid Chapters, or has been found anywhere, we invalidate by the authority of this present, most complete Constitutum.”

After Vigilius had accepted the synod’s sentence, he was released to Rome. Before that, however, in August he had seriously discussed with the emperor the administration of the entire province, and especially the restoration of the government of the city of Rome to a better condition.

Complying with his request, Justinian issued a noble sanction at Constantinople, dated on the Ides of August. By it he granted many concessions to the Italians and raised up their fortunes, which had been depressed by the long Gothic war that had exhausted them.

Concerning women dedicated to God, Justinian states:

> “Since the presumption of tyrannical ferocity has undoubtedly treated even unlawful acts as though they were permitted, we establish that, if anyone is found to have taken to himself women consecrated to God or wearing a religious habit, no property or dowries that may have been recorded for them are to remain with such men; they are to be restored to the monasteries, churches, or holy vocation to which the women were dedicated.”

When Vigilius brought this sanction back with him on his return to Italy, he was overcome by the pain of kidney stones and remained in Sicily until his death.

To return to the Fifth Synod: Gregory the Great spoke truly when he said that the Fifth Synod did not deal with faith but only with persons. Moreover, Gregory venerates not the Fifth but only the first four councils as the Gospels of God. Therefore, although this council possesses the highest authority, it does not possess authority equal to that of the other four.

For this reason Gregory, in letter 37 of book III to Constantius, bishop of Milan, who was attempting to restore Theodelinda, the most devout queen of the Lombards, to communion with the Church after she had been led astray by defenders of the Three Chapters, prudently replied:

> “You wrote that you did not wish to send my letter to Queen Theodelinda because the Fifth Synod was mentioned in it. If you thought that she might thereby be scandalized, it was rightly decided that it should not be sent. Therefore we now do as you wished, praising only the four synods and making no mention of the Fifth Synod.”

Constantius therefore judged that faith would not be lost through an improper and erroneous judgment concerning the Fifth Synod, and that the matter could for a time be tolerated by way of dispensation. Gregory approved this, although matters concerning the decrees of faith cannot be concealed by way of dispensation.
