Nevertheless, Vigilius’s successors, and especially Saint Gregory, approved the Fifth Synod, as will be clear from what follows.

---

## Note: [Col. 0611C]

Number 103, line 3. “Far be this from me, Augusta. I spoke badly before,” etc. “But now,” etc.

Baronius accuses, with very strong reasons, of being spurious the letter that Liberatus attributes to Vigilius (*Breviary*, chapter 22), since it is impious and infected with heresy. But if it could be shown that it was written by Vigilius, it would clearly have to be assigned to the period before his legitimate pontificate, during the schism and the intrusion into the See of Peter while the true pontiff, Silverius, was still alive.

For the solemn profession of faith in the four councils, together with the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo and the constitutions of his successors, which Vigilius customarily sent both to the emperor and to the patriarch of Constantinople, beginning when the legitimate successor and pontiff of Vigilius began to occupy that see after Vigilius’s death, is sufficient to dispel the disgraceful calumny directed against that pontificate. See letter 4 of Pope Vigilius.

> “I,” he says, “following in every respect what has been reverently defined concerning the faith by the Fathers of the four holy synods, by the letters of Pope Leo of blessed memory named above, and by the constitutions of our predecessors mentioned above, and condemning by the praiseworthy authority of the Apostolic See those opposed to their teaching, anathematize all who should perversely attempt to dispute or faithlessly doubt the exposition or correctness of that faith,” etc.

Would Pope Vigilius not have been devoted to curses and contempt in the sight of the whole world if such a letter as the one Liberatus thrusts upon him could have been produced with his signature—especially when the profession of faith prescribed the dogmatic letter of Leo the Great and the definition of the Council of Chalcedon?

The same must be thought of another letter to Menna of Constantinople, which would contradict Vigilius’s fifth letter, in which he recognizes the foundations of orthodox and apostolic faith in his four holy councils.

See Pagi, who makes the same observations in the notes selected by us.

The prudent policy of Pope Vigilius in the affair of the Three Chapters can be recognized from the material brought forward by the same Lord Archbishop Sommier, chapter 33, and from what Pagi considers in his treatment of Vigilius. Both also embrace the history of the controversy concerning the Three Chapters, following the footsteps of Cardinal Norisius in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, chapters 3 and following. See Pagi’s notes above.

---

## [Col. 0577]

### 102. Vigilius

Vigilius, a Roman by birth, son of the consul John, sat for seventeen years, five months, and twenty-six days. [Note: [Col. 0577] B: sixteen years.]

At the same time the patrician Belisarius waged war against Witigis, king of the Goths. [Note: [Col. 0577] C: *Witige*.] When that king fled by night, John, the master of the soldiers, surnamed “the Bloodthirsty,” pursued him, captured him, and brought him to Belisarius and to Vigilius at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0577] *“whom John pursued as he fled” is inserted.*] Then they gave him safe-conduct pledges in the Basilica of Julius. [Note: [Col. 0577] C: “of Julius.”] They promised to deliver him safely to the emperor Justinian. When they had brought him to Constantinople, the emperor rejoiced, made him a patrician and count, and sent him toward the Persian frontier, where he ended his life.

The emperor then asked Belisarius how he had dealt with the Romans and how Vigilius had been installed in the place of Silverius. After he had given his reply, the emperor and the empress thanked him. Having bestowed a dignity upon him, the emperor sent him again to Africa against Gontharis, king of the Vandals. [Note: [Col. 0577] C: *Gontharidem*, here and below; *Vandalorum*.] He was to do in Africa what he had done in Italy.

When he reached the borders of Africa, he killed Gontharis, king of the Vandals, under the pretext of peace, and Africa was brought under the imperial government. [Note: [Col. 0577] *Guntharum.*] Then the patrician Belisarius, returning to Rome with the spoils of the Vandals, presented to blessed Peter the Apostle, through the hands of Pope Vigilius, a golden cross set with gems, weighing one hundred pounds, on which he had inscribed his victories. [Note: [Col. 0577] See Baronius under the year 545; C: *Cerostrata*.]

He also gave two larger silver-gilt *cerostratae*, which still stand before the body of blessed Peter the Apostle. He distributed many other gifts and alms to the poor. The patrician Belisarius also built a hospice on the Via Lata and, on the Via Flaminia near the city, a monastery of Saint Juvenalis, to which he gave many estates and gifts. [Note: [Col. 0577] *Another.*] [Note: [Col. 0577] C: *hortas* or *ostia*.]

### 103

At the same time the empress Theodora wrote to Pope Vigilius:

> “Come and fulfill for us what, in accordance with your good will, you promised concerning our father Anthimus, and restore him to his office.”

Vigilius replied:

> “Far be this from me, Augusta. Before I spoke badly and foolishly; but now I absolutely cannot agree with you that I should restore a heretical and anathematized man. And if I am an unworthy vicar of blessed Peter the Apostle, how were my predecessors, the most holy Agapitus and Silverius, who condemned him?”

Then the Romans made their accusations against Vigilius because Silverius, the most blessed pope, had been deposed with Vigilius’s advice. They said:

> “We bring to your piety the report that he is acting wickedly toward your Roman servants and toward his own people, because we accuse him of murder.”

He became so enraged that he slapped his notary, who immediately fell at his feet and expired. [Note: [Col. 0577] C: “We report,” they say.]

### 104

He also gave his niece Vigilia to the consul Asterius, the son of a widowed woman. Because of this incident, he had Asterius seized at night and beaten until he died. [Note: [Col. 0577] C: “Vigilius [gave] his nephew.”] When the Augusta heard this, she sent the notary Anthimius with her orders and with a large force to Rome, saying:

> “Except if you find him in the Basilica of Saint Peter, spare him.” [Note: [Col. 0577] *If you find him in the Basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle, spare him.*]
>
> “For if you find Vigilius in the Lateran, in the palace, or in any church, place him immediately on a ship and bring him to us. If you do not do so, by Him who lives forever I shall have you flayed alive.”

When the notary Anthimius came to Rome, he found Vigilius in the church of Saint Cecilia on 22 November. At the people’s request, he was seized. It was Vigilius’s birthday, and he was distributing gifts to the people. They seized him, carried him down the Tiber, and put him on a ship.

The plebs followed him, shouting that they wished to receive a prayer from him. After he had given the prayer, the whole people answered, “Amen,” and the ship set out.

When the Romans saw that the ship on which Vigilius was sitting had begun to move, the people began throwing stones, sticks, and pots after him, saying:

> “Your hunger go with you! Your plague go with you! You acted wickedly toward the Romans; may you meet evil where you are going!”

Some of his supporters did indeed follow him from the church. [Note: [Col. 0579] *Certain ones.*]

### 105

When he entered Sicily and reached the city of Catania, he was permitted during the month of December to ordain presbyters and deacons. He then sent back to Rome Ampliatus, a presbyter, his own *vicedominus*, and Valentinus, bishop of Santa Rufina and Santa Seconda, to guard the Lateran and govern the clergy. [Note: [Col. 0579] C: “to the saints”; “the Laterans.”]

After taking leave of everyone, he entered Constantinople on the eve of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. The emperor came to meet him, and when they kissed one another they began to weep. The people sang before him all the way to the church of Hagia Sophia:

> “Behold, the Lord, the ruler, has arrived,” etc.

### 106

For two years there were disputes concerning the patriarch Anthimus. They showed Vigilius the written pledge of the emperor’s hand, demonstrating that he had promised to restore Anthimus to his office. But Vigilius would not consent to them in any way. Strengthened by such courage, he preferred to die rather than live. [Note: [Col. 0579] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 547.]

Then Pope Vigilius said:

> “As I see it, it was not Justinian and Theodora, the most pious rulers, who made me come to you. Today I know that I have found Diocletian and Eleutheria. Do as you wish, for I receive what my deeds deserve.”

Then someone slapped him in the face, saying:

> “Murderer, do you not know to whom you are speaking? Do you not know that you killed Pope Silverius and murdered the son of a widowed woman with heels and clubs?”

Vigilius then fled into the church of Saint Euphemia and held on to an altar column. He was dragged away from it and thrown outside the church. [Note: [Col. 0579] C: “outside.”]

The Augusta Theodora ordered a rope to be put around his neck and had him dragged through the entire city until evening. He was then placed in custody and given only a little bread and water. The Roman clergy who were with him were sent into exile to various places to cut stone in the mines.

### 107

Then the Goths made Baduila their king; he was called Totila. He descended upon Rome and besieged it. A very great famine arose in the city of Rome, so that the inhabitants even wished to eat their own children.

On the thirteenth day he entered the Roman city, in the fourteenth indiction, through the gate of Saint Paul. [Note: [Col. 0579] C: “On a certain day”; “the thirteenth.”] All night he had the trumpets sounded, until the entire people either fled or hid themselves in the churches, lest the Romans should end their lives by the sword.

When the king entered, he lived among the Romans as a father among his children. Then certain senators who had fled—Techeus, Albinus, and Basilius, patricians and former consuls—entered Constantinople and appeared before the emperor, afflicted and desolate. The emperor consoled and enriched them as Roman consuls deserved. [Note: [Col. 0579] C: Cintheus.]

### 108

At the same time the emperor Justinian sent Narses, his eunuch and chamberlain, to Italy. When he fought the Goths, God granted him victory; the king was killed, and a multitude of Goths were slain.

Then the clergy assembled and asked Narses to join them in petitioning the emperor that, if Pope Vigilius were still alive, or if any presbyters, deacons, or members of the clergy who had been deported into exile with Vigilius were still alive, they might return. [Note: [Col. 0579] *Presbyters and deacons.* See Baronius under the year 554.]

When the emperor received the report of Narses and of all the Roman clergy, he rejoiced, together with all his illustrious officials, because God had granted rest to the Romans. He immediately sent his commands to the various places where those exiles had been deported—to Gypsum and Proconnesus—and brought them before him. [Note: [Col. 0581] C: *Gyssa* and *Proconneso*.]

He said to them:

> “Do you wish to receive Vigilius, as he was your pope? I give thanks; if not, here you have [instead] your archdeacon Pelagius, and my hand will be with you.”

[Note: [Col. 0581] *If you wish to receive Vigilius, that he may be your pope, we give thanks; but if not, here you have Peter and the archdeacon Pelagius, on whose behalf my hand will be with you.*]

They all replied:

> “May God rule your piety. Restore Vigilius to us, and when God wishes him to pass from this world, then, with your permission, let your archdeacon Pelagius be given to us.”

[Note: [Col. 0581] C: “our archdeacon.”]

Then he dismissed them all with Vigilius. They came to Sicily, to the city of Syracuse. Vigilius, suffering severe pain from kidney stones because of his many afflictions, died there.

His body was carried to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla. He performed two ordinations in the month of December: forty-six presbyters, sixteen deacons, and eighty-one bishops in various places. The see was vacant for twenty-six days. [Note: [Col. 0581] C: three months; B: three months and five days.]

## Note: [Col. 0613C]

In the Farnesian Codex, number LXII, which is number LXI in the Velser Codex.

Holstenius, in his notes: Vigilius, returning to Rome, died on 10 January. Pelagius succeeded around the middle of April and was consecrated on Easter Day, 16 April. Under the year 556, the chronicle in a manuscript codex of the Queen of Sweden, written five hundred years ago, has the entry under Justin: “In the nineteenth year of Justinian and in the year 561 of the Incarnation.”

There it combines the year 561 of the Incarnation with Justinian’s twenty-ninth year, in accordance with our opinion, which maintains that Christ was born five years before the common era. For since Justinian’s twenty-ninth year fell in the common-era year 556, adding five years gives the year 561.

---

## Note: [Col. 0613C]

Line 3. At the same time Narses and Pope Pelagius, having reached an agreement, came from Saint Pancratius to Saint Peter the Apostle, conducting a litany with hymns and spiritual songs.

A litany, that is, a solemn procession, was ordered by Pelagius from the church of Saint Pancratius to the Basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle. Gregory I ordered a solemn litany to drive away the plague; see Gregory himself, book II of the letters; Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 1; and Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 25.

Justinian praised the use of litanies in Novel 123, chapter 22. Honorius ordered a solemn litany to be held every week on Saturday. Anastasius, in his life of Honorius, says:

> “He established a constitution in the Church and decreed that every week, on Saturday, a litany should go out to blessed Apollinaris and to blessed Peter the Apostle, and that the entire people should come forth with hymns and spiritual songs.”

Line 9.—Pelagius, holding the Gospels and the Lord’s cross over his head, ascended the ambo and satisfied the whole people and populace that he had committed no wrong against Vigilius. Pelagius purified himself in the ambo—that is, before the church’s pulpit—from the charge of Vigilius’s death by means of the holy Gospels and the Lord’s cross. Similarly, Leo III cleared himself by oath of the accusations brought against him, with twelve bishops present, in the church’s ambo; see Anastasius under Leo III; *Decree* “Auditum,” *Decree* “Omnibus,” 2, q. 5; *Decree* “Nos si,” in the same case, q. 7. Sixtus III likewise, accused by a certain Bassus, cleared himself in a synod; see *Decree* “Mandastis,” 2, q. 5.]

[Note: [Col. 0614C]

Line 6.—“They withdrew from his communion,” etc. Although Justinian favored Pelagius, as is sufficiently clear from the preceding events, in which he proposed Peter and Pelagius to the clergy [Col. 0614D] and added, “for whom my hand will be with you,” etc., nevertheless, because he had indicated that he intended to advance the servile practices introduced by King Theodoric concerning the election of the Roman pontiffs, the Roman clergy did not cease to defend its freedom in properly carrying out canonical elections.

Pelagius was a man of no contemptible integrity. Vigilius, on his return from Constantinople, had left him there as his *apocrisiarius*, as Liberatus says in his *Breviary*, chapter 22. When Totila was threatening the destruction of the City, Pelagius also performed great acts of generosity, recorded by Procopius, *Gothic War*, book III, chapter 8:

“At that time there was among the Romans and the holy men a certain deacon named Pelagius, who, having lived for a long time in Byzantium, had won for himself the greatest friendship with the emperor. Thus, surrounded by a very large amount of money, he had gone to Rome shortly before it was besieged. During the siege that followed, he generously distributed part of his money to those in need, undaunted; and since even previously he had been a good man among all the Italians, he gained, as was fitting, still greater glory for charity and benevolence toward everyone around him,” etc.

Thus, three occasions for disagreement between the clergy and the senate seem to have arisen in Pelagius’s election. The first was that Justinian, through Narses, who was then active in Italy, arranged for him to be elected pontiff; this presumption in sacred elections was contrary to ecclesiastical liberty. The second was that Pelagius’s rivals had fabricated a charge against him, as though he had hastened Vigilius’s death. The third, finally, was that part of the Roman clergy, together with certain provinces of the West, still persisted in defending the Three Chapters. Hence it rejected Pelagius’s communion and letters.

That Pelagius was elected by clergy who maintained the defense of the Three Chapters is clear from the fact that Victor of Tunnuna, who, together with the other Africans, stood in defense of the Three Chapters, says in his *Chronicle*:

“Pelagius, Roman archdeacon and defender of the three aforementioned Chapters, returns from exile with the permission of the emperor Justinian; and, condemning what he had previously defended with the greatest steadfastness, he is ordained bishop of the Roman Church by transgressors,” etc.

By “transgressors,” Victor means all those who defended the just condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Accordingly, the Roman clergy, divided into two parties at the beginning of Vigilius’s pontificate, was rushing toward schism. The bishops of Tuscia had also adhered to the opposing party. Pelagius sent them a letter rebuking them because they did not retain the pontiff’s name in the sacred diptychs:

“How do you not believe yourselves separated from the communion of the whole world if, amid the sacred mysteries, you do not retain, according to custom, the remembrance of the name in which, although unworthily, you see the stability of the apostolic see at the present time to stand through the succession of the episcopate?” etc.

He also wrote to other bishops of the West in order to dispel the calumnies that had been heaped upon him.

Line 7.—“At the same time,” etc. I think this addition was taken from Marcellinus, who in his *Chronicle* under the year 554 has the following:

“Pope Vigilius, released from exile by the Roman emperors and by Narses, had begun to return to Rome when he died in Sicily of stone disease. He was soon carried to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria. In his place Pelagius, the fifty-second pope, was ordained and sat for eleven years and ten months. Accused by the Roman people as a partisan against Vigilius, he celebrated litanies together with Narses, ascended the ambo at Saint Peter’s, placed the Gospel over his head, and cleared himself by oath [Col. 0615D] of the charge,” etc.

Line 17.—“And he caused all the golden and silver vessels to be restored,” etc. This restoration, promoted by the pontiff’s diligence and carried out by the notary Valentinus, proves the observation made above: namely, that everything belonging to the Roman Church had been collected by the notaries, recorded in some special catalogue, and kept by them, with the accounts of the gifts, their weights, and their donors noted. From these catalogues Anastasius was able to describe the offerings individually and add them to the deeds of each pontiff.

Pelagius could not easily have ordered the restoration unless catalogues had existed by which the vessels could be identified, together with the manner in which they had either been brought in or alienated elsewhere. The greatest fidelity was therefore required of these notaries; hence it is added concerning Valentinus that he was a man who feared God.

The dispersal of those vessels may have occurred either because of Vigilius’s prolonged stay in Constantinople or because the apostolic see, in order to provide assistance to Vigilius in exile, had pawned the sacred vessels. We frequently read that bishops, in order to undertake journeys for councils, gave sacred vessels in pledge to meet their own needs.

For this reason, in the *Encyclical* volume—that is, the volume preserving the encyclical letters written by bishops in support of the authority of the Council of Chalcedon—the synod of the bishops of the province of Helenopont praises the emperor Leo because, in the same controversy, he had forbidden the celebration of an ecumenical council. It adds this reason from among others (Part III of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 33, pp. 736, 757):

“For those who desire synods to be assembled are striving for nothing else than that, after selling the sacred vessels of many holy bishops, they may consume all the proceeds on costs, expenses, and the transport of animals; and that some of them, deprived of the light of this life during their journey or at sea, may be recognized as imposing this burden and sin upon those convening the council. Instead, command each priest, established in his own Church and remaining where he has been appointed, to celebrate prayers and supplications for the rule of your serenity,” etc.

We find the same provision enacted in other synods as well.

Another occasion for that dispersal arose from Theodoric’s edict, by which, after the death of Pope John I, he had ordered that all episcopal elections depend upon royal consent. Consequently, wicked men, heaping gifts upon courtiers, extorted consent by such means.

This simoniacal corruption had long been prevalent, to such an extent that Athalaric wrote as follows to John II (in Cassiodorus, book IX, letter 15, p. 590):

“But you, who preside in the honor of patriarchs over the other Churches, since our constitution has freed you from unlawful promises, must now, by imitating good examples, offer to the majesty pontiffs worthy of it, without any loss to the Churches. For it is unjust that ambition should have a place among you when, through divine consideration, we have closed it off from laymen.

“Therefore, if anyone should believe that a bishop of the apostolic Church or a patriarchal bishop is to be advanced, whether by himself or through his relatives or any persons subject to our service, by any ambition involving support, we decree that he himself must repay what he has received, and that he must in every way suffer what the canons have established.

“But if anyone should fear to publish what he has given or promised while the recipient is still alive, let the Church from whose support the bishop is found to have been ordained recover it from his heirs; and let the survivors nevertheless be branded with the mark of infamy,” etc. (The same, no. 16.)

Indeed, in a letter to Salvantius, prefect of the City, Athalaric ordered that the edict, engraved on marble tablets, be placed at the doors of the basilica of Saint Peter:

“So that this principal benefaction may remain attached both to the present age and to future generations, we command that both our determinations and the laudable decrees of the most distinguished senate be properly engraved on marble tablets and placed before the atrium of Blessed Peter the Apostle as a public testimony. For this is a worthy place to contain both the glorious reward due to us and the praiseworthy decrees of the most distinguished senate.

“We have sent the person concerned for this purpose, so that upon his return we may know that what we ordered has been accomplished. For what someone commands seems uncertain when the outcome of his affairs is reported to him only slowly,” etc.

From these words we obtain the confirmation of what we noted above: namely, that those charged with publishing any royal authority were required to report back concerning the matter carried out.

Pelagius’s words found here in line 12 refer to these public tablets:

“Pope Pelagius also added and said: ‘For I ask you to confirm my petition: if anyone is found worthy to be promoted in the holy Church, from the doorkeeper’s office up to the degrees of the episcopate, let him advance neither through gold nor through any promises. You all know that he is a simoniac,’” etc.

The final words refer to the edict then affixed to the doors of Saint Peter’s. He subsequently adds:

“But if anyone is learned in the work of God and possesses a good life, we command that he come to the first degree not through payment but through good conduct,” etc.

This last provision indicates the reform of the clergy begun under Agapetus, when, because of the invasions of the barbarians [Col. 0617A], literary studies had fallen into disuse. Cassiodorus communicated his plans for restoration to Agapetus, as he writes in the very preface to the *Institutions*:

“I endeavored, together with the most blessed Agapetus of the city of Rome, to arrange that, just as it is reported to have been established for a long time at Alexandria, and as it is now diligently reported to be expounded among the Syrian Hebrews in the city of Nisibis, the city of Rome, after providing the necessary expenses, might receive professed teachers for a Christian school; from this the soul might receive eternal salvation . . . But because of the wars raging and the exceedingly turbulent conflicts in the Italian kingdom, my desire could in no way be fulfilled, since a matter of peace has no place in troubled times,” etc.

Nevertheless, as academies were gradually introduced into Italy, it is credible that Pelagius issued this provision for the advancement of learning, so that only learned men would be promoted.

At the same time, Primasius, primate of Africa, seeing the provinces freed from the barbarians, promoted learning around the year 550. A letter of Junilius to Primasius survives, in which his requests concerning the restoration of studies are set out, together with a reply. Junilius writes that Primasius had asked (in *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*, p. 340):

“Was there among the Greeks anyone who burned with zeal for the study and understanding of the divine books?”

To this I replied that I had seen a certain man named Paul, Persian by race, who had been educated in the school of the Syrians in the city of Nisibis, where the divine law is taught by public teachers, just as grammar and rhetoric are taught among us in worldly studies, in an orderly and regular manner,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0617B]

Line 1.—Pelagius. Pope Adrian, in his letter to Charlemagne concerning images, writes the following about Pelagius:

“Much more, however, his most holy successors, Lord Pelagius and Lord John, building from the ground the church of the Apostles of wondrous greatness, painted various histories both in mosaic and in different colors, together with sacred images, and even to this day they are venerated by us.”

[Col. 0617C] Line 19.—“The basilica of the apostles Philip and James was begun.” Pelagius began this church, but his successor John completed it and consecrated it under the title of Saints Philip and James, according to the wording preserved, as Baronius testifies, in the ancient monuments of the Vatican basilica collected by Manlius:

“Pelagius began it; Pope John completed it.”

] [Note: [Col. 0617C]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

The catalogues of Lucca and Farfa, together with the Farnesian, Regian, Mazzarino, and Thuanean manuscripts of the *Bibliothecarius*, correctly reckon the vacancy of the see from the death of Vigilius, who died in Sicily around 10 January of the year 555, until the ordination of his successor Pelagius on Sunday, 18 April, as three months and six or five days, depending on whether the terminal days are excluded.

They assign Pelagius a tenure of four years, ten months, and eighteen days, not only in the Luccan and Farfense catalogues and in the Farnesian, Welserian, Cavensis, and other manuscripts of the *Bibliothecarius* generally, but also in his funerary inscription at the Vatican. This inscription is reported by Cardinal Baronius in the *Annals*, Gruterus in the *Thesaurus veterum inscriptionum*, Manlius and, following him, Aringhius in *Roma subterranea*, book II, chapter 8, the Roman Canon at Paul de Angelis, *Description of the Vatican Basilica*, p. 77, and various other historians and antiquarians. After several verses, it is marked as follows:

> HERE RESTS PELAGIUS, WHO SAT [AS BISHOP] FOUR YEARS, TEN MONTHS, EIGHTEEN DAYS. DEPOSITED ON 4 MARCH.

According to the *Bibliothecarius*, he died two days before his burial; it records that he died on 2 March. Pelagius’s death therefore belongs to the year 560 and the day 2 March.

Panvinio must consequently be corrected in his *Chronicle*, as must Holstenius, who follows him; they defer Pelagius’s death to the year 561. Aringhius likewise, writing with Baronius, says that Pelagius, elected in the year 555, died in 559. For the reckoning of years and months does not permit the terms to be extended or shortened in such a way as to correspond with the total expressed in the chronology of the stone epitaph, as Cardinal Norisius observes in his historical dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 9, section 1, at the end.

There is no need for us to linger over the investigation of the cause of the error by which, in certain catalogues and manuscripts of the *Bibliothecarius*, Pelagius’s years in office are given as eleven. We may suspect that the error arose from Marcellinus’s *Chronicle*, where, after the fourteenth year following the consulship of Basil, we read:

“Pope Vigilius, etc., died in Sicily after being struck by stone disease, etc.; in his place Pelagius, the sixty-second pope, was ordained and sat for eleven years and ten months,” etc.

For if the continuator of Marcellinus, from the Greek text of some chronicle that assigned to Pelagius ΕΤ Ι Δ—four years—painted ΕΤ ΙΑ instead of the letters ΕΤΙ or the sign Δ, the false number eleven could easily have emerged from the true number four. [Col. 0618B]

But let others investigate the cause of the error. For us it is enough to establish, from the genuine documents, the funerary inscription, and the corrections found in the manuscripts and in the oldest copies, that Pelagius I must be assigned four years, ten months, and eighteen days, in accordance with the catalogues and the text of the *Bibliothecarius*.

In the same place we read that after Pelagius’s death the see was vacant for three months and twenty-five days. Therefore his successor John III was elected pontiff on 27 July 560 and ordained on the following Sunday, which fell on 1 August.

HISTORICAL NOTES.

Line 6.—“They withdrew from his communion, saying that he had been involved in the death of Pope Vigilius,” etc. You will find the falsity of this popular error, and of the purification that followed from it, which Pelagius performed from the ambo and to which the *Bibliothecarius* adhered together with the common people, corrected in the notes of Pagius.

Cardinal Norisius treats the matter more fully in his dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 9. First [Col. 0618C], after considering and comparing the chronicle of Tunnuna and other documents and deeds, he concluded that this kind of canonical purification was voluntarily undertaken by Pelagius—not to remove from himself the charge that he had hastened Vigilius’s death, for Pelagius had been that pontiff’s faithful *apocrisiarius* and companion in the persecutions on account of the Three Chapters, but because he wished to avert the suspicion that he disapproved of the Fifth Synod after the condemnation of the Three Chapters, which he had previously defended. Many Western bishops believed that this condemnation constituted a betrayal of the sacred Council of Chalcedon.

Norisius carefully explains the whole matter in section 1, which he entitles “On Pelagius I.” He responds there to the reckless attacks of Peter Halloix, who congratulated himself on defending the lamentable cause of the Origenists and, with the utmost shamelessness, marked the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, the supreme pontiffs, and the most learned Fathers with his censorial stroke. Norisius’s arguments help to free Anastasius’s account of this passage from popular rumor, and he concludes as follows:

“Therefore, before the people in the ambo, he did not affirm under oath that nothing had been attempted by him against Vigilius; rather, he affirmed that he had established nothing against the faith of the Council of Chalcedon in the matter of the Three Chapters. Ignorance of the controversy concerning the Three Chapters led Anastasius, otherwise an ancient writer, into those stories to which the other writers gave credence.”

See also the more minor errors of the distinguished historians of our own or the immediately preceding age concerning the deeds of Pelagius I, which Norisius corrected on this occasion.]

[Note: [Col. 0618D]

Line 1.—“Pelagius, Roman by nation.” He was consecrated on 16 April, Easter Sunday, and, because of the exceptional gifts and virtues with which he was endowed, was raised to Peter’s chair.]

[Note: [Col. 0619A]

Line 1.—“He sat for four years,” etc. Pelagius, deacon of the holy Roman Church, Roman by nation and son of Vicarianus, was appointed successor to Vigilius after an interval of approximately three months between pontificates.

It is clear that he was ordained in April from his epitaph, which will be cited below, and specifically on the eleventh day of that month, which in the year 555 was a Sunday. It is incontrovertibly proved that he was consecrated in April of the year 555 by his sixth letter to the bishops of Tuscia, dated 15 February in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basil, vir clarissimus, which is the year 556. Thus, before April, and indeed already in February, when that letter was issued, he was Roman pontiff. The date of his ordination is deduced from the duration of his pontificate recorded in the epitaph just mentioned.

Line 2.—“And since there was no bishop to ordain him,” etc. Before his pontificate, Pelagius had been Pope Vigilius’s *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople before the emperor Justinian [Col. 0619B], with whom, as Procopius—quoted shortly below—says, he had won the greatest friendship.

While holding that office, he was the one who induced Justinian to condemn the Origenists, as appears from what was said under Vigilius. He returned from Constantinople to Rome, summoned by Vigilius in the year 544, before the emperor issued his first edict against the Three Chapters.

In 546 he was sent as an envoy to Totila, king of the Goths, who was besieging Rome, and softened him after the city was captured; from him he obtained whatever he wished. Procopius describes this in book III of the *Gothic War*, chapter 2:

“At that time, he says, there happened to be among the Romans and the holy men a certain deacon named Pelagius, who, having lived for a long time in Byzantium, had won for himself the greatest friendship with the emperor. Thus, surrounded by a very large amount of money, he had gone to Rome shortly before it was besieged. During the siege that followed, he generously distributed part of his money to those in need; and since even before that he had been a good man among all the Italians, he gained, as was fitting, still greater glory for charity and benevolence toward everyone around him [Col. 0619C].

“When the Romans were suffering every sort of unworthy and most grievous hardship because of hunger, they easily persuaded him to go to Totila and ask that he grant them a truce of a few days on these conditions: if within the period they had agreed upon no one came to their aid from Byzantium, they would immediately surrender themselves and the City to the barbarians.

“When Pelagius came to Totila with these instructions and was received by him with great kindness,” etc.

Totila entered the City and went into the temple of the Apostle Peter to pray. Meanwhile, however, the Goths cut down those whom they encountered. In this way, only twenty soldiers and sixty civilians were killed.

As Totila entered that temple, Pelagius himself came to meet him, carrying the Gospels of Christ in his hands. He fell down in supplication on his knees and said, “Spare your own people, O prince.”

Then Totila smiled broadly and addressed him as follows: “So you have come to beg me now, Pelagius?”

“Yes,” he replied [Col. 0619D], “since God has made me your servant; but from now on withdraw your hand from those who have fallen into your servitude.”

Overcome by these prayers, Totila immediately ordered the Gothic soldiers by edict to kill no more Romans and to abstain from plunder. Pelagius then obtained from Totila the freedom of the Roman captives. Totila also sent him, together with Theodorus, one of the city’s principal magistrates, as an envoy to Justinian to seek peace, as the aforementioned Procopius relates.

Later, Pope Vigilius summoned Pelagius to Constantinople so that he might assist him in the difficult matter of the Three Chapters. Under Vigilius he also fought steadfastly for the Three Chapters. For he is recorded as having subscribed to the *Constitutum* of Vigilius.

When he refused to subscribe to the Fifth Synod, he was sent into exile, as Victor of Tunnuna—whom we shall quote shortly—testifies. After learning of Vigilius’s death, Justinian recalled Pelagius from exile. Pelagius complied with the emperor, condemned the Three Chapters, and by this means was raised to the Roman see. These are Victor of Tunnuna’s words:

“Pelagius, Roman archdeacon and defender of the three aforementioned Chapters, returns from exile at the persuasion of the emperor Justinian; and, condemning what he had previously defended with the greatest steadfastness, he is ordained bishop of the Roman Church by transgressors.”

Victor speaks in this way because Pelagius had been an extremely obstinate defender of the Three Chapters.

These matters have been related at somewhat greater length so that it may be clear that Anastasius was mistaken when he wrote that the Romans withdrew from Pelagius’s communion because he was publicly known as the author of the evils that Vigilius had suffered at Constantinople. He added that Pelagius, holding the Gospels and the Lord’s cross over his head, ascended the ambo and thus satisfied the whole people and populace that he had committed no wrong against Vigilius.

How could this be true, when it is established that Pelagius had been Vigilius’s companion in his persecutions, had stood with and for him, had subscribed to his *Constitutum*, by which the Fifth Synod was invalidated, had consequently been driven into exile, and, as Victor says in his *Chronicle*, had defended the Three Chapters with the greatest steadfastness? Therefore Pelagius did not affirm under oath before the people in the ambo that he had attempted nothing against Vigilius; rather, he affirmed that he had established nothing against the faith of the Council of Chalcedon in condemning the Three Chapters.

When it became known at Rome that Pelagius had condemned the Three Chapters, all alike, both clergy and laity, separated themselves from his communion. Nor could a third bishop be found in all Italy by whom he might be consecrated; they detested him as a transgressor of the Council of Chalcedon.

Accordingly, he was consecrated by the bishops of Perugia and Ferentino and by Andrew, priest of Ostia, as the same Anastasius relates. Thus far from the truth are Anastasius’s statements that the Roman people were offended with Pelagius because he had been the author of Vigilius’s persecutions, and that, after Vigilius had been confined, the Roman clergy had been sent into exile to various mines.

For it is established from the same Victor of Tunnuna [Col. 0620C] that those who defended the Three Chapters were sent by the emperor to distant monasteries. Moreover, ignorance of the controversy concerning the Three Chapters led Anastasius, otherwise an ancient writer, into those stories to which many writers gave credence, as Cardinal Norisius says in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 1, where he made these observations.

Line 4.—“They ordained him pontiff.” We must not move on from Pelagius’s ordination until we first observe that a new custom had been introduced in his election: the emperor Justinian, who had already controlled Rome for four years, arrogated to himself and his successors the authority to confirm the Roman pontiff, following the example of the Gothic kings, who had drawn the confirmation of elections to themselves.

Hence, after Vigilius’s death, there was an interregnum of three months; after the deaths of subsequent pontiffs, it was also longer than usual, because confirmation had to be awaited from the emperor’s court. From Anastasius under Agatho we learn that the emperors did not confirm an election until the customary amount of gold had been paid.

Mabillon explains this third period in the election of pontiffs in the following words, in his preliminary commentary on the *Roman Order*, paragraph 17, drawing from Onuphrius Panvinius’s manuscript work on the various methods of creating the Roman pontiff:

“When the pontiff died, responsibility for the vacant apostolic see was entrusted to the three principal ministers of the clergy: the archpriest, the archdeacon, and the *primicerius* of the notaries. They immediately notified the exarch of the pope’s death; after the Goths had been expelled, the emperor established that exarch at Ravenna.

“After the proper rites had been performed for the deceased and a three-day fast had been completed, they deliberated on the election of a pontiff. The clergy, the nobles, the people, and the soldiers took part in this election—that is, the military detachments stationed chiefly at Rome and Ravenna to defend the remaining part of Italy against the Lombards.

“The election was then reported to the emperor, from whom approval of the election was requested and awaited. The matter was likewise written about to the exarch, the judges, the archbishop, and the *apocrisiarius* at Ravenna, so that they might favor the election.

“After the emperor’s approval had been given, the elected man was finally ordained at the confession of Saint Peter, and there he professed the faith. Soon afterward he sent his confession of faith to all the Churches.”

All these details are established by the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, whose formulas began to be used from that time, that is, after Pelagius’s election.

So Mabillon; the author of the criticism of Baronius agrees with him in everything except his assertion that this custom lasted until Charlemagne. For we shall see below, with that same author, that under Pepin, king of the Franks, the Church was freed from that servitude [Col. 0621B], although, under the emperor Louis the Pious, the custom was restored to its former condition and the ordination of the Roman pontiffs was again carried out in the presence of the emperor’s legates.

Line 17.—“At the same time the basilica of the Holy Apostles was begun,” etc. Anastasius, in Pelagius’s *Life*, testifies that Pelagius began the construction of the basilica of the Apostles Philip and James. “While it was being begun,” he says, “he died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Nones of March.”

Pelagius therefore died in the year 560, during the night between the final day of February and the first day of March, and was buried on the fourth day of that month, as is read in his epitaph. He had been ordained on 11 April of the year 555 and, according to the same epitaph, sat for four years, ten months, and eighteen days; he was buried on 4 March. Thus everything agrees.

We shall see in the account of John’s pontificate that the basilica of the Holy Apostles was completed by his successor John. It was called the basilica of the Apostles [Col. 0621C] Philip and James because its dedication took place on 1 May, a day sacred to the holy Apostles Philip and James. It was built in honor of the twelve apostles, as is read in the bull of John III, Pelagius’s successor, which Baronius cites under the year 369 and which will be discussed below.]

[Note: [Col. 0621C]

Line 2.—“And since there was no bishop to ordain him,” etc. Theodoric and his successors, the Gothic kings in Italy, had arrogated to themselves the tyrannical power of confirming the Roman pontiff after an election carried out by the Roman clergy.

When the emperor Justinian had freed Rome and Italy by his arms from the yoke of those same barbarians, he established a right for himself from their usurpation. The abuse of this right was prolonged and continued until Pepin and Charlemagne, through their victories and acquisitions in Italy, brought protection to the Roman Church so that it could recover its former liberty.

As long as that violent servitude oppressed the Church, the method of elections was as follows, according to Panvinio, whom Mabillon cites in his preliminary commentary on the *Roman Order*:

“When the pontiff died, responsibility for the vacant apostolic see was entrusted to the three principal ministers of the clergy: the archpriest, the archdeacon, and the *primicerius* of the notaries. They immediately notified the exarch of the pope’s death; after the Goths had been expelled, the emperor established that exarch at Ravenna.

“After the proper rites had been performed for the deceased and a three-day fast had been completed, they deliberated on the election of a pontiff. The clergy, the nobles, the people, and the soldiers took part in this election—that is, the military detachments stationed chiefly at Rome and Ravenna to defend the remaining part of Italy against the Lombards.

“The election was then reported to the emperor, from whom approval of the election was requested and awaited. The matter was likewise written about to the exarch, the judges, the archbishop, and the *apocrisiarius* at Ravenna, so that they might favor the election.

“After the emperor’s approval had been given, the elected man was finally ordained at the confession of Saint Peter, and there he professed the faith. Soon afterward he sent his confession of faith to all the Churches.

“All these details are established by the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, whose formulas began to be used from that time, that is, after Pelagius’s election.”

Line 6.—“They withdrew from his communion,” etc. Since Pelagius had received and approved, just as his predecessor had done, the condemnation of the Five Chapters, those who thought differently about these matters from the judgment of the Roman see were to be regarded as schismatics.

The pontiff’s first concern, therefore, was to bring everyone into that unity whose center is the apostolic see. Pelagius began by turning the clergy and people of the City away from their separation, removing from their minds the prejudice under which they labored: namely, that assent could not be given to the condemnation of the Three Chapters without simultaneously disapproving the holy Council of Chalcedon.

He then wrote to the bishops of Etruria in these terms:

“Having received the report brought to us by Jordan, the defender of our Church, we were sufficiently astonished that you had become so forgetful of apostolic authority that you wished your separation from the universal Church to be confirmed, God forbid, even with my consent; and that those whose duty it was to restrain popular ignorance by priestly teaching should wish to follow the judgment of the people in insult to the apostolic see.

“Nor do we grieve, in saying this, over an injury to ourselves, since, by the Lord’s gift, our purpose is to preserve, in gentleness and by preferring all else, every bond of fraternal peace. But, as we have said, I am profoundly astonished at your separation from the general Church, which I shall not be able to endure with patience.

“For when the most blessed Augustine, mindful of the Lord’s sentence by which he placed the foundation of the Church in the apostolic sees, says that whoever does not believe himself separated from the authority or communion of the bishops of those sees is in schism, how do you not believe yourselves separated if, amid the sacred mysteries, you keep silent concerning the memory of my name according to custom—in the one in whom, although unworthily, you see the stability of the apostolic see at the present time to reside through the succession of the episcopate?”

Pelagius I, Letter 18, to the bishops of Tuscia.

To remove the anxiety from their minds and the scruple by which they seemed troubled—because they considered that the Fifth Council, condemning the Three Chapters, could not be received without the Council of Chalcedon and the ancient faith likewise being condemned—he issued a declaration of his faith and renewed it in an encyclical letter sent to all the Churches. At its opening he says:

“Nothing whatsoever has been attempted against the faith of the Fathers or against the firmness of the four synods; rather, everything was done so that the firmness of those synods might stand with immovable solidity against all enemies.”

Letter 40, to all the people of God.

On the same subject he wrote at length to Gaul, to King Childebert and also to the bishop of Arles, specifically to dispel the false rumor that had arisen concerning the Fifth Synod.

To achieve more successfully the full realization of his wishes, which were directed toward the extinction of schism, he sought the assistance of secular power. In his second letter to Narses he recalled:

“This was established both by divine and by human laws: those who are separated from the unity of the Church and most unjustly disturb its peace are to be restrained even by secular authorities.

“Addressing King Childebert in exhortation (Letter 16), he arouses the fervor of his faith so that, as he says, throughout all the regions of your Gaul he may take care that those who sow scandals there do not, driven on by the shamelessness of your countenance, roam about as they attempted to do in these parts, and agitate some of our brother bishops or the peoples entrusted to them toward dissension.

“For, since they are not of the right faith, they pretend to defend the right faith, desiring through the pain of their oppression to make themselves familiar to Catholics for the fostering of scandals—especially among those who are ignorant of their frauds and deceits.”

He also advises Narses (Epistle 5, to Narses) that, if such restless men should find something objectionable to them in the decision of the general synod held at Constantinople during the recently elapsed first indiction, “they should send to the Apostolic See, as has always been done, some of their own number who could give and receive an account, and should not, with closed eyes, tear apart the body of Christ our God, that is, the holy Church. But,” he adds, “such men must be restrained by imperial or judicial authority, because the rules of the Fathers expressly established that, if any person in ecclesiastical office should resist the person to whom he is subject, or gather separately, or erect an altar, or cause a schism, he should be excommunicated and condemned. But if he should perhaps despise even this and persist in making divisions and schism, [Col. 0624A] he should be suppressed by the public authorities.” He adduces the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, Act IV, in the letter of the archimandrites, and of Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 72.

This holy pontiff enjoyed the praise and good fortune of seeing his labors crowned by the suppression of the schism throughout Africa, Illyricum, and Italy—indeed, throughout the entire Christian world—with the sole exceptions of the Churches of Istria and Venice, which were subject to the metropolitan of Aquileia. Victor of Tunnuna, *Chronicle*, under the years 554, 555, and 559.

In Gaul he not only preserved unity with the holy Roman See, but also, at Childebert’s request, constituted the bishop of Arles the vicar of the Roman See throughout Gaul; previously, because of the decline of Roman imperial authority in that ecclesiastical province, the bishop of Arles had been appointed by the Roman pontiffs only over that part belonging to the Romans.

[Col. 0611]

**109 Pelagius**, Roman by nation, son of John Vicarianus, sat four years

[Note: [Col. 0611] C: eleven years.]

ten months, and eighteen days. Since there was no bishop who could ordain him, two bishops were found—John of Perugia and Bonus of Ferentino [Note: [Col. 0611] C: Ferentinus]—together with Andrew, a priest of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0611] C: Ostia], and they ordained him pontiff. At that time there were no members of the clergy able to promote him, because the monasteries, the multitude of religious, and the learned nobility had withdrawn from his communion, saying that he had involved himself in the death of Pope Vigilius and therefore was being afflicted with such great punishments.

At the same time Narses and Pope Pelagius, having taken counsel together, proceeded from Saint Pancratius to Saint Peter the Apostle, with a litany, hymns, and spiritual songs. Pelagius, holding the Gospels and the Lord’s cross above his head, ascended the ambo and satisfied the whole people and populace that he had done no wrong against Vigilius.

Pope Pelagius further added and said: “For I ask you to confirm my petition: if anyone is found worthy of promotion in the holy Church, from the doorkeeper’s office up to the episcopal orders, let him advance neither through gold nor through any promises. You all know that such a man is a simoniac. But if someone is learned in the work of God and possesses a good life, we command that he advance, not through payment, but through good conduct, up to the first grade.”

At the same time he appointed his notary Valentinus, a man who feared God, and caused all the gold and silver vessels and vestments to be restored throughout all the churches. At the same time the basilica of the Apostles Philip and James was begun; when he began to have it built, he died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter. He held two ordinations in the month of December: twenty-six priests, nine deacons, and forty-nine bishops in various places. He also died on the second day of March [Note: [Col. 0613] C: the sixth day before the Ides of March], and the episcopate remained vacant for three months and twenty-five days.

**LXIII. JOHN III. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 559, THE 33rd YEAR OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN.**
