[Note: [Col. 0625C]

Line 3.—“He established that offerings, vessels, or lights should be supplied in those same cemeteries on every Sunday from the Lateran.” There were oratories in the cemeteries of the City, in which the sacrifice of the Mass was customarily celebrated on each Sunday. Therefore, so that the expense might not be lacking, John III established that offerings—that is, bread to be offered for the purpose of the sacrifice—*hamae* or *amulae*, that is, pitchers in which the wine and water for the sacrifice of the Mass were contained, and lights, that is, candles, should be supplied from the Lateran, that is, from the Lateran basilica. The same was established by Gregory III. Anastasius [Col. 0625D] says in his Life: “With these same institutions he arranged that, in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the feast days of those whose memorials were being celebrated—that is, of the holy apostles and martyrs—lights should be supplied for holding vigils, and that offerings from the patriarchium should be carried by the offertory-bearer for the celebration of Masses, through the agency of one whom the pontiff then in office had appointed for this purpose.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

Line 5.—“At the same time the Heruli,” etc. The more important deeds [Col. 0626B] of this pontiff are reported in similar words by Paul the Deacon (*Book XVIII*, p. 677); indeed, this entire passage has been copied confusedly from him and ought to be restored from the same source, as well as from Marius of Avenches, a distinguished writer and chronicler of this period, whose brief work appears among the writings of François du Chesne, volume I. He left the following note:

“In the second year of the consulship of Justin the Younger Augustus, indiction 1. In this year Narses, formerly *praepositus* and patrician, after so many tyrants had been overthrown—that is, the Gothic kings Baduilla and Teia, Bucellinus, commander of the Franks, and also Sindual of the Heruli—and after Milan and the other cities which the Goths had destroyed had been commendably restored, was removed from Italy by the aforementioned Augustus,” etc.]

Line 10.—“Then the Romans, moved by envy,” etc. This passage too has been copied from the same Paul, with only this difference: here the writers of the treacherous letter are called Romans, whereas Paul calls them commanders (in the same place, p. 677). In his *History of the Lombards*, Book II, chapter 5, p. 51, Paul the Deacon likewise observes that the Romans were the accusers and had been moved by envy. From that history of the Lombards by Paul the Deacon, Anastasius copied entire chapters into the successive deeds of the Roman pontiffs; and where Paul stopped, the deeds of the succeeding pontiffs are recorded in a bare and meager fashion [Col. 0626D]. What both Paul and the *Liber Pontificalis* relate about the invitation of the Lombards by Narses, even if some count it among fables, is nevertheless wrongly dismissed as such. For among the Colbert manuscripts there is a short work by Mellitus, bearing the title *A Brief Account of the Times*. He says that he completed it in the year 614, and the following is read in that account:

“Narses the patrician, after he had defeated Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy under the Emperor Justinian, terrified by the threats of Sophia, wife of Justin, invited the Lombards from Pannonia and led them into Italy,” etc.]

Line 31.—“The episcopate remained vacant ten months and three days,” etc. The lengthy interregnum arose from the Lombard invasion, about which Paul the Deacon writes in the same work, chapter 7, p. 57, and Sigebert more fully in his *Chronicle*. The invasion raged so fiercely that the pontiff was compelled to hide in the cemeteries, as is noted here. See the same author, Book XVIII, p. 778.]

[Note: [Col. 0627A]

Line 1.—“He sat twelve years,” etc. The period during which he began and ceased to exercise this apostolic office indicates that he held the pontificate for thirteen years and fourteen days. Anastasius acknowledges that he died on the third day before the Ides of July. Therefore, if he obtained the pontificate on 27 June, after an interregnum of three months and twenty-five days, in the year of Christ 559, it must necessarily be affirmed that the man who survived until July of the year 572 held the papal See for thirteen years and fourteen days.

Line 8.—“Then Amingus came,” etc. According to Agathias, Book IV, these events occurred in the twenty-ninth year of the Emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 555, during the pontificate of Vigilius and the reign of Theobald, king of the Franks. See Baronius, under the year 555, numbers 12 and 15.

Line 10.—“Then the Romans,” etc. Baronius refutes this history as fabulous and entirely fictitious under the year 567, numbers 11 and following. There, on the authority of the African grammarian Corippus, he shows that Narses had been recalled to Constantinople before the year 567, when the Lombards began to invade Italy from Pannonia, and had received great honor; he proves from Cedrenus, Corippus, and other writers that Longinus had been substituted in Narses’ place.]

[Note: [Col. 0627B]

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES**

The poverty of the documentation renders the See of John III obscure, although it was long-lasting, extending to nearly thirteen years—three or four days short of that period—according to the Librarian and the catalogues; Pagi also observes this, since neither an account of his deeds nor surviving letters are available. A monument from the fourth year of his pontificate survives in ancient Vatican marble, discovered among the ruins of the old basilica and indicating a place assigned for the burial of Marcellus, subdeacon of the sixth region.

**LOCVS MARCELLI SVBD. REG. SEXTE CONCESSVM SIBI ET POSTERIS EIVS A BEATISSIMO PAPA IOANNE QVI VIXIT ANN. PL. M. LXVIII DEP. P. C. BASILII. V. C. ANN. XXII IND. XI. VNDECIMV. KAL. IANVARIAS**

“Place of Marcellus, subdeacon of the sixth region, granted to him and his descendants by the most blessed Pope John, who lived approximately sixty-eight years. Deposited after the consulship of Basil, an illustrious man, in his twenty-second year, indiction 11, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.”

The eleventh indiction, running after the twenty-second year following the consulship of Basil, on 22 December, demonstrates the year 563 of the Christian era [Col. 0627D]. This was the fourth year of this Pope John’s pontificate, which began on the day of the Kalends of August, as we showed above at the end of the chronological note on Pelagius. The ancient chronicles, with their additions, leave us without information about Marcellinus five years earlier—that is, after the seventeenth year following the consulship of Basil, where they end.

The chronography of John Malalas likewise breaks off in this same eleventh indiction marked on the Vatican stone. He records that certain regions of Africa were occupied by the Moors in January and that Marcian, the nephew of the Emperor Justinian, was sent against them.

The Paschal Chronicle does indeed continue to the years of Phocas and Heraclius, but during the final years of Justinian and throughout the reign of Justin the Younger it records almost nothing beyond the names of the emperors and the indictional character for each year. Consequently, we can scarcely extract anything from either the Greek or the Latin chroniclers contemporary with these events that would illuminate the years of this pontiff [Col. 0628A].

Several copies of the Librarian assign the end of the See and life of John III to 31 July, but 23 July appears to be the correct reading. Since they assign him twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six or twenty-seven days—namely, thirteen complete years less three or four days—that total properly ends on 23 July 573, counting from the day of election that we established at the end of the chronological note on Pelagius, 27 July 560. The Lucchese catalogue places John’s death on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. If the reading were the tenth day before the Kalends of August, which is precisely 23 July, the date we have now established and confirmed from the indicated epochs, everything would agree exactly. Everyone can easily understand, however, that a difference of three days could have entered the numbers through the fault of copyists or reckoners.

**HISTORICAL NOTES**

Line 2.—“He restored the cemeteries of the holy martyrs,” etc. These cemeteries, together with the churches built over them [Col. 0628B], had evidently been devastated by the Goths during the year-long siege under Vitiges. See the notes given above on the Life of Saint Silverius, no. 99. Among the cemeteries and churches built over them, John seems especially to have devoted his attention to restoring the celebrated cemetery on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veran field, which is distinguished by the name of its founder, Saint Cyriaca, and by the basilica of Saint Lawrence buried there. For, while the buildings of the monastery adjoining the basilica were being restored, a lead pipe was found among our objects of antiquarian interest, bearing the letters:

**+ SALVO PAPA IOANNE STEFANUS PP REPARAVIT**

That is: “With Pope John safe, the *praepositus* Stephen restored it.”

The considerations that follow suggest that this inscription should be referred to this John, and that the restoration was carried out by the *praepositus* Stephen on his orders. First, during the year-long siege of the City by Vitiges, the principal aqueduct—through which the Julia, Marcia, Tepula, and Anio Novus waters flowed into the hills of the City and supplied branch pipes to the churches adjacent to Rome along the Tiburtine, Latin, and Appian Ways—was not only occupied by the Goths but also cut off and obstructed with rubble, preventing the waters from being supplied. Procopius, who was then in the City, described this in *The Gothic War*, Book II, chapter 3. Nine years later, in December of the year 547, when Rome was again captured by Totila, not only had the channels been broken, but Totila even considered razing the City entirely. Although his fury was somewhat moderated, he thought it sufficient to demolish one-third of the walls from the Porta Capena to the Porta Praenestina.

Although five years later Narses, sent to Italy, recovered the City, most of the buildings in that area still lay devastated by the Goths. Nor did sacred buildings readily obtain a restorer, because Pope Vigilius had been summoned to the East, sent into exile, and died on his return in Sicily two years after Rome was recovered by Narses; Vigilius was unable to reach the City alive. His successor Pelagius, troubled by disturbances for most of the first part of that five-year period, during which he was not pontiff for the entire time, began to restore the churches within the walls and to construct the title-church of the holy Apostles Philip and James, which, overtaken by death, he left to his successor John to complete.

Therefore, none of John III’s predecessors had been able to repair the ruins and damage inflicted on the cemeteries of the martyrs, the suburban churches built over them, and the channels of the Claudia, Marcia, Julia, and Tepula aqueducts, which had been broken during the twenty years of the Gothic War. Since John is said to have been a lover and restorer of the cemeteries of the holy martyrs, he should be thought to have begun with the restoration that was most necessary for keeping ministers there and providing services in those sacred places—namely, restoring the inflow of water and repairing the conduits for the use of the basilica, monasteries, praetorium, and bathhouse. We read that all these had been built beside the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls and the cemetery of Cyriaca by the blessed Hilary above, no. 71, and for the weekly residents there through the institution of Simplicius, no. 72.

The other Pelagius, who after Benedict’s three-year interval became the successor both of that man and of this John, restored the same Laurentian basilica from its foundations (below, no. 112). I therefore believe that the inscription on the lead pipe found there belongs to John III and that its restoration was arranged by the *praepositus* Stephen.

In John’s time there are found *praepositi* in charge of offices and construction works, both in the Eastern and in the Western Empire. The *praepositus* of the palace, Amantius, is mentioned by Marcellinus Comes under Justin; in the Alexandrian Chronicle he is called simply **Πραιπόσιτος** (“*praepositus*”). On the pavement of the basilica of Saint Paul, Peter the *praepositus* is recorded under Rusticius, an illustrious man, as consul—that is, in the year of Christ 520.

In Cassiodorus, Book II, several letters of King Theodoric addressed to Faustus the *praepositus* occur [Col. 0629B]. From their context it appears that the assignment of a thousand [units] for the maintenance of the baths belonged to his responsibility. In Book II, Letter 28, besides other more distinguished *praepositi* among the ministers of King Theodoric, we also find in this sphere, which concerned construction, a formula for appointing a *praepositus of lime* (Book VII, no. 17).

Stephens mentioned by contemporary writers also occur around this period, one of whom could have been the *praepositus* expressed in the pipe under Pope John. The Stephen mentioned by Senator, who in the aforementioned Letter 28, Book II, is elevated from head of an office—or *praepositus*—to the rank of *comes* of the first order, while retaining the privileges of his school, could honorably have been employed by John III to supervise the restoration of the Laurentian sacred building, if he lived into that pontificate.

Alternatively, it could have been that Stephen whom, after Totila had conquered the City, we read in Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book III, chapter 20, that Totila chose from among the Romans to serve as his envoy to the Emperor Justinian for the sake of peace and a treaty, while he was restoring many of the works of the City that he himself had conquered and his men had disfigured and devastated. Or Stephen should perhaps be understood as one of the ecclesiastical men: that restorer of the conduits of Saint Lawrence outside the walls. The deacon Stephen, whom Vigilius used as his *apocrisiarius* before the emperor, should not be excluded from the number, since several inscriptions demonstrate that Roman deacons undertook this responsibility, especially the inscription that Hilary, archdeacon and later pontiff, set up in the other church of Saint Lawrence near the Esquiline Gate, which we reproduced in the notes on Hilary, p. 169.

I have thought it worthwhile to record these matters in passing, so that the surviving antiquities of this otherwise document-poor age may also contribute to illuminating John’s pontificate and the restoration of the cemeteries undertaken under him after the Gothic disaster.

We also saw the remains of another cemetery excavated on the Esquiline in 1691, near the Liberian basilica [Col. 0629D], in the Peretti gardens, now called the Negroni gardens. They showed that this intramural cemetery could have been opened under Justin—perhaps because the Romans had been compelled to do so—within the boundary of the City, during the plague and the year-long siege under Vitiges, and amid the frequent attacks on the suburbs.

Among the other marble slabs found there that had closed the burial niches of the dead, I noted one that had first been used by Munius Modestinus to cover the ashes of Munia Modestina, his virgin daughter, in a pagan monument, as the inscription carved on its inner side showed; Fabrettus reported it on p. 144, no. 164. Later, after being carried away by Christians and placed in this cemetery for the burial of a Christian girl, its reverse surface was marked with the following inscription, which indicates the year 567 of the Christian era, the beginning of the eighth year of the pontificate of John III:

**+ HIC REQUIESCIT IN SOMNO PACIS FLORA QUAE VIXIT ANN. V. D. XXVIII**

**DEP. SUB. D. III. ID. AUG. IND. XV. P. C. DOMINI. N. JUSTINI PP AUG.**

“Here rests in the sleep of peace Flora, who lived five years and twenty-eight days. Deposited on the third day before the Ides of August, in the fifteenth indiction, after the consulship of our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus.”

She is said to have been deposited on the third day before the Ides of August, in the fifteenth indiction, after the consulship of our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus; these are the chronological markers of the year 567.

Line 23.—“The most holy pope remained in the cemetery of Saints Tiburtius and Valerianus, and lived there for a long time, so that he also consecrated bishops there.” These statements about John accord with the other matters considered by Cardinal Noris concerning the steadfastness of John III in defending the Fifth Synod against the schismatic bishops of Venice and certain of their Italian adherents, who were hostile to the Fifth Synod.

The plan of the schismatics was to suggest to Justin that Narses be recalled from Italy, so that they might preserve their schism under the Goths or Lombards, which the emperor was striving with all his strength and greatest zeal to destroy. See what Cardinal Noris writes in *Dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod*, chapter 9, section 3. Narses was rightly regarded as the scourge of the Goths and of every barbarian horde unleashed for the destruction of Italy. Once he had been removed from the care of Italy, matters would proceed according to the schismatics’ wishes.

Thus, having suborned envious men either at Rome or in the imperial court to construct accusations against Narses and advance them before Caesar, they hoped that, once the power of the prince hostile to the schism had been diminished, they would be free to persist in their ill-founded obstinacy under the protection of other kings. Therefore, just as they had erased the name of the Roman pontiff from the diptychs, so they tried to remove the more eminent ministers of the Roman Empire from Italy.

On the contrary, the most holy and equally provident pontiff John, understanding very well how important Narses’ presence and protection would be not only for the peace of the state but also for the unity of the Church of God, as soon as he saw that Narses, wearied by the accusations of the envious and by the devices of the schismatics who had suborned the Romans, had withdrawn into Campania, did not cease to act promptly [Col. 0630C] and recall him to the City.

For this reason, perhaps recognizing in them the same common enemies as Narses—those who were enemies of public peace and Catholic unity—he prolonged his stay in the cemetery of Tiburtius and Valerianus, which is considered part of the district of Callixtus, in order to avoid persecution, and consecrated bishops there.

From those whom he generally appointed as bishops throughout Italy, he consistently demanded that they swear and subscribe, in accordance with the decrees of the Fifth Synod, that they professed its teaching. Cardinal Noris demonstrates this from the clear documents of the letters of the great Gregory and of his predecessor Pelagius, writing about John in the cited section 3 of chapter 9, p. 89:

“Furthermore, in the most dangerous times, Pope John did not lose heart, but both sought help from the emperor for the declining Roman state and defended the Fifth Synod. For those who were consecrated as bishops of the cities swore to the decrees of the Fifth Synod and sent to the Apostolic See a written attestation of the faith they had given [Col. 0630D]. Gregory is a witness to this in Book III, Letter 2, to Constantius. ‘Indeed,’ he says, ‘if anything concerning the Three Chapters was named in any word or writing, your Fraternity remembers this well, although Laurentius, your Fraternity’s predecessor, sent the Apostolic See a very strict guarantee, to which men of the highest distinction, in the proper number, subscribed; among them I too, who at that time was holding the urban praetorship, subscribed likewise,’ etc.”

Noris demonstrates there with irrefutable arguments that this praetorship fell in the year 571, from p. 99. The same eminent writer gathered another testimony to the steadfastness of John III, together with the other predecessors in Peter’s See, both in approving and in requiring subscription to the Fifth Synod, from the letters of Pelagius II, which he cites on p. 85:

“Concerning John III,” he says, “who succeeded Pelagius I, this must here be stated; afterward we shall discuss the judgment of Benedict. Pelagius II, who was the fifth pontiff after Vigilius, testified in letters to Elias and the bishops of Istria [Col. 0631A] that his predecessors had approved the Fifth Synod and condemned the Three Chapters.”

And on p. 96, from Saint Gregory’s letter to Constantius, he adds these words: “Because, after such a division had been created for no reason, it was commanded that the Apostolic See should take care that the unity of the universal Church be preserved in every respect in the minds of priests.”

Then he concludes: “You see, therefore, that new bishops customarily sent an attestation by which they renounced the Three Chapters. Laurentius therefore sent his in the year 571, and Gregory the Great’s praetorship is more correctly assigned to that period. Thus, according to the same pontiff, from the time of Pelagius I, when in Italy many bishops had withdrawn from communion with the Roman pontiff on account of the Three Chapters, every time a new bishop was elected he condemned the Three Chapters in writing and sent a written attestation to the Roman pontiff. Consequently, Holloix must now be judged guilty of manifest falsehood, since he did not hesitate to assert that Benedict and his predecessor John had by no means condemned the Three Chapters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0631B]

Line 23.—“But Narses, having entered Rome,” etc. An inscription cut by Narses near Rome, while Justinian was still alive, in the preceding year, 564, on a bridge that he had restored over the Anio River, can still be seen:

“While our most pious and ever-triumphant lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in his thirty-ninth year, Narses, a most glorious man, formerly *praepositus* of the sacred palace, former consul, and patrician, after the Gothic victory, when their kings themselves had been overcome and overthrown in open battle with marvelous speed, and the freedom of the City of Rome and of Italy beyond the City had been restored, renewed the bridge of the Salarian Way, which the most wicked tyrant Totila had destroyed, after clearing the riverbed, in a better condition than it had once been.

“How well the path of the bridge, once curved, has been made straight,

“And the interrupted road has been continued.

“We tread the hard waters of the torrent beneath us,

“And it pleases us to behold the murmur of the angry water.

“Go, therefore, freely amid your rejoicing, Quirites,

“And let resounding applause sing Narses’ name everywhere.

“He who was able to bring the hard hearts of the Goths under control

“Taught the rivers also to bear a harsh yoke.”]

[Note: [Col. 0631C]

Line 1.—“He sat twelve years.” After the death of Pelagius, the episcopate remained vacant for four months and seventeen days, not, as it is read in Anastasius, three months and twenty-five days. For, since Anastasius himself establishes that John III, Roman by nation and son of Anastasius, an illustrious man, sat twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six days, and was buried in the basilica of Blessed Peter on the thirteenth day of July, it is likewise clear that the interregnum is incorrectly described in Anastasius and that John was ordained on the eighteenth day of July, on which Sunday fell in the year 560. Although John III’s pontificate was so long, his deeds are nevertheless almost unknown because the ancient monuments are lacking.

Line 4.—“He completed the church of the twelve holy apostles.” Of John III Anastasius writes: “He completed the church of the holy Philip and James and dedicated it.” Pelagius, John’s predecessor, had begun that basilica, as we said in connection with the same Anastasius. It is now called the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles.

For under the year 559 Baronius reports an ancient copy of a bull of John III, extracted, as he says, from Vatican manuscripts, preceded by this inscription:

“Copy of the bull of Pope John III, in which he says that he completed the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, begun by Pelagius, his predecessor, and left unfinished when death overtook him; that he constituted it a cardinal title; that he assigned to that basilica the boundaries of its parish; and that he endowed it with various gifts from his own wardrobe.”

Pope Adrian speaks of the same basilica in his letter to Charlemagne concerning images, saying that Pelagius and John built the Church of the Apostles from the ground up, a church of marvelous size, and painted various scenes both in mosaic and in different colors with sacred images; “and to this day,” he says, “they are venerated by us.” See what has been said about this church under Pelagius.

The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* likewise writes that John III established that offerings, vessels, or lights should be supplied in the cemeteries every Sunday. From this, in the case of Pope Stephen I, we inferred that the practice of offering in the cemeteries continued not only during the time of persecution but also long afterward. On this matter, see also what will be said under Gregory III.

Line 15.—“Then Narses went out from Rome,” etc., and line 17.—“When John learned this,” etc. In the year 568, the Lombards, invited by Narses—as distinguished writers have recorded—descended into Italy under their king Alboin, hostile to the peace of Italy, and occupied Aquileia and the neighboring towns of Venetia in almost a single assault. Thus the bishops of those cities, separated from the Roman Empire, attacked the Fifth Synod thereafter with greater security and insolence.

But in these most dangerous times Pope John did not lose heart. He both sought help from the emperor for the declining Roman state and defended the Fifth Synod. For those who were consecrated as bishops of the cities swore to the decrees of the Fifth Synod and sent to the Apostolic See a written attestation of the faith they had given, as Gregory the Great witnesses in Book III, Letter 2, to Constantius. From this it is inferred that Pope John required such an oath from Laurentius, the bishop-elect of Milan:

“Indeed,” Gregory says, “if anything concerning the Three Chapters was named in any word or writing, your Fraternity remembers this well, although Laurentius, your Fraternity’s predecessor, sent the Apostolic See a very strict guarantee, to which men of the highest distinction, in the proper number, subscribed; among them I too, who at that time was holding the urban praetorship, subscribed likewise.”

Mabillon, in volume I, part II of the *Museum Italicum*, and Papebrochius, in the *Exegesis on the Bishops of Milan* prefixed to volume VII of the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, have brought to light the previously obscure beginning of Laurentius’ pontificate. It fell approximately in January of the year 573. It follows that Laurentius sent Pope John a guarantee by which he affirmed under oath that he condemned the Three Chapters, a written declaration that Pope John had required from him. Since John had approved the Fifth Synod, he rightly defended the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

Line 31.—“And the episcopate remained vacant,” etc. Although Anastasius writes that after the death of John III the episcopate remained vacant for ten months and three days, it is nevertheless clear from Anastasius himself that the interregnum was longer. For he states that Benedict, his successor, sat four years, one month, and twenty-eight days and was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, in the Secretariat, [Col. 0632D] on the thirtieth day of July. If we count backward from that day, we find, according to Anastasius, that Benedict, Roman by nation, son of Boniface, called Bonus by the Greeks, was ordained on the third day of June in the year 574, on which Sunday fell in that year. Consequently, according to Anastasius himself, after the death of John III the See remained vacant for ten months and twenty-one days.

The cause of so lengthy an interregnum appears to be attributable to the disturbances caused by the Lombards, who were throwing Italy into turmoil. Benedict died without becoming distinguished by any deed that has come down to us.]

Line 1.—He held office for twelve years, twenty-seven days, and eleven months. Owing to the loss of ancient records, scarcely anything is known to us about the pontificate of John III, even though its duration extended to nearly thirteen full years. Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 20, records that, by his authority, the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius were restored to their sees; they had appealed to him after being removed by the synodal judgment of the Council of Lyons. When they appeared before Pope John, they declared that they had been removed for no valid reasons. He therefore sent letters to the king, ordering that they be restored to their sees; and the king, after first rebuking those responsible at length, carried out the order without delay.

[Col. 0623]

## 110. John, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, an illustrious man, held office for 12 years, 27 days, and 11 months

[Note: [Col. 0623] B: 13 years, less 14 days.]

He loved and restored the cemeteries of the holy martyrs. He decreed that offerings, ampullae [Note: [Col. 0623] C: amulae, “small vessels.”], and lights should be supplied in those same cemeteries from the Lateran on every Sunday. He completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James.

At that time the Heruli came to Tarsia [Note: [Col. 0623] C: Turcia or Tuscia, “Turkey” or “Tuscany.”] and raised up for themselves a king, Sindualt [Note: [Col. 0623] C: Sindual. See Baronius under the year 555.], and they oppressed all Italy. But when Narses went out against him, the king was killed, and he subjected the whole nation of the Heruli to himself.

Afterward Amingus, duke of the Franks, and Buccellinus came. In the same way they too oppressed Italy. But, with the Lord’s help, they too were killed by Narses. Thus all Italy rejoiced.

Then the Romans, moved by envy, made a representation to Justinian [Note: [Col. 0623] C: Justin. See Baronius under the year 567.] and Sophia, saying that it would have been better for the Romans to serve the Goths than the Greeks: “Narses, the eunuch, rules and does not subject us to servitude; and our most pious prince does not know this. Either free us and the city of Rome from his hand, or else we shall serve foreign peoples.”” [Note: [Col. 0623] See Paul the Deacon, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 5.]

When Narses heard this, he said: “If I have done evil to the Romans, may I meet with evil.” Then Narses left Rome, came to Campania, and wrote to the nation of the Lombards, telling them to come and take possession of Italy.

When Pope John learned that they had sent their representation against Narses to the emperor, he hastened to Naples and Pope John began to ask him to return to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0623] Baronius, in the place cited, proves that Narses had already been recalled to Constantinople.] Then Narses said: “Tell me, most holy pope, what evil have I done to the Romans? I shall go to the feet of the man who sent me, so that all Italy may know how I labored with all my strength for it.”

Pope John replied: “I shall go sooner than you will have left this land.”

Thus Narses returned with the most holy Pope John. Then the most holy pope remained in the cemetery of the saints Tiburtius and Valerian and lived there for a long time, even consecrating bishops there.

Narses, however, entered Rome and died after a long time. His body was placed in a lead coffin, and all his wealth was taken back to Constantinople. At the same time Pope John himself also died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the thirteenth day of July [Note: [Col. 0623] C: the third day before the Ides of July].

He carried out two ordinations during the month of December: twenty-nine priests [Note: [Col. 0623] C: thirty-eight], thirteen deacons, and seventy-one bishops [Col. 0625] in various places [Note: [Col. 0625] C: sixty-one]. The episcopate then remained vacant for ten months and three days.

# LXIV. BENEDICT. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 573, THE EIGHTH YEAR OF JUSTIN THE YOUNGER

[Note: [Col. 0633B]]

From the Farnesian manuscript LXIV.

No. 111. Line 1: Benedict, etc. He held office for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days; at that time the nation of the Lombards invaded Italy. Line 4: so that they might alleviate the scarcity caused by famine. And when Justinian had learned this. Line 6: and he sent ships laden with grain to Rome, etc. God of the land of Italy. Line 7: the most holy Pope Benedict, etc. In the secretarium, etc. One ordination during the month of December.

In Fabrotti, from the Freher manuscript.

Line 1: AB, four years; AB, twenty-eight days. Line 5: Justinian, AB. Line 10: B, twenty bishops.

From the Regius, Mazarine, and Thuan manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0633C]]

Line 8.—He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter in the secretarium. The *secretarium* is the sacristy of a church, in which sacred vessels are kept. The Greeks call it the *diakonikon* (διακονικόν), as in the Synod of Laodicea, canon 21; Agatho, chapter 66; canon *Non oportet*, 1 and 2; Distinction 23. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue*: “Thus, while passing through, Martin had his lodging in the secretarium of the church.” Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 18: “We, gathered together, were sitting in the secretarium of the basilica of blessed Peter, etc.” Leo of Ostia, *Cassinense Chronicle*, Book III, chapter 26: “Beside its apse he constructed a two-roomed building for storing the treasury of ecclesiastical service; this building is called the secretarium.”

Gregory I was buried before the secretarium. Anastasius, in his Life: “And he was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter before the secretarium.”

The Roman pontiffs stood in the secretarium before proceeding to the church. The same author, in the Life of Hadrian II: “From there they presented themselves, with sufficient humility, to the most holy Pope Hadrian, who was seated with the bishops and nobles in the secretarium of Saint Mary Major, according to the custom of the holy apostolic see; and they offered gifts and letters.”

Elsewhere, *secretarium* means the tribunal or court of a judge, as in Law 3, *Code*, “Where a senator or a man of rank”; or Ambrose, Sermon 4: “But perhaps you fear the judge whom you left in the tribunal.” Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 21: “Just as also in this ordering of the commonwealth, the person who is handed over to prison is sent out either from the judge’s tribunal or from his court.” Symmachus, Book X, Letter 36: “When the delegated authority of the prefect of the City had brought the rites of Bassus, which were to be examined, to the common tribunal.”

[Note: [Col. 0634C]]

Line 1.—Benedict. Since the Roman see had been vacant for ten months and three days because of the military disturbances, Benedict, whom the Greeks call Bonosus, was created pontiff on 16 May in the year of Christ the Redeemer 577.

During his time the Lombards, for the most part worshipers of idols, harassed the Church with savage persecution. They profaned holy places by breaking open the tombs of the holy martyrs, demolished buildings in the suburbs [Col. 0634D] of Rome, drove the holy bishop Cerbonius into exile together with his clergy, and put eighty peasants to death: forty because they refused to eat sacrificial meat, and the others because they refused to worship a goat’s head. During this persecution the miracles occurred that are recorded in Saint Gregory’s books of the *Dialogues* concerning Saint Cerbonius the bishop, Saint Sanctulus, and other priests.

The same line.—He held the see for three years. He held the pontificate for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. For he died in the year of our Redeemer 557, on the day before the Kalends of August.

[Note: [Col. 0635A]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The election of Benedict brought an end to the long vacancy of the see. The Librarian, as well as the Lucan and Farfense catalogues, defines it as ten months and three days. Pagius nevertheless argues that this calculation conflicts with the context of the same Librarian, in which he assigned the death of John III to 13 July, whereas from the same context we have assigned it to 23 July. Hence Anastasius states, and the catalogues mentioned agree, that the see was vacant for ten months and three days.

Benedict’s election therefore fell on 27 May 574, and his ordination on the following Sunday, which was 31 May. He is said to have held office for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days in the manuscripts of the Librarian, the Farnesian, Regius, Mazarine, and Thuan manuscripts.

This total may be reckoned from the day of his election, in which case his death must be placed on 25 July 578; or it may be reckoned from the day of his ordination, in which case his death must be assigned to 27 July of the same year, and his body would have been deposited at Saint Peter’s in the secretarium three days later, on 30 July—as we read in all the manuscripts of the Librarian.

I do not see why this corrected chronology, which is consistent in each of its assertions and in its measurements of the periods of John, his predecessor, and Benedict, his successor, should incur Pagius’s criticism.

The epoch of this pontificate is marked by an unfortunate event, namely, the Lombards’ spread throughout all Italy. Paul the Deacon connects it with the epochs of the Frankish kings and the Roman pontiffs in Book II, chapter [sic]:

“In those days when the Lombards invaded Italy, the kingdom of the Franks, after King Chlothar had already died, was ruled in four divisions by his sons. The first of them, Aripert, had his seat at Paris; the second, Gunthram, governed the city of Orléans; the third, Chilperic, held his throne at Soissons, in the place of his father Chlothar; and the fourth, Sigebert, ruled at the city of Metz. At this same time the Roman Church was governed by the most holy Pope Benedict, while blessed Paul [read: Paulinus] was patriarch over the city of Aquileia and its people. Fearing the barbarity of the Lombards, he fled from Aquileia to the island of Grado and carried away with him the entire treasury of his church.”

This narrative of Paul the Deacon illuminates the chronology and deeds both of Benedict, with whom we are here concerned, and of Pelagius II, his immediate successor, especially if there are added the matters that Cardinal Noris brought forward with his customary abundance of universal learning when discussing the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 9, section 3.

We shall be content to attend to the indication of Benedict’s pontificate, begun in May 574, as we established above, and completed in July 578, an unfortunate decade after the Lombards had been summoned from their Pannonian settlements in the preceding year—namely 567—for Italy’s destruction, and, in the preceding year 577, at the beginning of spring, had immediately spread over the region of Aquileia under their king and leader Alboin. They occupied Aquileia itself and the neighboring towns of Venetia in almost a single assault.

Thus, Noris adds, the bishops of those cities, separated from the Roman Empire, attacked the Fifth Synod thereafter with greater security and insolence.

[Col. 0636A] The connection between the epochs of the expulsion of the Goths, the Lombard invasion, and the four Frankish kings described by Paul the Deacon is also illustrated by their coins, which may be seen in the work of the distinguished V. C. le Blanc, *A Historical Treatise on the Coins of France*, published in French with illustrations of the coins of Aribert—whom the moneyers also represent as Niaribert and Charibert, and as Cherebert and Heribert—of Gunthram, who is read on the coins as King Gunthaera, with the name of his city, Senoni Civita, added; and of Sigibert, whose coins were struck at Marseille, as well as those of their father Chlothar, bearing the inscription VICTORIA GOTHICA. This inscription is not subsequently found on the coins of the sons, since the Goths had been completely expelled from imperial Italy by Narses.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

Line 2.—At the same time the nation of the Lombards invaded Italy, etc. We have already touched above, in the account of John, on the injuries that the Church, its unity, and its history suffered from this Lombard invasion, following the authorities collected by Cardinal Noris from contemporary writers.

With the same author as our guide, we have also presented a restoration of the chronology of these times, which had been badly handled even by the most distinguished writers of the age immediately preceding ours, drawing on his dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 9, sections 3 and 4. Likewise, we have set out the firmness of Pope Benedict in following the footsteps of his predecessors, in his approval of the Fifth Synod, and in requiring from bishops the customary oath; this firmness he made evident in the letters of Gregory the Great and Pelagius II.

Line 1.—Benedict, etc. The Greeks call this man not Benedict but Bonosus, from his surname, as Evagrius testifies in Book V, chapter 16.

Line 5.—Because Rome was endangered by famine, etc. Benedict’s prayers to Tiberius Augustus greatly benefited the city, which was suffering from a shortage of grain. For the emperor Justin sent many thousands of measures of grain from Egypt [Col. 0636C] and bestowed a great benefit on Benedict and all the citizens.

[Note: [Col. 0636C]]

Line 7.—In these labors, etc. He died, etc. Anastasius writes in his account of Benedict that during his time the nation of the Lombards invaded all Italy, and that at the same time there was a very severe famine, so that even a multitude of fortified settlements surrendered themselves to the Lombards in order to alleviate the scarcity caused by famine.

He adds afterward: “Placed amid these labors and afflictions, the most holy Pope Benedict died. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter in the secretarium, on the day before the Kalends of August.”

Benedict therefore died on 30 July 578, not in 579, as Papebrochius maintains. For in that latter year, on 18 February, Pelagius II, Benedict’s successor, was already seated, as is clear from his letter written on that day and read at the Synod of Grado, which will be discussed in the account of his pontificate.

Line 10.—And the episcopate remained vacant, etc. See Pagius’s notes on the number of the see.

[Note: [Col. 0636D]]

Line 2.—At the same time the nation of the Lombards, etc. The pontificate of Benedict I, extending over four years, fell during the Lombard persecution and the scourges of plague and famine by which Italy was devastated. Consequently, no records of him have come down to us. For the decretals that bear the name of this pontiff suffer from the defect of having been fabricated.

[Col. 0633]

## 111. Benedict, a Roman by nationality, son of Boniface, held office for three years

[Note: [Col. 0633] CB: four years. See Baronius under the year 568.]

He held office for one month and eighteen days. At that time the nation of the Lombards invaded all Italy, and at the same time there was a severe famine, so that even a multitude of fortified settlements surrendered themselves [Note: [Col. 0633] C: might surrender themselves] to the Lombards in order to alleviate the scarcity caused by famine.

When Justin, the most pious emperor, learned that Rome was endangered by famine and mortality, he sent to Egypt and sent ships laden with grain to Rome; thus God took pity on Italy.

Placed amid these labors and afflictions, the most holy and venerable pope died. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter in the secretarium on 30 July [Note: [Col. 0633] C: on the day before the Kalends of August].

He carried out one ordination [Note: [Col. 0633] C: during the month of December]: fifteen priests, three deacons, and twenty-one bishops in various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for three months and ten days.

[Col. 0639A] Line 8.—He built this above the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence, etc. When the body of Saint Lawrence was being sought by the workmen, those wondrous and fearful events occurred that Saint Gregory recounts in Book III, Letter 30, in these words:

“My predecessor of holy memory, likewise desiring to improve something at the body of the martyr Saint Lawrence, did not know where his venerable body had been placed. While the place was being excavated in search of it, his tomb was suddenly opened unintentionally. The monks and custodians who were present and working saw the body of that martyr, but did not dare to touch it in any way. Within ten days all of them died, so that no one could remain alive who had seen his holy and righteous body.”

## Observation of Philippe Labbé

At the end of the manuscript of the distinguished Parisian senator Claude Hardy, a man of great learning, which we have used until now, the following is written [Col. 0639B]:

“From blessed Peter until now there have been 444 years and 6 months, excluding the intervals of vacant episcopates. The end.”

From this it is most clearly shown that Anastasius the Librarian did not write all the Lives of the Roman pontiffs who flourished from the age of Pope Damasus to his own time, but assembled from various sources here and there the whole collection that appears under his name.

[Note: [Col. 0639B]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

We infer the cause of the long vacancy of the Roman see before Benedict’s election or ordination from the much shorter interval between his death and the election of Pelagius. “He was ordained,” says the Librarian, “without the command of the prince, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome.”

Ever since the Gothic kings had oppressed Italy’s liberty, greater sacrifices had been offered to public peace. To avert schisms, the clergy tolerated the Roman pontiff elected by them not being placed on the apostolic throne without consulting the prince. This tolerance was displayed to the emperors and to their exarchs sent to govern Italy, as the City was alternately rescued from Gothic servitude.

Since, therefore, at the death of John III disturbances and suspicions had already arisen everywhere, while Narses was beginning that disastrous web through the summoning of the Lombards that he had threatened, the election of his successor as pontiff was prolonged in that state of affairs, with storms threatening Italy and the Empire from every side. Numerous messages and replies were sent back and forth to the royal court of the Eastern Empire, which, after the Goths had been expelled, exercised unrestricted rule over the City.

But at Benedict’s death, when the Lombards surrounded and besieged the City so closely that there was power neither to send messengers to Caesar nor even to bring provisions into Rome, Pelagius was given authority over the apostolic see after a period of two months [Col. 0639D]. Nevertheless, three months and ten days are recorded as having elapsed before the election was publicly announced—a delay that could reasonably have seemed long enough to allow the expected opportunity to send a messenger east, if any hope of return and receiving a response had appeared.

Accordingly, after these one hundred days had elapsed from Benedict’s death, the election of the deacon Pelagius as Roman pontiff was celebrated on 17 November. The new ruler of the Church was subsequently initiated into the priesthood and received episcopal ordination on Sunday, 27 November.

He is said to have held office for ten years, two months, and ten days, both in the catalogues and in the copies of Anastasius. But it is clear that one year has dropped out of the epoch of Pelagius’s years and that it should read: “He held office for eleven years, two months, and ten days.”

This is made clear by his letter read at the synod celebrated at Grado on 3 November 579: “In the reign of the most serene Tiberius Constantine Augustus, in the fifth year of his reign, and in the same consulship, on 3 November, the thirteenth indiction,” a letter that had been dated 18 February of the same year.

For, if this is compared with the chronology and letters of Gregory the Great, who was the immediate successor of this Pelagius II and was ordained after a vacancy of almost seven months, on 3 September 590—as everyone agrees—it becomes clear that the beginning of Pelagius’s pontificate must be placed at the end of November 578. From there to his death on 7 February 590, there are eleven full years, two months, and ten days.

Regarding that Synod of Grado and the letter of Pelagius read there, with the chronological indications given, see above all Cardinal Noris in his dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, chapter 9, section 3. In this field he has outshone all chronologists, just as elsewhere he often and successfully did in demonstrating the most difficult and nearly hopeless boundaries and courses of time.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

[Col. 0640B] Line 3.—And much devastation was caused by them in Italy. Since the Eastern Empire was distracted by the Persian war, its rulers were slower to send assistance to Italy against the Lombards. The strength that the schism of those who refused to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Synod gained from the Lombard dominion, which had been extended, is sufficiently clear from Cardinal Noris’s dissertation cited above under Benedict and from the notes of Pagius and Sommier on this Pelagius.

Nevertheless, Pelagius persevered tirelessly in his pastoral care to bring back the sheep who had been led astray, even publishing a substantial treatise that blessed Gregory, his successor, praises while sending it to the bishops of Hibernia in Letter 36, indiction 10.

Indeed, the longer letter sent to the bishops of Istria is also said to be Gregory’s work: Paul Warnefrid, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 20, asserts that it was written in Pelagius’s name by blessed Gregory, who at that time was his deacon.

Gregory also adds that Pelagius, having experienced the obstinacy of the schismatics, resorted to other remedies—namely, to the authority of the exarch Smaragdus, so that he might restrain the obstinate and compel them to obey the apostolic see.

“As Pelagius was looking after ecclesiastical peace and the dignity of the holy Fifth Council,” says Noris, page 104 of his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, “he even employed force through Smaragdus, mindful of the sentence that his predecessor Pelagius had long before pronounced against those same Aquileian schismatics:

‘You must either be drawn from those same apostolic sees to salvation by whatever means may be necessary, or, so that they may not become the ruin of others, you may be restrained according to the canons by secular authorities.’

Thus one stirred up Narses against the schismatics, and the other Smaragdus.

Pelagius showed himself so thoroughly the defender of the Fifth Synod that in his third letter to the Istrians he condemned the Three Chapters, and in the same letter he also rejected Origen as a heretic together with the Fifth Synod; indeed, he declared him to have been the worst of all heresiarchs, thundering with apostolic voice:

‘For what is worse than Origen the heresiarch?’

After reciting the great praises bestowed on Origen, he concludes:

‘Nor did the favor of another’s testimony excuse him from his own guilt.’”

See in the same Noris the matters he carefully examines on this occasion: first, the fatherly clemency of the apostolic see in hearing the petitions of Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who requested that his metropolitan see be transferred to Grado. Pelagius granted this graciously at the beginning of his pontificate, hoping that by conferring benefits on him, although he was the leader of the schismatics, he might make him more respectful toward the apostolic see. Noris also discusses the repeated acts of fatherly charity performed toward the obstinate, on page 101.

He likewise treats with the greatest precision the title of the Aquileian patriarchate, which began to be used on this occasion, during the schism, in that metropolitan church. He presents the opinions of Baronius, Sirmond, and other distinguished authors concerning the origin of that primacy, which he handles with great learning, as is his custom, in chapter 10.

Line 7.—He built the cemetery of the blessed martyr Hermes. He built a basilica above the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence [Col. 0641A]. Pelagius continued the restoration of the sacred cemeteries begun by John III, as we showed in the notes to his Life.

The cemetery of Saint Hermes on the Salarian Way, within the first milestone from the City, is celebrated in the writings of ancient, medieval, and modern authors. It is mentioned in the ancient Martyrologies in the prolegomena (vol. CXXVII, cols. 123–124), where Basilla is also mentioned, and in the description of the City under Charlemagne, likewise given in the prolegomena (col. 365 of the same volume):

“On the Pincian Way outside the city, of Protus and Hyacinthus, on the right of Saint . . . . . and Saint Hermes.”

From medieval writings I have produced the history of Malmesbury, dating from around the end of the eleventh century, in a short work inserted in the same prolegomena (cols. 315–316 of the same volume):

“The fourth gate, and the Salarian Way, which is now called that of Saint Sylvester. There, beside the road, Saint Hermes rests, as do holy Basilla, Protus, and Hyacinthus,” etc.

Among more recent writers, besides Baronius in his *Martyrology* and *Annals*, Aringhius and Boldetti should be consulted, since they present the plan of this cemetery [Col. 0641B] and the inscriptions found there. See also what we have published about that cemetery in the notes to Saint Alexander.

Regarding the basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the walls, first built by Constantine above the venerable body of the saint and the cemetery of Cyriaca, and later restored from its foundations by this Pelagius, see Ciampini, both in Book I of *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, chapter 6, and in volume II of *Ancient Monuments of the Roman Church*, chapter 13.

He shows that it was restored from its foundations by Pelagius II, preserving the ancient plan and the east-facing orientation of the front, which were later changed by Pope Hadrian I and by Honorius III toward the west and the city walls in a new construction undertaken and repaired by them.

Ciampini also presents an image of the mosaic work added by Pelagius during his restoration above the triumphal arch of the presbytery, where it can still be seen, together with his likeness and name.

Through the generosity of the most eminent Prince Alexander Albani—whose bronze plates of the work in Ciampini’s museum, purchased from his heirs at a price, are preserved today—we obtained permission to have the same image, which Ciampini had ordered to be engraved so that it could be inserted among his mosaics, reproduced here [Col. 0641C].

We have inserted it so that this third volume of our edition [Note: [Col. 0641] “Our second volume comprises volumes three and four of the Vatican edition.” EDIT. PATROL.]—which began with Sylvester and indicated his image and the epoch of his pontificate, painted in the patriarchal basilica of Saint Paul during the age of Leo the Great, together with those of several successors—may also display at the end of the work the image and inscription of Pelagius II, likewise dedicated and preserved in our own age in the surviving mosaic of the patriarchal basilica of Saint Lawrence outside the walls.

The series is successfully brought down to this pontiff, so that the frontispiece of the fourth and final volume, which will follow this one, may be opened by Gregory the Great. His own name and the epoch of the beginning of his pontificate will also adorn this third volume, which we have completed.

At the end of the entry for Pelagius II, the Anastasius manuscripts present this statement:

“From the death of Saint Sylvester until this first Gregory there were 246 years.”

Papebrochius, in his *Historical Chronological Essay on the Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 88, no. 3, writes:

“Baronius, who had lost two years by introducing the successors of Vigilius into the apostolic see too early, and who saw that this Pelagius had certainly lived until the year 590, added those years to his pontificate, despite all the Anastasian manuscripts, including our own.”

Before Papebrochius, Noris had seen that serious errors had occurred in the chronology of the age of Pelagius II and Gregory the Great, both in Baronius and in Riccioli—and in the latter by a full four years [Col. 0642B], page 93—errors requiring medical treatment, which he himself, of course, applied.

Papebrochius then proceeds to observe that in the Palatine catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, and in the appendix added first to the Petavian manuscript, then to that of Queen Christina, and finally to the Vatican Alexandrian manuscript published by Schelestratius in volume I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, the following clause is read after Pelagius II:

“From blessed Peter until now there have been 444 years, 1 month, and 60 days, excluding the interval of the vacant episcopate.”

I think, however, that this clause belonged to Felix IV, at whom the catalogue ends, rather than to the appendix. Papebrochius correctly establishes that its numbers cannot possibly be reconciled with the interval from the martyrdom of blessed Peter to Pelagius II. They agree very closely, once the periods of vacancy of the see are deducted from the total interval, if they are referred instead to the time of Felix IV.

Finally, Papebrochius turns to another clause appended to Pelagius in all the Anastasian manuscripts, which we have reproduced here:

[Col. 0642C]

“From the death of Saint Sylvester until this Gregory there were 246 years. For this,” he says, “is most certainly true, since Sylvester died at the end of the year 335, and Gregory was ordained after more than half of the year 590 had passed.”

With such distinguished witnesses to the chronology and to the ancient documents of this volume, we shall place here, as a seal, the mosaic constructed by Pelagius II and preserved to our own age in the Laurentian basilica, so that the deeds of the pontiffs recorded during this interval may be consistently illuminated by contemporary monuments belonging to the same period, extending from Saint Sylvester to Saint Gregory the Great.

[Col. 0643] [Note: [Col. 0645A]]

Line 1.—He held office for ten years, etc. After Pope Benedict’s death, the see was vacant not for three months and ten days, as is read in Anastasius, but for four months; this can easily be demonstrated.

Since it is certain that Pelagius II, Benedict’s successor, died on 8 February 590 after having held office for more than eleven years, two months, and ten days, his ordination must necessarily be assigned to 30 November 578 according to our opinion, or to the year 579 according to those who maintain that he held office for only ten years.

But the latter cannot be said. For at the Synod of Grado, of which we shall speak shortly, celebrated in the same year 579 on 3 November, a letter of Pelagius II dated 18 February was read. It follows that his ordination took place on 30 November 578, and consequently, even according to Anastasius, the vacancy of the see after Benedict’s death lasted four months, since Anastasius himself states that Benedict died on 30 July and Pelagius on 8 February.

Pelagius II, therefore, a Roman by nationality and son of Winigildus, was ordained Roman pontiff on 30 November, the feast of the holy apostle Andrew, in the year 578.

He was ordained without the command of the prince, says the same Anastasius, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome and were causing great devastation throughout Italy. Thus it sometimes happened that, when necessity pressed, Roman pontiffs were consecrated without waiting for the emperor’s or exarch’s consent.

[Note: [Col. 0646A]]

Line 2.—“Because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome and were causing great devastation throughout Italy, etc.” The evils that followed from the Lombard domination throughout Italy in the case of the Aquileian schism are not enumerated here by the Librarian by name; only the general statement is made that much devastation was caused by them.

They are carefully investigated and arranged in narrative order by the eminent Cardinal Noris in his celebrated dissertation on the Fifth Ecumenical Synod. From there they were gathered by later writers, and by our authors of notes, Pagius and Sommier.

“It would be equally useful to consult one or the other of these, since from the same Norisian source they present us with a condensed summary of the sequence of events. The learned archbishop Sommier begins Book VI of his *History of Dogma*, chapter 39, with the concession made by Pelagius to transfer the metropolitan see of Aquileia from the city of Aquileia to the town of [Col. 0646B] Grado.”

The clergy of Aquileia, who had abandoned that city when the Lombards were bringing forces against it, had withdrawn to the town of Grado; and Elias, the archbishop, asked Pope Pelagius to transfer the metropolitan see there. Pelagius, in order to soften his attitude and attract him, together with his followers, to restoration to the unity of the Church through acceptance of the Fifth General Council, graciously granted this request.

Eighteen suffragan bishops of Aquileia held a council in the new metropolitan see. There the bull of Pope Pelagius was read, declaring that the fortress of Grado was established by him as the metropolitan see of all Venetia and Istria, and so forth. See Pagi’s notes, from the second note to the ninth.

[Col. 0637]

**112. Pelagius**, a Roman by nationality and the son of Vinigildus, held the see for ten years,

[Note: [Col. 0637] B, 12, two months, ten days [Note: [Col. 0637] B, 27].]

He was ordained without the emperor’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome and great devastation was being inflicted by them throughout Italy. At the same time there were such heavy rains that everyone said, “For the waters of the Flood are inundating us” [Note: [Col. 0637] *inundaverunt*, “inundated us”], and there was such a calamity as no one remembered having occurred since the beginning of the world. At the same time he covered the body of the blessed Apostle Peter with gilded silver panels. He made his own house a hospice for the poor [Note: [Col. 0637] “a hospice for poor old men”], and for the aged. He built a cemetery for the blessed martyr Hermes. Above the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence he built a basilica from its foundations and adorned his tomb with silver panels. He died and was buried at the blessed Apostle Peter on the seventh day of February [Note: [Col. 0637] C, the Ides of February]. He held two ordinations in the month of December: twenty-eight priests [Note: [Col. 0637] C, 82], seven deacons [Note: [Col. 0637] C, 8], and forty-eight bishops for various places. The episcopal see remained vacant for six months and twenty-five days. From the death of Saint Sylvester to this first Gregory there were 246 years.
