[Note: [Col. 0647C]

**Line 14.**—“At the same time he dedicated the Church of the Goths, which was in the Subura, in the name of the blessed martyr Agatha.” The antiquarians disagree about the precise location of the Subura. Martinelli recounts their opinions in a booklet published at Rome in 1638, in which he describes and illustrates the deaconry of Saint Agatha in the Subura. After setting these opinions before the reader, he proposes, as though divining the answer in an obscure matter, the view that before the enlargement of the city’s *pomerium* the Subura comprised the plain extending beneath the Palatine Hill toward the Amphitheatre of Titus; that, after the city had been enlarged, it was extended toward the Forum of Nerva, and from there ran through the valley situated between the Viminal and the Quirinal and Esquiline Hills. Marlianus supposes that the temple of Silvanus stood in this valley; and Fabritius reports that the temple of Silvanus was converted into a church dedicated to Saint Agatha, in these words: “The temple of Silvanus, now that of Saint Agatha, below the Viminal, on the Suburan Way.”

[Col. 0647D] The Goths had occupied this church, dedicated to the blessed Agatha, while Ricimer held the patriciate; and Ricimer himself had enlarged it with many ornaments, especially a marble apse, on whose gable he ordered the following inscription to be set in mosaic:

**FL. RICIMER V. I. MAGISTER UTRIUSQUE MILITIAE PATRICIUS ET EXCONSUL ORD. PRO VOTO SUO ADORNAVIT.**

“Flavius Ricimer, illustrious man, commander of both services, patrician and former consul in the regular order, adorned it in fulfillment of his vow.”

Caesar Baronius read this before the apse itself, weakened by age, collapsed in an unforeseen ruin. It is better to hear the account from Cardinal Baronius himself, under the year of Christ 472:

“This was that sacrilegious Arian, Ricimer, who, having usurped such authority over the Roman Empire, claimed for himself, by barbarian authority, a church in the City, despite the unwillingness of the very pontiffs of the Roman Church, so that he and his Arian Gothic soldiers might assemble there. It was the church of Saint Agatha, situated at the foot of the Quirinal Hill [Col. 0648C] opposite the Viminal. Although small, it was nevertheless adorned by that Arian himself in the Catholic manner; for he splendidly ennobled its apse with marble revetment and sacred mosaic images of the Savior and the twelve Apostles. The work remained until our own time, when, weakened by excessive age, the apse itself collapsed in an unforeseen ruin five years ago and was utterly destroyed.”

In the year of Christ 591, however, the blessed Gregory consecrated the church, which had been defiled by Arian superstition, according to the Catholic rite. Baronius narrates the event in these words:

“In this same year Pope Gregory dedicated the church of Saint Agatha situated at Rome, which the Arian Goths had usurped for themselves. Although, after they had been completely expelled and defeated and driven from the City and Italy, it had been left vacant, nevertheless, because it seemed to have been polluted by Arian leaven and was therefore regarded no longer as sacred but as accursed, Gregory, divinely inspired, resolved to purify it by sacred rites, make it fit for divine worship, and dedicate it to God. That this was done in this year is sufficiently clear from what he himself writes in the *Dialogues*, composed in the fourth year of his pontificate, when he says that it had happened two years earlier—that is, in this very year. What then occurred, worthy of admiration, he himself narrates in *Dialogue* III, chapter 30:

“‘Nor will I pass over in silence what the heavenly mercy also showed in this City two years earlier, for the condemnation of that same Arian heresy. From the events I recount, the people learned one thing, while the priest and the custodians of the church testify that they heard and saw another. The church of the Arians in that district of the City called the Subura had remained closed until two years earlier. It was decided that it should be dedicated in the Catholic faith, after the relics of the blessed martyrs Stephen and Martha had been brought into it, and this was done. For when we came with a great multitude of people, singing praises to the Almighty Lord, and entered that same church, while the solemnities of the Mass were already being celebrated and the crowd of people was pressing together because of the narrowness of the place, some of those standing outside the sanctuary suddenly felt a pig running back and forth between their feet. Each person felt it and pointed it out to those standing beside him. The pig then made for the doors of the church and filled all those through whom it passed with astonishment, but it could not be seen by anyone, although it could be felt. Divine mercy showed this so that it might be clear to all that an unclean inhabitant was leaving that place.

“‘When the celebration of the Mass was completed, we departed. But that same night a great noise arose in the roof of the church, as though someone were wandering about and running through it. On the following night the sound grew more severe, and suddenly resounded with such terror as though the entire church had been overturned from its foundations. Then it withdrew, and no further disturbance by the ancient enemy appeared there; but by the terrifying sound that he made, it became known that he had been forced to leave the place he had long occupied.

“‘A few days later, in perfectly clear weather, a cloud descended from heaven upon the altar of that church and covered it with its veil. It filled the whole church with such terror and such sweetness of fragrance that, although the doors stood open, no one dared enter. The priest, the custodian, and those who had come to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass saw the event but could not enter; they inhaled the sweetness of the wondrous fragrance. On another day, while lamps hung there without light, they were kindled by a light sent from heaven. A few days later again, after the solemnities of the Mass had been completed and the lamps extinguished, the custodian left the church. Shortly afterward he entered and found the lamps, which he had left extinguished, burning. Thinking that he had extinguished them carelessly, he now put them out carefully and, leaving, locked the church. But after three hours he returned and found the lamps he had extinguished lit again, so that the light itself plainly revealed that this place had passed from darkness into light.’”

Baronius reports these matters partly from himself and partly from the blessed Gregory. Yet in this account two things seem to have been written with less accuracy. First, he says that the Arian Ricimer adorned the church of Saint Agatha in Catholic fashion, embellishing its apse with sacred mosaic images of the Savior and the Apostles. Second, he says that the blessed Pope Gregory brought into the same church the relics of Saint Stephen and Saint Martha. If he had paid closer attention to what Pope Hadrian wrote to Charlemagne in a letter addressed to him, containing these words, he would not have allowed these matters to escape him:

“‘As for the church of the Arians, which Saint Gregory himself mentions in the *Dialogues*, Saint Gregory decided that it should be dedicated in the Catholic faith after the relics of the blessed martyrs Sebastian and Agatha had been brought into it; and this was done. The blessed Gregory himself also had it painted in various ways, both in mosaic and in colors, and erected venerable images there, which have been venerated from that time until now.’”

This testimony clearly shows that the sacred images of the Savior and the Apostles, added in mosaic to that apse and seen by Baronius before the apse collapsed, had been installed by the holy pontiff, not by an Arian, and not in those times when the use of images in churches was still uncommon. It also makes plain that the relics brought by the blessed Gregory into that church were those of Saints Sebastian and Agatha, as the better manuscripts of the *Dialogues* read, and not those of Saints Stephen and Martha, which Baronius copied from some corrupt exemplar.]

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

**Line 2.**—“Here he expounded forty homilies on the Gospels.” It was customary from ancient times for homilies of this kind to be read in churches. Accordingly, among the gifts presented to churches, we shall later read that under Stephen IV there was presented a book of eleven homilies. Sometimes a book of sermons is likewise said to have been presented—a book in which the sermons of the Fathers were customarily written out and then read before the congregation during the solemnities of Mass, as an explanation of the Gospel. The *Homiliary* is mentioned among the Fathers of the Council of Tours of the year 813, canon 17; of Mainz, in 847, canon 2; and frequently in other sources. The blessed Augustine demanded particular diligence in copying such works, in Letter 77:

“Order that each of the sermons you wish be written out separately, corrected, and sent to us.”

Compare also Beletus, chapter 59, and Durandus, Book VI of the *Rationale*, chapter 1, no. 32.

**Line 3.**—“And the *Pastoral Rule*.” Agnellus, in Book II of the *Pontifical History*, part II, p. 129, volume II of *Italian Historical Writers*, where he describes the life of Mariniani, bishop of Ravenna, mentions the reason for which the pontiff published the *Pastoral Book*:

“Consecrated at Rome by the most blessed Gregory, he was sent by him; and when he wished to escape from this see, saying that he could not, as pontiff, bear the weight of so great an honor, the most blessed Pope Gregory began to console him with words of encouragement, saying: ‘For your sake alone I shall make a little book. Keep it daily in your hands; always look into it; observe the words of that book, and you will be secure from every fear.’”

And he wrote and sent him the *Pastoral Book*. In the commonly printed edition, however, the *Pastoral Book* is dedicated by Saint Gregory to John of Ravenna, Mariniani’s predecessor. On this matter see Bacchinius’s notes in the same place.

**Line 4.**—“At the same time.” Anastasius copied these words, as was his custom, from Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 8:

“At this time also Romanus, patrician and exarch of Ravenna, hastened to Rome. When he was returning to Ravenna, he recovered the cities held by the Lombards, whose names are these: Sutrium, Polimartium, Horta, Tuder, Ameria, Perugia, Luceoli, and certain other cities. When this had been reported to King Agilulf, he immediately left Pavia with a strong army, made for the city of Perugia, and there for several days besieged Maurisio, the Lombard commander who had gone over to the Roman side. Having captured him without delay, he put him to death. At the arrival of this king, the blessed Pope Gregory was so terrified that he ceased expounding the temple described in Ezekiel, as he himself also relates in his homilies.”

**Line 7.**—“At the same time.” What Anastasius relates here about the apostolic mission established in England, Paul recounts in chapter 26 in these words:

“At this time the same blessed Gregory sent Augustine and Mellitus, and John with several other monks who feared God, to Britain; and through their preaching he converted the English to Christ.”

There are two matters that our author explains. Yet, when he transcribes these fragments word for word from Paul the Deacon into the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, he nowhere observes the order of events, and by stitching together deeds gathered here and there with little discrimination, he has cast more than Cimmerian darkness over the chronology. But more on this later.]

[Note: [Col. 0650D]

**Line 1.**—Gregory became pope in the year of the Lord 590, after the see had been vacant for six months and twenty-six days. Saint Gregory, whose grandfather was Pope Felix, the third of that name—not the fourth, as John the Deacon holds—had Gordianus as his father and a mother named Silvia, who was enrolled among the saints. He writes in Homily 38 that Tarsilla and Aemiliana, virgins dedicated to God, were his father’s sisters. He was educated in excellent morals and good letters; nevertheless, he remained ignorant of the Greek language. He himself declares that he was also a lawyer, in Letter 54 of Book II. The outstanding deeds of this pontiff may be seen year by year throughout his pontificate in volume V of the Councils.]

[Note: [Col. 0651A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

What the distinguished bishop of Verona, Francesco Bianchini, complained of in the notes on Pelagius II—Bianchini, whose role as the greatest champion and most vigorous defender of the Apostolic See is attested by this very edition of Anastasius, which he left incomplete because he was overtaken by death—what, I say, he complained of was that peace had supposedly been purchased by great sacrifices: namely, that Roman pontiffs elected by clergy and people should not be ordained until an order or confirmation had been sent by the emperors of the East. This consideration appeared highly opportune to Gregory, who strongly resisted receiving the papal insignia, as a reason for rejecting so great a dignity (John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 40 and following).

After Pelagius had died, while the bubonic plague was raging with great violence at Rome in the year 590, Gregory was immediately elected by the unanimous vote of the people. He had returned from Constantinople only a few years earlier and, grieving and lamenting, wrote to Maurice, whose favor he had secured while serving as *apocrisiarius* at the imperial court, begging him not to confirm his election. But it was difficult for Gregory to kick against the goad: the letters were intercepted by Germanus, prefect of the City, and did not dare resist the will of the divine Spirit. Nevertheless, these letters, however they were intercepted, are powerful evidence of the authority usurped by Odoacer and, as it were, transmitted by hand to the emperors, so that in those extremely difficult times the vicars of Christ appeared subject to the commands of princes.

Hence arose the long intervals between pontificates, until the same authority was transferred to the exarch of Ravenna in the time of John IV, while messengers were sent back and forth. Only when Italy was being more shamefully torn apart was the election of a pontiff hurried forward, as we saw in the case of Pelagius, Gregory’s predecessor, whom Anastasius regards as an extraordinary case because he was ordained without the emperor’s command.

Through intervals between pontificates of similarly long duration, compounded for the most part by the carelessness of copyists, there arose an excessive disturbance in the chronology of the succeeding pontiffs down to Saint Martin. This drew learned men into differing opinions. Among them, Sigonius, Panvinius, Baronius, Papebrochius, and Pagius very rarely agree; and since few or no monuments remained that could attest the facts, they were free either to shorten or to lengthen the periods of the pontificates and their intervals. For that reason I think I shall perform a worthwhile service if, using the *Book of the Pontiffs* as my guide, I restore, as far as I can, the chronology of the pontiffs, which has been ruined. With this as a kind of preface, I begin the notes.

While the letters confirming Gregory’s election were arriving from Constantinople, Although there was no place for an elected man in the administration of the Church, Gregory, as the disease grew, instituted the sevenfold litany; see Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book I, and Father Mabillon, *Roman Order*. At last, after six months and twenty-eight days, he was consecrated, though unwillingly, in the same year in which Pelagius died, 590, on September 3, as the more recent scholars consistently and correctly hold, especially Father Mabillon and Cardinal Noris. Bianchini is accustomed to swear by Noris’s words, and if I have learned anything about ancient matters and customs, I owe it to him.

This is supported by the Sunday Letter A, which in that year coincides with the stated day, and by the date of death, March 12, 604. These dates, as pivots, encompass the entire period of Gregory’s see: thirteen years, six months, and ten days. For the same number of years, months, and days is assigned to Gregory in all the manuscripts of Anastasius and in most catalogues. The final days, however, are not excluded, as Anastasius sometimes does.

Counting backward from the day of ordination to the death of Pelagius, there is a certain interval between pontificates—not, as in the commonly printed texts, six months and twenty-five days, but six months and twenty-eight days. This is not inconsistent with Bianchini’s view, which defined the interval as nearly seven months, although death prevented him from fully investigating the matter. For, fixing Pelagius’s date of death as February 7 and Gregory’s ordination as September 3, and thereby separating the two pontiffs by an interval of nearly seven months, he followed not the commonly printed text of Anastasius but the Royal, Mazarin, and first Thou manuscripts, which have six months and twenty-eight days. The third Ambrosian manuscript, in volume III of the *Italian Writers*, agrees with them. In fact, when the endpoints are included, exactly that amount of time is counted between February 7 and September 3.

It seems worth noting that one perceptible change of style among the many observable in the Anastasian manuscript, begun under some of Gregory’s predecessors, continues through several of his successors. From Vigilius through Honorius, the period of the pontificates and the intervals between them is consistently counted in the curial manner; afterward the Kalends, Nones, and Ides are restored. Moreover, as the very learned Ciampinus says in his *Examination of the Book of the Pontiffs*, Book III:

“From the deeds of Vigilius, the successor of Pope Silverius, down to Martin, exclusively, the style underwent some change; for it scarcely departs from the evangelical style, which is plain and open, without any embellishment or choice of words.”

Whether this occurred because of the disastrous conditions of Italy, when silence was imposed upon letters, or for some other reason, it has left many deeds of those pontiffs in the realm of conjecture. The situation is different with Gregory, whose chronology required little labor to establish. Among his other works there survive twelve books of letters, which provide their own indictions. Although some of them are found removed from their proper places, no more valuable monument for establishing the dates of his pontificate can be conceived.

For this reason, apart from Paul the Deacon, who incorrectly states that Gregory died while Phocas was reigning in the eighth indiction, in the second year of his reign—using VIII in place of VII—no difficulty arises either among ancient or modern martyrologists and scholars. Accordingly, when I, together with others, determine the day of his death as March 12, 624, I shall not delay in providing further support for the matter. For a fuller chronological examination of Gregory’s entire life, see Cardinal Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 8, section 4 and following.]

[Note: [Col. 0652C]

**Line 1.**—“Gregory.” Saint Gregory the Great, doctor of the Church, son of Gordianus the senator and Silvia, a most holy matron, a Roman of the most noble and ancient family of the Anicii, a monk, archdeacon and *apocrisiarius* of the Holy Roman Church, apostle of the English, under the emperors Tiberius Anicius, Constantine Maurice, and Flavius Phocas Augustus, held the see for thirteen years, six months, and eight days.

As the plague raged more fiercely in Rome from day to day, the City was being drained by continual funerals. Observing this, Gregory summoned the people to an assembly on the fourth day before the Kalends of September in the basilica of Saint Sabina on the Aventine. Filled with the divine Spirit, he said that those scourges were being inflicted because of the people’s sins and that God must be entreated with tears, prayer, and repentance for their former life, so that he might restrain his fury and anger.

Accordingly, on Wednesday, at first light, he ordered the clergy to go out from the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian with the priests of the sixth region; all the abbots with their monks from the church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, with the priests of the fourth region; all the abbesses with their communities from the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, with the priests of the first region; all the boys and girls from the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul, with the priests of the second region; all laymen from the church of the holy martyr Stephen, with the priests of the seventh region; all widowed women from the church of Saint Euphemia, with the priests of the fifth region; and all married women from the church of the holy martyr Clement, with the priests of the third region.

Coming out in this manner from each church and assembling at the church of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin, mother of Jesus Christ our Lord, they were to implore the Lord there with long weeping and groaning and beg forgiveness for their sins. Thus the practice handed down by him still remains: after the entrance of the Mass, the Church should implore the mercy of the Lord and of Christ nine times, through *Kyrie eleison* and *Christe eleison*.

Meanwhile the plague raged so violently from day to day that many, when they sneezed, and others, when they yawned, suddenly gave up their spirit. When this happened repeatedly, the custom was introduced—which is still observed today—of praying for those who sneezed by wishing them health, and of seeking protection for those who yawned by making the sign of the cross over their mouths.

Moved by these events, Gregory, in addition to the other remedies for heavenly anger, instituted the following year, 593, a solemn supplication on the day of the Resurrection. In a ceremonial procession he carried forth an image of the holy Virgin, Mother of God. According to tradition, this image had already been painted from life by the hand of the evangelist Luke and was being preserved with exceptional popular devotion in the church of the blessed Virgin at the Crib, situated on the Esquiline.

It happened that wherever the image was carried, the dreadful plague yielded to the weight of heaven and the desired health followed. While everyone was giving thanks to God for this, an angel was heard from heaven addressing the holy Virgin in these words:

“Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia,  
For he whom you were worthy to bear, alleluia,  
Has risen as he said, alleluia.”

When Gregory received this hymn in his ears, immediately, moved by the divine Spirit, he completed it in this manner:

“Pray for us to God, alleluia.”

From that time the antiphon remained in the Church as a solemn Easter expression of joy. Not long afterward, an angel was seen standing above the Mausoleum of Hadrian, sheathing a drawn sword.

**Line 11.**—“And dispose our days in your peace.” He ordered these words to be added to the Canon because Agilulf, king of the Lombards, when the City was without a garrison, brought his camp up to its walls and struck the whole city with immense terror. Gregory consequently ceased expounding the prophet Ezekiel, on whom he was preparing commentaries.

**Line 16.**—“Buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter.” In the outer portico before the basilica of Saint Peter, near the sacristy, which is now called Saint Mary of Fever. Leo, Simplicius, Gelasius, Symmachus, and several other Roman pontiffs were also buried there, as John the Deacon relates in Book IV of his *Life*. Later Gregory IV transferred Gregory’s body inside the basilica and placed it beneath the altar of the Apostle Andrew. The following epitaph was placed on his earlier tomb:

Receive, O earth, this body taken from your body,  
Which you may restore through God who gives life.  
The spirit seeks the stars; no laws of death will harm one  
For whom that death is rather a road to another life.  

The members of the supreme pontiff are enclosed in this tomb,  
He who always lived everywhere by countless good works.  
He overcame hunger with food and cold with clothing,  
And by sacred admonitions shielded souls from the enemy.  

He fulfilled in deed whatever he taught in speech,  
So that, speaking mystical words, he might be an example.  
With piety as your guide, you turn the English to Christ,  
Gaining new ranks for the faith from a new people.  

This was your labor, this your study, this your care, this the shepherding  
By which you offered abundant gains to the Lord from the flock.  
Made God’s consul by these things, rejoice in your triumphs,  
For now, without end, you possess the reward of your works.

Peter the Deacon, who was one of Gregory’s intimates, once affirmed under oath that he had often seen a dove sitting beside the ears of the pontiff while he was working by lamplight.

Throughout his life Gregory suffered from many illnesses. He was frequently tormented by stomach pains and suffered from gout and disorders of the kidneys. In addition to the matters mentioned above, this most holy pontiff established many practices in the Church: the blessing of branches and candles, which are blessed on Palm Sunday and on the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary; the blessing of ashes and their imposition on people’s heads on the first day of Lent; and the washing of feet mutually in imitation of Christ. He also established that antiphons should be sung, which are commonly called Introit chants. He instituted the Stations; arranged and approved the ecclesiastical office; introduced Roman chant and the college of singers; and did many other things that display the wisdom and charity of this most holy and vigilant shepherd.

[Col. 0654A] Yet all his deeds seem surpassed by what God deigned to accomplish through him in liberating the soul of the emperor Trajan, who had already been condemned to the fires of Tartarus for five hundred years, and in rescuing it through the prayers of the glorious pontiff and placing it among those to be saved. Apart from the testimony of the most authoritative writers who attest this and the common opinion of those who affirm the same thing, I have dispelled all objections and proved its truth in a special booklet published on this subject.

They relate that at the time when the martyr Hermenegild was crowned with martyrdom by his father Leovigild under Gregory, the tunic of Jesus Christ, which had fallen by lot to one of the soldiers, was found near the city of Zaphat, deposited there in a marble chest, during the episcopates of Thomas of Jerusalem, John of Constantinople, and Gregory of Antioch.

In the year of Christ 597, the seventh of Gregory’s pontificate, that deceiver Muhammad, the false prophet and ruin of the world, was born in Arabia.]

[Note: [Col. 0654B]

**Line 1.**—“A Roman by nationality, the son of Gordianus.” Gregory was born to Gordianus, a man of senatorial rank, and Silvia, a woman distinguished for her piety. His great-grandfather was Pope Felix—either the third, as Cardinal Baronius holds in his annotation on the *Roman Martyrology* under February 25 and in the *Annals* under the year 582, or the fourth, as we read in John the Deacon. Fathers of Saint-Maur support the latter reading with plausible arguments.

Besides our Anastasius, the life of Saint Gregory was written in Latin by Paul the Deacon, whose work the learned Mabillon published from manuscript codices under Gregory’s name, in the first volume of the *Saeculum*, p. 385; by John the Deacon, who, at the command of John VIII, composed Gregory’s life in four books; and finally by the most learned Fathers of Saint-Maur, who compiled Gregory’s life chiefly from his own writings; it appears in volume IV of Saint Gregory’s works. Gregory of Tours, Bede, and Ado, bishop of Vienne, also wrote certain things from his deeds. Saint Gregory is also mentioned by Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, of whom something will be said shortly below in the fifth note; and by Isidore, Ildefonsus, Sigebertus, Trithemius, and all the cataloguers of ecclesiastical writers.

**Line 2.**—“Here he expounded forty homilies on the Gospels.” Sigebertus writes of these:

“He wrote forty-two homilies on the Gospel to Marianus or Marinianus, bishop.”

But according to Anastasius we possess only forty, and he sent copies of them not to Marianus but to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina. Accordingly John the Deacon agrees with Anastasius, writing in Book IV, chapter 74, of the Gospel homilies:

“Moving through the Stations”—he is speaking of Gregory—“he publicly delivered twenty homilies on the Gospel at various times; he dictated the remaining twenty, but because his stomach was failing and he was continually weak, he allowed others to recite them.”

**Line 3.**—“Thirty-five books on Job.” Saint Gregory undertook this work chiefly at the urging of Saint Leander of Seville [Col. 0654D], with whom he had formed a friendship at Constantinople, when Leander was Pelagius’s *apocrisiarius* to Tiberius, while he himself was requesting assistance from Tiberius on behalf of Hermenegild. These commentaries on Job—properly called a storehouse of the whole moral teaching of the Gospel—were held in such esteem that, while Gregory was still alive, bishops began to have them read both at their tables and publicly at vigils. When the most modest pontiff learned of this, he prohibited the practice, sending them more urgent letters to that effect, which may be seen in the register of his letters.]

### The Same. On Ezekiel, Book XXII

He divided the Homilies on Ezekiel into two books. In the first, he explained the first three chapters of Ezekiel and part of the fourth in twelve homilies; in the second, he explained the fortieth chapter, concerning the vision of the temple to be built in Jerusalem, in ten homilies. Casimir Oudinus, in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, censures Saint Gregory because, while explaining the prophet Ezekiel, he made a great leap from the fourth chapter to the fortieth [Col. 0655A]. How unjustly he wrote this can be understood from Venerable Bede and John the Deacon, who report the reason why Saint Gregory explained only certain parts of Ezekiel’s prophecy. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book II, chapter 1, says:

> “He also expounded, in twenty-two homilies, the first and last parts of Ezekiel’s prophecy, which appeared to be more obscure, and demonstrated how much light they contain within.”

John the Deacon, however, Book IV, chapter 76, writes:

> “He also treated the first and last parts of Ezekiel’s prophecy, which appeared to be more obscure, at the request of the Romans.”

If, then, the Roman people asked Gregory to shed light, through his exceptional learning, only upon the more obscure passages, and if the supreme pope proposed only this to himself, Casimir wrongfully attacks Gregory for leaving the intermediate chapters untouched.

### The Same. On the Fourth Book of the *Dialogues*

The four books, arranged in the form of a dialogue between Gregory and Peter his deacon, contain the miracles of the Italian Fathers. That these are genuine works of Saint Gregory the Great, and not of Saint Gregory II, as some have thought, is demonstrated clearly—not only by the testimony of manuscripts but also by Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 1. There, while relating the Life of Saint Benedict the abbot, he says that he is writing about Benedict what he had learned from four of that saint’s disciples, two of whom had already died, while the other two were still alive. This can certainly not apply to Gregory II, unless we say that those surviving monks lived for approximately two hundred years.

Moreover, Saint Paterius, the secondarius and disciple of Gregory the Great, who composed an exposition of the Old and New Testaments from the sayings of the holy teacher, extracted far more material from the books of the *Dialogues*. Casimir Oudinus, however, treats the books of the *Dialogues*—a work especially useful for fostering piety—as of little value, as though they were teeming with old women’s tales.

Against Casimir’s injurious censures, the whole ancient scholarly tradition stands in opposition, to say nothing of the more recent age, which in every century has always held Saint Gregory’s learning and piety in this work in equal esteem. Since at this point I am adding only very brief notes to Anastasius’s text, it will be more useful to oppose Casimir with the judgment of Photius, whose acuity and diligence no one fails to recognize.

Photius therefore left the following statement in his *Bibliotheca*, codex 252:

> “The admirable Gregory composed many other books in Latin that were beneficial to souls and to the Roman people, and he delivered homilies in which he expounded the Gospels. Moreover, he composed in four dialogues the Lives of men who were distinguished in Italy, interweaving narratives that instructed in salvation. For one hundred and sixty-five years, those who did not understand the Latin language alone were deprived of the benefit arising from his labors. But Zacharias, who became successor to that apostolic man at a later time, translated into the Greek language the knowledge and benefit confined within the Latin language and generously made the gain common to the whole world. He undertook to translate into Greek not only the works called the *Dialogues*, but also other worthy labors of Gregory.”

Thus far Photius concerning Gregory’s works; his testimony must certainly be held in the highest regard in this matter. For either Photius wrote this before the solemn schism, as I myself believe—for Photius composed this work before he occupied the see of Constantinople, while he was serving as ambassador for Basil in Assyria, as he himself testifies in his letter to Tarasius, which is read in the Greek edition at the end of the work, p. 892, and is placed earlier, more correctly, in other editions—or he wrote it afterward.

If he wrote it before the schism, then this otherwise learned man, speaking so accurately about the books he had read, expresses an independent judgment, and Gregory ought rightly to be preferred to Casimir and all his followers. But if he wrote it afterward, then we must say that the reading of the *Dialogues* is certainly most salutary, since a man hostile to the Roman see nevertheless had to approve it with the highest praise. Let the reader consult what I shall write about Saint Zacharias in note 2.

### The Same. And the *Pastoral*

When Saint Gregory had for some time avoided the supreme dignity of the pontificate by hiding in a cave, and had been reproved by John, bishop of Ravenna, he wrote this *Pastoral*, explaining the gravity of the pastor’s office—a work that all who care for souls ought certainly to read continually. For this reason many synods commended the reading of the *Pastoral Care* to bishops, so that each might contemplate himself daily as in a kind of mirror.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, testifies in the preface to his little work 55 that in his day it was customary for this book, together with the book of the sacred canons, to be placed by the metropolitan in the hands of the bishop being ordained during the ordination itself. The bishop was solemnly adjured to conduct himself in living, teaching, and judging as it was written there, and he promised that he would do so.

### Line 4. And many other good works that we cannot enumerate

These include the *Book of the Sacraments*, the *Antiphonary*, the *Commentary on the First Book of Kings*, the *Exposition of the Song of Songs* and of the seven penitential psalms, and also the *Register of Letters*. These works may be consulted in the edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great by the Fathers of Saint-Maur.

### Line 10. He enlarged the prayer of the Canon

John the Deacon speaks of this addition in Book II of his Life of Gregory, chapter 17:

> “He also abridged the Gelasian Book concerning the solemnities of the Mass into a single volume, removing many things, changing a few, and adding some others for the exposition of the Gospel readings. In the Canon he inserted: ‘Order our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect.’”

### Line 13. He caused Masses to be celebrated over the body

I believe the meaning of the words “he caused Masses to be celebrated over the body of blessed Peter and blessed Paul the apostle” is either that Saint Gregory restored the ancient practice of celebrating the divine mysteries over the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul in their basilicas. Perhaps this practice had ceased while he was pope because sacred rites could not be celebrated in buildings that had deteriorated through age. For in the *Register of Letters* he orders Sabinianus, the subdeacon responsible for the Church’s affairs in Lucania and Bruttium, to arrange for beams from those provinces to be brought to Rome for the restoration of the apostles’ basilicas. See Book XII, letters 20, 21, 22, and 23.

Or perhaps Gregory confirmed by decree what had already been preserved by the customs and practice of the Roman Church: namely, that the sacrifice of the Mass should be offered over the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Saint Jerome, who preceded Saint Gregory by approximately two centuries, contrasted this Roman practice with Vigilantius, who had dared to abolish the veneration of the holy martyrs. “The Roman bishop therefore acts wrongly,” says the holy teacher in his book against Vigilantius, “who offers sacrifices to the Lord over the dead bodies of Peter and Paul—bones venerable according to us, but, according to you, worthless dust—and regards their tombs as the altars of Christ.”

Indeed, it had long before been decreed by Saint Felix, pope—whose ordination the illustrious and equally learned prelate Blanchinus fixed on 3 January in the year of Christ 269—that sacrifices should be celebrated over the tombs of any martyrs. Anastasius writes in his Life of Felix:

> “He established that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs.”

Hence the Acts of the Martyrs often show that altars were erected not only over the tombs of martyrs but also in the places where they exchanged mortal life for immortal life; these accounts may be consulted in the work of the most learned Ruinart.

The practice of celebrating the divine mysteries over the memorials of martyrs—or at least not without their relics beneath the altar—was therefore so ancient and solemn in the Roman Church that from it there spread to the other churches the custom of building no church and no altar without such relics.

It is sufficient to cite Saint Ambrose as an entirely adequate witness. In Letter 52 to his sister Marcella, he indicates that the dedication of churches with the relics of martyrs was a practice proper to the Roman Church. Speaking of himself, he writes:

> “When I wished to dedicate a basilica, they began, as though with one voice, to urge me, saying: ‘As in Rome, so dedicate the basilica.’ I replied: ‘I will do so if I find relics of martyrs.’”

He then found the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius and dedicated the basilica according to the Roman rite.

Whoever wishes to learn more about this subject should read the writers on liturgical matters, especially Cardinal Bona, Book I, chapter 19.

### Note: [Col. 0657B]

### Line 2. He expounded the homilies

Gregory composed forty homilies on the Gospels. Some of them, dictated by him, he ordered to be read by a notary to the assembled people; others he delivered himself. After correcting them, he sent them to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium. In their preface he writes:

> “During the solemn celebrations of Mass, I expounded forty readings from the holy Gospel, drawn from those that are customarily read on appointed days in this Church. The exposition of some of them, having been dictated, was read by a notary to the assembled people; but I myself spoke the explanation of others before the people, and it was recorded just as I spoke it.”

In the year 592 Gregory completed all forty of these sermons. The thirty-eighth is known to have been delivered in the basilica of Saint Clement in that same year, since, when recounting events that had then taken place, he reckons there two years from the time when the plague that had struck the City began. Since the plague raged in Rome in 590, this thirty-eighth homily was certainly delivered in 592.

### Line 3. On Ezekiel

The year 595 was disastrous for the whole of Italy. Agilulf, king of the Lombards, not only recaptured in a fit of fury the cities that had been taken from him by the Roman exarch of Ravenna, but also devastated the Roman territory with the greatest destruction, as is clear from Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 7.

Nevertheless, at this very time Pope Gregory, at the insistence of the people, interpreted in public the exceedingly difficult prophecies of Ezekiel. It may well seem astonishing that he could engage in such reflection amid so great a crisis in the City, and that the people, placed in the same danger, could demand such sermons from him.

Saint Gregory, however, was scarcely then torn away by force from what he had begun, once he had seen with his own eyes the City surrounded and the wounds, imprisonment, and slaughter of its citizens. These homilies on the prophet Ezekiel, recorded by notaries while he delivered them before the people, were afterward corrected by the same pontiff and sent to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

### The Same. Book XXXV of Job

Saint Gregory conceived the *Moralia on Job*, of which we have not yet spoken, at the request of Saint Leander and of the religious men with whom he lived at Constantinople while serving as apocrisarius of the apostolic see before the emperor Tiberius. He dedicated the completed work to that same Leander, bishop of Hispalis.

This work is a storehouse of evangelical moral teaching, and preachers, those who care for souls, and spiritual directors ought to read it carefully and continually.

### The Same. Book IV of the *Dialogues*

During this period the same most holy pontiff, worn out by labors and anxieties, withdrew for a short time into solitude. Having gathered accounts of the remarkable deeds of the holiest men of Italy—especially those who had lived in his own age—either because he himself knew them well or because he had received them from men of the highest reliability, he devoted the greatest care to these matters and presented them in the form of a dialogue. He used as his interlocutor Peter the deacon, a man who had been closely bound to him in friendship from childhood and whom he had taken with him into solitude.

He explains all this at greater length in the opening of the work. It is certain, from Gregory’s repeated testimony in the same work, that these four books of the *Dialogues* were completed in the year 593, the fourth year of his pontificate. While discussing the plague that afflicted Rome in the year in which he himself was made pope, he says in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapters 16 and 36, and elsewhere, that it had occurred three years earlier.

These books of the *Dialogues* were later translated from Latin into Greek by Pope Zacharias, as Anastasius relates in his Life of Zacharias and Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, codex 252. The same books were translated into Saxon by Alfred, king of the West Saxons, but this translation has perished.

Some authors, not only heterodox but also Catholic, have denied that the books of the *Dialogues* belong to Saint Gregory the Great, attributing the work instead to Gregory II, who was therefore called *Dialogus* by the Greeks.

They are refuted, however, by Saint Gregory the Great’s Letter 1 of Book II, in the eleventh indiction, addressed to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, and by the beginning of Book II of the *Dialogues*. There, when he is about to write the Life of Saint Benedict, he says that he received what he is going to relate about him from four disciples of that same saint, two of whom were still alive. Gregory II, who was 150 years younger, could certainly not have said this.

There are also the testimonies of authors who lived after Saint Gregory and who, in complete agreement, attributed the *Dialogues* to him. These include Saint Paterius, his disciple, in the *Book of Testimonies* collected from all the works of Saint Gregory; Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, who flourished in the year 630, in his *Collection* from the works of Saint Gregory, divided into five books; Saint Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, in Book I of his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 1; Julian, bishop of the same Church, in his *Prognostic of the Future Age*; Bede, Book II of his *History*, chapter 1; Paul the Deacon and John the Deacon in their Lives of Saint Gregory; and many others cited by Natalis Alexander, century VI, chapter 3, article 16, where he also answers all the objections of the opponents.

Gregory II was therefore wrongly called *Dialogus* by certain Greeks. The name clearly belongs properly to Saint Gregory the Great because of the publication of the books of the *Dialogues*.

Before his withdrawal, Gregory, while caring for the universal Church, sent many letters to different people concerning various matters. In Letter 39 of Book II, addressed to Peter the subdeacon of Campania, he wished a girl held in servitude, who desired to embrace the monastic life, to be redeemed with the Church’s money so that she could fulfill her vow.

In Letter 9 of Book III, addressed to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, he decreed against the Jews that their female or male slaves, if they fled to a church, should not be returned to them. In Letter 37 of Book II, addressed to Libertinus, prefect of Sicily, he ordered that Christian slaves purchased by a Jew named Nasas be restored to freedom, and that Nasas himself be punished because, in pursuit of profit, he had erected an altar in the name of the prophet Elijah and invited Christians to worship there.

When Gregory learned that certain idolaters and worshipers of angels—this was a Jewish heresy—were still to be found in a particular corner of Sicily, he admonished the local bishop, Eutychius, to labor vigorously for their conversion. He did so in Letter 60 of Book II, addressed to that bishop.

Finally, a letter of the year 593, Letter 64 of Book II addressed to the patrician Narses and issued in August of the eleventh indiction, indicates that Gregory was so occupied and oppressed by tribulations that, as he himself says, he had no opportunity either to read or to say much in letters, and that he had forgotten to eat his bread because of the sound of his groaning.

These circumstances seem to have caused him to seek retirement. All those letters were issued before September, except Letter 9 of Book III, which was issued in September, when the fourth year of his pontificate began and when he testifies that he wrote the books of the *Dialogues* in retreat.

I therefore infer that Gregory withdrew into solitude and began writing the books of the *Dialogues* around the end of September of that same year, 593. No letters appear in his *Register* for the months of October, November, or December—not because he wrote none during that retirement, but, as may be conjectured, because he wrote very few, and those did not survive.

In the same *Register*, before the month of May in the year 594, only three of his letters remain: two issued in January and one in April. This leads me to suspect that his retirement was not so brief as Baronius believes.

### Line 3. And the *Pastoral*

Meanwhile, not only did the remnants of the plague continue to afflict Rome, but the City was also shaken by the violence of the winds, attacked by the incursions of the Lombards, and oppressed by dreadful famine. The more Gregory saw these evils increase, the more vigorously he rose against them through courage of spirit.

At the very beginning of his pontificate he composed his outstanding commentary on the *Pastoral Care*, taking the occasion from a letter of the bishop of Ravenna, by which he had been reproved for wishing to flee pastoral responsibility by hiding himself.

That *Pastoral* of Saint Gregory was held in such esteem in Gaul that many councils of Gaul ordered bishops to read it, to follow its admonitions, and to carry out its precepts—for example, the Council of Tours, canon 3; the Second Council of Chalon, canon 4, held in 813; and the Council of Aachen, canon 4, held in 836.

Indeed, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, testifies in the preface to his little work 55 that in his time it had become customary for the *Pastoral* of Saint Gregory the Great, together with the book of the sacred canons, to be handed by the metropolitan to the bishop being ordained during the ordination itself. The bishop was adjured to conduct himself in living, teaching, and judging as it was written there, and the bishop himself promised that he would do so.

In this book Gregory teaches how great the burden of pastoral office is, how reluctantly it should be undertaken, and with what care it must be carried out. He divided the book into four parts.

In the first he explains what sort of person should come to the summit of the episcopate. In the second he teaches how a pastor ought to conduct himself in the exercise of government. In the third he explains how a pastor ought to teach. Finally, in the fourth he teaches that a pastor who fulfills his holy office should return to himself, and should not dwell upon the right things he has done but upon those he has neglected to do.

He concludes the book as follows:

> “Behold, good man: compelled by the necessity of my rebuke, while I strive to show what a pastor ought to be, I, an ugly painter, have painted a beautiful man, and I direct others toward the shore of perfection while I myself am still tossed about in the waves of sins. But, I beg you, in the shipwreck of this life let the plank of your prayer sustain me, so that, because my own burden weighs me down, the hand of your merit may raise me up.”

Thus was the holy pontiff greatest in humility.

That book of Saint Gregory was translated into Greek by Anastasius of Antioch not long afterward, but the translation has perished. Alfred—also called Aelfrid or Aluerd—king of the West Saxons, likewise translated it into Saxon in the ninth century.

### The Same. And many other good works

We still have to discuss the works wrongly attributed to Saint Gregory.

First, the *Exposition of the Seven Penitential Psalms* is not the work of Saint Gregory, nor of any author contemporary with him. From the manner in which royal and imperial authority is discussed in it, it appears that the commentary was published while Gregory VII was pope and Henry IV was emperor. What the author reproaches the emperor for—namely, that he had torn the Church apart through schism and disturbed the peace of the Church through simony—can be attributed more appropriately to him than to Maurice or Phocas.

Nevertheless, some believe that this exposition of the seven penitential psalms should be attributed to Gregory VII, as Peter Gussanvilla noted in the latest edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great.

### [Col. 0660A]

The *Commentary on the Books of Kings* also appears to be falsely attributed to Saint Gregory. It was unknown to Paterius, the notary of the Roman Church and disciple of Saint Gregory, and to all the ancients who either collected testimonies from Saint Gregory’s works, mentioned them, or were accustomed to cite their testimony.

Furthermore, the author of this commentary uses the commonly received version of Sacred Scripture, whereas Saint Gregory used the Itala and the version of Jerome. He also cites many passages in a manner unlike Saint Gregory, as the editor of his works, already mentioned, demonstrates in the preface to Volume III.

Moreover, the style differs from Gregory’s. Finally, Saint Gregory did preach sermons to the people on the Books of Kings, but because of his weakness he could not commit them to writing. They were recorded by a certain Abbot Claudius, but not according to the mind of the holy teacher, as Gregory himself complains in Letter 22 of Book X.

### Line 8. He sent the servants of God Mellitus and Augustine

In the discussion of Pope Eleutherius, we stated from Anastasius and from Bede, Book I, chapter 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, that the Gospel had once been publicly received by the Britons under their king Lucius.

But when, in the middle of the fifth century, the Britons had been expelled from the island by the Angles and Saxons, the island returned once more to the worship of idols. Gregory, who, as we said above, had considered the conversion of the Angles before his pontificate, undertook the mission in the year 596. He sent Augustine, whom he had appointed head of the monastery of Saint Andrew in Rome, to England with companions, and commended them in numerous letters to the kings of the Franks and to various bishops of Gaul.

These letters survive in Book V of Gregory’s *Register*, from Letter 52 through Letter 59.

In the year 597 Augustine was ordained bishop by Virgilius, bishop of Arles. He then returned to Britain and baptized Ethelbert, king of Kent. On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, in the first indiction, beginning on the Kalends of September in the year 597, more than ten thousand Angles were baptized, as Gregory writes in Letter 30 of Book VII, addressed to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, and issued in the following June.

After Augustine later reported to Saint Gregory that the harvest in England was indeed great but that the laborers were few, the same pontiff sent “many fellow workers and ministers of the word, among whom the first and chief were Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinianus.” Through them he also sent everything generally necessary for divine worship and the service of the Church: sacred vessels, altar cloths, ornaments for churches, priestly and clerical vestments, relics of the holy apostles and martyrs, and many books, as Bede writes in the cited chapter 29.

Bede also reports there the letter written by Gregory to Augustine, then bishop of Canterbury, issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth indiction, in the year 601 then current. In it Gregory says that he is sending Augustine the pallium and grants him its use only for the celebration of Mass; he also indicates how Augustine ought to establish bishops in Britain.

In the decretal letter sent by Saint Gregory to Augustine, who had consulted him on several matters—a letter also found in the cited chapter 27 of Bede and numbered 31 in Book XII of Gregory’s *Register*—there is mention of an apostolic vicariate granted to Augustine, not indeed in explicit words but by implication. This is inferred from Gregory’s seventh response to Augustine’s question, in which Augustine had asked how he should conduct himself with the bishops of Gaul and Britain.

Gregory replied:

> “We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul, because from ancient times, from the days of my predecessors, the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we certainly ought not to deprive him of the authority he has received.”

The dignity of vicar of the apostolic see was therefore joined to the pallium, and Gregory did not wish to take it away from the bishop of Arles.

That privilege, moreover, was personal and not perpetual, as is clearly inferred from the letter of Gregory to Augustine cited above. It is also certain that the archbishops of Canterbury were not made vicars of the Roman pontiff until long after this period, so that the bishop of that Church came to be called the born legate of the apostolic see.

Thus writes Baluzius in the supplement to Book V of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 42, no. 9, following what Marca says in Book VI, chapter 7, no. 3. Marca states that in the age of Saint Gregory it became customary for the Roman pontiff to adorn with the pallium metropolitan bishops to whom he entrusted his authority in the provinces—for example, the archbishop of Thessalonica, the metropolitan of First Justiniana or Bulgaria, and, in Gaul, the bishop of Arles.

There is not, however, a single settled opinion concerning the use of the pallium in the period with which we are concerned, as may be seen in Garnerius’s appendix to the notes on chapter 4 of the book *On the Roman Order*.

It is enough to observe here that Gregory subjected the bishops of Britain to Augustine of Canterbury in these words, which are read at the end of the seventh response:

> “We entrust all the bishops of Britain to your fraternity.”

### Line 10. He enlarged the prayer of the Canon

Gregory revised the ancient Gelasian Missal, or book concerning the Mass. For John the Deacon, in the Life of Gregory recited by Mabillon in the first century of the Benedictine history, writes in Book II, chapter 2:

> “He also abridged the Gelasian book concerning the solemnities of the Mass into a single volume, removing many things, changing a few, and adding certain others for the exposition of the Gospel readings.”

We have stated under Gelasius that both the Missals of Gelasius and of Gregory were still extant in the abbey of Centula, or Saint-Riquier, in the year 831.

From the *Pontifical Book* and from Bede, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1, it appears that Gregory added these words to the Canon of the Mass:

> “Order our days in your peace, and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect.”

John the Deacon likewise records this in Gregory’s Life.

In the Mass, another prayer for the dead follows, beginning, “To us also, sinners.” In this portion several saints are named who were not mentioned in the earlier part of the Canon. They were selected from different orders: among the deacons, Stephen; among the apostles, Matthias; among the disciples, Barnabas; among the bishops, Ignatius; among the supreme pontiffs, Alexander; among the priests, Marcellinus; among the clerics of the minor orders, Peter; and among married women, Felicity and Perpetua.

Since no virgins had yet been included, Gregory added Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, and Anastasia to this part of the Canon, as Aldhelm, bishop, writes in his book *On Virginity*, chapter 25.

### Note: [Col. 0661C]

### Line 8. He sent the servants of God Mellitus and Augustine, etc.

We stated in the discussion of Eleutherius that formerly Lucius, king of the Britons, had requested from that pontiff preachers of the Gospel and had obtained their dispatch. Through their efforts the faith of Christ was proclaimed in those regions and the Church was founded there.

Afterward, however, the Anglo-Saxons brought idolatry once more into that part of the island which they had taken from the ancient Britons. Saint Gregory, concerned for their conversion before he was made pope, had resolved to undertake that burden himself and preach the faith to them.

Since he was unable at that time to carry out his plan, he later returned to it after becoming head of the Church. He selected for this purpose the monk Augustine, whom he had appointed over his monastery of Saint Andrew, and sent him there with other companions of the mission.

He gave them several letters of recommendation to the kings of France, Theuderic and Theudebert, and to their grandmother Brunhild, as well as to various bishops of Gaul. He asked these persons to protect and assist the evangelical laborers in the hardships they were about to undergo.

God granted his blessing to them, as Gregory himself testifies in Book VII, Letter 30, addressed to the patriarch of Alexandria:

> “While the nation of the Angles, situated in a remote corner of the world, still remained in the unbelief of worshiping wood and stone, it pleased me, with the help of your prayers, that, by God’s authority, I should send to it in preaching a monk from my monastery. With the permission I gave him, he was made a bishop by the bishops of Germany, and, with their assistance, he was brought to the aforesaid nation at the end of the world. We have now received letters concerning its salvation and his work. Indeed, such miracles shine forth in that nation through him and through those who were sent with him that they seem to imitate the power of the apostles in the signs they display. On the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, which has just passed in this first indiction, more than ten thousand Angles were reported by that brother and our fellow bishop to have been baptized.”

For this reason the holy pontiff urged Augustine by letter to preserve humility and fear of God in his heart amid the joy and exultation produced by so great an accomplishment.

He also wrote to the king of that nation, asking him to listen to and support those who proclaimed the kingdom of Christ to his subjects and peoples.

He likewise sent a letter to the queen, comparing her with Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, because both Christian women had prepared the hearts of the nations they governed to receive evangelical truth. See Book IX, Letters 58, 59, and 60.

To draw those peoples more easily to the faith of Christ, Gregory also wrote to the other preachers of the Gospel whom he had ordered to assist Augustine. His instructions were as follows:

> “After long reflection with myself on the matter of the Angles, I considered that the shrines of idols in that nation should by no means be destroyed, but that the idols themselves should be destroyed within them. Let blessed water be made and sprinkled in those shrines; let altars be built and relics placed there. For if those shrines have been well constructed, it is necessary that they be changed from the worship of demons to the service of the true God, so that when the people see that their shrines have not been destroyed, they may remove error from their hearts and, recognizing and worshiping the true God, may gather more familiarly in the places to which they are accustomed.

> “And because they are accustomed to slaughter many oxen in sacrifice to demons, some solemnity should also be changed for them in this respect. On the day of the dedication or on the feast of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, let them make for themselves tents of branches around those same churches that have been converted from shrines, and let them celebrate the feast with religious banquets. Let them no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for food in praise of God and give thanks to the giver of all things for their nourishment. Thus, while some outward joys are reserved for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys.

> “For there is no doubt that it is impossible to cut off everything at once from minds that are hard. Whoever seeks to climb to a high place must necessarily be raised by steps or strides, not by leaps.”

(Book IX, Letter 71.)

Moreover, when granting Augustine the use of the sacred pallium, Gregory prescribed for him what foundations he should lay to establish that new Church:

> “We wish you to ordain twelve bishops in separate places, subject to your authority, so that thereafter the bishop of London may always be consecrated by his own synod and may receive the pallium of honor from this holy and apostolic see, which by God’s authority I serve. For the city of York, we wish you to send a bishop whom you yourself judge should be ordained, so that if that city and its neighboring places receive the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan dignity. Yet we wish him to remain subject to the arrangement of your fraternity.

> “After your death, he should preside over the bishops whom he has ordained in such a way that he is in no respect subject to the authority of the bishop of London. Henceforth there should be this distinction of honor between the bishops of the cities of London and York: the one who was ordained first should be regarded as senior.”

(Book XII, Letter 15.)

Augustine also asked the pontiff about certain matters of discipline and conduct. The pontiff replied to each question individually:

> **1.** “It is the custom of the apostolic see,” he says, “to give this instruction to bishops who have been ordained: of all the income that comes in, four portions are to be made. One is for the bishop and his household, for hospitality and reception; another for the clergy; the third for the poor; and the fourth for the repair of churches.”

(Book XII, Letter 31.)

Since Augustine had been accustomed to monastic discipline, Gregory therefore warned him not to live apart from the clergy, but to organize the new Church of England according to the model by which the early Church was established, in which no one possessed anything as private property but everything was held in common.

Regarding the remaining matters, he replied:

> **2.** Separate portions were to be given to clerics who were not promoted to sacred orders and who wished to marry. As for living in common, he said that those living together had no resources available for the hospitality they were to practice and for the almsgiving they were to perform except whatever surplus they had to distribute in pious works, since the Lord says: “What remains, give as alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.”

> **3.** Concerning ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies, he granted Augustine authority to gather customs from other Churches that he judged to be especially good, and likewise to compile a *Ritual* for the Churches of the Angles.

4. Concerning the punishment of those who bring harm upon the Church, one must imitate a householder:

> “For, as he says, we ought to maintain discipline among the faithful in the same way that good fathers customarily do among their carnal children: they strike them with blows on account of their faults, and yet they seek to have as heirs those whom they afflict with pain, preserving for those whom they appear to pursue in anger whatever they possess.” (The same work.)

5, 6, 7. He explains that two full brothers may each marry one of two sisters; nevertheless, he prohibits marriages between the daughters—or the sons—of two brothers or of two sisters. If, however, people entered such an unlawful marriage during the time of unbelief, he orders them thereafter to abstain, but does not for that reason exclude them from communion. By contrast, he commands that those who contract similar marriages after conversion be excommunicated.

8. Concerning the ordination of bishops, he forbids it from taking place without assistants, whom he says must be summoned from Gaul:

> “Indeed, in the Church of the English, in which you are still found to be the only bishop, you cannot ordain a bishop otherwise than with bishops. For when bishops come from Gaul, let them stand with you as witnesses at the ordination of a bishop … When, therefore, by God’s authority, bishops have likewise been ordained in places near one another, the ordination of bishops must in every respect not be carried out without three or four bishops assembled together.” (The same work.)

[Col. 0664A] 10. He teaches that pregnant women, as well as women who are giving birth or have given birth, together with their offspring—especially when there is danger of death—ought to be baptized. Under the New Law no fixed period is prescribed for women, so that, if they have given birth, they should be excluded. Men, however, ought not to approach sexual intercourse with them until their children have been weaned; in this matter he gave advice, not a command. And below:

> “But a wicked custom has arisen in the conduct of married people, namely, that women disdain to nurse the children whom they bear and hand them over to other women to be nursed. This seems evidently to have been devised solely because of incontinence: since they do not wish to practice self-restraint, they disdain to suckle those whom they bear.” (The same work.)

**Line 10.**—Here he increased the Canon in the prayer, etc. Before Gregory, Gelasius had taken care to arrange the divine office, and especially the Liturgy, in a better order. Saint Gregory revised the Gelasian Ritual, removing many things that he judged either to have been taken from apocryphal authors or to be disconnected and less suitable. After changing some things and adding others, he produced a single volume. John the Deacon says of it:

> “He abridged the Gelasian Book of the solemnities of the Mass into a single volume for the exposition of the Gospel readings, taking away much, changing a little, and adding certain things.” (Life of Saint Gregory, book II, chapter 17.)

This volume is called the Sacramentary, and in it the order of the Mass is arranged as follows: the Introit; the *Kyrie eleison*; the *Gloria in excelsis*, which bishops were accustomed to say on Sundays and feast days, while the other priests were not permitted to say it except on Easter Day; the Collect; the Apostle, or Epistle; the Gradual, or Alleluia; the Gospel; the Prayer over the Offerings; the Preface; the *Sanctus*; and the preparatory prayer before the consecration, which has fallen out of use.

Then comes the Canon, to which Saint Gregory added:

> “And dispose our days in your peace; and rescue us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among your chosen flock.”

In the prayer *Nobis quoque peccatoribus*, where mention is made of saints who have been selected according to various conditions, no virgin’s name had occurred. Blessed Gregory therefore inserted the names of the holy women Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, and Anastasia (Aldhelm, *On Virginity*, chapter 25).

After the *Agnus Dei* there are various prayers, both Collects and Secret prayers. There are various Prefaces for the different days of the year—Sundays, feast days, and weekdays. Finally, blessings for various matters and exorcisms are provided, which ought to precede the administration of baptism.

[Col. 0645]

**113. Gregory, Roman by nation, son of Gordianus, occupied the see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days**

[Note: [Col. 0645] B: nine days.] He expounded forty homilies on the Gospels; thirty-five books on Job [Note: [Col. 0645] * “on Job”]; twenty-two books on Ezekiel; four books of *Dialogues*; and the *Pastoral Rule*, together with many other good works that we cannot enumerate [Note: [Col. 0645] See Baronius, volume VIII, under the year 595].

At the same time the Roman patrician and exarch came to Rome, and, while returning to Ravenna, retained the cities that the Lombards held, namely Sutrium, Polimartium, Horta, Tuder, Ameria, Perugia, Luceoli, and many others. [Note: [Col. 0645] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 601, page 117.]

At the same time the most blessed Gregory sent the servants of God Mellitus, Augustine, and John, together with many other God-fearing monks, to preach [Note: [Col. 0645] * “to the people”] to the English, so that they might convert them to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Here he enlarged the prayer [Note: [Col. 0645] * “Preface”] of the Canon: “And dispose our days in your peace,” and so forth.

He made for the blessed Apostle Peter a canopy with its four columns, of pure silver. He arranged that Masses be celebrated over the bodies of the blessed Apostle Peter and the blessed Apostle Paul. At the same time he dedicated the church of the Goths, which was in the Subura, in the name of the blessed martyr Agatha.

He turned his own house into a monastery. He died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, before the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0645] * “Secretarium”], on 12 March.

He held two ordinations, one in Lent and the other in September: thirty-nine priests [Note: [Col. 0645] C: thirty-eight], five deacons, and sixty-two bishops in various places. The see then remained vacant for five months and eighteen days [Note: [Col. 0645] C: sixteen].

## LXVII. SABINIANUS. A.D. 604; IN THE SECOND YEAR OF THE EMPEROR PHOCAS
