[Note: [Col. 0665B]

**Line 3.**—He ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened and grain to be sold to the people at one solidus for thirty modii of wheat. Cardinal Baronius is less than fair toward Pope Sabinianus when, assigning his death to the year of Christ 605, he writes:

> “The written manuscripts suddenly bring forward a more terrible explanation of his death. Sigebert has summarized the tragedy of the whole affair in these words: ‘When Pope Sabinianus likewise detracted from the generosity of his predecessor Gregory, Gregory appeared to him three times in a vision and reproved him for his fault of stinginess and for this disparagement. When he did not repent, Gregory reproved him horribly a fourth time and, threatening him, struck him on the head. Afflicted by the pain, he died not long afterward.’”

Because of this, when he died—as Anastasius relates—his body was not carried through the middle of the city with funeral pomp to the basilica of Saint Peter, as was customary, but was cast out of the City through the gate of [Col. 0665C] Saint John and carried outside the walls as far as the Milvian Bridge; from there it was brought into the very church of Saint Peter, where it was committed to burial. For the Roman people had been angered against him because he had not distributed the Church’s wheat to the poor, as Gregory had been accustomed to do, but had put it up for sale at thirty solidi per modius.”

I do not know what documents Sigebert used in composing that little story, nor can I guess who those written manuscripts were in which Baronius read the same account, since he himself does not say. Sigebert was writing around the year 1101, almost five hundred years after Sabinianus’s death. His more hostile attitude toward the Roman pontiffs is sufficiently demonstrated by the part he took in the cause of Henry IV and Henry V against Gregory VII and his successors, Urban II and Paschal II.

For this reason Natalis Alexander, in chapter 1 of the seventh century of his *Ecclesiastical History*, after citing from Sigebert and Baronius the same material concerning Sabinianus, declares it apocryphal, since it rests upon no ancient testimony.

But what if it can easily be shown from Anastasius that Sabinianus was by no means ungenerous, since he opened the Church’s granaries and proved himself in no way unworthy of his predecessor Gregory, although Sigebert asserted that he had fallen far short of Gregory’s examples of generosity?

In the year 605 famine afflicted not only the City but all Italy, according to the testimony of Paul the Deacon:

> “That year,” he says, “the winter was exceedingly cold, the vines died in almost every place, and the crops, struck by blight, withered away everywhere.”

[Col. 0666B] Sabinianus ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened—clearly they had been closed—“and grain to be sold to the people for one solidus, thirty modii of wheat.” So Anastasius. I adhere to this reading, which I judge the more trustworthy and from which perhaps others departed under Sigebert’s influence.

The *modius* was a Roman measure, one-third of an amphora, holding two *congii* and two-thirds of a *congius*. I willingly accept the *congius* as the common measure: it was a well-known Roman vessel, and the Romans referred their other measures, both liquid and dry, to the *congius*. From it they called the gift distributed to the people through the generosity of the emperors a *congiarium*.

In the Farnesian palace there survives a *congius* that has escaped the ravages of time and the damage inflicted by ignorant men, wholly intact and elegant. It bears the names of a father and son of the Flavian family, together with the marks P. X, indicating ten pounds—namely, a weight of ten Roman pounds. It contains ten pounds of water, that is, 120 ounces, and seven and a half pounds of wheat, namely ninety ounces.

A *modius*, therefore, holds twenty-three pounds and four ounces of water, but twenty pounds of wheat. Sabinianus, having opened the Church’s granaries, therefore ordered six hundred pounds of wheat to be sold for one solidus.

The name *solidus* was adopted later by writers of the Latin language in monetary matters and began to be used only in the Constantinian age. The first writer known to me to use it was Lampridius, who substituted *solidus* for *aureus* in his *Life of Alexander Severus*.

A remarkable law is found in book X, title 76, concerning the price of silver brought into the treasury:

> “We order that, for the quantity of silver which anyone is about to bring into the treasury, he be given the right to bring in gold instead, so that for each pound of silver he may bring us five solidi.”

For each ounce of gold six solidi were counted, as the most eminent Cardinal Norisius, distinguished no less for learning and scholarship than for rank, clearly explains in his dissertation *On the Coinage of Licinianus Licinius*, volume II of the Verona edition, column 1150:

> “For, according to law 13, concerning receivers, issued by Valentinian the Elder in A.D. 367, and according to the rescript of Honorius mentioned above, issued in the year 395, seventy-two solidi made up a pound of gold. A solidus, however, was worth twenty-five denarii of Roman money, or, as they call them, julii, as the very learned J. Fridericus Gronovius teaches learnedly in book IV of *On Ancient Money*, chapter 25, and elsewhere frequently from Dio, book LV.”

By the law cited, five solidi were ordered to equal one pound of silver. Honorius—or perhaps he fixed the value of the solidus by establishing its weight—either defined it himself or caused Arcadius to issue the law in the name of both emperors. The law was promulgated at Constantinople under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.

This illuminates and explains a distinctive bronze coin of the third size preserved in the royal treasury at Paris. Its obverse shows the head of Honorius bound with a jeweled crown and bearing the inscription D. N. HONORIUS AUG.; its reverse shows a standing female figure holding scales in her right hand and a cornucopia in her left, with the letters EXAGIUM SOLIDI.

[Col. 0667B] *Exagium* means the same as an exact and just weight, or a form of precise weighing, as Cujacius says. A pound of silver, therefore, whose price is equivalent to five solidi, will be worth 125 julii; an ounce will be worth ten julii and five-twelfths. An ounce of gold, which six solidi comprise, will contain a value of 150 julii. At that time, namely, gold stood to silver as fourteen and two-fifths to one, approximately the same ratio as at present.

Returning, then, to the point from which we digressed: when Sabinianus ordered thirty modii of wheat to be sold for one solidus, he priced six hundred pounds of wheat at twenty-five julii. In a time of extreme grain scarcity this was an example of exceptional generosity, by which he provided timely assistance both for the needs of the churches and for the poverty of the poor. He ought therefore to have been greatly praised, not accused.

It can easily be inferred that this reading of Anastasius is preferable to the one used by Baronius. If the price established by Sabinianus for one modius of wheat had been thirty solidi, as Baronius reads, twenty pounds of wheat would have cost 750 julii. That would have been an enormous and intolerable price, and on that account the pontiff would not have ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened but closed, since the entire people would thereby have been deprived of the ability to buy wheat.

It also deserves notice that Baronius attributes to Anastasius the statement that, as the reason for carrying the dead pontiff’s body through the gate of Saint John outside the walls of the City to the church of Saint Peter, the people’s anger at the increased price of wheat is assigned. Anastasius does indeed relate that the funeral was carried outside through the gate of Saint John, but he neither notes that this was done contrary to custom nor supplies any reason for it, as is clear to anyone reading the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0667D]

**Line 2.**—“There was a famine.” These words too are taken from Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 30. After recounting Gregory’s death, he adds:

> “Sabinianus was ordained in his place to the office of the apostolate. At that time the winter was exceedingly cold, the vines died in almost every place, and the crops, partly destroyed by mice and partly struck by blight, withered away.”

The same account is found in Agnellus, in the passage cited immediately below, page 130.

**Line 3.**—“When peace had been made.” The following passage from Paul, in the same work, chapter 33, may shed light on this:

> “King Agilulf made peace with the patrician Smaragdus for one year, receiving twelve thousand solidi from the Romans. The cities of Tuscia, namely the King’s Bath and the Old City, were also invaded by the Lombards. At that time, in April and May, a star appeared in the sky, which they call a comet. Later King Agilulf again made peace with the Romans for three years.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668B]

**Line 1.**—“Sabinianus.” After the Apostolic See had been vacant for five months and nineteen days following the death of blessed Gregory, Sabinianus was elected on the Kalends of September in the year of Christ’s birth 604, not without tumult, as may be gathered from the decree of his successor Boniface. All Latins and Greeks alike confirm this. I therefore do not see on what authority Nicephorus Callistus writes that someone named Innocent was substituted for Saint Gregory.

**Line 2.**—“There was a severe famine in the city of Rome.” Concerning this famine Paul the Deacon says in book IV, chapter 9:

> “The winter was exceedingly cold, the vines died in almost every place, and the crops, struck by blight, withered away everywhere.”

During this famine, in detestation of avarice, the following miracle seems to have occurred. Under the pontificate of Sabinianus, Sigebert describes it in his *Chronicle* in these words:

> “At that time,” he says, “when a certain poor man asked sailors for alms and did not receive any, the shipmaster said: ‘Stop asking us for alms; we have nothing except stones.’ When the poor man replied, ‘Then let everything be turned into stones,’ everything edible that was on the ship was turned into stones, while retaining the same color and form as the objects had possessed.”

**Line 6.**—“When he had died.” Sigebert gives a more terrible account of the cause of the sudden death of Pope Sabinianus in the *Chronicle*, described in these words:

> “When Pope Sabinianus likewise detracted from the generosity of his predecessor Gregory, Gregory appeared to him three times in a vision and reproved him for his fault of stinginess and for this disparagement. When he did not repent, Gregory reproved him horribly a fourth time and, threatening him, struck him on the head. Afflicted by the pain, he died not long afterward.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668D]

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES**

That the Apostolic See was vacant after the death of Saint Gregory for no longer than five months and eighteen days is testified, besides the commonly printed manuscript of Anastasius, by four other manuscripts used by the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori: the Farnesian and Lucensian catalogues, the latter of which, through a copyist’s error, has twenty-three instead of eighteen days, an easy alteration of V into X.

This is reinforced by the authority of the Freherian manuscripts, the Royal, Mazarine, and both Thuanean copies. Although they count one day more, they include the day of death and do not disturb the chronology in the least.

Antonius Pagius attempted to criticize this unanimous authority of the catalogues and manuscripts, to which Ordericus also gives support, extending the interregnum to six months and one day. How successfully he did so will become clear from what follows.

I adhere to the agreement of the catalogues and manuscripts, as I see Papebrochius doing, and, counting from Saint Gregory’s death five months and eighteen days—or nineteen when the day of death is included—I find the letter D of the Sunday cycle marked before 30 August. I recognize without doubt that this is the very day of Sabinianus’s ordination.

Sabinianus, therefore, formerly Gregory’s representative at the imperial court of Constantinople, was ordained on 30 August in the year 604 and occupied the see for one year, five months, and eight or nine days, as all authorities consistently state.

But in the number of days there is an obvious error, arising either from double counting: the V, correctly used once for the months, being wrongly added again to the days, so that four became nine; or from the addition of a V. Whatever the origin of the error, Sabinianus’s two burials are mentioned in another Freherian manuscript.

When it first speaks of his burial at Saint Peter’s, it says that he was buried on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, namely 24 February. Then, speaking of the first burial, it says: “He was buried on the second day of February,” namely the second day, as one of the Ambrosian manuscripts expressly has.

The Roman numeral II must therefore be understood as the number two, not as an Arabic numeral, as is sufficiently demonstrated by the fact that copyists often did this. An example is found in the specimen of a very ancient parchment manuscript presented by the distinguished Muratori in *Italic Script*, where we read: “He made ordinations through the month of March: two priests, two deacons,” while the printed editions have: “He held one ordination through the month of March: two priests, two deacons.”

Baronius likewise interpreted II in this way, assigning Severinus, against the testimony of all the ancients, two months and eleven days.

Accordingly, according to this first burial in the Freherian manuscript—at the Lateran church—Sabinianus seems to have occupied the see not nine days beyond one year and five months, but four days. For from the day of his ordination, 30 August, to his burial on 2 February, counting the day of ordination in the customary manner, there are one year, five months, and four days.

This also casts considerable light upon the history of Anastasius. He relates that Sabinianus’s funeral was conducted in an entirely new manner, never heard of either before or afterward: it was carried outside the walls of the city through the gate of Saint John.

This account is certainly supported by some reason. Therefore, although I do not believe Sigebert’s old wives’ tale, which Sigonius and after him Baronius adopted, I nevertheless agree with Papebrochius that either bad weather, ice, or heavy rains prevented the pontiff’s body from being carried out immediately and by the customary route.

In any event, Sabinianus, having occupied the see from the day of his ordination, 30 August 604, for one year, five months, and four days, died on 2 February 606, as the manuscripts of Marquard Freher and one Ambrosian manuscript teach. His body, meanwhile deposited in the Lateran basilica, was carried to Saint Peter’s on the twenty-second—or, as other manuscripts have it, the twenty-fourth—of the same month.]

[Note: [Col. 0669D]

**Line 1.**—Sabinianus, son of Bonus, from Blera, a Tuscan, cardinal deacon and representative of the Apostolic See, was sent by Pope Saint Gregory to the emperor at Constantinople. Under the emperor Phocas Augustus he occupied the see for four months and nineteen days. He was created on the Kalends of September and consecrated on Sunday, the Ides of September.

**The same line.**—“From the city of Ulera.” Blera was a city of inland Tuscia according to Cato, Pliny, and Ptolemy; it is commonly called Bieda, and its remains are still found ten miles from Viterbo.

**Line 4.**—“For one solidus, thirty modii of wheat.” He certainly ordered grain to be distributed to the people, but not free of charge, as Gregory had done. Rather, he set the price at thirteen solidi for each modius.]

[Note: [Col. 0670A]

**Line 2.**—“There was a severe famine in the city of Rome.” During this period of scarcity, when the entire city was suffering from an immense shortage of grain, Sigebert of Gembloux relates in his *Chronicle*, under the year 607, that Sabinianus, detracting from the generosity of blessed Gregory by withholding food from the needy, was reproved by Gregory in a vision three times for his avarice. After a fourth and terrible rebuke, he was struck on the head and, afflicted by that pain, died shortly afterward.

Sigebert may perhaps have copied this account from the life of Saint Gregory written by Paul the Deacon, whose loss in his own time Baronius lamented. But that account is fabulous may be shown especially from the silence of John the Deacon. John certainly read Paul’s *Life*, as is evident from these words of John near the end:

> “His venerable merit, as long as the orbit of this world revolves, will always continue to increase, if I may confess the same with Paul, a most eloquent man.”

These very words also occur in the *Life of Gregory* written by Paul the Deacon. Yet John says not a word about Saint Gregory’s rebuke of Sabinianus, although, in many chapters near the end, when recounting Saint Gregory’s miracles, he describes numerous events of this kind. He ought surely to have included this example, which above all would have belonged to the praise of Saint Gregory, as no one can fail to see.

I am therefore easily led to believe that, in John the Deacon’s time, this story about Sabinianus’s rebuke was not present in Paul’s *Life*, and that it was subsequently sewn onto it by some idle person. Or, if it was present, John must certainly have judged it so contemptible, as resting on no reliable evidence, that he decided it should not be included in the fuller life of Saint Gregory prepared at the command of John VIII.

Sigebert, however, who adhered to the emperor Henry, persecutor and rebel against the Roman Church, and dared to write letters and pamphlets against Pope Saint Gregory VII, a man distinguished for the innocence of his conduct, inserted this little tale into his *Chronicle* as well, so that Sabinianus, the Roman pontiff, might be spoken of badly by later generations.

But this invention conflicts both with our Anastasius, who praises Sabinianus for increasing the clergy and the sacred lights in the basilica of Saint Peter, and with the reputation Sabinianus left behind among his own people, namely that of courtesy and benevolence. This is expressed in the Vatican epitaph, which Aringus quotes from Manlius in *Rome Subterranean*, book II, chapter 8:

> “Here he removed the faults of men with gentle speech;  
> He was not a judge against their sins, but their medicine.”

[Note: [Col. 0670C]

**Line 4.**—“For one solidus, thirty modii of wheat.” “Yet,” says Papebrochius in his *Chronological-Historical Essay*, “because certain copies of Anastasius seem to have stated that Sabinianus demanded thirty solidi for a modius of grain, someone invented the tale in which he is imagined to have been rebuked by his predecessor Saint Gregory, appearing at night, for his stinginess, struck on the head, and dying not long afterward.

“But no ancient writer who has described the life and miracles of Saint Gregory says anything of this—not even John the Deacon, who nevertheless filled the end of book IV with examples of this sort of vengeance, extending over twelve chapters.

“It is therefore astonishing,” Papebrochius continues, “that Baronius gave credence to this tale, rashly reported by Sigebert. Baronius also connects it with the fact that, after Sabinianus’s death, as Anastasius says, his funeral was carried out through the gate of Saint John and taken outside the walls of the city by the Milvian Bridge to the Vatican church. He thinks this was done contrary to custom in order to protect the body from harm feared from the angry people if the funeral were carried through the middle of the city, although many other causes for this novelty—and causes joined with some praise of Sabinianus—could be devised by a kindly conjecturer.”

**Line 6.**—“When he had died.” Nothing else concerning Sabinianus’s deeds has come down to us apart from what we have just reported from Anastasius, who adds that he occupied the see for one year, five months, and nine days, and was buried in the Church of the blessed Apostle Peter on the twenty-second day of February.

Therefore, since Regino in his *Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle*, Ordericus in book II, and Honorius of Autun likewise assign one year, five months, and nine days to the pontificate of Sabinianus, it follows from Anastasius himself that he was ordained on 13 September in the year 604 and died on 22 February in the year 606.]

**114. Sabinianus, Tuscan by nation, from the city of Ulera**

[Note: [Col. 0663] B: “Volaterra.”] son of Bonus, occupied the see for one year, five months, and nine days [Note: [Col. 0663] B: “five months, nineteen days”].

At the same time there was a severe famine in the city of Rome. After peace had been made with the Lombard people, he ordered the Church’s granaries to be opened and grain to be sold to the people for one solidus [Note: [Col. 0663] * “for thirteen solidi”; B: “thirty modii for one solidus”]—thirty modii of wheat.

In the church of the blessed Apostle Peter he provided lamps [Note: [Col. 0663] * “he added lamps”].

When he died, his body was cast out [Note: [Col. 0663] * “carried out”] through the gate of Saint John and taken outside the walls of the city by the Milvian Bridge. He was also buried in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter on the twenty-second day of February.

He filled the Church with clergy. He made twenty-six bishops in various places, and the see remained vacant for eleven months and twenty-six days.

This was the decree of Boniface III: the election of the Roman pontiff was not to take place until after the third day following the burial—that is, the interment—of the deceased. Canon *Nullus*, distinction 76; chapter *Bonae memoriae*, *On Elections*.]

[Note: [Col. 0673A]

**Line 2.**—“He obtained from Phocas.” Anastasius copied the same account from Paul Warnefrid, although he changed and inverted the words, whether by art or through ignorance. Paul writes there, chapter 37:

> “At the request of Pope Boniface, he decreed that the Roman and Apostolic Church should be the head of all the churches, because the Church of Constantinople was proclaiming itself the first of all the churches.”

**Line 5.**—“He issued a decree.” This proceeded from Boniface’s desire to restrain the ambition of future pontiffs in elections. The principal sees of the Church had become accustomed to having certain men as candidates, and these men sometimes struggled, not without the stain of schism, to be designated by the bishop while he was still alive.

In the Church of Antioch, when there was rivalry between Meletius and Paulinus over the episcopal rank, there were six candidates. For this reason Flavianus, a priest of that Church, at the command of the emperor Theodosius, summoned Meletius, Paulinus, and the other suitable men who desired the episcopal chair in order to avert the schism that had arisen. He also summoned the people of both parties and bound each man by oath, on the matter recalled by Socrates, book V, chapter 5:

> “When they had gathered all those who seemed suitable to exercise the episcopate—and there were six in number, among whom was Flavianus—they compelled them by oath that, when either of the two bishops died, none of them would seek the episcopal seat.”

Sozomen writes similarly in book VII, chapter 3:

> “When the people on both sides had been stirred up and an uprising was expected, a remarkable council prevailed by which they were recalled to concord. It was decided that those who thought or hoped themselves suitable to govern the episcopate of that place should bind themselves by oath. At that time there were five others besides Flavianus. They swore that they would neither seek the episcopate nor accept it if it were offered to them by election, so long as Paulinus and Meletius survived; but if one of them died, they would allow the other to hold the episcopate alone. After the oath had been sworn on these conditions, almost the entire populace returned to concord.”

At Rome, the archdeacon usually obtained the pontifical insignia, and those who held the archdeaconate were generally regarded as designated pontiffs.]

Line 2.—He obtained this from Phocas. Whatever Phocas granted, he did contrary to the custom of his predecessors [Col. 0673D], out of hatred for Cyriacus the bishop, who, he claimed, had obstructed him because Germanus, the patrician and rebel against the empire, had escaped the just punishment for his crime, as Theophanes says.

### Chronological Notes

The death of Pope Sabinianus was followed by a prolonged vacancy of the see, namely eleven months and twenty-six days; on this point nearly all catalogues, manuscripts, and authorities cited by Pagi agree. For that reason Pagi himself saw no reason to subtract anything from that interval. It is clear, however, that the vacancy must not be reckoned from 22 February, since that was not the day of death but of burial and therefore cannot be excluded. Otherwise 17 February of the year 607 results, which coincides with a Friday—the chronological obstacle into which Pagi fell because Sabinianus’s beginnings had been wrongly established. Treating a difference of only two days as negligible, he transfers Boniface’s ordination [Col. 0674A] to the Sunday corresponding to 19 February. This departs so far from chronological accuracy that it can readily be recognized that not Pagi serves Anastasius, but Anastasius serves Pagi.

The eleven months and twenty-six days should therefore be reckoned from the actual day of Sabinianus’s death, 2 February 606. When these are properly counted, excluding the final day, 29 January of the following year, 607, is obtained; since it is marked by the Sunday letter A, it clearly indicates the date of Boniface’s ordination. The pope held office for eight months and twenty-two days, as stated by the Freherian manuscripts and by the second Thuanus manuscript together with the first and second Ambrosian manuscripts—although in the first Ambrosian manuscript two years have elapsed before the months—as well as by several catalogues, especially the unpublished Blanchinian catalogue, Ordericus, and A. A. cited by Pagi. Therefore there is no reason to trust the common version and others that give twenty-eight days.

After the period beginning on 29 January had elapsed, the date that appears is not 12 November, as Anastasius has it, but 12 Kalends of November, that is, 21 October. That this was the day of Boniface’s burial, since he had died the preceding day [Col. 0674B], is demonstrated by the subsequent vacancy of the see, as I shall explain under Boniface IV, his successor. Here too Pagi is short by two days; hence he reluctantly places the pope’s death on 10 November, expressing wonder that the burial should have been delayed for two days.

I would not dare affirm whether this Boniface III, like his successor—as we shall see with complete certainty—and his predecessor Sabinianus, as we have already seen, was brought to the Church of Saint Peter several days later, or what reasons may have caused this. Yet from the calculation of the periods assigned to the vacancies and pontificates, I see that the years are fulfilled exactly, as I shall set before the reader under Boniface IV.

To this may be added an inscription from the Vitonian manuscript, first copied by Papebrochius and later by Antonio Pagi. Although it is extremely corrupt, it nevertheless confirms the account of Anastasius concerning Boniface III. It reads:

> HERE RESTS BONEFATIUS, WHO SAT [Col. 0674C]  
> SEVEN MONTHS, THIRTY-TWO DAYS.  
> BURIED ON THE DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF NOVEMBER,  
> WHILE THE LORD * P P AUGUSTUS  
> WAS REIGNING, IN THE SIXTH YEAR, INDICTIon XI  
> [Pagi adds: PHOCAS.] [Col. 0674D]

As you see, this inscription lacks the month, contains ten excess days, and assigns Phocas a sixth year, although from the day of his coronation, 23 November 602, he had counted only a fifth year. Nevertheless, together with Anastasius, it confirms 12 November as the day of burial at Saint Peter’s.

Do not suppose that this was the day of death. This is sufficiently shown by Papebrochius, who was the first to see the inscription, through his departure from the date marked by the era, as may be seen in his *Conatus historici*, and by Pagi, who accepted it but was forced to depart from the unanimous consensus of all authorities, just as he had done concerning the vacancy after Gregory. There he added fourteen days to arrive at Sabinianus’s death; here the certain date of the successor’s ordination forced him to subtract more than twenty days.

Without doubt, therefore, according to the calculations of Anastasius, Boniface III, having held office from the day of his ordination, 29 January 607, for only eight months [Col. 0674D] and twenty-two days, died on 20 October of that same year. On the following day he was buried in the Lateran church, and on the twelfth day of the following month he was buried in the church of Saint Peter. This chronology is confirmed by no monuments, since none survive from that extremely difficult period; nevertheless, it is established by the date of his ordination and by the duration of his successor’s pontificate.

[Col. 0675D]

Line 1.—Boniface. Under the emperor Phocas he held office for eight months and twenty-three days, according to Nicephorus; he was created and ordained on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, a Sunday.

Line 2.—So that the apostolic see of blessed Peter the apostle might be the head of all the Churches. Since the matter could not be settled under Gregory because of Maurice’s inertia, after Maurice’s death it was established under Boniface III by the emperor Phocas that the Roman pontiff should retain the first place in accordance with apostolic doctrine [Col. 0675A] and the most ancient tradition of the holy Fathers, while the bishop of Constantinople should hold the second.

Thus write Bede in his book *On the Reckoning of Time*, Paul the Deacon, and the eighteenth book of the *Roman History* appended to Eutropius. It was also added that the name “pope,” which had been established as more eminent than all episcopal titles, should be retained solely by the Roman pontiff, although previously it had been common to all bishops; while the other four bishops of the principal sees—Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—should be called patriarchs.

Moreover, the bishop of Constantinople continued to use the title “ecumenical,” which he had initially usurped, especially after Photius. He was accustomed to write: “N., by the mercy of God archbishop of New Rome, Constantinople, and ecumenical patriarch.” The Roman bishop, however, always abstained from this proud title, and called himself by no other than the humblest name, namely: “N., bishop, servant of the servants of God,” [Col. 0675B] or “bishop of the Catholic Church.”

### Note on Line 2.—He obtained this from Phocas

The bishops of Constantinople, who at first were subject to the bishop of Heraclea, in the course of time exercised metropolitan authority over Heraclea and other Churches in the opposite direction. Later, supported by imperial power, they were enrolled among the ancient patriarchs and, at the Second Council of Constantinople and at Chalcedon, obtained second place after the Roman pontiff, despite the opposition of Saint Leo. He rejected the canon issued at Chalcedon on this matter as spurious and fraudulently added after the council had concluded.

At length they began to usurp the title “ecumenical.” John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, displayed it with such arrogance that blessed Gregory, rightly disturbed by the proud novelty of the title, wrote several letters against him, both to the patriarchs of the East and to the emperor Maurice [Col. 0675C], though he achieved nothing with him. Since Maurice supported the title, John retained it until his death; Cyriacus, who succeeded John, likewise followed in his footsteps.

Boniface III obtained from Phocas a sanction providing that Cyriacus and the other patriarchs of Constantinople should no longer call themselves ecumenical. As Anastasius says at this point:

> “He obtained from the ruler Phocas that the apostolic see of blessed Peter the apostle should be the head of all the Churches—that is, the Roman Church—because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first of all the Churches.”

The sense of this imperial sanction is that Phocas declared by his judgment that the title “ecumenical” belonged not to the patriarch of Constantinople but to the Roman pontiff, the successor of blessed Peter. It does not mean, as some foolishly think, that Phocas first introduced the primacy of the Roman Church, since before Phocas the Roman pontiffs had exercised jurisdiction over the whole Church: in Africa, Egypt, and Asia, and even within the very boundaries of the patriarchate of Constantinople. Anyone who has touched even lightly upon ecclesiastical history knows this.

As for the title “ecumenical,” it is established that it was offered to Saint Leo the Great long before Phocas by the Council of Chalcedon. At that council petitions addressed to Saint Leo were read and entered in the synodal records; in them Saint Leo is honored with this title:

> “To the most holy, most God-beloved, ecumenical archbishop and patriarch of great Rome, Leo.”

Blessed Gregory, however, rejected the name “ecumenical bishop” and wished to be styled “servant of the servants of God,” an expression of his singular humility. This should not be understood as though Gregory failed to acknowledge the extensive jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs throughout the Church, which he repeatedly demonstrated in practice and declared in writing. Rather, he rejected the title “ecumenical” in the sense that it would assert that there was one bishop over the universal Church, as though no others in the whole world were bishops [Col. 0676A].

### Note on Line 2.—He obtained this from Phocas, etc.

This pope obtained from the emperor Phocas what Pelagius II and Gregory had been unable to obtain: that the bishop of Constantinople should no longer use the title “ecumenical.” For this emperor, at Boniface’s request—Boniface having won his favor while serving as apocrisiarius of the apostolic see at Constantinople—declared that only the Roman pontiff should be called ecumenical, or universal, bishop. Anastasius expressly testifies to this:

> “He obtained,” he says, “from the ruler Phocas that the apostolic see of blessed Peter the apostle should be the head of all the Churches—that is, the Roman Church—because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first of all the Churches” [Col. 0676B].

The emperor Phocas’s decree is also mentioned by Paul the Deacon in nearly the same words in Book IV, chapter 11, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*.

Baronius, Binius, and others maintain that Phocas issued this edict out of hatred for Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople, against whom he was embittered. This conjecture, however, does not seem acceptable, since Cyriacus died in October 606, and Thomas, a deacon of the great Church of Constantinople, succeeded him on 23 January 607, before Boniface was ordained Roman pontiff.

Since there is no evidence anywhere that the decree was issued out of hatred for Cyriacus, why should we not say that Phocas, knowing well that the Roman Church had always held by divine right the primacy over all the Churches of the world, judged the matter equitably—especially since it is clear that he was favorably disposed toward the Roman pontiffs, as appears in the case of Boniface IV?

This disproves Baronius’s claim that Cyriacus, consumed by grief because Phocas had issued that decree, died as a result.

[Col. 0676C] Line 10.—Who, having died. Since the epitaph of Boniface III, preserved in the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Vannes at Verdun, where several epitaphs of Roman pontiffs follow verses of Damasus, establishes that this pontiff died on 10 November 607, Anastasius’s statement that he was buried in the church of blessed Peter the apostle on 12 November must be interpreted as referring not to the day of his death but to the day on which he was committed to the earth. Boniface therefore held office for eight months and twenty-two days, as attested by three manuscript copies of Anastasius—one Colbertine and two Freherian—as well as by the later Corbie catalogue, Ordericus Book II, Luitprand, Abbo, and Hermannus Contractus.

[Col. 0676C] Line 2.—He obtained this from Phocas, etc.

The pontificate of Boniface III is made notable by the edict that this pope obtained from the emperor Phocas for the apostolic see [Col. 0676D]. We have already said, under Pelagius II and Gregory the Great, that the patriarchs of Constantinople, John the Faster and Cyriacus, usurped the title “ecumenical,” against which those pontiffs resisted with all their strength. Yet they were never able either to compel the patriarchs or to obtain the emperors’ consent that this offensive and inflated title be suppressed. Boniface III achieved this.

Not a few modern writers maintain that the emperor issued this edict in favor of the Roman Church out of hatred for the patriarch Cyriacus, who on certain occasions had prevented him from violating the Church’s immunity. But apart from being a mere conjecture, this rests on a very unstable foundation, for Cyriacus is known to have died before Boniface, who ascended the chair of Peter in 607, whereas Cyriacus had ended his life in 606.

Whatever may be said about this hypothesis, nothing is found in the ancient authorities who transmit the account that supports such a conjecture [Col. 0677A]. Anastasius says that the pontiff obtained from Phocas that the Roman Church should be the head of the Churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first among all the Churches. Paul the Deacon likewise relates the matter in nearly the same words in Book IV, chapter 11, of *The History of the Lombards*.

It must therefore be believed that the emperor, who knew that this was one of the prerogatives granted by Jesus Christ to the holy see—namely, to be the head of all the Churches of the world, a prerogative recognized from the beginning—rightly prohibited the patriarch of Constantinople from usurping it, since such usurpation injured the apostolic see [Col. 0678A].

[Col. 0671]

**115. Boniface**, a Roman by nationality, son of John Cataaudioce, held office for eight months and twenty-eight days. [Variant: B, 23.] He obtained from the ruler Phocas [variant: *Jocam] that the apostolic see of blessed Peter the apostle should be the head of all the Churches—that is, the Roman Church—because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first among all the Churches [Col. 0671]. See Baronius under the year of the Lord 606.

He issued a decree [Col. 0671] *that is, a decree; see Baronius in the same place] in the church of blessed Peter, where seventy-two bishops, thirty-four Roman priests, the deacons, and all the clergy assembled, under anathema, that no one, while a pope was alive—or while the bishop of his city was alive—should presume to speak of his successor or form a faction for himself, except on the third day after his burial, when the clergy and the children of the Church had assembled. Then the election should take place, and each person should have permission to choose for himself the priest he wished. [Variant: *“Let them have whom they wished.”]

After his death, he was buried in the church of blessed Peter the apostle on 12 November. He ordained twenty-one bishops in various places, and the episcopal see remained vacant for ten months and six days.

### Note on Line 3.—At the same time he requested from the ruler Phocas the temple called the Pantheon

In it he established the church of Saint Mary ever-virgin and of all the martyrs. This church was called Saint Mary at the Martyrs. Anastasius, under Paul, writes:

> “When he had recognized this, he fled into the church of the holy virgin Mary, Mother of God, which is called ‘at the Martyrs.’”

It was so called because the pontiff instituted there, to be celebrated on the Kalends of November, the solemnity of all the martyrs, which later became the solemnity of All Saints. Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 609, writes:

> “He converted the Pantheon at Rome, obtained from the emperor Phocas, into a church of Saint Mary and all the Martyrs; later, as Christian devotion increased, it was decreed that it should be celebrated in honor of all the saints.”

Later writers called it the Rotunda. Bertold, presbyter of Constance, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1087, writes:

> “Guibert the heresiarch did not cease from the perversity he had begun; rather, he fortified himself in the church of Saint Mary at the Martyrs, which they call the Rotunda.”

[Col. 0679A]

### Note on Line 3.—At the same time he requested from the ruler Phocas the temple called the Pantheon

With excellent judgment, the most holy pontiff Boniface IV consecrated in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary and all the martyrs the temple, famous throughout the world, that had been dedicated by pagan superstition to the worship of all the gods. He followed an example given—or perhaps even received—from earlier pontiffs, who converted profane temples into sacred ones while retaining a certain resemblance and apparent kinship between the old and the new worship. Thus temples sacred to Mars were assigned to blessed Martina, and those sacred to the brothers Romulus and Remus were likewise assigned to the honor of the brothers Cosmas and Damian.

The Pantheon was called the temple of all the gods. Antiquarians also used the term to indicate a figure carved on the reverse of certain ancient coins and filled with the symbols of several gods. On a large Egyptian bronze coin, which Peter Seguinius displays among his selected coins, one side shows the laureate head of Antoninus Pius, while the other shows a bearded head adorned with the insignia of the principal deities. Among these, the modius placed on the head signifies Serapis; the ram’s horn, Jupiter Ammon; the three-pronged pitchfork, Father Dis; and also Neptune; the serpent coiled around the same figure, Aesculapius; the radiant hair, the Sun or Osiris; and the cornucopia, the Nile. I once saw a gem engraved with a similar design. They call that a Pantheon.

Marcus Agrippa, son-in-law of Augustus, either erected the Pantheon from its foundations or completed what had been begun; certainly he adorned it with a portico, as the inscription placed on the front of the structure tells us:

> M. AGRIPPA. L. F. COS. TERTIVM. FECIT.  
> “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this.”

Dio speaks of it in Book LIII:

> “Agrippa also completed the Pantheon. It is perhaps so called because, in the statues of Mars and Venus, it contained many images of the gods; but in my view it derives its name from the fact that its convex form displayed the likeness of the vaulted heavens.”

Ludovicus Demontiosius, a man of consular rank, in his booklet entitled *A Gaul as Guest in Rome*, printed in Rome in 1585, advances his own ingenious conjecture concerning the construction of the Pantheon. He denies that the Pantheon originally had the form it now presents:

> “For although it rose high above the level ground,” he says, “today one descends thirteen steps”—

now one descends by two, thanks to Alexander VII, Supreme Pontiff, who removed the earth and splendidly restored part of the portico on the right, which had also collapsed—

> “into the portico, with many ornaments buried beneath the ground, and with them this passage of Pliny, which was overwhelmed in almost the same disaster. Therefore he attempted to assist both, so that we might display the temple itself as visible from its foundations and bring Pliny’s passage into the light from the dense darkness that has long enveloped it” [Col. 0679D].

I shall briefly review what this author clearly and abundantly describes, so as to demonstrate the form that the Pantheon once possessed.

First, it must be observed that the ancient symmetry now appears greatly altered. Since the temple’s width now equals its height, the structure becomes square in form, that is, of the Doric order, although the double portico, the temple entrance, the doorframes, lintel, opening, columns, and everything else belong to the Corinthian order. Here is a hermaphroditic form of architecture: the overall structure is masculine, the parts feminine. There is therefore no symmetry here, for symmetry is nothing other than the proportion of the parts to one another and of those parts to the whole [Col. 0680A].

Should the most celebrated structure, which Pliny lists among the outstanding works of the world, be condemned? Certainly not. It must instead be restored to the refined form of architecture. It must be judged that as much lies buried beneath the earth as is lacking for the proper symmetry of the Corinthian order, and that the present pavement should therefore be excavated to the depth corresponding to the difference between the Doric and Corinthian proportions.

Second, Pliny mentions the caryatids of the Pantheon. In Book XXXV, chapter 5, he says:

> “Diogenes of Athens adorned Agrippa’s Pantheon, and his caryatids on the columns of the temple are judged among the few outstanding works.”

Four of them, excavated from the earth beneath which they lay hidden, can still be seen: two on the Capitol and two in the Chigi palace, occupied by the duke of Bracciano. What, then, was their position in the temple? The column plinths are narrower than the proportions of the columns require; part of the plinth is therefore concealed by the mosaic pavement. The stylobates of the columns are likewise concealed. Vitruvius teaches in Book III, chapter 3, that stylobates ought to be added in works of this kind.

The width of the marble of the caryatids, however, is the same as that of the plinths and stylobates, and the kind of marble is also the same. Once the earth has been removed, the plinths and stylobates should therefore emerge intact, and the caryatids should be restored to their stylobates, from which ignorant hands had torn them [Col. 0680B].

Third, the Pantheon contained statues of all the gods. But where and in what order were they arranged? For sacred rites were not performed for all the gods in the same place. Sextus Pompeius states that the ancients performed rites for the heavenly gods in buildings elevated above the ground, for the earthly gods on the ground, and for the infernal gods in excavated earth.

Jupiter was therefore placed on the tribunal in an elevated position. The other celestial gods stood in the small shrines projecting from the solid part of the wall around the temple’s circumference. The earthly gods were situated in the spaces between the columns, while the infernal gods were in the excavated earth within the vault beneath the steps [Col. 0680C].

The steps, beginning at the threshold of the door, descended to a depth that completely absorbed the difference between the Doric and Corinthian orders mentioned above. Since the entire diameter of the temple’s width is 178 palms, and the diameter is divided into four parts, with one quarter assigned on each side to the steps extending from the outermost point to the innermost, two quarters remained empty in the middle for the temple floor. Thus, someone standing on the innermost step and looking up at the dome would see the innermost circuit of the dome’s squares correspond to the innermost circuit of the steps.

From this it is easy to infer that the architect intended to shape the lower part of the temple, in a certain way, into the form of the upper hemisphere, so that the lower parts would correspond to the upper. Otherwise the builder would have extended the pyramids of the dome, as in other rounded roofs where they converge at the finial, which is like the navel of the roof.

Moreover, the proportions of this temple were arranged so that the same symmetry of the steps was preserved on the exterior, in the convex part of the roof [Col. 0680D]. Thus not only did the lower parts correspond to the upper, but the exterior also corresponded to the interior.

This is how the most ingenious Gaul divined the form of the Pantheon from the rules of the art. Ammianus Marcellinus does not seem far removed from him when, in Book XVI, he calls the Pantheon “a circular region vaulted with beautiful height.”

I hope I shall give pleasure to readers by placing before their eyes the diagram drawn by this distinguished author. This will be all the more useful because the praised book is not easily available to everyone, and the description of the temple will be more evident from examining the diagram.

[Col. 0681A]

### Note on Line 4.—The Pantheon

Paul wrote the same thing at greater length in the same place, chapter 37, whereas Anastasius wrote it briefly:

> “The same emperor Phocas, at the request of another pope, Boniface, ordered that in the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, after the filth of idolatry had been removed, a church of blessed Mary ever-virgin and of all the martyrs should be made, so that where once there had been the worship not of all the gods but of demons, there might thereafter be the memorial of the saints.”

[Col. 0681A]

### Note on Line 1.—Boniface

On 18 September 607, after an interregnum of ten months and six days, Boniface, the fourth of that name, was created pope during the reign of Phocas. Concerning the emperor Phocas, Cedrenus and Nicephorus preserve the memorable report that when a monk asked, “Why have you imposed such an impious emperor upon the Christians?” God replied: “Because I could find no one worse than he, and the crimes of the people of Constantinople deserved him” [Col. 0681B].

### Note on Line 3.—He requested from Phocas, etc.

Thus that remarkable work, celebrated in the praises of so many ancient writers, erected by Marcus Agrippa during Augustus’s third consulship and consecrated to Jupiter the Avenger, was transferred to the service of the Christian religion after six hundred and thirty-two years.

[Col. 0682A]

### Chronological Notes

Regarding the interregnum between Boniface III and Boniface IV, all manuscripts and catalogues agree: ten months and six days. The same number is counted, inclusively as usual, from Boniface III’s death on 20 October 607 to Boniface IV’s ordination on 25 August 608. That 25 August was Boniface’s actual ordination date is demonstrated not only by the Sunday letter F, which recurs in that year, but also very clearly by the certain date of his burial and the certain duration of his pontificate, as will be explained below.

For the benefit of all who wish to follow the matter easily, and to show that Pagi’s insertion of a stroke, increasing or diminishing the periods prescribed by him whenever he wished, is useless, I think Anastasius’s and Pagi’s chronologies should be set before the reader. If to the sum of four years, five months, and fourteen days there are added the year 604, [lacuna], and eleven days, including Gregory’s day of death [Col. 0683A], the year 608 and the day 25 August are obtained—the date we have said was Boniface IV’s actual ordination, as Pagi himself acknowledges.

But according to Pagi’s chronology the figure is four years, five months, and ten days. Thus, apart from the difficulties demonstrated in their proper places, four days are missing to complete the periods. It is therefore clear that Anastasius rather than Pagi must be followed, although Pagi was otherwise a most learned man.

As for Boniface IV’s pontificate, not only do all authorities agree that he held office for six years, eight months, and thirteen days, but the inscription beneath his epitaph, which Baronius and more recent writers have taken from Mansi’s collection, confirms the matter. It reads:

> HERE RESTS BONIFACE THE YOUNGER,  
> WHO SAT SIX YEARS, EIGHT MONTHS, TWELVE DAYS.  
> HE WAS BURIED ON THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY,  
> WHILE THE LORD HERACLIUS WAS REIGNING,  
> IN HIS FIFTH YEAR.

[Col. 0683B]

This inscription excludes the day of burial; consequently, twelve days rather than thirteen are counted, so that Boniface IV died on 7 May and, according to Anastasius and the others who give thirteen days, was buried on the eighth of that month.

No clearer argument could be devised to demonstrate that the day of a pontiff’s death is one thing, and the day of his burial in the church of Saint Peter another. For most manuscripts and catalogues state that Boniface was buried at Saint Peter’s on 25 May. Although Antonio Pagi suspects that this may concern a translation of the relics, with due respect, he could not have been buried at that place seventeen days later; nor, if a later translation among several were being recorded, would a writer plainly contemporary with those events have used the word “buried” in the very text. Moreover, the translations carried out many years later are not unknown.

Therefore, although the burial ceremonies reported by Papebrochius must, together with Pagi, be regarded as apocryphal, Pagi nevertheless came closer to the truth concerning the papal chronology [Col. 0683C]. In the year 615, then, Boniface died on 7 May and was buried on the eighth in the Lateran church; on the 25th he was transferred to Saint Peter’s.

### Note on Line 4.—The temple called the Pantheon

The most holy Boniface, detesting the worship of idols, expelled Jupiter and all the gods from the building, so that the temple might rightly be consecrated to the Virgin Mary and all the saints. Because of its circular form, the Romans now call it the Rotunda.

Bede, a grave authority and almost contemporary with those events, committed to memory that this building was given to the Church of Christ by Phocas Augustus; after him, Walafridus did likewise in his book *On the Origin and Development of Ecclesiastical Matters*, as did others.

This most illustrious temple was dedicated by Boniface IV in the year 610, on 13 May. On that same day, the bodies of many holy martyrs were transported in twenty-eight heavily laden wagons from various cemeteries of the city of Rome and buried there beside the high altar. Nearly six hundred and thirty-two years after the building had been founded for the worship of idols, it was transferred to Christian worship and given the name Saint Mary at the Martyrs.

This day was exceptionally solemn and celebrated among the Romans, with crowds gathering from every direction, so that they caused a famine among the Roman people, since the supply of grain was more limited at that time. For this reason Pope Gregory IV judged that the celebration should be transferred to the Kalends of November, when provisions are usually more plentiful [Col. 0683D].

### Note on Line 4.—The temple called the Pantheon

Marcus Agrippa, a relative of Augustus and distinguished by his naval victory over Sextus Pompey, built this temple of solid construction for Jupiter the Avenger, or for Mars and Venus. Since images of all the gods were placed in it, it could be called in Greek **τὸ τῶν θεῶν κοινὸν ἱερόν**, “the common sanctuary of the gods.”

The building was held in such high esteem that it was counted among the most distinguished works of the City, and the Roman emperors diligently strove to preserve it for posterity. Hadrian restored it when it had become dilapidated through age, as Spartianus testifies in chapter 19. Antoninus Pius also restored it, as Capitolinus records in chapter 8, and Septimius Severus, as the inscription in Gruter, page 1, no. 1, indicates:

> THE EMPERORS CAESAR LUCIUS SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS …  
> AND EMPEROR CAESAR MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS PIUS …  
> RESTORED THE PANTHEON, DAMAGED BY AGE,  
> WITH ALL ITS ORNAMENTATION.

The temple became much more celebrated when, after all idolatrous superstition had been removed, it was consecrated to the one true God in honor of Saint Mary at the Martyrs. In a solemn rite, blessed Boniface IV purified it [Col. 0684B] and enriched it with the relics of holy martyrs from cemeteries outside the City, and it passed into the service of the Christian religion. Thus, after the multitude of demons had been expelled, a multitude of saints began to be commemorated there, as our author says at this point, and as Paul the Deacon says in Book IV, chapter 37. The same fact is expressed in a very ancient Vatican epitaph preserved by Manlius:

> Here lies blessed Boniface, fourth after Gregory,  
> Who was the just ruler of this see and church.  
> In Phocas’s time, seeing that the temple at Rome,  
> Had been the shrine of all the demons,  
> He purified it and dedicated it to all the saints.

### Note on Line 3.—At the same time he requested from Phocas

When Boniface saw that the emperor Phocas was favorably disposed toward the Roman pontiffs, he asked him to give him the Pantheon, a famous Roman shrine celebrated in the praises of so many ancient writers. It had been erected by Marcus Agrippa during his third consulship under Augustus and consecrated to Jupiter the Avenger; it had remained intact, since the Christian Romans had not demolished the dwelling places of the demons.

After obtaining it, Boniface cleansed it of the filth of its ancient idolatry and consecrated it in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, and all the holy martyrs, whose many relics were transferred there from cemeteries outside the City.

Anastasius and Bede recount these events in Book II, chapter 4, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. This church can still be visited at Rome and is called Saint Mary Rotunda because of the form of the building. Its dedication is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 13 May, where it is called the dedication of the church of Saint Mary at the Martyrs.

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, assigns the dedication to the first year of Boniface, whom he says:

> “Instituted there on the Kalends of November the solemnity of all the martyrs, which later, as Christian devotion increased, was decreed to be celebrated in honor of all the saints.”

On this matter Baronius should be consulted in his notes to the Roman Martyrology for 13 May and 1 November. He was unaware, however, that Pope Gregory III had consecrated this solemnity to the holy martyrs and later decreed that it should be observed by the whole Church in honor of all the saints, as Usuard records in his Martyrology. See also what will be said under Gregory IV.

Linea 7.—“When he had died.” According to Anastasius, Ordericus, book II, Abbo, Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle*, and several catalogues, Boniface held the see for six years, eight months, and thirteen days, and departed to God on 7 May in the year of Christ 615. Baronius reports that, according to monuments collected by Manlius from the Vatican Basilica, the following epitaph was inscribed on his tomb; at its end one reads:

> Here lies Boniface the younger, who held the see for six years, eight months, and twelve days; he was deposited on 8 May, under the reign of the lord Heraclius, in his fifth year.

Here only twelve days are counted beyond the eight months, [Col. 0685A] because 7 May, the day of his death, is excluded. From this it also follows that we have correctly assigned his ordination to 25 August, and that Anastasius’ account of the vacancy of the see after the death of Boniface III was incorrectly transmitted. Saint Boniface IV is commemorated on 25 May; on that day Papebrochius also gives his Life in the *Acta Sanctorum*.

[Note: [Col. 0685A]]

Linea 3.—“At the same time he requested from the emperor Phocas the temple called the Pantheon.” After cleansing this temple of the filth of idolatry, he consecrated it to the true God under the invocation of the most blessed Virgin Mary and all the holy martyrs. On that occasion he established a solemnity to be celebrated annually in the City on the Kalends of November, in honor of the same blessed Virgin Mary and all the saints and martyrs. Gregory IV later ordered it to be celebrated throughout the Church on that fixed day in honor of all the saints.

This temple was built by Marcus Agrippa, Augustus’ son-in-law, after the victory at Actium over Mark Antony and Cleopatra; today it is called Capo Figato. Agrippa dedicated it to Jupiter the Avenger, and it was called the Pantheon either because images of all the gods worshiped at Rome had been placed in it, or because its vaulted structure displayed the appearance of the heavens, which are the dwelling of God.

Although, after the conversion of the emperors, the other temples of the idols were demolished by Christians with great zeal, this temple remained intact, in accordance, as is believed, with a law of the emperor Honorius, which reads:

> Just as we prohibit sacrifices, so we wish the adornments of public buildings to be preserved.

(*Codex Theodosianus*, book 15, “Concerning Pagans.”)

It still stands intact at Rome and is called the church of the Rotunda.

[Col. 0677]

### 116. Boniface

Boniface, by nation a Marsian, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician, held the see for six years, eight months, and thirteen days. During his time there were extremely severe famines, pestilences, and floods. At the same time he requested from the emperor Phocas the temple called the Pantheon.

[Note: [Col. 0677] *From Phocas. See Baronius under the year of the Lord 607.*]

In it he established a church of Saint Mary ever-virgin and of all the martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0677] *Of the martyrs of Christ.*]

In that church the emperor offered many gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0677] *Presents.*]

He made his own house into a monastery and endowed it richly. When he died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 25 May. He held two ordinations in December: eight deacons and thirty-five bishops for various places.

[Note: [Col. 0677] *B: 25.*]

### LXX. Saint Deusdedit. Year of Christ 614, the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius

[Note: [Col. 0685B]]

#### From the Farnesian manuscript LXVII

No. 117, line 1: “he held the see for three years and twenty days”; “this.” Line 3: “Eleutherius, the patrician and chamberlain, came to Ravenna and killed all who had been involved in the killing of John the exarch and of the judges of the republic.” “He came to Rome.” Line 10: “a great earthquake in August, in the sixth indiction.” Line 11: “the outbreak of scabies,” etc.; “when he had died, he was buried.”

Line 5: “and those involved with the judges of the republic.” “And when he came to Rome, he was received most favorably by the most holy pope.” Line 6: “from Rome.” Line 7: “by John Campsivus, ‘Arcata’ [reading uncertain]”; in the same place, “the patrician.” Line 9: “peace was made.” Line 10: “a greater earthquake.” Line 11: “in the sixth indiction. He established that a second Mass should be celebrated among the clergy on the same day.” Line 11: “sixth indiction.” In the same line: “the disaster of scabies followed, so that no one could recognize his dead; and when he had died, he was buried” (he often uses this expression in the preceding material).
