[Note: [Col. 0687A]]

Linea 9.—“And when a *roga* had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout all Italy.” A *roga* is a distribution made by the emperor in place of a donation to the soldiers. Anastasius, in his Life of Severinus:

> And where are your *rogae*, which the lord emperor directed to be given to you in turn, stored by the holy man?

Gregory, book II of the *Letters*, letter 32:

> The Theodosians who remained here, receiving no *roga*, scarcely devote themselves to guarding the walls.

I said there that *roga* is also a distribution made by the Roman pontiffs to the clergy or the people. Anastasius, below in the same work:

> He left, for his obsequies, to the entire clergy one complete *roga*.

The same author, in the Life of Boniface V:

> He loved the clergy and gave his clergy a complete *roga*. He left to the entire clergy, for his obsequies, one complete *roga*.

The same, in the Life of John IV:

> He left a complete *roga* among the entire clergy.

The same, in the Life of Eugenius:

> He gave the clergy their customary *roga*.

The same, in the Life of Leo III:

> He greatly increased the *roga* for his clergy, especially in the presbytery.

In the same place: “He established a second Mass among the clergy.” On Sundays a single public Mass—that is, a solemn Mass—was customarily celebrated. See canon “And this,” *De Consecratione*, distinction 1. On this subject, see Dionysius the Areopagite’s letter to Demophilus and John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 27.

Leo the Pope established the celebration of a second Mass so that the people would not be excessively crowded, while preserving the practice of a single Mass; see canon “It is necessary,” *De Consecratione*, distinction 1. After him, Pope Deusdedit established a second Mass among the clergy—that is, in the Roman Church—as Anastasius testifies here. Perhaps the practice of a single public Mass had not yet disappeared from the Roman Church, which was always more tenacious of antiquity.

[Note: [Col. 0687C]]

Linea 9.—“He established a second Mass among the clergy.” Of those who have written treatises on liturgical matters, no one fails to struggle with this passage of Anastasius when the subject of repeating the Mass in the same church arises. Cardinal Bona, who should never be named without praise, in his excellent treatise *On Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 14, no. 4, had attempted to prove from Leo the Great’s letter to Dioscorus of Alexandria—where Leo orders the sacrifice to be repeated when the multitude of the faithful is so great that the basilica cannot receive them all at once—that the custom of offering the sacrifice several times on the same day had prevailed at Rome from that time onward. He then raises against himself the text cited above, saying:

> Concerning the holy pontiff Deusdedit, the author of the *Pontifical Book* writes: “He established a second Mass among the clergy.” On these words Peter of Urbevetano says in his scholia that perhaps at that time, following the Greeks, only one Mass was sung in the church, which according to the ancients was more edifying.

He immediately adds:

> Yet from the testimony of Leo just cited it is clear that the practice of repeating the sacrifice had been introduced into the Roman Church much earlier.

With due respect to this eminent author, however, if one wishes to defend Urbevetano’s interpretation—namely, that down to the time of the blessed Deusdedit the custom of celebrating only one Mass in each church had prevailed—Leo’s letter can easily be explained as commanding the sacrifice to be repeated only when a new congregation filled the basilica, in places where there was only one basilica, and by the same presbyter. Deusdedit, however, may then have been the first to establish that after the solemn Mass a second, private Mass should be celebrated among the clergy by another member of the clergy, whether or not a new congregation had assembled, and whether there was one basilica or several.

It was certainly then that the practice seems first to have been introduced into the Latin Church of celebrating several Masses in the same church and of constructing several altars for this purpose. It is beyond controversy that in the first centuries of the Church there was one altar in each basilica, and that only one Mass was celebrated upon it; both practices are retained by the Greek Church. All who attended that Mass were nourished by the sacred synaxis, especially those who served at the solemn Mass. Hence the Fourth Council of Toledo, in 635, decreed in canon 17:

> Let the priests and Levites communicate before the altar, the clergy in the choir, and the people outside the choir.

All the presbyters who were present, however, performed the sacred rite together with the presbyter who was celebrating, or with the bishop, offering and communicating together.

> It is the custom of the Roman Church that, at the accomplishment of Christ’s offering, the presbyters be present and, together with the pontiff, accomplish it by word and hand,

as Mabillon reports in part II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 1111, from Amalarius, book I, chapter 112.

Moreover, history teaches us that the ancient monks were accustomed to celebrate one Mass only, and that only on Sunday and feast days, when all the monks assembled.

> Certainly during Lent, except on Sundays, Mass was not sung in the time of Saint Benedict,

says Hindelmarus in his commentary on chapter 48 of the Rule, as reported by Mabillon in his first preface to the fourth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, no. 168.

> It is reported that formerly the Carthusians celebrated Masses only on Sundays and feast days,

according to Peter of Cluny, book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 28; Abbot Guibert, book I of *His Life*, chapter 11; and Peter of Blois, letter 86. Thus Cardinal Bona, book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 18, no. 11. In no. 8 he adds:

> Palladius relates in the Life of the blessed Arsisius that in the church of the mountain of Nitria there were eight presbyters, among whom only the first offered; and as long as he lived, the others neither offered, nor judged, nor delivered a sermon.

For this reason, according to Álvaro Pelayo, book II of *The Lament of the Church*, article 5, blessed Francis

> wanted the brothers to be content with one Mass in whatever place they were, knowing that the brothers would wish to justify themselves by Masses and reduce them to a source of gain, as we see happening today.

Pelayo was writing around the year 1330, approximately one hundred years after the death of blessed Francis, and was undoubtedly directing his attention and his finger to a letter written by blessed Francis to his brothers, in which we read:

> I also admonish and exhort you in the Lord that, in places where the brothers reside, only one Mass be celebrated each day, according to the practice of the holy Roman Church. But if there are several priests in a place, let one, out of the love of charity, be content after hearing the celebration of the other priest.

I know that modern sectarians misuse this authority to abolish the private Mass, which they intensely hate. Their response, however, does not seem acceptable to me when they regard the letter of blessed Francis as apocryphal. The testimony of Pelayo, who uses the same letter, stands against them; his testimony must not be rejected, since he is both an ancient witness and a member of the same order.

It must therefore be said that the ancient discipline of celebrating only one Mass was relaxed by blessed Deusdedit to the extent that, after the solemn Mass, only one additional Mass was sung among the clergy; it was not relaxed so far that Masses were multiplied according to the number of presbyters, as may perhaps have begun to happen in the time of blessed Francis and as later became customary. One cause of this, as the aforementioned Cardinal Bona says in book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 18, no. 9, was:

> Because the mendicant orders were founded and spread far and wide, the burdens of Masses multiplied, and therefore it became necessary for each priest to celebrate privately each day in order to satisfy them.

From this also we can easily understand the origin of the multitude of altars with which the churches of the mendicants are filled, and which one does not see in other basilicas, whether of monks or of clerics.

[Note: [Col. 0689B]]

Linea 3.—“The patrician Eleutherius.” Anastasius, once again reproducing Paul’s words, once again confuses the events. It must therefore be corrected from the same author, who writes in chapter 31:

> At this time John Consinus invaded Naples; a few days later Eleutherius, the eunuch patrician, assumed the imperial authority from that same city.

Consinus—or, as Anastasius calls him, Compsinus—invaded Naples and the other surrounding places and declared himself king. Batillus, in his *History of Bari*, maintains that this John Consinus was crowned with an iron crown in the city of Bari and then with a golden one among the Neapolitans, so that he might establish himself as king before the peoples of Italy. Eleutherius, however, brought him back into order. Of him Paul continues:

> After this the same Eleutherius, the eunuch patrician, assumed the imperial authority. While he was traveling from Ravenna to Rome, he was killed by soldiers in the fortress called Luceolis, and his head was carried to the emperor at Constantinople.

Anastasius inserted this episode among the deeds of Boniface V.

[Col. 0689C]

Linea 7.—“Intarta.” “*Intarta*,” says Hesychius, means “a tyrant, a rebel against the king.” It derives from ἀρταίρω, “I contend, I quarrel.” Festus likewise says: “*Antarium* is a war fought before a city,” namely, by citizens in rebellion. In the Acts of Saint Martina the virgin one likewise reads:

> O Alexander, and enemy of the Christians.

And in the *Fontanellensian Chronicle*, chapter 3:

> War was waged between Charles the exarch and Regenfrid the *intarta*.

From this arose the verb *intartarizare*, which occurs more than once later in these deeds.

Linea 10.—“At the same time.” Anastasius’ words must be illuminated by what Paul writes in chapter 42, where he records the deeds of Rothari, king of the Lombards:

> He waged war against the people of Ravenna and the Romans at the river Emilia, which is called the Scultenna. In that battle, when the rest of the Romans were turning their backs, eight thousand fell. At that time a great earthquake occurred at Rome, and there was a great flooding of the waters. After this came the plague of scabies, so that no one could recognize his dead because of the excessive swelling.

The unskilled compiler of the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, however, mixes together the times and events. While Deusdedit was pope, Adaloald the Lombard was ruling. Therefore, if the flooding and the plague of scabies occurred during the reign of Rothari, that account of Anastasius may perhaps have to be transferred to the deeds of Pope John IV or Theodore, since Rothari did not assume the Lombard kingdom before the year 636.

After gaining this victory, and increasing his dominion and wealth, Rothari consolidated the Lombard kingdom in Italy. He was also the first to devote his attention to issuing Lombard laws and to commit them to written records. Hence Paul writes in the same work, chapter 44:

> This Rothari, king of the Lombards, arranged in written form the laws which they had previously retained only by memory and custom, and ordered that the book itself be called an edict. It was already the seventy-seventh year since the Lombards had come into Italy, as the same king testified in the prologue to his edict.

This statement stands at the very beginning of the Lombard Laws.

[Note: [Col. 0690A]]

Linea 1.—“Deusdedit.” After the apostolic see had been vacant for five months and twelve days following the death of Boniface IV, Deusdedit, distinguished by outstanding virtues and holiness, was elected pontiff. In the Church a public hymn is sung about him on 8 November, declaring him to have been of such merit that, when he visited the sick, he healed a leper with a kiss and cleansed him of leprosy.

Linea 1.—“He held the see for three years and twenty-four days.” Three years less five days. Since his anniversary is commemorated in the Church on 8 November, once the calculation is made from the beginning of his pontificate, he is found to have held the see for the period stated above.

Linea 9.—“Roga.” It is a donation, so called from *erogare*, “to distribute.”

[Note: [Col. 0690B]]

### Chronological Notes

Although the commonly circulated manuscripts of Anastasius display no vacancy of the see, as does the Lucensian catalogue, the first Freherian manuscript has six months and five days; the second Thuanean has six months and twenty-five days, agreeing with the parchment Ambrosian manuscript and the Mazarine Regius manuscript; while the first and second Ambrosian manuscripts and the first Thuanean have seven months and twenty-five days. Finally, the Farfensian catalogue gives an interregnum of thirteen days, both after Boniface IV and after his two successors, Deusdedit and Boniface, everywhere incorrectly and with serious damage to chronology.

It is plainly evident that none of the interregna cited is correct. For no matter from where the counting of the days begins—whether from the day of death or from the day of deposition—it never reaches a Sunday except when the period is reckoned from the day of deposition in the Vatican, 25 May. This practice is indeed often found after Honorius, [Col. 0690C] though with a smaller discrepancy when counted from the day of death. Moreover, the certain dates of Saint Deusdedit’s death and pontificate cannot be displaced; consequently, one must either construct a new interregnum or resort to conjecture.

As for the duration of the see, both the manuscripts and the catalogues define it as three years and either twenty-three or twenty-four days. Other catalogues—such as five catalogues of Antonius Pagius, our previously unpublished Blanchinian catalogue, and the second catalogue of Mabillon—give three years and twenty days. Their opinion is supported by Martin of Troppau, the author of the *Fasciculus Temporum*, and Gotfridus of Viterbo, though they incorrectly make Deusdedit contemporary with the reign of Phocas.

Following their authority, I count backward from the day of death, or from the deposition on 8 November 618. Subtracting three years and twenty days, I arrive at 19 October 615, marked by the letter F, which coincided with a Sunday in that year. I therefore seem to have discovered the very day of his ordination, which Pagius also recognized as such.

Again, ascending from this day of ordination to the day of Boniface IV’s death, 7 May, I count five months and thirteen days—not twelve, as Pagius has it—for the day of Boniface’s death is included. Thus the Farfensian catalogue, which gives thirteen days, is less erroneous than the other catalogues and manuscripts, in which an interregnum has been devised arbitrarily.

Here I cannot sufficiently wonder at Garnerius’ negligence. In his learned notes on the *Book of the Popes*, he places the beginning of Boniface V, the successor of Saint Deusdedit, in the year 617 and consequently attaches to the decree of the pope’s election the fifth indiction, which corresponds to that year after September; he also admits, with Anastasius, that Saint Deusdedit died in November. Yet, wholly occupied with conjecturing the date of the compilation of the *Book of the Popes*, he failed to read in the same Anastasius the most certain indication of the pontiff’s period. Anastasius says that a great earthquake followed—in August, before the pontiff’s death—in the sixth indiction. John the Deacon likewise confirms this in his *Chronicle*, assigning it to the year 618; it was followed by the disease of scabies, or elephantiasis.

Therefore the death of Saint Deusdedit must necessarily be assigned to that year, just as the election of Boniface, his successor, must not be placed earlier in that same year as it was drawing to a close. Nor should it be postponed to the following year with Pagius, since the killing of Eleutherius and other arguments demonstrate this; I shall present them in the notes on the same Boniface.

Accordingly, Saint Deusdedit was ordained after a vacancy of five months and thirteen days, on 19 October 615. After holding the see for three years and twenty days, he died on 7 November and was buried on the following day, as Anastasius and the Roman Martyrology, corrected by Baronius, correctly state—namely, on the day of his deposition, 8 November.

[Note: [Col. 0691A]]

Linea 1.—“Deusdedit.” A cardinal presbyter of Saints John and Paul, the title of Pammachius, appointed by Pope Saint Gregory, he obtained the pontificate by the unanimous vote of all. Under the emperor Flavius Heraclius Augustus, he held the see for three years and nineteen days. He was consecrated on a Sunday, 21 October, in the year of the Lord 613.

[Col. 0691B]

*Deusdedit* was a compound name made from a noun and a verb, customary in those times. Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus writes to Deusdedit, a Ravenna scribe, and Saint Augustine writes to Quodvultdeus.

Linea 11.—“After this the plague struck the people.” In the year 613, in the month of August, the earth trembled with a great movement; a most loathsome pestilence followed the earthquake. This was scabies, called by the name elephantiasis. It so disfigured the faces of those afflicted that the living could scarcely be distinguished from the dead, nor could they be recognized. At that time the holiness of the pontiff manifested itself conspicuously to the people. For when the pontiff offered a kiss to a leprous man whom he met, he immediately restored him to his former health.

[Note: [Col. 0691B]]

Linea 11.—“After this the plague followed.” Pliny states in book XXVI of his *Natural History* that elephantiasis—the disease called by the Greeks σατυρίασμος, because it makes the face of the sufferer resemble the face of a satyr—was not present in Italy before the time of Gnaeus Pompey. But while the holy pontiff Deusdedit occupied the see, elephantiasis raged in the City with such violence that, as our author says, no one could recognize his dead.

Amid such a disaster among the people, pontifical charity came to the aid of those afflicted by the disease and was glorified by divine power. For when Saint Deusdedit kissed an elephantiasis sufferer whom he encountered, divine power working through him, he immediately restored the man to his former health. This remarkable deed, praised in the most ancient records of the Church, is commemorated annually in the Roman Martyrology on the sixth day before the Ides of November, his feast day, in these words:

> At Rome, Saint Deusdedit, pope, who was of such merit that by a kiss he healed a leper of leprosy.

[Note: [Col. 0691C]]

Linea 1.—“From his father Stephen, a subdeacon.” In the copy of Anastasius used by Baronius, the reading was:

> Deusdedit, son of Stephen, having been a subdeacon, held the see for three years.

On these words he writes:

> That a Roman subdeacon should be made Roman pontiff happened for the first time, without the example of his predecessors; this clearly indicates that great disturbances had arisen in the clergy. But, to omit other matters, the fact that Deusdedit was elected was brought about by his outstanding holiness, by which he shone forth wonderfully illuminated amid so much darkness.

Since learned men had hitherto been persuaded that subdeacons had never been elected Roman pontiffs, the passage was restored from the Regius edition of Anastasius and from various manuscript copies in this form:

> Deusdedit, from his father Stephen, a subdeacon.

Thus Deusdedit himself was not necessarily a subdeacon but the son of a subdeacon. Yet, since it is clear from Liberatus the deacon’s *Brief Account*, chapter 22, that Silverius was called a Roman pontiff “from the rank of subdeacon,” it remains uncertain which of the two readings should be preferred, since the correction of the former rests upon a false foundation. I think, moreover, that subdeacons could be elected until the time of Stephen III, called by others Stephen IV. In his Roman synod, held in 769, it was forbidden under anathema that anyone should ever presume that a layman, or one from another order, could be promoted to the sacred dignity of the pontificate unless, ascending through the distinct grades, he had first become a cardinal deacon or presbyter.

From these words it seems to me that subdeacons were excluded from the pontificate only at that time. For Liberatus, cited above, tells us that Silverius was promoted from that order to the pontificate, and no one objected that this rendered him ineligible. Anastasius, moreover, leaves it uncertain whether Deusdedit himself had also been only a subdeacon before his election. This seems more probable, since the later reading does indeed say that he was the son of a subdeacon, but does not deny that he himself had also been a subdeacon, whereas the earlier reading expressly states this.

Linea 9.—“He established a second Mass among the clergy.” The author of the *Pontifical Book* commends his love and generosity toward the clergy and writes:

> He established a second Mass among the clergy.

On these words Peter of Urbevetano says in his scholia, cited by Cardinal Bona in book I, chapter 14, no. 4, of *Liturgical Matters*:

> Because perhaps at that time, following the Greeks, only one Mass was sung in the church, which according to the ancients was more edifying.

Yet it is clear from Leo the Great’s letter 81 to Dioscorus of Alexandria that the custom of repeating the sacrifice had been introduced into the Roman Church long before Deusdedit. In that letter Leo orders the sacrifice to be repeated when the multitude of the faithful is so great that the basilica cannot receive them all at once; otherwise one part of the people would be deprived of its devotion if the custom of only one Mass were to be maintained.

He then says that it is entirely pious and reasonable that whenever the presence of a new congregation fills the basilica, the sacrifice should be offered again. The holy pontiff gave this command concerning the repetition of the sacrifice in accordance with the custom then prevailing at Rome:

> So that in all things our observance may agree.

And below:

> So that what has become established in our custom according to the form of the tradition of our fathers may not be neglected by your care.

The aforementioned Cardinal Bona discusses this matter at greater length. What Anastasius understands by these words, however, I leave for others to examine.

Linea 12.—“When he had died.” Anastasius writes of this holy pontiff:

> When he had died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the eighth day of November.

Marianus Scotus also gives this in his *Chronicle*. On the other hand, since Gotfridus of Viterbo, Martin of Troppau in his *Chronicle*, the author of the *Fasciculus Temporum*, and several catalogues of the Roman pontiffs state that Deusdedit held the see for three years and twenty days, it follows that we have correctly connected his ordination with 19 October 615 and that he died on 8 November [Col. 0692D] in the year 618.

His name is not found in the Martyrology of Galesinius or in the older martyrologies, but because of his distinguished virtues Baronius entered it in the Roman Martyrology, corrected by his apostolic authority, under 8 November.

[Note: [Col. 0692D]]

Linea 9.—“He established a second Mass among the clergy.” It is not sufficiently clear what the author of the *Pontifical Book* means by these words. Some indeed believe that he permitted the sacrifice of the Mass to be repeated on the same day in places where the churches could not contain the people because of their limited size. But Saint Leo the Great had established this, as we said in the account of his pontificate.

[Col. 0685]

### 117. Deusdedit

Deusdedit, a Roman by nation, son of Stephen, a subdeacon, held the see for three years and twenty-four days.

[Note: [Col. 0685] C: twenty-three; B: three years less five days.]

He greatly loved the clergy and recalled the priests and clergy to their former places.

[Note: [Col. 0685] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 615.]

At the same time Eleutherius, the patrician and chamberlain, came to Ravenna and killed all those who had been involved in the killing of John the exarch and of the judge [Note: [Col. 0685] *C: “of the judges.”] of the republic. He came to Rome and was received most favorably by the most holy Pope Deusdedit. He went out from Rome and came to Naples, which was held by John Compsinus, the *Intarta*.

[Note: [Col. 0685] “Areata”; B: “intacta.”]

Eleutherius the patrician entered Naples by fighting, killed the tyrant, and returned to Ravenna. When a *roga* had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout all Italy. He established a second Mass among the clergy.

At the same time a great earthquake occurred in August, in the eleventh indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0685] C: sixth.]

After this a plague struck the people, the outbreak of scabies, so that no one could recognize his dead.

[Note: [Col. 0685] C: “could.”]

When he had died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the eighth day of November.

[Note: [Col. 0685] C: “the Ides of November.”]

He left one complete *roga* for his obsequies to the entire clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0685] *Roga*, a donation, so called from *erogare*, “to distribute.”]

He held three ordinations: nine presbyters,

[Note: [Col. 0685] C: fourteen.]

five deacons, and twenty-nine bishops for various places. The episcopate then ceased for one month and sixteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0685] *Sixteen.*]

### LXXI. Boniface V. Year of Christ 617, the eighth year of the emperor Heraclius

[Note: [Col. 0693A]]

#### From the Farnesian manuscript LXXI

No. 118, line 1: “he held the see for five years and ten months”; “he established.” Line 6: “he completed the cemetery of Saint Nicodemus and dedicated it.” Line 10: “in the fortress called Luceolis, where he was killed by soldiers from Ravenna; his head, etc.” “When he had died, he was buried.” Line 16: “the episcopate ceased for thirteen days.”

#### From the Vallicellian manuscript

Line 1: “from the city of Naples, son of John; he held the see for five years and ten days.” He was exceedingly gentle, kind, humble, meek—this word is redundant in the manuscript—and merciful. He established that no one should be dragged from a church and that an acolyte should not presume to [Col. 0693B] raise [relics], unless a presbyter [did so]. Line 4: “and that in the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize.” Line 5: “but the following subdeacon” (read: “subdeacons”). He established that a will should be valid according to the command of the emperor. He completed the cemetery of Saint Nicodemus (read: “Saint Nicodemus”) and dedicated it. He loved the clergy and gave his clergy a complete *roga*.

Before the day of his ordination, Eleutherius, the patrician and exarch, having become *antara*—in the margin it is noted: “*antara*, as if ἄνταρας, but read *antarta*”—seized the kingdom. Coming from the Roman city to the fortress called Luceolis, he was killed there by soldiers from Ravenna. His head was carried to Constantinople to the most pious emperor.

When the most blessed pope had died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle, and he left to the entire clergy one complete *roga* for his obsequies. He held ordinations, etc. Line 15: “December”; twenty-six presbyters. Line 16: the word “number” is lacking in the manuscript. Same line: “thirteen days of the episcopate.”

#### In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript

Line 1: “Naples, son of John.” Line 2: A: “ten days.” Line 6: B: “Nicodemus.” Lines 8–9: A: “before the days of the ordination” [Col. 0694A] “of Boniface himself.” Line 10: B: “in the fortress called Luceolis, where he was killed by soldiers from Ravenna.” Line 12: A: “to Constantinople, to the emperor.” Lines 16–17: AB: “his episcopate ceased for thirteen days.”

#### From the Regius, Mazarine, and Thuanean manuscripts

Line 1: “Naples, son of John; he held the see for five years and ten days. He was exceedingly gentle, kind, humble, and merciful.” Line 3: “from the church”; “and that an acolyte should not presume.” Line 4: “unless a presbyter”; “and that an acolyte in the Lateran should not baptize.” Line 6: “it.” “He loved the clergy and gave his clergy a complete *roga*.” Before the day of his ordination, Eleutherius, the patrician and exarch, having become Antara (read: Antarta), seized the kingdom and, coming from the Roman city to the fortress called—line 11—Luceolis, was killed there by soldiers from Ravenna. His head was carried to Constantinople to the most pious emperor. When the most blessed pope had died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle and left to the entire clergy, for his obsequies, a [Col. 0694B] complete *roga*. Line 15: twenty-six presbyters, four deacons (M: ten), and twenty-nine bishops for various places; the episcopate ceased for thirteen days.

#### From another Thuanean manuscript

Line 1: “Naples, son of John.” Line 3: “so that no acolyte should not presume.” Line 5: “should not baptize.” Line 6: “Nicomedus, and he dedicated it.” Line 8: “and the *roga*.” Line 9: “the day of the ordination”; “Eleutherius the patrician and exarch became Antarta.” Line 10: “in the fortress.” Line 11: “Luceolis”; in the same place, “he was killed by soldiers from Ravenna.” Lines 12–13: “when the most blessed pope had died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle. He left.” Line 16: “the episcopate, thirteen days”; “deposited on 25 October.”

#### In Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript

Line 1: “Naples.” Line 3: “acolyte.” Line 6: “Nicodemus.”

[Note: [Col. 0695A]]

Linea 2.—“He established that a will should be valid according to the command of the emperor.” By the decree of Boniface V it was established that wills made according to the command of the emperor—that is, according to the laws—should be valid.

Linea 3.—“He established that no one should be dragged from a church.” The decree of Boniface V was that no one should be forcibly removed from a church. The same had previously been enacted by the constitution of Theodosius, book 3, *Concerning Those Who Flee for Refuge to a Church*. Augustine, on Psalm 150:

> Such fetters bind your hands, and those of the bishops as well. Surely they do not flee into the church while wearing fetters, and are they not released here?

In the same place: “He established that an acolyte should not presume to raise the relics of the holy martyrs unless a presbyter did so.” The decree of Boniface was that an acolyte should not be permitted to carry the relics of martyrs, but only a presbyter. Nevertheless, it was the ministry of deacons to carry the relics of the saints before the bishop on solemn days. Third Council of Braga, canon 5.

[Col. 0695B] Line 4.—He decreed that at the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize with a deacon, but with the subdeacons who followed. Baptizing belonged to deacons, as it did to priests. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 17: “The highest priest, who is the bishop, has the right of administering baptism; thereafter, the priests and deacons, yet not without the bishop’s authority, for the honor of the Church.” Jerome, *To the Luciferian*: “I do not indeed deny that this is the custom of the Churches: that the bishop should hasten to those who, in distant smaller towns, have been baptized by priests and deacons, in order to lay his hand upon them at the invocation of the Holy Spirit.” Boniface’s decree was a particular one: that in the Lateran basilica a deacon should not baptize with an acolyte, but with a subdeacon.

Line 10.—The fortress called Luceolis. Anastasius mentions it in his account of Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0695B]

Line 2.—“That the testament should be valid according to the command of the prince.” Why Boniface decreed this, what law concerning testaments he had in mind, and which prince the author of these Acts—whoever he may be—intended, is not clear to me. Did he mean the Roman laws of the ancient emperors, or some recent law promulgated on this matter by the emperor Heraclius? Certainly neither. For Roman citizens were all, without exception, unquestionably governed by Roman law in appointing heirs; and no one could assert, on any grounds whatever, that new laws concerning testaments had been enacted at this time by the emperor Heraclius. Or had it been doubted whether testaments written according to the laws of the princes were valid, so that the pontiff had to reply that they were valid? Nothing could be less likely.

Shall we perhaps suppose that Pope Boniface had turned his attention to Lombard law and declared a testament made according to it valid? But why would he at this time apply Lombard law to Romans, who were governed by the Greek emperors and the exarch of Ravenna solely by Roman laws? Moreover, no written law was published among the Lombards until the year 643, when King Rothari published his edict, in which, at numbers 157 and following, he issued several provisions concerning testaments—that is, in the year 643 or 644. For, according to Paul the Deacon, Rothari’s edict appeared in the seventy-seventh year of the Lombard kingdom; and according to his chronology—which Pagius vainly shortens in the *Critica* on the authority of Sigebert—Alboin reigned from the year 568 for three years and seven months; Cleph for one year and six months; then, after an interregnum of ten years, Authari for six years, Agilulf for twenty-five, Adaloald for ten, and Arioald for twelve; after that came Rothari. Rothari’s election fell in the year 636, but in the sixty-eighth year of the Lombard kingdom. Consequently, the eight years remaining until the completion of the seventy-sixth year would be years of Rothari’s reign corresponding to indiction II. These are the chronological signs contained in the very prologue of the edict.

Thus one or another diploma of the Cassinese *Bullarium* is not so weighty as Pagius thought in the year 626, that it could overturn Paul the Deacon’s account, which distinguishes the periods of Adaloald and Arioald, and moreover compel us to tamper with the royal edict and read “the eighteenth year of my reign” instead of “the eighth.” When A. Muratori saw this, in the preface to the Lombard Laws, volume I, part II of the *Rerum Italicarum*, I do not know why he moved the promulgation of the edict back to the year 638, despite the chronology of the Lombard kingdom, which Paul the Deacon and the royal edict themselves record with a difference of only one year. But this is incidental.

To return to our subject: since laws of this kind appeared a full eighteen years after the death of Boniface V, the pontiff could not possibly have had them in mind. Either, therefore, the author of the *Gesta pontificalia* is again suffering from chronological confusion and attributes to Boniface a decree belonging to one of his successors—for it later happened that Lombard law prevailed throughout all Italy alongside Roman law, and at that time I have no doubt that similar declarations could have been issued by the pontiffs—or, if one prefers to preserve complete confidence in Anastasius, we may conjecturally suppose that the pontiff approved one of the customs which the Lombards had used in place of laws down to Rothari: the custom they employed in making testaments. Perhaps also Agilulf or Adaloald had promulgated a special law concerning these matters for their own people and for the peoples of Italy, and the pontiff had confirmed it by his decree while minds were wavering between Roman law and these new laws—namely, that in those very places where Lombards administered their estates and where the Patrimony of Saint Peter lay, testaments made according to their customs or laws should be valid once confirmed by recognition in the royal chancery. Examples of such recognition occur in a deed of donation made by Berengar, preserved by Bacchinius, and the matter is established in diplomas published by Baronius, Mabillon, and others.

Which of these explanations is the more correct, I do not wish to decide. Let the choice rest with the reader.

Line 5.—“The subdeacons who followed.” That is, those who followed the deacons in their ministry. For when the deacon baptized, it was not acolytes or others who assisted, but subdeacons who served the one performing the sacred rite.

[Note: [Col. 0696C]

Line 1.—Boniface. On the fourteenth—or, according to another reading, the twenty-fourth—of December, in the year of the Lord 617, after an interregnum of one month and six, or sixteen, days, Boniface V, a Neapolitan by birth, was made pontiff. During his time lived Muhammad the Arab, a false prophet and scourge of the world, from whom the sect of the Muslims took its origin. In order to draw all peoples into his sect, he adopted something from nearly every religion: from the Jews, circumcision, worship of one God, and abstinence from pork; from the Christians, Christ, but created with the Arians, a mere man with the Nestorians, and crucified not truly but only apparently with the Manichaeans; from the pagans, worship of the moon or of some star. He taught that the law he proposed was extremely foolish and was to be propagated by arms, and he forbade it to be examined through disputation. See John of Damascus, *On Heresies*; Theophanes; and Cedrenus under Heraclius; Baronius, under the year 630.]

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

The vacancy of the see from the deposition of Saint Deusdedit is correctly given by the commonly circulated codex of Anastasius and by most other codices, both manuscript and printed, as one month and sixteen days, although some—for example, the two Freherian codices together with the Farfa catalogue—give thirteen days, omitting the month. The Regius and Thuanus codices give one month and fifteen days; another Thuanus gives only sixteen days.

The reason why the see remained vacant for so short a period is clear. Heraclius, from whom the command had to be sought, was being harassed by the Persians, who were holding his mistreated ambassadors bound in prison; Constantinople was suffering from famine and plague; the exarch Eleutherius, taking advantage both of the emperor’s extraordinary distress and of the interregnum, had seized tyranny, and had therefore been murdered by the people of Ravenna. Meanwhile Rome was being ravaged by the elephantine disease, which had recently broken out and was spreading. For these serious reasons the command seems neither to have been sought nor awaited.

Hence, apart from the codices and catalogues mentioned above, Hermannus Contractus, Marianus Scotus, and Sigebert place the election of Boniface V in the year 618, and so understand the vacancy not to have been long. Finally, Bede, an eighth-century writer, says in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation*, book II, chapter 7: “Boniface,” he says, “who presided over the Church after Deusdedit, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 618.” Pagius wants this passage, indeed the whole edition of Bede used by Baronius, to be corrupt, and urges recourse to the Chiffletian and Cambridge copies, which read “the nineteenth.” Yet, with due respect to that most learned man, I carefully examined several editions of Bede: the old Basel edition of 1563, the Antwerp edition printed under the care of Gravius at Cologne in 1612, and another edition published there in 1688, the most carefully corrected of all. Everywhere I found the year 618. I preferred to place greater trust in these editions, since they agree with so many codices and catalogues of Anastasius, than in the two copies corrected according to the judgment of recent editors, especially in the Chiffletian attempt to reconcile Bede with Fredegarius.

Antonio Pagius, however, favors the following evidence. Setting aside the authority of five of the seven older catalogues and of the most weighty writers cited in the *Critica* of Baronius, he embraced above all the sixth catalogue, written toward the end of the twelfth century, which gives a vacancy of one year and six days. Since that period does not fill the interregnum after Deusdedit, he draws forty days from his own repositories, thereby arriving at the day of Boniface V’s ordination; for the fixed duration of Boniface’s pontificate and the fixed beginning of Honorius convinced him that the latter could not have been delayed beyond Sunday, 23 December of the aforesaid year 619.

[Col. 0697C] I cannot deny that I was almost carried away into Pagius’s conjecture when I saw that, unless the entire chronology is to be ruined, a full year must be added between Deusdedit and Honorius. But the best codices plainly showed that, with Baronius, this year ought not to be added to the see of Boniface: the Farnesianus and Ambrosianus 3—while the others either remain silent or indicate a corrupt reading in the published passage, giving ten days instead of thirteen—as well as catalogue 2 of Mabillon. All agree with the epitaph written before Boniface was buried, which Baronius quotes in volume XII, appendix to volume XIII of Aringhus’s *Subterranean Rome*, book II, chapter 8, and which reads:

> He ruled the apostolic summit five and twice months, years,  
> And departed to the summit of great honor.

That is, according to the interpretation of Papebrochius, Pagius, and all the learned, Boniface sat for five years and ten months. I therefore acknowledged that the additional year had necessarily to be assigned to one or the other of the interregnums, either after Deusdedit or after Boniface V.

Why I departed from the learned Pagius, preferring to add it after Boniface without damage to the chronology of Anastasius, was determined both by the authorities supporting the ordination of Boniface and by the narrowness of the period between his death and the ordination of Honorius. These make it clear that Pagius had improperly delayed the beginning of Boniface’s pontificate, as I shall say in the discussion of Honorius. To this may be added the reasons recently mentioned, which persuaded men to disregard the imperial command even in the consecration of Pelagius II, although they were much less serious.

The chief reason that moved Pagius, however, is the two letters of Boniface to Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, and to his wife Ethelberga, which Bede recites after the ordination of Saint Paulinus, the first bishop of York. Bede says that Paulinus was ordained on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, that is, 21 July of the year 625 (*Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book II, chapter 9). Lest anyone think this an error—for in the *Epitome* the year is given as 622—Bede records the death of Paulinus on 10 October 644, the sixth day before the Ides (*ibid.*, book III, chapter 14), after he had held the episcopate, he says, for nineteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. Nothing more precise could be desired in this chronology.

In particular, Paulinus was ordained by Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, who succeeded Mellitus, recalled to heaven in the year 624, on 24 April. Before that, while administering the Church of Rochester, Justus had not possessed the authority to ordain bishops. Yet, although the date of Paulinus’s ordination is established, we are not thereby compelled to place the letters of Boniface after that ordination, since no chronological indication forces us to do so. We learn from Bede himself, in several passages of his *History of the English*, that he was accustomed to relate events belonging to the same matter without regard to their chronological order. The clearest examples are chapters 17 and 18 of book II, where one first reads that the pallium was sent to Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, and only afterward hears of the death of Justus, whom Honorius succeeded.

For this reason I regard it as certain that Boniface sent the two letters before Ethelberga, and with her Paulinus, departed for York. Everything contained in them had been arranged through messengers sent back and forth, as is evident to anyone who reads them. I have no doubt that the exhortation to Edwin and the letter to Ethelberga were carefully arranged by her most devout brother, King Eadbald, while negotiations were taking place concerning the marriage, the dispatch of a Catholic retinue for Ethelberga, and the ordination of a bishop for the Northumbrian people, so that they might carry the exhortation to Edwin with them. In that letter there is no mention of Saint Paulinus—not even of a bishop—but only of the preaching of the Gospel.

Moreover, since Bede was a very ancient writer who committed these events to writing more than a hundred years after they occurred, I do not see why his chronology should be preferred to all others. Indeed, I find it highly suspicious. For Bede says in the same chapter 9 that on the night of Saint Easter in the year 626—falling on 20 April—Ethelberga’s daughter Eanfled was born. What are we to make of this? Paulinus is ordained on 21 July of the preceding year to marry Ethelberga; he must still travel from Canterbury to York; then Ethelberga herself makes the journey with the new bishop and the entire royal retinue—a journey certainly lasting several days—and in the following year, on 20 April, gives birth to Eanfled, before nine full months have elapsed? Let posterity believe it.

Therefore, lest we assert something absurd while pressed by so many difficulties on every side, we assign the interregnum after Boniface and arrange the chronology of that pontiff with Anastasius as follows. Saint Deusdedit was deposited at Saint Peter’s on 8 November 618. After an interregnum of one month and sixteen days, his successor Boniface V was ordained on 24 December of that year, which A in the Dominical Letter shows to have fallen on a Sunday. He comforted his sheep, who were daily dying shamefully while the plague of scabies raged.

After sitting for five years and ten months, he died on 24 October 624 and was deposited the following day at Saint Peter’s, as the codices of Anastasius, both printed and manuscript, correctly attest. His death was followed by the longest interregnum, as I shall explain in the discussion of Honorius.]

Line 1.—Boniface. A Campanian by nation, a Neapolitan by birthplace, son of John Fumminus, the ninth pope from the native population, during the reign of the emperor Flavius Heraclius, he sat for five years and ten months. He was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, at the beginning of the year of the Lord 617. During this period Boniface wrote to Edwin, king of the English, and to Ethelberga, the queen, earnestly urging them to restrain their subjects from idols and the worship of idols. A copy of these letters, in which Boniface introduces himself as “the bishop, servant of the servants of God,” is preserved in Bede, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History of His Nation*.

[Note: [Col. 0698D]

Line 6.—“He completed the cemetery of Saint Nicomedes.” That is, he enlarged and restored the cemetery of Saint Nicomedes. The agreement among writers on subterranean Rome is that it was situated not on the Via Ardeatina, as Onuphrius wrote in his catalogue of cemeteries, but on the Via Nomentana, near the walls of the City. The church of Saint Nicomedes was also located there. Since it was collapsing from age, Hadrian I restored it, as Anastasius reports below. But through the ravages of time it was so leveled with the ground that in our own age scarcely any ruins of it are visible.

As for the cemetery, since it was unknown before Bosio, Bosio was the first to discover it, in 1601, near the walls of the City on the Via Nomentana. It comprises three or four paths and an equal number of chambers.]

[Note: [Col. 0699A]

Line 12.—“Who, having died, was buried.” After Boniface sent those letters to England, he did not survive for long. In the same year, 625, on 22 October, he died; and, as Anastasius records, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 25 October, after sitting for five years and ten months. This duration is given by Gotfridus of Viterbo in his *Chronicle*, by Liutprand, by the *Catalogue of Apostolic Names*, by the Colbertine manuscript of Anastasius, and by four of the catalogues prefixed to Baronius’s *Critica*. The matter is placed beyond doubt by his epitaph, quoted by Baronius, which ends with these two verses:

> He ruled the apostolic summit five and twice months, years,  
> And departed to the summit of great honor.

][Col. 0693]

118. Boniface, a Campanian by nation, from the city of Naples; he sat for five years and thirteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0693] B gives seven years, ten months, and one day.] He decreed that a testament should be valid according to the command of the prince. He decreed that no one should be dragged out of a church. He decreed that an acolyte should not presume to carry away the relics of holy martyrs unless he were a priest. He decreed that at the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize with a deacon, but with the subdeacons who followed. He completed and dedicated the cemetery of Saint Nicodemus [Note: [Col. 0693] *Nicomedis, “of Nicomedes.”]. For the blessed Boniface was exceedingly gentle and merciful toward all people. He loved the clergy and gave his entire dole to his clergy.

At the same time, before the day of his ordination, Eleutherius, the patrician and eunuch who had been made *Intarta* [Note: [Col. 0693] *Antara], seized the kingdom. When he came to the Roman city, he was killed by the soldiers of Ravenna in the fortress called Luceolis [Note: [Col. 0693] *in castro*, “in the fortress”; *a militibus Ravennaticis*, “by the soldiers of Ravenna.”]. His head was taken to Constantinople to the most devout emperor.

After he died, he was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 25 October. He left to all the clergy one full dole for his funeral expenses [Note: [Col. 0693] *pro obsequiis suis*, “for his funeral rites.”]. He held two ordinations in the month of December: twenty-seven priests, four deacons, and twenty-nine bishops in various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for six months and eighteen days.

LXXII. HONORIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 626, THE SEVENTEENTH YEAR OF HERACLIUS.

Line 5.—“He covered the royal doors at the entrance of the principal church, which are called the Middle Doors, with silver.” The royal doors are the larger doors of churches. John the Monk, in the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, speaks of a boar whom he calls extraordinary: “But he, having put aside his fierceness so that access might be granted to anyone entering, beat for a long time upon the royal doors mentioned above and smeared them with the foam of his mouth wherever he could make it adhere.” The basilica door is the same thing. Frodoard, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 820: “At Rheims, in the monastery of Saint Peter, at the basilica door.” The same writer, book IV of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 46, calls the principal door of the basilica of Saint Peter the royal door. Paulinus, letter 33: “Into the vast basilica of glorious Peter, through that venerable royal door, smiling from afar with its blue façade.” Anastasius, in his account of Conon: “He kept watch over those who had been sent from the army to guard the closed royal doors of the basilica.” The same, in his account of Gregory III: “From the arch of the altar as far as the royal doors.” The same, in his account of Leo III: “In the basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger, at the entrance of the manger, he made royal doors covered with the purest silver.”

Number 120, line 12.—“And the water-channel that brings water into the Sabbatine Lake, and beneath it the channel that conveys the water of the Tiber.” Honorius brought a channel—that is, an aqueduct—from Lake Sabbatena into the City, into the atrium of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle. Hadrian I restored the same channel. Anastasius, in his life of Hadrian: “The channel called Sabbatena, being exceedingly broken, through which water flowed by way of the Centenarium into the atrium of the church of blessed Peter the Apostle,” and so forth. Gregory IV also restored it. Anastasius, in his life of Gregory: “The channel called Sabbatena,” and so forth.

The Sabbatine channel is one that comes from Lake Sabatenus, which is called *Angularius*, in the law *Rutilia Polla*, in the Digest, *On Contracts of Sale*. Hence its name derives from the three angles presented by the Via Aurelia, which leads to the Vatican, as Platina taught us in his account of Hadrian. In the atria of churches there were *chantari*, or water fountains, whose waters were brought from outside at great expense through pipes for the use of the churches. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II: “He likewise repaired the church of Saint Laurence situated outside the walls, and, after a long time, brought water back into the same church through joined pipes.”

[Col. 0704A] Line 16.—“He made a church for blessed Adrian the martyr in the Three Fates, and dedicated it.” The Three Fates was a place in the City, mentioned by Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, book IX, near the end. This is also confirmed by another passage of Anastasius in his account of Hadrian: “In the church of the blessed Cosmas and Damian in the Three Fates he made a garment of *stauracin*.” And again: “He restored the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian situated in the Three Fates.” I do not claim another’s observation as my own; Lacerda already noted this, *Adversaria*, chapter 149, number 27.

Perhaps one should instead read “the Three Harvests,” that is, “three years,” according to the common speech of country people, who count years by harvests or crops. Virgil, *Eclogue* 1:

> After some years, when I see my little realm, I shall marvel at the ears of corn.

][Note: [Col. 0704A]

Number 119, line 1.—Honorius, a Campanian by nation, son of Petronius the consul, sat for twelve years, eleven months, and seventeen days. I submit for the consideration of learned readers a facsimile of a lead bull stamped with the sacred name of Pope Honorius, which is kept in my museum among many other lead bulls whose collection I have been pursuing for many years. If fortune should favor my wishes, if funds and life should be available, with God’s help, I shall publish a series of pontifical lead bulls, to which I shall append others of various kinds as an appendix. I expect their number to increase daily; from this, ecclesiastical scholarship will be enriched, and something will also redound to the honor and glory of the Holy See.

Although this kind of study may appear entirely barren and unattractive, it nevertheless has its own charms and usefulness. It is certainly neither ignoble nor fruitless to observe the practice, from the ancient centuries of the Church, by which the Roman pontiffs signed and sealed public diplomas in their own names on a lead bull, as an authentic mark of truth, passing a hempen or silk thread through the body of the bull and intertwining it with the membrane so that it could not be torn away without breaking it. One may also observe the variations that these same bulls underwent over the course of time, and record many other circumstances that would otherwise escape the notice of those attending to other matters.

[Col. 0703D] This bull of Honorius is older than any other represented by writers, with the sole exception of a bull of Saint Deusdedit, who preceded Honorius by only eleven years. That bull was recently published at Florence, among the Donian inscriptions, from the treasury of the noble and learned Baron Philipp von Stosch, by Antonio Francesco Gori, a man adorned with every kind of learning and rightly numbered among the very few who are said to have been born for the public good.

This bull demonstrates the antiquity of the Roman Church’s practice of impressing its seal in lead, against those who consider the practice to have been introduced only later and to have become fully established only in the ninth or tenth century. Polydore Vergil, book VIII of *On the Discovery of Things*, chapter 2, speaks as follows about Roman bulls:

> “I long sought to discover how the practice of sealing the letters of the Roman pontiff with lead came down to posterity, since lead is so precious that, I believe, it hides itself again in the bowels of the earth so that it may not become anyone’s booty, while only the Roman pontiffs use it. It is sufficiently established that Agatho, during whose pontificate the Holy See received a great increase of honor, impressed seals in wax with a ring. But afterward, when the Roman pontiff was granting many privileges and it was desired that the diplomas should last longer, Stephen III and then Hadrian I decided that apostolic documents should be sealed with lead. This was in the year of salvation 772, when Hadrian himself became pontiff, for no earlier lead seal is found.”

Our bull of Honorius must be placed between the year 621 and the year 638, the span covered by the pontificate of Honorius.

John Michael Heineccius reports in his book *On the Seals of the Ancient Germans*, part I, chapter 5, from Thomas Stubbs, as cited by Mabillon in book II, chapter 14 of *On Diplomatics*:

> “When a dispute arose between William of Canterbury and Thurstan of York, prelates, and the former brought forward the privileges of his Church in support of his claim, a question arose concerning the authenticity of the diplomas, because lead bulls were lacking from them. When the man of Canterbury said that lead bulls had not at that time been customary, the man of York produced diplomas of Popes Gregory I and Honorius, already furnished with lead bulls.”

But Dominicus Raynaldus, in Leo Allatius’s *On the Perpetual Agreement of the Western and Eastern Churches*, book I, chapter 6, not only mentions the bulls of Leo I, Gregory I, and Sergius I, which he says are preserved in the archive of the Castel Sant’Angelo, but goes back as far as the time of Saint Sylvester, whose lead bull he asserts is found in the Arezzo archive.

I would not dare to deny this, but neither would I concede it. I am entirely certain of this: Honorius I used a lead seal, and I possess one of his seals. From it I date not the beginning of the use of the pontifical seal in lead—for I believe that practice began much earlier—but rather the earliest point at which I have been fortunate enough to acquire a bull. Thus I can affirm that this bull is unquestionably genuine and belongs to Honorius I. The integrity and neatness of the letters, the small size of the lead disk, and the bare and solitary name “Honorius,” without any numeral identifying a second or third, demonstrate this most clearly. Bulls of the other Honorius, issued after the first, bear the Roman numeral II or III. For before the year 1000, the pontiff’s name was written by itself, without a numeral distinguishing several popes of the same name. The first pope to add a numeral to lead bulls was Leo IX, who became pope in 1048; he was followed by Victor II and all the others thereafter, including Honorius II, who ascended the pontifical throne in 1124.

It is therefore clear that Dominicus Raynaldus—and likewise John Palatius in his *Deeds of the Pontiffs*—had no secure foundation for assigning bulls stamped with the names Leo, Gregory, Sergius, and Sylvester to the first popes of those names. Popes bearing the same names may with equal right claim all seals stamped with those names, since, as I have said, before the year 1000 they lack a numeral. Perhaps the bull of Rieti (*bulla Reatina*) to which the same author assigns priority belongs to Sylvester II, elected pope in the year 999.

[Col. 0706A] I do not deny that the form of the letters can provide some indication of the period in which they were engraved. But we cannot rely on it with certainty, both because the pope’s name is generally represented by only a few letters, which can scarcely, or not at all, suffice to convey an idea of the script then in use, and because changes in letters ordinarily arise only over a long interval of time—so that within a century several popes bearing the same name may appear.

There would be one way to assign such unnumbered bulls securely to their respective popes: namely, if the bulls were still attached to their membranes. For then the identity of their author could easily be learned from reading, carefully inspecting, and examining the diploma. But to discover the author from the lead bull alone is, in my judgment, a futile labor.]

[Note: [Col. 0706A]

## No. 119, line 12 — On the Temple

This temple, from which Honorius, with the consent of the emperor Heraclius, removed the bronze plates—or, as the manuscripts of Regius, Freher, Mazarini, and both Thuani have it, the bronze tiles—and with which he covered the entire church of blessed Peter, is called “the Temple” at Rome, but in other manuscripts “the Temple of Romulus.”

The former temple, that of Rome—which was impiously worshipped as a goddess—was built by Hadrian and joined to the temple of Venus. Dio says the following about it in Book LXIX:

> “Hadrian himself, sending him [that is, Apollodorus the architect] the plan of the temple of Venus and Rome, thereby indicating that even enormous buildings could be constructed without his skill and assistance, asked whether the building was properly designed. Apollodorus wrote back that the temple ought to be made both lofty and concave, so that from the higher place there might be a more distinguished and conspicuous view all the way to the Sacred Way. It should be concave in order to receive the theatrical mechanisms, which could be assembled secretly inside it and then brought from there into the theater by a hidden route.”

Where such a temple stood, Anastasius himself can teach us. In his Life of Felix IV he wrote:

> “He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the city of Rome, in the place called the Sacred Way, beside the Temple of the City of Rome.”

It was therefore not far from the amphitheater, since, according to the description of Apollodorus the mathematician, the theatrical mechanisms were to be taken from there and brought back to the same place. For this reason many are convinced that the two enclosures still surviving in the gardens of Saint Mary the New are the ruins of this temple.

It was of such great renown that the coins of the emperors themselves were marked with it. Coins of this kind were recently dug up in our Piedmontese territory near Mondovì and are preserved in the royal treasury; perhaps one day they will be brought before the eyes of scholars.

But if you prefer the Temple of Romulus mentioned by Anastasius, this too enjoyed no little veneration among the Romans. Dionysius of Halicarnassus speaks of it in Book I, where he discusses the Lupercal:

> “Along the road that leads to the Circus there is shown a temple nearby, in which is the She-Wolf giving her breasts to two boys.”

It therefore stood at the Lupercal, in the eighth region, beyond the Curia, or at the Basilica Porcia, where the church of Saint Mary the Liberator now stands.

Meanwhile, from these pontifical Acts we learn that one or the other of these temples survived into the Christian sixth century, rich in bronze plates and statues, and perhaps preserved for so long by the rulers because it contained images of the ancient Caesars.

## No. 119, line 1 — Honorius

In the year of our Redemption 626, on the thirteenth day of May, Honorius of Campania was made Roman pontiff. During his pontificate the heresy of the Monothelites arose and spread.

Whether Honorius was a Monothelite is a serious question. The more probable opinion, however, is that held by almost all the orthodox scholars of our time: namely, that Honorius is cleared of every stain of having embraced the heresy.

The Monothelites opposed him, claiming him as their own. But Maximus, in his controversy with Pyrrhus, together with John IV, Martin I, Agatho, and several other Roman pontiffs, fought on his behalf and claimed Honorius for themselves.

See the very learned annotation of Severinus Binius in volume V of the Councils, under the Life of Honorius; Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, Book IV, chapter 11; and Baronius, under the year 633.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Necessity and the calamity of the times once persuaded the Roman clergy and people to dare to proceed with the election and consecration of Boniface V. From Anastasius himself, and from the agreement of all the catalogues and manuscripts, it is clear that this was not done in the case of his successor Honorius.

For if Honorius occupied the see for twelve years, eleven months, and sixteen days, and died (or was laid to rest) on 12 October, as everyone most consistently maintains, he was ordained on 27 October. Counting inclusively down to the day of his death, there are therefore exactly as many years, months, and days as the period of Honorius’s reign.

Since 27 October was a Sunday in the year 625, as the dominical letter F indicates, the interregnum consequently lasted one year and three days, not merely thirteen days, as almost all the manuscripts and catalogues have it, except the vulgate, which irrationally gives a vacancy of six months and eighteen days.

Antony Pagi correctly observed that the beginning of Honorius’s pontificate cannot be placed later than the year 625. He argues this from the pontiff’s letter to the bishops of Epirus, dated 12 December of indiction XIV, which survives in Holstenius’s *Roman Collection*, p. 248. Papebroch considers this letter corrupt because it contradicts itself as a result of a year having been subtracted from Honorius’s reign; Papebroch places its beginning in the year 626. Pagi therefore argues against Papebroch under the year 625, no. 16, as though he had not seen that collection.

Here, however, the error of Pagi—otherwise a most learned man—is evident. For although, following Anastasius, he fixes the burial (*depositio*) on 25 October, and moves Honorius’s death back by two days, he nevertheless admits that Honorius was ordained on 27 October of that same year.

What ears can endure the claim that only a single intervening day separated the death from the election and ordination of a pontiff—especially at a time when the emperor’s command was awaited from Constantinople—and that this occurred without any canonical election, indeed directly contrary to the decree of Boniface III, issued only a few years earlier, that a pontiff should not be elected until the third day after the deposition?

To this must be added the authority of the contemporary *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs. In the chapter “On the Election of a Pontiff,” under the heading “To the Exarch,” it reads:

> “When he who belonged to the pontifical memory had been summoned from these present cares to eternal rest, as commonly happens in human affairs, a great burden of sorrow overwhelmed us because we had been deprived of our own steward. But the accustomed goodness of our God did not abandon those who hoped in him, leaving us long in affliction. For while we remained in prayer for three short days, so that the heavenly favor might reveal to all minds whom it judged worthy,” etc.

Certainly, unless Pagi, misled by the passage in Bede, had extended the see of Boniface V beyond what was reasonable, he would not be caught in these difficulties.

Since the matter stands thus, the vacancy of the see between Boniface and Honorius is evident in itself: one year and three days. The error found in nearly all the manuscripts and catalogues, which give thirteen days, arose, as I think, from the Arabic numeral 13, written without points according to the ancient barbarous practice of a later age.

As for the day of Honorius’s death, or deposition, it is clear from Anastasius. That the year was 638 is agreed by all learned men, especially Papebroch in his *Historical Essay*, Sirmond in his *Synopsis* of the Collection, Anastasius, and Antony Pagi.

I have therefore thought that this uncertain year, which others have divided in different directions, should be restored in this manner. If this restoration does not please the reader, let the matter be investigated more successfully elsewhere.

## No. 119, line 1 — Honorius

Honorius, son of Petronius de la Mara, a man of consular rank, a Campanian, the tenth pope from the local population, sat in the chair of Peter under the emperor Flavius Heraclius for twelve years, eleven months, and seven days. He was created and consecrated on Sunday, 7 November, in the year 622.

In the published manuscripts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, the charge of the Monothelite heresy is unjustly brought against this most holy man, although it is entirely false that he ever subscribed to that heresy. On the contrary, it is clear that he condemned it, as is sufficiently evident from the Greek letters of Maximus the monk, his contemporary, who lived under Pope Martin, and from his dialogue against Pyrrhus, the Monothelite heretical patriarch of Constantinople, which is preserved in the Palatine Library.

That this same pontiff was always Catholic was also confirmed in writing by the Greek Emmanuel Calles, Cardinal John de Turrecremata in his book *On the Primacy of the Holy Roman Church*, and, in our own time, Albert Pighius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

Moreover, that the commonly circulated copies of the Sixth Council were corrupted by the Greeks, and that its canons, in which Honorius is condemned, are spurious, Anastasius the Librarian demonstrates from the Greek historian Theophanes Isaurianus in his own Latin history, which he composed from Theophanes, Nicephorus, and the abbot George.

These observations were made by Guglielmo Sirleto of Calabria when he was protonotary of the Apostolic See. Since he was endowed to the highest degree with learning, piety, and every kind of virtue, he deserved promotion to the college of cardinals, and his memory is now blessed.

**Line 11 — “He covered the church.”**  
He covered the Basilica of Saint Peter with bronze tiles taken from the Capitoline Jupiter.

**Line 13 — “He built the church of blessed Agnes.”**  
As the poem in the apse indicates.

## No. 119, line 2 — “But also many other things”

Among the many other deeds of Pope Honorius was this: he brought peoples who were strangers to the Christian religion to faith in Christ by sending ministers of the word of God to instruct them.

Bede testifies that Honorius sent Bishop Birinus to Britain, through whom the West Saxons received the Christian faith. He writes in Book III, chapter 7:

> “At that time the nation of the West Saxons, who in ancient times were called Gewissae, received the faith of Christ during the reign of Cynigils, when Bishop Birinus preached the word to them. He had come to Britain with the counsel of Pope Honorius, promising that, in the presence of the pope, he would sow the seeds of the holy faith in the innermost parts beyond the Angles, where no teacher had gone before. Therefore, by the command of that same pontiff, he was consecrated to the episcopal rank by Asterius, bishop of Genoa.”

## No. 119, line 3 — “During his pontificate he renewed,” etc.

Many admirable things are found in Anastasius concerning Honorius’s reverence for divine worship in arranging ecclesiastical affairs, and his generosity in building, adorning, and endowing churches.

He renewed almost the entire clergy; covered the Basilica of Saint Peter with bronze tiles taken from the Capitoline Jupiter; covered Saint Peter’s altar with silver; and added many other ornaments.

He rebuilt from the foundations the church of Saint Agnes the martyr. He restored the church of Saint Pancratius on the Via Aurelia, the church of Anastasius at the Aquae Salvianae, and the church of the Four Crowned Martyrs. He built the church of Saint Severinus near the city of Tibur with magnificent workmanship, and adorned it with silver, gold, porphyry, and marble stones, with wall inlay, stucco, and mosaic work.

He also restored the cemetery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter. He restored many other churches and built many anew. He was the first to establish that every Saturday the people should go with litanies from Saint Apollinaris to Saint Peter.

Still more remarkable is the fact attested by his epitaph and by another ancient inscription reported by Canisius in volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*: namely, that he extinguished the schism of Istria concerning the Three Chapters. This is no small distinction.

But since we have shown under Saint Gregory that this schism lasted until the pontificate of Sergius, either it was not completely suppressed under Honorius, or the schismatics fell back into it after Honorius’s death.

## No. 120, line 20 — “Who was also buried”

Pope Honorius finally died on 12 October 638, after, as Anastasius says, having sat for twelve years, eleven months, and seventeen days. The day of his ordination and the day of his death or burial have evidently been combined in the total, as often happens. It therefore becomes clear that, following the intention of Anastasius, we correctly connected his ordination with 27 October 625, since, according to the same witness, he died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on 12 October.

## 119 — Honorius

Honorius, a Campanian by nationality, son of the consul Petronius, sat for twelve years, eleven months, and seventeen days.

He clad the shrine (*confessio*) of blessed Peter with pure silver, weighing 187 pounds. He covered the royal doors at the main entrance of the church, called the middle doors, with silver, weighing 975 pounds. He also made two pairs of large silver *cerostata* (candelabra).

**[Note: “large *cerostata*.”]

They stand before the body of blessed Peter the Apostle, each weighing 272 pounds. He also made silver panels before the shrine (*confessio*) of blessed Andrew the Apostle, at the place mentioned above, weighing 73 pounds.

He adorned and embellished it on every side and placed many gifts there. He adorned her tomb with silver, weighing 252 pounds. Above it he placed a bronze, gilded canopy of marvelous size.

He also made four golden *gabatha* (bowls),

**[Note: C has three *gabatae*.]

each weighing one pound. He made the apse of the same basilica in mosaic,

**[Note: “mosaic work.”]

## 120

He established a regulation in the Church and decreed that every week, on Saturday, a litany should go forth to blessed Apollinaris and to blessed Peter the Apostle, and that all the people should assemble with hymns and songs.

He also built from the foundations a church for blessed Cyriacus the martyr, on the Ostian Way seven miles from the city, where he also offered a gift.

At the same time he built the church of the Four Blessed Crowned Martyrs, dedicated it, and offered a gift there.

He built the church of blessed Severinus from the foundations near the city of Tibur, twenty miles from the city of Rome. He himself dedicated it and offered many gifts there.

He renewed the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter on the Lavican Way.

At the same time he built from the foundations the basilica of blessed Pancratius the martyr on the Via Aurelia, two miles from the city, and adorned his tomb with silver weighing 120 pounds.

There he also established a mill on the wall at Trajan’s place beside the city wall, and an aqueduct which leads water into the Sabatine Lake, with another aqueduct beneath it which conveys the water of the Tiber.

He also made a silver canopy over the altar, weighing 287 pounds.

**[Note: C has 187 pounds.]

He made five silver arches, each weighing fifteen pounds. He also made three golden candlesticks, each weighing one pound, and offered many gifts there at the same time.

He built the church of blessed Hadrian the martyr at the Three Fates,

**[Note: C has “outside.”]

which it would be lengthy to enumerate.

**[Note: C has eleven,]
