## No. 121, line 2 — “The Lateran episcopal residence was devastated”

During his pontificate the Lateran episcopal residence was devastated by Mauritius the chartularius and Isaac the patrician and exarch of Italy, while the lord Severinus was still elected.

While Severinus was still elected—that is, elected but not yet consecrated—the episcopal residence, namely the Lateran patriarchium, was plundered by Mauritius the chartularius and Isaac the patrician and exarch of Italy.

The possessions of vacant churches were customarily plundered by the populace. This kind of plundering was called *levae*, from the verb *levare*, “to take away.” It was prohibited by Victor III.

Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book II, chapter 97:

> “The riots which they call *levae*, or plunderings, which he had learned were accustomed to occur here upon the death of an abbot, Pope Victor III most strictly forbade, so that they might not happen again.”

Peter Damian, Book V, letter 6:

> “By widespread report we have learned of the custom of the common people: when their bishop has died, they violently break into and seize the bishop’s house, plunder his possessions like robbers, invade the houses on his estates, and even cut down the vines and orchards with a savagery more brutal than that of beasts. Unless this is corrected by the discipline of ecclesiastical vigor, there is no doubt that the sword of sudden fury threatens those regions.”

The fury of the Roman populace in plundering the pontifical residences during a vacancy of the see did not cease.

Monstrelet, *Chronicle*, vol. I, chapter 62, concerning the election of John XXIII:

> “And immediately his entire house was forced open, and everything found there was carried away; indeed, neither door nor window remained, for everything had been removed.”

The Lateran Basilica is the first among the patriarchal churches of the city of Rome. It is so called because the house of the Lateran was converted into a church.

Jerome, *To Oceanus, concerning Fabiola*:

> “In the Basilica once belonging to the Lateran, which was cut down by the Caesarian sword.”

The Lateran episcopal residence, or patriarchium, is attached to the Lateran Basilica because it was there that the dwelling and palace of the ancient Roman pontiffs stood.

Anastasius, in his accounts of Vigilius and Stephen III:

> “When the Augusta heard this, she sent Anthemius the notary with her commands and with a greater force to Rome, saying: ‘Except in the Basilica of Saint Peter, spare no one. For if you find Vigilius in the Lateran, in the palace, or in any church, immediately put him on a ship and bring him to us.’”

Radevicus, *On the Deeds of Frederick*, Book I, chapter 10:

> “Hence, concerning the emperor Lothair, this was written in the Lateran palace above such a picture:
>
> ‘The king comes before the gates, first swearing the honors of the City;
>
> Then he becomes the pope’s man, and receives the crown from him who gives it.’”

Anastasius himself, in his account of Stephen IV:

> “There, after the bishop had given the prayer according to the ancient custom and bestowed peace upon all, they introduced him into the Lateran patriarchium.”

And they sealed the entire church treasury, or the episcopal *cymilia*.

The *cymilium* of a church is its vestry or treasury, in which sacred vestments, sacred vessels, and the church’s more valuable possessions are stored for safekeeping, as Anastasius himself explains here and below in the same work:

> “How he, together with the army, sealed the entire treasury of the episcopal residence.”

The same author, in his account of Vitalian:

> “They also took away the sacred vessels and the treasuries of the holy churches of God, leaving nothing behind.”

Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book V, chapter 11:

> “For the vessels and treasuries of the holy churches of God were also taken away by imperial command and through Greek avarice.”

## No. 121, line 2 — “The episcopal residence was devastated”

This plundering of the extremely wealthy Lateran patriarchium, which Anastasius mentions, and the slaughter perpetrated against the Romans by Mauritius the imperial chartularius, had the following origin, as we learn with complete certainty from the Acts of the Lateran Council under Martin I.

With the support of Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, the emperor Heraclius published the *Ecthesis*, in which both sides were ordered to remain silent concerning the controversy raised by the Monothelites: whether one or two operations were to be acknowledged and affirmed in Christ our Lord.

Previously Pope Honorius, Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, and other bishops of the principal sees had agreed upon a pact of silence in this matter, because at that time it could seem timely and expedient.

But after Honorius had departed from human affairs, the Monothelites converted the pact of silence into a means of consolidating their heresy, to such an extent that Sophronius judged that it had to be broken in defense of orthodox tradition and faith.

Sergius, on the other hand, stubbornly attached to his heresy and his purpose, carefully extracted from Heraclius the edict they called the *Ecthesis*, and once again held up the mask of pernicious hesitation before the radiance of religion.

The *Ecthesis* was sent to the patriarchs and the other bishops for subscription, according to the custom of those times.

When Isaac the exarch received it, he immediately sent it through Mauritius the chartularius to Pope Severinus, so that it might be confirmed. Among the Greeks, the office of the chartularius was to receive public documents, give them official force and authority, and then preserve them.

Severinus therefore received the *Ecthesis* and, in a Roman synod—perhaps assembled for his ordination—posted a sentence of condemnation against it.

Hence came Isaac’s threats and attacks against Severinus; hence the furious plundering of the Lateran patriarchium and the persecution directed against the clergy and Romans.

Cyrus of Alexandria speaks of the imperial mandate sent to Pope Severinus, requiring him to confirm the *Ecthesis*, in his letter to Sergius, quoted in the fifth session of the Lateran Council under Martin, volume III of Hardouin’s *Councils*, p. 803:

> “Eustachius, the glorious master of the soldiers, brought me the venerable letters of my distinguished lord, the God-honored blessed one. They contained a copy of the *Ecthesis* of our venerable faith, duly and most carefully composed and sent by our most pious and God-preserved lord and great prince to Isaac, the most excellent patrician and exarch of Italy, concerning our own faith. Our brother Severinus, most holy and, God willing, about to be ordained in Rome, must profess it.””

Nevertheless, that the *Ecthesis* was condemned by Severinus and the Roman synod is testified by Pope Martin. After reading Cyrus’s letter, Martin addressed the Lateran Fathers in these words:

> “They have fallen from their hope, lying against their own head. For it was neither received nor admitted at all, contrary to their vain expectation; rather, the *Ecthesis* of their most wicked and presumptuous novelty, which had been sent here, was condemned and anathematized by apostolic authority.”

Thus, in the first place, the *Ecthesis* was proscribed by an anathema in the Roman synod by Severinus, with the consent of the entire Roman clergy.

For this reason the pontifical Acts add:

> “When Isaac had learned this more accurately, he came to the city of Rome and sent all the leading men of the Church, each to a separate city, into exile, so that there would be no one from the clergy who could resist him.”

In fact, Severinus issued a decree against the Monothelites. It is praised in the profession of faith in the Roman *Liber Diurnus of the Pontiffs*, chapter 3, no. 6, in these words:

> “We also profess that we preserve all the decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, namely those of Severinus of holy memory, John, Theodore, and Martin; these are known to have cut away, in defense of the proper doctrine, all the scandals of the tares that arose in the royal city concerning new questions. We profess, in accordance with the movement of the natures, two natural operations as well, and we condemn under anathema whatever they condemned.””

From these facts, therefore, we know that Pope Severinus, together with his Roman synod, publicly attacked the Monothelite heresy in his decree, and that the Roman clergy, because they steadfastly adhered to him, were punished with exile.

**Line 3 — “While he was still elected.”**  
That is, according to the custom introduced long before, the emperor’s permission for the ordination was awaited. This is clearly indicated by the words of Cyrus in the letter cited above: “which our brother Severinus, who is being ordained in Rome, must profess.”

I therefore think that, together with Sergius’s *Ecthesis*, the imperial permission for the ordination was sent to Severinus, and that Mauritius the chartularius brought both documents to Rome. Perhaps he first delivered the *Ecthesis* to the pontiff; and when Severinus condemned it in the Roman synod, the patriarchium was devastated, its wealth plundered, and the entire clergy, through the action of the exarch Isaac, harassed by exile and mockery.

After recounting these events, the pontifical Acts add:

> “Afterwards the most holy Severinus was ordained.”

**Line 6 — “So much money.”**  
Honorius had donated an almost unbelievable quantity of gold and silver to the churches and left the Lateran treasury filled.

His Acts report that he offered 2,500 pounds of worked silver, apart from gifts of gold and other furnishings. Here, however, it is said that he enriched the Lateran treasury with an enormous sum of money.

The matter appeared advantageous and opportune to the emperor, exhausted by the expenses of war. He therefore seized the opportunity and ordered the treasury to be plundered, leaving the rest to Isaac to ravage.

## No. 121, line 1 — Severinus

After the death of Honorius, Severinus, a Roman by nationality, was made pontiff with the consent of the entire clergy. Perhaps he obtained no confirmation of his election from Heraclius; such confirmation was customarily exacted in a tyrannical manner.

**Same line — “He sat for months,” etc.**  
Baronius, under the year 639, no. 3, says that Anastasius assigns Severinus eleven months and four days.

That Severinus reached the year of the Lord mentioned above, which coincides with indiction XII, is clear from the fact that he condemned and anathematized Heraclius’s *Ecthesis*, promulgated in indiction XII, as can be seen in the Roman Council, fifth session.

We can infer that he did not go beyond this year from the Roman synod, which the Acts of that synod testify was assembled by Pope John, Severinus’s successor.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

All the catalogues and manuscripts unanimously define the vacancy of the see after Honorius as one year, seven months, and seventeen or eighteen days.

Baronius most learnedly conjectured the reason for this lengthy vacancy: namely, that the ordination of the new pontiff was delayed by the emperor and by the exarch Isaac the patrician until he approved the Greek doctrinal document called the *Ecthesis*.

He inferred this from the letter of Cyrus of Alexandria to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople.

From Anastasius we learn another cause of the very long interregnum. He reports that when Isaac the patrician heard that Pope Honorius had collected and deposited many treasures in the Lateran, he came to Rome, sent all the leading men of the Church into exile—namely, the cardinals, as Baronius and Calvisius understand it—and then carried away the Church’s treasure.

Baronius’s conjecture is strongly approved by Antony Pagi, who observes that the *Ecthesis* was issued in the same year in which the Lateran patriarchium was plundered and Isaac came to Rome. He therefore follows the opinion of the learned annalist step by step, despite the useless opposition of Combefis in *The History of the Monothelite Heresy*, disputation 1, section 11. Combefis attributes the delayed confirmation either to the emperor’s illness or to fear of a certain danger for the western part of the empire if the burden of the pontificate were placed upon an old Roman man unknown to them.

On the *Ecthesis* and Monothelitism, consult the notes of Pagi and Sommier on Saint Martin, no. 131.

The vacancy, therefore, having lasted so long for the reasons stated above, beginning on 12 October 638, ended on 28 May 640, as is shown by the dominical letter C belonging to the day of his ordination.

But although the interregnum before Severinus’s ordination was lengthy, the time he occupied the see was, by contrast, extremely short. For the pontiff, ordained on 28 May 640, died on the Kalends of August of that same year and was buried the following day, having held the chair of Peter for only two months and four days.

Such lengthy interregna should not, however, be understood according to the practice of our own age. The Apostolic See ordinarily did not remain deprived of its shepherd for more than three days. The clergy and people immediately agreed upon some distinguished man whom the Holy Spirit had inspired them to elect, as is clear from the *Liber Diurnus of the Pontiffs*.

Indeed, Anastasius himself, speaking of the Lateran plundering, says: “while the lord Severinus was still elected.” Earlier, in his account of Boniface V, when discussing the killing of the patrician Eleutherius, he had said: “before the day of his ordination.”

Moreover, we do not read that the emperor’s command, tolerated for the sake of public peace, was ever imposed on anyone other than a duly elected pontiff.

Indeed, when circumstances required it, an elected man performed the office of pastor even if, before confirmation, matters appeared otherwise—as is clear in the case of Gregory the Great, who, although not yet confirmed by Mauritius, celebrated the sevenfold litany and similar rites amid Rome’s greatest calamities.

Returning to the see of Severinus, I affirm that its duration was no more than two months and four days, although eleven months are found by error in Baronius.

## No. 121, line 1 — Severinus

Severinus, son of Labienus, a Roman, under the emperor Flavius Heraclius Augustus, sat from his ordination for one year, two months, and three days. He was created and consecrated on Sunday, the Kalends of June, in the year 637, and was confirmed in the pontificate by Isaac, exarch of all Italy. For the election of the clergy and people was considered void unless the emperors or their exarchs confirmed it.

**Line 4 — Mauritius.**  
Either hostile toward the Church, or incited by Heraclius, who was not well disposed toward it.

### No. 123, line 8

“And the episcopate was vacant for four months and twenty-nine days.”

While the see was vacant after Severinus’s death, a delegation of Scots arrived in Rome. They had sent it to Severinus concerning the date on which Easter should be celebrated and concerning the Pelagian heresy, as Bede relates in Book XII, chapter 18. The archpriest, the archdeacon, and the first secretary of the notaries—who at that time, during the vacancy of the see, were administering the Roman Church—opened their letter. So that the darkness of the question might not remain unresolved for long, they gave a reply and wrote that Easter must by no means be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon together with the Hebrews. They also warned them to beware of Pelagius’s blasphemy and foolish speech, which had repeatedly been condemned by the Church.

From this error certain English Protestants infer that the Britons’ first beginnings in the faith were not drawn from Roman doctrine at the command of the Roman pontiffs, but derived from Greece and Asia, since from the beginning of their newly emerging Church they celebrated Easter according to the Asiatic custom. But Protestant writers are shown to infer this incorrectly: the letter sent by the Scots to Severinus would not have been sent had they been outside communion with the Roman Church; and Bede himself, at the beginning of the letter that the Roman clergy sent back to the Scots, clearly states that only very recently, in those times, had this heresy arisen among them, and that not the whole nation but only some of them had become entangled in it.

### No. 121, line 2

“During his time the Lateran episcopate was devastated.”

During the interregnum, Isaac, patrician and exarch of Italy, and Mauritius the chartularius, having taken counsel with certain wicked men, plundered the Lateran patriarchium. Anastasius says that they incited “the Roman army, saying: ‘What benefit is there in the fact that so much money has been gathered in the Lateran episcopate by Pope Honorius, while this army has received no assistance from it, although your pay, which the lord emperor has ordered to be given to you at intervals, is deposited there by the holy man?’”

They used this pretext to incite the soldiers to plunder. Although Anastasius likewise asserts that Isaac “sent part of the substance itself to the royal city, to the emperor Heraclius,” Combefis nevertheless maintains in *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, Disputation I, §§11–12, that the plundering of the Lateran patriarchium should not be attributed to the emperor Heraclius. It is scarcely conceivable, he argues, that either Sergius or Heraclius—men who sought the name of Catholics and had hitherto been regarded as Catholics, and who had held the Roman see in great reverence because of Honorius—would have wished to treat it so badly in the case of Severinus.

### No. 121, line 3

“When the lord Severinus was still only elected.”

Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, in order more easily to propagate Monothelitism and to establish it more firmly, composed a formula or exposition of faith called the *Ecthesis*. He persuaded the emperor Heraclius to order that it be published in his name. It appeared in the year 638, without the knowledge of Pope Honorius, who died in that same year (*Lateran Council under Martin I*, secret. 1; Pagi, *Critical Notes on Baronius*, under the year 639, no. 8). Heraclius later rejected it after learning of the scandals that had arisen from it in the West.

The *Ecthesis* is Catholic insofar as it speaks about the mystery of the Trinity against Sabellius and Arius, and about the mystery of the Incarnation against Nestorius and Eutyches, up to the following words:

> “In no way do we permit anyone at all to say or teach that there is one or two operations in the divine Incarnation of the Lord. Rather, as the holy and universal councils have handed down, we confess that the one and same only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God, performs divine and human works; and that every operation appropriate to God and to man proceeds indivisibly and without confusion from the one and same incarnate God the Word, and is attributed to the one and same [person]. For although the expression ‘one operation’ was used by some of the Fathers, it nevertheless troubles the ears of certain outsiders, who suppose that it was uttered to the destruction of the two natures united in one substance in Christ our God. Likewise, the expression ‘two operations’ scandalizes many, since it has been uttered by none of the holy and eminent Fathers. It also leads to the confession of two wills opposed to one another: the God the Word willing to accomplish the most saving passion, while the incarnation effected in him goes against his will and fights against it. Thus two contrary wills would be introduced, which is impious and foreign to Christian doctrine.”

(*Lateran Synod under Martin I*, secret. 3.)

The clergy of Constantinople proposed this *Ecthesis* to the legates who had been sent from Rome to request confirmation of Severinus’s election from the emperor, so that the elected pope might subscribe to it. The legates then replied:

> “The Roman Church, which from ancient times until now, as the elder of all the Churches beneath the sun, presides over them all, has certainly received and obtained this position canonically from councils and apostles, as well as from the supreme authority of the apostles. It is subject to no writings or synodal documents whatsoever for the protection of the pontificate; just as all who are subject to it in accordance with sacerdotal law stand equally subject to it. … We also make this certain to you: we shall report everything that has been put before us and show the document to the one who is to be consecrated. If he considers that it is sound, we shall ask him to append his own signature to it.”

(St Maximus, Letter to Thalassius, in the collection of Anastasius the Librarian.)

A copy of the same *Ecthesis* was sent to the exarch of Italy so that he might arrange for the elected pope to subscribe to it. The sectarians undoubtedly thought that this would be done, as the patriarch of Alexandria writes to the chief of the Constantinopolitan sect (Cyrus’s letter to Sergius, in the Lateran Synod under Martin I, secret. 3). The pontiff, however, frustrated their hopes: instead of confirming the *Ecthesis*, he struck it with an anathema as pernicious (Martin I, letter, same place).

Moreover, the formula of profession that elected pontiffs used from that time until the Sixth General Council clearly demonstrates that Severinus and his successors condemned Monothelitism, and consequently the *Ecthesis*, which plainly confirms that heresy. The profession runs as follows (*Roman Book of the Pontiffs*, chapter 3, title 6):

> “We also profess all the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see—that is, of Severinus of holy memory, John, and the others—who are known, by their own teaching, to have cut off all the scandals of the tares against the new questions that arose in the royal city, and so forth.”

### No. 123, line 6

“Four bishops in various places.”

In one ordination he created nine bishops.

### Line 7

“Who was also buried.”

After condemning the *Ecthesis* at the synod, Severinus did not live long. For, as Anastasius writes, after he had sat for two months and four days, he was buried. He was a pontiff highly commended for singular piety and religion, kindness, generosity toward the poor, and munificence, on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

All copies of Anastasius, both printed and manuscript, assign him the same duration of office, as do Hermannus Contractus, Regino, Liutprand, Abbo, and Honorius of Autun. Since he was ordained on 28 May of the year 640, he died in that same year on 1 August and was buried the following day.

### 121. Severinus

A Roman by nationality, son of Abienus; he held the see for two months and four days.

> [Baronius says that Anastasius assigns him eleven months.]

During his time the Lateran episcopate was devastated by Mauritius the chartularius and Isaac the patrician and exarch of Italy, while the lord Severinus was still only elected. Before Isaac arrived, Mauritius, led by deceit against the Church of God, took counsel with certain wicked men and incited the Roman army, saying:

> “What benefit is there in the fact that so much money has been gathered in the Lateran episcopate by Pope Honorius, while this army has received no assistance from it, since your pay also, which the lord emperor has ordered to be given to you at intervals, is deposited there by the holy man?”

When they heard this, everyone was inflamed against the Church of God. They all came, from the least to the greatest, stirred up and armed—everyone found in the Roman city, from child to old man—to the aforesaid Lateran episcopate. They could not enter by military force, because those who were with the most holy lord Severinus resisted them.

### 122

When Mauritius saw this, because they had been unable to accomplish anything, he was led by deceit to make the army remain there inside the Lateran episcopate. They stayed there for three days. After the third day, Mauritius entered with the judges who had been found with him in the council, and they sealed all the church vestments, that is, the treasures of the episcopate, which various most Christian emperors, as well as patricians and consuls, had left to the blessed apostle Peter for the redemption of their souls, so that they might be distributed at the proper times as nourishment for the poor or for the redemption of captives.

> [They entered under the appearance of peace and sealed everything.]

Afterward Mauritius sent his letters to the patrician Isaac at Ravenna concerning what had happened—how he himself, with the army, had sealed all the vestments of the episcopate—and saying that they could plunder all the aforesaid property without any injury.

When Isaac had learned these things more accurately, he came to the Roman city and sent all the leading men of the Church, one by one, into exile in the various cities.

> [Baronius thinks that “the leading men” means the cardinals.]

He did this so that there would be no one from the clergy who could resist him. After several days Isaac the patrician entered the Lateran episcopate and remained there for eight days, until they had plundered all that property.

### 123

At the same time he sent part of that property to the royal city, to the emperor Heraclius.

> [A certain part of the property itself.]

Afterward the most holy Severinus was ordained, and Isaac returned to Ravenna. Severinus restored the apse of the blessed apostle Peter with mosaic work, since it had been ruined. He loved the clergy and increased everyone’s gift. He was a holy and kind man above all others, a lover of the poor, generous, and exceedingly gentle.

He created four bishops in various places. He distributed the full *roga* to all the clergy.

> [B: “he divided.”]

He was also buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. The episcopate was vacant for four months and twenty-nine days.

### No. 124, line 12

“He distributed the full *roga* to all the clergy.”

Since *roga* is principally understood in two senses—either as a gift or honorarium, which emperors customarily distributed to nobles and magnates, and even to the people, or which supreme pontiffs distributed to the clergy (hence the word’s etymology), or as an exaction or payment made under the name of a petition, which the clergy itself annually paid to the pontiff—the words of Anastasius may perhaps mean that John granted and remitted this sort of payment to the Roman clergy.

Nevertheless, this word occurs frequently in these pontifical biographies to express distributions. It is well established from Roman historians that the ancient Caesars distributed gifts to the soldiers. The Greek emperors likewise maintained this custom. When they sent crowned images through the provinces as proof that they had assumed the government, solidi struck with that design were scattered by the imperial officials wherever the emperor’s image was carried.

We shall discuss this later, when treating Philip the emperor. The author of the *Miscellany*, speaking of the emperor Tiberius II, says:

> “He took Anastasia as his wife, crowned her Augusta, and distributed a great *roga*.”

Gregory of Tours makes a related statement in *History*, Book VI:

> “Mauritius proceeded to the Circus, and after acclamations of praise had been given him and gifts distributed to the people, he was confirmed in the imperial office.”

The *Fuldensian Annals*, concerning Charles the Bald, state:

> “He corrupted the Roman Senate in Jugurthine fashion and joined it to himself, so that even Pope John, after placing the crown upon him, ordered that he be called emperor and Augustus.”

I am reluctant to transcribe more documents of this kind concerning imperial generosity, which rulers are found to have practiced even after the restoration of the Western Empire.

The Roman pontiffs likewise distributed these *rogae* to the people and clergy at their ordinations and on other more solemn days. Examples are readily available. Anastasius himself, in the life of Vigilius, page 108, reports that after the solemn celebration of Mass he gave gifts to the people. In the life of Theodore, page 126, he says:

> “After he had completed these things, he caused gifts to be distributed among the people.”

He is speaking of Pyrrhus of Constantinople, to whom the pontiff, after he had renounced Monothelitism at Rome, granted the honor of distributing a *roga* to the people according to the custom of the pontiffs.

Concerning Leo IV, who was the first to celebrate the Octave of the Assumption, the *Acts*, page 368, say:

> “A great multitude of the people had gathered for it, desiring to celebrate the solemnity of the new feast. When that magnanimous bishop saw this, he distributed several silver coins to all who were present at the celebration.”

The same pontiff, at the dedication of the Leonine city, page 383, is said to have done the following:

> “After the sacred offices had been completed, he honored and enriched all the nobles of Rome with numerous gifts, not only in gold and silver but also in silken cloaks.”

Concerning this *roga* distributed by elected pontiffs, William the Librarian provides an example in the life of Adrian II, where, after recounting visions that had preceded his future election, page 425, he says:

> “Some, according to apostolic custom, distributed gold coins in the Lateran basilica,” and so forth.

We read that princes traveling to the thresholds of the apostles also made such distributions. In the life of Benedict III, page 403, we find:

> “During his time the king of the Saxons, hastening to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, offered gifts. At the request of the most holy lord Pope Benedict, that he should make a public *roga* in the church of the blessed apostle Peter from a weight of pounds of gold or silver, the king of the Saxons gave gold to the bishops, presbyters, deacons, the whole clergy, and the Roman nobles, but small silver coins to the people.”

The pontiffs, however, distributed a fixed sum of money to the clergy: one full *roga* to all clerics, and another *roga* to those assigned to apostolic service. Thus we read in the life of Deusdedit:

> “He distributed one full *roga* among his officials and to the whole clergy.”

This distribution is recorded by Anastasius in almost every individual pontifical biography.

In other Churches, distributions were made to the clergy according to the revenues. There is a constitution of Felix IV preserved by Agnellus in the life of Ecclesius, bishop of Ravenna, page 96:

> “A fourth of the patrimony of the Ravenna Church—that is, three thousand solidi—shall be completed through the customary distributions to all the clergy, or to those to whom it is customary for distributions to be made.”

A double *roga* is also occasionally mentioned, as in the life of Boniface V, page 119. I think this happened especially when the apostolic see acquired new patrimonies or other property through the generosity of rulers and the faithful. For Felix, in the same constitution, also established that a fourth of newly acquired property was owed to the clergy of Ravenna, adding:

> “If anything should increase from rents or inheritances, by the will of our Lord, then, with the same Lord’s assistance, it too shall be added to the fourth portion, so that, once the lists have been arranged, what is distributed to each person cannot remain concealed … according to the places which God has established in justice and measure.”

### No. 121, line 1

“John.”

In the year of the Lord 636, John IV, of that name, was substituted for Pope Severinus. He was a steadfast and fearless defender of the orthodox faith. Yielding nothing to the threats of the exarchs and little disturbed by the exile of the cardinals, he assembled a council of bishops and, as Theophanes relates, anathematized the heresy of the Monothelites, in order to defend and free his predecessor Pope Honorius from the calumny of the heretics.

For this reason he took the greatest care to ensure that the writer who had been secretary to Pope Honorius and had written the letters addressed to Bishop Sergius would interpret their true and genuine meaning and transmit it to the emperor. When that writer faithfully fulfilled the task at the command of the blessed Pope John IV and set forth the legitimate meaning of the words of Honorius, he removed every sinister suspicion of heresy from Honorius.

### CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Concerning the consecration of this pontiff, Papebrochius maintains that confirmation began to be sought not from Constantinople but from the exarch at Ravenna. Pagi, in order to support his own opinion about the delayed ordination of Boniface V, says that this began with the election of Honorius, on account of the difficulties inflicted upon the Church after the death of St Deusdedit. For this reason he dates the beginning of the authority delegated by the Eastern emperors to the exarch of Ravenna to the year 625.

Garnerius, in his notes on the *Pontifical Book*, traces the exarch’s authority to the year 618, at the election of that same Boniface, since he observes that only a few days of interregnum occurred between St Deusdedit and Boniface.

But since much longer vacancies followed afterward, as we have seen, neither Garnerius’s nor Pagi’s conjectures should be accepted. Papebrochius’s opinion is different. Since it is clear that after John IV the emperor’s command from Constantinople was no longer awaited, it is not unreasonable to believe that John’s election too was confirmed by the exarch. The shorter interregnum preceding it supports this view.

Although Blanchinus says, in the life of Pelagius II, that one hundred days were more than sufficient to send a messenger to Constantinople and receive a reply, the 144 days that preceded John’s election appear all the more sufficient.

Whatever the truth may be in this matter, which is attested by no documentary monuments, it is certain that before the death of John IV the exarch of Ravenna received from the Eastern emperor the power to confirm the pontiff.

John IV, after a vacancy of four months and twenty-four days, as stated by the Freherian Codex 1 and Thuani Codex 2—which Pagi testifies that he saw in manuscript—was ordained in the year of Severinus’s death, 640, on 24 December, under the Sunday letter A, not after twenty-nine days, as the printed text and certain others incorrectly state, supported by Ordericus.

This is clear not only from the interregnum that preceded him—for the Kalends of August are separated from 24 December by four months and twenty-four days, counting the day of death—but also from the duration of John IV’s pontificate: namely, one year, nine months, and eighteen days, as recorded in most catalogues and codices, with which the authorities cited by Pagi agree.

The second Freherian Codex, the second Thuani Codex, and the Blanchinian catalogue, now published for the first time, nevertheless give nineteen days, differing by one day after the year and months. The Regius and Mazarin codices and the first Thuani codex would likewise give nineteen days, had the inattentive copyist not omitted the numeral and left only nine days to be read.

Indeed, if one counts one year, nine months, and eighteen days from the day of his ordination, 24 December 640, one arrives at 11 October as the day of John IV’s death, and at 12 October, the fourth day before the Ides, as the day on which he was buried at St Peter’s, according to Anastasius, if nineteen days are counted. It is customary for Anastasius and the catalogues sometimes to record the day of death and sometimes the day of burial, as a careful observer will find throughout.

### No. 121, line 1

“John, son of Venantius the scholastic, a Dalmatian of Jadera, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, held the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days; he was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the beginning of the year of Christ 639.”

Severinus had scarcely died when letters from the nation of the Scots were brought to Rome. John the deacon, elected Roman pontiff but not yet consecrated according to the custom of the city, could not reply to them alone. Hilary the archpriest and John the first secretary, who were maintaining the place of the apostolic see, therefore composed the reply with him; it is preserved in Bede.

From this letter we learn that it was the custom of the Roman Church for those who held the highest offices among the Church’s ministers to give a written reply to letters received before the lawful consecration of the bishop.

### No. 122, line 2

“He sent a great deal of money throughout Dalmatia, or Istria.”

Since a huge multitude of captives had been carried away from those regions by the Slavs, or Sclavi, who were ravaging Dalmatia, John IV, a Dalmatian by birth, took pity on the sufferings of his countrymen and redeemed them with a great amount of money. He did this all the more willingly because, through these works of charity, he was placing the Church’s treasure in a safer location—namely, in the bosom of the poor. For he had seen the ecclesiastical goods that Honorius had accumulated already being plundered by the sacrilegious greed of the imperial officials. Anastasius discusses this above, in the life of Severinus.

### No. 122, line 2

“During his time.”

Pope John, as Anastasius testifies, sent throughout all Dalmatia, or Istria, large sums of money from what remained of the treasures that the exarch Isaac had dissipated, as we said in the life of Severinus. He sent them through the most faithful and holy abbot Martin, for the redemption of captives whom the heathen had carried off.

Fearing that the relics of the saints in Dalmatia, his homeland, might be scattered by the invading barbarian enemies, he ordered the relics of the holy martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, and Maurus to be brought from Dalmatia and Istria, as the same Anastasius testifies. He deposited them in the Lateran Church, in a private oratory that he built in their honor beside Constantine’s baptistery. This remains intact to the present day and, from the year 1575 onward, after the image of the Virgin Mother began to shine there through miracles, was commonly called *La Madonna di San Giovanni*, as Octavius Pancirolus writes in Augustine Oldoinus’s life of John IV.

### Line 12

“Who was also buried.”

At last, after Pope John had held the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days, as Anastasius writes, he fell asleep in the Lord on 11 October of the year 642. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the fourth day before the Ides of October, that is, on 12 October.

The purity of Anastasius’s text concerning the duration of his pontificate is established by the fact that Regino, Liutprand, Ordericus, Book II, and the Vatican-Palatine catalogue assign him the same duration: one year, nine months, and eighteen days.
