### No. 125, line 7

“He rebelled against Isaac the patrician.”

Mauritius the chartularius is said to have *intartized* against Isaac the patrician and exarch of Ravenna. *Intartizare* means to rise up or rebel against a ruler. Anastasius uses the word in the life of Adeodatus:

> “During his time Mezentius, who was in Sicily with the Eastern army, rebelled and seized the kingdom as the instigator of rebellion.”

Hence *intarta* in Anastasius’s life of Deusdedit:

> “He went out from Rome and came to Naples, which was held by John Compsinus, who had rebelled.”

The same writer says in the life of Adeodatus:

> “And many of his judges were mutilated and brought to Constantinople, together with the head of the leader of that rebellion, namely Mezentius,”

of whom we spoke earlier.

The word is derived from the Greek **ἀνταίρειν**, “to rise against.”

### Line 12

He sent Donatus, master of the soldiers, and his treasurer to the city of Rome with an army. The *sacellarius* was one of the offices of the Constantinopolitan court: he was the prefect of the treasury, virtually its treasurer, from *sacellum*, which is a diminutive of *saccus*, the term by which the treasury is denoted. Augustine, on Psalm 146: “For *fiscus* means a sack, whence *fiscellae* and *fiscinae* are also so called.” And below: “The *fiscus* is the public sack.” The *sacellarius* is also reckoned among the offices of the Roman Church, as in the *Ordo Romanus* and in Anastasius’s accounts of Gregory II, Adrian I, and Leo III.

### No. 126, line 1

“Mauritius fled to Holy Mary at the Crib. When they seized him from the church, they put a *boia* around his neck.” According to Festus, a *boia* is a kind of bond. Arnold of Lübeck, in the *Supplement to Helmold*, book II, chapter 26:

> “When the bishop, after making the aspersion, had come to them, moved by compassion he sprinkled them with blessed water, using these words: ‘The Lord raises up those who are bowed down; the Lord releases the fettered.’ And immediately, with a great noise, the *boia* burst apart.”

Hence *inboiati*, “fettered.” Anastasius below, in the same account: “Likewise he sent all those who had been with him in the council to Ravenna, fettered.” And again: “Those who had been sent with him he ordered all to be thrown into prison, fettered and under strict guard.”

[Col. 0727D]

### No. 126, line 8

“But when Isacius saw the head of Mauritius, he rejoiced and had it set up on a stake in the Ravenna circus, as an example to many.” The heads of the condemned were displayed on stakes as an example. Bede, *History*, book 3, chapter 12:

> “Moreover, the king who had killed him ordered that his head and hands, severed from the body together with the arms, be hung upon stakes.”

The heads of the condemned, as of public enemies, were sent to the emperor. Anastasius, in his account of Adeodatus: “And many of his judges, mutilated, were brought to Constantinople, together with the head of that same rebel.” The same author, in his account of Gregory II: “His severed head was sent to Constantinople, to the emperor.” The head of Mauritius was placed on a stake in the Circus for public spectacle. Martyrs were led through the amphitheater and slaughtered there. Eusebius, book 5, chapter 1; Jerome, *On Sacred Scripture*, chapter 17.

### No. 127, line 1

“At that time Pyrrhus came from Africa, having been patriarch of Constantinople, to the city of Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles.” Pilgrimage by the faithful to the thresholds of the apostles was frequent. Anastasius, in his account of Leo IV:

> “When he saw that Christian people were being sent from everywhere to the most sacred threshold of the prince of the apostles, for the sake of prayer or devotion to him.”

Sidonius, book I, letter 5:

> “Meanwhile Rome also came into view, and I seemed about to drink in not only its appearance but even its naval battles; before I had touched its walls, I was overwhelmed at the triumphal thresholds of the apostles, and immediately felt every weariness driven from my feeble limbs.”

Odo of Cluny, *Life of Saint Gerald the Count*, book II, chapter 17:

> “He had made it his custom to visit Rome frequently.”

Gregory VI, in his address to the cardinals, as quoted by the continuator of Bede, book II, chapter 26:

> “Secure pilgrims occupied unfamiliar paths; lodged throughout the City, they feasted their eyes on ancient marvels; singing, they returned to their homeland with the gifts they had received.”

Hence, for the sake of security, *Romipetae*—pilgrims to Rome—were placed under the protection of the apostolic see. And by a constitution of Callistus II, if anyone captured pilgrims visiting the thresholds of the apostles, he was excommunicated. Canon *Si quis Romipetas*, 24, question 3.

### No. 127, line 6

“He made him distribute gifts among the people, and had a chair placed for him beside the altar, honoring him as priest of the Royal City.” For the sake of a largess, the Roman pontiff customarily scatters coins among the populace. Anastasius, in his account of Leo IV:

> “To all who were present at this solemn celebration, namely the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he distributed many silver coins.”

When Pyrrhus, formerly of Constantinople, came to Rome, the pontiff granted him this as an honor: that he should distribute a largess among the populace.

### No. 128, line 1

“At that time the bodies of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus were discovered; they had been buried in a sand-pit on the Nomentan Way.” The discovery of martyrs is celebrated with solemn ceremony. Ambrose, on Psalm 118, sermon 6:

> “For we celebrate the day on which the bodies of the holy martyrs were revealed to the people.”

Those bodies were those of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. The translation and elevation of relics were performed with even greater solemnity. Concerning the same martyrs, Ambrose, letter 85:

> “What more shall I say? We found them intact and transferred them in due order, as evening was already approaching, to the Basilica of Fausta. There were vigils throughout the night and the laying on of hands. On the following day we transferred them to the basilica which they call Ambrosian. We transferred two; a blind man was healed.”

Augustine also bears witness to this event in his book against the letter of Petilianus, chapter 16.

[Col. 0728D]

### Note

#### No. 125, line 4

**Mauritius the chartularius.** He called himself king at Rome. The events make clear what is expressed by the verb *intartizavit*: namely, the exiles inflicted upon the Romans by Isacius, and the persecutions which he daily contrived against the faith and the Catholics, gave Mauritius the opportunity to rebel. For this reason he had Roman nobles and the Italian army as his followers. We shall note more suitably elsewhere how vigorously that army always fought for the pontiff and for the preservation of the purity of the faith.

[Col. 0729A]

#### No. 126, line 2

**A *boia* around his neck.** That is, a bond. Festus writes concerning it: “*Boiae*, that is, a kind of bond, whether wooden or iron, are so called.” In this sense the word occurs in the *Acts of the Martyrs*: “Take the *boia* from my neck.” And Saint Jerome, book V on Jeremiah, chapter 27, writes on the prophet’s words, “Peace to you: bonds and chains”:

> “Or collars (*κλοιούς*), which in Hebrew are called *mototh*, ‘bonds,’ and in the common language are called *boiae*.”

Others call it *boga*. Isidore, discussing punishments established by law, says in book I, chapter 27:

> “A *boia* is the collar of the condemned, like the yoke of oxen. It belongs to the class of bonds.”

And Cantacuzenus, book I, chapter 49:

> “For if you order my father to come with a *boia*—that is, with collars thrown around his neck—and to remain imprisoned there.”

The same is found in the *Cassinian Chronicle*, book 4, chapter 68:

> “A certain soldier in Apulia was captured in a certain conflict by a most wicked man, bound with a *boia* and chains, and thrown into a pit.”

The same type of bond is to be understood in what is recorded in Vigilius, page 109:

> “And the Augusta Theodora had a rope put around his neck and dragged him through the entire city until evening. Then he was sent into custody.”

[Col. 0729B]

#### No. 129, line 1

**“Then,” etc.** These matters are described in the acts of the Lateran Council under Martin, where the following is read on page 702. It is useful to compare it with the words of Anastasius. In Migne, the sections of text entitled “Anastasius’s Text” and “Lateran Council, Secret Session I” are printed in parallel.

**ANASTASIUS’S TEXT**

> “Then the most holy Theodore wrote to Paul, patriarch of the Royal City, both asking and duly reproving him, and likewise, through the *apocrisiarii*, as has been stated, whom he had sent especially for this purpose, admonishing him in person and charging him to correct his own error and return to the orthodox faith of the Catholic Church. Neither the entreaties nor the reproofs could in any way recall him from his undertaking. Therefore he was struck by the apostolic see with the punishment of deposition.”

**LATERAN COUNCIL, SECRET SESSION I**

> “For his predecessors had not ceased, at various times, to write most carefully to the aforesaid men, both asking and duly reproving them, and likewise, through their *apocrisiarii*, as has been stated, whom they had sent especially for this purpose, admonishing them in person and charging them to return to the Catholic Church. Neither their entreaties nor their reproofs could in any way recall him from his undertaking. Therefore he was struck by the apostolic see with the punishment of deposition.”

Where Anastasius says “as has been stated,” referring to the *apocrisiarii* sent from the apostolic see, one should recognize the error of a careless copyist, since not even a single letter had been written about them in the *Life of Theodore*. It is nevertheless established from other sources that Pope Theodore pronounced a sentence of deposition against Paul of Constantinople. Thus, among other evidence, there is the monks’ petition to Pope Martin, read in the Second Secret Session of the Lateran Council, where we read:

> “Together with these matters, and with the *Typos*—through the importunate persuasion and falsehood of Paul, who had been deposed by your predecessor, the most holy Theodore…”

### Note

#### No. 125, line 1

**Theodore.** In the year of Christ our Redeemer 641, on the twenty-fifth of November, Theodore was made pontiff. At the beginning of his pontificate, Pyrrhus, bishop of Constantinople, voluntarily withdrew to Africa in order to escape the snare he had deserved because he was conscious of having administered poison to the emperor Constantine. There he found Maximus, abbot and martyr. After holding with him that famous disputation preserved in volume V of the Councils under Theodore, he came to know the truth of the faith and the error and perfidy of the Monothelites.

#### Line 4

**Mauritius the chartularius.** This is that Mauritius who, during the pontificate of Severinus, plundered the Lateran Church. Baronius, year 645, no. 5.

[Col. 0730A]

#### No. 126, line 2

**A *boia*.** That is, a bond.

#### Line 5

**Ficulas.** This is the church of Ficodensis, now called Cervia. Baronius, year 643, no. 5.

#### Line 15

**He sent Theodore the patrician and exarch.** It is established from letter 16 of Pope Martin that the heretical exarch Plato was sent to Italy before Theodore Calliopas. See Baronius, year 643.

#### No. 127, line 7

“Afterward he returned once more, like a dog, to the vomit of his own impiety.” When the emperor heard of Pyrrhus’s conversion, he sent Olympius, a most audacious heretic, as successor to the exarch Plato. Once Olympius reached Ravenna, he devoted every effort to accomplishing what he knew would please the emperor—namely, to restore Pyrrhus to his former error—and he did so. See Theophanes, year 20 of Heraclius; the Lateran Council under Martin; Baronius, year 648, no. 11 and following.

[Col. 0730A]

### CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

At last we have arrived at shorter intervals between pontificates, thanks to the exarch; and there can no longer be any doubt that confirmation was sought from Ravenna. This is shown quite clearly by the forty-three days between pontificates, wholly insufficient for messengers to be sent back and forth to Constantinople. Moreover, the *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs, scarcely mentioning the Eastern court while presenting much material concerning the exarch and archbishop, as well as the judges and the Ravennate *apocrisiarius*, shows that the practice of seeking an imperial command from Constantinople had fallen into disuse.

As for the date of this *Diurnus*, Garnerius leaves the matter uncertain. He asserts that it must certainly be sought within the 185 years from 567, when the exarchs were instituted, to 752, when they were expelled. Then, observing in title 6, in the promise of the *Fid. Ep.*, three definite chronological markers—Martin I, who died in 655; the Sixth Synod, which was completed in 681; and Constantine Pogonatus, who died in 685—he maintains that its date can be placed around this period.

[Col. 0730C]

Accordingly, the settled opinion of scholars is that this *Diurnus* was compiled forty years after John IV. Whatever the truth of the matter, after the death of John IV on 11 October 642, with only one month and twelve days intervening, as all unanimously affirm, Theodore, his successor, was ordained on 24 November of the same year, as the concurrent dominical letter F demonstrates.

The nearly universal opinion of the manuscripts is that he occupied the see for six years, five months, and eighteen days, except for the second Thuani manuscript, which increases the duration of his pontificate by one day and incorrectly subtracts all five months. The new Blanchinian Catalogue is also mistaken, omitting the number ten in the days. This becomes evident from the duration of the pontificate and from the day of the deposition, which all unanimously connect with 14 May.

Pagi, indeed, thinks that the reading of the Thuani manuscript—nineteen days—should be accepted, while supplying the months, so that Theodore, dying on 13 May, would have been buried on the following day. He observes that from 14 May there are certainly fifty-two days between pontificates, counted by Anastasius up to Martin’s ordination.

[Col. 0730D]

But if we count from the date of Theodore’s ordination, 24 November 642, to the date of his death, 13 May 649, six years, five months, and eighteen days—excluding the final endpoints, as we have sometimes seen Anastasius do—we shall find the calculation exact even without the reading of the Thuani manuscript.

Apart from the slight difference of one day, not only the manuscripts of Anastasius but also several martyrologies record Theodore’s deposition on 14 May, as Papebrochius testifies in his appendix to the aforesaid date and in his *Historical Endeavor*, and Pagi in his notes on this year, no. 2.

It is therefore clear, as I observed elsewhere, that Anastasius’s notation of the day of deposition should not be followed so scrupulously that the days of the pontiffs’ deaths must be extended or shortened, to the great detriment of pontifical chronology, unless every day is counted exactly. It is enough that, whether the endpoints are excluded or included, nothing is left over and nothing is lacking.

[Col. 0731A]

### Note

#### No. 125, line 1

**Theodore, son of Bishop Theodore.** He was born at Jerusalem. He was a Greek. Under the emperors Flavius Heraclius, Constantine Heraclius, and Constans Augustus, he occupied the see for six years, five months, and nineteen days; he was consecrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, a Sunday. Upon entering the pontificate, he carefully considered everything that he judged to belong to the dignity of the Christian religion, as a good shepherd should, displaying remarkable kindness toward everyone, but especially toward the poor.

#### No. 127, line 10

**“He condemned him.”** Theodore, having summoned a very large synod, went to the basilica of the prince of the apostles. Having taken a chalice, he dripped ink into it, and thus, with his own hand, carried out Pyrrhus’s deposition. It is necessary either that this custom had been observed before him in the deprivation of bishops, or that Theodore handed down this formula to later generations as an example—the latter seems more probable. Leo IX mentions this deposition in his letter to the bishop of Constantinople.

[Col. 0731B]

### Note

#### No. 127, line 1

**“Pyrrhus came from Africa.”** Pyrrhus the heretic, after a disturbance had been stirred up against him because of the suspicion that had arisen in Constantinople concerning him and the Augusta Martina—namely, that he had administered poison to the emperor Constantine—renounced the dignity of the patriarchate and withdrew to Africa, which he knew had defected from the emperor.

There, before the patrician Gregory, in an assembly of bishops and in the presence of a large gathering of citizens, he held with Saint Maximus the Abbot a celebrated disputation concerning the two wills in Christ. In it Pyrrhus was defeated and recanted his error. He then came to Rome and offered Theodore a statement of the faith in which he condemned the Monothelite heresy and its authors. Theodore received him into communion with the Church, but when Pyrrhus returned not long afterward to the same impiety, Theodore struck him with an anathema.

[Col. 0731C]

#### No. 129, line 6

**“He was struck by the punishment of deposition.”** The very learned Combefisius, in his *History of the Monothelites*, thinks that Paul was not deposed by Theodore at all. He was led to this opinion, contrary to Anastasius’s testimony, by two conjectures.

The first is that Saint Martin, in the Lateran Council, attributes the persecution inflicted by Constans and Paul upon Theodore’s *apocrisiarii* not to Paul’s deposition, but only to the admonition delivered to the *apocrisiarii* in the name of the apostolic see, urging Paul to withdraw from heresy. The second is that Benedict, bishop of Ajaccio, and other bishops, when pressing Paul’s condemnation in the Lateran Council, sufficiently indicate that no anathema had yet been imposed upon Paul.

But these conjectures are refuted by the explicit testimony of the Greek abbots and monks in a petition presented to the Lateran Synod under Saint Martin and read in the Second Secret Session. In confirmation of the deposition of Paul reported by Anastasius, it says:

> “Together with these matters, and with the *Typos*, which has now been made against the Orthodox faith through deception, not by the intention or purpose of our most pious emperor—this honorable title the very learned father of the *Annals*, Baronius, carefully noted when continuing his account of Constans in the year of Christ 649; although he was a heretic, this was not yet entirely known publicly, nor had he been condemned by the Church—but through the importunate persuasion and falsehood of Paul, who was deposed by your Holiness’s predecessor, Theodore, pope of holy memory, of your apostolic see, we submit him to the same anathema.”

[Col. 0731D]

### Note

#### No. 127, line 1

**“At that time Pyrrhus came.”** While Pyrrhus was residing in Africa, he held that famous disputation concerning the Catholic faith with Maximus, the orthodox abbot of Constantinople, who was then in Africa, in the year 645. Since Pyrrhus was spreading his heresy everywhere, he found in Maximus his principal opponent.

Therefore, at the urging of the African bishops and of Gregory the patrician, governor of the province, it was agreed that, in their presence, a public disputation concerning the public controversies should take place between them. That it occurred in the year 645 is shown by the title prefixed to the disputation, which says that the proceedings took place in July, in the third indiction.

Baronius reports it in Greek and Latin in the appendix to volume VIII and discusses it at length for that year from Theophanes and Anastasius. The disputation ended with Pyrrhus, convicted of his error, repenting and recanting his *palinode*. When he came to Rome and offered Pope Theodore a statement of the faith in which he abjured his error and professed the Catholic faith, he was received into the Catholic Church together with the title of patriarchate. Everything necessary was honorably supplied to him at the expense of the Roman Church. This is clear not only from Theophanes and Anastasius but also from the acts of the disputation itself.

### No. 129, line 1

“Then the holy Pope Theodore wrote to Paul, patriarch of the Royal City.” Paul, the usurper of the see of Constantinople, had indeed been able for a short time to suppress the poison he had swallowed by means of the drug of pretence; but as his conscience swelled daily, he finally vomited it up, even against his will.

His first accusers were the Cypriot bishops, together with Sergius, their archbishop. In 643 they assembled in a council and wrote a synodal letter to Pope Theodore—whom they call “the father of fathers” and “the universal pope”—concerning the Monothelite heresy which they themselves had condemned. This letter is preserved in the Second Secret Session of the Lateran Council.

At approximately the same time, Stephen, bishop of Dor, delegated by the Catholic prelates of Palestine, went to Rome on behalf of the Church of Jerusalem, which had been invaded by pseudo-bishops allied with Paul of Constantinople, the most determined supporter of the Monothelites. Theodore obtained for Stephen from the pope the vicariate authority of the apostolic see in those regions, so that he could condemn their leader, Sergius, bishop of Joppa, a Monothelite intruder into the see of Jerusalem, and restore to ecclesiastical order the bishops he had ordained after deposing them from their rank.

These matters are established from the petition of Stephen himself, presented to Pope Martin at the Lateran Council.

On the other side, the four African primates—each in his own province, namely Byzacena, Numidia, Mauritania, and the Proconsular province—summoned synods in 646 to confirm the Catholic doctrines which they had seen Maximus the Abbot defend so powerfully against Pyrrhus in the preceding year.

The records of these councils were read in the Lateran Council under Pope Martin, in the Second Secret Session. They included a synodal letter written on that occasion by three of them together—the bishops of Byzacena, Numidia, and Mauritania—to Theodore, the Roman pontiff. Since these African Fathers were preparing to send an embassy to Constantinople and to admonish Paul, the bishop of that city and leader of the Monothelites, they first wished to inform Theodore of the matter. In their letter they asked that their own writings to Paul be delivered to him by representatives of the apostolic see. They further requested that, if Paul did not correct his error, he should be condemned by the Roman pontiff with a sentence of excommunication.

The actual letter of the Africans to Paul has not survived. Only the letter separately sent to him by the Fathers of the Council of the Proconsular province of Carthage survives, together with another letter of the synod of Byzacena written at the same time to the emperor on this matter. These can be read in the same Second Secret Session of the Lateran Council.

Moreover, in the synodal letter of the African Fathers to Pope Theodore, the Fathers say that they wished to inform the pontiff of their embassy to Paul because

> “the ancient rules had established that whatever might be done in provinces, even remote or far distant, should not be taken up before it had been brought to the knowledge of the nourishing apostolic see, so that by its authority whatever just pronouncement had been made might be confirmed; and that the other Churches should derive from it, as from their native spring, the beginning of their preaching, while throughout the various regions of the whole world the sacraments of the uncorrupted faith of salvation should flow forth.”

[Col. 0733A]

Thus Pope Theodore, seeing the whole African Church united in one and the same judgment, and all of them crying out with one voice against Paul, bishop of Constantinople, as a Monothelite, sent *apocrisiarii* to Constantinople to Paul with extremely severe letters, which, as Baronius notes, have not reached us.

That this nevertheless happened is testified by the letter Paul sent to Theodore, quoted by Baronius under the year 646. In it Paul, responding to Theodore, set forth Monothelitism almost in the same manner as Sergius had done in the *Ecthesis*: asserting one will explicitly, in order to exclude opposition between wills in Christ. This was the sole pretext for those who, after Honorius had forbidden the expression, avoided expressly asserting one operation, while professing one will.

In that letter Paul professes that he follows Sergius and Honorius, as well as the entire assembly of the saints and doctors. When Theodore received it, he considered pronouncing a sentence of deposition against him, a step which the African bishops, indignant at Paul’s attacks upon the Church, were urging.

But Paul, in order to wound the faith treacherously and protect himself, already hated by the Catholics, composed a certain *Typos*, or formula and exposition of faith, and published it in the name of the emperor Constans. Under the pretended pretext of peace and union, it imposed silence on both Catholics and heretics, so that no one thereafter would dare to discuss either one or two wills, or one or two operations, in Christ.

The deceitful man also thought it expedient to remove the *Ecthesis* from the doors of the Church, as is clear from these words of the *Typos*:

> “For the perfect unity of the holy Churches of God and their common concord, and so that no opportunity might be left to those who wish to contend without end, we ordered the documents that had been placed in the *narthex* of the most holy Great Church of our God-preserved royal city, containing the questions mentioned above, to be removed.”

That the *Typos* was promulgated in 648 is established from Theophylact, first secretary of the apostolic see, who says in the Fourth Secret Session of the Lateran Council:

> “According to the command of your Beatitude, I have in my hands Paul’s letter and a copy of the *Typos*, recently—that is, in the past year—published at the persuasion of Paul himself.”

The Lateran Council was celebrated at the beginning of October in the year 649.

This is also established from the *Report of the Admonition* made between the lord Abbot Maximus and his companion and the princes in the Secret Session. Baronius quotes the following passage from it:

> “And through the *Typos*, which was recently, that is, during the sixth indiction, promulgated; this indiction continued until the Kalends of September of the year 648.”

[Col. 0733C]

Saint Pope Martin, in his letter to Saint Amandus, then bishop of Traiectum, recognizes that the attempt expressed by Paul through the *Typos* was far more wicked than all those that had preceded it.

Nor was this interpretation of the *Typos* held only by Catholics. Just as the *Ecthesis* composed by Sergius “appeared ridiculous not only to the orthodox, as Zonaras says when discussing Heraclius, but also to the followers of Severus,” so too the *Typos* fashioned by Paul was hated not only by Catholics but also by certain Monothelites.

Thus Theodosius of Caesarea, in his *Collation* with Maximus, said:

> “By the God who will judge me, when it was made I said, and now I say the same thing: the *Typos* was badly made and to the injury of many.”

Paul would not have set forth these schemes of impiety so confidently if he had not had Constans as his associate. The emperor left nothing unattempted in order that Monothelitism might be spread everywhere.

Paul therefore obtained in Constans an accomplice in his crime, expounded the *Typos*, and published it in Constans’s name, just as Sergius had issued the *Ecthesis*, confirmed by the authority and in the name of Heraclius.

Nevertheless, the orthodox Fathers not without reason attributed the whole crime expressed in the *Typos* to Paul, lest the emperor Constans’s spirit, provoked by insults—although he deserved them—should bring still worse evils upon the Church.

Thus Pope Martin, in the letter sent to him, calls him “the most pious lord,” “one who loves God,” “a sincere minister of Christ,” and “the best emperor.” In the same way, in the Sixth Synod, Constans is called “the emperor of holy memory,” so that his son Constantine Pogonatus might not, because of the insults directed against his father, abandon the defense of the faith he had undertaken and become an enemy of the Church, which proclaimed him its protector and restorer of ecclesiastical peace.

[Col. 0734A]

Here an opportunity presents itself to examine, together with the recent anonymous author of the *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, the “economy of silence” of Honorius, which resembles that proposed in the *Typos*. From the Seventh *Scrutiny* of this author, I have selected a few points here.

In both his letters Honorius approves and commends Sergius’s policy of silence, to be imposed on both Catholics and heretics, concerning both one and two wills and operations in Christ. He also tried to persuade Sophronius of this, as appears from fragments of his second letter.

The hatred with which the orthodox Fathers who bravely resisted the Monothelites pursued this policy of silence in every circumstance is demonstrated by the condemnation of the *Typos*. If the dispensation of silence is removed, you will find nothing condemnable in it. For all the thunderbolts hurled by the Fathers against the *Typos* are aimed precisely at this: they especially anathematized it because

> “together with the perfidious heretics it rejected the orthodox Fathers, and, together with the voices of wicked men—that is, with one will and operation—it likewise caused the doctrines of the orthodox to be denied, namely, the two wills and operations of the same Christ,”

as Saint Martin says in the Fifth Secret Session of the Lateran Council. He considered it no less absurd to prescribe silence on this point than to expunge from Christ one or two wills and operations.

For a similar reason Saint Maximus, in his *Collation* with Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea, attacks the policy of silence expressed in the *Typos*, as resembling that of Honorius:

> “What believer accepts a dispensation that causes the words to be silenced which, as I have said, God of all dispensed through the apostles, prophets, and teachers?”

For this reason the *Typos* itself was hated even by that same Theodosius, although he was a Monothelite, as we said in note 11.

A distinction must be made, however, between dispensations and policies of expediency that may be employed in matters of faith. They may concern either persons suspected of heresy or doctrines of faith.

If disagreement concerns persons, one should not too precipitately proscribe as a heretic someone who is brought before the apostolic see as such. Consequently, a dispensation or policy of expediency may be introduced with the utmost prudence, delaying his condemnation until the matter becomes more fully clear.

The Fathers who opposed emerging Monothelitism prudently used such a dispensation. Although they immediately condemned the heresy as it erupted, they spared the persons anathema until more severe remedies were ultimately required and the supporters of Monothelitism—Cyrus, Theodore, Sergius, and the others—were synodically condemned by Pope Martin.

But if disagreement concerns doctrines of faith, the matter proceeds quite differently. If a truth is attacked that is plainly contained in all the holy Fathers and flows abundantly from the sources of Sacred Scripture and the holy councils, no policy of expediency or dispensation of silence is then necessary. It must immediately be defined openly by those whose office requires it, unless it is found to have been defined already by their predecessors—especially when it is clear that, through the frauds of heretics, many of the orthodox are being driven headlong into their pits.

In this way the ancient Fathers proceeded whenever new heresies arose, as could be demonstrated by many examples.

Nor does it help, in defense of the economy of Honorius, to say that Honorius could commendably have introduced it as a matter still indifferent, since no conciliar definition or papal decree had yet clearly established that there were two wills and operations in Christ.

This cannot be said of the *Typos*, since the council of John IV had preceded it and had clearly defined this truth. I say that this does not help because nowhere did the Fathers who defeated Monothelitism, especially Pope Martin and Abbot Maximus, attack the economy of the *Typos* on the ground that it overturned the council of John IV. They attacked it because it destroyed the doctrine of Saint Leo, the Council of Chalcedon, the whole of Scripture, and all the Fathers.

The same argument also applies against the dispensation of Honorius, since it followed the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of Saint Leo. It therefore falls under the same censures as the economy, or *Typos*, of the emperor Constans.

[Col. 0735B]

Moreover, the Fathers attacked the economy of the *Typos* so fiercely because silence appeared to deny one or two wills. Thus Martin, Maximus, and all the other enemies of the Monothelites unanimously considered it exactly equivalent to define that one should not speak of one or two wills or operations in Christ and to deny every will or operation to Christ altogether.

This absurdity should no more be presumed from the economy of Constans than from the dispensation of Honorius. Therefore either both must be acquitted or both condemned.

Third, the doctrine of the ancient Fathers, who unanimously and openly assert that there are two wills and operations in Christ, is weakened no less by the economies of Honorius than by the dispensations of the *Typos*. If the authorities of the Fathers strongly compelled Pope Martin and Abbot Maximus to attack the economy of the *Typos* with such vehemence, why could those same authorities not have sufficed for the bishops of the Sixth Synod to expel the economy of Honorius, which supplied nourishment to the heretics?

[Col. 0735C]

The same anonymous author mentioned above reports and refutes other excuses in favor of the economy of Honorius, which there is no time to repeat here. The same arguments advanced to excuse the dispensation of Honorius can also be used to defend the *Typos*. Let this suffice, then, concerning economies and dispensations; more can be read on the subject in the work cited.

Pyrrhus of Constantinople, formerly patriarch, had falsely abjured his heresy at Rome in order to win over Pope Theodore and the Western bishops by pretending to hold the orthodox faith, and so that through their assistance and authority he might be restored. He returned to an open profession of heresy once the way to union with the Easterners had been opened to him through Plato, the exarch of Italy, as Theophanes for the twentieth year of Heraclius and the author of the *Synodal Booklet* testify.

Theophanes says:

> “When Pyrrhus had departed from Rome and reached Ravenna, he returned like a dog to his vomit” (2 Peter 2:22). “When Pope Theodore learned of this, he summoned an assembly of the Church, went to the tomb of the prince of the apostles, and, having requested the divine chalice, dripped life-giving blood from it into ink. Thus, with his own hand, he carried out the deposition of Pyrrhus and of those who communicated with him.”

Paul the Deacon of Aquileia, in *History*, chapter 18, and the author of the *Synodal Booklet* use nearly the same words, and they too mention the blood of Christ being dripped from the chalice into ink.

It is therefore certain, with Theophanes, Anastasius, and the author of the *Synodal Booklet* as witnesses, that Pyrrhus was struck by a sentence of anathema and deposition in the Roman Synod summoned by Pope Theodore in 648.

This practice of signing with a pen dipped in the Lord’s blood instead of ink was peculiar to the Greeks; nevertheless, it was employed by Pope Theodore in the condemnation of Pyrrhus, although Anastasius did not mention this fact. Baronius relates the same story from Nicetas, in the *Life of Saint Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople*, who, speaking of Photius’s condemnation at the Council of Constantinople, says under the year 869 in Baronius:

> “They subscribed to this condemnation not by a document written in ordinary ink, but—horrible to say, as I learned from those who know it—by dipping the pen in the very blood of the Savior, and thus condemned Photius.”

Combefis, in *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, Disputation 1, paragraph 13, writes that the aforementioned Theodore and the Constantinopolitan Fathers committed no sin more serious than this abuse, as though it were the Lord’s blood, and this irreverence; nor, he adds, did Basil commit a less serious sin when he wished a particle of the Lord’s body to be buried with him, as may be read there. The deed of Saint Basil is preserved in Amphilochius, whose fragment Aeneas, bishop of Paris, cites in his book *Against the Greeks*, *Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 81. Saint Gregory likewise relates in Book II, chapter 24 of the *Dialogues*, that Saint Benedict did the same: he ordered a young monk to be buried with the Lord’s body, reverently placed upon his breast. Edmond Martene also observes, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, Book I, chapter 5, article 4, that at the solemn dedication of churches three portions taken from the Lord’s body were enclosed in the altar with lime and cement; an anonymous author of the *Deeds of the Abbots of the Greater Monastery* relates that Pope Urban II did this at the dedication of the basilica of the Greater Monastery. Martene subsequently shows that the ancients did not consider that anything of the honor owed to Christ was thereby diminished.

Baronius thought that the *Typus* had been condemned by Pope Theodore at the same synod, together with Paul, bishop of Constantinople. But from Anastasius, Theophanes, and the author of the synodical booklet—who alone among the ancient writers speak of this Roman synod, and who do not contain even a word about either the *Typus* or Paul being condemned there, but speak only of Pyrrhus—it is inferred that the *Typus* was condemned neither at this synod nor afterward by Theodore. Since nowhere is it recorded that Theodore condemned the *Typus* after that synod, we must conclude, with the aforementioned Combefis, that the first condemnation of the *Typus* belongs to Pope Martin. Certainly, if Theodore had condemned the *Typus*, the emperor, when he learned of Martin’s election, would not have urged him to agree with the *Typus*, but would have asked him to rescind the decree issued against it. Perhaps, moreover, at the time of this Roman synod the promulgation of the *Typus* was still unknown; it had been carried out in the sixth indiction, and therefore before the Kalends of September in the year 648, the same year in which Theodore held this Roman synod.

As for Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, when Theodore, after issuing through his letters and his *apocrisiarii* the most affectionate admonitions and the most earnest warnings, had found that Paul’s wound was already desperate and could no longer be treated by flattery but only by the sword and fire of anathemas, he pronounced against him the sentence of excommunication and deposition near the end of his pontificate—that is, at the end of 648 or before May 649, in which month he died—but outside a synod. [Col. 0736D] That Paul was deposed by Theodore is established by the testimony of the Greek abbots and monks in the booklet presented to the Lateran Synod and read in the second secretary, where they say:

> “Together with them we submit to the same anathema the *Typus*, which has now been produced against the orthodox faith through deception, not from the purpose or intention of our most pious emperor, but through the importunate persuasion and false speech of Paul, who was deposed by Theodore, the predecessor of your holiness, the pope of your apostolic see, of most holy memory.”

That he was condemned outside a synod is inferred from Anastasius. After speaking of the synod at which Pyrrhus was condemned, Anastasius relates the translation of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus and other deeds of Pope Theodore, and then adds:

> “The most holy Pope Theodore wrote to Paul, patriarch of the imperial city, both entreating him and correcting him according to the canons; he also admonished and warned him in person through *apocrisiarii* sent especially for this purpose, so that he might correct his own composition and return to the orthodox faith of the Catholic Church. Yet neither the entreaties nor the corrections could in any way recall him from his undertaking. Therefore he was struck by the apostolic see with the punishment of deposition.”

Here there is no mention of any other synod held by Theodore.

As for the persecution stirred up by Paul against the *apocrisiarii* of the apostolic see, of which Pope Martin speaks in the fourth secretary of the Lateran Council and Anastasius in his account of Martin, it appears to have occurred in Theodore’s time, as Baronius proves under the year 648. Paul first plundered the altar and oratory in the house where the *apocrisiarii* of the Roman see had customarily lived. Then he stirred up persecution against those same *apocrisiarii*, who were at that time in Constantinople, and against the other orthodox people attached to them: some he handed over to prison, others he sent into exile, and still others he subjected to scourging. It does not seem possible to say that Pope Martin’s *apocrisiarii* suffered this persecution, since Martin himself, in letters written against Paul, bishop of Thessalonica, laments that his own *apocrisiarii* had been led astray.

**Line 9—“Who was also buried.”** After all these things had been carried out with such constancy and holiness, and after—according to the testimony of the same Anastasius—he had occupied the see for six years, five months, and eighteen days, he was taken from this life on 13 May 649. He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 14 May, that is, on the second day before the Ides of May. Since he had been consecrated on 24 November 642, it must be said, with certain manuscripts of Anastasius and certain catalogues, that he occupied the see for six years, five months, and nineteen days. His name is entered under 14 May in certain martyrologies, as may be seen in the Bollandist *Acts of the Saints* for that day. Concerning the books of Saint Gregory the Pope’s *Moralia*, which were discovered at Rome during Martin’s pontificate, see what is said under Martin.]

[**Note: [Col. 0737C]**]

**No. 127, line 1—“At that time Pyrrhus came from Africa.”** While the see of Constantinople was occupied by Paul, Pyrrhus, who had withdrawn to Africa, found there the holy abbot Maximus. He held with him a celebrated disputation on Monothelitism before the governor and several bishops of the province. They disputed concerning Pope Honorius, whom Pyrrhus claimed had plainly taught one will in Jesus Christ in his letter to Sergius. When Pyrrhus finally became convinced, together with Maximus, that greater credence regarding the true meaning of the letter should be given to the man who had written it in the name of Honorius, and who was still alive and was illuminating the whole West both by his other virtues and by the doctrines of the Christian faith, rather than to the Constantinopolitans, who interpreted it according to their own pleasure, Maximus recited the very words which the same writer later used in the name of Pope John, writing to the emperor Constantine about that letter:

> “We said that there is one will in the Lord—not of his divinity and humanity together, but of humanity alone. For when Sergius had written that certain people said there were two contrary wills in Christ, we said that Christ did not have two contrary wills, of flesh, I mean, and spirit, as we have after sin, but only one, which naturally signified his humanity.” (*Lateran Council*, first secretary.)

Maximus said that this was especially clear as the meaning of the letter because it mentions flesh and limbs, which do not belong to divinity. Then, showing how he anticipated the objection, he continued in the writer’s words:

> “But if someone says, ‘Why, when speaking of Christ’s humanity, did you not also mention his divinity?’ we answer, first, that the statement was made in response to the question; and, second, that here, as everywhere, we followed the usage of Scripture, which sometimes discusses his divinity—for example, when the Apostle says, ‘Christ the power and wisdom of God’—and sometimes his humanity alone, as when the same Apostle says, ‘What is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men.’” (Ibid.)

The outcome of this celebrated disputation was Pyrrhus’s conversion. He concluded it with these words:

> “Because I value my salvation more than all other things, I am ready to do this with complete satisfaction. I ask only that I first be considered worthy to venerate the churches of the apostles, and especially those of the chief apostles; then that I may see the face of the most holy pope and hand him the booklet containing the things that were absurdly done.” (Ibid., at the end.)

He certainly stood by his words. He came to Rome, where, by a solemn abjuration, he rejected the impious doctrines of the sectarians and, through a correct profession of faith, joined himself to the Catholic Church. He presented the authentic acts of his rejection to Pope Theodore before the clergy and people. In return, the pope, who recognized him as the legitimate bishop of Constantinople, wished to give him whatever was necessary to maintain the dignity of the imperial see.

But Pyrrhus departed from Rome and came to Ravenna, the seat of the exarchate. There, apparently at the exarch’s urging and led by the hope of recovering his see through the favor of the emperor Constans, who professed Monothelitism, he corrupted himself and returned to his vomit. When the pope first learned of this, he summoned a synod and condemned Pyrrhus by a rite no less novel than terrifying: he wrote the deposition of Pyrrhus and of those adhering to him with a pen sprinkled with the precious blood of Jesus Christ. (*Theophanes*, year 20 of the Emperor Heraclius.)]

[Col. 0721]

**125. Theodore, a Greek by nation, son of Theodore the bishop, from the city of Jerusalem, occupied the see for six years, five months, and eighteen days.**

[**Note: [Col. 0721]** B, 20.] He was a lover of the poor, generous, kinder than all others, and very merciful. During his time, when the sins of Maurice the *chartularius*—through whom the patrician Isaac had committed many evils—had increased against blessed Peter the Apostle, so that unquenchable fire might make them its heirs, the aforesaid Maurice, having taken counsel with those with whom he had previously devastated the Church of God, set himself up against the patrician Isaac. [**Note: [Col. 0721]** “Had increased against blessed Peter the Apostle”; **Note:** “so that it might make him its heir”; **Note:** “He set himself up,” B: “he made himself a tyrant.”] He sent throughout all the military camps situated around the Roman city, gathered the troops, and bound himself with them by an oath. [**Note: [Col. 0721]** “With one another by an oath.”] They swore that from then on none of them would obey Isaac or his men, who asserted that he had refused to assume kingship. [**Note: [Col. 0721]** “Who asserted that he wished to assume kingship.”]

When the patrician Isaac heard this, because the whole army of Italy had sworn an oath to Maurice, [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “Because Maurice and the whole army had sworn such oaths to one another,”] he sent Donus, his *magister militum* and treasurer, to Rome with an army. When he entered the Roman city, all the judges—that is, the Roman army—which had previously bound itself by oath to Maurice, were driven by fear to abandon Maurice the *chartularius*. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** B adds “the Romans.”] They all joined Donus. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “They all turned to Donus.”]

**126**

[**Note: [Col. 0723]** See Baronius under the year 643.] When Donus entered Rome, Maurice fled to Saint Mary at the Crib. They seized him from the church and put a fetter around his neck. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “A fetter, that is, a chain.”] Likewise, all who had been involved in his council were sent to Ravenna in fetters, through the hands of Maurinus the *scribo* and Thomas the *chartularius*. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** B: “Thomasius.”] While they were leading them away, they reached a place near Ravenna called Ficulas, twelve miles from the city. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “Ficudas,” B; it is the church of Ficodensis, today Cervia.] There they beheaded Maurice, because they had received this order from the aforementioned Isaac: that he was not to enter the city of Ravenna. After he had been beheaded, they lifted up his head and carried it to Ravenna. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** C: “They carried him.”]

When Isaac saw Maurice’s head, he rejoiced. He had it placed on a stake in the circus at Ravenna as an example to many. As for all those who had been sent with him, he ordered them, still in fetters, to be put in prison under strict guard while he considered how to punish them. But while these things were being done, Isaac was immediately struck down by divine judgment and died. Those who had been imprisoned came out and returned individually to their own places. When the emperor heard that Isaac had died, [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “Constans,”] he sent the patrician Theodore, the exarch surnamed Calliopas, to govern all Italy.

**127. At that time Pyrrhus came from Africa.** He had been patriarch of Constantinople and came to the city of Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** See Baronius under the year 645.] When he entered, he presented a booklet bearing his subscription to our apostolic see in the presence of all the clergy and people, condemning in that booklet everything that he or his predecessors had written or done against our immaculate faith. After he had completed these acts, he caused gifts to be distributed among the people [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “Among the people,”] and had a chair placed for him beside the altar, honoring him as the priest of the imperial city. Later he returned again, like a dog, to his own vomit of impiety. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “He returned.”]

Then the most holy Pope Theodore summoned all the priests [**Note: [Col. 0723]** See Baronius under the year 648.] and clergy in the church of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and condemned him under the bond of anathema, in accordance with the reward and retribution for his own transgression, adding the canonical punishment, namely deposition. [**Note: [Col. 0723]** C: “And decreeing it.”] The aforementioned Pyrrhus returned to the eastern regions.

**128.** At the same time the bodies of the holy martyrs Primus and Felicianus, which had been buried in a sandpit on the Nomentan Way, were recovered and brought into the city of Rome. They were deposited in the basilica of blessed Stephen the protomartyr [**Note: [Col. 0723]** “On Mount Caelius,”] where Theodore also offered gifts: three golden *gabathae*, silver panels before the confessio, and two silver arches. He built from the foundations a church for Saint Valentine on the Flaminian Way, beside the Milvian Bridge, dedicated it himself, and offered many gifts. He built an oratory for Saint Sylvester [**Note: [Col. 0723]** CB: “Sebastian”] within the Lateran episcopal residence, where he also gave gifts. He likewise built an oratory for the martyr Saint Euplus outside the gate of blessed Paul the Apostle, and adorned it.

**129**

[**Note: [Col. 0723]** See Baronius under the year 648.] Then the most holy Pope Theodore wrote to Paul, patriarch of the imperial city, both entreating him and correcting him according to the canons; he also admonished and warned him in person through the *apocrisiarii*, as stated, sent especially for this purpose, so that he might correct his own composition and return to the orthodox faith of the Catholic Church. Neither the entreaties nor the corrections could in any way recall him from his undertaking. Therefore he was struck by the apostolic see with the punishment of deposition. [**Note: [Col. 0725]** “Struck.”]

He conducted one ordination in the month of December: twenty-one priests, four deacons, and forty-six bishops in various places. He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the second day before the Ides of May, and the episcopate was vacant for fifty-two days. [**Note: [Col. 0725]** C: “One month and sixteen days.”]

## LXXVI. MARTIN. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 649, THE EIGHTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTINE

[**Note: [Col. 0743D]**]

**No. 130, line 5—“So that he might persuade the most merciful prince to set forth the *Typus*.”** The *Typus* is a pragmatic edict, Novel 113, chapter 1; canon 38 of the Synod in Trullo: “Τοῖς πολιμικοῖς καὶ δημοσίοις τύποις”—“civil and public *typoi*.” Balsamon, in canon 12 of the Council of Chalcedon, says: “Τὰ βασιλικὰ προστάγματα, πραγματικοὶ τύποι λέγονται”—“Imperial edicts are called pragmatic forms.” Hence Anastasius below, in the same place:

> “In this *Typus* he weakened all the words of the holy Fathers, together with the distinctions of the most wicked heretics.”

And below:

> “And if you find the province itself agreeing with the *Typus* set forth by us.”

And below:

> “Because the orthodox *Typus* has been made by us.”

*Typoi* are also agreements of peace between rulers. Paul the Deacon, Book XIX:

> “He also destroyed the peace established with the Bulgarians, disturbing the *typoi* which had been properly made by his father.”

**Line 10—“He himself ventured in the dispute so far that, overturning and plundering the altar of our holy see, which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia, in the venerable oratory…”** *Oraculum* means “oratory.” Anastasius below, in the account of Agatho:

> “In the oratory of blessed Peter the Apostle inside the palace.”

And again:

> “Inside the oratory of Saint Peter inside the palace.”

The same author, in the account of Sergius:

> “In the oratory of the blessed martyr Caesar, Christ’s servant.”

**Line 21—“So that the harmful sickness of their *ecthesis* might in no way tear apart the whole body of the Catholic Church.”** *Ecthesis* comes from the Greek ἔκτισις, “defection,” “loosening of the limbs,” “wasting,” *ectesis*, φθίσις, “a serious disease”; concerning this, see Book I, section “But it must be known,” of the *Digest*, title *On the Edict of the Aediles*.

**No. 131, line 2—“And he held a synod according to the institution of the orthodox Fathers, in the church of the Savior beside the Lateran episcopal residence.”** Roman synods were very often held in the Lateran church, which was called Constantiniana after its founder because it had been founded by Constantine. Anastasius, in his account of Sylvester, and below in this passage, says:

> “They seized the most holy Pope Martin from the church of the Savior, which is also called Constantiniana.”

It was also called the church of the Savior because it was dedicated to the Savior, and it had a silver gable on whose front the Savior was represented seated on a chair. Peter Damian, Book II, Letter 1, says of it:

> “Just as the Lateran church is distinguished by the name of the Savior, who is certainly the head of all the elect, so it is the mother, summit, and crown of all the churches throughout the world. It has seven cardinal bishops, and only they, after the apostolic pontiff, are permitted to approach that sacred altar and celebrate the mysteries of divine worship.”

**Line 4—“The bishops and priests being seated, the deacons and the whole clergy standing by.”** In a council the bishops and priests sit, while the deacons stand, according to the Council of Laodicea, canon 20, and canon 93, *Non oportet*, of the *Decretum*. John Chrysostom, *Homily 33 on Matthew*:

> “For your sake the presbyter sits; for your sake the deacon stands, laboring and afflicted.”

The Roman Council on the veneration of images, held by Gregory III, was conducted with the bishops and priests seated and the deacons standing. (Anastasius, in his *Life*.)

**No. 132, lines 9–10—“For while the most holy pope was giving him communion, he wished to kill him cruelly, as he had ordered his *spatharius*.”** A *spatharius* is one who carries the ruler’s sword. The Franks call it a *spatha*. Aymoin, Book I, chapter 12:

> “He extended his hand and cast his Frankish axe to the ground; it is called a *spatha*.”

Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II:

> “A gilded *spatha* and sword.”

Hence *spatharius* and *protospatharius*. Anastasius, in his account of Sergius:

> “Then he sent Zacharias, his savage *protospatharius*, with an order.”

And below:

> “Zacharias the *spatharius*, terrified.”

The same author, in his account of Gregory II:

> “Marianus, the imperial *spatharius*, who held the Roman duchy.”

Cassiodorus, Book III, *Variae*, Letter 43. The office of the *spatharius* was to carry before him the emperor’s unsheathed sword. The Frankish Annals say:

> “Before his tribunal an unsheathed sword was carried in the imperial manner.”

**Line 13—“And he was not permitted to see the pontiff when he gave communion to the exarch or gave him the peace.”** A bishop or pontiff gives the peace, that is, the blessing. Ambrose, *On the Death of Satyrus*:

> “Let us proceed to the tomb, but first, before the people, I shall say my final farewell, proclaim peace, and give the kiss.”

John Chrysostom, *Homily 29 on Matthew*:

> “For in the Church also the presiding bishop gives peace.”

]

[**Note: [Col. 0746A]**]

**No. 130, line 2—“During his time, Paul…”** The material which the Librarian includes here was again taken from the same Lateran Council and from the surviving letters in Anastasius’s own collections, published by Sirmond. Much material useful for illuminating the deeds of Saint Martin can be drawn from them.]

[**Note: [Col. 0746A]**]

**No. 130, line 1—“Martin.”** In the year of Christ 649, on the first day of July, after an interregnum of one month and sixteen days, Martin, of Tuscan origin, ascended the apostolic throne. Heretical innovators falsely accuse him of being a follower of the Novatian heresy because, in Letter 11 to Amandus, he taught that forgiveness should not be given to priests or deacons who sinned after their ordination. But if they had read, or even now read, the pontiff’s letter carefully and without prejudice, they would undoubtedly be ashamed of their own malice and ignorance.

When Amandus, bishop of Maastricht, disgusted by the corrupt morals of the clergy, had asked the Roman pontiff by letter to be released from the episcopate, Martin rightly refused him what he had requested to the detriment of the Church of Maastricht and admonished him to reform ecclesiastical discipline there. He ordered him to depose from their rank priests and deacons who had committed serious sins; and, if they repented and asked forgiveness, to absolve them but never restore them to their former ranks and dignities. It is therefore clear that Martin was speaking not so much about forgiveness of sins as about restoration to the sacred ministries. See Bellarmine, Book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 12.

**Same line—“He occupied the see for six years.”** Baronius, in the appendix to Volume II, correcting what he had thought in earlier editions concerning the duration of Saint Martin’s see, says that Martin governed the Church for five years, four months, and twelve days.

**No. 133, line 13—“Many miracles, and so forth.”** Pope Gregory II, writing in his letter to the heretical emperor Leo the Isaurian, adds the following concerning Saint Martin, among other things:

> “The city of Cherson and the Bosporus testify that blessed Martin is a saint, as do the whole north and the inhabitants of the north, who flock to his tomb and experience cures of diseases.”

**Line 16—“The episcopate was vacant for twenty-eight days.”** It is not probable that Saint Martin’s death could have been conveyed to Rome in so short a period; therefore this reading, which is absent from other manuscripts, appears to have entered the text by error.]

[**Note: [Col. 0746D]**

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.**]

With an inter-pontificate of 52 days established after Theodore in the notes on that same pope, it remains now to inquire into the beginning of his successor, Saint Martin, as well as his final day and the duration of his pontificate. That his beginning must be placed no later than the very year of Theodore’s death, 649, is clearly taught by the Lateran Council of 105 bishops celebrated by Martin himself in that same year against the Monothelite depravity. For the heading of the first secretary records: “In the name of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, in the ninth year of the reign of our Lord Constantine, the most devout Augustus, on the third day before the Nones of October, indiction 8.” Here we have two certain chronological markers of the aforesaid year—repeated also in the fifth and final secretary—the year of Constans, whom others correctly call Constantine, and the indiction.

Indeed, the very day of his ordination presents itself to a careful observer of the calendar. For, counting fifty-two days from the death of Theodore on 13 May, 5 July remains; that date is marked by the dominical letter D for that year and must therefore be assigned to the ordination of the holy pontiff.

As for the end of his pontificate, no clearer evidence could possibly be devised than that which is available. Various short Greek works, collected and translated into Latin by Anastasius the Librarian, are extant and are therefore called his *Collectanea*. From them the dates of the holy pontiff’s captivity, deportation, imprisonment, trial, and death are evident. For in a letter sent to the West by a most Christian man, and in the *Hypomnesticon* of the monks Theodosius and Theodore, concerning the struggles and death of the holy martyrs, Martin’s death at Cherson, the place of his exile, is related in identical words: in the month of September, on the sixteenth day, in the fourteenth indiction—that is, in the year 655, since the fourteenth indiction was running from the Kalends of September according to Greek usage.

In view of this, Antonius Pagius in his *Critique of Baronius* and Daniel Papebrochius in his *Chronological-Historical Endeavor* rightly wonder that the most learned cardinal, without taking any account of the cycle, overturned the most certain chronological foundations of this pontificate by shortening the dates of Martin’s captivity and deportation by two years, and that of his death by one year. We too may reasonably wonder at this. For the only excuse that could be offered—that Baronius had not seen the *Collectanea*, since they were published through the efforts of Sirmond after Baronius’s death—collapses completely under Baronius’s own testimony in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* for 12 November, where he properly boasts that such a precious manuscript had been bequeathed to the library of his congregation.

Since I know that the reader will find it most agreeable to inspect the persecution of the holy pontiff set out chronologically from the day on which it began, 15 June 653, until the day of his death, I shall place before his eyes a brief and careful account of it.

[Col. 0747C]

**653.**

**17 days before the Kalends of July, or 15 June, Saturday.** Calliopas enters the city of Rome with the army of Ravenna and Theodore the chamberlain. (Onuphrius calls this man Theodore Calliopas, the second exarch of Italy.)

**15 days before the Kalends of July, or 17 June.** Calliopas and the army, armed, sacrilegiously enter the Constantinian church. An order is presented to the priests and deacons, commanding that Martin be deposed and sent to Constantinople. Then the holy pontiff is led from the church to Calliopas’s palace.

**14 days before the Kalends of July, or 18 June, Tuesday.** The entire clergy visits the pontiff, and a large part of it promises that it will accompany him.

**13 days before the Kalends of July, or 19 June, Wednesday.** During the preceding night Saint Martin, taken away with only six attendants, reaches the harbor, from which he departs without any other retinue.

**On the Kalends of July.** He reaches Messina; and, sailing in great illness and without assistance of any kind, he comes to the island of Naxos in September, where he is compelled to remain for a year.

[Col. 0747D]

**654.**

**15 days before the Kalends of October, or 17 September.** He reaches the harbor of Byzantium near Euphemia. In the evening he is taken to the guardhouse and detained in that prison for 93 days. At last he is brought out and, treated most harshly, thrust into the prefect’s custody, or the workhouse of Diomedes, where he remains for 84 days—178 days in all.

**655.**

**7 days before the Kalends of April, or 26 March, Thursday of Holy Week.** He is deported from Byzantium to Cherson, the place of exile.

**On the Ides of May, or 15 May.** He reaches Cherson, where, after suffering many hardships for a period of four months, he dies on 16 September. He is buried outside the walls of Cherson, almost one stadium away, in the church of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin.

There you have the fully established final events of the holy pontiff, which cannot be doubted, since they are affirmed by contemporaries of those times, who agree with the letters of Martin himself. His beginnings likewise seem to me equally certain, on the basis of the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts and catalogues in establishing an inter-pontificate of 52 days. For this reason I would say that the duration of Saint Martin’s pontificate extended from 5 July 649 to 16 September 655, partly in Rome and partly in exile, were I not deterred from deriving the beginning of his successor Eugene from the time of Saint Martin’s exile. Accordingly, whatever must be said on this matter will be more appropriately established below, in the notes on Eugene.

Here I mention in passing that, from the notes of Pagius and Sommier on this pontiff, which I have gathered together, a complete history of Monothelitism and of its principal foundations can be had from the pontificates of Honorius and Martin: Heraclius’s *Ecthesis* and Constans’s *Type*, whose condemnation brought so many hardships upon Martin. Hence see below, no. 131.

[Note: Col. 0748B]

**No. 130, line 1.—Martin.** Son of Fabricius, from the city of Todi, now commonly called Todi in Tuscany. Under the emperor Flavius Heraclius Constans II Augustus, he was *apocrisarius* at Constantinople in attendance upon that same emperor Constans. He occupied the pontificate for 6 years, 4 months, and 17 days; he was elected on the day before the Nones of July and consecrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of October.

[Note: Col. 0748B]

**No. 130, line 5.—“To set forth the Type, which would destroy Catholic doctrine.”** After the emperor Constans, according to the custom of that age, had consented to the election of Saint Martin, he left nothing undone to extort from him confirmation of the Type. But the holy pontiff abhorred the crime and was so far from giving his assent to Constans that he instead summoned the Lateran Synod. It began on 5 October of that same year, 649, and was concluded on the vigil of All Saints, as is clear from the headings of the first and fifth, or final, secretary.

Martin could not be deterred from so holy a purpose either by the emperor’s letters or by the presence of Olympius himself, the exarch who had been sent into Italy to promulgate the Type. When Olympius came to Rome at the very time when the synod was being held, he first attempted to provoke a revolt through the army. When he saw that this had failed, he urged his sword-bearer to kill the pontiff while the exarch himself was receiving Communion from him during the solemn celebration of Mass. But the sword-bearer was divinely blinded, and the pontiff was delivered from this imminent danger as well. Olympius himself was afterward reconciled with him, as Anastasius relates; this was why, in his letter to the emperor Constans, Pope Martin did not mention this act of violence.

[Col. 0748D]

**No. 131, line 2.—“And he held a synod according to the institutions of the Fathers,” etc.** Thus Martin, as we have said, was in no way terrified and celebrated the synod. One hundred and five bishops attended it. First, various legations were heard and letters were read both from Eastern and Western prelates against the heresy of the Monothelites and its adherents. Then everything that could be found to have been written by such heretics against the Catholic faith was brought forward, together with the *Ecthesis* promulgated in the name of the emperor Heraclius and the *Type* promulgated in the name of the emperor Constans.

In particular, the writings of Theodore, bishop of Pharan, regarded as the founder of the Monothelite error, were read, since all who promulgated the heresy had received it from his writings. After these had been carefully examined, twenty canons were enacted from the teaching of the holy Fathers, in order to declare the true doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Word and to refute all heresies, together with an equal number of anathemas against those who held otherwise.

All the ancient heresiarchs were condemned, as were the authors and principal supporters of the Monothelite impiety: Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, bishops of Constantinople, together with their impious writings, as well as the *Ecthesis* of Heraclius and the *Type* of Constans. Everything was then confirmed by the subscriptions of all the bishops.

The synod acted with prudent policy toward the emperors Heraclius and Constans. It did not wish to condemn the *Ecthesis* and the *Type* under their names, nor to strike the rulers with an anathema: lest Constans create a schism, lest he promote the heresy more boldly, lest he bring persecution upon the Church, and finally lest every hope of detaching him from the heretics be destroyed by the anathema through which he would have been cut off from the Church.

The synod consisted of five secretaries, or consultations, or sessions, completed over an equal number of days. A *secretarium* was a small building or chamber attached to a temple or sacred building in place of an exedra, in which the church’s equipment was stored and in which priests and clerics put on their ecclesiastical vestments before proceeding to the sacred rites. We learn from the Acts of synods that synods were often held in such *secretaria*.

From this Lateran Synod Martin the pontiff and all the Fathers wrote a synodal circular letter to all the faithful everywhere concerning what had taken place there. It survives, composed with great diligence from the sacred Scriptures, and is fully worthy of so great a pontiff and so great an assembly of bishops.

Such was the authority of this synod that it was later mentioned, after the five general synods, in the professions of faith customarily made by the Roman pontiffs. Hence, in the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 2, title 9, three formulas of these professions are recited. In the third, which was made by the Roman pontiff after his ordination, the pontiff not only professes that he safeguards the five general synods and, in addition, the sixth, which had recently been convened, as the formula says, but also all the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, “especially those which were defined and decreed by Martin, of holy memory, universal pope, for the confirmation of the aforesaid five synods.”

Thus the practice of adding a confession of the Lateran Synod under Martin, after the assertion of the five universal synods, continued even after the sixth ecumenical synod had been promulgated.

## History of Monothelitism

Two letters of Pope Honorius, written in 634 to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, furnished abundant material for the notable controversy concerning Honorius’s orthodoxy, or unimpaired faith, and concerning his Monothelitism—especially since he is found implicated by an anathema in the Acts of the sixth general synod as they are now transmitted.

To explain this controversy, something must first be said here about the heresy of the Monothelites. Their principal error consisted in maintaining that there was in Christ a single operation and therefore a single will. They argued that the human nature was so united to the Word that, although it possessed a mind and other faculties that are appendages of nature, it nevertheless did not exercise an action proper to itself. Rather, there was one action only, proceeding from the Word as its principal cause and from the humanity as its instrumental cause.

This is established by the letter of Cyrus of Alexandria, the Monothelite patriarch, to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople and leader of the Monothelites. In that letter Cyrus professes that he had received this opinion from Sergius. Natalis Alexander adduces many other Monothelite testimonies in proof of the same matter in Century VII, chapter 2, section 1. There he also shows, from the testimony of Saint Maximus in his disputation with Pyrrhus, how great was the Monothelites’ fickle shallowness in setting forth or defending their error.

Various beginnings are assigned to this heresy. The author of the *Critique of Baronius* proves that it began to emerge around the year 616 from the fact that Saint Maximus, in the aforementioned disputation with Pyrrhus—the immediate successor of Sergius in the see of Constantinople—wishing to defend the innocence of Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, whom Pyrrhus had accused of being responsible for the origin of this evil, replies:

“Where was Sophronius when Sergius wrote to George, surnamed Arsa, a Paulianist, asking him to send authorities concerning one operation, and even adding to his letter that he himself was making these authorities serve the union of the Church with them? But blessed John, pope of Alexandria, took this letter away from Arsa with his own hand. Therefore, when he wished to depose him on account of it, he was prevented at that time by the Persian invasion of Egypt.”

Since the Persians afflicted Egypt in 615 and the following year, and Saint John the Almsgiver, patriarch of Alexandria, died in November 616, the beginning of the Monothelites cannot be placed later than that year.

[Col. 0750B]

Writers commonly, however, associate the beginning of Monothelitism with the year 622. In that year the imprudent emperor Heraclius became its midwife in the encounter he had in Armenia with Paul the One-Eyed, a follower of the heretic Severus, whom Sergius mentions in his letter to Pope Honorius, which is extant in action 13 of the sixth synod.

Indeed, others derive its beginning from the year 629, when, according to Theophanes in his *Chronicle*, Heraclius had another encounter at Hierapolis, not far from Edessa, with Athanasius, patriarch of the Jacobites. In both encounters the emperor offered the doctrine of one will and one operation in Christ.

But whatever may be the case concerning this second encounter, it is certain that in 622 Heraclius, deceived by the aforesaid Paul the Severian, consulted both Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, who was later transferred to the archbishopric of Alexandria, asking whether there were two wills in Christ or one. From them he received the answer that one will and operation must absolutely be affirmed in Christ.

Nor did Sergius, the patron of this sect, have much difficulty in drawing Heraclius over to his position under the attractive title of union, since the East was then deplorably divided into various sects. Yet the outcome did not correspond to his hope and expectation; indeed, Saint Maximus testifies in his letter to Peter the Illustrious that “the Catholic Church enjoyed concord and unanimity, as well as peaceful and tranquil faith, before the devil himself, the friend of disturbance, stirred up through his Monothelite ministers the dark cloud and the shrieking waves of the sea.”

The father of the Monothelites, then, was Sergius, a Syrian by race, born to Jacobite parents. From being a deacon he was made bishop of Constantinople in 610, after the death of Saint Thomas, patriarch of that same church. We read of him in a synodal treatise:

“When Heraclius, having undertaken by divine assistance the war against the Persians, brought the river Phasis under his power, a certain Acephalian—namely Paul the One-Eyed, concerning whom the preceding section has spoken—suggested to him the question of wills and operations. After he had communicated this question especially to Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, and both of them were in doubt, they reported it to Sergius of Constantinople. He, having convened a synod according to the heretical practice and examining the Acts of Mena point by point, wrote back to the emperor Heraclius that there was one will in Christ our God and Savior.”

That false synod of Constantinople was held in 626. Sergius himself relates that these things had taken place between Cyrus and himself in his letter to Pope Honorius, which Baronius cites under the year 633.

Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, was elevated to the episcopal see of Alexandria. When the emperor Heraclius issued an order against Paul the Severian which, among other things, prohibited the assertion that there were two operations in Christ, and sent it to the more prominent bishops—especially to Sergius of Constantinople and Cyrus of Alexandria—Cyrus initially hesitated. The following words of Saint Leo led him to withhold his assent:

“Each form operates, in communion with the other, what is proper to it.”

But, confirmed in his error by Sergius’s prompting, he cast off all scruple, as we learn from his own letter to Sergius. Sergius, who rejoiced greatly that the wicked doctrine he had taught the emperor Heraclius was being established by the emperor’s command, approved that order.

These might have seemed slight sparks of error, but they burst into a great conflagration when Cyrus of Alexandria, in 633, convened a conciliabulum at Alexandria under the pretext of uniting the Acephali with the Church. There he issued nine chapters, in the seventh of which he asserted:

“The same one Christ and Son operates things divine and human by one divine-human operation, according to Saint Dionysius.”

But Cyrus interpolated Saint Dionysius’s text and substituted “one” for “a new divine-human operation.” The other Monothelites followed this fraud.

After that false synod had been celebrated, Cyrus wrote to Sergius and attached to his letter the nine chapters fabricated and promulgated at Alexandria.
