Sergius sent Cyrus a congratulatory reply, inserted in the Lateran Synod under Saint Martin, secretary III. There he openly approved Cyrus’s chapters, praised them extravagantly, and asserted:

“The same one Christ operates things divine and human by one operation, because every divine and human operation proceeded from one and the same incarnate God the Word.”

Sophronius, still a monk and not long afterward patriarch of Jerusalem, came to that false synod of Alexandria. Saint Maximus says in his letter to Peter the Illustrious:

“Thus the divine and great Sophronius, coming to Alexandria at that time, immediately upon the first reading—for Cyrus had also given him those nine chapters of impiety to reconsider—uttered something mournful and immense, pouring forth springs of tears. He fervently begged, implored, and entreated him, prostrate at his feet on the pavement, to preach none of these things on the ambo against the Catholic Church of God, since they were plainly the impious doctrines of Apollinaris.”

Since Cyrus and Sophronius could not reach agreement, Sophronius went to Constantinople to plead his case before Sergius and to seek the abolition of the seventh chapter, in which only one divine-human will was decreed. But he could obtain nothing from Sergius.

Returning from Constantinople to Palestine, Sophronius was appointed, toward the end of 633 or the beginning of the following year, to replace Modestus, the deceased patriarch of Jerusalem. He immediately held a council of the Palestinian bishops, at which he composed the sacred encyclical customarily sent to the patriarchs. It was read at the sixth synod, action 11, and in it he abundantly proclaimed, with the most eloquent authorities of the holy Fathers, that there are two wills and operations in Christ.

“He sent his synodical acts to Honorius, Roman pope, and to Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople,” as we read in the synodal treatise.

Before Sergius received Sophronius’s synodical letter, he approached the Roman pontiff by letter and referred the entire matter to him as the bishop of the first see and supreme judge of the faith. In this letter, inserted in action 12 of the sixth synod, Sergius opened the way for a pernicious policy, or dispensation: namely, that henceforth neither one nor two operations should be mentioned in Christ, on account of the scandal arising from the use of those expressions. Instead, it should be said that one and the same only-begotten Son, true God, our Lord Jesus Christ, operated both the divine and the human, and every operation proper to God and worthy of man.

Honorius in turn sent Sergius a letter in which he praised him for removing the novelty of the term, which could cause scandal to the simple. He concluded his lengthy letter as follows:

“Let your Fraternity proclaim these things with us, just as we, exhorting you, unanimously proclaim them with you; exhorting you to avoid the newly introduced term ‘operation,’ whether singular or dual, and to proclaim with us one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, true God, who operated divinely in two natures, in orthodox faith and Catholic unity.”

Thus Honorius was easily persuaded to accept this dispensation of silence, which Sergius had tried in vain to persuade Sophronius to accept, and in this respect he was drawn to Sergius’s position, not without harm to the faith. This first letter of Honorius to Sergius is extant in action 12 of the sixth synod.

The situation had not yet reached such an extreme that no hope of reconciliation remained. Sophronius did not reject Honorius’s policy, either because he still recognized Sergius as the bishop of the imperial city, with whom one had to deal gently lest an offended spirit become more alienated from the faith, or because he considered that obedience due to the universal pastor, from whom, especially by virtue of the privilege of the apostolic see, correction of Sergius ought to be expected.

But when he saw that Cyrus did not cease preaching one will in Christ, he judged that this rashness had to be restrained and that efforts had to be made to remove the heresy of one will. For this reason he sent Stephen, metropolitan of Dor, to Pope Honorius, as is recorded in the Lateran Council under Martin I. There Stephen says that Sophronius himself had been unable to undertake this task because of the invasion of the Saracens. He later adds that “at the petition of nearly all the most reverend bishops and Christian peoples inhabiting the Eastern region,” he too had been invited to undertake this legation and had often explained to the holy men residing at Rome, according to the truth, everything that had been set in motion in the East.

[Col. 0752C]

Nevertheless, after being informed of these matters, Honorius wrote a second letter to Sergius, arguing the same point as in the first. He imposed silence upon Cyrus of Alexandria, who was preaching one will and operation in Christ, and he also wrote to Sergius so that he might admonish Cyrus to preserve the policy already established.

Honorius’s letter to Cyrus does not survive, but it is mentioned in Honorius’s letter to Sergius, of which a fragment was read in action 13 of the sixth synod. In this second letter to Sergius, Honorius therefore distinguishes the matter in these terms: “The term ‘one operation’ or ‘two operations,’ newly introduced, should be removed from preaching, because it is quite foolish to think or say that the Mediator between God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, either is or was one operation or two.”

With these matters established, the faith of Pope Honorius must be examined. For the voice of every heretic is that he fell into heresy, and this has also seemed so to certain Catholics, who say that human conjectures should not be indulged in on this matter but that one must stand by the judgment of the sixth ecumenical synod, in whose Acts, as we said at the beginning, he is found implicated by an anathema.

Baronius took a previously untried path. He maintained that the Acts of the sixth synod were not genuine and believed that this alone was sufficient to support the defense of Honorius. But since it had never entered the minds of ancient writers to accuse the Acts of the sixth synod of defect, or even to call them into doubt, much less to condemn other instruments of public authority as forged, Peter de Marca devised another defense of Honorius, as can be seen in his Life written by Baluzius and in his books on the harmony of the priesthood and the empire, prefixed by Baluzius.

Thus, in section 70, Baluzius says that Marca, while he was alive, promised to write a letter to Philippe Labbe in which he would entirely free Honorius from the stain of Monothelitism and show that nothing had been condemned in him at the sixth synod except negligence and the fact that he had acted inconsistently.

First, Marca had decided to prove by the clearest arguments that the Acts of that council were genuine and had not been corrupted by the Greeks, and that Honorius had been condemned there—not because the council thought that he had taught the heresy, but because he had evaded the consultation of Sergius of Constantinople and Cyrus of Alexandria with ambiguous replies and had not immediately condemned the heresy then newly emerging.

This gave the peoples of the East occasion to believe that the opinion of the Monothelites was not heretical, since the first see did not strike it with an anathema. Honorius, Marca held, had been deceived because those patriarchs promised that the entire East, where the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches prevailed, would return to the unity of the Catholic Church and embrace the decree of the Council of Chalcedon concerning the two natures united in Christ, if it could in some way be conceded that there had been one will in Christ.

Since this new opinion was then open to interpretation, because it had not yet been condemned by the Church, Honorius, in order more easily to recall the East from its ancient errors, departed from the strictest right through policy and dispensation.

This dispensation nevertheless turned out badly for him. For it resulted in the sixth synod pronouncing a sentence of condemnation against him, and the entire world became convinced that he had fostered the unsound opinion of one will, which he ought to have extinguished at its beginning.

For this reason, when the Roman pontiff Leo II speaks of Honorius, condemned at the sixth synod, he writes to the Spanish bishops:

“He did not extinguish the flame of the heretical doctrine when it was beginning, as apostolic authority required, but by neglecting it he nourished it.”

The same Leo expresses himself similarly in his letter to the emperor Constantine Pogonatus. The words are somewhat obscure in the Latin context, but in Greek they correspond remarkably with the words of the letter to the Spanish bishops according to Marca’s careful translation:

“He did not endeavor to cleanse this apostolic Church with the doctrine of apostolic tradition, but by profane betrayal allowed the pure Church to be stained.”

The emperor Constantine plainly teaches that Honorius acted inconsistently in this matter of the faith:

“Moreover, Honorius,” says the emperor in his edict, “who was pope of ancient Rome, was a confirmer of this kind of heresy, and yet he was also its opponent.”

“Honorius,” says Marca, “wrote things contradictory to one another, and in this way was a confirmer of the heresy.” These statements amount to the same position as Leo’s.

Marca added to this a passage taken from the second profession of faith customarily made by Roman pontiffs after the sixth synod. It is read in the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, page 32, where the pontiff says that he condemns “the authors of the new heretical doctrine, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople, together with Honorius, who supplied encouragement to their wicked assertions.”

Marca maintained that an episcopal negligence in a matter of faith was a crime punishable by deposition. In support of this position he cited the rescript of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, issued at Ravenna on 9 June, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. The emperor, as Marca writes, threatens according to the canons the loss of the episcopate for those who had acted sluggishly against the Pelagians, together with perpetual exclusion from communion, in addition to expulsion from the cities, which was a secular punishment.

The emperors add:

“For the guilt of those who either by concealing their agreement or by failing to condemn it have supplied harmful support is one and the same.”

The same thing is taught by Leo I and Innocent III in the Lateran Council. Hence Marca concluded that Honorius could have been condemned by the sixth synod not because he taught the heresy or assented to the Monothelites, but because of his negligence in condemning their error. For, as the emperors say, the guilt of those who either by concealing their agreement or by failing to condemn it have supplied harmful support is the same.

“For the faults of those in lower orders,” Saint Leo says in his third letter, “according to ancient practice, must be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish great pestilence while they dissimulate and fail to apply the necessary medicine.”

The silence of Honorius—or, as the Augusti call it, his concealment—is detected in the letters of Pope Leo II. Leo rebukes him for having nourished the heresy of the Monothelites by neglecting it and for having allowed, through his betrayal, the apostolic Church, which was pure, to be stained.

The same letters of Leo teach that Honorius supplied harmful support to this destructive doctrine, which he did not extinguish at its beginning, as apostolic authority required, but nourished through neglect. The emperor Constantine likewise said, in this sense, that Honorius was a confirmer of the heresy.

Moreover, Honorius’s own letters to the patriarch Sergius survive and were read at the sixth synod. Because that synod recognized that he had in some way evaded the issue in a matter of faith, it pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him as negligent. Negligence by a bishop in a matter of faith is an extremely grave crime, and the same Augusti cut off every hope of pardon for it.

This is how Baluzius presents Marca’s position in Marca’s Life.

This opinion was later explained more fully by Garnerius in the appendix to the notes on chapter 2 of the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, paragraph 6, and by Tamagninus, author of the *History of the Monothelites*, published at Paris in 1678 without the author’s name. They demonstrate at length that Honorius was justly condemned—not because he had been an advocate of one will in Christ or had taught one will in Christ, but solely because he favored those who taught it and supplied them with the opportunity to teach.

For nothing else was charged against Honorius than that he agreed with Sergius and thus fostered the heresy. He agreed only insofar as Sergius, under the fictitious name of peace, judged that the matter should be concealed. Thus both fostered the heresy out of a desire for concord: Honorius fostered another’s heresy because he did not destroy it, while Sergius fostered his own because he concealed it.

Both subscribed to positions similar to those contained in the two condemned imperial documents: Honorius to the *Type* of Constans, concerning which we have spoken in the section on Pope Theodore, in which nothing was commanded except silence; and Sergius to the *Ecthesis* of Heraclius, concerning which we have spoken in the section on Pope John IV, in which, besides an injunction of silence, a profession of one will was contained.

Honorius therefore sinned through that policy by which he wished silence to be maintained concerning one or two operations, although religious duty required that the two be openly defended. Otherwise the faith concerning the two natures—unconfused, unmixed, and undivided—which was being indirectly attacked by the remnants of the Eutychians, might waver.

There is no sin harmful to the Catholic faith that the Church cannot rightly punish. But if the person who sinned has been taken from the living, punishment can be imposed only by erasing his name from the sacred records, defaming his memory, and burning his books. These are the three measures that the sixth synod exercised against Honorius.

To erase a name from the sacred diptychs is, in the case of the dead, the same as casting someone out of the Church. To defame his memory means nothing other than condemning him because of the harm inflicted upon the faith. To burn his books is to declare them unworthy of being read.

In his letters Honorius asserts that none of the Fathers openly preached two wills in Christ, but that they professed this only in a sort of stammering fashion. After setting forth the controversy concerning one or two wills and operations in Christ, he says:

“Unless perhaps, as we have stated above, they taught some such thing while stammering, accommodating themselves to forming the minds and understandings of little ones, which ought not to be drawn toward ecclesiastical doctrines.”

From this he again infers that the expressions “two wills” and “two operations,” as new and recently introduced terms, threatened to cause scandals in the Church and ought not to be introduced among the faithful.

Yet it is certain that the holy Fathers preached two wills in Christ together with two operations, not by stammering but by clear definition, not to form the minds of little ones but to instruct the understanding of the wise. Consequently, such expressions were neither new nor recently introduced into the Church; they arose together with the Church’s most ancient Fathers.

Sophronius alone certainly produced six hundred statements of the Fathers, and both the Lateran Council under Martin I and the sixth general council present very many more. Honorius also seems to have proceeded with excessive contempt in this most serious controversy, on which depended the stability of the Council of Chalcedon and the overthrow of the Apollinarians, Eutychians, and other heretics who were then tearing the Church apart in the East.

He calls the persistence in Christ, after the union, of two wills and operations “light,” “foolish,” “idle,” and “grammatical.” These are his words, already quoted above:

“It is quite foolish to think or say that the Mediator between God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, either is or was one operation or two.”

And again:

“Whether, besides the works of the divinity, two operations ought to be called or understood derivatively, such matters must not reach us; let us leave them to grammarians, who are accustomed to claim for little ones elaborate names formed by derivation.”

Finally, he calls those who investigate the truth concerning one or two wills in Christ “vain weighers of natures,” “idle negotiators,” and so forth.

Nor can it be called foolish to assert what all the holy Fathers teach and everywhere proclaim to the orthodox; moreover, Sophronius, John, Martin, Maximus, Agatho, and six hundred other orthodox priests would have endured so many labors and persecutions in vain, if it were sufficiently foolish and trivial, according to Honorius’s judgment, to believe and profess the very thing for which they alone underwent all those labors. Again, it ought not to have been called “grammatical” to profess openly what was absolutely necessary for the defense of the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of Saint Leo, and for removing the disgrace inflicted upon the Church by the Alexandrian conciliabulum, of which all the heretics boasted. Finally, those who endured so many hardships and labors in order to purchase the innumerable souls of Christians whom the tyrannical cunning of Sergius, Cyrus, and the other heretics was dragging away ought not to have been called “idle traffickers.” Still less should he be regarded as a vain “weigher of natures” who, for the defense of the councils and the faith, undertook an exact consideration of Christ’s natures.

In the end, Honorius displayed excessive easiness, which he openly exhibits in his letters, both in assenting to Sergius’s counsels and in believing the many calumnies that Sergius fabricated in his letters. Sergius writes that Sophronius was the author of all the dissensions; Honorius not only does not rebuke this, but seems further to approve it. In the same letter to Honorius Sergius fabricated certain booklets of Menas addressed to Pope Vigilius, in which one will and one operation were proclaimed in Christ; he also published them everywhere, as Saint Maximus disclosed in his dialogue with Pyrrhus. Yet Honorius neither exposed the imposture nor removed the disgrace inflicted thereby upon Vigilius and upon the Roman See. Indeed, Honorius’s letters maintain a profound silence about this; thus, although by his office he was bound to blunt the charge in writing, he appears to have approved it by keeping silent.

Add to this the ease with which he swallowed Sergius’s similar calumny, invented against Sophronius—namely, that Sophronius, even when asked, could not produce a single testimony of the Fathers in favor of two wills in Christ—although this was not only false but wholly improbable: that a simple monk should have fiercely resisted patriarchs and bishops without being supported by any testimony either of Sacred Scripture or of the Fathers. What more is needed? Sergius asserts that none of the Fathers proclaimed two wills in Christ; Honorius asserts the same. Sergius assumes that scandals would arise from determining this controversy; Honorius makes the same assumption. Sergius insists upon silence as a suitable policy; Honorius confirms this as the best policy. Sergius strives to persuade Sophronius of it; Honorius likewise attempts to persuade Sophronius’s legates of it. Sergius mixes many things contrary to the faith into his letters; Honorius in no way attacks them. Sergius accuses the most holy Leo of being a supporter of heresy; Honorius in no way rebukes this. Sergius stirs up wars against the orthodox; Honorius praises Sergius.

What wonder, then, if the Fathers of the Sixth Synod assert that Honorius held the same opinions as Sergius, and if Leo II affirmed that, by neglecting it, Honorius had nourished the flame of heretical doctrine, as the anonymous author of the *History of the Monothelites*, Investigation VIII, says? Yet in Investigation V the same author vindicates the Honorian letter, which is read as condemned at the Sixth Synod, session 12, from every suspicion of heresy; likewise, regarding fragments of another letter, which are also brought forward in session 13 of the same synod, he demonstrates that Honorius’s doctrine was Catholic and entirely alien to Monothelite madness. In the words of Saint Maximus in his letter to Marinus: “Pope Honorius of Rome did not deny the duality of wills naturally present in Christ; rather, he confirmed it.”

This is the stumbling block and stone of offense against which not a few Catholics, together with the heretics, daily strike, although Honorius never agreed with the Monothelites, but was guilty only of fostering heresy through ill-considered dissimulation. On his policy, see what was said under Pope Theodore, where there is also discussion of the *Typos* of Constans.

**Line 9.—“And having made copies, he sent them throughout all the regions of the East and West.”** Martin sent the synodal acts to Africa, as is clear from the letter that he wrote to the Church of Carthage and to the bishops subject to it. He also sent them to Asia, to John, bishop of Philadelphia, as is shown by other letters of his addressed to John and to other Easterners. He likewise sent them to Gaul, to Clovis, king of Neustria and Burgundy, with legates. Through these legates he asked Clovis to send the leading Gallic bishops to Rome, so that an apostolic legation might be entrusted to them, by which they could act before the emperor in the East; and so that they might present to the emperor Constans what had been decreed at the Lateran Council together with the other synodal documents. This is clear from the pope’s letters to Saint Amandus, bishop of Tongeren. From those letters it is also evident that he sent the synodal acts to Sigebert, king of Austrasia, to whom the city of Tongeren belonged. Audoenus likewise testifies to this in the *Life of Saint Eligius*. He writes that this legation was sent to the Frankish king after the council had already been held, not before it, as Fridegodus states in the *Life of Saint Audoenus, Bishop of Rouen*; in this matter Audoenus deserves greater credence than Fridegodus.

In the letters to John, bishop of Philadelphia, mentioned shortly before, Martin appointed him vicar of the apostolic see in the East, so that he might assist the Churches of Jerusalem, Antioch, and other Churches in those regions when deprived of pastors or weakened by heretics. For this reason Martin wrote other letters to certain bishops, archimandrites, and distinguished men, asking them to be at John’s disposal and to obey him. He also wrote a letter to the Churches of Jerusalem and Antioch, announcing that the heresy of the Monothelites had been condemned at the council and that the ordinations of Macedonius of Antioch and Peter of Alexandria—who had invaded those sees without any canonical election—had been improperly performed.

He wrote not only to bishops and distinguished men, but also, together with the synod, to the emperor Constans himself. He did so with such moderation that he did not at all charge Constans with issuing the *Typos*, but attributed it to Paul, bishop of Constantinople, who had advised him. Nevertheless, Martin warned him that the condition of the state grows together with the careful preservation of orthodox faith, but declines when emperors and kings fight on behalf of the enemies of the faith. The letter’s superscription reads:

> “To the most devout and most serene lord, victor, triumpher, the son who loves God and our Lord Jesus Christ, Constans Augustus: Martin, bishop, servant of the servants of God, and the entire synod assembled in this city of Rome.”

From this it is clear that Martin and the synod rightly acted toward Constans with prudent diplomacy.

**No. 133, line 6.—“Then he was sent by the emperor,” etc.** When the emperor Constans learned that the Monothelites and the *Typos* had been condemned at the Roman synod by Pope Martin, he decided to drive Martin from the city. But, lest he be heard of throughout the Christian world as a tyrant and acquire the name of persecutor, he invented other charges against him, in order to give his exile and death a plausible appearance. Thus, with witnesses procured, he brought three charges against him: that Martin had changed the faith handed down by his ancestors; that he had plotted something against the Roman Empire with the Saracens; and that he had said something—I do not know what—against the veneration of Mary, the Mother of God. He further charged him with having irregularly and contrary to the canons intruded himself into the papal see.

After these charges had been fabricated against him, Calliopas, exarch of Italy, came to Rome in 653 with Theodore the chamberlain in order to carry out the emperor’s will. With an armed force he entered the Lateran basilica and palace. He feared neither the holiness of the place nor the courage of the Roman clergy, who defended their pontiff and struck his opponents with a dreadful anathema, crying:

> “Let whoever says or believes that Martin has changed, or will change, the faith even in one single point be anathema; and let those who do not remain steadfast in their orthodox faith unto death be anathema.”

Calliopas, I repeat, fearing none of this, expelled the holy pontiff from that same church. Martin did not resist; indeed, he expressly forbade his followers to use force. Although he was physically ill and afflicted with the pains of gout, he was taken from the palace and brought to the Roman harbor “on the night that dawns into Wednesday, which was the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, at about the sixth hour of the night,” as Martin himself writes in Letter 15 to Theodore.

Thus, on June 19, 652, which fell on a Wednesday, the holy pontiff was put aboard a ship. “We reached,” he says in the aforementioned letter to Theodore, “on the Kalends of July, Mesena—that is, Messina—where there was a ship, that is, my prison.” Nor was it only at Mesena, but also in Calabria, which is subject to the great city of the Romans, and in many islands, where our sins detained us for three months or more, that I received no compassion—except only on the island of Naxos, because there we remained for a year.”

Naxos, or Naxus, is one of the Cyclades in the Aegean Sea. Saint Martin remained there until the year 654.

[Col. 0757D] At last, as is recorded in a report by one of his disciples, “when that blessed man reached Byzantium on September 17, at the harbor near Euphemia, close to Arcadianon, the attendants left him lying on a pallet in the ship from morning until the tenth hour.” From there he was led to prison, where he was “shut up, entirely deprived of anyone’s conversation, for ninety-three days.” On the ninety-third day, which was Good Friday, they took him in the morning from custody to the chamber of the *sacellarius*, or treasurer of the imperial fisc—a high office in the Church of Constantinople, as Ducange demonstrates in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*. Saint Martin was therefore in prison from September 18, 654, until December 19 of that same year, when he was placed in the chamber of the *sacellarius* and interrogated by him before his accusers.

On that same day, December 19, a Friday, he was ordered to appear before the court. Many false witnesses overwhelmed him with calumnies, while the emperor and the nobles acted so that he would be declared guilty of treason and thus, with no one objecting, be placed in danger of death. They accused him of having entered into a conspiracy against the emperor with Olympius, recently exarch of Ravenna. Dorotheus, patrician of Sicily and one of the prominent false witnesses, said:

> “Even if he had fifty heads, he ought not to live, because he alone has overturned, ruined, and destroyed the entire West; and indeed he shared one counsel with Olympius and is the emperor’s murderous enemy and the enemy of Roman civilization.”

After the interrogations, the *sacellarius*, as recorded in the *Collectanea* of Anastasius, “ordered that the *psachnion* of the supreme, apostolic, and foremost shepherd of all Christians be removed from him without delay,” and so forth. “When the guard had cut the *psachnion* from the blessed man and removed the strap of his *campagi*, the *sacellarius* immediately handed him over to the prefect of the city, saying: ‘Take him, lord prefect, and cut him limb from limb at once.’”

The *psachnion* was a garment of the supreme pontiffs, as Ducange states under that word. The *campagus* was a type of footwear worn by those same pontiffs. Thus the *Hypomnesticon* says that Anastasius the *apocrisiarius* was given by Saint Martin one of his *campagi*, that is, leggings, “which no other human being wears except the holy Roman pope.”

Afterward the executioners fastened iron chains around his holy neck and threw him into a prison with murderers. From there they “transferred him to the prison called Diomedes, in the prefect’s praetorium. The most reverend pope spent eighty-five days in that same prison of Diomedes, after the first ninety-three—that is, 178 days altogether,” says the cited author of the report. He therefore remained in that prison until March 13, 655. From there, as the same source records, he was transferred to the house of a scribe named Sigolaba, and after two days was to be deported into exile to Cherson. He was transferred to the prison of Diomedes with such violence that his legs were torn and blood flowed.

The holy pontiff would then have been killed, had not Paul, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople, driven the sword from his neck, prompted by conscience. The event is related in the report mentioned above, composed by one of Saint Martin’s companions. After stating that the holy pontiff had been transferred to the prison of Diomedes, it says that the emperor visited the patriarch Paul:

> “For he was near death, and he told him what had been done to the most holy man; and Paul earnestly implored the emperor to let what Martin had suffered be enough, and not to make him endure anything more.”

Paul considered it unworthy that Martin—even if the emperor wished to persuade him that Martin was guilty of treason—should suffer such things. Groaning, Paul burst out:

> “Alas for me! Has this too been done to add to my legal troubles? Lord, is it not pitiful for a pontiff to suffer such things?”

Thus Paul moved the emperor to spare Martin’s life.

Meanwhile, the author of the same report states that Paul died. His death therefore occurred between December 10, 654—the day on which Martin was transferred to the prison of Diomedes—and March 13, 655—the day on which Martin was taken from there and exiled to Cherson. The emperor Constans appointed Pyrrhus, the former patriarch, in Paul’s place; we have discussed him under Pope Theodore. Yet Constans did not appoint him until he had learned from Martin’s own report, and from that of Plato, formerly exarch of Italy, who had received the *libellus* from Pyrrhus in Rome in 645, that Pyrrhus had acted voluntarily and had come to Rome intending, of his own accord, to renounce Monothelitism. This is confirmed by the appendix to the Acts of Saint Martin published by Sirmond in the *Collectanea* of Anastasius.

The emperor acted in this way because, while concealing his heretical mind, he did not wish to appear estranged from the faith of the Roman Church and from ancient discipline. On the other hand, in order to erase the mark of tyranny and show that he was not persecuting the Roman Church, he attacked Martin as though he were guilty of treason, as the cited report records. But God soon avenged Pyrrhus’s crime by inflicting death upon him. He died in the same year, 655, and Peter, infected with the same heresy, was appointed in his place.

After Saint Martin had been captured on June 19, 653, and deported to Greece, the archdeacon, archpriest, and chief notary governed the Roman Church, as is clear from the holy pontiff’s aforementioned Letter 15, written to Theodore from Constantinople. He says:

> “An order was delivered by Calliopas to the priests and deacons, containing the deposition of my humility: that I had irregularly and unlawfully usurped the episcopate and was not worthy to be installed in the apostolic see, but should in every way be sent to this imperial city, with another bishop substituted in my place—something that has never yet happened and, I hope, will never happen. For, in the absence of the pontiff, the archdeacon, archpriest, and chief notary represent the pontiff.”

This letter was written after September 17, 654, for Saint Martin arrived in Constantinople on that day. At that time he was still unaware of Eugenius’s election as Roman pontiff; otherwise he would not have said that it had never happened that another was elected in the absence of a pontiff, nor that he hoped it would never happen. On this, see what was said under Saint Gregory, no. 3, and under John IV, no. 4.

Eugenius, however, had been ordained pontiff on September 8 of that same year, 654. The Roman clergy feared that the emperor would impose upon them, against their will, a Roman bishop who was a defender of the same heresy as the emperor. They therefore judged that another pontiff should be elected, without Martin’s knowledge but with his subsequent approval. After Martin learned what the Roman clergy had done to forestall the emperor’s plots, he testified that the election pleased him, in a letter written from Cherson to a certain dear friend. He says:

> “Nevertheless, may God, through the intercession of Saint Peter, establish their hearts in the orthodox faith and strengthen them against every person who is a heretic or an enemy of our Church; and may he keep them immovable, especially the pastor who is now shown to preside over them.”

This letter was written after Easter of the year 655, when Saint Martin reached Cherson.

The title of this letter is: *To a Certain Dear Friend Concerning the Calamity of His Exile*. In it he says:

> “Sailing on Holy Thursday of the Lord’s Supper—which in the year 655 fell on March 26—we passed through the Pharos, traveling across various places on the Ides of May, and reached Cherson.”

On that island this pontiff, exhausted by hardships and hunger, departed to heaven to receive the crowns of the martyrs on September 16 of that same year, 655. At the end of his Acts, preserved in the *Collectanea* of Anastasius, we read:

> “The same most holy, thrice-blessed, apostolic Pope Martin, truly a recent confessor and martyr of Christ our God, died in that same exile at Cherson, according to the petition that he had offered with tears to the Lord God when he came out of the ship and set foot upon that land—namely, that he might finish his life there—fighting the good fight, completing the course of martyrdom, and preserving the good faith, in the month of September, on the sixteenth day. On that day, according to the annual cycle, the memory of the most blessed martyr Euphemia, who guarded the orthodox faith, is celebrated; it was the fourteenth indiction,” which began on September 1, 655.

The *Hypomnesticon* concerning Anastasius the *apocrisiarius*, p. 262, gives the same year, month, day, and indiction.

> “He was placed,” the Acts continue, “in the tombs of the saints outside the walls of the city of the Chersonites, about one stadium away, in the most precious and venerable church of the most holy Lady, to be honored above all the saints, the most chaste, immaculate, most blessed, glorious, and exalted Lady of all creatures, full of grace, who brings and grants joy; who by nature and truth is the Mother of God alone and ever-Virgin Mary, called Blachernas.”

The Greeks celebrate Saint Martin on the very day of his death, though more solemnly on April 13 or 14. His burial at Constantinople and his deposition at Blachernae are commemorated on September 20. At Rome, however, where his body was later transferred to the church named after him, Saints Sylvester and Martin in the Mountains, it is commemorated on November 12.

Anastasius is wrongly criticized by Baronius, and Ciaconius by Oldoinus, because they wrote that Martin performed two ordinations during the month of December. “He could certainly not have had two in December,” says Oldoinus, “if he lived at Rome in December only during the first year of his pontificate.” But since it is clear from what has been said that he spent the month of December at Rome during the first four years of his pontificate, one should not depart from Anastasius on this point. We shall discuss the duration of his see under Eugenius. Saint Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, celebrates his martyrdom in the *Life of Saint Eligius* and writes that his glory was no less than that of those who were taken away by pagan persecution. He adds that, in exile, Martin deserved by prayer alone to restore sight to a blind man.

[Note: [Col. 0760B]]

**No. 130, line 2.—“During his time Paul, bishop of the city of Constantinople,” etc.** From the *History of the Dogmas of the Holy See*, book VIII, chapter 5.

Paul, an intruded patriarch of the See of Constantinople, under the pretext of establishing peace and harmony between Catholics and Monothelites, had composed a formula of faith called the *Typos*. In order that it might appear with greater authority, he published it in the name of the emperor Constans. In that profession it was decreed as follows:

> “We decree that those subject to us who abide in our orthodox and immaculate Christian faith, who belong to the Catholic and Apostolic Church, shall not henceforth have permission to engage in controversy with one another concerning one will, or one operation, or two wills, or two operations, of any kind whatsoever . . . just as, before controversy arose, no one among all people up to the present has dogmatized one will and one operation, or two wills and two operations . . . But if any should presume to transgress these provisions, whether they are bishops or clerics, let them by every means be deprived of their priesthood or of their clergy,” etc.

(*Typos of Constans, in the Lateran Council, Secret Session 4.*)

**No. 131, line 2.—“He held a synod according to the institution of the orthodox Fathers in the church of the Savior.”** The emperor, exerting all his strength to compel Pope Martin to accept the *Typos*, sent him letters and ordered the exarch of Italy to lead an army to Rome, so that force might be used if necessary to accomplish this purpose. But all these devices were employed in vain; for no means could move the holy pontiff away from his ardent devotion to the Catholic faith.

Indeed, at the beginning of his pontificate he himself convened the Lateran Council. Its president first renewed the anathemas pronounced by earlier councils against the heretics in the mystery of the Incarnation; then, turning to the new form of heresy, he said:

> “If anyone does not anathematize Theodore, formerly bishop of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, etc.; and, in addition to these, the most impious *Ecthesis*, which was composed through the persuasion of the same Sergius by Heraclius, formerly emperor . . . and with them again the wicked *Typos*, recently composed through the persuasion of the aforementioned Paul by the most serene prince, the emperor Constans, against the Catholic Church—inasmuch as it promulgates that both the two natural wills and operations, divine and human, which the holy Fathers piously proclaim in Christ the true God and our Savior, and the one will and operation which the heretics impiously venerate in him are alike to be denied and bound to silence; and therefore determines that both the holy Fathers and wicked heretics are unjustly to be released from every reproach and condemnation, to the cutting away of the definitions of the Catholic Church, etc.—let such a one be condemned.”

(*Lateran Council under Martin I, canon 18.*)

After the council had been held, the pontiff wrote encyclicals in which he informed all the faithful of Christ about what had been defined through him. Among other things, they contain the following:

> “Most reverend bishops living in several different provinces—and, what is more remarkable, entire synods—by their written communications not only invite us to correct our own heresy, but even summon and protest against us ourselves, that is, against our apostolic see, urging us to rise up according to regular authority and not for so long a time permit the novelty of our opponents to devour the holy Catholic Churches of God.”

(*Pope Martin’s Encyclical Letter to All the Faithful of Christ.*)

On the same matter he wrote, in the name of the council, to the emperor Constans, demonstrating that the Monothelites, contrary to the mind of the holy Fathers and the definitions of the general councils, were making Jesus Christ an imperfect man. By claiming that his holy humanity lacked will and operation, they were mutilating it. They had imposed upon the faith of the emperor and of his grandfather Heraclius formulas composed contrary to the true faith. These formulas had disturbed the whole Church, offended the Christian people, and caused unbelievers to mock the great mystery of the Incarnation.

Because nearly all bishops and peoples had brought complaints and prayers to the holy see, asking it, by the supreme authority with which it was endowed, to restrain the growing evil and preserve the purity of the faith according to the traditions of the Fathers and the councils, Martin had convened their synod. At it, all those assembled had unanimously pronounced anathema—not only against the heretics, but also against the *Ecthesis* and *Typos* invented by them and produced by their perverse doctrine. The pontiff said that this had been done so that the emperor’s policy and counsel would not be blamed by the innovators. Finally, in the name of the same Fathers, he prayed and urged Constans to support the synodal decrees with his laws and to proscribe the heresy and its supporters.

(*Letter 3 to the Emperor Constans.*)

Many other letters of Martin of the same kind survive as witnesses to this matter, especially the letter to Amandus, bishop of Tongeren; Letter 4 to the Church of Carthage; Letter 11 to the Church of Jerusalem; and Letter 12 to Paul of Thessalonica. In the latter, Martin deprives Paul of communion and deposes him from episcopal dignity as a professor of Monothelitism, until he repents, detests the heretics condemned by the synod and their errors, and signs the Lateran Council. Finally, Letter 13 to the Church of Thessalonica conveys the same message to the clergy.

**Line 5.—“They condemned Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius,” etc., “who presumed to introduce novelties against the immaculate faith,” etc.** Heresy truly is a hydra: when its heads are cut off, new heads emerge. This has been confirmed by the experience of every age and is increasingly demonstrated in our own. Those who wish to appear Catholic pretend to defer to what the Catholic Church has defined in matters of faith; meanwhile, they try to bring forth error concealed under another name.

Among the Eutychians, or Acephali, those who in the seventh century wished to avoid the detestable name of heretics, while not departing from their meaning, signed the Council of Chalcedon and professed two distinct natures in Christ, divine and human. Yet in reality they denied those same natures and recognized in him only one will and one operation. For if will belongs to essence, or to an intelligent nature, and if operation gives it life, then whoever asserts that the human nature—which is an intelligent being—exists in Jesus Christ without its own distinct will, or that such a will lacks operation, thereby denies that the human nature truly and distinctly exists in Jesus Christ, without confusion and without mixture, as Saint Leo the Great and the Council of Chalcedon define.

The beginnings of Monothelitism must certainly be placed before the year 616. For during the lifetime of John the Almsgiver, who died in that year, we find that Sergius of Constantinople, born to Acephali parents, proposed to a certain George Arsamas, likewise an Acephalus, although of a different sect, that he should embrace the doctrine of one operation in Christ as a means of reconciliation between them. Maximus reports this in his disputation with Pyrrhus.

Nevertheless, this heresy did not spread throughout the East until several years later, namely in the years 622 and 629, as the conversations of the emperor Heraclius with the Acephali demonstrate: specifically, during his passage through Phasis, in conversation with Paul the One-Eyed of the Severian sect; and at Hierapolis near Edessa, with Athanasius the patriarch, as Theophanes teaches in his *Chronicle*.

All agree that Sergius of Constantinople was the patriarch of Monothelitism; Cyrus approached him after obtaining the Alexandrian see. Each of them convened conciliabula in his own patriarchate—Sergius in 626 and Cyrus in 633—in which each endeavored to have his errors confirmed.

The monk Sophronius, celebrated for holiness and doctrine, first strove with all his strength in Alexandria, and later in Constantinople, to restrain the advance of the growing evil. Finally he became patriarch of Jerusalem and convened a synod at which he proscribed the heresy. From that same synod came the most excellent synodical letter sent to the other patriarchs, which was read in session 11 of the Sixth General Council, since it splendidly proves by testimonies of the Fathers that there are two wills in Christ and an equal number of operations.

At the same time Sergius’s letter to Pope Honorius appeared. It has always been believed to be the very letter that was presented at the same Sixth Council and gave occasion for a judgment against the answer to that letter and even against the memory of the holy pontiff. I shall present it in the very same words, but divided into numbered sections and printed in different type, so that it may more easily be subjected to the criticism of the learned author whom I shall cite after the letter.

**Note.** Sergius’s letter and Honorius’s reply are presented in the notes under Agatho, where they may be found.

[Note: [Col. 0762C]]

**No. 131, line 14.—“In the *Typos* set forth by us.”** Paul the Monothelite, who occupied the Constantinopolitan see after Pyrrhus’s departure, saw himself compelled by Pope Theodore and the African bishops, under threat of anathema, to renounce his error. He devised a fraud by which this very cunning man could both protect his reputation and establish the Monothelite heresy.

He persuaded the heretical emperor Constans to publish a *Typos*, that is, an edict—for the term *Typos* designated whatever imperial constitutions were issued—in which silence concerning one or two operations in Christ would be imposed under the pretext of restraining controversies in matters of faith. He also persuaded him to order that the writings favoring Monothelitism, which had been affixed to the doors of the great church, be torn down.

Constans issued this deceptive *Typos* and sent Olympius the chamberlain and exarch to Italy, so that he might promulgate the *Typos* in the West and protect all the bishops whom he found consenting to it, as Anastasius relates here. But the impious constitution, issued by a lay prince who had no authority to judge controversies of faith, was rejected by 105 bishops assembled in the Lateran Council under Saint Martin. This was especially because it was clear that, by prohibiting the assertion of either one or two wills in Christ, the Catholic dogma was being condemned together with the heretical position.

[Col. 0737]

> **[Col. 0737] 130.** Martin, from the city of Todi in the province of Tuscany, held the see for six years, one month, and twenty-six days [Note: [Col. 0737] *B: three months and twelve days]. [Note: [Col. 0737] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 648.] During his time Paul, bishop of the city of Constantinople, puffed up by the spirit of pride against the sound doctrine of the holy Church of God, boldly presumed to oppose the definitions of the Fathers. Moreover, he sought, as a covering for his own error, through certain subterfuges [Note: [Col. 0737] through certain evasions], to persuade the most merciful prince to publish a *Typos* that would destroy Catholic doctrine. In this *Typos* he weakened all the words of the holy Fathers by mixing them with the expressions of the most wicked heretics [Note: [Col. 0737] with their decrees], namely, by defining and confessing neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ our Lord.

On account of this, while defending such perversity, he attempted to presume upon something that no earlier heretic had ever dared, and did so in such a way [Note: [Col. 0739] He broke out into such madness that he overturned the altar] that, overturning the altar of our holy see which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia, in the venerable oratory, he plundered it and forbade our *apocrisarii* to offer the adorable and immaculate host to God there or to receive the sacraments of communion.

These *apocrisarii*, moved by the command of apostolic authority, urged him to withdraw from such a heretical purpose. They also appeared to have been ordered to protest [Note: [Col. 0739] They moved him to abandon this heretical intention. They were also ordered to protest]. But he pursued them with various persecutions together with other orthodox men and venerable priests, imprisoning some, deporting others into exile, and subjecting still others to beatings [Note: [Col. 0739] C: subduing them].

Since these disturbances were troubling nearly the whole world, many orthodox people from various places are shown to have brought complaints against them to our apostolic see. They implored it to cut off, by apostolic authority, the device of such great wickedness and such enormous ruin [Note: [Col. 0739] so that it might be cut off], lest the illness of their harmful *Ecthesis* [Note: [Col. 0739] execution] be able to tear apart the entire body [Note: [Col. 0739] the whole body] of the Catholic Church.

> **131.** Then Martin, the most holy and most blessed bishop, sent for and gathered 105 bishops in the city of Rome and held a synod according to the institution…

[Note: [Col. 0739] instituted.]

In the church of the Savior beside the Lateran episcopal residence, the orthodox Fathers assembled according to the established practice. With bishops and presbyters seated, deacons and the entire clergy standing by, they condemned Cyrus of Alexandria, and Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, patriarchs of Constantinople, who had presumed to introduce novelties contrary to the immaculate faith. Since, in their haste to suppress that faith itself, they had contrived a confusion of heretical doctrines against the Catholic Church of God [Note: [Col. 0739] continued], they were struck by the punishment of anathema [Note: [Col. 0739] struck]. [Note: [Col. 0739] See Baronius under the year 649.] This synod is preserved today in the archive of the Church. He also made copies and sent them throughout all the regions of East and West, disseminating them through the hands of the orthodox faithful.

In those days the emperor sent Olympius, his chamberlain and exarch, into Italy to govern the whole of Italy, commanding him and saying:

“It is necessary, Your Glory, that you carry out what Paul, patriarch of this God-preserved city, has suggested to us. If you find the province itself consenting to hold to the *typos* [“formula”] set forth by us, you must compel all the bishops who are there, and the heretics among the possessors [Note: [Col. 0739] B, professors], the inhabitants, and the foreigners, to subscribe to the same [Note: [Col. 0739] Make all who are there—the bishops, possessors, and inhabitants—subscribe to the same].

“But if, as the glorious patricians Plato and Eupraxius have suggested to us, you are able to persuade the army stationed there, we command that Martin, who was our apocrisarius in the imperial city, be seized. Afterwards, have all the churches read the *typos* made by us orthodox, and let all the bishops of Italy subscribe to it. But if you find the army opposed in this matter, keep it quiet until you have gained control of the province and have been able to gather a larger army [Note: [Col. 0739] larger] for yourselves—also from the cities of Rome and Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0739] both from the city of Rome and from Ravenna]—so that you may be able to carry out as quickly as possible what has been commanded by us [Note: [Col. 0739] may be able].”

### 132

The aforementioned Olympius, coming to the city of Rome, found the holy Roman Church united with all the bishops of Italy, as well as the priests and clergy. Wishing to fulfill the commands given to him, and taking with him an army of strength [Note: [Col. 0739] an army by force], he attempted to introduce a schism into the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0739] into the holy Church]. This continued for a very long time. But almighty God did not permit him to accomplish what he was attempting.

Seeing, therefore, that he had been overcome by the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of God, he was compelled to abandon his evil intention, as it were, so that what he could not accomplish by armed force he might achieve by a heretical [Note: [Col. 0739] surreptitious] method, through the solemn celebration of Mass in the church of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, at the Manger [Col. 0741].

For while the most holy pope was offering him communion, Olympius wished to kill him cruelly, as he had ordered his sword-bearer to do. But almighty God, who is accustomed to protect his orthodox servants and rescue them from every evil, blinded the sword-bearer of Olympius the exarch. He was not permitted to see the pontiff when the pontiff offered communion to the exarch or gave him the kiss of peace [Note: [Col. 0741] the bread], so that the pope’s blood might be shed and the Catholic Church of God subjected to heresy [Note: [Col. 0741] subjugated]. The aforementioned armed servant later publicly acknowledged all this under oath.

### 133

When the exarch Olympius saw that God’s hand was protecting the most holy Pope Martin, he was compelled to make peace with the pontiff and to disclose to that most holy man everything that had been commanded him. Having made peace with the holy Church of God, he gathered an army and departed for Sicily against the Saracen people who lived there.

[Note: [Col. 0741] See Baronius under the year 650.]

Because of sin, a great slaughter befell the Roman army, and afterwards that same exarch died of illness. Then the emperor sent the exarch Theodore, known by the surname Calliopas, together with the imperial chamberlain Theodore, who was also called Pellurius [Note: [Col. 0741] Pelarius], with orders. They seized the most holy Pope Martin from the church of the Savior, which is also called Constantiniana, and brought him to Constantinople; but even then he did not consent to them. Afterwards the aforementioned most holy man was sent into exile, to a place called Chersona [Note: [Col. 0741] * B. Cherson]. There, as it pleased God, he ended his life in the peace of Christ as a confessor. He also performs many miracles down to the present day.

In the month of December he carried out two ordinations [Note: [Col. 0741] Baronius proves that only one was carried out]: eleven presbyters, five deacons, and thirty-three bishops in various places. He was buried on 17 September [Note: [Col. 0741] His burial is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October; B, 12 November], and the episcopate remained vacant for twenty-eight days.

## LXXVII. SAINT EUGENIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 652, THE ELEVENTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR CONSTANTS

[Note: [Col. 0763B]]
