[Note: [Col. 0763C]]

### Line 5

“So that on the day of his passing he might order that the *presbyteria* be distributed in full to the poor, the clergy, or the household.”

Eugenius ordered that on the day of his death *presbyteria* be distributed to the clergy, the poor, and the household—that is, provisions such as are customarily distributed to presbyters. Anastasius, in his account of Zacharias, says: “He greatly loved his clergy and gave them their annual *presbyteria* twofold and more.” The quantity of provisions assigned to presbyters and clerics varied according to the dignity of their order: whoever was higher in rank ought to be superior in the portion received. See the chapter *Statuimus*, *De majoritate et obedientia*. Anastasius calls it a blessing in his account of Conon: “He left a blessing in gold to all the clergy and monasteries, as his predecessor, Pope Benedict, had done.”

### Line 6

“During his time Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, sent a synodical letter to the apostolic see according to the earlier custom, but one exceedingly obscure and beyond the rule.”

At the beginning, Roman pontiffs and patriarchs were accustomed to send a synodical letter concerning their ordination to the emperor and the patriarchs, and patriarchs sent one to the apostolic see. Anastasius, in his account of Vitalian, says: “He sent his representatives with a synodical letter, according to custom, to the imperial city and the most devout rulers, making known his ordination.” The same author, in his account of Gregory III, says: “This most blessed man, according to ecclesiastical rite and the orthodox profession of his faith, sent a synodical letter to the Church of Constantinople, and at the same time sent another petition to the most serene Emperor Constantine.”

### Line 13

“In the holy basilica of the Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, which is called at the Manger.”

The basilica of holy Mary, called at the Manger, is one of the five patriarchal churches of the City and one of the seven customarily visited with solemn rite. It received this name from the chapel of the manger located within it. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II, says: “He established the hospice situated behind the apse of the holy Mother of God at the Manger as a monastery.”

It was first called the basilica of Liberius, after its founder—that is, Liberius, the pope who built it. According to Anastasius, after Sixtus III restored it and dedicated it to the Blessed Virgin Mary, it was called the basilica of Saint Mary. Then, from the chapel of the manger, it was called “at the Manger.” Concerning this, Anastasius, in his account of Gregory III, says: “He also made there, in the oratory called the Manger, a golden image of the Mother of God” [Col. 0765B]. The same author, in his account of Leo III, says: “He made in the basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger, at the entrance to the manger, royal doors clothed in the purest silver.” Finally, it was called the basilica of Saint Mary Major. The same author, in his account of Gregory IV, says: “And in it he made the holy manger in the likeness of the manger of the holy Mother of God, which is called ‘of the Major.’” The same author says this in his account of Sergius II.

[Note: [Col. 0765B]]

### Line 1

“Eugenius, a Roman by birth, from the region of the Aventine, a cleric from the cradle.”

That children were offered by their parents to the Church from infancy so that they might be admitted into the clerical order is so clear that it requires no proof. History teaches us that this custom prevailed not only in the earliest centuries of the Church but also in later times. Whether, however, such children were at the very beginning of infancy marked with the clerical tonsure and enrolled in the order of readers, and whether, once they had reached puberty, they were required to remain in the clerical service to which, at their parents’ request, they had given their names—these two questions do not seem so clear that they do not deserve illumination through somewhat more careful examination.

Morinus, in his excellent work *On Sacred Ordinations*, part III, exercise 15, *On the Clerical Tonsure*, chapter 3, explicitly teaches that children offered to the Church were immediately received among the clerics and endowed both with the tonsure and with the clerical state. In proof of this he brings forward the testimony of several authorities.

Pope Siricius, in letter 1, chapter 8, says: “Whoever from infancy has vowed himself to the service of the Church before the years of puberty ought to be baptized and associated with the ministry of readers.”

Zosimus, letter 1, chapter 1: “Let him become accustomed in the army of the Lord, first in the rank of readers, to the beginnings of divine service”; and elsewhere: “If from infancy he has given his name to ecclesiastical offices, let him remain among the readers by continuous observance until his twentieth year.”

The Third Council of Carthage, in 397, decreed: “It has seemed good that readers, when they have reached the years of puberty, be compelled,” and so forth.

The Second Council of Toledo, in 589, decreed: “Concerning those whom the will of their parents has from the first years of infancy bound to the office of the clergy, we decree that this is to be observed: as soon as they have been tonsured or assigned to the ministry of readers, they must be instructed in the house of the Church under the bishop’s supervision by the superior appointed over them” [Col. 0765D].

He finally concludes in chapter 4: “When boys were offered to the clerical state, they were at the same time initiated into the readership; nor were bishops then accustomed to tonsure those who had not been initiated into the orders.”

An example of this is supplied by the life of Saint Sulpicius in Surius, 17 January. Austregisilus, bishop of Bourges, obtained from Prince Theodoric permission to confer upon Saint Sulpicius the office of teaching in the Church. For he saw crowds gathering because of his learning. The king immediately granted that, once his hair had been cut, he might enter the clergy. Thus, promoted step by step to higher positions, he also obtained the levitical ministry.

The most diligent investigator of the ancient rites of the Church, Edmund Martene, strengthens Morinus’s opinion with several examples in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, volume II, book I, chapter 3, no. 3:

“From Cyril of Scythopolis, in the *Life of Saint Euthymius the Abbot*, *Greek Analects*, volume I, we read that Euthymius, when three years old, was offered to Otreius, bishop of Melitene. The bishop baptized the child whom he had received, tonsured him, made him a reader in the Church entrusted to him, and received and raised him in the episcopal residence.

“The Carthaginian readers mentioned by Victor of Vita, book V, chapter 9, were not much older. He records that they were driven into exile with Bishop Eugenius and the entire clergy—a clergy numbering more than five hundred, among whom there were very many child readers, since infancy does not extend beyond the seventh year.

“Felix of Nola, according to Saint Paulinus, began to serve God as a boy: ‘And from his earliest years he served as a reader.’ Saint Epiphanius, later bishop of Ticinum, as Ennodius writes in his life in Bollandus under 21 January, undertook the office of ecclesiastical reader when he was about eight years old.

“But the Roman order, as the same Morinus testifies, which contains all the ceremonies customarily observed in the Roman Church approximately seven hundred years ago and also much earlier, introduces the section on the orders as follows:

“‘In whatever school boys are found who sing the psalms well, let them be taken from there and raised in the school of singers, and afterwards let them become chamberlains. But if they are sons of nobles, let them immediately be raised in the chamber, and let them receive this authority from the archdeacon, so that they may sit upon the hairy cloth which it is customary to place upon the saddle of a horse. Then, as the book of the sacraments contains, let them be ordained, when and where appropriate, up to the office of subdeacon.’

“Above all, however, the tonsure was conferred upon them while they were still boys, as is clear from the prayer given there for the tonsure: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, who are our head and the crown of all the saints, look favorably upon the infancy of your servant N.,’ and so forth; also from the title of the prayer: ‘Prayer for tonsuring a boy.’”

To illustrate this institution, it is useful to present a very ancient object: namely, a golden ring recently discovered in a small marble container together with little bones and a golden chain. The ring is not inelegantly made. Its upper part, intended for a gemstone, is flattened and drawn out into a plate of the same gold; on it are engraved the letters: **MAXIM. AEVITA.**

The diameter of the circle is extremely small, barely fitting the thickness of the little finger of a two- or three-year-old child. Here Maximus is described with the title *levita*, “levite,” using the Greek letter lambda, Λ, in place of the Latin L.

This should not lead anyone to suppose that Maximus could at that childish age have been marked with the rank of deacon, which was not normally conferred until after puberty, and not even then in those times. Rather, the name *levite* was used in a broad sense to designate any member of the clergy, whatever order conferred honor upon him.

“The duties of the Levites were various,” says Morinus in exercise 12, *On Subdeacons*, chapter 2: “to assist the priests in sacrifice, to prepare and carry the sacred vessels, to spread and gather the veils, to sing the psalms, and to guard the doors of the temple. The number of Levites who ministered to the priests in the tabernacle and in the sacrifices was very large. In 1 Chronicles 23 it is written: ‘The Levites were numbered from thirty years old and above, and thirty thousand men were found. From these, twenty-four thousand were chosen and assigned to the ministry of the house of the Lord . . . Moreover, four thousand were gatekeepers, and an equal number were singers playing musical instruments.’ From this it is clearly demonstrated that those singers and gatekeepers were Levites.”

Since, therefore, the designation “Levites” passed into the ecclesiastical rite of the New Law to designate ministers of the altar from the rites of the Old Law, and since in the ancient rite lower temple ministers such as gatekeepers and singers were also included under the name Levites, those established in the minor orders could likewise have been called Levites in the first centuries of the Christian Church. Such was our Maximus, whose childish age could bear the title *levita* engraved on a golden ring, to indicate the name and office of its wearer [Col. 0767A], not for use as a seal, which would have been entirely unsuitable for that age.

The letters engraved on the ring are also correctly placed in their natural position, from left to right, not in the reverse order, from right to left, as seals have them [Col. 0768A].

[Col. 0767B] It is therefore clear that for many centuries the Church maintained the practice of receiving children offered by their parents into the clergy and admitting them to the tonsure and readership. For this reason, as Cardinal Bona says in book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 25, no. 18: “The result was that they became highly skilled in ecclesiastical matters, having been nourished in them from infancy.”

The Council of Trent, in session 23, chapter 4, wisely corrected this ancient discipline of the Church, which the customs of our age did not permit, by issuing the following decree:

“Those who have not received the sacrament of confirmation and have not been instructed in the rudiments of the faith, who do not know how to read and write, and concerning whom there is no probable presumption that they have chosen this way of life not through the fraud of fleeing secular judgment but in order to render faithful service to God, are not to be initiated with the first tonsure.”

Whether those once offered to the Church from infancy could return to the lay state, or whether they were compelled to remain in the clerical state, is a matter on which the practice of the Church varied at different times.

The Third Council of Carthage, cited above, seems by these words of chapter 19—“It has seemed good that readers, when they have reached the years of puberty, be compelled either to marry or to profess continence”—to have left it to clerics to remain in the clerical state or to withdraw from it.

The Council of Chalcedon, however, established otherwise in canon 7 (in the year 403):

“We decree that those who have once been appointed to the clergy or have chosen the life of monks may neither enter military service nor attain any worldly dignity; and that those who attempt this and do not repent so as to return to what they first chose for God’s sake are to be anathematized.”

The Council of Tribur, in 395, likewise decreed in canon 7:

“We decree that if a cleric brought up ecclesiastically in the Church, whether reading or singing before the people, later abandons the clerical habit and slips away from the Lord’s camp to which he has been enrolled, profane and apostate, returning to the world, he is to be canonically restrained by the bishop so that he may return to the bosom of Mother Church. If he persists in this indiscipline, so that he grows his hair long, he is to be compelled to be tonsured again, and afterwards he is neither to take a wife nor to approach a sacred order” [Col. 0767D].

The rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 59, concerning boys, was in conformity with the discipline of the ancient Church. “Saint Benedict the abbot commands that they be bound by the irrevocable force of their parents’ vow,” says Mabillon in the preface to the sixth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, “and Rabanus Maurus approves this in a special treatise which he composed against certain people who resisted the prescription of this rule.”

Hence, in the formulas for the offering of boys made by their parents, this condition is solemnly included: “so that from this day it may not be permitted him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the rule.”

Martene, in his commentary on this rule of the holy Father, chapter 59, cites the following formula from ancient manuscripts [Col. 0768B]:

“I hand over this boy in devotion to our Lord Jesus Christ before God and his saints, so that he may persevere all the days of his life and become a monk until his death.”

The condition was the same in this respect for clerics and monks, as is clear from canon 7 of the Council of Chalcedon cited above.

Everyone can see that this discipline arose from the power of the father, which parents once enjoyed over their children under Roman and Greek law. Thus Hugo Menard, in chapter 66 of the *Concordance of the Rule*, says:

“I say that this right derives from the natural power that parents have over their children. They can even sell them in a time of necessity; therefore they can also offer them to God, for the sake of devotion, into his perpetual service, both for their own salvation and for that of their children, provided that this is done with pure intention and devotion. This offering is an act of the highest virtue, which overcomes the natural love of parents for their children and also the natural desire to propagate their family, especially since, when one child has been offered, the other surviving children can die without offspring, and since by offering them to God the parents are deprived of the comfort they could have received from such children” [Col. 0768C].

The clemency of Charlemagne, however, brought some relief to this stricter discipline, as Thomassinus testifies in part I of *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 57. He cites a brief written statement of matters to be discussed with bishops and abbots, in which chapter 10 contains the following:

“Where has it been established in the canons or in the rule of any holy Father that anyone, whether cleric or monk, should become one against his will? Or where did Christ command, or any apostle preach, that a congregation of either canons or monks should be formed from those unwilling, reluctant, and worthless?”

This practice was entirely abolished, as the twelfth century drew to a close, by Celestine III. Following his prescriptions, Innocent III wrote in book 15, letter 116, to the bishop of Lyon:

“Concerning sons of minor age who have been offered to a monastery and have received the habit or tonsure: if, when asked by their superiors in their fifteenth year, they consent to remain in the intention of the religious life they have undertaken, the opportunity for repentance is to be closed to them. Otherwise, the possibility of returning to the world is not to be taken away from them, lest they appear to render forced service to God” [Col. 0768D].

Finally, the Council of Trent, in session 25, chapter 15, established concerning religious profession:

“In every religious order, both of men and of women, profession is not to be made before the completion of the sixteenth year.”

Concerning the reception of sacred orders, the same council decreed in session 25, chapter 12:

“No one in future is to be promoted to the order of subdeacon before his twenty-second year.”

Concerning the education of boys in seminaries, it decreed in chapter 18:

“Those are to be received into this college who are at least twelve years old, born of a legitimate marriage, and sufficiently able to read and write, and whose character and inclination give hope that they will perpetually serve in ecclesiastical ministries. It wishes the sons of the poor especially to be chosen, but does not exclude those who are wealthier, provided that they are supported at their own expense and show a desire to serve God and the Church” [Col. 0769A].

Thus the ancient institution of receiving into the clergy children offered by their parents—children who had been dedicated to the Church from the cradle—was rendered obsolete and completely abolished. Anastasius records that Saint Eugenius the pope had been such a child.

[Note: [Col. 0769A]]

### Line 1

“Eugenius.”

There are some who maintain that Eugenius was elected pontiff twenty days after Saint Martin had been driven into exile, while Martin was still alive, since the imperial ministers had declared him deposed—or rather, through the gravest calumny, unlawfully ordained.

In the account of the proceedings against Saint Maximus preserved in the collections of Anastasius, when Saint Maximus had said that the Monothelites had been struck with anathema at the synod held under Martin, Demosthenes exclaimed:

“The synod is not valid, since the one who celebrated it, Martin, has been deposed” [Col. 0769B].

Among the calumnies that they had fastened upon the holy pontiff was the accusation that he was guilty of treason. They likewise slandered Saint Maximus, to whom the following charge is recorded as having been made:

“You alone handed Egypt, Alexandria, Pentapolis, Tripoli, and Africa over to the Saracens.”

The supporters of the same opinion also cite what the holy pontiff wrote in a letter to someone especially dear to him, volume III of the Councils, page 688:

“Nevertheless, may God, through the intercession of Saint Peter, strengthen their hearts in the orthodox faith, confirm them against every person belonging to the heretical adversaries of our Church, and preserve them immovable—especially the shepherd who is shown to preside over them.”

But, to speak candidly, those who infer from this that Eugenius was substituted for Martin while Martin was still alive are gravely mistaken. The pontiff was speaking there about Pyrrhus, who at that very time had become an apostate and had again seized the throne of Constantinople [Col. 0769C].

For this reason, in the appendix to the Acts of Saint Maximus in the collection of Anastasius, we read:

“Moreover, it must be known concerning Pyrrhus that, when they had been informed by the thrice-blessed apostolic [man] and by Plato that he had voluntarily composed his written statement, they placed him upon this throne.”

And in the Acts of Saint Martin, in the cited volume of the Councils, page 683:

“Meanwhile, after Paul had died and Pyrrhus was attempting to remain in office, while certain members of the Church opposed and prohibited this in the palace, asserting that he had been anathematized by the most blessed Paul, and after much agitation had arisen . . . Pyrrhus again came forward.”

The shepherd of whom the pontiff speaks must therefore be understood as Pyrrhus. Martin was praying to God to avert from the Church the greater evils that seemed imminent because of Pyrrhus’s apostasy and his recovery of the Constantinopolitan throne.

For this reason I believe that greater attention should be paid to what the same most holy pontiff wrote in his letter to Theodore, page 677:

“An order was delivered by Calliopas to the presbyters and deacons, containing the rejection of my humility: that I had unlawfully and contrary to the law usurped the episcopate, that I was not worthy to be installed in the apostolic see, and that I was to be sent in every way to this imperial city, with another bishop substituted in my place. This has never yet been done, and I hope that at some time it will be done, because in the absence of the pontiff the archdeacon, archpriest, and chief notary represent the place of the pontiff.”

Between the sentence of exile and the writing of this letter, two years and two months elapsed. At that time, therefore, Eugenius was not yet pontiff; the Roman clergy certainly did not permit him to be elected before the death of Blessed Martin.

### Line 6

“Peter the patriarch.”

This man, the successor of Pyrrhus in the episcopate, added a new heresy to Monothelitism. He thought that both sides could be reconciled if it were taught that in Christ the Lord there was one substantial operation and two natural operations.

The first to undertake the refutation of this invention was Anastasius, a disciple of Saint Maximus. He published a denunciatory letter to the common college of monks established at Calaris. The letter stands at the beginning of Saint Maximus’s works; the following passage, on page 43, is relevant:

“Now, therefore, they have been transferred from nonexistence to absurdity: that is, from saying that there is neither one nor two, they have been led to proclaim two and one—that is, to introduce three wills and operations in one and the same Christ. Neither the language of the Fathers, nor the synodical language, nor the language of nature has decreed this; nor has the fury of the ancient heretics and those who came after them ever yet discovered it.”

The rest may be read there.

Peter, therefore, was widely regarded as famous for this inept attempt to unite things that had been torn apart by means of a compromise; and, what was far more unjust, he was believed to be thoroughly Catholic.

Accordingly, when Eugenius had been elected pontiff and sent apocrisarii with a synodical letter to Constantinople for the purpose of consecration, they—whether corrupted by gifts, deceived by negligence, or misled by the novelty of the matter—approved Peter’s doctrine as though it were orthodox, communicated with him, received from him the synodical letter addressed to Eugenius, and returned to the pontiff [Col. 0770B].

The communion entered into by the apocrisarii with Peter is discussed in the aforementioned account of the proceedings against Saint Maximus. The judges addressed him in these terms:

“What will you do when the Romans are to be united with the Byzantines? For behold, the Roman apocrisarii arrived yesterday, and tomorrow, on the Lord’s Day, they will communicate with the patriarch. Through this it becomes manifest to all that you are subverting the Romans. Indeed, once you had been removed from there, they immediately agreed with those who are here.”

And he said to them:

“Those who came—how will they prejudice the Roman see, even though they communicate, since they did not bring the letter to the patriarch?”

Concerning the fall of the apocrisarii, Anastasius says in the same place, page 44:

“Since, as has been said, they were unwilling to correct their statement, they also compelled the apocrisarii of their own elder Rome to agree with them in proclaiming in the same Lord Jesus Christ one will and operation over two—that is, three wills and operations—mixing together a taste like that of the tree of knowledge, just as these men, according to their desires, produce the faith from good and evil. Therefore, having deceived such men by letters of this kind, they sent them to the one who had dispatched them”—that is, to Eugenius.

Maximus uses the same phraseology when describing the invention introduced by Peter. In his letter to the bishop of Thessalonica, who had been caught in the same snares and was consenting to the pseudo-patriarch, the holy martyr burns with anger and rebukes him. Combefisius, in *History of the Monothelites*, page 661, records his words:

“For you not only remained uncorrected yourself, but you also deceived our aforementioned apocrisarii; and you did to them what the crafty serpent did to Adam, making him a deserter together with yourself.”

From this we learn that the fall of the pontifical legates occurred chiefly through the agency of the primate of Thessalonica.

These events make Peter’s letter deservedly seem exceedingly obscure. By what deceptions and evasions, we may ask, was that writing woven, since it produced so monstrous a disturbance and danger for the faith?

[Col. 0770D]

### Line 10

“Had sent such a synodical letter.”

The monks of Calaris, by no means unaware that they had to fight for the orthodox faith, whose violation they had recognized from Anastasius’s denunciatory letter, wrote to Eugenius and to the Roman Church.

Anastasius had earnestly charged them to do this in the same letter:

“Since, therefore, the affairs of the whole Catholic and Apostolic Church are in great danger on this account, we pray and beseech you, most holy men, not to disregard her in peril, but to help her as she is tossed by storms, knowing that in a time of tribulation there is a love which is born in the Holy Spirit. If it is possible, cross over more quickly, as if on another matter, to the pious and steadfast men of senior Rome, firm as a rock . . . who are our guardians and most powerful defenders of the truth. Beseech them with supplicating voices and tears on behalf of all Christians.”

To this the Bibliothecarius adds that, with the greatest justification, the entire clergy and Roman people were horrified by Peter’s heretical synodical letter and, after a disturbance had arisen, intervened so that it might be entirely rejected.

For it was customary that all denunciatory letters be read publicly in church, as we have discussed at length in the first dissertation *On Encyclical Letters*. Therefore the Roman populace, thoroughly aware of the ancient faith and tradition, became so enraged against Peter’s synodical letter that it did not permit even the pontiff.

### Line 12

“To celebrate Mass in the basilica of the holy Mother of God.”

It had long become customary for embassies from rulers and public letters to be heard in the basilica of the holy Mother of God at the Manger. Thus, in his account of Martin, Anastasius noted that Olympius, sent by the emperor, was received by the pontiff in that same basilica, where Olympius was plotting treachery against him.

I believe that the anathemas against the writings issued by the Easterners, who had abandoned the faith, were published there. For in the aforementioned account of the proceedings against Saint Maximus it is related that the *typos* was condemned by anathema in the church, in that same basilica.

The Acts state:

“For Troilus said to Saint Maximus: ‘Did you not anathematize the *typos*?’ He replied: ‘I have often said that I anathematized it.’ ‘You anathematized the *typos*; you anathematized the emperor.’ The servant of God replied: ‘I did not anathematize the emperor, but a document alien to the faith of the Church.’ And he said to him: ‘Where was it anathematized?’ He replied: ‘By the Roman synod, in the church of the Savior and in the church of the Mother of God.’”

After Martin had therefore published the anathemas against the *typos* in the Lateran secretariat, he subsequently presented them to the people and ordered them to be read in the church or basilica of Saint Mary Major.

That legates were likewise customarily received and heard in the same basilica is shown by the author of the Life of Adrian II, page 430:

“Then, while the most holy Pope Adrian was seated with the bishops and nobles in the secretariat of Saint Mary Major, according to the custom of the apostolic see, they presented themselves to him with great humility and offered gifts and letters”—namely, Basil and John, metropolitan of Caesarea, the legates of the emperor Basil [Col. 0771C].

Since, therefore, the practice then prevailed that Eastern legates should be heard in that basilica, the Roman clergy and people opposed Eugenius when he was about to celebrate solemn Mass there, lest anyone dare to read Peter’s synodical letter.

Eugenius was so far from accepting that synodical letter that, together with the synodical letter of his own apocrisarii, he annulled and rejected all the proceedings. This is suggested by the words of Troilus, who threatened Pope Eugenius, because Eugenius opposed him, in the following terms:

“Know, Lord Abbot, that if we obtain even a little respite from the confusion of the nations, we shall, by the Holy Trinity, join with you even the pope who is now exalted and insolent; and we shall melt down all those speaking in Rome, all your disciples, and all of you, each one in the place suited to him, just as Martin was melted down.”

Here the zeal of Eugenius, as well as that of the entire Roman clergy and people in rejecting Peter’s Constantinopolitan heretical writings, is clearly evident, since Troilus was driven to such threats.

[Note: [Col. 0771D]]

## Line 1.—Eugenius

After Pope St Martin had been deported to Cherson at the instigation of Theodore Calliopas, exarch, the Roman clergy designated Eugenius vicar of the Apostolic See, with the intention stated above. When reliable news of St Martin’s death was brought to Rome, no one else was sought to succeed him; rather, the man who had previously held the vicariate began to sit as true and legitimate pontiff in the year of the Lord 654, which was the thirteenth year of Constans.

## Line 2.—

He sat for two years, eight months, and twenty-four days. Understand this as reckoned from the time of Martin’s deportation to Cherson.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The disturbed chronology of certain pontiffs—especially those who, after Silvester, endured martyrdoms, deportations, exiles, and imprisonments imposed by emperors at the instigation of heretics—troubles more careful chronologists and compels them to adopt differing opinions, since they must rely chiefly on conjecture. I therefore think that this explains why their foremost scholar, Francesco Bianchini, who recently enriched this field with so many new monuments before the time of St Gregory the Great, when he comes to some such pontiffs, although using conjecture superior to that of others, nevertheless seems not to have placed the matter beyond doubt. Examples are the pontificate of Felix II, placed within the division of Liberius’s seat, and that of Vigilius, first an intruder while Silverius was still alive and afterward a legitimate pontiff, whose tenure he decrees must be shortened by a full year, from June of 537 to the same month of the following year, when Silverius died in exile on the island of Ponza. I shall have to use a method not unlike this in determining the chronology of Eugenius; for the beginning of his legitimate tenure must be taken from St Martin’s exile, as more recent scholars commonly affirm against Baronius’s opinion.

I have established that the two years, nine months, and twenty-four days attributed to Eugenius by almost all the manuscripts of Anastasius and by the better catalogues begin while Martin was still alive. I use as evidence Martin himself, who, while exiled at Cherson, says the following in his second letter to a friend:

> “May God establish their hearts in the orthodox faith … and keep them steadfast, especially the shepherd who is now shown to preside over them.”

From this it may safely be inferred that in 655, when Martin wrote this letter, Eugenius was the legitimate pontiff, and therefore that Martin had already abdicated the pontificate. When he abdicated, however, is uncertain. For, while he was stationed on guard at Constantinople after 18 September 654, he wrote to Theodore that a Roman pontiff had not yet been created, although the Monothelites wished this to happen:

> “An order was presented by Calliopas to the priests and deacons, containing the rejection [or, in another reading, expulsion] of my humility: that I had irregularly and unlawfully usurped the episcopate, that I was not worthy to be established in the Apostolic See, but should in every way be transferred to this imperial city, with a bishop substituted in my place—something that has never yet happened, and I hope will never happen. For in the absence of the pontiff, the archdeacon, archpresbyter, and chief notary represent the pontiff’s place.”

Since, moreover, in two letters written from Cherson to a friend, especially in the last one, which he wrote only a few days before his death, Martin confesses in more than one place that he had once been Roman pontiff—for example, in the first letter:

> “What shall we say of ourselves, who are his own servants, and at least for a moment ministered to him, yet remain in such exile and affliction?”

And in the second:

> “I marvel at the indiscretion and compassion of all who once belonged to me.”

It is evident that a new pontiff was already sitting at Rome. When the testimony just cited is joined to the passage brought forward from the same second letter, from which it is clear that St Martin regarded him as the legitimate pontiff, it becomes absolutely certain that Eugenius was sitting while Martin was still alive.

It therefore remains to establish the beginning of Eugenius’s tenure. This can be found only by counting backward from the date of his deposition, 2 June, which all authorities consistently maintain. All the better manuscripts—the two Freherian manuscripts, the Regius, Mazarine, and first Thuane manuscripts, the three most ancient Ambrosian manuscripts, as well as Luitprand and many other authorities—agree with the finest catalogues, namely the Palatine-Vatican, Bergomate, Lucense, second Corbeiensis, Farfense, and Veronese, in assigning Eugenius two years, nine months, and twenty-four days [Luitprand: twenty-three; Lucense: twenty-nine; Corbeiensis: nineteen; Farfense: fourteen], with only slight differences in the number of days.

Counting this period backward from 2 June, one reaches 9 August, which was a Sunday in the year 655. That year cannot be assigned to his ordination, however, since Martin, living at Cherson, already knew that his successor had been created. The ordination must therefore be referred to the preceding year, 654, when Sunday fell on 10 August, and the date of deposition must be included in the calculation, as we already know Anastasius usually did. Thus Eugenius was consecrated on 10 August of that year, 654, while Martin was still staying on the island of Naxos, and after two years, nine months, and twenty-four days he died on 2 June 657.

For this reason Sirmond’s opinion must be rejected. In his *Chronological Synopsis* appended to the *Collection of Anastasius*, he begins the tenure in September 653, while, like the others, assigning the deposition to 2 June after two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. For even if, in order to treat him indulgently, we began the period of the pontificate from the Kalends of September, we should certainly find the deposition falling, contrary to everyone’s testimony, on 24 June.

The opinion of Antonio Pagi, otherwise a most learned man, must likewise be rejected. He uses an interregnum of one year, two months, and twenty days found in several manuscript copies as a rule for establishing the date of Eugenius’s ordination, without noticing that these manuscripts and the printed copies, in the various readings of our edition, assign Eugenius a tenure of two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. The ordination would therefore have to be moved back by an entire month, to the great detriment of his conjecture.

Moreover—and this is least tolerable in a learned man—he wants the ordination to have taken place in the Roman Church, the mother and teacher of all the Catholic churches throughout the world, nearly two years before the date corresponding to 8 September 654. It would have been better to reject the addition of the interregnum, introduced by an unskilled hand, than to embrace it. I say “addition,” because the manuscripts and catalogues show that every interregnum is an interpolation: the second Thuane manuscript and any others that may exist, as well as certain catalogues, especially the Veronese, show no vacancy at all; finally, the Lucense catalogue gives an interregnum of twenty-eight days added by another hand.

And indeed, who would believe that the Roman See was vacant after St Martin, when at one and the same time two pontiffs are seen to have been established in it? Whether the latter legitimately occupied the see while Martin was alive, until Martin’s abdication is established, must remain undecided. It is nevertheless probable that he occupied it illegitimately for some time, although the surviving monuments of such great antiquity do not provide the means of distinguishing the two periods.

In any case, before Eugenius’s ordination, no more than five years, one month, and six days can be assigned to St Martin. That is the period demonstrably elapsed from his consecration on 5 July 649 to the ordination of his successor on 10 August 654.

This, then, is how I think the chronology of the two pontiffs should be arranged. Yet I admit, with the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori, in his notes on John the Deacon’s *On the Bishops of Naples* (*Italian Writers*, vol. I, part II, p. 303), that the acts of the holy pontiffs Martin and Eugenius are found in Anastasius enveloped in such darkness that they can scarcely be reconciled, unless light is supplied from elsewhere.

## Line 1.—Eugenius

Eugenius, son of Ruffinianus, a Roman from the first region, the Aventine, sat in the pontifical see for two years, nine months, and fourteen days. He was created and consecrated on Sunday, 10 August 654.

## Line 6.—Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, sent a synodical letter

After the death of Pyrrhus, who, following Paul, had again occupied the see of Constantinople amid very many disputes, Peter himself, also a heretic, was appointed by heretics. Wishing to reach an accommodation with Catholics and heretics alike through some new invention, he fabricated an unheard-of doctrine concerning Christ’s wills: namely, he asserted three wills in Christ, one subsistential will together with the Monothelites, but two natural wills together with the Catholics.

This is stated in St Maximus’s letter to Anastasius the monk, his disciple. In it he vigorously refutes this new error, as also in the letter of Anastasius the monk, disciple of St Maximus, to the common college of monks assembled at Calaris. Both letters are extant in the *Collections* of Anastasius Bibliothecarius, edited by Sirmond, volume three.

> “Peter,” he says, “preached one will above two—that is, three wills and operations—to be proclaimed together in the same Lord Jesus Christ.”

Peter therefore wrote his extremely obscure and evasive synodical letter to Eugenius in order to be received by him into communion. Eugenius not only did not admit it, but with even greater public rejection cast it out of the holy Church of God.

## Line 1.—Eugenius, Roman by nationality

When Pope St Martin was taken captive and carried into Greece on 19 June 653, the archdeacon, archpresbyter, and chief of the notaries governed the Roman Church, as we explained under his pontificate, until 8 September 654. On that day Eugenius, Roman by nationality, son of Ruffinianus, from the first region, the Aventine, a cleric from infancy, as Anastasius says, was ordained Roman pontiff, after the see had been vacant for one year, two months, and twenty days because of Martin’s absence, as is read in certain manuscript copies of Anastasius cited at the end of the royal edition.

This occurred without Martin’s knowledge but was later approved by St Martin, as we proved under no. 19 of his pontificate. Hence the opinion of those who maintain that Eugenius was merely Martin’s vicar before Martin’s death collapses. When a pontiff was dead or absent, a vicar was not placed over the Church; rather, it was governed by the three men just mentioned.

Baronius’s statement likewise collapses: he says that Eugenius sat only nominally until Martin’s death and then, when the previously expressed consent was renewed, began to sit legitimately. Eugenius, however, must be regarded as the legitimate pontiff from the day of his ordination, since that ordination was acceptable to St Martin.

Finally, there must be an error in Anastasius where he says that Martin sat for six years, one month, and twenty-six days. Apart from the fact that this would make him sit only until 31 August 655, which is demonstrably false from the date of his death, neither Anastasius nor the authors of the catalogues ordinarily attribute to pontiffs periods that elapsed after their abdication or deposition, as was seen in the cases of Silverius and Vigilius. Instead, they attribute such periods to their successors, however those successors may have been ordained.

## Line 3.—“For he was kind,” etc.

Platina calls Eugenius a man of extraordinary piety, religious devotion, gentleness, and generosity. Anastasius calls him kind, mild, gentle, affable to all, and distinguished for holiness. His name is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 2 June. Baronius writes in his notes that he was not only the successor of St Martin in the see but also in holiness.

## Line 6.—“During his time Peter, patriarch of Constantinople…”

Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, whom we said under Martin had been substituted in 655 for the deceased Pyrrhus, was a Monothelite heretic. Nevertheless, in order at least to display the appearance of a Catholic and thereby deserve to be received into communion by Eugenius, he sent him letters to Rome wrapped in evasions and perplexities. The clergy and people forbade them, and they were not received at all.

As was customary among his predecessors, Eugenius sent apocrisiaries to the emperor Constans with a synodical letter and notified him of his ordination. Anastasius is silent about this embassy, but St Maximus informs us of it in the *Account of the Proceedings held between the lord abbot Maximus and his companion and the officials in the secretary*. This account is included in the collections of Anastasius and was produced in 655, or at the latest in 656, since in the same collections it precedes the disputation between St Maximus and Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, which was held in 656, as Baronius correctly observed.

From this account we learn that Peter of Constantinople, wishing to agree with both Catholics and heretics, preached three wills in Christ: one subsistential will together with the Monothelites, but two natural wills together with the orthodox. We also learn that the Roman pontiff’s apocrisiaries, enticed by Peter, agreed to this new monstrous error. The words of this account may be read in Baronius under the year 657, no. 15.

The same fact is established by the letter of Anastasius the monk, disciple of St Maximus, to the common college of monks assembled at Calaris. It shows that the apocrisiaries of the Roman pontiff agreed with Peter’s error, which asserted two operations and one above two—that is, three operations and wills:

> “Since, as has been said, they refused to correct their own statement, they compelled the apocrisiaries of senior Rome to persist in their own sect. They proclaimed with him one will above two—that is, three wills and operations—to be preached in the same Lord Jesus Christ, concocting a taste like that of the tree of knowledge, just as these men bring forth the faith from good and evil, while desiring such things.”

Those apocrisiaries cannot have been the men whom Pope Vitalian sent to Constantinople, as Combefis maintains in *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, disputation 1, paragraph 15, because Vitalian is said to have become pontiff in July 657. Moreover, St Maximus’s disputation with the officials in the secretary belongs to 655, or at most 656. The reference, therefore, is to apocrisiaries sent by Pope Eugenius.

There can be no doubt that Eugenius, who rejected Peter’s synodical letter, also rejected what the treacherous apocrisiaries had done at Peter’s urging. Those apocrisiaries had brought Eugenius no letter from him. Hence St Maximus, whose words Baronius quotes in the place cited, concludes that if they were in communion with Peter, no prejudice would thereby be done to the Roman See:

> “These men who have come,” he says, “will in no way cause prejudice to the Roman See, even if they communicate with him, since they did not bring a letter to the patriarch.”

## Line 15.—“He was also buried…”

After Eugenius had created twenty-two bishops in two ordinations and had sat for two years, eight months, and twenty-four days, as is read in Anastasius, he died on 1 June 657 and was buried on 2 June, the fourth day before the Nones of June. From this it is clear that Anastasius calculated the beginning of his pontificate not from St Martin’s death, but from 8 September 654, when Eugenius was ordained while St Martin was still alive. Thus we were justified in saying that an error lies in Anastasius where he states that Martin sat for six years, one month, and twenty-six days, as we showed under no. 1.

## Line 3.—“For he was kind,” etc., “and more distinguished for holiness”

Ecclesiastical writers—Anastasius Bibliothecarius, Platina, and Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 2 June—speak of Eugenius as a man of admirable piety, sound religious devotion, graciousness, and magnificence. The Church venerates him as a saint and as a worthy successor of St Martin, not only in the Roman chair but also in the praise of holiness. He gave an outstanding proof of this when he rejected the synodical letter customarily sent by Peter, patriarch of Constantinople: it had been composed in obscure language and did not speak of two wills.

## [Col. 0763]

### 134. Eugenius

Eugenius, Roman by nationality, from the first region, the Aventine [the Aventine region], a cleric from infancy, son of Ruffinianus, sat for two years, eight months, and twenty-four days [B: it also maintains that he sat for six months and twenty-three days after St Martin’s death, in the year 655].

For he was kind, mild, gentle, affable to all, and more distinguished for holiness. He granted the clergy the customary gift (*roga*) and distributed alms to the needy. He also ordered that, on the day of his death, the *presbyteria* should be distributed in full to the poor, the clergy, or the household [in full]. See Baronius under the year 653.

During his time Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, sent a synodical letter to the Apostolic See, entirely obscure according to the former custom and beyond the rule, but not declaring the operations [not otherwise declaring the two operations] or wills in our Lord Jesus Christ. The people or clergy, inflamed because he had sent such a synodical letter, did not receive it at all [C: they received it]; rather, it was cast out of the holy Church of God with even greater public rejection.

The people or clergy would not even allow the same pope to celebrate Mass in the basilica of Holy Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God, called at the Crib, unless he himself promised that he would never receive it. He made twenty-one bishops in various places [B: twenty-two].

He was also buried at St Peter the Apostle on 2 June, the fourth day before the Nones of June. The episcopate was vacant for one month and twenty-nine days [C: twenty-three].

# LXXVIII. SAINT VITALIAN

## In the year of Christ 655, the fourteenth year of the Emperor Constans
