## [Col. 0779A]

### No. 133, line 12.—“And on that very day the emperor went to St Peter, for prayer, and offered a gift there”

When the emperor entered Rome, he immediately hastened to the basilica of St Peter for prayer and offered gifts. Augustine says on Psalm 140:

> “The emperor came to Rome. To what does the emperor hasten—to the emperor’s temple, or to the Fisherman’s memorial?”

The same author says on Psalm 65:

> “But it is better that, when the emperor comes to Rome, he should lay aside his diadem and weep at the Fisherman’s memorial than that the Fisherman should weep at the emperor’s memorial.”

### Line 14.—“On the Lord’s day he proceeded to St Peter with his army; all came out to meet him with candles, and he offered upon its altar a pallium woven with gold, and Masses were celebrated”

When the emperor approached the basilica of St Peter, the clergy came out to meet him with candles, and the emperor, according to custom, offered gifts. The honor of meeting emperors and princes as they entered the Church was paid by bishops and clergy; and an emperor ordinarily does not attend the sacred rites without making an offering. On this subject see in detail book 1 of *On Dukes and Counts*, chapter 17.

### Line 18.—“Likewise, on the Lord’s day, there was a station at St Peter”

Stations were held on the Lord’s day. Stations were established prayers which the faithful made standing in the individual churches of the city of Rome, especially on the Lord’s day, in memory of the Lord’s resurrection. Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*:

> “Now he will either make stations for some other one rather than for Christ, or also on the Lord’s day, when not even for Christ.”

### No. 136, line 1.—“And he uncovered the church of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs, which had been covered with bronze tiles”

The roof of the basilica of Holy Mary at the Martyrs was made of bronze tiles. The larger basilicas are roofed with bronze or lead. Hence Stephen of Tournai, letter 165:

> “The churches are covered with English lead and stripped of Roman [material].”

The *trullum*, that is, the gable or dome of the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, was roofed with leaden sheets, that is, plates. Anastasius, under Sergius:

> “He covered and fortified the *trullum* of the same church with cast leaden sheets.”

The same author, under Gregory III:

> “Likewise, in the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God, which is called at the Martyrs, he had the roof, demolished by long neglect, cleaned down to the sound material and restored it anew with abundant lime and leaden sheets.”

The basilica of St Mary at the Martyrs is the one called the Rotunda. Berthold of Constance, *Chronicle*, under the year 1087:

> “Guibert the heresiarch did not cease from the perversity he had begun; rather, he fortified himself in St Mary at the Martyrs, which they call the Rotunda.”

### Line 6.—“He imposed such affliction upon the people of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia through *diagrapha*, or head-counts, and through naval requisitions”

The Italians, Sicilians, and Africans were burdened by assessments and head-counts, that is, poll taxes or head taxes. An assessment was made for the purpose of imposing a head tax; this was called a census. *Capitatio* is a head tax, a levy imposed upon persons. See *Si minor*, *Code*, “On the Purchase of Property”; book 1 of the Theodosian Code, “On Fugitive Colonists.” Augustine, *Questions on the New Testament*, chapter 75:

> “The two-drachma payment is understood as a levy on persons or a tribute, not on estates; this is now called the ‘shabby gold,’ since the poor too are required to pay it.”

Tribute and the head tax differ in this way: tribute is an assessment on estates, whereas *capitatio* is an assessment on persons. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 13:

> “But fields burdened by tribute are less valuable, and the heads of men assessed for payment are less honorable.”

For this reason Sidonius calls tribute an “unshaped levy” in poem 7:

> “And let him demand that the unshaped levy be cut back.”

A naval requisition is the obligation to provide ships, which was imposed upon provincials. Marcus Tullius Cicero, *Against Verres*, book 5:

> “For that reason you did not demand a ship from the Mamertines, because they are federated allies.”

Not only were ships requisitioned, but also soldiers and rowers, pay and provisions. Livy, book 26:

> “The consuls proclaimed that private citizens should provide rowers according to their census and classes, as before, together with pay and provisions for thirty days.”

## [Col. 0780A]

### No. 135, line 1.—“Vitalianus”

Most of these events have been patched together from various fragments of Paul. This, indeed, was Anastasius’s usual practice. But events pertaining to the pontiffs that Paul had written while preserving their order were attached by Anastasius to one pontiff or another, and therefore must be assigned to their proper places so that the historical sequence may proceed.

Accordingly, after the words in no. 136, line 12, “He was killed in the bath,” the following passage from the Life of Adeodatus, no. 137, line 6, must be inserted here:

> “During his time Mezzetius, who was in Sicily with the eastern army, revolted and seized the kingdom. The army of Italy proceeded, some through the regions of Istria, others through the regions of Campania, and still others through the regions of Sardinia and Africa. In the same way they came through Sicily to the city of Syracuse. With God’s help, the unspeakable Mezzetius was killed. Many of his judges were mutilated and brought together to Constantinople, along with his head, the head of the rebel. Later the Saracens came into Sicily, took the aforementioned city, and carried out a great slaughter among the people who had fled into the camps or mountains. They likewise made immense booty, and, taking with them the bronze that had been brought there from the Roman city, they returned to Alexandria.

> “At the same time”—this should be taken from the Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane manuscripts, in the notes at line 12 of no. 136—“Pope Vitalian sent to Britain Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, both highly learned men, who enriched many churches of the English with the fruits of ecclesiastical learning. Among them Theodore, archbishop, described the judgments of penitents, namely, how many years each person ought to repent for each sin, with marvelous and discerning judgment. Not long afterward the venerable pope just mentioned ended his life.”

To this must be joined what we read in the same Life of Adeodatus, no. 138, line 5:

> “After his passing there were rains and thunder such as no human age remembers having occurred, so that men and animals even perished by lightning. Unless the Lord had been appeased by the litanies that were performed daily, people would not have been able to thresh grain or store it in the granaries. These evils increased so greatly that, as a result of the rains themselves, legumes grew again and reached maturity; and the astonished people wondered at this, etc.”

But in order to rescue Vitalian’s deeds from the confusion in which they are entangled, it will be preferable to arrange each event in its proper year and present his pontificate in a brief chronological scheme.

Thus, in 657, the first year of Vitalian and the seventeenth of Constans, St Maximus held a disputation at Constantinople with the emperor’s officials.

In 658, the second year of Vitalian and the eighteenth of Constans, after various incursions of the Saracens into the empire—concerning which Troilus had spoken in the aforementioned disputation with St Maximus, while Mavias and Hali were disputing the caliphate—Mavias, in order to overcome his opponent, made peace with the emperor Constans. The author of the *Miscella* discusses this at greater length in book 18. Theophanes, in his *Chronicle* under this year, writes:

> “This year, when an embassy from Mavia was received by the emperor, the Arabs, shaken by seditions and disturbances, made a pact with the Romans, namely, that each day they would pay the Romans one thousand coins, a horse, and a slave. Meanwhile, a great earthquake arose throughout Palestine and Syria in the month of Dios, in the second indiction, and caused great destruction.”

At about the same time, when Thomas, patriarch of Constantinople, had died, John succeeded him, according to Nicephorus’s testimony in his *Chronicle*. Likewise, as the author of the *Miscella* writes:

> “In the eighteenth year of the reign of Constans, Constans killed his brother Theodosius.”

In 659, the third year of Vitalian and the nineteenth of Constans, Constantine, Constans’s firstborn son, who had been declared Augustus six years earlier, admitted his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius into the imperial partnership as Caesars. At the same time Mavias, having defeated Hali, his rival for the caliphate, obtained sole rule over the Saracens and established the royal residence and treasury at Damascus. Theophanes and the author of the *Miscella* relate this. The latter wrote in book 19, page 136:

> “While the Arabs were at Saphin, the aforementioned Hali was killed by treachery, and Muhavias ruled alone according to royal custom, inhabiting Damascus and storing treasures of money there.”

In 660, the fourth year of Vitalian and the twentieth of Constans.

In 661, the fifth year of Vitalian and the twenty-first of Constans.

In 662, the sixth year of Vitalian and the twenty-second of Constans.

In 663, the seventh year of Vitalian and the twenty-third of Constans. In that year Constans, having become hated by the people of Constantinople, came to Italy and, as Anastasius says, in the sixth indiction—that is, according to the chronological designation of the current year—the author of the *Miscella*, page 137, gave the following account of the reason:

> “After the killing of his brother Theodosius, he was hated by the Byzantines, especially because he had disgracefully brought the most holy Pope Martin to Constantinople and banished him into exile in the regions of Cherson, and had cut off the tongue and hand of Maximus, the wisest confessor, and had condemned many orthodox people to beatings, exiles, and persecution because they would in no way assent to his heresy. He even handed over to tortures and exile the two Anastasii who had been disciples of Maximus the Confessor. Because of such deeds he became hated. Since he was very afraid, he wanted to transfer the empire to the city of Rome. For this reason he wanted to take the empress and his three sons away from Byzantium, unless Andreas the chamberlain and Theodore the patrician of the colony had prevented the plan. In fact, he spent six years in Sicily.”

Cedrenus, under Constans, says:

> “He decided to transfer the empire to Rome, since he was hated by the Byzantines because of the Monothelite heresy and other erroneous opinions concerning religion. He therefore sent men to bring his wife and children; but the Byzantines detained her with the children.”

In 664, the eighth year of Vitalian and the twenty-fourth of Constans, Anastasius’s account of what Constans did at Rome at this time was copied almost word for word from Paul the Deacon, book 5, chapter 11. In the same year John died, and Constantine the Deacon was elected bishop of Constantinople, according to the report of the patriarch Nicephorus in his *Chronicle*.

In 665, the ninth year of Vitalian and the twenty-fifth of Constans, Constans granted autocephaly to the bishop of Ravenna. A privilege concerning this survives in volume 2 of the *Writers of Italian Affairs*, page 146.

In 666, the tenth year of Vitalian and the twenty-sixth of Constans, the patriarch Constantine died. In his place Theodore, a Constantinopolitan presbyter, syncellus, and keeper of the vessels, was elected; according to the same Nicephorus, he was a most wicked Monothelite.

In 667, the eleventh year of Vitalian and the twenty-seventh of Constans, Theophanes reports that a rebellion took place by Sabor, commander of the Armenian army, against the emperor Constans.

[Col. 0781D] **Year 668, the twelfth of Vitalian, the first of Constantine Pogonatus.** For while Constans was still residing in Sicily, he was murdered in a bath. Concerning this, the author of the *Miscella*, book XIX, p. 137, writes:

> “In the twenty-seventh year of his reign Constans was treacherously killed in Sicily at Syracuse, in a bath called Daphne [lacuna] and when he had entered the aforementioned bath, a certain Andreas, son of Troilus, entered with him as his attendant. When [the emperor] had begun to be anointed with Gallic perfume, Andreas took a bucket and struck him on the head with it, then immediately fled. But when the emperor lingered in the bath, those who were outside rushed in and found the emperor murdered.”

Troilus was the father of Andreas the murderer, and he is mentioned in the account of the proceedings against St. Maximus. Meanwhile, while Sabores was raging through the East with the utmost tyranny, Mezzetius seized power in Sicily. Concerning him we must hear Paul the Deacon, in the same work, chapter 12:

> “After Constans the emperor had been killed at Syracuse, Mecetius seized the kingdom in Sicily, but without the consent of the eastern army. Against him, therefore, soldiers of the Italian army came—some through Istria, others through the regions of Campania, and still others from the regions of Africa and Sardinia—and attacked Syracuse with great force, depriving him of life. Many of his judges were beheaded, and many were brought to Constantinople; with them the head of the false emperor was also carried away.”

Anastasius transcribed this account almost verbatim, except that he asserts that the event took place with the approval of the eastern army, whereas Paul says that it occurred without the consent and will of the eastern army. Moreover, what Anastasius calls *Intarta*, Paul calls “false.” The historian then proceeds to relate the Saracen invasion, so that it must have occurred either in the present year or, at the latest, in the following one. We shall discuss this below from Theophanes.

In the same year Paul continues his account of the deeds of Pope Vitalian in the following manner, chapter 30:

> “Therefore, after Constans Augustus had been killed in Sicily, and Mecentius the tyrant who had succeeded him had been punished, Constantine, son of Constans Augustus, assumed the government of the Roman kingdom, and ruled the Romans for seventeen years. In the time of Constantine, Theodore was archbishop …”

—with the remainder as it is read in the other manuscript copies of Anastasius. That all of this must be referred to the present year is expressly attested by Bede, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1:

> “Theodore was ordained bishop: he was ordained by Pope Vitalian in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 668, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April. Thus, together with Adrian, he was sent to Britain on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. When they had travelled together by sea to Marseilles and from there by land to Arles, and had delivered to John, archbishop of that city, letters of recommendation from Pope Vitalian, they were detained by him until Ebroin, mayor of the royal palace, granted them permission to proceed wherever they wished.”

**Year 669, the thirteenth of Vitalian, the second of Constantine.** Theophanes and the author of the *Miscella* assign the Saracen invasion of Sicily to this year. [Col. 0782C]

**Year 670, the fourteenth of Vitalian, the third of Constantine.** The aforementioned author records that Constantine achieved a victory over the Saracens.

**Year 671, the fifteenth of Vitalian, the fourth of Constantine.** The same author writes for this year:

> “In the fourth year of Constantine a rainbow appeared in the sky in the month of March, and all flesh trembled, so that everyone said that the end was at hand. In the same year, having built a great fleet, the enemies of Christ—namely, Muhammad and Qays—sailed to Sicily and Lycia, and a pestilence occurred in Egypt.”

Paul the Deacon adds, chapter 31:

> “Shortly thereafter, in the month of August, a comet appeared in the eastern region with exceedingly brilliant rays; then it turned back upon itself and disappeared. Soon after, a severe pestilence arose from that same eastern region and devastated the Roman people. In this year Vitalian also died.”

After Vitalian’s death Paul the Deacon says that the following events occurred, which he relates after narrating the Saracen invasion of Sicily, book V, chapter 15:

> “At that time there were rains and thunder so tremendous as no human being had previously remembered, so that countless thousands of men and animals were killed by lightning. In that year the vegetables, which had been unable to be gathered because of the rains, grew again and were brought to maturity.”

Anastasius wrongly appended these events to the account of Adeodatus and, committing an intolerable chronological error of at least four years, says that they occurred after Adeodatus’s death. If they are assigned to the deeds of Vitalian, we obtain an orderly sequence of events, and everything falls into place with its proper times and persons. This is all the more convincing because the *Miscella* likewise relates that the same atmospheric disturbance occurred at the beginning of Constantine’s reign.

**Line 2.—“Here he sent his representatives.”** When Vitalian had been elected pope in accordance with the established custom, he sent a letter to the emperor requesting permission for his ordination. Attached to this synodical letter was the decree of election, together with the signatures of the clergy and leading men, so that its legitimacy might be recognized.

In the election of Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, Theophanes preserved a copy of the decree issued in the year 714, in the *Chronicle*, p. 322. It reads as follows:

> “By the suffrage and consent of the devout presbyters, deacons, and the entire sacred clergy, of the holy senate, and of all the Christ-loving people of this God-protected imperial city: by divine grace, which always cares for what lies within and supplies what is lacking, Germanus, the most holy metropolitan and president of the metropolitan see of Cyzicus, is transferred to be bishop of this God-preserved City and Queen of Cities. This was done in the presence of Michael, the most holy presbyter and apocrisiary of the Apostolic See, together with the other priests and bishops present, while Artemius was emperor.”

Anyone can easily discern from these Anastasian records that a similar formula was customarily used in the election of the Roman pontiffs.

**Line 4.—“Renewing the privileges of the Church.”** The highly honorable reception given to the apostolic envoys, and the renewal of the privileges which the Apostolic See had long enjoyed, sufficiently indicate that Constans greatly approved Vitalian’s zeal against the Monothelites, whose madness he certainly weakened by his replies.

We may infer this from the fact that, after the heretic Peter’s death, three patriarchs succeeded him—Thomas, John, and Constantine—who are called Catholics without objection in the Acts of the First Session of the Sixth Synod, and not even the legates of the Apostolic See offered any opposition to them.

Therefore, although after Honorius the Eastern Church had separated from the Western and at Constantinople the names of the Roman pontiffs had not been inserted in the sacred diptychs, scarcely had Vitalian been raised to the pontificate when this ecclesiastical custom was restored throughout the East. Once accepted under Vitalian, it continued until George of Constantinople, a Monothelite bishop.

When George made seditious efforts to erase Vitalian’s name from the ecclesiastical diptychs, Constantine Pogonatus opposed him. In a letter to Pope Donus he wrote:

> “Both this most sacred patriarch and Macarius, the most holy patriarch of Theopolis, made repeated demands of us that the most blessed Vitalian should be removed from the diptychs … For they did not agree that the patriarchs who subsequently held office in the aforementioned holy Roman Church should be commemorated until an agreement and satisfaction had been reached concerning the words disputed between the two sees … But we did not agree to this, namely, that the same Vitalian should be removed from the diptychs.”

Without doubt, those three patriarchs did not refuse to send synodical letters to Vitalian. The matter is treated in Session 13 of the Sixth Synod:

> “George the deacon and chartophylax said … ‘My lord, the book, or register, containing copies of the synodical letters issued by Thomas, John, and Constantine, of holy memory, formerly patriarchs of this imperial city, is now here, together with the authentic sealed synodical letter issued by Thomas, of holy memory, formerly patriarch, to Vitalian, of holy memory, formerly Roman pope. Although he wished to send it to him because of the continually impending invasion of the impious Saracens—which, as you know, lasted for two years, during which he held the pontificate—he was unable to send it. At your command, therefore, I immediately bring it forth.’”

Indeed, when Anastasius discusses the Sixth Synod under Pope Agatho, he says:

> “Then they removed from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, and from the church paintings their images, or removed them from the doors where they might have been; namely, Cyrus, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, through whom the error against the orthodox faith has continued to spread until now.””

Thus the names of the patriarchs Thomas, John, and Constantine were left in the diptychs, for the Sixth Council considered them Catholics. It is therefore no wonder that an emperor who was not entirely orthodox received the apostolic envoys with great courtesy and honored Vitalian himself by renewing his privileges.

**Line 7.—“Here he preserved the ecclesiastical rule.”** Anastasius omits, not without culpable negligence, the deeds of Vitalian, from which the pope’s extraordinary zeal in defending the faith shines forth.

Peter was patriarch of Constantinople and the author of a monstrous heresy; he defended the invention of a threefold operation in Christ. He had already experienced the zeal of Pope Eugenius and the steadfastness of the Westerners who condemned that same impiety. In order to defend it, he sent Pope Vitalian a letter full of fraud and of convoluted, deceptive argument, falsifying the testimonies of the holy Fathers.

Concerning this the Fathers of the Sixth Synod say, Session 13:

> “Likewise, from another register, the letter of Peter, formerly bishop of the imperial city, to Vitalian, of holy memory, who was Roman pope, was read. Its beginning is: ‘Your letter of unanimity and holy brotherhood has brought us spiritual joy.’”

I suppose that Vitalian had written salutary admonitions intended to turn Peter away from the impiety he had conceived. [Col. 0784B] But the obstinate heresiarch persisted in defending what he had once taken into his mind, in the aforementioned letter to Vitalian. For the Acts add:

> “When that letter was being read, containing various testimonies of the Fathers, those who represented Agatho, the most holy Roman pope, said: ‘We inform your Glory that the testimonies of the Fathers contained in the present letter, Peter’s letter now being read, have been cut down and mutilated by Peter himself, because he wished to display his own intention concerning one will and one operation—that is, one substantial operation.’”

As soon, therefore, as Peter’s letter was brought to Rome, it was publicly read in an assembly, examined, and convicted of fraud. Consequently, the legates, fully aware of all these matters, hastened to Constantinople with sufficient and suitable memoranda for exposing the patriarch’s machinations.

The judges acknowledged this in the full synod and said:

> “We have carefully established, in accordance with what your Reverence has stated, that such testimonies as are contained in the present letter have been placed there in mutilated form. If it pleases your holy and universal council, let the reading of such a letter proceed no further.”

The reason why the emperor, although otherwise a Monothelite, dismissed the pope’s representatives kindly and honorably was surely that he feared the Italian army, which he knew to be most devoted to the pope.

**Line 8.—“Constantine.”** It should read “Constans,” who had come to Rome because of the disputes known to have arisen between Rome and Constantinople.

Since he himself was devoted to the heresy, while, on the contrary, the leading men of Rome and Italy were fiercely opposed to it, the prince, with savage intent, harassed many Italians with grievous burdens and afflictions. Meanwhile Vitalian, neither rebellious against the prince nor negligent in defending the faith, endured these vexations with unconquered courage.

He was even the instigator of the Italian army, so that they might suppress the tyrants who, after Constans’s murder, successively ravaged the empire. His son Constantine speaks of this fairly clearly in a letter to Pope Donus, where he says that he undertook Vitalian’s defense against the efforts of George of Constantinople and the obstinacy of Macarius of Antioch:

> “This also was because of the affection shown to us by that same Vitalian while he was still alive, in his admonition concerning the tyrants.”

The pope was therefore worthy of being honored with the eulogy that he had carefully preserved the ecclesiastical rule in the most difficult circumstances.]

[Note: [Col. 0784D]]

**Number 135, line 1.—“Signiensis.”** He was so called from the city of Signia among the Hernici, situated thirty miles from Rome on the Via Lavicana.

**Line 2.—“Six months.”** Five months less four days after thirteen years. This is evident from the beginning and end of the pontificate he undertook.

**Line 6.—“Golden Gospels.”** The crafty emperor offered these gifts to the Church in order to pretend that he was a Catholic. See Baronius, 655, no. 5 and following.

**Number 136, lines 12 and 13.—“He was killed in a bath.”** In the twenty-seventh year of his reign and in the year 668 after the birth of Christ. See Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Baronius, year 668, nos. 1 and 2.

**Lines 13 and 14.—“He ended his life.”** In the year of Christ 669, which was the second year of the emperor Constantine Pogonatus. Theodore, bishop of Constantinople, a Monothelite, erased him from the sacred diptychs of the Greeks without the emperor’s knowledge, as is evident from Constantine’s letter to Pope Donus.]

[Note: [Col. 0785A]]

## Chronological Notes

Once the pontificate of St. Eugenius has been correctly established, and its end has been assigned to the year 657 together with the most learned men Panvinio, Papebrochius, and Pagius, it is not difficult to determine the beginning of Vitalian’s pontificate.

For although the codices, catalogues, and authors generally assert that after Eugenius’s death the see was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days, counting one month and twenty-eight days from the day of Eugenius’s death, or deposition, 2 June 657, brings us to 30 July of the same year. This date is indicated for Vitalian’s ordination by a letter of Dom A. from that year.

Although Luitprand, without discussing the vacancy of the see, connects Vitalian’s death with 6 February and, being a week later, namely 6 August, seems to require that his ordination be placed on that date, we reject his opinion because it is singular. Bollandus cites this opinion of Luitprand under 27 January, no. 7; nevertheless, relying on the martyrologies—not many, nor very ancient, as he says—which commemorate Vitalian on 27 January, he himself demonstrates in no. 1 that his death should be fixed on that day.

Thus, once the beginning and end of Vitalian’s pontificate are known, the remaining matters are clear. For the common agreement of the catalogues and codices, as well as of the authorities cited by Pagius under the year 669, no. 2, establishes his pontificate as fourteen years and six months—apart from a difference of two or three days. The months were not complete, but were short by two or three days; nevertheless, they disregard this in using the round number, as is clear when the duration of the see is reckoned from 30 July 657, since 30 January 672 completes it.

Moreover, it is sufficiently clear that the catalogues and codices use the round number while disregarding this difference, since the date of Vitalian’s ordination must either be moved back to the time of St. Martin or postponed to the year 660 so that it will coincide with a Sunday, if six complete months are counted.

If I may offer my own opinion, I think that an error arose because Vitalian’s date of death was recorded as the sixth day before the Kalends rather than the fourth day before the Kalends of February in the martyrologies and codices, owing to the ease with which IV was changed into VI, as I have noted elsewhere. I shall discuss this in the notes on Adeodatus.

I do not understand what Papebrochius intends in his argument with these words: “The catalogues generally count no days beyond fourteen years and six months,” which would postpone Vitalian’s death to the end of January. For if a period of three days remains over, what more days ought to have been counted? I understand his conjecture even less: that number 6 should be read as divided, so that five months and one day are assigned to it. For the twenty-seven days that intervene between the day of death and the deposition seem to me completely to destroy this conjecture. [Col. 0785D]

Furthermore, the Bergamo catalogue, which gives as many days as months in place of six months, shortens Vitalian’s pontificate by one year and leaves a gap in the months, namely: thirteen years, [lacuna] months, six days. It should therefore not be preferred to all the others, which agree.

In any case, Onuphrius in the *Chronicle of the Pontiffs*, as well as the more careful chronologists, rightly connect Vitalian’s death with the year 672; there is no reason for me to disregard their authority.]

[Note: [Col. 0785D]]

**Number 135, line 1.—“Vitalian.”** An Italian by nationality, he was born at Suertia, a fortress in the Abruzzi, the son of Anastasius Pontratius. He was the eleventh pope who was a native of the kingdom. Under the emperors Flavius Heraclius Constans and Constantine Augustus, he held the pontificate for fourteen years, five months, and twenty-nine days.

As soon as he was ordained pope, he immediately sent his legates [Col. 0786A] to Constantinople to the emperor, announcing his ordination. They renewed the privileges of the Roman Church and returned to Rome with gifts: the emperor sent to St. Peter a Gospel book written in golden letters and adorned with precious gems.

**Line 7.—“The ecclesiastical rule.”** Vitalian, devoted to divine worship, both composed the ecclesiastical rule and ordered the chant, introducing, as some maintain, organs for the sake of concord.]

[Note: [Col. 0786A]]

**Number 135, line 8.—“In his time Constans Augustus came.”** Cedrenus assigns the reason why Constans came from Constantinople to Italy to the eighteenth year of his reign:

> “He decided,” he says, “to transfer the empire to Rome, since he had become hateful to the Byzantines because of the Monothelite heresy and other corrupt opinions concerning religion.”

In addition to this reason, Cedrenus gives another: namely, that Constans had decided to go to Italy in order to escape, by changing his residence, from the unwelcome shadow of his brother Theodosius, which had appeared before his eyes in sleep in the dress of a deacon and, as though offering him a cup full of blood, had said: “Drink, brother.”

For Constans had murdered his brother Theodosius. Out of envy he had already arranged for him to be ordained deacon by Paul, the heretical patriarch, and, when Theodosius offered him the blood of Christ, Constans had drunk it.

Zonaras goes further and says that Constans left Constantinople because of the hatred conceived against him by its citizens, both on account of his brother’s murder and because of the sacrilegious acts committed against St. Martin the pope and the abbot Maximus, the most courageous champions of Catholic truth against Monothelism.]

[Note: [Col. 0786B]]

**Number 135, line 2.—“Here he sent his representatives,” etc.** Immediately after his ordination, Vitalian sent his representatives, or apocrisiaries, with a synodical letter, according to custom, to the imperial city, to the most devout princes, Constans and Constantine his son, whom his father had already proclaimed Augustus in the year 654, announcing his ordination, as Anastasius says.

With letters for both emperors, Vitalian’s apocrisiaries brought a letter of exhortation which he had sent to Peter, bishop of Constantinople. The letter itself is not extant, but it is mentioned in Peter’s reply to Vitalian, which was read in the thirteenth session of the Sixth General Synod. From that reply it is clear that Peter had not faithfully reproduced the testimonies of the Fathers, but had altered their words and appended them to his letter, because he wished to display his own intention concerning one will and one operation. This fraud was exposed in the same session, by both Greeks and Latins.

Vitalian therefore sent his synodical letter to both emperors, not to Peter. He did so because the emperors appeared to have acted against Catholics less from obstinate treachery toward the Catholic faith than from the persistent influence and incitement of the impious patriarchs; and also because Vitalian could at least in this respect incline them favorably toward the interests of the Church.

With the same policy, at the Lateran Synod Martin himself and the other Fathers, while honoring Constans—although he was an extremely hostile enemy of the faith—attacked the patriarchs, not Heraclius or Constans, although one had been among the authors of the Monothelite heresy and the other its most ardent defender.

Moreover, as will soon be said, Constans sent gifts to Vitalian, which the pope was obliged to accept as a matter of duty, lest he embolden the emperor against the Church. For if Martin and Eugenius acted with such humanity toward Constans while he raged furiously against the faith, as the anonymous author of the *History of the Monothelites*, Investigation 3, says, why should Vitalian have acted so harshly as to reject the emperor’s gifts, when some dawn of repentance—so beneficial to the faith—was already beginning to shine in Constans?

This was indeed remarkable, but entirely true. Martin, Eugenius, and Vitalian refrained from condemning Constans, although he had undertaken every possible evil against the Church. What crimes so wicked and sacrilegious could be imagined that might be compared with what Constans perpetrated against the faith and against its supreme leaders, namely the Roman pontiffs? Yet Martin, Eugenius, and Vitalian not only refrained from imposing an anathema on him; they also praised him and exercised every kind of courtesy in order to win his favor and bring him back to a better course.

For the same reason, when Constans came to Rome, he received every sign of kindness from Vitalian, as we shall see in the following number.

The envoys, or apocrisiaries, of Pope Vitalian returned from Constantinople to Rome with gifts sent by the emperor Constans to St. Peter—namely, a Gospel book written in golden letters and adorned with precious gems. Anastasius testifies to this in these words:

> “Through the same envoys the emperor Constans sent to Blessed Peter a golden Gospel book, adorned all around with white gems of marvelous size.”

As has just been said, Vitalian ought not to have rejected this gift, lest he embolden the emperor against the Church. For Baronius’s assertion that Constans renounced the heresy immediately after the beginning of Vitalian’s pontificate, and that otherwise he would not have accepted the Mass offering through the representative, rests on no evidence. Neither Anastasius nor any other ancient writer mentions any renunciation of the heresy by Constans.

**Line 7.—“Here he preserved the ecclesiastical rule,” etc.** After Deusdedit, archbishop of Dorovernum, or Canterbury, died in the year 664, Egbert, king of Kent, and Oswiu, king of Northumbria, sent the presbyter Wighard to Rome so that he might be ordained in Deusdedit’s place.

“When he reached Rome,” Bede says, book IV, chapter 1 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, “where Vitalian at that time presided over the Apostolic See, after he had explained the reason for his journey to the aforementioned apostolic pope, not long afterward both he himself and nearly all his companions who had come with him were destroyed when a pestilence broke out.”

For this reason Pope Vitalian did not wish to appoint another so quickly without consulting the kings. He therefore wrote to Oswiu, king of Northumbria, and explained both Wighard’s death and the difficulty of choosing a successor.

Bede, book III, chapter 29, quotes Pope Vitalian’s letter. Among other things, Vitalian says that through Oswiu’s envoys he sent to his wife Eanfled, his spiritual daughter, “a cross containing a golden key made from the most sacred chains of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.”

To King Oswiu, through the same envoys, Vitalian sent “relics of those same apostles and of the holy martyrs Laurence, John, Paul, Gregory, and Pancratius.” In the same letter he congratulated Oswiu on his faith and urged him to ensure that Easter be celebrated in the island at the proper time, according to apostolic tradition.

Worcester, however, assigns this embassy and Wighard’s death to the year 667, or confirms that date by the ordination of Theodore.

Vitalian therefore sought a suitable bishop whom he could send to England to undertake the office. He found Theodore, a Greek monk from Tarsus, upright in character, venerable in age, and instructed in secular and divine literature in both Greek and Latin. In the year 668 he ordained him archbishop for the English, as Bede testifies, book IV, chapter 1:

> “He was ordained,” he says, “by Pope Vitalian in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 668, on Sunday, the seventh day before the Kalends of April. Thus, together with Adrian the monk, he was sent to Britain on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.”

But Theodore remained at Arles until Ebroin, mayor of the palace of Clotaire III, king of Neustria and Burgundy, granted him permission to proceed wherever he wished, as Bede says in the same place.

After Theodore had been ordained archbishop of Canterbury, while he was still in Gaul and staying with Agilbert, bishop of Paris, he learned among other things from him that Gregory the Great had granted Augustine, the first bishop of the Cantuarians, many privileges of papal authority, by which jurisdiction over all the churches of Britain had been granted to him. Since the Church was still new everywhere, he had not been able to exercise that jurisdiction.

Theodore therefore wrote to Rome before proceeding to England and humbly asked Pope Vitalian to grant him everything that would benefit the entire island, and especially the church of the Anglo-Saxons. Pope Vitalian replied and granted his requests, as may be read in the letter quoted by William of Malmesbury, book I *On the Bishops*; for these letters are absent from the editions of the councils.

Strengthened by this privilege of the Apostolic See, Theodore extended his authority over all the churches of the Anglo-Saxons, as may be seen in the writers of English history.

In the same year, 667, John, bishop of Lappa in Crete, having suffered injustice at the hands of Paul, archbishop and metropolitan of Crete, by whom he had been deposed in a provincial synod, appealed to the Roman pontiff. He came to Rome in December, and after his case had been examined was restored to his see by Vitalian. Vitalian also rebuked Paul the metropolitan for violating the canons and for not allowing a bishop who had appealed to Rome the opportunity to travel there. This is established by four letters of the same pope written on the matter.

Hieronymus Rubeus, in book IV of the *History of Ravenna*, reports from the records of that church that Maurus, then bishop of Ravenna, was excommunicated by Pope Vitalian because, having been summoned by him to Rome to give an account of his conduct, he had refused to appear.

Relying on the power and friendship of the exarch, Maurus proceeded in his madness so far as to pronounce the same sentence of anathema in return against Vitalian. All the bishops of Italy, terrified by this monstrous crime, therefore joined with Vitalian and completely stripped Maurus, as unworthy, of the priesthood.

But he persisted in his fury and, even at the time of his death, charged all the clergy of the Church of Ravenna never to submit to the Roman pontiff. For this reason his successor, Adeodatus, excluded him entirely from ecclesiastical communion—namely, from the customary suffrages offered for the dead—and from commemoration in the sacred diptychs. Concerning Reparatus, the successor of Maurus, see what will be said under Pope Donus.

**Line 8.—“In his time,” etc.** Just as St. Martin the pope, as we have already said, used a policy of accommodation toward Constans at the Lateran Council, so also did Vitalian when Constans came to Rome.

Since the emperor at that time was at least outwardly Catholic and acted courteously toward Catholics, peace among the churches and tranquility in the faith became possible. Constantine Pogonatus, son of Constans and completely Catholic, was also very favorably disposed toward Pope Vitalian and later brought about the Sixth General Synod.

Constans remained in Rome for twelve days. Although he made no pretext of a religious purpose and appeared to act amicably toward Pope Vitalian, he plundered whatever was precious, both in the City and elsewhere in Italy, sparing neither buildings nor their sacred vessels and treasures, as Anastasius adds in the account of Vitalian:

> “Constans remained in Sicily until the year 668, when, after the sixteenth day of September, he paid the penalty for his crimes; for in that year he was killed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0788D]]

**Number 135, line 2.—“Here he sent his representatives with a synodical letter.”** St. Vitalian, following the example of his predecessors, Saints Martin and Eugenius, also devoted great care to the affairs of the emperor Constans.

Although Constans was an open supporter of Monothelism and was implicated in the anathema pronounced by the Holy See against the adherents of that sect, Vitalian nevertheless, immediately upon ascending the pontificate, sent him legates with a synodical letter according to custom. He did not act in this way toward the patriarch Peter, to whom, as a heretic, he wrote only a letter of exhortation in order to lead him to conversion.

Moreover, he received the same emperor in Rome with great honor, going out to meet him with the clergy, accepting the gifts he gave to the basilicas with expressions of gratitude, and omitting nothing that might bring him to fulfill the common hope of Catholics—namely, to bring him back to their side.

It was certain to everyone that the emperors had been made open and manifest enemies of the orthodox faith not by an inclination toward error, but by the impulse and instigation of the patriarchs of Constantinople. This indulgence of the Holy See toward the emperors, especially when the correction of the times had brought an increase of difficulties, gave rise to the great love with which Constantine Pogonatus, son and successor of Constans, embraced the Apostolic See, as we shall see.

**Line 7.—“Here he preserved the ecclesiastical rule and authority in every respect, as was customary.”** While the holy pontiff was granting their rights to those who appealed to the Holy See, he heard the complaints of John, bishop of Lappa in Crete, who had appealed to the Holy See from the judgment of Paul, archbishop, and his suffragans on that island.

It was found that the archbishop’s investigation and judgment departed from the rules of the Church. For, as the pontiff says in Letter 1 to Paul of Crete:

> “The same Bishop John was sent into custody … and, contrary to the commands of the canons, he was also urged to provide a surety. Then, according to the force of the canons, at the time when he requested permission to come to us, your fraternity ought to have released him by your letters. You not only refused canonically to release him for the thresholds of the Prince of the Apostles, but answered him indecently, saying: ‘Because you are not making a proper request.’”

Accordingly, after sharply rebuking the archbishop, the pope absolved the bishop who had appealed and whose innocence he had established. By an apostolic decree he annulled Paul’s sentence and restored John to his see. All these matters are plainly evident from the aforementioned letter:

> “What the holy Fathers have decreed—are these things indecent? Or do things pleasing to you seem decent? Therefore, having found the aforementioned Bishop John equally free from blame, we decree and confirm by the authority of this decision of ours that everything done and completed by you and your synod against the institutions of the canons and the decrees of the laws, as well as the sentence pronounced against him, is void and empty. Whatever is found to have been taken from him, let your Dilection cause to be restored to him, together with his Church, preserving him in every respect without loss … so that, just as the other bishops of your Dilection [act] with the fear of God for the benefits of their churches, so may he also …”

He made Vaanus, an administrator of the emperor on the island of Crete, and George of Syracuse, metropolitan in Sicily, participants in this matter, urging them to contribute their assistance toward restoring Bishop John to his see.

Concerning Oswiu, king of Northumbria in England, who had asked the Apostolic See to determine on what day holy Easter ought to be celebrated in that kingdom, together with the faith that had been restored there, Vitalian first commends the zeal with which he burned for the conversion of his subjects. Then, proceeding to the matter itself, he says:

> “It is fitting that your Highness, since you are a member of Christ, should constantly follow in all things the pious rule of the Prince of the Apostles, both in celebrating Easter and in all the matters handed down by the holy apostles Peter and Paul. For just as the two lights of heaven illuminate the world, so their teaching daily enlightens the hearts of believing men.”

(*Letter 5 to Oswiu*)

Later, as a controversy of this kind intensified in the same kingdom, it was decided that a gathering of ecclesiastics should be held [Col. 0790A] before the king, at which each party would present the reasons for its own custom. When they had assembled, the authority of Saint Peter was asserted on the one side: he had decreed that Easter should be celebrated on the first Sunday occurring after the fourteenth day of the moon in March—for Christ rose on one of those days. On the other side, a tradition was defended that had partly originated with the Apostle John, who always celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, and partly with certain Asians, who celebrated it on a Sunday even when that Sunday coincided with the fourteenth day of the moon. This was contrary to the custom of the Romans, who, so as not to celebrate Easter with the Jews when Sunday coincides with the fourteenth day of the moon, transfer it to the following Sunday.

Then, as champion of the Roman custom, he addressed his opponent:

> “I do not deny that those servants of God and beloved of God loved God with rustic simplicity but devout intention; nor did such failure to observe Easter greatly harm them so long as no one had appeared who could show them the decrees of a more perfect [Col. 0790B] discipline that they ought to follow. I certainly believe that, if a Catholic calculator had then come to them, they would have followed his instructions in the same way that they are proved to have followed the commandments of God which they knew and had learned. But you and your companions, if, after hearing the decrees of the apostolic see—indeed, of the universal Church—and these having been confirmed by the sacred writings, you refuse to follow them, you will perish without any doubt. For even if your fathers were holy, should their small number from one corner of a remote island be preferred to the universal Church of Christ, which exists throughout the world? And if your Columba—indeed, ours—was holy and powerful in miracles, if he belonged to Christ, could he be preferred to the most blessed Prince of the Apostles, to whom the Lord said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’?”  
> *(Synod of Pharensis, in Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, book III, chapter 25.)*

Hearing this, King Oswiu, who, as I have said, was present, turned to the Roman opponent and said:

> “‘Were these words truly spoken by the Lord to that Peter?’  
> “He replied: ‘Truly, O king.’  
> “The king said: ‘Can you produce anything of such power having been given by the Lord to your Columba?’  
> “He replied: ‘Nothing.’  
> “Again the king said: ‘If both of you agree without any dispute that these things were principally spoken to Peter, and that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to him by the Lord?’  
> “They answered: ‘Both of us do.’  
> “Then he concluded: ‘And I tell you that this is the doorkeeper whom I do not wish to contradict. Rather, insofar as I know or am able, I desire to obey his statutes in everything, lest, when I come to the gates of the kingdom of heaven, there be no one to open them, since the one who is shown to hold the keys has turned away from me.’”

When the king had said this, all the distinguished men sitting or standing there, together with the lesser persons, gave their approval; and, renouncing the less perfect discipline, they hastened to transfer themselves to what they had learned to be better. *(Ibid.)*

[Col. 0790D] For this reason I gladly bring forward here the prophecy of Isaiah that is read in Vitalian’s praised letter to Oswiu. I think it may be applied to blessed Peter and his successors, subordinated to Christ, whose vicars they are:

> “I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness, and have taken you by the hand, and preserved you; and I have given you as a light to the nations and as a covenant to the people, to open the eyes of the blind and to bring the bound man out of confinement, from the prison-house, him who sits in darkness” (Isaiah 42).

“See,” the pontiff continues, “most excellent son, how clearer than light it is that not only you, but also all the nations spoken of by the prophets are to believe in Christ, the creator of all.” *(Letter 5.)*

[Col. 0775]

### 135. Vitalian

Vitalian, by nationality from Signia, of the province of Campania, son of Anastasius, sat fourteen years and six months.

[Note: [Col. 0775] B, 5, less 4 days. See Baronius under the year of the Lord 655.]

He sent legates, together with the customary synodical letter, to the royal city and to the most devout rulers, announcing his ordination. When they had been received, they returned after renewing the privileges of the Church. Through these same envoys, the clemency of the rulers had sent to the blessed Apostle Peter golden Gospel-books adorned all around with white gems of remarkable size [Note: [Col. 0775] C, “of the rulers”; “adorned,” feminine]. He preserved the ecclesiastical rule and vigor in every respect, as was customary.

During his pontificate, Constantine Augustus came from the royal city by the coastal route to Athens, and from there to Tarentum, then to Beneventum and Naples, in the sixth indiction. Afterwards he came to Rome, that is, on the fifth day of July, a Wednesday, in the aforesaid indiction. The apostolic pontiff went out to meet him with his clergy at the sixth milestone from the city of Rome and received him.

On that same day the emperor went to Saint Peter, where he offered worship and a gift. On Saturday he went to Saint Mary and likewise offered a gift. On Sunday he proceeded to Saint Peter with his army. Everyone went out to meet him with candles, and he offered upon the altar a pallium woven with gold [Note: [Col. 0775] “a golden-woven pallium”]; Masses were celebrated.

Again, on Saturday, the emperor came to the Lateran, bathed, and performed the rite there in the Basilica of Julius [Note: [Col. 0775] C, “having gladly dined there”]. On Sunday there was likewise a station at Saint Peter. After Masses had been celebrated, the emperor and the pontiff took leave of one another. He remained in the Roman city for twelve days.

>[Col. 0777] |

### 136

He removed everything made of bronze that had served to adorn the city. He also stripped the church of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs, which had been covered with bronze tiles, and sent it to the royal city together with the various other things he had removed.

Afterwards, on Monday, he left the Roman city and returned to Naples. From there he proceeded by land to Rhegium [Note: [Col. 0777] “From there he proceeded by the Tyrrhenian Sea to Rhegium”], entering Sicily in the seventh indiction. He lived in the city of Syracuse and inflicted such suffering upon the people, inhabitants, and landowners of the provinces of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia—through written assessments, quotas, and naval levies over many years—as had never been known in the world. They were even separated from their wives, or children from their fathers [Note: [Col. 0777] “from their parents”], and endured many other unheard-of afflictions, so that no one retained any hope of life. They even took away the sacred vessels and treasures of the holy churches of God, leaving nothing behind.

Afterwards, on the fifteenth day of July, in the eleventh indiction, the aforesaid emperor was killed in a bath. Not long afterwards the aforementioned most holy man ended his life.

He carried out four ordinations: twenty-two priests, one deacon, and ninety-seven bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 0777] B, 18]. He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, and the episcopal see remained vacant for two months and thirteen days.

No. 137, line 9.—“And with God’s help he was killed, and Mezentius should not be named.” Mezentius should not be said or named because he seized the kingdom in Sicily through tyranny. The same applies to Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, who was deposed for heresy at the Sixth Synod in Trullo. Anastasius, in his account of Agatho, says: “And after these things he exhorted [them], and Macarius, who should not be named, by the holy synod.” The same applies to the Saracens. Anastasius, in his account of John V, says: “He made peace with the nation of the Saracens, which should not be named.” Likewise, in his account of Gregory II: “In the meantime Constantinople was besieged for two years by the Agarenes, who should not be named.” The same applies to the heretic Philippicus, in the same place: “by Philippicus, who should not be named.” Likewise, in his account of Stephen III: “According to what had been sent by the aforesaid Alstulphus, the tyrant, who should not be named.” Likewise, in his account of Leo III: “The wicked Paschal, the primicerius, who should not be named, came to meet him without a cloak.”]

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II: “For seven days water held Rome in its grip. Accordingly, litanies were frequently held by the lord pope.” At other times they were held as thanksgiving for peace. Anastasius, in his account of Zacharias: “And thus, by God’s favor, he returned with the palm of victory to this city of Rome. He gathered the whole people and addressed them, so that, to offer thanks to almighty God, they should all leave the church of the Mother of God, called ‘at the Martyrs,’ and proceed together with a general litany to the blessed Prince of the Apostles; and so it was done.” At other times they were held to obtain help against enemies. Anastasius, in his account of Stephen III: “This most blessed man decreed that, for the safety of the province and of all Christians, a litany should be held every Saturday, with every other occupation laid aside.”]
