[Note: [Col. 0794C]

### Chronological Notes

The ancient writers recount the acts of the pontiffs Adeodatus and Donus so sparingly that, had a few details not been supplied by Anastasius, I too could have regretted the lack of information about them, especially about Vitalian, their predecessor. Baronius, under the year 669, number 2, says: “We regret that both the writings and the acts of so great a pontiff have, for the most part, perished completely, buried in oblivion through the misfortune of the times.”

What is more regrettable is that, in the judgment of recent scholars, their periods seem to have been described less accurately by Anastasius. Hence, more than others, Papebrochius, Bacchinius, and Pagius each constructed a chronology according to his own judgment. Yet each of them, departing from Anastasius’s traces and supporting his opinion on no foundation other than conjecture, seems to have cast more darkness over this history than had previously covered it, as is evident from the errors detected in Pagius, who criticized the others.

In any case, Adeodatus, Vitalian’s successor, began to sit in the same year 672 in which Vitalian ceased to sit, as recent scholars acknowledge; and he sat for four years, two months, and five days, as I shall demonstrate more fully below. That Vitalian’s death cannot be placed before the aforesaid year is evident from the terms of office of his successors after Adeodatus—Donus and Agatho—which rest upon chronological indications that are nearly certain.

The election of Donus in particular would be confirmed as having taken place in the year 676 by the comet that appeared in the East in August, as Hermannus Contractus and Calvinus, among others, observe. But Antonius Pagius, under the year 677, number 9, together with Chiffletius, contends that it appeared in 677. They say that Bede refers it to that year in *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book IV, chapter 12, connecting it with the eighth year of Ecgfrith, king of the Northumbrians, although Bede discusses it under the year 688 in connection with the expulsion of Saint Wilfrid.

Whatever may be the truth concerning this scholarly controversy, and whether that comet appeared earlier or later, Vitalian’s year of death ought not to be postponed; rather, Anastasius’s statement “when he had been elected” must be interpreted more broadly.

Therefore, it appeared either in 676 or in the following year, 677. If in 676—which is made very probable by the severe weather that followed Adeodatus’s transition and by the other calamities reported by the authors—Vitalian’s year of death was 672. But if the comet appeared in 677, as the learned Chiffletius and Pagius, together with Bede, believe, then, lest the whole sequence of Anastasius collapse and conflict arise with the acts of the Sixth Synod, the entire period of Donus must be included in that reckoning.

Since this is so, we must first examine the very day of Vitalian’s death, then the ordination, pontificate, and death of Adeodatus; these confirm the foregoing against Baronius’s interpretation. For Baronius interprets Anastasius’s statement about Vitalian, following the killing of Constans—“Not long afterwards the aforementioned most holy man ended his life”—which is also related by Paul the Deacon in book V, chapter 11 of *The History of the Lombards*, and by John the Deacon in *The Archbishops of Naples*, number 33, as meaning that the pontiff died only a few months later. Thus, contrary to all the manuscripts and catalogues, he assigns seven years to Adeodatus, beginning his reckoning earlier because he understood the year 676 from another source to set a limit beyond which he could not go.

Above I explained two opinions concerning the six months added to the fourteen years assigned to Vitalian, both of which lead to Vitalian’s death. The first held that the months should be understood as incomplete months, although they were stated as a rounded number. Panvinus follows this opinion, saying that Vitalian sat from 30 July 657 to 27 January 672—fourteen years, five months, and twenty-nine days—which in fact results when the first and last days are included, as anyone who counts them can see.

The second opinion—that an ignorant hand had changed *iu Cal* into *ui Cal*—is not obscurely indicated as being defended by Bollandus. For, in his preliminary commentary on Saint Vitalian under 27 January, he states that the death of this holy pontiff on that day is recorded in many, though neither numerous nor very ancient, martyrologies.

Thus, if 29 January is taken instead of the twenty-seventh, it is clear that from 30 July 657 to 29 January 672 there are fourteen years and six complete months, including the days of ordination and death. Which of these opinions should be preferred is uncertain. The second is made more probable both by the inconsistency in determining the day of death—for Luitprand postpones it to 6 February—and by Anastasius’s new method of reckoning periods by rounded numbers.

After Vitalian’s death, according to Anastasius, the see remained vacant for two months and thirteen days; according to the first and third Colbertine catalogues, for two months and fourteen days. Accordingly, by measuring either the same period from 27 January—two months and fourteen days, excluding the first and last days—or from the twenty-ninth—two months and thirteen days, including the day of death—the day of Adeodatus’s ordination becomes evident: 11 April of the aforesaid year 672, as the Sunday letter C makes clear.

That one should not depart at will from whichever interval between pontificates is found in the manuscripts and catalogues is shown sufficiently by Antonius Pagius’s own example of error, under the years 669, number 4, and 676, number 2. For, mistakenly believing that 22 April 672 fell on a Sunday, although it was a Thursday, he insists that it must be assigned to Adeodatus’s ordination and adds twelve days to the vacancy of the see. This addition drew him into further and further chronological errors, as we shall see.

I mention this opportunely so that complete confidence may not be placed in a man of such great learning in every matter. For Pagius the younger, who preferred to reckon by blood relationship rather than by the calendar cycle, also fell into error, as will become clear below in his notes. Therefore, if we do not wish, with the Pagii, to place the pontiff’s ordination on a Thursday, or to become entangled in other errors, we must not depart from the manuscripts and catalogues of Anastasius unless evident reason or some document persuades us that this should be done.

Accordingly, this pontiff was ordained on 11 April 672 and governed the Church no longer than until 17 June 676, as all the manuscripts and catalogues, and the most authoritative writers cited by Pagius, teach. They consistently assign to Adeodatus four years, two months, and five days.

It follows that the day of burial indicated by Anastasius, 26 June, must be distinguished from the day of death, so that 26 June was the transfer of the pontiff from the Lateran Church—where he must have been laid immediately after his death—to Saint Peter. This is suggested by the interval between pontificates after Adeodatus’s death, which is reckoned from the aforesaid day of death, not from his burial at Saint Peter.

This is certainly neither new nor unheard-of. We saw above, in the case of Sabinianus, on page 13, that the same thing was done when the corpse could not be carried out because of bad weather. Moreover, Anastasius himself shows that this happened here. He says:

> “After his passing there were such great rains and thunderclaps as no human age remembers, so that even men and cattle perished from lightning. And unless the Lord had been appeased by the litanies that were held daily, people would not have been able to thresh,” etc.

Then, after adding much else, he says:

> “He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.”

It is as though he were saying that, because of the frequency of the rains, the clergy could not take the opportunity to carry out the corpse before that day. This is made probable for those living in Rome by the long road separating the two basilicas from one another.]

[Note: [Col. 0796B]

No. 137, line 1.—Adeodatus. An Italian by nationality, son of Jovinianus, a Roman by origin, formerly a monk of Saint Erasmus on Mount Caelius of the Order of Saint Benedict; under the emperor Flavius Heraclius Constantinus Augustus, he sat for four years, five months, and sixteen days, and was consecrated on the third day before the Ides, a Sunday.

No. 138, line 5.—“Such great rains and thunderclaps.” A comet, which the Greeks call *cometen* (“comet”), announced many evils impending at that time; it appeared for three continuous months, together with great rains and frequent thunderclaps.]

[Note: [Col. 0796B]

No. 137, line 1.—Adeodatus, a Roman by nationality. That Adeodatus, a Roman by nationality and son of Jovinianus, was ordained Roman pontiff from the monastic state in the same year, 672, and indeed on 22 April, a Sunday, after the pontifical see had remained vacant not for two months and thirteen days, as it is read in Anastasius through the error of the copyists, but for two months and twenty-five days, can be demonstrated from Anastasius himself.

For he adds that Adeodatus sat for four years, two months, and five days, and died or was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, that is, on 26 June. If from that day in the year 676, when he died, one counts backward four years, two months, and five days, one reaches 22 April 672, on which day he was therefore ordained according to Anastasius. Consequently, Anastasius could not have written that the see had been vacant for two months and thirteen days after Vitalian’s death, since he himself asserts that Vitalian died on 27 January.

Of the deeds of this pontiff nothing survives except a diploma by which he confirms the privilege that Crotbertus, bishop of Tours, had granted to the monastery of Saint Martin. Its entire substance is that the bishop of Tours, in whose diocese the monastery of Saint Martin is situated, should have no authority over it except to confer holy orders upon the monks and grant the sacred Chrism.

John Launoy, in his *Assertion of the Inquiry into the Privilege of Saint-Médard*, mentioned in the account of Pope Gregory, attacked this document with twelve arguments. But Radulphus Monsnyerus, in his book *On the Rights of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours*, showed that these arguments were vain and futile; and Charles Cointius, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* under the year 676, where he weighs and compares the arguments of both men, rightly concludes that nothing occurs in that privilege contrary to the form of the privilege presented by Marculfus in book I, chapter 1. Launoy therefore wrongly believed it to be spurious and surreptitious.

[Col. 0797A] Anastasius states in his account of Adeodatus that this pontiff sat for four years, two months, and five days. The same is read in two manuscript copies of Anastasius, the Colbertines, as well as in Luitprand, Orderic in book II, Regino, Hermannus Contractus, the Vatican-Palatine catalogue, and others. He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 26 June. From these facts we have deduced that he was ordained on 22 April 672 and died on 26 June 676, as is clear to anyone who counts.]

[Note: [Col. 0798A]

No. 138, line 5.—“After his passing there were such [Col. 0797] great rains.” Paul the Deacon also recalls this violent storm in book V, chapter 15 of *The History of the Lombards*:

> “At that time,” he says, “there were such great rains and such great thunderclaps as no human being had ever remembered before; so that countless thousands of men and animals were killed by lightning. In that year, the legumes that could not be gathered because of the rains sprouted again and were brought all the way to maturity.”]

[Col. 0791]

### 137. Adeodatus

Adeodatus, a Roman by nationality, from the monks, son of Jobinianus [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “Jovinianus”], sat for four years, two months, and five days [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “seven years, two months, and seventeen days”].

He was of such great stature [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “of such great magnitude”], and so gentle and kind, that he willingly received every person, from the greatest to the least. He showed compassion to strangers [Note: [Col. 0791] “he showed compassion”], so that each person obtained without doubt whatever he requested [Note: [Col. 0791] “might obtain”].

He also increased the *roga* for everyone.

During his pontificate, Mezzetius [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “Mezentius”], who was in Sicily with the eastern army, acted as a tyrant [the text has *intartizavit*; Note: [Col. 0791] B, “tyrannized”] and seized the kingdom. The army of Italy then proceeded through different parts of Istria; others through parts of Campania; and still others through parts of Sardinia and Africa. In the same way they came through [Note: [Col. 0791] “into”] Sicily, to the city of Syracuse. With God’s help he was killed, and Mezzetius should not be named [Note: [Col. 0791] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 668]. Many of his judges were mutilated and brought to Constantinople, together with the head of that same usurper.

Afterwards the Saracens came into Sicily, took the aforesaid city, and inflicted great slaughter upon the people [Note: [Col. 0791] “Only a few of the people escaped, having fled to very strongly fortified camps and to the mountain ridges. They also carried away enormous booty and all the bronze ornament, together with objects of various kinds, which Constantine had brought from Rome by ship”]. They likewise took enormous booty and, carrying away the bronze that had been transported there from the city of Rome, returned to Alexandria.

### 138

He appropriately restored and dedicated the church of Blessed Peter, which is on the Portuensian Way beside the field of Merulus. He also enlarged with many new buildings the monastery of Saint Erasmus situated on Mount Caelius, in which the aforementioned most holy man seemed to have grown up [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “to have assembled”]. He also acquired estates [Note: [Col. 0791] “and acquired many estates there”] and, during his lifetime, established an abbot or community there.

After his passing there were such great rains and thunderclaps as no human age remembers, so that even men and cattle perished from lightning. And unless the Lord had been appeased by the litanies that were held daily, people could not have threshed or stored grain in the granaries.

These evils increased so greatly that, because of the rains themselves, legumes sprouted again and reached maturity; on this account the people were amazed. He carried out one ordination in the month of December: fourteen priests, two deacons, and forty-six bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “forty-three”].

He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, and the episcopal see remained vacant for four months and fifteen days [Note: [Col. 0791] B, “six months”].

From the time of the ordination of Saint Pope Gregory up to this point there are ninety-five years, five months, and fourteen days.

## LXXX. DONUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 676; IN THE NINTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE POGONATUS

[Note: [Col. 0797B]

### From the Vallicellian manuscript

No. 139, line 2: “above Saint Peter the Apostle,” etc., as in Reg., Maz., and Thuan.; with these, lines 3, 5, 7, and 17 also agree. Line 8: “he divided, and established monks in the monastery already mentioned” [read: “and now established monks in the monastery,” etc.], as in the cited manuscripts. Line 10: “having separated the autocephalous [monks], he subjected himself again to the former apostolic see” [read: “the autocephalous [Church] again subjected itself to its former see”]. Line 12: “While this pope was elected, during the month of August.” Line 14: “they penetrated the heavens.” “At the sight of this, all the people, rising, wondered what it could be.” After this apparition, etc., as in the said manuscripts.

### In V. L. Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript

Line 18: “on the third day before the Ides.” B, “the third day before the Kalends of April.”

### From the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuani manuscripts

Line 1: “he sat for two years.” Line 2: “above Saint Peter,” [Col. 0797C] “which is called Paradise, and is…” Line 3: “with white and large marble stones, magnificently constructed.” Line 5: “Likewise the church of Saint Euphemia.” Line 7: “in the Boetian monastery.” Line 8: “he divided them and established Roman monks in the monastery.” Line 10: “having separated the autocephalous [Church].” Line 12: “While this pope was elected…” Line 14: “rising, all the people wondered what it could be.” After that apparition, a great mortality followed in the eastern region. He carried out one ordination. Line 17: “six places.”

### From another Thuani manuscript

Line 5: “whom he divided among various places.” Line 14: “penetrated the heavens.” In the same line: “rising.” Line 15: “on account of which there was a great mortality.”

### In Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript

Line 1: “Conus.” Line 3: “but the church.” Line 6: “namely the clergy, various…” In the same line: “he found.” Line 9: “of Ravenna.” Line 12: [Col. 0798C] “during the month of August.”]

[Note: [Col. 0797C]

Line 6.—“He found in the city of Rome, in the monastery called Boetianum…” Nestorian Syrian monks. He divided them among various monasteries. Monks who have fallen into heresy are transferred, as a penance, to stricter monasteries: canon *Si episcopus*, distinction 50; canon *De lapsis*, question 16. The same penalty applies to clerics. Anastasius, in his account of Leo II, says:

> “Nevertheless, since the defenders of the evils of heresy mentioned above were unwilling to depart from their purpose, they were confined in various monasteries.”

Line 9.—“During his time the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church on account of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former apostolic see.” Reparatus, archbishop of Ravenna, subjected himself to the apostolic see. Before him the archbishops of Ravenna had become so arrogant, relying on the privilege of Constans Caesar, that they themselves consecrated the bishops subject to them and were consecrated by three bishops under their authority, without seeking any confirmation from the Roman pontiff. On this matter see Hieronymus Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, book IV, under the year 648.

Line 12.—“A star appeared in the East, from cockcrow until morning, for three months.” Cockcrow means midnight. Anastasius, in his account of Leo II, says: “And only after cockcrow did it gradually begin to clear.”

Line 15.—“On account of which matter.” Here *capitulum* means a thing or cause, because a cause is the head of a matter. Anastasius, in his account of Zacharias, says: “And other matters which he had promised.” At other times *capitulum* means a question concerning a definite matter. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II, says: “Questioned about certain matters, he resolved each question with an excellent answer.”

Sometimes *capitulum* means an article of litigation, as in the penultimate law, paragraph 1, title *On Things Lent and Oaths*: “Let the case or article be decided”; and in the paragraph “Those Present” of the same law: “By other matters or articles, or parts of the litigation.” The head is the summary of every matter. Plautus, in *The Ass*: “Today I was the head of finding this silver.” Hence the diminutive *capitulum*.

*Capitulum* is also used of a slave. Slaves do not have a head, that is, status or personhood; but they are said to have a *capitulum*, as though they were lesser in head or diminished in head. Plautus, in *The Ass*: “Today I shall write that you have satisfied this little head for the injury.” The same author, in *The Curculio*: “When they have stolen something, they drink hot wine with their little heads covered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0799C]

Line 12.—“While he was elected, during the month of August, a star appeared in the East, from cockcrow until morning, for three months, whose rays penetrated the heavens … and afterwards, turning back upon itself, it disappeared.”

Anastasius calls this a star, but Bede, in book IV, chapter 11 of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, calls the star that appeared during Donus’s pontificate by its proper name, a comet:

> “In the year,” he says, “of the Lord’s Incarnation 678, which was the eighth year of King Ecgfrith’s reign, a star appeared in the month of August, which is called a comet. It remained for three months and rose during the morning hours, displaying before itself a lofty column of radiant flame.”

This comet began to appear in August. It was seen in the region of the sky facing east. It rose approximately three hours before sunrise. At sunrise it disappeared, the sun’s rays intercepting it from view. Its rays, penetrating the region of the sky, presented the appearance of a tail, or beam, or column. After three months the comet disappeared.

It is sufficiently remarkable that Anastasius recorded all these circumstances in such an unfavorable age, when the study of the sciences had declined into a worse condition, and in view of the purpose of an ecclesiastical historian, whose task does not include attending to astronomical subtleties.

Nevertheless, these details are not enough for an astronomer who wished to reduce the phenomena of that comet to exact calculations. He would need more information: namely, the point in the sky at which the comet was situated when it first appeared; its longitude and latitude; the path along which it traveled; and the speed at which it moved.

The earlier appearance of a comet after the Christian era is not recorded by Sir Isaac Newton in Book III, Proposition IX of the *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*: that appearance was observed in 1101 or 1106, “whose star was small and dim (like that of 1680), but the radiance that issued from it was very bright and extended eastward and northward like a huge beam,” as Hevelius reports from Simeon of Durham, the monk. In 1337 Nicephorus Gregoras, historian and astronomer of Constantinople, reports another comet, whose path among the fixed stars he describes fairly accurately, as Edmund Halley notes in his *Cometography*; but he records the circumstances of time in such a way that they cannot be subjected to astronomical calculation. In 1472 Regiomontanus observed another comet, terrifying in its size and coma, which was observed to traverse forty degrees of the great circle within one day; and, as Halley likewise observes, it was the first comet whose particular details sufficient for calculation have reached us. In 1577, when Tycho observed the heavens with instruments most ingeniously devised for that purpose, the comet presented itself to his eyes; and he was able to bind it so closely to astronomical laws that already then astronomers began to hope that comets could be philosophized about in the same way as planets. This was finally accomplished by that eminent geometer and philosopher, the knight Sir Isaac Newton, in 1680, when that prodigious comet fell from the heavens toward the sun almost perpendicularly. Seen for four complete months, it was exceptionally suitable for establishing the theory, position, orbit, and motion of comets.

I judge that historians have recorded the appearances of comets rarely and less exactly because of the prejudice of philosophers, led by Aristotle, who thought that these were fires accidentally kindled in the sublunary region and that it was not worthwhile to commit to writing the paths of such vapors wandering through the air. But after the industry of modern astronomers, aided by instruments constructed for this purpose—especially the longer optical tube—discovered that comets were not sudden fires, as Seneca had already said (*Natural Questions* VII.22), but belonged among the eternal works of nature, namely, that they were planets in equal number, which describe, depart along, and return upon their elliptical—or, if one prefers, parabolic—orbits around the sun, one of the foci being the sun, at fixed intervals, no comet now appears in the heavens without finding an observer prepared for it and wholly intent on noting accurately everything that contributes to a complete theory of it.

The first to formulate this hypothesis was Giovanni Domenico Cassini, beginning in 1666. Reflecting that two different comets could not have these three conditions in common—(1) the same nodes, (2) the same inclination of their orbit to the ecliptic, and (3) the same velocity at their perihelia—and observing from a comparison of observations of several comets that these three conditions sometimes occurred perfectly in two comets, he judged that they were not two comets but one and the same comet returning to us after completing its orbit. Hence Halley easily believed that the comet he himself observed in 1682 was the same one observed by Kepler in 1607, by Peter Apian in 1531, and, in the preceding century, in the summer of 1456; and that it would appear again in 1758, since its revolution is completed within a period of seventy-five years.

Cassini likewise compared the comet observed in 1702 with the one he himself had observed in 1668 and judged that they were the same, as was also the comet seen in 1566, in 1362, and in 410, as well as the comet reported in the year 70 by Flavius Josephus, *The Jewish War* VII.12. It was also the comet Aristotle saw in 373 before the Christian era, projecting its tail toward the sun like a beam. Thus, from the year in which Aristotle saw it—a year not difficult to establish because several chronological indicators coincide—to 1668, it had completed its orbit sixty times, by dividing the 2,040 years between Aristotle’s observation and Cassini’s observation by 34.

By this calculation Cassini judges that he has sufficient grounds for affirming that the period of this comet’s revolution does not exceed thirty-four years, though not for denying that it may be shorter than that interval; for if its period is assumed to be half that, or even half of that half, the calculation still holds. Although this interval, reduced to shorter limits, is nevertheless not sufficient for observing the comet’s return more exactly—because its appearance is usually invisible owing to its excessive proximity to the sun, as happens with Mercury, which completes its orbit within eighty-eight days but is nevertheless seen only once every thirty-three years—if the comet appears again in 1736, Cassini’s hypothesis will be strengthened by the firmest conjecture. See Cassini’s report submitted to the Paris Academy of Sciences concerning the year 1702.

Now, if, going backward as far as the time of Pope Donus, I apply the stated Cassinian interval of thirty-four years, or seventeen, or eight and a half, to the elapsed periods, beginning from the year 1702, I shall find that the comet’s appearance in Donus’s time occurred in the year 674 after the birth of Christ, according to the common era. If this reasoning were certain, then the various records of the comet that appeared under Donus would all be fixed to the same year, 674: that of Funccius to 673, those of Alsted to 674 and 675, that of Calvisius to 676, that of Rockenbach to 677, and that of Bede to 678. These records are cited by Stanislaus Lubieniecki in the second part of his *Theatrum Cometarum*, no. 146. Chronologists would then also have a new method for calculating dates from cometary records and for assigning them, with sufficiently probable evidence, to those historical events.

## Notes

### Column 0801B, line 2 — “Here he built an atrium”

These words are taken from Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 31:

> “In those days Pope Donus wonderfully paved with white and large marble the place of the Roman Church called Paradise, in front of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.”

### Column 0801B, line 9 — “The Church of the Ravennans”

After the rise of the Monothelite heresy, on account of which the Churches of the East and West came into conflict with one another, the bishop of Ravenna began to assert himself. Relying on the power of the exarchs—who, in the name of the Greek emperors, governed the provinces still remaining in Italy after the Lombard invasion—he sought to claim autocephaly, and, once he had seized it, defended it stubbornly against the statutes and examples of his predecessors.

Many letters addressed to Martinian of Ravenna survive in the books of Gregory the Great. From them it is perfectly clear that the see of Ravenna was entirely subject to the Roman Church: it sought confirmation from Rome of the decree issued concerning episcopal elections; it received the pallium from Rome; and it received from Rome the rule concerning the days on which it might use it.

Saint Peter Chrysologus had clearly shown this subjection in his letter to Eutyches, where he writes that he considers it impious to reply on anything in the disputed matter without consulting the apostolic see. John III likewise wrote to the bishop of Ravenna, in Baluze’s fifth volume of *Miscellanea*:

> “We know that it accords with reason that we adorn with the pallium those whom, through the divinely inspired mercy of God, the honor of the priesthood illuminates in those cities in which it is also established that the pontiffs who held office in former times were granted this privilege by the apostolic see. Therefore, by our present authority, we grant to Your Charity the use of the pallium, as your predecessors are known to have possessed it; and we wish all those matters concerning the privilege of your honor to remain in force which, as is established, were preserved for your Church in earlier times, so that you may in no way grieve that any of its privileges have been diminished.”

John, who governed the Church of Ravenna in the time of Gregory the Great, likewise wrote frankly to the pontiff about this same subjection and about the privileges received from the apostolic see. His letter is found in Book II, no. 55:

> “Because, for greater satisfaction, I have placed in the venerable archives all the privileges granted to the holy Church of Ravenna by your predecessors, arranged according to the times of the consecrations of my predecessors, and have nevertheless found them authentic, it is now in the power of God and of Your Holiness to order whatever, once the truth is known, you may command to be done. For, desiring to obey the commands of my lord the apostle, although ancient custom prevails, I have taken care to abstain until a second command.”

Among the concessions of earlier pontiffs this bishop had produced a letter of John III. The holy pontiff replies concerning it in the same place, letter 54:

> “And that you know this custom of the universal Church well, you have made most clearly known to us in your letters, in which you transmitted to us the decree of our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope John, together with the documents submitted to us, containing all the customs granted to you and to your Church by the privilege of our predecessors, which ought to be preserved.”

Accordingly, the emperor Constans, in order to bring into the West as well the schism and heresy then spreading widely through the Eastern Church, granted autocephaly to the bishop of Ravenna. In the chronological account of the pontificate of Vitalian, we stated that this occurred in the year 665. Maurus, bishop of Ravenna, had extorted this privilege from Constans, who was an author of the schism and of the disputes that arose between the two Churches of the West concerning the right of autocephaly.

The emperor had written to Maurus concerning this privilege as follows:

> “But now also, for the greater cheerfulness of his mind, we decree by this present pious command of ours that it remain more secure and free from every superior episcopal condition, and that it devote itself solely to prayer for the purpose of imploring our imperial power; and that it in no way be subject to the patriarch of the ancient city of Rome, but remain *autokephalēn* [αὐτοκεφαλήν], ‘autocephalous.’”

At the end it bears a characteristic mark showing that the document was issued in 665 or 666. Meanwhile, as the schism grew stronger, Pope Vitalian displayed the vigor of the apostolic see and resisted the schismatic bishop. Agnellus, himself a schismatic, writes the following in the *Life of Maurus*, p. 143:

> “He had many troubles with the Roman pontiff, many conflicts, many disturbances, and many disputes. Many times he reached Constantinople so that he might turn his Church away from the yoke and jurisdiction of the Romans. And it was done: the Church of Ravenna was withdrawn, so that thereafter its pontiffs would never go to Rome for consecration. The future pastor of the Church of Ravenna would have no other government over him, nor would he ever be under the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff; rather, they would consecrate his elect by three of his own bishops, and the pallium would be brought from the emperor of Constantinople.”

This, then, was the autocephaly of Ravenna. Pope Donus therefore brought it about that the bishop of Ravenna returned to his former subjection, that the schism was quieted, and that peace among the Italian clergy revived.

### Column 0802C, line 11 — “Reparatus”

He was elected by imperial privilege and, under the pretext of autocephaly, consecrated by his own bishops without apostolic approval. Agnellus says this in his *Life of Reparatus*, chapter 1, p. 148:

> “He was ordained bishop of Ravenna by three of his suffragans, just as the Roman pontiff is accustomed to be consecrated.”

Nevertheless, Reparatus issued a decree, concerning which Agnellus writes in the same place:

> “And he decreed that, at the time of consecration, the one elected at Rome should return to Rome within no more than eight days.”

Thus the bishops of Ravenna were thereafter compelled to return to their former obedience toward the Roman see.

### Column 0802C, line 12 — “While he was elected”

Anastasius copied this from Paul the Deacon, as we noted above. But since the events occurred in 671, as is evident from the order of the narrative both in Paul and in the author of the *Miscella*, while Donus was not elected before 676, these fragments of the record must be referred to Vitalian and assigned to the year 671, in accordance with the chronological arrangement established above.

### Column 0802D, line 1 — “Donus”

Some call him Domnus, others Domnion, and others Conus or Cunon. He was made Roman pontiff in 676, on the Kalends of November themselves.

## Chronological Notes

After the death of Pope Adeodatus, which I have shown must be assigned to 17 June 676, the see was vacant for four months and fifteen days. Thus all manuscripts and catalogues agree unanimously, except the fifth Colbertine catalogue, which has four months and five days. Disregarding its isolated authority, therefore, I see that Donus was ordained on 2 November of the same year, 676; the Sunday-letter of that year, E, demonstrates that this date agrees with the ordination.

The interregnum must be counted from the aforementioned day of Adeodatus’s death, 17 June, not from his deposition on the 26th. Onuphrius and Pagius clearly show this by doing otherwise. Onuphrius lengthened Adeodatus’s tenure by eleven days and subtracted nine days from the interregnum, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts and catalogues.

Pagius, therefore, departing from the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts, catalogues, and authors, follows one Colbertine catalogue. Recognizing perhaps that it was corrupt, although it agrees with the others in determining the lengths of the pontificates of Vitalian and Adeodatus, he understood it to suffer from a gap of ten days; he nevertheless wrongly joins it to the second Colbertine catalogue, which has no vacancy of the see at all.

Then, following that guide, he proceeds to Donus’s ordination by two months and five days. Although he omits the day of the deposition, he nevertheless does not derive the date from the Colbertine before the Kalends of November. Thus, contrary to the universally accepted custom of the Church—a custom of which he was otherwise its greatest defender and champion—he supposes that the Roman pontiff was ordained on a Saturday. Acknowledging that he has handed down a difficult matter, he nevertheless defends his earlier error in another lapse, scarcely tolerable in Baronian criticism:

> “Donus,” he says (*676 and 678*, no. 2), “was consecrated Roman pontiff on the first day of November, the feast of All Saints.”

Today everyone knows that this feast is celebrated on the Kalends of November. But who does not know that the dedication of Saint Mary at the Martyrs was carried out by Boniface IV in the month of May, and that the martyrologies therefore read, on 13 May: “The Nativity, or Dedication, of Saint Mary at the Martyrs”? Indeed, Pagius himself had admitted under the year 607, no. 3, that he had seen this in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, Rotger, and the Roman Martyrology.

He could have learned from another martyrology that the transfer of this feast to the Kalends of November was made in the ninth century by Gregory IV. This is stated in the martyrology of the abbot Francesco Maurolico, which recounts the history fully in these words:

> “On the Kalends of November, the feast of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of all the holy martyrs, which Pope Boniface instituted as a solemn and universal feast to be celebrated every year, so that the Pantheon—the temple that Marcus Agrippa had dedicated to Jupiter and all the gods—might rightly be designated by Christians for the Savior and all the saints, after it had been obtained from the emperor Phocas. Pope Gregory IV later transferred this solemnity to the Kalends of November.”

I mention in passing that other learned men were similarly deceived, among them the illustrious Archbishop of Caesarea, Claude Sommier, as may be seen above. I could easily have removed his error when translating that passage of his *Dogmatic-Pontifical History* into Latin; but since the same celebrated work circulates among scholars in French, I decided that nothing should be changed.

Returning, therefore, to the point from which I digressed, I assert against Pagius’s opinion that Donus was ordained on 2 November 676. After the interregnum had elapsed from Adeodatus’s death on 17 June of the same year, that is the date reached. Baronius and all more recent writers are right to hold that Donus’s pontificate began in that year.

The matter is otherwise concerning the length of his tenure. The manuscripts and authors disagree by one full year: some assign him one year, others two, while there is no disagreement concerning the months and days. Following the example of Panvinius, I maintain that Donus held the see for two years, five months, and ten days, so that his tenure extended from 2 November 676 to 11 April 679, the date assigned by Anastasius to his burial. I rely on the authority of the Royal, Mazarin, first Thuane, and third Ambrosian manuscripts.

I see two reasons that compelled more recent writers to follow manuscripts assigning one year: the absolution of Wilfrid of York at the Roman council, and the beginning of that council, which gives the month of October, indiction VII. These certainly indicate the year 678. I shall resolve these difficulties more appropriately in the discussion of Agatho, so that I will not be compelled, as they were, to add a complete year extracted from the acts of the sixth council to Agatho’s tenure from his own records.

But the imperial letter of Constantine to Donus, as the emperor himself testifies in his sacred letter to Gregory, patriarch of Constantinople, had been given while Donus was still alive. The emperor continues that, when Donus departed this world, the holy Agatho, recently elected pope, received it and sent legates there, and so forth.

Although we read that Donus, who survived the imperial letter by eight complete months, accomplished nothing—whether because he was hindered by illness, or because it was conveyed late to Rome by Epiphanius, the secretary, through whom Anastasius says it was sent to his predecessor Pope Donus in the Life of Agatho—it is nevertheless easier to believe that Rome heard nothing about the imperial letter for eight complete months than that Constantinople heard nothing for four full months, from Donus’s death on 11 April until the imperial letter was issued on 10 August, either about Donus’s death or Agatho’s election.

For from Anastasius himself we know that elections were sometimes held in a much shorter interregnum; that an imperial command was requested from Constantinople, before authority had been granted to the exarch; that the command was brought to Rome; and finally that the pontiffs were ordained. What negligence, then, on the part of the exarch Theodore! Why did he not send to the most pious emperor, who had served the apostolic see so well, news of the deceased pontiff and the consecrated successor during at least the forty-five days that intervened between Agatho’s ordination and the issuance of the imperial letter? But I shall discuss these matters more suitably below.

### Column 0804C, line 1 — “Donus”

Donus, also called Domnus, son of Mauricius, a Roman, held the see for two years, five months, and ten days, under the emperor Flavius Constantine V Augustus Pogonatus. He was consecrated on Sunday, the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the year 676.

### Column 0804C, line 2 — “The atrium of the blessed apostle Peter”

Pope Donus, concerned for honor and divine worship, built the vestibule of Saint Peter, called Paradise, as a four-sided portico of marble. According to Platina, the marble was taken from the pyramid that stood in the Vatican opposite Hadrian’s Mausoleum. See Paul the Deacon, Book III of the *History of the Lombards*.

During the pontificate of Pope Donus, Dagobert, the eighteenth king of the Franks, died. His soul was seen by demons to be carried to the island of Lipara, where there is a fiery abyss, to be purified; but immediately it was rescued from the hands of the spirits through the assistance of Saints Dionysius, Martin, and Mauricius. For during his life the king had always honored them as patrons and had made them more honored in their churches. The authorities are Platina in the *Life of Pope Donus*, Robert Gaguin, Book III of the *Life of Dagobert*, and the abbot Boniface Simoneta.

### Column 0804D, line 9 — “In his time, the Church of the Ravennans”

Maurus, archbishop of Ravenna, had acknowledged his Church’s subjection to the Roman Church at the beginning of his episcopate. For, when Saint Martin was presiding at the Lateran Council summoned to deal with the Monothelite heresy, he was present through Maurus of Cesena, bishop, and Deusdedit, a Ravennate presbyter.

But after the impious Constans had sacrilegiously attacked the holy pontiff Martin, Maurus seized the opportunity created by the emperor’s hatred of the Roman Church, which arose because the Church had condemned his heretical *typos*, in order to exempt his own Church from obedience to the Roman see. Thus, in the time of Pope Vitalian, Maurus, inflated by the pride inherent in his character, obtained—at the destruction of himself and his followers—a privilege by which Constans, lacking ecclesiastical authority, wickedly removed the Church of Ravenna from the power of the Roman see.

The emperor says to Maurus in the diploma, or “decree,” as it was called, which the distinguished Bacchinius published from the Este manuscript in the *Life of Maurus* in Agnellus’s *Pontifical Book*:

> “We decree that it remain more secure and free from every superior episcopal condition, and that it devote itself solely to prayer for the purpose of imploring our imperial power; and that it in no way be subject to the patriarch of the ancient city of Rome, but remain *autoképhalē* [αὐτοκέφαλην], ‘autocephalous,’ and that its holy Church after him remain so.”

From these words it is easy to understand what Maurus, resisting secular power, obtained—both wickedly and futilely. He secured exemption not from the right of primacy by which the pontiff presides over the entire Church, but from patriarchal jurisdiction. As soon as Vitalian understood that Maurus was withdrawing himself from that jurisdiction, he called him back to obedience with the sword of anathema.

But this obstinate man dared, in a horrible crime, to pronounce anathema against the pontiff himself. Agnellus, a writer strongly attached to the schismatic party, reports this in the *Life of Maurus*.

Bacchinius, praised for his account, shows from Agnellus’s own testimony that Maurus’s successor Reparatus cleared the Church of Ravenna from the disgrace of this schism toward the end of his life. Agnellus, however, wishing to extend the thread of his narrative a little farther, asserts that Reparatus did not subject himself to the Roman see.

Sigonius, Rubeus, and others agree with Agnellus’s testimony. They additionally suppose that Reparatus went to Constantine, son of Constans, and obtained for himself and his Church the same autocephaly that Maurus had obtained from Constantine’s father.

But Bacchinius, cited above, overturns their opinion by Agnellus’s own testimony. He observes that the privilege obtained from Constantine was a very extensive immunity both from taxes and from the lay court, granted to the bishop and clergy of the Church of Ravenna; among them a *staurophoros*, that is, a “cross-bearer,” is expressly named. It was not, however, a privilege of autocephaly, or exemption from the patriarchal jurisdiction of the Roman see over the Church of Ravenna.

This is especially clear since Sigonius writes under the year 669, in his *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, that Constantine, deterred by his father’s example, by his life, and by the circumstances of his death, was a most ardent supporter of the Roman Church. How could Constantine be regarded as the Roman Church’s most ardent supporter if, by renewing the decree of autocephaly, he had confirmed the Church of Ravenna in schism, torn away from its head? But I shall speak further of the autocephaly of the bishops of Ravenna in the discussion of Agatho’s successor, Saint Leo II.

### Column 0806A, line 2 — “Here he built the upper atrium of the blessed apostle Peter”

Paul the Deacon preserved the memory of this benefaction for us in Book V of *The Deeds of the Lombards*:

> “In those days Pope Donus wonderfully paved with white and large marble the place of the Roman Church called Paradise, in front of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.”

Anastasius further reports that Donus restored and dedicated the churches of the apostles on the Ostian Way and the Church of Saint Euphemia on the Appian Way. I do not know, however, whether this Church of Saint Euphemia is the same one that Oldoinus, I do not know on what authority, says was built by Pope Adeodatus, Donus’s predecessor, at the foot of the Esquiline Hill; it had already been weakened by age when Sixtus V leveled it to the ground for the adornment of the city.

Finally, Donus found in the city of Rome, in the monastery called Boetianum, Syrian Nestorian monks. According to the same Anastasius, he divided them among various monasteries, assigning them to penance and entrusting the Boetian monastery to Roman monks. He held one ordination, consisting of ten presbyters and five deacons; he ordained six bishops in various places.

### Column 0806B, line 9 — “In his time, the Church of the Ravennans”

When Maurus, the bishop of Ravenna whom we discussed under Vitalian, died outside the communion of the Church, as Rubeus writes in Book IV of his *History of Ravenna*, Reparatus was appointed in his place. He too, resisting the apostolic see, attempted to accomplish through an imperial rescript that the Church of Ravenna should not be subject to Rome.

At the end of his life, however, he repented of what he had done, subjected himself to Pope Donus, and died under him, according to Anastasius. The successor of Reparatus was Theodore, exceptionally obedient to the Roman Church. He is also found to have attended the Roman synod under Agatho; indeed, Anastasius under Agatho testifies that he came to Rome for no other reason than to subject himself to the pontiff.

Later, however, Felix, likewise bishop of Ravenna, separated himself from obedience to the Roman pontiff by schism under Pope Constantine; the outcome of that affair will be stated in its proper place.

## 139. Donus

Donus, a Roman by nationality, son of Mauricius, held the see for one year, five months, and ten days. He built the upper atrium of the blessed apostle Peter, which is called Paradise, in front of the church, as a four-sided portico paved with large marble slabs. He also restored and appropriately dedicated the Church of the Apostles on the Ostian Way. Likewise, he dedicated the Church of Saint Euphemia on the Appian Way.

He increased the clergy in various orders and honors. In the city of Rome, in the monastery called Boetianum, he found Nestorian Syrian monks, whom he distributed among various monasteries—[B.,] namely, for penance. In that monastery he established Roman monks.

During his pontificate, the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church on account of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former apostolic see. The bishop of that Church, named Reparatus, immediately died, as it pleased God. [See Baronius under the year 678.]

While he was elected, in the month of August, a star appeared in the eastern quarter, from cockcrow until morning, for three months. Its rays penetrated the heavens. At the sight of its rising, all the provinces and peoples wondered [what it might be]; afterward, returning into itself, it disappeared. After this apparition a great mortality followed in the eastern region. [After that appearance, a great mortality followed in the eastern region.]

He held one ordination: ten presbyters, five deacons, and six bishops in various places. He was also buried at the blessed apostle Peter on the third day before the Ides of April, and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and fifteen days.

# LXXXI. SAINT AGATHO. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 678, THE ELEVENTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE POGONATUS

### From the Farnesian Manuscript

No. 140, line 1: “a Sicilian by nationality, he held the see for two years, six months, and four days.”

Line 11: “John the deacon, and Constantine the subdeacon, Theodore the presbyter of Ravenna.”

### From the Vallicellian Manuscript

No. 140, line 2: “four days.” “He was,” etc., as in the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, with which lines 3 and 4 also agree.

Likewise in lines 7 and 11. Line 5 reads as in the cited manuscripts, except for the following: “the earlier decree,” omitting “unless … and with his knowledge,” etc., which are found in line 4 of no. 146.

Line 6: “through Prophania, the glorious secretary, sent to his predecessor.” Line 8: “to love,” an error for “to direct.” Line 9: “and he did not delay to ordain.” “Accordingly, he sent Habundantius of Paternus, John of Reggio, and John of Porto, bishops.” Line 12: “servants of God, monks.”

The Vallicellian manuscript immediately adds the following—whereas the printed editions and the other manuscripts put several other things first, although these disturb the order of the narrative and occur in the following section:

> “The aforesaid envoys of the apostolic see, entering the imperial city on 10 November, in the ninth indiction, with the Lord giving them assistance and the prince of the apostles accompanying them, were received by the imperial prince in the oratory—read ‘in the oratory,’ rather than ‘in the little palace’—of the blessed apostle Peter within the palace, presenting to him the pontiff’s documents. When he had received them, he admonished and exhorted them not to act wickedly or in anger, but, through a peaceful settlement, abandoning philosophical assertions, to give satisfaction according to the pure faith of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers, confirmed by synodal decrees. He also gave them time to reconsider their writings, granting them everything sufficient for their support” (the manuscript has “sufficient,” singular), “etc.,” as in line 15 of the following number, in the same place.

Line 16: “in the house which they call Placidiani”—read “Placidia”—on the 18th day of the month mentioned above. “On Sunday,” etc. Line 17: “to Blachernas,” read “Blachernas.” Line 18: “to receive jointly,” so that it might be peaceful, etc.

No. 141, line 1: “In his time, in the eighth indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse in the month of June, on the eighteenth day.”

No. 142, line 6: “After this, the patricians Hypatius and the entire Senate.” “And having held…”

No. 142, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, and likewise in lines 2, 10, 12, and 13.

Line 5: “when they had prostrated themselves and worshiped, the rest of the princes, together with our men.”

“After this, all the patricians, and all the illustrious men, with the entire Senate”; “and after an inquiry had been held by his Piety, concerning which party’s exposition ought to be approved, the legates of the apostolic see”; line 14: “and, saying that they shared the will in the Lord Jesus Christ, as became clear before the prince and the synod.”

Elsewhere the pious prince, defender of the Catholic faith, presided in the secretary’s office. The word *to* [τὸ, “the”] before “presided” is also found in the margin of the edition. I am surprised that Holstenius notes here: “No manuscript recognizes this reading.” In the dispute brought before the manuscripts themselves, he thus found that these words had recently been falsely added.

No. 143, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript has “on 22 November.” Line 2 agrees with the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, as does line 15.

Line 5: “and George the chartophylax having been summoned.” Line 6: “he brought forth the codices from the library of the Church of Constantinople”; “and the documents produced and reread were found to be entirely authentic.” Line 12: “on the fourteenth day.”

No. 144, line 3: “The Western bishops subscribed the synodical letter, numbering 120.” Line 15: “on the twentieth day of February.”

No. 144, line 2: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “the synodical letter of the most blessed Pope Agatho.”

The same line: “with the sayings of the Fathers inserted, in which the bishops of the Western party subscribed.” “And when, after this, he had exhorted him…”

Line 6: “in no way to confess one or two wills”—the verb “to confess” is omitted—“or operations in Christ.”

Line 8: “to read the document in which one will and heretical doctrines had been written and subscribed by his own hand: most openly,” etc., as in the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts.

Lines 10 and 21 agree with the cited manuscripts.

Line 12: “Patriarch George replied that, if he embraced that faith which the apostolic see teaches, in accordance with the writings of Pope Agatho or of the venerable holy Fathers.”

Line 14: “in writing.” Line 15 agrees with the cited manuscripts, except for the words “sent by the most blessed pope”; “on that day, Gregory.”

No. 145, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, and likewise in lines 6, 10, 13, 14, 20, 23, and 26.

Line 3: “so that he might place himself on whichever side he wished.” “The patriarch George withdrew,” etc., as in the cited manuscripts.

Line 19: “Epiphanius and Anastasius, from among the presbyters, thrust into exile.”

At the final line: “they acclaimed,” etc., as in the said manuscripts, except for the following variant readings:

### From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane Manuscripts
Num. 140, line 2, day 4: He was so benevolent and mild toward everyone. Line 3 and 4: “of Ravenna.” Line 5: “He received an imperial order, in accordance with his petition, by which the amount customarily paid for the ordination of pontiffs was reduced, but on this condition: if an election had taken place, the person elected was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been introduced into the royal city according to custom, and unless the ordination was to proceed with the knowledge and command of that emperor.” He also received an imperial order from the most pious princes. Line 6: “through the profane gloss sent by the secretary to his predecessor.” Line 7: “that he ought to [sacredly—abbreviated *sac.*].” Line 9, distinction: “Thus he sent” A. Line 10: “Regianus and John, bishops of Porto.” Line 11: “John, deacon; Constantine, subdeacon; Theodore [title abbreviated].” Lines 12 and 13: “monks.” In manuscript M the following is added at the end of the page, in a more recent hand: “namely, clerics of different orders; he increased them beyond what was appropriate to their honors. Here, contrary to custom, he became treasurer of the Church of Rome, and personally administered the office of treasurer, sending out, namely, writs in the name of the collectors, overshadowed by his own hand; when he was detained by illness, he appointed a treasurer according to custom.”

Num. 141, line 1: “During his times, indiction VIII.” “Likewise a greater and most grievous mortality followed in June, July, August, and September in the city of Rome, such as is recorded never to have existed in the times of any other pontiffs, so that even parents with their children, brothers, sisters, or children were carried on litters to the tombs.” Afterwards it did not cease to ravage the suburban districts and camps all around. The envoys of the Apostolic See mentioned above, entering the royal city on 10 November, indiction 9, were received, with the Lord giving comfort and with the prince of the apostles accompanying them, by the prince in the oratory of blessed Peter the Apostle within the palace, presenting to him the pope’s writings. When he had received them, he admonished them and urged them not to dismiss the matter in anger or fury, but through a peaceful settlement, abandoning [the abbreviated phrase is uncertain: *ph.*], with pure faith, the sacred writings and the opinions of the Fathers approved by faith [the remaining abbreviations are uncertain]. He also gave them time to reconsider the writings, granting them everything. Line 15: “in the house called Placidia, on the 18th day of the month,” and “on the following Sunday.” Line 18: “so that he might receive them collectively.”

Num. 142, line 1: “On 12 November, in the basilica also called the Trullus.” Line 2: “with Constantine Augustus presiding, and George with him.” Line 5: “When they had bowed down and worshiped, the matter was brought before the prince, together with our men” (namely clerics; the additions mentioned above under Num. 140, line 13, after the word “monks,” are inserted here. In the Regal manuscript, however, the reading is better than in M: “such as is recorded never to have existed in the times of other pontiffs”). After this, five patricians and all the illustrious men entered with the entire synod, and, after his Piety had investigated which party [was meant], the legates of the Apostolic See said—. Line 10: “let the authority of the See be set forth.” When they heard this, they rejoiced. Line 12: “for they did not think that they could overcome by truth, except through [the abbreviated phrase is uncertain].” Line 13: “which are added in the books themselves.” Line 14: “to say that there is one will in the Lord Jesus Christ.” Line 17: “saying that there is one will.” Line 18: “On another day, Constantine.” In the same line: “presiding in the inquiry concerning the books themselves, he thus rejected the false things as false” [the remaining wording is abbreviated and uncertain].

Num. 143, line 1: “On 22 November.” Line 2: “The envoys of the Apostolic See, presenting the place of the most blessed Agatho, the pope, arrived, and the synod ordered them to sit.” To whom—. Line 6: “to them, so that they might—.” Line 7: “bring them down.” In the same place: “and when they were read, they were found to be most genuine.” Line 12: “the 14th day.” Line 15: “those who professed two natures, two wills, and two operations in Christ.”

Num. 144, line 2: “of the most holy Pope Agatho.” Line 3: “with the words inserted.” In the same place, subscription: “120.” When, after this, he had exhorted them, and no one was saying—. Line 6: “or operation.” Line 8: “for reading, in which there were heretical doctrines,” and so forth, as in the oration. Line 11: “where his subscription was.” Line 12: “that he would embrace it according to the writings of Pope Agatho, or of the holy venerable pontiff”; he replied that he would respond in writing concerning what had been brought forward. Line 15: “February, on the Lord’s day, in the oratory of blessed Peter.” In the presence of the emperor and patriarch together, they received the envoys of the Apostolic See, rereading the suggestions sent for their commendation by the most blessed pope mentioned above (M reads “subscribed”), and directed by him. George, the venerable patriarch, professed in writing two natures—. Line 21: “and they say that there are two wills and two operations.”

Num. 145, line 1: “together with the prince.” Line 3: “so that each might go to whichever party he wished: George the patriarch withdrew with his men to the orthodox party, but Macarius with his men to the other, heretical party.” Line 6: “which, having done, they presented to the prince; it was read, and Macarius was admonished. When questioned, he answered that he remained in the same perfidy.” Line 10: “Basil, bishop of Crete, removed his stole from him, and they anathematized him and cast him outside the synod.” Line 13: “casting him out”—this is read consistently in this form, as in the other ancient books. Line 14: “they were amazed.” By this it was signified that the [abbreviated *s. h.*] had been driven out—. Line 16: “of the monastery of Baiae.” Line 18: “Leontius, one of the presbyters; Polychronius, one of the deacons; and Anastasius, one of the presbyters, were thrust into exile in Rome.” Line 21: “from the writings of the churches, or from the paintings, or from the doors, wherever the names of the patriarchs could be found—namely Macarius, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and also Peter, through whom this error had continued to spread until now.” Line 23: “by the grace of God, all—.” Line 25: “which was in the royal city.” In the same line: “On the Lord’s day of Easter, in the church of Holy Sophia, the public Mass was celebrated with the prince and patriarch; it was celebrated in Latin, and all [were] one—.” Final line: “acclamations.”

“During the times of this venerable pope, in indiction 7, the moon suffered an eclipse in June on the 18th day. Likewise, a very great and grievous mortality followed in July, August, and September in the city of Rome, such as is recorded never to have existed in the times of other pontiffs, so that even parents with their children, and brothers or sisters, were carried two by two on litters to the graves. In the same way the same mortality spread outside, throughout the suburban districts and camps. This pope also increased the clergy with various honors beyond what was appropriate. Nevertheless, contrary to custom, he became treasurer of the Roman Church, and personally administered the office of treasurer, sending out, namely, documents concerning what had been received, shaded over by his own hand, through the *nomenclator* (read: *nomenclator*). When he was detained by illness, he appointed a treasurer according to custom. He left [something] to all the clergy.” These words, or nearly the same, are included under Num. 140 and Num. 141.

[Note: [Col. 0815C]

Num. 140, line 14.—“Here, contrary to custom, he became treasurer of the Roman Church, and personally administered the office of treasurer, sending out, namely, what had been received, shaded over by his own hand through the *nomenclator*: when he was detained by illness, he appointed a treasurer according to custom.”

Theodore, archbishop of Ravenna, was made treasurer of the Roman Church contrary to custom. The treasurer of the Roman Church is the prefect of the Church’s treasury. Treasurers are overseers of the chest, or treasury, of the prince. See the final law of the title “Concerning receivers, overseers, and treasurers.” Concerning them, Sidonius, Book VII, chapter 7: “To the treasurers, weights and measures having been assigned.” Jerome, in his letter to the Romans, on the words “Erastus greets you, the treasurer of the city”: “Here he calls him *arcarius* from *arcarius*.” The Ravennate is said to have carried out the office of treasurer personally, issuing through the *nomenclator* documents concerning what had been received or collected. *Suscepta* or *desuscepta* are certificates for money received or for grain collected from the treasury, given to those who paid by the collectors; concerning these there is Title 6 of Book X, that is, concerning the officials assigned to receive grain or taxes.

Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 10: “After the page concerning what had been received had been submitted.” The same, Letter 44 of the same book: “As for the other things that are with us, send from them what has been received, for remembrance of the future.” He says, “through the *nomenclator*.” Among the offices of the Roman Church was that of *nomenclator*. The *Roman Order*: “After the horse, these are the men who ride: the deputy steward, the wardrobe officer, the *nomenclator*, and the treasurer.” The *Frankish Annals*, under the year 802: “The leaders of this faction were Pascal, the *nomenclator*, and Campulus, the treasurer.” Anastasius, in his Life of Constantine: “Cosmas, the treasurer; Sisinnius, the *nomenclator*.”

The archbishop of Ravenna, a rival of pontifical dignity, had his own *nomenclator*, as is clear from this passage: “There was also a *nomenclator* among the offices of the magistrates.” Symmachus, Book X, Letter 43: “When he, while I was pursuing him with protection, had asked for aid, and, relying on the support of a single *nomenclator*, might proceed as in a peaceful city.”

Num. 141, line 17.—“So that he might also send caparisoned horses from the palace.” Caparisoned horses were sent to pontifical legates as a mark of honor. *Caballus* means “horse”; hence *caballarii*, “horsemen.” Otto of Freising, *On the Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, Book II, chapter 24: “But concerning the horsemen of your nobility.” *Caballicata* means riding. Liutprand, Book III, final chapter: “When he had arrived there, he sent caparisoned horses about on every side, as they commonly say.” And *caballicare* means the same as *equitare*, “to ride.” The same author, Book II, chapter 4: “According to the statement of Count Burkhard, if I do not make all the Italians use only one spur and ride misshapen mares, I am not Burkhard.” Anastasius himself, in his Life of Conon: “He also granted him permission to use the cloak for riding.” Justinian granted Constantine, a deacon and administrator of the patrimony of Sicily, permission to use a cloak for riding—that is, a horse covered with a cloak—which was not appropriate for clerics; see the chapter “Clerics,” concerning the life and honorable conduct of clerics, and Bernard, Letter 42.

Num. 142, line 1.—“In the basilica called the Trullus, within the palace.” The Sixth Synod was held at Constantinople in the Trullus. The Trullus is the emperor’s palace, as this author reports in the Life of Leo II. The synod was held in the secretariat of the basilica adjoining the Trullian palace. Anastasius here writes: “On another day the pious prince, defender of the Catholic faith, sitting in the secretariat,” and so forth. A little later in the same place: “On the following day, with the synod sitting in the same secretariat.”

Line 6.—“After this the patricians, consuls, and all the illustrious men entered.” The Greek word ὕπατοι means “consuls.” Suidas: “ὕπατοι are those who administer the commonwealth of the Romans.” “Consuls,” that is, those who administer the Roman state. The illustrious men are senators. Anastasius, in his Life of Constantine: “With the patricians and all the illustrious men.” Among the ancients, “illustrious” meant men of rank. Plautus, *Pseudolus*: “Famous mistresses of the highest men.” The same author, *Persa*: “To wealthy, illustrious, mighty Jupiter.”

Num. 143, line 5.—“And George, deacon and chartophylax of the Church of Constantinople, having been summoned, was ordered to bring the books from the Church’s library into the midst, according to their information.” The *chartophylax* of the Church of Constantinople was the keeper of the Church’s record office or archive. Concerning him, see Codinus, *On the Offices*, chapter 1 of the ecclesiastical master; Balsamon, Book VII of the Greek Law; the same author on canon 18 of the Council of Nicaea; and Meursius, *Glossary*, under the word Καρτοφύλαξ.

Num. 145, line 9.—“At that hour the holy synod, together with the prince, ordered his stole to be removed from his neck; and Basil, bishop of the Church of Crete, rising up, removed his stole and, anathematizing him, cast him outside the synod.”

Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, was deposed in the Trullian Synod for heresy by the removal of his stole. In the same way Constantine, the antipope, was deposed by the removal and cutting of his stole. Anastasius, in his Life of Stephen IV: “Again the aforesaid Constantine was brought into the midst, and, after the most sacred canons had been read, was deposed in this manner. For Maurianus, a subdeacon, approached, removed the stole from his neck, threw it before his feet, and cut its fastenings.”

The solemn deposition of bishops was carried out by removing the insignia bestowed at ordination, such as the stole, ring, and staff, according to the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27, and the canon “A Bishop,” Question 3. Benedict, the invader of the Apostolic See, was deposed by Leo VIII through the cutting off of the pallium and the breaking of the pastoral staff, while he was allowed to retain the diaconate. Regino, *Chronicle*, Book II: “Then Leo the apostolic, having assembled a synod of many bishops, deposed Benedict, the invader of the Roman See, by the judgment of all from the rank he had invaded; he cut off the pontifical pallium which Benedict had put on himself, seized the pastoral staff from his hand, broke it into pieces before everyone, and, at the emperor’s request, allowed him to retain only the rank of deacon.”

By the same law Formosus, bishop of Porto and usurper of the Apostolic See, after his death was dragged from his grave by Sergius, the Roman pontiff; his pontifical garments were removed, three fingers were cut off, and he was thrown into the Tiber. Liutprand, Book I, chapter 8: “For after Formosus had died, the man who had been appointed pope after Formosus was expelled, and Sergius was made pope through Adalbert. Once he had been installed, he ordered Formosus, as an impious man ignorant of sacred doctrine, to be dragged from his tomb and placed, clothed in priestly garments, upon the Roman pontifical throne. He also said to him: ‘When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman See through the spirit of ambition?’ When this had been completed, he ordered him at once to be stripped of his sacred garments, three fingers to be cut off, and his body to be thrown into the Tiber.” Leo of Ostia says the same in Book I, chapter 9.

In the same way the deposition of magistrates is carried out by removing the insignia of their appointment, according to the law “Judges,” in the Code, “Concerning Dignities.” This is what John Chrysostom says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 53: condemned criminals, before being subjected to punishment, are stripped of the ornaments of their dignity, ἀφαιρούμενοι τῆς τῶν ἀξιωμάτων τιμῆς, “having removed the honor of their offices.”

Likewise, soldiers are cashiered by the removal of military insignia, according to the law in the Digest, “Concerning Those Branded with Infamy,” and chapter 2, “Concerning Punishment,” in the Sixth Book—that is, the belt or military sash and spurs. This was observed in the degradation of Andrew Herkle, an English knight, because he defected to the Scots, as Thomas Walsingham records under Edward II, in the year 1323: “First, he was degraded by having his spurs cut off at his ankles with an axe; then, in turn, he was ungirt of the military belt, and his shoes and gloves were removed.” In the same way, bishops are restored by having their pontifical insignia returned, according to the canon “A Bishop.”

Line 20.—“Then they removed from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, or erased their figures from the church paintings and from the doors where they could be found—namely Cyrus, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, through whom this error against the orthodox faith had continued to spread until now.”

In the same synod, the names of the patriarchs condemned for heresy were removed from the church diptychs, and their images were erased from the doors and from other places in the church where they had been. Thus, when John Chrysostom was deposed, his name was removed from the church diptychs, but after his death it was restored by his successor Atticus. See Socrates, Book VII, chapter 25, and Theodoret, Book V, chapter 35.

The images of schismatic patriarchs were removed, just as the images of tyrants were removed. Ambrose, *On Interpellation*, chapter 9: “See how in cities the images of good princes remain, while the images of tyrants are erased.” The same author, on Psalm 38: “If anyone possesses images of a tyrant who, already defeated, has perished, he is rightly condemned.” The same, *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 49: “If anyone possesses an image of a tyrant, is he not liable to condemnation?”

The image of the heretical emperor Philippicus was not admitted by the Romans into the Church. Anastasius, in his Life of Constantine: “At that time the Roman people had decided not to accept in any way the name, documents, or image of the heretical emperor; consequently, neither was his likeness brought into the church, nor was his name mentioned at the solemn celebration of Mass.”

Num. 146, line 1.—“Here he received an imperial order, according to his petition, as he had requested, by which the amount customarily paid for the ordination of a pontiff was reduced.”

The Roman pontiffs were compelled, like the lesser bishops, to pay a fixed sum of money to the Gothic kings for confirmation. Cassiodorus, Book VIII, Letter 35. After the Goths had been expelled, the burden once imposed remained easily in force under the Greek emperors. Gregory, in the Fourth Penitential Psalm, and John the Deacon, in his Life of Gregory, Book I, chapter 39, report that Gregory regretted having endured this disgraceful burden. Matters did not improve for the pontiffs who followed him, until this burden was remitted to Agatho by Constantine Pogonatus, as is reported here; from this passage the canon “Agatho” in Distinction 63 was taken.]

[Note: [Col. 0818C]

Num. 140, line 3.—Theodore, archbishop of Ravenna. When Agatho was about to celebrate a synod of the Western bishops, he sent a summons to the bishops, among them Theodore of Ravenna. When Theodore received it, he announced it to his clergy, as was customary with such encyclical letters; as a result, he set out for the synod summoned at Rome.

Although Agnellus continually spreads the poison of the schism he supported throughout his narratives, he nevertheless recounts the matter faithfully in the Life of Theodore, chapter 4, page 153:

“After a short time, the bishop himself, keeping grief in his heart and intending to harm his priests, remembered the wrong they had done him. Since he could not, as he wished, enrich his relatives from the property of the Church, he secretly sent a message to Pope Agatho at Rome, as though he wished to discuss with him the cause of the holy Churches of God in the Catholic faith, asking him to order Theodore to come there.

He immediately wrote a letter that Theodore, the bishop, should hasten to Rome for the holy and undefiled Catholic faith. Theodore displayed the letter before all his priests, read it, and replied, saying to them: ‘What do you think? You have seen the apostolic letter, and you know what it contains. What do you think? I shall do nothing apart from your will. We have one counsel, brothers; let there be one will and one mind: shall we go, or shall we remain?’

They answered simply, not knowing the hidden plan: ‘We ought all to submit to the danger of death for the orthodox faith and the holy Church of God.’

When he reached Rome, he subjected himself and his Church to the Roman pontiff. The Roman pontiff rejoiced, having recovered what his predecessors had lost; he received him gladly, agreed to whatever he requested, and granted what he asked, according to his will.”

You can see Agnellus’s prejudiced mind: he invents cunning and fraud in Bishop Theodore, although he himself had already affirmed that a decree concerning the matter had previously been issued, requiring the bishop to be elected at Ravenna to go to Rome for consecration. Certainly no one familiar with the customs of that age can doubt that Agatho restored the rights of his Church in the synod of the Westerners and secured some definition there. Indeed, the summons itself from the primate to the synod, and the consent of the entire Ravennate clergy, sufficiently demonstrate that the dispute concerning autocephalous rights had already been annulled and removed, and that Agnellus, carried away by partisan zeal, wrongly censured Theodore’s moderation.

Line 12.—Theodore, presbyter of Ravenna. Agnellus calls him in the same place the archpresbyter of the Ravennates. Since he was sent in the name of Agatho and of the council of the Westerners to the synod of the Easterners, it is manifest that the rights of the Apostolic See over the Ravennate Church had already been fully satisfied.

Num. 141, line 1.—“Indiction VIII.” Anastasius also took these words from Paul the Deacon, Book VI, chapter 5, who writes:

“During his times, in indiction VIII, the moon suffered an eclipse. A solar eclipse also occurred at nearly the same time, around the tenth hour of the day, on the fifth day before the Nones of May. Immediately afterward a most grievous plague followed for three months, namely July, August, and September. So great was the number of the dying that even parents with their children, and brothers with their sisters, were carried two by two on biers to the tombs near the city of Rome.”
