Line 18.—“Admonishing them in that very matter.” In the memorandum given to the legates of the Apostolic See, whom he had furnished with books and reliable testimonies of the holy Fathers, the pontiff had taken care that, whenever the Easterners appealed in the synod to the faith and judgments of the Fathers, they should compare them with these authoritative copies and firmly reject whatever they found to disagree with them.

The Monothelite trickery had already long since been discovered in the synodical letter of Peter written to Vitalian. Consequently, the diligence of the legates was not without reason fortified by these aids of truth, so that they might have them ready for the debate to be undertaken with the Monothelites. Nor did the outcome disappoint the pontiff; for, as Anastasius testifies below, when an investigation was made using the books themselves, it was found that false things had recently been added.

Num. 145, line 26.—“He celebrated in Latin.” To make the union between the Churches of the East and West fully manifest, John, the legate and bishop of Porto, celebrated the solemn rites of Mass according to the Latin rite, and indeed with unleavened bread. Hilarus the monk noted this in his dialectical treatise on the mystical bread of the Greeks and the unleavened bread of the Latins:

“Concerning the Sixth Synod,” he writes, “I read among the Fathers that, after the heresy of the Monothelites had been condemned, on the eighth day of Easter at Constantinople, in the church of Holy Sophia, thanks were given to God in Latin, while all the Greeks praised the manner of the Latin sacrifice.”

Num. 146, line 2.—“The amount was reduced.” This servitude was imposed by the Gothic kings upon those elected as pontiffs, so that they could obtain permission to carry out the ordination only after a fixed sum had been paid into the royal treasury. Cassiodorus treats this matter at length in Book IX, Letter 11, page 589.

Indeed, after the Gothic yoke had been shaken off in Italy and Italy had been recovered for Justinian, the pontiffs were required to pay the same sum of money to the emperors of the East as the price of consecration. Gregory, in the Fourth Penitential Psalm, and John the Deacon, in his Life of Gregory, Book I, chapter 39, report how Gregory bore this burden with grief. Constantine Pogonatus remitted this burden, whatever its precise character, while retaining for himself the right to subscribe the decree that still had to be requested for pontifical consecration.

Likewise, Agnellus reports in the Life of Maurus, bishop of Ravenna, that the Ravennate Church paid a fixed sum to the imperial treasury through the archdeacon. He writes that the deacon Benedict drew from the sole patrimony of the Church of Ravenna located in Sicily:

“Besides fifty thousand modii of wheat, without any other grain or legumes, red and purple ramskins, embroidered casulae and silk cloaks, and other vestments, vessels of bronze and silver, and thirty thousand gold solidi, of which he carried fifteen thousand to the Constantinopolitan palace and sixteen thousand to the church archive.”]

[Note: [Col. 0820A]

Num. 140, line 1.—Agatho. It is established from the letter of the emperor Constantine, which he sent to Pope Donus on the day before the Kalends of August, in indiction 6, in the year of the Lord 678, that Agatho ascended the apostolic throne around the same time, after the death of Donus. It is also established that, at the command of the Western bishops, various councils were held in Italy, Gaul, and England, after they had learned what the emperor had written to Donus concerning the convocation of an ecumenical council on the Monothelite question.

During Agatho’s pontificate, the preaching of the Gospel among the Grisons and the Southern Saxons was begun by Wilfrid, bishop of York, and completed through the efforts of Willibrord.

“Two years, six months.” It is more truly established from what I noted above concerning the Life of Pope Donus, and from the ecclesiastical tables that commemorate and represent him as having died in indiction 10, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the year 682, that Agatho occupied the pontifical See for approximately three years and five months, more or less.

It is clear from a letter of Constantine sent to Agatho at the stated time that Agatho was still alive in December of indiction 10. This letter is preserved at the end of the eighteenth session of the Sixth Ecumenical Council.

Line 5.—“Here he received an imperial order.” This is preserved among the preliminary materials of the Sixth Council.

Line 9.—“And he sent Abundantius, and so forth.” The men who acted as legates in the name of the Apostolic See were Theodore and George, presbyters, and John, a deacon. These three, carrying out the office of apostolic legates, presided over the individual sessions of the ecumenical council, as is plainly established by the acts of that council.

The others whom Anastasius indiscriminately names together with the legates of the Apostolic See were deputed by the Roman council, specifically so that they might present the synodical letter they had received to the emperor and publicly declare before him what the judgment of the Western bishops was concerning the wills and operations of Christ.

Num. 141, line 8.—“On the tenth day of November.” Anastasius is mistaken. Since, after the arrival of the legates in the city, Emperor Constantine wrote that sacred letter mentioned above to George of Constantinople on the fourth day before the Ides of September, it is necessary to affirm that both delegations arrived in the city either around the end of August or at the beginning of September.

Add to this that the ecumenical council itself is said to have begun on 7 November under the presidency of the legates of the Apostolic See, who were already present. The text can be corrected if, instead of “10 November,” we read “10 September.”

Num. 142, line 1.—“On the twenty-second day of November.” From this point to the end of the Life of Agatho, Anastasius gives a brief summary of the synodal acts. It contains several things that are missing from the Sixth Synod itself, while, conversely, several things written in the surviving synodal acts are absent from it.

Num. 144, line 1.—“On the following day,” and so forth. Everything that follows up to the passage “But Macarius with his men,” and so forth, is absent from the synodal acts.

Num. 145, lines 19 and 20.—“They were sent into exile in the city of Rome.” Anastasius is mistaken. They were sent to Rome not to undergo exile, but to pursue the appeal they had lodged against the emperor, as is clear from the letter of the emperor Constantine to Pope Leo, preserved at the end of session 18 of the acts of the Sixth Council.

Moreover, there is no example by which the city of Rome was ever assigned as the place of exile for banished heretics.

Num. 146, line 2.—“By which the amount customarily given was reduced.” The Arian and impious Gothic kings had first established by tyranny that no Roman bishop should be ordained unless, with the king’s prior consent, he had paid a fixed sum and amount of money.

After the Gothic kings had been overthrown, the Eastern emperors demanded payment of the same contribution. This is clear from the complaint of Saint Gregory, who complained most bitterly about the matter in his *Commentaries on the Fourth Penitential Psalm*: although he had been lawfully called and elected to the pontificate, he had not been permitted to perform his office until he had redeemed it from the emperors with money.

The emperor Constantine IV, while still retaining the right of confirmation that had been usurped by tyranny in ancient times, abolished this most unjust exaction of money. When the Church was freed from the other tyrannical servitude by which elected pontiffs had to be confirmed by the emperors, we shall explain in the Life of Pope Benedict II.

Final line.—“One year,” and so forth. Anastasius’s statement concerning the interregnum of the pontifical See is confirmed by canon 2 of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, from which it is clear that Leo II, Agatho’s successor, was still alive in the year 684, when the aforementioned Council of Toledo was held.

Since everyone agrees that Leo held the pontificate for no more than ten months and seventeen days, it is necessary to affirm that, between the death of Agatho and the beginning of Leo’s pontificate, an interregnum of that length intervened.]

[Note: [Col. 0821B]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

As regards the interval between the death of Donus and the next pontificate, if we exclude the Ambrosian manuscript I and the Veronese catalogue, which give three months and fifteen days, while the sixth Colbert manuscript records no days, all the others—both manuscripts and catalogues—consistently establish two months and fifteen days.

Therefore, counting an interpontificate of two months and fifteen days from the date of Donus’s death, 11 April 679, the date 26 June is reached, with the Sunday letter B indicated, and this accordingly belongs to the ordination of Agatho.

From that point to his death, or deposition, recorded by Anastasius on 10 January, in addition to the two full years and six months unanimously assigned to Agatho’s See, the number is not four or three days, as several manuscripts and catalogues inconsistently have, but fourteen days, as in the fourth and sixth Colbert catalogues, on whose authority Pagius relies, and also in another Corbeian catalogue and the newly published Veronese catalogue. All these correctly give two years, six months, and fourteen days.

Accordingly, Saint Agatho was consecrated on 26 June 679 and remained in office until 10 January 682.

I have now completed the chronological part of the task. What remains is to defend the manuscripts and catalogues that assign such narrow limits to this pontificate that the great abundance of events surviving from his times seemed to the most learned men incapable of being contained within them.

The principal writers are Baronius, Papebrochius, Benedict Bacchini, and Antonius Pagius. Agreeing concerning the year and day of his deposition, they contend that the beginnings of his pontificate must be placed a year earlier, namely in 678.

Rather than linger over refuting their opinions one by one, which would depart entirely from my purpose, I shall set out as briefly as possible the sequence of events that led more recent scholars away from Anastasius. The diligent reader may later compare it with the learned dissertations of Papebrochius in the *Historical-Chronological Attempt*, of Bacchini in Agnellus’s *Book of the Ravenna Pontiffs*, and of Antonius Pagius in the *Baronian Criticism*, especially under the years 677, 678, and 679; I shall explain it as far as I am able.

There are altogether two matters that compelled them to move the date backward.

1. The opening of the Roman council under Agatho, which in all the collections after the Regal manuscript edited by Sirmond has the following:

“In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, while our most pious lords Constantine, the senior emperor and Augustus, was reigning in the twenty-sixth year, and in the tenth year after his consulship, and Heraclius and Tiberius, his brothers, the Augusti [variant: ‘new Augusti’], were also reigning in their twenty-second year, in the seventh indiction, in the month of October, with Agatho, the most holy and thrice-blessed apostolic universal pope, presiding.”

2. The other matter is the synodical subscription of Saint Wilfrid, archbishop of York, to another Roman council, which is read in session 4 of the Sixth General Council:

“Wilfrid, humble bishop of the holy Church of York in the island of Britain, legate of the venerable synod constituted throughout Britain, have likewise subscribed this petition, which we unanimously composed on behalf of our apostolic faith.”

I shall briefly untie the first of these knots here. I shall deal with the second, since it is connected with the narration of events, after I have explained everything.]

The aforementioned opening of the Roman council contains four chronological indicators [Col. 0822B] that conflict with one another and plainly refer to four—or at least three—different years: 677, 678, 679, and 680. For the tenth consulship of Constantine Pogonatus, by which he reckons his tribunician powers, indicates the year 677 in the month of October, as Pagius most learnedly observes in *Ep. hypat.*, part III, chapter 4. This reckoning began with the year of Constans’s murder, 668, on 15 July, according to Anastasius and other ancient and modern writers, although Pagius prefers an unspecified day after 16 September and before 7 November; in this matter I agree with him, for I have no need to oppose him on this single point.

The seventh indiction, recurring in the month of October, corresponds to the year 678. The twenty-sixth year of Constantine, who had been proclaimed Augustus by his father Constans in April of the year 654, indicates the year 679 after 26 April of that month. Finally, the twenty-second year of Heraclius and Tiberius, beginning between 26 April and 9 August, corresponds to the year 680, since they are said to have been made Caesars in 659 [Col. 0822C].

I pass over the incongruous designation of Heraclius and Tiberius as “new Augusti,” since they not only never advanced to the dignity of Augusti, but, as Theophanes observes, were even stripped of the dignity of Caesar by their brother Pogonatus—although this occurred in the following year, when he took his son Justinian as his associate in the empire. Moreover, although the councils show that new Constantines were acclaimed as Augusti on account of their merits, as Ducange observes (*Dissert. de num. inf. aevi*, chapter 29), it is by no means clear that the same men were called new Augusti as a mark of honor. Pagius therefore rightly expunges such titles and restores in their place those found in the proceedings of the Sixth Council.

Since this is so, I cannot help wondering that these learned men were driven by such matters, inserted into the records by an ignorant later hand, both to reject the authority of Anastasius and to correct so many ancient writers. I wonder at it all the more because, in the collections of the councils, immediately after this council is reported—whether in the year 680 or 679—another account is at once produced from a manuscript codex of Malmesbury, in which the case of Wilfrid is treated, although it is silent in the first account; and it is called another example of the same council, or at least another session. The understanding of both accounts depends upon what will be said below.

I now come to the second point, namely Wilfrid’s subscription. I shall first set out that part of the history relevant to the matter from Bede and Radmer, compared with the edition of Stephen published by Mabillon (*Saecul. IV Bened.*), from whom Pagius derives his material.

Saint Wilfrid was deprived of the bishopric of York by King Ecgfrid because of the private hostility of Queen Ermenburga. While Wilfrid was absent, three bishops were ordained in his diocese by Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. The holy man returned and was astonished by these developments. He complained to the king without success and appealed to Rome. Then, gently rebuking some of those present who mocked his misfortunes with laughter, he said:

> “Ah, sons! May you pass long years in prosperous happiness [Col. 0823A]. But know that hostile fortune will very soon dissolve these joys of yours. You will not see this year pass before you repay with bitter grief the mockery that you now direct against me.”

So says Eadmer, chapter 4.

He then relates the death in battle of Ecgfrid’s youthful brother Eswini, or Elfwin. Henschenius, following the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, says that this occurred in the year 679. Mabillon therefore rightly assigns Saint Wilfrid’s expulsion to the preceding year, 678, as Bede had earlier done (*Hist. Angl.*, book IV, chapter 12), together with the author of the catalogue of the bishops of York transmitted by Simeon of Durham and published by Selden.

Pagius rejects both authorities: Bede, because in the same year 678 he placed the appearance of the comet about which modern scholars dispute—some maintaining that it appeared in 676, others in 677, and others finally in 678, as I said in the notes to the catalogue of Adeodatus—and Simeon’s catalogue, because in another edition of the same catalogue, derived from the manuscript library of Labbe, he reports the expulsion in the year 678 [Col. 0823B].

Pagius also argues from the contrary testimony of Eddius, a contemporary and companion of Saint Wilfrid. Eddius agrees with Eadmer, saying in chapter 23:

> “On this anniversary day, you who now laugh at my condemnation out of envy will then weep bitterly in your own confusion.”

He teaches that “anniversary day” may also be understood after many years, on the authority of the sermons of Saint Leo.

But there is no room here for such refined learning, since the aforementioned chronicle makes it clear that the battle between Ecgfrid and Alred took place in 679. Many ancient and modern writers, however, connect Saint Wilfrid’s expulsion with the preceding year, 678, and must therefore be corrected—especially Eadmer and Malmesbury, unquestionably the foremost authorities in narrating English affairs. I follow them. But I return to Saint Wilfrid.

After being expelled from his see, from which the aforementioned catalogue says that he was an exile for ten years, he boarded a ship and arrived in Frisia in the same year. He spent the entire winter there, greatly benefiting that people, for he preached the Gospel [Col. 0823C] to them.

When spring arrived, he continued his journey to Rome through Gaul. Eadmer shows that he did not reach Rome immediately, reporting that he visited Dagobert, a king who was his very close friend, and afterward Berther, duke of Champagne (Reims). It is not credible that he made only brief stays at either court, as Pagius rightly observes. Pagius also says that he did not reach the city before the beginning of October, and on this point I agree with him.

When he arrived at Rome, his case was already well known, for Archbishop Theodore had sent ahead the monk Coenwald with his instructions. Many citizens went out to meet him:

> “He was received with great favor by the people,” says Eadmer, “and was reverently led into the basilica of blessed Peter. At that time the apostolic see was governed by Agatho, of blessed memory, a just and simple man, and by no means lacking in skill in ecclesiastical affairs. In the presence of this pope and many bishops, when the case of blessed Wilfrid had been examined in the presence of his accusers, the judgment of all established that he had been accused without fault and that he was worthy of the episcopate. At that time, while the same pope was convening a synod of 125 bishops at Rome against those who taught that the Lord and Savior had one will and one operation, he ordered blessed Wilfrid to be summoned and, seated among the bishops, to state his faith and that of the province from which he had come.”

Bede relates the same matter clearly in book V, chapter 20, as do Eddius Stephen and Malmesbury. In Malmesbury one may read the decree of the first council, expressed in these words:

> “Let the bishop beloved of God, Wilfrid, receive the bishopric which he formerly held; and let those whom he shall choose as his assistants, with the consent of the council to be assembled there, be ordained and advanced as bishops by the most holy archbishop, while those who, in his absence, were irregularly thrust into the episcopate are expelled far away; and so forth. Those who do not accept these decrees are forbidden to do so. After these decrees had been issued, the rejoicing bishop was also ordered, by command of the pope, to sit among the 130 holy bishops who were deliberating against those who taught one operation,” and so on.

It is therefore evident that two councils were held in two different years. The first was held in October, as stated in its opening—although that opening is otherwise full of errors. Eddius, chapter 50, shows that the second was held on the third day of Easter, and therefore in the following year.

Accordingly, on the basis of the history that we have so far narrated, supported by the authority of ancient writers who agree remarkably with one another, and contrary to modern authors who distort the chronology by a full year, we hold it certain that Saint Wilfrid was expelled from his see in 678; that he arrived in Rome in the following year, in an uncertain month; that there he was acquitted at a council of fifty Fathers in October of that same year, 679; and that finally he took part in the council held on Tuesday of Easter in the year 680, namely 27 March, against the Monothelite heresy, under Pope Agatho and 125 bishops [Col. 0824B].

Since this is so, it is not difficult to discover why the aforementioned opening of the Roman council became corrupt. In it the indiction is reckoned, according to Roman custom, from the Kalends of January, so that the seventh indiction corresponds to the whole of the year 679, to which Constantine’s twenty-sixth year is assigned. The tenth year after the consulship, however, is reckoned not according to Pogonatus’s new alteration in the calendar, but according to the old custom, from the year following the consulship, 669.

As for the fourth chronological marker, namely the years of Tiberius and Heraclius, it is not surprising that an error occurred, since the Greeks do not record the year in which the dignity of Caesar was conferred upon them. That year must be extracted from the proceedings of the Sixth Council—unless perhaps the person who copied the council’s proceedings into a codex and scattered them with so many additions deliberately made the same two-year error in recording the years of the Caesars, as learned men will recognize.

Nothing, however, confirms the matter better than the constitutions and acts of these councils, which I realize must be examined more carefully. In the first Roman council, held in October 679, the Fathers decreed matters concerning the disturbed discipline of the English Church, particularly because three bishops had been ordained in Saint Wilfrid’s diocese while he had been expelled. Together with these decrees they sent John, monk of Saint Martin and archchanter of the Church of Saint Peter. They also gave him a copy of the Lateran Council held by Saint Martin against the Monothelites.

In another synod held by the same Fathers in the same month—or rather, in another session of the same synod—Saint Wilfrid was acquitted. As we have seen, he was ordered to sit with the other 125 bishops who were arriving in Rome day by day for the council and to give judgment with the rest.

Indeed, on 17 September of the following year, 680, a council was held in England called the Council of Hæthfelth, after its location. Bacchinius, unaware that Bede was using the Caesarean indiction, improperly departs from Pagius, who is correct. At this council Martin’s council was received, and a profession of faith was made. Bede writes (*Hist. Angl.*, book IV, chapter 18):

> “The venerable John, archchanter of the Church of Saint Peter and abbot of the monastery of blessed Martin, who had recently come from Rome at the command of Pope Agatho, was present at this synod and jointly confirmed the decrees of the Catholic faith.”

Bede also states in the same chapter that the principal reason John was sent to England was to investigate the faith of that island. He further relates that John later died on his return journey to Rome and that the decrees of the synod were carried to the city by another person.

Nothing concerning discipline was done at that council, for it had been disturbed by royal command. The bishops therefore had to overlook it. This explains why Saint Wilfrid is not mentioned, although his innocence and holiness were known both to Archbishop Theodore, to the other English bishops, and finally even to Ecgfrid himself, despite Wilfrid’s expulsion through the jealousy of Queen Ermenburga.

As for Wilfrid himself, while John was departing for England, Wilfrid remained in Rome by order of the pope and attended the council held there in 680. Eddius, Bede, Malmesbury, and Eadmer preserved for us the splendid testimony that he gave there on behalf of himself and his island, in these words:

> “Wilfrid, the bishop beloved of God, of the city of York, appealing to the apostolic see concerning his case, and absolved by that authority from matters certain and uncertain, and seated with 125 other fellow bishops “in synodo judicii sede” (‘in the synod’s judicial seat’) [Eadmer: “in synodi judiciaria sede” (‘in the judicial seat of the synod’)], confessed the true and Catholic faith and confirmed it by a written declaration [Eadmer: ‘and confirmed it by a subscription’] on behalf of the whole northern part of Britain and of the islands of Ireland, inhabited by the peoples of the English, Britons, Scots, and Picts.”

After this Roman synod had concluded, the legates were not sent immediately to Constantinople, for the professions of faith from beyond the mountains were awaited. Although Anastasius teaches that Agatho did this as soon as possible—and that he did not delay arranging it—once I learned, especially from the exiled Martin, that the journey from Rome to Constantinople took two months, or at most a few additional days, I see that the legates were sent only at the beginning of July 680 and arrived at Constantinople on 10 September, according to recent learned writers. Thus the events beyond the mountains were awaited for more than three months.

The legates were not sent until a full year of Agatho’s pontificate had elapsed. But whether they arrived then or not, the legates of the councils of Gaul took part in the Roman council, as is clear from the synodal letter brought to Constantinople by Agatho’s legates: two bishops and the deacon Taurinus; and one legate of the British synod, which had not yet been held, namely Wilfrid.

If they undertook the office of legates through private letters, they are to be understood as legates of their own synods. If not, it is probable that they were declared legates by the pope himself, who had been thoroughly instructed by these bishops concerning the faith of Gaul and Britain.

There can certainly be no doubt that they subscribed as legates of their own synods, and even less doubt that the correct faith was not yet known anywhere, as the synodal letter itself testifies:

> “And especially because, in the midst of the peoples both of the Lombards and Slavs, as well as of the Franks, Gauls, Goths, and Britons, many of our fellow servants are known to exist who do not cease to labor earnestly to learn what is being done in the matter of the apostolic faith. Insofar as they remain united with us in harmony of faith and think in agreement with us, they can be of great benefit; but, God forbid, if they suffer any scandal in a matter of faith, they are found to be equally hostile and opposed.”

Moreover, both the Gallic bishops and Wilfrid call themselves in their subscriptions legates of a synod established throughout the provinces of Gaul or throughout Britain, and these statements certainly agree with the synodal letter.

Now that I have narrated what bears upon our subject, it remains for me to show that these matters accord with the see of Agatho, which, contrary to the opinion of modern writers, I have argued must be begun in the year 679 [Col. 0825D].

Saint Agatho was consecrated pope on 26 June 679. Not long afterward, through Epiphanius, the *gloriosus a secretis*, he received the imperial letter that Pogonatus had sent in August of the previous year to his predecessor Donus. It is not known whether it was returned to Agatho. It is uncertain whether the delay of eight months was caused by the emperor, by the pope’s illness, or perhaps by both.

According to this imperial letter, which concerned the convocation of the Sixth General Council against the Monothelites, Saint Agatho instructed all the bishops of Italy by letter to come to Rome as soon as possible. Once they had assembled, he intended to define the article of faith then under dispute and to send his definition to the East, confirmed by the synod, through his legates. These legates would preside in his name at the general council and ensure that the same definition was established there.

The bishops obeyed the apostolic commands, and a large part of them was already residing at Rome in October, when Wilfrid’s case was examined synodally [Col. 0826A]. Deodatus, bishop of Toul, who had recently come from Gaul with Wilfrid, was also present.

In the same month it was decided that John the abbot should be sent to Britain. Through his agency and in his presence, the Council of Hæthfelth was held in England the following year, 680.

Before this English council, however, a council of 125 bishops was held at Rome on 27 March of the same year. Although everything was ready, the legates were detained at Rome for at least another three months, in expectation of the return from beyond the mountains of those whom Agatho had sent to discover whether all peoples everywhere rejected the Monothelite depravity. In this way, with the confirmation of the entire Western patriarchate, the whole East and the general council of the entire Catholic world—at which the same Roman pontiff would preside through his legates—might decree the true faith defined by Agatho.

Since those men did not return at the appropriate time, Agatho finally ordered the legates to depart for Constantinople with his letters and the synodal letter. All who had taken part in the council subscribed that synodal letter. The rest is sufficiently clear [Col. 0826B].

Thus, in agreement with the manuscript and printed codices of Anastasius, and supported also by the authority of catalogues and highly reputable ancient authors, I overturn the opinion of modern writers that clings to the exceedingly corrupt date of the first Roman council. Whether I have undertaken this correctly will be shown by the reading of the learned dissertations of those same writers, especially Pagius, whom one will see entering upon a new path and being delayed at every step by obstacles that he attempted to overcome by criticizing the whole of antiquity.

[Note: [Col. 0826B]

**No. 140, line 1.**—Agatho, a Sicilian by nationality. Son of Pannonius Amon, from the fortress of Aquila in the Sicilian valley, in the province of Further Abruzzo; a monk of the order of Saint Equitius and cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church under the emperor Constantine V, Pogonatus Augustus. He occupied the see for two years and six months. He was consecrated on the seventh day before the Ides of June, on a Sunday, in the year of Christ 679, the eighty-second pope reigning in the Christian era.

**No. 145, line 1.**—“With the synod in session.” This is the Sixth General Council, of 289 bishops, added to the Councils of Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the two Councils of Constantinople, upon which the whole of Christian faith was founded.

The First Council was held at Nicaea by 318 Fathers, under Pope Sylvester and the emperor Constantine the Great, against Arius, who posited different substances within the Trinity.

The Second was held at Constantinople by 150 Fathers, during the pontificate of Pope Damasus and the reign of the emperor Gratian, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God.

The Third was held at Ephesus by 200 Fathers, under Pope Celestine and the emperor Theodosius the Younger, against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Nestorius called the Virgin merely the mother of a human being, since he made one person belong to the flesh and another to the divinity, and taught separately that one was the Son of God and the other the son of man [Col. 0826D].

The Fourth was held at Chalcedon, a city opposite Byzantium, by 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo I and the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople. Eutyches did not hesitate to assert that, after assuming human nature, Christ did not consist of two natures but was contained solely within the divine nature.

The Fifth was held at Constantinople against Theodore and all the heretics who said that the Virgin Mary had given birth only to a human being, not to God and man. At this synod it was established that the blessed Virgin should be called *Theotokos*, “God-bearer,” because she gave birth to true God and man.

The Third Council of Constantinople followed these, against the Monothelites, under Agatho, concerning whom Anastasius writes here.]

[Note: [Col. 0826D]

**ANNOTATION OF THOMAS ACETUS.**

**No. 140, line 1.**—“A Sicilian by nationality.” It is established among all authorities that Calabria was called by the name Sicily, and that the kings of Calabria and Sicily were styled kings of both Sicilies. Indeed, in earlier centuries part of Calabria, the part nearest Pharos, was called by the name Sicily, as is clear from Thucydides, book III, who describes Messana and Rhegium as the wealthiest cities of Sicily.

This led certain writers, confused by the name, to assign some pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church who belonged to Calabria to Sicily, without distinguishing from which Sicily they came. One of the pontiffs wrongly transferred to Sicily was Agatho, who was Rhegian. This may be seen in Marafictus, *Chronicle of Calabria*, book I.]

[Note: [Col. 0827A]

**No. 140, line 9.**—“And he sent Abundantius of Paternus.” After the barbarians who had ravaged the Roman Empire had been subdued, Constantine Pogonatus, in order to establish peace in the Church, which had already been torn apart for many years by the Monothelite heresy, sent a letter to Pope Donus, whom he still believed to be alive, asking him to send men equipped with the authority of the apostolic see, through whom the heresy might be overthrown at the universal synod to be convened at Constantinople.

But when Donus had died, the letter was delivered to Saint Agatho. After he had convened at Rome a council of 125 bishops, the vote of the Fathers selected John, bishop of Porto; Abundantius, bishop of Paternus; and John, bishop of Rhegium or Rhegion, to go to Constantinople as the synod’s legates and bring the Monothelite controversy to an end.

Therefore the others whom our author lists confusedly—namely the priests Theodore and George, the deacon John, the subdeacon Constantine, and the monks—do not belong to the legation sent by the Roman synod to the emperor, but to another legation that Saint Agatho sent to Constantinople in his own name.

The priest Theodore of Ravenna, whom Anastasius also mentions in this passage, acted in place of Theodore, archbishop of Ravenna. All this is clear both from the first session and from the subscriptions of the same Sixth Universal Council [Col. 0827C].

These two legations departed together, as we understand from the letter of the same emperor Constantine to George, bishop of Constantinople, in which the following words are read:

> “Agatho, the most holy pope, recently ordained in the apostolic see of the aforementioned ancient Rome, receiving such pious imperial letters from us, has now sent Theodore and George, priests beloved of God, and John, the deacon beloved of God, clothed with his own person; and in the name of his entire council, John, Abundantius, and John, venerable bishops, together with the other clergy and monks.”

Moreover, in the letter that Agatho sent to Constantine through his legates, which was read in the Fourth Session of the Sixth Synod, there is a notable passage that greatly helps to remove every suspicion of the Monothelite heresy from Pope Honorius. I gladly transfer it into this annotation:

> “For this is the rule of true faith,” says the most holy pontiff, after vigorously combating the error of the Monothelites, “which this spiritual mother of your most tranquil empire, the apostolic Church of Christ, has truthfully maintained and defended in prosperity and adversity alike. Through the grace of almighty God she will be shown never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor, corrupted by heretical innovations, to have succumbed. Rather, as she received it from her founders, the leaders of Christ’s apostles, from the beginning of the Christian faith, she remains undefiled to the very end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, which he declared in the holy Gospels to the Prince of his disciples: ‘Peter, Peter,’ he said, ‘behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you as one sifts wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.’
>
> “Let your tranquil Clemency therefore consider that the Lord and Savior of all, whose faith this is, who promised that Peter’s faith would not fail, instructed him to strengthen his brothers. It has always been known to all that the apostolic pontiffs, my predecessors, confidently did this. Though my littleness is unequal and least among them, nevertheless, for the ministry entrusted to me by divine favor, I desire to follow in their footsteps.”

With what confidence could Saint Agatho have asserted that none of the Roman pontiffs had departed from orthodox faith if Honorius had embraced the same Monothelite heresy that Agatho condemned in his letter to the emperor and confirmed in his own writing?

**No. 145, line 17.**—“But Macarius with his supporters.” Anastasius reports that Macarius, patriarch of Antioch and leader of the Monothelites, together with his adherents who were then still alive, was sent to Rome to live there in exile.

But since it is nowhere read that the emperors of the East ever assigned Rome as the place of Macarius’s exile, the reason why Macarius and his companions were sent to Rome must certainly be established as something other than what Anastasius describes. They were not sent to live in exile in the city, but to pursue the appeal that Macarius and the others infected with the same heresy had lodged before the Roman pontiff.

This is stated in the emperor’s *sacra* to Leo II. After writing that Macarius and his Monothelite companions had been stripped of priestly dignity by the General Council, Constantine adds:

> “They all jointly prayed our Serenity in written petitions that we should send them to your Beatitude. Thus we acted, and we sent them to you, entrusting their entire case to your paternal judgment.”

If anyone, together with the most learned Baronius, argues that this letter from Constantine to Leo II is a forgery, I do not refute him at present. Nevertheless, he must regard it as no less certain that Macarius and those who had fallen away from the faith of the Fathers concerning the two wills of Christ were sent to Rome to be subjected to the judgment of the apostolic see [Col. 0828C].

Indeed, in the letter that Constantine sent to the Roman synod through the same legates sent by the synod to Constantinople, the same thing is asserted concerning Macarius and his companions in these words:

> “By the common judgment of this universal assembly they were rejected from priestly dignity and handed over to the examination of the most holy pope.”

Anastasius then narrates the condemnation of Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria, and of Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, patriarchs of Constantinople, who had professed Monothelitism and had already died. He relates specifically the erasure of their names from the diptychs and of their images from the church paintings.

For in the seventh century it was established as a solemn custom of the Churches not only to write the names of orthodox bishops in the diptychs, according to ancient practice, but also, as a mark of honor, to paint their images in basilicas, in their porticoes or at their doors. The learned Bacchinius observes this in his notes to the Life of Bonus, bishop of Ravenna, who lived in this seventh century.]

[Note: [Col. 0828D]

**No. 140, line 9.**—“And he sent Abundantius of Paternus, etc.” Agatho not only held a council at Rome against the Monothelites; he also ordered synods to be assembled in various regions where the Monothelite heresy was to be condemned—in Italy, Gaul, and England—as is clear from the letters of Agatho to the emperor cited shortly above.

The Gallican and Milanese synods preceded the Roman synod. At the former, Felix of Arles, Adeodatus or Deodatus of Toul, or of the Leuci—of whom we have just spoken—and Taurinus, deacon of the Church of Toulon, were chosen to attend the Roman synod. At that synod the orthodox faith was to be confirmed, the Monothelite heresy condemned, and a legation to Constantinople for the Ecumenical Council appointed [Col. 0829A].

The Milanese synod was convened at approximately the same time as the Gallican one. It was presided over by Saint Mansuetus, bishop of Milan, and the same Mansuetus was delegated from it to the Roman synod together with Anastasius, bishop of Ticinum.

This synod also wrote a synodal letter to the emperor. It is found in volume VI of the Councils, page 601, and, as Paul the Deacon says (*History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 4), it gave substantial support to Agatho’s Roman synod.

As for the English council, it was summoned by Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, so that what had been decreed elsewhere in Gaul and Italy against the Monothelites might also be established in England. It belongs to the year of Christ 680, for Bede writes in his Recapitulation:

> “In the year 680 a synod concerning the Catholic faith was held in the field of Hæthfelth, with Archbishop Theodore presiding; John, the Roman abbot, was present.”

It is true that Bede writes in book IV, chapter 17, that this council was held on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the eighth indiction. This misled Baronius and others: because the eighth indiction begins on the Kalends of September in the year 679, they believed that the council had been held on 17 September of that year.

But Bede was there using the Constantinian indiction, which begins on 24 September. He therefore confirms what he wrote in the Recapitulation, namely that the council was convened in 680, specifically on 17 September. From it, as the aforementioned Bede says in chapter 18:

> “A copy of the Catholic faith of the English was carried to Rome and received with the greatest gratitude by the apostolic pope and all who heard or read it.”

In Anastasius it is erroneously read that the legates of Pope Agatho and of the apostolic see entered Constantinople on 10 November, in the ninth indiction—that is, in the year 680. Yet the first session began on 7 November of that year, in the ninth indiction, with the legates of Pope Agatho present. This could not have happened if the legates had entered the imperial city only on the tenth day of that month [Col. 0829C].

In Anastasius, therefore, “10 November” must be corrected to “10 September.”

Anastasius then adds:

> “And he [that is, the emperor] granted them a period for reviewing the writings and provided them with everything necessary for their support and expenses, in the house called Palcidia, on the eighteenth day of the aforementioned month [that is, September]. On Sunday they were summoned in procession to the holy Mother of God at Blachernae, with such honor that even from the palace the imperial piety sent richly caparisoned horses with an escort and thus received them.”

The legates therefore arrived on 10 September. On 18 September the emperor provided them with everything necessary for their support. When Sunday arrived, namely 23 September, they were summoned in procession.

**No. 141, line 6.**—“The aforementioned legates of the apostolic see, who had been sent,” etc. On the same day on which the legates arrived and were sent by the Western synod, the emperor sent a new imperial letter to George, patriarch of Constantinople, for arranging the affairs of the synod and summoning to it the bishops subject to the throne of Constantinople. It is said to have been dated on the fourth day before the Ides of September.

Another error in Anastasius must also be corrected. He says that on 22 November the legates of the apostolic see were received in the basilica. Since the acts of the synod state that the first session, with the apostolic legates present, began on 7 November, this cannot be true.

The text of Anastasius, rather than the acts themselves, has been corrupted. The author of Baronius’s critical work infers this from the chronological notes of the earlier sessions. The second session, he says, was held on 10 November; the third on the 13th; the fourth on the 15th of the same month; and the fifth finally on 7 December, as the acts record.

The error therefore lies in Anastasius. Otherwise all the dates of the earlier sessions would have been corrupted, which is unbelievable, since the contrary is asserted without foundation.

[Col. 0830A] Besides the legates of the apostolic see and of Agatho, who presided over it, and the delegates of the Western synod, the following attended the synod: two Eastern patriarchs, George of Constantinople and Macarius of Antioch; Peter, vicar of the patriarch of Alexandria; George, a priest representing the Church of Jerusalem; and with them a very large number of Eastern bishops, although the writers do not agree sufficiently concerning their number.

Photius, in his little book on synods, counts 170; Theophanes and Cedrenus count 289; but only 166 signatures are found appended to the final synodal session.

The emperor Constantine Pogonatus also attended, together with certain magistrates selected by him. Hence the council is said to have been held under the presidency of the most pious and Christ-loving great emperor Constantine.

Although the apostolic legates presided over it, the most religious prince may nevertheless be said in a certain sense to have presided, as defender of the faith and guardian of the judicial order [Col. 0830B], but not as judge of controversies concerning the faith.

The magistrates who are frequently called “most glorious judges” in the synod were present as protectors of the synod and of the freedom of the parties.

**No. 142, line 2.**—“With Constantine in the chair,” etc. Thus the Sixth Ecumenical Council began at Constantinople on 7 November 680, in the third year of Pope Agatho, the twenty-seventh year of the emperor Constantine Pogonatus, and the thirteenth year after his consulship, in the Trullo—that is, in the *secretarium* of the palace or basilica called the Trullo.

Ducange explains what the Trullo was in *Constantinopolis Christiana*, paragraph 32 and following of book III, while describing the Church of Saint Sophia. The council was held in that building, which Anastasius calls a basilica in his account of Agatho and a palace in his account of Leo II.

The Roman pontiff’s legates sat on the emperor’s left; Macarius of Antioch and George of Constantinople on his right. Nothing contrary to ecclesiastical custom was committed in this arrangement of the session. At the Council of Nicaea, Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, also sat first on the right, while Hosius and the other legates of Saint Sylvester sat on the left.

At the Council of Chalcedon the legates of Saint Leo sat on the left, while Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, sat on the right, with the Gospels placed in the middle. Nor is this surprising, since in the Church the left is more honorable than the right, as we observed when discussing the Council of Nicaea.

In the middle of the synod, according to ancient custom, the most holy Gospels of God were placed upon an ornamented throne, thereby representing Christ himself. The legates of the Apostolic See then began to speak and explained the reason for their arrival. They complained that four bishops of the see of Constantinople—Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—as well as Cyrus of Alexandria and Theodore, bishop of Pharan, had introduced a new heresy into the Church concerning one will and one operation in Christ.

Accordingly, at the emperor’s command, the leading representative of that faction, Macarius, bishop of Antioch, gave the response on behalf of the opposing side to the legates of the Apostolic See. Together with others speaking for the see of Constantinople, he replied that they had introduced no novelty, but had instead put forward what had been received from the holy synods and the holy Fathers. After hearing them, the emperor declared that he would not permit himself to remain present at the synod unless they proved everything that they had proposed. Macarius promised that he would do so. Thus, in this first session and in the two that followed, nothing else was done except that the acts of three ecumenical synods—the synods of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the Fifth—were read.

In the fourth session, two dogmatic letters were read: one from Agatho and the other from the Western synod, addressed to the emperor Constantine. In them, the Catholic doctrine of two wills and two operations in Christ was demonstrated from the rules of faith. In the fifth and sixth sessions—the latter held on 12 February of the following year, that is, in the year of Christ 681—Macarius, patriarch of Antioch and the most obstinate Monothelite, produced testimonies of the holy Fathers that appeared to assert one will in Christ. The legates of the Apostolic See, however, replied that Macarius and his associates had mutilated these testimonies and fraudulently transferred to Christ’s will what the Fathers had clearly said about the divine will.

In the seventh session, held on 13 February, the legates recited testimonies of the holy Fathers who proclaimed two wills and two operations. The emperor then asked George, patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius of Antioch whether they agreed with the definition of Pope Agatho. They requested a copy of the definition and time to compare the passages cited from the holy Fathers with the books of the Church of Constantinople.

In the eighth session, held on 7 March, George of Constantinople, questioned by the emperor, replied that after carefully collating the texts with authentic copies, he had learned that the testimonies of the holy Fathers cited in Agatho’s reports agreed with them. He therefore declared that he accepted the reports of Pope Agatho and of the Western synod and followed the same faith.

George gave an outstanding proof of orthodoxy in that same session when he requested that the name of Pope Vitalian be restored to the sacred diptychs. It had been removed through the evil practices of Macarius of Antioch, and the emperor granted his request. The synod commended his faith with a festive acclamation: “Many years to George, the orthodox patriarch.” All the bishops subject to the see of Constantinople declared together with George that they shared his belief, accepted Agatho’s letter, professed the faith, and anathematized the heresy.

In that same eighth session, Macarius of Antioch, together with the abbot Stephen, a most wicked Monothelite, not only obstinately persisted in his error but also brazenly declared that he would not abandon it even if he were cut limb from limb and thrown into the sea. Indeed, he shamelessly boasted that, in order to establish his heresy, he had corrupted the writings of the Fathers. The entire synod therefore broke out with these words:

“He has plainly shown himself to be a heretic. Anathema to the new Dioscorus. Let such a man be deposed. Cast out the new Dioscorus. Evil years to the new Apollinarius. He deserves to be excluded from the episcopate. Strip him of the pallium placed around him.”

Finally, in the ninth session, held on the following day, 8 March, a sentence of deposition was pronounced both against Macarius and against the aforementioned abbot Stephen. The dignity of the bishops and clerics who had renounced the error was preserved, on condition that they present written professions of faith to the synod under oath. After the synod, the emperor sent Macarius of Antioch, the abbot Stephen, Polychronius, who will be discussed below, Anastasius the Monothelite, and other disciples of Macarius into exile at Rome, as Anastasius relates. On this matter, see what will be said under Leo II.

[Col. 0831D] In the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth sessions, held in the same month of March, the written recantations of certain men who were retracting their error were received. The letter of Sophronius, formerly bishop of Jerusalem, to Sergius of Constantinople was also read and approved; likewise, the writings of Macarius and other heretics were read but condemned. When the nobles, or magistrates, asked whether Macarius should be restored to his see if he happened to retract his error, the holy synod declared that the divine rule absolutely did not permit him to sit any longer in the teacher’s chair. The letters of Sergius, the leader of the Monothelites, to Cyrus and to Honorius were also read, as was the first letter of Honorius, Roman pontiff, to Sergius.

In the thirteenth session, held on 28 March, sentence was pronounced against the Monothelite heretics, specifically against Sergius, Pyrrhus, Peter, and Paul, formerly bishops of Constantinople, and likewise against Cyrus of Alexandria and Theodore, bishop of Pharan. Honorius the pope was condemned together with them—not indeed as a heretic, but as a supporter of heretics, as we demonstrated in our treatment of his pontificate. In the same session, the second letter of Pope Honorius to Sergius was read. The letter of Pyrrhus of Constantinople to Pope John IV was also read; because it appeared to support the impiety of the Monothelites, it was handed over to the fire in the presence of the synod.

The synodal letters of Thomas, John, and Constantine, formerly patriarchs of Constantinople and successors of the Monothelite Peter, were likewise reread. Nothing contrary to the orthodox faith was found in them. Therefore the holy synod decreed:

“These three men of holy memory—Thomas, John, and Constantine—are to remain in unity and are to be recited in the sacred diptychs of the holy churches, since they were found in all things spotless and beyond reproach with respect to our right Christian faith.”

In the fourteenth session, held on 2 April, the written statements of Menas, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, to Pope Vigilius, and the letters of Vigilius to the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora were read. The legates of the Apostolic See exclaimed that these were not by Vigilius and that the book of the acts of the Fifth Synod had been falsified. When the codices of that Fifth Synod were examined, in which those letters of Vigilius appeared, it became clear that they had formerly been absent from the ancient copies and that three new gatherings had been added not long before at the beginning of the synod.

In the seventh session, which contains those two letters of Vigilius, the fifteenth gathering had been altered, and a four-leaf section without a title had been inserted before the sixteenth gathering; in that section were found the two statements, or letters, said to be by Vigilius. For this reason the Fathers decreed that the papyrus volume which had been falsified should be cancelled at the places where the additions had been made, and they pronounced an anathema against the statements said to have been written by Vigilius to Justinian and Theodora.

But, as Baluzius says in the new *Collection of the Councils*, volume I, in the preface to the acts of the Fifth Synod, this does not assign authority to those letters of Vigilius. They are not called false, but falsified and corrupted by those who wished to misuse their testimonies to confirm their opinion concerning one will and one operation in Christ. This, then, is why they were accused of falsification: namely, because the section dealing with one operation in Christ had been added by the Monothelites. Baluzius, already cited, discusses this matter more fully.

In the fifteenth session, held on 26 April, Polychronius, a presbyter and monk, disciple of Macarius of Antioch and of the abbot Stephen, was summoned into the public hearing and questioned about the faith. He revealed himself not only as a Monothelite but also as a magician and a public impostor. He requested that a tablet bearing this proposition—“Whoever does not confess one will and one God-human operation is not a Christian”—be placed upon a dead man, promising that he would raise him in order to prove the truth of his faith, which he falsely claimed had already been confirmed by heavenly visions.

When Polychronius had drawn a large crowd after him by this promise of a miracle, the synod was compelled, lest the sacrament of the faith be placed in danger by the insolence of a most frivolous man, to undergo—even though the condition was disgraceful—the proposed test. In the presence of the Fathers, the emperor, and the entire people, the corpse of a recently deceased man was placed before Polychronius. For several hours Polychronius played the part of the treacherous impostor, whispering into the dead man’s ears; at last he confessed his inability. Then the people cried out:

“Anathema to the new Simon. Anathema to Polychronius, the deceiver of the people.”

After this he was brought back into the synod’s meeting place. Since he refused to renounce the heresy, he was stripped of every priestly rank and office as a deceiver of the people and an obvious heretic, and was placed under the bond of anathema.

[Col. 0833A] In the sixteenth session, which is recorded as having been held on 9 August, another heretic named Constantine, a presbyter of the Church of Apamea, received permission to speak. He declared that he had come to instruct the synod and proposed a certain compromise by which the Monothelites and the Catholics might be reconciled: namely, that Christ should be said to have two operations but one will, in such a way that Christ would be asserted to have abandoned the human will together with the flesh and blood at the time of the cross.

The synod rejected and condemned this assertion as belonging to the Manichaeans, and Constantine himself received the same sentence of condemnation. In the same session, George, bishop of Constantinople, requested that, if possible, the persons of his predecessors Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter not be anathematized by name. The synod rejected his request. George assented to the synod.

Acclamations followed:

“Many years to the orthodox and peaceful emperor Constantine, the new Theodosius, the new Marcian, the new Justinian, preserver of the right faith.”

“Many years to Agatho, the Roman pope,” and so forth.

Anathemas were added against each heretic and supporter of heretics by name: Theodore of Pharan, Sergius, Cyrus, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, Aspergius, metropolitan of Perge in Pamphylia; and, finally, against all heretics and those who support heretics.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth sessions, held on 11 and 16 September, the definition of faith was issued and promulgated, confirmed by the subscriptions of all the Fathers. Afterward the emperor asked whether it had been promulgated with the subscription of all the bishops. They all cried out together:

“We all believe this; there is one faith. We all hold the same belief. We all subscribed in agreement and acceptance. We all believe in orthodoxy. This is the faith of the apostles; this is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the orthodox.”

The acclamations were then repeated, and an intensified anathema was pronounced against Theodore of Pharan, Sergius and Honorius, Pyrrhus and Paul, Cyrus and Peter, Macarius, Stephen and Polychronius, and all who had proclaimed, or proclaimed and taught, or would proclaim, one will and one operation in the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, our God.

After the emperor had thanked the holy synod for extinguishing the heresy, a speech of acclamation composed for his majesty was publicly read. In it the Fathers also asked him to confirm the council by an edict, so that no one might contradict what had been done or undertake a new controversy.

By unanimous agreement the Fathers also wrote a synodal report to Agatho, the supreme pontiff, and sent it with the acts of the synod through their legates. They asked him to confirm the synod and its canonical decrees by apostolic authority, in these words:

“We have clearly proclaimed with you the splendid light of the orthodox faith. We ask your paternal holiness to confirm it once more through your honorable rescripts.”

But before either the emperor’s and the synod’s letters or the synod itself could be conveyed to Rome, Pope Agatho had already died. We shall therefore speak of his confirmation under Leo II, his successor. On the heresy of the Monothelites, see the discussion of Pope Honorius, no. 12 and following.

It must now be shown, on the authority of the author of the *Baronian Criticism*, that the acts of the Sixth Synod, as they are now preserved, have not been interpolated, contrary to the opinion of Baronius. When he saw that Saint Maximus the Martyr and other men of great piety and authority had removed the stain of heresy from Honorius, yet found him implicated by an anathema in the acts of this council, Baronius supposed that those acts had not come down to us in an authentic form. He persuaded many learned men of this opinion.

But, as the same author of the *Criticism* says, it does not now seem possible to call into question the authenticity of the acts of the Sixth Synod as we possess them. This is shown by Combefisius in his *History of the Monothelites*, in the *Apology for the Acts of the Sixth Synod*; Lupus in his dissertation *On the Sixth General Synod*, concerning the eighteenth session; the recent anonymous author of the *Inquiry into the History of the Monothelites*, inquiry 6; Natalis Alexander in dissertation 2 of the seventh century; Garnerius in the appendix to the notes on chapter 2 of the *Roman Pontiffs’ Book of Days*; and others.

Baronius says that there was no reason for Honorius to be condemned, since his two letters contain nothing that is not Catholic. But in our treatment of his pontificate we showed that, although he was free from error, he was nevertheless condemned at the Sixth Synod because he had sinned through that policy of his by which he wished silence to be maintained concerning one or two operations, even though at that time religious necessity required that the two operations be openly defended.

[Note: [Col. 0834A]

No. 140, line 5.—“Here he received the imperial command,” etc. Constantine Pogonatus, an orthodox prince who was striving to restore peace to the Church, which had been troubled by the Monothelites, judged that the best way of settling the matter would be to hold a general council at Constantinople. Accordingly, he sent a letter to Donus, which was afterward delivered to Agatho, his successor. In it the emperor urged the Roman pontiff, in accordance with his paternal concern, to confound the demon who was the author of the division by which the Church was then being afflicted. He then said:

“We exhort your paternal Beatitude to send men clothed with the authority of your Apostolic See and of its council, possessing the full authority thereof, so that, meeting with the most holy patriarch presently here, etc., they may search out the truth and adhere to it through the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

(*Letter of the Emperor Constantine to Donus.*)

So that the pontiff might carry out this pious proposal of the emperor, he ordered councils to be held in various provinces of the West and convened one at Rome. From it he chose the legates of the Holy See and those who were to represent the Western patriarchates at the general council that was to be held at Constantinople. The office of legate was entrusted to two presbyters and a deacon of the Roman Church. The bishops of Porto, Reggio, and Paterno were ordered to represent the Western patriarchate. (*Letters of Agatho and of the Roman Council to the Council of Constantinople, Sixth Council, session 4; and Constantine’s letter to George, archbishop of Constantinople, Sixth Council, part I.*)

He then sent two letters to the emperor: one in his own name as pontiff and successor of Saint Peter, and the other in the name of the Western Church, represented by the council held at Rome. In the former he explained what authority he had delegated to his representatives:

“They are to make it their sole concern to explain what this their spiritual mother—the Church of the empire established by God—believes and proclaims, in which they too have been instructed from infancy. They have been charged only with this: that they presume to add, remove, or alter absolutely nothing, but sincerely narrate the tradition of this Apostolic See as it was established by the apostolic pontiffs who preceded us.”

(*Agatho’s First Letter to the Augusti.*)

As for the controversy concerning the two natures, he affirmed that the tradition of the Apostolic See had never differed from the Gospel:

“We affirm all things as twofold in the one and same Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, according to the evangelical tradition. We affirm that our same Lord Jesus Christ has in himself, just as he has natures, natural wills and operations—namely, divine and human: a divine will and operation which he possesses eternally in common with the consubstantial Father, and a human will and operation which he assumed from us temporally together with our nature.

“This apostolic teaching was handed down by the blessed apostle Peter, whose true confession was revealed by the Father in heaven. With his protection assisting it, this Apostolic Church of his has never deviated from the path of truth in any matter of error, nor has it yielded, corrupted by heretical novelties. Rather, from the beginning of the Christian faith, it received this teaching from its founders, the chief apostles of Christ, and to this day it remains in uncorrupted faith, according to the Lord’s own promise which he declared in the holy Gospels to the chief of his disciples.”

(*Ibid.*)

Then, having confirmed the indefectibility of the Holy See by the words of Jesus Christ—“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may never fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brethren”—he warned the emperor to observe that, in accordance with these promises of the Savior to Saint Peter, his successors, the Roman pontiffs, had always confirmed the other bishops in the Catholic faith, as was known to everyone. He therefore wished to follow the example of his predecessors.

For this reason he asserted the truth of the two wills and two operations of Jesus Christ, adducing authorities from Holy Scripture, the councils, and the Fathers, which he interpreted at great length. He cited the heretics who had dared to think otherwise and showed the variations within their own teaching. He then urged the emperor to defend the justice of his cause and those whom the Holy See was sending to defend it.

Finally, concerning the archbishop of Constantinople, he spoke as follows:

“If the bishop of the Church of Constantinople chooses to hold and proclaim with us this rule of apostolic doctrine, there will be abundant peace for those who love the name of God, and no stumbling block of dissension will remain. But if—and may this be far from happening—he prefers to embrace the novelty recently introduced by others and to entangle himself in doctrines alien to the rule of orthodox truth and to our apostolic faith, rather than avoid them as harmful to souls, he should know what account he will have to render for such contempt at the divine judgment of Christ. My apostolic predecessors have continually exhorted and admonished him concerning this, but he has delayed until now.”

(*Ibid.*)

In the second letter, written in the name of the Fathers of the council, the Fathers likewise testified that the teaching of the Holy See concerning the two wills and operations of Jesus Christ was inviolably to be preserved. They declared that those who had departed from the Apostolic See to attend the council had not come to debate doubtful matters, but to present certain and immutable doctrines:

“We have determined to send representatives from the order of our humility to the footsteps of your strength, which is protected by God. They are to offer the suggestion of all of us—that is, of all the bishops throughout the northern and western regions—in which we have already set forth a preliminary confession of our apostolic faith. They have not come, however, to dispute uncertain matters, but to present certain and immutable doctrines in a concise definition.”

(*Synodal Letter of the Roman Council to the Augusti.*)

Then, declaring who were to be regarded as Catholics and who as heretics, they said:

“Whoever among the priests sincerely desires to proclaim with us the things contained in this confession of our humility, as one in agreement with our apostolic faith, we receive as spiritual brothers and as our fellow bishops. But those who refuse to confess these things, as enemies of the Catholic and apostolic confession, we judge to be liable to everlasting condemnation; nor do we permit such men ever to be received into the fellowship of our humility unless they have been corrected.”

(*Ibid.*)

From the testimonies cited it is evident that the Holy See defined and established the article of faith that was to become the subject of the decision to be made in the general council against the Monothelites. This is especially clear from the pope’s letter to the emperor, in which he indicated that he had charged his legates to follow exactly the tradition of the Holy See, which his predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, had always taught:

“They have been charged only to narrate sincerely the tradition of this Apostolic See, as it was established by the apostolic pontiffs who preceded us.”

He immediately explained what that tradition was: the two natural wills, and so forth.

“This is the tradition held by the apostolic Church of Christ, the mother of your empire.”

The entire Western Church declares the same thing when it says that those who were to represent it at the council carried with them a profession of faith and had been ordered not to dispute it at all, but to use it as a certain and immutable rule for defining the matter:

“We have already set forth a preliminary confession of our faith, so that they may present it in a concise definition as certain and immutable.”

Earlier it had said that this doctrine, derived from the source of the immeasurable light, had reached the Roman Church through the holy apostles Peter and Paul and had been spread from there through their successors, the Roman pontiffs, and preserved incorrupt throughout the provinces of the West and the North:

“The light which, from the true source of light, through the blessed ministers Peter and Paul, chief of the apostles, and their apostolic successors, has been preserved step by step down to our littleness. They are to offer the suggestion of all the bishops throughout the northern and western regions.”

No. 142, line 11.—“They introduced their books, various volumes, and the synods which they had falsified.” (*From the illustrious archbishop of Caesarea, Claudius Sommier, *History of Pontifical Dogma*, book VIII, chapter 12.*)

From the evidence of Agatho’s letters and of the Roman synod to Constantine Pogonatus, it can plainly be discerned that not even the slightest mark of Monothelite heresy can be attached to Pope Honorius. For if this pontiff had been, at the very least, a supporter of such an error, with what confidence could Saint Agatho have affirmed before the whole Church that no trace whatever, however slight, of error had ever been found in the Apostolic See, and that his predecessors had always confirmed the brethren in the faith of Saint Peter, which was never to fail, as everyone knew?

“This Apostolic Church of Peter has never deviated from the path of truth in any matter of error. He who promised that Peter’s faith would not fail instructed him to strengthen his brethren; and it is known to all that the apostolic pontiffs, the predecessors of my insignificance, have always done this.”

(*Letter of Agatho to Constantine, Sixth Council, session 4.*)

Hence the distinguished author rightly argues that Honorius’s letter, about which the modern writers have amassed so much material, was a response to another letter of Sergius that was entirely Catholic. I shall therefore present its examination, together with the observations of Father Desirant, which he gives in book VII, chapter 17 and following of his *History of Pontifical Dogma*, below, after I have, as promised, brought forward both the letter of Sergius and that of Honorius.

[Col. 0836C]

## Letter of Sergius

### 1

We are bound to you, most holy men, by such complete unanimity of spirit that we strive to have you, most sacred ones, present in all our counsels and actions. If the great distance between places did not separate us, we would do this every day, surrounding ourselves with the fortified and walled counsel of your honored and harmonious brotherhood. Nevertheless, since speech and writing grant us, without labor, what we desire, we shall immediately explain the matters for which we are writing:

### 2

Some time ago, when our lord and great emperor, strengthened by God, was leading an army against the Persians, on account of the struggles entrusted to him by God for the Christ-loving commonwealth, and had reached the regions of Armenia, one of the leaders of the impious faction of Severus, a certain Paul, accursed, appeared in those parts and approached His Piety. He put forward an argument on behalf of his wandering heresy.

His most pious and royal greatness—who, together with other gifts of God, had deserved to be enriched with knowledge of divine doctrines—refuted and exposed his depraved impiety and, as its true defender, set forth in opposition the right and immaculate doctrines of our holy Church. Among these he also mentioned one operation of Christ, our true God.

### 3

After some time, the same emperor, strengthened by God, arrived in the province of Lazica and remembered the dispute which, as we have said, he had held with that heretic Paul, in the presence of Cyrus, the most holy man who at that time held the metropolitan see of the same province of Lazica, but now governs great Alexandria.

When the aforementioned most holy man heard this, he replied to His Serenity that he did not know precisely whether it was necessary to assert one or two operations of Christ, our true God. Therefore, at the command of His Piety, that most holy man asked us by letter whether it was necessary to speak of one operation or two in our Savior Christ, and whether we knew of any holy and blessed Fathers who spoke of one operation.

### 4

Accordingly, in our reply we informed him of what lay within our knowledge. We also sent him the acclamatory discourse of Menas, formerly the most holy patriarch of this royal city preserved by God, which Menas had presented here to Vigilius, your predecessor of holy memory. It contained various testimonies of the Fathers concerning one operation and one will of our Savior Christ, our true God.

### 5

Nevertheless, in these replies of ours we promulgated nothing at all as our own, as you, most sacred and harmonious men, can readily know by rereading the copies of what was sent.

### 6

From that time onward, silence was observed concerning this question.

### 7

Shortly before this, through the cooperation of the grace of God, who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and prompted by the pious zeal of the most powerful and invincible great emperor, Cyrus, patriarch of the great city of Alexandria, our common brother and fellow priest of God, lovingly and modestly exhorted those in the great city of Alexandria who were languishing in the heresy of Eutyches and Dioscorus, and also of Severus and Julian—men hateful to God—to approach the Catholic Church.

After many discussions and labors, which he undertook in this matter with great prudence and a most salutary policy, he arranged, by heavenly grace, what he had hastened to accomplish. Certain doctrinal articles were established between the two parties. In these all who had previously been divided into different groups and had reckoned the heretics Dioscorus and Severus as their forefathers were united with the holy and only Catholic Church.

Now the entire Christ-loving people of Alexandria has become the flock of Christ, our true God, and almost all Egypt with them, as well as Thebaid, Libya, and the other regions belonging to the Egyptian administration. These regions, which formerly, as we have said, they regarded as divided into an immeasurable multitude of heresies, have now, by God’s good pleasure and through the zeal of the aforementioned most holy bishop of Alexandria, become all of one language and one voice, and in unity of spirit they confess the doctrines of the right Church.

Among the things said and established there is one article concerning one operation of Christ, our great God and Savior.

### 8

When these things had occurred, Sophronius, the venerable monk who, as we have learned by report, has been ordained bishop of Jerusalem—for up to this time we have not yet received his synodical letter in the customary manner—was then staying in Alexandria with the aforementioned most holy pope while he was arranging, as we have said, that admirable unity, by God’s good pleasure, among those who had formerly been heretics.

When Sophronius was treating these same articles with him, he opposed and contradicted the article concerning one operation, saying that it ought to be held that Christ our God had two operations.

### 9

The aforementioned most holy pope, especially when he produced testimonies of certain holy Fathers who, scattered through various short works, asserted one operation, also said, by way of further explanation, that our holy Fathers often, in order to win the salvation of many souls, when such questions arose, appeared to employ policies pleasing to God and appropriate to the circumstances. They did not agitate the finer points of the Church’s correct doctrines.

He also said that, in the present circumstances, when the salvation of so many thousands of peoples lay before them, it was necessary not to quarrel contentiously over this matter, because, as has been said, such an expression had also been used by certain holy Fathers, and nothing contrary to right faith was thereby harmed.

But Sophronius, beloved of God, in no way accepted such a policy.

### 10

Since he joined this matter to us in a letter from the same most holy fellow minister and continued to press the issue among us, urging that, after the union had been achieved, the expression “one operation” should be removed from such articles, we judged this very difficult.
