For how could it not be difficult and extremely burdensome, when removing and overturning it would destroy that entire harmony and unity which had been successfully established both in the great city of Alexandria and throughout all the subordinate provinces—regions which until then had never consented even to mention merely the name of our divine and praiseworthy pope Leo or of the holy, great, and universal Synod of Chalcedon, much less proclaim them with a glorious and great voice in the sacred mysteries of the Mass?

### 11

After we had held many discussions with the aforementioned venerable Sophronius on this subject, we finally exhorted him to produce testimonies of holy and approved Fathers—those, namely, whom we all commonly acknowledge as teachers and whose doctrines and law the holy Churches of God recognize—which explicitly and in their own words taught that two operations were to be spoken of in Christ.

But he was wholly unable to do this.

### 12

We, however, observing that a quarrel was beginning to flare up among certain people here and knowing that the divisions of heresies had always arisen from disputes of this kind, judged it necessary to devote every effort to calming and cutting off such a superfluous conflict of words.

### 13

We therefore wrote to the aforementioned most holy patriarch of Alexandria that, after he had, with God’s help, established unity with those who had long been in the process of returning, he should henceforth permit no one to speak of one or two operations in Christ our God.

Rather, in accordance with the teaching of the holy and universal councils, he should confess that the one and same only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the true God, operated both divinely and humanly, and that every operation proper to God and every operation proper to man proceeded indivisibly from the one incarnate God the Word and was referred to the one and same subject.

### 14

The reason was that, although the expression “one operation” had been used by certain holy Fathers, it nevertheless seemed foreign and disturbed the ears of some who suspected that it was being uttered for the destruction of the two natures of Christ our God, united without confusion according to hypostasis—a thing which has never happened and never existed.

Likewise, the expression “two operations” might scandalize many, since it had been put forward by none of the holy and approved teachers of the Church. Moreover, it entailed proclaiming two wills opposed to one another, as though God the Word wished the saving passion to be fulfilled, while his humanity opposed and resisted his will, thereby introducing two contrary wills. This is impious.

It is indeed impossible for two wills, simultaneously and contrary to one another with respect to the same thing, to subsist in one and the same underlying subject. For the salutary teaching of the Fathers who bear God has established as a matter worthy of careful attention that the Lord’s intellectually animated flesh never separately, and from its own appetite, carried out its natural movement contrary to the will of the Godhead united to it according to the subsistence of the divine Word; rather, it did so when, in the manner, and to the extent that God the Word himself willed. And, to put it more fully: just as our body is governed, ordered, and directed by our intellectual and rational soul, so also in the Lord Christ his entire human constitution was always moved in all things by the divinity of the Word himself and was subject to God’s movement.

According to Gregory of Nyssa, who says the following against Eunomius [Col. 0839B]:

> Insofar as the Son was God, he is certainly impassible and immortal. But if some suffering is spoken of him in the Gospel, he brought this about through his humanity, which received the suffering. For the Godhead truly accomplishes through the body that surrounds it the salvation of all, so that the suffering belongs to the flesh, but the operation to God.

Therefore, seeing that this dispute was beginning to flare up, we judged it necessary rather to follow always the statements of the holy Fathers and the definitions issued synodically. We should neither reduce to a universal dogmatic rule and law what was rarely said by certain Fathers who did not have this matter in mind, as though they were setting forth a clear and unambiguous doctrine concerning it—such as their statement about one operation—nor, again, should we proclaim as an ecclesiastical dogma the two operations that no reputable Fathers at all have stated, but which certain Fathers now put forward.

[Col. 0839C]

### 15

Finally, it was agreed and resolved that the venerable Sophronius mentioned above should henceforth initiate no discussion concerning either one or two operations, but should be satisfied with the aforesaid sound, careful, and well-trodden tradition and teaching of the holy Fathers.

### 16

Thus the frequently mentioned venerable man, content with these things and assuring us that he would observe them, asked that we also provide him with a written response concerning them, so that, as he said, he might show the letter to those who might perhaps wish to question him about the matter mentioned above. We gladly did so, and he indeed departed from there on these terms.

### 17

Recently, however, our most devout and God-crowned lord, residing in the city of Edessa, sent us a devout imperial letter commanding that we should extract those paternal testimonies contained in the dogmatic book, as has been said, composed by Menna of holy memory for Vigilius, most holy bishop, concerning one operation and one will, and that we should send these to his God-instructed serenity. We also carried this out.

But, remembering what had been stirred up earlier and knowing the disturbance that had begun from such agitation, we made a suggestion to his most devout serenity through our modest memorandum, and likewise in a written communication to the most excellent imperial sacellarius, explaining all the subtlety of this chapter, the things that we had undertaken in this matter, and that one ought not to scrutinize such an inquiry, but should remain within the well-worn teaching of the Fathers, which all unanimously confess concerning this question: namely, that the only-begotten Son of God, who is truly God and man at the same time, performs both divine and human acts, and that from the one and same incarnate Word of God, as we have already stated, every divine and human operation proceeds inseparably and indivisibly.

For Leo taught us this, plainly declaring:

> Each form acts in communion with the other what properly belongs to it.

In response to these matters we received from his most gentle authority a rescript of the pious command, containing provisions suitable for the preservation of his serenity by God.

### 18

Since all these things had proceeded in this way from the beginning, we judged it both reasonable and necessary to give your Fraternity and your unanimous Blessedness an account of the matters partly mentioned above.

### 16

Through the copies that have been sent by us, we also exhort you, most sacred brethren, to read all these things.

> **Note, reader:** It is clear from the letter of Honorius that Sergius did not send more than one copy. Therefore, in the genuine letter of Sergius, this passage must be read as follows: “Through the copy that has been sent by us to the aforesaid Sophronius, we also exhort you, most sacred brethren, to read all these things.”

### 20

And, continuing now also in the God-pleasing and most complete charity that is in you, if you find anything more or less than this, complete it through the grace given to you by God, and signify through your holy words, together with your desired welfare, whatever may seem good to you concerning these matters.]

[Col. 0840B]

## HONORIUS’S RESPONSE

### 1

We have received the letter of your Fraternity.

### 2

Through it we have learned that novel opinions and new questions of terminology have been introduced by a certain monk named Sophronius, now constituted bishop of the city of Jerusalem by popular report, against our brother Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, who was proclaiming to those converted from heresy one operation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### 3

When Sophronius therefore came to your Fraternity and laid down such a complaint, he was instructed in many ways and asked that what you had taught him should be disclosed to him in written words.

### 4

Having received a copy of the letter sent to that same Sophronius, and having observed that your Fraternity had written with sufficient foresight and care, we commend you for removing the novelty of the expression, which could generate scandal among the simple.

### 5

We ought to walk in the way to which we have come. Indeed, with God as our guide, we have come to the measure of the true faith, which the apostles of truth have extended by the cord of the holy Scriptures. We confess the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, performing divine acts through the humanity naturally united to the Word of God, and the same Lord performing human acts through the flesh ineffably and uniquely assumed, distinctly, without confusion, and without change, in the fullness of divinity.

He who flashed forth in the flesh full of divine miracles is himself the one who, having become flesh, is fully God and man. One mediator between God and human beings suffers passions and reproaches in both natures: the Word made flesh who dwelt among us. He himself is the Son of Man descending from heaven, one and the same—just as it is written, “the Lord of majesty was crucified”—while it remains established that the divinity cannot undergo any human sufferings, and that the flesh was assumed not from heaven but from the holy Virgin, the Mother of God.

For Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.

He thereby plainly instructs us that the flesh was ineffably and uniquely united to the divinity, so that it might be seen to be joined distinctly and without confusion, and yet indivisibly, so that, while the differences of both natures remain wondrously and astonishingly, their union may be recognized.

### 6

Agreeing with him, the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> We speak wisdom among the mature—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed. Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age understood. For if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty.

The divinity plainly could neither be crucified nor experience or endure human sufferings. But because of the ineffable union of the human and divine nature, God is therefore said to suffer, and humanity is said to have descended from heaven together with the divinity.

### 7

Hence we also confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ, because our nature was assumed by the divinity—not guilt: namely, the nature that was created before sin, not the nature corrupted after transgression.

For the Lord Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh and took away the sin of the world, and from his fullness we all receive. By assuming the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a man, because, having been conceived without sin by the Holy Spirit, he was also born without sin from the holy and immaculate Virgin, the Mother of God, experiencing no contagion of corrupted nature.

### 8

In the sacred writings we recognize that the term “flesh” is used in two ways, for good and for evil, as it is written:

> My spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh.

And the Apostle says:

> Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.

And again:

> With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.

And:

> I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin, which is in my members.

Many other such passages are customarily understood unequivocally in the evil sense.

In the good sense, however, the prophet Isaiah says:

> All flesh shall come to Jerusalem and shall worship before me.

And Job says:

> In my flesh I shall see God.

And elsewhere:

> All flesh shall see the salvation of God.

There are also various other passages of this kind.

### 9

Therefore the Savior did not assume, as we have already said, a corrupted nature that resists the law of his mind. Rather, he came to seek and save what had perished—that is, the corrupted nature of the human race.

For there was no other law in his members, nor a different or contrary will opposed to the Savior, since he was born above the law of the human condition.

### 10

And although it is written:

> I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me;

and:

> Not what I will, but what you will, Father;

and other passages of this kind, these do not concern different wills, but the dispensation of the humanity assumed.

These things were said for our sake. He gave us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps, as the gracious Teacher instructed his disciples that each of us should prefer not his own will, but rather the Lord’s will in all things.

### 11

Therefore, walking along the royal road, avoiding on the right and on the left the traps set around us by the hunters, lest we especially strike our foot against a stone, leaving to the Idumeans—that is, to earthly people—and to the heretics what belongs to them, and not trampling at all upon the earth—that is, their perverse teaching—with even the footprint of our understanding, may we reach the goal toward which we are striving, namely, our ancestral boundaries, walking in the path of our guides.

And if some people, so to speak, stammering, attempt to set forth explanations and fashion themselves as examples for those being instructed [reading uncertain], so that they may imbue the minds of their hearers, one ought not twist these matters into ecclesiastical dogmas. Neither synodal decrees that examined this matter nor canonical authorities appear to have explained it, so that anyone might presume to proclaim one or two energies of Christ God—energies that neither the evangelical or apostolic writings nor any synodal examination held concerning them appear to have defined.

Unless, perhaps, as we have already said, certain people taught something while stammering, accommodating themselves to the formation of the minds and understanding of little ones. Such things must not be drawn into ecclesiastical dogmas, which each person, being rich in his own understanding, appears to explain according to his own opinion.

### 12

For the sacred writings are filled with clear demonstrations that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son and Word of God, through whom all things were made, is himself the one operator of divinity and humanity.

### 13

Whether, however, because of the works of divinity and humanity, the resulting operations should be called or understood as twofold does not concern us. We leave such matters to grammarians, who customarily claim for little ones the refined derivation of names.

### 14

For we have not learned from the sacred writings that the Lord Jesus Christ and his Holy Spirit have one operation or two. Rather, we have learned in many ways that he operates.

For it is written:

> If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.

And elsewhere:

> No one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit.

There are different distributions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are different distributions of ministries, but the same God, who operates all things in all people.

### 15

If there are many distributions of operations, and God performs all of them in all the members of the complete body, how much more can these things be fully applied to our head, Christ the Lord? Thus head and body may be one perfect whole, so that it may come perfectly, as it is written, “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

If the Spirit of Christ operates in many ways in others—that is, in his members—in whom they live, move, and exist, how much more fitting is it for us to confess that, through the Mediator between God and human beings himself, fully, perfectly, in many ways, and ineffably, he operated through the communion of both natures?

### 16

We ought therefore to think and hope according to the sanctions of the divine words, rejecting those things that are recognized as novel expressions capable of generating scandals in the holy churches of God.

Otherwise, offended by the expression “two operations,” we might be thought, by following the Nestorians, to hold insane opinions. Or, if we should decide that one operation of our Lord Jesus Christ must be confessed, we might appear, to astonished ears, to profess the foolish madness of the Eutychians.

Let us take care lest the ashes and revived fires of those whose empty weapons have been burned should again renew the flame-spewing fires of their questions. Let us simply and truly confess the Lord Jesus Christ as one operator of the divine and human nature.

It is preferable that vain philosophers, idle dealers in the weighing of natures, and swollen with pride against us, should resound with the voices of frogs, rather than that the simple Christian people, humble in spirit, should remain unfed. Let no one deceive the disciples of the fishermen through philosophy and empty deceit.

For, following their teaching, all their rocky arguments, crafty disputes, and wandering controversies have been shattered within their nets.

### 17

Let your Fraternity proclaim these things with us, just as we unanimously proclaim them with you. We exhort you, avoiding the introduction of the expression “one operation” or “two operations,” which is a novel expression, to proclaim with us the one Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, the truest God, who in two natures operated divinely and humanly, in orthodox faith and catholic unity.

**Subscription:** May God keep you safe, most beloved and most holy brother.]

[Col. 0842D]

## NOTES ON THE LETTER OF SERGIUS  
*(From the same book, chapter 17, as above.)*

The letter of Sergius, which I have presented, was always regarded as the legitimate offspring of this patriarch until the Reverend Father Desirantius, a celebrated theologian of our age and doctor and professor of the University of Louvain, was commanded by Clement XI of holy memory, an impartial judge of his virtues, to expose all its falsifications.

For that most learned man, carefully examining Sergius’s letter itself and the response of Honorius, as well as the acts of the Sixth Council that condemned both letters together with their authors, finally recognized that the letter of Honorius had been produced at the council in an authentic Latin form with a Greek translation. Sergius’s letter, however, had been presented neither in an autograph nor in an authentically transcribed copy, but only as an extract from a copy found in the registers of the patriarchate of Constantinople. These registers had certainly been falsified and corrupted by the pseudo-patriarch Paul, Sergius’s successor after Pyrrhus.

He likewise observes from the character of the response that this letter of Sergius had originally been catholic, and that heretical additions had been inserted into it. These additions were the reason why the meaning of Honorius was perverted. Although Honorius’s response is in itself good and legitimate, it becomes bad and condemnable when considered in relation to this letter of Sergius, whose response has always been believed on account of empty rumors and testimonies resting on no foundation.

He teaches that the cause of this corruption must be attributed to the fraud of Macarius, the pseudo-patriarch of Antioch. For when Macarius sent papers to the emperor to be produced at the Sixth Council, he included Sergius’s letter, entitled:

> Copy of the letter of Sergius of Constantinople to Honorius, Roman pontiff,

and joined to it the letter of Honorius, inscribed:

> Extract from the letter of Honorius, Roman pontiff, to that same Sergius.

Because neither of these copies was authentic, the council ordered them to be compared with the autographs. This was done improperly. For Honorius’s copy was found to correspond exactly to the Latin autograph. But no attention was paid to whether the title appended by Macarius was legitimate—namely, whether this Latin letter of Honorius was truly a response to the copy of Sergius that Macarius had produced.

The copy of the alleged letter of Sergius was not compared with Sergius’s genuine letter, but only with the registers of the patriarchate of Constantinople, which the keeper of the archives had brought to the council. In those registers there was inserted a letter in the name of Sergius, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, to Honorius, formerly Roman pontiff, and the copy transmitted by Macarius agreed with it in every respect.

But those registers had been derived not from autographs but from spurious and false documents. This is beyond doubt in the case of the letter under discussion. For who would believe that the latest Monothelite patriarchs wished to adulterate this letter by inserting into it heretical meanings that it had not previously contained?

The opposite would have occurred if they had corrupted it in order to bring it back to a better meaning and make Sergius appear catholic. For then the Fathers of the council, who were not unaware of Sergius’s wickedness, would have exposed their fraud and examined the dubious reliability of the registers. That should not have happened, however, once they had found what they were seeking: Sergius convicted of error.

Within a very brief period, three Monothelite patriarchs had successively occupied the see of Constantinople. All of them boasted that Pope Honorius agreed with them, yet they never proved that this was so.

On the contrary, the successors of Honorius demonstrated that the matter was otherwise. Saint Maximus, disputing in Africa with Pyrrhus, one of those patriarchs, convicted him so thoroughly that he abjured his error at Rome. Yet, in order to regain the favor of the heretical emperor Constans, he returned to his vomit.

Pyrrhus was aware, both from his debate with Maximus and from other sources, of whatever the Catholics felt concerning the defense of Honorius. Therefore, when the pseudo-patriarch Paul and he possessed the letter of Honorius and the archives of Constantinople, they easily added whatever they pleased, especially since they had wished Saint Maximus and Pope Saint Martin, who could have exposed the fraud, to perish in exile.

The Sixth Council itself was so persuaded of Honorius’s innocence during its first eleven sessions that it declared blasphemous the proposition that counted Honorius among the sectarians, as though he had acknowledged one will in Christ.

In the following session, however, Sergius’s letter was produced. It was truly heretical, but it was not examined closely enough to make clear whether Honorius had given his response to that letter. Let the acts of the council be read and reread: one finds that this question was never brought back for examination.

The synod praises him and accepts the letter as genuine, then, without investigating anything further, proceeds to other matters. Yet this should have been confirmed by witnesses of unimpaired faith, who would have affirmed that the letter inserted into the patriarchal registers was either the autograph or a copy of the genuine letter to which Honorius had replied.

Such caution would not have been necessary if Honorius had inserted the entire letter into his response, or at least its summary and substance, which was believed truly to be Sergius’s. In that case, the response itself would have been both testimony and confirmation of the fact under dispute.

But since this was not done at all, and since everything contained in that letter is entirely catholic, the response must likewise be regarded as a response to a catholic letter.

This, in summary, is Desirantius’s account of Sergius’s letter. He then examines its articles more closely, saying that the length of the disputed letter plainly shows that it is not the letter to which Honorius responded, since Honorius’s response indicates what was contained in Sergius’s short letter of only a few articles.

The first article, which serves as its beginning, is reflected in Honorius’s response, where the pontiff commends Sergius for having had recourse to the Roman pontiff in doubtful matters.

The second is spurious. For it is not credible that Heraclius, who relied exclusively on Sergius’s services in religious matters, rebuked Paul the One-Eyed, whose friendship he cultivated for the purpose of defending Monothelitism, besides having him as a protector at the imperial court, as Saint Maximus showed to Pyrrhus:

> When Sergius wrote from Theodosiopolis to Paul the One-Eyed, a follower of Severus, he also sent him Menna’s little book, together with that of Theodore of Pharan, with his own approval.

*(The Disputation of Saint Maximus with Pyrrhus.)*

Moreover, these sectarians attributed the origin of the controversy to the dispute of the monk Sophronius with Cyrus of Alexandria in the year 633:

> Sophronius, who shortly afterward became patriarch of Jerusalem, caused us—namely, Pyrrhus and Sergius—to do this, for he raised that discussion concerning operations at an inopportune time.

*(The same work.)*

They therefore could not attribute its origin to a meeting between the One-Eyed man and the emperor, since that meeting had taken place many years earlier, when the emperor was fighting the Persians in Armenia.

The third is an addition. For it is clear from Sergius’s letter to Cyrus, then bishop of Phasis, which was read in the twelfth session of the council, that Cyrus had approved Heraclius’s decree concerning the non-recognition of two operations in Christ, sending it to Arcadius, bishop of Cyprus. It is therefore falsely asserted that Cyrus replied that he did not know whether he should confess one operation or several.

The fourth is likewise an addition. For Pope Honorius mentions neither Menna nor Vigilius in his response. It is therefore easy to understand that Sergius had written nothing to Honorius about matters preceding Sophronius’s opposition.

Moreover, while Sergius was still alive, he circulated corrupted copies of his letter to Honorius, in which he merely reported that Pope Vigilius had been informed about Menna’s acclamations. Later, his successor Pyrrhus, before leaving Constantinople, wrote to Pope John that such acclamations—or Menna’s discourse—had been presented and shown to Vigilius by Constantine the quaestor:

> I am amazed that, although you are patriarchs, you dare to lie. Your predecessor wrote in his letter to Honorius that Vigilius had indeed been informed about that little book, but that it had not been offered or shown to him. Yet in your letter to Pope John you said that it had been offered and shown, and even read by Constantine the quaestor. Whom, then, are we to believe—you or the one whose successor you are? Both cannot have spoken the truth.

*(The same work.)*

Finally, this letter testifies that Menna himself offered that discourse to Vigilius. Sergius never wrote this.

The fifth is spurious. For how could Sergius have dared to write that nothing had been published by him, as though it came from him, concerning the question, when he had written about it to Cyrus, commended in his letter Heraclius’s decree mentioned above, and cited in the same letter testimonies in favor of one will and one operation, falsely attributed to Menna and Saint Cyril of Alexandria?

Moreover, this article mentions several copies sent to Honorius. Yet in his response the pontiff speaks of no copy other than the single copy of the letter that Sergius pretended to have written to Sophronius.

The sixth is likewise spurious. Instead of remaining silent about the controversial matter, Sergius had, on the contrary, attempted everywhere to pour out his poison before Sophronius appeared on the scene, in order to infect the Church, as Saint Maximus reproaches Pyrrhus:

> What, then, he says, after Sergius had set forth his disease publicly in many ways and had corrupted and devastated the greater part of the Church—if Blessed Sophronius admonished him with the humility appropriate to his character, falling at his feet and recalling the life-giving sufferings of Christ God, which contained every form of supplication, and imploring him not to renew the voice of the heretics, once rightly extinguished by the holy Fathers of earlier times—was he the author of this scandal?

*(The same work.)*

For this reason it is credible that Sergius’s genuine letter, after the beginning contained in the first article, begins with the seventh article. In the opening he promises that he will immediately narrate the matter, which naturally connects with the seventh article, beginning with the words, “Since a short time ago.”

And indeed, by establishing in this article the beginning of the controversy at the time when Cyrus was patriarch of Alexandria, he plainly contradicts the assertions in the preceding articles that the controversy began while Cyrus was still bishop of Lazarus.

The interpolators had inserted into this article the claim that the two sides had agreed on certain articles, one of which concerned the single operation of Jesus Christ. For it is clear from Honorius’s response that Sergius had informed him in his letter that none of the holy Fathers of the Church had taught one or two operations.

It therefore cannot be the case that Cyrus and his recently converted disciples had drawn up an article of faith concerning the same matter. I would say the same about the eighth and ninth articles of the letter: namely, that Honorius’s response makes it clear that Sergius had written nothing at all to him about the celebrated articles of their agreement, but only that Cyrus had generally proclaimed one operation to those who had recently been converted.

Article 10 is an addition. For Honorius declares at the end of his letter that he holds the same view as Sergius. Would he really have responded in that way to a letter informing him that it would be difficult and burdensome to remove the article concerning one operation, on which agreement had been reached in the union of the recently converted with Cyrus, after he had taught that belief in one operation was the insane opinion of the Eutychians?

The eleventh belongs to the genuine letter. But it falsely states that Sergius urged Sophronius to produce testimonies from the Fathers concerning two operations, and that Sophronius was unable to do so. For Sophronius’s synodical letter to Sergius shows that he produced a hundred such testimonies. The Lateran Council held by Pope Martin I testifies that he produced six hundred in two books written on this matter.

*(Sophronius’s Synodical Letter to Sergius, in the General Council VI, act 11; the Libellus of Stephen of Dora, in the Roman Council under Martin I, secret 2.)*

The same judgment should be made concerning the twelfth article, which genuinely belongs to Sergius’s letter but is false. For Sergius, the leader of his sect, far from attempting to destroy it, was exerting all his strength to support Cyrus’s teaching concerning one operation.

The thirteenth plainly contradicts the tenth. There Sergius had said that it would be exceedingly difficult and burdensome to compel Cyrus to remove the expression “one operation.” Here, however, we read that Sergius wrote to Cyrus instructing him not to allow it to be mentioned.

[Col. 0846A]

The next two articles, 14 and 15, belong to the genuine letter. In them Sergius attempts to persuade Honorius to believe that the question concerned merely a matter of terminology, as Catholics in the East had already agreed.

Honorius, believing this to be the case, replies that the matter should be referred to the grammarians:

> We leave such matters to grammarians, who customarily claim for little ones the refined derivation of names.

*(Letter of Honorius to Sergius.)*

The sixteenth is genuine. But the claim that Sergius wrote Sophronius a letter, a copy of which he sent to Honorius, is contradicted by Sophronius’s synodical letter sent that year to the patriarchs. From it it is clear that Sophronius could not have colluded with Sergius concerning such a question, nor could he have requested such a letter from him in order to defend his own silence on the matter.

The seventeenth is spurious. For it is clear from Honorius’s letters that Sergius’s letter contained no question concerning the inquiries of the emperor Heraclius. Thus the alleged discourse of Menna, or another text of Saint Leo relevant to the controversy, must have been reproduced.

The eighteenth belongs to the genuine letter. The same is not true of the nineteenth. For Honorius mentions only one copy of the letter. Yet Pyrrhus and Paul, when they had decided to place in the archives of Constantinople a copy of Sergius’s letter fabricated in such a way as to prove Honorius a Monothelite, pretended that everything mentioned in that corrupt copy had been sent to Honorius. They failed to notice that Honorius’s response, speaking of a single copy, exposed their stratagems.

It cannot be denied that the twentieth and final article agrees with the letter to which Honorius responded.

I ask only this of those who wish the letter published in Sergius’s name to be entirely his own offspring: let them agree concerning the orthodoxy of Honorius’s response. For there the faith concerning the wills and operations of both natures is clearly acknowledged.

When he speaks of one will of Jesus Christ, he understands the human will, distinct from the will of other human beings, who, as Honorius explains together with Blessed Paul, feel in their members a law warring against the spirit:

> There was no other law in his members, nor a different or contrary will opposed to the Savior, because he was born above the law of the human condition.

*(The same work.)*

For the rest, if this holy pontiff appears blameworthy in any respect, he can at most be blamed for excessive ease in granting assent to Sergius’s proposal that both sides should remain silent for the sake of peace. Sergius was not acting sincerely, as history teaches, and as is also detected from his letter, which is full of falsehoods.

As for Honorius’s letter, it is certainly a composition of the noblest and most Christian sentiments. I consider it worthy of defense that he approved silence. For, regarding the subject of the dispute as merely a question of terminology, concerning which neither Scripture nor the Church appeared to have spoken, he referred it to grammarians and sophists as their own concern, judging it unworthy of an ecclesiastical decision.

> It is not proper, he says, to twist these matters into ecclesiastical dogmas, which neither synodal decrees examining this matter nor canonical authorities appear to have explained. . . . These things do not concern us; we leave them to the grammarians. . . . For we have not learned from the sacred writings that the Lord Jesus Christ and his Holy Spirit have one operation or two. . . . Let us simply and truly confess the Lord Jesus Christ as one operator of the divine and human nature, judging it preferable that vain philosophers, idle dealers in the weighing of natures, and swollen with pride against us should resound with the voices of frogs, rather than that the simple Christian people, humble in spirit, should remain unfed.

*(The same work.)]

[Col. 0805]

### 140. Agatho

Agatho, a Sicilian by nation and formerly a monk, occupied the see for two years, six months, and three days.

[Note: [Col. 0805] B.: three years, eight months, and fifteen days.]

He was so kind and gentle that he was also found to be cheerful and pleasant toward everyone.

During his pontificate, Theodore, archbishop of Ravenna, presented himself to the Apostolic See after the passage of many years. Agatho received the imperial command of the most devout rulers, the Augusti Constantine Heraclius and Tiberius, sent through Epiphanius, the glorious secretary, to his predecessor, Pope Donus. The command invited and urged him to send priests or envoys to the imperial city in order to bring about the union of the holy Churches of God, and he did not delay in arranging this.

[Col. 0807]

He therefore sent Abundantius, bishop of Paternus; John, bishop of Rhegium;

[Note: [Col. 0807] Another copy reads: Regianus.]

and John, bishop of Portus;

[Note: [Col. 0807] Another copy reads: bishops.]

the priests Theodore and George; John the deacon; and Constantine; Theodore the priest;

[Note: [Col. 0807] Another copy reads: the subdeacon.]

a Ravennate; and religious servants of God, monks.

He promoted them—namely, the clergy—through various ranks and with honors beyond what was due.

Here, contrary to custom, a treasurer of the Roman Church was appointed;

[Note: [Col. 0807] “He was made treasurer.”]

and he personally administered the business of the treasury, issuing from what had been received through the nomenclator documents marked by his own hand [reading uncertain]. When detained by illness, he appointed Arcadius according to custom.

### 141

During his pontificate, in the eighth indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse on June 28. Likewise, a major and extremely severe mortality followed in the aforementioned month, July, August, and September in the city of Rome, such as had not occurred even in the times of the other pontiffs.

[Note: [Col. 0807] “to have been.”] It is recorded that parents with their children, and brothers and sisters, were carried two by two [Note: [Col. 0807] * “in pairs.”] on beds to the graves. Afterwards, however, the plague did not cease ravaging the areas outside, throughout the suburbs and the military camps [Note: [Col. 0807] * “In the same way the same plague spread outside, around all the suburbs and the military camps.”].

The aforementioned representatives of the Apostolic See, who had been sent, entered the imperial city on the tenth day of November, in the ninth indiction. With the Lord offering comfort [Note: [Col. 0807] C: “comforting.”] and the prince of the apostles accompanying them, they were received by the emperor in the chapel of the blessed apostle Peter within the palace, and presented him with the pope’s letters. After receiving them, he admonished and exhorted them that, not through schism or fury but by peaceful deliberation, they should set aside philosophical assertions and give satisfaction through synodal decrees concerning the pure and proven faith of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers. [Note: [Col. 0807] See Baronius under the year 680.]

After granting them time to reconsider their writings, he provided them with everything sufficient for their support and expenses, in the house called Placidia. On the eighteenth day of the same month, a Sunday, they were summoned in procession to Blachernae, to the holy Mother of God, with such honor that imperial devotion even sent horses with ornate trappings from the palace as an escort, and thus received them. At the same time he admonished them to present, in peaceful argument, the testimonies of the venerable Fathers.

142

[Note: [Col. 0807] See Baronius at the place cited above.] On the twenty-second day of November, in the basilica called the Trullus, within the palace and under royal ceremonial, the representatives of the Apostolic See were received by Constantine Augustus, George, patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius of Antioch, who were seated there; afterwards, one hundred and fifty metropolitans or bishops of the eastern regions were received. They bowed prostrate, and the emperor ordered them to sit together with our representatives.

After this the patricians, the consuls, and all the illustrious men entered [Note: [Col. 0807] * “five patricians and all the distinguished men, together with the entire senate.”] and, after an inquiry by His Piety [Note: [Col. 0807] C: “by the assembly”], he asked which party’s exposition ought to be approved. The legates of the Apostolic See said:

“Truth and reason require that the authority of the Apostolic See be expounded openly [Note: [Col. 0807] * “that the authority be expounded openly.”] by the party of those who assert one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.”

When they heard this, they became pleased and said that they were ready. Having received permission, they immediately brought in their books, various volumes, and the synods that they had falsified. For they did not try to prevail by the truth [Note: [Col. 0807] * “they thought they could prevail”], but [Note: [Col. 0807] * “unless”] by lies and various fabrications that they themselves had added to their books [Note: [Col. 0807] * “to the books themselves”]. When these were read one by one, they were found to be liars: they said that there was one operation and one will, and they had falsified, in the Fifth Synod, Pope Vigilius’s letter to Mennas, patriarch of Constantinople, as well as Mennas’s own memorandum, in newly added quires, asserting one will and one operation. This became clear before the emperor and the synod.

On the following day, the pious emperor, defender of the Catholic faith, presiding in the secretarium [Note: [Col. 0807] * “seated as president”], examined the books themselves and found that the newly added passages had indeed been falsified.

> [Col. 0809]

43 On the twelfth day of December [Note: [Col. 0809] C: “November”], the synod being seated with His Piety, the representatives of the Apostolic See were received, and he ordered them to sit in the synod [Note: [Col. 0809] * “the synod ordered them”]. They appeared as representatives of the most holy and blessed Pope Agatho. They were told to bring before the synod all the books that they knew to pertain to the matter of the faith, and this was done.

George, deacon and keeper of the archives of the Church of Constantinople, was summoned and ordered, according to their information, to bring out from the church library the codices for examination. When they had been brought and read, both sets were found to be identical [Note: [Col. 0809] * “found to be entirely authentic”], containing two natures and two wills and operations in the Lord Jesus Christ. Macarius, confounded before the synod, was proved to be a liar.

Then the imperial piety forbade George the patriarch to receive Macarius or his men in his church, barring Macarius from proceeding. This was his first downfall.

On the thirteenth day [Note: [Col. 0809] * “fourteenth”] of February, with the blessed apostle Peter assisting, so that the light of truth might appear, the statements of the venerable Fathers John of Constantinople, Cyril, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Dionysius, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Leo were brought before the synod. They declared, for the satisfaction of the emperor and the synod, that Christ possesses two natural wills [Note: [Col. 0809] * “two natures and wills”] and operations.

144 On the following day, the synod sat in the same secretarium together with the emperor. The synodical letter of the most holy Pope Agatho was reread, and the Fathers’ statements were inserted and confirmed point by point [Note: [Col. 0809] * “with the statements inserted”]. In this synodical letter one hundred and twenty-five bishops of the western party subscribed [Note: [Col. 0809] C: “120”].

After this Macarius was exhorted by the holy synod, the pious emperor, and the entire senate—not merely to be called upon, but to profess whether he confessed one or two wills or operations—but he would not listen at all. Rather, he refused to say that the Savior possessed either one or two.

[Note: [Col. 0809] See Baronius under the year 681.]

Then the most pious and serene emperor produced a volume for rereading, in which Macarius’s vain heretical doctrine had been written and signed by his own hand, expressly affirming one will in the Lord. Beneath his signature was that of Theodore, the former patriarch, in accordance with the same tenor [Note: [Col. 0809] * “in which Macarius’s one-will doctrine and heretical teachings had been written and signed by his own hand, expressly affirming one will in the Lord. After his subscription came that of Theodore”].

George the patriarch was asked whether he embraced the faith taught by the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0809] * “whether he would embrace it in writing”], in accordance with the writing of the venerable Pope Agatho and of the holy and venerable Fathers. He replied that, once permission had been granted, he would answer in writing [Note: [Col. 0809] * “in the document”] concerning the matters at issue.

They departed on the seventeenth day of February, a Sunday. Within the chapel of Saint Peter in the palace, with the senate and the patriarch present [Note: [Col. 0809] * “the emperor and the patriarch standing together with the legates”], the emperor received the representatives of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0809] * “received”] and reread another petition sent by the most holy pope in their commendation [Note: [Col. 0809] * “condemnation”]. On that day the most holy patriarch George professed in writing that he believed and preached that there are two natures and two wills and operations in the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the Apostolic See believes, anathematizing those who say that there is one nature, one will, or one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

145 On the twenty-fifth day of February, while the synod sat together with the pious emperor and the legates of the Apostolic See, they ordered Macarius to appear. The emperor gave permission for the parties to divide themselves as each wished [Note: [Col. 0809] * “into whatever party each person wished”]. George, patriarch of the imperial city, stood with his followers on the orthodox side; Macarius, however, stood with his followers on the other, heretical side.

They brought forward George the patriarch’s profession, which he had made, presented it to the emperor, and reread it [Note: [Col. 0809] * “and they presented it”]. Macarius was then asked what he thought or believed. He replied that he remained in the same perfidy that he had previously professed [Note: [Col. 0809] * “in that same perfidy”], and would in no way assent to the orthodox faith [Col. 0811].

At that moment the holy synod, together with the emperor, ordered the stole to be removed from his neck. Basil, bishop of the Church of Crete, sprang up, took his stole away, and, after anathematizing him, threw him outside the synod, together with his throne. The Roman clerics of the holy synod seized his disciple Stephen by the neck and expelled him.

At that moment so many very black spider webs fell in the midst of the people that everyone wondered and said that the filth of the heresies had been expelled. With God’s help, the holy Churches of God were united.

In Macarius’s place Stephen [Note: [Col. 0811] Theophanius] was appointed patriarch of the Church of Antioch: he was abbot of the monastery called Baiae on the Sicilian island. [Note: [Col. 0811] See Baronius under the year 681, p. 560.]

Macarius, together with his supporters—that is, Stephen; Anastasius, formerly a presbyter; Leontius, formerly a deacon; Polychronius; and Epiphanius, formerly a presbyter—were confined and sent into exile in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0811] * “were thrust into exile”].

Then they removed from the diptychs of the Churches the names of the patriarchs, and from the church paintings their images, or removed them from the doors wherever they might be found: namely, Cyrus, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, through whom the error had continued to sprout against the orthodox faith until that time [Note: [Col. 0811] * “had sprouted”].

So great was the divine grace granted by almighty God to the representatives of the Apostolic See that, to the joy of the people and of the holy council assembled in the imperial city, John, bishop of Porto, celebrated the public Mass in Latin in the church of blessed Sophia on the Sunday of Easter’s octave [Note: [Col. 0811] * “on Easter Sunday in the church”], before the emperor and the patriarch. Thus all together acclaimed, in Latin voices, the praises and victories of the most pious emperors on that day.

146

[Note: [Col. 0811] See Baronius at the place cited above.] Here he received an imperial decree according to his petition, as he had requested; by it the amount customarily given for the ordination of a pope was disclosed. It was nevertheless stipulated that, if an election should take place after the emperor’s death [Note: [Col. 0811] * “after his death”], the person elected was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been brought into the imperial city according to ancient custom, and the ordination was to proceed with their knowledge and command.

He distributed one donative to the entire clergy, and two thousand one hundred and forty solidi for the lamps of the apostles and of Saint Mary at the Praesepe [Note: [Col. 0811] C: “60”].

He held one ordination: ten presbyters, three deacons, and eighteen bishops in various places. He too was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the fourth day before the Ides of January, and the episcopate remained vacant for one year, seven months, and five days.

LXXXII. SAINT LEO II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 683, THE SIXTEENTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE POGONATUS.
