No. 147, line 4.—“Also a scholastic by language.” By the term scholastici, “scholastics,” advocates are meant, because of their devotion to eloquence, which is cultivated in the schools. Book II, chapter On the Profits of Advocates, book XII, speaks of the official scholastics. The Synod of Sardica, canon 12: “The scholastic from the marketplace.” Or scholasticus is understood as an eloquent man. Basil, Letter 241: “If a certain scholastic, So-and-so, pleads a case … [there are] public courts and laws” [the printed Greek is corrupt]. Augustine, Against Julian, book 2: “Surely the scholastic hearers, that is, those who make petitions in the judges’ audience hall?” Elsewhere scholasticus means an eloquent person. Augustine, On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 9: “The scholastics must be earnestly admonished that, clothed in Christian humility, they learn not to despise those whom they know avoid faults of conduct more than faults of speech.” [Col. 0851B] The same author, On John, chapter 7: “For those who have a case and wish to petition the emperor seek some legal scholar, by whom petitions may be composed for them,” and so forth. The same author, Sermons on Time, sermon 78: “And because the unlearned and simple cannot ascend to the height of the scholastics.” Salvian, On the Government of God, book I, preface: “They did not strive to do this so that they might be regarded as wholesome and beneficial, but as scholastics and eloquent men.”

No. 149, line 1.—“In his time, as the imperial command of the most merciful emperor continued, the Church of Ravenna was restored under the ordination of the Apostolic See, so that, when the archbishop died, the one who had been elected should come to the Roman city to be ordained according to ancient custom.”

By the constitution of Constantine Pogonatus, the Church of Ravenna was restored to the ordination of the Apostolic See, so that the elected archbishop was to be ordained by the Roman pontiff. Earlier, in the time of Pope Donus, Reparatus, archbishop of Ravenna, had submitted himself to the ordination of the Apostolic See, as Anastasius reports under Donus: “In his time the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church on account of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former Apostolic See.”

Later, however, in the time of Leo II, so that the matter might be more secure, the constitution of Constantine Pogonatus provided that the elected archbishop of Ravenna should seek ordination or consecration from the Roman pontiff, because by the privilege of Caesar Constans he had been ordained by three bishops of his own jurisdiction and had sought the pallium from the emperor. (Jerome Rubeus, History of Ravenna, book IV.)

Line 4.—“He established the provision contained in the archive of the Church: whoever has been ordained archbishop must not pay any customary charge for the use of the pallium or for various ecclesiastical offices.”

Maurus, archbishop of Ravenna, with the permission of Caesar Constans, withdrew himself and his successors from the Apostolic See in such a way that he himself ordained the bishops subject to him, was ordained by three bishops of his province, and sought no confirmation [Col. 0851D] from the Roman pontiff; instead, he received the pallium from the emperor. (Jerome Rubeus, History of Ravenna, book IV.)

When the archbishop of Ravenna returned to the faith and obedience of the Apostolic See, Leo II issued an edict that the pallium was to be requested from the Roman pontiff, and that no customary payment—that is, no tax—was to be paid for it. Nothing may be given or received for the granting of the pallium: canon Novit, distinction 100.

Line 6.—“And also, so that the anniversary of Maurus, once a bishop, or a memorial Mass, might not be celebrated, they restored to the Apostolic See the decree of autocephaly that they had obtained for themselves, in order to remove scandals.”

Leo II prohibited the celebration of the anniversary of the ordination of Maurus, the schismatic archbishop of Ravenna, who was very hostile to the Apostolic See, as Rubeus testifies in the cited passage; and he also prohibited the celebration of an agenda, that is, a Mass for the dead.

The anniversary day of bishops’ ordination used to be celebrated. See canons Solemnitates 1 and 2, On Consecration, distinction I; Augustine, Sermon 32, On the Words of the Lord: “Tomorrow dawns the anniversary of the ordination of the aged Lord Aurelius; he asks and admonishes, through my humility and your charity, that you graciously come with devotion to the basilica of Faustus.”

The annual agenda of bishops, that is, a Mass for the dead, was also customarily celebrated. Bede testifies concerning the bishops of London buried in the church of Saint Paul, Ecclesiastical History of the English, book I, chapter 3: “Almost in the middle of it there is an altar dedicated in honor of blessed Pope Gregory, at which, every Saturday, the agendas of those men are solemnly celebrated by the presbyter of that place.”

An agenda is a solemn sacrifice for the dead. Peter of Cluny, book II, letter 17, On the Death of His Mother: “At last, when the mournful prayer had ended, I began the agenda.” Tertullian commends the practice of celebrating an annual sacrifice for the dead, On Monogamy: “And he offers on the annual days of her falling asleep.”

Both the anniversary of ordination and that of death were removed from Archbishop Maurus because he died in schism.

The typus, that is, the principal form of autocephaly, obtained by the archbishop of Ravenna from the emperor, was restored to the Apostolic See so that it would not become the occasion of renewed litigation. Autocephaly means exemption. Anastasius, under Donus, in the passage cited shortly above: “The autocephalous are those who acknowledge no superior”; they are likewise called acephalous. Hence acephalous are called clerics who obey no bishop.

The Synod of Paris, in Gratian, canon Nulla, distinction 93: “Ancient ecclesiastical custom called such persons acephalous, that is, without a head.”

The First Council of Mainz, canon 22: “Concerning wandering clerics, or acephalous men, that is, those who are without a head, neither in the service of our Lord, nor under a bishop, nor under an abbot.”

Geoffrey of Vendôme, book II, letter 27: “We are not acephalous, because we have Christ the Savior as our head, and after him the Roman pontiff.”]

[Note: [Col. 0852C]

No. 147, line 1.—Leo. It is clearly inferred from the second canon of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo that Leo was made pontiff in the year of the Lord 683.

He sat for ten months and seventeen days. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, on which day he is recorded in the ecclesiastical registers as having been numbered among the saints. He sat for ten months and eighteen days. Baronius, Annals, 684, no. 1.

No. 148, line 6.—Honorius. Baronius holds that, in those acts presented to Pope Leo, the name of Honorius was fraudulently added by Theodore through deception.

(From Labbe.) In the year of Christ 582, at the beginning of January 10, in the tenth indiction, Pope Agatho died, or at least was buried, after a pontificate of three years, six months, and twenty-five days, when the Third Council of Constantinople, or Sixth Ecumenical Council, had already been completed on September 16, while the ninth indiction was still running among the Latins. Leo II was elected Roman pontiff shortly after Agatho’s death. When Constantine the emperor heard of Agatho’s death and Leo’s election, he wrote to Leo on April 13—not December, as the common version reads—a letter that survives in Greek and Latin at the end of Session XVIII.]

[Note: [Col. 0852D]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

Since we already know from the shorter interregna that the power of confirming the pontiff was granted by the emperors of the East to the exarch of Ravenna, we must investigate another change introduced by Pogonatus through the two interregna, longer than the others, that followed Agatho and his successor Leo. To accomplish this more easily, we must recall what the most learned authors have handed down concerning the changing history of papal elections.

Mabillon, following Panvinio’s footsteps, divides this history into six periods. First: from Saint Peter to Constantine the Great, when the election was made in a sacred manner by the votes of the clergy and the assembly of the faithful; Blanchini discusses this amply above from Cyprian’s letter. Second: from Constantine to Justinian, when the authority of the emperors of the West, and later that of the Gothic kings, was added to the election of the pontiff; this is treated sporadically in the notes on the pontiffs elected amid contention.

Third: from Justinian to Charlemagne. When the pontiff died, the archpriest, archdeacon, and chief notary assumed care of the Apostolic See and immediately announced the pope’s death to the exarch. After the proper rites had been performed for the deceased and a three-day fast completed, the clergy, nobles, people, and soldiers assembled together—not all soldiers indiscriminately, but the military garrisons, for these were stationed especially at Rome and Ravenna to protect the Italian region against the Lombards—and elected the pontiff. Confirmation was then requested from the court at Constantinople, after a fixed payment had been made; once the command had been brought from there to Rome, the pontiff was consecrated.

Fourth: from Charlemagne to the election of Formosus. Adrian granted Charlemagne the right for himself and his successors to elect, although they did not actually do so, being content with confirmation, following the example of the emperors of the East, while otherwise leaving election free to the clergy and people.

Fifth: from Formosus to Otto the Great. Sixth: from Otto to Frederick Barbarossa, or Alexander III, in whose time and through whose care election devolved upon the cardinals alone. These periods do not pertain to the time of Anastasius; accordingly, they may be examined in Mabillon, from whom I have taken this material.

I therefore return to the third period of elections, in which we are now engaged. Blanchini, comparing Mabillon and Pagius, says that this period extended not to Charlemagne, as Mabillon holds, but to Pepin, following Pagius: “Under Pepin, king of the Franks,” he says, “we shall see below, together with the same author, Pagius, that the Church was freed from that servitude.”

I confess with Blanchini that Pagius’s opinion should be preferred. This will become clear from the interregnum after Zacharias and from the free elections of his successors, Stephen II and Paul. Just as these bring the third period of elections to an end, so they will complete this fourth volume, in which we shall have embraced almost the whole history of that period.

This third period of changing elections, moreover, underwent two notable changes. I indicated the first above in the notes on Pachecus, when the emperor granted the exarch of Ravenna the power to confirm the pontiff. The second was the unusually long interregnum following Agatho’s death, a practice that had already fallen out of use; its explanation must be offered here.

Constantine Pogonatus, because of his piety and devotion toward the Holy See, wished first to free it from the payment mentioned above, as Anastasius testifies under Agatho, 146: “Here he received an imperial decree according to his petition, as he had requested, by which the amount customarily given for the ordination of a pontiff was relieved.”

Then, as the same sacred document makes clear, he removed from the exarch the power to confirm the pontiff and recalled it to Constantinople: “Nevertheless, if an election should take place after his death, the person elected was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been brought into the imperial city according to ancient custom, and the ordination was to proceed with their knowledge [another reading: his knowledge] and command [another reading: their information and order].”

Finally, scarcely five years later, he freed the clergy and people of Rome even from this necessity of confirmation: “Here he received the imperial commands of the most merciful Constantine, addressed to the venerable clergy and people and to the most fortunate army of the city of Rome, by which he granted that the person elected to the Apostolic See should immediately and without delay be ordained pontiff.”

From this it seems possible to establish the epoch of the restoration of freedom in ordinations in the year 684, under Pope Benedict. But because, as we shall see, it was necessary to approach the exarchs on account of disputes, I believe, with the most learned Pagius and Blanchini, that this should still be postponed by about seventy years, namely to the time of Pope Zacharias, or Pepin, king of the Franks.

Now that we have seen the origin of the long interregnum after Agatho and Leo II, each case must be examined separately in its proper place.

Almost all manuscripts and catalogues incorrectly report that the Apostolic See was vacant after Agatho for one year, seven months, and five days. For although all the same manuscripts and catalogues—except Colbert manuscripts 1 and 2, which differ by two days, and the Corbie manuscript, which differs by one—consistently report that Agatho’s successor Leo sat for ten months and seventeen days, it is perfectly clear from Anastasius himself to which year those months belong. Thus the error becomes apparent not only concerning the duration of the pontificate but also concerning the incorrectly recorded interregnum.

“During his time,” says Anastasius, “on the sixteenth day of April, in the eleventh indiction, the moon underwent an eclipse. After the Lord’s Supper, almost throughout the night, it labored with a bloody appearance.”

Two chronological markers are expressly given here: the eleventh indiction and Thursday in Holy Week, which coincided with April 16. Together they indicate the year 683, when Easter fell on the twenty-ninth day of that month. In that same year Calvisius, examining the eclipse in question, says: “It began at the middle of the tenth hour and ended about an hour and a half after midnight; for it lasted almost four hours. True latitude, 12° 50′; semidiameter of the moon, 17° 26′; sum of the semidiameters, 62° 53′; remaining arc, 50° 3′; eclipsed digits, 19° 18′; the sun at 29° Aries.”

Antonius Pagius also observes another indication of the same year in Anastasius, no. 149: the dedication of the church of blessed Paul beside Saint Bibiana on February 22. In the year 683 this fell on a Sunday, as the Dominical Letter D shows. Since this is so, the error concerning the interregnum is obvious. The eclipse occurred only one year and three months after Agatho’s death, while the dedication of the church of blessed Paul was even nearer, only two months away.

Moreover, Leo’s death is assigned in the best manuscripts and catalogues, especially the Veronese, to July 3, while in others there is only a difference of six days, with the death assigned to June 28. It therefore cannot be removed from the same year 683 unless someone wishes, on his own conjecture, to assert that Leo sat longer; for the lunar eclipse in April, which made the year famous, is separated from July of the following year by fourteen months.

Accordingly, without disturbing anything supported by the authority of so great an antiquity, the following appears to be the proper conclusion concerning the interregnum after Agatho, the ordination of Leo II, his pontificate, and the day of his death.

Agatho died on January 10, 682. The See then remained vacant for seven months and six days, as stated by the excellent Veronese catalogue. From this catalogue, as from all the other manuscripts and catalogues, the year of vacancy must plainly be expunged as completely superfluous. Thus, on Sunday, August 17 of that same year, Leo II was ordained—excluding, of course, the day of death and the day of ordination. He sat for ten months and seventeen days and died in the following year, 683, on July 3. The ordination and death are therefore separated by ten months and seventeen days if the day of ordination is included, as the calculation requires, since it was excluded from the interregnum; and the day of death must likewise be removed from the following interregnum.

Against this entirely sound chronology of Leo there seem to militate four letters of the same pontiff, handed down to Peter the Regionary and dealing with one subject: first, to all the bishops of Spain; second, to Quiricus; third, to Simplicius the count; and fourth, finally, to King Erwig. Although Baronius considers them spurious, more recent scholars rightly defend them, especially Pagius under the year 683, numbers 12 and following.

It is established that these letters had not yet reached Spain on the day before the Nones of November in the year 683, when the Thirteenth Synod of Toledo was being held, although, according to our chronology, the fifth month after Leo’s death was already passing.

But if we examine the matter attentively, every difficulty disappears. Before Leo could prepare what was necessary, a large part of his pontificate had elapsed; and, unless I am greatly mistaken, the Regionary had not yet departed from the city when the pontiff began to suffer from illness and was soon taken away—or at least, when the pontiff’s death became known, he could not complete the journey he had undertaken.

I do not rest this assertion on a mere conjecture. Benedict II, scarcely elected, wrote a brief letter in which the following very strong arguments in support of my view are found:

“Benedict, presbyter and, in God’s name, elected, etc. In accordance with what your zeal knows, the lord Pope Leo, whose memory is apostolic, had resolved to go to the province of Spain, to the most excellent …, in order to carry out, with the greatest devotion and zeal for piety, the ministry entrusted to him for the strengthening of our apostolic faith.”

And below:

“Adorning with vigilance and skill the office of piety that you have undertaken, hasten to complete it.”

Those who regard this letter as idle, and therefore spurious, have not properly examined its meaning.

Furthermore, Leo’s second letter, mistakenly addressed to Quiricus, was actually given to Julian, archbishop of Toledo, who had succeeded Quiricus three years earlier, namely on January 28, 680. This unusual manner of proceeding deserves particular notice, especially against not a few recent writers who, instead of illuminating the Spanish Church—then flourishing exceedingly—have cast the greatest darkness over it from every side. For Leo, in addition to the letter sent to all the prelates of Spain, delivered a separate letter to the archbishop of Toledo, as primate of the kingdom. I mention this only in passing, since, God willing, my dissertations on the antiquity of the Spanish Church will soon appear. In them many monuments of antiquity [Col. 0855C] will be brought forward, clearly demonstrating the primacy of the Churches of Spain before the Saracen invasion, without the aid of the pseudo-chronicles, against the most learned recent writers who confuse the apostolic vicariate with the primacy.

[Note: [Col. 0855C]]

**No. 147, line 1.—**Leo, called “the Younger,” was from Cedella in the territory of the Sicilian Valley, in the province of Further Abruzzo; he was the son of Paul Meneius, a physician, and, having been a regular canon, became a cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, the thirteenth pope native to the kingdom. He was consecrated by three bishops—the bishops of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri—although until that time it had been customary for him to be consecrated by the bishop of Ostia alone.

[Note: [Col. 0855C]]

**THOMAS ACETUS’ NOTE**

**No. 147, line 1.—**A Sicilian by nation. From what we noted in the case of Agatho, it is sufficiently clear that the name Sicily also included Calabria. There is moreover a constant tradition that Saint Leo was born at Rhegium [Col. 0855D], whatever Ciaconius and Scipio Mazzella may say. Although they admit that the place belonged to the kingdom of Naples, they nevertheless maintain that he was born in the Abruzzi, deceived by the similarity of the words. For instead of *Aprutiis*, they ought to have read “in the Sicilian Valley, in Bruttium,” where there is a place near Rhegium also called the Sicilian Valley. See Gabriel Barrius, *On the Location and Antiquity of Calabria*, which, enlarged by our notes, you will soon receive, God willing.

[Note: [Col. 0855D]]

**No. 148, line 1.—**“Here he received the holy Sixth Synod . . . in which Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, and Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter were also condemned.” Five letters written by Blessed Leo II survive: one was addressed to the emperor Constantine Pogonatus, who, having sent a copy of the acts of the Sixth Synod to the pope, had requested it from him for confirmation of the synod; and four others were sent to Spain [Col. 0856A]—the first to the bishops of Spain, the second to Quiricus the bishop, the third to Count Simplicius, and the fourth to King Erwig. All four have substantially the same content: namely, that the pope was sending to Spain Peter, a regional notary, who would bring with him the definition of faith of the Sixth Synod, the synod’s acclamatory address to the emperor, and the emperor’s edict ordering the bishops to subscribe to the synodal definition.

Cardinal Baronius regards all these letters as spurious. Since the eminent father of the Sacred Annals was the first to pursue the course of cleansing every stain from the memory of Honorius by asserting that the acts of the Sixth Synod had been interpolated and shamefully corrupted through the fraud of Theodore, patriarch of Constantinople, he was obliged, in support of his assertion, to reject Leo’s letters, in which Honorius was said to have been anathematized. He also had to acknowledge that the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* had grievously erred in relying on those same acts when he says: “in which Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, and Pyrrhus, [Col. 0856B] Paul and Peter were also condemned.” So that the reasons by which Baronius attacks the authenticity of Leo’s letters may not require the reader to consult the *Annals*, I shall summarize them briefly.

First, it must be held as absolutely certain that Honorius’s faith was sound and blameless, and that nothing appears in his letters to Sergius capable of suggesting any suspicion of conspiracy in the Monothelite heresy. This is clearly shown by Blessed Maximus the Martyr in the dialogue he held with Pyrrhus the Monothelite. Wherever, therefore, mention is made of the condemnation of Honorius, it must be said that an error lies there, whether through the malice of a falsifier or the carelessness of a copyist.

The first indication that Leo’s letters are spurious is supplied by their false chronological datings. The emperor’s sacred letter to Leo bears this notation: “Sent in December, in the tenth indiction.” If Leo was not proclaimed pope until the eleventh indiction, in August 683, as Anastasius reports, the emperor could not have addressed a letter to him seventeen months [Col. 0856C] before his election.

Moreover, the emperor writes that he had sent a letter of exhortation to Pope Agatho, asking him to send certain persons to Constantinople to represent him at the council that was soon to be held. Yet it is clear from the emperor’s own letter to George, bishop of Constantinople, from Agatho’s replies to the emperor, from the synodal acts, and from Anastasius, that Constantine did not address a letter to Agatho, but to Donus, Agatho’s predecessor.

Leo’s letter in reply to the emperor is likewise corrupted by a similar error in its dating. It is said to have been dated on the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction. But if, in the body of the letter, Leo states that he received the emperor’s imperial rescript together with the synodal acts in July, during the recently concluded tenth indiction, how can the same letter be dated on the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction—a date which would place the letter three months before the time when it was received?

[Col. 0856D] Leo’s letters sent to Spain are disfigured by almost the same anachronism. They assert that the synod held concerning the Monothelites had been completed in the ninth indiction, whereas it is certain that it was completed in the tenth indiction, as its final acts make so evident that no doubt on the matter can remain.

In his letter to the bishops of Spain, Leo says that he selected archbishops from the councils subject to the Holy See to send to the emperor. Yet among the subscriptions to the synod no archbishop can be found who had been sent from Rome and attended the synod.

Furthermore, since the synod was completed before Agatho’s death, how could Leo claim to have sent archbishops to the synod who were different from the legates whom Agatho had sent in advance?

A letter is unhappily represented as having been given by Leo to Quiricus, although it is evident that Quiricus had died long before Leo—seven years earlier, in fact—and that Julian had been substituted for him. Julian is recorded as having subscribed the Twelfth Council of Toledo, held in 682 [Col. 0857A], whereas the name of Quiricus appears only in the subscriptions of the Eleventh Council of Toledo, held in 675. Nor can another Quiricus, distinct from the bishop of Toledo, be invented, since the pope ought to have written to the primate and metropolitan when, after writing a general letter to all the bishops of Spain, he wished to write separately to one of them.

There is no mention of Count Simplicius in that long list of counts recorded as having attended the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, twenty-two in all.

In the letter addressed to King Erwig, two things are altogether unacceptable. First, it says that the emperor Constantine sent letters to Agatho, whereas it has already been shown that they were sent to Donus. Second, it says that the emperor’s letter was written in the ninth indiction, whereas the letter sent to Donus is found dated in the sixth indiction, on the day before the Ides of August.

To all this must be added that those letters clearly state that not the synodal acts themselves were being sent to Spain—“for, because of the difference of language, they were written in Greek and had not yet been carefully translated into Latin speech” [Col. 0857B]—but only the definition of the synod, the emperor’s edict, and the Fathers’ acclamatory address to him: plainly only a very small part of the acts. Yet the bishops at the Eleventh Council of Toledo, held in 684, testify that they had received the complete acts of the synod together with Pope Leo’s letters of invitation, “through which the entire order of the proceedings, and the acts of the several sessions, became clearly known to our understanding just as they had been conducted.”

These, then, are Baronius’s arguments that Leo II’s letters are spurious.

Those who regard the five letters of Leo as genuine, however, are not satisfied with these arguments. First, they agree entirely with Baronius that Pope Honorius was far removed not only from every guilt of heresy but also from every suspicion of guilt. John IV defended his cause most ably in his apology for Honorius addressed to Constantine, son of Heraclius; so too did Anastasius the Librarian in the preface to his *Collection* addressed to John the Deacon [Col. 0857C], which Baronius did not see, since it was brought out of darkness after his death by Sirmond. Nor could he have seen the *Pontifical Book of Daily Office*, which Garnerius was the first to publish.

What Leo censures in Honorius is that unhelpful policy by which he granted silence to Sergius, an exceedingly deceitful man who used that indulgence as a pretext for peace and tranquility in the Eastern Churches. This is clearly indicated in the letter to the bishops of Spain by these words:

> “He extinguished the flame of the heretical doctrine when it was beginning—not as apostolic authority required—but, by neglecting it, he nourished it.”

If the chronological notes do not correspond exactly to the times when the letters were written, this should be attributed partly to the copyists, who generally transcribed them from copies, and especially to the chronology of this pope, which the author of the *Pontifical Book* transmitted to us damaged and defective. Philip Labbeus opportunely applied a physician’s hand to its restoration in an observation published by him after [Col. 0857D] the life of this pontiff in volume VII of the *Councils*. That observation will be reproduced in full below.

Once Labbeus’s correction is accepted, the passages that seemed misplaced to Baronius are easily restored. Agatho died in the year of Christ 682, on January 10, in the tenth indiction, and Leo II was immediately elected. Upon hearing of Agatho’s death and of Leo’s replacement of him, in March or April of the tenth indiction, Constantine wrote a letter to Leo. The legates whom Agatho had sent to Constantinople returned to Rome in July, bringing the letter together with the acts of the Sixth Synod. One of them was John, bishop of Porto, who took part in Leo’s consecration, which was carried out in August of the same tenth indiction.

Meanwhile Leo ordered the synodal acts to be examined. After they had been carefully considered and diligently discussed, he replied to the emperor in May of the following year, 683, in the eleventh indiction. Wherever, therefore, we read in Constantine’s letter, “sent in December, in the tenth indiction,” we should read “in April, in the tenth indiction” [Col. 0858A]. And in Leo’s letter, wherever we read “on the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction,” we should read “on the Nones of May, in the eleventh indiction.”

No chronological error occurs in Leo’s letters sent to Spain. Leo says that the synod held concerning the Monothelites had been completed in the ninth indiction, whereas in reality all the sessions relevant to the substance of the doctrinal matter had been completed before the beginning of the tenth indiction, specifically in sessions 17 and 18, held on September 11 and 16, at the beginning of the tenth indiction. Those dates may also be referred to the ninth indiction by Western reckoning, since the West began counting the tenth indiction from September 24.

The letter to the bishops of Spain does indeed say that archbishops were chosen by the pope from provinces subject to the Holy See. But this may perhaps be attributed to the copyist, if he wrote “archbishops” where the original had “bishops.” Archbishops were present as well, as Pagius correctly observes in his note on this passage of Baronius: the archbishop of Corinth was present, Basil of Crete, and John, archbishop of Rhegium [Col. 0858B] in Calabria. Leo could call these men “sent by us,” since they had been sent by the Roman See.

The letter given to Quiricus assumes in good faith that he was still alive, since news of his death had not yet reached Leo. The date of Quiricus’s death should not be calculated from his subscription to the Eleventh Council of Toledo in 675, but from the time of the Twelfth Council of Toledo, held in 682. Julian, perhaps substituted for Quiricus a few months after his death, is recorded as having subscribed that council.

Nor should an alleged fabricator of the letters be thought so inept that, if he wished to deceive by fraud, he would neglect to read the episcopal subscriptions to the councils held at that time and address forged letters to men whose names appeared in the catalogues. The same may be said of Count Simplicius.

In the letter to King Erwig, however, Leo writes that the emperor had sent sacred letters to Agatho in the ninth indiction, although it is certain that they were sent to Donus in the sixth indiction, on the day before the Ides of August [Col. 0858C]. Pagius replies that errors often creep into numerical notations, and that codices bearing such notations should not therefore immediately be rejected. The letters may be said to have been addressed to Agatho because, after Donus’s death, Agatho received them and replied to the emperor concerning them.

But perhaps Constantine, who had previously written to Donus, could, after receiving news of Donus’s death, have written again on the same matter to Agatho, Donus’s successor. Must the existence of letters be denied merely because they do not survive?

Finally, if the bishops of Spain at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo testify that they received all the acts of the synod, whereas Leo denies in his letters that the complete acts could be sent by him, they may mean that they received what belonged to the substance of the synodal proceedings—namely, the definition of faith issued by the synod, which was the most important and essential part of the acts of the Sixth Synod.

Leo wrote to Spain in 683, but died on June 18, 684, during the twelfth indiction . . . The Fourteenth Council of Toledo was held in 684. Within the space of a year, the acts of the synod could have been translated from Greek into Latin, sent to Spain with Peter the notary, and suitably communicated by Peter to the bishops of Spain, so that they might subscribe the definition of faith.

These are the considerations that appear capable of defending Leo’s five letters against the charge of spuriousness. Whether they actually do so, let the prudent reader judge.

[Note: [Col. 0858D]]

**OBSERVATION OF PHILIP LABBEUS, S.J.**

In the entire succession of the Roman pontiffs, scarcely anything appears more confused in the writers of ancient and recent memory than the beginning, deeds, and death of Pope Leo II. Therefore, to satisfy myself and my readers, I shall touch briefly upon the matter beforehand and set it out *ἀκροστιγῶς*—in outline.

In the year of Christ 682, at the beginning of January 10, in the tenth indiction, Pope Agatho died, or at least was buried, after occupying the see for three years, six months, and twenty-five days. By then the Council of Constantinople III, or the Sixth Ecumenical Council, had already been completed on September 16 [Col. 0859A], although the ninth indiction was still running according to the Latin reckoning.

Leo II was elected Roman pontiff shortly after Agatho’s death.

After hearing of Agatho’s death and Leo’s election, the emperor Constantine wrote a letter to Leo on April 13—not in December, as the standard edition reads—which survives in Greek and Latin at the end of Session XVIII.

In July of the tenth indiction, the legates sent by Pope Agatho in 680 to the general council returned and brought back its acts together with Constantine’s letter.

On August 15 of the tenth indiction, Leo II, having received confirmation, was ordained pope, among others by John, bishop of Porto, who had been one of the legates. It must therefore be said that Leo occupied the see for one year, ten months, and fourteen days.

Nevertheless, his consecration is commonly assigned to August 15 of the following year, 683 [Col. 0859B], toward the end of the eleventh indiction. If this is correct, it must be admitted that Leo II, although elected by the Romans and meanwhile fulfilling the papal office in a manner worthy of it, consented to his consecration only after scarcely—or not even—about a year and six months, whether from the greatest humility of spirit or for other reasons.

In the year 683, in the eleventh indiction, on April 16, after the Lord’s Supper, the moon labored through almost the entire night with a bloody appearance. It did not begin to emerge from the darkness until cockcrow—that is, shortly after midnight—when Friday of Holy Week had already begun, as Anastasius testifies. This eclipse therefore occurred during the pontificate of Leo, whether he was merely elected or had also been consecrated, depending on the method used for reckoning.

In May of that indiction—not the tenth, but the eleventh—after leisurely examining the acts of the Sixth Synod together with the emperor’s letter, which the returning legates had brought in July of the preceding year, Leo, whether still merely elected or already solemnly ordained in the preceding year, replied to the emperor [Col. 0859C] and approved the proceedings of the Sixth Ecumenical Council. Some also place Leo’s death in June of this year.

Toward the autumn of 683, when the twelfth indiction had already begun, as it is reasonable to believe, Leo sent the acts of the Ecumenical Council to Spain through Peter, regional notary of the Holy Roman Church, together with the surviving letters. But since the Thirteenth Council of Toledo had already been completed on November 4 and the Fathers had returned to their cities, the reading of the acts was postponed until November of the following year, when the Fourteenth Council of Toledo was held, in the Spanish era 722.

Meanwhile, on January 28 of the year 684, while the twelfth indiction was running, Leo died. Benedict II succeeded him on August 20. Benedict wrote to the same Peter, the regional notary, and to King Erwig, and died on May 7, 685, in the thirteenth indiction.

Those chronologists who maintain that Leo died in 683 place the beginning of Benedict’s pontificate in 683 as well, and assert that the pontificate of one or the other was extended by a year [Col. 0859D]. But there is no need to break through the limits established by us and by others. Since Peter the regional notary, sent to Spain by Leo in 683, remained there after the completion of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo until the annual meeting of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, where the Spanish bishops subscribed the acts of the Ecumenical Synod; and since, after hearing of Leo’s death, Peter perhaps pressed less urgently the matters entrusted to him by Leo, Benedict, Leo’s successor, shortly after his election or ordination, exhorted him by the extant letter to carry out the ministry entrusted to him with the greatest devotion, for the firmness of the apostolic faith. He did so in November of 684, as may be understood from canon 2 of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo.

[Note: [Col. 0859D]]

**No. 148, line 1.—**“Here he received the holy Sixth Synod.” From the quoted words of Anastasius it is clear that Agatho’s legates and the representatives of the Western Synod, who presided at the Sixth Synod in Constantinople [Col. 0860A], returned to Rome before the ordination of Leo II, contrary to Baronius’s opinion. John, bishop of Porto, was one of the legates and also one of those who ordained Leo II.

Accordingly, Leo himself says in his letter to the emperor Constantine, written after August of the year 682:

> “We received the legates of this apostolic See, together with the persons who had departed with them, in the recently elapsed tenth indiction— which continued until the Kalends of September of that same year, 682—in July, together with the imperial rescripts of your Clemency and the synodal acts, rejoicing and exulting in the Lord with great joy.”

The papal legates therefore remained in Constantinople for two years, attending to the prosperous condition of the Roman Church, or for other reasons unknown to us. But when they received news of Agatho’s death and of the election of Leo II—which Leo himself communicated to the emperor by letter—they departed from Constantinople, bringing the synodal acts and the emperor’s letter to Leo [Col. 0860B]. They reached Rome in July of the tenth indiction, and therefore in the year 682. There John of Porto, together with two other bishops, consecrated Leo pope on August 17.

Consequently, in the heading of the emperor’s letter to Leo, which Baronius assigns to the year 683, the statement that it was sent to Leo on December 13, in the tenth indiction, must be corrected. At that time Agatho had not yet died. It should read either May 13 or June 13, and so forth.

After receiving the synodal acts and the emperor’s letter, the pope sent him a letter confirming the Sixth Synod. It is said to have been dated on the Nones of May, in the tenth indiction, but this date is absent from the Greek text and is therefore an addition, to be treated as worthless. For Leo’s own words show that it was written after the tenth indiction, and therefore after August.

Leo confirmed the Sixth Synod in these words:

> “Therefore the holy, universal, and great Sixth Synod, which [Col. 0860C] your Clemency, by God’s will, diligently convoked, and over which you presided in the service of God, followed in all things the apostolic rule and the approved teaching of the Fathers. And because it proclaimed the definition of the true faith—which the apostolic See of blessed Peter the Apostle, whose ministry we perform although unworthy, has reverently received—therefore we too, and through our office this venerable apostolic See, agree concordantly and unanimously with what it has defined, and confirm it by the authority of blessed Peter.  
> 
> “Just as, upon the solid rock which is Christ, we have received firmness from the Lord himself, and therefore receive and firmly proclaim the five holy universal councils—the Council of Nicaea, the First Council of Constantinople, the Council of Ephesus, the Council of Chalcedon, and the Second Council of Constantinople—which the whole Church of Christ approves and follows, so likewise we receive with equal veneration and judgment [Col. 0860D] the holy Sixth Council recently celebrated in the imperial city through the pious zeal of your serenity, as the follower and interpreter of those councils. We decree that it is to be numbered worthily among them, as having been assembled by one and the same equal grace of God. We likewise judge that those who gathered faithfully in it, the priests of the Church of Christ, are to be enrolled among the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church.”

After this, Saint Leo sent the synodal acts to Spain so that they might be ratified by the assent of the Spanish bishops. He therefore wrote to Erwig, king of Spain, to the bishops of that kingdom, to Quiricus the bishop, and to Count Simplicius. All the letters had the same general content: since the Ecumenical Synod had been completed, Leo was sending to Spain, through Peter the regional notary, the definition of the same faith, together with the synod’s acclamatory address to the emperor and the emperor’s edict, so that these might be strengthened by the subscriptions of all the bishops to whatever had been established in the Ecumenical Council.

Baronius believed these letters to be spurious [Col. 0861A] because they testify that Pope Honorius had been condemned by the Sixth Synod and by Leo himself. But Saint Leo censures Honorius not for heresy, but only for negligence and culpable connivance. In the letter to the bishops of Spain he says:

> “Theodore, Cyrus together with Honorius, have been condemned to eternal punishment. Honorius did not extinguish the flame of heretical doctrine when it was beginning, as apostolic authority required, but by neglecting it he nourished it.”

In the letter to King Erwig, repeating the same point, he says:

> “Theodore of Pharan, and so forth, have been deprived of union with the Catholic Church, and together with them Honorius of Rome, who consented to the immaculate rule of tradition that he had received from his predecessors being stained.”

Other arguments for and responses to the charge of spuriousness may be read in Baronius’s critical discussion. We shall speak of the Council of Toledo at which the acts of the Sixth Synod were received when we come to Benedict II, Leo’s successor.

**Line 7.—**“And Macarius together with his disciple Stephen [Col. 0861B].” We have already stated, in the life of Pope Agatho, that Macarius, bishop of Antioch, Stephen the abbot, and other Monothelites, after being condemned and deposed at the Sixth Synod, were sent to Rome into exile, as Anastasius records.

Baronius argues that the emperor’s letter to Pope Leo II mentioned at no. 3 is spurious because its chronological notation contains an error. But, as we have said, that error must be attributed to the copyists.

He then says that Constantine asserts in it that letters had been sent to Pope Agatho to convene the universal council, whereas it is clear that they had been sent to Donus, his predecessor. This argument has no force. The emperor is speaking in abbreviated historical form: Agatho himself received the letters that the emperor had sent to Donus after Donus’s death, and he dealt with them. Constantine could therefore quite naturally write to Leo II that he had sent letters to Agatho.

But suppose that letter is spurious. How, then, did Baronius use it in the year 681 to accuse Anastasius the Librarian of falsehood when Anastasius wrote that Macarius [Col. 0861C], bishop of Antioch, had been deposed by the Sixth Synod and sent to Rome with his followers into exile by the emperor—especially since Baronius himself, in the year 685, reports that at the First Session of the Second Council of Nicaea Peter the priest, representative of Pope Adrian and of the Apostolic See, said:

> “Macarius, condemned by the Holy Sixth Synod, was an exile at Rome,”

along with the other words that we quoted in Benedict II, no. 9.

Nor can it be said that no example exists of the city of Rome being assigned as the place of exile for those condemned to exile. Callinicus, patriarch of Constantinople, was blinded by the emperor Justinian and sent into exile at Rome, as Baronius himself admits under the year 703, no. 2. This is confirmed by the Greek life of Callinicus, which Lambecius says is preserved in the imperial library, volume VIII, p. 210. Its title is:

> “Memorial of Callinicus, patriarch of Constantinople, who, after having his eyes torn out, was sent to Rome into exile, where he was shut up in a certain wall and died miserably.”

Finally, Baronius deduces from that letter that Macarius and his followers were sent to Rome because they had appealed to the Apostolic See. This is wholly unbelievable, since the Sixth Synod, which had deposed him, declared in its final session that in defining the Catholic faith it followed Agatho’s letter and the synodal letter of the Roman council. It therefore cannot plausibly be said that Macarius appealed to the Apostolic See.

It seems to me, then, that the only conclusion that can be drawn from the letter is that Macarius, seeing that the emperor had decided to send him into exile, requested to be sent to Rome. This did not displease the emperor, who left it to the judgment of the Roman pontiff to restore him to his see if he should repent:

> “They all together,” he says, “begged our serenity in written petitions that we should send them to your blessedness. Thus we acted, and sent them to you, entrusting their entire case [Col. 0862A] to your paternal judgment.”

And in the same emperor’s letter to the Roman synod, found at the end of the last session of the Sixth Synod:

> “By the common judgment of the universal dispute, they were deprived of sacerdotal dignity—Macarius and his followers—and were handed over for examination to the most holy pope.”

Thus Benedict II later wished to restore Macarius to his see, as we shall relate in his pontificate.

**No. 149, line 2.—**“The Church of Ravenna was restored,” and so forth. Leo obtained from the emperor Constantine imperial commands by which the Church of Ravenna was restored under the authority of the Apostolic See. The emperor ordered that, after the death of the archbishop of Ravenna, whoever was elected in his place should, according to ancient custom, come to Rome to be ordained.

So Anastasius reports. He adds that Leo established that archbishops should pay nothing either for the use of the pallium or for various Church offices—something that, as we stated in the life of Pope Vitalian, Saint Gregory had formerly established at the Second Roman Synod [Col. 0862B].

Leo also prohibited the celebration of anniversaries or memorial observances for Maurus, formerly bishop of Ravenna, who had died in schism against the Roman Church, as we discussed under Pope Vitalian.

**No. 150, line 1.—**“In his time,” and so forth. According to Calvisius in his chronological work, this eclipse occurred on April 16, which in the year 683 coincided with the Lord’s Supper, since Easter was celebrated that year on April 19. Since, according to Anastasius, it occurred during the time of Leo II, it necessarily follows that Leo was already pope on April 17, 683. Consequently, the interval between pontificates was only seven months, as Onuphrius Panvinius wrote, following Martin of Poland in his little work *On the Wonders of Rome*, in his ecclesiastical chronicle. It follows also that Saint Leo was ordained on August 17 of the same year, 682, after the see had been vacant for seven months and seven days. This will be established more certainly at the account of his death.

Leo was the son of Paul and a Sicilian by nation.

**Line 4.—**“Here he held one ordination,” and so forth. This passage [Col. 0862C] greatly perplexed learned men. Looking to the Saturday of the Ember Days immediately after Pentecost, which cannot be reconciled with June 27 regardless of which year of Leo’s pontificate is assumed, some read May 27. But they were mistaken, for that Saturday does not occur even in May. Others did read June, but in place of the 27th they inserted the 4th, on which, in the year 684, the Saturday of the Ember Days after Pentecost occurred.

But apart from the fact that we have proved Leo to have died in 683, the author of Baronius’s critical discussion, in my judgment more correctly, writes that Anastasius’s text should not be disturbed, and that Leo held this ordination on June 27, a Saturday, even though it was not an Ember Day. For just as, on account of his princely dignity, the Roman pontiff has been granted the privilege of consecrating bishops alone, without other bishops, so for the same reason he was also permitted to ordain deacons, priests, and bishops on every Saturday.

That Roman pontiffs [Col. 0862D] were not bound by the common rules in conferring orders is shown by Alexander III. Writing to the bishop of Bath, he says:

> “No one except the Roman pontiff is permitted to ordain subdeacons on Sundays.”

He confirms this in a letter to the bishop of Hereford:

> “No bishop, except the Roman pontiff, is permitted to ordain anyone to the subdiaconate except on the Ember Days, on Holy Saturday, or on the Saturday before Passion Sunday.”

Furthermore, the same author continues, it should not be thought that Leo II ordained nine priests, three deacons, and twenty-three bishops in a single ordination. Anastasius indicates that during his pontificate he held one general ordination, and that during the time he lived as pope he ordained nine priests, three deacons, and twenty-five bishops, but on different days.

He himself suggests that this is Anastasius’s genuine meaning, both here and in the accounts of the other pontiffs. For in the life of John VI he says:

> “He held one ordination of priests or deacons [Col. 0863A]: that is, nine priests and two deacons. He also made fifteen bishops in different places.”

Here the word “ordination” can refer only to the priests and deacons, not to the bishops.

Anastasius confirms the same point in the life of Sergius I:

> “He ordained ninety-seven bishops in different provinces. He also held two ordinations in the month of March: eighteen priests and four deacons.”

Here the word “ordination,” and the month of March, refer only to the priests and deacons, not to the bishops.

Hence, in the lives of the pontiffs in which no mention is made of the ordination of priests and deacons, one never reads expressions such as “he held an ordination in the month of . . .” or “during Lent,” because the time and month referred only to general ordinations, at which priests and deacons were consecrated.

In the life of John I we find only:

> “He ordained thirteen bishops in different places.”

In the life of Sabinian:

> “He filled the Church with clergy; he made twenty-six bishops in different places [Col. 0863B].”

The same wording appears in the lives of Eugenius I, Benedict II, John V, and Conon.

It is true that in the life of Anterus we read:

> “He held one ordination in the month of December, [ordaining] one bishop.”

But apart from the fact that Anterus is there placed before Pontianus, the passage is corrupt. It should be read, with a Freherian manuscript:

> “He made one bishop in the city of Fundi in Campania, during the month of December.”

Furthermore, the Roman pontiffs were obliged to ordain all the bishops of the suburbicarian provinces who had been canonically elected by clergy and people, without being able to delay their consecrations for long, lest the Churches remain deprived of their pastors.

If bishops had been consecrated by the Roman pontiffs only on the general ordination days on which priests were ordained, what would we have to think of Gregory, who, during the sixteen years he occupied the see, would have consecrated bishops only once—and then 150 on one and the same day? What would we have to think of Adrian I, who, during the twenty-four years in which he governed the Roman Church, would have ordained bishops only twice, and 185 of them within two days [Col. 0863C]?

All these conclusions are plainly absurd. It must therefore be said altogether that the Roman pontiffs consecrated bishops not only on Sundays and on the Saturdays of the Ember Days, but also on all other Sundays whenever necessity required, and that they did not consider themselves bound by the common law assigning sacred ordinations to the Saturdays of the Ember Days. Thus the annotator of Baronius correctly observes.

It might perhaps be objected that the aforementioned letters of Alexander III to the bishops of Bath and Hereford concern only subdeacons, whose order had not yet been counted among the sacred orders, and that therefore the Roman pontiffs could indeed confer the minor orders on any Saturday or Sunday, but not the major orders. This is refuted by the fact that, after the subdiaconate had been included among the major orders, and while certain bishops still conferred it indiscriminately on various Sundays, the Dalmatian Council, held in 1191, decreed in canon 2 as follows:

> “We also forbid any bishop to presume to promote anyone to the sacred orders except during the Four Ember Seasons, in accordance with the constitution of the holy Fathers. For only the Roman pontiff may ordain subdeacons on Sundays.”

From this it also follows that at that time the subdiaconate was counted among the sacred orders. Although the council speaks only of subdeacons, the privilege of the Roman See regarding the ordination of deacons and priests on any Saturday or Sunday is not thereby abolished, since examples from before that council are available to us, proving that Roman pontiffs also ordained deacons and bishops outside the Four Ember Seasons.

The matter of bishops has already been discussed above under Pope Simplicius, where, in the final note, we observed that Pope Agapetus ordained Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, on 13 March 536, a Thursday. For deacons, and consequently for priests, we have the example of Gelasius II, who was consecrated Roman pontiff on Sunday, 10 March 1118, the Sunday after the March Ember Saturday. On that same day of his consecration, “he promoted Peter Rufus, cardinal deacon; Baron, subdeacon; and me, Pandulf, the porter, who wrote this, to lector and exorcist, and ordained several others in the minor orders,” as Pandulf says in his Life of Gelasius, reported by Papebrochius in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt*.

Accordingly, Innocent III writes in Edmund Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, vol. II, p. 283:

> “Only the Roman pontiff, who is consecrated before the evangelical hymn and afterwards himself begins and completes the solemnity of the Mass as the consecrated pontiff, is permitted to celebrate ordinations on the day of his consecration.”

From these statements we learn that the power to consecrate deacons and priests on any Saturday or Sunday, and even on the day of his own consecration, although that day was not a Sunday, was reserved to the Roman pontiff alone. The Dalmatian Council therefore speaks only of subdeacons because at that time only they were at issue. As I have said, many bishops thought that they were permitted to confer the subdiaconate on any Sunday, just as had been permitted before that order was counted among the major orders; the council forbids this and declares that the power was reserved to the Roman pontiff alone.

**Line 8.—“He was ordained by three bishops.”** The same Anastasius writes that Leo II was ordained by three bishops:

> “This most holy man, mentioned above, was ordained by three bishops, namely Andrew of Ostia, John of Porto, and Placentinus of Velletri, because the Alban Church had no bishop.”

Sigonius’s opinion therefore collapses. In his *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 682, he says that before Leo II the privilege had belonged exclusively to the bishop of Ostia, so that, with the other bishops excluded, he alone consecrated the Roman pontiff. Since Anastasius explains that the bishop of Velletri was substituted for the Alban bishop, whose see was vacant, this proves that previously the custom had been for the Alban bishop, together with the bishops of Ostia and Porto, to assist at the ordination of the Roman pontiff.

Mabillon confirms this: Roman pontiffs, he says, were customarily ordained by three bishops. He makes this statement in his preliminary commentary on the *Roman Order*, on the basis of one of the two little works on Ordination that he published. In that work, as in the *Roman Order*, three bishops are mentioned in the ordination of the pontiff. The little work was undoubtedly written before the pontificate of Leo II.

Indeed, even before the Council of Nicaea, the ordinations of bishops at Rome appear to have been carried out by three bishops. This may be inferred from the case of Novatian, who summoned three drunken bishops to Rome, kept them shut up until the tenth hour, and compelled them, by a kind of shadowy and empty laying-on of hands, to confer the episcopate upon him. Pope Cornelius writes this in his letter to Fabian of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43. If one bishop had then been sufficient to consecrate the Roman bishop, Cornelius would certainly have been content with one. Thus Mabillon, as cited above.

It is likewise clear from Anastasius that the same practice continued afterwards. Under Pope Pelagius I he writes that a third bishop could not be found anywhere in Italy to perform the consecration; Pelagius was therefore consecrated by the bishops of Perugia and Ferentino, together with Andrew, presbyter of Ostia. This establishes that the ordination of the Roman pontiff had always customarily been performed by three bishops. See what was said above under Mark.]

[Note: [Col. 0864D]

**No. 148, line 1.—“Here he received the holy Sixth Synod.”** After Agatho died shortly after the celebration of the Sixth General Council, Leo II succeeded him. Leo received an imperial letter in which the emperor recalls how Agatho’s letter had been received at the council:

> “As though we had looked upon Peter himself, the prince of the apostolic choir and bishop of the first see, with the eyes of our minds, declaring divinely the mystery of the whole dispensation and through those letters presenting these words to Christ: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God.’ For his sacred letter [Agatho’s] expressed the whole Christ to us in its exposition. We received it all with willing and sincere hearts and embraced it, as it were Peter himself, in the arms of our soul.”  
> *(Letter of Constantine Pogonatus to Pope Leo.)*

In the same imperial letter the emperor speaks of the dissenters in these words:

> “Macarius refused to assent to the most sacred letters of Agatho, raging against the chief and prince Peter as though against the very coryphaeus … All of them—Macarius and the adherents of his heresy—jointly petitioned our serenity in written supplications that we should send them to Your Beatitude. We therefore did so, sending them to you and entrusting their entire case to your paternal judgment.”  
> *(Ibid.)*

The emperor also sent letters to the bishops of the West, informing them that the synod had regarded both them and the supreme pontiff as present:

> “For you too were present, speaking divinely both in spirit and in writing together with the universal prince of shepherds himself. We received not only letters directed to us from his blessedness, but also letters from your holiness, which were brought forward and read, and which displayed the true style of truth and depicted the orthodox faith … As though it were the voice of the divine Peter himself, we were struck with wonder at Agatho’s report.”  
> *(The same, to the synod of the apostolic see.)*

Leo, replying to the emperor, writes:

> “To the King of kings, in whose power are the kingdoms of the world, we, the small together with the great, give thanks, because he has bestowed an earthly kingdom upon you in such a way as to permit you to seek heavenly things all the more. For it is greater that you trust with a mind fixed upon God than that you reign through the honor divinely bestowed upon you. The former benefits you; the latter benefits your subjects … We have received the legates of this apostolic see, your mother, the Roman Church, together with the imperial letters of your clemency and the acts of the synod, rejoicing and exulting in the Lord with great gladness … For we have learned that the holy, universal, and great synod has felt and decreed the same things as the whole council sitting in attendance upon this holy apostolic see, whose ministry we exercise … and that it has confessed these things together with us … By the synodal judgment and the authority of the imperial edict, as by the two-edged sword of the Spirit, the error of the new perversity has been pierced together with the ancient heresies … Since, therefore, the holy, universal, and great Sixth Synod proclaimed the definition of the true faith most fully, and the apostolic see of blessed Peter reverently received it, we too, and through our office this venerable apostolic see, agree with it harmoniously and unanimously in the things defined by it, and confirm them by the authority of blessed Peter, as upon the solid rock, which is Christ, having received firmness from the Lord himself.”  
> *(Leo II to the emperor Constantine.)*]

[Note: [Col. 0865C]

**No. 149, line 2.—“The Church of Ravenna was restored.”** Constans had usurped certain rights of investiture. He had granted autocephaly to the Church of Ravenna in such a way that it nevertheless had to request the pallium from the imperial court, as was noted above. Although the privilege concerning this matter had in practice become obsolete, Leo nevertheless wished Constans’s privilege to be abolished by a new imperial rescript. Anastasius reports here that this was done.

Agnellus gives the same account in his *Life of Theodore of Ravenna*, p. 153:

> “After Pope Agatho died, he [Theodore] fulfilled all the agreements with his successor Leo, and they established among themselves that whichever elected man the priests of Ravenna brought from Ravenna to Rome, Leo should consecrate him; that he should remain in Rome at the time of his consecration no longer than eight days, and should not come there again; that, on the feast of the Nativity of the Apostles, he should send a legate from among the priests, and that the bishop of Ravenna should remain undisturbed; and many other articles, which we cannot set down, were confirmed by the hand of Leo together with the priests.”

[Col. 0866A] **Line 6.—“He ought to pay.”** It appears that the bishop of Ravenna was required, at his consecration, to pay a certain sum to the apostolic see, since the emperor freed the Ravennates from that burden.

**Line 7.—“The bishop’s anniversary.”** The clergy of Ravenna celebrated the anniversary of Maurus, who had died in schism. Leo II took this badly and ordered the practice abolished. I think this was certainly one of the articles of the agreement made between Leo and Theodore, which Agnellus mentions when he recounts Maurus’s obstinacy. See the same author, chapter 3, p. 144.

**No. 150, line 4.—“One ordination during the month of June.”** An old law or custom was in force whereby ordinations were generally performed during the December fast, as is clear from the many sermons of St Leo the Great delivered at that time. The apostolic see, however, is said to have been exempt from that law. Hence Leo performed ordinations during the fast in which the fourth Ember Season was celebrated, on 28 June. Accordingly, the Dalmatian Council decreed in canon 2:

> “We also forbid any bishop to presume to promote anyone to the sacred orders except during the Four Ember Seasons, in accordance with the constitution of the holy Fathers. For only the Roman pontiff may ordain subdeacons on Sundays.”

Pandulf, in the *Life of Gelasius II*, which is reported by Papebrochius in his *Chronological-Historical Attempt*, says of Sunday, 10 March 1118:

> “He promoted Rufus, cardinal deacon; Baron, subdeacon; and me, Pandulf, the porter, who wrote this, to lector and exorcist, and ordained several others in the orders.”]

[Note: [Col. 0866B]

**No. 149, line 1.—“During his time, when the imperial decree was in force.”** Although Reparatus, bishop of Ravenna and the immediate successor of the schismatic Maurus, submitted himself again to the apostolic see toward the end of his life, as I said under Donus, every pretext of autocephaly ceased only under St Leo II, when his *typus*, or decree, was removed in order to eliminate the scandals.

This *typus* chiefly contained two provisions: namely, that the archbishop should be consecrated by three suffragan bishops of the Church of Ravenna, and that the use of the pallium should be received not from the pontiff but from the emperor. Theodore, who succeeded Reparatus, was consecrated in the Church of the Apostles at Ravenna by his own bishops—if any confidence may be placed in Agnellus, a writer especially favorable to the schism of Ravenna.

That same Theodore, whose memory Agnellus pursues with curses, but whom Rubeus rightly praises with the highest commendation for piety, presented himself to the Roman see during the time of St Agatho, after many years had passed, as Our Author reports under Agatho. I think this happened on the occasion of the council of 125 bishops convened by Agatho at Rome against the Monothelites. This is suggested both by the fact that Theodore attended and signed the acts of that synod and by Agnellus’s account in chapter 4 of his *Life of Theodore*: Agatho, he says, ordered Theodore by letter to come to Rome for the sake of the holy and undefiled Catholic faith.

Agatho, however, was overtaken by death and did not put an end to the schism of the bishops of Ravenna. He left the completion of this affair to St Leo II, who resolved it under the following four conditions listed by Our Author. First, the elected archbishop was to go to Rome for ordination. Second, he was not to pay anything by custom for the use of the pallium. Third, he was to abstain from celebrating the commemoration of Maurus, who had died in schism. Finally, he was to restore the *typus* of autocephaly.

By the words “when the imperial decree was in force,” Anastasius seems to suggest that the Church of Ravenna was restored to obedience, or to the patriarchal jurisdiction of the Roman see, by an imperial decree of Constantine. But it is much more likely that this schism was extinguished by St Leo’s ordinance and that the conditions to be observed between the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Ravenna were imposed by Leo himself.

Agnellus says nothing about an imperial command. Indeed, in the passage cited above, he states that Theodore departed from the clergy of Ravenna for Rome with feigned intentions, while secretly fostering plans with the Roman pontiff. Moreover, once the emperor had learned of the pontifical decree, he amply demonstrated in his letters—called imperial letters (*divales*)—that it greatly pleased him, as the aforementioned Rubeus rightly observes in his *History of Ravenna* under the year 693. See that work. See also the learned Bacchinius in Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, p. 149, Milan edition.]

[Col. 0847]

### 147. Leo, a Sicilian by nationality, son of Paul, sat ten months and seventeen days [Note: [Col. 0847] B: eighteen.] He was a most eloquent man, sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in the Greek and Latin languages, outstanding in singing and psalmody, and refined by the most subtle exercise in their meanings. He was also a scholastic in speech, polished by extensive reading [Note: [Col. 0847] *polished.*], an exhorter to every good work, impressing upon many a most flourishing knowledge [Note: [Col. 0847] *and he fervently impressed their knowledge upon the people*], a lover of poverty, and a provider for the needy [Note: [Col. 0847] *provision for the needy*], solicitous not only through the piety of his mind but also through the labor of his zeal.

### 148

[Note: [Col. 0847] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 633, vol. VIII, p. 316, in defense of Pope Honorius.]

Here he received the holy Sixth Synod, which had recently been celebrated by God’s providence in the imperial city. It was written in Greek, with the most devout and merciful great prince Constantine conducting and presiding within his royal palace, which is called the Trullus, together with the legates of the apostolic see and two patriarchs, namely the patriarchs of Constantinople and Antioch, and 150 bishops.

At this synod Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, and Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter, as well as Macarius with his disciple Stephen, and also Polychronius, a new Simon, were condemned—those who said or preached that there was one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ, or who thereafter might preach or defend that doctrine.

But now, as the same synod translated most carefully into Latin declares, two wills and two operations of Christ, the steward of our salvation and our God, are to be proclaimed. Nevertheless, the aforementioned defenders of the evil heresy, because they were unwilling to abandon their purpose, were confined in various monasteries [Note: [Col. 0847] *the principal ones among the aforementioned defenders—namely Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and Anastasius—because they were unwilling to abandon their purpose, were confined at Rome in various monasteries.*]

This most holy man [Note: [Col. 0847] *Leo*] admitted two men to communion. They had been sent from the imperial city to Rome together with the aforementioned Macarius and the others, because they had not yet been anathematized by the synod [Note: [Col. 0847] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 683]. They were Anastasius, presbyter, and Leontius, deacon of the Church of Constantinople. This took place on the holy day of the Epiphany. They set forth their faith in written statements of their own, in accordance with the determination of the holy synod, anathematizing all heretics [Note: [Col. 0847] *the two heretics*], as well as the aforementioned men, their accomplices, whom the holy synod or the apostolic see had anathematized.

### 149. During his time, when the imperial decree of the most merciful prince was in force, the Church of Ravenna was restored

[Note: [Col. 0847] *of Ravenna*] under the authority of the apostolic see, so that, when the archbishop died, the man elected according to the ancient custom should come to the city of Rome to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0847] *for ordination*].

He issued a decree preserved in the archive of the Church: whoever was ordained archbishop was not to pay anything by custom for the use of the pallium or for various ecclesiastical offices. He also prohibited the celebration of the anniversary or memorial service of the former bishop Maurus [Note: [Col. 0847] *and he prohibited the celebration of the anniversary of the former bishop Maurus or of his memorial service*]. They also restored to the apostolic see, in order to remove scandals, the *typus* of autocephaly that they had claimed for themselves.

He built a church in the city of Rome near St Bibiana, where he deposited the bodies of the saints Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice, together with those of other martyrs, and dedicated it to the name of blessed Paul the Apostle. By the command of this gracious pontiff, a church was built near the Golden Veil in honor of blessed Sebastian, and likewise another in honor of the martyr George.

[Col. 0849]

### 150

During his time, on the sixteenth day of April, in the eleventh indiction, the moon underwent an eclipse. After the Lord’s Supper, for almost the entire night it appeared blood-red, and only after cockcrow did it gradually begin to clear and return to its normal appearance [Note: [Col. 0849] C: condition.].

He performed one ordination during the month of June [Note: [Col. 0849] *May*], on the twenty-seventh day: nine priests, three deacons, and twenty-three bishops in various places. He was also buried at St Peter the Apostle on the fifth day before the Nones of July [Note: [Col. 0849] B: the fourth day before the Kalends of July]. The episcopate remained vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days.

This aforementioned most holy man was ordained by three bishops, namely Andrew of Ostia, John of Porto, and Placentinus of Velletri, because the Alban Church had no bishop.
