[Note: [Col. 0869B]

**No. 151, line 3.—“And singing.”** Along with monasticism, various systems of melody were introduced. Accordingly, in both Churches, the first training of clergy and monks consisted in learning the Psalter by heart and singing it. Thus Our Author wrote under Leo II:

> “Outstanding in singing and psalmody, and refined by the most subtle exercise in their meanings.”

Cyril of Scythopolis likewise writes in Cotelerius, *Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. III, p. 258, that this was the monks’ first instruction, until they had learned the Psalter and the rule of psalm-singing. He repeats this more than once elsewhere.

Anastasius observes the same thing in the Lives of the succeeding pontiffs, especially under Sergius II, p. 343:

> “Then the bishop entrusted him to the common school of singers to be instructed in the letters, so that he might be trained in the honey-sweet melodies of song.”

**No. 153, line 4.—“Without delay.”** A new regulation was issued concerning pontifical consecration: the elected man was not to await the imperial approval at all, but was to be consecrated on the following Sunday.

Benedict had indeed waited for that imperial permission, as appears from the letter he sent to Peter the notary before his consecration, while Peter was then in Spain. The letter bears this heading:

> “Benedict, presbyter and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see, to Peter, regional notary.”

Similarly, at the time of his election, John IV had written to the bishops of Scotland:

> “Hilary, archpresbyter and acting in place of the apostolic see; John, deacon and, in the name of God, elect; likewise the chief notary and acting in place of the holy apostolic see; and John, servant of God, counselor of the same holy see.”

Thus they governed the Church together with the Elect, as we observed above under Martin I. The elected men were therefore honored only by the title of Elect and did not assume the name of pontiff until after their consecration.

Accordingly, Anastasius had written above in the *Life of Severinus*:

> “The Lateran episcopal residence was devastated by the exarch Isaac while Lord Severinus was still elect.”

Paul I likewise wrote in his first letter:

> “Paul, deacon and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see.”

When necessity pressed, however, the command of the emperors was sometimes not awaited, and the elected man was immediately consecrated. Anastasius writes under Pelagius II:

> “He was ordained without the emperor’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome.”

Although the pontiffs appeared to possess this as a privilege granted by the emperors, the impotence and avarice of the exarchs caused them in practice not to escape this burden, as the acts of the following pontiffs show.

Meanwhile, from this imperial concession arose the practice that Benedict’s successor was consecrated without delay. For Our Author writes in his Life:

> “After the lapse of many pontifical terms, or years, according to the ancient custom, he was elected by the whole body in the Church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana, and was then brought into the episcopal residence.”]

[Note: [Col. 0870D]

**No. 151, line 1.—“Benedict.”** In the year 684, on 20 August, Benedict was created pontiff, after the pontifical see had been vacant for one month and twenty-two days.

**The same line.—“He sat ten months.”** It is inferred from Benedict’s death, whose sacred anniversary is commemorated in the Church on 7 May, that he sat for eight months and seventeen days.

**No. 153, line 1.—“Here he received the imperial commands.”** The emperor Constantine restored the Roman Church to its former liberty, granting it permission to consecrate the pontiff freely and no longer to await any imperial confirmation, which certain Eastern emperors had claimed for themselves on the example of the Gothic kings.

**Line 5.—“He received locks of hair.”** By *mallones* he means curls or locks of hair. For Greek μαλλός (*mallos*) means the same as Latin *vellus*, “fleece.” It is therefore clearly understood that, when the emperor Constantine offered the hair of his sons to the pontiff, he wished them to honor, love, and respect the Roman pontiff as a father, and to obey and comply with his admonitions all the more earnestly. See Baronius under the year 684.]

[Note: [Col. 0871A]

### CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Since I have discussed the interregnum after Leo sufficiently in the preceding note, I seem to have only this remaining task: to examine the chronological data found in the manuscripts and catalogues.

After Leo’s death, recorded on the third day of July, the apostolic see was vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days. All the manuscripts, both printed and unprinted, agree on this, although the Regius, Mazarin, Thuane I, and two Ambrosian manuscripts—the first and the third—together with two Colbertine catalogues, the first and the third, give one day fewer. In every other respect, however, these Colbertine manuscripts differ either in determining the number of days or even in determining the number of months.

I therefore see that we must adhere to those manuscripts with which the outstanding Veronese Catalogue, often used by me in doubtful matters, agrees above all others. This catalogue now occupies the first place among the minor works in the Prolegomena to volume IV of the work of the distinguished Father Joseph Blanchini. Through his singular kindness I have made use of the same manuscript in preparing these chronological notes.

Thus, counting eleven months and twenty-two days from the day of death of Leo II, 3 July 683, and excluding, as I said above, the day of death itself, we arrive at Sunday, marked by the Sunday letter B, 26 June of the following year, 684, a date suitable for Benedict’s ordination.

That Benedict’s pontificate must begin from this date is clearly demonstrated by the long succession of his successors, whose terms of office are for the most part confirmed by dates of certain character. Thus the ages of Leo II and of his successors are correctly established from the properly fixed beginning of Benedict’s pontificate. Pagi appears correct in this, and I shall follow him hereafter, since he properly establishes the pontiffs’ terms, although at times he removes ordinations from their proper dates, as we shall see.

Benedict sat for ten months and twelve days, according to all the manuscripts and catalogues except the Corbeian manuscript, which adds one day, and the Lucan manuscript, which says nothing about this pontiff.

Anastasius therefore correctly places his death on the eighth day before the Ides of May—that is, 8 May 685. The numeral eight, omitted through the carelessness of a copyist, is not found in the Regius, Mazarin, or Thuane manuscripts, nor in the first and second Ambrosian manuscripts. The chronological signs mentioned by Anastasius and by Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 6, must be referred to that year. Clavisius wrongly guesses that they belong to the preceding year.

Anastasius indeed states that this pontiff sat for ten months and twelve days and died on 8 May. In his time, between 25 December and 6 January, an obscured star appeared; in February another star declined from west to east; and finally, in March, Vesuvius erupted.

Since Calvisius, together with Anastasius, refers Benedict’s death to the year 685, while correctly deriving the beginning of his pontificate from the preceding year, I ask that most audacious writer first: how are the three mentioned months to be counted within the ten-month period in the year 684? Then I ask again whether it is more evident that there is nothing but darkness in the history of the pontiffs (Calvisius, under 683), or that there is nothing but darkness in Calvisius’s mind.

Moreover, because Paul the Deacon, as I said, mentions these chronological signs, he provides me with a very timely opportunity to assert that Anastasius, whom people commonly call “Anastasius,” though it might be better to call him the *Liber Pontificalis*, composed by many contemporary authors, is not safely believed by some to have been a plunderer of the Deacon, who, as the eighth century was drawing to a close, was committing the deeds of the Lombards to writing.

Paul the Deacon, after reporting those chronological signs in chapter 6, narrates in the following chapter the descent of the Saracens into Africa and finally, in chapter 2, the death of Constantine. Pagius clearly shows, on the authority of the Arabic writers Elmacin and Nowairi, that Paul is mistaken in these matters. He teaches that the invasion of Africa belongs to the year 691, whereas Constantine died in 685, as no one fails to recognize—six years earlier.

This is why the distinguished Francis Bencini also unsuccessfully emends Anastasius from Paul’s History, where he transfers the period of bad weather from Adeodatus to Vitalianus [above, pp. 68–69]. For how can Anastasius’s words be reconciled:

> “Unless the Lord had been appeased through the Litanies that were held daily, people could not have threshed grain or stored it in the granaries”—

how, I ask, can these words, clearly indicating harvest time and therefore correctly narrated by Anastasius after the death of Adeodatus, which occurred in June, be reconciled with the death of Vitalianus, which belongs to the end of January?]

[Note: [Col. 0872B]

**No. 151, line 1.—“Benedict.”** He was called the younger, son of John, a Roman, a cardinal presbyter of the Roman Church from the regular clergy of the Lateran. He sat for ten months and twenty-one days and was consecrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, on a Sunday, in the year of Christ 684.

**No. 153, line 1.—“Here he received the imperial commands of the most merciful Constantine.”** Moved by the fame of this most holy pontiff Benedict, Constantine V never ceased, day and night, to think about restoring the dignity and authority of the Roman Church.

Accordingly, in the following year, 684, when Benedict succeeded Leo as pontiff, Constantine judged that something was still lacking from the Church’s increased greatness and restored to it its ancient freedom in electing the pontiff. In a letter sent to the Roman clergy, people, and army, he permitted the man elected as pontiff in a legitimate assembly to be consecrated without awaiting the confirmation usurped by the emperor or the exarch.

Pope St Gregory deplores this sort of temerity most bitterly. He says that the Church of God is being held captive by an earthly prince through greed for profit, and he attacks the emperor for unlawfully usurping such rights in his exposition of the fifth Penitential Psalm, at the verse “All day long my enemies reproached me.”

Odoacer the Herulian, an Arian and king of Italy, first devised this practice, and Pope Gelasius I resisted his efforts. After the Goths were driven out, the Eastern emperors most unjustly claimed for themselves the right that had been wrongly usurped.]

### Number 151, line 1.—Benedict, etc.

From a letter of Pope Benedict to Peter the Regionary, we understand that either at his election or shortly beforehand the custom we observed under Gregory, John IV, and Saint Martin had ceased—namely, that when the apostolic see was vacant or the pontiff was absent, the administration of the Church lay with the archpresbyter, the archdeacon, and the primicerius of the notaries. For whereas at that time only those three were named in the inscriptions of letters, with the name of the elected pontiff added if one of those three had been chosen, in this letter Benedict alone is named as the elected man. This clearly shows that the administration of the Church rested not with others but with Benedict himself, although he had not yet been ordained, and consequently that the former custom had ceased either at his election or shortly before it.

John VI asserts in the decree of Benedict’s absolution, concerning which see number 7 in the account of his pontificate, and Wilfrid himself before the synod assembled at Rome, in Eddius, chapter 43, that Benedict issued a decree in favor of Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York, while he was still the elected Roman pontiff:

> “May you, with the abundant benevolence of your piety, deign to confirm everything concerning uprightness and piety that your most blessed predecessors, the apostolic Lords, Saint Agatho, Benedict the Elect, and Blessed Sergius, unanimously decreed with regard to my smallness.”

### Number 153, line 1.—“He received the imperial commands,” etc.

We stated in the account of Agatho that the emperor Constantine had taken from the exarchs of Ravenna and drawn back to himself the authority to confirm those elected as Roman pontiffs. But Constantine entirely abandoned that subjection under Pope Benedict, as Anastasius testifies in his account of Benedict, where he says: “He received,” etc. Nevertheless, Justinian II, son and successor of Constantine Pogonatus, seems to have paid no attention to this command, since under Pope Conon the exarch’s confirmation was again required, as will be seen in that place.

### Line 5.—“He received locks of hair.”

The same emperor Constantine gave his sons Justinian and Heraclius to Benedict II as sons; Anastasius indicates this in these words. For at that time the custom prevailed that, by such a presentation of hair, someone was offered to another as a son. We learn this from Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 53, where he says:

> “Charles, prince of the Franks, sent his son Pepin to Liutprand, king of the Lombards, so that, according to their custom, he might receive his hair. Cutting his locks, Liutprand became his father, and sent him back to his father enriched with many royal gifts.”

Thus the pious emperor wished his sons to know that they had the Roman pontiff as their special father, whose admonitions they ought all the more earnestly to obey and whom they ought to love and revere as a father.

By *mallones* are meant curls, ringlets, or intertwined locks; for *mallo* means wool, fleece, or hanging hair, as may be seen in the *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin* under the word *mallones*.

Mabillon observes in the preface to the first part of the third century of the Benedictine order, number 17, that among Europeans the tonsure of laymen differed according to age: there was one for boys and another for adults. Boys wore their hair uncut for some time; afterward the bishop cut the curls from their heads—or at least the spiritual father who performed this act was called such—as is clear from the words of Anastasius and Paul the Deacon just cited.

From that time the Frankish kings seem to have worn their hair arranged in a circle:

> “For previously,” says Agathias, who lived in the sixth century, “it was customary for the kings of the Franks to keep their hair uncut from childhood, with curls of hair flying on both sides over their shoulders, while the hair in front was parted from the forehead.”

Indeed, in wax images of the Carolingian kings the hair appears leveled in a circle and reaching to the shoulders.

That rite of cutting boys’ hair seems to have originated among pagans, most of whom offered the first hair cut from their boys to one of their gods. Whether this custom was practiced among boys from the beginning of the Christian religion is uncertain, since scarcely any examples of it are found before the eighth century, when it is said to have been performed as a customary practice.

Several prayers for cutting the hair and tonsuring a boy are found in the *Roman Ordinal*, distinct from those assigned for making someone a cleric. The former seem to have been used in that solemn rite by which boys were first tonsured outside the clerical order, from which the clerics were distinguished by the crown-shaped tonsure.

Thus Mabillon, in the work cited.

---

### Number 151, line 1.—“Benedict,” etc.

Hardly had he been elected as the successor of Leo II to the chair of Saint Peter when, without awaiting the consecration—which at that time did not take place until the imperial command or approval had been brought from Constantinople—he himself began to administer the Church. Before him, when the see was vacant or the pontiff was abroad, its administration had been entrusted to the archpresbyter, the archdeacon, and the primicerius of the notaries. He was also granted this distinction: he saw the apostolic see freed from subjection to imperial confirmation, as Anastasius relates.

### Number 152, line 3.—“He made a covering over the altar with nails and little rods, and around it a purple-gold border.”

*Palergium* was Phrygian work, an ancient craft, from the Greek *palai* [παλαί, “anciently”] and *ergon* [ἔργον, “work”]. Anastasius below, in the same place: “And around it a silk palergium.” *Fastellis* is incorrect for *hastillis*. *Hastillae* were little golden or silver rods. Anastasius, in his account of Leo III:

> “He also made over the greater altar four true silk curtains, with rods and roses embroidered in gold.”

Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book II, chapter 103: “With an onyx rod.” Bulenger, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book I, chapter 45. Elsewhere *hastilia* means vine supports. Pliny, book XVII, chapter 23:

> “The slenderness of the individual vines was strengthened by rods tied around them,” commonly called *échalas*.

### Number 153, line 1.—“He received the imperial commands of the most gracious Constantine the Great, addressed to the venerable clergy, the people, and the most fortunate army of the Roman city, by which he granted that whoever had been elected to the apostolic see should immediately and without delay be ordained pontiff.”

By a constitution of Constantine Pogonatus it was granted that the election of the Roman pontiff should be free and that the elected man should at once be ordained, without awaiting the emperor’s consent. According to the ancient custom, the Roman pontiff was not ordinarily ordained until the consent of the emperor at Constantinople had first been obtained. In Agatho’s time the tax customarily paid for the pontiff’s ordination was indeed remitted; but the burden of awaiting the prince’s consent remained, canon 63, distinction 4, until this burden was removed by the present constitution.

### Line 4.—“He, together with the clergy and the army, received the locks of hair of the Lord Justinian and Heraclius, the sons of the most gracious prince,” and also the command indicating that those same locks had been sent.

Constantine Pogonatus offered to Benedict the pontiff the locks of his sons’ hair, so that Benedict might be their spiritual father by adoption. According to Lombard custom, adoption was performed through the cutting of the hair. Aimon, the monk, book IV, chapter 57:

> “Charles Martel, prince of the Franks, had made a treaty with Liutprand, king of the Lombards, and sent him his son Pepin, so that, according to the custom of faithful Christians, he might first cut his hair and thus become his spiritual father.”

The same is found in Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 13: *Mallones capillorum* means curls of hair, from the Greek *mallos* [μαλλός], which in Latin means fleece. In our language: *tresses de cheveux*, “tresses of hair.” Marcus Tullius used “the fringes of curls” in *Against Piso*:

> “He had carefully arranged hair, and the dripping fringes of his curls.”

### Line 14.—“He distributed thirty pounds of gold to all the clergy, monasteries, deaconries, and mansionarii.”

Anastasius similarly says in his account of John V:

> “He distributed to all the clergy, monasteries, deacons, and mansionarii one thousand nine hundred solidi.”

The same author says of Gregory II:

> “He distributed to all the clergy, monasteries, deacons, and mansionarii two thousand solidi.”

The Roman pontiffs customarily distributed money to churches, monasteries, deaconries, and mansionarii. Deaconries were stations or charitable places established by pontiffs in which provisions were distributed to the needy. That there were several wealthy ones in the city is testified by Anastasius in his account of Hadrian:

> “He established three deaconries outside the gate of the blessed Prince of the Apostles.”

The same author says in his account of Gregory III:

> “Likewise, the deaconry of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, granting everything that belongs to the use of the deaconry, and establishing that it should perpetually serve for the support of the poor in the ministry of the deaconry.”

I have discussed these matters more fully in book IV of my work on Gregory, letter 24. Mansionarii are church wardens or custodians of sacred buildings; they are treated at length in the same work on Gregory, book III, letter 51. For this reason the Roman pontiffs customarily distributed money to them for the protection and repair of sacred buildings.

---

### Number 153, line 1.—“He received the imperial commands.”

When the Roman see was vacant after the death of Simplicius in the year 487, Odoacer, king of the Heruli and of Italy, at the urging and counsel—as he falsely claimed—of Simplicius himself, enacted through Basil, the praetorian prefect, a law that no election of the supreme pontiff should take place without consultation with and consent of the king of Italy.

Although this constitution of a lay ruler, wholly opposed to the sacred canons, was condemned by the Church in the year 502 at the fourth Roman synod under Symmachus, where King Odoacer’s law, which undermined ecclesiastical liberty in the election of the pontiff, was repealed, the Arian kings of the Goths nevertheless usurped this tyrannical right of confirming the pontifical election. They further compelled the newly elected pontiff to pay a certain sum of money as the price of confirmation.

After the Goths had been driven from Italy by the patrician Narses, Justinian and the other emperors of the East claimed this most unjust right for themselves, down to Constantine Pogonatus. No pope was consecrated at the confession of Saint Peter until his election had been approved by the emperor. In the meantime, as I said above in the account of Severinus, the Roman Church was administered by the archpresbyter, the archdeacon, and the primicerius of the notaries.

But when Saint Agatho was seated, Constantine remitted the amount of money—as Anastasius writes in his account of Agatho—that was customarily paid for the pontiff’s ordination, while retaining for himself the gratuitous confirmation. Before his death he entirely abandoned this as well, restoring the Roman Church to its former liberty under Benedict II:

> “He received commands from Constantine by which he granted that whoever had been elected to the apostolic see should immediately and without delay be ordained pontiff.”

Therefore, because the freedom of the election had been restored, Anastasius observes in his account of John V, the successor of Benedict:

> “After the lapse of many pontiffs, or many years, he was elected according to the ancient custom by the general body in the Church of the Savior, which is called the Constantinian Church, and thereafter was brought into the episcopium.”

### Line 5.—“He received locks of hair.”

That is, he received the curls of the hair of Justinian and Heraclius, the sons of Constantine Pogonatus, which had been sent to him. For the Greek *malloi* [μαλλοί] means in Latin curls, ringlets, or intertwined locks; *mallos* [μαλλός] means wool, fleece, or hanging hair.

Constantine Pogonatus therefore sent the curls of his sons to Benedict II, and the pontiff received them together with the clergy in solemn procession. According to the custom of that age, when a father sent his sons’ curls to the pontiff, he offered them to the pontiff as sons; and when the pontiff accepted the curls, he acquired the title of their father.

This custom can readily be understood from Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 53, where, concerning Charles, prince of the Franks, he writes:

> “Charles, prince of the Franks, sent his son Pepin to Liutprand, so that, according to the custom, he might receive his hair. Cutting his locks, Liutprand became his father, and sent him back to his father enriched with many royal gifts.”

Sometimes, too, the offering of hair was a symbol of the religious servitude that someone undertook. Anastasius the Librarian, in the preface to the Eighth Council, writes the following about the king of Bulgaria, who before the papal legates Paul of Populonia and Formosus of Porto professed himself the servant of blessed Peter and of his successor, the Roman pontiff:

> “The prince’s piety had grown so great, and his affection of veneration toward blessed Peter was so abundant, that one day he took hold of his own hair with his own hand and, while all the Roman envoys looked on, handed himself over to them, saying: ‘Let all princes, and all the princes of the land of the Bulgarians, know that from this day forward, after God, I shall be the servant of blessed Peter and of his vicar.’”

There are also records of hair cut by bishops and placed upon an altar to confirm donations made to churches. An example may be found in the charter of William, count of Warenne, in which the count says:

> “And from that point I invested her—that is, I invested the Church—with the hair of my head and of my brother Ralph of Warenne, which Henry, bishop of Winchester, cut from our heads with a knife before the altar.”

In ancient ritual books there are prayers for cutting the hair distinct from those assigned in the same books for initiating someone through clerical tonsure. See the *Roman Ordinal* and the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great* with the notes of the most learned Father Menard.

### [Column 0867]

#### 151

Benedict, a Roman by nation, son of John, sat for ten months [B: eight months and seventeen days] and twelve days. From the beginning of his life he served in the Church, and from childhood and later in the dignity of the presbyterate he displayed himself in the divine Scriptures and in singing as befits a man worthy of his name, in whom the grace of heavenly blessing truly overflowed—in his name as well as in his deeds—so that he was worthy to attain the government of the pontificate. He loved poverty, and was humble, gentle, patient, and most generous with his hand [B: “most generous”].

#### 152

He restored the church of the blessed apostle Peter and also that of the blessed martyr Lawrence, which is called the Lucina church. Likewise, in the church of the blessed Valentine on the Via Flaminia, he made a covering over the altar with nails and little rods [variant: *fistellis*], and around it a most precious gold-embroidered *palergium* [variant: *per largum*].

Similarly, in the church of blessed Mary at the Martyrs, he made another porphyry covering with a cross and four little gems embroidered in gold, and around it a most beautiful silk border; and in the aforesaid title of Lucina he made another covering decorated with silk. He also made two golden ministerial chalices, each weighing one pound.

#### 153

He received the imperial commands of the most gracious Constantine the Great, addressed to the venerable clergy, the people, and the most fortunate army of the Roman city, by which he granted that the *person who had been elected to the apostolic see should immediately and without delay be ordained pontiff.

He, together with the clergy and the army, received the locks of hair [that is, curls; see Baronius, year 684, at the end] of the Lord Justinian and Heraclius, the sons of the most gracious prince, together with the command indicating that those same locks had been sent.

In his time a star appeared at night near the vigils [possibly “Vergiliae,” the Pleiades], and remained visible by day in a clear sky between the Nativity of the Lord and the Epiphany, completely obscured, as though the moon were beneath a cloud. Likewise, in February, after the feast of Saint Valentine, a star came out in the west at midday and declined toward the eastern regions.

After this, Mount Vesuvius [the manuscript reads “Mount Baebius”; possibly Vesuvius], which is in Campania, erupted during the day in March, and all the surrounding places were devastated by the dust of its ash.

He enlarged the clergy, in its various orders, with honors on the holy day of Easter. Immediately afterward he fell ill and died several days later. He distributed thirty pounds of gold to all the clergy, monasteries, deaconries, and mansionarii. He made twelve bishops in various places. He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 8 May, and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and fifteen days.

### [Column 0877C]

### Number 154, line 3.—“After the lapse of many pontiffs or many years, according to the ancient custom, he was elected by the general body in the Church of the Savior, which was called the Constantinian Church, and thereafter was brought into the episcopium.”

According to the ancient custom, the election of the Roman pontiff was ordinarily held in the Church of the Savior, which is the Lateran basilica; and the Lateran palace, joined to the basilica, was the seat of the pontiffs.

Anastasius himself says in his account of Conon:

> “The clergy, assembled together, were waiting before the doors of the Constantinian basilica,” etc.

The same author says in his account of Stephen III:

> “With a sincere mind and praises, they all carried him into the basilica of the Savior, which is called the Constantinian Church; and from there they entered within and, according to custom, brought him into the patriarchate.”

For this reason the election of Ursicinus, made during the schism against Damasus, was rejected, because it had been made *en apokrypho topo* [ἐν ἀποκρύφῳ τόπῳ, “in a hidden or unusual place”], namely in the basilica of Sicininus (Socrates, book IV, chapter 24; Ammianus, book XXVII).

### Line 11.—“And also other imperial commands remitting not a few grain assessments from the patrimonial estates of Sicily and Calabria.”

The Roman Church possessed an extensive patrimony in Calabria and Sicily, which bore the burden of the head-tax, like the other estates of both provinces. The emperor Leo imposed a tax on the persons of Sicily and Calabria, *pholoi kephalikoí* [φόλοι κεφαλικοί, “head taxes”], as Cedrenus says in his account of Leo.

But this burden was remitted by the constitution of Constantine Pogonatus. He said “grain heads” for “head-tax,” because it was imposed on each head, just as *capita* are called the fodder for pack animals because it was supplied to soldiers in fixed amounts, according to the number of heads—that is, according to the number of animals—*Law of the Provinces*, title “On the Distribution of Military Grain,” book XII. Ammianus, book XXII:

> “They commonly call the fodder of pack animals ‘heads.’”

In the time of Conon, Justinian II also remitted to the defenders of the patrimony of the Roman Church in Bruttium and Lucania the annual grain assessments that had been paid. Anastasius, in his account of Conon:

> “In his time imperial piety, through its sacred command, remitted two hundred grain assessments, which the guardians of the patrimony in Bruttium and Lucania paid annually.”

### Number 155, line 5.—“Because of the violation of the ordination of the Church of Turris,”

which the archbishop of Caralis, Cironatus, had carried out without the authority of the pontiff.

The island of Sardinia became the property of the Roman Church through the donation of Constantine (Anastasius, in his account of Sylvester). Hence, by custom, the Roman pontiff claimed for himself the right of ordaining the bishops of Sardinia, disregarding the archbishop of Caralis, who was the metropolitan. But because the archbishop of Caralis claimed, by metropolitan right, that he possessed the right to ordain the bishops of the whole island, he was suspended from this right—that is, prohibited from exercising it—by a constitution of Martin. And because the bishop of Turris had been ordained by the metropolitan of Caralis without the consent of the Roman pontiff, his ordination was declared invalid.

### [Column 0879B]

### Number 154, line 5.—“When he was a deacon.”

That is, he served in the office of the *Dominicus cursor*, the papal courier, for the promulgation of Agatho’s doctrinal letter. Together with the acts of the Sixth Synod, he also brought to Rome many privileges granted to the apostolic see. For it was the duty of the deacon who served as *Dominicus cursor*—who at Rome also held custody of public documents—to promote and carry out such matters. We have demonstrated this at length in the *Prolegomena* to the discussion of encyclical letters.

### Number 155, line 3.—“He established peace.”

The emperor Justinian the Younger made peace with the Saracens, which proved wholly disastrous to the Eastern Empire. Thus both Justinians, the Elder and the Younger, greatly weakened the strength of the empire through careless administration. The Elder opened the way for the northern barbarians to invade the kingdoms of the West; the Younger, together with the peace mentioned here by Anastasius, laid the foundations of Saracen power.

Among the measures that help preserve a monarchy for a long time, Maecenas had advised Augustus to guard the boundaries of the empire more carefully and diligently, and to support the frontier soldiers with honors, gifts, and pay, since the safety of the empire seemed entrusted to them. Justinian the Elder reduced this military force and opened the way for the northern peoples to seize the kingdoms of Europe.

Procopius aptly noticed this in his *Secret History*. After recounting the dismissal of this army, he adds:

> “Thus, with the soldiers weakened in many ways and deprived of what they needed, their spirit became so alienated from military service that the affairs of the Romans and of Italy completely fell into ruin.”

Shortly afterward he says:

> “Since the subject of soldiers has brought this to mind, it may be added that in former times the Roman emperors established frequent companies of soldiers throughout the remote regions. These troops chiefly guarded the boundaries of the Roman Empire, especially in the eastern provinces, and from there held back the incursions and force of the Persians and Saracens. They were also called frontier troops.”

Just so Justinian the Younger suffered from this negligence, as the author of the *Miscellany* writes, page 139:

> “When Justinian was still young, about sixteen years old, he arranged everything in his own affairs recklessly.”

Accordingly, when Mavia invaded the provinces of the empire and ravaged them with impunity, the people from Lebanon called Mardaites, driven together into a force by sound counsel, broke the Saracen assault.

When Theophanes in his *Chronicle* had recounted Mavia’s fortune and victories, he continued as follows:

> “The Mardaites attacked Lebanon and held everything from Mount Maurus to the Holy City, and they also occupied the summits of Lebanon. Many slaves and captives shamefully joined them, so that within a very short time their number grew to many thousands. When Mavia heard this, he and his counselors were greatly afraid, so much so that, judging the Roman Empire to exist under God’s protection, they sent envoys to the emperor Constantine [Pogonatus] to arrange peace.”

Thus, in the year 685, during the pontificate of John V, Abimelech finally offered peace to Justinian on the condition that he disband the Mardaites’ force. Theophanes writes for that same year:

> “This year Abimelech sent envoys to Justinian to establish peace. Peace was made on these conditions: the emperor would suppress the force of the Mardaites breaking forth from Lebanon and prevent their raids; Abimelech, for his part, would pay the emperor one thousand gold coins each day, together with a horse and a slave; and the two princes would divide between themselves, in equal shares, the revenues of Cyprus, Armenia, and Iberia. Having issued an edict, the emperor removed the Mardaites, twelve thousand in number, from their native place, thereby mutilating Roman power.”

The evils that followed immediately are enumerated in this manner:

> “For all the cities situated on mountain summits and inhabited by Arabs, from the boundary of Mesopotamia to the Fourth Armenia, became weak in their fortifications and empty of inhabitants because of the raids of the Mardaites, who afterward returned. From that day to this hour, every kind of disaster and every adversity has poured into Roman territory through the agency of the Arabs.”

The author of the *Miscellany* gives a similar account.

### [Column 0880C]

### Number 154, line 1.—“John.”

According to Anastasius, John V, bearing this name, was substituted for Benedict on 22 April in the year of the Lord 685. He was the first to be consecrated Roman pontiff without awaiting the emperor’s authority from Constantinople, and he took part in the Holy Sixth Synod, honored by the office of apostolic legate.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Concerning the interval between pontificates after Benedict—two months and fifteen days—and concerning the period during which John sat, namely one year and nine days, the agreement of the catalogs, manuscripts, and authors is so great that nothing more certain seems capable of being devised.

Moreover, Anastasius himself supplies clear evidence for the age of this pontiff, further confirming the chronology of his predecessors. He says:

> “In his time the Lord Justinian Augustus reigned, his father having died at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction.”

Since the fourteenth indiction marks September of the year 685, and John’s entire period of rule includes only one September, there can be no doubt that this pontiff was already seated in the year 685. Therefore, when the interval between pontificates of two months and fifteen days is counted from 8 May of that same year, the day on which Benedict died, it reaches Sunday, 23 July, which must be assigned to John’s ordination.

Then, when one full year and nine days of his pontificate are counted, we arrive at 2 August of the following year, 686, which Anastasius connects with his death.

As for why the intervals between pontificates became shorter after Benedict, I have explained this sufficiently in the notes on Leo II.

That John was the very first to make use of the benefit of the confirmation of the elected pontiff being relaxed by Pogonatus is plainly evident from Anastasius, who says:

> “After the lapse of many pontiffs or many years, he was elected according to the ancient custom by the general body in the Church of the Savior, which is called the Constantinian Church, and thereafter was brought into the episcopium.”

For this reason I confess that I have been unable to follow Pagi’s reasoning. From the intervals between pontificates, which were generally two months—he cites the year 681, number 15—he conjectures that Justinian paid no attention to the privilege granted to Benedict, but rather preserved the privilege granted to Agatho.

If that were so, confirmation would have had to be requested at Constantinople, and the interval between pontificates would not have been sufficient for letters to be sent back and forth. Besides, the interval before John’s pontificate, who clearly used this privilege, exceeds most of the subsequent intervals in number of days.

Therefore, as I think, in a matter insufficiently established it would have been better to refrain from conjecture. I shall explain more appropriately in the notes on Conon, John’s successor, what causes led to the exarch’s authority not being disregarded until the time of Pepin.

### [Column 0881B]

### Number 154, line 1.—“John.”

Son of Ciriacus, an Antiochene and a Syrian, cardinal archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church under the emperors Flavius Heraclius Constantine V and Justinian II the Younger Pogonatus Augustus. He was created on the eighth day before the Kalends of August and consecrated on the third day before the Kalends of the same month, in the year in which the emperor Constantine V Pogonatus died in the seventeenth year of his reign.

---

### Number 154, line 14.—“He was consecrated by three bishops.”

Before Saint Leo II, Sigonius writes in *On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 682, that the Roman pontiff was consecrated by the bishop of Ostia alone. The distinguished Mabillon rejects this opinion in his preliminary commentary on the *Roman Ordinal*, chapter 18, on the testimony of another treatise on ordination that he published. In it, as in the *Roman Ordinal*, three bishops are mentioned in the pontiff’s ordination:

> “One bishop comes and says a prayer over him, and departs; another comes likewise. A third comes and consecrates him.”

Furthermore, the words of the treatise show that it was undoubtedly written before the pontificate of Leo II. If Leo’s ordination is carefully considered, as it is written in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, a strong argument against Sigonius’s opinion may also be drawn from it:

> “The most holy man mentioned above,” says the author of the *Book of Pontiffs* in his account of Saint Leo II, “was ordained by three bishops: namely, Andrew of Ostia, John of Porto, and Placentinus of Velletri, because the Alban Church had no bishop.”

Since the author gives the reason why the bishop of Velletri was substituted for the bishop of Alba—namely, that the see of Alba was vacant—this shows that it had previously been customary for the bishop of Alba, together with the bishops of Ostia and Porto, also to assist at the ordination of the Roman pontiff.

Certainly, we infer that episcopal ordinations performed by three bishops had taken place at Rome even before the Council of Nicaea from the case of Novatian. He summoned three drunken bishops to Rome, confined them until the tenth hour, and compelled them, through a kind of shadowy and empty laying-on of hands, to confer the episcopate upon him. Pope Cornelius writes of this in his letter to Fabian of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43. He would surely have been content with one bishop if one alone had then sufficed to consecrate the Roman bishop.

These observations are taken from Mabillon in the place cited, where he also has more concerning the ordination of the pontiff. Pagi may likewise be consulted under the same year, 682; in number 6 he corrects Sigonius’s error.

---

### [Column 0882B]

### Number 154, line 14.—“This pontiff was consecrated,” etc.

It follows that the Alban see was still vacant at the time of John V’s ordination, just as it had been vacant at the time of Leo II. This is inferred from Anastasius, who says that the bishop of Velletri was one of Leo II’s ordainers because the Alban see was then vacant.

Before his pontificate, John V was a deacon of the Roman Church, and he was one of Pope Agatho’s legates to the Sixth General Synod, which he presided over together with others.

### [Column 0875]

#### 154

John, a Syrian by nation, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, sat for one year and nine days.

[Note: [Col. 0875] B: eleven.] A man very energetic, endowed with learning, and wholly moderate. After the lapse of many pontificates, or years, he was elected by the whole body, according to ancient custom, in the Church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana; and from there he was brought into the episcopal residence [Note: [Col. 0875] B: *episcopium*, “episcopal residence.”]. While he was a deacon, he was sent by Pope Agatho of holy memory to the imperial city with other priests, representing the Apostolic See at the holy Sixth Synod, which by God’s providence was assembled or celebrated there. When it had been completed, he was released by the most clement emperor and brought back great joy to the Church: namely, he confirmed both the holy Sixth Synod itself and the decree of the most clement emperor confirming that same synod. He also brought other imperial commands relieving numerous grain obligations imposed on the patrimonies of Sicily and Calabria, as well as an order concerning grain and other things, which the Roman Church had previously been quite unable to pay annually [Note: [Col. 0875] “could pay.”]. He was consecrated by three bishops—those of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri—just as his predecessor Pope Leo had been.

**155.** In his time the lord Justinian Augustus reigned. His father died at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction. This most clement emperor, with the Lord’s help, established peace for ten years on land and sea with the Saracen people, whose name should not be spoken. The province of Africa was also subjected to the Roman Empire and restored.

After many years had passed, because of the violation of the ecclesiastical ordinance of the Church of Turris [Note: [Col. 0877] B: “in Sardinia.”], which Citonatus, archbishop of Cagliari, had carried out without the pope’s authority—for anciently the ordination of that see belonged to the Apostolic See, and the right of ordaining it had been granted to that Church only for a time—the archbishops were later suspended from that right by papal commands because of their arrogance, in accordance with the decision of Pope Martin of holy memory. After a council of priests had been held, he restored and confirmed under the authority of the Apostolic See the newly appointed bishop who had been ordained by that archbishop; their written instrument is kept in the Church’s archive [Note: [Col. 0877] “is retained.”].

This most holy man was confined by a prolonged illness, so that he could scarcely complete the ordinations of priests. He left one thousand nine hundred solidi to the entire clergy, monasteries, deacons, and *mansionarii*. He appointed thirteen bishops in various places. He was also buried at blessed Peter the Apostle, on the second day of August; and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and eighteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0885C]]

No. 156, line 3.—“In whose election.” After the concessions made to the Romans by Constantine Pogonatus, of which we have spoken, the pontiffs were consecrated on the following Sunday after their election; they then informed the exarch of Ravenna about it through legates. For this reason the following order was observed in the creation of pontiffs. Three days after the death of the pontiff: “The priests and clergy, having taken counsel, unanimously entered the Lateran episcopal residence and elected him.” The election was announced to the nobles and the army, who received the elected man with acclamations and praises. The decree of election, signed by the clergy, was presented to them, and they likewise signed it:

“But when the army saw the unanimity of the clergy and the people subscribing to his decree [lacuna], they subscribed to his decree with devoted mind.”

The Italian soldiery was always ready and constant in obedience to the pontiff, though not rebellious toward the emperor, unless injury to the faith or to the pontiff occurred; for these causes it never failed to fight with unconquered steadfastness.

“And immediately all the judges, together with the leaders of the army, came likewise to greet him, and all together acclaimed him in his praise.”

Afterward legates were sent to the exarch:

“And they likewise sent messengers, together with clerics and some of the people, to the excellent exarch Theodorus, as is customary.”

Line 24.—“He recovered the Acts of the holy Sixth Synod.” Either Pope John or Conon had heard that, because of the emperor Justinian’s ill-considered conduct, the Monothelites were growing insolent against the Acts of the Sixth Synod. Therefore they acted with Justinian through salutary letters and also through threats, so that the synodal decrees might retain their full authority. Stirred by these admonitions, the emperor sought the autograph copy of the synodical book, found it, and, by letters sent to Conon, professed his observance of it.

On this occasion I think that the deacon Agatho was elected, just as he himself declares in his peroration to the Sixth Synod: he says that in the imperial palace he had most carefully prepared and copied several exemplars of that same synod. Meanwhile, that Conon suffered many things while this profession was being demanded is indicated by Nicholas I in Letter 8 to the emperor Michael:

“Our predecessors, languishing for so many years under the diseases of various heresies, did not seek a medicinal remedy. Rather, like desperate men or men possessing an impenitent heart, they voluntarily cast from their very jaws the medicine offered to them, while they killed in two ways the ministers who offered such great salvation: either they killed them spiritually by making them participants in their error, as happened in the time of Conon, pope of revered memory, who existed after the Sixth Synod.”

The letter of Justinian is indeed addressed to Pope John, either because John had first warned the emperor to suppress these new attempts of the Monothelites, or because the name Conon was changed through the error of copyists, or finally because Anastasius, as was familiar to him, attached to Conon what ought to have been referred to John.

Moreover, that Pope Conon was treated harshly either by Justinian or by the exarchs on account of the Monothelites is proved, besides the words of Nicholas cited above, by the persecution that Justinian launched against Felix of Ravenna, of which Agnellus speaks in Felix’s Life. For the faction of the Monothelites grew so powerful under Justinian that it savagely harassed the orthodox in the West.

No. 157, line 16.—“To John, the new exarch.” He is mentioned in the Life of Felix of Ravenna by Agnellus, and he likewise subjected the people of Ravenna to extraordinary vexations.]

[Note: [Col. 0886D]]

No. 156, line 1.—“Conon.” Since the emperor Justinian regretted that the Apostolic See had recovered its customary freedom in choosing the pontiff, he ordered that no pontiff should be created without the exarch’s consent. From this there first arose the evil that those aspiring to the pontificate tried to obtain it by corrupting the exarch with gifts or other services.

Therefore, when on this occasion a schism had arisen between Theodorus and Peter, Conon was elected in the year of the Lord 686, on 20 October, by the unanimous consent of the entire clergy, despite the military forces’ resistance.

Saint Kilian was ordained by this pontiff and brought Eastern Francia to the faith of Christ.

Lines 23 and 24.—“Here he received the imperial command.” It is clear from the letter of Nicholas I to the emperor Michael that the emperor Justinian the Younger was not sound in the faith and opposed Conon, since he had once compelled Conon’s legates, who had been sent to Constantinople, to betray their trust. Nicholas’s words are these:

“You killed the ministers who offered such great salvation in two ways, because either you killed them spiritually by making them participants in your error, as happened in the time of Conon of revered memory.”

For this reason it is sufficiently clear from what we shall say below that the emperor Justinian felt the divine power angry with him and that everything began to deteriorate. Theophanes records that at this time the Syrians suffered a great famine and that the peace made with the Bulgars was again broken.]

[Note: [Col. 0887B]]

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES**

The practice of having the elections of Roman pontiffs confirmed by the emperors, introduced because necessity demanded it—to restrain private ambition and curb the disputes of the multitude—proceeded with such a fortunate outcome that for more than one hundred and fifty years no schism disturbed the tranquillity of the Church.

Indeed, from the year 530, when Justinian, counting his fourth tribunician power, confirmed the election of Pelagius and extinguished the brief schism of a few days involving Dioscorus, until John’s death in 686 [Col. 0887C], the Church suffered no other schism except those of Silverius and Vigilius; the latter succeeding the former and governing the Church with the utmost holiness, Vigilius completely erased the stain of schism.

But scarcely had the piety of Constantine Pogonatus, in the year 684 or the following year, as I have said, restored the former freedom of the clergy, people, and army, when disputes returned and private ambition revived tumultuous elections. Thus, when John, who alone had benefited from Pogonatus’s favor, died after a pontificate of one year, the electors divided into two parties: some raised Peter the archpriest, others the priest Theodorus, to the See of Peter. The dispute would not end unless a third man, Conon, was elected; first the clergy and priests, and afterward the people and soldiers, consented to his election.

Hardly had this first schism been removed when private ambition on the part of one man stirred up another, more violent one. Conon, suffering from poor health, bequeathed whatever gold he possessed to the clergy and monasteries. Since this legacy had not yet been paid—for the pontiff was still alive—the archdeacon Paschal secretly wrote a letter to John Platyn, the exarch who had recently come to Ravenna, promising to give him the amount of gold bequeathed if he would lend his assistance so that Paschal himself might become pontiff.

The promises did not displease the exarch. When an opportunity arose to send his judges to Rome, he instructed them to ensure that, after Conon’s death, Paschal would be raised to the See of Peter. They came to the City and, successfully carrying out the business entrusted to them, drew many over to their side. But lest the audacious Paschal ascribe the supreme dignity of the Church, once received, to his ambition and greed, when Conon died and the matter of electing a successor began, a division arose among the people: one party elected the archpriest Theodorus, another the archdeacon Paschal. Consequently, to calm the schism, a third man, Sergius, had to be elected; he succeeded Conon.

Two facts especially useful for clarifying the elections of the pontiffs become known from this history. First, in these times the exarchs of Ravenna had no authority to confirm pontiffs, as had been customary before John V. Second, during the same period it remained customary to send legates to the exarch with the decree of election, as had been done before Pogonatus’s privilege.

I shall briefly examine both points, and then proceed, in accordance with my purpose, to the chronology. I begin with the authority of the exarch.

No one is unaware how reverently the emperors of the East took care over the creation of pontiffs. For, unlike the Gothic Arian kings, when they ruled Italy, they did not dare to interfere in elections. They permitted them to be made by the clergy and people and were content to confirm the elected men before they were ordained.

Such confirmation, signified by a sacred or imperial command, was considered so necessary for as long as the practice prevailed that we do not read of any pontiff being consecrated without it, except Pelagius II, because Italy was being afflicted by innumerable evils. Saint Gregory, who succeeded Pelagius, clearly shows that the consecration of the elected man took place at the emperors’ discretion, with their assent; or, if their assent was not given, another equally free election could be held. When he wished to avoid the pontifical insignia, he secretly sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, imploring him with many prayers never to give his consent to the people.

This authority, first delegated to the exarchs and later taken away by Pogonatus, as we have seen above, was never again acquired by them after Constantine, whatever others may think. The one thing they could do—and which the Arian Goths had formerly done, as did certain less religious princes in a later age—was to terrify the electors, clergy, and people by force and arms, so that they would elect a pontiff whom some private interests favored.

That this was done by the exarch John so that Paschal might be elected against Sergius is taught by Anastasius (no. 159):

“He also did not cease secretly to send his messengers to Ravenna, and by promising money or various other gifts to persuade John the patrician and exarch, surnamed Platyn, to come secretly to Rome with his judges, no one knowing.”

Then, reporting that John came secretly to everyone, Anastasius continues:

“When he had come secretly, unknown to all, and found that everyone had consented to the most holy Sergius, he was unable to support Paschal.”

Thus, unlike the period before Pogonatus, the clergy and people were not forbidden by a law of confirmation to ordain the man they had elected. Once the election had been made by unanimous consent, however, it deprived those who opposed it of every hope of preventing the ordination, which required no confirmation.

What I said about the second point—that after the election of the pontiff messengers or legates were customarily sent to the exarch of Ravenna, as had been the custom before the power of confirmation was removed—is established by the same Anastasius (no. 136), who says:

“They likewise sent messengers, together with clerics and some of the people, to the excellent exarch Theodorus, as is customary.”

That is, soldiers. From this it is clear that the clergy, people, and army sent their legates to Ravenna according to the ancient custom, as is plainly taught in the *Diurnus Pontificalis* (*On the Election of a Pontiff to the Exarch*):

“Having solemnly drawn up his decree and confirmed by the subscriptions of our hands the desires of our hearts concerning his election, through the bearers of this letter we send to you the most holy bishop N., the venerable priest N., the regional notary N., likewise the regional subdeacon N., and N. and N., honorable citizens; and from the flourishing and most fortunate Roman army, the most eminent consul N., or the magnificent military tribunes N. and N., our fellow servants.”

Since this is so, when I said, together with Pagius and Blanchinus, that the custom of sending legates to Ravenna continued until Pepin, I was not asserting, in agreement with Pagius, that the legates were sent to seek confirmation—a servitude from which Pogonatus had freed the Church. It seems, with very plausible conjecture, that the practice of sending them began [Col. 0889A] because of the double election rejected both in the creation of Conon and in that of Sergius, so that, when the exarch—who represented the emperor of the East in the Western Empire—signed the decree of election, the one Father and Pastor of all might be acknowledged by everyone through the general consent of all, and so the schism might be completely abolished.

Although no ancient authority proves whether Ravenna was approached in the elections of Sergius’s successors, it is nevertheless credible that this was done as long as the exarchate existed—not because the clergy and people were compelled by any law or necessity, but solely as an act of obedience. If this was a form of servitude, it was a very mild and agreeable one, freely sought in order to avoid schisms. In this way Pepin freed the Apostolic See, as will be explained in its proper place.

Having briefly discussed the election after Pogonatus, against the conjecture of Peter de Marca, *De Concordia*, book VIII, chapter 9, no. 10, quoted by Antonio Pagius in his own words, I now come to Conon’s chronology, as Pagius does in the year 686, no. 8.

The published codex of Anastasius reckons the vacancy after John as two months and eighteen days; the other codices and catalogues agree with it, except the Lucensian, according to which the see was vacant one month less and one day more.

Before proceeding, however, I must briefly touch on the weakness of the conjecture just praised. Pagius derives it from the intervals between pontificates, as may be seen in the years 681, no. 5, and 686, no. 8; he supposes that these intervals before Zacharias were longer than they really were. For, apart from the first three after Benedict, John, and Conon—which are said to have lasted nearly three months—and the singular interval after John VII, which appears in the codices as three or even four months, all the remaining six are either one month with a few days or less than two months.

Therefore, to tell the truth, I do not understand why the interval of two months and fifteen days after Benedict did not make Pagius suspicious. Was it necessary to wait at Ravenna for confirmation of the election of John V, when the much shorter intervals between pontificates demonstrate that such confirmation was expected?

Since I have discussed these matters above, I proceed with the rest concerning Conon. If, beginning from John’s death on 2 August 686, we count two months and eighteen days, excluding the day of death itself because it belongs to John’s pontificate, we arrive at 21 October of the same year. Since that day was a Sunday, it belongs to Conon’s ordination.

From this it follows that he sat for only eleven months, as all the catalogues correctly state, especially the Corbeiensis, which were being written at this time, and the Farnesian, Ambrosian I, Thuanus II, and Vallicellian codices. Therefore no credence should be given to the published text, which has, besides those eleven months, twenty-three days, nor to the other codices that exceed it by three days. This becomes evident from the date of Conon’s death, recorded in the Veronese and Lucensian catalogues and in almost all the codices as 21 September 687. Those that give the twenty-second refer rather to his burial than to his death.

Thus Conon was ordained on 21 October 686, and after sitting for eleven months, he died on 21 September of the following year.]

[Note: [Col. 0889D]]

No. 156, line 1.—“Conon.” A Thracian, son of Benedict, a native of Tomi, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church. After Peter and Theodorus, elected in the schism, had been expelled, he sat for eleven months; he was created and consecrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, a Sunday, in the year of Christ 686.

No. 157, line 2.—“Two hundred grain-obligations.” In the year 687, having learned of Conon’s consecration, the emperor wrote him a second letter, in which he declared that he would relieve two hundred estates whose annual payments had been made by the custodians of the patrimony of Bruttium and Lucania, and that the families of that patrimony and of Sicily should be restored, since they were being held by the military as pledges.

Conon made Constantine, a deacon of the Church of Syracuse, rector of the patrimony of Sicily, and granted him many privileges beyond custom.]

[Note: [Col. 0890A]]

No. 156, lines 22 and 23.—“They sent to the excellent exarch Theodorus, as is customary.” Justinian II, distressed that Constantine Pogonatus had restored to the Roman Church the ancient freedom of the assemblies in choosing a pontiff, imitated his grandfather Constans in this matter rather than his father Constantine. He ordered that no pontiff should be created without the exarch’s consent, and opened a new source of evils within the clergy, since those aspiring to the pontifical dignity tried to obtain it through an exarch won over by gifts or corrupted by offices.

Hence new disagreements and disputes arose in the choice of the pontiff. For when John V died, a schism broke out for several days between Theodorus the priest, favored by the army, and Peter the archpriest, favored by the clergy. It was finally extinguished when Conon was elected by everyone’s votes, and messengers were sent to Ravenna to the exarch Theodorus to announce his election.

Bacchinius, in his notes to the Life of Theodorus, bishop of Ravenna, learnedly observes that this Theodorus was a different man from Theodorus Calliopa, who administered the exarchate twice. Calliopa had a deceitful and impious character, as is shown by his sacrilegious actions against Pope Martin; this Theodorus, however, was gentle in character and devout toward sacred buildings, for he visited Saint Mary at Blachernae daily for religious purposes—a church outside the walls of Ravenna—and wished to be buried there with his wife Agatha.]

[Note: [Col. 0890B]]

No. 156, line 3.—“In whose election there was no small contention.” When Pope John V died, the city was split into two parties. The clergy supported Peter the archpriest, while the judges and the army favored Theodorus the priest. Finally, by common agreement, the clergy united in the election of a third man, namely Conon, a Thracian by origin, who had been educated in Sicily and later came to Rome, where he attained the dignity of the priesthood.

His venerable gray hair, simple spirit, peaceful character, religious life, and sacred learning made him most worthy of this position, as Anastasius writes. He adds:

“After some days they too were persuaded—the judges, namely, and the leaders of the army—and they consented to the person of the aforesaid most holy man, subscribed to his decrees with devoted mind, and likewise sent messengers, together with clerics and some of the people, to the excellent exarch Theodorus, as is customary.”

From this it is evident that what we observed concerning Benedict II is true: the emperor Justinian, son and successor of Constantine Pogonatus, established, according to the earlier custom, that the consecration of the Roman pontiff should not take place without the confirmation of the exarch of Ravenna. The Romans therefore remained free from the burden of sending the decree of election to Constantinople, but remained subject to examination by the exarchs until the exarchate itself disappeared in the following century, as de Marca notes in book VIII of *On Concord*, chapter 9, no. 10.

Conon, therefore, was consecrated on 21 October 686, which fell on a Sunday. It is true that Anastasius says that after the death of John V the episcopate ceased for two months and eighteen days. But either Anastasius is corrupt at this point and we should read nineteen days, or he excluded both the day of death and the day of burial from the interval between pontificates. This must be said if Conon’s ordination is to be placed on a Sunday.

Whatever the case, either in the period of John V’s see or in the interval after his death, an error of at least one day must have entered the chronology of his death; this does not affect our chronology, provided that Conon’s ordination is assigned to a Sunday.

We know from the words of Anastasius cited above what rite was observed in Conon’s creation before he was consecrated. Anastasius had already said that the priests and clergy unanimously elected Conon at the Lateran. Then all the judges, together with the leaders of the army, came to greet him and acclaimed him in his praise. When the army saw the unanimity of the clergy and people, they consented to the election and signed the decree with them. Finally, together with the clergy and people, they sent their messengers to the exarch, as was customary.

The election was therefore first made by the clergy; then came the greeting and acclamation by the judges and leaders. The consent of the army followed. Finally, everyone signed the decree, which was sent to the exarch and sometimes also to the emperor.

From this and other matters that the same author relates concerning Pope Valentinus, Mabillon, in his commentary on the *Roman Ordinal*, section 18, explains the rite customarily observed before the eleventh century in the consecration of the Roman pontiff.

The election of a pontiff was followed by his institution, carried out in two actions: ordination and enthronement. Ordination customarily took place in the Vatican Basilica of Saint Peter, and enthronement in the Lateran. In these matters the order was not fixed. Although consecration usually preceded enthronement, sometimes enthronement came first, as we have seen in the case of Conon; the same occurred in the election of Valentinus, as we shall relate below.

Line 23.—“Here he received the imperial command,” etc.

“Although Anastasius says this,” writes Baronius under the year 686, “it is nevertheless clear from the letters of Pope Nicholas to the emperor Michael that Justinian was not sound in the faith, and that this same emperor opposed Conon, since he forced Conon’s legates, who had been sent to Constantinople, to betray their trust. But hear Nicholas’s words as he inveighs against wicked emperors who have treated the Roman Church badly:

‘You killed the ministers who offered such great salvation in two ways, because either they killed them spiritually by making them participants in their error, as happened in the time of Conon of revered memory,’ etc.

These words indeed indicate that Justinian began to adhere to a different faith from the Roman pontiff, and therefore it is clear that he felt the divine power angry with him,” etc.

Thus Baronius. But since neither Anastasius nor the other historians mention that crime, and since, on the other hand, no one committed to writing that Justinian felt the divine power angry with him and was cast down from the throne because he had defected from the faith—indeed, Agatho, a deacon of the Church of Constantinople, says in his peroration entitled *The Scribe’s Peroration on the Acts of the Sixth Synod*, where the rash undertakings of the tyrant and fool Bardanes against that same holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod are also reported—since, I say, Agatho says that those evils occurred because of Justinian’s wicked and bloodthirsty disposition from the beginning, then in the aforesaid Letter 8 of Pope Nicholas, where we read “of Conon of revered memory,” it seems that we should read “of Constantine of revered memory.”

It was under Constantine’s pontificate, not Conon’s, that the tyrant Bardanes—who had seized the empire under the name Philippicus—persecuted the orthodox who refused to sign the document he had composed for abolishing the Sixth Synod, as we shall say in its proper place.

Accordingly, it was not Conon’s but Pope Constantine’s legates whom Philippicus, not Justinian, compelled to betray their trust. For, according to Anastasius, Justinian permitted Conon to preserve the Sixth Synod forever intact and unshaken, the synod which his father Constantine had convened. See what is said under Pope Constantine.]

[Note: [Col. 0892B]]

No. 157, line 3.—“So that the family of the aforesaid patrimony, which was being held as a pledge by the military, might be restored.” The family of an ecclesiastical patrimony is the flock of slaves assigned to cultivate the land. The slaves of the Church, and even freedmen—that is, manumitted slaves—are said to belong to the Church’s *familia*, canon 8, cause 12, question 2; just as the freedmen of private persons are said to belong to the *familia* of their patron, *Cum pater*, section *Fidei*, *De legatis* 2.

Line 4.—“Beyond custom, without the consent of the clergy, in opposition to the ecclesiastics, he appointed Constantine, a deacon of the Church of Syracuse, rector of the patrimony in Sicily.” According to custom, subdeacons of the Roman Church were sent by the pontiff, not without the consent of the clergy, to administer the patrimony of the Roman Church in Sicily; see canon *Pervenit*, cause 11, question 1, and canon *Valde necessarium*, distinction 94. Thus Conon is criticized because, contrary to custom and without the consent of the clergy, he placed a deacon of the Church of Syracuse over the patrimony of the Roman Church in Sicily.]

[Col. 0881]

**156. Conon, originating from a father named Tracesius.**
[Note: [Col. 0881] “A Thracian by birth,” B.], educated in Sicily; afterward, coming to Rome and serving that Church, he attained the honor of the priesthood. He sat for eleven months and twenty-three days.

During his election, when a bishop was being sought, no small dispute arose, because the clergy were supporting Peter the archpriest, while the army supported Theodore the priest. [Note: [Col. 0881] “All [the army] in favor of Theodore.”] The clergy, assembled before the doors of the Constantinian basilica, held their ground, because those who had been sent from the army to guard the imperial basilica were watching the closed doors [Note: [Col. 0881] “gates,” omitted in some witnesses] and absolutely permitted no one to enter. The entire army, meanwhile, had likewise assembled in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr [Note: [Col. 0881] “had assembled”]; neither side consented to the other: the army would not yield to the clergy, nor the clergy to the army, on behalf of the aforementioned priests.

But when messages sent by both sides [Note: [Col. 0881] “messages having been sent by both sides”; B has “replies”] went back and forth for a long time without accomplishing anything toward agreement, the priests and clergy, having taken counsel, entered unanimously into the Lateran episcopium and chose and proclaimed a third person, the aforementioned pontiff [Note: [Col. 0881] B: “Conon”]. In him there were truly an angelic appearance, venerable gray hair, truthful speech, advanced age, [Col. 0883] a simple disposition, peaceful manners, and a religious life. He had never involved himself in secular lawsuits or affairs [Note: [Col. 0883] “had never entangled himself in secular lawsuits and affairs”].

Immediately all the judges, together with the chief men of the army, came to greet him, and all together acclaimed him in his praise [Note: [Col. 0883] “in praise of him.”] When the army saw the unanimity of the clergy and people subscribing to his election, after several days they too yielded and consented to the person of the aforesaid most holy man. With devout mind they subscribed to his election and sent messengers, together with members of the clergy and people, to the most eminent Theodore the exarch, as was customary. [Note: [Col. 0883] See Baronius, under the year of the Lord 686.]

He received the imperial command of the lord Justinian, by which Justinian indicated that he had found the acts of the holy Sixth Synod and had them in his possession—the synod which his father, the lord Constantine of pious memory, had convened with God’s help. His Piety promised that he would perpetually guard and preserve that synod inviolate and unshaken.

### 157

In Conon’s time the imperial Piety, by a sacred command, remitted two hundred annona-assessments, which the guardians of the patrimony annually paid in Bruttium and Lucania. He also sent another command that the household of the aforesaid patrimony and of Sicily should be restored, since it was being held in pledge by the army.

Here, contrary to custom and without the consent of the clergy, through the instigation of evil men and against the wishes of churchmen, he appointed Constantine, a deacon of the Church of Syracuse, as administrator of the patrimony in Sicily [Note: [Col. 0883] “in the opposition of churchmen”]. He was a perverse and evasive man [Note: [Col. 0883] perhaps “a depraved man”]; Conon also granted him permission to use a cloak for riding.

Not long afterward a revolt arose against him among the citizens on account of disputes concerning the patrimony. He was shut away by the provincial judge under strict custody, because he was found to have sent instructions for setting the judges against one another [Note: [Col. 0883] “to have been sent”]. The most holy man, held by a prolonged illness, so that he could scarcely complete even the sacred ordinations [Note: [Col. 0883] “of priests”], died.

He left a blessing in gold for all the clergy and monasteries, just as his predecessor, Pope Benedict, had done. His archdeacon, seeing that the same pontiff was constrained by illness and led by greed for the aforesaid legacy [Note: [Col. 0883] B adds: “which the pontiff had left to the clergy and monasteries”], while it had not yet been paid, wrote to Ravenna to John, the glorious new exarch. Promising him its payment [Note: [Col. 0883] B: “he promised”], he sought to have his own person elected to the pontificate.

He also charged this to his judges, whom he appointed at Rome, and sent them to administer the city, so that after the pontiff’s death the person of that archdeacon might be elected. He ordained sixteen bishops in various places.

He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on 21 September [Note: [Col. 0883] B: “22 October”], and the episcopate was vacant for two months and twenty-three days [Note: [Col. 0883] B: “thirteen days”].
