[Note: [Col. 0903A]]

No. 158, line 7.—During his priesthood he diligently celebrated the solemn rites of Mass throughout various cemeteries. In the cemeteries there were oratories, or altars, at which stations and gatherings of Christians took place for the sake of prayer, and Masses were celebrated.

Anastasius, in Gregory III: “He also established that an annual station should be held in the cemetery of Saint Petronilla.” Hence, in the time of Decius, Christians were forbidden to set foot in cemeteries. The deacon Pontius, in the Life of Cyprian, in Surius, September 14: “They also ordered that no assemblies should be held in any places and that they should not enter cemeteries.”

Socrates, Book II, chapter 23, relates that the people of Alexandria withdrew into a cemetery for the sake of prayer so as not to communicate with George the false bishop:

“Τῇ ἑβδομαδι μετὰ τὴν ἁγίαν Πεντηκοστὴν ὁ λαὸς νησθεύσας ὑζῆλθε παρὰ τὸ κοιμητηρίον εὔξασθαι.”

“On the week after holy Pentecost, the people, having fasted, went out to the cemetery in order to pray.” The same is found in Theodoret, Book II, chapter 14.

No. 159, line 2.—“And entering, he greeted and kissed the aforementioned most holy elect.” When Theodore and Paschalis had been elected in opposition, Sergius was elected in order to dissolve the schism. Theodore was one of the two elected during the schism; he approached Sergius with prostration and a kiss.

Cardinals and bishops are admitted as brothers to the kiss. Supreme pontiffs—and even exempt abbots themselves (Chapter *Cum olim*, under “On privileges”)—and bishops, because of the reverence due to their rank, are admitted to the kiss of the prince.

Ambrose, Letter 27, concerning the embassy to Maximus the Tyrant, seated at Trier: “When he sat in the council chamber, I entered; he rose so that he might give a kiss.”

Hilary of Poitiers, Against Constantius: “You receive priests with the kiss by which Christ also was betrayed.”

Laymen, at the ordination of the Roman pontiff, kiss his feet. Anastasius, in the life of Valentinus: “Then, with fitting praises of glory and the fullness of honor, he was led by them to the Lateran patriarchium and placed upon the pontifical throne, while the entire Roman senate joyfully kissed his feet,” etc.

Even cardinals, at the ordination of a pontiff, lower themselves to kiss his feet. Radevicus, On the Deeds of Frederick, Book II, chapter 66: “Then, as is customary, the lord cardinals and the Roman clergy—all who were present and those who later gathered—and the greater part of the Roman people kissed his feet.”

Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, when consulted concerning Cadalo, the antipope, and Alexander II—who should be judged the true pontiff—says in Book III, Letter 4: “I give my hands, I kiss his soles, and I call not only him the apostolic one but even an apostle, if you command.”

Even emperors kiss the feet of the pontiff. Justinian II kissed the feet of Pope Constantine. Anastasius, in the life of Constantine: “On the day when they saw one another, the most Christian Augustus, with the kingdom upon his head, prostrated himself and kissed the pontiff’s feet.”

Siginolfus, prince of the Beneventans, received a blessing from Sergius II after first kissing the pontiff’s feet. Anastasius, in the life of Sergius II: “When the prelate had received him, he prostrated himself on the ground, humbly kissed his precious feet, and, having received a blessing from him, departed from his presence.”

Finally, at the election of the Roman pontiff, there was an ancient custom of kissing the feet of the elect. The same author, in the life of Leo IV: “Preserving the ancient custom, they all kissed his feet.” Likewise, in the life of Benedict III: “And proceeding, they began to kiss his footprints.”

Line 23.—“The aforementioned Paschalis, however, not long afterward was deprived of the office of archdeacon because of certain incantations and groves which he worshiped, or lots which he practiced with other diviners, with the judgment of God and of the blessed chief of the Apostles Peter intervening.”

Paschalis, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was deposed because of certain incantations and the worship of groves, which he worshiped with other worshipers. There were people who made vows and prayers at trees or springs.

Synod of Auxerre, canon 3: “It is not permitted to fulfill sacred vows among brambles or trees, or at springs.”

*Respectare* is a frequentative verb, equivalent to “to worship” or “to look upon with reverence.” Velleius Paterculus, Book II: “Having obtained permission to touch his hand, he returned to the little boat, gazing at Caesar without end, and was brought to the bank of his people.” Hence *respectores*.

No. 160, line 8.—“Sent into the little granary, which is called the fleshly scebrum, into this Roman city, for confirmation.”

*Scebrum* means a granary. Hence Ingulphus should be corrected in the Chronicle of Croyland: “By the Lord’s generosity he began to abound in all good things, so that in treasures and scauræ, as well as in lands and tenements, double compensation was later returned to him for the things first lost.” In place of *scauris*, read *scebris* or *scearis*.

Line 13.—“Sending the emperor Sergius the magistrianus to Rome in contempt of the aforementioned pontiff.”

The *magistriani* were *agentes in rebus*, so called because they served among the palace offices under the authority of the master of offices. Ambrose, On Duties, Book II, chapter 27: “The form of the rescript was being read; the directive established by the master of offices was present, and an agent in affairs was in attendance.”

No. 162, line 3.—“After prayer had been made, he removed the impressed seal, opened the little case, and found inside a plumarium of holoseric silk laid over it, which is called a stauracis.”

The silver casket containing a portion of the wood of the Lord’s cross had been sealed. Cases containing relics were customarily sealed.

Gregory of Tours, On the Miracles of the Martyrs, Book I, chapter 33: “But when Abbot Venantius had removed the seal from the cabinet, he found the chest locked.”

A plumarium of holoseric silk had been placed over the wood of the cross. A *plumatium* was a veil of silk cloth woven in the form of birds’ feathers. Ambrose, Letter 27: “When I was conferring with his companions, lest they should allow the old man to be cast out without clothing, without a plumarium.”

This is what they called *opus plumarium*, or *plumatile*. Plautus, in the *Epidicus*: “Cumatile or plumatile.” *Plumatum.* Petronius, in the *Satyricon*: “Clothed in a golden Babylonian plumatum.” Gregory of Tours, On the Miracles of the Martyrs, Book I, chapter 97: “There stands a table covered with snow-white cloths and adorned with plumarium work.”

Hence *plumarii* are craftsmen who weave this kind of garment. Book 2 of the Code, “On exemptions for craftsmen,” Book X. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, Book III, chapter 10: “Linen-workers or plumarii.” The same author, chapter 13 of the same book: “They will make linen-workers, or weavers of tunics, plumarii.”

This kind of garment was extremely costly. Vopiscus, in the life of Carinus: “Why should I speak of linens brought from Egypt; of those from Tyre and Sidon, translucent because of their fineness, glittering with purple, renowned for the difficulty of their plumarium work?”

Not only garments but also cuirasses were customarily woven with scales or iron plates in the form of feathers. Virgil, *Aeneid* XI:

> Whom a hide, bristling with bronze scales wrought into feathers and fastened with gold, covered.

Veils woven with plumarium work were also customarily placed before the doors of houses. Anastasius, in Gregory IV, at the end: “One linen, plumatum veil before the doors.”

He says that it was made of holoseric silk, which is called stauracis. Stauracis veils are truly made of silk or purple cloth, woven with various flowers or figures; they were imported from Tyre and were therefore also called Tyrian. See Anastasius, on stauracis or Tyrian cloth.

Line 6.—“From it he drew four petals, in which gems had been enclosed.”

A *petalum*, from the Greek πέταλον, is a golden crown worn by priests or by those descended from priests, such as the Apostle John and James, the brother of the Lord.

Concerning John, Eusebius, Book III, chapter 25: “Ὡς ἐγενήθη ἱερεὺς, τὸ πέταλον πεφορηκώς.”

“When he became a priest, he wore the petalum.”

Concerning James, Epiphanius, *Panarion*, heresy 29: “Ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ πέταλον ἐστι τῆς κεφαλῆς ἐξῆν αὐτῷ φέρειν.”

“But it was also permitted him to wear the petalum of the head.”

Line 7.—“And he found the ineffable portion of the saving wood of the Lord’s cross” [Col. 0905A], “which from that time, for the salvation of the human race, is kissed and adored by all the Christian people on the day of the Exaltation of the holy Cross in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantinian.”

On the day of the Exaltation of the Lord’s Cross, solemn worship of the cross by kissing was instituted in the Lateran basilica. Pagans too were accustomed to kiss images of the gods; hence images of the gods appeared worn down by kisses. Lucretius, Book I:

> Then beside the bronze gates  
> The images stretch forth their right hands,  
> Often worn thin by the touch of those greeting  
> And passing by.

No. 163, line 18.—“He covered and strengthened the *trullus* of the same church with cast leaden sheets.”

A *trulla* is a hollow wine vessel. Marcus Tullius, *Against Verres*, Book 6: “There was also a wine vessel made from one enormous gem.” Apicius, *On Culinary Matters*, Book IV: “As many lagana as you have placed, fill just as many trullae, and pour wine over them.”

Hence, shortly before, *detrullare* means “to pour out from a trulla.” “And it is fitting to pour alternately from the trulla into a dish.”

A *trulla* is hollowed out and has a golden handle. Hence *trullus* could signify a vault or chamber of a church, because it was shaped like a trulla. From this came *trullus*, the name of the imperial palace at Constantinople.

The roof of the church was made of sheets—that is, leaden boards. Anastasius, in Gregory III: “Likewise, in the basilica of the holy Mother of God which is called ‘at the Martyrs,’ he had the roof, destroyed by long neglect, thoroughly cleaned and restored anew with abundant lime or leaden sheets.”

Line 22.—“The basilica of Saint Aurea at the mouths [of the Tiber].”

This is the basilica of Saint Aurea, virgin and martyr, at the mouths of the Tiber. The Roman Martyrology, August 24: “At the mouths of the Tiber, Saint Aurea, virgin and martyr.”

Hence a corrupt passage in Anastasius, in Leo III, should be corrected: “He entirely repaired anew the roof of the church of blessed Aurea situated at the mouth.” Read “of Aurea.” This correction is supported by Leo IV, in canon *Igitur*, 23, question 8: “The supreme prelate celebrated Mass in the church of blessed Aurea” [Col. 0905C].

The name Aurea was attributed to Petronilla, daughter of the Apostle Peter. Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 758, reports that her monument bore the inscription: “Aurea Petronilla.”

No. 164, line 1.—“Here he established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, the clergy and people should sing: AGNUS DEI, QUI TOLLIS PECCATA MUNDI, MISERERE NOBIS”—“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

Anastasius calls Pope Sergius the author of this institution, namely, that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung during the celebration of Mass. Alcuin mentions this institution in *On the Divine Office*, chapter 40.

Others, however, maintain that this institution was made at the Council of Nicaea, which they prove from the Arabic version of that council itself.

Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, in the supplement to Sigebert, reports that in the year 1183 the Virgin Mary appeared to a woodworker and gave him a seal engraved with her own image and that of the newborn Christ, marked around with this inscription: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.”

Line 2.—“He established that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which the Greeks call Hypapante” [Col. 0905D]—“a litany should go out and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.”

Among the Greeks, *Hypante* or *Hypapante* is the feast of the meeting, which among the Latins is called the feast of the Purification because of Simeon’s meeting with Christ.

Paul the Deacon, Book XVI, in the life of Justinian: “In that same year the Hypapante of the Lord began to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.”

Siffrid, priest of Meissen, *Epitome*, Book II, under the year 551: “Under Pope Pelagius and the Emperor Justinian it began at Constantinople that the Hypapante of the Lord—that is, the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary—should be solemnly celebrated.”

The same is found in Anastasius, *History*: “In the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign the Hypapante of the Lord began, to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.”

[Note: [Col. 0905D]]

No. 158, line 11.—“Paschalis the archdeacon.” [Col. 0906A] We noted above, in connection with Boniface III, that he had established in a synod of seventy-two bishops that no one, while the pontiff or the bishop of his city was alive, should presume to speak of a successor or form a faction for himself, except on the third day after his burial. The reason and necessity for that enactment, designed to prevent the evils arising from the canvassing of candidates, are seen even more clearly in the election of Sergius.

According to Anastasius’s account in his Life, Conon had bequeathed a fixed sum of gold for distribution to the clergy as a *roga*, or *presbyterium*, as it was called; the archdeacon was generally in charge of distributing it. Thus Paschalis the archdeacon, while Conon was ill, did not distribute that gold at all, but promised it to John the exarch on condition that he support him in the election.

Hence the schism arose between Paschalis the archdeacon and Theodore the archpriest. Concerning the authority of the archdeacon in governing the clergy, see Agnellus in the Life of Theodore of Ravenna. For, speaking of a severe shortage of grain, he relates:

“When the priests could not find [Col. 0906B] where to buy it, they went to him and begged him to give them assistance. He then summoned the archdeacon, named Theodore … and said to them: ‘Tell the priests of the Church and the entire clergy: why are you being consumed by poverty and hunger? If you give up the whole fourth part of the Church’s income and receive for the entire course of the year only a gift in place of that fourth part, according to the pontiff’s provision, I shall now relieve your poverty.’

“After being harshly pressed for a long time, and as hunger grew worse, they consented; and from that time the fourth part was taken away from the clergy of that Church, down to the present day. He also removed the custom of the Church, which had been written in separate volumes for each office, and consumed it by fire.”

All these things, of course, had been kept by the archdeacon of Ravenna.

## No. 159, line 18.—To be given as a pledge

In the public necessities of the Church, bishops gave sacred vessels as pledges, and even persons who were bound to the service of the Church. Thus Conon, when those who were staying in Sicily [Col. 0906C] to administer the patrimony of Saint Peter had been held as pledges by the military, took care to ransom them. Hence Anastasius writes in his Life of Conon:

> “He sent another order that the household of the aforesaid patrimony, and of Sicily, which was being held as a pledge by the military, should be restored.”

Likewise, when Pope Agapetus, in order to undertake a journey to Constantinople for the needs of the Church, had pawned the sacred vessels to the imperial treasurers, Senator, having learned of the matter, ordered that they be restored, as is read in Cassiodorus, book XII, letter 20, p. 774:

> “Therefore, having been reminded by our command and made secure by the royal order, return the vessels of the saints, together with the bond of the acknowledgment, to the agents of Saint Peter the Apostle without any delay, so that, returned with profit and obtained swiftly, the desired ministries may be seen restored to the hands of the Levites and reported throughout the whole world. Let what was its own be given back, since it has justly received it through generosity.”

James II, king of Aragon, abolished the pledging of persons in the year 1269:

> “We do not wish that the person of anyone should be pledged, or that anyone should be seized or detained in our land for another’s debt on account of any pledge . . . since, when a neighbor is pledged for a neighbor, it is enough that the property, and not the person, be pledged.” [Col. 0906D]

## No. 160, line 14.—Magistriani

Whenever imperial commands had to be carried out with greater speed, magistriani were sent. For this reason, long ago the emperor Leo, in order to suppress the disturbances that Timothy Aelurus, the Eutychianist, had stirred up in Egypt, sent magistriani throughout the world to the bishops, so that by encyclical letters all might reply with one faith and one mind concerning what ought to be decreed against the seditious heretics.

## Line 15.—Boniface the counselor

Among the Roman clergy and the pope, the dignity of counselor of the Apostolic See was among the more distinguished offices. Whoever held this function stood beside the pope and the clergy like an assessor in more serious and public controversies; and whenever the see was vacant, he governed the Church together with others.

Gregory the Great speaks of this office, book II, letter 54 [Col. 0907A]. For in the controversy concerning the privileges of the Church of Ravenna, the more important investigation was entrusted to the counselor of the Apostolic See. Indeed, when Copronymus, in a letter to Charlemagne, complained about Christopher, counselor of the Apostolic See, Pope Paul I wrote a defense of him to Charles, which is found, and among other things he says:

> “For they assert in the very substance of their writings that our beloved son Christopher, primicerius and counselor, without our authority and as though we were unaware of it, made those reports which we had repeatedly directed to him, and had read back other matters in place of those sent by him and by you; and in this we produce God as witness and judge, that it is in no way so. For that counselor has never done, or presumed to do, anything outside our will, since he was and is the sincere and most approved faithful servant both of our predecessor and brother, the lord Pope Stephen, and of ourselves; and we are satisfied with his [Col. 0907B] unstained faith and firm constancy of heart.”

From this it is clear that the counselor assisted the pontiffs by his learning and judgment in disputes concerning faith and discipline. Accordingly, this Boniface was chosen to refute Macarius of Antioch, whom the Sixth Synod had punished with exile, as is read in the legitimate first act of the Seventh Synod, p. 63:

> “For Macarius the heretic, sent into exile by the Sixth Synod, was in exile at Rome; and our holy father, Pope Benedict, gave him a period of forty days, and every day he sent to him Boniface the counselor, teaching him divine Scripture in admonitory words; but he never wished to be corrected. He did this in order to persuade and correct him.”

Therefore the emperor Justinian, observing that confirmation of the Trullan canons had been refused by Sergius, wished—apparently at the suggestion of Boniface the counselor—to have both men brought to Constantinople, so that they might give an account of the deed.

## No. 161, line 4.—The heart of the military force of Ravenna

When Zacharias, the imperial protospatharius, attempted to arrest Pope Sergius in order to send him captive to the emperor, the Italian military stood in the pope’s defense and did not withdraw from Sergius until the unjust imperial officer had departed. That military was chiefly stationed in those cities which were under the authority of the bishop of Ravenna, and which Agnellus lists in his *Pontifical*, part II, especially since various disputes subsequently broke out between the pontiffs and the bishops of Ravenna. [Col. 0907C]

## No. 163, line 15.—The most ancient image of the apostles

It appears from this that the ancient use of sacred images, and their placement in churches, was already established. On this subject Ciampini should be consulted in his work on mosaics.

## No. 164, line 7.—The synod of Aquileia

Anastasius copied this, as he did several other things, from Bede, who says in his book *On the Six Ages*:

> “A synod was held at Aquileia. Through ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope [Col. 0907D] Sergius, it too consented to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

Paul the Deacon likewise, book VI, chapter 14, after recounting that Tiberius had seized the empire in the ninety-eighth year, writes:

> “At this time a synod was held at Aquileia, which, through ignorance of the faith, etc.”

What follows is identical with what we have cited from Bede.

---

## Note: [Col. 0907D]

## No. 158, line 1.—Sergius

According to Molanus, in his *Index of the Saints of Belgium*, Saint Hubert, bishop of Liège, was consecrated by this pontiff. He was the most worthy successor of Saint Lambert the Martyr, noble by birth. In order to keep his subjects firmly established in observance of the Catholic faith and obedience to the holy Roman Church, from which they had received the holy Gospel, and to bind their descendants by the same bond, he gave them the public seal of Saint Lambert the Martyr, engraved with his image and marked with this inscription:

> “Holy Liège, daughter of the Roman Church.” [Col. 0908A]

## No. 160, line 1.—The council

The Constantinopolitan Quinisext Council.

## Line 2.—Legates of the Apostolic See

Understand by this those Greek bishops who had been established in the East as vicars of the Roman pontiff.

## No. 161, line 25.—For even the one who had sent him, etc.

The prefect Leontius, having received the empire from the Greeks, mutilated Justinian by cutting off his nose and banished him to Cherson in the year of Christ 694, which was the tenth year of Justinian’s reign. Cedrenus, Theophanes, and Zonaras, as well as other Greek annalists, describe the circumstances of the event.

By the just judgment of God, the impious Justinian deservedly suffered this punishment. After, at the urging of the patriarch Callinicus, he had sanctioned new canons and thoroughly disfigured the Eastern Church by them, he worked with the greatest zeal either to inflict the same disgrace upon the Roman Church or, at least, if the supreme pontiff resisted the emperor’s command, to have the pope forcibly taken from Rome to the royal city. [Col. 0908B]

## No. 164, line 7.—In his time the synod of Aquileia, etc.

Paul the Deacon writes the same thing, book V, chapter 14.

---

## Note: [Col. 0908B]

## Chronological Notes

When Conon, after exercising the pontificate for eleven months, died on 21 September 687, an interregnum of two months and twenty-three days preceded the ordination of his successor, as all the manuscripts teach, except the Mazarin manuscript, which adds the day. The third and fifth Colbertine catalogues and the Veronese catalogue agree with it. Nevertheless, all agree remarkably: when the day of death is excluded, there are twenty-three days, and when it is included, twenty-four days, in addition to the two months of the interregnum.

Accordingly, Sergius, Conon’s successor, after the ambition of his rival the archdeacon—which was joined with crime—had been frustrated, was ordained pontiff on 15 December of the aforesaid year, 687, as the F. lit. Dom. demonstrates. He administered the Apostolic See longer than his predecessors and closed the seventh century. In the first year of the eighth century already in progress, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, or 8 September, he died, in the fifteenth indiction, as the common, Freherian, and Cavense manuscripts correctly state. This indiction corresponds to the year 701, the year of Sergius’s death. [Col. 0908C]

The remaining manuscripts that I use give the fourteenth indiction, which indicates September of the preceding year, 700. But since all these same manuscripts agree with the others in assigning to Sergius’s pontificate a duration of thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days, it is perfectly clear that those manuscripts which give the fourteenth indiction are erroneous. This is evident both from the correctly established reigns of his predecessors and from a document that Antonio Pagi reports as received from Bede, confirming the beginning of Sergius’s pontificate (Pagi, 689, no. 5).

This is the epitaph of King Caedwalla, which ends as follows:

> “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction, while the apostolic man, the lord Pope Sergius, was pontiff in the second year.”

If Sergius was in his second year in April 689, there can be no doubt that the beginning of his see must correctly be reckoned from the year 687, namely from the final month of that year, December, as I stated above. Moreover, there is absolutely no authority, either in the manuscripts or in the catalogues, by which Sergius’s death can be moved back by a whole year.

The Bergomas catalogue, which alone supports this opinion, gives twelve years instead of thirteen. Since it agrees with the others in determining the reigns of his successors—reigns based on definite chronological markers—it does not provide assistance to the other manuscripts but instead harms its own position by revealing a further error from which it suffers.

The first, second, and third Colbertine manuscripts, as well as the Palatine-Vatican, Lucan, and Farfensian manuscripts, have a lesser defect: they omit the month. The Veronese manuscript also began to be less careful from this point onward, no longer recording the death-days of the pontiffs. In the case of Sergius, however, it is not merely careless but plainly erroneous, adding a full year to his pontificate contrary to the testimony of all the others. [Col. 0909A]

As for the addition of one day found in all the Colbertine manuscripts except the second and fifth, and likewise in various other catalogues, I repeat what I said concerning the interregnum: the entire difference disappears according to whether the day of death is included or excluded.

Thus, concluding from beginning to end, I state that Sergius, ordained on 15 December 687, sat for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days, and exchanged life for death on 8 September 701.

---

## Note: [Col. 0909A]

## No. 158, line 1.—Sergius

The son of the merchant Tiberius, a native of Antioch, he came to Rome during the pontificate of Adeodatus and was received into the Roman clergy. Soon afterward he became a regular canon, and then, made by Pope Leo II a cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna at the Two Houses, he acquired such renown that, when Conon died, he was substituted in his place. He was elected on the twelfth day before the Kalends and consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the beginning of the year 687. [Col. 0909B]

---

## Note: [Col. 0909B]

## No. 158, line 18.—They proceeded to the sacred palace

The sacred palace to which most of the clergy and the leading men of the army proceeded from the Lateran, in order to deliberate on ending the schism between Theodore the archpriest and Paschal the archdeacon, was situated not on the Palatine, where the former imperial residences had stood, but not far from the title of Saint Sixtus, at the place where the Appian Way diverges from the Latina.

There stood very large buildings called the Sacred Palace, intended for the use either of the pontiff or of the emperor, whenever the latter happened to be in Rome. Within the Sacred Palace there was an oratory or church of Saint Caesarius. This church was distinguished under the title of Saint Caesarius in the Palace, as is testified both by several ancient monuments and by the acts of the sacred Council of Trent, where Christopher Cardinal Madrucius is subscribed as priest of Saint Caesarius in the Palace. [Col. 0909C]

Sixtus V removed this church from the number of the titles because, having collapsed through extreme antiquity, it was entirely inaccessible in his time. Nevertheless, it was rebuilt not long afterward, during the pontificate of Clement VIII. In addition, so that its former dignity might remain intact and preserved for posterity, he again enrolled it among the titular churches. I make these observations from the most learned Baronius (*Annals*, to the year 603, no. 2).

## No. 160, line 1.—The emperor Justinian ordered that a council be held in the royal city

The bishops of the pseudo-synod testify in their preface to Justinian II that this little council was held to supplement the Fifth and Sixth Synods, which had issued no canons concerning discipline, in the same Trullo of Constantinople where the Sixth Ecumenical Council had been convened ten years earlier.

For this reason Theodore Balsamon, the patron of schismatics, calls it σύνοδος πεντεκτη, that is, the Quinisext Synod. Our author says that legates of the Apostolic See attended it and were deceived into subscribing to it. This should not be understood as though Sergius had sent legates representing him to that assembly, which he condemned. Rather, the meaning is that a representative of the Apostolic See was present—one who had lived in Constantinople since the time of the first Justinian, attended to matters of faith and discipline, and could exercise no jurisdiction without orders.

Basil, archbishop of Gortyna in Crete, was then the sole holder of this legation and subscribed to the little council in the name of the Roman Church. Besides him, Balsamon contends, in order to give the erratic synod—for this is what the ancients called it—the authority of an ecumenical council, that there also subscribed a certain bishop of Ravenna acting in place of the Roman synod, together with the bishops of Thessalonica, Sardinia, Heraclea, and Corinth, who were then papal legates, as is found written in the ancient collections of canons. [Col. 0910A]

But, to say nothing of the papal legation, with which the bishop of Heraclea was never honored, the surviving acts of the Trullan assembly themselves expose Balsamon’s falsehood. The ordinary bishop of Corinth, the legate of the Apostolic See, and likewise the bishops of Ravenna, Heraclea, and Sardinia were absent from it. A blank document was left for them so that they might later sign the dissolved synod in their names:

> “The representation of Heraclea, Sardinia, Ravenna, and Corinth.”

In a higher place the pseudo-synod likewise left a blank document for Pope Sergius, as the head of all priests:

> “The representation of the most holy pope of Rome.”

But Sergius rejected it. For although some of the more than one hundred canons that it contains are highly praiseworthy, others are extremely objectionable.

In canon 3—without pursuing each one individually—the eighty-five canons of the apostles are ordered to be received, although Gelasius had placed all of them among the apocrypha by a solemn decree accepted throughout the world.

In canon 13, the law of ecclesiastical celibacy is shaken, and the most chaste discipline of the Roman Church is censured, by which ministers of sacred things are forbidden the use of marriage.

Canon 55 condemns the Saturday fast, a practice celebrated in the Roman Church from ancient custom.

Canon 67 prescribes abstinence from blood and from strangled animals, for clerics under penalty of deposition and for laypeople under penalty of excommunication—as though we ought always to nourish ourselves with milk, which we first began to suck as infants.

But anyone who wishes to know more about this synod should consult the father of ecclesiastical annals, Baronius, under the year of Christ 692.

## Line 4.—Which was also defined, as it were, synodally

This passage may also be added to the proofs that the most learned prelate Ciampini brought forward in his *Examination of the Pontifical Book*, chapter 6, to demonstrate that Anastasius the Librarian was not the author of all the Lives of the pontiffs written in that *Pontifical*, although they were printed under his name.

For the author of this Life of Sergius I writes in this passage things that directly contradict what Anastasius reports in the prefaces to the Seventh Synod addressed to John VIII and to the Eighth Synod addressed to Adrian II. It will be preferable to place Anastasius’s words here, so that anyone may see at a glance whether the statements concerning the more than one hundred canons of the erratic synod found here could have proceeded from the same pen as the statements about them in both prefaces.

In the first preface Anastasius writes:

> “The rules which the Greeks claim were issued by the Sixth Synod are admitted by the principal see in such a way that none of them is received if it is found contrary to the earlier canons, or to the decrees of the holy pontiffs of this see, or certainly to good morals, although all of them have hitherto remained wholly unknown among the Latins, since they have not been translated. Nor are they found in the archives of the other patriarchal sees, although they use the Greek language, evidently because none of those sees was found, when they were issued, either to have promulgated them, or to have consented to them, or even to have been present. Although the Greek Fathers who were present at the Sixth Synod are said by the Greeks to have promulgated them, they cannot prove this by any reliable evidence.”

In the other preface he says:

> “The Greeks also display numerous and highly presumptuous chapters of rules, almost all of them very contrary to ancient tradition, which they claim were promulgated by the Sixth Synod, although the Sixth Synod brought forward nothing except the rule of faith. But the rules which they claim to be its own are known to have been drawn up among them long after the Sixth Synod, privately and on their own authority.”

## No. 163, line 7.—Here lies the body of blessed Leo, the most approved Father and pontiff

The body of Saint Leo the Great is said to have been the first of the confessing pontiffs to be brought into the Vatican Basilica as an honor and deposited in the vestibule of that same basilica.

After Saint Leo, so many pontiffs were buried there that his tomb lay hidden beneath the tombs of the others. When Pope Sergius was divinely warned, the body of the holy pontiff was transferred from the more obscure place to a more dignified one, namely to an oratory on the right side of the greater apse, near the altar of Saint Peter, as the author of *Subterranean Rome* testifies.

This was the first translation of Saint Leo’s body—other translations occurred in subsequent centuries—and it is related by Anastasius. It is confirmed by an ancient epitaph, which the distinguished Mabillon published among other inscriptions found in the basilica of Saint Peter (*Analecta*, vol. III). The following text has been corrected according to the Oxford manuscript:

> Here lies first the body of this apostolic man,  
> who was worthy of a tomb in Peter’s citadel.  
>   
> Hence the company of distinguished poets and nobles whom you see here,  
> their limbs are covered beneath this splendid house.  
>   
> But long ago, while the great shepherd Leo guarded  
> the flock and the enclosure of Christ’s people,  
> he was the doorkeeper of the citadel.  
>   
> From the tomb he reminds us of what he did while still alive:  
> that the lurking wolf might not ravage God’s fold.  
>   
> The books sent forth in defense of right doctrine bear witness,  
> books honored by devout hearts and feared by the evil crowd.  
>   
> The wolf roared, and the frightened hearts of the beasts trembled;  
> the sheep obeyed the commands of their shepherd.  
>   
> Yet here he lay beneath the final marble of the church,  
> which is now concealed by many tombs of pontiffs.  
>   
> Sergius the bishop, driven by divine love,  
> transferred him from there to the front of the sacred house,  
>   
> adorning the gleaming tomb with precious marble,  
> in which those who ask behold heavenly wonders.  
>   
> And because he once excelled through wondrous virtues,  
> the pontiff’s final glory will be greater.

At the foot of this epitaph, Mabillon records the following chronological addition:

> “He sat in the episcopate for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. He was deposited on the third day before the Ides of . . .”—supply “April”—“and was transferred here again by blessed Sergius on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the indiction [the supplied text is defective].”

The Bollandists (*April*, vol. II, p. 21) give an account of the elevation and translation of the body from a manuscript catalogue of the church of Saint Peter. Read it if you desire further information about the translations of Saint Leo. See also the notes of the illustrious prelate Blanchini on Saint Leo.

## No. 164, line 4.—What they call the Hypapante

From Ἀπὸ τῆς ὑπαντῆς, or ὑπαπαντῆς, or ὑπαπαντήσεος—that is, “from the meeting” or “encounter,” which took place when the old man Simeon and the widow Anna met the Lord as the child Jesus was brought into the temple by his parents Mary and Joseph—the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary is called by the Greeks Hypante or Hypapante.

Some call it the Hypante of the Lord; others, the Hypante of Simeon and Anna. Theophylact Simocatta, however, calls it, in a rounded expression, Τεσσαρακοστὴ ἡμέρα τῆς γενεθλιακῆς πανηγύρεος τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ Ἰησοῦ, that is, “the fortieth day of the birthday celebration of the great God Jesus.”

According to the command of the ancient Law, a woman who had given birth to a male child was purified after forty days in the tabernacle, and afterward, following the construction of the temple by Solomon, in the temple, with the sacrifices prescribed by the Law. [Col. 0911D]

Therefore the most blessed Virgin, who conceived by the Holy Spirit, after forty days had elapsed from her saving childbirth, wished to conform herself to other women who had given birth, although, as the most pure Θεοτόκος (“God-bearer”), she had no need whatsoever of purification. I have shown this in the notes to the *Hebrew Republic according to Sigonius*, which appear in volume IV of the *Milan Collection*, pp. 224, annotations 58 and 59.

Among writers on ecclesiastical affairs there is general agreement that the feast of the Hypapante was instituted among the Greeks before it was instituted among the Latins. Cedrenus, under the ninth year of Justin the Great, reports its institution when Antioch collapsed after being shaken by a great earthquake.

Anastasius the Librarian, following Theophanes, assigns it to the time of Justinian:

> “In the fifteenth year of Justinian, in the month of October, there was a mortality at Byzantium; and in that same year the Hypapante began to be celebrated at Byzantium on 2 February.”

The same account is given by Landulf the Wise in his *Life of Justinian*, by Sigebert in his *Chronicle* under the year 542, and by the Martyrology of Usuard. Under 2 February it reads:

> “The Hypante of the Lord, and the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, a feast which began in the time of the emperor Justinian at Byzantium, or Constantinople.”

Those who assign greater antiquity to this feast wish to recall Saint Methodius, first bishop of Olympus and Patara, coastal cities of Lycia, and afterward bishop of Tyre in Phoenicia, who gained the crown of martyrdom at the beginning of the fourth century.

Father Combefis reprinted, in his *Amphilochius*, a homily preached on this feast by Saint Methodius, with the following title prefixed:

> “By Methodius, bishop of Patara and martyr, on Simeon and on Anna, on the day of the Hypapante, and on the holy Θεοτόκος.”

They further add Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, likewise a fourth-century writer and a great interpreter of the Church’s rites, who also spoke about the ceremony involving candles at this feast. They add several other Eastern Fathers who lived before Justinian, whose catalogue may be seen in the Bollandists, volume I for February. [Col. 0912B]

For this reason, the authors of this opinion assert that Justinian instituted this new feast at Constantinople when the city was being exhausted by continual funerals; or that he restored by a new decree what other Churches, especially the Church of Jerusalem, already possessed as an ancient feast. In this way Sixtus V, by a new constitution, did not so much institute a new feast of the Presentation of Mary—celebrated in many homilies of the Greek Fathers and not unknown to the Latins—as restore an ancient one, while thereafter requiring it to be celebrated more solemnly in the Church.

On this feast processions are held according to ancient custom with burning candles. Saint Ildefonsus, who flourished in the year 644 (*Sermon on the Purification*), and Saint Eligius, bishop of Noviomagus in Gaul, who died in 665 (*Homily 2 on the Purification*), write that this practice arose from the extinguished superstition of the sacred rites of Februus, that is, Pluto, transformed from superstition into true religion.

For the sake of obtaining rest for the dead, the Romans in the month of February used to appease the spirits around the tombs with expiations and sacrifices, with candles and torches lit, as Macrobius testifies (*Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 13).

Cardinal Baronius believes, in his notes on the Martyrology, that Gelasius opened the way for the ceremony of lights when he abolished the Lupercalia, which were celebrated at Rome in the month of February. His conjecture seems to have little solidity, since in Gelasius’s defense against the senator Andromachus, where he attacks at length the games of the Luperci as no less superstitious than licentious, not a word occurs concerning the rite of lights.

The author of the *Pontifical Book* states in this passage that Pope Sergius was the originator of this procession, and the Roman *Ordo* agrees with him. But since the custom of carrying lights on the day of the Purification already existed both in Spain and in Gaul, as is clear from the homilies of Saints Ildefonsus and Eligius, who preceded Sergius’s pontificate, it follows that Sergius either first introduced this practice into the Roman Church or, more probably, determined the route of the procession for that day, from the church of Saint Adrian to Saint Mary Major. Bede reports that in this procession the clergy and the entire people carried burning candles given by the pontiff. [Col. 0912D]

## Line 7.—The archbishop of the Church of Aquileia, and the synod that he convened

The Church of Aquileia, together with the bishops of Venetia and Istria, long fought against the Fifth Ecumenical Council. It denied that anyone could proscribe the three chapters, which, as they claimed, had not been proscribed by the Fathers of Chalcedon.

Paulinus, the usurper of the see of Aquileia and instigator of the disturbances, held a little council at Aquileia with his schismatic bishops against the Fifth Council, which had pronounced an anathema against the three chapters. This occurred around the year 557, while Vigilius occupied the Roman See.

Our author testifies in this passage that another pseudo-synod was held in the same matter while Sergius was sitting at Rome, that is, around the year 698. Eventually the people of Aquileia, instructed by Sergius, accepted the venerable Fifth Synod and returned to the unity of the Catholic Church after renouncing the schism.

Cardinal Noris, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 6, paragraph [uncertain in the source], believes that no new little council was convened under Sergius, contrary to the account of Anastasius, and that Bede agrees with our author. For in his *Chronicle of the Six Ages*, under the seventh year of the reign of Tiberius Apsimar, when Sergius governed the Roman Church, Bede says:

> “A synod was held at Aquileia. Through ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.”

Noris interprets this to mean that Bede is referring to the council held by Paulinus against the Fifth Synod, whose error and corrupt judgment concerning the Fifth Synod remained in force for a long time, until the people of Aquileia, instructed by the admonitions of Sergius, accepted it together with the other Churches after abandoning their error.

The learned cardinal proves this from the fact that Maximus, bishop of Aquileia, is recorded as having subscribed to the Lateran Synod held in 649. Furthermore, under Pope Saint Agatho, who preceded Sergius’s pontificate by only five years, the other suffragan bishops of Aquileia were present at the Roman Synod with Agatho and subscribed the synodical letter. From this it is inferred that they had accepted the Fifth Synod. [Col. 0913B]

There are, however, two reasons why I do not agree with the learned Noris, and why I believe that two pseudo-synods were convened at Aquileia: one in 557 by Paulinus, and the other in 698 by Peter, who then occupied the see of Aquileia.

The first point is that the synod convened by Paulinus was held to judge the Fifth General Synod, which he rejected as undermining the Council of Chalcedon through its condemnation of the three chapters. This is clear from fragments of letters of Pelagius I, first brought out of obscurity by Lucas Holstenius.

In the third fragment one reads:

> “It was never permitted, nor will it ever be permitted, that a particular synod be convened to judge a general synod.”

The synod mentioned by Bede, however, was merely hesitant through ignorance of the faith to receive the Fifth General Synod. To reject a universal council is one thing; not to accept it because of ignorance is another. The first is to despise a universal council through contumacy; the second is to hesitate to receive it through ignorance.

A clear testimony to the second point is supplied by Paul, a writer from the province of Aquileia and a deacon of the Church of Aquileia, who died in the eighth century. If Bede had been mistaken in identifying this synod, Paul would certainly have corrected him rather than copying his words.

Paul therefore asserts that a synod was convened at Aquileia while Sergius was seated at Rome. After recounting that Tiberius Apsimar had seized the empire, he adds:

> “At this time a synod was held at Aquileia. Through ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to assent to it together with the other Churches of Christ.” [Col. 0913D]

I had already made these observations concerning the second Aquileian pseudo-synod against the Fifth Ecumenical Council when the most learned dissertation on the schism of the Church of Aquileia by the distinguished Father Bernardo Maria de Rubeis came into my hands. In chapter 5, section 19, he demonstrates that Bede was referring to a synod different from that of Paulinus.

As for the opposing argument drawn both from the subscription of Maximus of Aquileia to the Lateran Synod and from the synodical letter of the Roman Synod under Saint Agatho, to which Agatho of Aquileia subscribed together with his suffragans, the same most learned writer replies that Maximus and Agatho belonged not to the Church of Aquileia but to the Church of Grado.

It is not surprising, however, that they subscribed as Aquileians, for they were Catholic metropolitans of that Church, although they had been ordained on the island of Grado. At that time the metropolitan see of Aquileia had not yet been divided in two; this occurred later through the authority of Gregory II.

“There was one metropolitan see,” says the cited author, “which was torn by schism: one body with two heads, one schismatic and the other Catholic; healthy members adhered to one, diseased members to the other. The Catholic metropolitan was called Gradensis because he was elected on the island of Grado; the schismatic was called Aquileiensis because John, opposed to the Catholic Candianus, had been ordained in the old Aquileia. Each acted as bishop of Aquileia and claimed rights over the entire metropolitan province.

“The schismatic enjoyed the favor of the Lombards; the Catholic was supported by the Roman pontiffs, the exarchs, and the most Christian republic of Venice.”

Anyone who desires further information about the history of this schism should read the same dissertation, which sheds much light upon the Aquileian schism.
