## Note: [Col. 0914A]

## No. 159, line 22.—The pontiff was ordained

Paschal, a deacon of the Roman Church, sent letters to John, the new exarch of Ravenna, so that he might more easily obtain the pontificate after Conon’s death. He offered him the quantity of gold that Pope Benedict had left and that Conon had ordered to be distributed both to the clergy and to the monasteries, provided that John’s assistance secured his election to the pontificate. [Col. 0914B]

Seven days after the death of the blessed Conon, as was customary, discussion began concerning the election of his successor. Since the people were divided into two factions, a schism arose. One party favored Theodore the archpriest, the other Paschal the archdeacon. One elected Theodore, the other Paschal.

Theodore, with the people who supported him, occupied the inner part of the patriarchium. Paschal occupied the outer part, from the oratory of Saint Silvester and the basilica of the Julia house, which looks over the Campus. Since neither wished to yield the place to the other, the leading judges and commanders of the Roman army, together with a large part of the clergy, especially the priests, proceeded to the Sacred Palace. After deliberating at length about what should be done, with God’s consent they unanimously chose a third candidate: Sergius, a priest of the holy Roman Church, a Syrian by nation and an Antiochene by birth, son of Tiberius, brought up at Palermo in Sicily, whom Pope Adeodatus had adopted into the Roman clergy and whom Leo II had ordained priest.

They therefore took him from the midst of the people and brought him into the oratory of the blessed Caesarius, martyr of Christ, which was within the palace. From there they led him to the Lateran episcopal residence amid acclamations of praise.

Theodore willingly yielded to Sergius, the legitimate pontiff. Paschal, persistent in schism, was compelled to greet Sergius, but he sent men of his faction to Ravenna and summoned the aforementioned John, surnamed Platyn, the exarch, to Rome so that he might assert for Paschal the papal name and dignity.

When the exarch saw that Sergius had been placed in the See of Saint Peter by legitimate suffrages and common consent, he could not support Paschal. Nevertheless, he demanded from Sergius the one hundred pounds of gold that Paschal had promised him.

When Sergius protested that he had neither made such a promise nor possessed enough for the Church to pay the sum, he ordered the chalices and crowns that had hung from ancient times before the sacred altar and the confession of blessed Peter to be taken down and given as a pledge, in order to move the exarch. But the man, greedy for money, was no more moved by this, nor did he cease troubling the Church until he had received the one hundred pounds of gold.

Not long afterward Paschal was convicted of magic. By the judgment of the pontiff he was removed from the office of archdeacon and confined in a monastery, where, remaining unrepentant, he died after five years. These facts are established by Anastasius.

### No. 160, line 1

He ordered a council to be held in the royal city. Since no canons had been issued at the Fifth and Sixth General Synods, the Emperor Justinian convened the Trullan Synod for the restoration of discipline and the reform of morals, to supplement the Fifth and Sixth Synods. Those bishops who assembled there indicate the purpose of the synod in their address to the emperor:

“Since, however, the two holy and universal synods—namely, the Fifth and the Sixth—did not at all compose sacred canons, as did the other four universal synods … therefore, by order of Your Piety, we have assembled in this God-observing and imperial city and have written sacred canons.” [Col. 0915A]

Hence this synod was called the Quinisext, because it was made as a supplement to both synods; others also called it the Erratic. It was called Trullan because it was held in the Trullus of the great palace, as Balsamon relates. See what has been said about the Trullus under Agatho. But whence did the Greeks derive the idea that an ecumenical synod could not be held without issuing canons, when, as Pope Leo teaches, such synods are held to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith?

There are three opinions concerning the year in which this synod was celebrated. Some, together with Bishop Tarasius, who was seated at Constantinople during the time of the Seventh General Synod, maintain that it was held four or five years after the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, and therefore in the year 686. But this opinion cannot be sustained: for canon 3 says that it was celebrated while the fifth indiction was in progress, whereas in the year 686 the fourteenth indiction was in progress. Moreover, what follows will make it clear that its date must be placed under the pontificate of Sergius, who was ordained pope only in December of the year 687.

Finally, it is evident that Tarasius was mistaken from the fact that he also asserts that those who subscribed under Constantine Pogonatus to the Sixth Synod were the same men who subscribed under Justinian to the present synod. For Paul, bishop of Constantinople, subscribed to this synod, whereas George subscribed to the Sixth. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, subscribed to this synod, whereas at the Sixth the same Peter was still a presbyter and vicar of the Alexandrian patriarch. Anastasius, bishop of Jerusalem, subscribed to this synod, whereas at the Sixth George subscribed in the name of the Church of Jerusalem. Finally, to say nothing of the others, George, bishop of Antioch, subscribed to this synod, whereas at the Sixth Macarius, patriarch of that Church, was present and delivered the sentence of deposition. [Col. 0915C]

The second opinion is that of Theophanes, who writes that this synod was held in the year 699 from the Incarnation according to the Alexandrian reckoning. That year began on the Kalends of September in the year 706 of our era. Accordingly, he also thinks that the synod began then, and adds that twenty-seven years elapsed from the Sixth Synod to the Trullan Synod. He ridicules “those who assert in their writings that the capitular formulas of the Sixth Council were published four full years later,” thereby referring to Tarasius and disparaging his opinion.

But the date he proposes is far less probable, since Paul, bishop of Constantinople, who presided over this synod, died in the year 693 and left the see vacant for Callinicus, as Theophanes himself testifies. Secondly, after speaking of the Trullan Synod, the author of the Synodical Book says:

“When Leontius had seized the empire and had banished Justinian to Cherson after cutting off his nose, Artemius, who is also called Anastasius, succeeded Leontius.” [Col. 0915D]

Therefore the Trullan Synod was convened not in the year 707, but before the year 695, when Justinian was deposed by Leontius. Thirdly, Anastasius explicitly asserts that this synod was convened while Sergius I was administering the Roman Church, and his testimony ought to be trusted. For in his Life of Sergius he accurately relates what happened at Rome when Justinian Augustus first ruled, including the efforts to compel Sergius to subscribe to the decrees of the Quinisext Synod. It therefore seems certain that he was well informed about the date of this synod. Bede, moreover, who lived in that age, in his book On the Six Ages, and Paul the Deacon, who flourished in the following century, in Book VI of On the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 11—both earlier authorities than Theophanes—support Anastasius.

Since, then, the celebrated third canon of the Trullan Synod says that it was held in the past year 6109, and since the defenders of both opinions admit that this passage is corrupt and must be corrected from Theophanes to the year 677 from the Incarnation according to the Alexandrian reckoning, so that it should read “in the year 6199,” while that year of the world according to the Constantinopolitan era ended with August of the year 691, the Trullan Synod was likewise convened in that year. For on the Kalends of September of that year the year 6200 began, and the fifth indiction was in force. The synod was held under those conditions, and the cited canon was composed before the beginning of February in the year 692.

The author of the Critique of Baronius discusses this matter at greater length in the dissertation on the Greco-Roman Era prefixed to the first volume. There he explains extensively that Constantinopolitan era of the world, as well as the other Greek eras, both those reckoned from the creation of the world and those reckoned from the Incarnation.

Matthew Blastares, in the preface to his Nomocanon concerning the Trullan Synod, writes:

“The chief members of that synod were Paul of Constantinople; Paul—read Peter—of Alexandria; George of Antioch; Anastasius of Jerusalem; John of New Justinianopolis; Basil of Gortyna, metropolitan of the island of Crete, acting on behalf of the whole holy synod of the Roman Church. For after the emperor’s subscription, each of the patriarchs and metropolitans signed his own name and dignity in the ancient books.” [Col. 0916B]

Yet Anastasius the Librarian, in the preface to the Seventh Synod addressed to Pope John VIII, asserts that the patriarchs were not present even through legates. The author of the Synodical Book writes that 240 bishops attended this synod; Balsamon and Zonaras give the number as 217. In the manuscripts now available, however, only 211 signatures are found, among them men whom integrity, learning, and holiness rendered commendable.

Baronius and Binius, and even the recent anonymous author of *A Selection of the Acts of the Universal Church, or a New Summary of the Councils*, write that Callinicus, the successor of Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, was the author and president of this synod. But this is said against the manifest evidence of the subscriptions, against the testimony of the cited Balsamon, and against Nicephorus in his *Chronicle* and Theophanes, who connect Paul’s death with the year 693 and Callinicus’s accession.

Lupus nevertheless followed Baronius’s opinion in his dissertation on the cause and date of the Trullan Synod, where he adds: “I suppose that his name—namely, Callinicus’s, as a man of disreputable character—was erased by later supporters of the synod and that Paul’s name was inserted.” Yet none of the ancients accuses Callinicus of any crime, and it is gratuitously asserted that Paul’s name was substituted for Callinicus’s. Callinicus will be discussed below.

That an apostolic legation was present at this synod is expressly testified by Anastasius in his *Life of Pope Sergius*, where he writes:

“During the time of this pontiff, the Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the royal city. Legates of the apostolic see also assembled there and, having been deceived, subscribed.”

Recent historians explain this legation in various ways; among them, Marca seems to have treated the matter most precisely in Book V, chapter 18, of *On Concord*. He observes that the Roman pontiffs were accustomed to send legates to Christian emperors to conduct the affairs of the universal Church. These legates, called *apocrisiarii* and *responsales*, were constantly present in the prince’s retinue. They pursued the particular causes of the Roman Church before him and pleaded matters concerning faith and discipline; nevertheless, they exercised no portion of jurisdiction except by special delegation.

This precaution was not useless for avoiding the machinations of the patriarchs of Constantinople. Always intent on enlarging their see, they might have extorted, through the emperor’s terror and threats, the legate’s assent to establishing innovations, so that an alteration supported in some measure by the authority of the apostolic see might at least not appear entirely without color.

Nevertheless, by their prudence the Roman pontiffs could not prevent themselves from falling into the very snares against which they so carefully guarded. For at this Trullan Synod, to give some appearance of legitimacy to the new decrees enacted there, it assumed the title “ecumenical,” on account of the authority of the Roman see that had been invoked. The legates—or *apocrisiarii* or *responsales* of the apostolic see—who served as spokesmen before the Emperor Justinian, were present at this synod.

Certainly Pope Sergius had not sent legates equipped with his instructions to that gathering, since he condemned it as unlawful, as will shortly be seen. Basil, bishop of Gortyna in the province of Crete and metropolitan, alone performed that legation at the time. Accordingly, at the end of the synod’s canons he describes himself as “legate of the entire synod of the Roman Church,” following the example of the three legates of Agatho and the Western Synod, who assumed this title at the Sixth Synod. [Col. 0917A]

One hundred and two canons were issued at this synod, as testified by Saint Tarasius, the Seventh Synod in its refutation of the Iconoclast assembly, Photius in his *Nomocanon*, and the author of the Synodical Book. Many of them are excellent and in large part breathe the ancient discipline of the Church.

Therefore, although many are rightly praised and deserve praise, they were not all rejected by the Roman Church, but only five: canon 2, which decrees that eighty-five canons and constitutions bearing the name of the apostles are to be admitted; canon 13, which shakes the law of ecclesiastical celibacy and censures the most chaste discipline of the Roman Church, by which sacred ministers are forbidden marital relations. Indeed, this canon anathematizes those who forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons union and intercourse with their lawful wives.

Canon 55 was likewise not approved, since it condemns the Saturday fast, which is especially celebrated in the Roman Church. Nor was canon 67 approved, which forbids clerics, under penalty of deposition, and laypeople, under penalty of excommunication, to eat blood or anything strangled, and imposes this abstinence as though it were still binding by divine Scripture. Nor was canon 82 approved in every respect, which forbids Christ the Savior to be depicted in the image of a lamb, as he was shown to the Fathers in figure, and requires him instead to be depicted in human form, in which all the figures were finally fulfilled. [Col. 0917C]

The other canons that we have rightly called worthy of praise were not rejected by the Roman Church, as will be clear to anyone who reads and examines them. To speak only of the first and last: the first teaches that the faith confirmed by the six ecumenical councils and handed down by the apostles must be preserved inviolate.

The last contains excellent laws and instructions for hearing confession, and explains how prudently a priest ought to act toward penitents. He must consider the nature of the sin, the sinner’s ardent desire for conversion, and the remedy appropriate to the illness. He must examine whether the evil arises from habit, weakness, or a perverse inclination. Finally, it belongs to his pastoral office to bring back the wandering sheep; therefore he must neither drive the sinner over the precipices of despair nor loosen the reins so far as to lead to dissolution of life and contempt.

For all the canons of the Trullan Synod, both those approved and those rejected, Lupus should be consulted in his notes and scholia on the canons of the Council of Trullo.

### No. 161, line 1

“Then Zacharias, etc.”

Anastasius writes that Justinian the emperor sent everything enacted at the synod to Rome, for Sergius the pontiff to confirm or to subscribe in the place of honor, as head of all priests. For when Justinian sent Pope Sergius the acts of this synod, contained in six volumes, signed by the bishops and confirmed by the imperial hand, a blank sheet was left in the council’s register before the other patriarchs and after the Emperor Justinian, so that Sergius might fill it with his subscription.

In exactly the same way, blank sheets were left for the absent bishops of Thessalonica, Ravenna, Sardinia, and Heraclea, so that they might subscribe to the acts after the synod had been dissolved. The register notes this in the same words: “The place of the Thessalonian; the place of the Ravennate; and of the others.” [Col. 0918A]

But Sergius refused to confirm the acts:

“He himself was also compelled,” says Anastasius, “to subscribe, but he consented in no way, because certain chapters had been appended to it outside ecclesiastical custom. These had been defined as though synodally and written in six volumes, and so forth.”

That most blessed pontiff absolutely refused to yield to the same Justinian Augustus, and would not receive those volumes or allow them to be opened for reading. Rather, he rejected and cast them aside as invalid, choosing to die rather than consent to the errors of innovations. These canons will be discussed again under John VII.

Since, therefore, Sergius, unmoved by the pleas of the Emperor Justinian, rejected the canons of the Quinisext Synod, the emperor sent Zacharias, his protospatharius, to Rome to carry the pontiff to Constantinople. But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions, despising the emperor’s wicked orders, did not permit them to be carried out. Accordingly, when a multitude of soldiers gathered from every direction, Zacharias the protospatharius, fearing for his own safety, immediately took refuge with the pontiff. He prostrated himself at his feet, humbly begged forgiveness, and implored him not to surrender him to the fury of the soldiers.

The pontiff ordered him to take courage. Then he went out to pacify the army, sat before the basilica of the pontiff Theodore with the doors thrown open, and, after calming the soldiers and people, gave thanks because they had taken up arms with such eagerness for his safety. Nevertheless, the soldiers were unwilling to leave the city before they had driven Zacharias from it, weighed down with insults and terrified by fear.

These matters are established from Anastasius’s *Life of Sergius*, Bede’s *On the Six Ages*, and Paul the Deacon’s Book VI of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 11.

### No. 162, line 11

“He made a thurible.”

Cardinal Bona shows in Book I, chapter 25, number 9, of *On Liturgical Matters* that the use of these or similar vessels, in which incense and various fragrances are burned during the solemn offering, arose from apostolic tradition and the example of the Mosaic law. It was customary among every nation, however barbarous and unfamiliar with true religion, to believe that no sacrifice could be properly performed without incense or at least some fragrant fumigation.

The Magi revered and professed Christ as God with incense. In a similar way, the poets considered the offering of incense inseparable from the confession of divinity. Ovid says:

“I shall establish temples for you; I shall render you the honor of incense.”

Constantine the Great, according to the same author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* in the Life of Sylvester, offered two thuribles of the purest gold. Ambrose indicates that the practice of censing the altars during the solemn divine office is very ancient when, in his commentary on Luke 1, he says:

“And would that an angel might also stand by us as we cense the altars and bring forward the sacrifice!”

Bona, cited above, discusses this matter further.

Anastasius relates with what ornaments he adorned the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul and other churches of the city. He also writes that Sergius established that litanies should be recited annually from Saint Adrian’s on the feasts of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, and Saint Simeon, whom the Greeks call the Hypapante and the Latins the Purification.

Albinus Flaccus says the same in his book *On the Divine Office*. Sergius placed a portion of the Lord’s cross, hidden in a silver capsule in a more secluded place, in a more honorable and celebrated location. He appointed ninety-seven bishops in various provinces. He held two ordinations in the month of March and ordained eighteen priests and four deacons.

These words of Anastasius refute the opinion of those who assert that the feast of the Dormition, or Assumption, of the Blessed Virgin Mary began to be celebrated only in the eighth century. For, as Francis Maria Florentius observes in his notes on the Hieronymian Martyrology, under 18 January, the feast of the Assumption was celebrated before the time of the Emperor Maurice, and therefore before the end of the sixth century—indeed, on the eighteenth day of January.

He proves this both from that Martyrology, attributed to Saint Jerome and published by him, and from other sources that he cites. He discusses at length the institution of this feast and believes that it was transferred by the Emperor Maurice from 18 January to 15 August.

John Mabillon adds, in Book II, page 118, of *Gallican Liturgy*, that there are two calendars: the Corbie Calendar, which he says was written scarcely more than a century after Maurice, in which under the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February—18 January—is recorded “the deposition of the holy Virgin Mary”; and another very ancient calendar from Fleury, in which that deposition is noted on the same day.

Florentius, cited above, proves from Book XVII, chapter 28, of Nicephorus Callistus that the feast was transferred by the Emperor Maurice to 15 August. There Nicephorus writes:

“The same emperor—namely, Justinian—first established that the Savior’s Reception, that is, the Meeting or Hypapante, which we call the Purification of the Virgin, should be honored as a feast throughout the whole world, just as Justin had done with the holy Nativity of Christ. Not long afterward Maurice ordered that the Dormition of the holy Mother of God should be celebrated on the fifteenth day of August.”

From these words Florentius infers that, since Nicephorus added nothing about an established date in his accounts of the enactments of Justinian and Justin, but precisely designated 15 August in the enactment of Maurice concerning the feast of the Dormition, he evidently indicated that the feast had been transferred to that day of August rather than newly instituted.

But if Nicephorus reports the truth about Maurice, it nevertheless seems to me that he is mistaken when he says that the Emperor Justin established that the feast of Christ’s Nativity should be celebrated throughout the whole world. For under Pope Julius we showed that long before Justin the feast of Christ’s Nativity was solemnly celebrated both in the West and in the East, either on 25 December or on 6 January. It was Justinian, not Justin, who in the year 551 enacted a law establishing its observance on 25 December. Earlier he had given the same order concerning the feast of the Purification, assigning it to 2 February, as is clear from these words of Theophanes, Book XVI of his *History*, and of Landulf Sagax in the *Life of Justinian*:

“In the fifteenth year of Justinian’s reign, in the month of October, a plague occurred at Byzantium. In that same year the Hypapante began to be celebrated at Byzantium on the second day of February.”

I have found nothing elsewhere concerning Justin’s enactment. If it is genuine, one could say that it was renewed by the Emperor Justinian because it had not been observed.

On the feast of the Purification, see the *Critique of Baronius* under the year 542; on both feasts, consult the same Mabillon cited above and Edmund Martene, Volume IV of *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church in the Celebration of Divine Offices*. On the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, see what will be said under Innocent IV.

### No. 164, line 1

“He established, and so forth.”

Pope Sergius established that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, the clergy and people should sing: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us,” says the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

Sergius established that “have mercy on us” should be said three times. But after many adversities had overtaken the Church, as Innocent III says in Book VI, chapter 6, of *On the Mysteries of the Mass*, or, as others write, to remove a schism, it was decreed that the third petition should be “grant us peace.” This rite was accepted everywhere except in the Lateran basilica, where the ancient custom of saying “have mercy on us” three times is still observed.

For, as John the Deacon observes in chapter 6 of his book *On the Lateran Church*, this basilica represents the type of the heavenly Church:

“In it,” he says, “at Mass there is not sung, ‘Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace,’ because there the highest peace of the righteous will itself be Christ.”

Cardinal Bona, in Book II, chapter 16, number 5, of *On Liturgical Matters*, confesses that he has nowhere read which pontiff made this change, namely, the singing of “grant us peace.”

“But if Robert, abbot of the Mount, is truthful,” Bona says, “the blessed Virgin brought this petition for peace from heaven in the supplement to Sigebert’s Chronicle.”

For, as Robert relates, in the year 1183 the Virgin appeared to a certain woodworker laboring in a forest and gave him a seal bearing her image and that of her Son, with this inscription: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace.” She ordered him to carry it to the bishop and tell him that those who desired peace for the Church should make seals of this kind and carry them as a sign of peace.

### Line 7

“During his time the Church of Aquileia …”

Around the year 698, while Tiberius Apsimarus was emperor and Pope Sergius was seated at Rome, the schism of the Church of Aquileia concerning the Three Chapters came to an end.

For Paul the Deacon, in *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 14, after relating that Tiberius seized the empire—which occurred in the year 698—writes:

“At this time a synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance of the faith, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to agree with that council together with the other Churches of Christ.” [Col. 0920B]

Nearly the same words occur in the account of Sergius in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, commonly but mistakenly attributed to Anastasius, who was alive at precisely this time. Paul the Deacon lived not long afterward.

Cardinal Norisius, however, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 1, argues from Bede’s passage in *On the Six Ages* that this Aquileian synod was the synod convened by Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, against the Fifth Synod in the preceding century. Bede says:

“A synod held at Aquileia, because of ignorance of the faith, hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to agree with that council together with the other Churches of Christ.”

From the adverb “until,” the learned cardinal says it can be inferred quite clearly that Bede is speaking of a council convened before Sergius.

But apart from the fact that it is improbable that Paul the Deacon failed to understand Bede’s meaning, even if this were granted, it would not follow that the schism of the Church of Aquileia had been completely extinguished before Sergius, since Bede states in the same passage that that Church, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, consented to agree with the Fifth Council together with the other Churches of Christ.

We answered the arguments of the same cardinal under the pontificate of Saint Gregory.

The acts of Saint Aldhelm, abbot of Malmesbury in England, preserved by Surius under 25 May, report that Pope Sergius suffered a calumny, as though he were guilty of sexual misconduct—namely, that he was the father of a recently born child. When Aldhelm, who was then staying at Rome, baptized the child, Sergius ordered the child, in the presence of those standing by, to declare whether the man whom popular rumor named was his father.

The child replied that he had not been begotten through the agency of the man whom the foolish crowd falsely named. Thus the pontiff was freed from the disgrace. But Baronius rightly calls this story into question. It is not actually found in the Life of Saint Aldhelm composed by William of Malmesbury, although it is read in another Life of Saint Aldhelm written by an anonymous monk of Malmesbury who lived shortly before William of Malmesbury, as Henschenius, who published it, shows under 25 May.

Mabillonus reproduces the Life of Aldhelm written by William of Malmesbury in Part I, fourth century of the Benedictine era.

### Note on No. 160, line 1

“During these times, therefore, the Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the royal city, at which legates of the apostolic see also assembled.”

The subscriptions of these legates do not appear, unless perhaps the following subscription of Basil, bishop of Gortyna in Crete, is to be accepted:

“Basil, bishop of Gortyna, metropolitan of the Christ-loving island of Crete, and acting in place of the entire synod of the holy Roman Church, have defined and subscribed.” (*Quinisext Council*) [Col. 0921A]

Therefore, following Peter Marca, one ought to understand Anastasius, when he speaks in the name of the legates, to mean an *apocrisiarius* or administrator who customarily remained at the Constantinopolitan court by order of the pontiff, conducting the affairs of the holy see and attending to whatever other matters might arise. He nevertheless lacked jurisdiction, so that he could not decide matters, especially important ones, without a special mandate. He possessed only the right to report them and await the pontiff’s highest commands.

The Emperor Justinian II subscribed first to the decrees of the council. At the top of the list of all the Fathers, a place was left for Sergius’s subscription, with these words written there: “The place of the most holy Roman pope.” The rest is sufficiently clear from Anastasius, both in this section and in the following one.

### Note on No. 160, line 12

“Moreover, he rejected them as invalid.”

What chiefly moved the pontiff to reject that council was the presumption of the Eastern bishops, who, with the intention of overthrowing the celibacy of priests and deacons, defined as follows:

“Since we have learned that it has been handed down as a canon of the Roman Church that those promoted to the diaconate or presbyterate must profess that they will no longer unite themselves to their wives, we, observing the ancient canon of apostolic perfection and order, wish the lawful marriages of those in sacred orders to remain firm and stable from now on as well. We in no way dissolve their union with their wives or deprive them of their mutual intercourse at the proper time.

“Therefore, if anyone is found worthy to be ordained subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter, he must not at all be prevented from being admitted to such a rank if he lives with a lawful wife. Nor, at the time of ordination, should he be required to profess that he will abstain from lawful intercourse with his wife.

“If anyone, therefore, moved contrary to the apostolic canons, dares to deprive any of those in sacred orders—we mean priests, deacons, or subdeacons—of union and intercourse with a lawful wife, let him be deposed. Likewise, if any priest or deacon dismisses his wife under the pretext of piety, let him be separated from communion; and if he persists, let him be deposed.” (Canon 13.) [Col. 0922A]

Moreover, this council had other canons that could by no means be accepted: the canon that orders the admission of the eighty-five canons bearing the name of the apostles; the canon that forbids fasting on Saturdays during Lent, or in the Roman Church; the canon that orders clerics to abstain from strangled animals and blood under penalty of deposition, and laypeople under penalty of excommunication; and finally the canon that forbids depicting our Lord Jesus Christ under the figure of the lamb indicated by John the Forerunner, since the Savior ought to be represented only in human form, through which he fulfilled all the other figures. (Canons 2, 55, 67, and 82.)

### 158

Sergius, by nation a Syrian, of the region of Antioch, born of a father named Tiberius at Panormus in Sicily, held the see for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days. [Col. 0891; Note: B gives fourteen years.]

He came to Rome under Pope Adeodatus of holy memory and was enrolled among the clergy of the Roman Church. Because he was diligent and capable in the office of singing, he was handed over to the senior singers for instruction [Note: B reads “pious singers”], and was made an acolyte. Advancing through the orders, he was ordained priest by Pope Leo of holy memory at the title of Saint Susanna, which is called “at the Two Houses” [Note: “which” is read in place of “who”].

During his priesthood he diligently celebrated the solemn Masses in various cemeteries. After seven years, Conon, the bishop of the apostolic see of blessed memory, died. As usually happens, the Roman people of the City divided into two factions: one faction elected Theodorus the archpresbyter, while the other elected Paschal the archdeacon.

The archpresbyter Theodorus, together with the people who favored him, anticipated the others and occupied the inner part of the patriarchium. Paschal occupied the outer part, from the oratory of Saint Sylvester, as well as the basilica of the Julian house, which overlooks the Campus. [Col. 0893; Note: B reads “the basilica.”]

Since neither would yield his place to the other, but both persisted fiercely [Note: “unanimously”], each seeking to overcome the other, the leading judges and the army of the Roman soldiery, together with a large part of the clergy [Note: “the seditious clergy”], and especially a multitude of priests and citizens, went to the sacred palace. After deliberating for a long time about what should be done and how the dispute between the two contending electors might be brought to an end [Note: “intention”], by God’s favor they agreed upon the person of the aforementioned Sergius, then a venerable priest.

They lifted him from among the people and brought him into the oratory of the blessed martyr Caesarius, which was within the aforesaid sacred palace. From there they led him to the Lateran episcopal residence amid acclamations of praise [Note: “acclamations”]. Although the doors of the patriarchium were secured and closed from within, the faction that had chosen the aforementioned venerable man prevailed, since it was the stronger, and entered.

### 159

When he had entered, one of the two electors—that is, Theodorus the archpresbyter—immediately yielded and humbled himself. He entered, greeted the aforementioned most holy elect, and kissed him.

But Paschal’s hardness of heart in no way allowed him to do this, until, compelled and ashamed, willingly or unwillingly, he entered and greeted his lord and elect.

Paschal also secretly continued sending messengers of his own to Ravenna. By promises of money and various other gifts, he persuaded John the patrician and exarch, surnamed Platyn, to come secretly to Rome with his judges, without anyone knowing.

He came so secretly that neither the standards nor the military banner of the Roman army went out to meet him at the proper place according to custom, except from near the city of Rome. [Note: “from within.”]

When he arrived and found that everyone had agreed upon Sergius the most holy, he refused to support him. Nevertheless, the same exarch, through the wretchedness of that Paschal, inflicted expense and loss upon the Church of the blessed apostle Peter: he demanded from the Church one hundred pounds of gold, which had been promised him by the aforesaid Paschal.

The most holy elect Sergius protested that he had promised neither to give it nor possessed the means to give it. To move the hearts of those who saw the matter to compassion, he had the canthari (cups) and crowns that from ancient times had hung before the sacred altar and the *confessio* (shrine) of the blessed apostle Peter taken down and handed over as a pledge.

But even this did not soften the exarch’s hardness, until he received, as stated, one hundred pounds of gold. [Note: B reads “pounds.”]

Although, as has been said, the most wretched Paschal inflicted expense and loss upon the Church of Christ [Note: B reads “the same” and “inflicted”], nevertheless, with Christ’s favor, Sergius the priest and elect was ordained pontiff in the see of the blessed apostle Peter.

Not long afterward, the aforesaid Paschal was deprived of the office of archdeacon on account of certain incantations and sacred groves [Note: “little groves”] that he worshiped, or lots that he handled with other diviners [Note: “observers”; B reads “inspectors”]. By the judgment of God and of the blessed Prince of the Apostles, Peter, he was shut up in a monastery, and after five years died unrepentant because of the hardness of his heart.

### 160

[Note: See Baronius under the year 692, page 611.]

During his time, therefore, the Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the royal city, at which legates of the apostolic see also assembled and, having been deceived, subscribed.

He himself was also compelled to subscribe [Note: “the pope himself”; B reads “Sergius himself”], but he consented in no way, because certain chapters had been appended to it outside ecclesiastical custom. These had been defined as though synodally and written in six volumes. They had been subscribed by three patriarchs—namely, the Alexandrian, Constantinopolitan, and Antiochian—and by the other consuls [Note: B reads “prelates”] who had assembled there at that time [Note: “at that time”]. They had also been confirmed by the imperial hand.

The emperor directed the volumes, sent to Lucellum, which is called *scebrum carnale* [Note: B reads *chartale*; the passage is corrupt], into this city, for Sergius the pontiff, as head of all priests, to confirm them or to subscribe in the place of honor. But that most blessed pontiff, as has been said, absolutely refused to yield to the same Justinian Augustus, and would not receive those volumes or open them for reading [Note: “to reading.”]

Rather, he rejected and cast them aside as invalid, choosing to die rather than consent to the errors of innovations.

The emperor, sending Sergius the *magistrianus* to Rome in contempt of the aforementioned pontiff, took with him to the imperial city John, the God-beloved bishop of Portus, or Boniface, counselor of the apostolic see.

161 Then he sent Zacharias, his formidable *protospatharius*, with orders likewise to convey the aforesaid pontiff to the imperial city. But, through God’s mercy going before him, with the blessed apostle Peter, Prince of the Apostles, giving assistance and preserving his Church unharmed, the hearts of the army of Ravenna, of the duchy of the Pentapolis, and of the surrounding regions were stirred not to permit

[Note: [Col. 0895] “so that they would not permit.”]

the pontiff of the apostolic see to go up to the imperial city. When a multitude of soldiers gathered from every side, Zacharias the *spatharius*

[Note: [Col. 0895] B: “protospatharius.”]

—terrified and trembling lest he be killed by the military crowd—asked that the city gates be closed and that the pontiff be kept inside.

[Note: [Col. 0895] “by the pontiff.”]

He himself took refuge in the pontiff’s chamber

[Note: [Col. 0895] “at the pontiff’s feet.”]

and, trembling, tearfully begged that his pontiff have mercy on him and not permit anyone to attack his life. The army of Ravenna, entering through the gate of the blessed apostle Peter, came with arms and a crowd

[Note: [Col. 0895] * “a considerable crowd.”]

to the Lateran episcopal residence, burning to see the pontiff, whom they had learned—through spreading rumor—had been carried away during the night and put on a ship

[Note: [Col. 0895] * “had heard.”]

. Since the doors of the patriarchium, both lower and upper, were closed, they threatened that, unless they were opened more quickly, they would cast them down to the ground

[Note: [Col. 0895] B: “they threatened.”]

. Overcome by the extreme anguish of fear and despair of his life, Zacharias the *spatharius* entered beneath the pontiff’s bed

[Note: [Col. 0895] “beneath the bed.”]

and hid himself, so that he lost his mental composure and sense. The most blessed pope comforted him, saying that he should in no way be afraid.

Then the same most blessed pontiff went outside the basilica of the lord Pope Theodore, the doors having been opened, and sat on the seat

[Note: [Col. 0895] “sitting on the seat.”]

which is commonly called “among the Apostles.” He honorably received the whole body of the soldiers and people who were coming out to meet him; and, giving them a fitting and gracious reply, he soothed their hearts.

Although they, moved by zeal for love and reverence both for God’s Church and for the most holy pontiff, did not withdraw from guarding the patriarchium

[Note: [Col. 0895] “would not withdraw.”]

until they drove the aforesaid *spatharius* out of the Roman city with insults and abuse

[Note: [Col. 0895] “had expelled him.”]

. For the man who had sent him was also deprived of his kingdom at that very time, the Lord rendering recompense. Thus God’s Church, with Christ’s favor, was preserved undisturbed together with its bishop.

162 This most blessed man found in the sacristy of the blessed apostle Peter a chest lying in a very obscure corner, so blackened by the age that had passed that it would not have appeared silver even if it were; God revealed it to him. After praying, he removed the impressed seal and opened the little chest. Inside he found a quilted covering of pure silk placed over it, called a *stauracis*. Having removed this, he saw beneath it a cross adorned with various precious stones. When he drew out four panels, in which gems of marvelous size were enclosed, he found an ineffable portion of the saving wood of the Lord’s cross. From that day onward, for the salvation of the human race, it has been kissed and venerated by all the Christian people on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana.

He made an image of the blessed apostle Peter, which is in the women’s section. He made a large golden censer with columns and a cover, which he hung before three golden images of the blessed apostle Peter; on feast days, while the solemn celebrations of Mass are being held, incense and the fragrance of sweet odor are offered to almighty God therein with great abundance.

In the apse of the aforesaid basilica he placed a silver *apallarean* seat

[Note: [Col. 0895] “appellarian.”]

weighing 120 pounds.

[Col. 0897] In the aforesaid basilica he made six silver lampstands (*fari*), each weighing thirty pounds; they are above the beams at the entrance to the confession.

163 Around the altar of the aforesaid basilica he made eight *tetravila*

[Note: [Col. 0897] “beams.”]

—four of white cloth

[Note: [Col. 0897] “four white ones from them.”]

and four of scarlet

[Note: [Col. 0897] “four scarlet ones.”]

. He diligently renewed and repaired the roof and the chambers surrounding that basilica, which for a long time had been damaged by dripping water and rubble

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “scattered or ruined.”]

. He renewed the mosaic which had partly been destroyed on the front of the atrium of the same basilica. Likewise he renewed the mirrors of that church which are above the seat, as well as the larger royal arches.

He took the body of the blessed Leo, a most approved Father and pontiff, which had been placed in a hidden part of the lower secret chamber

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “in the lower hidden chambers.”]

of the aforesaid basilica, and, after more carefully making a tomb, reburied it in a public place in the said basilica, as had been revealed to him; he also adorned the place itself.

He made a large golden paten bearing gems of white color

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “white gems.”]

and, in the center, a cross of hyacinth and emerald, weighing twenty pounds. He diligently renewed and repaired the roof and all the chambers around the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, which had been worn out by age over a long period. Likewise he had beams brought from Calabria and renewed those which he found to be extremely old in the same basilica. He replaced the very old image of the apostles which stood above the doors of the same basilica.

He made an ambo and a *cyburium*

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “cyborium.”]

in the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, where he also offered many gifts. He covered and strengthened the *trullum* of the same church with sheets of lead cast for the purpose.

He made the *cyborium* of the basilica of Saint Susanna, which had previously been wooden, from marble; he also donated there various golden and silver treasures and immovable properties

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “there.”]

. He roofed and renewed the basilica of Saint Euphemia, which for a long time had stood uncovered. He roofed the basilica of Saint Aurea at Ostia

[Note: [Col. 0897] * B: “at Ostia on the Tiber.”]

, which likewise had been uncovered or ruined, and renewed it through his own efforts. He rebuilt from the foundations the oratory of the apostle Saint Andrew, which is situated on the Lavican Way

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “on the Lavican Way.”]

.

164 He decreed that at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body the following should be sung by clergy and people:

> Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.

He also established that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity, and the Dormition of the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which the Greeks call the *Hypapante*—a litany should go out from Saint Hadrian, and the people should assemble at Saint Mary’s.

[Note: [Col. 0897] See Baronius, under the year 632, at the end.]

In the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr, which is called the title of Lucina, he made four silver arches.

During his pontificate the archbishop of the Church of Aquileia and the synod gathered under him—those who, as people in error, hesitated to accept the holy Fifth Universal Council—were instructed by the admonitions and teachings of that same most blessed pope and were converted. They accepted the venerable council with satisfaction

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “having been satisfied.”]

. Those who had previously been held under the reproach of error, enlightened by the teaching of the apostolic see, reconciled in peace with the truth, were released to return to their own homes

[Note: [Col. 0897] * “returned.”]

.

He made many golden and silver coverings or vessels for use and adornment in various churches of Christ. He ordained Damian archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and Clement of the Frisians

[Note: [Col. 0897] “of the Frisians.”]

. He ordained Berechyald

[Note: [Col. 0897] B: “Berectuald.”]

archbishop of Britain. In various provinces he ordained ninety-seven bishops. He also held two ordinations in the month of March: eighteen priests and four deacons.

He too was buried at the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Ides of September

[Note: [Col. 0897] B: “the fifth day before the Ides.”]

, in the fifteenth indiction, while Tiberius Augustus was reigning; and the episcopate was vacant for one month and twenty days.

No. 165, line 7.—“He sent the priests to the camp, in which they had gathered together.” Pope John sent priests to restrain the tumult of the soldiers who were at the camp, that is, in the military encampment beside the city. *Fossata* are military camps, because they were fortified with a rampart or ditch. Anastasius, below, in the same place: “And he made a camp as far as the place called Horrea.” The same author, under Stephen III: “The Franks, entering the enclosed places, carried off the entire camp of the Lombards after the slaughter had been completed.” The same author, under Gregory IV, concerning the fortification of Ostia: “And from outside, not far from the same walls, he surrounded the city itself with a higher ditch.” Hence fortifications arranged along the frontier were called camps, because they originated from camps.

The Frankish Annals, under the year 801: “Another Saracen ambassador from Africa, sent by Amir Abraham, who was in command at the frontier of Africa.” The praetorian cohorts likewise established a camp beside the city walls. Tacitus, *Annals* VI, concerning Sejanus, prefect of the praetorian guard: “Previously he had increased the limited power of the prefecture by bringing the cohorts scattered throughout the city together into one camp.” Hence the praetorian soldiers, although they serve within the city, are considered absent from the state’s affairs; see *Digest* 50.16, laws “Limites” and “Qui mittuntur,” concerning causes of majority.

No. 166, line 6.—“And he made him return to his own country with his army.” *Hostis* means an army, so called because it is drawn up against the enemy. Aimoin, continuator, book V, chapter 22: “The Saracens, leaving Baira and following Louis’s army behind them.” The same author, chapter 28 of the same book: “From there he sent as large an army as he could with Carloman.” William of Tyre, book IX, chapter 3: “So that meanwhile he might be able to remain in the kingdom with his armies, he alleged.” Ivo of Chartres, letter 28: “Nor ought I to send excommunicated persons into the army.” Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 32: “In those days many of the Roman nobles were killed out of greed; the rest, divided among the armies, became tributaries, so that they might pay the Lombards a third part of their crops.”]

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

No. 165, line 4.—“The army of all Italy.” Theophylact, exarch of Italy, hostile to the pontiff, attempted to attack his person; but in vain, since the Italian army resisted him. Its zeal and constancy in defending the faith and the pontiffs often shone forth. It was composed of the people of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and Venice, who from that time had adopted the salutary policy of reclaiming Italy to freedom from the yoke of the Lombards and the tyranny of the exarchs. Agnellus records that Aistulf had at times summoned them as auxiliaries.

No. 166, line 1.—“Gisulphus.” Anastasius copied the following from Paul, book VII, chapter 27. He writes:

> “Finally, in this period, Gisulphus, leader of the Beneventans, captured Sora, a Roman city, and likewise the towns printed as *Hispinos* and *Arcom* [the latter perhaps *Arcanum*]. This Gisulphus, in the time of Pope John, came into Campania with all his forces, causing fires and plundering, captured many prisoners, and encamped as far as the place called Horrea; and no one was able to resist him. To him the pontiff sent priests with apostolic gifts, redeemed all the prisoners from their hands, and made the leader himself return with his army to his own country.”

Line 10.—“White curtains.” Among the furnishings of churches were curtains of various colors and considerable value. They were hung especially to cover altars and the tombs of martyrs, in order to increase reverence for them. We read that in former times the tribunals of judges and emperors were covered with curtains.

Concerning the chamber of the Eastern emperor, Cyril of Scythopolis, in Cotelerius, volume III of the *Monuments*, relates that Saint Sabas met the emperor and was brought before him; he says, on page 299:

> “When the emperor was inside the curtain, he saw a certain angelic form going before him.”

The use of curtains in sacred contexts was extremely common among the nations, since at the time of sacrifices and solemn festivals curtains were drawn before altars and images. Hence Apuleius, relating how, when he entered the temple to fulfill the vows of Isis,

> “while the gleaming curtains were drawn apart on either side, we sought the venerable sight of the goddess.”

Book XI of the *Metamorphoses*, p. 383.

Likewise, having been consecrated through Isiac initiation and about to perform priestly duties before a large crowd, he stood inside a curtain, as he says on page 398:

> “Thus adorned in the likeness of the sun, and with the image set opposite, when suddenly the curtains were drawn back, I entered the sight of the people. And from this I celebrated a most festive birthday, with pleasant feasts and auspicious banquets.”

The Hebrews too had extremely precious curtains, with which the tabernacle was covered, and curtains for the doors of the Holy of Holies; these were kept in the treasury, hanging from a silver beam. Josephus discusses them in book XIV of the *Antiquities*, chapter 13:

> “The treasurer, Eleazar the priest, handed over this beam to him—not with hostile intent, since he was just and good, but because the custody of the temple curtains had been entrusted to him; these curtains, hanging in this city, shone with marvelous beauty and the most precious workmanship.”

The same curtains were widely used in the basilicas and buildings of Christians, with ornaments and figures representing various images of the saints or histories, as we see very frequently noted in these pontifical records. The altar, which generally had four columns and a *ciborium*, was adorned with curtains hung between the columns; Anastasius often reports that these were white and embellished with costly woven decoration. Curtains were also extremely common as ornaments of the tombs in which martyrs or other saints rested, to shade the place for the sake of veneration.

Gregory of Tours writes of the tomb of Saint Martin, book IV, chapter 1:

> “I approached the place of the tomb without presumption, threw myself upon the ground, and poured out a prayer; then, more secretly, from the hanging curtains, having inserted a single thread beneath my garments, I traced the sign of the cross with it.”

And in chapter 2:

> “Again I approached the tomb to seek healing; and when I touched the hanging curtains, the pulse of my vein immediately stood still.”

For this reason the curtains sent by the faithful to be hung at the altar were received with solemn and festive ritual, as Saint Gregory the Great teaches, book IX, letter 38, p. 342. There he discusses curtains offered and their reception:

> “You sent them [the curtains] from a purest and most sincere heart to the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles; they were received in the presence of all the clergy and hung there. For my son, the venerable man Lord Symmachus, who delayed giving me your letter because I was ill from the pain of gout, gave me your writing only after a long time, when the curtains had already been received. Later, however, we found in your Excellency’s letter that they ought to have been carried with a litany to the church of the blessed Peter.”

Gregory immediately adds concerning the use of curtains:

> “I trust also in his mercy, because he whose body you covered on earth may, through his intercession, protect you from all sins in heaven.”

Long before this, Tertullian had spoken of their variety, workmanship, and cost in his book *On the Dress of Women*:

> “But also the walls with Tyrian and hyacinthine hangings, or those royal curtains which elaborate art, unraveling and transforming them, uses in place of painting.”

Concerning white curtains used at the tombs of martyrs in the fourth Christian century, Paulinus says in *Natale* 3:

> “Now the golden thresholds are adorned with snowy curtains.”

And in *Natale* 6:

> *Cedo, alii pretiosa ferunt donaria, ne quae / Officii sumptu superent, quae pulchra tegendis. / Vela ferant foribus, seu puro splendida lino, / Seu coloratis textum fucata figuris.*  
> “Come, let others bring costly gifts, lest beautiful coverings exceed the expenditure of duty. Let them bring curtains for the doors, splendid either with pure linen or with woven work dyed in colored figures.” [The syntax of the first couplet is compressed; the printed Latin is retained above.]

[Col. 0925D] But especially from the fourth century onward, curtains representing sacred histories came into use. Whoever wishes to learn more about this should consult the distinguished Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, p. 462.]

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

No. 165, line 1.—“John.” On 28 October in the year of the Lord 701, after a vacancy of one month and twenty days, John, sixth of that name, was created pontiff.

Line 2.—“He was in the time of Tiberius.” Justinian, having returned from exile, entered the city secretly through an aqueduct and, after many insults had been inflicted upon him, deprived him at once of life and empire. This appears to have happened by God’s just judgment, so that the man who had risen against the Roman pontiff through his chamberlain Theophylact and his exarch, as Anastasius describes above, should suffer at the hands of Justinian—who, because of the persecution of Pope Sergius, had his nose cut off and for the same reason

[Col. 0926A]

was deprived of imperial dignity—the same deprivation of life and empire.

It likewise appears to have occurred by the same divine judgment that Callinicus, patriarch of Constantinople, who, relying greatly on the number of bishops, had defiled the Eastern Church with the canons of the aforesaid assembly and had risen against the Roman Church, was bound by that same emperor, deprived of his eyes, and sent into exile at Rome; so that he who had raised his head so proudly against the Roman pontiff might receive from the same man, humbled, the necessities of life. This is drawn from the annals of Theophanes and Cedrenus.

Line 7.—“At the camp.” That is, at the military encampment. Baronius, under the year 702, no. 2.

No. 166, line 1.—“Gisulphus.” The same account is found in Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 26 of the new edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0926A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The man who compiled the deeds of the pontiffs from Sergius to Gregory III, besides being unlearned in letters, as Ciampinus observed (*Examination of the Book of the Pontiffs*, section 3),

[Col. 0926B]

neglected chronological reckoning to such an extent that he long and greatly troubled later chronologists. Moreover, manuscripts and catalogues, whether by their silence or by their discrepancies, have drawn different scholars into different opinions.

Two pontiffs in particular, John VI and Sisinnius, seem, according to the chronology of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, to have been ordained outside Sunday; and Antonius Pagi taught that this had happened, although elsewhere we have found him deceived on this matter. It will therefore not be surprising to uncover new errors of his. Since both pontiffs must be discussed in their proper places, I shall speak here about John and later about Sisinnius in the notes concerning him. First, therefore, we must hear Pagi’s teaching concerning pontifical ordinations.

He teaches that these began to be held, after Constantine had defeated Maxentius and peace had been restored to the Church, either on Sundays or on more solemn days (under the year 68, no. 20). Hence he often reproves Baronius for holding the opposite view, beginning with the very ordination of Silvester, namely in the year 314, the year in which peace was restored, which he moves back to the last day of January from the Kalends of February, to which Baronius had attached it.

The first part of this teaching—namely, that pontiffs were ordained on Sundays—was handed down by other learned men before Pagi and followed by many after him. Above all, Blanchini, whose footsteps I follow, maintains that not only Roman pontiffs but also other bishops were ordained on Sundays (*above, in the notes on Saint Linus*). Affirming that this is proved by historical records, he offers as an example from the *Book of the Pontiffs* the bishop of Terni ordained by Zacharias on a Sunday.

Indeed, what strengthens Blanchini’s opinion still further and deserves notice is that the same *Book of the Pontiffs*, while recounting Zacharias’s journey, in section 209 and following, lists the individual days in sequence; yet when it reaches Sunday, it does not mention it in the same way as it would have acknowledged the day of a bishop’s ordination. Then, moving on to other matters, it continues: “On that same Sunday,” and so forth.

Whether all the other bishops were ordained on Sundays is not for me or for this place to investigate. I therefore return to pontifical ordinations.

Among the more solemn days mentioned by Pagi, on which he believes the consecrations of pontiffs were held, there are undoubtedly the Nativity of the Lord, the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the nativity of Christ’s precursor. Yet the fact that Sundays were preferred to those days which I name above, because they concern the pontiffs of this fourth volume

[Col. 0926D]

[among us, the second volume. Editor of the *Patrologia*]

, is made clear by Boniface V, John IV, and Stephen III: either by anticipating the ordination when those feast days preceded, or by passing them over when they followed.

Boniface V, who was ordained without the emperor’s authorization, for the reasons mentioned on page 26, under the year 619, was ordained on 24 December, the day before the Nativity of the Lord, in accordance with the accepted custom. Similarly, John IV was consecrated in the year 640 two days before the same solemnity, namely on 23 December, when Sunday coincided with it.

If those two pontiffs make clear that not even the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity was considered suitable for celebrating ordinations, Stephen III shows that, when some more solemn day occurred, it had to be passed over so that the coming Sunday might be awaited.

For in the year 752, when Zacharias died on 15 March and a certain Stephen was made pontiff but died before his ordination on the fourth day after his election, another Stephen was immediately elected. Although the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation coincided with a Saturday, which would have preceded the ordination—since the emperor’s authorization no longer delayed it—the ordination was nevertheless postponed until the following day, the twenty-sixth, so that it might be performed on the proper day.

[Col. 0927B] I have already said that I must refrain from other examples, some of which will be available to us in the fifth volume.

Since this is so, I wish it to be held firm and certain that Roman pontiffs, after peace had been restored to the Church, were customarily ordained only on Sundays. This is taught by the ancient Roman *Ordo* preserved by Mabillon, which, as Mabillon himself testifies, was attributed by Felix Contelorius to Cencius incorrectly, since Cencius should be considered merely a copyist of an ancient ritual.

The words of the *Ordo*, no. 81, are as follows:

> “After this, on the next Sunday, the elected man goes with all the orders of the sacred palace and the Roman nobles to the church of the blessed Peter. There, at the high altar, as the *Ordo* prescribes, he is consecrated by the bishop of Ostia in particular and by the other bishops of the curia.”

Consequently Pagi’s opinion collapses: he maintains that John VI was ordained on 28 October, the feast day of the blessed apostles Simon the Cananaean and Thaddeus, which in the year 701 fell on a Friday.

[Col. 0927C] That he was ordained on the immediately following Sunday, 30 October, is demonstrated with complete clarity by the interval between pontificates after his death, as I shall show below. Meanwhile I shall examine the vacancy of the see after Sergius.

After Sergius’s death, all the manuscripts and catalogues unanimously affirm that the see was vacant for fifty days, or one month and twenty days, as part of them reads, with no other discrepancy appearing. Therefore, if the fifty days are counted from the day of Sergius’s death, fixed by Anastasius as 8 September, one scarcely reaches 29 October. Accordingly, either Anastasius gave the day of burial instead of the day of death, as Baronius and Aringhius think, reading the fifth day before the Ides, that is, 9 September; or—and this seems more probable to me and does not conflict with the Martyrologies—Sergius died during the night preceding the ninth day, so that uncertainty remained whether twenty-three or twenty-four days should be assigned to his see, in addition to the years and months. Yet there was no uncertainty about assigning 9 September as the day of his deposition.

[Col. 0927D] In this way the fifty days properly complete the interval between pontificates and lead to Sunday, 30 October, on which John was undoubtedly consecrated, counting the days in the customary manner with the final day excluded.

John held the see for three years, two months, and twelve or thirteen days, as the Bergomian catalogue and the first and third Ambrosian manuscripts state, while all the others agree in a remarkable way. I therefore place his death on 11 January of the year 705, led to this date by the correct calculation of the duration of his see: most of the manuscripts, contrary to their custom, are silent about the year, while all attest the day.

The Farnesian, Regal, Mazarin, Thuane II, and three Ambrosian manuscripts give the third indiction, with Tiberius Augustus reigning; these most certainly indicate the year 705. I take the day of his death to be the eleventh, whereas Pagi takes it to be the ninth because of a discrepancy of two days in placing his ordination. Which of us has calculated more carefully and correctly will become clear in the following note.]

[Note: [Col. 0928A]

No. 165, line 1.—John VI was Greek by country and descent, son of Paternus, also called Petronius. Under the emperor Tiberius Absimarus Augustus he held the pontificate for three years, two months, and twelve days. He was elected on the fourth day before the Kalends and consecrated on the third day before the Kalends of November. He died at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of January in the year 705. The see was vacant for one month and eighteen days. Some hold that he suffered martyrdom, but it is not known from whom he suffered martyrdom; nor is it clear that he was buried at the catacombs of Saint Sebastian on the Appian Way, as some assert.]

[Note: [Col. 0928A]

No. 165, line 2.—“The chamberlain Theophylact came,” etc. John VI illuminated the beginnings of his pontificate by two acts of kindness and generosity that brought him great esteem and glory.

The first of these acts was to protect Theophylact,

[Col. 0928B]

the exarch, who had come to Rome at the command of the emperor Tiberius. The reason for his coming is uncertain, since history is silent; but, as may easily be inferred, he had not come to serve the interests of the holy see or of the pontiff. For when the army of Italy learned this, they immediately rushed upon him and would have inflicted much harm on the exarch had not the pontiff intervened and settled the tumult. Anastasius relates the second act in the following number.

No. 166, line 1.—“While Gisulphus, duke of the Lombard people,” etc. Gisulphus, duke of the Lombards, passing through Campania, was laying it waste completely, since no one resisted him. Therefore the pontiff sent bishops to him with gifts, freed all the captives from his hands, and compelled him to return with his troops to his own territory.]

[Note: [Col. 0928B]

No. 166, line 1.—“Then, while Gisulphus …” Paul the Deacon also relates that Gisulphus, duke of the Beneventans, entered the borders of Campania with a strong army, raided the territory of the Romans, and carried off a great number of people as booty. Pope John VI redeemed them with many gifts. Paul writes in book VI, chapter 27:

[Col. 0928D]

> “Finally, in this period, Gisulphus, leader of the Beneventans, captured Sora, a Roman city, and likewise the towns of Arpinum and Arcanum. This Gisulphus, in the time of Pope John, came into Campania with all his forces, causing fires and plundering, made many prisoners, and encamped as far as the place called Horrea; and no one was able to resist him. To him the pontiff sent priests with apostolic gifts, redeemed all the prisoners from their hands, and made the leader himself return with his army to his own territory.”

Camillus Peregrinus, in the reprinted *History of the Lombard Princes*, volume II of *Italian Historical Sources*, p. 324, criticizes Paul the Deacon and Anastasius because they relate this incursion of Gisulphus under John VI, whereas he wishes it to have occurred under John V. Yet both Paul and Anastasius retain their credibility, as the distinguished Joseph Antonius Saxi clearly proves in his notes on Sigonius’s *Kingdom of Italy*. There, after examining the chronology of the dukes of Benevento under the years 695 and 704, he shows that the devastation caused by Gisulphus belongs to the time of John VI, although he admits that it is uncertain whether it occurred in 702, as Baronius writes, or in 704, as Sigonius relates, since the documents do not provide enough evidence to decide which opinion should prevail.]

[Note: [Col. 0928D]

No. 166, line 1.—“Then, while Gisulphus …” In the year 702 Gisulphus, duke of Benevento, invaded the Roman territories as a raider and, gathering considerable booty there, returned home. Before returning, he captured many prisoners. Pope John commended apostolic charity: he sent priests with apostolic gifts to Gisulphus while he was staying in camp, redeemed all the prisoners from his hands, and made him return

[Col. 0930A]

with his army to his own territory, as Anastasius in his Life and Paul the Deacon, book VI of the *History of the Lombards*, chapter 27, relate.]

[Col. 0921]

165 John VI, a Greek by nation, held the see for three years, two months, and twelve days. He lived in the time of Tiberius Augustus. During his pontificate Theophylact, chamberlain, patrician, and exarch of Italy, came from the region of Sicily to the city of Rome. When the army of all Italy learned of his arrival,

[Note: [Col. 0921] “when it learned.”]

it gathered tumultuously at this Roman city, wishing to harass the aforesaid exarch. On account of him

[Note: [Col. 0921] “on behalf of his person.”]

the pontiff, so that he would not be afflicted, placed himself in the middle

[Note: [Col. 0921] “in the middle of the camp, that is, the soldiers’ encampment.”]

, closed the city gates, and sent priests to the camp, where they had gathered together, and by salutary admonitions quieted their tumultuous uprising.

But when certain infamous persons had drawn up an indictment against some inhabitants of the city of Rome and had handed it to the aforesaid exarch so that they might be stripped of their possessions, these men were punished with the penalty deserved by their deed

[Note: [Col. 0921] * “with a punishment worthy of their offense.”]

.

166

[Note: [Col. 0921] See Baronius under the year 702.]

Then, while Gisulphus

[Note: [Col. 0921] B: “Gisulphus.”]

, duke of the people of the Lombards at Benevento, was coming into Campania with all his forces, carrying out much burning and plundering, and taking not a few captives, and while he was making a camp as far as the place called Horrea

[Note: [Col. 0921] * “had made [a camp]”; B: “had established a camp.”]

, there was no one who could resist him. The aforesaid pontiff sent priests with apostolic gifts, redeemed all the captives from his hand, and made him return with his army

[Note: [Col. 0921] B: “with his host, that is, army.”]

to his own territory.

He newly made an ambo in the basilica of the blessed apostle Andrew, which is situated below the church of the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles. Above the altar of the church of Saint Mark he made a covering, and in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, between the columns on the right and left of the altar, white curtains. He held one ordination of priests and deacons, namely nine priests and two deacons. He also ordained fifteen bishops in various places. He too was buried at the blessed apostle Peter; and the episcopate was vacant for one month and eighteen days.
