[Note: [Col. 0931C]

No. 167, line 9.—“He also made images throughout various churches; whoever wishes to know them will find his likeness painted in them.” Statues and images of emperors were worshiped and were placed everywhere in temples and in the forum. Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book VI, chapter 9: “Only the heads of princes, cast in bronze, and faces fashioned from bronze or marble, are worshiped by human beings.” The same author, *On Interpellation*, chapter 9: “See how in cities the images of good princes endure, while the images of tyrants are erased.” Corippus, *On the Praises of Justinian*, book III:

> Painted everywhere,  
> Justinian was there; the lord delighted in the painting,  
> And they rejoiced when they saw the image of their father.

No. 168, line 1.—“In his time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored, in the proper right of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the right of the Church and was being destroyed by that same people, having been inscribed in golden letters” [Col. 0931D]. A royal donation written in golden letters to the Church is mentioned. Pachymeres, in *Andronicus Palaeologus*, book V, chapter 20, records imperial diplomas sealed with a golden bull:

> Ὁ βασιλεὺς αὐτίκα προστάττει, καὶ λόγος ἐκτίσθεται χρυσοβούλλειος.

“The emperor immediately gives the order, and a diploma is drawn up, sealed with a golden bull.” The same author, *Andronicus*, book I, chapter 2:

> Αἱ γάρ διὰ χρυσοβουλλείων λόγων πίστεις.

“For the guarantees given by diplomas sealed with golden bulls.”

Line 7.—“He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the circus before the entire people.” Leo and Tiberius, usurpers of the empire, were butchered in the circus while the people stood by. Assemblies and councils were held in the circus. Livy, book IX: “With all the peoples holding a council at Anagnia, in the circus which they call the Maritime.” Ammianus, book XXVIII, concerning the Roman people: “For them the circus and theatre were temple and dwelling, assembly and every hope, because popular largesses were distributed there” (John Chrysostom, *On Various Passages of Both Testaments*, sermon on the Circus). For this reason emperors, on entering upon the empire, proceeded to the circus for the purpose of distributing largesses (Gregory of Tours, book V, chapter 30, and book VI, chapter 30).]

[Note: [Col. 0932C]

No. 167, line 10.—“His likeness painted in them.” When the pontiff ordered various images to be painted in the churches in mosaic work, he took care that his own image should be added. Ciampinus observes this in his work on mosaics, and Agnellus repeatedly bears witness to it when he records images of this kind commissioned by the archbishops of Ravenna. Those who were portrayed while alive were customarily represented in the likeness of one praying.

No. 168, line 1.—“Aripertus.” Anastasius copied this from Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapters 2 and 28: “At this time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the right of the Apostolic See but had long been taken away by the Lombards, and sent this donation, inscribed in golden letters, to Rome.” Concerning the pontificate of John and the year in which this donation occurred, Hermannus Contractus noted the following in his *Chronicle*, edited by Canisius: “In the year 707. At this time Aribert, king of the Lombards, gave to Saint Peter and to Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, formerly seized and held by the Lombards, by a privilege written in golden letters.”

Line 4.—“Justinian.” This too is taken from Paul, chapter 31: “But Justinian, who, having lost the principate, was living in exile in Pontus, recovered the kingdom with the aid of Tervel, king of the Bulgarians, and killed the patricians who had expelled him. He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the Circus before the whole people. But he sent Gallicinus, patriarch of Constantinople, to Rome after having had his eyes torn out; and he appointed Cyrus, the abbot who had supported him in exile in Pontus, bishop in Gallicinus’s place.” Concerning the army restored by Justinian from Constantinople to the empire, his cruelty and savagery, consult the author of the *Miscella*, page 142; but concerning what the emperor undertook against the people of Ravenna whom he discovered to be supporters of the conspiracy, Agnellus treats at length in the *Life of Felix of Ravenna*, chapter 2, page 160.

No. 167, line 1.—“John VII.” John VII assumed the pontificate in the year of Christ 705, on the first day of March. It happened to this newly elected man, almost miraculously, that a Greek, placed in the Apostolic See from among the other cardinals through the efforts of Greeks, inherited the apostolic spirit and by no means yielded to the heretical emperor who sought confirmation of the Constantinopolitan council mentioned above.

No. 168, line 10.—“The tomes.” Understand the canons of that Constantinopolitan council, mentioned above under Sergius.]

[Note: [Col. 0933A]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

The catalogues and codices, with great agreement, define the vacancy of the Apostolic See after the death of John VI and up to the ordination of the other John as one month and eighteen days, except for the Veronese catalogue, which counts one day fewer because it excludes the terminal days, and the plainly corrupt third Colbertine catalogue, which counts thirty days altogether. Since we have correctly established the date of the predecessor’s death as 11 January, the date of John VII’s ordination is self-evident: counting downward from 11 January 705 through one month and eighteen days of interregnum, one reaches the Kalends of March, which in that same year 705 fell on a Sunday, as the dominical letter D confirms. Pagius was likewise compelled to assign the Kalends of March to John’s ordination because he found no feast day that suited his chronology.

But what then? Just as he moved the predecessor’s ordination and deposition back by two days, so he now stands two days apart from those same Kalends of March. To recover that interval he uses a plainly unusual device, which I think should be presented in his own words so that it may be clearer to the reader. “But,” he says concerning the interregnum, “in place of eighteen days, nineteen days should be read, with the day of death also excluded both from the see of John VI and from the interregnum; and this error, it seems, should be attributed to Anastasius.” Here the most learned man makes two mistakes, because he removed the ordination from Sunday. He declares the entire series of catalogues and codices erroneous and draws one day from their evidence in order, if possible, to fill the gap; and since one day is still lacking, he commands that the day of John VI’s death be made to disappear. Yet if he ordered that day to disappear after Sergius, he ought not to have opposed the agreement of the codices and catalogues. For, counting fifty days from 9 September, he would end at 29 October, the final day of the interregnum preceding the ordination of John VI; but in such a way that he excluded the day of death, or deposition, itself from the interregnum and joined it to Sergius’s pontificate.

If such agreement among all the codices compelled Pagius correctly to establish the date of the ordination on the Kalends of March, their equal consistency in defining the day of death—18 October—proves that John’s death cannot be moved from that date [Col. 0933D], whatever the remarkable disagreement about the duration of his see may otherwise suggest. Indeed, all the codices and catalogues that I have seen assign John VII two years of pontificate; but as regards months and days they differ greatly among themselves. The Veronese catalogue and the sixth Colbertine have eight months; the Bergomense, Lucchese, Farfense, and three Colbertines—the fourth, fifth, and seventh—together with the vulgar codex, both Freherian codices, the second Thuane, the Cavensis, and the Farnesian, have seven months; the Palatine-Vatican, the second and third Colbertines, together with the Regius, Mazarine, first Thuane, and also first Ambrosian codices, supported by Liutprand, have six months. Of these various opinions, the one that assigns John seven months is unquestionably preferable. Likewise, among the competing views concerning the number of days, the one counting seventeen should be chosen. For John VII, ordained in 705 on the Kalends of March, after sitting two years, seven months, and seventeen days, was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 18 October—in the sixth indiction, or the year 707, as Anastasius reports.]

[Note: [Col. 0934A]

No. 167, line 1.—“John VII, born of Plato, son of Janidega, a native of Rossano in Magna Graecia, also called Calabria, the fourteenth pope from the native population, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New, sat two years, seven months, and twelve days; he was elected and consecrated on Sunday, the Kalends of March.”]

[Note: [Col. 0934A]

No. 168, line 1.—“In his time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored in the proper right of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which for a long time had been deprived of the right of the Church and was being held by that same people, having been inscribed in golden letters.” The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, or rather Paul [Col. 0934B] the Deacon, from whom Anastasius easily transcribed it into the *Book of the Pontiffs*—or, if someone else was its author or interpolator—presents here an illustrious document of the most ancient possession of temporal dominion in favor of the holy Roman See. Anyone who is not excessively hostile to that See will readily acknowledge this with me.

This donation, or restoration, of the Cottian Alps is said to have occurred in the year 704, during the pontificate of John VII, not long before the lifetime of Paul the Deacon, who reports the event and flourished until about the year 770. He not only states that the donation was committed to writing, but that it was written in golden letters—something he himself could have seen with his own eyes.

This was not a donation of some estate, farm, garden, or olive grove, of the sort of which innumerable examples are supplied by our marbles and church inscriptions, as the most illustrious prelate and most experienced scholar of ecclesiastical affairs, Francesco Bianchini, correctly noted in his preface to Anastasius (vol. I, no. 43 and following). The loss of Bianchini’s papers—which he was unable to illuminate with his notes to the very end—is understood and lamented by these pages, to the great detriment of readers [Col. 0934C]. Rather, it was a donation of an immense tract of land extending from the Gallic frontier through the Allobroges and Segusium as far as Bobbio, formerly reduced by Nero to a Roman province, as Suetonius states in his *Life of Nero*. Likewise, the kingdom of the Alps, after the death of Cottius, he reduced to the status of a province.

It is also noteworthy that these lands are not called simply “the Alps,” but “the patrimony of the Alps.” The use of this designation is mixed in ancient documents: it denotes both goods dedicated to blessed Peter through the piety of the faithful and goods bound by royal rights.

This distinguished monument of the rights of the Roman Church is wonderfully illuminated and confirmed by the records of Anastasius, from the donations, restitutions, and recoveries of lands and patrimonies made to the holy Roman Church by Lombard and Frankish kings during the course of this century. It is useful to cite one or two examples in advance, to confirm the point.

Under the year 714, in the *Life of Gregory II* preserved by Anastasius—who perhaps likewise copied it from Paul the Deacon—we read of the unlawful usurpation of the same Cottian Alps and the just restoration that followed shortly afterward, made by Liutprand. “At that time,” says Anastasius, “King Liutprand confirmed the restoration of the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which King Aripert had made and this man had reclaimed, returned at the admonition or rebuke of so great a man, Gregory II.” Here one sees the same word “patrimony” repeated. This was not done by chance but, as can readily be understood, by deliberate design, to declare the transfer of property from royal rights to the rights of the holy See.

In the year 715 the Lombards deceitfully seized the fortress of Cuma, which certainly belonged to the dominion of the Roman Church. The pontiff demanded the possession unjustly taken from him. When he had tried in vain to recover it by entreaties, he used the allied forces of the Neapolitan ruler and redeemed it by paying him money:

“Also at that time,” says Anastasius in the *Life of Gregory II*, “the fortress of Cuma had been invaded by the Lombards through the deceit of peace. When this was heard, everyone became sad. The most holy pontiff exhorted and admonished the Lombards to return it; if they did not comply, he denounced in his letters that they would incur divine wrath for the deceit they had practiced. He even wished to give them many gifts so that they would restore it. But they, in their arrogant minds, neither allowed themselves to heed the admonitions nor to make the restitution.

“Therefore the same holy pontiff grieved exceedingly and entrusted himself to divine hope. He called upon the duke and people of Naples for assistance, and, by writing to him every day, presented to him how they should proceed. Obeying his command, they assembled in council and, by force, entered the walls of the fortress under cover of the silence of night. John the duke, with Theodimus the subdeacon and rector, together with the army, killed nearly three hundred Lombards and their castald, and captured alive more than five hundred others, whom they led as prisoners to Naples. Thus they were able to recover the fortress. For its redemption the most holy pope himself gave seventy pounds of gold, as he had previously promised.”

From this testimony, which I wished to reproduce in full, it clearly follows that at that time the Roman Church possessed, by undisputed right, lands and fortresses. To retain them or recover what had been lost, the holy pontiffs spared no effort, using at one time prayers and threats, and at another arms and money:

“You have seen, reader,” writes Baronius in his commentary on the passage of Anastasius just quoted, “that the holy pontiff, like Gregory the First, by no means despised ecclesiastical property invaded by enemies, nor ceased trying to recover it, however nearly impossible the conquest of the place might seem. Rather, what he could not recover with his own forces he arranged to recover with the arms of others, and with every effort he was present with counsel, assistance, and money; he even used the services of a subdeacon of the Roman Church. But observe the order in which he proceeded: first he dealt with the matter through paternal admonitions; then he terrified the contemptuous with ecclesiastical censures; finally, against those who despised all these measures, he proceeded with arms and arranged for the fortress to be stormed. Thus God wished a pontiff distinguished for both doctrine and holiness to undertake so great an enterprise, and by his example to sanction a discipline by which his successors, instructed by him, would reclaim ecclesiastical property from unjust possessors, even if arms were necessary when the other remedies were despised.”

But I shall discuss this matter more fully and more appropriately when the subject of Adrian I arises.]

[Note: [Col. 0935C]

No. 168, line 15.—“But John, timid through human weakness.” Justinian the Younger, restored to the empire through Tervel, king of the Bulgarians, ordered Tiberius Absimarus to be put to death. Having secured his affairs through the slaughter of many, he sent two metropolitans to John VII so that the canons of the wandering synod might be submitted to the supreme judgment of the Apostolic See. He requested that whatever in them seemed worthy of approval to the pontiff should be established by him [Col. 0935D], and that whatever required correction should be corrected.

Although this request of the emperor appeared reasonable, the pontiff nevertheless judged that it belonged to the dignity of the chair of Peter not to approve what had been decreed by the little council. Accordingly, he sent the canons of that synod back to the emperor through the aforesaid metropolitans, without confirming them even in part. This is why our author here reproaches John for being timid through human weakness: fearing to make himself disagreeable to the emperor, he was afraid to separate the wheat from the chaff.]

[Note: [Col. 0935D]

No. 168, line 1.—“In the time of Aripert.” While John VII was seated, Aribert, or Aripert, the second king of the Lombards bearing this name, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had belonged to the right of the Roman Church but had long been taken away by the Lombards, and, as Paul the Deacon testifies, sent this donation, inscribed in golden letters, to Rome [Col. 0936A]. Paul, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 28, writes: “At this time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the right of the Apostolic See but had long been taken away by the Lombards, and sent this donation, inscribed in golden letters, to Rome.” In the same book, chapter 43, he writes that Liutprand, son and successor of Ansprand, confirmed that restoration made to the Roman Church.

Anastasius indeed says that this occurred while John VI was seated. Hermannus Contractus, however, in the Canisian edition of his *Chronicle*, connects the donation with the year 707, when John VII was still seated; for under that year he writes: “In the year 707, at this time Aribert, king of the Lombards, returned to Saint Peter and Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, formerly seized and held by the Lombards, by a privilege written in golden letters.”

The Cottian Alps—so called after King Cottius, who conquered them—begin, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, chapter 10, at the town of Segusio. In the Bordeaux Itinerary, however, their beginning is placed at the town of Ebredunum in the modern Dauphiné; for it reads there: “Station at Hebridunum, 16 miles. From there the Cottian Alps begin,” and below: “City of Secussio, 16 miles. From there Italy begins.”

But the Paul the Deacon cited above, book II, chapter 16, when enumerating the provinces of Italy, writes that the Cottian Alps—so called after King Cottius, who lived in Nero’s time—extend from Liguria eastward to the Tyrrhenian Sea and are joined on the west to the borders of Gaul. In that province, which he counts as the fifth of Italy, he says that there are Dertona, the monastery of Bobbio, and also the cities of Genoa and Savona.

As for King Cottius, however, Paul the Deacon is mistaken when he says that he lived in Nero’s time. Ammianus, in the passage cited, states that he “was received into the friendship of the emperor Octavian,” namely Augustus. Paul the Deacon then says, in chapter 18, that the ninth province of Italy is in the Apennine Alps, “which take their origin where the Cottian Alps end,” and concludes: “There are those who say that the Cottian and Apennine Alps constitute one province; but Victorinus’s History refutes them, since it calls the Cottian Alps a province in their own right.”]

[Note: [Col. 0936D]

No. 168, line 10.—“The tomes which previously …” Here, speaking of Justinian’s restoration to the empire—which, as was stated shortly before, occurred around the end of that same year 705—the author writes:

“As soon as he entered the palace and regained his own empire, he sent, through two metropolitan bishops, the tomes which he had previously sent to Rome under Sergius, the pontiff of blessed memory. In them various chapters contrary to the Roman Church had been written. Through them he also sent a sacred letter by which he adjured and exhorted John VII, the designated pontiff, to assemble a council of the Apostolic Church, to establish whatever seemed right to him, and to exclude by refusing whatever was contrary.”

Thus Justinian not only requested from Pope Sergius, as stated above, confirmation of the Quinisext Synod and was refused; he also requested it from John VII, who, as Anastasius adds, “timid through human weakness, without correcting these tomes, sent them through the aforesaid metropolitans to the emperor, after which he did not remain long in this life.”

Anastasius therefore blames John VII for not wishing to sift the canons of the Quinisext Synod and separate the wheat from the chaff. Nor is this without foundation, says Lupus in his notes and scholia on the canons of the Council in Trullo. For concerning this synod the synodical booklet truly says: “It issued the canons omitted by the Fifth and Sixth Synods and cleansed the Churches of every Greek—that is, pagan—and Jewish, indeed even heretical, tradition.” This synod contains good things mixed with bad, and the useful is not corrupted by the useless; therefore they could have been separated, says Lupus.]

[Note: [Col. 0936D]

No. 168, line 1.—“Aripert, king of the Lombards, [restored] the donation of the patrimony.” After the Lombards acquired Italy, the Cottian Alps also came under their dominion—that region which lies between Sedunum and Ebredunum, on the far side of these mountains in Cisalpine Gaul.

These Alps once belonged to the holy See, of whose patrimony they formed a part. Since the Lombards had retained them for a very long time, usurping them without any right, their king Aripert restored them to Saint Peter and to his successor John VII, and sent him the donation, marked with golden letters, as Paul the Deacon testifies (*On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 28):

“At this time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged to the right of the Apostolic See but had long been taken away by the Lombards, and sent this donation, inscribed in golden letters, to Rome.”]

No. 168, line 10.—“The tomes which previously under Lord Sergius …” The canons of the Trullan, or Quinisext, Synod, sent by Justinian the Younger to John VII so that he might reject whichever ones he wished while approving the rest—and which the pontiff was ordered to bring intact to Constantinople—are recounted clearly enough by the Librarian.

What should be noted, however, is that some accuse the pontiff on this occasion of weakness and timidity, while others say that there would have been nothing improper in separating the many useful things from the far fewer useless ones (Christophorus Lupus, notes and scholia on the Trullan canons).

For the rest, if the matter is brought before a fair judgment, the pontiff could not have acted with greater prudence than by approving absolutely nothing that had been fabricated by an assembly arrogating to itself the name of an ecumenical council, without the Roman pontiff’s knowledge whatsoever of its convocation or celebration—especially since the spirit of arrogance and envy toward the Apostolic See prevailed in it. Does not that same holy See every day reject and condemn entire books because several bad propositions are mixed with many good ones, without nevertheless drawing up an itemized catalogue of everything that ought to be rejected and condemned?]

[Col. 0929]

167. John VII, a Greek by nationality, son of Plato, sat for two years, seven months, and seventeen days. He lived during the times of Tiberius Augustus and Justinian, formerly emperor, and was a most learned man, eloquent in speech. He made an oratory of the holy Mother of God within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, whose walls he adorned with mosaic painting. There he spent a great quantity of gold and silver and erected, on the right and left, the likenesses of the venerable Fathers. He restored the basilica of Saint Eugenia, which for a long time had been stripped of its roof and ruined. He also labored on the cemeteries of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Mark and of the holy pontiff Damasus. He also made images throughout various churches; whoever wishes to know them will find his likeness painted in them. He likewise adorned with paintings the basilica of the holy Mother of God, which is called the Ancient Basilica, and there newly made an ambon. Above that same church he preferred to establish an episcopal residence, so far as lay within his means

[Note: [Col. 0929] * he wished to construct it], and there completed the period of his pontificate. He made a splendid golden chalice weighing twenty pounds, which he also adorned with precious gems.

168. In his time Aripert, king of the Lombards, restored in the proper right of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps [Note: [Col. 0929] * “of the Coctian Alps.” B: “of the Cottian Alps.”], which for a long time had been deprived of the right of the Church and was being held by that same people, having been inscribed in golden letters. [Note: [Col. 0929] See Baronius under the year 704.] In his time Emperor Justinian, coming from the region of Khazaria [Note: [Col. 0929] * “Gazaria”], through the regions of Bulgaria with the aid of Tervel, king of the Bulgarians, as far as the imperial city, regained his own kingdom, from which he had been cast out. He also captured Leo and Tiberius, who had usurped his position, and had them slaughtered in the middle of the circus [Note: [Col. 0929] “in the Circus”] before the entire people. He regained the principate from which he had previously been violently expelled. As soon as he entered the palace and regained his own empire, he sent, through two metropolitan bishops, the tomes which he had previously sent to Rome under Sergius, pontiff of blessed memory. Various chapters contrary to the Roman Church had been written in them. Through the same men he also sent a sacred letter by which he adjured and exhorted the designated pontiff to assemble a council of the Apostolic Church, to establish whatever seemed right to him, and to exclude by refusing whatever was contrary [Note: [Col. 0929] See Baronius under the year 705.]

But John, timid through human weakness, did not correct these tomes at all; through the aforesaid metropolitans he sent them back to the emperor, after which he did not remain long in this life. He made eighteen bishops in various places. He was also buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s, before the altar of the oratory of the holy Mother of God, which he himself had built, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the sixth indiction, while Justinian was governing the Roman state. The episcopate then ceased for three months.

LXXXIX. SISINNIUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 708, THE FIFTH YEAR OF JUSTINIAN’S SECOND REIGN.

[Note: [Col. 0937C]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

Since, as I have shown, the deposition of John VII is correctly recorded by Anastasius as having occurred on 18 October, we can more easily reach the two matters that must be examined concerning the brief pontificate of Sisinnius, lasting only a few days: namely, the interregnum preceding his ordination and the duration of his see.

I see first that Sisinnius’s deposition must be established [Col. 0938C]. Some codices are silent about it; others place it incorrectly; finally, two Freherian codices and the Farnesian, together with the vulgar text, set Sisinnius’s deposition on 7 February. Those that are silent are the second Thuane and Cavensis codices, and the fourth Ambrosian, together with the Lucchese catalogue.

Those that place it incorrectly are more numerous. The Regius, Mazarine, Thuane, and three Ambrosian codices of superior quality say that Sisinnius was deposed on the eighth day before the Ides of November, that is, on 6 November. The error is obvious. These same codices have the sixth indiction, like the others, which indicates November of the year 707, and a vacancy of the See after Sisinnius of one month and nineteen days, so that according to this chronology his successor Constantine would have been ordained on 25 December, which fell on a Sunday in that same year 707. I am reluctant to see learned men embrace this opinion.

For since Constantine still counted his first year in 709, as I shall show below in the notes on him, it is clear that he was not ordained before the year 708, and therefore I rightly call the aforementioned codices corrupt. Accordingly, the vulgar text and the three other codices that place Sisinnius’s deposition on 7 February, following the example of Baronius and Pagius, are to be preferred to all the rest, so that we need not resort to guesswork by clinging to the silent codices.

Thus the two depositions—those of John VII and Sisinnius—are separated from one another by three months and twenty days. Within this interval it is necessary to place the interregnum after John and the see of Sisinnius.

Indeed, I may seem to be looking for a knot in a rush; for, with three months of interregnum according to most catalogues and the codices listed, counting from the day of John VII’s death, 18 October 707, one reaches 18 January of the following year, 708, which Baronius and Pagius assigned to Sisinnius’s ordination. Then, after the passage of twenty days—the period during which they commonly report that Sisinnius sat [Col. 0939B]—one arrives at 7 February, assigned as the date of Sisinnius’s deposition.

Yet it seems that we should heed neither the most learned cardinal, whose view causes the ordinations of pontiffs to wander outside Sundays, nor his learned critic. The latter, after establishing his axiom concerning ordinations—that they took place either on Sundays or on more solemn feast days—now wishes Sisinnius to have been ordained neither on a Sunday nor on a feast day.

As for his thinking that the feast of the Roman Chair should be traced back so far, there is certainly reason for wonder. But that he should count among the more solemn feasts a celebration which, even after its institution by Paul IV, is observed neither as a precept nor out of devotion, as they say, and that the man who blames Baronius for removing ordinations from Sundays and feast days should himself hold this view—I cannot wonder at it enough.

Accordingly, I shall first settle the remaining matters concerning the chronology; afterward I shall discuss the Roman Chair against Pagius and the others who were misled by the martyrologies of the ninth century.

Three or four complete months of interregnum, [Col. 0939C] neither of which leads to a Sunday—I have no doubt that they must be judged false. Likewise, the period of the see, defined in most catalogues and manuscripts as twenty days, since it is reckoned from no Sunday and equals the interval between that Sunday and 7 February, I think must be rejected. To this must be added the inconsistency of the catalogues—for the Palatine-Vatican assigns Sisinnius seven years and fifteen days, using the very words it employs for Constantine; the second Colbertine gives thirty days, the third twenty-five, and the seventh one year and two days—which compels me to say that nothing certain can be affirmed about either the interregnum or the see of this pontiff.

Unless, perhaps, the thirty days are to be assigned to the see, as in the second Colbertine catalogue; for, counting that much time backward from the day of his deposition, 7 February, one arrives at 8 January, which coincides with a Sunday. From there to the death of John on 18 October, only two months and twenty days are counted. Therefore, if ten days were added to the period of the see, they would have to be subtracted from the interregnum. And in fact I regard only this as certain: from John’s death to Sisinnius’ death exactly three months and twenty days elapsed. How the period of the see is to be separated from the interregnum I leave to others to determine.

For the rest, I shall never be persuaded that this pontiff was ordained on a Wednesday, contrary to the custom already established, unless perhaps the gouty humor by which he was so grievously afflicted prompted him to choose that day, so that, after being painfully brought to it through a prolonged three-month interregnum, he might suffer less and give no expectation of a more favorable day. But I shall now finally demonstrate, as I promised, that the reason which moved Pagius—namely, the feast of the Roman Chair—ought not to be considered at all.

# Dissertation on the Roman Chair

**Summary.**—I. The memorable origin of the Chair of Antioch.—II–III. Its feast instituted at Rome on 22 February to abolish the *Feralia*, or meals of the dead.—IV. No other feast of the Chair was celebrated at Rome.—V–VI. As is demonstrated by the authority of manuscripts belonging to the very basilica of Saint Peter.—VII. And by Bede’s genuine Martyrology, vindicated against Florus’s additions, together with those additions of Florus.—VIII. Also by the celebrated Martyrologies of Wandalbert and Sens.—IX. Paul IV instituted the feast of the Roman Chair in 1558 and praises the martyrologists in his constitution.—X. Their genealogy is presented.—XI–XII. The foundation of the Roman Chair is, with Blanchinus, referred to 25 April.—XIII. What was formerly believed to be celebrated on 22 February together with the Chair of Antioch.—XIV–XVI. The false origin of the same feast on 18 January derives from Transalpine Martyrologies; today, relying on Paul IV’s constitution, the feast is rightly celebrated, but on a day that is not its own.

## I

The feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, celebrated from the very beginnings of the Church no less than the Nativity of the Apostles [Col. 0940B]—but distinct from the martyrdom of Saints Peter and Paul—certainly had a great and memorable beginning. For, as William Durandus says (*Book* VII, chapter 8):

> “The Church solemnizes the Chair of Saint Peter because, as is reported, he was exalted at Antioch with cathedral honor. Some say that this exaltation was brought about by Theophilus, prince of Antioch—Maurolycus calls him the prefect—whose deceased son Peter raised after fourteen years, and whose people he converted. For this reason they built a church there, in the middle of which they placed a lofty Chair, and raised Peter upon it so that he could be heard and seen by all; he sat there for seven years. The Church therefore solemnizes this honor because at that time the prelates of the Church began to excel in rank and to be exalted in honor. For then the Psalmist’s words were fulfilled: ‘Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people’ (Psalm 106). Hence the ancient Fathers of the Church, especially Saint Augustine (Sermon 15, *On the Saints*—unless that sermon belongs to someone else, as the Maurist Fathers thought), celebrated this same feast with great praise.”

## II

When this took place especially at Antioch is not sufficiently clear. But that the celebration of this feast was instituted at Rome in February, in order to abolish the superstition of bringing food to the graves of the dead, is testified by the sermon just cited:

> “Since religious observance has rightly introduced this solemnity into the Churches,” he says, “I wonder why among certain unbelievers such a pernicious error has today grown so strong that they bring food and wine to the tombs of the dead, as though souls departing from their bodies required bodily food.”

For this reason such a celebration was formerly called the Feast of Blessed Peter of the Meals. For it was not only the pagans who embraced that superstition; Jerome Macer, on the authority of Saint Augustine, likewise reports this concerning Christians:

> “The Feast of the Meals,” he says. “The Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, on which day Christians, especially in Africa, were accustomed to feast. Concerning them Saint Augustine says in Book VI of the *Confessions*, chapter 2: ‘When he had brought to the memorials of the saints, as is customary in Africa, porridge, bread, and unmixed wine.’ This custom was introduced by pagan superstition: on precisely the same day they were accustomed to place food upon the tombs of the dead.” (*Hierolexicon*)

That this superstition continued among Christians for a long time is confirmed by the Second Council of Tours, held in the year 570, canon 22:

> “There are also those who on the third day of the feast of the Chair of our lord Peter the Apostle offer food to the dead (Sirmondus reads *in trinitas* in the Beauvais manuscript), and, returning home after the Masses, return to the errors of the pagans.”

## III

From these documents the very day on which the feast was instituted can plainly be recognized. For in the rural Calendar edited both by Gruterus and by Bucherius in *On the Doctrine of Time*, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March—that is, 21 February—one reads *Feralia*, when meals were brought to the tombs, because people thought that the souls fed on them during the night preceding the feast. [Col. 0941A]

On the day of the feast itself, 22 February, the same Calendar has *Caristia*. As Dufresne observes in his *Glossary*, this word has the same meaning as *cara cognatio* (“dear kinship”), which occurs on the same day in the calendar of Polemius Silvius:

> “So called,” he says, “because at that time, even if there had been hatred between living relatives, it was put aside at the time of death.”

Moreover, in that same calendar the feast of the Chair itself is indicated by these words: “Burial of Saint Peter and Paul.” Some have wrongly interpreted this as referring to the apostles’ martyrdom. Tillemontius (*Ecclesiastical History*, volume I) elegantly refutes their opinion, and Father Conrad Janningus likewise attacks it in his commentary on 29 June, preliminary commentary, numbers 24 and following, by pointing to what is read in the same calendar on the third day before the Kalends of July—that is, 29 June:

> “Peter at the Catacombs, Paul on the Ostian Way.”

These entries plainly demonstrate their martyrdom.

In any event, that Silvius designates the day of the Chair by the name “Burial” is established both by Bollandus’s observation and by Bucherius’s ancient Martyrology, entitled *The Burial of the Martyrs*. It begins as follows:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Christ was born at Bethlehem of Judah.”

There the Nativity of the Lord is numbered among the burials; likewise, a little farther on, the Chair is listed among those same burials:

> “IN THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, the birthday of Peter of the Chair.”

This most ancient Martyrology, written in the time of Liberius, was transferred by that great defender of ancient monuments, Francis Blanchinus, from Bucherius’s *On the Doctrine of Time* into the prolegomena to this work, so that it might be available to those reading our text.

## IV

I have used the authority of Polemius Silvius’s calendar and of the ancient Martyrology to establish the very ancient institution of the Chair of Antioch on 22 February. To avoid dwelling too long on a matter sufficiently familiar to learned men, I must now show more fully that there was once only one feast of the Chair at Rome.

Having carefully examined as many Antiphonaries, Responsories, Sacramentaries, and volumes of that kind as I could see—especially those published through the work and study of the venerable Cardinal Tomasius—I found in them only the feast of the Chair on 22 February. The Antiphonary arranged by Saint Gregory for the cycle of the year; the Chartres Antiphonary, which Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, among many other precious objects, gave as a gift to the basilica of Saint John the Baptist at Monza; the Capitular Book of the Gospels; the *Comes*, or Lectionary—all extremely ancient and all pertaining to the very basilica of Saint Peter—display no other Chair besides the one mentioned on 22 February.

There do indeed exist manuscript Antiphonaries and Lectionaries of Saint Gall in which one reads, on 18 January, “The Chair of Saint Peter.” But Walafrid Strabo, a ninth-century writer (*On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 25), confirms—as the same cardinal warns in his preface—that the Roman Antiphonary, after it had been transported beyond the Alps, received numerous additions from Gallican masters.

To establish the truth of this, let us consider the manuscript of that same monastery of Saint Gall, which underwent no additions and in which there is an *Order of the Catholic Books that Are Read in the Roman Church*. In that manuscript one can read:

> “From the Nativity of the Innocents until Septuagesima, etc. From the Purification of Saint Mary, etc. At the Chair of Saint Peter the readings are those used on the nativity of all the apostles.”

Since no other Chair occurs, either before or afterward, the evidence is clear.

## V

To establish still more clearly that there was only one feast of the Chair, it is also worth observing that the Responsory and Antiphonary arranged by Gregory the Great, into which no Gallican additions entered, displays the rites customarily used in the Roman Church in the twelfth century, when the piety of monks and the religious devotion of bishops had already introduced another feast of the Chair beyond the Alps, on 18 January. I shall explain its origin and development below. Nevertheless, this book agrees exactly with the Ritual of the Canon Benedictus, who describes the rites of his basilica with great fidelity.

The Responsory has the following for 18 January:

> “On the feast of Saints Aquila and Prisca, Responsory, etc.”

But for 22 February:

> “At the Chair of Blessed Peter, at Vespers we sing the Antiphons ‘BEHOLD THE PRIEST.’”

The Ritual of the aforementioned Canons, however, describing the rites of the feasts individually (in Mabillon, *Order* XI), says, when it reaches the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany:

> “But on weekdays, if there is no feast, the Antiphon is sung,” etc.

This is the clearest proof that the feast of the Roman Chair was unknown in its own basilica. Later, in the exposition of the rites of the Purification, Septuagesima, and Sexagesima, it says:

> “At the Chair of Saint Peter it is read as on the day of his nativity; nevertheless, at Vespers and at Matins it is sung: ‘BEHOLD THE GREAT PRIEST.’ The station is in his basilica.”

What more could be desired concerning the singular feast of the Chair of Saint Peter?

## VI

To all these arguments an even stronger one may be added: namely, the Calendar, or Martyrology, according to the ancient custom of the canons of the Vatican Basilica of Saint Peter. It is expanded from the ancient Martyrology that I presented from Bucherius and from the Calendar of Polemius Silvius. This calendar is prefixed to the Responsory and Antiphonary of the Roman Church for the cycle of the year, which the venerable Cardinal Tomasius reports to have been written in the twelfth century.

In it, the limits of Septuagesima, Lent, and Easter are indicated in various verses according to ancient custom. Above all, the final stage of Septuagesima, which falls on the vigil of the Chair of Antioch, is indicated in the first verse of this couplet:

> “Forestalling the Chair, it grants the later [day?] to be free.”

The second verse reads:

> “Winter retreats before the enthroned Simon Peter.”

The higher limit, however, coinciding with 18 January, when today we celebrate another Chair, is not indicated by the Vatican Calendar as a special feast of the basilica. Indeed, the feast itself is not even mentioned, since it was then unknown; instead, in its place we find:

> “Aquila and Prisca.”

Nor should anyone wonder that no monument of the Vatican Basilica—whether ancient or from the later Middle Ages—exists in which the feast is mentioned that so many ancient Transalpine manuscripts display. For, to use Morinus’s words, the Romans:

> “The later compilers of the Sacramentaries do not compose Sacramentaries on their own initiative, but copy them; and when they add something, they do not express it in their own words, but transcribe it as they see it expressed” (Joannes Morinus, *On the Sacrament of Ordination*, part 3, exercise 9, chapter 1).

Thus Saint Gregory the Great, arranger of the Sacramentaries, and Benedict, canon of Saint Peter and describer of the Ritual, added to the ancient Sacramentaries and Rituals those celebrations whose rites had become established in the basilica during their age. But those which bishops and monks had introduced into their own churches either from piety or from zeal, although they were wholly unknown at Rome and might have brought greater glory to the prince of the apostles and to his basilica, they did not mention. For they did not compose Sacramentaries on their own initiative; they copied them.

## VII

But in proving the feast days of the Roman Church, do I use only Roman authors? On the contrary, outsiders themselves offer stronger support for the truth of the matter. [Col. 0942D]

The venerable Bede, Florus, and Wandalbert, who followed the monuments of antiquity when publishing their Martyrologies, are entirely silent concerning the Chair on 18 January.

No one is unaware that Bede, the venerable presbyter of England, published a Martyrology expanded from the ancient Roman Martyrology, which all the Churches everywhere embraced. He published it at the beginning of the eighth century, when Pagius believes that the feast of the Roman Chair was already celebrated.

Likewise, everyone knows that Florus, deacon of Lyons, a century later—that is, toward the end of the ninth century—expanded Bede’s Martyrology.

The learned Henschenius and Papebrochius published Bede’s genuine Martyrology and Florus’s additions in volume II of the *Acta Sanctorum* for March, after searching through the most select libraries throughout Europe, especially those at Rome. They used three particularly choice manuscripts: the Vatican manuscript; the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus in the Baths, from the Vallicellian Library, which Baronius used; and a third from the exceptionally well-equipped Barberini Library.

Father Sollerius, continuator of the *Acta*, added new labors to that edition in his preface to Usuard’s Martyrology (volume VI for June). Finally, Father Joseph Blanchinus, a great investigator of ancient monuments like his uncle, collated and corrected Henschenius’s edition against the thousand-year-old manuscript of the distinguished Chapter Library of Verona.

Nevertheless, neither Bede’s Martyrology nor Florus’s additions, transmitted on the authority of so many celebrated manuscripts, has anything on 18 January besides the Nativity of Saint Prisca; nor is any other Chair mentioned in them except the one that was truly celebrated at Rome and throughout the Catholic world on 22 February.

## VIII

Bede’s Martyrology is further supported by the Martyrology of Sens, belonging to Saint Columba and later to the queen of Sweden, which the aforementioned Father Sollerius compares in authority with the three select Roman manuscripts mentioned above; and by the celebrated Martyrology of Wandalbert, a monk of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, who wrote it around the middle of the ninth century. Neither of these presents the feast of the Roman Chair.

These facts compelled Sollerius, straining all his strength and resources to assert the Chair, to anticipate the objection of learned men:

> “Nothing,” he says, “stands in the way of Bede’s, Florus’s, and Wandalbert’s silence, unless someone wishes by the same reasoning to argue against the commemoration of almost innumerable saints.”

I assure that most religious man of my good faith: I shall not use their silence to abolish feasts, but to uncover the true origin of feasts.

Would it not have been culpable negligence on the part of the Vatican clergy to organize their rites in so many Sacramentaries and manuscripts cited above while mutilating them of their chief ornament—the memory of the apostolic see first established at Rome?

Would not the Venerable Bede, who undertook to enlarge the ancient Roman Martyrology so that, if possible, no day would remain without being illuminated by the illustrious name of some saint, have inflicted a serious loss through that untimely silence upon the Roman see, which he honored with such singular devotion?

Finally, would not Florus, who first of all expanded Bede’s Martyrology, have wasted his labor by passing over in silence a feast that ought to have been counted among the Roman feasts above all others?

## IX

From this everyone can see that before the ninth century had fully matured, when the younger martyrologists attached the feast of the Roman Chair to 18 January, no mention of that rite occurs either at Rome or elsewhere.

Afterward, however, it is clear that the feast was solemnly celebrated in several parts of the Christian world, especially in Gaul and Spain, and perhaps even in the city of Rome itself. Paul IV is the witness: in 1568 he ordered it to be celebrated, as Maurolycus says—or rather, he restored it to its ancient celebration after it had fallen into disuse, as the learned men Cardinal Baronius (*Notes on the Martyrology*, 18 January) and Joannes Bollandus (*Acta Sanctorum*, 18 January) observe.

The pontiff’s words are:

> “Indeed, although the city itself owes far more to that same Peter, who founded it by establishing in it an episcopal Chair so that it might be joined to the heavenly kingdoms, than to those by whose efforts the foundations of its walls were first laid, among whom the one who gave it its name stained it with fraternal slaughter, nevertheless it does not observe and celebrate the feast of that Chair—which, according to the testimony of our most ancient holy Fathers, was on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February and is solemnly celebrated on that day in various parts of the Christian world, especially in Gaul and Spain—but celebrates only the feast of the Chair of Antioch, which, according to the testimony of those same Fathers, was on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. It is as though our Savior, who often chose the weak in order to confound the strong, without regard for our weakness, had reserved for our own times the celebration—or rather the restoration to its ancient celebration—of the feast of the Chair on which the apostle Peter first sat at Rome.”

From Paul’s words three facts become known:

1. In his own age the feast of the Roman Chair was not celebrated at Rome.
2. The most ancient Fathers testify that the Roman Chair fell on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, on which day it was then celebrated among foreigners, especially among the Gauls and Spaniards.
3. The origin of the Roman Chair is nothing other than the beginning of the establishment of the Roman pontificate.

## X

Although I have abundantly established the first point through monuments of antiquity from the first eight centuries of the Church, I would not dare deny that the feast may also have been celebrated for some time at Rome during the ninth or tenth century.

I am moved by the words of Paul just cited, in which he decreed that the feast of the Chair should be celebrated—or rather restored to its ancient celebration—on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, which is the second point. I understand that their genealogy, or, better, their respective ages, must be examined so that greater confidence may be given to these statements.

Father Joan Baptista Sollerius, in his preface to Usuard (volume VI for June, from number 12 through 160), places three as the principal figures of all: Eusebius, or Jerome, or both together; the Venerable Bede; and the unknown author of the Martyrology discovered at Ravenna by Ado.

He makes Rabanus, Ado, Notker, and Usuard their successors. He teaches that Rabanus was either contemporary with Florus, deacon of Lyons, who expanded Bede’s Martyrology around the year 830, or, more probably, that he composed his own Martyrology after examining Florus’s additions. He proves that Ado, bishop of Vienne, worked on his own Martyrology at the same time and from the same source. He demonstrates that Notker had also seen Rabanus’s Martyrology. Finally, he readily affirms that Usuard, a monk who wrote after the others, around the year 875, examined all the works of his predecessors.

## XI

Therefore, unless I am mistaken, we have grasped the origin of the Roman Chair—namely, when it first entered the Martyrologies of the Fathers just mentioned.

But since the most learned Parisian canon Claude Castellan asserts that this same feast was particular to Gaul before Charlemagne, while at Rome and throughout Italy it was entirely unknown, and since Paul IV says that its true origin was derived from the beginning of the Roman pontificate, I shall do worthwhile work if I show that the beginning of the Roman Chair was not correctly placed in Gaul on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

The great defender of pontifical chronology, Blanchinus, establishes with such invincible arguments that the beginnings of the Roman Chair must be referred to 25 April that it would seem idle to demonstrate the same matter again in this work. (See the notes on Saint Peter.)

But what if he had seen what the learned Father Joseph Blanchinus, his brother’s son, produced from the outstanding library of his native Verona, which he so often examined and stripped bare? He brought forth an ancient Sacramentary [Col. 0944D]—see *Patrologia*, volume LV—in which, on 25 April, there is not merely the Greater Litanies, as in other books, an argument of very uncertain significance, but an entire Mass of Saint Peter. And so that no doubt might remain that the beginning of the Roman Chair must be taken from that day, the margin bears the note:

> “AT THE DEDICATION.”

I confess, however, that when this most precious monument was first communicated to me by that distinguished man, with his customary generosity and courtesy, I rejoiced exceedingly. For I saw that it provided an invincible argument for establishing the beginnings of the Roman Chair together with the catalogue of Felix IV and the third Colbertine manuscript, on 25 April—the day on which I saw the Greater Litanies and the station at Saint Peter indicated in all the Sacramentaries and manuscripts. Yet I could not grasp the mystery.

## XII

In particular, I often read in the Roman Order of the frequently praised Canon Benedict, number 58:

> “When the Litany and the other offices have been completed, he ascends to the basilica of Saint Peter, where the station is; and there the lord pontiff sings Mass.”

Likewise, in the excerpts of Peter Manlius, also a canon of Saint Peter, chapter 27, concerning the daily stations:

> “At the Greater Litanies, on the day of Saint Mark; at the Dedication of the churches of the apostles Peter and Paul”—namely, 18 November, on which day the Calendar and Martyrology make the entry—“at the Chair of Saint Peter.”

In Onuphrius Panvinius’s book *On the Stations of the City of Rome*:

> “On the day of Saint Mark, at the Greater Litanies, the ancient station.”

But concerning the stations on Monday at Saint Paul, on Tuesday in the Lateran Basilica, and on Wednesday at Saint Peter during the three-day Litanies at the time of the Rogations:

> “The recent station.”

All these things led me to follow Blanchinus’s opinion step by step. Yet just as I did not see him rejecting 18 January, so from the distinction he makes between the founded Chair and the declared primacy I understood clearly that some doubt still remained in his mind about the point from which the beginnings of the Roman Chair ought to be derived.

Now, however, after examining both Bede’s genuine Martyrology and the Sacramentary of Leo the Great, I think there can no longer be any doubt, with Blanchinus, concerning the beginnings of the founded Roman Chair; and it seems highly probable that they can be referred precisely to 25 April.

## XIII

As for the feast of the Roman Chair, Paul IV decreed on 18 January that it should be celebrated, or restored to its ancient celebration, following, as he says, the example of the lesser Churches. This in no way prevents us from celebrating it on a day other than the day of its foundation, just as it is known that the day of 29 June was once prefixed in the Gelasian manuscript, and as I have already pointed out was also done with the Chair of Antioch.

For the Roman pontiffs did not institute the celebration of the latter on the day on which the enthronement took place at Antioch, but on the day on which Christians, following pagan custom, celebrated the superstitious feast of the meals.

Moreover, the highly respected twelfth-century writer Beletus states in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, chapter 83, that both Chairs were celebrated at Rome on one and the same day:

> “At this time,” he says, “the Chair of Saint Peter is customarily celebrated, both the one that was at Rome, which is later in time, and the one that was at Antioch. But the one that was at Antioch is certainly more solemn than the other, as the collect of this day itself, which is about the enthronement that took place at Antioch, sufficiently testifies; it is also called the feast of Blessed Peter of the Meals.”

And below:

> “When holy men had noticed this and wished to extinguish that custom completely, they instituted a feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, both of the one that was at Rome and of the one that was at Antioch, on the very day on which those abominable practices were carried out by the pagans, so that by this solemn feast the feast of that depraved custom might be entirely extinguished.”

This agrees neither poorly with the sermon of Saint Augustine—or of another ancient Father—mentioned above, which treats both Chairs together, nor with the Vatican manuscripts cited earlier, which mention the feast of the Chair only once, although the established rite of the Litanies and of the other ceremonies customarily performed on the anniversary of the founded Chair, 25 April, remained in force.

## XIV

It remains to discuss the origin, beyond the Alps, of the founded Roman Chair, which is attested as having been referred to 18 January by the manuscript Antiphonary of Saint Gall in Switzerland, by the additions to Bede’s Martyrology, and by many later manuscripts.

The Gallican masters, as Walafrid Strabo calls them, undoubtedly had before their eyes the Calendar of Polemius Silvius, in which one reads on 22 February:

> “Burial of Saint Peter and Paul.”

Since they placed the apostles’ martyrdom on that same day, they attempted to establish on it the beginning of Saint Peter’s Roman pontificate. Nor was it difficult for them to find some catalogue or manuscript which, like our manuscript from Cava, assigned to Peter’s see, in addition to twenty-five years, one month and five days.

Therefore, counting backward one month and five days from the day which they believed to be the day of his martyrdom, they arrived at 18 January. Since they were either bishops or monks, they wished that day to be held sacred to the founded Chair in their own churches or monasteries.

This is how it happened that in other churches—where religious devotion and piety encouraged people to add as many saints’ names as possible to their Martyrologies—the feast of the Roman Chair began to become celebrated.

I shall present highly conspicuous examples that demonstrate the matter more clearly than daylight. The contracted Hieronymian Martyrologies, as the aforementioned Father Sollerius calls them, which he adduces above all others, are the Rheinau and Reichenau Martyrologies. Like the ancient Roman Martyrology, the Martyrology of the queen of Sweden, and many other excellent Martyrologies, they had on 18 January “At Rome, Saint Prisca.”

Then they underwent an addition, with such carelessness on the part of the compiler that he left the future discovery of it even to the blind. Let both be examined:

**Rheinau Martyrology:** “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February: At Rome, Saint Prisca. Also at Rome, the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, and in Pontus, Mary.”

**Reichenau Martyrology:** “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February: At Rome, the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, and in Pontus, Mary. Also at Rome, Saint Prisca.”

## XV

I pass over the obvious addition at the beginning of one and at the end of the other, resulting from the repetition of “At Rome”; the point is self-evident.

What does that commemoration in the Reichenau Martyrology mean—for the Rheinau manuscript is mutilated for the two months of February and March—concerning the Chair of Antioch, the Nativity of the Chair of the Apostle Peter? Does it not expose the first memory of the Roman Chair as an interpolation?

But I am disputing something as clear as sunlight. Henschenius and Papebrochius, in their preface to Bede’s Martyrology, assert that these two Martyrologies were compiled by adding from other sources whatever pleased their compilers.

The same is true of the others cited by Sollerius, including the Gellone Martyrology published in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume XIII. Although the editor assigns it the greatest possible antiquity, he cannot place it beyond the ninth century. It too was compiled at the same time, when its writers were attempting to select saints’ names from here and there so that the days of the months might all be filled. This is revealed by the striking similarity they share.

I would not dare affirm that Bede’s Martyrology was the principal source from which the martyrologists of that age derived their material. This much I know for certain: only very rarely do copies of Bede’s text from the archetype display that addition, as is evident from the many manuscripts examined by Henschenius and Papebrochius; of these, only the Tournai manuscript, intended for the use of the monastery of Saint Martin, records the memory of the Roman Chair.

## XVI

In any event, whoever first introduced this addition into the Martyrologies did so with such success that I have found it even in one Italian Ambrosian Calendar.

Yet this interpolation was made with the same carelessness as in the Transalpine Martyrologies just mentioned. There are, in fact, two ancient Calendars that preserve the superstitious practice of the Egyptians’ days according to the custom of the ancients, published by the distinguished Ludovico Muratori (*Italian Writers*, volume II, part 2): the Ambrosian and the Sitonian.

The former certainly surpasses the latter in antiquity and is almost entirely astronomical, except for the first four months, in which the Paschal limits and other matters relating to the principal solemnities are indicated. Both, pertaining to the Milanese Church, display its feasts.

The Ambrosian Calendar, however, recites the names of saints only in January; in the following three months it mentions them rarely, and thereafter not at all. It lists more than the other, more recent calendar, so that it often clearly appears to have received additions.

And lest I assert this without evidence, the very day, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, provides the proof. It has:

> “Prisca the virgin. At Rome, the Chair of Saint Peter.”

Here the addition is obvious, both because it names Rome nowhere else except in this place and because it adds “Saint” to the apostle Peter, just as on the Kalends it had added “Martina the virgin,” also an interpolation. It does not do this except twice or three times in other additions of this kind, such as “Saint Benedict,” “the burial of Saint Ambrose,” and “Saint Zeno,” apart from the few persons whom the ancient Martyrologies honor in this way.

The Sitonian Calendar, on the other hand, although much more recent, mentions the Chair of Saint Peter in its proper place, namely 22 February, whereas the Ambrosian does not.

Since this is so, those very ancient Breviaries and the manuscript Roman Martyrology in which Baronius read the feast of the Roman Chair on 18 January (*Notes on the Martyrology*, that day) cannot be older than the ninth or tenth century of the Church.

Accordingly, whether the feast of the Chair was celebrated at Rome on 18 January at that time or was not celebrated—since the pope could have instituted it on whatever day he pleased, as happened with many other feasts celebrated outside their proper day—there was no need for Paul IV to investigate the matter more subtly, especially since, as he himself says, the aforementioned day, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, was celebrated in various parts of the Christian world.

Thus he did not disdain to follow even the example of the lesser Churches, so that, to the glory of the prince of the apostles, the rite of the Roman Chair might be celebrated on one and the same day throughout the Catholic world and especially in the city of Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0947A]

Line 1.—Sisinnius. Son of John, a Syrian, under the emperor Justinian II Augustus; he sat for twenty days; he was created on the fifteenth day before the Kalends, and consecrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.]

[Note: [Col. 0947A]

Line 1.—Sisinnius was Syrian by nationality. In the time of Benedict II, after Constantine Pogonatus had abolished the most unjust right of confirming the elected pontiff—a matter discussed above under Benedict—the Greeks devised new methods by which they could govern the Roman Church according to their own will.

They took care to enroll Greeks and Orientals into the sacred college of the clergy of the City, and from these, chiefly through the agency of the exarchs, the pontiff was elected.

Benedict had as his successor John, fifth in order by that name, a Syrian by nationality; John had Conon, a Thracian; Conon had Sergius, a Syrian; Sergius had John VI and then John VII, both Greeks; John VII had this Sisinnius, a Syrian; Sisinnius had Constantine, likewise a Syrian; and, with only Gregory II intervening, Gregory III, a Syrian, was elected. After him Zacharias, a Greek, was placed over the Roman see.

Yet the pontiffs elected for this reason were so far from diminishing even in the slightest degree their apostolic gravity and religious devotion that no one resisted the unjust demands of the Greeks more vigorously than they did.]

[Col. 0937]

**169. Sisinnius**, Syrian by nationality, son of John, sat for twenty days. He lived in the time of the emperor Justinian Augustus. He was so constricted by gouty humor that he could not present food to himself with his own hands. Nevertheless, he was firm in spirit and concerned for the inhabitants of this city. He also ordered lime to be fired for the restoration of the walls. [Note: [Col. 0937] *Calcarias*: “lime.”]

Nevertheless, he died a sudden death. He ordained one bishop on the island of Corsica. He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle, on 7 February, in the sixth indiction, under Justinian Augustus, and the episcopate remained vacant for one month and twenty-nine days. [Note: [Col. 0937] B, or thus.]

### Notes

**No. 170, line 6 — Felix.** Here Anastasius recounts the wrongs inflicted upon the people of Ravenna, because they had dared to do certain things without consultation and rashly. He suppresses, however, the rebellion made against Justinian, which Agnellus reports at length, since on account of it the archbishop Felix, after his eyes had been torn out, lived for some time in exile in Pontus. The security-oath that was to be handed over to him by the same man was similar, or perhaps more extensive, to that found in the *Roman Diurnum*, which the elected metropolitans used to make. I say that it was more extensive in the case of the Ravennate bishops, since it had to include those chapters which the same Agnellus asserts were agreed upon under Leo II, in the *Life of Theodore of Ravenna*, chapter 4, p. 153. See Bacchinius, *Observations on the Life of Felix of Ravenna*.

**No. 171, line 2 — To ascend to the imperial city.** Anastasius gives a lengthy account of the journey and actions of the pontiff and his companions. Paul the Deacon, however, in book VI, chapter 31, writes the following about Justinian: “He ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, received him honorably, and sent him back. Having prostrated himself upon the ground, he asked him to intercede for his sins, and he renewed all the privileges of his Church. When he sent an army into Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, that same venerable pope strongly forbade him to do this, but nevertheless could not prevent him.”

If this is compared with Agnellus’s narrative, in which he reveals that Justinian was extremely hostile to the Ravennans and to the City, and inflicted many hardships upon the nobles whom he knew to be guilty of his expulsion from the empire, we may perhaps infer the reason for the journey that the pontiff undertook to Constantinople. Namely, Pope Constantine appears to have been summoned by Justinian so that, after complaining of the security-oath denied him by Felix of Ravenna, the matter might be examined in his presence. Among the privileges granted to the Apostolic See, Justinian confirmed the decrees of Constantine Pogonatus concerning the subjection of the Church of Ravenna to the Roman Church.

As for Paul’s assertion that Justinian was warned by the pontiff not to direct his soldiers and forces against Philippicus, because he had detected treachery, the event itself confirmed it, and demonstrated that the warning had been given with the greatest prudence.

**No. 174, line 3 — Justinian was murdered.** The author of the *Miscella* and Theophanes recount the unhappy fate of Justinian, caused by the tyranny of Philippicus and the treachery of his own army. Agnellus, in the same *Life of Felix of Ravenna*, reports the matter and attributes its cause to what the emperor had done against the Ravennans. He names as the author of the rebellion Joannicius, who shortly beforehand had said to assassins and traitors: “Tomorrow, at this same hour at which it is now, you will kill your emperor, and he will be with me before the most just Judge … On another day, at the hour he had foretold, they rushed upon the emperor and, unable to endure the wickedness of his people, killed him.”

Agnellus also adds the manner of the death and the mockery inflicted upon the prince, whose head was carried throughout the whole of Italy. But here, as elsewhere, the untrained historian records a trivial popular tradition.

**Line 4 — And Philippicus the heretic.** Anastasius copies what Paul says in chapter 32: “The army that had been sent against Philippicus went over to Philippicus’s side, and made him emperor. Coming against Justinian at Constantinople, he fought with him at the tenth milestone from the city, defeated and killed him, and obtained his kingdom.”

Justinian’s excessive cruelty moved the peoples to defect, as Paul observes there. In chapter 33 he adds: “But Philippicus, who was also called Bardanes, ordered Cyrus … who had been removed from the pontificate, to return to Pontus to govern his monastery. This Philippicus sent Pope Constantine letters containing an evil doctrine, which he rejected with the counsel of the Apostolic See. Because of this he made paintings in the portico of Saint Peter, representing the proceedings of the six holy universal synods. For when such paintings existed in the imperial city, Philippicus had ordered them removed; and the Roman people decreed that they would accept neither the name of the heretical emperor, nor his documents, nor the image of the solidus.”

Two councils must therefore be examined more carefully: one, illegitimately held at Constantinople; the other, celebrated at Rome by the pontiff.

## On the Constantinopolitan Conciliabulum Held Concerning the Sixth Synod

While Philippicus was living in exile at Cherson on account of his attempted tyranny, he was chosen emperor by the Chersonites, who had heard that Justinian was preparing and arranging a large fleet against them.

Agatho the deacon discusses Philippicus’s first movements and the treachery of the imperial army in his peroration to the Sixth Synod, published by Combefisius in the *Appendix to the Library of the Fathers*. He writes:

“Indeed, when the very large army which he had distributed by sea into various squadrons in order to attack and plunder the city of Cherson and utterly destroy and wipe out its people rebelled against him from that place and made an assault, that same army, in a fanatical and indiscriminate tumult, rashly and without any legitimate examination or vote, appointed as emperor and proclaimed as prefect a certain man who at that time was living in exile in those regions under the pretext of tyranny, named Bardanes, a Pergamaean by birth and son of Nicephorus.”

Philippicus had been formed in the school of the Monothelites, from whom he had absorbed the stain of heresy; but he was confirmed still more strongly in error by a certain impostor-monk. Concerning him, the author of the *Miscella*, p. 145, writes as follows:

“Before he became emperor, there was a certain recluse in the monastery of Callistratus, a diviner (*astronomos*, ἀστρονόμος) and a heretic, who said to Philippicus when he came to him: ‘The empire has been reserved for you.’ But Philippicus was troubled; and the recluse said: ‘Thus God commands. Why, then, do you resist? I say this because the Sixth Synod was wrongly conducted. If you become emperor, cast it out, and the empire will be made strong and long-lasting for you.’ He then swore to him that he would do this. But when Leontius had succeeded Justinian, Philippicus went up to the recluse, who said to him: ‘Do not hurry; it will happen to you.’”

Theophanes likewise writes in his *Chronicle*, p. 319:

“Moreover, long before he obtained the empire, a certain recluse, gifted with the art of prophecy and infected with heresy, lived in the monastery of Callistratus. Whenever Philippicus came to him, he foretold: ‘The empire has been reserved for you.’ When Philippicus was shaken by such words, the recluse added: ‘If God so commands, will you oppose him? I declare only this: the Sixth Synod was most wickedly conducted. If you ever become emperor, proscribe it and annul it, and a fortunate and long-lasting empire will follow you.’ Having given his oath, he undertook to carry out the deed.”

The recluse was a disciple of Stephen the abbot and of Macarius of Antioch, the most obstinate Monothelite. As Agatho the deacon says:

“Having long possessed within him—not only through the preceding teaching and tradition of his parents, as he himself said, but also through a certain false doctrine and most profane heresy opposed to this holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod—the man had been a disciple from his earliest age of the abbot Stephen, the disciple of Macarius.”

Such monkish impostors, devoted to judicial astrology, remarkably often drove the unwary mad. This was a particularly familiar rust of that iron age of the Church among men consecrated to God. Hence Paschalis the archdeacon, who had sought the pontificate under Sergius, was deprived of the office of archdeacon, according to Anastasius:

“For certain incantations and lights which he worshipped, or lots which he handled with other observers, by the judgment of God and of blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles, he was deprived [of office].”

Meanwhile Philippicus, having been raised to the empire, chose that monk as his companion and promoter of his treachery.

“Immediately, without any delay, using imperial power and authority, before his own entrance, he ordered the image of that same holy Sixth Synod, which had been displayed, to be thrown down; otherwise, he said, he would not endure entering the imperial palace, since it was not his, unless matters had first been arranged in this way,” as Agatho says. He immediately adds:

“After a very short time, when he had also found those whom we mentioned placed in the imperial palace, he cast out the volumes of the Acts of that same holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod, written by my own hand, brought them into public view, and consigned them to a secret fire and destroyed them.”

Patriarch John writes similarly in his synodical letter to the pontiff:

“He dared to burn the volumes of the Acts of the aforementioned holy Sixth Synod, deposited in the palace, believing—as it seemed to him—that by doing so he would also erase the word of truth.”

These things occurred in the year 711. Soon afterward he convoked a conciliabulum at Constantinople, so that the Sixth Synod might be subjected to anathema by a more solemn decree.

In the year 712, therefore, this council was assembled at Constantinople. Theophanes writes of it:

“An insane conciliabulum against the holy ecumenical council was held. After Cyrus was expelled during the sixth year of his patriarchate, John was made patriarch of Constantinople; Andrew, metropolitan of Crete, and Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, openly subscribed and anathematized, with all their colleagues, the aforementioned holy ecumenical synod held against the Monothelites.”

At that gathering they first dealt with condemning the Council of Chalcedon, as John the patriarch hints in his letter to the Roman pontiff, published by Combefisius in the same place. In it John asks pardon because he himself had presided over that predatory synod, and among other things says:

“Indeed, some were already murmuring that the holy Catholic Council of Chalcedon itself ought to be abolished, since, as regards agreement in doctrine, it depended upon that synod and, so to speak, had its root and confirmation in the said holy Sixth Synod.”

Nevertheless, they did not then dare to attack the decrees of the great Council of Chalcedon, although they hurled anathema against the Sixth Synod and all the Fathers who had sat in it. Nicephorus writes in his *History*:

“After this Philippicus administered the empire disgracefully and negligently, and condemned those Fathers who had assembled in the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, rejecting what they had decreed concerning the two wills and operations of Christ the Lord. In this he found as an accomplice John, patriarch of Constantinople, and Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, along with many other priests and senators.”

An encyclical decree was subsequently issued, by which all bishops were required, under threat of the gravest penalty, to profess and subscribe. Agatho the deacon briefly relates this:

“After he had persecuted many orthodox Fathers, sent some of them into exile, and especially those who refused, at his command, to subscribe to the composed and promulgated statement of faith, as though it were a volume intended to abolish this holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod.”

The synodical booklet of Pappus says the same:

“But Philippicus, who was also called Bardanes, having departed from Cherson, occupied it together with the imperial fleet, killed Justinian with swords at Damatrys, and, gathering a wicked synod at Constantinople, renewed the impiety of the Monothelites.”
