The subscriptions of John of Constantinople, of Germanus, who later succeeded him in the patriarchate, and of Andrew of Crete, the presidents of this conciliabulum, whose learning was renowned, had such force that they dragged many into subscribing to this formula, although they believed that those men had done so in order to avoid greater evils. Whether rightly or wrongly, we shall discuss more suitably in the dissertation on ecclesiastical economy.

## The Roman Synod Under Constantine

Anastasius writes that Philippicus sent an imperial letter to Constantine containing a written statement of evil doctrine; Paul merely says that he sent Pope Constantine letters containing evil doctrine. On this point both agree: the pontiff rejected them with the counsel of the Apostolic See.

We believe that a synod is indicated here, convoked by the pontiff, in which Philippicus’s heretical letter was examined. Whoever wishes to consult what we discussed in our first dissertation concerning encyclical letters will have no doubt that confirmation by the Apostolic See was always required whenever a new profession of faith, declaration, or similar matter concerning the public good of the Church was published, so that unity might shine forth in the establishment of doctrine or discipline throughout the entire ecclesiastical structure.

The volume of treachery, as Agatho calls it, had already been sent to the metropolitans of the East, so that they might command their suffragans to make both a profession and a subscription. The emperor judged that this needed to be promoted still more urgently among the Westerners, knowing that the decrees of this kind had to await their final and necessary strength from the head.

Since it had become customary for encyclicals of this kind to be proposed in a synod of the Westerners, or at least in a synod of the Apostolic See, which was assembled from the neighboring provinces as necessity required, a synod was gathered at Rome. As was proper, the bishops condemned the heretical volume, declared Philippicus’s wicked attempts, and proclaimed him everywhere a heretic.

The first decree was subsequently that images of all the councils, together with the Sixth Synod and its decrees of faith, should be placed in the atrium of Saint Peter, as may reasonably be inferred. For the principal decrees of councils were accustomed to be written on panels so that they might become known to the people. That this was done in the case of the Eighth Synod is shown by the *Breviary* preserved among its Acts, in which it is asserted that the synodical proceedings were placed at the Church of Saint Sophia. Likewise, the condemnation of Anastasius was placed on panels near Saint Peter for public use and display; Holstenius published a copy of it in his Roman collection.

Meanwhile the Roman people openly refused obedience to Philippicus, as though by a popular decree. “The people decreed,” in Paul the Deacon’s words, “that they would not accept the name or documents of the heretical emperor … Hence neither was his image introduced into the church, nor was his name pronounced at the solemn Mass.”

Indeed, to make the people’s zeal for orthodox faith still clearer, they steadfastly rejected the customary distribution which, when the image of a new emperor was carried ceremonially through the City, the officials were accustomed to distribute to the people, since the solidus displayed the image of the current emperor. Hence Paul specifically relates that the people rejected the image of the solidus.

Finally, in order to carry out the synodal decree, the Romans also fought with arms against Peter, who had been sent by the emperor to govern the Roman duchy and who was attempting by force and sacrilege to publish in Rome the impious formula, which Anastasius calls an order, and to compel everyone to make a profession and subscription, as our author reports.

Moreover, the hostile arms remained in use until the *scholasticus*, the chamberlain, patrician, and exarch of Italy, came to Rome and brought with him the sacred letter of Anastasius, the orthodox emperor, to the pontiff. In it Anastasius openly declared to all that he was a preacher of the Catholic faith and a confessor of the holy Sixth Council.

These are almost Paul the Deacon’s words in the same place:

“He”—Philippicus—“after ruling for one year and six months, was attacked by Anastasius, who was also called Artemius. Anastasius expelled him from the kingdom and deprived him of his eyes, but did not kill him. Anastasius sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, in which he declared himself a supporter and preacher of the Catholic faith and of the holy Sixth Council.”

These, then, are the Acts of this Roman synod under Constantine.

**No. 174, line 9 — Archbishop Felix.** Agnellus reports that Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, was released from exile, indeed enriched and heavily endowed with gifts, and sent back to his own see. He also lists the gifts bestowed upon him.

**No. 175, line 1 — The two Saxon kings.** Paul has the same account in chapter 37:

“In those times many noble and common people of the English nation—men and women, leaders and chief men—were accustomed to come to Rome, moved by divine love.”

**No. 176, line 17 — Anastasius the orthodox Augustus.** Concerning his election, we should hear Agatho the deacon, who was living at that time:

“For on the Sabbath of holy Pentecost, in the eleventh indiction, a sudden uprising against him occurred at twilight, contrary to expectation, by the army that had been assembled in Thrace because of the invasion of the neighboring nation of the Hungarians and Bulgarians, with great slaughter and destruction of the Christians who remained in Thrace, caused by his fault because he had not kept the agreements. The barbarous tyrant himself was captured, removed and expelled from the empire, and suddenly deprived of his eyes. Thereafter, during the time of his life, he walked in darkness, in the blindness of his foolish heart, as the language of the Psalms says.

“On the following day, on holy Pentecost itself, by the inspiration and grace of the most holy and life-giving Spirit, he was proclaimed emperor, pious and orthodox, under the name Philartemius. Afterward, with his name changed, he was called Anastasius. Previously he had belonged to the staff of the *a secretioribus*. By the judgment and votes of the sacred senate, the entire priestly register, and the lovers of Christ who were present there, together with the armies and the entire people of the city, he was first proclaimed in the most holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of God and crowned by the pontiff and patriarch John at the holy and venerable altar. At the same time, the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod was openly proclaimed and acknowledged by all the most holy pontiffs who were present there, together with the pious clergy. They took the greatest care for the peace and concord of the most holy Churches existing everywhere.”

### Chronological Notes

Although a less careful reckoning of times and the uncertain testimony of the Codices compel the most distinguished chronologists to conjecture, nevertheless, with the support of an ancient monument, matters that had seemed either dubiously asserted or rashly preferred to another opinion are sometimes established.

The same is true of the beginnings of the pontificate of Constantine. For since the two difficulties mentioned above have made the chronology of the preceding three pontiffs extremely laborious, and continue to do the same in determining the periods of this pontiff and of Gregory II, an ancient monument elsewhere demonstrates which opinion should be followed. It teaches that the dates for Anastasius’s deposition found in the commonly circulated Codex are to be preferred to those read in the manuscript Codices.

The monument survives in the frequently cited Veronese catalogue, contemporary with the period. It reads:

“In the first year of his pontificate”—that is, Constantine’s—“the 150th year of the recurring cycle of Victorius is completed, in the seventh indiction, in its first year, while Tiberius was reigning together with his father Justinian.”

Three facts become known from this precious monument, especially since the Victorian period had not yet fallen out of use among the Italians. I shall briefly pursue them because they touch upon my purpose.

The monument is distinguished by three chronological markers: the cycle, or Victorian period; the indiction; and the emperor.

The 150th year of the recurring Victorian period begins with the Kalends of January in the Dionysian year 709. For, as the learned Cardinal Noris demonstrates against Scaliger in *On the Paschal Cycle of Ravenna*, chapter 2, the beginning of this period must be taken from the year of the Passion of Jesus Christ, the leap year 28, whose Kalends of January fell on a Thursday and whose Easter fell on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, with lunar cycle 16. After the entire cycle had revolved, the year 559 was completed; in that year the Kalends of January fell on a Wednesday and Easter on the Ides of April, with lunar cycle 9.

Therefore, in the following year, 560, a new revolution began, and its 150th year began to run with the Dionysian year 709. According to the monument quoted above, the first year of Pope Constantine was then in progress.

The seventh indiction, which began in September of the year 708, unquestionably coincides with the 150th year of the Victorian period and with the Dionysian year 709.

As for the emperor, the monument does not number the years, but it attests to the otherwise neglected co-rule of Tiberius, his son, which Baronius records under the year 703 from the Greek annalists Theophanes and Cedrenus. Baronius also states there that, as soon as Justinian recovered the empire, he crowned Tiberius and his wife Theodora with the imperial crown. Paul the Deacon had transmitted this concerning Tiberius in the following words in *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 32:

“Justinian, in this second reign, ruled together with his son Tiberius for six years.”

From this the year of each emperor is easily recognized. Since it is clear from Anastasius that the pontiff returned from Constantinople to Rome in the year 711, on the twenty-fourth day of October, and that the slaughter of Justinian, whose empire Philippicus had usurped, was announced at Rome three months later, there is no doubt that Justinian was killed in December of that same year, 711. Consequently, he began to reign again with his son Tiberius in December of the year 705. Pagius also correctly observes this, against the opinion of the most learned cardinal, who adds two years to the empire.

Therefore, in the 150th year of the recurring Victorian period and the Dionysian year 709, the fourth year of both emperors was in progress. Let these observations be understood as contributing to a fuller understanding of the ancient monument.

Now, relying upon its testimony, I shall pursue those matters that concern the pontificate of Constantine.

Rightly, as is evident, I wondered that certain learned men thought Constantine’s reign should be reckoned from December of the year 707, for in that case his first year could by no means have been counted as 709. To establish the matter correctly, however, one must look to the interregnum after Sisinnius in the following year, 708. When this pope died suddenly and was buried at Saint Peter’s on 7 February 708, the apostolic see remained vacant for one month, as all the manuscripts and catalogues unanimously report; and for eighteen days, as the Lucchese catalogue and four Colbertine manuscripts read, or nineteen, as the first Colbertine, the Royal, Mazarin, Thuane, and two Ambrosian manuscripts—the first and third—have it. The authority of the remaining manuscripts, which add ten days, must be rejected, as the date of Constantine’s death teaches.

Accordingly, after an interregnum of one month and eighteen days, counting 7 February, the day of Sisinnius’s death, as excluded—or nineteen days, counting it as included—the date 25 March is reached; and since in that leap year it fell on a Sunday, it is clear that this date must be assigned to the pope’s ordination. For, after sitting seven years and fifteen days, according to the agreement of all the catalogues and manuscripts, with only a difference of a few days in some of them, he died on 9 April, the thirteenth indiction, which indicates the year 715. This is correctly reported by the common text of Anastasius and by the second Freherian, Cavensis, and Farnesian manuscripts; the Lucchese catalogue agrees with them, clearly distinguishing the date of death from that of burial, while it records Constantine’s death on 7 April. From the day of his ordination, 25 March 708, to the day of his death, or burial, 9 April 715, exactly the same number of years is counted.

A careful chronologer will observe that the manifest contradiction in the other manuscripts—which persist in the error they began and extend the pope’s death by many months—must be attributed to the stupidity of the copyists. I shall not take care to wrap the understanding of others once more in the same entanglements from which it has at last been freed. Concerning Constantine, enough has been said.

[Note: [Col. 0962A]

No. 170, line 1.—Constantine, son of John. A Syrian; under the emperors Justinian the Younger and Philippicus Bardanes Augustus, he sat for eight years, one month, and twenty days. He was created on 23 December and consecrated on 25 December, Christmas Day, at the beginning of the year 708; during his pontificate there was a great famine.

Line 7.—“He refused to make the securities.” It was then customary for bishops, before they were consecrated, to submit a statement of their faith and obedience and deposit it in the papal archive. They called this making the “securities” in the scrinium.

No. 174, line 17.—“Deprived of his sight.” After he had looked into a concave bronze vessel made red-hot; from it a fiery ray emerges, which very easily strikes and blinds the eyes.]

[Note: [Col. 0962A]

No. 170, line 7.—“He refused to make the customary securities in the scrinium.” Among medieval writers, a person was said to “make securities in the scrinium” when he placed in the archive a written statement of his faith and obedience. Thus the word *cautio*—the security which Felix refused to furnish according to the custom of the archbishops of Ravenna—does not here mean a financial guarantee concerning money to be sent to Rome, as some have incorrectly written. Rather, it signifies an affirmed and sincere faith expressed in certain prescribed formulas, by which the newly ordained archbishop of Ravenna swore that he wished to be subject to the Roman pontiff—not merely with that common reverence by which all bishops are subject to him, but also with the special subjection by which the metropolitan bishops of Ravenna were subject to the Roman pontiff as patriarch of the West.

Anastasius adds: “But because of the power of the judges, he set it forth as he preferred.” That is, Felix, supported by the authority of the judges of the exarchate—or even of those judges who exercised jurisdiction at Rome in the emperor’s name—set forth the matter according to his own judgment, in a manner more favorable to the liberty of the Church of Ravenna. I therefore think that, at his ordination, Felix refused to furnish Pope Constantine with the same securities which the bishops of Ravenna supplied after the schism had ended: securities that removed every pretext for autocephaly and resembled those found in the *Liber Diurnus*. Rather, he either added something to them or, more probably, wished to remove from them some element that expressed the patriarchal right of the Roman Church over the metropolitan see of Ravenna.

This security, however, after being deposited by the pope at the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, was found many days later blackened and seemingly scorched by fire, as Anastasius relates here. The matter entrusted by the pope to God and commended to the patronage of the prince of the apostles was thus declared by a divinely produced sign, as a certain indication of the divine will: namely, that God was displeased with Felix’s ungrateful profession, in which he did not express that the Church founded by Saint Apollinaris at Peter’s command was subject to the Roman Church in its capacity as the patriarchal Church of the West.

No. 171, line 2.—“That most holy man, obeying the imperial commands.” He did so after prayers had been offered and every form of security had been provided by letter. Justinian the Younger, now restored to a better disposition, summoned Pope Constantine to the imperial city, issuing orders that wherever the pope stopped he should be received by the magistrates exactly as though the emperor himself were present.

Sigonius gives an elegant account of the events related by Anastasius (*On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 711), and I do not hesitate to transfer his words here:

“Constantine,” he says, “departing from Hydruntum at the beginning of spring, was treated with every kind of generosity in all the Greek towns through which he passed. As he approached Constantinople, Tiberius, Justinian’s son, and Cyrus the patriarch, together with all the patricians and citizens, went out seven miles to meet him. They brought him into the city, seated upon richly decorated horses with his entourage and dressed, according to custom, in the papal cloak, after celebrating the day as a festival; and they lodged him in the house of Placidia, where accommodation had been prepared.

“When Justinian learned of the pope’s arrival, he sent him a second sacred letter from Bithynia, offering thanks and asking him not to regard it as burdensome to come to Nicomedia, since he himself would proceed there from Nicaea. Constantine therefore set out for Nicomedia and was received there also with great honor. Not long afterward Justinian arrived. The meeting of pope and emperor in those regions, unheard of in human memory, stirred all the neighboring peoples to come and see so rare a spectacle on earth.

“Thus, surrounded by a very great multitude of every kind, the emperor entered the city and approached the pope, who was waiting for him according to an arranged plan. Wearing his crown in the customary manner, he prostrated himself at the pope’s feet and kissed them. After they had exchanged solemn embraces, he addressed him with particular kindness and generosity, while all present expressed immense applause out of joy, and our people rejoiced no less because of the notable harmony between the rulers and their Churches.

“Then each withdrew to his own residence, and on the following days they passed the time in various discussions concerning the ordering of the Church and the empire. When the emperor said that he wished to send a fleet and army against Philippicus, the pope strongly dissuaded him from doing so. But all his speech was fruitless.

“Afterward both agreed that on Sunday the pope should celebrate the divine service. When the ceremony had been completed with the greatest splendor, the emperor, having first been cleansed of his former sins, received the Lord’s Body from him, confirmed all the ancient privileges of the Roman Church, and then sent him back to Rome.”

Thus far Sigonius. Yet, owing to the scarcity of the sources, it is not certainly known for what principal reason the emperor summoned the pope to Constantinople. From what Anastasius reports in the following Life of Saint Gregory II, however, it may be inferred that a controversy long agitated between Latins and Greeks was involved, concerning the canons added to the Fifth and Sixth Ecumenical Councils, and that the pope’s presence was intended to bring the matter to an end. Anastasius writes there:

“With the holy man Constantine the pope, he proceeded to the imperial city, and when questioned by the emperor Justinian about certain chapters, he resolved each question with an excellent answer.”

No. 175, line 4.—“He also disputed on behalf of the Church of Ticinum.” That the ordination of the bishop of Ticinum had from ancient times belonged to the metropolitan of Milan is shown so clearly by two surviving examples that Sigonius writes incorrectly (*On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 715) that Benedict, archbishop of Milan, had wished to transfer the consecration of the bishop of Ticinum to himself in order to establish a new right, but, opposed by all the examples of antiquity, had withdrawn defeated.

The first example is drawn from the action of Saint Crispinus, bishop of Ticinum. Feeling his strength broken by age and recognizing that the day of his departure was near, he brought Saint Epiphanius to the bishop of Milan and begged him, after Crispinus had departed from this life, to place Epiphanius over the priesthood of Ticinum. The request was fulfilled by the bishop of Milan immediately after Crispinus had gone to heaven, as Saint Ennodius—who himself was also bishop of Ticinum—testifies in the Life of Saint Epiphanius.

The second example is found in the Life of Saint Ambrose, written in the same age by the presbyter Paulinus, where we read: “After he had been ordained priest of the Church of Ticinum, he fell ill.”

But at the Roman synod under Constantine, Archbishop Benedict was defeated in the case because, as our author says, “from ancient times the bishop of that same Church of Ticinum belonged, and still belongs, to the apostolic see for consecration.” These ancient times cannot be carried back farther than the period when the kings of the Lombards established their seat at Ticinum.

For when the Lombards invaded Italy, Honoratus, bishop of Milan, terrified by the ferocity of the new people, withdrew to Genoa with most of the clergy and the leading men. After him, several Milanese archbishops are said to have been elected there, until Saint John Bonus, undeterred by the savage domination of the Lombards, returned to his own see and brought the Ligurian exile almost to an end after the lapse of a century.

When Benedict brought suit at the Roman council to recover the ancient right of consecration of the bishop of Ticinum, a century and a half had passed since Honoratus’s departure. For this reason our author maintains that from ancient times it had belonged to the Roman pontiff to consecrate the bishops appointed over Ticinum, the royal city; hence Benedict withdrew defeated by the judgment of the Roman synod.

Paul the Deacon also writes that this was the outcome of the controversy (*History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 29). He further adds that the venerable Archbishop Benedict was a man of outstanding holiness, whose reputation for goodness spread throughout Italy.

The holiness of this archbishop was so great that his name was entered in the catalogues of the saints, and the Ambrosian Church annually celebrates his memory with solemn rites on 11 March. Indeed, in the register of the archbishops of the Milanese Church, published by decree of the provincial council and preserved in the fourth part of the *Acts under Saint Charles*, Saint Benedict is said to have belonged to the Crispi family.

This statement is not accepted by the very learned Papebrochius (*May*, volume VII, in the *Exegesis on the Bishops of Milan*), because at the time when Saint Benedict lived—that is, in the eighth century—the use of hereditary surnames was not known; it became common only after the eleventh century. On this basis he believes, following Puricellus, that Peter Galesinius was the first to add the surnames of noble families to the ancient names of bishops.

Yet long before Galesinius, who lived in the sixteenth century, some manuscript episcopal catalogues contain archbishops who flourished before the eleventh century written with family surnames. This is especially true of the manuscript catalogue of Philip of Castro Seprio, which he brought down to his own time, namely the year 1331. When I was in Milan, I myself read its copy in the library of the distinguished monastery of Saint Ambrose.

Galesinius, therefore, was not the first to append individual episcopal surnames to catalogues. I do not, however, wish this to be understood as though I thought surnames—especially among the prelates of the Churches—were in use before the eleventh century. I mean only that the origins of the ancient bishops could have been preserved so firmly in the noble families of Milan—for Puricellus likewise testifies to this in the Life of Saint Lawrence of Litta—through the continuous tradition of ancestors, that, supported as it were by the safeguard of domestic history, each family might reasonably have assigned to itself a descendant bearing the family name once surnames had been added.

The Crispi family could accomplish this more easily than the others, since Saint Benedict had adorned the see of Milan for many years—indeed, for forty-seven years—with such holiness of life that his reputation, as Paul, whom I have just cited, testifies, spread throughout all Italy.

No. 176, line 16.—“They announced that Philippicus the heretic had been driven from the imperial throne.” Through the rebellion raised against Justinian, Bardanes, called Philippicus, gained the empire with the aid of the inhabitants of Cherson. After expelling Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, and replacing him with John, a deacon and chartulary of the administration, he carried out what he had sworn to the pseudo-monk impostor who had foretold the empire to him: namely, the abolition of the Sixth Ecumenical Council.

It was not difficult to drive Bardanes into this crime. From childhood he had listened to the abbot Stephen, a Monothelite and disciple of Macarius, teaching, and through this corrupt instruction he had absorbed the heresy deeply into his mind. Having therefore convened a conciliabulum, he sacrilegiously pronounced anathema against the Sixth Synod. He also ordered its image, which had been painted in the vestibule of the palace between the Fifth and Sixth Schools, to be erased before he entered the city, as is read in the *Peroration of Agatho the Deacon*, in Combefis’s *History of Monothelitism*.

Bardanes consequently expected to possess the empire for the long period that the demoniac had foretold to him. But shamefully deceived by the impostor, he was blinded a little more than a year later by Rufus, prefect of the Opsikion, and was then driven into exile by Artemius, who was called Anastasius after he had been consecrated emperor.]

[Note: [Col. 0965D]

No. 170, line 5.—“Here he ordained Felix.” At the very beginning of Pope Constantine’s pontificate, after Damian, bishop of Ravenna, had died, Felix was appointed in his place. Although reluctant, Felix went to Rome, as was customary, in order to receive consecration from the pope; he made a profession of faith and promised obedience. But when he returned to Ravenna, he violated that promise at the instigation of the citizens and again separated himself from the apostolic see by schism.

For this reason the emperor Justinian, angered against him, sent the patrician Theodore with an army to Ravenna. After capturing the city, Theodore stripped the rebels of their property and sent them in chains to Constantinople, where they were punished with death. Archbishop Felix himself was deprived of his sight and deported into exile in Pontus.

This is Anastasius’s account. In his Life of Pope Constantine, however, he adds that after Justinian was killed, Felix was released from exile and, although blind, restored to his Church after rendering the customary obedience to the Roman pontiff. Jerome Rubeus, in his *History of Ravenna*, even testifies that Felix shone with outstanding holiness and that he was distinguished by miracles.

From that time the prelates of that city displayed complete obedience to the Roman pontiffs, down to the beginning of the eleventh century, as we shall see under Paschal II.

No. 171, line 1.—“At the same time he sent, etc.” What Pope Constantine did at Constantinople is hidden by the scarcity and silence of the sources. Baronius nevertheless concludes that the controversy concerning the canons of the Council in Trullo was then being debated there, because, although no other question was at that time being disputed between the Eastern and Western Churches, Anastasius nevertheless writes in the Life of Gregory II:

“Gregory, then a deacon of the Roman Church, went with the holy man Constantine the pope to the imperial city, and when questioned by the emperor Justinian concerning certain chapters, he resolved each question with an excellent answer.”

It is regrettable that this answer is either concealed from us or has perished.

Christian Lupus, in his scholia and notes on the Trullan canons, p. 1078, infers from the words of Anastasius quoted above that Constantine was the first of the Roman pontiffs to approve the canons of the Trullan Synod, since they did not conflict with the decrees of the Roman Church. He also concludes that Constantine obtained from Justinian what Justinian had requested from John VII, and that for this reason Justinian confirmed all the privileges of the Roman Church by new edicts.

For earlier, as I said in the second section, he had restored the Roman Church against the resurgent autocephaly and rebellion of the archbishops of Ravenna. This apostolic confirmation of the Trullan canons provided Pope Adrian I of Rome and Saint Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, with a distinguished basis for bearing witness to those canons.

Adrian I, says Lupus, approved only those canons of the Trullan Synod that had been promulgated lawfully and orthodoxly. He adds that those are gravely mistaken who think that the confirmation of these canons made by the Seventh Synod in its first canon is authentic, since the Roman Church never confirmed all the canons of the Seventh Synod.

Hence the confirmation of the Trullan canons by Pope Constantine remained unknown not only to the Roman Church but also to the other patriarchal Churches, with the exception of Constantinople; consequently, it had to be renewed by John VIII, as we shall see in his Life.

No. 175, line 1.—“In his time there were two kings, etc.” The second year of Pope Constantine’s pontificate was made especially illustrious by the abdication of Coenred, king of the Mercians, and Offa, king of the East Saxons. In the year 709 they abandoned their kingdoms for Christ and went to Rome, where they assumed the monastic habit. When they came to the threshold of the apostles, Pope Constantine received them with the greatest kindness, rejoicing that, after renouncing earthly kingdoms, they wished to serve Peter the fisherman.

This is established from Bede, both in the *Epitome* and in the *History*, book V, chapter 20:

“In the year 709,” he writes in the *Epitome*, “Coenred, king of the Mercians, after reigning for five years, went to Rome.”

In the *History* he writes:

“In the year of Osred’s reign—which ended in 709—Coinred, who had ruled for some time with great distinction in the kingdom of the Mercians, abandoned the scepters of the kingdom with still greater distinction. For he came to Rome, where, with Constantine holding the pontificate, he was tonsured and became a monk; and at the threshold of the apostles he remained in prayers, fasts, and almsgiving until his final day. Ceolred, son of Æthelred, succeeded him in the kingdom; Ceolred had held that same kingdom before Coinred.

“With him there also came the son of Sigehere, king of the East Saxons, named Offa, a young man of most beloved age and beauty, and one greatly desired by his entire people to take up and preserve the scepters of the kingdom. Led by an equal devotion of mind, he abandoned his wife, lands, relatives, and homeland for Christ and for the Gospel, so that in this life he might receive a hundredfold and in the age to come eternal life.

“Accordingly, when they reached Rome and the holy places, he too was tonsured and, completing his life in the monastic habit, attained the long-desired vision of the blessed apostles in heaven.”

No. 176, line 17.—“Anastasius, orthodox Augustus.” In the year 713, the impious Bardanes, or Philippicus, after holding the empire for one year and six months, was driven from and deposed from the empire on 3 June, as Paul the Deacon (*History of the Lombards*, book VI, chapter 33) and Bede (*On the Six Ages*) relate. Philarthemius, who changed his name and was called Anastasius, a pious and orthodox man, was appointed and crowned in his place on the following day, the feast of Pentecost.

Through the patrician Scholasticus, chamberlain, whom he sent to Italy as exarch, he sent a profession of his faith to Pope Constantine, as Anastasius relates in the Life of Constantine. When Pope Constantine therefore heard that a Catholic emperor was reigning in the East and had received from him, through the exarch, a profession of orthodox faith, he wished Anastasius to be received into Catholic communion and entered in the register of orthodox emperors, so that the whole Church might pray for him.

He also sent to him, as was customary, the presbyter Michael, an *apocrisiarius*, or ecclesiastical legate, to receive his answers on ecclesiastical matters, as Theophanes reports. Such a legation seemed absolutely necessary, so that at Constantinople there might be someone who, by the authority of the apostolic see, could reconcile to the Catholic Church the bishops who had fallen during Philippicus’s persecution and were now penitent.

Since many had assented to the condemnation of the Sixth Synod only because they had been shaken by fear, their repentance was very easy. Pope Constantine, through his *apocrisiarius*, extended a hand to these shipwrecked men and hastened to assist them as quickly as possible. John, bishop of Constantinople, had requested this of Constantine, as head of the Christian priesthood, in the letter cited below.]

[Note: [Col. 0966D]

No. 170, line 5.—“Here he ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna.” The archbishops of Ravenna had long been contriving to withdraw themselves from the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs, at least in matters concerning their ordination and the rights of the Roman Church as patriarchal Church of the West.

In this respect they undoubtedly imitated the archbishops of Constantinople, who had eventually emerged as patriarchs because their city had become the imperial residence. Following their example, the Ravennate archbishops became persuaded that they too might obtain something similar because the exarch resided in their city.

For this reason Archbishop Felix, who had been deeply displeased at being ordained by Pope Constantine, carried his attempt at independence farther than any of his predecessors. No sooner had he been ordained at Rome and returned to Ravenna than he threw off the yoke of the Holy See and drew the leading citizens into his schism.

But alas for his unhappy boldness! The emperor, greatly offended by it, decided to punish him rather than support him. He therefore sent an army to Ravenna. Although the city had prepared in vain to resist, the archbishop and his partisans were captured; the emperor ordered the latter to be killed and condemned Felix, after depriving him of his sight, to exile.

No. 174, line 4.—“And its sacred letter with the exposition of the corrupt doctrine.” Scarcely three months after Constantine had returned to Rome, from which he had been absent for a year, he learned that an Armenian named Bardanes had been proclaimed emperor and called Philippicus, and that by his order the emperors Justinian and Tiberius had been killed.

This usurper, “because from early childhood,” as Agatho the deacon says (*Collection of the Councils*, p. 1405), “he had been a disciple of the abbot Stephen, the disciple of Macarius, immediately using the authority and imperial power, ordered the image of that holy synod—the Sixth General Council—which had been placed many years earlier in the vestibule of the imperial palace, to be thrown down.”

Afterward he sent a sacred letter to Constantine; Anastasius discusses it fully in numbers 174 and 176, and the illustrious Archbishop Sommier cites it in *History of Dogma and the Pontiffs*, book VIII, chapter 21.

To strengthen his crime still further against the Sixth Council, “he arranged,” says Theophanes in his *Chronicle*, “for an insane conciliabulum to be held against the holy Ecumenical Council. John, patriarch of Constantinople, Andrew, metropolitan of Crete, and Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, openly subscribed to it and, together with all their colleagues, condemned by anathema the aforesaid holy Ecumenical Synod that had been held against the Monothelites.”

But the tyrant did not long enjoy the fruits of his impiety and defection. His dissolute life and negligence in administering the empire brought him hatred and contempt from the leaders of the praetorian guard. They therefore expelled him from the palace and stirred up a general revolt against him.

Then, with the agreement of all the orders, they elected Philarthemius, who wished to be called Anastasius, a man of high reputation and, above all, a Catholic. Philippicus, deprived of his sight and driven into exile, was removed.]

No. 175, line 1.—“In his time there were two Saxon kings.” While Audax, archbishop of Ravenna, was seeking a condemnable freedom from the jurisdiction of the Holy See, two lay princes came to Rome in order to strip themselves of the legitimate freedom they enjoyed and offer it to Christ Jesus in the presence of his vicar, the supreme pontiff.

They were Coenred, king of the Mercians, and Offa, prince of the East Saxons. Following the command of the Gospel, they abandoned the crowns and kingdoms of this world, aspiring only to the heavenly kingdom. Accordingly, when they arrived at Rome, they served at the tombs of the apostles, and there they ended their days holily under Pope Constantine, who gave glory to God both for the conversion of such great princes and for the honor that the Holy See received from it.

“Pope Constantine,” says Bede, “rejoiced that, having renounced earthly kingdoms, they were serving Peter the fisherman.” (*Epistle* and *History*, book V, chapter 20.)

No. 176, line 20.—“The exarch, coming to Rome, brought with him the sacred letter of the emperor Anastasius.” As soon as Anastasius ascended the imperial throne, he sent a letter to Constantine in which he openly professed the Catholic faith and indicated that he adhered to the Sixth Synod.

He further decided that, since the patriarch of Constantinople was sending his synodical letter to the Roman pontiff, he should attach to it an account of what had been done against religion during the period of the tyranny.

“When he had thus decided and agreed,” writes Agatho the deacon in his epilogue, “letters of defense were composed by John, the most holy pontiff of this city, to Constantine, the most holy and blessed pope of Old Rome. These were sent, according to custom, together with the synodical letters, and they duly informed him of everything that had previously been written.”

The notable beginning of the patriarch John’s letter is especially significant, for it offers an analogy through which the pope’s role in the Church is clearly recognized:

“He himself, the Maker of our nature, having arranged by his workmanship that the head should be placed over the whole body, and having situated in it the principal instruments of the senses, caused every movement and perfection of the remaining members to arise from it and to be preserved. If any one of them should be injured or afflicted by some difficulty, he ordained that he should not merely take modest care of them, but that, even when a natural affection and sympathy toward the extremities was offended, he should attend through the ministry of the hands, under the direction of the eyes, to what was suffering.

“We may compare your apostolic pontificate to this, O most holy head of the Christian priesthood. Recognizing you canonically as the head, we rightly seek through you relief from the illness that has befallen our ecclesiastical body, from a pestilential and destructive tyrannical power affecting our souls.

“For you also, as is proper to the head, will not despise us who suffer unwillingly, nor send us away from the relationship that is innate and firmly joined to us . . . especially since the disease did not arise from any fault of the body, but was produced from outside by a violent and unexpected calamity.” (John of Constantinople, *Letter to Pope Constantine*.)

He then explains the destructive plans of the tyrant and his adherents, which had proceeded as far as abolishing the Council of Chalcedon, while they had condemned the Sixth Ecumenical Council that confirmed and upheld it. He leaves no stone unturned in excusing those who, adapting themselves to the necessities of the time, appeared in some measure to have complied with him, since, had they acted otherwise, the man who possessed the power of arms would have brought affairs to an even more deplorable end.

He relies on the examples of several holy Fathers and calls God himself as witness both to his own intention and to that of his colleagues:

“Moreover,” he says, “the religious *apocrisiarius* of your most holy see, who resides here, to whom in this time of extreme necessity we have given satisfaction by oath, has received satisfaction from us by an oath in this time of extreme necessity, as we disclosed to him the pure affection that we possess for the orthodox faith.” (Ibid.)

He continues, excusing himself and his people:

“We judged that we ought for a short time to yield to the impulses of the man, so that in matters of greatest importance the confession of the faith might be preserved inviolate, if not in words, at least in intention. We say this not as people wishing to overturn the expressions already defined synodically and confessed by the whole Church of God for so long a time—namely, that in the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, according to the pious understanding known from the holy Fathers, there are two natural wills and two natural operations.

“To say that Christ, in the other nature, is endowed with the power of willing and operating is nothing other than to understand two natural wills and two natural operations.” (Ibid.)

He proceeds by emphasizing the happiness of the Church, which had obtained a Catholic emperor burning with zeal for the good cause. Then, turning to the holy pontiff, he says:

“You, therefore, O sacred head, extending to us the hand of a gracious summons, by the customary ecclesiastical exchange of mutual letters—namely, counter-synodical apostolic letters—apply the remedy of charity . . . For since you are the disciple and successor of the one who heard from the Lord, ‘I have prayed for you,’ and so forth, you ought diligently to introduce what supports and strengthens correction, and still more readily to grant what belongs to a gentle and merciful spirit.” (Ibid.)

He supports such prayers by the example of Aaron, who was reproved by his brother:

“For Aaron,” he says, “when he yielded to the impulse of the ancient people and had assisted them in making an idol, was indeed reproved by his brother. But when he asserted in his defense that he had done this because he had been compelled by force, he received no rebuke from God and was not deprived of the dignity of the priesthood.” (Ibid.)

The pope conceived such joy at the election of the excellent emperor that he immediately sent to him the presbyter Michael, an *apocrisiarius*, or resident at the imperial court, with authority to reconcile to the Church all the bishops and other ecclesiastics who were penitent and whom the fear of the tyrant Bardanes had compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of the Sixth Council. Baronius teaches this from Theophanes, under the year 713:

“Pope Constantine wished to have Anastasius, received into Catholic communion, entered in the register of orthodox emperors, so that the whole Church might pray for him. He also sent to him, as was customary, the presbyter Michael, cardinal *apocrisiarius*, to receive his ecclesiastical replies.”]

[Note: [Col. 0969B]

No. 171, line 7.—“Cosmas the treasurer, Sisinnius the nomenclator.” The treasurer (*sacellarius*) and the nomenclator are counted among the offices of the Roman Church.

The treasurer is the custodian of the church treasury. Anastasius, in the Life of Constantine: “He was made subdeacon and treasurer.” Likewise, in the Life of Gregory II: “Under the blessed memory of Lord Pope Sergius he was made subdeacon and treasurer.” Likewise, in the Life of Stephen IV: “Together with Sergius, who was then treasurer.” Likewise, in the Life of Leo III: “Likewise Campulus the treasurer.” Likewise, in the Life of Adrian II: “There he was greeted by Paul, keeper of the books, Joseph, keeper of the vessels, and Basil the treasurer, all dressed in ecclesiastical vestments.”

The treasurer is distinguished from the *arcarius* in Anastasius’s account of Paul the deacon and *vicedominus*, and Peter the *arcarius*. The nomenclator is an attendant who informs the pontiff of the names of those approaching the Roman pontiff. I have discussed both offices in the Life of Agatho, under Anastasius.

The treasurer of the fisc is an administrator, or prefect, of the treasury. Baldric, in his letter to the emperor Henry III: “Just as your generosity has a treasurer who, when matters arise, provides for daily expenses, so I too am their treasurer,” and so forth.

John the Deacon, book II, chapter 23: “The same Gregory, according to his custom, ordered the treasurer to invite twelve pilgrims to dinner.” A little later: “After summoning the treasurer, he asked why he had presumed to invite a thirteenth person contrary to his command.”

No. 172, line 3.—“The presbyter Sergius the abbot, and Sergius the ordainer.” He calls him “the presbyter abbot” because at the beginning each monastery had a single presbyter, its own abbot, from whom the monks received the sacraments and heard Mass.

Augustine, in Letter 81, wrote to the abbot and fellow presbyter of the monks of the island of Capraria. He likewise says in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapter 33: “I myself have seen the hospices of the saints at Milan, accommodating not a few people, over which one presbyter presided, an excellent and most learned man.”

John, bishop of Jerusalem, in Letter 60, writes that he ordained Paulinianus presbyter of the Bethlehemite monastery because blessed Jerome, the superior of that monastery, in his humility could not endure to administer the sacraments to the brothers. Anastasius likewise, below, in the Life of Stephen III, speaks of “Fulrad, abbot and presbyter.”

The ordainer (*ordinator*) is the master of the order of the Mass, or the instructor of those being ordained. Instruction of the candidates precedes ordination; and after ordination the ordainers give them an official booklet containing the *ordo*, that is, the arrangement of the ecclesiastical office. Council of Toledo IV, canon 25; the canon *Quando*, Distinction 38.]

### Line 10

There he received the imperial seal through Theophanius, the *regionarius*. Here “imperial seal” means an imperial decree secured by a seal; elsewhere *sigillum iconiae*, or “seal of the image of blessed Mary,” means the inscription attached to the image. Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel, in the supplement to Sigebert, under the year 1183:

> “In the preceding year Our Lady, the mother of mercy, holy Mary, appeared to a certain woodworker while he was working in a particular forest, and [Col. 0970A] offered him the sign of her own image and that of her Son, our Savior, whose inscription was: ‘The Lamb of God,’” etc.

### Line 14

The patrician Theophilus, *extraticus* of the *caravisiani*, came to meet him and received him with the greatest honor. For *extraticus*, read *strategus of the scaravisiani*, that is, commander of a cavalry squadron. The word derives from the barbarous Latin *scara*, which means the same as a cavalry squadron. Aimoin, book IV, chapter 26:

> “In the tenth year, Dagobert assembled a picked troop of warriors from Francia, which we may call a *turma* or wedge.”

Hincmar of Reims, to the bishops of his diocese, chapter 3:

> “The lines of warriors whom in the vernacular we call *scarae*.”

*Scala* is incorrectly read for *scara* in William the Breton, *Philippid*, book X:

> “They cling laterally to the king in the king’s *scala*.”

Hence *scaritae*: soldiers selected into a *scara*. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 37:

> “There Theodoric came with the *scaritti* and ten thousand men.”

It is a plausible conjecture that the *scaravisiani*, or *scaritae*, the soldiers mentioned here, were Frankish soldiers who served in *scarae* for Greek pay. We know from Cedrenus, in his account of Constantine Monomachus, that Franks served the Greeks in the East; indeed, the Byzantine emperors used Franks and Germans as their bodyguards, and these men carried battle-axes. See Nicetas in his account of Alexius Comnenus.

### Line 19

The pontiff and his principal attendants entered together with imperial saddlery, saddles and bridles gilded, and also with *mappulae*. Here *sellare* is distinguished from *sella*. *Sellare* appears to mean a *housse* (saddle-covering) laid over the saddle for adornment. Anastasius, in his Life of Stephen III:

> “He also hurried beside him as far as a certain point in the place of the *vicestrator*, next to his saddle-covering.”

Anastasius likewise calls this covering a *pallium* in his Life of Conon:

> “He also granted him permission to use a cloak when riding.”

The pontiff and the cardinals used gilded bridles and saddles. Bernard of Clairvaux, letter 42, to William of Sens, makes the same observation about the bishops of his age:

> “The naked cry out; the famished cry out; they complain and say:
>
> ‘Tell us, pontiffs: what is gold doing on the bridle?’”

The Council of the Lateran under Innocent III, chapter *Clerici*, *On the Life and Honesty of Clerics*, forbids clerics to use gilded bridles, saddles, breast-straps, and spurs.

The pontiff and the cardinals, riding in solemn procession, used *mappulae*. These are small white linen cloths, concerning which Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 19, writes:

> “One day he sent someone, as usual; but the monk who had been sent, after receiving an admonition from the holy women, accepted some *mappulae* when they asked him to do so, and hid them in his bosom.”

And below:

> “He said to him: ‘Was I not present there when you received the *mappulae* from the servants of God?’ He immediately fell at his feet, repented of having acted foolishly, and threw away the *mappulae* that he had hidden in his bosom.”

The use of *mappulae* was common to the bishops and deacons of the Roman Church. Gregory, book II, letter 54. From this comes canon *Illud*, distinction 93.

### Line 21

The Apostolic Pontiff, having left the palace with a *camelaucum*, as he was accustomed to proceed in Rome, hastened as far as the Placidia residence, where he was staying. A *camelaucum*, or *camelaugum*, is the cap worn by the pontiff. The word derives from the Greek καῦμα, “heat,” because it serves to ward off heat. Suidas:

> Καμηλαῦκιον παρὰ τὸ καῦμα ἐλαύνειν  
> “A *camelaucum*, because it drives away heat.”

The *Etymologicum Magnum*:

> Καύσια ὥριτας μὲν καμελαῦκιον παρὰ τὸ ἐλαυνεῖν τὸ καύμα  
> “The *causia* [with *ὥριτας μὲν*, of uncertain sense in the supplied text] is called a *camelaucum* because it drives away heat.”

Achmes, *Oneirocritica*, chapter 219:

> Τὸ καμηλαύκιον ἐπὶ βασιλεὺς εἰς τὴν Αὐγούσταν, καὶ εἰς τέκνον κρινέται  
> “The king’s *camelaucum* is interpreted with reference to the Augusta and to his children.”

The *camelaucum* was a head-covering common to kings and private persons, though differing in color. Usage subsequently established that among Romans *camelaucum* properly meant the pontiff’s cap. Papias: “The *camelaucus* is the pope’s garment.”

[Col. 0971A]

### Number 174, line 6

For this reason, inflamed with zeal for the faith, the entire assembly of the city of Rome erected in the church of blessed Peter an image containing the six holy and universal synods, which the Greeks call *votarea*, or—as others read it—*pancarea*.

This was the image of the six universal councils, which the Roman people erected in the church of blessed Peter. The heretical emperor Philippicus had removed it; Theodosius restored it at Constantinople. Anastasius, in his Life of Gregory II:

> “As soon as Theodosius entered the imperial city, he immediately raised again in its former place that venerable image on which the six holy synods had been depicted and which Philippicus had removed without even mentioning it.”

### Number 175, line 1

In his time two kings of the Saxons, coming with many others to pray at the shrines of the Apostles, ended their lives speedily, as they desired. This passage must be understood of the Anglo-Saxons, in the year of Christ 689. In those times pilgrimage by the English to the thresholds of the Apostles was frequent, as Bede reports, book V, chapter 7:

> “At this time many from the English nation, both nobles and commoners, laymen and clerics, men and women, were accustomed to do this eagerly.”

The same writer had earlier stated, in book IV, chapter 23:

> “He also took care to go to Rome, because at that time this was regarded as a sign of great virtue.”

Likewise Anastasius, in his Life of Benedict III:

> “In his time a king of the Saxons, whose name was …, came for the sake of prayer; leaving all his possessions, he abandoned his own kingdom and hastened to Rome, to the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul, with a multitude of people,” etc.

[Col. 0971B]

### Number 176, line 10

“And more than twenty-five on both sides were wounded and died.” *Plagare* means “to inflict a wound.” Augustine, *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 11: “He challenged or wounded the Lord.”

### Line 11

“Until the pontiff sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord, and thus the opposing factions were pacified.”

Litanies, or processions, were conducted with the Gospels and crosses carried before them. It was customary to go out to meet a bishop with the Gospel. Ekkehard the Younger, *On the Calamities of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 1:

> “He immediately prepares the basilica and altar, prepares carpets and a walkway covered with a cloak, and orders the bishop to be received with the Gospel, together with some priests who were present.”

And below:

> “Not long afterward it also happened that Peter of Verona, returning from the palace, unexpectedly came to a similar place of hospitality. The brothers received him and offered him the Gospel, which was the best thing they possessed.”

The same work, chapter 9:

> “Everyone agrees that, in order to receive a bishop with the Gospel, all should meet him together, even if he has not been enrolled as a brother. The bishop is received; Victor offered him the Gospel. When the bishop had kissed it, Victor withdrew.”

The custom of carrying crosses at litanies is extremely ancient. The Novel of Justinian 123, chapter 32, forbids litanies to be conducted without crosses. At litanies it was customary for the golden cross offered by Charlemagne to be carried before the pontiff; Anastasius discusses this in his Life of Leo IV.

The clergy also solemnly went out to meet princes and rulers with crosses. Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 9:

> “Ebraccharius came as far as the city of Venice. The royal bishop had sent his own clerics to meet him, with crosses and psalmody; they escorted them as far as the city.”

The emperor Lothair was met with crosses and standards, that is, banners. Anastasius, in his Life of Sergius II:

> “His Holiness sent venerable crosses and likewise standards to meet him; as is customary when receiving an emperor or king, he caused him to be received with the greatest honor.”

[Note: [Col. 0971D]]

### Number 176, line 4

“It happened that a certain Peter sent a decree to Ravenna concerning the duchy of the city of Rome … And it happened that Christopher, who was duke …”

Christopher is the first person who appears in Anastasius explicitly designated by the title “duke of the city of Rome.” I would gladly investigate what this new title of duke signified; what dignity and jurisdiction it carried; what functions it involved; what succession of dukes existed; what the boundaries of the Roman duchy were; and what cities belonged to it—if there were anywhere a glimmer of hope of extracting and establishing anything certain by which the *Liber Pontificalis* might duly be illuminated. But everything is shrouded in darkness, slippery, and uncertain, so that one cannot safely rely on it. Contemporary authorities are silent on the matter, and later writers lack the support of ancient records. I shall attempt to illuminate Anastasius from Anastasius himself.

All Italy obeyed the emperors before barbarian peoples invaded it and devastated everything with sword and fire. The last people to occupy most of Italy were the Lombards. After gaining possession of the principal Italian provinces, they left the Greek emperors nothing except the region extending from the Po to the Adriatic Sea, between the Apennines, the Pentapolis, and the sea. This region was called the Exarchate of Ravenna, after the model of the Exarchate of Africa. Longinus was appointed to it by the emperor Justin II as Narses’ successor in the year 567. They also left the emperors that part of Italy washed by the Tyrrhenian Sea as far as Sicily, except for the duchy of Benevento, which the Lombards likewise held.

The exarch resided at Ravenna. From there he sent to the other lands subject to the emperor in the East both the sacred commands of the prince and his own administrators, who were designated by various names: masters of the soldiers, treasurers, record-keepers, and others.

Concerning a duke and duchy of Rome, there is profound silence in the *Liber Pontificalis* throughout this period, down to approximately the year 711. When Roman magistrates are mentioned, they are designated either as judges or as the Roman army, as in the Life of Theodore, no. 125; or as the clergy, people, and army of the Roman city, as in the Life of Benedict, no. 153:

> “Here,” Anastasius says, “he received the imperial commands of the most merciful Constantine the Great addressed to the venerable clergy and people, and to the most fortunate army of the city of Rome.”

They are also called the judges and leaders of the army, as in the Life of Conon, no. 156; or the leaders of the judges and of the Roman military force, as in the Life of Sergius, no. 158.

Thus, during the pontificate of Constantine, Christopher is the first duke mentioned, on the following occasion. The heretical emperor Philippicus, a hater of sacred images, had sent a certain Peter to obtain the Roman duchy. The Roman people, who, as Anastasius says, “had determined in no way to accept the name of the heretical emperor, or his documents, or the image of his coin; consequently neither was his likeness brought into the church, nor was his name pronounced at the solemn celebration of Mass,” were inflamed with zeal for the faith. They refused to receive that Peter and presented themselves armed to Duke Christopher, so that under his leadership they might fight against Peter and prevent him from entering the city and exercising the magistracy.

The fighting took place on the Sacred Way. When many men on both sides had fallen wounded, the pontiff sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord to pacify the factions. The party of Peter was already being so hard pressed [Col. 0972D] that there was no hope of survival for it, when, at the pontiff’s command, the opposing party, which was called Christian, withdrew.

From this I learn that military affairs and the entire administration of military matters belonged to the duke. I infer that he also administered civic affairs from the fact that, when Pope Zacharias left Rome, he entrusted the city to Duke Stephen for its government (Anastasius, Life of Zacharias, no. 213). I likewise believe that, while the see was vacant, the duke exercised great care to prevent disturbances from arising in the city and protected the election of the new pontiff by the authority of his rank and by the support of arms. For in the Life of Hadrian, no. 292, I read that Hadrian, on the very day on which he was elected, caused the judges of this Roman city, both clergy and military, to be recalled from exile. They had been sent into exile at the passage of Lord Pope Stephen by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta. After Stephen’s death, Afiarta had been placed in charge of governing the city during the interregnum and had sent the leading citizens into exile.

Thus Christopher was the first duke of the city of Rome, when the Roman people refused any longer to obey the heretical emperor, as I have reported above from Anastasius. Following his example, the other peoples, according to the same Anastasius, no. 184, each elected dukes for themselves everywhere in Italy.

I present the succession of the Roman dukes from Anastasius:

- Christopher, duke, from the year 711 (Anastasius, Life of Constantine, no. 176, near the end).
- Peter, duke, from the year 713 (Anastasius, Life of Constantine, no. 176, near the end).
- Basil, duke, from the year 717 (Anastasius, Life of Gregory II, no. 183, near the end).
- Marinus, the *spatharius*, duke, from the year 718 (Anastasius, Life of Gregory II, no. 183, around the middle).
- Peter, duke, from the year 720 (Anastasius, Life of Gregory II, no. 184, around the middle).
- Stephen, duke, from the year 740 (Anastasius, Life of Zacharias, no. 207).

Besides those already named, a certain Gratiosus is also mentioned, at that time a *chartularius* and later a duke, in the Life of Stephen IV, nos. 269 and 288; and John, duke and brother of Lord Pope Stephen, in the Life of Hadrian, no. 297. But I am persuaded that either they were not dukes with the ordinary authority of dukes, like those mentioned above, or that one of them was elected amid a disturbance raised by factious citizens, while the other, supported by his relationship to the pontiff, usurped the title of duke. This is because, beginning with Stephen III, the power of the dukes ceased with the establishment of the Roman patriciate; an opportunity to discuss its dignity and office will arise below.

I have no doubt, therefore, that the dukes were abolished when Pippin was first anointed king of the Franks and was elected patrician of Rome by Stephen III, on account of his outstanding services to the Roman Church, especially because of the donation made to it of the Exarchate of Ravenna. Anastasius, no. 253, affirms that authentic documents of this donation existed in the Roman archive in his own time.

In a letter sent by Stephen III to Pippin before Pippin again descended into Italy to wrest the Exarchate of Ravenna from Aistulf, king of the Lombards—who had seized it—and to hand it over to the pontiff, Stephen recalls the donation of the Exarchate made to blessed Peter by Pippin. He both justly demands that it be fulfilled and earnestly begs for its fulfillment. He says in letter 3:

> “Let it grieve you on behalf of the holy Church of God and of blessed Peter, and let it be your duty to hand over to him for possession what you promised to offer to blessed Peter by your donation. Remember, and always hold firmly in your hearts, what you promised to that same doorkeeper of heaven. … See to it that you hasten to hand over everything that you promised him and pledged by your donation. … Know that, just as the prince of the Apostles firmly holds your donation in a written deed, so it is necessary that you fulfill that very deed.”

Tome VIII of Labbe’s *General Councils*, Venetian edition, p. 381.

While the dukes governed Rome, supreme authority over the city of Rome and the Roman duchy belonged to the pontiff. This is clearly taught by Anastasius, whose testimony alone I use in this note.

Anastasius reports in the Life of Sisinnius, no. 169, that Sisinnius ordered lime to be burned for the restoration of the city walls but was prevented by death from accomplishing anything. In the Life of Gregory II, no. 177, he says:

> “At the beginning of his pontificate he ordered lime to be burned, and, beginning at the gate of Saint Lawrence, he had decided to restore the walls of this city. After completing part of the work, he was hindered by the disturbances and various tumults that arose.”

What clearer proof of supreme authority over a city could there be than fortifying it and constructing walls around its perimeter?

The same Gregory, no. 187, encourages the exarch, who was staying in Rome, frightened and disturbed by the defection of certain cities to Tiberius the usurper; he also sends leading men of the Church and troops to his aid. Gregory III, no. 204, has the walls of the city of Centumcellae, which had been almost destroyed from their foundations, rebuilt with great strength. Zacharias, about to leave Rome and go to Luitprand, king of the Lombards, for the salvation of the people of Ravenna, leaves the city of Rome to Stephen, patrician and duke, for its government, no. 213.

From these facts it is manifest that supreme authority over the city and duchy rested with the pontiffs, even though the dukes exercised judicial authority.

I do not have a thorough knowledge from Anastasius of which cities and fortresses constituted the Roman duchy. I understand, however, that Centumcellae belonged to the Roman duchy from the construction of its walls ordered by Gregory III. Likewise, the fortress of Gallese, recovered under the same Gregory, belonged to it; for Anastasius says, no. 203, that the Roman duchy was attacked daily by the duchy of Spoleto on account of it.

Similarly, under the same king, four cities were taken from the Roman duchy: Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera. Anastasius says this in his Life of Zacharias, no. 207:

> “Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera.”

I do not pronounce so confidently about the other places. Anastasius does say in the Life of Zacharias, no. 210:

> “For he also restored to blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, by title of donation, the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken away for nearly thirty years, and likewise the territory of Narni, that of Auximum, and that of Ancona, as well as Numania and the valley called the Great Valley, situated in the territory of Sutrium; and he confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years.”

But that Anastasius was not intending here to enumerate the places properly belonging to the Roman duchy is shown by his inclusion of Ancona, Auximum, and the Sabine patrimony, which are clearly known to have lain outside the duchy.

Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, asserts that the Roman duchy included the city of Rome and Portus, Centumcellae, Caere, Blera, Maturanum, Sutrium, Nepi, Castellum Gallesii, Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia, Narni, Otricoli, Signia, Anagni, Ferentinum, Alatrium, Patrica, Frosinone, and Tibur. In my opinion, he took this enumeration from the charter of confirmation issued by Louis the Pious to Paschal in the year 817, although Anastasius says nothing about it in his Life of Paschal.

[Col. 0947]

## 170. Constantine

Constantine, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, occupied the see for seven years and fifteen days.

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: six years and fifteen days.]

He lived during the reigns of the emperors Justinian, Philippicus, and Anastasius. He was a very gentle man. In his time a great famine afflicted the city of Rome for three years. Afterward such abundance prevailed that the abundance of fertility caused the want of the earlier scarcity to be forgotten.

He ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna. Felix refused to provide the customary guarantees in the registry according to the practice of his predecessors; instead, through the influence of the judges, he forced the matter through as he wished.

[Note: [Col. 0947] “He wished.” B: “He prevailed.”]

His guarantee, deposited by the pontiff in the most sacred confession of blessed Peter the Apostle, was found a few days later burned by the earth, as though by fire.

[Note: [Col. 0947] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 708.]

For the citizens of Ravenna, puffed up with pride, were punished with a penalty worthy of vengeance. The emperor Justinian sent the patrician Theodore, the *primicerius* of the army of the island of Sicily, with a fleet of ships. He captured the city of Ravenna, held the aforesaid arrogant archbishop bound in a ship, shackled all the rebels whom he found there, seized their wealth, and sent them to Constantinople.

By the judgment of God and the sentence of Peter, prince of the Apostles, those who had been disobedient to the Apostolic See were put to death by a bitter death.

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: “See.”]

The same archbishop, deprived of his sight and receiving a punishment worthy of his deeds, was sent into exile in the region of Pontus.

## 171. In the same period

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: “In his time.”]

In the same period the emperor mentioned above sent a sacred letter to Pontiff Constantine, by which he ordered him to come up to the imperial city.

[Note: [Col. 0947] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 709.]

The most holy man obeyed the imperial commands. He immediately had ships prepared in order to undertake the sea voyage, and he departed from the Roman harbor on the fifth day of October, in the ninth indiction.

He was followed by Nicetas, bishop of Silva Candida; George, bishop of Portus; Michael; Paul; George the priest; George the deacon; George the *secundicerius*; John, first *defensor*; Cosmas, the *sacellarius*; Sisinnius, the *nomenclator*; Sergius, the *scriniarius*; Dorotheus and Julian, subdeacons; and a few clerics from the other orders of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0947] Michael.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: Cosmas.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: “not a few.”]

## 172

When he came to Naples, he found there the patrician and exarch John, surnamed Rizocopus. John had come to Rome and slaughtered Saul the deacon and *vicedominus*, Peter the treasurer, Sergius the abbot-priest, and Sergius the ordainer.

[Note: [Col. 0947] B: “Paul.”]

Proceeding to Ravenna on account of his abominable crimes, he there met a most disgraceful death by the judgment of God.

George the priest was left at Naples. The pontiff, with his companions, proceeded to Sicily. There the patrician and *extraticus* Theodore, detained by illness, came to meet the pontiff. He greeted and received him with great reverence and immediately obtained a cure.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “and *strategus*.”]

Departing from there, the pontiff passed through Rhegium and Cortona and crossed the sea to Gallipoli, where Nicetas, bishop, died. While he was delayed at Hydruntum because it was winter, he received there the imperial seal through Theophanius, the *regionarius*. The seal contained the provision that wherever the pontiff was announced to have arrived, all the judges should receive him with such honor as though they were seeing the emperor himself in person.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “Wherever.” “Might be met.”]

From there they departed and reached the regions of Greece. On the island called Caea, the patrician Theophilus, *extraticus* of the *caravisiani*, met him and received him with the greatest honor. He embraced him, as the imperial command stipulated, and completed the journey that had been begun.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “and *Strategus*.” B.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] B: *curavisiani*.]

Sailing from that place, they came to Constantinople at the seventh milestone. There the emperor Tiberius, son of Justinian Augustus, came out with the patricians and all the illustrious men; Cyrus the patriarch came with the clergy and a multitude of the people. Everyone rejoiced and kept a festival.

The pontiff and his principal attendants entered the city with imperial saddlery, saddles and bridles gilded, and *mappulae*. The Apostolic Pontiff, wearing a *camelaucum*, as he was accustomed to proceed in Rome, left the palace and hastened as far as the Placidia residence, where he was to stay.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “Camelaucum.”]

[Note: [Col. 0949] “where he was going to lodge.”]

## 173

Lord Emperor Justinian, hearing of his arrival and filled with great joy, sent from Nicaea in Bithynia a sacred letter full of thanks.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “A letter.”]

He requested that the pontiff come to Nicomedia, while he himself would come from Nicaea.

[Note: [Col. 0949] “would come.”]

This was done. On the day when they saw one another,

[Note: [Col. 0949] B: “saw each other.”]

the most Christian Augustus prostrated himself with his crown upon his head, kissing the pontiff’s feet. Then they fell into one another’s arms,

[Note: [Col. 0949] “mutuo” (for *mutuum*).]

and great joy arose among the people, all of whom looked upon the great humility of the good ruler.

On Sunday he celebrated Mass for the emperor. The prince received Communion from his hands and, asking the pontiff to pray for his sins, renewed all the privileges of the Church. He then released the most holy pope to return to his own see.

The pontiff departed from Nicomedia, worn down by frequent illnesses. At length, with God granting him health, he reached the port of Gaeta safely. There he found priests and a very great multitude of the Roman people. On the twenty-fourth day of October, in the tenth indiction, he entered Rome, and the entire people exulted and rejoiced.

## 174

While going and returning through various places, he ordained twelve bishops.

After three months, a mournful report resounded: Justinian, the most Christian and orthodox emperor, had been murdered, and the heretic Philippicus had been elevated to the imperial throne. Constantine received from him a sacred letter containing a statement of his false doctrine, but rejected it in consultation with the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0949] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 711.]

For this reason, inflamed with zeal for the faith, the entire assembly of the city of Rome erected in the church of blessed Peter an image containing the six holy and universal synods, which the Greeks call *votarea*.

[Note: [Col. 0949] *Pancarea*.]

He restored a golden paten weighing twelve pounds.

At the same time Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, was brought back from exile. Moved by repentance, although deprived of the sight of his eyes, he nevertheless returned to his own see. There he made the customary declarations that are made by all in the bishops’ registry, together with a confession of faith, and thus earned absolution and reconciliation.

[Col. 0951]

## 175

In his time two kings of the Saxons, coming with many others to pray at the shrines of the Apostles, ended their lives speedily, as they desired.

[Note: [Col. 0951] “With speed.”]

Benedict, archbishop of Milan, also came with a vow to pray and to present himself to his own pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 0951] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 711.]

He also argued on behalf of the Church of Ticinum, but was defeated, because from ancient times the bishop of that Church both had belonged and still belonged to the Apostolic See for consecration.

## 176

At this time the Roman people had determined in no way to receive the name of the heretical emperor, or his documents, or the image of his coin. Consequently, neither was his likeness brought into the church, nor was his name pronounced at the solemn celebrations of Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0951] “Of the emperor Philippicus.” B: “was pronounced.”]

It happened that a certain Peter sent a decree to Ravenna concerning the duchy of the city of Rome and received a document concerning this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0951] “That it should be sent, and a document concerning it.”]

When it became known that this same Peter had obtained his advancement under the name of the heretical emperor, a large part of the Roman people, inflamed with zeal for the faith, decided in no way to accept him as duke.

While Christopher, who was duke, and Agatho with his men were fighting over this matter, civil war broke out. They engaged one another on the Sacred Way before the palace, and more than twenty-five men on each side were wounded and died, until the pontiff sent priests with the Gospels and the crosses of the Lord, and thus the factions were pacified.

The party of Peter was so hard pressed that there was no hope of survival for it. But at the pontiff’s command the other party, which was also called Christian, withdrew.

Thus the party supporting Peter, the defender of the heretic, prevailed, as though the opposing side, having been worn down, withdrew.

[Note: [Col. 0951] “Thus the party of the heretical supporters of Peter did not prevail but, having been worn down, withdrew.”]

Not many days afterward, letters arrived from the island of Sicily reporting that the heretic Philippicus had been driven from the imperial throne and that Anastasius the Orthodox Augustus had assumed the royal scepters to govern.

[Note: [Col. 0951] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 713.]

Then there was great rejoicing among the orthodox, while a day of darkness spread over all the heretics.

After some time,

[Note: [Col. 0951] “time.”]

Scholasticus, chamberlain, patrician, and exarch of Italy, came to Rome and brought with him a sacred letter from the emperor Anastasius. In it the emperor declared to everyone that he was a preacher of the true orthodox faith and a confessor of the holy Sixth Council. He presented the letter to the pontiff and then proceeded to Ravenna.

While these things were taking place, Peter obtained the duchy, promising that he would not attempt to oppose anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0951] B: “that he would by no means henceforth oppose the Romans.” B adds: “of the city.”]

He conducted one ordination: ten priests, two deacons, and sixty-four bishops in various places.

He too was buried at blessed Peter the Apostle on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction, while Anastasius was Augustus. The see remained vacant for forty days.

## Notes

### No. 177, line 7 — Concerning certain chapters

Gregory accompanied Pope Constantine, who was hurrying to Constantinople, and Justinian questioned him about the chapters. These appear to have been none other than the Trullan canons, toward the promulgation of which the emperor had devoted prolonged effort, as we read in the Life of Sergius, page 151. Some think that on that occasion certain of the Trullan canons were approved and confirmed by the Roman pontiff. We do not wish to decide the matter without certain evidence.

### No. 178, line 1 — John of Constantinople

This man had presided over the conciliabulum held at Constantinople under Philippicus and had subscribed to those decrees which, as we have noted, were promulgated by an encyclical letter and accepted by many. This Anastasian epitome, however, concerns the Life of Constantine, to whom John wrote a synodical letter. Therefore, after the words “He proceeded to Ravenna” in the account of Constantine’s deeds, page 163, line 1, the following should be added; these words have been wrongly inserted into the Life of Gregory:
