“During his time John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodical letter, and the same pontiff used replies addressed to him.”

For John could not have written a synodical letter during the time of Gregory II, since he died before Gregory was raised to the pontificate. Constantine died in 715, whereas John of Constantinople died in 714, and Germanus succeeded him. Theophanes records the following in his *Chronicle*, page 322:

“In that same year, the second of the reign of Artemius, also called Anastasius, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eleventh day of August, Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan see of Cyzicus to Constantinople, and a decree concerning that transfer … was promulgated.”

Agatho the Deacon, a contemporary author likewise, makes this absolutely clear. After recounting the elevation of Anastasius to the imperial office, he adds:

“And shortly afterward, when it had seemed so to him and he had consented, a letter of defense was written by the most holy pontiff of this city, John, to Constantine, the most holy and blessed pope of Old Rome. These letters, indeed, were sent according to custom with the synodical letters. As was fitting, they informed him of all that had previously been written.”

From this we learn more fully about the Roman synod mentioned above that Constantine sent a threatening letter to John, reproaching him for what had been done at the predatory Constantinopolitan synod; and that John, in addition to the customary synodical letter, sent Constantine an apology, so that whatever he had wrongly done might be attributed to the most salutary remedy of ecclesiastical economy. Agatho also suggests that John wrote to the pontiff—as was proper—for he ought to have answered the Roman synodical letter, lest he appear contumacious.

John’s letter is printed in volume III of Hardouin’s councils, page 1838, under the heading:

“Letter of the most holy archbishop John of Constantinople to Constantine, the most holy Roman pope, an apology concerning what was stirred up during the tyranny of Barda against the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod.”

### No. 179, line 1 — Liutprand

Our author excerpted this from Paul the Deacon, book 6, chapter 43:

“At that time King Liutprand confirmed the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church.”

### Line 6 — Emperor Anastasius

Paul, preserving the chronological order, narrated this before the aforementioned confirmation of the donation, chapter 36, as follows:

“At this time the emperor Anastasius sent a fleet against the Saracens toward Alexandria. Its army, turning toward another plan, returned from the middle of its journey to the city of Constantinople, sought out Theodosius the Orthodox, elected him emperor, and compelled him to accept and confirm the imperial throne. Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a serious battle near the city of Aerea; after receiving an oath from him, he compelled him to become a cleric and had him ordained a presbyter. As soon as he himself had received the kingdom, he immediately restored in the imperial city to its former place that venerable image in which the holy synod had been depicted and which had been removed by Philippicus. In those days the river Tiber flooded so greatly that, overflowing its bed, it inflicted much destruction upon the city of Rome; it rose in the Via Lata to a height of one and a half [units], and the waters spread out and joined from the gate of Saint Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge.”

### Line 16 — That venerable image

Both Paul and his copyist Anastasius attribute to Theodosius the restoration of the image of the Sixth Synod. Agatho, however, who was present at the events, plainly attributes this work to Anastasius. Therefore both historians must be corrected, and in place of Theodosius the following should be written:

“Immediately after the aforementioned Anastasius entered, together with the other matters which likewise must be referred to the deeds of Constantine …”

For after describing the election of Anastasius, Agatho continues in the passage so often cited:

“Since, after the removal of the synodal image mentioned above, that impious and deranged criminal Bardanes, who had ordered it to be removed, commanded the five holy and ecumenical synods to be depicted in the vault called the Melion, and himself alone to be placed in the image’s midst with Sergius set up beside him, it was altogether necessary and most fitting that, after those two persons had been removed from it, a representation of the same holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod should be made on the column together with the other five. A common festival and joy, and a spiritual exaltation in the Lord, arose for the whole assembly of the Church that loves God, because of the establishment and peace of the most holy Churches.”

### No. 182, line 4 — The detestable Agarenes

With certain changes, the whole of no. 182 has been copied from Paul the Deacon, book 6, chapters 46–47.

### Line 12 — The three sponges sent

What our author says about the sponges is omitted by Paul. Among the ancients, the use of sponges was common. They were frequently used at tables and even employed in sacred contexts, particularly for polishing the lamps standing before the altar, as is made certain by what is recorded below concerning Paschasius. They were kept in silver vessels intended for the service of the altar. For we read that Paschal dedicated a silver basin for holding a sponge there, for the nocturnal services.

I think that sponges of this kind were sent because they had been soaked in oil used at the tombs of the martyrs.

**Bencinus**

### No. 183, line 24 — Under Prince Leo

Leo seized the empire after deposing Theodosius. He alone resisted when the soldiers, having expelled Anastasius, acclaimed Theodosius emperor. The author of the *Miscella*, book 20, page 146, says:

“Leo, when he was governor of the East, because he supported Artemius, was not subjected to Theodosius.”

There were very frequent deposings of emperors of this kind. Nicephorus observes the following in his *Chronicle*, after narrating the deposition of Theodosius:

“While conspiracies against the emperors were continually made in this manner, and while, as tyranny grew stronger, the condition of the empire and the state was neglected and gradually slid into a worse condition, the study of letters also began little by little to be extinguished and perish, and military discipline was no less ruined. Thus it came about that the Roman empire was attacked with impunity by wars, and that killings indiscriminately, abductions of people, and destructions of cities occurred everywhere. To the accumulation of these evils was added the incursion of the Saracens, who, having undertaken a land expedition against the imperial city, gathered from the peoples subject to them an innumerable force of infantry and cavalry. At the same time they moved a vast fleet of approximately 1,800 ships, under a leader named Muslim—for that was how they called him in their native language. When these events became known, the military commanders and civil magistrates, observing Theodosius’ inexperience and knowing that he was unequal to resisting such forces of the enemy, began to press and urge him to abdicate the empire and allow himself safely to be compelled into the ranks. He did not refuse the condition, but, while the year of his reign was still in progress, 717, he voluntarily abdicated. Then they began deliberating about choosing a successor, and at that moment Leo the patrician was proposed, who at that time commanded the eastern forces. Therefore, as emperors are accustomed to be, he was received with solemn ceremony, entered Byzantium through the Golden Gate, and received the imperial crown in the Great Church.”

### No. 183, line 9 — Liutprand of the Lombards

Concerning him Paul says, book 6, chapter 49:

“At that time Liutprand besieged Ravenna, attacked the fleet, and destroyed it.”

### Line 13 — So that they might kill the pontiff

This refers to Leo the Armenian, who, with hopes of the imperial power, had previously been ensnared by Jews into destroying the images and had issued earlier edicts for abolishing them. When he recognized that Pope Gregory was strongly opposed to him in this matter, he tried to have him killed through the men whom Anastasius lists here.

### No. 184, line 1 — By orders

Concerning these edicts promulgated by Leo the Isaurian, Paul has the same account in book 6, chapter 49. When Anastasius copies Paul, he mixes together the emperor’s heretical edicts without distinguishing the earlier from the later. Leo therefore published two decrees.

In the first, which appeared in 716, he had forbidden the veneration of images. The words of Stephen the Deacon of Constantinople in the *Life of Saint Stephen the Younger* must be understood as referring to this decree. There we read:

“After the tenth year of his reign that new Balthazar breathed into the Church that Manichaean heresy and, so to speak, that of the Aphthartocites, scarcely unlike it. Calling together the people subject to him, this inhuman beast, roaring before everyone in the manner of a lion, illustrious in the name of Leo and with an angry heart, as though from Mount Etna, belched forth and uttered that pitiable voice: ‘Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped.’”

Theophanes, under the relevant year, and the author of the *Miscella*, page 150, explain more fully where Leo derived his error. Theophanes plainly shows, page 340, that he began by prohibiting the veneration of images before proceeding to order their destruction:

“That impious man was not only involved in error concerning the relative veneration of venerable images, but also, being a most wicked man, abhorred the intercessions of the most holy Mother of God and of all the saints, and their relics, after the manner of his Arab teachers. From that time he rashly undertook hostility against the blessed patriarch Germanus of Constantinople, condemning all his predecessors, emperors, prelates, and Christian peoples as idolaters because of their veneration of the holy and venerable images, while through excessive unbelief and rusticity he was unable to understand or discuss their relative honor.”

### Line 4 — Therefore the pious man, looking upon the matter

That is, Pope Gregory, in the matter of the sacred images, convened a synod at Rome, some fragments of which Hadrian I preserves in his letter to Charles concerning images. Just as Philippicus, by publishing his volume of faith, compelled everyone to pronounce an anathema against the Sixth Synod and was therefore declared a heretic by the pontiff, so the synodical letter of Pope Gregory stirred the Italian army so strongly to defend the faith that, unless Gregory had opposed it, it would almost have deliberated about choosing a new emperor.

**Bencinus**

### Line 8 — Of the Venetians

The Venetian republic, already distinguished at this time for its arms, generally stood in defense of the pontiff. Ursus was then in charge of it, and he was closely connected with Gregory and often stood by him. Therefore, when King Liutprand occupied the exarchate of Ravenna, Gregory wrote to Ursus so that he might come to his aid. The pontiff’s letter is found among his other letters.

### Line 12 — All the dukes everywhere in Italy chose

This was the first period of Italian liberty, in which the Italians, beginning to free themselves from the yoke of the barbarians and the Greeks, laid the foundations of the Western empire, later restored. Theophanes speaks of this movement in Italy, page 342:

“Moreover, that holy and divine Germanus, defender of the decrees of true religion, flourished at Byzantium against Leo, who derived his name from his deeds, and fought against his satellites as against wild beasts. Likewise, in Old Rome, the man holy and apostolic in every respect, the confessor of Peter, chief of the apostles, Gregory, distinguished for his learning and glorious deeds, flourished. He withdrew Rome, Italy, and the whole of the West from Leo’s obedience, both civil and ecclesiastical, and from his rule.”

### No. 187, line 2.—“Named Tiberius”

If Anastasius is reporting the truth, two tyrants must be distinguished. One, at the beginning of Leo’s reign, seized power as tyrant in Sicily; the other, around the year 728 or 729, made himself emperor in Tuscany and was also called Tiberius.

The author of the *Miscella*, p. 150, under the year 718, where he is discussing the second year of Leo’s reign, deals with the first:

> “Sergius, protospatharius and praetor of Sicily, having heard that the Saracens were besieging the imperial city, there crowned as emperor a certain Constantinopolitan, one of his own men, the son of Gregory Onomagulus. Changing his name, he called him Tiberius. He made appointments and appointed his own rulers on the advice of the aforesaid Sergius. But the emperor, hearing this, sent Paul, his own chartularius, whom he appointed patrician and praetor of Sicily, giving him two spatharii as auxiliaries and very few men for his service, together with orders for the rulers of the West and sacred messages to be recited to the people.

> “When they had entered at night into a swift *dromon*, they came out in the region of Cyzicus and, traveling from place to place by land and sea, suddenly arrived in Sicily. When they had entered Syracuse, Sergius heard of it and was struck with terror. Reflecting on his own transgression, he fled to the neighboring Lombards of Calabria.

> “The people, however, gathered; and, after the sacred messages had been read, they were convinced that the imperial government still stood and that the city was more ready to resist the nations. When those men also related what had happened concerning the two *stolae* [perhaps official robes or insignia], they praised Leo as emperor, but handed Basil Onomagulus and the rulers who had come from him, bound, over to the praetor. He himself beheaded Basil together with his particular praetor, and sent their heads, preserved in *pusca* (vinegared water), to the emperor by the spatharii. Of the rest, he sent some into exile after they had been scourged, others after their hair had been cut off, and still others after their noses had been cut away. Thus it came about that a great establishment of correction was made in the West. Sergius, meanwhile, after receiving and requesting a promise of impunity from the praetor, went out to him; and in this way all the regions of Hesperia obtained peace.”

The other tyrant in the region of Tuscany, likewise called Tiberius and mentioned by Anastasius at this point, was surnamed Petasius. He induced Etruria to revolt, although he was crushed by the Roman army with Pope Gregory’s cooperation.

### No. 188, line 1.—“The wickedness of that same emperor became manifest”

Most of what Anastasius records here is taken word for word from Paul the Deacon, at the end of chapter 49. Accordingly, in the year 730 the emperor promulgated an edict ordering that the venerable images be removed and burned throughout the entire empire.

The place, time, and circumstances he left to Theophanes, who, under the aforesaid year, writes:

> “Moreover, on the seventh day of the month of January, in the thirteenth indiction, the irreligious Leo held a session against the sacred and venerable images in the tribunal of the nineteen *accubitores*. He had summoned the most holy patriarch Germanus, believing that he could persuade him finally to subscribe to his decree concerning the abolition of the sacred images. But that courageous servant of Christ in no way yielded to Leo’s abominable plan; rather, distributing the word of truth with upright understanding, he resigned the episcopate. . . .

> “On the seventh day of that same month of January they appointed Anastasius, a man of false name, the blessed Germanus’s disciple and chancellor, in his place. Since he was moved by ambition for secular power and assented to Leo’s impiety, he was made a false bishop of Constantinople. Meanwhile Gregory, the holy bishop of Rome, . . . deposed Anastasius together with his documents, rebuked Leo himself by letters as an irreligious man, and stirred Rome together with all Italy to revolt from his rule. Thereafter the tyrant, inflamed each day with greater fury, began persecutions against the holy images, so that many clergy and monks, and devout laymen, having risked their lives for the true decrees of the faith, were rewarded with the crown of martyrdom.””

Stephen, in the *Life of Stephen the Younger*, gives further information about the persecution stirred up against the Catholics.

Meanwhile the Lombard rulers, Luitprand and afterward Aistulf, were attempting to invade all Italy, which was being harassed by such conflicts, and were daily occupying many places belonging to Roman territory. Gregory secretly entered into an alliance with Charles Martel. Later pontiffs did the same, as we shall note in its proper place.

### Line 14.—“Admonishing the emperor with salutary counsel”

Gregory II published several letters concerning the holy images. Only two are now extant, and they are read at the beginning of the Seventh Synod.

Indeed, Anastasius noted above that after Leo’s earlier decrees the pope issued an encyclical to the entire Catholic world in which he declared the emperor a heretic; from this the first movements of the Italian armies arose. Theophanes also suggests that the same letter was circulated throughout the East, where he says that John of Damascus pronounced an anathema against Leo:

> “Gregory rebuked him in letters which everyone knows, sent to him; and finally John [of Damascus], together with the bishops of the whole East, bound the impious Leo with an anathema.”

## Note

**[Col. 0995D]**

### No. 177, line 1.—“Gregory”

After the apostolic see had been vacant for forty-two days following the death of Pope Constantine, Gregory II of that name was elected pope, with the complete agreement of the clergy and people, on 22 May 714, under the emperor Anastasius. This is contrary to Panvinio’s view in the *Fasti*.

The point is proved above all by the statement of Anastasius the Librarian. When he reckons that Gregory occupied the see for sixteen years, eight months, and ten days, and says that he died on 11 February, it is necessary to affirm that he began to sit in the year 714. Anastasius confirms the same point when he writes that John, bishop of Constantinople, sent a letter to Gregory.

If this is true, it must plainly be conceded that Gregory held the pontificate at the stated time. For Theophanes makes it clear that the aforesaid John was removed from his episcopate by the emperor Anastasius in the second year of that emperor’s reign, which was A.D. 714.

This pope is improperly called “the Dialogist” by older Greek writers and by some more recent Latin writers as well, although that title truly belongs, on the basis of the books written in dialogue, only to Gregory I. Gennadius, in his exposition for the Council of Florence, chapter 5, section 16, and chapter 3, sections 5 and 6, either does not distinguish between the two popes named Gregory or wrongly thought that both should be called by this title. For in chapter 5 he calls Gregory II “the Dialogist,” but in chapter 3 he gives the title to Gregory I. See Baronius, under the year 726, no. 31.

### Line 11.—“He ordered lime to be burned”

And this because of the Lombards, who were lying in wait for the City. See Baronius, under the year 715, no. 2.

### No. 178, lines 8–9.—“Here in Germany through Boniface”

Concerning the deeds nobly accomplished by Saint Boniface, father, apostle, and martyr of Germany, the venerable and most learned Nicolaus Serarius, theologian of the Society of Jesus, provides much information in *Moguntina Historia*, book II.

### No. 179, line 1.—“At that time Luitprand”

The same is reported by Bede, Paul the Deacon, and Oldradus in his letter to Charlemagne, where he states that these events were carried out by Luitprand himself in his first year.

### No. 182, line 21.—“Meanwhile, during those days, Constantinople”

Concerning Constantinople, besieged by the Saracens for two or three years and freed through the aid of the Virgin Mother of God, Theophanes gives more information after Bede and Paul the Deacon. Saint Gregory also mentions the matter in his letter to Saint Germanus, bishop of Constantinople.

**[Col. 0996B]**

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The order of events now leads us to the time of Saint Gregory II. If all his acts had survived, he could rightly be compared with Saint Gregory the Great, [Col. 0996C] from whom I began, as the most learned father of the *Annals*, Bollandus, asserts. (*Preliminary Commentary on the Life of Gregory II*, 13 February.)

Antonius Pagius and other recent writers determine the certain length of this pope’s life and pontificate against the opinion of Panvinius and Baronius. Papebrochius did the same before them, although, by anticipating the ordination, he separates the death from the deposition by several days, as is customary.

It will soon become clear that we must not depart from their view. For of the three matters considered in determining the age of any pope, two—the interval between pontificates and the end, or day of death—are certain by the unanimous agreement of all. The second matter, namely the duration of the pontificate, is enclosed between them and consequently becomes evident by itself.

Before I set out these three matters, however, I shall, for the sake of learning, resolve the remarkable disagreement found in the catalogues and manuscripts concerning the years, months, and days.

[Col. 0996D] The catalogues and manuscripts divided into two groups present Gregory’s years as either fifteen or sixteen. Eleven of them stand for fifteen years, while thirteen, supported by Luitprand, give sixteen years.

The Bergomian catalogues and five Colbertine catalogues, together with two Freherian manuscripts, one Thuanean, the Farnesian, and one Ambrosian manuscript, give fifteen years. All the remaining four of our catalogues and two Colbertine catalogues, as well as four of our manuscripts and three Ambrosian manuscripts, give sixteen years.

A similar disagreement is found in the number of months. Seven, eight, and nine months are inconsistently assigned to Gregory’s pontificate. Finally, there is an even greater discrepancy concerning the days: ten, eleven, twenty-two, twenty-four, and twenty-nine are found recorded in various places.

These differences would certainly make the chronology of this holy pope very laborious. But since, as I said a little earlier, his beginning and end are clear, it is easy to determine the interval between them. The matter therefore stands as follows.

After Constantine’s death on 9 April, as we saw above, the manuscripts correctly record that the same interval between pontificates lasted forty days, without any disagreement. [Col. 0997A] Counting these from the aforesaid day brings us to 19 May. The dominical letter F shows that in the year of Constantine’s death this was a Sunday; consequently, the beginning of Saint Gregory II must be reckoned from the very day of his ordination, 19 May 715.

The end, or death, of this pope is likewise consistently transmitted by all the manuscripts as 11 February, in the fourteenth indiction. This undoubtedly indicates the year 731, both because the same fourteenth indiction, which was current in the second year of Gregory’s pontificate, is associated by Anastasius with the celebrated lunar eclipse followed by the great flooding of the Tiber in the fifteenth indiction, and especially because Gregory II vigorously defended the sacred images against Leo the Isaurian and the other iconoclasts. I shall shortly establish the beginning of that madness and of the sacrilegious audacity of the Easterners.

[Col. 0997B] Saint Gregory therefore governed the apostolic see with the greatest holiness throughout the entire interval between these two extremes, from 19 May 715 to 11 February 731—that is, fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-four days. This is correctly given by four Colbertine catalogues, one of the Thuanean manuscripts, two Freherian manuscripts, and the Farnesian manuscript, together with the *Acta*, in Pagius.

This total includes both the day of his ordination and the day of his death. Nor is this certain reckoning of his age disturbed in the least by the Martyrologies, which commemorate the passing of the holy pope on the following day or two days afterward. On these matters see Bollandus under 13 February, in the preliminary commentary on his Life.

Having completed what concerns Gregory’s age, I shall touch, in accordance with my purpose, on several matters that confirm it. These are the war declared by the impious Leo against the sacred images, which Baronius discusses at length under the year 726, and the two letters of Gregory II written on that occasion to the emperor. They make the pope’s chronology especially clear.

Baronius correctly teaches, against Theophanes and despite the opposition of certain recent scholars who seek to defend Theophanes’ opinion, that Leo was elevated to the imperial power in the year 716, on 25 March, while the fourteenth indiction was still current.

[Col. 0997C] The first of Gregory’s letters supports Baronius’s opinion:

> “While you are reigning in the fourteenth indiction, and also in the fourteenth, fifteenth, first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth [indictions], we carefully preserve in the holy Church, at the threshold of the confession of the holy and glorious prince of the apostles Peter, the letters which we have received from you.”

Baronius cites this under the year 726.

Pagius likewise uses this passage to support his own view and that of recent writers. He says that Leo, who was proclaimed emperor in 717, wrote the letter in the fourteenth indiction, which was current in that year. To prevent the matter from being blamed on a copyist, he adds below:

> “Gregory mentioned letters written to him by the emperor in the fourteenth indiction, namely in the first year of his reign.”

I confess that I am astonished at the negligence of this learned writer. Having finally noticed that Gregory’s letters had not yet been assigned to their proper year, he failed to see that the fifteenth indiction was current in 717 until the Kalends of September. Moreover, if one letter was given for each indiction, as Gregory affirms, then by the ninth indiction not eleven but ten letters would be counted.

[Col. 0997D] Furthermore, under the year 741, no. 4, Pagius correctly analyzes the long reign of Copronymus according to Theophanes. Because the chronology conflicts with his own opinion, however, he entirely confuses it and declares Theophanes’ *Chronicle* corrupt, without seeing that he thereby distorts a vast sequence of events reported both by Theophanes and by the author of the *Miscella*.

Therefore, if everything is to proceed consistently, the beginnings both of the Isaurian and of the Copronymian period must be moved back by one year, after rejecting the defective notation of the indictions.

Since I have arranged these matters in the *Imperial and Pontifical Chronology*, I shall continue with the remaining points concerning Gregory II that I promised.

Leo the Isaurian, therefore, after the tenth year of his reign, as we read in the *Life of Saint Stephen the Monk and Martyr*, began his criminal undertaking by tearing down the image of the Savior that had been placed above the bronze gate.

[Col. 0998A] But he did not promulgate public edicts for the destruction of all images everywhere until the fourteenth year of his reign, A.D. 730. Anastasius is an advocate of this view. He reports the invasion of the Lombards, followed by the donation of the Castle of Sueri to Saint Peter in 728, and then, in 729, the appearance of a comet in the western sky. Bede also reports the comet in that same year, saying that another was seen in the East. Anastasius then writes:

> “After this, the wickedness of that same emperor became manifest. Because of it he persecuted the pope, compelling all the inhabitants of Constantinople, by force and by blandishments, to remove everywhere the images of both the Savior and his holy Mother, and of all the saints, and—as it is cruel to say—to burn them in the middle of the city and to whitewash all the churches that had been painted.”

The abdication of Saint Germanus also confirms this chronology with the greatest certainty. It occurred after he had opposed the emperor’s audacity and impiety without success. Pagius discusses it learnedly under the year 730, beginning with no. 1.

[Col. 0998B] Accordingly, we should more correctly place the beginning of the war against the images in 730 rather than 726. Nevertheless, since the ancient authors teach us that this war began as soon as Leo’s monstrous crime emerged, we set the beginning of the persecution in 726 and maintain that it was publicly promulgated four years later, namely in 730.

Perhaps I shall be mocked for so frequently opposing Pagius. He teaches that the edict for the public destruction of the images was promulgated in 726:

> “Therefore, just as formerly the pagan emperors promulgated edicts against the Christians in the years marked by their decennial vows, so Leo the Isaurian, in the tenth year of his reign, stirred up persecution against the Orthodox and declared war on the sacred images—and this before the Kalends of September, when the tenth indiction began.”

(*Annals*, 726, no. 1.)

Yet, with due respect to the Isaurian, who according to Pagius himself began to reign on 25 March 717, on the Kalends of September 726 he was in the fifth month of the tenth year of his reign. Therefore he could not have promulgated the edict in imitation of the pagans in a year dedicated to his decennial celebrations. For decennial vows were proclaimed after the decade had been completed and a new decade had begun. Examples of this may be seen in Cardinal Noris, *Chronological Dissertation on Decennial Vows*.

[Col. 0998C] It is indeed true that, according to the chronology of Baronius, which I follow, Leo was in his eleventh year, which would have been especially suitable for celebrating decennial vows. But since I have shown that the promulgation of the edict belongs to the year 730, all the learning concerning the decennials collapses.

Once these matters are understood, the date of the two letters of Saint Gregory also becomes clear. Pagius discusses them learnedly under the years 726 and 730 against Cardinal Baronius, who wants them to have been written before the events about which they speak had taken place.

They were written, therefore, after Saint Gregory had received the synodical letter of Anastasius, who had been intruded by the emperor into the patriarchal see after Saint Germanus had been expelled—namely, in the fourteenth indiction, which began with the Kalends of September 730. For Anastasius makes it clear that the holy pontiff first sent a letter to him and afterward to the emperor.

Pagius, the nephew and copyist of Antonius, and Sommier speak explicitly about these matters; their notes should be consulted below, sections 184 and 188.

[Col. 0998D] Why Leo appears not to have written to Gregory after the year 726 is also clear. When the holy pontiff counts the emperor’s letters written in each year, he means Catholic letters. But after the ninth indiction—that is, after 726, when the persecution of the images began—they were no longer Catholic. Consequently, if Leo sent any letters, as he certainly did when he recognized that Italy had formed an alliance against him and wished a council to be summoned, there was no reason for them to be preserved. Gregory detested him as a most wicked heretic, as is confirmed by the council held at Rome, a fragment of which survives, and by the two aforementioned letters written a few months before Gregory’s death.

The sequence of events may be read in the historical annotators.

## Note

**[Col. 0998D]**

### No. 177, line 1.—“Gregory II”

Gregory II, a younger Roman, [Col. 0999A] son of Marcellus, was made cardinal deacon of the Roman Church from the monastery of Saint Benedict by Pope Constantine. He sat under the emperors Flavius Anastasius, Artemius, Theodosius of Adramyttium, and Leo the Isaurian, and occupied the see for fourteen years, ten months, and twenty-one days. He was elected on the twelfth day before the Kalends and consecrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. He had been initiated into the sacred ministry under Pope Sergius and was placed in charge of the chapels and the library.

### No. 188, line 1.—“For after this the wickedness of the emperor became manifest”

Leo began to think more intensely about abolishing the sacred images and sent a letter concerning the matter to the pope. Gregory replied to him with the dignity appropriate to the matter, explaining that the sacred images were honored in the Church according to the ancient practice of the Catholics and that he could neither abolish their veneration at his own discretion nor was it proper for him to do so as part of his office.

Gregory also repeatedly warned him to observe carefully both what he was doing and how far he was proceeding. It was not the emperor’s role to establish anything new concerning the faith, but to defend by every means what had been decreed by the Fathers from ancient times.

## Note

**[Col. 0999B]**

### No. 178, line 8.—“Here in Germany, through Bishop Boniface, he preached the word of salvation”

Here in Germany he preached the word of salvation through Bishop Boniface, and by the teaching of light converted to Christ that people which sat in darkness.

Boniface, consecrated bishop by Gregory II and sent to Germany for the conversion of the people, was the first bishop of Mainz. The ordination and mission of bishops for the conversion of unbelievers belong to the Roman pontiff.

By this authority Boniface was sent by Gregory II to Germany. Sergius ordained Willibrord, called Clement, and sent him to convert the Frisians; he was the first bishop of Utrecht. Anastasius discusses him under Sergius; so do Bede, book V, chapter 12, and Sigebert in his *Chronicle* under the year 697.

Gregory I sent Augustine to England, with great success, for the conversion of the English. Gregory himself discusses this in book V, letters 53 and following; Bede does so in book IV, chapters 23 and following.

### [Col. 0999C] No. 181, line 11.—“And they killed nearly three hundred Lombards together with their castald”

A *castaldus*, or *gastaldus*, among the Lombards is the governor of a city or castle.

Paul Warnefrid, *On the Origin of the Lombards*, book V, chapter 29, writes:

> “He ordered that Alzoron himself, after his title of rank had been changed, should be called a castald instead of a duke.”

Rainerius the gastald of the city of Sora is mentioned by Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book II, chapter 32. Tacipertus the castald and Ramingus the castald of Tuscany are mentioned by Anastasius under Zacharias.

Sometimes *gastaldus* means a procurator. Urban II, in canon “Salvator,” 1, question 33, writes:

> “In the name of defender, an advocate, his castald and judge.”

Pandulf the gastald is named in the inscription of John VIII, letter 215. The same man is called the judge of Capua in letter 217 of the same pope.

### No. 182, line 11.—“In the preceding year, three sponges were sent to them by the aforesaid man as a blessing, to be placed on the pope’s table for use”

Before the year in which the Saracens, under their king Addiramen, invaded Gaul, [Col. 0999D] Gregory II sent three sponges to Duke Eudo of Aquitaine as a blessing. They were of the kind used to wipe the pope’s table. After they had been cut into pieces and distributed among the soldiers, all who received them emerged safe and unharmed from the battle in which Charles Martel and Eudo, with their united forces, routed the Saracens utterly.

Sponges were used for wiping tables, as is proved by the following passage, which Martial illustrates in book XIV, epigram 144:

> “By fortune this sponge is given to you, useful for wiping tables.”

They were also used for wiping floors, as in *Digest* 33.7, “The Question,” section “Likewise, the pole,” concerning legacies of equipment.

Marcus Tullius, *For Sextius*, says:

> “You remember, judges, that the Tiber was filled with the bodies of citizens, the sewers were repaired, and the blood was wiped from the Forum with sponges.”

Hence the Egyptian virgin who, pretending to be foolish, served the others out of humility, was called **σπόγγος τῆς συνοδίας**, “the sponge of the monastery.” [Col. 1000A] Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 40.

### Line 17.—“Here he instituted that during Lent, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the churches, which had not previously been done”

Even during Lent, the apostles had instituted a perpetual release from fasting in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection.

Gregory, in *Gospel Homily* 16, writes:

> “Although there is still another matter that can be understood concerning the season of Lent, from the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks. These amount to forty-two days; when the six Sundays are subtracted from them as days of abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence.”

Besides Sundays, Thursday too was customarily exempt from the Lenten fast. But Gregory the Younger restored fasting even on Thursday, as well as the solemn celebration of Mass—that is, of the offices—throughout Lent. Anastasius, in this passage, and the *Micrologus*, concerning the observances of the Church, chapter 50, bear witness to this.

### [Col. 1000B] No. 183, line 7.—“Ten baskets weighing twelve pounds”

The baskets were silver vessels in which vessels—that is, sacred implements—were stored.

Anastasius, under Benedict III, writes:

> “Two *exafoci* baskets of the purest silver, weighing four and a half pounds.”

The passage is very corrupt. It seems that it should be restored as **canistra exaphodia**, from the Greek **ἐφόδιον**, meaning sacred provisions for a journey, or viaticum.

The Council of Nicaea, canon 12, refers to them because they were baskets in which the Lord’s body was stored. Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus concerning blessed Exuperius, writes:

> “There was no one richer than he who carried the Lord’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in glass.”

From this the more corrupt passage of Anastasius under Leo III should also be restored:

> “A basket of the cede of Cafoli, weighing twelve and a half pounds.”

The same applies to the passage under Paschal:

> “The aforesaid pontiff made two *Enafoti* baskets of silver.”

And likewise to the passage under Gregory IV:

> “He also offered two *enna fodia* baskets.”

In former times drinking vessels were placed on tables in silver baskets. Servius, commenting on the passage in book I [Col. 1000C] of the *Aeneid*,

> “Who load the tables with dishes and set out the drinking cups,”

explains that among the ancients cups were not handed directly into people’s hands but were placed on tables. Even today, among many peoples, cups are set out in silver baskets, which are called *siccaria* baskets.

### No. 186, line 18.—“And he placed before the body of the apostle a mantle, an armilausa, a belt, a sword, and a gilded blade, together with a golden crown and a silver cross”

Luitprand, king of the Lombards, overcome by the pope’s entreaties, laid down his royal garments and ornaments before the altar of Saint Peter: his mantle, armilausa, belt, and sword.

A *mantum* is a short little cloak that covers the shoulders and reaches only to the hands. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 24, writes:

> “The Spaniards call it *mantum* because it covers only the hands; for it is a short covering.”

Here the mantle is placed among royal ornaments. Radevicus places it among pontifical garments, *On the Deeds of Frederick*, book II, chapter 62:

> “Many of our men say that they saw the chancellor [Col. 1000D] leave the city on the eleventh day without a mantle, without a stole, without a white horse, and without any protection of clothing, with skins covered by a royal cloak and with a black *almutium* reaching down to the cistern.”

The *armilausa* is placed among royal garments. It is a military garment that covers the arms—that is, the shoulders—and reaches to the knees, so that the wearer may move more freely.

Paulinus, letter 7, to Severus, writes:

> “Let him keep his armilausa, his boots, and his *buccae*.”

The same author, letter 13 to the same man, writes:

> “Moreover, his face blushed no less than the armilausa.”

Isidore explains the etymology of *armilausa* from arms in *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 22:

> “It is commonly called *armelausa* because it is divided and open in front and behind, closed only around the shoulders, as though *armiclausa*, with the letter c removed.”

Suidas writes:

> **Ἀρμιλαύσιον παρὰ τὸ ἄρμα, τὸ ἐπάνω τῶν ὁπλων**  
> “*Armilausion* comes from *arma*, that which is above the arms [shoulders].”

The armilausa is joined with the *balteum*, which is a military belt.

Paulinus, letter 7 to Severus, writes:

> “We are girded not with a belt but with a rope.”

It was an ancient custom to place a belt of offering upon the altar. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 61, writes:

> “At a certain time a devout man placed upon the altar of that basilica a belt made of the purest gold and most carefully fashioned with all its equipment, praying that the power of the martyr might deign to be present in his affairs.”

He says that it was a silver cross. Emperors wore a golden cross around their necks. Ditmarus bears witness concerning Charlemagne, book IV:

> “Taking the golden cross that had hung around his neck, together with part of his still-unspoiled garments, he placed the rest away with great reverence.”

## Note

**[Col. 1001A]**

### No. 178, line 1.—“In his time John of Constantinople, etc.”

When the election of Gregory became known in the East, John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodical letter according to custom, as Anastasius himself reports. He says:

> “In his time John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodical letter, and the same pontiff responded to him by letter.”

Some, with Baronius, believe that Gregory rejected John’s synodical [Col. 1001B] letter and regarded him as a heretic. They therefore suppose that the emperor Anastasius, after receiving Pope Gregory’s letters, restored John to his rank and deposed him from the throne, and that Theophanes mentioned this deposition.

But not only Theophanes, but also Anastasius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, or in his translation of Theophanes, explicitly state that the patriarch John died after occupying the see for three years. Since only Zonaras mentions the deposition of this John, much greater credence must be given to Theophanes.

[Col. 1001C] From what we said concerning Pope Constantine, it is clear that John was not a Monothelite. Consequently, Gregory II could not have rejected his synodical letter. As soon as the tyrant Philippicus had been removed, John communicated his policy to Pope Constantine, apologized for it, and had not a few associates in it, among them Germanus, his successor in the see of Constantinople, and Andrew of Crete, men of great virtue.

It is not surprising that Baronius overlooked this, since he had not seen John’s letter to Constantine, published by Combefisius.

This John, then, according to the passages cited from Theophanes and Anastasius, and also according to Nicephorus in his *Chronicle*, died after occupying the see for three years. Thus he died in the year 715. In that same year, on 11 August, Saint Germanus, metropolitan of Cyzicus, was transferred to the government of the church of Constantinople.

Theophanes records this under the Alexandrian year of the Incarnation 707, which begins on the Kalends of September in the Dionysian year 714; the years of the emperors likewise begin on that day:

> “In the second year of the reign of Artemius, who was also called Anastasius, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eleventh day of August, Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan see of Cyzicus to Constantinople.”

We shall have to speak of him more than once below, because he resisted the emperor in defense of the holy images and was sent into exile.

### [Col. 1001D] Line 8.—“Here in Germany, etc.”

In the year 718 Saint Boniface, who had crossed from England into Frisia, went to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles. On 30 November, the day sacred to Saint Andrew the Apostle, Pope Gregory orally granted him the authority to announce the Gospel to the nations in Germany and declared him his legate.

For this reason both Willibald in his *Life* and Othlonus, who also wrote a *Life* of Boniface—the two works being reproduced by Mabillon in *Saeculum III of the Benedictines*, part II—take the beginning of his episcopate from that day. They use “episcopate” improperly for the office of preaching and call him a bishop because Gregory II made him a herald of the faith and legate of the apostolic see throughout Germany.

After receiving the apostolic letters concerning his legation, dated 15 May 719, Boniface came to Thuringia. From there he sailed to Frisia, and [Col. 1002A] while there sowing the seeds of the divine word, he drew very many people away from the error of idolatry, as Othlonus says in book I, chapter 10, of his *Life*. He remained there for three years and afterward preached in Hesse and Thuringia with the greatest success.

Later he informed Pope Gregory through one of his companions of the successful outcome of the preaching he had undertaken. Immediately invited to Rome by apostolic letters, he hastened there by long and rapid journeys. On the day before the Kalends of December he was ordained bishop by the same pope, in the year 723, as is established by a letter of Pope Gregory addressed, on the day after Boniface’s ordination, to all the Christians living in Germany; Willibald preserves it.

Gregory therefore consecrated Boniface as a bishop attached to no particular see, so that he might be strengthened by the authority of the apostolic dignity and might be more readily accepted by all in the office of preaching.

Gregory required Boniface to swear a solemn oath concerning the preservation of the integrity of the faith and the unity of the Church, and concerning the perpetual observance of [Col. 1002B] singular obedience to the pontiffs of the apostolic see. Boniface secured this oath with his own signature and, according to custom, placed it above the body of Saint Peter, as the aforementioned Othlonus reports in chapter 14.

I have said that Boniface was consecrated bishop but attached to no particular see. To understand this, one should observe with Serarius, note 25 on the *Life of Saint Boniface*, that two kinds of bishops and archbishops must be distinguished:

> “For some have a definite see, a definite place, and a fixed location; and their bishops or archbishops are named from that place. Others, however, have no definite see and no certain or fixed location. This latter kind is generally found among those peoples and in those provinces that have only recently begun to be incorporated into the faith of Christ.

> “Since those who announce the Gospel to them must run here and there and do not yet possess a flock gathered in any particular territory or city, they receive from the apostolic authority the episcopal power to ordain priests and place them in various locations, or even the archiepiscopal [Col. 1002C] power to create bishops. Meanwhile they wander among uncertain settlements, gathering for Christ Jesus, the true and supreme Shepherd of souls, as many sheep as they can from every direction.

> “These men are called, strictly and simply, bishops, or more generally bishops and archbishops of that region in which they labor and seek out the Lord’s flock.”

So writes Serarius.

That Saint Boniface was a bishop of the latter kind is clear from the two authors of his *Life*. Gregory sent Boniface back equipped with various letters of recommendation to Duke Charles, mayor of the palace of the Franks; to bishops and others of every rank, both clergy and laity; and to the clergy, nobles, and entire people of the Thuringians and Saxons, so that he might continue to discharge the apostolic office he had begun.

From a letter of that same Gregory to the clergy and people, which Othlonus reports together with five others, [Col. 1002D] book I, it is clear that the pontiff instructed Boniface not to presume to perform illicit ordinations; not to admit to sacred orders a bigamist, or one who had not married a virgin, an illiterate man, anyone defective in any part of his body, one formerly subjected to public penance, a curial official, anyone bound to any condition of servitude, or anyone branded with any mark of infamy; not to lay hands indiscriminately upon Africans; not to conduct ordinations except on the Saturday of the Four Ember Days; not to confer baptism outside Easter and Pentecost, except upon those in danger of death; to strive to increase the ministries, furnishings, and patrimonies of the churches, and never diminish them; and to distribute ecclesiastical revenues and offerings into four portions.

Those instructions seem to have been taken from a letter of Pope Gelasius I, his ninth, addressed to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, in the year 494, concerning which we dealt in that same place; as Cointius shows for the individual matters in the year 723, no. 17 and following, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*. [Col. 1003A] Yet Gregory, speaking of precautions against illicit ordinations, mentions Africans, about whom Gelasius is silent, and Gregory gives this reason: some of them had been proved to be Manichaeans, others to have been repeatedly rebaptized. Before crossing into Spain, the Saracens occupied Africa, and the displaced Africans, pouring into Europe, began to seek their livelihood through ecclesiastical orders. But because most of them were recognized as either Manichaeans or Donatists, a general law was enacted, as Baronius writes under the same year 723, forbidding any African to be ordained in any way by any bishop. There can be no doubt that by “Africans” Gregory means Donatists, since they were present in great numbers in Africa and stubbornly defended Anabaptism.

In the year 726, Gregory, consulted by Boniface on various matters, answered each point in a letter beginning *Desirabilem mihi*, said to have been given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, during the reign of the most pious lord Augustus Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, in the tenth year of his reign; and also under Constantine the great emperor, in the seventh year of his reign and the tenth indiction. From this indiction, which was current in November of the year 726, combined with Leo’s tenth imperial year, it is evident that the beginning of Leo’s reign was correctly assigned to the year 717.

For many centuries this practice of the Church and monasteries prevailed: boys, or infants, offered by their parents were permanently bound to monastic life, and were not permitted to renounce that state of life either before or after the years of puberty. There are quite a few examples of this practice among the Franks on both sides of the Rhine. When Boniface consulted Gregory about it, Gregory replied in these words:

“You have also added”—namely, in the seventh consultation—“that if a father or mother should hand over a son or daughter, during the years of infancy, within the enclosure of a monastery, to the discipline of the Rule, may they, after completing the years of puberty, leave and marry? We altogether avoid this, because it is unlawful that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.” [Col. 1003C]

What Gregory permits in his second response—that if a woman, overcome by illness, is unable to render the marital debt to her husband, the husband, if he cannot remain continent, may marry—must be understood as referring to a permanent impediment that was unknown when the marriage was contracted. Natalis Alexander reports Gregory’s responses to Boniface’s other consultations in the eighth century. Gratian wrongly attributed this letter to Gregory III. The remaining matters relating to the apostolate of Saint Boniface will be examined under Gregory III and Zachary.

**No. 179, line 16.—“That venerable image.”** When Artemius, later called Anastasius, had been crowned emperor on the fourth day of June in the year 713, as we said above, and had held the empire for two years and eight months, the soldiers revolted and chose another emperor for themselves, named Theodosius. Artemius was deposed and thrust into a monastery. Therefore Theodosius was proclaimed emperor around the beginning of the year 716. Since he was a Catholic, he made it his first concern to restore what the emperor Philippicus had destroyed: the noble monument on which the six ecumenical councils had been depicted. By doing this he so silenced the mouths of the heretics that all controversy about the faith ceased in that city.

Thus Baronius, following Anastasius in his account of Gregory II. But I am firmly convinced that Anastasius was deceived in this matter. Agatho the deacon expressly asserts, in the oft-cited peroration, both in his account of Agatho and in that of Conon, that it was the emperor Anastasius, not Theodosius, who restored in the imperial palace the image of the Sixth Council erased by Philippicus. As an eyewitness, Agatho deserves greater credence than Anastasius. After saying that Anastasius was called a pious and orthodox man and emperor, and that, with his approval and consent, Patriarch John had written to Pope Constantine, he adds:

“After the previously declared destruction of the complete image of the councils, with the image of the Sixth Council erased, that wretched and insane Bardanes, who had impiously ordered its abolition, had commanded himself to be depicted in the aforementioned chamber of Melios, standing upright in its midst together with Sergius, with only the five ecumenical councils remaining. Therefore, once both such persons had been removed from there, it was entirely necessary and most fitting that the same holy and ecumenical Sixth Council, together with the other five, should again be depicted there in its place; and that the entire God-loving assembly of the holy Church should rejoice together in common celebration and gladness, exulting spiritually in Christ and triumphing over the tranquillity and peace granted to the most holy Churches.”

See what was said about this act of Bardanes, or the emperor Philippicus, in the account of Pope Constantine. There, together with Baronius, we observed from Theophanes that he sent Michael, a priest of the Roman Church and *apocrisiarius*, to the emperor Anastasius, although Baronius here says that he was sent by Gregory II.

**No. 181, line 1.—“The fortress of Cumae as well.”** We have said that Pope Sisinnius seriously considered restoring the walls of the city of Rome and for that reason ordered lime-kilns to be fired. Anastasius asserts that Gregory II attempted the same thing at the beginning of his pontificate, but was prevented by various disturbances. The same author reports what those disturbances were and how they diverted him from his purpose. The Lombards, he says, seized and carried off a fortress belonging to the Roman Church under the pretext of peace. Since they could be moved neither by fear of divine vengeance nor by the gifts offered by Pope Gregory to induce its restoration, Gregory recovered it with the help of the duke and people of Naples, paying seventy pounds of gold for its redemption, as he had promised.

Paul the Deacon gives the same account in book VI, chapter 40, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*. He informs us that the fortress, which Anastasius does not name, was the fortress of Cumae, which the Lombard duke of Benevento had seized from the Church. The same Paul the Deacon, in chapter 42, also reports that at that time King Liutprand of the Lombards confirmed the restoration of the Cottian Alps already made to the Church while John VII was seated on the papal throne, as was said there. Bede adds, in *The Six Ages*, that Liutprand reclaimed the Cottian Alps from the Roman pontiff, but, upon the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, confirmed their restoration by Aripert.

**No. 182, line 4.—“At the same time the accursed race of the Hagarenes.”** By comparing Anastasius’s words in the Life of Gregory, where he says that the Saracens fought against Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, with what Paul the Deacon writes in book VI, chapter 46, of *The Deeds of the Lombards* concerning the Saracens’ entry into Aquitaine, the author of the *Critique of Baronius* rightly concludes that the battle took place in the year 725 and that Eudo won the victory with the help of a sponge sent to him by Gregory II. Anastasius says, speaking of Eudo’s letter to the pontiff:

“Adding that in the aforesaid year, when three sponges had been sent to them by the aforesaid man as a blessing—sponges such as are placed upon the pontiff’s table for use at meals—at the hour when the battle was joined, Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, distributed them to his people in small portions for them to consume; and not one of those who partook of them was wounded or killed.” [Col. 1004D]

Here Anastasius is speaking of the sponge with which the pontiff’s table was wiped, sent to Eudo and distributed as a blessing for the army. Frodoardus also speaks of the victory won through the aid of the sponge, in his book on the Roman pontiffs, under Gregory II:

> Foreign triumphs too, brought from afar,  
> The pope’s victorious Franks celebrate:  
> The sponge protects them from the Hagarenes’ arms,  
> While those who share the iron are neither wounded  
> Nor harmed by the weapon, a few lying prostrate,  
> Empty of such protection.

Frodoardus’s words plainly demonstrate that this battle between the Hagarenes, or Saracens, and the Franks, fought under Gregory II, was different from the battle fought in 732 under Gregory III. Concerning sponges, consult the *Thesaurus of the Latin Language* and Calepinus, under the word *spongia*, where you will find that the ancients prized sponges and used them in place of scrapers and towels for rubbing down and cleaning the body. Martial, book XIV, epigram 149, says that it was customary to use them to wipe tables:

> Perhaps this sponge is given to you for wiping tables.

**No. 188, line 1.—“After this he became famous,” etc.** In the earliest periods after the rise of the Christian religion, while pagan fury against it was still burning and superstition concerning idols still lay hidden in people’s minds, the use of sacred images was not as frequent as it later became. Nor, Dionysius Petavius observes in book XV of *Theological Dogmas*, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 13, were images found in temples and basilicas. Since images belong to the category of things that are not altogether necessary for salvation and do not pertain to the very substance of religion, it lies within the Church’s authority either to employ them or to set them aside, according to what it judges more expedient. Such things are commonly said to belong to positive law.

From this arose the reproach of the unbelievers expressed in these words by Minucius Felix, page 25:

“Why do they have no altars, no temples, no recognized images?”

Octavius replies to him, page 95:

“Do you think that we conceal what we worship because we have neither shrines nor altars? What image of God could I fashion, when, if you judge rightly, man himself is God’s image? What temple could I build, when this whole world, fashioned by his work, cannot contain him? And when I occupy a wider space, shall I enclose the power of such majesty within a single little building? Is it not better that he be dedicated in our mind and consecrated in the deepest part of our heart?”

Accordingly, some people then thought that it was not lawful to build temples to God, because this practice had not yet been established among the Christian people, and because, while the pagans still held power, it was not permitted; they regarded it as impious and unlawful. Concerning sacred images, too—and images very different from idols—most people seem to have held a similar opinion. Christians were gradually disabused of both views after experience and reason, their teacher, showed them that neither practice should be condemned, but that both could contribute to piety.

Therefore, once peace and freedom had been restored, they did not hesitate to build basilicas—or, as they eventually began to call them, churches—and altars in honor and worship of God, indeed magnificently and at great expense. Neither the former practice and ancient custom nor the authority of even great men deterred them from doing so. In the same period the Church also began to employ images of Christ and the saints, whose use had not previously become widespread, once there was no longer any danger of idolatry and once it seemed useful both for spreading the memory of Christ, the martyrs, and the other saints, and for encouraging the faithful, through their example, to steadfast piety.

It is by no means established that this was done in every place according to the same policy and at the same time. In some places it occurred earlier, in others later, according to the capacity and character of the nations and what those who governed them judged expedient. This must be observed all the more carefully because it applies to the interpretation of many ancient examples and testimonies that Protestants misuse in attacking the Church’s practice. Catholic theologians who resist them are sometimes excessively disturbed when it is established that images were rejected and condemned by the Orthodox, although this can suitably be explained according to the circumstances of place and time. Therefore, in the controversy over images, greater account ought to be taken of the examples and practices of the later Church than of those of the earlier Church.

While pagan superstition was still spreading with full force, it seemed preferable during those first centuries of the Church to suppress and omit many things that were not in themselves useless, and might even be beneficial, because there was a danger that the outward appearance of certain rites would cause offense by its similarity to practices celebrated by the pagans. This was done lest the images of Christ and the saints be taken by the ignorant and inexperienced for the idols to which they had been accustomed, and lest their minds be kept too closely attached to the custom and memory of empty images. It is therefore credible that Christians made little use of images during approximately the first four centuries, throughout which the accursed worship of demons in idols and the most savage persecution of the Christian name continued their course.

Only in the fifth century, after gaining freedom, when the Church began in a certain sense to stretch out her limbs, did images begin to be publicly displayed in most places and set up in temples and chapels. Until then, although they were used to some extent, they had not been employed indiscriminately or frequently. These and many other points about the use of images in the ancient Church are made by the Petavius cited above. Natalis Alexander demonstrates at length, in the eighth century, dissertation 6, that this use and veneration of images of Christ and the saints not only does not conflict with God’s law, but is consonant with religion and useful for arousing the piety of the faithful.

At the beginning of that same eighth century there arose in the East a dreadful monster, namely the heresy of the Iconoclasts, which declared war on the venerable images. The seventh synod, in its first and fifth sessions, testifies that its precursors had been pagans, Jews, Marcionites, Manichaeans, and Theopaschites. The Jews began this impious war in the year 723, when, at the command of Jezid, the Arab caliph, they removed the images of Christ and the saints from the Christian churches throughout the borders of his entire kingdom. Baronius reports this for that year from Theophanes and from the account of John the monk, vicar of the Eastern bishops, preserved in the same seventh synod, session five. From session four of that synod it is clear that this impiety passed from the Hebrews to the Christians through the agency of Constantine, bishop of Nacolia in Phrygia Salutaris. Expelled by his own diocesans, Constantine insinuated himself into the court of the emperor Leo the Isaurian and inflamed him against the holy images. The Jews also—those to whom Leo the Isaurian had sworn that, once he had been elevated to the empire, he would grant whatever they asked, and who had prophesied that he would become emperor—incited him to abolish the holy images and their veneration as though they were remnants of idolatry. This is testified by the Greek historians Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Constantine Manasses.

Just as pagan emperors had formerly issued edicts against Christians on the occasion of their decennial anniversaries, so Leo the Isaurian, as Zonaras says, having begun the tenth year of his tyranny, raised a persecution against the Orthodox in the twenty-sixth year of the Christian era after 700, that is, in 726, and declared war on the sacred images.

“After the tenth year of his reign”—that is, after it had begun, says Stephen the deacon of the Church of Constantinople in the Life of Saint Stephen the Younger, monk and martyr, which he wrote around the year 808 and which the Benedictine monk James Loppinus published in Greek and Latin in volume I of the *Greek Analecta*—“that new Belshazzar, Leo the Isaurian, breathed into the Church the Manichaean heresy and one perhaps not greatly unlike that of the Aphthartodocetists, if I may so speak. And so, having summoned the people subject to him, this inhuman beast, roaring like a lion before them, a notable bearer of the name Leo, belched forth and uttered from his angry heart, as though from Mount Etna fire and sulfur, this pitiable declaration: ‘Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped.’”

That this occurred only after Leo’s tenth year had begun, and not after it had ended—as Stephen the deacon seems to imply—is also clear from the anonymous author published by Combefisius among the writers of Byzantine history who wrote after Theophanes. In an invective composed to refute those who opposed the sound faith and the teaching of the holy and Orthodox Fathers, he testifies that Leo began to resist the truth in the ninth indiction, which coincided, until the Kalends of September, with the tenth year of his reign. This anonymous author was alive in the year 770.

[Col. 1007A] The monk Theosterictus, a disciple of Saint Nicetas, abbot of Medicius in Bithynia, famous for his defense of the sacred images and who died in exile in 824, observes that this heresy was most bitter from its very beginning. He wrote the life of this saint within the first five years after his death; Bollandus recited it under April 3. In it he says:

“Consider also this point: other heresies arose from bishops and lesser priests, but this one proceeded from the emperors themselves—you know, however, how great the difference is between kings and priests. Those other heresies grew by teaching and contradiction and gradually gained strength; this one, however, was exceedingly powerful from the beginning because of imperial authority.”

Nevertheless, a great disturbance was stirred up by the people as soon as Leo’s decree for the abolition of images appeared. Fearing for himself, the emperor concealed his sacrilegious design.

“‘My opinion,’ he said, ‘does not aim at their complete destruction. I say only that they ought to be placed higher, so that no one may touch them with his mouth and thus in some way offer insult to things worthy of honor.’”

By these tactics he was planning to abolish all veneration of images.

In the same year 726, Leo Augustus wrote to Pope Gregory that, if he wished to have the emperor’s favor, he should remove the images of the saints; Gregory II, in turn, wrote back to the emperor. This is testified by Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 49, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, as well as by Anastasius and Theophanes. But those letters have perished.

Afterward, when the emperor could obtain nothing from Gregory, he repeatedly plotted against the life of the holy pontiff through his exarchs, dukes, and other officials. But the Romans and Lombards, piously allied, preserved him unharmed from their treachery and attacks by their united strength:

“Romans and Lombards bound themselves together, as if by a chain of faith, like brothers, all desiring to endure a glorious death in defense of the pontiff, never willing to allow him to suffer harm, fighting for the true faith and the salvation of Christians,” says Anastasius.

The pontiff, as the same author adds,

“Giving thanks for the people’s good will according to the purpose of their minds, addressed them all in gentle speech, urging them to advance in good works toward God and to remain steadfast in the faith, and admonishing them not to abandon their love and loyalty to the Roman Empire.”

The emperor was hostile to Gregory II not only because of the new opinions that Gregory rejected, but also because he would not allow a new tax to be imposed in the Roman province. For this reason the emperor arranged for Gregory to be killed, first through Marinus, the *spatharius* and duke of the Romans, and afterward through Paul the patrician and exarch.

“Paul the exarch,” says Anastasius, “by the emperor’s command, attempted to kill that same pontiff because he prevented him from imposing a tax in the province.”

That tax was a form of capitation similar to the one imposed upon Sicily and Calabria, of which Theophanes speaks.

With all the steadfastness he could muster, [Col. 1007D] Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, resisted the impiety of Leo the Isaurian. Through one of the Church’s principal ministers he informed Leo that images had been produced from the beginning, after Christ’s ascension into heaven; that he would gladly die for them; and that anyone who dishonored Christ’s image cast the insult back upon the one whom it represented. He therefore set before Leo the tradition and practice of the holy Church and the honor paid to images, approved by the councils. He recalled the solemn promises Leo had made, when he was inaugurated emperor, not to overthrow the rites of the Church. He earnestly entreated him, by all that was sacred, not to permit the overthrow of the sacred images during his reign, adding that anyone who committed this crime would be a precursor of Antichrist. At last he left no stone unturned in attempting to draw him back from the impiety he had conceived.

These facts are established from another Life of the same Saint Stephen the Younger, monk and martyr. Baronius and others wrongly attribute it to Saint John Damascene; John Billius therefore appended it to the works of that saint, although it is in fact the genuine offspring of Metaphrastes, as Allatius teaches in his dissertation *On the Symeons*, page 126.

But the holy patriarch accomplished nothing. Indeed, in the year 730, on “the seventh day of January, the thirteenth indiction, the third day of the week,” says Theophanes under that Christian year, “the irreligious Leo held a ‘silence’”—that is, a meeting of the leading men convened by imperial command to deliberate on affairs of state—“against the holy and venerable images in the tribunal of the nineteen couches. He had summoned the most holy patriarch Germanus, believing that he could persuade him at last to subscribe to his decree abolishing the sacred images. But the brave servant of Christ did not yield in the least to Leo’s abominable design. Rather, rightly dividing the word of truth, he resigned the episcopate.”

Then the emperor sent satraps to the patriarchal residence,

“commanding them to drive the holy man out with blows and insults,”

as Stephen the deacon says in the aforementioned Life of Saint Stephen the Younger. Germanus withdrew to the Platanium, his ancestral house, intending to lead a private life. But shortly afterward, on Leo’s orders, he was carried from his house to a monastery far away and strangled, nearly a hundred years old, Stephen the deacon adds.

“After he had been expelled and had become a participant in monastic life, one could see the whole city, deprived of the Father’s honey-sweet teaching, giving vent to no small weeping and lamentation. Thus that day was not a day but darkness, weeping upon weeping, and woe upon woe, as the prophet says. In those same miserable days the impious Anastasius”—the disciple and fellow chamberlain of Saint Germanus—“seized the pontificate with the hand of impiety” (he was ordained, as Anastasius and the author of the *Miscella* write, on the twenty-second day of that same month of January) “by the force of soldiers, not by the suffrage of divine piety. He handed over everything belonging to the Church to the emperor’s palace.”

Saint Germanus was then in his ninety-fifth year, as is read in a letter written by Pope Gregory in that same year. He wrote various works, most of which remain unpublished. He is commemorated in the Greek *Menaea* on May 12.

“Then the tyrant,” the same author continues, “having received unrestricted power to disclose the heresy, immediately attempted to pull down and consign to the fire the holy and lordly image of Christ our God, which had been placed above the imperial courts and, because of its appearance, was called the Holy Bronze Image”—*Aenea*—“and he did accomplish this. Meanwhile, while it was being removed, honorable women, strengthened by divine zeal, rushed forward bravely. Seizing the ladder, they threw to the ground the *spatharius* who was removing the image and, having torn him apart, put him to death.

“After this they immediately hurried to the patriarchal residence and attacked the impious Anastasius with stones, saying: ‘Most impure head and enemy of the truth, did you invade the priesthood for this reason, that holy and sacred anathemas, or offerings, should be destroyed?’ Unable to endure this victory over himself, the profane man fled from the sight of the devout women and took refuge with the tyrant, persuading him to kill those holy women by the sword. This was done. They had entered into battle for Christ’s image and received from Christ himself the prize of victory, rejoicing with all the victorious saints in the kingdom of heaven.”

The martyrdom of these devout women and men is commemorated in the *Menaea* on August 9.

That image was preserved in the church dedicated to the Mother of God, called Chalcopratiana from the district of the city in which it had been built. Hence it is called sometimes Chalcopratina, sometimes Aerea or Aenea, and sometimes Antiphonetes, as though one should say “sponsor” or “surety.” Combefisius published, in his *History of the Monothelite Heresy*, page 613, a pious account of the Lord’s image at Chalкопrate, in which the origin of devotion toward that image is explained and the reason for its being called Antiphonetes is made clear.

Combefisius there conjectures that women had been permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and the altar area in that church, whereas in other churches throughout the East only ministers entered there, except when the emperor was about to make an offering, or when monks were being consecrated to God. He conjectures, I say, that under Leo the devout women arrogated to themselves entrance into the area in order to deter the emperor’s sacrilegious minister from his impious attempt. They wisely judged that what had been permitted for the sake of religion ought not, in this situation, to be preserved when it was being used against religion. Therefore, as a reward for that zeal, entry into the altar area of that church was made free for women, since they had forestalled so great a crime and pulled away the ladder.

Meanwhile the emperor Leo, having sent an edict ordering the images to be removed, promised Gregory II his favor if he subscribed to the impious definition; otherwise he threatened to expel him from his rank as quickly as possible. Gregory immediately prepared himself against the hostile disposition of the prince and warned the armies of the Pentapolis and Venice to guard themselves against that impiety:

“Accordingly,” says Anastasius, “the armies of the Pentapolis and Venice, moved by this, opposed the emperor’s command, and declared that they would never submit to the death of that pontiff, but would fight manfully all the more in his defense.”

The minds of all turned toward protecting the pontiff and withdrew from obedience to the exarch. Each, by his own choice, appointed leaders over himself, as the same Anastasius testifies:

“They subjected Paul the exarch—or those who had sent him—and his accomplices to an anathema, despising his appointment. Everywhere in Italy they all chose their own leaders, and thus all strove to preserve both the pontiff’s immunity and their own.”

From that time the Roman province, like the others, had a duke chosen according to its own judgment—that is, by the selection of the nobles—who exercised the same authority in administering the state as the dukes sent by the emperor.

The Italians wished to break out into open revolt and create a new ruler. But the pontiff intervened and, at the urging of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, restored friendship with Eutychius the exarch and, according to Anastasius, restored his authority in the city of Rome:

“Once the emperor’s wickedness became known, all Italy resolved to choose an emperor for itself and take him to Constantinople. But the pontiff restrained this plan, hoping for the prince’s conversion.”

And below:

“He admonished them not to abandon their love or loyalty to the Roman Empire.”

From this it is clear that Theophanes, and the Greek authors Zonaras and Cedrenus who followed him—being generally poorly informed about events in the West—wrote incorrectly that Pope Gregory had withdrawn Rome, Italy, and the other western provinces from Leo’s obedience and empire. For, besides what we have reported from Anastasius, Paul the Deacon also writes in book VI, chapter 49, of *The Deeds of the Lombards* that Gregory kept the peoples in the obedience and loyalty owed to the empire. More on this shortly.

In that same year 730, Gregory was informed by Saint Germanus, patriarch, about Leo’s heresy. Gregory replied in a letter inserted in the fourth session of the seventh synod. After receiving Leo’s own letters, he wrote two dogmatic letters to him worthy of the supreme pontiff. Theophanes speaks of them, writing that Gregory openly rebuked Leo in letters “known to many.” Baronius reproduces those letters under the year 726, believing that they were written then. But from what follows it will clearly be established that they were given in the year 730.
