When Leo saw that the Romans, Campanians, people of Ravenna, and inhabitants of the Pentapolis had defected from him and that discussions were under way about depriving him of the empire, he wrote again to the same pontiff and requested that a general council be convened. Gregory had broken off all correspondence with him because Leo had attempted to take his life. Nevertheless, Gregory replied to his letter and mocked him for insolently insulting and threatening him.

“You have written,” Gregory says in his first letter, “that a universal council should be convened, and that proposal has seemed useless to us. You are a persecutor of images, an insulting enemy, and a destroyer. Stop, and grant us this favor: be silent; then the world will enjoy peace and scandals will cease. . . . Do you not perceive that this attempt of yours, by which you have risen up against the images, is a turbulent, insolent, and arrogant crime? While the Churches of God enjoyed profound peace, you have raised battles, hatreds, and scandals. Stop and be quiet; then a synod will be entirely unnecessary. Write to everyone and to every region of the world to which you have been a cause of offense that Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, and Gregory, pope of Rome, have erred concerning the images; and we shall set you free from this matter, so that no sin or lapse may be attributed to you, since we have received from God the power to loose both heavenly and earthly things.”

Before this he had set out the limits prescribed for pontifical and imperial authority:

“You know, emperor, that the doctrines of the holy Church belong not to emperors but to pontiffs, who are accustomed safely to expound doctrine. For this reason pontiffs, abstaining from the affairs of the state, have been placed over the Churches. Therefore emperors likewise should abstain from ecclesiastical matters and attend to what has been entrusted to them.”

[Col. 1010B] It is certain that these dogmatic letters of Gregory to Leo were given in the year 730. In the first he says:

“You have stripped the Churches of God, which the holy Fathers had clothed and adorned; you have despoiled and stripped them bare, although you had such a pontiff—our lord, I mean, our brother and fellow minister Germanus. You ought to have obeyed his counsels as those of a father and teacher, and as those of an elder endowed with great experience both in ecclesiastical and civil affairs. For that man is now in his ninety-fifth year, having served every patriarch and emperor.”

Thus, when that letter was written to the emperor, Germanus was no longer in Constantinople and had resigned the pontificate. Yet Baronius himself admits that he resigned it only in the year 730.

Moreover, in that letter Gregory mentions the image of the Savior called Antiphonetes and the killing of the *spatharius* sent by the emperor to remove it, after he had struck the face of the Savior’s image three times with an axe. He also mentions the martyrdom of those holy women who, unable to endure that wicked deed, killed the *spatharius*. This occurred after Anastasius had occupied the see of Saint Germanus, as was soon demonstrated from the Acts of Saint Stephen the Younger. It therefore occurred in January of the year 730, in which year Gregory II’s aforementioned letters were written, after the beginning of September, when the fourteenth indiction began.

Not content with this, Pope Gregory held a synod at Rome. There, sitting and presiding with the neighboring bishops, he condemned the heresy of the Iconomachists and confirmed the Catholic faith concerning the holy images. Only one fragment of this synod survives, quoted by Pope Adrian I of Rome in his first letter to Charlemagne. Cedrenus and Zonaras also mention this synod. From them Baronius concludes that Gregory, seeing that the emperor had become thoroughly heretical, cursed him with an anathema at this synod, then caused the Romans and Italians to withdraw from his obedience, and forbade them to pay him tribute. Bellarmine, book V of *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 8; Sigonius, book III of *On the Kingdom of Italy*; and many others write the same.

**No. 189, line 8.—“With Leo and the emperor Constantine.”** While Saint Gregory was seated on the papal throne, a son was born to the emperor Leo in the year 718. He was later called Constantine and was given the additional title Copronymus because he defiled the sacred font when he was immersed as an infant. Saint Damascene, the noble defender of the sacred images, calls him “Cabalinus”—from horse dung—in his *Demonstrative Oration on the Sacred and Venerable Images*, because the most impure man took delight in its smell and touch.

In the year 720, on the third indiction, on Easter Day itself, as Theophanes writes, the emperor Leo made him his co-emperor. Therefore his years are reckoned from March 31, on which day Easter fell in that year.

[Note: [Col. 1011A]

### No. 178, line 1.—“In the time of this man John, bishop of Constantinople, etc.”

As soon as it was first heard at Constantinople that Gregory II had been raised to the highest dignity, John the patriarch wrote him a synodical letter, to which the supreme pontiff likewise sent his reply. Some more recent writers, who have neither seen nor considered the patriarch’s apology, portions of which we have presented in our account of Constantine, have regarded him, on Zonaras’s authority, as a Monothelite. For this reason, they say, Gregory rejected his synodical letter, and afterward the emperor Anastasius drove him from his see. But apart from the fact that his apologetic letter makes this opinion wholly improbable, other very authoritative writers, better informed about these matters than Zonaras, explicitly report that Patriarch John died after occupying the see for three years, and that Germanus, bishop of Cyzicus, was appointed his successor (Theophanes, *Anastasius*, in the same version; Nicephorus, *Chronicle*).

### [Col. 1011B] Line 8.—“Here in Germany through Bishop Boniface, etc.”

The more illustrious herald of the Gospel in the age of Gregory II was undoubtedly the Englishman Winfrid, later famous under the name Boniface, who is regarded as the apostle of the Germans. He had taken monastic vows; then, preferring the ministry of a preacher of the Gospel to the dignity of abbot that had been offered to him, he fled to Gregory’s feet to obtain authority to announce the Gospel to the nations. The pontiff, moved both by the testimony of the bishop of Winchester, whose subordinate Boniface was, and by Boniface’s personal merits, which became evident in frequent conversation, granted him an apostolic diploma. By it he gave him power to preach the faith to idolaters and ordered him, according to the rite of the Roman Church, to baptize those who were converted and to inform the Holy See of everything that appeared necessary for completing the work he had undertaken.

> “Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Boniface, a religious priest. The evident and pious intention of your religious purpose, burning in Christ, and the most sincere report of your approved faith, which has been brought to us, requires that we employ you as a fellow minister in the administration of the divine word, whose care we undertake through the grace of God,” etc. (Gregory II, Letter 1, to Boniface).

And indeed, after carrying out his ministry with very happy success in Frisia, Hesse, and Thuringia, Boniface reported this to the pontiff, who wished him to come to Rome to give an oral account of his affairs. He therefore came, and afterward, having been made a bishop, returned with letters of recommendation from Gregory to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Franks; to the bishops; to the clergy of the second rank; to the nobles; to the magistrates; and finally to the peoples of the provinces that I have just mentioned (Gregory II, Letters 2–7).

He later sent him another letter (Letter 8), beginning: “Moved by the anxious care of the charge entrusted to us, and also by evangelical instruction, etc.,” in order to support him in his apostolic ministry and encourage him to persevere. In a decretal addressed to him, in which he responds to certain points of discipline, he first commends him for consulting, concerning matters pertaining to the Church, the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and of the episcopate. Then he says that he is not making a decision as though from himself, but under the inspiration of him who gave speech to many and made even children eloquent:

> “In your letter,” he says (Letter 13), “you appended certain chapters, asking how this holy apostolic Roman Church holds or teaches these matters. You have done very well, since the blessed apostle Peter was the beginning both of the apostolate and of the episcopate; and, because you have consulted us concerning the condition of the Church, we say—not from ourselves, but by the grace of him who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent—how the doctrines of apostolic vigor ought to be held,” etc.

In this decretal Gregory restricts the impediment to marriage to the fourth degree of consanguinity. To a man who has a wife incapable of marital relations he permits the taking of another wife, provided that he also supply support for the first. He permits priests to purge themselves by oath of crimes of which they had been lightly accused and for which there were no certain witnesses.

He prohibits priests, even if unworthy, from repeating the sacrament of confirmation; consecrating a second chalice in the sacrifice of the Mass; eating food offered to idols; permitting marriage to sons whom their parents had dedicated to a religious life; and rebaptizing those who had already been baptized with the legitimate form. He nevertheless wishes children who have been taken from their parents to be baptized, unless it is clear that they had already been baptized after their abduction. He does not wish the Eucharist to be denied to lepers on the pretext that eating with them is forbidden. He says that it is foolish to withdraw from monasteries or churches infected with contagion, as though God’s hand could thereby be avoided. He teaches that one ought not to shun the customary association and table of ecclesiastics and illustrious men who are rife with vices, since such contact often contributes more to recalling them to their duty than correction and reprimand do.

### No. 179, line 1.—“At that time Liutprand, etc.”

In the time of this holy pontiff many supreme rulers testified to their exceptional reverence for the Holy See. Theodo II, duke of Bavaria, whom Saint Rupert, bishop of Salzburg, had converted to the Catholic faith, was the first of all the German princes to come to Rome out of piety, in order to visit Saint Peter and his successor, the supreme pontiff.

But in piety King Ina of the English must be preferred to Theodo. He not only came to Rome to visit the tombs of the apostles, as Bede records (*Ecclesiastical History of the English*, Book V, chapter 7), “after he had held the rule of that people for thirty-seven years”; before departing from the city, he is also said “to have granted a penny from each household of his kingdom to blessed Peter. This was long called by the English Romescot, but in Latin Peter’s penny” (Ranulf of Chester, Book, chapter 24).

While Ina was in Rome, he obtained permission from the pontiff to build a house that they called the School of the English.

> “To this house,” says Matthew of Westminster, “the kings of England and the royal family, together with bishops, priests, and clerics, were to come to be instructed in Catholic doctrine and faith, so that nothing harmful or contrary to Catholic truth might be taught in the English Church; and, strengthened in stable faith, they might return to their own country. He also built a church” (for the English clergy to serve, and in which the English who died in Rome were to be buried). “And in order that all these things might obtain the strength of perpetual stability,” he continues, “it was established by a general decree throughout the entire kingdom of the West Saxons, in which the aforesaid Ina reigned, that every year one penny from each household should be sent to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, so that the English residing there might receive from it the support necessary for life.”

Anastasius speaks at length of Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, imploring the aid of the Apostolic See against the Saracens and obtaining an astonishing victory after the pontifical blessing; of the Lombard king Liutprand restoring to the Apostolic See the Cottian Alps, which he had recently invaded; and finally of the usurpations of the Lombards in Benevento. The most illustrious archbishop Sommier sets these matters forth in the French language, recounting together the services rendered by princes to the Holy See.

### No. 184, line 4.—“The emperor therefore later issued orders that no image …”

III. The archbishop Sommier gives a lengthy account of the history of the Iconoclasts, which I shall present in full below, at No. 188, in the notes of Pagius. For the moment I shall excerpt it from the same archbishop’s *Dogmatic History*, Book VIII, chapter 24.

The law and institution of the Iconoclasts was to reject the veneration of images of Christ and the saints and to accuse the invocation of the saints and their relics of superstition. Leo the Isaurian is commonly regarded as the heresiarch. Constantine Manasses says of him:

> “The accursed emperor was giving birth to those absurd and novel plans against Christ; but he could in no way bring forth the offspring of his wickedness, since a timid spirit recalled him from his purpose.”

Indeed, before giving birth to the crime he had conceived, in the very year in which he was made emperor and afterward every year, he always sent Gregory Catholic letters. Gregory himself testifies to this in his first letter to the emperor:

> “We carefully preserve your letters, received over eleven indictions, deposited in the holy church at the threshold of the confession of Saint Peter, holy and glorious prince of the apostles, where also are preserved the letters of the predecessors who loved Christ and ruled piously.”

In those letters Leo had promised the pontiff that he would never depart from the rules of the orthodox faith.

> “But after the tenth year of his reign that new Balthasar … uttered that pitiable cry and declared: ‘Since the making of images is an idolatrous art, they ought not to be worshiped’” (Jacob Loppin, *Analecta*, vol. I, *Life of Saint Stephen, Monk and Martyr*).

Nevertheless, the emperor remained silent for some time because of the disturbances that had arisen at Constantinople over this matter, while the holy patriarch Germanus was working above all to avert the impious deed. At last, however, he disclosed his mind in the senate and dared to persuade the pontiff to eliminate the sacred images. Thinking that the supreme pontiff’s paternal admonition wounded his majesty, he repeatedly sent men to Rome to kill him.

He expelled Saint Germanus from the patriarchal residence, threw down the image of Christ that Constantine the Great had erected in the vestibule of the palace, and sent orders everywhere to his subjects, especially those living in Italy, that they should consume the sacred images by fire—shameful even to say—and should kill the pontiff if he resisted.

Then Saint Gregory was obliged to strengthen Catholics everywhere in the faith by his letters against the heresy. By God’s singular favor it happened that he heard that everyone had bound himself by oath to defend the faith and the life of the pontiff. The Lombards also, whom the impious emperor was trying to draw to his side, generously rejected his gifts and made a pact with the Italians in order to defend the pious cause.

Their king Liutprand, indeed, enticed by the hope of obtaining the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento and promised assistance by the exarch—assistance that he truly did obtain—made a pact with the exarch and in turn gave him aid for the conquest of the city of Rome. But when the exarch surrounded Rome with his forces, and the pontiff was deprived of all human assistance—for the allied forces of Italy were insufficient—God protected him. By fasts and prayers, both private and public, the pontiff had rendered God favorable to himself.

Trusting in him, he left the besieged city and went to the hostile king. By his gracious speech he so moved him that the king, overcome, fell at the pontiff’s feet and promised that he would harm no one. Thereafter, full of obedience and reverence, he did everything that the *Liber Pontificalis* recounts with sufficient clarity.

### No. 188, line 13.—“By warning letters, unless they converted to the Catholic faith, etc.”

When Leo perceived that the provinces of Italy belonging to the West had defected from the empire and that all the dukes had chosen leaders of their own, threatening to elect a new Augustus whom they would bring to Constantinople, he wrote to the Roman pontiff asking him to summon an ecumenical council.

But the pontiff, despising the emperor’s plan, replied:

> “You have written that a universal council should be summoned, and this seemed to us a useless undertaking … You are a persecutor of images, an insulting enemy, and a destroyer. Stop, and grant us this favor: be silent. Then the world will enjoy peace and scandals will cease … Suppose that we had obeyed you, that bishops from the whole world had been assembled, and that the senate and council had taken their seats. Where is the lover of Christ and pious emperor who, according to custom, ought to sit in the senate, count those who speak correctly, and dismiss those who babble things contrary to the truth, when you, emperor, waver and imitate barbarians?” (Gregory II, Letter 1 to Leo).

Meanwhile the pontiff wished a synod to be held at Rome. There, after defending the veneration of sacred images and the invocation of the saints by the authority both of Sacred Scripture and of the Fathers and by the custom introduced into the Church through the piety of the faithful, he condemned the contrary doctrine as an insane opinion and a most pernicious heresy.

> “The Lord Gregory II, junior pope, in his holy council, with the same supreme and most blessed Lord Gregory pope presiding in person, likewise said … because we see many disturbing the ordinances of the Church with troubled minds, we wish, to restrain the madness of error, to say something further from the ancient documents,” etc. (*Fragment of the Roman Council III*, in the letter of Adrian I to Charlemagne).

Only a fragment of this council survives in Adrian I’s letter to Charlemagne. Greek writers contemporary with these events—Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Zonaras—nevertheless report, as do most recent writers who follow them, that Leo was excommunicated in that council and that the Italians were released from their oath of allegiance to him.

> “Gregory,” says Zonaras, “who at that time governed the Church of Old Rome, rejected association with the ruler of New Rome, namely the emperor Leo, and with those who followed him; he bound them together with the emperor by a synodical anathema, prohibited the payment of the taxes that had until then been sent from there, and made a pact with the Franks.”

Other more recent writers, however, think otherwise. They teach that Leo was neither excommunicated nor deposed in that synod. They say that he was not separated from communion because the Latin writers Paul the Deacon and Anastasius the Librarian, who knew these affairs that were taking place at Rome better than the Greeks, are silent about the matter.

Nor, they maintain, was he deposed—a position that seems more probable—for these same Latin authors explicitly report that Gregory the pontiff continually resisted the will of the people and of the Italian armies to raise a new Augustus in Leo’s place, since Gregory had come to hope that the emperor might at some point be converted.

> “The entire army of Ravenna,” says the Deacon (*Book VI, chapter 49*), “and likewise that of Venetia, resisted such orders with one mind; and unless the pontiff had forbidden them, they would have undertaken to set up an emperor over themselves.”

And Anastasius says (No. 184):

> “All Italy formed a plan to choose an emperor for itself and bring him to Constantinople, but the pontiff restrained this plan, hoping for the conversion of the ruler.”

What we know with certainty about the same matter is clear from Gregory’s frequently cited first letter:

> “We invoke Christ, the prince of the whole army of creation, seated in heaven, who is above all the armies of the heavenly powers, that he may send a demon against you, as the Apostle says, ‘to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.’”

From these words it seemed impossible to understand anything other than excommunication.

As for Gregory’s dogmatic letters, in the first he admonishes the emperor concerning the reason God forbade the Israelites to worship images: namely, to turn their minds away from idolatry, on account of which he was sending the peoples of the Promised Land into destruction. When Moses asked the Lord to grant that he might behold him through a visible image, God did not grant him this favor. But in the fullness of time the Son of God, clothed in human flesh, made himself visible in all the mysteries he had accomplished for our redemption.

Those who had seen Jesus Christ represented him by the same image through which they had recognized him. Likewise, the images of the saints James, Stephen, and the other martyrs had been produced by those who had seen them. Catholic worship, however, was not confined to such images, nor was hope placed in them. Rather, Gregory said that when Catholics looked upon the image of Jesus Christ, they turned to Jesus Christ himself and said:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, help us, save us.”

Likewise, when looking at the image of the blessed Virgin, they said:

> “Holy Mary, Virgin Mother of God, intercede for us with the Lord, that he may save us.”

And similarly with the other images of the saints.

Leo had brought upon himself universal hatred and even the contempt of little children learning their catechism by declaring war on the sacred images. Gregory wished to use, as Roman pontiff, the power and authority that he had received from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in order to punish Leo:

> “But since,” he says, “you have brought a curse upon yourself, keep it for yourself together with your counselors, whom you embrace … Write that Gregory, Roman pope, has prayed concerning the images; and we shall make you free from this care, so that there may be no sin or fall on your part, since we have received from God the power to loose both heavenly and earthly things.”

He continues by teaching that bishops, not emperors, define doctrine. He declared himself before God and men absolved from the charge of idolatry that the emperor attributed to him for venerating images. He declared that he and his successors, the Roman pontiffs, would always be arbiters and mediators of peace between East and West, whatever evils Leo might threaten.

And if Leo should send to Rome, as he boasted, men who would overthrow the image of Saint Peter, Gregory said that he did not claim to know what would happen. Nevertheless, he protested that he would be innocent of the future shedding of blood, for which the emperor alone would be responsible.

In the second dogmatic letter he testifies to Leo of the profound grief with which he was afflicted because Leo persisted in error. He then sets before him the examples of his predecessors, who, together with the pontiffs, had arranged for councils to be held.

He says that it was not emperors but pontiffs who defined the doctrines of the faith. Just as the pontiff does not interfere in the affairs and duties of the imperial household, so the emperor ought not to interfere in ecclesiastical matters, choose or consecrate ministers of the altar, celebrate the sacred mysteries, or finally partake of them without the ministry of priests.

In political affairs, secular rulers punish crimes by confiscation of property, capital punishment, or exile. In the Church, however, after confessing their crimes, people are punished by fasts, vigils, and prayers; afterward they are admitted to communion in the body and precious blood of Jesus Christ and are fully reconciled with the Lord.

Emperors distinguished by religion and piety were, like other men, willingly subject to such laws. Leo, by contrast, after rebellion and crimes, used force and arms to afflict the supreme pontiff and plotted against his life. Finally, since he had always rejected the pontiff’s salutary admonitions and instructions and was certainly devoted to the perverse and condemnable doctrine of the heretics, he would undoubtedly have his share with them unless the merciful God called him to repentance.

### [Note: Col. 1015C]

### No. 181, line 10.—“With Theodimus the subdeacon and administrator.”

Theodimus was a regional subdeacon and administrator, in the name of the Apostolic See, of the diaconia of Saint Andrew at Naples. In those places where the Roman Church possessed estates, diaconiae had been established, in which alms were distributed by a subdeacon who administered the patrimony. For, as many letters of Saint Gregory the Great teach us, it was the duty of subdeacons to care for the poor of the diaconia.

This Theodimus was buried at Naples, in the same church of Saint Andrew, called “at the Nest.” On a marble tablet before the altar there is the following funerary inscription:

> “O holy apostle Andrew, gladly receive the bones, decayed by corrupting putrefaction, of one who flees to your aid and, out of longing for your favor, made the walls of your court shine with wondrous beauty.
>
> “With your aid, may wretched flesh, once the bonds of hell have been broken, be able to rise again from here, and, on the day of judgment, when criminal sins have been trampled down, may it receive divine joys through your intercession, martyr Andrew.
>
> “Here in peace lie the remains of Theodimus, regional subdeacon and rector of the Holy Apostolic See, and steward of this diaconia of blessed Andrew.
>
> “If anyone should presume to violate this tomb, he shall be bound by the chain of anathema.”

### No. 182, line 17.—“He instituted that during Lent, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Masses should take place in the churches, which had not been done.”

What Walafrid Strabo, a contemporary of Anastasius, reports (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 120) can shed light on this passage of Anastasius, although the two accounts appear in some respects to conflict. Anastasius says that Gregory II instituted fasting and the celebration of Mass on Thursday, which had not previously been customary. Strabo, however, says that Gregory II instituted a proper Mass, whereas previously, on Thursday, the Mass of the preceding Sunday had been repeated.

Strabo’s words are:

> “Because Melchiades, the thirty-third in order to govern the Roman see, decreed that no Christian should in any way fast on Sunday or Thursday—for pagans frequently observed something resembling fasts on those days—therefore blessed Gregory, in arranging the offices of the year, left Thursday within Lent vacant, so that, because it was festive like Sunday, it might also be celebrated with the office of Sunday.
>
> “But because this Thursday afterward began, like the others, to be devoted to fasting, Gregory the Younger”—that is, Gregory II—“decreed that it should be solemnized with Masses and prayers; that is, that it should have its own proper Masses, as the other weekdays of Lent do, and, gathering materials from various places, he increased the offices of that day.”

The *Micrologus*, who wished to conceal himself under a humble name, nearly transcribed Strabo’s words and added (chapter 50):

> “Especially from the Sunday Gospels, passages are still found assigned to Thursdays.”

Cardinal Bona (*Liturgical Matters*, part I, chapter 18, no. 12) reconciles Anastasius with Strabo in this way. He thinks that Anastasius means that Thursday was held without any special honor until Gregory II decreed that during Lent fasting and Mass should be observed on it, as on the other regular weekdays.

Strabo, however, means that outside Lent Thursday long remained without its own solemn office, and that if anyone wished to celebrate the sacrifice privately on that weekday, he used the Mass of the preceding Sunday.

If anyone finds the explanation given by Strabo less convincing—namely, that Saint Gregory I left Thursday vacant in arranging the offices because pagans frequently observed something resembling fasts on that day, although his assertion can be supported by canon 15 of the Council of Narbonne in 589, where, against certain people who superstitiously celebrated the day called Thursday, it was decreed that, unless some feast occurred, that day should pass without any religious rite—let him read Abbot Grimold in the preface to the *Book of Sacraments* published by Pamelius (volume II of the *Liturgies*). Grimold assigns a much clearer reason why certain days lack an office in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great:

> “As we have learned from the report of some people,” says Grimold, “the apostolic lord completely abstains from stations on those days, because, wearied by keeping stations on the other weekdays, he rests on those days, so that, free from the commotion of the people, he may more freely distribute alms to the poor and attend to external affairs.”

Grimold’s statement is confirmed by the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory in the same edition of Pamelius. Where certain days are noted as vacant, these words are added:

> “The lord pope gives alms.”

Christian Lupus, in his notes on the Trullan canons (canon 52), thinks Strabo was mistaken when he said that Saint Gregory I had left Thursday within Lent vacant in arranging the offices. He held that on all the days of Lent, except Good Friday and Holy Saturday, the Latin Church celebrated the full sacrifice of the Mass.

To support his opinion this distinguished author adduces two arguments. The first is chapter 4 of Innocent I’s letter to Decentius of Gubbio, where it says:

> “The tradition of the Church holds that during these two days the sacraments of the Church are not celebrated at all.”

But I do not see what can be established from this passage of Innocent, since the sole purpose of the holy pontiff there is to show that one must fast not only on Friday but also on Saturday; he is not enumerating the days without liturgy on which the Roman Church lacked Masses.

The second argument is that Masses assigned to Thursdays are found in the Sacramentary of blessed Gregory the Great. But this learned man did not notice that Grimold warns that everything in Gregory’s Sacramentary marked with little strokes was added after Gregory’s time, including the Masses assigned to Thursdays.

Indeed, it is certain that in the ancient books of the Sacraments, as well as in the Lectionaries and Calendars, no Mass or Gospel is found assigned to Thursday, either during Lent or outside Lent, throughout the entire year—except, after Saint Gregory II, during Lent alone and in the octave of Easter. This may also be seen in the Calendar published by Fronto; consult him in the places mentioned above, paragraph 6.

### Line 21.—“Meanwhile, they besieged Constantinople for two years.”

Besides the Latin writers, the Greeks Theophanes and Nicephorus mention this famous siege, in which Masalmas, commander of the Saracens, blockaded Constantinople with land forces, while the caliph Suliman blockaded it with his fleet. During the first year of the siege, Suliman died on 2 October and was succeeded in the caliphate by Omar II, the twelfth caliph according to Langlet’s chronological tables, as Elmacin writes in his *Saracen History*. Theophanes and Nicephorus testify that the imperial city was liberated through the special protection of the Mother of God.

The city, dedicated to the Mother of God, venerated her with intense devotion in many places, but most frequently of all at Blachernae, where an august church had been dedicated in her name. The Greek Church annually commemorates the city’s deliverance in the Menaion on 18 Kalends of September. In the *Menologion* of Basil Porphyrogenitus, first printed at Urbino in elegant form, the event is expressed in the following Latin translation:

> “In the reign of Leo the Isaurian, a numerous army of Saracens came and surrounded Constantinople by land and sea, intending to crush that city by siege. When they perceived that the emperor was being driven into the straits of necessity and believed that he was prepared to come to terms with them, they thought that they could also impose a garrison upon the city.
>
> “But the Lord, who resists the proud, rendered their plan useless. When the prince of that people discovered that he was accomplishing nothing, he asked that he at least be permitted to enter through the Bosphorus Gate while mounted on horseback. Although others entered without difficulty, his horse alone rose up and could not pass inside.
>
> “Then, raising his eyes and seeing above the gate an image of the Mother of God, he understood that this had happened to him because he had uttered blasphemies against her. Thus they returned without accomplishing their purpose. When they reached the Aegean Sea with their ships, they perished, struck by a violent hailstorm.”

The Greeks commemorate this favor each year with the celebration called **τῆς ἀκαθίστου**, “of the one who is not seated”: they remain standing throughout the entire night, singing hymns and songs without sitting. See Codinus, *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople* (chapter 12, no. 10), and note 13 on that work in the royal edition. See also the most learned Father Combefis in the *Supplement to the Library of the Holy Fathers* (volume II), where he made public a historical oration on the liberation of Constantinople, from which further material concerning this matter may be gathered.

### [Note: Col. 1017D]

### No. 182, line 12.—“Having sent three sponges, which were placed for the use of the pontiff’s table.”

After the three sponges sent to him by Pope Gregory II had been cut into pieces and distributed individually among the soldiers—sponges “which were placed for the use of the pontiff’s table,” or, as other manuscripts read, “which pontiffs used for the use of their table”—Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, destroyed 375,000 Saracens, without losing a single one of his own men who had received a portion of those sponges.

I think it necessary to explain what should be understood by these sponges said to have been used at the pontiff’s table. Francis Pagius, in his *Brief Account of the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, in the Life of Gregory II, says that Anastasius is speaking here of a sponge with which the pontiff’s table was wiped, which was sent to Eudo and distributed as a blessing for the army. He adds the following comment:

> “Concerning sponges, one should consult the *Thesaurus of the Latin Language* and Calepinus, under the word *spongia*, where one will find that the ancients counted sponges among their luxuries, using them in place of scrapers and linen cloths for rubbing and cleaning their bodies.”

It was excellently done, then, for Saint Gregory II to send Eudo, in place of a blessing, sponges that he had used as luxuries and with which, in place of a scraper, he had rubbed and cleaned his body.

No less successfully did Joseph Maria Suaresius, bishop of Vaison, a man otherwise of extensive and distinguished learning, explain this obscure passage of Anastasius in a short work on the annual washing of the great altar of the basilica of Saint Peter. There he says:

> “Writing was erased with a sponge, as Suetonius reports in chapter 20 of his *Life of Caligula*. Hence Augustus replied to his friends that his Ajax had lain upon a sponge, according to the same Suetonius, chapter 85. Those three sponges therefore signified that the Agarenes would be erased unto destruction, and the piety of the commander and soldiers preserved them safe and unharmed.”

That is, the soldiers of Eudo, among whom portions of the sponges were distributed, would have been erased—not the Agarenes, whom the sponge did not touch.

I think the most illustrious bishop Jean-Christophe Battel struck the matter exactly in his book published at Rome in 1702, in which he explains and illustrates the rite of the annual washing of the high altar of the Vatican basilica on Maundy Thursday. After recounting the sacred and secular uses of sponges and mentioning the deed of Eudo, described by Eudo himself in a letter addressed to Gregory II, he adds:

> “But what the ancient use of sponges at the pontiff’s table may have been has until now been unknown to us. This, however, we certainly and plainly know: in our times such sponges are no longer placed either at the pontiff’s spiritual or bodily table. Nevertheless, we reasonably suppose that sponges of this kind used to be employed when the pontiff celebrated solemn Mass, for wiping the vessels of the sacred table, which are now wiped with purificators and linen cloths.
>
> “For such was, and still is, the use of sponges among the Greeks, both in solemn Mass and in the washing of the holy table on Maundy Thursday, as we have shown above. Indeed, the patriarch customarily distributes to the people, as a blessing, sponges used in washing the sacred table, since they are believed to have drawn holiness and divine power from contact with the altar, as Goar explains in his notes on that rite, no. 13.
>
> “Anastasius records that Gregory II did the same when he says that he sent the sponges of the pontifical table to the duke of the Franks as a blessing.”

But if I may add something to Battelli’s explanation, I would not think it improper to understand the sponges sent by the pope—mentioned by Anastasius in that context as being for the pope’s use at table—as having been among those which the pope himself had used in the solemn washing of the altar on which he celebrated Mass. It is a most ancient rite of the Vatican Basilica, which that same basilica still religiously retains and observes: on the day of the Lord’s Supper, to wash the high altar with wine, sweep it with sprinklers, and finally wipe it carefully, first with sponges and then with small cloths.

The ancient collectors of rites remember this rite: Isidore of Seville, Book I, *On Divine, or Ecclesiastical, Offices*; Alcuin, *On Divine Offices*; Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; and Rabanus Maurus, Book II, *On the Instruction of Clerics* [Col. 1019A]—men who flourished from the sixth through the eighth and ninth centuries. This high altar of the Vatican Basilica stands above, as they say, the confession of Saint Peter, or the lower chapel in which the sacred relics of Saints Peter and Paul are venerated. Apart from the supreme pontiff, no one may celebrate Mass upon it unless the supreme pontiff has granted him permission, and even then only after a special bull has first been issued and affixed near the altar itself, as the *Roman Order* prescribes, no. 15, in Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 455. Peter Amelius, article 17, under the title “On the Circumcision of the Lord,” says:

> “The Roman pontiffs have always been accustomed to celebrate this Mass. … Note also: if the pope is in the city on this day and does not celebrate, but has the Mass said by some cardinal in the church of Saint Peter, before the cardinal vests, the bull is to be presented explaining how the pope dispenses with the requirement, so that he may celebrate upon the altar of Saint Peter. It hangs before the royal doors throughout the whole day; and likewise in all the other Masses celebrated upon it.”

What wonder, then, if this altar is properly [Col. 1019B] called the pope’s altar? But is the altar the same thing as the table? Both terms are used interchangeably. Anastasius, in the *Life of Stephen IV*, no. 294, says:

> “He decreed that every Sunday the solemn Mass should be celebrated upon the altar of blessed Peter by the seven cardinal bishops serving weekly, who observe the solemnities of the Mass in the church of the Savior.”

There was, moreover, in the Lateran church a wooden table held in great honor and formerly consecrated by the frequent liturgies of blessed Peter. The *Roman Order*, designated no. 10, in the aforementioned Mabillon, vol. II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 99, states:

> “If the pontiff is at the Lateran, after the *Credo in unum Deum* has been sung, and before he enters to offer the sacrifice, the deacons lift the table from the altar—here one is distinguished from the other—with the coverings folded over it; and with reverence and every devotion it is carried back from there to the chapel of Saint Pancratius, beside the canons’ cloister, because that is the place of reservation. It is kept there with every precaution until Saturday.”

[Col. 1019C] We therefore have the sponges, the pope’s table, and the sacred use of sponges in wiping that same table. What more do we seek for a fuller understanding of Anastasius’s text? That the sponges could have been sent by the pope to the pious Frankish duke Eudo as something consecrated, or as though they were holy relics—having in some way been consecrated through contact with the altar placed above the tomb of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—is demonstrated by many similar examples from that period: cloths laid upon the body of blessed Peter, and keys taken from the body of Saint Peter, which Gregory the Great mentions more than once in letters sent to eminent men; and the golden keys of which Gregory of Tours speaks in Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*:

> “Many also make golden keys for the venerable grating of the blessed tomb; those who carry them receive them first as a blessing, and by them they heal the infirmity of the afflicted.”

**No. 188, line 1.—“For after this the emperor’s wickedness became clear.”** Natalis Alexander, in Dissertation 1 on the *Ecclesiastical History of the Eighth Century*, vol. V, p. 733, denies that Gregory II, because of the abolition of the veneration of sacred images, led the peoples of Italy away from obedience to the emperor Leo the Isaurian and forbade them to pay him tribute thereafter. He relies on the authority of Paul the Deacon, Book VI, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 49, who says:

> “All the armies of Ravenna and of Venetia alike resisted such commands with one accord; and, unless the pope had restrained them, they would have attempted to set up an emperor over themselves.”

He also relies on Anastasius, who says, no. 184:

> “When the emperor’s wickedness became known, all Italy resolved to choose an emperor for themselves and bring him to Constantinople; but the pope restrained this plan, hoping for the prince’s conversion.”

And no. 185:

> “With gentle speech he entreated them all to advance in good works toward God and to persevere in the faith, but he warned them not to abandon their love for, or their loyalty to, the Roman Empire.”

He also [Col. 1020A] quotes letters sent by Gregory himself to Leo, in which the pontiff threatens neither to turn the peoples away from allegiance to the emperor nor to obstruct the payment of tribute, but declares himself unarmed and defenseless and says that, if an attack should occur, he will withdraw to nearby Campania and invoke Christ, asking that the fate which befell the incestuous Corinthian offender under blessed Paul might befall the emperor. Yet, he adds, it was wholly unbecoming for a most holy bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures, to involve himself in popular disturbances, urge the people toward revolt, and withdraw them from the obedience owed even to a heretical emperor.

Francis Pagi agrees with Natalis in the *Life of Gregory II*, where he says:

> “So far was Gregory from driving the Italians and Romans to revolt, or preventing them from paying their tax, that he kept the armies of Ravenna and Venetia, which were prepared for rebellion, within their allegiance.”

He then repeats the same evidence that Natalis had used.

I readily concede that matters stood thus before the emperor’s wickedness became manifest [Col. 1020B], as Anastasius says. The most holy pontiff wished patiently to endure the injuries inflicted upon him by the impious emperor, even at the risk of his life, and to try every remedy of gentleness and kindness, so as to win the emperor’s good will and turn him back from the fury with which he was raging against the sacred images. He kept the peoples of Italy, subject to the Eastern Empire, in their allegiance when they were contemplating revolt; he restrained them from appointing a new emperor whom they would bring from Constantinople; and, after the exarch had been expelled from Ravenna by the Lombards and was staying in Venetia, he commended him by letter to Ursus, duke of Venetia, so that Ursus might support him and restore the city of Ravenna to its former condition. He wrote two letters to Leo in order to break his obstinate spirit and lead him to better counsels.

Leo had threatened to send someone to Rome to shatter the image of Saint Peter and take Gregory away from there as a prisoner. [Col. 1020C] Gregory, however, replied that the pontiffs sat at Rome for the sake of restoring peace, like an unimpaired wall and a dividing barrier between East and West, and as arbiters and moderators of peace:

> “But if you send anyone to overthrow the image of Saint Peter, know this: we declare to you that we are innocent of the blood which they will shed; rather, this will fall back upon your neck and upon your head.”

The holy pontiff had foreseen what would happen if the emperor dared to attempt anything by force of arms. For, as Anastasius relates, the people of the Pentapolis and the armies of Venetia, prepared to resist the emperor’s commands, had chosen leaders for themselves. Concerned for the immunity both of the pontiff and of themselves, “the Romans and Lombards bound themselves together, as it were, by a chain of faith like brothers, all desiring to endure a glorious death in defense of the pontiff and never willing to allow him to suffer harm while contending for the true faith and for the salvation of Christians”—or, according to another reading, “while contending for salvation.”

And to whom could the Roman people [Col. 1020D] more fittingly entrust their salvation and faith than to the Roman pontiff, whose heart was set on nothing more than relieving the poverty of the needy with a most generous hand, opening the Church’s granaries to the poor when famine threatened, embracing everyone with gentle speech, enlarging the city with churches and monasteries, and adorning the churches with gifts of gold and silver? Gregory had undertaken the restoration of the city walls; he had reunited the Cottian Alps, which had been severed from the patrimony of the Church, to that patrimony; and he had recovered for the Roman duchy the fortresses seized by the Lombards, sometimes by force, sometimes by prayers, and sometimes by gifts.

It is therefore not surprising that, having cast off the empire of the heretical Leo—who threatened old Rome with the plundering, slaughter, and fires which he had carried out in the new [Rome]—the Romans entrusted themselves, their lives, and their possessions to their most holy bishop.

These events occurred toward the end of Gregory II’s pontificate; those matters, however, which Natalis Alexander reports from his authorities took place before the emperor’s wickedness had been declared to the whole world [Col. 1021A]. Leo seized the empire in the year 716, and Gregory wrote to Leo about the year 727:

> “For ten years,” he says in his letter to Leo, “by God’s kindness you walked rightly and made no mention of the sacred images; but now you say that they occupy the place of idols.”

Thus, in the year 726, Leo began openly to rage against the sacred images and to produce those monstrous acts of savagery and folly which Gregory reproaches him for in the said letter. For this reason the peoples of Italy began to shake off the yoke of the Greek Empire, trample underfoot the emperor’s laurelled insignia, and seize the cities subject to him.

From the year 727 onward the emperor’s wickedness became more conspicuous: he tore the sacred images from the churches and burned them in fire, slaughtered eminent citizens who opposed his impiety, and afflicted holy bishops with exile and death. Thus, in the year 730, toward the end of Gregory’s pontificate, the events occurred which the Greek historians Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Theophanes also record. The pontiff subjected Leo as a public heretic to anathema; all [Col. 1021B] the peoples of Italy vindicated themselves by just arms from the emperor’s tyranny; and Gregory assisted them with his counsel, authority, and protection.

Natalis, who was generally hostile to the authority of the Roman See, either paid no attention to this distinction of time or refused to do so; Pagi followed him, carried away by an excessive zeal for criticism. Let the most careful reckoner of years, Baronius, be heard under the year 730:

> “Until this time Gregory had often held back the reins of the rebellious people, lest they rebel completely against the emperor, so long as there could still be some hope that, after being repeatedly warned, he might revoke the edict he had promulgated concerning impiety; Gregory cared nothing that, on the emperor’s account, his own life was repeatedly placed in danger. But when he could neither recall him from his undertaking by words or writings nor restrain him by benefits from sliding into worse things, he judged that the time had come to bring the axe to the root of the unhappy tree. By apostolic authority he cries, ‘Cut it down!’ Awakened by that thunderclap [Col. 1021C], the faithful of the West immediately broke entirely from Leo’s empire and clung to the apostolic pontiff.

> “Thus Gregory left to later generations a worthy example: heretical princes must not be allowed to rule in the Church of Christ if, after repeated warnings, they are found to persist in error with an obstinate mind. For then occurred what all the Greek historians affirm, and Theophanes himself says: in the fourteenth year of the emperor Leo, Leo was deprived by Gregory of the collection of the taxes of Italy. Cedrenus and others attest this. Zonaras reports that these things were done at Rome—as it is reasonable to believe—in a synod, and that in the same council the emperor himself was punished with anathema.”

[Note: [Col. 1021C]

**ANNOTATION OF THOMAS ACETUS.**

No. 188, line 1.—“After this the emperor’s wickedness became clear.” Leo the Isaurian, the impious Iconoclast, became so violently insane—burning or defacing [Col. 1021D] the images of the saints here and there—that he rashly wrote to Saint Gregory II, the supreme pontiff, who was attempting to call him back from his error, saying that he would also send someone to Rome—as Baronius reports under the year 726—to shatter the bronze image prominently displayed of the most holy apostle Peter.

This statue of the prince of the apostles, which in the judgment of the most serious authorities is extremely ancient, is rightly believed to have been cast from the metal of the statue of Jupiter Capitolinus, at the command of Saint Leo the Great, after Rome, in the year 452 of the redeemed world, had been delivered from the impending scourge of Attila, king of the Huns, through the patronage of that same most holy apostle, and had regained peace.

Nevertheless, it was transferred from the very ancient oratory of Saint Martin, built through the efforts of that same Saint Leo near the Vatican Basilica, where it was first installed, to another [oratory] of the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus—as Matthew Vegius says, who flourished under the pontificate of Martin V—and from there, under Paul III, to the front portico of the same basilica, as the contemporary writer Tiberius Alpharanus records [Col. 1022A]; finally, under Paul V, it was moved to the place where it is now seen.

This celebrated image likewise enjoyed an ancient cult, especially through the kissing of its foot, which appears smooth and worn from the extremely frequent contact of lips. Indeed, Cardinal Caesar Baronius, whenever he visited the basilica of the prince of the apostles, venerated this statue by kissing it twice: first, when he approached the apostles’ confession, saying these words while kissing it, “I believe in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church”; then, when he departed from the confession, saying these other words: “Peace and obedience.”

Nor did we think we should pass over the remarkable miracle of an instantaneous healing which God, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, effected by a kiss impressed upon this statue with living faith, at the time when this Anastasian Codex was being printed.

In the Jubilee year 1725, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, during the pontificate of Benedict XIII, Joannes Kouvalschi, a soldier from the province of Silesia who had fought in the Turkish war, was horribly wounded while Belgrade was being stormed [Col. 1022B]. He fell from a certain rock into a deep pit, so that the vertebrae of his spine were dislocated through the violence and confusion of the fall. He could no longer walk or stand, for his legs and hips, rendered almost dry and useless by the paralysis that had contracted them, failed him.

The wretched man moved—or rather dragged himself as best he could—using certain wooden supports fitted to his hands, for about eight years. Then a light shone into the dwelling of his mind, and he seemed to see that he should be sent to Rome to be healed of his infirmities. He therefore made a vow and, not without the special providence of God, eventually reached Rome. He fasted for three days and, after receiving sacramental absolution from the Reverend Father Alexander Morichoni of the Society of Jesus, penitentiary for the Polish language, was refreshed by Holy Communion in the Vatican Basilica.

He then approached the statue of the prince of the apostles and prayed for a while. He wished to kiss the sacred foot but could not. He therefore asked some pilgrims who were standing nearby [Col. 1022C] for assistance, and with their help kissed the foot of the statue in living faith, asking to be restored to health through the intercession of Saint Peter.

What a marvelous power of faith! At once his feet and the soles of his feet were strengthened, and he began to walk and praise God, just like that cripple who had been lame from his mother’s womb, who sat begging for his livelihood at the Beautiful Gate of the temple and was healed by blessed Peter, as can be seen in the Acts of the Apostles.

The prodigy of this instantaneous healing was widely circulated, and our reverend chapter of the Most Sacred Vatican Basilica ordered it to be published in the Vatican press, on the basis of authentic proofs and documents preserved in our archive, through the care and diligence of the most learned man Dominicus Baptista, priest and beneficiary. His Eminence Annibal, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Albanus, called Saint Clement, archpriest of the same basilica, also ordered an image of the statue to be engraved in copper with this inscription:

> **TO THE BRONZE STATUE OF THE PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, PLACED IN THE VATICAN [Col. 1022D] BASILICA AND FREQUENTED BY THE MOST ANCIENT VENERATION OF THE CHRISTIAN PEOPLE. IN THE JUBILEE YEAR 1725, DURING THE PONTIFICATE OF BENEDICT XIII, GOD GLORIFIED THE MERITS OF HIS APOSTLE BY THE SIGNAL MIRACLE OF RESTORING HEALTH TO A PARALYTIC WHO HAD IMPLORED THE AID OF BLESSED PETER. ANNIBAL, CARDINAL OF SAINT CLEMENT OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, CAMERLENGO AND ARCHPRIEST OF THAT MOST SACRED BASILICA, CAUSED THIS TO BE REPRESENTED ON A COPPER PLATE BY ENGRAVED TYPE, TO INCREASE THE FAME OF THE APOSTOLIC PATRONAGE AND THE RELIGION OF CHRIST’S FAITHFUL. IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1727.**

We too, who by the favor and munificence of that same eminent archpriest had been admitted—although unworthy—among the beneficiary clergy of the same basilica of the prince of the apostles, saw that young man walking and glorifying the Lord. Therefore we faithfully bear witness to the truth. And lest the memory of this most illustrious [Col. 1023A] deed should perish with the passage of time, we thought it should be inserted into this Anastasian codex, for the greater glory [Col. 1024A] of the Most High, whom we proclaim wondrous in his apostle Peter.]

[Col. 0973]

**177.** Gregory II, a Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, occupied the see for sixteen years, eight months, and twenty days.

[Note: [Col. 0973C] C, 9, distinction 11.]

He lived during the reigns of the emperors Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine. From childhood he was brought up in the patriarchium under Pope Sergius of holy memory; he was made subdeacon and treasurer, and entrusted with the care of the library [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “he undertook its care.”]. He was then advanced to the order of deacons. He went with the holy pontiff Constantine to the imperial city, and, questioned by the emperor Justinian about certain articles, answered each question with an excellent reply. For he was a chaste man, learned in divine Scripture, eloquent in speech and steadfast in spirit, a defender of ecclesiastical affairs and a most vigorous opponent of those who opposed them [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “of opponents.”].

At the beginning of his pontificate he ordered lime to be prepared, and, beginning at the gate [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “portico.”] of Saint Lawrence, had decided to restore the walls of this city. After completing part of the work, however, he was hindered by the various unforeseen disturbances and tumults that arose.

**178**

[Note: [Col. 0975] See Baronius under the year 714, vol. IX.]

During his pontificate John, bishop of Constantinople, sent him a synodical letter, and the pontiff likewise made use of written replies to him. He roofed most of the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “Peter.”], which had fallen, bringing beams from Calabria; he built a new altar; and he restored the silver ciborium, which had been damaged by the collapse [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “which had been shaken by the collapse.”]. [Note: [Col. 0975] Baronius, year 710.]

He likewise repaired the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls, which, with its beams broken, was already near collapse, and after a long interval brought water back into the same church through joined pipes. He renewed various churches lying in ruins, which it would take too long to enumerate in order.

Through Bishop Boniface he preached the word of salvation in Germany and converted that people, sitting in darkness, to Christ by the teaching of light. He restored the monasteries beside the basilica of Saint Paul, which had been reduced to desolation, and, appointing monks as servants of God, re-established a community there after a long interval, so that they might render praises to God there day and night.

He founded a hospice—which is situated behind the apse of Saint Mary the Mother of God at the Cradle—and made it a monastery. He also appointed monks to the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew, called Barbara, which had been reduced to extreme desolation and contained not even a single monk [Note: [Col. 0975] C: “in which not even one monk lived.”], so that both monasteries might sing praises to God every day and night in honor of the holy Mother of God.

**179** At that time King Liutprand confirmed, at the admonition—or rebuke—of so great a man, the restoration of the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps [Note: [Col. 0975] “Coctian Alps.”] which King Aripert had made and Liutprand himself had reclaimed. [Note: [Col. 0975] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 715.]

During his pontificate a sign appeared in the moon in the fourteenth indiction, and it was seen to be blood-red until midnight. At that time Theudo [Note: [Col. 0975] “Theodo.”], duke of the Bavarian people [Note: [Col. 0975] “Bavarian.”], was the first of that nation to come to the threshold of the blessed apostle Peter, fulfilling a vow of prayer.

At that time the emperor Anastasius sent a fleet of ships prepared in the region of Alexandria against the Hagarenes, who had been destroyed [Note: [Col. 0975] “were to be destroyed.”] by God. They, however, turning to another plan before reaching their destination, returned halfway along the route to the imperial city. They sought out Theodosius the Orthodox, chose him as emperor, and compelled him to accept and confirm the imperial throne.

Anastasius therefore went with the citizens and with as many of the army as he could gather to the fortified city of Nicaea. There he fought the fleet in which Theodosius had become emperor, and nearly seven thousand of the army were killed. The defeated party of Anastasius then sought a pledge of immunity. After giving it, he became a cleric and was ordained a priest.

As soon as the aforementioned Theodosius entered the imperial city, he restored to its former place [Note: [Col. 0975] “restored to its former place and inscription”] the venerable image on which the six holy councils had been depicted and which Philippicus, whose name must not be spoken, had removed. Thus, through the fervor of his faith, every dispute ceased in the Church.

**180**

[Note: [Col. 0975] Baronius, year 717.]

At that time the river called the Tiber, overflowing its channel, spread across the plains. It swelled with a flood of many waters and entered through the gate called Flaminia [Note: [Col. 0977] “flowed out.”]. In the meantime it rose above the city walls in some places and extended through the streets beyond the basilica of Saint Mark, so that in the Via Lata the water of that river had risen to a height of one and a half men. The waters spread from the gate of the blessed apostle Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge, and near the lower places flowed back into the channel of the river [Note: [Col. 0977] B: “the waters of the same river flowed back.”].

It overturned houses and devastated fields, uprooting trees and crops. Indeed, at that time most of the Romans could not even sow. Great tribulation threatened because of this. For seven days the water held Rome submerged.

The lord pope therefore repeatedly caused litanies to be sung. When he persisted in prayer and litanies, on the eighth day God took pity and removed the water, and the river returned to its own channel in the fifteenth indiction.

**181** At that same time the fortress of Cumae had been seized by the Lombards through a deceitful pretense of peace. When this was heard, everyone was plunged into grief. The most holy pontiff exhorted and warned the Lombards to return it, declaring in his letters that, if they did not comply, they would incur divine anger because of the deceit they had committed [Note: [Col. 0977] B: “he protested.”]. He also wished to give them many gifts so that they would restore it, but, with their minds swollen with pride, they neither allowed themselves to heed the warnings nor to return it. [Note: [Col. 0977] See Baronius under the year of the Lord 715.]

Therefore the same holy pontiff was deeply grieved and entrusted himself to divine hope. While the Neapolitan duke and the people were occupied with the fortification, he presented to them daily, by writing, how they should conduct the duchy [Note: [Col. 0977] “he provided.”]. Obeying his command, they took counsel and entered the walls of the fortress by force [Note: [Col. 0977] B: “by stealth,” or “as if by cunning”] under cover of the silence of night.

John, together with the subdeacon and governor Theodimus, and with the army, killed nearly three hundred Lombards and their castald, or royal official [Note: [Col. 0977] “castaldo”]. They also captured more than five hundred alive and led them as prisoners to Naples. Thus they were able to recover the fortress. For its ransom the most holy pope himself, as he had previously promised, gave seventy pounds of gold.

**182** He covered and repaired the holy church of Jerusalem, which had long remained exposed, and the surrounding porticoes, shaken by age, by bringing in beams. He also made a marble ambo in the same church and endowed it with various linens and furnishings.

At the same time the unspeakable race of the Hagarenes, after they had held the province of Spain under occupation for ten years, attempted in the eleventh year to cross the river Rhône and seize Gaul, where Eudo was in command. He summoned the Franks in a general mobilization against the Saracens, and they surrounded and killed them. [Note: [Col. 0977] C: “warning.”]

For 375,000 were killed in a single day, as the letter sent to the pontiff by that same Eudo, duke of the Franks, stated. They said that only 1,500 Franks had died in that battle [Note: [Col. 0977] “the letter said.”]. He added that, in the preceding year, when the three sponges sent to them by the aforesaid man as a blessing—sponges which are placed for the use of the pope’s table—were being distributed by Eudo, prince of Aquitaine, in small portions among his people for them to consume at the hour when the battle was joined, not one of those who partook of them was wounded or killed.

At that time, in a certain place in Campania, burnt wheat, barley, or legumes fell from the sky as though in the form of rain. During Lent he instituted the practice that, on Thursday, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place in the churches, something that had not previously been done.

He rebuilt from the foundations the oratory in the patriarchium dedicated to the blessed apostle Peter, ornamenting it with various metals [Note: [Col. 0977] C: “he built it.”]. He covered the walls surrounding the altar with silver and painted the twelve apostles; these weighed 180 pounds.

Meanwhile, in those days, Constantinople was besieged for two years by the unspeakable Hagarenes [Note: [Col. 0979] C: “unnamable.”]. But, with God opposed to them, most of them were killed there by famine and war, and they withdrew in confusion during the reign of Leo. It was also said that 300,000 people of that city, of different sexes and ages, were destroyed by the necessity of the plague [Note: [Col. 0979] “Of the population of that same city, 300,000 of different ages perished when the plague ravaged them.”].

**183**

[Note: [Col. 0979] Baronius, under the year 717.]

At that time the pontiff’s mother, Honesta by character and by name, was taken from this life. After her death Gregory built his own house anew in honor of Saint Agatha, martyr of Christ, adding rooms from the foundations and whatever structures were necessary for a monastery [Note: [Col. 0979] “for the monastery.”]. He offered urban and rural estates there for the needs of the monks [Note: [Col. 0979] B: “to them.”].

In the same church he made a silver ciborium for blessed Agatha, weighing 720 pounds [Note: [Col. 0979] C: “22”]; six silver arches, each weighing fifteen pounds; ten baskets, each weighing twelve pounds; and he gave many other gifts.

At that time the fortress of Narnia was seized by the Lombards. King Liutprand of the Lombards, having conducted a general mobilization, advanced to Ravenna, besieged it for several days, and, seizing the fortress, carried away many captured ships and countless possessions. [Note: [Col. 0979] Baronius, year 726.]

After several days Basil the duke, Jordanes the chartularius, and John the subdeacon, surnamed Lurion, took counsel to kill the pontiff. Marinus, the imperial *spatharius*, who held the Roman duchy and had been sent from the imperial city at the emperor’s command, approved this plan. But they could not find the opportunity, because by God’s judgment he was struck down and became paralyzed, and thus withdrew from Rome.

Afterward Paul was sent to Italy as patrician and exarch. They again considered how they might complete this crime. Their plan became known to the Romans, who, stirred to action [Note: [Col. 0979] B: “moved”], killed both Jordanes and John Lurion. Basil, however, became a monk and ended his life shut away in a certain place.

The exarch Paul, acting on the emperor’s command, attempted to kill the same pontiff. He hindered him from imposing a tax upon the province, and was considering stripping the churches of their possessions, as had been done elsewhere, and appointing another in his place. After him another *spatharius* was sent with imperial commands, so that the pontiff might be removed from his see.

Again the patrician Paul, to complete such a crime, sent some men whom he was able to seduce from Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0979] “from among the people of Ravenna”], together with their commander, and also some men from the fortresses. But the Romans were roused, and the Lombards everywhere gathered for the defense of the pontiff: the men of Spoleto at the Salarian Bridge, and the Lombard dukes on both sides surrounding the Roman borders. Thus they prevented the attempt.

**184** Thereafter the emperor sent commands decreeing [Note: [Col. 0979] “the emperor Leo”] that no image of any saint, martyr, or angel should be kept anywhere [Note: [Col. 0979] “he had ordered them all to be removed and burned”]. For he declared them all accursed; and if the pontiff complied with this, he would have the emperor’s favor, but if he prevented it, he would be deposed from his rank.

Thus the pious man, seeing the prince’s profane command, armed himself against the emperor as against an enemy, rejecting his heresy and writing everywhere to warn the Christians to beware, since such impiety had arisen [Note: [Col. 0979] “which had produced such impiety,” B]. Accordingly, all the people of the Pentapolis and the armies of Venetia, stirred to action, resisted the emperor’s command. They declared that they would never consent to the death of that pontiff, but would fight manfully for his defense.

Thus they subjected Paul the exarch, and the one who had sent him [Note: [Col. 0979] B: “the one who had issued that edict”], and their accomplices, to anathema. Despising his appointment, they everywhere chose their own leaders throughout Italy [Note: [Col. 0979] B: “they chose death”], and all alike concerned themselves with the immunity both of the pontiff and of themselves.

When the emperor’s wickedness became known, all Italy took counsel to choose an emperor for itself and bring him to Constantinople. But the pontiff restrained this plan, hoping for the prince’s conversion.

Meanwhile, during those same days, Exhilaratus, duke of Naples, deceived by diabolical instigation, occupied parts of Campania with his son Adrian [Note: [Col. 0981] B: “Andrian”], urging the people to obey the emperor and kill the pontiff. Then all the Romans followed him, captured him, and killed him together with his son. After this [Note: [Col. 0981] “Afterward”], they also attacked the duke Peter, who said that he had written against the pontiff to the emperor [Note: [Col. 0981] B: “The Romans, being disturbed, said that he too had written against the pontiff.”].

**185** Accordingly, when dissension arose in the region of Ravenna, some consenting to the impiety …

[Note: [Col. 0981] “to wickedness.”] […] of the emperor; others held with the pontiff and the faithful; when contention arose among them, they killed Paul the patrician.

To the Lombards surrendered the fortresses of Aemilia—Ferorianus, Montebelli, and Verablum [Note: [Col. 0981] Frentana, Montella, Venafrum.]—together with their towns, Buxo and Pernicteta [Note: [Col. 0981] Persiceda; C, Praecutio.]; likewise the Pentapolis and the city of Auximana surrendered themselves. After some time the emperor sent to Naples Eutychius, a eunuch and patrician who had formerly been exarch, so that he might accomplish what the exarch Paul, the spatharii, and the other counsellors of evil had been unable to do. But even then, with God’s prompting [Note: [Col. 0981] “command,”], the wretched plot did not remain hidden; the wicked plan became clear to everyone, for they were attempting to violate the churches of Christ and to destroy everyone and plunder the possessions of all [Note: [Col. 0981] “all places.”].

When he sent his own man to Rome with letters in which it was stated that the pontiff was to be killed together with the leading men of Rome, once their most savage madness was recognized, they immediately wished to kill the patrician himself who had been sent [Note: [Col. 0981] “the Roman sentence immediately wished to kill the envoy of that patrician.”], had not the pontiff’s excessive protection prevented it. Nevertheless, they anathematized Eutychius the exarch, binding themselves, great and small alike, by a solemn oath never to permit the pontiff, a champion of the Christian faith and defender of the Churches, to be harmed or removed, but declaring that they were all prepared to die for his safety.

The patrician then promised the Lombard leaders and king great gifts on every side [Note: [Col. 0981] “promised,”], urging through his legates that they desist from assisting the pontiff. He replied [Note: [Col. 0981] “from the written reply,”] that, despising the man’s detestable deceit, the Romans and Lombards had bound themselves together as brothers by the chain of faith, all desiring to endure a glorious death in defence of the pontiff and never permitting him to suffer injury while he fought for the true faith and the salvation of Christians [Note: [Col. 0981] “while they fought.”].

With matters thus situated, that father [Note: [Col. 0981] “pope,”] chose to distribute to the poor with the most generous hand whatever he found, adopting prayer and fasting and daily beseeching God with litanies. Thus he remained always strengthened by a hope greater than human hope, while nevertheless giving thanks for the people’s goodwill and purpose of mind. With gentle speech he urged everyone to advance in good works toward God and to persevere in the faith, but he also admonished them not to cease loving or remaining loyal to the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0981] Baronius, under the year 728, at the end.]. In this way he softened the hearts of all and eased their continuing grief.

### 186

At the same time, in the eleventh indiction, the Lombards deceitfully seized the fortress of Suerius, which remained in the possession of those same Lombards for one hundred and forty days [Note: [Col. 0981] B, forty days.]. But, through the pontiff’s many successive letters and admonitions sent to the king, and although many gifts had been given, the king of the Lombards—stripped at least of all his resources—restored and donated the fortress, issuing the aforesaid donation to the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

At that time, in the twelfth indiction, in the month of January, for ten or more days a star called Antifer [Note: [Col. 0981] C, Aurifer; cf. Lucifer.] appeared in the western sky with rays. Its rays faced toward the northern regions and extended as far as the middle of the heavens [Note: [Col. 0981] Baronius, under the year 729.].

At that time the often-mentioned patrician Eutychius and King Liutprand again devised a wicked plan: after gathering their armies, the king was to subdue the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, while the exarch was to attack Rome and carry out what he had previously been ordered to do concerning the person of the pontiff. The king came to Spoleto, received oaths and hostages from both dukes, and withdrew with his entire cohort [Note: [Col. 0983] “with his whole army.”] into Nero’s Field.

The pontiff went out to meet him and, when presented before him, did everything he could to soften the king’s mind by pious admonition. He even prostrated himself at the king’s feet, and the king promised that he would injure no one. Thus he was moved by the pious exhortations to such deep remorse that he removed the garments he was wearing and laid before the body of the apostle his cloak, armilausia [Note: [Col. 0983] “bracelets,” or B, “armillary garment.”], belt, sword, gilded blade, golden crown, and silver cross.

After prayer had been offered, he asked the pontiff to receive the aforementioned exarch into reconciliation and peace; this was done. The king then withdrew, abandoning the evil plans he had undertaken with the exarch.

### 187

While the exarch remained in Rome, a certain deceiver named Tiberius, surnamed Petasius, came into the Tuscan region, to the fortress of Manturianum [Note: [Col. 0983] Mantuarianum; C, Maturanum.]. He attempted to usurp for himself the rule of the Roman Empire. He deceived people of lesser standing as well, so that the inhabitants of Manturianum, Luna, and Blera [Note: [Col. 0983] Blerans, C.] gave him their oaths.

When the exarch heard this, he was disturbed. The most holy pope encouraged him and sent with him the leading men of the Church and an army. When they arrived at the fortress of Manturianum, Petasius was killed there. His severed head was sent to the emperor in Constantinople, but even then the emperor did not grant the Romans full favour.

### 188

After these events the malice of that same emperor became evident, and for this reason he persecuted the pontiff. He compelled all who lived in Constantinople, by force [Note: [Col. 0983] “by strength,”] and by persuasion alike, to remove wherever they were found the images both of the Saviour and of his holy Mother, as well as those of all the saints, and to burn them in the middle of the city—something dreadful to relate—and to whitewash all the painted churches.

Because many among the city’s inhabitants prevented this crime from being carried out, some were beheaded, while others suffered punishment by having parts of their bodies cut off [Note: [Col. 0983] “in some part of the body.”]. For the same reason the emperor deprived Germanus, bishop of the holy Church of Constantinople, of his episcopate, because he had refused to consent to him, and appointed in his place the presbyter Anastasius, his accomplice [Note: [Col. 0983] “to his place.”].

When Anastasius sent to Rome a synodical letter, the holy man found him consenting to such a heresy. He therefore did not judge that he should ordinarily be called either brother or fellow priest, but in admonitory letters he ordered that, unless he returned to the Catholic faith, he should also be excluded from priestly office. He likewise admonished the emperor in writing, offering salutary counsel that he should turn away from such execrable misery.

### 189

He made an outstanding golden chalice decorated with various precious stones, weighing thirty pounds; likewise a golden paten weighing twenty-eight pounds and one half. He left to all the clergy, the monasteries, the diaconia, and the mansionarii 2,160 solidi, and 1,000 solidi for the lights of the blessed apostle Peter.

He carried out five ordinations: four in the month of September and one in June. There were thirty-five presbyters, four deacons, and 150 bishops in various places. He was also buried at the church of the blessed apostle Peter on the third day before the Ides of February, in the fourteenth indiction, during the reign of the emperors Leo and Constantine.
