The episcopal see remained vacant for five days and one month.

**Number 203, line 1:** “the fortress, for which…”

**Number 204, line 2:** “the others.” Line 4: “to build.” In the same place: “as they were preserved,” and “according to…” Line 15: “the priest”; “and the episcopal see was vacant for four days. The rest is missing in Penia’s manuscript.]”

[Note: [Col. 1035B]

## OF BINIUS AND LABBE

**Number 190, line 1.** Gregory. In the year 731, on 16 February, Gregory III, an excellent pontiff, was elected. Saint Boniface, the apostle of the Germans, consulted him once through legates and once by coming personally to Rome concerning the propagation of the faith among the gentiles and heretics. [Col. 1035C]

He sat for ten years, eight months, and twenty days. He died in the year 741, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. Baronius correctly writes, in the year cited above, that he sat for ten years, nineteen months, and twelve days.

**Number 191, line 1. Persecution.** During this persecution, Aemilianus, bishop of Cyzicus, Basil, Procopius of Decapolis, and the monk Theophilus are recorded in the Greek menologion as having been exiled.

**Number 193, line 2. He sent other writings, etc.** Adrianus says the same in his letter to the emperor Constantine:

> “Both Gregorys, the most holy Roman pontiffs of their times, were cast into great tribulation. They often admonished the great-grandfather of Your Serenity not to allow the venerable images to be removed from their position, but their salutary prayers did not move his mind in the least.”

**Number 194, line 1. He brought the columns granted to him.** He also confirmed in deed the use of the sacred images, which he had defended in writing against Leo [Col. 1035D], when he erected in the church of the blessed Peter images of the Saviour, the Mother of God, the apostles, and the holy Virgins, images of great value.

**Line 7. He made an oratory.** In this oratory the same pontiff honourably placed the relics of all the saints that he could gather from throughout the Christian world. He did this because Leo the Iconoclast despised the relics of the saints.]

[Note: [Col. 1035D]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

After the day of February on which, as we see, the death of the holy pontiff Gregory II is consistently placed, the see was vacant for thirty-five days, as recorded by the three Catalogues—those of Colbert and Verona—and by all the manuscripts, both ours and the Ambrosian, except the fourth, which, together with the commonly printed versions, the other Freherian manuscript, and the Cavense, gives one month and five days. Pagius wishes these accounts to agree with the first, but he did not observe [Col. 1036B] that, if a month is counted, namely two days of March and five days, the sixteenth of that month coincides with the ordination, which is impossible because it fell on a Friday. On the other hand, if thirty-five days are counted, allowing for the two-day deficiency of February, one arrives at 18 March, namely the Sunday marked G in the calendar, on which Saint [Col. 1036C] Gregory III was ordained; and this was in the year of his predecessor’s death, 731.

Indeed, seeing that thirteen days must be removed either from the interval between pontificates or from the period during which Gregory sat, I long hesitated whether, following the fifth and seventh Catalogues, I should make the interval twenty-two days and say that Gregory was ordained on 4 March. For the period of his see, which is read in most manuscripts and Catalogues as ten years, eight months, and twenty-four days, would then be completed remarkably on 28 November 741, the year of his death. Or should I instead, with Pagius, follow the Catalogue of Regino and, taking twenty-four days as belonging to the pontificate, make the interval eleven days?

But when I saw that no historical record contradicted the removal of those thirteen days from wherever they might be taken, and furthermore noticed that they were counted inconsistently—for one repeatedly finds nine, twelve, twenty, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four, and twenty-five days—I therefore judged that Regino should be preferred together with Pagius. It is also relevant that Regino flourished at the beginning of the tenth century, whereas the copyists of the Catalogues belonged to the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. The seventh of these is generally found to be corrupt, while the fifth clearly shows that its copyist did not understand the marks of his exemplar; for, although an interval of thirty-five days occurs there, one again finds twenty-two days.

Since this is so, Gregory III is therefore memorable, like his predecessor, both for the restoration of the churches of the City and for his continued defence of the sacred images. While he was attending the funeral of that same predecessor as an act of service, he was elected by all, moved by divine inspiration, as Anastasius says. (See Pagius’s notes below.) He was ordained on 18 March, after an interval of thirty-five days, in the year 731. He governed the Church during extremely troubled times until the fourth day before the Kalends of December, or 28 November, when, as recorded in the Martyrologies, he died in the year 741, after sitting for ten years, eight months, and eleven days.

His death was preceded by one month by that of Charles, mayor of the palace of France. “His sons,” says the Pithoean annalist, [Col. 1037A] “Carloman and Pippin, under the pretext of the office of mayor of the palace, take up the kingdom of all France and divide it between themselves.” I gladly place this epoch here because of the outstanding services of the Frankish kings toward the apostolic see, which originated with Pippin, the son of Charles. For the remaining matters concerning Gregory, read the notes on Zacharias.]

[Note: [Col. 1037A]

**Number 190, line 1.** Gregory III, son of John, a Syrian, cardinal presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, during the reign of the emperor Leo III the Isaurian, sat for ten years, eight months, and twenty-four days. He was created on the third day before the Nones of March and consecrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. In the year 731 he entered upon the pontificate with the consent of all.]

[Note: [Col. 1037A]

**Number 190, line 15. While he was before the bier, etc.** Gregory’s mastery of the Greek and Latin languages; his knowledge of the divine Scriptures; his understanding of the psalms, which he held in his memory [Col. 1037B]; his eloquence; his zeal for preserving the faith; his courage and steadfastness; his wisdom and singular gentleness; his love of poverty; his pious concern for redeeming captives and relieving orphans, widows, the poor, and all the needy; and his inclination toward religious men made him worthy of the highest pontificate. Thus Anastasius testifies:

> “When his predecessor had departed from this world, while he was occupied in attendance upon his predecessor, the Roman men, or the whole people, from the greatest to the least, moved by divine inspiration, suddenly raised him by force and elected him to the order of the pontificate.”

Frodoardus writes the same in his fragment on the Roman pontiffs:

> “While attending the funeral rites of his father, he was hurried from the bier  
> and summoned, once chosen, to the highest rule.”

Although Gregory III was elected pontiff immediately after Gregory II died, his ordination was nevertheless postponed until 18 March [Col. 1037C], the thirty-fifth day after his predecessor’s death, because confirmation had to be sought from the exarch of Ravenna. The Roman Church was freed from this servitude after the death of Gregory III, as will be seen in the pontificate of his successor Zacharias.

From these words of Anastasius and Frodoardus, it also seems possible to infer the form of the letters that the Roman clergy used to write after the election of a pontiff to the exarch, the judges, the archbishop, and the apocrisiarius of Ravenna. In those letters they reported that the election had taken place and requested its confirmation. This form, which survives in chapter 2 of the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs*, cannot have been written after the death of Gregory II, specifically to request the confirmation of Gregory III, because he was elected immediately after his predecessor’s death and while he was occupied in attendance upon his predecessor, as Anastasius says, or while he was attending his predecessor’s funeral rites, as Frodoardus writes. The person whose confirmation was requested in those letters, however, was, according to the same text, only three days removed from the death of his predecessor.

Moreover, [Col. 1037D] at the time of Gregory’s election, while the see was vacant, the administration of the Church lay with the elected pontiff, not with the archpresbyter, archdeacon, and primicerius of the notaries, as we proved in the case of Benedict II. I therefore consider it very probable that this form, which Papebrochius appended to the pontificate of Gregory II in his *Chronological-Historical Endeavour*, believing that it had not yet seen the light, was actually written long before Gregory III.

**Number 191, line 5. Admonitory letters.** At the beginning of his pontificate, Gregory judged that he had to defend the veneration of the sacred images, which the emperors Leo and Constantine were attacking. He therefore immediately wrote letters to them, exhorting them to abandon so perverse an opinion.

The presbyter Gregory, who carried the letters, did not dare to deliver them, for fear of the persecution in which the emperor Leo at that time drove many people—bishops and patricians as well as persons of every rank—into exile or handed them over to death. He returned to Rome without accomplishing his mission [Col. 1038A] and brought the letters back intact to the pontiff.

For this reason the pontiff received him with the greatest severity. He would even have been deposed at the synod held at Rome on this matter, had not the intervention of the Fathers of that synod softened the pontiff’s anger. He did so, however, on the condition that the same presbyter Gregory should again travel to Constantinople with the same letters.

But the emperor ordered that he be detained in Sicily, that the writings be taken from him, and that he be sent into exile. Anastasius records all these events.]

### No. 194, line 1—“Here he granted,” etc.

The most holy pontiff Gregory opposed the emperor’s impiety concerning the veneration of sacred images and the honoring of holy relics not only in writing but also by his actions. For Anastasius adds to what was said above that he erected, in the basilica of Saint Peter, with magnificent workmanship, images of the Savior and the apostles on one side, and of the Mother of God and the holy virgins on the other. In the same place he built an oratory in which he honorably deposited, for veneration, sacred relics gathered from everywhere. He also decreed that the anniversaries of the saints should be celebrated daily with sacred offices and Masses by monks serving the Lord there from three monasteries. Finally, he instituted that a priest celebrating Mass in that oratory should insert the following clause into the canon after the words “and all your saints”:

> “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world.”

He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory. But Gregory established this specifically for that oratory and therefore, as Walfrid notes in chapter 22, it is not recorded in the canon that is said generally.

Cardinal Bona, *Rerum liturgicarum*, book III, chapter 11, no. 2, testifies that among the great number of manuscript Missals that he examined he found only one in which these words had been added: it is preserved in the Barberini Library, Codex 1858. Edmund Martene, *De antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, book I, chapter 4, article 8, no. 16, nevertheless observes that the Colbert Codex 2585, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint-Denis in France, contains a similar clause. It reads:

> “And also of those martyrs whose solemn triumph is celebrated today in the sight of your glory.”

Furthermore, when Innocent III was questioned about this matter by William, abbot of Saint Alban’s, he by no means disapproved of these and similar additions, as Matthew Paris writes in his *Lives of the Abbots of Saint Albans*. On the canon of the Mass, see what was said under Gelasius.

### No. 202, line 12—“In his time,” etc.

In the year 740, Luitprand, king of the Lombards, laid siege to Rome because Trasamund of Spoleto and Godescalc of Benevento, dukes hostile to him, were in friendship with the Roman pontiff. Therefore Gregory, in the year 741, sent a double embassy to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Frankish kingdom, carrying the keys of Saint Peter and portions of the chains, and wrote him a double letter, with the purpose that he might free them from such great Lombard oppression, as Anastasius says. Anastasius, however, mentions only one embassy, carried out by Anastasius, bishop, and Sergius, presbyter.

But we learn from the Continuator of Fredegar, who writes in chapter 110, that Gregory sent Charles a double embassy—not only imploring Charles’s aid against the Lombards, but also against the emperor, who, as Baronius says, had stirred up the king of the Lombards against the Roman Church:

> “At that time,” says the Continuator, “the blessed pope Gregory sent twice from Rome to the aforesaid prince—namely Charles—the keys of the venerable tomb, together with the chains of Saint Peter and great and countless gifts; or rather, something such as had never before been heard of or seen in any former age of embassies.”

The same Anonymous gives the following explanation for this double embassy:

> “This arrangement having been made, so that he might withdraw from the emperor’s side and confirm the Roman consulship—or patriciate—for the aforesaid prince Charles.”

That Gregory requested aid from Charles not only against the Lombards but also against the emperor is expressly stated in the *Annals of Metz*, preserved in Duchesne’s collection of the Frankish historians:

> “In the year 741, Charles, the prince, after subduing the peoples situated all around, while arranging within the boundaries of his rule those matters that belonged to peace, received twice in the same year an embassy sent from the apostolic see by the most blessed pope Gregory. The envoys offered him the keys of the venerable tomb of the prince of the apostles, Peter, together with his precious chains and great gifts—something that had previously been sent by no bishop of the Roman city to any Frankish prince. The aforesaid bishop Gregory also sent him a letter, by decision of the Roman leaders, stating that the Roman people, having abandoned the emperor’s dominion, wished to turn to Charles for their defense and to his unconquered clemency.”

From this it is also clear that the double embassy belonged to the year 741 and that Gregory asked Charles to withdraw from the emperor’s side.

No ancient writer reports what Charles replied to Gregory III’s embassies and letters. But the Continuator of Fredegar teaches us that they were most welcome to Charles. In his Appendix he writes:

> “He received the embassy itself with wondrous and magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and sent to Rome, with great rewards and with the envoys who had come with him, Grimo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sygobert, a recluse of the basilica of the martyr Saint Denis, to the thresholds of Saint Peter and Saint Paul.”

Since this embassy was most welcome to Charles, there can be no doubt that through his envoys he declared war on King Luitprand unless he promptly withdrew from Roman territory. Deterred by these threats, Luitprand returned to Pavia, from which he had come, though, as Anastasius reports, he retained the four towns he had occupied. These were later restored under Zacharias, Gregory’s successor, as we shall say in that place.

There is likewise no reason to doubt that Charles promised aid to the pontiff; but since he died in the same year, 741, he could not provide it.

Moreover, from the words of the Continuator of Fredegar and the Annalist of Metz it follows that Gregory III offered Charles the consulship—or, as the author of the critical notes on Baronius explains at length, the patriciate—since the latter says that the Roman people, having abandoned the emperor’s dominion, called Charles to their defense.

The dignity of patrician was conferred upon those who were chosen to defend Churches and the poor against the violence of the powerful, as is clear from the formula reported by Paul the Deacon in a Vatican manuscript of his *History of the Lombards*, by which a prince appointed someone patrician:

> “For this reason we grant you this honor, so that you may administer justice to the Churches of God and to the poor, and thereafter render an account before the Most High Judge. Then let the emperor clothe him with a mantle, place a ring on his right index finger, and give him, written in his own hand on cotton, the words: ‘Be a merciful and just Patrician.’ Then let him place a golden circlet upon his head and dismiss him.”

The patriciate involved a certain extraordinary right of protection, as Marca explains, *De Concordia*, book I, chapter 12, no. 1. This was the protection that those who were not otherwise obliged by their office to provide it ordinarily granted to Churches not subject to them, against the public or private violence of the powerful. Although princes were bound by office to protect the Churches established in their kingdoms, that ordinary right of protection depended upon jurisdiction.

This extraordinary right of protection was granted to eminent men called patrons, defenders, protectors, and advocates. They provided particular Churches with special protection and defense, in addition to the protection expected from kings as part of the public order.

But the patriciate of the Roman Church, or the title “Patrician of the Romans,” included two things: the jurisdiction by which the kings of the Franks, with the consent of the pontiff and the Roman people, exercised authority in the City; and the protection, or defense, that they had promised to the Roman Church, a defense established by agreements made with the Roman pontiffs.

Marca assigns the beginning of those agreements concerning protection with the Roman Church to this period, when Gregory III entrusted himself and his Church to the protection of Charles, duke of the Franks. He writes that this protection was later confirmed by new laws issued by Pippin, king of the Franks, and Stephen II, Roman pontiff, who conferred the dignity of patrician upon Pippin and his sons.

Thus, in these most difficult times, Charles Martel was called Patrician of the Romans and Defender of the Church. Besides the Continuator of Fredegar already cited, this is clearly implied by the emperors Charles the Great and Louis the Pious.

In the division of his kingdom among his sons in 806, Charles the Great states:

> “Above all, however, we command that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly it was undertaken by our grandfather Charles and by Pippin, our father of blessed memory, and afterwards by us; and that with God’s help they strive to defend it against its enemies, and ensure that it possesses its justice, insofar as it concerns them and reason requires.”

Louis the Pious says the same in the division of his kingdom, which Goldastus published in volume II of the *Imperial Constitutions*, and Baluze in volume I of the *Capitularies*, under the year 837. The author of the critical notes on Baronius, however, more correctly considers it to have been made in 835:

> “Above all we command and enjoin that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as formerly it was undertaken by our great-grandfather Charles, by our grandfather Pippin, by Charles, our father of blessed memory and emperor, and afterwards by us.”

From these statements it must be concluded that Charles Martel was the first of all Frankish princes—or of any other nation—to undertake the patronage of the City and of the Roman Church. Anyone wishing to learn more about this matter should consult the cited work of Marca and the critical notes of Baronius under the year 740.

From Gregory III’s embassy to Charles Martel, who at that time exercised the entire administration of France, the origin of apostolic nuncios in France seems to have arisen. It was then that representatives of the Roman see first appeared in France, dealing twice with Charles Martel so that he might provide the Romans with aid and counsel.

Those who held the Roman pontificate after Gregory III, says Cointius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of France* under the year 740, no. 7, sent envoys to France more frequently. Matters eventually reached the point that, besides the legates sent from Rome when new circumstances arose, a representative of the apostolic see remained continually in the king’s retinue; and not rarely this office was conferred by the Roman pontiff upon the man whom the king had appointed archchaplain of his palace.

### Note: Column 1040C

### No. 192, line 1—“The synodal decree”

This synodal constitution was issued in the second Roman synod under Gregory II. Adrian I preserved several fragments of that synod in his letter to Charles concerning the holy images.

### Line 15—“Among the other enactments”

Anastasius asserts that this celebrated encyclical document, published by the Roman synod, was appended to the other papal decretals. He therefore presupposes the existence of a codex in which the decretal letters of the pontiffs were inserted as authoritative testimony, and which was carefully and reverently preserved in the apostolic archives.

Indeed, in the time of Pope Gregory I, such a codex was being sought in the provinces in order to maintain the strength of faith and discipline. The monk and recluse Secundinus had requested from Gregory the transcription of papal decrees. In replying to him, Gregory says in book VII, letter 54:

> “Concerning the ordinances of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, your charity asks whether anything was added after the most blessed man Hormisdas; but you should know that the ordinances of the bishops were set forth down to the time of Pope Vigilius.”

Whenever more solemn decrees were published by the pontiffs, they were appended to the body, or Codex, of the Decretals together with the assent and confirmation of whatever synods happened to be held. This was what the present synod decreed.

Another example of the same practice is recorded in the *Deeds of Leo IV*, where we read:

> “He also ordered these chapters to be written after the other decrees of the pontiffs in the sacred canons, so that they might henceforth be preserved inviolate by all.”

### Note: Column 1041A

### No. 194, line 13—“Masses of the anniversaries”

Masses of the anniversaries, or birthdays, of the martyrs are the Masses of the solemn day of their final struggle, because on that day they were born to Christ.

Anastasius, in his life of Gregory III: “On the day of their anniversaries,” that is, of the holy apostles and martyrs.

The same author, in his life of Adrian: “On the anniversary of the pontiff.”

Ambrose, sermon 72:

> “As they say, when the vintage is approaching, we prepare the anniversary of his martyrdom.”

Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chapter 3:

> “For the dead we make offerings; for their anniversaries, on the annual day.”

### “He added this to the canon of the Mass”

The canon of the Mass is the solemn prayer by which the Lord’s body is consecrated.

The *Roman Order concerning the Sacrifice of the Mass*, chapter 12:

> “The prayer which, because of the regular celebration of the sacraments, we call the canon or action according to Roman custom.”

Gregory should be understood in this sense in book VII, letter 63, where he says that you established that the Lord’s Prayer should be said immediately after the canon.

Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book II, chapter 94:

> “When he had reached that place in the canon where the names of men are customarily recited.”

### No. 195, line 1—“He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory, in which, making a pergola, he displayed gifts of various kinds”

Pope Gregory built an oratory beside the basilica of blessed Peter and erected in it a pergola, in which he displayed various gifts offered by him. In churches, offerings are displayed in a pergola.

Anastasius, below in this passage:

> “And above the same apse, three silver crosses, and the other things intended for the decoration of the pergola or for the altar hangings.”

Tertullian alludes to this in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 7:

> “With various pergolas built one above another, and with each god assigned by as many stairways.”

A *pergola* is a place or appendage of a building from which one looks out into a public area. During the Second Punic War, Fulvius was punished with prolonged imprisonment because he was seen looking into the forum from his pergola with a wreath of roses. Pliny, book XXI, chapter 3:

> “Lucius Fulvius, during the Second Punic War, was said to have looked out from his pergola into the forum in daylight with a wreath of roses; by authority of the senate he was led to prison and was not released before the end of the war.”

The same author, book XXXV, chapter 10, writes that Apelles displayed painted panels in a pergola and hid behind them to hear the judgments of passers-by:

> “He also displayed his finished works in a pergola for passers-by, and, hiding behind the panel itself, listened for the faults they noticed.”

Slaves were likewise displayed for sale in a pergola. Plautus, in *The Pseudolus*:

> “Therefore tomorrow I shall have you carried in a basket to the pergola.”

### Line 2—“Two golden gabathae; five others, called saxicae”

*Gabathae* are hollow dishes of gold, silver, or bronze in which oil burned.

Anastasius, in his life of Honorius:

> “He also made four golden gabathae, each weighing one pound.”

Papias indicates the etymology of the name: “A gabatha is a dish, a vessel, as though hollowed out.”

Hence Phocas was mocked by the Greens as though, in his madness, he used a gabatha instead of a cup. Anastasius, in his *History*:

> “Phocas held a circus game, and the Greens dared to attack him with insults, shouting: ‘You drank from a gabatha; you have lost your senses again.’”

There is a certain type of gabatha called *saxica* or *saxisca*. Anastasius, in his life of Benedict III:

> “One saxica gabatha of the purest silver, weighing three pounds.”

Perhaps the term means “Saxon,” because they were invented in Saxony, a province of Germany, just as *Saxonicia* denotes a type of garment derived from the Saxon people.

The author of *Questions on Both Testaments*, chapter 127:

> “Is not even an ordinary man’s tunic, although clean, nevertheless dirty and forbidden for an emperor? Likewise, a Saxonicia is improper for a senator.”

Or perhaps they were sold and made in Rome in the district of the Saxons. There was indeed a district of the Saxons in the City, mentioned by Anastasius in his life of Leo IV:

> “At the very beginning of his pontificate, a powerful fire attacked the district of the Saxons.”

There are other gabathae called *interrasiles*. Anastasius, in his life of Leo III:

> “Nine interrasile gabathae, weighing eleven pounds.”

They were called *interrasiles* because they were, as it were, scraped smooth—that is, plain and simple, without engraving.

The same author, in his life of Gregory IV:

> “Five interrasile gabathae with their feet.”

Thus *interrasile* gold means gold scraped and leveled. Pliny, book XII, chapter 19:

> “Vespasian Augustus was the first of all to dedicate in the temples of the Capitol and Peace crowns made of cinnamon enclosed in smooth gold.”

The same author supports this interpretation in book XVII, chapter 23:

> “The bark having been scraped so that it may be covered; hence they also want the smooth thing to be pressed down into the furrow.”

Gabathae were made in the shape of lions or other beasts. The same author, in the same place:

> “Likewise, he has a saxica gabatha in the form of a lion.”

Gryphons and other beasts were engraved on gabathae. Anastasius, in his life of Leo III:

> “Silver gabathae bearing gilded gryphons.”

And in the same place:

> “A saxica gabatha in the form of a lion.”

Gabathae hung in the pergola before the altar. Anastasius, in his life of Leo III:

> “He also made fifteen gabathae of the purest gold, set with gems, hanging in the pergola before the altar.”

The gabatha was a kind of dish known to the ancients. Martial, book VII, epigram 47:

> “Gabathae pass rapidly by, and platters fly.”

### Line 4—“Two pairs of gilded amulae hanging. Five fibulatoria”

The matter of arms, or *amulae*, was discussed above. *Fibulatoria* are ecclesiastical garments, such as dalmatics and similar vestments, fastened with clasps.

Anastasius, in his life of Leo IV:

> “Five larger and smaller fibulatoria.”

Trebellius Pollio, in his life of Claudius:

> “Clasped cloaks.”

A *fibula* is a fastening of gold, silver, or bronze by which garments are secured. In this sense Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, says that a connective device is applied like a fibula to join the parts of speech:

> “For it has also applied art, as it were a connective fibula, to bind the discourse together.”

Hence *fibula* may mean the garment itself that is fastened with a fibula. Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book I, chapter 28:

> “Also with phialae, humuli, bocae, and fibulae of the purest gold.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

> “You fasten the purple garment beneath with a golden fibula.”

Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* I:

> “But now the fibula releases your gathered garments.”

Related to these are *campestria*, or *succinctoria*, with which young men girded themselves when exercising in the Campus Martius; hence the name *campestria*.

Augustine, *City of God*, book XIV, chapter 16:

> “And they made for themselves campestria, that is, girdings for the genitals. The word *campestria* is indeed Latin, but it was derived from the fact that young men who exercised naked in the field covered their private parts; hence the common people call those who are girded in this way *campestrati*.”

Hence *campestrati* means those who have *succinctoria*. Liutprand, book VI, chapter 4:

> “Two boys were brought in naked but campestrati, that is, wearing girdings.”

### Line 7—“One pair of silver aquamaniles”

An *aquamanile* is a vessel from which water is poured for washing the hands.

Anastasius, in his life of Sixtus III:

> “Silver aquamaniles, each weighing eight pounds.”

Paul, in book 3 of the *Digest*, title *On Legacies of Household Goods*:

> “Water vessels, basins, aquamaniles.”

Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People*, book II:

> “We call a little water vessel an aquamanile because water is poured from it into a trulleum.”

An *aquamanus*, according to Anastasius below in his life of Leo III:

> “He made two pairs of aquamani, gilded with beaten gold.”

### Line 8—“And a golden necklace with hanging gems”

A *collare* is a necklace of gems, an adornment of women’s necks.

Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> “And around her neck a beaded necklace.”

Ammianus, book XX:

> “He was ordered to produce the diadem; and when he denied ever possessing anything belonging to his wife’s neck or head, it was demanded of him.”

### Line 9—“And he covered the front of the altar and the confession with silver rods”

*Regulae* are rods of gold, silver, bronze, or iron, from which curtains are drawn before an altar or sacred images.

Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 61:

> “Many deceived them on the journey by their commerce, selling bronze rods that had somehow been colored so as to imitate the appearance of tested and assayed gold.”

In other passages Anastasius calls them *regulares*. In his life of Stephen IV:

> “For he also made three silver regulares over the curtains through which they enter toward the altar, where the images are set in the front.”

The same author, in his life of Adrian:

> “At the entrance of the presbytery of the church, where he also made a regular of silver covered with silver, he placed the three aforementioned images upon the same regular. In the upper curtain, that is, in the middle of the presbytery, he made another regular covered with silver.”

The same author, in his life of Leo III:

> “Four small curtains of stauracium, hanging from the regular before the images.”

And below:

> “He also made six silver columns and two regulares of the purest silver, together weighing eighty pounds.”

The same author, in his life of Paschal:

> “He also made, before the vestibule of the altar, a regular covered with sheets of silver.”

### Line 12—“Five small silver crowns”

The golden or silver crowns, or small crowns, were offerings frequently presented by the faithful, as below in this passage:

> “And also a small golden crown with a cross hanging above the altar.”

*Coronula* is a diminutive of *corona*; a further diminutive of *coronula* is *cornula*. Matthew Paris, under the year 1247:

> “And a golden cornula, which is commonly called a garland.”

From this came the vernacular word *cornette*.

### No. 196, line 1—“Here, in the church of the holy Mother of God at the Crib, he made around the columns a regular of candelabra, in the likeness of the church of the blessed apostle Peter”

A *regular of candelabra* is a line or row of candelabra arranged in order.

### Line 9—“White silk curtains adorned with blatta, that is, with a blatta border”

*Blatta* means the same as purple.

Trebellius Pollio, in his life of Claudius:

> “When his wife asked him to wear a single purple silk cloak, he replied: ‘Far be it that threads should be weighed against gold; for at that time a pound of silk cost a pound of gold.’”

Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 38:

> “Therefore he received from the emperor Anastasius the documents of the consulship, and in the basilica of blessed Martin he was dressed in a purple tunic and a cloak.”

### No. 197, line 1—“And he built a monastery beside the same title of the holy martyrs Stephen, Lawrence, and Chrysogonus, appointing there an abbot and a congregation of monks, ordered to offer praises to God in that title by day and by night, after the pattern of the offices of the church of the blessed apostle Peter”

The basilica of the holy martyr Chrysogonus is a cardinal title. Gregory III founded a monastery there and appointed an abbot and a congregation of monks to celebrate the divine office by day and night, following the example of the church of blessed Peter.

From the church of blessed Peter the custom spread to all the other secular and regular churches of celebrating the divine offices at their appointed hours, day and night. These are called the canonical Hours, because the divine offices are recited at fixed times: namely, matins, prime, terce, sext, none, and vespers.

Anastasius, in his life of Adrian:

> “Moreover, in the basilica of blessed Eugenia he newly built from the foundations a monastery of women there and established that they should continually sing praises to God there, namely at prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and matins.”

Augustine, *On Time*, sermon 55:

> “And therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, rise early for the vigils; above all, gather at terce, sext, and none.”

The same author, sermon 78, *On Time*:

> “Yet I ask and urge you more earnestly, brothers, to strive to rise early for the vigils and to come faithfully to terce, sext, and none.”

Gregory III is likewise said below to have restored a monastery beside the Lateran basilica so that the offices might be celebrated there by day and night, after the pattern of the offices of the church of blessed Peter. Adrian also established that the canonical Hours should be celebrated in the monastery of Pope Honorius as in the Lateran church.

Anastasius, in his life of Adrian:

> “And he appointed them to celebrate the offices in the basilica of the Savior, also called Constantiniana, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate: namely, matins, prime, terce, sext, and also none and vespers.”

The same is said below concerning the monastery of Saint Lawrence.

### Line 5—“Separated, that is, from the jurisdiction of the presbyter of the aforesaid title”

Gregory III founded a monastery in the church of the holy martyr Chrysogonus, which is a cardinal title, but exempted it from the jurisdiction of the cardinal presbyter of that title. For the general custom in the City is that no monastery should be subject to a cardinal title: chapter *Dilectus*, *Extra*, *On Chapels of Monks*.

### No. 198, line 5—“He also newly made the roof and likewise the chamber of the apostle Andrew at Saint Peter, and painted it”

It is an ancient custom for churches to be painted.

Anastasius, below in this passage:

> “Here he also rebuilt from almost the foundations the basilica of the pontiff and martyr Saint Calixtus, which had been destroyed, with new structures and a roof, and painted it all.”

And below:

> “Likewise, he rebuilt and painted from the foundations the basilica of the holy Mother of God called at Aquiro, where previously there had been a deaconry and a small oratory; he made it longer and broader.”

I discussed this more fully in Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 17.

### No. 202, line 3—“He also restored anew from the foundations and painted the dining halls that had been placed in ruins at Saint Peter”

An *accubitum* properly means a dining couch on which one reclines for a meal.

Lampridius, in his life of Heliogabalus:

> “He did not easily recline on couches unless they had hare’s fur or the down feathers from beneath partridges’ wings. Often changing the mattresses, he spread cushions for his poorer friends instead of couches.”

Sometimes *accubitum* meant a dining room in which couches were arranged.

Anastasius, in his life of Leo III:

> “He also made in the Lateran patriarchate a dining hall of marvelous size, in which he placed couches.”

And below, in the same passage:

> “He also made a building in the atrium, in which he likewise placed couches.”

The same author, in his life of Leo IV:

> “For the dining hall which Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built from the foundations, and all the furnishings that he had prepared there, had been destroyed through excessive age and the neglect of his pontifical predecessors. On the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, neither the lord Gregory nor the lord Sergius of holy memory ever dined there. But that most blessed and supreme bishop Leo IV, with joy and great delight, newly restored all the furnishings and provisions that had been destroyed there and magnificently returned them to their former use.”

Accordingly, the corrupt passage in Gregory IV should be restored:

> “He also made beside the couches, for the rest of the pontiff, a small but honorably built lodging, where, after the morning prayers or the offices of the Mass, his limbs might sleep.”

Read “beside the couches,” which were, namely, beside the basilica of blessed Peter.

### No. 203, line 1—“In his time the fortress of Gallese was recovered, for which the Roman duchy was daily attacked by the duchy of Spoleto, at the payment of considerable sums of money”

In the time of the Lombards, Italy was divided into duchies. Individual provinces were called duchies, such as the Roman duchy, the duchy of Spoleto, and the duchy of Friuli.

Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 52:

> “Around this time, after Grasulf, duke of Friuli, had died at Forum Julii, Hago undertook the government of the duchy. At Spoleto also, after Atto had died, Theudelapius was made ruler of that city.”

During this period the Roman territory suffered greatly at the hands of Luitprand, king of the Lombards, because of Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, who had fled to Rome while pursued by the king. Four cities were taken from the Roman duchy by siege: Ameria, Horta, Polymartium, and Blera. Anastasius discusses this in his life of Zacharias.

### No. 204, line 4—“And he decreed that, according to the constitution made by the college of priests before the sacred body of blessed Peter, for celebrating the solemn vigils and Masses of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, of the holy apostles, of all the holy martyrs and confessors, and of the perfect righteous resting throughout the whole world, vigils should be celebrated by monks in the oratory dedicated to their name within the church of the apostle Peter under the principal arch, and the solemn Masses by the weekly priests”

This constitution contains two provisions. The first is that the vigils of the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors resting throughout the world should be celebrated by the weekly priests.

In the church of blessed Peter there were weekly priests who celebrated Masses by turns. Anastasius discusses them in his life of Hilary, where I have spoken of them.

### Line 11—“And by the same constitutions he arranged that, in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the days of their anniversaries, lamps for celebrating vigils and offerings from the patriarchate should be carried by the offertory-bearer to celebrate Masses, through the priest whom the pontiff then in office should appoint”

Gregory III established that on the anniversaries of the apostles and martyrs, lamps for celebrating the vigils and offerings—that is, bread and wine—for celebrating the Masses should be carried from the Lateran patriarchate to the cemeteries by the *oblationarius*. This had previously been established by John III, as is evident from Anastasius in his life of John.

The *oblationarius* is a subdeacon who received the offerings—that is, the bread and wine intended for the sacrifice of the Mass—from the pontiff’s hand and then handed them to the archdeacon.

The *Roman Order concerning the Office of the Mass*:

> “The subdeacon receives the offerings from the pontiff and places them in the linen cloth carried behind him by two acolytes.”

And below:

> “Then the archdeacon receives the two offerings from the oblationarius and gives them to the pontiff,” and so forth.

### No. 205, line 3—“He established the venerable Vulcarius as archbishop in the regions of France at Vienne, giving him the pallium”

An archbishop is said to be established by the giving of the pallium because through the pallium the fullness of pontifical office is conferred. Chapter *Nisi*, *On the Authority and Use of the Pallium*.

### Note: Column 1045C

### No. 14, line 7—“Here he built an oratory within the same basilica”

The more cruelly the impious emperor Leo the Isaurian raged in the East against the sacred images and their defenders, the more earnestly the holy Gregory III labored in the West to establish the Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration of the saints in writing and in action.

Once and again, through representatives of the apostolic see, he sent threatening letters to Leo, by which he sought to recall him from heresy and impiety. After summoning a synod of ninety-three bishops in the basilica of Saint Peter, he struck the iconoclasts with the sword of anathema.

On one side of the same basilica he placed images of the Savior and the apostles, and on the other an image of the Mother of God and of the holy virgins, all executed with magnificent workmanship. In the same place he built an oratory in which he honorably deposited, for religious veneration, the relics of saints gathered from throughout the world.

Among these was the body of the blessed presbyter Gabinius, with an altar established for him, to which Sardinia and Corsica sent an annual tribute. There was also an altar of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, together with her image embracing her Son.

These altars remained in Gregory’s oratory until the time of Pope Eugene III, as a Roman canon who was present at the time testifies in his *Description of the Vatican Basilica*. At Eugene’s command the ancient altars were then destroyed and a new one was erected there from the foundations.

To enrich this oratory more and more each day through the intercession of the heavenly beings, Gregory decreed that their anniversary celebrations should be solemnly observed every day by sacred offices performed by the monks of three monasteries serving God in the Vatican basilica.

A priest celebrating the sacred rite in the same oratory was to recite, after the words of the canon “and all your saints,” the following:

> “Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world.”

So Anastasius writes in this passage. Walfrid Strabo, a writer of the same period, agrees fully with him in chapter 22:

> “Gregory III, building an oratory in the basilica of blessed Peter in honor of all the saints, and establishing that offices and Masses should be celebrated there daily in their veneration, instituted that the priest should say in the canon: ‘Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world.’ Since this pertains specifically to that celebration, it is not recorded in the canon that is said generally.”

Since the words instituted by Saint Gregory III were to be said only in the aforesaid oratory by the priest performing the divine office, it plainly follows that nothing at all was added to or changed in the canon after Saint Gregory the Great. The canon consists of the very words of the Lord, apostolic traditions, and the institutions of the holy pontiffs.

This is carefully observed by the most illustrious archbishop of Ravenna, Jerome Crispi, distinguished no less by rank than by learning, in the second edition of his *Golden Dissertation on the Mysteries of Evangelical Law*, p. 110. The work was first composed for the advancement of that clergy and was twice committed to the Roman press for the common good.

### Note: Column 1046C
### Number 202, line 12 — “In his time, etc.”

Leo was contemplating vengeance against Italy, and especially against the pope, whom he considered a supporter of Italy’s revolt. He therefore appointed as commander of the fleet he had equipped Manes, the stronger of his generals. “But the emperor,” says Theophanes in his account of Leo, “was raging against the pope, and against Rome’s and Italy’s defection; and he dispatched a great fleet against him, appointing Manes, commander of the Cybrrhaeote forces, as its chief.”

Meanwhile, the pontiff had taken measures for his own affairs by preparing an embassy to Charles Martel, prince of the Franks, from whom he requested assistance both for the Holy See and for the Roman people, who were rejecting Leo’s rule. The Annals of Metz speak of this embassy before other sources (in Duchesne, *Collection of Frankish Histories*), where the following is read:

“In the year 741, Charles, prince of the Franks, received twice in that same year the embassy sent from the Apostolic See by the most blessed Pope Gregory … The aforesaid bishop Gregory had also sent him a letter, by decree of the Roman nobles, because the Roman people, wishing to abandon the emperor’s domination, had desired to turn to his protection and unconquered clemency.”

From the same Charles he had also demanded assistance against the Lombards (Letters 5 and 6), who were oppressing Italy and inflicting many hardships upon the Holy See.

But God, without any human aid intervening, miraculously protected the See against Leo’s wrath. For a violent storm attacked his fleet between the empire and Italy; it scattered part of it upon the rocks and buried part in the deep waves. Yet Leo did not thereby return to a better course. Rather:

“Then” (Theophanes, at the place cited), “the enemy of God, raging still more fiercely, when he was held by the Arab view against the images, imposed a head-tax upon a third part of Sicily, or Calabria. He ordered those estates called the patrimonies of the holy chief apostles—estates which formerly paid half a measure of gold to the churches and three talents of silver to the public treasury—to be assessed. He also ordered the male children to be counted and registered, as Pharaoh once did with those who were of Hebrew descent.”

Thus, while this new Pharaoh ruled the empire, it suffered plagues no less terrible than those by which Egypt was once afflicted under the ancient Pharaoh. The Saracens invaded it and devastated its provinces. Famine and pestilence subsequently completed their desolation; and, as the calamity increased, a dreadful earthquake overthrew its principal cities and crushed most of the inhabitants beneath the ruins.

Moreover, this emperor, the chief author of all evils, inflicted the worst of them upon his subjects: he left them as his successor his son Constantine Copronymus, who far surpassed his father both in impiety and in every kind of crime.

### Number 205, line 2 — “Bishops in various places, etc.”

Bishop Boniface, who had formerly been sent to convert Germany, had reported to the pontiff by letter how matters there had proceeded. Therefore, as a mark of gratitude and esteem, the pontiff bestowed upon him the dignity of archbishop and sent him the pallium, indicating when he was to use it:

“We have sent you the gift of the sacred pallium, which, receiving it by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, you shall put on; and, as one among the archbishops, we decree, with God as author, that you shall be recognized. But learn, instructed by the apostolic command, how you are to use it. Thus, when you celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, or when it happens that you consecrate a bishop, use it only at that time.” (*Gregory III, Letter 1, to Boniface.*)

He also granted him authority to create bishops according to the laws of the sacred canons:

“We command that, according to the statutes of the sacred canons, wherever the multitude of the faithful has increased, you should, by the authority of the Apostolic See, ordain bishops—yet with pious consideration, so that the dignity of the episcopate may not be cheapened.” (*Ibid.*)

He teaches that those whom the pagans had baptized in another manner ought to be baptized in the name of the most holy Trinity. He orders Boniface to prohibit Christians from eating horseflesh and to impose a severe penalty upon transgressors. Prayer should be made for the dead, and the priests should mention them in the sacrifice of the Mass. Counsel should be given that no one marry more than twice. For parricide, penance should be imposed for as long as life remained, and communion should be given to such persons only at the point of death. Those who sold slaves to the pagans for sacrifice were to be treated like homicides. The consecration of a bishop was always to be performed in the presence of two other bishops. He warns him concerning all these matters.

After Boniface himself had come to Rome, the pope gave him, on his departure, three letters. The first was addressed to all the bishops, priests, and abbots whom he might encounter on the journey; the pope urged them not to detain or delay any member of their ecclesiastical jurisdiction who might wish to travel with Boniface to convert the unbelievers.

The second was addressed to the nobles and people of the recently converted provinces. He begged them to support Boniface’s ministry by their own authority and to expel from their territories all those whom superstition and idolatry had left behind there.

The third was addressed to the bishops of Bavaria and Germany. In it he stated that he had declared Boniface his apostolic vicar in their dioceses, had granted him authority to convene synods wherever he considered it useful, and to report to the Holy See whatever had been done in them.

When Boniface returned to his mission, he visited Bavaria, where he found every kind of corruption among the clergy, owing to the scarcity of bishops. Only one man governed that vast province, and he possessed neither a cathedral city nor a territory. Therefore Boniface established three others there, with the agreement of the dukes and nobles, and founded four cathedral sees: Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg, and Passau. He reported all this to the pontiff.

The pontiff, disapproving of none of it, replied:

“Because you have indicated that you went to the nation of the Bavarians and found them living outside ecclesiastical order, since they had no bishops in the provinces except one named Vivilo, whom we ordained some time ago; and because, with the consent of their duke Orilo—that is, of the nobles of that province—you ordained three bishops and divided that province into four parts, that is, into four parishes, so that each bishop might have his own parish: you have acted well and with sufficient prudence, brother, because you have fulfilled the apostolic command in our place, and have acted just as we commanded you.” (*The same, Letter 7, to the same Willibald, in the* Life of Saint Boniface, *chapter 31.*)

When Gregory appointed Boniface archbishop, he established no metropolitan see in those provinces, since he did not wish Boniface to be attached to any particular episcopate, but rather to assume general care of them all.

### [Column 1023]

#### 190. Gregory III

Gregory III, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, sat for ten years, eight months, and twenty days.

*[Note: B, column 9, day 12; C, day 25.]*

He was a very gentle and exceptionally wise man, sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in the Greek and Latin languages, retaining all the psalms in order by heart, and refined by the most subtle exercise in their meanings. His speech, too, was polished in reading; he encouraged every good work and preached salutary things most fruitfully to the people. He was an unaltered guardian of the Catholic and apostolic faith, continually strengthening the hearts of the faithful by his admonitions, an emulator and most powerful defender of orthodox faith, a lover of poverty, and a provider for the needy.

*[Note: “for the provision of the needy.”]*

He was concerned for them not only through the piety of his mind but also through the labor of his zeal. He redeemed captives, gave generously to orphans and widows, and supplied what was necessary. He loved religious observance according to the Christian rule.

*[Note: “and the Christian rule.”]*

Those who wished to live religiously and possessed the fear of God—or, according to another reading, “wished to possess the fear of God”—he cherished in his heart.

*[Note: “guide,” B.]*

By God’s favor he reached the sacred order of the priesthood. The Roman men—or rather, the entire people, from the greatest to the least—moved by divine inspiration, suddenly seized him by force and elected him to the pontificate when his predecessor had departed this world, while Gregory had been occupied before the bier in performing the service owed to his predecessor.

*[Note: “had been found there.”]*

#### 191

He lived in the time of the emperors Leo and Constantine, during the persecution stirred up by them for the deposition and destruction of the sacred images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God, of all the holy apostles, and of all the saints and confessors. Against this persecution, so that they might come to their senses and withdraw from their error, this most holy man sent admonitory writings established by the authority of the Apostolic See,

*[Note: “according to the authority and institution of the Apostolic See,”]*

just as his predecessor of holy memory had also sent them, through the priest George.

*[Note: B, “Gregory.”]*

*[Note: Baron, annals of 734.]*

But George, led by human fear, did not deliver those same writings to the emperor. On his return, bringing the matter back with him to the city of Rome, he disclosed it to the most holy pontiff and confessed that he had made himself guilty. The pontiff wished to deprive him of the priestly order with a grave threat. When the council was sitting,

*[Note: “when he was sitting in council,”]*

the council and the nobles alike begged that he not be deposed, but rather that the same priest be subjected to penance. After a fitting penance had been imposed upon him, the pope sent him a second time, with the same written letters, to the imperial city.

But the policy of those emperors, wickedly intensified,

*[Note: “argued,”]*

caused those same venerable writings to be detained in the island of Sicily and did not permit them to pass to the imperial city. It also banished the bearer himself into exile for nearly a full year.

#### 192

*[Note: Baron, annals of 732.]*

Therefore, moved by a still greater ardor of faith, the pontiff, together with the assembly of priests, decreed a synodal judgment while they were seated before the sacred confession of the most holy body of the blessed apostle Peter. Present were the supreme and venerable pope; the archbishops, namely Antonius, archbishop of Grado, and John, bishop of Ravenna; ninety-three other bishops of this part of Hesperia; the priests of this holy Apostolic See; the deacons standing with the whole clergy; the noble consuls; and the rest of the Christian people.

They decreed that if anyone thereafter, despising the faithful practice preserved by the ancient custom and by the Apostolic Church, should act against the veneration of the sacred images—namely, those of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; of his ever-virgin, immaculate, and glorious Mother Mary; of the blessed apostles; and of all the saints—and should prove to be their deposer, destroyer, profaner, or blasphemer, he should be excluded from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the unity and structure of the whole Church. All solemnly confirmed this by their subscriptions, and they sanctioned that it be added among the other established regulations of the worthy orthodox predecessors, the pontiffs.

#### 193

After this aforementioned synodal decree had been completed, Gregory again sent other similar admonitory writings for the restoration of the sacred images, through the defender Constantine. These too were detained in the same manner as the earlier writings. Their bearer was held under the strictest guard for nearly a full year. Afterwards, they forcibly took the writings from him and, after that long imprisonment, sent him away with insults and threats.

Indeed, the entire population of this province of Italy likewise sent unanimous petitions to the same princes for the restoration of the images. These too were taken away, like the earlier writings, by Sergius, patrician and *exarch*

*[Note: C, “and devastation,”]*

of the island of Sicily. The bearers were detained for nearly eight months and were sent back in the same way, with insulting reproaches.

Again, the lord pope prepared exhortatory letters for the restoration of the sacred images mentioned above and for the firmness of the orthodox faith. He sent them through the defender Peter to the imperial city, both to Anastasius, the usurper of the see of Constantinople, and to the emperors Leo and Constantine.

*[Note: “to the imperial city.”]*

#### 194

He received from Eutychius the exarch six movable columns of onyx and brought them into the church of the blessed apostle Peter. He placed them around the presbytery before the confession, three on the right and three on the left, beside six other ancient columns equal to them in height.

*[Note: B, “lithoparian”; C, “philoparian.”]*

Upon them he placed beams and covered them with the purest silver. On one side were represented the figures of the Savior and the apostles, and on the other side those of the Mother of God and the holy virgins. He placed silver lilies and lamps above them.

*[Note: “lamp,” or “phara.”]*

They weighed altogether seventy pounds.

*[Note: “seven hundred.”]*

He made an oratory within the same basilica, beside the principal arch on the men’s side. In it he placed, in honor of the Savior and his holy Mother, the relics of the holy apostles and of all the holy martyrs, confessors, perfected, and righteous persons resting throughout the whole world.

He instituted that the feasts of their vigils should be celebrated there daily in order by the monks serving there from three monasteries, and that Masses for their anniversaries should be celebrated in the same place.

*[Note: “who were present”; “he instituted.”]*

In the canon of the Mass he added the following, to be said by the priest:

“Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the presence of your majesty, Lord our God, throughout the whole world.”

*[Note: “He added this to the canon of the Mass.”]*

#### 195

He had this institution inscribed on stone tablets in the same oratory. There he made a screen and donated gifts of various kinds: two golden basins; five other stone basins; four hanging crosses; likewise ten similar crosses; two pairs of hanging, gold-plated vessels; and five clasps.

*[Note: “similar.”]*

He placed above the altar a hanging golden crown adorned with gems and a cross; a golden paten and chalice set with gems; and one silver water ewer.

He also provided an image of the holy Mother of God wearing a golden diadem with gems, a golden necklace with hanging gems, and six sapphire earrings. He covered the face of the altar and the confession, with their small rails, in silver. On the three sides of the altar he placed three silver crosses, weighing altogether thirty-six pounds.

He provided two silver baskets, a daily silver chalice, five small silver crowns, and one silver chalice hanging in the apse of the oratory. Above the same apse he placed three silver crosses, together with the other objects assigned to the decoration of the screen or to the altar furnishings.

#### 196

In the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, he made a circular lampstand over the columns, after the model of the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

*[Note: B, “lampstands.”]*

In the holy oratory there, which is called the Manger, he also made a golden image of the Mother of God embracing the Savior, our Lord and God, adorned with various gems.

*[Note: “adorned with gems.”]*

It weighed five pounds.

He renewed the roof of Saint Chrysogonus the martyr, as well as the vault or paintings of the walls. He made a silver ciborium with five arches, weighing altogether 220 pounds. There he offered four silver crowns, two *pharacanthara*, one silver paten, one silver chalice, and altar cloths, together with white silk veils ornamented with purple hanging all around.

#### 197

He also built a monastery beside the same titular church of the holy martyrs Stephen, Laurence, and Chrysogonus. There he appointed an abbot and a community of monks, organized to offer praises to God in that titular church by day and by night, according to the pattern of the offices of the church of the blessed apostle Peter. It was separated from the jurisdiction of the priest of the aforementioned titular church.

In this monastery, for its support, the same most holy man generously gave estates, gifts, and household dependents. Various other faithful people and lovers of our Lord Jesus Christ also most devoutly bestowed estates and gifts upon the same monastery of Saints Stephen, Laurence, and Chrysogonus.

In the same way he renewed the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist, Saint John the Baptist, and Saint Pancras, which had been established beside the church of the Savior in ancient times

*[Note: “built,”]*

and had been left entirely destitute through excessive neglect of the monastic order.

*[Note: “monastic.”]*

There he donated estates and gifts, and whatever he found alienated from the monastery he restored to the same place after paying the price. He also appointed a community of monks and an abbot to perform daily the sacred offices of divine praise in the basilica of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, which is called the Constantinian basilica beside the Lateran. These offices were arranged by day and by night according to the pattern of those of the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

#### 198

He also re-silvered an ancient image of the holy Mother of God and covered it with the purest silver; it weighed fifty pounds.

He made a large golden paten with various stones, weighing twenty-six pounds, and likewise a chalice with gems, weighing thirty-four pounds. He also made golden Gospels with gems, weighing fifteen pounds.

He newly made the roof and vault of the church of Saint Andrew the apostle at Saint Peter, and painted the vault. In the same basilica he made a golden image of the blessed apostle Andrew set with gems, weighing eight pounds, and inside the confession he covered it with silver, which he gilded with the purest gold.

He also rebuilt from the foundations the basilica of Saint Calixtus, pontiff and martyr, which had almost been destroyed. He constructed it with new masonry and a roof and painted it entirely. There he donated a silver paten and chalice and an altar vestment.

#### 199

He newly constructed the roof of the basilica of Saints Processus and Martinianus, placing beneath it a foundation of very strong masonry behind the venerable bodies of those saints, for the strengthening of the walls of the holy basilica.

In the church of the blessed martyr Genesius he newly restored the roof. There he also erected an altar in the name of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, and donated a silver paten and chalice, as well as a silver crown with six dolphins and a small golden crown with a hanging cross above the altar.

#### 200

In the basilica of the holy Mother of God called “at the Martyrs,” he had the roof, which had collapsed through ancient neglect, thoroughly cleared and restored anew with abundant mortar and lead sheets. Whatever had been scattered around the roof he rebuilt with new brilliance.

#### 201

He built from the foundations, lengthening and widening it, and painted the basilica of the holy Mother of God called “in Aquiro,” in which previously there had been a deaconry and a small oratory.

He also enlarged, with more substantial construction from the foundations, the deaconry of Saints Sergius and Bacchus situated at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, where previously there had been a small oratory. Granting everything that belonged to the use of the deaconry, he decreed that it should serve perpetually for the support of the poor in the ministry of the deaconry.

#### 202

In the cemetery of Saint Petronilla he instituted that an annual station be held. There he offered a golden crown, a silver chalice and paten, and various other objects belonging to the adornment of the church.

He newly restored from the foundations and painted the couches that had been placed in ruins near Saint Peter.

*[Note: B, “the couch.”]*

He newly repaired the roof of the basilica of Saint Mark, situated outside the walls of this Roman city on the Appian Way, after it had collapsed.

In the church of the blessed apostle Paul he replaced five beams and repaired and restored the entire roof of the basilica, from the altar arch to the doors. He also replaced five beams in the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger.

He newly built the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter beside the Lateran, as well as the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Januarius, Urbanus, Tiburtius, Valerianus, and Maximus. He newly completed their roof, which had been lying in ruins.

*[Note: “he rebuilt the roofs lying in ruins.”]*

*[Note: “he rebuilt.”]*

During his time, a very large part of the walls of this Roman city was restored. He also provided from his own resources the maintenance of the craftsmen and the price of the lime to be purchased.

#### 203

During his time the fortress of Gallese was recovered. On its account the Roman duchy was daily being attacked by the duchy of Spoleto. He was able to settle the matter by giving two considerable sums of money to their duke Trasamund, so that the wars and disputes might cease, and he ordered that the fortress be joined to the structure of the holy commonwealth and to the body of the Roman army beloved by Christ.

#### 204

He made altar vestments in the church of the Savior,

*[Note: “at the altars of the churches of the holy Savior,”]*

of the Mother of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of Andrew and the others in various churches.

He also had the ruined walls of the city of Centumcellae rebuilt with great strength almost from their foundations. He established that, according to the decree made by the college of priests before the sacred body of the blessed Peter for celebrating the solemn vigils and Masses of Christ our Lord Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, of the holy apostles, and of all the holy martyrs, confessors, perfected, and righteous persons resting throughout the whole world, vigils should be celebrated by monks in the oratory dedicated to their name inside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, beneath the principal arch, and the solemn Masses by the weekly priests.

According to the same institutions, he arranged that in the cemeteries situated all around Rome, on the anniversaries of the saints, lamps for the vigils and offerings from the patriarchal treasury should be carried by the offertory-bearer, so that Masses might be celebrated by whichever priest the pontiff in office at the time should appoint.

#### 205

He held three ordinations during the month of December: twenty-four priests, three deacons, and eighty bishops in various places. He also appointed the venerable Vulcarius archbishop in the region of the Franks, in the city of Vienne, after giving him the pallium.

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. His episcopal see was vacant for four days.

[Note: [Col. 1067A]]

Num. 206, line 1.—Zacharias. After an interval between pontificates of only four days following the death of Gregory III, Zacharias was elected pope: specifically, on the first day when the leading men gathered in the Lateran patriarchate to deliberate together about the election. For during the preceding three days the proper funeral rites were being paid to the deceased pontiff, and it was not possible to deliberate about the election. [Col. 1067C] This hurried and peaceful election seems to have resulted both from the merits of Zacharias and also from the fact that the tyranny of the exarchs had been weakened: for the Italian army had by no means obeyed the heretical emperor Leo, and had openly defected from Copronymus.

Num. 208, line 7.—Against the Roman duchy. Rome and its duchy easily came from the Greeks to the Roman pontiff because of Leo’s heretical edicts, when the peoples refused obedience to the heretical emperor. The Roman duchy, which is frequently mentioned in the preceding deeds and whose governors were appointed by the emperors, consisted of the city of Rome together with its castles, towns, and even fortified places in the regions of Tuscia. These were Portus, Centumcellae, Caere, Bleda, Maturanum, Sura, Nepet, the Castle of Gallese, Orta, Polimartium, Ameria, Tuder, Perusia, Narnia, and Otricoli. In Latium there were Signia, Anagnia, Ferentinum, Alatrium, Patricum, Frusino, and Tibur. That this duchy was under the discretion of the Roman see during the time of Gregory II is also clear from the fact [Col. 1067D] that the Roman army, while the pontiff himself was governing, suppressed the seditious men and the tyrant Tiberius, and compelled Liutprand to restore the places he had usurped in this duchy. Thus, from the time of Gregory II and his successors, clearer indications of supreme temporal dominion appear.

Num. 213, line 5.—John, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna. Agnellus reports in the Life of John how Ravenna was captured by the king of the Lombards through treachery. He is silent, however, about the benefits conferred on the Ravennates by Pope Zacharias, which Anastasius describes here. Compare Agnellus, p. 170.

Num. 217, line 15.—A peace was made. Zacharias, following the custom of supreme rulers, made peace with Rachis, who, after the death of King Liutprand, had assumed the Lombard government.

Num. 221, line 1.—Carloman. He was Pippin’s brother; both were sons of Charles Martel. Popes Gregory II and Gregory III had long before entered into treaties with the Franks, and Zacharias had renewed them. In the year 746, when Pippin consulted him as to which brother seemed more worthy of the royal dignity—whether the one who, languishing in idleness, contributed nothing to the common welfare of the peoples, or the one who thought day and night about the safety and protection of the kingdom—he replied that he certainly believed that king should be chosen who served the kingdom’s advantage and the safety of the peoples. When asked, he issued a decree [Col. 1068C] that they should substitute Pippin as king.

Thus the Bertinian Annals, under the year 749, report that Burchard and Fulrad were sent to ask about transferring the kingdom to Pippin: “Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Folrad, chaplain, were sent to Pope Zacharias to inquire about the kings in Francia, who at that time did not possess royal power, whether that was right or not. And Pope Zacharias instructed Pippin that it would be better for the one who possessed power to be called king than for the one who remained without royal power, so that the order might not be disturbed. Therefore, by apostolic authority, he ordered Pippin to be made king.”

And under the year 750: “Pippin was elected king according to the custom of the Franks, and was anointed by the hand of the holy and venerable archbishop Boniface, and was raised by the Franks to the kingdom in the city of Soissons. But Childeric, who was falsely called king, was tonsured and sent to the monastery of Sithiu.”

The continuator of Fredegar likewise wrote under the year 751: “And the land rested from warfare. At that time, with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, a report having been sent and authority received from the apostolic see, the illustrious Pippin was elevated to the royal throne by the election of all Francia, with the consecration of the bishops and the submission of the nobles, together with Queen Bertrada, as the ancient order demands.”

The Annals edited by Pithoeus have the following: “In the seven hundred and fifty-second year from the incarnation of the Lord, Pope Zacharias, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, instructed the people of the Franks that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Therefore King Childeric, the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent to a monastery. Pippin, however, was anointed in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface the archbishop and was elevated with the honor of the kingdom.”

The epoch of the royal line of the Carolingians should therefore begin in the year 752, as Antonius Pagius proves at length under that same year in his *Critica*.]

[Note: [Col. 1069A]]

Num. 206, line 1.—Zacharias. In the year 741, on 5 December, which was the eighth day after Gregory’s death, Zacharias was unanimously elected pope. He sat for ten years, etc. The number of years, months, and ten days assigned above is correctly calculated from the beginning and end of his pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 1069A]]

## Chronological Notes

The patrimonies of the apostolic see ought to be reclaimed by the supreme pontiffs, both by right of patrimony, as that prelate who had deserved exceptionally well of the same see used to say (Blanchinus, *Anastasius*, no. 34, on Saint Sylvester), and by another and more compelling right flowing from divine laws, according to which things sacred to God are to be administered, possessed, retained, vindicated, and recovered by the supreme priest from sacrilegious usurpers whenever they are occupied.

Hence these two greatest pontiffs—of the first, the interval before his pontificate still remains to be examined; of the second, its beginnings, see, and death—namely Gregory III and Zacharias, both celebrated for the innocence of their conduct and the holiness of their lives, attempted, the one by force of arms and the other by action, to recover the cities of Ameria, Horta, Polimartium, and Blera, which King Liutprand of the Lombards had taken from the holy see.

Gregory had lost them because he had protected Trasamundus, duke of Spoleto, within the walls of the City from Liutprand’s fury. When he had tested the treachery of the Lombard king, whose strength had been increased by the Roman army so that he might more easily recover his duchy and the cities of the Church, Gregory sent an embassy twice to Charles Martel, whom he calls the under-king of Francia, requesting aid so that, by their arms, he might assert the rights of the Church. Meanwhile Charles and Saint Gregory died a few days apart.

But what was to be desired from the all-good and all-great God occurred: Zacharias immediately succeeded Gregory, and Pippin succeeded Charles—the latter outstanding in the conduct of affairs, the former in the glory of arms. [Col. 1069C] For after several years Pippin extended the patrimonies of the holy see in every direction. Zacharias, scarcely elevated to Peter’s see, negotiated through envoys with the king of the Lombards for the restoration of the cities, and aided him with Roman troops against the treacherous Trasamundus, after the king had promised to restore them. When the king did not keep his promises, Zacharias went fearlessly and boldly to his camp in the territory of Spoleto, and did not return to Rome until the patrimonies that had been seized long before had been restored, together with the four cities taken two years earlier, of which he himself personally took possession. Then he entered Rome, where, devoting himself to sacred duties, he gave thanks to Christ, the vindicator of the Church.

These events were accomplished by the two pontiffs within three years, as can be seen in my arrangement in the *Pontifical Caesarean Chronology*—unless someone prefers to enter the labyrinths of the Deacon and the Franks, from which even Pagius, a man of such learning, was unable to emerge. But, lest I seem to stray too far from my purpose, I turn to the reckoning of the dates.

After Saint Gregory III died, as was stated in his notes, on 28 November, the day on which he is commemorated in the martyrologies, the pontificate was vacant for four days—not eight, as is read in some codices and catalogues. This is correctly given by the common text and by two Freherian codices, the Cavensis, and the fourth Ambrosianus; all the others, especially the Colbertine codices, except the seventh, say nothing of an interval between pontificates. Thus, counting four days from the day of death, 28 November, which belongs to Gregory’s see, one arrives at 3 December. As the letter A of the Sunday cycle shows, this fell on a Sunday in the year 741 and must therefore be assigned to Zacharias’s ordination.

Zacharias sat for ten years, three months, and thirteen days, as correctly stated by the Lucensis Catalogue and the second Freherian codex. Two Colbertine catalogues incorrectly count one day and one month more than the others.
