For from the day of death, 15 March 752, on which Anastasius testifies that Zacharias was buried and which the martyrologies confirm, it is clear that this pontiff [Col. 1070A] sat for ten years, three months, and thirteen days, with both the day of his ordination and the day of his death included.

Since this is so, Pagius must in no way be heard when, on his own authority, he wants Saint Zacharias to have been ordained on 30 November, the feast of Saint Andrew. To pass over what I have often discussed elsewhere—perhaps to the point of weariness—about the Sundays proper for ordination, and what I shall have to recall in the following note, how can a period of four days be inserted between the 28th and the 30th? I cannot embrace this not only in my mind, but not even in thought.

Although Regino, whom alone Pagius ought to have followed in establishing Gregory’s pontificate, may have included the day of burial in the total—a fact that seems new to Pagius, although it is customary in all the codices and catalogues—it may indeed be possible, because of the constraints that press upon us, to count the interval between pontificates from that point. But how will the greater difficulty arising elsewhere be overcome?

The elections of the Roman pontiffs took place only on the third day after the burial, both because of the constitution of Boniface III, cited elsewhere, and because of the praiseworthy custom of the Roman Church. Therefore, unless someone wishes to ruin the monuments of the ancients, the Roman ordines, and the *Liber Diurnus* of the pontiffs, he will say at most that the election took place on 30 November.

If someone were to connect this election with the ordination—as though the elected man were sent to the Lateran patriarchate, as was customary, and from there hurried with all speed to the Vatican, with all the other ceremonies performed that the *Ordo* and the *Diurnus* teach—he would appear not to know the ancient rites sufficiently. For during this period the *enthronement* (*ἐνθρονισμός*) preceded the consecration and took place immediately after the election.

To avoid asserting this without evidence, Anastasius himself, speaking of the successor of Saint Zacharias, who had been elected in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib, says (no. 227): “All of them, with sincere devotion and acclamations of praise, carried him into the basilica of the Saviour, which is called Constantiniana, and from there they entered within and introduced him into the patriarchate according to custom.”

He says it still more clearly of Valentine [Col. 1070C] (no. 455), likewise elected in the basilica of Saint Mary: “Then, with fitting praises of glory and the full dignity of honor, he was led by them to the Lateran patriarchate and placed upon the pontifical throne.”

The consecration took place on another day—namely Sunday—whose arrival was awaited after the enthronement had taken place. Anastasius himself testifies to this in the same passage: “When the day of his consecration had dawned brightly and the light was already shining, all the Romans together led the aforesaid bishop from the palace to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and, with the help of divine majesty, they consecrated him supreme pontiff upon the high throne.”

Thus the enthronement took place on the day of the election itself in the Lateran patriarchate; then, on another day—without doubt Sunday—the consecration took place in the basilica of Saint Peter. From this point the age of the consecrated man began to be counted. For the time when he was merely elected and, in some fashion, enthroned belonged to the interval between pontificates. Consequently, Pagius, who correctly taught this in connection with the year of Christ 67, now undermines his own position by adopting the opposite doctrine.

The ordination of Saint Zacharias has therefore been vindicated and restored to its proper day, as was right. For when, ordaining the bishop of Interamna on a Sunday, he gave the greatest defender of pontifical antiquity the occasion to assert that bishops were not ordained except on Sundays (Blanchinus, *Anastasius*, no. 2, on Saint Linus), it must not even be imagined that Zacharias himself was not consecrated on a Sunday.

Since, I say, Zacharias’s ordination has been vindicated, it is necessary not to pass over in culpable silence the final year of his pontificate, distinguished by two memorable events. The year of the holy pontiff’s death is made memorable by the end of the exarchate of Ravenna and the beginning of the Carolingian kings, who deserved so well of the apostolic see.

The period of the exarchate, which comprised approximately 184 years—from the year 567, when the patrician Longinus came to Italy, to 751, when the patrician Eutychius departed for Constantinople—came to an end around July of that year, 751, when King Aistulf captured Ravenna. Bachinus learnedly observes this in his notes on Agnellus (*Part 2, on the schism of Maurus*), where he produces a charter issued in the palace of Ravenna on the fourth day of July, in the third year of our most fortunate reign, under indiction 4. Thus the exarchs were expelled from Italy approximately nine months before the death of Saint Zacharias.

Pagius connects the beginning of the Carolingians with the month of the pontiff’s death, March; under the year 752, from numbers 1 to 11, he establishes this epoch with considerable learning. No arguments are needed concerning the year itself, for we have the Frankish annals as witnesses. Here are the very words from the Pithoean Fulda Annals: “752. Pope Zacharias, by the authority of Saint Peter the apostle, instructed the people of the Franks that Pippin, who exercised royal power, should also enjoy the dignity of the name. Thus King Childeric, who was the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks, was deposed and sent to a monastery. Pippin, however, was anointed king in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface the archbishop and was elevated with the honor of the kingdom” [Col. 1071B].

The Bertinian annals, which are silent about this year, say under 754: “Stephen, they say, confirmed Pippin with holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Charles and Carloman.” If he confirmed him, then Pippin had previously been inaugurated.

On this matter Pagius should be consulted in the place cited, where, against Cointius and Mabillon, he most eloquently proves the epoch of Pippin and the deposition of Hyldricus, or Childeric III, the last of the Merovingians.]

[Note: [Col. 1071B]]

## Ciaconius

Num. 206, line 1.—Zacharias, son of Polychronius Pontinius, was born in Siberena of Magna Graecia, now called Calabria. He was a regular canon, then a monk of Saint Benedict, and soon afterward was made by Pope Gregory III a cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church. Under the heretical and most impious iconoclast emperor Constantine Copronymus Augustus, the fifteenth pope residing in the empire, he sat for ten years, three months, and fourteen days: he was created on the Kalends of December and consecrated on the third day before the Nones of the same month in the year 741. He is counted among the best and holiest pontiffs.

[Note: [Col. 1071C]]

## Annotation of Thomas Aceti

Num. 206, line 1.—A Greek by nationality. Although the writers agree that Zacharias came from Magna Graecia, which is now Calabria, they nevertheless disagree about the place. Some do not identify his homeland; others assign him to Sybaris, as Ciaconius and Ferracius do. Nevertheless, this pontiff came from the city of Siberena, commonly called Santa Severina, as constant tradition relates and as appears from the Breviary of the Lateran Canons, where it reads: “Zacharias, born in the city of Siberena in Calabria.” See Baronius with his notes.

[Note: [Col. 1071C]]

Num. 207, line 1.—He found all Italy in turmoil. The holy pontiff found all Italy disturbed by the arms of the Lombards, and Liutprand, their king, preparing for war against the Roman duchy, from which he had already taken four cities—Horta, Polimartium, Ameria, and Bleda. Therefore, “having sent an embassy to the aforesaid king of the Lombards,” as Anastasius says, “he proclaimed salutary words to him. Inclined by the admonitions of the holy man, he promised to return the aforesaid four cities which he had taken from the Roman duchy.”

But while King Liutprand still failed to restore the aforesaid four cities, Zacharias judged that he ought to go to meet him at Interamna, in the territory of Spoleto, in the year 742. Thus, accompanied by the entire Roman clergy, he left the city and directed his journey there.

When the king learned this, unwilling to allow himself to be surpassed in courtesy, he sent a legate to meet him and escort him as far as Narnia, where most of the dukes and soldiers received him. As he approached Interamna, the king came to meet him with the rest of the company of nobles and soldiers. He traveled for some distance with him in pleasant conversation, and then dismissed him to a palace prepared for him. [Col. 1072A]

The following day, when they had again come out for a conversation, the holy pontiff so softened the king’s mind that he granted him everything he requested and restored to the same holy man the aforesaid four cities, which he himself had taken two years earlier through the siege conducted on behalf of the aforementioned duke of Spoleto, Trasamundus—that is, on his account.

“And he confirmed them by a donation,” says the same Anastasius. He adds that the king voluntarily restored to the pontiff the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken from the Roman Church thirty years earlier, and moreover, by a deed of donation, reconveyed to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the patrimonies of Narnia, Ancona, and Auximum, together with the valley of the Sutrine territory called Magna. He also confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years and restored to the aforesaid pontiff all the captives whom he held.

Finally, the four cities were restored, and the pontiff returned to Rome.

### No. 213, line 1.—“While the aforesaid king was oppressing the province of Ravenna excessively” [Col. 1072B]

In the following year, 743, the same king Luitprand attempted to bring the exarchate of Ravenna under his authority and prepared to besiege Ravenna. Therefore the pope, at the request of Eutychius the exarch and John, archbishop of Ravenna, proceeded to that city, leaving the Roman city under the administration of the patrician and duke Stephen. Before departing from Rome, he sent envoys bearing gifts to Luitprand, begging him to abandon his plan and return the fortress of Cesena to the people of Ravenna. But when he could obtain nothing, he came to Ravenna, where the Ravennates received him with abundant tears, crying out and saying: “He has come, he has come, our Father, who has left his sheep and hastened to free us who are lost.”

From that city he sent the priest Stephen and Ambrosius the primicerius to King Stephen, so that they might announce his arrival to him. He himself entered the territory of the Lombards and followed as an attendant behind his messengers, whom the said king refused to receive. [Col. 1072C] But when the pope had reached the Po on 28 June, the king sent his nobles to receive him. With them he reached Ticinum, where the king was residing. The king came outside the city walls to meet him; then, in order to celebrate the solemn Masses of the vigil of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he proceeded to his basilica, which is called “at the Golden Heaven,” and afterward, when the offering had been completed, entered the same city.

On the following day, Zacharias the pontiff was invited to celebrate the Nativity of that prince of the apostles. He celebrated the solemn Masses, and there they mutually received food together. On the next day the king invited him to his palace. The pope was received there honorably and begged him no longer to oppress the province of Ravenna, but to return the cities he had taken, together with their territories, and likewise the fortress of Cesena. Although reluctantly, the king replied that he would do so. He escorted him as far as the Po and sent him away, giving him men from among his leading nobles to restore the territories of Ravenna, especially Cesena. [Col. 1072D] After these places had been recovered, the pope returned to Rome and, having given thanks to God, again celebrated the Nativity of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

All this is established by Anastasius. From these facts Marca concludes, in book III of *On Concord*, chapter 11, no. 5, that it could not be demonstrated more clearly that at this time the supreme pontiffs retained responsibility for the imperial government and that imperial officials presided over the administration of affairs at Ravenna and Rome, so that every hope of preserving Italy had been placed in the supreme dignity of the pontiff. “From these facts,” says Baronius, “see, under the year 743, how unjust are the complaints of the Easterners against the Roman pontiff, alleging that he stripped the Eastern emperors of the Western empire.”

### No. 219, line 7.—“This most blessed Zacharias, according to ecclesiastical custom”

According to the rite of the Church, Pope Zacharias sent to the Church of Constantinople in 742 the synodical letter of his orthodox profession of faith, and another petition through his *Responsales* to the emperor Constantine. But these men found Artabasdus, the usurper and rebel, inside the palace of the imperial city. After the eyes of both Artabasdus and his sons had been put out, Constantine Copronymus, although a heretic, received the envoy of the Apostolic See, and sent him back to Rome. “And, in accordance with what the most blessed pontiff Zacharias had requested, he sent to the same most holy pope and to the holy Roman Church, for perpetual possession, a written grant of two estates called Nymphas and Nornias, which belonged by right to the commonwealth,” says Anastasius. This donation took place in 743, as the deposition of Artabasdus demonstrates.

Moreover, an *estate* (*massa*) is the same as a *manse* or *mansa*, and designates a definite portion of land, as Du Cange explains in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under the entries “Mansus” and “Massa.” From this Baronius’s annotator observes that it is clearly evident that Gregory II did not shake off the yoke of the empire and consequently did not strike Leo the Isaurian with an anathema. [Col. 1073B] For Zacharias would not have had any dealings with Constantine, who was worse than his father Leo, if Constantine had been excommunicated by his predecessor and punished by the imposition of tribute.

### No. 221, line 1.—“In his time, etc.”

In 747, Carolomannus, mayor of the palace of France, “committed the kingdom, together with his son Drogo, into the hands of his brother Pippin, and came to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, intending to remain there in the monastic order,” as the continuator of Fredegar testifies. He is supported by the annalist of Metz, the Nazarian annalist, the Petavian annalist, the annalist of Masiacum, and the author of the Chronicle of Saint-Denis.

Anastasius reports the same event, understanding by the word “clericate” the monastic state; in this sense the word is commonly used elsewhere as well. Hence those writers must be corrected who assert that Carolomannus first went to Cassino and became a monk there. For Herkempertus writes that he went to Rome and was made a monk by Pope Zacharias, and that after some time he proceeded from there to Cassino. In the intervening period, however, he built on Mount Soracte a monastery in honor of Saint Sylvester, where he is said once to have hidden during the persecution that took place under Constantine, as Eginhard writes in his annals under the year 746. He reports the same event here in his *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 2; Adrevaldus, too, follows him in book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 14. Adrevaldus adds that many nobles from Francia, traveling to Rome to fulfill their vows and interrupting the leisure that Carolomannus especially enjoyed at the monastery of Mount Soracte, compelled him to change his residence. It follows from this that Carolomannus was clothed in the monastic habit at Rome by Pope Zacharias himself.

### No. 223, line 9.—“King Ratchis, abandoning his royal dignity”

Rachis, king of the Lombards, disregarding the twenty-year peace that he had established with the Roman pontiff, invaded the Pentapolis, laying waste to everything with sword and fire, and surrounded Perugia with a siege. When Pope Zacharias heard this, he took certain members of his clergy and, trusting in divine assistance, went to the same city. He appeased Rachis with gifts and prayers and induced him to lift the siege. Indeed, by his sacred exhortations he instilled in him such disgust for secular life that, after renouncing the kingdom together with his wife Thesia and his daughter Rattruda, Rachis professed the religious life under the rule of Saint Benedict: he in the monastery of Cassino, and the women in a convent for women which they built and endowed not far from Cassino. This is established by Anastasius in his *Life of Zacharias*, by Leo of Ostia in the *Cassinese Chronicle*, chapter 8, and by Sigebert in his *Chronicle*, where he testifies that Rachis renounced the world in 749. The same year is also given by the anonymous monk of Nonantula in the *Life of Saint Anselm, the First Abbot of Nonantula in Italy*, preserved by Mabillon in *The Benedictine Centuries*, part I, century IV.

[Col. 1074A]

### No. 226, line 1.—“This most blessed pope, etc.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in his *Life of Zacharias*; Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 252; and John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 75 of his *Life of Saint Gregory*, report that Zacharias translated the books of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory the Great from Latin into Greek. John writes:

> “These books—that is, the *Dialogues*—Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, most learned in both Greek and Latin, in the time of the emperor Constantine, after approximately 175 years”—John the Deacon counts at least fifteen years too many—“translated into the Greek language and disseminated among the Eastern Churches, although the crafty perversity of the Greeks, in the passage concerning the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, cunningly scraped away and removed the name of the Son.”

For Gregory had left written in the final chapter of book II of the *Dialogues*: “Since it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son.” But in the Greek text circulated under Zacharias’s name one reads: “Therefore it is plainly evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father [Col. 1074B] and remains in the Son.”

[Note: [Col. 1074B]]

## SOMMIER

### No. 210, line 5.—“The aforesaid four cities, etc.”

The historian expressly notes that the cities were returned to the pontiff together with their inhabitants. This certainly indicates something other than mere useful ownership, whatever later writers may assert when they contend that during this period the Roman pontiff exercised no royal right or supreme authority, since everything continued to remain with the emperors.

They ought nevertheless to have observed that it was not to the emperor, or to any of his officials, that the Lombard king restored the cities and the places belonging to them in the Roman duchy, together with the captives taken during the war. The restoration was made solely to the pontiff and the Apostolic See, and it was ratified and confirmed by a solemn donation signed by the king before the altar. The king took the document from the altar and, after signing it, placed it again upon the altar. [Col. 1074C] The possession was therefore of the same kind as that which one pontiff entered into, and not that of someone dependent in any fashion upon the emperor.

### No. 221, line 1.—“Carolomannus, son of Charles, king of the Franks”

For a long time the mayors of the palace of France had arrogated supreme power to themselves, and nothing remained to the descendants of the great Clovis except the royal name. But Pippin, surnamed the Short, the last of the mayors of the palace, eventually undertook the great task of assuming for himself the royal dignity, title, and right.

To carry out this plan and make its outcome firm and valid, he understood that, besides the consent of the nobles of the kingdom, it was necessary to support it with the authority of the Apostolic See, lest subject peoples should imagine that they could change their kings at will:

> “Eginhard,” says Marca, “in his *Annals*—*Marca, Hispanic History*, book III, chapter 4—adds the authority of the Apostolic See, so that peoples would not think that changes of kings had been permitted to their own discretion. To this he adds the consent of the nobles and the unbroken succession [Col. 1074D] of both lines of kings, whose negligence and inertia had been fatal to the Christian commonwealth.”

A highly opportune occasion presented itself for winning the favor of the holy See toward Pippin’s affairs, since Pippin alone could have subdued the Lombards and supported religion, which was endangered everywhere. A very recent author observes that Pippin employed the services of Saint Archbishop Boniface to carry out the undertaking and to test what Zacharias’s position in the matter would be (P. Daniel, *History of France*, under Pippin).

For this reason Pippin sent to the pontiff Boniface himself, one of his priests, so that he might consult him about various matters pertaining to his ministry. Among other things Boniface wrote:

> “With earnest prayers I beseech the holiness of your paternal piety mercifully to receive this priest of mine. He has certain secrets of mine which he ought to disclose only to your piety, some of them orally . . . . He must bring back to me the answer and counsel of your fatherhood on the authority of Saint Peter the Apostle, so that, after hearing and considering all these matters, I may, with God’s help, endeavor to do whatever may please you.”  
> (*Life of Boniface*, book II, chapter 9.)

The pontiff gave an oral answer to Boniface’s priest concerning these secret matters, and the outcome showed that his response favored Pippin’s plan.

“In the meantime,” says Zacharias (letter 12, to Boniface), “your aforesaid bearer, Lul, together with his other companions, made known to us, clearly reporting both orally and in writing, everything that had been entrusted to them by your holy brotherhood. We have sent back to your brotherhood an answer concerning these matters, both orally and in writing.” [Col. 1075A]

And in fact, as we learn from the Chronicle edited by Pithoeus, the *Fulda Annals*, and the *Loisel Annals*, the matter occurred as follows:

> “Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad the chaplain were sent by Pippin to Rome to consult Pope Zacharias about the case of the kings who were in Francia at that time. They possessed only the name of king and no royal power, for all of it was held by the mayor of the palace. Therefore he asked that it be decided which of them ought justly to be called and be king: the one who sat safely at home, or the one who bore responsibility for the whole kingdom and the burdens of all its affairs.
>
> “Through these men the said pontiff sent word that it was better for the one to be called king with whom supreme power resided. By his authority he ordered that Pippin be constituted king. In accordance with the sanction of the Roman pontiff, Pippin was called king of the Franks, and, to confer this dignity of honor upon him, was anointed with sacred unction by the hand of the holy and blessed Boniface; according to Frankish custom he was raised to the throne of the kingdom in the city of Soissons.
>
> “But Childeric, who falsely bore the name of king, was shaved and sent to a monastery. He was the last of the Merovingians to rule the Franks.”

Besides the three authors mentioned above, who wrote about the transfer of the Frankish kingdom from the first dynasty to the second, and besides Eginhard, Pippin’s secretary to Charles the Great, who says that Pippin was made king from prefect of the palace through the authority of the Roman pontiff (*Life of Charlemagne*), the same account is also found in the heading of a short work composed by a contemporary writer of Pippin. Mabillon saw a copy of it in Papebrochius’s possession and quotes the very words in his *Diplomatic Work*, taken from the end of Gregory of Tours’s book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. They read:

> “If you wish to know, reader, in what period this little book appears to have been written and published in praise of the precious holy martyrs, you will find that it was in the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the time of the most fortunate, peaceful, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of the blessed memory of the former prince Charles, in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign, in the name of God . . . .
>
> “The aforesaid most flourishing lord Pippin, the pious king, was raised to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier by the authority and command of the holy and revered lord Pope Zacharias, by the anointing with holy chrism of the blessed priests of Gaul, and by the election of all the Franks.”
>
> (*At the end of Saint Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors*, and in Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book 5, table 22.)

To tell the truth, I cannot sufficiently marvel at certain modern writers, both Protestants and some of our own people—Natalis Alexander, *section* 8, *dissertation* 2—who accuse the ancient testimonies concerning the truth of this matter of falsity, although no suspicion whatever can attach to them.

The same pontiff, Zacharias, granted Pippin the power to nominate the bishops of the Frankish kingdom, in order to apply a healing hand to the abuses and excesses of those times whenever elections had to be conducted. This occurred while Pippin was still mayor of the palace, for he received such a concession at the Council of Soissons, held in 744, eight years before he ascended the royal throne.

> “After Pippin had laid before Zacharias, the Roman pope, the needs of this kingdom, in a synod attended by Boniface the martyr, he obtained his consent that, as bishops died, he might, through the diligence of men whom he had found most reliable, remedy the harshness of the times.”
>
> (Lupus, abbot of Ferrara, letter 81, to Amulo, archbishop of Lyon.)

[Col. 1076A]

[Note: [Col. 1076A]]

## ALTASERRA

### No. 211, line 6.—“On that Sunday, after the solemn Masses had been completed, he invited the same king to dinner in order to receive the apostolic blessing”

Here “blessing” means refreshment or dinner, either because the meal begins with the blessing of the table or because it is given in the manner of an *eulogia*, that is, a blessing.

*Life of Louis the Pious*: “When, at the beginning of spring, he was being sent away by his father, he was asked why, although he was king, he was so poor in household resources that he could not offer even a blessing unless it had been requested of him.” And below: “After they had shared together in the blessing of bread and wine, the emperor returned to the city.”

Council of Melphia under Urban II: “So that bishops and abbots may retain tithes from vineyards, fields, and crops that they cultivate for their own use or that of the brothers, for a blessing or for receiving guests.” Canon, *Questions* 16, question 1.

### No. 213, line 22.—“The cloud itself accompanied them, covering the way to the basilica of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna”

To *conviare* means to travel along the road together with another. Anastasius, below in the same codex: “After this, the same king, going from place to place, accompanied that holy man and escorted him as far as the Po.”

### No. 214, line 3.—“These men entered the territory of the Lombards, into the city called Imola”

Imola is a city of Emilia, formerly Forum Cornelii, later called Imola after the city’s fortress, whose name was Imola. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 18: “And the Forum of Cornelius, whose fortress is called Imola.”

Forum Cornelii was a city of Gallia Cisalpina, later called Lombardy. Martial, book III, epigram 4:

> “If anyone inquires in what land, in what city, we are,  
> You may tell him that I am from the Forum of Cornelius.”

Forum Cornelii was an episcopal city, formerly a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Milan. Hence Ambrose, bishop of Milan, appointed one of the suffragan bishops as visitor of the vacant church. He himself bears witness in letter 44, to Constantius his fellow bishop:

> “I commend to you, my son, the Church that is at the Forum of Cornelius, so that you may visit it frequently in the near future, until a bishop is appointed for it.”

Today it belongs to the metropolitan see of Ravenna. Gregory, book VI, letter 39, where I discussed it.

### Line 12.—“With them he reached Ticinum, where the king himself was residing; passing outside the walls of the same city, at the ninth hour of prayer, he proceeded to his basilica, called ‘at the Golden Heaven,’ to celebrate the solemn Masses of the vigil of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles”

The ninth hour of prayer is mentioned because the sacred office is distributed among fixed hours: matins, the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours, vespers, and compline. Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 16.

### No. 218, line 1.—“Here in the Lateran patriarchate, before the basilica of blessed Theodore the pope, he newly built a dining hall, which he adorned with various marbles and glass, metals, mosaics, and painting; he also decorated with sacred images both the oratory of Saint Sylvester and the portico”

The passage is corrupt. In place of *vitio*, read *vitreis*, “with glass.” In ancient times the walls of buildings were faced with glass joined by bitumen, in place of plaster. Vopiscus, in *Firmus*: “For he is said to have faced a house with square pieces of glass set in bitumen and other substances.” Seneca, letter 86: “But who nowadays would tolerate bathing in such a way? A man seems poor and dirty to himself unless his walls shine with large and costly discs, unless the ceiling is concealed by glass.”

### Line 11.—“Here in the church of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, he made hanging curtains between the columns from silk cloths”

Curtains between columns were used to adorn churches, made of silk cloths or hangings. Anastasius, in his *Life of Hadrian*: “Also, through the various arches, fifty-seven Syrian curtains.” And below: “Twenty curtains of Syrian cloth, and twenty of linen.” The same author, in his *Life of Leo III*: “And larger silk curtains, stamped, having a *periclysis*, and a cross of *bathin*, or *fundatum*.” Read *blathin*.

The same author, immediately below, says: “Moreover, through the silver arches he made Easter curtains with a *periclysis* of *stauracin*.”

Among the ancients, images were also arranged between columns. Cicero, *Against Verres*, book III: “Where are those statues now, Verres? I mean those which we recently saw arranged at your house beside every column, in every intercolumniation, and finally in the open air, like a forest.” Indeed, forests were also planted between the columns of larger buildings—that is, rows of trees planted for ornament. Horace, book I, letter 10:

> “Of course, a forest is cultivated among the varied columns.”

### Line 13.—“Here in the church of the aforesaid prince of the apostles he arranged all the books belonging to his household, which are read at matins throughout the cycle of the year, in the work of a book cabinet”

Zacharias placed his own books in a cabinet of the Roman Church. An *armarium* is a library of books. See “But if a library,” *On Legations*, book III. Pliny, book II, letter 17: “A cabinet was built into its wall, giving it the appearance of a library.” Sidonius, book II, letter 9: “You would have thought you were looking at either the bookstands of grammarians, the tiers of an Athenaeum, or cabinets built up by booksellers.”

By analogy Lupus of Ferrara called it the cabinet of Saint Martin, letter 16: “We earnestly beg you to send us the commentaries of Boethius on Cicero’s *Topics*, which Amalricus has in a parchment codex in the cabinet of Saint Martin.” Ekkehard the Younger, *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 10: “They go into the cabinet, but into the narrow treasury of Gallus.”

Elsewhere *armarium* is a place where things are stored for safekeeping. Jerome, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book IV, chapter 15: “They contain them in cabinets, boxes, and small chests.”

### Line 14.—“Here he newly organized the cultivated estate of Lauretum, adding also the estate of Fonteiana”

A *cultivated estate* (*domus culta*) is an estate or farm equipped with buildings, colonists, and agricultural tools.

Anastasius, immediately below in the same work:

> “And he established the cultivated estate of the same place for blessed Peter, to remain in perpetuity by right; this cultivated estate is called that of Saint Cecilia to the present day. He assigned this cultivated estate for his own use—that is, for the use of the lord’s household. Here he established another cultivated estate fourteen miles from this Roman city, a patrimony of Tuscany, and bound it by his ordinances to remain for the use of the Church.
>
> “Through his own diligence he acquired by right of blessed Peter the estates called Antrus and Formias, and he established them as cultivated estates. Concerning all the cultivated estates, under penalty of anathema, he decreed that none of his successors in the pontificate, nor any other person, should in any way be permitted to alienate those cultivated estates from the use of the Church.”

The same author, in his *Life of Hadrian*: “This most blessed prelate newly built and established four cultivated estates.”

Leo III established his own estates as cultivated estates, according to the *Life of Louis the Pious*:

> “At that same time, when Leo the pope was afflicted by an adverse illness, they attempted, without awaiting any judge, to seize for themselves and restore to themselves all the estates which the Romans call cultivated estates and which had recently been established by that same pope, as well as those which they falsely claimed had been taken from them contrary to law.”

### No. 222, line 1.—“Moreover, at the same time it happened that several Venetian merchants came to this Roman city and, extending the markets of their commerce, appeared to buy a multitude of slaves, both male and female, whom they were also attempting to take to Africa for sale to a pagan people”

The shameful commerce of the Venetians is noted: they bought slaves of both sexes in order to sell them to pagans in Africa. The pontiff prohibited this. This type of trade was common. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 1:

> “From this populous Germany innumerable bands of captives were often carried away and sold for a price to the peoples of the south.”

An even more disgraceful form of commerce was that in which slaves were customarily castrated by merchants from Verdun. These were called *carsamantian slaves*, and they were sold to the Saracens in Spain. Liutprand of Cremona, book VI, chapter 3:

> “I offered the emperor four *carsamantian* slaves, more valuable than all the others. The Greeks call a *carsamantian* a boy who, after his male organs and member have been cut off, is made a eunuch. Merchants from Verdun customarily produce such slaves for enormous profit and take them to Spain.”

### No. 223, line 2.—“As with the other towns of the Pentapolis”

Flaminia is a province of Italy in which are Ravenna and the five principal cities called the Pentapolis, according to Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 19. Hence Anastasius earlier said: “Ravenna and the cities of the Pentapolis and Emilia.”

### No. 224, line 7.—“Therefore, in the venerable patriarchate, that most holy pope found the most sacred head of the blessed martyr George enclosed in a box, and in it he also found a written label, inscribed in Greek letters, indicating that it was the head itself”

A *pittacium*—that is, a slip or label—is attached to boxes containing the relics of saints. It is a label or brief inscription indicating whose relics they are.

Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 36: “For there is a tomb there, adjoining this one on the left; on the upper front of it is written: ‘Of Galla, of holy memory.’”

A *pittacium* is a small written label. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 23: “He publicly displayed a written label of the law.” Its diminutive is *pittaciolum*. Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book III, chapter 23: “A little label foolishly prepared and signed by your hand.” Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, book IV, chapter 23: “They called those little labels the phylacteries of the Decalogue.” John the Deacon, book II, chapter 45: “And, writing a prayer on a little label, he gave it to one of his deacons.”

Elsewhere *pittacium* means a band used for binding wounds. Cornelius Celsus, book III, chapter 10: “Two strips whose width and length correspond to the forehead.” Vegetius, *Veterinary Art*, book I, chapter 22: “On the wound you should place a strip, so that it may close it more carefully.”

### No. 226, line 1.—“This most blessed pope decreed that on frequent days the cost of provisions, which is still called almsgiving, should be carried from the venerable patriarchate by the cellarers and distributed to the poor and pilgrims who remain at Saint Peter’s, etc.”

The *paracellarii* are the superintendents of the cellar of the Lateran patriarchate. From it daily stipends were distributed to the poor and pilgrims.

Anastasius, in his *Life of Hadrian*: “And fifty loaves, together with two measures of wine and a cauldron full of stew, should be distributed every day by the hands of one especially trustworthy cellarer to those same poor.”

Hence the cellar of the Lateran patriarchate is called the *paracellarium*. Anastasius, in his *Life of Hadrian I*:

> “The wine, and likewise the various legumes, which annually grow on the estates and lands of those cultivated estates, should similarly be carefully brought into the cellar of your holy church and stored separately. Also, of the pigs that have been fattened annually on the farms of the aforementioned cultivated estate, one hundred head should be slaughtered and stored in the same cellar.”

[Note: [Col. 1078D]]

### No. 223, line 1.—“In those same times, Ratchis”

After King Luitprand had died, and after the brief reign of his nephew Hildeprand, who was removed from the throne in his seventh month, Rachis, duke of Friuli, was chosen with the favor of all the Lombards. He was highly esteemed for the firm strength of his body, a quality greatly valued among that people; but he was far more commendable for his outstanding piety. After renouncing his royal dignity, he embraced the monastic life in the monastery of Cassino and observed it until his final day, as Leo, cardinal bishop of Ostia, relates (*Cassinese Chronicle*, book I, chapter 8).

I do not hesitate to include this historian’s words, although he is later than our Anastasius, since the events he narrates here place the matter in a favorable light:

> “In those days also,” says the cardinal of Ostia, “Rachis, king of the Lombards, went with a powerful army to capture the city of Perugia and attacked it vigorously on every side. Pope Zacharias proceeded to that city and, by many prayers and admonitions, and by granting him many gifts, compelled him to return to his own territory. Remembering the pope’s admonition attentively, the king, not long afterward, moved by divine inspiration, abandoned his royal dignity and glory. After he had reigned for five years and six months, he came devoutly to Rome with his wife and daughter, to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.
>
> “There the aforesaid Zacharias, prelate of the Apostolic See, cut his hair and made him a cleric; he also clothed him, together with his wife and daughter, in the monastic habit. Soon, having been sent by that same pontiff to this monastery of Saint Benedict, he arrived there and placed himself under regular instruction. After a sufficiently religious and God-pleasing life, he met the end of his life there.
>
> “To this day there remains a vineyard quite near the monastery, commonly called the Vineyard of Rachis. Some of our people believe that Rachis both planted and cultivated it. His wife, named Tasia, and his daughter Rattruda, with the permission and assistance of the aforesaid abbot, built at their own expense a convent for women not far from Cassino, in a place called Pallumbariola. After endowing it with many possessions, they lived there under strict supervision and rigorous observance of the rule and brought their lives to an end.”

### No. 226, line 1.—“This most blessed pope, through his exceedingly prudent diligence”

There is an ancient complaint by John the Deacon, in book IV, chapter 75 of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, and after him by all Catholics, that the translation of the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory, which Pope Zacharias prepared in Greek, had been corrupted.

John says in the passage just cited:

> “These books Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, most learned in both Greek and Latin, in the time of the emperor Constantine”—that is, Constantine Copronymus—“after approximately 175 years”—more accurately, 158—“translated into Greek and disseminated among the Eastern Churches, although the crafty perversity of the Greeks, in the passage concerning the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, cunningly scraped away and removed the name of the Son.”

The Greek translation was indeed corrupted, as can still be recognized in the final chapter of book II. Where the Latin *Dialogues* read, “Since it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son,” the Greek has:

> Φανερὸν οὖν ὑπάρχει, ὅτι τὸ παράκλητον Πνεῦμα ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς προέρχεται, καὶ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ διαμένει.

The meaning is: “Therefore it is plainly evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.”

Some suspect that Photius, a highly skilled craftsman of corruptions, was the author of this corrupted reading, because in his *Bibliotheca* he praises the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory with extraordinary commendation, as though, when passing judgment on books he had read, he were already forging weapons with which he would one day attack the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

But while Photius was praising Gregory, it seems to me far more likely that he was not then preparing such machinations. First, as I said in my *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, Photius wrote his *Bibliotheca* at the time when he was an envoy for Basil in Assyria, before he seized the see of Constantinople. Secondly, Photius praises not merely the writing of the *Dialogues*, but all Gregory’s works, exalting them as much as he can, and rightly so.

If Photius had sought support for establishing his schism from Gregory’s corrupted *Dialogues*, why would he do so when Gregory says in so many other places that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son? In the Creed that he promulgated at the beginning of his pontificate he says: “The Holy Spirit, neither begotten nor unbegotten, but co-eternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

In the *Moralia*, book I, no. 30, he says: “While speaking of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from himself”—that is, from the Son. In book V, no. 65: “Who, proceeding from the Father and receiving from that which belongs to the Son,” and so forth. Still more plainly, in homily 26 on the Gospels, near the beginning: “He proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Therefore the final chapter of book II was not corrupted by Photius, but by some other Greek of the Greek faith. Otherwise, by praising all the writings of blessed Gregory, and especially his homilies on the Gospels, he would have supplied rather than removed weapons to the Latins, who could easily have used even his confession to assert the supreme authority of Gregory’s teaching and demonstrate from Gregory’s writings the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

[Note: [Col. 1080A]]

### No. 226, line 20.—“He was buried at Saint Peter the Apostle on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction”

Once again I am engaged with Natalis Alexander, who, in dissertation II of volume V of his *Ecclesiastical History of the Eighth Century*, stubbornly denies, against a cloud of witnesses unanimously affirming that the transfer of the Frankish kingdom from Childeric, the last of the Merovingian kings, to Pippin, the first of the Carolingians, was carried out by apostolic authority, that Childeric was deposed and Pippin made king at the urging or by the agency of Zacharias, the Roman pontiff. He calls it a fable in article 5, chapter 7 of that same century.

I shall briefly summarize the arguments on which he relies and the manner in which he attempts to evade the clearest testimonies of the ancient writers.

Natalis first lays this down as a foundation: that the ancient annalists do not agree whether Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation to the kingship took place on the authority of Stephen or of Zacharias. He shows that it cannot be attributed to Stephen because, after Zacharias died on March 15, as Anastasius relates, in the fifth indiction—which indicates the year of Christ 752—Stephen III was inaugurated as pope toward the end of that same month; yet he did not set out for Francia until November, in the seventh indiction, which had begun on the Kalends of September—that is, in the year 753—when Pippin had already been reigning for a year and a half.

Nor, however, can it be attributed to Zacharias, whom Anastasius calls a most gentle and kindly man, adorned with every virtue, and who therefore was such a devotee of justice and piety that he could not, without committing the greatest injustice, have forcibly driven from his ancestral throne and thrust into a monastery an innocent young man who, because of his age, had not yet had the opportunity to prove what sort of person he was—Childeric, who was scarcely eighteen years old. Add to this Anastasius’s silence in the Life of Zacharias concerning an affair so celebrated throughout the world and so highly favorable to the dignity and authority of the Apostolic See—something which the papal author would certainly not have wished silently to pass over.

But Zacharias did not know who the true king of the Franks was; indeed, he appears to have regarded Charles Martel, Pippin’s father, as king. This is indicated by his letter to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, and in Letter 5 to the same man he calls Charles’s sons “princes of Gaul.” Almost all writers, moreover, make Stephen the author of Childeric’s deposition and of Pippin’s absolution from his oath, leading to his becoming king—not Zacharias.

To the numerous procession of writers who handed down the same event to posterity, Natalis replies that the number of writers is of no weight in establishing authority when they are convicted of falsehood by the most certain documents. He points out the source from which they drew their fictions: namely, Einhard, from whom they all received the same story and enlarged it with new inventions. Einhard himself, in the Life of Charlemagne, admits that he does not know the facts concerning Charles’s birth and infancy, because there were no reliable authorities who had written about them, and that he knew even less about what preceded his birth.

Natalis further claims that the things Einhard spread about the slothfulness of the Merovingian kings were false; that many things may have been fabricated by him to flatter the Carolingian kings; that they did not grow the beards they were supposed to have promised to grow, since nearly all of them died beardless; and that the royal magnificence they displayed toward churches and monasteries sufficiently refutes the exaggerated account of their poverty, according to which they possessed nothing except a villa producing a very small income and the precarious means of subsistence supplied to them by the palace mayor.

He says that the ancient Frankish annalists do not agree about the date: some place Pippin’s accession in the year 750, others in 753; some say that he was anointed king by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, others by Stephen, the Roman pontiff. They also err concerning the place, saying that it happened at Soissons, whereas Pippin was anointed king by Stephen at the monastery of Saint-Denis in the territory of Paris, after Childeric had already died, as Anastasius writes in the Life of Stephen. Finally, Natalis says that Pippin was elevated to the kingship by the authority of the pontiff according to Frankish custom, although the Franks did not customarily request and receive kings from the Roman pontiff, but placed them upon a shield at the assembly of the kingdom and acclaimed them.

What certainty, he asks, can be drawn from these contradictions? Thus Natalis mixes everything together, right and wrong alike, in order unsuccessfully to defend a bad cause against pontifical authority.

I, however, reply that scarcely anywhere in the whole of history does an event occur whose establishment is supported by the faith and authority of so many writers, conspiring together with such unanimity. I mean an event so widely known that, at almost the very time when it occurred, it was committed to writing by Franks, Germans, Lombards, Italians, and Greeks alike.

I have no time here to thrust upon the reader, who is hastening toward Anastasius’s text, a lengthy heap of citations, which he may consult, if he wishes, in the collectors of Frankish and German histories. I shall cite only two authors, whose undeniable reliability it would be shameless—or rather evidence of a deranged mind—to diminish. One of them, however, Cointius, whom Alexander praises, wrongly considers interpolated; the other both of them deceitfully conceal and pass over with malicious silence.

Leaving aside Einhard, the annalists of Lorsch, Fulda, Lorsch [Loiselianus], and Metz, Paul the Deacon, Theophanes, Anastasius, the Monk of Engolism, Ado of Vienne, Egilward, and Regino of Prüm—authors either contemporary or nearly contemporary with the event, since they all wrote before the year 1000—I present first the author of the continuation of the history written at Childebrand’s command. That this author was Nibelung is revealed by the following subscription, which was read in the manuscript codex of D. Petavius:

> “Up to this point the illustrious man Childebrand, count and uncle of the aforesaid King Pippin, caused the account to be written. From this point onward the authority of the illustrious man Nibelung, his son and likewise count, succeeds.”

Nibelung writes as follows:

> “The land rested from wars for two years. During that time, after a report had been sent to the Apostolic See with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, and authority had been received from it, the eminent Pippin, by the election of all Francia, was elevated to the throne of the kingdom, with the consecration of the bishops and the submission of the nobles, together with Bertrada, as the order of antiquity requires.”

The most learned Mabillon provides us with a second, exceedingly clear document in Book V of *De re diplomatica*, page 384: namely, the subscription of an anonymous writer to the book *On the Glory of the Confessors* by Saint Gregory of Tours. Mabillon acknowledges that he had obtained his copy from the Reverend Fathers Henschenius and Papebrochius, in whose possession the autograph existed:

> “If you wish to know, reader, in what period this little book seems to have been written and published for the precious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find that it was in the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the reign of the most fortunate, peaceful, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of the late prince Charles of blessed memory; in the sixteenth year, in God’s name, of his most fortunate reign, in the fifth indiction; and in the thirteenth year of his sons, Charles and Carloman, likewise kings of the Franks—who, through the hands of the most blessed lord Stephen, pope of holy memory, together with their aforesaid father, the most glorious lord Pippin, king, were consecrated with sacred chrism by divine providence and through the intercession of the most holy Peter and Paul.

> “For the aforesaid most flourishing lord Pippin, the pious king, had been elevated to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier, by the authority and command of the lord Zacharias, pope of holy memory, through an anointing with sacred chrism by the hands of the most blessed priests of Gaul and by the election of all the Franks. Afterwards, through the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on one day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—where the venerable man Folrad is known to be archpriest and abbot—he was anointed and blessed king and patrician, together with the aforesaid sons, Charles and Carloman, in the name of the holy Trinity.

> “In that same church of the blessed martyrs, on that same day, the aforesaid venerable pontiff blessed Bertrada, the most noble and devout wife of the aforementioned most flourishing king, who was clothed in royal garments, with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. At the same time, he confirmed the princes of the Franks with his blessing and the grace of the Holy Spirit, and bound them all by such a prohibition and law of excommunication that they should never presume to choose a king in perpetuity from another man’s loins, but only from those whom divine mercy had deigned to exalt and whom it had resolved to confirm and consecrate through the intercession of the holy apostles and by the hands of their most blessed vicar, the pontiff.

> “For this reason we have briefly inserted these matters, on the final little page of this book, for your charity, so that through the report of succeeding generations and of the common people, posterity may be able to know the lineage forever.”

In this splendid testimony we have such an exact designation of all the circumstances—the place, the time, and the persons—that it seems to have been composed by divine providence itself for the refutation of the quibbles of crafty men.

Childeric’s deposition and Pippin’s elevation to the throne must therefore be attributed both to Zacharias and to Stephen. Pope Zacharias granted the request of the envoys sent to him by the Frankish people—Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and Fulrad the chaplain—who asked him to declare whom he judged worthy of the kingdom: the man who bore the name of king but did nothing else, as Childeric did, or the man who discharged all the affairs of the kingdom, as Pippin did. He declared Pippin king by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter and ordered him to be anointed king by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz; this was done at the city of Soissons.

Again, three years later, Pippin was anointed with chrism and crowned by Pope Stephen at the monastery of Saint-Denis, together with his wife Bertrada and his sons Charles and Carloman. In this way the writers are reconciled: some attribute Pippin’s elevation to the throne to Zacharias, others to Stephen.

If a discrepancy of dates appears in the annals of writers from different nations, while all agree completely about the event itself, it should either be disregarded or can be resolved if the different events that preceded and followed it are carefully assigned to their proper years.

Pippin’s elevation to the throne must certainly be placed in the year 751 of Christ, the fourth indiction. The events that occurred in the various years of Pippin’s reign agree with this date with complete precision.

The council of Verneuil was held by the authority of King Pippin at the palace of Verneuil on July 11, in the year of Christ 755, and in the fourth year of King Pippin. The anonymous writer mentioned above records that his little book was written in the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord and in the sixteenth year of Pippin’s reign. Sirmond, in his notes on the aforesaid Council of Verneuil, makes the third year of Pippin’s reign coincide with the year of Christ 754, the sixth with 757, and the tenth with 761.

Pippin died in the year of the Lord 768, after seventeen years of reign. Those who assign Pippin fifteen years of reign appear to begin the count from his anointing as king by Pope Stephen.

I set these matters before the reader arranged by years and indictions:

- In the year 749, the second indiction, envoys were sent to Pope Zacharias at Rome.
- In the year 750, the third indiction, the envoys returned to Francia with Pope Zacharias’s sacred replies.
- In the year 751, the fourth indiction, Pippin was anointed king in the city of Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz.
- In the year 752, the fifth indiction, on March 15, Pope Zacharias died.
- In the year 752, the fifth indiction, on March 27, Stephen III was elected pope.
- In the year 753, the seventh indiction, on November 15, Pope Stephen set out for Francia.
- In the year 754, the seventh indiction, on July 28, Pope Stephen anointed Pippin, his sons Charles and Carloman, and his wife Bertrada as kings and queen.
- In the year 757, the tenth indiction, on April 24, Pope Stephen died.
- In the year 768, the seventh indiction, on September 24, King Pippin died after seventeen years of reign.

I shall now answer one by one the arguments Natalis has brought forward against this account.

First, it is false that Zacharias called Charles Martel king of the Franks in any of the letters sent to Boniface. On the contrary, he plainly recognized Pippin as mayor of the palace, addressing him in Letter 7 as: “To the most excellent and most Christian lord Pippin, mayor of the palace.” Although in Letter 3 he had called Carloman and Pippin “princes of the Franks,” this was plainly as a mark of honor, since they were the sons of Charles Martel, the mayor of the palace, whom Gregory III had called a sub-king in Letters 5 and 6 sent to him.

The deposition of Childeric and the substitution of Pippin as king does not, as Natalis would have it, cast a shadow over Zacharias’s well-established piety and justice. The matter was requested by a solemn embassy on behalf of all the orders of the Franks, because of Pippin’s outstanding virtues and, on the other hand, the slothfulness of the Merovingians, especially Childeric, who is called “the Stupid” by the authorities.

Anastasius is silent about this in the Life of Pope Zacharias. He was chiefly intent on recording matters relating to the government, adornment, titles, and donations of the churches, and so it seemed best to him to pass over an event celebrated throughout the world. But he recounts the matter fully in his *Ecclesiastical History*, which he wrote after Nicephorus, George Syncellus, and Theophanes.

Einhard professes that he does not know the matters relating to Charlemagne’s birth and infancy and therefore passes them over in silence. But he does recount Pippin’s elevation to the throne, which occurred before everyone’s eyes and was celebrated on everyone’s lips, and he narrates its causes according to the rules of history.

What he reports about the Merovingians’ appearance—that they went about with flowing hair and lowered beards—sufficiently confirms the matter. Natalis distorts this when he says that they had “promised” to grow their beards. The expression means not that they cultivated long beards, which would hardly suit men who died at twenty or twenty-four years of age, but that they did not shave their beards and wore the hairs growing on their chins uncut.

This is sufficiently confirmed by the seals of the Merovingians, which represent their faces as having a wild and rough appearance, both in Mabillon, Book V of *De re diplomatica*, and in John Heineccius, *On the Seals of the Ancient Germans*, Book I.

The fact that those same Merovingians were content with the possession and revenues of a single villa does not invalidate the magnificent donations made to churches and monasteries. These donations were indeed made in their name, but by the authority of the mayors of the palace, who were responsible for the administration of the kingdom and its royal resources.

Childeric’s tonsure, his removal to a monastery, and Pippin’s absolution from his oath are attributed by the writers to Pope Stephen, who was present in Gaul and could carry out in person what Zacharias, being absent, could not adequately direct.

It is false, however, that in the Life of Stephen III Anastasius writes that Childeric died upon Stephen’s arrival in Gaul, as Natalis asserts.

Finally, no author says that it was the custom of the Franks to request their kings from the Roman pontiff. Rather, at this particular turning point, when the transfer of the kingdom from one royal line to another was under consideration, the Franks thought it expedient to seek the counsel of the Roman pontiff, so that, with his authority obtained, they might carry out what they were planning. Once this had been secured, they established Pippin as king according to the custom of their nation by placing him upon a shield.

For the reader whose palate relishes such delicacies, I present an impression of a quite singular lead bull of King Childeric of the Merovingian line, whose fading and almost effaced letters I restored only with difficulty.

[Col. 1047]

206 Zacharias, a Greek by nationality, son of Polychronius, sat for ten years, three months, and fourteen days.

[Note: Col. 1047: B, “10 days.”] A most gentle and gracious man, adorned with every virtue; a lover of the clergy and of all the Roman people; slow to anger and swift to show mercy; returning evil to no one for evil, nor inflicting vengeance according to desert, but from the time of his ordination becoming pious and merciful toward all. Even to those who had formerly persecuted him he returned good for evil, advancing them to honours and enriching them with resources.

207 He found the whole province of Italy

[Note: Col. 1047: “of Italy.”] greatly disturbed, together with the Roman duchy, through the persecution of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, on account of Duke Trasamund [Note: Col. 1047: “Transamund.”] of Spoleto, who had taken refuge in this city of Rome while the same king was pursuing him. Since the aforesaid Trasamund had not been surrendered by his predecessor Pope Gregory of blessed memory [Col. 1049], by Stephen, formerly patrician and duke, or by the whole Roman army, the king laid siege to the city and, on Trasamund’s account, took four cities from the Roman duchy: namely Amelia, Orte [Note: Col. 1049: “Ortas.”], Bomarzo, and Blera. Thus the king returned to his palace in the month of August, in the seventh indiction. Duke Trasamund, however, having taken counsel with the Romans and assembled the general army of the Roman duchy, entered [Note: Col. 1049: “entered,” singular.] the territory of the duchy of Spoleto by two routes. Immediately, through fear caused by the multitude of the Roman army, the Marsians, the Forconians, and the Balvensians [Note: Col. 1049: “the Valvensians and the Pennensians.”], or Prinians, submitted to Trasamund. Then, entering through Sabine [Note: Col. 1049: “Persianimense, or Ravennese.”] territory, they came to the city of Rieti. Its people [Note: Col. 1049: “from whom.”] likewise immediately submitted.

208 Thereafter they proceeded and entered Spoleto

[Note: Col. 1049: “they entered the territory of Spoleto.”] in December of the aforesaid indiction. There was great disturbance between Romans and Lombards, for both the Beneventans and the Spoletans supported the Romans [Note: Col. 1049: “were joined to them.”]. But because Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, refused to fulfil what he had promised the aforesaid pontiff, the patrician, and the Romans concerning the recovery of the four cities lost on his account and the other terms which he had pledged; and because the aforesaid king was preparing, at the prompting [Note: Col. 1049: “after a summons of the army had been made.”] of the army, to move against the Roman duchy: amid these events Pope Gregory of blessed memory was removed from this world by a divine summons, and by divine will the aforesaid most holy Zacharias was elected to the pontificate. Almighty God bestowed on him such grace that he did not hesitate even to lay down his life for the salvation of the Roman people. He therefore sent an embassy to the aforesaid king of the Lombards and preached salutary counsels to him. Moved by the admonitions of this holy man, the king promised to restore the aforesaid four cities which he had taken from the Roman duchy [Note: Col. 1049: B, “from the duke.”]. When, after mobilizing troops to seize Duke Trasamund of Spoleto, he joined forces for this purpose, the Roman army went forth [Note: Col. 1049: “went forth,” singular.] at the holy man’s exhortation to assist the aforesaid king. Trasamund, seeing his own betrayal, left the city of Spoleto and surrendered himself to the king.

209 When the same king

[Note: Col. 1049: B, “Liutprand.”] delayed restoring, in accordance with his promise, the four cities already mentioned [Note: Col. 1049: B, “the aforesaid four.”], the aforesaid pontiff, truly the shepherd of the people entrusted to him by God, placing his hope in God, left this city of Rome with priests and clergy and proceeded confidently and boldly to the place called Interamna, where the king was staying in the territory of Spoleto. When he came to the city of Orte, and the king learned of his arrival, he sent his envoy Grimoald, who met him and escorted him as far as the city of Narni. At the arrival of the holy man, the king sent his dukes, his grandees, and a great army [Note: Col. 1049: “and a large army.”], and himself received him about eight miles from Narni. On Friday they brought him to the basilica of the blessed Valentine, bishop and martyr, situated in the aforesaid city of Interamna in the duchy of Spoleto [Note: Col. 1049: “Spoletan.”]. Before the doors of this basilica the king, with his other nobles and his army, received the holy man. After they had prayed and exchanged greetings [Note: Col. 1049: “having exchanged greetings.”], and he had been admonished by divine discourse, the king, prompted by affection, went with him for about half a mile after leaving the church, in attendance upon him; and on that Friday each remained in his own tents.

210 On Saturday, when they met again, the holy man, filled with divine grace, addressed the king with God-pleasing

[Col. 1051] admonitions, preaching to him [Note: Col. 1051: “him.”] that he should cease from hostile action and bloodshed and always pursue the things of peace. Moved by his pious words, and admiring the holy man’s constancy and admonition, the king granted, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, everything the pope asked. He restored to the holy man, with their inhabitants, the aforesaid four cities which he himself had taken two years before by siege on account of Duke Trasamund of Spoleto. He confirmed this by a deed of donation in the oratory of the Saviour, situated within the church of the blessed apostle Peter and built in his name. He also restored to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a deed of donation, the Sabine patrimony, which had been taken away for nearly thirty years, as well as the territories of Narni, Osimo, Ancona, and Numana [Note: Col. 1051: B, “Bomarzo.”], and the valley called Magna, situated in the territory of Sutri. The king confirmed peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years. Moreover, by letters sent both into his Tuscia and beyond the Po, he restored to the most blessed pontiff all captives whom he held from various Roman provinces, together with Ravenna’s captives: the consuls [Note: Col. 1051: B, “men of consular rank.”] Leo, Sergius, Victor, and Agnellus [Note: Col. 1051: “Agellus.”].

211 In the aforesaid basilica of the blessed Valentine, at the request of that same king, he ordained another bishop in the place of the deceased bishop of Cosenza

[Note: Col. 1051: C, “of Cosenza”; B, “of Constantine.”]. While the king and his judges were present at this consecration, such prayers, in the sweetness of divine inspiration, issued from him that, seeing the holy man pour forth prayers, many of the Lombards were moved to tears. On that Sunday, after the solemnities of Mass had been completed, the most blessed pontiff invited the king to dine and receive the apostolic blessing. There he took food with such sweetness and cheerfulness of heart that the king said he could never remember having dined so well [Note: Col. 1051: C, “having eaten”; B, “having eaten by himself.”]. On the following day, Monday, as the king bade him farewell, he assigned to attend upon him his nephew Agiprand [Note: Col. 1051: B, “Aldeprand.”], duke of Chiusi, Tacipert the castald, Raming [Note: Col. 1051: B, “Raning.”], castald of Tuscia, and Grimoald, who were to serve the holy man as far as the aforesaid cities and deliver those cities to him; and this was done.

212 First they came to the city of Amelia, then to Orte. When they had reached the fortress of Bomarzo and had received it, the journey by circuit through the territories of the republic to the city of Blera, by way of Sutri through the Lombard territory of Tuscia, was long, whereas the nearer way was by the fortress of Viterbo

[Note: Col. 1051: “Laternium.”]. Therefore Grimoald, the king’s envoy, escorted the most blessed pontiff to Blera, which Raming the castald and the aforesaid envoy Grimoald delivered to him. Thus, by God’s favour, he returned to this city of Rome bearing the palm of victory. Gathering all the people, he exhorted them to hasten, in a general litany, from the church of the Mother of God called “at the Martyrs” to the blessed Prince of the Apostles, in order to render thanks to almighty God; and so it was done.

213

[Note: Col. 1051: Baronius, year 743.] These things having been completed in the tenth indiction, in the following, eleventh indiction, the aforesaid king grievously oppressed the province of Ravenna and was preparing to advance and besiege the city of Ravenna. When his intended action became known, the most excellent patrician and exarch Eutychius, together with John, archbishop of the church of Ravenna, all the people of that city, and the cities of the Pentapolis and Aemilia, sent a written supplication to the holy man [Col. 1053], asking him to come to [Note: Col. 1053: “meet.”] their deliverance. The holy man sent an embassy and gifts to entreat the king, through Bishop Benedict, the vicedominus, and Ambrose, primicerius of the notaries, asking him to cease his advance and restore the fortress of Cesena to the people of Ravenna; but the king would not permit it. Seeing his harsh obstinacy, the aforesaid most holy man, armed with the trophy of faith, left the city of Rome under the governance of the aforesaid Stephen, patrician and duke. Not like a hired man, but like a true shepherd, leaving his sheep, he went to rescue those that were perishing. As he set out, commending himself in prayer, together with his priests, clergy, and companions on the road, to Peter, prince of the apostles, by the will of almighty God a cloud covered them during the day so that they were not scorched by the heat, until they reached the place where they pitched their tents; in the evening it withdrew [Note: Col. 1053: “departed.”]. On the next day it likewise stood over them as a divinely appointed protection. The aforesaid most excellent exarch came out to meet him as far as the basilica of Saint Christopher, situated at the place called ad Aquilam, about fifty miles from the city of Ravenna. The cloud travelled with them, covering them, as far as the basilica of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Ravenna. Then a sign occurred: fiery ranks in the clouds preceded the holy pontiff as he went to the city of Pavia. When he left Ravenna, men and women of different sexes and ages, giving thanks to almighty God and shedding tears, received the holy pontiff, crying out: “Welcome [Note: Col. 1053: ‘He comes, he comes.’], our shepherd, who left his own sheep and has come to rescue us, who were about to perish.”

214 From the same city of Ravenna the pope sent Stephen the priest and Ambrose the primicerius to the aforesaid king to announce his arrival. Entering the territory

[Note: Col. 1053: “territories.”] of the Lombards at the city called Imola, these men learned that certain persons were attempting treachery [Note: Col. 1053: B, “betrayal.”] against the holy man in order to prevent his coming there, and by a letter written in the silence of night they informed him. When the aforesaid pontiff learned this, at daybreak on Saturday, not terrified by fear of death but relying on Christ’s aid, he boldly left Ravenna and entered Lombard territory [Note: Col. 1053: “territory.”], arriving one and a half days after his envoys. The king, grieved at their prior arrival, had refused to receive them. The supreme pontiff himself reached the Po on the twenty-eighth day of June, where the king sent his nobles to receive him. He came with them to Pavia, where the king was staying, and, passing outside the walls of the city, went at the ninth hour to the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles Peter, called San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro, to celebrate the solemn Masses of his vigil. After the offering had been completed [Note: Col. 1053: “after the libation had been completed.”], he entered the city and remained there.

215 On the next day, invited by the aforesaid king to celebrate the feast of that Prince of the Apostles in the aforesaid church, he celebrated the solemnities of Mass. There they greeted one another and took food together; then they returned to the aforesaid city. On the following day the king invited the holy man, through his nobles, to come to his palace. Received by the king with great honour, he addressed him with salutary counsels, beseeching him no longer to oppress the province of Ravenna by military action, but rather to restore to it the cities of Ravenna which he had taken, together with the fortress of Cesena.

[Col. 1055]

216 After much hardness of heart, the aforesaid king was persuaded to enlarge the boundaries of the city of Ravenna as they had formerly been held [Note: Col. 1055: “which he had formerly held.”]. He restored two-thirds of the territory of the fortress of Cesena to the republic. He retained the remaining third of that fortress as security, under an agreement that by the Kalends of June, when his envoys returned from the royal city, he would restore that fortress and the third part which he held as a pledge to the republic. After this the king himself accompanied [Note: Col. 1055: “escorting the holy man”; B, “having accompanied.”] the holy man from place to place as far as the Po. There, bidding him farewell, he gave him leave to return [Note: Col. 1055: C, “for his return.”] with due arrangements, assigning to attend him his dukes, chief men, and other persons who would restore the oft-mentioned territories of Ravenna and the fortress of Cesena; and so it was done.

217 God worked wonderfully and freed the peoples of Ravenna and the Pentapolis from the oppression and calamity in which they were held; and they were filled with grain, oil, and wine. When he returned to Rome, giving thanks to God with all who were with him [Note: Col. 1055: “giving thanks.”], he again celebrated with all the people the feast of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul. He devoted himself to prayer, asking almighty God to grant mercy and consolation to the people of Ravenna and Rome against that plotter and persecutor, King Liutprand. Divine clemency did not despise his prayers, but removed that king from this world before the date fixed above, and all persecution ceased. There was joy not only among Romans and the people of Ravenna but also among the Lombard nation, for they deposed from the kingdom his nephew Aldeprand, whom he had left as king, because he was ill-disposed, and the Lombards chose as king Ratchis, who had been a duke. When a report was sent to him [Note: Col. 1055: C, “an embassy.”], the most blessed pontiff immediately secured peace: the king, moved by reverence for the Prince of the Apostles and inclined by his prayers [Note: Col. 1055: “the king.”], and peace having been made for twenty years, all the people of Italy were at rest.

218 In the Lateran patriarchate, before the triclinium of Pope Theodore of blessed memory, he made anew

[Note: Col. 1055: C, “restored.”] a triclinium, which he adorned with various marbles, glass, metals, mosaic work, and painting. He also decorated both the oratory of Saint Sylvester and the portico with sacred images. There he ordered all his property to be brought in through Ambrose, primicerius of the notaries. From the foundations he made a portico and tower before the Lateran archive; there he installed bronze doors and railings and adorned the entrance with an image of the Saviour [Note: Col. 1055: C, “a screen of the Saviour.”]. Ascending the stairs, he constructed above that tower a triclinium and bronze railings. There he painted a representation of the whole world, adorned it with various short verses, and restored almost the entire patriarchate anew, for he had found the place in great poverty. In the church of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul he made hanging curtains between the columns of Syrian [Note: Col. 1055: “silken.”] cloth. In the church of that Prince of the Apostles he arranged in the work of the bookcase all the books belonging to his household which are read at Matins through the cycle of the year. He newly established the cultivated estate of Lauretum [Note: Col. 1055: C, “the hidden Laurentum.”], adding also the estate of Fonteiana [Note: Col. 1055: B, “Fontiniana.”], called Paunaria [Note: Col. 1055: B, “Paunasia.”].

219 He established twenty pounds of gold yearly for the purchase of oil, so that the profit from it might be applied to the apostolic lamps

[Note: Col. 1055: C, “lamps.”], and confirmed this endowment under the bond of anathema. He made an altar-cloth for the altar of Saint Peter, woven with gold and depicting the Nativity of our Lord God and Saviour Jesus Christ, and adorned it with precious gems. He also made four purple silk curtains, which he adorned with wheels [Note: Col. 1055: C, “with Rhodian [ornaments]”; B, “with vows.”] [Col. 1057] and various ornaments woven in gold. He likewise made, from his own resources, a crown of the purest silver with dolphins, weighing one hundred and twenty pounds. In accordance with ecclesiastical rite and the orthodox confession of his faith, this most blessed man sent a synodical letter to the church of Constantinople, together with another petition addressed to the most serene Emperor Constantine.
