When the representatives of the Apostolic See went to the imperial city, they found within the palace of imperial power a certain usurper and rebel named Artabasdus [Note: Col. 1057: “Artavastus, C.”]. For when the emperor himself had hastened to fight the nation of the Hagarenes, the aforesaid Artabasdus at once won over the people remaining in the imperial city by gifts and seized the imperial throne. Afterwards the aforesaid Emperor Constantine assembled a multitude of eastern armies [Note: Col. 1057: C, “the aforesaid.”], marched upon Constantinople, attacked it bravely, and besieged it from outside; he captured the city and recovered the former height of his rule.

220 Immediately he put out the eyes of the aforesaid Artabasdus and his sons and made many of his rebellious followers exiles from their own homes. After this, seeking the envoy
[Note: [Col. 1057] *missos*, “messengers/envoys,” accusative plural; no witness is specified.] of the apostolic see, who had happened to arrive there during the time of the disturbance, and, having found him, released him to the apostolic see; and, in accordance with what the most blessed pontiff had requested, he sent to that same most holy and blessed pope, for perpetual possession by right of the holy Roman Church, a written donation of two estates, called Nymphas and Normias [Note: [Col. 1057] *massis*, “estates,” instead of *mansis*, “holdings/estates”; no witness is specified.], which belonged to the public domain.

### 221

[Note: [Col. 1057] See Baronius under the year of Our Lord 747.] During his time Caroloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks, abandoning the glory and earthly power of the present life, came in devotion to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with some of his faithful companions. He dedicated himself to that same apostle of God and, promising that he would remain in a special [Note: [Col. 1057] *spirituali*, “spiritual,” instead of *speciali*, “special”; no witness is specified.] habit, received from that most holy pontiff the yoke of the clerical state. Among many other gifts he offered blessed Peter the apostle, before the Confession, a large silver arch weighing seventy pounds. After some time he departed for the monastery of blessed Benedict, situated in the territory of the people of Aquino, in which he solemnly professed under oath that he would end his life.

### 222

Moreover, at the same time it happened that several Venetian merchants came to this city of Rome. While extending their markets for trade, they were seen to purchase a multitude of slaves, both male and female, whom they were attempting to take to Africa, to the pagan people. When the same most holy Father learned of this, he prohibited it, judging that it was not just that those washed in the baptism of Christ should serve pagan peoples. He gave the Venetians the price which they were proved to have paid for their purchase, redeemed them all from the yoke of slavery, and released them to live in the manner of free persons.

### 223

At that very time Ratchis [Note: [Col. 1057] Rarchisus. B, Rachis.] king of the Lombards set out with great indignation to capture the city of Perugia, as he had the other towns of the Pentapolis, and, surrounding it, was vigorously attacking it. When the most holy pope heard this, relying immediately upon divine hope, he took with him some members of his clergy and the leading men and reached that city as quickly as possible [the text prints *quanto opus* and queries the conjecture *quantocius*, “as quickly as possible”]. By presenting the king with very many gifts and earnestly pleading with him, with the Lord’s assistance he removed him from the siege [Note: [Col. 1057] *obsidione* for *obsessione*, both “siege”; no witness is specified.] of that city. By proclaiming saving teaching to him, he also succeeded, by God’s authority, in inclining his mind toward a special devotion. [Note: [Col. 1057] See Baronius under the year of Our Lord 750.] After some days, that same king Ratchis abandoned his royal dignity and went reverently with his wife and sons to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Having received a prayer from the aforesaid most holy pope and become a cleric, he was clothed in the monastic habit together with his wife and sons.

> [Col. 1059]

### 224

Finally, during his time our Lord God was pleased to reveal a great treasure in this Roman city through that same life-giving pontiff. In the venerable patriarchate, that most holy pope found the head of the holy martyr George stored in a chest. In it he also found a label [Note: [Col. 1059] *pittacium* instead of *pictacium*, both “label/document”; a spelling variant with no witness specified.] likewise written in Greek letters, identifying it as the head itself. The most holy pope, exceedingly joyful and satisfied, immediately gathered the people of the Roman city and had it carried with hymns and spiritual songs to the venerable deaconry bearing his name, situated in this Roman city, in the second region, at the Golden Veil. There Almighty God deigns to perform innumerable miracles and benefits, to the praise of his name, through that same most holy martyr [Note: [Col. 1059] *dignatus est*, “has deigned,” instead of present *dignatur*, “deigns”; no witness is specified.].

During his time Theodore the elder died and, son of Megistus [Note: [Col. 1059] C reads *regis*, “of the king”; B reads *magnifici Cataxanti*, “of the magnificent Cataxanti.”] Cataxanti, for the forgiveness of his sins, left to blessed Peter the estate which he had inherited from his father and enjoyed by inheritance. It lay five miles from this Roman city, on the Tiburtine road, and was known to contain an oratory of Saint Cecilia [Note: [Col. 1059] C reads *Ecclesiae*, “of the Church,” instead of *Caeciliae*, “of Cecilia.”]. That most blessed pope adorned it with buildings of great construction and paintings, and enlarged its boundaries on every side. He gave suitable compensation to those who appeared to hold possessions near that place; he used force against no one, but, as befits a father, bought all the estates around that place by friendly agreement and payment. He established the cultivated estate as belonging by perpetual right to blessed Peter. This cultivated estate is called Saint Cecilia’s to the present day.

He also built there an oratory of Saint Abbacyrus [Note: [Col. 1059] C reads *abbatis Cyri*, “of Abbot Cyrus,” instead of *Abbacyri*, “of Abbacyrus.”], where he deposited many relics of the saints. He assigned that cultivated estate to his own use, namely, to the lord’s administration [*dominicae traditionis*; the precise administrative sense is uncertain]. He established another cultivated estate fourteen miles from this Roman city, in the patrimony of Tuscia [Note: [Col. 1059] The reading *in patrimonio*, “in the patrimony,” replaces accusative *patrimonium*; no witness is specified.], and bound it by his ordinances to remain for the use of the Church, together with the places which appear to have been granted to blessed Peter from the bequest of Anna, of the late primicerius Agatho [Anna’s relation to Agatho is not stated explicitly] [Note: [Col. 1059] *tam loca, quam annua relicta quaedam*, “both places and certain annual bequests,” is the alternative reading; it does not name Anna.]. By his own efforts he acquired for blessed Peter the estates called Antro and Formias, and established them as cultivated estates.

### 225

And, concerning all the cultivated estates mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1059] *domibus cultis*, “cultivated estates,” replaces the contracted *domocultis*; no witness is specified.], he issued apostolic documents establishing them and, gathering the priestly college, decreed under anathema that none of his pontifical successors, nor any other person whatsoever, should in any way be permitted to alienate those cultivated estates from the use of the Church. He made an exceedingly fine garment for the altar of blessed Andrew the apostle at blessed Peter’s.

### 226

That most blessed pope established that, on frequent days, the cost of provisions—what is still called almsgiving—should be carried from the venerable patriarchate by the assistant cellarers [Note: [Col. 1059] *a cellariis*, “by the cellarers,” instead of *a paracellariis*, “by the assistant cellarers”; no witness is specified.] and distributed to the poor and pilgrims who remain at blessed Peter’s. He likewise established that the same alms of provisions should be distributed to all the needy and sick residing throughout the districts of this Roman city.

During his time it happened that suddenly the covering [Note: [Col. 1059] *tegumentum* instead of *tegumen*, both “covering/roof”; no witness is specified.] of the church dedicated to blessed Christ’s martyr Eusebius fell. That most holy man, striving with all his strength and carefully laboring, repaired and restored what had fallen, just as it had formerly been, and restored it excellently.

This distinguished pontiff brought many holy places into better condition. He made excellent vestments for the altars of those churches of God. He loved his clergy greatly and gave them annual provisions in double measure and more; embracing everyone like a father and a good shepherd, caring for them beneficially, and allowing no one at all to be troubled. During his time, therefore, the people entrusted to him by God lived in great security and joy.

By his very prudent care, this most blessed pope translated the four books of the Dialogues which Pope Gregory of blessed memory [Col. 1061] had composed from the Latin language into Greek, and through the history contained in that reading he enlightened many who did not know Latin.

He held three ordinations during the month of March: he created thirty priests, five deacons, and eighty-five bishops in various places. He was buried at blessed Peter’s on the Ides of March, in the fifth indiction, and the see was vacant for twelve days.

## XCIV. STEPHEN II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 752, THE TWELFTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE COPRONYMUS

[Note: [Col. 1101A]

From the Farnesian manuscript, XCV.

Num. 228, line 9: *pari modo fundasse dignoscitur ex Zenodochium in plantana*, “he is likewise known to have founded … a guesthouse in Plantana” [the printed *ex Zenodochium* has an irregular construction].

Num. 233, line 12: *achiropyta*, “not made by hands.”

Num. 234, line 5: “and by strengthening.”

Num. 241, line 6: Wildecharius; line 8: Boniface, the secundicerius.

Num. 243, line 18: “the exarchate of Ravenna,” printed *exarchatum Rabenae*. Line 20: “he asked to depart to spend the winter.”

Num. 246, line 4: “he departed from this light.” Moreover, the most Christian Pippin.

Num. 249, line 14: “he inflicted damage.” Therefore he removed from the right of blessed Peter that castle of Narni which he had previously returned through the Frankish messenger. Thus impiously, etc.

Num. 250, line 14: “the imperial messengers, namely Gregory.”

Num. 255, line 13: “the aforesaid Ratchis.”

[Col. 1101B]

Num. 256, line 11: “in the tenth indiction; Paul, by birth …,” etc. [*indict. X Paulus nat.* begins the next biographical entry].

### From the Vallicellian manuscript

Num. 227, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, in the same place: “five years, twenty-nine days.” Line 3: “as the cited manuscripts read.” Line 6: “Pope Zacharias of blessed memory.” Line 7: “the whole people chose him.” Remaining there for two days. Lines 7–8: “as the cited manuscripts read.” Line 10: “after this, the whole people of God gathered inside the basilica of the holy Mother of God, the virgin Mary, in good spirit and with one voice, and chose for themselves the aforesaid most blessed pontiff.” Line 15: “with proclamations of praise [he was] carried into the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantinian, and thence into the venerable patriarchate” [the compressed source reads *basilica salv q. appel Cons depor*; *venerabilem* is marked sic].

Num. 228, line 2: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and so likewise at lines 5, 8, 9, and 11. Line 3: *praedicatorum*, “of the preachers,” [Col. 1102A] incorrectly. Line 4: “also the strongest defender of those men.” Immediately thereafter. Line 6: “they remained, and disordered, everything.” Line 7: “arranging them inside and outside.” Line 9: “it is recognized.”

Num. 229, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 2: “he bestowed gifts.” Line 3: “with the deacons who were outside.” The same manuscript also has *diaconiae*, “deaconries/of the deaconry.” Lines 4–5: “as the cited manuscripts read.”

Num. 230, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “Meanwhile, among the good works which he was performing, the Lombard king Aistulf inflicted a great persecution on this Roman city and the cities subject to it. But, in the third month of his ordination, that same most blessed pope sent his own brother, namely a most holy…” Line 5: “the primicerius, with gifts, to that same Lombard king named Aistulf, in order to arrange and confirm the treaties of peace.” “When these men joined him…” Line 8: “as though they might more easily obtain this from him, arranging a treaty with him for a period of forty years and confirming it.” Lines 11–12: “as the manuscripts Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane read, with which line 13 also agrees.” Line 15: *per unumquique*, “through each one,” with incorrect case. [Col. 1102B] Line 16: “he was eager to take away.”

Num. 231, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscripts agree with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 3–4, and also at lines 4, 5, 6, 8, and 9.

Num. 232, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at line 12. Line 2: “to that same most blessed pontiff.” There also: “and likewise other things.” Line 3: “he reported, adding words of exhortation,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Line 5: “that imperial messenger the aforesaid pope immediately sent with his brother Paul, the aforesaid deacon, to the most wicked king Aistulf at Ravenna.” Line 7: “with the response, and adding to him.” Line 9: “as the cited manuscripts read”—except for the pronoun “to him,” which is absent from our manuscript [Col. 1103A]—and likewise at line 14, where *adveniret*, “he should arrive,” stands for *conveniret*, “he should come together/come.”

Num. 233, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at line 2 there, and at lines 4, 14, and 15. Line 10: “they besought the almighty Lord.” Line 11: “he went forth in a litany with the most sacred image of our Savior Jesus Christ, which is called *archeropsita*, “not made by hands,” and together with it he brought forth various other sacred mysteries.” Line 17: “with ashes, with great weeping and wailing they besought the most merciful God. He also bound and fastened [this] to the venerable cross of our Lord God.” Line 19: “had torn apart.”

Num. 234: The entire number 234 is absent from the Vallicellian manuscripts.

Num. 235, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “Therefore, while that same most holy man was entreating the already-mentioned pestilential king of the Lombards, giving innumerable gifts on every occasion, on behalf of the flocks entrusted to him by God and the lost sheep—namely, on behalf of the entire exarchate of Ravenna and the whole people of this province of Italy [Col. 1103B], whom that impious king had torn away through diabolical fraud and possessed,” etc., as below at line 8. Line 9: as the manuscripts Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane read, with which line 10 also agrees. There also at lines 11, 12, 13, and 16.

Num. 236, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 2: “through whom.” There: “he should order [them] to be summoned” (“he should make [them]”). The word *faceret*, “he should cause [them to be summoned],” is a variant reading wrongly introduced into the text beside *juberet*, “he should order.” Line 4: as the manuscripts Regius and Mazarine read. Line 6: “of the aforesaid pope.” “Afterward, however,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here.

Num. 237, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 6 and 13. At the same line, also there and at line 15. Num. 238, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with [Col. 1103C] Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. There: “the mercy of almighty God.” Line 2: as the cited manuscripts read, and likewise at lines 7 and 8. Also at line 9 there, and at line 12. Line 3: “they followed him.” Line 4: “and would by no means allow him to walk.” “Then the most blessed man, relying upon the power of God…” Line 9: “bringing [him] to the apostles.” Line 11: “the leading men as well as the rest of the clerical order,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here.

Num. 239, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 5, 6, 8, and 11. Line 2: “as if [it were] a fiery sword.” Line 6: “Aistulfus the king sent his messengers to him.”

Num. 240, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “When he came to the city of Pavia and was presented to the aforesaid king…” Line 2: “he asked with abundant tears that…” Line 4: “he was able to obtain this,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here, with which lines 5 and 6, 10, 11, and 12 also agree. Line 7: *ut prae. P. Franciam p. r.*, “that the aforesaid pope might proceed to Francia, he asked …”; *Ad h. c. B. virum rex, interrog. si ei Franciam prop. esset vol.*, “at this … the king questioned the blessed man whether he wished to proceed to Francia” [both readings are compressed]. Line 10: “he revealed his intention.”

[Col. 1103D]

Num. 241, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, except for the word “Rodigandus,” and likewise at line 9. Line 5: “or, with the clergy, George, bishop of Ostia, and Quilcharius, bishop of Nomentum.” Line 7: “and Gemulus.” Line 8: “Boniface, the secundicerius.” Line 10: “setting out on his journey, he departed for Francia.”

Num. 242, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: *Post ejus absol. adh. nit. supra scripturis rex*, “after his departure, the aforesaid king still strove …” [the abbreviated, irregular *supra scripturis* is retained here as printed], etc., as the manuscripts Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane read here. Lines 3–4. Also lines 5 and 7, as the cited manuscripts read. Line 6: “of Mauritius, in which he is established, and so forth,” as the cited manuscripts read here. Line 8: “he remained for some days.” “Then Floradus the abbot and others gathered in the aforesaid monastery of Agannum,” etc., as those manuscripts read here.

Num. 243, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 3: “and his son named Charles to meet the pope.” Line 7: “as the Mazarine manuscript reads throughout.” Line 8: “in a certain part of the place.” Line 9: “Then the aforesaid pope, with all his companions, loudly giving glory and praise to almighty God,” [Col. 1104A] etc., as the cited manuscripts read here up to the words “he departed.” Line 11: “on the sixth day of the month of January, on the most sacred solemnity of the Lord’s Epiphany,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read. Line 12: with which line 16 also agrees, and likewise lines 18 and 21. Line 18: “it was pleasing.” Line 19: “the winter season was approaching.” “The same pope with all his companions to Paris, at…”

Num. 244, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: *ven monast. cum rege convivante post aliquantos*, “in the venerable monastery, while dining with the king, after some …” [compressed], etc., as the manuscripts Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane read here, with which line 8 also agrees. Line 9: “they hoped.” There: “on the following day he was suddenly found restored to health.” Line 10: as the cited manuscripts read, except for line 11, namely: “which is called Carisiacus.” Line 12: “at the holy admonition of so great a father.” Lines 13 and there: as those manuscripts read.

Num. 245, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “Meanwhile Aistulfus [went] to Carloman, brother of *Papini* (sic; Pippin), who was in the monastery of blessed Benedict,” etc., as the Mazarine manuscript reads here throughout; in the other manuscripts, however, as in Regius and Thuane. Lines 5 and 11: as the cited manuscripts Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane read, and likewise at line 7, except for the following: line 9 [Col. 1104B] *comperto A. ingenio decertabat, tota se virtute isdem Pipinus professus est decorare*, “having discovered A.’s stratagem, he struggled; that same Pippin professed that he would honor [himself/him] with all his strength” [the fragment’s construction is uncertain].

Num. 246, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at line 3. Also at the same line, 5, 9, 14, 17, and 19. Line 2: “Caroloman.” There: as the cited manuscripts read, except for the word “himself,” which is absent from our manuscript.

Num. 247, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 3, 4, 8 and 9, 10, and 15. Line 5: “he should return” (with the word “rights” omitted), but “he,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Line 7: as only Regius and Thuane read. Line 11: “they remained, awaiting their king.” When King Aistulfus heard that only a small number of those Franks had arrived—men who had come to guard their own fortified places—he trusted in his strength, suddenly opened the fortified places, and at dawn fell upon them with a great many troops. “But the just man,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read at line 15. Then, occupying the upper margin of several preceding pages of our manuscript, there appears this inscription, painted in large red letters: “Peter William, librarian at Acey [*Acejum*], [Col. 1104C] while he was staying there in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142.” Line 17: “having escaped by flight from their hands” [the source then has *invaserit* (sic), uncertain], etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Line 21: “taking away.”

Num. 248, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at line 4. Line 7: “the matter might be brought to an end.” “When King Pippin heard that they desired peace and were promising an agreement by a written treaty,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here.

Num. 249, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 2: “when they had been separated from one another, King Aistulfus, falling into perjury, delayed returning what he had promised on oath.” “But when the pope had arrived at Rome, after some time Aistulfus, filled with violent rage, not only failed entirely to fulfill what he had promised, but also made a general mobilization; and with the whole people of his Lombard kingdom…” Lines 9, 10, and 12: as the cited manuscripts read.

[Col. 1104D]

Num. 250, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript has the same reading as Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, except for the following. Line 2: “but the most blessed pontiff also.” Line 3: “sending his messengers to Francia, together with a man named Uvarnarius, who…” Line 5: “everything that had been done and everything that Aistulfus had carried out,” etc., as the cited manuscript reads here. Line 7 also agrees with them. At line 14, except for *prothoa secretis*, “chief of the secretariat.” Line 15: “sent to the aforesaid Pippin; after these had been received, the said pope,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Lines 20, 22, and 23: as those manuscripts read. At the same line 22: “when they learned this.” Line 23: “Marseilles.”

Num. 251, line 2: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “from the imperial messengers themselves, namely George, the chief of the secretariat.” Line 3: *A. S. missos, celeriter praenominatum Fr. reg. assecutus est*, “[the] messengers of the Apostolic See … he quickly overtook the aforesaid king of the Franks” [the opening is abbreviated]. Line 5: “he found [him] in the city. Line 14: “of their sins.” “He also asserted this.” Line 18: “he reached Rome.”

Num. 252: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 4: “to return the cities.” There: “he would return.” “Thus, after it had again been confirmed.” Line 6: “Aistulfus himself restored the aforesaid cities.” Line 7: as the cited manuscripts read here.

Num. 253, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 5, 6, 7, 10, and 11. Line 8: “with the messenger of Aistulfus,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here.

Num. 254, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane. Line 2: “with the holy donation sent concerning them by their king.” Line 3: “to that apostle of God and to his vicar, the pope.” Line 5: “He himself handed over Ravenna (*Ravennam*), Ariminum, Pensaurum, Concam, Fanum, Cesenas, Senogallias, Aesis, Forum Populi, Forum Livii, with the castle of Salsubio (*Castro Salsubio*), Montem Feletri, Accerrem, Agiomontem, Montem Lucati, Serram, the Castle of Saint Marinus (*Castellum Sancti Marini*), [Col. 1105B] Boibium, Orbino, Callis, Luceolis, Egubium, and Comaclum [the place-name forms are retained as documentary readings]. And likewise,” etc. Line 9: *quae a duce Spolitano per*, “which by the duke of Spoleto through …,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Line 13: “who had been sent by that same Aistulfus into the region of Tuscia.” Line 14: “the entire multitude of the army.” Line 15: *arripere usus [lege ausus] est fastigium*, “dared to seize the supreme position” [read *ausus*, “dared,” instead of printed *usus*, “used”]. “Ratchisus, despising him, formerly…” Line 17: as the cited manuscripts read, except for: “or, gathering the rest of the multitude of the Lombard army.”

Num. 255, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at lines 5, 7, 10, and 13. Also there at lines 17 and 18. Line 2: “so that he himself might be royal.” Line 3: “to fulfill [the wishes] of the aforesaid pontiff.” Line 6: “the words ‘and good shepherd’ are absent from the manuscript.” There: “with the aforesaid Folradus”; and likewise a little below. Line 11: as those manuscripts read. Line 16: *in ejus deposuit occurrere adjutorium*, “he … to come to his aid” [*deposuit*, literally “put down,” is syntactically uncertain]. “Thus, with the support of the most blessed pontiff…”

Num. 256, line 1: The Vallicellian manuscript agrees with Regius, Mazarine, and Thuane, and likewise at line 4. Line 6: “as a good shepherd laying down his life for them,” [Col. 1105C] “all,” etc., as the cited manuscripts read here. Only the following should be excepted: “to pursue Scripture with every effort … and in opposition to the Church of God … and of all Christians … after setting everything aside and neglecting it, he decreed that it should be done … of Saint Lawrence, situated above Saint Clement … of Saint Soteris … completing his course … and he was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of May … bishops in various places” (the number omitted) … etc.

### In Fabrottus, from the Freherian manuscript

Num. 227, line 1: In A and B the number is missing. Lines 1–2: A, twenty-nine days. Line 5: “they ordained him in the order of the diaconate.” Line 14: A and B, “they chose.” Line 16: B, “and from there they came to the patriarchate.”

Num. 228, line 9: A and B, “in the same way.” Line 10: A and B, “in the Platana”; B, “arrangement.”

Num. 229, line 2: A and B, “the gifts which,” and “he associated.” Line 4: B, “Silvester for a long time.” Line 5: B adds:

“During his [Col. 1105D] time Huhmac, duke of Aquitaine, came to the threshold of the apostles and promised that he would remain there. But afterward, deceived by diabolical fraud and beguiled by cunning, he broke his vow and, departing, joined the Lombards through a wicked exhortation. But, as he deserved, he ended his life by a death worthy of him, being killed by stones.”

Num. 230, line 7: A and B, “who were the aforesaid men.” Line 9: A, “a treaty of the pact.” Line 10: B, “postponing that very treaty of peace.” Line 16: A and B, “he was eager to take away.” At the same line 16: A, *sui jurisdictione*, “under his jurisdiction”; the witness printed *h.* has *sui jurisditioni*, “to his jurisdiction.”

Num. 231, line 7: B, “he sent back to his own people.” Line 9: “by the example which he frequently,” B. Line 10: A, “commending this cause of insult.”

Num. 232, line 1: B, “while these things were being done, he came to Rome”; A, “he joined Rome.” Line 7: B, “having received them, he sent them away with an empty response, adding to the same…” Line 8: B, “the wickedness of the nation, the man.”

Num. 233, lines 7–8: A, “by his most merciful clemency.” Line 12: A and B, “acheiropoietos.” Line 13: B, “adding the mysteries” [Col. 1106A]; A, “bringing forth the mysteries.” Line 18: B, “they prayed for the treaty, namely the one which the wicked king of the Lombards had torn apart.”

Num. 234, line 2: A and B, “to pursue Scripture with effort.” Line 5: A and B, “and by strengthening the whole Church of God,” etc. Line 6: A and B, “to guard himself”; B adds:

“But while he was urging all priests toward heavenly things, he attracted them to earthly honors. In order that all might be found adorned in the Church of God, he gave tunics, chasubles, or whatever was suitable to each person, as an honor. He freed others by payment of a price, those who had been handed over to moneylenders, so that the whole Church of God might rise to the highest honor. This most blessed man…”

Line 8: “on one Sabbath”; B reads *alio et alio*, “on another and another.” Line 9: B, “of the apostles”; “he made *rugas* [barriers or railings; the architectural term is uncertain] before the church of holy Mary ever-virgin, which is called at the Manger, and covered them with silver; they weighed thirty pounds.”

Num. 235, line 1: “He restored the basilica.” Line 3: “what had fallen; he also made an altar cloth for the holy [Col. 1106B] Mother of God, which is called at the Martyrs, and, carrying it there in a litany, he himself covered it with his own hands. Therefore, while that same most holy man,” etc., B. Line 4: “the king many times.” Line 6: “the entire exarchate,” etc. Line 8: B, “he saw that he could obtain nothing concerning this matter.” Line 12: B, “they sent their messengers to the king of the Franks.” Line 16: “written with excessive grief.” At the stated line 16, B: “written.”

Num. 236, line 1: “Then also, in the same letter, he asked that his men,” etc. Line 3: B, “the whole province was being oppressed; suddenly a messenger came.” Lines 4–5, after “named”: A reads *Trottigangus*; B reads *Oroctigangus abbas*, “Oroctigangus the abbot.” Line 6: B, “to fulfill the pope’s will.” Line 7: B, *ejus venit, ea ipsa*, “of him … he came … those very things” [fragmentary].

Num. 237, line 3: B and A, “immediately from the imperial city the aforesaid…” Line 5: B, “and the messenger of the wicked Lombard king whom he had brought.” Line 6: A and B, “inserted to the Lombard king.” Line 7: A and B, “he was about to hasten.” Line 8: A and B, *pro quo*, “for which/on whose behalf,” and *de praesenti direxit*, “he sent immediately.” Line 11: B, “the Franks came, namely Chrodigangus.” At the same line, A, “Aucharius”; B, “Autharius.” Line 15: B, “the lost sheep.”

[Col. 1106C]

Num. 238, line 1: *Tunc consol est idem*, “then that same man was consoled” [*consol* is abbreviated], etc., “mercy.” Line 7: A, “bringing.” Lines 7–8: A and B, “of weakness.” At the stated line 8, B, “he undertook the journey.” Line 10: A and B, “from the bosom of this church.” Line 11: B, “from the leading men of the military.” Line 12: B, “he began his journey.”

Num. 239, line 6: “to the city of Pavia.” Line 8: B, “concerning recovering.”

Num. 241, line 1: “Chrodigangus.” Line 2: A and B, “of the Lombards.” Line 4: B, “there he released and dismissed.” Line 5: B, “the priests and clergy.” Line 6: B, “Vilcharicus”; A, “Vinlcharicus.” At the same line 6, A, “a bishop surnamed Leo.” Line 8: A and B, “Boniface, the secundicerius.” Line 9: “or, as the others.”

Num. 242, line 1: A, “the wicked king of the Lombards.” Lines 3–4: B, “he came to the fortified places.” Line 8: B, “in which place.” Line 9: B, “days, where Ambrosius the primicerius, seized by a fever, died; gathering in the aforesaid…”

Num. 243, line 3: B, “not a few thousands.” There, B, “Charles.” Line 11: A, “with the said king”; B, at line 13, “[Col. 1106D] in the oratory.” Line 20: A and B, “in Paris.”

Num. 244, line 2: “while Pippin was staying.” Line 7: “concerning him.” Line 10: “of admonition.”

Num. 245, line 2: B, “devoted.” Line 3: “to him with arguments.” Line 5: “when he had come there.” Line 6: A and B, “causes.”

Num. 246, lines 4–5: A and B, “the number of the year of his death is absent.” Line 8: A and B, “possessions.” At the same line, B, “rights”—this occurs twice—and a third time, “it was done according to the admonition of the most blessed pope.”

Num. 247, line 3: A and B, “through which, and vigorously.” Line 8: A and B, “trusting in the almighty.” Line 9: “he undertook his journey.” Line 11: B, “gathering together.” Line 17: B, “undertaking flight.” Line 19: B, “he shut up several.”

Num. 248, lines 6–7: B, “when the preaching was imminent.” Line 11: B, “the king receiving.”

Num. 249, line 3: B, “that treacherous man.” Line 5: “when the pope had come,” B, “after several…” In the preceding line, namely line 4, after the word “delayed,” the following appears in manuscript B:

“The most Christian and God-beloved king of the Franks also sent his messengers to him: his brother Jerome and [Col. 1107A] his other leading men, together with a considerable number of people, who were to remain in his service until he returned to Rome.

“When the most holy pope had come to Rome, to the field called Nero’s, he found priests there singing psalms with crosses and giving immense thanks to the Lord. Likewise, he found a great and mixed crowd of people, both men and women, crying out and saying: ‘Our shepherd has come, and after the Lord, our salvation.’

“After some period of time, that adversary, filled with violent rage,” etc., “and Aistulfus, an enemy of his own soul, with God opposed to him, by no means fulfilled what he had promised. Meanwhile, that same most blessed pope, always meditating on the things of God, caused the offices which had for a long time been neglected at night to be performed during the nocturnal hours, and likewise restored the daytime offices during the daytime hours, as they had been in ancient times.

“To the three monasteries which from ancient times perform those offices in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, he added a fourth. He established monks there who would join [Col. 1107B] in that office and appointed an abbot over them. He bestowed many gifts there, both all the things necessary for the monks in the monastery and the immovable properties outside, which he established for the chanting of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, or for the aforesaid three monasteries, to remain there to the present day.

“But that same wicked Aistulfus, king of the Lombards, fulfilled through the hardness of his heart what he had ordered to be done by his mobilization. For, with the whole of his Lombard kingdom,” etc. Line 14: “the sacred cemeteries”; B, “he inflicted devastation.” Line 15: “he removed.” “Therefore he removed from the right of blessed Peter that castle of Narni which he had previously returned through the Frankish messenger,” A and B.

Num. 250, line 3: B, “ordering his messengers to undertake the journey and sending them to Francia.” Line 4: A, “Warnarius, here at Rome.” Line 9: B, “to fulfill”; “but concerning this.” Line 10: B, “he reached the region of the Lombards.” Line 13: B, “they gathered in this place.” Line 14: B, *protus a secretis*, “chief secretary.” Line 17: B, “having doubts, they did not believe.” [Col. 1107C] At the same line 17: “believing; with them the messenger of the apostolic see, having received the pope’s permission, undertook the journey to go to Francia.” Line 23: B, “in Marseilles.”

Num. 251, line 4: A and B, “the most Christian king.” Line 5: B, “he promised that he would give him many imperial gifts if [he returned] Ravenna.” Line 18: after the word “joined,” the following appears in manuscript B:

“At the same time, the most holy man, the aforesaid pope, made in the church of the holy Mother of God Mary an image of that same Mother of God, made of the purest gold, seated on a throne and bearing on her knees the countenance of our Savior God Jesus Christ. He adorned it with many precious stones, namely hyacinths, emeralds, *brasini* [a named type of gemstone, uncertain here], and white stones. Among the other two images of that same Mother of God Mary, which had long stood there before the altar, he placed it in the middle; and he also had those silver images gilded. But when…”

Num. 253, line 3: A, “from the archive.” Lines 6–7: B, “immediately he himself happily [went] to Francia.” Line 11: “he came to Rome.”

[Col. 1107D]

Num. 254, line 7: “with the castle of *Sassusio*”; B and A read *Sustibio*. Line 8: A reads *Bobio*. Line 10: “invaded.” At the same time that most blessed pope built above the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle a tower, which he partly gilded and partly covered with silver. In it he placed three bells, to summon the clergy and people to the service of God. Line 11: B, “by divine inspiration.” Line 14: A, *universum exercituum*, “the whole … of the armies”; B, *universam exercitus*, “the whole … of the army,” with different gender and number constructions. Line 18: B, “very much transalpine,” that is, “or the rest of the Lombards,” etc.

Num. 255, line 16: B, “they arranged to meet.”

Num. 256, line 1: “the pontiff, and recovered those cities.” Line 7: B, “he completed. Meanwhile.” Line 9: “two priests”; A and B, “fifteen in various places”; B, “twenty in number”; “and while he was in Francia, he gave the pallium to Chrodigangus, a most holy bishop, and ordained him archbishop; and when he was buried,” etc. Line 11: B, “the fifth day before the Kalends of May.” Line 12: B, “the episcopate [was vacant] one month, five days”; A, “thirty-five days.”

The following exact forms clarify the preceding apparatus readings. Farnesian: no. 241 *Wildecharium*, “Wildecharius”; *Bonifacium secundicerium*, “Boniface the secundicerius”; no. 255 *Radchiso*, “Ratchis.” Vallicellian: no. 228 *dinoscitur*, “it is recognized”; no. 239 *ingneus*, “fiery” (printed spelling); no. 241 *Rodigando*, “Rodigandus”; *Quilcharium … Numentanum*, “Quilcharius … of Nomentum”; *Bonifatium*, “Boniface”; no. 246 *Karolmannus*, “Carloman”; no. 247 *clusas/chasas*, “fortified passes/barriers.” Freherian: no. 230 A *sui jurisdictione*, “under his jurisdiction,” and the witness printed *h.* reads *sui jurisditioni*, “to his jurisdiction,” with distinct case and spelling; no. 233 AB *acheropsita*, “not made by hands,” B *mysteria adjiciens*, “adding mysteries,” A *mysteria ejiciens*, “bringing forth mysteries”; no. 234 AB *confortendo*, “strengthening,” printed for *confortando*; no. 241 *Chrodigango*, “Chrodigangus,” B *Vilcharicum*, A *Vinlcharicum*, distinct name forms; no. 250 A *Warnario bic Roma*, “Warnarius … here at Rome” [printed *bic*, apparently *hic*]; no. 253 A *archivo*, “archive/from the archive.”

[Col. 1108A] From the Royal, Mazarine, and Thuane manuscripts.

The source abbreviates many of these readings. Their abbreviated forms are retained where needed to distinguish readings or show where an expansion remains uncertain.

**No. 227.** Line 1: *St. n. R.*, “Stephen, Roman by birth.” Line 2: *6. di. 29*, “6; twenty-nine days” [the numeral 6 is printed without a unit here]; *Hic p.p.s. obitum*, “Here … after … death” [compressed abbreviations]; M reads *transitum*, “passing,” instead of *obitum*, “death.” Line 3: *sub doctrina apostolicae traditionis suorum praedecessorum beatae memor. Gregorii et Zachariae pontificum perm.*, “remaining under the teaching of the apostolic tradition of his predecessors, the pontiffs Gregory and Zacharias of blessed memory.” Line 6: *b. mem. papa Zach Steph.*, “Pope Zacharias of blessed memory … Stephen.” Line 7: *c. pop elegit*, “the whole people elected.” Lines 8–9: *a suo som surg.*, “rising from his sleep.” Line 10: *post hoc v.*, “but after this.” Line 11: *basil s. D.*, “the basilica of the holy [Mother] of God”; there, *ubi omn mis D. petentes, et ipsius Domini Genitricis virg Mar b. a. cons. u. p. b. sibi eliegerunt P.*, “where all, seeking the mercy of God and of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of the Lord himself, with good spirit and one voice elected for themselves the aforesaid blessed pope” [the abbreviated reading prints *eliegerunt*]. Line 15: *laudum pr. in basilica S. et exinde intra venerabile patriarchium i.*, “with proclamations of praise into the basilica of the Savior, and thence into the venerable patriarchate” [the final verb is abbreviated *i.*].

**No. 228.** Line 2: *conservabat*, “he preserved.” Line 5: *rest qu.*, “the remaining …” [abbreviated]. Line 6: *man et ordinata omnem inutilitatem*, “remaining … and ordered … every uselessness”; M reads *utilitatem*, “usefulness,” for *inutilitatem*, “uselessness.” Line 7: *intus et foris*, “inside and outside.” Line 8: *quae pr. pr.*, “which …” [the two *pr.* abbreviations are unresolved]. Line 9: *pari modo*, “in the same way.” Line 10: *depositum illic faci.*, “had … placed there” [abbreviated verb]. Line 11: *v. eis dec t.*, “... for them ...” [a compressed reading whose remaining abbreviations are uncertain].

**No. 229.** Line 1: *foris muros quoque h.*, “outside the walls also, he ….” Line 2: *et multa contulit dona*, “and he bestowed many gifts.” Line 3: *diaconis … foris ex.*, “to the deacons … situated outside”; M reads *diaconiis*, “to the deaconries,” instead of *diaconis*, “to the deacons”; *ut perenniter permanerent*, “so that they might remain perpetually”; also *idem d.*, “the same d. …” [abbreviated], for *id est*, “that is.” Line 4: *Silv et pr. apost.*, “Silvester and the prince of the apostles.” Line 5: *permansura m.*, “to remain …” [the noun is abbreviated].

[Col. 1108B] **No. 230.** Line 2: *extit illico idem beat.*, “there arose … immediately that same blessed man ….” Line 4: *m. germanum suum, sanctiss.*, “... his own brother, the most holy ….” Line 5: *prim et plures*, “the primicerius and several others.” Line 6: *ad eund Longob Aist r.*, “to the same Aistulf, king of the Lombards”; M reads *eundem reg Longob nomine Aistulphum*, “the same king of the Lombards, named Aistulphus”; *ob pacis ordinanda, atque confirmanda f. m. Qui viri ad eum jungentes*, “he sent [them] to arrange and confirm treaties of peace. These men, coming to him ….” Line 8: *quo fac pro ea re apud eum impetrantes in XI annorum spatia pacti, et ordinantes foedus cum eo firmaverunt*, “obtaining this matter from him more easily, they agreed for a span of eleven years and, arranging the treaty, confirmed it with him.” M reads *quo facilius pro eadem re apud eum imp in 40 ann spatia impetrantes, et ordinantes f. cum eo conf.*, “obtaining more easily from him concerning the same matter … obtaining a span of forty years and, arranging the treaty, confirming it with him” [*imp* is left abbreviated before the repeated *impetrantes*]. Lines 11–12: *multas etiam praefato beato viro vel omni pop.*, “many also to the aforesaid blessed man or to all the people ….” Line 13: *dirigebat. Cupiens quippe e contrario c.*, “he was sending. For desiring, on the contrary, c. …” [the final abbreviation is unresolved]. Line 15: *caput solidos auri an auferre*, “to exact gold solidi per head annually” [the amount is not given in this excerpt].

**No. 231.** Line 1: *isdem s. P. perniciosam scevitiam regis, accersitis ad se ven.*, “that same holy pope … the king’s destructive cruelty, having summoned to himself the venerable …”; M spells “cruelty” *sevitiam* instead of *scevitiam*. Lines 3–4: *eid misit cr. regi*, “he sent to that same cruel king.” Line 4: *cum quiete*, “with quiet/peace.” Line 5: *confirmanda*, “to be confirmed.” Line 6: *sprevit munera*, “he spurned the gifts.” Line 8: *ad praefatum venerabilem papam d.*, “to the aforesaid venerable pope ….” Line 9: *juxta quod cr. cons omnipotenti Deo suam pop.*, “according to what … the almighty God … his people …” [the compressed middle abbreviations are uncertain].

**No. 232.** Line 1: *dum haec ag. pervenit Romae*, “while these things were being done, he arrived at Rome.” [Col. 1108C] Line 2: *beatissimo pap.*, “to the most blessed pope”; in the same line, *et alia*, “and other things.” Line 3: *adnectens verba, ut scilicet reip loca diab ab eodem rege us.*, “adding words, namely that the places of the commonwealth, diabolically usurped by that same king ….” Line 5: *cum suo germano Paulo praedicto ad regem misit praedictum Aistulphum nequissimum Ravennam*, “with his brother, the aforesaid Paul, he sent [him] to Ravenna to the aforesaid most wicked king Aistulphus.” Line 7: *Q. s. inani eos abs r. adjungens eidem imperiali misso*, “having received them, he dismissed them with an empty answer, adding to the same imperial messenger ….” Line 9: *profecturum urbem, reversique Romam, ac praes eidem beatiss pap ei narr nisi s. eg. Tunc beatissimus papa agnito*, “that he would proceed to the City; and returning to Rome, and present before that same most blessed pope, they related to him only … [*s. eg.* unresolved]. Then the most blessed pope, having learned ….” Line 12: *cum pr imp m.*, “with the aforesaid imperial messenger.” Line 13: *eis saepius tribulatis scripserat, has Italiae in partes modis omnibus conveniret, et de morsibus filii iniquitatis R. h. u., etc. Italiae prov.*, “he had written, as they were so often afflicted, that he should by all means come to these parts of Italy, and from the bites of the son of iniquity … [*R. h. u.* unresolved], etc., the province of Italy.”

**No. 233.** Line 1: *in sua nequitia*, “in his wickedness.” Line 2: *rex Aistulphus*, “King Aistulphus”; there, *et frendens*, “and gnashing his teeth.” Line 4: *sub sese d. Rursusque beatissimus Pater congr.*, “under himself … [*d.* unresolved]. And again the most blessed Father, having assembled ….” Line 10: *omnip Deum depr.*, “they implored almighty God.” Line 11: *processit in let*, “he went forth in a litany”; there, *imagine Salvatoris Domini nostri Jesu Chr.*, “with the image of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ.” Line 12: *acheroposita*—M reads *acheropsita*—*n. simulque cum ea al. div sac ministeria ejiciens*, “called ‘not made by hands,’ bringing forth together with it other various sacred ministries/objects” [the printed noun is *ministeria*, “ministries,” distinct from *mysteria*, “mysteries,” in other readings]. Lines 14–15: *sac gestans, nudis p.*, “bearing sacred …, with bare feet.” Line 15: *pl. perg ad eccl.*, “... going to the church” [*pl.* unresolved]. Line 17: *cinere, maximo fletu, et* [Col. 1108D] *ululatu misericordissimum Deum deprecati sunt. Allegavit quoque, et connexuit ad cr. Domini nostri*, “with ashes, very great weeping, and wailing, they implored the most merciful God. He also bound and fastened [it] to the cross of our Lord.” Line 19: *diruperat*, “he had broken”; M reads *diripuerat*, “he had plundered/torn away.”
]

Num. 235, line 3: Accordingly, while that most holy man was entreating the aforesaid pestilential king of the Lombards, repeatedly presenting innumerable gifts, on behalf of the flocks entrusted to him by God and the lost sheep—namely, on behalf of the entire Exarchate of Ravenna and all the people of that province of Italy, whom that impious king had torn away by diabolical deceit, and possibly [the text continues], etc.—as far as line 8. Line 9: and from the emperor’s predecessors. Line 10: and the lord [Zacharias?]. Line 11: to the most excellent and good king. Line 12: asking him to come to his aid. Line 13: endured from the Lombards; and that venerable Father, inspired by divine grace. Line 16: from excessive grief.

Num. 236, line 1: Even thereafter he did not cease sending [messengers] to make his own men [go] to Rome. Line 2: make [it so]. Line 4: suddenly there arrived a messenger of the aforesaid king of the Franks named Rotdingandus (M: Rodingandus). Line 6: the aforesaid Father himself [sent?]. Afterwards he also sent other messengers, his personal attendants, announcing those same things.

Num. 237, line 1: Charles from the Lombards, as has been said, [so that]. Line 2: so that they might also seize Curanum (M: Ciccanum; and thus it has been corrected in the margin of the Codex Regius): immediately from the royal city came the aforesaid imperial [messenger], carrying with him the letters of the blessed Father concerning the death of the [king], whom the impious king of the Lombards had sent along with [him], and [other matters]. Line 6: in which there was a letter to the king of the Lombards, stating that the same pope was about to hasten to Ravenna because of the recovery of the city. Line 8–9: he sent his aforesaid messenger to the same king concerning him and those who were with him, and concerning the [other] matter. When he had returned, and the [other] messengers of King Pippin the Frank had arrived—namely, Rotdingandus (M: Rotingandus), abbot, and Antharius, a distinguished man of the palace of the pope. Line 13: they delivered [him] to his king in Francia. Same line: they found [him]. Line 14: about to hasten. Line 15: [on behalf of] the sheep.

Num. 238, line 1: Then the most blessed Father consulted [them]. Line 2: to the most blessed [Father]. Line 4: and they did not allow him to walk about. Then that blessed man, commending himself to the protection and power of God and of his holy Mother, and to the blessed apostles’ [protection]. Line 7–8: overcome by weakness, he undertook the journey with difficulty. Line 9: to the blessed [Father]. Same place: and with him the entire clergy of this holy Church, who were [present]. Line 11: the bishops and barons, etc., of the clerical order, as well as the military forces of Christ, began the journey. Line 12: heavenly service.

Num. 239, line 1: Accordingly, when he had reached the borders of the Lombards, one night a sign appeared in the heavens, [namely]. Line 5: before him at Ticinum. Line 6: the city of Pavia. Same line: Aistulph sent his messengers to him. Line 8–9: or the remaining places belonging to the commonwealth, which [were]. Line 10: which, so that no one might tremble with fear, [were]. Line 11: from the purpose of asking for such things.

Num. 240, line 1: When he came to the city of Pavia (M: but when he came), and, having approached the king, [he presented] many gifts and entreated him exceedingly, and asked him with tears streaming down (M: he entreated him) and with abundant tears. Line 4: this imperial messenger also, [presenting] great gifts, [said] this [same thing] (M: these matters). Line 5–6: but he could obtain nothing. Line 7: so that the aforesaid Father might send [someone] to Francia concerning the recovery of [the places] which Aistulph had taken, if he wished to go to Francia; but that man [said] that neither [the pope] nor [anyone else]. Line 9: he wished to give him his [own] [answer]. Line 10: he growled. Line 11: he called his own nobles to him, with the intention of declaring [his decision].

Num. 241, line 1: On the following day, through Bishop Rotdingus, he asked the pope whether he wished to go to Francia. He replied: “If it is your will, let me [go].” Line 5: or clergy—Georgius and [H.]—Quilcharius, Bishop of Nomentum, and Seon. Line 7–8: Grimulus. Line 8: secundicerius. Line 9: and the remaining [men], on the fifteenth day of the month of [N.], from the city of Pavia.

Num. 242, line 1: After his departure, the evil king, having learned of this journey, [acted], but the pope was by no means unaware of it, and therefore, with secrecy, [proceeded]. Line 3–4: he arrived secretly. Line 5: at a monastery of Christ, [named]. Line 6: in which it had been arranged that he would meet with the Frankish king. Line 7: The blessed Father, safe and sound, [arrived] with all those who were with him. Line 8: He stayed there for several days. Then, at the aforesaid monastery, there met him Abbot Florardus of Aginnum and Rotardus, a distinguished man sent by King Pippin, asking the pontiff to go to their king, whom they found in great [joy].

Num. 243, line 1: When King Pippin heard of the pontiff’s arrival, he hastened to meet him, together with his wife, sons, and nobles, for whom there were almost one hundred thousand [men]. Line 3: he sent his son Charles to meet the pope. Line 7: he received the same pope, for whom he acted as escort (M: standard-bearer). Line 9: Then the aforesaid pope, raising his voice and offering glory to almighty God and praises with hymns and spiritual songs together with all his men, proceeded with the said king to the palace of Ponticon, in the sixth indiction. Line 12: on the sacred day of the Lord. There, when they had sat down together in the oratory, the blessed Father immediately approached the king with tears. Line 16: who in the presence [of the pope]. Same line: by oath, the blessed Father [promised?] that he would obey with all his strength all his commands and admonitions. Line 18: to restore Ravenna and the other places belonging by every right to the commonwealth. Line 19: because winter was immediately approaching, he [asked] the same pope. Line 20: he arranged for him to winter at Paris.

Num. 244, line 1: After some days, with the king accompanying him to the monastery, by the favor of God the same King Pippin was consecrated by that pope, together with his two sons, as king of the Franks. Afterwards the pope, afflicted by severe illness and infirmity, was so weakened that all, both his own people and the Franks who were present, despaired of his life. But through the mercy of our God. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction. He carried out one ordination in the month of March: two priests, two deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places; and the episcopate ceased for thirty-two days.

Num. 227, line 1.—Stephen. On the twelfth day after the death of Zacharias, 27 March in the year of the Lord 752, Stephen II was elected.

[Note: [Col. 1115B]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

After the holy pontiff Zacharias had been deposited in the Vatican basilica on the Ides of March in the year 752, the see remained vacant for twelve days, as all the manuscripts and catalogues unanimously attest (except the Colbertine manuscripts, six of which are silent about the interregnum and a seventh of which lengthens it by one day). Indeed, the same number of days runs out to the twenty-sixth of the month, on which it is established that Stephen was ordained as successor. This follows both from the duration of his pontificate—five years and twenty-nine days, as recorded by the Lucan catalogue and three Colbertine manuscripts, while the first Freherian, Regius, Mazarin, Thuaneus, and three Ambrosian manuscripts count one day fewer than the other manuscripts—and from the date of his deposition, usually recorded as the sixth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 26 April, in the tenth indiction, which indicates the year 757, although the common text, and also some manuscripts, show a difference of one day or even two.

Since these calculations proceed correctly, as Pagius also asserts in the year 757, section 1, it is necessary for me to explain somewhat more fully the two remaining points that I had to observe concerning this pontiff against Pagius himself: namely, that the ordinations of the Roman pontiffs cannot be separated from Sundays, and that the date of the restoration of the freedom of ordinations must be placed in the year 684.

As for the first point, the very analysis of the twelve-day interregnum plainly shows that Sundays were preferred to all the more solemn feast days, as I said concerning John VI. And, not to linger uselessly over words, Anastasius says that on the third day after Zacharias’s deposition the clergy and people customarily chose for themselves a certain Stephen; and on the day of the election itself, 17 March, a Friday, they sent him to the Lateran patriarchate, or enthroned him—things which I have already shown to be identical in the case of Zacharias. He remained there for two days, that is, on that Friday and on Saturday. On the third day, namely Sunday—clearly intended for the ordination—while he had scarcely awakened and was sitting down to arrange his personal affairs, he suddenly became deranged and fell silent as he sat; on the following day, Monday, he died.

Anastasius does not include this man among the pontiffs, since he was not consecrated, as is clear from the Life of Adrian I, no. 292, where he calls the next pope “the second,” whom we call the third. Nevertheless, because Panvinus and Cardinal Baronius count him and call him the second, when the election of the other Stephen is reached it remains uncertain whether the election was held, as usual, on the third day after the deposition, or immediately, as Anastasius seems to suggest when he tells us that everyone assembled at Saint Mary at the Praesepe and with one voice elected Stephen, whom, on the basis of the foregoing, I call the second, or alternatively the third.

However this may have been, lest I seem to be deceiving Pagius, I pursue the analysis just as though the electors had awaited the third day. Accordingly, on Wednesday, 22 March, Stephen was elected pontiff and enthroned in the Lateran patriarchate. What follows? Was his consecration then carried out four days later, on the day sacred to the Annunciation of the Lord’s Incarnation, in accordance with Pagius’s frequently cited axiom, according to which the ordinations of pontiffs were customarily performed on Sundays or on more solemn days? Certainly not. The following Sunday, which was owed to the pontiff’s ordination, was awaited; and—what must especially be noted—it was awaited at a time when there can no longer be any doubt that the Church enjoyed the full freedom to ordain, without the confirmation of the exarchs, who had been expelled in the preceding year.]

What arguments, then, do I use to prove that the ordinations of pontiffs were performed only on Sundays, when Anastasius himself confirms in explicit words what I am investigating? In treating the consecrations of the intruder Constantine after Saint Paul and of Stephen III, or IV, he openly makes clear that they were performed only on Sundays. Although these two matters belong to the fifth volume, I nevertheless wish to touch on them here, so that what I have hitherto [Col. 1116D] argued concerning ordinations may cling to a new support. In the year 767, on June 28, Saint Paul I died in the basilica of Saint Paul, where he had been residing at that time. “And the episcopate,” says Anastasius, “was vacant for one year and one month,” during which time—as it is read in Codex Freherianus 2—“Constantine, violator and invader of the Apostolic See, held it.” For on July 28 of the following year, 768, the presbyters Sergius and Waldipert, together with the Lombards, entered Rome; they killed Toto, duke of Nepi, who had installed his brother Constantine; and, after several hours, as Anastasius continues, “the judges of this Roman army . . . secured Constantine under guard, together with his surviving brother Passivus and Bishop Theodore.” Thus ended the invasion which Anastasius properly calls [Col. 1117A] an inter-pontificate. Nor should one quarrel with him because, while he seems very carefully to record the time of the invasion, he appears to have made the inter-pontificate shorter by ten days; for, as he individually counts the remaining days, he leaves no doubt about any of them, as we shall see in its proper place.

Accordingly, in the aforesaid year 767, on June 28, with Sunday falling on that date, Toto, duke of Nepi, seized by the desire to create as pontiff his lay brother Constantine and surrounded by a throng of factionaries, entered Rome. He arranged for his brother to be elected in his own house, and then hastened with him to the Lateran patriarchate; after making him a cleric, he enthroned him there by the utmost sacrilege, while Paul was still alive. Paul died shortly afterward, on that same day. The following day, Monday, was sacred to the feast of the Apostles. What could have been more convenient for Toto, who trampled upon the sacred canons and supported his brother, installed by armed force, than to have the brother whom he had enthroned on the preceding day consecrated as quickly as possible on the next day in the basilica of Saint Peter, so that he might appear to be the legitimate pontiff? Since, however, there was no memory of a [Col. 1117B] consecrated pontiff outside a Sunday, those same six days had to be awaited under arms.

“​​When Sunday arrived,” says Anastasius, “the pontiff hastened again with a multitude of armed troops to the basilica of blessed Peter, and there he was consecrated by George, bishop of Praeneste, and two other bishops, Eustathius of Albano and Citonatus of Porto.” This example of an intruded pseudo-pontiff—who, just as the canons had been violated in other respects, would likewise have been ordained through a violation of the rites, not only on a more solemn day but on any other day whatsoever, unless the pontifical consecration had coincided with Sunday—confirms my position more strongly than any other example that could be produced. Moreover, when the same Anastasius treats of the ordination of Stephen III, or IV, although this does not contradict Pagius, since no feast intervened between the election and Sunday, he nevertheless speaks so absolutely of an ordination performed on Sunday that he clearly reveals the custom of those times. [Col. 1117C]

“On Saturday,” he says, “at dawn, one day before the ordination of the aforesaid most blessed pope Stephen.” And below: “Thus, on the following Sunday, the aforesaid most blessed Stephen received the consecration of the pontificate.” Perhaps more evidence will be available if someone rises to defend Pagius against this opinion.

The second matter that remains for me to prove is the epoch at which the freedom of ordaining the Roman pontiffs was restored. I stated, in my notes on Leo II, that it could be dated from the year 684, when Pogonatus, with the generosity and reverence that he showed toward the Apostolic See, granted Benedict the pontiff by an imperial decree that thereafter the clergy and people should not await any command from the prince, but should consecrate the elected pontiff without delay. Yet, together with the most learned men Pagius and Blanchinus, and against Mabillon’s opinion, which carries this epoch down to Charlemagne, I preferred to extend it approximately seventy years, namely to the beginnings of Pippin, king of the Franks. In agreement with Pagius, I place these at March 1, 752, [Col. 1117D] while Zacharias was still pontiff.

But this must be held firm and certain: after Constantine Pogonatus, when the Romans sent their envoys to Ravenna after the election of a pontiff had taken place, they did so more as a gesture of obedience than to seek confirmation. The ordination of Zacharias himself will serve as an example: it was carried out after an inter-pontificate of four days, before Pippin had become king, and without consulting the exarch. Hence Pagius says that the custom of seeking confirmation continued until Gregory III, Zacharias’s predecessor (Annals, 731, no. 20). Yet he supports this only by private authority, producing no document other than a conjecture based on the Westerners’ aversion to the Isaurian Iconoclast; and although these considerations may be highly probable, they do not establish the certainty that the epoch of no longer seeking confirmation of the pontiffs should be fixed in the age of Gregory III.

For this reason I embraced the opinion of the most learned prelate Blanchinus [Col. 1118A], who, when the alternatives of Mabillon’s and Pagius’s opinions were presented to him, preferred the latter, although he followed it with some difference in the number of years. He says that the matter should be examined down to the reign of Pippin, whereas Pagius refers it to the time of Charles Martel. Thus, interpreting Blanchinus’s thought, I assert that the freedom of pontifical ordination began in the very year of Saint Zacharias’s death, when Pippin was inaugurated as king—that is, in 752. For the exarchs had been expelled since July of the preceding year, and the emperors of the East had no involvement whatever in Italy. This cannot be asserted on the basis of the brevity of the inter-pontificate after Gregory III, both because the exarchate had not yet been expelled and because, owing to the wars that were breaking out, the ordination may have been carried out hastily.

In any event, during those sixty-eight years that elapsed from the imperial decree of Pogonatus, namely from the year 684 onward, the Roman clergy and people sent their envoys to the exarch, I say, more as an act of obedience than in order to seek confirmation, since no law obliged them to do so. And if there had been no [Col. 1118B] schisms—as I have noted elsewhere—which taught that legitimate elections needed to be more firmly secured, they would not even have gone for the sake of obedience. Once that servitude, which the Church had undertaken for the sake of peace under the auspices of the most pious Pogonatus, had been cast off, we nowhere read that it was taken up again; those who think otherwise, in order to accommodate the Augusti, are merely divining.

There will, however, come times when we shall see the pontiffs themselves grant the emperors of the West the power, out of gratitude, to intervene in the elections of pontiffs.

[Note: [Col. 1118B]

No. 227, line 6.—“A certain Stephen.” He was an Italian by nationality, the cardinal presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, whose father was Roman. Under the emperor Constantine Copronymus, he sat in the chair of Peter for four days, having been created on March 25. On the fourth day after his election he was overcome by a severe drowsiness. On the following day, when he awoke and had begun at last to put his household affairs in order, he suddenly became mentally deranged and lost his voice. On the next day he was seized by apoplexy [Col. 1118C] and died. Before he had received consecration, on March 28, the see was vacant for one day. The historians of the pontificate do not include him among the pontiffs, either because he was not consecrated or because he lived for such a very short time. This was not rightly done, since he had been lawfully elected and was regarded as a man of tremendous spirit and courage. He therefore should not be removed from the number of the pontiffs, even if he had lived for only one hour.]

[Note: [Col. 1118C]

No. 227, line 6.—“A certain Stephen,” etc. After Pope Zacharias died, a certain presbyter named Stephen, a Roman by nationality, was immediately elected Roman pontiff by the people and admitted to the Lateran patriarchate. He remained there for two days; on the third day, after rising from sleep and arranging his domestic affairs, he suddenly became deranged while sitting and fell mute, and on the following day he died, says Anastasius, who does not count him among the Roman pontiffs.

Onuphrius, in [Col. 1118D] his Ecclesiastical Chronicle and in his notes on Platina, followed by Baronius, counts this Stephen among the Roman pontiffs. But this opinion has all the ancient writers opposed to it, as well as all the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, none of which records the name of this presbyter Stephen, because he was merely an elected pontiff and was never ordained. For although it was customary for the elected man immediately after his election to be brought into possession of the patriarchate, he was nevertheless neither simply called nor actually a true pontiff before he had been ordained. Hence Anastasius and Frodoard, in the Fragment on the Roman Pontiffs, whom we have often cited, and who died in the sixty-second year of the tenth century, call the Stephen who follows him Stephen II, and similarly number the remaining pontiffs of that name, preserving the sequence of the numbers. They certainly would not have done this if this Stephen had then been counted among the Roman pontiffs as an elected pontiff.

Therefore, to avoid confusion, we shall call the Stephen [Col. 1119A] who follows the present one Stephen II, but with this qualification: according to others, he is Stephen III; and we shall proceed in the same way with the others, down to Stephen X.

No. 232, line 11.—“He sent his envoys to the royal city.” Stephen II was made pontiff in extremely difficult circumstances. At the very beginning of his pontificate, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, having broken the treaty that he had made with the Roman Church, decided to attack Rome. At that time the Romans had not yet abandoned their obedience to the emperor.

For after their extensive lands had been invaded and after the heresy of the emperor Leo, the Roman pontiffs honored the rule of Leo and Constantine Copronymus, did not abandon the care of the state, and the city of Rome, although afflicted by the calamities of war under King Aistulf, acknowledged the authority of that same Constantine. Constantine sent John the Silentiary to Rome with letters to the pope and to Aistulf himself. John went to Ravenna with Paul, the brother of Pope Stephen, but was unable to obtain from Aistulf the restoration of the provinces that had been taken from the Roman Empire.

Therefore Pope Stephen [Col. 1119B] asked the emperor through envoys “that, in accordance with what he had repeatedly written to him, he should come by every means with an army to protect these parts of Italy and free this city of Rome, or the whole Italian province, from the bites of the son of iniquity,” says Anastasius.

No. 235, line 8.—“Seeing that no aid remained from imperial power,” etc. When no hope of assistance from the East remained and King Aistulf was besieging Rome in order to subject it to his rule and invading the cities of the Roman Church, Stephen offered public prayers for the safety of the City and judged that the only aid for its salvation was to implore the arms of Gallic piety.

“Secretly,” says Anastasius, “he sent his letters through a certain pilgrim, addressed to Pippin, king of the Franks, by which he urged him to send assistance.” After receiving these letters, Pippin sent the abbot Droctegangus to Rome. Just as other apostolic messengers followed the aforesaid pilgrim, so other royal envoys followed Abbot Droctegangus: [Col. 1119C] Bishop Chrodegang and Duke Autchar. In the meantime Droctegangus had departed from Rome toward Francia, carrying letters to the king and the nobles.

No. 239, line 5.—“When he had drawn near,” etc. Pope Stephen, encouraged by the arrival of the royal envoys, Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, and Duke Autchar, left the city of Rome on October 14, in the seventh indiction, according to Anastasius, and therefore in the year 753. With them he set out for Lombardy and from there for Francia, as he had requested.

Passing through Pavia, he was entirely unable to obtain from King Aistulf the restoration of the things that had been taken away. Therefore, on November 15 of the aforesaid seventh indiction, he departed from the city of Pavia and set out on his journey to Francia. Continuing the journey he had begun, he reached the monastery of Agaunum, or Saint Maurice, where he remained for several days.

That most celebrated [Col. 1119D] monastery of Agaunum, now called Tornatense after the small town founded there, was situated in the kingdom of Burgundy, not far from Octodurum. On this subject, the second volume of the Baronian Critique should be consulted. To that monastery came Fulrad, a presbyter and chaplain—or archchaplain—of the palace, and Duke Rotard, sent by King Pippin. They asked the pontiff to proceed to their king. They escorted him to the king with great honor, together with all who were with him.

No. 243, line 1.—“When that same king heard,” etc. After Christmas Day, King Pippin immediately went to the royal estate of Pontigon, situated in the district of Perthe, not far from Victoriacum, to meet the pope, together with his wife, his sons, and his leading men. He had sent his eldest son Charles ahead, with his nobles, to meet him. He himself, with his wife Bertrada and his other son Carloman, presented himself at the third milestone. [Col. 1120A] Dismounting at the pope’s sight and bowing himself to the ground, he received him together with his wife, sons, and nobles, and even for some distance performed for him the service of a groom, as Anastasius testifies.

The pontiff proceeded to the aforesaid palace on January 6, on the most sacred solemnity of the Manifestation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and therefore in the year 754. As far as the year is concerned, Anastasius, who wrote this account, is supported by the later author of the appendix to the Continuation of Fredegar and by the annalist of Metz.

While the pontiff was staying in the said palace of Pontigon, on the following day he entreated King Pippin to defend the cause of blessed Peter and of the Roman state. King Pippin promised the pontiff that he would take every measure to restore the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights of the state, as the Annals of Metz testify.

Line 19.—“But because the winter season was approaching.” From the palace of Pontigon Pope Stephen proceeded to the monastery of Saint Denis near Paris:

“But because [Col. 1120B] the winter season was approaching,” Anastasius adds, “he caused the most holy pope, together with all his companions, to proceed to Paris, to the venerable monastery of blessed Denis, in order to winter there.”

Then King Pippin “sent an embassy to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asking that, out of reverence for the most blessed Peter and Paul, he should not move hostilely through the regions of Rome, and that, because of his request, he should not do those superstitious and impious things contrary to the order of the law that he had never before done at Rome,” says the anonymous author who added the second appendix to the Continuation of Fredegar. Beginning the year from the Kalends of March, he adds:

“When the aforesaid King Pippin had not obtained through his envoys what he had requested, and Aistulf had scorned to do this, after the year” 753 had elapsed, Pippin ordered all the Franks, as was the custom of the Franks, to come to him on the Kalends of March at the royal estate of Brennacum, situated in the district and kingdom of Soissons on the river Vidula, [Col. 1120C] commonly called Braine.

No. 244, line 11.—“At the place which is Carisiacum.” Pippin later went to Carisiacum at the request of Pope Stephen, and there, as Regino writes in his Chronicle, Pippin celebrated Easter in the year 754. Easter was celebrated on April 14. As I have said, Regino writes that Pippin celebrated it at Carisiacum in the year when Stephen II was in Francia, although he wrongly assigns that year to 751.

Carisiacum is now commonly called Quirsi or Chirsi in French. It is a place on the river Oise, then a royal estate, situated a few leagues from the city of Noyon. On this subject one should read the dissertation published by Mabillon in Book IV of On Diplomatic Matters, p. 258.

Pope Stephen was also brought there, and there Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman made him a promise that the possessions seized by the Lombards would be restored to the Roman pontiff, as the same Anastasius testifies in his account of Hadrian I.

[Col. 1120D] Line 3.—“King Pippin and his two sons were anointed as kings.” War was being prepared against Aistulf on every side, but the expedition was delayed for a time because of Pope Stephen’s grave and dangerous illness. Stephen was ill around the end of July in the monastery of Saint Denis, as is clear both from Anastasius and from Stephen himself, in his letter preserved by Hilduin in the Areopagitica. A narrative of the anointing of Pippin, his sons, and his wife by Stephen follows that letter:

“In this year,” says Hilduin, “which is the seven hundred and fifty-fourth from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August”—that is, July 28.

Stephen, therefore, having been healed through a remarkable miracle by the intercession of Saint Denis the martyr, anointed Pippin, his sons Charles and Carloman, and his wife Bertrada as kings of the Franks on July 28. In the year 754 that date fell on a Sunday; for such ceremonies were customarily performed on Sundays or on more solemn feasts.

Pippin was therefore anointed king twice: first by Saint Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, as was shown in the account of Pope Zacharias; and a second time by Pope Stephen, as testify the annalists of Bertin, Loisel, Metz, and others, as well as Anastasius.

When anointing Pippin, Charles, and Carloman as kings, Stephen called them patricians of the Romans, as is inferred from the letter written to them that survives in the Carolingian Code, no. 9. Its heading is as follows:

“To the most excellent lords, his sons, Pippin the king and our spiritual co-father, and likewise Charles and Carloman, kings and both patricians of the Romans: Pope Stephen.”

The annalist of Metz, however, removes all doubt about the matter. Under the year 754 he writes:

“He ordained”—that is, Stephen—“according to the custom of the ancestors, by sacred anointing, Pippin, the most pious prince, as king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, and likewise crowned his two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same honor and with a fortunate succession.”

Since in this letter, and quite frequently in the heading and text of other letters, Stephen calls Pippin his spiritual co-father, and since in a letter to the same Pippin, numbered 8 in the Carolingian Code, he also calls Charles and Carloman his spiritual sons and their mother Bertrada his spiritual co-mother, no other explanation of this matter can be offered than that Stephen II raised Charles and Carloman from the sacred font before anointing them as kings.

Therefore, says Cointius in the Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks under the year 754, no. 58, those are mistaken who maintain that Charles was baptized at Mainz by Boniface, the bishop of that city.

No. 245, line 1.—“Meanwhile, the most wicked Aistulf.” While Pippin was at Carisiacum with Pope Stephen, his brother Carloman, then a monk of Monte Cassino, also came there from Italy. He tried with all his strength and fought vigorously to overturn the cause of the holy Church of God, “as Aistulf had sent him for this purpose,” says Anastasius.

More plausible, however, is what Einhard writes in the Annals under the year 753: namely, that Carloman undertook that embassy unwillingly, since he did not dare to disregard his abbot’s commands, nor did his abbot dare to resist the orders of the king of the Lombards, who had imposed this upon him.
