The annalist of Lorsch and many others likewise write that Carloman undertook this embassy at the command of his abbot.

But Pippin, as he had already promised the pontiff, undertook the protection of him and of the Roman Church.

No. 248, line 13.—“He would immediately restore the cities of Ravenna.” In the meantime Pippin had sent envoys to King Aistulf and had not obtained from him what he had requested. He therefore marched against him with an army, as the author cited in the second appendix to the Continuation of Fredegar and Anastasius relate. Anastasius says that this expedition occurred in September, when the eighth indiction had already begun, and therefore in September of that same year, 754.

Before his own arrival, King Pippin sent several of his nobles, together with part of the army, to guard the Frankish passes, or the Alpine defiles. Finally, crossing the Alps with his entire army, he defeated Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in battle in the very mountain passes. Pursuing him in flight, he besieged him at Pavia.

The pontiff, fearing a new shedding of Christian blood, negotiated with Aistulf. After receiving from him an oath and hostages for the restoration of Ravenna and the other cities, he returned to Gaul.

No. 249, line 1.—“And after peace had been made,” etc. After these matters had been brought to a most successful conclusion, King Pippin, victorious, returned to Gaul, while Pope Stephen returned to Rome. There he was received by his people with the greatest joy and publicly offered the customary praises worthy of God in the basilica of Saint Peter for so many and such great benefits.

Jerome, the brother of King Pippin, accompanied Stephen to Rome, according to the annalist of Fulda. The annalists of Loisel, Lorsch, Bertin, and Regino, however, add to Jerome Fulrad, one of Pippin’s envoys. “Pippin himself,” says the annalist of Lorsch, “returned to his kingdom and sent Pope Stephen back to Rome with Fulrad, the presbyter and chaplain, and a considerable force of Franks.”

Stephen reached Rome before the end of the year 754, as will become clear from what follows. Paul Aemilius adds that Pippin brought glory home with him, since he was the first of all mortals to undertake, without personal grief, a foreign war against a people renowned for its achievements, for the sake of religion, and to bring it to completion without personal advantage.

Line 6.—“Filled with vehement fury,” etc. As that year was drawing to a close, Jerome, the brother of King Pippin, and Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, returned from Rome to Francia with the letters cited in the Carolingian Code, no. 7. Through these letters Pope Stephen complained to Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, that Aistulf was not at all keeping his promises and had restored nothing either to the Roman Church or to the Roman state.

In those letters the pontiff says of Aistulf:

“He has not allowed even a space of one palm of land to be restored to blessed Peter, to the holy Church of God, or to the Roman state, although they”—that is, Pippin and his sons—“had freely confirmed by a written deed of donation that cities and places should be restored to blessed Peter, to the holy Church of God, and to the Roman state.”

From these words one may also infer that, when peace was arranged between Stephen and Aistulf, Pippin imposed this condition upon Aistulf: that he restore what had been taken from both the Roman Church and the Roman state, not from the Roman Empire, as some incorrectly write.

Aistulf not only failed to restore what had been taken from the Roman Church, but after Fulrad and Jerome had returned to Gaul, he immediately began to trouble Pope Stephen through spies, or scouts, and through plunderings or devastations.

Moved by this, Stephen arranged for the letters found as no. 9 in the Carolingian Code to be carried without delay by Willharius, or Wilearius, bishop of Nomentum, to the aforesaid kings. In them he urged them to compel Aistulf to restore to the Roman Church and the Roman state what he had taken away and what Pippin had decided to donate to the Apostolic See:

“For,” he says, “as we first declared to your Christian devotion, the wicked King Aistulf, after the devil entered his treacherous heart, made void everything that he had promised by oath to restore to blessed Peter through our envoys, and he was unwilling to return even a space of one palm of land to blessed Peter . . . For he was not content merely with refusing to restore the possessions of blessed Peter as he had determined; by his command he also did not cease, and does not cease, to carry out spying, plundering, or devastation in the cities and places of blessed Peter . . . Therefore I ask you, most excellent sons protected by God, and I beseech you most earnestly: let the cause of the holy Church of God and of blessed Peter grieve you, and deliver to him what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by donation.”

Line 9.—“Besieging it for a period of three months.” At the beginning of the year 755, King Aistulf, having assembled a huge army once more, surrounded the city of Rome with a siege. He devastated and burned all the surrounding places, sacred and profane alike; cast the holy images into the fire; profaned the most sacred Body of the Lord; tore monks apart with blows; violated nuns; slaughtered the remaining clergy and laypeople of both sexes; killed infants torn from their mothers’ breasts; and, in short, practiced every kind of impiety and cruelty.

In these desperate circumstances Stephen suddenly sent envoys to King Aistulf concerning the observance of the agreements. But when they brought back nothing peaceful, he placed all his hope, after God, in the kings and people of the Franks. He ordered Warner, the abbot sent to him by Pippin and who had performed the duty of a soldier with distinction in defending the City, to travel by sea with his envoys, Bishop George and Count Thomeric, so that he might reach Francia more quickly and safely. He instructed him to report all these matters to Pippin and to implore him by everything sacred finally to fulfill what he had once promised.

Through those envoys he sent two letters to Francia: one in his own name to King Pippin; the other in his own name and in the name of all the Romans afflicted by these troubles, to Pippin and his sons, as well as to the bishops, abbots, presbyters, monks, dukes, counts, and all the other Franks. From these letters it is clear that Rome was already under siege on the Kalends of January.

No. 250, line 2.—“By sea,” etc. As the Lombards were pressing the siege more fiercely, Stephen, in a new and extraordinary example—one that had not previously been used by his predecessors and was not afterward used by his successors—wrote in the name of Saint Peter the Apostle himself to the same kings, Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, or rather to the entire body of the Franks.

He earnestly entreated all of them, in words carefully composed to arouse the greatest possible compassion, to come to the aid of the afflicted Church and city of Rome. Just as all the peoples who had taken refuge with the most powerful nation of the Franks had been saved, so they should hasten to free the holy Church of God and its people from the oppression of their enemies.

From the letters to King Pippin it is clear that the Church and the Roman people had placed all their hope in the most Christian king and in the Franks as their liberators:

“Help us,” he says, “and come to our aid with the greatest speed, most Christian king . . . I beg you, lest we perish, lest at some time the nations throughout the whole world say: ‘Where is the confidence of the Romans, which, after the Lord, they had in the kings of the Franks?’ . . . Save us before we perish, most Christian king . . . Consider, son, consider, and reflect deeply. By the living God I adjure you, because the souls both of us and of the entire Roman people, after God and his chief apostle, depend upon your excellence protected by God and upon the people of the Franks entrusted to you by God . . . For we have entrusted the holy Church of God and the people of our Roman commonwealth to no one else, but only to your most beloved Excellence, to your sweetest sons, and to the entire people of the Franks, by the command of God and of blessed Peter, to be protected.”

No. 252, line 6.—“He restored the aforesaid cities.” When Pippin learned of King Aistulf’s treachery, he burned with both anger and grief and, by a new decree, summoned fresh levies from the people for war. Then he marched with his army against the Lombards, drove Aistulf into the Alpine passes, and besieged him at Pavia.

He refused ever to grant pardon to Aistulf, although Aistulf pleaded for forgiveness for having broken the treaty, until he had handed over to the Roman pontiff Ravenna with the entire exarchate, the Pentapolis, and twenty cities included within those provinces.

“He compelled Aistulf,” says Anastasius, “to confirm the agreement that had been made between the parties during the eighth indiction that had elapsed,” and he sent the written donation to Rome, to Pope Stephen. This therefore took place after August of the year 755, in the month of September, when the ninth indiction began.

On his return to Francia, Pippin left in Italy Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, so that he might receive from Aistulf the cities included in the agreement and immediately transfer the cities once received into the power of the Roman pontiff, as Anastasius relates.

No. 254, line 1.—“And the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various [cities],” etc. Fulrad, advancing into the exarchate and the Pentapolis with Aistulf’s representatives, received all the cities except Ferrara, Faenza, and several others. After taking hostages from each city and bringing its leading men with him, he went to Rome and deposited in the confessio of Saint Peter the keys of the individual cities together with the tablets of the donation made by King Pippin.

At Ravenna, on an ancient tablet, this inscription may still be read, as reported by Papirius Masson in Book II:

“PIPPIN THE PIOUS, THE FIRST, OPENED THE WAY FOR THE ENLARGEMENT OF THE CHURCH AND THE EXARCHATE OF RAVENNA WITH THE MOST EXTENSIVE [lacuna].”

The remaining words have been worn away. But that inscription was placed long after Pippin’s death and after he had acquired imitators, since it calls him the first to enlarge the Church.

There is disagreement among writers about what Pippin’s donation contained and which cities it included. For, besides the cities listed by Anastasius, Leo of Ostia, in the History of Monte Cassino, Book I, chapter 7, extends the same donation over wider boundaries.

Whatever the truth may be, this much seems certain to Baronius’s annotator: from that time onward the Roman pontiffs exercised full administration in civil affairs, both at Rome and in the exarchate of Ravenna, unless they were occasionally prevented by rebellions.

“For from the time when Pippin granted the exarchate of Ravenna to the prince of the Apostles and to his successors,” he says, “the Romans completely shook off the rule of the heretical emperor Constantine Copronymus, who was unable to defend them against the Lombards, and established a commonwealth whose head was called the Roman pontiff and whose defender and protector was called Pippin, king of the Franks.”

Hence, when Stephen II speaks in his letters about Aistulf and the affliction of the city of Rome, he nowhere mentions the emperor and calls the Romans his people, as can be seen in his letters 3, 4, and 6 to King Pippin. Pope Paul, Stephen’s successor, and Hadrian I use the same forms of expression: Paul in letters 2 and 7 to Pippin, and Hadrian in letter 4 to Charlemagne, written in the year 775.

It is irrelevant that in the subscriptions of these letters the pontiffs mention the years of the emperor Constantine. They are said to have been issued “while the most pious Lord Augustus Constantine, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning,” in his thirty-second year or in some other year of that emperor. The Roman council of 743, likewise, is said to have been held in the second year of the emperor Artabasdus and the thirty-second year of King Liutprand. It does not follow from this that Rome was subject to Liutprand, king of the Lombards.

The Roman pontiffs mentioned above therefore used these formulas at that time as chronological markers, and they implied no subjection.

No. 255, line 1.—“At this, the aforesaid Desiderius,” etc. After Aistulf, king of the Lombards, died in the year 756, Pope Stephen suppressed the disturbances that had arisen among the Lombards over the succession. He helped Desiderius, duke of Tuscany, obtain the kingdom, establishing a treaty with him and securing Frankish assistance for him on the condition that he restore to the Roman Church the cities that Aistulf had retained, contrary to the treaty, until his death and that were included in Pippin’s donation, as Anastasius the Librarian testifies.

These cities were Faenza, Imola, and Ferrara, with their territories; Osimo, Ancona, and Humana, with their territories; and Bologna, as is clear from Stephen’s letters to King Pippin concerning this matter. These letters were sent through Abbot Fulrad, Bishop George, and John the sacellarius. In them Stephen asked Pippin to make a treaty of friendship and peace with Desiderius once Desiderius had fulfilled his promises.

Stephen, however, received only the duchy of Ferrara, while King Desiderius retained the other cities contrary to his promises.]

[Note: [Col. 1124D]

### No. 233, line 10

“But on one of the days, proceeding with great humility and devout care in a litany with the most sacred image of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, which is called *Anteropsita*.”

In the litanies, the image of Christ the Savior, customarily carried about together with the cross, was called *anteropsita*, a word perhaps compounded from the Latin *ante* (“before”) and the Greek ὄψις (“sight,” “spectacle”), because it appeared to be carried before the litany. Bede, *History*, book I, chapter 26, says of Augustine, the first bishop of the English, and his companions:

> “But they, endowed not with demonic but with divine power, came bearing a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord Savior painted on a panel; and, singing litanies, they supplicated the Lord for eternal salvation, both their own and that of those for whose sake and to whom they had come.”

And below:

> “It is reported that, when they approached the city, they were accustomed to chant this litany with united voice, carrying the holy cross and the image of the great King, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The image of the Savior was held in the greatest veneration among the faithful. On 9 November the commemoration is celebrated of the image of the Savior which, after being crucified by the Jews, poured forth an abundant flow of blood; concerning this, see the *Roman Martyrology*. Hence numerous churches throughout the world have been dedicated to the Savior, both at Rome and elsewhere. Augustine, book I *Against Julian*:

> “Therefore mothers also daily throughout the whole world run, not only to Christ—that is, to the child—but to Christ himself, that is, also to the Savior, with their little ones.”

### Line 13

“And at the same time receiving with it various other sacred mysteries, and carrying the holy image himself upon his own shoulder together with the other priests, that most holy pope, both he himself and the entire populace proceeding barefoot, went to the church of the holy Mother of God called ‘at the Manger,’ with ashes placed upon the heads of all the peoples, proceeding amid the greatest wailing.”

In the litany the pontiff proceeded barefoot with the clergy and the people; both he and the presbyters carried upon their shoulders the image of Christ and various relics of the saints. It was the duty of deacons, on the feast days of martyrs, to carry the relics of the saints upon their shoulders. *Council of Braga III*, canon 5.

### No. 237, line 3

“Immediately John, the imperial *silentiarius*, came from the royal city.”

In the palace there was a corps of *silentarii*, who kept watch in the imperial court. Anastasius is recorded as having been raised from the corps of *silentarii* to the imperial throne. Evagrius, book III, chapter 31. Ambrose, in the funeral oration for Valentinian:

> “In the evening the *silentiarius* departed.”

### No. 242, line 3

“Therefore, with excessive speed, God going before him, he reached the fortifications of the Franks.”

*Clusae* are the passes of the Alps through which passage is open. The *Frankish Annals* say:

> “To those very narrow places in the mountains which they call *clusae*.”

Anastasius below, in the same passage:

> “To guard the Franks’ own fortifications.”

And below:

> “And he completely overthrew the fortifications of those same Lombards.”

The Lombard *clusae* are said to have been overthrown because the *clusae*, to make them safer, had been fortified with defensive works. The same author below, in the account of Adrian:

> “The aforesaid Desiderius and the entire multitude of the Lombard army were stationed in those very fortifications, prepared to resist bravely; they had attempted carefully to strengthen them with structures and various walls.”

Liutprand, *History*, book I, chapter 2:

> “For it was separated from us by certain exceedingly difficult barriers, which they call *clusae*.”

The same author, book V, chapter 18. Regino calls them *clausurae* in *Chronicle* I:

> “He sought the Thermopylae, that is, the Lombard fortifications.”

Radevicus, *On the Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 3:

> “He penetrated their fortifications, which they had made in narrow places by cutting through the dense forests.”

Cassiodorus, *Variae* II.19, calls them *clusurae*:

> “We command that grain be supplied without hesitation to all Goths and Romans, and to those who preside over the harbors and fortifications, with sixty soldiers permanently stationed in the Augustan fortifications, just as it has also been decreed for the others.”

Cujas, *Observations* III.24.

### Line 5

“And having begun his journey, he reached the venerable monastery of Saint Maurice, martyr of Christ.”

Around the year 600, King Sigismund of Burgundy founded a monastery dedicated to Saint Maurice at Agaunum in the Allobroges. Aimo, book II, chapter 4:

> “Saint-Maurice in Chablais on the Rhône.”

### No. 243, line 5

“And in his own palace, in the place called Pontigone.”

When Pope Stephen III came into Gaul to seek assistance against the Lombards, Pippin received him in his own palace, which was called Ponticone or Pontigone. Ponticone or Pontigone was a royal estate in the district of Châlons, famous for the Council of Pontigon, which Aimo mentions in book V, chapter 33 and which is included among the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, edited by Jacques Sirmond. Gregory of Tours calls it Ponticone in book IV, chapter 23, and book VI, chapter 37. The same author does so in *Miracles of Saint Martin*, book IV, chapter 40. Frodoard, in his *Chronicle* under the year 952, calls it the Pontigon royal estate—that is, the fiscal estate.

### Line 8

“And, acting in the capacity of groom, he proceeded beside his saddle for some distance.”

Pippin performed the office of groom for the pontiff, riding beside his saddle. A *strator* is one who covers his master’s horse with a saddle and supports him as he mounts. In the imperial court, grooms belonged among the palace offices. Spartianus, in his *Life of Antoninus Caracalla*:

> “When his groom was lifting him onto the horse, he stabbed him in the side with a dagger.”

Pontius the Deacon, in the *Life of Cyprian*, in Surius, 14 September:

> “Two officials came to him, one a groom of the office of the most exalted *proconsul* Galerius, and the other a horse-groom from the guards of that same office.”

The duty of the grooms was to inspect the military horses supplied by the provincials. *Codex*, single law, “On Grooms.” Ammianus, book XXIX:

> “Constantine the groom dared to change a few military horses from those here, for the inspection of which he had been sent to Sardinia.”

Louis the Younger also, taking hold of the bridle of Nicholas I’s horse, led the mounted pope on foot in the manner of a groom.

### No. 244, line 11

“In the place called Carisiacus.”

Carisiacus was a royal estate, famous for the Council of Carisiacum, which survives among the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, and for the death of Charles Martel. Fredegar, in his *Chronicle*, chapter 110:

> “And coming to Carisiacum—Crécy-sur-Oise—the palace estate above the river Oise, he was seized by a violent fever and died in peace.”

### No. 250, line 15

“Receiving them, therefore, the most blessed pope announced to them the movement of the aforesaid king of the Franks.”

Sometimes the departure or movement of an army was announced by a military signal. Ammianus, book XXI:

> “By a signal, the order was given to march into Pannonia.”

The same author, book XXIII:

> “Sent through the military units by an expeditionary signal.”

More often the signal for departure was given by a trumpet. Curtius, book III:

> “It was handed down by ancestral Persian custom that they should proceed only after sunrise, when the day was already bright.”

The signal was given from the king’s tent by a trumpet. The same author, book V:

> “When he wished to move the camp, the trumpet gave the signal.”

And below:

> “He himself, during the third watch, proceeded in silent formation, without even giving a signal by trumpet, along the indicated route of the paths.”

### No. 254, line 1

“And placing in the confession of blessed Peter the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities belonging to the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the deed of donation concerning them issued by their king, he handed them over to that apostle, to his most holy vicar the pope, and to all his successors the pontiffs, to possess and administer perpetually.”

Pippin, king of the Franks, through Abbot Fulrad, granted to Peter and his successors the exarchate of Ravenna, taken by force from Aistulf, king of the Lombards, as a token of the donation, after the keys had been placed upon the confession—that is, the tomb—of blessed Peter. The handing over of keys is a symbol of surrender or donation.

The *Frankish Annals*, under the year 800:

> “Aran, the Saracen prefect of Huesca, sent the keys of the city, together with other gifts, to the king, promising that he would surrender it.”

Concerning the surrender of golden keys, by which Capua was granted to the emperor Basil by the prince of the city, Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book I, chapter 39:

> “When, therefore, the prince of Capua, secretly favoring Basil, the Constantinopolitan emperor, sent him golden keys, by this act he surrendered to the empire both himself and the city of Capua, indeed his entire principality.”

Charles the Great received the keys of the Jerusalem sepulcher from the patriarch as a token of blessing. The *Frankish Annals*, under the year 801:

> “On that same day the priest Zacharias, whom the king had sent to Jerusalem, came to Rome with two monks whom the patriarch had sent with him to the king; for the sake of blessing they brought the keys of the Lord’s sepulcher and of the place of Calvary, together with a banner.”

### Line 8

“Eugubium, or Comiaclum.”

Eugubium, today Comiaclum, is an episcopal city of Umbria which came to the Apostolic See through Pippin’s donation together with the exarchate of Ravenna. Anastasius, in his account of Adrian:

> “Or Comaclium, of the exarchate of Ravenna.”

## Note

### No. 235, line 10

“Lord Gregory.”

According to Anastasius, therefore, both Gregory II and Gregory III, as well as Zacharias, entered into treaties with the kings of the Franks. In the case of Gregory II, historical evidence is not available, many records having been erased by the injuries of time. But concerning Gregory III, Fredegar’s continuator, an almost contemporary writer, reported the following in chapter 110:

> “At that time blessed Pope Gregory twice sent from Rome to Charles Martel an embassy, such as had never before been sent in any time heard of or seen, with the keys of the venerable sepulcher, the chains of Saint Peter, and great and countless gifts; and, after a compact had been concluded that he would withdraw to the emperor’s party, he conferred the Roman consulship upon the aforesaid prince Charles.”

Concerning the embassy received and its proceedings, he adds:

> “He received that embassy with wonderful and magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and, with great rewards, sent to Rome, to the thresholds of Saints Peter and Paul, together with his fellow envoys, Grimoald, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, and Sygobert, a recluse of the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr.”

The annalist of Metz gives the same account:

> “In the year 741, Prince Charles, after subduing the peoples situated all around, while he was arranging matters of peace within the boundaries of his rule, received twice in that same year the embassy of the most blessed Pope Gregory, sent from the Apostolic See. They presented him with the keys of the venerable tomb of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and with his precious chains, together with great gifts—something previously sent by no bishop of the Roman city to any Frankish prince. The aforesaid bishop Gregory had also sent him a letter, by decree of the Roman princes, stating that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s rule, wished to turn to Charles’s protection and unconquered clemency.”

I believe that the only decree of the Roman princes was the decree by which they had elected Charles Martel consul. We have seen above that decrees of elections, with subscriptions, were customarily employed in this period.

### Line 15

“Secretly through a certain pilgrim.”

For at that time Aistulf, king of the Lombards, was harassing and oppressing the pontifical territory with invasions to such an extent that every access to the kings of France was obstructed. Therefore Pippin sent Bishop Rodingang and Duke Autchar to Italy so that they might accompany the pope Stephen, who was intending to travel to France.

### No. 239, line 8

“To seek the city of Ravenna.”

Aistulf held Ravenna. Hence, when Stephen continued his journey toward Pavia, the king ordered that he should not pass through Ravenna or through the exarchate. For this reason Agnellus’s slanderous falsehood in his *Life of Sergius of Ravenna* is exposed, where he tells certain old wives’ tales about Stephen’s entering Ravenna in order to plunder the treasury of that Church. On this matter, see his *Life of Sergius*, chapter 4, page 172, and Bacchini in his observations on the same work.

### No. 244, line 4

“Kings have been anointed.”

For establishing the royal era of the Carolingians, which ancient and modern chronologists attach to the year 752, it is useful to reproduce an annotation found in an old manuscript codex of Saint Gregory of Tours’ *Book on the Glory of the Martyrs*, published by Mabillon, book V of *On Diplomatics*, page 354, plate 22:

> “If you wish to know, reader, in what period this little book seems to have been written and published for the precious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 767, in the time of the most fortunate, most peaceful, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of the blessed-memory former prince Charles, in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign, in the fifth indiction, and in the thirteenth year of his sons, those same kings of the Franks, Charles and Carloman (who, by the hands of the man of holy memory, the most blessed Lord Pope Stephen, together with the aforesaid father and lord, the most glorious man, King Pippin, were consecrated with sacred chrism, by divine providence and through the intercession of Saints Peter and Paul). For that aforesaid lord, the flourishing, pious King Pippin, by the authority and command of the lord of holy memory, Pope Zacharias, and through the anointing with sacred chrism by the hands of the priests of Gaul, and through the election of all the Franks, had already been raised to the throne of the kingdom three years earlier.

> “Afterward, by the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on a single day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius (where the venerable man Folrad is known to be archpriest and abbot), he was anointed and blessed as king and patrician, together with the aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

> “In that same church of the blessed martyrs, on one and the same day, the aforesaid venerable pontiff blessed Bertrada, the noble and most devout wife of the aforesaid flourishing king, most devotedly attached to the holy martyrs, after she had been clothed in royal robes, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. At the same time he confirmed the leaders of the Franks with the blessing and grace of the Holy Spirit, and bound them all by this prohibition and law of excommunication: that they should never dare in perpetuity to choose a king from the loins of another, but only from those whom divine mercy had deigned to exalt and whom, through the intercession of the holy apostles, it had determined to confirm and consecrate by the hands of their vicar, the most blessed pontiff.

> “For this reason we have briefly inserted these things in the final little page of this book for your charity, so that the posterity of generations to come may be able to know them for ever through the reports of the succeeding ages and of the people.”

The *Annals of Bertin*, under the year 753, likewise say:

> “Pope Stephen came to France, seeking assistance and support for the rights of Saint Peter. Likewise Carloman, a monk and brother of the aforesaid King Pippin, came to France at the command of his abbot, as if to disturb the Apostolic petition.”

And under the year 754:

> “Stephen confirmed Pippin as king by holy anointing, and with him anointed his two sons, Lord Charles and Carloman, as kings, in the year of the Lord 754, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.”

### No. 247, line 11

“The fortifications of the Franks.”

Concerning these, the *Annals of Bertin* say:

> “King Pippin, traveling into Italy at the Apostolic invitation and seeking the justice of blessed Peter the apostle, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, seeking to prevent the aforesaid justice, made for the Lombard fortifications and came to meet King Pippin and the Franks. They joined battle, and, with the Lord’s help and through the intercession of blessed Peter the apostle, King Pippin emerged victorious with the Franks. In that same year, 755, Pope Stephen was led to the Holy See by the messengers of Lord King Pippin, together with Fulrad and the others who were with them.”

The remaining matters related by the aforementioned annalist correspond exactly to what is contained in the papal deeds.

## Note

### No. 236, line 4

“Rodingang, abbot, already sent in the name of the aforesaid king by the Franks.”

Rodingang was the abbot whom Pippin sent to Rome to Stephen to answer the letters that the pontiff had sent him through a foreign pilgrim, so that he might pass more safely through the Lombard territory, which was hostile to the Roman pontiff. In the two letters preserved in the *Carolingian Codex*, he is called Droctegang. The tenth letter contains the following:

> “The present Abbot Droctegang has been presented at the sacred threshold of your protector, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and before our presence.”

And the eleventh letter:

> “As we sent through the present religious Abbot Droctegang and his companions.”

Which monastery Droctegang was abbot of is entirely uncertain to me. In the life of Saint John, abbot of Gorze, published by Bollandus under 27 February, it is suggested that Droctegang governed the abbey of Gorze, situated in the diocese of Metz.

But the illustrious deeds and holiness of life of Rodingang, or Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, have made the matter much clearer. This was the same man whom Pippin later sent to Stephen, as is read in the following section of Anastasius. Concerning this Bishop Chrodegang, Paul the Deacon relates in his book *On the Bishops of the City of Metz* that he was born in the district of Hasbain, to Sigramnus his father and Landrada his mother, from the highest Frankish nobility—for King Pippin was Rodingang’s maternal uncle, as is read in the charter of donation cited by the distinguished Father Calmet, volume I of his *History of Lorraine*, written in French, page 281, in the proofs—and that he was raised in the palace of Charles the Mayor, becoming that ruler’s *referendary*, that is, keeper of the royal ring; and finally, in Pippin’s time, he attained the episcopal dignity of the city of Metz.

Indeed, in the manuscript of Anastasius, both in the Thuane manuscript and in another Ambrosian one, he is said to have been adorned by Stephen with the dignity of the pallium, in these words, which are enclosed in parentheses in that codex:

> “And while he was situated in France, he bestowed the pallium upon Rodingang, the most holy bishop, and ordained him archbishop.”

Lambecius attests this in book II, chapter 8, of his *Imperial Library*.

As for his embassy to Stephen III, which Anastasius reports at this point, the aforementioned Warnefrid gives the following account:

> “Since he was wealthy in every respect, he was specially chosen by King Pippin and the entire assembly of the Franks, and sent to Rome; and, as the wishes of all earnestly desired, he summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul.”

In the Chronicle of Lorsch, not only is Rodingang’s embassy mentioned, but his zeal is also praised, by which he obtained from Pippin that the exarchate of Ravenna and the other patrimonies which the Lombards had seized by force should be restored to blessed Peter:

> “Among other highly memorable deeds,” says the *Chronicle*, “he summoned Pope Stephen to Gaul and girded Pippin, with all the strength of the Franks, against the tyranny of the Lombards; he devoted constant zeal and effort to having the exarchate of Ravenna and many patrimonies of blessed Peter restored to the Roman See.”

### No. 245, line 1

“Meanwhile the most wicked Aistulf sent Carloman.”

Aistulf resolved to send this embassy to Gaul with the intention of subverting the cause of the Roman Church. Carloman, Pippin’s brother, who at that time was living as a monk in the monastery of Monte Cassino, accepted it reluctantly, since he was compelled to undertake it by the virtue of obedience by his abbot Gratianus. The abbot feared that, as had happened previously, the monastery, restored with such great labor, might again be destroyed by the Lombards. This is attested by Einhard, Aimo, Leo of Ostia, and other ancient writers.

It will not be unhelpful to produce one or two testimonies concerning this matter. Einhard, in his *Annals* under the year 753, gives the following explanation of Carloman’s journey:

> “Because neither he dared resist the commands of his abbot, nor his abbot the orders of the king of the Lombards, who had commanded him to do this.”

Leo of Ostia, also treating the affairs of Monte Cassino, gives the same account in book I, chapter 7:

> “Afterward, when Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asked him to go to his brother Pippin, king of the Franks, on certain affairs of his kingdom, and when his abbot likewise requested that this be done, he consented reluctantly and eventually departed. When he had remained there for some time, prevented by the very cause for which he had come, he died. His brother Pippin afterward placed his body in a golden coffin and, together with many other gifts, sent it back here, that is, to his monastery.”

I have chosen to append these authorities to this passage because, contrary to the testimony of the ancients, shameless men in our own time have dared to write that Carloman undertook his journey to Gaul on behalf of Aistulf because he himself disapproved of the pontiff’s cause, ambition, and desire to rule.

There was certainly no ambition or desire to rule in the most holy pontiff Stephen. He was concerned solely that Pippin should defend the cause of blessed Peter’s justice, which the perjured Aistulf was overthrowing by force and crime.

Certainly, concerning Carloman’s stay in Gaul, our author reports the following:

> “When he had joined them there, he strove with all his strength and contended most vigorously to subvert the causes of the holy Church of God, in accordance with the instructions of the aforesaid Aistulf, that tyrant whose name ought not even to be spoken, by whom he had been sent. But, through the Lord’s mercy, he was entirely unable to bend to this the most steadfast heart of his brother, the most Christian King Pippin of the Franks.”

But if we possess the testimony of the ancients that Carloman reluctantly undertook the embassy on behalf of Aistulf, how can it be consistent to say that he approved Aistulf’s cause and disapproved that of the pontiff? If he vigorously defended Aistulf’s side before his brother Pippin, it should rather be thought that he did so lest the monastery of Monte Cassino, to which he had devoted himself, should again be exposed to the savagery of the Lombards. Who does not see that this would have happened if Carloman, as their ambassador, had dealt perfunctorily with their affairs before Pippin?

### No. 242, line 9

“Abbot Fulrad, and so forth.”

*Summary of the History of Dogma*, book VIII, chapter 34.

On his journey toward France, Stephen gave answers on various questions of discipline. Concerning marriage, he declared:

- that when a concubine was dismissed and taken as a legitimate wife, this did not constitute a double marriage;
- that a marriage could not be dissolved because impotence arose after the celebration, or because another illness supervened, except in the case of leprosy or demonic possession;
- that a man who changed his dwelling could not likewise change his wife while the woman to whom he had been lawfully married was still alive;
- that it was not lawful to marry the godmother either of one’s baptism or of one’s confirmation;
- that one who had repudiated one wife could not be joined to another;
- that penance ought to be imposed on those who, after vowing virginity but before entering a monastery, marry;
- that religious men and women who marry must be separated from communion;
- that a widow who marries after professing religious life must be confined to a monastery for the remainder of her life;
- that spouses should be separated if either suffers from leprosy, lest they produce leprous offspring;
- that a man who, uncertain whether he had been ordained a priest, had celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass and administered baptism, but thereafter renounced the ministry and married, must be shut up in a monastery to do penance for the rest of his life; and that the same must be done with the woman whom he married, provided that she had not been unaware that the man had performed the office of priest;
- and finally, that a woman who, believing her absent husband to be dead, married another must return to her first husband, if he survives, under penalty of excommunication.

#### II. Concerning baptism

He decreed that anyone who, having water available, baptizes with wine is to be excommunicated; but if he has no water and the child is in danger, he will be free from punishment. Baptism by immersion is valid. A priest who, uncertain whether he has been validly ordained, administers baptism in the meantime must be punished by penance until the end of his life.

#### III. Concerning the clergy

Finally, he decreed:

- that a bishop condemned for definite offenses by the unanimous agreement of the bishops of his province could not be judged again by others;
- that in clerical cases the bishop of the diocese should associate with himself six colleagues from neighboring dioceses, to be chosen by the accused if he is a priest, or three if he is a deacon; but that the bishop himself should hear and determine the cases of other clerics;
- that a priest who had been convicted and had confessed with his own mouth that he had committed the crime of sexual immorality before ordination should be forbidden the sacred Mass, but not the other functions of the priesthood;
- and that clerics and monks should not wear their hair long.

The same pontiff granted Abbot Fulrad authority to build monasteries wherever he could in France. The privilege reads as follows:

> “By this Apostolic authority, granting and conceding to you, our beloved son Fulrad, and to all your other successors the abbots, license and power to build monasteries wherever you wish in the province of France, we prohibit by this authority any bishop of any Church or any other priest from exercising any jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monasteries, except the Apostolic See.”

(*Privilege of Stephen II granted to Abbot Fulrad.*)

### No. 244, line 3

“King Pippin, by the same most holy pontiff, and so forth.”

While arms were being prepared on both sides, and the same was being done in France, the pontiff anointed the king, his sons, and his wife. Hilduin relates the matter clearly in the *Areopagitica*:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 754, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, blessed Pope Stephen anointed the flourishing King Pippin as king of the Franks, together with his two sons Charles and Carloman. He also consecrated Bertrada, the wife of the illustrious King Pippin, clothed in royal robes, in the name of God through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit of the Holy Spirit. Blessing the nobles of the Franks with Apostolic blessing, he bound them by the authority of blessed Peter, given to him by the Lord Jesus Christ, true God, and charged them never, throughout succeeding ages, to presume in any way to establish over themselves a king from another stock, unless from the lineage of those whom Divine Providence had deigned to choose to guard the most holy Apostolic See and to raise to royal power through him, namely the vicar of Saint Peter, indeed of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to consecrate with the most sacred anointing.”

Nor did he merely ordain, as the annalist of Metz says, that Pippin, the most devout prince, should be anointed king of the Franks with sacred anointing according to the custom of his ancestors. Rather, so that he might commend the protection of the Apostolic See to them more and more strongly, he also declared Pippin a patrician of the Romans and crowned his two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same fortunate honor.

### No. 254, line 4

“To possess and administer perpetually.”

Before Stephen departed from King Pippin, he testified to him that no reliance could be placed either in words or in writing upon the Lombard king and his people, since they would not have kept their promises if the Frankish army had returned across the Alps, unless the peace treaty that was being made had been put into execution:

> “King Aistulf, writing from Rome, says: ‘By flattering speeches, persuasions, and oaths with their judges, they deceived your prudence, and you believed those who spoke falsely rather than us who asserted the truth.’”

(Stephen II, letter 3, to Pippin and his sons.)

And indeed, what the pontiff had foretold happened. For Aistulf, freed from the fear and danger of losing his territory, deceived the commissioners whom Pippin had left in Italy to prevent him from seizing what belonged to others. As Stephen continues in the same place, Aistulf nullified everything that he had promised under oath to restore to blessed Peter through Pippin’s messengers, and he refused to return even a space of land one palm wide to blessed Peter.

What is more, Aistulf, having drawn up a powerful army, besieged Rome and omitted nothing cruel or impious that he did not order to be perpetrated in the neighboring places. Therefore, in such extreme circumstances, lacking counsel, the pontiff again turned to Pippin and the Frankish people and earnestly demanded that they fulfill what they had promised:

> “What you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by the donation, you ought to secure for him to possess.”

(Same author, letters 3 and 4.)

Moreover, so that he might penetrate their hearts more deeply and obtain assistance as quickly as possible, he sent to the Franks a letter written in the name of Saint Peter in these words:

> “Through the word of evangelical preaching that we have received, your hope of future reward is surely joined to us in this Apostolic Roman Church of God entrusted to us. Therefore I, Peter, the apostle of God, who regard you as adopted sons, exhort and appeal to the devotion of all of you to rescue from the hands of adversaries this Roman city and the people entrusted to me by God, as well as the house where I rest according to the flesh, and to free them from the pollution of the nations. I solemnly admonish you to liberate the Church of God entrusted to me by divine power, because they are suffering the greatest afflictions and oppressions from the most wicked people of the Lombards.”

(Same author, letter 5, to the Franks.)

When Pippin heard this, he crossed the Alps with the greatest speed and besieged Ticinum for a second time, in order to recall Aistulf from the siege of the city and defend the royal seat. He did not return to France until he had seen everything fully accomplished. The remaining details are sufficiently clear in Anastasius.

## Note

### No. 244, line 2

“The same most Christian King Pippin and his two sons were anointed kings of the Franks by the same most holy pope through the grace of Christ.”

In that same year, namely 754—or rather, on that same day, 28 July—on which Pope Stephen anointed Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman as kings, he declared those same men patricians of the Romans. The confirmation of the kingdom and the conferral of the patriciate were one and the same ceremony.

I first infer this from the letters of Pope Stephen. The first letter written to Pippin, before Stephen went to Gaul, bears this title:

> “To the most excellent lord, his son, King Pippin, from Pope Stephen.”

For Pippin had been declared king by Stephen’s predecessor Zacharias and consecrated by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, but had not yet been created a patrician. The third letter written by the same Stephen after his return from Gaul bears this other title:

> “To the most excellent lords, his sons, King Pippin, our spiritual fellow-father, and likewise Kings Charles and Carloman, both patricians of the Romans, from Pope Stephen.”

The same point is most clearly stated by the anonymous author whom I quoted from Mabillon in the notes on Zacharias:

> “Afterward, by the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on one day, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, Pippin was anointed and blessed as king and patrician, together with the aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman, in the name of the Holy Trinity.”

What Stephen conferred upon Pippin by conferring the patriciate, insofar as the obscurity of the matter permits—and it has been made still more obscure by the preconceived positions and partisan interests of various sides—I shall attempt to explain briefly.

When the Roman republic had been thrown into disorder, its ancestral institutions had been overthrown, and imperial power had been established in the hands of the emperors of Constantinople, the dignity of patrician was granted to those whom the favor of the prince raised to the highest offices of the empire.

The most eminent Norisius observes, in dissertation 4 of his *Pisan Cenotaphs*, that access to the dignity of patrician was especially open to those who had served well as commanders of the army in war. Idacius, in his *Chronicle* at the beginning of the reign of Valentinian III, says:

> “Felix is appointed patrician from the office of commander of the army.”

And under the ninth year of that same emperor:

> “Aetius, commander of both armies, is appointed patrician.”

In imperial rescripts sent to illustrious men, those who were also called commanders of both armies are designated by the title of patricians. Novel 24 of Theodosius is sent to Aetius, count and commander of both armies, and patrician; Novel 2 of Majorian is sent to Ricimer, illustrious man, count and commander of both armies, and patrician.

In Gruter’s large collection of inscriptions, page 1076, the following is read:

> **FL. FELIX. V. C. MAGISTER. UTRIUSQ. MILITIAE. PATRICIUS. ET. EXCONS. OR. ET. PANDUSA. EJUS. INL. FEMINA. VOTI. COMPOTES. DE. PROPRIO. FECERUNT.**

“Flavius Felix, a man of senatorial rank, commander of both armies, patrician and former ordinary consul, and Pandusa, his illustrious wife, having fulfilled their vow, made this at their own expense.”

But that Asterius who corrected, with consular authority, the manuscript of Virgil preserved in the Medicean Library lists the patriciate among the more honorable titles, although he had not been commander of the army. At the end of the *Bucolics* the following is read:

> **TURCIUS RUFIUS APRONIANUS ASTERIUS V. C. ET INL. EX COMITE DOMEST. PROTECT. EX. COM. PRIV. LARGIT. EX PRAEF. URBI PATRICIUS ET CONSUL ORDIN. LEGI ET DISTINXSI CODICEM FRATRIS MACARII V. C.**

“Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius, illustrious and noble man, former *comes domesticorum*, protector, former *comes* of the private largesses, former prefect of the city, patrician and ordinary consul, read and divided into sections this codex of his brother Macarius, an illustrious man.”

Asterius’s consulship falls in the year 494, from which one may infer the antiquity and value of that singular codex. Corrected by Asterius in that year, but written much earlier, it seems to precede the famous Tiburtine Cornutian charter signed by the consuls Leo Augustus IV and Probianus, an illustrious man, namely in the year 471, which was regarded as the oldest of all by the eminent scholars Suaresius, Mabillon, and Blanchini.

Anastasius calls Belisarius a patrician and calls many exarchs of Ravenna patricians: John, Eleutherius, Isaac, Paul, Romanus, Theodore, and Eutychius.

[Col. 1133B] The dignity of the patriciate was inferior to the dignity of the consulship. I learn this from Cassiodorus, who, in Book VI, chapter 2, when reciting the formula of the patriciate, says: “He precedes prefects and men of the other dignities, yielding only to one splendor, which we know is sometimes also assumed by us”; by this he means the consulship.

That the emperors subsequently attached to the dignity of the patriciate the duty of protecting and defending churches and the poor against the violence of the more powerful is taught by the formula by which the emperor created a patrician, reported by Paul the Deacon in his *History of the Lombards* from the Vatican manuscript, and copied by Pagius in the *Life of Gregory III*: “We grant you this honor, that you may uphold the law for the churches of God and for the poor, and thereafter render an account before the Most High Judge.” Then the emperor should put a mantle upon him, place a ring on his right index finger, and give him, with his own hand, a written document on cotton. “Be a merciful and just patrician.” Then he should place a golden circlet upon his head and dismiss him.

From this, Peter de Marca, Book I of *On Concord*, [Col. 1133C] chapter 12, infers that patricians enjoyed, by a certain extraordinary right, the responsibility of conducting the affairs and defense of churches not subject to them. Since it is the prince’s ordinary right to protect the churches established within his dominion against the violence of the powerful, through the conferral of the patriciate he granted an extraordinary right of protection to the leading men among the citizens; for that reason they were called defenders and advocates, by virtue of which they were to provide defense and protection to particular churches.

I pass over that point, but I deny what he adds: that the Roman patriciate comprised two things, namely the jurisdiction by which kings held power over the city with the consent of the pope and the Roman people, and the protection or defense that they promised to the Roman Church. Thus he wrongly concludes: “The patriciate of the Romans, therefore, in addition to command over the City and the Roman duchy, comprised that defense which had been established by agreements entered into with the Roman pontiffs.”

[Col. 1133D] Agreements were indeed entered into and confirmed by solemn oath between Pope Stephen and King Pippin concerning the defense and protection of the Roman Church. But that Stephen granted Pippin jurisdiction over the city of Rome and the Roman duchy, I consistently deny; and de Marca, whom Pagius rashly followed, invented this for himself by his own ingenuity, without any foundation.

For he himself never saw the charter of the agreements in which he could have read of such a grant; nor is there any trace of it either in the letters sent by Stephen to Pippin or in the *Life of Stephen* written by Anastasius, who saw the charter and knew that in his own time it was kept in the archive of the holy Roman Church.

Two things were agreed between Stephen and Pippin. The first was that Stephen would confer upon Pippin the singular and distinguished honor of the Roman patriciate, previously granted to no one, by virtue of which Pippin would assume the protection, defense, and advocacy of the Roman Church, of all the patrimonies of blessed [Col. 1134A] Peter, and of all the rights and full claims of justice belonging to the apostolic see. The second was that Pippin, by virtue of this protection, would exert all his strength so that the Church’s rights would be restored, the exarchate of Ravenna would be wrested from the hands of the Lombards, and it would be handed over to the Roman pontiff.

The first point is clearly shown by Stephen’s letters to Pippin. In Letter 3:

> “What none of your ancestors deserved to receive, you have received; and the prince of the apostles, making you, above all other kings and nations, his special possession, has entrusted all his causes to you. You will render an account to God of how you have fought for the justice of that doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven.”

A little earlier he had said:

> “For this reason the Lord, through my humility and by the mediation of blessed Peter, anointed you as kings, so that through you his holy Church might be exalted and the prince of the apostles might receive his justice.”

And in Letter 4:

> “Since, as has been stated above, we have entrusted, by God’s command, to no one else but solely to your most loving Excellency, to your most dear sons, and to the entire Frankish people, the holy Church of God belonging to blessed Peter and our Roman people of the commonwealth, for protection.”

The second point is likewise established by the same letters. Letter 3:

> “For when we were brought before your honey-sweet presence, we entrusted all the causes of the prince of the apostles to your hands, since, inspired by God, you deigned to lend an ear to our petitions, and you promised blessed Peter that you would exact his justice and provide for the defense of the holy Church of God.”

A little later:

> “For this reason I ask you, most excellent sons protected by God, and I earnestly beseech you: may you grieve on behalf of the holy Church of God and the cause of blessed Peter, and may you deliver to him for possession what you promised would be offered to blessed Peter by your donation.”

And below:

> “Swiftly and without hindrance, return to blessed Peter, by your donation, the cities, places, and all the hostages and captives that you promised him; or return everything that the donation itself contains.”

And Letter 6:

> “May you deign to grant full justice to that same Church of God . . . so that you may command that the remaining cities, which had been joined under the authority of a single dominion, together with the established boundaries, territories, places, and wooded lands, be restored in their entirety to your spiritual mother, the holy Church. I ask you, son, I ask you before the living God . . . to command that everything which you promised to blessed Peter under oath be fulfilled, and, just as you began, to grant him full justice.”

These alone were the agreements established between Stephen and Pippin, and no others. Nowhere in those letters is there a single word about a grant to Pippin of command over the City or the duchy, although there had been frequent opportunity to speak of such a matter, especially in the straits in which Rome found itself, besieged by the Lombards. The pope could have implored Pippin’s aid for that city in whose dominion he would supposedly have called the king to share.

Anastasius, moreover, accurately recounts the oath and the promise made by Pippin to Stephen to fight for the Church of God and to restore—or donate—the exarchate of Ravenna to the Roman Church, but he says not a word about that fancied grant of jurisdiction.

> “Pippin,” Anastasius says in the *Life of Stephen III*, no. 243, “by the oath presently given, satisfied that same most blessed pope by obeying with all his strength all his commands and admonitions, and, as it should please him, by every means returning the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights or places of the commonwealth.”

And in no. 245:

> “The same most excellent Pippin, king of the Franks, declared with all his strength that he would fight for the cause of the holy Church of God, just as he had previously promised the aforesaid most blessed pontiff.”

And in no. 253:

> “Of all the cities received, he sent a written donation for possession to blessed Peter, to the holy Roman Church, and to all the pontiffs of the apostolic see in perpetuity; this donation is still kept to the present day in the archive of our holy [Col. 1135A] Church . . . The aforesaid venerable abbot Fulrad, priest of the Ravennates, joining forces with the envoys of the aforesaid King Aistulf and entering each of the cities, both of the Pentapolis and of Emilia, received them and took hostages from each one, carrying with him the leading men together with the keys of the city gates, and proceeded to Rome. He placed the keys themselves—both those of the city of Ravenna and those of the various cities of that exarchate of Ravenna—together with the donation concerning them sent by their king, at the confession of blessed Peter; and he handed them over to that apostle, to his most holy vicar the pope, and to all his pontiff-successors, to possess and administer forever.”

He then lists individually the cities which, in the king’s name, the abbot Fulrad, the king’s envoy, handed over to Pope Stephen for the Roman pontiffs to possess and administer perpetually, delivering their keys. He reserved for the king no dominion over them, nor any appearance of dominion or of any right whatsoever, but granted—or, more truly, restored—all rights and claims of justice to Peter and Peter’s successors.

What more need be said? If Stephen, by conferring the patriciate, had granted Pippin some right over the city of Rome, could he have spoken in his letters to Pippin in terms more explicit than those by which he declared his full dominion over the City and over the Roman citizens? Yet he speaks of “his” Roman commonwealth, “his” people, and “his” Roman city.

In Letter 3:

> “For our entire people of the Roman commonwealth is afflicted, together with us, by great sorrow and the most bitter tears.”

In Letter 4:

> “We have entrusted the holy Church of God and our Roman people of the commonwealth for protection.”

[Col. 1136A] In Letter 5:

> “Therefore provide for my Roman people entrusted to me by God . . . provided only that you protect my special people and my Roman city . . .”

This manner of speaking is clear evidence not of jurisdiction alienated or divided, but of jurisdiction always wholly retained and preserved by the pope.

The first Frankish emperors themselves also spoke in their acts of the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church, but never of jurisdiction over the City or the Roman duchy supposedly granted to them by the popes.

Charlemagne, in the division of his kingdom made among his sons in the year 806, says:

> “Above all, we command that these three brothers jointly assume the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as that care was once assumed by our grandfather Charles, by King Pippin of blessed memory, and afterward by us; and that, with God’s help, they strive to defend it against its enemies and ensure that it obtain its justice, insofar as it pertains to them and as reason demands.”

And Louis the Pious, likewise in the division of his kingdom, which Baluzius reports in volume I of the *Capitularies*, in the year 837, says:

> “Above all, we command and enjoin that these three brothers jointly assume the care and defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as that care was once assumed by our great-grandfather Charles, by our grandfather Pippin, by our father, the emperor Charles of blessed memory, and afterward by us.”

I thought it appropriate to discuss these matters concerning the Roman patriciate briefly in my notes on the *Life of Stephen*. Anyone who desires fuller information should consult the excellent treatise entitled *Defense of the Rights of the Church over Comacchio*, where its most learned author—who has rendered outstanding service not only to the Roman Church but to the entire republic of letters—long ago elucidated this same argument with the distinction it deserves.

[Col. 1083]

### 227

Stephen II, a Roman by nation, the son of Constantine, occupied the see for five years and twenty-eight days. After the death of his father, he was left as a young child in the venerable Lateran palace, where, under the predecessors of the pontiffs of blessed memory, he remained for instruction in the apostolic tradition.

[Note: [Col. 1083] Under the instruction in the apostolic tradition of his predecessors, the pontiffs Gregory and Zachary.]

They advanced him individually through the ecclesiastical orders and ordained him to the order of deacon.

[Note: [Col. 1083] B: *clerical.*]

After Zachary, the lord pope of blessed memory, had died, the entire people chose a certain presbyter named Stephen for the pontificate and placed him in the Lateran patriarchate. He remained there for two days; on the third day, after rising from sleep and sitting down to arrange his household affairs, he suddenly became deranged and fell silent while seated, and on the following day he died.

After this, the entire people of God assembled inside the venerable basilica of the holy Mother of God at the Praesepe. There, beseeching the mercy of the Lord our God and of that lady, our holy and ever-virgin Mother of God Mary, they chose the aforesaid most blessed man as their pontiff, with good will and in unanimous agreement. With sincere devotion and acclamations of praise, they carried him into the basilica of the Savior called Constantiniana; from there they entered within and, according to custom, brought him into the patriarchate.

### 228

For this same most blessed pope was a lover of the churches of God, preserving ecclesiastical tradition with firm constancy.

[Note: [Col. 1085] *He preserved.*]

He was a swift helper of Christ’s poor and a preacher of the word of God with great steadfastness. He visited widows and orphans with exceptional care.

[Note: [Col. 1085] Baron: with almsgiving, that is, rather than by bodily presence.]

He was also a most courageous defender, through God’s power, of his flock. He immediately restored the four xenodochia situated in this Roman city from ancient times, which had remained abandoned for a long period. In them he arranged every provision, organizing the various functions both inside and outside; he also bestowed many gifts upon them, confirming these by a charter of privilege under threat of anathema.

In the same way, he is known to have newly founded a xenodochium at Plantana.

[Note: [Col. 1085] B: Plataria.]

There he established a house for one hundred of Christ’s poor and decreed that their daily food should be provided.

### 229

Outside the walls of this Roman city, beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he also built two xenodochia. He bestowed many goods upon them and joined them to the venerable deaconries existing there outside the walls, so that they might remain permanently:

[Note: [Col. 1085] *So that they might remain permanently.*]

namely, the deaconry of the holy Mother of God and the two deaconries of blessed Silvester. He secured their perpetual continuance by apostolic privileges.

### 230

[Note: [Col. 1085] Baron, annals, year 752.]

Meanwhile, when a great persecution had arisen in this Roman city and in the cities subject to it from Aistulf, king of the Lombards,

[Note: [Col. 1085] B: Aistulf.]

and the king’s fierce violence was threatening, the same most blessed pope, in the third month of his pontifical consecration, immediately sent his own brother, the most holy deacon Paul, together with Ambrosius the *primicerius*, and many gifts, to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, to arrange and confirm a treaty of peace.

[Note: [Col. 1085] *And more gifts.*]

When these men approached him and presented the gifts, so that they might more easily obtain their request from him, they arranged and confirmed with him a treaty of peace for forty years.

But that arrogant king of the Lombards, overcome by the cunning of the ancient enemy, broke the peace treaty after scarcely four months, falling into the guilt of perjury. He heaped many insults upon the aforesaid most holy man and the entire Roman people and sent him various threats.

Since he desired, with God opposed to him, to invade this entire province, he endeavored to impose a burdensome tribute upon the inhabitants of this Roman city:

[Note: [Col. 1085] *to add.*]

he greedily sought to exact one gold solidus annually from each person.

[Note: [Col. 1085] *To take away.*]

He insolently asserted that this Roman city and the camps subject to it ought to be brought under his jurisdiction.

### 231

When the same most holy pope saw the destructive violence of the aforesaid king threatening in full force, he summoned to himself the venerable abbots of the holy monasteries of Vincentius and Benedictus and sent them in his place to the most cruel king. Through them he earnestly requested that the peace treaty be confirmed and that quiet be secured for the people of God on both sides.

The king received them but held them in utter contempt. He spurned their counsels

[Note: [Col. 1085] *Gifts.*]

and, to the detriment of his own soul, dismissed them in confusion and without accomplishing their mission to their monasteries, warning them not to approach the most holy pope.

When that chief Father heard this, he immediately—as he frequently used to do—commended and entrusted his own cause and that of the people committed to him to the almighty Lord our God, and made known to his divine Majesty this sorrowful lamentation.

### 232

While these things were taking place, John, the imperial *silentiarius*, arrived in Rome.

[Note: [Col. 1087] *He came.*] He brought to the same most holy pontiff a royal command, and at the same time carried another appended command addressed to the aforesaid impious king, ordering him to restore to their rightful lord the places of the commonwealth that he had seized through diabolical cunning.

The same most holy pope immediately sent this imperial envoy, together with his aforesaid brother, the most holy deacon Paul, to the wicked Aistulf at Ravenna. After receiving them, Aistulf dismissed them with an empty reply. He attached to the imperial envoy a certain impious man of his own nation, imbued with diabolical counsels, to proceed to the royal city.

[Note: [Col. 1087] *about to depart.*]

[Note: [Col. 1087] B: that is, joining him.]

When the envoys returned to Rome and were brought before the same most holy pope, they reported that they had accomplished nothing.

Then the aforesaid most holy man, having learned the evil king’s plan, sent his own envoys and apostolic messages to the royal city together with the aforementioned imperial envoy. He begged the imperial clemency that, in accordance with what he had often written to him, the emperor should come by every means with an army to protect these regions of Italy and free this Roman city and the entire province of Italy from the bites of the son of iniquity.

### 233

Meanwhile, persisting in his wickedness,

[Note: [Col. 1087] *In his evil conduct.*]

the aforesaid most savage king of the Lombards burst into violent fury and, roaring like a lion, did not cease directing deadly threats against the Romans. He asserted that all of them would be slaughtered by one sword unless, as stated above, they submitted themselves to his authority.

Again

[Note: [Col. 1087] *Rursumque* / *Rursusque*: “again.”]

the aforementioned most holy Father, having assembled the entire Roman community, admonished them with paternal affection, saying:

“Dearest sons, I beg you: because of the burden of our sins, let us implore the Lord’s mercy. He will be our helper, and in his most provident mercy he will free us from the hands of our persecutors.”

The entire people obeyed these saving admonitions. They assembled unanimously and, shedding tears, entreated our almighty Lord.

One day, as he was proceeding solemnly and anxiously in a litany procession with the most sacred image of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, called *antheropsita*,

[Note: [Col. 1087] Perhaps *acheropita*, “not made by human hands.”]

and receiving with it various other sacred objects,

[Note: [Col. 1087] *Sacred mysteries.*]

the same most holy pope himself carried the holy image on his shoulder together with the other priests. He and the entire populace proceeded barefoot to the church of the holy Mother of God, called the Praesepe. Ashes were placed upon the heads of all the people; they advanced with the loudest wailing,

[Note: [Col. 1087] B: *with lamentation.*]

beseeching our most merciful Lord. To the cross of our God he bound and attached the pact which the impious king of the Lombards had broken.

### 234

This most blessed pope diligently gathered all his priests and the clergy in the Lateran patriarchate. He admonished them to search the divine Scriptures with all their strength and devote themselves to spiritual reading, so that they might prove effective in every reply and argument against the adversaries of the Church of God.

Nor did he cease, by continually admonishing and correcting the entire people of God, urging them to act soberly and devoutly and to guard themselves from every depravity.

This blessed man decreed that, for the salvation of the province and of all Christians, a litany should be held every Saturday, with no neglect or postponement. One Saturday it was to be held at the holy Mother of God at the Praesepe, another at the blessed apostle Peter, and another at the blessed apostle Paul.

### 235

[Note: [Col. 1087] Baron, annals, year 753.]

This most blessed pope restored the basilica of Saint Lawrence, situated above Saint Clement’s in the third region, which had lain in ruins for a long time. He also restored the roof of the cemetery of Saint Soteris, which had collapsed.

Thus, while the same most holy man repeatedly entreated the aforesaid pestilential king of the Lombards, offering countless gifts, on behalf of the flocks entrusted to him by God and of the lost sheep

[Note: [Col. 1089] B: *citizens.*]

—that is, on behalf of the entire army of Ravenna

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Exarchate.*]

and all the people of this province of Italy, whom that impious king had deceived and possessed through diabolical fraud—and while he obtained nothing from him in this matter, especially when he saw that no assistance was forthcoming from imperial power,

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Moreover.*]

then, just as his predecessors, the pontiffs of blessed memory, Lord Gregory, another Gregory, and Lord Zachary, had sent to Charles, the most excellent king of the Franks, requesting aid because of the oppressions and invasions which they too had suffered in this Roman province at the hands of the wicked Lombard people, so now this venerable Father, inspired by divine grace, secretly sent his letters through a certain pilgrim to Pippin, king of the Franks. They were written with profound grief over this province.

### 236

He also then ceased sending to him, so that the Frankish king himself would send envoys here to Rome and thereby summon him to his presence.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *He still did not cease sending.*]

When this province and its cities were being gravely oppressed by the king of the Lombards, suddenly there arrived an envoy of the aforesaid king of the Franks, an abbot named Rodigangus,

[Note: [Col. 1089] B: Rodigandus.]

through whom he sent word that he would fulfill the entire will and request of the aforesaid most holy pope.

Afterward another envoy, a familiar associate of his, arrived, announcing the same things.

### 237

Since, as stated above, the ancient Roman city and all the camps were being harassed by the Lombards, and since he had also seized the fortress of Ciccanum, which belonged to the colonists of the holy Church of God, the aforesaid John, the imperial *silentiarius*, immediately arrived at the royal city with envoys of the same most holy pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *He came from the royal city.*]

He brought with him what the envoy of the wicked king of the Lombards had carried away, as well as an imperial command in which it was inserted

[Note: [Col. 1089] *it was.*]

that the most holy pope was to proceed to receive the city of Ravenna and the cities belonging to it.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *to it.*]

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Was to proceed to the king.*]

For this reason Pope Stephen immediately sent to that blasphemous king his own envoy, both for his own safety and for the safety of those who were to travel with him.

When John returned at once, the envoys of the aforesaid Pippin, king of the Franks, also arrived: namely, Bishop Rodigangus

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Rhotingandus.*]

and Duke Autcharius. Their purpose was to lead the aforementioned most holy pope—according to the request he had sent—to his king in Francia.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Into Francia.*]

They found the pope himself ready to proceed to the aforementioned king of the Lombards, in order to recover all the Lord’s lost folds.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *Sheep.*]

### 238

Then the same blessed pope, taking counsel, went out from this Roman city toward the blessed apostle Peter on the fourteenth day of October, in the seventh indiction.

[Note: [Col. 1089] *perceiving.*]

Many Romans and people from the other cities followed him, weeping and wailing, and they would scarcely allow him to walk at all. But that most holy man, trusting in God’s power and in the protection of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed chief apostles, steadfastly undertook the arduous journey for the salvation of all, though he was afflicted by bodily weakness. He commended and entrusted the entire Lord’s people to the good shepherd, our Lord, and to Peter, chief of the blessed apostles.

Taking with him from this holy Church certain priests, as well as leading men and others of the clerical order, and also some of the military nobility, he continued the journey he had begun, with Christ going before him. Along the route the Lord granted him great serenity of sky.

### 239

When he had reached approximately the fortieth mile within Lombard territory,

[Note: [Col. 1089] *When he had arrived at the Lombard frontier.*]

a great sign appeared in the sky during one night, like a globe of fire [Col. 1091] inclining toward the south, from the regions of Gaul toward the regions of the Lombards.

Accordingly, one of the Frankish envoys, namely Duke Autcharius, went ahead as quickly as possible to Pavia and waited for him there.

When the aforesaid most blessed pope had already approached the city of Pavia, the aforementioned most wicked king Aistulf sent his envoys to him, solemnly warning him not under any circumstances to dare say a word to him about requesting the city of Ravenna and the exarchate belonging to it, or about the remaining places of the commonwealth which he or his predecessors, the Lombard kings, had invaded.

But the pope sent him this reply: he asserted that he would not remain silent about making such a request out of fear of any kind.

[Note: [Col. 1091] *He would not remain silent about such a request through fear of anything.*]

### 240

When he arrived at the city of Pavia and was brought before the aforesaid wicked king, he presented him with many gifts. He earnestly entreated him, and with abundant tears begged him to return the Lord’s sheep whom he had taken away and to restore what belonged to each rightful owner.

But he was unable by any means to obtain this from him. The imperial envoy likewise made the request, presented him with imperial letters, and could obtain nothing.

The aforementioned Frankish envoys, however, pressed Aistulf vigorously to release the most holy pope so that he could proceed to Francia.

For this purpose, Aistulf summoned the aforementioned blessed man and asked whether it was his desire to go to Francia.

[Note: [Col. 1091] *to him.*]

[Note: [Col. 1091] *Whether he wished to go to Francia.*]

The pope did not conceal his answer but openly declared his wish. At this, like a lion, the king gnashed his teeth. He therefore secretly sent his attendants to him on various occasions, so that they might somehow divert him from such an intention.

### 241

On another occasion, in the presence of the most holy Bishop Rodigangus, the aforesaid king of the Lombards asked the same blessed pope whether he wished to travel to Francia,

[Note: [Col. 1091] *Whether he wished to go to Francia.*]

and addressed him as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1091] *He replied:*]

“If it is your will to release me, it is entirely my will to go.”

Then the king released him. Taking with him priests and clergy from this holy Church of God—namely, George, bishop of Ostia; Wilearius, bishop of Numentum;

[Note: [Col. 1091] *Villarius.*]

the presbyters Leo, Philip, George, and Stephen; the archdeacon Theophylact; the deacons Pardus and Gemmulus; Ambrosius the *primicerius*; Boniface the second; and the *regionarii* Leo and Christopher, together with others—he departed from the city of Pavia on the fifteenth day of November of the aforesaid seventh indiction and set out on his journey to Francia.

### 242

After his release, the Lombard king mentioned above still attempted to turn him aside from the journey. This did not escape the notice of the most holy man. Therefore, with God going before him, he reached the Alpine passes with great speed.

[Note: [Col. 1091] *He arrived.*]

[Note: [Col. 1091] B: *mountain passes, that is, the narrow defiles of the Alps.*]

When he entered them with those who were with him, he immediately rendered praises to almighty God.
