Continuing the journey he had begun, he reached the venerable monastery of Saint Maurice, martyr of Christ, where it had likewise been arranged that he should meet the king of the Franks. With the Lord’s consent, the same most blessed pontiff arrived there safely with all who were with him.

After they had stayed there for several days, Abbot Fulrad and Duke Rothardus,

[Note: [Col. 1091] Rothaldus.]

sent by the aforementioned most excellent Pippin, king of the Franks, arrived at the venerable monastery. They asked the most holy pontiff to proceed to their king.

They led him to the king with great honor, together with all who were with him.

### 243

When that king heard of the arrival of the same most blessed pontiff, he hurried greatly to meet him, together with his wife, his sons, and his leading men. He also sent his son, named Charles, with some of his nobles, nearly one hundred miles to meet the pope, who was like an angel.

[Note: [Col. 1091] *For this reason and at nearly one hundred.* B: “offering.”]

The king himself, at his palace in a place called Ponticone, descended from his horse at a distance of nearly three thousand paces [Col. 1093] and prostrated himself on the ground with great humility. Together with his wife, sons, and nobles, he received the same most holy pope.

He went before him for some distance, performing the service of a stirrup-holder (*vicestrator*).

Then the aforesaid beneficent man, together with all his companions, offered glory and unceasing praises to almighty God in a loud voice, with hymns and spiritual songs.

[Note: [Col. 1093] B: *in a lofty voice.*] All proceeded together with the king to the aforementioned palace on the sixth day of January, on the most sacred solemnity of the Epiphany of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

There, after they had sat together inside the oratory, the same most blessed pope immediately tearfully entreated the aforementioned most Christian king to settle the cause of blessed Peter and of the Roman commonwealth through a treaty of peace.

The king immediately satisfied the same most blessed pope by swearing to obey with all his strength all his commands and admonitions, and by promising, as the pope desired, to return by every means the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights or places of the commonwealth.

[Note: [Col. 1093] *Or the other places belonging to the commonwealth, by every means.*]

But since the winter season was at hand, he arranged for the same most holy pope and all his companions to go to Paris,

[Note: [Col. 1093] *Paris.*]

to reside there at the venerable monastery of Saint Denis during the winter.

[Note: [Col. 1093] *To winter there.*]

### 244

When this had been done and he had arrived at the same venerable monastery accompanied by the aforementioned most Christian Pippin,

[Note: [Col. 1093] *With him.*]

with the Lord’s consent,

[Note: [Col. 1093] See Baron, under the year 754.]

after several days the same most Christian King Pippin, together with his two sons, was anointed king of the Franks by the grace of Christ through the same most holy pope.

Afterward the most blessed pope became seriously ill from the excessive strain of the journey and the changeability of the weather, so that all his own people and all the Franks present there despaired of him.

[Note: [Col. 1093] *The Franks present there despaired of his life.*]

But the ineffable clemency of our Lord God, who does not abandon those who hope in him and desired to preserve the most Christian lord, intervened.

[Note: [Col. 1093] *wishing every human being to be saved, while him . . .*]

Although they had hoped to find him dead in the morning, he was suddenly found well on the following day.

King Pippin, released with the admonition, favor, and prayer of the venerable pontiff, proceeded to a place called Carisiac,

[Note: [Col. 1093] B: Parisiacus.]

where he assembled all the leading men of his royal power. Instructing them by the admonition of so great a Father, he resolved with them to complete what, with Christ’s favor, he had once decreed together with the same most blessed pope.

### 245

Meanwhile the most wicked Aistulf sent Carolomannus, the brother of the most benevolent King Pippin, from the monastery of Saint Benedict, where he had been living devotedly as a monk for a long period,

[Note: [Col. 1093] *To his brother Charlemagne.*]

persuading him through diabolical arguments to go to the province of Francia in order to oppose and resist the cause of the redemption of the holy Church of God and of the Roman commonwealth.

[Note: [Col. 1093] *To place him in the province of Francia so that he might obey him.*]

When he arrived there,

[Note: [Col. 1093] *When he had reached it.*]

he strove with all his might and fought even more fiercely to overturn the cause of the holy Church of God, in accordance with the purpose for which he had been sent by the aforementioned unspeakable tyrant Aistulf.

But by the Lord’s favor he was entirely unable to bend the firm heart of his brother, Pippin, the most Christian king of the Franks, in this matter. Rather, when that excellent King Pippin discovered the trickery of the most wicked Aistulf, he declared with all his strength that he would fight for the cause of the holy Church of God, just as he had previously promised the aforementioned most blessed pontiff.

### 246

Then, after taking counsel together, the same most holy pope and the aforementioned king of the Franks placed Carolomannus in a monastery there in Francia, in accordance with his having devoted himself to living a monastic life—
[Note: [Col. 1093] * They placed him at Vienne.] There, after a few days, he departed this life by divine calling in the year of the Lord 755. [Note: [Col. 1093] See Baronio, year 754.] Moreover, the most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks, as a faithful servant of blessed Peter and obeying the salutary admonitions [Note: [Col. 1093] * commands.] of the aforesaid most holy pontiff, sent his envoys [Col. 1095] to the most wicked Aistulf, king of the Lombards, concerning the terms of peace and the restoration of the rights of the holy Church of God and the Roman Republic. Twice, and then a third time, in accordance with the admonition of the aforesaid most blessed pope, he entreated him and promised him many gifts, asking only that he peacefully restore what belonged to each rightful owner. But that man, with sin pressing upon him, delayed obeying.

Thereupon that distinguished king of the Franks, seeing that in no way could he soften the stony heart of the most savage Aistulf, resolved to undertake a general expedition against him. When the wedges of the Frankish armies had already advanced through nearly half the journey, the same most holy man again entreated the aforesaid most kind king Pippin to send another embassy to the savage Aistulf, king of the Lombards, so that, if possible, he might at last, even belatedly, calm his ferocity and persuade him most beneficially to restore what belonged to its rightful owners without the shedding of human blood. And so it was done: once again that most kind king of the Franks sent his envoys to the same Aistulf.

247. But that most blessed pope, as a true father and good shepherd, lest Christian blood be shed, sent him letters of apostolic admonition and supplication. Through them he solemnly adjured and implored him, invoking with great force every divine mystery and the day of future judgment, to restore peacefully, without any shedding of blood, the rights belonging to the holy Church of God and the Roman Republic. But because of his iniquity he refused to yield. Instead, he sent threats and expressions of anger to the aforesaid pontiff, to the most excellent king Pippin, and to all the Franks.

Then, trusting [Note: [Col. 1095] relying.] in the mercy of almighty God, the aforesaid Pippin, king of the Franks, set out on his journey. He sent some of his nobles ahead of his own arrival, together with military men, to guard the Frankish passes [Note: [Col. 1095] B, closed places.]; and there they took up positions at a distance, awaiting the arrival of their own king.

That arrogant Aistulf, hearing that the Franks who had come to guard their passes were few, trusting in his own ferocity [Note: [Col. 1095] strength.], suddenly opened the passes and at dawn fell upon them with very numerous armies. But the just Judge, the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, granted victory to those very few Franks. They overcame and slaughtered that multitude of Lombards, so that Aistulf himself, seized by flight, could scarcely have escaped their hands had he not fled without arms as far as the city of Pavia, where, fearing the Franks, he withdrew with some of his men. The Franks, however, entering the passes, seized the entire Lombard encampment [Note: [Col. 1095] the encampment, that is, the camp.] after completing the slaughter, carrying away much booty.

248. The most Christian king of the Franks, Pippin, then arrived with the aforesaid most blessed pope as his companion, and together they reached the walls of the city of Pavia. The Frankish armies besieged it and pressed it vigorously for several days [Note: [Col. 1095] constricted it.].

Then that most blessed and co-angelic pope entreated the most kind king Pippin that this evil should not proceed any further [Note: [Col. 1095] come to pass.], and that Christian blood should not be shed. By salutary preaching he urged that the matter should be brought to an end peacefully.

The most Christian king Pippin, hearing and fulfilling the admonition of that same most blessed Father and good shepherd, entered into a peace pleasing to God. They confirmed in writing the treaty between the Romans, Franks, and Lombards, and the Frankish king took away the Lombard hostages. Aistulf himself, together with all his judges, promised under a terrible and most solemn oath, and confirmed in the written treaty, that he would immediately restore the city of Ravenna together with various other cities.

[Note: [Col. 1095] * The king Pippin, hearing that they longed for peace and were promising in a written treaty to honor their agreement, said to the supreme Pontiff: “Let it be according to your command, most blessed Father.”]

249. After peace had been made between the Romans, Franks, and Lombards, King Pippin returned to his own territory, taking the Lombard hostages with him. When they had separated from one another, that faithless man Aistulf, king of the Lombards, fell into the customary guilt of perjury and delayed restoring what he had promised under oath.

For while the aforesaid most holy pope was returning to Rome, after some time had passed that adversary and enemy of his own soul, Aistulf, filled with violent fury and with God opposed to him, not only failed to fulfill what he had promised, but also raised a general uprising with the entire Lombard people of his kingdom and came against this city of Rome. He besieged it for three months, surrounded it on every side, and attacked it vigorously each day. Everything outside the city he devastated with sword and fire, destroying and consuming it utterly.

That pestilential Aistulf pressed on all the more fiercely, hoping that he might capture this city of Rome. He even dug up many bodies of saints and carried away their sacred memorials [Note: [Col. 1097] * cemeteries.], to the great detriment of his soul.

250. When the aforesaid deeds of Aistulf had been performed impiously, they were reported as quickly as possible to the ears of the aforementioned king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1097] * were heard by his ears.]. The most blessed pontiff also arranged for his envoys to travel by sea and sent them to Francia, together with a certain religious man named Warnerius, who had been sent here to Rome by that same Frankish king.

Through his apostolic reports he informed the aforesaid most Christian Pippin, king of the Franks and worshiper of God, in detailed fashion [Note: [Col. 1097] * subtly, in his reports.], of everything that had happened and of all that that cruel tyrant Aistulf had perpetrated. He strongly and firmly adjured him, invoking the divine day of judgment, to fulfill everything that he had promised to blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 1097] * adjuring him on the day of divine judgment to fulfill everything that he had promised to blessed Peter.].

The most Christian king Pippin, moved by the fervor of faith, once again undertook a general expedition with God’s strength and entered Lombard territory [Note: [Col. 1097] came there.], utterly overthrowing their passes.

When the aforesaid most Christian king Pippin of the Franks was approaching the aforementioned Lombard passes, imperial envoys arrived in this city of Rome [Note: [Col. 1097] * came to this city]: namely, Gregory the protosecretary [Note: [Col. 1097] proto a secretis, “chief secretary”], and John the Silentiary, who had been sent to the aforementioned Frankish king.

The most blessed pope received them and informed them of the expedition of the aforesaid Frankish king. They were indeed doubtful that this could be believed. The envoy of the apostolic see, who accompanied them, dismissed them to go to Francia [Note: [Col. 1097] Dismissed them, that is, sent them away.]. Traveling by sea, they soon reached Marseilles. When they entered the city, they learned that the aforementioned Frankish king had already entered Lombard territory, in accordance with the exhortation of the aforesaid most blessed pope and the promise that he had offered to blessed Peter under oath.

When those imperial envoys learned this, they became sad and attempted by deceit [Note: [Col. 1097] * by trickery.] to detain the envoy of the apostolic see at Marseilles, so that he would not hurry to the aforementioned king, and they mistreated him severely [Note: [Col. 1097] * very severely.].

251. But, through the intervention of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, their cunning trickery was reduced to nothing. Accordingly, one of them—namely Gregory the protosecretary [Note: [Col. 1097] Proto a secretis, “chief secretary”]—went ahead of the envoy of the apostolic see and quickly caught up with the aforementioned king of the Franks. He found him in Lombard territory, not far from the city of Pavia.

Gregory repeatedly entreated him and promised that imperial gifts would be granted to him, so that he might grant the city of Ravenna, as well as the other cities and fortresses of that exarchate, to imperial authority. But he could in no way bend the resolute heart of the aforesaid most Christian and most kind faithful servant of God and lover of the apostle blessed Peter, namely the aforementioned Pippin, king of the Franks, so that he would assign those cities and places to imperial authority.

That worshiper of God, the most gentle king, asserted that under no circumstances could those cities be alienated in any way from the power of blessed Peter, the right of the Roman Church, or the pontiff of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1097] B, “allow.”]. He also affirmed under oath that he had entered the struggle so many times through no man’s favor, except for love of blessed Peter and the forgiveness of sins. He further declared that no abundance of treasure could persuade him to take away what he had once offered to blessed Peter.

Having given this answer to the imperial envoy, he immediately dismissed him to return to his own country by another route. The envoy reached Rome without accomplishing anything.

252. While the aforesaid most kind king Pippin of the Franks was besieging and pressing the city of Pavia, the most savage Lombard king Aistulf, in order that Pippin might grant him pardon and withdraw from the siege, professed in every way that he would restore the cities that he had previously refused to return, as they had been written into the treaty.

After confirming the earlier treaty, which had been made between the parties during the preceding eighth indiction [Note: [Col. 1099] B, “agreed upon.”], he restored the aforementioned cities, adding also the fortress called Comiaclum [Note: [Col. 1099] B, Comaclum.].

253. Concerning all these cities that had been received, he sent a written donation, to be possessed by blessed Peter, the holy Roman Church, and all the pontiffs of the apostolic see in perpetuity. It is preserved to this day in the archives of our holy Church.

To receive those cities, the most Christian king of the Franks sent his counselor, namely the venerable abbot and presbyter Fulrad. Immediately that distinguished king [Note: [Col. 1099] the king himself.] returned successfully to Francia with his armies.

The aforementioned venerable abbot and presbyter Fulrad, arriving in the territory of Ravenna with envoys of the aforesaid King Aistulf and entering each of the cities, both of the Pentapolis and of Emilia, received them and took hostages from each one [Note: [Col. 1099] * taking them from each city.]. He also brought with him the leading men, together with the keys of the city gates, and arrived at Rome.

254. He placed the keys both of the city of Ravenna and of the various cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, together with the above-mentioned donation issued by their king, at the confession of blessed Peter. He handed them over to that same apostle, to his most holy vicar the pope, and to all his successors, the pontiffs, to possess and administer perpetually.

These were: Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Cesena, Senigallia, Jesi, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, together with the fortress of Sussubium, Montefeltro, Acerragio, Monte Lucari, Serra, the fortress of Saint Marinus, Bobbio, Urbino, Cagli, Luculos, Gubbio, and Comacchio.

Also included was the city of Narni, which had been seized by the duke of Spoleto [Note: [Col. 1099] * by the duke of Spoleto.] from the Roman side over the course of many years.

While these things were being done, the unfortunate Aistulf went to a certain place for worship and was struck by a divine blow; he died. Then a certain Lombard duke named Desiderius, who had been sent by that same wicked Aistulf into the territory of Tuscany, heard that Aistulf had died. He immediately gathered the entire multitude of the armies of Tuscany and attempted to seize the throne of the Lombard kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1099] See Baronio, year of the Lord 756.]

Ratchis, the former king and afterward a monk, who was the brother of the aforementioned Aistulf, regarded him with contempt. Together with many other Lombard nobles, he rejected Desiderius. Gathering a great number of Transalpine troops and the remaining Lombard forces, they set out to fight against him.

255. At this point the aforesaid Desiderius earnestly entreated the most blessed pontiff to bring him aid, so that he might be able to assume the royal dignity. He promised under oath to fulfill the entire will of the aforesaid most blessed pontiff. Moreover, he professed that he would restore to the Roman Republic the cities that remained and would even give abundant gifts.

Then that eminent Father and good shepherd, after consulting with the often-mentioned venerable presbyter and abbot Fulrad, counselor of the most Christian king Pippin of the Franks, sent his own brother—namely Paul the deacon—and his counselor Christopher, together with the aforesaid Fulrad, into the territory of Tuscany to the aforementioned Desiderius.

Speaking with him, they immediately obtained from Desiderius, in a written document and under a terrible oath, his profession that he would fulfill the promise set out above.

After this had been accomplished, he at once sent his envoy, namely the venerable presbyter Stephen, with letters of apostolic exhortation to the aforesaid Ratchis and to the entire Lombard people. The aforesaid venerable Fulrad also hastened with some Franks to assist Desiderius, and he arranged for a larger number of Roman troops to come to his aid if necessity required it [Note: [Col. 1101] to come to his assistance.].

With the acceptable prayers of the aforesaid most holy pontiff supporting him, almighty God arranged matters so that, without any danger to souls, the aforesaid Desiderius, through the intervention of the aforementioned co-angelic pope, assumed the royal dignity that he desired. [Note: [Col. 1101] Ratchis, however, returned to the monastery.]

256. While these things were taking place, the most holy pontiff sent his envoy and took possession of the cities that the aforementioned King Desiderius had promised to restore to that most blessed pope: namely Faenza with the fortress of Tiberiacum [Note: [Col. 1101] B, Tiberianum.], as well as Gabellum [Note: [Col. 1101] * Caballum.] and the entire duchy of Ferrara.

With God’s approval he enlarged the Roman Republic. As a good shepherd, giving his life for the entire Christian people entrusted to him—namely, the rational sheep—he rescued everyone from the snares of their enemies. Completing his course and bringing all things to a useful conclusion, he ended his life by God’s calling and departed to eternal rest.

He carried out one ordination in the month of March: eleven priests, two deacons, and twenty bishops in various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for thirty-five days.

He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction. The episcopate remained vacant for thirty-two days.

## XCV. SAINT PAUL. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 757, THE SEVENTEENTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE COPRONYMUS.

From there, his blessedness transported her venerable and holy body, together with the marble sarcophagus in which it had been enclosed and on which the following words had been carved: ‘To Aurea Petronilla, his sweetest daughter.’ [Col. 1140A] It is therefore beyond doubt that the carving of those letters is recognized as having been made by the hand of blessed Peter the apostle himself, out of love for his beloved daughter. No. 257, line 1.—Paul. On 28 May 757, Paul, the brother of his predecessor Stephen, obtained the pontificate by the greater number of votes against Theophylact.

No. 258, line 14.—“Letters of admonition.” These letters, and Paul’s preceding letters to the emperor Constantine and King Pippin, are missing. The former letters are mentioned in Pope Hadrian’s letter to the emperors Constantine and Irene.

No. 260, line 13.—“Greek chant.” When the impious emperor Copronymus had issued an edict forbidding monks to remain in the East, a great multitude of Greek monks had gathered in Rome. Since they possessed the Greek language as their distinctive language, he wished those placed in the same monastery to perform the services that they had been accustomed to perform in their Eastern monasteries—namely, to render the singing of the psalms and the other ecclesiastical offices in their own language.]

[Note: [Col. 1141B]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Now that the exarchs had disappeared, and the Lombard kings not only had not succeeded to whatever rights had belonged to them, but had also been remarkably hard pressed by Pippin, king of the Franks, who was full of obedience and reverence toward the supreme pontiffs, there was no reason for the apostolic see again to remain vacant somewhat longer, or not immediately after the election to receive its newly consecrated pontiff.

But internal dissension, which we learn from Anastasius himself, was the cause of the longer interregnum. I gladly set it out here in his own words, both to confirm what I have taught elsewhere concerning enthronement preceding consecration and to make clear that in those times it was customary to consider the election of a successor only after the burial at Saint Peter’s. Pagius did not sufficiently notice this when he found an opportunity to place consecrations outside Sunday.

Anastasius, therefore, speaking [Col. 1141C] of the election and consecration of Saint Paul, who was the full brother of the recently deceased pontiff, reports the causes of the interregnum: namely, the dissension of the electors. The greater part of them adhered to Paul, who had never departed from the Lateran patriarchate, while the others adhered to the archdeacon Theophylact in his own house.

“After he had been buried there,” he says, “with great honor in the basilica of blessed Peter, immediately that same assembly of the people, which held with the aforesaid most blessed Paul, then a deacon, because it was stronger and more powerful, elected him to the summit of the pontificate. After this, those who had gathered with the aforesaid archdeacon dispersed. And thus, with God’s approval, that same most holy man was consecrated pontiff in the sacred apostolic see of blessed Peter.”

All these events took place after the death of Stephen, in the year 757. Concerning the duration of the interregnum, there are two opinions in the manuscripts and catalogues. Most authors report that the see was vacant for one month and five days, or twenty-five days, as do the catalogues of Lucca and Farfa, six Colbertine manuscripts—the fifth Colbertine manuscript, mistakenly, has twenty-two days—and two Freherian manuscripts, as well as the second Thuanean manuscript and two Ambrosian manuscripts, the first, very ancient manuscript, which ends here, and the fourth.

Others, however, count thirty-two days of interregnum, as do the commonly circulated text, the Regius, Mazarinus, first Thuanean, second and third Ambrosian, and Farnesian manuscripts, although none of the catalogues supports them.

In either case, we are led to the date of Saint Paul’s ordination, 29 May, which in the year 757 fell on a Sunday. The only difference between the two opinions is that the first—thirty-five days, namely, the opinion followed by the authors under Pagius—counts the interregnum from the day of the death of Stephen II, or III. The duration of his pontificate shows that this occurred on 24 April, and that date is included in the total. The second, thirty-two days, counts the interregnum, according to custom, from the day of his burial, excluding it from the total.

I therefore believe that these two learned opinions concerning the interregnum can be reconciled in this way, for the benefit of those who favor the first: the interval of two days between Stephen’s death and burial completes the gap.

Thus Saint Paul the Deacon, the brother of his predecessor, once the popular dissension had subsided, was consecrated on 29 May in the year 757 and began his pontificate. By the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts and catalogues, he reigned for ten years and one month—that is, until 28 June 767.

The author of the Life, whoever he was, does not mention the burial of this pontiff, but carefully recounts everything that concerns his piety, without any chronological indication. From another source, however, his year of death is certain. For the Annals of Bertin, speaking under the year 767 of Pippin returning from his expedition into Aquitaine, state: “And he returned to Bourges, and there he was informed of the death of Pope Paul.”

Indeed, Anastasius himself gives the actual day of his death in the Life of Stephen III, or IV, the consecrated successor, which can be inferred from the deposition of the usurper Constantine. I have discussed this sufficiently and more than sufficiently in the preceding note, where I also touched upon the days that elapsed between the overthrow of the usurper and Stephen’s ordination, days that Anastasius omitted.

Anastasius’s words are as follows: “On the twenty-eighth day of the month of July”—which fell on a Thursday—“in the sixth indiction”—the year 768—“in the evening, at the very twilight, on the eve of the vigil of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, they occupied the Salarian Bridge” (the Lombards, and so forth). “On the following day”—Friday—“crossing the Milvian Bridge, they came to Rome and did what I have related above: they cast out the usurper Constantine, a deserter, from the Lateran patriarchate and threw him into prison.”

Marianus Scotus in his Chronicle agrees with this remarkably, although Pagius vainly objects: “Constantine was deposed on Friday, in the month of July—not from the order of the pontificate, which happened later, but from the dignity that he had usurped.”

Therefore, if attention is paid to what Anastasius says concerning the interregnum after Saint Paul—“The episcopate remained vacant for one year and one month”—to which the second Freherian manuscript appropriately adds, “during which Constantine, the transgressor and invader of the apostolic see, existed,” and likewise to what the same Anastasius says in the Life of Stephen III, or IV, concerning Constantine—“He held the apostolic see under invasion for the space of one year and one month”—then there can be no doubt at all that Saint Paul died on 28 June 767.

For from that date until 29 July of the following year, 768, one year and one month are counted, just as the ten years and one month during which the holy pontiff governed the Church extend from 29 May 757 to the aforementioned day of his death.

These notes on the chronology of Saint Paul I, who closes this fourth volume, had not yet been sent to the press when the often-praised Father Joseph Blanchinus, ever vigilant in illuminating pontifical history, gave me an outstanding document excerpted from the manuscript of the celebrated capitular library of Verona. It splendidly confirms the death of that same Saint Paul and the deposition of the pseudo-pope Constantine and the election of Stephen III, or IV.

Since he does not permit anyone to be deprived of his proper praise, he testified to me that he had received it from the most learned archpresbyter and chancellor of the distinguished chapter of Verona, Bartholomew Campagnola. His remarkable expertise in reading and examining ancient manuscripts and charters for the public benefit is admired by excellent judges, V. C. Ludovicus Muratorius and Bishop Blanchinus. Blanchinus says that Campagnola, at the request of the illustrious and most learned Count Otholino Otholinio, copied that document with the greatest fidelity and gave it to him on 28 May of the current year, 1735.

The aforesaid document is the almost complete first session of the Roman council under Stephen III, or IV. From its third and fourth sessions Lucas Holstenius extracted a venerable fragment, and another is read in the *Spicilegium* of Acherius. From these sources the same material has been transferred into later collections of councils, whereas previously everyone had derived from Anastasius only a bare memory of this council.

From this newly discovered document there finally emerge the twelve [Col. 1143B] Frankish bishops whom Sirmondus did not reproduce in full from the Panvinian papers and who consequently deceived the Sammarthani, Antonius Pagius, and other writers, even the most vigilant. There are also all those bishops whom Anastasius says were assembled from Campania, Tuscany, and the province of Italy, forty in number. Ughellus and all who wrote before this day recognized scarcely three or four of them as having been mentioned elsewhere by Anastasius.

I would publish the whole document here, unless I intended to publish it more appropriately in the following volume, for the purpose of illuminating the Life of Stephen III, or IV. Meanwhile, so that learned men may not take this amiss, and so that the directors of the most select libraries of Europe—famous both by name and through their writings—may be encouraged to bring similar discoveries to light, I shall publish this outstanding document separately from Anastasius, together with several notes, for the greatest benefit of ecclesiastical history.]

[Note: [Col. 1143C]

No. 257, line 1.—Paul. Son of Constantine, a Roman, full brother of Pope Stephen the Younger, made cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Zacharias. Under the emperors Constantine and Leo Augustus, he was elected and consecrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 757, in the Lateran patriarchate. He learned conduct and ecclesiastical doctrine under the pontiffs Gregory III and Zacharias, by whom he was admitted, together with his brother, to the order of deacons.

After his brother’s death, however, Paul was substituted in his deceased brother’s place because of the integrity of his life and his learning. There was no precedent for the succession of two brothers in the supreme priesthood, nor was such a thing ever seen afterward.]

[Note: [Col. 1143C]

No. 257, line 17.—“They elected him to the summit of the pontificate.” When Paul was made pontiff, he sent a letter to Pippin, king of the Franks, informing him of the death of his brother Stephen and of his own election. He also indicated that he would continue the friendship with the Franks that Stephen had begun, asking Pippin to do the same.

These were the first letters sent by Paul, since they were written before his ordination. Their heading is as follows: “To the most excellent lord, his son Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, Paul the Deacon, and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see.”

This letter is correctly placed first in order in Labbe’s collection of councils; in the Carolingian Codex it is number 13.

Here there is an opportunity to inform the reader about the author of the Carolingian Codex. In 1613 Jacob Gretzer published at Ingolstadt the letters that the Roman pontiffs Gregory III, Zacharias, Stephen II, Paul, Stephen III, Hadrian, and the pseudo-pope Constantine sent to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, to Pippin, to Charlemagne, and to his brother Carloman.

These letters had once been collected into a single volume through the study and care of Charlemagne himself, and they number ninety-nine in all. In the year 791 Charlemagne had them recopied, because they had already become partly worn out through excessive age. This is clear from an ancient inscription written in capital letters, which was prefixed to the collection by the very man who, at his command, copied them into a single body.

This collection is called the Carolingian Codex after its author, Charles the Great. Lambecius, in Book II of the *Imperial Library*, chapter 5, testifies that it was extracted from an ancient manuscript of that same library. He adds, however, that the person who copied the Codex and sent it to Gretzerus arrogated to himself excessive freedom in correcting and changing certain passages. It would therefore be worthwhile to collate that first edition in its entirety with the cited authentic exemplar.

Finally, all those letters precede the year 791, since their collection was made in that year. They are also found in Duchesne, volume III.]

Num. 261, line 12.—“Here, while he was in the church of Saint Paul.”

In the same year, 767, Pope Paul, while staying during the summer in the church of the blessed apostle Paul because of the oppressive heat, was seized by bodily illness and summoned to heaven, there to receive from God the reward of his labors. He died on the twenty-eighth day of June, after having occupied the see for ten years and one month, as Anastasius writes—as also Martinus Polonus and Luitprand do. Because of the honor that he had constantly and devotedly shown to the apostle Paul, he wished to be the first to be buried in that same basilica of Saint Paul. After several months had passed, however, he was transferred to the Vatican and buried in the oratory that he himself had built near the high altar. His name was entered by Baronius in the Roman Martyrology under 28 June, the day on which he completed his mortal life; previously, however, his name had been recorded under 27 January by Peter de Natalibus, *Book* III, chapter 30, by the Carthusians of Cologne in the *Additions to Usuard*, and by Canisius, Maurolycus, Felicius, and Galesinius.

[Note: Col. 1144C]

Num. 258, line 5.—“Cells of the poor and sick.”

A *cella* is a dwelling or little house of poorer people. Martial, *Book* III, epigram 30:

> “Whence have you your little toga and the rent of your dark cell?”

A prostitute’s *cella*, that is, the brothel where she stands for sale. Petronius, in the *Satyricon*:

> “By now the prostitute had demanded an as for the cell.”

Cells for slaves. Columella, *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 6:

> “For the slaves, cells facing the equinoctial midday should be made, as the best provision for their health.”

[Note: Col. 1144C]

Num. 258, line 13.—“Therefore he sent his messengers more than once to the aforesaid emperors Constantine and Leo with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition.”

The most holy pontiff Paul labored greatly over the extremely serious matter of the veneration of the sacred images against which the Constantinopolitan emperors Constantine Copronymus and his son Leo had declared a wicked war. In order to recall those impious emperors from their perverse opinion, he repeatedly sent messengers to them and composed several letters filled alike with entreaties and admonitions. The passage of time, the negligence of men, and their carelessness have deprived us of copies of those letters. Besides Anastasius, Pope Adrian mentions them in the second session of the Second Council of Nicaea.

Our Librarian, however, says not a word about the letters that Paul sent into Gaul to King Pippin. To construct the history of this pontiff, he ought apparently at least to have indicated them, if he did not wish to quote them—especially since Paul was no less concerned to defend ecclesiastical doctrine against the heresy of the Iconoclasts than to protect the possessions and provinces of the Apostolic See, namely the Pentapolis and the Exarchate of Ravenna, which had recently been added to the rights of that see by King Pippin’s donation, from the injuries and plots of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and from the threatened attacks of Constantine and Leo.

These letters survive in the *Codex Carolinus*, thirty-one in number.

If anyone, relying on Anastasius’s silence, were to deny that these letters belonged to Paul, he would reveal his own disgraceful error and ignorance. The letters indisputably exist, each bearing Paul’s name, in authentic codices: in the Imperial Library, from which Gretser copied them, and in the Vatican Library, from which Onuphrius Panvinius extracted the arguments of the individual letters, which Baronius quotes in order under the year of Christ 767. The order arranged according to the proper sequence of years differs from that which the letters have in the *Codex Carolinus*.

How poorly, then, Natalis Alexander argues from the similar silence of Anastasius in the *Life of Pope Zacharias* that the deposition of Childeric and the elevation of Pippin to the kingship of the Franks were falsely attributed to the authority of Zacharias! By the same reasoning, from Anastasius’s silence he could have declared incredible and wholly untrustworthy the letters of Paul to Pippin, although their existence is otherwise undeniable. From this the prudent reader may judge Natalis’s disposition, his zeal for the Holy See, and also the force of a negative argument in cases of this kind.

[Note: Col. 1145B]

Num. 158, line 13.—“He sent his messengers more than once with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition, etc.”

The letters that the holy pontiff wrote to the emperor on this matter, expressly mentioned by Pope Adrian I in his letter to Constantine and his mother Irene, the Augusti, have certainly not survived. The letters that he wrote on the same occasion to King Pippin are likewise missing. In them he asked Pippin to use his authority to intercede with the Iconoclast emperor and turn him away from persecuting the Church. This much is clear from Paul’s seventh letter to Pippin: he knew very well that the persecution of the Greek emperor and his unjust plans against the Apostolic See arose from the fact that the pontiff defended the orthodox faith and the venerable tradition of antiquity, which that impious man was attempting to destroy:

> “For, as Your Excellence has been most fully informed, those most wicked Greeks persecute us for no other reason than the holy and orthodox faith and the pious and venerable tradition of the Fathers, which they desire to destroy and trample underfoot.”  
> (*Paul, Letter 7 to King Pippin*, *Codex Carolinus* 34.)

Constantine had adopted the following plan against the Apostolic See: he wanted the Exarchate of Ravenna returned to his possession. Pippin, after conquering the Lombards, had lawfully brought it under his own power and had granted it to the Roman pontiff to possess with full authority and useful dominion.

The emperor understood perfectly well that he could never attain his desired end so long as the Franks supplied the pontiff with resources and assistance, and unless he drew the Lombard king to his side by enticing him with the prospect of gain. To accomplish both objectives, he left nothing unattempted. For this reason he sent envoys into Francia who, moving every stone in order to damage the pontiff’s reputation, sought to withdraw King Pippin from the alliance he had made with him.

At the same time he maintained agents in Ravenna and throughout the Exarchate who stirred up the peoples to revolt against the pontiff. He also ordered that the marriage of his son Leo, whom he had taken as a partner in the empire, to Pippin’s daughter Giselide be proposed. And lest the difference in religion—which, as he claimed, the pontiff was putting forward as a reason for defection—prove an obstacle, he requested that a religious conference be held in Francia. At it his envoys, whom he intended to send for that purpose, were to present the case for the orthodoxy that he wished to be observed throughout the empire.

Nevertheless, neither the conference held near Paris nor all the schemes that Copronymus devised and employed against Pippin accomplished anything toward detaching that excellent prince from the Catholic faith and the defense of the Holy See. (*Paul, Letters 20 and following to Pippin*, in the *Codex Carolinus*; Ado, *Chronicle*; Einhard, under the year 767.)

Therefore Constantine turned elsewhere and lent his ears to the king of the Lombards, who promised to join him in a treaty against the pope. The agreement was concluded on these conditions: they would fight with united forces so as to bring Ravenna and Hydruntum under their own dominion; the Lombards would possess the former, while the Greeks would possess the latter together with the neighboring region; and the emperor would immediately send a very powerful fleet to Italy for this purpose.

Copronymus did not, however, carry this out. He persuaded himself that the troops he had in Sicily and the neighboring regions would be sufficient to recover Ravenna without Lombard assistance. At that time King Pippin was unable to help the pontiff, since he was occupied in war with the dukes subject to him in Bavaria and Aquitaine.

But the pontiff, having timely discovered Constantine’s plans, immediately disclosed them to King Pippin, so that Pippin might compel the Lombard king himself, together with the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, to protect the Holy See, along with the other neighboring peoples, should the Greeks happen to take up arms against it:

> “Deign at once to send your messenger to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, so that, if necessity is announced, he may grant us assistance against the incursion of those same enemies. Commanding the Beneventans and Spoletans, or the Tuscans who dwell near us, that they themselves come to our aid.”  
> (*Paul, Letter 7 to King Pippin*, *Codex Carolinus* 34.)

When the emperor learned this, he attempted none of the things he had planned. The king of the Lombards, however, continually harassed Paul throughout his pontificate. First, he refused to return to the Holy See the cities of Bologna, Imola, Ancona, and others, which he had promised to restore in order to obtain its support against Ratchis, who was contesting the Lombard kingdom with him. Then he brought war into the Pentapolis and devastated it. Finally, he expelled the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento, who depended upon the Holy See, and installed others who were subject to himself.

When the pontiff justly complained of these actions, Desiderius prolonged the discussion with words, promising that he would fully carry out the treaty concluded at Pavia between Stephen and Aistulf, provided that Pippin arranged for the hostages whom he had taken into Francia to be returned to him.

Paul, however, seeing that Desiderius believed he was mocking him, outwitted him in turn. Under the pretext of sending envoys to demand the hostages, he ordered those same envoys to expose the Lombards’ treachery to the king and to implore his assistance. Among all princes, Pippin alone was able to recall the treaty-breaking Lombard to his duty and support the subjects of the Church:

> “It is evident that, above all kings and powerful men, you abound in pious works … Therefore, so that the struggle of your pious activity may be brought to fulfillment, it is fitting that we frequently send apostolic letters to you, as the liberator of this holy Church of God and of its special people.”  
> (*Paul, Letter 2 to Pippin*, *Codex Carolinus* 15.)

For this reason Pippin became ever more devoted to the Holy See and sent two of the principal commanders of his court to Desiderius. They informed him that the king himself would come into Italy with a powerful army unless he satisfied the pontiff.

Terrified by this unexpected development, the Lombard returned to Paul part of what he had retained from the rights of the pontiff, and promised that he would restore everything else that remained in his possession:

> “When Remedius, your Germanus, and Autcharius, the most glorious duke, had joined us, he established between them and Desiderius, king of the Lombards, that throughout the coming month of April he would restore to us in full all the rights of your patron, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—namely, all the patrimonies, rights and places, boundaries and territories of our various cities, belonging to the Roman republic. Accordingly, the same king of the Lombards is known to have restored some of these rights to us; and he professes and absolutely promises that he will restore all the remaining rights to us.”  
> (*The same author, Letter 3 to Pippin*, *Codex Carolinus* 17 and 19.)

[Col. 1147A] Desiderius, however, did not keep his promises. Secretly, as we have said, he negotiated with the emperor so that, having entered into an alliance with him, he might bring arms against the pontiff’s rights. Although his schemes came to nothing, instead of restoring to Saint Peter and his successor the cities and territories that he had seized without any right—as he had promised King Pippin whenever Pippin pressed him to do so—he was planning new invasions.

Therefore he remained a source of trouble to the holy pontiff for as long as he lived, as his final letter openly makes clear:

> “Let Your most excellent Christian character know for certain that, unless the boundaries of our cities that were invaded by those same Lombards and our patrimonies are restored to us, they will plot to invade even those things which they first restored.”  
> (*The same author, Letters 17 and 19*, *Codex Carolinus*.)

[Note: Col. 1147A]

Num. 260, line 13.—“Of Greek chant.”

Pope Paul had received fugitive monks who had fled from all Greece because of the persecution of Constantine Copronymus, and he built for them the monastery of Saint Stephen in Rome as a dwelling.

Theophanes speaks in the following manner of the persecution especially stirred up by Copronymus against the monks, p. 373:

> “He also declared that monasteries—the sacred buildings constructed for the glory of God and as refuges for those seeking salvation—should become common and profane houses for soldiers infected with the perversity of his opinion. He assigned the monastery of the Dalmatians, the most renowned coenobium in Byzantium, as lodging for soldiers. He also overturned from their foundations other sacred buildings, such as those celebrated under the names of Callistratus, Dius, and Maximinus, as well as other religious houses of monks and residences of virgins. Whenever he discovered that men distinguished either by military skill or by rank, previously especially necessary to him and familiar with his secret lusts and disgraceful acts, were devoted to the monastic life, he condemned them to certain death, supposing that their confessions would bring shame upon him.”

The monk Saint Stephen the Younger was responsible for their migration to the West, as we read in his *Life*, volume I of Loppin’s *Greek Analecta*, p. 456:

> “Since, as he said to the monks, three portions of those among us who do not share communion with this wicked heresy remain, I advise you to hasten into those regions. For there is no other place subject to the Dragon that does not follow his empty talk.”

That monks came to Rome among other places is likewise reported by the deacon Stephen in the same *Life*:

> “Then one could see Byzantium deprived of its monastic order and Nazarene habit, as though it had been led away into captivity. One man was making for the Euxine Pontus; another for Cyprus; another was preparing to depart for Rome.”

For the rest, if you wish, consult Theophanes.

[Note: Col. 1147C]

Num. 260, line 1.—“This most holy prelate built a monastery in his own house.”

Concerning the church and monastery founded by Paul I, there is preserved in Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 761, a *Constitutum*, or privilege, issued by that same pontiff in the Roman synod. It clearly confirms what Anastasius relates here.

After Paul had spoken in that *Constitutum* about several cemeteries of holy martyrs, some collapsed through age and others destroyed by the sacrilegious violence of the Lombards, he adds the following:

> “Therefore, seeing the same holy places neglected through sloth, and greatly lamenting this, worn down by the deepest sorrow, I judged it appropriate, with God’s assent, to remove those holy martyrs, confessors of Christ, and virgins from those ruined places. We brought them into this Roman city with hymns and spiritual songs, and built a church anew from its foundations in their honor—inside the walls, in the house that came to me by hereditary succession, in which I am known to have been born and raised. There I placed and buried their most holy bodies.
>
> “In that place I established a congregation of monks under a special rule, in honor and in the name of the blessed Pope and martyr Stephen and the blessed Pope and confessor of Christ Sylvester, whose venerable bodies rest there. I determined that the monastery should belong to male monks; namely, I decreed that psalmody should be performed there perpetually.”

Since Anastasius states that this perpetual psalmody was in the Greek manner, it may easily be inferred that Paul entrusted this monastery to Greek monks who, driven from their homes by the persecution of the Iconoclasts raging in the Eastern Empire, came to the City.

For the impious emperor Copronymus, burning with the greatest hatred against monks, whom he recognized as vigorous opponents of his heresy and powerful defenders of the sacred images, issued an edict around this time forbidding monks to live within his dominion and threatening every kind of punishment.

Thus, as they migrated in different directions, all who came to Rome were kindly received by Pope Paul and given this most fully equipped monastery, where they could perform the Church’s offices according to their rite and honor appropriately the remains of Christ’s martyrs and confessors resting there.

The magnificence of this monastery’s foundation can be understood not only from what our author reports about it but also from the words of Paul’s own *Constitutum*, issued, as I said above, in the presence of the priesthood and confirmed by the council:

> “And behold,” Paul says, “with the Lord’s mercy, we have founded this monastery in their honor and have enriched it most generously with various estates and goods, urban and rural properties, and all necessary equipment. We have granted everything sufficient for the arrangement of the lights, the diligent offering of sacrifices, and the uses of the monks residing there: namely, estates, farms, farmsteads, tenant holdings, vineyards, gardens, olive groves, houses, guesthouses, saltworks, watermills, fisheries, and the remaining landed properties situated in different places and cities, together with the property of the servants who minister there.
>
> “We have also added and confirmed under the authority and jurisdiction of our monastery certain monasteries and venerable places with all their possessions and with everything generally and wholly belonging to them.”

Nor can Paul’s *Constitutum* be condemned as suspect of falsity merely because the chronological notations do not fit the copy published by Baronius under the year mentioned. At its end the following subscription appears:

> “Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, while our lord Constantine Augustus, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the forty-first year since he began to reign with his father, and in the twenty-first year after his consulship, in the fourteenth indiction.”

Since Constantine Copronymus was declared his father’s partner in the empire on the last day of March in the year 720, and on the eighteenth day of June in the year 741, assuming the consulship according to custom, succeeded his father Leo and his impiety, his forty-first year of empire cannot coincide with the twentieth year of his consulship. For the consulship exceeds the imperial reign by one year.

Paul’s *Constitutum*, however, which Baronius calls a worthy monument of the holy pontiff, should not for that reason be accused of being forged:

1. Because the chronological notation recorded incorrectly in Baronius’s copy may perhaps agree correctly with the original preserved in Rome by the nuns of Saint Sylvester, who had replaced the monks because of the changing circumstances of the times. I was not permitted to see it, especially since the diploma of Paul printed in type contains a slight error, easily introduced by the hands of copyists.

2. Because the sequence of the *Constitutum* agrees both with our historical author and with the account attached to the letter in which Stephen III wrote about the recovery of his health, granted him by God through the blessed martyr Dionysius. There the monastery is called that of the Holy Martyrs in the School of the Greeks and is said to have been nobly built by Paul, his brother. It is preserved among Hilduin’s *Areopagitica* in volume V of Surius.

3. Finally, because many ancient diplomas, which everyone accepts with unwavering confidence, would have to be rejected, since scribes have very often erred in copying chronological notations, as scholars acknowledge.

[Col. 1149] In the Roman-Vatican edition the notes of the various commentators end here.

[Col. 1135]

> [Col. 1135]

### 257

Paul, a Roman by nation, the son of Constantine, occupied the see for ten years and one month. From early childhood he was entrusted, together with his own elder brother Stephen, his predecessor as pontiff, to the Lateran patriarchate for instruction in ecclesiastical discipline, during the time of Lord Gregory II, the younger pontiff. Later he was consecrated by Lord Zacharias, the most blessed pope, in the order of the diaconate, together with the brother mentioned above.

When that same brother and predecessor of his, the pontiff, was approaching the end of his life, the people of this Roman city were immediately divided with him. Some, supporting Theophylact the archdeacon, gathered and remained in his house. Others sided with that same blessed Paul the Deacon; a very large part of the judges and people supported him, as did those supporting the aforementioned Theophylact the archdeacon.

The most holy man himself did not withdraw at all from the Lateran patriarchate, but continued steadfastly, with the other faithful, to serve his sick brother and predecessor, the pontiff.

When the brother and predecessor mentioned above had departed this life and had been buried with great honor in the basilica of the blessed Peter, the same assembly of the people that had supported the aforementioned Paul, then still a deacon, immediately elected him to the summit of the pontificate, because it was stronger and more powerful. After this, those who had gathered around the aforementioned archdeacon were dispersed.

Thus, with God’s assent, that same most holy man was consecrated pontiff in the sacred Apostolic See of the blessed Peter.

### 258

He lived during the reigns of the emperors Constantine and Leo. He was gentle and exceedingly merciful, never returning evil for evil to anyone. If he heard anyone nearby suffering harassment at the hands of wicked agents over a small matter, nevertheless, moved by compassion, he brought him the mercy of consolation. [Note: Col. 1137: B reads “he heard [them] afflicted” (*tribulatuos audiebat*).]

As many have testified, at night he himself went around among the cells of poor and sick people lying there, who could not rise at all from their own beds, and among other needy persons, together with his attendants, moving through the silence of the night. He supplied them most generously with food and brought them help and support.

He also visited the prisons and other places of confinement during the same secret hours of the night. If he found anyone shut up there, he bought him back from the danger of death and released him to go free.

He also freed many who, bound by debts and afflicted, were being oppressed by their creditors, redeeming them from the yoke of servitude by paying the debt itself. He brought aid to widows, orphans, and all the needy. He was, moreover, a most courageous defender of the orthodox faith.

Therefore he repeatedly sent his messengers to the aforesaid Augusti, Constantine and Leo, with apostolic letters of entreaty and admonition, seeking the restoration and confirmation to their former state of veneration of the most sacred images of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy Mother, and of all the blessed apostles, prophets, martyrs, and confessors.

### 259

This most blessed pontiff also devoted himself continually, with all his spiritual zeal, to the holy cemeteries. Seeing that many sites of those holy cemeteries had been neglected, that the ancient remains had suffered extensive demolition, and that they were already close to ruin, he immediately removed the bodies of the saints from those ruined cemeteries.

Bringing them into this Roman city with hymns and spiritual songs, he took care that some of them should be reburied with fitting honor in the titular churches, the deaconries, the monasteries, and the other churches.

### 260

This most holy prelate built from the foundations, in his own house, a monastery in honor of Saint Stephen, martyr and pontiff, and of the blessed Sylvester, likewise pontiff and confessor of Christ. There he also built an oratory in the upper part of the same monastery and buried their bodies with great veneration.

Within the enclosure of the monastery he newly built from the foundations a church of marvelous beauty. He adorned it with mosaic and marble, lavishly supplied its decoration with gold, silver, and various precious materials, and also made there a silver ciborium, of an unspecified number of pounds [amount omitted in the source]. In it he buried, with the greatest reverence, the innumerable bodies of saints that he had removed from the aforementioned demolished cemeteries.

In that same monastery he bestowed many estates, possessions, and urban and rural properties, enriching it excessively and abundantly with gold, silver, other valuable goods, and every necessity. There he established a congregation of monks and decreed that it should be a coenobium of psalmody in the Greek manner. He ordained that praises should be offered there assiduously and without interruption to our almighty God and to all the saints resting there, under severe prohibitions.

### 261

He newly built a church within this Roman city, on the Via Sacra, beside the Temple of Romulus, in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. At that place the two most blessed princes of the apostles, at the time when they were crowned with martyrdom for Christ’s name, were seen to bend their knees while offering prayers to our Redeemer.

At that place, even to the present day, their knees are known to be marked, as a testimony for every generation that will come at the end, in a certain very hard rock.

He also newly built, outside the walls of this Roman city, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, an oratory in honor of the holy Mother of God, beside the oratory of Pope Leo and near the entrance doors of Saint Petronilla and the blessed apostle Andrew. He adorned it with mosaic and various metals. [Note: Col. 1137: *oraculum*, that is, “oratory.”]

There he installed an image of the holy Mother of God in a statue of gilded silver weighing one hundred pounds. In that oratory he also built a burial place for himself.

Here, while staying in the church of the blessed apostle Paul during the summer because of the intense heat, he was overtaken by bodily illness and ended his life there, where he was also buried.

His unburied corpse remained there for almost three months. [Note: Col. 1139: variant reading, “buried” (*humatum*).] Afterwards all the Roman citizens and the other peoples gathered, transported his body by boat across the river Tiber, and carried it to Saint Peter with the honor of psalmody. They buried him in the oratory that he had built as mentioned above.

He held one ordination in the month of December: twelve priests, two deacons, and three bishops in various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for one year and one month.
