### 262

Stephen III, a Sicilian by nation, son of Olivus, sat for three years, five months, and twenty-eight days. He was a vigorous man, learned in the divine Scriptures, imbued with ecclesiastical traditions, and a most steadfast perseverer in their observances. When he had come from the island of Sicily to this Roman city, Lord Gregory, pope III of holy memory, entrusted him to the monastery of Saint Chrysogonus, which he was then newly founding; there he was made both cleric and monk. Later, Lord Pope Zacharias removed him from that monastery and ordered him to serve in the chamber of the Lateran patriarchate.

[Note: [Column 1149] B reads *auferens*, “removing”; B also reads *suo praeferens*, “setting him over his own.”]

Afterward he consecrated him priest in the title of the church of Saint Cecilia. Nevertheless, because of his modest chastity, he retained him in his office at the Lateran. The other pontiffs also—namely, Lord Stephen and Paul, most blessed pontiffs—likewise retained this most holy Stephen in their service because of his pious conduct.

### 263

While his predecessor, Lord Pope Paul, was staying at the church of Saint Paul during the summer season because of the severity of the heat, and was there overtaken by a severe illness from which he also died, this same most blessed Stephen continued day and night in the service of that pontiff, his predecessor, and in no way withdrew from his bedside until he gave up the spirit.

But while Pope Paul lay ill and had not yet breathed out his spirit, a certain duke named Toto, formerly an inhabitant of the city of Nepi, immediately gathered with his brothers Constantine, Passivus, and Paschal a multitude of troops and a crowd of country people, both from Nepi itself and from other cities of Tuscia. Entering this Roman city through the gate of Saint Pancratius and standing armed in the house of the aforementioned Toto, they suddenly elected there Constantine, the brother of that Toto, who was a layman. Many of them, wearing breastplates and acting as brigands, brought him armed into the Lateran patriarchate.

### 264

When they had ascended with him into the *vicedominium*, they immediately summoned Bishop Georgius.

[Note: [Column 1149] B reads “Gregory.”]

They compelled him to confer upon that Constantine the clerical prayer. He absolutely refused to do this; falling prostrate on the ground at Constantine’s feet, he earnestly adjured him by every divine mystery to yield and withdraw from that purpose of impious presumption, lest through him such an unheard-of novelty should arise in the Church of God.

While he was uttering these words of adjuration, many of those wicked men who had made the same impious election became enraged, rose up against him, and threatened him severely. Seized by fear, he gave him the clerical prayer, and thus made a cleric, Constantine invaded the Lateran patriarchate.

When the next day dawned, Monday, he was consecrated subdeacon and deacon by the same bishop in the oratory of Saint Lawrence within that patriarchate, contrary to the ordinances of the holy canons.

### 265

Thus he compelled the entire people to give him the sacrament. When Sunday arrived, he hurried again with a multitude of armed troops to the basilica of Saint Peter, where he was consecrated pontiff by the same Georgius, bishop of Palestrina, and by two other bishops: Eustratius of Albano and Citonatus of Portus.

[Note: [Column 1149] *Citomalo*.]

He held the apostolic see, which he had invaded, for a year and one month.

[Note: [Column 1149] Baron, *Annals*, 768.]

When Christopher, the *primicerius* and counselor, saw this, he and his son Sergius, then serving as *sacellarius*, preferred to die rather than behold such an impious novelty and wicked presumption perpetrated in the apostolic see. Continuing daily in weeping and tears, they pretended that they wished to become monks and asked Constantine to release them, saying that they intended to go to the monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and there assume the monastic habit. After Christopher the *primicerius* had received their oath, Constantine believed them and released them.

[Note: [Column 1149] *absolvit*, “he released”; that is, “he dismissed them.”]

### 266

As they hastened onward and reached the borders of the Lombards, the abbot of the aforementioned monastery wished to bring them into that monastery. But Christopher the *primicerius* and his son Sergius, formerly *sacellarius* and afterward *secundicerius*, turned aside from the road and earnestly adjured Theodicius, duke of Spoleto, to take them across the Po to Desiderius, their king of the Lombards, since they were striving thereby to accomplish the liberation of the holy Church of God.

[Column 1151]

The duke of Spoleto brought them to his king. When they had been presented before him, they earnestly begged the king to grant his assistance so that this error of novelty might be cut away from the Church of God. While the aforementioned Christopher the *primicerius* and his son Sergius were staying with that king, the aforesaid Constantine, invader of the apostolic see, carried out ordinations of priests and deacons—eight priests and four deacons—and within the course of that same year and one month he also made eight bishops in various places.

### 267

[Note: [Column 1151] Baron, *Annals*, 767.]

The aforementioned Georgius of Palestrina, who had consecrated him deacon and pontiff, was overtaken not many days after Constantine’s consecration by a severe and very grievous illness. He became immobile and afterward could no longer celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass. His right hand withered and became contracted. He was unable even to bring it to his mouth, and thus, trembling and languishing, he ended his life.

While these things were happening, the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius, released by the king of the Lombards, reached the city of Reate. Sergius and the priest Waldipertus went ahead with the people of Reate and Forcona and with other Lombards of the duchy of Spoleto. They suddenly and unexpectedly reached this Roman city on the twenty-eighth day of July, in the sixth indiction, at evening, in the very twilight of night, on the vigil of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, and seized the Salarian Bridge.

### 268

On the following day they crossed the Milvian Bridge and came to the gate of Saint Peter; then, proceeding onward, they approached the gate of Saint Pancratius. Certain relatives of the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius were watching and guarding that gate. When they saw that Sergius himself had approached it, they signaled to him and immediately opened the gate.

Thus Sergius and Waldipertus, together with the Lombards, entered the Roman city. They climbed along the city walls carrying a small banner, fearing the Roman people. The Lombards did not dare descend from the little platform at all, but remained there in great trembling.

### 269

When Toto and his brother Passivus heard this, not knowing the plan and deception that the traitors had devised against him, they ran with some men to the aforesaid gate. Demetrius the *secundicerius*, or Gratiosus, then a *chartularius* and afterward duke, also hastened with them; these men too had been involved in the plot with the aforementioned most wicked traitors.

As they approached those Lombards, one of them, named Racipertus, who appeared more warlike than all the others, met Duke Toto and attacked him. Toto rushed upon him, struck him violently, and killed him. When the Lombards saw this, they turned to flight and tried to escape. But Demetrius the *secundicerius* and Gratiosus, standing behind the aforementioned Toto, struck him in the back with spears; thus they prevailed against him and killed him.

Passivus, however, fled into the Lateran patriarchate and announced to his brother Constantine what had happened.

### 270

When Constantine heard this, he fled with the aforementioned Passivus, Bishop Theodorus, and his *vicedominus* into the basilica of the Savior. They descended to the fountain and entered the church of Saint Venantius, where they remained for a short time. Then, considering that they could be better saved, they went up into the wardrobe. Entering within the oratory of Saint Caesarius, they shut the doors behind them and remained there.

After several hours the judges of the Roman militia arrived, drove them out of the oratory, and placed them under guard.

On the following Sunday, the priest Waldipertus, without the knowledge of the aforementioned Sergius, gathered some Romans and went to the monastery of Saint Vitus. From there they took the priest Philip. They chose him and acclaimed him joyfully with the cry: “Philip pope! Saint Peter has chosen him!” In the customary manner they led him to the basilica of the Savior.

There, after the bishop had given the prayer according to ancient custom and he had given peace to everyone, they brought him into the Lateran patriarchate. There likewise he sat on the pontifical chair and, giving peace again as was customary, went up and took possession of the table, as pontiffs were accustomed to do; some of the leading men of the Church and the chief men of the army sat with him.

### 271

After a short while the aforementioned Christopher the *primicerius* arrived on that same day. When he learned the circumstances of Philip’s election, he immediately ascended in great anger.

[Note: [Column 1151] *succensus*, “inflamed”; delete *in*.]

He affirmed under oath before all the Romans, saying that he would not enter Rome at all until the priest Philip had been expelled from the Lateran patriarchate. Then the aforementioned Gratiosus hastened with some Romans and expelled the priest Philip from that patriarchate. Philip descended by the staircase leading to the bath and, with great reverence, returned to his monastery.

On the next day the aforementioned Christopher the *primicerius* gathered the priests in the three aforesaid [orders; the reading is uncertain], the leaders of the clergy, the chief men of the army, the entire army, the honorable citizens, and the whole assembly of the Roman people, from greatest to least. They all reached agreement with one mind and one consent concerning the person of the aforementioned most blessed Stephen.

They went to the title of the blessed Cecilia, where he was serving as a priest, and elected him pontiff. With acclamations and praises they carried him to the Lateran patriarchate. After everything had been duly completed concerning his election, with God as author, he assumed the summit of the pontificate.

### 272

While this same most holy man was still only elected, some wicked men who did not have God before their eyes and did not fear the terrible future judgment, prompted by certain pestilential instigators of evil—for whom the Lord repaid deeds deserving of such a fate—seized Bishop Theodorus and his *vicedominus*.

[Note: [Column 1153] B reads *Constantini, quod*, “of Constantine, which.”]

They cruelly tore out the bishop’s eyes and cut out his tongue, which is even impious to mention.

They likewise tried to tear out Passivus’s eyes and displayed such godlessness toward them that they did not even allow them to be carried to their own homes, where their people could have cared for them. Instead, after taking away all their possessions, households, and estates,

[Note: [Column 1153] B reads *ablatis*, “having taken away.”]

they had one of them—namely Bishop Theodorus—shut up in the monastery of Clivus Scaurus. There, burning with hunger and thirst and crying out for water, he gave up his spirit.

They sent Passivus to the monastery of Saint Silvester. As for Constantine, the invader of the apostolic see, when he had been brought before the assembly, they attached heavy weights to his feet, made him sit on a woman’s saddle on a horse, and carried him before everyone to the monastery of Cellanovas.

On Saturday at dawn, the day before the ordination of the aforementioned most blessed Pope Stephen, some bishops, priests, and clerics gathered in the basilica of the Savior. The aforementioned Constantine was brought before the assembly again. After the most sacred canons had been read, he was deposed. The subdeacon Maurianus removed the *orarium* from his neck, threw it at his feet, and severed its fastenings.

Thus, on the following Sunday, the aforementioned most blessed Stephen received consecration to the pontificate. The entire Roman people made a penitential confession and supplication before the divine mercy, confessing that they had all sinned by accepting communion from the impious ordination of the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the apostolic see, because they had not resisted him. This confession was therefore read aloud in the ambo of the basilica of Saint Peter by Leontius the *scriniarius*.

### 273

After this, all the armies of the Roman city, Tuscia, and Campania gathered. In Campania was Gracilis the tribune, an ally of the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the apostolic see, through whom many evils had been perpetrated in part of Campania. They strongly blockaded that city, seized Gracilis from it, and brought him here to Rome. They shut him up under strict guard, and he remained confined there for several days.

Later certain wicked Campanians who had come here to Rome, encouraged by other men even more wicked and impious, took Gracilis from that confinement, pretending to be carrying him to a monastery. When they had reached the Colosseum, they tore out his eyes there and cut out his tongue.

[Note: [Column 1153] B reads *auferentes*, “taking away.”]

After several days had passed, when the Tuscans and Campanians had gathered here in Rome, they plotted with the aforementioned Gratiosus and his stronger associates, through whose authority such evils were being committed and who did not fear God. At first light he went with a wedge of troops from Tuscia and Campania to the monastery of Cellanovas, where the aforementioned Constantine, invader of the apostolic see, had been confined. They expelled him from the monastery, tore out his eyes, and left him lying blind in the street.

[Note: [Column 1153] B reads *perrexerunt*, “they went.”]

### 274

When these deeds had been accomplished, certain men rose up, saying that the aforementioned priest Waldipertus, born of Lombard stock, had entered into a conspiracy with Theodicius, duke of Spoleto, and some Romans to kill the aforementioned Christopher the *primicerius* and other Roman leaders, and to hand the Roman city over to the Lombard people.

Therefore a certain Christopher the *vicedominus* was sent with a multitude of people to seize him. When Waldipertus learned of this, he fled into the church of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, which is called “at the Martyrs.” The same *vicedominus* dragged him from there. Waldipertus was carrying an image of the Mother of God. They had him shut up in a most terrible prison called Ferrata, in the larger cellar.

After a few days they expelled the priest Waldipertus from that prison and threw him onto the ground beside the boundary of the Lateran field. They gouged out his eyes and cruelly and impiously cut out his tongue. They sent him to the hospice of Valerius, where he later died as a result of the excavation of his eyes.

### 275

At the beginning of his ordination, when this most holy bishop had assumed the summit of the pontificate, he sent to the regions of Francia, to the distinguished men Pippin, Charles, and Carloman, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, the aforementioned Sergius, then *secundicerius* and *nomenclator*. Through his apostolic letters he begged and exhorted their excellencies to send some bishops who were knowledgeable and highly trained in all the divine Scriptures and in the institutions of the holy canons, in order to hold a council in this Roman city concerning the impious presumption and rashness of this new error.

[Note: [Column 1155] *praesumptione*, “presumption.”]

The aforesaid Constantine, usurper of the apostolic see, had dared to perpetrate this.

[Note: [Column 1155] *invasor*, “invader.”]

### 276

When the aforementioned Sergius hastened to the Frankish regions, he found that the most Christian King Pippin had already departed from this life. Continuing on the journey he had begun, he reached his sons Charles and Carloman, brothers, kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans.

After presenting them with apostolic letters, he was kindly received by them. They showed him worthy hospitality and, in any case, obtained from their excellencies everything for which he had been sent.

[Note: [Column 1155] Baron, *Annals*, 769.]

The most Christian kings sent twelve bishops from the Frankish regions, men highly learned in the divine Scriptures and in the ceremonies of the holy canons, and exceptionally approved.

When they reached this Roman city in April, in the seventh indiction, the aforementioned most holy Pope Stephen immediately gathered various bishops of Tuscia and Campania, as well as some from this province of Italy.

### 277

When all these men had been gathered, a council was held in the basilica of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ beside the Lateran palace. The same most blessed pope presided. With all the bishops sitting together, Constantine, the invader of the apostolic see, was brought before the assembly, his eyes already blinded.

They carefully questioned him about why, although he was a layman, he had presumed to invade the apostolic see and perpetrate such an erroneous and wicked novelty in the Church of God. Before everyone he declared that he had suffered force from the people, had been elected by the people’s power, and had been compelled to be brought into the Lateran patriarchate because of the injuries and prejudices that Lord Pope Paul had inflicted upon the Roman people.

Falling to the ground with his hands extended on the pavement, he lamented that he was guilty and had sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea. He asked to obtain the pardon of mercy from that priestly council. They had him lifted from the ground, but on that day they pronounced no sentence concerning him.

On the following day they brought him forward again and questioned him about the same impious novelty. He replied that he had done nothing new, saying: “For Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, although a layman, was made archbishop; and Stephen of the city of Naples, likewise a layman, was suddenly consecrated bishop.”

While Constantine continued to speak in this way, all the priests, angered by zeal for ecclesiastical tradition, had his neck struck with slaps and expelled him from the same church.

### 278

Then, after all the records of his acts had been uncovered,

[Note: [Column 1155] B reads *combustis*, “burned.”]

they burned in the midst of the presbytery of that church both those records and the council which had been issued in writing concerning his purported confirmation. When this had been done, the most holy Pope Stephen threw himself on the ground with all the priests and the Roman people. Crying, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), they confessed with great weeping that they had all sinned because they had received communion from the hands of Constantine. Thus penance was imposed on all of them.

Then the most sacred canons were brought forward and carefully examined, and that priestly council pronounced, under the prohibition of anathema, that no layman, nor anyone from another order, might ever presume to be promoted to the sacred honor of the pontificate unless, having ascended through the distinct grades, he had become a cardinal deacon or priest.

### 279

They also decreed in that council that many other matters which required canonical correction concerning him should be amended.

[Note: [Column 1155] *correctione*, “correction.”]

Concerning the bishops, priests, and deacons whom Constantine himself had consecrated, it was promulgated in that council as follows: those bishops, if any of them had previously been a priest or deacon, were to return to the former grade of their rank. If they were acceptable to the people of their city, then, after a decree of election had again been made in the customary manner with clergy and people, they were to come to the apostolic see and receive from the same most holy Pope Stephen the consecration of blessing.

[Note: [Column 1155] *susciperent*, “they should receive.”]

The priests and deacons whom Constantine had consecrated were likewise to return to the status in which they had previously been. Thereafter, if any of them proved acceptable, the aforesaid most blessed pontiff was to consecrate them priests or deacons.

[Note: [Column 1155] B reads *consecraret*, “should consecrate”; another reading is *conciliaret*, “should reconcile.”]

He decreed that those among them who were to be consecrated

[Note: [Column 1155] B reads *consecrandi*, “to be consecrated.”]

were by no means to ascend to a higher rank

[Note: [Column 1155] B reads *potiorem*, “more eminent.”]

or be promoted to the summit of the pontificate, lest such an impious error of novelty should spring up in the Church of God.

### 280

The aforesaid most blessed Pope Stephen himself cried aloud before the entire priestly college, saying that he would in no way involve himself in, or wholly decline, the consecration of those priests or deacons.

[Column 1157]

Concerning laymen who had been consecrated priests or deacons by Constantine, it was promulgated that they must remain in religious habit for all the days of their life, whether in their own homes or wherever they might be.

When these judgments had been promulgated, those bishops who had been ordained by Constantine immediately returned, in accordance with the sentence of the council, to the former grade of their rank; after being elected anew by clergy and people and the customary decree having been made, they hastened to the apostolic see and were consecrated by the same most holy pope. But those priests and deacons remained so until the death of that pontiff and were never consecrated by him.

[Note: [Column 1157] See Baronius, *Annals*, 769.]

For it was decreed in that council that everything which Constantine had done in ecclesiastical sacraments and divine worship was to be repeated,

[Note: [Column 1157] B reads *iterari debuissent*, “ought to have been repeated.”]

except for sacred baptism and holy chrism.

### 281

When all these things had been promulgated, various testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the sacred images of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy and glorious Mother, our Lady Mary ever-virgin, and of the blessed apostles and of all saints, prophets, martyrs, and confessors, were immediately brought into the same council. After they had investigated many matters carefully, they decreed that all Christians should venerate these sacred images with deep devotion to their honor, as had been observed and practised concerning their honor by all the pontiffs, predecessors of this apostolic see, and by all venerable Fathers down to that time, and as had been handed down to all as a memorial of devout compunction. They condemned and anathematized that execrable synod recently held in the regions of Greece for the destruction

[Note: [Column 1157] *deponendis*, “for removing.”]

of these same sacred images.

When everything promulgated in that council had been completed, the same most blessed pontiff gathered all the priests, clergy, and people, and they proceeded to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, walking barefoot with hymns and spiritual songs. There Leontius the *scriniarius* ascended the ambo and read aloud to the people all that had been done in the council. Three bishops also—Gregory of Silva Candida, Eustratius of Albano, and Theodosius of Tivoli—ascended the ambo of that aforesaid church and pronounced the bond of anathema against anyone who should at any time presume to transgress anything of all that had been decreed in the council.

### 282

After these things had been accomplished, it happened after some time that Sergius, archbishop of the city of Ravenna, departed this life. Immediately Michael,

[Note: [Column 1157] B reads *Michael*.]

the *scriniarius* of that church, who held no sacerdotal rank, went to Rimini to Maurice, duke of Rimini. This same most wicked Maurice gathered an army with the counsel of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, hastened and entered Ravenna, chose the aforesaid Michael by force, and installed him as bishop of the church of Ravenna. They carried Leo the archdeacon, who had been elected to the rank of archbishop, to Rimini, where Maurice caused him to be confined under strict guard.

Then Michael, Maurice, and the judges of Ravenna immediately sent to the aforesaid most blessed pontiff, promising him abundant gifts if he would consecrate Michael archbishop. But the most blessed bishop was not induced by the promise of any gift to consecrate Michael, declaring that this could by no means be done while the aforesaid Michael held no sacerdotal rank.

### 283

He repeatedly sent him letters and envoys of entreaty and admonition, and likewise to the citizens, that he should withdraw from that unjust purpose. But he would in no way obey the apostolic admonitions. Giving many gifts to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, including treasures and ornaments of that church together with other various valuables, he held its bishopric by force for a year and more,

[Note: [Column 1157] B reads *invasum*, “invaded.”]

stripping it and reducing it to great poverty.

But since the most wicked adherents of Michael could in no way bend the steadfast constancy of mind of that most holy pontiff, and while envoys of the most excellent Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, were present in person, the same most blessed bishop again sent his own envoys, as well as the aforesaid Frankish envoys, and admonished all the Ravennates. They immediately rose against Michael and expelled him with disgrace from the bishopric. Sending him bound here to Rome, they elected the oft-mentioned Leo, archdeacon of that church. Leo hastened to this apostolic see with the priests and clergy of the church of Ravenna, and was ordained and consecrated to the honor of the archbishopric by the same most holy Pope Stephen.

### 284

For the same aforesaid most blessed bishop was an observer of ecclesiastical tradition, and he renewed the former rite of the Church in its various clerical dignities. He decreed that every Sunday the solemn rites of Mass should be celebrated at the altar of Saint Peter by the seven cardinal weekly bishops who observe them in the church of the Savior,

[Column 1159]

and that “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*) should be said. He also made three regular silver railings over the steps by which one enters the altar, where images are set in the front: one in the basilica of Saint Peter the apostle, another in the basilica of Saint Paul, and another at Saint Andrew the apostle.

The same most blessed pontiff diligently endeavored to send envoys and admonitory letters to the aforesaid most excellent Charles, king of the Franks, and to his brother Carloman, likewise king, while the often-mentioned Christopher the *primicerius* and Sergius the *secundicerius* pressed and contended in this matter, to exact from Desiderius, king of the Lombards, the rights

[Note: [Column 1159] *Justitiis*, that is, “rights.”]

of Saint Peter, which he refused in hardness of heart to restore to the holy Church of God. Therefore Desiderius himself, burning with an excessive fury of indignation against the aforesaid Christopher and Sergius, sought to destroy and eliminate them.

### 285

By his malicious contrivance he therefore pretended that he was about to hasten here to Rome to Saint Peter, as if for prayer, so that he might seize them. Secretly sending gifts to Paul the *cubicularius*, surnamed Afiarta, and to his other impious followers, he persuaded them that they ought to bring Christopher and Sergius into apostolic displeasure. Paul agreed with him and secretly labored for their destruction.

When the aforesaid Christopher and Sergius learned this and learned that the insolent King Desiderius was hastening to Rome, they immediately gathered a multitude of people from Tuscia, Campania, and the duchy of Perugia. With that assembly of people they manfully prepared to resist King Desiderius. Indeed, closing the gates of this Roman city, they built another one from them, and all stood armed for the defense of their own city.

### 286

While these things were happening, the aforesaid King Desiderius suddenly arrived at Saint Peter with his Lombard army.

[Note: [Column 1159] *Conjunxit*, that is, “he arrived.”]

He immediately sent envoys to the aforesaid pontiff, asking him to come out to him; and this was done. When the pontiff had been presented to him and they spoke together concerning the rights of Saint Peter, the most blessed pontiff returned and entered the city.

The aforesaid Paul and his most wicked followers, having taken counsel with the said king of the Lombards, sought to seduce the Roman people into rising against Christopher and Sergius so that they might kill them. When this was reported to Christopher and Sergius, they gathered the people and went up armed into the Lateran to seize those who were plotting against them.

### 287

[Having been notified?] in the customary manner,

[Note: [Column 1159] B reads *nuntiantesque mox salvati*, “and immediately announcing, [they were] saved.”]

the entire multitude of people who had come with them made an assault and entered armed into the basilica of Pope Theodore, where the aforesaid pontiff was seated. He sharply rebuked them for having presumed to enter that holy patriarchate armed and, speaking with them, ordered them to withdraw.

On the following day the aforesaid pontiff again went out to Saint Peter to speak with the same king. When they had been presented together, Desiderius, setting aside the matters concerning the rights of Saint Peter, pressed only for the deception of Christopher and Sergius. He therefore shut all the doors of Saint Peter and allowed none of the Romans who had gone out with the most holy pontiff to leave that church.

Then the venerable pontiff sent Andrew, bishop of Palestrina, and Jordan, bishop of Signia, to the city gate that leads out toward Saint Peter, where Christopher and Sergius were staying with a multitude of people. He charged them to declare that they should either enter a monastery to save their souls, or endeavor to hasten to him at Saint Peter. But, fearing the malignant savagery of the aforesaid king of the Lombards, they did not dare go out to him, asserting that they would sooner surrender themselves into the hands of their Roman brothers and fellow citizens than into those of a foreign people.

When the people who were with them heard these things sent by the aforesaid pontiff through the mouths of the aforesaid bishops, their hearts were immediately broken and troubled, and each one began to withdraw from them.

### 288

For a certain Gratiosus, a duke and now a kinsman of the aforesaid Sergius, pretending that he was going to his own house, gathered several Romans and proceeded with them to the Porta Portuensis. Finding the gate closed, they dared to remove it from its hinges, and thus during the night they went out to the aforesaid pontiff.

Christophorus and Sergius, realizing that they had been placed in a position of great treachery, first Sergius himself, during that same night, at the hour when the bell sounded, descended over the wall and hurried to Saint Peter’s. The Lombard guards seized him at the steps of the church of Saint Peter and led him to their king. Christophorus, Sergius’s father, followed him, and both were presented before the aforesaid pontiff. Wishing to preserve them safely,

> **[Note: [Col. 1159]** *almus conser.* = “the kindly protector,” abbreviated.**]**

he ordered them to become monks. Afterward, having celebrated Mass

> **[Note: [Col. 1159]** *missionem B.* = “the dismissal” (the reading of manuscript B).**]**

for the aforesaid king, that same most blessed pontiff entered Rome, leaving the aforementioned Christophorus and Sergius in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, wishing to bring them safely **[Col. 1161]** into Rome in the silence of night, because of the ambushes of their enemies.

But when the sun appeared to be declining toward sunset, the aforementioned Paul the chamberlain, together with the multitude of the people and his other most wicked accomplices, immediately gathered and hurried to Desiderius, king of the Lombards. They entered into an impious plan with him, removed those same Christophorus and Sergius from the church of the blessed apostle Peter, and, hastening with several Lombards as far as the city gate, there tore out their eyes.

Thus the aforesaid Christophorus was led to the monastery of Saint Agatha, where, after three days, he ended his life because of the pain caused by the tearing out of his eyes.

> **[Note: [Col. 1161]** *effalitione* in manuscript B; *effossione*, “the gouging out [of the eyes],” in another reading.**]**

Sergius, however, was carried to the monastery of the Clivus Scauri and afterward taken to the Lateran storehouse, where he remained until the death of the aforementioned pontiff.

> **[Note: [Col. 1161]** See Baronius, year 770.**]**

### 289

All these evils came about through the wicked instigations of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. For that most holy pontiff held one ordination in the month of December: five priests, four deacons, and bishops in various places, numbering [lacuna]. He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle’s, and the episcopate remained vacant for eight days.

## XCVII. SAINT ADRIAN

### In the year of Christ 772; in the thirty-second year of Constantine Copronymus

> **Exact transmitted reading(s), No. 303:** `lin 1, summittere. lin 9, quanti vitales. lin 12, perpetrari, occupari.`

**No. 306, line 2:** “his blessedness.” Line 3, “of Sabina.” Line 6–7, **[Col. 1199C]** “that he should hasten to come for a mutual conference.” Line 9, “for this very matter to direct [someone] to him.” Line 11, “but rather remaining.” Lines 13–14, “concerning which, amid very great weeping.”

> **Exact transmitted reading(s), No. 308:** `lin 6, resisterent. lin 14, concalcari. lin 20, alicujus. ibid., ablatas.`

**No. 309, line 1:** “they were satisfying [the claim] immediately.” Line 2, “he allowed [them] to return to Francia, sending them back with him.” Line 6, “taken away”; and elsewhere, wherever *abstulta* occurs. Lines 6–7, “by his own struggle.”

**No. 327, line 1:** “cultivated estates (*domocultae*).” Line 4, “existing.” Line 5, “compensations.”

[Col. 1163]

290. Adrian, a Roman by nationality, son of Theodore, from the district of the Via Lata, sat for twenty-three years, ten months, and seventeen days. A very distinguished man, sprung from a family of the noblest lineage and born of the most powerful Roman parents, he was elegant and exceedingly dignified in appearance, steadfast and very strong in orthodox faith, and a defender of his fatherland and of the people entrusted to him. Manfully resisting, with God’s strength,

[Col. 1165] the enemies and assailants of the holy Church of God and of the commonwealth, he was also most compassionate and generous in consoling all the poor and needy; and he observed ecclesiastical tradition and the institutions of the holy Fathers.

291. For this most blessed man, after his father had died and he had been left as a small child to his most noble mother, was carefully nourished and educated by his father Theodore [Note: [Col. 1165] B: Theodulus], formerly consul and duke, and afterward primicerius of our holy Church, after the death of the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 1165] * holy] mother. From the earliest childhood of his life, while he was still a layman, he devoted himself with the greatest earnestness to spiritual disciplines, charity, and modesty, persevering diligently in the church of Saint Mark, which appears to have been near his home. There he frequently offered praises to our God by day and night; clothed in sackcloth, he afflicted his body with fasts, and willingly distributed alms to the poor and destitute, with discerning generosity and according to the strength of his means. The merits of his good conduct frequently resounded in the ears of all the Romans, so that the reputation of his nobility and chastity was thereby spread far and wide. When Pope Paul, of holy memory, observed the spiritual conduct, works, and outstanding character of this pious man, he ordered him to become a cleric; appointing him regional notary in the Church, he afterward made him subdeacon.

292. When, after the death of Pope Paul, the lord Stephen II [Note: [Col. 1165] B: III], the younger pope, had been elevated to the summit of the pontificate, he too, observing the merits of the same most blessed Adrian’s spiritual conduct, advanced him to the order of deacon. From that time, distinguished in many spiritual disciplines, he devoted the greatest care both to proclaiming the divine and evangelical words skillfully and clearly to the people and to carrying out ecclesiastical tradition. Thus the grace of the Holy Spirit shone in his heart, so that he was found effective and capable in all things. And so it happened that, when the aforesaid Pope Stephen departed this life, this distinguished and most holy man and worshiper of God, Adrian, was immediately elected [Note: [Col. 1165] B: elevated] to the sacred summit of the pontificate, while he was loved by the Roman people with the most ardent affection.

On the very day of his election, at once and in that same hour, he caused those judges of this Roman city—both from the clergy and from the military—who had been sent into exile by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta, and by his other impious accomplices at the death of Pope Stephen, to return. He also caused those who had been left behind, confined and shut up in strict custody, to be released; and, while all were rejoicing together with him, he received his pontifical consecration under God’s auspices.

293. Therefore, at the very beginning of his consecration, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, sent messengers to his blessedness: namely, Theodicius [Note: [Col. 1165] B: Theodoricus], duke of Spoleto; Tunnus [Note: [Col. 1165] B: Tunnorum], duke of the royal city of Ebura; and Prandulus, his chamberlain. Through them he sent words of persuasion, saying that he wished to bind himself to him, as it were, in the bond of charity [Note: [Col. 1165] * “to be joined”].

The most blessed bishop replied to them as follows:

“I indeed desire to have peace with all Christians, including your king Desiderius, and I shall strive to remain in that covenant of peace which has been confirmed among the Romans, Franks, and Lombards. But how can I trust your king in view of what my predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen, of holy memory, reported to me more fully concerning his treacherous faith? He said that Desiderius had lied to him about everything that he had promised him under oath, upon the body of blessed Peter, concerning the restoration of the rights of the holy Church of God; and that, merely by his wrongful [Note: [Col. 1165] * unjust] scheme, he had caused the eyes of Christopher the primicerius and Sergius the secundicerius, his son, to be torn out, thereby satisfying his will against those two leaders of the Church. Thereby he brought us still greater harm and injury [Note: [Col. 1165] * inflicted it].

“For he contributed no benefit to the apostolic causes. Moreover, my predecessor told me this because of the affection he had for me, his little one: when he afterward sent his messengers to Desiderius—namely, Anastasius, the first defensor, and Gemmulus the subdeacon—exhorting him to fulfill what he had expressly promised to blessed Peter, Desiderius sent back this reply through those same messengers:

“‘It is enough for the apostolic Stephen that I have removed Christopher and Sergius, who were ruling over him; he need not seek the rights owed to him [Note: [Col. 1165] * ‘need not seek’]. For certainly, if I do not help the apostolic one himself, great destruction will come upon him, since King Carloman of the Franks, being a friend of the aforementioned Christopher and Sergius, is ready to hasten to Rome with his armies to avenge their death and to capture the pontiff himself [Note: [Col. 1165] * ‘to hasten’].

“Behold what the faith of your King Desiderius is, and with what confidence we could enter into alliance with him.”

294. As the most blessed Bishop Adrian continued speaking in this way to the messengers of King Desiderius, they assured him even more firmly, under oath, that their king would fulfill for that distinguished bishop and supreme shepherd all the rights that he had not rendered to the aforesaid lord Pope Stephen, and that he would remain joined with him in an unbreakable bond of charity.

Trusting their oaths, his blessedness sent his own messengers to King Desiderius to accomplish all these matters: namely, Stephen, regional notary and treasurer, and Paul the chamberlain, together with the rest concerning this matter. When they departed from this Roman city and reached Perusia, they brought the message [Note: [Col. 1167] “message,” that is, “report”] that the aforementioned Desiderius had taken the city of Faenza and the duchy of Ferrara, or Comacchio, from the exarchate of Ravenna—territories which King Pippin, of holy memory, and his sons, the most excellent Frankish kings and Roman patricians Charles and Carloman, had granted and offered to blessed Peter.

Not even two months had passed since that most holy man had attained the summit of the pontificate when the same most savage Desiderius seized those cities, surrounding on every side the city of Ravenna and Casales, occupying all the Ravenna estates [Note: [Col. 1167] “lands”], and taking away all provisions, as well as the households, livestock, and everything else that appeared to be held in those estates.

295. When no hope of survival remained either for Archbishop Leo or for the aforesaid people of Ravenna, who were in great distress and want of food, they sent their messengers here to Rome: namely, the tribunes Julian, Peter, and Vitalian [Note: [Col. 1167] singular: “tribune”]. With much weeping they begged the same most holy pontiff to come to their aid in whatever way he could, and to strive to recover those cities [Note: [Col. 1167] “to recover them”], asserting that, unless those cities were restored, they could not live [Note: [Col. 1167] “would not be able to live”].

Then, while the aforesaid messengers were still in Rome, the glorious pontiff sent Stephen the treasurer and Paul the chamberlain to the aforementioned king concerning this matter, together with a letter of entreaty, asking him to return those cities. In his letter he sternly rebuked him for having changed his mind about the promise he had sent through his messengers, and also because he had not returned blessed Peter’s rights as he had promised. Moreover, he had taken away those cities which his predecessors, the most blessed pontiffs Stephen, Paul, and the other Stephen, had held.

296. When the aforesaid most holy pontiff had sent such messages to the insolent Desiderius, entreating, admonishing, and adjuring him, Desiderius replied that, unless the glorious bishop first joined him in person so that they could speak together, he would not return those cities.

In those days it happened that the wife and sons of the late King Carloman of the Franks fled to the same king of the Lombards with Autchar. Desiderius strove eagerly and persistently to have the sons of Carloman assume the Frankish kingdom [Note: [Col. 1167] B: “assume it”]. For this reason he tried to entice the most holy bishop to hasten to him, so that he might anoint the sons of the aforesaid Carloman as kings. He desired to introduce division into the Frankish kingdom, to separate the most blessed pontiff from the charity and affection of the most excellent Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, and to subject the whole Roman city and all Italy to the power of his Lombard kingdom.

But with God’s favor he could not obtain this in any way, for the aforementioned Bishop Adrian stood firm like an adamant stone. Paul, who was still with the same Desiderius concerning this matter, repeatedly promised him firmly that he would lead the most blessed pope to him, saying: “Even if it should be necessary for me to put a rope around his feet, I shall bring him to your presence as best I can.”

And so it happened that, while Paul was on that journey, it became publicly known that he had caused Sergius the secundicerius, who was blind and was in the storeroom, to be killed. The most holy bishop feared that news of this might reach Paul’s ears, and that Paul might either return to the same king or turn aside from the journey into Lombard territory and perpetrate further evil with Desiderius in Roman territory and in the territory of Ravenna—for Paul was very dear and faithful to Desiderius.

Therefore the aforesaid most holy pope secretly and with the utmost discretion sent word through the tribune Julian to Leo, archbishop of the city of Ravenna, that, when Paul returned from Desiderius, he should detain him either at Ravenna or at Ariminum [Note: [Col. 1167] B: “should detain him”]. This was done: when Paul returned from that journey, he was seized at Ariminum and held in custody.

297. Then the same most blessed pontiff began carefully to investigate the death of the aforesaid Sergius the secundicerius. He summoned all the keepers of the storerooms and questioned them closely about how Sergius had been removed from that storeroom.

They replied: “At the first hour of the night, Calventinus the chamberlain came with Tunisso the priest and Leonatius the tribune, residents of the city of Anagni. While the lord Pope Stephen was still alive, eight days before he departed this life, he removed Sergius and handed him over to the aforesaid Campanians.”

Immediately the same chamberlain was brought forward and questioned as to who had ordered him to remove Sergius from the aforesaid storeroom and hand him over to the Campanians. He replied that Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta, Gregory the regional defensor, John the duke, brother of the lord Pope Stephen, and Calvulus the chamberlain [Note: [Col. 1169] * Calventius] had ordered him to deliver Sergius to them.

298. The same most holy bishop sent his messengers into Campania, to the city of Anagni, and had the aforementioned Tunisson [Note: [Col. 1169] * Lavisson] and Leonatius brought before him. Presented to the apostolic presence and subjected to severe constraint, they confessed, saying that the order to seize and kill the aforementioned Sergius had come from Paul the chamberlain, Gregory the regional defensor, John, brother of the aforesaid lord Pope Stephen, Calvulus, likewise a chamberlain, Malignus, an accomplice, and the aforesaid Paul.

At once the most holy pontiff sent his faithful ministers with the aforementioned Campanians, ordering them to show the place where they had killed and buried Sergius. They hastened to Merolana, to a painted arch beside the road that leads to the church of the holy Mother of God at the Praesepe. There, near the same arch, they opened a grave and showed the body of Sergius lying there, with his throat bound by a rope and his whole body wounded by blows. It was therefore unmistakably clear that he had been strangled and buried in the earth while still half alive.

When all the primates of the Church and the military judges saw this, they went together with the entire people to the Lateran patriarchate. Prostrating themselves at the apostolic feet, they earnestly begged the glorious pontiff to order vengeance and correction for so great and unheard-of a sacrilege: they had presumed to torture and cruelly kill a man who had repeatedly been burned with torments, something never before recorded. They declared that, unless the guilt of such a crime were expiated, this impious presumption of wicked audacity would spread excessively throughout the Roman city, and that wicked men would thereby take courage to attempt still worse deeds.

Then the aforesaid most holy bishop, at the urging of the judges and of the whole Roman people, ordered Calvulus the chamberlain and the aforementioned Campanians to be handed over to the prefect of the City, so that he might examine them as murderers before the entire people. They were led from the Elephant [Note: [Col. 1169] B: “from the aforesaid patriarchate into prison”] into the public prison, where they were examined before the whole people.

299. Thus the Campanians confessed in that examination just as they had previously. Calvulus, however, hardened his heart and scarcely admitted that everything was so; nevertheless, in that same prison he lost his spirit by a cruel death [Note: [Col. 1169] “released his spirit”]. To remove the guilt of such intolerable crimes, the Campanians themselves were sent into exile at Constantinople.

300. After this, the aforesaid most blessed pope ordered the bodies of Christopher and of the aforementioned Sergius, his son, to be taken up, and had them honorably buried in the church of blessed Peter.

The record of the examination—how the aforementioned Calvulus the chamberlain and the Campanians confessed the guilt of their own crimes—was sent by the glorious pontiff to Ravenna, so that it might be read aloud in full to Paul. When Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, received this record, he immediately, without apostolic authority, handed Paul over to the consul of the city of Ravenna. Examined before all the people of Ravenna, Paul had the same proceedings read aloud to him, and, thus revealing himself guilty of so great a sacrilege, confessed that he had committed the crime.

Paul was examined in this way, yet no information about it was given to the aforesaid most holy pontiff, either by the archbishop or by certain people of Ravenna; his holiness learned of it through others. While this was taking place, the distinguished shepherd and excellent pontiff, desiring to save the soul of the aforementioned Paul so that he would not perish forever, caused his petition to be written to the great emperors Constantine and Leo Augustus. He explained the impious killing of the blind Sergius and begged their imperial clemency to order that Paul be received for the correction of so great a crime and kept in exile in the regions of Greece [Note: [Col. 1169] B: “that they should order it”].

301. His blessedness sent this same petition to Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, so that he might send Paul into exile at Constantinople, either through Venice or by whatever other means he could, together with the aforesaid apostolic petition.

The archbishop, however, plotting intensely against Paul, seized upon an impious pretext and replied to the distinguished pontiff: “It is not expedient to send Paul there, because Desiderius, king of the Lombards, is holding the son of Mauricius, duke of the Venetians, captive in his power, lest Mauricius, wishing to recover his son from that king, hand Paul over to him as a substitute.”

Behold the cunning pretext that the archbishop of the Church of Ravenna employed so that he might destroy Paul; and so he sent that petition back to the apostolic see.

302. After this, when the most holy bishop sent Gregory, his treasurer, to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to entreat and exhort him to restore the cities he had taken, he ordered Gregory firmly to warn Leo the archbishop to preserve Paul and, when he returned from Ticinum, to bring Paul back with him here to Rome.

When the aforesaid Gregory the treasurer had hastened to the city of Ravenna, he firmly and steadfastly protested before the archbishop and the judges of Ravenna, by apostolic command and in the presence of Anuald the chartularius, then residing there—a Roman citizen who had been sent there by the apostolic see—that Paul was to be kept safe and unharmed until Gregory returned from Ticinum. He declared that he had been ordered by the apostolic authority to take Paul with him to Rome and present him safely before the apostolic presence.

After making this protest to the archbishop, Gregory began his journey toward Ticinum. Immediately the aforementioned archbishop summoned the consul of the city of Ravenna and ordered him to kill Paul. When the aforesaid treasurer returned and reached Ravenna, he found that Paul had already been killed. He severely rebuked the archbishop for daring to act in this way against Paul contrary to the apostolic command.

After several days, the archbishop himself, troubled in conscience, sent his messenger Julian the tribune to the aforementioned most holy pope, begging that apostolic letters and words of consolation be sent to him, as though it were thought that he bore no blame for Paul’s death, since the blood of an innocent man had been avenged. But he could not in any way turn aside the most holy pope [Note: [Col. 1171] B: “incline”]. The pope replied: “Let him see for himself what he has done to Paul.”

303. “For I certainly desired to save Paul’s soul and had decided to subject him to penance. For this reason I sent my treasurer here to bring him away.

“Now, when the aforementioned Desiderius, king of the Lombards, swollen with the arrogance and boastfulness of pride, seized the aforesaid cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, he immediately sent a multitude of troops and caused them to occupy the territories of the cities—namely, Senigallia, Montefeltro, Urbino, Gubbio, and the other Roman cities—perpetrating many murders, plunderings, and burnings throughout those territories.

“For, when he sent a general army into the city of Blera in Tuscia, and the people of Blera, trusting in the peace, went out in general with their wives, children, and servants to gather their crops, the Lombards suddenly fell upon them. They killed all the leading men who were useful [Note: [Col. 1171] * ‘who were of use] in that city, carried away much booty both of people and of livestock, and devastated everything around them with sword and fire.

“In the territory of the Roman city and in that of the other cities as well, the same Desiderius ordered many evils and plunderings to be committed; he also caused the fortress of Utriculum to be occupied.”

304. Therefore, time and again the most blessed bishop sent letters of entreaty [Note: [Col. 1171] * “letters of supplication”] and messengers to the same Desiderius, begging him to turn back from such evils and to return the cities he had taken.

But he was not only unwilling to return the cities he had occupied; he also refused to withdraw from that wickedness, continuing, as has been said, to inflict many cruel and intolerable evils upon the territories of the Romans.

305. Then the aforesaid most holy pontiff summoned the religious abbot of the monastery of the holy Mother of God, situated in the territory of Sabina, together with twenty elderly monks, servants of God, and sent them to Desiderius to entreat him.

When they hastened to him, as those servants of God reported, they fell at his feet before the Lombard judges and, with tears, begged him on behalf of the aforesaid vicar of blessed Peter to turn back from such evils and return to blessed Peter the cities he had taken. But they could not bend his stony heart in the least. Thus those servants of God returned without result.

Desiderius then sent his messengers to the aforementioned most blessed pontiff: namely, Andrew the referendary and Stabilis the duke, saying that he ought to join him in person for a conference. The glorious shepherd received them and replied:

“Say this to your king on my behalf: I firmly promise you before almighty God that, if he returns to me the cities of blessed Peter which he has taken during my pontificate, then immediately—whether at Ticinum, Ravenna, Perusia, here at Rome, or wherever he wishes—I shall hasten to his presence. I shall join and speak with him concerning whatever pertains to the salvation of the people of God on both sides.

“If he has any doubt about this, let him know that I must not join him until he has returned those cities. After he has returned them, if I do not join him to speak, he may occupy them again. But if he does not first return those cities and do us justice, let him know with certainty that he shall never see my face.

“Therefore, behold, after your mounted messengers, I shall endeavor to send my messengers to your king, so that, if he wishes to return the cities, they may receive them. As soon as my messengers have received those cities and returned to me to announce this, I shall immediately hasten to his presence, wherever he wishes, as I have said, to speak with him.”

306. When the Lombard messengers hastened away and returned to their king, his blessedness immediately sent his own messengers to Desiderius to receive those cities: namely, Pardus, the religious abbot appointed over the monastery of blessed Sabas, and Anastasius, the first defensor.

When they were presented before him, they too fell at his feet and, pouring forth tears, begged him to return the aforementioned cities. They promised him, under oath and by apostolic authority, that, if he returned them, the glorious pontiff would immediately hasten to him to confer with him.

But they could not soften his iron breast or his exceedingly hard mind [Note: [Col. 1173] “bend”]. Receiving nothing, they returned without result.

Nevertheless, the aforesaid pontiff did not cease sending messengers to him for this very purpose, both priests and men from each of the religious orders. But they could obtain nothing from him. Rather, he persisted in his wickedness and caused evils and great threats to be inflicted everywhere upon many cities and territories of the Romans, sending word to the distinguished pontiff that he would come with all the armies of the Lombards to besiege the Roman city.

Because of this, the most holy pontiff, together with his people, was plunged into great weeping; he ordered the gates of the Roman city to be closed and caused other gates to be built in their place [Note: [Col. 1173] “closed in the wall”].

307. While he remained in great distress and tribulation, compelled by necessity, he sent his messengers by sea, with apostolic letters, to the excellent Charles, the God-protected king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans. He begged his excellence, just as his father Pippin, of holy memory, had done, to come to the aid and assistance of the holy Church of God and of the afflicted Roman people and province of the exarchate of Ravenna, and to demand from that king Desiderius the full rights of blessed Peter and the cities that had been taken.

[Note: [Col. 1173] See Baronius under the year 773.]

But when the wicked Desiderius could not by any crafty stratagem persuade the aforesaid most holy pontiff to come to him so that he might anoint the sons of the aforesaid Charles the Great as kings, and when he wished to separate the glorious pontiff from the charity and affection of the often-mentioned most Christian King Charles the Great, then, driven by obstinacy and audacity, he departed from his palace with Adalgisus, his own son, and the Lombard army. He brought with him the wife and sons of the aforementioned late Carloman, as well as Autchar, who, as has been said, had fled to him.

He now strove to hasten to Rome, sending his messengers without the knowledge of the aforementioned pontiff—namely, the aforementioned Andrew the referendary and two others of his judges—to announce his arrival.

When they reached Rome and were presented before the apostolic presence, the pontiff gave them this reply:

“Unless he returns to blessed Peter, as he has already promised me, those cities which he took during my pontificate, and renders full justice to our party, there is no need for him to undertake the exertion of coming here, for it cannot happen that I should first be presented before him.”

308. When the same Desiderius received this reply, he did not turn back because of it, but continued on the journey he had begun toward Rome. When the most holy and distinguished shepherd himself learned that his arrival was approaching [Note: [Col. 1173] “had approached”], he gathered the entire people of Tuscia, Campania, and the duchy of Perusia, together with some men from the cities of the Pentapolis, and fortified this Roman city. All were armed and ready, so that, if the king arrived, they might resist him bravely, with God’s help and that of blessed Peter, supported by the prayers of the aforementioned most holy bishop.

His holiness also caused the churches of blessed Peter and Paul to be stripped of their ornaments [Note: [Col. 1173] “to be adorned,” that is, “stripped of their ornamentation”], and brought all their treasures and furnishings into this Roman city. He ordered all the doors of the church of blessed Peter to be closed and secured from within with iron bars, so that, if the insolent king arrived without the pontiff’s permission and authorization, he would have no access into the church unless, by force of arms and to the destruction of his soul, he broke down those doors.

After arranging all these matters, he drew up in writing a formula of anathema and sent three bishops to King Desiderius: Eustratius of Albano, Andrew of Praeneste, and Theodosius of Tibur. Through the same word of obligation and exhortation he protested to him and adjured him by all the divine mysteries not to dare, in any way, to enter or set foot within the territory of the Romans without the pontiff’s absolution—not he himself, nor any Lombard, nor even Autchar the Frank.

When the same word of obligation had been received through the aforementioned bishops, the Lombard king, immediately and with great reverence, withdrew in confusion from the city of Viterbo and returned to his own territory.

After this, messengers of the often-mentioned Charles, the excellent king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, came to the apostolic see: namely, George, the most holy bishop; Gulfard, the religious abbot and counselor; and Albinus, the king’s favorite. They inquired whether the aforementioned king of the Lombards had returned the cities taken and all the rights of blessed Peter, as he falsely reported when sending messages to Francia, asserting that he had returned everything.

>[Col. 1175] **309** And they were presently satisfied that nothing had been returned by him. The same foremost pontiff, reporting to them everything that had taken place, released them to return to Francia, sending his own envoys with them to the aforementioned most excellent king of the Franks, bearing apostolic admonitory letters. He earnestly adjured him to fulfill what he had promised to blessed Peter together with his father, King Pippin of holy memory, and to ensure that the redemption of the holy Church of God was accomplished; likewise, he urged him to cause everything seized by the treacherous king of the Lombards—both the cities and the remaining rights—to be returned to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, without conflict [Note: [Col. 1175] “by his own conflict”; another reading: “without conflict.”] [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “cause him to do so.”].

Accordingly, the Frankish envoys, hastening together with the envoys of the apostolic see, turned aside to the aforesaid Desiderius. They steadfastly entreated and exhorted him, as they had been commanded by their king, to return peacefully to blessed Peter the aforementioned cities that he had seized, and to restore the rights belonging to the Roman people [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “to restore them.”]. But they were completely unable to obtain any of this from him, for he declared that he would return nothing at all. Having received this answer, the aforementioned Frankish envoys returned to their own land.

**310** The envoys of the apostolic see likewise hastened back, reporting everything more precisely and announcing to the aforementioned most excellent and God-protected King Charles the Great the evil purpose of the aforesaid Desiderius. Immediately that most gentle and truly most Christian king of the Franks sent his own envoys to Desiderius, entreating him, as before, to return peacefully the cities he had seized and to restore in full the rights belonging to the Roman people. Moreover, he promised that fourteen thousand gold solidi would be granted to him, a payment in gold and silver. Yet neither his entreaties nor his gifts could bend that most savage heart. Since they obtained nothing, the Frankish envoys returned to their aforementioned most Christian king.

Then God-protected King Charles the Great gathered the entire multitude of the armies of his Frankish kingdom [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “army.”]. He sent part of that army to occupy the mountain passes; he himself, with many of the bravest Frankish warriors, approached those same passes by way of Mount Cenis, and then withdrew with his armies and took up position within Frankish territory.

The aforementioned Desiderius, however, and the entire multitude of the Lombard army [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “army.”] stood firmly at those passes to resist, striving carefully to fortify them with constructions and various walls. But when the aforementioned most Christian king of the Franks approached those passes, he immediately sent his envoys once more to Desiderius, entreating him, as before, to accept the aforesaid amount of solidi and peacefully return the cities. He absolutely refused to comply.

While King Desiderius persisted in such stubbornness, the aforementioned most Christian king of the Franks, desiring to receive the rights of blessed Peter peacefully [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “to restore them.”], sent word to the Lombard king that he should hand over to him only three hostages—the sons of Lombard judges—in exchange for returning those cities, and that he would then immediately return home with his Frankish armies without inflicting any harm [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: “without an accompanying military force.”] or engaging in battle. But even this could not bend his wicked mind.

Therefore Almighty God, seeing the unjust treachery and intolerable stubbornness of that wicked Desiderius, sent terror and powerful trembling into his heart, and into that of his son Adalgisus and of all the Lombards, just as the Franks were about to return home on the following day. That same night, abandoning their tents and all their possessions, they all indiscriminately took flight, with no one pursuing them. When the Frankish armies saw this, they pursued them and killed many of them.

Desiderius himself, fleeing as quickly as possible at a rapid pace with his judges, reached Pavia and there sought to shut himself in with his judges and a multitude of the Lombard people. He fortified the walls of that city to resist the Frankish armies and prepared, together with his Lombards, to defend his own city.

His son Adalgisus [Note: [Col. 1175] Another reading: Aldegisus.], taking with him the Frank Autchar and the wife and sons of the aforementioned Carloman, entered the city now called Verona, because it appeared to be the strongest of all the Lombard cities.

**311** The remaining Lombards, dispersed, returned to their own cities. For before Desiderius and his Lombard army went to the passes, certain prominent men among the Spoletans and Reatines fled for refuge to blessed Peter, presented themselves to the aforementioned most holy Pope Adrian, and, swearing according to Roman custom in the faith of that prince of the apostles and of the aforementioned most holy pontiff, were tonsured.

[Note: [Col. 1175] “Tonsured,” because the Lombards wore their hair loose.]

All the others from that duchy of Spoleto also eagerly desired to give themselves over in service to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church. But, fearing their king, they did not dare to do so. Thus, when they had fled from the passes and all those from the various cities of the duchy of Spoleto had returned from there, they immediately came together in a general assembly to the aforementioned life-giving pontiff [Col. 1177]. Falling at his feet, they earnestly entreated his thrice-blessed holiness to receive them into the service of blessed Peter and of his holy Roman Church and to have them tonsured according to Roman custom.

**312** Receiving them, he proceeded with them into the church of blessed Peter. There, all together, from the greatest to the least, they promised by an oath under the bond of a pledge [Note: [Col. 1177] “bond.”] to that apostle of God, in the service of him and of his aforementioned vicar, the most holy Pope Adrian, and of all his pontifical successors, that they would remain faithful, together with their sons and their entire descendants.

After the oath had been given, they were all tonsured according to Roman custom. Immediately that thrice-blessed, good shepherd and father, rejoicing with them all, appointed as their duke the noble Hildeprand, whom they themselves had freely chosen. He had earlier taken refuge at the apostolic see with the others.

**313** Thus, with God’s approval, the aforementioned foremost pontiff brought the entire duchy of Spoleto under the jurisdiction and authority of blessed Peter through his own exertions. Likewise, all the inhabitants of the duchies of Fermo, Osimo, and Ancona, as well as those of the castle of Felicitas [Note: [Col. 1177] Fulcinatis.], returning after fleeing from the Lombard passes, hastened to the aforementioned most holy pontiff and gave themselves over to his thrice-blessed holiness. After swearing an oath that they would remain faithful in the faith and service of blessed Peter, of his vicar, the aforementioned life-giving Pope Adrian, and of his pontifical successors, they were tonsured according to Roman custom.

**314** The aforementioned most Christian King Charles of the Franks then set out with his entire army and, reaching the city of Pavia, surrounded and fortified it on every side. Immediately sending to Francia, he had his most excellent wife, Queen Hildegard, and his noble sons brought to him at Pavia. When he learned that the aforementioned Adalgisus had fled to Verona, he left a large part of his army at Pavia and himself hurried with some of the bravest Franks to that same city of Verona.

When he arrived there, Autchar and the wife and sons of the often-mentioned Carloman voluntarily surrendered themselves to the most gracious King Charles. His Excellency received them and returned once more to Pavia. Immediately sending out divisions of his fighting forces, he seized the various Lombard cities situated beyond the Po and brought them under his authority.

After that Frankish king had remained for six months in the siege of Pavia, he felt a great desire to hasten to the threshold of the apostles. Since the most sacred Paschal festival was approaching, he took with him various bishops and abbots, as well as judges, dukes, and counts, together with very large armies, and hastened here to Rome by way of Tuscany. He arrived so quickly that he presented himself at the apostolic threshold on Holy Saturday itself.

When the aforementioned most blessed Pope Adrian heard of his arrival—how suddenly the Frankish king had come—he was filled with great astonishment and wonder. He sent out to meet him all the judges, nearly thirty thousand in number, from the Roman city to a place called Novae, where they received him with the *bandora* [Note: [Col. 1177] *Bandora*, a military standard.].

**315** When he had approached to within approximately one mile of the Roman city, he sent out all the military schools together with their patrons, as well as the boys who were going to learn letters. Carrying branches of palm and olive and singing all the praises with the voices of their acclamations, they welcomed the Frankish king.

His Holiness sent venerable crosses—that is, standards—to meet him, as is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician, and had him welcomed with immense honor. When that most gracious, God-appointed King Charles the Great of the Franks and patrician of the Romans saw those most sacred crosses and standards coming to meet him, he descended from the horse on which he was seated and hastened on foot with his judges toward blessed Peter.

The aforementioned life-giving pontiff had risen at dawn on that same Holy Saturday and proceeded with all the clergy and the Roman people to blessed Peter to receive the Frankish king. He awaited him with his clergy on the steps of the apostolic hall.

**316** When the same most excellent and gracious King Charles arrived, he kissed one by one all the steps of the most sacred church of blessed Peter. Thus he reached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the atrium above the steps beside the doors of the church.

After receiving him, they embraced one another, and that most Christian King Charles took the right hand of the aforementioned pontiff. They then entered together into the venerable hall of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. The entire clergy and all the religious servants of God sang praises to God and loudly acclaimed his Excellency:

> Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, etc.

Thus, together with that pontiff, the Frankish king, all the bishops, abbots, and judges, and all the Franks who had come with him approached the confession of blessed Peter [Col. 1179]. They prostrated themselves there and offered their vows to our almighty God and to that prince of the apostles, glorifying the divine power because, through the intercessory merits of that same prince of the apostles, it had granted such a victory.

When this prayer had been completed, the Frankish king earnestly entreated the aforementioned life-giving pontiff to grant him permission to enter Rome, so that he might fulfill the vows of his prayers throughout the various churches of God. Both that most holy pope and the aforementioned most excellent Frankish king then descended together to the body of blessed Peter. Strengthening themselves mutually by an oath [Note: [Col. 1179] “Oaths.”], the Frankish king immediately entered Rome with that pontiff, together with his judges and people, on the same Holy Saturday.

**317** They entered together into the Basilica of the Savior beside the Lateran [Note: [Col. 1179] Lateran.]. There the most excellent king remained with all his people until the aforementioned thrice-blessed pontiff celebrated the sacrament of holy baptism. Afterwards the most blessed king returned to blessed Peter.

**318** On the following day, as holy Sunday dawned, during that most sacred Paschal festival, the most holy prelate sent all the judges and the entire military retinue to the same king. Receiving him with great honor, they accompanied the king as he proceeded with all the Franks who had come with him to the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger.

After the solemn celebration of Mass, he went with the aforementioned pontiff to the Lateran patriarchium, and there they dined together at the apostolic table.

On the following day, Monday, in the same manner, the illustrious Father and outstanding pontiff celebrated the solemn Mass in the church of blessed Peter according to custom and had praises rendered to almighty God and to the aforementioned most excellent King Charles of the Franks and patrician of the Romans.

On Tuesday, as customary, he had Mass celebrated for the same king in the church of the apostle Paul.

On Wednesday, the aforementioned pontiff went out with his judges, both of the clergy and of the military, to the church of the apostle blessed Peter. There, meeting together with the same king for a conversation, he steadfastly entreated him, admonished him, and sought to exhort him with paternal affection to fulfill in every respect the promise that his father, King Pippin of holy memory, and that most excellent Charles himself, together with his brother Carloman and all the Frankish judges, had made to blessed Peter and to his vicar, the holy-memory Lord Pope Stephen the Younger, when he had gone to Francia to grant various cities and territories of this province of Italy and to hand them over to blessed Peter and all his vicars for perpetual possession.

When he had the promise made in Francia at a place called Carisiacum read aloud to him, all that was attached to it pleased him and his judges. Of his own free will, with a good and willing heart, the aforementioned most excellent and truly most Christian King Charles of the Franks ordered another promise of donation to be written by Etherius, his religious and most prudent chaplain and notary, after the model of the earlier one.

In it he granted those same cities and territories to blessed Peter and promised that they would be handed over to the aforementioned pontiff, with the boundaries specified as the donation itself shows: from Luna, with the island of Corsica; then to Surianum; then to Mount Bardone, that is, to Verceto; then to Parma; then to Reggio; from there to Mantua; and to Mount Silicis [Note: [Col. 1179] Another reading: “bridge of Silicis.”]. He also granted the entire exarchate of Ravenna, as it had existed in ancient times, together with the provinces of Venetia and Istria, and the whole duchies of Spoleto and Benevento.

**319** After this donation had been made, the most Christian Frankish king confirmed it with his own hand and had all the bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts subscribe it [Note: [Col. 1179] Another reading: “had it subscribed.”].

They placed it first upon the altar of blessed Peter and afterwards inside his holy confession. There, both the Frankish king and his judges handed it over to blessed Peter and to his vicar, the most holy Pope Adrian, promising under a terrible oath that they would preserve everything contained in that donation.

The most Christian king of the Franks also had a copy of the donation written by the same Etherius. He placed it with his own hands inside the church, above the body of blessed Peter and beneath the Gospels, which are kissed there, as the firmest security and for the eternal remembrance of his name and of the Frankish kingdom. His Excellency carried other copies of the same donation with him, written by a registrar of this holy Church of ours [Note: [Col. 1179] *Apparem*, that is, copies.].

Returning with his armies to Ticinum, the most excellent Frankish king fought vigorously and besieged the city of Pavia. While God’s anger raged fiercely against all the Lombards who were in that city, and many were dying from illnesses or the devastation of mortality, the most excellent king, by God’s will, captured that city, as well as Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and all those who were with him, and subjected the entire Lombard kingdom to his authority [Col. 1181]. He took the aforementioned Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and his wife with him to Francia.

The aforementioned most blessed pontiff was indeed a lover of churches.
