**320** This angelic man made in the church of the apostle blessed Peter a garment of extraordinary beauty, of gold and gems, depicting the story of how blessed Peter was freed from his chains by an angel.

Likewise, in that basilica, from the entrance to the *rugae* as far as the confession, he covered the pavement with the purest silver, weighing 150 pounds. In the same basilica, beside the greater doors, he made silver curtains of extraordinary size from *stauracin* or *quadrapol* textiles.

He also made throughout all the arches of the basilica of that prince of the apostles sixty-five hangings from Tyrian and embroidered textiles. Finally, his Blessedness made a great *pharus* in the same church of blessed Peter, in the form of a cross, hanging before the presbytery and containing 1,370 candles. He established that this *pharus* should be lit four times a year: at the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, on the feast of the apostles, and on the feast of the pontiff.

**321** The aforementioned most holy prelate also made a cast silver chalice weighing five pounds, which he placed in the presbytery in place of the one that had perished during the time of Lord Pope Paul.

In the church of the apostle blessed Andrew, situated beside the church of the apostle blessed Peter, that thrice-blessed pontiff likewise newly made a *ciborium* of the purest silver, weighing 135 pounds.

In the church of the apostle blessed Paul he also covered the body of that teacher of the world with silver plates weighing thirty pounds.

**322** He added these because the silver that had originally been there was found to be badly broken.

Likewise, in the basilica of the apostle blessed Paul he made beside the principal doors a great curtain of *quadrapol* textiles, modeled on the curtain that he had made in the church of blessed Peter. He also made another great curtain of *quadrapol* textiles, hanging beneath the great arch beside the altar. Throughout the various arches of that church he made seventy hangings of *quadrapol* textiles.

The atrium of that church of blessed Paul, which had previously lain desolate, where oxen and horses entered to graze because of the grass growing there, the same most holy pontiff, inspired by God, had paved with beautiful marble.

In the church of the holy Mother of God at the Manger he made two vestments for the main altar: one of the purest gold and gems, depicting the Assumption of the holy Mother of God, and another adorned around its edge with *blattin* [Note: [Col. 1181] Another reading: *blattis*.], made of *stauracin* [Note: [Col. 1181] *Stauracio*.].

In that church he also made great curtains of *quadrapol* textiles [Note: [Col. 1181] *Quadrapolis*, or *quadruplis*.], modeled on the one he had made in the church of blessed Peter.

**323** Likewise, throughout the various arches of that basilica of the holy Mother of God, he made, in the same manner, forty-two hangings of *quadrapol* textiles.

In the Basilica of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, beside the Lateran, he similarly made a *stauracin* vestment or a great curtain of *quadrapol* textiles. He also made throughout the various arches fifty-seven Syrian hangings, all of *quadrapol* or *stauracin* textiles.

In the church of the martyr blessed Lawrence outside the walls, where his holy body rests, he made a *stauracin* vestment; and in the Major Church he likewise made another vestment.

He also renewed the roof of that basilica of the martyr blessed Lawrence, which had already been stripped, together with its broken beams.

In the basilica of blessed Valentine he similarly made a *stauracin* vestment. In the basilica of blessed Pancratius he made another vestment of *stauracin* in the same manner.

In the church of blessed Mark, whose roof, already weakened by age, appeared close to collapse, he removed the ancient beams, put in others, newly constructed the roof and the surrounding portico, and restored the church itself.

Adding twelve pounds of silver, the same most blessed pontiff newly constructed the three arches that had been extremely old. He also made in that church a *stauracin* vestment for the main altar. Throughout the various arches of the same church he made twenty-seven hangings of *quadrapol* textiles, and he also made a crown of the same *quadrapol* textiles, hanging beneath the beam.

**324** The roof of the basilica of blessed Lawrence [lacuna] at Taurellum, being exceedingly old, he replaced all its beams with new ones and restored it. He also made and offered a *quadruplum* vestment for the altar of that church.

The basilica of blessed Felix at the Pincian Hill was in ruins, and its roof had been stripped. After newly constructing the roof, he renewed the church itself and made and offered a *quadrapol* vestment for its altar.

He also renewed the roof of the basilica of Saint Lawrence called that of Damasus. There he made a *stauracin* vestment for the altar and another vestment behind the altar, where the body of Saint Damasus rests.

He renewed the surrounding portico of the basilica of the apostles on the Via Lata, which his predecessor, Lord Pope Paul, had begun but not completed. By God’s favor, the aforementioned most blessed pontiff repaired everything and also restored the main roof.

When the same most blessed pontiff saw that the apse of that church was already close to collapse, he had the apse reinforced with iron bars and thus renewed it. He made a *stauracin* vestment for the main altar of that church.

**325** He also renewed the cemetery of the blessed Peter and Marcellinus on the Via Labicana, beside the basilica of blessed Helena. He newly constructed its roof—that is, the roof over Saint Tiberius and over those same saints, Peter and Marcellinus—and newly made its steps descending to their most sacred bodies, since there was no longer any descent to those holy bodies.

In the basilica of blessed Adrian he made silver *cerostata* weighing twelve pounds, together with two silver *laudunae* [Note: [Col. 1183] Another reading: *laudanae.], weighing eight pounds, which he placed above the *rugae* of the presbytery, where there is a silver arch.

He also made two *stauracin* vestments: one for the altar of blessed Adrian and another for the altar of Saint Martina. In the same church he made fifteen hangings of *quadrapol* textiles.

Finally, he newly constructed the roof of the titular church of blessed Prisca, which was already about to fall and lay in ruins; there he also made a *stauracin* vestment.

In the church of the blessed Cosmas and Damian at the Three Fates he made a *stauracin* vestment, together with a curtain before the apse of *quadrapol* textiles. He also made twenty hangings of the same *quadrapol* textiles and twenty linen hangings.

Throughout the various titular churches and other churches, and all the deaconries, and however many sacred buildings exist within the walls of this Roman city, that most holy pontiff, inflamed by divine inspiration, made and offered vestments from textiles—that is, *stauracin* or Tyrian textiles.

**326** Like a good shepherd, he restored and adorned all the churches of God, both outside the walls of this Roman city and within the walls, for the praise of God. He also renewed the walls and towers of this Roman city, which had been ruined and destroyed down to their foundations, and usefully restored everything around them.

He spent as much as one hundred pounds of gold on the wages of those who built the wall, on their provisions, and on lime and various necessities.

This most blessed prelate, inflamed by divine inspiration, established a community of monks in the monastery of Saint Stephen called *Catabarbara Patriciana*, situated at blessed Peter the apostle. There he appointed a suitable person as abbot.

He decreed that they should offer continuous praises in the church of blessed Peter, as did the other three monasteries, so that two monks at the side of that church might sing praises to our God. For that monastery had been left in great sloth, neglect, and carelessness, and no divine office was being performed there with due worship.

**327** This most blessed prelate newly established and endowed four cultivated estates.

The first was called Capreorum [Note: [Col. 1183] Another reading: Capracorum.], situated in the territory of Vejano, approximately fifteen miles from the city of Rome. It appears that he had originally held the estate of Capracorum itself, together with several other estates attached to it, through the hereditary succession of his parents. Since these had once been his own, he also appears to have bought various other estates, farmsteads, and estates from different persons, giving appropriate compensation in exchange, and added them to that cultivated estate.

He established by apostolic privilege, under the obligation of great anathemas, that this cultivated estate of Capracorum, with its estates, farms, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, water mills [Note: [Col. 1183] *Aquimolis*.], and everything belonging to it, should remain perpetually for the use of our brothers, the poor of Christ. The wheat and barley that annually grew on the lands of that cultivated estate were to be carefully brought to the granary of our holy church and stored separately.

The wine and various legumes that annually grew on the farms and lands of the aforementioned cultivated estate were likewise to be carefully brought to the *paracellarium* of our holy church and stored separately.

**328** Likewise, of the pigs that were annually fattened in the farmsteads of the often-mentioned cultivated estate, one hundred head were to be slaughtered and stored in the same *paracellarium*.

His thrice-blessedness decreed and promulgated under the strongest obligations and prohibitions that every day one hundred of our brothers, the poor of Christ—even if there should be more of them—were to assemble in the Lateran patriarchium. They were to be placed in the portico beside the staircase leading up into the patriarchium, where those poor are depicted.

Fifty loaves of bread were to be distributed, each loaf weighing two pounds; likewise, two measures of wine, each measure weighing sixty pounds; and cauldrons full of porridge. These were to be distributed every day by the hands of one most faithful *paracellarius* to those poor. Each person was to receive a portion of bread and a portion of wine—that is, a cup holding two *calices*—as well as meat from the porridge.

Thus his life-giving Blessedness, together with the priestly college, decreed and promulgated that none of the produce or other resources of the aforementioned cultivated estate should be distributed or spent for any other purpose, but that everything should be devoted and perpetually expended solely for the proper support and daily nourishment of our aforementioned brothers, the poor of Christ.

The other three cultivated estates were: Galeria, situated on the Via Aurelia, approximately ten miles from the city of Rome, near Santa Rufina, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, water mills, and everything belonging to it; another Galeria, situated on the Via Portuensis, approximately twelve miles from the city of Rome, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, and water mills, together with the monastery of blessed Lawrence, situated on the island of the Roman port, its associated vineyards, and the *lecticaria* called Asprula; and Calvisianum, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, water mills, and everything belonging to it, situated on the Via Ardeatina, approximately fifteen miles from the city of Rome.

His thrice-blessedness established by apostolic privilege, under strong obligations of anathema, that these three cultivated estates—Galeria, Calvisianum, and the other Galeria—should remain perpetually for the use and proper benefit of our holy Church.

**329** Along with all the spiritual endeavors that the same thrice-blessed and life-giving pontiff undertook for the growth, benefit, and advancement of the holy Roman Church, for the restoration of the churches of God, and for the improvement of divine worship, it is certain that he also devoted great care and loving affection to the holy and venerable patriarchal residence.

Therefore, out of his exceedingly fervent love, for the honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for the adornment of that holy patriarchium, he newly constructed and built there a tower of extraordinary beauty, adorned with an adjoining portico that descends to the bath.

There he also had a covered walkway—namely, his sun terrace—constructed most beautifully with bronze grilles. He also very usefully renovated the portico itself, which had fallen into ruin through age. He adorned that tower and all the buildings newly constructed by him with paintings and marble.

**330** Thus the same thrice-blessed and truly foremost Father, good shepherd, and outstanding prelate, burning with such love toward his nourisher, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, made and offered in that apostolic hall all its adornment: splendid garments of gold and gems, various textiles, and other ornaments of gold and silver.

He also renewed all its great steps leading up into the atrium, as well as the two porticoes leading up into the same church, on both sides. He renewed the entire pavement of the church wherever the marble had been broken, using other, beautiful, superior marble.

In the porticoes on both sides of the aforementioned church, where broken beams remained and the roof had come close to collapse, he installed new beams and restored the roof by newly constructing it.

His Blessedness also made six images covered with silver plates. He placed three of them above the *rugae* at the entrance to the presbytery of the church, where he also made a silver-covered *regulare* and placed the three images upon it. In the middle was one bearing the painted face of the Savior; on either side were images bearing the painted figures of the angels, one of blessed Michael and the other of blessed Gabriel.

On the upper *ruga*, that is, in the middle of the presbytery, he made another silver-covered *regulare* and placed the remaining three images upon it. In the middle was the represented face of the holy Mother of God; on the two sides were one image bearing the painted face of the apostle blessed Andrew and another of Saint John the Evangelist.

All six images, as stated, were made most beautifully from silver plates and gilded. On these images he placed one hundred pounds of silver.

**331** But after twenty years had passed, the aqueduct called the Sabbatina had become badly broken. Through it water flowed through a *centenarium* into the atrium of the church of the apostle blessed Peter and also into the bath situated beside that church, where our brothers, the poor of Christ, who annually used to come to receive alms and bathe during the Paschal festival, and by which various mills were operated through a *genuculum* mechanism.

[Note: [Col. 1185] * *macinabant* (“they were grinding”).]

The water from the same aqueduct no longer flowed either into the atrium of Saint Peter or within the city, since the aqueduct itself, as stated, lay demolished: one hundred arches of that great aqueduct, built to a considerable height, had been pulled down and destroyed from their foundations, so that no hope now seemed to remain of rebuilding or restoring either those arches or the ruined aqueduct. But this most blessed and holy bishop, gathering a multitude of people, personally prepared to construct and restore it. He devoted such care and attention to the work on the aqueduct that he renewed and restored it anew from its foundations. Immediately, too, the conduit through which water from that aqueduct flowed into the atrium of Saint Peter—whose lead, through excessive neglect, had already been secretly removed from it over much of its length—was rebuilt by that distinguished shepherd. He added a quantity of lead to the battered remainder and reconstructed the conduit. With God’s aid, he thus caused water to flow abundantly, as in ancient times, into the atrium of Saint Peter, into the aforementioned bathhouse, and even within the city, that is, at the grinding-place where the mills operated.

At the same time, the same most blessed pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul three images from silver plates, [Col. 1187] which are placed above the screens at the entrance to the presbytery: one bearing the painted face of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and on either side painted images bearing the likenesses of angels. They weighed twenty-four pounds. He also made in the basilica of the Apostles on the Via Lata twenty curtains of Syrian purple cloth and twenty of linen. In the church of the blessed martyr and levite Lawrence outside the walls of this Roman city, he likewise made twenty curtains of Syrian purple cloth and twenty of linen. In the church of the blessed Mother of God at the Martyrs, he similarly made twenty curtains of Syrian purple cloth and twenty of linen. Likewise, throughout the various titular churches, this most holy pontiff made, for each title, twenty curtains of *stauracin* or Tyrian cloth and twenty of linen; together these amounted to four hundred and forty Syrian curtains.

### 332

That distinguished pontiff made images from gilded silver plates, bearing the likeness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. One was placed above the entrance to the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, where the silver doors are located; it weighed fifty pounds. He also made, in the various diaconiae, six *stauracia* or Tyrian curtains for each diaconia, making ninety-six curtains in all.

Likewise, the same holy bishop had the aqueduct called Jobia [Note: [Col. 1187] *Jovia*.], which had lain severely broken down from its foundations for a period of twenty years, restored. In the same way, in the basilica of the blessed martyr Pancratius, outside the walls of this Roman city, he made thirty-eight curtains of *stauracium* or Tyrian cloth and thirty-eight of linen. In the basilica of the blessed protomartyr Stephen on the Caelian Hill, he made twenty curtains of *stauracium* or Tyrian cloth and twenty of linen. In the basilica of the blessed Apollinaris, likewise, he made ten curtains of *octaplum* and ten of linen. In the basilica of the blessed martyr Valentinus, situated outside the walls of this Roman city, he similarly made twenty-two curtains of *stauracium* or *octaplum* and twenty-two of linen.

### 333

When the aqueduct called Claudia appeared to have been demolished over many years, so that its water—used for bathing in the Lateran baths and customarily flowing on the holy day of Easter into the baptistery of the church of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and into several other churches—had been reduced to a small flow within the city, the distinguished and angelic bishop, gathering a multitude of people from the regions of Campania, hastened with all his strength personally to construct and restore that aqueduct. He devoted such care and attention to its construction that he renewed and restored it anew. Immediately he caused water from it to flow abundantly, as in ancient times, into the aforesaid baths and within the city.

During his time, Leoninus, consul and military commander, later a monk for the forgiveness of his sins, died; the text then refers, in a grammatically incomplete phrase, to three *unciae* of the Aratiana estate [Note: [Col. 1187] *Aricinae*.], which he had inherited from his parents. The estate lay sixteen miles from this Roman city on the Via Ardeatina, and the church of the blessed Edistus is known to have stood there. The most blessed pope adorned that church with buildings of substantial construction and enlarged it. To the three *uncia* of the aforementioned Aratiana estate, he added another six *uncia*, purchased from Count Peter, from Agnete, widow of Agatho the Scriniarius, and from Theodata, formerly the widow of Dominicus the Prefect [Note: [Col. 1187] B, *praefectori* (“prefect”).]. He also acquired boundaries on every side. Offering suitable compensation and using force against no one, but rather, as befits a father, purchasing all the estates adjoining that place by amicable agreement, he established the cultivated estate as belonging perpetually by right to Saint Peter. To this day it is called the cultivated estate of Saint Edistus.

### 334

Likewise, the estate called Acatiana, which appears to have been situated beside that cultivated estate, was granted by the same Leoninus to Saint Peter. Then the same thrice-blessed bishop, in the great basilica called that of the holy Mother of God, which stood beside the basilica of the blessed martyr and levite Lawrence, where his holy body rests outside the walls of this city of Rome, offered fifteen curtains of *stauracium* or *quadrapolis* and fifteen of linen.

### 335

He newly restored the roof of the title-church of the blessed Clement, which was already about to collapse and lay in ruins in the third region. Likewise, he renewed the basilica of the blessed confessor and pontiff Sylvester, situated at the Orpheus, which already lay in ruins and whose roof had collapsed; after making a new roof, he renewed the church.

In the same way, in the most famous and renowned basilica throughout the world, the venerable basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, the same distinguished pontiff observed that the ancient beams there had become extremely old over the course of many years. He therefore sent his treasurer Januarius, whom he knew to be a suitable man, and, with a multitude of people, replaced fourteen beams there. He also newly restored the entire roof and porticoes of that basilica.

### 336

This same beneficent bishop, filled with divine inspiration and moved by compassion, observed that the aqueduct called the Virgin had been demolished over many years and was full of ruins, with scarcely any water entering the city of Rome. Like a most kindly and devout shepherd, he restored it anew and brought forth such an abundance of water that he almost satisfied the entire city.

Finally, he newly restored the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyr Januarius, situated at the gate of the blessed martyr and levite Lawrence. In the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, outside the Porta Portuensis, he made and offered a garment of *stauracium*.

### 337

This angelic man, inflamed by divine inspiration, established three diaconiae outside the gate of the blessed prince of the apostles: one belonging to the holy and glorious ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary our Lady, situated in the Atrium [Note: [Col. 1189] B, *attio*.]; another belonging to the aforementioned immaculate Lady, situated outside the gate of the blessed apostle Peter at the head of the portico; and a third diaconia called that of Saint Sylvester, beside the hospice of Saint Gregory.

Finding the aforementioned diaconiae in hidden places, without the fruit of mercy, this beneficent man restored them anew. There he offered many gifts, both movable and immovable, for the salvation of his soul. He established that every week, on Thursday, they should proceed with psalm-singing [Note: [Col. 1189] *Psallentio*, that is, “singing of psalms”.] from the diaconia to the bathhouse, and that there, through orderly administration, the poor should be comforted and alms distributed.

Moreover, this frequently mentioned most holy bishop, seeing that the beams in the basilica of the chosen vessel, the blessed apostle Paul, had become ancient through the passage of time and were about to collapse, did as he had done above in the basilica of Peter, prince of the apostles. He arranged everything through his most faithful treasurer Januarius, with a multitude of people. The thrice-blessed shepherd himself also frequently attended the work in person and completely restored the basilica anew. He replaced thirty-five of its principal beams and newly restored it all around.

### 338

This thrice-blessed and apostolic man, having discovered through the most careful investigation that the monastery of Pope Honorius was falling into extreme desolation through a certain negligence, was moved by divine inspiration. He rebuilt and endowed it anew, appointed an abbot and other monks who lived there according to the rule, and established that they should celebrate the offices in the basilica of the Savior, also called the Constantinian basilica, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate: namely, the offices of Matins, Prime, Terce, None, and Vespers.

One choir consisted of the monks from the monastery of Saint Pancratius, who had formerly sung there alone in both choirs; the other consisted of the monks of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Andrew and Saint Bartholomew of Pope Honorius. Thus, singing together in devout praises, they might joyfully resound with hymnic choirs, offering glorious melodies to the Lord and frequently commemorating the name of the venerable pontiff, composing his memorial for all ages in their songs.

### 339

This same most holy bishop founded from the ground and built a church in the cultivated estate called Capracorum, which he had offered from his own property to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles and his nourisher, for the support of the poor. He also adorned it splendidly and dedicated it, in that saint’s name, to God his creator. In it he deposited relics from the garments of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, of the same Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, of the twelve apostles, and of other venerable martyrs.

Going to this most sacred church with his entire senate and the Roman people, they celebrated together with great glory and rejoicing. He distributed the customary great alms there to Christ’s poor and transferred and introduced into the church the bodies of holy martyrs and pontiffs: the body of Saint Cornelius, martyr and pontiff; the body of his successor, Saint Lucius, martyr and pontiff; likewise the body of Saint Felix, martyr and pontiff; and the body of Saint Innocent, confessor and pontiff. The beneficent holy pontiff honored them as patrons in the Lord, out of love for the holy apostolic see over which they had presided, as was fitting.

He also newly restored the roof of the title-church of the blessed martyr Susanna, situated between two houses beside Saint Quiriacus, which was already about to collapse and lay in ruins. In the same way, he restored anew the title-church of the blessed martyr Cyriacus and the church of Saint Lawrence at Formosa.

### 340

He also renewed the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantinian basilica, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate and lying in ruins, together with its four-sided porticoes, atria, and fountains, just as he had done with the churches of the blessed princes Peter and Paul. In it he replaced fifteen principal beams.

Likewise, this beneficent bishop, finding the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the deserted region of the Palatine, restored it anew and endowed it in every respect. He joined it to another monastery situated beside it, namely that of Saint Stephen, called Baganda. He appointed monks and established that in the title-church of the blessed pontiff and confessor Mark they should perform the offices—that is, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers—for the repose of his soul.

In the aforementioned basilica of Saint Mark he also made six other silver arches, weighing fifty-five pounds in all. Likewise, he repaired the ministerial chalices proceeding from the Catholic Church, made of the purest gold, weighing nine and a half pounds.

[Col. 1191]

### 341

This farsighted man, considering the salvation of a great multitude of people, repaired the portico along the bank of the river that leads to the blessed apostle Peter. It had been narrow and confined, although travelers passed along it to reach that blessed prince of the apostles, Peter. Placing more than twelve thousand tufa blocks in the foundations along the riverbank, he repaired the portico from the ground to the top of the roof, on a marvelous scale, and restored it as far as the steps of Saint Peter.

He also restored the diaconia of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, the Greek School, called Cosmedin. Formerly short in its buildings and lying beneath ruins, it had a huge monument of Tiburtine tufa hanging over it. Over the course of a year, after gathering a great multitude of people and burning a pile of much timber, he demolished the monument. He also cleared away the heap of rubble, built it from its foundations, and greatly enlarged the aforementioned basilica on every side. Establishing three apses in it, the distinguished bishop rebuilt the true Cosmedin on a very grand scale.

He likewise repaired the title-church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, which is called that of Lucina, as well as the church of the blessed Martin situated beside the title-church of Saint Sylvester. He also repaired the basilica of the blessed martyr Agapitus, situated outside the walls beside Saint Lawrence. These churches, decaying from ancient times, had collapsed under the weight of their ruins; the distinguished bishop, fervent in the love of the Holy Spirit in all things, renewed them entirely from the ground with their porticoes, in great splendor.

He likewise renewed anew the buildings of the title-church of Saint Sixtus and of the basilica of Saint Adrian. He also completely restored from the ground, with great splendor, the basilica of the blessed martyr Pancratius, which had been destroyed by extreme old age and overwhelmed by ruins, together with the monastery of Saint Victor situated there.

Likewise, the distinguished bishop restored on every side the basilica of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, which had entirely decayed from ancient times, and placed twenty principal beams in the repaired roof of that church.

### 342

In the same way, he renewed the basilica of Saint Eusebius on every side. He newly made the chamber of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, which had been completely destroyed and demolished, by carving it in the ancient manner and using various colors.

He newly restored the portico leading to the blessed apostle Paul, from one gate together with the church of Saint Euplius as far as the aforementioned basilica of Saint Paul. He also newly constructed the portico leading to Saint Lawrence outside the walls, from the gate as far as that same basilica.

This same beneficent Father newly restored on every side the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence, where his holy body rests, adjoining the great basilica that the same bishop had formerly built. He likewise renewed completely the church of Saint Stephen situated beside them, where the body of Saint Leo, bishop and martyr, rests, together with the cemetery of Saint Cyriaca and its ascent.

He also entirely restored the basilica of Jerusalem, situated in the Sessorian district, magnificently replacing its ancient beams, which had decayed, throughout the whole building. Likewise, he newly restored the entire church of the Apostles called Eudoxia at the Chains.

He also renewed with the greatest care the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda, situated in the episcopate of Silva Candida, which had decayed through ancient age, together with its baptistery. Likewise, he newly restored, together with its baptistery, the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter situated on the Via Appia at the place called Silice, beyond Saint Thomas the apostle and not far from the thirtieth milestone. It had been overwhelmed by desolation and ruins, and he adorned it with a structure of great size.

### 343

Likewise, he entirely restored anew the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated at the Three Fates, because its beams, similarly decayed through extreme old age, had collapsed.

He newly renewed in every respect the church of Saint John the Baptist, situated beside the Porta Latina, which had been overwhelmed by ruins. He also newly restored the church of the Apostles outside the Porta Appia, at the third milestone, in the place called the Catacombs, where the body of the blessed martyr Sebastian rests with others; it too had been overwhelmed by ruins.

He newly repaired the title-church of Pudentiana, that is, the church of Saint Potentiana, which lay in ruins. He also restored the basilica of Saint Theodore, situated within the Velum beside the cultivated estate of Sulpitianus, as well as the basilica of Saint Peter situated on the Merulana estate, which had been ruined from the passage of many years, renewing it from the ground.

### 344

During his time, the deceased Mastalus, the primicerius, left instructions that, for the sake of his soul, his property should be distributed by the aforementioned pontiff to Christ’s poor. Accordingly, by common agreement, the heirs of the aforementioned Mastalus gave and sold to that great bishop, together with estates and farmsteads belonging to the church of Saint Leucius, the share that pertained to them. It was situated on the Via Flaminia, approximately five miles from the city of Rome, and they also gave two hundred gold *solidi mancusos*. The heirs of the same Mastalus likewise gave his province to Christ.

The share of Gregory the secundicerius, which he was known to possess in the aforementioned farmsteads of Saint Leucius, was granted by that Gregory to the same beneficent bishop in recognition of the honor of the secundicerius. When the church of Saint Leucius had perished, surrounded by great ruins and thickets, the bishop restored it anew and built there, for Saint Peter his nourisher, a cultivated estate of marvelous size. He granted it in perpetuity and enlarged its boundaries both from the inheritance of Paschalis and through an exchange made with the heirs of the late Lucia and of John the primicerius, as well as with those of various places.

In the basilica of the blessed Petronilla at Saint Peter the apostle, he made six silver arches weighing fifty pounds. He completely restored the title-church of Saint Praxedis, which had partly collapsed. He also newly restored the basilica of Saint Eugenia, both inside and outside.

### 345

In the same way, he newly restored the basilica of Saints Gordian and Epimachus, together with the cemetery of the same church of Saints Simplicius and Semilianus, and of the martyrs Quartus and Quintus, and of the blessed Sophia, together with the cemetery of Saint Tertullian outside the Porta Latina.

He also restored anew the church of the blessed Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, as well as the basilica of Saint Zeno, together with the cemetery of Saints Urban the pontiff, Felicissimus, and Agapitus, and of the martyrs Januarius and Cyrinus, all adjoining one another outside the Porta Appia. They had decayed from ancient times.

Likewise, he restored completely from the ground and on every side the title-church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary called that of Callistus across the Tiber. In the same way, he newly restored the title-church of Saint Marcellus situated on the Via Lata. He also renewed the basilica of the cemetery of the holy martyrs Hermes, Protus, and Hyacinthus, a basilica of marvelous size.

He restored with remarkable grandeur the cemetery of Saint Felicity on the Via Salaria, together with the churches of Saint Silvanus the martyr and of Saint Boniface the confessor and pontiff, which adjoined one another on a single site.

He also renewed the basilica of Saint Saturninus, situated on the aforementioned Via Salaria, together with the cemetery of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria. He renewed the cemetery of Saint Hilaria and also newly restored the cemetery of the Jordanians, namely those of Saints Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, and of the seven holy Virgins.

Likewise, on the same Via Salaria, he renewed the cemetery of Saint Sylvester the confessor and pontiff and of many other saints, which lay in ruins. He also newly restored the church of Saint Felix situated outside the Porta Portuensis.

At the same time, he renewed together the basilica of Saints Abdon and Sennen and that of the blessed Candida, along with the other cemeteries of the saints situated there.

This distinguished bishop also newly restored the aforementioned basilica of the blessed martyr Adrian and the basilicas of Saints Cosmas and Damian. He established diaconiae in which he did many good works for his perpetual memorial, granting them fields, vineyards, olive groves, male and female servants, various livestock, and movable property, so that, from their revenues and the regular receipts accruing to the diaconiae, Christ’s poor might be fed.

### 346

In the aforementioned diaconia of Saint Adrian he offered twelve silver baskets, one large vessel, one cup, one paten, one chalice, and one offertory vessel, weighing sixty-seven pounds.

Likewise, through exceedingly diligent care and industry, he built anew from its foundations the aqueduct of Sabbatina and brought flowing water to his patron, the blessed apostle Peter. He supplied both the fountain of the basilica, which was filled by means of vehicles, and the atrium of that basilica, as well as a bathhouse, for the use of the pilgrims serving there.

He also newly restored the basilica of Saint Secundinus, situated in the city of Praeneste, where his body rests, although it lay in ruins.

### 347

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed first martyr Stephen, situated on the Caelian Hill, whose structures had decayed through ancient time, he newly renewed the enormous beams within it, of immense bulk, and also magnificently restored the porticoes inside and outside.

Moreover, in the basilica of the blessed Eugenia, which his beneficence had restored some time before, he continued to care for it diligently. There he newly built from the foundations a monastery for women and established that they should continually sing praises to God there, namely at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Matins. He offered many gifts there—fields, vineyards, houses, male and female servants, various livestock, and other movable goods—and endowed it with them.

He also renewed all the roof-work of the title-church of Pammachius of Saints John and Paul, which had decayed over the years that had passed.

### 348

This distinguished priest, out of his great love for the confession of the blessed Peter, adorned its entire interior with the purest gold, arranged in plates and in various scenes, adding a weight of three hundred pounds. On the upper doorpost of that sacred confession he placed thirteen pounds of pure gold, and likewise twenty-five pounds on the lower threshold of the confession of that apostle.

He carefully renewed the altar-front above the same confession and at the right and left beside the steps of that confession, adding one hundred and thirty-six pounds of silver [Note: [Col. 1193] B reads *cariosum*.]. He also most brilliantly adorned its scenes with eighteen pounds of the purest gold.

At the same time, he renewed ten *canthara* in that church of God and the Apostle, adding one hundred pounds of silver to them. Before the silver doors he made twelve silver baskets, weighing thirty-six pounds. Likewise, in the tower he made twelve silver baskets, weighing forty-five pounds there. In that same church of the blessed Peter he made, among various crowns, silver dolphins weighing one hundred pounds.

### 349

In the church of the blessed apostle Paul, after the model of those he had placed in the church of Saint Peter, he placed silver dolphins weighing one hundred and eighty pounds. Likewise, in the church of the Savior called the Constantinian basilica, he made silver dolphins weighing thirty pounds.

In the church of Saint Peter he also made twelve silver baskets in various chapels, weighing forty pounds in all. He made screens in the presbytery, on the men’s and women’s sides, of the purest silver, weighing one hundred and thirty pounds. He also made other screens at the head of the presbytery before the confession, of silver, weighing one hundred and four pounds in all.

In the church of the holy Mother of God Mary across the Tiber he made five silver baskets, weighing fifteen pounds in all.

In the basilica of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, on the altar of that Manger, he made plates of the purest gold painted with scenes, weighing one hundred and five pounds in all. Inside the aforementioned confession, he made two silver panels, weighing fifteen pounds in all.

### 350

He newly restored the church of the blessed martyr Agnes, or the basilica of the blessed Emerentiana, and likewise the church of the blessed Nicomedes situated outside the Porta Nomentana, as well as the cemetery of the blessed martyr Hippolytus beside Saint Lawrence. These had decayed from ancient times.

In the same way, he restored the church of the blessed martyr Stephen, situated beside the aforementioned cemetery of Saint Hippolytus. In the confession of the blessed apostle Paul he made an image of the purest gold, in the form of the Gospel books, placed inside above the most sacred body of that apostle; it weighed twenty pounds.

### 351

This distinguished bishop, foremost in every good work, newly dedicated and established the monastery of Saints Adrian and Lawrence, which had been decaying in ruins from ancient times and was being inhabited by laypeople like a crypt. That excellent bishop restored it anew in the name of the aforementioned saints, Adrian and Lawrence. There he donated many things, both gold and silver, as well as fields, estates of dependents, various livestock, and movable goods.

He established that in the basilica of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary at the Manger, and in the other monasteries established there, those who sang praises to God day and night should recite the customary offices.

There, in the confession of the blessed martyr Lawrence outside the walls, the farsighted bishop made an image of the purest gold in the form of the Gospel books, containing the likeness of that blessed Lawrence; it weighed fifteen pounds.

### 352

In the church of the Savior called the Constantinian basilica, he made three golden bowls (*gabatae*) before the vestibule of the altar, weighing ten pounds. In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God at the Manger, he also made silver dolphins among various crowns, weighing twenty-four pounds.

That outstanding and eminent bishop made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter at the body an image that had formerly been of silver—of the Savior, the holy Mother of God, and the holy apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew—of the purest gold and of marvelous size, weighing two hundred pounds.

### 353

This most distinguished bishop and powerful preacher of the true faith sent his representatives—namely, Peter, a priest of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, a devout and venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabas, called Cella Nova—to the emperor Constantine and his mother Irene.

Through his apostolic letters he exhorted them and faithfully preached to them concerning the restoration of the sacred images, explaining how, on the basis of the testimonies of Scripture and the tradition of reliable Fathers, they had been orthodoxly venerated from ancient times up to that day in the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church.

The aforementioned emperors venerated and embraced that apostolic letter and caused a council of three hundred and fifty bishops to be assembled at Nicaea. In accordance with the teaching of the apostolic letter, these bishops indeed believed. Publishing their judgment, they decreed and defined through the universal synod, by unanimous assertion, that images should be honored and erected.

The aforementioned envoys brought that synod back with them in the Greek language, together with the document signed by the sacred imperial hands. The distinguished bishop ordered it to be translated into Latin and placed in the sacred library, thereby making there an everlasting memorial worthy of the orthodox faith.

This same eminent pope adorned the altar of the blessed apostle Paul, together with the doors of that confession, with pure gold and sacred scenes, decorating it magnificently; it weighed one hundred and thirty pounds. He also completely restored the roof-work of the title-church of the Four Crowned Saints, which was in ruins, placing many beams there.

He made a paten and chalice of the purest gold in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter for the daily offices; together they weighed twenty-four pounds.

Likewise, the most blessed man made in the church of the holy Mother of God Mary at the Manger a paten and sacred chalice of refined gold, weighing twenty pounds.

In the title-church of Eudoxia, namely that of the blessed apostle Peter at the Chains, he made twelve baskets weighing thirty-six pounds, and thirty-five dolphins among various crowns, weighing eight pounds. He also newly repaired the church of the blessed Sabina, situated in the territory of Ferentinum.

This beneficent bishop made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul a paten of refined gold together with a sacred chalice; together they weighed twenty pounds.

### 354

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr Lawrence outside the walls, he made a paten and sacred chalice of the purest gold; together they weighed fifteen pounds.

Then the administrator of the diaconia of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, because of fear of the temple that appeared to stand above it, overturned it and destroyed that basilica from its foundations over the same church. Since he was entirely unable to restore it, the farsighted bishop, moved by compassion and love for those martyrs, restored it from its foundations on a larger scale and in an exceedingly splendid form.

When the most compassionate bishop heard that the basilica of the monastery of the blessed martyr Anastasius of Christ, together with its baptistery, *egumenarchium*, and other buildings, had been burned through the negligence of the monks in the silence of night, from its foundations to the top of the roof, he ran there quickly at first light. He found it still burning, with only the martyr’s shrine removed and lying in the middle of the courtyard. All the other sacred objects and liturgical vessels, both in the church and in the vestiarian treasury, had been consumed by the fire.

With immense grief, he and his ministers vied with one another in extinguishing the fire. Immediately, with all his strength, he rebuilt from the fiery ruins and restored to a better condition the aforementioned church, together with the treasury, the *egumenarchium*, and the other buildings. He also supplied it with more sacred objects, liturgical vessels, and ornaments than those that had been burned there.

### 355

This bishop, protected by God, as it is said, saw that the walls of this Roman city had long lain in ruins and that, in many places, towers had been overturned to the ground. Through his most diligent effort, he assembled the whole cities of both Tuscia and Campania, together with the Roman people and their suburban inhabitants, as well as the whole ecclesiastical patrimony. Preaching to everyone and distributing provisions from the apostolic expenditures and stores, he restored the entire City in its circuit, renewing and adorning everything.

In particular, on the main altar of the church of the blessed apostle Peter he made various scenes of the purest gold, weighing five hundred and ninety-seven pounds. Inside the confession he made an image in the form of the Gospel books from refined gold, weighing twenty pounds in all, and grilles before the same confession of the purest gold, weighing fifty-six pounds.

Thus, for the altar and within the sacred confession on every side, he made an image in the form of the Gospel books, together with work on the lower and upper doorposts, the grilles, and around the body, all in refined gold, weighing one thousand three hundred and twenty-eight pounds.

### 356

In the twentieth year of the aforementioned eminent pontiff, in the month of December, in the fifteenth indiction, the river Tiber, having overflowed its channel and risen, spread across the countryside. Because of the extreme inundation, it entered the gate called Flaminia, tore the gate from its foundations, and carried it as far as the arch called the Three Faccicelae. Meanwhile, in some places it also overtopped the walls.

Beyond the basilica of Saint Mark, it overturned the portico called the Palatine. Spreading through the streets as far as the bridge of Antoninus, it overturned the wall itself and, having passed out, joined its channel again. Thus, on the Via Lata, the water of that river rose to a height of more than two human statures; and the waters descended as far as the gate of the blessed Peter and the Milvian Bridge, then subsided as the force of the river abated.

It overturned houses and devastated fields, tearing out and uprooting trees and crops. Indeed, most of the Romans were unable to sow at that time, and consequently a great tribulation threatened.

When the distinguished bishop heard this—because for three days the river ran through the city as though through a channel—he gave himself over to profound lamentation. He remained prostrate on the ground in prayer, and the merciful Lord, moved by his prayers, brought the flood to an end after three days.

The water nevertheless kept Rome invaded for many days. The distinguished bishop, moved by divine inspiration, carried food by small boats to those remaining on the Via Lata, so that they would not die of hunger, since the extreme height of the waters prevented them from leaving their dwellings. Afterwards, when the water had dried up, he consoled all those in that district of the Via Lata in his house.

The same most sacred bishop also carefully brought from the city of Perugia large bronze doors of marvelous workmanship and erected them beautifully at the tower in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

In the title-church of his nourisher, the blessed Mark, he made a paten and sacred chalice of the purest gold, weighing eleven pounds. He also made four silver chalices, weighing twelve pounds.

357. Furthermore, in the basilica of the blessed Cosmas and Damian he likewise presented a paten and chalice of refined gold, weighing together eleven pounds. He also bestowed in the deaconry of Saint Adrian a paten and chalice of pure gold, weighing together eleven pounds. He made two silver arches in the deaconry of the martyr Saint Adrian, weighing twenty pounds, and three silver arches in the basilica of Saint Martina, weighing thirty pounds. Indeed, in the church of the ever-virgin Mary, which is called “at the Martyrs,” he renewed the silver ciborium, which had been consumed by age; he added sixty pounds of silver to it and newly restored it to its former place. He also made a silver arch in that venerable church, weighing twelve pounds.

This most blessed pontiff did all these things usefully and anew, applying himself both to alms for the poor and to the adornment of the holy churches. Having completed his course and most diligently preserved the orthodox faith, he ended his life at God’s summons and departed to eternal rest. He conducted two ordinations in the month of March: twenty-four priests, seven deacons, and 185 bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction. He lived in the time of King Charlemagne.

From the Royal, Mazarine, and Thuane manuscripts.

No. 358, line 1: Leo, born a Roman. Same line: twenty days. Line 2: in the patriarchal vestments (M: *patriarchii*). Line 3: especially learned. Line 4: he was a man of character. Line 5: where he neither [spared] the foremost monks nor the servants of God. Line 6: with them. Line 7: the Scriptures, so that through care for the poor they might redeem their souls by almsgiving.

[Col. 1209]

358. Leo III, a Roman by birth, son of Azuppius, held office for twenty years, five months, and seventeen days. From childhood he had been nourished and educated in the wardrobe of the patriarchium, and spiritually instructed in every ecclesiastical discipline. Learned both in the psalter and in the sacred divine Scriptures, he was made a subdeacon and advanced to the rank of priest. For he was a chaste man, eloquent in speech, and steadfast in spirit. Whenever he found some eminent monk or servant of God engaged in divine discourse and prayer, he never ceased to devote himself wholly to him. He was exceedingly cheerful in almsgiving and, moreover, a most assiduous visitor of the sick, preaching to them from the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1209] “the Scriptures”], so that they might redeem their souls [Note: [Col. 1209] “that, through concern for the poor, they might redeem their souls”] by almsgiving.

359. Many, assenting to his preaching, secretly distributed to the poor, day and night, whatever he commended for Christ’s sake, frequently offering to God the saving fruit of souls [Note: [Col. 1209] alternatively, “offering”]. While he thus shone especially in that wardrobe office, and himself directed its most diligent administration, he was most lovingly cherished by all. Therefore, by divine inspiration and with one accord and will, he was chosen by all the priests and nobles, by all the clergy, and likewise by the magnates and the entire Roman people, through God’s prompting, on the feast [Note: [Col. 1209] “birthday/feast-day”] of the blessed first martyr Stephen. On the following day, the feast [Note: [Col. 1209] “birthday/feast-day”] of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, he was ordained pontiff in the apostolic see, to the praise and glory of almighty God.

He was a defender of ecclesiastical interests, a most valiant assailer of adversaries, extremely gentle, and an illustrious and benevolent lover of that Church: slow to anger and swift to compassion, repaying evil to no one for evil and granting no vengeance according to desert. Rather, pious and merciful, from the time of his ordination he strove to do justice to all [Note: [Col. 1209] “he seemed”]. [Note: Baronius, year 796.] He greatly increased the roga—that is, the stipend—of his clergy in the presbyterium [Note: [Col. 1209] “roga, that is, stipend”]. In the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, his patron, he made a golden thurible before the entrance of the altar, weighing seventeen pounds; and in the confession of the same apostle, gold curtains of the purest gold with various gems, weighing forty-nine pounds. He also made three large silver crowns, weighing three hundred and seven pounds, and white figured-silk curtains having in the middle a cross of chrysoclavus [Note: [Col. 1209] “chrysoclavo”], together with one border of fundatum.

360. He entirely renewed the repaired roofs of the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle—that is, the principal nave, another nave above the altar, the quadriporticus, and the font—as well as the area before the silver doors. He also entirely restored anew the tower with its chambers, from bottom to top. Above all, he placed in the gable beneath the larger arch, for the adornment of the aforementioned Church, an image of the Savior, painted with the others in marvelous beauty. Likewise, in the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle and in the basilica of the Savior, he made and set up corresponding images [Note: [Col. 1209] “instar, that is, similar images”]. He also entirely restored, by his beneficent care, the repaired roofs of the title of blessed Anastasia, which through neglect had decayed from ancient times and were nearly falling.

361. Likewise he diligently renewed the title of Saint Sabina. In this church the same eminent bishop made five silver crowns, weighing fourteen pounds; two baskets, weighing three and a half pounds; and nine pierced bowls, weighing eleven pounds [Note: [Col. 1209] “intersatiles”].

In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, called at the Manger, he made a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing six hundred and eleven pounds; silver curtains at the entrance of the presbyterium, weighing eighty pounds; and one large white silk curtain having a border and a cross of fundatum. On the most sacred major altar he made a cloth of chrysoclavus, bearing the history of the Nativity and of Saint Simeon, and in the middle a chrismon.

In the vaulted chamber of the same church and in the quadriporticus, he also provided three silver crowns, weighing there one hundred and forty-five pounds and nine ounces [Note: [Col. 1209] “one hundred and fifty-five”]. Meanwhile, in the basilica of the blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he made three silver images—the Savior, the blessed apostle Peter, and Saint Lawrence—together weighing fifty-four and a half pounds; and on the sacred altar a silk cloth of chrysoclavus, bearing the history of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.

He also renewed the roofs of the blessed martyrs Felix and Audactus near Saint Paul the Apostle; of the basilica of Saint Menna; of the title of the blessed martyr of Christ, Vitalis; and of the cemetery of the blessed Sixtus and Cornelius on the Appian Way. Likewise, he renewed the cemetery of Saint Zoticus on the Labican Way.

[Col. 1211]

362. He likewise restored the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, situated in Fonticana, which had decayed through age. In the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the world, this bishop made a confession and gold curtains of refined gold with precious gems, like those of Saint Peter the Apostle, weighing one hundred and fifty-six pounds. Above the sacred altar he made a golden image bearing the Savior and the twelve apostles, weighing seventy-five pounds; and he newly made the vaulted chamber of that basilica after the model of Saint Peter’s.

He also made three silver crowns, one weighing two hundred and twenty pounds; fifteen large stamped figured-silk veils, having a border and a cross of batthin or fundatum; forty-three large mixed veils of quadruple fabric, hanging in arches; twenty small stamped veils, decorated with quadruple fabric and hanging in smaller arches; ten small veils of stauracin hanging in arches, and another ten, of which three have a border of chrysoclavus; four veils of matching Alexandrian thread; and one rotating alithine veil, having a rotating border with lattices, a jewelled cross in the middle, and four matching wheels of Tyrian thread.

363. In the basilica of Saint Andrew at Saint Peter the Apostle he made silver curtains, weighing eighty pounds. In the basilica of the Savior, called Constantinian, he made a vaulted chamber of marvelous size.

This beneficent bishop made, for the major altar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, a cloth of chrysoclavus adorned with precious gems, bearing very large representations of the Savior granting to the blessed apostle Peter the power of binding and loosing, and of the Passion of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, resplendent on the feast of the apostles.

364. He also made, on the altar in the title of Eudoxia, a Tyrian cloth having large griffins, two wheels of chrysoclavus with a cross, and a border of batthin and chrysoclavus.

In the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle he made a silver lararium before the presbyterium, with thirty silver bowls and an octagonal basket in the middle, weighing sixty-three pounds. In the silver fountains, both around the altar and in the presbyterium, he set silver candleholders weighing there two hundred and twelve pounds.

On the altar of blessed Petronilla he placed one cloth of stauracin, having a border of purple silk or chrysoclavus. In the basilica of the Savior, also called Constantinian, he made a cloth bearing the history of the Crucified One and of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with a border of chrysoclavus. In the basilica of Saint Clement he made one cloth of stauracin with a border of chrysoclavus. He also made very beautiful veils of stauracin in the silver arches of the church of the Apostle of God.

365. In the title of blessed Susanna, where he had been ordained priest, this eminent pontiff found the church partially ruined and its walls decayed for a very long time. Out of great love he enlarged the building, excavated deeply and laid a very firm new foundation; after clearing the level ground, he wonderfully raised upon those foundations a church with a very spacious apse, marvelous mosaic summits, a decorated apse and presbyterium, and a pavement adorned with beautiful marbles.

On the right and left he also built its porticoes with marble columns. He established a baptistery there and offered the following gifts: three gold bowls of fundatum, weighing four and a half pounds; two jewelled gold crosses, weighing one pound; silver rods, weighing three pounds and seven ounces; one silver lamp, weighing five pounds; and three silver images, weighing thirty-five pounds.

366. He made the confession of that altar from the purest silver, weighing one hundred and three pounds and two ounces; eight silver columns, two gammadia, two arches, five silver crosses, and fifteen bowls, together weighing one hundred and fifty pounds; and a diacopton cross, weighing fourteen pounds.

He made a basket of cedar wood (cede cafotii), weighing twelve and a half pounds; one large silver crown with thirty-two dolphins, weighing thirty-two pounds; one silver basket weighing eighteen pounds, and another silver basket likewise weighing eighteen pounds; gilded silver straining vessels, weighing four pounds and three ounces; silver bowls with gilded griffins, weighing two pounds; and two silver crowns with eighteen dolphins, weighing nineteen pounds.

Moreover, the same eminent bishop made in that church one cloth of chrysoclavus with a chrysoclavus border; another cloth of batthin with a cross of chrysoclavus in the middle; four jewelled panels of chrysoclavus; and four gammadia of chrysoclavus in that cloth, with a border of chrysoclavus.

367. In the Lateran patriarchium he made a great triclinium, surpassing all triclinia in the splendor of its size. He laid its most solid foundations, adorned the circuit of its light with marble, and paved it with patterned marble.

He decorated its chamber with various columns—both porphyry and white, sculpted with vessels and lilies—and with doorposts. He adorned the chamber with a mosaic apse; and in the two wings he decorated two apses, painting diverse histories above the marble incrustation around the whole circuit.

In the basilica of blessed Prisca he made one gilded, fundatum chalice and three crowns, one with ten dolphins and the other two numbering nine; also eight bowls, together weighing twenty-nine pounds; and a white figured-silk cloth ornamented around with Byzantine purple, with a cross of chrysoclavus at the front.

[Col. 1213]

368. While this venerable and most holy bishop lived in the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church according to ecclesiastical order, maintained the rite of orthodox faith, and magnificently adorned great buildings both in the patriarchium and in various churches [Note: [Col. 1213] Baronius, year 799], it happened one day that he was proceeding, as usual, in the litanies which all call the Major Litanies.

There the people ought reverently to come out to meet him, and he was to celebrate with the priests the annual litanies and solemnities of the Mass, offering prayers to almighty God for the safety of the Christian people [Note: [Col. 1213] “Christian”]. According to ancient tradition, the notary of the holy Roman Church had proclaimed that litany in the church of the blessed martyr of Christ George on his feast-day. All men and women then gathered in devout companies at the church of the blessed martyr of Christ Lawrence, called Lucina, where the aforesaid station was held.

369. When the venerable pontiff had left the patriarchium, the wicked and unspeakable Paschal, primicerius, met him without a chasuble and hypocritically begged his pardon, saying: “Because I am ill, I have come without a chasuble.” The most holy bishop pardoned him; Campulus the sacellarius did likewise.

In their treachery they proceeded together in pontifical attendance, speaking to him sweet words that were not in their hearts. These evil, wicked, perverse, false Christians—utter pagans and sons of the devil—satanically banded together. Filled with evil intent, they stood secretly armed on the road before the monastery of Saints Stephen and Silvester, founded by Pope Lord Paul. Suddenly leaping from their ambush, they rushed upon him impiously to slaughter him—horrible to relate—without any reverence, with Paschal standing at his head and Campulus at his feet, according to their wicked plan.

All the people around him, unarmed and prepared for God’s service, were terrified by the weapons and took flight. The ambushers and workers of evil, in Jewish fashion, disregarding every divine and human claim to honor, seized him like beasts, threw him to the ground, stripped him by tearing his garments, and cruelly tried to gouge out his eyes and wholly blind him. His tongue was cut off, and, as they then believed, they left him blind and mute in the middle of the street.

370. These malignant men, Paschal and Campulus, true pagans and impious men, dragged him to the church of that monastery before the confession. Before the venerable altar itself they again more cruelly tore out his eyes and tongue, beat and mangled him with various blows and clubs, and left him half alive, rolling in blood before the altar. Afterwards they kept him under guard in that monastery.

Fearing that he might be stolen away by Christian men, they devised a wicked plan. As the hegumen of the monastery of Saint Erasmus [Note: [Col. 1213] “Gerasimus”] testified, the malignant Paschal, then primicerius, Campulus the sacellarius, and Maurus Nepesinus secretly summoned him by night and sent him to the said monastery of Saint Silvester with many wicked accomplices in their crime.

They then removed him by night from there [Note: [Col. 1213] “dragging him away”] and brought him to the monastery of Saint Erasmus, shutting him in close and narrow custody. But almighty God, who in foreknowledge had long borne their malice patiently, wonderfully destroyed their wicked designs.

For, through God’s cooperation and the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, while the aforesaid pope was being committed to custody in the monastery of Saint Erasmus by those executioners, by the Lord’s will and the intercession of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he recovered his sight and his tongue was restored for speech.

371. To show his customary mercy and a great miracle upon his servant, almighty God caused faithful Christian men—namely, the chamberlain Albinus and other God-fearing faithful men—to remove him secretly from that enclosure and bring him to the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where his most sacred body rests.

Hearing and seeing the wonders of God, who had rescued the innocent and just pontiff from the hands of his enemies, they all glorified the Lord God, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone performs great wonders and has not forsaken those who hope in him” [Note: [Col. 1213] Psalm 35]. In him, however, he fulfilled his mercy, so that God’s glory and his wonders might be made manifest in him, as he promised those who hope in him; as the Psalmist says:

“The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” [Note: [Col. 1215] Psalm 26.]

And again:

“Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” [Note: [Col. 1215] Psalm 118].

Truly the Lord rescued him from darkness, restored his light and his tongue for speech, made all his limbs sound [Note: [Col. 1215] “him”], and wonderfully guided and strengthened him in every undertaking.

As great as was the joy of faithful Christian men, so greatly were those men distressed by grief and sadness: not knowing what to do and believing themselves in danger, they sought to kill themselves. When they found nothing else to do, they plundered and destroyed the house of Albinus, faithful servant of Saint Peter the Apostle and of the pontiff.

As the aforesaid pontiff entered the hall of Saint Peter the Apostle, the glorious duke Winichis of Spoleto immediately met him with his army. Seeing the supreme pontiff able to see and speak, he reverently received him and brought him to Spoleto, glorifying and praising God, who had made him illustrious through such wonders.

On hearing this, Roman faithful from diverse cities came to him; and with bishops, priests, Roman clergy, and civic leaders from some of those cities, he proceeded to the most excellent Lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

As soon as that most Christian, orthodox, eminent, and most merciful king heard, he sent Archbishop and chaplain Hildivald and Count Ascharius to meet him. Afterwards he sent his own son, the most excellent King Pippin, with other counts. When the great king himself met him, he received him venerably and honorably, as the vicar of Saint Peter the Apostle, with hymns and spiritual songs; embracing, they kissed one another with tears.

As the aforesaid pontiff began “Glory to God in the highest,” and all the clergy joined, a prayer was given over the whole people. Then the most gracious Lord Charles, great king, beholding the pontiff, gave thanks to God, who through the intercession of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul had worked such great wonders upon his servant and reduced the aforesaid wicked men to nothing.

372. The most serene king kept him with himself in great honor for some time. On hearing this, the aforesaid wicked men and sons of the devil, after committing dreadful and wicked burnings on the possessions and property of Saint Peter the Apostle, attempted—God opposing them—to bring false accusations against the most holy pontiff and to send them after him to the said king; but they were utterly unable to prove them [Note: [Col. 1215] “were able”], for they uttered such unspeakable charges in order by their plots and wickedness to humiliate the holy Church.

While the aforesaid pontiff was residing with the most merciful great king in great and fitting honor, archbishops, bishops, and other priests came from every direction, together with the counsel [Note: [Col. 1215] “son”] of that most pious great king and all the eminent Franks. With God as guide, they honorably sent him back [Note: [Col. 1215] “returning”] to Rome and his apostolic see with the immense honor that was fitting [Note: [Col. 1215] “dismissed”].

Through each city they escorted him to Rome, receiving him as though he were the apostle himself. Then, in overwhelming joy, the Romans received their shepherd on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle: all the chief clergy with all clerics, the magnates and senate, all the soldiery, and the entire Roman people, with nuns, deaconesses, most noble matrons, and all women; likewise all the schools of foreigners—the Franks, Frisians, Saxons, and Lombards.

All assembled at the Milvian Bridge with standards, banners, and spiritual songs, received him, and led him to the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, where he celebrated the Mass. All partook together in faith of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

373. On the following day, celebrating according to ancient custom the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, he entered Rome with great joy and gladness and went into the Lateran patriarchium.

Some days later the most faithful envoys who had come with him in pontifical service—Hildivald and Arno, most reverend archbishops; Cunibert, Bernhard [Note: [Col. 1215] “Bealiard”], Hattho, and Tesse, most reverend and holy bishops; Flaccus, bishop-elect; and the glorious counts Helmgoth, Rothegar, and Germanus—sat in the triclinium of Pope Leo himself.

For more than one week, questioning those most execrable criminals about what grievance Paschal and Campulus and their followers had had against their pontiff [Note: [Col. 1215] “against the pontiff”], they found that they had nothing to say against him.

374. The aforesaid envoys of the great king therefore arrested them and sent them into Francia.

Shortly afterward the great king entered the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle and was received with great honor. He caused archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the nobility of the Franks and Romans to assemble in that church. The great king and the most blessed pontiff sat together and caused the most holy archbishops and abbots also to sit, while the other priests and the Frankish and Roman nobles stood, in order that the charges made against the beneficent pontiff might be refuted [Note: [Col. 1217] B, “examined”].

All the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, after unanimous deliberation, said:

“We do not dare judge the apostolic see, which is the head of all God’s churches; for all of us are judged by it and by its vicar, while it is judged by no one, as has been the custom from ancient times. But as the supreme pontiff himself shall decide, we will obey canonically.”

The venerable bishop said:

“I follow the footsteps of my predecessor pontiffs, and I am ready to clear myself of such false accusations as have wickedly arisen against me.”

375. On the next day, in the same church of Saint Peter the Apostle, with all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots present together, all the Franks in the service of the great king, and all the Romans, the aforesaid venerable pontiff, embracing the four holy Gospels of Christ in their presence, ascended the ambo before all and said in a clear voice under oath:

“I have no knowledge of these false accusations which the Romans who wickedly persecuted me have laid upon me, nor do I know that I committed such deeds.”

When this had been done, all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and all the clergy, after a litany, gave praises to God, to the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary our Lady, to blessed Peter prince of the apostles, and to all God’s saints.

376. Thereafter, on the feast-day of our Lord Jesus Christ, all again gathered in the aforesaid basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle. The venerable beneficent pontiff then crowned him with his own hands with a most precious crown [Note: [Col. 1217] “Charlemagne”].

Seeing the great protection and love which he had shown toward the holy Roman Church and its vicar, all the faithful Romans cried out unanimously in a loud voice, by God’s will and that of blessed Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven:

“To Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor, life and victory!”

[Note: See Baronius, year 800.]

Invoking many saints before the sacred confession of Saint Peter the Apostle, they said this three times, and he was constituted emperor of the Romans by all. Immediately the most holy bishop and pontiff anointed with holy oil Charles and his most excellent son, the king, on that day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When Mass had been completed, after the celebration of the Masses, the most serene Lord Emperor offered a silver table with its feet, weighing [lacuna].

377. In the confession of that Apostle of God he offered, together with his most excellent son the king and his daughters, various vessels of the purest gold for the service of that table, weighing [lacuna]; also a gold crown with large gems, hanging above the altar, weighing fifty-five pounds; a large gold paten with various gems, weighing thirty pounds; a large chalice with gems and two handles, weighing fifty-eight pounds; likewise a large fundatum chalice with a cup, weighing thirty-seven pounds; and another large fundatum chalice, weighing thirty-six pounds.

Upon the most sacred altar of Saint Peter the Apostle, and also in the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle, he offered a smaller silver table with its feet, weighing fifty-five pounds, with various silver vessels of marvelous size pertaining to the use of that table.

378. In the basilica of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, called Constantinian, he offered a cross with hyacinth gems, which the beneficent pontiff ordered to be carried in front in the litany at the request of that most pious emperor; likewise an altar with silver columns and a ciborium; and a Gospel-book of the purest gold adorned with gems, weighing [lacuna].

In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God Mary at the Manger, he offered large silver siclae, weighing [lacuna].

Afterwards, when the most wicked criminals—Paschal and Campulus and their followers—were brought before the most pious Lord Emperor, with the noblest Franks and Romans standing around and all reproaching them for their evil schemes and deeds, Campulus rebuked Paschal, saying:

“An evil hour was it when I saw your face, since you then sent me into this danger.”

The others did likewise; each condemning the other, they disclosed their own crimes. When the most pious emperor recognized them as so cruel and wicked, he sent them into exile in regions of Francia.

The aforesaid most holy pontiff made beside the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, in the great triclinium, a marvelously beautiful apse decorated with mosaic, with two shining apses on the right and left above marble and painting. He also finely made a pavement laid with marble patterns and other large buildings, both at the ascent of the stair and behind that triclinium.

In the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle he made a cloth of chrysoclavus adorned with precious gems, bearing the history of the Lord’s Resurrection; and between the silver arches, very beautiful white silk veils and veils of stauracin.

After his return, out of great affection, he made for this patron a completely new marble presbyterium of great beauty, finely carved and erected. Above the major altar he also made four alithine figured-silk tetra-veils, with chrysoclavus stars and roses.

[Col. 1219]

379. On the same altar he made a Tyrian cloth with representations of the crucified Lord. In the church of the blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the world, he made four alithine figured-silk tetra-veils; a white chrysoclavus altar-cloth bearing the history of the holy Resurrection; another chrysoclavus cloth bearing the history of the Lord’s Nativity and of the Holy Innocents; and another Tyrian cloth bearing the history of the blind man enlightened and the Resurrection.

The same most holy bishop made in the basilica of blessed Mary at the Manger a white chrysoclavus cloth bearing the history of the holy Resurrection, and another cloth with roundels of chrysoclavus, bearing histories of the Annunciation and of Saints Joachim and Anne.

In the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls, he made a white rose-patterned cloth with chrysoclavus, and another white cloth of chrysoclavus stauracin with pearls over Lawrence’s holy body.

In the title of Callixtus he made a chrysoclavus cloth of Byzantine batthin, bearing the history of the Lord’s Nativity and of Saint Simeon.
