No. 426, line 1: “seven months.” Line 2: “in the patriarchium of the Savior, that is, the Lateran.” Lines 3–4: “distinguished by birth, devoted to holy discipline, and diligent.” Line 4: “already dead.” Line 5: “his lord Pope Leo succeeded him”; elsewhere, “observing.” Line 6: “he led him by his humble conduct to the order of subdeacons, and thus he reached the rank of the priesthood.” Thus it happened, as in line 5 of the following number.

No. 427, lines 5–6: “the aforementioned lord Pope Leo immediately, with fervor.” Line 7: “he was raised to the height of the pontificate.” “All of them with one affection.” Line 8: “leading [him] to the blessed Peter.” Line 9: “consecrated pope of the city. This most holy man, already placed at the height of the pontificate.”

[Col. 1257B] No. 428, line 2: “he undertook the journey to Francia for the Church”; elsewhere, “the lord.” Line 3: “when he had arrived in Francia”; elsewhere, “and with rejoicing was received by the aforesaid prince and the people of the Franks, as the tongue can scarcely recount”; “and the Lord deigned to grant him such favor …” Line 6: “he might obtain”; same line: “so that that same prince, out of love for him, …” Line 7: “the … omits ‘which he had …’; ‘a cross of his own.’” Line 8: “through the page of the decree.” Line 10: “held captive”; elsewhere, “which he restored to the holy Roman Church.” Line 12: “he brought back.” “Here, by a divine voice,” etc., as in line 14 of the following number.

[Col. 1258A] No. 429, line 13: “He held ordinations in the month of December, priests …”

From another Thuane manuscript:

No. 426, line 4: “already dead.” Line 6: “he practiced humble conduct.”

No. 427, lines 5–6: “the aforementioned.” Line 6: “immediately”; elsewhere, “that same most holy man.” Lines 7–8: “all with one affection.” Line 9: “pope of the city.”

No. 428, line 3: “when he reached Francia.” Line 4: “to recount.” Line 5: “he granted generously, so that … whatever he had requested from him.” Line 7: “court.” Line 8: “through the page of the decree.” Line 10: “all exiles”; elsewhere, “whom he restored to the holy Roman Church.”

No. 429, line 1: “he likewise made a silver …”; line 2: “number … and in the monastery mentioned above”; line 4: “with gems, weighing 10 pounds. He also made in Saint Theodore in the Sabellum …”

In Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript:

[Col. 1258B] No. 426, line 6: “he practiced humble conduct, and …”

No. 427, line 9: “pope of the city.”

No. 428, line 2: “of the Church, of Francia.” Lines 4–5: “so much for him.” Line 6: “he obtained.”

No. 429, line 6: “he also made in Saint Theodore in the Sabellum.”]

[Col. 1255]

### 426

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Marinus, held office for seven years and seven months

[Note: [Col. 1255] B: “seven months”; 3.]

From his earliest youth he was nourished and educated in the Lateran patriarchium under the late lord Pope Adrian. Born of a noble lineage and most illustrious family, while still a child he devoted himself most diligently to learning the knowledge of sacred discipline.

When the aforementioned lord Pope Adrian of blessed memory had died, lord Pope Leo succeeded him. Observing that the aforesaid lord Stephen possessed good conduct and humility, he promoted him to the order of subdeacons.

### 427

Seeing that he devoted himself more and more to spiritual studies, with the Lord’s favor he advanced him to the rank of deacon. From that time, endowed in many ways with spiritual studies, he showed the greatest care both in proclaiming divine and evangelical words skillfully and clearly to the people and in carrying out ecclesiastical tradition.

Thus the grace of the Holy Spirit shone in his heart, so that in everything he was proved effective and capable. And so it happened that, when the aforementioned lord Pope Leo departed this life, this eminent and most holy man Stephen, who was loved by the Roman people with the most fervent affection, was immediately elected to the sacred height of the pontificate.

They all, with one affection and equal love, led him to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, and, by God’s providential ordering, he was consecrated pope of the world.

### 428

Once this most holy man had assumed the pontificate, he undertook a journey to Francia to the most pious and serene lord Emperor Louis, in order to confirm the peace and unity of the holy Church of God.

When he reached Francia, he was received by the aforesaid most pious prince and by the people of the Franks with such honor and exaltation that it can scarcely be described in words. The Lord deigned to grant him such favor that he obtained in every respect everything he is known to have requested from him.

So greatly did this most pious prince love him that, beyond all the gifts he granted him, he conceded from his own treasury, for perpetual use by the blessed apostle Peter, a royal estate in the territory of Francia through a charter of grant

[Note: [Col. 1257] B reads “through a charter of receipt.”]

The same sacred bishop, taking as his example our Redeemer, who for our sake deigned to descend from heaven and rescue us from the captivity of the devil, brought back with him, out of mercy for the Church, all the exiles who were held captive there because of their crimes and the transgressions they had committed against the holy Roman Church and against lord Pope Leo.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter “in Chains” he made a thurible of silver, gilded on top, weighing …

### 429

Likewise, he made a silver basin weighing … pounds. Similarly, he made silk curtains with a *periclysis* of *fundatum*, number …

He also made in the same church a *chrysoclave* vestment with gems, displaying the story of the blessed apostle Peter.

Likewise, he made *fundatum* curtains, number …

And in the monastery mentioned above he made a gold chalice adorned with gems, weighing … pounds, and a silver paten gilded on top, weighing … pounds.

Likewise, he made a gold cross adorned with gems, weighing … pounds.

The aforesaid venerable and distinguished pontiff also made in Saint Theodore in the Sabellum a gold cross adorned with gems and a silver chalice, weighing … pounds.

The aforesaid venerable and distinguished pontiff also made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter “in Chains” a paten and a silver chalice gilded on top, weighing … pounds.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a silver crown with its pendants, weighing … pounds.

Indeed, in the oratory of the holy martyr Barbara in the Subura he made a *fundatum* vestment. Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed Helena he made a *fundatum* vestment.

This man, taken from this light by divine calling, departed to eternal rest. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

He held one ordination in the month of December: nine priests, four deacons, and five bishops in various places. The episcopate was vacant for two days.

## C. PASCHAL. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 817; OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS, 4; OF LEO THE ARMENIAN, 4

[Note: [Col. 1271A]

[Col. 1259]

### 430

Paschal, a Roman by nationality, son of Bonosus, held office for seven years, five months

[Note: [Col. 1259] * three], and sixteen days [Note: [Col. 1259] * seventeen].

From the earliest age of his life he was devoted to divine worship and, in the patriarchium of the most holy Church, was imbued with the studies of divine and saving Scripture. He was especially instructed both in the Psalter and in the sacred pages of the New and Old Testament. Elegant and perfect in every virtue, he was first made a subdeacon and afterward honorably consecrated as deacon and priest.

He was a holy, chaste, pious, innocent, great-hearted man, devoted in speech and full of modesty; with great cheerfulness and joy he appropriately distributed among the poor in alms everything he possessed. In divine conversations he most frequently devoted himself, with diligent observance day and night, to religious and holy monks; and in prayers, vigils, and daily fasts he flourished humbly and honorably.

When his predecessor, the three-times-blessed lord Pope Leo, saw him so vigilant in study and devoted to religion, he entrusted to him for governance the monastery of the blessed Stephen the protomartyr beside the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

For it is written: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” [Note: [Col. 1259] Matthew 5].

He corrected, with sober and useful moderation, the gains of this temporal life for the sake of eternal life, and religiously adorned in his subjects both the example of good living and the correction of piety.

He also usefully prepared and supplied the necessities of hospitality for pilgrims and the lame who, for love of the blessed apostle Peter, came from distant regions to his threshold; and secretly and cheerfully distributed to them what they needed.

Every day he continued to grow in the work of God, until his predecessor, lord Pope Stephen, departed from this light to eternal blessedness.

When, therefore, the reputation of such good works spread especially far and wide, and almighty God consented that the governance of his Church should be suitably and moderately arranged under his pious direction, he was raised to the apostolic see, by one agreement and one identical will, with divine counsel intervening, by all the priests and nobles, the entire clergy, the leading men, and all the Roman people, to the praise and glory of almighty God.

For he was a most appropriate observer of the precepts of the Fathers, the institutions of pontiffs, the canons, and the sanctions of the laws; from the time of his ordination he was a most noble promulgator of every norm of justice; slow to anger and quick to show mercy.

Returning no evil for evil, nor inflicting vengeance according to anyone’s offense, he was always merciful, showing loving devotion to all the citizens and proving himself a lover and governor of the Roman people entrusted to him by God.

Of all the churches of God he was, with the greatest zeal and care, according to his customary religious devotion, a worshiper, restorer, and most devoted adorn­er in every respect.

### 431

This most blessed prelate searched out and found many bodies of saints. He carefully and honorably reburied them within the city for the honor and glory of God.

He also greatly enlarged the *rogam* for all his clergy in the presbytery and stored the whole treasure in the heavenly treasury, especially for captives and exiles. He redeemed with gold and silver not only men and women from overseas regions but also searched for them along distant roads, finding them throughout the regions of Spain and in individual places; like a good and true shepherd, he led them back to their own people.

He made for the sacred altar of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a vestment of extraordinary size, very beautiful and richly decorated, woven of gold and gems, representing the story of how that same apostle was delivered from chains by an angel.

In the same venerable basilica, before the entrance leading to the body, in a place enclosed by iron, he established an altar and most honorably placed in it the venerable body of the blessed Sixtus, martyr and bishop. Above it he also suitably constructed an arch decorated with mosaic.

In the same most sacred church of the blessed apostle Peter, beside the entrance leading to the blessed Petronilla, he beautifully built an oratory of the greatest size and beauty.

He decorated the columns and the vaulted spaces of the quadrified structure with mosaic and beautiful metals. In it he also honorably and memorially reburied the bodies of the most blessed martyrs Processus and Martinianus, for the honor and glory of almighty God.

In whose apse, a most beautiful gilded image of silver, with various scenes amid marble constructions
[Note: [Col. 1259] B: “incrustations.”]

…he set in orderly fashion; they weighed sixty-two and a half pounds. Likewise, silver lilies, weighing seventeen pounds and two ounces; and seven bowls of the purest silver, weighing altogether thirteen and a half pounds and two ounces. He also made three gilded silver images in the same venerable place: one of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and two of the blessed martyrs Processus and Martinianus, weighing altogether thirty-six pounds. He also offered, for the adornment of the aforesaid oratory, another image of the purest gold, weighing thirteen pounds and three ounces. Likewise, eight baskets of the purest silver, weighing altogether forty-three pounds.

### 432

Likewise, he installed there a silver basin for the sponge used in the nocturnal services, weighing seven pounds and nine ounces. Indeed, in the same venerable place he appropriately adorned keys in the form of a cross, made of the purest gold and embellished with wondrously beautiful gems; they weighed [lacuna]. There also he arranged a railing, overlaid with silver plates, weighing twenty pounds. Above it he set two silver arches and four *gammadiae*, which together weighed sixty pounds. He also surrounded the altar’s *propitiatorium*, adorned with silver plates, and most nobly encircled its sacred confession inside and out with its little rails; these together weighed [lacuna].

Above the altar of those most blessed martyrs he also installed two coverings, one of *fundatum* with a cross of *chrysoclavus*, and the other splendidly adorned with *quadrapulum*. He likewise adorned seven large coverings of *fundatum*, bordered with a *periclysis* of *blatthin*. Nor, we think, should this be passed over in silence: at that same time, through the devil’s cunning and the negligence of certain people of the English nation, their entire settlement—which in their language is called a *burgus*—

[Note: [Col. 1261] B: “*baxus*.”]

—was consumed by an overflowing blaze of fire, so thoroughly that not even traces of the former habitation could be found in that place. The fire’s raging conflagration also devastated almost the whole portico leading to the basilica of the prince of the apostles.

### 433

When the thrice-blessed pontiff perceived these things, as it were at the sounding of the night-watch, he suddenly ran barefoot and unshod, out of love for the Church of the blessed apostle Peter and because of the utter devastation of those pilgrims. Such mercy of almighty God attended his arrival that He did not permit the fire’s advance to cross the place where that angelic pontiff had first taken his stand. But while he entreated God’s clemency and the multitude of faithful who were present strove with him, the line of fire was extinguished through God’s mercy. Thus it happened that, continuing throughout the whole night until dawn, it remained halted in that place.

Afterward, when the most blessed shepherd considered the poverty of those pilgrims, which had arisen through the treachery of diabolical fraud, he bestowed upon their needs such gifts and benefits as he had always been accustomed to provide. He supplied abundantly gold and silver, clothing for their bodies, all other necessary provisions, and also a plentiful supply of timber, so that they could use it to restore their dwellings as they had previously been in that place. He also restored the portico, which had been ravaged by that same disaster, more suitably and more firmly than it had been before.

### 434

This distinguished and venerable pontiff made, in the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and his patron, coverings of *chrysoclavus* for the arches of the presbytery, bearing a narrative of the apostles’ miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through them, forty-six in number.

The church of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Praxedes, once built in ancient times but now so weakened by extreme age that it threatened to collapse from its foundations, was likewise raised by that same venerable pontiff into a better condition than before. Foreseeing its ruin and caring for the church, he was often there with vigilant attention. He moved it to another place not far away and rebuilt it better than it had previously been. He adorned its apse with mosaic work in various fitting colors. In the same way, he completed and beautifully decorated its triumphal arch with the same metals, in a wondrous manner.

This most blessed and distinguished pontiff, searching with pious concern for the many bodies of saints that had long lain in cemeteries, lest they remain neglected, gathered those he found and, with great reverence, transported and reburied them in the aforesaid church of Christ’s martyr Praxedes, which he had wondrously renewed and built. The whole Roman people accompanied the procession, while bishops, priests, deacons, and clerics sang praise to God.

While these things were being carried out through the innermost vigilance of the most holy and angelic prelate’s heart, so that the saints’ bodies deposited there might aid him by their prayers before the almighty Lord, who is continually pleased by them above the stars, he built on that site, from its foundations, a monastery, which he dedicated under the name of the holy virgin Praxedes. There he also gathered a Greek community and introduced it, so that day and night it might diligently offer, in Greek chant, psalmody and praises to almighty God and to his saints resting there.

Indeed, by bestowing upon the venerable monastery numerous estates, urban and rural properties and holdings, he enriched it excessively and abundantly. Moreover, in the same church he made an oratory of the holy martyr of Christ, Zeno, where he placed his most sacred body and magnificently adorned it with mosaic work.

### 435

In the same church he made a silver ciborium weighing eight hundred and ten pounds; indeed, he splendidly adorned the sacred altar’s *propitiatorium* with silver plates. Finally, he beautifully constructed and decorated its confession, enclosing it inside and out with its little rails; these together weighed three hundred pounds.

Above the same venerable altar he made a golden *spanoclystum* of yellow gold, adorned with various stones, weighing five pounds, two ounces, and a half. On the same sacred altar he made a covering of *chrysoclavus*, adorned with various narratives and of wondrous size and beauty. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he offered another covering of *chrysoclavus*, made of gold and gems, bearing a narrative of virgins with blazing torches, magnificently fashioned and decorated.

Finally, for the sacred body of the same virgin he offered an image made of embossed silver plates, weighing ninety-nine pounds. This most kindly prelate made, in the aforesaid monastery, an oratory of the blessed Agnes, virgin of Christ, adorned with wondrous beauty.

Finally, he rebuilt from its foundations the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, called *Dominica*. It had been built long ago and was already close to ruin; the aforesaid pontiff, through diligent vigilance, rebuilt and renewed it larger and better than it had previously been. He also magnificently adorned its apse with mosaic work.

There he offered many gifts, namely a silver ciborium weighing three hundred and thirty-two pounds. He elegantly adorned the sacred altar’s *propitiatorium* with silver plates. He likewise completed and marvelously adorned its confession, inside and out, with its little rails; it weighed one hundred and fifteen pounds and three ounces.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a bowl of the purest gold, weighing two pounds and eight ounces. He also made a silver arch and two small columns with two *gammadiae*, weighing [lacuna]. 

### 436

Indeed, on the sacred altar he made a covering of *chrysoclavus*, adorned with a narrative of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ and of wondrous beauty. Again, in the place mentioned above, he made a most beautiful covering of *stauracium*, with a border of *blatthin*. Likewise, another covering of Byzantine *blatthin*, bearing a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of the holy Mother of God and angels standing in attendance, with a border of *staurax*.

Similarly, another covering of *staurax*, bearing peacocks and, in the middle, a cross of *blatthin*. Moreover, two coverings of *quadrapulum*, bearing in the middle a cross of *blatthin*. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he made a covering woven with gold, with a border of *blatthin*. One red silk cover. He also made, around the altar, four red silk coverings with *gammadiae* and crosses of *quadrapulum*.

This venerable prelate offered on the beam before the altar’s vestibule three Tyrian coverings and five of *quadrapulum*. In the larger arches of the same church he made twenty coverings of *quadrapulum*, and in the arches of the presbytery four small coverings of *stauracium*; likewise, at the entrance to the presbytery, two Tyrian coverings.

This most kindly pontiff made, at the entrance of the aforesaid church, large curtains of *quadrapulum*, very splendidly adorned with a border of *fundatum*.

For this servant of Christ almighty, our Lord, and the aforesaid pontiff, continually foreseeing and diligently caring for the churches of God, came one day, intent on prayer, to the church of the holy virgin of God and martyr of Christ, Cecilia. Seeing that its walls, already badly shaken by extreme age, were threatening to fall even from their foundations—walls that had decayed through the defect of age over a long period and had remained for ancient times almost shattered by ruin—he applied himself to the work and began to build a new church on that site with magnificent workmanship, striving to complete it much better than it had been.

### 437

Nor do we think that the following should be passed over. One day, while he was going to the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that he might celebrate the vigils before that blessed apostle Peter according to his customary practice and, seated before his confession as Sunday dawned, might chant the morning praises, he was suddenly overcome by sleep. He saw a maiden standing beside him, of virginal appearance and adorned in angelic garments, who uttered these words:

“We give you many thanks, because you have abandoned the contest that you had long undertaken concerning me, lending your ears to reports spread abroad by deceptive accounts”—

[Note: [Col. 1263] B: “because you had long been willing to lend an ear to the uncertain report which had been spread about me through deceptive accounts,” or similar.]

—“for you were so devoted to me that we could speak to one another with our own mouths.”

The aforesaid pontiff, listening carefully and attentively to these words, began to inquire who she was who spoke to him in this way and by what name she was called. She replied:

“If you seek my name, I am called Cecilia, the servant of Christ.”

Then the supreme prelate said to her:

“How can I believe this, since a report was formerly spread that the body of the venerable martyr of Christ, Cecilia, had been secretly taken away by the men of the Lombard king Aistulf, when he was hostilely residing in Rome?”

When the venerable pontiff had told her this, the servant of almighty God said:

“It is entirely true that the Lombards sought me eagerly, desiring to find me; but, through the aid of my Lord Jesus Christ and the help of my Lady, the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, they were unable either to find me or to carry me farther away from here as they wished. Therefore, just as you have begun to seek how you may find me, do not cease devoting yourself to constant labor, because it has pleased the Lord God, for whose honor I suffered, that you should find me and place me in the church that you have newly built.”

Having said this, she vanished from the eyes of the one who was looking.

### 438

Then that venerable pontiff, after the morning praises had been completed, began to search here and there, with even greater effort, for where her most sacred body lay buried, in accordance with the judgment of so certain and undeniable a revelation. While he diligently sought it, God granting his efforts, he found it in the cemetery of Praetextatus, situated outside the Appian Gate. It was clothed in garments of gold, together with the body of her venerable spouse Valerian, and with the linen cloths of the martyr herself, full of the blood with which she had been struck by the wicked executioner and consecrated as a martyr of Christ the Lord, who reigns forever.

Those linen cloths, with which the blood of the holy martyr had been wiped, were found wrapped at the feet of that body, full of the most sacred blood from the executioner’s threefold blow. He handled all these things with his own hands, gathered them, and with great honor placed the body of that virgin, together with her dearest spouse Valerian, and the martyrs Tiburtius and Maximus, as well as the pontiffs Urban and Lucius, beneath the sacred altar inside the walls of this Roman city, in a church dedicated in the name of that holy martyr, for the praise and glory of almighty God.

For the honor and help of these saints, he built a monastery in honor of the virgins and martyrs Agatha and Cecilia, beside her church, in the place called the Lying Hills.

### 439

In it he established a congregation of monks serving God, to chant day and night the daily praises of the almighty Lord in the aforesaid title of Saint Cecilia. For the support of the community, the provision of lamps, its practical needs, and the stipends of the monks—and also out of the love and affection that he appeared to bear toward his predecessor, Pope Leo III of blessed memory—he took the hospice of Saint Peregrinus, situated by the blessed apostle Peter in the place called the Naumachia.

That hospice had been built by the same predecessor but, through the negligence and abandonment of its administrators, appeared to be wasting away in poverty. Therefore, providing for it with pious assistance, he confirmed by a document of his authority, for the aforesaid congregation of monks in the same monastery, the hospice together with its estates, farmsteads, holdings, tenants, houses, households, and everything that had justly and reasonably been given to it by his predecessor according to the provisions of the laws, as well as everything that he himself had piously added for the enlargement of the aforesaid monastery—fields, vineyards, houses, and rural dependents.

### 440

This most holy prelate, out of love for the venerable saints, had the apse of their church decorated with mosaic work, and made a ciborium of wondrous size in silver, weighing five hundred and a half pounds and eight ounces.

He then beautifully completed and decorated the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar, or its confession, inside and out with its little rails, made of silver plates; these together weighed sixty-four pounds and five ounces. For the sacred body of the same virgin he offered an image made of silver plates, weighing ninety-five pounds.

He also made, before the vestibule of the altar, a railing covered with silver plates and equipped with two columns. There he placed one arch and two *gammadiae*, weighing altogether one hundred and a half pounds. He offered there three gilded silver images, weighing altogether forty-eight and a half pounds.

The aforesaid prelate also made twenty-six large silver chalices for the arches of the same church, weighing altogether one hundred and nine and a half pounds. Likewise, in the place mentioned above, he offered two silver baskets, weighing two pounds and eight ounces, and a bowl of the purest gold, weighing three pounds.

The aforesaid pontiff made two *enafoti* baskets of silver, weighing ten pounds, three silver bowls weighing five pounds, and a gilded silver censer weighing one pound.

This most kindly prelate offered on the sacred altar a covering of Byzantine *blatthin*, bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the narrative of how the angel crowned the blessed Cecilia, Valerian, and Tiburtius; it was adorned with a border of *chrysoclavus* of wondrous beauty. Likewise, there he made a covering of *fundatum alythinum*, having around it a border of *oloverus*.

### 441

Out of love for the same virgin he made another covering of *fundatum porphyreticum*, bearing in the middle a cross woven with gold and handsomely decorated. Indeed, on the aforesaid altar he offered a white covering, marked with little roses, bearing in the middle a cross of *blatthin*, with *psillia* and a border of Byzantine *blatthin*, most beautifully adorned. He also offered on the aforementioned altar a covering of *quadrapulum*.

The venerable pontiff made four *alithynus* coverings hanging around the altar, bearing crosses and *gammadiae* of *fundatum* and *quadrapulum*. For the small shrine where he deposited the venerable head of the same virgin, he made a small Tyrian covering with a border of *blatthin*. In the place mentioned above he offered a covering of green *fundatum*. He also made another covering of *stauracium* with a border of *oloverus*, and a covering of *blatthin* with a border of *fundatum*.

He also made, in the shrine containing the body of the aforesaid virgin, a covering of *quadrapulum* with a border. Moreover, another covering of *staurax* with a border of *oloverus*.

In the aforesaid church he made twenty-five Tyrian coverings with borders of Byzantine *blatthin*. Likewise, four green coverings with borders of *oloverus*. In the place mentioned above he offered three *alithynus* coverings with borders of *blatthin*, and likewise two small *fundatum* coverings with borders of *blatthin*. Similarly, two Tyrian coverings with borders of *fundatum*.

This venerable and distinguished pontiff made twelve *fundatum* coverings for the arches of the aforesaid church, and fourteen of *quadrapulum*. He also made twelve small coverings for the presbytery arch, with borders of Byzantine *blatthin*. This venerable prelate, protected by God, made at the entrance of the same church a large curtain of *quadrapulum* and *staurax*, most beautifully adorned.

### 442

The same aforesaid pontiff, taking vigilant care for the monasteries built all around and inquiring into what each possessed, discovered the monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, situated beyond the aqueduct of the Lateran patriarchal residence, utterly desolate in all its resources. The community of women servants of God living there was so destitute through poverty that they could chant no praises to almighty God and his saints.

Moved by compassion through his inquiry, the venerable shepherd arranged matters so that the servants of God could live well and religiously. He gathered monks there and established a community, enriching the monastery with many resources. He greatly and sufficiently increased it with dependents, holdings, vineyards, houses, and urban and rural properties, so that the resident community, putting aside every necessity, might chant night and day, in melodious fashion, praises and hymns to God alone and to his saints in the venerable church of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ situated beside the Lateran.

### 443

Moreover, in the oratory of the most blessed martyrs Processus and Martinianus, situated within the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which he himself had also built, he offered an image of the purest gold bearing the face of the holy Mother of God, weighing ten pounds and four ounces.

There he also made a covering of Byzantine *blatthin*, bearing two panels of *chrysoclavus* with the faces of the blessed Peter and the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus, and a border of *chrysoclavus*, decorated with wondrous beauty.

There also he offered a silk covering bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the image of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and a border of Byzantine *blatthin*, most beautifully fashioned. Indeed, for those same saints he offered nine silk coverings with borders of *quadrapulum* and Byzantine *blatthin*. In the place mentioned above he made six small Tyrian coverings with borders of *fundatum*. A wondrously made gilded silver censer, weighing one pound.

In the oratory of the most blessed martyrs Sixtus and Fabianus, the aforesaid pontiff made three silver bowls, weighing five pounds and six ounces. Before the image of that oratory he also made a covering of *chrysoclavus*, magnificently decorated.

Above their venerable altar he made a covering of *alithynus*, bearing in the middle a cross of Byzantine *blatthin* and likewise a border of *blatthin*. In the same way, in the aforesaid oratory, the aforementioned pontiff offered a silk covering bearing in the middle two crosses of *chrysoclavus* and a border of *stauracium* adorned with various pearls. There he also made another covering of *fundatum*, bearing in the middle a cross of *blatthin*.

He also made, for the adornment of the aforesaid oratory, four *alithynus* coverings with borders of Byzantine *blatthin*, and likewise four silk coverings with borders of *quadrapulum* and *oloverus*.

### 444

This most kindly prelate made, in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way, a Tyrian covering bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of our Lord Jesus Christ and those of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian with their three other brothers, together with a cross woven with gold and a border of *oloverus*, most beautifully fashioned and decorated.

Finally, above their sacred altar he offered a Tyrian cover, magnificently decorated. Indeed, before the vestibule of that altar he made three Tyrian coverings with borders of Byzantine *blatthin*.

The venerable pontiff also made, in the monastery of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ situated in the territory of Reate, a covering of *chrysoclavus* with a narrative of how our same Lord Jesus Christ shines in heaven with the archangels and apostles, adorned with wondrous beauty and various pearls.

Likewise, in the aforesaid monastery, for the adornment of the sacred altar, he offered another covering of *fundatum*, bearing crosses of Byzantine *blatthin* and a border of *chrysoclavus*, magnificently decorated. In the same way, in the church of the blessed martyr Menas he made a covering of *quadrapulum* with a border of Byzantine *blatthin*.

This most holy and angelic prelate offered in the church of the blessed apostle Peter at Centumcellae a gilded silver chalice and paten, weighing four pounds and three ounces.

### 445

Indeed, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, his protector, he made a Gospel book with Byzantine *blatthin* and silver, weighing eight pounds and eight ounces.

The most kindly prelate also made, in the monastery of the blessed protomartyr Stephen at Saint Peter’s, four white silk coverings bearing in the middle a cross woven with gold, with various pearls and a border of *blatthin*, magnificently decorated.

Likewise, in the place mentioned above, the aforesaid pontiff offered a covering of *fundatum*, bearing in the middle a cross woven with gold and a border of *chrysoclavus*. Finally, in the aforesaid monastery, the aforementioned prelate made a covering of *fundatum*, bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the face of the holy Mother of God and those of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and a border of *blatthin*.

There he offered two coverings of *stauracium*, bearing in the middle crosses of *chrysoclavus* and borders of *blatthin*. He also made, for the adornment of that oratory, a large covering of *quadrapulum*, bearing in the middle three crosses woven with gold and a border of *blatthin*.

In the deaconry of the holy archangel, the aforesaid pontiff offered a covering of Byzantine *blatthin*, bearing in the middle a cross of *chrysoclavus* and a border of *chrysoclavus*, most beautifully fashioned.

### 446

Indeed, in the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia he made a silver basin, in which he placed the precious head of the same virgin; it weighed eight and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr Quiriacus at the Baths, the aforesaid prelate offered eight *fundatum* coverings.

This pontiff, supported by God, made in the oratory of the holy Archangel—which his predecessor, the lord Pope Leo, had once established and built—a white silk covering bearing in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus* with a narrative of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and a border of *chrysoclavus*, magnificently decorated.

There he also offered another covering of *fundatum* with a border of Byzantine *blatthin*. The aforesaid pontiff likewise made in the aforementioned oratory another covering of *quadrapulum*, embroidered around with a narrative of the Mother of God, most beautifully fashioned and decorated.

### 447 [Col. 1269]

Moreover, that same supreme and orthodox pontiff, moved by divine inspiration, saw that the church of the holy and undefiled Virgin Mary, our Lady, at the Manger had formerly been so constructed that women, standing near the pontiff after his throne, appeared close beside him at the sacred solemnities of Mass. Thus, if the pontiff wished to speak with those attending him, he could not do so without their intervention because of the women’s very close crowding. Seeing that there was ample room there by which he could move the throne, he applied himself unceasingly to the work of raising the seat, which had been lower down, so that he might pour out prayers to the Lord more freely insofar as he could modestly avoid the company of the people.

Finally, he made the throne, better than it had formerly been, beautifully adorned with the finest marbles, and constructed approaches on every side by which one might ascend to it. Raising the pavement of the altar, he paved it with most precious marbles. Before the confession of the sacred altar he erected six purple columns, above which he placed a beam of white marble; joining them on the right and left with purple marbles and adorning them with carvings, he decorated them most suitably. He also restored the presbytery of that church with diverse marbles, improving it beyond its former state.

He wondrously adorned the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar, or confession, inside and out with its little rails, in the purest gold, weighing one hundred seventy-four pounds and six ounces. Likewise, he most beautifully made and gilded the altar of that basilica with silver plates and various scenes, weighing three hundred eighty-five pounds. The most kindly and distinguished prelate also offered there six bowls of the purest gold with various gems, weighing twenty pounds and six ounces. He further ordained that lamps should always burn before the most holy altar by day and night.

Supported by divine inspiration, he offered in the aforesaid basilica eight silver arches with sixteen columns, weighing altogether two hundred eighteen pounds and eight ounces. He also made before the vestibule of the altar large silver rails, weighing seventy-eight pounds. He also offered there six silver *canthara*, weighing altogether sixty and a half pounds. Likewise, in the larger arches of the aforesaid church he made forty-two large hanging silver chalices, all together weighing two hundred eighty-one pounds. Out of love for that Virgin, our Lady, the venerable prelate also offered there four silver crowns, weighing sixty-two and a half pounds and three ounces; likewise, two silver baskets, weighing thirteen pounds. He also made there a gilded silver image with the face of the blessed Mother of God Mary, weighing seventeen pounds and three ounces.

The servant of Christ the almighty Lord offered on the most holy altar of the aforesaid basilica two coverings of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, with borders, adorned with various gems and pearls and magnificently decorated.

### 448

He also offered there another covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of how our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized by John in the Jordan, with a border of *chrysoclavus*, magnificently adorned. Likewise, there he made a covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with a border of *chrysoclavus* and adorned with various pearls.

Led by divine love, the most blessed and venerable aforesaid pontiff likewise made there, on the aforesaid altar, a covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of how the blessed Mother of God Mary was assumed bodily, with a border of *chrysoclavus* and various pearls, handsomely fashioned and decorated. That most kindly prelate also made there another covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of the Ascension of Christ our Lord, suitably decorated. Likewise, there, out of love for the same Virgin, he made another covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a narrative of how the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, adorned and decorated with various pearls. There also he supplied another covering of *chrysoclavus*, with the history of the palms, modestly fashioned and decorated.

### 449

Moreover, there the aforesaid pontiff made another covering of *oloverus*, with a border of *fundatum*. Likewise, for daily use he offered two coverings of *fundatum*, with borders of *quadrapulum*, most beautifully adorned.

Moved by divine inspiration, that most holy prelate made in the larger arches of the aforesaid basilica fourteen coverings of *fundatum*, fourteen of *quadrapulum*, and likewise fourteen of *imizilum*. Out of love for the same our Lady, the servant of our Lord Jesus Christ made, in the arches of the presbytery of the aforesaid church, twenty-six coverings of *chrysoclavus*, bearing scenes of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Nativity and Assumption of that same undefiled Virgin. Likewise, in those same arches he offered twenty-four coverings of *quadrapulum*, embroidered around with various scenes.

The servant of Christ the almighty offered high up, in view of the apse, a wonderfully decorated Alexandrian cloth. He also offered on the principal beam of that basilica a large covering of *fundatum*, having seven bands of *chrysoclavus* and a border of Byzantine *blatthin*. For the adornment of that basilica he also made, on that beam, six coverings of *quadrapulum* and four of *imizilum*. Near the vestibule of the altar, in the apse, he made twelve coverings of *quadrapulum* and, there, six coverings of *blatthin*.

The venerable prelate also made at the entrance of the aforesaid basilica a large Alexandrian curtain, handsomely decorated with various scenes. Likewise, for daily use he offered there another Alexandrian curtain, wonderfully adorned. The most kindly and distinguished pontiff offered in the aforesaid basilica six white silk coverings on the principal beam, with borders of *fundatum*. There he also installed, most splendidly, four other white coverings of Byzantine *blatthin*. In the apse of that basilica he also placed six white coverings with borders of *fundatum*.

### 450

Because that same thrice-blessed shepherd frequently devoted such care and vigilance to the condition of God’s holy churches, he also most wonderfully made and decorated the altar of the Manger in the aforesaid basilica, and the venerable confession, on all sides in the purest gold with various scenes, weighing one hundred thirty-four pounds and four ounces. Likewise, there, in gilded silver with various scenes, ten [unspecified objects], weighing two hundred fifty-four pounds and four ounces. There the aforesaid pontiff also offered three bowls of the purest gold with various gems, weighing eight pounds and ten ounces. He also placed there coverings of *alithynus* with borders of Byzantine *blatthin*.

Out of the great affection of his heart, this holy bishop made in the church of the blessed Cecilia a covering of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a wonderfully depicted and adorned narrative of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. That venerable and distinguished pontiff, protected by God, made the *propitiatorium* of the sacred altar of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where his most sacred body rests, a *spanoclistum* of yellow gold, painted with various scenes and wonderfully decorated, weighing two hundred pounds. Likewise, in the aforesaid church, out of love for that apostle of God, his patron, he offered forty-six coverings of *chrysoclavus* in the arches of the presbytery, bearing a narrative of the Passion and Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian on the Sacred Way, he made a silk covering, most beautifully fashioned and decorated.

### 451

The most benevolent bishop also made, in the basilica of the blessed Mary, ever-Virgin Mother of God, our Lady, at the Crèche, two goblets of gold adorned with various gems, weighing six pounds. There he likewise offered an apostolic goblet of purest gold, weighing five pounds. In the same place he made eight silver *pharacanthara*, weighing together eighty-two pounds. Out of love for that same Lady of ours, he also offered in the aforesaid basilica four columns and one arch, weighing together sixty pounds.

The oft-mentioned pontiff made in the venerable altar of that church a white vestment bearing in its midst a cross of *chrysoclavus*, sewn around with various gems and beautifully adorned; and he attached there another vestment of Byzantine purple, likewise with a cross of *chrysoclavus*, most honorably decorated with various stones. He also made, for the adornment of the aforesaid church, curtains of *chrysoclavus* across the arches of the presbytery, bearing the story of the Passion and Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. He also offered on the great beam of the oft-mentioned church six other curtains with a border of *quadrapulum*. In the beams of that basilica he made seven *fundatum* curtains. He also offered four silk curtains around the altar of the aforesaid church, bearing a border of *quadrapulum*.

The venerable bishop also made in the church of the blessed Mother of God, called the Dominica, silver hangings weighing sixty-six pounds. He likewise made in the church of the blessed Mother of God, Mary our Lady, situated at Savina in the episcopal residence, a *fundatum* vestment with a border of Byzantine purple.

Finally, he died by divine calling. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter. He held two ordinations, one in December and the other in March: priests …, six deacons, and bishops in various places … in number. His episcopate was vacant for four days in January, in the first indiction.

## CI. EUGENIUS II

824 years after Christ; in the twelfth year of Emperor Louis; the fourth year of Michael Balbus.

[Note: [Col. 1275B]

From the Codex Regius, the Mazarine, and the Thuane manuscript.

No. 452, line 1: “Bonomund, he held office for four years.” “This venerable and distinguished man,” line 4: “for many days and nights”; line 6: “orphans and widows”; line 7: “throughout”; in the same place: “For he himself”; line 8: “what else, except”; lines 16–17: “the martyr’s ciborium”; line 17: “pounds … .” The rest is missing.

|

[Col. 1276B] From another Thuane manuscript.

Line 1: “Eugenius. For this venerable man”; line 4: “of this prelate’s pontificate”; line 6: “orphans”; line 8: “was very much … .”

In Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript.

Line 1: “from his father …”; line 4: “pleasing for many days.”]

[Col. 1275]

### 452

Eugenius, a Roman by nationality, the son of Boemund, held office for four years [Note: [Col. 1275] B: three years], two months, and twenty-three days.

This venerable and distinguished man was very simple and humble, endowed with knowledge, outstanding in speech, handsome in appearance, generous to those who asked, and disdainful of the world. He thought day and night only about what was pleasing to Christ. During the time of this aforementioned pontiff, considerable abundance had spread not only through all Rome but also through nearly the whole world. For whatever he justly received from his subjects, he distributed unceasingly to everyone—not only to the poor and widows, but also to the rich.

There was also the greatest peace and rest throughout the Roman world in his days. Since he was a friend of complete peace, what else did those under him do except what he himself practiced through his honorable conduct? And they in turn conducted themselves likewise.

For he was archpriest of this most holy and universal Church. In it he governed his office with extraordinary distinction for no brief time. Afterwards, having been elected by all the Romans in pious recognition of his merits, he became pontiff after the death of the most holy lord Pope Paschal.

During his priesthood he held the church of the blessed martyr Sabina, situated on the Aventine Hill. By God’s providence, after the pontifical dignity had been bestowed upon him, he brought it to better condition and adorned it everywhere with paintings. In his days the Roman judges who were being held captive in Francia returned. He allowed them to enter their ancestral possessions and gave them substantial resources from the Lateran patriarchate, since they had been deprived of nearly all their means.

In the aforementioned church of the blessed martyr Sabina he made a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing … pounds. The same venerable bishop, in the same place, offered …

## CII. VALENTINUS II

827 years after Christ; in the fourteenth year of Emperor Louis; the seventh year of the Emperor Michael Balbus.

[Note: [Col. 1277A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript.

No. 453, line 1: “the son of Leontius; he held office for one month and ten days.” Line 5: “he examined closely, and with great …”; line 6: “in noble fashion”; line 8: “with the nectar of inspiration”; line 15: “of example.”

No. 454, line 9: “modest in purpose.”

[Col. 1279A] No. 455, line 15: “into the see.”

From the Codex Regius, the Mazarine, and the Thuane manuscript.

No. 453, line 1: “the son of Leontius; he held office for one month and ten days, and the see was vacant for four days.” Line 2: “This man was filled with the Holy Spirit and remained suffused with grace.” “Empty,” as in line 5. Line 6: “he avoided.” “When Lord Pope Paschal saw him adorned with good character, he appointed him archdeacon of this holy Roman Church.” “When Lord Eugenius had died, Valentinus, the archdeacon, ascended the highest summit.” “For he was generous,” as in no. 456, line 4.

[Col. 1280A] No. 456, line 6: “adorned by Christ, he was called to heavenly things”; lines 7–8: “of the most blessed work.”

From another Thuane manuscript.

No. 453, line 1: “Valentinus.” The complete Life of Valentinus is missing.

In Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript.

No. 453, line 1: “Valentinianus.” Line 6: “in noble fashion.” Line 8: “full of inspiration.” Line 9: “with trappings.” Line 10: “appointing.”

No. 454, line 10: “Moreover, what …”; line 11: “by merits, and outstanding …”; line 13: “the assembly of the Romans.”]

[Col. 1275]

### 453

Valentinus, a Roman by nationality, the son of Peter, from the district of the Via Lata, held office for forty days. This man was filled with great holiness and great blessedness, and remained suffused with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

While he was living in this Roman city—which, by God’s authority, possesses the dignity of supreme priesthood and royal excellence—he was born of freeborn and devout parents and, for the study of the elementary disciplines, was entrusted to a diligent teacher. With ample understanding he examined closely the sacred writings of divine law and retained them in the memory of his intellect. He avoided the empty and disgraceful games of boys in the manner of the noble. He uttered no unsuitable or dishonorable stories from his own mouth and engaged in no unlawful actions; but from the earliest flower of infancy he was devoted to pious modesty and sobriety, and, filled with the splendid spirit of divine inspiration, he kept his lips adorned amid every ornament of speech and wisdom.

He was also outstanding in the abundance of his words, and by the luminous merits of his works he revealed the elegance of his mind. Above all, in accordance with the eminent saying of the Teacher of the Nations, he showed himself to all without giving offense, gladly and with a kindly spirit. By placing no stumbling block of opposition before anyone, he earnestly endeavored in spirit to extend to his neighbors the due measure of perfect love. And in accordance with the command of the Lord’s voice, he carried his loins girded with chastity and lamps

[Col. 1277] burning in his hands, shining brightly in speech and likewise sparkling in the performance of his teaching, with the magnificent testimony of an example worthy of praise.

### 454

With the heavenly power of God also aiding him, when he had already reached the beginning of mature age, and when the favor of his goodness and discernment spread far and wide like the fragrance of fragrant incense, and had clearly struck the ears of the most blessed prelate, the lord Paschal of pious memory, through the truthful report of the faithful—and when he had learned, as the people unanimously praised him, that Valentinus was truly distinguished and renowned in every respect—the pontiff immediately advanced him through the ecclesiastical ranks to the dignity of subdeacon from the Lateran palace and ordered him to serve him.

Recognizing his manner of life, patience, and character, he loved him greatly above the others. The aforementioned man, with divine grace from above favoring him—grace to which he had devoted himself with complete devotion of mind and integrity of virtue—shone with the light of truth and wisdom. He was approachable in speech, distinguished in teaching, notable in appearance, modest among his brethren in pious devotion, and faithful to his neighbors.

Supported by a discerning heart, he did not involve himself in affairs by which anyone might be saddened, even slightly. Moreover, when the aforementioned pontiff saw him adorned with so many good qualities and such great merits of his works, as well as with an elegant and distinguished bodily appearance, he consecrated him as a levite of his apostolic see. Because of the merit of his life, which shone splendidly, and because he was loved with great affection by all the people of the Church and by the illustrious Roman people gathered in great numbers, he bestowed many goods and benefits upon him with lavish generosity, and afterwards made him archdeacon.

When this prelate, at Christ’s command, was ascending to the heavenly heights, Eugenius was raised by everyone to pontifical honor and placed in the apostolic see. Recognizing clearly that Valentinus was adorned with all the virtues mentioned above, Eugenius retained him throughout his life as one of his dearest companions and rejoiced in his heart as a father rejoices in his own son; he wished him constantly to remain before his eyes.

When the term of this prelate’s passing light had been completed and divinely ended, the entire Roman assembly entreated the Lord with repeated fasts and prayers at the summit of the sacred see, asking that he might graciously reveal to their minds who would be worthy of the honor of so great a see. But once the divine majesty had been appeased, whom else would it show by the hidden command of its power that they should choose from the priestly roster, except the man whom it had adorned from his mother’s breasts with so many of the virtues described above and with the fairest flower of learning, and whom it had raised as a steadfast and faithful fosterling in all things, granting him as ruler to the most holy see?

### 455

Therefore, when the venerable bishops, the glorious nobles of Rome, and the entire population of the great City had gathered together in the Lateran palace, so that what had already been divinely revealed to their hearts and held equally by all might resound in the single voice of many, Valentinus was unanimously acclaimed with strong approval:

“Valentinus, the most holy archdeacon, is worthy! Valentinus is worthy to be adorned with the insignia of the supreme pontificate!”

After these honeyed words, they all immediately remained united in a single bond of peace and hurried to the church of the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady—the clergy, the nobles of Rome, and the people together—where they found him, as usual, rendering manifold thanks and praises to the Lord.

Although he immediately resisted them strongly and for a long time, declaring in a resolute voice that he was unfit for so great a government, he was elected to the papal see by the joyful acclamations of the beloved people and of both Roman military orders. Then they led him from there to the Lateran patriarchate with fitting praises of glory and the fullness of honor, and placed him on the pontifical throne.

When the entire Roman senate kissed his feet with joy, and all that had to be fulfilled had been duly and reverently performed, great sobriety and great rejoicing prevailed among the people of every sex and age. As the clear day of his consecration was already dawning, all the Romans together led the bishop from the palace to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles; with divine majesty assisting, they consecrated him supreme pontiff on the lofty throne.

### 456

He immediately ascended the heights of the life-giving see of the blessed apostle Peter, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom. After piously offering divine praises and sacrifices to God, he returned to the palace amid great joy, accompanied by a large and magnificent assembly of Romans. After taking sumptuous meals, he enriched the sacred clergy, the senate, and the Roman people with many and varied gifts of great generosity [Note: [Col. 1277] * “very generously”].

He was renowned for generosity, distinguished in action, eloquent in speech, compassionate toward all, and always ready to offer timely assistance to those enduring poverty. Adorned with these manifold virtues, he was called by Christ to heavenly things and, overcome by bodily illness, passed away in a precious death. With the fruit of a life and work both desirable and most blessed, he joyfully ascended into the presence of the supreme Majesty, rejoicing and exulting with the Lord forever.

## CIII. GREGORIUS IV

827 years after Christ; in the fourteenth year of Emperor Louis; the seventh year of the Emperor Michael Balbus.

[Note: [Col. 1291A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript.

No. 463, line 3: “the elephant.”

No. 466, line 7: “octagonal”; line 9: “octagonal.”

No. 470, line 12: “with the breath of the heart.”

No. 471, line 1: “two pairs.” In the same place: “nineteen white [ones].” Line 2: “in the same image.” Line 4: “73.” Line 5: “golden finger-rings.” Line 13: “small lions.”

No. 472, line 2: “at the triumphal arch”; line 3: “in the regular [arrangement].” Line 5: “sixteen outside the altar.” “Likewise five curtains hanging inside around the altar, having twenty-five straps.”

No. 474, line 6: “adorned with wondrous [stones].” Line 8: “the marvelous richness of the embossing.” Line 10: “before which the greater circuit surrounds.”

No. 475, line 9: “beside the acolyte.”

No. 478, line 12: “there, stationary, is missing.” Line 14: “wherever it is suitable for them, with all things.” Line 20: “or a curtain before the doors.” Line 24: “of the apostle Peter; and the episcopate was vacant for fifteen days.”

From the Codex Regius, the Mazarine, and the Thuane manuscript.
