[Col. 1279]

### 457

Gregory IV, a Roman by nationality, the son of John, held office for sixteen years. He was an energetic and most kind man, filled with holiness and piety, adorned with learning, pleasant in speech, more modest than all others in conversation, most firm in the Catholic faith, just in his deeds, and a most diligent investigator of the divine writings. He was also an indefatigable visitor of the holy churches, a father of the poor, and a nourisher of all widows. Desiring nothing earthly and abandoning the worldly profits of the present life, he acquired eternal rewards in heaven by merits worthy of them.

This most blessed pontiff was noble by birth, but more illustrious in holiness; handsome in appearance and more beautiful in faith. These praises of his virtues did not shine only during his pontificate; while he was still in the vigor of youth, he tirelessly strove to perform such deeds. This did not remain hidden from the Romans for long, as it is written:

“For no one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but so that it may shine for all who are in the house” [Note: [Col. 1279] Matthew 5].

His holy activity began to resound more fully from day to day throughout the entire city of Rome, as the Gospel teaches: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known” [Note: [Col. 1279] Matthew 10].

Finally, because of these innumerable good deeds, he was made not only subdeacon but also priest [Note: [Col. 1279] *that is, cardinal presbyter] by the most holy lord Paschal, pope of this sacred see. He remained established in the condition of his priesthood, chastely and modestly, remembering what Holy Scripture records when it says: “Let the priests of God be clothed with righteousness” [Note: [Col. 1279] Psalm 131], that is, let them be occupied with nothing else except prayer, reading, and fasting.

While he was devoted to these things, the aforementioned pontiff Paschal was removed from this life in human fashion, and Eugenius, chosen by God as bishop, attained the dignity of the sacred summit. Remaining in it for a short time, he too died. After him Valentinus obtained the summit of the episcopate, charged with feeding the flocks, but was removed from this present life with great speed.

### 458

At last all the Romans began to think more intently not only about the pontiffs who had been lost so suddenly, but also about the future one, so that they might recognize a man illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, under whose teaching and rule the entire nobility of the senate could live in due order.

The Creator of all, the helper in times of need and in tribulation, kindled the hearts of all those nobles with his own inextinguishable holy light and turned their minds toward the pious deeds of the most blessed Gregory IV. They all agreed in one spirit and one soul.

When they had elected him, he was brought into the Lateran patriarchate; they had forcibly taken him from the basilica of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian, for he said that he would be useless for such a ministry. But because he could not resist so immense a multitude, they led him to the place mentioned above with hymns and spiritual songs.

### 459

But since we cannot investigate everything he did in a swift account, let us, though briefly, bring to everyone’s knowledge those things which he offered to sacred and venerable places with an undivided mind and pious devotion.

Moreover, after his election and consecration, he began to show the greatest concern for the saints and their churches, so that, with the Lord’s protection, he might quickly restore them to their former condition through renewed adornment. This was done. At that time he had the church of the blessed martyr Saturninus, situated outside the Salarian Gate, rebuilt with new structures from its foundations, since it had fallen because of extreme age and long decay; he also adorned it with various paintings. There he offered one *fundatum* vestment.

When he had completed these things mentioned above, the mind of the pontiff began with the utmost zeal to attend to other works for the saints. Since he was then kindled by divine love, he took the body of the blessed Gregory, pontiff of this universal Church, through whom the grace of the Holy Spirit introduced throughout the whole world an inexhaustible gift of wisdom, from the place where it had previously been buried, and transferred it with the highest honor not far away to another newly built place within the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

He adorned its sacred altar everywhere with silver panels and dedicated the oratory under the saint’s name. He also painted its apse with gilded mosaic. Into that oratory he transferred the bodies of the blessed martyrs Sebastian, Gorgonius, and Tiburtius from the cemeteries in which they had previously lain. He placed each of them at a separate altar. For them, during his pontificate, he decreed that the monks assigned to perform the office in the church of the blessed apostle Peter should not cease singing praises there to the almighty Lord every day.

In the same oratory he offered eighteen large or small silk curtains; three vestments over the altar beneath which the body of the most holy Pope Gregory rests; one with *chrysoclave*, bearing the story …; and over each of the aforesaid martyrs’ altars, one *fundatum* vestment.

Finally, he offered three images silvered above and also covered with gold, bearing the face of the Lord and painted images of those whose particular bodies, buried there, possess power through miracles and virtues.

### 460

When these works had been completed, the venerable pontiff suddenly turned his attention and mind to others. At that time he demolished from its foundations the church of the blessed Mark, confessor and pontiff, which he had undertaken to govern during his priesthood and which had remained under his jurisdiction and authority until he attained pontifical dignity. Because of its extreme age it seemed repeatedly on the point of collapse. With the help of almighty God, he rebuilt it from the foundations and afterward brought the whole structure to a better state of worship and beauty through new construction. He also painted the apse of the aforesaid basilica with mosaic overlaid with golden colors, with the greatest delight.

He made all its roofing new, and whatever he had previously recognized as worthless in it he afterward preferred to make precious.

### 461

After completing all these things for the remedy and future recompense of his soul, he offered in the often-mentioned church the following gifts, to remain there for future times:

One golden crown, which still hangs above the altar today, with very fine gems and a golden cross in the middle, likewise with precious gems; three goblets of the purest gold hanging before the aforesaid altar; twelve engraved silver goblets made by the work of angels; and five other engraved goblets with their feet.

In the same place he offered three gilded censers, twelve silver baskets, nine large and small silver crowns, three silver crosses, each weighing one pound, and four candle-stands silvered above.

He also made, for the praise and adornment of the confessor so often mentioned, a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing one thousand pounds. He likewise adorned his altar with silver panels, wishing through the exercise of temporal things to attain eternal rewards in heaven.

The aforementioned venerable pontiff also offered there one *fundatum* vestment bearing points around its circumference. He also made another *olovero* vestment [Note: [Col. 1281] B: *holosericum*, “silk”], bearing gems and golden apples in the middle and a band of *chrysoclave* around it. Indeed, the most holy bishop offered an *olovero* vestment with griffins and unicorns, and another vestment with *chrysoclave* around it, bearing in the middle the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### 462

The venerable pope, already often mentioned, offered in the aforesaid church a vestment with griffins and *chrysoclave* around it, bearing in the middle the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. He also offered another vestment with *chrysoclave*, bearing four wheels of *chrysoclave* across its middle and the Nativity and Baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The aforementioned pontiff offered another vestment with lions, bearing the Lord’s Resurrection in *chrysoclave*. He offered eight smaller *fundatum* vestments placed over the altars, which are known to be around that church.

He offered four white silk curtains: one with Tyrian purple all around, bearing a cross in the middle and *gammadia* of *chrysoclave*; another of *stauracium*, bearing in the middle a cross of *olovero* and *gammadia* of Tyrian *olovero*; and the third and fourth likewise.

He offered four *rodinum* curtains surrounding the sacred altar, one of which bears a cross of *chrysoclave*. He offered twenty-six *fundatum* curtains and likewise linen curtains, hanging across the arches of the church.

He offered three Alexandrian curtains hanging before the great doors, bearing human figures and horses. He offered one Alexandrian curtain and four others bearing points of *fundatum*. He offered one *octapulum* curtain. He offered eight other *fundatum* curtains bearing around them a border of purple. He offered six other curtains with eagles, bearing around them a border of Tyrian purple. He offered five additional *fundatum* curtains bearing lions and a border of Tyrian purple.

He offered other Alexandrian curtains, one of which bears wheels and roses in the middle, while another bears trees and wheels; these hung before the doors of the church. He also offered a small *olovero* curtain bearing in the middle a man with a horse. He offered fourteen curtains with silver *spaniscus*. In the same place he offered ten small *olovero* curtains, each bearing ducks.

Protected by divine inspiration, he offered in the aforesaid basilica one silver hand-washing ewer.

[Col. 1283]

### 463

He also made in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian one *fundatum* vestment bearing in the middle a painted scene with *chrysoclave*.

In the church of the blessed Abbacyrus and the Archangel at the Elephant.

This bishop, chosen by God and distinguished, offered in the basilica of the blessed martyr Eustachius one *fundatum* vestment bearing in the middle a scene in *chrysoclave*.

The often-mentioned bishop made another *fundatum* vestment in the church of the blessed martyrs Sergius and Bacchus. In the same way he made another *fundatum* vestment in the church of Saint Silvester, situated on Mount Soracte.

After all these things had been completed and carefully carried out, he made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter fourteen curtains with *chrysoclave*, bearing various scenes from the Gospels and the passions of the blessed Peter and Paul, as well as of the apostle Andrew. These hung among images cast in gold and silver on the beam silvered above, before one approached the sacred confession, exceedingly beautiful to human eyes and especially distinguished.

### 464

The magnificent bishop also made porticoes on either side in the church of the blessed martyr George of Christ, and adorned them with various paintings for the adornment of that basilica. With the Lord’s help, he carefully restored the apse of the same deaconry from its foundations.

This most loving pontiff, when he carefully observed that the secretariat of the same venerable deaconry was decaying because of excessive age, rebuilt it anew in honor of that place and for love of others.

The most holy pope therefore offered the following gifts in the same place: one *fundatum* vestment with *chrysoclave*, bearing images of the Savior and of the martyrs Sebastian and George; two large and eighteen small *fundatum* curtains.

In the confession of that basilica he made silver hangings covered with gold. In the same way he newly restored the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyr Adrian, situated on the Sacred Way, since it had decayed through excessive age.

### 465

He also made in the Lateran patriarchate a dining hall of marvelous size, decorated with a mosaic apse, as well as two other apses situated to the right and left beneath the *paracellarium*, painted with various scenes.

The most holy pope also made in the church of the blessed confessor Clement a *fundatum* vestment with lions and a border of *octapulum*. In the same way, in the deaconry of the blessed martyr Theodore, he made a *fundatum* vestment bearing lions and a border of *octapulum*.

In the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he made a *chrysoclave* vestment bearing the story of Zacchaeus. He also made another *fundatum* vestment with griffins, in honor of the holy Mother of God among the martyrs.

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed protomartyr Stephen on the Caelian Hill, he made a *fundatum* vestment with *gammadia*. He also made in the deaconry of the blessed Mother of God on the Via Lata a *stauracium* vestment with a border of purple.

In the same way, in the church of the blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, at the Crèche, he made a gold-woven vestment bearing the Nativity, Baptism, Presentation, and Resurrection. At the top of the scene it bore three hundred and eighty white gems, fifty hyacinth-colored gems, and twenty-two green gems; around it were *alvavira* bearing the name of Lord Gregory IV, pope.

He also made in the deaconry of the blessed martyr Adrian at the Three Fates a *fundatum* vestment. The aforementioned bishop also made in the church of the blessed apostles at the Chains a *fundatum* vestment bearing lions with griffins. He likewise made another *fundatum* vestment in the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Martin, bearing lions with trees.

466. Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed martyr Eusebius he provided a garment of *oloverum*, bearing eagles, with a border of *quadrapulum*. The aforesaid bishop also offered in the basilica of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, across the Tiber, a Tyrian garment bearing a scene of the Nativity of the Lord and of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. Indeed, in the deaconry called Cyriacus he likewise offered a garment of *fundatus*. Likewise, in the deaconry of blessed Mary on the Via Lata he offered a garment of *fundatus* in the same manner.

This illustrious and venerable pontiff, trusting in divine inspiration, made in the church of the blessed Mark, confessor of Christ and bishop, a gilded octagonal paten, bearing in its center the face of our Lord, and on its two sides the face of the blessed Mark himself and that of the same bishop; it weighed six pounds. In the same manner he offered there a gilded octagonal chalice of *fundatus*, with leaves, weighing six pounds; he also arranged for a silver cup to be offered there, weighing six pounds. The aforementioned pontiff himself also offered two *ennafodion* baskets, weighing fourteen pounds together.

Indeed, in the church of the teacher of the nations, the blessed apostle Paul, the often-mentioned pontiff offered a garment of *chrysoclavus*, bearing a scene of our Lord God, and in his service, on the right and left, archangels and apostles in worthy number, of marvelous size and beauty, most beautifully adorned and woven with various stones and pearls.

467. This most kind and illustrious pontiff, while as a good and true shepherd he exercised the greatest care and vigilance everywhere for the condition of the holy Church of God, observed the poverty of the Romans: when they needed to grind wheat for food, they had no means of doing so. Trusting in divine assistance, he therefore undertook, with diligent labor, to rebuild the structure called the Sabbatine, which for many years already seemed broken and ruined, just as it had been built in ancient times, so that it might now, as formerly, flow freely to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and to the Janiculum.

He also made in the deaconry of the blessed Mary, ever-Virgin, in Cosmedin, a Tyrian garment bearing a scene of the Lord’s Nativity and of Christ, our true God, rising again.

[Col. 1285] For the honor and glory of the blessed virgin Susanna, the most holy bishop offered in her church a garment of *fundatus*, with a border of Tyrian cloth.

468. In the church of the blessed martyr and deacon Cyriacus he made a garment of *fundatus*, bearing a border of *stauracius*. Likewise, in the church of the blessed virgin Pudentiana, a garment of *fundatus*, with a border of *quadrapulus*. He offered to the blessed martyr Vitalis a garment of *fundatus*, bearing eagles and a border of *quadrapulus*.

The aforesaid pontiff made in the church of the blessed martyr Anastasia a garment of *fundatus*, bearing eagles and a border of *oloverum*. Indeed, the aforementioned bishop offered in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lucia, called Orphea, a garment of *fundatus*, with a border of *octapulus*.

Finally, the most holy pontiff made in the title of the blessed martyr Chrysogonus a Tyrian garment bearing a scene of Daniel, with a border of *stauracius*. The most blessed pope offered in the title of Pammachius a garment of *stauracius*, with a border of *quadrapulus*. He also made in the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia a garment of *fundatus*, bearing eagles and griffins, with a border of *oloverum*.

Likewise, in the title of Aemiliana he offered a garment of *fundatus*, bearing eagles and a border of Byzantine *platta*. At the same time, in the church of the blessed martyr and pontiff Sixtus, he made a Tyrian garment bearing a scene of Daniel, with a border of *oloverum*.

469. He made in the basilica of the blessed martyr a garment of *fundatus*, with a border of *oloverum*. In the title of Damasus he made a garment of *stauracius*, bearing a border of Byzantine *blatta*. He also made a garment of *fundatus* in the church of the apostles James and Philip. Likewise, in the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Marcellus he made a garment of *fundatus*. In the same manner, in the basilica of the blessed Lawrence in Lucina, he made a garment of *stauracius*. Likewise, in the church of Saint Valentine he made a garment of *fundatus* and *gammadia* of *octapulus*.

470. When all these things, recorded above, had been more freely completed and brought to perfection by the fourth pope of this undefiled See, Gregory, with God’s favor, he was unwilling to remain idle. After caring for the flocks, he began to devote himself without distinction to the cultivation and improvement of venerable places, so that in his time they might be strengthened by a new form of cultivation. Through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, Peter, this was accomplished according to his desire.

While he was turning such matters over in his episcopal mind and pondering them anxiously, he suddenly remembered that it was not right for the church of the holy Mother of God, which according to ancient custom is still called that of Calixtus across the Tiber, to remain without the service of monks—especially since signs, not insignificant miracles, and various acts of power frequently occurred there. At last, divinely pierced in heart and strengthened and supported by the help of almighty God, he founded a monastery from its foundations beside the aforesaid basilica and adorned it with new buildings.

He also gathered there canonical monks who would perform the office in that place and, day by day and through the following nights, sing praises and thanksgiving to almighty God with the inward breath of their hearts. As we see at the present time, the exceptional shepherd enlarged this work with great struggle and great zeal, making it extremely solid. For where formerly there had been no notable cultivation, now, by God’s providence, there are beautiful dwellings for monks. And where recently the places seemed full of brambles and filth, cells have now been built in which Christ’s sheep, together with all that serves their needs, dwell and sleep most generously after the offices of praise.

At that time the aforesaid church had been broken down in several places around it by long age, but he restored it everywhere with extremely strong defenses. In it he made a holy manger modeled on the manger of the holy Mother of God called Major, and adorned it with sheets of gold and silver.

For the remedy and forgiveness of sins he offered these gifts: a golden image bearing a scene of our Lady, with various precious gems—thirteen larger hyacinths, ten green stones, twenty-nine larger white stones, twenty larger *alamandina* stones, and small white stones around the crown of the head, variously arranged in *philopares*.

471.

[Note: [Col. 1285] A very corrupt passage.]

It has two pairs of *cercelli*, containing eighteen precious white gems, eight green stones, and four hyacinths. Likewise, on the same image it has two most precious green *murenae*, from which eleven pendants hang. It also has a three-stranded golden *murena*, containing seventy-three various white gems and thirty-three *buticulae*. It has a *murena* from which thirteen hyacinth gems hang; nine golden *digitiae* hang from a golden thread. It also has a threaded *murena*, from which fourteen hyacinth gems hang.

The sign of Christ has two little ships and three *murenae*. All the *murenae*, with their comb-like fittings. Pure gold *gabathae*, finely worked in *philopares*. A Christ-image, hanging from three chains, with *lilio* [uncertain] and a hook [lacuna], with an inscription concerning the gifts of God and of Saint Mary, which is called the Manger across the Tiber, of Pope Gregory IV, who offered three stone *gabathae* with a pure heart.

The sign of Christ has a scene in the form of a lion with a mane, with various works of pure gold hanging from four little chains and one hook. It also has a stone *gabatha* in the form of Leo IV, with various scenes of serpents, and in the middle a standing pine, gilded, with four little lions; these hang from three little chains and one hook.

It also has stone *gabathae*, from each of which gilded works hang from three little chains and four hooks; one of them has glass gems. This Pope Gregory IV also offered these willingly.

472. Indeed, the aforementioned bishop offered in the church of the teacher of the nations, the blessed apostle Paul, a *fundatus* curtain hanging on the triumphal arch, bearing in the middle the Annunciation and the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, one *oloverum* veil hung on a rod beneath a silver image, bearing a scene of an emperor.

There he also made two other small *fundatus* veils, which hang around the altar and have twenty-five straps. The veils hanging in the presbytery number twenty-four; the *fundatus* veils hanging on the major arches number forty. For the canopy of that church he made four veils.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr of Christ George he made six *fundatus* veils, bearing around them *gammadia* of *octapulus*. This God-protected and illustrious pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Sabas a garment of *oloverum* with lions, bearing a border of *octapulus*. He also made, in the monastery of the martyr Saint Anastasius, in the same manner, a garment of *stauracius*, with a border of *quadrapulus*.

At the same time, in the monastery of Saint Andrew, which is called on the slope of Scaurus, he made one garment of *stauracius*, with a border of *octapulus*. In the monastery of the martyr Saint Agatha, which is situated above the Subura, he made one garment of *oloverum*, with a border of *octapulus*. Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Erasmus he made one garment of *stauracius*, with a border of *octapulus*.

Indeed, in the deaconry of Saint Lucia, situated at the Seven Ways, he made one garment of *oloverum*, with a border of *octapulus*. In the oratory of Saint Lucia, situated in the monastery of Serenatus, he made a garment of *oloverum* with lions, bearing a border of *octapulus*. In the same manner, in the monastery of Saint Sylvester he made a garment of *oloverum*, with a border of *octapulus*. In the same manner, in the monastery of Saint Sylvester he made one garment of *oloverum*, with a border of *octapulus*. There he made a garment of *fundatus* with griffins, bearing a border of *blatthin*.

473. Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Praxedes he made one garment of *oloverum*, with a border of *stauracius*. This God-protected and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, *chrysoclavus* veils for the arches of the presbytery, bearing a scene of the blessed apostle Paul himself, and around them a gold band, numbering twenty-seven.

This God-chosen and illustrious bishop offered in the church of the blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, which we call that of Calixtus and Cornelius, two silver crowns, each with twelve dolphins, weighing twelve pounds together.

At the same time, in the deaconry of the blessed martyr of Christ George, he made one silver crown with twelve dolphins, weighing six pounds. This God-protected and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, which we call that of Calixtus and Cornelius, four silver baskets bearing the inscription “Holy Mother of God, Pope Gregory IV,” weighing twenty-four pounds.

On the altar of the same church he also made silver panels, weighing 113 pounds. In the same holy place, within the enclosure of the church, the same venerable pope made an elaborate and beautiful reconstruction. Formerly the altar had been situated in a low place, almost in the middle of the apse. Around it the people of both sexes gathered, while the pontiff celebrated the sacred mysteries with the clergy mixed indiscriminately among the people.

474. Moreover, the holy bodies of the blessed Calixtus, Cornelius, and Calepodius, buried in the central area of the church and lying behind the people, were not being honored fittingly. The same most devout pope did not endure this lightly. Applying his usual careful zeal and deepest diligence, he began a wondrous work and completed it most excellently.

After excavating a hidden chamber, he lifted the aforesaid holy bodies with the greatest reverence and honorably concealed them in the western part of the same church, that is, in the circuit of the apse. Around them he raised a massive mound, constructed and adorned a tribunal with dressed stones for the ministers, and above the confession, facing toward the rising sun, fitted panels of marvelous fragrance with an elaborately decorated structure.

Below the rising base of the altar, of marvelous proportion and ornament, he erected in clearly visible silver, in honor of the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, a structure raised higher than the former one, between beautiful steps of fine workmanship. In front of it he built a spacious presbytery from the foundations, elaborately constructed. On its northern side he placed stones around the enclosure of the matrons.

Adding beauty to the altar and honoring the Mother of the Lord with worthy gifts, he made there a *chrysoclavus* garment with Byzantine *blatta*, bearing a scene of the Nativity and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. In addition, he made an image of the blessed Mother of God Mary, cherishing the image of her donor.

This God-protected and illustrious pontiff made six silver *amae*, which precede the procession at all stations, weighing thirteen pounds; two cups, each weighing ten pounds; and eight *gemmiliones*, each weighing two pounds.

475. After all these things had been suitably completed by the aforementioned pontiff, with God’s favor, he restored to their former condition and adornment the things in the church of the blessed apostle Peter outside the walls that had long seemed ruined by age.

He newly adorned almost the entire portico over the oratory of the holy Mother of God Mary, called the Middle Portico, with beams and other kinds of wood, for the beauty of the basilica. He also completed, with new workmanship and distinguished adornment, another portico in front of the silver doors.

Likewise, on the front of the paradise of the aforesaid principal church, he decided with great speed to paint and restore in mosaic everything that had been destroyed on that wall since ancient times. He also renovated the portico of the same basilica, which is seen above its steps, by which the people ascend freely in fulfillment of their vow of prayer.

Beside the acolyte’s quarters he made a small but honorably constructed lodging for the pontiff’s rest, where, after the morning prayers or the services of the Mass, his limbs could sleep; and he adorned it with exceptional paintings.

Among the other examples of good works, in the Lateran patriarchate he also made, for the pontiff’s benefit and use, near the oratory of the holy martyr of Christ Lawrence, a sufficiently suitable dwelling, where there was excellent rest and from which the pontiff, going out with his clergy, could offer due praises to almighty God.

After these things, the buildings recorded above—buildings already ruined and nearly collapsing under the weight of time, which seemed to have been constructed beneath the palace by the ancient Fathers—the often-mentioned most blessed Pope Gregory raised and arranged anew from their foundations, with new adornment and workmanship.

He so newly rebuilt the descent facing the *paracellarium*, by which people had previously ascended and descended as though at night, that thereafter no darkness could impede passers-by as before. From that place all the way to the oratory of Saint Lawrence, he restored everything that was old. He also added new structures, among them three heated rooms.

He also entirely renovated from the foundations the bathhouse situated beside the *paracellarium*, and adorned it with marble and other suitable works. Previously, because of its great age, it seemed likely to collapse, unless the mind and excellent zeal of so great a pontiff had decided to restore it to its former state.

Likewise, in the church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana, he made a woven-gold garment bearing a scene of the palms and the Lord’s Supper.

476. Likewise, in the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, and of Saints Cornelius and Calixtus, which they call Across the Tiber, he made six baskets, weighing eighteen pounds together; one cup, weighing eight pounds and four ounces; a *cantharus* with a censer, weighing three pounds; and one *siclon*, weighing three pounds.

When all these things had been completed and carried out exactly, since—as has been said—the holy, venerable, and memorable simplicity of this man, always intent upon the service of almighty God, was likewise unceasingly concerned for the future salvation of the people and the liberation of the fatherland, lest, God not permitting it, they should somehow be captured by enemies; and since, in the time of this most holy Father and pope, the impious, wicked, and God-hated race of the Agarenes had risen from its territories and, ranging around almost all the islands and regions of all lands, was savagely carrying out the plundering of people and the desolation of places, and has by no means ceased doing so to this day—the most merciful bishop, having great fear of these unusual and avoidable dangers lest the people entrusted by God and by the blessed apostle Peter to him, who lived in the cities of Portus and Ostia, should suffer loss through the tribulation and plundering of the most wicked Saracens, drew deep sighs from his heart and began prudently to inquire how he might help and liberate the city of Ostia.

At once almighty God placed this counsel in his heart: that he should build anew from its foundations, on that spot, a city in which he might save the people, since what had been built in earlier times now seemed ruined, shaken by long age.

He did as he had been divinely inspired. In the aforesaid city of Ostia he built another city from the ground, extremely strong, fortified it everywhere with higher walls, gates, locks, and portcullises, and above them skillfully constructed stone-throwing engines for attacking enemies if they should come. Outside, not far from those same walls, he surrounded the city with a deeper ditch, so that they might not easily reach the walls.

477. When the aforesaid city had earned the beginning of its new construction, the most holy pope himself remained there for many days. Taking as his own share a considerable section of the walls, together with his men, he raised it from the foundations.

Until, with God’s favor, the frequently mentioned city was brought to the legitimate completion of its entire construction, he continually endured many labors and struggles in his holy heart. For this newly built city he also established a name to remain forever: it was to be called by all, whether Romans or other nations, by the name proper to it, namely Gregoriopolis.

And rightly did it take its name from its founder, because—something we read no pontiff had done before—this man, fortified by the help and power of almighty God, constructed and arranged the work already mentioned, for the people and the liberation of the fatherland, with marvelous beauty of workmanship.

478. With these works remaining in their proper places, the same angelic and exceptional bishop made in the basilica of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ, beside the Lateran patriarchate, a garment with *chrysoclavus*, bearing on the front of the altar a scene of the most blessed John the Baptist and Evangelist.

Around the altar, likewise joined together as a single piece, he made what were also like *chrysoclavus* veils, with certain paintings in the form of griffins, their horns painted on their foreheads.

He also made in the monastery of the most blessed martyr of Christ Lawrence, called Pallacinis, six silver baskets and two covered *cerostata*; one silver cup and one *ama*, likewise of silver.

In the oratory of the most holy Pope Gregory, situated within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made four silver columns, containing forty pounds of silver.

After all these things, this venerable pontiff ordered a sufficiently worthy house to be newly built from the ground in the estate called Draconis, surrounded on every side by porticoes from the upper stories. In it both he and future pontiffs, with all who serve them, might remain there in a stable manner for as long as they wished.

Likewise, in another estate called Galeria, he made another large and spacious house, sufficiently distinguished, for the use and benefit of the pontiffs, where, whenever necessary, they might be most generously lodged together with all who serve them.

The same nourishing and illustrious pontiff, burning with heavenly love, made in the basilica of the holy, undefiled Virgin and Mother of God, our Lady Mary, which is called “At the Martyrs,” a canopy of the purest silver, weighing four hundred pounds together. He also made one crown of the purest silver, weighing ten and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed confessor and pontiff Marcellus he made three crowns of the purest silver, weighing together [lacuna].

Indeed, in the deaconry of the martyr Saint George he made an Alexandrian veil bearing twelve pheasants, and one linen quilted veil before the doors.

After this most blessed pontiff had ruled the Roman and apostolic See most gloriously for sixteen years, he was taken from this light and passed to eternal rest. He held five ordinations in the month of March and December, namely, [lacuna] priests, [lacuna] deacons, and 185 bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

## CIV. SERGIUS II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 844, OF LOTHAR 3, OF MICHAEL 3.

[Col. 1293]

479. Sergius, a Roman by nation, son of Sergius, of the fourth region, sat for three years. Born of an illustrious mother, he was reared by her with chaste nourishment, and she began with great diligence to educate him. He did not fear to despise childish amusements, so that no one could hear or see anything obscene or lustful in him. Thus he seemed to excel in pious conduct before everyone and began to shine in the morals of the greater nobility, fortified and instructed by his mother’s pure admonitions.

His mother therefore rejoiced daily and cheerfully gave thanks to almighty God, who by heavenly assistance had granted her such a child. In the twelfth year of his age his mother died and departed to the Lord. Left by his mother—for his father had long been blind—he lived with his own people in his ancestral home.

At that time the blessed and distinguished Pope Leo III held the primacy of the Church of the city of Rome. Remembering the nobility of this exceptional boy and recalling the distinction of his parents, he ordered him to be brought to his presence with great affection.

When he had been brought in, he began to observe him with cheerful face and serene mind, and the boy pleased his heart beyond measure. The bishop then entrusted him to the school of singers to be educated in the common literary disciplines and to be instructed in the honey-sweet melodies of song.

480. This same distinguished and diligent boy quickly acquired the whole skill of literary training, so that he surpassed all the boys of his school. When the excellent pontiff heard these things, he was filled daily with inexhaustible joy at the boy’s favorable progress. He then appointed him an acolyte in the holy Roman Church.

In the twentieth year of his pontificate, when Leo had died in office, Stephen took up the priesthood of the Roman Church; Sergius himself loved him with great affection of heart. When Stephen observed that Sergius was exceptionally quick in the divine Scriptures, he immediately granted him the office of subdeacon.

After he had administered the governance of his episcopate for a short time, Paschal assumed the helm of the Church. Under him, this man, prudent in every respect and adorned with life, learning, and morals, was consecrated priest of the title of the blessed confessor and pontiff Sylvester. He excelled above all in mercy, zeal, vigilance, and every excellent discipline.

When Paschal died, Eugenius received the summit of the episcopate. After Eugenius had remained in the pontificate for three years, Valentinus was consecrated pontiff of that See; after his death, Gregory assumed the summit of the Church. Since the aforesaid man was greatly loved by Gregory, he ordained him archpriest in the holy Church.

481. After he had governed the Church with great diligence for sixteen years, he reached the end and died. Then the nobles and leading men of the city of Rome, together with the whole people of the Church, gathered in one place to choose a pontiff. As usually happens in such circumstances, one called out one candidate and another another. Suddenly, by God’s providence and pierced by divine inspiration, they began to discuss more carefully the religious character of Sergius, the aforementioned archpriest, so that all cried out that he was worthy to obtain the governance of the pontificate.

When their decision concerning this man had been confirmed, each person returned to his own place. Then suddenly a certain deacon of that Church, John, broke out into such madness and insanity that, after persuading a rather ignorant and rustic people, he gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men and entered the Lateran patriarchate by force, breaking down the doors with weapons of war and transgressing the tradition of law and order. As a result, everyone who was within the walls of the patriarchate was filled with astonishment and fear.

After that disorder had lasted with him for about an hour, the crowd of ignoble people, seized by fear, abandoned him and disappeared. When these things had occurred, all the princes of the Romans were indignant. By common agreement they gathered together in the basilica of the blessed confessor and pontiff Martin, coming quickly and with a great mounted retinue.

They brought out Sergius, the archpriest whom we mentioned above, a man approved in every virtue, from the church with great honor and with a great crowd of people accompanying him. Amid resounding praises, hymns, and spiritual songs, he was elected and led to the Lateran patriarchate.

On that same day such a quantity of snow fell throughout the city that everything appeared white. Many said that this was a sign of joy and brightness.

### 482

The aforesaid deacon John was expelled from the patriarchate with great disgrace by the leading men of this Roman city, who ordered him to be thrust under stricter guard into confinement because of that impious and dreadful presumption of such great rashness which the aforementioned deacon John had dared to commit. The leaders also wished to condemn him in a council of bishops and deprive him of his office. Others even wished to tear him limb from limb with swords and kill him. But the kindly and most diligent bishop Sergius prevented this, unwilling, in accordance with the evangelical command, to repay anyone evil for evil.

[Note: [Col. 1295] Romans 12.]

At last, when all the priests, nobles, dignitaries, and all the people of the Church were rejoicing, that most holy man was ordained and consecrated pontiff in the apostolic and most sacred see of blessed Peter.

### 483

For he was distinguished by birth, pure in faith, freer in preaching, humble before God, renowned among men, cheerful in countenance and even more cheerful in mind; a governor of churches, a cultivator of peoples, a supporter of the poor, a shelter for widows and a comforter of the needy, a giver to the dispersed and a preserver of those gathered together; a despiser of empty and worldly things, eager for and enamored only of the riches of wisdom.

When news of this most sacred consecration reached the ears of the invincible Emperor Lothair Augustus, he sent Drogon, archbishop of the Church of Metz, together with his most excellent son Louis, toward Rome with a great Frankish army. He also ordered several archbishops and bishops, abbots, and counts to set out with them.

When they entered the territory of the city of Bologna with their armed forces, they inflicted such slaughter and carnage upon the people that those who had been terrified by tyrannical cruelty throughout the cities and countryside abandoned their own places and hid themselves in remote regions and hiding places. While they were carrying out this savage wickedness everywhere, through each city, village, and field, they came to the bridge of Capella.

At that time the sky was so clear that no one could see a cloud or any sign of rain anywhere in the air. Suddenly, however, a considerable mass of black clouds formed, and, surrounded by stormy showers and flashes of lightning, some of Drogon’s advisers from among the leading men were struck and killed by a thunderbolt.

### 484

When the Franks saw this terrifying sign, they were all seized by extreme fear. Yet they did not in any way lay aside the fierceness of their minds, but hastened toward the City with savage intent.

When the aforementioned most blessed Pope Sergius learned that their arrival was drawing near, he sent all the judges to meet the most excellent King Louis at a distance of nearly nine miles from this Roman city. They received him with standards and great resounding praises.

When he had approached to within almost one mile of the City, he sent out all the military schools together with their patrons. All sang praises worthy of the most noble king, while the most accomplished Greek soldiers sang imperial praises. With the sweet-sounding voices of those praises, they received the king gloriously.

His Holiness sent venerable crosses and likewise standards to meet him; in the manner customary for receiving an emperor or king, he caused him to be received with immense honor. When King Louis saw the most sacred crosses and standards coming to meet him, he became cheerful and rejoiced greatly.

Then, with all his people and with all the Roman judges and military schools leading the way, he hastened toward blessed Peter. [Col. 1297] The aforementioned life-giving pontiff awaited the same king on the steps of that apostolic palace, together with his clergy, on that very Sunday after Pentecost.

When the king arrived and everyone ascended the steps of that most sacred church of blessed Peter, he approached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the atrium above the steps beside the church doors with all the clergy and the Roman people.

Then, embracing one another, King Louis took the right hand of the aforementioned pontiff, and they entered farther into the atrium and reached the silver doors. In that atrium, one of the soldiers was seized by a demon and grievously tormented in the sight of all the Franks.

Then the life-giving bishop ordered all the doors of blessed Peter to be closed and bolted, and, prompted by the Holy Spirit, said to the king:

“If you have come here with a pure mind and sincere intention, for the safety of the commonwealth, of the whole world, and of this church, enter these doors at my command. Otherwise, neither through me nor by my permission will these gates be opened to you.”

### 485

The king immediately replied that he had come with no evil intention, perversity, or malicious design. Then, at the bishop’s command, they placed their hands upon the aforesaid doors and opened them.

Thus they entered that venerable hall of blessed Peter, while all the clergy and all the religious servants of God sang praise to God and his excellence, acclaiming with extended voice:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and so forth.

Then the king himself, together with the same pontiff, all the bishops, abbots, and judges, and all the Franks who had come with him, approached the confession of blessed Peter. Prostrating themselves there, they gave thanks to our almighty God and to that prince of the apostles.

After the aforesaid life-giving pontiff had pronounced a prayer over the people, they all returned together from the church.

On the following continuous days, however, they afflicted all the suburbs with destructive devastation, tearing up fields, crops, and meadows like a thunderbolt’s assault. While this was happening, the pontiff himself, protected by God, had heard from certain people that they wished to enter this famous City under the pretext of hospitality; but he absolutely refused to allow this, fortifying and closing the gates.

### 486

On the following Sunday, all the archbishops and holy abbots, and all the Franks who had come with him, were gathered in the same basilica of the prince of the apostles, together with all the noble and distinguished Romans.

Then the life-giving pontiff himself anointed Louis, son of Emperor Lothair, with holy oil, crowned him with a royal and most precious crown, and appointed him king over the Lombards. Giving him a royal sword, he ordered him to gird it on.

When the celebration of the Mass was finished, everyone returned from the church rejoicing with the king.

Thereafter, day after day, the archbishop of the Church of Metz, Drogon, whom we mentioned above, stirred up a great conflict against the most holy pontiff and all our bishops, dignitaries, and nobles—both he himself and all the archbishops and bishops who had assembled with him against this universal Church, the head of all the Churches of God, without the authorization or summons of its metropolitan.

They were: Gregory, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna; Angelbert, archbishop of the Church of Milan; Joseph, bishop of the Church of Eporecia; Aginus, bishop of the Church of Verona; Almaricus, bishop of the Church of Como; Hortchaudus, bishop of the Church of Vercelli; Sigifridus, bishop of the Church of Reggio; Toringarius, bishop of the Church of Concordia; Odelvertus, bishop of the Church of Aosta; Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Lucca; John, bishop of the Church of Pisa; Peter, bishop of the Church of Volterra; Gausprandus, bishop of the Church of Pistoia; Cantio, bishop of the Church of Siena; Lupus, bishop of the Church of Tescina; Sisismundus, bishop of the Church of Teramo; Pico, bishop of the Church of Ascoli; Fratellus, bishop of the Church of Camerino; Gisus, bishop of the Church of Fermo; Racipertus, bishop of the Church of Nocera; Amadeus, bishop of the Church of Penne; Donatus, bishop of the Church of Fiesole; and others.

The counts Boso, Adalgisus, John, Vuldo, Vernardus, Wifridus, Maurinus, and others also contended with them.

### 487

But, by the inspiration of divine grace, they were unable to overcome either the words or the wisdom of that life-giving pontiff. Such heavenly power was with him that no one could confound or constrain him in argument. Overcome by him, they departed ashamed and covered with confusion.

When they saw this, they laid aside in every way all the anger and ferocity that they had maintained in their minds.

After these events, they asked the aforesaid pontiff that all the Roman primates should promise fidelity by oath to King Louis. The most prudent pontiff by no means permitted this, but began speaking to them as follows:

“If you wish them to make this oath only to the lord Lothair, the great emperor, I consent and permit it. But that it be made to Louis, his son, neither I nor all the Roman nobility consents.”

### 488

Then at last, seated together in the same church—the most blessed pontiff, the great king, and all the archbishops and bishops, while the remaining priests and the nobles of the Romans and Franks stood—they promised fidelity to Lothair, the great emperor, forever Augustus.

After this, the archbishops Ebbo and Bartholomew, who had been deprived of their office and expelled from the Church by the most holy pontiff because of their crimes, asked the pontiff to deign to reconcile them and grant them the pallium.

But that bishop said that they were not even worthy to receive communion among the clergy; they would have permission only to communicate among the common people.

At the same time, while King Louis himself was staying in Rome, Siginolfus, prince of the Beneventans, came to Rome with a great army.

[Note: [Col. 1299] Platina, under “Sergius.”]

When the aforementioned king had received him honorably, Siginolfus explained to him everything for which he had come. The king, with a grateful heart, granted and conceded to him whatever he had requested.

When the Franks, Lombards, and Beneventans had gathered together, an immense multitude of people was formed, so that Rome appeared surrounded on every side; by their multitude all the crops were destroyed.

Siginolfus himself ardently desired to see the pontiff and receive his blessing from him. When the bishop had received him, Siginolfus prostrated himself on the ground and humbly kissed his precious feet. Having received his blessing, he returned cheerfully from his presence, giving thanks to God.

### 489

When all these matters had been completed, the most excellent King Louis returned with great joy to Pavia, where from the beginning of his principate he had governed the summit of power.

Then all the people, rejoicing with their wives and children—the Roman senate and people—having been freed from such a great plague and redeemed from the yoke of tyrannical savagery, revered the most holy bishop Sergius as the author of their salvation and the restorer of peace.

He, however, attributed the deed not to his own virtue but to the divine gift.

Since the tongue cannot adequately explain in order everything that he did, let us pass to the things that he offered in holy places and begin to relate them briefly.

At the very beginning of his pontificate, burning with heavenly love, he completed a work of extraordinary beauty in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana. He marked out with his own finger a larger circuit for the sacred altar, which had formerly been narrowly constructed there, and completed it from its foundations. He splendidly adorned it with beautiful columns and with marble carved above in a circle. There the sacred people now continually stand abundantly in the administration of the sacred office.

When this had been completed, the life-giving pontiff offered in the same basilica, for the beauty and adornment of this distinguished work, twenty white silk hangings decorated around the edge with embroidered gold. Likewise, twenty other very fine hangings embroidered with gold and decorated around the edge with purple.

There also, with Christ’s cooperation, he constructed a marvelous confession and splendidly adorned it with silver panels covered with gold. Consecrating it with his own hands, he placed relics in it.

He also completed another very fine work before the doors of this venerable basilica: for he made the sacred thresholds, formerly hidden from the people, fully visible to everyone, constructing there beautiful and ornamental arches from their foundations, which he also decorated brilliantly with various paintings.

### 490

The distinguished pontiff, protected by God, for the remedy and future recompense of his soul, magnificently and especially adorned with silver and gilded panels the chamber of the manger of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is joined to the basilica of blessed Mary, God’s Mother and our Lady, now called Major. The panels bore the history of blessed Mary, God’s Mother. No pontiff, throughout so many years, had thought to bring it to such a splendid appearance.

This bishop, while carefully caring for all the churches, also completed from its foundations the basilica of the holy Archangel, situated on the summit of Mount Fajano [Note: [Col. 1299] Perhaps Gargano.], making it larger than it had previously been. He ordered it to be brightly painted with radiant pictures and newly restored its damaged roof.

There he offered four garments of *imizilo* and likewise four hangings.

The life-giving and most blessed pope also restored from its foundations, with God’s merciful favor, the school of singers, formerly called the Orphanotrophium, which, because of extreme age, appeared almost ruined and broken down, to a better condition than before.

He also completed from its foundations the basilica of the blessed martyr Romanus, situated not far outside the City, beyond the Salarian Gate. He decreed that it should be the parish church of the saints Sylvester and Martin.

He also built the basilica of the holy martyr Theodore, which is seen to be situated in the territory of the Corani, thirty miles from the city of Rome, and splendidly adorned it with gleaming paintings.

### 491

In the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter he made a garment of gold-and-silk brocade, bearing in the middle an image of the Savior and, to his right and left, shining figures of all the holy apostles. He also adorned it with the most precious green, blue, and white gems.

Thus this most accomplished pontiff, protected by God and most blessed, in pious devotion and solicitous through his ardent love for Saints Sylvester and Martin, rebuilt from its foundations in a better and more beautiful condition the church consecrated in their holy names. He had diligently governed it from the beginning of his priesthood until he was raised to the summit of the pontificate; through long ages it had decayed from the failure of old age and had long remained shattered by ruins and torn apart.

He also painted its apse with immense devotion in gold and colors laid over mosaic.

For the honor of almighty God and of the same most blessed bishop Sylvester, he dedicated and placed beneath the sacred altar the body of Saint Sylvester together with the most blessed Fabian, Stephen, and Soter, martyrs and bishops; the martyr Asterius with his most sacred daughter; Saints Cyriacus and Maurus; Largus and Smaragdus; Anastasius and Innocentius, bishops; Saints Quirinus and Leo, bishops; and the martyrs Artemius, Nicander, and Crescentianus. With them he placed the blessed women Soter and Paulina, as well as Memmia, Juliana, Quirilla, Theopiste, and Sophia, virgins and martyrs, and the blessed widow Quiriaca, together with many others whose names are known to God alone.

### 492

After magnificently completing these works, with a grateful heart and an attentive mind he offered in the same church the following objects, to remain there perpetually:

A very precious golden crown with green, blue, [Col. 1301] and white gems, which to this day is seen hanging above the altar; it has in the middle a cross of the purest gold, likewise with precious gems.

Also four *gabathae* of the purest silver covered with gold, hanging before the vestibule of the sacred altar; and two open-work *gabathae* gilded and furnished with bosses.

Two very fine golden crosses with gems; and one other silver cross similarly made.

In the same basilica he offered three gold-covered thuribles; two silver patens of the purest silver, gilded.

One gilded silver strainer, which he uses in the sacred office.

One silver crown with little bells, having in the middle a cross with a dove.

This most blessed pope, burning with heavenly love, offered in the place mentioned above three pairs of silver hand-washing vessels.

Also two silver sextarii; four larger silver crowns with dolphins, weighing [lacuna] pounds; two larger silver chalices, likewise gilded; a larger silver paten covered with gold, bearing in the middle an image of our Lord Jesus Christ; three pairs of *cerostata* (candlesticks), silver-plated above; three silver baskets; one gilded paten with chalice; one silver cup, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

For the honor of that venerable basilica he offered twelve bronze chandeliers and likewise six pairs of bronze *rugae*.

This distinguished man made, for the glory and honor of the holy confessors whom we mentioned above, a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

### 493

He also magnificently adorned the confession of the sacred altar with silver panels covered with gold, weighing [lacuna] pounds, so that through the sacred intercession of those saints he might possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

This most merciful and kindly bishop offered in the place mentioned above three images covered with silver and gold: one bearing the image of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the other two of the saints Sylvester and Martin, seated above the vestibule of the sacred altar.

In the basilica mentioned above he offered a garment of gold-and-silk brocade bearing the history of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with green, blue, and white gems.

He also made another most precious garment embroidered with gold and silk, bearing in the middle the image of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, and, to his right and left, images of the saints Sylvester and Martin, likewise with green, blue, and white gems.

Indeed, the most holy bishop offered three Alexandrian curtains woven in a most precious workmanship.

Twenty-four gold-embroidered hangings, decorated around the edge with purple, which hang in the arch of that basilica.

Fifteen other gold-embroidered hangings with a purple border.

Four white silk hangings surrounding the sacred altar; one of them has in the middle a cross and *gammadiae* of gold-and-silk brocade, and the others are decorated around the edge with purple.

This distinguished and most blessed pope, protected by divine inspiration, built from the foundations beside that basilica, to the praise of the Creator, a monastery in honor of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, Sergius and Bacchus, and Saints Sylvester and Martin.

In it he established a congregation of monks serving God, who, for daily praises, prayed day and night to the Lord our God in the aforementioned church.

After this most blessed pontiff had gloriously governed the Roman and apostolic see for three years, he was taken from this light and departed to eternal rest.

He held one ordination in the month of March: eight priests, three deacons, and twenty-three bishops in various places.

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

Therefore, in the second year of his pontificate, the aforementioned city had its beginning, and in the sixth year of his consecration the city was completed on every side. On that day there was immense peace and joy for all the clergy and nobles.

When this city had been completed, the bishop was distressed that the people had not at all come to inhabit it. At that same time the people of Corsica arrived, having abandoned their cities, lands, and possessions because of fear of the Agarene people.

The supreme bishop gave this city to them with immense joy, enriched them with many riches, and granted them many possessions [Col. 1340D].

After the Saracen plundering, he also made larger silver doors in the church of blessed Peter.

He also made a silver crucifix between the columns, weighing sixty-two and a half pounds.

He also held a council attended by sixty-seven bishops, at which he ordered the decrees of the pontiffs to be reread. At it the cardinal Anastasius was condemned on account of his crimes.

During his time, as in number 554, line 1:

Number 554, line 1: “Daniel, an unjust and foolish master, blinded…” (M., “and blinded, foolishly”), “hastened to go to the most serene Emperor Louis, and reported many useless words to him concerning Gratianus, the most eminent master of the soldiers, alleging that he himself ought to make a division between kingdom and priesthood and ought to transfer the empire to Constantinople.”

When the emperor heard this matter, he came quickly to Rome. When the bishop heard of the king’s arrival, he began to wonder and received him at blessed Peter. They began to discuss the aforementioned matter together, but found it completely false.

The man himself who had gone to Francia for the purpose of making the accusation was handed over to Gratianus’s authority. When these things had been completed, as in line 15 of the following number, the emperor departed, and Saint Leo IV, pope…

Here the Life of John the Englishman is inserted in both manuscripts. But since this story was refuted long ago, we have decided that it should be removed here, lest malicious people should afterward seize from it an opportunity for slander. If anyone is displeased that we have omitted this Life, let him consult the Royal manuscript; there he will read the interpolated words of Martin of Troppau, which foolish men inserted into the manuscripts of Anastasius.

The opening apparatus continues from the preceding section. Abbreviated readings remain fragments; uncertain expansions are marked locally. In the inventories, *fundatus* denotes a rich figured textile (its precise weave is not specified), *stauracius* a cross-patterned textile, *spaniscus* a named cloth whose precise type is uncertain, and *chrysoclavus* gold-woven ornament. *Periclysis* is a border; *blatta/blatthin* is purple cloth; *pharus/phara* denotes a lamp fixture; *clamacterios* are hanging fittings of uncertain form. *Solarium* denotes an upper terrace or gallery; the Confession is the shrine over a saint’s tomb.

Thus it is recorded in Penia’s hand:

“Benedict III succeeded Leo IV in the year of the Lord 855, with no other pontiff intervening; from this it is evident that the remarkable fiction and shameless lie concerning a certain woman invading the Roman pontificate after Leo IV and bearing the name John VIII is false. Neither this ancient book nor the noble writers of earlier centuries make any mention of her.”

[Col. 1303]

## 494

Leo IV, a Roman by birth, son of Radoaldus [Note: [Col. 1303] Platina has “Radulphus”], sat for eight years, three months, and five days. He was an exceedingly Catholic and apostolic man, possessed of great patience and great humility; generous, devout, innocent—or benevolent—an ardent lover of justice and most zealous governor of the people, and also an unfailing student of the divine Scriptures, always devoted to vigils and prayers.

In his most blessed breast there dwelt, in accordance with what is read in the holy Gospel, both the cunning of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove [Note: [Col. 1303] Matthew 10]. For he was filled with the beauty of every holiness: a lover of religious men and of those who continually served God in all things, a nourisher of the poor, and one who despised himself.

At first, for the study of letters, he willingly went from his parents to the monastery of the blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, which lies outside the walls of this Roman city beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, until he had fully learned the sacred writings. There he learned not only letters but also the practice of holy conduct. Although he was then still a boy, he remained there not as a boy but as a perfect monk. By the example of his devout conduct, the others living under the same monastic rule served almighty God with greater devotion. He was among them as one of them.

And because “a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” [Note: [Col. 1305] Matthew 5], [Col. 1305] so the reputation of this most holy man could not remain hidden for long. His fame, or reputation for holiness, spread here and there, clearer than daylight, and through the reports of many faithful people it soon reached the ears of the once most blessed father and pope Gregory. When the excellence of his chastity and worthy conduct had been recounted to him, Gregory immediately ordered him to leave the monastery in which he was piously living, brought him to the bosom of holy Mother Church, and commanded him to remain familiarly in his service at the Lateran patriarchate.

## 495

He also made him a subdeacon because of the fame of his praiseworthy life. Although he changed his place and rank, he nevertheless bound his life and conduct even more firmly than before to the service of our supreme Creator and multiplied them through good works.

When Pope Gregory of this most sacred see died, Sergius, archpresbyter of the holy Roman Church, became its prelate. He consecrated as priest this Leo—of whom we have reported something above—namely, the most blessed pope, and bestowed upon him the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs. While Leo excelled in good conduct there and supplied the needy with what they required, refreshing pilgrims, the poor, and those possessing little not only by word but also with bodily nourishment, Sergius, who then presided over the Roman see, was taken from this present life. In his time, too, the churches of the most blessed princes Peter and Paul were utterly plundered by the Saracens.

## 496

Since every Roman strength had therefore languished and been crushed by this calamity or misery, the entire assembly of the Romans confessed that it could in no way escape the danger of death through two circumstances or perils: namely, the sudden death of the pontiff and the devastation inflicted upon the holy churches and all the territories of the Romans.

When all the Roman nobles, with equal devotion and common agreement, were considering the future pontiff—who could rule or govern so holy and inviolable a place in the fear of almighty God—the fame and merit of the most blessed prelate were immediately revealed by everyone and spread throughout the whole city. For the pontiff who had died had not yet been carried to his appointed burial.

## 497

And behold, everyone, from the last to the first, with one voice and complete unanimity, demanded that Leo the venerable priest become their future pontiff. They declared through many oaths and acclamations that they did not wish to have any other prelate over them except this man, of whom we have spoken so often.

We believe that the hearts of all who desired him were inflamed and united by nothing other than divine love and the clemency of divine power. Then all of them, as noted above, went joyfully and with great eagerness to the church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs, where he lived. They forcibly removed him against his will and brought him with hymns and distinguished praises to the Lateran patriarchate. Preserving the ancient custom, they all kissed his feet.

No human being can briefly recount how great the harmony and unanimity were in his pontifical election. What divine power accomplished, at the time of his election, against those Saracens who had committed so abominable a crime, through the aid of the apostles and the intercession of his own holy prayers, it is neither improper nor blameworthy to record in the present writing, whether for fear of the future or for the sake of remembrance.

For when they all wished, after committing the crime of iniquity and plunder, to return to the African region from which they had come [Note: [Col. 1305] *Reverti*, “to return,” deponent infinitive, instead of *revertere*, active infinitive.], they were, as we learned from a reliable report, sunk by the violence of winds and storms in the vast expanse of the sea, God permitting it. Thus the ancient miracle of the Egyptians was newly achieved through the prayer of the apostles.

The Romans too, as we have said, rejoicing together in the election of the new pontiff, began again to be greatly troubled because they did not dare to consecrate a future pontiff without imperial authority. They were especially afraid for the city of Rome, lest it should again, as formerly, be besieged by other enemies. Struck by this fear and the impending danger, they consecrated him as prelate without the prince’s permission, preserving his faith and honor in every way and in all things after God.

## 498

Since human judgment is not sufficient to estimate, nor speech adequate to report, how great in goodness and piety this most blessed pontiff was, let us return to the things which, trusting in the love of God, he offered to the churches of the saints, and let us recount them from the beginning of his pontificate.

This distinguished and renowned prelate, burning with heavenly love, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter one crown of the purest silver, weighing twenty-four pounds; two pierced bowls (*gabathae*), weighing two pounds; seven curtains—two of *fundatus*, two of *stauracius*, and three of *spaniscus*.

There he also offered, for the splendor and glory of that venerable basilica, one Alexandrian curtain of remarkable beauty, bearing a scene of peacocks carrying figures above them, another scene of eagles, wheels, and birds with trees.

The distinguished and most prudent pope offered in the basilica of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs, where he had most diligently fulfilled the office of priest, three baskets of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds; likewise one pair of handwashing vessels (*aquamanile*) of the purest silver; a pitcher with a thurible, weighing [lacuna] pounds; and twelve *fundatus* curtains, which can be seen hanging in the arch of the church for its adornment.

[Col. 1307]

He also made thirty-four white silk curtains in the same basilica. For the splendor of the sacred altar he made a silk vestment having a *periclysis* of *chrysoclavus*. He also made a white vestment with roses, having seven wheels and, in the middle, a panel of *chrysoclavus* with the image of a man wearing five green gems on his head. He also made a white *chrysoclavus* vestment with six wheels.

In the aforesaid basilica, for the honor and glory of the sacred altar, he made thirty-three curtains bearing crosses and gamma-shaped ornaments of gold-woven decoration, gems, and golden bosses. He made one embroidered curtain bearing the image of a man seated upon a peacock. He also made three curtains bearing a scene of the holy Mother of God. He made fourteen other *fundatus* curtains, and two others with a vestment of purple cloth.

## 499

This exceptional and most blessed pope made in the basilica of the holy Mother of God, situated in the district called that of the Sardinians, a *fundatus* vestment bearing a scene of the holy Mother of God, worked in *chrysoclavus*, with prophets.

This God-beloved and most prudent pope constructed marble seats at the entrance of the patriarchate, which none of the pontiffs had undertaken to complete. The *solarium* which Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built, when it was seen overturned and ruined because its beams had broken through excessive age, he restored anew, more beautifully and in improved form.

This distinguished and devout prelate, relying upon heavenly love, decreed that at the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, on his feast day, the praises should be sung publicly in the evening by all the clergy and the schola.

In the time of this blessed prelate, an earthquake occurred in the city of Rome in the tenth indiction, so that all the elements seemed to have been shaken, as everyone could see.

This often-mentioned and most diligent pontiff, in accordance with ancient custom and by canonical authority, decreed and established that, while the sacred solemnities of the Mass were being celebrated in the church, no layman should presume to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except the sacred people who appeared to be appointed for the administration of the sacred office.

## 500

This most blessed pontiff, after the slaughter and plunder committed by the savage race of the Hagarenes in the churches of the holy Apostles, directed his attention daily to restoring those churches, so that he might repair everything that had been taken away by impious hands, hoping for the reward of eternal future recompense.

Therefore, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he offered a fixture of the purest silver, called *buttonem* in the text [its precise form is uncertain], with silver bowls hanging from seven small chains.

For the illumination of that basilica he made a bronze lattice with seventeen silver baskets. He also restored a *pharus* of remarkable size for the splendor and glory of the oft-mentioned church. In it he also offered a crown of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

He made twenty-five *fundatus* curtains, hanging more beautifully around the sacred altar. He also made ten curtains bearing scenes of lions, which can be seen hanging before the entrance of the sacred Confession. He made forty-six other *fundatus* curtains, glittering between the columns on the right and left of that venerable basilica. He also made thirty-three *fundatus* curtains hanging in the arch for the adornment and decoration of the presbytery.

Moreover, this beneficent pope arranged for eighteen other *fundatus* curtains to hang in various places of the same basilica, and four other curtains to hang before the doors of the sacred basilica.

## 501

This distinguished and prudent prelate, relying upon heavenly love, made in the basilica of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs a *chrysoclavus* vestment bearing a scene of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with images of the aforesaid martyrs and of the beneficent prelate himself.

The mind of this aforesaid beneficent prelate shone with such great divine love that, in his special time, he willingly wished to restore anew, with all his heart, all the innumerable goods that had previously been taken away by impious hands from the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

For the dignity and honor of that aforesaid church, he therefore made two crowns of the purest silver, composed with marvelous workmanship, hanging from silver chains and adorned with gems and gilded bosses. One weighed 132 pounds and the other 130. One had thirty-seven silver *clamasteria* hanging beneath it, and the other, similarly made, had forty.

And because he was always richly adorned by the divine gift and strove successfully to exercise worthy care and concern for everything, he made in the oratory of Saint Andrew the apostle at Saint Peter’s two large *fundatus* curtains and five smaller ones, decorated around the edges with purple cloth.

## 502

This venerable and distinguished pontiff, protected by God, made in the monastery of Saint Anastasius, for the eternal redemption of his soul, one silk *fundatus* vestment bearing a scene of eagles. Likewise, he made two *fundatus* curtains, trimmed around the edges with purple cloth.

In the same way he made one *fundatus* vestment in the monastery of Saint Praxedis.

This aforesaid prelate, from the day on which, relying upon divine power, he ascended the sacred see of the apostle Peter with complete benevolence, immediately strove eagerly and willingly to restore to memory all the former or ancient usages and orders of the sacred palace which, during the times of his predecessor pontiffs, had fallen into disuse and been abolished through varying custom, or to arrange everything in a better condition than it had recently been.

For the dining hall which Lord Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built from its foundations, together with all the furnishings he had prepared there, had been destroyed through excessive age and the forgetfulness of preceding pontiffs. On the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, neither Lord Gregory nor Lord Sergius of holy memory dined there at all.

But the same most blessed and supreme prelate, Leo IV, restored anew, with [Col. 1309] joy and great delight, all the furnishings and provisions that had been destroyed there, and splendidly restored them to their former use.

He also restored a cross of the purest gold adorned with gems, which Charles, emperor of the Franks and Romans of pious memory, had offered in the basilica of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, now called the Constantinian basilica, during the time of Lord Leo III, pope of holy memory. It had been customary for this cross to precede the most sacred pontiff during litanies, and it remained in this use until the time of Pope Paschal of holy memory. Then, through diabolical suggestion and instigation, it was extorted by wicked men and secretly stolen by thieves at night.

Thereafter none of his predecessor pontiffs—neither Lord Paschal, Lord Eugenius, Lord Valentinus, nor Lord Gregory, nor even Lord Sergius—remembered to restore it and repair it for the use of the holy Church of God at Rome [Note: [Col. 1309] *pararet*, “he might prepare,” instead of *repararet*, “he might restore,” marked with an asterisk.].

But the aforesaid magnificent prelate made it anew of the purest gold, skillfully adorned it with pearls and hyacinth-colored and green gems of remarkable size, and splendidly restored it to its former use in the Roman Church of the holy Mother of God.

## 503

This eminent and distinguished prelate was a preacher proven in knowledge and learning of the divine Scriptures. He shone with such a reputation for blessedness and holiness that he worked miracles before the sight of all the people of this Church founded in Christ.

In the first year of his pontificate, beside the basilica of the blessed martyr Lucy, situated in Orphea [Note: [Col. 1309] Platina: “Orthea”], a serpent of a dreadful kind arose in certain gloomy and hidden caverns. In Greek it is called *basiliscus*, in Latin *regulus* (“little king”). By its breath and its gaze it swiftly killed all who approached those caverns and delivered them to the danger of death, so that astonishment and fear seized everyone as they marveled at the serpent’s powers and destruction.

## 504
