When the most blessed and distinguished pontiff heard of this slaughter and ruin of the people, he turned to prayer and did not cease to implore the Lord with fasts, that He might free all from such destruction. While this was taking place, the illustrious and celebrated day arrived on which the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary is celebrated.

Then the aforesaid universal pope went on foot, as is customary, from the patriarchate to the basilica of the holy martyr Adrian, with hymns and spiritual songs, the sacred icon proceeding before him, and with all the clergy. Returning from there with the whole company of the faithful, he hastened, amid God’s praises and accompanied by a great crowd of people, to the basilica of the blessed Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, called *ad Praesepe*.

When he reached the place where, as we have said above, that most deadly basilisk lay in gloomy caverns, he ordered all the clergy and people to stand still. Hastening to the caverns, he stood fearlessly over the serpent’s opening, from which its pestilential breath issued. He raised both his eyes and his hands to heaven and, with abundant tears, entreated Christ, who is God above all things, to drive the dreadful race of the serpent from that place by His power. Having said a prayer over the people, he went on to offer the praises of God in the basilica mentioned above.

From that day the deadly basilisk itself was so driven away and cast out from those dens that thereafter no trace of its harm appeared in those places. This beneficent pope also performed another miracle, which we shall briefly begin to recount.

## 505

At the beginning of his pontificate mentioned above, a violent fire invaded the Saxon quarter. By the force of its flames it began fiercely to consume everything. Great crowds of people gathered there, wishing to extinguish the flames of the conflagration; but the fire was carried higher into the air by gusts of wind, consuming and destroying everything, so that it came near the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, burning and ravaging the houses of the Saxons and Lombards and the portico.

When he heard this, the most blessed pontiff anxiously hastened there and placed himself in the path of the advancing fire. He began to entreat the Lord to extinguish the flames of the blaze; and, making the sign of the cross with his own fingers, he prevented the fire from spreading its flames any farther. Unable to withstand the power of the blessed pontiff, it reduced its extinguished flames to ashes.

This God-beloved and most prudent pope made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter forty-five *fundatus* curtains, trimmed round about with purple cloth. The same distinguished pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Martin adjoining the basilica of Saint Peter, for the praise and glory of the shrine of that blessed Martin, a vestment of remarkable beauty. It bore a scene of the saint mentioned above lying on a bed, with an image of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ; likewise an image of the holy martyr Agatha, having at her feet an image of the beneficent pontiff himself, adorned with seventeen hyacinth-colored gems. In the same oratory he also made four curtains, one of which had three wheels of *chrysoclavus*.

## 506

In the basilica of the four holy brothers he made one *fundatus* vestment bearing a scene of those holy martyrs and an image of the beneficent prelate himself, adorned with twelve gems; likewise four *fundatus* curtains.

This venerable and distinguished pontiff made in [Col. 1311] the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his patron, one pierced basket of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds. There he offered crowns of the purest silver, weighing [lacuna] pounds. Relying upon heavenly love, this most blessed and distinguished pope offered to the blessed apostle Peter, for the splendor and glory of that most sacred basilica, one double-nozzled lamp of the purest silver, weighing forty-five pounds.

The same most blessed prelate made in the church of Saint Sylvester, confessor and pontiff, situated on Mount Soracte, one *fundatus* vestment with four corners, two Tyrian and two *fundatus*. In the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the same most holy and blessed prelate also made eighteen gold-woven curtains hanging in the arch of the presbytery and bearing a scene of the blessed apostle Peter. In the oratory of Saint Leo, confessor and pontiff, situated beneath the aforesaid church, he made one *fundatus* vestment bearing a scene of eagles. There he also offered one silver crown, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

## 507

There he also made twenty *fundatus* curtains, trimmed on both sides with purple cloth. He offered to the blessed apostle Peter sixteen silver chalices placed around the altar, weighing [lacuna] pounds; and also a hanging chalice with little chains and dolphins, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

After the Saracens’ plundering of this church, the aforesaid most holy and angelic prelate also made over the body of the blessed apostle Peter three silver images in all. The one in the middle bore an image of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, its head adorned in the form of a cross with hyacinth and green gems. Another, set at the Savior’s right, bore the faces of the blessed apostle Peter and blessed Petronilla. Another, set at the left, bore a painted face of the blessed apostle Andrew together with the face of the aforesaid supreme prelate. They weighed 104 pounds.

There he made twelve bronze lamps placed above the entrance to the sacred altar. This most blessed pope often desired with great earnestness to rebuild every ruined place of the saints. Thus he restored more perfectly, for the salvation of his soul and its future recompense, the monastery of the Corsae, situated beside the basilica of the blessed martyr and pontiff Sixtus, which had been laid waste by the deeds of certain wicked men and converted to secular habitation. There he established a community of handmaids of God to render daily praise to almighty God; he enriched it with gifts, adorned it with wealth, restored by sacred decrees all that had been taken away from it, and more fully confirmed these things with his holy hands.

This often-mentioned and most blessed pope brought many to knowledge of the truth through the discourse of his preaching, and daily displayed saving works to all.

Textual forms in the opening apparatus: no. 513 *auri obr*, “refined gold” (abbreviated); nos. 514/515 *rotas*, “roundels,” and *effigiis*, “images”; nos. 527/531 *gilium/giliis*, “lily/lilies”; no. 530 *blattaha*, “purple cloth,” as spelled; no. 531 *arcora/arcos*, alternative inflections/forms for “arches”; no. 536 *grammad*, “gamma-shaped ornaments,” abbreviated. In Penia’s Cavense readings: no. 506 *optulit*, “offered,” as spelled; no. 511 *monacos*, “monks,” as spelled; no. 525 *turabulum*, “thurible/censer,” as spelled; no. 528 *cyburium*, “ciborium,” as spelled; no. 531 *giliis*, “lilies”; no. 547 *parium*, “pair.”

### 508

He also ordered that the eighth day of the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God—which previously had by no means been celebrated at Rome—should be observed with sacred vigils and morning praises, while he spent the night with all the clergy in the basilica of that same ever-Virgin, our Lady, situated outside the walls beside the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence. A great multitude of the people had also gathered there, eager to celebrate the solemnity of the new festival. When this magnanimous bishop saw this, he distributed several silver coins among all who were present for the celebration.

The same most blessed man made in the church of that same Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary one *fundatum* vestment. He also made there forty-five curtains. In the oratory of that church, called [the oratory] of the blessed Barbara, he likewise offered one *fundatum* vestment. That pre-eminent bishop, chosen by God, also made one *fundatum* vestment in the oratory of Saint Eugenia.

### 509

This diligent, most holy, and in every respect illustrious and pre-eminent pontiff, with God’s help, generously and with pure intention gave one *fundatum* vestment to the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, situated outside the walls beside the church of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Within the precinct of this church, in the oratory of the blessed martyr Leo, he made one *fundatum* vestment.

That most gentle pontiff, keen in every good work, also offered one *fundatum* vestment in the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated within the aforementioned monastery called Corsarum. In the place mentioned above he offered one *fundatum* vestment in the oratory of Saint Caesarius.

### 510

The same most benevolent man newly made a golden cross. As has been customary since ancient times, this cross was carried by subdeacons before the horse of preceding pontiffs; with God’s help, he renewed it more splendidly in gold, silver, and gems.

He offered one *fundatum* vestment in the church of the blessed martyr Nympha, which appears to be situated in the city of Portus. Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian, which appears to be in Silva Candida, he made one *fundatum* vestment. In the same place he also offered three *fundatum* curtains, ornamented around the edge with *blatthin*.

This most blessed pope regularly visited the tombs of the most sacred martyrs with devout mind and ardent heart. For them he continually pleaded, by sacred vigils and prayers, on behalf of the people of the orthodox faith.

### 511

One day, when he had reached the tomb of the blessed martyr Lawrence and was completing his prayer according to his custom, he began to inquire more carefully and said: “How many monks here daily offer praises to almighty God?”

Then all who were present told the blessed pontiff that two monasteries had been built there by certain pontiffs, but that, because of extreme poverty, they had been reduced to desolation. Immediately that beneficent pontiff, moved by a heavenly impulse, restored the monastery now called that of Saint Stephen and Cassian, and fully adorned the place with gifts and wealth.

In it he also trained a number of Greek monks in holy discipline, so that day and night they might offer praises to the Almighty and to that same martyr.

That bishop, protected by God and venerable, constructed within the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter an oratory of extraordinary beauty and supreme elegance. He magnificently adorned it by surrounding it with fine marble, and gloriously decorated its apse with gold mosaic overlaid with color. In it he placed the venerable body of the blessed confessor and pontiff Leo; above it he constructed a sacred altar, and, relying on his love for Christ’s name, completed a ciborium with a gilded cross, so that he might secure for himself a worthy place in heaven.

### 512

After all these works had been undertaken and completed—their names having already been written or mentioned individually above—the same distinguished shepherd and Father, although he exercised a useful and worthy care and concern for all the churches of God and was more attentive than anyone else to every good work, nevertheless drew long sighs from the depths of his heart.

For every day he saw the most sacred altar of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, violated, and reduced to such dishonor and degradation by the treacherous Saracens, enemies of God. Moreover—and we say this with grief and sorrow—he saw Christian people from every direction being sent to the most sacred threshold of that aforesaid prince for the sake of prayer and devotion, and therefore unable fully to accomplish their vows as in former times.

Accordingly, trusting in the help of almighty God and strengthened by counsel and courage, he adorned not only the sacred confession but also the front of the aforementioned altar, with gold and silver panels, in a manner sufficiently seemly and honorable, as the work dedicated there visibly demonstrates in every respect.

Therefore he newly dedicated the principal front of the venerable altar with panels of the finest gold, surrounding it entirely with very many excellent and precious gems, and restoring it to its former, better condition and beauty. On these golden panels, as has been said, not only does the image of our Redeemer shine forth, but also his venerable Resurrection and the representation of the sacred and life-giving cross.

### 513

The faces of Peter, Paul, and Andrew likewise shine and gleam on the aforementioned panels. Among them were depicted the most holy pontiff Leo IV, as well as his special son, the lord emperor Lothair, persons dear to God and worthy of veneration throughout all ages, for future remembrance or reward.

Finally, he made a panel of enamel, weighing 216 pounds of refined gold.

He also restored the confession of the frequently mentioned altar to its ancient honor and condition, with panels prepared from the purest silver, with equal devotion of heart. On them we see the Savior seated on a throne, wearing precious gems on his head; on his right are cherubim, and on his left are depicted the faces of the apostles and the others.

He also made the *rugae* of the sacred confession from silver, bearing the faces of the most blessed Peter and Paul; they weighed 208 pounds.

That pontiff, beloved of God and most prudent, made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter eleven curtains woven with gold, hanging from the arches and elegantly ornamented around the edge with *blatthin*.

In the oratory of the pontiff Saint Leo, within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he also made one white silk vestment with stamped decoration, with *gammadia* and *periclysis* of *blatthin*, together with two larger and eight smaller white curtains.

In the monastery of Saint Caesarius, situated in the palace, he made one *fundatum* vestment and eight curtains.

### 514

That bishop, protected by God and venerable, made, for the repayment and reward of his soul, one *fundatum* vestment and eight curtains in the cemetery of the blessed martyr Agatha, situated outside the gate of the blessed martyr Pancratius.

Who could say, or adequately describe, how many gifts this pope, protected by God and most diligent, offered with devout mind to the holy places?

In the oratory called that of Pope Paul, he offered one vestment of extraordinary beauty, decorated with eagles, bearing a scene with a cross of *chrysoclave* and *gammadia*.

In the oratory of Saints Processus and Martinianus he made one vestment of considerable splendor, with wheels and human figures, and a scene with a cross, likewise of *chrysoclave*, and *gammadia*.

In the basilica of Saint Petronilla he completed another vestment of radiant appearance, bearing a wheel and an eagle, with a cross of *chrysoclave* and *gammadia*.

### 515

In the oratory of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin, our Lady Mary, situated in the *mediana*, he offered one vestment likewise with wheels, eagles, and a cross of *chrysoclave*, with *gammadia*.

In the oratory of Saint Hadrian he made one vestment with wheels and figures of people, with a cross likewise of *chrysoclave* and *gammadia*.

The same frequently mentioned and most blessed pope offered in the basilica of the martyr Saint Sebastian, situated at Frascata, one vestment of exceptionally precious brilliance, with a cross of *chrysoclave* and *gammadia*.

That supreme and pre-eminent bishop made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter one *cortina* of *holosericum*, with many scenes of immense splendor, for the adornment and glory of that most sacred basilica.

When the most blessed man and pontiff Leo IV, with the Lord’s assistance, had more fully bestowed these and the other things that have been written, through love and devotion, upon various holy places of the faithful, he began, in consultation with Jesus Christ the Lord, to consider the condition of the city of Rome and the restoration of its walls, which after long age and excessive antiquity appeared completely broken and ruined.

He feared that, if they remained for long in such neglect and forgetfulness, they might more easily, with the Lord’s permission, be captured or perhaps stormed by enemies. Therefore, lest this evil occur in the future, as the twelfth indiction approached he took care, with complete eagerness of mind, to renew all the walls of the city of Rome and restore them to their former use and beauty.

[Col. 1315] He not only ordered the walls mentioned above to be rebuilt with swift activity, but also hastened to command that the gates, by which the whole city is often closed, be rebuilt with new workmanship and very strong timbers, because of fear and terror of the enemy.

So that all these things might be completed quickly and brought to effective and beautiful completion, the aforementioned apostolic man went about among the walls and gates not only on horseback but also on foot, personally, with his faithful followers, so that no delay or postponement might arise in their restoration.

Therefore, as has already been said, while the venerable pontiff exercised the greatest care and concern for the city of Rome among all his responsibilities, he everywhere newly brought everything to a better and renewed condition. He also ordered fifteen towers—which he found utterly ruined around the circuit of the city—to be restored with new construction.

### 516

He prudently and wisely arranged for two of these towers to be built beside the Portuensian gate, at the very bank of the Tiber—that is, beside the river’s shore—in a way that no one previously could have imagined or considered.

Since through this place not only ships but also people had formerly been able to enter easily, whereas now scarcely even small boats could pass through it, this was done because of the future danger posed by the Saracen enemies and for the safety of the city of Rome.

He therefore took care to secure these towers not only with stones but also with iron chains, so that, if necessity required, no ship could pass through that place.

This newly constructed work provides a defense for the city of Rome and, to those who see it, not a small but a great wonder, because it was accomplished with great wisdom, subtle prudence, and dignity.

### 517

That pope, protected by God and most blessed, also gathered within the walls of this nurturing City many bodies of saints that had long lain hidden, with the greatest care and deepest devotion of heart, for the honor of almighty God.

For, diligently searching, he found the bodies of the four holy martyrs called the Four Crowned Ones. For love of them, he rebuilt from the foundations, with the merciful favor of heavenly power consenting, the basilica consecrated to their name.

When he had been elevated to the summit of the pontificate, he had governed it with the wisest moderation. Yet, shaken by the passage of long ages, weakened by old age, and almost broken by ruin, it had long appeared ancient, dilapidated, and disrupted. He restored it to a more splendid and beautiful condition.

For the praise of almighty God, he placed beneath the sacred altar their most holy bodies together with those of Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphronius, Castorius, Simplicius, Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus—the four brothers; likewise Marius, Audifax, and Abachus; Felicissimus and Agapitus; Hippolytus with his household, eighteen in number; Aquilinus, Aquila, and Prisca; Narcissus and Marcellinus; Felix and Symetrius; Candidus and Paulina; Anastasius and Felix; Apollonius and Benedictus; Venantius and Felix; Diogenes and Siberaelis; Festus, Marcellus, and Superantius; Pudentiana and Benedictus; Felix and Venantius.

He also placed there the head of Saint Protus, together with Saint Cecilia, Saint Alexander, Saint Sixtus, Saint Sebastian, and the most sacred virgin Praxedis, as well as many others whose names are known to God.

Over this he constructed, for the glory of the Creator, a ciborium of marvelous workmanship and extraordinary beauty, made of the purest silver overlaid with gold, with green and hyacinth-colored gems, weighing 313½ pounds.

In the same place he offered in that church four red curtains hanging around the altar.

The same most holy bishop also made in the aforementioned oratory of the blessed Barbara, constructed within the church of the Four Crowned Ones, a silver crown weighing twelve pounds.

He also offered in the same oratory ten silver *gabathae*, weighing … pounds.

Furthermore, in the oratory written above he made three *fundatum* vestments, having in the middle crosses with *gammadia*, and twelve curtains.

### 518

The aforementioned venerable pontiff also made in the basilica of the blessed pontiff Stephen, at the third milestone on the Latin Way, one *fundatum* vestment with a cross in the middle, and six curtains.

There he offered a paten and a small sacred silver chalice, weighing one and a half pounds.

The most blessed bishop also offered in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles a silver-gilt apostolic censer, bearing the name of the lord Pope Leo IV, weighing four pounds.

There, in the oratory of the blessed confessor and pontiff Gregory, he also made one *fundatum* vestment with *gammadia*, and one cross made of woven silver.

Likewise, there in the oratory of the blessed martyr Pastor he made one vestment in the same manner.

In the oratory of the blessed Mother of God, situated by the ambo, he made one vestment in the same manner.

In the oratory of the holy and exalted Cross he made one vestment likewise.

In the oratory situated by the font he similarly made one vestment, together with *quadrapulum* curtains.

### 519

That venerable and illustrious pontiff made in the church of the Four Crowned Ones, above the main altar, one *fundatum* vestment with a cross in the middle and *gammadia*, and, around it, one *fundatum* border.

In the oratory of Saint Barbara, in the same place, he likewise made one *fundatum* vestment.

In the oratory of Saint Sixtus he made one vestment in the same way.

In the oratory of Saint Nicholas he likewise made one vestment with an eagle.

In the same church he also made one linen *cortina* with a cross in the middle and, around it, a *fundatum* border of extraordinary size.

Adorned with pious conduct and these sacred works, the pope offered in the frequently mentioned church, which he had founded out of love, a paten of the purest silver overlaid with gold, decorated with the trophy of the cross, the image of the Savior, and the figures of the holy Mother of God and the holy apostles, in a beautiful design, weighing seven pounds.

Likewise, he offered a sacred chalice covered with gold, bearing an icon of the Evangelists and a cross, weighing four pounds.

He also offered a *cantharus* of the purest silver, gilded, around which a recessed sign of the cross can be seen, with figures of the prophets and an icon of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr.

He also offered one apostolic censer of the purest silver, and four gilded *gabathae* for the splendor of that venerable basilica, weighing two and a half pounds.

[Col. 1317]

### 520

After all these things had been accomplished, he adorned the confession together with the sacred altar with silver panels weighing ninety-three pounds, and decorated it with figures of the saints.

Above it he also offered a crown of the purest silver with very precious gems, having a cross in the middle; it can still be seen hanging above the same altar.

There he also offered forty-three *fundatum* curtains.

The same frequently mentioned and illustrious bishop, inflamed by heavenly love, offered in the monastery of Saint Silvester, Saint Benedict, and Saint Scholastica, called “at the Lake,” three *fundatum* vestments and likewise seven *fundatum* curtains.

After the Saracen plundering, the same most blessed bishop also made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter a crucifix of extraordinary size, constructed of the purest silver, gilded, and decorated with hyacinth-colored gems. It weighed seventy pounds and had seven additional white gems, one of them larger.

### 521

We shall not act improperly if we clearly insert into this work, for everlasting remembrance, the things that, among the other events, were wondrously done and accomplished in the twelfth indiction through the constant prayers and tears of the most holy bishop, prayers heard by the Lord, so that present and future generations may more easily recognize how great a holiness this man possessed in this troubled life.

After the impious and mournful, misery-filled plundering that the Saracens had carried out, at the devil’s urging, against the first of all churches—the holy Roman Church—they wished once again, as before, to inflict similar damage upon the Roman territories and the church of the most blessed apostle Peter, and then to return victorious to the places from which they had departed.

But, because of the care and diligence of the supreme shepherd, which shone forth and remained watchful, they were entirely unable to accomplish this.

Nevertheless, so that the faithful might rightly become still more faithful in the Lord, and might not doubt that his signs and venerable miracles had newly proceeded from ancient examples, it must first be recalled what divine mercy pitifully did to them at that time, and by how many miseries and calamities that pestilent people was deservedly crushed and scattered.

Accordingly, remembering the former profit or plunder they had gained, they cruelly resolved, with a multiplied force of wicked men and many ships, to come to attack the city of Rome while the twelfth indiction was in progress.

They also remained for many days in a place called Tozarum, near the island of Sardinia. Departing from there, they attempted to enter the Roman port, but God did not aid them.

### 522

Their wicked and impious arrival greatly terrified the Romans. But because almighty God has always preserved his Church inviolate, and does not cease to preserve it thereafter, he then stirred the hearts of all the Neapolitans, Amalfitans, and Gaetans, among the others, so that together with the Romans they would rise up and fight bravely against them.

Immediately, leaving their own regions, they arrived with their ships before the worthless Saracens—

[Note: [Col. 1317] “They arrived” (*conjunxerunt*), that is, “they reached [them].”]

—and made their sudden arrival known to the most blessed pontiff Leo IV. They declared that they had come for no other reason than to emerge victorious over the pagans, with the Lord’s help.

Then the venerable pope ordered some of them first to come to him at Rome, wishing especially to learn from them whether their arrival was peaceful or not; and so it proved to be.

Among them came Caesar, son of Sergius, master of the soldiers, who had been appointed over the army. The pope received them kindly in the Lateran palace and inquired the reason for their coming.

They testified that they had come for no other purpose than the one written above.

Trusting their words, the charitable apostolic bishop soon hastened to the city of Ostia with a great company of armed men, and received all the Neapolitans with profound and exceptional devotion.

When they saw the supreme bishop, they prostrated themselves at his feet on the ground, reverently kissed them, and gave thanks to the almighty High-Throned One, who had resolved to send them such a bishop to strengthen them.

So that they might become victorious over the sons of Belial, they earnestly begged that they might be worthy to receive the Lord’s body from his sacred hands.

He sang Mass for them with his own voice in the church of the blessed Aurea, and all received Communion from his hands, as has been said.

Before this took place, he had gone with them, with the help of Christ, as far as the aforementioned church, with hymns, litanies, and distinguished songs.

There also, kneeling, he entreated the Most High that by his prayers he might deign to deliver the enemies of the Christians into the hands of those who resisted them.

### 523

For them he also offered this prayer with many tears, saying:

“God, whose right hand raised the blessed apostle Peter as he walked upon the waves, lest he be drowned, and rescued his fellow apostle Paul from the depths of the sea when he was shipwrecked for the third time, hear us graciously and grant that, through the merits of both, the arms of these your faithful servants, fighting against the enemies of your holy Church, may be strengthened and made powerful by your almighty right hand, so that, after triumph has been received, your holy name may appear glorious among all nations. Through our Lord, etc.”

On the following day, after the venerable bishop had returned from the city just mentioned, those accomplices and partners in crime appeared beside the shore of the sea at Ostia with many ships.

The Neapolitans attacked them and wished to fight bravely; they even wounded some of them, and would then have won a triumph if one obstacle had not arisen too quickly.

For while they were fighting each other with intense attention, suddenly a wind arose so strong and overwhelming that no one in these times can remember anything like it. It immediately separated both fleets.

At first the Saracen ships came as far as the seashore; then, as the wind blew and the sea rose in storms, they were scattered, and after a little while, their strength broken, they returned.

For we firmly believe that almighty God had brought forth this wind from his treasury, and that it did not permit them to go out to cause harm.

For these new and mystical miracles, which the Divinity has deigned to show and demonstrate to us in our times, although we are unworthy, the mercy of our true God must always be glorified and praised. He permitted them to see the place they desired, yet, lest they be able to seize it, drove them far away by the power of his might. Later, through the intercessions and merits of the most blessed princes Peter and Paul, the depths of the sea, as well as hunger and the sword, relentlessly destroyed many of them.

### 524

Of these, many who were suffering from hunger on certain of our islands were killed by our people.

The others were captured alive, for the sake of truth and testimony, and brought to Rome. So that their great number might not be seen, the Roman nobles ordered many of them to be hanged on wood near our Roman port.

We ordered some others to be kept alive in chains, solely so that they might recognize, more clearly than daylight, both the hope we have in God and his ineffable goodness, as well as their own tyranny.

After this, lest they live among us idly or without hardship, we ordered them sometimes to carry whatever seemed necessary to the wall that we had begun to build around the church of the most blessed apostle Peter, and sometimes to various works of the craftsmen.

### 525

For these benefits, as has already been recounted, the blessed pontiff offered in the basilica of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, after the plundering by the Agarenes, thirteen arches of the purest silver. Of these, two, which he placed on the right and left sides in the presbytery, were of extraordinary size and weighed … pounds.

The same most blessed bishop also made in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter one gold-woven vestment, bearing a scene of how the blessed Peter preached to the holy Roman Church, with seven white gems—that is, pearls—eleven green gems, and twenty-seven hyacinth-colored gems.

In the church of the blessed apostle Andrew he made a ciborium over the altar out of marble, and a silver chalice, with twelve hanging crowns on the same ciborium, weighing … pounds.

He also made there the bell tower, and placed a bell with a bronze hammer and a gilded cross.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter he also offered a censer of the purest gold, decorated with various gems.

In the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated at Saint Lawrence outside the walls, he made one vestment bearing a scene of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and an image of the aforesaid beneficent pontiff.

### 526

In the church of the Four Crowned Ones he also made eleven silver baskets, weighing twenty-four pounds.

In the church of the blessed apostle Peter he offered a cross of the purest gold, decorated with hyacinth-colored and white gems and emeralds, of extraordinary size. It stands on the right side beside the main altar.

There he newly renewed the staff and silver-plated it, the staff in which the aforementioned cross is contained. It weighed eleven and a half pounds of silver and bore the name of the lord Pope Leo IV.

In the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen he also offered a gold-woven vestment with four hyacinth-colored gems.

The same aforesaid beneficent and supreme bishop, moved by immense love and devoted to good conduct, made in the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, situated outside the walls of the city of Rome, one vestment of pure silk with eagles. It had three gold-woven panels on each side, depicting the martyrdom of the aforesaid martyr and the image of the aforesaid pontiff.

### 527

In the church of the holy martyrs, the Four Crowned Ones, he also made three gilded silver images: one bearing the face of the Savior, and the other two bearing the faces of the saints Claudius and Nicostratus. They weighed fifty-two and a half pounds.

In the same church he offered one silver crown weighing twenty-five pounds.

On the screen of that church, which stands before the main altar, he hung a silver lily with crystal apples and a buttercup.

In the same place he also made seven silver baskets, weighing twelve pounds.

That most gentle man established, in his own residence—which he had ordered to be built from the foundations and which appeared to have come to him by right of his parents—a monastery of women servants of God in honor of Saints Symetrius and Caesarius.

There he also bestowed gifts: a paten and a sacred gilded silver chalice, bearing various gems, weighing … pounds.

In the same place he offered incense vessels (*thymiamateria*) together with one *cantharus*, weighing … pounds.

Furthermore, that beneficent pontiff offered in the monastery mentioned above three baskets of the purest silver and Saxon *gabathae*, weighing together twelve and a half pounds.

There he made, for the repayment and reward of his soul, three *fundatum* vestments, each having an enclosed embroidered panel.

There he made a crown of the purest gold with green and hyacinth-colored gems, which hangs above the altar, weighing … pounds.

[Col. 1321]

### 528

That bishop, protected by God and venerable, burning with heavenly love, offered in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated outside the walls of this city of Rome beside Saint Lawrence, one *fundatum* vestment having in the middle a gilded panel with an image of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ and of that beneficent pontiff.

In the church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he offered a silver censer with its gilded cover, having chains and knobs around it, weighing six pounds.

In the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, across the Tiber, the aforementioned bishop restored the apse, which projected as though about to collapse because of excessive age.

In the church of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, for the honor and strength of that church, he made a *butron* of the purest silver, hanging in the presbytery before the main altar, weighing 149 pounds.

He also made in the church of the blessed martyr Sebastian, situated at Frascata, a basket of the purest silver, weighing two pounds, bearing the name of the beneficent bishop and of Saint Sebastian.

After these things had been suitably completed and accomplished following the grievous and unjust plundering by the Saracens, the catholic and wholly praiseworthy bishop, for the adornment and praise of the church of the prince of the apostles, Peter, made above his venerable altar a ciborium, columns, and gilded lilies of extraordinary size and beauty, made of the purest silver and weighing 1,606 pounds.

Above the ciborium he also offered four crowns and sixteen chalices of pure gold, weighing … pounds.

Of silver, as above, for the honor and glory of the ciborium, he made forty-six chalices and crowns, weighing twenty-two pounds and seven ounces.

For the extensive beauty of the ciborium he also made above its columns four baskets of the purest silver, weighing forty-two pounds.

There, around the altar, he also made fourteen white stamped-silk curtains, having *fundatum* borders.

### 529

There he also offered fourteen additional linen curtains, having around them a border of stamped white silk.

In the same place he made two arches of the purest silver, weighing fifty pounds.

In the oratory of Saint Sylvester within the Lateran palace he made one *fundatum* vestment, having in the middle a small panel of *chrysoclave*, and four *fundatum* curtains.

In the church of Jerusalem he made one *fundatum* vestment and likewise four *fundatum* curtains.

In the deaconry of the Virgin Saint Mary, situated at Cyro, he also made a silver crown on the inside, surrounded by golden knobs.

In the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated at Frescata, he offered one *fundatum* vestment, having in the middle a small enclosed gilded panel, and four *fundatum* curtains.

In the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, situated at Morenico Narrano, he likewise made one *fundatum* vestment and four *fundatum* curtains.

In the same manner, in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, situated at Maruli, he offered one *fundatum* vestment, having in the middle a small enclosed gilded panel, and four *fundatum* curtains.

### 530

That bishop, protected by God and venerable, offered in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated at Saint Lawrence outside the walls, one linen *cortina*, having around it a *fundatum* border and, in the middle, a cross likewise of *fundatum*.

In the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which appears to be in Silva Candida, he offered one red vestment, having around it a silver border, a cross in the middle, and four curtains with eagles.

In the church of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter he offered a silver crown, surrounded on the outside with scenes and gilded, weighing seven pounds.

That pope, protected by God and most blessed, trusting in heavenly love, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, before the confession of the sacred altar, on the right and left sides, for the adornment of that basilica, six angels of the purest silver, weighing sixty-four pounds.

Above that ciborium he made *oleae* hanging around the altar, having four gilded panels and four *gammadia*.

In the same place he made four arches standing in the presbytery, of the purest silver, weighing one hundred pounds.

That most blessed pontiff offered in the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated in a place called Sublacus, approximately forty miles from the city of Rome, one *fundatum* vestment and likewise three *fundatum* curtains.

The same aforesaid bishop also made in the church of the blessed martyrs of Christ, Gervasius and Protasius, situated within the city called Fundana, one *fundatum* vestment having in the middle one cross of gold-woven material, and one *fundatum* curtain.

The same aforesaid bishop also offered in the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Caesarius, situated within the city called Terracina, one *fundatum* vestment having in the middle a cross with *gammadia* and a *periclysis* of *blatthin*, bearing the name of the lord Pope Leo IV, and likewise five *fundatum* curtains.

He also offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter four arches of the purest silver, weighing eighty-four pounds.

In the basilica of the blessed martyr Rufina at Silva Candida he made one *fundatum* vestment, having in the middle a cross of *periclysis* and, around it, *blatthin*, bearing the name of the lord Pope Leo IV.

### 531

The same most blessed prelate also made in the church of the blessed Clement, martyr and pontiff, six bowls (*gabathae*) of the purest silver: three, indeed, with *filopares* bearing the sign of Christ; two likewise with representations of palm trees; and one chased vessel, which is *saxisca*, weighing altogether four pounds.

The same most blessed and illustrious pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed Peter the apostle, his spiritual nourisher, three arches with columns and lilies of the purest silver, weighing altogether 102 pounds.

That venerable pontiff himself made in the basilica of Saint Caesarius, which is situated at Terracina, one *vestis* of *quadrapulum*, ornamented around the edge with *blatthin*, and bearing in the middle a cross of *chrysoclavus*, with an inscription naming Lord Leo IV, pope.

He also made in the basilica of the blessed Peter the apostle three arches of the purest silver with columns and lilies, weighing sixty pounds.

He also made in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which is situated in the city of Porto, one *vestis* of *spaniscus*, ornamented around the edge with *fundatum*, and in the middle with a silver cross; likewise three *vela* of *spaniscus*, ornamented around the edge with *fundatum*.

He also made four gilded silver panels on the step before the confession of the blessed Peter the apostle, and two lambs, which together weighed forty-four pounds.

In the place mentioned above he offered porphyry-colored crowns of remarkable size, ornamented with the purest gold and twelve dolphins, bearing an inscription naming that beneficent prelate himself, weighing three and a half pounds of gold; also ten arches of the purest silver, which together weighed 181 pounds; and forty-eight linen hangings, which hang from the arches in the place mentioned above and are ornamented around the edge with *fundatum*.

### 532

Now, after everything written above, I wish to explain in this present account, for everlasting remembrance, what works and how great were the works that the most exalted and venerable prelate, moved by zealous and devout care for the defense of the universal Mother Church, dedicated honorably and nobly within a short period of time.

Accordingly, while all the Roman nobility remained in profound mourning because of the devastation that the impious and malevolent Saracens had inflicted some time before—and because they might thereafter have committed worse acts unless the church of the blessed Peter the apostle were quickly fortified on every side—the same beloved pontiff began to feel great anxiety for all the Romans. He thoughtfully sought how and by what means he might remove such resentment or fear from their hearts.

While he was repeatedly laboring long over these matters, God revealed to him the following plan: he should make this matter known as clearly as daylight to his beloved and special son, the lord Lothair Augustus, so that, with the Lord’s favor, through his assistance and counsel he might complete the desired work. His predecessor, Pope Leo III, had begun to build that city for the church of the aforementioned apostle and had already laid its foundations in many places. After his death, however, some men had removed them, so that not even the entrance could be seen where the aforesaid wall had previously been begun. If life permitted, the pontiff hoped, with Christ’s support, to bring this desired work to completion.

When the most pious and serene Caesar learned of this, he was immediately filled with great joy and exultation. He earnestly begged the aforementioned prelate, who was in every respect his spiritual father, to complete as quickly as possible the construction of so great a work through diligent labor. For this purpose he sent him, together with his brothers, a considerable number of pounds of silver, so that, as has been said, such a profitable work should by no means remain uncompleted.

At this welcome message the distinguished prelate became extraordinarily joyful. From that time onward he began to be very anxious about the undertaking. He summoned all the faithful of the holy Church of God and personally asked their counsel as to how so great a structure of walls could quickly be completed. It then seemed good to everyone that he should arrange for workers to come in turn from every city, from all the public estates, and from the monasteries—which was indeed done.

### 533

Accordingly, in the second year of his pontificate, the aforesaid city began to be built. In the sixth year after his consecration, the entire city was completed on every side with great and marvelous works.

When, through the many labors and struggles of the most blessed prelate, the whole work of the walls had been completed and finished according to his desire, he began to give manifold and innumerable thanks to almighty God, who had deigned to hear and fulfill his daily prayers for the new construction of the walls.

For no human tongue can briefly recount how great and what kind of care, zeal, and anxiety the pious and praiseworthy shepherd devoted each day and night to the work until it was built. Since, apart from the duties required by the sacred commands, he did nothing other than what has been written above, neither cold nor wind, rain, nor severe or moderate disturbance of the weather could in any way make him sluggish in going from day to day.

Rather, now here, now there, he hurried watchfully and anxiously among the various works on the walls, so that our almighty Redeemer, through the pious intercession of the apostles Peter and Paul, might swiftly fulfill his good purpose and desire—which we now all behold.

At last, when all the works of the new city had been completed and perfected, as we have often related, the most blessed pope, always praiseworthy in every respect, ordered—with great devotion of spirit and joy of heart—that the aforesaid city, which was called Leonine after the name of its founder, should remain forever firm and strengthened.

[Col. 1325]

After litanies had been sung and the psalter recited, all the bishops and priests resident in the city, together with him, and all the orders of clergy of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, were to walk barefoot around the entire circuit of the walls, carrying ashes on their heads with hymns and spiritual songs. He also ordered the cardinal bishops to have water blessed, so that during the prayers, as they passed along the wall, they might diligently sprinkle that water everywhere for the sake of sanctification. They humbly carried out what he had commanded.

### 534

The venerable pontiff himself delivered three prayers over that same wall, with many tears and sighs, asking and beseeching that the aforesaid city might be preserved forever by the aid of Christ and remain safe and undaunted from every assault of its enemies through the protection of all the saints and angels.

He first made his prayer over the gate that faces Saint Peregrinus. Its beginning and ending are as follows: + + +

> O God, who entrusted to your apostle Peter, when you gave him the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the pontifical authority to bind and loose: grant that, through his intercession, we may be freed from the bonds of our sins; and make this city, which we have newly founded with your help, remain forever secure from your anger, and grant it new and manifold triumphs over the enemies on account of whom it was built.

The same pious pope also delivered a second prayer over the postern gate where, in a wondrous manner, a fortress rises above it—the gate called Saint Angelus. The text of that prayer is as follows:

> O God, who from the very beginning of this world have deigned to guard and preserve this holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church from its enemies, graciously cleanse away the written bond of our iniquity, and permit this city, which we have newly dedicated to your holy name through the intercession of your apostles Peter and Paul, always to remain secure and undaunted from all the snares of its enemies. Through our Lord, etc.

He sang the third prayer over another postern gate facing the Saxon settlement; because of them it is called the Saxon postern. This third prayer contains the following form in particular:

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty and merciful God, that, crying out to you with our whole heart, through the intercession of your apostle Saint Peter, we may obtain the forgiveness of your mercy. And concerning this city, which I, your servant Leo IV, bishop, with your help have dedicated by a new work, and which is called Leonine after my name, we continually beseech your majesty’s clemency: command that it may always remain unharmed and secure. Through our Lord, etc.

### 535

In that city, in accordance with the promise of his desire which he had vowed to God, he distributed a great dole to Romans and to people of various nations on the day of the highest solemnity.

Then, as has been stated, he proceeded with the other priests and all the Roman nobles to the church of the blessed Peter the apostle, accompanied by prayers and divine praises, and solemnly celebrated Mass for the salvation of the people and for the city’s safety and perpetual stability.

After completing the sacred offices, he honored and enriched all the nobles of Rome with many gifts, not only in gold and silver but also with silken cloaks.

There was great joy for everyone on that day, namely the twenty-seventh day of June, the day before the vigil of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Throughout the entire city of Rome as well, boundless joy and countless celebrations of exultation took place.

Therefore it is more worthy and fitting that, for so great a prelate and shepherd, we should continually implore the almighty Lord with our whole and pure heart in our prayers. Through him, with Christ’s power assisting, we know that this astonishing and honorable work was rapidly completed and brought to its conclusion for the salvation of all Christians. May the pontiff flourish here for a very long time, and there, together with all the saints, may he deserve to possess eternal rewards forever for his innumerable struggles and labors.

### 536

The most blessed pope himself made in the church of Saint Sinzigus, which is situated in the city of Blera, one *vestis* of *fundatum*, bearing in the middle panels of *chrysoclavus* with an image of the Savior, who has three green gems on his head, and images of Saint Sinzigus and the most blessed prelate; and four *vela* of *fundatum*.

In the church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs he made two silver candle-stands (*cerostata*) of the purest silver, weighing five pounds and six ounces, and four silver bowls (*gabathae*), weighing [the number is defective in the supplied text] pounds.

He made in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which is situated at Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls, twenty-seven *vela* of *fundatum*.

Likewise, the aforesaid prelate made in the church of the blessed Clement, martyr and pontiff, a crown (*regnum*) which hangs above the high altar, sculpted from the purest gold without gems. It has in the middle a gold cross with gems set into that cross, five glass ornaments, and four additional hanging glass ornaments; it weighed fifty pounds.

He also offered in the church of the blessed Hippolytus the martyr, which is situated on the island of Porto and is called Arsis, one *vestis* of *fundatum*, bearing one *gammadia* woven with silver, and four *vela* of *fundatum*.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, which is situated within the city called Anagni, he offered one *vestis* of *fundatum* with *gammadia* woven in gold, and four *vela* of *fundatum*.

### 537

But lest, after the matters explained and recorded above with truthful testimony and precise descriptions, we pass over the remaining works in silence—which would be wholly inappropriate—I wish to make known, as clearly as daylight, other works of the most blessed pope, although they were very numerous, accomplished through the powerful assistance of Jesus Christ’s mercy.

[Col. 1327]

While the mind and spirit of the supreme prelate unceasingly labored in good and God-worthy works, he began to undertake a very great struggle concerning the city of Porto, seeking how and by what means it might remain safe and free from enemies and from the sons of Satan both in his own time and in future generations.

After he had long kept this plan silently in his pontifical heart, the almighty and exalted Father, who never ceases to help his faithful in just and pious thoughts, stirred the hearts of the Corsicans. Terrified by fear of the Saracens, they had become exiles from their own territories and wandered here and there without their native soil. They were to come as quickly as possible to the Roman See for refuge and salvation—and so it happened.

When they came to the most sacred threshold of the prince of the apostles, they were immediately presented to our thrice-blessed lord, Pope Leo IV.

### 538

After he and his nobles had prudently inquired of them what necessity then threatened them and for what reason they had come, they set out their necessities, calamities, and troubles in order, as if with one voice, before the aforesaid pontiff. They declared that they would live all their days in the obedience and service of him and of his successors in the pontificate.

When the benevolent prelate understood this, he was immediately lifted up in great exultation and joy, giving thanks to God for having sent him such men, who could dwell forever in the aforementioned city.

After hearing their many promises, the distinguished pope replied to them in a clear voice, together with his nobles:

“If you take care in your deeds to fulfill what you have told us in words, we have excellent places where you will be able to live, provided only that you prove good and faithful to us and to our pontifical successors.

“For the city that we shall give you is strongly fortified and defended. With the protection of our Redeemer’s aid, we have restored it to its former dignity with new gates and buildings in places of great necessity.

“If, as we have said, you wish to remain there, we shall grant you vineyards, lands, and meadows, so that you may suffer no want. We shall also give you, until you have enough from your own labor, what you and your wives and children need to live in full abundance: oxen, horses, and other animals as well, as we have said, if you carry out everything with good will.”

When the Corsican people heard these promises, they became even more joyful and immediately asked the pious pontiff to send men who would show them the city and the particular lands. This was done.

Everything pleased them, and they all calmly promised that, if our pope and lord should deign to grant them everything through which they had been conducted, they would hasten with their entire households and possessions into the service of Saint Peter, as his servants and those of his successors, with complete eagerness.

### 539

After surveying the city and all the possessions, they returned with the same envoys to the venerable pontiff.

When they arrived, as has been said, and reported the joyful and prosperous news—that the Corsican people had openly declared that they would live and die in those same places—the pontiff summoned everyone so that they might likewise testify unanimously in accordance with the envoys’ report.

For the sake of the eternal reward and memory of the most serene and great emperors Lothair and Louis, and also of his own eternal reward, he issued them a pontifical charter according to what he had promised. Its terms and stipulated condition were that it should remain firm and stable only so long as they remained obedient and faithful in all things to the prelates of the holy See and to the Roman people.

If, God forbid, they did not inviolably observe the entire series of the charter’s provisions, it was decreed in the same charter that it should stand void and empty.

The lands given to them and assigned by the pontifical envoys—both those belonging by proprietary right to the Church and those belonging to venerable monasteries, indeed also those of individual neighboring owners—are specifically recorded in the pontifical privilege granted to them.

Behold how great and how frequently displayed was the mercy of the often-mentioned prelate. He not only loved his Roman nobles for the defense of the city, but invited people from wherever he could gather them to their aid and protection, loving the defense of his homeland and the security of the people entrusted to him more than temporal and perishable profits, for the sake of which we already remember that many have continually lost both their lives and the possessions in which they delighted.

### 540

After all these matters, which have been woven together above in brief style, the holy and venerable prelate, greatly rejoicing, carried out other works not unlike them.

The very ancient cities of Horta and Ameria had walls and gates that, because of the extreme age of the times, had fallen to the ground and remained utterly abandoned. At one time thieves, at another robbers, entered them more easily through their open approaches, with no guard resisting them.

The most diligent prelate, recognizing the great neglect of these cities, restored the cities we have named to their former place and condition through divine favor. At his urging and by his care, he strengthened them with new walls and gates scarcely different from the earlier ones.

Now, within those cities, the inhabitants live in greater security from the ambushes of their enemies, while, as has been said, thieves and robbers, faced with closed walls and gates, will henceforth be able to inflict neither harm nor theft by night or by day.

After these works had been carefully completed, he made in the church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs one crown (*regnum*) of the purest gold, hanging above the high altar on golden chains. It had a sculpted golden cross in the middle, bearing fourteen gems: five fixed in that cross and nine others hanging there. Six were white and three hyacinth-colored. Together they weighed one and a half pounds and an ounce.

[Col. 1329]

Likewise, in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, which is situated in the district of the Sardonians, he offered one gilded silver chalice and paten, bearing an inscription naming Lord Leo IV, pope, weighing altogether four pounds and five ounces.

That distinguished and eminent prelate, after completing countless works of the highest splendor in the basilica of the blessed Peter, keeper of heaven’s keys, raised up the doors that the Saracen race had destroyed and stripped of their silver. He adorned them with many silver panels on which luminous and salutary histories were sculpted, and restored them to a better appearance than they had formerly possessed.

Thus all who wished to enter that same basilica might offer praises to almighty God and to his holy prelate, and ask that the many years of his life might be prolonged. Through this work of such brilliance and such weight of beauty, he adorned God’s hall with silver weighing seventy pounds.

This supreme and God-beloved pope, at the beginning of his pontificate, when the portico on the left side of the basilica of the blessed Peter had collapsed through excessive age, renewed it with swift and distinguished care.

### 541

He also renewed the roof and structure (*sarta tecta*) of that principal church, raising it with great beams and bold workmanship and restoring it resplendently.

When he saw that the portico adjoining the church of Saint Andrew was about to collapse, he likewise restored it anew in better form.

He also renewed and adorned the chamber which is seen before the silver doors of the aforesaid hall, relying upon immeasurable love.

He made many churches of pious workmanship in the same manner. If we wished to commit them to writing, the tongue would not suffice to recount them, nor would the limbs of writers be able to sustain the task.

While the most blessed pontiff was completing many distinguished works throughout the various churches of God, he renewed more splendidly and securely the portico that stands before the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, situated beside the basilica of Saint Lawrence Outside-the-Walls.

In the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, situated in the district of the Sardonians, at the thirtieth mile from the city of Rome, he offered four Catholic books: one of the Gospels, one of the Books of Kings, one of the Psalms, and one of Sermons.

In the church of the blessed Martin, confessor and pontiff, outside the gate of the blessed Peter the apostle, he made one silver chalice with chains, weighing four pounds and two ounces.

In the church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs he made two censers (*thymiamateria*) of the purest silver, weighing two pounds and one ounce.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed Petronilla he made three *vestes* of *fundatum* and twelve *vela*: four of *fundatum*, three of *spaniscus*, and five linen.

In the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which the most blessed pontiff himself had newly built from its foundations above the Saxon settlement, he offered three *vestes* of *fundatum* and likewise four *vela* of *fundatum*.

### 542

The most blessed pontiff also made in the basilica of the blessed Peter the apostle twenty-seven silver-plated candlesticks, which stand in the presbytery, weighing altogether forty pounds.

He also covered the beams at the entrance and in the middle of the presbytery with the purest silver, weighing sixty-seven pounds and three ounces.

Burning with zeal for his heavenly homeland, he adorned the churches of Christ in due order with splendid metals and ornaments. Afterward he made in the hall of the blessed Peter the apostle, prince of the apostles, one crown of the purest silver with four silver chains, bearing forty-two dolphins and weighing altogether twenty-three pounds.

This pontiff too, always relying on Christ’s aid and inspired by God, made around the altar of the blessed Peter the apostle four silken hangings of green (*prasinus*) cloth. They bore panels of *chrysoclavus* with images of the Savior, the apostles Peter and Paul, and the beneficent prelate himself, as well as crosses and *gammadia* of *chrysoclavus* in the middle, with roundels containing beautifully executed images of the apostles. On feast days these are hung there as an adornment.

### 543

In the same manner, in the place mentioned above, he made other white rose-colored silk hangings, magnificently decorated with latticework, shading the sacred things at Easter.

He also offered there another smaller crown with four chains and ten dolphins. It had a lily and a hook and weighed two pounds.

The spirit of this most blessed prelate, always devoted to God, continually strove with immense love to adorn the churches of Jesus Christ with precious ornaments for the salvation of eternal life.

What none of his pontifical predecessors had thought to do, he—undoubtedly burning with and impelled by the Holy Spirit—decreed that two crowns of the purest gold, shining with the illustrious faces of Christ and the saints, should be made in the church of the prince of the apostles, Peter, beside the altar beneath which his most sacred body rests. They were to hang on the right and left, adorned with golden chains, bosses, and green gems. Together they had sixty dolphins and weighed twenty pounds.

He also made in the same church a silver crucifix, painted with marvelous workmanship. It stands on the left side of the entrance between the great columns and shines with immense splendor. It weighed sixty-two and a half pounds.

The most blessed pontiff also made in the oratory of the blessed Andrew the apostle, which adjoins the church of Saint Peter, one silken *vestis* bearing a scene of eagles. In the middle was a panel of *chrysoclavus*, in which images of Christ and his disciples shone on the right and left, together with an image of the beneficent prelate himself.

After the completion of the entire work, and with appropriate ornaments, he likewise made in the church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs a *vestis* of the same silk, with a panel of *chrysoclavus*, bearing the scene or miracle in which the Lord Christ, feeding five thousand people abundantly with the nourishment of five loaves and two fish, performed the miracle.

### 544

[Col. 1331]

Amid these matters recorded above, the most holy prelate, often mentioned, began to devote particular care and concern to the rectors of the individual churches—namely, the bishops, priests, and deacons—and to the entire Christian militia.

Wishing, as was indeed done, to establish with Christ’s help a new rule based on ancient authorities concerning how each of them should lead a chaste and sober life and please God in all things, to whom we must always render irreproachable service, he finally, through a revelation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and together with the counsel of the most serene emperors Lothair and Louis, summoned a holy and venerable synod in the church of the blessed Peter the apostle.

This took place in the thirty-fifth year of their imperial rule and the seventh year of the pontificate of the aforesaid prelate, in December, on the eighth day, in the second indiction.

At it sat both the Catholic and apostolic man himself and sixty-seven other bishops with him. Four of these bishops had been sent by the emperors: Joseph of Évora, Notting of Brescia, Peter of Spoleto, and another Peter of Arezzo.

Among them also sat Paul, deacon of the holy Church of Ravenna, acting in the place of his archbishop John, without the priests, deacons, and clergy of the holy Mother Church.

### 545

Then, in the presence of all, he ordered forty-two chapters to be read by the deacons of the holy and universal See. These chapters were clearly understood to pertain to the salvation and benefit of all Christian people.

He also ordered that these chapters be entered in the sacred canons after the other decrees of the pontiffs, so that in the future they might be preserved inviolate by everyone, and so that all bishops might have the example of this authority before their eyes and be better able to instruct and teach their subjects.

In this synod, after the other proceedings, Anastasius, cardinal priest of the title of the blessed Marcellus, was canonically deposed by everyone because for five years he had abandoned his parish contrary to the institutions of the canons and had remained in another parish up to that time.

Since he had been unwilling to come either to the two councils convened on his behalf, or in response to apostolic letters, or when summoned by three bishops—namely Nicholas, Petronacius, and John—the holy synod therefore rightly deposed him by unanimous consent, according to what the sacred canons prescribe concerning such matters, and deprived him of priestly office, in the year, month, day, and indiction noted above.

### 546

After the principal determination of this council, the spirit of the most blessed prelate, always inflamed by the fire of heavenly love, again began to show great zeal for restoring the ornaments and vessels of all the churches of God.

In the church of the blessed Peter, keeper of the kingdom of heaven, he made one two-nozzled lamp of the purest silver, weighing sixteen pounds.

Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Martin, which adjoins the church of the prince of the apostles, he made another cast, two-nozzled silver lamp, weighing twenty-seven and a half pounds.

In the same way, in the monastery of Saints John and Paul he made another silver lamp like those mentioned above, weighing twenty-two and a half pounds. On Sundays and feast days it shines with a great radiance of light beside the lectern where the sacred readings are read.

The same most holy pope made cast silver rails with latticework at the entrance to the presbytery and before the confession of the blessed Peter the apostle, his beloved. Shining with beautiful splendor, they arouse admiration in the minds of those who see them. Two of them weighed 642 pounds, while the other two weighed 580 pounds.

In the church of Saint Vincent, which is situated at Frascati, he offered one *vestis* of *fundatum*.

But, as we have often said, the mind of this most serene prelate, filled above all with love for the most blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, and for the supreme church whose throne he governed by divine dispensation, always desired to complete many ornaments.

He made over its holy altar a *vestis* of *chrysoclavus*, bearing in the middle a scene of the Savior shining amid angelic faces and handing the apostle Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven. On the right and left shone the glorious passion of Peter and Paul.

Among them the prelate himself offered a painted image of the city that he had ordered to be built through Peter’s intercession, together with a cross glittering with gold and gems.

Around and above the altar were silken cloths woven with a precious scene of eagles; two of them are seen to be gilded.

### 547

In the place mentioned above he offered four *vela* with *chrysoclavus*. In them the prelate himself is depicted offering to the image of the Savior, shining amid angelic faces, the city that he had prepared from its foundations.

Since we have now described, however briefly, the ornaments that the aforesaid pontiff offered to the church of the blessed Peter, we shall next make known for eternal remembrance, in summary, what he accomplished in the church of the most blessed apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, after the impious devastation of the Hagarenes.

He made over his most sacred body a *ciborium* of marvelous beauty, adorned with silver columns and possessing an immense weight of silver, weighing 946 pounds.

But since the benevolent mind of that pontiff, both before and after providing various ornaments for all the churches, always took care to offer something excellent and more precious to the blessed Peter, he offered him three *oleae masoricae*—of admirable beauty, woven of silk and colored—which were to hang around the high altar on feast days.

He also made in the church of Saint Marcian, situated at Domucella, which is called Balnearola, one *vestis* of *fundatum* and two *vela* of *spaniscus*.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed Lawrence, martyr of Christ and Levite, he offered twenty-four *vela* of *fundatum*, which hang from the arches beneath the larger columns.

He also made in the church of the blessed Clement, martyr and pontiff, one pair of silver ewers (*aquaemanilia*), bearing on them a sculpted representation of a human head with a vine, and another scene, weighing three pounds.

[Col. 1333]

Likewise, the most blessed and beneficent prelate offered in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in Aemilia, which is called the Via Aurelia, one *vestis* of *fundatum*.

Similarly, in the church of Saint Stephen, in the place mentioned above, he offered another *vestis* of *fundatum*.

That distinguished and beneficent prelate, protected by the heavenly right hand and persevering always with a sincere heart in God’s service, after many good deeds, adorned and painted with many beautiful colors the church of Saints Sylvester and Martin, which his predecessor, Lord Sergius, had newly built from the foundations. Its beauty still provides great wonder to human eyes.

He also covered and adorned its venerable and sacred altar with the purest silver, weighing 116 pounds.

### 548

After the beautiful and praiseworthy works in various churches of God that the magnificent prelate carried out with complete devotion of spirit, he ensured that the Christian people would no longer perish in the fortress of Centumcellae at the hands of enemies, as often used to happen.

For forty years that city had remained with its walls destroyed and without its native inhabitants. Like beasts, the people who had been driven from their homes because of fear of the Saracens wandered through the dark forests and unknown mountains, abandoning their own dwellings, as had happened up to that time.

There, too, because of fear of their enemies, they were unable by day or night to obtain sleep for their eyes or even the slightest rest according to human custom.

Since the pious and praiseworthy prelate felt daily compassion for their burden and their intolerable distress—beyond measure and beyond what can be believed—he continually entreated the Lord, creator of all things, with many tears and countless prayers, asking that by the gift of his grace God might deign to show him where the city of Centumcellae could be moved for the safety and liberation of the frequently mentioned Christian people.

The prelate himself went there and carefully examined and surveyed the places adjoining it. But wherever a site seemed suitable for building a city, there was a shortage of water, which is always very necessary for human beings.

### 549

Having therefore traversed all the places, as we have said, he at last reached, by God’s merciful favor, an excellent and very strongly fortified site. His spirit was especially encouraged by it, because it provided an abundant supply of water for strengthening the people, as well as the other necessities of human life, including fully adequate watermills. Yet it is worthy that all the people should faithfully remember and acknowledge how and by what order divine clemency revealed this to him: the work so long sought was accomplished by divine counsel and deliberation.

One night, while the illustrious bishop was lying in his own bed according to custom and thinking, as he usually did, about divine works, he was brought in a dream to the place already foreseen and appointed, situated twelve miles from the city of Centumcellae. In the revelation, as though in bodily presence, he showed each individual site in order to a certain Peter, master of the soldiers, indicating where churches and where gates were to be founded and built with pontifical assistance. Since, because of the narrowness of the site, only two gates could be built there, he marked them with his own fingers in that secret revelation.

When morning came, he began to have great doubts concerning the dream he had seen. He immediately ordered the aforementioned Peter to come into his presence, related to him everything he had seen in his sleep, and gave him many silver mancuses, so that, having hired the people of the city of Centumcellae, he might complete the city with them as quickly as possible.

And now, with God as its guide, everything shines forth built just as the praiseworthy pope had marked it out with his own hand in the dream. He gave it the name Leopolis, after his own name. After its construction had begun, he affectionately went there with a multitude of his faithful to see and inspect the building. At last, when he saw the gates and churches in the very places he had indicated, and when, with Christ protecting him, his desire had been fulfilled, he gave boundless thanks to almighty God, who had deigned to show him such a site—one where the people would remain safe and where even stones and sand would be supplied in abundance, so that the newly built structure might grow without labor for the workmen.

### 550

Rejoicing in all these things, the aforementioned pontiff went around the city of Leopolis on foot, with litanies and prayers, and consecrated it perpetually with three prayers, in the manner of the Trinity. He duly performed the office of the Mass, as was his custom, and ordered holy water to be sprinkled over the walls. Out of the greatness of his love, he also distributed a considerable *roga* with his own hands to the whole people, commending both the people and the city divinely shown to him to almighty God, so that it might never be captured or invaded by enemies.

After completing all these things, he returned to his own see with immense joy and eagerness, Christ assisting him. On the fifteenth day thereafter, the entire circuit of the walls was completed and finished, in the eighth year of his episcopate, in the second indiction.

### 551

He also offered many gifts in the churches he had built there.

In the church of Saint Peter, seven larger and smaller silver *gabathae* cast in silver, weighing altogether sixteen pounds and one ounce; one gilded *canthara*; three gilded *baucae*; larger *fibulatoria*, and five smaller ones; one gilded silver cross with a gem; another gold cross having a *monocossis* in the middle; and another silver cross, one in number, having forty gems; one gilded gold censer; one right-hand-shaped object of stone [*dextram saxiscam*]; twelve golden crowns; one *gabatha*; and

[Col. 1335] two ostrich eggs.

He also made in the same church of the aforementioned city two silken vestments: one of them has in the middle a panel of *chrysoclavus*—gold embroidery—and the other has in the middle a cross and four small circles with *gammadia*; and eighteen *fundati* hangings; one crucifix of the purest silver, weighing seven pounds.

Likewise, in the church of Saint Leo, mentioned above, he offered one gilded paten, one silver chalice, and two vestments: one of *fundatum*, ornamented around the edge with *oloverum*, having in the middle a wheel of *chrysoclavus* and *gammadia*, and the other of *spaniscus*. Likewise, seven Catholic books: the *Histories of Solomon*, an Antiphonary, a Psalter, a Sacramentary, [books] of deeds and sermons, and also a Gospel with silver covers.

He adorned the most sacred altar of God, which stands above the most holy body of the blessed apostle Peter, with gilded silver plates bearing the miracles on the right and left of that chief of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 1335] Perhaps *luminaribus*—“with lights.”] They now glitter with immense splendor like the stars of heaven and weigh altogether eighty-four pounds and five ounces.

### 552

After the insignia of so immense an undertaking and the divine works accomplished—works which, inspired by the mercy of the eternal God, that most holy pope performed in various places for the salvation of Christians—he endeavored daily, out of his excessive love for the heavenly homeland, to adorn the church founded by the Lord’s word upon the firm rock, glorious and radiant under the holy name of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, with the most precious ornament of all metals.

There he also completed, in celebrated workmanship, a silver lectern embossed with figures and standing on four feet. At its summit a lion’s head shines forth. It weighs thirty-one pounds and eleven ounces. He also took four *cerostata*, which for a long time had been erected in the middle of the presbytery on feast days by the supreme pontiffs, and, with wise judgment, encased them in the purest silver.
