He decreed that they should remain erected there forever—something none of his predecessors had thought to do. They weighed altogether fifty-five pounds.

In the same place he made a pair of larger silver *cerostata*, weighing forty-eight pounds and ten ounces. Lamps of pure silver, shining beside the high altar, sit in them; these weigh altogether forty-nine pounds. He also made seven other silver-plated *cerostata*, weighing twenty-five pounds and three ounces. Likewise, he made seven other iron *cerostata* with four sides, covered above with silver, weighing twenty-one pounds and three ounces.

Above the altar itself he placed a garment woven with gold, shining throughout with white pearls, and having on the right and left gemmed panels with golden circles around them, in which the distinguished name of that bishop was inscribed.

### 553

He also restored with remarkable buildings the monastery of Saint Martin, which was on the point of collapsing from great age, and wholly adorned it to a condition better than it had previously possessed. In it he offered a white, rose-patterned vestment, depicting the Savior with the apostles and the Virgin, with the name of Lord Leo IV inscribed. He also offered five white, rose-patterned hangings, one of them having thirteen *gammadia*, and three gilded silver almonds.

In the church of the Four Crowned Saints he made one *fundatum* vestment.

Moreover, the same supreme and orthodox pontiff, moved by divine inspiration, made in the basilica of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, silver chalices of the purest silver, which hang above the principal arch, and also below the larger columns, on the right and left, eighty-three in number. Together they weighed 441 pounds.

In front of the entrance to the sacred altar he also made a beam of extraordinary beauty. After the wicked plundering of the savage nation, he adorned it with the purest silver. Sacred and venerable images of God sit upon it; it weighs sixty pounds.

He also offered one gilded silver censer in the church of the blessed apostle Peter situated in the city of Leopolis.

Likewise, in the church of holy Mary, the Mother of God, situated in the district of the Sardians, he offered gilded silver *gabathae* with a basket, weighing . . . .

Similarly, in the venerable monastery of Jerusalem, which is situated beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter, he made a *fundatum* vestment with small circles, ornamented around the edge with a band of *chrysoclavus*, together with two *imizinus* hangings and three *fundati* hangings.

The venerable and illustrious pontiff, protected by God, made a *propitiatorium* for the sacred altar of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, where his most holy body rests: a *spanoclistum* weighing seventy-two pounds of silver and eighty of gold.

### 554

In his time, a certain Daniel, master of the soldiers, blinded by the weight of wickedness and folly, hastened to the feet of the most serene lord Emperor Louis. He did not hesitate to tell him many false and useless things, which could in no way be believed, about Gratian, the most distinguished master of the soldiers and the excellent superintendent and counselor of the Roman palace.

He persistently accused Gratian out of malicious hatred of falsehood, saying to the emperor:

“Gratian, the superintendent of the city of Rome, whom you believe to be faithful toward you, said to me alone, secretly, while he was murmuring excessively against the Franks in his own house: ‘The Franks do nothing good for us and offer no assistance; rather, they violently take away what belongs to us. Why do we not summon the Greeks and, making a peace treaty with them, drive the Frankish king and people from our kingdom and dominion?’”

When the aforementioned emperor heard this, immediately inflamed with immense fury, he arranged to come swiftly to Rome, even without sending letters to the Roman pontiff and senate.

[Col. 1337] Nevertheless, when he arrived, Lord Pope Leo received him honorably, as was customary, sitting above the great steps of the blessed apostle Peter, and began to appease him with honey-sweet words of preaching.

### 555

One day the emperor himself, together with the most holy pontiff Leo, all the Roman nobles, and likewise the leading Franks, was seated in the house that Pope Leo III of blessed memory had built beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter. There he held a hearing concerning the accusation just mentioned.

Then Daniel, armed with an evil countenance and filled with a false thought, said before everyone:

“This Gratian took counsel with me to take this Roman land from your power and hand it over to the Greeks.”

Immediately Gratian—not only he, but all the Romans as well—said before the emperor:

“You are lying. What you say is in no way true.”

When the emperor and all the Roman and Frankish nobility recognized that the aforementioned Daniel had made such an accusation against Gratian through falsehood and envy, the most merciful emperor, unwilling to act against the institutions of the ancient Augusti concerning the Romans, established that they should be judged according to Roman law.

During that judgment, Daniel, reproved by the statements of many, admitted with his own mouth that he had falsely accused Gratian. Therefore he was handed over to the aforesaid Gratian before everyone, so that Gratian would have the power to do with him whatever he wished.

But after the emperor had repeatedly asked Gratian, with much humility and supplication, to spare Daniel who had been handed over to him, Gratian consented. Having immediately received complete pardon, Daniel willingly accepted it, and thus was freed from the danger of death.

When these matters had been completed, the emperor departed. The most holy lord Pope Leo IV, after not many days, fell asleep in the Lord on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

He held two ordinations: one in December and the other during March. He ordained nineteen priests, eight deacons, and sixty-three bishops in various places.

*(Here some falsely insert John VIII, a woman.)*

## C VI. BENEDICT III. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 855, THE 16TH OF EMPEROR LOTHAR, THE 14TH OF MICHAEL III

No. 557, line 6: “the assembly at the title of Calixtus.” Line 8: “he recognized the companies.”

No. 558, line 9: “the decree.” “Nicholas.” Line 10: “Mercurius, and the master of the soldiers, meeting Arsenius, bishop of Gubbio.”

No. 559, line 13: “he made the oath of fidelity to the beneficent [Benedict].” Line 17: “insulting and boasting of such men’s” [Col. 1356C] “strength and virtue.”

No. 560, line 4: “which neither barbarians nor pagans are heard to have accomplished among legates, or nations.”

No. 561, line 9: “by the command of the Augusti.”

No. 562, line 7: “with guards and fortresses he.”

No. 563, line 1: “on the following day.”

No. 564, line 8: “seeing the arrival.”

No. 566, line 3: “Benedict, the elected one, was dwelling there, they came together with one soul.” Line 10: “with softer words, in the same manner.”

No. 570, line 4: “the purest,” which weighed. Line 5: “the censer.” Line 7: “the intention of his mind.”

[Col. 1356D] No. 571, line 3: “hypapanti.”

No. 572, line 1: “the title of Saint Cyriacus.”

No. 574, line 3: “one *gabalus*.” “Chazarus.” Line 7: “one clean [garment].”

No. 575, line 4: “one sword.” Line 9: “gold.” “To the people,” five.

No. 576, line 1: “for the holy man greatly.” Line 11: “six priests.”]

[Col. 1345]

### 556

Benedict III, a Roman by nation, son of Peter, sat for two years, six months, and ten days.

This blessed man, born of most beloved parents, endowed with heavenly dew and growing rapidly through zeal for divine letters, was entrusted by his father’s decision to be educated. Just as a sponge very quickly absorbs water, so he learned the readings of the sacred books, understood and received their rudiments, laid them in the foundation of his mind, and propagated them through invisible roots.

When an exceedingly famous report about him was widely circulated, he was brought to the Lateran patriarchium and assigned to the clergy. He was wise in speech, distinguished in learning, sober in conduct, peaceful in conversation, compassionate toward all, and obedient to everyone—in short, most kind.

When Pope Gregory the beneficent saw that he was skilled in learning and useful, he appointed him subdeacon of the holy Roman Church. In that order he underwent many struggles of sacred discipline, for he conquered the flesh, the prince of this world, and all his utterly wicked arguments.

Then Gregory, the bishop, died and departed to the Lord. Sergius, the bishop, assumed the governance of the Roman Church; when he died, Pope Leo assumed the apostolic see. Pope Leo, loving Benedict deeply for his most fortunate deeds and moved by a heavenly prompting, ordained him priest with great honor, assigning him an eminent title.

His blessedness shone and flourished so far and wide that everyone called him most blessed in word and deed. It was clearly recognized that divine wisdom dwelt in him, because he nourished everyone with his generous and pure affections and adorned them more brightly than light. He rejected the delights of the fleeting and passing world and distributed to the needy and poor whatever he possessed. Strong through fasting, constant in prayer, he remained ever watchful and spent every day in the praises of God.

### 557

When Leo, the bishop, had been taken from this light and died, immediately all the clergy of this Roman see protected by God, all the nobles, the entire senate and people, gathered together, beseeching the mercy of the Lord to deign to show them a blessed shepherd who could rule the apostolic summit peacefully.

Then, divinely inflamed by heavenly light, with one accord and one effort they proclaimed that Benedict should be elected pontiff, because of the many sacred works in which he excelled.

Immediately, with eager zeal, the entire people and assembly of the populace hastened under the heavenly title and found him pouring forth prayer to almighty God, as was his custom. Rising and seeing the dense crowds of the people, he understood what was happening and grasped it in his mind. Meanwhile, bending his knees with many tears, he earnestly entreated everyone in a mournful voice, saying:

“I beg you, do not lead me away from my church, because I am not capable of sustaining or bearing the burden of so great a dignity.”

### 558

But they in no way consented. Rather, drawing him away from that title by force, with hymns and spiritual songs, with great exultation and ineffable joy they led him into the Lateran patriarchium and placed him upon the pontifical throne, as is the custom of pontiffs and ancient practice demonstrates.

[Note: [Col. 1345] From this it is perfectly clear that Benedict, not a female John VIII, succeeded Leo IV.]

Therefore the City rejoiced, the Church exulted, the old men shared in the joy, and the virgins, celebrating, sang divine praises. The poor were enriched, the needy made wealthy, captives consoled, the weak rose up, and the sick were healed and hurried forward with swift steps. For the sadness that had been spread over them was dispelled, and a flowering tranquillity appeared established.

When these matters had been completed, the clergy and all the nobles composed a decree, confirmed it with their own hands, and sent it, as ancient custom required, to the unconquered Augusti Lothar and Louis.

The legates who carried the decree were Nicholas, bishop of the Church of Anagni, and Mercurius, master of the soldiers. Meeting Arsenius, bishop of Gubbio, they began to converse with him. By crafty words he began to soothe and soften their hearts; they abandoned their fidelity to the blessed elected man and sought to confirm with them a plan that they should adorn the deposed and anathematized Anastasius with the papal insignia—something divine mercy in no way permitted.

They went to Louis, the most merciful Caesar, and delivered the decree. Carrying in their minds the double intention they had conceived, they returned to Rome. Announcing the arrival of the imperial envoys, they presented the distinguished elected man with letters containing the response of the Augusti.

They said to all the clergy and the assemblies of the state, desiring to carry out the plan which, as we have said, they had arranged at Gubbio with Arsenius, through dreadful machinations:

“All of you, together with us, must go out to meet the imperial legates, so that you may prove yourselves obedient to the commands of the Augusti.”

### 559

After several days, the envoys whom they had announced hastened to Horta, which lies forty miles from Rome. Adelbert and Bernard, counts, entered the town and joined a certain priest named Anastasius, who had once been condemned, with Arsenius compelling the bishop to do so. In the holy synod presided over by Leo, the bishop of blessed memory, Anastasius had been duly excommunicated, deposed, and bound by anathema according to the promulgations of the sacred canons.

Not having God before their eyes and desiring tyrannically to overturn his commandments, they were plainly considering how they might raise the expelled and anathematized Anastasius to the apostolic dignity, against tradition and all the decrees of pontiffs and holy men.

The envoys whom we mentioned above—Bishop Nicholas and Mercurius, master of the soldiers—had carried to the most merciful emperor our decree concerning the election of Benedict. Having conceived this plan in their minds, they left Rome with certain other nobles, namely Gregory and Christopher, masters of the soldiers, and went out as though to meet the emperor’s legates.

As they hastened toward the city of Horta, they despised and forgot the oath of fidelity they had sworn to the beneficent Benedict and joined themselves to the condemned elected man. On this pretext, after the deposed priest, many others likewise left the city, contemplating a council—according to the prophet’s saying [Note: [Col. 1347] Psalm 20]—which they could not establish.

Then, leaving the city, they reached the basilica of the blessed martyr Lucius near Horta, insulting others and boasting of their own strength. Raduald, bishop of Porto, and Agatho, bishop of the city of Todi, were with them; they had secretly departed from Rome. Entangled in the earth’s darkness, they joined themselves to that anathematized man, darkened in understanding, mind, and soul.

### 560

When God’s servant Benedict, the elected pope, heard this, he endeavored to send the venerable and prudent bishops G. G. and Majon, full of every kind of knowledge, to those imperial envoys with certain letters. When the envoys seized them, they bound them at the prompting of the anathematized priest Anastasius and handed them over to guards—something that neither barbarians nor pagans are said to have done even among legates.

Afterward, Benedict, the often-mentioned minister of Christ, the elected pope, sent the distinguished *secundicerius* of the holy apostolic see, Adrian, and Duke Gregory to meet them.

### 561

On the following day, while carrying out their mission, they instructed all the clergy, the entire senate, and the whole people to go beyond the Milvian Bridge to meet the emperor’s commands.

Then the Romans, knowing nothing of the deceit or trickery, agreed and unanimously left the city, proceeding beyond the Milvian Bridge.

As they hastened toward the basilica of the aforementioned martyr, the Roman clergy and nobles met the deposed and anathematized priest-bishop, together with the men mentioned above as legates. Riding together with them, they hastened through Nero’s Field toward the walls of the City.

They also led away the distinguished *secundicerius* Adrian, surrounded by guards. They seized Gratian, superintendent of the sacred patriarchium, and Theodore, the *scriniarius*, and kept them shut up, holding them fast with spears. This had in no way been commanded by the Augusti or ordered according to their will; rather, it was done through the wretched presumption of the deposed priest.

Entering the City by force with the imperial legates, he suddenly invaded the basilica of the chief of the apostles, which he ought not to have entered, despising God’s judgment. He boldly perpetrated such great and terrible evils through his accursed action as not even Saracen hands had dared or imagined carrying out there.

For he smashed the images and burned them in the fire. He destroyed the synod which Pope Leo of blessed memory had ordered to be painted above the doors of the sanctuary, and with a double-bladed axe threw down to the ground the icon of the Lord Jesus Christ and of his ever-virgin Mother, which he ought not to have touched. At this detestable deed all the orthodox worshipers of the faith shed tears, groaned, and were filled with sadness and grief.

### 562

After these events, the deposed Roman priest himself entered by hostile force and quickly hastened to the Lateran with his most wicked followers. By secular power and many kinds of weapons, the tyrant opened its doors and entered the patriarchium like a bloody man. He sat upon the throne, which he ought not even to have touched with his hands, and ordered a certain bishop of Bagnoregio, named Romanus, to eject the most blessed Benedict from the pontifical throne on which he was seated—the Benedict whom the entire Roman people, as we have said, had elected.

Like a barbarian, he also seized and stripped off the pontifical garments in which Benedict was clothed, and filled him with many insults and blows.

Then the deposed Anastasius sought, by human rather than divine power, to hand the most merciful elected Benedict over to guards who would bind him more tightly—namely John and Adrian, formerly priests, who had been condemned and deposed by Bishop Leo for their crimes and removed from all priestly office.

Immediately the whole City was filled with wailing and abundant weeping and lay shaken by a heavy murmur. At once all the bishops, the clergy, and the people of God entered the Holy of Holies. Beating their breasts and shedding copious tears, they lay prostrate on the ground inside the vestibule and before the altar, praying to the majesty of God to free them by his victorious right hand from the darkness of so great an error.

It was then the course of the seventh day.

### 563

On the following day, the aforementioned bishops, together with all the clergy and people, assembled at the title of Aemiliana. The frequently mentioned legates of the Augusti also arrived there, raging and swollen with great pride.

They attacked the apse where the bishops were seated with the clergy, singing psalms. Like ferocious lions, they climbed into it, raised their spears, and tried to strike them, threatening them with their swords and saying:

“Consent, and by your agreement let Anastasius be substituted for the pontifical dignity.”

But, filled with the Holy Spirit, they replied:

“We will never consent to one who has been deposed and bound by anathema by a holy bishop and blessed synod. In every way we reject him and separate him from the assemblies of God.”

Then the enraged men declared that they wished to punish them with blows and tortures. But the most blessed bishop of God almighty and those who were with him, disregarding their threats and menaces, remained unmoved.

When the aforementioned Franks saw their steadfastness, they withdrew from them filled with anger and entered a certain chamber of the basilica. There they devised various plans and brought in the bishops of Ostia and Alba, who had been forced to come. They struggled to bring them back through gentler speech and flattering entreaties, and afterward surrounded them with harsh threats, saying even in shrill voices:

“You cannot possess life at all; you will be subject to capital punishment unless you grant Anastasius the favor of consecration.”

But those men declared that they would first hand themselves over to death and be torn limb from limb rather than grant the blessing of consecration to one who had been deposed and condemned by anathema.

They accused the envoys and showed them all the writings of sacred response, explaining how they could in no way establish that deposed man in the order he demanded. Immediately, however, while they were speaking with them more privately, the fury that had swollen within the envoys diminished, and they seemed to have been driven from their minds.

### 564

At dawn on the third day, all the bishops, together with the clergy and people, gathered in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana. There the entire people and multitude of the populace cried out in a loud voice:

“We want the most blessed Pope Benedict! We desire him!”

The aforementioned legates heard this and were astonished.

Seeing that the unity of Christ and the blessed harmony of the people could not be bent toward Anastasius by any device, they summoned the bishops and other priests together with the clergy into a chamber of the patriarchium. There they sought to engage them in an extensive dispute. But the bishops overcame the boldness of the envoys with arguments and teachings so convincing that the envoys’ ill-omened purpose appeared crushed and confounded.

When the envoys saw this, they said to the venerable bishops:

“Take your elected man and lead him into whatever basilica you wish. We shall now eject from this patriarchium Anastasius, whom you call deposed. Let us observe a three-day fast with prayers, and afterward let whatever the heavenly mercy reveals be fulfilled.”

But the beneficent bishops cried out:

“Let the invader and deposed Anastasius be expelled from our presence and driven from this patriarchium; then we shall do what you urge.”

### 565

Immediately the aforementioned Anastasius was expelled and driven from the patriarchium with great shame, so that all the worshipers of the orthodox faith might render many kinds of thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ.

The bishops, together with all the clergy and people, took the most blessed Benedict from the basilica in which the clerics reside and led him away, because the most savage Anastasius had placed him there under guard.

With complete eagerness and exultation they descended with him into the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana. When they came out from there, they placed him, amid acclamations, upon the horse on which Bishop Leo had been accustomed to sit.

With a great crowd of people preceding him, they led him into the basilica of the Mother of God, which is called “at the Manger.” There, devoting themselves to fasting and prayers for three days and nights, they entreated the supreme majesty of the Lord with many tears.

### 566

When the fast had been completed, all those who had joined themselves to the anathematized and deposed man, moved by divine prompting and inflamed by God’s favor, came together unanimously in the aforementioned basilica where, as we have said, the most blessed Benedict was staying. Approaching, they began to kiss his feet and said:

“We have gone astray and departed from you with an unsteady foot. But, like a most holy shepherd, receive the flocks wandering through the woodland; gather the weary little lambs into your bosom and shelter us beneath your wings.”

Immediately Benedict, protected by God, stretched out his arms and eagerly desired to embrace them all with pure minds and a kind heart, adorning them with kisses. He also said to them:

“Rejoice, my beloved, and rejoice all the more, because Christ, the Son of God, has deigned by his power to unite the Church which had been divided.”

As he said this and preached similar things, the imperial legates also came there. They spoke privately with the elected man in healing and gentler words.

Suddenly, however, all the bishops, the entire clergy, and the innumerable multitude of the Roman people led him from that basilica with hymns and spiritual songs and introduced him into the Lateran patriarchium. They placed him upon the pontifical throne from which he had been expelled.

At last the entire Church rejoiced with him, and all the people resounded with loud acclamations.

Moreover, at dawn on the Lord’s Day, he was led by the bishops, clergy, and nobles into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. In the sight of everyone, while the imperial legates watched, he was consecrated and ordained pontiff upon the apostolic see, as custom and ancient tradition dictate.

The bishop of Porto, however, was barred from the church and in no way performed upon him the ordination he ought to have performed, because he had joined himself to the anathematized man and had fallen into—and remained in—the abyss of perjury.

[Col. 1351]

### 567

After the sacred solemnity of the Mass had been celebrated, he returned to the church, ordained pontiff in the Lateran patriarchium.

He was exceedingly gentle and adorned with every sacred work, handsome in appearance and radiant in mind, sweet in speech, and gracious in teaching. But since we are not able to recount everything in order, let us extend our pen to the things he offered in various holy places.

At the very beginning of his pontificate, burning with heavenly love, he had an icon of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer made in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana. It was of the purest silver overlaid with gold, worked in openwork, and represented Christ trampling a lion and a dragon beneath his feet. It weighed sixteen and a half pounds.

In the basilica of holy Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God and our Lady, which is called “at the Manger,” he offered one exceedingly precious golden crown weighing four pounds.

In that same basilica the baptistery had remained destroyed for a long time. Hoping for future recompense from the Lord, he restored it with swift zeal and arranged for it to be brought back to its former condition.

That distinguished and most blessed pope also offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter a *canthara* of the purest silver and gold, worked with incised decoration, into which incense is placed. There he also offered seven candlesticks with horns, made of the purest silver and shining with a golden color.

568. In the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, he also magnificently adorned the tomb that had been destroyed by the Saracens, weighing 103 pounds. In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God across the Tiber, he offered one hanging, ornamented around its border with *oloverum* and having in the middle a cross of *chrysoclave*. In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God called Antiqua—which Pope Leo had built from the foundations beside the Sacred Way—he made thirteen hangings of *fundatum*, with a border of *blatthinum*. He also offered and bestowed golden keys in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence, situated outside the city walls.

In the fifth month of the consecration of this distinguished pontiff, that is, in January, on the [lacuna] day, the river called the Tiber left its channel and spread across the plains. It swelled with a flood of many waters and entered the Roman city through the little gate called Saint Agatha at the hour of the day [hour unspecified in the source]. Meanwhile, it rose above the ground in certain places and entered the church of Saint Sylvester, so that, because of the great quantity of water, it climbed all the steps leading into the basilica of Saint Dionysius except one that was higher up. From there it spread over the street called the Via Lata and entered the basilica of the holy Mother of God Mary. There the water rose so high that, because of its great quantity, even the doors of that church could not be seen.

From there it climbed through streets and alleys as far as the slope of the money-changer. Then, turning back, it entered through the portico situated before the church of Saint Mark, in the month and on the sixth day mentioned above, the Epiphany of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh. From there, rushing onward, it began to run into the sewer beside the monastery of Saint Sylvester and Saint Lawrence the martyr, which is called Pallacini. From that day onward the water gradually began to diminish, and after causing great damage the river returned to its channel. For it overturned houses, laid waste fields, tore up crops, and uprooted shrubs.

When these things had been accomplished, the aforesaid most blessed pope, constrained by immense love, made in the church of the Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated across the Tiber, a hanging for the principal altar, of *chrysoclave*, bearing a representation of the Assumption of that same Mother of God.

569. He also offered in the monastery of the holy martyr of Christ Anastasius, which is called at the Salvian Waters, one *gabatha saxica* of purest silver, weighing three pounds. Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, formerly called Antiqua but now situated beside the Sacred Way, he made a hanging with *chrysoclave*, bearing a representation of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh.

In the monastery of the blessed Martin he likewise made two baskets of *afocium*, of purest silver, weighing four and a half pounds. The venerable and distinguished pontiff also made one *fundatum* hanging in the church of the blessed martyr Cyriacus, situated on the Ostian Way. In the same manner, in the church of the blessed martyr Felix, situated at the Pine Trees, he made one *fundatum* hanging with griffins.

The excellent bishop made five chalices of purest silver in the titular church of the blessed martyr Chrysogonus; together they weighed eleven and a half pounds. In the titular church of Callixtus he also made one *ama* of purest silver, weighing ten pounds. There he likewise made four *gabathae*, weighing nine and a half pounds, and nine baskets, weighing eleven pounds in all.

For the praise and glory of that church he made one Gospel book covered with silver and gold, weighing fifteen pounds. There he also made one curtain, one basket, and one arch with two *gammadia*, of purest silver, weighing forty pounds altogether. In the church of the blessed martyr Balbina he offered a Gospel book of purest silver.

570. In the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, he also made one hanging of *chrysoclave*, adorned with extraordinary size and beauty. In the church of the blessed apostle Peter, chief of the apostles and his foster-father, inflamed by immense love he made, for covering the *billicum confessionis*, one covering of purest gold, weighing three pounds.

In the monastery of the holy martyrs of Christ Sergius and Bacchus, which is called Callinicus, he made two chalices of purest silver, one paten, one strainer, one basin, and one censer, weighing four pounds altogether.

[Col. 1353]

That distinguished and most blessed pontiff, setting observance upon the heavenly foundation of his mind, took pleasure in nothing earthly or transitory, but only in spiritual and salutary works; and in all things pertaining to salvation he daily remained steadfast with excellent discernment.

571. Adorned with these sacred benefactions, he offered to the prince of the apostles and doorkeeper of the people one hanging of wondrous beauty, woven with gold, shining in workmanship and ornament, bearing the life-giving representation of the Annunciation and of the *Hypapante*—how the only-begotten Son of God entered the Temple and sat in the midst of the teachers.

Yet this same aforesaid and most blessed bishop, inflamed by immense love and supported by God’s help, made in the basilica of the blessed and excellent preacher, the apostle Paul, a *regnum* of purest gold, *spanoclistum*, with its chains, having in the middle a golden cross; also a *spanisca*, which continually hangs above the same altar, weighing two pounds and one ounce.

He also offered in the same basilica one basin of very pure silver, weighing nine ounces. That distinguished and most blessed pope made seven silver crosses, which in the customary manner had long preceded the processions through all the Catholic churches. Since they had been broken by extreme old age, this distinguished and most holy bishop restored them anew and brought them back to their former condition; together they weighed fifty-one and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the basilica of the holy martyr of Christ, the blessed Sebastian, situated in the place called Frascata, that excellent father offered one *fundatum* hanging having in the middle a cross with *gammadia* of *quadrapulum*. In the same manner, in the basilica of the blessed and excellent preacher, the apostle Paul, he made one red hanging of *arodina*, with *chrysoclave*.

572. In the titular church of the holy martyr Cyriacus he also made one *fundatum* hanging. The most blessed pontiff, inflamed with love, made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his foster-father, one *pharus* of silver, of extraordinary size, weighing [lacuna] pounds and [lacuna] ounces.

This most blessed pontiff, filled with divine inspiration, made in the church of the blessed Levite Lawrence, outside the walls of this Roman city, one *fundatum* hanging with *chrysoclave*, adorned with extraordinary size. He also renewed the principal roof-work of the church of the blessed apostle Peter, his foster-father—that is, the main nave and the other nave above his body—by placing seven great beams upon them and raising them with brilliant, bold craftsmanship.

In the titular church of the blessed martyr Cyriacus he offered one Gospel book of purest silver, for the praise and glory of that church. When these things had been accomplished, the aforesaid most blessed pope, constrained by immense love, rebuilt from the foundations the principal apse of the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, our Lady, situated across the Tiber, which had fallen into ruins, and raised it to a better state.

He adorned the windows with colored glass and decorated them with mosaic painting. He also entirely renewed the portico and baptistery, together with the sacristy, restoring everything throughout. He completely restored the cemetery of the blessed Mark, confessor and pontiff, situated outside the Appian Gate, which had already fallen into ruins.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, whose roof had become so old that it was close to collapse, he removed the ancient beams and put others in their place, newly restoring the roof itself, the surrounding portico, and everything else.

573. In the basilica of the distinguished teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, so often mentioned above, the same most holy bishop Benedict ordered a net of the most beautiful workmanship to be made with wondrous artistry, entirely of *alvaberi* gems and golden bosses, containing enclosed gilded plaques decorated with enamel—twenty-one of the larger kind, together with other smaller ones—as well as eleven golden *amendulae* and ten hanging *chrysoclave* gems.

With great love he ordered these to be made and, offering them in honor of the Apostle, commanded that they hang continually above the most sacred altar.

Moved also by a heavenly impulse, and with the purest heart unceasingly exercising care for the great holy church as a worthy minister of Christ, he learned that the volume containing the readings of the true preaching of Paul the apostle and of the other apostles and prophets, arranged in due order and customarily read by subdeacons at all the stations of the churches, had been removed or lost from the holy church above the ambo.

Overcome by great and vehement concern, he took care to prepare a similarly worthy volume. In it he ordered to be added the Greek and Latin readings from Scripture that subdeacons customarily read on Holy Saturday of Easter and likewise on holy Pentecost. Adorning it suitably with silver tablets of wondrous workmanship, he willingly offered it to the holy Roman Church.

574. In his time Michael, son of the emperor Theophilus and emperor of the city of Constantinople, out of love for the apostles, sent a gift to the blessed apostle Peter through Lazarus, a monk highly skilled in the painter’s art and by race a Chazarian: namely, one Gospel book of purest gold with various precious stones; likewise, one chalice of gold encircled with stones, decorated with extraordinary beauty by a hanging net of precious white gems; two hangings of *oloverum*, with a cross of *oloverum*; likewise, one border of *chrysoclave*; and the small coverings of the same chalice, as is the custom of the Greeks.

He also sent one hanging of clean imperial purple for the principal altar, decorated on every side with a representation, grilles, and roses of *chrysoclave*, of great beauty, as well as one veil of *stauracium*, with a cross of *chrysoclave* and Greek letters in gold.

[Col. 1355]

575. In his time a king of the Saxons, named Causa, came for the sake of prayer. Abandoning all his possessions, he left his own kingdom and hastened to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul with a great multitude of people. He offered to the blessed apostle Peter a crown of purest gold, weighing four pounds; two vessels of purest gold, weighing [lacuna] pounds; and a sword bound with purest gold.

He also offered two small images of purest gold; four *gabathae saxicae* of gilded silver; one *saraca* of *oloverum* with *chrysoclave*; white, stamped silk shirts with *chrysoclave*; and two large *fundatum* hangings.

At the request of the most holy lord Pope Benedict, this Saxon king made a public *roga* in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, distributing gold, or silver by pounds, to the bishops, priests, deacons, the entire clergy, and the Roman nobles, while giving small silver coins to the people.

Afterward, when his purpose of prayer had been completed, he returned to his own kingdom; and a few days later he ended his life and departed to the Lord.

576. Finally, since that same bishop took great care of the holy churches of God and always rejoiced, with pious devotion and zeal, in their restoration, he made and renewed, beside the lectorium, a silver *pharus cantharus* standing on four feet, which had formerly been taken away by the Saracens from the basilica of the keeper of the heavenly kingdom, his foster-father. On feast days and Sundays a lamp and candles were placed in it for the adornment of that basilica. It weighed [lacuna] pounds.

For he was always intent upon the love of divine worship, a lover of peace, and a cultivator of all heavenly works through chaste conduct.

He established that whenever a bishop, priest, or deacon died, the pontiff, together with all the bishops, priests, and deacons, as well as the remaining clergy, should assemble for the burial of his body and the commendation of his soul. Likewise, they were to do the same when the pontiff departed from this life. He not only taught this but also practiced it.

His successor, following his example in this matter of piety, as in other things, imitated him as a most devoted heir. He held one ordination in the month of December: five priests, one deacon, and sixty-six bishops in various places.

He was buried before the doors of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

CVII. NICHOLAS I. A.D. 858; [in the reign] of Louis II, year 3; of Michael III, year 17.

[Note: Col. 1377]

NOTE OF ONUPHRIUS PANVINIUS ON PLATINA, AFTER NICHOLAS I.

Up to this Nicholas, the Lives of the Roman pontiffs were written by Anastasius, monk and librarian of the holy Roman Church, who flourished under him and under his successors Adrian II and John VIII. What follows was compiled by a certain William, another librarian, and appears in the book circulated under the name of Damasus.

[Note: Col. 1377A]

In Fabrotti, from the Freher manuscript.

No. 577, line 6: *alimentis* (“nourishments”); line 13: *hortatu ad* (“at the exhortation to”).

No. 578, line 7: *mortis calicem* (“the cup of death”).

No. 579, line 17: *solphistico* (“sophistical”).

No. 580, line 9: *ovanti cum eo* (“rejoicing with him”).

No. 581, line 14: *numero 6* (“numbering six”).

No. 583, line 7: *hora diei 10* (“at the tenth hour of the day”).

No. 584, line 9: *oportunum fieret, legenaum quotiens*, for *obediens* (“obedient”), as elsewhere in no. 478, line 14.

No. 587, line 1: *temere excommunicabat* (“he excommunicated rashly”).

No. 588, line 6: *eidem archiepiscopo* (“to that same archbishop”).

No. 589, line 5: *retradidit* (“he restored”); line 6: *Luthardo episcopo* (“to Bishop Luthard”); line 8: *circumspectione dederunt* (“they gave with circumspection”).

No. 590, line 6: *contulit justus* (“the righteous one bestowed”); line 7: *miseremini mei, miseremini mei* (“have mercy on me, have mercy on me”); line 14: *antecessorum* (“of the predecessors”); line 17: *scandalia* (“stumbling-blocks”).

No. 591, line 3: *in bibliothecari jacent* (“they lie in the library”); line 19: *vestatarium* is lacking.

No. 592, line 3: *tituli Vastivae*, from F. B. Vitali.

[Col. 1377B]

No. 594, lines 10 and 11: *quod in Ignatio* (“which [is] in Ignatius”).

No. 595, line 1: *ubi aliis abjectis* (“when the others had been cast aside”).

No. 598, line 17: *neque excommunicata a papa ligata* (“nor [those] excommunicated and bound by the pope”); line 18: *curaverat* (“he had cared for”).

No. 600, line 8: *in eis nuscas*.

No. 602, line 11: *bene doctos* (“well taught”).

No. 608, line 24: *marcham illam custodientem* (“guarding that frontier district”).

No. 611, line 4: *amplum mirae magnitudinis* (“a large [object] of remarkable size”).

No. 612, final line: *apostoli, et cessavit episcopatus ejus annos 9, menses 7, dies 19* (“of the apostle, and his episcopate ceased after 9 years, 7 months, 19 days”).

From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuanus manuscripts.

No. 577, line 1: *ex patre Theodosio* (“from his father Theodosius”). “He sat for six years, nine months, thirteen days.” Line 2: *claruerunt* (“they shone forth”). “Accordingly Sergius, having heard his reputation, ordained him subdeacon. Leo ordained him deacon. Therefore, when Benedict had died, the aforesaid pontiff Nicholas, who was still serving in the office of deacon, with the other deacons, etc.” As in no. 578, line 8.

No. 578, line 8: *propriis man[ibus] illum tum collocavit* (“then placed him there with his own hands”). [Col. 1377C] *Eo tempore invict[issimus]* (“at that time the invincible [emperor]”).

No. 579, line 2: *condolens ad eam r. e.* (“grieving, [he returned] to it”); line 3: *effundebant* (“they poured forth”); line 4: *vigil[iis] instantes, incessabili Dominum* (“persisting in vigils, [imploring] the Lord without ceasing”); line 5: *quem pont[ificatus] culm[ine] subl[evarent*] (“whom they might raise to the summit of the pontificate”); line 7: *in qua per aliquot horarum spatium conf[abulantes] sid[ereo]* (“in which, conversing for a space of several hours, [under] celestial [splendour]”); same line: *un[animes] eum apost[olicae]* (“unanimously [they declared] him [bishop] of the apostolic [see]”); line 8: *continuo ad aulam pr[incipis apostolorum]* (“immediately to the hall of the prince of the apostles”); line 9: *indignum se esse tanti reg[iminis] gubernanda* (“that he was unworthy to govern so great a rule”), for *gubernacula suscep[ turum]* (“to undertake the helm”); line 10: *extrahentes* (“drawing [him out]”); line 11: *in apost[olico] solioque pos[uerunt]* (“and set [him] on the apostolic throne”); line 12: *in basilica beati Petri apost[oli] ded[uctus]* (“led into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter”); line 13: *apostolica sublimatus in s[ede]* (“raised to the apostolic see”); line 14: *apostoli beati Petri cel[ebravit]* (“he celebrated [mass] over [the body] of the blessed apostle Peter”); line 15: *spiritual[ibus] in patr[iarchium] Later[anense] iterum perductus e[st]* (“with spiritual [songs] he was again led to the Lateran patriarchate”); line 16: *gratulatur* (“rejoices”). “On the third day of his consecration … with sophisticated eloquence”; line 17: *conv[ivio] sophistico famine* (“at a banquet, in sophisticated speech”); line 18: *consurgit* (“he rises”). “When these things had been done.”

No. 580, line 1: *imper[ator] Urbe disc[essit]* (“the emperor departed from the City”); line 3: *ad eum* (“to him”); same line: *L[atini] R[omani] nominis propr[iis]* (“of the Latin Roman name, with his own [nobles]”); line 4: *quem cum audisset* (“when he had heard [of him]”) [M.: *vidisset*, “had seen him”]; same line: *in adventu* (“on his arrival”); line 5: *cum quo imperiale ingressus tentorium sal[ubribus]* (“entering the imperial tent with him, [they enjoyed] wholesome [conversation]”); line 7: *spirituali sumps[it] alacritate* (“he partook with spiritual cheerfulness”). “Accordingly, when they had been satisfied and the tables removed,” [Col. 1377D] *pl[ura] ser[enissimus] imper[ator]* (“the most serene emperor [gave] many [gifts]”); line 9: *Augustus ejus amore* (“the Augustus, through love for him”) [Col. 1378A] *fretus* (“relying”). “Mounting the imperial horse’s saddle, he went along with him in rejoicing delight.” Line 11: as above; same place: *dulcissimisque se osculis* (“and with sweetest kisses”). Line 12: *luciflue* (“radiantly”) [M.: *dulciflue*]. Line 13: *cum quibus pr[ofectus] fuerat, septus* (“surrounded by those with whom he had set out”); line 15: *jejunii s, vigiliisque dicatus, et diu c[ultui] intentus* (“devoted to fasts and vigils, and long intent upon worship”). “Of this distinguished pontiff,” as line 4 of no. 583.

No. 583, line 4: *pont[ificatus] tempore* (“in the time of [his] pontificate”); same place: *ind[ictione] 5* (“indiction 5”); same place: *per camp[estria] d[edit]* (“it spread across the plains”); line 6: *in urbem Romam, quam hora diei decima tr[anscendit]* (“into the city of Rome, which it crossed at the tenth hour of the day”); “it passed through certain places and entered the church”; line 8: “it entered the monastery of Saint Sylvester, so that from the steps”; line 10: “and entered the basilica”; line 11: *tantum intum[uit]* (“the water rose so high”); line 12: *prae multitudine aq[uarum]* (“because of the multitude of waters”); line 13: *exinde rediens, ingr[essus] est per p[orticum] qui est positus* (“then returning, it entered through the portico which is situated”); line 15: *quod vocatur Palatini* (“which is called Palatini”). “From that day onward the water gradually began to diminish, and after much damage had been done the river…” Line 17: “December”; same place: “the Nativity.” Line 18: “the Evangelist; on another occasion that same river…” Line 19: “as above. In his time,” as line 1 of no. 585.

No. 585, line 2: *quorum nomina haec sunt* (“whose names are these”); line 3: *et Samuel, et alii duo* (“and Samuel, and two others”); line 4: *Lasavir*; line 5: *ex auro puro* (“of pure gold”). [Col. 1378B] “Of gold, with stones and other gifts.” Then: “Finally, the aforesaid pontiff deposed John of Ravenna from the pontifical office, because, having been summoned three times on account of his crimes, he had scorned to come to the apostolic see. On hearing what the supreme pontiff had done, the archbishop went to Pavia and begged Emperor Louis to help him. The emperor, however, sent word to the pontiff to hear the case. The aforesaid pontiff held a council with archbishops, bishops, and clerics in the house called Leoniana, and heard that archbishop in the presence of the imperial envoys. The archbishop said that he was guilty and, with the whole council, sought [M.: ‘and mercy’] mercy from the supreme pontiff; he gave himself over to the laments of distress and excessive tribulation, and with tears implored whomsoever he could, saying,” as no. 590, line 7.

No. 590, line 7: *summi pontificis* (“of the supreme pontiff”); line 9: *ref[erens] pontifici, et sponsionis illius, quas lamentabili voce* (“reporting to the pontiff both that undertaking and the things which, in a lamentable voice”); [Col. 1378C] *dabat suggestionis* (“he offered as a petition”) [M.: *suggestiones*, “petitions”], *ad liquidum expon[ens]* (“setting them forth clearly”); lines 10 and 11: *qui non vult mortem peccat[oris]* (“who does not will the death of the sinner”); line 11: *imit[atus] et miser[icordiam] m[otus] prael[atus] arch[iepiscopus]* (“the aforesaid archbishop, imitating [him] and moved by mercy”); line 13: *scripta, quae* (“the writings which”); line 14: *antecessorum* (“of the predecessors”); line 15: *Leonina* (“Leonine”); lines 15 and 16: *pr[esul] et opt[imates] residebat, c[um]* (“the bishop and nobles sat, with”); line 18: *manu tenens* (“holding in [his] hand”); line 19: *jur[avit], sic om[nia]* (“he swore, thus all [things]”); lines 19 and 20: *suae sponsionis* (“of his undertaking”); line 21: “When these things had been done,” same place: “in the basilica of the Saviour”; line 25: *Leonina* (“Leonine”).

No. 591, line 1: “Then all the Emilian bishops brought an accusation against that same archbishop. The aforesaid pontiff commanded him, saying: ‘With every excuse set aside, except severe bodily illness, which wholly prevents you from coming,’” as lines 9 and 10. Line 10: *semel in sing[ulis] annis p[raesentes] st[are]* (“to appear once in every year”); same line: *nisi forte et morandi* (“unless perhaps [there is cause] for remaining”); lines 11 and 12: *per Aemil[iam] nisi post elect[ionem] D[ei] c[lementis] et p[er] ep[iscopum] apostol[icae] sed[is] praesulem non habeas consecr[andi] licentiam* (“through Emilia, unless after the election of merciful God and through the bishop, the prelate of the apostolic see, you have permission to consecrate”). “But those whom…” Line 14: *non recipiunt* (“they do not receive”); line 16: *nec ullum m[odum]* (“nor any means”); line 17: *temptes* (“you attempt”); line 18: *vel chartulas acquisitas, et poss[essiones] aliquo modo* (“or documents acquired, and possessions, in any manner”); [Col. 1378D] *occupes* (“you occupy”); line 19: *aut vestararii, R.* (“or [of] the vestry official, R.”) [M.: *vester*, “your”]; [Col. 1379A] line 21: “and the emperor”; line 22: “shepherd of the whole Church”; line 23: “we all say and think the same things”; same line: “then with that same archbishop”; line 24: “you report”; line 25: “having been satisfied with nectar, he…” “But the Church of God,” as line 9 of the following number.

No. 592, line 10: *vocatur* (“is called”); line 11: *decoraverat* (“he had adorned”); line 13: *speciebus* (“with forms/ornaments”). “In his time the glorious king of the Bulgarians, with the whole kingdom entrusted to him, was baptized at his preaching and himself requested an archbishop. But this most blessed pontiff pacified the whole world; he expelled Photius, the intruder and neophyte, as an adulterer, and there established an archbishop according to the rite of the holy Roman Church. He held one ordination in the month of December,” as no. 612, line 11.

No. 612, lines 13 and 14: “and the prince [having] departed from this light to the Lord. When he had died…” Line 17: “of the apostle, and his episcopate ceased after 8 years, 7 months, 9 days.”

No. 577, line 13: *coruscare. Cujus ortatu ad* (“to shine forth. At whose exhortation to”).
