[Col. 1357]

577. Nicholas, a Roman by nationality, son of Theodorus the regional official, sat for nine years, two months, and twenty days. His distinguished and most blessed deeds shone forth to all from the beginning of his childhood, and he was eminent in unblemished conduct. For he was so adorned with the beauty of sacred works that nothing in games, nor anything in which boys customarily take dishonourable delight, pleased him. He devoted himself to patience and sobriety, fragrant with humility and exceptional purity. His father, being a lover of the liberal arts and possessing a most noble intellectual capacity, instructed him in chaste elementary learning and life-giving rites, and adorned him with the study of letters and the best arts, so that no branch of sacred learning remained which he had not conceived in his inmost heart and brought within his knowledge.

[Note: Col. 1357] For.: *cunctis* (“all”).

He grew in body and in wisdom, illustrious, endowed with modesty, and adorned with learning. Whenever he saw men of approved conduct in any place, he eagerly sought to attach himself to them and warmly rejoiced in them. When he frequently came with his most prudent father to a certain most blessed man, who through the illumination of the Holy Spirit preached many things to the faithful, that man declared that he would ascend to a lofty summit. For, discerning the greatness of his inward beauty and the shining sweetness of his mind, at that man’s direction he was brought into the clerical order, so that what he had perceived by divine prompting might be fulfilled in time to come. When Bishop Sergius heard that he had mounted to the heights of supreme activity, he brought him from his parents’ house, lodged him in the patriarchal residence, and established him in the grade of subdeacon through the grace of blessing. There, living by marvellous observances, he was nourished by heavenly ardour. When Pope Sergius had been taken from this corruptible life, Bishop Leo assumed the helm of the Roman Church. Seeing in him very often the fruits of perseverance, he consecrated him deacon with great affection. While he ministered in that rank, so great a grace was granted him from above that all could see him shining with the perfections of supreme activity. He was loved by the clergy, praised by the nobles, and greatly loved by the people.

578.

[Note: Col. 1357] Behold: Benedict, not the female pope Joan, succeeds Leo IV.

When Pope Leo had died, Benedict, a man of wonderful blessedness and most sacred pontiff, protected by heavenly aid, was set over the Roman see; he associated Nicholas with his own administration because he loved him more than his blood relatives, so that he delighted never to be without him even for a moment. Whatever he judged conducive to the usefulness of ecclesiastical affairs, he promulgated jointly with him and committed to decision, contemplating the resources of his most prudent judgment and the manifest strength of his intellect. For the observance of both always brought about more useful results by his own exertion. When he had been brought to the end of life, Benedict drank the cup of the precious company; and Nicholas, still a deacon, carried him on his own shoulders with the other deacons as far as the basilica of the most blessed apostle Peter and then laid him in the tomb with his own hands, showing the reward of affection which he bore towards him and the integrity of his love.

579. At that time the invincible Caesar Louis had departed from Rome. When he learned of Benedict’s death, grieving, he swiftly returned to it. The Romans, having lost so great a shepherd, shed tears with most sorrowful lamentation. When the clergy, the magnates, and the class of nobles had assembled, they persisted in fasts, prayers, and vigils, and unceasingly implored the Lord in contest, that he might deign to show them a man such as the one they had lost, whom they might raise to the summit of the pontificate.

While these things were taking place, they gathered with all the people in the basilica of the blessed Dionysius, confessor and pontiff. There, after conversing for a space of several hours, kindled by a heavenly splendour, they unanimously decreed that he should be bishop of the apostolic see; and they immediately hastened with swift step to the hall of Peter, prince of the apostles, where he had taken refuge and lay hidden. For he said that he was unworthy to undertake the helm of so great a government.

But those present rushed upon him, drew him by force from that basilica, and brought him with sacred acclamations into the Lateran patriarchal residence, where they set him on the apostolic throne. Afterwards, escorted by the gatherings of the noblest men and by all the people into the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he was consecrated in the presence of the Caesar, raised to the apostolic see, and made pontiff; he blessedly celebrated the solemnities of Mass above the most sacred body of the apostle. Surrounded by dense ranks of nobles and people, with hymns and spiritual songs he was led again into the Lateran patriarchal residence. At last he was crowned: the City exulted, the clergy rejoiced, and the senate and the whole people offered splendid congratulations.

On the third day of his consecration, dining with Augustus at a banquet in sophisticated speech, he shone in prudent eloquence and, full of radiance, feasted in Christ. When the preparations for the banquet had ended, he rose and, kissing Caesar as his special and, as it were, dearest son, enfolded him in immense love.

[Note: Col. 1357] *ophistico*, that is, “prudent.”

580. After these things had taken place, the most serene emperor departed from the City and took up his residence in the place called Quintus.

[Col. 1359]

On hearing this, the most blessed bishop, compelled by the fullness of his affection and love, hastened to the same place with the magnates and nobles of the Latin Roman name. When the most excellent Augustus saw him—or, according to M., when he had seen him—he came out to meet him on his arrival; taking the bridle of the pontiff’s horse in his own hands, Caesar led it on foot for the distance of an arrow’s flight.

Entering the imperial tent with him, they enjoyed wholesome conversation with one another; and, with the tables adorned with feasts, they partook together of food with spiritual cheerfulness. When they had been satisfied and the tables removed, the most serene Caesar bestowed many gifts on the blessed bishop. Having received them, the bishop mounted his horse and tried to return whence he had come.

Augustus, relying on his affection, mounted the saddle of the imperial horse and went along with him in exultant delight. When they had reached a very spacious stretch of road, the emperor dismounted and again, as we have recalled, led the pontiff’s horse; approaching one another with sweetest kisses, they exchanged radiant congratulations. Caesar returned to the tent and resumed the journey he had begun.

The bishop entered Rome, surrounded by the assembly of nobles with whom he had set out, and was exalted by his life-giving manner of life. For he was handsome in appearance, comely in form, learned in speech, humble in utterance, distinguished in conduct, devoted to fasts and divine worship, generous to the poor, protector of orphans, supporter of widows, and defender of all the people. But since we cannot commit to this writing all the sacred works he performed, let us return to what he offered to holy places.

581. This most blessed bishop, filled with divine inspiration, made in the deaconry of the holy Mother of God Mary, our Lady, called Cosmedin, one all-silk hanging of *stauracium*, bearing a representation with eleven large lions. There he made one white rose-patterned veil, ornamented around its border with Tyrian purple, of extraordinary size. In the said deaconry he offered one gilded *gabatha saxica* of purest silver, weighing two pounds and four ounces.

In the basilica of the Saviour, which took its Constantinian name from Constantine’s name, he made crosses of purest silver which hang before the image of the substantial flesh of our same Lord Jesus Christ. On feast days wax figures are customarily set on them for the praise of that church; they weigh four and a half pounds.

Likewise, in the basilica of Mary our Lady, ever-Virgin, called at the Manger, he made one seated silver *cantharus* of Parian work, weighing eight pounds and four ounces. This pontiff, protected by God and filled with heavenly favour, offered in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, his foster-father, one *gabatha* of purest gold, most precious with gems, weighing three pounds and eight ounces.

In the confession of that most sacred basilica he made one neck-ornament of purest gold, weighing two pounds. Likewise, in the said church he made six crosses of very pure silver, together weighing thirteen pounds and five ounces; and in the same manner two crosses of purest silver in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, Teacher of the Gentiles, together weighing four pounds.

In the basilica of the martyr Saint Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he also made two crosses of purest silver, together weighing four pounds.

582. In the first year of his pontificate, a certain golden crown, adorned with most precious gems and weighing eight pounds and four ounces, was brought to His Blessedness. With great love he raised it on golden chains above the most sacred altar of his basilica, for its glory. Moreover, in the aforementioned church of the blessed apostle Peter, his foster-father, he made nine *gabathae* of purest silver, together weighing twelve and a half pounds.

583. This venerable and distinguished pontiff, protected by God, made in the principal church called Saint Dionysius, in the monastery of Saints Stephen and Sylvester, which the lord Pope Paul of holy memory had newly founded, four *stauracium* veils for the honour and glory of the sacred altar.

In the time of this distinguished pontiff, namely on the thirtieth day of October, in the eighth indiction, the river called the Tiber left its bed and spread across the plains. It also swelled with a flood of many waters and entered the city of Rome through the little gate called Saint Agatha, at the [lacuna] hour of the day. It passed through certain places and entered the church of Saint Lawrence, called Lucina’s.

From there it extended itself and entered the monastery of Saint Sylvester, so that, owing to the abundance of water, not one of the steps ascending to the basilica of Saint Dionysius could be seen, except one that was higher up. From there it spread across the street called the Via Lata and entered the basilica of the holy Mother of God Mary which is there; and the water rose so high that even the doors of that church could not be seen because of the height of the waters.

From there it climbed through streets and lanes as far as the Clivus Argentarii. Then, overflowing back, it entered through the portico situated before the church of Saint Mark. Rushing onward, it began to run into the sewer beside the monastery of Saint Lawrence the martyr, called Pallacini.

From that day onward the water gradually began to diminish, and after doing much damage the river returned to its bed. For it overthrew houses and walls, laid waste fields, tore up crops, and uprooted shrubs.

In like manner, on the twenty-seventh day of December, the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, in the aforesaid indiction, the same river called the Tiber again left its channel and entered the Roman city; all [happened] as above.

[Col. 1361]

**584** In like manner the illustrious and most blessed pontiff made, in the monastery of Saint Valentine, situated in the territory of Narnia beside Interamna, one gold-woven vestment bearing a scene of lions and, around it, *myzinum*.

Likewise, the venerable and illustrious pontiff prepared from its foundations for construction and restoration the structure of the watercourse called the Tocia, which by then had become excessively damaged through the passage of many years, and through which water flowed by the *centenarium* into the city of Rome.

Moreover, in the church of the same Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, called Cosmedin, he built a large and spacious hospice, especially suitable for the assistance and benefit of the pontiffs, so that, whenever necessary, he might lodge there most generously with all who serve them.

In like manner, in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and his foster-father, he offered curtains for the arches of the presbytery, with a gold border, bearing a scene of lions—forty figures in number. In the same church he also presented a chain, skilfully made of the purest silver, weighing four pounds.

For in the oratory of the holy Cross, which is situated within the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, he made one silver *gabatha*, weighing two pounds. This most sacred pontiff also made, in the basilica of the teacher of the nations, blessed Paul the apostle, one silver candelabrum weighing two pounds and six ounces. Moreover, in the titular church of blessed Eusebius, confessor of Christ, he made above the ciborium a cross with a curtain of the purest silver, weighing four pounds.

**585** In the time of this pontiff, Michael, son of the emperor Theophilus of the city of Constantinople, sent gifts to blessed Peter the apostle, out of love for the apostles, by bishops whose names are these: Methodius the metropolitan and Samuel the bishops; and two others who had been deprived of the episcopal dignity, whose names are these: Zacharias, and another Theophilus; and another, an imperial layman named Arsavir—

[Note: [Col. 1361] Lasavir.]

—a *protospatharius*. That is, he sent a paten of the purest gold, with various precious stones, white, green, and hyacinth-colored. Likewise, a golden chalice surrounded with stones, with hyacinths hanging around it on a golden wire, and two fans (*repida*) in the form of peacocks, with shields and various precious stones, hyacinth-colored and white, weighing together . . . pounds.

Likewise, a gold-bordered vestment with white gems, bearing scenes of the Savior, blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and the other apostles, with trees and roses on both sides of the altar, and inscriptions spelling out the emperor’s name, of marvelous size and beauty.

When they had presented many other gifts to the pontiff, they immediately delivered the words of the embassy entrusted to them. The emperor of the Greeks, moreover, having found a pretext concerning the removers of the sacred images, requested through the aforesaid legates that envoys of the Apostolic See be sent to Constantinople. He was ostensibly advancing the case of Ignatius the patriarch and of Photius, the usurper of the Church of Constantinople: for he desired, as later became evident, cunningly and through hostility to have that same holy man Ignatius condemned by the judgment of the Apostolic See, and to substitute the neophyte Photius for him in the Church.

**586** At that time the supreme pontiff, still unaware of the emperor’s most evil intention, sent two bishops there, namely Raduald and Zacharias. He ordered them to settle synodally whatever question might arise concerning the sacred images, and only to investigate formally the case of Ignatius the patriarch and of the neophyte Photius, and to report back to him.

I shall briefly pass over below how, disregarding the decrees of the holy pontiff, and corrupted there by how much and what kind of insane bribery, they acted in the manner of Vitalis and Mesenus. Meanwhile many people of Ravenna, who were suffering disadvantages in their possessions and lawful rights at the hands of John, archbishop of that city, came to this most blessed pope to be freed from such great oppressions. Hearing their cries with fatherly compassion, he repeatedly admonished the archbishop through his legates and letters to desist from such actions. But that man, in confusion of mind and **disregarding**—

[Note: [Col. 1361] *contemnens*, “despising.”]

—the admonitions of the merciful Father, did not fear to add worse things to those he had previously committed. The more the supreme prelate’s gracious attention admonished him to come to his senses, the more he turned toward the world’s worse practices and did not cease adding iniquity to iniquity.

**587** For he rashly excommunicated some, turned others away from visiting the Apostolic See, and seized the property of still others without legal judgment. He also took away very many estates of the holy Roman Church. He despised the pope’s envoys and, as far as he could, emptied the glory of blessed Peter the apostle. He even broke the decrees of the law of Saint Peter whenever he found them in anyone’s possession, and transferred them to the jurisdiction of Saint Apollinaris.

For he deposed, without canonical judgment, priests and deacons not only subject to himself but also established throughout Emilia and belonging to the Apostolic See. Some he caused to be thrust into prison, others into foul workhouses; others he compelled by written statements to confess crimes they had not committed. He also suppressed ecclesiastical institutions without the consent of the Apostolic See. When summoned by the supreme pontiff to Rome for a synod, he repeatedly declared that he ought not to appear.

Nor is it surprising that he later acted in this way, since at the beginning of his consecration, following the example of his predecessor Felix, he falsified the bonds and little documents customarily kept in the archives by the archbishops of Ravenna, and composed some barbarous writings and others that were false.

[Col. 1363]

**588** At that time the aforesaid pope summoned him three times by letter to the synod; and when he scorned to come, he was deprived of communion by the holy synod. Then, going to Pavia, he brought a complaint to the ears of the emperor Louis Caesar and sought worldly assistance. At that point, when the emperor granted him distinguished envoys, he came to Rome with them, filled with the swelling of pride.

But the merciful pontiff, because the envoys had communicated with the excommunicated man contrary to the rules of the sacred canons, gently reproved them. When they lamented what they had done, the pope, whom God was preserving, sent word to the same archbishop that he should appear on the Kalends of November at the synod from which he had been excommunicated, display full satisfaction, and put an end to such great transgressions.

But he refused and withdrew by going back. And behold, the people of Emilia and the senators of the city of Ravenna, together with an innumerable crowd, hurried with tears to the feet of this blessed Roman prelate and begged him not to disdain, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ, to go to Ravenna for their recovery, so that, after examining everything, he might restore them to complete freedom.

**589** Accordingly, the most blessed pope himself set out for Ravenna. When the archbishop John learned of his arrival, he immediately undertook the journey as far as Pavia in order once again to trouble the emperor’s ears. Then the excellent prelate mercifully restored to all the people of Ravenna, Emilia, and the Pentapolis the properties they had lost through the seizure of Archbishop John and his brother Gregory, and confirmed by a decree of his command what he had **restored**—

[Note: [Col. 1363] *retrancidit* should read *retradidit*, “restored” or “returned.”]

When the aforesaid archbishop, as has been said, arrived at Pavia, the citizens of that city, together with their bishop Liutard, consecrated by the Roman pontiff, heard that the archbishop had been excommunicated by the supreme pontiff. They then placed themselves under such vigilant restraint that they would neither receive him in their houses nor allow his men to buy anything, lest through such commerce they should at least appear to share in conversation with them and thereby incur the mark of excommunication.

Rather, whenever they saw some of the archbishop’s attendants walking through the streets, they shouted: “These men are among those excommunicated; it is not lawful for them to mix with us.”

Then, seeing that he could not by this means carry out the schemes of his will, the archbishop repeatedly asked to be aided by the emperor. Through an intermediary the Augustus sent him this reply: “Let him go, lay aside the arrogance of his pride, humble himself greatly before the pontiff, to whom both we and the whole Church incline, and submit the neck of obedience and subjection; for otherwise he will in no way obtain what he desires.”

When the archbishop heard this, he began to be distressed. Again, seeking imperial envoys through importunate pleas, he came to Rome. But the most blessed pope, who knew what had happened, despised all his arrogance as a spider’s web and remained firm and immovable in the sentence previously pronounced.

Nevertheless, the most holy pope spoke to the same imperial envoys with great gentleness in these words:

**590** “If our beloved son, the lord emperor, knew well the actions and character of this Archbishop John, he would not only not trouble us on his behalf, but would even send him to us, whether he wished it or not, so that he might correct himself.”

Then, as that distinguished pope had decreed, many bishops of the provinces assembled together, and he sent word to the same archbishop that he should appear in person, make full satisfaction concerning himself, and properly amend the things in which he had transgressed.

When the archbishop heard this and saw that no one could help him, overcome, he withdrew into the lamentations of anguish and excessive tribulation. He implored those whom he could with tears, saying: “Have pity on me, I beg you; have pity on me. Entreat the mercy of the supreme prelate, that he may have mercy on me. For behold, I am ready to carry out everything he orders.”

Some who saw and heard this reported it to the supreme bishop, explaining in full the appeals he made in his lamentable voice. Then the most compassionate pope, imitating the Lord who does not desire the death of a sinner, moved by mercy, resolved to receive the aforesaid archbishop, who had at last turned toward the path of humility.

Immediately he seized the written pledge and the documents of his oath, which at the time of his consecration he had filled with incomplete and confused expressions, as they appeared there, and, writing them in his own hand, composed them according to the custom of his predecessors. He then climbed to the house called the Leonina, where the most blessed prelate was seated with bishops, priests, nobles, and many dignitaries in attendance.

There he placed the aforesaid writings, which he had prepared, upon the life-giving cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, upon his sandals, and upon the sacred codex of the four holy Gospels. Holding them in his hands, and with the innumerable people who had assembled listening, he freely swore in a clear voice that he would faithfully observe and fulfill them all the days of his life, as was contained and read in those writings of his declaration.

He also read them aloud himself in the presence of all and handed them to the supreme prelate. When these matters had been completed, on the following day that distinguished and principal pontiff descended with all the bishops and the entire clergy into the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantiniana. There, at the command of the supreme pontiff, the aforesaid archbishop appeared and cleared himself of the charge of heresy with which he was accused. The pope restored him to communion and graciously granted him permission to celebrate the solemn rites of the sacred Mass.

On the following day, while the same supreme and universal pope presided in the same Leonina house, and the most holy college of priests and fellow bishops was seated according to custom, the same archbishop appeared and, at the command of the supreme prelate, took his seat.

**591** Then the bishops of Emilia appeared, presenting written complaints against the same Archbishop John and saying that they suffered many prejudices and burdens imposed by that archbishop. Some people of Ravenna and Emilia also testified to the same things, as anyone who investigates will be able to find in the records lying in the library.

When the pontiff, protected by God, heard this, he declared together with the holy synod that such actions were contrary to ecclesiastical rule. With the holy synod acclaiming that all these transgressions ought to be corrected, he decreed in gentle speech that this should be done, lest the Lord’s flock entrusted principally to him be abandoned through negligence to be torn by wolves’ bites.

“Nevertheless, O Archbishop John,” said the distinguished prelate, “so that all the things being reported may henceforth be more easily corrected through specific correction, we command you that, removing every excuse except serious bodily illness that completely prevents you from coming, you diligently hasten to the Apostolic See once each year, unless perhaps you receive permission from the Apostolic See to delay.

“We also decree that you shall not consecrate bishops in Emilia unless, after the election of the duke, clergy, and people, you have received by letter from the prelate of the Apostolic See permission to consecrate them. You shall in no way prevent those bishops whenever they wish to come to the Apostolic See. Nor shall you at any time demand from them any payment not prescribed by the sacred canons.

“We further command that you compel those bishops in no way to offer or perform for the Church of Ravenna that evil custom which some call the *tricesimalis*, nor attempt in any way to exact from them that practice which is contrary to the privilege of bishops.

“Furthermore, we command you never to seize or impose a title upon the property of any person, however acquired or possessed, by whatever device or document, until you have legally proved in the presence of the Apostolic See, its envoy, or the *vestararius* of Ravenna that it belongs to you.”

When this had been enjoined and commanded by the most blessed pope to Archbishop John, the holy synod rose and acclaimed three times:

“Right is the judgment of the supreme prelate; just is the decision of the whole shepherd of the Church; the salutary institution of Christ’s disciple pleases everyone! We all say the same things, we all understand the same things, we all judge the same things.”

Then, after both the same archbishop and the entire holy synod had been nourished by the food of the sacred word and satisfied by the nectar of the sweetest flavor from the most blessed prelate, each returned to his own place after receiving the pontiff’s permission.

**592** At that time this distinguished pope, whom God was preserving, had [lacuna] carved of the purest silver in the church of the blessed Mother of God Mary, called Cosmedin, weighing five pounds and two ounces. In the titular church of Vestina he also made an *icona* bearing an image of blessed Vitalis the martyr, weighing four and a half pounds.

He also made, around the sacred altar in the basilica of blessed Anastasius, martyr of Christ, four curtains with a purple border (*periclysis*). In the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, in the oratory of Pope Saint Gregory, he offered three gold-woven vestments ornamented all around with *oloverum*.

This most blessed and distinguished pontiff offered in the church of the teacher of the nations, blessed Paul the apostle, a vestment of marvelous beauty woven with gold and bearing hyacinth-colored, white, and green gems around it, together with carbuncles, with a pure mind. There also he made and offered two curtains similarly woven with gold and adorned with gems.

The church of the Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, formerly called the Old Church and now called the New, which Pope Lord Leo IV had built from its foundations but had not decorated with paintings, this most blessed prelate caused to be painted with beautiful and varied colors, increasing its splendor, and adorned it with many objects, with a pure heart.

**593** As I stated a little earlier, a certain schism had grown up in the holy Church of Constantinople. For Ignatius, the most reverend patriarch, had been expelled from that Church’s see, and Photius, a neophyte from the laity and the military who had been tonsured, had suddenly been substituted there as bishop, contrary to the decrees of the reverend canons.

But because Michael, emperor of the Greeks, was speaking abusively of Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople—whom, during the time of Pope Lord Leo IV, they had exalted with praises—and praising the usurper Photius, he humbly consulted the Roman See through Arsavir the *spatharius*, that is, his envoy, and through his letters, asking that this most blessed and distinguished pope send his envoys there to investigate the matters being reported.

Since the supreme prelate desired ecclesiastical order to remain inviolate, he did not refuse to do this. He wished to uproot the heaps of weeds (*zizania*) down to the root, lest through negligence any blemish should arise in the holy Church of God.

**594** Then he sent from his own side two bishops, Raduald, as has been mentioned, bishop of Porto, and Zacharias of Anagni, whom he considered suitable for this task. He ordered and commanded them to investigate only the matter of the election of Ignatius and the substitution of Photius, and to report back to him. Meanwhile they were to avoid communion with the neophyte Photius until, on their return, they had taken care to provide a definite account of everything.

But when they departed, disregarding what they had been ordered, they not only communicated with the neophyte Photius contrary to the sentence forbidding this, but, corrupted by gifts, they supported him and his consecration and, after convening a general synod, deposed that same man Ignatius the patriarch once again.

This can easily be found in the records they compiled at Constantinople; and it was truthfully established through the envoys—namely Leo the *a secretis* and others—as well as through the letter of the aforesaid emperor.

When those envoys returned, they highly praised what they had done concerning Photius and condemned with many objections those who had acted wickedly against Ignatius the patriarch. The rector and universal head of the Church, the distinguished and discerning prelate of the Apostolic See, considered these things at Rome with holy attention. But when he heard what had been done contrary to his arrangement, he did not immediately believe it, until he had examined everything according to the mystical understanding of his sacred wisdom.

Meanwhile he composed letters of his sacred authority both to Michael, emperor of the Greeks, and to Photius himself—letters preserved in the archive of this see—and entrusted them to Leo the *a secretis*, commanding and declaring that he would consent neither to the deposition of Ignatius the patriarch nor to the substitution of Photius until, after the truth had been recognized, the legitimate case had received its conclusion in his presence.

[Col. 1367]

**595** While some were saying that the decision of the prelate in this matter had been one thing, and others were acclaiming that Ignatius had been unjustly deposed, the same supreme pontiff continually prayed to the heavenly judge that, through his mercy, it might be revealed to God’s Church that he had not consented to such things.

Then, relying upon divine zeal, he summoned a council of bishops. In it it became most clearly evident that he had not consented to the deposition of Ignatius and that the envoys of the Apostolic See had deviated in these matters.

Finally, with the holy synod, that most merciful prelate deprived the aforesaid Bishop Zacharias, who was then present, of priestly rank—indeed, of ecclesiastical communion—because he was found to have exceeded the apostolic prohibitions in many respects, just as blessed Pope Felix had deprived the bishops Vitalis and Mesenus, who had been compelled to consent to Peter of Alexandria when he was stained by heretical filth.

The case of Bishop Radoald was suspended; afterward the pious pope condemned him together with the holy synod for violating his commands even in Gaul, breaking the excommunication, and evading canonical judgment.

**596** Accordingly, this distinguished man and pontiff devoted to holy zeal ordered that a certain deacon named Pepon, who had appealed to the Apostolic See from Bishop Pandulph and had been unjustly deposed, be restored to his office. Since he had been judged without a fixed number of bishops, indeed without proof of a crime, and since the deacon himself had been judged without a confession from his own mouth, he annulled the entire sentence of judgment and, through apostolic mercy, brought the case back onto the path of rectitude.

While this most excellent prelate was governing the Apostolic See, Louis Augustus presented these gifts to the holy apostle Peter, namely—

[Note: [Col. 1367] Something appears to be missing here.]

This most merciful pontiff was so diligent in keeping watch over the Lord’s flock that, whenever some scandal arose in the holy Church, he gave neither rest to his body nor sleep to his limbs until peace had been restored through his envoys or letters and the people of tranquility had recovered their benefit.

**597** For King Lothar, having abandoned Queen Theutberga and taken Waldrada, his concubine, in marriage, although he had consulted the Roman See and the same pious pontiff carnally concerning these matters, was wallowing in the corruption of lust and the wantonness of the flesh.

When the supreme pontiff considered within himself how he might drive this evil from the Church of God, lest that king pollute others with the plague of this disease, he began to be afflicted for a very long time. He grieved deeply in his heart and groaned over these errors, especially when he heard that Theutgaud of Trier and Gunther of Cologne, archbishops, together with Hagano of Bergamo and the other bishops, had given the king such authority that he could more freely reject Theutberga and lawfully unite the concubine Waldrada to himself in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Some call them Thietgaud and Gunther.]

The most blessed prelate discovered that those whom he ought to have had as helpers and guides before the Lord had instead become, by giving such authority, traitors delivered to perpetual fire.

Therefore, without delay, he immediately sent his envoys to Francia, ordering and warning them that, after convening a synodal assembly in the city of Metz, they should inquire why that king rejected Theutberga or joined Waldrada to himself in marriage. After investigating and discovering the truth, they were to bring the matter to a legitimate conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Some have *Thietberga*.]

**598** When the envoys of the Apostolic See arrived there, they began to investigate the matter. Among other things they heard this from Lothar: “Whatever I have done, I have done on the advice of these bishops.”

The aforesaid Theutgaud and Gunther, archbishops, were there as the principal men. The holy pope had already discovered that they were the authors of such a great crime. They asserted and declared that the union which King Lothar had formed with Waldrada the concubine was legitimate, and they promised that they could defend what they had said when they came before the distinguished lord pope.

Although the envoys of the Apostolic See had been misled in many respects, as they returned toward Rome they reported to the supreme pontiff what they had heard and learned from the king and from the archbishops Theutgaud and Gunther.

While the most pious prelate awaited the arrival of the archbishops, behold, by the direction of heavenly mercy, Theutgaud and Gunther came to the city of Rome and requested to be presented at the feet of this prelate in the sacred presence.

The most excellent prelate received them graciously. They offered him a written statement, saying that they had done neither more nor less than the document itself declared. When he examined it most carefully, he found in it no small amount of obscenity, expressed in profane and unheard-of language. Since these things exceeded the episcopal order, they bound the archbishops as though they were madmen.

Finally, after a synod had been convened in the Lateran palace, beside the apostles, the same archbishops were found, as has been said, to have incurred the mark of condemnation. This was especially because they proclaimed themselves the authors of so great a divorce and did not deny—but publicly declared in a loud voice—that they had dissolved the sentence which the pope had pronounced against Ingiltrud, the wife of Boso.

She had abandoned her husband Boso for seven years and had been excommunicated, bound, and anathematized by the pious pope of the supreme see; yet they had arranged for her to return to him and had communicated and maintained fellowship with her, indeed had spoken with her. They had also falsified at will the letter of the pious pontiff, as is demonstrated by the badly composed records deposited in the archive of this see.

Then, when that holy prelate judged and decreed together with the synod, they were deprived of priestly honor. They deservedly incurred the penalty of deposition.

In this synod the merciful prelate immediately annulled the Synod of Metz, where those proceedings had been arranged against the will of God and against his own will, and promulgated certain necessary chapters for the holy Church.

**599** After these matters had been completed, together with the aforementioned Bishop Hagano—who, as certain bishops wrote to that fellow angelic prelate, was called *Heliu* on account of the unskilled speeches that resounded in the aforesaid profane proceedings submitted by Theutgaud and Gunther, because Hagano himself had presided as their author and had composed such things with those same archbishops in unsuitable and mendacious language—and after Archbishop John, whose memory is discussed earlier in the text, had been summoned together with his own brother Gregory, who were held liable because they had forgotten the many transgressions of the oath they had sworn, those same deposed men, without seeking the lamentations of penance and without yet grieving over the great crime they had committed against the wife of King Lothar, began, together with Hagano, John the bishop of Ravenna, and his brother Gregory, to perpetrate against the Roman See—and especially against the supreme pontiff and the people subject to him and entrusted by the Lord Jesus Christ to blessed Peter the apostle, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven—many abominable, many hostile, many sacrilegious deeds, exceeding the bounds of Christianity, openly and secretly, fraudulently and shamelessly.

Their wickedness crossed mountains and seas; and, setting their mouths against heaven, they cruelly tore apart the Lord’s people and deceived innocent souls through a viperous conspiracy. The past evils were not enough for them; at the devil’s persuasion they did not refuse to commit new and unheard-of acts worse than those they had previously done. For they audaciously dared to touch what had been separately forbidden to each of them and had been prohibited synodally according to the gravity of their crime. They carried out, despite God, what no one ought to attempt—alas, how shamefully!

**600** This friend of Christ kept written lists with him of all the lame, blind, and wholly disabled people living in the city of Rome, and carefully provided them with their daily food.

For the other poor who possessed the ability to walk or had physical strength, he wisely devised a method by which he could feed them in turn. He ordered that tokens (*bullae*) bearing his name be made and commanded that these be given to them. By the sign of the tokens it could more easily be known how many were to eat on the first weekday, how many on the second, how many on the third, and on the remaining weekdays.

On the tokens given to them, he had two knots made on each token for those who were to be fed on the first weekday, and so on through Saturday, so that however many weekdays there were, that many knots would be on each token. He enclosed nuts in the places where the knots were made, so that there would be no poor person in the City who was not fed from his alms on at least one day of the week.

Meanwhile King Charles offered the holy apostle a vestment made of the purest gold and gems, bearing green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems.

The most holy and radiant pontiff, grieving that the people were oppressed by so many calamities, invoked God alone with countless prayers and praised him with endless proclamations, yet did not abandon care for the churches of God. Rather, amid tribulation and temporal trial, he fittingly increased it.

For he renewed the *secretarium* in the basilica of the Mother of God Mary, called Cosmedin, and there made a dining hall of beautiful appearance with fireplaces, to her honor and glory.

**601** In like manner, while renewing the portico beside the same *secretarium*, he constructed an oratory in honor of Saint Nicholas, where the merciful man placed very many gifts.

That benevolent shepherd also renewed the cemetery of blessed Felix the martyr and the *confessio* on the Portuensis Way. He also beautifully and marvelously restored the cemetery on the same road at Ursus Pileatus, where the bodies of the holy martyrs of Christ, Abdon and Sennen, had rested; it had already fallen into ruins.

On the Appian Way, at the cemetery of Saint Sebastian, martyr of Christ, in the Catacomb where the bodies of the apostles had lain, he renewed the building, which had stood in ruins for many years, with better workmanship. He made it into a monastery, gathered monks from wherever he could under the rule of an abbot, and ordered that food and other necessary stipends be provided.

**602** In this pontiff’s time, when many people came running to the reputation of his holiness, certain men from the English people came to Rome. In the oratory of blessed Gregory, pope and confessor of Christ, constructed at Frascati in the church of the prince of the apostles, they placed one silver panel weighing . . . pounds.

The aforesaid most merciful pontiff caused five gold-woven curtains to be made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom. They hang for the adornment of that basilica from the beams within the vestibule of so great a building, and are ornamented all around with excellent *oloverum*. He offered them for the palm of eternal life.

During the time of this most blessed prelate, consultations from so many and such great provinces were directed to the Apostolic See—after the clear light of his distinguished teaching had become known—that no one can remember anything comparable ever having reached it from ancient times.

As a prelate well supplied with the nourishment of the sacred word, he abundantly refreshed each person, gave them mystical precepts and laws, satisfied them with blessed instructions, taught them, and sent them back to their own places blessed and instructed.

Whatever he learned or heard from anyone was being done wrongly, he preferred to correct out of regard for God alone. He devoted himself to grievous laments and countless prayers, so that Almighty God, through his mercy, might transform such conduct through good and distinguished examples as though it had never existed.

The same occurred when a report arrived from the island of Sardinia. Having also learned this through members of his household who were Sardinian by birth, he received the report in these words:

**603** The judges of that island, together with the people subject to their administration, were contracting incestuous and unlawful unions with their near relatives and blood relations, just as they had been accustomed to do in the time of Pope Lord Gregory IV.

Then, instructed by the Holy Spirit, he composed letters of his preaching, sweet as honey yet terrible to transgressors, whose radiance shone throughout the whole world. He also summoned and sent vigorous men: Paul, bishop of Populonia, and Saxo, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saints John and Paul. He sent them there to call that Sardinian people back from so great an error.

When they went, they found some of them strongly opposed and refusing to receive the admonitions of discipline. Nevertheless, according to the authority of the supreme prelate’s command, they excommunicated and anathematized the Sardinians who heard them, until they fled from the evil of incestuous unions and sought the remedies of penance, as is contained and inserted in the register of that prelate in the letters which the same legates had carried to Sardinia.

Thus, after delivering abundant preaching, they returned to Rome.

**604** Moreover, a certain Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, deposed Rothad, bishop of the city of Soissons, who had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, contrary to the regulations of the Council of Sardica, and ordered him to be kept in strict custody.

When the most blessed pope had received three written petitions concerning this deposed man, together with his declaration of innocence, he admonished the archbishop by letters and ordered him to send the deposed Rothad to Rome with his envoys for a hearing.

Rothad came to this Roman city according to the command of the blessed pope and remained here for approximately nine months, but no one at all ever appeared on the accusers’ behalf to contend with Rothad before the most holy prelate or to accuse him.

Then, on the day of the vigil of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, when, according to the customary practice of this Apostolic See, the prelate was accustomed to celebrate the offices of the Mass with the clergy and people in the basilica of the Mother of God at the Manger, the merciful pope assembled everyone and spoke publicly from the ambo concerning Rothad. He explained how Rothad had been deposed after appealing to the Apostolic See and how, throughout all those months, none of his accusers had appeared in his presence.

Finally, with the consent of the bishops, priests, deacons, and the entire assembly, he decreed that Rothad was worthy to be clothed in priestly garments: no one had accused him throughout all those months, he had appealed to the judgment of the Apostolic See, and he should not be deprived of his honor.

There Rothad, clothed in episcopal vestments, promised that he would answer his persecutors at all times. After waiting a number of further days, namely until the feast day of the holy virgin Agnes, which falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, still no one appeared against Rothad, who had now been restored as bishop, to argue any charge.

### 605

When the most blessed prelate had therefore assembled with everyone in the basilica of that virgin outside the walls of the city on the Nomentan Way, the same Bishop Rothadus handed the supreme pontiff a written statement of his defense and undertaking—the undertaking by which he had promised that he would always answer his accusers. At the distinguished prelate’s command it was read aloud before all who were listening. There too the terms of his restoration were reread; and, after everyone’s consent had been given, in the church of Saint Constance beside the same basilica of the holy virgin, the often-mentioned Rothadus, now restored as bishop, solemnly celebrated the office of the Mass by decree of this most blessed prelate.

On the following day, when the synod had assembled again in the house called Leoniana, and Rothadus had been defended—as is contained in the written statements acknowledged by him, inserted in two gatherings of four leaves each, sent and presented at different times, and deposited in the archive of this see—he was restored to his former rank, as has been stated above, so that priests, and especially those who appealed to the apostolic see, would not thereafter suffer such dangers. He was sent back to his own see with the apostolic sanctions, so that, vested in episcopal insignia, if he should be challenged, he might henceforth answer his accusers before the prelate of the apostolic see.

Together with him, the most holy prelate, preserved by God, immediately sent Arsenius, bishop, apocrisiarius and envoy of this gracious apostolic see—both for Rothadus’s restoration and for the dissolution of King Lothair’s union, and also for preserving peace and concord among the kings of Gaul. Once peace had been restored, Arsenius was to unite them without resistance to the bosom of holy Church, and to carry out more diligently and abundantly certain necessary measures established in the Church of Gaul according to apostolic tradition.

### 606

Nevertheless, the same pope restored Seufredus, bishop of the see of Piacenza, to his own see after he had been driven from it through the treachery of a certain deacon, Paul, doing so through his legates. He also rebuked that deacon—who, while the see’s rightful ruler was still alive, had dared to invade it—by an appropriate reprimand, together with his followers.

[Col. 1373] In order completely to cut off that deacon’s disastrous and wicked presumption, and out of his zeal for holiness and for the peace of God’s Church, he commanded that already-mentioned deacon neither ever again to attempt anything of the kind nor, whether Seufredus lived or died as bishop, to presume either to reclaim or to accept the see of Piacenza.

For this distinguished and illustrious pontiff, with piety as his guide, foresaw the sufferings and needs of all and, compassionating everyone mercifully, quickly came to the aid of the needy. In imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who descended from on high to the lowest depths in order to redeem the human race, he endured immense labors among the people.

### 607

Therefore, seeing the lame and the blind, as well as those afflicted by various punishments, lying in the portico of the blessed apostle Peter beside the bank of the Tiber and unable to go forward to relieve their thirst, and divinely considering the benefit of the various peoples who came from every direction to the apostolic threshold on account of their sins, he ordered—sparing his body not at all—that the aqueduct, which had stood in ruins for many years and for that reason no longer carried water to the blessed apostle Peter, be restored with very great effort to a condition better than before. Thus it became not only beneficial to the physically disabled but also an outstanding work for everyone visiting the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, as it is still clearly visible and maintained to the adornment of the Leonine city.

Moreover, the city of Ostia, which blessed Pope Gregory of revered memory had long ago built for the salvation of many, lest the wicked nation of the Saracens surround or destroy the people of God, was lying in ruins. Moved by a stronger divine inspiration, this most holy prelate ordered it to be rebuilt with a stronger and firmer structure and restored it to a better condition. He also fortified it with very strong gates and towers, placing in it men ready for battle, so that thereafter no attack by a foreign people could dominate it or inflict any harm upon its citizens—unless, God forbid, through negligence.

**[Note: [Col. 1373] “Of blessed memory.”]**

### 608

Meanwhile, as the merits of this most blessed man were everywhere overflowing throughout the world, through the power of the Most High God, who daily performs great signs and wonders through his servants, the king of the Bulgarians, recognizing the teachings of Christianity and the holy faith, was found worthy to be baptized. He who had previously raged cruelly while serving the creature now submitted his neck to the Creator during this pontiff’s time and began to command with expansive religious devotion; he also displayed great piety.

In August, in the fourteenth indiction, he therefore sent his legates to this catholic and truly orthodox prelate. He bestowed considerable gifts both upon the holy places and upon the supreme pontiff himself, asking his apostolate what it would be more salutary for him to do, and what ought to be done concerning the remainder of the Bulgarian people, who still lacked holy baptism, so that they might receive the sacraments of the faith.

When the most blessed pope heard this, he was filled with great joy and offered abundant praise to Christ. Rejoicing with the whole Church divinely entrusted to him, he poured forth in a devout mind and also in a suppliant voice countless praises to our God, who in these last times had wrought so great a miracle.

After receiving the legates of the Bulgarian king, now bearing the name Michael, the holy pope honorably retained them with him. Meanwhile he appointed as envoys of the apostolic see Paul, bishop of Populonia, and Formosus, bishop of Porto, men of great holiness. Instructing them with honey-sweet admonitions and teachings, he decided to send them to preach to that people.

Since the road through the Bulgarian kingdom extended by land as far as Constantinople, and since the same pope had already made known throughout the East, once and twice, by apostolic letters, whatever decision he had reached concerning the holy Church of Constantinople, he likewise sent Donatus, bishop of Ostia, Leo, a presbyter of the holy Roman Church, and Marinus, a deacon of the holy apostolic see, suitable apostolic envoys. Paul and Formosus were to convert the Bulgarian people to the faith; the others were to announce in every respect what the apostolic see had deliberated concerning the Church of Constantinople. This was accomplished in the name of the Lord, with the help of Saint Peter and Saint Paul.

But while the aforesaid venerable bishops Paul and Formosus were staying in Bulgaria, the reverend Bishop Donatus, the presbyter Leo, and Marinus, minister of the apostolic see, were on their way to Constantinople. Behold, between the borders of Bulgaria and Constantinople they encountered a certain Theodore, who was guarding that region. He did not allow them to proceed any farther; rather, he heaped countless insults upon them and abused the legates of so great a see to such an extent that he even struck the heads of the horses on which they were riding, saying: “Our emperor certainly has no need of you.”

### 609

The same emperor is reported to have said to the legates of the Bulgarian king: “Unless the envoys of the apostolic see had come through Bulgaria, they would never see either my face or Rome during their lifetime.”

After remaining there for forty days, when they learned that the emperor of the Greeks had ordered this, they turned back. They were compelled to return to Rome and report these same events.

Meanwhile, the apostolic envoys sent by the aforementioned king of the Bulgarians were received with eager spirit and great devotion. They began to teach the people salutary admonitions, and, from the least to the greatest, washed them with God’s grace in the sacred font. They handed over the entire rite of the Christian faith to the Bulgarians as a customary practice, just as they had been instructed by the most holy pope.

The glorious king of the Bulgarians, enticed by the steadfastness of this devout Father’s admonitions, began to burn with such zeal for the faith that, expelling all foreigners from his kingdom and using only the preaching of the apostolic envoys, he resolved to be continually refreshed by the pastures of eternal life. He also requested that one of them, Formosus—a bishop distinguished in life and conduct—be given to him as archbishop.

He then sent his legates to Rome again and, among other matters, made the same request to the most blessed pope, asking his holiness for presbyters to instruct that people. When the pope learned of these things, he rejoiced greatly. Giving infinite thanks to God, he examined a considerable number of presbyters in his presence and sent to Bulgaria those whom he found worthy of the grace of preaching. With them he sent the bishops Dominic of Treviso and Grimoald of Polimartium, so that, since Bishop Formosus ought not to abandon the people entrusted to him, one of those presbyters who might be found worthy could finally be chosen in the Lord’s name for the archbishopric and sent to the apostolic see for consecration.

### 610

Meanwhile the most blessed pope, most diligent corrector of vices and worshiper of God, decreed that, when the bishops themselves entered Bulgaria, Paul of Populonia—whom we mentioned above—and Grimoald himself, as bishops in Bulgaria, should carry out whatever pertained to divine ministry for the instruction of that people. He also decreed that the often-mentioned venerable bishops Formosus and Dominic should travel again to Constantinople because of the schism that had arisen there, about which I have already spoken at length.

But while these things were taking place, God’s judgment struck Michael, emperor of the Greeks, with a fitting vengeance and killed him by a wicked murder. When Basil was ruling in Constantinople, God wished to bring to a good conclusion the unceasing labors that this holy pontiff had endured for the holy Church of Constantinople. As report has it, the neophyte and usurper Photius was expelled as an adulterer, and, in accordance with the decree of the apostolic see, the patriarch Ignatius was restored to the Constantinopolitan throne.

This most pious and catholic pope, executor of divine works, did not put his own interests first, but those of God; he placed them first and sought them. With the help of Saint Peter, he took care to wage the Lord’s wars spiritually, with the highest balance of administration. He moderated all those set over others with great foresight, lest they harm their subjects, admonishing them as a father; and he also decreed pastorally that subjects should obey their superiors according to each person’s privileges.

Anyone who wishes to recognize his holy zeal will be able to find it more clearly than daylight in his letters, which he sent throughout the world with careful balance. He placed his soul in his hands and thought of nothing but heavenly things. Devoting himself night and day to fasts, vigils, and prayers, he gave neither rest to his body nor sleep to his limbs.

For if we wished to insert into written records all the works of holiness that he, filled with Christ’s grace, accomplished through virtue and faith, and taught and fulfilled by his conduct and life, perhaps parchment would run out before speech. Yet, before turning our pen to the end of his life, let us return to the things he bestowed upon the holy places.

### 611

This outstanding pope, out of love for the prince of the apostles, Peter, his foster-father, made in his basilica hangings of stauracius, of fundatus, and of other beautiful and varied colors, numbering [lacuna]. He covered all the larger beams facing the presbytery around the entire circuit; these splendidly adorn and enhance it and, through their remarkable size, give it still greater honor.

There too, something which no one had attempted after the Saracen devastation, he made a silver arch and placed it, better than it had formerly been, upon the more elevated beam standing before the ciborium in the center, weighing [lacuna] pounds. He also fashioned three silver images: one representing the Lord Savior and two depicting angels. Gilding them with nine pounds of gold, he placed them there; one weighed eighty pounds, another seventy pounds, and the third likewise weighed seventy pounds.

He also made one golden cross adorned with precious gems, weighing [lacuna] pounds. He placed it on the summit of that same arch; and, in keeping with the breadth of its beauty and magnificence, he hung there one golden crown, two silver crosses, two silver chalices, and two silver staups.

On the purple marble slabs that hold silver folds before the body of the blessed apostle Peter, he placed, offering them, two silver crosses, one on the right and one on the left, weighing [lacuna] pounds.

### 612

In the Lateran patriarchium he ordered a most beautiful and exceedingly splendid house to be built. There he constructed an oratory of the holy Mother of God and, out of love for eternal life, the most blessed pontiff himself offered clothing and suitable ornaments with radiant vows.

The same man, protected by God and surrounded by heavenly grace, renewed many holy places threatened with collapse, bestowed various gifts upon various churches, and splendidly increased their resources.

In the ciborium of the Constantinian basilica he hung four excellent hangings of siforium and fundatus. Then he offered to the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven excellent hangings of the same number in the ciborium. He did the same in the church of the teacher of the nations. In the church of the holy Mother of God at the Praesepe he acted likewise, for the rewards of eternal recompense. In the church of Saint Lawrence, martyr of Christ, outside the walls of the City, he likewise gave four excellent hangings for the ciborium.

During the time of this blessed prelate there was such abundance and supply of food that this prosperity consigned to oblivion every memory of the famine that had occurred during the days of his predecessor.

He held one ordination in the month of March: seven presbyters, four deacons, and sixty-five bishops for various places.

After he had ruled the apostolic see most victoriously, as a true athlete of God, in a catholic and principal manner, he departed from this light to the Lord on the Ides of November, in the first indiction.

What should I say? Not only did various nations of humanity, using their full reason, mourn his departure, but even the elements of the world themselves, insofar as the inclemency of the air was concerned, wept for a long time and remained in sorrow over the death of so great a man. After his death, his body was buried before the doors of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

## CVIII. ADRIAN II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 867; OF LOUIS II, 12; OF THE EMPEROR BASIL, 1

No. 613, line 1: “Talarus, bishop, held the see for five years, eleven months, and twelve days.” Once, when he had customarily received denarii from Pope Sergius among his fellow presbyters, he returned home and ordered his equerry that, from those denarii, he should distribute three to each of the multitude of pilgrims whom he found before the door of that same house. **[M.: “three denarii each.”]** When the man asserted that not even one denarius for each would suffice for a third of them **[as in line 14]**, he himself took the denarii and distributed three to each.

When the generous priest’s equerry marveled at this excess, because money had not only failed to run out but remained over, he again bestowed three on each member of his household from what was left. When six remained, he said: “You see how generous the Lord is, who mercifully reserved three for me and three for you from that quantity of forty.”

When he was being led to the Roman pontificate from the church of the Mother of God our Lady, which is called at the Praesepe—see No. 614, lines 33–34—he was carried to the Lateran patriarchium in eager competition by the clergy, nobles, and people. When the envoys of Louis the emperor heard this, they took it badly, indignant because, although they were present, they had not been invited and had not been deemed worthy to participate in the election of the future pontiff desired by them. After they understood that this had been omitted not out of contempt for the Augustus but entirely with a view to the future—so that the custom of waiting for the envoys of princes in the election of Roman prelates would not grow through such encouragement—they entirely quieted the indignation of their minds and themselves approached humbly to greet the elected man.

No. 614, line 38: “through consideration of the time this was omitted.” Line 40: “they had carefully calmed all indignation” **[M.: “having contrived”]**, “and approached for salvation.” Line 41: “they approached.”

When Louis, the most Christian emperor, heard this, he immediately wrote an imperial letter to all the Romans, as in No. 615, line 9.

No. 615, line 11: “he praised the prelate because they had performed such a great service”; through this letter, evidently, it became known. Line 12: “for the consecration of the Roman pontiff, in whatever manner.” Line 13: “they eagerly desired unanimously.” Line 14: “to take away from the Roman Church.” Line 15: “During his time a synod was held at Constantinople for the expulsion of Photius and the restoration of Patriarch Ignatius. The legates of the Bulgarians, in the presence of Emperor Basil and the legates of the four apostolic sees, held a lengthy dispute over whether they ought to be subject to the Roman or to the Constantinopolitan Church. Later, the legate of Michael, king of the Bulgarians, presented the supreme pontiff Adrian with royal letters and royal gifts, as in No. 639, at the beginning.”

No. 639, line 8: “by choosing.” Line 9: “for the archiepiscopal office, the supreme pontiff sent a certain subdeacon Silvester to be chosen by the Bulgarians, together with the bishops Leopardus of Ancona and Dominic of Treviso. Afterwards, through the Easterners, as in the following number, line 5.”

**[Col. 1395]**

### 613

Adrian, a Roman by nation, son of Talarus, formerly bishop of the third region, held the see for five years. Descending through a close family connection from the pontiffs Stephen IV and Sergius the Younger, of blessed memory, while he was distinguished by remarkable deeds he received the ministry of the subdiaconate from Gregory IV, of venerable memory, prelate of the apostolic see.

Afterward, having been familiarly received into the Lateran patriarchium and having conducted himself commendably, he was ordained presbyter to govern the title of Saint Mark, confessor and priest of Christ. He lived so blamelessly and ministered so manfully that he was revered by everyone not merely as one who had become a presbyter but as one who would become pontiff.

For in Christ and in his Mother, at whose Praesepe he devoted himself to continual prayers, he had such confidence that, while doing good, he did not grow faint, nor did he fear incurring any danger, generously distributing with the greatest discernment everything he could possess.

One day, having received the customary forty denarii from the most holy Pope Sergius among his fellow presbyters, he returned home. As he wished to enter the doors of his house, he was completely unable to do so because of the multitude of pilgrims who had confidently gathered there, as was their custom, like grain to a common granary. Moved by compassion, he told his equerry, his steward:

**[Note: [Col. 1379] “to his equerry, his steward.”]**

“Nothing is common to me without so many brothers, and such a small amount of money is not mine alone.”

When the man replied that one denarius for each could not suffice even for a third of the poor, he said: “By the power of Christ, who satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, I shall distribute not one denarius to each but three denarii to each.”

Saying this, he went outside to the doorway, received the money from his equerry, and distributed three denarii individually to all the pilgrims as they came out. When the equerry marveled at this abundance, because the denarii had not only failed to run out but had remained over, the generous presbyter brought the remainder into the house and nonetheless distributed three coins individually to every member of his household.

When six likewise remained, he said: “See how generous and gracious the almighty Lord is, who distributed the quantity of forty coins in threes to our brothers and preserved three for me and three for you by equal fortune.”

### 614

He was moreover so hospitable and generous that he may rightly be compared with blessed Job, for compassion grew with him from infancy and came forth with him from his mother’s womb.

He did not despise the passerby because he lacked clothing; indeed, he warmed his sides with the fleeces of sheep. Nor did he eat even his morsel alone, since he ate it with orphans and the needy. He was, as it were, an eye to the blind and was proved to be a foot to the lame. To report the abundance of his virtues in writing, he was a father to the poor and a comforter of the widow’s heart. His door stood open to travelers, and the door of his house was not closed to anyone asking anything of him.

Thus, from every clerical rank, from the entire senatorial order, and from the harmonious assembly of the people, he would have been compelled to assume the supreme pontificate after the death of Pope Leo IV, just as after the death of Pope Benedict III, unless he had modestly evaded it through various devices and carefully contrived excuses.

**[Note: [Col. 1379] Note again that Benedict succeeded Leo IV.]**

But when Pope Nicholas, most holy and of apostolic memory, had departed from human affairs, and Adrian was at that time passing beyond his seventy-fifth year, all the citizens of the Roman City, together with those who happened to be present from outside, poor and rich alike, the clerical order and the entire mass of the people—of every age, profession, and sex—desired Adrian and eagerly wished Adrian to be given to them as prelate and shepherd.

No one was found throughout the vast extent of the City who did not desire from the depths of his being that Adrian be promoted to this height, except anyone who wished either himself or one of his own to be advanced.

The nobles, although they appeared divided in body into two parties, nevertheless burned with one mind and equal ardor toward him. The cause of their division was nothing other than their excessive affection for so great a man: each party was so eager that he be preferred to it that, if one party chose him, the other would be utterly at a loss; nor was the other party willing to hold back, except because it supposed that the former was directing its votes toward someone else.

This was especially so because many monks, most religious priests, and faithful laymen, through visions sent from heaven, had for a long time not merely suspected but openly proclaimed that Adrian would become pontiff. Among them, some saw Adrian reclining in the apostolic see with the pallium spread over his shoulders; others saw him celebrating Mass with the apostolic insignia; some saw him distributing gold in the Lateran basilica in the apostolic manner; and many had seen him seated upon the horse used by the most holy Pope Nicholas when he went to Saint Peter, clothed in the pontifical pallium, returning to the City before the nobles and followed by the remaining crowds and entering the patriarchium.

But when it became clear through evident signs that both parties were directing themselves toward this same man, such unity of minds and bodies came upon them that everyone seemed to possess one heart and one spirit toward the same priest of the Lord. Thus, with due reverence for Jesus Christ our Lord, he could in a certain way be called the cornerstone, because by his appearance—indeed, by his coming—he dissolved the enmities of their hearts and made the two parties one.

When all had therefore gathered, both the bishops with the entire clergy and the leading men of the City with the peoples obeying them, Adrian was seized and dragged from the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, which is called at the Praesepe, and was carried in eager competition to the Lateran patriarchium by the multitude of nobles and people.

When the envoys of the prince heard this, they took it badly, indignant—not because they did not want so great a man as pontiff, for they eagerly desired him, but because, while they were present, the Romans had not invited them as citizens, nor allowed them to take part in the election of the future prelate whom they themselves desired.

When they received the explanation that this had been omitted not out of contempt for the Augustus but entirely with a view to the future—namely, lest the practice of waiting for the envoys of princes in the election of Roman prelates should take root through such encouragement—they entirely calmed the indignation of their minds and themselves approached humbly to greet the elected man.

### 615

When they went up and down through the Lateran patriarchium, they were surrounded by such great shouts from the entire people, who cried out that the man long desired by them should be given for consecration, that none of them could hear the words of his companion speaking beside him.

It was indeed possible to see each individual possessing such powerful love for the pontiff who was to be consecrated as no one could have thought he had ever seen or would ever see. Finally, all of them eagerly strove before those same legates to seize him, drag him forward to the summit of the pontificate, and carry him away, until they were somewhat calmed by the senators’ conciliatory words and counsels.

When the most Christian emperor Louis heard of the desire of all these people and learned that they had confirmed their decision by their subscriptions, he rejoiced greatly. He desired from the depths of his heart that so great a servant of the Lord, desired and desirable to all peoples—Romans and foreigners alike—should be placed over the Christian people.

He immediately wrote an imperial letter praising all the Romans for having chosen a prelate worthy of so great an office. Through that letter it became known that no reward of any kind was to be promised to anyone on account of his consecration, since the emperor himself ardently desired it to take place, moved not by the suggestion of his own men but rather by the unanimity of the Romans. Above all, he declared that he loved what had been taken away to be restored to the Roman Church, not taken away from it, and that nothing should be lost.

Therefore, after prayers, vigils, and almsgiving had been properly completed on Saturday, the same venerable priest was led on Sunday, according to custom, by the whole assembly to the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. This took place on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first indiction and the nineteenth year of the aforementioned Augustus. Through the most reverend bishops—Peter of Gabii, Leo of Silva Candida, and, third, Donatus of Ostia, since the bishop of Albano had died, while Formosus of Porto had been sent by the most blessed Nicholas to preach and instruct the Bulgarians—he was found worthy to receive, in the Lord’s name, the blessing of the supreme pontificate, for the consolation of the many sons of holy God’s Church who, while the tyranny of factions raged more freely than usual, were driven into various exiles and afflicted with various hardships between the departure of one pontiff and the substitution of another.

### 616

At the celebration of his Mass there was such an extraordinary multitude, all striving to receive communion from his hand, that Theutgaudus, archbishop of Trier, and Zacharias, bishop of Anagni—because they had been stripped of the priesthood by Lord Nicholas and had also been deprived of communion—together with Anastasius, who had formerly been stripped of the presbyterate by the pontiffs Leo and Benedict and had been accustomed to receive communion among the laity, received ecclesiastical communion after making appropriate satisfaction.

He then immediately returned to the Lateran patriarchium and abolished a custom by which the prices of various gifts brought from different places were collected, retaining only what was sufficient for the needs of the tables. He said:

“It is not pious to sell for a price what we receive freely, or to value irrational coins more highly than rational brothers, for whom Christ’s precious blood was shed. Rather, I beg you, let these shameful commercial exchanges of prices be held cheap; let us give freely what we have received freely, according to the Lord’s command, and let us share Christ’s offerings with his guests and the poor, for whose sake we know that these things have been divinely granted to us.”

Immediately he also sent the bishops Dominic and Grimoald, whom his predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, had ordered to go to their native Bulgaria and had released from his service at the very moment of his departure. Since they had delayed going when they saw the death of so great a Father, he sent them to carry out the same embassy. He ordered that certain letters which Nicholas had selected for dispatch be issued under his own name, thereby showing that he shared the same will and zeal. As far as the storm of troubled times permitted, the pious heir fulfilled the devout Father’s desire.

### 617

After these men had been dismissed from the City, he immediately took care to recall the exiles—namely, Gauderinus, bishop of Velletri, Stephen, bishop of Nepi, and John, surnamed Hymmonides—whom the most shameless falsehood, accusing them before the serene Augustus, had banished from their homes and fatherland. He said that he could not appear to be a good shepherd of God’s Church unless he received back the sheep whom an unfaithful man had proscribed through his deceit from the faithful holy Church.

The Augustus was gladdened by this religious appeal and, together with his most Christian wife, not only honorably sent back to the City those for whom the supreme pontiff had sent, but also ordered that all whom anyone had imprisoned in dungeons as guilty of a private quarrel and treason against imperial majesty should be released and allowed to return.

### 618

After this, the supreme pontiff adorned the basilica of Saint Nicholas with various paintings, as his predecessor had desired. The most holy Pope Nicholas had built it from its foundations with such magnificence, together with three constructed aqueducts, that it surpassed all the Lateran basilicas in beauty.

Adrian followed the example of Nicholas’s conduct so diligently that the enemies of Saint Nicholas, who were striving in every way to undermine all his deeds, began to write and publicly call him “Nicolaitan.”

Because he recognized that some of those enemies, conceiving injustice, were about to give birth to the pain they had conceived, he retained them near him, as it were tares among the wheat, in a stewardly manner until the time of maturity. A false rumor therefore arose and was believed: that he wished to undermine all the acts of his predecessor, which Nicholas had established out of divine zeal but which his enemies were defaming according to their own desires.

### 619

As a result, all the bishops of the western regions sent solemn and honorable letters, continually urging the supreme pontiff to honor the religious memory of Adrian as a pontiff of orthodox and true philosophy.
