When, for several days, certain Greeks and servants of God from other peoples who were then living in Rome had secretly withdrawn from the company of this most holy Pope Adrian, on the Friday of Septuagesima this most holy bishop summoned them, according to custom, for refreshment, in greater numbers than usual.

With his own hands he humbly poured water over the hands of all of them, set out food, and served drinks. Moreover, something no pontiff before him was known to have done, he reclined at table with them in order to make them more ready for the meal, while spiritual songs continually rang out with praise throughout the entire time.

### 620

When he had risen from the meal, he fell on his face before everyone and said:

“I ask and humbly entreat you, fathers, brothers, and sons, to pour forth prayers to the Lord for his holy catholic Church. Pray for our most Christian son, Louis, emperor Augustus, that almighty God may make the nation of the Saracens subject to him for our perpetual peace.

“Pray also for me, frail and weak, that Christ may grant me such strength to govern the multitude of his Church in holiness and justice—he who entrusted to the blessed apostle Peter the governance of all whom he redeemed. For since, blinded by the dust of secular cares, I often perceive spiritual things less clearly, may your continual prayer, all the purer because it is farther removed from the world’s impurities, obtain divine assistance for me.”

When they cried out that the one who ought rather to pray for them was he, since he was more acceptable to God insofar as he alone labored more fervently for all, he was moved by inward compassion and said with tears:

“To pray for those who are very good, dearest ones, is to render thanks to God. I ask you, therefore, while holding in your prayers my lord, father, and predecessor, the most holy and orthodox Pope Nicholas, to offer common thanks to the Lord. In his compassion for his Church, God chose him and, like Joshua, armed him with the shield of protection and strengthened him with the sword of spiritual power, so that he might exclude the world’s most swollen uproars.”

**[Col. 1385]**
621. When all the servants of the Lord had heard this—namely, the men of Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, some of whom were serving as envoys of the rulers of the world—they were struck dumb with prolonged astonishment and burst into a loud acclamation, saying:

“Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, who has ordained that such a man should be placed over his Church; who knew that, keeping before his eyes the reverence due to his father and predecessor, he would pasture the Lord’s flock with rod and staff, and would not tear apart but fulfill the testament of the Fathers. Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, who has not placed an apostate pope upon the seat of his apostle; who laid the foundations of his house not upon sand but upon the firmest rock; who made you succeed the most holy Pope Nicholas and not depart from his decrees.

“Long live our lord Adrian, the supreme pontiff and universal pope, appointed by God!” This was said three times.

When he had signaled for silence with his hand, the supreme prelate intoned:

“Eternal memory to the most reverend, most holy, and orthodox lord Nicholas, the supreme pontiff and universal pope, appointed by God!” This was said three times.

“Perpetual life and unfading glory to the new Elijah!” This was said three times.

“Eternal salvation to the new Phinehas, deserving the insignia of the eternal priesthood!” This was said three times.

“Peace and grace to his followers!” This was said three times.

622. Thereupon Lambert, son of Vinton, duke of Spoleto, entered the city of Rome at the time of the consecration of this venerable pontiff, contrary to custom and like a tyrant. Treating it as though it had not rebelled, he distributed the city among his satellites for plunder, sold the houses of the leading families for many gifts, and spared neither monasteries nor churches. Indeed, he allowed girls of the noblest families, both within and outside the City, to be indiscriminately seized by his satellites.

Because of these offenses, he was overwhelmed by complaints before the most devout Augusti of the Romans, lost his duchy, and incurred the anger of the princes and the hatred of almost all the Gauls, being judged in truth an enemy of the apostolic see. Soon the Roman pontiff, freed from so great a tyranny, deprived Aistaldus, Walter, Hilpianus, Odo, and Teopertus, together with all the other plunderers and robbers, of all ecclesiastical communion until they returned what they had stolen and made lawful satisfaction to him.

Teopertus, however, took care to restore what he had taken without much difficulty. Aistaldus, a man devoted to God and exceedingly brave in war, turned with complete humility toward the prelate who had struck him; accepting his favor after promising to satisfy every Roman demand, he also received hope of recovering communion. He would indeed have been able to regain it, had he not afterward become privy to the conspiracy of the Lamberts and, fleeing with excommunicated and rebellious men, preferred to make for Benevento.

623. When these matters had been settled, after Michael, emperor of the Greeks, had killed Bardas Caesar, his own supporter and, as they say, the plotter of his downfall, he adopted Basil as his colleague and made him emperor. Since the new emperor Basil was honored with the greatest devotion by the Catholics, as one who had always favored them, Michael was killed by his own eunuchs, whether with his son’s consent is uncertain.

As soon as Basil had assumed power, he first satisfied everyone, as reported, by explaining that he had not been party to Michael’s death. Then, in accordance with the ruling of the Roman Church, he expelled the usurper Photius and, with the support of the people, restored Ignatius as patriarch. From both sides—namely, from the patriarch Ignatius and from the neophyte Photius—he sent envoys to Rome through his spatharius Basil, so that, in the presence of the supreme bishop, they might contend in turn and, with justice supporting them, either justify Photius or condemn him forever.

But by divine judgment the sea swallowed Photius’ highly eloquent party, while it preserved the very simple party of Ignatius together with the imperial envoy. No one from the neophyte’s side escaped except a certain little monk named Methodius. Later, accepting neither Photius, on whose behalf he had come, nor Ignatius, against whom he had come, nor even the rights of the universal Church, to which he had come, he was summoned three times, branded three times for his treachery, and departed after being anathematized once.

624. Basil, the emperor’s envoy, and John, metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia, had been sent to Nicholas. Accordingly, when the most holy Pope Adrian was seated with the bishops and nobles in the secretariat of Saint Mary Major, according to the custom of the apostolic see, they presented themselves before him with due humility and offered gifts and letters.

After these had been received, they returned many thanks to the holy Roman Church, through whose efforts the Church of Constantinople had risen cleansed from schism. Then, after innumerable praises, they said with one voice:

“Your most devoted son, the emperor Basil, and Ignatius, restored to the patriarchal office through your agency, after the Church of Constantinople had expelled the usurper Photius through your intervention, found in his archive a book heaped up with the greatest falsehood against the character of the holy Roman Church and of the most holy Pope Nicholas.

“They completely expelled it from their city, sealed as though it were truly contagious, and sent it to you as the supreme head, to whom Christ has granted power in heaven and on earth to loose and bind. We ask you to receive and examine it, and to observe from it the fraud which our slippery Photius was able to inflict upon the innocent people of Constantinople, when he sharpened his audacious tongue against this holy Roman Church, which has neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

“Publicly proclaim to everyone what the Church of God ought to think of this robbery, which he secretly fabricated under the name of a synod. If, with the pontiff’s consent, the assembly of both parties was able to bring forward a decision against the apostolic see and its pontiff—because Photius had no voice—it could perhaps hasten a sentence, but it could not weigh a judgment. He was, however, judged twice and condemned twice by the apostolic see.”

*[Col. 1387]*

625. And because he trusted in his own strength and did not fear to utter falsehoods against our most holy pontiff Nicholas, he plainly set his mouth against heaven and stretched out his tongue to pass over the earth. Therefore we admit the book of his little council for examination, so that its author, fabricator of falsehood, and inventor of perverse doctrines may be judged for a third time.

The metropolitan came out, presented the book, and hurled it to the ground, cursing it and saying:

“You, accursed at Constantinople, be accursed again at Rome. You were fashioned by Photius, the minister of the devil, the new Simon, compiler of falsehood. You were crushed by Nicholas, the minister of Christ, the new Peter, lover of truth.”

And the spatharius, striking the book with his heel and with his sword, nevertheless said:

“I believe that the devil dwells in this little work, because through the mouth of his accomplice Photius it belches forth what he cannot say himself. For it also falsely contains the subscription of our emperor Basil after that of Michael, whom he persuaded to subscribe at night while exceedingly drunk. The restoration of Ignatius declared that it was not Michael’s, and our satisfaction, if it pleases you, confirmed this by oath.

“For the name of Basil, who has always been a Catholic, could not have been falsely inserted into his deadly inventions by one who, by changing the script, was able to write the names of many absent bishops together with those of his few accomplices. The entire body of those bishops is as free from this subscription as it is ignorant of its contents.

“Indeed, when that little council was supposedly assembled—because in truth it never was—none of the people of Constantinople recognized it. But because provincials from the surrounding regions ascend to Constantinople, as to the imperial city, for various affairs, the most obstinate Photius smeared his falsehood with the medicine of truth, as he had been trained to do from the beginning.”

626. Since he made the citizens of certain most holy bishops subscribe in place of those bishops—though, as common report has it, they were deserters blinded by gifts—it is for this reason that the scripts of the subscriptions appear different. Some wrote with a sharper pen, some with a broad one, and others, pretending to be decrepit, wrote with a thicker hand, staining the parchment, so that through the fraud of those present the simplicity of the absent might be mocked; and so that the whole body might more easily believe that what falsehood had made different through dissimilar letters was genuine.

But you will immediately see the scripts when you compare the dissimilarity of the subscriptions. You will not recognize the fraud, however, unless you send to Constantinople, as that entire Church begs you to do.

Then the supreme pontiff ordered men skilled in both languages to examine the book for several days and to have everything contained in it faithfully made public before the synod. The synod diligently investigated all of it everywhere.

627. For the venerable pontiff, with the support of the entire senatorial and popular assembly, convened a sacred council at the blessed apostle Peter’s in defense of his Church and of his predecessor.

First, after the truth had been clearly heard from the envoys of Constantinople, he read the letters of his predecessor concerning this matter and cleared his predecessor’s sullied reputation. Then he struck Photius, his little council, and his accomplices with a third anathema.

Finally, after the matter had been strengthened by the subscriptions and judgments of the others, he removed the book of the wicked doctrine from before the steps of the doors, where it had been trampled under everyone’s feet. A pyre received it as fuel for the fire and consumed it almost before it could be thought half-burned, with a great stench and a pitch-black color.

Although naturally the fire ought to have been extinguished by the downpour of rain, its flame grew stronger against the rain as though against drops of oil. At this, the astonishment of the miracle dissolved the hearts of both Latins and Greeks into praises of God and of the most holy Pope Nicholas, as well as of Adrian, the supreme pontiff.

Afterward, in accordance with his predecessor’s instructions, he sent Donatus, bishop of Ostia, and Marinus, a deacon, to Constantinople with his predecessor’s letters; then he sent the same letters, bearing only his own name, together with a memorandum. He also associated with them Stephen, bishop of Nepi, and ordered them diligently to suppress every scandal in the Church of Constantinople and to restore to their own churches those ordained by Methodius and Ignatius, once they had given the satisfaction of the written statement they had received from the archive.

They were also to admit the Photian clergy to communion under the same, though stricter, satisfaction, but to defer the judgment of the priests until the sentence of the apostolic see, while the judgment of the most holy Pope Nicholas remained in force.

Thus, after penetrating the laborious circuits of many winding routes, they finally reached Thessalonica, with Christ as their guide. There the emperor Basil sent Eustathius, the candidate-spatharius, to meet the holy Roman envoys with the duty of conveying his greetings.

628. Conducting them with great honor along the successive stages of their journey, they reached Selymbria. There they were received by Sisinnius, the imperial protospatharius, and Theognistus, the patriarchal eugumenus, who had been a diligent intercessor at Rome before the most holy Pope Nicholas for the restoration of Ignatius. They were provided with forty horses from the imperial stable, a complete silver service for the table, and officials to serve them at every wish.

At the Round Castle, where there is a church of remarkable size dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist, they received lodging on Saturday through imperial favor.

On Sunday, which was 15 September, in the third indiction, they mounted individual horses with golden saddles through the emperor’s devotion. Met by all the military schools—namely, the spatharii, candidates, strategoi, mandators, and the other palace orders—and by all the clerical orders wearing the planeta, they came to the Golden Gate.

There they were greeted by Paul, keeper of the books, Joseph, keeper of the vessels, and Basil the treasurer, all dressed in ecclesiastical garments. […] They were solemnly preceded by the patriarch of Constantinople and followed by the entire people with candles and lamps.

Thus descending to the palace of Irene, they were honorably received in the house called the Great Golden Hall by John the secretary, the candidate-spatharius, and Strategius the candidate-spatharius, who had been appointed to attend them. Through these men they received imperial messages, which certainly suggested most devotedly that they should not take offense at being unable to be received on the following day, since the emperor’s birthday celebration was imminent.

After that celebration had been happily completed, the emperor sent all the palace orders to meet them. With these preceding them, they approached the emperor in the Chrysotriklinos, where he immediately rose to greet them. They offered him the apostolic letters, which the emperor himself received and kissed.

He carefully asked about the condition of the Roman Church, the health of the lord Adrian, the supreme pontiff, and the whole order of the clergy and senators. After affectionately kissing the envoys, he dismissed them to convey the apostolic command to Patriarch Ignatius.

*[Note: [Col. 1389] “He dismissed,” that is, “he sent away.”]*

They returned to the emperor on the following day, and he addressed them as follows:

“The holy Roman Church, the holy mother of all the Churches of God, by the faithful care of the most holy lord Nicholas, universal pope—as can be clearly understood from his letters, by whose authority our present father Ignatius, who had been violently expelled by the Photians, has recently, with the Lord’s help, been restored to his proper see—has cared for the holy Constantinopolitan Church, torn apart by the various waves of schism through the ambition of the most obstinate Photius.”

629. “Therefore, together with all the Eastern patriarchs, metropolitans, and bishops, after awaiting for two years the judgment of our holy mother, the Roman Church, we ask for God’s sake that God’s business be carried out manfully and that, at last, by the authority of your sacred college, the scandals of the pestilential Photian evasion be driven away, so that the desired unity and tranquility may be restored, as the most holy Pope Nicholas decreed.”

*[Note: [Col. 1389] This was the eighth ecumenical synod.]*

The envoys of the holy apostolic see replied:

“That is why we have come; that is why we were sent. But we can never admit any of your Easterners into our synod unless, after presenting a written statement whose form we have taken from the archive of the holy apostolic see, they have given us satisfaction.”

The emperor and the patriarch said:

“Since you assert that this requirement of presenting a written statement is new and unheard of, it is necessary for us to see its form and wording.”

Without delay, the form of the written statement was produced and, translated from Latin into Greek, was explained for everyone’s information. Some of them presented their statements and took their seats in the holy synod; those who refused to present them outside the synod were left without honor. But, day by day, tempered by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, they returned to the unity of the sacred synod after first providing the required statement of satisfaction.

Photius, that usurper, was brought into the synod to give an account of the many crimes he had committed. All the letters of the holy Roman Church against him were read. The sentence of deposition and anathema previously issued against him by the apostolic see was repeatedly hurled at him by all. In his presence, the profaned volumes of the wicked little council—those in which he had barked in a whispering voice against the most holy Pope Nicholas—were burned in the fire, and the lamp of truth and innocence shone forth.

He entered upon the noose he had once prepared for another, now glorified, and by the power of reason was reduced to the utmost helpless silence. The door of communion had been opened to him, and he had been instructed that he would be received after giving the required written satisfaction; yet, like a blind man at noon, he turned away from it.

Finally, after everything had been beneficially completed—the record of which comprises the text of the synod’s ten sessions—the envoys of the holy Roman Church entrusted the synod’s text to Anastasius, librarian of the holy apostolic see, for careful examination, lest Greek frivolity had inserted anything false against it, before they subscribed to it.

Anastasius, who was most eloquent in both languages, examined it with the greatest diligence. They found that everything which the most holy lord Pope Adrian had added, in praise of our serene Augustus Caesar, to the letter of his predecessor concerning the impending arrival of Bishop Arsenius had been excised.

630. Therefore they complained with the loudest cries that the letter of the apostolic see had been fraudulently mutilated, declaring that they would in no way subscribe to the synodal acts unless the integrity of the entire letter were joined to the synodal record.

While the Romans were contending in this way, the Greeks replied in a loud voice that the synod should deal not with the praise of the emperor but with God alone, and they showed utter hostility toward the imperial title of our Caesar.

At last the matter reached this point: after the condition of the apostolic will had been inserted, they subscribed to the defined judgments in a less than definitive manner, reading as follows:

“I, acting as the representative of my lord Adrian, the most holy and universal pope, presiding in this holy synod, have consented to everything, as it is written above, until the will of that eminent prelate, and I have subscribed with my own hand.”

631. After these matters had been completed, certain Greeks approached the emperor and tearfully complained that the Church of Constantinople had been brought under Roman control through the written statements that had been presented. They admitted that, because of uncertainty about the subscriptions, everything decreed in the synod had to be reconsidered and all the remaining errors confused; they pretended that they could not recover their former freedom unless the statements were returned to them.

At once certain statements were withheld by the custodians, since the envoys of the holy Roman Church, foreseeing what was to come, had entirely removed the statements of the more distinguished bishops. Consequently, those men, incredibly dismayed, relied upon the faithful assistance of Suppo, the archminister, and Anastasius, the most eloquent librarian of the apostolic see.

While they pressed the matter in different ways, not without great danger and exertion,

*[Note: [Col. 1391] “Pressing,” that is, “persisting and urging.”]*

they finally managed, though only with difficulty, to recover the statements; but because of their excessive strictness they incurred the emperor’s fierce anger.

632. Accordingly, on the third day after the most sacred synod, together with its writings, had been wholly completed in a codex, revised with every refinement, in the Church of Holy Sophia, they were craftily summoned by the emperor to a house. There, together with the representatives of the patriarchs—those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—and with Patriarch Ignatius, who was seated there with some others, they were ordered to sit and heard that the princes of the Bulgarians had sent letters and gifts through Peter and others.

They accepted the embassy, especially because the emperor was present. After the greetings, Peter, the Bulgarian envoy, began:

“Lord Michael, prince of the Bulgarians, hearing that you had gathered from various regions by apostolic authority for the benefit of the holy Church of God, received this with gratitude. He gives many thanks to you, who have been sent from the apostolic see, because, as you passed through his country, you deigned to visit him with your letters.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“Because we know you to be sons of the holy Roman Church, we neither ought nor wished to pass you by without greeting you. The holy apostolic see embraces you as its own members.”

633. The Bulgarian envoys said:

“Until today we were pagans, and only recently have we approached the grace of Christianity. Therefore, lest we appear to be in error in any respect, we desire to learn from you, who represent the supreme patriarchs, to which Church we ought to be subject.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“To the holy Roman Church, to which you, Peter, together with the entire kingdom of your people, were surrendered by your senior to the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and from whose successor, the distinguished Pope Nicholas, you deserved to receive both rules of life and bishops and priests—to that Church you ought to have belonged and ought still to belong. This is also shown by the fact that you both accepted the priests we requested and have retained them until now with fitting reverence.”

*[Note: [Col. 1391] “Senior,” that is, “lord, king.”]*

The Bulgarian envoys said:

“We confess that we requested and received priests from the holy Roman Church and still possess them, and we resolve to obey it in all things. But determine with these representatives of the patriarchs whether we ought more reasonably to be subject to the Roman or to the Constantinopolitan Church.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“The matters concerning which the holy apostolic see had ordered us to determine with the Easterners, with the Lord’s help, we have determined. But since we received no mandate concerning your case, we neither determine anything nor think that anything should be determined to the prejudice of the holy Roman Church. Indeed, since your entire country is everywhere filled with our priests, we proclaim, so far as depends upon us, by a definitive judgment, that you ought to belong to no one except the holy Roman Church.”

634. The representatives of the Eastern patriarchs said to the Bulgarians:

“When you seized that country, to whose authority was it subject, and did it have Latin or Greek priests? Tell us.”

The Bulgarian envoys said:

“We conquered that country by force of arms from the authority of the Greeks, and there we found not Latin but Greek priests.”

The Eastern representatives replied:

“If you found Greek priests there, it is clear that the country belonged to Constantinople by virtue of ordination.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“You ought not to derive an argument from the Greek priests, because diversity of languages does not confuse the ecclesiastical order. For although the apostolic see itself is Latin, nevertheless, in many places, according to the custom of the country, it has always appointed and continues to appoint Greek priests; it neither should nor ought to regard this as a diminution of its privilege.”

635. The representatives of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“Even if you prove that the ordination of Greek presbyters belonged to your jurisdiction, you will never be able to deny that the country belonged to the Greek kingdom.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“Just as we do not speak falsely when we say that the ordination of Bulgaria belongs to us in another manner, so we certainly do not deny that the same Bulgaria was once part of the Greek kingdom.”

*[Note: [Col. 1391] Not by the law of kingdoms, but by that of sees.]*

“But you ought to understand that the rights of sees arrange one thing, while divisions of kingdoms permit another. We are not speaking about the division of kingdoms but about the rights of sees.”

636. The representatives of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“We wish to learn what you mean when you say that Bulgaria belongs to you in another manner.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“The apostolic see, as you will be able to learn from the decretal letters of the most holy Roman prelates, canonically organized and possessed both Epirus—the New and the Old—together with all Thessaly and Dardania, in which the city of Dardania is still shown today, and whose country is now called Bulgaria by these Bulgarians.

“Accordingly, the apostolic see did not now take from the Church of Constantinople, as is alleged, the jurisdiction which it had formerly abandoned because of the incursion of the pagan Bulgarians; rather, it recovered that jurisdiction from these Bulgarians, now made Christians.”

“Second, since the Bulgarians, who subjected the country to themselves by the law of nations and have retained for so many years what they seized, have specially entrusted themselves to the patronage and ordination of the apostolic see, as we said above, they ought, and not unjustly, to be subject to us, since they voluntarily chose us as their teachers.

“Third, because the holy apostolic see, at the command of the most holy Pope Nicholas, formerly converted these same Bulgarians from various errors to the truth of the Catholic faith, with much labor and with the grace of Christ leading the way: both through several of our own number who are here and who dedicated many churches there and created priests, and through Paul, Dominic, Leopard, and Formosus, venerable bishops, as well as through our co-bishop Grimoald, whom these Bulgarians have admitted in our presence that they have retained until now, together with many of our priests.

“Behold, for more than three years the apostolic see has held, holds, organizes, and governs them. Therefore it does not follow that the Roman Church should be stripped, without the knowledge of the Roman supreme pontiff, of those things with which it is visibly endowed here and now.”

The representatives of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“Declare which of these methods you now wish to apply.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church replied:

“The holy apostolic see neither chooses you as judges in its own case, since you are in fact inferior parties, nor has it chosen you through us, since it alone has the special right to judge concerning the whole Church. Nor has it commissioned us to pronounce a judgment in this matter.

“Therefore, since we have received no instruction from it concerning what is to be done, we reserve the judgment of this case in its entirety for its own examination—for the one who, through the abundance of his books, is able to bring forward much in defense of his position. From that see your entire judgment is despised with as much ease as it is pronounced with lightness.”

637. The representatives of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“It is highly improper that you, who reject the empire of the Greeks and cling to alliances with the Franks, should preserve the rights of ordination in the kingdom of our prince.

“Therefore, since we have learned that the country of the Bulgarians formerly belonged to the authority of the Greeks and possessed Greek priests, we judge that it should now be restored through Christianity to the holy Church of Constantinople, from which it had withdrawn through paganism.”

The envoys of the holy Roman Church cried out:

“The judgment which you, though neither chosen nor admitted, have just now hastened rather than pronounced—whether through arrogance, favor, or whatever it may be—we wholly rescind by the authority of the Holy Spirit until the definitive judgment of the holy apostolic see, so that it may in no way deserve even to bear the name of a judgment.

“And we adjure you, Patriarch Ignatius, by the authority of the holy princes of the apostles, before God, all his angels, and all those present, to guard your diligence from every ordination in Bulgaria, in accordance with this letter of your most holy restorer, the lord Adrian, supreme pontiff, which we now offer you, and to send none of your men there.

“Let not the holy apostolic see, which restored your own position to you, appear through you to lose what belongs to it. Rather, if—which we do not believe—you think that you have a just complaint, do not fail solemnly to bring it before the holy Church that restored you.”

Then Patriarch Ignatius received the apostolic letter. Although, despite repeated urging, he had delayed reading it, he replied:

“Far be it from me to become entangled in these presumptions against the dignity of the holy apostolic see. I am neither so youthful that I can be deceived nor so senile that I rave, so as to omit myself what I ought to condemn in others.”

With this, that conversation came to an end.

638. Yet the imperial agitation, although it outwardly pretended to offer hope, increased. Nevertheless, summoning the envoys of the holy Roman Church to dinner, the emperor honored them with excellent gifts and entrusted them to Theodosius the spatharius for their conveyance, though not with the vigilance that was appropriate.

They were escorted as far as Acodyrcharium and then negligently dismissed without any provision. A few days later, while traveling by ship, they fell, alas, into the hands of the Slavs. They were stripped of all their possessions and of the authentic copy in which all the subscriptions had been recorded. They themselves would have been beheaded had their captors not feared those who had escaped from the group.

At length they were freed from exile by apostolic and imperial letters and returned to Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction. Before the most holy supreme pontiff and the nobles they reported everything we have related above.

They were able to show no other documents than the record of Ignatius’ proceedings, the statements they had received from the Slavs, and the remaining statements which they had earlier entrusted at Constantinople to Suppo, the archminister, and Anastasius, the most prudent librarian of the holy apostolic see. Through the latter’s foresight,

*[Note: [Col. 1393] Perhaps, “through the care of the present one.”]*

the Roman Church had obtained the copy of the lost synod which he had secured permission to have written.

639. Earlier, Formosus, bishop of Porto, and Paul, bishop of Populonia, venerable bishops who, together with the others, had been sent at the command of the most holy Pope Nicholas for the purpose of preaching, returned from the Christianization of the Bulgarians and from the complete submission by which they had specially bowed their devoted necks to the holy Roman Church. They refreshed the apostolic see and presented to the supreme pontiff an envoy of Michael, king of the Bulgarians, named Peter.

That envoy offered royal letters together with royal gifts, earnestly asking the supreme prelate either to send back Marinus, a deacon whom he knew well, consecrated as archbishop, or to send from among the cardinals a man of his own Church, outstanding in wisdom, character, and life, to be chosen as archbishop for the Bulgarians, whom, after their approval, he would later elevate to the archiepiscopal ministry upon his return.

But because Marinus had, as we said, been assigned as the Constantinopolitan envoy, the supreme pontiff sent the Bulgarians a certain Silvester to be chosen. When the Bulgarians sent back Silvester with Leopard of Ancona and Dominic, bishop of Tarvisium, together with letters concerning the archbishop—or earnestly asking that Bishop Formosus of Porto be returned—the pope received them with great speed.

Among other matters he wrote back that, whomever the royal devotion named expressly, the pontifical provision would undoubtedly supply to the Bulgarians as archbishop.

640. The king of the Bulgarians, however, unable to endure any longer the delays of his expectations, was drawn toward the emperor of the Greeks on account of the children of Theodora, who were plotting to seize the kingdoms from one another in turn. He sent the same Peter, whom he had received late from Rome without obtaining what he desired, together with others from his retinue, to Constantinople to inquire to whom Bulgaria ought principally to belong.

There our envoys proved that it belonged by right to the Romans. But afterward, having been persuaded by gifts and promises from the Easterners and the Constantinopolitans, they accepted Greek priests, as Grimoald, the bishop who admits that he had been rejected by them, records. They expelled our priests.

That same Bishop Grimoald, having abandoned without the knowledge of the apostolic see the office of preaching entrusted to him and returned to Rome exceedingly wealthy, sent to the apostolic see, in his own defense, a large volume of letters filled with frivolous allegations, as though under the pretext of a considered judgment, and involving the presidents of the synod.

In this affair, since the bishop asserts in his letter that he was expelled by the Bulgarians, while the presbyters say that they were not driven out by Greeks or Bulgarians but were deceived by the bishop, it certainly seems beyond doubt that there is an appearance of mutual treachery beneath it—

*[Note: [Col. 1395] The passage is corrupt.]*

until Christ, the examiner of reins and hearts, brings this to light in the examination of his servants.

*[Note: [Col. 1395] Some words seem to be missing.]*

*[Col. 1379]*

**CIX. JOHN VII, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 872.**

**CX. MARINUS, IN THE YEAR 882.**

**CXI. ADRIAN III, IN THE YEAR 884.**

**CXII. STEPHEN VI, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 885, THE SEVENTH YEAR OF CHARLES THE FAT, THE NINETEENTH OF THE EMPEROR BASIL.**

*[Note: [Col. 1403]*

From the Royal, Mazarine, and Thuane codices.

Number 641, line 1: before “Stephen” is prefixed “John VIII, Martin II, and Adrian III.” But these belong to another author. See the testimonies concerning Anastasius. Line 1: “from his father Adrian, from the Via Lata; he sat for six years and nine days, and the episcopate was vacant for five days.” In his time the Normans, joined by the Danes, devastated almost all Gaul. Because of fear of them, the body of blessed Martin of Tours was carried to Auxerre and placed in the church of Saint Germanus.

But when the monks quarreled over the offerings and attributed to their own saint the miracles that occurred, a leper was placed between Martins—Martin and Germanus—for the sake of settling the dispute. He was cured only on Martin’s side; the following night he returned and was cured on Germanus’s side—not because Germanus lacked power, but because he honored his guest.

Everything else is lacking. With this Stephen, the Mainz edition of Anastasius, published in 1602, comes to an end. In both codices there follow the Lives of other pontiffs, down to Martin V. But since it was assigned to us only to revise Anastasius and to provide an opportunity for a purer edition to those who have more leisure, we stop here and willingly leave this task to them to complete.

*[Col. 1405A]* From Penia, from the Cavensis codex.

Number 642, lines 14 and 15: “multitudine dom.” [“by a multitude of lords,” uncertain expansion].

Number 644, line 7: “facunditate.” Line 29: “orders,” the choirs of the saints, who carry the vows of the faithful and the priest’s prayers for the people to the ears of the Lord of hosts.

*[Col. 1406A]*

Number 646, line 16: “one witta” [a band or fillet].

Number 648, line 1: “the prelate [in] a silk delothera” [a garment; term uncertain]. Line 7: “the next was at hand.”

Number 649, lines 13 and 14: “eptaticum.”

Number 650, line 20: “a support to assist him”; lines 23 and 24: “he admonished concerning heaven.”]*

*[Col. 1397]*
641. Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Hadrian, from the district of the Via Lata, sat for four years, seven months, and fourteen days. This most blessed pontiff was born of a noble Roman family. As he grew by God’s grace, he was instructed in sacred doctrines through the zeal and care of Zachary, his most holy bishop, kinsman, and librarian of the Apostolic See. When the younger pontiff Hadrian of blessed memory saw that he excelled in good character and was ardent in literary studies, he took him from his illustrious father and, with God’s favor, advanced him to the rank of subdeacon. He appointed him among his other personal attendants, serving in the Lateran patriarchate, and after receiving this honor Stephen himself led an admirable life.

642. For he was chaste in body, benevolent in spirit, cheerful in countenance, prudent in speech, generous in wealth, eloquent in talent, a consoler of the sorrowful, and a nourisher of orphans and the poor; in short, he was adorned with the flowers of every virtue. Therefore this same most eminent prelate, persevering in the service of the holy Roman Church and devoting himself ever more intensely to particular responsibilities, became well known to Pope Marinus of revered memory and was beloved by his household; he was accordingly summoned especially to serve him. Since Marinus observed his chastity, prudence, and fidelity in every respect, he appointed him his chamberlain on account of the merit of his faith and prudence, and, recognizing his disciplined spiritual life, ordained him priest of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs. He did not permit him to be separated from him in any way during his lifetime.

After Pope Hadrian of memorable recollection, who had succeeded that most blessed Pope Marinus, had died, Stephen was at the river Scultiuna, in a village called Viulzachara. At that time the Roman citizens had suffered many hardships, both from devastation by locusts and from the barrenness caused by lack of rain, as well as from famine. Believing that they could be relieved through the holiness of this venerable man, a gathering was held by God’s mercy, consisting of the most holy bishops, the entire clerical order, the noble senates, and a company of distinguished men. With everyone acclaiming him, together with the whole people and a multitude of the common folk of both sexes, they said:

“We all desire, all seek, and all ask that the priest Stephen, worthy of God, preside over us as pontiff; for without doubt we believe that through his holiness we can be freed from the dangers threatening us.”

At that time the aforementioned pontiff Hadrian had left in Rome John, the venerable bishop of Ticinum, as the envoy of the excellent Emperor Charles for the protection of the City. All therefore joined with the imperial legate and came unanimously to the house where the benevolent Stephen was engaged with his father in holy conversation. Then, breaking down the doors, they seized and led the elected pontiff of God—who resisted vigorously—to the same title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs entrusted to him. His father and both groups acclaimed him, while he and his father declared themselves unworthy of so great an honor.

There all the schools of the holy Roman Church joyfully joined together and, dragging the venerable elect, brought him to the Lateran palace under Christ’s leadership, with every honor and due reverence. Before he reached the sacred palace, such an inundation of rain came down from heaven that, by its abundance, it restored the earth, which had long been dry. Thus, by an evident judgment, God showed that through the merits and prayers of so great and benevolent a man he wished to be reconciled to all the people.

When he had taken his seat in that palace, the nobles of both orders rejoiced and began to show him the fidelity due to him. On the following Sunday, the whole Roman Church honorably conveyed him to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 1399], where the consecrated pontiff celebrated the solemn Mass according to custom. Returning with due honor and reverence to the Lateran palace, he began to adorn his ministry with marvelous works.

643. Then, together with the venerable bishops, the Augustal legate, and the honorable senate, he went throughout the sacred palace’s treasury and vestiaries. He found them so thoroughly devastated that scarcely any of the sacred vessels with which the pontiffs were accustomed to have tables furnished on feast days could be found. Of the remaining wealth there was absolutely nothing. Indeed, when he found the treasures of the vestiaries stripped, he searched the shrines and found almost nothing of the many gifts and church ornaments.

Nevertheless, the famous golden cross which the patrician Belisarius had established in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, was still there, as were many golden altar hangings belonging to the most sacred altars, together with the other precious ornaments. For this reason the most blessed pope took care to investigate the matter before so many witnesses, so that everyone might know that no such thing had been attempted during his time.

644. He was therefore afflicted with deep grief, because when the vestiaries had been devastated, the granaries and storerooms were likewise found empty. He had nothing with which to distribute provisions to the clergy and the schools, nor anything from which to ransom captives or feed orphans and widows during the severe famine that was threatening. What was he to do?

He turned to the family estates possessed by his illustrious parents, took from them, and distributed to the poor with a generous hand as far as he could. Thus, by God’s mercy, it came about that through his efforts he alleviated the want caused by famine. Searching here and there for ministers and household members, he attached to his service men who excelled in holiness of life, sincerity of faith, instruction in wisdom, abundance of eloquence, and uprightness of character.

When he sat down to dine, he summoned orphans every day, whom he nourished as sons. When he summoned nobles and fed them with bodily food, he refreshed them with spiritual feasts. He bore such fear of God before the eyes of his mind and devoted himself so intensely to divine praises that a sacred reading was recited at his meal every day. He celebrated the solemnity of Mass daily, devoted himself to prayer by night and day, and never ceased from psalmody except when he wished to accomplish the duties of the people who appealed to him, in order to raise up the oppressed and assist the afflicted.

Observing the people’s insolence and the blindness of their hearts, occupied in the church with empty and wicked tales and idle conversations, and hearing that some, according to common report, used magical arts and incantations, he admonished the people while celebrating Mass with this address:

“We admonish your filial devotion, dearest ones, that when you gather in the most sacred temple of God, you diligently strive to attend to the purpose for which you have come. For if you truly believe that the place to which you gather is God’s temple, you ought undoubtedly to do there what pleases him whose temple it is and to which you have come. Although God is everywhere, he ought nevertheless to be sought especially in his temple; and whatever he deigns to inspire, whatever pleases him, ought there to be sought.

“God is merciful, yet he arranges to bestow his mercy on each person in such a way that he grants it to those who ask, not to the ungrateful; and he grants it to each person with the greater generosity of compassion the greater the sighs and the more ardent the spirit with which that person has implored it, as he himself says:

“‘Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much’ [Note: [Col. 1399] Luke 7:47].

“For the temple of God is a place of prayer, as he himself says elsewhere: ‘My house is a house of prayer for all nations’ [Note: [Col. 1399] Isaiah 56:7; Mark 11:17]. And the Psalmist says: ‘Holiness adorns your house, Lord’ [Note: [Col. 1399] Psalm 92].

“Indeed, if it is a house of prayer, one ought there to do what the name indicates: to pray, sing psalms, confess sins, wash away offenses with bitter tears of the eyes and sighs of the heart, and confidently implore pardon for the sins committed. There, especially, is the divine regard. Angelic orders stand there, interceding for the people; they carry our prayers to the ears of the Lord of hosts.

“With what face, I ask, does one stand in the most sacred temple of God who persists in empty tales and idle words? For if an account must be given on the day of judgment for every idle word [Note: [Col. 1399] Matthew 12:36], an account will especially be demanded and punishment exacted for those words that are obstinately uttered in the sight of so many saints, in a place dedicated to God. With what hope, I ask, does one think to obtain pardon for past sins who not only neglects to wash away his sins but rather strives to increase them? Fear him who, making a whip of cords, drove the sellers and buyers from the temple [Note: [Col. 1399] John 2:15]. It is surely more tolerable to engage profitably in business than to chatter meaninglessly and idly.

645. “When you gather in the place of prayer, stand in silence and beseech God with an attentive heart, so that he may accept the petitions of the priest who prays for you and hear his prayers. Keep before your eyes the Lord’s admonition when he says:

“‘When you stand at prayer, forgive whatever you have against another, so that your heavenly Father may also forgive you your sins’ [Note: [Col. 1399] Matthew 6:14].

“If you meditate on these things and, inspired by divine grace, put them into practice, instructed in evangelical and apostolic teachings, then, having obtained mercy from almighty God, illuminated by the lamps of good works, you will deserve to be presented with joy before Christ and crowned with the saints.

“Furthermore, dearest ones, we wish you to know that when the Lord was establishing his law for his people, with Moses as witness, he said: ‘You shall not allow a sorcerer to live’ [Note: [Col. 1401] Exodus 22:18].

“In this City, which I say with grief, there are some who not only do not attack sorcerers but rather protect and encourage them. Through them they do not shrink from consulting demons by means of certain incantations, forgetting the divine law and the teaching of the Apostle, which thunders:

“‘What partnership has light with darkness, or what fellowship has Christ with Belial?’ [Note: [Col. 1401] 2 Corinthians 6:14–15.]

“In this respect, by consulting demons in the manner of the gentiles while despising Christ, they confess that they are in no way Christians. Let each person consider how horrible and profane it is that a Christian should worship demons while despising Christ, so that he may recoil from committing such a crime.

“Therefore, whoever henceforth attempts to defile himself with such contamination, we judge, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, to be alienated from the life-giving body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until he repents of so great a disgrace. Whoever despises such salutary prohibitions and, persisting in the same deadly obstinacy, neglects to repent, let him be an eternal anathema from God the Father and Jesus Christ his Son.”

646. Since this outstanding prelate was such a man and persevered to the end in the things appropriate to divine worship, such grace was divinely granted to him that whatever he was able to possess he gave to the holy churches, and he ransomed captives. He was solicitous for the salvation of all, for when the fame of his name and deeds had spread through both the eastern and western regions, almost everyone hurried to him to receive his blessing.

It would take too long to recount among the other gifts that he bestowed on various churches. To mention a few of the many: when in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where he himself rests in his sacred body, he saw that incense was scarcely offered once during the nocturnal praises, he established that it should be burned at every reading and responsory.

In the pergola of that basilica, the reverend pope, out of love for blessed Peter, his nourisher, placed one golden cantharus, with precious pearls, gems, and enamel, together with its hanging weight. In the same venerable basilica of Saint Peter he offered one golden crown with various pearls, one sword with a golden scabbard, and one jeweled belt. He also presented in that basilica one garment decorated with gold and white gems; four silk hangings around the altar; and forty books of homilies by blessed Gregory.

In that same venerable basilica, the most holy pope, the vigorous eradicator of every vice, found the evil custom that the priests who offered sacrifice to the Lord there daily were accustomed to pay an annual fine. This custom had been broken by Pope Marinus of holy memory, his predecessor, but through the intrigues of certain men had revived during the time of Pope Hadrian III. Under solemn and forceful oath he ordered that no one should ever accept from them either this payment or any other tribute, but that they should be permitted to perform their office with every honor, as priests ought.

The same most sacred prelate, for his everlasting remembrance, observed that during the nocturnal vigils in the major church called Saint Mary, the holy and exalted Mother of God, at the Crèche, the customary lamps were lacking. He offered silver lamps with their lamp-bowls and ordered them to burn continually during the vigils.

The same most gentle pontiff also made in that basilica four hangings around the major altar: two of Byzantine purple silk (*sericum pigacium*), a third peacock-colored (*pavonatile*), and a fourth Alexandrian (*Alexandrinum*), all ornamented around the edge with *oloverum*.

647. Finally, the aforementioned most holy pope, protected by God, made in the church of blessed Paul, the apostle and teacher of the nations, for the redemption of his soul, one crown of the purest gold with various white, green, and hyacinth-colored gems. In the middle of the crown he placed one small golden cross hanging with its chains, and one silk garment above the main altar, decorated with gold and gems.

In the same basilica of the illustrious Teacher of the Nations he made four *belothera*, one of them woven with gold. The aforementioned venerable and renowned pontiff made in the church of the Lord Savior, called the Constantinian, one gold-woven garment for the main altar, with various pearls.

648. Likewise, in the same basilica the aforementioned most reverend prelate presented four silk hangings of Byzantine purple (*blatthin byzantea*) around the main altar, two of them eagle-patterned (*aquilata*) and two basilisk-patterned (*basilisci*), ornamented around the edge with *oloverum*; and ninety lion-patterned silk hangings (*vel[a] leonata*) for each arch of the presbytery.

For the future remedy of his soul he presented there one gilded cantharus; one book of commentaries; one book of the Prophets; and two books of Deeds.

Since he was concerned for the condition of God’s churches, lest those that were already in ruins should collapse during his time, he rebuilt from the foundations the church of the blessed apostles James and Philip, which had been consumed by extreme old age and was close to ruin. He adorned it with a chalice and a gilded paten inscribed with his name in Greek and Latin letters. In addition, for his perpetual salvation he presented in the same basilica of the Apostles one linen curtain and three silk *velothera* around the altar.

For the oratory of Saint Thomas, situated in the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew beside the basilica of the Apostles, he made one garment.

That outstanding and most prudent pope, knowing that the basilica of the Four Crowned Martyrs, in which he exercised the priestly office, had little adornment, offered there, out of reverence and love for those same saints, a golden cross above the altar with gems and enamel, a hanging cloak for the crown, and two pairs of silver-clad candelabra.

Out of his great love for them, the same benevolent pope also presented there one gilded cantharus, one *salomon*, one golden crown with extremely precious gems, one garment with gold and white gems, one book of Sermons, one book of Deeds, and one book of the Gospels with the epistles.

This eminent prelate, led ever more strongly by divine zeal and moved by love for those same saints, had made in their basilica fifteen baskets of extraordinary beauty, worked from the purest silver and weighing thirty pounds altogether; he also gave one codex of blessed John Chrysostom.

649. The same benevolent pope made in the title of Saint Marcellus, martyr and pontiff, one silver basket weighing three pounds; one golden cross; twenty-six linen hangings; one linen curtain; one book of Histories; and twenty homilies of Saint Gregory.

He also sent to the church of the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, situated at Manturianum, one book of Kings and one silk garment for the altar.

The aforementioned most gentle pope made in the monastery at the Clivus Scauri one golden cross. Ever solicitous for all the churches, that most pious Father also presented in the monastery of Saint Sylvester on Mount Soracte one silver censer and one silver *cantulla*.

More and more inflamed by divine love, he made in the title of Saint Pudentiana one book of Sermons; and in the title of blessed Anastasia, one book of Sermons and Epistles, [with *stolarum*, uncertain].

In the church called Jerusalem, in the *susurrio*, he offered one book of Kings and Solomon. Keeping the reverence due to blessed Gregory, his predecessor, before the eyes of his heart, the same supreme pontiff gave in that blessed Gregory’s hospital, in the portico of the apostle Saint Peter, one book of the sermons of the saints.

He also gave one Heptateuch in the school of singers, formerly called the Orphanotrophium.

650. The same distinguished prelate and most vigorous preacher of the true faith restored to the church of Ravenna, for the remedy of his soul, twelve pounds of gold and … pounds of silver, which had been taken away through the intrigues of certain persons. Likewise, in the church of Imola he restored seven pounds of gold and … pounds of silver that had been taken away. He also returned to the church of Bologna one silver paten, keeping God before his eyes.

Indeed, for everlasting reward, through various cardinals he distributed relics of the saints among the different titular churches and, elsewhere, throughout various monasteries, where they shine with many miracles. He placed the greater part of them with due honor in the church called “at the Apostles.” Since that church had been consumed by age and was close to ruin, the same most holy pope rebuilt it from its foundations and adorned it with many gifts and ornaments.

His whole intention was always to do what was acceptable to God. When the plague of locusts, which in the time of his predecessor Hadrian had almost consumed the entire region, began to hatch in multiplied broods and had filled everything, the same most holy pope took pity on the afflicted people. First he announced that whoever caught a sextary of them and brought it to him would receive five or six denarii.

When the people heard this, they began to run here and there, catch the locusts, and bring them to the most merciful Father to be purchased. But when he was unable to destroy them by this method, he fled to the mercy of the Lord. He went to the oratory of blessed Gregory, where that saint’s bed is kept, beside the church of the prince of the apostles, and there gave himself to prayer with tears.

After praying for a long time, he rose, blessed water with his own hands, and ordered the mansionarii, saying:

“Take it and distribute it to each person, instructing them to go around their fields in the name of the Lord and sprinkle this water over the sown fields and vineyards, asking God for his aid and assistance.”

After this was done, such mercy from almighty God followed that wherever that water had been sprinkled, not a single locust remained.

When the neighboring people throughout the region heard this, they streamed into the City and begged that they too be helped. They cried out that the whole land was covered with locusts like dust. The most pious pope kindly admonished them that they ought to seek help from heaven against the scourge threatening them, and immediately, joyful … [lacuna].

What follows is missing.

## Appendix to the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 1405]

### Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from Blessed Peter to Saint Paul I, made public from the excellent manuscript of the most distinguished chapter of Verona

[Col. 1405B]

**Blessed Peter**, son of John, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, first sat in the episcopal see at Antioch for seven years, then at Rome for twenty-five years, two months, and three days. He lived during the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero, under whom he also suffered martyrdom.

He wrote two Epistles, which are called canonical, and the Gospel of Mark, because Mark was his hearer and his son through baptism. After the complete source of the four Gospels, which were confirmed at Peter’s inquiry, while one accords in Greek, another in Hebrew, and another in Latin [the text is grammatically uncertain].

He held three ordinations in December: seven deacons, ten priests, and three bishops. He was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the temple of Apollo, beside the place where he was crucified, near the Neronian palace, in the Vatican, in the territory on the Via Aurelia, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

### II. Linus

Linus, Italian by nationality, son of Herculanus, held office for twelve years, three months, and twelve days. He lived during the time of Nero, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio to the consulships of Capito and Rufinus. He was crowned with martyrdom.

By order of blessed Peter, he was buried in the Vatican on the ninth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 1405C].

### III. Cletus

Cletus, Roman by nationality, from the Vicus Patricius, son of Aemilianus, held office for seven years, one month, and twenty days. He lived during the times of Vespasian and Titus, from the consulship of Domitian and the ninth consulship of Vespasian to the consulships of Domitian XVII and Clement [Note: [Col. 1405D] Let someone more fortunate correct this].

He was crowned with martyrdom. By order of blessed Peter, in the month of December he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome. Most of all the pontiffs who followed celebrated their ordinations in December. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter in the Vatican on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

### IV. Clement

Clement, Roman by nationality, from the district of Mount Caelius, son of Faustinus, held office for eleven years and ten days. He lived during the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Tragalis and Italicus to the ninth consulship of Vespasian and Titus. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He assigned faithful notaries to the Church, so that each of them might diligently investigate the deeds of the martyrs throughout his own district [Col. 1405D]. He also wrote two Epistles.

He held two ordinations [Note: [Col. 1406D] Supply “two”]: ten priests, two deacons, and five bishops in various places [Col. 1406B]. He died a martyr during the time of Trajan. He was buried in Greece on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, and the episcopate was vacant for eleven days.

### V. Anacletus

Anacletus, Greek by nationality, from Athens, son of Antiochus, held office for twelve years, ten months, and seven days. He lived during the time of Domitian, from the tenth consulship of Domitian and Sabinus to the seventeenth consulship of Domitian and the consulship of Clement.

He built a memorial for blessed Peter and arranged a place where the bishops might be buried. He too was buried there on the Ides of July.

He held two ordinations: five priests, three deacons, and six bishops in various places. The episcopate was vacant for seventeen days.

### VI. Evaristus

Evaristus, Greek by nationality, an Antiochene, son of a Jew named Judas, from the city of Bethel, held office for seventeen years, seven months, and two days. He lived during the times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan, from the consulship of Valens and Vetus to the consulships of Gallus and Bradua. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He divided the titular churches in the city among the priests and ordained seven deacons to attend the bishop when he preached, for the sake of the style of truth [Col. 1406C].

He held three ordinations: seventeen priests, nine deacons, and fifteen bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. The episcopate was vacant for nineteen days.

### VII. Alexander

Alexander, Roman by nationality, son of Alexander, from the district of Caput Tauri, held office for twelve years, seven months, and two days. He lived during the time of Trajan, up to the consulships of Aelianus and Vetus.

He incorporated the Lord’s Passion into the priests’ preaching. He was crowned with martyrdom. He established that water for sprinkling should be blessed with salt.

He held three ordinations: six priests, two deacons, and five bishops. He was buried on the Via Nomentana, where he was beheaded, on the fifth day before the Nones of May. The episcopate was vacant for thirty days.

### VIII. Xystus

Xystus, Roman by nationality, son of Pastor, from the district of the Via Lata, held office for ten years, two months, and one day. He lived during the time of Hadrian, up to Verus and Anniculus. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He established that the sacred vessels should be touched only by ministers [Col. 1406D]. He also decreed that any bishop who had been devoted to the Roman Apostolic See, and who returned to his parish, should not be received unless he carried a formal letter of greeting from the Apostolic See [Col. 1407A] [Note: [Col. 1407D] Perhaps read “when he returned”].

He established that during the liturgy the priest should sing the hymn before the people: “Holy, holy, holy.”

He held three ordinations: eleven priests, three deacons, and three bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the seventh day before the Kalends of April. The episcopate was vacant for two months.

### IX. Telesphorus

Telesphorus, Greek by nationality, formerly a hermit, held office for eleven years, two months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Marcus.

He established that a fast of seven weeks should be observed for Easter. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He arranged that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ and that at the beginning of the Eucharistic sacrifice the angelic hymn should be sung: “Glory to God in the highest”—but only at night on the Nativity of the Lord.

He held four ordinations: twelve priests, eight deacons, and thirteen bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the fourth day before the Nones of January. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.

[Col. 1407B]

### X. Hyginus

Hyginus, Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher, from Athens, held office for ten years, three months, and seven days. He lived during the times of Verus and Marcus, from the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus to the consulships of Orfitus and Camerinus.

He organized the clergy, distributed the ranks, and held three ordinations: fifteen priests, five deacons, and six bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the third day before the Ides of January. The episcopate was vacant for three days.

### XI. Anicetus

Anicetus, Syrian by nationality, son of John, from the village of Amisa, held office for nine years and three months. He lived during the times of Severus and Marcus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to the consulships of Praesens and Rufinus.

He established that the clergy should not grow their hair long. He held five ordinations: eight priests, four deacons, and nine bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.

### XII. Pius

Pius, Italian by nationality, son of Rufinus, brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquileia, held office for fifteen years, four months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus.

During his episcopate [Col. 1407C], Hermes wrote a book containing the command that the angel of the Lord gave him when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd. He commanded that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.

He established that a heretic coming from the Jews should be received and baptized. He held five ordinations: nineteen priests, twenty-two deacons, and twelve bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the fifth day before the Ides of July. The episcopate was vacant for fourteen days.

### XIII. Soter

Soter, Campanian by nationality, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, held office for eight years, two months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the time of Severus, from the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus to the consulships of Cethegus and Clarus.

He established that no monk should touch consecrated *pallae* [Note: [Col. 1407D] Read “consecrated *pallas*”], nor place incense inside the church.

He held three ordinations: nineteen priests, nine deacons, and eleven bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate was vacant for eleven days.

### XIV. Eleutherius

Eleutherius, Greek by nationality, son of Abundius, from the town of Nicopolis, held office for fifteen years, three months, and two days [Col. 1407D]. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Commodus, up to the consulships of Paternus and Bradua.

He received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he become a Christian through his command. He established that Christians, especially the faithful, should reject no ordinary food that God had created, provided that they are rational [the transmitted wording is uncertain].

He held three ordinations: twelve priests, eight deacons, and fifteen bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the ninth day before the Kalends of June. The episcopate was vacant for sixteen days.

### XV. Victor

Victor, African by nationality, son of Felix, held office for fifteen years, three months, and ten days. He lived during the time of Caesar Augustus, from the second consulship of Commodus and the consulship of Glabrio to the consulships of Lateranus and Rufinus.

He established that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as Eleutherius had also done. He organized the successive clergy. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He also established that, in case of necessity, if water were found in a river, sea, or spring, any person coming from paganism should be baptized, provided that Christian belief had been declared.

He held a council concerning Easter, or concerning the first day, with Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, regarding the moon.

He held two ordinations: four priests, six deacons, and twelve bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. The episcopate was vacant for twelve days.

### XVI. Zephyrinus

Zephyrinus, Roman by nationality, son of Abundius, held office for eighteen years, three months, and ten days. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Severus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Gallicanus to the consulships of Praesens and Stricato.

He established that, in the presence of all the faithful clergy and laity, whether deacon or priest, ordination should be performed.

He also issued a regulation concerning the church: that glass patens should be placed before the priests in the church, with ministers carrying them above, while the bishop celebrated Mass before him, with all the priests standing nearby [Note: [Col. 1407D] Read: “that the patens … should be in the church, with ministers supporting them” [Col. 1408D]. “While,” etc. And below, read *adstarent*; shortly afterward, for *inter*, read *interest*, and supply *quod ante ex ea*].

Thus Masses were to be celebrated, except that the clergy alone would exercise the bishop’s right in this matter. With everyone present, from that consecration the priest would receive from the bishop the already consecrated crown, which he was to hand on to the people.

He held four ordinations: fourteen priests, eight deacons, and thirteen bishops. He was buried in the cemetery beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

### XVII. Callistus

Callistus, Roman by nationality, son of Domitius, from the district of the city of the Ravennates, held office for five years, eleven months, and ten days. He lived during the times of Marinus and Theodolus Obillus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Alexander. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He established that a fast should be held three times a year on Saturday, of grain, wine, and oil, according to the prophecy of the fourth, seventh, and tenth [months].

He built a basilica across the Tiber and the cemetery on the Via Appia called Callistus. He was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, on the day before the Ides of October.

He held five ordinations: sixteen priests, four deacons, and eight bishops. The episcopate was vacant for sixteen days.

[Col. 1408C]

### XVIII. Urban

Urban, Roman by nationality, son of Pontianus, held office for nine years, one month, and two days.

He established sacred silver vessels and placed twenty-five silver patens. He was also a renowned confessor during the time of Diocletian. He converted many to baptism, including Valerian, the bridegroom of Saint Cecilia.

He held five ordinations: nineteen priests, seven deacons, and eight bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. The episcopate was vacant for thirty days.

### XIX. Pontian

Pontian, Roman by nationality, son of Calpurnius, held office for five years, two months, and twenty-two days. He was crowned with martyrdom.

He lived during the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelinianus. At that time the bishop Pontian and the priest Hippolytus were deported by Alexander into exile on the island of Sardinia, called Bucina, during the consulship of Severus and Quintianus. There Pontian, weakened by beatings with clubs, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

He held two ordinations: six priests, five deacons, and seven bishops [Col. 1408D]. Blessed Fabian brought him back and buried him in the cemetery of the Catacombs. The episcopate was vacant for ten days.

### XX. Anterus

Anterus, Greek by nationality, son of Romulus, held office for twelve years, one month, and nineteen days. He was crowned with martyrdom during the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus.

He collected the deeds of the martyrs and deposited them in the church. Because of a certain priest named Maximus, he was made a martyr. He ordained one bishop in the Campanian city of Fundi.

He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the third day before the Nones of January. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.

### XXI. Fabian

Fabian, Roman by nationality, son of Fabius, held office for thirteen years, one month, and ten days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived during the times of Maximus and Africanus up to the second consulship of Decius and Quadratus [Col. 1409A].

He divided the regions among the deacons and appointed seven subdeacons to supervise the seven notaries, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs faithfully and successfully. He also ordered that many structures be built throughout the cemeteries.

He held five ordinations: twenty-two priests, eight deacons, and thirteen bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.

### XXII. CORNELIUS

Cornelius, a Roman by nationality, held office for 2 years, 3 months, and 10 days. He was crowned with martyrdom. During his episcopate, Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church and, in Africa, Nicostratus [Note: Supply “ordained”]. After this, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius together with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned as faithful members to the Church.

Afterward, Bishop Cornelius was driven into exile at Centumcellae. There he received from Cyprian a letter written concerning the confirmation of his martyrdom, which Cyprian had composed while in prison, and also concerning the reader Celerinus. During his episcopate, at the request of a certain matron, he secretly removed the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul from the Catacombs. First, the body of blessed Paul, once recovered, was placed by blessed Lucina on her estate on the Ostian Way, near the place where he had been beheaded. Bishop Cornelius received the body of blessed Peter and placed it near the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of holy bishops, in the Temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican, at the site of Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

He conducted one ordination: eight presbyters. After this, he traveled secretly to Centumcellae. At that time Decius learned that he had received a letter from blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. He ordered Cornelius to leave Centumcellae and commanded that he be brought before him at night, saying to him:

“Have you decided that you should neither regard the gods, nor the commands of your ancestors, nor fear our threats, so that you accept and send letters against the commonwealth?”

Cornelius replied: “I received letters concerning the Lord’s crown, not against the commonwealth.”

Then Decius ordered that his mouth be beaten with leaded clubs and that he be led to the temple of Mars to worship, or else be beheaded. This was done. Blessed Lucina buried his body near the cemetery of Callistus, on her estate, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October. His episcopate remained vacant for 66 days.

### XXIII. LUCIUS

Lucius, a Roman by nationality, son of Porphyrius, held office for 3 years, 8 months, and 10 days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Gallus and Volusian, up to the third consulship of Valerian and Gallicanus. By God’s will he returned unharmed from exile to the Church.

He ordered that in every place two presbyters and three deacons should remain with the bishop for the sake of testimony. Valerian beheaded him on the fourth day before the Nones of March. As he was proceeding to his passion, he entrusted authority to Stephen, the archdeacon of his Church.

He conducted two ordinations: four presbyters, seven deacons, and seven bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. His episcopate remained vacant for 35 days.

### XXIV. STEPHANUS

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Jobius, held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 5 days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Gallicanus and Maximus, up to the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallicanus.

He decreed that priests and Levites should not use sacred vestments in daily life except in the church. He conducted two ordinations: six presbyters, five deacons, and two bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. His episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

### XXV. XYSTUS

Xystus, a Roman by nationality, formerly a philosopher, held office for 1 year, 10 months, and 22 days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Valerian, from the second consulship of Maximus and Glabrio up to the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. At that time there was a great persecution under Decius. Four days after the passion of the same blessed Xystus, his archdeacon Laurence suffered martyrdom.

He conducted two ordinations: four presbyters, seven deacons, and two bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. His episcopate remained vacant for 2 years.

### XXVI. DIONYSIUS

Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose parentage is unknown, held office for 8 years, 5 months, and 4 days.
