He lived in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus.

He divided churches and cemeteries among the presbyters and established parishes and dioceses. He ordained seven bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. His episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

### XXVII. FELIX

Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantius, held office for 4 years, 1 month, and 25 days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Claudius and Paternus up to the third consulship of Aurelian and the consulship of Capitolinus.

He decreed that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of martyrs. He conducted two ordinations: eight presbyters, three deacons, and eleven bishops. He too was buried in his own cemetery on the Aurelian Way, on the third day before the Kalends of June. His episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

### XXVIII. EUTYCHIANUS

Eutychianus, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Marinus, from the city of Luna, held office for 1 year, 1 month, and 2 days. He lived in the time of Aurelian, from the third consulship of Aurelian and Marcellinus until the Ides of December, in the consulship of Carus for the second time and Marinus.

He decreed that among the fruits offered upon the altar only beans and grapes should be blessed. During his episcopate he personally buried 342 martyrs in various places. He conducted five ordinations: fourteen presbyters, six deacons, and nine bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. His episcopate remained vacant for 8 days.

### XXIX. GAIUS

Gaius, a Dalmatian by nationality, of the family of the emperor Diocletian and son of Gaius, held office for 11 years, 4 months, and 9 days. He lived in the time of Carus and Carinus, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, beginning with the second consulship of Carus and Carinus, until the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth consulship of Diocletian and the second of Constantius.

He decreed that if anyone were deemed worthy to become a bishop, he should ascend gradually from the doorkeeper through each rank to the higher offices. He divided the regions among the deacons. Fleeing the persecution of Diocletian and living in the crypts, he rested as a confessor.

He conducted four ordinations: sixteen presbyters, nine deacons, and six bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. His episcopate remained vacant for 11 days.

### XXX. MARCELLINUS

Marcellinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, held office for 8 years, 2 months, and 16 days. He lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, from the tenth day before the Kalends of July, beginning with the consulship of Diocletian and Constantius for the second time, until the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian.

At that time there was a great persecution, so that within 30 days 17,000 people were crowned with martyrdom. In connection with this, Marcellinus himself was led to sacrifice in order to burn incense; and he did so. A few days later, moved to repentance, he was beheaded by the same Diocletian. His body lay in the street together with those of other martyrs for 26 days, as an example to Christians.

Then the presbyter Marcellus secretly collected the bodies and buried them on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. He conducted two ordinations: four presbyters, two deacons, and five bishops. His episcopate remained vacant for 7 years, 6 months, and 25 days, while Diocletian was persecuting the Christians.

### XXXI. MARCELLUS

Marcellus, a Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, held office for 5 years, 7 months, and 21 days. He lived in the time of Maxentius, from the fourth consulship of Maxentius and Maximus until after that consulship.

He established the cemetery on the Salarian Way and set up 25 titular churches in Rome, as if they were dioceses, for baptism, penance, and the burials of martyrs. He ordained 25 presbyters, 2 deacons, and 21 bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. His episcopate remained vacant for 21 days.

### XXXII. EUSEBIUS

Eusebius, a Greek by nationality and a physician, held office for 5 years, 1 month, and 3 days. He lived in the time of Constantine. At that time the Lord’s cross was discovered. He found heretics in Rome.

He conducted three ordinations: thirteen presbyters, three deacons, and fourteen bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the fifth day before the Nones of October. His episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

### XXXIII. MELCHIADES

Melchiades, an African by nationality, held office for 4 years, from the ninth consulship of Maximinus until the second consulship of Maxentius, in the consulship of Volusian and Rufinus.

He decreed that no Christian should under any circumstances fast on Sunday or Thursday, because the pagans observed a sacred fast on those days, and Manichaeans had appeared in the City. From that day he also established that consecrated offerings should be sent throughout the churches from the bishop’s consecration; this is called the fermentum.

He conducted one ordination: four presbyters, four deacons, and eleven bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the fourth day before the Ides of September. His episcopate remained vacant for 16 days.

### XXXIV. SILVESTER

Silvester, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufinus, held office for 22 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He lived in the time of Constantine and Volusian, from the Kalends of February until the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Constantius and Volusian.

He was in exile on Mount Soracte, shaken by Constantine’s persecution; afterward he returned with glory and baptized Constantine Augustus. He issued a decree concerning the whole Church. With his consent, a council was held at Nicaea in Bithynia with 318 bishops, whose signatures were entered; another 208 were weak or infirm. They set forth the complete faith and condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius.

In the city of Rome he assembled 277 bishops and condemned Callistus, Arius, and Photinus. He decreed that chrism should be prepared by bishops, and granted bishops the privilege of sealing the baptized because of heretical persuasion. He also decreed that no layperson should bring a charge against a cleric.

He established that deacons should wear dalmatics, and that the altar sacrifice should not be celebrated in silk or dyed cloth, but in linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a shroud. He decreed that anyone wishing to serve in the Church should be a reader for 30 years, an exorcist for 30 days, an acolyte for 5 years, a subdeacon for 5 years, a deacon for 7 years, and a presbyter for 3 years, having been tested in every respect; only then should he ascend to the episcopate. No one should seize the place of a superior or predecessor, nor should any cleric or faithful person who objected be disregarded.

In the month of December he conducted six ordinations: 42 presbyters, 36 deacons, and 65 bishops.

During his episcopate Constantine Augustus built the Constantinian basilica and others, which he furnished. There he placed gifts and a gold canopy. He gave there, both in sacred vessels and in various forms of gold, 480 pounds; 7,626 pounds of silver; seven bronze candelabra enclosed in silver, each weighing 300 pounds; 151 pounds of spices each year; and established estates producing annually 1,500 solidi for the lamps.

At the font where Constantine Augustus was baptized by Saint Silvester, a font made of porphyry metal, he placed ornaments: 82 pounds of gold; 3,813 pounds of silver; a golden censer with 48 green gems; 200 pounds of balsam for the light during the days of Easter; and estates producing annually 7,122 solidi for the lamps at that font.

During his episcopate Constantine Augustus, at the request of Bishop Silvester, built the basilica of blessed Peter. He enclosed the tomb containing Saint Peter’s body with bronze on every side, extending five feet in each direction, and adorned its upper part with porphyry columns and other columns of glass [Note: Read “vitineis,” vine-colored or made of vine wood]. He also made the far end of the basilica’s canopy of gleaming gold, and placed bronze above the body, which he enclosed.

He made a gold cross weighing 150 pounds, corresponding to the dimensions of the place. On it was written: “Constantine Augustus and Helena Augusta encircle this royal house, this hall shining with a similar radiance” [Note: Supply “surround”]. The inscription was written in pure black letters on the cross itself.

He made seven bronze candelabra enclosed in silver, each weighing 300 pounds. Likewise, for the building, Constantine Augustus offered to blessed Peter, from the diocese of the East, estates producing annually 3,788 solidi; 215 pounds of balsam; 800 pounds of nard oil; 100 pounds of cyprinum oil; 650 pounds of spices; 50 medimni of pepper; 50 pounds of cloves; 100 pounds of saffron; 100 units of spun linen; 1,022 bundles of paper; and 1,000 bundles of papyrus.

At the same time Constantine built a basilica for blessed Paul, whose body he enclosed in the same manner as that of blessed Peter. For this basilica he offered the following gift: all the gold, silver, and bronze vessels, and a gold cross over the site, just as in the basilica of blessed Peter. He also gave estates producing annually 4,070 solidi; 1 pound of balsam; 200 pounds of nard oil; 170 pounds of spices; 1 pound of cassia; 30 pounds of storax; 150 pounds of liquid storax; 500 bundles of papyrus; and 300 sacks of linen.

At that time blessed Constantine Augustus built a basilica in the Sessorian palace, where he enclosed a piece of the wood of the holy cross in gold and gems. He also gave it the name Jerusalem and built many other churches of the saints.

These churches are: the church of Saint John the Martyr; the basilica of Saint Laurence the Martyr; the basilica of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus, presbyter, and Peter, exorcist, between the two laurel trees, where his mother, Helena Augusta, was also buried; in the city of Ostia, a basilica for blessed John the Baptist; and a basilica in the city of Albanum. Within the city of Capua he built a basilica which he also named Constantinian, and he built a basilica in the city of Naples.

All these basilicas, which Constantine Augustus built, he richly adorned with gold and silver and endowed with substantial properties in various provinces. Blessed Bishop Silvester ordained during the month of December 44 presbyters, 26 deacons, and 65 bishops at various times and places.

He was buried on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, three miles from the city of Rome, on the day before the Kalends of January. His episcopate remained vacant for 8 days.

### XXXV. MARCUS

Marcus, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 2 years, 8 months, and 20 days. He lived in the time of the consuls Constantine, Nepotianus, and Fecundus, beginning on the Kalends of February.

He decreed that a bishop should use the pallium and should be consecrated by that same bishop of the city of Rome. He conducted two ordinations: 25 presbyters, six deacons, and 17 bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the day before the Nones of … His episcopate remained vacant for 20 days.

### XXXVI. JULIUS

Julius, a Roman by nationality, son of Rusticus, held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 7 days. He lived in the time of Constantius [Note: Read “Constantii”] and Felicianus and Maximus.

He decreed that no cleric should bring a case into public court. He conducted three ordinations: 18 presbyters, four deacons, and nine bishops. He was buried at the cemetery of Calepodius. His episcopate remained vacant for 25 days.

### XXXVII. LIBERIUS

Liberius, a Roman by nationality, son of Augustus, held office for 6 years, 4 months, and 8 days. He lived in the time of Constantius.

Constantius sent him into exile because he refused to consent to the Arian heresy, and he remained there for three years. Then, with the advice of the priests, he appointed the presbyter Felix as bishop in his place.

Afterward the aforesaid Liberius, in his own council, together with 48 bishops, condemned the two presbyters Ursatius and Valens because they had agreed with Constantius in the heresy. A few days later, moved by zeal, Ursatius and Valens asked Constantius Augustus to recall Liberius from exile and to allow him to share in one communion only, except for rebaptism. Liberius consented.

After he had been recalled from exile, he lived in the cemetery of Saint Agnes with the sister of Constantius Augustus, so that he might return to the city as though at her request. But she refused to plead for him because she was faithful in Christ.

Then Constantius, together with Ursatius and Valens and others who were from the dregs of the Arian party, recalled Liberius to Rome. After holding a council with the heretics, they expelled Felix from the episcopate. Felix lived on his small estate, where he also rested in peace on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Liberius entered the City on the fourth day before the Nones of August and consented to Constantius the heretic—heretical, yet Liberius was not rebaptized. At that time there was a great persecution in Rome, so that Catholic clerics were denied entry to churches and baths.

Accordingly, all the years of Felix are counted within this tenure. Liberius conducted two ordinations: 18 presbyters, five deacons, and eight bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the fifth day before the Ides of September. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### XXXVIII. FELIX

Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, held office for 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days. He declared Constantius a heretic and as having been rebaptized. He was crowned with martyrdom. He built a basilica on the Aure lian Way, where he also rests.

He conducted one ordination: 21 presbyters, five deacons, and 18 bishops. He was buried on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December. His episcopate remained vacant for 17 days.

### XXXIX. DAMASUS

Damasus, a Spaniard by nationality, son of Antonius, held office for 18 years, 3 months, and 11 days. He lived in the time of Julian.

He dedicated the Platonium in the Catacombs, where the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul had lain, and adorned it with verses. He was accused of adultery and, after a synod had been held, was cleared by 219 bishops. They also condemned the deacons Concordius and Callistus, his accusers, and cast them out of the Church.

He conducted five ordinations: 31 presbyters, 11 deacons, and 41 bishops. He too was buried on the Hadrianic Way, in the basilica that he himself had built, on the third day before the Ides of December. His episcopate remained vacant for 26 days.

### XL. SIRICIUS

Siricius, a Roman by nationality, son of Tiburtius, held office for 15 years. He issued a decree concerning the Church, sent it throughout the provinces, and established that, without the consecrated bishop of the place, no presbyter might consecrate [Note: Read “without a consecrated [bishop]”].

He decreed that a heretic should be reconciled through the laying on of hands. He conducted five ordinations: 31 presbyters, 16 deacons, and 32 bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. His episcopate remained vacant for 20 days.

### XLI. ANASTASIUS

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Maximus, held office for 3 years and 24 days. He decreed that when the Gospels were being read, priests should not sit but should stand bowed. He also decreed that no cleric from overseas should be received unless he presented a signed document from five bishops, because of the Manichaeans.

He conducted two ordinations: nine presbyters, five deacons, and eleven bishops. He was buried at the site called Ursus Pileatus on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. His episcopate remained vacant for 21 days.

### XLII. INNOCENTIUS

Innocentius, an Albanian by nationality, son of Innocentius, held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 22 days. He decreed that a fast should be observed on Saturday, because the Lord was placed in the tomb on Saturday and the disciples fasted.

He conducted four ordinations: 30 presbyters, 12 deacons, and 54 bishops. He was buried at Ursus Pileatus on the fifth day before the Kalends of July. His episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

### XLIII. ZOSIMUS

Zosimus, a Greek by nationality, son of Abramius, held office for 7 years, 9 months, and 24 days.

He issued a decree that deacons should have their left shoulders covered with linen pallia; that wax should be blessed throughout the parishes; and that no cleric should be served a drink in a public cup, except in the homes of the faithful, especially of clerics.

He conducted one ordination: ten presbyters, three deacons, and nine bishops. He was buried beside the body of blessed Laurence the Martyr on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. His episcopate remained vacant for 11 days.

### XLIV. BONIFACIUS

Bonifacius, a Roman by nationality, son of the presbyter Jucundus, held office for 3 years, 8 months, and 6 days.

He was ordained amid a disputed election together with Eulalius. There was dissension in the clergy for 4 months and 15 days. After a synod was held, Eulalius was deposed by 252 presbyters because he had been ordained unjustly. With the consent of all, Bonifacius sat as bishop, while Eulalius was appointed bishop in the city of Nepi.

He decreed that no woman should touch the sacred cloth or place incense in the Church unless she were a minister; that no slave should be made a cleric; and that neither a person legally bound [Note: Supply “Duriae”] nor anyone bound by any obligation should be admitted.

He conducted one ordination: thirteen presbyters, three deacons, and 36 bishops. He too was buried in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. His episcopate remained vacant for 9 days.

### XLV. CAELESTINUS

Caelestinus, a Campanian by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 9 years, 10 months, and 17 days.

He decreed that the 150 Psalms should be sung before the sacrifice, which had not previously been done. Previously only the letter of the apostle Paul and the holy Gospel were recited, and Masses were celebrated.

He conducted three ordinations: 32 presbyters, 12 deacons, and 46 bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the eighth day before the Ides of April. His episcopate remained vacant for 21 days.

### XLVI. SIXTUS

Sixtus, a Roman by nationality, son of Sixtus, held office for 8 years and 19 days.

He was accused by a certain Bassus and, by command of Valentinian Augustus, after a synod and a thorough inquiry, was cleared by 256 bishops. They also excluded Bassus from communion.

He built the basilica of Saint Mary beside the market of Livia and adorned the confession of the blessed apostle Peter with silver. During his episcopate Valentinian Augustus richly adorned the basilicas of blessed Peter and Paul with gold and silver. In the Constantinian basilica he made a silver gable that had been taken away by barbarians. Valentinian Augustus also offered many gifts to numerous other Roman basilicas.

Bishop Sixtus conducted three ordinations: 28 presbyters, 12 deacons, and 52 bishops. He too was buried on the Tiburtine Way at Saint Laurence. His episcopate remained vacant for 22 days.

### XLVII. LEO

Leo, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Quintianus, held office for 21 years, 1 month, and 13 days.

He renewed the furnishings of the Roman Church after the Vandal war. Together with many bishops he set forth the correct Catholic faith, which is preserved today in the archive of the Roman Church, because of the heresy of Eutyches and Nestorius, who were condemned during his episcopate.

He conducted seven ordinations: 72 presbyters, 30 deacons, and 175 bishops. He restored the basilicas of blessed Peter and blessed Paul the apostles after the divine fire, and built many other basilicas.

For the sake of the Romans, he went to Attila, king of the Huns, and freed all Italy. He established a monastery near blessed Peter the apostle. He decreed that the holy sacrifice and the rest should be mentioned during the action. He also decreed that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-covering unless she had been tested in virginity for 40 years.

He established guardians over the tomb, who are called chamberlains. He too was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the third day before the Ides of April. His episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

### XLVIII. HILARUS

Hilarus, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Pinianus, held office for 3 years, 3 months, and 10 days.

He made many vessels and various ornaments for the apostles Peter and Paul, and adorned the Constantinian basilica, Saint Laurence, and Saint Mary.

He conducted one ordination: 25 presbyters, six deacons, and 22 bishops. He too was buried at Saint Laurence beside the body of Saint Sixtus. His episcopate remained vacant for 10 days.

### XLIX. SIMPLICIUS

Simplicius, a Tiburtine by nationality, son of Castinus, held office for 15 years, 1 month, and 7 days.

He established weekly stations at Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Laurence, so that presbyters might remain there for those seeking baptism and penance: from the third region at Saint Laurence; from the first region at Saint Paul; and from the seventh region at Saint Peter.

He conducted three ordinations: 58 presbyters, 11 deacons, and 82 bishops. He was buried at blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Nones of March. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### L. FELIX

Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of the presbyter Felix, held office for 8 years, 11 months, and 17 days.

He conducted two ordinations: 28 presbyters, five deacons, and 31 bishops. He was buried near blessed Paul. His episcopate remained vacant for 5 days.

### LI. GELASIUS

Gelasius, an African by nationality, son of Valerius, held office for 4 years and 8 months. He lived in the time of King Theodoric and Zeno Augustus.

He wrote five books against Nestorius and Eutyches. He also composed hymns in the manner of blessed Ambrose and wrote two books against Arius. He composed the prefaces of the sacraments in carefully guarded language.

He conducted two ordinations: 32 presbyters, two deacons, and 67 bishops. He too was buried near blessed Peter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December. His episcopate remained vacant for 7 days.

### LII. ANASTASIUS

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter, held office for 1 year, 11 months, and 24 days.

He built the confession of blessed Laurence. At that time [Note: For “hic,” read “eo tempore”], many members of the clergy and many presbyters withdrew from communion because he had communicated, without their advice, with a Thessalonian deacon named Photinus.

He conducted one ordination: eleven presbyters and eight bishops. He was buried at blessed Peter on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### LIII. SYMMACHUS

Symmachus, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Fortunatus, held office for 15 years, 6 months, and 27 days. He lived in the time of Theodoric the heretic and Anastasius Augustus.

He loved the clergy and the poor. Laurentius was ordained together with him amid a disputed election. When the dispute arose, they decided that both should go to Ravenna for judgment before King Theodoric. When they arrived, they found this equitable judgment: whoever had been ordained first, or wherever the greater part had consented, should sit in the apostolic see. Equity, however, favored Symmachus.

Then blessed Pope Symmachus appointed Laurentius bishop in the city of Nuceria [Note: Read “Nucerina,” Nucerian]. After four years, certain members of the clergy and certain senators, moved by zeal, accused Symmachus. They sent accusations against blessed Symmachus to the heretical King Theodoric, secretly recalled Laurentius to Rome, created a schism, and separated part of the community from Symmachus’s communion, asking the heretical king for Peter of Altinum as visitor.

Then blessed Symmachus assembled 115 bishops. After a synod had been held, he was cleared of the false charge, while Peter of Altinum and Laurentius of Nuceria were condemned. Symmachus then sat in his see with great honor.

At that time the patrician Festus began carrying out killings within the City among the clergy who communicated with blessed Symmachus. He removed consecrated women from their dwellings, stripped the female sex, beat them with clubs [Note: Read “cecidit,” struck down], and killed many priests there.

Blessed Symmachus lived from the consulship of Paulinus until the consulship of Senator, from the tenth day before the Kalends of December until the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

He built the basilica of Saint Andrew the apostle at Saint Peter and richly adorned it and many others with gold and silver. He was a builder of churches. He enlarged the clergy, tripled the presbyteral allowance, and tripled clothing and food for the poor, as well as many other good works that would take too long to recount.

He conducted four ordinations: 98 presbyters, 16 deacons, and 119 bishops. He too was buried at blessed Peter on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### LIV. HORMISDA

Hormisda, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus, from the city of Frusino [Note: Read “Frusinone,” Frusino], held office for 9 years and 17 days.

Through his letters he engaged in contests against Anastasius, the heretical emperor. Among the many things Anastasius sent to him, he wrote this: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” Struck by a divine bolt of lightning, he perished.

The orthodox Justin then assumed the empire and sent word to the apostolic see. Pope Hormisda made many ornaments of gold and silver in the Roman Church and its numerous basilicas. He also conducted ordinations of presbyters and bishops in various places.

He too was buried at blessed Peter on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Maximus the Younger. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### LV. JOANNES

Joannes, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius, held office for 2 years, 4 months, and 15 days, from the consulship of Maximus until the consulship of Olibrius the Younger.

King Theodoric sent him as an embassy to Emperor Justin at his request, because Justin, out of his great love for the Christian religion, wished to destroy the heretics. Thereupon the angry King Theodoric wished to destroy the Christians of Italy.

Then Pope Joannes, together with religious men and the consuls, accepted the embassy’s instructions [Note: Read “acceperunt,” “they accepted”]: that the churches in the Greek regions should be restored to their heretics. If this were not done, King Theodoric would put all Italy to the sword.

When they entered [the text here reads uncertainly “om. sis.”] Constantinople with Pope Joannes, men came out to meet them from the twelfth milestone in honor of the apostles. They desired, after blessed Pope Silvester, to receive in the Greek regions the vicar of Saint Peter, who had deserved this position since the time of Constantine.

Emperor Justin bowed before blessed Joannes, from whose hands he was crowned. Then Theodorus, an illustrious man, together with the other nobles who had come with blessed Pope Joannes, granted the requests and, because of the Roman bloodshed, restored their churches to the heretics.

While Bishop Joannes and the illustrious men were staying in Constantinople, King Theodoric seized two senators, Boethius and the patrician Symmachus, killed them with the sword, and ordered them to be hidden.

When Pope Joannes came with the aforementioned illustrious men, Theodoric received them deceitfully and wished to put them to the sword. Fearing Emperor Justin, however, he nevertheless burned them all in custody, so that blessed Joannes, worn down in imprisonment, died at Ravenna on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

Then, 98 days later, King Theodoric was struck by lightning and perished.

Blessed Joannes brought gold from Greece. He adorned many basilicas with gems, silver, and gold. He conducted ordinations of bishops in various places. His episcopate remained vacant for 58 days.

### LVI. FELIX

Felix, a Samnite by nationality, son of Castorius, held office for 4 years, 2 months, and 13 days, from the consulship of Maburtus until the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, from the fourth day before the Ides of July until the fourth day before the Ides of October.

He was ordained by order of King Theodoric and died in the time of King Athalaric on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of … [lacuna]. He was buried at blessed Peter. His episcopate remained vacant for 3 days.

He conducted two ordinations in the month of February: 52 presbyters, four deacons, and 29 bishops.

### LVII. BONIFACIUS

Bonifacius, a Roman by nationality, held office for 2 years and 26 days. He lived in the time of Athalaric.

He was ordained together with Dioscorus amid a disputed election. Dioscorus was ordained in the Constantinian basilica, while Bonifacius was ordained in the basilica of Julius. There was dissension in the clergy and senate for 28 days.

At that time Dioscorus died. Then Bonifacius, moved by zeal and deceit and with great bitterness, reconciled the clergy under the bond of anathema by a signed document. He deposited that document in the archive of the Church, as though condemning Dioscorus.

He assembled a synod in the basilica of blessed Peter and issued a decree that he should appoint his successor, with the signed documents of the priests and an oath before the confession.

At the same time another synod was held, and the priests decided, out of reverence for the holy see, that the decree had been made contrary to the canons. Pope Bonifacius himself confessed that he was guilty because he had confirmed Vigilius as deacon with his signature.

Then he burned that decree in the presence of the priests and the senate. He too was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes. His episcopate remained vacant for 2 months and 15 days.

### LVIII. JOANNES THE YOUNGER

Joannes the Younger, a Roman by nationality, held office for 2 years and 4 months. He lived in the time of King Athalaric and the Catholic Emperor Justinian.

He himself sent his see, in a document written in his own hand, to the apostolic see together with great gifts.

Pope Joannes conducted one ordination: fifteen presbyters and 21 bishops. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. His episcopate remained vacant for 6 days.

### LIX. AGAPITUS

Agapitus, a Roman by nationality, son of the presbyter Gordianus, held office for 11 months and 18 days.

Theodahad sent him on an embassy to Emperor Justinian at Constantinople. There he died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. His body was transported in a lead coffin to Rome, to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, where he was also buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

He conducted ordinations in the city of Rome: four deacons and [lacuna] bishops. His episcopate remained vacant for 28 days.

### LX. SILVERIUS

Silverius, a Campanian by nationality, son of Hormisda, Roman bishop, held office for 1 year, 5 months, and 11 days.

He was elevated by the tyrant Theodahad without the deliberative decree, which the priests had not signed in his favor according to custom. Once he had been ordained under force and fear, they signed in order to preserve the unity of the Church.

After two months, however, Theodahad the tyrant was destroyed by divine will. Silverius conducted one ordination: fourteen presbyters, five deacons, and 18 bishops. His episcopate remained vacant for [lacuna].

LXI.—VIGILIUS, a Roman by nation, son of the consul John, sat for seventeen years, six months, and twenty-six days. At that time he was accused before the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora. They then sent the notary Anthemius to Rome, saying that he should be spared only in the basilica of Saint Peter. He found him in the basilica of Saint Cecilia on her feast day; seizing him, he took him to Constantinople. For two years there were disputes concerning the patriarch Anthimus, because he had promised to restore him to his rank. Vigilius said that he would not restore him, because my most holy predecessors Agapitus and Silverius had condemned him.

[Col. 1417C] “And now I see that Justinian and Theodora did not make me come to them; but today I know that I have encountered Diocletian and Eleutheria. Do as you wish: for I am receiving what is worthy of my deeds.” Then someone struck him in the face, saying: “Murderer, do you not know to whom you are speaking? Do you not know that you killed Pope Silverius?”

He said this because Vigilius had been accused by the Romans in the following terms: that, being carried away in fury, he had struck his notary, who immediately fell at his feet and died; that he had killed a widow’s son with heels and clubs; and that Pope Silverius had been deposed on his advice.

Then, fleeing into the basilica of Saint Euphemia, he grasped the altar’s horn; dragged away from it, he was sent into custody, and the clergy who were with him were sent into exile. At the same time Justinian sent his eunuch Narses to Italy, and, after a battle had been fought with the Goths, victory accompanied him; the Gothic king Totila was killed.

Then the Romans asked Narses to join them in petitioning the emperor for a privilege, and they obtained it. [Note: [Col. 1417D] Perhaps read *quo*, “by which” or “whereby.”] On his return Vigilius came to Sicily, where he died from his many afflictions. His body was brought to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus. He held two ordinations: forty-six priests, sixteen deacons, and eighty-one bishops. The episcopate was vacant for three months and five days.

LXII.—PELAGIUS, a Roman by nation, son of John, sat for four years, ten months, and eighteen days. Since there was no bishop who could ordain him, two bishops were found—John of Perugia and Bonus of Ferentino—and Andrew, a priest of Ostia; they ordained him pontiff.

At that time there were no members of the clergy who could advance him, because a multitude of religious persons had withdrawn from communion with him, saying that he had involved himself in the death of Pope Vigilius.

At the same time, after the Litany had been given, Pope Pelagius went from Saint Pancratius to [Col. 1418A] Saint Peter, holding the Gospels and the cross of the Lord above his head. Ascending the ambo, he satisfied the people, because he had done no wrong against Vigilius. He added: “I ask you: if there is anyone who is found worthy to be promoted in the holy Church, let him advance by no means; for that is simony.”

At that time the basilica of the apostles Philip and James was begun. Meanwhile he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter. He held two ordinations: twenty-six priests, nine deacons, and forty-nine bishops. The episcopate was vacant for two months and twenty-five days.

LXIII.—JOHN, a Roman by nation, son of Anastasius, sat for twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six days. He restored the cemeteries of the holy martyrs, and decreed that offerings, vessels, and lights should be supplied in those same cemeteries every Sunday from the Lateran. He completed the church of Philip and James. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter. He held two ordinations: thirty-seven priests, [Col. 1418B] thirteen deacons, and sixty-one bishops. The episcopate was vacant for ten months and thirteen days.

LXIV.—BENEDICT, a Roman by nation, son of Boniface, sat for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. At that time the nation of the Lombards invaded Italy. When the emperor Justinus learned that the Romans were endangered by famine, he sent to Egypt and dispatched ships laden with grain to Rome.

While suffering in that affliction, blessed Benedict died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, in the secretarium. He held one ordination: fifteen priests, three deacons, and twenty-one bishops. The episcopate was vacant for three months and ten days.

LXV.—PELAGIUS, a Roman by nation, son of Unigild, sat for ten years, two months, and ten days. He was ordained without the prince’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the city. He clothed the body of blessed Peter with gilded silver panels. He was buried there in the same basilica. He held two ordinations: twenty-eight priests, eight deacons, and forty-eight bishops. The episcopate was vacant for [Col. 1418C] six months and twenty-five days.

LXVI.—GREGORY, a Roman by nation, son of Gordianus, sat for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He expounded forty homilies on the Gospels; he also expounded thirty-five books on Job, twenty homilies on Ezekiel, the *Pastoral Rule*, four books of the *Dialogues*, and much else.

He sent the servants of God Mellitus, Augustine, and John to preach to the nation of the English. In the prayer of the canon he added, “And order our days in your peace,” and so forth. He made for blessed Peter a ciborium with four silver columns. He arranged for Masses to be celebrated over the bodies of blessed Peter and Paul.

At that time he dedicated the church of the Goths in the Subura in the name of blessed Agatha. He made his own house into a monastery. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter before the secretarium.

He held two ordinations, one in Lent in the month of February and the other in the seventh month: thirty-nine priests, five deacons, and sixty-two bishops. The episcopate was vacant for five months and nineteen days.

[Col. 1418D] LXVII.—SABINIAN, a Tuscan by nation, son of Bonus, sat for one year, six months, and eighteen days. At that time there was a severe famine. After peace had been made with the Lombards, he ordered thirty modii of wheat to be sold for a solidus. He added lights in the church of blessed Peter, and was buried there. He made twenty-six bishops. The episcopate was vacant for ten months and twenty-six days.

LXVIII.—BONIFACE, a Roman by nation, son of John, sat for eight months and twenty-two days. He obtained from the prince Phocas that the See of the blessed apostle Peter should be the head of all the Churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing itself first of all.

Together with the bishops and clergy, under threat of anathema, he decreed that no one, when a pontiff died—or when a bishop of his own city died—should presume to speak or form a faction for himself until the third day after his burial. [Note: [Col. 1418D] Supply “and then”: “and only then should an election be held.”] The clergy being assembled, an election was to take place.

When he had died, he was buried [Col. 1419A] in the basilica of blessed Peter. He made twenty-one bishops. The episcopate was vacant for ten months and six days.

LXIX.—BONIFACE, a Marsian by nation, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician, sat for six years, eight months, and thirteen days. He asked the prince Phocas for the temple called the Pantheon; there he made a church of blessed Mary, in which church the prince offered many gifts. He made his own house into a monastery. After his death he was buried at Saint Peter. He held two ordinations: eight deacons and thirty-six bishops. The episcopate was vacant for six months and twenty-five days.

LXX.—DEUSDEDIT, a Roman by nation, sat for three years and twenty days. He loved the clergy greatly. He established a second Mass for the clergy. At that time a major earthquake occurred on 8 August. After this a plague followed among the people: an eruption of scabies, so that no one could recognize his own dead.

After his death he was buried at Saint Peter, and for the expenses of his funeral he left the clergy one complete *roga*. He held three ordinations: fourteen priests, five deacons, [Col. 1419B] and twenty-nine bishops. The episcopate was vacant for one month and sixteen days.

LXXI.—BONIFACE, a Campanian by nation, from the city of Naples, son of John, sat for five years and ten days. He decreed that a testament should be valid according to the prince’s command; that an acolyte should not presume to lift the relics of the saints unless he were a priest; and that at the Lateran an acolyte should not baptize with the deacons, but [there should be] subdeacons following.

He was very gentle and merciful, and gave his clergy one complete *roga*. He was buried at Saint Peter. He held two ordinations: twenty-six priests, four deacons, and thirty-eight bishops. The episcopate was vacant for thirteen days.

LXXII.—HONORIUS, a Campanian by nation, son of the consul Petronius, sat for twelve years, eleven months, and seventeen days. He did many good things. He renewed all the furnishings of blessed Peter, covered his confessio with 185 pounds of gold, and constructed many other things there.

In his time sixteen beams were raised in the church of blessed Peter. [Col. 1419C] He covered its basilica with bronze panels, which he took from the temple called the Pantheon at Rome, with the consent of the most pious emperor Heraclius.

He decreed that every week, on Saturday, a litany should go out from the church of Saint Apollinaris, which he himself had built in the portico of that church at Saint Peter. He also built the church of the blessed martyr Agnes three miles from the city of Rome, where he also rests. He built the church of blessed Pancratius two miles away, and constructed, adorned, and enriched many other basilicas.

He held ordinations: priests, deacons, and bishops. He too was buried at Saint Peter. The episcopate was vacant for one year, seven months, and eighteen days.

LXXIII.—SEVERINUS, a Roman by nation, son of Abienus, sat for two months and two days. He renewed the apse of the blessed apostle Peter with mosaic. He loved the clergy and increased everyone’s gift; he was generous to the poor.

He made bishops in various places and left the clergy one complete *roga*. He too was buried at Saint Peter, on 2 August. The episcopate was vacant for four months and nineteen days.

LXXIV.—JOHN, a Dalmatian by nation, son of Venantius, sat for one year, nine months, and nineteen days. He sent large sums of money throughout Dalmatia and Istria for the redemption of captives. He also built and adorned many basilicas. He held one ordination. He left the entire clergy one complete *roga*. He too was buried at Saint Peter. The episcopate was vacant for one month and thirteen days.

LXXV.—THEODORE, a Greek by nation, son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Miletus, sat for six years, five months, and eight days. He was generous and loved the poor. He built many churches. He held one ordination. He too was buried at Saint Peter. The episcopate was vacant for fifty-two days.

LXXVI.—MARTIN, from the city of Todi, sat for six years, one month, and twenty-six days. [Col. 1420A] He assembled 105 bishops at Rome in the church of the Savior and condemned heresy. This synod is preserved today in the archive of the church. He died in the city of Cherson and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin.

LXXVII.—EUGENIUS, a Roman by nation, sat for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter. The episcopate was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days.

LXXVIII.—VITALIAN, a Campanian by nation, son of Anastasius, sat for fourteen years and six months. In his time Constantine Augustus came from the imperial city along the coast to Athens, then to Tarentum, then to Beneventum and Naples, in the sixth indiction.

Afterward he came to Rome on 5 July, a Wednesday, in the indiction stated above. The Apostolic One went out to meet him six miles from Rome. On that same day he came to Saint Peter and offered him a gift; the next day he went to Saint Paul and offered a gift there; and on Saturday he went to [Col. 1420B] Saint Mary and likewise offered a gift.

On Sunday he proceeded to Saint Peter with his army and offered upon its altar a pallium woven with gold. On the following Saturday the emperor came to the Lateran and dined there. On Sunday there was a station at Saint Peter; after the Masses had been celebrated, the emperor and the pontiff took leave of one another.

He removed everything that had been used to adorn the city. He also stripped the church of blessed Mary at the Martyrs, which had been roofed with bronze tiles, and sent it to the imperial city together with various other things he had removed.

For a second time he departed from the city of Rome, returning to Naples. From there he proceeded by land to Rhegium, then entered Sicily in the seventh indiction and stayed in the city of Syracuse. He imposed such affliction upon the people and landowners of the provinces of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia through *diagrapha*—that is, assessments or quotas—and through forced transport by sea, for many years, such as had never previously been known, that even wives were separated from husbands and children from parents.

[Col. 1420C] Subsequently, on 10 July, in the twelfth indiction, the aforesaid emperor was killed in a bath. Not long afterward blessed Vitalian ended his life. He held four ordinations: twelve priests, one deacon, and ninety-seven bishops. He too was buried at Saint Peter on 27 January. The episcopate was vacant for two months and thirteen days.

LXXIX.—ADEODATUS, a Roman by nation, from the monks, son of Jobinianus, sat for four years, two months, and five days; he was extremely gentle. In his time Mizizius [Note: [Col. 1419D] Read *Mezentius*.], who was in Sicily with the eastern army, usurped (*intartizavit*) and seized the kingdom, and the army of Italy proceeded in divisions through Istria, while others went through Campania, and likewise through Sardinia and Africa.

In the same way they came to Sicily, to the city of Syracuse; with God’s help the man who must not be called Mizizius was killed. Many of his judges were mutilated and brought to Constantinople, together with the head of that usurper.

Afterward the Saracens came and seized Sicily, carrying out a great slaughter among the people. [Col. 1420D] Taking away with them the bronze that had been transported there by sea from Rome, they returned to Alexandria.

After Pope Adeodatus had died, there were such rains and thunder as no human age is remembered to have known, so that people and animals even perished by lightning. But through litanies the Lord was propitiated toward them.

He held one ordination: thirteen priests, … deacons, and forty-six bishops. The episcopate was vacant for four months and fifteen days.

LXXX.—DONUS, a Roman by nation, son of Mauricius, sat for one year, five months, and ten days. He paved the atrium of blessed Peter, which is in front of the church within the four-sided portico, with great marble slabs. He also built and adorned other churches. He increased the clergy in its various orders.

In Rome, on the mountain called Boetiana, he found Nestorian Syrian monks, whom he distributed among various monasteries; on the aforesaid mountain he established Roman monks. At his election, in the month of August, a star appeared in the eastern region for three months. Its rays penetrated the heavens; at its appearance all nations marveled.

Afterward a great mortality followed in the East. He held one ordination: ten priests, five deacons, and … bishops. He too was buried at Saint Peter on 10 April. The episcopate was vacant for three months and fifteen days.

LXXXI.—AGATHO, a Sicilian by nation, from the monks, sat for two years, six months, and fourteen days. He was so kind and gentle that he was cheerful toward everyone.

He received the imperial command of the most pious princes, the emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, sent to his predecessor Pope Donus, inviting him to send priests or his legates to the imperial city for the unification of the holy Church of God.

He sent Abundantius of Paternus, John of Reate, and John of Porto, bishops; Theodore and George, priests; John, a deacon; and Constantine, [Col. 1421B] a subdeacon.

In his time, in the ninth indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse in June, on the eighteenth day, and a very severe mortality followed. Later, when the aforesaid legates entered the imperial city, they were kindly received by the prince and presented to him the pontiff’s documents.

When he had received them, he admonished them—not in anger but in peaceful discussion—that, abandoning philosophical assertions, they should satisfy him with the pure faith of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers, approved by synodal decrees. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Read: “he admonished them … that, abandoning philosophical assertions, they should satisfy him with the pure faith of the holy Scriptures and the Fathers, approved by synodal [decrees].”]

Then, when the prince was seated with George, patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius of Antioch, the legates of the Apostolic See were received, followed by 150 metropolitans and bishops of the East. He ordered them to sit after they had worshiped. After an inquiry had been held, the legates of the Apostolic See said:

“Appropriate truth and reason require that, on behalf of those who assert one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ, the authority of the Apostolic See should be set forth.” [Note: [Col. 1421D] Read: “the authority should be set forth.”]

When they heard this, they rejoiced and said that they were ready. At that very hour they brought in their books and various volumes, and the synods which they had falsified, since they were not striving to prevail by truth but by various commentaries that they themselves had recently added to their books.

On the following day the legates of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1422D] Supply “were received.”] presented themselves as representing blessed Pope Agatho. They were told to bring before the synod all the books that they knew pertained to the matter of faith. George, the chartophylax of the Church of Constantinople, was summoned, and this was done.

When [Note: [Col. 1422D] Supply “the codices”] had been reread, they found them to contain two natures, two wills, and two operations. Macarius was exposed as confused and a liar.

The statements of the venerable Fathers John of Constantinople, Cyril, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Dionysius, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Leo were introduced before the synod; these statements affirmed two natures, wills, and operations in Christ.

One birth was before the ages and timeless, from the incorporeal Father; the other was that of him descending from heaven and becoming incarnate in the Virgin. The wills are conjoined with the divine and human natures, because the voluntary exists according to the nature of each. The operations are conjoined with the divine and human unity, because they exist effectively in each nature according to that nature. [Note: [Col. 1422D] This passage is riddled with serious textual errors.]

Then the patriarch George professed that he believed and preached two natures, two wills, and two operations, just as did the Apostolic See.

But since Macarius persevered in his heresy, at that hour the holy synod ordered his orarium [Note: [Col. 1422D] Read *orarium*, “stole,” or “prayer-cloth.”] to be removed. Bishop Basil of Crete sprang up, took the orarium from him, and, after anathematizing him, threw him outside the synod. The Romans expelled his deacon Stephen from the holy synod by the neck.

At that hour so many very black spiderwebs fell into the midst of the people that everyone marveled that the filth of the heresies had been expelled.

The abbot Theophanius was ordained in Macarius’s place. Macarius and his associates were deported to Rome into exile. Then they removed from the diptychs and from the paintings the names of the pontiffs—namely, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—through whom the error of faith had continued to sprout until now.

It was arranged, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, that Bishop John of Porto should celebrate public Mass in Latin on the octave of Easter in the church of Saint Sophia, and that the emperor’s praises and victories should be acclaimed aloud.

Blessed Agatho received an imperial command by which the amount customarily given for the ordination of pontiffs was reduced. Nevertheless, if an election had taken place, the elected man was not to be ordained until a general decree had first been brought to the imperial city, according to ancient custom.

He left his entire clergy one *roga*, and gave 2,160 solidi for the lights of the Apostles and for Saint Mary at the Crib. He held one ordination: ten priests, three deacons, and eighteen bishops. He too was buried at blessed Peter on 10 February. The episcopate was vacant for one year, seven months, and six days.

LXXXII.—LEO, a Sicilian by nation, son of Paul, sat for ten months and seventeen days. He was a most eloquent man in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in chant, refined by the most subtle practice in their meanings, and a lover of the poor.

He received the sixth synod, which had recently been celebrated in the imperial city by God’s providence, with the most pious prince Constantine presiding, together with the legates of the Apostolic See and the two patriarchs, of Constantinople and Antioch. In it Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, and Macarius were condemned.

In his time, when the imperial command of the most clement prince was carried out, the Church of Ravenna was restored under the authority of the Apostolic See, so that whoever was elected there should come to Rome to be ordained.

He issued a decree that an archbishop who had been ordained should not, by any custom, have to pay anything to the various offices of the Church for the use of the pallium. In his time, on 16 April, in the eleventh indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse; after the Lord’s Supper and cockcrow it gradually became clear again.

He held one ordination in June: nine priests and twenty-three bishops. He too was buried at Saint Peter on 3 July. The episcopate was vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days.

LXXXIII.—BENEDICT, a Roman by nation, son of John, sat for ten months and twelve days. In this man the grace of heavenly blessing overflowed, and he adorned the Church.

He received two imperial commands from the most clement prince Constantine, addressed to the clergy and Roman people, directing that whoever was elected to the Apostolic See should be ordained pontiff without delay.

Together with the clergy and army, he received the locks of hair of the lord Justinian and Heraclius, his sons, along with the command indicating that they had sent their hair. In his time a star appeared between the Lord’s Nativity and Epiphany, entirely darkened like the moon. Likewise, in February, a star rose in the west at midday and declined toward the eastern regions. After this Mount Bebius, which is in Campania, erupted.

He left thirty pounds of gold to the entire clergy. He made twelve bishops and was buried at Saint Peter on 8 May. The episcopate was vacant for two months and fifteen days.

LXXXIV.—JOHN, a Syrian by nation, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, sat for one year and nine days; he was a very vigorous man.

After the time of many pontiffs, he was elected by the whole body according to ancient custom in the church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana. While he was a deacon, he had been sent by holy Pope Agatho to the imperial city on the matter of the faith, for which the Church expressed great joy.

He was consecrated by three bishops: of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri. In his time the lord Justinian reigned at Nicaea in September, in the fourteenth indiction. This pious prince established peace with the nation of the Saracens for ten years; Africa too was subjected to the Roman Empire.

He left the entire clergy 1,900 solidi and made thirteen bishops. He too was buried at Saint Peter on 2 August. The episcopate was vacant for two months and eighteen days.

LXXXV.—CONON, a Greek by nation, son of Tracessius, brought up in Sicily, sat for eleven months. He received an imperial command from the lord Justinian Augustus, indicating that he had found the proceedings of the holy sixth synod and possessed them, and that his father, of pious memory, Constantine, had produced them with God’s help; he promised to preserve them forever.

In his time imperial piety, through a sacred command, reduced by 200 the total of grain allowances paid annually by the patrimonies of Brixia and Lucania. [Note: [Col. 1423B] There is a textual error here.]

He left the entire clergy a blessing in gold, like his predecessor Pope Benedict.

When his archdeacon saw the pontiff constrained by illness, he was moved by desire for the aforesaid legacy, which had not yet been paid out, and wrote to the glorious John at Ravenna, promising a payment so that his own person might be elected to the pontificate. He also entrusted this to his judges, whom he sent to Rome to arrange the city, so that after his death that same archdeacon might be elected pontiff.

He made sixteen bishops. He was buried at Saint Peter on 21 September. The episcopate was vacant for two months and twenty-three days.

LXXXVI.—SERGIUS, a Syrian by nation, sat for fourteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days.

LXXXVII.—JOHN, a Greek by nation, from Plato, sat for three years, two months, and twelve days. The episcopate was vacant for one month and seventeen days.

LXXXVIII.—JOHN, a Greek by nation, sat for two years, eight months, and seventeen days. The episcopate was vacant for three months.

LXXXIX.—SISINNIUS, a Syrian by nation, sat for twenty days. The episcopate was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days.

XC.—CONSTANTINE, a Syrian by nation, sat for seven years and fifteen days. The episcopate was vacant for forty days. In the first year of his pontificate, 150 years of Victor’s recurring cycle were completed, in the seventh indiction, the first year, while Tiberius was reigning with his father Justinian.

XCI.—GREGORY, a Roman by nation, sat for sixteen years, seven months, and twenty-four days. The episcopate was vacant [Col. 1424B] for thirty-five days.

XCII.—GREGORY, a Roman by nation, sat for ten years, ten months, and nine days. The episcopate was vacant for eleven days.

XCIII.—ZACHARIAS, … fourteen days. The episcopate was vacant for twelve days.

XCIV.—STEPHEN, a Greek by nation, sat for five years, one month, and twenty days … The episcopate was vacant for fifty days.

XCV.—PAUL sat for years …  

[Col. 1423]

FRAGMENT OF THE CATALOGUE OF PONTIFFS, ENDING WITH VIGILIUS

It now appears again from the Verona manuscript, of remarkable antiquity, together with a mutilated narrative of events falsely asserted concerning Pope Anastasius, and the Life of Blessed Symmachus, fabricated by the faction of the schismatics through the work of the patrician Festus and others favoring the antipope Laurentius. My uncle Franciscus Bianchini had published all this only in part, in volume III of the *Anastasius Bibliothecarius* (C).

[Col. 1423C] …  

… sent to Emperor Anastasius through the bishops Cresconius and Germanus, so strongly supported by the authority of the heavenly Scriptures that anyone who reads it attentively in the fear of God recognizes how vainly such a wicked schism has thus far persisted between the Churches of the East and Italy.

LII. Symmachus sat for fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. With him Laurentius, a priest of the Roman Church, had been ordained bishop; and so savage a discord had invaded the clergy and Roman people that neither regard for divine things nor fear of the emperor could restrain the factions from their mutual collision.

Then both men—Symmachus and Laurentius—were compelled to seek the imperial court, intending to submit to the emperor’s judgment. There Symmachus prevailed through large sums of money; Laurentius was sent to govern the Church of Nuceria, a city of Campania, compelled by many threats and promises.

After several years Symmachus was accused before the king of many crimes. The king summoned him to court under the pretext of Easter, because he had not celebrated it with the whole community, in order to demand an account for the discrepancy in the festival … [Col. 1424C] He ordered him to reside at Ariminum. While he remained there for some time with several of his clerics, walking in the afternoon [manuscript: “before noon”] along the seashore, he saw women passing by, with whom he was accused of wrongdoing and who were seeking the imperial court by royal command.

Pretending not to know what he had seen, at midnight, while everyone was asleep, he fled with only one confidant and returned to Rome, shutting himself inside the precincts of the blessed apostle Peter.

Then the priests and deacons, as well as the other clergy whom he had brought with him, approached the king and testified that Symmachus had fled without their knowledge. Through them the king sent commands both to the senate and to the clergy concerning his condemnation, so to speak.

He was also accused by the entire Roman clergy of having squandered ecclesiastical estates contrary to the decree observed by his predecessors, and of having thereby entangled himself in the bonds of anathema. For the Easter days, the venerable man Peter, bishop of Altinum, was requested by almost everyone from the king as visitor of the Roman Church. After the holy festival, a synod assembled in the city of Rome by order of the king and at the wish of the senate and clergy, to judge his excesses.

This was undertaken by certain bishops and senators … so that … Symmachus … might be subjected to a hearing. Some openly cried out in his defense that no Roman pontiff could be heard by anyone, even if he were such as he was accused of being. But more distinguished bishops, both out of regard for religion and because of the royal command, judged that a matter of such importance, already almost universally known, could in no way be abandoned without examination.

Since the synod, amid this disagreement, was providing ever more fuel for discord between the factions, it finally decided that the written accusation presented by Symmachus’s accusers should be received and formally read among the records.

This having been done, Symmachus was immediately summoned by the bishops to appear for judgment. But when his attendance had been refused by the clerics who kept watch over him, the bishops admonished him a second and a third time, according to the rules, to come to the synodal hearing; he did not deign to give any answer.

Then several bishops, seeing that they were making no progress in the case, admonished the clergy who had withdrawn from Symmachus’s fellowship once and again to return to him, leaving the investigation aside. They replied that they could by no means do this before he was either acquitted, if innocent, after a regular inquiry into such grave crimes, or, if found guilty, deposed from the priesthood.

But when the bishops saw that the delays of the … were increasing the party divisions more and more, they made what decisions seemed useful to them concerning Symmachus’s person, and thus left the city in the utmost confusion.

The more distinguished clergy and senate, who had avoided Symmachus’s fellowship, sent a petition [Col. 1425C] to the king on behalf of Laurentius, who at that time was staying at Ravenna to avoid Symmachus’s violence and persecution, asking that he himself preside over the Roman Church, where he had formerly been ordained supreme pontiff.

For this too was established by the canons: that each person should remain where he was first consecrated bishop; or, if he had been removed from there by certain devices, he should be recalled by every means.

Thus Laurentius came to the city and held the Roman Church for approximately four years. The civil wars fought during that time and the many murders committed need not be set forth in the present account.

While the factions clashed with one another in mutual disagreement and frequently sought royal protection for their causes, Symmachus finally sent a petition to the king through Dioscorus, a deacon of Alexandria, asserting that great prejudice was being done to him, especially concerning the titles of the churches that Laurentius held within the city.

The king’s mind was softened by this representation, and he sent commands to the patrician F… [Col. 1426A], instructing him to restore all the church titles to Symmachus and to allow there to be one pontiff in Rome.

When Laurentius learned this, he did not wish to distress the city through prolonged conflict. Of his own accord, and without delay, he withdrew to the estates of the aforesaid patrician Festus [manuscript: “report” for “delay”; *e* for *i*]. There, under great restraint, he met the end of his life.

Symmachus, however, although victorious, was afterward discolored by rumor concerning many matters—especially the more obscene one which people commonly called the “Conditaria”—and also concerning ecclesiastical orders, which he distributed openly after receiving money for them. Because of these matters the Roman Church remained in schism until the end of his life.

He built and adorned the church of blessed Martin near Saint Sylvester with money from the illustrious Palatinus, and dedicated it at that man’s very insistence. He also renewed several cemeteries [manuscript: *cymeteria*], especially that of Saint Pancratius, and constructed many new buildings there.

LIII. Hormisda sat for nine years and seventeen days.

LIV. John sat for two years, nine months, and sixteen days.

LV. Felix sat for four years, two months, and twelve days.

LVI. Boniface sat for two years and twenty-six [Col. 1426C] days.

LVII. John sat for two years, four months, and six days.

LVIII. Agapitus sat for eleven months and eight days.

LIX. Silverius sat for nine months.

LX. Vigilius sat for eighteen years, two months, and nine days. He died at Syracuse on Monday night, 7 June, in the third indiction. [Note: [Col. 1425C] This catalogue was therefore written in the year 555.]

The Bulgarians 168. They are instructed in the Christian faith 609, 616; they withdraw from the Latin Church 639. See “Legates of the Bulgarians.” By what arguments it is proved that Bulgaria is subject by right of the sees to the Roman pontiff 635. Michael, king of the Bulgarians, asks Pope Nicholas I to send him priests whose work will convert his whole kingdom to the faith of Christ; when they are sent, the king receives them honorably, and they baptize every Bulgarian without exception 608–609. He then asks the pope to assign him an archbishop, ibid.

He sends legates to the Eighth Synod convened at Constantinople. When they asked the Fathers to which Church the Bulgarians ought to be subject, Constantinople or Rome, the pope’s legates answered: Rome, because that Church had sent the first priests there and they were still present 632–633. The Greeks, however, maintained that the Bulgarians ought to be subject to Constantinople. The Roman legates replied that Epirus in both its parts, Thessaly, and Dardania—which is now Bulgaria—had formerly been subject to the Roman Church 635–636. For this reason Emperor Basil dismissed the pope’s legates with insufficient courtesy 638. Indeed, they were stripped by Slavs, so that the copy of the council held there was lost; Anastasius the Librarian, who had copied it, later restored it 638. Finally, because the dispatch of an archbishop was excessively delayed, the Bulgarians submitted to the Church of Constantinople and the Latins were expelled 640. The king of the Bulgarians 608.

Carloman, son of Charles, king of the Franks—or rather, of Duke Charles, namely Martel—, who, together with some of his companions, abandoned worldly glory and was made a cleric by Pope Zacharias, then went to the monastery of Saint Benedict 221; sent as ambassador by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, to Pippin, king of the Franks, to obstruct Pope Stephen’s efforts; there, at the pope’s command, he settled in a certain monastery of France and died not long afterward, in the year 725 245. Carloman, king of the Franks—that is, king of Austrasia—brother of Charles the Great, king of the Franks; Stephen IV asks him to come to the defense of the Church against Desiderius, king of the Lombards 284, 285. He and his brother Charles, later called the Great, are called kings of the Franks and patricians 294, 296. Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to whom Carloman’s wife had fled with her sons, asks Pope Adrian to anoint them kings of the Franks, so that he might stir up disturbances in that kingdom and make the pontiff hated by Charles the Great; but the pope refuses to fulfill Desiderius’s wicked request 296. Charles the Bald 600. Charles the Great sends ambassadors to Adrian I; when they learned that the cities had not been restored by Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as he had assured Charles that he had done, they unsuccessfully attempt to move him by gifts and entreaties 308–310. Therefore Charles, a truly most Christian king, having crossed the Alpine passes, bursts into Italy; Desiderius and his men miraculously flee to Ticinum. His son Aldegisus, however, with the sons of Carloman, who had fled from France to Desiderius, goes to Verona. The people of Spoleto and others, abandoning Desiderius, ask the pope to tonsure them 310, 311. After capturing Verona, with Aldegisus and Ticinum under siege, Charles goes with part of his forces to Rome 314. All Rome meets him: the clergy with crosses, boys with palm branches. At the sight of them he dismounts and proceeds on foot to the church of Saint Peter; before reaching the pope, he kisses all the steps of Saint Peter. Charles and the pope rush into one another’s arms; everyone acclaims: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” All the Franks prostrate themselves before the altar of blessed Peter and give thanks for the miraculous victory. Charles asks permission to enter the City and visit its churches 315, 316. At Easter he dines with the pope; when the pope asks that the old donation once made by Pippin be confirmed, Charles orders a new and larger document to be written, in which the provinces of Venetia and Istria are named, and places it as an offering upon the altar of Saint Peter 317, 318. Returning from there to Ticinum, after capturing it he brought the entire Lombard kingdom under his authority and took Desiderius captive with him to France 319. He returns to Rome with Pope Leo III. The Romans receive him honorably, and in the church of Saint Peter, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the pope crowns him with a most precious crown, while the people acclaim: “To Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, life and victory!” After the saints had been invoked, this was repeated three times. He was also anointed with sacred oil together with his son. He offered to Saint Peter a silver table and many other gifts 372, 376. He sends Paschal and Campulus, the authors of the blinding of Pope Leo, into exile in France 373. He also offered the customary cross carried before the litanies and processions 376, 378. Desiderius, prefect of Tuscia, begs the pope’s help so that he may become king of the Lombards, promising that he will restore the duchy of Ferrara and Faventia. Pope Ratchis, therefore, orders the king, who has become a monk, to lay down his arms and return to the monastery 255. But after obtaining the kingdom he did not keep his promises, and took the duchy of Ferrara away from the pope 292. The wife of Caroloman, who was the brother of Charlemagne, fled to him with her sons; he refuses to return her unless the pope comes to him, for he wanted the pope to crown Charlemagne’s sons kings of the Franks, in order to stir up a schism in Francia and bring all Italy under his control 296. Pope Adrian sends twenty monks to him, asking that he not proceed to ravage the Roman territories; but they obtain nothing 305, 306. Charlemagne also sends his own legates with gifts, but in vain 310. When Charlemagne came into Italy, Desiderius’s army fled in panic, and Desiderius himself withdrew to Pavia, ibid. After Pavia was captured, Charlemagne took Desiderius and, having extinguished the Lombard kingdom, carried him away to Francia 319. Desiderius, king of the Lombards 254, 265, 283 ff. He ravages the territory of the Church 303 ff. He flees to Pavia 311. He is carried away to Francia 319.

Constantine gave many things to the churches but attempted to carry even more with him to Constantinople; he was killed in Sicily 136. The Roman Church is universal and head of all the churches 486. So that it might be recognized and called the head of all the churches, Pope Boniface III obtained this from Emperor Phocas, because the patriarch of Constantinople had begun calling himself universal 606. Aripert restored the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church 168. King Liutprand confirmed that donation 179. The Frankish kings Pippin, Charles, and Carloman restored to it the duchy of Ferrara, Ravenna, Faenza, and so forth 256, 294. The legates of Emperor Basil call the Roman Church “having neither spot nor wrinkle” 624.

When Charlemagne came to Rome for religious reasons, he kissed all the steps of the Church of blessed Peter as he ascended 316 [Col. 1462]. In the same church King Louis, son of Lothar, together with the Franks, venerated the confession of Saint Peter prostrate 485. The zeal of the Roman people in defending the Catholic religion was so great that they did not allow the pope to receive a synodical letter from Peter, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople 134. Their same zeal was shown against the heretical emperor Philippicus 174. They slaughtered the duke of Naples and his son because he had attempted to kill the pontiff in the name of the emperor of the East 184. Even when threatened with death by the Franks, they refused to receive Anastasius, who had been deposed from the episcopate, as pope; by their shouts they compelled the Franks to agree to the legitimate pope 564.

Roman doorkeeper and martyr 25. Roman patrician and exarch 113. The Roman pontiff is judged by no one 374, and judges every bishop, ibid.; he alone has the right to judge the entire Church 636. When Vigilius became pope, he steadfastly denied that he would fulfill the promise made to the empress Theodora, wife of the Emperor Justinian—that is, to restore Patriarch Anthimus—saying: “Earlier I spoke foolishly; now I in no way consent to the recall of a heretical man” 103. He is driven from Rome and honorably received at Constantinople; when he resisted the empress, he was struck in the face 106. The empress ordered him, with a rope thrown around his neck, to be dragged through the streets of the city as far as the prison, while his clergy were condemned to the mines.
